title: Amazon’s AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 11 Live Feeds on One Screen
summary: Personalized multiview livestreams — the ability to watch multiple video feeds on one screen — have become a popular and much-requested feature by customers, particularly for sports. Now AWS, Amazon’s cloud-services division, is launching a new service that will let streamers deliver up to 11 feeds in a single personalized channel. On Thursday, AWS took […]
content:
Personalized multiview livestreams — the ability to watch multiple video feeds on one screen — have become a popular and much-requested feature by customers, particularly for sports. Now AWS, Amazon‘s cloud-services division, is launching a new service that will let streamers deliver up to 11 feeds in a single personalized channel.

On Thursday, AWS took the wraps off new capabilities in its suite of video services: per-viewer dynamic multiview, AI-generated metadata generation to facilitate monetization opportunities based on what’s happening on screen, and automated backfill of unfilled ad inventory. AWS is showcasing the new capabilities at IBC 2026, running Sept. 11-14 in Amsterdam.

The new capabilities will make it possible to deliver “truly personalized live TV,” said Samira Bakhtiar, general manager of telco, media, entertainment, games and sports at AWS. “AWS helped build the streaming era. Now we’re helping to build the intelligence era. Every frame of live video is personalized and understood.”

Popular on Variety

The new AWS Elemental MediaPackage Dynamic Multiview lets viewers choose their own multi-camera layout from a single set of encoded sources, delivered to any device over standard HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) or Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) — without per-layout encoding costs

India’s JioHotstar is already using the AWS multiview feature to present quad-view features for its coverage of Indian Premier League (IPL) cricket matches. “AWS Elemental MediaPackage Multiview lets us deliver multiple synchronized camera angles within a single stream, putting our subscribers in control of how they experience live sports,” Akash Saxena, CTO of JioHotstar, said in a statement. “The server-side composition approach scales this premium experience to over 100 million viewers without multiplying origin complexity or CDN costs, giving us a true differentiator in India’s competitive OTT landscape.”

AWS says that existing approaches to implementing multiview features have forced trade-offs. For example, tiled encoding limits reach to High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC)-capable devices, while client-side compositing demands custom software development kits for each device. Server-side compositing requires pre-encoding every layout combination (each costing as much as a new channel).

By contrast, AWS MediaPackage Dynamic Multiview stitches multi-camera and multi-feed layouts on demand from encoded sources, delivered as a single adaptive bitrate stream through HLS or DASH. Sources encode one time through AWS Elemental MediaLive. Then, Elemental MediaPackage assembles layouts in the compressed domain with no reencoding. The output reaches more than 95% of consumer devices with a single digital rights management (DRM) key and requires no SDK, per-device builds, or new vendors, according to AWS.

Also being introduced by AWS is Elemental Inference Contextual Metadata, which uses AI to extract metadata from live video in real time. That can then be used to power personalized video experiences and contextual ad decisioning.

In addition, the AWS Elemental MediaTailor Yield Optimization capability provides automated backfill of unfilled ad inventory using Amazon Publisher Services (APS) demand, aimed a maximizing ad revenue. The new suite of capabilities also includes AWS Elemental MediaTailor Low-Latency Ad Insertion, which provides personalized ad insertion to low-latency streams using Apple’s HLS interstitials.

According to AWS, its cloud services are used by streaming services to nearly 2 billion customers worldwide. Media companies that use AWS include Fox, Amazon MGM Studios, Disney, HBO, NBCUniversal, Sony and Netflix.

Amazon in 2015 bought Elemental Technologies, a video-encoding and content delivery technology company, for a reported $500 million in cash.

title: ‘Why Did I Get Married Again?’ Review: Taraji P. Henson Joins the Gang for a Tyler Perry Sequel That Sells the Next Generation Short
summary: It’s been nearly 20 years since “Why Did I Get Married?”, the original Tyler Perry movie that first introduced these characters and their variously troubled relationships — and 16 years since the sequel to that film, “Why Did I Get Married Too?”. So it feels only normal, at the start of this latest outing for […]
content:
It’s been nearly 20 years since “Why Did I Get Married?”, the original Tyler Perry movie that first introduced these characters and their variously troubled relationships — and 16 years since the sequel to that film, “Why Did I Get Married Too?”. So it feels only normal, at the start of this latest outing for the gang, that we should be treated to some fairly heavy exposition.

“Why Did I Get Married Again?” certainly doesn’t stint on it: As the film begins, we catch up with fiery Angela (Tasha Smith) and her husband Marcus (Michael Jai White), a now somewhat cowed figure who has quit his womanizing in practice but kept the macho attitude. The pair are preparing to host a dinner ahead of the marriage of their daughter Jasmine (Armani Greer) to football player Wesley (Everett Osborne), who happens to be the son of their friend Roselyn (Taraji P. Henson, new to the franchise but treated by all and sundry as if she had been part of the adventure all along).

Tasha and Marcus have of course invited their old friends from the first two films, Shelley (Jill Scott) and Troy (Lamman Rucker), and Diane (Sharon Leal) and Terry (Tyler Perry), who all have children of their own, in their early twenties. Meanwhile, Shelley’s old troublemaker ex, Mike (Richard T. Jones), turns up for some reason, this time dating a much younger woman who happens to be the ex of Angela and Marcus’s son Marcus Jr. (Da’Vinchi).



It seems like an overly convoluted set-up — not least because the younger generation don’t bring much to the film apart from narrative developments that reflect the older generation back to them. So, Marcus Jr. is a hot-headed skirt-chaser like his old man, and Diane and Terry fret that their son T.J. (Jaden Michael) may conversely be a little mild. The film is fundamentally uninterested in the younger people as characters, however, which gives it a strange flavor: The kids constantly provide the (rather thin) action, and the older lot then argue, worry or wryly chuckle about these events, saying things like, “Marcus Jr. is just like you used to be, Marcus.”



That is to say, the film’s exposition-speak continues long after its opening scenes, permanently relating to the audience what is happening, who is who, and why it concerns the franchise’s veteran characters. That doesn’t make for very enjoyable watching, and it compounds a tonal problem raised by the multi-generational approach: Where the older characters are cheerfully upfront and confrontational about their problems, the younger people have grown up in a world that sees things differently, and therefore appear bland. You have to feel sorry for Marcus Jr., portrayed as the lone bad egg among the dreary new set, whose greatest sin is trying to get with his spoken-for ex-girlfriend a couple of times, only to get a furious dressing-down from Angela in front of everybody.



A lightly macho tone prevails, even as Perry writes a handful of quite sensitive scenes for his female characters, such as Shelley’s fears about her aging mother, or Roselyn’s anguish about her son rejecting her. That leads to a curious scene in which Marcus somehow bests the insanely buff Wesley at weightlifting, which seems like nothing so much as wish-fulfillment — and to an even more curious treatment of the character of T.J., who appears to be written as homosexual without this ever being stated. Stranded in a no-man’s land where everybody deplores toxic masculinity but the guys still need to be given something to do, the film doesn’t manage to contrive any actual fun.

Popular on Variety

Netflix money oozes from every pore of “Why Did I Get Married Again?,” most visibly when the gang head to Lake Como for the nuptials. The ladies duly appear at brunch in a variety of chic ensembles and statement jewelry, and the wedding itself is suitably plush, but all of this merely adds to the film’s strange detachment from reality — an overstuffed chamber-piece with a tenuous connection to actual life and concerns.



Among the performers, Smith rules the roost as the no-nonsense Angela, and Jones acquits himself tolerably on comic relief duties as the pathetic Mike. Henson, apparently acting in another film entirely, gives us a character unable to submit to true love in the face of her perceived duties; alone of all the actors, she gets close to something truthful, but that still sits quite uncomfortably with the ambient tone of woolly half-jokes and that’s-life sermonizing.

That spirit finds its most naked expression in a drably conceived scene toward the film’s conclusion, in which the older characters gather in a semi-circle to literally explain everything to the younger generation (who are also seated in a semi-circle). Everybody takes turns to speak their hard truth or life lesson or warm expression of love. A wedding dance scene — interspersed with bloopers to remind you that you have been watching a comedy — caps off proceedings with something like relief, the assignment finally completed.

title: Jack Quaid Jokes He’s a Supermodel After Starring in New Bonobos Campaign: ‘I Guess I Can Add That to My Resume’
summary: Jack Quaid isn’t giving up his acting career, but the “Boys” star jokes he’s on his way to becoming a supermodel now that he stars in the Fall 2026 campaign for menswear brand Bonobos. “I guess I can add that to the résumé,” he cracks. The campaign is an episodic video series featuring Quaid in […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Jack Quaid isn’t giving up his acting career, but the “Boys” star jokes he’s on his way to becoming a supermodel now that he stars in the Fall 2026 campaign for menswear brand Bonobos.

“I guess I can add that to the résumé,” he cracks.

The campaign is an episodic video series featuring Quaid in an office setting, where he manages to keep himself — and the Bonobos clothing he’s wearing — together even when thrown some curveballs.

“I’ve been a fan of the brand for a while now,” Quaid tells me. “I remember wearing a lot of their stuff in the earlier days when they had a brick-and-mortar store near me in L.A. Sometimes as an actor brands reach out and you’re like ‘Yeah, I can sort of see myself partnering with them,’ but with Bonobos, it just felt like the perfect fit. It’s clothes I actually wear.”

Popular on Variety

In the first episode, Quaid talks to camera and introduces himself as the “Weekday Warrior Consultant.”

“That’s not my actual job title. HR keeps rejecting it but that’s what people call me around here because I wear these — the Weekday Warriors,” he says as the camera pans to his pants. “Great-fitting, no-worries work pant. No wrinkles, no hassles.”

He goes on to brag that he got others in the office to wear the $119 pants. “But out there,” he says, looking out a window, “there are guys walking around in bad-fitting wrinkly pants that were a ‘great deal’ online — not on my watch.”

Future episodes will center on the Weekday Warrior Dress Shirt, Jetsetter Dress Shirt, Everyday Oxford Shirt, Unconstructed Blazer and Knit Blazer. Real Bonobos employees are also featured in the campaign.

Quaid admits he wasn’t always one to think about fashion too much.

“I’ve come a long way,” he says. “Starting out in like high school, middle school, everything was like a graphic tee with a ‘Family Guy’ quote on it. Nothing against ‘Family Guy,’ but when all of your shirts have a ‘Family Guy’ quote on it, it’s time to maybe have something more basic.”

But now, Quaid says, “I consider myself pretty fashionable. I still hang out with a lot of the people I went to high school with, and they’re like, ‘Hey, you dress a lot better than you used to. I feel like I can trust them because they’ll be very honest with me. I’m happy that I’m finally in good graces with the fashion gods when it comes to my high school friends.”

title: NBCUniversal’s Split From Comcast Will “Allow Us To Move Faster,” Media Group Chief Matt Strauss Says
summary: NBCUniversal Media Group Chairman Matt Strauss is extremely bullish on the company’s forthcoming split from Comcast. “There is genuine excitement” about the move inside the company, Strauss said Thursday at an investor conference hosted by BofA Securities. “We feel really good about our trajectory and our growth, and I think the independence is going to […]
content:
NBCUniversal Media Group Chairman Matt Strauss is extremely bullish on the company’s forthcoming split from Comcast.

“There is genuine excitement” about the move inside the company, Strauss said Thursday at an investor conference hosted by BofA Securities. “We feel really good about our trajectory and our growth, and I think the independence is going to allow us to move faster. It’s like a catalyst for us.”

Comcast revealed the plan in June to separate its Philadelphia-based pay-TV, broadband and wireless business from NBCU. The move follows the spinoff of most of NBCU’s cable networks into a separate company, Versant Media, and is in line with what Warner Bros. Discovery was planning before agreeing to be acquired by Paramount.

Strauss said being solo will give NBCU “the ability to be more flexible when it comes to partnerships” such as the company’s landmark distribution agreement with YouTube, which was reached earlier this summer.

Watch on Deadline

“That’s the type of innovation that we’re looking to continue driving,” Strauss said. “So, I wouldn’t say that the independence changes how we’re looking at media. I think it just gives us more flexibility to move quicker. We’re not trying to build a broadcast business sitting next to a streaming business. We’re trying to build a digital-first new media company where we’re trying to get the maximum return for our investment across the portfolio.”

The split is expected to take about a year to complete. While execs don’t publicly characterize it this way, it was motivated in part by Comcast’s sagging stock price, which reflects growing concern about pressure on broadband growth. Strauss didn’t address M&A at the conference, but Comcast Co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts told investors on their second-quarter earnings call in July that conversations are already under way with potential deal partners.

BofA media analyst Jessica Reif Ehrlich, who moderated the discussion, interjected her enthusiasm for NBCU at regular intervals during the session. She closed by asking Strauss, who oversaw the launch of Peacock in 2020, what he envisions the streaming service becoming over the next five years.

“There is a tremendous opportunity to reimagine the experience for streaming,” he replied. In particular, he said, focusing on ways to “super-serve” fans by supplementing the main programming with games, podcasts and other personalized offerings will be crucial.

One example in that veing that NBCU hopes to replicate, Strauss said, is Love Island USA.

Episodes ran six days a week over the summer, and while NBCU employed the typical algorithmic tools to try to keep viewers engaged with other programming, execs soon had a realization. “What we found is that at the end of the episode, many of those fans didn’t want to watch another show. They wanted to continue engaging with Love Island. So what happens? They leave our platform. They go to social media. They’re looking for clips, for games, for podcasts, and that is engagement that we built, but we’re not monetizing, because we’re not really providing that level of experience outside the premiumness of the content. And so, we’ve started to look at this several years ago. Well, what does it mean to be an entertainment platform?”

Spurred by the data point that 30% of Love Island viewing is on mobile devices, NBCU built out a vertical video offering on Peacock, introducing it last year. “We’re not creating the behavior,” Strauss said. “We’re tapping into the behavior, but we’re moving that engagement back to our platform.”

The management team, he said, is “starting to think differently about ways that you could drive engagement, where when you finish an episode, it’s not the end. It’s the beginning. And then we can introduce more ways for you to engage and give you more things that you love and continue to drive growth and monetization.”

title: Spain’s Mediapro Group To Become Imagina After Reorganization
summary: Spain’s Grup Mediapro will relaunch as Imagina on January 1, 2027, following a major company review. The decision to relaunch comes after “several months of reorganization” and was announced internally yesterday at an all-staff meeting. “The change revives a name the group has used before across its more than 30-year history, reflecting its intent to […]
content:
Spain‘s Grup Mediapro will relaunch as Imagina on January 1, 2027, following a major company review.

The decision to relaunch comes after “several months of reorganization” and was announced internally yesterday at an all-staff meeting.

“The change revives a name the group has used before across its more than 30-year history, reflecting its intent to look ahead while staying grounded in its past,” the company said in a note to press.

Imagina was previously the parent company of Mediapro, following the latter’s 2006 merger with producer Globomedia.

The news follows a tumultuous 2026 for the Spanish sports media and entertainment giant, during which it cut 189 staff. Senior execs such as General Manager Laura Fernández Espeso, The Mediapro Studio’s international content chief, Ran Tellem, and business chief Miguel Cardenal all left.

Watch on Deadline

Mediapro’s new management, Executive Chairman Sergio Oslé and CEO Carlos Núñez, said the company expects EBITDA to grow between 50% and 60% against 2025, along with positive cash flow generation.

This was thanks to the company-wide review that took place over the first months of 2026 and ultimately “brought its resources in line with today’s market realities.”

“The next step is to drive new projects that deliver unique experiences to audiences around the world, funding this growth with more than €100 million [$116 million] the company itself will generate over the next three years,” the company stated.

Oslé and Nũnez were installed following the departures of founding partners Jaume Roures and Tatxo Benet. They are now presiding over a business that handles production of numerous major sporting events, sells broadcast rights to the likes of Spain’s La Liga outside of North America, MENA and India, and has a content production unit that is behind the likes of The Head.

Southwind Media Capital, which is part of China’s Orient Hontai Capital, owns Mediapro, which has its main offices in Madrid and Barcelona. Southwind bought a majority stake in February 2018, with former bosses Roures and Benet retaining minority stakes.

title: ‘Le Faux Soir’ Trailer: Arieh Worthalter & Mélanie Thierry Star In WW2 Belgian Resistance “Media Hack” Drama – TIFF
summary: EXCLUSIVE:  Michaël R. Roskam‘s ensemble World War Two Belgian resistance drama Le Faux Soir world premieres as a Special Presentation in Toronto this weekend, before heading to San Sebastian as the closing film, and Deadline can unveil the trailer.   Set in Belgium in November 1943, the drama is inspired by the events surrounding daily […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Michaël R. Roskam‘s ensemble World War Two Belgian resistance drama Le Faux Soir world premieres as a Special Presentation in Toronto this weekend, before heading to San Sebastian as the closing film, and Deadline can unveil the trailer.

Set in Belgium in November 1943, the drama is inspired by the events surrounding daily newspaper Le Soir, which became a vehicle for Nazi Germany propaganda following its invasion of the country in 1940, resulting in it being nicknamed “Le Soir Volé” (The Stolen Soir).

In the world’s “first media hack”, a group of Resistance fighters hatch a wild but dangerous plan to print a fake edition of Le Soir, packed with articles mocking the occupier.

Arieh Worthalter (The Goldman Case) leads a cast also featuring Mélanie Thierry (Da 5 Bloods, Memoir of War), Karim Leklou (Beating Hearts, Jim’s Story), Mara Taquin (The Mohicans, On the Edge), Bouli Lanners (Nobody Has to Know, The Night of the 12th), Julien Frison (The Night of the 12th) and François Damiens (Dog on Trial, La Famille Belier).

Watch on Deadline

The production marks Roskam’s first feature film since Racer and the Bird, which played as a Special Presentation in Toronto in 2017, with credits in between including Apple+ drama Golden Globe-nominated Black Bird, with Taron Egerton, Paul Walter Hauser and Greg Kinnear.

Le Faux Soir is produced by Jean-Yves Roubin and Cassandre Warnauts at Belgium’s Frakas Productions; Alice Girard and Vincent Maraval at French production combo Goodfellas/Rectangle Productions; and Roskam’s Harbor Men Pictures; in association with Anonymous Federation et Rossel (Bernard Marchant). Cinéart has taken Benelux rights.

Goodfellas is handling international sales.

title: EST N8 Picks Up Manila-Set Crime Thriller ‘Jaguar’ With Elijah Canlas, David Call, Sid Lucero & Gabby Padilla
summary: EXCLUSIVE: EST N8 has acquired worldwide rights to Jaguar, a Manila-set crime thriller from director Dean Colin Marcial, a Berlinale Talents Lab alumnus whose work has screened at Toronto, SXSW, Tribeca and Sitges film festivals. The ensemble cast is led by award-winning Filipino actor Elijah Canlas – known for indie breakout hits Kalel, 15 and […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: EST N8 has acquired worldwide rights to Jaguar, a Manila-set crime thriller from director Dean Colin Marcial, a Berlinale Talents Lab alumnus whose work has screened at Toronto, SXSW, Tribeca and Sitges film festivals.

The ensemble cast is led by award-winning Filipino actor Elijah Canlas – known for indie breakout hits Kalel, 15 and Sunshine – along with U.S. actor David Call (Tiny Furniture; James White), Sid Lucero (Lav Diaz’s Norte, The End of History) and Cinemalaya Best Actress winner Gabby Padilla (Kono Basho).

Also featuring in the cast are Ruby Ruiz, who starred in Prime Video series Expats, Soliman Cruz (To The North), Venice best actor winner John Arcilla (On The Job 2: The Missing 8) and Isabel Sandoval (Lingua Franca). The film also marks the feature acting debut of Dilaw Obero, the frontman for Filipino rock band Dilaw.

Watch on Deadline

The film follows a young security guard in Manila who accidentally witnesses a high-profile murder involving an American movie star. Described as a combination of Filipino genre cinema with American indie grit, the film explores themes including class, power and corruption.

Supported by Purin Pictures and Film London, and winner of the Mocha Chai Laboratories Post-Production Grant at the QCinema Project Market, the film is produced by Braden Friedman (Little Accidents), Bam Manlongat (Under Parallel Skies) and Marcial.

Executive producers include A/Vantage Pictures founder Jason Michael Berman, whose credits include Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest and Ben Affleck’s Air; Galileo Mondol (The Creator) and veteran Filipino producer Moira Lang (The Blossoming of Maximo Oliveros, Norte, The End of History).

EST N8 will launch international sales on the title at the upcoming Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) Market. The deal for worldwide rights was brokered by Sophie Shi for EST N8, and Bianca Grimshaw with Rebecca Theodore at Granderson Des Rochers LLP on behalf of the filmmakers.

“I was just blessed to work with an amazing cast and director that always collaborated to elevate the scenes in the film,” said Canlas, who won several Best Actor awards for his role in Jun Robles Lana’s Kalel, 15 and stood out in Antoinette Jadaone’s social drama Sunshine.

“I feel like audiences are craving for unique and fresh ways of telling a story and that’s what we aimed for with Jaguar: a film that follows an ordinary Filipino worker that spirals into unknown territory.”

Sophie Changhui Shi, EST N8 Head of Studios, said: “Jaguar hits the sweet spot for international distributors – it’s an auteur-driven crime story with visceral genre elements and an exceptional festival pedigree that showcases the extraordinary creative energy coming out of Southeast Asian cinema right now.”

“Dean Colin Marcial and his team have crafted a story deeply rooted in the local atmosphere while possessing universal tension, further elevating high-concept Asian genre cinema on the world stage. We are thrilled to introduce this raw, electric thriller to global buyers at TIFF.”

Marcial noted: “We set out to shoot an incendiary crime story that’s a snapshot of present-day Manila – the bleeding edge of east & west. Sophie and the rest of the EST N8 team share our vision for the film and are champions of the emerging SEA New Wave.”

Jason Michael Berman said: “I really believe Jaguar announces Dean as a great new talent. It’s also a genuinely cross-cultural film – pairing a prolific American actor with some of the biggest Filipino stars, and standing as a terrific U.S.-Philippines co-production.

“Partnering with the team at EST N8 to launch Jaguar on the international stage at TIFF ensures that this collision of indie filmmaking and Filipino genre reaches the wide global audience it was made for.”

The international sales push and global rollout strategy for Jaguar will be led by EST N8 executives Jan Paul Villanueva (EVP, Acquisitions & Global Distribution), Cathy Ni (Head of Sales) and Shams Pasha (Sales & Marketing Executive).

EST N8’s TIFF Market slate also inclues B-EST Pictures’ Thai horror debut Tame, Chan Chun-hao’s Taiwanese thriller Dead End, Rezwan Shahriar Sumit’s IFFR Big Screen Award winner Master, and Tetsuya Mariko’s Dear Stranger, starring Hidetoshi Nishijima and Gwei Lun-Mei.

title: Alicia Keys, Yeonjun & Others Join Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean For Hugh Jackman-Hosted 2026 Global Citizen Festival In NYC
summary: UPDATE: Alicia Keys & friends, Victoria Monét, Yeonjun, and Yoshiki have joined the lineup for this year’s Global Citizen Festival. Taking place on September 26 in Central Park, they join previously announced performers Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend,Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey and Tomorrow X Together. Additionally, Bill Nye, IZA, Jordan Fisher, Katie Couric, Lais Ribeiro, Marcus Samuelsson, Naomi Watanabe, Nomzamo Mbatha, PJ […]
content:
UPDATE: Alicia Keys & friends, Victoria Monét, Yeonjun, and Yoshiki have joined the lineup for this year’s Global Citizen Festival. Taking place on September 26 in Central Park, they join previously announced performers Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend,Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey and Tomorrow X Together. Additionally, Bill Nye, IZA, Jordan Fisher, Katie Couric, Lais Ribeiro, Marcus Samuelsson, Naomi Watanabe, Nomzamo Mbatha, PJ Sin Suela, and Vladimir Duthiers will make appearances, with more names to be announced in the coming weeks.

PREVIOUS, August 13: The 2026 Global Citizen Festival in New York’s Central Park next month will feature a line-up including Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean celebrating the 30th anniversary of Fugees’ album The Score, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend, Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey, and Tomorrow X Together.

Taking place on Central Park’s Great Lawn on Saturday, September 26, the festival will be hosted by Hugh Jackman, and feature appearances by Rachel Brosnahan and Gayle King, with more to be announced in the coming weeks.

Watch on Deadline

The line-up was announced today by Global Citizen, considered the world’s largest movement to end extreme poverty.

Following the success of the first-ever FIFA World Cup Final Halftime Show, which was produced by Global Citizen and helped raise $60 million for the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, this year’s festival will raise awareness for what the organization says are three core issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty across the world. The goals as stated are to create opportunities for 2 million children to go to school, support 1.5 million smallholder farmers, and provide electricity for 2.5 million homes.

Tickets to the Global Citizen Festival are free and can be secured by visiting the Global Citizen app and earning points by completing “action journeys” related to the core issues. Points can be redeemed by entering the free ticket lottery or making a $25 charitable donation to instantly secure a ticket. Funds raised will go to New York City’s City Parks Foundation to support their youth education programming and parks initiatives across all five boroughs, as well as to organizations helping those experiencing homelessness across the city.

“It’s time to gather once again on the Great Lawn, in the middle of New York City, to tell the world an end to extreme poverty is possible,” said Jackman, Global Citizen Ambassador, in a statement.

title: Andrew Scott to Receive Mill Valley Film Festival’s Acting Award for ‘Elsinore’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Andrew Scott will receive the Mill Valley Film Festival’s Acting Award for his latest performance in “Elsinore.” Scott stars in the Focus Features film portraying Ian Charleson in his celebrated performance as Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, before the actor, known for starring in “Chariots of Fire,” died at the peak of the AIDS crisis […]
content:
Andrew Scott will receive the Mill Valley Film Festival‘s Acting Award for his latest performance in “Elsinore.”

Scott stars in the Focus Features film portraying Ian Charleson in his celebrated performance as Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, before the actor, known for starring in “Chariots of Fire,” died at the peak of the AIDS crisis in 1990.

Directed by Simon Stone and produced by Scott, “Elsinore” tells the deeply emotional and inspirational true story of the late Charleson, a gifted actor whose greatest challenge becomes his greatest triumph. “Facing his own mortality with unflinching honesty, wit, and grace,” the film’s synopsis explains, “Charleson delivers a courageous performance that becomes a source of healing and inspiration for those around him.” Focus will release “Elsinore,” also starring Oscar winner Olivia Colman, in theaters on Nov. 20.

MVFF49 takes place Oct. 1-11 across venues in Marin County and the Bay Area. The California Film Institute, a nonprofit that also runs the DocLands Documentary Film Festival, presents the festival. Scott’s Actor Award presentation will take place on Saturday, Oct. 3, at 7 p.m. at the Smith Rafael Film Center as part of MVFF49’s Spotlight program, which recognizes standout work by film artists at any stage in their career.

Popular on Variety

“Devastating and miraculous, Andrew Scott gives the performance of a lifetime as an actor racing mortality to claim Hamlet before the curtain falls,” said Mark Fishkin, founder and director of the Mill Valley Film Festival, in a statement. “Olivia Colman quietly breaks your heart as the only one who knows the truth. Urgent, unforgettable, and deeply moving.”

The festival’s artistic director Rose Kuo added: “Andrew Scott’s interpretation of Ian Charleson’s Hamlet, the most death-haunted of tragic heroes, is witty, superbly passionate, and profoundly moving, becoming a meditation on mortality and the art of acting itself.”

Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis declared that playing Charleson in “Elsinore” is “the role of Scott’s career” and could land him his first best actor Oscar nomination, recognition that has eluded the actor thus far, including a notable snub for his shattering turn in “All of Us Strangers.”

The Mill Valley award is the latest accolade for Scott, who previously won SAG-AFTRA’s Actor Award for his role in “Fleabag” and three Olivier Awards for “Vanya,” “A Girl in a Car with a Man” and “Present Laughter.” In 2024, he earned Emmy, Golden Globe and Critics’ Choice nominations for starring in Netflix’s “Ripley.” He also became the first person to win Critics Circle lead actor prizes in both film and theater in the same year for “All of Us Strangers” and “Vanya.”

Scott most recently starred in Focus’s “Pressure,” opposite Oscar winner Brendan Fraser, as well as the third installment of the “Knives Out” franchise, “Wake Up Dead Man” and Richard Linklater’s “Blue Moon,” which earned Scott the Berlin Film Festival’s Silver Bear award (for best supporting performance), ahead of the film’s Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations. Next year, he stars in “A Place in Hell” for Neon, alongside Michelle Williams and Daisy Edgar-Jones. He recently wrapped production on Netflix’s “Walk the Blue Fields” opposite Emily Blunt, and Justine Triet’s next film, “Fonda,” alongside Mia Goth.

title: Gaza Doc ‘NAZA,’ From ‘No Other Land’ Directors, Earns Record-Breaking 24.5-Minute Venice Ovation as Producer Jonathan Glazer Leads Applause
summary: “NAZA,” the new documentary from “No Other Land” directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, earned a massive 24.5-minute ovation at its Venice Film Festival premiere on Thursday. This marks the longest-ever standing ovation in Venice, besting the 22 minutes for “The Voice of Hind Rajab” last year, and perhaps the longest at any film festival […]
content:
“NAZA,” the new documentary from “No Other Land” directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, earned a massive 24.5-minute ovation at its Venice Film Festival premiere on Thursday.

This marks the longest-ever standing ovation in Venice, besting the 22 minutes for “The Voice of Hind Rajab” last year, and perhaps the longest at any film festival period.

The film shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis. The hot-button doc, which was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, features revelatory interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers.



“NAZA,” a term that appears throughout the documentary, is an acronym for collateral damage used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians it expects will be killed in an airstrike.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four directors of “No Other Land,” which won the 2025 best documentary Oscar and depicts the Israeli government’s efforts to force Palestinians from their homes in the southern West Bank.

Popular on Variety

In an interview with Variety ahead of the doc’s premiere, Abraham said: “As Israelis, we found ourselves wanting to use the kind of position that we have — the access that we have to people in our own society who went into the military — to look at that system as it carried out what all human rights organizations are saying is a genocide.”

The film, which is the only documentary feature in this year’s Venice’s competition lineup, is produced by British newspaper The Guardian and James Wilson (JW Films) and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer. Wilson and Glazer are the Oscar-winning team behind the film “The Zone of Interest.”

Last year, Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania’s Gaza-set “The Voice of Hind Rajab,” about the death of a 6-year-old girl killed by Israeli military fire while attempting to flee Gaza City with her family, elicited a 22-minute standing ovation, which stands as the fest’s longest. Ben Hania is part of Venice’s Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury that will be selecting the award winners on Saturday.

title: ‘Naza’ Review: Two of the ‘No Other Land’ Filmmakers Deliver a More Devastating Exposé of Israeli Genocidal Policy, This Time in Gaza
summary: The irksome controversy over “No Other Land” upon winning both the Berlinale Documentary prize and the Academy Award was never really about the film. It was hardly the first strong documentary to call attention to Israel’s official policy of ethnic cleansing, and there were no revelations to be had. But coming just four months after […]
content:
The irksome controversy over “No Other Land” upon winning both the Berlinale Documentary prize and the Academy Award was never really about the film. It was hardly the first strong documentary to call attention to Israel’s official policy of ethnic cleansing, and there were no revelations to be had. But coming just four months after the October 7th Hamas attack, tensions were high, misinformation was rife, and Israel’s decades-long conflation of anti-Zionism and anti-Semitism had burrowed deep into the Western psyche. Simplistic media pieces marveled that Palestinian and Israeli filmmakers were working together, and film festivals claiming “not to take sides” were able to hide behind their programming and have it both ways.

The distance between then and now is saturated with the blood of more than 73,000 people, though casualty figures fail to account for the deliberate infliction of trauma on those who survive. This is the space that “Naza” seeks to fill, and in its systematic, neutral-toned way of conveying information about Israel’s policy-driven perpetration of genocidal war crimes, it’s a more effective and urgent documentary than “No Other Land.” It also makes sense that it’s directed by only the Israeli half of that film’s directing team, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who have assumed the responsibility of revealing their government’s hidden activities in a way that would have been impossible had their fellow filmmakers joined them.

Popular on Variety

The setup is simple and remarkably effective: Over the past three years, they filmed Abraham talking to members of the Israeli military elite at night, on Tel Aviv rooftops. Each of the 24 service members is seen in obscured profile, their voices modified to make identification impossible. Asked about their duties, they describe in detail, frequently using sketchpads, how they executed their orders in Gaza. Some were involved in surveillance, several were guiding lethal drones from the safety of their Tel Aviv headquarters, and others were on the ground. All participated in erasing not just the human presence in Gaza, but the buildings themselves.

“Naza” is the army word for “collateral damage.” Rather than talk about the murder of non-combatants, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) use the term “naza,” obviating the need to think of dead civilians as men, women and children. This erasure of human costs is not a policy that originated with Benjamin Netanyahu: For decades, the Israeli government has stocked its jails and morgues with Arab men in order to use them as bargaining chips in prisoner exchanges. Six Israelis for 291 Syrians; one dead IDF soldier for 65 prisoners and 40 bodies; one Israeli hostage for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners. The message, disseminated not just within Israel but among the diaspora, is that one Israeli, alive or dead, is worth untold numbers of Arabs.

Understanding that this is policy is crucial for comprehending how Israeli soldiers are expected to dutifully erase entire villages without questioning orders. By saying “200 naza” rather than “200 non-combattants killed,” the dehumanization process is handily condensed to four letters. And yet, despite being miles away from the drone attacks, the soldiers directing the strikes hear everything. The IDF listens to all Gazan phones, so they know where people are and whether children are home. They know who’s in an apartment just before the missiles hit, and they hear the screams after the explosions. They even coined a phrase — “Where’s Daddy?” — to describe listening in on a child’s phone, determining when their father will be home, and then sending a missile to kill them all. As one solider matter-of-factly says about a 12-year-old, “You hack her phone, and then you kill her.”

That’s the part most difficult to comprehend: It’s easy to use the term “naza” because it’s a cold statistic, but how is it possible to listen to people in agony and still accept that this is a necessary operation? “You feel like God, because you hear everything they say,” explains one of the people interviewed. In many cases, the soldiers have had Arabic training, so they can’t hide behind incomprehension, as so often happens on Western news broadcasts that show distraught Arab women but don’t bother to subtitle what they say.

The geographic distance (Gaza is a mere 37 miles from Tel Aviv) offers another form of psychological detachment, but as one IDF member says, they didn’t need psychologists — they were fully into it. Raised on video games where the more you killed the more points you got, these soldiers just transferred those dopamine highs to real life: Strikes that were successful were fun. What’s more, they’re just following orders. “My role is technical” and “You have to trust the system” are two of the familiar lines used to disguise the moral somersaults needed to perpetrate atrocities.

It’s not as if they don’t understand the ethical implications. The same man who says it was fun also openly admits to knowing Israel is committing genocide. Presumably the reason he agreed to speak with Abraham is because he feels some iota of remorse, though that concept never comes up. Someone else expresses revulsion at seeing dogs devour bodies left to rot, but the disgust doesn’t seem to extend to the killings themselves. (Conversely, the organization Breaking the Silence, composed of former soldiers actively calling attention to Israel’s policy of ethnic cleaning, was featured in Avi Mograbi’s 2021 documentary “The First 54 Years.”)

For those still unwilling to accept the word ‘genocide’ in the context of Palestine, “Naza” makes clear that the Israeli government believes there are no innocents in Gaza, which is why snipers can so nonchalantly pick off starving people waiting at food distribution points. But genocide is not only the elimination of human lives, it’s also the deliberate destruction of property, to cover up ethnic cleansing and ensure that no one from the eliminated population will come back. Despite official Israeli denials, this too is revealed, as those involved on the ground talk about the premeditated flattening of any structure that could harbor human life.

Abraham and Szor intersperse these chilling testimonies with shots from the rooftops of the Tel Aviv skyline at night. Without seeing faces, we glimpse people in their apartments, watching TV, preparing meals, heading to sleep. The device allows the viewer a momentary space to breathe before the next wrenching description, but it also reflects on the large percentage of Israelis who also “trust the system.” Though not stated in “Naza,” this faith in the righteousness of eliminating the Palestinian people from their lands doesn’t come from the ruling Likud party, but can be found in the very DNA of Zionist philosophy.

Given the film’s extremely effective structure, it would be difficult to insert information not elicited from the rooftop conversations, though it would have been useful had the filmmakers been able to get at least one soldier to talk about the government’s fear-mongering following the horrific October 7th atrocities, with discredited tales of beheaded babies and likely exaggerating reports of sexual violence (about which Azadeh Moaveni has persuasively written in the “London Review of Books”). Will “Naza” change minds, now that it’s becoming increasingly difficult to disguise what’s happening in Gaza and the West Bank? It has more of a chance than “No Other Land,” though by giving festivals claiming to be apolitical a free pass just for programming the film, we too contribute to a campaign designed to obfuscate the reality so unflinchingly revealed here.

title: Role Model and Hydro Flask Launch Limited-Edition Drinkware Collection Inspired by ‘Chuck Timely & The Hourglass’
summary: Hydro Flask announced a collaboration with singer-songwriter Role Model (Tucker Pilsbury), featuring stylish drinkware inspired by his third studio album, “Chuck Timely & The Hourglass.” To celebrate its launch, Role Model released a promotional video with his friend and longtime collaborator Ky Newman teasing the limited-edition collection, which is timed with the opening night of […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Hydro Flask announced a collaboration with singer-songwriter Role Model (Tucker Pilsbury), featuring stylish drinkware inspired by his third studio album, “Chuck Timely & The Hourglass.”

To celebrate its launch, Role Model released a promotional video with his friend and longtime collaborator Ky Newman teasing the limited-edition collection, which is timed with the opening night of Role Model Presents: Chuck On Tour.

“Being able to outfit the whole band and crew with reusable bottles cuts down on waste to really make an impact while we’re on the road,” Role Model said. “We also got to run with the creative for this campaign, so it just felt like me and Ky doing what we normally do.”

Limited-Edition Hydro Flask x Role Model SHOP ONLINE

The collection features eight Hydro Flask bottles that were selected and designed in partnership with Role Model, including variations of top-selling bottles such as the 32 oz Wide Flex Straw Cap and the 400 mL Micro Hydro.

This marks the second artist-inspired drop released through the Hydro Flask x Universal Music Group partnership, which aims to promote reusable drinkware throughout the music industry.

“Hydro Flask has always led with joy. Role Model brings that same spirit to music, and our partnership was a natural fit,” said Larry Witt, the president of Hydro Flask. “Since launching our partnership with UMG, we’ve seen a strong response from fans and artists. Our new campaign with Role Model shows that reusables can be part of everyday life, and that making a positive impact can be simple, easy, and even a little fun.”

The full collection is available now on the Hydro Flask website.

title: ‘The Office’ and ‘King of the Hill’ Producer Greg Daniels on Opening Doors For a Whole Generation of Writers
summary: When Greg Daniels wants to be friends with you, he won’t invite you to grab a drink at a local bar. He’ll ask you if you want to write comedy. “It’s kind of like my invitation to play tennis or hang out,” he says. “I’ve worked with some really amazing collaborators, and I’ve sought them […]
content:
When Greg Daniels wants to be friends with you, he won’t invite you to grab a drink at a local bar. He’ll ask you if you want to write comedy.

“It’s kind of like my invitation to play tennis or hang out,” he says. “I’ve worked with some really amazing collaborators, and I’ve sought them out. It’s been the highlight of my social life.”

Early in his career, that meant approaching Larry David and pitching a ton of ideas for “Seinfeld,” one of which became the Season 3 episode “The Parking Space.”

“My goal was to just get into that room, and find out how he’s doing ‘Seinfeld,’” Daniels says. “And I was given a 20-minute window to pitch him over the phone, so I pitched him, like, 11 episode ideas. He bought a story that happened to my dad in the streets of New York when I was a kid. So I got a chance to go in there and write three drafts of that with him, and hear all of his thoughts.”

Popular on Variety

Daniels, who is getting a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame Sept. 10, also was a huge fan of James L. Brooks’ work growing up, so when he moved to L.A., a priority became landing a job at “The Simpsons.” The success of that “Seinfeld” episode helped secure him the job — and then get that chance to sit in a room and pitch jokes to the legendary Brooks.

“I just wanted to do something that I felt was sophisticated and funny and human,” he says.

After “The Simpsons,” Daniels partnered with Mike Judge — then riding high on the success of “Beavis and Butt-head” — to create “King of the Hill,” and the two set out to do something different in tone from “The Simpsons.”

“I respect Mike’s genius,” he says. “I just love the way he looks at the world and his writing style.”

Then, as a fan of the U.K. “The Office,” Daniels met with creators Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant, mostly because, “I just wanted to know how they did the original British show,” he says. “I really wanted to meet them and find out their process more than actually adapt the show. But we kind of hit it off, and I thought well, maybe for HBO, this would work, and I agreed to adapt it.”

The series ended up going to NBC, of course, and in the process, Daniels created an American “Office” that has become a multi-generational hit, as Gen Z fans rediscover the series and binge it on streaming. (It also spawned the spinoff “The Paper”).

It’s that career trajectory and impact on TV storytelling over the course of multiple decades that made Daniels an easy candidate for a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. It’s an honor, he says, since the attraction still reminds him of his early days as an aspiring writer in Los Angeles.

“It’s very meaningful for me because when I came out here in 1985, I used to walk up and down the boulevard and find all my heroes,” he says. “It’s crazy to be on the street too! I think I’m on the same block as Bob Newhart and John Belushi, which is kind of cool.”

Daniels also takes pride in the recognition because, as he notes, “I’ve been lucky enough to have a lot of shows that have shot in L.A.” That’s notable since most of his shows haven’t actually taken place in the City of Angels, but through Hollywood magic, Van Nuys has doubled for Scranton, Pa., in “The Office,” while Pasadena and environs often doubled for Pawnee, Ind., in “Parks and Recreation.” And now, the Valley, downtown and even the L.A. Times offices fill in for Toledo, Ohio, in “The Paper.”

“To be shooting now, again, on the Universal lot, and be able to work with the same crew that I’ve had before on other shows, it’s really great to have that long history,” Daniels says.

His impact on Hollywood also extends to the successful writers and producers that have gone on to big things after learning at the School of Greg Daniels. That is especially true with the list of writers who spent time on “The Office” — including Mike Schur, who co-created “Parks and Rec” with Daniels before moving on to shows like “The Good Place” and “Brooklyn Nine-Nine.”

Other prolific “Office” alums include Mindy Kaling, who not only starred on the show but also wrote more scripts than anyone else on that series, and then went on to create “The Mindy Project,” “Never Have I Ever” and more.

“Greg is an incredibly funny writer and a great producer, but what makes him so special is how much he loves teaching younger writers,” Kaling says. “He’s impossibly patient and has this professorial quality that makes you want to learn from him. He empowered me to find my voice and taught me how to be a showrunner.”

Then there’s Gene Stupnitsky and Lee Eisenberg (“Jury Duty”), Justin Spitzer (“Superstore”), Paul Lieberstein (“The Newsroom”), Jennifer Celotta (“Barry”), B.J. Novak (“Vengeance”), Randall Einhorn (“Abbott Elementary”) and others.

“He’s taught a generation of writers a new way to think about character, dialogue, scene and story structure — writers who have then spread that knowledge to dozens of shows,” Lieberstein says. “Nobody is better at casting actors and finding writers than Greg. He sees past all the standard markers of talent, to what’s great inside a person, what an actor can truly offer — and that has lead him to cast people and give them the roles that have made them some of the biggest untraditional stars of today.”

For Michael Koman, who co-created the “Office” spinoff “The Paper” with Daniels, he’s learned by example in a wide variety of ways. “Like pretty much everyone who works in, or watches, television, I admire Greg,” he says. “I respect his talent and his capacity for hard work, and the good sense that he brings to the endless stream of decisions that he’s asked to make almost constantly. On top of that, you have all of the cool things he’s made, the people he’s worked with, the legacy he’s built, his massive effect on American comedy, his brilliant family, and the loyalty he’s earned through decades of high-quality work and decency.

“Every show Greg has made he has used as a ladder for people that he recognizes as talented and funny to move up in the world,” he adds. “Our whole culture is populated by people that Greg hired, trained, mentored and showcased.”

What is the hallmark of a Greg Daniels show? “I tend to think of it as I’m a link in a sort of character comedy chain that goes back to a lot of shows that I loved growing up, like ‘The Odd Couple,’” he says. “And maybe the storytelling that I heard growing up from my dad, who shaped my taste.”

And then it was “King of the Hill” that helped define Daniels’ series alchemy.

“What I really liked doing and kind of developed on ‘King of the Hill’ was having an emotional story that was kind of hidden for most of the episode, underneath the plot’s story,” he says.

What he wanted to break out of was how sitcoms traditionally treated emotional storylines as pro forma: “It was always like someone’s going to hug, and then they had something called a ‘treacle cutter,’ which was the joke that got you back to comedy, land after the hug. It never felt as earned. If I have a style, it’s probably based on paying attention to the emotional story and trying to do it in an earned way that’s hidden behind the comedy until it comes in.”

Saladin Patterson, who serves as showrunner on the recent Hulu revival of “King of the Hill,” calls Daniels both the smartest and funniest person he knows. “His curiosity and excitement towards problem-solving become contagious and this encourages everyone around him to be the best versions of themselves,” Patterson says. “You couldn’t ask for better qualities in a leader.”

With “The Office,” Daniels wound up enjoying the mockumentary format and what the show’s character confessionals allowed him to do creatively.

“That adds a lot of complexity,” he says. “There’s this idea that they’re aware they’re being filmed in half the scenes, but in another portion of the scenes, they’re not aware they’re being filmed. For the actors and the writers, that’s another layer to play with. So for something that’s so relatable and simple, set in this office, it’s super complex because it has all these abilities to talk to people’s perspectives and points of view, and then catch them unaware — to see how they present themselves to the world, how they actually are. It’s got a stylishness that isn’t necessarily apparent on a single frame.”

And now he’s getting to revisit that format with “The Paper,” which is set in the same universe as “The Office” but follows the staff of a small Toledo newspaper as new editor Ned Sampson (Domhnall Gleeson) attempts to revive the troubled publication.

“I am very happy,” Daniels says. “It’s another assemblage of a cast that is all amazingly unique and talented. It’s just a joy to be going to the set and working with them.”

But unlike “The Office,” which aired as many as 28 half-hours in a single season, “The Paper” has produced just 10 episodes a season for Peacock. That’s the reality of this streaming age, but Daniels would love to produce more.

“It’s a great art form, the character comedy, and it takes a lot of episodes to really get to know everybody. Then you’re really locked in, and you’re excited for any new story involving these characters that you love so much,” he says. “There’s a great cast on ‘The Paper,’ and we’re always leaving lots of wonderful ideas and scenes on the cutting-room floor. If we had more episodes, we’d be able to explore more with the ensemble, so I think that it would be great.”

But even as the business has changed, Daniels still loves what he gets to do. “I’ve had such a nice time in this business,” he says. “A lot of my best memories are things that were in the writers’ room, or times on set where the actors kept breaking. I hope that other young writers get a chance to have a whole career in it the way I have.”

And if they’re really lucky, perhaps Daniels will call them up to hang out and make some comedy. But leave the tennis racquet at home — and just bring a laptop.

Greg Daniels receives a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame at 11:30 a.m. PT on Sept. 10. Location is at 6357 Hollywood Blvd., Hollywood; go to walkoffame.com to watch a livestream of the ceremony.

Greg Daniels Looks Back at Writing for Some of the Most Iconic Series on TV

Greg Daniels began his career out of Harvard working alongside writing partner Conan O’Brien on sketch comedy shows like “Saturday Night Live” — then reinvented himself as a comedy series scribe on “The Simpsons.” He co-created “King of the Hill” and adapted “The Office” into one of the most iconic TV series of the 21st century. Here are some of the key shows from his five-decade career so far.

“Not Necessarily the News” (HBO; Daniels’ tenure: 1985-87)

Daniels’ and O’Brien’s first job out of college was this early HBO parody of both news programs and the political and public figures in the headlines. “We sat in a room and watched unedited news footage from ABC, hours and hours of it,” Daniels says. “We saw some stuff that you couldn’t see on network TV because it was too graphic, and tried to make it funny.”

“The Wilton North Report” (Fox, 1987-1988)

After Fox canceled its “The Late Show” talker (hosted by Joan Rivers, then Arsenio Hall), it attempted to create a late night comedy news magazine hosted by two radio DJs and featuring segments from both comedy writers and filmmakers. Some of the segment producers came from the world of documentaries — a world that Daniels would later mine with mockumentaries like “The Office.” The show itself “blew up so spectacularly,” Daniels recalls. He also appeared on-air briefly in a rare on-camera moment.

“Saturday Night Live” (NBC; Daniels’ tenure: 1987-1990)

“The excitement of the music starting, and it’s live, and working with all those talented people,” Daniels recalls. “The caliber of the actors like Dana Carvey, and working with Robert Smigel — and it was such an eye opener to observe Lorne too. Oh, and it’s where I met my wife!” (That’s longtime TV exec Susanne Daniels, who began her career as Lorne Michaels’ assistant and development executive before moving on to eventually run networks like The WB and Lifetime.)

“The Simpsons” (Fox; Daniels’ tenure: 1993-1998)

Daniels wrote early memorable episodes like “Homer and Apu” (which landed him an Emmy nom for the song “Who Needs the Kwik-E-Mart?”), “Bart Sells His Soul” and “Lisa’s Wedding,” which earned the series an animated program Emmy. “I was anxious and excited to see James L. Brooks in the ‘Simpsons’ room, and he is so brilliant and generous with his laughter,” Daniels says. “It was always a treat to pitch stories to him.”

“King of the Hill” (Fox/Hulu, 1997-2010 and 2025-present)

When Daniels co-created the family comedy with Mike Judge, he wanted to make sure it didn’t copy “The Simpsons” formula. And instead, it created its own lane as a more grounded, and emotionally rich, animated series about a quirky Texas family and their friends. The show’s recent revival earned critical raves and recently returned for a second season. “It was fun to be back with the cast and the characters, to be writing scenes again for Hank and Peggy Hill, it was like seeing old friends,” he says.

“The Office” (NBC, 2005-2013)

“I loved the show so much,” he says of getting the keys and adapting it for NBC. “I was always telling the cast, if all we get to do is the pilot, that’s enough. It’ll be amazing, we’ll enjoy it so much. And then we got another five episodes, and I was like, ‘my God, guys, it’s going to air somewhere!’ It really was a long while before it looked like it was going to be a big deal, but it was so worth it creatively for everybody.”

“Parks and Recreation” (NBC, 2009-2015)

Daniels and Mike Schur were originally tasked with writing a spinoff of “The Office,” but “Parks and Rec” quickly became its own thing — and a bit of a counterweight to the themes of “The Office.” “We decided that, OK, if ‘The Office’ is about private business, this is about government,” he says. “And we also were like, well, ‘The Office’ is kind of dreary. Let’s try and make this one happier and less bittersweet. It was super fun as we built a whole world and shot in it.”

“Upload” (Prime Video, 2020-2025)

A sci-fi fan, Daniels had been sitting on the idea for “Upload” for decades, going back to his days on “SNL.” Then he started writing it as a book during the 2008 writers’ strike. After “The Office” ended, he finally began crafting it as a series. “For me to go out of the box of comedy and do something so cinematic, VFX-heavy and expensive was a stretch,” he says. “It was a long process to get it to the screen. But it was really fun to almost do a live-action cartoon, because it was half in a digital world and a lot of cartoony things can happen in that world. I’m very proud of it.”

“Space Force” (Netflix, 2020-2022)

Daniels reunited with his “The Office” star Steve Carell for this comedy, which wasn’t meant to be a statement on politics — but he realizes now was probably hampered by how divided this nation is. “I feel like we weren’t giving anybody the show that they wanted,” he says. “The country was a little divided, obviously, and half of them were very wary of being made fun of, and the other half was like, ‘go after them much harder than you’re going after them.’ But we were making a character comedy.”

“The Paper” (Peacock, 2025-present)

In finally finding a way to revisit the world of “The Office,” Daniels and co-creator Michael Koman thought that a documentary crew following the attempts to revive a local newspaper would be fruitful. “I felt it was important to reference the original format of the show and not just do another mockumentary,” Daniels says. “I had taken to much wonderful inspiration from the original format that I thought it would be cool to keep it in the same world. And then there was the notion of paper being the connecting tissue.” Pun intended!

title: Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Netflix’s Cannes Film Festival winner La Bola Negra will begin its platform release on Oct. 16 with the Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo directed title booked at AMC Century City and AMC Burbank in Los Angeles, and at the Angelika Film Center (35mm) and The Paris Theater (35mm) in New York. A bold tapestry […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Netflix’s Cannes Film Festival winner La Bola Negra will begin its platform release on Oct. 16 with the Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo directed title booked at AMC Century City and AMC Burbank in Los Angeles, and at the Angelika Film Center (35mm) and The Paris Theater (35mm) in New York.

A bold tapestry spanning nearly a century of Spanish history, La Bola Negra tells the story of three generations of men whose lives are intimately connected through desire, pain, and love.

The film will continue to expand in its second and third week in the top DMAs in the U.S. and Canada before expanding wider across the country on November 6 (running list of markets below).

The other 35mm locations where the pic will screen include TIFF Lightbox Toronto, Alamo Drafthouse Brooklyn, Landmark Nuart Los Angeles, Music Box Chicago, Coolidge Corner Boston, Angelika Film Center Dallas, Rialto El Cerrito, Hollywood Theatre Portland, The Tara Atlanta, the Sun-Ray Tampa, The Tower Sacramento and VIFF Vancity Vancouver.

Watch on Deadline

Calvo and Ambrossi (aka the Javi’s), along with members of the cast, will participate in select in-theater Q&As in both Los Angeles and New York. Ambrossi and Calvo won the Best Director Award at Cannes back in May. The film most recently held its North American premiere at the Telluride Film Festival to a rapturous reception. It will screen next at TIFF.

As previously reported, Netflix will be reporting grosses for La Bola Negra, David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, Peter Berg’s Mosquito Bowl, Danny Boyle’s Ink, Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew and animated title Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. The hope here for La Bola Negra is to pop a solid per theater average during its run. Netflix’s first No. 1 ranking film at the domestic weekend box office was late August 2025’s Kpop Demon Hunters Singalong with an estimated $19M.

title: Kristen Ciccarelli’s ‘Crimson Moth’ Book Series In Development For TV Adaptation With ‘The 100’s Kim Shumway Penning Script
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Georgia Lee (The Expanse), Joe Henderson (Lucifer) and Chad Kennedy have acquired the rights to the internationally bestselling fantasy romance Crimson Moth series by Kristen Ciccarelli. The trio are developing the project for television with Kim Shumway (The 100) adapting. The script is currently being shopped to buyers. In addition, Wednesday Books, an imprint […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Georgia Lee (The Expanse), Joe Henderson (Lucifer) and Chad Kennedy have acquired the rights to the internationally bestselling fantasy romance Crimson Moth series by Kristen Ciccarelli. The trio are developing the project for television with Kim Shumway (The 100) adapting. The script is currently being shopped to buyers.



In addition, Wednesday Books, an imprint under St. Martin’s Publishing Group, a division of Macmillan Publishers, has acquired books three and four in the bestselling Crimson Moth series in a major deal. Book three, Dark Descent, is slated for publication in August 2027. Foreign rights have already been sold in Brazil, the UK, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Sweden, and more.

Ciccarelli’s Crimson Moth series began with Heartless Hunter, a cat-and-mouse romance between a witch hiding in plain sight and the witch hunter determined to uncover her. A breakout BookTok favorite, the Crimson Moth series became an instant bestseller, has been translated into 24 languages, and has sold over one million copies in the USA and Canada alone.

Watch on Deadline

The Crimson Moth books fall into the vein of the popular romantasy genre that includes the likes of Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing in the works as a TV series adaptation at Prime Video and Jennifer L. Armentrout’s From Blood and Ash in the works with Sony Pictures Television. Hulu and 20th Century recently set a deal to develop a television series adaptation of Sheila Masterson’s The Poison Daughter. Devney Perry’s Shield of Sparrows, which is the first in a planned romantasy trilogy saga, is becoming a feature film with Amazon MGM and Premeditated Productions.

The film/tv deal for Ciccarelli was brokered by UTA, with book deal representation under Danielle Burby at Mad Woman Literary (U.S.) and Taryn Fagerness at Taryn Fagerness Agency (foreign).

title: Snoop Dogg Set To Host 2026 VMAs
summary: West Coast will be representing at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. MTV announced today that Snoop Dogg will host the show as it returns to the West Coast for the first time since 2017. Last year, Queens-raised LL Cool J fronted the show from New York. Snoop’s VMAs stint follows a string of big-ticket, […]
content:
West Coast will be representing at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards.

MTV announced today that Snoop Dogg will host the show as it returns to the West Coast for the first time since 2017. Last year, Queens-raised LL Cool J fronted the show from New York.

Snoop’s VMAs stint follows a string of big-ticket, live televised event appearances for the rapper. Those include his Summer and Winter Olympics commentary for NBC, a run as a coach on The Voice, his New Year’s Eve special on NBC and taking part in an all-star West Coast collaboration with Dr. Dre during the 2022 Super Bowl Halftime Show.

“MTV and the VMAs have been part of my story since the beginning,” the hip-hop star said in a statement. “Some of the biggest moments of my career happened on that stage and on MTV – they gave hip hop a place to be loud, fearless and seen by the whole world. So to come back now and host the VMAs, all these years later, that’s a full-circle moment for me. And doing it with my brother Van Toffler makes it even more special. Van was there during those early MTV days when we were changing the culture in real time, and we’ve got a whole lot of history together. Now we get to make some new history. The VMAs have always been about those moments you don’t forget – and trust me, we’re gonna give y’all a few more. See you at the VMAs.”

Watch on Deadline

For this year’s VMAs, Madonna received 11 nominations, including Video of the Year for “Confessions II — The Film,” Artist of the Year and Song of the Year for “Bring Your Love.”

Following Madonna with nine nominations is Taylor Swift, whose “The Fate of Ophelia” scored nominations in categories like Video of the Year, Best Pop and Best Cinematography, among many others. Swift is also nominated as Artist of the Year.

Nirvana will be honored with the Video Vanguard award.

The VMAs are produced by Gunpowder & Sky. Van Toffler serves as producer. Jesse Ignjatovic of Den of Thieves, Barb Bialkowski and Bruce Gillmer serve as executive producers alongside Barry Barclay and Floris Bauer. Melanie Block serves as co-executive producer and Gary Lanvy as co-producer. Snoop Dogg is executive producer alongside producers Sara Ramaker and Jasmin Ratansi. Jen Proctor is executive talent producer.

Live from Los Angeles, the VMAs will air on Sunday, Sept. 27 (7:30-9:30 p.m. ET/4:30-6:30 p.m. PT) on CBS. It will be simulcast on MTV and streamed on Paramount+ (Premium) in the U.S. The show will also be available globally the next day on Paramount+ and MTV.

title: HBO’s ‘Task’ Adds Rose Rollins & Carol Santiago To Season 2 Cast

Based on an original idea by Brad Ingelsby, Task is set in the working-class suburbs outside of Philadelphia. In the first season, we saw […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: HBO is expanding its recurring cast for Season 2 of Brad Ingelsby’s acclaimed crime drama series Task starring Mark Ruffalo, with Rose Rollins (Long Slow Exhale) and Carol Santiago as the latest additions.

Based on an original idea by Brad Ingelsby, Task is set in the working-class suburbs outside of Philadelphia.

In the first season, we saw Ruffalo’s Tom Brandis form a task force to track down a crew of masked robbers, led by a working-class family man, that were carrying out a series of violent crimes in the Philadelphia area.

In Season 2, Brandis takes the helm of a new task force, but the deeper the operation runs, the harder it is to tell who’s the target.

Watch on Deadline

Cast also includes Mahershala Ali as Eddie Barnes; Julianne Nicholson as Lori Ross; Harry Melling as Brennan Boylan; Adam Nagaitis as Luke Clemmons; Aminah Nieves as Nataly Zamora ; Edgar Ramírez as Miguel Contreras; Martha Plimpton as Kathleen McGinty; Silvia Dionicio as Emily Brandis; Tim Blake Nelson as Denny Coughlin; Jharrel Jerome as Jordan Barnes; Brían F. O’Byrne as Charlie Boylan; Bethlehem Million as Lisa Barnes; Kevin Dunn as Vince Runyan; Andrew Russel as Ethan Brandis; Alaíde as Maria Delgado; Rocío Guzmán as Yvonne Delgado; Regina Nava as Fernanda and Stephanie Sigman as Carmen Belandria

Rollins will play Evie Barners, the deeply devoted wife to Eddie Barnes (Ali) and Santiago will portray Ana Salazar, an expectant mother and a friend to Maria (Alaide).

Task is created by Ingelsby, who returned to HBO following his work on Emmy-winning crime drama Mare of Easttown. Ingelsby is also writing, showrunning, and exec producing alongside Paul Lee and Mark Roybal for wiip, Jeremiah Zagar, Ruffalo, and Ron Schmidt. Nicole Jordan-Webber and Karen Wacker are co-executive producers.

Rollins is repped by The Burstein Company, Innovative Artists, and Meyer & Downs. Santiago is repped by Louis Giovino of ATB Talent Agency and Lucius Robinson of WSM Talent.

title: ‘All Of A Sudden’ Trailer: Ryusuke Hamaguchi Returns With Parisian Drama That Japan Submitted To The Oscars
summary: Here’s the first trailer for Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s latest All of a Sudden, Japan’s entry into the 2027 Oscar Best International Feature race. The Japanese-French-language drama premiered to an 11-minute standing ovation at Cannes and went on to win a Best Actress prize for both of its stars, Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto.
