content:
Here’s the first trailer for Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s latest All of a Sudden, Japan’s entry into the 2027 Oscar Best International Feature race.

The Japanese-French-language drama premiered to an 11-minute standing ovation at Cannes and went on to win a Best Actress prize for both of its stars, Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto.

Set in France and Japan, All of a Sudden follows Marie-Lou (Efira), the director of a care facility for the elderly, who is determined to introduce an innovative philosophy of care rooted in listening and respect for residents’ dignity, despite resistance from members of her staff. Her path is profoundly reshaped by an encounter with Mari (Okamoto), a Japanese theater director battling cancer. As the two women form a deep friendship, they join forces in a shared struggle to make the impossible possible.

Watch on Deadline

Hamaguchi co-wrote the screenplay with Léa Le Dimna, loosely adapting the book of writings by Makiko Miyano and Maho Isono titled When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher with Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist.

The film is produced by David Gauquié, Julien Deris, Jean-Luc Ormières and Renan Artukmaç for France’s Cinefrance Studios; Hiroko Matsuda, Kosuke Oshida and Yuji Sadai for Japan’s Office Shirous and Bitters End; Bettina Brokemper for Germany’s Heimatfilm; and Joseph Rouschop for Belgium’s Tarantula.

Neon will open the film in U.S. theaters on November 25.

Check out the trailer above.

title: Mike McFarland, ‘One Piece’ and ‘Dragon Ball Z’ Voice Actor, Dies at 56
summary: Mike McFarland, a voice actor from the English-dubbed versions of “One Piece” and “Dragon Ball Z,” died on Wednesday following a battle with brain cancer. He was 56.  McFarland was a voice-acting veteran, first playing Master Roshi and Yajirobe in “Dragon Ball” and “Dragon Ball Z” and Buggy the Clown in “One Piece.” His other […]
content:
Mike McFarland, a voice actor from the English-dubbed versions of “One Piece” and “Dragon Ball Z,” died on Wednesday following a battle with brain cancer. He was 56.

McFarland was a voice-acting veteran, first playing Master Roshi and Yajirobe in “Dragon Ball” and “Dragon Ball Z” and Buggy the Clown in “One Piece.” His other roles include Jean Kirstein in “Attack on Titan,” Jean Havoc in “Fullmetal Alchemist” and Teppei Sugo in “Psycho-Pass.”

“Mike brought so much to all of us who knew him, and to all of the anime fans that knew his work,” anime streaming service Crunchyroll said in a statement. “He was an incredible talent, a good friend to so many of us and will be sorely, sorely missed.”

Popular on Variety

Kicking off his career in 1997 as one of the first voice actors in Texas hired by Funimation Entertainment, McFarland became a prominent figure in the anime world. He worked as line producer, ADR director and ADR script adapter for many Animated Dubbing Vision films and series from Funimation/Crunchyroll. These titles include Sky Master in “Heaven’s Lost Property,” Goemon Ishikawa in “Lupin III: The Woman Called Fujiko Mine” and other Lupin III films, as well as George in “Case Closed.” His more recent work includes Hiroshi Odokawa in “Odd Taxi,” Big Bad Wolf in “Date A Live IV” and E.G. Mine in “Trigun Stampede.”

McFarland had been suffering with health issues since January 2025 after he was forced to drop out of Central Florida Comic Con due to a brain tumor. Fellow voice actors J. Michael Tatum and Brandon McInnis created a GoFundMe crowdfunding campaign to help McFarland afford a live-in medical assistant. He underwent multiple surgeries, but the tumor turned out to be a glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer.

title: Tom Hardy Reunites With Helen Mirren at ‘Mobland’ Premiere as Guy Ritchie Says: ‘It’s Been Nothing Other Than a Pleasure to Work With These Monsters of Creativity’
summary: After plenty of behind-the-scenes drama on Paramount+ hit “MobLand,” which saw Tom Hardy almost booted off the series, the cast and creatives reunited for the premiere of Season 2 in London, Thursday night. Leading trio Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren — who play crime couple Conrad and Maeve Harrigan opposite Hardy’s fixer Harry Da Souza […]
content:
After plenty of behind-the-scenes drama on Paramount+ hit “MobLand,” which saw Tom Hardy almost booted off the series, the cast and creatives reunited for the premiere of Season 2 in London, Thursday night.

Leading trio Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren — who play crime couple Conrad and Maeve Harrigan opposite Hardy’s fixer Harry Da Souza — posed together with Hardy on the black carpet outside the Odeon Luxe theater in Leicester Square before heading inside to take the stage alongside co-creator Guy Ritchie and exec producer David Glasser.

Introducing the director and cast to the audience, Glasser – who was believed to have lost patience with Hardy after the actor requested script changes and was late to set – heaped plenty of praise on the star, calling him “the captain of our ship.”

Popular on Variety

“Without further ado, the captain of our ship, and the man who really, really pushed the envelope for us to get this to where we want to do Season 1 and Season 2, and was with it from the beginning and stayed with it to the bitter end of us getting through this incredible season, ladies and gentlemen — Tom Hardy,” Glasser announced as Hardy joined Ritchie, Brosnan and Mirren on stage.

After the cast and audience sang “Happy Birthday” to Ritchie, who turns 58 today, the director spoke movingly about the cast, saying they’ve been “magnificent, it’s been nothing other than a pleasure to work with these monsters of creativity.”

“Lady Helen — Dame Helen, fantastic Helen, Queen Helen — has been nothing other than an inspiration and a force of creativity,” Ritchie said. Super positive all day long, super creative all day long. Pierce Brosnan, your lordship, I can say exactly the same about Pierce and my old brother Tom Hardy.”

“I’m going to come and give a quick cuddle,” Ritchie added before darting across the stage and hugging Hardy.

“They’ve all been a magnificent cast,” Ritchie continued. “It’s been nothing other than a pleasure to work with these monsters of creativity. It’s been nothing but a pleasure. And David, thank you very much. David actually is a visionary. There you go. That’s a surprise. I don’t know. It’s a surprise. He actually is. David is a force of creativity. Good for you, David. Well done.”

When asked what she was most excited for the audience to see in Season 2, Mirren replied “Madder, badder, better,” before turning to Hardy and repeating: “Madder…badder…better. Chaotic, cool, funny. Frightening, funny.”

Brosnan added: “Yeah, very mangled, very strange. And there’s frailties within these characters as well, which makes them very human. But we get on like a great company of actors.”

Mirren also praised the show’s writer, Jez Butterworth, saying he provided them with “incredible material.”

“And the beautiful poetry of Jazz Butterworth, the poetic element in the script is so incredible. It just heightens it out of the sort of the normal. It’s incredible material for us to work on.”

Before introducing the cast, Glasser gave some insight into how the show first got off the ground, saying he and the Paramount+ team flew to Ritchie’s country house in the U.K. to pitch him on the show. “He said yes on the spot…” Glasser recalled. “Over a great bottle of wine while he was cooking some amazing lamb.”

Glasser also revealed that when they were just eight weeks away from shooting Season 1, he, Ritchie and Hardy were still trying to “figure out what the show is” which is when they brought in Butterworth. “We call upon a dear friend, Jez Butterworth, and we say to Jez, ‘We’re eight weeks out of production. Here’s the idea. Here’s the early concept. Let’s go make something of it.’ And you can only imagine being eight weeks out what that was like. It was insane.”

By Season 2, however, the relationship between Hardy, Butterworth and Glasser deteriorated to the point that reports emerged claiming Hardy had been kicked off the show. Those reports turned out to be premature, and Variety confirmed the trio’s “creative differences” were being worked out in order to bring the actor back for Season 2 re-shoots as well as Season 3, which is set to start shooting later this year.

Last week Paramount+ officially confirmed Hardy would indeed return as fixer Harry Da Souza in the popular gangland series.

title: Jack Innanen on Paul Baker’s ‘Adults’ Season 2 Arc and Wanting a Season 3 Halloween Episode
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from Season 2 of “Adults” now streaming on Hulu. It’s Season 2, Paul Baker; we’re doing a classic sitcom.  In only eight episodes, the second season of FX’s “Adults” has managed to capture the spirit of a classic sitcom that has felt somewhat elusive since the slow death […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from Season 2 of “Adults” now streaming on Hulu. It’s Season 2, Paul Baker; we’re doing a classic sitcom. In only eight episodes, the second season of FX’s “Adults” has managed to capture the spirit of a classic sitcom that has felt somewhat elusive since the slow death of the 22-episode season. The raunchy friend group comedy, created by Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw, follows Paul Baker (Jack Innanen), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele), Billie (Lucy Freyer) and Samir (Malik Elassal). While Samir’s parents are away, the friends are bunking together and navigating their twentysomething lives in his childhood home in Queens, New York. Following the premiere of the second season (but before the promise of a third), Innanen spoke with Variety about Paul Baker’s arc this season, the limits of delivering sitcom goodness within an eight-episode season and his hopes for a Season 3.

Other then a few network sitcoms, the 22-episode season has fallen out of fashion with the rise of streaming services. Now, fans are lucky to get 10 episodes in one season. “Adults,” with the addition of Paul Baker’s origin story prequel episode, now clocks in at an uneven 17 across two seasons. “If we had 22 episodes, we could do ‘stuck in the elevator’ episode,” Innanen says. “We could do the beach episode. We could do so many fun filler episodes. But it’s just born too late.”

But the show has the trappings of a classic sitcom, despite its shortened airtime.

Popular on Variety

Courtesy of FX

This season kicks off with the camera winding its way through the Queens house as Issa delivers the meta line, “It’s Season 2, Paul Baker; we’re doing a oner.” The first season set a high bar for guest stars, with Julia Fox playing herself, but the sequel season ups the ante with Raven-Symoné entering as Anton’s sister Talia, to the tune of her own personal laugh track.

“I love that shit, and I’m so glad that they sprinkle it in here and there,” Innanen says. “I think of it like a fun wink, and it’s not overdone. It’s very aware that it’s a sitcom, and I feel like that makes it even more fun and even more — hate to use the term, but Gen Z in the way of appreciating that everyone has deep media literacy.”

Season 2 gives a look into previously undiscovered sides of the group, including Anton’s volatile relationship with his family. Innanen recalls someone saying this season explored the characters’ “inner opposites.”

“That Anton is so externally charming, that he’s a monster to these people, and he prides himself so much in work, but can’t admit that to himself or to others,” Innanen says. “I think that was everyone’s arc this season. What are their inner opposites and how do they contest that, and how does that manifest in the relationships in the house? Which I think served the Paul Baker-Anton arc very well.”

The Paul Baker-Anton arc, of course, was one of the most anticipated plotlines to resolve in Season 2. The first season ended with Anton marrying Paul Baker to keep the Canadian in the country, concluding a season’s worth of intense eye contact with a heated just-married kiss. This season picked up with the introduction of Paul Baker’s alter ego: “Baker,” whose fratty tendencies are at odds with the sexually fluid soft-boy Paul Baker his friends (and audiences) know and love.

Amita Rao, Lucy Freyer, Owen Thiele, Malik Elassal, Jack Innanen in “Adults” Season 2 ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection

“It weirdly paired a complex I have within myself where I was like there are different sides of me, maybe, that I’m ashamed of or that I don’t show around other people, and that was something to deal with,” Innanen says of playing into his character’s duality.

“Also, I will be honest, I was scared about it tainting viewers’ perception of Paul Baker, which I think played into it completely,” he adds. “There’s this shameful side of him, but I was scared people were gonna be like, “Oh, is he a total frat bro? Can he still be Paul Baker with this Baker side of him?” Which I think they thread very well in the show, but it was fun, therapeutic and nerve-wracking.”

Paul Baker’s friends are thrown off by the existence of another friend group that knows Baker, which results in a series of identity crises. For Innanen, these opposing identities playing together was necessary. There’s a moment he loves, where Paul Baker asks if he is a piece of shit because of his alter ego, and Anton says, “No, parts of you are shitty.”

“I think what everyone wants, I’ll speak for myself, is to open your chest up and be like, ‘This is who I am, completion. Yes or no? Do you still love me in spite or even because of these things?’” Innanen says. “I think Anton does that in that scene. I think that was a really good way to jumpstart, where here are the things that Paul Baker’s ashamed of, and this kind of ugly multitude to him, and for Anton to be the one who says, ‘It’s OK, you’re OK, we’re all like this, I love you still.’ We couldn’t have had that without the Baker story. I think that they actually served each other in a very beautiful way.”

Paul Baker and Anton get their happy resolution, in the end, with a balloon-covered real kiss in the Season 2 finale. With the two finding some stability, Innanen wants to see what a future season would bring.

Jack Innanen and Owen Thiele in “Adults” Season 2 ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection

“Malik had said something really beautiful, where he said that there’s a finite amount of love in the house, and it just transmutes different ways,” Innanen says. “I’m curious what that does for everyone else, with the Paul Baker-Anton relationship in a stable place, what does that mean for everyone else? We’ll have to see.”

Innanen is also hoping for a holiday special in Season 3. “We need the filler episodes,” he says. “I desperately want a Halloween episode. I got lunch with Ben and Rebecca, and they were telling me all the ideas for a Halloween episode.” One of his ideas is a group costume gone wrong. (Think The Beatles, but John Lennon is shot — or Billie insists on being Yoko Ono.)

And speaking of things you might find in a classic sitcom: “I need to know what our other bottle episode is because the bottle episodes — chicken dinner and raccoon — those are the most fun episodes to film,” Innanen says. “That’s the highlight of my year, every year, is the two weeks when we do the bottle episode.”

Even when they aren’t purposefully contained for a bottle episode, the characters spend a lot of time in the house (partially a constraint of the fact that while the show is based in New York City, the production is filmed in Toronto). But that means both Innanen and Paul Baker are intimately familiar with the house.

“It feels almost like my childhood home where I can tell you where everything is, because there’s been so much time in there,” Innanen says. “It feels like the house is that other character where we get to play around and it mutates and we find new fun things in each room. I love that house.”

Lucy Freyer, Owen Thiele, Amita Rao, Jack Innanen, Malik Elassal in “Adults” Season 2 ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection

STD tests. Baby photos of Malik because this is Samir’s childhood home, after all. Podcast equipment to hint at a fictional podcast hosted by Anton, Issa and Billie. The fridge in particular, Innanen says, is full of Easter eggs.

“One thing I saw people picked up on, which I thought was very sweet — because the set dec people fucking killed it, and props killed it too — they added Paul Baker to the chore chart this season, which I thought was really fun. That was one of the first things I came in and saw on the fridge,” he says. “I almost want people to be able to walk through and pick apart the fridge.”

And it’s not just the characters who have hidden Easter eggs. “I have cheese and salami and Sour Patch Kids and water bottles and my scripts, my sides, hidden all over the house,” Innanen says. “And I, dead serious, opened up a drawer this season, and there was the most disgusting bag of cheese and crackers I had left from the last season was hidden really well.”

“Boy’s gotta eat,” Innanen says with a laugh about snacking during the long day they spent shooting the possum scene this season. “We shot that scene for like 12, 14 hours, I think,” he says. “It’s a long time to be kissing your friends, but we shot that for a long time to get it as right as we could, because, at least for me, it felt like the most important scene for Paul Baker this season.”

The scene in question is a foursome between Issa, Paul Baker, Anton and a possum that has found its way into the room. Innanen says the choreography was “unexpectedly rigorous,” but finding the moment where Paul Baker grabs Anton’s leg to keep him from leaving made for one of his favorite moments from the season.

Jack Innanen, Amita Rao, Owen Thiele in “Adults” Season 2 ©FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection

The night of the foursome eventually proves the catalyst for Paul Baker and Issa’s mid-season breakup, but that can’t keep her down. “I get very envious of Issa, because I think Issa is the only one where everything rolls off her back and she’s in the driver’s seat,” Innanen says. The other characters, on the other hand, don’t catch many breaks. The finale ends in a rare moment where everything seems to be resolved — at least relationship-wise.

Innanen says he was happy Paul Baker and Anton got to consummate their slow burn after two seasons, even as the finale introduced a new possible relationship in the house. “I think that they did it in such a beautiful way, and I’m glad that they had it where every relationship knot is tied, like no one feels left out, and then there’s a new cliffhanger,” he says. “I fucking want Season 3 so bad so that we can explore that, and I’m really geeked about that.”

title: Australian Director Darren Dale Bows True Crime ‘2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback,’ Acquired by Netflix for the World, Just Before TIFF
summary: Australian docuseries “2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback,” which world premiere at Toronto Sept. 10 as part of TIFF’s Primetime strand, has just been the subject of a preemptive Netflix buy for the world.   That speaks well for a four-part series examining the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Kumanjayi Walker by Northern Territory police officer […]
content:
Australian docuseries “2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback,” which world premiere at Toronto Sept. 10 as part of TIFF‘s Primetime strand, has just been the subject of a preemptive Netflix buy for the world.

That speaks well for a four-part series examining the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Kumanjayi Walker by Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe in the remote community of Yuendumu, tracing how the 2.6 seconds between the first shot and the last upended the lives of those involved as well as the national discourse.

In his directorial debut, Darren Dale uses archival footage, courtroom testimony and intimate interviews with both families to reconstruct the case from multiple perspectives.

Popular on Variety

Produced by both Dale and Jacob Hickey for Blackfella Films, “2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback” is co-commissioned by SBS and NITV, with major investment from Screen Australia’s First Nations department and Screen NSW, and produced in association with All3Media International. The series arrives on the heels of Dale’s 2012 production “The Tall Man,” about the death of an Aboriginal man in police custody on Palm Island, and his AACTA-winning drama “Total Control,” which also premiered at the Primetime strand at TIFF in 2019.

“Primetime introduces audiences to the best in global, episodic storytelling,” said Geoff Macnaughton, TIFF’s VP of market programming and theatrical. “International programmer Jason Ryle discovered ‘2.6 Seconds’ during the summer. We’ve programmed other Blackfella Films productions at TIFF, including ‘Total Control’ in 2019, which went on to win best TV drama at the AACTA Awards. We’re excited to see how audiences respond to ‘2.6 Seconds’ this September.”

Variety spoke with Dale about making the series and what he hopes international audiences take away from it.

What led to your covering this case? And what did filming the series reveal to you about Australia?

Dale: We made a film in 2011, “The Tall Man,” about the death of Mulrunji Doomadgee in police custody on Palm Island. In 2019 you have nearly the same thing play out again, a young Aboriginal man dead at the hands of police. What struck me was the disparity in how Aboriginal people are treated by the justice system when a calamitous event like this happens. It was about trying to make the country care: to see that this young man’s life is as valuable as if it were anyone’s own grandson, son, brother. Two men, eight or nine years apart, from two very different places, come together in a room, and within a short space of time one of them is dead. What led us to that point? For me the project was: How do we make the country care, how do we make the world care?

The series centers around a moment, expanded over four episodes. How did you decide what needed to be unpacked in order for an audience to understand what happened in that moment?

Dale: We live in a world where conversations quickly turn to binaries: people jump to certainty rather than sitting with what’s difficult. Either the cop is the villain or the victim had it coming. I thought if we ever want to truly understand, we have to be curious about the moments we’re uncertain about. So the series looks at both men, and both sides: what it’s like to be a young police officer in Alice Springs, where 90% of whom you police is Aboriginal, and you’re seeing the fallout of domestic violence, alcohol, substance abuse, alongside a young Aboriginal man’s own life and circumstances. We never wanted the film to shout. Everyone in it speaks with real grace and humility. It’s true crime, but told with composure. This case has already been pored over in a murder trial and a coronial inquest, so the job was bringing those threads together for a contemporary audience to actually feel what happened, and make their own assessment. It’s easy to look away now; algorithms feed us what we want to see. The series asks what we’ve all been complicit in by looking away.

You’ve spent most of your career as a producer. What put you in the director’s chair for the first time?

Dale: I’m deeply fascinated by these stories, by what documentaries can do as a window into ourselves. Andrew Boe, the writer, had been the barrister on the Kwementyaye Doomadgee case that “The Tall Man” was based on, and we’d stayed in that conversation for years. I went to Alice Springs, sat in on the coronial inquest hearings, and met the family. After that, I couldn’t see how I’d hand this to another director and have them just plug in; the complexity and the emotion of it made that feel wrong. I raised directing it myself with SBS, half-expecting pushback, and they said it was music to their ears. Two and a half years later, here we are premiering two episodes at TIFF.

For an international audience who knows nothing about Kumanjayi, what do you hope they take away?

Dale: Two things. I hope it puts an uncomfortable spotlight on Australia and how race relations play out here: we’re an island continent, easy to feel remote, but just as connected to the world as anywhere else. I want people to understand the conditions First Nations people still live in in Central Australia, and how present the effects of colonisation still are. But I also think there are parallels everywhere in how marginalised groups are treated. This story is an invitation to care, to have empathy for someone else’s experience, to ask what leads a country to a point where a man can walk into a room and, within two minutes, another young man is dead on the floor, and that’s allowed to happen. It’s been told and told, but do people actually care? I think people everywhere, whatever the divide, feel the margins more than ever, and this asks all of us to question ourselves.

title: The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More For Sale
summary: After the Toronto Film Festival last year yielded the highest-grossing fest acquisition ever at the box office with Obsession ($512 million worldwide), and with the arrival of a new market, the million-dollar question heading into this year’s TIFF that kicks off Thursday is whether there will be a spike in independent feature sales. There’s a […]
content:
After the Toronto Film Festival last year yielded the highest-grossing fest acquisition ever at the box office with Obsession ($512 million worldwide), and with the arrival of a new market, the million-dollar question heading into this year’s TIFF that kicks off Thursday is whether there will be a spike in independent feature sales.

There’s a mix of great promise, and also a harsh reality.

Watch on Deadline

Let’s start with the debbie-downer news.

Despite what’s bound to be a record post-Covid year at the domestic box office with a potential $10 billion (alongside the best summer we’ve ever seen at $4.76 billion), small and mid-sized independent features aren’t sure bets at the box office, or in the awards race. Yes, there are diamonds in the rough, but the Obsession effect is largely felt to be an anomaly.

Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in ‘Obsession’ Focus Features / Everett Collection

Many have pointed to the pandemic for slaughtering a number of independent cinemas, but let’s face it, even with streaming easing, the format has made moviegoers more discerning about what’s worth their attention and dollars outside the home. Some believe those theaters that have closed weren’t even worth $20M at the box office.

What’s changed in the streaming era and post-Covid are booking patterns. Exhibitors no longer have the patience to give indie films a full-schedule two-week run in order for realize word of mouth. It takes a powerful arthouse distributor such as A24, Neon, Focus Features or Searchlight to muscle the strength of a potential awards or adult holdover (a la A24’s Sundance pickup The Invite, which grossed more than $55M worldwide). Quite often indie pics are on split schedules. Furthermore, if a movie (any movie) isn’t doing $3,000-$4,000 a screen in a weekend, that screen is in serious jeopardy.

Most of the evening primetime slots at TIFF this year at Roy Thomson Hall, the Princess of Wales and Royal Alexandra Theatre aren’t occupied by major studio or streamer titles like the days of yore. Instead, there are a plethora of indie sales titles (scroll down for our hot list of those). In years past, evening primetime slots were tee-offs for studios’ award contenders: think 20th Century Fox’s The Martian, Netflix’s Frankenstein and Roma, Focus Features’ The Danish Girl, Universal’s Green Book and The Fabelmans, Warner Bros’ The Joker and A Star Is Born… the list goes on.

This year there is Apple’s Being Heumann, which is opening the fest tonight, and Amazon MGM Studios’ anticipated I Play Rocky from Green Book director Peter Farrelly on Saturday night. In 2018, Green Book won TIFF’s highest prize, the People’s Choice Award, which has a history of being an Oscar bellwether.

‘Being Heumann’ Apple TV

While sellers salivate over a film being fast-tracked into awards season upon acquisition — TIFF has a history for this with such titles as The Wrestler selling to Searchlight, Still Alice selling to Sony Pictures Classics, and I, Tonya to Neon — the reality of the situation is it’s a hard needle to thread. Black Bear took the Sydney Sweeney boxing title Christy off the sales-market table a year ago and decided to make the pic its first U.S.-distributed theatrical release. Haste made waste at the box office; it grossed less than $2M stateside after its early November bow. In addition, coming out of Venice and into TIFF, Searchlight jumped on Mona Fastvold’s Shaker origin period title The Testament of Ann Lee, which didn’t shake up any Oscar noms or church collections with $2.5M domestic.

The new market does take some pressure off buyers: There’s no rush to release a finished movie into awards season especially if it receives a hot reaction. Moreover, a seller doesn’t need to worry about sour reviews slowing a sales auction.

For all of the movies acquired out of TIFF in the past, there were also often other secret seller screenings for buyers, and big sales percolating. Case in point: the $30M global sale orchestrated by CAA Media Finance and Miramax in 2022 for Alexander Payne’s The Holdovers, which wound up being a serious Oscar frontrunner with five noms, including Best Picture, scoring a Supporting Actress win for Da’Vine Joy Randolph.

“We were already treating Toronto like a market,” one seller says.

This year, the TIFF market runs alongside the festival from today through September 16 at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre. It count some 150-plus exhibitors with an advisory committee that includes CAA Media Finance co-head Roeg Sutherland, Mubi SVP Global Distribution Arianna Bocco, Sony Pictures Classics co-founder and co-president Michael Barker, and more. The idea is to provide a vital pit-stop for foreign sellers to get a movie financed in time to roll cameras by early Q1.

Says one indie label boss: “Calendar-wise, it make sense a lot of sense to have the TIFF market. One of the frustrations out of [November’s American Film Market] is that by the time you did presales to finance a project, those contracts aren’t signed and I can’t actually go to bank. I can’t do anything until later next year. Whereas in Toronto, you can spend your fall putting your finance plan together and boom go into production at the start of January.”

The notion is that AFM would then become the pit-stop for closing contracts on projects that launched at TIFF.

Other good vibes at this year’s market: financier Black Bear is looking to acquire finished projects. Sumerian surprised with its buy of Channing Tatum drama Josephine at Sundance, so sellers are curious about its future endeavors. Warner Bros’ genre label Clockwork is looking for the right buy; specifically titles that can make $15M-$20M at the domestic box office. We’re hearing that Paramount+ and Peacock (the latter looking for fare to appeal to the Bravo audience) are ready to jump into the fray as a pay-one provider and partner with theatrical distributors who need them. For too long, Hulu has been the one-stop pay-one shop on several indie acquisitions.

One minus among some sellers this edition is that TIFF now has a reduced Press & Industry screening schedule due to the market eating into showings. Previously, titles received two P&I screenings; now it’s just one. “But that could also force some buyers to go to public screenings,” says one agency seller, looking at the bright side.

With that, below are some hot titles to look out for at this year’s TIFF. Note, the list only includes films that are up for sale and playing in the festival’s official selection. Not listed are Venice hot titles not playing at TIFF, i.e., the Luc Besson-written Father Joe, Kornél Mundruczó’s Place to Be starring Ellen Burstyn, Taika Waititi and Pamela Anderson; the Casey Affleck-directed Company, and the late Bernardo Bertolucci co-written pic The Echo Chamber starring Alicia Vikander, Luca Marinelli and Susan Sarandon.

TIFF Hot List 2026

(all times ET; photos courtesy TIFF)

ALPHA GANG — Following their hot Sundance title Sasquatch Sunset, David and Nathan Zellner arrive in the Great White North with a sci-fi comedy about alien invaders, hellbent to conquer Earth, but in the form of a 1950s biker gang. Those getting leathered up are Léa Seydoux, Dave Bautista, Kelvin Harrison Jr, Lily-Rose Depp, Doona Bae, Riley Keough, Chris Pine and Cate Blanchett. CAA Media Finance is selling U.S.; mk2 is handling foreign. World premiere: Sunday, September 13, 9:30 p.m. at Princess of Wales

‘Bucking Fastard’ Lena Herzog

BUCKING FASTARD — Werner Herzog’s first narrative feature in seven years bottles up Rooney and Kate Mara and shakes them up as Jean and Joan Holbrooke, “two sisters who dress the same, sort of look the same, and often say the same things at the same time. This we learn in the opening scenes, which find them in court as the defendants in a highly unusual court case,” writes Deadline’s Damon Wise in his review. The pic is already 72% fresh out its Venice premiere. Gersh is handling U.S. sales. Premiere: Monday, September 14, noon at TIFF Lightbox

CLOSING NIGHT — American Horror Story franchise thespian Cody Fern makes his feature directorial debut with a story about an internationally renowned movie star (Sarah Paulson) who invites her estranged family to the opening night of her Broadway play after decades of silence, and old wounds resurface almost as quickly as old habits. Her emotionally fragile sister (Naomi Watts) remains determined to hold on to a lifetime of resentment, while her nephew (Toby Wallace) sees an opportunity to forge a relationship with his famous aunt. Pic also stars Dianne Wiest and Odessa A’zion. CAA Media Finance is selling US.; mk2 is handling foreign. Premiere: Saturday, September 12, 2:45 p.m. at Princess of Wales

‘Evil Genius’

EVIL GENIUS — Courteney Cox’s second feature as a director is produced by Jason Bateman and Michael Costigan and follows the infamous “pizza bomber” case exploring deception, desperation and the blurred line between victim and villain. Along for extra pepperoni in this comedy crime caper are David Harbour, Patricia Arquette, Michael Chernus, Garret Dillahunt, Ryan Eggold, Gregory Alan Williams, Tom McCarthy, Owen Teague, Harlow Jane and Danielle Macdonald. Sales agents are Arregate Flims and August Night Pictures. Premiere: Saturday, September 12, noon at Roy Thomson Hall

THE FACE OF HORROR — The TIFF Midnight Madness movie comes from Viva genre filmmaker Anna Biller, who has adapted the Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan into a Technicolor 14th-century England gore tribute. In the pic, a ghost in medieval England rises from her grave to seek revenge on her husband. Jonah Hauer-King, Kristine Frøseth, Ellie Bamber, Leo Suter, Ben Radcliffe and Bella Heathcote star. WME Independent is selling U.S.; Embankment is handling international. Premiere: Friday, September 11, 11:59 p.m. at the Royal Alexandra

GIRL GROUP — After her feature directorial debut Debs, Rebel Wilson returns to TIFF with this pic about a washed-up former pop star who is kicked out of her own girl group’s reunion and sentenced to court-ordered community service. She seizes the chance to stage a comeback by coaching a group of misfit teen girls for a major record label audition… only to push them too far, forcing her to confront the toxic industry that made her and the self-destruction she can’t escape. Wilson stars with Randall Park and Lilah Pate. UTA Independent Film Group is handling U.S. sales. Premiere: Friday, September 11, 5:30 p.m. at Roy Thomson Hall

THE HOUSEWIFE — Ben Shirinian’s feature debut stars Naomi Watts, Tye Sheridan, Michael Imperioli, Luke Evans, Lena Olin and Debi Mazar in a story about a New York Times journalist who tracks down a potential Nazi officer living secretly in Queens. When he befriends the suspect’s elegant and charming wife, the implications of his investigation become much more unsettling. CAA Media Finance is selling U.S.; Neon International is handling foreign. Premiere: Thursday, September 10, 8:45 p.m. at Royal Alexandra

THE IDIOT(S) — Co-directed by Polish filmmaker Małgorzata Szumowska and DP Michał Englert, the movie follows newlyweds Fyodor Dostoevsky (Johnny Flynn) and Anna (Aimee Lou Wood) on their European honeymoon, which leads them to Baden. The trip turns into an unexpected and explosive years-long stay as they struggle and overcome obstacles in pursuit of Fyodor writing his masterpiece The Idiot. Vicky Krieps and Christian Friedel also star. CAA Media Finance is selling U.S.; the Match Factory is selling foreign. Premiere: Tuesday, September 15, 9:30 p.m. at Princess of Wales

THE JULIA SET — Chase Infiniti’s big feature follow-up after One Battle After Another has her cast as Julia, a talented mathematician working in a competitive academic environment. She is recruited by T.A. Pascal into an elite prep course for the world’s most challenging math competition, the Putnam Exam. Evan Wood filmmaker Niki Byrne writes and directs. Gersh is selling U.S. Premiere: Friday, September 11, 6:15 p.m. at Princess of Wales

THE LIFE AND DEATHS OF WILSON SHEDD — The feature written and directed by Tim Blake Nelson is based on actual events: When a teacher in an abusive marriage takes a job leading creative writing classes at a maximum security prison, she begins to fall for a charismatic inmate. The consequences call into question not only the nature of punishment and retribution but also the limits of our humanity. Amanda Seyfried, Scoot McNairy, Wunmi Mosaku, Devyn Tyler, Missi Pyle, Grant Harvey, William Jackson Harper and Nelson star. WME Independent is selling U.S. co-repped with D Squared Films; WestEnd is handling foreign. Premiere: Sunday, September 13, 9:30 p.m. at Roy Thomson Hall

‘Magazine’

MAGAZINE — An intern at an elite magazine navigates sex and power in the cutthroat New York magazine world of 2011. Lily McInerny, Jake Lacy, AnnaSophia Robb and Lukita Maxwell star in the pic from from journalist-turned-filmmaker Alexandra Pechman, who has written for Vogue, New Yorker, Vanity Fair and the New York Times. UTA Independent Film Group is selling U.S.; Film Constellation is selling foreign. Premiere: Friday, September 11, 12:15 p.m. at TIFF Lightbox

‘Onwards & Sideways’

ONWARDS & SIDEWAYS — From John Madden, who directed the seven-time Oscar winner Shakespeare in Love, the pic stars Laura Linney and Rhys Ifans as strangers whose lives become entwined when both are diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. Rory Kinnear and Monica Dolan also star. CAA Media Finance is selling U.S.; Kaleidoscope reps foreign. Premiere: Sunday, September 13, 2 p.m. at Roy Thomson Hall

PRIMA FACIE — Suzie Miller adapted her play for the big screen. It follows a rising star lawyer in London who represents sexual assault defendants. After she is raped by a colleague, she finds herself at the center of a patriarchal legal system she often controlled. Cynthia Erivo stars and produces under her Edith’s Daughter label. Pic also stars Daniel Ings, Noma Dumezweni, Toheeb Jimoh, Elizabeth Dulau, Harry Treadaway, Khalid Abdalla, Elliot Levey, Simon Russell-Beale and Sarah Junillon. UTA Independent Film Group is co-repping U.S. with CAA Media Finance; Embankment is handling foreign. Premiere: Sunday, September 13, 5:45 p.m. at Roy Thomson Hall

‘Rogue Trooper’

ROGUE TROOPER — Moon filmmaker Duncan Jones arrives with this adult animation about a genetic infantry soldier accidentally dropped behind enemy lines in the midst of a secret military operation. Aneurin Barnard, Jack Lowden, Daryl McCormack, Reece Shearsmith, Matt Berry, Jemaine Clement, Diane Morgan, Hayley Atwell and Sean Bean are the voice cast. CAA Media Finance is handling U.S. Premiere: Saturday, September 19, 11:59 p.m. at Royal Alexandra

THE SURGEON — The action thriller written and directed by Roshan Sethi, from John Wick producer Thunder Road, follows a former surgeon who is kidnapped and given an impossible choice. Sethi co-created the Fox series The Resident. Michelle Yeoh stars alongside Martin Freeman, Laurie Davidson, Yuri Kolokolnikov and Joseph Mydell. WME Independent is selling U.S.; Legendary 193 is selling foreign. Premiere: Saturday, September 12, 8:30 p.m. at Royal Alexandra

TRASH MOUNTAIN — The dark comedy from director Kris Rey produced by Jurassic World filmmaker Colin Trevorrow follows a young gay man living in Chicago who returns to his hometown in Missouri following the sudden death of his hoarder father. Caleb Hearon, Zooey Deschanel, Jacki Weaver, Jaboukie Young-White, Kyle Marvin and Holmes star. CAA Media Finance and WME Independent are co-repping U.S; WME is also handling foreign. Premiere: Friday, September 11, 6:15 p.m. at Scotiabank 1

UP AGAINST IT — From British actress-turned-director Trudie Styler, “post-marital acrimony and parental devotion make strange bedfellows” for a divorced couple whose daughter develops a rare form of leukemia. The doctors tell them that their best bet at saving her is to produce a second child who could provide a transfusion. The ex-spouses balk at the idea — and their new partners don’t fancy it either — but they may have no choice but to bury the hatchet (in bed). Antonio Banderas, Forest Whitaker, Úrsula Corberó, Eva Birthistle, Arinzé Kene and Eden Hamilton star. CAA Media Finance is selling U.S.; Beta Cinema has foreign. Premiere: Thursday, September 17, 5:30 p.m. at Roy Thomson Hall

VINTAGE VIOLENCE — From The Code director Eugene Kotlyarenko, the Midnight Madness title stars Cole Sprouse as a disgraced live-streamer who discovers a trove of rare vintage denim in a Colorado mine. He follows it to Tokyo — and straight into the arms of a woman who may be using him. Caught between desire and betrayal, he finds himself entangled in black market turf wars, yakuza, and a past that refuses to stay buried. Kiko Mizuhara, Nijiro Murakami, Pierre Taki and Hio Miyazawa also star. WME is handling U.S. sales; Best Friend Ever has international. Premiere: Saturday, September 12, 11:59 p.m. at Royal Alexandra

title: ‘The Muppet Show’ Special Got Viewership & Emmys  – Where Is The Disney+ Series Order?
summary: The Muppet Show has become the unlikely flag bearer for The Disney Company at the 2026 Emmy Awards. The Disney+ special won the most trophies of any program across the Disney portfolio, four, after the first two ceremonies last weekend, accounting for more than a quarter of the company’s overall haul with an excellent 67% […]
content:
The Muppet Show has become the unlikely flag bearer for The Disney Company at the 2026 Emmy Awards. The Disney+ special won the most trophies of any program across the Disney portfolio, four, after the first two ceremonies last weekend, accounting for more than a quarter of the company’s overall haul with an excellent 67% conversion of its six nomination.

With no Disney series among the top contenders in the categories awarded on the Sept. 14 main telecast, it is safe to say that The Muppet Show will be the top Emmy performer for the company this year.

The variety special, which premiered on February 4, has been a top ratings performer too. Back in February, Disney touted a multi-platform viewership of nearly 8 million within eight days of The Muppet Show‘s airing on ABC and launch on Disney+, with the official Muppets account calling the special “a smash-hit.”

The Muppet Show, featuring the beloved Muppets ensemble, executive producer Seth Rogen and special guest stars Sabrina Carpenter and Maya Rudolph, had been intended as a backdoor pilot which, in success, would spawn a new Muppet Show television series. The setup was jokingly alluded to in the special by Kermit who says, “It’s the return of The Muppet Show back on the very stage where it all started, and then ended, and is maybe starting again, depending on how tonight goes.”

Watch on Deadline

Seven months, millions of views and four Emmys later, there has been no pickup, begging the question: what more does the backdoor pilot need to do to get a series order?

According to sources, it is not for the lack of trying, and the reasons have been creative.

The Muppet Show revival comes from three main production entities, 20th Television, The Muppets Studio and Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg’s Point Grey Pictures, which has been driving the effort to bring Kermit & Co. back.

I hear there have been difficulties cracking a premise for an ongoing Muppet Show series that Disney (Disney+ and 20th TV), The Muppets Studio and Point Grey will all be on board for.

There are no active series conversations about at the moment, sources said.

That could change if the Emmy wins give the process new momentum and motivates all sides to find a winning series format.

Until then, the Muppets special will be known for getting Grammy winner Carpenter halfway to EGOT. (As an executive producer, she was recognized in Outstanding Variety Special, Pre-Recorded.)

title: Get Ready For “Mariska Unleashed”: 78th Annual Emmys Host & Producers Tease Telecast At Blue Carpet Rollout
summary: While crews toiled away building out the Peacock Theater ahead of Monday’s 78th annual Emmy Awards, host Mariska Hargitay sparkled in the sun as she rolled out the blue carpet alongside the show’s producers. She may have spent nearly three decades investigating heinous crimes on NBC’s Law & Order franchise, but she knows how to […]
content:
While crews toiled away building out the Peacock Theater ahead of Monday’s 78th annual Emmy Awards, host Mariska Hargitay sparkled in the sun as she rolled out the blue carpet alongside the show’s producers.

She may have spent nearly three decades investigating heinous crimes on NBC’s Law & Order franchise, but she knows how to have fun, too.

“What I’ve done, the material that I’ve been living in, it’s hard and it takes a toll,” she told Deadline on Thursday morning’s carpet rollout and press preview. “So do something completely different, I’m telling you, I count the moments to get in the room with [the Emmys writers], and it’s been soul filling.”

Mariska Hargitay takes us inside the #Emmys writers room ahead of Monday’s ceremony for a taste of what to expect from her hosting style pic.twitter.com/3Tk6Qzs1OX — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 10, 2026

Hargitay is also executive producing the telecast with Jesse Collins, Dionne Harmon and Jeannae Rouzan-Clay of Jesse Collins Entertainment. Harmon tells Deadline that Hargitay’s hosting style will be “a complete 180 from Olivia Benson.”

Watch on Deadline

“The show should be called like Mariska Unleashed,” laughed Collins. “That should be like the after-school special [version].”

Hargitay is the first woman to helm the show in 15 years. She’s also a departure from the typical choice for an awards show host in that she’s primarily a drama actress rather than a late-night host or stand-up comic. Recent Emmys hosts include Nate Bargatze, Eugene and Dan Levy, Anthony Anderson, and Kenan Thompson.

However, the producing team thinks Hargitay isn’t getting enough credit for her comedy chops.

“Everyone’s been saying she’s not a comedian, but I think we feel otherwise,” Rouzan-Clay added. “She’s kind of a comedian.”

The Jesse Collins Entertainment trio also teased a few other moments during the live ceremony, confirming both the Charlie’s Angels and Buffy the Vampire Slayer reunions that were hinted in Wednesday’s presenters announcement.

Collins also revealed that Noah Kahan will perform Paul Simon’s “Bridge Over Troubled Water” during the in memoriam.

#Emmys host Mariska Hargitay joins the producers to roll out the blue carpet for Monday’s ceremony pic.twitter.com/mGDJ39FzEh — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 10, 2026

This year’s ceremony drew some minor heat for cutting some of the acting, writing and directing categories from the main broadcast, instead handing them out during the non-televised ceremony over Labor Day weekend. However, the extra room in the telecast will go toward “letting a lot of things breathe,” Collins said.

“[It’s] really giving our hosts time to truly host the show,” he told Deadline. “But even across the board, presenters have more time. We’re just trying to make it so that the show has a great pace…and really just make the show feel different.”

He adds: “It’s a very tough thing, and the decisions were made, and we think in the end people will see that they were the right choices, and the show will be great.”

title: Odeya Rush, Annarah Cymone & Neela Jolene Join Justin Long & Iris Apatow In Killer Bee Movie ‘Stung’, Filming Wraps
summary: EXCLUSIVE: VMI Worldwide, Verdi Productions and Source M+P have wrapped killer bee movie Stung in Rhode Island. From writer-director Colin Minihan, the film follows Jess (Iris Apatow), Maya (Odeya Rush) Brooke (Annarah Cymone) and Rachel (Neela Jolene) “as their innocent girl’s night sleepover spirals into a living nightmare when their home is overtaken by a […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: VMI Worldwide, Verdi Productions and Source M+P have wrapped killer bee movie Stung in Rhode Island.

From writer-director Colin Minihan, the film follows Jess (Iris Apatow), Maya (Odeya Rush) Brooke (Annarah Cymone) and Rachel (Neela Jolene) “as their innocent girl’s night sleepover spirals into a living nightmare when their home is overtaken by a massive swarm of African killer bees. Under the watchful eye of their pathetic neighbor Derek (Justin Long) not even he can save the girls from their fate”.

Teddy Parker, Kayln Harper, James Baccile, Tom DeNucci, Kea Ho and Rob Goon will also be appearing in the film. VMI Worldwide will be at TIFF discussing the film with buyers.

The film was shot entirely in Rhode Island and produced by Andre Relis, Chad A. Verdi, Jib Polhemus, Chad Verdi Jr., Paul Luba and Jessica Russo, with Michelle Verdi, Sera Verdi, Anthony Gudas serving as executive producers.

Watch on Deadline

Rush is best known for Lady Bird, Goosebumps and Fox Hulu series Memory of a Killer. Iris Apatow can currently be seen in the Amazon Prime feature Pretty Lethal and on the final season of the Hulu drama series Tell Me Lies. She will also be appearing in Lionsgate’s upcoming feature The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Cymone is best known for Netflix series The Midnight Club. Colin Minihan’s most recent feature, Coyotes, starred Justin Long and Kate Bosworth.

President of Verdi Productions, Chad A. Verdi stated: “Stung is an intense horror story with entertaining characters at the center of it, and Colin has terrific instincts for building tension and keeping audiences on the edge of their seats. The script and concept grabbed my attention right away and never let go. It’s the kind of original, high-concept material that interests Verdi Productions. Iris, Odeya, Justin, Annarah, Neela and the rest of the cast brought the characters to life in a way that made a bizarre concept such as killer bees realistically terrifying.”

Odeya Rush is represented by Verve and MGMT Entertainment.

title: Jeremiah Watkins Unveils Third Hour Stand-Up Special ‘Crazy Pizza’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Comedian Jeremiah Watkins has just released his third full-length special, Crazy Pizza, on YouTube. Watch it above. Taped at The Comedy Vault in Batavia, Illinois, the special finds Watkins navigating life as the father to an alleged serial killer toddler and his wife’s anger in the bedroom, while riffing on alternatives to hitting your kids, his […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Comedian Jeremiah Watkins has just released his third full-length special, Crazy Pizza, on YouTube. Watch it above.

Taped at The Comedy Vault in Batavia, Illinois, the special finds Watkins navigating life as the father to an alleged serial killer toddler and his wife’s anger in the bedroom, while riffing on alternatives to hitting your kids, his recent vasectomy, and all of the other toppings that go on his Crazy Pizza.

Watkins, the special’s writer, performer and director, exec produced alongside Avery Pearson, Amy Zvi, Shannon O’Halloran, Thousand Percent, and Wildline. Pearson is also credited as producer, along with Jesse Chieffo and Chris McMillan. Liz Valaitis and Anna Rogers associate produced; Thousand Percent, Saxy Turtle Productions and 4933 Productions are the production companies.

For Watkins, Crazy Pizza follows the self-released Daddy and his debut hour, Family Reunion, which can be found on Prime Video. Co-host of the Trailer Tales Podcast, he’s also known for his series Stand-Up on the Spot, which sees comics performing off the cuff based on audience suggestions, as well numerous online sketches. Most recently, he taped a short set for Comedy Central Stand-Up Selects that will be unveiled this fall.

Watch on Deadline

In addition to stand-up, Watkins is known for his acting, voice acting, and impressions. Via Cartoon Network’s DC Superhero Girls, he’s among the select actors who have voiced the iconic DC character, The Joker. Additional credits include Carpool Karaoke, Roast Battle, Lights Out with David Spade, Netflix’s Historical Roasts, Jimmy Kimmel Live!, HBO’s Crashing, Nickelodeon’s The Casagrandes, Churchy, Big Bruh, and Dr. Phil LIVE.

Watkins has 1.5M+ followers across social platforms and has amassed 93.5M+ views across all of his YouTube shows, with nearly 2M likes and 147K+ shares/comments. He is repped by Mgmt Entertainment, Gersh and Knol Hanly Garrett.

title: Netflix Taps ‘Friday Night Lights’ Director Peter Berg for NFL Gameday Openers, the First Narrated by Kyle Chandler
summary: Peter Berg is directing the show opens for all four of Netflix’s NFL gameday livestreams this season — and for the first one, debuting Thursday, he drafted Kyle Chandler, star of the “Friday Night Lights” TV series, for an assist on the play. Berg directed the 2004 movie “Friday Night Lights,” about a high school […]
content:
Peter Berg is directing the show opens for all four of Netflix‘s NFL gameday livestreams this season — and for the first one, debuting Thursday, he drafted Kyle Chandler, star of the “Friday Night Lights” TV series, for an assist on the play.

Berg directed the 2004 movie “Friday Night Lights,” about a high school football team in Texas, and Chandler portrayed Coach Taylor in the TV series adaptation that first aired on NBC.

The first of Berg’s NFL pregame teasers debuts Sept. 10 during Netflix’s broadcast from Melbourne, Australia, featuring the Los Angeles Rams vs. the San Francisco 49ers (coverage begins at 3:30 p.m. PT). He’ll also direct openers for Netflix’s other NFL gamedays (Green Bay Packers vs. Rams on Thanksgiving Eve; Packers vs. Chicago Bears and Buffalo Bills vs. Denver Broncos on Christmas Day; and a Week 18 game on Jan. 9, 2027, with the teams TBA).

Popular on Variety

Berg’s Sept. 10 opener, “For the Love of Football,” runs 2 minutes and intercuts scenes of kids’ football teams (and their coaches) with footage from NFL games — giving it an overt “Friday Night Lights” vibe.

“And so it begins. Right here, right now. Today,” Chandler says at the beginning of the clip. “You are going to win. You’ll use your eyes to win. Your eyes will show you the truth. You’ll recognize it whether you like it or not.”

Later, Chandler says in the voiceover, “You’ll play with your eyes clear and your heart full. If you can do that and then do it again and again, I assure you, you cannot lose… Clear eyes, full hearts. Can’t lose.”

Apart from the NFL gameday teasers, Berg was already in business with Netflix. He directed, wrote and produced the movie “The Mosquito Bowl,” bowing in theaters on Oct. 30 ahead of its Nov. 25 release on Netflix. The sports drama is based on the bestselling novel of the same name by Pulitzer Prize winner Buzz Bissinger, based on the true story of four top American top college football stars who set aside their fame to enlist in the Marines following the attack on Pearl Harbor during World War II.

Watch Berg’s “For the Love of Football,” which opens the Rams-49ers game on Sept. 10:

title: Steve Carell Almost Played ‘The Office’ Creator Greg Daniels’ Dad in Biopic About the 1968 Olympics
summary: Steve Carell and writer Greg Daniels got so close while making “The Office,” they became like family. So much so that Daniels once wanted Carell to play his dad Aaron in a biopic he wrote about him almost 20 years ago. “He’s a very colorful person and he actually was in the Olympics in 1968, […]
content:
Steve Carell and writer Greg Daniels got so close while making “The Office,” they became like family.

So much so that Daniels once wanted Carell to play his dad Aaron in a biopic he wrote about him almost 20 years ago.

“He’s a very colorful person and he actually was in the Olympics in 1968, and I wrote a movie for Steve to play him, like on spec during the writers strike of 2008,” Daniels told me at his Hollywood Walk of Fame star unveiling on Thursday morning. (Writers were allowed to write uncommissioned spec scripts during the 2008 strike.)

What was his sport?

Popular on Variety

“He had a very rare sport. That’s how he was able to do it,” Daniels explained. “It was the demonstration sport of Mexico, basically like jai alai but with paddles and so he managed to wrangle his way in with some friends.”

The elder Daniels competed as an amateur athlete in the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City.

“The Office” creator Greg Daniels reveals Steve Carell almost played his dad in a biopic Daniels wrote nearly 20 years ago:



“He’s a very colorful person and he actually was in the Olympics in 1968, and I wrote a movie for Steve to play him, like on spec during the writers… pic.twitter.com/BrEQsBC3Rx — Variety (@Variety) September 10, 2026

Carell, along with Conan O’Brien, spoke at the star unveiling. “Everyone told me not to do ‘The Office,’” Carell said. “[They said] it will not work. The original is too good. It is a waste of time. And mostly, it is just going to stink. And then a crazy thing happened. It didn’t stink because of Greg Daniels.”

During our chat, Daniels put the kibosh on fans’ hopes for any sort of “Office” revival or reboot. “I don’t think we need to find out what all the characters are doing so much because of the way the show ended,” he said. “It seemed like people liked the ending and you’re just sort of risking a lot to open it up again.”

Daniels adapted “The Office” from the British series of the same name. It premiered in 2005 before ending after nine seasons in 2013.

title: James Talarico Blasts ‘Government Censorship’ After ABC Pulls His Jimmy Kimmel Interview Over FCC Concerns: ‘Dangerous Form of Cancel Culture’
summary: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate running for senator in Texas, has spoken out after ABC pulled his sit-down with Jimmy Kimmel over FCC concerns. The interview will instead be posted to the “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” YouTube channel on Thursday night. “Government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party,” […]
content:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate running for senator in Texas, has spoken out after ABC pulled his sit-down with Jimmy Kimmel over FCC concerns. The interview will instead be posted to the “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” YouTube channel on Thursday night.

“Government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party,” Talarico told MS NOW, calling the FCC’s threats against certain broadcast programs (including ABC’s “The View”) “the most dangerous form of cancel culture.”

“People at the top, powerful politicians, powerful media executives, censoring what we watch, what we read, what we say,” Talarico continued. “That, again, should be a concern to everyone who believes in the First Amendment and believes in the freedom of speech.”

Popular on Variety

He told Symone Sanders Townsend of MS NOW’s “The Weeknight” that he still has hope ABC will air the Kimmel interview across its broadcast channels. “I’m still hopeful that we can have this interview on the air,” he said. “So we’ll see what happens tonight.

Kimmel announced on his show Wednesday night that ABC had decided to preempt his chat with Talarico because of concerns about Trump’s FCC, which is led by Brendan Carr. The government agency is currently locked in a dispute with ABC over whether “The View” qualifies as a “bona fide news program” exempt from the “equal time” rule. The FCC also played a key role in Kimmel’s brief suspension in 2025 over Charlie Kirk comments.

“Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” Kimmel said on his show Wednesday night.

It’s not the first time a late-night show has preempted an interview with the Texas Senate candidate. In February, Stephen Colbert said CBS executives pulled his interview with Talarico from air over concerns about violating the equal time rule, which requires broadcast stations to give equal time to political candidates when they appear on-air. While there are exemptions to the rule, Trump’s FCC has been aggressive about clamping down on broadcast programs perceived as liberal. (Before the ABC drama, the agency went after “Saturday Night Live” over a brief cameo by Kamala Harris.)

Ultimately, Colbert put his Talarico interview on YouTube, with the clip garnering 9.5 million views. The Talarico campaign raised $2.5 million in the 24 hours after Colbert revealed he was barred from airing the interview.

title: The Legend of Patricia Summersett’s ‘Zelda’: Voice Actress Behind Nintendo’s Iconic Princess on Franchise’s 40th Anniversary, Upcoming Live-Action Movie
summary: “The Legend of Zelda” turns 40 this year, but the titular princess at the center of the franchise doesn’t look a day over whatever ethereal age the Nintendo video game franchise needs her to be for any given game. The magic of the fantasy character is in large part thanks to actress Patricia Summersett, who […]
content:
“The Legend of Zelda” turns 40 this year, but the titular princess at the center of the franchise doesn’t look a day over whatever ethereal age the Nintendo video game franchise needs her to be for any given game.

The magic of the fantasy character is in large part thanks to actress Patricia Summersett, who has been voicing the English-dub version of Princess Zelda since 2017’s “Breath of the Wild.” But Summersett says she crafted the now-iconic voice without knowing it was Zelda she was portraying.

“One of the funny things about how that voice was created was that I based it on the specs in the script — but not knowing that it was Zelda because it was secret,” Summersett tells Variety. “I had auditioned for multiple characters, so I went with the archetype that felt like it rested in my body the best at the time. And I knew that my regular voice was too low for a young princess character, so I sort of pitched it up. I found the place that it sat right on my vocal cords. And then I was like, I think she needs to be a little bit more classic English, that was part of the description as well as it could be anything, because it’s a fantasy world. Then I brought it in for the audition, and we worked around with it for a while. But of course, I still didn’t know what it was. So it happened organically, but I had very good reason to try very hard for the audition because, I just moved and I was really focused on doing some sort of good audition. So whatever that translated into, I can’t be sure, except that I’m glad I didn’t know what it was because that might have changed the outcome and I might have tried too hard on something.”

Popular on Variety

In addition to “Breath of the Wild,” Summersett has also voiced Zelda in “Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity,” “The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom and “Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment,” but can’t confirm one way or another yet if she’s involved in the upcoming “Ocarina of Time” remake set to release in November, or if she has anything to do with the live-action “Zelda” movie slated for April 2027.

And though she has done additional video-game voice acting and on-screen roles, Summersett says playing Zelda is one of the most physically comfortable experiences in her career.

“Yes, actually, it takes a little warming up for me to get into any range that it’s going to sit at, but I always feel a sense of deep relaxation after the recording sessions because it’s soft and you have to be kind of relaxed when you’re hitting that range,” Summersett says. “Even if she’s a thoughtful, heady character, the voice itself has to remain relaxed. So you get a sense of feeling very, very nice and warm afterward. Also, holding your center of energy at a sort of young, wide-eyed, youthful place that has a big heart is a pleasant feeling. Not all characters get to be like that.”

See below for more from Variety’s interview with Summersett about her career and the 40th anniversary of “The Legend of Zelda.”

With the 40th anniversary of “The Legend of Zelda” this year, is it causing you to reflect on your own career and part in the IP?

Absolutely. I mean, particularly when fans and media and everything are drawing up the anniversary dates and asking all these questions about it, I, of course, by default, get asked these questions too and it gives me a good reason to reflect on everything. It being the 40th anniversary, it’s interesting to think about the fact that I have been part of the franchise for essentially a quarter of it and that is something I never could have predicted in my life. I’m finding I’m really appreciating the longevity of any project these days, as there’s so much change around in the world and technologies and to have any sort of consistency with these wonderful stories over a series of several years and these wonderful characters, is just a real gem. I’m really happy about it, and I’m very happy for the “Zelda” fans right now with everything that they have coming and the way that it just keeps seeming to grow and expand and keep innovating. It’s just an awesome thing to be associated with in any way.

Do you recall landing the role for “Breath of the Wild” and what the audition process was like?

It happened for me at such a fascinating time in my career where I had made this big leap. I’d been acting for 10 years, but I decided to move to LA. I’d done Canada, I’d done London and I was like, “It’s time to go to California.” In retrospect, I’m kind of shocked at how this was one of the first things that I auditioned for when I got there. But I had packages ready to go and I came in probably with a certain amount of fresh blood. The project was secret; I did not know what it was, and so, like a lot of video games, it was presented as an RPG fantasy-style game with code names and everything like that. So, I just went in, balls to the wall, hoping to make a good impression and to land anything anywhere and just have a sign to tell me that I’d come to the right place. And in the end, it was that I landed. And it was so shocking to find out after I signed the NDAs and everything and that it was like, OK, here we go.

Had you already played the older “Zelda” games when you (unknowingly) auditioned for the part? Were you a big fan?

I absolutely had. I wasn’t a die-hard fan, but I’d grown up with the NES in my house. I’d played the original “Zelda.” I’d played “Ocarina of Time,” and was very familiar with the franchise and very familiar with Nintendo as well because I was more of a “Mario” player growing up. My sister and I were really big into the original “Mario” and “Mario 3.” So coming from that, as soon as I did discover what it was, it was like having an adrenaline rush. Like drinking five Red Bulls or something. Skydiving. I knew it was powerful.

What is your relationship with the “Legend of Zelda” fandom like these days?

Right now, what defines the franchise for me from the outside and just as Patricia, is very much fans and fan interactions because I do a lot of comic cons. I’ve traveled the world with it. It’s now been almost 10 years of that, which is just bananas to me. But to hear what the stories mean to other people, to have people come up to me and play the ocarina, play “Zelda’s Lullaby,” all over the world, you see the universal love of this story everywhere. So what a crazy thing for me to experience in that way, in terms of coming to a character that had this incredible legacy before I arrived.

You cannot play the past and thankfully, all the training that I’ve ever had before landing this role has taught me that you’ve got to come with the script at hand, the people that are in the room and, of course, you can be informed. I mean, when I did discover that I got the role, I went straight into “Hyrule Historia.” I taught myself “Twilight Princess” Hylian. I did a bunch of things to try to reinforce and just sit with the character. But when it comes to the actual recording, you’ve got to just let all that go. Take the direction that is in front of you, and trust that they cast you because you have the essence of what they’re looking for. It’s not some ethereal thing out there. They’re looking for the human in you and what you breathe life into.

Aside from your most recent work on “Zelda,” what projects are you involved with now?

I am working on several video games right now, which I’m so thrilled about. Obviously, I can’t talk about them. The other things that have really come around for me when I think of anniversaries — it’s so fascinating because “Zelda’s” having its 40th anniversary, I’m now in my 40s as well and I’m seeing a lot of things come back around to me that I had started in my 20s. So the things that I’m working on are almost stemming back from these early roots.

I’m going back into music. I’m going to go back into the recording process with my band, but we’ll probably change the name and just do a completely new iteration of it. I’m going back into the writing process, starting to write essays. So it’s a lot of indie stuff that I feel really strongly that I just need to do. Some of it involves going out into nature and being completely untapped from technology. And on the same stroke, the other part of it requires me going directly into interactive technology, hard core, like buying things like Mi.Mu gloves, Imogen Heap’s little creation, and then combining those and seeing where they sit in the middle.

So I’m just kind of interested, as an artist right now, in reflecting what that landscape is on the outside of even the video game world or whatever else I’m doing. Just creative projects that reflect my experience right now, which is it’s a very interesting world to be living in right now, where we have a lot of things at our fingertips, but a lot of fractured energy.

With the “Ocarina of Time” remake coming up, I’d like to know how you approach doing the voice acting for a “Zelda” remake vs. a new game. Are you playing Zelda in “Ocarina of Time?”

Oh, I have no idea for “Ocarina of Time.” I wouldn’t be able to speak to that. It’s not a released game, so whether or not I was a part of it, I wouldn’t be able to say anyway. What I could say about “Ocarina of Time” is that I’m excited for people who are “Zelda” fans because they’ve been waiting for that for a long time. So no, I can’t say that I’m involved in that at all. But I can say that, in a way, I’m as excited as the fans for what everybody’s going to get for an adaptation that people have literally been asking for for, I don’t know, probably since the original came out.

The “Legend of Zelda” live-action movie is set to release next year with Bo Bragason in the role as Princess Zelda. Do you have any thoughts on the best way to adapt the character of Zelda for the big screen?

In a way, I’d be the last person to weigh in on how I think it would be best adapted, because I’m not that kind of filmmaker or expert that they’ve assembled. In terms of different versions of Zelda, I wouldn’t be able to know because it hasn’t been released how it might affect how I feel about Zelda in general. I just leave a lot of room open for all sorts of different interpretations that different people bring to it. In the same way that somebody brings something to a new Harry Potter series or a James Bond or something of that nature that has a kind of cyclical storytelling element with different repeating archetypes.

It’s hard to get video game adaptations right, but we also live in a time now where we’re finding that there are major successes with those adaptations. We’ll see. A lot of people are really excited for it. I’ll be very, very curious to see what they do with it and excited along with everybody else for the people involved because it’s such a massive project and they’re so lucky to be involved in such a cool franchise, too. Just sort of wishing them the best and I’m sure it’s going to be great. But people will always have very strong opinions about it, regardless.

Sometimes for these film and TV adaptation projects, they try to incorporate and make nods to the video games by also incorporating the voice actors from the games. Have you been asked to be part of the “Zelda” movie?

I couldn’t answer that one way or another. Of course, I’m a walking NDA, sort of on the nomad land of the world. I mean, I love it when they do that for voice actors for sure and I hope that becomes a thing that is always implemented in the future as all the technologies sort of meld and video games want to be more like film and film wants to be more video games. That acknowledgment is lovely, but I couldn’t say one way or another.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: Rams Vs. 49ers In Australia: How To Watch & Livestream First NFL International Game Of 2026 Online & On TV

content:
The first international game of the 2026 NFL season will be live from Melbourne, Australia, where the Los Angeles Rams will host their NFC West rivals, the San Francisco 49ers.

As the road to Super Bowl LXI begins, the first Thursday night football game will be thousands of miles away at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

The Rams have stacked up their team ahead of the new season, hoping to make it all the way to the championship game, which is set to take place on their home turf, SoFi Stadium.

What time does the Rams vs. 49ers game start?

The Los Angeles Rams vs. San Francisco 49ers game starts at 8:35 p.m. ET and will take place at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in Australia.

Watch on Deadline

Where will the Rams vs. 49ers game air on TV?

The first international game of the 2026 NFL season will stream on Netflix. The game will be available in over 200 countries and to Netflix subscribers worldwide in English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and German.

How to watch the Rams vs. 49ers game for free?

Fans of the Rams and 49ers in their local markets can watch the game on local stations without signing up for Netflix. Los Angeles-area residents can watch the game on KNBC 4 starting at 5 p.m. PT, while San Francisco-area residents can root for their team watching on KNTV 11 starting at 5 p.m. PT.
