The jury — made up of French director Chloé Barreau, Hungarian producer Júlia Berkes and Italian writer, cultural curator and film-industry professional Caterina Mazzucato — praised “Before the War” in a statement. “For its intense and vibrant direction, for the powerful and expressive talent of its lead actor, and for the mastery of its mise-en-scène, thanks to superbly crafted images in which bodies, faces and gestures create an impressive physical tension while provincial Italy becomes the stage for violent passions,” they said.

“Before the War” stars the director’s brother Piero Usberti as Guido and Luàna Bajrami as Sonia. The drama’s cast also comprises Massimiliano Balduzzi, Sebastien Halnaut and Cisky Capizzi.

In its statement, he Critics’ Week jury went on to praise “Before the War” for being a film “that relies as much on silence as on words, where sound and music become a battlefield in their own right to explore urgently contemporary themes: toxic masculinity, impossible desire and the individual’s profound loneliness.” They called it “a raw, evocative and deeply cinematic feature, both classic and innovative, revealing a strong and distinctive directorial voice.”

“Before the War” is produced by Thibault de Gantes, Lucas Le Postec (L’Heure d’été), Francesco Virga, Adele Dell’Erario, Marco Serrecchia (MIR Cinematografica) and Beatrice Bordone Bulgari (Eolo Film Productions). It’s being sold internationally by The Party Film Sales.

London-based Chilean-Indian director Shalini Adnani’s debut feature “Our Share of Sand,” about a 12-year-old girl named Maya who returns to rural India to reconnect with her estranged father, won the section’s audience award.

Fiction-documentary hybrid “The End of Times,” a political piece co-directed by Bibiana Rojas Gómez and Juan David Cárdenas that uses artificial intelligence and explores colonialism and capitalism in Colombian history, scooped both the best technical contribution award and a special mention.

Chinese drama “Zoom In, Zoom Out,” by Dong Jie — about a young video game designer who embarks on a journey to seek his missing roommate Gao following a clue hidden in an online game — scored the prize for the most innovative film in the selection, awarded by a separate jury.

Venice Critics’ Week general delegate Beatrice Fiorentino said in a statement that the section’s main winners “perfectly reflect the breadth of our program, from its most accessible works to its most radical, while above all recognizing the section’s profoundly contemporary character, firmly rooted in the complexities of the present.”

title: Ella Rubin, Sarah Sherman, Marcello Hernandez and More Rock Out at Chanel’s NYFW Party
summary: Chanel brought springtime bloom to New York Fashion Week. The luxury fashion house celebrated the launch of their new Coco Mademoiselle Crush Absolu fragrance on Thursday night, where everyone from “Sterling Point” stars Ella Rubin and Keen Ruffalo to “SNL” cast members Sarah Sherman and Marcello Hernandez rocked out to the indie band Balu Brigada […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Chanel brought springtime bloom to New York Fashion Week.

The luxury fashion house celebrated the launch of their new Coco Mademoiselle Crush Absolu fragrance on Thursday night, where everyone from “Sterling Point” stars Ella Rubin and Keen Ruffalo to “SNL” cast members Sarah Sherman and Marcello Hernandez rocked out to the indie band Balu Brigada at Balthazar in their finest attire,.

While the new bottle was the star of the night, guests arrived with plenty of Chanel leather in tow. Paige DeSorbo, for one, showed off a new metallic lambskin handbag she picked up at the Venice Film Festival earlier this week. “I walked by Chanel and this was in the window, and I said, ‘No one can have this but me!” she muses to Variety.

Popular on Variety

Keen Ruffalo and Amélie Hoeferle attend the Chanel Party at Balthazar WireImage

Sarah Sherman attends the Chanel Party at Balthazar WireImage

Others brought a more sentimental touch. Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast — in the final days of her pregnancy (“I’m ready to pop!”) — carried her mother’s decades-old black quilted Chanel bag. “I think it was just such a big investment piece for her,” she says. “I knew it meant so much to her, so whenever I carry her purse, it feels really meaningful to me.” Sherman also thought of her mother while getting ready for the event, recalling her mom’s go-to scent as the original Coco Mademoiselle. “I’m a Patchouli girl!” As for the newest iteration? She only has one word to describe it. “Girl.”

After walking a carpet shielded from the hectic SoHo street by the restaurant’s deep-red streeteries, attendees made their way into the restaurant where they were met with floating trays of cheeseburgers, salmon crudo, shrimp cocktail, buckets of fries and an endless stream of white wine and champagne.

Sherman and fellow “SNL” castmember Veronica Slowikowska huddled in a red leather corner booth over dirty martinis, while Marcello Hernandez and girlfriend Ana Amelia Batlle Cabral mingled at the bar with Adam DiMarco. Photographers, meanwhile, made the rounds among some of Hollywood’s newest breakout stars, including “Sterling Point’s” Amélie Hoeferle, Rubin and Ruffalo, as well as “The Shards” stars Igby Rigney and Hayes Warner. One surprise guest, podcast host Adam Friedland, seemed perfectly at ease — even without an interlocking-C accessory in tow. “They just told me to come here. I don’t know what I’m doing,” he joked in his usual deadpan. “What is this event? I thought it was a runway. Is it a runway? I’m gonna be useless.”

Pierre Beasley and Henry Beasley of Balu Brigada perform during the Chanel Party at Balthazar WireImage

Nara Smith and Iris Law attend the Chanel Party at Balthazar WireImage

Terrence O’Connor attends the Chanel Party at Balthazar WireImage

Downstairs, a more clandestine party unfolded. The waiting area outside the bathroom was transformed into a series of photo ops, including a deep-maroon couch beneath Chanel signage and, across the room, a backlit alcove with a vintage rotary phone made for posing. The bathroom itself, wrapped in mirrors and stocked with Chanel beauty products, became a gathering point for the fashion set, who crowded in for mirror selfies.

As the night wore on, Balu Brigada’s live set gave way to a more mellow DJ soundtrack as pavlova, chocolate mousse and mini profiteroles made the rounds. On their way out, guests were ushered through the restaurant’s boulangerie, where croissants, éclairs and other baked goods were packed up for the road. Because, yes, it’s 2026 and models eat carbs!

title: New James Bond Movie: First Draft of the Script Is Done, Says Steven Knight
summary: With so much of the frenzied James Bond interest centered on who might be taking over from Daniel Craig as 007, something many believe is going to be announced imminently, the matter of the all-important script has largely been ignored. Well, according to Steven Knight, that key element is now complete. Speaking to Zoe Ball […]
content:
With so much of the frenzied James Bond interest centered on who might be taking over from Daniel Craig as 007, something many believe is going to be announced imminently, the matter of the all-important script has largely been ignored.

Well, according to Steven Knight, that key element is now complete.

Speaking to Zoe Ball on the U.K.’s Greatest Hits Radio, when asked if he’d done the script draft, Knight replied: “I’m nodding silently.”

The prolific screenwriter, who created “Peaky Blinders,” “A Thousand Blow” and “House of Guinness” and helped write the new Oasis documentary “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” described writing Bond as “more than bucket list,” adding he felt he was “doing my duty for King and country by taking this thing on.”

Popular on Variety

He added: “I’m absolutely loving doing it. It’s an honor to be asked. And believe it’s going to be so good. I really do believe it’s going to be amazing.”

Earlier in the week, Knight appeared to hint that he knew who had been cast as Bond in the 26th instalment and franchise reboot, being directed by Denis Villeneuve and coming from Amazon MGM Studios.

Asked by BBC Radio 4’s “Today” program whether he’d written the film with the chosen actor in mind or based on what he knew about the character he replied, “It’s a bit of both.” He added: “It does make life a little bit easier if you know who that person is, but also you have to write the character, not the actor.”

The update comes just days after Gary Oldman claimed that the crucial casting decision had been made and said he was hoping his “Slow Horses” co-star Jack Lowden — among the hot favorites — would be the one getting the call.

“It’s been rumored that [Lowden] is on the shortlist,” Oldman said in an interview with Canada’s “The Morning Show.” “We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack.”

title: Jay Baruchel & Michael Dowse Talk Falling In Love With ‘The Stunt Driver’ Ken Carter, Upcoming Sitcom Project, Baruchel’s WWII Fighter Pilot Passion Project
summary: For Michael Dowse, the filmmaker behind The Stunt Driver, there’s a meta aspect to his journey with the Canadian sports comedy. The film, examining the dogged pursuit of a seemingly impossible dream, was in effect just that for him — a “white whale” that he chased for 12 years. And now, he’s harpooned it: The film […]
content:
For Michael Dowse, the filmmaker behind The Stunt Driver, there’s a meta aspect to his journey with the Canadian sports comedy.

The film, examining the dogged pursuit of a seemingly impossible dream, was in effect just that for him — a “white whale” that he chased for 12 years. And now, he’s harpooned it: The film premieres at the Royal Alexandra Theatre, as part of the Toronto Film Festival, tonight.

The Stunt Driver tells the true story of Ken Carter, Canada’s underdog answer to Evel Knievel, whose life goal was to nail a mile-long jump in a rocket car across the St. Lawrence River. Jay Baruchel plays the stuntman, in his third collaboration with Dowse — a friend of 20+ years — following the cult hockey comedy Goon and FXX comedy Man Seeking Woman.

Beautifully shot on 16mm and 35mm film, at multiple aspect ratios, The Stunt Driver is inspired by The Devil at Your Heels, the 1981 documentary on Carter from Robert Fortier, and makes Fortier a central character, using the making of the doc as a central structural device in telling the story.

Watch on Deadline

This was in part a practical decision: Knowing he wouldn’t have the budget to practically capture all of Carter’s athletic exploits, Dowse resolved to build the film around doc footage and other archival material. The final product speaks to the amazing results that can come in art, when adapting to constraints.

Ahead of their premiere, Dowse and Baruchel spoke with Deadline about a film that will make you all in love with Carter — a piece that is as sweetly heartfelt as it is funny. They also talk Montreal Canadiens fandom and cast standout Joe Cobden, while hinting at a new sitcom they’re developing together as a starring vehicle for Baruchel, and the Second World War fighter pilot epic that he’s dying to make.

DEADLINE: Michael, you’ve called The Stunt Driver your “white whale.” What first grabbed you about Ken Carter’s story?

MICHAEL DOWSE: I was drawn by the spectacle of it all, the period and the character. I fell in love with Ken — with his hope, with his sense of humor. He was a dreamer. So it was really the character that cemented it, and what he had to go through. Then, when I started digging into it, I just thought this would be a really interesting film, if I can somehow incorporate Bob Fortier and the different aspect ratios. It just got me really excited. But yeah, it was mostly Ken that drove me to it, just because there’s so much you could do with a character like that.

DEADLINE: What were the first steps you went through when you sat down to write?

DOWSE: Well, I think the first step was, you sort of write down the documentary verbatim. You follow the structure of the documentary, and what you discover is that it can’t be the same thing when you adapt it to a feature film. You have to combine things. Like, there’s three different car tests. There’s so many different attempts in the actual real story that we tried to combine it. Really, you had to consolidate a lot of things to make the story flow, and once you started thinking about the necessities of your budget and what you had to do, it really did lead to the invention of, “Let’s use Bob Fortier as more of a character. Let’s use these three different aspect ratios. Let’s play around with this, and let’s really bob and weave in and around the footage.” So, a long process, but it definitely is a thing where you have to collapse a lot of characters and events into more of a streamlined story that’ll be more palatable for a feature film.

DEADLINE: Can you expand a bit on arriving at your basic visual approach — framing the film around the making of The Devil at Your Heels, and moving between different aspect ratios?

DOWSE: It comes from necessity. The first time we got a breakdown of the script, it was an insanely expensive movie that we would never be able to make. So the first step was like, well, we have to use the stunt footage. We have to use a lot of that footage and we have to bob and weave around this stuff because we can never launch our own rocket car off a 90-foot ramp as they do in the [doc]. So that was the first step. And then when you really start to dig into what that means, you start to play around with, what happens if you jump from 16 to 2:39, and what does that access give you when you jump out to an anamorphic world that’s your reality behind the doc footage?

So I got excited by the idea of flipping the world of a documentary. Normally, the documentary is the truth, but because Ken was such a showman and had such a great relationship with Bob and was so aware of the camera, I got really interested in terms of what we could do behind the documentary in our 2:39 aspect ratio. And then obviously, having Jay as an actor, it just opens that world up completely in terms of where you can go.

DEADLINE: Jay, how familiar were you with Ken Carter’s story when Michael approached you?

JAY BARUCHEL: Anything I know about Ken is a function of being friends with Dowse. We’ve known each other for over 20 years, and way back at some point when we were trying to build our first movie together, Goon, I think we’d had these conversations about, if you could do anything in the world, what would it be? He mentioned making a feature of Devil at Your Heels back then, and then of course I fell in love with that movie, Ken himself, everything he represents. So when Mike was like, “I wrote a script finally, and enough time has passed that I think you’re old and fat enough…” [Laughs]

DOWSE: Old enough.

BARUCHEL: “You’re old enough to do this now, maybe…” Because never in a million years did it once occur to me that I would ever play Ken Carter. In all the times I watched that movie and talked about the movie with friends, I never once imagined myself in him. And so when Dowse pitched it to me, I wish I had a better term than “left field.” It was lovely and unexpected. And then I read his incredible script. I called or texted him at page 40 or 50. I was just like, “I love it. It’s an amazing script. I have to do it.” I just knew that the other 50 to 90 pages would also be good. And they were.

Now that I’m talking about his script, I’d just like to take the chance to say…Mike’s being very Calgary about all of it and writing everything off as a function of technical restrictions. But he sees Ken in a way that only he could see him. I think he’s doing himself a bit of a disservice. Like, the documentary’s wonderful, but the depth that Mike sees and how he frames Ken, in terms of what he means to our culture specifically, as well as anybody that ever felt stuck where they were…Dowse is an incredible artist, so he brings something really beautiful to it, and it’s one of the best scripts I ever read.

DEADLINE: What did you understand immediately about Ken as a character, and what took longer to unlock in your performance?

BARUCHEL: The way I like to say it is, I was born in 1982, so that means that there were still men like Ken Carter around when I was a boy, and there just aren’t those guys anymore. And for a bunch of reasons that are good: We’ve eradicated adult illiteracy and all of these things. But the margins were way more severe when he was a kid. So that creates a particular brand of person — a guy who has had to fight for everything he’s ever gotten, and a guy for whom his entire sense of his worth is tied specifically to one f*cking crazy thing that he can screw up the courage to do.

You can’t find — at least I haven’t found — any interviews with Ken talking about how much he loves jumping cars. He just says he does it, and that he’s good at it, but you never hear him talking about what a kick he gets out of it or anything. Acting scares the f*ck out of me, and I know that the only reason that I’m on this Zoom call with you is because of this particular weird thing that I can suck up the courage to find a way to do. So I feel like I got him right away.

What took a sec to figure out was the fun of the physicality, and adopting his gait, and trying to figure out his particular eye situation and all of these different things.

DOWSE: Jay just puts the film on his back. I love this performance, I love what he does with the character. He brings so much shape to it. It’s not just a mimicry or an aping of the real guy; he really makes it his own and does such an amazing job that he better get the recognition he deserves.

DEADLINE: Tonally, The Stunt Driver is something special — very funny but also sweetly sincere. I’d equate It, as a compliment, to an earnest Ricky Bobby. How did you calibrate that balance?

DOWSE: It’s a continuation of everything that I’ve been doing in a lot of my films, where you take what might be considered broad characters and really try to ground them and give them heart. I think the key for me is that you want to get people laughing with them and falling in love with them. You set people up with the left hand of, get people laughing: They’re funny characters, they’re approachable, they’re accessible. And then you knock them with a bit of tragedy or conflict. And that’s definitely the approach I took on this one. The difference here is that it’s a real guy, so the stakes are even higher in terms of, you don’t have free will to just do whatever you want. You have to stay within the guidelines to a certain degree of, this is a real guy, and these things happened.

I think that the starting point for us of Ken Carter, he was an incredible person. He was brave, he was idiosyncratic. He was a bunch of things. There was ups and downs. He wasn’t a simple person you could put in a box. So it allows you to play with the tone a little bit. And for me, it was about, you have to take this character seriously because he takes what he’s doing quite seriously. But that doesn’t mean he can’t be the life of the party and he can’t be funny.

So I really just try to use comedy to be a gateway to the likability and how much you’re invested in the character, and then you can have a lot of leeway with where you go with that. And obviously we’re following the guidelines of this story, of actually what happened, but it’s a tone that I love and it’s a tone that I think is really effective. I think people respond to it because they love the character.

DEADLINE: Was financing the film a long road? Were there many false starts?

DOWSE: There was just one false start. Telefilm came in and gave us their full support, and then SODEC, which is the Quebec version of Telefilm, did the same thing. So we had enough money to get going and get started. But even then, it gets eaten up a lot by the ramp and by the period and the scale of it all. We were lucky enough to find one location where we could shoot about 80% of the film, so that made it easier. But there was just a ton of constraints. I say this a lot, but I feel like because you have to build the ramp and you have to build the rocket car, you kind of turn into Ken Carter himself, trying to deal with the same problems. But we only had one delay, which was trying to go in the spring and we just weren’t ready. And you just have to, a lot like Ken Carter himself, pull the plug and know that three months later, we’ll be back up and get going.

DEADLINE: This is your second Canadian sports film together, following Goon. How deep does sports fandom run for both of you?

BARUCHEL: We watch a lot of hockey and I think there’s at least 10 to 15% meathead in both of us. [Laughs]

DOWSE: That’s generous.

BARUCHEL: [Laughs] But yeah, no. I’m a religious hockey fan, and I wasn’t a huge fan of stunt driving. I obviously have a respect and appreciation for it now, but half of what Mike and I talk about at any given time is hockey.

DOWSE: The Montreal Canadiens, to be specific.

DEADLINE: What has made for a strong friendship and collaboration between you, over three projects now?

BARUCHEL: I think number one, we just get on really well. We enjoy each other’s company, and there’s enough points of common interest to sustain a friendship over two decades. And we are diametrically opposed on some movies and stuff like that. But we have, I think, enough of the same ideas in movies and television that we complement each other. And any places where we don’t, I think that’s only to the project’s benefit. I think Dowse has ideas I could never, and I would like to think vice versa, as well.

DOWSE: 100%.

BARUCHEL: And there’s just an easy shorthand. We’re working on something else right now. We’re writing this sitcom together for him to direct and me to star in, and the writers’ room for that sh*t is just the happiest thing in the world. It’s just us hanging out, making each other laugh, getting Tim Hortons. It’s all very on the nose, man. We get on super good, and I’m lucky that a guy that I get on with is also the best director around.

So it’s a really, really cool thing. Even if our movies and sh*t sucked, it would still be fun to do it. [Laughs] The added benefit is that we make awesome sh*t together. Stunt Driver, for me, is— and there’s no hyperbole, whatsoever, when I say —the best thing I’ve ever done. And it’s certainly my favorite. It is absolutely my favorite of anything I’ve ever done.

DEADLINE: Jay, you’ve expressed real excitement about, and commitment to, the telling of distinctly Canadian stories as a primary point of focus in your career. That has led you down a great road with films like BlackBerry, and now The Stunt Driver. What is this pursuit really about for you?

BARUCHEL: For as long as I’ve had a career in the U.S., I’ve had a career in Canada, too. I never had my foot out of here completely, and so for every big Hollywood studio movie that people might recognize me from, from a long time ago, there’s two or three independent Canadian movies that are out there. So I’ve been building this resume the whole time and just trying to do stuff that I give a sh*t about. And it’s a very simple criteria I have, which is would I watch this? Would I f*ck with this? Is this the kind of thing that I’d be interested in? And failing that, is it going to be a meaningful way to spend my time? And as long as one of those boxes are checked — ideally both — but as long as at least one of them are checked, then I know it’s something I should do.

At a certain point, if you do it long enough and the sh*t’s good, the world starts to notice. And so I’m very, very proud. I’m very proud of the story that BlackBerry has had, and I’m really even more so excited about the story that this is going to have. At this point in my life… Look, I’m very lucky to have any gig. Anybody is. But truly, at this point in my life, any boxes I have left to check are just about putting my country’s stories on film.

DEADLINE: Joe Cobden, who plays documentarian Bob Fortier, is a real standout in The Stunt Driver.

BARUCHEL: He’s so good.

DEADLINE: He’s someone I hadn’t seen before; you share great comedic chemistry. Talk about how he came to the project and what he brought.

DOWSE: Joe has, I think, 27 movies at TIFF this year, so he’s very seasoned. He’s also Foghorn Leghorn in [Coyote vs. Acme], which is incredible.

BARUCHEL: [Laughs] What? Is that true?

DOWSE: [Laughs] Oh, yeah. He’s all over the place. It’s like, if you squint, you’ll see Joe in your movie. He’s incredible; I didn’t even have to read him. I just saw him on the list and was like, “Yeah, yeah, he’s perfect.” And I think he just came in with Bob Fortier’s voice and owned the part.

On paper, when you look at that schedule, it’s a very thankless part because he’s behind camera a lot of the times. Just to be on set, but he’s not necessarily shooting all the time. It’s sometimes just his voice, but he needs to be present there. And he just really embraced it and really was a big fan of the doc and the story. And we were lucky to have him. He was incredible. A lot of actors would have a problem with that part because he’s on set a lot, but maybe not in a lot of the footage, but his presence in the movie is so important. And Bob’s story is as much of the story, right?

BARUCHEL: I’ve known Joe, I think since I was 18 or 19, and I’m 44. I’m from Montreal, and when he moved to Montreal from Nova Scotia 20+ years ago, he just took the city by storm. He’s such an accomplished, incredible performer — theater performer, historian, filmmaker. He just is truly a real polyglot, renaissance man, whatever, and is a lovely guy. Again, just someone whose company we enjoy and somebody who is interested in and cares about the same things as Dowse and me. So we didn’t have to find our sea legs. We kind of all just had a shorthand and were able to figure it out by the time the first setup was ready to go on day one, which is important when you’ve only got f*cking 20 days to make a movie. You don’t have a bunch of time to figure yourself out. So the better you’re with people that you know and trust and have a preexisting relationship with. You kind of just build on that. And so what you’re seeing on screen between Joe and me is a sort of friendship or relationship of 20+ years, finally on camera.

DOWSE: Guys, I’ve got to jump. I got a crew staring at me; I got to start my day.

BARUCHEL: See you, Mike.

DEADLINE: A few final questions, Jay. One of the most compelling thematic ideas in your film is the distinction between a stunt driver and a daredevil — real craft versus reckless delusion. When in your own career did you know for yourself that you were a stunt driver, not a daredevil?

BARUCHEL: That’s a lovely question that is hard to answer without sounding like a bit of an arsehole. But I think when I kept getting gigs down in L.A. I started acting in Montreal when I was 12 and never thought I would continue into adulthood. I thought I would get to 18. If I was lucky to have saved any money, I would go and live on my own, write a bunch of scripts, try to get some independent horror sh*t going until my money ran out, and then that would be that. Whatever. So I already had made peace with it being done and that I was onto the next piece.

Then, I was lucky enough to get work down in L.A., and it begat more work, which then generated work for me up here. I take none of it for granted though, right? And I’m very happy to be talking to you on the week that this movie I adore is premiering at TIFF – on a really great slot, on a great night, at a great theater and all this sh*t. But I also know that it could all go away at any minute. [Laughs] This time next year, or far quicker than that.

My mom always raised me with a sense of, never get too used to any of it. Know your value, know you’re good, but know that nothing is guaranteed for anybody, and there but for the grace of God go I kind of thing. At 44, the fact that when I started, they were still putting actual film canisters into cameras and actually checking gates and all of this sh*t, and that I’m still here, makes me breathe a bit easier. But it’s a freelance gig. And so every time a gig is done, it is in theory potentially the last one ever. So just like every jump could f*cking kill you, it’s impossible to get completely comfortable, I think.

DEADLINE: What has been your process in managing the fear that comes with your line of work?

BARUCHEL: I wish I could liken it to something where the stakes were a bit lower because I am by no means comparing what I do to these following two gigs that you have to be really hard to do, which is a fireman or a sailor. Like, a sailor has to fear the ocean enough to respect it so that you don’t f*ck about — because that could be that. Same with a fireman. But you can’t be so scared of it that you can’t do the thing, and live with the thing, and you have to like it as well and get something out of it. So that’s kind of how I compare it.

Also, my mind is so nuked from 30 years of acting that there’s basically three places in the world I’m comfortable: It’s my house, my cottage, and a film set. And everything else, I’m really outside my comfort zone. Like, I just went and picked up my suit that I’ll be wearing on Friday, and just being out and about in public is really difficult for me, just because I don’t do well in crowds and I’m super uncomfortable. But you put me on a set with a bunch of lights and a camera aimed at me, it’s my secret little sanctum. There’s a calm to be found there for me.

DEADLINE: The film is ultimately about chasing an impossible dream. What’s yours, at this stage of your life?

BARUCHEL: Oh boy. Well, because I’m a movie nerd, it’s all going to be down to some movie that I hope I get to make one day. So I wrote this script called Malta Spitfire, which is based on a true story. I’ve optioned these two books and synthesized them into one screenplay: It’s a big Second World War fighter pilot epic about a Montreal boy that was Canada’s deadliest ace in the war and one of the RAF’s deadliest spitfire pilots. He led quite a crazy life and he’s an Anglo boy from Montreal. It’s a story that means a lot to me.

His name is George Beurling. I have been singularly obsessed with him for years. When I turned 40, my wife and I went to Malta for my 40th so that I could location scout for a movie that might never get made. [Laughs] But yeah. That’s my Stunt Driver, from the director’s seat anyway.

title: ‘Before The War’, ‘Our Share Of Sand’ Scoop Top Venice Critics’ Week Prizes
summary: Italian-French director Tommaso Usberti’s Before the War, a coming-of-age tale exploring contemporary masculinity, has scooped the Grand Prize at the 41st Venice International Film Critics’ Week. In other key feature film prizes, Chilean-Indian London-based director Shalini Adnani’s Our Share of Sand, a family drama reflecting on inequality and environmental crisis, won the Audience Award. Bibiana […]
content:
Italian-French director Tommaso Usberti’s Before the War, a coming-of-age tale exploring contemporary masculinity, has scooped the Grand Prize at the 41st Venice International Film Critics’ Week.

In other key feature film prizes, Chilean-Indian London-based director Shalini Adnani’s Our Share of Sand, a family drama reflecting on inequality and environmental crisis, won the Audience Award.

Bibiana Rojas Gómez and Juan David Cárdenas’s The End Of Times – a radical essay film using archive footage and AI to reflect on memory and colonialism – won the Best Technical Contribution as well as Special Mention within the Grand Prize category.

Set in the northern Italy’s Po Valley, Before the War revolves around a young man raised in a violent, racist and macho milieu, and his encounter with Sonia, a young Kosovar immigrant.

Watch on Deadline

The international jury – composed of French director Chloé Barreau, Hungarian producer Júlia Berkes and writer, cultural curator and film-industry professional Caterina Mazzucato – praised the film for its intense direction, the performance of the lead actor and its mise-en-scène.

“A film that relies as much on silence as on words, where sound and music become a battlefield in their own right to explore urgently contemporary themes: toxic masculinity, impossible desire and the individual’s profound loneliness. A raw, evocative and deeply cinematic feature, both classic and innovative, revealing a strong and distinctive directorial voice,” read their jury statement. .

The film also won the Luciano Sovena Award for Best Producer “for managing, with limited means, to portray an Italy of those on the margins, between realism and magic, violence and tenderness, romanticism and racism. A dialogue between registers that is also reflected in the winning production (or rather co-production), which best embodies the spirit and mission of Luciano Sovena, to whose memory this award is dedicated”.

It is produced by Thibault de Gantes and Lucas Le Postec at L’Heure d’été; Francesco Virga, Adele Dell’Erario, Marco Serrecchia at MIR Cinematografica and Beatrice Bordone Bulgari at Eolo Film Productions.

The Venice International Film Critics’ Week is an independent and parallel section organised by the Italian National Film Critics Union (SNCCI).

The selection was curated by General Delegate Beatrice Fiorentino together with the selection committee composed of Matteo Berardini, Marianna Cappi, Francesco Grieco and Marco Romagna.

title: Gary Oldman Clarifies James Bond Comments: “I Do Not Know, But I’m Hoping It’s Jack”
summary: Gary Oldman has reflected playfully on creating headlines around the world with his comments about the James Bond casting process. In an interview with Canadian broadcaster Global over the weekend, Oldman claimed that 007 had been selected. Oldman added that he hoped his Slow Horses co-star Jack Lowden would get the role. “It’s been rumored […]
content:
Gary Oldman has reflected playfully on creating headlines around the world with his comments about the James Bond casting process.

In an interview with Canadian broadcaster Global over the weekend, Oldman claimed that 007 had been selected. Oldman added that he hoped his Slow Horses co-star Jack Lowden would get the role.

“It’s been rumored that he’s on the shortlist. We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack.”

It was not clear from Oldman’s comments whether he meant that Lowden had been cast as Bond, or whether he was talking more generally about Amazon MGM Studios alighting on Ian Fleming’s secret agent.

Watch on Deadline

Well, now we know. Speaking during a Visionaries session at TIFF, Oldman told Josh Horowitz that he does not know who will be playing Bond — but he stands by his suggestion that the role has been cast.

Gary setting the record straight on the Bond speculation 🙂‍↕️ pic.twitter.com/aXTGtZPbrq — Agus (@riverscoat) September 11, 2026

“There’s six people on a shortlist. I heard a rumor that they’ve picked James Bond, but they haven’t announced it yet, which is their prerogative,” Oldman said. “So I do not know [who has got the part], but I’m hoping it’s Jack.”

The Oscar winner joked that he had a “red phone” to the “Bond people” and, even if he did know the identity of 007, he would not reveal the state secret.

Oldman added that he learned his lesson after letting slip about the greenlight for The Dark Knight Rises, the third film in Christopher Nolan’s Batman trilogy. “I got reprimanded for that,” he said.

Asked if he would consider playing a Bond baddie, Oldman replied: “Don’t do drugs and Bond villains.”

Odds on Lowden becoming Bond shortened after Oldman’s remarks. Deadline reported over the summer that auditions were taking place for James Bond in August. Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, as well as director Denis Villeneuve, informed talent who had been shortlisted.

At the time, we reported that Harris Dickinson, Callum Turner, and Jacob Elordi fit the idea of Bond that Amazon MGM Studios had in mind.

title: ‘Bling Empire’ Star Dorothy Wang Launching Wedding Series On YouTube
summary: EXCLUSIVE: From Married At First Sight to Say Yes To The Dress, wedding shows remain a popular fixture on television. And now YouTube. Dorothy Wang, one of the stars of Netflix reality series Bling Empire: New York, is launching her own wedding on the Google-owned streaming service and has teamed up with Rich Kids of […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: From Married At First Sight to Say Yes To The Dress, wedding shows remain a popular fixture on television. And now YouTube.

Dorothy Wang, one of the stars of Netflix reality series Bling Empire: New York, is launching her own wedding on the Google-owned streaming service and has teamed up with Rich Kids of Beverly Hills exec producer Gennifer Gardiner to facilitate the vows.

Dorothy’s I Do is a five-part wedding docuseries that will launch on September 27 and roll out episodes weekly.

It marks the latest high-profile project to debut on YouTube as stars and producers eye plans to increasingly produce for the free streamer.

Watch on Deadline

The series will follow Wang and her husband, Brandon Yankowitz’s journey from the anticipation and preparation leading up to their wedding through their lavish celebration in Florence, Italy.

The wedding took place in October 2025, bringing together family, friends and stars such as Nicky Hilton, Sai De Silva, Tina Leung, Lilly Ghalichi, Farrah Aldjufrie and Tinx. The three-day event was held at the Collegio alla Querce with a reception at Florence’s Palazzo Corsini and an afterparty that featured DJ Devin Lucien and a performance from Saweetie.

I Do is produced by Wang and Yankowitz’s newly launched production company, Chez Yankowitz, with Gennifer Gardiner, who has also worked on shows including MILF Manor and Growing Up Hip Hop, exec producing.

Wang and Gardiner previously worked together on Rich Kids of Beverly Hills when the former was a castmember. Wang will also host a TikTok Live to promote the show.

title: Scott “Kid Cudi” Mescudi Stars Opposite Barbie Ferreira In His Next Directorial Feature ‘Wrong Number’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Scott “Kid Cudi” Mescudi has recently been teasing his second directorial effort in a year, on the heels of the addiction drama Doe. And we can now tell you that it’s Wrong Number, a horror thriller where he stars opposite Barbie Ferreira (Mile End Kicks). Currently in production in Los Angeles, Wrong Number centers on Ibn (Mescudi), […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Scott “Kid Cudi” Mescudi has recently been teasing his second directorial effort in a year, on the heels of the addiction drama Doe. And we can now tell you that it’s Wrong Number, a horror thriller where he stars opposite Barbie Ferreira (Mile End Kicks).

Currently in production in Los Angeles, Wrong Number centers on Ibn (Mescudi), a lonely self-help author whose unexpected romance with a mysterious woman named Eliza (Ferreira) turns into a waking nightmare when he becomes the target of an unseen stalker and the prime suspect in a string of murders.

Pic’s cast also includes Lucy Barrett (Deep Water), Dewayne Perkins (The Blackening), Clifton Powell (Ray) and Laura Harrier (Michael).

Watch on Deadline

Mescudi is directing from his own script and exec produces alongside Karina Manashil under their Mad Solar banner. Mark Webber, Anthony Baldino, and Ryan Lacen are producing, after working with the multi-hyphenate on his debut feature, Doe. Casting is by Obsession‘s Skyler Zurn, with Mescudi also penning the film’s score.

“A lot of people know that im a huge horror buff. And it was only a matter of time before I’d jump into the genre myself with my own stories,” Mescudi wrote in a statement to Deadline. “WRONG NUMBER is a fun ride, an original story that has all the elements of an epic horror thriller, and I can’t wait for you all the experience it. So thankful to have this amazing cast and team with me on this wild journey. There will be blood!!”

Mescudi is eyeing to release both of his directorial efforts next year. Deadline was also first to report on Doe, a film exploring themes of addiction and survival, where he stars alongside Mark Webber, Leah McNamara, Brandon Scott and Brandon Perea.

“Directing my second film in a year is unreal,” Mescudi said. “I’m learning more and more each day and I’m just ready for the challenge. I’m hyped to see people become fans of my filmmaking in the same ways they are with my music. I’m putting the industry on notice, Mad Solar bout to shake it up.”

Previously best known for his work as an actor and Grammy-winning musical artist, Mescudi’s recent screen credits include Happy Gilmore 2, M. Night Shyamalan’s Trap, Paramount+’s Sonic the Hedgehog spin-off series Knuckles and John Woo’s Silent Night. Upcoming, he stars opposite Willow Smith in the animated feature Slime from Jeron Braxton. He is repped by Three Six Zero and Brillstein.

Best known for roles in the likes of Euphoria, Faces of Death and Nope, Ferreira is repped by Authentic Talent & Literary Management, Untitled, and Felker, McGinnis & Ryan.

Barrett is repped by Wendy Powell at Active Artists Management and Ian Stack at Stride Management; Perkins by CAA, Artists First, and attorneys Amber Payne and Isaac Dunham; Powell by Opus Entertainment; and Harrier by CAA and Entertainment 360.

title: Sandra Bullock Rejected ‘Every Pervert’ in Auditions ‘Asking Me to Drop My Pants’ and Stopped Acting in Rom-Coms When ‘I Was Getting So Much S— For Them’
summary: Sandra Bullock joined her friend and fellow actor Jennifer Aniston for a chat as part of the “Practical Magic 2” star’s Interview magazine cover and revealed that she made the intentional decision to step away from the romantic comedy genre in the mid-2000s because “I was getting so much shit for them.” Aniston asked Bullock […]
content:
Sandra Bullock joined her friend and fellow actor Jennifer Aniston for a chat as part of the “Practical Magic 2” star’s Interview magazine cover and revealed that she made the intentional decision to step away from the romantic comedy genre in the mid-2000s because “I was getting so much shit for them.”

Aniston asked Bullock if there was ever a moment where she “made a deliberate choice about the kind of career [she] wanted,” to which the Oscar winner cited two examples. The first was before she a working actor: “I was in New York, I was a waitress, I was auditioning for every pervert that existed asking me to drop my pants. I was like, ‘Nope, not the role for me.’ I was working my way up. Every working actor thinks you will never work again so you just take what you can get and make the most of it.”

The second was when Bullock was already a box office star: “The only time I was intentional about my career was when I said, ‘I need to stop right now with the rom-coms,’ because I was getting so much shit for them. And I took a role in this film called ‘Crash‘… I wanted to start flexing other muscles.”

Popular on Variety

Bullock was a rom-com regular for much of her early career with hits like “While You Were Sleeping” (1995) and “Two Weeks Notice” (2002) and other offerings such as “Two If by Sea” (1996) and “Forces of Nature” (1999). She’d continue to flex her genre muscles in star vehicles like the 1998 romance “Hope Floats” and 2000’s blockbuster comedy “Miss Congeniality.” But after 2002’s “Two Weeks Notice” with Hugh Grant became a hit, Bullock stepped away for two years and returned with a dramatic role in “Crash.” Now her fans know this was a deliberate choice on Bullock’s part.

“It’s a very risky feeling to say, ‘I’m going to drop what feels like my comfort zone, which is comedies, and let’s see if they’ll take me seriously in the dramatic world,'” Aniston told Bullock. “The industry tends to pooh-pooh comedies, but they’re not as easy as they look.”

“Now more than ever, I miss that. I want to do nothing but that now,” Bullock responded.

Bullock isn’t the only rom-com icon to walk away from the genre amid fame and box office glory. Matthew McConaughey also made the deliberate choice to stop acting in rom-coms and even left Hollywood and moved his family in Texas to distance himself from the box Hollywood was trying to keep him in. He even turned down a $14 million offer to return to the genre.

As for Bullock’s decision to temporarily ditch the rom-com genre in favor of dramatic work, it ultimately paid off with “Crash.” The movie won her the Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding ensemble in a motion picture, and the movie went on to win the Oscar for best picture. Bullock would return to rom-coms in 2009 with “The Proposal,” one of her biggest hits, and “All About Steve,” which won her the Razzie for worst actress. But that year also included the release of “The Blind Side,” which won her the Oscar for best actress. Bullock’s most recent rom-com was 2022’s “The Lost City” with Channing Tatum, which was a post-pandemic box office hit with $192 million worldwide.

title: Court to Hold Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement Conference in Late October
summary: A court will hold a two-day settlement conference in the Paramount-Warner Bros. antitrust case in late October. The conference is a standard part of civil procedure and does not indicate whether a deal is in the offing. A magistrate judge, Thomas Hixson, has been tasked with overseeing the settlement discussions and to determine whether it […]
content:
A court will hold a two-day settlement conference in the Paramount-Warner Bros. antitrust case in late October.

The conference is a standard part of civil procedure and does not indicate whether a deal is in the offing. A magistrate judge, Thomas Hixson, has been tasked with overseeing the settlement discussions and to determine whether it will be possible to avoid a trial, which is scheduled for next March in Oakland.

Paramount has been pushing for a deal with California Attorney General Rob Bonta, and has been hoping to get it done before Oct. 1. That’s the date that it will begin paying a $7 million daily “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. shareholders.

Popular on Variety

Bonta, in turn, has said he is open to a settlement but only if it includes “robust structural remedies” — that is, presumably, spinning off a significant chunk of the combined assets.

California and 11 other states allege that the $111 billion merger will illegally reduce competition in the theatrical and basic cable markets, and Bonta has been looking for terms that would address concerns in both markets.

Bonta’s office was set to have settlement discussions with Paramount on Aug. 24, but Bonta canceled the talks the night before, accusing Paramount of leaking details to the press. Paramount denied it, and has since been somewhat quieter about exerting pressure on Bonta to make a deal.

At a scheduling conference on Friday, the parties were ordered to submit dates by next Tuesday that will work for in-person discussions at the end of October.

A settlement could come through the court-supervised process or outside of it. So setting the court settlement conference for late October does not foreclose the possibility of an earlier deal.

Paramount has entered into a stipulation agreeing not to close the transaction until after the trial, which is set for March 2. However, the company subsequently asked a court to require the plaintiffs to put up a $1.88 billion bond to cover the costs of a delay in case the deal is approved.

A hearing on that request is set for Sept. 24. The states have argued that Paramount is seeking to renege the agreement it made to hold off on closing with no bond.

title: ‘Back to Buenos Aires’ Review: Marco Bechis’ Return to the Screen Covers Similar Ground to Earlier Works but is Only Fitfully Effective
summary: The return of Marco Bechis to filmmaking after 10 years is a welcome surprise, and the terrain he covers in “Back to Buenos Aires” is a familiar one for the veteran Chilean-Italian director who himself was caught up in the nightmare of Argentina’s military dictatorship. Set in the present, with frequent flashbacks, the film tells […]
content:
The return of Marco Bechis to filmmaking after 10 years is a welcome surprise, and the terrain he covers in “Back to Buenos Aires” is a familiar one for the veteran Chilean-Italian director who himself was caught up in the nightmare of Argentina’s military dictatorship. Set in the present, with frequent flashbacks, the film tells the story of an Italian doctor involved in Argentina’s resistance in the 1970s who reluctantly goes back to the country to give testimony about his three-plus years in the Garage Olimpo concentration camp. Stylistically looking like an uneasy hybrid between horror and film noir, Bechis’ return fails to satisfy on multiple levels, including the emotional one, though there are a few memorable scenes and the crux of the tale is potent.

It’s no coincidence, of course, that the prison where Mariano Guerra (Adriano Giannini) was held, Garage Olimpo, is also the name of Bechis’ 1999 film. “Back to Buenos Aires,” however, is a very different movie, less visceral and more hallucinogenic, but also less gripping. It’s a film that tries to come to terms with survival guilt, avoiding pat judgments but hinting rather too strongly at the possibility of redemption through confession. Pervaded by silences that mirror the decades of silence that allowed war criminals to walk among us, the story unfolds through a back-and-forth of past and present, keeping pace with the revelations and Mariano’s increasingly fraught state.

Popular on Variety

Multiple messages on Mariano’s answering machine in Italy ask him to return to Buenos Aires to testify, but he keeps ignoring them, incapable of coming to grips with his Argentine past. The pressure is building, making him more and more edgy, until he finally agrees to go — cue a stunning sequence of shots filmed from his plane seat. Once landed, he and other witnesses pile into a van, but recognition doesn’t lead to conversation, which Mariano avoids at all costs. (One can’t help compare the loquacious Iranian survivors in “It Was Just an Accident” with the nearly mute Argentines here.) Housed in what looks like an old-fashioned congress center, the group take meals together but barely talk, for doing so would force them to revisit the trauma of the past as well as confront their own actions while in prison.

Even before we know the details, it’s clear that Mariano’s resistance to testifying springs from the shame of collaboration. That guilt, eating away at him for decades, comes boiling to the surface when he’s visited by Evelyn (Veronica Gerez, in a poorly written role), the daughter of a woman who disappeared during the dictatorship. He rejects her request for information about her mother, though not convincingly since his nerves are so shot he can barely avoid trembling. Even when the lawyer (Marcelo Chaparro) for those testifying has him look through photos to see if he can identify some of the people who ran Garage Olimpo, he feebly claims not to recognize anyone.

Bechis plays with the claustrophobia of the congress center as well as the courthouse, both locations lit with a deadening flatness that contrasts sharply with the few outdoor scenes, especially when Mariano spies a short, balding man leaving the courthouse and, in great agitation, follows him to the hospital where he works. It comes as no great surprise that Dr. K (Adrian Fondari), as he was known in Garage Olimpo, was Mariano’s chief tormentor, the man who wore down his will to such a degree that he became a passive collaborator when so many other prisoners were killed.

Bechis accompanies these scenes with flashbacks to when medical student Mariano (Eduardo Hoy) was working for the Resistance together with Muneca (Olivia Nuss), whose daughter Evelyn is the woman in the present putting pressure on him to reveal what he knows about her mother’s disappearance. The scene where Muneca is taken away is one of the most effective in the film, especially when it melds past and present. This shift between the two time periods creates an effective dialogue as we learn what actually happened in the prison, less graphically represented than in “Garage Olimpo” but still conveying the brutality inside.

Back in the present, the testimony of Amalia Mendez (Ana Celentano), her dignity unbowed as she recounts the sexual assaults she endured, helps to center the film at a moment when it really requires a strong, articulate voice. Mariano is just too shaky, his trauma too much on the surface, making us question how he ever remained a functional doctor. Multiple elements in “Back to Buenos Aires” don’t quite come together, starting with the peculiar mise-en-scène, which evokes horror movies — empty dully lit corridors, eerie silences, isolated characters — and film noir with shadows cast by old-fashioned blinds and lots of cigarettes. Flashback sequences are inevitably given a very brown tone, since no evocation of the 1970s would be considered believable unless brown predominates.

title: After Taylor Frankie Paul’s ‘Bachelorette’ Scandal, ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Just Isn’t Fun Anymore
summary: SPOILER WARNING: The following story contains plot details from Season 5 of “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.” From its very first moments, “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” has been inextricable from the toxic entanglement between #MomTok influencer Taylor Frankie Paul and her on-again, off-again boyfriend Dakota Mortensen. Two years ago, the show began […]
content:
SPOILER WARNING: The following story contains plot details from Season 5 of “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.”

From its very first moments, “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” has been inextricable from the toxic entanglement between #MomTok influencer Taylor Frankie Paul and her on-again, off-again boyfriend Dakota Mortensen. Two years ago, the show began with a violent encounter between the pair as captured on police officers’ body cameras. (The incident resulted in Paul’s arrest and subsequent guilty plea for aggravated assault.) Then, earlier this year, a planned season of “The Bachelorette” starring Paul — a bit of crossover corporate synergy between ABC and “Mormon Wives” streamer Hulu, both owned by Disney — was canceled after more graphic, harrowing footage of the same fight was leaked to TMZ.

Paul’s new venture may have been scuttled, but her flagship star vehicle remains intact. This week, “Mormon Wives” returned for an abridged Season 5, almost entirely filmed before production went on hiatus in March amid Paul’s public relations furor. The new information revealed in the five episodes is minimal. We learn the eventual winner of the final rose on the unaired “Bachelorette” season, making it even less likely the competition will ever see the light of day. We also learn how irrelevant the victor’s identity is, because Paul slept with Mortensen again the very night she returned from filming. Paul and Mortensen, by her own admission, have “an addiction” to one another and their toxic relationship. Most pairings formed during the “Bachelor” franchise don’t last; Paul’s was doomed before it even began.

Popular on Variety

But watching Season 5, something else becomes clear: “Mormon Wives” itself has a seemingly unbreakable dependence on the Paul-Mortensen saga, a tragedy that’s at once the show’s driving force and its greatest liability. What has already incurred a quite literal cost to ABC is now exacting a more metaphorical toll on the hit reality show, which is being swallowed whole by its most volatile element. In the season’s closing minutes, cast member Mikayla Matthews expresses her amazement that the friend group known as #MomTok has mutated from a source of “empowerment” into something much darker. Yet viewers have watched this process unfold in almost real time, making it anything but mysterious. Paul and Mortensen can’t quit each other, “Mormon Wives” can’t quit Paul — and the ensuing tragedy has turned what was once an addictive work of pop sociology into a grim spectacle that’s the opposite of fun.

Season 5 makes some token attempts at milking other sources of intrigue, like a half-hearted conflict between “Dancing With the Stars” alumni Jennifer Affleck and Whitney Leavitt or Jessi Draper’s recovery from what she characterizes as excessive plastic surgery. Paul and Mortensen are nevertheless inescapable — partly because the exes are trapped in an endless cycle, and partly because their dynamic is echoed in so many other pairs within the cast. No one sinks to the same depths as Mortensen, who claims to have sent Paul a sex tape of himself with another woman and, it’s strongly implied, likely weaponized the TMZ footage in retaliation for Paul drawing a boundary. In context, however, the couple comes off less like an exception and more like a tone-setter for a larger study in cautionary romantic tales.

Affleck’s husband Zac, arguably the show’s secondary antagonist, complains about his wife wanting to pose for Sports Illustrated even as her fame allows him to drop out of medical school and drive a CyberTruck. Miranda Hope’s ex-husband Chase McWhorter, fresh off a DUI, clearly yearns to be on camera and is duly rewarded for his confrontational stunts. Layla Taylor dates McWhorter’s brother Mason, showering him with gifts and vacations while he’s unable to return the favor.

“Mormon Wives” has always held interest for how the cast’s lucrative internet fame — which predates, though is accelerated by, the show — inverts the traditional gender dynamics instilled by their religion. But five seasons in, that fascination has curdled into discomfort. “Mormon Wives” isn’t just depicting unhealthy partnerships; in many cases, it’s exacerbating them, creating a perverse incentive for malcontents like McWhorter to stick around in return for exposure that’s still conditional on the women in their lives. In some cases, this tension exists among the women themselves: Paul has the most followers of anyone in the cast, and Draper expresses concern fans will inevitably take her side against her well-meaning friends.

Unlike the stars of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” the other reality smash set in the same area, the “Mormon Wives” are much younger and remain more entrenched in the Mormon community. Where Housewives like Heather Gay have proudly emancipated themselves from their marriages and the social expectations that came with them, the “Mormon Wives” feel like they’re still mired in the worst heterosexuality has to offer. (Though Layla Taylor has recently shared that she’s now dating a woman.) Paul and Mortensen, who she often refers to as her “baby daddy,” are in some ways far from traditional matrimony. They’re still stuck performing their dysfunction in public — a process that’s gone on so long it feels irresponsible to keep centering. But if “Mormon Wives” isn’t about terrible men exploiting women, what is it about? That’s one question among many for an upcoming spinoff set in Orange County to answer.

The only way to win this game, it seems, is not to play. Following her Broadway debut as Roxie Hart in “Chicago,” Leavitt announced her plans to leave the cast after Season 5. But even before her official exit, Leavitt already feels physically and emotionally distant. Well-spoken and level-headed, she’s almost unrecognizable from the volatile villain she came off as in Season 1. She’s also barely willing to engage with Affleck, whose issues with Leavitt have the subtext of Affleck’s less successful music career. (I have little faith the flamingo-inspired single “Pink Back” will be Affleck’s breakout.) Whatever issues Affleck claims to have with Leavitt’s behavior, she seems more jealous that Leavitt was able to leverage her talents into an escape hatch, leaving Affleck to share such dire sentiments as “I feel like Zac doesn’t understand me.” The “Mormon Wives” may have a sincere belief in religious concepts like Heaven, but for now, the show feels more like purgatory.

title: ‘Le Faux Soir’ Review: Fake News Tells the Truth in an Earnest, Slow-Paced Period Piece
summary: “Le Faux Soir” sources its high concept — hijacking state media propaganda’s fake news to tell the truth — from Second World War history. In 1943, disgruntled anarchist and poet Marc Aubrion (Arieh Worthalter) is recruited by the Belgian Resistance, which publishes its own underground newspaper. Marc’s brainwave is to reach outside the bubble of […]
content:
“Le Faux Soir” sources its high concept — hijacking state media propaganda’s fake news to tell the truth — from Second World War history. In 1943, disgruntled anarchist and poet Marc Aubrion (Arieh Worthalter) is recruited by the Belgian Resistance, which publishes its own underground newspaper. Marc’s brainwave is to reach outside the bubble of their already-captured readership by printing a fake edition of “Le Soir” — a once-venerable newspaper publishing Nazi propaganda under direct Gestapo supervision — to reach citizens the Resistance otherwise never would. A stolid two-plus hours directed with some surface frills by Michaël R. Roskam (“Bullhead,” “The Drop”), “Le Faux Soir” will appeal to elderly audiences hungry for low-impact prestige period fare with a reassuring message.

Looking like Jon Hamm in full “Mad Men” hangover mode, Worthalter draws on the surly, unceasingly confrontational energy he brought to 2023’s “The Goldman Case,” once again an outraged citizen revolting against an unjust state. Under the Gestapo’s occupying eye, Worthalter has limited his protest activities to writing scatalogically insulting poetry against them, then distributing it surreptitiously by tucking it into randomly pulled volumes from library stacks. His clumsily administered provocations draw the attention of a more organized Resistance coalition, who want to make use not of his poetry but his skills as a printer.

Popular on Variety

Marc’s idea of hijacking official media — not in service of organized theft but for a demonstration of the power of the press — kickstarts a familiarly structured heist drama. “The Nazis call these weapons of war,” printer Wellner (François Damiens) solemnly intones when showing off his roller presses, a piece of dialogue iterated three times lest anyone miss the point. Admittedly, the emphasis on that power isn’t just metaphorical but quite literal, with the film indulging a novel fetishism of both the technical aspects of printing — with much focus on obtaining linotypes, montages of type being set, scenes of pages being brushed against blocks of type, and so on — as well as the administrative side of newspaper publishing, with extended discussion of the circulation, distribution and storage logistics of what’s effectively a one-off issue. Anyone who’s worked in print media may feel unexpectedly pandered to (or like their grave is being walked over).

This recurring emphasis on logistics, however gratifying it may be to a shrinking and specialized viewership, isn’t particularly riveting. As onscreen title cards count down the 22 days to the big operation, Roskam tries to add additional verve to the proceedings with zooms, tracking shots, the occasional rolling timpani of Christophe Chassol’s loudly deployed score (which sometimes cutely syncs up with blocks of type being hammered), and even a “Reservoir Dogs”-style shot of four men walking out of a building in slow motion. But at 133 minutes, the film is supremely attenuated, each hurdle registering less as an exciting kink in a heist gaining momentum and more as a series of problem-solving administrative meetings. Admittedly, that’s a workable understanding of publishing, but it still doesn’t make for high drama, and the pace never quickens.

The film’s belief that truth will convert people if only it can reach them (surprisingly akin to “Disclosure Day”) is meant to be comforting. Clearly, there’s a metaphorical suggestion from the past to draw upon: instead of staying within liberal echo chambers, journalists who value truth must think unorthodoxly about audience outreach and targeting to recapture the attention of a misled populace. This is an inadvertently ironic message to place within a prestige period piece that, however jazzed-up on the margins, targets elderly, nostalgic audiences who value the importance of a good, firm handshake as much as these characters do.

Regardless, the suggestion rings false. Consumers have chosen their ideological siloes, and penetrating them is a conundrum that can’t be solved by bromides about the power of the press. It’s also a message that’s complicated, if not undermined, by the real-life, present-day “Le Soir” serving as one of the film’s production companies. No matter how blameless or hands-off their involvement might have been, it unavoidably renders the film self-burnishing sponsored content.

title: They’re Talking!: Paramount & AGs Settlement Talks Set For Next Month; Bonta Downplays Significance As “Standard Course”
summary: Paramount Skydance and the coalition of a dozen state Attorneys General fighting to stop David Ellison’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery will be having settlement talks after all. Well, settlement-ish talks Under the routine procedure of the federal court system, a judge in Oakland today instructed the battling parties to sit down together […]
content:
Paramount Skydance and the coalition of a dozen state Attorneys General fighting to stop David Ellison‘s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery will be having settlement talks after all.

Well, settlement-ish talks

Under the routine procedure of the federal court system, a judge in Oakland today instructed the battling parties to sit down together for “two consecutive days in the end of October”

The ” in-person settlement conference” is scheduled to start at 10 am PT in a month and a half, per Magistrate Judge Thomas S. Hixson.

Of course, none of this changes the fact that a Paramount disputed antitrust trial is still set to start on March 2, 2027. In fact, none of this means much at all unless Team Para, WBD and the AGs led by California’s Rob Bonta actually want to put their swords down and strike a deal, “structural remedies” and all.

Watch on Deadline

To that, Bonta’s office Friday bluntly told Deadline: . “A court-ordered settlement conference means the judge required both sides to meet, but it does not indicate a settlement is in progress. This is standard course in a case of this magnitude.”

title: Gustavo Dudamel Takes New York Philharmonic Baton With Help From Lizzo, Liev Schreiber & More
summary: Gustavo Dudamel officially took the baton Thursday as conductor and artistic director of the New York Philharmonic, leading a concert at Radio City Music Hall that was packed with special guests. Liev Schrieber served as the night’s host, while St. Vincent, Joaquina, Aaron Tveit and Lizzo took turns collaborating with the orchestra. (Lizzo showed off […]
content:
Gustavo Dudamel officially took the baton Thursday as conductor and artistic director of the New York Philharmonic, leading a concert at Radio City Music Hall that was packed with special guests.

Liev Schrieber served as the night’s host, while St. Vincent, Joaquina, Aaron Tveit and Lizzo took turns collaborating with the orchestra. (Lizzo showed off her classical training as a flutist along with singing a couple of her best-known hits; you can watch a video of her below.)

In his years leading the LA Philharmonic, Dudamel cultivated relationships with pop stars and entertainers, lending his voice to animated feature Trolls World Tour and routinely booking splashy performances at the Hollywood Bowl. Last summer, he appeared with members of the New York Philharmonic at the World Cup halftime show, which also featured Madonna, Justin Bierber and the Muppets.

Musical segments with guest artists were interspersed with performances of 21st century pieces by composers Philip Glass, Jessie Montgomery and Arturo Márquez. The night opened with George Gershwin’s “Overture to Strike Up the Band.”

Watch on Deadline

Schreiber, who proclaimed his roots as a native of New York’s Lower East Side, ribbed Dudamel as a “New Yorker by way of Venezuela” before offering a playful tribute. “Let’s face it: Gustavo Dudamel is not an easy person to describe – but God help me, I’m going to try,” he said. “Imagine if you added a teaspoon of Billy Joel, an ounce of Jean-Michel Basquiat, a cup of Tito Puente and a dash of Barbara Streisand. And absolutely nothing of Lionel Messi. Then add several thousand volts of electricity, an unreasonable amount of hair, and a capacity for the English language that still remains gloriously unchanged. Bake the whole thing into one giant musical arepa, and give it a baton. You’d be close.”

Turning more serious, Schreiber said Dudamel fits in with the city’s “idea of existential creativity.” Comparing the task of getting orchestra members to work together with the New York Knicks’ recent NBA title run, he declared, “Out of unity and cohesion, history is made.”

The New York Philharmonic, whose home at Lincoln Center was recently upgraded in a significant renovation, was founded in 1842. Its past conductors have included luminaries like Arturo Toscanini, Gustav Mahler, Leonard Bernstein, Pierre Boulez, and Zubin Mehta. Dudamel was appointed in 2023 but is only now taking over because of how drawn-out these transitions tend to be in the classical music world, which relies on annual subscription revenue and plans programs years in advance.

While the orchestra’s main residence at David Geffen Hall offers dramatically improved acoustics compared with predecessor Avery Fischer Hall, the far larger Radio City adds Sphere Immersive Sound. The same technology found at Sphere in Las Vegas has been added to Radio City in recent months by the venues’ shared parent company.

The system, dubbed Sphere Immersive Sound, uses 3D audio “beamforming” and wave field synthesis. The result is a consistent experience wherever an audience member is seated in the 6,000-seat theater.

Joaquina, a Grammy winning singer-songwriter from Venezuela, told Deadline by email prior to the concert that she was struck by what she heard at the soundcheck for Tveit, a Tony winner for Moulin Rouge. “I thought it was incredible how his voice sounded and blended with the orchestra,” she said. “I don’t think I’ve heard music being experienced in such a carefully crafted and intentional way in a venue in a very long time.”

title: Josh Giuliano Sets ‘Occupant’ With Blumhouse Atomic Monster Following TIFF Premiere Of Horror Debut ‘River’; Focus Features Distributing
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Following last night’s TIFF world premiere of his buzzy debut feature River, Josh Giuliano already has his next project — another horror film with a distributor on board and major backing. He’s set to write and direct Occupant for Blumhouse Atomic Monster, Divide/Conquer and Spooky Pictures, with Focus Features distributing. Focus holds worldwide rights to the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Following last night’s TIFF world premiere of his buzzy debut feature River, Josh Giuliano already has his next project — another horror film with a distributor on board and major backing.

He’s set to write and direct Occupant for Blumhouse Atomic Monster, Divide/Conquer and Spooky Pictures, with Focus Features distributing. Focus holds worldwide rights to the project and has set Universal Pictures International to handle international distribution.

Plot details for Occupant are being kept under wraps.

Producers are Jason Blum for Blumhouse Atomic Monster, Greg Gilreath and Adam Hendricks for Divide/Conquer, and Steven Schneider for Spooky Pictures. Executive producers include Daniel Bekerman, Derek Bishé, Neil Mathieson, Allie Steffler, Sam Zimmerman, and Jeremy Kulyk. The film is set up in association with Closer Media.

Watch on Deadline

Giuliano came to Blumhouse Atomic Monster through Zimmerman, who oversees the slate after joining earlier this year from Shudder. A fan of his work, he got the ball rolling on the Occupant partnership after connecting the filmmaker with Divide/Conquer’s Gilreath and Hendricks, who have a first-look deal with Blumhouse Atomic Monster on which we were first to report last December. The project reunites many of the parties behind Curry Barker’s breakout Obsession, one of the films igniting recent fervor around young digital native filmmakers. That one was also released by Focus, becoming the studio’s top-grossing film ever at over $512M worldwide.

Coming off a massive summer with Obsession and the Atomic Monster-produced Kane Parsons debut Backrooms, Blumhouse Atomic Monster is taking the same approach with Giuliano as they did with Barker; they set up Barker’s next project Anything but Ghosts at Focus after flipping for his debut feature, though they don’t have a producing credit on Giuliano’s first film as they did on Barker’s. (Spooky Pictures’ Schneider was part of the producing team, alongside Nick Antosca and Alex Hedlund.)

Premiering as part of TIFF’s Midnight Madness program, Giuliano’s River stars Jane Levy, Jessica Rothe and Max Mattern as three estranged siblings who reunite in their hometown after the death of their father. They set out to scatter his ashes at his favorite spot on a remote river, but when their boat breaks down, the trip devolves into a waking nightmare. Dane DiLiegro also stars.

An alumnus of the American Film Institute’s directing program, Giuliano’s shorts have won awards at genre festivals like Fantasia, Fantastic Fest, and FrightFest. He is represented by CAA, Kaplan/Perrone Entertainment, and Marios Rush.

title: Jimmy Kimmel In Talks To Renew Deal At ABC
summary: Earlier this week, tabloid reports had Jimmy Kimmel standing down from his late-night ABC show after his contract ends in May. That was not true, as evidenced by the fact that it has emerged that Kimmel is in talks to renew his deal for another year, Deadline has confirmed. Kimmel and Disney are in those […]
content:
Earlier this week, tabloid reports had Jimmy Kimmel standing down from his late-night ABC show after his contract ends in May.

That was not true, as evidenced by the fact that it has emerged that Kimmel is in talks to renew his deal for another year, Deadline has confirmed.

Kimmel and Disney are in those talks at the moment. The wrinkle? ABC reportedly is keen to cut the budget of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, a move that is becoming increasingly commonplace in late-night television.

This is what happened to The Late Show with Stephen Colbert before CBS axed the entire franchise. Late Night with Seth Meyers has also seen its fair share of cuts recently including the axing of the 8G band with Meyers taking particularly long breaks to cut down on the number of production weeks.

Disney is keen to make cuts across the board. In August, Deadline broke the news that Disney was offering longtime executives early retirement. This came after it started rounds of layoffs, first announced in April, with the elimination of 1,000 jobs with more cuts coming in July, particularly on the Pixar and Nat Geo fronts.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: List Of Hollywood & Media Layoffs From Paramount To Warner Bros Discovery To CNN & More

Deadline also understands that the television division is expecting a restructure in the near future, led by Debra OConnell, who was named Chairman of Disney Entertainment Television in March.

One would imagine even with some cuts to the budget, Kimmel would be keen to continue, at least for a couple more years to see out a certain President, who would likely crow and take credit if the comedian left before him.

Kimmel and his wife Molly McNearney, who is also an exec producer of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, discussed the topic of retirement recently on Dax Shepard’s Armchair Expert podcast.

Shepard asked Kimmel if he would regret retirement. “I know people who’ve been in that situation. It’s funny. People make a big show of like ‘I’m done and I’m tired doing this’, and then they make a lesser comeback trying to do the same thing. That’s always a bummer. I always look at that and go, Oh, is that going to be me?,” he said.

“Do you ever think to yourself, ‘How would I explain this to me at 25 years old, just giving up, just letting it go?’ I know that 25-year-old me will be like, ‘Are you crazy?’ I would have just been so excited to work at a place that had a snack table that was free,” he added.

McNearney admitted that Kimmel gets asked this question a lot but “I feel like it changes”.

Puck broke the news of Kimmel’s renewal talks.

title: United Artists, Amazon MGM & Steven Spielberg’s ‘Mandela Catalogue’ Sets Summer 2028 Release
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The next big YouTube-born horror IP for the big screen we told you about, the Mandela Catalogue from the Scott Stuber-led United Artists, Amazon MGM Studios and Steven Spielberg’s Amblin, is getting a summer release date of June 9, 2028. As Deadline reported, Mandela Catalogue creator Alex Kister is directing the feature off a screenplay […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The next big YouTube-born horror IP for the big screen we told you about, the Mandela Catalogue from the Scott Stuber-led United Artists, Amazon MGM Studios and Steven Spielberg‘s Amblin, is getting a summer release date of June 9, 2028. As Deadline reported, Mandela Catalogue creator Alex Kister is directing the feature off a screenplay he adapted with Tyler Clifton.

The trio of studios beat 11 other bids for films rights to the popular YouTube horror series, which has closed over 100 million views across its official episodes alone, making it one of the largest original analog horror franchises on the streaming portal. The property is regarded as one of the defining titles in the analog horror genre, alongside Local 58 and The Backrooms.

Launched in 2021, Mandela Catalogue is set in the fictional Mandela County, WI, which is invaded by shape-shifting, nearly immortal creatures called Alternates.

Watch on Deadline

Spielberg and Holly Bario are producing for Amblin Entertainment alongside Aaron B. Koontz for Paper Street Pictures and Stuber and Nick Nesbitt for United Artists. Kister and Clifton are also producing. Annie McCreery will oversee the project for United Artists. Maria Fortese will oversee for Amblin.

The only other title on June 9, 2028 so far is an untitled Universal event movie.

Following the success of this past summer’s genre titles from YouTube creators — Curry Barker’s Obsession ($512 million global box office) and Kane Parson’s Backrooms ($394.1M global), particularly among the Gen-Z crowd — Hollywood has been on a crusade to keep such fare humming.

title: Sebastian Stan on Why ‘Fjord’ Is Being Called a ‘MAGA Movie’ and How Making ‘The Batman 2’ Feels Like ‘F—ing Godfather Part 2’
summary: Sebastian Stan has been running around the city of Toronto. We’re sitting in a restaurant, having lunch between his multiple studio visits for various publications. It’s busy and bustling around us, the way TIFF tends to transform every hotel and restaurant over its 11-day period. Stan settles in at the table and digs into a […]
