“As a distributor, I released most of his eighties films including Oshima’s ‘Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence,’ Frears’ ‘The Hit,’ Roeg’s ‘Insignificance,’ Bertolucci’s ‘Sheltering Sky’ etc., and before that I wrote as a film pundit the cover article for the Sex Pistols movie ‘Rock n Roll Swindle’ for Time Out ( a movie I adored), which he produced with Julien Temple directing. All inspiring!!!

“And his company HanWay sold a lot of our productions including ‘Made in Dagenham’ and ‘Carol.’ He wasn’t just the Oscar winner of ‘Last Emperor’ (with an Italian director and Irish star set in China!) he was much, much more.

“Without Jeremy (and a little help from John Boorman) I would never have had the nerve at 27 to make ‘The Company of Wolves’ with the Irish director-writer Neil Jordan and the iconic feminist and anarchic writer Angela Carter. Jeremy showed with his first movie success ‘The Shout’ (with Polish friend and collaborator Skolimowski) that boundaries were there to be ignored or broken. And that movies are an international and all-embracing experience.

“Myself and my producing partner Elizabeth Karlsen look up to his guiding star still moving across the galaxy and inspiring filmmakers from all nations and genders with his extraordinary body of stellar work. Hoping to take guidance from a groundbreaking guru whose love of world cinema defied any easy categorization.”

Producer and publisher Charles Finch said, “He made great movies and was a loyal, dear friend. His father, Ralph, made a film with my father, Peter, called ‘No Love for Johnnie.’ We spent plenty of time talking movies, cars and praising the devilled kidneys as Wilton’s.”

On social media, Edinburgh Film Festival CEO and director Paul Ridd said that the “loss of Jeremy Thomas is enormous, to film culture and to the world,” adding that he was “such a beautiful man and a extraordinarily generous supporter” of the festival.

Adrian Wootton, chief executive of Film London and the British Film Commission, said that Thomas’ passing was, “Such terribly sad news for Jeremy’s loved ones, family, friends, colleagues, the filmmakers and for the British Film Industry he did so much for.”

Across a career spanning more than half a century, Thomas produced 80 features, championing the work of both international cinema and daring auteur filmmakers in the process. In 1988 he won the best picture Oscar for Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor.”

title: Andrew Scott Gets Candid at TIFF About ‘Elsinore’ and People Against Gay Actors Playing Straight Roles: ‘That’s Just Prejudice’
summary: Could Andrew Scott make history? That is the big question concerning the Irish actor’s towering performance in “Elsinore,” which debuted in Telluride before playing the Toronto International Film Festival. Directed by Simon Stone, the film features Scott as Ian Charleson, a Scottish actor whose career has slowed down since featuring in “Chariots of Fire.” The […]
content:
Could Andrew Scott make history?

That is the big question concerning the Irish actor’s towering performance in “Elsinore,” which debuted in Telluride before playing the Toronto International Film Festival. Directed by Simon Stone, the film features Scott as Ian Charleson, a Scottish actor whose career has slowed down since featuring in “Chariots of Fire.” The year is 1989, and when Daniel Day-Lewis walks offstage during a production of “Hamlet” at London’s National Theater, Charleson sees it as an opportunity to show the world what he’s made of as an actor — even as his body is being ravaged by AIDS, and against the advice of his doctor (Olivia Colman), who warns him that the stress could further worsen his health.

As Variety’s Clayton Davis wrote, “The casting is too perfect to be accidental. Scott is himself a celebrated London Hamlet, here playing a man whose Hamlet was his last act of defiance. ‘Elsinore’ is, at its heart, a love letter to actors — to the craft as vocation, to the courage of standing in the light when the body is failing. And a milestone waits inside the role. No openly gay man has ever won the Oscar for best actor, and Scott could very well become the first.”

Popular on Variety

Scott was widely seen as “snubbed” for his embodiment of Richard Rodgers in “Blue Moon” and the haunted Adam in “All of Us Strangers.”

On Saturday, Sept. 12, Scott took the stage at the Royal Alexandra Theatre to roaring applause as part of TIFF’s “In Conversation” series to discuss his much-heralded turn in “Elsinore” and his storied career. The talk was moderated by Keith Bennie, TIFF’s vice president of public programming.

The talk began with Bennie asking Scott, 49, who was sporting a striking purple jumper, about the internet’s obsession with him.

“I don’t have the internet. I never see it,” he joked, before adding, “It’s actually wild: You never know what feral things people [will say].”

“Elsinore” is the first film Scott has ever produced, so he said it “took a huge amount of encouragement and support and vision from so many people” to bring it to fruition. It was also a very personal project for Scott, who is openly gay and has been acting in theater since the ‘90s, including his aforementioned turn as Hamlet in 2017.

“You go through stages with it, and the film is so incredibly personal for me, which is the reason why I chose to produce this one,” he explained. “It’s set in the theater and about the representation of gay actors in the ‘90s, and it’s about family. So many things that I really relate to.”

Scott made his acting debut as a teenager in “Korea,” an Irish film that premiered at TIFF in 1995. And it was a formative experience for him, since he was given a crash course in how to conduct himself on a film set by watching his co-star, screen veteran Donal Donnelly, who led with authority but treated people with dignity and respect.

“Depressing. No, it was extraordinary. I was 17, and it was the first film I’d ever made,” offered Scott. “I learned how to be on a set because [Donnelly] was incredibly kind and fun with everybody… He wasn’t in any way cruel or anything like that.”

When Scott was a child, he had a speech impediment, which, in a roundabout way, is how he “fell in love with acting.”

“When I was a kid, I had a speech impediment — I had a very strong sort of lisp— so I had to go to elocution lessons at seven or eight,” he shared. “It had a drama section to it where you could improvise in front of the other kids.” Performing poetry and monologues in front of a crowd, however small, “amplified something that was dormant” in him.

At one point during the talk, Bennie shared a scene of Scott’s priest acting alongside Phoebe Waller-Bridge in the second season of “Fleabag,” which became an internet sensation and earned his character the nickname “The Hot Priest.”

“If you had got a script that said, ‘The Hot Priest,’ you’d be like, ‘This is dodgy,’” joked Scott. “It was just called ‘The Priest’ and then the internet took over.”

Scott, however, was immensely proud of “The Hot Priest” craze in the sense that it helped ease some of his own anxieties about whether the audience would accept a gay actor in a role as a woman’s love interest.

“I guess there was a fear that I wouldn’t be able to get cast in those roles. That’s what everybody said,” he confessed. “But I knew, because when I did plays, that the people that were waiting at the stage door, they knew my sexuality and they did not care.”

He continued: “I feel very proud that that was quite a big moment because people were like, ‘The actor is gay. Whoa!’ And it is like this idea that the audience is stupid. We go to see ‘Batman,’ and it’s like, ‘Oh my god! He is not a bat?’”

And if you don’t like Scott in those types of roles, that’s on you.

“That’s just prejudice,” said Scott. “And we won’t cater to those people, or I’m certainly not going to.”

About an hour in, the talk swung back to “Elsinore,” a film — and performance — that people will be talking about throughout awards season.

“It’s about how we use our time, and he was enormously fun, attractive, beautiful, amazingly gifted actor,” Scott said of playing Charleson. “And the film is about the support that he got and the courage that he displayed. The reason I was so attracted to it, I think, is because it doesn’t end well for any of us, and quality of time is what he chose… I know what an Olympian, absolutely exhausting task that is [to play Hamlet]. I did it 150 times… The idea that he did it when he was so unwell, it always just gets me.”

Scott, who got choked up while discussing the film, also lamented how difficult it was for Charleson to act, or even exist, at a time when gay men, particularly those with HIV/AIDS, were being viciously discriminated against.

“There weren’t any gay actors — for no reason,” he remarked. “That was taken away from them.”

title: Pierce Brosnan Thinks the Next James Bond Will Be ‘Someone That None of Us Know About’: ‘There Are Lots of Good Hats in the Ring’
summary: Ever since Denis Villeneuve’s forthcoming James Bond film was announced, the million-dollar question has been: Who will take on the role of the iconic spy? Now, former 007 Pierce Brosnan is offering his thoughts.  In a recent interview with The Times, the actor, who played the character in four films from 1995 to 2002, said […]
content:
Ever since Denis Villeneuve’s forthcoming James Bond film was announced, the million-dollar question has been: Who will take on the role of the iconic spy? Now, former 007 Pierce Brosnan is offering his thoughts.

In a recent interview with The Times, the actor, who played the character in four films from 1995 to 2002, said that “there are lots of good hats in the ring” and “lots of great actors” being considered. “I see it. I follow it. They could probably just go left-field and pick someone that none of us know about.”

When it comes to names, Brosnan remained neutral: “I wouldn’t pick anyone,” he continued. “My wife told me not to say anything and I’ve said too much. Because once I say something it goes [everywhere] and I get hanged.”

Popular on Variety

Brosnan also explained that he hasn’t revisited his own Bond films since their release. “I have no desire to see myself in Bond,” he said. “I’m just a member of the audience now awaiting the next Bond and wishing him well.”

This isn’t the first time the actor has waded into the Bond waters — back in Aug. 2025, while speaking with the Radio Times, Brosnan joked that he’d return as a senior citizen Bond.

“I don’t think anyone wants to see a craggy, 72-year-old Bond, but if Villeneuve had something up his sleeve I would look at it in a heartbeat,” Brosnan said. “Why not? It’s great entertainment. It could be lots of laughs. Bald caps, prosthetics… who knows?”

Variety previously reported that Amazon MGM Studios enlisted casting director Nina Gold to find the new secret agent. Her credits include the Netflix series “The Crown,” five films in the Star Wars franchise, “Les Misérables,” “The Martian” and “Conclave.” In 2025, she was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Hamnet.”

While the final casting for the film has not been confirmed, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and Jack Lowden have all been reported as among those in the final running.

title: ‘Dancing with the Stars’ Pro Emma Slater Pulls Out Stops By Performing with Savannah Bananas Ahead of Tuesday’s Premiere
summary: Emma Slater isn’t leaving anything to chance before the season 35 premiere of Dancing with the Stars. Partnered with Savannah Bananas second baseman Jackson Olson for the season that begins Tuesday on ABC, the popular pro doubled down on her pre-season publicity tour by performing with his exhibition baseball team. Slater and Olson joined the […]
content:
Emma Slater isn’t leaving anything to chance before the season 35 premiere of Dancing with the Stars.

Partnered with Savannah Bananas second baseman Jackson Olson for the season that begins Tuesday on ABC, the popular pro doubled down on her pre-season publicity tour by performing with his exhibition baseball team.

Slater and Olson joined the Bananas at Grayson Stadium in Georgia to dance to “Rewrite the Stars” from The Greatest Showman soundtrack. The stakes are high going into the new season; there’s a double elimination planned for the first week.

Hulu’s Get Real podcast host Amanda Hirsch revealed during the Sept. 10 episode that one male and one female will be sent home following the two-night premiere on Sept. 15 and 16.

Watch on Deadline

“This is the first time since 2018 that one male celebrity and one female celebrity will be sent home after the two-night premiere,” Hirsch said during the episode. “That hasn’t happened in many years.”

Most of the celebrities from the 35th season have been stepping up their social media game before the premiere. But it’s old hat for Olson; besides playing infield for the Savannah Bananas, he is a prolific content creator known for his macro baseball insights and tales about family, relationships and food.

Other celebs competing for the mirror ball this season include The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air star Tatyana Ali; Bachelor alum Tyler Cameron; former boy band member Taylor Hanson; actress Julia Stiles; actress Jenna Dewan; cooking star Giada De Laurentiis; Paralympian Ezra Frech; Olympian Amber Glenn; comedian and podcaster Connor Wood; Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt’s husband, Connor Leavitt; Love Thy Nader star Sarah Jane Nader; Grey’s Anatomy star Harry Shum Jr. ; Guillermo Rodriguez from Jimmy Kimmel Live; Traitors star Maura Higgins; and Summer House‘s Ciara Miller.

title: ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts, And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival
summary: Douglas Sirk , the master of so many great female-driven melodramas of the 50’s (Imitation Of Life, Magnificent Obsession) might have been jealous of Cody Fern’s directorial debut that just had its World Premiere at the Toronto Film Festival. It is what Sirk’s and other movies of the era were once dubbed, “women’s films” that […]
content:
Douglas Sirk , the master of so many great female-driven melodramas of the 50’s (Imitation Of Life, Magnificent Obsession) might have been jealous of Cody Fern‘s directorial debut that just had its World Premiere at the Toronto Film Festival. It is what Sirk’s and other movies of the era were once dubbed, “women’s films” that didn’t hold back on the all the drama that threatened to rip families apart. They also were made in a Hollywood, one once ruled by producer Ross Hunter, that gave great dynamic roles to women who could light up the boxoffice with them.

Watching Closing Night, a movie about mothers and motherhood in its most unattractive light, at least on the surface, reminded me of a time when this kind of soapy melodrama was a big seller at the box office. I am not sure Closing Night will play as well as those films of a bygone era, but if casting counts this one has the goods. It is not often the kind of material comes along that offers such go-for-broke roles for actresses these days like this one does, but Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts, Dianne Wiest, and Odessa A’zion have risen to the occasion and play this dysfuntional family dynamic to the hilt. It is hard to turn away when this level of talent is pouring it all out on the screen.



It all starts with Broadway star Sandra Vale (Paulson) on stage in her latest hit play, even if the performance isn’t up to snuff, she’s having trouble and this we gather is a star who has never failed a role. However she is determined to go on despite the producers concern and insistence that maybe she can’t . Reluctantly she sees a doctor, takes a cognitive test, and refuses to accept the truth that she is suffering the early signs of dementia. This is a strong woman who is in denial, who can’t understand what is happening to her but it also turns into a moment of self-reflection, a dangerous one as it turns out.

Watch on Deadline

She ignites a firestorm as she invites her estranged family to the opening night of her play, one that turns disastrous, not just on stage when she collapses, but in the hospital room where the worst fears of her eccentric and unbalanced sister, April (Watts) come true when she realizes Sandra has contacted and met her son, Theo (Toby Wallace) who is living with the clueless Lucy (A’zion) and has no idea he is about to find out some hard facts about his family. Enter vitriolic Grandma, Diane (Wiest) who arrives to really stir things up with more secrets and lies that only now are going to explode out in the open after decades of holding them at bay.

In a plot that unfolds like a stage play (this could have headed to Broadway itself) revelations seem to come at a quick pace, and the startling truths of a fractured family come pouring out before it all takes a sharp turn in tone with a surprising decision Sandra has in store.

Fern, a producer on American Horror Story where he met Paulson, has created ultimately a vivid story about motherhood in all its rich but dark degrees of betrayal, anger, regrets, and some pretty bad choices in retrospect, things that may never be forgiven but now don’t have much time even to try.

This is a movie all about performance and Fern has given these amazing stars some pretty dishy roles. Paulson is excellent as the daughter who left family behind to pursue a career at a cost that only now is just getting revealed. Watts seems to have fun playing the loopy sister who has never gotten her act quite together but has tried to be a decent mom to Theo. Wiest is simply dynamite as you might expect when she gets a role to really let loose with, and that she does as the mother who runs a small town beauty parlor and isn’t apologizing for her parenting skills. Wallace and A’zion, possibly pregnant herself, add their own degree of spice to the proceedings but the main attraction here are three stellar female stars in the kind of movie they just don’t make anymore. Well, they just did.

Producers are Nancy Grant, Rosalie Chicoine Perreault,Will Howarth, Matilda Comer.

Title: Closing Night

Festival: Toronto – Special Presentations

Director: Cody Fern

Screenplay: Cody Fern and Devon Bostick

Cast: Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts, Dianne Wiest, Toby Wallace, Odessa A’zion.

Running Time: One Hour and 55 Minutes.

Sales Agent: CAA (U.S.); Mk2 (International)

title: ‘The Face of Horror’ Review: Anna Biller’s Medieval Ghost Story Is A Technicolor Fever Dream Of Love, Betrayal & Vengeance — Toronto Film Festival
summary: A decade after her sophomore feature The Love Witch, Anna Biller has returned from a whole other era with another technicolor fever dream of female rage. In The Face of Horror, the writer/director updates the Kabuki ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, which she deconstructs for the medieval era with help from stars Kristine Frøseth, Jonah Hauer-King, […]
content:
A decade after her sophomore feature The Love Witch, Anna Biller has returned from a whole other era with another technicolor fever dream of female rage.

In The Face of Horror, the writer/director updates the Kabuki ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, which she deconstructs for the medieval era with help from stars Kristine Frøseth, Jonah Hauer-King, Ellie Bamber and Bella Heathcote.

The film begins with the knight Edward (Hauer-King) asking Eleanor’s (Frøseth) father for her hand in marriage, which the patriarch rejects over the suitor’s scoundrel, thieving ways. Unable to take “no” for an answer, Edward kills Eleanor’s father, before deceitfully promising her to exact vengeance on his killer and convincing her to marry him so that he can protect her.

As months go by, Edward has grown disgusted with a postpartum Eleanor, instead courting the recently widowed noblewoman Isabel (Heathcote), who devises a plot to kill Eleanor so they can be together. With Edward’s conscience and Eleanor’s livelihood hanging in the balance, the film culminates in a bloody final act filled with ghostly horror and vengeance.

Watch on Deadline

Kristine presents a perfectly subdued performance as the sweet, naive Eleanor, desperate for the love of her own husband, so much so that she’s prepared to go through great lengths to fit his vision of beauty.

As Edward, Hauer-King is a villainous medieval fuckboy with little redeeming qualities. But plagued by the threat of eternal damnation, the actor delivers a tortured portrayal of the weak knight as he struggles to outrun his toxic nature and be redeemed after being haunted for his actions drives him to the point of madness.

Bamber gives a surprise breakout performance as Eleanor’s strong-willed sister Beatrice, whose love for her sister leads to a quest for vengeance that will have audiences cheering, as well as crying.

The final product should be worth the decade-long wait for Biller fans, as she weaves a stunning cinematic ode to Hollywood’s technicolor era and the tragic beauty of the original Kabuki tale, featuring an emotionally volatile narrative with strong operatic performances from its cast that walk the line between camp and Shakespearean drama.

With The Face of Horror, Biller has provided another fix for cinephiles craving some good old-fashioned filmmaking with a contemporary feminist heartbeat.

Title: The Face of Horror

Festival: TIFF

Section: Midnight Madness

Director-screenwriter: Anna Biller

Cast: Jonah Hauer-King, Kristine Frøseth, Ellie Bamber, Leo Suter, Ben Radcliffe, Bella Heathcote

Sales agent: Embankment Films

Running time: 2 hrs

title: Glen Basner & Roeg Sutherland Open Their Global Sales Playbook: “You Have To Reset Yourself Every Two Weeks” — TIFF: The Market
summary: Glen Basner and Roeg Sutherland opened their global sales playbook at TIFF: The Market. The duo discussed the realities of working in the modern-day independent film business during a conference session at TIFF’s newly-minted market. They also got into the weeds on the dos and don’ts of packaging indie film projects. Sutherland, CAA’s Co-Head of […]
content:
Glen Basner and Roeg Sutherland opened their global sales playbook at TIFF: The Market. The duo discussed the realities of working in the modern-day independent film business during a conference session at TIFF’s newly-minted market. They also got into the weeds on the dos and don’ts of packaging indie film projects.

Sutherland, CAA’s Co-Head of Media Finance, said that a fast-changing market is nothing new, but the pace of change has accelerated. “It’s cyclical, [but] what is happening now is that things are changing so much quicker than they ever have. Instead of having to reset yourself every six months, you have to reset yourself every two weeks.”

He added: “Things will be uncomfortable, but we work in independent film; everything’s uncomfortable pretty much all the time.”

Watch on Deadline

Sutherland said that when the business is changing super-fast it also creates huge opportunity.

“Studios are not developing the way they used to, which presents an unbelievable opportunity to the independent community. All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes.”

Basner, CEO of FilmNation Entertainment, talked about challenges around packaging indie film projects, and specifically distributors’ attitude to risk.

“This is my biggest complaint about the independent distribution community right now,” he said. “There’s a very traditional approach to packaging. They’re worried about how much risk they’re taking, and so they know they need to mitigate that by selling their movie to pay television, and specifically to streamers. The only problem is that we’re [then] building movies for the streamer companies. That may work great on streaming, but it’s not the same thing as building a theatrical proposition.”

He continued: “We are trying to evolve to say, ‘how do we make the best possible film so that it can compel people, in an undeniable way, to see it in a movie theater?’ And if they do go and see it, then it’s going to work in home video, it’s going to work on pay TV, it’s going to work on free television.”

To warm applause Basner also sounded an optimistic note about theatrical. “I see all the films that are premiering at festivals like TIFF, and I’m going to have a really busy next four months sitting in a movie theater watching great movies.

“Filmmakers are finding a way, not just to get their films made, but to tell their stories from their own unique perspective… and audiences are responding. I think 2027 is going to be a great year at the theatrical box office.”

title: Gary Myers Dies: NASCAR Driver, Patriarch Of Racing Family Was 76
summary: Gary Myers, the former NASCAR driver, stock car legend and patriarch of a noted racing family, died Thursday, September 10, following an extended period of ill health. He was 76. His death was announced on Facebook by his son, racecar driver Burt Myers. “Last night I lost my hero,” Burt Myers wrote. “He fought so […]
content:
Gary Myers, the former NASCAR driver, stock car legend and patriarch of a noted racing family, died Thursday, September 10, following an extended period of ill health. He was 76.

His death was announced on Facebook by his son, racecar driver Burt Myers.

“Last night I lost my hero,” Burt Myers wrote. “He fought so hard but was so tired. My daddy is in Heaven and can finally do the things he wanted to do the last several years. Thank God for the times we had. He taught me everything I know. Selfishly I want him here but I know he is much better off now. I miss him so much. I love you Daddy!”

The Myers are a four-generation racing family that also includes Gary’s son Jason Myers, whose Facebook page also posted a tribute. “Last night we lost our patriarch,” the statement reads. “Gary was Jason’s best friend. He taught him and Burt everything they know and touched so many people along the way. To know him, was to love him. Rest easy, legend. You will be with us always.”

Watch on Deadline

Gary Myers was the son of racer William “Billy” Myers, who died in 1958, and the nephew of NASCAR driver Bobby Myers, who died in 1957. Gary Myers’ grandson is driver Slate Myers.

The Myers family is most closely associated with Bowman Gray Racing Stadium in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, where they have raced for more than 60 years.

Over his career, Gary Myers competed in the NASCAR Winston Cup Series, the NASCAR Grand National East Series, and the NASCAR Featherlite Modified Tour. He won 38 races at Bowman Gray and was the 1996 SMART Modified Tour Champion. He first raced professionally in 1974, competing in 46 NASCAR Cup Series Races over the next four years.

“We lost one of our heroes – Gary Myers,” SMART Modified Tour said in a statement. “Gary was a Founding Member of the SMART Modified Tour & its 1996 champion. He had 15 wins. Gary’s sons, Burt & Jason, as well as grandson, Slate, are winning racecar drivers as well. Our thoughts & prayers go out to the entire Myers family.”

A statement from the Bowman Gray stadium reads, “Our Bowman Gray family is saddened by the loss of Gary Myers. Gary earned 38 wins at Bowman Gray in Modified competition, in a career that also saw him make starts in the NASCAR Cup Series and Grand National Series. Our thoughts are with his wife Pam, sons Burt and Jason, grandson Slate, and the entire Myers family.”

In addition to sons Burt and Jason and grandson Slate, Myers is survived by wife Pam, Complete information on survivors was not immediately available.

title: ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Review: Giddily Genre-Crossing Comedy Sees Right Through Taron Egerton’s Nice-Guy Act
summary: Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” — another story of a young man’s desires getting violently over-satisfied — to start it all up again. Merging romantic comedy, body horror and gender-war satire as casually as its handsome, outwardly affable […]
content:
Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” — another story of a young man’s desires getting violently over-satisfied — to start it all up again. Merging romantic comedy, body horror and gender-war satire as casually as its handsome, outwardly affable protagonist gets women into bed (and then, crucially, out of it), this limber first feature from British writer-director Jonathan Schey is alternately silly, nasty fun for much of its running time, carried by a performance of witty good sportsmanship from Taron Egerton, though it’s occasionally hobbled by sexual politics that are slightly less progressive than it seems to think.

Following a hot-ticket premiere at Toronto — where a queue snaking fully around two city blocks proved the value of that deliciously grabby title — “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” has all the makings of a viral conversation piece once it gets out into the real world, though its genre bait-and-switch move may divide viewers, as the initial promise of a smart, relatable modern-romance study takes a hard-left turn into supernatural territory, complete with inflamed STI imagery to make David Cronenberg proud. (Hey, depending on who you’re talking to, that’s modern romance too.) But that harder-edged novelty should serve Schey’s film well in a market that’s less accommodating of old-school romcoms: As a debut, it’s especially slick and canny, heavily indebted to recent Scandi relationship comedies in its arch tone and playful style, and Schey could follow it down any number of plausible commercial paths.

Popular on Variety

It’s the poster for Agnès Varda’s feminist touchstone “Cléo from 5 to 7” on his bedroom wall that immediately raises questions about personable, clean-cut Adam (Egerton), and you can practically see them whirring through the mind of Liv (“How to Have Sex” star Mia McKenna-Bruce, in a too-brief cameo) when she wakes up in his bed one sunny Sunday morning. Great film, sure, but is he actually a fan? He might be: He’s urbane and intelligent, works as an associate in a private London gallery dedicated to showcasing female artists, and carries his things around a blue Mubi tote that will get a guffaw of recognition from any industry-adjacent audience.

But it could as easily be a performative signal, like the books by Ottessa Moshfegh and Edna O’Brien on his shelf or the adorably scruffy, heterochromic dog named Alana (yes, after Haim) that he walks every day in Victoria Park — accessories that advertise to women his sensitivity, his sophistication, his sharing of their interests. We’ve already seen that Adam is a smooth operator in that regard. In the film’s opening scene, he picks up Liv at a club by intervening when another man is pestering her, pretending to be her boyfriend to fend him off; it’s a nice-guy ploy that secures a one-night stand, though she’s baffled by his standoffishness in the cold light of day.

That’s just his routine, however. His WhatApp is a sea of young women similarly seduced and abandoned: The only member of the opposite sex he’ll go out with more than once is his lesbian bestie Emma (Charly Clive), who rolls her eyes at his exploits, but also, as a shacked-up woman with a baby on the way, vicariously lives through them a little. Significantly less forgiving, however, is Sofia (a scintillating Jessica Henwick), the cynical academic type he tries to pick up at the theater, and who calls him out on pretty much all his shit from the get-go, spitting out the script’s most immediately quotable line: “Men don’t actually like women — they just want women to like them.”

Against all odds, she invites Adam back to her place, where her take-control attitude both confuses and excites him, and the night gets blurrier from there. The next morning, she‘s the one who’s ghosted him, and from then on, nothing quite feels right, even though he’s suddenly sending out pheromones that appear to make him absolutely irresistible to women. Even by his promiscuous standards, his body count soars; simple eye contact, it seems, is enough to seal the deal. So why isn’t he having more fun? Why does it feel like he isn’t actually doing the work here? And what’s that purply welted rash forming down in his crotch? Schey deftly builds this uncanny turn of events by degrees, in such a way that we’re initially unsure if Adam is simply delusional, but also isn’t shy of exploring its most extreme possibilities for darkly farcical purposes. Suffice it to say that incest isn’t off the table.

Egerton’s initially cocksure, steadily more frantic performance does much to sell this absurd pivot, lending proceedings a recognizable human factor throughout: We all know men a bit like Adam, who aren’t the worst but are also pretty far from the best, who may not be overtly toxic themselves, but don’t recognize the toxicity inherent in their advantaged social status. “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” allows us to feel a little sorry for him, while also relishing the spectacle of him being put through the wringer a bit — especially as the film’s grosser horror instincts take over.

It’s just a bit of a shame that Schey’s script winds up advocating for a pretty staid alternative to his behavior in Emma’s thoroughly domesticated monogamy and imminent parenthood: There are safe, fun, equitable ways to, well, be a horny little devil, and this lively, zesty, thoroughly enjoyable comedy could spend a little more time exploring the options and playing the field.

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Aim at Trump’s New Hair — and Paddy Young Says the Punchline Was ‘Taken From Me by Our Legal Team’
summary: U.S. President Donald Trump’s new hairstyle was heavily mocked in “Saturday Night Live U.K.’s” Weekend Update segment. “This week, President Trump stepped off Air Force One sporting a different hair color,” quipped co-anchor Ania Magliano. “He appears to be trialling a new shade of brown. Or, he’s shat his head.” “People are questioning, does the […]
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s new hairstyle was heavily mocked in “Saturday Night Live U.K.’s” Weekend Update segment.

“This week, President Trump stepped off Air Force One sporting a different hair color,” quipped co-anchor Ania Magliano. “He appears to be trialling a new shade of brown. Or, he’s shat his head.”

“People are questioning, does the carpet still match the drapes?” added Paddy Young. “I wouldn’t know, that’s between the president and the punchline that just a second ago was taken from me by our legal team. Thank you, legal team, it was almost funny.” It’s unclear whether this moment was a joke, or whether the legal department actually did intervene.

Elsewhere, Prince George’s first day at the prestigious Eton College was imbued with some dark humor. “How will he survive being stuck in a place famous for producing sexual abusers? By leaving it and going to Eton College,” Magliano said to “ooo”s from the audience.

Popular on Variety

Recent anti-migrant protests taking place in the U.K. were also under the microscope, including that of far-right activist Danny Tommo. “On Saturday, members of Tommo’s group Patriot Platform yelled obscenities, threw stones, spat and then said goodbye to their families and headed to the protest,” Magliano joked.

“Who is this Danny Tommo?” responded Young. “Before launching Patriot Platform he is reported to have tried his luck as both a bricklayer and a web designer. However, neither worked out as he had the physique of a web designer and a mind of a brick.”

The first episode of “SNL U.K.” Season 2 was hosted by Jeff Goldblum.

title: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Jazz Number to Open ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2: ‘Hoping You’ll Like Me More Than Nando’s or Marmite’
summary: Jeff Goldblum kicked off his hosting duties on “Saturday Night Live U.K.” by employing his musical skills in a jazzy number about spending time in London. “Can you believe this is Saturday night, first of all?” Goldblum asked the live audience after making his grand entrance. “And me, I’m hosting this gosh darn ‘SNL U.K.’ […]
content:
Jeff Goldblum kicked off his hosting duties on “Saturday Night Live U.K.” by employing his musical skills in a jazzy number about spending time in London.

“Can you believe this is Saturday night, first of all?” Goldblum asked the live audience after making his grand entrance. “And me, I’m hosting this gosh darn ‘SNL U.K.’ triumphant second season first episode! So, for the occasion, may we perform something we’ve just composed special for you tonight?”

The American actor, who has his own jazz band in addition to starring in franchises like “Wicked” and “Jurassic Park,” then took a seat behind the piano and began to sing a tune chock-full of U.K. references. “I’m hoping to be your precise cup of tea and that you’ll like me more than Nando’s or Marmite,” Goldblum sang. “Even if I still bomb, I will keep calm and carry on because I’m hosting from London tonight.”

Popular on Variety

Goldblum danced around the stage and even made a reference to his “Wicked” role, singing: “Despite a few wicked flaws, I am the Wizard of Oz!”

Musical guest CMAT then came out to help Goldblum with the lyrics, holding cue cards that read “Life Finds a Way,” in reference to his famous “Jurassic Park” line. “I don’t recognize it,” Goldblum said — but then the band begin to play the “Jurassic Park” theme and he remembered who he was. “I get it now, I can do it!”

“Life finds a way, when you’re live on Saturday,” he concluded with a big finish. “Like Sainsbury’s Local, we’re all feeling vocal. And I’m hosting right here, in London tonight!”

title: Camera-Shy Chrissie Hynde on Finally Allowing a Definitive Doc to Be Made About ‘The Pretenders,’ Bowing in Toronto: ‘I Just Wanted to Be in a Band. I’ve Never Graduated Beyond That Initial Interest in It’
summary: At this late date, what the Pretenders accomplished is no mystery achievement. But it’s also a story that has never been extensively chronicled on film until “The Pretenders,” a Joss Crowley-directed doc that premieres Sunday at the Toronto International Film Festival. The band released what might rightly be considered the best rock ‘n’ roll debut […]
content:
At this late date, what the Pretenders accomplished is no mystery achievement. But it’s also a story that has never been extensively chronicled on film until “The Pretenders,” a Joss Crowley-directed doc that premieres Sunday at the Toronto International Film Festival. The band released what might rightly be considered the best rock ‘n’ roll debut album of all time in Janauary 1980, and Crowley’s film covers the lead-up to that — Chrissie Hynde looking and acting like a biker chick in late ’70s Akron before moving to and finding her real gang in the U.K. — and the tumultuous few years that followed, with further masterpieces arriving alongside band dismisals and deaths. Although the focus is on the original lineup and the first five years, it brings us into the present day of Hynde, still one of the greatest to ever pick up a guitar. As delightfully plain-spoken as Hynde is when you get her to sit down and talk, she can be difficult to get into that chair, as a naturally camera-shy personality, so Crowley’s film is particularly useful in further immortalizing a subject who never wanted to be anything more than an ordinary musician, whether “rock goddess” was quickly and eternally thrust upon her or not. Variety spoke with Crowley and the charmingly tart-as-ever Hynde in advance of the Toronto premiere. Most of the time with modern music documentaries, it’s the artist or their company instigating the doc, and usually co-producing it. But it sounds like that’s not necessarily what happened this time because, Joss, you’ve talked about the difficulty in talking Chrissie into it. Joss Crowley: I’ve been trying to work with Chrissie and tell the Pretenders’ story for over 10 years, and kept knocking at the door; didn’t get an answer. It was just a question of right time, right place, and Chrissie came round to the idea of meeting me. We sat down and talked about some of the docs I’ve made, and about other things, trying to find some mutual interests. I wasn’t really sure when I left that meeting how it had gone, but within about a week, we sat down and recorded our first interview, at the end of 2023. Chrissie, you needed less than a week to think about it and get underway after that first meeting? Chrissie Hynde: Well, we had to have a go and see how it would go, and I think I must have laid down some sort of ground rules, so I was willing to go into it — that it would be (visually focused on) archive footage, and really talk about the band and not focus too much on me, and it wouldn’t be about “women in rock” or any of that kind of thing. It would just be a story of the band. I was kind of keen to have it done because, as we all know, there’s documentaries on everything and everyone now. And in fact, someone else had already made a documentary on the Pretenders, which had nothing to do with me or my entire organization. I was starting to get calls from some of my old friends saying, “Oh, I’m gonna do your documentary on Tuesday.” And I’d be like, “We’re not doing a documentary!” This other team had gone in to people I know and made it sound like it was an official documentary. So I thought, “Well, if that’s happened once, that’s gonna happen again.” Either you want to do it and you want your story out, or you don’t, which I didn’t particularly, but if it’s going to be out, I’d rather know that it’s true. Chrissie Hynde in ‘The Pretenders’ Courtesy TIFF At the very end of the film, you’re heard talking a little bit about why you did it and you mention that you especially wanted to do it for James Honeyman-Scott [who suddenly died at the height of the band’s success in 1981], in some way. Hynde: For me, a rock band is all about electric guitar, and I think he was one of the great guitar heroes. Over the years when I see lists of the greatest 100 rock guitar players, I never see Jimmy’s name. That’s all he was interested in, music and playing the guitar, and I thought he didn’t get his due and that would be important for him. He’s not here, so I thought I could do it for him. It feels like the way the documentary turned out was kind a nice compromise in the end, since you didn’t want to be on-camera at all, but you were talked into being seen for the very last interview, so there’s a little bit but not a lot. You acquiesced a little bit. Hynde: Yeah. I haven’t seen it, and I probably won’t. Someone said, “Oh, don’t say that! That sounds negative.” But I think a lot of people don’t like watching themself or listening to themself talk, and I don’t have to watch it, and there you go. It’s not negative. I mean, I’ve already lived through it, so I don’t think I wanna go through it all again.

I think so many people feel this way, and most people that I’ve ever had a conversation about it with do: they don’t like the sound of their speaking voice. I mean, I’ve had to get used to my singing voice because, you know, that’s kind of my shtick. But my speaking voice, when I hear it back, I’m always pretty horrified. And everyone I talk to feels the same way… People expect if you do it for a living, that you must like it, but that’s not necessarily true.

One of your quotes in here is, “I like being in a band, I just don’t like being observed. It’s a real problem.” A lot of people will relate to that, wanting to have a voice — figuratively — while not liking the attention that comes with it.

Hynde: I think so, because I think I represent just ordinary people, and that’s how I feel and that’s how I go through my life. You know, I get the public transport. I don’t live in a gated community. I’m just exactly the same way I always was, and I don’t want that taken away from me. I like hanging out. I’d rather sit on a doorstep and eat a slice of pizza than go to a fancy restaurant. I’ve always been like that, but I think most people are.

Popular on Variety

It has become more common in documentaries to have the subjects entirely off-screen. I was recently watching Paul McCartney’s Wings documentary, and his interviews in it are all audio-only, which is great most of the time. But at the same time you’re kind of like, “Well, just show him to me for 10 seconds.”

Hynde: Are you talking about “Man on the Run”? I loved that. In fact, I watched it sitting next to Paul when it was screening. He was singing along! I guess he’s so used to seeing himself. It was very moving for me to see Linda in the early days, even before I met her, and how cool and how beautiful she was… We’ve seen so many documentaries, it’s a matter of kind of getting away from the format. But, certainly, archive footage — we were lucky to have any for ours, because this was way before people had camera phones or were thinking much about taking photos.

Crowley: There was a big archive breakthrough when we found this cameraman, Andy Watt, who’s from Hereford, like the band really, and he joined the original band on tour about three months before Pete left and Jimmy died. [Bassist Pete Farndon was dismissed in1982 and died the following year; Honeyman-Scott died two days after Frandon’s firing.] He was able to document two weeks on the road in North America with the band, and that footage has never been seen. We found all 20 tapes of it, and they were in very poor condition and pretty much unusable, but fortunately we found a retired engineer who was able to bring them back to life. Another thing that really helped the device was doing the interviews with Stan, the old tour manager, who read his diaries aloud, and we could suddenly see Jimmy and Pete in and around the band in the period where we focused the story, which is those five years between the end of the ’70s and the early ’80s.

You start the movie with Stan Tippins, now an elder gent, reading these diaries for the camera. It seems like his participatino was really, no pun intended, a tipping point.

Hynde: I’d love to see that stuff, with the Stan diaries. All the time that we were with Stan, he often mentioned, “Now I’m gonna go write my diary,” but no one ever saw them. Joss and I had dinner with Stan and Lynne Honeyman-Scott, Jimmy’s sister, and (original drummer) Martin Chambers, and it never even occurred to me that Stan would be willing to be actually filmed, reading his diaries. I’m dying to see all that part, so maybe I will have to watch it at some point. Stan was so important in the early band. He was our scout leader or something. We were new at this, and he had been a singer in Mott the Hoople [prior to Ian Hunter]. We loved him, because was like having a farmer in a band. He would say things like, “I don’t know why you would wanna take drugs when you could have a nice, juicy pear.” I suppose you could say we were laughing behind his back, but he was the wise man of the operation.

When it came to your interviews, Chrissie, there ae some topics that are tricky or touchy, inevitably. It’s clear on camera when you are willing to get into something and when you aren’t. Joss asks you about Ray Davies, and you say, “I’d rather not get into it. There’s a lawsuit waiting to happen.” But it’s cool that we at least see you address not wanting to discuss something, whereas a lot of docs would just leave that out. And then, of course, you do get into a lot of tough stuff with the early ’80s with everything that happened with the band. Was it cathartic in any way to talk about the hard times of the band, or is it always just difficult?

Hynde: First of all, talking about, for example, Ray Davies — I mean, anything with him or with anyone in my family — I don’t think it’s right to talk about other people because it’s an invasion of their privacy. I’ve never done that, and I don’t think that’s a very dignified thing to do. If people ask me, “Oh, are your kids musical?” I say, “Well, if you ever meet them, you ask them. I don’t wanna talk about it.” Not because I don’t love them, but because this is kind of an invasion of their privacy. And I’ve never talked to any journalist and given a list of things that they’re not allowed to ask. Because if I don’t wanna talk about it, then I can say, “Let’s not talk about it.” But not for any other reason than that. Because certainly as a Kinks fan, I mean, who doesn’t wanna talk about Ray Davies? He’s fucking amazing. But I just don’t do that.

I can’t remember what Joss asked me about the grisly stuff in the ’80s, because I haven’t revisited that. But the other thing is, when you have a story that’s in public or when you become famous or whatever, your story isn’t that much more interesting than just an ordinary person’s. I mean, nobody hasn’t had bereavements and fuck-ups and disappointments and victories, and all these things that happen in a person’s life. I think there’s too much emphasis on the extraordinary life of celebrities.

You’ve been clear from the beginning of your career up till now that you never wanted to be a poster girl or an emblem or spokesperson for anything.

Hynde: Being in a rock band… I mean, who didn’t wanna be in a rock band? Did you wanna be in a rock band?

Of course.

Hynde: Are you now?

No, sadly.

Hynde: But you wanted to be. So, I’ve offered some music, and that’s all I’m offering. Everyone that I grew up with wanted to be in a rock band. That was my generation. We were all very ordinary kids. People didn’t get into bands to become celebrities. They just wanted to be in a band. I’ve never graduated beyond that initial interest in it.

Surely you’ve grown in a thousand ways since the band’s early days, but the film kind of presents you as somebody who sort of had either a certain idealism or just a basic attitude about certain things and stuck to it.

Hynde: I also had some great people that I’ve met in my life who were inspirational. Lemmy never changed. Lemmy was always the same. and that’s kind of been my motto. That’s why I don’t do fashion magazines. Well, there’s many reasons I don’t! But I always think, “Well, if you wouldn’t ask Lemmy to do it, don’t ask me.” Because he’s kind of, I suppose you could say, my style icon, if there is such a thing in the case of someone who was in Motörhead.

Neil Young’s another. He’s never changed. You might not have ever met him, but anyone who’s listened to his music, you have met him. He’s exactly what you think he’s going to be. Bob Dylan, I mean, ia obviously more of an enigma, because he’s a little bit more of a trickster and a comedian. But he offered the world all that music and I’m not sure that he got into it to be the spokesman of his generation, which was the mantle that he had to carry. And in the case of Willie Nelson, Neil Young, Bob… First name basis, did you get that? [Laughs.] Paul McCartney’s the best example because he was in the fucking Beatles, and yet he’s still doing exactly what he was doing. If his band hadn’t made it that big, I reckon if he was still in Liverpool and he got married and had some kids, he’d probably still be playing in a band in a local bar somewhere, because that’s what he likes.

Joss, is there any way to put in a nutshell what you wanted to capture about Chrissie in this film? And did it change at all as you spent so many hours with her?

Crowley: To answer the first question, it’s the story of the Pretenders, which I know is obviously very much about Chrissie, but also about the rest of the band. But with Chrissie, I because I spent so many hours with her, I just wanted to make sure her personality came across in the film. Because I think that’s what documentary does perhaps better than any other medium, is that it brings personality to the screen. And so if it felt awkward at times, that’s OK. When it was successful, great. When the band was successful, great. And everything in between, and when it was emotional and sad, it had to be there. We were talking about voices earlier on, and I’ve had to get used to hearing my voice a bit because it was important to hear questions that I put to Chrissie that she didn’t want to answer, or at least didn’t want to answer initially and then came round to answering later on. Because that, I think, tells you as much about Chrissie as a perfectly articulated answer. So that was something I guess I warmed up to, the idea of keeping my questions in, which I haven’t done in previous documentaries. That was a good way to unlocking a bit more about who Chrissie is.

The other question: in terms of hours, we would meet monthly, for a few hours…

Hynde: Seems like most of my life. No, Joss did prompt me, but mainly I just imagined a certain time, an event that happened, and I would just talk about it for an hour, and then have a few cups of tea and leave. And then he’d have to figure it out. Definitely the early sessions were much more like that, and as it evolved, it became a bit more interview-based, I suppose, and it had a different rhythm to it.

I didn’t want to ask my mates to sit down in front of a camera, because I find it uncomfortable, so I thought, “Well, why would I expect them to do it?” So I made a real point of just having talk over {i.e., audio-only interview]. But then you have to think about, if you’re on stage, what are you prepared to do? But then you also have to think about the audience: What do they want? And I’ve been in the audience as much as I’ve been on stage, if not more. I know the audience wants a certain thing. And [for a documentary] I know the audience wants to see people sitting down talking to camera. I know I want to see that.

Crowley: There were two things that Chrissie said to me early on in the process. She said, “Make it good, and make it different.” And I think we’ve achieved that. But you can’t make something different for the sake of it being different. It has to work for the story that the film tells. And Chrissie doesn’t like cameras. Chrissie doesn’t like having her photograph taken. It was really hard to find archive as well because lots of times cameramen or camera crews weren’t allowed access to the band. It was hard on a lot of levels. So the fact that I managed to to convince Chrissie to go on camera for the final interview, it just sort of works. I think it’s an achievement of the film and also a reflection of how much she doesn’t want to be on camera all the time.

You probably did get much more intimate stuff by allowing her to just speak into a microphone. And we get to luxuriate in the sound of her voice as she’s digging deep on some of that stuff…

Hynde: Oh, God, when you said “luxuriate in the sound of her voice,” I’m cringing.

You often say you don’t like to be a symbol of anything, but is anything you represent to the public that you kind of allow for yourself as being OK?

Hynde: Well, of course I like being a sex symbol, but…

Glad you brought that up, because that was something that struck me watching the movie — that to some people you were and are a sex symbol, and at the same time, there is Shirley Manson talking about how what you got out of it was loving seeing you be androgynous, so…

Hynde: I was being facetious! [About being a sex symbol.] I’m just, you know… I’m a man of the people.

One thing that hasn’t changed that you represent: being against rock turning completely consumerist. Every time I see a music star doing a product commercial, I think of your song “How Much Did You Get for Your Soul?”

Hynde: Yeah. They’re all at it, aren’t they? Well, you know, fuck ’em.

Joss, do you have a favorite moment in the movie?

Crowley: Favorite part of the production of making the film, I guess, was when Stan opened his diaries for the first time, and he found the first time he met Chrissie in rehearsals, because it was such a breakthrough for me. I think he summed up quite a lot about, about Chrissie and the band in a few words. Do you know the bit I’m talking about? I can’t remember exactly what he says, but it’s something like, “She has quite a lot of fun, but underneath she might be a bit nervous.”

Hynde: Oh, God, I hate to think what’s in those diaries. Fuck me. But we love Stan, so there you go.

Chrissie, we can’t ask you if you have a favorite moment in the movie…

Hynde: I saw my manager, Ian Grenfell, yesterday and I said, “Hey, is this gonna come across really negative if I say I haven’t watched it?” And he goes, “Don’t worry about it, because that horse has bolted. People already know [to expect] you haven’t watched it. And a lot of people do not watch their documentaries.” So I was relieved that I don’t have to tough it out… I’ve been very inspired in the last couple of days, seeing Noel and Liam (Gallagher, from Oasis) out there. They’ve got a documentary out and they’re on the front line going for it. But I just don’t have that kind of drive.

I’m sure you’ll be in Toronto, Joss. Are you going, Chrissie, or will you be avoiding the premiere?

Hynde: Yeah, I am going. And then Martin’s going. It’s gonna be me and Martin there on the red carpet, so that should be… Well, it won’t be a beauty contest.

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s British Return in Cold Open: ‘Don’t Tell Me You’ve Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!’
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s recent much-publicized return to England was mocked in the cold open of the first episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2. The cold open began with Larry Dean as King Charles II and Emma Sidi as Queen Camilla relaxing at Balmoral Castle in Scotland (“I do love our weekends […]
content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s recent much-publicized return to England was mocked in the cold open of the first episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2.

The cold open began with Larry Dean as King Charles II and Emma Sidi as Queen Camilla relaxing at Balmoral Castle in Scotland (“I do love our weekends away. No responsibilities, just like every other day,” says Camilla.)

They are then interrupted by the arrival of Harry (Jack Shep) and Meghan (Ayoade Bamgboye). With much of the skit consisting of them being in a close embrace — to the disgust of King Charles — there were countless one-liners making fun of their decision to return to the U.K.

“What do you two want?” asked an infuriated Charles. “Don’t tell me you’ve spent that Netflix money already.”

Popular on Variety

“Daddy, it was $16 million,” replied Harry. “How long was it supposed to last?”

“What a waste you’ve become, you’re lucky your father is not around to see this,” Charles responded, a line which received a large reaction in the room.

Meghan’s lifestyle brands were also riffed on, with her presenting an ice tray to Camilla. “I made it myself,” she said. “I can give you the recipe. I’m a whizz in the kitchen.”

“She hires the best chefs,” Harry added.

George Fouracres, who received acclaim for his acute portrayal of former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, also made his first appearance as Prime Minister Andy Burnham, wearing his trademark black rimmed glasses.

“I’m the new PM. And I’m nothing like the last one,” he said. Making fun of Burnham’s raft of policies over the summer and his attempts at being relatable despite being in high office, the skit ended up with him saying: “I will buy everybody a pint, because I want you to like me. I need you to like me.”

The first episode of “SNL U.K.” was hosted by Jeff Goldblum, who performed a jazzy number about spending time in London during his monologue.

title: Huge L.A. Job Losses If Paramount Exits California, County Warns; Ellison-Led Company Slams AGs & WGA’s Antitrust Action In Official Rebuke
summary: There will be harsh job losses and severe economic pain if Paramount carries out its threat to leave California over the antitrust action a coalition of blue state Attorneys General are pursuing to stop David Ellison’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery, an internal L.A. County report estimates. “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters […]
content:
There will be harsh job losses and severe economic pain if Paramount carries out its threat to leave California over the antitrust action a coalition of blue state Attorneys General are pursuing to stop David Ellison‘s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery, an internal L.A. County report estimates.

“At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out f California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years in California across all industries and losses of between $1.01 billion and $2.03 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031,” L.A. County’s Economic Development Corporation says in a leaked September 10 document.

Simultaniously, as Paramount brass are scheduled to sit down for court-ordered settlement talks with a the AGs next month, a filing in federal court late Friday made clear, Ellison’s crew thinks their debt heavy acquisition of WBD shouldn’t even be up for discussion, antitrust, employmentwise or otherwise.

Watch on Deadline

With constant leaks out of the Melrose lot that Ellison is contemplating a move to the redder horizons of Tennessee, Georgia or Texas if the AGs don’t holster their legal pistols and start negotiating by October 1, this week’s EDC document from the County offers zero anesthesia “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output.”

In even more terse tone that a previous duo of LA. County missive, the latest four-page report adds: “Note that since this employment would be lost to California permanently, these figures are more appropriately expressed as full-time jobs instead of job-years.” Then there is the real estate and ancillary blast radius of Para and WBD leaving town. A shuttering of soundstages, closing of vendors and more that would result in “permanently” decimating the physical and economic foundations built up over 100 years of Hollywood.

Bleak, to say the least.

Even more bleak when one considers the EDC’s own math figure on the upside of one big ParaBros.

“Paramount’s post-merger production commitment of 30 features a year for three years would generate a total of between 1,020 and 2,760 job-years in California across all industries and between $377.7 million and $1.01 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031,” the finding (first reported by Politico) asserts with a spotlight on Ellison’s biggest big screen promise.

Rob Bonta and Letitia James Getty Images

At the same time, in the mix of the AGs long anticipated July 13 filed antitrust action, Paramount’s September 11 filed Defendants’ Answer to Complaint and Defenses basically insists California AG Rob Bonta, NY AG Letitia James and pals just get outta ParaBros’ corporate way and stick to their side of the street. Slicing the AGs as being out of their jurisdiction, the presumption pitched here is the antitrust suit “amounts to a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.”

Supercharging the usual litany of agreements and disagreements that characterize such perfunctory responses, Oracle scion Ellison’s lawyers use the filing to pre-argue (bordering on pre-relitigating) their POV on ParaBros ahead of the March 2, 2027 trial and a boatload of bond hearings, ticking fee kick off and a possible SCOTUS intervention. “Paramount’s proposed merger with Warner Bros. (the ‘Merger’) will enhance competition, not diminish it,” they state in the 25-page document.

In language we’ve all heard over and over since the AGs took to the legal barricades, Para’s Beth Wilkenson-led legal Seal Team continue: “The Merger will benefit movie theaters by bringing more films to the big screen. It will benefit cable companies by providing more high-quality content on TV in the face of declining cable subscriptions. It will benefit content creators by increasing investment in, and production of, films and TV shows. And for all these reasons, it will also benefit consumers, not only with more high-quality content in theaters and on cable, but also with a better combined streaming offering to create real competition against dominant tech giants like Netflix, Disney, and Amazon.”

That sounds a lot like Paramount’s declaration of July 13 that the AGs big move “distorts settled antitrust law and is based on a misrepresentation of competition in the entertainment industry today,” doesn’t it?

There’s that, and then there’s the real blade being unsheathed in the September 11 filing: “Plaintiffs’ entire theory of leverage falls apart—models that ignore the real world have no basis in a court of law.” A sentiment stuck in further with: “Day by day, the weak case against this Merger gets even weaker.”

Bonta’s usually media quick and to the point office was silent when Deadline reached out for a response to Paramount’s official response. As for that L.A. County report …no one was saying nuthin.

title: ‘Twilight’ Star Kellan Lutz Leading Faith-Based Survival Thriller ‘The Rescue’, Sales Launch At TIFF
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Premiere Entertainment Group is introducing faith-based survival thriller The Rescue, which has Kellan Lutz (Twilight franchise) attached, to international buyers at the TIFF market. The synopsis reads: “After a violent storm leaves a rescue team stranded on a frozen Alaskan mountain, survival becomes a test not only of endurance, but of faith, as hope […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Premiere Entertainment Group is introducing faith-based survival thriller The Rescue, which has Kellan Lutz (Twilight franchise) attached, to international buyers at the TIFF market.

The synopsis reads: “After a violent storm leaves a rescue team stranded on a frozen Alaskan mountain, survival becomes a test not only of endurance, but of faith, as hope is pushed to its breaking point.”

The film is scheduled to begin production in New Zealand in January 2027.

Lutz, known for his roles in the Twilight franchise and The Expendables 3, will lead the ensemble cast, which is currently coming together.

The film will be directed by Darren Simmonds and Jared van Berkel from a screenplay written by van Berkel. Simon Ambridge, Anton Steel and Jared van Berkel will produce.

Watch on Deadline

“The Rescue has everything international audiences respond to: a recognizable star, an expansive survival story, and a powerful emotional message,” said Elias Axume, CEO of Premiere Entertainment Group. “Kellan is the perfect actor to lead this film, and we’re excited to introduce it to buyers at TIFF.”

Kellan Lutz is represented by Innovative Artists.

title: Taylor Frankie Paul Says She’s “Stayed In, Single & Celibate” Since Her Season of ‘The Bachelorette’ Was Yanked
summary: Taylor Frankie Paul revealed on social media Saturday that she’s “stayed in, single and celibate” since ABC decided to table her run as The Bachelorette. Paul, who can currently be seen in the fifth season of Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Morman Wives that dropped Sept. 10, also said she will not allow anyone “intimate […]
content:
Taylor Frankie Paul revealed on social media Saturday that she’s “stayed in, single and celibate” since ABC decided to table her run as The Bachelorette.

Paul, who can currently be seen in the fifth season of Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Morman Wives that dropped Sept. 10, also said she will not allow anyone “intimate access to me again unless he’s my person and that’s a promise to myself.”

“We got to see me breaking … shortly after I was sought to be destroyed and instead it ricocheted,” continued Paul. “Maybe my prayers are heard after all. Such a long way to go but baby steps.”

Paul also shared photos of a “magazine cover I never got a chance to share but was one of the most fun shows.” She also teased that maybe it was time to “release the tapes” and joked about a “bachelorette round two.”

Watch on Deadline

Paul revealed in the new season of Morman Wives that she chose participant Doug Mason at the end of The Bachelorette, which was pulled three days before its March 22 premiere after a 2023 video surfaced of her throwing a stool at her ex Dakota Mortensen.

“And yes, he did get down on one knee and proposed, which I was shocked,” Paul said of Mason, who has since released a statement that says, in part, “I’m just sending out prayers to Taylor because that was her moment and her moment was blocked. All we can do right now is be hopeful.”

In May, Disney’s reality TV chief Rob Mills told Deadline that the network is taking it “day-to-day” on whether or not to release Paul’s season. “It’s a good question,” he added. “On a personal level … we want to make sure she’s OK.”

Mills previously told Deadline in April that “The Bachelor franchise is one that is obviously is very important to us and that’s going through its own growing pains right now. Those are our crown jewels to continue to polish.”

title: May El-Toukhy On Venice Golden Lion Win & Riccardo Scamarcio Remembers Jeremy Thomas — Winners Press Conference
summary: Venice Golden Lion winner May El-Toukhy is not surprised that some pundits considered her win a surprise this evening. “It doesn’t surprise me that some people would say ‘Oh, did she get it?’ Because that’s part of everyday life as a woman in this industry,” she responded to a question about her win being called […]
content:
Venice Golden Lion winner May El-Toukhy is not surprised that some pundits considered her win a surprise this evening.

“It doesn’t surprise me that some people would say ‘Oh, did she get it?’ Because that’s part of everyday life as a woman in this industry,” she responded to a question about her win being called a surprise by some in the media.

El-Toukhy, the Danish director of the night’s big winner Woman Unknown, says she is used to being counted out, and that before the lineup was confirmed, she was very low on Venice prediction lists.

“I was far down on predictions,” she said. “There were like 40 films predicted, and I was 39 or 40 every time. By now I’m pretty used to that. That’s a systemic issue. When I look to those lists, we would be four women, and I would feel that I had to compete with those four women and not my male peers, and that’s a systemic issue, and that’s something that all of us need to think about, including journalists, the media, my male peers. How can we make it easier for women to be part of this industry? I don’t have the feeling that my male colleagues aren’t interested in having women in the industry, but still, there are structures in place that we haven’t found a way to solve.”

Watch on Deadline

Venice jury head Maggie Gyllenhaal described the winning film, about sexual shame and political paranoia in postwar Denmark, as “a brilliantly made movie that felt like a laser beam”.

Danish actress Mathilde Arcel scored the festival’s Best Actress prize for her turn in the drama-thriller as a woman with secrets to hide who desperately tries to avoid mob justice.

It’s rare at the Venice festival for the same film to win the top prize and an acting award, but Gyllenhaal explained that it’s possible when the jury votes unanimously for the Golden Lion winner’s lead actor or actress to get the acting prize, which happened in this case.

Elsewhere this evening, the filmmakers behind Special Jury Prize winner Naza, the hard-hitting film about the IDF’s killing of Gazans, said they hope the film will reach an audience in Israel, before also touching on the IDF’s (Israeli Defence Force) comments criticizing the film.

Director Yuval Abraham commented: “It’s definitely important to show it [the film] to Israelis in as wide a way as possible. I hope we will be able to. It’s important as Israelis that we recognize what our government has done in Gaza…In terms of the IDF comments, our reporting in the film is rigorous. It’s being done in partnership with the Guardian…To me, it seems like an attempt to not face reality. In just these 10 days of the festival, Israel, our country, has killed multiple Palestinian children in Gaza. This is the reality described by Palestinian journalists from the very start. And I think it’s important we we talk about it.”

Italian actor Riccardo Scamarcio won the Orizzonti sidebar prize best actor for his performance in The House of the Monkey. The actor was asked by Deadline about his previous collaboration with the revered UK producer Jeremy Thomas who passed away last night.

A visibly emotional Scamarcio said of Thomas: “He was a pirate. He was a free man, a great man of cinema. He made movies that are part of the history of cinema, and he behaved like an independent producer, like the father of the movie he produces, protecting directors and creators. But he did so protecting the freedom of the artists to express themselves. When I heard the news this morning, I was glad to come to Venice to get my award, but I cried for Jeremy.”

Iranian actress Laleh Marzban won best actress in the Orizzonti section for the film Falling House. The performance was commended by Deadline’s journalist at the press conference Melanie Goodfellow who asked the actress how she thought the film would be received in her homeland due to “its brave challenge to the government” and a patriarchal system.

“This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective. If we give our small contribution, maybe we will reach our objective. I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.”

You can see the full list of winners here.

title: ‘SNL UK’ Cold Open Lampoons Harry & Meghan’s Return: “Don’t Tell Me You’ve Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!”
summary: Saturday Night Live UK returned for its second season — and wasted no time getting stuck into Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. The Sky series cold opened with a sketch (watch above) in which the Duke and Duchess of Sussex (as depicted by Jack Shep and Ayoade Bamgboye) visited the King and Queen in Scotland’s […]
content:
Saturday Night Live UK returned for its second season — and wasted no time getting stuck into Prince Harry and Meghan Markle.

The Sky series cold opened with a sketch (watch above) in which the Duke and Duchess of Sussex (as depicted by Jack Shep and Ayoade Bamgboye) visited the King and Queen in Scotland’s Balmoral Castle.

Larry Dean’s King Charles III was aghast at his child’s reappearance. “Don’t tell me you’ve spent all your Netflix money already,” he asked incredulously.

“It was $60 million. How long was it meant to last?” Prince Harry replied.

Queen Camilla, as played by Emma Sidi, was rather warmer in her reception. “Hello, sweet Harry. And beautiful Meghan, as brown as ever,” she exclaimed.

Watch on Deadline

The latter remark was an apparent reference to the Duke and Duchess’ interview with Oprah Winfrey, in which they revealed that an unnamed member of the royal family had concerns about how dark their unborn son Archie’s skin might be.

Markle, who has hosted two seasons of an unsuccessful Netflix lifestyle series, responded: “Hey Step Queen. I brought you a gift … It’s ice. I made it myself. I can give you the recipe.”

The reunion was interrupted by new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham (George Fouracres), who was wearing his signature yellow Manchester badge and offered to buy the nation a beer.

“I’m the new PM, and I’m nothing like the last one. Harry, Megan, I’m here to tell you that just because you’re normal folk doesn’t mean your life has to be crap. That is the Burnham promise,” he said.

SNL UK‘s Season 2 premiere was hosted by Jeff Goldblum, who opened with a musical number from the show’s London studio.

The second season will run for six episodes before taking a break and returning in early 2027. Chicken Shop Date host Amelia Dimoldenberg and Stath Lets Flats creator Jamie Demetriou will guest-present the second and third episodes.

All of SNL UK’s cast members have returned, including Hammed Animashaun, Bamgboye, Dean, Celeste Dring, Fouracres, Ania Magliano, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Shep, Sidi and Paddy Young. New cast member Freddie Meredith also made his debut.

SNL UK is produced by Universal Television Alternative Studio’s UK production team and Broadway Video. Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer. James Longman is lead producer.

title: Paramount Leaving California Will Devastate Los Angeles Economy, Leaked Report Finds
summary: A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Paramount Skydance out of California. A copy of the report published by Politico reads, “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out of California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years […]
content:
A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Paramount Skydance out of California.

A copy of the report published by Politico reads, “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out of California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years in California across all industries and losses of between $1.01 billion and $2.03 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031.”

Reps for Paramount had no comment on the matter.

Popular on Variety

In August, news broke of Ellison’s plan to take Paramount Skydance out of the Golden State if California Attorney General Rob Bonta and a coalition of other state AGs did not come to the bargaining table and settle their lawsuit to stop the $111 billion merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Ellison gave the AGs until Oct. 1, or he would start packing. The company is considering states such as Georgia, Texas and Tennessee.

The report went on to outline some big-picture stats for if and when Paramount Skydance completed the move: “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output.”

On Oct. 1, Paramount Skydance will have to start paying a “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders of $7 million a day until the deal closes. The trial between Ellison and the AGs is scheduled to start on March 2, meaning that without a settlement, Paramount is on the hook for about $1.3 billion to WBD shareholders.

In late August, progress toward a settlement seemed promising after Bonta and Ellison scheduled a meeting on Aug. 24. In a last-minute move, Bonta canceled the meeting, accusing the Paramount camp of leaking details of their discussions. Paramount denied the accusations, but Bonta did not relent, saying in a statement he won’t return to settlement talks until they put a “lid on their lying leaks.”

title: ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Review: Giddily Genre-Crossing Comedy Sees Right Through Taron Egerton’s Nice-Guy Act
