summary: Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” — another story of a young man’s desires getting violently over-satisfied — to start it all up again. Merging romantic comedy, body horror and gender-war satire as casually as its handsome, outwardly affable […]
content:
Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” — another story of a young man’s desires getting violently over-satisfied — to start it all up again. Merging romantic comedy, body horror and gender-war satire as casually as its handsome, outwardly affable protagonist gets women into bed (and then, crucially, out of it), this limber first feature from British writer-director Jonathan Schey is alternately silly, nasty fun for much of its running time, carried by a performance of witty good sportsmanship from Taron Egerton, though it’s occasionally hobbled by sexual politics that are slightly less progressive than it seems to think.

Following a hot-ticket premiere at Toronto — where a queue snaking fully around two city blocks proved the value of that deliciously grabby title — “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” has all the makings of a viral conversation piece once it gets out into the real world, though its genre bait-and-switch move may divide viewers, as the initial promise of a smart, relatable modern-romance study takes a hard-left turn into supernatural territory, complete with inflamed STI imagery to make David Cronenberg proud. (Hey, depending on who you’re talking to, that’s modern romance too.) But that harder-edged novelty should serve Schey’s film well in a market that’s less accommodating of old-school romcoms: As a debut, it’s especially slick and canny, heavily indebted to recent Scandi relationship comedies in its arch tone and playful style, and Schey could follow it down any number of plausible commercial paths.

Popular on Variety

It’s the poster for Agnès Varda’s feminist touchstone “Cléo from 5 to 7” on his bedroom wall that immediately raises questions about personable, clean-cut Adam (Egerton), and you can practically see them whirring through the mind of Liv (“How to Have Sex” star Mia McKenna-Bruce, in a too-brief cameo) when she wakes up in his bed one sunny Sunday morning. Great film, sure, but is he actually a fan? He might be: He’s urbane and intelligent, works as an associate in a private London gallery dedicated to showcasing female artists, and carries his things around a blue Mubi tote that will get a guffaw of recognition from any industry-adjacent audience.

But it could as easily be a performative signal, like the books by Ottessa Moshfegh and Edna O’Brien on his shelf or the adorably scruffy, heterochromic dog named Alana (yes, after Haim) that he walks every day in Victoria Park — accessories that advertise to women his sensitivity, his sophistication, his sharing of their interests. We’ve already seen that Adam is a smooth operator in that regard. In the film’s opening scene, he picks up Liv at a club by intervening when another man is pestering her, pretending to be her boyfriend to fend him off; it’s a nice-guy ploy that secures a one-night stand, though she’s baffled by his standoffishness in the cold light of day.

That’s just his routine, however. His WhatApp is a sea of young women similarly seduced and abandoned: The only member of the opposite sex he’ll go out with more than once is his lesbian bestie Emma (Charly Clive), who rolls her eyes at his exploits, but also, as a shacked-up woman with a baby on the way, vicariously lives through them a little. Significantly less forgiving, however, is Sofia (a scintillating Jessica Henwick), the cynical academic type he tries to pick up at the theater, and who calls him out on pretty much all his shit from the get-go, spitting out the script’s most immediately quotable line: “Men don’t actually like women — they just want women to like them.”

Against all odds, she invites Adam back to her place, where her take-control attitude both confuses and excites him, and the night gets blurrier from there. The next morning, she‘s the one who’s ghosted him, and from then on, nothing quite feels right, even though he’s suddenly sending out pheromones that appear to make him absolutely irresistible to women. Even by his promiscuous standards, his body count soars; simple eye contact, it seems, is enough to seal the deal. So why isn’t he having more fun? Why does it feel like he isn’t actually doing the work here? And what’s that purply welted rash forming down in his crotch? Schey deftly builds this uncanny turn of events by degrees, in such a way that we’re initially unsure if Adam is simply delusional, but also isn’t shy of exploring its most extreme possibilities for darkly farcical purposes. Suffice it to say that incest isn’t off the table.

Egerton’s initially cocksure, steadily more frantic performance does much to sell this absurd pivot, lending proceedings a recognizable human factor throughout: We all know men a bit like Adam, who aren’t the worst but are also pretty far from the best, who may not be overtly toxic themselves, but don’t recognize the toxicity inherent in their advantaged social status. “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” allows us to feel a little sorry for him, while also relishing the spectacle of him being put through the wringer a bit — especially as the film’s grosser horror instincts take over.

It’s just a bit of a shame that Schey’s script winds up advocating for a pretty staid alternative to his behavior in Emma’s thoroughly domesticated monogamy and imminent parenthood: There are safe, fun, equitable ways to, well, be a horny little devil, and this lively, zesty, thoroughly enjoyable comedy could spend a little more time exploring the options and playing the field.

title: ‘Babies’ Review: Lauren Miller Rogen Film Is A Witty, Heartfelt Exploration Of Childless Adulthood & Chosen Family – Toronto Film Festival
summary: After years of fielding questions about whether she wants to be a mom, Lauren Miller Rogen gives the definitive answer in the form of her witty, heartfelt comedy Babies. Written and directed by Miller Rogen, Babies stars Anna Kendrick and the auteur’s husband Seth Rogen as the happily married Aaron and Annie, a couple without kids of their […]
content:
After years of fielding questions about whether she wants to be a mom, Lauren Miller Rogen gives the definitive answer in the form of her witty, heartfelt comedy Babies.

Written and directed by Miller Rogen, Babies stars Anna Kendrick and the auteur’s husband Seth Rogen as the happily married Aaron and Annie, a couple without kids of their own who are constantly asked about why they don’t have any.

When their friend Eliza (Kate Berlant) leaves her husband Luke (Dan Stevens), she and her young daughter move in with couple, giving them a chance to test drive being parents. Rogen’s Aaron hilariously compares it to receiving a Baskin Robbins sample.

Rogen and Kendrick share the kind of onscreen chemistry that makes you think they could be pretty great parents — or if you are a parent, it might make you jealous of their child-free dynamic. Either way, they swap quips back and forth in the same effortless way they express love and care for one another.

Watch on Deadline

Berlant and Issa Rae play their longtime friends Becky and Eliza, both at different stages of parenthood with very different parenting styles.

As Eliza, Berlant gives a hilariously high-strung performance as the recently single mom trying to figure out her divorced life.

Rae plays the seemingly perfect working mom, who has her hands full with a snarky teen daughter, a baby on the way and a gallery she’s starting with Annie.

Stevens and Zach Cherry complement their onscreen spouses with their own unique takes on fatherhood — Stevens as the unreliable co-parent who adores his daughter while neglecting his wife, and Cherry as the constantly reliable dad who is cooler than his daughters can admit.

The talented ensemble of seasoned actors is adequately matched by their child co-stars, each brimming with personality.

It’s safe to assume the film came from a personal place for Miller Rogen, who along with her husband, has taken numerous questions from the media over the years about their decision not to have kids.

“What fucking business is it of yours?” Rogen asks in one voiceover, a question he’s likely been holding in during many an interview over the years.

The film also deals with the pain and uncertainty of a sick parent, mirroring the filmmaker’s own experience with her late mom’s Alzheimer’s, which inspired the couple’s Hilarity for Charity nonprofit.

A sincere comedy about the ups and downs of life, Babies offers a balanced critique of parenthood that gives good parents their due while also celebrating the beauty of chosen family, being able to go to the movies alone in the middle of the day and smoke a joint in your own home.

title: Netflix Developing ‘Diablo’ Animated Series
summary: The Diablo video game is coming to Netflix. Blizzard Entertainment chief Johanna Faries revealed at BlizzCon in Anaheim Saturday that the streamer is adapting the game as an animated series. Here’s the description of the project, per Variety: “After decades of bringing entire universes to life through our games, we’re partnering with some creative powerhouses […]
content:
The Diablo video game is coming to Netflix.

Blizzard Entertainment chief Johanna Faries revealed at BlizzCon in Anaheim Saturday that the streamer is adapting the game as an animated series.

Here’s the description of the project, per Variety: “After decades of bringing entire universes to life through our games, we’re partnering with some creative powerhouses to tell even more stories beyond gaming across new screens. A new animated series set in the world of ‘Diablo’ is in development with Netflix. More details will be shared in the future, but this is only the beginning, with even more taking shape across our universes.”

BlizzCon is a fan event staged by Blizzard, the video game developer behind such titles as World of Warcraft, Overwatch, StarCraft and Diablo.

Watch on Deadline

Diablo made its original debut in 1996. There have since been three other editions released in 2000, 2012, and 2023. Blizzard also announced that Diablo V will bow in the spring of 2029.

title: FCC Chairman Slams James Talarico as Running a ‘Hoax’ With Jimmy Kimmel Interview, Which ABC Punted to YouTube, to Get ‘Clicks and Donations’
summary: Brendan Carr, the Trump-aligned Republican chairman of the FCC, accused James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, of running a “hoax” to garner attention and campaign donations by sitting for an interview with Jimmy Kimmel — which ABC put on YouTube instead airing it on broadcast TV to avoid a potential clash […]
content:
Brendan Carr, the Trump-aligned Republican chairman of the FCC, accused James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, of running a “hoax” to garner attention and campaign donations by sitting for an interview with Jimmy Kimmel — which ABC put on YouTube instead airing it on broadcast TV to avoid a potential clash with the FCC.

In a post on X Saturday night, Carr wrote that Talarico is “just running the same hoax he did a few months ago on Colbert for the purpose of getting clicks and donations — he’s banking on people not understanding the statute or operating as partisan lemmings.”

Carr’s post included a meme mocking Talarico and Kimmel. That depicted Kimmel riding a bike with Talarico tucked into a baby backpack carrier on the TV host’s shoulders; Kimmel then inserts a stick into the spokes, causing the bike to crash.

Popular on Variety

Variety has reached out to Talarico’s press office for comment.

Kimmel on Wednesday announced on his ABC late-night show that the interview Talarico would be on YouTube and not TV, saying the decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense.”

The concern was that the FCC might retaliate against ABC over Talarico’s appearance under the agency’s equal-time rule, which requires broadcast programs give equal airtime to political candidates (unless they are “bona fide” news programs). Late-night shows and daytime talk shows have long been considered exempt from the rule. But earlier this year, Carr kicked off a formal review of whether ABC daytime talk show “The View” qualifies for an exemption to the equal-time rule. The FCC chairman has alleged that talk shows like “The View” function as partisan mouthpieces for Democrats and should be subject to agency regulations like the equal-time rule and a prohibition on “news distortion,” given they are using publicly licensed TV spectrum.

Talarico characterized ABC’s decision to abstain from putting his interview with Kimmel on TV as effectively a form of censorship by the U.S. government. “Government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party,” Talarico said in an interview with MS NOW. The Democrat called the FCC’s threats against broadcasters over “The View” and other programming “the most dangerous form of cancel culture.”

In February, Stephen Colbert said CBS executives pulled his interview with Talarico from air over concerns about violating the equal time rule, which requires broadcast stations to give equal time to political candidates when they appear on-air. (CBS said it didn’t block the interview but provided the show “legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule.”)

Carr, in his Saturday-night commentary, was responding to a comment on X by an organization called University Democrats at UT Austin, which asked rhetorically, “So I can’t watch Talarico on Kimmel but I have to watch Ted Cruz on GameDay?” That’s a reference to an appearance on ESPN’s “College GameDay” Saturday by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who was on-air for almost 10 minutes. Cruz, who was lobbying for the Protect College Sports Act legislation to regulate collegiate sports practices, was loudly heckled and booed by the fans in attendance.

Carr, who was appointed chairman of the FCC by Donald Trump in 2025, noted that the FCC’s equal-time rule doesn’t apply to ESPN’s “GameDay” because Congress applied it to broadcast tv stations, not cable programs. In addition, he pointed out correctly, the statute only applies to “legally qualified candidates” running for office.

He also argued that the equal-time statute “does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast tv. It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others.”

Carr, explaining why broadcast and cable networks are regulated differently by the FCC, continued, “Broadcasters are unique. The FCC gave them free licenses worth many billions of dollars to use a public resource (spectrum). They are given a government sanctioned monopoly on their broadcast frequencies, too. If anyone else wants to use that same public resource (spectrum) for the purpose of expressing their own views, the government will not let them — it will eject anyone else that tries to use a broadcaster’s licensed spectrum.”

The Supreme Court has ruled that “holding broadcasters to their public interest obligations is not censorship or any sort of 1A [First Amendment] violation,” Carr wrote. “And Congress has charged the FCC with ensuring that broadcasters meet those public interest obligations, as required by their licenses. The agency should do so.”

Of course, today, most Americans watch “broadcast” television networks like ABC on cable, satellite or internet pay-TV services.

In resopnse to Carr’s post, UT Austin’s University Democrats responded, “ok brandon.”

title: Chris Rock’s Hollywood Send-Up ‘Misty Green’ Hits TIFF With Rosalind Eleazar’s Knockout Lead Performance
summary: Roughly two-thirds through “Misty Green,” Rosalind Eleazar takes a breath and lets a rendition of “One Night Only,” from the musical “Dreamgirls,” rip. The characters around her go quiet, and the crowd at the Toronto International Film Festival, where Chris Rock’s film made its world premiere, seemed similarly enraptured. But when Rock and his cast […]
content:
Roughly two-thirds through “Misty Green,” Rosalind Eleazar takes a breath and lets a rendition of “One Night Only,” from the musical “Dreamgirls,” rip. The characters around her go quiet, and the crowd at the Toronto International Film Festival, where Chris Rock‘s film made its world premiere, seemed similarly enraptured.

But when Rock and his cast took the stage for their post-screening Q&A, the crowd made their appreciation for her work known with cheers and applause.

Onstage, Eleazar explained why she fell in love with Misty and was “really desperate” to play the part.

Popular on Variety

“It was such a raw and honest take on the darker side of our industry,” Eleazar said about reading the script for the first time (and charming the crowd with her British accent). “She’s such a complex and such a contradictory and flawed character, and I’m sort of drawn to characters that are difficult to love, and the way that Chris wrote the individual relationships with such precision and nuance.”

“The moment I read the script in London, I was desperate to do this part. So I did whatever I could,” Eleazar said, before realizing what she’d accidentally insinuated, since Misty Green will indeed do anything for a role. Rock and the crowd chuckled as she hastily recovered: “Normal things! Just like Zooms and stuff.”

Eleazar — recently named one of Variety’s 10 Actors to Watch for 2026 — is a best actress contender that dares anyone in the room to argue otherwise. Each scene feels fit for her Oscar clip package, much Cate Blanchett delivered in each beat of “Blue Jasmine.” Misty is a fading, award-winning actress clawing back her career, but self-sabotaging along the way. Eleazar plays her with the danger of Pam Grier and the polish of Tracee Ellis Ross.

”I love a messy woman,” Rock said, explaining why he crafted the complex character in the first place. “I like to make things I haven’t seen: I haven’t seen it with a woman, I haven’t seen it with a Black woman.”

As Rock explained in his Variety cover story, the role was a tricky one to cast because of its risqué nature, but Eleazar was game as could be.

“I know she’s a lovely lady and demure tonight, but you have these meetings, and you have to think to yourself: ‘OK, is she gonna smoke the cigarette in her underwear on the balcony? Is she gonna get on the floor and fight for the money? Like on the day you can just say you’re not doing it, and what the fuck am I gonna do?”

With “Misty Green,” Rock, who wrote and directed the film, crafted a dramatic satire that cuts to the bone. The film functions as a tour of Los Angeles’ most potable artistic hot spots, but doubles as an autopsy of the business, especially for artists of color. He skewers “Hollywood” without ever quite naming names. “Call Kevin,” one actor barks. “Is it Hart?” The film keeps daring you to fill in the blanks.

Most importantly, Rock hands Eleazar showcase after showcase, and she cashes in on every opportunity. A sequence built around a screen test for “The Devil Wears Prada” is the funniest, sharpest stretch of acting in the film — until the next one that follows it. When Misty sings a version of Radiohead’s “Creep” in the lounge at the Hollywood Roosevelt, the ache lands similarly to Carey Mulligan’s “New York, New York” solo in “Shame.” By the time Eleazar reaches “One Night Only,” it’s her “La La Land” audition moment.

Now, for the Oscar-shaped elephant in the room. Only one Black woman has won the lead actress Oscar: Halle Berry, for “Monster’s Ball,” in 2002. Now, 24 ceremonies later, could Eleazar be the most credible candidate to become the second? She’s more than worthy.

And then there’s Daniel Kaluuya. The “Judas and the Black Messiah” Oscar winner has been away from screens for too long, and “Misty Green” is the argument for why the business can’t afford to keep letting that happen. He plays Misty’s brother, who grapples with his mental health. A single scene near the finale is enough to shatter your heart.

Adam Driver turns up for a stretch that is, improbably, the best thing he does all year — better even than his work in “Paper Tiger” — as a Hollywood type that walks the fine line between pimp and producer. One scene, which finds him snorting a line off Misty’s thigh, is pure, gleeful provocation.

Rock’s entire ensemble is superb. Anna Kendrick gives her sharpest turn since “Up in the Air” as Misty’s best friend, a fellow actress drawn to Black men even as she dates the family-approved white ones. Topher Grace plays Misty’s talent agent, forced to deliver the hard truths about her erratic behavior. Rock casts himself as Jordan Green, a Hollywood director who knew Misty at her peak. Colleen Camp has a small, sly role, her second A24 film this year after “Club Kid.” Anthony Anderson plays a police officer, whose deadened delivery drives the film toward some of its most uncomfortable scenes.

“Misty Green” has plenty of laughs, but it curdles by the end — à la “Requiem for a Dream” — with scenes that drag Misty into the darkest depths of the business.

Nonetheless, Rock is building toward something less comfortable than a takedown of Hollywood vanity. The film is ultimately about is redemption and an examination of mental illness — and how thoroughly the country has failed to fund it, understand it or train anyone, its police most of all, to meet it. Anderson’s cop and Kaluuya’s brother are two ends of the same failure, and the movie sits in the space between them.

For the upcoming Oscar race, Eleazar is a top-tier best actress contender in waiting. Kaluuya belongs in the supporting conversation on the strength of a single scene. And Rock, long underrated behind the camera since “Top Five,” has finally made the movie that earns his name a place in the screenplay and directing chatter.

“Misty Green” opens in U.S. theaters on Oct. 9.

title: Mahershala Ali Finally Made His ‘Blade’ Film With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’
summary: Bassam Tariq and Mahershala Ali finally made their “Blade” movie. On Saturday night, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” made its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival before its theatrical release on Sept. 25. Tariq’s film centers on Latif (Ali), a devout Muslim hitman who, following the sudden death of his wife, goes […]
content:
Bassam Tariq and Mahershala Ali finally made their “Blade” movie.

On Saturday night, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” made its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival before its theatrical release on Sept. 25. Tariq’s film centers on Latif (Ali), a devout Muslim hitman who, following the sudden death of his wife, goes on the run with his teenage daughter (Adia, a revelation), 10-year-old son (Jahleel Kamara) and newborn baby on the hunt for breast milk and after running afoul of not only his boss but also Hwan (an unrecognizable John Cho), the gun-toting leader of an anti-pornography Christian cult.

And yes, Ali dispatches his enemies with a long blade.

Popular on Variety

Tariq (“Mogul Mowgli”) was hired by Marvel Studios to direct “Blade” — with two-time Oscar winner Ali in the starring role — all the way back in 2021, but backed out of helming the project in 2022 due to production delays, staying on as an executive producer. The film was then stuck in development hell, and by July 2026, Ali confirmed it was dead in the water. So, Ali put the sword-fighting skills he’d learned training for the superhero to good use in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” a powerful meditation on religion, family and the ties that bind.

Following its premiere, Tariq, Ali and the cast participated in a Q&A at the packed Princess of Wales Theatre.

“It just all felt like the worlds were colliding all the time, every day and in every scene on that set,” Ali said of making the intense film. “Bassam gave us a lot to carry. I’m really grateful for the task and all the duties involved in playing this character. There’s something very special in working with my children in the film… The experience, the part, it’s all a bit of an emotional blur. And I’m still learning about it.”

In addition to Ali’s magnetic performance, which deserves serious awards consideration, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” marks a breakout turn for Adia as his rebellious daughter struggling to balance her faith and teendom. And Adia had nothing but praise for her onscreen dad who she says allowed her to reach such great emotional depths.

“Mahershala is such an incredibly generous soul in his scene work but also off camera,” Adia shared. “He really gave me the space to share myself off camera and on camera in a way that I’m not sure a lot of people get, so it made it a lot easier to approach the work — especially really tough scenes.”

As for Ali’s fight scenes, he and Tariq gave a shout-out to Adam Hart, the film’s stunt coordinator, who choreographed the sequences in a short amount of time. “I’m so blown away with what he was able to choreograph and pull off within the time that we had,” said Ali. “It was a beautiful experience. Bassam and I met many years back, and I had had a year-plus of doing martial-arts training, and then I had over a year off of that. Bassam came to me with this incredible script and I had to do what I had to do and had my process in terms of getting to a yes. Once it was time to go, it just happened to be Ramadan and I was fasting and training a bit in L.A., and as soon as Ramadan was done, we started shooting.”

title: ‘Animal Hospital’ Leads Roblox Innovation Awards 2026 Winners as Roblox Unveils 20th Anniversary Event
summary: The Roblox Innovation Awards (RIAs) unveiled its 2026 winners during a ceremony in San Jose Saturday with new title “Animal Hospital” taking home several top honors. Part of the 12th annual Roblox Developer Conference, this year’s RIAs were hosted by Roblox’s head of the developer community, Justin Sousa (widely known as “JParty” to Roblox users). […]
content:
The Roblox Innovation Awards (RIAs) unveiled its 2026 winners during a ceremony in San Jose Saturday with new title “Animal Hospital” taking home several top honors.

Part of the 12th annual Roblox Developer Conference, this year’s RIAs were hosted by Roblox’s head of the developer community, Justin Sousa (widely known as “JParty” to Roblox users).

The RIAs honor Roblox developers, artists, studios and creators across 20 categories. This years results were calculated based on 319 million votes.

“What I love most about this list is how different all of these winners are,” Sousa said. “There isn’t one definition of a great Roblox game anymore, and that’s the point. From tactical shooters and terrifying forests to word games, football, fashion, audio, and one particularly suspicious medical facility, the boundaries of what can be built on Roblox keep moving because this community keeps moving them.”

Popular on Variety

The RIAs were held at the conclusion of this year’s Roblox Developers Conference, during which Roblox made several big announcements, including the reveal of Roblox’s upcoming 20th anniversary event, “The Hunt.”

Per Sousa, “Roblox has been around for two decades now, and it shows in the breadth of ingenuity creators bring to the table. For those who missed the RIAs live, we also announced a special event to celebrate Roblox’s 20-year anniversary, beginning on September 17—The Hunt: Roblox 20. But more on that later.”

See below for the full list of winners announced during the 2026 Roblox Innovation Awards.

Best Shooter

Game: RIVALS

Studio: Nosniy Games

A polished, competitive FPS built around intense 1v1 duels to 5v5 battles. RIVALS is easy to jump into and very hard to put down.

Best Use of Audio

Game: DOORS

Studio: LSPLASH

In DOORS, sound isn’t just atmosphere—it’s part of how players understand the world, anticipate what’s coming, and occasionally realize they’re in serious trouble.

Best Plugin

Plugin: UGC Makers Toolbox

Creator: Onogork

A creator-built toolbox designed to make the process of building UGC easier. This is exactly the kind of thing we love seeing developers build for other developers.

Best Puzzle Game

Game: Finish The Word

Studio: Table Game X

A wonderfully simple idea with surprisingly stressful consequences: Keep the word chain alive, think fast, and don’t be the one who runs out of answers.

Best Innovation in a Branded Game

Partnership: Steal a Brainrot x GOAT (Sony Pictures)

Studio: Do Big

A collision of one of Roblox’s biggest cultural phenomena with a major entertainment property in a way that feels native to the experience rather than bolted onto it.

Best Party & Casual Game

Game: +1 Speed Keyboard Escape

Studio: SecretVerse Studio

Let’s chill … or maybe not? Fast, accessible, and delightfully chaotic, this is the kind of game where “one more round” can quickly turn into 10.

Best Innovation in Tech

Game: TTK

Studio: Sable Digital

An ambitious tactical shooter pushing on what high-fidelity combat can look and feel like on Roblox, from helmet cams and optics to sophisticated squad-based gameplay.

Best Sports Game

Game: FIFA Super Soccer

Studio: Play! Football

Football? Soccer? Who cares! FIFA Super Soccer brings the game’s energy, competition, and global appeal to Roblox.

Best Action Game

Game: Jujutsu Shenanigans

Studio: Tze’s Shenanigans

Fast combat, big abilities, destructive chaos, and exactly the right amount of shenanigans.

Best UGC Creator

Creator: Valkenheim

A creator whose distinctive work continues to show just how much personality and imagination can fit into an avatar.

Best Innovation in Creative Direction

Game: Animal Hospital

Studio: Animal Anomaly

From the creepy hospital setting to the decidedly abnormal patients, Animal Hospital’s creative identity captures players’ attention almost immediately.

Best Survival Game

Game: 99 Nights in the Forest

Studio: Grandma’s Favourite Games

Build a camp, gather resources, and rescue the missing kids. Survive this fantastic party game and stop whatever is watching from the forest over 99 very long nights.

Best Strategy Game

Game: Mini War

Studio: M&M Community

Start with a small country, build its economy, raise an army, and decide whether diplomacy or total domination is the better path to victory.

Best RPG

Game: Piggy: Intercity

Studio: Piggy: Intercity

Piggy goes open world with exploration, characters, base building, and player choices that shape a journey through an infected world.

Best Classic Game

Game: Natural Disaster Survival

Studio: Stickmasterluke

Survive the flood, dodge the meteors, and stare in awe at the ones who make it through. Some Roblox lessons are timeless.

Best Video Star

Video Star: Laughability (YouTube)

Being a star has its perks. Thanks for the stories, humor, and unique creator-driven PoV!

Best New Game

Game: Animal Hospital

Studio: Animal Anomaly

The night shift at this animal hospital gets weird fast. Animal Hospital is a wonderfully unsettling mix of treating patients, spotting anomalies, and trying to survive until morning.

People’s Choice

Game: Animal Hospital

Studio: Animal Anomaly

Apparently the community agrees: Questionable veterinary practices make for a pretty great Roblox game.

Best Studio

Studio: Nosniy Games

A studio that continues to combine craft, polish, and a deep understanding of what makes players want to come back for one more game. Developers of games like Treasure Quest, Super Golf, and, of course, RIVALS, named this year’s Best Shooter. Also some pretty cool d00ds.

The Builderman Award

Game: Animal Hospital

Studio: Animal Anomaly

And the final award goes to Animal Hospital, where working the night shift gets weird … fast.

title: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Chris Rock Tells the Story of a Party-Girl Actress, Brilliantly Played by Rosalind Eleazar, in The Best Movie About Hollywood in Years
summary: "Misty Green" is an amazing slice of showbiz sociology, riveting in the details of what a contemporary Hollywood actress — even a successful one — is up against. Rock isn’t casting stones. The warped values he depicts are there in the industry and in Misty herself.
content:
The title character of “Misty Green,” Chris Rock’s explosively entertaining, savagely authentic drama about life in the Hollywood of today, is a television actress who had a moment — in fact, she was close to the top of the heap. But that was then and this is now. Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar (“Slow Horses”) with doleful charisma and a casual fury, is in her late 30s. She’s a vivid and acclaimed actress and singer who was popular enough to have won the Emmy for best supporting actress for her cult thriller series “Red Eye.” She was on the cover of Cosmo. People still talk about her show in reverent tones.

Yet it’s funny how time passes. At an audition, Misty is seated next to a young actress who’s awed to meet her, because “Red Eye” was her mother’s favorite show. Misty still has her looks, her talent, and her drive (everything you need, right?). And she’s still out there working it. But her career has been in a slump, and that kind of downhill mojo can take on a life of its own. Suddenly you look up and you’re a has-been.

Popular on Variety

It doesn’t help that Misty is an unapologetic party girl. She likes to drink, drug, and fuck whoever to the point that it’s getting more than a bit self-destructive. The night before that audition, she gets a text from Zack (Adam Driver), an oily tech power-player sleazebag who always has a harem of women around him, which he maintains by keeping them well-supplied with cocaine. Misty hooks up with him for a night of clubbing, snorting, and screwing in the bathroom stall, and the next morning she’s a wreck. But her hellbent hedonism, and the recklessness that grows out of what’s really an orgiastic form of self-medicating, didn’t happen by accident.

Misty is pissed off. The big picture of her career is that the industry, because of its values (and because of her defiant nature, though that’s the very quality that made her a star), is slowly but surely choking off her options. She’s Black, which is no deal-killer but still, in the eyes of too many, puts her in a box. She’s getting “old.” And she has slept around enough, and acted thoughtlessly enough, flying off the handle, that she has left a trail of enemies. There are too many people who look at her and think she’s trouble. In the new corporate Hollywood run by algorithm, trouble means not fitting into the machine. At the same time, Misty has been at the game for so long that she’s become a round-the-clock liar. She deceives and manipulates to survive, and that’s part of her performance vibe — she’s always acting. She’s a star, a diva, and a mess.

Last year, a lot of people clutched pearls over whether the title character of “Marty Supreme” was “likable” enough. Misty Green makes Marty look like an Eagle Scout. The movie, however, isn’t apologizing for its heroine’s bad behavior or making excuses for her. She has made her own bed. What’s mesmerizing about “Misty Green” is that Misty is part of an entertainment industry that has cut so many corners, and has so many pathologies, that it’s hard to separate the corruption she’s up against from her own self-inflicted damage. As a filmmaker, Chris Rock wants us to know Misty as if we were in her skin (he has cited the films of John Cassavetes, like “A Woman Under the Influence,” as one of his role models). At the same time, “Misty Green” is an amazing slice of showbiz sociology, riveting in the details of what a contemporary Hollywood actress — even a successful one — is up against. Rock isn’t casting stones. The warped values he depicts are there in the industry and in Misty herself.

In the eyebrow-raiser of an opening scene, we meet Misty in the fabulous beachfront apartment she’s been living in for four years. It belongs to the wealthy player she was the mistress of, who has just died; his wife walks in in a rage and demands that Misty leave. But then she recognizes Misty (like everyone, she was a fan of “Red Eye”), which provokes a suddenly sympathetic reaction. She’ll let Misty stay in the apartment for one more week. This scene, with its machine-gun insults and effusive obscenity, establishes several key things: that Hollywood is a place where people like Misty let themselves be used; that it’s a place that will toss you out; and that the sway of celebrity may be fickle, but it’s still all-powerful.

Misty is broke, without a home, and without too many prospects. (That audition is for a “street” role — in other words, what a Black actress is expected to do.) Yet she’s still Misty Green! And the movie, set against the ticking countdown clock of that week, uses Misty’s crisis of survival to take a spiritual inventory of Hollywood.

I knew it when I saw “Top Five,” the last movie he directed (12 years ago!), but now it can be shouted from the rooftops: Chris Rock is a major filmmaker. He is, of course, flexing different muscles here than he is as a stand-up comedian, but part of his delicious gift as a writer-director is that he draws on the extraordinary empirical powers that drive his stand-up. Like all the greatest comedians, he’s really a philosopher-detective, and the beauty of “Misty Green” is that it’s not some stylized “satire” of the new entertainment culture. The movie has laughs, a lot of them dark, but Rock has insisted that people call it a drama, and I get why he’s touchy on the point. The lure of “Misty Green” is its authenticity.

You feel that in your bones when Misty goes into the audition, and there at the table is Rhonda (Tracie Thoms), the veteran casting director who’s known her for so long that she can’t see who Misty is anymore. (A rival actress praises Misty to the heavens, all as a sly way of putting her down.) You feel it when Misty is dishing with her best friend, Naomi (Anna Kendrick), an actress who’s getting out of the business by marrying a finance dude (Rich Sommer) she’s far from in love with — and, in fact, she still yearns for random erotic encounters. But if that sounds chortle-worthy, it’s really expressive of the L.A. state-of-mind of the “Real Housewives” era, where everything is transactional. And you feel it in Misty’s encounters with Zach the demon of temptation, who’s both lover and pimp — one of those character roles that Adam Driver, with his quick-hit hustler’s aggression, is perfect for. Zack offers Misty 200 grand to go to Dubai and party with the royalty there. He’s asking her to prostitute herself, but the point is that Zack – and Dubai — is now part of the Hollywood chain.

Rock has cast himself in the movie as well. Acting with a jovial diffidence, wearing a porkpie hat he never takes off, he plays Jordan Green, a film director Missy once worked with (on an update of “Cinderella”), until she came in one day so high on coke that she punched a crew member. So Jordan is another burnt bridge, except that Rock, an infectious presence (even if he isn’t quite an actor), invests him with empathy and gives him a lot of fun lines (like his explanation of why “all Civil Rights movies suck”). Rock, with his scolding amusement, is there, in a way, to expound on the subtle racism of latter-day Hollywood, and to give Misty a break because of it. Jordan is directing a reboot of “Dreamgirls,” to be shot in Vancouver, and maybe this could be Misty’s second chance.

The other major character is Misty’s brother (also named Jordan), who is bipolar and turns violent whenever he goes off his meds. He’s played by Daniel Kaluuya, in his first screen performance in four years, and Kaluuya is a force. When Jordan erupts at a waiter for not bringing the bill to him, we see that his mental illness carries an echo of Nina Simone’s “irrational” rage. She was bipolar too, but this, the movie says, is the mad despair that a sensitivity to entrenched racism can drive you to. And Misty’s loyalty to her brother — to that side of him — is part of her undoing.

Yet Misty still has the goods. At the Roosevelt Hotel cabaret, she does a performance of Radiohead’s “Creep,” and it’s hypnotic. “Dreamgirls” would be perfect for her, and she and Jordan know it. Rosalind Eleazar shows us Misty’s duplicity, but she acts with such unguarded emotion that we’re desperate to see her burn through her problems and succeed. When she finally does her “Dreamgirls” audition, and sings “One Night Only,” it carries the film’s payload of hope and despair. Chris Rock is right: This is a drama. Yet “Misty Green” is put together with so much observational exuberance that it leaves you both daunted and exhilarated.

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Peter Farrelly’s Sensational Biopic Of The Making Of Stallone’s Classic Is Just As Inspiring As The Original Movie Itself – Toronto Film Festival
summary: It is no spoiler to say I am going to reveal the final moments of Peter Farrelly’s fantastic crowd pleasing biopic chronicling the making of the 1976 classic, Rocky, that not only made Sylvester Stallone a major star, but also became one of the greatest behind the scenes stories in Hollywood history. Stay all the […]
content:
It is no spoiler to say I am going to reveal the final moments of Peter Farrelly‘s fantastic crowd pleasing biopic chronicling the making of the 1976 classic, Rocky, that not only made Sylvester Stallone a major star, but also became one of the greatest behind the scenes stories in Hollywood history. Stay all the way through the very last of the credits and you will be rewarded with the only scene in this saga not recreated for the movie.

Introducing Stallone for the first time on The Tonight Show to promote Rocky, Johnny Carson tells a bit of the incredible backstory of Stallone turning down hundreds of thousands of dollars for his screenplay in order to insist he star in the movie he wrote for himself( even though he was completely unknown at the time). “If someone were to actually make a movie about the making of Rocky nobody would believe it,” Carson prophetically said.

Well, someone has done that and the film that has resulted is a winner in every way, a movie that in fact manages to carry the same emotional wallop as the original Rocky and containing a performance from Anthony Ippolito that is so uncanny I didn’t for a minute think he was anyone but the actual Stallone. It feels like they just used de-aging technology so Stallone could play himself a half century younger. But make no mistake, Ippolito’s powerful, moving, and inspiring portrayal is not a mere imitation. This guy inhabits Stallone in every way, delivering an authentic portrait that will blow you away.

Watch on Deadline

Farrelly has said he would not have made the film without Stallone’s blessing, which he got, and he has, with Peter Gamble’s beautifully structured and crafted screenplay, made one of the best movies ever made about Hollywood moviemaking and the sheer mechanics of getting anything made. Certainly it is one of the most entertaining.

In a year that marks the 50th anniversary of Rocky, a film that spawned five sequels and three more films in the Creed spinoff series with Michael B. Jordan, I Play Rocky brings us full circle right back to the beginning and manages to slyly recapture the fresh spirit that birthed it. This film has turned the making of Rocky into its own Rocky-like moment of triumph.

Starting with Ippolito on screen as “Mike Stallone” auditioning for a nameless role, one of those aspiring actors working any menial job he can to support his dreams of making it in the industry, Gamble’s script shows us in linear fashion exactly how this impossible dream happened. From scraping the bottom of the barrel, even doing soft porn (a hilarious audition scene that really happened), finding a puppy he names Butkus, meeting his eventual wife Sasha ( a perfect AnnaSophia Robb) at the movie theatre he works, and finally getting a break to meet big time producers Irwin Winkler (PJ Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell) who sadly inform him Jan Michael Vincent got the job so the role of his brother has to go to someone else, all the ups and downs of the life of an actor trying to just get by and keep going are here.

On his way out the door he tucks a script he wrote called Paradise Alley (eventually a movie Stallone got made) under a pile that says “weekend reading”. Their assistant knew the ruse but read the script and praised it which caught the producers’ attention. They tell him he has real talent as a writer and to come up with some ideas. Sitting at a bar wondering how he was going to get by he sees a Muhammed Ali fight and bingo, the idea for Rocky comes pouring out of him, written in longhand in only three and a half days and handed to Sasha to type, Chartoff/Winkler (both Byrne and Kebbell are really wonderful in these parts) spark to it and manage to sell to a skeptical studio head, Sandy Maddux (a terrific and scene stealing Tracy Letts in a composite of studio execs at the time). “Boxing pictures? Nobody makes boxing pictures,” he barks. The only hangup is he won’t sell it to them unless he stars in it.

In a series of scenes where the price keeps going up with seemingly no ceiling, Sly holds his ground, “I won’t sell it for $1 million. Not $10 million,” he swears and you can see the passion of a man who believes in himself, willing to “go the distance” just like Rocky to prove it. Finally after knocking the budget down to just $1 million with clauses designed to get Stallone fired so they can get Ryan O’Neal or an actor on that level when it inevitably behind schedule, the saga of the actual filming begins and it has all been recreated with tender loving care, from the cinematography to production design, costume, music, editing, and one riotous scene after another that are not just about the making of this one film against all odds, it is really about the making of just about every film, a love letter to movies that in its own way is on par with Truffaut’s Day For Night.

A scene in Philadelphia at the meat packing plant where they find the local union head has gotten wind they are shooting without permits turns into an amusing nail-biting moment where all the equipment and cast and crew has to be immediately hidden before he gets there. Another scene, the recreation of the iconic run up the Philly steps show us one of the first uses ever of the now indispensible Steadicam (using the original I am told) as it reinvented that aspect of moviemaking.

But the emotional knockout is delivered in the filming of a scene with Burgess Meredith (played by Robert Morgan) as Mickey who tells him he will agree to train him, after first rejecting him. The key scene just wasn’t working and director John Avildsen (a great Jay Duplass) tells him they have to do it again, but how? It needs a stronger emotional hook or it fails. Stallone then proceeded to completely make up a five minute take on the spot that is masterfully delivered. Ippolito brought me to tears watching him play it, quite tricky since this improv is now scripted but has to feel spontaneous. The entire cast with Ippolito is ideal, with special shoutouts to Keki Seto as Talia Shire and Stephan James as Carl Weathers, both taking on Stallone’s iconic Rocky co-stars in style.

There are so many highlights in a movie that pulls off a tall task in bringing the same feeling we got the first time we saw Rocky. Farrelly, who won and deserved a couple of Oscars including Best Picture for Green Book, a film that tugs at the heartstrings without ever being anything less than simply human, has now made another film that makes us feel good about life and ourselves. Like Frank Capra used to do, he has made a movie that gives us hope. It couldn’t come at a better time.

Producers are Toby Emmerich, Christian Baha, Peter Farrelly, Paul Currie, Michele Weiss

Title: I Play Rocky

Festival: Toronto – Special Presentations

Distributor: Amazon MGM Studios

Release Date: November 6, 2026

Director: Peter Farrelly

Screenwriter: Peter Gamble

Cast: Anthony Ippolito, AnnaSophia Robb, Toby Kebbell, P.J. Byrne, Jay Duplass, Matt Dillon, Stephan James, Tracy Letts, Kiki Seto

Running Time: 2 hours and 8 minutes

title: ‘Misty Green’ Review:  Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down And Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival
summary: I have to confess I am a sucker for down-on-your-luck Hollywood stories, especially movies about actresses who once had success and are now scraping the bottom. Of course there is the classic of classics, Sunset Boulevard, but there are many more. A personal favorite is The Star which got Bette Davis an Academy Award nomination […]
content:
I have to confess I am a sucker for down-on-your-luck Hollywood stories, especially movies about actresses who once had success and are now scraping the bottom. Of course there is the classic of classics, Sunset Boulevard, but there are many more. A personal favorite is The Star which got Bette Davis an Academy Award nomination as a has-been who walks around Hollywood carrying her Oscar saying things like “Come on Oscar. Let’s go get drunk”. Jane Fonda got nominated as well playing a down-and-outer in Hollywood in The Morning After. For sleazy fun there’s Connie Stevens in The Sex Symbol, Kim Novak in The Legend Of Lylah Clare (“Tell them Lylah is coming!”), and a great Natalie Wood in a real favorite, Inside Daisy Clover to name just a handful. The lure of Hollywood and the dark side of those who chase the dream has been fascinating subject matter for filmmakers throughout Hollywood history and now it is Chris Rock‘s turn.

Rock was doing a group voice over session and noticed a couple of once successful actresses from hit sitcoms who were now doing this kind of day work to keep the lights on and it got him thinking about a scenario that eventually became his latest idea for a film, Misty Green. It has been 12 years since his last, and most critically acclaimed turn behind the lens with 2014’s Top Five. Earlier this century he tried his hand directing 2003’s Head Of State and 2007’s I Think I Love My Wife (I quite liked that one) although neither of those two were box office hits.

Watch on Deadline

Now he is back and if Misty Green will be remembered for anything it is the remarkable performance of British actress Rosalind Eleazar, a co-star currently for Slow Horses, but soon will be known as well for playing the title role in this story of an L.A. based television actress, a once upon a time Supporting Actress Emmy winner, now going through tough times, various addictions, family problems, and standing in her own way of reviving her career because she won’t lower herself to audition. This is the kind of material that could lend itself to show business cliches (we have seen it a hundred times), but Rock has created a character, specifically a Black actress on the skids, the kind of character we don’t get to see portrayed on screen as opposed to the long list of similar stories listed above with white stars.

This is all about Misty. We meet her best friend Naomi (Anna Kendrick) who tries to encourage her , even helping with a self tape audition Misty resists; we meet her frustrated agent Randy (Topher Grace) who complains because on the last job she punched a co-star ; we meet friend and would be filmmaker Zach (Adam Driver) whose drug induced invitations and sleazy job opps are not what Misty needs, but still can’t resist because she needs the cash; and we meet her brother Jay (Daniel Kaluuya) whose is in and out of jail, a mess, but someone she loves and wants to help. These are the people around her and they also include Jordan (Rock plays him), a working director she with whom she has a past, and with whom she might have a future dream role if she can get her act together.

Misty Green is also a pretty depressing portrait of L.A., the land of the haves and the have nots as Rock sees it, a fairly empty place dreamers head towards with no idea how to navigate a life worth living. Really this scenario isn’t particularly fresh, but I have to say when I heard the brief synopsis I was all in. It is a bit uneven though in execution and Rock, in his role, plays it seriously until resorting to some dialogue and use of the N word that resembles his old stand up rather the guy he’s playing here. But is all lifted way up high by Eleazar who makes this all worth the ticket. She’s mesmerizing in one of the best performances by an actress this year. You believe her, you may even know her.

Among the rest of the cast the standout is Kaluuya who is heartbreaking as a young man who simply has never been able to get out of his own way, despite the best intentions. Driver gets the sleaze of his role just right, though it is a one-dimensional character. In the large cast there are some familiar walk ons such as Anthony Anderson as a cop, and even Ice T as himself.

The Los Angeles locations are well chosen giving a sense of what the city really is behind the fake glamour. Rock is a very smart performer , you can’t have doubts about that, and he has a keen eye for the underbelly of show biz, so even in a movie that is not the sum of all its parts, many of those parts are pretty good and he has delivered a film that will be remembered as the one that gave us a glimpse of the movie star Rosalind Eleazar is about to become.

Producers are Peter Rice, Rock, Victoria Thomas, and David Worthen Brooks.

Title: Misty Green

Festival: Toronto – Gala Presentations

Distributor: A24

Director/Screenplay: Chris Rock

Cast: Rosalind Eleazar, Anna Kendrick, Adam Driver, Chris Rock, Daniel Kaluuya, Topher Grace, Rich Sommer, Amy Landecker, Anthony Anderson.

Rating: R

Running Time: 1 hour and 44 minutes

title: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr Accuses James Talarico Of Running A “Hoax” With Jimmy Kimmel Sit Down; YouTube Interview Nears 7 Million Views
summary: As Jimmy Kimmel’s interview with James Talarico nears 7 million views on YouTube, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr weighed in on Saturday evening, accusing the Texas U.S. Senate candidate of orchestrating a “hoax” to drive up “clicks and donations.” Earlier this week, Kimmel told viewers that he would be sitting down with an interview with Talarico […]
content:
As Jimmy Kimmel‘s interview with James Talarico nears 7 million views on YouTube, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr weighed in on Saturday evening, accusing the Texas U.S. Senate candidate of orchestrating a “hoax” to drive up “clicks and donations.”

Earlier this week, Kimmel told viewers that he would be sitting down with an interview with Talarico for his ABC late night show, but that it would be posted to YouTube and not broadcast because of the FCC’s crackdown on its equal time rule.

In a post on X, Carr accused Talarico of “just running the same hoax he did a few months ago on Colbert for the purpose of getting clicks and donations—he’s banking on people not understanding the statute or operating as partisan lemmings.”

He also posted a meme of Talarico riding on a bicycle on Kimmel’s back before Kimmel puts a stick in the spokes and it crashes to the ground.

Watch on Deadline

Ok, fine. I’ll weigh in.



1. The Equal Time statute doesn’t apply to GameDay for several reasons.



For one, when it passed the statute, Congress applied it to broadcast tv stations—not cable programs like GameDay.



For another, Congress stated that the statute only applies to… https://t.co/r3KP7RvQL8 pic.twitter.com/m5IbEl8Ngr — Brendan Carr (@BrendanCarrFCC) September 13, 2026

A Talarico campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Kimmel interview had drawn 6.8 million views as of Saturday evening.

In February, Stephen Colbert posted an interview with Talarico to YouTube, telling viewers that he was warned by network executives about featuring the candidate on the broadcast. That interview generated 9.6 million views on YouTube. Like the Kimmel interview, the YouTube views were well over the average audience for the actual late-night broadcast.

In an interview this week, Talarico characterized the Kimmel incident as government censorship and a form of “cancel culture.” He also posted the interview to X, calling it “the interview Trump’s FCC doesn’t want you to see.”

For decades, daytime and late-night TV talk shows have operated on the assumption that they were exempt from the FCC’s equal time rule, which requires broadcasters who feature candidates to provide comparable time to their rivals, if it is requested. News coverage and news interviews have been exempt from the requirements, and the rule also does not apply cable or streaming, where the FCC’s authority is limited.

But in January, the FCC under Carr, appointed by Donald Trump, issued guidance to broadcasters that TV talk shows actually may not be exempt, a move that critics saw as a regulatory effort to crack down on daytime and late-night hosts the president does not like. Within weeks, the agency launched an investigation of ABC’s The View after it featured Talarico as a guest.

Until now, Carr had yet to weigh in on Kimmel’s latest criticisms and the decision to move the interview to YouTube. The late night host called the FCC’s equal time enforcement threats an effort to “make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept.”

On Thursday, a White House spokesperson said that Kimmel was “play acting” to “create a false narrative,” and that Carr “has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate.”

Carr has denied that the FCC’s stricter enforcement of the equal time rule was an attempt to censor guests.

On X, Carr posted, “The Equal Time statute does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast tv. It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others. Indeed, when the statute applies, it simply requires broadcast stations to offer comparable time and placement. And comparable does not necessarily mean an interview by the same person on the same program either.”

Carr’s comments were in response to a post from University of Texas Democrats, who noted the appearance of Sen. Ted Cruz (D-TX) on ESPN’s College GameDay on Saturday. The group posted on X, “So I can’t watch Talarico on Kimmel but I have to watch Ted Cruz on GameDay?”

The FCC chairman noted that the equal time rule would not apply to Cruz’s appearance because it was on a cable network and because the regulation covers only legal qualified candidates, or contenders who are in the midst of an election campaign. Cruz is not up for reelection this year; Talarico’s Republican rival is Ken Paxton.

ABC is challenging the FCC’s enforcement of the rule when it comes to The View, pointing out that the agency affirmed its exemption from the regulation in a 2002 letter.

The network also has sued the FCC on First Amendment grounds. It claims that the agency’s order that its eight owned stations submit to early license renewals is a form of regulatory retaliation, due to the Trump administration’s dislike of its news coverage and other content including The View and Kimmel.

In his post, Carr again defended the FCC’s regulatory efforts as within the bounds of the agency’s authority.

He wrote, “In exchange for that free and exclusive right to use spectrum, broadcasters made a deal with the American people. They agreed to operate, not in their own narrow interests, but in the public interest. There are various rules and policies that they must follow. This sets them apart from newspapers and cable shows and podcasts. But some broadcasters want to break their deal with the American people. They want to keep their free access to billions of dollars worth of spectrum, of course. They are less eager these days to abide by their public interest obligations.”

ABC’s legal team has argued that the FCC is engaging in selective enforcement, as its January guidance did not target conservative talk radio, and wrote that the equal time rule is unworkable for shows like The View as it puts network stations on the hook for time to potentially dozens of candidates on the ballot. Kimmel said this week that he would love to interview Paxton, but “our affiliates in Texas would have to give equal time to as many candidates as there are on the ballot. There’s about 10 candidates on the ballot.”

title: ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh  Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival
summary: After supporting roles in blockbusters like Wicked, Michelle Yeoh has her first all out starring role since winning the Best Actress Oscar for Everything Everywhere All At Once three years ago. Considering her expertise in martial arts and kick ass action (Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon for starters), her latest effort in the genre is a […]
content:
After supporting roles in blockbusters like Wicked, Michelle Yeoh has her first all out starring role since winning the Best Actress Oscar for Everything Everywhere All At Once three years ago. Considering her expertise in martial arts and kick ass action (Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon for starters), her latest effort in the genre is a lot of fun, but not for squeamish stomachs since The Surgeon makes The Pitt look like Paw Patrol. This medical thrill ride holds nothing back in exploring the human anatomy as weaponry that even John Wick would envy. Maybe we should call this one John Sick. Who needs a gun when you bring on instant death just by pulling out the colon and squeezing for 30 seconds. This movie from writer/director Dr. Roshan Sethi (A Nice Indian Boy) is a manual for turning bad guys inside out – literally.

There can be no doubt what attracted Yeoh, a supreme action star as well as serious actor, to the role of Eliza, a world renowned surgeon who has followed her Monastic code of medicine for 40 years and now is retiring. Early on a phone call from her insurance company says it all: “Should we continue insuring your hands?” and the answer is no, no longer necessary. But those plans to take it all easy are rudely interrupted when she is abducted at gunpoint by criminals and ordered to operate on their gravely ill leader, Sean (Martin Freeman). Apparently she is the only hope this crime boss has, and his henchmen, notably Cole (Yuri Kolokolnikov), an imposing Russian bad guy is watching closely to make sure she does what she is ordered to do as she cuts him open, starts removing organs, and proceeds to make the weakest among us want to reach for the barf bag. Prosthetics supervisor Suzi Battersby leaves little to the imagination. Congratulations, Suzi.

Watch on Deadline

Eliza senses once she has done the job she will be killed, but they have come to play with the wrong doc. She does make one demand, that they crank up the Thin Lizzy songs, her preferred music to cut by. It doesn’t take long before she uses her exceptional ability to turn every key body part into a death sentence, particularly in a clock ticking demonstration of how lethal her hands can be when she sets about slicing and dicing with her scalpel. Yeoh’s martial arts skills really come into play in battling these guys by manipulating their mobility in delightfully paralyzing ways.

We get a little more info on Sean in a flashback to her initial meeting with him where they talked about his dire diagnosis and knew she was likely his only ticket to live. So how could he accept she had hung up her scrubs?

In the tight 92 minute running time, Dr. Sethi shows his own bonafides by making a truly original action flick that may be the most informative trip inside the body since Fantastic Voyage. Although Freeman creates a fairly dimensional character while the other baddies are strictly stereotypes, it is Yeoh that makes this enterprise worth watching. She not only still have the action chops, she is completely believable and authentic as a doctor who has seen it all and possesses extraordinary talent in the profession. Her last stand in the operating room is one to behold.

Shout out to fight choreographer Laurent Demanioff for the dazzling moves. There can be no doubt this film, which had its world premiere tonight at the Toronto International Film Festival, is a tailor made vehicle guaranteed to turn up the temperature for Yeoh fans everywhere all at once.

Producers are Basil Iwanyk, Erica Lee, Diarmaid McGrath, Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Neil Shah, Steve Klinsky, Adam Kolbrenner, John Schoenfelder, Russell Ackerman.

Title: The Surgeon

Festival: Toronto – Centerpiece

Director/Screenwriter: Dr. Roshan Sethi

Cast: Michelle Yeoh, Martin Freeman, Laurie Davidson, Yuri Kolokolnikov, Joseph Mydell

Running Time: One Hour and 32 Minutes

Sales Agent: WME; 193(International Sales)

title: Bill Dubuque Crime-Drama ‘M.I.A.’ Canceled At Peacock After One Season
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Peacock has canceled the Miami-set crime-drama series M.I.A. after one season. The series, from creator, writer, and executive producer Bill Dubuque, premiered on May 7 with all 9 hour-long episodes. Following the show’s premiere, there was a lot of buzz around M.I.A. It received an extra push from NBC with a special airing on the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Peacock has canceled the Miami-set crime-drama series M.I.A. after one season. The series, from creator, writer, and executive producer Bill Dubuque, premiered on May 7 with all 9 hour-long episodes.

Following the show’s premiere, there was a lot of buzz around M.I.A. It received an extra push from NBC with a special airing on the network on May 14. In a unique move, M.I.A. was one of the few shows that was set in Miami and was also shot there. Details regarding the reason for the cancellation are unknown.

In M.I.A., running drugs is a family affair for Etta Tiger Jonze (Shannon Gisela). But when the family business is threatened, she is thrust into a life she never expected, forcing her to use her wits to survive as she navigates Miami’s criminal underground.

The cast also included Cary Elwes, Danay Garcia, Brittany Adebumola, Dylan Jackson, Alberto Guerra, Maurice Compte, Gerardo Celasco, and Marta Milans.

Watch on Deadline

Karen Campbell served as the show’s showrunner, writer (102), and executive producer. Alethea Jones directed the first two episodes of the series and executive produced. Additional directors and their episodes include: Gwyneth Horder-Payton (103), Marizee Almas (104, 105), Ben Semanoff (106, 107), and John Dahl (108, 109). MRC is the studio, and Paramount Global Content Distribution is the distributor.

title: Tom Nicoll Looks Beyond Male Influencer Culture in TIFF Title ‘Salvation’: ‘I Don’t Think Anyone’s Ever Been Insulted Into Changing Their Mind’
summary: Scottish writer-director Tom Nicoll is unveling at Toronto his buzzy debut “Salvation.” It tracks an aspiring online life coach whose attempt to reinvent himself and then sell that transformation to others pulls him in increasingly desperate directions. The psychological and blackly comic thriller world premieres in TIFF’s Discovery section, having already been selected for the […]
content:
Scottish writer-director Tom Nicoll is unveling at Toronto his buzzy debut “Salvation.” It tracks an aspiring online life coach whose attempt to reinvent himself and then sell that transformation to others pulls him in increasingly desperate directions.

The psychological and blackly comic thriller world premieres in TIFF’s Discovery section, having already been selected for the BFI and British Council’s Great 8 showcase at Cannes. MetFilm Sales recently boarded world sales on the film, which stars Liam Harkins, Stephen McMillan, Kathleen McDermott and Conor McCarron.

Set largely in Greenock, a post-industrial Scottish town, “Salvation” follows Danny Carlton, played by Harkins, as he emerges from a self-improvement retreat convinced he has found the way forward. Having been transformed, at least in his own mind, by charismatic guru Marshall Allison (Kevin O’Loughlin), Danny sets off to build a life coaching business of his own. The problem is that virtually nobody wants what he is selling while the money he has spent and borrowed pursuing it grows.

Popular on Variety

For Nicoll, the film was never primarily about finding easy targets in the world of male influencers.

“I suppose, in general, in my life, I’m interested in that idea of what people find purpose in, what people choose to do with their lives, what they find value in, what they choose to put their energy into,” he told Variety. With Danny, that became a question of “what is lacking” to compel someone’s move towards a culture offering answers, status and self-optimization.

“I don’t think anyone’s ever been insulted into changing their mind,” Nicoll explained. “It’s easy to point and laugh at someone.” A sweeping satire of the influencer sphere might provide “easy jokes” for five or ten minutes, he argues, but understanding why somebody is susceptible is the harder and more interesting motivation to pursue.

We see Danny’s excitement and defence of his new found answers among a doubtful circle of family and acquaintances. His confidence might be misplaced, but he isn’t cynical. When he tells Scott, a depressed young man played by Stephen McMillan who comes to see him, all he’s learnt and how he wants to help he’s genuine.

“He really means that when he’s saying that Marshall saved him from a very dark place,” says Nicoll. “That is, I think, a crucial part of the character.” Over the course of the film, “the economic imperative kind of takes over,” altering the relationship between Danny and Scott as the former discovers the wordplay he absorbed as self-help can turn into a tool for manipulation.

The result is a chain of unequal relationships: Marshall has power over Danny, while Danny gains power over Scott. For Nicoll, that dynamic goes beyond any single strain of digital culture.

“Most people could probably relate to the idea of when you go online and someone’s telling you how to eat better or exercise better or be happier, be in a better relationship,” he said. At a moment of insecurity, the promise that somebody else knows how to sort it can prove hard to resist.

Nicoll had previously directed Liam Harkins in short “Lighting Tests” and wrote Danny around a rare combination he saw in the actor: an outwardly conventional masculinity alongside vulnerability, sensitivity and comedic timing.

“I had the idea for the story and thought he would be perfect for the role,” said Nicoll, who sent drafts back and forth to Harkins roughly a year before shooting. “I knew that on a production standpoint, he would just be the rock that could build the production around.”

The relationship at the film’s centre needed warmth as well as exploitation. The director recalls nervously arranging a Zoom between his two leads prior to filming, preparing questions in case conversation petered out.

“I think I probably said about three things in the hour,” he says. “They were just chatting, getting to know each other, and then just talking about the characters.” A later read-through of three key scenes confirmed the chemistry: “It was an amazing one of being like, ‘Oh, we’ve got something here.’”

That closeness is gradually squeezed by the film’s visual language. Working with cinematographer Alex Grigoras, Nicoll chose a 4:3 frame. “We always knew it was going to be a film of faces,” he says. The format offered intimacy and, as Danny’s choices reduce, claustrophobia. Centering him clarifies his self-absorption. He is initially, “the centre of his own world.”

The use of long lenses compress the spaces around him, particularly in the interiors, while stillness releases giving way to unsettled camerawork as the predicament deteriorates.

Composer Salla Luhtala’s score pushes in almost the opposite direction. At the start, as Danny leaves the retreat filled with new conviction, the music enlarges his modest circumstances matching the way he sees himself.

“It’s like the world is his oyster. That’s what he feels like,” Nicoll explained. “It should feel like he’s reborn. It should feel like new momentum. It should feel like the new life is calling him.” Rather than standing outside Danny and mocking the fantasy, Nicoll wanted audiences pulled into it.

“Salvation” is as Indie as it gets assembled through self-financing and crowdfunding, with Screen Scotland boarding late and providing £45,000 ($60,750) through its Production Growth Fund. Shot around Greenock and Glasgow, the production initially completed 15 days before returning months later for a few more days.

“That’s the nature of independent filmmaking, I suppose,” he says. But the enforced pause became “an amazing opportunity,” allowing a chance to clarify the story and add “scale and cinematic scope at the right moments.”

Nicoll looked to an American independent tradition for ways of making those limitations feel like choices. Sean Baker’s “Red Rocket” and earlier work were reference points, as was Kelly Reichardt’s “Old Joy”: films capable of retaining a distinct voice without requiring vast resources.

And what of that word “Salvation”?

“It’s the kind of underpinning, I think, of a lot of these self-help ideas,” says Nicoll. “You can be saved from this thing, and you can move into a kind of hallowed place, or a place free of this previous pain or this previous deficiency. And I don’t know if I believe in that.”

The film isn’t interested in providing a clean, moralistic conclusion. The director prefers films that resist “easy answers,” leaving open the question of whether Danny is capable of deep reflection or likely to place explanations for everything that has happened to him elsewhere.

For a film that Nicoll describes as “an independent film in its bones,” there is buzz around it. MetFilm Sales’ acquisition adds a strong international sales push to a run that has included Great 8 and selection as one of Screen International’s Rising Stars Scotland 2026.

“It’s been pretty wild,” Nicoll said. “It’s pretty much close to best-case scenario” for a film made this way. More importantly, he adds, “it is the film I wanted to make.”

The recognition offers the possibility of scaling up, something the writer-director is keen to pursue as he looks to move beyond the indie and micro-budget level. He has several scripts in various stages, including larger-scale thriller and horror projects. “Ambition can be talked about just as it relates to budget, but I think it’s about your approach to characters and characterisation, and how deep you’re willing to go in terms of excavating what it is to be human,” he says. “That’s what ambition is about in filmmaking to me, and that’s what I would want to take going forward, no matter the level of budget.”

title: Yoon Dan-bi’s Toronto and San Sebastian Film ‘The World Before’ Gives Its Camera a Soul and Its Island a Voice
summary: Seven years after “Moving On,” Korean filmmaker Yoon Dan-bi returns with “The World Before,” a coming-of-age film about desire and first love. Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s Toronto Film Festival Platform world premiere, Yoon discusses how capturing the authenticity of change worked its way at every stage of the production. “I want to […]
content:
Seven years after “Moving On,” Korean filmmaker Yoon Dan-bi returns with “The World Before,” a coming-of-age film about desire and first love.

Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s Toronto Film Festival Platform world premiere, Yoon discusses how capturing the authenticity of change worked its way at every stage of the production.

“I want to make films about things that can’t be described in one sentence,” says Yoon. “In my previous movie I wanted to capture nostalgia, here I wanted to capture the restlessness, that fever you experience when innocence turns into desire.”

The coming-of-age story follows 17-year-old Jin and her unexpected reunion with childhood friend Du-jae, who returns for his grandmother’s funeral on a remote Korean island. For Yoon, narrating the chapter that marks the end of childhood and the beginning of adulthood required focusing on her character’s inner turmoil, but also very much on their physicality.

Popular on Variety

“As well as emotion, I’m very keen on observing people’s movement,” she explains. “When the feeling of desire is born, how does it affect movement? How do they let their guard down when they love, hug each other, unexpectedly hold hands? I wanted to portray that desire in a very realistic way, without being overtly sexual.”

That attention changed drastically how she used the camera. While ‘Moving On’’s stationary and observational lens blurred the line so well between reality and fiction that many commented it felt it was a documentary, Yoon tried another technique in “The World Before.”

“The camera moves around a lot as if it had its own soul,” says Yoon. “I wanted to move it unexpectedly to create a rhythm. For example, there’s a scene on the beach with Jin and Du-jae where you see the light coming in, then the sun goes behind the clouds and comes out again. It was all natural light when we were shooting,” she pauses to laugh. “My crew told me this effect can be done in post production, but I tend not to believe them and I prefer to wait.”

Yoon is grateful to her crew, who she says had a hard time rescheduling shoots, staged across two islands during the hot, humid months of the Korean summer, when a typhoon came around. They also had to carry all the equipment without cars as Soan-do, one of the islands located in Wando County off the southern coast, had no bridge connecting to the mainland. “We wanted rain scenes,” she adds, “but it didn’t rain that summer.”

Still, Yoon loves the aesthetics of this period which she describes as the season of growing up. Lulled by the chant of cicadas, the island’s bright stillness offers the perfect contrast to the movement Yoon chases – light inching on naked skin and leaves blowing in the wind.

“Soando feels very much like how the countryside used to be in Korea,” Yoon notes. “The main labor there is fishing abalone and seaweed, they’re pretty much self sufficient. The villagers offered help and invited us for food, which helped the actors to adapt to island life quickly. But looking back, I realized I went with a sort of prejudice, I thought everyone would want to escape but it turns out they all wanted to stay there.”

The correction found its way into the character: “Jin likes living on the island and doesn’t even consider leaving,” Yoon says. Other surprises made it into the film as well – a local grandmother was cast for the opening scene after the villagers pronounced her the best singer among them ; an improvised moment between the young leads watching ants by the roadside, became one of the movie’s authentic snippets of life. But those additions are only possible because the script is written to accommodate them.
