title: Angelina Jolie and Salma Hayek Pinault on Their New Film ‘Without Blood’ and Spending ‘A Lot of Time Talking About Our Pain, Our Losses, Our Traumas’
summary: In “Without Blood,” written and directed by Angelina Jolie, Salma Hayek plays Nina, a woman who spends her adult life looking for the three men responsible for the wartime murder of her father and brother when she was just a child. In two of the cases, her revenge is fatal. But then she meets the […]
content:
In “Without Blood,” written and directed by Angelina Jolie, Salma Hayek plays Nina, a woman who spends her adult life looking for the three men responsible for the wartime murder of her father and brother when she was just a child.

In two of the cases, her revenge is fatal. But then she meets the third accomplice, Tito (Demián Bichir), now a clerk in a newspaper kiosk at a train station.

The movie is in many ways a two-hander featuring Nina and Tito talking over drinks with flashback scenes chronicling both of their sometimes harrowing lives.

“I was afraid that I couldn’t play this part, and also I was afraid to go so far every day at work and go into this really difficult place,” Hayek says during a joint interview with Jolie. “At the beginning, I wasn’t sure that Angelina was directing. I thought she was just producing. I’m like, ‘Oh no, I don’t want to suffer like that. I don’t want to.’ And then she started talking to me about the importance of the piece. And then you have to understand that Angelina is an extraordinary director.”

Popular on Variety

Salma Hayek Pinault stars in “Without Blood.” Courtesy Image

“Without Blood” is an adaptation of Italian writer Alessandro Baricco’s novella of the same name. Like the book, the movie doesn’t specify the time or the location where the story takes place, nor identify the war at the center of the story. The characters speak English and Spanish.

“I wanted it to be that anyone watching it from anywhere could identify with it,” Jolie says. “Even if it wasn’t an actual war or a conflict, there’s something beautiful in the book where it says, ‘We return to where we break.’ So part of the conflict and the idea of the film is that anybody can identify with something in your life where something happened where it broke you and changed you, and how much you wish you could sit across from that person and have answers and have some kind of say your piece and hope that they could see you and hope that it gives you some kind of healing or closure. Of course, sometimes it doesn’t give you what you think you’re looking for or doesn’t heal those.”

This isn’t the first time Jolie has made a film about war and conflict. Her directorial debut was the Bosnian war drama “In the Land of Blood and Money” in 2011. “Unbroken” (2014) told the story of American prisoners-of-war during World War II. The life of Cambodian author and human rights activist Loung Ung under the rule of the Khmer Rouge was the subject of “First They Killed My Father” in 2017.

“In ‘First They Killed My Father,’ we had trauma therapy tents because a lot of people there had been through war and I’ve learned that everybody’s been through some level of trauma,” Jolie says. “What we did on this was the time spent with everybody discussing it. We all ended up spending a lot of time talking about our pain, talking about our losses, our traumas. Obviously, community can be very, very healing.”

Jolie and Hayek Pinault first worked together five years ago when they co-starred in the Marvel movie “Eternals.” Next, Jolie will serve as a producer on Hayek Pinault’s directorial debut, “Arena,” an epic romantic adventure that the “Frida” star also wrote.

“In a way, she’s my partner,” Hayek Pinault says. “I’ve written two different scripts with two different pens that she gave me. It’s a really good, enriching and artistic relationship. That is hard to find. It’s such a gift.”

I asked Jolie if she’s ever been tempted to direct lighter material like a comedy. “We’ve laughed a lot. We fantasized about making different comedies together,” Hayek Pinault says.

Jolie laughs, “My comedies tend to be a bit dark. I think I have a dark sense of humor.”

Hayek Pinault turns to Jolie and says, “You’re funny. So funny. She just keeps it a secret.”

Jolie isn’t sure she has what it takes to helm comedy. “I don’t know how good I’d be. You have those things that we think, as an actress, you like to try everything and then you get to a point you realize other actors are good at certain things and there are many who are better at comedy than I am. But I do think I’m a pretty good straight person, like the ‘Maleficent.’ I’m a good straight.”

“Without Blood” is in theaters now.

title: Paramount and California AG Bonta Reportedly in ‘Advanced Talks’ to Settle Antitrust Suit
summary: David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance is in “advanced talks” with California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the 12-state antitrust suit that’s holding up its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing anonymous sources. A Paramount spokesperson declined to comment. A rep for Bonta’s office said, “Potential settlement talks are confidential. […]
content:
David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance is in “advanced talks” with California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the 12-state antitrust suit that’s holding up its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing anonymous sources.

A Paramount spokesperson declined to comment. A rep for Bonta’s office said, “Potential settlement talks are confidential. We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”

Per the Journal’s report, the talks are “ongoing and there is no guarantee that an agreement will be reached.” Paramount and the California AG have “discussed compromises including Paramount agreeing to operate the two companies’ movie studios separately for a period rather than immediately combining them,” according to the WSJ article.

Popular on Variety

However, Bonta has previously said that running the two companies separately — but under common ownership — would be a mere “behavioral” remedy, and that he is looking for a structural remedy that would entail separate ownership.

RELATED STORY: Who is Rob Bonta and Why is California’s Attorney General Suing to Block Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger?

A judge has scheduled a trial in the matter for March 2027. Paramount had requested that the 12 states — and the Writers Guild of America, which also has filed an antitrust suit seeking to block the Paramount-WBD deal — post a $1.88 billion bond to cover its potential losses from a “ticking fee” payable to WBD shareholders (starting as of Oct. 1 at a rate of $7 million per day) if Paramount ends up prevailing in court. A hearing on the bond motion is set for Sept. 24.

Ellison’s $111 billion pending deal for Warner Bros. Discovery is being bankrolled in part by his mega-billionaire father, Larry Ellison, as well as the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. On Thursday, the FCC approved Paramount’s petition to allow 49.5% of its equity to be held by foreign entities if the Warner Bros. Discovery is consummated.

David Ellison has internally told Paramount execs he’s seriously considering relocating the company’s operations — including, over a longer time horizon, its studio — out of California if Paramount is unable to close the Warner Bros. deal by the end of September. He’s floated the possibility of moving the company to Tennessee, Texas or Georgia.

title: ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Says No GenAI Was Used In Making Of Show: “There Hasn’t Really Been A Need”
summary: Despite VisionQuest‘s subject matter as the first solo outing of the title artificial intelligence, the Marvel series kept things strictly human-made. Series creator Terry Matalas recently confirmed there was no GenAI used in the making of the Disney+ series, which debuts Oct. 14 on the streamer, noting there wasn’t “a need” for the tech. “No, […]
content:
Despite VisionQuest‘s subject matter as the first solo outing of the title artificial intelligence, the Marvel series kept things strictly human-made.

Series creator Terry Matalas recently confirmed there was no GenAI used in the making of the Disney+ series, which debuts Oct. 14 on the streamer, noting there wasn’t “a need” for the tech.

“No, not at all. There hasn’t really been a need,” Matalas told ScreenRant. “All the designs nod to how our current form of AI processes things… That felt like a fun way for us to comment on it.”

Production designer Will Hughes-Jones explained that his team employed human creativity to emulate the flawed look of AI software renderings.

Watch on Deadline

Set after the events of WandaVision (2021), VisionQuest follows the resurrected android Vision (Paul Bettany) as he goes on a journey of self-discovery with help from AI personas embedded into his programming, all while a bounty is placed on his head.

In May, Disney pulled the plug on its $1B investment in OpenAI’s Sora, putting an end to the use of Disney’s extensive character catalogue in the text-to-video app.

title: Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings
summary: They’re talking! Or are they? And what are they actually talking about? Does everyone need to chill out? Paramount and state attorneys general are talking, we are told. However, the discussions that are occurring over coming to a deal in the battle over Paramount’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery are far from advanced. […]
content:
They’re talking! Or are they? And what are they actually talking about? Does everyone need to chill out?

Paramount and state attorneys general are talking, we are told. However, the discussions that are occurring over coming to a deal in the battle over Paramount’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery are far from advanced.

In fact, sources tell us, the conversations that are occurring between David Ellison’s team and California AG Rob Bonta’s crew are centered on laying out the agenda for their already scheduled mid-October court ordered settlement discussions. “This is part of the process before you get the principals onboard, it’s pretty straightforward,” declares an individual with direct knowledge of the state of affairs. “The end is not nigh.”

Earlier this week, a federal judge made it official and ordered Para, WBD and the AGs to appear for a two-day settlement conference October 14-15 in a San Francisco courtroom.

Watch on Deadline

Core to the discussions will be scenarios like Paramount potentially operating the film and TV studios of Paramount and Warner Bros. separately, at least for a period of time after the close. Bonta has said a “behavioral remedy” like the company agreeing to release at least 30 films a year, will not satisfy the plaintiffs. Along with studio consolidation, cable network concentration is a key part of the states’ complaint, with speculation centering on some way of moving some of the 50-plus cable networks out of the combined portfolio to avoid running afoul of antitrust limits.

Eyebrows (and hopes) were raised late Friday about a potential resolution of Paramount’s legally waylaid WBD merger. The Wall Street Journal reported tonight that Paramount is in “advanced talks” with California’s Bonta over a settlement of the antitrust suit being brought by the Golden State AG and 11 other states.

Shares in Paramount, which are down 23% in 2026 to date amid mounting uncertainty about the fate of the merger, jumped 5% in after-hours trading. WBD stock, which is also underwater for the year, rose 6% after hours.

After Donald Trump’s DOJ and other major jurisdictions approved the mega-merger with no conditions, the dozen attorneys general filed a much-expected antitrust suit against Para and WBD on July 13. The case, set to go to trial on March 2, 2027, has seen an explosion of threats that Paramount would move to a red state, “blackmail” accusations by Bonta and a media war in the court of public opinion. It could also cost Ellison and his Oracle founding father Larry Ellison some sweet cash with a $7 million a day ticking fee set to WBD shareholders to start on October 1.

In that context, talk of advanced talks is just another piece of that PR puzzle.

“I get why some want this to look bigger than it is, there’s a lot of pressure here,” an insider notes. “This is too big, too much on the line for anyone to rush a deal,” the source added. “Hold your horses. No one wants to waste anyone’s time.”

As with initial talks last month, it is mid-level staff that are in communication as the brass stay above the fray, as it is, we hear.

Paramount had a blunt “no comment” on whether negotiations with the AGs were going on and what the status of them are at present.

Having called out Paramount previously for alleged leaks that scuttled the last set of behind the scenes talks, Rob Bonta’s office today were 100% by the book. “Potential settlement talks are confidential,” a spokesperson for the CA AG told Deadline In the non-answer answer they added: “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”

While there appeared to be reason for optimism (mild as it is at this stage) there are many caveats to consider — and not just because there is a big Paramount+ streamed UFC fight out of L.A. this Yom Kippur weekend.

Getty Images

The latest word of discussions follows an ill-fated sequence in August. Bonta canceled negotiations hours before they were set to take place, accusing Ellison of “playing games” ahead of those meetings. “Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” Bonta said at the time.

Even as recently as Thursday of this week, when Bonta made an appearance at the Atlantic Festival in New York, the top cop of California said the fate of the deal “lies at the feet” of Ellison and the Paramount team. A follow up sit-down on MS Now, Democrats’ favorite cabler newser, contained much of the same even as Paramount leaks tried to up the ante on the Melrose lot packing up for Tennessee, Texas or Georgia.

Sources tell us Bonta had a “conversation” with fellow ParaBros antitrust plaintiff NY AG Letitia James while out on the East Coast this week. To that, it is not clear if AG Bonta is back on the West Coast tonight.

The leverage has been heavily on the side of the AGs since a string of rulings in the case by a federal judge favored the plaintiffs. Even when it came to setting a date for the antitrust trial, the judge landed on early March, which was a lot closer to the AGs’ preference of April than to Paramount’s stated desire for November.

Despite momentum in the case, high-profile Democrats in California, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and L.A. Mayor Karen Bass, have publicly pressured Bonta multiple times to settle the case. The ambitious Newsom and reelection-fighting Bass fear damage to the industry, L.A. and the state if the deal remains pending for several months. At the same time, of course, a damning August report delivered to L.A. County from the region’s Department of Economic Opportunity says the $80 billion debt ladened merger will likely cause the loss of thousands of jobs, adding to the pain for a region already facing a downturn in production and other headwinds.

The job loss and economic pain could be much greater if Paramount makes good on their threat to leave L.A., says a September 10 report to the County from the Economic Development Corporation. On the flip side, that same leaked EDC report, which Paramount commissioned, also told the powerful Board of Supervisors that ailing Hollywood would be boomtown if ParaBros went though with jobs and productions galore.

As well, the ParaBros court calendar is looking pretty full even before those official settlement talks of next month and the spring 2027 trial. A hearing will be held next week in Oakland on Paramount’s request for a $1.88 billion bond from the plaintiffs to cover “extraordinary losses” the company anticipates due to having to pay those pricey ticking fee during litigation. On September 25, the blue state AGs have to respond to a motion from red state Iowa and Montana to take the validity of the antitrust suit to the Supreme Court.

title: John Wilson Lays Down ‘The History of Concrete’ With ‘The Weight’, ‘Shaun The Sheep’ In Packed Indie Weekend – Specialty Preview
summary: It’s a busy specialty weekend with fewer new studio releases. Well-reviewed Depression-era western The Weight starring Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe in wide release joins comedic doc The History of Concrete by John Wilson in an exclusive engagement. GKids opens Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom and Johnny Knoxville statrs in R-rated Tiny […]
content:
It’s a busy specialty weekend with fewer new studio releases. Well-reviewed Depression-era western The Weight starring Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe in wide release joins comedic doc The History of Concrete by John Wilson in an exclusive engagement. GKids opens Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom and Johnny Knoxville statrs in R-rated Tiny Fugitives. From TIFF, Angelina Jolie’s drama Without Blood and doc You Had To Be There (full title below) how a 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell changed the comedy world.

The Weight from Vertical opens in wide release on 1,504 screens. Director Padraic McKinley’s feature film debut stars Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe. Certified Fresh at 93% on Rotten Tomatoes, it premiered at Sundance, see Deadline review. Opened the Deauville Film Festival earlier this month with Hawk receiving the Deauville Talent Award celebrating exceptional artists in cinema.

Watch on Deadline

Referenced as harkening back to classics such as William Friedkin’s Sorcerer and John Huston’s Treasure of the Sierra Madre, The Weight is set in Oregon in 1933 as Samuel Murphy (Hawke) is torn from his daughter and sent to a brutal work camp. Warden Clancy (Crowe) tempts him with early release if he smuggles gold through deadly wilderness, but betrayal festers within the crew, and Murphy questions how far he’ll go to see his child again.

Preview events this week included an AMC Dolby Cinema Early Access screening program at 200+ theaters and an Alamo Drafthouse simulcast screening across the chain’s markets followed by a live Q&A with Ethan Hawke, co-star Julia Jones and McKinley from the Booklyn location.

Magnolia Pictures drops Sundance-premiering The History Of Concrete by the host of HBO series How To With John Wilson at the IFC Center in New York. The comedic documentary is loosely structured around and inspired by cement, the world’s most widely used building material and the bedrock of Wilson’s beloved New York City. He bounces from Rome to check out the Pantheon, built in 126 AD (the world’s largest unreinforced concrete dome), to a concrete convention in Vegas, with long digressions into Hallmark moviemaking, tattoo taxidermy and New York’s underground music scene — interspersed with musings on his career path and Zoom meetings with perplexed potential investors in the project.

Wilson’s HBO series ran for three seasons from 2020-2023. The History of Concrete sits at 100% RT score (off 41 reviews). Based on presales, it’s looking like the best opening for a documentary in IFC’s 21-year history, as per Magnolia. The distributor went heavy on the NYC premiere Wednesday with a concrete truck wrapped in the film’s title treatment parked outside the theater, and a 125-pound poster made entirely from concrete in the lobby. Expands to 20 markets including LA next week.

Greenwich Entertainment is out with You Had To Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (In a Canadian Kind of Way) by Nick Davis at Film Forum in NYC. Eugene Levy, Martin Short, Jayne Eastwood and more reminisce about the 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell, where Short, Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Paul Shaffer and other entertainment icons got their start. Premiered at TIFF, See Deadline review. Executive produced by Judd Apatow. Adds LA and other markets next week.

Without Blood from Brainstorm Media, directed by Angelina Jolie and starring Salma Hayek and Demián Bichir, opens on 350 screens. Jolie also produced and penned the screenplay based on the book of the same name by Italian writer Alessandro Baricco. A young woman seeks a reckoning decades after surviving the brutal murder of her family during a wartime conflict. Premiered at TIFF, see Deadline review.

Moderate/Wide: GKids is releasing StudioCanal and Aardman production Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom on 2,173 screens. The film is currently Certified Fresh at 98% on RT. Official synopsis: “The residents of Mossy Bottom Farm are looking forward to Halloween – until the clumsy Farmer trashes the Flock’s beloved pumpkin patch! When Shaun turns MAD SCIENTIST to fix the problem, things rapidly spiral out of control… With The Farmer missing and a wild beast roaming the woods of Mossingham, all the ingredients are in place for a monstrously fun family adventure.”

Indie distributor Inaugural Entertainment opens raunchy R-rated comedy Tiny Fugitives starring Johnny Knoxville, in about 300 theaters. Co-written and directed by Michael Lewen, it follows a reckless, fiercely determined group of twelve-year-olds who hatch a chaotic plot to escape reality and spend the rest of their lives at sleepaway camp. Standing between them and permanent freedom is Bob (Knoxville), the camp’s deranged, relentless, 50-year-old lifer counselor. With Aaron Harris (Matlock), Isa Bernal Steiner, Jai Soundar, Alyssa Gervasi, with Blake Anderson (Workaholics) and Jay Baruchel (How to Train Your Dragon).

Sundance-premiering The Musical by Giselle Bonilla, written by Alexander Heller and starring Will Brill (Tony-winner for Stereophonic ), Gillian Jacobs and Rob Lowe (who also produces) is out on 250 screens. Convinced he’s a big fish stuck in a small pond, bitter playwright Doug Leibowitz has been marking time as a theater teacher until he can get to New York. But when he finds his ex has been dating the person he hates most in the world, the school principal, his plans shift to secretly staging the most inappropriate play possible at the middle school. Unapologetic Partners, Blue Harbor Entertainment and Variance Films are partnering on the release.

Live-action biblical drama Daniel And The Fiery Furnace from EKKL Entertainment arrives on 1,493 screens this weekend. Written and directed by Matthew and Daniel Kooman, this is the origin story of the prophet Daniel against the backdrop of exile in Babylon.

Limited: Watermelon Pictures opens Traces of Home by Colette Ghunim at the Angelika in NYC. The doc follows the filmmaker on a journey of self-discovery as she sets out to reunite her parents with the ancestral homes they were forced to flee as children in Palestine and Mexico. Filmed over five years and featuring animation and archival footage. Executive produced by Melissa Barrera and John Leguizamo. Winner of the Grand Jury Prize in U.S. Competition at DOC NYC last November and Best Documentary Feature at San Diego Latino Film Festival. Expands to Laemmle Royal and Laemmle Glendale in LA next week.

As Alex Gibney’s Musk makes headlines, the Oscar-winning documentarian has another film out this weekend — Knife: The Attempted Murder Of Salman Rushdie opens in 18 theaters via Abramorama. Featuring the writer and his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths and inspired by Rushdie’s memoir Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder, it explores his recovery from a 2022 attack at a speaking engagement where was stabbed 15 times. With personal footage that has never been seen by the public, the doc follows the writer on his physical and spiritual recovery.

Quiver Distribution debuts Berlin-premiering coming of age drama Sunny Dancer on about 20 screens. A group of teenagers find friendship at a summer camp for cancer survivors. Stars Bella Ramsey, Neil Patrick Harris, James Norton and Jessica Gunning with a score by Este Haim.

Fourth Act Film opens SXSW-premiering documentary First They Came For My College directed and produced by Patrick Bresnan about a right-wing takeover of liberal arts school the New College of Florida orchestrated by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. World Premiered at True/False and screened at DC/DOX, IFF Boston, SFFILM and the Florida Film Festival, where it won the Feature Documentary Audience Award. Starts at the Hippodrome in Gainesville, Fla. and rolls out to about 30 markets, hitting DCTV in New York City on Sept. 25.

More to come

title: ‘Magazine’ Review:  Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY’s Literary World – Toronto Film Festival
summary: Perhaps the title of this Toronto Film Festival premiere says it all. Magazine is a period piece set in a pre-digital world as the long proud tradition of print publications is about to end in favor of quick hits and screen-reading in a new and strange universe ruled by social media, not the once smart […]
content:
Perhaps the title of this Toronto Film Festival premiere says it all. Magazine is a period piece set in a pre-digital world as the long proud tradition of print publications is about to end in favor of quick hits and screen-reading in a new and strange universe ruled by social media, not the once smart and thriving intellectual world of New York City publishing. It is this period circa 2011 that debuting feature filmmaker Alexandra Pechman tackles here in a style reminiscent of movies made by Whit Stillman, some influences of Noah Baumbach, but I would go back even to 1977’s now nostalgic look at a struggling indie Boston newspaper, Joan Micklin Silver’s Between the Lines.

There are echoes of all of them in this slight but well-cast story of the monthly New Yorker-lite magazine called Platen, a safe place for authors with audacious stories to tell, ruled by a staff of bright pseudo-elitists that viewed now look like a tribe long ago and far away. That it has been just 15 years since the setting of this movie, only shows how far we have — and haven’t — come in a rapidly-paced environment that no longer stops to smell the roses, value content over Kindles, words over hits.

Watch on Deadline

The focus of Pechman, though is all on the fresh faced, eager, non-paid summer interns getting their first taste of the then-real world of niche publications, because that is what Platen is all about. As in any movie like this we have our protagonist, Nora (Lily McInerny) as she stands eagerly in front of the building, checking her watch, careful not to be exactly on time for her first day as an intern. She clearly has visions of belonging in this place, and whatever college preparation there was, this is the real deal. She is welcomed by other interns including the warm and fun Tabitha (Shrinking’s Lupita Maxwell) and nerdy Leonard (a funny Daniel Zolghadri), along with the more colorful Daphne (Iris Apatow). And then at the corner desk in front there is the guy who clearly sets his sights on Nora almost immediately, editorial assistant Thomas (Joshuah Melnick), the kind of Lothario who eyes his prey instantly, although we don’t quite know that yet. We will.

Nora finds out soon as she ends up in Thomas’ bed in no time, a new relationship that probably isn’t such a wise move for a young woman whose big hope is that a prized position might open up at Platen during her time there. She proves proficient at copy reading, correcting mistakes, menial work, but is it enough to stand out? Pechman sets this all up between the various characters, each with hopes of getting the gig that doesn’t yet exist, and then soon brings in the lively Greer (Ruby Cruz) to add to the mix as she and the others vie for the job that does eventually surface. She and Nora become friends but it is clear Greer may be a stronger candidate than any of them.

Lording over everything is Mickey (an amusing Jake Lacy), the publisher who offers wisdom to the newbies like, “a magazine is like a snapshot of a single moment in time, and then it’s gone.” It is a prophetic line considering how fast the world is leaving this kind of enterprise behind. Beyond the competition for full-time employment and the unfortunate sexual advances of Thomas (this is all clearly pre #MeToo) and the subplot of that relationship, what we have is a group of young hopefuls getting their first taste of a world they would very much like to live in permanently. Not all of them will, but you have the feeling this bunch, especially Nora, will find their own path after a memorable summer and a taste of the realities of being a tiny fish swimming upstream in the big city. In the meantime, why not just dance?

Pechman has made a handsome-looking, well-appointed film for her first feature, one that in style feels oddly out of time as much as the subject matter does. What it undoubtedly will be remembered for its engaging young cast. It is nice to know this kind of independently made small slice of life is still getting financed. It is like a little antidote to The Devil Wears Prada, but it works on its own modest terms.

Producers are Pechman, Anne Alexander and Tess Cohen.

Title: Magazine

Festival: Toronto (Discovery)

Director-screenwriter: Alexandra Pechman

Cast: Lily McInerny, Lukita Maxwell, Joshuah Melnick, Iris Apatow, Ruby Cruz, Daniel Zolghadri, AnnaSophia Robb, Delaney Rowe, Jake Lacy, Sasha Bhasin, Alex Edelman

Sales agent: UTA

Running time: 1 hr 45 mins

title: World Premiering at San Sebastián, Igor Legarreta Describes His Third Film ‘The Blind Ants’ as a Coastal Western Set in the Basque Country
summary: “The Blind Ants” (“Inurri Itsuak”), the third feature by director Igor Legarreta (“All the Moons,” “When You Stop Loving Me”), had it world premiere on Sept. 18 at the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival. Part of the Zinemira section, which is dedicated to Basque productions, the film is competing for the Irizar Award for […]
content:
“The Blind Ants” (“Inurri Itsuak”), the third feature by director Igor Legarreta (“All the Moons,” “When You Stop Loving Me”), had it world premiere on Sept. 18 at the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival. Part of the Zinemira section, which is dedicated to Basque productions, the film is competing for the Irizar Award for Basque Cinema. It will be in Spanish theaters on Oct. 9, distributed by Buena Vista International Spain.

Set in the Basque Country in 1930, the film tells the story of an English ship that is stranded on the shores of Biscay during a violent storm. Holding tons of valuable coal, the local people of Algorta scramble to rescue some of it in order to help them survive a harsh winter. The Jauregui family decides to risk it all and brave the unrelenting storm in order to keep some of the black gold. Their decision leads to tragic consequences that will change them forever.

“We launched a production company in the Basque Country with a clear vision: to combine our strengths with local talent to create films that are artistically ambitious and uncompromising in their production values. We achieved this with “Inurri Itsuak”: a Basque-language film with international appeal and high production value that tells a story as deeply rooted in the local context as that of Ramiro Pinilla. Partnering with Playtime for international sales and Buena Vista for distribution in Spain will help the film reach the widest possible audience, Lazona Zinema producer Luis Ferrón told Variety.

Popular on Variety

‘The Blind Ants.’ Photo Credit: Imanol Nabea

“The Blind Ants” stars Urko Olazábal (Goya Award for Best Supporting Actor for “Maixabel,” nominated for Best Lead Actor for “Soy Nevenka”), Itziar Ituño (“Money Heist,” “Intimacy,” “Irati”), Josean Bengoetxea (“Balenciaga,” “Errementari,” “Loreak”), Miren Gaztañaga (“The Last Romantics,” “Ane,” “The Platform”) and Carlos Santos (“The Nuclear Bunker,” “Invisible,” “1992”).

It is produced by leading Basque producer Lamia Producciones, Lamia Films, Lazona Zinema, Lazona Producciones, Buendía Estudios Bizkaia, Bruja del Norte AIE, and Sideral Cinema. It is co-produced with Caviar Antwerp.

Igor Legarreta. Photo Credit: Esteban Delaiglesia



Variety caught director Legarreta before the premiere.

The film is based on Ramiro Pinilla’s book. Was it difficult to adapt it into a narrative film?

Igor Legarreta: Adapting a novel is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, you have all the necessary materials: plot, characters, theme… But on the other hand, you have to transfer a literary universe to a very different world such as cinema. It is a long and complex process where you must try to separate yourself from the initial material, but without ever betraying it.

I would like to point out that Pinilla’s novel conveys his love for both literary and cinematographic fiction, especially for the American fiction of the first half of the twentieth century. The film aims not to betray that love, and I truly believe that there are not many films with the character and visual strength of “Blind Ants.”

What attracted you to the story?

Legarreta: Undoubtedly, the experience that reading the novel provides. It is a literary gem that has not received the acclaim it deserves. I find many emotional connections with the story of the Jaureguis: life on the Basque coast, the small universe of the caserío [the Basque farmhouse], willpower as a weapon to continue fighting…. In the end, it is the story of a Basque family and its unwavering struggle not to lose its dignity.

Did you shoot the film entirely in the Basque Country?

Legarreta: Yes, the film was entirely shot in Bizkaia, in the Basque Country. We tried to preserve that coastal atmosphere. It is not for nothing that I have sometimes defined “Blind Ants” as a coastal Western.

This is a big Basque period production co-produced with Belgium’s Caviar. Can you tell me about how the project came together?

Legarreta: As often happens in cinema, travel companions are added little by little. The arrival of Robin (Caviar) and the subsequent incorporation of Kris and his entire team (Loom) helped us to grow the project in size and ambition. They are also part of the Jauregui family.

You’ve worked with Itziar Ituño on some of your previous projects. Can you tell me about your working relationship with her?

Legarreta: I’ve known Itziar since the time we were making short films at university, when she was taking her first steps as an actress and I as a director. Then, for some time, our paths separated until we met again in “All the Moons” (2021). Working with her is always a pleasure. She is a very close person, generous in her way of working, the kind of actress that is always part of the crew. Perhaps that’s why she has an enormous capacity to connect with real emotions and with real life.

Tell me about the rest of the actors.

Legarreta: It was a challenge to bring together a family as extensive and particular as the Jaureguis. We had to find a group of actors that could give us a real sense of family. And I think we succeeded. I had never worked with most of them, and in some way, they joined the project as we were making up that family. It has been a wonderful team that managed to take that bond beyond the filming.

Any particular challenges while shooting the film?

Legarreta: Half of the novel takes place during a stormy night on a cliff. When it came to filming, we decided to build a huge set to be able to shoot in the best conditions. We had to guarantee full safety in the scene, while we needed to have absolute control over all the elements. It was a real technical and creative challenge where the production design led by Mikel Serrano shines through in the film.

title: ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name
summary: "Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been" tracks the unique fusion of glory, injustice, fleeting opportunity, dashed dreams, resilience, and latter-day recognition that defines her story. The movie, like Love’s life and career, is a one-of-a-kind ride, and by the end you don’t just feel like you know and understand this remarkable artist. You feel closer to the center of the mysteries of pop.
content:
“Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” is a documentary about one of the greatest singers in the history of pop music, but it’s also a stunning meditation on the issue of identity in pop. Darlene Love recorded her most defining songs in the early ’60s, when she was part of the Phil Spector hit factory. She led a group called the Blossoms, who Spector recruited, in 1962, to sing “He’s a Rebel,” the track that became the prototype for the Wall of Sound. The song was supposed to have been sung by the Crystals, but they were 3,000 miles away in New York, and Spector, eager to rush the song into production, figured it didn’t matter — he could just credit the Crystals (which he did), and no one would know.

Darlene Love sings “He’s a Rebel” with a saucy majesty that builds in power, until it becomes almost lordly in its reverence-for-the-bad-boy. (It’s no accident that Kenneth Anger, in “Scorpio Rising,” transposed the song so that she was singing about Jesus.) Her voice is as big as the Wall of Sound she helped to create. She sang lead on another Crystals track, “He’s Sure the Boy I Love,” did the background vocals on many other Spector songs — and, in 1963, sang “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” the greatest pop-music Christmas song ever recorded. She was credited on that one, but “The Phil Spector Christmas Album” had the misfortune to be released on Nov. 22, 1963, the day JFK was shot. The record fizzled; after a few weeks, Spector suppressed any further distribution of it. The album was essentially lost (until it was reissued by Apple Records in 1972). So even though Darlene Love had been billed on the album’s greatest track, her name remained lost as well.

Popular on Variety

Thirteen years ago, Morgan Neville’s documentary “20 Feet from Stardom” paid tribute to rock ‘n’ roll’s most fabled back-up singers (the majority of whom were Black), and to how they spent their careers standing in the shadows. Darlene Love was one of those singers, and she featured prominently in the film; when it won the Oscar for best documentary, it was Love who stood up at the Academy Awards and gave an indelible speech. “20 Feet from Stardom” captured a very particular situation: The artists it was about didn’t get to be stars, but the movie suggested that in an alternate universe they might have been.

Darlene Love, however, has lived a special, heightened version of that conundrum. She hovered in the background, not getting the recognition she deserved. At the same time, she was a star. Not a maximal one, but if being a true pop singer means singing lead on some of the most magical recordings of the 20th century, Love did that. She was out there in front, spearheading the sound. It was her name that was erased, so in a strange way her identity got erased too. You knew that voice in your sonic bones, but it was in front of you and invisible at the same time.

Darlene Love didn’t need an alternate universe (she lived in both universes), and “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” tracks the unique fusion of glory, injustice, fleeting opportunity, dashed dreams, resilience, and latter-day recognition that defines her story. The movie, like Love’s life and career, is a one-of-a-kind ride, and by the end you don’t just feel like you know and understand this remarkable artist. You feel closer to the center of the mysteries of pop.

Love is 85 now, but in the documentary, which is built around a present-day interview with her (though there’s also a ton of great archival footage), she’s ageless. Under a wig of orange-blonde curls, her face beams, her smile dances, her laugh rings out, her personality is funky and vivid, and she simply doesn’t seem old. Love got to know Paul Shaffer when David Letterman fell in love with “Christmas (Baby Please Don’t Come)” and decided, in 1986, to feature Love singing it on his late-night show (a performance that became an annual ritual). The documentary presents Love along with Shaffer and his band in a studio of the Power Station, where she performs updated renditions of several of her key songs. Her voice is extraordinary, the force and quality of it undimmed. And Love proves a great narrator of her own legend. She knows what she was robbed of (not just credit but the life she could have had), yet she has transcended bitterness.

The film’s director, Barry Avrich, takes us back to the age of radio (he pays nifty homage to it in the opening credits), when you would hear a voice coming out of that box, and the voice took hold of you. Love, born Darlene Wright in 1941, shuttled between Los Angeles and Texas and spent her first 15 years in church, dunked in gospel as much as Aretha or Ray Charles were. She joined the Blossoms in the late ’50s, and they sang backup on a host of classics, starting with Sam Cooke’s “Everybody Likes to Cha Cha Cha” and then on “Chain Gang” and “Rockin’ Robin,” “Monster Mash” and “Johnny Angel.”

From there, they moved on to Phil Spector. They worked for him as back-up singers, in addition to being swapped in for the Crystals and Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, for whom Love sang lead on the sublimely lilting “Why Do Lovers Break Each Other’s Hearts.” Spector was a holy terror even then (though he was also a genius), and the name game he played with his female soul singers, moving them around as if they were interchangeable game-board pieces, was designed to do several things at once. It made Spector himself the star. (He was the first producer to do that.) It enabled him to withhold royalties. And in the largest sense, it was his (racist) way of treating all his talent like indentured servants.

Love became a magnetic presence on “Shindig!,” the great rock ‘n’ roll TV show that allowed its performers to be wild and woolly (Shaffer offers a great reminiscence of it). She led the Blossoms in back-up vocals on pop songs from “Monday, Monday” to the Beach Boys’ “In My Room,” and she went on tour with the other Spector singers, falling into a serious relationship with Bill Medley of the Righteous Brothers. Onstage, she had a toothy insolence.

Her career was a string of missed opportunities, including one that sounds like a conspiracy theory, though as presented in “I Know Where I’ve Been” it’s a fascinating one. Love was originally set to record “River Deep, Mountain High” for Phil Spector. At the last minute, he changed the singer to Tina Turner — and the song was, of course, a legendary commercial flop, the one that effectively ended Spector’s reign. The theory presented is that Turner’s rendition of it had too much R&B grit to succeed on the pop charts of 1966. Whereas Love, who had a much smoother pop-soul croon, would have made it a hit. Ah, the seduction of alternate-universe thinking! The documentary reveals how Spector became a creepier presence with the years and continued to shadow her, at one point buying out a contract she had with someone else. There’s no doubt that Spector’s great songs made her career, but the way he designed it they also nipped it in the bud.

Love was still singing in the early ’70s (we hear her do a spellbinding rendition of “I’ll Be There”), but as the age of peak R&B wound down, so did her opportunities. She was married several times and had four children, two of whom got involved in the L.A. gang-banger scene and wound up in prison. (They have since emerged and triumphed.) Love wound up cleaning houses. Yet she was not forgotten. Bruce Springsteen and Steven Van Zandt, both fans from way back, took an interest in her (they are interviewed extensively). She wound up reviving her career by doing nostalgia-act performances on cruise ships. This ultimately led to the 1984 jukebox musical revue “Leader of the Pack,” which she was featured in as it began performances in the Greenwich Village club the Bottom Line; it became a sensation. The documentary hints that it was also successful when it moved to Broadway (which isn’t the case; it flamed out there), but Darlene Love was relaunched.

And as much as that, she was recognized. The exultant Letterman performances of “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” featuring bigger choirs each year, helped a great deal, and so did her 2011 induction into the Rock ‘n’ Roll Hall of Fame. Suddenly, everyone knew who Darlene Love was. “I Know Where I’ve Been” completes the journey. It’s a film that leaves you staggered — at the soul-stirring splendor of her voice, at the forces of the time, both big and small, that marginalized her, and at our awareness of what might have been, which should never stand in the way of our awe at what was.

title: Gerrit Graham Dead: ‘Star Trek’ & ‘Phantom of the Paradise’ Actor Was 76
summary: Gerrit Graham, the actor known for roles in Phantom of the Paradise (1974) and Star Trek, has died. He was 76. The actor died of lung disease and other health complications on Tuesday in Rhinebeck, NY, according to Variety. Born Nov. 27, 1949 in New York City, Graham trained at Columbia University, where he was […]
content:
Gerrit Graham, the actor known for roles in Phantom of the Paradise (1974) and Star Trek, has died. He was 76.

The actor died of lung disease and other health complications on Tuesday in Rhinebeck, NY, according to Variety.

Born Nov. 27, 1949 in New York City, Graham trained at Columbia University, where he was head of the school’s Columbia Players theater company. He made his onscreen debut in Brian De Palma’s 1968 sophomore feature Greetings.

Graham was most known for his performance as glam rocker Beef in De Palma’s 1974 rock musical horror Phantom of the Paradise. He also played separate roles in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and Star Trek: Voyager.

Over the years, Graham had roles in such films as Beware! The Blob (1972), Demon Seed (1977), Used Cars (1980), National Lampoon’s Class Reunion (1982), TerrorVision (1986), Chopping Mall (1986), Police Academy 6: City Under Siege (1989), C.H.U.D. II: Bud the C.H.U.D. (1989), The Little Mermaid (1989), Child’s Play 2 (1990), This Boy’s Life (1993), My Girl 2 (1994) and more.

Watch on Deadline

On TV, Graham appeared in episodes of Dynasty, Starsky & Hutch, Laverne & Shirley, The A-Team, The Dukes of Hazzard, The Twilight Zone, St. Elsewhere, Miami Vice, Dallas, Tales from the Crypt, The Wonder Years, Seinfeld, Family Matters, Babylon 5, Law & Order and more.

Also a writer, Graham penned two episodes of The Twilight Zone and wrote songs with the Grateful Dead’s Bob Weir.

title: Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit: Nina Shaw & Patricia Glaser Honored On Day Of Big Ideas, Big Insights; Watch The Video Presentations
summary: Deadline’s inaugural L.A. Law Summit honored two powerhouses of the profession with awards Thursday for Patricia Glaser and Nina Shaw “If you’re perceived, and underline the word perceived, as good, the sky’s the limit in Los Angeles,” Glaser told a packed house at Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit on Thursday at the conference with Los Angeles’ […]
content:
Deadline’s inaugural L.A. Law Summit honored two powerhouses of the profession with awards Thursday for Patricia Glaser and Nina Shaw

“If you’re perceived, and underline the word perceived, as good, the sky’s the limit in Los Angeles,” Glaser told a packed house at Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit on Thursday at the conference with Los Angeles’ legal and creative heavy hitters to examine the big ideas and big topics for Hollywood “It is truly a meritocracy, and we should be really proud of that.”

In a similar spirit, Shaw spotlighted the power of character and the work when she told the September 17 conference: “I’m honored to be part of a legal community that strives to make the world better by supporting the arts. While while much of the work that we do is not known outside of these rooms, we know our contributions matter.”

When it comes to Glaser and Shaw, as generations of clients and projects, those contributions matter a lot.

So, among a legion of lawyers from the top firms in town on panels and in the audience, if Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit is going to have the Glaser Weil Fink Howard Jordan & Shapiro founding parter and the Del Shaw Moonves Tanaka Finkelstein Lezcano Bobb & Dang founding partner in the house, then the esteemed lawyers should be honored for their wide reaching contribution to their profession and the industry

That’s exactly what went down this week as litigator Glaser received the Visionary Award and Shaw received the Game Changer Award. Introduced respectively by Glaser Weil’s Gali Grant and Black List founder Franklin Leonard (after a note from WBTV boss Channing Dungey, Glaser and Shaw both addressed the other attorneys in the glass walled conference room at Deadline’s West LA HQ, along with the agents, creators and executives there too.

Take a look at the Visionary Award presentation for the Glaser Weil founding partner here:

Watch the Game Changer Award ceremony for Shaw and her speech to the L.A. Law Summit here:

Beginning with a quote from JFK and remembrance of the recently deceased Glaser Weil parter Roger Howard, the fast paced L.A. Law Summit saw discussions on IP, M&A (can you say ParaBros?), the Creator Economy and, of course, AI. Introduced by Deadline Editor-in-Chief Nellie Andreeva, the sessions were moderated by Deadline’s Executive Editor Dominic Patten, Political Editor Ted Johnson and Senior TV and Labor reporter Katie Campione.

Earl Gibson III

The day kicked off with Power and Nemesis co-creator Courtney Kemp, Blank Rome’s Cheryl S. Chang, Greenberg Glusker’s Chad R. Fitzgerald and Davis Wright Tremaine’s Nicolas Jampol dived into the intricacies of IP in a multi-platform market. Then Stubbs Alderton & Markiles’ Cathleen Green and Davis Wright Tremaine’s Carrie Casselman joined WME Chief Legal Officer Courtney Braun and the always closing Macro CEO Charles D King to talk M&A.

After lunch, Range Media Partners‘ Jack Whigham, Del Shaw’s Ethan Cohan, Greenberg Glusker’s Matt Dysart and Emmy-winning director-producer Anthony Hemingway centered on the true art of the deal and examined what it really means to be a Creator in 21st Century Tinseltown. Deadline’s first L.A. Law Summit ended on a bang with CAA‘s Chief Compliance Officer and Deputy General Counsel Tammy Brandt, Glaser Weil’s Jesse Levin and Blank Rome’s Craig Weiner taking on the facts, fictions and future of AI for the industry and society.

More coverage of Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit will be coming next week.

Deadline’s inaugural L.A. Law Summit was sponsored by Blank Rome LLP, Davis Wright Tremaine LLP, Greenberg Glusker LLP, Del Shaw Moonves Tanaka Finkelstein Lezcano Bobb & Dang LLP, Glaser Weil Fink Howard Jordan & Shapiro LLP, and Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP.

title: ‘Lollipop Chainsaw’: Cult Japanese Video Game Getting The Live Action Feature Treatment
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Cult Japanese video game Lollipop Chainsaw is heading to the big screen. Deadline can reveal that a live action feature version is in the works as the game’s creators look to establish “a new model for building globally recognized entertainment franchises from Asia.” The latest Lollipop Chainsaw video game launches soon alongside an animated […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Cult Japanese video game Lollipop Chainsaw is heading to the big screen.

Deadline can reveal that a live action feature version is in the works as the game’s creators look to establish “a new model for building globally recognized entertainment franchises from Asia.” The latest Lollipop Chainsaw video game launches soon alongside an animated series.

Set before the events of the original game and envisioned as an R-rated action comedy, the Lollipop Chainsaw film follows protagonist Juliet Starling, a San Romero High School cheerleader born into a legendary family of zombie hunters. When a catastrophic zombie outbreak engulfs her school, Juliet must fight her way through the undead to save her friends, protect her family, and somehow keep her boyfriend Nick close – even if doing so ultimately requires some highly unconventional arrangements.

Unveiled today at the Tokyo Game Show, the movie comes under license from Dragami Games and is being put together by an international creative and production team comprising Nada Holdings boss Joe Teng (As One), former ZDF Studios drama boss Robert Franke and his Orange Chariot indie, Throne Inc MD Takafumi Yuki, Ambitious Entertainment’s Kirk Shaw and Non Stop TV’s Patricio Rabuffetti.

Watch on Deadline

Released in 2012, Lollipop Chainsaw has over the years become a cult hit that has sold more than 1.5 million copies worldwide. A remastered edition, Lollipop Chainsaw RePOP, came out two years ago.

Dragami Games President Shohei Sato said: “We are truly excited to see our vision take another important step with the franchise’s first live-action feature film. We are especially pleased to be working with such an experienced and passionate international team— one that understands what makes Lollipop Chainsaw special while embracing the opportunity to create something new.”

Franke added: “We are making a film that feels unmistakably true to the spirit of Lollipop Chainsaw while standing completely on its own. Longtime fans will recognize the attitude, irreverence, and glorious excess they love, while newcomers can simply enjoy an unforgettable action-horror comedy. Our ambition is to create a film that entertains audiences everywhere, whether they’ve played the game or not.”

title: Kohner Agency Lays Off Its Talent Agents Due To “Profound & Unprecedented Economic Pressures”
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The Kohner Agency is downsizing. Its three talent agents have been laid off. The talent department will stay open to service existing contracts and collect commission only. Owner and President Pearl Wexler stresses that the agency, which has been in business for almost 90 years, is not closing. Its literary department is staying put, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The Kohner Agency is downsizing. Its three talent agents have been laid off. The talent department will stay open to service existing contracts and collect commission only.

Owner and President Pearl Wexler stresses that the agency, which has been in business for almost 90 years, is not closing. Its literary department is staying put, and Wexler herself will continue to represent acting and literary clients.

“It is with a heavy heart that we must announce a restructuring of our talent representation team, necessitated by the profound and unprecedented economic pressures currently facing the broader entertainment industry,” The Kohner Agency said in a statement to Deadline, which you can read in full below.

The post-Covid, post-Peak TV industry consolidation has been particularly hard on smaller, boutique talent agencies, which have found it hard to survive with a marquee, signature client who commands a big, steady paycheck as a star on an established series. Agencies that shut down in the past couple of years include A3 and KMR. That has further limited opportunities for up-and-coming actors to get an agent.

Watch on Deadline

Founded by Paul Kohner in 1938, The Kohner Agency is the second oldest in Los Angeles behind WMA (now WME) with long traditions in talent representations. Its early clients include Marlene Dietrich, Greta Garbo, Maurice Chevalier, Billy Wilder, Henry Fonda, John Huston, Ingmar Bergman, Lana Turner and Liv Ullmann.

Wexler has owned and run the agency for the past 25 years.

title: Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’
summary: World-premiering in San Sebastián main competition, Javier Ruiz Caldera’s time-warping drama ‘5 More Minutes’ (‘5 Minutos Más’) suggests one way an on-the rocks relationship may come closer together again: by plunging them into the makings of a global apocalypse. Writer-star Berto Romero (“The Other Side”) and Belen Cuesta (“The Endless Trench”) play a couple who […]
content:
World-premiering in San Sebastián main competition, Javier Ruiz Caldera’s time-warping drama ‘5 More Minutes’ (‘5 Minutos Más’) suggests one way an on-the rocks relationship may come closer together again: by plunging them into the makings of a global apocalypse.

Writer-star Berto Romero (“The Other Side”) and Belen Cuesta (“The Endless Trench”) play a couple who are trying to repair their frayed marriage, retreating to an idyllic vacation home in Spain’s exquisite Girona countryside. There they are handed the keys by Carlos, a property manager, played by the ever-popular Javier Cámara (“Talk to Her”) in a rare, less simpático role. Not long after he hands over the keys, time jumps back five minutes.

Actor-writer Berto Romero and Belen Cuesta in ‘5 More Minutes’ QUIM VIVES

As time continues to jump back for them, again and again, they grow increasingly paranoid. Catalonia has always looked to France for inspiration. This is a film which melds the great French and Catalan tradition of questioning the civilized manners of the bourgeoisie, rcast in a thouroughly modern genre blender, part excriciating comedy, part min-bending sci-fi, and part a shockingly violent thriller, driven by the logic of nightmares.

Popular on Variety

A potential breakout, “5 More Minutes” is produced by Movistar Plus, El Terrat, part of The Mediapro Studio, and Ikiru Films. Filmax handles domestic distribution in Spain and internatonal sales.

Ruiz Caldera and Romero both spoke to Variety in the run-up to San Sebastian’s world premiere.

What was it about this project that compelled you to take it on, particularly after your previous film?

Ruiz Caldera: I always want my next film to differ from the previous one and present a new challenge. Berto Romero’s script offered that, combining the genres I love most: fantasy, thriller and irresistible humor. I immediately wanted to make it.

The choice of music framing the film is striking. What informed the decision to open and close with Roy Orbison’s “In Dreams,” and what did you hope that musical motif would evoke?

Ruiz Caldera: Finding the right song was difficult. We wanted something hypnotic and mysterious that signaled this wasn’t simply a comedy. Then “In Dreams” clicked. Many will remember it from David Lynch’s “Blue Velvet,” and I hope that association adds an intriguing layer.

The performances feel remarkably spontaneous despite the film’s highly choreographed structure. How much latitude did you allow the actors to improvise, particularly Belén Cuesta, whose role is especially dialogue-heavy?

Ruiz Caldera: We rehearsed extensively and improvised during preparation, but the actual takes were highly choreographed. The film consists of five-minute takes, so everything had to be timed precisely. Making it look spontaneous was the goal, and Javier Cámara, Belén Cuesta and Berto Romero made that possible.

The film navigates an unusually delicate tonal terrain between black comedy, suspense and the fantastic. How did you calibrate those elements without allowing one to undermine the others?

Ruiz Caldera: Humor helps release tension before catching the audience off guard again. Given the characters’ extreme situation, black humor also feels natural—a way of protecting themselves from anxiety and fear.

The setting in Girona plays a significant atmospheric role. What drew you to this particular location, and how did its familiarity and natural beauty inform the film’s darker impulses?

Ruiz Caldera: It was shot in a beautiful valley in Girona, Catalonia, at a friend’s house I’ve known since childhood. It’s a paradise – an ideal setting for a nightmare.

The decision to construct the film around precisely five-minute takes presents a formidable formal and technical challenge. What motivated this constraint, and how did you coordinate the cinematography, production design, costume, sound, visual effects and production teams to sustain identical conditions across every sequence?

Every sequence shot had to last exactly five minutes, no more or less. We wanted audiences to genuinely feel the weight of those five minutes without relying on editing. After months of testing, every sequence was filmed at exactly 6:35 p.m., with identical light. Close coordination between cinematography, art, costume, sound, visual effects and production made the technical feat possible.

How has the involvement of Movistar Plus, a producer with El Terrat and Ikiru, helped to empower “5 More Minutes” in production terms. And how should it help its distribution potential in Spain?

Romero: I have worked with Movistar Plus on several productions over the years and have built a strong relationship of trust with their creative and production teams. The same is true of El Terrat, with whom I have worked in film and television for more than two decades. Together with Ikiru Films, they have supported the project from the beginning and given us complete creative freedom.

For distribution in Spain, having Filmax on board gives us great confidence. Their experience, knowledge of the market, and ability to connect films with audiences are a major advantage. Together with the support of Movistar Plus, El Terrat and Ikiru Films, we have a strong foundation to give ‘5 More Minutes’ visibility and reach a broad audience.

“5 More Minutes” blends sci-fi, survival thriller and excruciating (in the best sense) comedy. What attracts you to genre mixes?

I have always been drawn to stories that blend genres. Life itself is a good example: it can move from comedy to horror, thriller or drama in a matter of seconds. To me, that feels natural.

I like to follow the story I want to tell and let the genres emerge organically. I come from stand-up comedy and television, where I have worked for 30 years, so my way of seeing the world is naturally influenced by humor. At the same time, I have always loved genre stories, especially horror, thrillers, science fiction and fantasy.

I think my writing is a mix of everything I enjoy, filtered through my own view of life. With ‘5 More Minutes,’ I never set out to make a comedy. But in the end, humor, much like life in ‘Jurassic Park,’ found a way.

A considerable number of top Spanish directors – Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Alberto Rodríguez – use genre. Is there something about Spain or Spanish cinema which explain this predilection in auteurs?

I don’t feel qualified to speak for other writers or define a characteristic of Spanish cinema. For me, it is simply a personal preference as a storyteller. I find it fascinating to use genre conventions, subvert them and take audiences somewhere they don’t expect. I think this fascination with genre is more international than uniquely Spanish, though that may just be my own bias. In my case, it is a purely instinctive and irrational impulse when I write.

title: Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release
summary: “Ninjago Legends: Duskfall” is premiering in Korea this weekend ahead of a worldwide release on Lego’s YouTube channel. The anime-style shorts feature some of “Ninjago’s” most beloved characters as they encounter new challenges and new battles while bringing back some familiar voices from the original show as well as “Ninjago Dragons Rising.” The series of […]
content:
“Ninjago Legends: Duskfall” is premiering in Korea this weekend ahead of a worldwide release on Lego’s YouTube channel.

The anime-style shorts feature some of “Ninjago’s” most beloved characters as they encounter new challenges and new battles while bringing back some familiar voices from the original show as well as “Ninjago Dragons Rising.”

The series of three interconnected shorts, each three-minutes long, premiered Friday at a “Ninjago Legends” Duskfall” fan event at the Park Mall Yongsan in Seoul. The shorts will be released on the Lego Group’s YouTube channel on Saturday, Sept. 19.

The three shorts are titled “The End Begins,” directed by David Cazeaux and Charles Lefebvre, “Terminus,” directed again by Cazeaux and Lefebvre, and “Epilogue,” directed by Cazeaux, Lefebvre and Hugo Cierzniak.

Popular on Variety

Andrew Francis reprises his role as Cole alongside Kelly Metzger as Nya and Vincent Tong as Kai. Also returning to the franchise are Brian Drummond as Diviner and Runt, Adrian Petriw as Scott and Sabrina Pitre (the voice of Sora in “Dragons Rising”) as a reporter.

In a trailer for the shorts series, it opens with a female voice saying “Kai, if you make it out of this, promise me you’ll walk away.” It then cuts to plenty of action before Kai, in his red ninja outfit, says: “Save the Elementals, I’m coming.”

The female voice then says: “We’re not fighting demons or monsters anymore, they call us warriors. Protectors. Ninja.”

Created to mark the fifteenth anniversary of the “Ninjago” franchise, the shorts offer fans who’ve grown up the show an opportunity to watch the characters in a new way, with many hoping the anime-style shorts will be expanded into a full series. Ninja, watch this space.

title: Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare
summary: Celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, Portugal’s preeminent Queer Lisboa – International Queer Film Festival kicked off Friday with a vast program showcasing the latest in LGBTQ cinema, from established filmmakers to new voices, and a look back at the underground counterculture and revolutionary works of activist filmmakers on both sides of the Atlantic. Lisbon’s […]
content:
Celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, Portugal’s preeminent Queer Lisboa – International Queer Film Festival kicked off Friday with a vast program showcasing the latest in LGBTQ cinema, from established filmmakers to new voices, and a look back at the underground counterculture and revolutionary works of activist filmmakers on both sides of the Atlantic.

Lisbon’s oldest film festival, Queer Lisboa launched in 1997 at the Cinemateca Portuguesa as the Lisbon Gay and Lesbian Film Festival, opening with the 1950 short film “Un chant d’amour,” the only film ever directed by French novelist and playwright Jean Genet, whose works included “Querelle de Brest,” famously adapted by Rainer Werner Fassbinder.

Ana David and João Ferreira Credit: Joana Linda/Nuno Ferreira Santos

The festival’s origins at the Portuguese Cinematheque is one of the factors that has distinguished it from other queer festivals across Europe, Queer Lisboa artistic director João Ferreira tells Variety.

Popular on Variety

“From the very beginning, I would say that the festival was not envisioned as a kind of niche or festival only for the LGBTQ community because of the institutional support that it already had from day one. So I think it’s a very particular case for a queer festival in Europe. It was certainly not the case with some festivals that started more or less at the same time, like Madrid or Paris.

“The audience was from the very beginning, a very broad audience and an audience interested in film, a cinephile audience,” Ferreira adds. “But of course, also because in the first three years it was organized by the Portuguese chapter of ILGA [the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association], it also had this very important community aspect to it.”

The Man I Love Courtesy of Cannes Film Festival

The festival’s perception of queer cinema has never been based merely on narrative, Ferreira notes. “It was much broader than that. We were interested in a queer gaze at the world. We were interested in a camp aesthetic. So we were looking for very different kinds of films that could fit in this idea.” It was a view that shaped what the festival ultimately became, he adds. “Then the festival was called the Gay and Lesbian Film Festival, but the idea was already queer at the time, the way we looked at film.”

With a total of 94 feature, documentary and short films, the 30th edition of Queer Lisboa takes place at its regular venues, the Cinemateca Portuguesa and Cinema São Jorge, running Sept. 18-26.

Boasting a strong lineup that includes some of the year’s top LGBTQ titles, the festival opens with the Portuguese premiere of Rami Malek-starrer “The Man I Love” from Ira Sachs, whose previous films, “Passages” and “Peter Hujar’s Day,” likewise screened in Lisbon. Leah Nelson’s acclaimed animated drama “Tangles” closes the event.

Papaya ‘Papaya’ was among the first films to receive Screen Brasil distribution support. Credit: Priscilla Kellen

With nearly a dozen sections, including five competition categories and six non-competitive sidebars, the festival offers a broad showcase. New this year is Queer Family, dedicated to kids and their families, with a focus on culturally enriching independent films that explore themes of inclusion and identity. Two Brazilian features make up the program, Allan Deberton’s Berlinale award-winner “Gugu’s World” and Priscilla Kellen’s animated “Papaya.”

It’s been a long-standing goal to attract younger audiences, says Ana David, programmer and director at Queer Lisboa.

Gugu’s World Courtesy of Jamille Queiroz

The new section is aimed directly at families and the festival has already received positive feedback from interested parents.

“We’ll see if it’s the kids bringing their parents, or if it’s the parents bringing their kids. It’s important for us to work with young audiences who will also become the adult audiences of the festival in the future,” David says. The new section also provides the opportunity for parents and their children to have an intergenerational experience and to even talk about things after the screening, she adds.

The festival has already sold a large amount of tickets for the Queer Family screenings. “We think it’s going to work out really well,” David says.

With the increasing growth and appeal of LGBTQ cinema, Queer Lisboa has sought to find a balance between popular mainstream works, new discoveries and the more radical experimental films that have long defined queer cinema.

“We want this spectrum, the big films and very small films,” says Ferreira. “It’s part of our joy as programmers to discover these smaller and more independent, sometimes more DIY filmmakers and filmmaking, and we try to put all that in the program. It is challenging.”

While it’s much easier now to acquire films than it was 30 years ago, it’s become more difficult to filter through the huge amount of available titles and curate the 90-plus films that the festival presents, Ferreira adds.

Bound Courtesy of Queer Lisboa

Offering a rare treat for its 30th anniversary is an expanded Retrospectives section with 19 titles, including such works as the Wachowskis’ 1996 debut film “Bound”; Sally Potter’s “Orlando” (1992), Lisa Cholodenko’s “High Art” (1998), Patrice Chéreau’s “The Wounded Man” (1983), Kim Longinotto and Jano Williams’ British doc “Shinjuku Boys” (1995) and, from West Germany, Frank Ripploh’s 1980 classic “Taxi to the Toilet” (“Taxi zum Klo”).

This year’s showcase is especially interesting as Queer Lisboa is hitting 30 at the same time BFI Flare in London turns 40 and San Francisco’s Frameline turns 50, David notes. Those festivals, along with Paris’ Chéries-Chéris, “served as inspirations for the birth of Queer Lisboa.”

“It speaks to the longevity of queer cinema, but also the festivals that have for a long time now been promoting and expanding on the knowledge and appreciation of queer cinema,” David notes.

Orlando Courtesy of Queer Lisboa

For Queer Lisboa, it was an opportunity to look back at early films that are rare exhibitions in Portugal even if they’re already considered canon films within queer cinema. “We wanted to offer some classic titles that people know and can engage with the retrospective, but then also offer something new for them to learn about and that can expand on their knowledge,” David adds.

An important element of that is to present the films in restored or digitized versions.

It’s the first time that “Orlando” screens at the Cinemateca Portuguesa, David points out. “And they actually have a 35mm print, so it’s amazing that we can offer an excuse for this film to be shown.”

“And to take it out of the closet,” Ferreira quips.

Fatucha Superstar Courtesy of Queer Lisboa

Also presented will be a newly restored version of João Paulo Ferreira’s 1976 subversive queer musical comedy “Fatucha Superstar,” inspired by Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Jesus Christ Superstar.”

Made in the wake of the revolution that swept away Portugal’s authoritarian dictatorship, the film blasphemously ridicules in ultimate kitsch fashion one of the main pillars of the former regime, the apparition of Our Lady of Fátima and the Christian symbolism that surrounded it.

Along with Óscar Alves, João Paulo Ferreira was part of the rebellious and independent gay filmmaking movement that produced the first queer films in post-revolution Portugal. Together they founded the film collective Cineground and screened their Super 8 films in Lisbon’s queer bars and night clubs in the 1970s.

Maspalomas Maspalomas Film Factory Entertainment

Among the returning talents and exciting discoveries this year are Portuguese filmmaker André Godinho and the world premiere of his debut feature “Nothing Left,” described as a Portuguese queer version of “Punishment Park”; and German artist duo Benjamin Ramírez Pérez and Stefan Ramírez Pérez with the world premiere of “Life Is About Losing Everything,” their hybrid doc on the life and work of Canadian poet Lynn Crosbie, likewise a first feature. Both films unspool in the Queer Art Competition, which showcases experimental, boundary-busting works that “explore the limits of cinematic languages, genres, and narratives.”

Other highlights include Swiss-French feature “Summer Drift,” by Céline Carridroit and Aline Suter, and the European premiere of “Public Access,” David Shadrack Smith’s look at the people who transformed New York City TV into a groundbreaking space for self-expression during the 1970s and 80s.

This year’s diverse lineup includes special screenings of Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” while the fest’s non-competitive Panorama sidebar presents such recent international festival hits as “Jim Queen“; “Maspalomas;” “Outerlands“; and “Prosecution.”

Strange River Courtesy of Queer Lisboa

Competing in this year’s Queer Lisboa feature film competition are:

“Black Burns Fast,” by Sandulela Asanda (South Africa)

“On the Road,” by David Pablos (Mexico)

“Strange River,” by Jaume Claret Muxart’s (Spain, Germany)

“La Gradiva,” by Marine Atlan (France, Italy)

“Iván & Hadoum,” by Ian de la Rosa (Spain, Germany, Belgium)

“Julian,” by Cato Kusters (Belgium, The Netherlands)

“London,” by Victor Di Marco and Márcio Picoli (Brazil)

“Raging,” by Ryan Machado (Philippines)

The entire Queer Lisboa program can be explored here.

title: ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’
summary: A dog is indeed a man’s best friend. A New Directors contender at the San Sebastián Film Festival, “Morro” explores the unlikely bond between a man and the dog he inadvertently adopts. It is Rodrigo Garcia Saiz’s (“Lluvia”) sophomore feature and, by his own account, his most personal film to date. The titular Morro is […]
content:
A dog is indeed a man’s best friend.

A New Directors contender at the San Sebastián Film Festival, “Morro” explores the unlikely bond between a man and the dog he inadvertently adopts. It is Rodrigo Garcia Saiz’s (“Lluvia”) sophomore feature and, by his own account, his most personal film to date. The titular Morro is a dog, reflecting Garcia Saiz’s own lifelong connection with the animal.

“I’ve always had a connection with dogs and I also wanted to reflect on the violence in Mexico since I left it,” says Garcia, who now resides in Madrid. “But not so much about showing the violence itself, but about what happens to the people who stay. And how an animal that doesn’t judge, that asks for nothing but love and gives love, could help.”

Popular on Variety

“Morro” revolves around Mateo, a vet in rural Mexico, who lives quietly with the unresolved guilt of losing his son. In a town where violence simmers beneath the surface, his fragile routine is disrupted when he treats Morro, the injured dog of a local drug lord. Caring for the animal sparks a wordless, judgment-free bond that slowly gives Mateo a renewed sense of purpose.

“So the premise is really: Who saves whom? I started researching, went into conflict zones, and discovered this story, which is loosely based on the experience of someone I met through a friend.”

“At first, he was a little hesitant because he didn’t really want to tell us the whole story. But little by little, he opened up. I gradually gained his trust, and he started telling me things, and I began putting the story together with another screenwriter [Carlos Armella] and some other collaborators. It was really exciting to realize that what I had in my head actually happens in real life. So I made the story very much my own and it became a story that really came from my heart.”

He’s quick to point out that his film is not about drug trafficking and violence is never explicitly shown. “The violence is more in the moral and physical context.”

Finding the right dog to fit the part was a challenge as he didn’t want a trained one, but as luck would have it, he found the right dog, which bonded with his lead actor, Gustavo Sánchez Parra (“Amores Perros,” Michael Rowe’s Cannes-winning “Leap Year”), who even took him home.

“He looked a little like the dog from the story I researched. And when I saw him, I fell in love with him because he had such a beautiful expression. He could also believably be a drug dealer’s dog, but at the same time, he’s such a gentle, sweet animal.”

He also chose to film in 35mm with his DP Alfonso Herrera Salcedo (“Spectre”), a bold choice. “Shooting on 35mm was also a way of going back to basics. The set became almost like a church where everyone had to be quiet. There were no cell phones because the film stock is obviously very expensive, and you can’t just improvise, especially when you’re working with an animal and such a great actor. Everyone had to be completely focused and attentive. I’m really grateful that Kodak, PhotoKem and others supported me so much, because I feel the film has a very particular spirit – and that also comes from our decision to shoot it on 35mm.”

His next project is even more personal: “I’m working on a film that deals with my relationship with my father, who died on my tenth birthday.”

“Morro” is produced by Calouma Films, alongside Central Films and The 42 Film. Paola Cortés (“Lluvia”) Alberto Müffelmann (“I’m No Longer Here”), Julia Cherrier (“The Intruder”) and Pablo Guerrero (“New Order”) serve as producers.

The 74th San Sebastian Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26.
