Ultimately, Affleck ended up casting Kerry Washington after getting to know each other during the 2023 Hollywood strikes. “She’s very polished, but she’s also very warm. I thought, Oh my God, she’s amazing for this,” he said.

Co-written by Affleck, Connor O. McIntyre and Billy Ray, Animals stars Affleck as Los Angeles mayoral candidate Mark Kimball, whose son is kidnapped, giving him and wife Abigail (Washington) a few hours to get their hands dirty and come up with the ransom money.

title: Aaron Sorkin Says Jeremy Strong Treated ‘Social Reckoning’ Co-Stars “The Way He Imagines Mark Zuckerberg Treats People”
summary: As Jeremy Strong delivers his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg, Aaron Sorkin has shed some light on the method actor’s process for this role. The Social Reckoning writer/director was “not shocked” that Strong didn’t tell him about writing an email to Zuckerberg, confirming that the Oscar-nominated actor stayed in character as the Meta founder and CEO […]
content:
As Jeremy Strong delivers his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg, Aaron Sorkin has shed some light on the method actor’s process for this role.

The Social Reckoning writer/director was “not shocked” that Strong didn’t tell him about writing an email to Zuckerberg, confirming that the Oscar-nominated actor stayed in character as the Meta founder and CEO between takes.

“Jeremy does a lot of his own work. He does a tremendous amount of work before he shows up on your set,” he explained to NYT’s The Interview. “He did not speak in his own voice on the set or walk the way Jeremy walks.”

Sorkin continued, “I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him.’ And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.”

Watch on Deadline

Strong previously revealed that he emailed Zuckerberg before making the film to tell him he takes “this responsibility very seriously, and the veracity of it seriously, and I’m approaching it with respect.”

After The Social Network (2010) recounted Zuckerberg’s creation of Facebook and the controversy that ensued, screenwriter Sorkin returned to write and direct the upcoming sequel, which premieres Oct. 9, focusing on a 2021 document leak that exposed harm Facebook caused on society.

In The Social Reckoning, Facebook engineer Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) goes to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) with the social media platform’s most guarded secrets. Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Billy Magnussen and Betty Gilpin also star.

title: Movistar Plus Announces 2027 Slate, Including JA Bayona & Fernando León Projects, At San Sebastián
summary: Movistar Plus debuted some of the projects that will feature as part of its 2027 content slate, including two projects executive-produced by JA Bayona and a new comedy series by Fernando León de Aranoa (The Good Boss), this morning at the San Sebastián Film Festival. The León series will be titled The Castaway. León has […]
content:
Movistar Plus debuted some of the projects that will feature as part of its 2027 content slate, including two projects executive-produced by JA Bayona and a new comedy series by Fernando León de Aranoa (The Good Boss), this morning at the San Sebastián Film Festival.

The León series will be titled The Castaway. León has directed the series from screenplays he also wrote. The series has been produced by León, Jaume Roures and Patricia de Muns. Starring are Belén Cuesta and David Verdaguer.

Also on the TV side, Movistar will next year debut a series created by Cristóbal Garrido and Adolfo Valor (The Brief Life), which offers a fictionalized account of the 1991 Barcelona Olympics. The streamer has said the show will detail the preparations for the opening ceremony of the Olympic Games. The series has been produced in collaboration with Charlie Pisco Producciones and Kubik Films. Starring are David Verdaguer, Paula Malia, Silvia Abril, Andreu Buenafuente, Maria León, Alex Brendemühl, Pau Durá, and Jorge Usón.

The two JA Bayona projects will be non-fiction features. The streamer did not provide any specifics about those projects during this morning’s presentation, which was led by Movistar Plus CEO Alfonso Gómez Palacio and Director of Content Juan Andrés García Ropero.

Watch on Deadline

The two execs also committed to expanding their support of homegrown filmmaking talent. This will first be addressed by Movistar Plus debuting one new Spanish film every week on its platform in 2027.

“The Spanish film industry is experiencing an extraordinary moment, and we believe Movistar Plus has a responsibility to contribute to its continued growth,” Ropero said. “We are looking for projects with quality, personality, and a unique perspective. We want stories that no one else dares to tell.”

Other standout projects announced by the streamer today include A Family Visit, directed by Sandra Romero (As Silence Passes By), 250 Meters, directed by Daniel Monzón (Outlaws), and a series from the Moriartis, produced by Carles Porta, with Anna Castillo, Pol López, and Eduard Fernández attached to star.

title: ‘Resident Evil’ Breaks Franchise Opening Records & Even Some Cumes With $108.3M WW; Also Zach Cregger’s Highest – Global Box Office
summary: TriStar Pictures/Constantin Film/Davis Films’ Resident Evil rang up a massive $108.3M worldwide, not only the best start the franchise has ever seen, but also Zach Cregger’s biggest start as filmmaker surpassing the $70M WW reported opening of last year’s Weapons. In addition, the opening alone for Resident Evil beats the global final of the original […]
content:
TriStar Pictures/Constantin Film/Davis Films’ Resident Evil rang up a massive $108.3M worldwide, not only the best start the franchise has ever seen, but also Zach Cregger‘s biggest start as filmmaker surpassing the $70M WW reported opening of last year’s Weapons.

In addition, the opening alone for Resident Evil beats the global final of the original 2002 movie ($102.9M) as well as the last title, the failed reboot Welcome to Raccoon City ($41.9M). Currently, 2016’s Resident Evil: The Final Chapter stands as the highest grossing title in the series with $312M (51% of that coming from China or $159.5M).

Also, get this but this zombie shoot-em up paced like Scream 7, in fact even better (that pic opened to a franchise best $63.5M and $97M worldwide. Comps to Scream 7 were iffy on Thursday night, until they became real. For a horror pic this year at the worldwide B.O., it’s the second best after Backrooms‘ $118M.

Watch on Deadline

In terms of pure international debuts for a horror movie YTD, Resident Evil‘s $48.3M is the best for the genre, higher than Backrooms‘ $36.6M. Resident Evil is 66% over Weapons, 33% above A Quiet Place: Day One, and 18% ahead of Alien: Romulus on a like-for-like basis at current exchange rates.

What’s impressive is that the movie expanded its audience beyond the Milla Jovovich movies. UK at $5.8M was the top territory (in reported, 2010’s 3D charged Afterlife bowed to $2.5M there). Mexico followed at $5.6M (higher than Afterlife‘s reported $3.2M).

Metropolitan had French speaking markets, while Constantin had Germany speaking markets. France did $2.6M (higher than Final Chapter‘s reported $1M start). Germany counted $2.5M (higher than Final Chapter‘s reported $1.3M),

Other top markets were Australia ($2.6M), Spain ($2.3M), Brazil ($2.0M), Italy ($1.7M), Saudi Arabia ($1.6M), UAE ($1.4M), Indonesia ($1.4M), Malaysia ($1.3M), Taiwan ($1.2M), the Philippines ($1.2M), and India ($1.1M).

And there’s 13% of foreign markets left to go, and they’re big territories for the franchise, i.e. Thailand (Sept. 24), Japan (Oct. 9) and China (still to be dated). South Africa is opening on Sept. 23 while Central Asia is Sept. 24.

Final Chapter‘s $159.5M in the Middle Kingdom is looked at as an anomaly: Just a perfect place in time and space for a Resident Evil in regards to the types of U.S. action movies that fared well in China, in addition to the game’s popularity. Japan was the second highest territory for Final Chapter at $36.4M.

In addition today, A24’s highest grossing movie ever, Backrooms, clicked past the $400M mark at the global box office.

We’ll have more updates later.

title: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Review: A Riveting South Korean Popcorn Thriller About a Real Assassination
summary: Hur Jin-ho’s star-studded “The Assassin(s)” turns the holes in a public investigation into an imaginative mystery along the lines of Oliver Stone’s “JFK.” Like Stone’s provocative thriller, Hur crafts a clockwork political saga sure to spark curiosities about the attempted assassination of strongman South Korean prime minister Park Chung-hee in 1974, which resulted in the […]
content:
Hur Jin-ho’s star-studded “The Assassin(s)” turns the holes in a public investigation into an imaginative mystery along the lines of Oliver Stone’s “JFK.” Like Stone’s provocative thriller, Hur crafts a clockwork political saga sure to spark curiosities about the attempted assassination of strongman South Korean prime minister Park Chung-hee in 1974, which resulted in the death of his wife, first lady Yuk Young-soo, as well as a young bystander.

The film ties these events into larger concerns surrounding freedom of the press and some inventive government conspiracies. Your mileage may vary when it comes to the extent of these fabrications, even though “The Assassin(s)” begins with a disclaimer hinting at its own fictions. Regardless, its drama is solid and propulsive, beginning with a group of journalists being harangued by the KCIA (Korean Central Intelligence Agency) for publishing troublesome investigations en route to the botched assassination (intentionally so, according to the film’s internal logic).

The three most prominent characters are charismatic and sympathetic in equal measure. Two of them are journalists at the Dong-sung Daily, who mount a heroic stand against government forces at a time of severe censorship. Fiery rookie Young-il (Lee Min-ho) — the younger brother of a connected official — is assigned to cover the prime minister’s Liberation Day speech when the shooting goes awry, leading him to witness the events first-hand. The older, world-weary Jae-hwan (Park Hae-il) leads the City Desk, and investigates the event from a distance with the help of his police source, diligent detective Cheol-goo (Yoo Hai-jin).

Popular on Variety

The local policeman isn’t just present on the day, but tries to stop the eventual assassin from entering the auditorium for the prime minister’s speech, until he’s directed otherwise by senior authorities. He’s punished regardless by suits who refuse to listen, galvanizing the characters’ investigations into a larger collusion.

With a murderer’s row of supporting actors — like Park Hoon as a vicious KCIA goon harassing the Dong-sung workers, and Bae Seong-woo as the paper’s editor, trapped between maintaining journalistic integrity and bowing to censorious demands — the film establishes and unravels its drama at lightning speed. Hur judiciously constructs scene after scene that pulls and pushes the various probes closer to and further from the mysterious truth, which feels at once obscured and hidden in plain sight. As the puzzle pieces shift slowly into place, these revelations are jaw-dropping (once again, in their highly fictitious context), leading to a journalistic urgency.

Like any good cover-up movie, “The Assassin(s)” luxuriates in process and proficiency, following its cops and journalists sleuthing about to ask questions and peek at documents, poking their noses where they shouldn’t. It’s an invigorating kind of cinema, and Hur knows exactly how and when to tighten the screws, bringing his characters face to face with critical dangers, and with identities shrouded in mystery. These unspool in the form of action scenes where the stakes aren’t just personal safety, but the larger ideals of a nation under political suppression. Its tale of a Zainichi assassin (an ethnic Korean in Japan), as well as fraying political tensions between the North and South, take its characters far and wide, in a follow-the-money treasure hunt dangerously close to the halls of power.

To spin total concoctions into something so riveting is — for better or worse — an admirable cinematic skill, one Hur uses to turn a tale of forensic malfeasance into mass entertainment of considerable quality. (At Toronto, where the film premiered, it was the second runner-up for the International People’s Choice Award.) There are unanswered questions about these events to this day, and while “The Assassin(s)” isn’t the answer anyone was looking for, the movie taps into a national mood of frustrated anti-authoritarianism, while playing melodramatic tribute to those willing to speak truth to power. The result is rousing, popcorn-munching fun.

title: ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny Scores Her Dream Internship in Alexandra Pechman’s Warmly Nostalgic Study of a Bygone Literary Scene
summary: In an era when glamorous writing jobs have acquired the unreality of folklore, it feels fitting that Alexandra Pechman’s alluring and affectionate feature debut, “Magazine,” should portray its literary world as a fairy tale. Set in a faraway time — summer 2011 — when office flirtations were fun, ambition was a given and purses hung […]
content:
In an era when glamorous writing jobs have acquired the unreality of folklore, it feels fitting that Alexandra Pechman’s alluring and affectionate feature debut, “Magazine,” should portray its literary world as a fairy tale. Set in a faraway time — summer 2011 — when office flirtations were fun, ambition was a given and purses hung crossbody, the film follows Nora (Lily McInery), an aspiring poet who lands a competitive internship at Platen, a fictional literary magazine à la The Paris Review. Nora’s time in the office, and the relationships that blossom — and one that withers — over the course of that formative span give shape to this earnest, appealing movie about idealism lost but innocence preserved.

Pechman, who worked in magazines during the era she depicts, drew on her own experiences to write “Magazine.” But the movie — like “Almost Famous” for the n+1 crowd — is less interested in realism than in evoking the shiny, spiky atmosphere of that recent past. Stacked with pitch-perfect needle drops and nods to a sartorial moment, it overflows with warm nostalgia even as it shades its romantic outlook with a shrewd understanding of how it feels to be a young woman in a workplace that inspires reverence while courting disillusion.

Popular on Variety

That experience is evergreen and “Magazine” captures its thrills and anxieties with deep affection and sharp attention. The story opens on Nora’s first day of work, as she loiters outside the Platen offices, waiting for the clock to tick a few minutes forward. Thomas (Joshuah Melnick), an assistant editor, has told her to arrive a little after 10 a.m., and when she opens the door five minutes past the hour, she’s confident that the plum (yet naturally unpaid) position awaiting her will be her entry into a rarefied dream career.

At first, the bright, airy Platen offices seem to confirm the fantasy. As appointed by production designer Valeria De Felice, the workspace is a literary dreamscape, lined with Persian rugs and bookcases displaying a rainbow of magazine spines. Skipping inside, Nora joins a cadre of shambling interns whom the editorial staff regard with a mixture of bemusement and disdain. Among them are the self-assured Tabitha (Lukita Maxwell), who, in heeled booties and smudged eyeliner, is clearly a soon-to-be pal, and the curmudgeonly Leonard (Daniel Zolghadri), who can’t resist pointing out that Nora must come from money if she can afford to move to New York for an unpaid role.

Actually, Nora is living on scholarship funds she won from her unnamed college — but that detail hardly matters. In the mythopoetic world of “Magazine,” money is basically irrelevant. When one coded-wealthy nepotism hire gets fired for neglecting work, the ousting occurs in a passing line of dialogue. And although Thomas — who, as Leonard bitterly notes, has been blessed with good looks and great taste in books — resides in a soaring Manhattan loft owned by his mother, his eventual caddish streak has more to do with his fragile professional ego than his privilege.

Indeed, in her devotion to sparkle, Pechman declines to probe too deeply into any of the industry’s more hurtful or exploitative dimensions. It’s not that her movie is blind to the hazards; the plot hinges on Nora’s discovery that her bosses aren’t immune to the cliché of hitting on their dewiest interns. But even as she and Tabitha are drawn into such dalliances and then bruised by them, the movie is less interested in passing judgment than in conjuring the freshman thrill of being young, curious and unguarded.

That can, at points, make “Magazine” seem overly gentle. In its allergy to cynicism, it sometimes comes off like a starry-eyed love story, not between people, but between Nora and the life she has envisioned for herself. As our heroine is drawn deeper into the Platen scene, mingling with haughty editors and attending parties alongside authors of niche renown — one is played by a very funny Alex Edelman — we admire her passion while nervously taking note of her naiveté.

It’s hardly a surprise when she falls into a relationship with Thomas, whose freckled smirk toggles between mischievous and manipulative. Amiable and self-absorbed in equal measure, he is happy to sleep with Nora so long as nobody finds out and she asks nothing in return. That Thomas has no intention of helping Nora professionally is obvious to us but less so to her, though it is expressed by one of the film’s more unusual and beguiling characters: Daphne (Iris Apatow), a worldly socialite who advises Nora not to have sex with her superiors; they’ll only prove useful if you entice them and then remain out of reach.

That advice — to use one’s femininity to play the players — sounds straight out of Samantha’s mouth in “Sex and the City”: a third-wave theory women can take or leave. Daphne’s strategy is well beyond our naif’s capacity, but in “Magazine,” the sophisticate’s worldview proves apt. As Nora’s feelings for Thomas butt up against her wish for a full-time offer at Platen, her romanticized notions of the people and place come crashing down. As it turns out, the magazine is not an enchanted realm, but a game with particular rules. Nora can either learn to play or walk away.

“Magazine” is the story of a young woman losing her religion, of youthful certainty clouding with doubt. Pechman brightens Nora’s awakening with notes of optimism: friendships gained, memories forged, lessons learned. There’s no major wreckage here, nor is comeuppance meted out to the wrongdoers. Where other filmmakers might have come down harder on the scene, casting Nora’s experience as evidence of entrenched dysfunction and storm clouds hovering on the horizon, Pechman holds fast to good cheer. But if the movie’s instinct for lenience makes it smaller, it never dims its shine.

title: ‘Angh’ Review: Toronto’s Platform Award Winner Is a Lush Lament for an Indian Tribe in the 1960s
summary: Expanding on his 2021 short film, Theja Rio’s debut feature “Angh” forces its way into the hidden crevices between indigenous identity and colonial modernity. This tension unfolds with riveting restraint in a story set in 1960s Nagaland — the eastern Indian state on the Burmese border — following the principled chief of a waning tribe, […]
content:
Expanding on his 2021 short film, Theja Rio’s debut feature “Angh” forces its way into the hidden crevices between indigenous identity and colonial modernity. This tension unfolds with riveting restraint in a story set in 1960s Nagaland — the eastern Indian state on the Burmese border — following the principled chief of a waning tribe, and the arrival of an American missionary. “Angh” won the top prize in the Platform competition at this year’s Toronto Film Festival, thus qualifying it for the Best International Feature Oscar.

Lush, impenetrable forests play host to the tale of Anghba (Anghlong Konyak), addressed reverentially as “old chief” by his kin who have, willingly or otherwise, been excommunicated. After the death of his wife from disease, his son Amao (Sobino Rengma) — a silent boy searching for his voice — remains the only other member of his Konyak tribe. However, Amao’s curiosity about modern, western clothing and a nearby bustling community of Baptist converts threatens their existence.

Popular on Variety

Right from its opening scene, “Angh” frames the arrival of colonial missionaries as a strange, almost alien absurdity. With bow and arrow in hand, Anghba finds his hunt for a wild boar across a riverbank interrupted by a raft floating downstream, as former tribespeople surround a jovial American preacher (Douglas Henshall), much to the chieftain’s chagrin. These impositions are gradual and incredibly well-meaning, although even their medicinal intentions come laced with the word of a foreign lord and savior, whose crucifixes and tales of forgiveness are at odds with the local rituals.

Images often associated with barbarism on screen, like beheading the dead to memorialize them, are approached with an uncanny gentleness. This places the audience alongside the Konyaks, and subverts the traditional, colonial cinematic gaze in the vein of Filipino maestro Lav Diaz. The film’s cast is mostly made up of tribal non-actors, but Anghlong Konyak is its captivating center, as a man whose stubbornness against change sits alongside a lingering grief over his fading way of life.

The story of the rest of post-independent India lives far away from the film’s peripheries; Rio’s concerns, instead, are hyper-focused on a local tale of transformation and thorny resilience. To the average viewer living in a westernized society, Anghba may come off as obstinate, which feels entirely in tune with the film’s intent. However, his raging protectiveness over what might be lost — language, attire, ritual, even memory — grows more pronounced as Rio veers further into phantasmagoria by way of dreams and visions.

Together with his cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz, the director crafts an inviting 16mm atmosphere, transforming the textural flaws of celluloid into a living fabric, where dirt, scratches and punctures may as well be insects zipping across the screen, as though this is where the medium belongs. “Angh,” in this way, feels truly alive, and at one with nature — a harmony that’s slowly interrupted as the story unfolds, en route to fiery and devastating conclusions.

With disarming simplicity, “Angh” challenges closely held notions of default filmic perspectives, offering a whole new world for us to consider through its soulful ruminations, while forcing us to reflect on the cost of our own unassuming norms. It is, in effect, a lament for things which have been lost, a quiet memorial that beats with righteous fury over how easily we let entire ways of life simply slip away — or rather, how we allow them to be snatched in the guise of progress.

title: Jhené Aiko Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Westside Whimsy’
summary: Jhené Aiko has scored her first No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 with her fourth record “Westside Whimsy.” Aiko bows atop the chart with 74,000 equivalent album units, making it the first R&B album by a woman to top the Billboard 200 this year and the first to reach No. 1 since SZA’s “SOS” […]
content:
Jhené Aiko has scored her first No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 with her fourth record “Westside Whimsy.”

Aiko bows atop the chart with 74,000 equivalent album units, making it the first R&B album by a woman to top the Billboard 200 this year and the first to reach No. 1 since SZA’s “SOS” in May 2025. This year, the only other R&B album to hit No. 1 was Bruno Mars’ “The Romantic.”

Popular on Variety

“Westside Whimsy,” which touts features from Kendrick Lamar, Tyga and Larry June, arrived without much notice after Aiko announced the project less than a week before its release. It marks her sixth album to hit the Billboard 200, dating back to her first entry, “Sail Out,” in 2013. She last released her third album “Chilombo” in 2020, which debuted at No. 2 and earned three Grammy nominations including album of the year, best progressive R&B album and best R&B performance for “Lightning & Thunder.”

Aiko’s latest is the only album this week to debut in the Billboard 200 top 10. Ella Langley, who is expected to achieve the longest-running No. 1 on the Hot 100 tomorrow with “Choosin’ Texas,” falls to No. 2 with “Dandelion,” moving roughly 60,000 equivalent album units. Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” comes in at No. 3, followed by Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem” at No. 4 and Noah Kahan’s “The Great Divide” at No. 5.

Rounding out spots six through 10 are Drake’s “Iceman,” Ariana Grande’s “Petal,” Rod Wave’s “Don’t Look Down,” Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” and Kahan’s “Stick Season.”

title: ‘History Of Concrete’ Rocks IFC Center As ‘Daniel And The Fiery Furnace’ Brings Biblical Heat To Top 10 — Specialty Box Office
summary: John Wilson’s The History Of Concrete had a record-breaking IFC Center debut, grossing $90k in three days for the top doc opening and the second-highest weekend gross in the NYC theater’s 21-year history after only Parasite ($119k in 2019). Nearly every available ticket sold for the entire weekend, including for shows added Saturday afternoon for […]
content:
John Wilson’s The History Of Concrete had a record-breaking IFC Center debut, grossing $90k in three days for the top doc opening and the second-highest weekend gross in the NYC theater’s 21-year history after only Parasite ($119k in 2019). Nearly every available ticket sold for the entire weekend, including for shows added Saturday afternoon for last night and today.

It was a wild weekend. “We knew last week we had pre-sold about $60k in tickets and were on target for a really big weekend. And we kept adding in shows, and they kept selling out. Every show, every ticket,” says Neal Block, head of distribution and marketing at Magnolia, which acquired the film out of Sundance. On Friday, I thought we could get to $75k. But we kept selling out. including morning shows, and the grosses kept inching higher.”

He attributes the surge in large part to Wilson, host of acclaimed documentary comedy series How To With John Wilson (EP Nathan Fielder) that ran on HBO for three seasons (2020-2023). Wilson also co-founded and helps run Low Cinema, a 42-seat micro-theater in Ridgewood, Queens, so is something of a local celebrity. Fans and the press have been curious about his next project and he’d been working on this film for some time. Block also said the distributor limited exposure to the film with few screenings between Sundance and opening weekend to build anticipation.

Watch on Deadline

He said demos skewed young – not Gen Z Backrooms young, but 20s to mid 40s. The film expands next week to about 40 screens in 15 markets including LA and Brooklyn. Rolls out to 50 markets on a few hundred screens Oct. 2.

Magnolia’s been having a nice run. Late Fame by Kent Jones starring Willem Dafoe crossed $500k this weekend on 30 screens for an estimated $523k cume. The film opened August. 7 and hung in, playing well with an older arthouse demo. Maddie’s Secret by and starring John Early opened in June, topping out at $1.2 million.

Looking now at a rare happening as two films from faith-based distributors vied at the domestic box office. Angel Studio’s Runner is no. 6 on 2,472 screens for a week 2 gross of $3.18 million and a hefy cume near $12 million. Daniel And The Fiery Furnace from EKKL Entertainment, a PG-rated origin story of the Prophet Daniel starring Elijah Alexander and Mena Massoud and directed by Daniel and Matthew Kooman, opened at no. 7 with $3.14 million on 1,520 screens.

This is a broad market of films — straight from the Scriptures, to inspirational and values-based fare, to something like Angel’s latest, a more mainstream action-comedy thriller with a help-save-a-young-girl’s-life premise starring Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson.

Daniel is one of the first releases by Michael Scott’s new EKKL label, a sort of rebrand of his Pinnacle Peak Pictures. Scott had also co-founded the Pure Flix streaming service that Sony acquired in 2020.

He calls faith-based a genre, like horror, with an equally enthusiastic fan base. Fans see it as “good and clean” cinema and it can bring multiple generations to the theater together, clapping and cheering as a story “the audience holds near and dear” comes to life. The films are fairly critic-proof.

Women 35+ are typically the key drivers. Daniel skewed more male with lions and fiery furnace action. The film, which was shot in northern India near the Pakistan border, is meant to be the first in a series from the Book of Daniel.

EKKL also has a sister streaming service with audiobooks, podcasts, film content, and prayer and devotion.

More top ten: Panning for gold, Vertical’s The Weight cracked the no. 9 spot opening weekend. Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe star in Padraic McKinley’s feature film debuting on 1,504 screens. Vertical notes strong play at major chains nationwide topped by NY (AMC Lincoln Square & 34th Street, Alamo Brooklyn) and LA (AMC Century City & Burbank) as well as strong sales in San Francisco, Chicago, Dallas, Phoenix, Nashville, West Palm Beach, Minneapolis and St. Louis. Art house audiences turned out on stellar reviews. Outdoorsy markets solidly over-performed from Twin Falls, Idaho, to Traverse City Michigan, Rapid City South Dakota and Billings Montana.

The survival epic set in 1933 Oregon features stunning, forests and an unforgiving wilderness beautifully captured by McKinley on hand-held digital equipment.

Moderate/limited releases:A solid showing for If I Go Will They Miss Me, with an estimated $352k at 251 theaters in week 2 for a cume topping $400k. It debuted to $40k last week exclusively at AMC Century City. The Sundance-premiering Rich Spirit release starring Danielle Brooks and J Alphonse Nicholson and directed by Walter Thompson-Hernandez is garnering Awards attention for Brooks. Continues its theatrical run into October.

Greenwich Entertainment documentary You Had to Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (In a Canadian Kind of Way) opened to $20k at an exclusive run at NYC’s Film Forum, selling out multiple shows and repping one of the theater’s biggest 2026 doc openings.

The TIFF premiering romp tells the story of the 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell, featuring an eye-popping cast of future comedy titans: Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Andrea Martin, Gilda Radner, Dave Thomas—with Victor Garber as a hippie Jesus and Paul Shaffer as musical director.

A hit with film festivals over the last year, You Had to Be There was promoted to theater fans through partnerships with Broadway World, Playbill, and The Public Theater, and to comedy fans through partnerships with The Magnet Theater, Asylum Theater, and The Second City. Expands to about 100 theaters next week.

Wide: Roadside Attraction’s Buddy kicked out another $1.93 million on 1,532 screens in week 4 for a $24.8 million cume. It is now Roadside’s third highest grossing film.

Neon’s Hope is eyeing an estimated $997k in week 2 from 1,400 locations and an estimated domestic cume through Sunday of $7.3 million. A police chief and hunters pursue a mysterious creature terrorizing a remote South Korean village.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom from Gkids, a StudioCanal and Aardman production, bowed to $1.9 million for the beloved animated franchise on 2,183 screens. When the Farmer destroys the flock’s beloved pumpkin patch, Shaun turns mad scientist to fix the problem, only for events to spiral out of control as a wild beast roams the woods of Mossingham. The film features the voices of John Sparkes and Justin Fletcher and is directed by Matthew Walker and Steve Cox. Rated PG.

The Uprising from Focus Features and Blumhouse grossed an estimated $1.2 million from 2,069 theaters in North America in week 2 for an estimated cume of $5.78 million. The medieval historical epic starring Andrew Garfield was written and directed by Paul Greengrass.

title: Chad Gilbert Dead: New Found Glory Guitarist Was 45
summary: Chad Gilbert, the New Found Glory founding member and lead guitarist, has died. He was 45. On Sunday, Gilbert’s wife Lisa Cimorelli announced that he “passed away peacefully in his sleep,” following his emergency brain surgery in March when three tumors were discovered and his metastatic pheochromocytoma was upgraded to stage 4 adrenocortical carcinoma. “On […]
content:
Chad Gilbert, the New Found Glory founding member and lead guitarist, has died. He was 45.

On Sunday, Gilbert’s wife Lisa Cimorelli announced that he “passed away peacefully in his sleep,” following his emergency brain surgery in March when three tumors were discovered and his metastatic pheochromocytoma was upgraded to stage 4 adrenocortical carcinoma.

“On the morning of September 20th, Chad Everett Gilbert passed away peacefully in his sleep,” wrote Cimorelli in a joint statement with the band. “He left this world surrounded by friends and family and took his final breaths with his wife and mother by his side, just as he wished. We are devastated and shocked by how quickly he left us, yet so grateful for how peacefully and smoothly he went. The amount of visitors that crowded the hospital lobby at a moment’s notice is a testament to how beloved and cherished Chad was, and always will be. He was a legendary musician, but his favorite accomplishment was being a husband and father. His biggest dreams came true. He is survived by his wife, Lisa, his daughter, Lily, his mother, Jackie, and his brother, Brian.”

Cimorelli added, “Chad’s guitar playing, songwriting, humor, and relentless drive helped shape New Found Glory for nearly three decades. Through more than a dozen albums, endless tours around the world, and more accolades than we ever could have imagined, Chad challenged all of us to grow as musicians, performers, and human beings. While we are devastated to lose him, we are so grateful for the incredible life he lived, the memories we shared, and the brotherhood we had. His influence will always be part of New Found Glory and his spirit will be felt on every stage we stand on, with every note we play. Rest in peace, Chad. We love you forever. Lisa, Jordan, Ian, Cyrus, and Dan”

Watch on Deadline

Gilbert first underwent surgery to remove a pheochromocytoma cancerous tumor in 2021, before undergoing another operation in 2022 and chemotherapy the following year.

Born March 9, 1981 in Coral Springs, Florida, Gilbert formed New Found Glory in 1997 with Jordan Pundik, Steve Klein, Ian Grushka and Joe Moreno. He left high school after 11th grade when New Found Glory was signed to Drive-Thru Records, releasing their debut album Nothing Gold Can Stay in 1999.

In addition to performing with band Shai Hulud and recording solo music as What’s Eating Gilbert, he also produced music for A Day to Remember and H2O.

title: JoAnna Garcia Swisher Thanks ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Team For Giving Her “Somewhere To Belong”
summary: As Sweet Magnolias comes to an end, JoAnna Garcia Swisher is grateful for all the friends and fans she made in Serenity, South Carolina. On Sunday, the actress reflected on the “really beautiful chapter of my life” as she penned a heartfelt statement after Netflix canceled the series following five seasons. “How do you say […]
content:
As Sweet Magnolias comes to an end, JoAnna Garcia Swisher is grateful for all the friends and fans she made in Serenity, South Carolina.

On Sunday, the actress reflected on the “really beautiful chapter of my life” as she penned a heartfelt statement after Netflix canceled the series following five seasons.

“How do you say goodbye to something that became so much more than a job? Seven years. Five seasons. A million tiny moments that somehow became a whole life,” she began on Instagram. “Sweet Magnolias came into my world during a chapter that held some of my deepest loss and, somehow, some of my greatest joy. I lost both of my parents during those early seasons, and in a time when I wasn’t always sure how to keep moving forward, Serenity gave me somewhere to go. These people gave me somewhere to belong.

“They made me laugh when I was sure I had forgotten how. They let me be sad when I needed to be. They showed up. Again and again and again. And maybe that’s what I will carry with me most. This show was always about showing up for the people you love. About friends becoming family. About life not turning out exactly the way you planned, and choosing to build something beautiful anyway. Somewhere along the way, while we were telling those stories, we started living them too.”

Watch on Deadline

Swisher continued, “To every single person who made this show, and every single person who watched it, loved it, shared it, and found a little piece of themselves in Serenity…thank you. You will never fully know what you gave me. Five seasons. Seven years. One really, really beautiful chapter of my life. I’m not quite sure I’m ready to close it. But I am so incredibly grateful I got to live it. Thank you, Serenity. Pour it out.”

The post comes after Deadline exclusively announced on Friday that Netflix has canceled the series after five seasons. Meanwhile, the streamer has greenlighted a new series from Sweet Magnolias EP/showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson and Swisher.

Loosely based on Lauren Edmondson’s novel Ladies of the House, the new series also centers on a trio of women. Swisher is attached as an EP, and she’s being eyed to star.

In Ladies of the House, when the charismatic owner of a winery dies unexpectedly, his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives. Good friends and good wine will aid in the journey to hang on to the winery, but what matters most is that they find a way to hang on to each other.

title: Jessica Chastain Thriller ‘The Savant’ Getting 2027 Release On Apple TV After Year On Hold
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The release of The Savant is back on. A year after Apple TV put the thriller starring Jessica Chastain on hold three days before it was slated to premiere on Sept. 26, 2025, the streamer has rescheduled it for spring, 2027. The exact timing, which is still being finalized, will make the series eligible […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The release of The Savant is back on. A year after Apple TV put the thriller starring Jessica Chastain on hold three days before it was slated to premiere on Sept. 26, 2025, the streamer has rescheduled it for spring, 2027. The exact timing, which is still being finalized, will make the series eligible for the 2027 Emmys, I hear.

As Deadline reported at the time of the postponement, The Savant‘s last-minute benching was due to its storyline about preventing extremist attacks and some imagery, including sniper attacks, that were considered potentially triggering two weeks after the assassination of right-wing political activist Charlie Kirk.

“After careful consideration, we have made the decision to postpone The Savant,” an Apple TV spokesperson said in a statement to Deadline at the time. “We appreciate your understanding and look forward to releasing the series at a future date.”

Watch on Deadline

While there was skepticism whether the series would ever see the light of day, Apple TV had consistently held the line that The Savant was delayed but not axed and will be released. It is now happening.

From writer/executive producer/showrunner Melissa James Gibson, Fifth Season and Anonymous Content, The Savant follows an undercover investigator known as “The Savant” (Chastain), who infiltrates online hate groups to stop domestic extremists before they act.

The cast also includes Cole Doman, Jordana Spiro, Trinity Lee Shirley, Toussaint Francois Battiste, and guest star Pablo Schreiber. James Badge Dale appears in a major recurring role.

Chastain and Kelly Carmichael executive produce via Freckle Films alongside Alan Poul, Melissa James Gibson, and Matthew Heineman, who also directs. David Levine and Garrett Kemble serve as executive producers for Anonymous Content. Stanley serves as a consultant.

title: Ke Huy Quan Says His $100,000 ‘Indiana Jones’ Residual Check Was ‘Life-Changing’ As a Child Actor: It ‘Didn’t Make Any Sense’
summary: Ke Huy Quan shared in his new memoir, “Never Say Die,” the feeling of receiving his first residual check of $100,000 for “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” as a child actor. Because Quan was just 12 years old when he booked the role of Short Round in the 1984 film (his first major […]
content:
Ke Huy Quan shared in his new memoir, “Never Say Die,” the feeling of receiving his first residual check of $100,000 for “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” as a child actor.

Because Quan was just 12 years old when he booked the role of Short Round in the 1984 film (his first major role as an actor), he didn’t realize he would receive residuals in addition to his base pay.

“One afternoon, I walked into the kitchen and found my parents standing together at the table,” Quan wrote in the memoir via Entertainment Weekly. “Mom was holding an envelope with my name printed across it. Dad had the papers that had been inside.”

He continued, writing, “They were both smiling, the kind of smile that comes from surprise and disbelief mixed together. They handed everything to me. It was a check from Lucasfilm. It was for almost $100,000, an amount that didn’t make any sense to me.”

Popular on Variety

“Back then, almost no actors got a piece of a movie’s profits,” Quan continued. “Even today, only the biggest stars do. That a kid like me, making his first film, would be included in something like that was unheard of. And ‘Temple of Doom’ wasn’t some small movie no one was expected to see. It was the sequel to a massive hit, a movie everyone knew would make a lot of money. That made their gesture even more generous.”

Quan noted that the “small share was life-changing for my family.”

As a child, Quan also starred in Richard Donner’s 1985 film “The Goonies” as Data. He returned to the spotlight in 2023 after decades for “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” winning the Oscar for best supporting actor. His memoir, released Tuesday, details his early life fleeing Vietnam with his father, time in refugee camps, his life as a child actor and his triumphant return to the screen.

title: ‘My Hero Academia’ Reworks ‘You Say Run’ Theme With Electric Callboy for 10th Anniversary
summary: Toho Co., Ltd. has set a 10th-anniversary version of “You Say Run,” the “My Hero Academia” theme, pairing composer Hayashi Yuki with German band Electric Callboy, with a global release set for Sept. 22. The reworked track debuted live at the “My Hero Academia in Concert” show in London on Sept. 20 ahead of the […]
content:
Toho Co., Ltd. has set a 10th-anniversary version of “You Say Run,” the “My Hero Academia” theme, pairing composer Hayashi Yuki with German band Electric Callboy, with a global release set for Sept. 22.

The reworked track debuted live at the “My Hero Academia in Concert” show in London on Sept. 20 ahead of the wider rollout. Electric Callboy, known for songs including “Hypa Hypa” and its Babymetal collaboration “Ratatata,” features Kevin Ratajczak and Nico Sallach, who connected with Hayashi after he wrote English lyrics for the anniversary version. Toho’s music team had been looking for international artists who could bring powerful shouts and melodic vocals in keeping with the show’s high-energy tone, which led to the Electric Callboy pairing.

“We are beyond excited to have this opportunity to add our vocals to ‘You Say Run,'” said Ratajczak. “The melody of ‘You Say Run’ is so powerful and uplifting – we just absolutely love this song.”

Popular on Variety

Sallach said working on the track was pure fun and a huge honor to collaborate on, adding, “We can’t wait for everyone to hear it! We really hope you’re as excited for it as we are.”

The new version folds the song’s original orchestral arrangement into Electric Callboy’s blend of EDM and pop hooks, arriving a decade after the anime first premiered. “‘You Say Run,’ one of the signature tracks representing ‘My Hero Academia,’ has been reborn with an unprecedented surge of energy by fusing with the incredible vocals of Electric Callboy,” said Hayashi. “I am deeply honored and thrilled to share this special sound born from the intersection of our shared energy.”

Bones Film also unveiled a new illustration to mark the release, showing Izuku Midoriya (“Deku”) performing a “Smash” in a nod to the cover art of the anime’s original Season 1 soundtrack.

“I truly hope the song crosses borders and genres, reaches as many hearts as possible, and resonates passionately with everyone,” said Hayashi. “And while the track is absolute perfection, the cover art is top-tier too. Plus Ultra.”

The release marks a decade since “My Hero Academia” debuted, and the franchise remains among anime’s biggest global hits. Horikoshi Kohei’s manga concluded in August 2024 after selling more than 100 million copies globally, and the anime spans eight seasons, 170+1 episodes and four feature films. The new song is part of the ongoing “My Hero Academia The Animation 10th Anniversary” project, which will continue through 2026 with further announcements on the anniversary’s dedicated website.

“You Say Run -10th Anniversary Ver.-” by Hayashi Yuki featuring Electric Callboy streams globally and across major platforms starting Sept. 22.

“My Hero Academia” is a Japanese anime series based on the manga by Horikoshi Kohei, set in a world where about 80% of the population has a superpowered ability known as a Quirk. It follows Izuku Midoriya and his classmates at U.A. High School as they train to become heroes who protect society from disasters and Quirk-wielding villains. The anime released its eighth and final season in fall 2025.

Formed in Germany in 2010, Electric Callboy has built a global following on genre-blending hits such as “Hypa Hypa,” “We Got the Moves” and the Babymetal collaboration “Ratatata.” Known for a sound that mixes pop and metalcore, the band is currently building momentum around its new album, “Tanzneid.”

title: Ben Affleck Almost Cast Ex-Wife Jennifer Garner in ‘Animals’ Before Deciding ‘We Don’t Wanna Do That’: ‘You Just Get Baggage’
summary: Ben Affleck originally wanted to cast his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner, as the leading lady in his latest directorial effort, “Animals,” until a scheduling conflict meant he’d have to step into the role opposite her. “I thought, God, Jen Garner would be amazing for this role,” he told Entertainment Weekly. “It also has the added benefit […]
content:
Ben Affleck originally wanted to cast his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner, as the leading lady in his latest directorial effort, “Animals,” until a scheduling conflict meant he’d have to step into the role opposite her.

“I thought, God, Jen Garner would be amazing for this role,” he told Entertainment Weekly. “It also has the added benefit of, like, both of us will see our kids more because we do a week and a week and back and forth. I thought, well, we can coordinate our schedules around it.” He also noted that he thought Garner could “bring something interesting that she hasn’t [done], that I kind of know she can do, that I don’t think she had a chance to do in one movie.”

Initially, Matt Damon was attached to star as Mark Kimball, the male lead. But because of scheduling conflicts and another film in the same genre slated for a similar release window, Affleck tabled the film two weeks before production was set to begin. When it was time to revive “Animal,” Damon was set to star in another project: “The Odyssey.”

Popular on Variety

“Matt was unfortunately doing another lesser film, obviously, with Odyssey,” Affleck joked. “He chose a smaller director and a smaller film and a smaller role for his career, and I think he’s gonna suffer for it. He’ll regret this choice.”

Affleck stepped in for Damon, and the former couple ultimately decided they didn’t want the “baggage” that would come with the on-screen pairing: “I talked to Jen, and she was like, ‘We don’t wanna do that. You just get baggage,’” he said.

“I would love to work with her, frankly,” he continued. “She’s fabulous, and we’re really good friends, and I’m profoundly grateful to her, and we have a great thing. I still would wanna work with her in the future, but what you don’t wanna do is take the audience’s baggage and have it work against you, you know?”

Co-written by Affleck, Connor O. McIntyre and Billy Ray, “Animals” stars Affleck as a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped, giving him and his wife, Abigail (Kerry Washington), a few hours to come up with the ransom money.

“Animals” premieres on Oct. 9 on Netflix.

title: NYU Langone Privately Bought the Site of a Landmark AMC Theater — New Yorkers Are Now Fighting to Save It
summary: “We came to this place for magic.” On a rainy Sunday afternoon, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal stood in solidarity with more than 100 New Yorkers outside AMC Kips Bay 15. In his best Australian accent, he recited Nicole Kidman’s iconic AMC Theatres ad in a loving tribute to the neighborhood’s longstanding cultural institution. But […]
content:
“We came to this place for magic.”



On a rainy Sunday afternoon, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal stood in solidarity with more than 100 New Yorkers outside AMC Kips Bay 15. In his best Australian accent, he recited Nicole Kidman’s iconic AMC Theatres ad in a loving tribute to the neighborhood’s longstanding cultural institution. But despite a record-breaking summer at the box office, the Kips Bay multiplex is expected to close at the end of this year.

“I’m a lifelong resident of Kips Bay, and I came out here to support my favorite theater that I’ve been going to since I was a child,” said Lucy Di Lorenzo, one of the many Gen-Zers who attended the protest.

Popular on Variety

The site of the Kips Bay AMC, the chain’s second-largest multiplex in Manhattan, was privately purchased by NYU Langone over a year ago. But several city officials at the protest told Variety they didn’t learn about the deal until after it had gone through.

“NYU is a neighbor, and we’ve worked with them in many different capacities, so it was surprising that we had to reach out to them to find out that they were the ones looking to acquire the land behind us,” New York State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez explained after the protest. “It’s not unreasonable to ask NYU to be proactive in engaging with the community.”

The “Save the Kips Bay AMC Theater Rally” was organized by the Eleanor Roosevelt Independent Democrats, a local political club representing several communities across the Lower East Side, East Village and Midtown East. Judith Gross, the group’s president, says her members are “devastated” by the news but remain hopeful they can get through to AMC Theatres and NYU Langone.

“I’m hoping AMC and NYU see what we’ve done here,” Gross said. “This neighborhood is not a campus for NYU and its medical offices. We’re guiding the whole community to protest these takeovers of what little community space we have left.”

Several local businesses have joined Gross’ rallying cry, including Paddy Reilly’s Music Bar, the staple Irish pub located just around the corner from AMC Kips Bay. After promoting the protest on social media, the bar offered a free drink to anyone who came in afterward with a selfie from the rally.

“It’s very important because we have a lot of young people in this neighborhood who love to go to the movie theater,” said Desi Murray, who has owned Paddy Reilly’s for the past three years. “It would be a big loss for the community.”

Paddy Reilly’s is celebrating its 40th year in business. Inside the bar, several locals mourned the potential loss of a community gathering space that’s been around even longer.

“We’ve been here since ’73,” a patron named Cesar told his buddies at the bar. He took a sip of Guinness. “There has always been a theater here.”



As the pub-goers clamored over how surprisingly funny “Resident Evil” was and how great Robert Pattinson’s Batman is, the fate of their favorite local movie theater remains in limbo. It’s a conflict playing out on a much larger scale with the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, which many of Hollywood’s most prominent voices are arguing would diminish opportunities and resources for creatives.

“And right here, the same thing is happening,” Gonzalez explained. “We’re getting a big new partner coming in, potentially kicking this out, limiting options to see the movies in our neighborhood. And all we’re asking for, whether it’s in Hollywood or right here in Pittsburgh, is for everyday people to be included and have our voices heard.”



In a statement to Variety, NYU Langone has responded to the protests: “NYU Langone is committed to providing high-quality, accessible healthcare to the communities we serve. We have been exploring opportunities to expand clinical services and improve access to care as we continue to see growing demand at our Manhattan campus.



When the owner of the Second Avenue property approached us most recently regarding a potential sale, we recognized that the site’s proximity to our hospital could help support those long-term community healthcare needs. The purchase remains under contract and is not expected to close until early next year. Years before NYU Langone was approached about the property, AMC and the landlord entered into a lease granting either party a right to terminate at any time.



We will provide updates on our clinical plans when the transaction is finalized.”

title: Charlize Theron on ‘The Odyssey’ Becoming Universal’s Highest-Grossing Movie and Raising Millions to Fight Femicide in Africa With CTAOP
summary: Last week, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” became Universal Pictures’ highest-grossing film of all time, grossing $1.68 billion and counting. “I feel like I got a great invitation to the best party in town, and I don’t know how I got it, but I’m really glad I got invited,” Oscar winner Charlize Theron told Variety on […]
content:
Last week, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” became Universal Pictures’ highest-grossing film of all time, grossing $1.68 billion and counting.

“I feel like I got a great invitation to the best party in town, and I don’t know how I got it, but I’m really glad I got invited,” Oscar winner Charlize Theron told Variety on Saturday night. (For the record, Theron stars in two of the studio’s top 10 movies, with 2017’s “Fate of the Furious” coming in at No. 6.)

But the box office milestone wasn’t really the figure Theron had at the top of her mind. She was more focused on how much money she could raise for her foundation, the Charlize Theron Africa Outreach Program — which works to strengthen the health and safety of youth in Southern Africa. CTAOP hosted its 6th annual block party on the Universal backlot with a guest list that included January Jones, Nick Kroll, Patton Oswald, Skye P. Marshall, Jeannie Mai, Heather Gay, Natalie Martinez, chef Andrew Zimmern, Thaddeus LaGrone, Aggy K. Adams, Shudu Musida, Naledi Masilo, Michelle De Leon, Max Talisman, as well as NBCUniversal Entertainment chairman Donna Langley.

Popular on Variety

“Universal truly is my family,” Theron said. “I owe so much to Donna Langley, and to Michael Moses and Peter Cramer. All of them have stood by me for my entire career.”

Speaking of family, Theron is also expected to reprise her role as the villainous Cipher in “Fast Forever,” the final installment of the “Fast and Furious” franchise. Vin Diesel declared the film’s script is “the best [he’s] read in decades,” but he hasn’t shared a copy with Theron yet. “He’s very secretive,” she explained.

But what would a happy ending look like for someone like Cipher?

“That is a difficult thing,” Theron said, pondering the character’s fate. “She’s a tricky bitch. She’s messy. I don’t know. I’m sure Vin will come up with a great way for her to … I almost said die, but I guess she doesn’t have to die, right?” (With a spinoff series in the works at Peacock, it’s safe to say any fate is possible for the massive ensemble cast.)

Kid Cudi and Charlize Theron attend Charlize Theron’s Africa Outreach Program’s annual block party. Getty Images for CTAOP

January Jones and Charlize Theron Getty Images for CTAOP

Now back to the topic at hand: next year, CTAOP will turn 20 and, to date, has served over 80 organizations, reached over 4.8 million youth and granted $16.5 million to local grassroots organizations.

“The success of CTAOP is understanding the importance of a community here — because without this community, other communities on the ground can’t do the work,” Theron said about CTAOP’s supporters.

“It’s also just good for the soul to see that people care,” she continued. “It’s such a misconception that Americans don’t care about what’s going on in the rest of the world. If anything, I think they do. There’s a big percentage of the population that understands that less than 1% of [America’s] overall budget going to foreign aid and saving millions and millions of lives is a good thing. And I really hope we can get back to those times, because people are dying.”

Here, Theron grew particularly impassioned, explaining that people try to oversimplify the situation. “The truth is, we’re taking so many steps back,” she said. “To not think that all of this is going to affect us in the long term makes it hard to not see the geopolitical side of it. If you take away the humanitarian out of it — what’s important to you? Is it the safety of wanting to know that you’re safe here in America? Then you should care about other people as well.”

As CTAOP works toward that 20th anniversary, Theron said her “ridiculous hope and dream is to say we don’t have to do this anymore. It’s solved. But I don’t think that that’s going to be the case.”

“If anything,” she explained, “I think we’re leaning into a year where we really have to spend real money toward organizations that really, really work on the ground with gender-based violence. The femicide happening in South Africa right now is beyond brutal.”

The horrors for women and girls are prevalent everywhere, Theron said, but her native South Africa is particularly devastated by it.

“Every morning, I get on my feed and I hear of another young woman’s body that was found in a dump in East Rand, where I grew up. And it’s like nobody cares. Nobody’s talking about these things,” Theron added, growing impassioned. “The value of women’s lives should matter. And when you find a young woman’s body in a dump, that should be the most important thing that we’re talking about.”

Scroll for a look inside the starry celebration, which raised more than $1 million for the organization.

Inside Charlize Theron’s Africa Outreach Program’s annual block party on the Universal Studios backlot. Getty Images for CTAOP

Natasha Lyonne and Carolyn Michelle Smith Getty Images for CTAOP

Charlize Theron with Nick Kroll and Lily Kwong. Getty Images for CTAOP

“Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” star Heather Gay Getty Images for CTAOP

The Six Compound showed off their break dance skills to kick off the event. Getty Images for CTAOP

Charlize Theron and Thando Dlomo, who co-hosted the event. Getty Images for CTAOP

Rodney Franks co-hosted the event, which included a live and silent auction that $1 million. Getty Images for CTAOP

Max Talisman and Steven Clark Getty Images for CTAOP

Jeannie Mai Getty Images for CTAOP

Siphosihle Benge delivered her personal testimony as a graduate from CTAOP’s Youth Leaders Scholarship program. Getty Images for CTAOP

title: ’60 Minutes’ Patrick Clancy Interview Provides a Surprisingly Thoughtful Take on Much-Watched Trial
summary: Credit is merited when it’s due: CBS News’ newly minted “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat landed a thoughtful, emotional interview with the person who may have elicited more speculation than anyone else this year. Patrick Clancy is the grieving father of three children killed in January 2023 by his then-wife, Lindsay Clancy. (During the criminal […]
content:
Credit is merited when it’s due: CBS News’ newly minted “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat landed a thoughtful, emotional interview with the person who may have elicited more speculation than anyone else this year.

Patrick Clancy is the grieving father of three children killed in January 2023 by his then-wife, Lindsay Clancy. (During the criminal trial about whether Lindsay was sane or not when she committed the crime, she testified to killing them while in the throes of post-partum psychosis. Because of one holdout juror who’s proclaimed he was convinced of her guilt, the Massachusetts judge reluctantly had to declare a mistrial earlier this month.) As the “60 Minutes” segment points out, Patrick Clancy has been the subject of predictably intense scrutiny, with much of the TikTok commentariat convinced he did the deed.

Whether or not Patrick Clancy came off as credible is up for debate. To this viewer (someone who has literally never used TikTok and is generally skeptical of citizen journalism) he was the picture of bereavement; to others, it may be a judgment call. But he read to me like a person who’d been through, to say the very least, a horrible ordeal, doing the thing that he needed to do to silence the relentless commentary — if that could even be possible. And “60 Minutes” deserves credit for letting him share his side of things after social media has adjudicated his guilt.

Popular on Variety

Douthat, until recently slotted into the New York Times opinion desk as one of the providers of that newspaper’s conservative perspective, can count this as his first “60 Minutes” story. That, between his bearing and his interests, he’s not a natural for TV may have worked in his favor here: Had the Clancy family tragedy happened in a previous era, a true-crime-hungry newsanchor might have pushed harder than Patrick Clancy was willing to go into the gruesome details of the night. (This would’ve been a classic Diane Sawyer or Connie Chung interview, and, as such, might have pushed into more uncomfortable territory.)

What’s been most interesting, to this viewer of the trial from afar, about the story is Patrick’s ability to forgive his ex-wife for what she has admitted to doing to their family. Douthat asked about that: Patrick has forgiven Lindsay, even though she did not ask for it. Were Douthat, perhaps, a more seasoned question-asker on camera, he might have asked how often the two speak and what else passes between them. Douthat let opportunities like this go.

Regardless, landing this interview is a win for CBS News at an interesting time: The network’s news division, run by former opinion journalist Bari Weiss, has tended toward a thumb-on-scale favoritism toward establishment narratives, even as the establishment itself seems to be tilting toward derangement. On Tony Dokoupil’s first night as “CBS Evening News” anchor, during the U.S. attack on Venezuela that resulted in the capture of that nation’s president, Nicolás Maduro, the “Evening News” featured a lengthy and incurious interview with Pete Hegseth. I was similarly unimpressed — during the debut of Weiss’ newly overhauled “60 Minutes” one week ago — by that episode’s “big get,” Norah O’Donnell’s interview with an Air Force officer shot down over Iran. Taking nothing away from his experience, her questions seemed overly deferent to the U.S. military’s narrative.

With that in mind, Douthat deserves praise for being genuinely thoughtful and curious about how Patrick Clancy is doing these days. This was the interview every TV outlet sought, and “60 Minutes” can be doubly proud: Its name and heritage may well have helped book the most-talked-about figure of the moment, and its on-camera talent was more open to deep questions than to relitigating the legal case. The question remaining is whether, in weeks between massive gets that exist entirely outside the narrative of an increasingly unpopular presidency whose functionaries Weiss courts, “60 Minutes” can maintain this momentum.

title: Ke Huy Quan Reveals “Life Changing” Gesture From Spielberg & Lucas When He Was A Kid
summary: Ke Huy Quan was 12 years old when he made Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. In his new memoir, Never Say Die, excerpted in Entertainment Weekly, the Oscar-winning actor reveals that producer George Lucas and director Steven Spielberg took care of him in way he didn’t know about until after filming had concluded. […]
content:
Ke Huy Quan was 12 years old when he made Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom.

In his new memoir, Never Say Die, excerpted in Entertainment Weekly, the Oscar-winning actor reveals that producer George Lucas and director Steven Spielberg took care of him in way he didn’t know about until after filming had concluded.

“One afternoon, I walked into the kitchen and found my parents standing together at the table,” Quan writes. “Mom was holding an envelope with my name printed across it. Dad had the papers that had been inside.

“They were both smiling, the kind of smile that comes from surprise and disbelief mixed together. They handed everything to me. It was a check from Lucasfilm. It was for almost $100,000, an amount that didn’t make any sense to me.” Quan had already been paid his fee for the project.

Watch on Deadline

But the film made more than $300M worldwide, and the director and producer made sure the kid shared in that bounty.

“Back then, almost no actors got a piece of a movie’s profits. Even today, only the biggest stars do. That a kid like me, making his first film, would be included in something like that was unheard of. And Temple of Doom wasn’t some small movie no one was expected to see. It was the sequel to a massive hit, a movie everyone knew would make a lot of money. That made their gesture even more generous.”

The actor added, “That small share was life-changing for my family.”

title: Spanish Government Pledges to Continue Audiovisual Hub Through Spain Crece Fund
summary: Spain plans to press on with its commitment to the country’s audiovisual industry, said Óscar López, Minister for Digital Transformation and Public Administration. Speaking at the conference titled The New Script of the Audiovisual Industry at the San Sebastian Festival, López said Sunday that his Ministry would continue supporting its audiovisual industry through the Spain […]
content:
Spain plans to press on with its commitment to the country’s audiovisual industry, said Óscar López, Minister for Digital Transformation and Public Administration. Speaking at the conference titled The New Script of the Audiovisual Industry at the San Sebastian Festival, López said Sunday that his Ministry would continue supporting its audiovisual industry through the Spain Crece Fund.

That looks likely to feature further strategic investment via SETT, the Ministry’s sovereign venture capital fund.

“When a public policy works, it should be maintained without a deadline. It is the golden age for our audiovisual sector,” he said, pointing to a series of record-breaking figures.

Popular on Variety

López spoke just hours before “La Bola Negra,” from Spain’s Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, won the 2026 TIFF People’s Choice Award, a coveted audience prize at the annual film festival in Toronto. which, according to Variety, is largely seen as an indicator of legs on the road to the Oscars stage.

Four Spanish series seasons and three movies feature in Netflix Top 10s of the streaming giant’s biggest non-English hits ever, more titles than from any other country in the world.

“We had the talent, the ideas and the locations. What was missing was political will and a significant injection of capital,” López continued. He pointed to the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan as a key driver of the sector’s development, describing it as “an unprecedented institutional commitment commensurate with the scale of the challenge” that made it possible “to design an economic transformation on an unprecedented scale.”

“And here we are, €1.6 billion later, reaping the benefits and expanding our horizons,” he said.

Statistics Reveal Spain’s Dramatic Growth

Spain is now the European Union’s largest production market, while audiovisual production in the country grew by 31% in 2025. Spanish productions also account for nine of the 11 most-watched series in Europe, according to the figures cited by the minister.

Employment in the sector has doubled since 2020, rising from 30,900 workers to more than 64,000 in 2025.

López noted that “the industry will soon benefit from the €450 million in investments mobilized by SETT (Spanish Society for Technological Transformation), in companies such as Lazona, Good Films and Aurora Media.”

High Praise for SETT, the Venture Capital Fund of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation

Speaking at the first of three panels, Good Film Studios founder Miriam Segal praised Spain’s studios, talent and international potential. Having worked across the U.S., UK and Europe, she said she “didn’t know about this incredible” industry infrastructure or the government’s “extraordinary passion and commitment” to the sector. For the first time as an independent producer, this support has enabled her to offer pay-or-play deals to actors. Ánima Kitchen’s José Carlos Garcia thanked SETT for supporting the company’s vision, enabling growth, talent recruitment and plans for three high-end animated films in five years, adding that SETT would help expand Ánima’s animation leadership.

Europe Panel: A Roadmap to the Future

The panel brought together perspectives from Spain, Greece and Denmark on how Europe can remain culturally diverse while competing globally. They agreed there is no single European audiovisual model, with Carla Redondo of Spain’s Ministry of Digital Transformation describing this diversity as “one of the true strengths” of Europe. Spain highlighted incentives, investment, talent and infrastructure, while Greece stressed using international productions to build local capacity and training. Esben Snoer Iversen Denmark’s Culture Ministry emphasized regional cooperation and flexible funding as the media landscape evolves. Speakers also called for greater administrative harmonization and support for emerging creative industries. As Leonidas Christopoulos of Ekkomed put it, “it’s all about the stories”: strong content ultimately drives international competitiveness.

Linear Television is Not Dead

The third panel explored how broadcasters and platforms are adapting to a rapidly changing audiovisual landscape. Said Mediaset’s Fernando Hernaiz” “Television is not dead” but has evolved into a broader “ecosystem” spanning linear channels, streaming, production and distribution. “We have a capacity to adapt,” he said, noting that television is now “technology, creation, scripts and business.” Audience fragmentation and measurement remain major challenges, while the panelists, including RTVE’s Alfonso Morales, Atresmedia’s Miguel Langle and Movistar Plus’ Clara Ruipérez called for regulation that keeps pace with platforms and social media. Investment, promotion and strong storytelling were seen as essential to making Spanish content travel internationally.

Sneak Peek at the Olsberg-SP Data

Spain Film Commission’s Juan Manuel Guimerans and Leon Forde of Olsberg SPI gave a sneak peek of the Olsberg study of the country’s audiovisual sector based on official data, which estimates €20 billion in direct production expenditure between 2020 and 2025, generating nearly €18 billion in gross value added and supporting around 64,000 jobs. Direct investment grew 45%, while gross value added rose 38%. More than half of employment generated by the sector comes through related industries and supply chains, including construction, hospitality and transport. Forde stressed that data is essential for effective policymaking but remains fragmented across the complex industry. They described audiovisual as an “ecosystem” where “all [species] are indispensable,” requiring continued investment and balance. A more detailed report will be presented on Sept.22.

John Hopewell contributed to this article.

title: Chile Film Industry Surges 20.5% Compared to Previous Season, New Catalog Reveals (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: CinemaChile unveils its 2026-2027 catalog at the San Sebastián Festival on Sept. 21 where it has much to celebrate, with eight titles screening across seven sections, led by Pablo Larrain’s “My Sad Dead,” a 4-part Netflix series that has been combined to make a roughly three-hour feature that competes for the Golden Shell. Unsurprisingly, the […]
content:
CinemaChile unveils its 2026-2027 catalog at the San Sebastián Festival on Sept. 21 where it has much to celebrate, with eight titles screening across seven sections, led by Pablo Larrain’s “My Sad Dead,” a 4-part Netflix series that has been combined to make a roughly three-hour feature that competes for the Golden Shell.

Unsurprisingly, the catalog proves that this tiny county of some 20 million inhabitants continues to punch above its weight, with the catalog reporting a 20.5% growth in Chile’s film industry compared with the 2025-2026 period.

Said Gabriela Sandoval, a CinemaChile board member: “We have gone from 156 to 188 titles, which is clearly great news and demonstrates the strength of Chilean cinema, which has continued to grow over the past five years.” In 2021, Chile reported 139 titles.

Popular on Variety

Sandoval notes that the latest figures bring further positive developments: Of the 188 films, 66 are directed or co-directed by women, while 100 are productions or co-productions featuring leading industry professionals.

“The work of female directors and producers is not only growing, but their films are also shining around the world,” she said, pointing to the Chilean filmmakers and producers attending this year’s San Sebastián Festival.

Also notable is that more than 80% of the titles are international co-productions, linking Chile with 23 countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Spain, France, Italy, Germany, the U.K., the U.S., South Korea, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Qatar.

Given the country’s size, this is to be expected. As Pablo Larrain’s producing partner and brother Juan de Dios Larraín pointed out at a talk held at the Guadalajara Film Festival in April, it was precisely the size of Chile’s market that has forced them and their peers to look outward in order to make their films.

“Co-production isn’t just helpful—it’s essential to Chilean cinema. There’s really no other way to do it. You can’t finance a film purely through the Chilean market; the numbers just don’t add up. So, from early on, going out and seeking funding became a fundamental part of the process – it’s built into the system,” he said.

“In a way, that limitation forces growth. It pushes you to adapt, collaborate and think beyond your own borders from the very beginning,” he added.

Noted Sandoval: “The catalogue is a snapshot of an increasingly diverse, internationalized and connected sector, where new voices coexist with established filmmakers.”

“Beyond the growing number of titles, the 188 films offer a clear picture of the Chilean audiovisual sector today: active, diverse and deeply connected to the world.”

She added: “San Sebastián is especially significant for presenting the catalogue because that same picture is reflected in the Festival’s programming. Chilean cinema appears across sections, formats and generations, from Official Selection to New Directors, Horizontes Latinos, Perlak, Zabaltegi, Made in Spain and Zinemira. This breadth reflects what CinemaChile wants to show: there is no single way to define Chilean cinema today.”

Aside from Larrain’s film in main competition, New Directors features Thomas Woodroffe’s debut “Erratics” (“Bloques erráticos”) vies for the main prize in the festival’s New Directors compeition and Horizontes Latinos includes two films by established female directors, Manuela Martelli’s “The Meltdown” (El deshielo”) and Dominga Sotomayor’s “The Dog” (“La perra”).

Zabaltegi features Felipe Luis’ Cannes-winning short “For the Opponents” (“Para los contrincantes”) while Perlak presents John Malkovich-led “Wild Horse Nine,” shot on Easter Island and starring Chilean actresses Mariana di Girolamo and Paola Giannini.

Made in Spain screens “This Body of Mine” (Este cuerpo mío”) by Chilean-born director Afioco Gnecco, partly shot in Chile. Zinemira features the animated feature “Winnipeg, the Seed of Hope” (“Winnipeg, el barco de la esperanza”).

title: Karan Johar’s Dharma Productions Confirms Film on Indian Spymaster Rameshwar Nath Kao, Targets 2028 Release (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Karan Johar’s Dharma Productions is teaming with Leo Media Collective on a theatrical feature about Rameshwar Nath Kao, founder of India’s Research and Analysis Wing, targeting an Aug. 11, 2028 release timed to the Indian Independence Day holiday weekend. R&AW, India’s primary external intelligence agency, was established in 1968 to consolidate the country’s foreign intelligence […]
content:
Karan Johar‘s Dharma Productions is teaming with Leo Media Collective on a theatrical feature about Rameshwar Nath Kao, founder of India’s Research and Analysis Wing, targeting an Aug. 11, 2028 release timed to the Indian Independence Day holiday weekend.

R&AW, India’s primary external intelligence agency, was established in 1968 to consolidate the country’s foreign intelligence operations, which had previously been handled by the Intelligence Bureau.

The untitled film is currently in development. The announcement was made on Sept. 21, marking 58 years since R&AW’s founding, with the makers eyeing the 2028 release date to coincide with the agency’s 60th anniversary. The project was initially announced in early 2020.

Popular on Variety

“Leo media has painstakingly been researching and dramatising this narrative with passion for the past two years, we want this film to be a gripping story based on true facts to pay homage to R&AW and honour their milestone year with a solid motion picture … all of us at Dharma are so excited to get going,” Johar said.

The espionage actioner is based on Nitin Gokhale’s book “Gentleman Spymaster,” with production slated to begin by mid-2026. Casting, director and other key details have not been disclosed, though an as yet unnamed A-list actor is attached to lead the project.

The story spans 1955 to 1971, tracing the lead-up to R&AW’s formation and its first mission during the 1971 war against Pakistan. Kao is widely regarded within Indian intelligence circles as a formative figure in the country’s espionage apparatus, with successive R&AW chiefs having credited his strategic approach.
