title: Robin Williams’ Daughter Calls for Fans Creating AI Videos of the Actor to ‘Have Some Shame’: ‘Leave Him Out of Your Delusional Bulls—’
summary: Zelda Williams is calling for fans to stop circulating AI-generated videos of her late father, Robin Williams, nearly a year after she last took to social media to ask them not to send her augmented content featuring the actor. In a statement posted to X on Monday, the “Lisa Frankenstein” director wrote that a “supposedly […]
content:
Zelda Williams is calling for fans to stop circulating AI-generated videos of her late father, Robin Williams, nearly a year after she last took to social media to ask them not to send her augmented content featuring the actor.

In a statement posted to X on Monday, the “Lisa Frankenstein” director wrote that a “supposedly ‘private video’” circulating of her father “is clearly AI, and not even particularly convincing AI,” she wrote. “Anyone who claims to be a fan who believes it clearly listened to his movies on mute because that voice is robotic and terrible. That said, a human made a robot create it, and to you I say: leave him out of your delusional bullshit and let him rest. If you cannot make your case without making a dead man make it more convincing for you, then tell me: who’s the one manipulating the public thru media now?”

Zelda continued: “I hate this cesspool of an app. It’s mostly bots and people willingly being duped by bots at this point so not sure why I feel the need to come back to clarify, but I love him, so I will. Just because he’s gone does not mean he’s now your puppet. Have some shame.”

Popular on Variety

The iconic comedian, who starred in films including “Jumanji,” “Good Will Hunting,” “Dead Poets Society,” “Hook,” “Mrs. Doubtfire,” and more, died in 2014 at the age of 63. In recent years, his likeness has become a popular target for AI recreation as users continue to create and share augmented videos of the actor.

This isn’t the first time Zelda has voiced her feelings about AI; Back in Oct. 2025, she wrote “Please, just stop sending me AI videos of Dad” on Instagram. “Stop believing I wanna see it or that I’ll understand, I don’t and I won’t. If you’re just trying to troll me, I’ve seen way worse, I’ll restrict and move on. But please, if you’ve got any decency, just stop doing this to him and to me, to everyone even, full stop. It’s dumb, it’s a waste of time and energy, and believe me, it’s NOT what he’d want.”

Just last month, she revived her father’s Instagram account with siblings Zak and Cody in an attempt to “fight back against rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness on here.”

title: Netflix Partners With British Library, Sets Talks Series With Florence Pugh, Zoe Kazan and More
summary: Netflix has teamed with one of the most famous cultural institutions in the U.K., the British Library, to help “more people discover the books behind some of the world’s most popular films and series,” it says. The new national partnership, which will include local libraries across the U.K., comes as 2026 marks the National Year […]
content:
Netflix has teamed with one of the most famous cultural institutions in the U.K., the British Library, to help “more people discover the books behind some of the world’s most popular films and series,” it says.

The new national partnership, which will include local libraries across the U.K., comes as 2026 marks the National Year of Reading, an initiative aimed at reversing the sharp decline in reading for pleasure across the U.K.

Alongside dedicated funding from Netflix to support the British Library’s literary conservation and archives, this new partnership will see collections of books that have been adapted into Netflix films and series donated to 100 public libraries across the U.K. The collections will include titles including “Frankenstein,” “Pride and Prejudice”, “Heartstopper,” “One Day,” “The Thursday Murder Club” and “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.”

Popular on Variety

In addition to the donated collections, Netflix and the British Library will host a programme of events also streamed to libraries across the country about how books are brought to the screen. The programme has already included Q&As with the stars of “Frankenstein,” “The Thursday Murder Club”, and “The Seven Dials Mystery.” On Monday night, Florence Pugh, Zoe Kazan, Christopher Abbott and Mike Faist discussed the making of “East of Eden.”

“Every great adaptation starts with a great story. We are proud to bring these stories to audiences all over the world, but we also know the experience does not have to end when the credits roll,” said Anne Mensah, Vice President of Content, U.K. at Netflix.

“Books and screen adaptations can introduce audiences to different worlds, ideas and voices. Through our partnership with the British Library, we hope to help more people discover the books behind the shows and films they love, while supporting the public libraries that make reading accessible to communities across the country.”

The U.K. National Literacy Trust’s 2025 Annual Literacy Survey found that children’s enjoyment of reading had fallen to its lowest recorded level. Howvever, it also showed that books linked to favourite films and TV series can encourage reluctant readers. The same is true for adults, with Nielsen BookData finding that 12% of adult fiction bought by occasional readers was discovered through, or chosen because of, a film or television adaptation.

‘’We are delighted to be partnering with Netflix. With this partnership we’re helping to bring Netflix’s exciting literary adaptations to new audiences across the U.K. via our Living Knowledge Network of public libraries,” Helen Schulte, the British Library’s head of culture programmes. “We’re so grateful to Netflix for partnering with the Library and providing much needed philanthropic support for conservation, helping to preserve the treasures we care for as the U.K.’s national library.”

title: Oscar Winner Barbara Kopple On ‘Union Town,’ Her Third Towering Film On American Labor – Camden Film Festival
summary: Fifty years ago, a young director named Barbara Kopple came out with her first film, a documentary she thought would be little seen. “When I started making the film, I thought, ‘Oh, my parents will see it and their friends and maybe a museum will show it,’” she recalls. That film was Harlan County U.S.A., […]
content:
Fifty years ago, a young director named Barbara Kopple came out with her first film, a documentary she thought would be little seen.

“When I started making the film, I thought, ‘Oh, my parents will see it and their friends and maybe a museum will show it,’” she recalls.

That film was Harlan County U.S.A., about a long running strike at a coal mine in southeast Kentucky, and it was immediately hailed as brilliant, earning Kopple an Academy Award. She would earn a second Oscar for her 1991 documentary American Dream, about a strike at a Hormel Foods plant in Minnesota.

Kopple has made many other documentaries in intervening years – on actor Gregory Peck, singer Sharon Jones, and country band the Chicks (formerly the Dixie Chicks), among others. But she returns to the theme for which she is best known – working people in America — in her new documentary Union Town. It just held its U.S. premiere at the Camden International Film Festival in Maine after bowing at the Venice Film Festival earlier in September.

Watch on Deadline

UPS workers walk a ‘practice picket line’ on July 7, 2023, in New York City, ahead of a possible strike. TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images

Union Town follows the battle for better wages and working conditions on three fronts in New York City — at UPS, at Amazon, and among “deliveristas” – that is, people who work for apps like DoorDash making food runs for customers.

“I think that they [labor organizers] have a big fight on their hands, but I think that they’re road warriors and I feel an awful lot of hope,” Kopple tells Deadline in an interview at the Camden Opera House, where Union Town screened. “Each time they win something, it’s glorious. It’s wonderful. And they get a little closer and a little closer. And what else can you do? You have to keep fighting… Looking at the people that they work with who can hardly make a living or people who die in the plants because there’s no air conditioning [in summer] or no heat in the winter, it’s just a very human thing to do, so you can’t stop.”

In the past four decades, union participation in America has dropped by about half. “[But] they’re still there. They’re still there,” Kopple says of unions. “And if you don’t have them, you don’t have anything.”

Director Barbara Kopple with Antonio Rosario, a Teamsters union organizer, at the U.S. premiere of ‘Union Town’ at the Camden International Film Festival on Sept. 19, 2026 in Camden, Maine. Matthew Carey

She points to Antonio Rosario, a veteran of a 1997 strike at UPS who serves as the Teamsters lead union organizer for Amazon workers in the northeast. At one moment in the film, Rosario is with his young sons at the dinner table and holds a bundle of sticks in his hands to illustrate the importance of worker solidarity.

“Tony is trying to show them the difference that if you have a lot of people together, it takes too much to break it,” Kopple explains. “And if you just have one stick, you can break it. And that’s what it is. It’s people who have your back. It’s people who will help you and it gives you a sense of strength that you can change.”

Of the three groups seen in the documentary, deliveristas face the worst conditions and pay – they work year-round in every kind of weather, driving their bikes through snow in winter, for instance. Kopple documents the case of Victor Hidalgo, a 24-year-old man who was working for a pharmacy delivery company in 2024 when a New York Fire Department vehicle hit his bicycle, killing him. At a Q&A following the U.S. premiere, Kopple said Hidalgo’s aunt urged her to put him in the documentary.

“She said, ‘I don’t want anyone to ever forget Victor,’” Kopple recounted. “’Please come and film the funeral. Please come and let people know that these things really happen.’”

A DoorDash delivery person prepares to bike in the snow in New York City. Noam Galai/Getty Images

Deliveristas rely on tips as a major source of income, but customers often don’t give them much (one deliverista recalls a person opening his hand to deposit a tip and placing in his palm a piece of candy). What’s worse, the tips they receive through the app may not go to them; in 2025 DoorDash reached a nearly $17 million settlement in New York after being accused of effectively taking workers’ tips. (Per the New York Attorney General’s office, “Customers were misled into believing their tips would directly benefit Dashers. Instead, DoorDash would keep the tips meant for Dashers and take it out of their guaranteed pay. DoorDash would guarantee pay to a delivery worker, and then only actually pay them whatever the tip did not cover.”).

“What it does if people get to see this film is maybe they’ll give big tips. Maybe they’ll talk to the people who deliver or at least understand them,” Kopple says. “Ever since UPS got their contract, every time I see a UPS truck, I stop and I talk to the driver and I say, ‘So how’s your contract? How’s work?’ And they’re looking at me like, ‘Who’s this crazy person?’ But it’s wonderful to do it… [It shows] somebody cares. Somebody’s out there who cares about them. They’re not invisible.”

Producer Peter Palandjian, Teamsters union organizer Antonio Rosario, director Barbara Kopple, and producer Hannes Hosp attend the ‘Union Town’ photocall at the Venice Film Festival on September 9, 2026. Aurore Marechal/Getty Images

Autlook is handling worldwide film sales for Union Town. The 2024 documentary Union, about the successful effort to organize workers at an Amazon facility in Staten Island, NY, struggled to find U.S. distribution (it was clear Prime Video wouldn’t touch it). That film by Stephen Maing and Brett Story is now streaming through Criterion.

Kopple says it’s “too soon to tell” about potential distribution of Union Town. “This was the third time the film has ever shown, and I had just finished it maybe two weeks before Venice. So, it’s totally at the beginning. I mean, I hope it gets great distribution and gets shown far and wide.”

title: Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios
summary: Here is a concession no one really asked for — the settlement of state attorneys generals’ anti-trust lawsuit over the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger includes a provision ensuring that Paramount will keep Pluto TV or another free, ad-supported streaming service for the next five years. While Pluto TV is protected, the settlement spells out […]
content:
Here is a concession no one really asked for — the settlement of state attorneys generals’ anti-trust lawsuit over the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger includes a provision ensuring that Paramount will keep Pluto TV or another free, ad-supported streaming service for the next five years.

While Pluto TV is protected, the settlement spells out which cable brands Paramount will have to divest if it fails to keep carriage negotiations for the Paramount and Warner Bros. basic cable networks at arm’s length. The list includes two Par nets that already had been put on the block twice, BET (and its various sub-channels) and VH1, as well as Comedy Central, with the company’s flagships MTV and Nickelodeon out of danger.

Overall, television feels a little like an afterthought in the settlement, illustrated by California AG Rob Bonta’s opening remarks at his Monday morning press conference. He spent more than six minutes laying out the agreed-upon terms for film production and had only two lines about TV, one about the establishment of “a news editorial independence board to support CBS News’ and CNN’s continued editorial independence” and one that “Paramount and Warner Brothers are required to continue negotiating their cable packages separately.”

Watch on Deadline

With state AGs’ action focused on protecting jobs, there is nothing in the agreement that would prevent Paramount from combining some of its post-merger TV studios — Warner Bros. Television, Paramount TV Studios and CBS Studios — that will result in layoffs. Or any guidelines on the number of positions that will inevitably be cut when Paramount merges Paramount+ with HBO Max as the company had said.

Movies and basic cable were the focus of AGs’ legal battle because those were the areas where there were strong anti-trust concerns. (The combined HBO Max-Paramount+ would become a major SVOD player but will not have dominance in the space.)

Still, the complete omission of the TV (or film) studios is surprising as is the lack of mention of Paramount’s pay cable network Showtime, which, like the basic cable nets, negotiates carriage agreements. That would allow Paramount to bundle it together with WBD‘s market leader HBO in dealings with operators.

Emphasizing that, the settlement’s statement about separate negotiations for Paramount and WBD’s basic cable channels carries the following disclaimer: “For the avoidance of doubt, this paragraph does not apply to other Combined Entity offerings (e.g., premium cable channels, streaming services, or broadcast)”

The omissions are especially glaring given the attention Pluto TV got despite it not being considered in real danger and it having no counterpart on the WBD side.

The Curious Case Of Pluto TV

Over the past year, Paramount’s leadership has been bullish about Pluto TV, vowing to invest in the AVOD platform and grow it, which they have done in the form of a slew of library content acquisitions and making Pluto part of the company’s backend tech stack convergence alongside Paramount+ – a complex, lengthy process which has largely been completed.

Long before the Ellisons arrived on the scene, Pluto’s star had started fading as rivals Tubi and Roku became more popular. Pluto, although it had been a pioneer of FAST when it was founded in 2014, fell back in the market-share race. Its co-founder, Tom Ryan, and other core staffers exited the company.

Even so, the new regime has expressed optimism about aiding the potential of Pluto, which had been largely neglected for the previous couple of years.

“I am a big believer in the FAST space,” Paramount Chairman and CEO David Ellison said on the company’s Q4 2025 earnings call. Pluto TV was talked up to advertisers at the Paramount upfront presentation in May as a key piece of the company’s ad strategy, with upgrades ongoing and more underway.

Most recently, Paramount noted that “Paramount+ and Pluto TV remain at the center of how audiences discover and engage with our programming as we build an entertainment platform for the future” in its Q2 2026 letter to investors, with the company’s executives saying on the earnings call that “we do expect that Pluto will return to growth in back half of the year.”

Basic Cable Haves & Have Nots

According to the settlement with the 12 state AGs, “Paramount and Warner Brothers are required to continue negotiating their cable packages separately — a negotiate-separately condition, preserving the competition that exists between them today,” Bonta said Monday, adding, “It will mimic them being separate companies, even post-merger.”

As to how that separation will be ensured, the statement is a little vague, noting that there will be a “monitor” and a “state committee” that would assess any complaints.

If Paramount is caught in a “material violation,” following a six-month cure period where the company can “come into compliance,” they will have to sell one or more of the following linear networks: BET (Black Entertainment Television, including BET, BET Gospel, BET Her, BET Hip-Hop, BET Jams, and BET Soul), VH1, Comedy Central, Smithsonian, Destination America, and Science.

After Skydance’s acquisition of Paramount, the company’s new leadership has shared their intention to revitalize legacy cable brands such as MTV, Nickelodeon, Comedy Central and BET. The inclusion of two of the four on the potential divesture list is somewhat surprising but Paramount still has kept crown jewels MTV and Nickelodeon out of reach.

Additionally, the company already has Comedy Central’s biggest program, South Park, locked into a Paramount+ streaming deal for the foreseeable future and just folded BET+ into Paramount+.

The rest of the channels on the list are very small and, amid linear ratings declines, Paramount likely won’t mind divesting them anyway.

Dade Hayes contributed to this report.

title: ‘Forgotten Island’ Review: H.E.R. And Dave Franco Give Life To Gorgeously Animated And Frenetic ‘Toon
summary: You have to give points to DreamWorks’ latest animated feature, Forgotten Island, just simply for being an original from a studio system that rewards familiarity. And it comes from writer/directors Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado who proved with their own sequel, 2022’s Puss In Boots: The Last Wish that you could find clever ways to […]
content:
You have to give points to DreamWorks’ latest animated feature, Forgotten Island, just simply for being an original from a studio system that rewards familiarity. And it comes from writer/directors Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado who proved with their own sequel, 2022’s Puss In Boots: The Last Wish that you could find clever ways to renew and energize existing IP, rather than just settling for what the audience expects.

I suspect this one though will have the most appeal to a teenage female audience as it is centered on the BFF relationship of two young girls, besties since grade school in the Phillipines, who have lived a life of memories (they have matching charm bracelets to prove it) since being little kids inseparable from each other. Now on the cusp of seeing life taking them down separate paths, they are about to embark on their greatest adventure together ever. But will they even be able to remember it? That is the hook here as the opening of the film introduces us to the wild and wacky Jo, and the more serious-minded Raissa with dreams of being a scientist one day.

At home in Manila they both dream of a mythical place that in their minds absolutely exists. During their lives they have been fed epic stories by the beloved elder Lola (Dolly DeLeon) which are vividly shared with her class by Jo. The film jumps ahead to the end of their high school years where Jo (the older version voiced by singer H.E.R.) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) are at that inflection point. Raissa is accepted into Caltech in America and is going to be leaving, while meanwhile Jo is stuck in a menial job at a fast food joint. This will be their last night and they are going to make the most of it when they come upon a magical portal on the beach, the portal it turns out to, Nakali, that Forgotten Island.

Watch on Deadline

Next thing you know they have landed there, with absolutely no idea of just how they got to the place of their imaginations. They are about to find out in this play on memory and the importance of it in all of our lives. With colorful new appearances (Raissa now has wings and half a head of hair) they have gone down the kind of rabbit hole that infamous characters like Alice and Dorothy have tread in literature and movies before, but this place is something else. In quick and whirring succession they meet some real doozies starting with Weredog, Raww (voiced with style and fun by Dave Franco), who claims he had just spent the previous 12 hours with both of them. He is a bit of a mess, embarrassed by his ever-changing appearance from human to dog and back again, mostly dog though. He will be their self-appointed guide thorugh Nakali, but he has competition from another new acquaintance, Bungi (Manny Jacinto) a cycloptic giant blue baby still stuck (literally) to his mother after all these years. We also meet the more restrained cave dwelling Batiba (terrifically voiced by Jenny Slate) who is agoraphobic to her core, but lives with a collection of knick knacks it turns out have been stolen from other peoples memories, just not her own since she is deathly afraid of venturing out into the world. She promises to help Jo and Raissa get back to their own world in return for their own memories.

Along the way we meet Daju (Jo Koy) leader of a tree brigade; King Truffle Wuffle (Ronny Chieng) lording over his own feifdom; and the impossibly vain and slick Prince Mermahn (Kevin McCann). As in every single cartoon aimed at kids there is also a villainess, and here it is The Dreaded Manananggal (Lea Solonga) who can magically divide herself down the middle and other horrific talents. She’s the wicked witch and evil queen of the piece but of course there is a reason she got to be so bad and we will find out in due time.

Jo and Raissa must navigate all of this in order to get back to where they came from in this uber frenetically-paced journey. Crawford and Mercado (who clearly has added the Filipino flavor to this story) pack way too much visually, especially in the first half perhaps sensing today’s younger moviegoers have a bit of attention deficit. I thought this thing, beautifully animated with different styles creeping in and out and as colorful as it could possibly be, would never slow down to take a breath. But finally in the second half when the girls’ own hopes and dreams come front and center, and the emotional elements take charge, it does cool its jets just enough to take it all in. The main theme of saving our memories, and keeping them close comes through loud and clear and there is nice resoloution to all of this. The busy soundtrack has lots of catchy tunes, old and new, including an original or two from H.E.R. herself.

Is this an animated movie I will keep in my memories? Not likely, but I think its younger (much) target audience will indeed be the ones who will find some cool things to remember and some sharp life lessons about the value of friendship.

Producer of the DreamWorks Animation production is Mark Swift.

Title: Forgotten Island

Distributor: Universal

Release Date: September 25, 2026

Director/ Screenwriters: Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado

Cast: H.E.R., Dave Franco, Liza Soberano, Jenny Slate, Manny Jacinto, Dolly DeLeon, Jo Koy, Ronny Chieng, Kevin McCann, Lea Solanga

Rating: PG

Running Time: 1 hr 47 mins

title: Top UK YouTubers Launch Alliance Pushing For Better Conditions For Content Creators
summary: Top UK creators have banded together to launch an independent alliance championing their interests. YouTube UK is backing Creator Voices, which consists of The Sidemen’s rep Jordan Schwarzenberger, DamienTalksMoney, Jade Beason, TLDR News, Grace Andrews and Brandon B. The alliance is being unveiled today at a YouTube Festival in London. Creator Voices said its members […]
content:
Top UK creators have banded together to launch an independent alliance championing their interests.

YouTube UK is backing Creator Voices, which consists of The Sidemen‘s rep Jordan Schwarzenberger, DamienTalksMoney, Jade Beason, TLDR News, Grace Andrews and Brandon B. The alliance is being unveiled today at a YouTube Festival in London.

Creator Voices said its members will “leverage their collective reach” and “advocate for institutional recognition and deeper integration with traditional creative bodies.”

The move comes after thousands of creators including Amelia Dimoldenberg put their names to a first-of-its-kind report from YouTube that found its creator ecosystem contributed more than £2B ($2.67B) to the UK economy in 2023. That figure rose to £2.8B last year, according to a newer Oxford Economics Impact Report, which said the number could support more than 60,000 equivalent jobs.

When the report came out, its authors said they wanted the job of content creator to be given government recognition along with better industry representation and access to finance. Since then, digital creators have become an even more crucial cog in the traditional entertainment machine. Dimoldenberg, for example, will host Saturday Night Live UK this weekend, just a fortnight after Hollywood superstar Jeff Goldblum.

Watch on Deadline

“The UK boasts one of the most dynamic creative ecosystems in the world, and digital creators are adding an extraordinary new dimension to that heritage,” said YouTube UK boss Alison Lomax. “While YouTube is proud to support the convening of this independent collective, the voice and vision belong entirely to them. Connecting digital talent with established creative leaders will unlock significant economic growth, foster fresh storytelling and showcase the best of modern British culture on a global stage.”

Earlier this year, we told you how UK content creators like Dimoldenberg, Beason and Munya Chawawa were helping shape the TV industry behind the scenes.

title: Rima Das, Shan Zuolong, Shim Eun-kyung Named to Busan’s New Currents Jury
summary: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has confirmed Indian director Rima Das, Chinese producer Shan Zuolong and Korean actor Shim Eun-kyung as the three jurors for its New Currents Award, a prize that has served as a launchpad for emerging Asian directors. Debut feature films screening in BIFF’s Competition or Vision sections are eligible […]
content:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has confirmed Indian director Rima Das, Chinese producer Shan Zuolong and Korean actor Shim Eun-kyung as the three jurors for its New Currents Award, a prize that has served as a launchpad for emerging Asian directors.

Debut feature films screening in BIFF’s Competition or Vision sections are eligible for the award, which comes with a KRW20 million ($14,400) cash prize.

Das, a filmmaker based in Assam, India, is known for an intimate visual style built around themes of resilience and the human bond with nature. Her films have played at more than 150 festivals and picked up over 75 prizes internationally. Her credits include “Village Rockstars” (2017), “Bulbul Can Sing” (2018), “Tora’s Husband” (2022), “Village Rockstars 2” (2024) and “Not a Hero” (2026), titles that have found berths at festivals including Toronto and Berlin in addition to Busan. “Village Rockstars” took best feature film honors at India’s National Film Awards and went on to become the country’s Academy Awards submission in 2018. “Village Rockstars 2” was honored with the Kim Jiseok Award during BIFF’s 2024 edition, while “Not a Hero” received a Crystal Bear special mention in Berlin’s Generation KPlus section this year. Das belongs to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and has sat on festival juries before.

Popular on Variety

Shan’s credits as a producer trace back to “Kaili Blues” (Bi Gan, 2015), which took the best emerging director prize at Locarno, and “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” (Bi Gan, 2018), an Un Certain Regard selection at Cannes. His later slate includes “Love Is a Gun” (Lee Hong-chi, 2023), honored with Venice’s Lion of the Future for best debut feature; “The Botanist” (Jing Yi, 2025), a Grand Prix winner in Berlin’s Generation section; and “Resurrection” (Bi Gan, 2025), which took the Special Prize at Cannes and also received BIFF’s Busan Award for Artistic Contribution when it played in the festival’s inaugural Competition section last year. He joined the Producers Branch of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 2026.

Shim swept best actress honors at several of Korea’s top ceremonies for “Sunny” (2011) and “Miss Granny” (2014); her “Miss Granny” performance specifically earned wins at the Baeksang Arts Awards and the Chunsa International Film Festival, along with the Buil Film Awards. She went on to build a career in Japan as well, becoming the first Korean actor to claim the Japan Academy Film Prize for best actress, for her role in “The Journalist” (2019). Her latest credit, “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” (2025), took the Golden Leopard at Locarno, a run that also brought her the Kinema Junpo Best Actress Award.

The 31st BIFF will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and other venues throughout the city. The 21st Asian Contents & Film Market will take place Oct. 10-13.

title: From Memory to Horror: Eight New Gen Basque Filmmakers to Track
summary: For a new generation of Basque filmmakers coming into focus at San Sebastián, stories often begin with something unresolved: an argument a child cannot remember, the working lives buried in an industrial landscape, a language whose influence reaches beyond the words spoken on screen. “My films grow from spending time with people and places, allowing […]
content:
For a new generation of Basque filmmakers coming into focus at San Sebastián, stories often begin with something unresolved: an argument a child cannot remember, the working lives buried in an industrial landscape, a language whose influence reaches beyond the words spoken on screen.

“My films grow from spending time with people and places, allowing fiction to emerge from those encounters,” Ekain Albite tells Variety. His “Akira” is taking shape between the Basque Country and Georgia. Joana Moya’s upbringing on Bilbao’s industrial Left Bank informs her interest in “who we are beyond work and how the land and its materiality shape us.” For Gemma González Martínez, Basque identity provides a point of departure rather than a limit. “Being Basque gives me a very strong awareness of language, identity, memory and belonging,” she says. “But I don’t see it as a boundary. It is my starting point.”

Across their work, identity, memory and place are testing grounds. “I want cinema to provoke questions rather than provide answers,” says Asier Urbieta. Mikele Landa sees another possibility in that process: “I am tremendously interested in the use of memory as a matter to imagine possible futures, as a tool of resistance.”

Popular on Variety

Their routes to a first feature are varied, spanning journalism, cultural production, television, camera crews and years working on other directors’ films. San Sebastián has been part of that trajectory for several: Landa entered Ikusmira Berriak in 2024, Moya followed in 2025 and Albite joins the program this year. With new works from Nitya López and Gemma González Martínez in Zinemira, and Javier Giner entering with buzz in New Directors, the festival offers a meeting point for eight filmmakers with breakout potential.

Nitya López

After assistant directing-team jobs on “Ane,” “The Good Boss” and “Maixabel,” López makes his feature debut with a problem no amount of production experience can resolve: how to film a memory he doesn’t have. In Zinemira entry “Family Drill” (“Simulacro”), Iraia Elias and Miguel Garcés help him stage the parental confrontation behind a separation that happened when he was four. Rehearsing possible versions of the event raises questions about what he wants from the reconstruction. The Ibarrangelu-born filmmaker’s earlier directing credits include short “Deadly Draw” and “Aloka(h)iru,” an EITB series co-created with Alba Lozano.

Joana Moya

Moya’s geology training gives her an unusual qualification for “La Koreana,” a debut feature project in which the mountain has a history of its own. The arrival of Manuela, who comes from Andalusia to a mining settlement in 1960, opens a story that eventually breaks through into 1890. Lazona Zinema and Sirimiri Films, headed by “20,000 Species of Bees” director Estibaliz Urresola, are producing; last year’s Sideral Award at Ikusmira Berriak brought a €10,000 ($11,600) international distribution minimum guarantee. For the director, whose short “Salt Covers All” reached Hot Docs, the workers’ struggle concerns a still-familiar “search for dignity, time and freedom.”

Mikele Landa

Could the grammar of Euskera affect where a filmmaker makes a cut? That is the kind of question occupying Landa as she develops “Senda” with Gariza Films. “I wonder how much one’s mother tongue can shape a director’s particular way to approach filmmaking,” she explained. Her plans include using translation to inform the film’s construction, and casting sessions to continue its research and writing. An EQZE alum with Basque public bradcaster EITB and Berria journalism experience, Landa has taken the project through Noka Mentoring and Ikusmira Berriak. San Sebastián awarded it the Casa Wabi–ESCINE residency prize in 2024.

Ekain Albite

Albite’s filmmaking grew out of collaboration at Barcelona film school ESCAC, where he formed Colectivo Negu with Adrià Roca, Nicolau Mallofré and Mikel Ibarguren. After making shorts together, the group directed “Negu Hurbilak,” which received a Special Mention from the Filmmakers of the Present jury at Locarno in 2023.

He now takes sole directing responsibility with “Akira,” his first feature as a solo director and an Ikusmira Berriak 2026 project. Set between the Basque Country and Georgia, the film centers on a Georgian scrap dealer whose familiar world is unsettled by the arrival of a relative and a journey into the night. “It explores exile and the quiet unraveling of familiar worlds within an endless night,” Albite says. “I’m excited to extend my work beyond one territory and discover how cinema can bring distant lives together.”

Asier Urbieta

Who answers for a death when the territory itself changes hands? Urbieta built his 2025 fiction feature debut “Pheasant Island” around that question, bringing Goya Winner Jone Laspiur (“Ane”) and Sambou Diaby into a drama shaped by the Spain-France frontier. It played last year’s San Sebastian as well as Göteborg. “I’m particularly interested in the border, both as a physical and psychological space,” he says. His next film, “Islandia,” will see Urbieta shoot a single continuous take. “It’s an enormous technical challenge, but also a way of putting the characters, the actors and myself at risk — and that interests me greatly,” he told Variety.

Gemma González Martínez

Having led Ladyred Producciones since 2010 and founded women’s culture platform KulturFemme, González Martínez brings her documentary feature debut “Daughters of the Sea” (“Las hijas del mar”) to Zinemira. The film finds affinities between Jeju’s women divers and women whose work connects them to the Basque coast.

“I’m especially excited by projects that allow unexpected international collaborations to emerge,” she says. Already in development are a further “Daughters of the Sea” chapter spanning the Basque Country, Galicia and Brittany, and “Mirror Mirror,” a documentary series examining cultural ecosystems in different countries. Her slate gives that international ambition a concrete next step.

Javier Giner

Giner’s journey from Barakaldo to a feature premiere has included film school in Los Angeles, employment at MGM and international relations work at El Deseo, where he also assisted Pedro Almodóvar.

Following autobiographical series “Yo, adicto,” his debut “This Solitude” (“Esta soledad”) lands in New Directors. Oriol Pla and Marina Salas play a separated couple for whom earning a living and caring for family leave little room to recover their footing. Giner wrote the film with Luisa Matienzo; Filmax has set an Oct. 30 Spanish theatrical release. It brings a long industry apprenticeship, and TV breakout into a new phase.

Norma Vila

Bilbao-born Norma Vila makes the leap to features with “Carapace” (“Salitre”), a psychological horror film that turns empty-nest anxiety into something disturbing and physical. Starring Nagore Aranburu (“Querer,” “Sundays”) and Haizea Carneros, the film follows a mother whose terror of losing her teenage daughter begins to infect both their home and relationship. Vila came up through camera crews before directing prize-winning fantasy shorts “Jules D.” and “El fin de todas las cosas.” Now her debut lands directly in Sitges’ Official Fantastic Competition before opening San Sebastián’s Horror and Fantasy Film Festival. It marks Vila as a potentially distinctive new Basque genre voice.

title: Inside the Basque Production Boom: Who Owns the Growth?
summary: The Basque Country has become an increasingly attractive place to make films and television. In Bizkaia alone, audiovisual employment rose 50.5% between 2014 and 2024, while the number of companies linked to the sector climbed from 284 to 448. In 2025, the Bilbao Bizkaia Film Commission supported 219 shoots with an estimated economic impact of […]
content:
The Basque Country has become an increasingly attractive place to make films and television.

In Bizkaia alone, audiovisual employment rose 50.5% between 2014 and 2024, while the number of companies linked to the sector climbed from 284 to 448. In 2025, the Bilbao Bizkaia Film Commission supported 219 shoots with an estimated economic impact of €138.1 million ($158.45 million).

The boom has also complicated a simple question: What, exactly, is a Basque production? Is it a project that shoots in the territory, one backed by a Basque company, one made in Euskara, or one whose creative control, intellectual property and long-term economic value remain there?

For Xabi Berzosa of San Sebastian-based Irusoin, the legal answer is relatively simple.

Popular on Variety

“From a legal standpoint, if a film is produced by a Basque production company, it’s Basque. That’s simply how it is defined.”

Then he offers the complication. Irusoin is a co-producer on Nanni Moretti’s latest film “It Will Happen Tonight,” alongside such companies as Fandango and BTeam Prods.

“The film is Basque, as well as Italian and French,” Berzosa says. “It’s shot in Italy and in the Basque Country, in Italian. … We don’t really feel that’s a portrait of Basque filmmaking nowadays, of course, but legally it’s Basque.”

For filmmaker Koldo Almandoz, whose Basque-language feature “The Last Goodbye” plays out of competition in San Sebastian’s Official Selection this year, the answer lies somewhere beyond legal definitions. It has to do, he says, with “the soul,” with “the culture, the language, the crews and the intention of the films.”

He is blunter about productions arriving primarily because of tax incentives. “You can call it co-production, but we all know that it’s like they are working as commission agents,” he says. “I don’t consider those Basque productions.”

Iker Ganuza, president of producers’ association EPE-IBAIA and a producer at Lamia Producciones, approaches the same question from an industrial perspective. “A Basque production is not simply a production filmed in the Basque Country,” he says. For Ganuza, the key questions are where decisions are made, where intellectual property remains, how much Basque talent and business are involved and how much value stays in the region.

If he had to choose one criterion, it would be “deep-rooted business and creative presence, along with decision-making capacity.”

That word — deep-rooted — sits uneasily beside an industry that is increasingly mobile. Berzosa puts the principle more simply. “Productions that come for financial reasons will leave for financial reasons.”

None of the producers argues that attracting international productions is a mistake. “Major international productions have obviously a very positive impact,” Ganuza says. “They create jobs, generate economic activity, and boost international visibility.”

But, he adds, “once filming wraps up, the intellectual property, business decisions, and much of the future value leave the country.” “Both activities are important, but they are not the same.”

Berzosa makes a similar distinction between servicing and co-producing. “The obvious solution is to service that shooting,” he says. “You are hired, they come and they go.”

With Moretti’s film, Irusoin instead became a co-producer, gaining ownership and a deeper involvement in the project. Services, Berzosa says, “help people to work and to have continuity,” but “they don’t develop a local established industry for the long term.”

Almandoz worries about what happens to that local infrastructure if conditions change.

“If sometime these fiscal advantages disappear, all these little home companies we had, that were working for us, now absorbed by bigger companies, are they gonna stay, or are they gonna go… to Madrid or Barcelona or Paris?”

He is not predicting collapse. “People are working. There’s an industry. We are growing. We are learning a lot.”But, he adds: “We want to pass from zero to 100 in three years, and I don’t think it’s the way.”

Language adds another layer. For Berzosa, a film written, shot and released in Euskara is one particularly clear example of a production with cultural weight, but it is not a requirement for something to qualify as Basque. Ganuza likewise argues that the language must be specially protected, while cautioning against making it the sole measure.

“We can tell Basque stories to the world and also produce universal stories from the Basque Country.” The broader challenge, then, is not simply how to attract more production, but what remains when those productions leave.

Ganuza says the next phase must focus on making sure international investment strengthens local companies rather than displacing them.

“The main problem is not a lack of opportunities,” he says. “It is precisely the opposite: there is a huge opportunity, and we must ensure that growth does not leave behind the companies that have built this sector right here.” That may ultimately become a useful measure of success, and one relevant far beyond the Basque Country.

“We have to start talking about where we want the Basque film industry to be in 2030,” Ganuza says, “not just how many film shoots we’ll have next year.”

title: Werner Herzog’s ‘Ghost Elephants’ Lands Home Entertainment Deal With Buffalo 8 (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Buffalo 8 Distribution has acquired home entertainment rights to “Ghost Elephants,” the documentary written, directed and narrated by Werner Herzog. The deal, negotiated at the Toronto Film Festival market, pairs Buffalo 8 with Sobey Road Entertainment for the film’s home entertainment rollout, with release dates and platform details to be unveiled separately. The agreement was […]
content:
Buffalo 8 Distribution has acquired home entertainment rights to “Ghost Elephants,” the documentary written, directed and narrated by Werner Herzog.

The deal, negotiated at the Toronto Film Festival market, pairs Buffalo 8 with Sobey Road Entertainment for the film’s home entertainment rollout, with release dates and platform details to be unveiled separately.

The agreement was negotiated by Buffalo 8 CEO Matthew Helderman and Sobey Road Co-Managing Partner Terrence Battle.

“Few filmmakers have shaped documentary cinema like Werner Herzog,” said Nikki Stier Justice, head of distribution at Buffalo 8. “We are honored to partner on ‘Ghost Elephants’ and help extend the reach of this extraordinary film through home entertainment.”

Popular on Variety

The film follows Dr. Steve Boyes, a conservation biologist and National Geographic Explorer, on a search spanning more than a decade for an elusive, rarely documented elephant population in the mist-covered highlands of Angola, one some speculate may descend from the largest land mammal on record. Boyes is joined by National Geographic Explorer Kerllen Costa and three KhoiSan master trackers, Xui, Xui Dawid and Kobus, on an expedition that combines scientific inquiry with ancient knowledge.

Herzog described the expedition as more than a search for an elusive animal, calling it “an exploration of dreams, of imagination – weighed against reality.”

“Ghost Elephants” premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2025 before its North American premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, followed by selections at AFI Fest and IDFA. The film received a special mention from the FAI Persona Lavoro Ambiente Foundation at Venice and the Programmers Award for Documentary Feature at the Virginia Film Festival. Herzog’s narration also earned a 2026 Emmy nomination for outstanding narrator.

The documentary is produced by Herzog and Ariel Leon Isacovitch. It is a production of National Geographic Documentary Films, Sobey Road Entertainment, Skellig Rock, Inc. and The Roots Production Service.

Sobey Road’s slate also includes “Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery,” produced with ABC News Studios and CBC; “Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It”; and “Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes.”

title: Inside the 2026 San Sebastián-CAA Media Finance Creative Investors’ Conference
summary: Acme AI & FX’s Ryan Kavanaugh, Laura Austin-Little at Black Bear International, Neon’s Elissa Federoff, StudioCanal’s Ron Halpern and Sumerian Pictures’ Rob Williams are confirmed for San Sebastián’s fifth Creative Investors’ Conference, co-organized with CAA Media Finance. They will join CAA Media Finance’s Roeg Sutherland, Killer Films’ Christine Vachon, Patrick Wachsberger at 193 and Sumerian […]
content:
Acme AI & FX’s Ryan Kavanaugh, Laura Austin-Little at Black Bear International, Neon’s Elissa Federoff, StudioCanal’s Ron Halpern and Sumerian Pictures’ Rob Williams are confirmed for San Sebastián’s fifth Creative Investors’ Conference, co-organized with CAA Media Finance.

They will join CAA Media Finance’s Roeg Sutherland, Killer Films’ Christine Vachon, Patrick Wachsberger at 193 and Sumerian Pictures’ Rob Williams, among U.S. delegates.

The Creative Investors Conference also features sessions with some movers and shakers on the Latin American film-TV scene, Pablo and Juan de Dios Larraín, at San Sebastián to talk up game-changing TVOD platform Pijama, and Rodrigo Teixeira of RT Features, behind “Paper Tiger” and Oscar-winning “I’m Still Here,” and now ever more embracing global cinema. At his session, From Local to Global, he looks set to explain why.

Popular on Variety

From 2022, speakers like Sutherland, Wachsberger and Goodfellas Vincent Maraval have laid it on the line on how to confront challenges in the U.S. (cost, contracting budgets, unreliable tax breaks) and Europe (most recently, the need to scale), plus more promisingly, an evolution in U.S. theatrical audiences.

An update on all these issues looks likely to be on the table on two central panels, The New U.S. Landscape and Europe’s Current Challenges & Opportunities. Maraval will deliver a Goodfellas’ insight on the market, which promises to be as ever bracingly iconoclastic.

There’s also a new kid on the block and at the conference: Spain’s SETT, a sovereign venture capital fund at Spain’s Ministry of Digital Transformation, which has sunk invested €215.6 million ($252.3 million) into Spain’s film, TV, vid game and new technology sectors, sparking matching private sector investment of a further €230 million ($269.1 million). María Coronado, SETT director of audiovisual, looks set to explain why, other panelists, including private-sector partners, the benefits of SETT co-investment.

In a further development, the San Sebastian Festival is partnering with the Marché du Film-Festival de Cannes and its Investors Circle program to bring a select delegation of private investors to San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference. Participants will take part in the Conference program, dedicated educational workshops, and receive private mentoring and exclusive exchanges with top international industry professionals.

“At a time when so much is changing in the film industry, it is so important to host a Conference like this, to welcome these experts to share their insights with each other and with the festival’s industry badge-holders, as well as having important networking sessions and meetings between the global experts and the Spanish film industry,” said San Sebastian Film Festival Director Jose Luis Rebordinos.

title: Muse Entertainment Unveils ‘Doula: A True Crime’ Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Here’s a trailer for Doula – A True Crime, a Canadian doc series from The Walrus and the Whistleblower filmmaker Nathalie Bibeau about a bizarre criminal case of a woman who faked pregnancies. The three-parter, which will premiere on Canadian pubcaster CBC on October 7, looks into the story of Kaitlyn Braun, who aged […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Here’s a trailer for Doula – A True Crime, a Canadian doc series from The Walrus and the Whistleblower filmmaker Nathalie Bibeau about a bizarre criminal case of a woman who faked pregnancies.

The three-parter, which will premiere on Canadian pubcaster CBC on October 7, looks into the story of Kaitlyn Braun, who aged 24, reached out to more than 40 doulas with the same shocking story: that she had been sexually assaulted and was in her third trimester carrying a stillborn child.

We can reveal Boat Rocker Studios has acquired the international distribution rights to the Muse Entertainment-produced show and will launch it at MIPCOM Cannes next month.

The doc is notable for including the first interview with Braun, who was hit with 53 criminal charges after doulas, who had helped her and provided pro bono services such as hours of phone and video calls and round-the-clock in-person care, began to question her narrative.

Watch on Deadline

After piecing together the pattern that had formed over nine months between June 2022 and February 2023, many found others like themselves and started a grassroots campaign for to alert authorities through a viral TikTok counter-offensive.

In the trailer, we hear from several doulas shaken by their experience. “I can’t tell you I was assaulted, that’s not really what happened and I can’t tell that I was scammed, that doesn’t encompass what she did to me. I have to tell you the whole story so you understand,” says one. “I have no felt fear like that in my entire life,” says another later in the trailer.

The one-minute clip ends with a camera making its way up a porch, where it is met by Braun, who smiles as she opens the door and says, “Hello!”

The film was made over several years, and attempts to go beyond the sensationalist reporting that followed the story at the time. Braun conversed with Bibeau several times over extensive interviews and phone calls, offering insight into her actions and motivations.

“Everyone knew that Kaitlyn Braun had committed crimes. I wanted to understand why,” said Bibeau, writer, director and producer of Doula: A True Crime. “The deeper I went, the less the story yielded to easy conclusions. Kaitlyn’s deception played on empathy, and the harm it caused was real.

“But the very thing that made the harm possible was also what I needed to understand her. I’m drawn to the places where human behaviour resists a clean moral frame. And this story lives in one of those places – where empathy doesn’t get in the way of truth, but brings us closer to it.”

Jonas Prupas, Managing Director of Unscripted and executive producer at Montreal-based Muse, said the story “could easily be reduced to its more sensationalist elements,” but that Bibeau had made it “into something nuanced, surprising and deeply human.”

Mellany Welsh, SVP and Global Head of Distribution & Brands at Boat Rocker Studios, added the doc offered international buyers “a story they won’t find anywhere else.”

Muse – known for the likes of Sullivan’s Crossing, The Kennedys and Nose Deep – made the show for CBC and CBC Gem, with the series premiering on October 7 at 8am ET on CBC. Prupas and Courtney Dobbins are exec producers for Muse. For CBC, Sally Catto is General Manager, Entertainment, Jennifer Dettman is Executive Director of Unscripted Content, and Michelle McCree is Senior Director and Commissioning Editor of Documentary.

A CBC and BBC podcast titled Kaitlyn’s Baby launched last year.

title: ‘Trump TV’ Promo Uses Clips From ‘The Simpsons,’ ‘Seinfeld,’ ‘Friends,’ ‘The Dark Knight’ & Many More
summary: Donald Trump has defied copyright complaints from Neil Young, Ariana Grande, Beyoncé and everyone in between for unauthorized use of their music. Today, it posted a promo video for Trump TV that made use of footage from Friends, The Simpsons, Family Guy, Home Alone, Modern Family, Breaking Bad, The Dark Knight, The Office, SpongeBob SquarePants, […]
content:
Donald Trump has defied copyright complaints from Neil Young, Ariana Grande, Beyoncé and everyone in between for unauthorized use of their music. Today, it posted a promo video for Trump TV that made use of footage from Friends, The Simpsons, Family Guy, Home Alone, Modern Family, Breaking Bad, The Dark Knight, The Office, SpongeBob SquarePants, Parks and Recreation, That ’70s Show and more.

Among the studios and networks whose IP is used in the promo are Warner Bros., Fox, Nickelodeon, Sony Pictures Television, Disney and NBCUniversal. It’s not a terribly unusual move for the president, who routinely posts AI videos that lift scenes from hit films like Top Gun. It is, however, somewhat unique in its breadth. And perhaps that is the point.

Trump TV is a promotional effort launched after the president banned Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. The administration billed it “The Essentials Station.” Another (grammatically-challenged) administration pitch for the service was, “Not every big moment has made it on your tv, now it can.” The service provides a live feed of official events, seemingly without the razzle dazzle of which the president is so fond. The New York Times dubbed it “essentially a form of state television.”

Watch on Deadline

IT'S LIVE. 📺🦅



TRUMP TV IS STREAMING NOW. 24/7, updated in real time, with top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place.



Not every big moment has made it on your tv, now it can.



📲 https://t.co/3KwWkBZ69m pic.twitter.com/g4v7n2J04s — The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 21, 2026

The advent of Trump TV comes after the president denied Politico, CNN and MS Now access to the White House over the weekend, prompting outcry from other media and a lawsuit from the trio.

CNN had the White House pool assignment for Monday and was scheduled to be the primary network for coverage. The other TV networks declined to replace CNN in protest of the move, and as a result, there was no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveled to New York.

The lack of network-level production is apparent. Video posted on the White House YouTube channel this weekend includes a long, very unTrumpy nine-minute recount of a ribbon cutting. It includes long takes of the president shaking hands with attendees before proceeding to make his remarks. Those, however, are drowned out by the engines of Marine One in the background.

title: Post-Merger Paramount May Overdeliver On Settlement Terms With 36-Film 2027 Slate Amid Speculation About Duplication & WB Leadership
summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta can rest easy: A merged Paramount Warner Bros. Discovery would already account for 36 movies on the release schedule for 2027. Note, that’s an organic number of theatrical releases which were always set to happen even before the union of the storied studios came together. As for 2028, the combined […]
content:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta can rest easy: A merged Paramount Warner Bros. Discovery would already account for 36 movies on the release schedule for 2027.

Note, that’s an organic number of theatrical releases which were always set to happen even before the union of the storied studios came together. As for 2028, the combined entity currently accounts for 25 theatrical releases, hence another five titles are needed to meet the state AGs’ agreed-upon settlement term of 30 films in the merger’s first two years of existence. That should be easy, it’s still early, and awards season fare often gets dated later rather than sooner.

Beyond 2029, the AGs’ demand from the merged entity is for 32 films annually over three years. It’s on Ellison to make sure this union isn’t a repeat of Disney-Fox. Missing the annual theatrical release quota could cost Paramount — per the pact with the AGs — its 49% investment in Miramax. In addition, per Bonta, “For each film that they fail to make, should they fail to make any, $30M is paid to be split three different ways, but 90% of it goes to workers.”

Watch on Deadline

Despite all the pom pom waving that the house of Harry Potter and Batman are now one with the house of Transformers, Star Trek and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, the question becomes, how will Ellison’s Paramount wrangle this beast?

If merged today, both studios combined would count $838.3M at the YTD domestic box office (Jan. 1-Sept. 20) for an 11% market share, ranking fourth behind Universal ($1.78 billion), Sony ($1.22B) and Walt Disney ($1.03B) — global annual numbers were not available at the time of this report for Paramount or Warners. However, Universal leads all studios with around $5B WW, followed by Disney with $4B-plus WW.

Rumors that both studios would have to operate separately were wrong. We hear that as Ellison eyes his early corporate structure that one or two executives would oversee overall theatrical and film strategy and likely one or two executives would oversee each film brand. Note that this is all fluid and still in the works.

In addition, how the new conglomerate plans to deal with the duplication of marketing and distribution groups is in wait and see mode. Per the release breakdown below, there are plenty of weekends where the studios are dating against each other on the same weekend. In most instances, it’s a matter of counterprogramming — e.g. May 21, 2027, when family animated Warners pic Bad Fairies opens against a new James Wan Paranormal Activity film. However, it’s arguably unprecedented for a major studio to shell out on marketing for two big films from two big labels in the same weekend. Note: It hasn’t been uncommon of late for a big studio to face-off against its adult specialty label — e.g. Universal going up against a Focus Features title.

The one glaring tentpole-on-top-of-a-tentpole frame is June 30, 2028 where Paramount’s feature take of video game Call of Duty is up against DC’s Dynamic Duo. Also, there’s the situation of some serious summer stacking. July 2027 has James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow followed by Crawl 2 (granted, it’s a counterprogrammer) followed by Ocean’s Prequel and A Quiet Place III.

Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides and Zendaya as Chani Warner Bros.

On the bright side, before this year is over, the combined entity has a possible billion dollar hit and award contender in Warner Bros/Legendary’s Denis Villeneuve Dune: Part Three, which could create another Barbenheimer effect at the box office in its competition with Disney/Marvel Studio’s Avengers: Doomsday on Dec. 18.

While the studios can operate separately, Bonta says when it comes to negotiating and creating a marketplace where there isn’t reduced competition, “We basically ensure the status quo competition with negotiations (remaining) separately. It’s as if the companies never merged. They can’t bundle their basic cable channel assets. They can’t use them together to reduce competition…They have to remain separate and independent in their negotiations, and when they’re working with the cable companies. Same with the theatrical release.

“Usually, when you see [a deal that] reduces competition, you see people paying more for less. So you see less output, less quality. And you see higher prices. We address that by making sure that the fees remain flat, for the three years between the merch company and the exhibitors, the theaters. And then the requirement, this incredible, massive requirement for production output, cures for the less part, instead of paying more for less. You have the flat fee requirement with massive increase in production. So that’s how we address the concerns about reduced competition,” explained California’s AG this morning.

The multi-billion dollar question as far as box office goes is whether Warner Bros. Motion Picture Chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy make the jump to the new entity. De Luca told us earlier this year that no matter which way the merger went (Netflix or Paramount), “We’re hoping to stay the course.” Last year was a banner year for the duo with $4.3 billion WW. This year, there haven’t been as many hits, but the longtime production partners are known for their excellent relationships with filmmakers like their recent Oscar winners Paul Thomas Anderson, Ryan Coolger as well as Alejandro Inarritu and Zach Cregger, to name a few.

Rumors have swirled about DeLuca and Abdy heading over to Sony, or Netflix (that latter rumor fueled around town after their longtime comms chief Katie Martin Kelly departed Warners for the streamer). The reality is that the duo have a four-year extension on their contacts until 2030 to run Warners. A world where the pro-theatrical De Luca and Abdy continue to stay at the helm of their ship isn’t out of the question.

Ellison said in a memo to Paramount staff today, “We are tentatively planning to close in approximately two weeks.”

Get ready…

Here’s how the release schedule looks at this point in time for mid-October 2026 through the end of 2028. Those movies with the same release dates are in bold.

title: ‘Gangs of London’ Producers Claim They’re Owed $20 Million From Vice Over Pulse Films Sale
summary: The founders of “Gangs of London” producer Pulse Films claim they are owed more than $20 million over the sale of the studio to Vice Media in 2021. Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford, who founded Pulse Films in 2005, allege Vice still owes them $20.43 million after acquiring their 22% stake in the company for […]
content:
The founders of “Gangs of London” producer Pulse Films claim they are owed more than $20 million over the sale of the studio to Vice Media in 2021.

Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford, who founded Pulse Films in 2005, allege Vice still owes them $20.43 million after acquiring their 22% stake in the company for $53.24 million.

At the time of the acquisition, which brought Vice’s shareholding to 100%, the duo received $10 million in cash as well as a secured loan note for the remaining $43.24 million. Vice paid the initial instalements but in Sept. 2022 missed a payment of $5 million as well as subsequent payments, leaving a debt of just over $20 million.

Popular on Variety

Under the terms of the secured loan note, Benski and Clifford were entitled to force a sale of Pulse in order to reclaim the money. However they claim Vice misled them into waiving their rights after fraudulently promising the parent company was solvent and about to be sold for a significant sum, which would enabled their debt to be repaid.

The “true state of affairs,” they claim, was that Vice was “financially distressed” and “no genuine sale process capable of generating full repayment was underway.” Vice media filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy the following year.

Benski and Clifford have not yet filed suit but earlier this month their motion for pre-action discovery, filed against Pulse Films, was denied by a judge in London’s High Court, who said the request for discovery before a lawsuit was even filed placed a “disproportionately heavy burden” on the company. Pulse Films said complying with the request would have cost more than £440,000 and involved reviewing over 264,000 documents.

The judge said in his decision that while “it is not obvious to me that there is concrete evidence of dishonesty” this was effectively a question for a court to decide once a lawsuit has been filed.

Variety has contacted reps for Benski, Clifford, Pulse Films and Vice.

title: ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office

Warner Bros.’ “Practical Magic 2” moved to second place in its sophomore weekend, generating $2.03 million to bring its running total to $7.5 million. Studiocanal claimed […]
content:
Sony’s franchise reboot “Resident Evil” stormed to the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, debuting in first place with £4.2 million ($5.6 million) across its opening frame.

Warner Bros.’ “Practical Magic 2” moved to second place in its sophomore weekend, generating $2.03 million to bring its running total to $7.5 million. Studiocanal claimed third position with the debut of Aardman’s animated adventure “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom,” which banked $2.2 million in its opening session.
