A true story of a Nazi-hunting case in mid-1960s New York City, Ben Shirinian‘s debut feature is most absorbing as a character study of a woman lying to herself, at least as much as she’s lying to everyone else. It’s the procedural thriller around her, probing at that deception, that feels undercooked, with neither Tye Sheridan’s investigating journalist nor Michael Imperioli’s immigration officer much of a foil for Watts’ more layered protagonist.

This is ambitious material for a new filmmaker, and while Shirinian (a native of Montreal, where this mostly Queens-set film was shot) directs it with handsome gravity, he has a tendency to double down on signposting that’s already in the script by Alyssa Hill, also a first-timer. Still, with its burnished period production values and tony cast — also including an oddly underused Luke Evans and a briefly potent Lena Olin — this is the kind of older-skewing upscale drama that could do respectable arthouse business outside the awards corridor.

Popular on Variety

From the start, there’s a nervous brittleness to Hermine’s permanently pasted-on smile, though there could be any number of reasons for that. Having moved to the States with her husband Russell (Evans) after they met in post-WWII Austria, she has lived in New York for nearly a decade, but is aware she doesn’t quite fit in — beginning with her still-strong Germanic accent — and as the film begins, her looming U.S. citizenship interview is causing her much anxiety. But perhaps she frets too much: The local church women have embraced her as one of their own, her oatmeal raisin cookies are much in demand, and when the dreaded interview comes around, she easily impresses official Anthony DeVito (Imperioli) with her earnest-sounding American Dream spiel.

“You can be anyone you want to be,” she says in praise of her new home country — our first, unsubtle clue that everything is not entirely as it appears. When New York Times reporter Joseph Lelyveld (Sheridan) turns up on her doorstep requesting to speak with her husband, she seems less surprised than you might expect: He hasn’t told her that he’s acting on a tip from famed Austrian Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal (an oddly sidelined figure in the film’s version of events), but perhaps she wouldn’t be entirely surprised if he did.

Shirinian and Hill engage in some labored obfuscation — chiefly by delaying our first encounter with Russell to a suspicious degree — to engineer a narrative twist of sorts, but it’s more trouble than it’s worth: Viewers needn’t be acquainted with the facts of the real-life case to guess the truth well ahead of time, not least because the character of Hermine, and Watts’ simultaneously tricky and disarming playing of her, is so clearly the film’s driving force. A woman whose story, once tested, changes so often you wonder which version she believes, she’s sufficiently interesting to anchor the film without any need for strategized reveals and reversals.

Sheridan’s callow journo, by contrast, never feels like more than an information-gathering device, not helped by the phonily expositional nature of much of his dialogue — which occasionally goes so far as to insult the audience’s intelligence. (“After the war?” he asks gormlessly, when Hermine mentions that she married in 1958.) A suggested ripple of May-December attraction between his and Watts’ characters initially intrigues, but goes largely unexplored. “The Housewife” has little interest in perverse or ambiguous territory as it pivots, in its third act, to a somewhat cursory courtroom drama.

Even Watts’ hitherto finely measured character gradations are suddenly a bit compressed in this denouement, though Olin, as a Holocaust survivor bearing crucial, ugly truths, gets two scenes to quietly burn everything down. Shirinian brings “The Housewife” in at a brisk 102 minutes, though after the coy slow burn of its first hour, the rest could use as much breathing room. Just as the film gets risky, it rushes to the finish line — and away from its most riveting, unreliable perspective. But it’s a welcome reminder of what Watts, who’s been either ill-used or unchallenged in too many of her recent film vehicles, can do with a role that steps up to her adaptable, slightly unknowable screen presence.

title: Judge in Paramount-State AGs Case Still Has Questions, Schedules Hearing on Settlement Terms
summary: Paramount’s deal with the 12 state attorneys general to settle their antitrust lawsuit over the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is not official just yet: The judge in the case has some “outstanding questions” about the settlement, which requires her approval before it takes effect. In an order issued Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted […]
content:
Paramount’s deal with the 12 state attorneys general to settle their antitrust lawsuit over the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is not official just yet: The judge in the case has some “outstanding questions” about the settlement, which requires her approval before it takes effect.

In an order issued Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted the parties’ motion to vacate the hearing about Paramount’s previous motion to require the states (and the WGA) to post $1.88 billion bond to cover the company’s financial losses in the event it prevailed in court. That had been scheduled for Sept. 24. (The proposed settlements Paramount entered into with the states and the WGA makes that moot.)

However, Martinez-Olguin said in the order that the court “does not yet rule on the remainder of the motion to enter consent decree and dissolve the stipulation not to close” the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger.

Popular on Variety

“To address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties’ proposed consent decree, as well as the implementation of the proposed consent decree, the Court SETS a hearing for 11:00 a.m. PST on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote. The hearing will take place via Zoom.

RELATED: What’s in the Paramount Settlement With States: Commitment to Not Sell Studio Lots, Additional $300M Yearly Investment in U.S. Film Production, CNN Oversight and More

Paramount declined to comment. The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the states’ coalition suing Paramount and WBD over the merger, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On Monday came the announcement of Paramount’s settlement with the 12 Democratic state attorneys general, leaving only the judge’s approval of the proposed consent decree as the last checkbox needed for the Paramount-WBD merger to close. In a memo to staff, Paramount CEO David Ellison said he expected the Warner Bros. pact to close in around two weeks.

The lawsuit filed by Bonta and the other AGs had alleged the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. would have excessive power in markets for wide-release and “tentpole” theatrical movies as well as basic cable. Previously, Bonta had asserted that only “structural” remedies (i.e., divestitures) would be sufficient to call off the lawsuit but the resulting settlement includes no such provisions.

Among the top-line terms in Paramount’s settlement with the states: Paramount is prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in the state for at least five years, and is obligated to invest at least an additional $300 million on film production in the U.S. annually — for a total of $1.5 billion over five years. The combined Paramount-WB also must release at least 30 movies for theatrical distribution in the first two years (something Ellison has repeatedly promised he would do) and at least 32 in years 3-5, with a 45-day window for wide-release films. The merged Paramount-Warner Bros. also will be subject to monitoring by a “news editorial independence board,” which will establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles for” for CNN and CBS News.

The terms of the proposed settlement would conclude at the end of the fifth calendar year that follows the closing. That means if the Paramount-WBD merger closes before the end of this year as expected, the commitment period for the settlement would run through Dec. 31, 2031.

RELATED: Rob Bonta Sued Paramount to Counter Political Influence, Then Fell Victim to It

title: Rob Bonta Sued Paramount to Counter Political Influence, Then Fell Victim to It
summary: When Rob Bonta sued to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in July, he said he was doing so because the Trump administration had failed to act for political reasons. “They are greenlighting deals that their own antitrust section at U.S. DOJ knows and believes are unlawful, and they’re overriding them in the White House with […]
content:
When Rob Bonta sued to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in July, he said he was doing so because the Trump administration had failed to act for political reasons.

“They are greenlighting deals that their own antitrust section at U.S. DOJ knows and believes are unlawful, and they’re overriding them in the White House with political decisions,” he said. “They are not just missing in action, they are making things worse for Americans … So our role is more important.”

A mere two months later, Bonta has had to abandon his case in exchange for only modest conditions — largely due to political interference.

Popular on Variety

Gov. Gavin Newsom weighed in early and often, suggesting that it would be better for Bonta to settle than risk going to trial and subjecting the industry to a prolonged period of uncertainty.

Paramount also laid on the pressure, lining up political and industry supporters and threatening to flee to Tennessee if no deal was reached by Oct. 1. Amid a historic production slump, political leaders feared the optics of a major studio leaving Hollywood. And in the end, the one-two punch of Newsom and Nashville proved too much for Bonta to withstand.

“I think Bonta, in the legal case, had the upper hand,” said Abiel Garcia, a former California deputy attorney general. “He got cut at the knees on every other issue.”

Bonta is not alone among state attorneys general in seeking to fill the void left by the Trump DOJ on antitrust enforcement. On a series of cases — HPE/Juniper Networks, Ticketmaster, and Nexstar/Tegna — Bonta has joined multistate coalitions in defying the DOJ’s hands-off approach.

In that context, Newsom’s involvement in the Paramount case has raised concerns elsewhere about whether state AGs are just as vulnerable to political influence.

“My governor has never, publicly or privately, given me any feedback on any antitrust case,” Phil Weiser, the Colorado attorney general, pointedly told CFTN News last week.

Paula Blizzard, the head of the California A.G.’s antitrust section, was also asked about Newsom’s push for a settlement at a panel discussion at George Washington University. She noted that A. G.s are “separately elected as independent officials.”

“That’s probably all I can say,” she added.

Bonta argued that antitrust enforcement was a necessary check on “billionaires currying favor with the president so he’ll do their bidding.” Paramount CEO David Ellison has indeed courted the president’s support for more than a year, appearing with him at UFC events as he sought to win him over.

But of course, from Paramount’s perspective, it was Bonta — not Trump — who was acting “politically.” In his press conference announcing the case, Bonta mentioned Trump’s name seven times — and Ellison’s only once — while invoking the “no kings” anti-Trump rallying cry.

Some observers also thought Bonta’s antitrust case was marginal, at best. And it got harder as the Directors Guild of America, IATSE, and then Cinema United — representing the supposed victims — came out for a settlement.

But Paramount’s clout can be measured by the fact that it prevailed in the suit without winning a single favorable ruling in court. And when it appeared to be struggling, the Trump-led DOJ and two Republican state AGs sought to intervene, challenging in effect whether states should be allowed to enforce antitrust violations at all.

In that kind of fight, Bonta needed allies — and he was left without many in the end.

“It seems the attorney general overestimated the political support he was going to receive from the governor and other luminaries in his party,” said Bill Kovacic, a professor at GWU. “That’s a reminder of the power companies have to shape opinions by throwing their economic weight around.”

title: Tyra Banks’ Show & Tell: Ex-‘ANTM’ Host Hits Netflix With ‘Reality Check’ Video Edits; Streamer Wants Defamation Suit Dismissed
summary: Back in her America’s Next Top Model days, Tyra Banks used to love to tell viewers and contestants that “every hallway is a runway.” Looks like when it comes to the supermodel and her legal showdown with Netflix and the directors of the docuseries Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model, every filing is a […]
content:
Back in her America’s Next Top Model days, Tyra Banks used to love to tell viewers and contestants that “every hallway is a runway.” Looks like when it comes to the supermodel and her legal showdown with Netflix and the directors of the docuseries Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model, every filing is a battlefront too.

In today’s case, that battlefront includes video receipts.

Facing an effort by Netflix to toss out Banks’ June-filed defamation suit over her depiction in the three-part docuseries directed by Daniel Sivan and Mor Loushy, the ANTM creator and her Clare Locke lawyers hit back hard Tuesday with an opposition filing full of some pretty stark video to back up their case that Netflix and the Reality Check filmmakers “through selective deletion, rearrangement, and other editing techniques” distinctly altered Banks’ words and reaction.

Specifically, Banks and her attorneys point to the de facto non-response the model is shown giving to whether or not she knew about a sexual assault of ANTM participant Shandi Sullivan. Today’s filing and accompanying videos also spotlights a 2004 chat with Sullivan over infidelity — a conversation that in Reality Check comes across as instigated by Banks.

Watch on Deadline

Take a look at what was shown in Reality Check and what was actually filmed:

In case you missed it, the opposition filing describes the comparison: “After conveying to viewers Sullivan’s story of sexual assault, Banks was asked on camera, ‘You remember the story with Shandi?’ Banks nodded and said, ‘Um … I do remember her story.’ Episode 1 airs the question. It airs the “Um.” It removes the nod from between them, cuts the answer, and goes to black. Banks is left apparently unable to say whether she remembers the assault of a contestant on her own show. The nod was not cut off. It was cut out.”

Citing “willful misconduct,” today’s opposition to Netflix and the directors’ anti-SLAPP motion insists that the “Defendants held the full footage, understood that it contradicted the impressions they were creating, and cut it for the purpose of conveying those false impressions.”

To that, there’s the apparent cheat on that cheating conversation from 22 years ago:

In today’s L.A. Superior Court filing, Banks’ team says: “As originally broadcast, Sullivan asks Banks whether she has ever cheated or been cheated on. Banks answers, sees Sullivan tearing up, and asks whether she is okay. The Docuseries deletes Sullivan’s question, reverses the order, and adds a commentator to tell viewers that “it is not a coincidence that she starts talking about cheating” and that she has “producers in her ear.” Sullivan raised the subject. The Docuseries say Banks did.”

Suing Netflix, 89 Blocks Holdings, EverWonder Studio, Netflix Music, Loushy and Sivan for false light, defamation by implication, breach of contract and false endorsement, Banks received blowback after Reality Check debuted in February. As Banks claimed earlier in the summer in her initial complaint, that fallout resulted in “loss of future business opportunities, loss of business income, other compounding losses,” “severe reputational harm” and “significant mental anguish.”

With both sides dug in, the matter of the Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher-represented Netflix’s dismissal will be heard in a Los Angeles court October 30.

Asked for a response to Banks’ filing today, Netflix presented the statement it released more than two months ago when the all started.

“Directors Daniel Sivan and Mor Loushy are respected documentarians who thoroughly interviewed the people behind America’s Next Top Model,” a Netflix spokesperson said today, like before. “Tyra Banks was given the opportunity to speak openly about her experience and the creators fairly presented her perspective alongside those of every other participant shown in this documentary. We stand behind Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model and will continue to vigorously defend it.”

title: Kit Harington Thinks There Still Could Be A Jon Snow Spinoff, Says He Now Feels More Comfortable With ‘GOT’ Character
summary: Kit Harington said recently that, after calling off the Game of Thrones spinoff centered on Jon Snow in 2024, “I feel more comfortable with that character and that world again and where it sits in my life.” The actor explored the idea on the Happy Sad Confused podcast this past weekend. Harington recalled that GOT […]
content:
Kit Harington said recently that, after calling off the Game of Thrones spinoff centered on Jon Snow in 2024, “I feel more comfortable with that character and that world again and where it sits in my life.”

The actor explored the idea on the Happy Sad Confused podcast this past weekend.

Harington recalled that GOT was really his second big project after Warhorse, and the huge success of the show — where people were screaming “Jon Snow!” to him on the street — felt a little confusing.

“You had this like bifurcation,” Harington recalled about meeting fans, “like, ‘I’m not that guy. No one’s that guy, but I’m certainly not that guy. I’m sorry.'”

Watch on Deadline

The actor said he needed some space.

“I think I needed to do some other stuff like outside of it and it’s been a number of years and I’ve done all these different things. Some have been seen more widely than others. But I’ve done enough of them now that I don’t feel defined by just that character.”

But even when he announced in 2024 that the show was no longer being developed, the actor left the door open a crack.

“There may be a time in the future where we return to it,” he offered.

Harington isn’t exactly saying he’s pursuing the project again, but he sounds more open to the idea.

“Now I’ve gone and done all these other things, and now I feel more comfortable with that character and that world again and where it sits in my life,” he told Happy Sad Confused host Josh Horowitz.

“I still think there’s a world in which something could work. I wouldn’t have gone into it in the first place if I didn’t. But I was very insistent at the start — and they were as well, HBO and George R.R. Martin — of like: ‘If we don’t find the right thing, let’s not do it. It’s much better if we don’t.’ After a little while of thinking about it — it kind of was me — [I said], ‘This isn’t quite the right [story].’”

Word of the potential series centered on Harington’s character got out in June 2022. Following the leak, author George R.R. Martin revealed that the series had Snow as a working title and that it had writers/showrunners on board, brought in by Harington.

At a December 2022 GoT convention, Harington theorized what could be happening to Jon Snow after he killed Daenerys at the end of the mothership series.

“I think if you asked him, he would’ve felt he got off lightly,” Harington said. “At the end of the show when we find him in that cell, he’s preparing to be beheaded and he wants to be. He’s done. The fact he goes to the Wall is the greatest gift and also the greatest curse.”

title: Judge Sets Hearing On State AGs’ Settlement With Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery
summary: A federal judge has set a hearing for Thursday on the proposed settlement between state attorneys general and Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin set the hearing for 11 a.m. PT via Zoom. She wrote in an order Tuesday that the hearing would be to “address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and […]
content:
A federal judge has set a hearing for Thursday on the proposed settlement between state attorneys general and Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin set the hearing for 11 a.m. PT via Zoom.

She wrote in an order Tuesday that the hearing would be to “address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties proposed consent decree, as well as the implementation of the proposed consent decree.”

The parties have filed a motion to approve the consent decree, which lays out a series of settlement conditions to resolve the lawsuit brought by the state AGs in July. Among the provisions are Paramount commitments to release at least 30 movies per year, and another to create an independent board to oversee CNN and CBS News adherence to journalistic standards.

Watch on Deadline

The judge also canceled a scheduled hearing on whether to require the state AGs to post a bond as the litigation proceeded.

The judge said in a separate order that she would decide in “due course” on whether to dismiss the lawsuit brought by the Writers Guild of America to block the merger. The WGA said it also reached a settlement with Paramount to end its litigation.

title: NY Mayor Zohran Mamdani Blasts Paramount-WBD Deal As “Shameful Monument To Corruption”
summary: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a day after continuing his congenial dealings with President Donald Trump, blasted the “federal leaders” supporting the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. “America is free only when the media is competitive, independent, and accountable to the people,” Mamdani posted on X Tuesday. “This merger strikes a chilling blow against that freedom […]
content:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a day after continuing his congenial dealings with President Donald Trump, blasted the “federal leaders” supporting the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

“America is free only when the media is competitive, independent, and accountable to the people,” Mamdani posted on X Tuesday. “This merger strikes a chilling blow against that freedom – and hands even more power to billionaires like David Ellison to decide what Americans see and hear, all while lifting scrutiny off the federal leaders who pushed it through.”

Paramount on Monday reached a settlement with attorneys general from 12 states, including New York, as well as with the Writers Guild of America in dual antitrust lawsuits filed last July. The agreements remove the final barriers keeping Paramount from closing the controversial $111 billion transaction, which will remake Hollywood and likely result in sizable layoffs.

Trump has yet to weigh in publicly on the deal, though Larry Ellison, the Oracle billionaire who is a key funder of the deal and CEO David Ellison’s father, is an ally of the president.

Watch on Deadline

Mamdani in his post saluted New York AG Letitia James “for the protections she secured for workers.” He closed with a withering line about the regulatory process, though he didn’t make the target of his scorn completely clear. “This decision is a shameful monument to corruption and a betrayal that the American people won’t soon forget,” he wrote.

The social media missile stood in contrast with Monday’s atmosphere at Gracie Mansion, where Mamdani hosted Trump at the mayoral residence during his visit for the United Nations General Assembly. Their joint news conference showcased their mutually respectful, at times almost playful, dynamic. Behind closed doors, they said they discussed topics like affordable housing and immigration.

Trump repeated his hope that Mamdani would be “a great mayor.” Mamdani defended the decision to engage peaceably with Trump despite their many policy disagreements. “I committed over the course of the campaign, as well as while being in office, that I would meet with anyone, work with anyone that could deliver for New Yorkers,” he said. “So having a conversation about potentially building 12,000 homes, about the importance of our Haitian neighbors here in this city, those are conversations that are worthwhile to have.”

Even though the president has mounted constant attacks on “radical” and “Communist” Democratic candidates in November’s midterm elections, he has appeared to be charmed by the young mayor of his home town. They have met two previous times at the White House.

Presidential visits to Gracie Mansion have been rare, the New York Times noted. Harry Truman attended a luncheon there in 1949 for a ceremony during construction of the UN’s headquarters building. John F. Kennedy and Ronald Reagan appeared there in 1962 and 1981, respectively.

title: Doc Talk Podcast: Oscar-Nominated Filmmaker Sam Green On ‘The Oldest Person In The World’
summary: The oldest human being alive right now, in case you’ve been wondering, is Ethel Caterham of Shipton Bellinger, Hampshire, England, who turned 117 in August. She succeeded to the title of oldest person in the world after the death of Inah Canabarro Lucas, a Brazilian nun who died in 2025 at the age of 116. […]
content:
The oldest human being alive right now, in case you’ve been wondering, is Ethel Caterham of Shipton Bellinger, Hampshire, England, who turned 117 in August. She succeeded to the title of oldest person in the world after the death of Inah Canabarro Lucas, a Brazilian nun who died in 2025 at the age of 116.

Oscar-nominated filmmaker Sam Green has been thinking a lot about holders of this singular record — not just recently but going back a decade. The result of his 10-year exploration is the documentary The Oldest Person in the World, which just began its theatrical run in Los Angeles and San Francisco after opening September 10 in New York City. It expands to additional cities in the coming weeks.

Green (The Weather Underground, 32 Sounds) joins the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss his film, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival and has screened at SXSW, True/False in Columbia, MO, Full Frame in Durham, NC, and internationally at CPH:DOX, the Thessaloniki Documentary Film Festival in Greece and DOXA in Vancouver, BC, among many others.

Watch on Deadline

Green explains how editor Aaron Wickenden coaxed him into making the documentary the most personal of his career. In part that ensued through the inclusion of one of the younger people of the planet, comparatively speaking – Green’s vivacious son, Atlas – and through the filmmaker’s reflections on his own mortality after he received a worrisome medical diagnosis.

The director also speaks to many moments of humor in the film, some of which spring organically from the hoopla generated by one of the record holders celebrating a birthday, for instance, or by being recognized by the people at Guinness World Records as the oldest human extant. (The film begins with a birthday party for Susannah Mushatt Jones of New York City, then the oldest person in the world, who slept through almost the entire party, despite the urging of a Brooklyn city official who told the crowd in advance, “We want to get as much soundbite out of her as possible.”).

According to a synopsis of The Oldest Person in the World, “What begins as a portrait of longevity becomes a poignant meditation on the passage of time, the randomness of fate, and the joy and profound human experience of being alive.”

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

title: Finnish Film Affair: Survival, Horror, Dystopian Pics Unpacked by Nordic Genre Lab Participants: ‘The Base of Nordic Talent Is Deep’
summary: Home to some of the Nordics’ hottest genre talents making waves at top international festivals – Hanna Bergholm and Ilja Rautsi whose respective “Nightborn” and “Red Snow” were snagged by Shudder – Helsinki will no doubt vibrate this week to the beat of some of the most jaw-dropping and entertaining genre projects taking part in […]
content:
Home to some of the Nordics’ hottest genre talents making waves at top international festivals – Hanna Bergholm and Ilja Rautsi whose respective “Nightborn” and “Red Snow” were snagged by Shudder – Helsinki will no doubt vibrate this week to the beat of some of the most jaw-dropping and entertaining genre projects taking part in the inaugural Nordic Genre Lab.

“Alma,” a Finnish thriller penned by Rautsi, “Trespassers,” a Swedish “Deliverance” from “Midsommar” producer Patrik Andersson, and “Whistler,” the first-ever Faroese horror pic, are among eight high-end genre films in development to be showcased at the Helsinki Intl. Film Festival’s industry confab Finnish Film Affair, running Sept 23-25.

Popular on Variety

Between Thursday and Friday, the Nordic Genre Lab titles will be pitched live to 500-plus delegates, attend workshops and receive mentorship from Two Magpies Entertainment’s Claire Willats, former Netflix commissioner, and genre expert Todd Brown, former XYZ Films head of acquisitions.

Claire Willats, Todd Brown, Laura Laaksonen Courtesy of Claire Willats, Miguel Bueno, Ville Juurikkala

Under their former Netflix and XYZ gigs, the two senior industry executives collaborated on the original Norwegian version of “The Trip,” starring Noomi Rapace and Aksel Hennie, and the acquisition of the Netflix hit “The Platform.” Through her London-based banner Two Magpies Entertainment, Willats is attached to Norwegian “Troll” helmer Roar Uthaug’s upcoming supernatural horror “Amara.” As for Toronto-based Brown, his next ambitious genre bet is Johnnie To’s “Two Gun Cohen,” which is in early development.

When approached by head of program Laura Laaksonen to join her in the intensive training venture Nordic Genre Lab, the two international power players signed up, eager to contribute to strengthening the Nordic genre ecosystem and boost the career of emerging genre talent.

“Nordic genre remains very strong, in my view,” Todd told Variety. “The base of talent is deep, and the Nordics in general do a remarkable job of balancing class and critical quality with audience accessibility. You continue to not only see a high volume of projects at global festivals but also see those perform commercially.”

However, he argued, “There still isn’t much in the way of institutional knowledge of genre within funding bodies or a way for these creators to really connect, support and learn from one another in the way they can within the arthouse world.” Which is why he’s hoping with his Nordic Genre Lab colleagues “to help fill that gap.”

Willats, co-founder of the event with Laaksonen, added: “I think there is a huge appetite for Nordic genre in the global market. If you look at streamers like Netflix, “Troll” is still the number one film not in the English language. We are hoping the lab can help draw more focus on the wealth of talent in the Nordics, and we hope to repeat this next year and include Sámi, Icelandic and Greenlandic projects, which are unfortunately not represented this year,” she stated.

Together with Norwegian producer Einar Loftesnes (“The Tunnel,” “Kraken”), Willats and Brown selected the eight titles out of 29 submissions, based on the originality of the project, quality of the team, the writing and stage of development.

The finalists represent “an extraordinary range of genre filmmaking, from folk horror rooted in Faroese landscape to dystopian survival thriller in Norway and from animated psychological horror to dark political satire from Finland and more,” said Willats.

Among the participants, Jón Hammer (“Trom”), producer of Gudmund Helmsdal’s “Whistler,” said, “We set out to make the first Faroese horror feature, and the first in what we hope will become a series of Faroese genre films, so the opportunity to develop ‘Whistler’ further with the guidance and expertise of such strong mentors is incredibly exciting for us.”

Pauliina Piipponen of Finland’s Making Movies, producer of “Alma,” helmed by Pete Riski (“Icebreaker,” ”Dark Floors”) said, “Taking part in the Nordic Genre Lab comes at a very good moment for the project as we’re now moving further into the creative development and the international financing and production strategy.”

Juha Fiilin (“Joy Eternal”), director and producer of the Finnish anime horror “Echo Chamber,” hopes to build on the program to strengthen his film’s market potential, ink Nordic distribution and global sales. “Horror is a perennially attractive genre, but the recent successes of ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms’ prove a maturing of the audience. People are ready for high-quality character work in genre films,” he added.

Nordic Genre Lab is backed by Nordisk Kulturfond, the Finnish Film Foundation and Nordisk Film & TV Fond.

Full rundown of the Nordic Genre Lab Projects:

“Alma” (Pete Riski, Finland)

Produced by Academy-Award shortlisted and Golden Globe nomination Making Movies (“The Fencer,” “My Sailor, My Love”), the ambitious €4 million ($4.5 million) project is penned by genre wiz Ilja Rautsi (“Red Snow,” “Nightborn,” “Hatching”).

Set between two-timelines World War II Finland. We follow Alma (16), who gains telekinetic powers to save her father from the retreating Nazi army in Lapland. Then in the present day, the same character -aged 96- meets her granddaughter for the first time, and they must escape Alma’s past sins, exploring the cost of gaining power.

“’Alma’ deals with war and its consequences through three generations of women, combining a historical setting with themes of trauma, power and responsibility that feel particularly relevant today,” says Pauliina Piipponen, who produces with Kai Nordberg and Kaarle Aho.

“Echo Chamber” (Juha Fiilin, Finland)

Anime psychological horror penned by Adam Cullen. First pitched at Cartoon Next 2025.

“Echo Chamber” combines tone and artistic sensibilities of prestige drama with the anime-inspired spectacle of chilling body horror, viscerally rendered as only hand-drawn animation can deliver it,” says Fiilin of Fiilin Good Films who produces with Debbie Stepgens. “It’s a mature, thoughtful horror where a curse forces together two sisters estranged by their grief, but that curse inadvertently provides the circumstances and opportunities for them to learn what it is like to grieve together. To see that it is bittersweet and healing; not just bitter.”

“Linden Lane 6” (Josefina Rautiainen, Finland)

From the prolific It’s Alive Films, behind Oscar submissions “Euthanizer, “The Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic” and Finnish hit “100 Litres of Gold.”

“It’s a timely and provocative genre film that reverses the traditional roles of men and women in order to explore sexual harassment, manipulation, and abuse from the opposite perspective,” says producer Anita Hyppönen. “By changing these familiar dynamics, the film shows that abuse is often less about desire and more about power and control.”

“Long Way Home” (Kjersti Helen Rasmussen, Norway)

Produced by Njål Lambrechts for Truewest.

Character-driven dystopian road movie in which, after an electromagnetic pulse wipes out all electricity across Western Norway, Tea (22) and her neighbor Herman set out on a dangerous journey through a frozen and increasingly lawless landscape to reach her childhood home, confronting both the chaos around them and the darkness within.

“At its core, it’s a coming-of-age story,” says Rasmussen. The physical journey home becomes an inner journey from dependency to independence, while the society around the characters faces its own test of trust, solidarity and community. The future I portray is both dark and hopeful. Systems will fail and people will fall, but it is in the darkness that we discover the light and what it costs to choose it,” she says.

“Sauna Diplomacy” (Teemu Niukkanen, Finland)

Debut feature from the director of the 2017 Sundance selected short “Fucking Bunnies” and Canneseries winning series “Money Shot.” Produced by Tack Films’ John Lundsten, behind the 2017 Palme d’Or nominated short “The Ceiling.”

Dark comedy, set in 1970, during the height of Finlandization. A Finnish diplomat is ordered to host a high-ranking Soviet official at his summer cottage for the weekend. What begins as an awkward diplomatic retreat descends into humiliation, manipulation, and psychological power games.

“The Evil Eye” (Kristian Lidegaard, Denmark)

Penned by Kristian Lidegaard and Sissel Dalsgaard Thomsen, produced by Manna Film (“Kalak,” “The Quiet Migration”).

Online found-footage horror film in which the main character, Oliver, is both the villain and the creator of the film we are watching. Obsessed with Lucas, a successful young swimmer who bullied him as a child, he secretly films and infiltrates his victim’s life, sharing disturbing “films” on a closed online forum until the line between observer and destroyer disappears entirely. “Told entirely through iPhones, POV glasses, surveillance cameras, screen recordings, social media and an uncensored private forum on the dark web, the film is both instantly recognizable and radically unique. As stories of online abuse and violent digital communities surface worldwide, the film’s horror feels contemporary, borderless and disturbingly real,” says producer Maria Møller Kjeldgaard.

“Trespassers” (Johannes Persson, Sweden)

From the director of the horror pic “Feed,” starring Molly Nutley, Sofia Kappel. Written by Melina Maraki (“Summer of 1985”); produced by “Midsommar” producer Patrik Andersson, with Mylla Films co-founder Jakob Abrahamsson.

Backwoods horror-thriller in which four young people from a failed anti-establishment movement travel to the vast wilderness of Northern Sweden to reconnect with nature, but after a river rafting accident leaves them stranded, they discover they are not alone, and not welcome on land controlled by a group that has isolated itself for centuries with its own terrifying beliefs.

“Whistler” (Gudmund Helmsdal, Faroe Islands)

Produced by Outlier Projects’ Jón Hammer (“Trom”), formerly at Zentropa.

Helmsdal’s “Brother Troll” bowed at 160 festivals and won best short at the Arizona Int’l Film Festival. Survival folk horror from the set on the bird cliffs and grazing lands of the Faroe Islands, where four marine biologists race to catch the last ferry after their guide’s fatal climbing accident, only to find themselves hunted across forbidden grazing land by a reclusive farmer who uses a bone whistle to command a pack of grotesque half-human creatures.

title: ECAM Incubator Title ‘The Woodworm’ Explores Female Identity in the Shadow of an Artist Father
summary: In “The Woodworm” (“El Corquim”), the feature debut of Laura Obradors, a teenage girl’s search for an identity of her own runs up against the authority of her father, a successful artist in creative crisis. Developed through Madrid’s ECAM Incubator, the project examines the power exercised inside a family and the artistic prestige that can […]
content:
In “The Woodworm” (“El Corquim”), the feature debut of Laura Obradors, a teenage girl’s search for an identity of her own runs up against the authority of her father, a successful artist in creative crisis.

Developed through Madrid’s ECAM Incubator, the project examines the power exercised inside a family and the artistic prestige that can shield it from scrutiny.

Produced by Sergio Adrià’s Espurna Films, with Sandra Hermida on board as co-producer, the film centers on 17-year-old Clara, whose desire to be seen and loved is complicated by a growing impulse to escape the expectations surrounding her.

“Clara always seems to crave something from the outside world: to be seen, accepted, acknowledged, adored,” Obradors told Variety. “But at the same time she has an internal and contradictory impulse that wants to push her to break free from these attachments and become more independent, mature, and free.”

Popular on Variety

Inspired by the life of a close friend, the project grew from the filmmaker’s interest in the conflicting feelings that can coexist in a daughter’s relationship with her father. For Obradors, that relationship also provides an early encounter with the rules and expectations of a wider masculine world.

“Somewhere between these two polarities is a world that inspired me to make this film — an attitude, an action, where preservation and destruction coexist,” she said.

Clara grows up within a family structure shaped by power, submission and male pleasure, with few alternative points of reference. Questioning what she has learned about femininity and intimacy means confronting the guilt attached to that questioning.

Her father Ricard’s profession brings another layer to those dynamics. As both a parent and a painter, he has the power to shape a person’s understanding of the world and the images through which that world is represented.

“For a long time, we’ve seen the artist as a kind of genius and almost a divine figure,” Obradors said. “That idea can sometimes make us forget that artists are also responsible for what they create and for the power they have.”

Adrià, whose producing credits include “Upon Entry” and Gerard Oms’ “Away,” was drawn to the decision to place Clara’s experience at the center of the film.

“It’s not a film about how he deals with his inner demons or impulses: it’s all about her, focusing on the construction of female identity in a hostile and male-dominated environment,” he said.

That perspective will also inform the film’s visual approach. Adrià describes a world filtered through adolescence, where people, places and situations can appear idealized, magical or unsettling. The beauty of the landscape will sit alongside the cruelty unfolding among the characters.

Espurna, which Adrià founded in 2023, is developing the project as part of its commitment to auteur-driven, original-language Catalan cinema with international potential. Obradors previously directed the shorts “Si amanece, nos vamos” and “Las chicas,” the latter produced by Espurna.

At the time of the interview, “The Woodworm” was on its fourth script draft, following participation in Mexico’s Cine Qua Non Lab and ECAM’s La Incubadora. It has received development support from the Catalan Institute for Cultural Enterprises, with selections for Cannes Focus COPRO’ and ECAM Forum’s Films to Come helping broaden its industry reach.

Obradors said the development process had allowed her to gain distance from the material’s origins, “put reality at the service of the film rather than the other way around.”

Hermida, whose credits include “Society of the Snow,” “A Monster Calls” and “The Impossible,” mentored the project through La Incubadora alongside director and screenwriter Carlos Marqués-Marcet, who took a new director Goya for “10,000 km.”

The team is seeking co-producers, distributors and sales agents across Spain, France, Portugal and Belgium, and are in attendance at San Sebastián and will be at Les Arcs Industry Village.

For Obradors, the title offers a way into Clara’s domestic world: an insect weakening a structure from within, and all the while difficult to detect.

“It’s a space of repression, silent and invisible, where suffering, fear, and guilt live,” she said. “Clara feels like an intruder, especially when she comes into conflict with the different images of herself that have been constructed around her.”

title: ‘Fluorescent, Dirty and Sexy’: Eire Cid’s ‘The Imaginary Kings’ Presented at Madrid Film School (ECAM) Incubator
summary: Of the five projects at the 9th Incubator program of the Madrid Film School (ECAM), Eire Cid’s debut feature “The Imaginary Kings” (“Los Reyes Imaginarios”) centers on the angst of male urban youth. “It is an irreverent and visceral project, with a stylized, anti-naturalistic aesthetic. Fluorescent, dirty and sexy, heavily influenced by urban culture,” Cid […]
content:
Of the five projects at the 9th Incubator program of the Madrid Film School (ECAM), Eire Cid’s debut feature “The Imaginary Kings” (“Los Reyes Imaginarios”) centers on the angst of male urban youth.

“It is an irreverent and visceral project, with a stylized, anti-naturalistic aesthetic. Fluorescent, dirty and sexy, heavily influenced by urban culture,” Cid tells Variety.

The story revolves around Rude, a tattooed teenager living with his father in a working-class neighborhood. Sensitive yet volatile, he embodies a masculinity that is both aggressive and fragile. Haunted by the sudden death of his pal El Rubio, Rude drifts through trap music, betting, fights, porn and poppers. When he falls for Valeria, she makes him happy but also forces him to confront his grief.

Popular on Variety

“However, he is unable to connect with his own pain and vulnerability, and to do so, he will have to break,” Cid explains.

“At the heart of the story is doubt and the possibility of change. That is why we also call it a ‘coming-of-empathy’: a journey toward empathy, much like the one I experienced while writing characters I initially hated as a feminist, but ultimately came to understand,” she says.

For producer Bea Villar of Brava, “Los Reyes Imaginarios” is a film primarily “for teenagers whose stories are rarely told … and that is at the heart of Brava.“

“From the beginning, Eire and I shared the same goal: to connect with young people at a time when dangerous ideas about what it means to be a man are resurfacing and to open a dialogue around them,” she noted, expressing her admiration for how Cid stepped outside of her comfort zone to tell this story.

“The setting is also fundamental: a working-class neighborhood in Vigo surrounded by betting shops and bars, with the port cranes in the background. The choice of Vigo was not accidental. Like other European port cities, it carries the legacy of declining industrial masculinity. In many ways, the city reflects the film’s male characters, Villar asserts.

The project itself has been on quite a journey in its development. It participated in the 4th Edition of the Film Academy’s Rueda Program, the inaugural incubation and development program at the Madrid University School of Arts TAI, the Navarra Residency, the AGAG Mentorship Program for Women Screenwriters and the CREA Conecta Lab.

The writing process was mentored by such acclaimed filmmakers and writers as Alberto Guntín (“Matalobos”), Belén Funes (“A Thief’s Daughter”), Lola Mayo (“Dolemite”), Golden Leopard winner Albert Serra (“Story of my Death”) and Silvia Herreros de Tejada (“La Ruta”).

Plans are to shoot it late next year in Vigo, a port city in northwestern Spain. “Vigo is pivotal to the story because, like other European industrial cities, it carries the legacy of a frustrated working-class masculinity shaped by the decline of the shipbuilding industry and offshoring,” says Villar. “That heritage is very present in ‘The Imaginary Kings’ as an intergenerational burden.”

title: Sister Group Strikes Partnership With Branded Entertainment Company Common Interest, Makes Minority Investment
summary: Sister Group, Jane Featherstone and Elisabeth Murdoch‘s ever-growing transatlantic powerhouse, has entered the branded entertainment business by forging a strategic partnership with London-based company Common Interest, in which it has also taken a minority investment. The partnership with Common Interest, the communications and entertainment group founded by Anthony Freedman, brings together what it describes as […]
content:
Sister Group, Jane Featherstone and Elisabeth Murdoch‘s ever-growing transatlantic powerhouse, has entered the branded entertainment business by forging a strategic partnership with London-based company Common Interest, in which it has also taken a minority investment.

The partnership with Common Interest, the communications and entertainment group founded by Anthony Freedman, brings together what it describes as “brand creativity, entertainment execution and access to world-class production talent.”

The two groups are already collaborating on projects with the goal of building a slate of projects that are connected with brand partners from the very start.

Popular on Variety

Founded in September 2023, Common Interest now spans brand experience, entertainment-led communications, cultural intelligence and IP development. The group currently numbers eight companies: 21st Century Brand, Amplify, Baby Teeth, CultureLab, Knock Three Times, Otherway, Seed and Wonder. Baby Teeth, the creative company building entertainment and IP for brands and talent, recently created and produced “Finding Jamie,” a microdrama series for the Jamie Oliver Group in partnership with Life360.

“We immediately found a cultural and creative kinship with Anthony and the exceptionally talented teams he has assembled across Common Interest,” said Murdoch and Featherstone. “Their deep commitment to entertainment and brand strategies that people actually care about, mirrors the values of creative excellence, authorship and risk-taking intrinsic to Sister. We’re not just aligned on paper, but underway on some great ideas where the potency of that combination is very apparent.”

The partnership comes at moment the two companies describe as “structural change,” with brands now welcomed into the entertainment industry conversation from the early stages of development and as audiences increasingly “embrace brand-led content and entertainment across a variety of formats.”

“Advertising is looking for new ways to reach audiences, and entertainment has never been more open to working with brands as a genuine creative partner,” said Freedman, Founder and CEO of Common Interest. “Each needs what the other has, and the appetite for that is already visible, from Barbie to LEGO to Kraft Heinz’s new partnership with Disney. This partnership is more than a meeting of minds, it’s a real commitment from both sides, to prove that brands can be part of shaping entertainment without compromising on what audiences love.”

The Sister Group currently spans companies across TV and film (Sister Pictures, Dorothy St Pictures, Yes Yes Media, Locksmith Animation, South of the River, Unanimous Media), podcasting (Campside Media), publishing (Zando, AWA), music and live experiences (KOKO), and digital-first production (After Party Studios). The Group recently announced a partnership with journalist and broadcaster Amol Rajan as the producer and distributor of his new Creator Economy venture.

The deal with Common Interest was managed by Chris Fry, COO and CFO, Sister Group and Common Interest group’s chief financial and operating officer Deepa Shah.

title: Robert Pattinson Says ‘The Batman 2’ Is ‘So Ambitious’ and a ‘Different Take’ on the Franchise: ‘It’s a Real Left Turn From the First’
summary: Robert Pattinson is opening up about “The Batman: Part II” — and how it is a totally “different take” on the franchise than the first film was. “It’s so ambitious. I mean, I sort of said the other day on something that the first one was a different take on a Batman movie, and this […]
content:
Robert Pattinson is opening up about “The Batman: Part II” — and how it is a totally “different take” on the franchise than the first film was.

“It’s so ambitious. I mean, I sort of said the other day on something that the first one was a different take on a Batman movie, and this one is another,” he told Collider in a recent interview. “It’s a real left turn from the first one, but somehow it keeps elements of the kind of feel of it. But it just feels really ambitious, and I’m excited to see how it turns out.”

Set to hit theaters on Feb. 18, 2028, “The Batman Part II” is Matt Reeves’ follow-up to 2022’s “The Batman,” in which audiences were first introduced to the “Primetime” star as Bruce Wayne. Scarlett Johansson and Sebastian Stan will star alongside Pattinson in the film, along with supporting cast members Charles Dance, Brian Tyree Henry and Sebastian Koch. Still, the film’s plot details remain under wraps.

Popular on Variety

Variety previously reported that Reeves completed the sequel’s script in June 2025, though the film was originally announced in 2022 — just a month after the first film debuted in theaters. When “The Batman Part II” premieres, it will have been six years since the first did.

DC Studios co-chief James Gunn previously defended the release delays by explaining how it’s “fairly common” for big-budget titles to have lengthy gaps before a sequel is released.

“To be fair, a 5-year gap or more is fairly common in sequels,” Gunn wrote on Threads last year. “7 years between ‘Alien’ and ‘Aliens.’ 14 years between ‘Incredibles.’ 7 years between the first two ‘Terminators.’ 13 years between ‘Avatars.’ 36 years between ‘Top Guns.’ And, of course, six years between ‘Guardians Vol 2’ and ‘Vol 3.’”

title: Liz Murdoch & Jane Featherstone’s Sister Group Takes Stake In Common Interest
summary: Liz Murdoch and Jane Featherstone’s Sister Group has taken a minority stake in brands and advertising specialist Common Interest. The two organizations have agreed a strategic partnership and are already working together. Founded by Anthony Freedman, agencies including Amplify, 21st Century Brand and Baby Teeth are part of Common Interest. Sister Group, meanwhile, houses Black […]
content:
Liz Murdoch and Jane Featherstone’s Sister Group has taken a minority stake in brands and advertising specialist Common Interest. The two organizations have agreed a strategic partnership and are already working together.

Founded by Anthony Freedman, agencies including Amplify, 21st Century Brand and Baby Teeth are part of Common Interest. Sister Group, meanwhile, houses Black Doves prodco Sister Pictures, unscripted outfit Yes Yes Media, Locksmith Animation, and factual specialist Dorothy Street among others.

Sister Group and Common Interest said they are already collaborating on projects and will build a slate of IP that exists on multiple platforms and is backed by brands.

It is the third deal in recent months for Sister Group, which Murdoch and Featherstone set up in 2019, and has Lucinda Hicks as CEO. It has already acquired After Party Studios and cut a programming deal with Amol Rajan.

Watch on Deadline

Freedman said: “This partnership is more than a meeting of minds, it’s a real commitment from both sides, to prove that brands can be part of shaping entertainment without compromising on what audiences love.”

“Connecting Sister’s creative diversity and track record in storytelling with Common Interest’s deep knowledge of brand strategy, culture and commercial relationships can demonstrate what’s possible when you stop treating entertainment and brand as different conversations,” added Hick.

In a joint statement, Murdoch and Featherstone said that Common Interest is a natural fit with Sister. “Their deep commitment to entertainment and brand strategies that people actually care about, mirrors the values of creative excellence, authorship and risk-taking intrinsic to Sister. We’re not just aligned on paper, but underway on some great ideas where the potency of that combination is very apparent.”

title: Trump Insists White House Ban On CNN & MS Now  “Lawful Under The First Amendment”; TRO Hearing Showdown Set For Wednesday
summary: Coming right up against a deadline set by a federal judge, the Justice Department tonight defended Donald Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds. The response comes despite an outcry across media outlets that the restriction is a flagrant violation of the First Amendment. Leaning onto a Wednesday hearing […]
content:
Coming right up against a deadline set by a federal judge, the Justice Department tonight defended Donald Trump‘s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds. The response comes despite an outcry across media outlets that the restriction is a flagrant violation of the First Amendment.

Leaning onto a Wednesday hearing on a temporary restraining order, the administration argued for Trump and top White House aides in its opposition filing that the “President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”

Adding to that, and sidestepping Trump’s previous quip that there was no particular reason for the ban the Department of Justice is now claiming that CNN, MS Now and Politico have “engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security” over stories on the construction of Trump’s much criticized ballroom. Swiping at past rulings on White House access, the DOJ is also maintaining that “While the D.C. Circuit has held that some areas of the White House grounds constitute a nonpublic that decision is wrong and should be overruled.”

After Trump banned the three outlets on Friday, CNN, Politico and MS NOW jointly sued the president and top staffers, claiming violations of the First and Fifth amendments.

Watch on Deadline

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” their lawsuit stated.

Late Tuesday, the DOJ laid out POTUS’ POV.

“The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation’s Commander-in-Chief,” the 19-page document from Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate and others at the DOJ states. “Plaintiffs CNN, MSNOW, and Politico have long been granted privileged access to White House grounds. But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum “standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including” by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.'”

Snapping at UN credentialed CNN reporters while in NYC today, Trump has found himself out of the usual spotlight.

Shortly after the filing on Monday, the five major TV networks that make up the White House TV pool said that they were suspending coverage in solidarity, leaving a void in video of Trump at the White House and other events. The pool is made up of CNN, NBC News, ABC News., CBS News and Fox News. Other outlets, like The New York Times, have protested the ban in other ways, like withholding their use of images from the White House.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly has scheduled a hearing for Wednesday afternoon on the outlets’ motion for the TRO. Trump has already signaled that he expects the judge to rule in the networks’ favor and plans an appeal. Even though he appointed the judge in his first term, Kelly sided with then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta after the network sued the Trump administration for revoking his hard pass in 2018.

The three outlets’ legal team, led by Theodore Boutrous Jr., bolstered their case earlier on Tuesday when they noted a new D.C. Circuit decision on access to the steps of the Capitol. The judges ruled that the eastern steps of the Capitol were a “nonpublic forum” but speech regulations had to be “viewpoint neutral.”

Trump has complained about the three outlets’ coverage of him, telling reporters, “There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories.”

title: Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ World Premiere Was A Royal Affair With Prince William & Kate Middleton
summary: Tom Cruise and Digger took over London’s Leicester Square Gardens on Tuesday for the world premiere of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s dark political comedy. The Warner Bros/Legendary pic is due to hit screens internationally on September 30 and on Imax and across North America beginning October 2. The event, a Royal Film Performance, was attended by […]
content:
Tom Cruise and Digger took over London’s Leicester Square Gardens on Tuesday for the world premiere of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s dark political comedy. The Warner Bros/Legendary pic is due to hit screens internationally on September 30 and on Imax and across North America beginning October 2.

The event, a Royal Film Performance, was attended by Prince William and Princess Catherine of Wales and was hosted in aid of the UK’s Film & TV Charity.

Tom Cruise's #DiggerMovie takes over the entirety of London's Leicester Square for the world premiere pic.twitter.com/cBZ9Ig5rBg — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 22, 2026

William and Kate greeted Cruise and González Iñárritu first on the carpet, and after a chat met the rest of the cast, with González Iñarritu escorting Prince William and Cruise escorting Princess Catherine down the line. Cruise’s co-stars in attendance included Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons.

Also in attendance were Emma D’Arcy, Emmanuel Lubezki, Sophie Wilde, J.J. Abrams, Hannah Waddingham and Salma Hayek. Click for Deadline’s red carpet photo gallery.

Prince William and Princess Catherine of Wales walk down the carpet at the world premiere of Tom Cruise’s #DiggerMovie pic.twitter.com/JRgroQFCrM — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 22, 2026

Tom Cruise and Alejandro G. Iñárritu greet Prince William and Princess Catherine of Wales at the world premiere of #DiggerMovie in London pic.twitter.com/M3dRZ1vSWl — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 22, 2026

Prince William and Princess Catherine of Wales chat to Tom Cruise, Sandra Hüller, Riz Ahmed, Emma D’Arcy and more at the #DiggerMovie world premiere in London pic.twitter.com/s6UGxZHqVG — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 22, 2026

Once inside, Cruise introduced the movie, thanking the Royal Family.

“We “want to thank the Royal Highnesses for supporting this event,” he said onstage. “And just to tell them that we love them and we really appreciate what they do for the arts for this country and for the world, thank you.”

He also praised producers Mary Parent and Michael Sharp before turning to González Iñarritu.

“You are one of one and I have so admired your films from the very first one, and to have the opportunity to work with you has been one of the great dreams of mine and pleasure, and you’ll see this character and what he’s created,” he said. “I’ve never seen anything like it. His mind is just extraordinary.”

Then it was González Iñarritu’s turn.

“We all know how incredible actor he is, but I think for me the most surprising thing is, how generous, how the positive energy that he brought every day to the set,” said the director. “His enthusiasm is contagious — it’s actually uncomfortable,” he added, making Cruise laugh.

“I think he shared his experience, his enthusiasm with all of us every day in a very challenging role that you will see something that he has never done like that, at least I never saw how capable he was to understand every inch of his body, of his voice, of the tone, of the volume of the pauses of the thing as precise as when he jumped into the plane and he knows that one second can be dead or alive.”

Tom Cruise presents #DiggerMovie at the world premiere in London: “I’ve never seen anything like it” pic.twitter.com/5x3PfRPue7 — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 22, 2026

The Royal Guards play a song at the #DiggerMovie world premiere as Prince William and Princess Catherine of Wales enter the movie theater pic.twitter.com/YoqbIS9Dci — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 22, 2026

Director Alejandro G. Iñarritu praises Tom Cruise at the #DiggerMovie world premiere and makes the star laugh by joking that his positivity is “uncomfortable” pic.twitter.com/aCrXnivID2 — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 23, 2026

In Digger, Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, an oil baron and the world’s most powerful man, as he embarks on a frantic mission to prove he is humanity’s savior before the environmental disaster he unleashed destroys everything.

title: ‘Reasonable Doubt’ Drops Season 4 Trailer Revealing Shooting Victim
summary: For fans of Hulu’s Reasonable Doubt, the shooting victim teased in the Season 3 finale, when Monica (Brandee Evans) stormed into The Stewart Firm, has been revealed in the first trailer for Season 4. The new season premieres with three episodes October 6, with new episodes dropping weekly on Tuesdays through November 4. The trailer […]
content:
For fans of Hulu‘s Reasonable Doubt, the shooting victim teased in the Season 3 finale, when Monica (Brandee Evans) stormed into The Stewart Firm, has been revealed in the first trailer for Season 4. The new season premieres with three episodes October 6, with new episodes dropping weekly on Tuesdays through November 4.

The trailer shows Jax (Emayatzy Corinealdi) in the hospital fighting to survive with the help of many life-saving machines. She also has the support of her loved ones, like her husband, Lewis Stewart (McKinley Freeman), who is shown at her bedside, and Corey Cash (Morris Chestnut), who also visits, asking Jax to keep fighting.

Chaos has erupted in her absence, with her old firm moving into action to poach her clients in her greatest time of need. In a voice-over, Cory says, “This is not the end of your story; it can’t be.”

Watch on Deadline

Monica shot Jax because she blames her for destroying her career and reputation. So if all goes well, I’m going to guess that Monica has some karma waiting for her.

Season 4 is about survival, truth, and rebuilding under pressure. Every character will be forced to confront consequences they can no longer outrun as Jax’s fate hangs in the balance, driving the entire story forward in the new season.

The official synopsis: After a brutal attack leaves Jax’s family and newly minted law firm shaken, nothing feels certain, especially their future. With Jax’s most loyal client at the center of a spiraling media disaster, The Stewart Firm is thrust into a high-stakes battle where every move could mean survival … or collapse of the firm. As grief lingers and pressure mounts, one question looms: Can they rebuild in time, or will the cost of moving forward too quickly be everything they stand to lose?

Reasonable Doubt is created, written and executive produced by Raamla Mohamed Hunter. Kerry Washington executive produces alongside Pilar Savone for Simpson Street, Larry Wilmore for Wilmore Films, Tamara Gregory, Anton Cropper, Lena Cordina and Erika L. Johnson. Shawn Holley, Jon Leshay and Zahir McGhee serve as co-executive producers. The series hails from Onyx Collective and is produced by 20th Television, a part of Disney Television Studios.

Watch the trailer above.

title: ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Recap: Viral Hits Night Ups Ante While Bringing Katseye, Tinashe & ‘Heated Rivalry’ To Ballroom Floor
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details from Tuesday night’s episode of Dancing with the Stars. The Dancing With the Stars ballroom is back in business, and all of the remaining Season 35 contestants are competing during the same live show for the first time Tuesday night. Last week, ABC split up the premiere into two […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details from Tuesday night’s episode of Dancing with the Stars.

The Dancing With the Stars ballroom is back in business, and all of the remaining Season 35 contestants are competing during the same live show for the first time Tuesday night. Last week, ABC split up the premiere into two nights, women and men, with two eliminations.

There’s still 14 people left in the competition, so things are really just getting started. Harry Shum Jr and Maura Higgins tied for the top scores across both nights last week, but no one scored above a 7. The judges have made it clear they’re not going easy on anyone this season.

Watch on Deadline

Speaking of the judges, the forces that be are also putting some rules on them this year. After going over time on Wednesday night’s broadcast last week, the third judge to speak each night will have to keep it short, summing up their thoughts in just one word. Jury is still out on whether cutting time from the judges is a positive change to a dance competition series, so we’ll see if they keep this going in the weeks to come.

Week 2 is all about the viral hits, so each of the couples are dancing to a song that made the rounds on social media recently.

Let’s dive in.

Actress Jenna Dewan with Val Chmerkovskiy. Last week, Carrie Ann Inaba told Dewan that she wasn’t always using her partner to his fullest potential, so she’s determined to get on the same page as Chmerkovskiy for a jive to “Animal” by Katseye on Week 2. They came out swinging, and Inaba was quite impressed with the kinetic resistance at play. “That’s what I’m talking about!” Inaba said. SCORE: 21 out of 30

Reality star Ciara Miller with Brandon Armstrong. Miller had an intense start to her DWTS journey, putting up an ambitious display of vulnerability during her first performance. Going into Week 2, she seems to be feeling much more secure in her place in front of the camera. Now that she’s feeling braver, she’s tackling a tango to “No Broke Boys” by Disco Lines & Tinashe. “Ciara has entered the building!!!” Inaba declared after the routine. “You are in it to win it. Watch out everybody!” SCORE: 18 out of 30

Reality star Tyler Cameron with Sharna Burgess. The former Bachelorette star surprised himself with his performance last week and is really leaning into the experience in the second week. He finds himself getting his confidence back, and he’s ready to perform a salsa to “Girls” by The Kid Laroi. Burgess delivered an impressive and crowd-pleasing routine, but all three judges agreed there was barely a lick of a salsa to be found among the various wild lifts (which Julianne Hough slyly, or not so slyly, suggested viewers use for a viral trend). SCORE: 16 out of 30

Actress Julia Stiles with Ezra Sosa. Stiles took the judges’ corrections seriously, and she wants to implement as many as she can in a tango to “The Door” by Teddy Swims. She speaks during her intro package about “reclaiming my relationship with people watching me” after having a complicated relation to fame growing up. The judges can see her effort to go outside of her comfort zone, but they want her to really let go. Basically, keep doing what you’re doing! SCORE: 16 out of 30

Savannah Bananas midfielder Jackson Olson with Emma Slater. Olson says he’s “fired up to get better” after the judges hammered his technique last week. This week, he’s dancing a foxtrot to “That’s So True” by Gracie Abrams, a song he’s used many times on his own social media. This is his first form dance, meaning he’ll need to stay in frame, so he’s determined to stay smooth and impress the judges. “Woah, improvement,” Inaba said, almost in disbelief. SCORE: 18 out of 30

Chef Giada De Laurentiis with Alan Bersten. A humble queen, De Laurentiis tells her pro partner she knows he was shocked they didn’t go home last week — and that’s OK! She’s open to the process and is ready to improve for her salsa to “Bella Ciao” by Becky G. It’s a challenging week, and she doesn’t quite land every step, but she went out there and gave it her all. “It still feels a little timid,” Derek Hough tells her. “Next time, I want a little bit more power.” SCORE: 12 out of 30

Comedian and podcaster Connor Wood with Rylee Arnold. The first time Wood went “big time” viral was a video with his grandma, so basically he owes his career to Grammy, he says. Let’s hope he can go viral again this week with a tango to “12 to 12” by Sombr in honor of her. The dance style is certainly out of his comfort zone, and the judges are keen to point that out, but not at the expense of acknowledging the effort he’s clearly putting in. “There were a lot of mistakes tonight, and you know that…but the good bits were excellent,” Tonioli said. SCORE: 15 out of 30

Paralympian Ezra Frech with Daniella Karagach. After coming out swinging with a fantastic first week, Frech is taking on what Karagach says will be his most difficult dance style of the entire competition — a cha cha to “Low” by Flo Rida. It becomes clear in training that several accommodations will be needed, but they take it on with ease, and they smash it. “Ezra, I am absolutely blown away,” Derek said. “This is your superpower.” SCORE: 21 out of 30

Actress Tatyana Ali with Jan Ravnik. The Fresh Prince of Bel Air star is happy with her lively performance last week and, this week, she’s getting much more vulnerable and reflective in a foxtrot to “What Was I Made For?” by Billie Eilish. The judges are quite impressed, with Inaba calling it “touching.” SCORE: 18 out of 30

Olympian Amber Glenn with Pasha Pashkov. Glenn couldn’t dance a tango to “All the Things She Said” by Harrison without a nod to Heated Rivalry, which is the entire reason the song went viral in the first place. She struggles with the concept of dancing in frame, but she’s determined to do the routine justice. Needless to say, she nailed it. “Best tango of the night. Period,” Tonioli said. Hough didn’t even have to say his one word, trading it for what appears to be the pair’s secret handshake instead. It ended with a salute. SCORE: 21 out of 30

Late-night sidekick Guillermo Rodriguez with Witney Carson. Rodriguez might have a tough time getting serious this week for a paso doble to “Where Have You Been” by Rihanna (his favorite artist!). He says he’s going to think of his wife yelling at him to keep from laughing. And there wasn’t even a smirk! Not to mention, what a technical improvement over Week 1. “Guillermo, I appreciate that you just didn’t rely on shtick in that dance,” she said. SCORE: 12 out of 30 (The judges got booed for that one.)

Musician Taylor Hanson with Britt Stewart. Inaba said she’d be keeping an eye on him last week, so Hanson is eager to impress on Week 2. Now that he has a sense of the show, he’s ready to get to work and really dig in this week to learn a cha cha to “Cake By the Ocean” by DNCE. He might not be used to moving those hips that way, but he pulls it off, kind of. Now he needs to learn how to use his arms and finish his movements correctly. “But, I like the way you’re working,” Tonioli said. Inaba called it “frenetic.” SCORE: 15 out of 30

Actor Harry Shum Jr. with Jenna Johnson. After impressing the judges and scoring atop the leaderboard in his debut, Shum Jr. is feeling some pressure approaching a Viennese waltz to “Iris” by the Goo Goo Dolls. It’s a very technical dance, so it’s something new, but he’s taking it on with confidence. “Overall it wasn’t bad,” Tonioli said, but both she and Inaba encouraged him to bridge the gap between his performance in the emotional, more expressive moments versus when in frame. SCORE: 18 out of 30

Reality star Maura Higgins with Mark Ballas. After tying for the top spot on the leaderboard last week, Higgins was truly in shock, and she’s feeling the pressure to pull off a cha cha to “September” by Earth, Wind & Fire. Things get emotional in practice, but you’d have never guessed she was nervous when she stepped on the dance floor. “It was a little safer this time,” Inaba said, but that’s OK. She’s committed to learning the technique, and they agree that’ll take her far. SCORE: 19 out of 30

Who goes home?

Sadly, someone has to hit the road. This week, it’s Giada and Alan. The remaining 13 couples are back in the ballroom next Tuesday for Yacht Rock night.

title: Will a U.S. Federal Tax Threaten Europe’s Production Boom? European Producers Don’t Think So: ‘The U.S. Is Falling Behind’
summary: One of the hottest topics at this year’s Creative Investors’ Conference at the San Sebastián Film Festival is the likelihood and the effects of a U.S. federal tax credit for film production. Speaking at a panel titled “Europe’s Current Challenges and Opportunities,” Lorenzo de Maio of De Maio Entertainment said he doesn’t believe the measure […]
content:
One of the hottest topics at this year’s Creative Investors’ Conference at the San Sebastián Film Festival is the likelihood and the effects of a U.S. federal tax credit for film production. Speaking at a panel titled “Europe’s Current Challenges and Opportunities,” Lorenzo de Maio of De Maio Entertainment said he doesn’t believe the measure would be a threat to the booming European production market.

“I’m Italian but live in Los Angeles, and [the tax credit] is one of the few things uniting Republicans and Democrats,” he said jokingly. “A stackable federal credit added to state credits is a very interesting opportunity because the U.S. has lost so much of its production capabilities.”

“There’s a lot of capacity in the world, so the U.S. is falling a litte behind, honestly,” he continued. “Imagine if [a country like] Spain didn’t have incentives… It’s time for the U.S. to have it. It’s not controversial and will help rebuild some of the craftspeople that have left the business. The beauty of supporting the system is that you create new filmmakers, storytellers, companies, and cultural opportunities for co-productions. A whole ecosystem that thrives is something the U.S. lost a little bit, and it would be helpful to bring it back, but I don’t think it’s a threat.”

Popular on Variety

De Maio also spoke about another pressing topic at this year’s conference, which is co-organized with CCA Media Finance: the increase in U.S. private equity making up for a steep decline in pre-sales. “There are definitely new sources of equity coming in,” he said. “The fun of it for us is we can be quite open. With most of our [Fremantle] companies, we will look at equity or debt; we can cash flow. So what works for the project is usually the right answer if you have that flexibility, and there are so many opportunities to co-pro within Europe and so many ways of doing. The complexity is there, but it’s worth navigating it because it’s a thriving industry.”

Why Not Productions’ Pauline Lamy echoed that thought, saying that having U.S. equity come into the European market is “a new thing” for the company. “Because we can not presell a lot of films because of their language, having that type of money is really helping us make films at a bigger scale. ‘Fjord’ needed that; ‘Emilia Pérez’ needed that. A lot of films couldn’t work without this mixed system.”

Speaking of Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or-winning film, Lamy said the co-production model between Romania, France, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland felt a “natural” fit for the project.

“We are an independent cinema company and filmmaker-driven, so we try following filmmakers through all their projects,” she said. “Of course we are always trying to push them, but we would never force them to make a film in another language to have a bigger audience. Sometimes it happens; you can think about ‘Fjord,’ from a Romanian director who always worked in his own country, but with this story, you have characters who are in Norway and speak in English, so he could have an English-speaking cast and then have a bigger audience. It’s not a strategy; it depends on the project and the director.”

De Maio noted how “60% of European movies only open in their own territory,” so it is not worth forcing unnecessary co-productions for movies that might remain limited to their home turfs. “It is not about conquering the market but how we honor the DNA of the market.”

“We really have to think about what works for it,” he continued, offering Pablo Larraín’s Chile-Italy co-production “Maria” as an example. “That was a natural co-production. But we have local movies, and it’s not natural to force that. So we look at the DNA of the movie and let financing come from that.”
