title: ‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse Review: The ’50s Absurdist Comedy Is Too Smug in Its Peak-Bleak View of Venal Humanity, but Jefferson Mays and Melinda Page Hamilton Are Worth the Visit
summary: When an “Amadeus” revival opened at Pasadena Playhouse in February, it was such a spectacular success on every level that you wouldn’t have minded if the keepers of the venerable San Gabriel Valley venue just turned over the keys to the place for a while to the two Tony winners most responsible for making it […]
content:
When an “Amadeus” revival opened at Pasadena Playhouse in February, it was such a spectacular success on every level that you wouldn’t have minded if the keepers of the venerable San Gabriel Valley venue just turned over the keys to the place for a while to the two Tony winners most responsible for making it a smash: star Jefferson Mays and director Darko Tresnjak. And that’s kind of what the Playhouse has done. That dynamic duo is already back in Pasadena with “The Visit,” which has opened a mere seven months after “Amadeus” first hit the boards there. With a good number of cast and crew members carrying over from the previous production to rock us again after “Amadeus,” this looks, for the moment, like as close a thing to an official house company as you can get in a major theater nowadays.

But is “The Visit” as much fun as “Amadeus”? Let’s just say for the moment that this followup production is destined to be more polarizing than that across-the-board crowd pleaser, although it’s not even a bit less lively. Like Peter Shaffer’s play before it, it is a vintage black comedy — even more vintage, as it was written by Swiss playwright Friedrich Dürrenmatt in 1956, although it’s been subject to a lot of Engligh adaptations and re-writes in subsequent decades. It loosely belongs to the theater of absurdism, which means that there is increasing room as the tragicomedy proceeds for Tresnjak to play around with the initially realistic trappings and have some fun with surrealist, grotesque and/or anachronistic elements. But what it really belongs to is the theater of fatalism, where things line up along the way to increasingly convince us that society, government and individua people themselves are inevitably subject to corruption and venality. So your enjoyment of the play may finally be subject to how much you feel you already do or don’t know that.

Popular on Variety

Given that Mays is widely regarded as one of the most charismatic and capable actors in modern theater, would it surprise you to learn that he is not really the star of “The Visit”? Well, he is, certainly in billing, and in the fact that he is the clear protagonist, as Anton Schill, a humble shopkeeper in postwar (or is it 2020s?) Europe whose past comes back to haunt him. But Mays is playing almost more of a mouse than a man. So, talk about a turnaround from Salieri. As much scenery-chewing as the actor was doing in “Amadeus” — and it was a glorious meal — that’s how little he’s doing here. Mays admitted in a recent interview that he wasn’t sure he was right for the role, and you can see why he might have thought so, given the character’s passivity. But it takes a skilled actor to successfully put his mojo on mute, too. So if you know what he’s capable of, there’s some pleasure in watching him at first seem to embody the milk of human kindness, before he succumbs more of an emblem ofBut the the milquetoast of human depravity.

Melinda Page Hamilton in ‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse Jeff Lorch/Pasadena Playhouse

But the obvious centrifugal force of “The Visit” is the female lead, a character named Claire Zachanassian who may be the richest woman in the world, and who has an even greater surfeit of personality than money. She’s played here to perfection by Melinda Page Hamilton, whose stage appearances and recurring TV roles have not made her a household name — yet she has such presence that, from her first scene forward, you’re convinced that she must be one anyway. She gets off a train and breezes into the downtrodden European town where she spent her impoverished girlhood like she is some charming ane cunning combination of Lauren Bacall, Madonna and a demonically possessed Daisy Buchanan. Her intentions for the hometown she is nostalgically revisiting are cloaked at first, but her barbed banter is so much fun, you can almost half-wish she doesn’t mean anything sinister with her visit, even if she clearly does. After all, her musclebound handlers have brought along with them an empty casket, and this is the sort of play where a coffin that appears in the first act is definitely going to go off in the third. (Not literally; although “The Visit” has been produced in as a hefty three-parter in some productions, it’s mercifully cut down to a single act in Pasadena.) You can never take your eyes or ears off Hamilton, even when the plot gives her increasingly schematic things to say and do in the second half.

About that plot. There is a big revelation less than halfway into the show, one that might even count as a plot twist, and thus something not to be spoiled… if not for the fact that virtually every synopsis in the last 70 years has included it in the first sentence. So we’ll assume most patrons know it going in and won’t hold a discussion of it against us here, though stop right now if you think you might. Cutting to the chase, Claire has earmarked the aforementioned casket for Anton, despite the fact that he was her lover in their youthful days, and they are sharing sweet memories of their lusty romps in the woods within minutes of her arrival. After some more talk of the bucolic days gone by, Claire suddenly announces at a town meeting that she will rescue this on-the-skids burg with a donation of one billion (what the currency is goes unspecified), with one condition: that they deliver her a dead Anton. For reasons eventually to be revealed, she represents pure vengeance, even if she does talk like someone out of a ’30s screwball comedy, or “Truth or Dare.”

Up to the point that she delivers the townspeople this ultimatum — a deal with the devil, or with an especially cocktail-party-friendly Cruella de Vil — “The Visit” has kind of been a rollicking good time. For much of the audience, it will remain that all the way to the end, even with some somber moments along the way that aren’t played for laughs. But the basic problem with the play — if you’re spoilsport enough to see it as one — is that once Claire makes her modest proposal to save the town, there won’t likely be any doubt in a single audience member’s mind that things are going to pan out exactly as she wants them to. Because it’s that kind of a show: one that is just a little too self-pleased with itself for offering the bleakest possible vision of what civilized people can and probably will do, offered a way out of their misery or mundanity. So there’s not that much to happen in the last two-thirds of the drama than for your ribs to be constantly nudged with the idea of how easily the most respectable citizens among us will give in to modest proposals and, indeed, murder. It rings true, don’t get me wrong! But it also rings awfully predictable, in a way that maybe it didn’t in the late ’50s and ’60s, when it was a little easier for defiantly grim morality tales to seem transgressive in the mainstream.

‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse Jeff Lorch/Pasadena Playhouse

The story might have at least a modicum of suspense if any of the upstanding townspeople were seen as struggling with the idea of murdering a trusted friend. But after an initial vote of “no way” to Claire’s offer, everyone seems to have become completely transformed by the next morning. The program notes reference “Invasion of the Body Snatchers,” which seems like an apt analogy, except that that film would be a lot less riveting if the entire city turned into pod people instantly, followed by an hour of Kevin McCarthy slowly deciding he should accept his fate. To give some credit here, there is one scene in which a cleric openly debates with himself whether to go along with the greedy mob or not, but within a couple of minutes he’s come to terms with the creeping evil, too. It’s realistic, sad to say, that a population would find a way to justify throw all of its collective principles away and commit a horrific crime; it’s just a little less realistic — or good for the purposes of a full-length drama — that this would all happen in a virtual instant.

There are other huge dramatic implausibilities, if we want to get picky about it. The opening scenes of “The Visit,” when it is in its most realistic mode, have the townspeople convinced that Anton is actually their ticket to riches, not a future scapegoat, because of his past romance with Claire. And he seems to be firmly convinced of this, too, as they get together alone in the woods and share reminiscings of those tender or erotic moments of yore. But once Claire reveals the backstory of why she is out to bring the wrath of God down on him, her reasoning seems… well, still a little psychopathic, but somewhat justified, by the standard of modern feminist morality tales. To say he did her wrong is an understatement. So is Anton supposed to be mentally compromised or deranged, rather than the harmless soul we first meet him as, to have imagined that Claire would have come back after all these decades with a positive picture of him, instead of a lust for blood? It makes no sense. Maybe that’s a fault of the condensation, and the picture would be clearer in the three-and-a-half-hour version (!) Tony Kushner adapted for the London stage at the turn of the decade. But there’s some basic sense missing here that can’t be explained away with the idea that it’s just a surrealist fable.

With all that said, there are still a lot of pleasures in this production that remain failsafe, even after the ride toward a way-too-inevitable outcome is firmly on its tracks. For instance, the way that Tresnjak, wardrobe designer Charlotte DeVaux Shields and set designer Alexander Dodge have conspired to make sneakers into the embodiment of complicity and evil is fairly ingenious. Somehow, the show’s supporting cast members manage to make their way onstage without giving away their footwear until, at some key moment, their colorful shoes are lit up in what looks like a flurorescent glow, revealing that they, too, have gone along with the body snatchers. (Everyone should see it coming a mile away, but even I LOL-ed when the town cleric showed that he, also, has succumbed to the Air Jordan pandemic.) There are an increasing number of moments like that throughout the production in which it seems to have suddenly jumped into the present day, and some work, some don’t. It is a little jarring when, still pretty early in the show, you hear the first example of disco bumper music, like they suddenly piped in a little bit of David Byrne’s score for “Here Lies Love” to cover the scene change. But by the end, the use of modern-day cameras and video screens to bring the action fully into the 2020s seems justified enough, if you buy into Tresnjak’s time-tripping aesthetic at all.

‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse Jeff Lorch/Pasadena Playhouse

The show’s creepiest characters — no contest here — are a couple of aging, balding, blind eunuchs (played by Jake Levy and Lauren Worsham)who seem to be part of Claire’s entourage for no good reason, other than to figure into the tale of woe she eventually tells, which finally explains why they know their way around the town so well despite being sightless visitors. Their presence brings “The Visit” almost right up to the edge of horror, which is where thematically it kind of belongs, despite all the zingers, smirks and guffaws. The play seems to want to flirt with the idea of Grand Guignol, even if remains more firmly rooted in the land of Samuel Beckett.

But the swing being taken here is bold enough that there’s no reason to want to take the Playhouse keys back from Tresnjak, if he has more offbeat revival aspirations where this one came from. And with lead performances like Mays’ and Hamilton’s, the production is — sorry to do this here — worth your visit. If the initial impulse is that Mays doesn’t have as much to do here as is worthy of his talent, he is so firmly enmeshed in the character of a nebbish caught up in a sub-Kafkaesque nightmare, he makes you feel deeply for his fate, even if Maurice Valency’s adapted script kind of seems to want you to not feel so bad about it. And Melinda Page Hamilton? She’s so captivating, in both her rages and her funnier, more casual cruelty, that I’d follow her Claire to just about any soiree where the multi-billionaire elite meet, even if I did spot a coffin there with my name on it.

“The Visit” runs through Oct. 4 at Pasadena Playhouse, located at 39 South El Molino Ave. in Pasadena. Phone: 626-356-7529. For tickets and more information, visit http://www.pasadenaplayhouse.org.

title: Rolf de Heer Named President of Tokyo Film Festival Jury
summary: The Tokyo International Film Festival has named Australian director Rolf de Heer president of the international competition jury for the festival’s 39th edition. De Heer has spent more than 40 years in Tasmania, Australia, directing, writing and producing films across a broad range of genres and subjects. His 1993 feature “Bad Boy Bubby” won the […]
content:
The Tokyo International Film Festival has named Australian director Rolf de Heer president of the international competition jury for the festival’s 39th edition.

De Heer has spent more than 40 years in Tasmania, Australia, directing, writing and producing films across a broad range of genres and subjects. His 1993 feature “Bad Boy Bubby” won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival, along with the festival’s Fipresci Prize. Four of his films have made the official selection at Cannes, among them “Ten Canoes” (2006), winner of the Special Jury Prize in the Un Certain Regard section.

This year’s World Focus lineup at TIFF will include Australia Spotlight, a dedicated showcase of Australian cinema mounted with the Australian Embassy in Japan. The series will screen de Heer’s “The Survival of Kindness” (2022), a competition entry at the 73rd Berlin Film Festival that went on to win the Fipresci Prize there.

Popular on Variety

“For any of us attending the Tokyo International Film Festival, it is a privilege,” de Heer said. “For me, as a filmmaker, it is even more so. The more films I manage to make, the fewer films I manage to see, especially on the big screen. But as a part of this jury, I have the duty, the obligation, to see at least 15 films and talk about them with other filmmakers.”

Hisamatsu Takeo, festival director of TIFF, said he was delighted to welcome de Heer as jury president. “With his distinctive perspective and unwavering commitment to filmmaking, de Heer has spent decades opening up new possibilities in cinema,” Hisamatsu said. “We look forward to the fresh dialogue and discoveries that his wealth of experience and deep insight will bring to this year’s Competition and its diverse selection of films.”

De Heer trained at the Australian Film, Television and Radio School and has since written or co-written 14 screenplays that reached the screen as feature films. His director’s credits run to 15 and a half features spanning a range of budgets and genres, and he has produced or co-produced 16 fiction films and five documentaries.

Career highlights include “Dingo” (1991), starring Colin Friels and jazz musician Miles Davis; “The Tracker” (2002), which began de Heer’s collaborations with Australian Aboriginal actor David Gulpilil; and “Charlie’s Country” (2013), for which Gulpilil won the best actor award at Cannes. “Alexandra’s Project” (2003) earned Helen Buday a best actress award at the San Sebastian Film Festival after the film screened in competition at the Berlin Film Festival.

The 39th TIFF will run Oct. 26-Nov. 4. TIFFCOM, the festival’s industry market, will take place Oct. 28-30.

title: ‘Game Changer’ Host Sam Reich on Season 8’s 23-Contestant, 90-Minute, Non-Chili’s-Sponsored Finale and ‘Acid Trip’ Season 9 Episode Plans
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 8 finale of “Game Changer,” now streaming on Dropout. “Game Changer” capped off its eighth season Monday with a finale episode that was not at all sponsored by Chili’s but ended with its winner taking home between $3,000 and $5,000 (host and Dropout CEO Sam Reich […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 8 finale of “Game Changer,” now streaming on Dropout.

“Game Changer” capped off its eighth season Monday with a finale episode that was not at all sponsored by Chili’s but ended with its winner taking home between $3,000 and $5,000 (host and Dropout CEO Sam Reich isn’t sure) in Chili’s gift cards. Combine that with the fact the Season 8 finale (a talent show competition) is the longest episode of the Dropout series to date (coming in at just under 90 minutes) and boasts the largest number of contestants (23) and you’ve got a wildly unprecedented undertaking for Reich and the “Game Changer” team.

The episode, titled “Last Talent Standing,” features nearly two dozen contestants performing in a talent show with a “Squid Game”-esque twist that “killed off” eliminated competitors who then joined a panel of judges led by guest stars Kumail Nanjiani, Maria Bamford and Gianmarco Soresi.

Popular on Variety

“What you see in this 90-minute episode is extraordinarily faithful to everything that actually occurred,” Reich tells Variety. “There is not a single go that we lifted out of the show completely.”

(It should be noted the episode does cut Katie Marovitch’s answer to the way she’d like to fake die upon her elimination, which was deemed “too dark” for Dropout’s standards. “Yeah, I think Katie and I will probably take that one to the grave, so to speak,” Reich says.)

Reich was willing to let the cameras roll indefinitely to capture the seemingly endless talents (from Japanese fan dancing to mind reading) of the Dropout players. But what he wasn’t up for was making another two-part episode.

“Most ‘Game Changer’ shoots go as long as they need to,” Reich says. “The difference between this season and prior seasons is, if you’re looking for how we’ve creatively pivoted, we’ve done episodes that we’ve split in two. Many. In fact, if you look at other two-parters, the sum of their parts is not as long as this 90 minutes was. I have finally landed against two-parters, and the reason is that I feel like we set up expectations and then there’s no way to surprise people as much with the second half. So their experience of watching an episode, waiting a week — actually two weeks — and then watching the second half is always going to be a funny kind of payoff where that second half better be, in some ways, profoundly different from the first half in order to still feel like ‘Game Changer.’ And I would rather wallop people with one experience. So now that we can afford to, that’s basically what this comes down to. We’re just doing longer episodes here and there.”

Though Reich says he’s done breaking episodes into two parts, there is still a limit to how long he’s willing to let an episode go based on his initial plans in a writers’ room vs. what happens during the actual production.

“There were game mechanics that we had to abandon because the day was immediately running so long and the biggest game mechanic that we had to abandon was mini games that were going to happen in between rounds and those mini games were going to be all players squaring off in the same talent,” Reich says. “For instance, we were going to reach the end of round one and then the players were going to go heads up on beatboxing or heads up on best Scottish accent or heads up on runway walk — which Oscar did do for us later in the episode — and we were quickly running so, so long that was not possible. Winners of those games were going to get a ‘one free death’ or ‘resurrection’ certificate. Our thinking was they could use them on themselves or they could unselfishly use them on someone else, which might also create a funny dynamic.”

Reich says that those planned aspects had to be cut out to account for the lengthy production day, but there was a key mechanic he made sure could stay in no matter how long the episode got.

“There is a distinction between what I am willing to do and what, like a ‘Squid Game’ or a ‘Beast Games’ is willing to do and part of that for me at this point is trying to figure out, if I’m going to do an elimination game, ways that eliminated players are going to stay involved,” Reich says. “So turning eliminated players into judges was important to me for that reason.”

Once the game got down to its final four contestants — Jacob Wysocki, Kimia Behpoornia, Kaylin Mahoney and Oscar Montoya — Reich says the competition hit its “tipping point,” as the desire to end the very long production day and go home warred with everyone’s goal to commit to the bit. This led to moments like Wysocki trying and failing to eliminate himself to, as he (the only “straight white guy” left at that point) put it, “give voices to people who matter” and so he could “go smoke a joint in my car.”

“The meta game of ‘Game Changer’ at any point is that probably everyone is just trying to create the best possible episode, regardless of if that means they’re winning,” Reich says. “I think everyone’s sort of producer brain is — meaning all of my players, and this is what makes for such a good show — probably a little higher than their game-player brain. Not all the time, but sometimes. Which means that I can count on players doing the funny thing, even if that means getting eliminated. Jacob, I think he was sort of saying to himself, ‘I don’t need to win this. The day is already going long. I want for one of my friends to win it,’ and just no one would allow it. And that was, in some ways, the tipping point of the episode, where we went from running long to that being the spirit of the day. To everyone wanting to hang in there as long as possible.”

Ultimately, Montoya walked away the proud owner of a Chili’s gift card with “under $5,000″ on it, courtesy of Dropout, not Chili’s — though that was not for lack of Reich trying to get Chili’s involved.

“I absolutely did,” Reich says. “Granted, I could have probably pressed on that more than I did. There was something about the fact that all of that happened and we weren’t sponsored by anybody, which is also funny. Just like if this ends up being the result, it’s just the result.”

As Dropout has grown, the company has set a steady pace with production and release cycles for its expanding slate of TV shows, which also includes “Dimension 20,” “Make Some Noise” and “Very Important People.” That means that even though “Game Changer” Season 8 has just concluded for viewers, the episodes were shot so long ago now that Reich’s focus has shifted to the ninth season, which begins production in three weeks. And he is trying to limit how the response to Season 8 affects new ideas.

“I’m so deeply entrenched in Season 9 that even to turn back and reflect on it, it’s tricky,” Reich says. “It requires me extracting my brain from one Frankenstein and putting it in another Frankenstein. There’s a natural sort of built-in tweak to ‘Game Changer,’ which is the show itself is such an experiment and we’re lucky to have fans who really care about it. But for the most part, I try to tune out the noise and to remain faithful to the experiment. And what to me that means is every season, it is a show that, like a cat, will always be exploring the perimeter of what it can do because it’s always looking for new things to exploit. And because the show gets bigger and bigger, there’s more at its disposal to be able to exploit season after season. So every season we have this conversation with ourselves, which is sort of like, what do we want to see a little bit more of? What do we want to see a little bit less of? And in some ways, every season is a response to the season that came before it.”

The focus between Seasons 7 and 8 was pushing the boundaries for game design, and Reich says he’s “really proud of what we came up with” for Season 8’s episodes, which has “some of the truest games that we’ve ever done with the show.”

Now going into Season 9, Reich says these episodes are planned to be “by a mile, the strangest stuff we’ve ever done.”

“It is just like whatever those game design impulses were [for Season 8], [Season 9] hasn’t left them entirely in the gutter, but it is like an acid trip,” Reich says. “The show benefits not at all from consistency. So we’ll continue to reinvent it, and it’ll continue to shape-shift and that’s part of the fun of being on this ride.”

title: ‘Gremlins 3’ Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros.
summary: Warner Bros. has delayed “Gremlins 3” from Nov. 19, 2027, to Oct. 6. 2028. David Zaslav, the CEO and president of Warner Bros. Discovery, first revealed the project during an investor call in 2025. Steven Spielberg is returning as executive producer alongside Maiden Voyage’s Eleanor Columbus. “Harry Potter” filmmaker Chris Columbus is set to produce […]
content:
Warner Bros. has delayed “Gremlins 3” from Nov. 19, 2027, to Oct. 6. 2028.

David Zaslav, the CEO and president of Warner Bros. Discovery, first revealed the project during an investor call in 2025. Steven Spielberg is returning as executive producer alongside Maiden Voyage’s Eleanor Columbus. “Harry Potter” filmmaker Chris Columbus is set to produce and direct. Hannah Marks is writing the script from an original draft by Chris Columbus, Zach Lipovsky and Adam Stein.

Kristie Macosko Krieger and Holly Bario are producing under Amblin Entertainment alongside Michael Barnathan and Mark Radcliffe of 26th Street Pictures. The official title, plot details and casting have not been disclosed.

Popular on Variety

Joe Dante’s original 1984 “Gremlins,” which played a role in creating the PG-13 film rating, was a horror comedy following a young boy named Billy who receives a cute, furry yet mysterious creature called a Mogwai. The two become fast friends, but Billy’s new pet comes with two strict rules: Never get the Mogwai wet and never feed it after midnight. Of course, those regulations are broken. The gremlin then multiplies and creates chaos in Billy’s small town during the holiday season.

The first “Gremlins” was a box office smash, grossing $212 million worldwide against a budget of about $11 million. The 1990 follow-up, “Gremlins 2: The New Batch,” only mustered $41 million by the end of its run but is considered a cult classic.

“Few titles are as beloved and iconic as ‘Gremlins,’ and we’re beyond excited to bring it back for both lifelong fans and a whole new generation,” Warner Bros. Pictures’ president of development and production Jesse Ehrman said in a statement at the time of the announcement of “Gremlins 3.” “It’s a privilege to be working alongside Steven [Spielberg], Chris [Columbus], and the entire creative team, and we look forward to audiences experiencing the next installment of the magic, mayhem and heart of Gremlins on the big screen in 2027.”

title: Rolf De Heer To Head Competition Jury At Tokyo Film Festival; ‘The Survival Of Kindness’ To Play In Australia Spotlight
summary: Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) has announced that Australian director Rolf de Heer will serve as president of the International Competition jury at this year’s edition of the festival. De Heer’s 2022 film The Survival Of Kindness, which was selected for competition at the Berlinale, will screen in Tokyo as part of an Australia Spotlight, […]
content:
Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) has announced that Australian director Rolf de Heer will serve as president of the International Competition jury at this year’s edition of the festival.

De Heer’s 2022 film The Survival Of Kindness, which was selected for competition at the Berlinale, will screen in Tokyo as part of an Australia Spotlight, a special showcase of Australian cinema presented in cooperation with the Australian Embassy in Japan.

Based in Tasmania, de Heer has a career spanning more than 40 years and widespread international acclaim, starting with Bad Boy Bubby (1993), which won the Special Jury Prize and FIPRESCI Prize at Venice. Other early career highlights include Dingo (1991) with Colin Friels and jazz legend Miles Davis; The Quiet Room (1996) and Dance Me To My Song (1998), both selected for Competition at Cannes.

In total, four of his films have screened in Official Selection at Cannes Film Festival, including Ten Canoes (2006), which won the Special Jury Prize in Un Certain Regard.

Watch on Deadline

Mid-career highlights also include The Tracker (2002), which also played in Venice competition and marked de Heer’s first collaboration with Australian Indigenous actor David Gulpilil; Alexandra’s Project (2003), which won best actress at San Sebastian for Helen Buday’s performance; The King Is Dead! (2012); and Charlie’s Country (2013), which won Gulpilil a Best Actor award at Cannes.

De Heer said: “For any of us attending the Tokyo International Film Festival, it is a privilege. For me, as a filmmaker, it is even more so. The more films I manage to make, the fewer films I manage to see, especially on the big screen.

“But as a part of this jury, I have the duty, the obligation, to see at least 15 films and talk about them with other filmmakers! And not just any old 15 films, but the 15 films in Competition, drawn from films made all over the world by all sorts of extraordinary filmmakers! And to do this in a city that plays host to one of the most formidable film cultures in the world! Can life ever get much better than this?”

Tokyo Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu said: “We are delighted to welcome Rolf de Heer as President of the International Competition jury at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival. With his distinctive perspective and unwavering commitment to filmmaking, de Heer has spent decades opening up new possibilities in cinema. We look forward to the fresh dialogue and discoveries that his wealth of experience and deep insight will bring to this year’s Competition and its diverse selection of films.”

Tokyo International Film Festival will take place October 26 to November 4, with the TIFFCOM contents market running October 28-30.

title: Barry Diller Drops Bid To Acquire Full Control Of MGM Resorts
summary: People Inc. Chairman Barry Diller has withdrawn a proposal to acquire full ownership of MGM Resorts. The media company will retain its 27% stake in the casino operator, he said in a statement Wednesday, though it remains “open and interested” in potential strategic alternatives to the original transaction. “There are lots of ingredients that go […]
content:
People Inc. Chairman Barry Diller has withdrawn a proposal to acquire full ownership of MGM Resorts.

The media company will retain its 27% stake in the casino operator, he said in a statement Wednesday, though it remains “open and interested” in potential strategic alternatives to the original transaction.

“There are lots of ingredients that go into a proposal of this kind on its way to completion,” Diller said. “We didn’t feel the mix was coming together in the way we had hoped and have decided not to pursue taking the company private at this time. What is undimmed is our belief in the future of MGM Resorts.”

As a minority investor, he added, People has “total confidence in both the management and the company’s prospects.”

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Peter Bart: Barry Diller’s New Memoir Might Be The True Final Reckoning

Diller announced the bid in June, writing in a letter to the MGM Resorts board of directors that its shares were undervalued. Acquiring full ownership represented “a compelling opportunity to support MGM’s next phase of growth and help unlock its full value,” Diller said at the time.

Diller, who had significant tours of duty in Hollywood at Paramount and Fox before entering the digital media business, made an offer to buy Paramount before Skydance ultimately acquired it in 2025. He has indicated a willingness to buy CNN, which Paramount soon will control, though the network is not leaving the portfolio as of now.

People Inc. became the corporate name of what had been IAC (InterActive Corp.) earlier this year. IAC had acquired People magazine as part of a larger deal for Meredith, its corporate parent, which had bought the title when Time Warner was selling off its publishing business.

title: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
summary: A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount’s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference. The video call, which has […]
content:
A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference.

The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood. According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday.

The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures.

Watch on Deadline

“It feels like a scramble,” one source said.

To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it.

“It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.”

Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed.

Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told.

The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers).

But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that.

“We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery.

Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt.

On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove-like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule.

The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18.

At Paramount, the latter epic would fall into the arms of global marketing and distribution guru (and former WB senior ranking theatrical suit) Josh Goldstine, who led the Dune franchise across two movies to a $1.12B global gross and eight Oscars.

We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution.

“There could be more fear on the Paramount side,” says one source in the know when it comes to marketing. How’s that? Goldstine will be back together with the team he built at Warners, meaning Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford.

There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff.

Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching.

The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership.

“Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.”

And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal.

What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.”

Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.”

For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground.

Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros.

Beams one optimistic Warner exec, “The new merger gives us the all the financial resources to compete on a level with the big streamers.”

title: As YouTube Remains Streaming’s Alpha Dog, It’s Adding Even More Unlikely New TV Tricks
summary: It’s been clear for a while that YouTube’s biggest screen in terms of viewing is the TV – but don’t expect the tech giant to just sit back on the couch. On the contrary, it is embracing the idea of adding more and more counter-intuitive features to the living room experience. At its annual Made […]
content:
It’s been clear for a while that YouTube‘s biggest screen in terms of viewing is the TV – but don’t expect the tech giant to just sit back on the couch. On the contrary, it is embracing the idea of adding more and more counter-intuitive features to the living room experience.

At its annual Made on YouTube event Wednesday, the company unveiled nearly three dozen new features for creators, viewers and brands, the latest of what CEO Neal Mohan said were 3,000 new product updates in 2026 to date. Viewers on TVs can now post comments; view “posts” (still images and texts posted to channels by creators); and watch series on YouTube Shorts.

These interactive elements are a key reason why YouTube has topped the Nielsen charts for three years straight with, as of July, 14.2% of all viewing via a TV in the U.S., executives say. (Of course, being available for free doesn’t hurt either.)

Watch on Deadline

“Consumption is moving away from being passive, and people want to be engaged,” Kurt Wilms, senior director of product management, YouTube on TV, told reporters after the New York event.

Asked to elaborate, he clarified, “I wouldn’t call it passive. I would call it, like, lean back. I’m watching it. Something maybe happens in the show. And then I’m like, ‘Oh, well, I want to read the comments, or I want to leave a comment myself, or, wait, what did she just talk about a different video? I wanna go to her channel and see.’ So now, instantly I become a leaned-in viewer. And so I think it flows, ebbs and flows between two. We don’t think of them as a hard line.”

Though its presence on landscape televisions seems counterintuitive, Shorts has been a runaway hit in the living room, with viewers watching more than 2 billion hours of its programming on TVs each month.

Even inside the company, the reaction to the notion of adapting features from the mobile and web experience is often, “Is this meant for the TV?” Wilms said. “But we’re hearing viewers ask for it and creators ask for it.”

The rollout of expanded capabilities is rooted in a mission to preserve the DNA of the first iteration of the site, which launched in 2005. (The first comment posted on “Me at the Zoo,” the first video ever uploaded, the company breezily noted on Wednesday, was a succinct “Lol.”)

“We didn’t want it to feel broken,” Wilms said of the app when it is viewed on a TV.

Although Shorts seems like a left-field stunner, in retrospect its success made perfect sense. “The first thing everyone was telling me about Shorts on the TV is there was no good way to watch this content with friends or family,” Wilms said. “The TV unlocked communal viewing for Shorts in a way that just wasn’t possible before.”

The strategy of “bringing all these content formats that you might not think would resonate with viewers on the TV” has been a particular focus over the past two years, Wilms said, citing gaming videos, podcasts and shorts. “We saw it again actually around the same time with video comments,” he recalled. Viewers told the company, “‘I want to read the comments on TV,’ and we were thinking, ‘Really?! You want to read the comments on the TV?!'”

While YouTube has not put numbers to it, Wilms estimated that the amount of viewers reading comments on TVs rivals the number doing so on the web. Similar to Shorts and comments, the Posts functionality resulted from consumer and partner research.

“It’s all born out of creator and viewer feedback,” he said. “And we’ve seen time and time again when we bring [features] to the big screen, they’re successful.”

Rather than bucketing viewers according to those who lean back and those who interact, Wilms says the company’s research shows a more blended experience.

“One of the things when we talk to viewers that we hear about a lot is, we call it modes – like, a viewer is in a mode,” Wilms said. “It might be, at night you want to use YouTube on your television as your home stereo and use it for music. Another mode might be you’re with your family and your kids, and you want to use YouTube as a way to watch with them. And so another mode that we’ve heard about is, ‘Oh, I don’t know totally what I want to watch, but I want to sit down and kind of get some quick bites, and so I go into this Shorts mode.”

Enter microdramas, the booming sector that has spawned a host of startup studios along with optimism that the major component of the Asian entertainment ecosystem will gain similar adoption elsewhere.

Microdramas “have been incredibly successful on YouTube,” Wilms said. “There are more than 6.5 billion views of this content on YouTube already this year. On TV screens specifically, microdramas are growing 90% year over year.”

Execs see more upside ahead. “Microdramas in particular, they’re fast paced, they’re action packed, they’re quick, and so in the industry as a whole, I think viewers are resonating to this type of content, so I assume it’s gonna continue to grow,” Wilms added. Overall, we see a lot of success of bite-sized content that could be personalized to your taste. …. People are seeing it as a place to spend breaks in their day.”

title: Asia Video Content Spend to Hit $15 Billion in 2026 as Streaming and Local Film Draw Capital, Media Partners Asia Report Finds
summary: Spending on video content in seven major markets across Asia is expected to climb to $15.1 billion in 2026, according to Media Partners Asia’s “Asia Video Content Dynamics 2026” report. Streaming and local film account for nearly all new spending as television budgets shrink. The study covers India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and […]
content:
Spending on video content in seven major markets across Asia is expected to climb to $15.1 billion in 2026, according to Media Partners Asia‘s “Asia Video Content Dynamics 2026” report. Streaming and local film account for nearly all new spending as television budgets shrink.

The study covers India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. MPA puts 2025 spending across the seven markets at $14.8 billion and projects it will reach $15.4 billion by 2031.

Television still takes about 60% of the total, against 30% for online video and 10% for film. Korea, at $6.9 billion, and India, at $5 billion, together made up roughly 80% of 2025 investment.

Popular on Variety

“The viewership data shows demand is intact. Premium VOD engagement continues to grow across India, Korea and Southeast Asia, streaming now leads content investment in India, and local stories are winning at the box office from Hanoi to Jakarta and Mumbai. This is a story of reallocation rather than retreat as capital moves toward streaming and local film, where both audiences and returns are growing,” said Myat Pan Phyu, an analyst at MPA.

The money picture is less rosy. The region’s media businesses have big audiences and plenty of creative talent, yet the report finds that this reach is not reliably turning into healthy profits. Many long-established companies trade well under their equity book value. In MPA’s view, the firms that build value will be the ones that spend capital wisely, trim costs and defend the content that genuinely sets them apart.

India hit a turning point last year. Online video claimed 46% of the country’s content investment in 2025, edging past TV at 42% and taking the lead for the first time. Indian viewers logged 420 billion hours of online video over the year. JioHotstar holds a 58% share of premium VOD viewing in the country and has more than 180 million paying subscribers.

In Korea, TVING ranks a clear second in the market behind Netflix. Indonesian platform Vidio, which leads its home market with more than 6 million paying subscribers, has been EBITDA-positive since the fourth quarter of 2025.

Sports rights are what set streamers apart, according to MPA. Cricket helped push JioHotstar’s connected-TV reach up 26% during the 2026 Indian Premier League cricket tournament, while exclusive KBO baseball coverage took TVING from 5.3 million to 6.5 million subscribers. Coupang Play has built the widest premium sports offering in Korea. Vidio spreads Indonesian football, the Champions League and the Premier League across its pricing tiers. In Vietnam, the FIFA World Cup lifted premium VOD viewing by 22% this year.

The report picks out local film as the clearest opportunity for growth in the region. In Vietnam, box office grew 20% to $213 million in 2025, with homegrown titles taking 69% of receipts. Indonesian box office rose 10.5% to $325 million, 60% of it from local films. India set a box office record of $1.41 billion. In Korea, a stronger domestic lineup is fueling a sizable theatrical rebound in 2026.

Television looks weaker. People are still watching, but the revenue keeps slipping. Thai TV advertising dropped 18% to $422 million in 2025, and MPA says several markets are carrying more broadcast capacity than their ad income can support.

Producers are feeling the squeeze too. Broadcasters and streamers have grown choosier about what they order, which hurts companies that live on production fees. Value is moving toward integrated studios and toward producers that own IP, have repeat buyers or earn money from several sources. Production in Korea costs more than anywhere else in Asia, and drama margins there have been compressed to between 5% and 10%. Southeast Asia is cheaper, but tighter commissioning is hitting it as well.

“Asia’s video industries are not short of audiences or creative capability. They are short of structures that convert both into sustainable returns. As the margin for error narrows, management quality will become decisive. Companies that rationalize legacy costs through restructuring and the adoption of new technologies such as AI, collaborate where independent investment no longer makes sense and protect the content that gives viewers a reason to stay will increasingly outperform, and the valuation gap between winners and losers will widen,” said Stephen Laslocky, vice president at MPA.

Of the seven markets, MPA sees India and Korea as furthest along the road to consolidation. India set the pace with a definitive transaction – the 2024 merger of Reliance’s Viacom18 and Disney’s Star India that created JioStar – and more M&A could follow. Korea is looking to the proposed TVING-Wavve combination to unlock value. Southeast Asia has lagged, though the firm sees clear scope for collaboration and consolidation in the Philippines, Thailand and Indonesia.

Separately, MPA estimates that reorganizing CJ ENM into four clearly defined businesses could support an equity valuation far above the company’s current market value.

title: Sean Gunn Says He’s ‘Too Old’ and ‘Retired’ From Playing Rocket Raccoon in ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’: It ‘Hurts After a While’
summary: Sean Gunn has proclaimed himself “retired” from doing the on-set motion capture for the fan-favorite “Guardians of the Galaxy” character Rocket Raccoon. The actor explained that he feels he’s aged out of standing in for the Marvel character due to the physical demands of contorting himself into the shape of the small animal on a […]
content:
Sean Gunn has proclaimed himself “retired” from doing the on-set motion capture for the fan-favorite “Guardians of the Galaxy” character Rocket Raccoon. The actor explained that he feels he’s aged out of standing in for the Marvel character due to the physical demands of contorting himself into the shape of the small animal on a recent episode of The Brandon Davis Show.

“Since I’ve turned 50 a couple of years ago, I am retired from playing Rocket,” he said. “Not that they’ve called. But if they did, I don’t think that I could do the motion reference anymore for Rocket. I think I’m too old.”

He continued: “Everyone thinks it’s my knees, but it’s really my feet and my ankles. I’m in a catcher’s crouch, and I’m pivoting a lot on my points of contact with the ground. I’m doing a lot of pivoting in my ankles and feet. And over the years, I think it had a little bit of an effect on my physiology.” He also noted that it “hurts after a while.”

Popular on Variety

While Bradley Cooper famously voiced the character, it was Gunn who performed the aforementioned on-set motion capture for the animated raccoon. Gunn did this for the character in all three of the “Guardians of the Galaxy” movies, the first of which premiered in 2014. The sequel, “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” followed in 2017 and “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3” premiered in 2023.

On-screen, Gunn also played the Marvel character Kraglin Obfonteri in “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” “Avengers: Endgame,” “Thor: Love and Thunder,” “The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special” and “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.”

title: ‘No One Achieves Anything Alone’: Inside Variety’s Power of Women Event With Jennifer Hudson, Sharon Stone, Pearlena Igbokwe and Melissa McCarthy
summary: Jennifer Hudson, Pearlena Igbokwe, Melissa McCarthy and Sharon Stone were the guests of honor at the starry Variety Power of Women presented by Lifetime event in Beverly Hills Wednesday night, during which the musician, executive and actresses were commended for both their outstanding accomplishments and their dedicated commitment to a number of key causes. The […]
content:
Jennifer Hudson, Pearlena Igbokwe, Melissa McCarthy and Sharon Stone were the guests of honor at the starry Variety Power of Women presented by Lifetime event in Beverly Hills Wednesday night, during which the musician, executive and actresses were commended for both their outstanding accomplishments and their dedicated commitment to a number of key causes.

The annual event, hosted by multi-hyphenate comedian Iliza Shlesinger, brought a long list of influential talents to a packed Beverly Hills Hotel for an evening centered on both the Power of Women honorees and the accomplished women profiled in the annual Women’s Impact Report, which highlights leaders in the entertainment industry. And while Hudson, Igbokwe, McCarthy and Stone all have much to brag about, each of the women used their time on stage to turn the focus to the charities they were supporting and highlight the many different ways the term “powerful” can be applied.

Following introductory remarks from Variety‘s co-president and publisher Dea Lawrence, co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh and co-editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton — plus a show-stopping opening performance of “I Will Always Love You” by Hudson — the first honoree of the night was Igbokwe, introduced by Queen Latifah. The chairman of NBCUniversal’s Television Studios, NBC Entertainment & Peacock Scripted, Igbokwe spent more than 35 years helping shape the medium of television across prestige cable, broadcast, studios and now streaming. She used her speech to support the nonprofit A Better Chance.

“A Better Chance not only introduced me to Kent Place but also supported me when I got there with test-taking workshops, mentoring, and sometimes emotional encouragement — resources I would not have had otherwise. This set me up for an Ivy League education, transforming the trajectory of my life and that of my entire family,” she said. “So yes, my origin story started with hard work, but someone had to give me an opportunity. No one achieves anything alone.”

After an introduction by Molly Sims, Paige DeSorbo took to the podium next to receive the Courage Award presented by the Purina Purple Leash Project, a charity that helps create pet-friendly shelters for survivors of domestic abuse. DeSorbo discussed opening up about her experience surviving an abusive relationship as a teenager, why she decided to speak about it on her podcast “Giggly Squad and how her cat, Daphne, helps her feel safe.

“Daphne has been there for the version of me that nobody else sees,” she said. “She just curls up on my chest and purrs and everything, for a second, feels right again. No context needed. No story to tell. Just presence. I think that’s the incredible thing about our pets. They don’t need us to explain what we’re going through. They just stay. They give us a sense of safety and remind us that we are loved, even when we don’t feel our strongest. And that’s why the Purple Leash Project means so much to me.”

“The Jennifer Hudson Show” was honored with the Variety Changemaker Award, presented by Waymo. Hudson, along with many of the show’s producers, accepted the award after an introduction by the company’s chief marketing officer, Suzanne Philion. Later in the evening, Hudson also took to the stage to spotlight the Jennifer Hudson Foundation and her show once more.

“Our mission was always to highlight and accentuate the positive, and that is what we strive to do at ‘The Jennifer Hudson Show’ each and every day,” Hudson said. “That brings me to power. Power is an interesting idea. I think we’ve been taught to shy away from embracing power. We are told to be strong, never told to be powerful. But power can be good, and in the right hands, power can change the world for the better. And what better hands than those of a woman?” She continued: “Power can open doors, create a seat at the table, build a platform, protect a neighbor and lift a voice. So I am honored to be in a room where we’re celebrating power, good power.”

Next, McCarthy’s former “Gilmore Girls” collaborator Lauren Graham welcomed her to the stage, and the “Bridesmaids” star used her time to shine the light on the Joyful Heart Foundation and two of the women in her life she considers powerful: Mariska Hargitay and Gloria Steinem. Steinem passed away earlier this month. “When I say powerful, I don’t mean tough or strong, though they certainly are. For me, the greatest display of power are those willing to roll up their sleeves and help bring change,” she said. “I am humbled to support the Joyful Heart Foundation, and I am honored to be a part of this room tonight. And I hope that we all can leave here inspired to roll up our sleeves and make a difference.”

An acoustic rendition of “Motivation” by Normani helped lead in Emmy Award-nominated actress, writer, producer and entrepreneur Issa Rae, who received the Variety Entertainment Entrepreneur of the Year Award, presented by U.S. Bank senior executive vice president Courtney Kelso.

“I can decide who I’m around for the most part, who I work with, who I champion, who I invest in, whose stories I help tell, who I platform, who I respond to,” said Rae. “I can use the power I do have to pour into my little community to make sure whatever success I’m lucky enough to have doesn’t stop with me. And even when I’m tired, pissed off, or deeply uninspired by what’s happening around me, I can honestly say that nothing can stop me from trying to figure out where I can be useful, because as discouraged as I may get, I’m never going to stop trying.”

Sharon Stone closed out the night, taking the stage following remarks from actor and podcaster Marc Maron. The Academy Award-nominated, Emmy and Golden Globe-winning actress and producer reflected on her career and how she’s become the on- and off-screen icon she is today.

“You have to claw your way to the top. So, for those of us who got here, it’s the top of our heads that broke that glass ceiling that you’re all getting the benefits of,” she said. “And I have gone the distance. I have gone the distance from being a sex symbol … and I did it by keeping both of these tired feet that hurt from wearing four-inch heels on poured concrete floors. I kept them firmly planted on terra firma because there is no gray in the red, white and blue. So the power that I feel in the power of women, I get because I am standing in the middle of you, and I do not stand alone when I stand here.”

title: Issa Rae Is ‘Never Going to Stop’ Using Her Power for Good, Even as Mergers and AI Disrupt Hollywood: ‘This Is All Men’s Fault’
summary: Issa Rae received the Entertainment Entrepreneur of the Year Award at Variety’s L.A. Power of Women event on Wednesday in Beverly Hills. The award was presented by U.S. Bank senior executive vice president Courtney Kelso and honored the Emmy-nominated actress, writer, producer and entrepreneur. Rae created, executive produced and starred in HBO’s “Insecure,” which ended […]
content:
Issa Rae received the Entertainment Entrepreneur of the Year Award at Variety’s L.A. Power of Women event on Wednesday in Beverly Hills. The award was presented by U.S. Bank senior executive vice president Courtney Kelso and honored the Emmy-nominated actress, writer, producer and entrepreneur.

Rae created, executive produced and starred in HBO’s “Insecure,” which ended its run in 2021. Kelso welcomed Rae to the stage, saying the comedian has “put her own community here in L.A. front and center across her incredible ventures.”

Rae began her acceptance speech by joking that she hadn’t written anything inspirational, as she’d been distracted by everything happening across the nation, “the industry [eating] itself,” climate disasters, politics and the rise of AI. But she did identify one force that continues to create instability: “This is all men’s fault. Rich, white men to be specific” she joked, drawing laughter from the audience.

“It is hard to feel like a powerful woman when men keep fucking everything up,” she said.

She then took a serious tone when detailing the struggles she’s faced, sharing that “it’s hard to feel inspired when you feel helpless and useless.”

As a writer, Rae said she experiences those feelings often, but she has also learned that she can direct her energy toward the things she knows she can control.

“I can decide who I’m around, who I work with, who I champion, who I invest in, whose stories I tell, who I platform, who I respond to,” she said. “I can use the power I do have to pour into my little community to make sure whatever success I’m lucky enough to have doesn’t stop with me.”

She shared that “even when I’m tired, pissed off or deeply uninspired by what’s happening around me, I can honestly say that nothing can stop me from trying to figure out where I can be useful. Because as discouraged as I may get, I’m never going to stop trying.”

Rae concluded her speech by saying, “Maybe that’s all any of us can do — is just figure out where we have some power and use it the fuck for good, please. So that’s what I’m going to do. I hope you guys do too.”

Rae’s on-screen credits include Greta Gerwig’s “Barbie,” Cord Jefferson’s “American Fiction,” the “Black Mirror” episode “Hotel Reverie” and “A Black Lady Sketch Show,” which she also executive produced. She also voices Jessica Drew in Sony Pictures’ “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” and Angela in the HBO Max series “Young Love.” As a producer, Rae worked on the 2023 film “Gray Matter” and executive produced the HBO Max series “Rap Sh!t.” She also produced “One of Them Days,” starring Keke Palmer and SZA. She is set to write and executive produce a new HBO comedy pilot, which is an untitled “male friendship show.”

title: Isabel Sandoval, Tricia Tuttle, ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Producer Anup Poudel Join QueerFrames Mentor Lineup as Lab Unveils New Cohort, Southeast Asia Expansion (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: QueerFrames Screenwriting Lab, a training initiative for emerging queer, trans and nonbinary filmmakers, is expanding into Southeast Asia for its fourth annual edition, bringing together storytellers from India, the Philippines, Vietnam, Singapore, Indonesia and the diaspora. The 2026 cohort features eight fiction feature projects, with queerness woven into the core of each story. The selected […]
content:
QueerFrames Screenwriting Lab, a training initiative for emerging queer, trans and nonbinary filmmakers, is expanding into Southeast Asia for its fourth annual edition, bringing together storytellers from India, the Philippines, Vietnam, Singapore, Indonesia and the diaspora.

The 2026 cohort features eight fiction feature projects, with queerness woven into the core of each story. The selected filmmakers are Alec Berame and Joshua Caesar Medroso from the Philippines, Saurav Mahind and Sanju Kadu from India, Minh-Anh Vo Dinh from Vietnam and Canada, Megan Teo from Singapore, Kurnia Alexander from Indonesia and Rachel Leyco from the U.S. Their scripts take on identity, intimacy, masculinity, belonging and personal freedom through love stories, thrillers, horror and dramedies that blend genres.

Launched in 2023, QueerFrames has worked with 22 queer and trans filmmakers from the region since its founding. The Lab pairs craft-focused screenwriting development with mentorship from filmmakers, producers, programmers and industry leaders, taking participants from an early draft to a project that is ready for the market.

Popular on Variety

The 2026 edition will open with an in-person screenwriting retreat in Hua Hin, Thailand, running Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, followed by an Industry Day in Bangkok on Oct. 3 held in partnership with the French Embassy in Thailand, Alliance Française Bangkok and the French Regional Audiovisual Cooperation. The Lab will then continue with virtual sessions through March 2027.

Netflix and the French Institute in India are backing the 2026 edition, with additional support from Purin Film Fund in Thailand and Momo Film Co in Singapore.

This year’s mentors include Anup Poudel, who produced Nepal’s Oscar contender “Elephants in the Fog,” winner of the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at Cannes; Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle, returning to the Lab; Filipino filmmaker and actor Isabel Sandoval; “A Useful Ghost” director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke; Indian screenwriter Gazal Dhaliwal; and Momo Film Co chief Tan Si En. Writer-directors Vishnu Sinha, adjunct faculty at Columbia University, and Paromita Dhar return as Lab instructors.

“With this year’s expansion into Southeast Asia, QueerFrames is bringing together a wider community of storytellers who are pushing beyond familiar narratives and exploring queer lives across cultures, genres and lived experiences,” said Rafiul Alom Rahman, director of QueerFrames Screenwriting Lab. “Our hope is to build not just stronger projects, but lasting connections and infrastructure that enable these filmmakers to thrive.”

“Some of the most powerful stories come from places and experiences that have been left out of the frame,” said Poudel. “QueerFrames offers writers the space to develop those stories with courage, specificity and creative freedom.”

Mathieu Béjot, cultural attaché for film, audiovisual and digital content at the French Institute in India, pointed to the partnership’s longevity. “Our longstanding partnership with QueerFrames reflects that commitment, and we are delighted to continue supporting a new generation of queer filmmakers from South and Southeast Asia as they develop their work and connect with the wider international film ecosystem,” Béjot said.

Among the 2026 projects: Berame’s “Hisap Sebatang Before Ciao! (Each/Other)” follows a Filipino diplomat navigating a geopolitical crisis while hiding a quiet romance with his counterpart from Malaysia. Vo Dinh’s “Anglerfish” centers on two men whose seaside getaway is upended by a stranger’s arrival and a string of grisly deaths. Teo’s “Pack” follows a closeted professional boxer who turns to underground pit-fighting to transition. Leyco’s “Winning” is a spoken-word dramedy about a broke queer artist who wins the lottery and slowly becomes the gambling-addicted father she despises.

Mahind’s “Starvation” follows Namya, a gay drifter who pickpockets closeted men until one of his marks comes back looking for closeness instead of revenge. Kadu’s “Under Such a Sky” follows a closeted gay man who breaks his pattern of chasing straight men through a bond with four kids from his swimming class. Medroso’s “Lasto (Last Two)” follows a debt-ridden gay uncle and his niece tracking down the thief who robbed them of their winnings from a “lasto” game. Alexander’s “Jatuh Cinta yang Lurus (A Straight Way to Love)” follows a gay filmmaker who returns to the town that once cast him out, only to find that reconnecting with the friend who was also his first love threatens the life he rebuilt after leaving.

title: Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked By Judge, Who Orders CNN, Politico & MS NOW Credentials Restored
summary: The Trump administration must restore press credentials for staffers at CNN, Politico and MS NOW, a federal judge ruled early Thursday morning, delivering a rebuke to the president’s efforts to ban the outlets from the White House grounds. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, granted a temporary restraining order to the media outlets, […]
content:
The Trump administration must restore press credentials for staffers at CNN, Politico and MS NOW, a federal judge ruled early Thursday morning, delivering a rebuke to the president’s efforts to ban the outlets from the White House grounds.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, granted a temporary restraining order to the media outlets, after they sued Trump and other top administration officials, claiming violations of the First and Fifth amendments. The temporary order is set for a duration of 14 days. Generally, such orders are given to allow the court to consider a case more thoroughly.

Trump has previously sought to revoke the credentials of individual reporters, but his latest ban was a sweeping effort to punish the media for negative reporting on him. Although the government later claimed national security concerns, attorneys for the outlets said that was a post-ban rationalization, violating their due process rights.

Watch on Deadline

Earlier today, a collection of more than four dozen media groups and news outlets urged the judge to rule to end Trump’s ban. They included Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents’ Association and 49 other media organizations. Among those signing on to the brief were the Associated Press, Reuters, NPR, the National Press Club, CBS, NBC, ABC, Fox News and the Dow Jones Co.

After CNN was restricted from the network TV pool rotation at the White House earlier this week, four other networks — ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and Fox News — said that they would suspend their participation in an act of solidarity.

title: Meta Introduces New VR Glasses With Access To Content From YouTube, Prime Video, HBO Max, Disney+ & More
summary: Meta today announced a new generation of VR glasses that it promised will “define a new era for virtual reality,” creating an all-in-one productivity and media device. Meta VR Glasses will deliver cinema, TV and sports content in one device with access to Prime Video, YouTube, Peacock, HBO Max, and Paramount+, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, […]
content:
today announced a new generation of VR glasses that it promised will “define a new era for virtual reality,” creating an all-in-one productivity and media device.

Meta VR Glasses will deliver cinema, TV and sports content in one device with access to Prime Video, YouTube, Peacock, HBO Max, and Paramount+, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, Tubi, the NBA, MLB, ESPN, MLB, NBC Sports, TNT Sports and UFC, some with virtual and 3D enhancements. The frames are set to be released in Spring 2027 at a price point of $1300.

Like Apple’s Vision Pro — to which they bear more than a passing resemblance — you can watch movies, TV and sports on “theater-sized” virtual screens, video chat with your friends or work in an app environment similar to that on your phone.

Meta VR Glasses will be operated with hand gestures or by moving your eyes to icons on the screen.

Watch on Deadline

Thankfully, Meta VR Glasses are five times lighter than their predecessor, the clunky Meta Quest 3. That’s primarily because the device is split in two: the frames and a pocket-sized device called a “puck.” The VR Glasses handle sensors and display. The puck, connected by an optical tether, handles compute, battery and storage and can be slipped into (or clipped onto) a pocket or bag.

The device’s TV app promises “the best media lineup of any VR device,” plus offerings from the 3D media catalogs of Peacock, HBO Max and Paramount+.

Even before the glasses launch, through a partnership with Disney+, subscribers to that service will be able to stream movies like The Avengers, Black Panther and more in 3D on Meta Quest headsets. There will also be themed immersive viewing environments from Disney franchises like Tatooine and the Avengers Tower.

Hundreds of movies will be available to rent or buy later this year on Meta Quest, with thousands of titles available by Meta VR Glasses’ launch next spring. Those will eventually include 3D films from Lionsgate and “first time in 3D” blockbusters from James Cameron and Lightstorm Vision.

Sports apps, like NBA, MLB and ESPN will be available on the device, with ESPN offering “Immersive Sports,” billed as “a front-row seat, 8K streaming, and 180-degree views.” Immersive Sports will launch with college football this year on Meta Quest, with more sports to come in 2027. Meta VR Glasses launch will being over 100 immersive live sports events each year from MLB, NBC Sports, TNT Sports and UFC.

title: Ryan Murphy “Just Finished” Writing ‘Glee’ Reboot Script, Says Original Cast Is “Enthusiastic”
summary: More than a decade later, Ryan Murphy likely has Journey stuck in his head again as he prepares for a McKinley High reunion. The 2x Golden Globe winner revealed on Wednesday that he “just finished” a Glee reboot script, noting that most of the cast is “very enthusiastic” about the potential reunion for the Fox […]
content:
More than a decade later, Ryan Murphy likely has Journey stuck in his head again as he prepares for a McKinley High reunion.

The 2x Golden Globe winner revealed on Wednesday that he “just finished” a Glee reboot script, noting that most of the cast is “very enthusiastic” about the potential reunion for the Fox musical comedy series that ran for six seasons from 2009 to 2015.

“Well, funny you ask, cause I just finished the script an hour ago,” he told Entertainment Tonight. “So, we have a script. Brad [Falchuk], Ian [Brennan] and I, who wrote all the first two seasons, have written something. I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members. It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Murphy added, “Nobody’s read it, so I don’t know, we’ll see. I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, cause we were very close when we were making it.”

Watch on Deadline

According to sources, the project, from 20th Television, has not been set up at a platform yet.

The update comes just two months after Murphy teased a potential Glee return. “That show is interesting because it’s come back around. So many young people now watch it. And I’m like, ‘Maybe we should revisit that show,'” he told People.

Don't stop believin' in a 'Glee' reboot!



Ryan Murphy confirms he wrote a new script, and the original cast is "enthusiastic" about returning. pic.twitter.com/SVk9ng2JG4 — Entertainment Tonight (@etnow) September 24, 2026

Created by Murphy, Falchuk and Brennan, Glee followed high school show choir coach Will Schuester (Matthew Morrison) and his team of talented outsiders as they worked toward their goal of becoming national champions while dealing with the drama of high school by performing covers of hit songs.

title: In ‘Tenzing,’ Jennifer Peedom Ensures the Iconic Himalayan Mountaineer Is Finally ‘the Protagonist of His Own Life’
summary: Tenzing Norgay was the first person to summit Mount Everest alongside Edmund Hillary. The Apple Original film “Tenzing,” opening Zurich Film Festival, reframes the story of that first ascent. “It’s often reduced to a familiar shorthand: Hillary conquered Everest, assisted by a Sherpa. But Tenzing had more experience on Everest than anyone else on that […]
content:
Tenzing Norgay was the first person to summit Mount Everest alongside Edmund Hillary. The Apple Original film “Tenzing,” opening Zurich Film Festival, reframes the story of that first ascent.

“It’s often reduced to a familiar shorthand: Hillary conquered Everest, assisted by a Sherpa. But Tenzing had more experience on Everest than anyone else on that 1953 expedition. He wasn’t just helping another man achieve his dream. He had his own dream,” says director Jennifer Peedom.

“The ambition was to restore that subjectivity and allow him to be the protagonist of his own life, not a supporting character in someone else’s heroic story. Importantly, this doesn’t require diminishing Hillary. I think their partnership becomes much more interesting when you understand the stature of both men and what each brought to that rope.”

Popular on Variety

Genden Phuntsok stars, joined by Tom Hiddleston as Hillary, Thinley Lhamo, Caitríona Balfe and Willem Dafoe, who plays Colonel John Hunt.

“I needed someone with tremendous emotional depth, physical strength, warmth and humor, but also a kind of quiet authority. Tenzing is not a character who announces everything he’s feeling, so I needed an actor who could carry a lot internally,” recalls Peedom, adding that Phuntsok was “completely fearless.”

“He has this extraordinary, contained force. Culturally, there were things he understood because he grew up on the Tibetan Plateau, at altitude, in a landscape and culture with real connections to Tenzing’s own world.”

She adds: “It was wonderful to see actors with very different histories and methods – Genden, Tom and Willem – meet each other as equals inside the world of the film.”

Peedom was struck by Tenzing’s journey – even before Everest.

“We tend to focus on the final achievement, but the obstacles he had to overcome just to get to the starting line were immense,” she notes.

He first tried to join an exhibition in 1933 and finally got his first opportunity in 1935, initially as a porter. Over the next two decades, he built his experience and reputation until, by 1953, he was one of the most experienced Everest mountaineers in the world.

“I found that incredibly moving in my research. He wasn’t a man who was given an opportunity and then proved himself on the mountain. He had to fight for the opportunity in the first place.”

Peedom is well aware that, for the longest time, the achievements of the Sherpas were completely ignored. She made a short “The Sherpas’ Burden” and feature doc “Sherpa.”

“In a sense, ‘Tenzing’ is another chapter in the same exploration. What happens when you move the person who has traditionally been at the edge of the frame into the center of the story?”
