title: ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Magic Of Returning To ‘Big Bang’ Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about the Season 1 finale “Spoiler: Filmed In Front Of a Live Studio Audience” of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe. The Big Bang Theory single-camera spinoff Stuart Fails To Save the Universe went full-circle in the Season 1 finale by turning multi-camera and returning to the […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about the Season 1 finale “Spoiler: Filmed In Front Of a Live Studio Audience” of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe.

The Big Bang Theory single-camera spinoff Stuart Fails To Save the Universe went full-circle in the Season 1 finale by turning multi-camera and returning to the stage where the original series was filmed.

After getting trapped in a comic book in the penultimate episode, the multiverse-hopping quartet of Stuart (Kevin Sussman), Bert (Brian Posehn), Denise (Lauren Lapkus) and Kripke (John Ross Bowie) found themself in a multi-camera sitcom in the finale, complete with a laugh track.

And, in the trippiest moment in a season chockfull of meta references, in the finale, Stuart, Denise, Bert and Kripke witnessed a curtain call for a taping of the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe sitcom where they see identical versions of themselves played by the real-life stars of the HBO Max series: Sussman, Posehn, Lapkus and Bowie.

Watch on Deadline

Still shocked, the four walked out of the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe soundstage, which is revealed to be Stage 25 on the Warner Bros. lot that housed Big Bang. (The stage is currently home to CBS spinoff Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, which co-creator Lorre and Prady executive produce.)

“So now what?,” Denise asked in the final seconds of the episode.

“I don’t know but I’ve got to believe that the answer is out there somewhere,” Stuart said in a X-Files-esque “The truth is out there” manner, prompting Bert to follow up with “In Burbank?” and Kevin to reply, “or Studio City?,” a reference to the city Warner Bros. is based in and the neighboring area.

The finale’s back-and-forth shift between single- and multi-camera involved Stuart Fails To Save the Universe building a multi-camera version of Stuart’s comic book like the one used in Big Bang on the Universal lot where the Warner Bros. TV-produced Big Bang spinoff films its interiors and some exteriors. (The final exterior scene was filmed outside of the real Stage 25 on the Warners lot.)

The episode paid homage to the mothership series in other ways too, including incorporating Big Bang‘s signature animated atom transition, complete with the whooshing sound, using its audience warm-up Mark Sweet, who had worked with Lorre since his 1997 ABC comedy Dharma & Greg, and having the characters sit around a coffee table eating takeouts.

In an interview with Deadline, the Stuart Fails creators/executive producers Zak Penn, who comes from genre background, and sitcom veterans Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady, break down how they pulled off the single-camera/multi-camera transitions, how it was filming outside Stage 25, the various Big Bang easter eggs and that ending (where exactly is the answer?).

They also address the several digs at CBS, broadcast television and multi-camera sitcoms, the black consciousness adversary introduced in the finale and its implied alliance with Kyle (Ryan Cartwright). The trio gives some clues about the recently picked up Season 2, which already is being written, including when it would premiere.

How ‘Stuart’ Brought ‘Big Bang’ (& Its Laugh) Back

DEADLINE: Where did the idea to have our heroes be in a multi-camera sitcom come about? Did you want to pay homage to Big Bang?

PENN: Yeah, that was definitely part of it. These guys [Lorre and Prady] have a lot to say about it, so it was pretty fertile ground. I don’t think we said at the beginning of the season, we must comment on the sitcom, that wasn’t a goal.

LORRE: If our characters on their adventure, on their journey, could be trapped into a comic book, they could certainly be trapped into a sitcom. I mean, we’ve gone past any boundaries of rationale, and this is a spectacularly cool thing to do, let’s do it. Can we explain it? We’re gonna try, we’re certainly going to try.

DEADLINE: You used both single-camera and multi-camera versions of the comic book set in the episode. For the multi-cam one that you had to build, did you use any pieces of the original Big Bang set?

PRADY: We didn’t use the original sets, but you’re right, we had to build. The only way to do this, because a multi-cam set looks different than a single-cam set, is we had to build the set two times. We had our single-cam comic book store that we’ve been using all season with four walls and a ceiling, and on the next stage over at Universal, they built the multi-cam version of that set and the multi-cam version of the stockroom.

But they also had to build the interior of a multi-cam soundstage, they had to build audience risers, the sound booth and the lighting booth that sits behind the audience, the camera alley, all of those features of multi-cam stage, they had to build. Our amazing production team actually went over to Georgie and Mandy, which was in production at the time, so that they could copy it and and get it right. And it was also a change for the director of photography.

The camera moves in multi-cam are completely different, the cameras go onto dollies, you have dolly moves that don’t exist in single-cam, and all of that had to be duplicated. So it was a pretty, pretty complicated task.

DEADLINE: How many scenes did you have to film twice in both formats? There were scenes that switched between single- and multi-cam.

PENN: Probably one third, two thirds, maybe more single-cam. Every time you see that, we had to do it twice, we had to shoot it on both stages, but there wasn’t a live studio audience there for that part of it. The live studio audience was only there when we needed to see the live studio audience.

LORRE: For the curtain call.

PENN: Because it would have been so boring to watch these little snippets of scenes, it just wouldn’t have made sense to anyone.

DEADLINE: Bert makes a comment on the show that the laugh is fake. You just said that the live studio audience was not used for the actual taping of the scenes beyond the curtain call, so the spoiler in the episode’s title is not accurate.

PRADY: It’s pretty perverse. One of the things that we battled forever on Big Bang Theory was people saying that this was a laugh track when it was a live studio audience. So here, in fact, the laughter that you’re hearing during the scene, the laugh that Kripke is hearing, those are old laughs from a The Big Bang Theory audience eight or nine years ago. Yes, all of those ironies.

(L-R): Ryan Cartwright, Brian Posehn, Kevin Sussman, Lauren Lapkus & John Ross Bowie in ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ S1 finale HBO Max

Dinging CBS As “Old TV Thing”, Sitcoms As “Void”

DEADLINE: Speaking of ironies, the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe sitcom within the series is promoted as “Coming to CBS this fall.” Is this just a line of dialogue, or is there some truth here? Can you license this show to CBS, home of Big Bang and all other spinoffs, for a linear run?

LORRE: That’s a question you’d have to ask HBO. I wouldn’t think so. It was just an opportunity to make a cheap joke about the end of network television.

DEADLINE: Yes, the punchline to that was Kyle asking “What is CBS?”, and Kripke explaining it as an “old TV thing,” a dig at broadcast and CBS. Did you write that, Chuck? They’re still employing you.

LORRE: I want to bite the hand that feeds me, Elvis Costello.

DEADLINE: There was another shot, about a meaningless void and sitcoms being the same thing. Is this how you all feel about multi-cam comedies these days?

LORRE: Not at all. No, it was a joke, Nellie. It was an opportunity to try and make the audience laugh.

PRADY: It’s certainly what Kripke thinks.

LORRE: It might be what Kripke thinks of situation comedies, but the history of this genre is just rich with genius, going back to Lucy and Norman Lear and Cheers and Friends and Frasier. It’s ridiculous to try and put down a genre that has done such great work over decades.

PRADY: We’re in awe of the genre.

LORRE: It’s much harder to do this than it is to shoot a little movie. It’s much harder to make 200 people laugh, even if they’re related to you.

DEADLINE: Chuck, any plans to do another multi-cam sitcom? I saw CBS Entertainment President Amy Reisenbach recently, and she said that the door is wide open for you.

LORRE: That’s very sweet of her. I love that woman. I’ve been doing this an awful long time, and Amy is just terrific. She’s been a really big supporter of Georgie and Mandy out of the gate, she’s been nothing but helpful and supportive of us trying to put on a show.

DEADLINE: But no current plans for you to do a new sitcom?

LORRE: No. My current plans are to take a nap right after we’re done talking.

(L-R): Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie in ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ S1 finale

Behind The Curtain Call

DEADLINE: The level of meta play in the finale — I don’t know if mushrooms or something else was involved in coming up with the sitcom idea, but the idea to have…

LORRE: It’s not drugs, it is called imagination. It’s something that will go away shortly with the advent of AI sitcoms. But, for the time being, it’s making sh*t up is what’s happening.

DEADLINE: But the idea to have the characters looking at actors carrying their real names playing the same characters; talk about how this whole thing made sense.

PENN: This is a place that we hadn’t gone, and going there seemed kind of scary, like, how are we going to make this work? And then, how are we going to write our way out of it? I think that was the approach the whole season is what something we could do that would be funny, but also, let’s not just do oh, and now they go to a universe where everybody’s a bird or whatever, like trying to come up with something to top what we had done, and this seemed like the place to go.

DEADLINE: Did Brian pay extra because everyone got a straightforward intro when Mark Sweet brought out the cast, he’s the only one who got “hilariously funny”?

PRADY: So the cast is allowed to bribe us, and we have a whole set.

PENN: Yeah, Brian paid us, you’re right. Brian gave us $1,500, and the rest of the cast gave us like 100 bucks, or someone gave us wine. We couldn’t split it. That was Mark Sweet, right? Whatever he chose to say.

PRADY: We were writing the kinds of things Mark Sweet said, which, when we sat down to write it, Chuck and I had heard it so many times, we channeled Mark Sweet, who’s playing himself as the audience warm-up guy, without even thinking about it.

LORRE: It was really easy. We’ve been listening to Mark since 1996, since Dharma & Greg. Thirty years, he’s been doing the same act.

PRADY: He’s got turns of phrase like, “you know him, you love him.” There’s a whole bunch of stuff that we just know. It’s years of listening to Mark and literally writing what we’ve heard him say.

(L-R): John Ross Bowie, Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman & Brian Posehn in ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ S1 finale HBO Max

The Magic Of Stage 25

DEADLINE: You filmed the final scene outside of WB’s Stage 25, where Big Bang was shot. How was that?

LORRE: That was a fun night.

DEADLINE: Was it really rainy, or did you make everything wet?

PENN: No, that’s a classic wet-town.

LORRE: I loved how we ended it. It’s a really delicate thing to bring a season to an end, or a series to an end, which we’ve certainly been through. It’s a real lot of hoping and wishing and praying that you get it right. I thought we brought the 10 episodes to a wonderful — hopefully, a reason to anticipate Season 2 as well as pleasurable to watch.

PENN: There was a bit of magic that night, watching the actors walk out through that door and onto the lot. It definitely felt there was something in the air.

LORRE: Yeah, something special happened that night.

PRADY: What was really strange that night, because we were shot at Stage 25, which was obviously the Big Bang stage, and walking in and using that stage, like using that as a place to stand and as a place to use the restroom and stuff. I found it very surreal, personally, to walk onto stage 25 with all that muscle memory of the years of Big Bang. 12 years there.

The Answer, The Adversary & ‘Young Leonard’

DEADLINE: Speaking of the ending, the final line “I’ve got to believe that the answer is out there.” Was that an X-Files reference?

LORRE: It does echo a little bit of The X-Files, doesn’t it? “The answer is out there, in Burbank, or maybe Studio City.” Yeah, it is something of a variation on that, I suppose, I hadn’t really thought about it.

PRADY: Not on purpose.

LORRE: Just a chance to say Burbank, because whenever you get a chance to say Burbank, you should.

DEADLINE: So where is the answer? Is it in Burbank, in Studio City or somewhere else?

LORRE: The answer is in Episode 1 of Season 2.

DEADLINE: The adversary, that whole swirly consciousness thing we saw at the end, do we know what it is? Don’t tell me the answer is going to be in 201.

PENN: The answer will be in 201.

DEADLINE: Is Ryan’s character working for the adversary? Because the thing said to him “I gave you one job.” Is Kyle a bad guy?

PENN: That version of those two characters work for the adversary.

PRADY: But not all versions.

PENN: But not the other ones you’ve seen that season. And then there’s another group led by, as far as you know, led by Stuart Prime. That’s the Stuart who shows up periodically to give them clues or hints to try to help them on their way.

DEADLINE: Would that be a major point in Season 2, who’s behind this?

PENN: Unquestionably, it’s going to be dealt with. We didn’t want to spend the whole season doing a bunch of mythology shows where we break down every single thing about what’s going on. We just wanted to set some stuff up.

LORRE: The truth is out there.

DEADLINE: The final shot includes banners for Two and a Half Women and Young Leonard. Chuck, were there spoofs of any of your other sitcoms’ titles that you considered and discarded?

LORRE: I don’t think so. I think, just the idea that we’re not quite in the universe where we started this series is the implication of those posters.

PRADY: It’s not quite our world.

LORRE: It’s close.

PRADY: But also in this world, Stuart is a multi-cam as opposed to in our world where it’s a single-cam. So we wanted to show that we were two or three degrees off of our universe.

DEADLINE: Two and a Half Women and Young Leonard are not bad ideas. Have Warner Bros. TV executive reached out about possibly doing them as shows?

LORRE: No, they haven’t come to us with anything like that, nor should they.

(L-R): Kevin Sussman & Lauren Lapkus in ‘Stuart Fails To Save the Universe’ S1 finale HBO Max

Season 2: Everything We Know

DEADLINE: You are in the writers’ room, right? Have you already mapped out Season 2?

LORRE: We started working last week on fleshing out Season 2, which hopefully, I think production begins in January or February. Like Season 1, we’re hoping to write all the episodes before we start, giving all the departments a lot of lead time to do the remarkable stuff they did in Season 1, which was truly benefited also by us being allowed to stay in Los Angeles and do this here with the best crews in the world.

PRADY: Yeah, it’s worth saying in every episode that we had the most amazing production team: sets, costumes, props, art direction, photography, lighting, sound. Every person on that stage was a gift, and everyone’s coming back.

LORRE: Yeah, everybody’s coming back. One of the little miracles that happened was we got a tax break from the state of California, which allowed us to stay here, stay in Los Angeles, which allowed us to have the best crews.

DEADLINE: Can you do the show on yearly cadence? There are a lot of special effects but can Season 2 premiere next summer or next fall? When will it be ready?

LORRE: We’re hoping certainly by next fall. We’re shooting to also participate in Comic-Con again next year. We did it this year, and it was great, it was a great way to launch the first season. When the show actually will debut on HBO, we don’t know. But hopefully, we’ll at least have an episode or two finished

to do Comic Con.

PENN: It’s not going to be like two years between seasons. It’s going to come out next year.

LORRE: Next year, yeah.

DEADLINE: Will Season 2 be similar in structure, the gang going to a new universe each episode or will you revisit some of the more popular worlds from the first season?

LORRE: We’ll try and put together 10 great episodes, and that’s the goal, to not run dry.

PRADY: You don’t have to follow a strict rule.

LORRE: You can return to a universe, there’s no rule against that. We’re not bound to say we couldn’t go back to some place they’ve already been if there was a great reason to do so.

PRADY: Right. We don’t sit here and say okay, well we have to do fan service, so more centaurs. But if more centaurs is really funny and has a story that can be told, then there’ll be more centaurs. But we make fun of our own mythology as we’re going, so I think there’s no real rules about what we’re going to do. We just try to do something that’s interesting.

DEADLINE: Will you also keep the idea of original Big Bang stars coming back? And I assume that the characters of Leonard, Howard, and Sheldon will stay off limits because if one of them shows up, he will fix the machine, and its show will be over.

LORRE: We’re hopeful that we can have some guest starring opportunities again in Season 2, but we haven’t figured that out quite yet. It was a lot of fun working with Mayim [Bialik] and Melissa [Rauch], Kunal [Nayyar], Kaley [Cuoco]. Having them do something that they never did on The Big Bang Theory, giving them an opportunity to stretch a little bit, that’s been built into this from the beginning, and I hope we can keep it going.

DEADLINE: Is there any chance of seeing different versions of Jim Parsons’ Sheldon, Johnny Galecki’s Leonard or Simon Helberg’s Howard?

PRADY: Tune in next season.

LORRE: There’s always a chance. We’re not going to limit ourselves as to cameos. If it’s possible and it can be done, great. That was a lot of fun for us, and I think it was a lot of fun for the folks who came and played with us for a couple of days.

DEADLINE: What’s the verdict on the custom opening credits? Have fans liked it, skipped it, didn’t care? Will you keep that in Season 2?

LORRE: I haven’t talked to fans recently but we enjoyed it, we thought it was funny.

PRADY: Our families liked it.

LORRE: We thought it was adding value to the show to have different credits, different opening titles every week and break some rules with what we’re used to seeing on all television.

PRADY: Maybe we’ll mix it up and, if we can come up with something even crazier, maybe we’ll do that. But don’t quote me on that.

DEADLINE: Length-wise, will you keep the episodes brisk and short again next season? [Half of the Season 1 episodes, including the finale, were 15-18 min each]

LORRE: As long as they need to be. And I’m keeping my fingers crossed that some of these shorter episodes we can get on Quibi.

PRADY: That has been the goal from the beginning.

LORRE: Because kids want to watch these shows on their phones while they’re at the supermarket. That was pitched to me.

DEADLINE: Quibi was ahead of its time, let’s just say that.

LORRE (sarcastically): Sure.

Lessons Learned

DEADLINE: What did you learn from the first season? Anything that you want to do differently in Season 2?

PENN: I learned a lot about sitcoms personally.

LORRE: Special effects take a long time.

PRADY: Be patient with special effects.

LORRE: Be very patient. I had panic attacks all through Season 1 that some of the special effects that we were asking for were not going to work. They all did but it took time. It’s an arduous process to build stuff that doesn’t exist.

PENN: That was the part I was comfortable with.

LORRE: He is very comfortable with it; Zak said, It’ll be fine, it’ll be fine. Just let them, It’s not finished yet. It was the thing you hear over and over and over again but it was really gratifying when that stuff works.

PENN: There wasn’t a lot that didn’t work, honestly. People might like some episodes more than others.

LORRE: That’s inevitable.

PENN: But normally, in doing a sci-fi show, you would find like, oh, we couldn’t pull this off, but that never happened to us. I mean, everything got pulled off. The crew, we say it over and over again, but they nailed it. There was never an episode where we walked in and said, Okay, the departments couldn’t really make this work. Let’s write around it. Never happened.

LORRE: It took quite a bit for us to figure out how to do the falling through the void sequence, but we got there. There was some trial and error because we didn’t know. It’s one thing to write on a laptop, the character Bert and and Kripke are falling through an endless void, it’s easy to write down. It’s much more difficult to make it a reality, and I think ultimately we got there.

DEADLINE: Uh-huh. Ask your actors, they told me they were traumatized filming that scene.

PRADY: Well, that was another benefit.

LORRE: Traumatized is part of show business.

PRADY: I do know that the actors, in all their interviews, kept saying there was a lot more running, they found a lot more running than they thought. Maybe more walking in Season 2.

title: Hannah Einbinder Speaks Out After UN Arrest, Calls For U.S. To “Bring An End” To Israel Attacks On Gaza
summary: Following her arrest Thursday at a demonstration outside the United Nations General Assembly, Hannah Einbinder doesn’t want her message to get lost in the headlines. The Emmy-winning Hacks star urged the U.S. government to “bring an end” to Israel’s attacks on Gaza after she was detained for protesting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s arrival at the […]
content:
Following her arrest Thursday at a demonstration outside the United Nations General Assembly, Hannah Einbinder doesn’t want her message to get lost in the headlines.

The Emmy-winning Hacks star urged the U.S. government to “bring an end” to Israel’s attacks on Gaza after she was detained for protesting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu‘s arrival at the UN building in New York.

“If the pictures of my friends and me getting arrested in protest of Netanyahu’s shameful visit to New York draw attention to anything, let it be to the devastating genocidal war Israel is waging against the people of Palestine and Southern Lebanon — to the settler attacks, the home demolitions, the bombing of people as they sleep; to the crimes that happen every SINGLE day but garner almost no international press coverage,” she began in a statement on her Instagram Story.

“The U.S. government has the power to bring an end to all of this killing, pillaging, and land theft, yet instead it chooses to welcome the butcher of Gaza with open arms. The fact that the orchestrator of all this bloodshed is roaming freely in our cities is an indictment of BOTH REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS who enable and protect architects of genocide like Netanyahu,” Einbinder continued. “Let us not mistake the spectacle for the story: genocide is the headline, and it is time for it to end.”

Watch on Deadline

Einbinder and Susan Sarandon were among as many as 100 anti-war protesters detained while blocking Bibi’s entrance to the UN, where he spoke with global leaders at the UN General Assembly.

Also present at the demonstration were Cynthia Nixon, Elliot Page, Chelsea Manning, Glennon Doyle, Sarah Sherman, Mary Beth Barone, Indya Moore and Caleb Hearon, protesting Netanyahu and the ongoing strikes on Gaza in the Israel-Hamas conflict.

“Free, free Palestine! Stop the genocide!” protesters chanted at the demonstration organized by the Jewish Voice for Peace, as well as, “Netanyahu, you can’t hide! We charge you with genocide!”

title: Robert Pattinson Thinks Matt Reeves’ ‘The Batman’ Would Be “Tough” To Fit Into James Gunn’s DCU
summary: With sequels in the Batman and Superman franchises on the horizon, a DC team-up between the Dark Knight and the Man of Steel doesn’t seem to be in the immediate future. Robert Pattinson admitted it “would be kind of tough” to make his version of Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves’ The Batman movies fit into […]
content:
With sequels in the Batman and Superman franchises on the horizon, a DC team-up between the Dark Knight and the Man of Steel doesn’t seem to be in the immediate future.

Robert Pattinson admitted it “would be kind of tough” to make his version of Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves‘ The Batman movies fit into James Gunn‘s DCU, which he launched with last year’s Superman.

“I think it would be kind of tough to have this version of Bruce outside of [Reeves’] world,” he told LADbible. “It’s one of the only characters I guess because of the length of the shoots but also it’s such a specific kind of [style], the tone of it gets inside you.”

Pattinson added, “I remember that happened to me the last time I did it, it took a while. You’re just in the dark, the whole time. Both mood-wise and light-wise, I can’t see anything for like months. It does affect you like you feel strange afterwards.”

Watch on Deadline

Gunn revealed last July that the script for The Batman: Part II was finished, following several delays. Last August, a letter to Warner Bros. Discovery’s shareholders revealed that filming on the sequel would begin filming in the spring.

Warner Bros. recently pushed the movie’s release date to Feb. 18, 2028 as Reeves continued to tease the sequel with camera test footage of Pattinson in costume.

Meanwhile, Gunn wrapped filming on his Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow last month, which joins Superman (2025), Supergirl (2026) and Clayface, premiering Oct. 23, in Gunn’s expanding DCU.

title: ‘Halima,’ First Finnish Pic Ever by Black Female Filmmaker, Bags Fiction Project Prize, ‘Sauna Diplomacy’ Named Best Genre Project at Finnish Film Affair
summary: Former BBC journalist Naima Mohamud’s heartfelt and warm comedy “Halima,” about a 10-year-old Somali girl trying to fit in Finland in 1998 took home Helsinki’s Finnish Film Affair’s top prize for Best Fiction on Thursday evening. The award was handed out by the jury, including U.S. producer and executive Jodi Hildebrand (formerly at Condé Nast […]
content:
Former BBC journalist Naima Mohamud’s heartfelt and warm comedy “Halima,” about a 10-year-old Somali girl trying to fit in Finland in 1998 took home Helsinki’s Finnish Film Affair’s top prize for Best Fiction on Thursday evening.

The award was handed out by the jury, including U.S. producer and executive Jodi Hildebrand (formerly at Condé Nast and Marvel Studios), the British Film Institute’s Phoebe Hall and FEST-New Directors festival director Fernando Vasquez, who said: “The director’s energetic and authentic voice shone through in the pitch and translates into what promises to be a compelling lead performance. This is a 90s tinged snapshot of a Finland we haven’t seen on screen before, by a fresh Finnish voice.”

“11 Hours” Courtesy of Fenomen

Produced by It’s Alive Films (“Euthanizer,” “The Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic,” “100 Litres of Gold”), Finland’s regular provider of artistically daring and original scripted content, Mohamud’s debut feature marks a milestone as the very first Finnish feature film directed by a black woman. “But it’s also the first film not directed by Teemo [Nikki], co-owner of the company,” said It’s Alive’s co-founder and producer Jani Pösö at his pitch, while reminding the 500-plus delegates that their films are “entertaining takes on deadly serious subjects.”

Popular on Variety

“This is the same here, and we simply had to make this movie,” added Pösö, who produces with Finland’s No-Office Films, in co-production with Ireland’s Vico Films.

“This story was inspired by my family, and my experience of growing up in Finland, where no one had seen black people!” said Dublin and Helsinki-based Mohamud, who studied filmmaking at London Metropolitan University and USC (University of Southern California) in Los Angeles. The feature, which won Best Pitch at the Haugesund New Nordic Films in 2024, is now in post-production with a delivery set for the fall 2027.

At Thursday’s awards ceremony, which closed the showcase day at Helsinki Film Festival’s industry confab Finnish Film Affair, the jury also handed out the €3,000 ($3,400) Best Nordic Film Award from the Amos Anderson Fund to the Norwegian suspense drama “11 Hours” by Emilie Beck, best-known for Netflix’s “Royalteen” and TV2 Norway’s hit “Escaping Bolivia.”

Inspired by true events, the pic chronicles the traumatic 11 hours that daycare director Sara, her employees and 11 children had to endure when an armed man took them hostage.

“This pitch made us all immediately lean forward in our seats,” said the jury. “Using the form of a ripped-from-the-headlines hostage thriller to illuminate a complex and layered social story, it’s a film we can’t wait to see more of.”

Toplining an A-list Norwegian cast including Ingrid Bolsø Berdal (“La Palma,” “Detective Hole”), Jan Gunnar Røise (Dag Johan Haugerud’s “Sex”), Oddgeir Thune (“Loveable,” “Home for Christmas”) and Sofia Tjelta (“Delete Me”), the feature, produced by Fenomen Studios and Maha Film, will be released domestically in September 2027 via Scanbox.

In other main categories, the new €2,500 ($2,800) Best Genre Project, sponsored by Post Control Helsinki & Angel Films, crowned Teenu Niukkanen’s “Sauna Diplomacy,” the only comedy among eight projects that competed in the high-profile inaugural Nordic Genre Lab.

“We believe that the project was a clear stand out,” said jury members Noëmie Devide (Goodfellas), Sydney Brumfield (Searchlight) and screenwriter Espen Auka, who felt the concept was “very original, fun and commercially viable.”

Set in the summer of 1970, the story turns on the diligent civil servant Heikki who decides to host a high-ranking Soviet diplomat at his family’s lakeside cottage. But the seemingly harmless weekend turns into a game of manipulation, and power games.

“It’s set during Finlandization, when Finland during the Cold War was a pre-western democracy, as long as the Soviet Union would tell us what to do!,” quipped Niukkanen (“Fucking Bunnies,” “Money Shot”), a self-proclaimed creator of content with “bad taste, done with good taste.”

“I recommend reading Teemu’s script! It’s fuckingly funny – topical, rowdy, thrillingly violent, yet a much-needed guide on how to stand up against tyrants,” said Oskari Huttu, who produces with John Lundsten for Tack Films. The project in development has been pre-bought by Nordisk Film for the Nordics, with production set to kickstart in 2028.

Elsewhere, the €3,000 AVEK Best Documentary Award handed out by IDFA’s Isabel Arrate Fernandez, director Einari Paakkanen and the Estonian Film Institute’s doc specialist Filipp Kruusvall, went to Anna Antsalo (“Walk the Tideline”) for her film “Darkness Counts,” produced by Venla Hellstedt.

“The award for best documentary project goes to a project that turns the greatest enemy of filmmaking – darkness – into a visually captivating element,” said the jury.

Reflecting the Finnish Film Affair’s ever-expanding collaborations with key European markets to facilitate networking and business opportunities for Finnish and Nordic professionals, an extra four industry awards were given out on Thursday.

In a tightly fought series competition, the six-part comedy thriller “Body in the Closet” from “Bloodsuckers’” Elin Grönblom grabbed the Midpoint Series Consulting Award. The series produced by Mia Oikanen for Warner Bros Int’l Television Production Finland tells of a shy theater prop master who accidentally becomes a killer while trying to please everyone around her, especially her narcissistic mom. “Yes, there are murders, but no one cares about the murderer and murdered people – they only care about themselves!” said MFA graduate Grönblom in her entertaining pitch.

The Midpoint Institute also granted its Feature Consulting Award to the courtroom drama in development “Big Deal,” helmed by Hedda Mjøn for Oda Kruse, in which four character’s lives are irrevocably changed by a single trial. SF Studios has boarded the Norwegian, Finnish, Estonian co-production.

The inaugural Producers Network Award from the Marché du Film went to the Finnish project in development “Babyface” by Aleksi Delikouras (“Nerd:DragonSlayer666”), a modern-day “Karate Kid” in which a 13-year-old boy befriends the eccentric pro wrestler Killer Joe. “I want to offer a different image of masculinity, and show that vulnerability is not a weakness,” said Delikouras in his pitch.

Finally It’s Alive Films’ psycho horror “Linden Lane 6” from rising talent Josefina Rautiainen picked up the Göteborg Film Festival Award. The story focuses on a novelist who moves into a building, strangely inhabited only by woman – 13 of them. The project in development is being produced by Anita Hyppönen, recipient as well of the Connecting Cottbus Producers Exchange accolade.

Commenting on the overall industry event, Searchlight’s Sydney Brumfield, who was in Helsinki for her Nordic Genre Lab duty, said Finnish Film Affair organizers “did an excellent job in selecting the projects because the quality was amazing.”

Her views were shared by Tonje Hardersen, head of the Norwegian Int’l Film Festival. “It’s been a very strong year and many projects stood out,” said the seasoned Norwegian executive, who had Emilie Beck’s “11 Hours” in her list of top projects.

title: ‘Unabomber’ Review: A Portrait of the Terrorist as a Young Man, Given a Hokey TV-Movie Gloss
summary: The Unabomber may be a figure of enduring public fascination, but it’s hard to see that extending to “Unabomber,” Netflix’s unimaginatively titled and prosaically assembled drama about how domestic terrorist Ted Kaczynski was radicalized, and how he was caught. Alternating between a standard-issue procedural thriller, dramatizing the FBI’s final year of investigation on the case, […]
content:
The Unabomber may be a figure of enduring public fascination, but it’s hard to see that extending to “Unabomber,” Netflix‘s unimaginatively titled and prosaically assembled drama about how domestic terrorist Ted Kaczynski was radicalized, and how he was caught. Alternating between a standard-issue procedural thriller, dramatizing the FBI’s final year of investigation on the case, and psychologically revealing flashbacks to the 16-year-old Kaczynski’s freshman year at Harvard, Janus Metz‘s film has some built-in intrigue from its subject matter alone, but rote dialogue and autopilot true-crime styling do little to fire the imagination. Meanwhile, the dual timelines never spur or inform each other in any meaningful way; the sense that two disparate but half-baked Unabomber projects have been unhappily welded together is hard to shake.

The more interesting of the two is the college-set narrative, which meets the streamer’s seemingly insatiable appetite for making-of-a-murderer biopics — call them true-life villain origin stories, if you will — and serves up a novel casting coup: Jacob Tremblay, the guileless child star of “Room” and “Wonder,” as the teenage Kaczynski. Portrayed as a butter-wouldn’t-melt prodigy unprepared to function in the real adult world, he’s pitted against Harvard professor Henry Murray, whose avuncular approach masks more manipulative intent as he enlists the vulnerable student as a subject in an experimental psychological study.

Popular on Variety

Played by Russell Crowe, who cruises through the film while remaining its most compelling figure, Murray is presented in Sam Chalsen and Nelson Greaves’ script as the unwitting architect of Kaczynski’s psychosis — and the spur behind his repeated targeting of academic figures with his bombings. Yet the film’s own case is pretty tenuous, and does little to counter Kaczynski’s later assertion that the experience, while unpleasant, wasn’t formative. Still, there’s more going on here than in the film’s 1990s-set section, which lumps Shailene Woodley with the stock role of fictional FBI agent Joanne Miller, battling institutional sexism and investigative complacency as she rather conveniently pieces together the Unabomber puzzle all on her own.

There’s certainly little in the film to match the intensity of Tony Stone’s underseen 2021 biopic “Ted K,” starring a genuinely disquieting Sharlto Copley in the title role, which worked precisely because it didn’t try to crack or psychologize Kaczynski in the ways that “Unabomber” does to increasingly banal effect. While Miller pores over Kaczynski’s famous manifesto, correctly concluding that its linguistic quirks will lead the authorities to him, the upshot of Murray’s study four decades before is that the young Kaczynski shows signs of schizophrenia. Neither qualifies as a eureka moment likely to make slumping viewers sit bolt upright on their couch.

The most complex story wrinkle here is the fact that Murray’s study, heavily rooted in his contentious “personology” theory of personality, is so patently unethical and specious — recruiting the young Kaczynski, among others, to debate his personal philosophies against a purposely combative and abusive opponent, solely for the purpose of observing how the hapless subject collapses under stress. Administered by Murray with his research partner Christiana Morgan (Annabelle Wallis), it’s written as a dastardly setup that serves to place Kaczynski in the most sympathetic possible light — while also showing the roots of his disconnect from society.

As such, Kaczynski is characterized as little more than a twitchy grab-bag of symptoms, played by Tremblay with a fractured little-boy-lost affect that is never altogether convincing. When most under pressure, the performance retreats into a slightly one-note register of antisocial stridency — not that the hokey script, with all its heavily underlined tells and forced connections, calls for anything more finely shaded. Meanwhile, over at the FBI, Miller has the obtuse skepticism of her boorish partner Leo (a thankless role for Alexander Ludwig) to contend with while drawing perfectly logical conclusions from the evidence at hand; we vaguely feel for her, while also suspecting that the case can’t have been quite so simple.

Metz, the Danish director of “Borg vs. McEnroe” and “All the Old Knives,” directs “Unabomber” in workaday style — beginning with a wholly unnecessary reenactment of the 1994 bombing that killed New Jersey ad exec Thomas J. Mosser (Michael Buie), which cues an archival recap of Kaczynski’s misdeeds for the benefit of anyone tuning in who might be unfamiliar. It’s an intro straight out of the Netflix true-crime playbook, which the film glossily follows throughout, while never seeming all that true. There’s little understanding to be gained from “Unabomber,” or even much tension from its fictionalized rejigging of the case — just the lurid draw of what we already know.

title: Silver Lion Winner ‘Miss Violence’ Director Alexandros Avranas to Helm Greek Adaptation of Globoplay’s Hit Series ‘The Others’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Alexandros Avranas, who won the Venice Film Festival Silver Lion for best director for the harrowing drama “Miss Violence,” will helm the Greek adaptation of Globoplay’s hit series “The Others.” The project, which is currently in production, follows the format sales agreement signed between Alpha TV and Brazilian media powerhouse Globo in late 2024. Created […]
content:
Alexandros Avranas, who won the Venice Film Festival Silver Lion for best director for the harrowing drama “Miss Violence,” will helm the Greek adaptation of Globoplay’s hit series “The Others.” The project, which is currently in production, follows the format sales agreement signed between Alpha TV and Brazilian media powerhouse Globo in late 2024.

Created and written by top Brazilian TV creatve driving force Lucas Paraizo, “The Others” follows two neighboring couples who clash after a fight between their teenage sons, triggering an escalating conflict with absurd consequences. What begins as a trivial disagreement reaches new proportions regarding how far a lack of dialogue can drive people.

The series is one of the most successful Globoplay original series to date, following in the footsteps of Paraizo’s hit medical drama “Under Pressure,” which was sold to more than 60 countries. In Brazil, the success of the franchise was consolidated with the premiere of its third season this year.

Popular on Variety

Nikos Psarras (Petros) – Paschalis Terzis (Ektoras) – Marina Kalogirou (Melina)

The Greek adaptation of the series is produced by Primavisione and stars Maria Nafpliotou (“Café 404”), Charis Fragulis (“Afterlov”), Nikos Psarras (“The Fire Bracelet”), and Paschalis Terzis. In addition to “The Others,” Greece will also get a local adaptation of the telenovela “All The Flowers,” with the same production company and broadcasting channel.

Charis Fragkoulis (Alexandros) – Maria Nafpliotou (Sophia) – Sotiris Gkoros (Manos)

To follow the start of production, author Lucas Paraizo visited the set in Greece: “I was on the set of the Greek version of ‘The Others’, a series I created, and had the pleasure of watching the shooting of one of the most important scenes of the first season: the scene where the characters Cibele and Wando face off over their sons’ fight,” he said.

“I had the pleasure of witnessing the enthusiasm of the cast, crew, and director Alexandro Avranas, whom I’ve been a fan of since he directed the feature film ‘Miss Violence,’” he added. “I am curious to see this new version of the series and am sure it will be a success in Greece, as it was in Brazil, countries that have a lot in common.”

“The Others,” courtesy of Globo

The deal reinforces Globo’s positioning in the format rights market. Recently, the major banner saw a Peruvian version of “Her Own Destiny” and a Portuguese adaptation of “Her Own Destiny.”

“The start of filming for the Greek version of ‘The Others’ is another important step in our international formats strategy,” said Angela Colla, Head of International Business at Globo. “The partnership with Alpha TV proves the strength of Brazilian narratives that transcend borders. The essence of Lucas Paraizo’s text is about human relationships, and we are excited to see how this story will resonate with the Greek audience.”

Christos Kompos, Program Director at Alpha TV, said that their adaptation of “The Others” “underscores Alpha TV’s unwavering commitment to delivering cinematic, top-tier drama to the Greek market.”

“Partnering with a global powerhouse like Globo gives us the creative foundation to produce something truly exceptional,” he added. “Lucas Paraizo has written a narrative that holds a direct mirror to modern society, showing how quickly community ties can fracture when people stop talking to one another. Under the visionary direction of Alexandros Avranas and led by a phenomenal ensemble cast, we are elevating this incredible Brazilian psychological drama into a culturally distinct, high-end production. It is a privilege to collaborate with Globo to breathe new life into a story that is as globally relevant as it is locally poignant.”

title: Taylor Swift Still Has Unfinished Business With Her Exes — Thank God! — While Also Mooning Over Her Groom in ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’: New Tracks Review
summary: If you’re a Taylor Swift fan, one of your deepest fears this year might have been that the pop superstar will be so wrapped up in a long, rapturous honeymoon that she’ll neglect to bring us down by continuing to write about the bums that got away, or any lingering regrets that were accumulated on […]
content:
If you’re a Taylor Swift fan, one of your deepest fears this year might have been that the pop superstar will be so wrapped up in a long, rapturous honeymoon that she’ll neglect to bring us down by continuing to write about the bums that got away, or any lingering regrets that were accumulated on the way to the skybox. So it will come as some relief that three of the four new tracks on “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” prove she has no intention of turning in her Tortured Poets membership card any time soon.

Meanwhile, the fourth track, “Cleveland!,” establishes that she also has no intention of stopping writing about marital bliss, in the giddiest form possible, with an unrepentant sunniness so blinding it could almost blot out the memory that she’d ever written an elegy in her life. You’ve been warned.

However it’s packaged, these four tracks essentially constitute a new EP — something she really hasn’t formally given us since 2008’s “Beautiful Eyes” — more than they feel like any kind of obvious addendum to “The Life of a Showgirl,” despite reassembling the same trio of Avengers (Max Martin, Shellback and herself) for the task. Call if what you want: as much as the world loves Swift as the 21st century’s quintessential album artist, it’s refreshing to get something fast and easily digestible from her between pop opuses, too. Here’s how these four tracks taste at first bite:

“Patient Zero.” When Swift thinks of a certain recent ex in her past, she does not think of Tim McGraw. She thinks of hospitals, and/or pandemics. One has to suspect that if “Patient Zero” has a real-life inspiration, it’s the same guy who inspired her to write that she was dying, emotionally, in “You’re Losing Me,” the scary post-“Midnights” bonus track that appeared to be about her longest-term relationship going into its last throes on life support. But as harrowing as “You’re Losing Me” was, “Patient Zero” is absolutely chipper, since she’s singing about being long since recovered from the malady and remembering it only for the sake of warning the fellow’s current paramour about how his good-guy act won’t be nourishing in the end.

The sound is very different from anything on “The Life of a Showgirl,” so it makes some sense to learn that this and the other tracks were recorded after that album was already out (and very long after it was recorded). The dry drum sound heard on much of “Showgirl” is replaced here with electronic percussion, while the key bit of instrumentation is a violin, or something built to emulate one. If you didn’t know better, you might guess this was a stray Jack Antonoff track, since it doesn’t bear any of the obvious Martin/Shellback hallmarks. There’s a bittersweet, lopingly mid-tempo feel to it that we haven’t heard in, well, a fortnight.

Fans will point to her telling the ex’s new gal that she should take the sisterly advice from “someone who had him and walked away,” which does narrow down the possibilities of who it could be about IRL, if anyone. And from that, prompt the cries of “She’s married, and she still hasn’t gotten over it?” The point is kind of that she has. But good for her for keeping that memory mill alive; she’s going to need it to keep writing songs that aren’t all white picket fences. Plus, we love a T-Swift who forgives — maybe — but never, ever forgets.

title: Gaussian Scout, Pixentinel Take Top Prizes at San Sebastián’s Zinemaldia Startup Challenge
summary: SAN SEBASTIÁN, Spain — Finland’s Gaussian Scout (formerly listed Virtual Location Scouting) and Spain’s Pixentinel claimed the top prizes at the 2026 Zinemaldia Startup Challenge, the San Sebastián Festival’s flagship technology competition. Gaussian Scout, a browser-based virtual location scouting platform being developed by Finnish cinematographer Antti Ahokoivu, won Best European Project with its €10,000 and […]
content:
SAN SEBASTIÁN, Spain — Finland’s Gaussian Scout (formerly listed Virtual Location Scouting) and Spain’s Pixentinel claimed the top prizes at the 2026 Zinemaldia Startup Challenge, the San Sebastián Festival’s flagship technology competition.

Gaussian Scout, a browser-based virtual location scouting platform being developed by Finnish cinematographer Antti Ahokoivu, won Best European Project with its €10,000 and also picked up the €3,000 Special Mention for Entrepreneurship. Spanish streaming-operations startup Pixentinel took the €30,000 Best Spanish Project award. Rather than simply flagging when a live stream has broken, Pixentinel aims to determine where a failure originated supplu evidence to the diagnosis and, where possible, automatically trigger a response. The proposition is aimed at broadcasters and streaming operators feel the hit of short interruptions during live programming can become lost viewers and revenue.

Ahokoivu admitted the double win came as a surprise after travelling from Finland with a project that is still pre-commercial somewhat a side project to his Cinematorgraphy work. More important than the prize itself, he said, was seeing people engage with the idea. “People come to talk and are interested about it,” he told Variety. “You get more confident that there is something interesting.”

Popular on Variety

The technology grew directly out of Ahokoivu’s work as a cinematographer and his experience trying to get different departments to understand a location in the same way before a shoot. “Having some tools that you can visualise things with, that you talk about the same things, what we’re going to do, helps so much,” he said. The prize money will now help Gaussian Scout move into tests on real productions and further develop the cloud-based system that will eventually allow users to upload and work with their own digital twins.

The 2026 Zinemaldia Startup Challenge offered €30,000 for the Best Spanish Project, €10,000 for the Best European Project and a €3,000 Special Mention for Entrepreneurship. The competition is the centerpiece of the Festival’s Zinemaldia & Technology initiative and is organized by the San Sebastián Festival in collaboration with Tecnalia, ALÍA and Vicomtech.

The Spanish competition also forms part of Spanish Screenings: Financing & Tech, supported by Spain’s Ministry of Culture through ICAA, the Ministry for Digital Transformation and Civil Service, ICEX, the Málaga Festival and the San Sebastián Festival. Prior to the win announcement the ten finalists, five Spanish and five from elsewhere in Europe, pitched their projects with each given a strict 10 minutes to present and field questions.

We profile the companies below:

European Finalists



GaussianScout (Virtual Location Scouting Finland)

Cinematographer Antti Ahokoivu is developing this browser-based tool intended to make remote location scouting more spatially informative than conventional photographs. Ahokoivu’s starting insight was simple: flat images rarely communicate the true proportions and geometry of a filming location for the disparate teams. GaussianScout, formerly listed as Virtual Location Scouting, brings Gaussian splats, XGRIDS scans, photogrammetry and related 3D capture methods into a shared environment where filmmakers can explore spaces, frame potential shots, even measure spaces accurately. Script-import tools are also planned. The project is still pre-commercial, with a subscription launch is targeted for autumn 2027.

Graphrs (Germany)

Berlin-based Graphrs wants to become the “operating system for video production,” orchestrating everything from scheduling and staffing to shoots and AI-assisted content creation in a single platform. Co-founder and CEO Thomas Brömme pitched the product as infrastructure for companies producing video repeatedly across multiple markets, currently backed by a network of around 20 camera teams. Brömme cited names including TikTok, UNIQLO and the WHO as examples of its client base.

SuperScout (United Kingdom)

SuperScout, founded by Gabriel Isserlis, turns filmmakers’ accumulated location research into private, searchable, map-based databases. Isserlis gave the example of working alongside a Disney location scout and seeing how painful it was to retrieve alternatives when a booked location suddenly became unavailable and showing how this scout was able to find an alternative location scouted 6 years prior quickly and getting the production day back on track. The platform stores previous scouts, imagery and location data so teams can find options instead of starting again. At Zinemaldia, SuperScout said it was being used across 14 countries, including by the BBC, and that 11 customers had also invested in the company. English Heritage is a confirmed institutional customer.

TheGreenShot (Belgium)

Belgium’s TheGreenShot automates sustainability measurement and carbon reporting for film, television and other entertainment productions. Co-founder Max Hermans described the opportunity as replacing today’s scattered spreadsheets with software able to ingest accounting, supplier, expense and on-set data and turn it into customised reporting at scale. The pitch argued that its advantage over horizontal carbon platforms such as Greenly or Watershed is deep entertainment-industry specificity. Its public customer roster includes HBO, Chanel and Banijay, while Hermans announced Fremantle as a new customer during the Zinemaldia pitch.

THELMA (Finland)

Finnish startup THELMA is building an identity-protection service for actors, influencers and other public figures whose image, voice or likeness may be impersonated or reused without permission online. Founder Aleksi Hyvärinen described a workflow of finding suspected misuse, preserving evidence, helping initiate action and then reporting outcomes back to the customer. The business is already testing a subscription model, with pitch pricing of roughly €350 per month for individuals and €499 for agencies.

Spanish Finalists



Volum (Spain)

Barcelona-based Volum Technologies is commercialising years of i2CAT research into real-time volumetric communication. Its HoloMIT technology captures, compresses, streams and renders people as live 3D representations, allowing remote participants to appear “there” rather than as flat video, as long as you don a headset of course. The company spun out of i2CAT in 2025 following more than €3.7 million of research investment and is now developing an ecosystem spanning an SDK and products such as HoloBooth and HoloTotem. Volum’s broader ambition is to make holographic presence as accessible as videoconferencing, using relatively standard cameras rather than specialised studio-scale capture infrastructure.

Pixentinel (Spain)

Pixentinel is developing an operational-intelligence layer for live streaming that, it was proposed, goes beyond detecting outages to diagnosing their likely cause and automatically triggering responses. Its system analyses video signals in context, attaches evidence and confidence scores to detected problems and can activate webhooks when intervention is required. The pitch is aimed at broadcasters, streaming platforms and telecom operators whose existing monitoring stacks generate fragmented alerts that engineers must manually correlate and react to. Pixentinel’s core proposition is therefore reducing the time between a streaming failure starting and an operations team understanding and deploying a fix for it.

intoreality.tv (Spain)

Barcelona-based Into Reality offers a white-label immersive streaming platform that lets traditional 2D feeds coexist with VR180 and VR360 video. Viewers can switch cameras, audio streams and perspectives across phones, computers, tablets and VR headsets, effectively becoming their own live-event director. The platform can be embedded into a customer’s website or deployed as a standalone audiovisual service, with AVOD, subscription and pay-per-view monetisation models. Into Reality has also licensed i2CAT’s Sync-X technology, expanding its ability to deliver synchronised multicamera and multiscreen experiences for entertainment, culture, sport and live events.

HaMo Real-Time Animation System (Spain)

HaMo Animation is building patented hardware and software for animating digital characters live, combining the responsiveness of traditional puppetry with real-time virtual production. HaMo showed the technology works with 2D, 3D, realistic and stylised characters and has already been used for promotional content around “Tad and the Magic Lamp” enabling the IP to be used live in front of Spanish distributors. The stated ambition is to productise and sell the hardware, with consumer applications potentially following in the future. José Luis Farías demonstrated the system live arguing that speed and production cost distinguish it from AI-generated animation workflows starting to appear.

Dymensium (Spain)

Valencia-based Dymensium is developing a volumetric-capture pipeline built around Gaussian Splatting, particularly 4DGS for moving subjects. Founder Jacinto Nicolás framed the pitch around the rapid evolution from NeRFs to Gaussian techniques and a workflow spanning capture, Gaussian generation, cleaning and integration. Its studio uses 120 synchronised cameras and targets film, VFX, games and immersive media, where directors can reposition the virtual camera after capture. Dymensium also pointed to Gaussian Splatting’s emerging use in major film production namely in James Gunn’s “Superman” as evidence that the underlying technology is moving into commercial workflows.

title: ‘The Lion King’ Director Rob Minkoff To Develop & Exec Produce Family Pic ‘Storm Dogs’ From Tilly Norwood Creator Particle 6
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Rob Minkoff, co-director of Disney’s classic animated hit The Lion King, is in advanced discussions to develop and executive produce Storm Dogs, an upcoming family adventure title from Tilly Norwood creator Particle 6. Minkoff, who also directed Stuart Little, will be the creative lead on the upcoming feature film and will work closely with […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Rob Minkoff, co-director of Disney’s classic animated hit The Lion King, is in advanced discussions to develop and executive produce Storm Dogs, an upcoming family adventure title from Tilly Norwood creator Particle 6.

Minkoff, who also directed Stuart Little, will be the creative lead on the upcoming feature film and will work closely with Particle 6 CEO Eline van der Velden on developing the story, characters and screenplay ahead of production.

Based on an original idea from Van der Velden, the story is set in an English village during a devastating storm. When two-year-old Poppy is unexpectedly separated from the adult caring for her, five different dogs must overcome their instincts, and one another, to bring her safely home.

Set over the course of 24 hours, the film follows the unlikely pack as it carries Poppy across flooded fields, damaged bridges and a countryside transformed by the storm. What begins as a desperate journey gradually turns five mismatched dogs into a family and forces Poppy’s dog-fearing mother to see them in an entirely new light.

Watch on Deadline

The film will combine live-action performances with photorealistic animated characters. Human roles will be filmed “conventionally”, according to a statement, while the dogs and Poppy will be created through an approach that brings together live-action performance, traditional filmmaking techniques and emerging AI tools. Production is slated for 2027.

The Particle 6 creative team says it is developing a “performance-driven process that translates an actor’s facial expressions, physicality, timing and emotional choices into the animated characters.” This, it says, will enable the actor shape and complete the performance.

“Rob has helped create some of cinema’s most enduring animal characters,” said Van der Velden. “His understanding of character, comedy and emotional storytelling makes him an extraordinary creative partner for Storm Dogs. This film presents a challenge that would be extraordinarily difficult to achieve through conventional production alone: a toddler and five dogs carrying much of the story through extreme weather and hazardous terrain. By bringing performers, filmmakers and emerging tools together, we can attempt something unusually ambitious while keeping every creative decision in human hands.”

Minkoff added: “I have spent much of my career looking for ways to create animal characters who are funny, emotionally truthful and completely alive. When I visited Particle 6 in London, I found a group of filmmakers who care deeply about story, character and performance. They are also serious about exploring how new production methods can expand how filmmakers’ imaginations are realised on screen. Storm Dogs is a wonderful opportunity to develop that approach together in the service of a story with real jeopardy, heart and humor.”

Van der Velden added: “I’m not interested in AI as a replacement for human creativity. But I believe it has extraordinary potential to transform the process of making motion pictures, to help filmmakers manifest what they imagine with greater freedom and fewer limitations. We are still in the pioneering phase of this transformation, and I’m thrilled to have the opportunity to help define how it can be used responsibly.”

Particle 6 made waves at the Zurich Film Festival last year when its AI actor Tilly Norwood was launched at the festival’s flagship industry event Zurich Summit, sparking a global debate about the use of AI in the entertainment space. Van der Velden is returning to speak to the Summit this year to reflect on the aftermath of that viral story. As previously announced, Tilly Norwood is set to star in her own feature Misaligned, which is being developed at Particle 6.

title: Zee 5 Global Releases ‘Hi’, Romantic Pic Starring Nayanthara & Kavin
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Zee 5 Global is today saying Hi to its latest movie premiere. The Indian content-focused streamer will premiere the pic, which stars Nayanthara and Kavin, today. The pic is billed as “an unconventional yet heartwarming romance that offers a fresh perspective on modern relationships.” Directed by Vishnu Edavan, the film follows a young man […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Zee 5 Global is today saying Hi to its latest movie premiere.

The Indian content-focused streamer will premiere the pic, which stars Nayanthara and Kavin, today. The pic is billed as “an unconventional yet heartwarming romance that offers a fresh perspective on modern relationships.”

Directed by Vishnu Edavan, the film follows a young man (Kavin), who refuses to give up on finding love despite heartbreak and rejection, and a young woman (Nayanthara) grappling with family challenges while trying to escape an unwanted marriage. When their paths cross, they embark on a heartfelt journey of love, acceptance, and self-discovery.

The film also stars Tamil cinema veterans Radhika Sarathkumar, Prabhu and K. Bhagyaraj, who passed away in June, making Hi his final performance on-screen.

Watch on Deadline

Above you can watch the trailer for the film, which is from Zee Studios, Seven Screen Studio and Rowdy Pictures, the latter of which Nayanthara runs with filmmaker Vignesh Shivan.

The movie released in cinemas in late August and will now stream in all Zee 5 territories, including the U.S. and Canada.

Siju Prabhakaran, Chief Business Officer at Zee 5 Global, said: “At Zee 5 Global, we are committed to bringing audiences stories that are rooted in emotion and connect with viewers across markets. With Hi, we are delighted to present a refreshing take on love, relationships and the complexities that come with them.

“The film brings together Nayanthara and Kavin in a heartfelt story that balances romance, humour and emotion. We look forward to bringing this film to audiences across our global markets and hope it resonates with viewers worldwide.”

Nayanthara said of her role: “The character I play in Hi is someone who is independent, resilient, and deeply grounded in her convictions, yet she carries her own fears and emotional complexities.

“That balance of strength and vulnerability is what made the role so meaningful to me. She is protective of the people she loves, thoughtful in her choices, and someone who learns that opening her heart can be both challenging and beautiful.

Kavin added: “What I loved most about Hi was that it gives us a male protagonist who is unapologetically vulnerable, emotionally honest, and unafraid to wear his heart on his sleeve. In a world where men are often expected to hide their emotions, my character embraces them, making him incredibly real and relatable. He is a young man navigating love, rejection, self-doubt, and the fear of not being enough, all while holding on to the hope of finding a meaningful connection.”

title: ‘American Idol’s Luke Bryan, Lionel Richie, Carrie Underwood & Ryan Seacrest Return For Season 25
summary: American Idol might be moving to a new location but it will have the same judges and host as before. Luke Bryan, Lionel Richie and Carrie Underwood are returning as judges for Season 25 of the music competition show alongside host Ryan Seacrest. Bryan announced the news on stage at a show in Nashville, Tennessee. […]
content:
American Idol might be moving to a new location but it will have the same judges and host as before.

Luke Bryan, Lionel Richie and Carrie Underwood are returning as judges for Season 25 of the music competition show alongside host Ryan Seacrest.

Bryan announced the news on stage at a show in Nashville, Tennessee.

It marks the third year that the trio of Bryan, Richie and Underwood will judge the contestants together; Seacrest has hosted since the start and has been the sole host (he co-hosted with Brian Dunkleman in Season 1) since 2003.

Idol was renewed for Season 25 or Season 10 on ABC in July but the judges deals always take a couple of months after that.

Auditions kicked off last month with the traditional Idol Across America tour, a virtual search for singers taking place across the country.

However, the big news in Idol-land is the move to Georgia. Bryan and Underwood both live in Tennessee, so it’s closer for the pair of them but Richie lives in LA and Seacrest splits his time between LA and New York.

Richie recently underwent a heart procedure for atrial fibrillation and canceled some tour dates but is expected to begin a residency in Las Vegas next month.

The show is produced by Fremantle and Sony Pictures Television’s 19 Entertainment with Megan Michaels Wolflick as showrunner.

Idol introduced a number of changes last season including social voting for the first time, moving Hollywood Week to Nashville, Tennessee, premiering on a new night in Monday (rather than Sunday) and started streaming live on Disney+.

title: ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews Each In Box Office Weekend Where There’s Something For Everyone
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Here’s what’s cool about this weekend. Without any wide entry opening to north of $30M, it’s going to be a fantastic late September frame at the box office. It wouldn’t be shocking if the marketplace sees the best late September weekend since 2018 when all films totaled $106.4M. From a pure box office standpoint […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Here’s what’s cool about this weekend.

Without any wide entry opening to north of $30M, it’s going to be a fantastic late September frame at the box office. It wouldn’t be shocking if the marketplace sees the best late September weekend since 2018 when all films totaled $106.4M. From a pure box office standpoint –forget about budgets for a minute and marketing costs– we’ve got four wide openings aimed at various demos in Disney/Marvel Studio’s Avengers: Endgame: Encore (fanboys), A24’s Primetime (Gen-Z and Robert Pattinson fans), Paramount’s Brad Pitt dog movie Heart of the Beast (flyover states and men/women adults), and Universal/DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island (families).

Heading into this weekend, it was believed that No. 1 could be a fight between Avengers: Endgame: Encore and the second weekend of Sony/Constantin’s Resident Evil, respectively at $25M-$30M and $21M-$24M.

Watch on Deadline

But there are curveballs: It’s the year of Pattinson in The Drama and beggers getting out of here memes in The Odyssey, and though A24 is eyeing $12M-$16M for his latest movie Primetime about To Catch a Predator‘s Chris Hansen and his case gone wrong, the $15M net production has a shot at a $20M opening in North America at 2,814 theaters.

“It could be a three way fight for No. 1,” says one distribution source.

We’re hearing that previews tonight for the first feature narrative title from documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim are chasing Avengers: Endgame: Encore‘s $3M+ previews with a figure between $2M-$3M. Previews for the R-rated Primetime began at 4PM today and Rotten Tomatoes reviews and critics are great at 86% certified fresh and 85%. Encore‘s showtimes began today at 2PM.

Those previews for Primetime are ahead of Pattinson pics The Drama ($1.7M, $14.3M opening), and possibly Mickey 17 ($2.5M, $19M opening), in addition to the Gen-Z summer horror surprise Obsession ($2.6M, $17.1M opening). The A24 financed-by-foreign sales-movie is bowing abroad this weekend in France, Germany, Austria, Taiwan, Iceland, India, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Meanwhile, Avengers: Endgame: Encore, boosted by four extra minutes of the Russo Brothers’ upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, has preview cash that could possibly surpass that of Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith‘s re-release which was $3.4M (that turned into a $25.4M opening). We heard presales for Encore were ahead of Revenge of the Sith‘s re-release. The asterisk here is that sometimes these re-releases could be front-loaded, so we’ll see how Encore plays out. The Russo Brothers Encore is booked in around 3,000 theaters, boosted by Disney/Marvel Studio’s new certification on 1,300 premium large format screens, Infinity Vision, plus 390 Imax hubs. Encore will share Imax and PLFs with Resident Evil.

Overseas outlook for Encore is $25M in what’s bound to be a $50M WW weekend give or take. While James Cameron’s Avatar remains the No. 1 movie of all-time at $2.92B worldwide, Avengers Endgame is No. 2 with $2.799B WW (and Spider-Man Brand New Day No. 3 with $2.5B). There is a $124M WW box office gap between Avatar and Avengers Endgame. Disney is in wait-and-see mode to see if Endgame could reclaim the all-time top spot before Doomsday‘s Dec. 18 opening. Unlike Revenge of the Sith‘s one week play, there’s no endgame for Encore at the fall box office.

Paramount’s Heart of the Beast leaves audiences moved and crying, including Deadline chief critic Pete Hammond. Film reviewers aren’t shrugging it at 89% certified fresh on RT. Tracking outlook is $17M-$20M at 3,400 theaters. Previews began today for the PG-13 David Ayer directed movie at 2PM and we hear from sources they’re around $1.8M (that includes Monday Mystery screenings). That figure is just north of what Pitt’s fall 2019 sci-fi drama Ad Astra did in previews at $1.5M ($19M opening). The movie cost a net $82M before global marketing with dueling edits by Ayer and Pitt’s (Ayer’s won). Internationally, the film will open this week in 63 markets (or 95% footprint) including Australia, Brazil, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Spain, and the United Kingdom. Expectation abroad is $15M for what could be a $35M WW opening. The hope is that older men and women find the film. Like Primetime, this survival tale about a Special Forces veteran and his combat dog who are stranded in the Alaskan wilderness, sells itself upon viewing.

Forgotten Island from Puss in Boots: Last Wish filmmakers Joel Crawford and Januel P. Mercado is looking at $13M-$15M at 3,500 sites. Typically, late September is home to a family animated movie, i.e. Abominable, Cloudy With a Chance With Meatballs, The Wild Robot, the list goes on. Blurb for Forgotten Island: Two best friends become stranded on the mystical world of Nakali, where their only escape might cost them their shared lifetime of memories. Previews today stateside began at 2PM and are estimated between $800K-$1M, we hear. Pic has a staggered offshore rollout. Last weekend, $1.5M was made in Mexico, Australia and New Zealand. An additional 31 markets this weekend will bring Forgotten Island‘s count to 34 markets with an additional $10M in store.

Resident Evil‘s cume through Wednesday stands at $76.8M.

title: ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Sets Brooklyn Week With Guests Mamdani, Springsteen, Fellow Late-Night Hosts & More
