content:
As Jimmy Kimmel returns to his late-night post, he’s ready to take the show across the river for Brooklyn Week once again.

On Thursday, ABC announced that Jimmy Kimmel Live! will head to Brooklyn Academy of Music’s Howard Gilman Opera House for the eighth Brooklyn Week, which will kick off next Monday with an all-star lineup.

This year’s guests for Brooklyn Week include New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Mahershala Ali, Billy Crystal, Pete Davidson, Robby Hoffman, Paul McCartney, Seth Meyers, Tom Morello, John Oliver, Bernie Sanders, Bruce Springsteen and Howard Stern, with musical guests De La Soul, Goose, TV On the Radio, and Springsteen & Tom Morello.

All five shows will tape in front of a live studio audience at BAM, to air every weeknight at 11:35pm ET on ABC and stream the next day on Hulu.

Watch on Deadline

Jimmy Kimmel Live is produced by 12:05 AM Productions LLC, in association with Kimmelot and 20th Television. Kimmel, Erin Irwin, Molly McNearney, Jennifer Sharron and David Craig serve as executive producers, with Douglas DeLuca and Danny Ricker as co-executive producers.

Brooklyn Week comes after ABC denied “inaccurate” reports that Jimmy Kimmel Live! is ending in 2027 after 24 seasons.

title: Produced by J.A. Bayona, Netflix Documentary Series ‘Beyond Society’ Examines What Happens After the Survivors of the 1972 Andes Plane Crash Return to Uruguay
summary: The Netflix documentary series “Beyond Society” (“Más Allá de la Sociedad”) had its world premiere at the San Sebastián International Film Festival on September 23. The three-part doc series, created by Juan Antonio Bayona (“Society of the Snow,” “The Impossible,” “A Monster Calls”) and Carlos Torres (“Pajares & CIA,” “Crims”), picks up where Bayona’s film […]
content:
The Netflix documentary series “Beyond Society” (“Más Allá de la Sociedad”) had its world premiere at the San Sebastián International Film Festival on September 23. The three-part doc series, created by Juan Antonio Bayona (“Society of the Snow,” “The Impossible,” “A Monster Calls”) and Carlos Torres (“Pajares & CIA,” “Crims”), picks up where Bayona’s film “Society of the Snow” ends.

“Through the creative process and all the research required for ‘Society of the Snow,’ Juan Antonio had come across many stories and felt that something was still beating, which was the story of what happened after the rescue. So what was clear to us was that our story begins where the others always end: with the rescue of the survivors. Another point is how cinema can end up changing memory and how fiction can impact reality,” said Carlos Torres at a press conference held before the premiere in San Sebastián.

Popular on Variety

J.A. Bayona’s 2023 film, “Society of the Snow,” recounts the story of the 1972 Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 crash in the Andes Mountains, where 16 of the 45 people onboard were able to survive by resorting to cannibalism. To date, it is the most-watched film on streaming across all of Europe.

The new documentary spans the last 50-plus years in Carrasco, Uruguay, where the families of both the dead and the living have had to co-exist.

“Our intention with the series was to go up to the mountain and leave it buried there. We wanted to close a very long but very beautiful journey. Beyond the film, which ended the moment they were rescued, there was another kind of survival, which was returning home and surviving, on the part of the survivors, and surviving the loss of a loved one. And something I’m very interested in, which is reflected in the documentary, is when reality is mixed with fiction, how all that pain and suffering can become stories we tell ourselves,” Bayona said at the press conference.

Interviewing some of the living survivors, the relatives of the deceased and the journalists who covered the story, the series illustrates the emotional toll the tragedy took on the small Uruguayan town of Carrasco, where both the survivors and the deceased were from. The accident caused a rift between the families of the living and the dead. The series examines how being able to tell one’s version of the story can change the way one faces it.

For some, it was a celebratory return of the people they thought they’d lost. For others, the media frenzy and the return of the survivors were a constant reminder of having lost their loved ones.

“We can’t shy away from difficult stories. We had to understand that we were telling the story of 45 families. You can’t always please everyone, but we had to find the essence of each of their pain, their way of life, and understand that nobody survived everything and nobody died from it, and 54 years later we’re still talking about it,” added Torres.

“Listening to and understanding the person in front of you, trying to understand why they behaved as they did. Grief is very personal, very subjective. We had to understand how each person manages pain, since pain is also very subjective. An event can cause great pain to one person while another copes with it much better. All forms of grief are valid, and the beautiful thing about this story is that in the end there was finally a reunification between the two sides. For me especially, as a film director, I liked that it was brought about by fiction, little by little, as I said, through the passing of the years, the generational change, finding a voice for everyone who was there. That finally allowed people who hadn’t talked about the tragedy in 50 years to be able to understand each other, to put themselves in the other’s shoes, and finally come together, like what we experienced when we screened the film in Montevideo,” added Bayona.

“I think that looking at the past is a shock, it’s like a mirror, confronting yourself with who you are, with what you have become. I’m often asked, what if this tragedy had happened in the age of social media? I think human beings are the same with or without social media. It was 1972 and it was a huge story. I don’t think we make documentaries to give lessons, but sometimes it’s about learning. I imagine you can always learn by looking at how things were handled, and not repeat those same mistakes,” said Torres.

“We tried to understand the point of view and behavior of everyone involved in this story over the last 50 years, and doing that was one of the driving forces for us to make this series, to be able to show how fiction has been making its way into this story, which is surely one of the first media tragedies in our society, since it was covered by the whole world. We told the story hoping that our work could give meaning to the tragedy,” concluded Bayona.

“Beyond the Snow” is directed by Torres and produced by Bayona, Belén Atienza (“Society of the Snow,” “The Impossible”) and Sandra Hermida (“Society of the Snow,” “Three Goodbyes”). It will be available on Netflix on December 18.

title: In Finnish Body Horror ‘Tick Fever,’ Lyme Disease Is the Least of Your Worries (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: No one likes ticks – least of all “Tick Fever” director Sebastian Granskog. “Every Finn has learned to live in fear of ticks since the summers of their childhood. It’s a tiny insect that latches onto your body, breaks through your skin, starts drinking your blood and grows bigger as it takes what it wants […]
content:
No one likes ticks – least of all “Tick Fever” director Sebastian Granskog.

“Every Finn has learned to live in fear of ticks since the summers of their childhood. It’s a tiny insect that latches onto your body, breaks through your skin, starts drinking your blood and grows bigger as it takes what it wants from you,” he explains.

“They’re pretty much the perfect metaphor and monster for a horror movie,”

Producer Mia Palmgren agrees: “When Sebastian mentioned ticks, it instantly clicked. How has there not been a horror film about these little monsters before?”

Popular on Variety

In upcoming “Tick Fever” – an absurd body horror about “bloodsucking ticks, growing anxiety and a relationship way past its due date,” says Palmgren – they represent the anxiety the lead characters feel.

“And, as is usually the case with anxiety, the more you try to fight it, the stronger it grows,” adds Granskog.

The film, presented for the very first time at the Finnish Film Affair, is produced by Palmgren for Character House, also behind “A Mother” and comedy “Wingman the Movie: All In,” the third most-watched film in Finnish theaters in 2024.

Its leads, Victor and Stella, are a codependent couple who can’t live together but also can’t break up. Actors Elias Salonen (“Kalevala: The Story of Kullervo”) and Anna Böhm (“Valhalla Project”) portray them in the exclusive first concept art for the film.

“It’s pretty much over between them, but the world is a scary, anxiety-inducing place, so they keep trying to hold onto their relationship. Eventually, fear and anxiety start to seep through the cracks of their safe bubble and manifest as a tick that latches onto Victor,” explains Granskog.

Victor tries to get rid of it, slowly losing his grip on reality and pushing Stella further away.

“They need to decide if they’re going to keep doing this to themselves or just let go of each other and move on.”

“I was in a relationship like this in my early twenties,” chimes in Laura Laaksonen, who also produces the film.

“It was sucking the life out of me, but I just couldn’t leave. I found Stella’s story incredibly relatable. She doesn’t want to admit the relationship has failed because she thinks that would mean admitting that she has failed too.”

Laaksonen says: “What fascinates me about body horror is how the threat can come from within, and how the characters’ attempts to regain control can make things worse. Beyond the gore, there’s room to explore who these people are and what drives them. That emotional depth is what makes the physical horror so compelling to me.”

The team – as well as the Finnish Film Affair, which spotlighted similar films with Nordic Lab Genre this year – agrees: the world needs more Nordic horror.

“We have so much to offer and so much to draw from. Our nature, our wacky mythology, our deadpan dark humor,” says Granskog, with Palmgren adding: “We have quite a dark sense of humor up here in the Nordics, and when it’s mixed with horror in the right way, it creates a brilliant sweet spot where you’re never quite sure whether to laugh or look away.”

“Sebastian brilliantly balances horror, relationship drama and social satire in this film, and the world he has created is horrifyingly relatable.”

Palmgren has already worked with Granskog before on the horror short “The Locker Room,” but “Tick Fever” will be their first feature film together. It’s currently being set up as a co-production between the U.K. and the Nordics.

And speaking of that Nordic sense of humor, for Granskog, “graphic and funny” go hand in hand.

“As a horror fan, gore has me giggling in my seat when I’m watching a movie. I would love to make this film with practical effects. I hope we can accomplish that, at least mostly,” he admits.

Palmgren adds, “Sebastian has made it pretty clear that he wants the tick to be made with practical effects. I don’t look forward to seeing giant ticks come to life on set. Or maybe a little bit.”

title: ECAM Incubator Film Project ‘Our Raised Skin’ Explores the Male Body and the Fear of Its Touch
summary: Director Paolo Natale’s experimental hybrid documentary/video-essay, “Our Raised Skin” (“Nuestra Piel Levantada”), is currently in advanced development as part of Madrid Film School’s (ECAM) incubator program. It’s one of the five projects selected for La Incubadora’s ninth edition. “The film reflects on and questions self-perception, asking at what point in childhood we go from being […]
content:
Director Paolo Natale’s experimental hybrid documentary/video-essay, “Our Raised Skin” (“Nuestra Piel Levantada”), is currently in advanced development as part of Madrid Film School’s (ECAM) incubator program. It’s one of the five projects selected for La Incubadora’s ninth edition.

“The film reflects on and questions self-perception, asking at what point in childhood we go from being children to patriarchal men,” says Natale.

Even though Natale says the film is not autobiographical, he draws from the fact that he, his father and his grandfather all suffered from the same compulsive eating disorder.

Popular on Variety

“Our Raised Skin” is produced by Manuela Gutiérrez Arrieta, Juan Carlos Ballesteros, Nabil Ejey and Mubox Studio. Gutiérrez Arrieta and Natale studied together at ECAM and they have received development funding from the Region of Murcia and La 7, Murcia’s regional television channel. They are seeking other sources of funding in Spain and Italy, where Natale is from. They are planning to shoot at least parts of the film in the summer of 2027.

Director Paolo Natale and Producer Manuela Gutiérrez Arrieta, ‘Our Raised Skin’



Variety interviewed Natale about the film.

You say the film is about male bodies and the fear of its touch. Can you elaborate?

Paolo Natale: This film is written from a very specific and precise observation of the dynamics that drive relationships of power and violence against bodies within the family, but drawing on reality is just one further layer, and I believe the project straddles the line between situational portrayal and theatrical staging. I’ve always been aware, ever since my childhood, that I had a problem with food. Or rather, an emotional problem that was managed through food and, consequently, a sense of the violence directed at obese bodies and all that this entails in various spheres. I didn’t know how to put this into words until I was 23. I gradually realized that there was a pattern, passed down through the male figures in my family via their upbringing. A way of managing emotions that involved food. I’ve internalized this, just as my father did.

It’s very common for men with eating disorders to feel shame and guilt. This is something that often leads to delayed diagnoses. We tend to associate bigorexia with men. All men are taught that they must achieve a certain physique in order to exert power over others — a strong body with which to capitalize on everything. However, emotional hunger or binge-eating disorders are different. Softness and flaccidity are frowned upon, and there is still a great deal of silence surrounding these issues among men.

Why did you decide not to do a regular narrative feature film?

Natale: I feel more at home with a documentary-style approach, so to speak. I’m also interested, from a cinematic perspective, in films that manage to navigate different layers and textures, whether on a formal, aesthetic or narrative level. I like films that are unsettling in that sense, and that’s what I want to make. I almost always value the risk and the intentions more than the result itself. I like and am moved by films that are mistakenly regarded as cinematic exercises, as imperfect films from an industrial point of view. The ‘small, fragile films’ are far removed even from standardized forms of funding, although sadly most of us find ourselves swept in the same direction.

You mentioned that as a child you heard orange fat overflowing and and flooding everything. What do you think it meant?

Natale: Fat is something that is present in our bodies from the moment we are born until we die. Our fat is political. It is a viscous substance with which we must come to terms. It is also guilt and pain, but above all, for me, it represents life itself. All bodies store fat, no matter how much of a calorie deficit you create. Fat has been present throughout human history.

What do you mean when you say you want to make the aesthetic political, while reflecting on the ethics of aesthetics and representation?

Natale: I am someone who is quite concerned about the issue of representation, cinematic formats and their use. I am a little tired of canonically beautiful, sharply defined images, of that sense of neatness. What does an image need to have to be considered cinematic? What must it possess to attain that status? What hierarchy lies behind these images? What constitutes an ‘elevated’ image?

I believe we find ourselves immersed in a contemporary context overflowing with canonically beautiful images, featuring naturalistic lighting and well-defined faces and bodies. Neat digital images and unjustified uses of film that reflect a social and class-based hierarchy of images. While high-resolution images seem to possess a certain power, low-resolution images bear witness to a technological failure and amateur production.

I wish to champion imperfection, placing at the center those images that show signs of fading, blurred and out of focus. I wish to approach male bodies from a place of acceptance of ‘flaw,’ thereby eschewing the norms and fetishism of visual capitalism.

title: Rio Film Festival Head on Bookending Fest With ‘La Bola Negra’ and ‘Club Kid,’ Expanding Premiére Brasil: ‘I Don’t Want a Festival By-the-Book’
summary: If you ever attended a major film festival in the last three decades, chances are you came across an auburn-haired woman sporting fashionable big glasses and pristinely curated outfits from some of Brazil’s most exciting up-and-coming fashion designers. This is Ilda Santiago, the artistic director of Brazil’s leading Rio Film Festival. The programming veteran has […]
content:
If you ever attended a major film festival in the last three decades, chances are you came across an auburn-haired woman sporting fashionable big glasses and pristinely curated outfits from some of Brazil’s most exciting up-and-coming fashion designers. This is Ilda Santiago, the artistic director of Brazil’s leading Rio Film Festival. The programming veteran has spent decades working to narrow the bridges between her hometown and international cinephilia, working tirelessly to secure some of the year’s buzziest titles for her festival as competition grows fiercer and fiercer.

Santiago has excelled at the task this year. The upcoming edition, running between October 1-11, will open with perhaps the buzziest title at Cannes this year, Los Javis’s “La Bola Negra,” and close with the second buzziest, Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid.” With over 270 features in the program, the festival will welcome 16 national Oscar submissions, including Brazil’s own “Gugu’s World,” “La Bola Negra,” Lukas Dhont’s “Coward,” and Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose,” starring Sandra Hüller in a transformative performance. Other major films to play at the festival include Beth de Araújo’s “Josephine,” Diego Luna’s “Ashes,” and Benjamin Naishtat’s “Glaxo.”

Popular on Variety

The festival’s homegrown talent strand, Premiére Brasil, has expanded into several sub-strands, with over 100 films vowing for the coveted Redentor Trophy. World premieres include Brazilian closing gala “100 Days,” the first live-action film by “Rio” helmer Carlos Saldanha; lauded docmaker Lucia Murat’s “The Hinterlands of Our Memories,” chronicling the country’s tough military dictatorship; and Pedro Waddington’s “Fernanda,” a documentary on the life of Oscar-nominated Brazilian acting legend Fernanda Montenegro (“Central Station”).

South Korea is this year’s country of focus at RioMarket, the festival’s industry sidebar running October 1-10. This year’s event will feature lengthy discussions on burning topics such as AI, diversity, TikTok, and awards strategies, with more being announced soon.

La Bola Negra La Bola Negra Courtesy of Movistar Plus

Speaking with Variety ahead of kicking off this year’s edition, Santiago says the festival’s opening and closing films “translate our desire to be in communication with younger audiences.” “These are films that are not hermetic; they have an interesting visual language and a well-constructed sense of dramaturgy. They are, from a macro point of view, more commercial films; they can reach wider audiences. We, as a festival, want to put forward new talent, but solid talent, because it’s not just about being young and new.”

The programmer noticed a rise in contemporary stories told through a lens of the past, but that also say something about where we are moving to as a society. “We have short-term memory as a society,” she points out. “Many times, we don’t know about our own stories. ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘Coward,’ ‘Prima Facie’ tell stories that use dramaturgy to usher in societal issues we might have either forgotten or not spoken about enough.”

Santiago and her team also purposefully wanted to program films that give the public a “sense of inner calm.” “I don’t think we should walk out of every film feeling like the world is going to end. Cinema has this capacity to get us out of our comfort zone, but also usher us into a place of hope and belief in humanity. Cinema isn’t there just to drive us to madness. We need to lean into this duality of the form.”

Asked about what the festival slate can tell us about the current state of Brazilian cinema following back-to-back banner years with Walter Salles’s “I’m Still Here,” and Kleber Mendonça Filho’s “The Secret Agent,” Santiago mentions how several docs are telling the stories of some of Brazil’s greatest, including Montenegro, singer Elza Soares and Dior muse Vera Valdez.

“These are people who make us proud to be Brazilian. I am a very, very proud Brazilian and I do what I do out of a desire to bring our stories and culture to the world and bring the world to my country. Brazil is a curious country; Rio audiences are very curious and very open to different ideas.”

Premiére Brasil has grown exponentially over the years, turning into an umbrella that sees sidebar sections focused on coming-of-agers, documentaries, genre, and more. “With Premiére Brasil, I think about carving pathways for audiences to understand the films that are coming out from our country,” says Santiago.

“We started with the competitive strands, and we have found out that we needed new ways of organizing all the work that was coming out,” she adds. “We have several entry points for audiences to connect with Brazilian cinema. When I think about the selection, I think about consistent high quality, and allowing Brazilian audiences to understand Brazilian cinema isn’t one singular thing. Our cinema is plural. I don’t want audiences to say they are going to the cinema to watch a Brazilian film; I want them to seek genre films, dramas, coming-of-agers, which just so happen to be Brazilian.”

“100 Days,” courtesy of Rio Film Festival

This year, Santiago worked on championing national coming-of-agers. “They used to be quite the American monopoly for a long time,” she notes. “If we want to attract young generations to cinemas, they need to see themselves on screen. We need to foment a cinemagoing habit from an early age, when they are teens.”

Another focus point this year is the festival’s strengthened relationship with Spain and the Spanish film industry. Not only is a major Spanish film opening the festival, but leading Spanish producer Esther García is also presiding over the jury. “This is a relationship we need to pay great attention to,” says Santiago. “It’s a natural pathway for Brazilian producers.”

“Today, I see young people in Brazil actively trying to learn Spanish, which is something I didn’t see ten years ago,” she says. “There’s this latent desire from a new Brazilian generation to be connected with their Latin heritage and cultural identity.”

Santiago says the Latin world used to feel “a bit foreign” to Brazilians, but today, the country widely recognizes itself as part of the cultural identity. “Brazilian cinema wants to be in conversation with Latin cinema, and Latin cinema wants to tap into the huge market that is Brazil. Spain consolidates a lot of Spanish-speaking cinema, and I believe it is the ideal partner to allow us to grow as an industry and build more and more partnerships with the world.”

The festival also platforms some of Brazil’s most anticipated series. After premiering hit crime series “Tremembé” last year, the festival will screen Amazon MGM Studios’ “Marília Mendonça: All the Feels,” a highly awaited documentary about superstar singer Marília Mendonça, who died in a tragic plane crash in 2021. Other major series to screen at the festival include Aly Muritiba’s “City of God: The Fight Rages On” and Leonardo Lacca and Marcelo Lordello’s “Delegado,” produced by Mendonça Filho and Oscar-nominated Emilie Lesclaux.

Santiago says she “doesn’t want to make a festival by-the-book.” “I want a festival that can face the issues of our contemporary world,” she adds. “I’ve been in the industry for over 30 years. I’ve seen VHS turn into DVDs, turn into digital, turn into streaming. I believe a festival needs to not only understand new formats, but work on the best way of welcoming them and embedding them into the identity of the festival. I am far from conservative in this sense.”

“Something very special about the festival is the trust audiences have in us,” she emphasizes. “Audiences are willing to take a chance, and this allows us to be a bit bolder with the programme, and to take risks. And it’s important to know how to take risks, because audiences don’t want just the obvious. Yes, they want ‘La Bola Negra,’ but that is the gateway to another ten films they might not be aware of and will come to love and be challenged by.”

title: Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Mizoguchi Retrospective, Anime Award Symposium and Teens Cinema Workshop Milestone
summary: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival has announced a slate of cultural programs running alongside its main competition, headlined by a 13-film retrospective honoring Mizoguchi Kenji on the 70th anniversary of his death, a symposium exploring a potential new international anime award, and a 10th-anniversary celebration of its Teens Cinema Workshop. The Mizoguchi tribute, staged […]
content:
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival has announced a slate of cultural programs running alongside its main competition, headlined by a 13-film retrospective honoring Mizoguchi Kenji on the 70th anniversary of his death, a symposium exploring a potential new international anime award, and a 10th-anniversary celebration of its Teens Cinema Workshop.

The Mizoguchi tribute, staged as TIFF/NFAJ Classics in collaboration with the National Film Archive of Japan, runs Oct. 27–Nov. 1 at the Archive’s Nagase Memorial Theatre Ozu. All 13 films screen with English subtitles across 12 programs, with an emphasis on newly restored prints. The standout presentation is “The Water Magician” (1933), receiving its first screening in Japan in a new digital restoration carried out with support from the Yanai Initiative, a joint project of Waseda University and UCLA. The retrospective also includes live benshi narration and musical accompaniment alongside guest talks.

The full screening schedule spans “Osaka Elegy” (1936), “Sisters of Gion” (1936), “The 47 Ronin” (Parts One and Two, 1941–42), “The Story of the Last Chrysanthemums” (digital restoration, 1939), “Yang Kwei Fei” (1955), “New Tales of the Taira Clan” (digital restoration, 1955), “Street of Shame” (digital restoration, 1956), “Gion Bayashi” (1953), “Ugetsu” (digital restoration, 1953), “Sansho the Bailiff” (digital restoration, 1954) and “A Story From Chikamatsu” (digital restoration, 1954).

Popular on Variety

At the festival’s market TIFFCOM, Tokyo Anime Next will stage a one-hour symposium on Oct. 30 titled “Toward the Launch of a New Anime Award in 2027,” examining the case for an international prize led by the Japanese animation industry. Speakers include Shimizu Akira, director of the Association of Japanese Animations and president and representative director of A-1 Pictures, with TIFF Animation programming advisor Fujitsu Ryota moderating. The TIFF Animation section will also present three separate symposia featuring directors from Japan and abroad, with details to follow.

The TIFF Teens Cinema Workshop, which offers secondary school students hands-on filmmaking training, marks its 10th year with a special Nov. 3 event at Toho Cinemas Chanter. Past lead mentors – directors Suwa Nobuhiro (2017), Sugita Kyoshi (2019), Seta Natsuki (2021) and Hayakawa Chie (2022) – will participate in screenings and discussions. The workshop has also shifted from its traditional August schedule to March going forward. A new companion program, TIFF Teens Cine Club, offering participants deeper engagement with film through both making and watching, is planned, with details to be announced. Both programs are co-hosted by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government.

Rounding out the education strand, the fourth TIFF International Symposium on Film Education takes place Oct. 31 at the National Film Archive of Japan, under the theme “Developing Educators and Building Support for Film Education.” The free event includes guests from France, with consecutive interpretation in Japanese, French and English.

The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival runs Oct. 26–Nov. 4. TIFFCOM runs Oct. 28–30.

title: BBC Boss Matt Brittin On Expected Service Closures: “No Program Or Channel Will Exist Forever”
summary: BBC director-general Matt Brittin has hinted that the broadcaster is preparing to close TV and radio networks as it looks to save money and better serve audiences online. In an interview that will air over the weekend, Brittin told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the BBC’s ambition to save £500 million ($662M) “may well mean” […]
content:
BBC director-general Matt Brittin has hinted that the broadcaster is preparing to close TV and radio networks as it looks to save money and better serve audiences online.

In an interview that will air over the weekend, Brittin told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the BBC’s ambition to save £500 million ($662M) “may well mean” that services are shut.

The former Google executive said the BBC “wouldn’t guarantee any program or any channel will exist forever. The tight financial situation means that we’re having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like.”

Brittin’s comments follow Deadline reporting on Wednesday that the BBC is expected to announce the closure of TV and radio networks as early as next week. There is speculation about the future of BBC Three, but nothing is confirmed at this stage.

Watch on Deadline

“We wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever”



BBC Director General Matt Brittin has said that the BBC's financial situation "may well mean" that some channels and radio stations will have to close.#BBCLauraKhttps://t.co/JZziQESjYy pic.twitter.com/m6Iv4cWEsU — BBC Politics (@BBCPolitics) September 25, 2026

Brittin told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “We might have some channels and services where maybe 100,000 people are watching the broadcast service, but 500,000 are getting those programs on iPlayer. When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.”

He added that the BBC had to go “in different ways to reach audiences and we’re locked into yesterday’s model of how people consume content and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow’s world.”

The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap.

Up to 2,000 jobs are at risk under the savings strategy, while the BBC is also involved in tense negotiations with unions over employee pay rises. Unions have rejected two BBC offers, meaning the risk of industrial action is increasing.

title: International Insider: Deep BBC Cuts Begin; Ali G Under Fire; San Sebastian Report
summary: Once again with feeling, Insiders. Jesse Whittock at the helm this week with a roundup of the biggest news and views from the TV and film world. Off we go, and sign up to the Insider newsletter for the full experience here. BBC Cuts Begin It starts now: There’s an argument that this is one […]
content:
Once again with feeling, Insiders. Jesse Whittock at the helm this week with a roundup of the biggest news and views from the TV and film world. Off we go, and sign up to the Insider newsletter for the full experience here.

BBC Cuts Begin

BBC boss Matt Brittin Carl Court/Getty Images

It starts now: There’s an argument that this is one of the bleakest periods in the history of the BBC. The UK broadcaster said in February it would seek £500M ($661M) in further cost savings on top of a previously announced £1.5B, and ever since there has been a drip, drip of news and rumor about where they will come from. The reality started to materialize more starkly this week. First it emerged 41 roles were going from BBC Sport before Jake revealed that major cuts to the TV and radio networks business could see the closure of a channel such as youth-skewing BBC3 as soon as next week. Deadline then revealed another 150 in the BBC’s tech division were expected to take voluntary redundancy. Collectively, the tech and sports exits could save around £17M, which barely touches the sides of overall savings required. This is an indicator of how deep things are going to go over the next few years. The broader picture is the BBC’s licence fee model, where Brits pay around £180 a year for its content and channels, which is under extreme threat. Around 94% use BBC services, but less than 80% are paying for them. This has caused a funding crisis that has become something of a lightning rod for culture wars debates over the future of the BBC. Some want the broadcaster gone completely, while for others it’s the crown jewel in British soft power around the world. Stay tuned to Deadline over coming weeks, as further cuts emerge. On top of all of this are tense conversations being held with unions over staff pay. Hate to say it, but this feels bleak.

Ali G Under Fire

Watch on Deadline

Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G Amazon MGM Studios

“Microwaving a relic”: Ali G was once a cultural phenomenon in the UK, propelling creator Sacha Baron Cohen to Hollywood with his suburban rude boy ways. Even back then, though, there was extreme discomfort within the Black British community about the character, who Baron Cohen claims is a pastiche of young men who culturally appropriate Black culture. They saw him as laughing at them, not with them, and that view has only amplified since Ali G’s heyday in the 1990s, so it was, to say the least, a big surprise when it emerged Baron Cohen was stepping back into his sneakers and reprising the character in MGM Studios’ Ali G: Who Iz I?. There was a wave of backlash when a trailer dropped for the film last month, and a host of Black creatives have now gone on record to criticize the pic. Dane Baptiste, creator of BBC shows Sunny D and Bamous, said Baron Cohen was “microwaving a relic from a generation ago” and was a step backwards in the post-Black Lives Matter era. Bob Hearts Abishola creator Gina Yashere and Paradise City actor Curtis Walker were among others calling out the character, though Deadline managed to speak with Colton Dunn, the Superstore actor who is one of three Black writers who worked on Ali G: Who Iz I?. Dunn called Ali G “a tool to expose racists,” and denied the character itself is racist.

The Deadline Interview: Abiba Coulibaly

Abiba Coulibaly

Next month will see the end of one of the UK’s most interesting cinema projects, when the Brixton Community Cinema closes its doors for the final time. The pop-up, pay-what-you-can cinema began in south London in 2022 and grew a reputation for eclectic and thought-provoking programming, so creator Abiba Coulibaly’s announcement of the closure took people by surprise. And the reason she is ending things now? You’ll have to click through to Zac’s exclusive chat with the film programmer to find out. >>>Read The Interview

San Sebastian Report

San Sebastian International Film Festival San Sebastian International Film Festival

Pitt stop: San Sebastián ends on Saturday with Le Faux Soir, the latest feature from Belgian filmmaker Michaël R. Roskam. High-profile visitors to the Spanish fest this year included Brad Pitt, who screened Heart of the Beast, and the veteran actor also shared some interesting thoughts about the indie film space. Check those comments out here. The festival’s Creative Investors’ Conference also returned for its fifth year. Topics discussed at the event included AI and Brazil’s current production boom. Check out our coverage of the conference here, and check back on Saturday to see who wins the festival’s top prize. This year’s San Seb is longtime festival director José Luis Rebordinos’s last in charge, as Maialen Beloki, the festival’s current deputy, will succeed him in January.

The Essentials

Susan Sarandon and Olivia Colman Darren Tieste/Josh Telles for Deadline

🌶️ Hot One: Oscar winners Susan Sarandon and Olivia Colman have joined Paddy Considine, America Ferrera, Alex Hassell and Kit Harington in Channel 4 thriller series Army of Shadows.

🌶️ Another: Sky has found its Mikael Blomkvist and Lisbeth Salander for the upcoming TV adaptation of Stieg Larsson’s The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo in the shape of David Oyelowo and Viola Prettejohn.

🔥 Fiery Third: Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to The Great Dictator, Matthew Sweet’s biography of the flamboyant and eccentric late author Dame Barbara Cartland.

🤓 De Heer today: The Tokyo International Film Festival has named Australian director Rolf de Heer as president of the International Competition jury.

⛺ Fest latest: The 2026 edition of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea International Film Festival has been cancelled, with the event postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027.

🗣️ Interview: The new boss of the UK’s influential Royal Television Society told Max the charity should shout louder about the nation’s “powerhouse” TV industry.

📦 Care package: Shaftesbury founder Christina Jennings issued an “urgent call to action” to the Canadian kids’ TV industry as she announced a significant package of financial support at the Ottawa International Animation Festival.

😎 Roll out the red carpet: Tom Cruise and Digger took over London’s Leicester Square Gardens on Tuesday for the world premiere of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s dark political comedy.

🚨 Sound the alarm: France’s film and TV sectors issued an open letter decrying a proposed €47M ($53M) cut in public funds for state broadcaster France Télévisions.

🤝 Done deal: Independent Talent Group has bought into UK sport talent agency Tongue Tied Management.

💰 Another deal: Patrick Spence has taken control of AC Chapter One, completing a management buyout from Anonymous Content and UK agencies Casarotto Ramsay and United Agents.

🍿 Box office: Resident Evil rang up a massive $108.3M worldwide, the best start the franchise has ever seen.

🎥 Trail: For You Can See Everything, A24’s much-anticipated Elizabeth Holmes doc.

Photo of the Week

John Phillips/Getty Images for Netflix

Bookish – Florence Pugh was among the stars at the British Library this week as the institution unveiled a partnership with Netflix aimed at helping people discover books.

title: Noel Hedges Joins Boat Rocker Studios In Global Acquisitions Role
summary: EXCLUSIVE: International TV industry veteran Noel Hedges has found his next gig. We can reveal Hedges has joined Canada’s Boat Rocker Studios as Senior VP, Global Acquisitions and Content Strategy. The role will be based in Boat Rocker’s London, UK office. This comes after Deadline was first with the news Hedges had exited Lionsgate earlier […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: International TV industry veteran Noel Hedges has found his next gig.

We can reveal Hedges has joined Canada’s Boat Rocker Studios as Senior VP, Global Acquisitions and Content Strategy. The role will be based in Boat Rocker’s London, UK office.

This comes after Deadline was first with the news Hedges had exited Lionsgate earlier this year. A well known face at international markets, he has more than 25 years’ experience with senior roles at the likes of DRG, ITV Studios, Cineflix and eOne, prior to its acquisition by Lionsgate.

In his newly created role, Hedges will seek to increase the long-term value of Boat Rocker’s content portfolio through IP acquisitions, rights ownership deals and co-production partnerships. He will report directly to Jon Rutherford, Boat Rocker’s President, Global Content & Rights. Hedges will start with the company in early October and be at MIPCOM with the Boat Rocker team.

Watch on Deadline

“In addition to his wealth of experience, Noel is extremely well-regarded throughout the industry, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the Boat Rocker Studios team,” said Rutherford. “This is an exciting time for our company as we continue to execute on our strategic priorities, with a clear focus on investing in great IP and maximizing its value across our business.”

Boat Rocker’s projects include Netflix’s Bet and Geek Girl; BBC, Binge and RTÉ co-production Mix Tape; BBC Scotland and Sky New Zealand series The Ridge, Apple TV’s Invasion and Palm Royale, BBC America and CTV drama Orphan Black and kids series The Next Step.

“I’m excited to join Boat Rocker at a time when the company is investing so deliberately in distinctive, high-quality IP,” said Hedges. “I look forward to working with the team to source ambitious projects and strengthen and expand Boat Rocker’s already impressive content portfolio.”

Earlier this week, we reported that Boat Rocker had landed rights to Doula: A True Crime, an upcoming CBC doc series launching in Cannes at MIPCOM.

Following Blue Ant Media’s reverse takeover of Boat Rocker Media last year, Ivan Schneeberg, David Fortier and John Young formed a new business to take over Boat Rocker Studios and effectively relaunched the business. It has Toronto, London, L.A., New York and Hong Kong.

title: BBC Studios Names Mediawan’s Sally Habbershaw President Of Global Distribution
summary: BBC Studios has a new global distribution chief in place. Sally Habbershaw is exiting Mediawan after less than a year to become President of Global Distribution at the BBC’s commercial arm. Her London-based role will see her overseeing BBCS’s worldwide content sales business, reporting into Zai Bennett, BBC Studios Global Content CEO and Chief Creative […]
content:
BBC Studios has a new global distribution chief in place.

Sally Habbershaw is exiting Mediawan after less than a year to become President of Global Distribution at the BBC’s commercial arm.

Her London-based role will see her overseeing BBCS’s worldwide content sales business, reporting into Zai Bennett, BBC Studios Global Content CEO and Chief Creative Officer.

BBC Studios has been without a sales boss for most of the year, as the U.S.-based Janet Brown exited in January as part of a plan to move distribution closer to the mothership in the UK. Habbershaw takes up her “newly expanded” post on September 29.

“Sally is one of the most accomplished and respected executives in the business and her experience across content investment, distribution, platforms and production makes her uniquely positioned to lead our global content distribution operation,” said Bennett.

Watch on Deadline

“She brings a rare combination of commercial leadership, creative instincts and deep global market expertise, alongside an exceptional track record of building partnerships and delivering growth across some of the industry’s most successful content businesses. I look forward to working with her as we continue to maximise the value and reach of our outstanding content portfolio.”

Habbershaw was the subject of news this time last year in the run up to MIPCOM Cannes, when she replaced Valerie Vleeschhouwer at France’s Mediawan. She was named Chief Distribution Officer at the Adolescence producer.

Last year, Deadline revealed that Habbershaw was exiting her New York-based role as Americas sales chief at All3Media International to move back to the UK, though she subsequently joined Paris-based Mediawan.

Further back in her career, Habbershaw held senior roles at A&E Networks, AMC Networks, Viacom and several Paramount-owned businesses. She is also a BAFTA Board member and Deputy Chair of BAFTA North America.

“After twenty years in the US and, more recently, in France, coming home to do this work here matters to me,” said Habbershaw. “The content and the brand speak for themselves. What made the opportunity irresistible is the moment and the people.

“Zai has built a leadership team that is ambitious, thinks differently and is set on making a real impact. I’ve spent my career on the other side of the table from the BBC, so I arrive with a clear view of its strengths and of the work ahead.”

Habbershaw’s hire is the latest major development this year in an international TV market that has seen Habbershaw’s former company, All3Media, merge with Banijay. Fair to say it’s been a period of change for the sales business as a whole ahead of MIPCOM.

title: Percy Hynes White & Jeff Wahlberg Lead Lovers-On-The-Run Thriller ‘Crime Novella’, Roland Emmerich Exec-Producing & First Look Revealed
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Percy Hynes White (My Old Ass), Jeff Wahlberg (Euphoria), Zlatko Burić (Triangle of Sadness), Bobby Soto (The Tax Collector) and Ava del Cielo (House of Cards) have been cast in writer-director Omar de Soto’s feature directorial debut, Crime Novella, which was shot on 35mm film. Written, directed and produced by de Soto, the romance […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Percy Hynes White (My Old Ass), Jeff Wahlberg (Euphoria), Zlatko Burić (Triangle of Sadness), Bobby Soto (The Tax Collector) and Ava del Cielo (House of Cards) have been cast in writer-director Omar de Soto’s feature directorial debut, Crime Novella, which was shot on 35mm film.



Written, directed and produced by de Soto, the romance crime-thriller “tells the story of two lovers on the run to save their relationship, discovering how far they’ll have to go to stay together.” Below is a first look image.

Production wrapped this summer with filming taking place on location in Albuquerque, New Mexico, Los Angeles, Las Vegas and Mexico. In addition to de Soto, the movie is produced by Paul Bennett IV of Replica and Marco Shepherd (Midway) of Centropolis Entertainment, which financed the feature. Roland Emmerich is executive producer. Jessica Olthof and Helena Martel Seward are co-producers.

Producers describe the film as “a modern descendant of Badlands and Wild at Heart with a transgressive spirit”.



Omar de Soto, husband of master of disaster Emmerich, said: “I couldn’t have asked for a more fitting cast. Cash and Valentine have always been the heart of this film, and Percy and Jeff understood the world I was trying to build from the beginning. Percy and Jeff are intoxicating onscreen. You simply cannot take your eyes off them. Zlatko, Bobby and Ava each brought their own special sauce and made our whimsical world feel lived in. I’m incredibly proud of this cast and deeply grateful to my producers and crew who believed in the film and helped us make it on our own terms. This is their moment.”



Hynes White is best know for his role in Netflix’s hit Wednesday, where he portrayed Xavier Thorpe in season 1. He also starred in the coming-of-age Sundance comedy-drama My Old Ass. Wahlberg most recently appeared in season 3 of HBO’s smash, Euphoria.



Burić won Best Actor at the 35th European Film Awards for his role in Ruben Östlund’s satirical black comedy Triangle of Sadness, which won the Palme d’Or at the 75th Cannes Film Festival in 2022. He has previously worked with Emmerich and Centropolis Entertainment on the disaster epic 2012. Soto had a leading role with Shia LaBeouf in David Ayer’s The Tax Collector. Del Cielo’s notable credits include Netflix’s House of Cards, From Dusk Till Dawn: The Series and Get Shorty, streaming on MGM+.



Hynes White is repped by Innovative Artists and Oscars Abrams Zimel & Associates (OAZ), and Sloane, Offer; Wahlberg is repped by Innovative Artists, Leverage Management, Sloane Offer; Burić is repped by Art Management; Soto is repped by Innovative Artists, Anonymous Content and Goodman, Genow; and Del Cielo is repped by Mitchell & Associates Talent. CAA reps Emmerich and Centropolis Entertainment.

Watch on Deadline

Crime Novella, credit: Centropolis

title: Endemol Shine North America CEO Sharon Levy Exits After Nearly a Decade
summary: Sharon Levy is exiting Banijay’s Endemol Shine North America after nearly a decade at the company — including most recently as CEO. The restructure comes following this summer’s completion of the $8 billion merger between Banijay and All3Media, with Banijay Americas CEO Ben Samek overseeing the combined company’s U.S. entity. “Sharon has played an integral […]
content:
Sharon Levy is exiting Banijay’s Endemol Shine North America after nearly a decade at the company — including most recently as CEO.

The restructure comes following this summer’s completion of the $8 billion merger between Banijay and All3Media, with Banijay Americas CEO Ben Samek overseeing the combined company’s U.S. entity.

“Sharon has played an integral role in building ESNA into the creative powerhouse it is today, and her influence has been felt across Banijay America and the wider Banijay group,” a Banijay Americas spokesperson said in a statement. “She has built a varied and healthy slate of titles that continue to thrive year-over year, spanning global franchises, creative IP extensions and scripted hits.”

Popular on Variety

As CEO, Levy led the indie Endemol Shine North America shingle’s output, which has included unscripted fare like “Lego Masters,” “MasterChef” and “Deal or No Deal,” as well as Netflix’s scripted series “Ripley.” She first joined Endemol Shine North America in 2017 as president, unscripted and scripted TV.

In 2021, Levy was named chief content officer, and then upped to CEO in 2023 at Endemol Shine North America as it shifted from its dual role as a studio and Banijay Americas’ holding company to solely an independent production company.

Besides the Emmy Award-nominated “Lego Masters” and the “MasterChef” and “MasterChef Junior” franchises on Fox, Levy’s oversight at Endemol Shine included Fox’s TBS’ revamped “Wipeout,” USA/Peacock’s “The Courtship,” the revived “Extreme Makeover: Home Edition” for ABC, “Fear Factor: House of Fear” at Fox, “Deal or No Deal Island” at NBC and “The Summit” on CBS.

Prior to her time at Endemol Shine, Levy was executive vice president of original series for Spike TV for seven years, where she led acquisition, creation and production of the network’s entertainment with shows like “Ink Master,” “Bar Rescue,” “Auction Hunters” and “Deadliest Warrior.”

Deadline was first with the news of Levy’s departure.

title: Global Citizen Festival 2026 Canceled Due to Extreme Weather Affecting New York City
summary: Global Citizen Festival has been canceled due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City. The event was slated to take place on Saturday at the Great Lawn in Central Park, with performances from Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend and more. But organizers shared that they had to make the […]
content:
Global Citizen Festival has been canceled due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City.

The event was slated to take place on Saturday at the Great Lawn in Central Park, with performances from Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend and more. But organizers shared that they had to make the difficult decision to call off the festival for the first time in 14 years.

“Forecasts predict dangerous conditions and circumstances in which we cannot safely bring tens of thousands of Global Citizens, artists, crew, vendors, partners, and staff onto the Great Lawn, let alone all of the equipment required,” said organizers. “Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we’ve had to cancel. We have spent this week working through countless contingencies, which were ultimately not possible, and cancelling is a decision we have not taken lightly.”

Those who purchased tickets will be refunded automatically, while those who acquired tickets through a donation will also be refunded. Options will be provided via email today for those who donated. Food that was meant to be available at the festival will be donated to local organizations in New York City.

Popular on Variety

“The Festival is one day, but the actions you took and the impact you created will reach far beyond Central Park,” continued the statement. “Conflict, extreme weather, and rising costs are forcing millions of families from their homes, disrupting education, threatening food supplies and pushing communities back into extreme poverty, but we have seen what is possible when we take action together.”

Additional performers for Global Citizen Festival included Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey, Tomorrow X Together, Victoria Monét, Yeonjun, Yoshiki and Alicia Keys with friends. Hugh Jackman was set to host.

Along with Global Citizen Festival, the three-day All Things Go NYC Festival was canceled just hours before doors were set to open on Friday afternoon due to the extreme weather conditions affecting the city.

title: ‘Princess Diaries’ Star Heather Matarazzo Reveals She May Lose Health Insurance If She Doesn’t Work Again Soon: ‘Lots of Actors’ Are in the ‘Same Boat’
summary: “Princess Diaries” star Heather Matarazzo revealed she may not qualify for health insurance if she doesn’t find work soon. The actress, who starred alongside Anne Hathaway in the “Princess Diaries” films as Lilly Moscovitz, replied to a post from “Atypical” actor Jack Haven that revealed they needed work in order to qualify for health insurance […]
content:
“Princess Diaries” star Heather Matarazzo revealed she may not qualify for health insurance if she doesn’t find work soon.

The actress, who starred alongside Anne Hathaway in the “Princess Diaries” films as Lilly Moscovitz, replied to a post from “Atypical” actor Jack Haven that revealed they needed work in order to qualify for health insurance through SAG-AFTRA.

The guild offers a health plan for its members that requires a “minimum earnings” threshold be met to qualify. However, booking projects in the entertainment industry is often unpredictable and fluctuates, which leads to larger gaps between employment opportunities and ultimately makes meeting that threshold more difficult.

“I’m in a bit of an emergency situation,” Haven shared in a YouTube video this week. “I need to make $4,000 by the end of the month in order to qualify for SAG health insurance starting in January.”

Popular on Variety

The actor shared their skills and said they will do “pretty much any job,” encouraging anyone open to hiring them on a production under SAG to contact them over email.

Matarazzo replied to a post about Haven’s plea, writing, “I am literally in the same boat right now. Lots of my fellow actors are. I remember a time when we didn’t have to earn a minimum to qualify for insurance. Glad to see that Jack has gotten an offer that will let them to qualify for 2027.”

As detailed on the SAG Health Plan’s eligibility page, the minimum threshold is expected to rise by approximately $900 each year until 2030. This year, members were required to earn $28,933. SAG-AFTRA did not respond immediately to comment.

Matarazzo’s most recent project was the 2025 short film “Paper Tiger.” She also starred “Welcome to the Dollhouse,” “The Devil’s Advocate” and “Scream 3,” as well as multiple episodes of Netflix’s “Wednesday.”

title: Liza Soberano and H.E.R. on Why Dreamworks Animation’s ‘Forgotten Island’ Story of Friendship Resonated With Them
summary: Dreamworks Animation knows how to tell stories about friendships, whether it’s between a boy and a dragon in “How to Train Your Dragon” or Donkey and Ogre in “Shrek” or a robot and bird in “The Wild Robot.” Its latest feature, “Forgotten Island,” anchors its story in two best friends who face being separated when […]
content:
Dreamworks Animation knows how to tell stories about friendships, whether it’s between a boy and a dragon in “How to Train Your Dragon” or Donkey and Ogre in “Shrek” or a robot and bird in “The Wild Robot.” Its latest feature, “Forgotten Island,” anchors its story in two best friends who face being separated when one has to go abroad to college. One final night together puts their friendship to the test.

Liza Soberano and H.E.R. lead the voice cast as Raissa and Jo, who find themselves stranded in the mystical world of the forgotten island of Nakali. They come to find that their only way home might come at the expense of a lifetime of memories and emotions. Written and directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, the film is produced by Mark Swift.

Popular on Variety

“Forgotten Island,” out now in theaters, centers around Filipino folklore, but its beating heart is the universal story of two teenage best friends who share memories and experiences.

Speaking with Variety, Soberano says the story was one that hit home. Growing up in the Philippines, she understood the theme of “losing” a family member or a friend who needed to go overseas for a better quality of life and to make a better living for themselves. Soberano explains, “I’ve seen all the different permutations of how that could affect family and loved ones that you’re leaving behind.”

The story struck a deeper chord when she left a successful career in the Philippines to make it in America. “I also went through that journey and that experience three years ago,” she says. She was particularly torn about leaving behind her little sister. “It was really heartbreaking because I was afraid of, I was afraid of us not being close anymore — not just in proximity, but in the relationship itself. I was afraid that we would grow apart. But through this, I actually discovered that there are so many reasons to not grow apart. You have to really fight for the relationship and fight for the closeness, no matter how far you physically are from one another. I find a lot of comfort in that, and this movie has taught me so much about it.”

Similarly, H.E.R., who grew up near Vallejo, California, also found the story relatable. “I left when I was 17 to move to New York and it wasn’t as far away — just across the country. But it felt super far. My sister was eight at the time, and I was 17 and she wanted her big sister around.”

While friendship is the beating heart of the film, “Forgotten Island” also captures the Filipino experience through cultural details that resonated deeply with its cast.

H.E.R. recalls seeing the Filipino elements in the film for the first time. “Seeing the Filipino sun for the first time — even before seeing the full film — made us so emotional. I remember that day very well. I remember seeing ‘pasalubong’ written on the screen, and I thought, oh my gosh, this is as Filipino as it gets. The petroleum jelly, all those little details, just really made me feel like, wow, I’m so proud to be Filipino. This is reminding me of home right now.”

Soberano agrees, saying, “It was the despedida — the farewell party. That was such an accurate depiction of what it’s like to be at a Filipino house party. There’s so much chaos going on. You have the lolas and the lolos being grumpy at everyone, telling them to either eat, sit down or go sing — and not to be ‘magulo.’ Then you have the little kids doing their own thing, hiding under the tables and creating chaos everywhere. And, of course, you have the titos and titas either playing mahjong on the side or singing karaoke. I thought that was such a beautiful depiction of Filipino energy, but you also feel the love coming from everyone at the party.”

Aside from starring in the film, the pair also lend their voices to the film’s soundtrack. Their voices capture the nostalgia, warmth and joy that radiate from their characters and the movie as a whole.

Angela Leus, senior vice president of Film Music at Universal Pictures, previously told Variety that neither she nor the filmmakers wanted to assume that H.E.R. would create an original song. “Everything needed to come from an organic place,” Leus says. “But when H.E.R. saw the film, she was so inspired that she decided to write something — and she was even more inspired to bring in Liza.”

Speaking about the song, Soberano admits she felt “major impostor syndrome being there.” She asked herself, “What did I do in my life to deserve this?” She adds, “I just felt so honored and blessed to be part of it.”

H.E.R. echoes the sentiment, saying, “She killed it. There was no need to be nervous because it was just fun. The fact that we were singing as Jo and Raissa just wraps it all up. Then we shot the video in Manila and made it kind of like a travel vlog, continuing that love letter to the Philippines. I’m just grateful to be in this process, especially with Liza. I love these characters. I love this film. I’m forever grateful for it.”

title: ‘South Park’ Season 29 Premiere Hits 4.2 Million Viewers in Three Days and Jumps 33% in Rating After Renaming to ‘South America’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s latest stunt has paid off. The Season 29 premiere of “South America” — renamed from “South Park” as a parody of Donald Trump’s controversial initiatives to rename major landmarks — hit 4.2 million viewers in three days. That total accounts for viewership across Comedy Central and Paramount+ in the U.S. […]
content:
Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s latest stunt has paid off. The Season 29 premiere of “South America” — renamed from “South Park” as a parody of Donald Trump’s controversial initiatives to rename major landmarks — hit 4.2 million viewers in three days.

That total accounts for viewership across Comedy Central and Paramount+ in the U.S. alone. The episode’s audience was relatively even with the previous season premiere, which reached 4.3 million viewers in three days, while making strong improvements among viewers age 18-49. In that demographic, the episode scored a 0.97 rating after three days, up 33% from Season 28’s 0.73 rating, and a share of 4.77, up from 20% from last year’s 3.96. Between Monday and Friday, the “South America” premiere was the most-watched cable telecast of the week among adults 18-49, excluding sports programming.

Unsurprisingly, the first episode since renaming to “South America” drove conversation on social media. On the day of its premiere, the series ranked as the No. 1 most social cable comedy, and went on to generate 11 million views and one million engagements in three days. It garnered 63,000 online mentions in three days, a 40% increase from what the Season 28 premiere achieved in the same amount of time.

Popular on Variety

In a statement earlier this month, Parker and Stone said, “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of ‘South Park’ to ‘South America,’” referencing the fact that the tech companies have honored Trump’s name changes on their maps. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation.”

title: Global Citizen Festival Canceled Due To Nor’easter Threat Of Extreme Weather For New York City
summary: The organizers of the annual Global Citizen Festival in New York City’s Central Park have canceled this year’s event due to the Nor’easter-caused extreme weather forecast for this weekend. “Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York […]
content:
The organizers of the annual Global Citizen Festival in New York City’s Central Park have canceled this year’s event due to the Nor’easter-caused extreme weather forecast for this weekend.

“Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York and NYC Parks, to cancel this year’s Global Citizen Festival,” organizers said. “Forecasts predict dangerous conditions and circumstances in which we cannot safely bring tens of thousands of Global Citizens, artists, crew, vendors, partners, and staff onto the Great Lawn, let alone all of the equipment required.”

The statement continued, “Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we’ve had to cancel. We have spent this week working through countless contingencies, which were ultimately not possible, and cancelling is a decision we have not taken lightly.”

Watch on Deadline

The annual festival, which raises money and awareness to end extreme poverty around the world, was to have taken place this year on Saturday, September 26, on the Great Lawn in Central Park. Hosted by Hugh Jackman, the festival was to have featured appearances by Alicia Keys, Yeonjun, Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend, Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey and Tomorrow X Together, among many others.

Following the success of the first-ever FIFA World Cup Final Halftime Show, which was produced by Global Citizen and helped raise $60 million for the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, this year’s festival was designed to raise awareness and raise funds for childrens’ global educational opportunities, smallholder farmers and electricity for 2.5 million homes.

According to Global Citizen, the organization over the last six weeks has secured $208.8 million in financial commitments to help more than 2 million children access education and stay in school, and support 7.5 million people, including smallholder farmers, women, youth, and indigenous communities. Ireland and Canada committed $151.6 million to help children get in and stay in school; and Burundi, Chad, Ethiopia, Kenya, Guinea, Rwanda, Somalia, Sudan, and Zimbabwe, the Minderoo Foundation, and the Green Climate Fund will support small farming businesses.

“The Festival is one day,” the organization said, “but the actions you took and the impact you created will reach far beyond Central Park. Conflict, extreme weather, and rising costs are forcing millions of families from their homes, disrupting education, threatening food supplies and pushing communities back into extreme poverty, but we have seen what is possible when we take action together.”

Tickets to the Global Citizen Festival were free and could be secured by visiting the Global Citizen app and earning points by completing “action journeys” related to the core issues.

“You took action to earn your tickets,” today’s statement said. “You made plans, booked travel, and in many cases came to New York from across the country and around the world to be with us in Central Park, and we are sincerely grateful for your commitment to our mission.”

Festival tickets that were purchased outright will be refunded automatically. People who made a donation to secure tickets can also receive refunds, with email instructions being sent to outline options.

Food that was due to be available at the Festival will be donated to local organizations serving the people of New York City.

“We are enormously proud of what we have achieved together this year – one of the most impactful years for our movement around the world – and we are deeply grateful to every artist, world leader, partner, crew member, vendor, global citizen, and our team,” Global Citizen said, adding that the festival “will be back in Central Park next year.”

title: ‘Scrubs’ Zach Braff Gives Discouraging Ken Jenkins Return Update, Teases More Dr. Cox, Turk Mental Health Arc In Season 2
summary: Dr. Kelso may not return to Sacred Heart after all. When ABC announced the Season 2 cast of the Scrubs revival, including OGs coming back, Ken Jenkins’ name was not among them despite being on show creator Bill Lawrence’s wish list. “Dr. Kelso will be back next year,” Lawrence told Deadline in February, ahead of […]
content:
Dr. Kelso may not return to Sacred Heart after all. When ABC announced the Season 2 cast of the Scrubs revival, including OGs coming back, Ken Jenkins’ name was not among them despite being on show creator Bill Lawrence’s wish list.

“Dr. Kelso will be back next year,” Lawrence told Deadline in February, ahead of the Season 1 premiere. “It just didn’t work out this year but it will next year.”

That may have been too big of an ask for the 86-year retired actor Jenkins who portrayed former Sacred Heart Chief of Medicine Dr. Kelso for Scrubs‘ entire nine-season original run.

During a joint video interview with Scrubs‘ three stars/executive producers Zach Braff (J.D.) Sarah Chalke (Elliot) and Donald Faison (Turk), Braff provided an update on the status of Jenkins’ potential return.

“The fans want this so much, and I so respect that, we do too, but I think we just also need to be respectful of his age,” he said. “I’ll keep trying, but I think, for currently where he’s at, it’s a bit of a big ask, I’ll just say that.” (You can watch the video below.)

While Jenkins may not be able to make it, Season 2 has a stong contingent of original cast members returning as guest stars, led by John C. McGinley (Dr. Cox) and Judy Reyes (Carla), along with Neil Flynn (The Janitor), Krista Miller (Jordan), Robert Maschio (The Todd) and Scott Foley (Sean), who joins in Season 2 as a romantic interest to former flame Elliot (Chalke).

McGinley’s Dr. Cox is front and center in the opening episodes of Season 2 as his former pupils rally to find treatment for his autoimmune disease.

“We all find the story of all of his mentees rallying around to cure and and treat him really interesting and something we want to continue,” Braff said. “We want to keep Dr. Cox, Johnny C around, and we’ll continue to do that in different ways because the audience loves him, and we love him, and he’s such a valuable part of the show.”

Braff admitted that “it’s a little tricky” because McGinley is a series regular on Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence’s newest series, HBO’s Rooster, which started production on its second season in Los Angeles just a couple of weeks after Scrubs began filming its second season in Vancouver.

“We’ll have to navigate all that but I think this season is about us navigating being teachers, being the leads of the hospital, and and passing down our knowledge,” Braff said. “We’re navigating dating new people while being co-workers, and Turk’s battling some struggles with his mental health, we introduced that in the pilot. Having J.D. come back was certainly a temporary cure for that, but I think that what we’re going to start to explore is how that doesn’t just take away your melancholia. That there’s more work to do than just have your friend come back to town.”

Does that sets up Turk for a more dramatic arc?

“Absolutely,” Faison said. “I think that monologue in the pilot surprised not only myself but a lot of people. And it’s something worth, let’s explore it and find out how far the rabbit hole goes.”

title: Starz’s Black Rodeo Drama Casts Eight In Recurring Roles
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Starz is rounding out the recurring cast for its upcoming Black rodeo drama series with the addition of Patrick Cage (One Of Them Days, Mayor of Kingstown), Mpho Osei-Tutu (Outer Banks, Reasonable Doubt), Keith Arthur Bolden (The Ms. Pat Show, Reasonable Doubt), Tracey Bonner (Raising Dion, Sweet Magnolias), Cris Ruiz (Beyond the Gates, Captain […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Starz is rounding out the recurring cast for its upcoming Black rodeo drama series with the addition of Patrick Cage (One Of Them Days, Mayor of Kingstown), Mpho Osei-Tutu (Outer Banks, Reasonable Doubt), Keith Arthur Bolden (The Ms. Pat Show, Reasonable Doubt), Tracey Bonner (Raising Dion, Sweet Magnolias), Cris Ruiz (Beyond the Gates, Captain America: Brave New World), Derek Delafonte (Paper Made, Reasonable Doubt), Demián Castro (Lioness, Sound of Hope: The Story of Possum Trot) and Christina DeRosa (Black-ish, Bad Moms).

The eight-episode family drama comes from Demascus showrunner Kirk A. Moore, Breaking Bad exec producer Mark Johnson and Counterpart Studios.

Watch on Deadline

The series, said to be “infused with hip hop swagger and country soul”, unfolds in Southeast Texas, where rodeo isn’t just what you do – it’s who you are. At the center are three siblings bound by the legacy their mother built and the unfinished business their father left behind. Driven by their own ambitions and drawn into each other’s orbit, alliances shift, relationships tangle, and nothing stays private for long.

Cage will play Tennessee. An ex-military man and engineer by profession, Tennessee explores new business opportunities with Rodney that aren’t exactly aboveboard. Tennessee is also a loving single father to a young son. With his business up and running, an unexpected spark ignites his love life.

Osei-Tutu will portray TJ, the shady owner of a local eight-liner casino, where Sebastian is a frequent client. He also has a past with Sebastian’s father, Elias, and his Uncle LeRoi.

Bolden is LeRoi Louis, the Clarke siblings’ favorite and only uncle. Though he ran the streets of Trinity City with Elias back in the day, he stepped up as the father figure in the siblings’ lives after Elias went away. LeRoi appears to be a dedicated member of the family, but he’s haunted by a deep secret that may one day catch up to him.

Bonner will play Neo Leland. Quick-witted, feisty, and loving, Neo is the owner of Neo’s Soul Kitchen. She’s Anaya’s closest friend, and also happens to be LeRoi’s on-again,-off-again girlfriend for over a decade. She’s in danger of losing her beloved restaurant after some financial setbacks. Good thing she has Anaya in her corner.

Ruiz will portray Rafael Morales, Francisco’s hot-headed, younger brother. While Francisco is the CEO of the family company, Rafael is mostly a follower and has already had several run-ins with the law. But when he feels like Francisco is distracted and leaving the business open to rivals, Rafael decides it might be time to assert himself and take the lead.

Delafonte is Playboy Ray, a cocky, obnoxious, and supremely talented all-around cowboy. Playboy Ray is one of the few multi-event riders in the city, and the rider everyone loves to hate. That’s his charm. His unexpected return to the rodeo reignites a long-standing beef as Julius’ biggest rival.

Castro will play Lieutenant Mescal. Observant, overworked and understaffed, Lieutenant Mescal is willing to do the hard work to solve any case – even if it means clashing with the mayor. He proves to be a threat to multiple people as he tries to piece together the truth behind Trinity City’s recent string of crimes.

DeRosa will portray Natalia Morales, Francisco’s supportive wife who believes strongly in family. She’s also second in command (COO) at Morales Timber, and not afraid to assert her opinion. Natalia believes everyone has a role in the Morales family and works to preserve their respected name – God bless anyone who gets in her way.

Previously announced cast includes DeWanda Wise as Anaya Clarke-Reagan, Shannon Wallace as Sebastian Clarke, Tian Richards as Rodney Clarke, Curtiss Cook as Elias Clarke, Lauren E. Banks as Wynter, Marcus Emanuel Mitchell as Julius Calhoun, Liv Symone as Jojo Calhoun, and Jason Dirden as Greg Reagan.

Moore serves as showrunner and executive producer. Johnson and Myki Bajaj executive produce via Gran Via Productions, along with Tony Hernandez, Elise Henderson and Lilly Burns of Counterpart Studios. It will be overseen by Starz execs Giovanna Desselle and Christina Jokanovich.

Cage is repped by Anonymous Content, CESD, and Goodman, Genow, Shenkman, Smelkinson, & Christopher. Osei-Tutu is repped by Aligned Stars Agency and GS Entertainment Managemen Bolden is repped by Sean M. Butler at Citizen Skull Management and Atlanta Talent & Model Agency. Bonner is repped by Stewart Talent and Jackson Entertainment Management. Ruiz is repped by J Pervis Talent Agency. Delafonte is repped by Formation Talent Agency and Sweeney Entertainment. Castro is repped by Privilege Talent and Established Artists. DeRosa is repped by Tay Smith at Smith Young Talent Agency and Roger Paul of Roger Paul Inc.
