title: White House Blocks CNN From Covering Trump On Air Force One As TV Pool Network
summary: The White House has blocked CNN from flying on Air Force One as the TV pool network traveling with Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday. A CNN spokesperson confirmed reports that the network was pulled from as a scheduled network providing TV coverage of the president. Because of space limitations, much of […]
content:
The White House has blocked CNN from flying on Air Force One as the TV pool network traveling with Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday.

A CNN spokesperson confirmed reports that the network was pulled from as a scheduled network providing TV coverage of the president. Because of space limitations, much of the coverage of the president is pooled, with video, photo, audio and print information shared to a wider circle of outlets.

Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds last week, but a federal judge ordered credentials reinstated on Thursday, concluding that it was a violation of due process rights.

The judge did not rule on a related action by the White House: On Sunday, after the president issued the ban on the three outlets, the Trump administration also pulled CNN from the TV pool rotation. The other four networks in the rotation — CBS, NBC, ABC and Fox — declined to replace CNN, suspending coverage for most of the week, an act of protest that meant a dearth of video images from the White House.

Watch on Deadline

The TV pool resumed earlier on Friday when CNN was reinstated, but now the network is being blocked again.

title: Chris Hansen Finally Saw ‘Primetime’, Still Not A Fan: “So Detached From Reality”
summary: After weeks of providing A24’s Primetime with free press, Chris Hansen has finally seen the Lance Oppenheim-helmed thriller. On Friday, the former To Catch a Predator host teased his reaction after catching a screening of the movie, which is now in theaters, based on Esquire‘s depiction of Hansen in the 2007 article “Tonight on Dateline […]
content:
After weeks of providing A24‘s Primetime with free press, Chris Hansen has finally seen the Lance Oppenheim-helmed thriller.

On Friday, the former To Catch a Predator host teased his reaction after catching a screening of the movie, which is now in theaters, based on Esquire‘s depiction of Hansen in the 2007 article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die” with Robert Pattinson portraying him.

“It was so bizarre and so in-and-out of reality,” said Hansen in a video shared on X. “Obviously, I’m not objective because the character is me, but it was so detached from reality or anything I’ve experienced then or now doing the investigations. I’m not sure what the point of it was.”

At the Venice Film Festival premiere, Pattinson recently said that he hopes Hansen sees the film as “some kind of compliment” from those he’s inspired.

Watch on Deadline

Meanwhile, Hansen’s official review of the film comes amid a rollercoaster of reactions he’s had to the project, including contemplating legal action and purchasing ad space before upcoming screenings of the movie to promote his true-crime streaming network TruBlu, where he continues his sting investigations.

Well….I saw Primetime. My reaction tonight 7p eastern on my podcast/YouTube channel Have A Seat With Chris Hansen ! pic.twitter.com/dMEErgVriH — Chris Hansen (@chrishansen) September 25, 2026

After Hansen recently confirmed he’s “going to see” the movie, following an invite from the production team to a private screening, he appeared last month on Fox News, claiming he was asked to sign “a very restrictive agreement” to attend the advanced screening.

The form was an NDA that all preview audiences are asked to sign a week in advance to view in an unreleased film, in order to prevent spoilers and protect IP. Hansen reportedly refused to sign, and therefore, wasn’t allowed to screen the film.

Now in theaters, Primetime follows Chris Hansen (Pattinson) as he attempts to make television history with NBC’s To Catch a Predator (2004-’07), a hidden camera show that set up stings for adult men seeking sex from minors online.

title: International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt “Campaign Of Threats” Against ‘NAZA’ Directors
summary: The International Documentary Association is coming to the defense of NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. The nonprofit organization posted a letter to its website urging the Israeli government to stop what the IDA terms a “campaign of threats” against the directors, whose film is sharply critical of Israel’s conduct of the war in […]
content:
The International Documentary Association is coming to the defense of NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

The nonprofit organization posted a letter to its website urging the Israeli government to stop what the IDA terms a “campaign of threats” against the directors, whose film is sharply critical of Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians.

“IDA calls on the Israeli government to withdraw its threats against filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor,” the letter says. “We also call for an end to the public campaign of intimidation against them.”

The letter continues, “Since NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, senior Israeli officials have moved against its directors. The Culture Minister has accused them of treason and sought to revoke their citizenship. The Prime Minister has announced bills to revoke the citizenship of anyone who ‘slanders IDF soldiers’ and to raise defamation damages twentyfold.” (Read the full letter form the IDA below).

Watch on Deadline

‘NAZA’ The Guardian/mk2

READ: ‘NAZA’ Review: Israeli Military Accused Of Depraved Indifference To Palestinian Life, Using AI To Kill In Gaza – Venice Film Festival

The documentary, which holds its North American premiere Saturday at the New York Film Festival, is based on the account of 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers, who were interviewed at the height of Israeli military operations in Gaza. The military personnel, whose identities are concealed to protect their anonymity, describe callous disregard for Palestinian civilian life as the Israel Defense Forces pursued Hamas targets in the occupied territory. Whistleblowers allege the IDF set acceptable totals of civilian Palestinian deaths in attacks targeting suspected Hamas militants, in one case authorizing the killing of up to 500 civilians in pursuit of one target.

The IDF, as Deadline has reported, has denied allegations in the film. The International Documentary Association writes, “The Israeli military disputes the film’s account, and it is entitled to do so. But as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Israel is bound by Article 19, under which restrictions on expression must be provided by law and be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim. Revoking citizenship, imposing punitive damages, or opening security investigations in response to a documentary does not meet that test. The UN Human Rights Committee recognizes the protection of journalistic sources as part of freedom of expression, and the filmmakers’ right not to disclose the identities of their sources must be upheld.”

The letter has gained more than 250 signatories so far, including from actors Javier Bardem and Mark Ruffalo, as well as many prominent figures in the documentary field including Oscar winners Laura Poitras, Rob Epstein, Dan Cogan, Alex Gibney, Roger Ross Williams, Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy, Orlando von Einsiedel, Dan Lindsay, and Ezra Edelman, and Oscar nominees Geeta Gandbhir, Liz Garbus, Connie Field, Guy Davidi, Rémi Grellety, Kellen Quinn, Joe Berlinger, Kirstine Barfod, Laura Nix, Sam Bisbee, Alexander Nanau, Joslyn Barnes, Raoul Peck, Kirby Dick, Amy Ziering, Carl Deal, and Tia Lessin, as well as former Sundance Film Festival director Tabitha Jackson, filmmakers Kirsten Johnson, Susan Lacy, Robert Bahar, Alison Klayman, Marjan Safinia, producer Ina Fichman, and many others.

The IDA’s letter includes several bullet-pointed items: “IDA calls on the Government of Israel to:

“withdraw the threats to revoke Abraham’s and Szor’s citizenship, and abandon the proposed legislation;

“respect the filmmakers’ journalistic right to refuse to disclose the identities of confidential sources

“reject changes to public film funding that penalize filmmakers for critical work or international recognition.

“We also call on everyone taking part in the public debate to reject the intimidation of the filmmakers and their families.”

Deadline has been alerted to a planned protest against NAZA outside Lincoln Center in New York City, where the film will screen on Saturday. According to organizers of the demonstration, they intend to “show documented footage from the October 7 massacre, alongside material challenging the film’s claims.” A nor’easter storm moving up the east coast may complicate any plans for an outdoor demonstration.

Here’s the IDA letter, from the organization’s executive director, Dominic Asmall Willsdon.

title: ‘SNL’ Promotes Keri Powers & Rebecca Schwartz
summary: There’s some changes behind the scenes at Saturday Night Live. The show has promoted two of its long-running figures: Keri Powers and Rebecca Schwartz. Powers has been promoted to sole head of its talent department and is responsible for host, musical guest and guest star bookings for the NBC show. She joined the show in […]
content:
There’s some changes behind the scenes at Saturday Night Live.

The show has promoted two of its long-running figures: Keri Powers and Rebecca Schwartz.

Powers has been promoted to sole head of its talent department and is responsible for host, musical guest and guest star bookings for the NBC show. She joined the show in 2014 and had previously worked for Paramount Pictures and CAA.

Her promotion follows the departure of Brian Siedlecki, who was the booker and spent 30 years in the role.

Separately, Rebecca Schwartz has been promoted to producer. She was part of the talent team and has been with the show since 2015.

Watch on Deadline

The moves come as SNL returns for Season 52 on Saturday with Jalen Brunson as host and Katseye as musical guest.

There wasn’t a huge amount of change coming into the season. Chloe Fineman left, as revealed by Deadline, and Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter joined as featured players. Ashley Padilla and Jane Wickline were promoted to reparatory status.

The cast now includes Michael Che, Mikey Day, Andrew Dismukes, Marcello Hernandez, James Austin Johnson, Colin Jost, Ashley Padilla, Sarah Sherman, Kenan Thompson and Jane Wickline with Belo-Osagie, Reiter, Tommy Brennan, Jeremy Culhane, Ben Marshall, Kam Patterson and Veronika Slowikowska as featured players.

title: Tilly Norwood Would Love to Work With Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, ‘but Only If It Were Their Digital Twins’ on an ‘AI Production’
summary: A year after announcing AI actress Tilly Norwood at Zurich Film Festival’s Summit, Particle 6 founder and Norwood creator Eline van der Velden returned to the Swiss event to look back at the backlash her creation has faced since. Asked if she could have ever predicted the furore around Norwood, van der Velden said not […]
content:
A year after announcing AI actress Tilly Norwood at Zurich Film Festival’s Summit, Particle 6 founder and Norwood creator Eline van der Velden returned to the Swiss event to look back at the backlash her creation has faced since. Asked if she could have ever predicted the furore around Norwood, van der Velden said not in her “wildest dreams.”

“But I had programmed her to become the most famous AI actress, so I don’t know how she did it, but she did, which is slightly scary,” she added.

“It’s such an odd conundrum, the sort of negativity and then the positivity at the same time,” she continued. “At Particle 6, we’ve grown eight-fold. We have four departments; we’re big in AI advertising, film and TV, we’re doing a lot of co-productions and original commissions. We do a lot of AI consultancy, bringing AI workflows into other studios and production companies.”

Popular on Variety

Over the course of the last year, said the exec, “a lot of people have realized that AI is coming, and that was the point of Tilly.” “I built her as a physicist actress; I felt like I needed to bridge the gap in communication between the tech and the entertainment industry.”

“As opposed to writing a boring white paper about what was happening with AI, I thought: Let’s create something to show people that will engage them and make them sit up and take action so that the creative industry can stay ahead as opposed to being completely and utterly taken over by the tech industry,” noted van der Velden.

After a few minutes trying to sort out a tech blip with the “traditional technology,” e.g., a problem with the HDMI cable, van der Velden introduced Norwood herself on stage, opening her creation to moderator and audience questions. Asked who she would like to work with, Norwood said Tom Holland and Olivia Colman, “but only if it were their digital twins joining me in an AI production.”

Norwood also spoke on the backlash, calling it “quite an introduction.” “My name kind of went everywhere. It’s funny. Nobody hated me particularly; they just sort of hated the future.”

When asked if she had met U.S. agents for representation, Norwood displayed the ironclad media training of an A-list Hollywood star. “Well, I’m certainly in a unique position there. I mean… The industry is still figuring out what to do with AI, so it’s not quite like having a traditional agent in Hollywood just yet. I mostly work on AI films, so it’s a bit of a different lane.”

Van der Velden also spoke about possibly getting Norwood an agent, saying the studio soon realized that they “don’t really need” an agent for the actress. “I think she’s big enough as it is. We get loads of offers in, we’ve said no to anything where she would be in a traditional film, because that’s not what she’s made for. We don’t need it at the moment, so if that makes people happy, that’s fine by me.”

“But also what saddens me about that is that it means that the traditional industry can’t participate in this new tech and that means they fall behind,” she added. “Is it a positive? Is it a negative?”

After watching Norwood’s now infamous malfunction while speaking with Piers Morgan on live TV, when the AI actress randomly began speaking Cantonese, van der Velden said: “Look, I think it’s all not to be taken too seriously. We built Tilly to be a funny interface that gets people alert to where the tech is at. The point is: China’s a big partner. Do we need regulation? What are the guardrails? Those are the conversations I want people to have coming here.”

Van der Velden also spoke about Particle 6’s latest project, “Storm Dogs.” Yesterday, the studio announced that “Stuart Little” and “The Lion King” filmmaker Rob Minkoff joined the AI film as an executive producer. Minkoff will work with CEO van der Velden and the studio’s team over the coming months to develop the story, characters and screenplay ahead of production.

“Storm Dogs,” an original idea from van der Velden, is a family adventure comedy-drama set in an English village during a devastating storm. The film will combine live-action performances with photorealistic animated characters. Human roles will be filmed conventionally, while the dogs and toddler will be created through an approach that brings together live-action performance, traditional filmmaking techniques, and emerging AI tools. The project is currently in early development, with production targeted for 2027. Distribution has not yet been announced.

The exec said that Minkoff was one of the first people to reach out to her following Norwood’s announcement.

“Yeah, so what was amazing about this backlash last year is actually it meant that a lot of talent reached out to us very secretly,” she said. “We were signing tons and tons of NDAs. Everyone was scared to take the hit, and I totally understand. Fortunately, we were in a position where we’d already taken the hit, so it didn’t matter anymore.”

Of “Storm Dogs,” she said, what is “great” about it is that they can now “animate mouths in a way that we’ve never been able before and give us expression to the animals that’s never been possible before. It is really enhancing the storytelling. And so that’s how I see it. It needs to aid the storytelling and the creative work that we’re making if we’re going to use AI.”

title: One Year On, Does AI Actress Tilly Norwood Have An Agent? “We Get Loads Of Offers, But No, We Don’t Need It” — Zurich Summit
summary: One year ago, AI ‘actress’ Tilly Norwood blew up at the Zurich Summit when she was introduced to the industry. The line that emerged from the event at the time was that agents were circling the AI creation. One year on, Norwood returned to the Summit with her creator Eline van der Velden from AI […]
content:
One year ago, AI ‘actress’ Tilly Norwood blew up at the Zurich Summit when she was introduced to the industry. The line that emerged from the event at the time was that agents were circling the AI creation.

One year on, Norwood returned to the Summit with her creator Eline van der Velden from AI firm Particle 6.

Deadline’s Diana Lodderhose, moderating a session with the duo, asked van der Velden whether her creation had found an agent in the year since she went viral and has become a regular media fixture.

Van der Velden said: “We’ve realized we don’t really need her to have a rep. I think she’s big enough as it is. We get loads of offers in. We’ve said no to anything where she would be in a traditional film because that’s not what she’s made for. But yeah, we don’t need it at the moment. So if that makes people happier, that’s fine. But also, what saddens me about that it is that it means the traditional industry can’t participate in this new thing, and that means they fall behind. And so, you know, is it a positive? Is it a negative? I don’t know.”

Watch on Deadline

She said Particle 6 had grown four-fold since it was launched and said that the industry was increasingly accepting that AI is here to stay.

Deadline’s Andreas Wiseman followed up with a question to Norwood herself who joined via video link. Wiseman asked Norwood whether she had met with the major U.S. agencies or Hollywood studios. She didn’t confirm, noting: “I’m certainly in a unique position there. I mean, the industry is still figuring out what to do with AI, so it’s not quite like having a traditional agent in Hollywood just yet. I mostly work on AI films, so it’s a bit of a different lane.”

Van der Velden teased footage of Norwood’s first project, an AI comedy-drama titled Misaligned, which is in production, and showed longer footage of Particle 6 kids movie Storm Dogs, which Deadline revealed yesterday is being developed and exec-produced by The Lion King director Rob Minkoff.

Norwood and van der Velden kicked off the session with a light video poking fun at Norwood’s recent high-profile tech glitch during an interview with Piers Morgan where she began speaking in Chinese. Norwood joked that the episode probably helped Morgan’s ratings.

The tech is clearly still being worked through. While Norwood generally gave answers in the right ball park to questions today, she did at least once give a wonky answer to moderator Lodderhose.

title: ‘Sunshine’ Director Antoinette Jadaone Launches Ilaya Ilaya; Women-Led Slate Headed By Angelica Panganiban, Kaila Estrada, Eugene Domingo & Maris Racal
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Filipino filmmaker and producer Antoinette Jadaone, whose credits include Berlinale award winner Sunshine, is launching a new production outfit Ilaya Ilaya with a slate spanning genre films, television originals and immersive theatre. Jadaone will run the company with longtime collaborator and producer Reign Anne De Guzman (Sunshine, That Thing Called Tadhana), who has collaborated […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Filipino filmmaker and producer Antoinette Jadaone, whose credits include Berlinale award winner Sunshine, is launching a new production outfit Ilaya Ilaya with a slate spanning genre films, television originals and immersive theatre.

Jadaone will run the company with longtime collaborator and producer Reign Anne De Guzman (Sunshine, That Thing Called Tadhana), who has collaborated with her since they both worked at Star Cinema, where Jadaone was a script continuity supervisor and De Guzman a production assistant.

Through their new outfit, the duo aim to champion Filipino cinema, women-led stories, unappreciated genres, and filmmakers whose work struggles to find support outside traditional studio systems and festival funding cycles.

Leading the slate is Birdsong – a found-footage horror film directed by Pam Miras (Medusae) and written by Glenn Barit (Cleaners), with Irene Villamor (The Loved One) on board as creative producer. The film follows an ornithologist who travels to a remote mountain in search of a mythical bird, while also seeking closure over her partner’s disappearance a decade earlier.

Watch on Deadline

The project recently won the Kantana Sound Studio Asian Project Award at the Bangkok International Content Market 2026. “It’s our first time working with Pam Miras as a director, and it is in a genre that is male-dominated,” said Jadaone. “We really love the way Pam handles experimentation in her films.”

Ilaya Ilaya is also developing supernatural comedy Chandra Catacutan And The Curse Of The Fuchsia Moon, set to star Eugene Domingo (Sisa). The film is directed by Tim Rone Villanueva, whose credits include Child No. 82: Anak ni Boy Kana, which caught Jadaone’s attention when it screened Cinemalaya film festival last year.

Domingo plays the eldest daughter of a manananggal – a creature from Philippine folklore that can separate its upper torso from the lower part of its body. In Villanueva’s project, the children of the creature are reunited when she suffers a stroke mid-air and fails to return to her lower half. Jadaone says Villanueva’s work showed the kind of resourcefulness and pop culture fluency she wants Ilaya Ilaya to champion.

The slate also includes Crème de la Crème, a coming-of-age whodunnit to be directed by Irene Emma Villamor. Written by Glenn Barit from a story by Natts Jadaone, the film is partly inspired by a 2006 incident at Philippine Science High School in which two male students laced a classmate’s water jug with mercury nitrate, preventing her from attending the graduation march.

Jadaone herself is returning to directing with Boldstar, a dark comedy starring Angelica Panganiban (That Thing Called Tadhana) and produced by Bianca Balbuena (Sunshine, Filipiñana). The project won the CJ Entertainment Prize at the Asian Project Market in 2019 and was later selected for the Berlinale European Co-Production Market in 2020.

Balbuena said Boldstar emerged from the momentum of Jadaone’s 2020 film Fan Girl and a period of political anger over misogyny and the treatment of women in public life. After several delays, including Panganiban’s pregnancy, Jadaone’s work on Sunshine, and Balbuena’s leadership role at the now defunct Anima Studios, the team is now reviving the project.

“The project feels very ripe and momentous now, especially after Antoinette’s Crystal Bear win in Berlinale and sold-out local screenings of Sunshine,” said Balbuena.

Beyond film, Ilaya Ilaya is expanding into television, with Jadaone showrunning an as-yet-untitled romcom series for Netflix Philippines. Plot and casting details remain under wraps, but the project is co-written with Fatrick Tabada (Flower Girl), marking Jadaone’s return to the genre that helped establish her as a local favorite nearly a decade after Love You To The Stars And Back. Jadaone previously worked with Netflix on Replacing Chef Chico.

“We’re thrilled to partner again with Antoinette Jadaone, whose creative vision and signature ‘kilig’ storytelling have resonated with Filipino audiences everywhere,” said Vitto Lazatin, Director of Content at Netflix Philippines.

Rounding out the slate is an immersive stage adaptation of Sunshine, to be directed by Mikko Angeles (Bar Boys: The Musical) and written by Mika Regis (Unica Hijas), with Racal returning to the role in her stage debut.

The project is envisioned as a choose-your-own-adventure experience that places audiences inside Sunshine’s world, expanding the film’s questions around agency, complicity, and choice beyond the screen.

“When you’re watching a film, you’re there to just watch Sunshine make decisions,” said Jadaone. “But what if Sunshine’s story was something you could hold and influence as an audience member?”

Commenting on the slate overall, Jadaone said: “Before we were filmmakers, we were lovers of Philippine cinema. We want to be more intentional now about telling stories and working with people who demonstrate a genuine love for Philippine cinema.”

De Guzman added: “What I’m most looking forward to is being able to tell stories that we really believe in. Hopefully, through Ilaya Ilaya and the stories we make together, we can get more Filipinos to appreciate and fall in love with Philippine cinema.”

title: ‘Ghost Song’ Review: Fatih Akin Doesn’t Find Top Form in This Supernatural Romance, but at Least It Has Beautiful Ghosts
summary: Since hitting an artistic peak with the back-to-back festival triumphs “Head-On” and “Edge of Heaven” in the mid-2000s, German-Turkish auteur Fatih Akin has darted all over the map in genre, style and form — occasionally striking commercially, as with the Diane Kruger thriller “In the Fade” and the local hip-hop biopic “Rhinegold,” without ever matching […]
content:
Since hitting an artistic peak with the back-to-back festival triumphs “Head-On” and “Edge of Heaven” in the mid-2000s, German-Turkish auteur Fatih Akin has darted all over the map in genre, style and form — occasionally striking commercially, as with the Diane Kruger thriller “In the Fade” and the local hip-hop biopic “Rhinegold,” without ever matching the rigor and impact of those earlier standouts. That pattern doesn’t change with his latest, the star-crossed supernatural romance “Ghost Song,” which opened this year’s San Sebastian Film Festival. The film, about two 20-year-olds carrying on their early courtship across the mortal divide, is earnest and a little clunky as it takes a simplistic inspirational approach to complex metaphysical questions. But it is accessible and attractive, shot in glistening monochrome, and could well be a youth-skewing hit for the filmmaker.

The choice to shoot in inky black-and-white, making prominent use of major German city landmarks, practically begs for comparisons to Wim Wenders’ “Wings of Desire,” another atmospheric romantic fantasy about a love spanning the mortal and ethereal realms — with Akin’s film the Hamburg-set, GenZ-focused homage to Wenders’ Berlin classic. Placing the two side by side doesn’t flatter the thinner, less lyrical new work, but it’s a marketable resemblance, while “Ghost Song” asserts its own identity with an expression of Muslim faith, as interrogated and interpreted by its young, multicultural characters. The fact that “Ghost Song” has simultaneously been adapted into a graphic novel by Akin and artist Bea Davies is a further indication of its generational targeting.

Popular on Variety

Farasha (luminous first-timer Mariam Dawoud) is a Syrian refugee who has settled and assimilated in Hamburg with her family, following an interstitial stint in Turkey. Though she chooses to wear a traditional headscarf, in other respects she lives as a modern, independent-minded woman, following in the footsteps of her late father by studying physics at university, while keeping at least one haram secret that would scandalize her mother: a butterfly tattoo on her stomach.

At a graduation party in Hamburg’s imposing Telemichel tower, she meets and immediately sparks with fellow grad Faris (Eren M. Guvercin), a tousle-haired, German-born Muslim of Turkish descent. With her very tipsy bestie Una (Carlotta von Falkenhayn), they decide to continue the party elsewhere and pile into his car; in circumstances deliberately (and somewhat luridly) parceled out over the course of the film, an accident sees the vehicle plunge into the Elbe river.

Faris wakes up in hospital to find that Farasha has drowned, and the police have questions; Farasha, meanwhile, comes to in a different way, finding that she can still walk the Earth, but no one can see or hear her. No one, that is, except her father, who informs her that for 40 days — in line with the mourning period in certain Muslim traditions — she can visit the living in their dreams. Still lovestruck and not yet fully accepting of her death, she seizes the opportunity to spend more time with Faris, cuing a strange and increasingly dangerous courtship.

“Ghost Song” rests on the idea that, in just one evening, Farasha and Faris made such a deep soul connection that even death can’t quite sever them. It’s an intensely romantic notion not really borne out by these wan characters, however individually charismatic the young actors playing them. Nor by Akin’s naïve, slightly purple writing, which keeps sentimentally reiterating the characters’ devotion to each other — mining tension from the question of which will ultimately make the biggest sacrifice for the other — but says little of any spiritual or philosophical substance. More moving is the film’s observation of Farasha’s family through this nightmare: A literal out-of-body scene in which she watches them ritually clean and prepare her corpse for burial is the film’s most layered and haunting.

Where the film veers into the superficial or kitsch, however, it can fall back on its lush mood and widescreen visual riches. Being a ghost has rarely looked quite this pretty on screen, as Tom Tykwer’s regular DP Frank Griebe — working for the first time with Akin — makes a chiaroscuro lovers’ playground of even Hamburg’s unlovelier spots, finding as much intimacy in a brutalist monument as an ordinary darkened bedroom. Iridescently illustrated title cards disrupt the stark monochrome, as do the moments leading into the closing credits — the characters’ worlds flooding into color with a crucial, life-or-death choice.

title: Nas, Jeremy Pope, Ashlee Simpson and More Toast Krug’s New Champagne-and-Sound Experience at L.A.’s Larrabee Studios
summary: Krug is pairing Champagne with live music at Larrabee Studios. The luxury Champagne house is opening the doors to one of Los Angeles’ most storied recording studios this month for “The Art of Blending Krug & Sound,” a three-night experience at Larrabee Studios that will turn guests’ tasting notes — or, more precisely, whatever memories, […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Krug is pairing Champagne with live music at Larrabee Studios.

The luxury Champagne house is opening the doors to one of Los Angeles’ most storied recording studios this month for “The Art of Blending Krug & Sound,” a three-night experience at Larrabee Studios that will turn guests’ tasting notes — or, more precisely, whatever memories, emotions and sensations their Champagne inspires — into an original song created in real time.

The experience will take place Sept. 28-30 inside Larrabee’s Studio 6, with 14-time Grammy-winning mixing engineer and studio owner Manny Marroquin (who most recently worked on Rosalía’s highly lauded “LUX”) leading the experiment alongside producers Scott Tibbs, Nick Rosen and Mike Bennett. Rather than simply putting on a playlist while everyone drinks, the producers will use guests’ reactions to each pour as raw material for a composition assembled live over the course of the evening.

Problem, Manny Marroquin Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com

Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com

Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com

At the center of the evening are Krug 2013 and Krug Grande Cuvée 169ème Édition, while Chef Oscar Torres of VERSE will serve a multi-course dinner paired with additional pours including Krug Grande Cuvée 173ème Édition and Krug Rosé 29ème Édition.

“Larrabee has always been a place where creativity comes to life through exchange,” Marroquin said. “Partnering with Krug gave us the opportunity to invite guests into that process, where every conversation, every shared moment and every glass of Champagne becomes part of the music we’re creating together. No two evenings will ever be the same.”

The public run was preceded Thursday night by a splashier VIP preview, where Nas, Ashlee Simpson Ross, Evan Ross, Jeremy Pope, Sabrina Claudio, producer Dahi, pianist Chloe Flower and others gathered inside Studio 6 to test-drive the concept before it opens to paying guests.

Over the course of the evening, guests sipped through the Krug lineup and wrote down emotions, sensations and words each cuvée brought to mind, which Tibbs, Rosen and Costa then translated into an original composition created live in the room. Words like “red,” “invigorating,” and “nostalgia” informed two lively songs played on cello, piano and drums.

Chloe Flower Kyle Goldberg/BFA.com

In between, the studio played tracks with their own Larrabee history, including John Mayer’s “Gravity” and Portugal. The Man’s “Feel It Still.” The finale came courtesy of Flower, who surprised the room with a live piano performance as a jeroboam of Krug Grande Cuvée 163ème Édition was brought out for one last pour.

The collaboration isn’t entirely out of left field for Krug. The Champagne house has long experimented with the relationship between music and taste, working with musicians and composers — most recently Max Richter — to explore how sound can affect perception and emotion while drinking.

And if drinking Krug inside a recording studio sounds suspiciously like the kind of night normally reserved for people with a platinum record on the wall, that’s part of the draw. The intimate sessions offer rare public access to Studio 6, with a limited number of reservations available through Tock.

After the three-night run wraps, the collaboration will spill over into Larrabee’s neighboring restaurants VERSE and Mensano, where Torres will offer a month-long Krug Grande Cuvée pairing inspired by the project.

Find out more about “The Art of Blending Krug & Sound” here.

title: Finnish Hit ‘100 Litres of Gold’ Gets Another Round With Sequel ‘200 Litres of Gold’ That’s a ‘Little Bit Darker, a Little Bit Funnier and a Little Bit Bigger’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Box-office hit “100 Litres of Gold” – last year’s Finnish Oscar submission – is getting a sequel, downing additional “200 Litres of Gold” as the boozy saga about Finnish beer sahti continues. “In the first one, the sisters were making sahti for their sister’s wedding. Now, they are making it for the Finnish Sahti Championship. […]
content:
Box-office hit “100 Litres of Gold” – last year’s Finnish Oscar submission – is getting a sequel, downing additional “200 Litres of Gold” as the boozy saga about Finnish beer sahti continues.

“In the first one, the sisters were making sahti for their sister’s wedding. Now, they are making it for the Finnish Sahti Championship. To win, they need to tolerate each other and overcome rival sahti makers – and their father,” says director Teemu Nikki.

“Needless to say, things don’t go too smoothly, resulting in physical and mental damage.”

Popular on Variety

Obviously, no one’s going to stay sober for long. But the comedy also stems from other sources, and the relationships between the sisters, and their father, are “even more complex than before,” says Nikki.

There’s also a new nemesis in town: the sahti makers from another village.

“They are two ladies who are as crazy as our sisters. There’s a lot of trash-talking and arm-wrestling.”

Elina Knihtilä and Pijo Lonka return as Pirkko and Taina.

“They’re close, for sure. But how well they’re able to take on life’s challenges, both together and alone, is part of the story’s theme,” notes Lonka.

“Actors have to find a way to love the characters they play, and these women were easy to love. They’re human. They’re not one-dimensional; they’re vulnerable, flawed and sometimes childlike. But with all their imperfections, you can relate to them and grow close to them.”

It was liberating to get a role like that, she says.

“It doesn’t happen very often for women. It’s great to show such a wide spectrum of emotions without holding back, and the person to thank for that is Teemu.”

“100 Litres of Gold” has already made waves abroad, with Dennis Lehane working on a U.S. remake.

Nikki and producer Jani Pösö are no beginners – with their production company It’s Alive Films, they have already created the likes of “The Blind Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic,” awarded in Venice, or their first Oscar submission “Euthanizer.” They’re also behind Naima Mohamud’s “Halima.”

However, no other film has come close to the box-office results of “100 Litres of Gold,” the most-watched local film in 2025.

“It still feels a bit strange that it did so well. It’s like we kept on hitting our heads against a wall until it finally collapsed,” laughs Pösö.

“In a way, I think we’ve become better filmmakers. Everything just clicked, from marketing and distribution to acting. Elina has been with us since the very first short we made, she has been fantastic in every role, and we finally got to work with Pirjo.”

They are happy to see this unlikely franchise grow.

“We are not sequel guys. But Teemu said: ‘I’m thinking of this as ‘The Godfather,’ and ‘The Godfather Part II’ was better than the first one,’” jokes Pösö.

“It’s a little bit darker, a little bit funnier and a little bit bigger. We find out that one of the sisters is not doing great; her liver has basically exploded. As in all our films, things get pretty serious in the end, even though it’s fun. It’s also totally independent, so you can watch it without having seen the first one. But the second one will make you want to watch the first one, and vice versa,” he says.

“With all franchises, there comes a moment when you need to stop. But a third one is certainly possible.”

title: Naima Mohamud Explains Why Finland Needs a Film Like ‘Halima’: ‘It Was a Long Time Coming’ (EXCLUSIVE)

content:
Finnish-Somali director Naima Mohamud’s debut feature, “Halima,” was named Best Fiction Project at the Finnish Film Affair.

It’s not the first award for the film, which has consistently generated buzz also outside of the country. But it’s the first Finnish feature film directed by a Black woman.

Produced by It’s Alive Films, No-Office Films and Vico Films and currently in post-production, it’s set in 1998 in Finland. Halima is a 10-year-old imaginative Somali girl who’s obsessed with Leonardo DiCaprio and Aqua (the band behind hit “Barbie Girl”), and wants nothing more than to be a pop star. The only trouble is, her family is always on the move, she has never had a friend and her mom refuses to talk about her dad.

Popular on Variety

“To be honest, I really think that a film like ‘Halima’ was a long time coming. We Somalis have been living in Finland for over 35 years, yet most Finns still don’t know anything about us, our culture or how we interact at home. None of those things,” Mohamud tells Variety.

“This film might help someone with a Somali neighbor finally get a glimpse. I hope that’s what this film does: opens up Finns to understanding Somalis.”

But Halima, who’s all about pop, is an outsider also in her own family.

“She has all these dreams of becoming a big star, which confuses her mom. She gets in trouble at school because of her imagination, and her mom just can’t understand the dancing and obsession with music. But she has bigger fish to fry, she has to support the family and make sure everyone’s okay, so she accepts it in her own way.”

Other kids aren’t that forgiving. Luckily, Halima is still young enough not to listen to haters – for now.

“She loves Lene, the lead singer of Aqua and she wants her bangs. Her hair is different, so when she cuts it, of course it looks weird. She’s okay with it, though, until other kids start bullying her,” says Mohamud.

“She’s still a child who’s not too self-conscious, but she’s slowly starting to understand that maybe this is embarrassing? Maybe I really look horrible?”

Some directors find it hard to see things from a child’s perspective. But not Mohamud.

“I’m still a kid!,” she laughs.

“I’ve always understood kids, so I had a great time working with them. I really enjoy this innocence of childhood. The older you get, the more you overthink. You start doubting yourself too much. Kids don’t have that. Halima thinks she can dance, and in her mind, she’s brilliant. When I decided to become a filmmaker at 14, I also didn’t think it was impossible – or that it would take so many years.”

She adds: “I like that ‘childish’ way of thinking, that everything is possible. You want something, and you go for it. I was just a very curious kid, too. I’d wonder: ‘Would my backpack fit in the school mailbox? What would it feel like to jump out of the window in the middle of class and roll around in the snow? Let’s find out!”

She wants to give Halima a moment of triumph in the film.

“There’s triumph, but it’s mischievous,” smiles Mohamud, whose goal is to make “joyful films.”

“I like happiness, and I like feeling happy. I love watching deep, serious films the same way I love looking at beautiful pieces of art. But I don’t want to spend my time making them,” she admits.

“It’s so important to know who you are as a filmmaker. I’ll just give you an example: recently, I wrote a short film about a reclusive Muslim scholar who’s asked to wash the dead body of a stranger who died alone. The experience helps her heal her own grief. It’s a very serious film, and I knew I could never direct it.”

“Camphor” will be directed by Ayla Amano.

“That film needed a poetic soul, and that’s not me – at least not as a director. I’d probably make the characters tell a few jokes and it would be so inappropriate. Even in film school, my classmates were all about the French New Wave. I loved James Cameron,” she admits.

“It’s just who I am, and I’m not going to change. I make films that I hope make you feel good when you leave the cinema. A tear here or there is great, but at the end, I want people to say: ‘You know what? Life is amazing.’”

title: ‘Backrooms’ Director Kane Parsons Distances $400M Hit From Horror Moniker: “I Don’t View It As A Horror Project”- Zurich Summit
summary: Kane Parson’s $400M hit Backrooms, spinning off his web-series inspired by “creepypasta’ horror content on the internet, is invariably and understandably billed as a horror. The director told a panel at the Zurich Summit on Saturday, however, that he does not see it as being aligned with the genre. “I didn’t direct like a horror […]
content:
Kane Parson’s $400M hit Backrooms, spinning off his web-series inspired by “creepypasta’ horror content on the internet, is invariably and understandably billed as a horror.

The director told a panel at the Zurich Summit on Saturday, however, that he does not see it as being aligned with the genre.

“I didn’t direct like a horror film. I don’t view it as a horror project. I think that’s just naturally been the path of least resistance from a marketing perspective and it’s what seems comfortable to people as a framing device,” he said,

Parsons acknowledged that A24, which spearheaded the adaptation the web-series and distributed the movie, would not like his comments, but added he hoped to be able to avoid this sort of framing in the future.

Watch on Deadline

“I’m going to try to stay as oblivious to those labels as possible… I think I have more creative control now with future projects so those sorts of structures will probably be a little less forceful in the future,” he said.

Parsons was talking on a panel on the $4.7 billion resurgence at the U.S. box office this summer, alongside Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences CEO Bill Kramer; President & Chief Content Officer Mattel Studios and Barbie producer Robbie Brenner and Sony Pictures Classics co-head Michael Barker.

Kramer, Brenner and Barker all acknowledged the role played by Backrooms in the box office resurgence, alongside Obsession, which was also born out of the YouTube space.

“Backrooms was an amazing example… and speaks to one of the things that’s happening with our industry…. your fandom travelled from YouTube to the theaters,” said Kramer.

“Young people want to go back to movie theaters. Fandoms shift. Theatrical can inform a fandom. YouTube can inform a theatrical fandom. It’s all connected in a way that I don’t think we thought was possible, and that for me was a big takeaway of this summer, and it gives me great hope for the film industry.

Barker described the box office success for Backrooms as symptomatic of a wider shift for the film business.

“If you look at the history of the motion picture business, there are these major inflection moments of transition. When I was 15 years old, Easy Rider came out in the middle of the Vietnam War, in the middle of a right-wing president, that spoke volumes to people in the moment. It spoke to young people, and they responded in huge numbers, and it affected the movies that were going to be made afterwards,” he said.

“I think this is that moment this summer with Obsession and Backrooms. What we haven’t talked about is what is in those movies that speaks to the population in the moment, and some of it’s very scary stuff… we’re in that moment for sure.”

Barker suggested the box offices was also being impacted by a phenomenon set in motion by the pandemic and the rise of the platforms, which has resulted in audiences in their teens, 20s and 30s being exposed to wider cinema content.

title: Taylor Swift Breaks Spotify Record With “Patient Zero” Surprise Release
summary: The previously unreleased song released by Taylor Swift yesterday as part of The Life of a Showgirl: Encore record has already scored some records of its own. Spotify says that one of the four Swift songs released yesterday – “Patient Zero” – immediately became Spotify’s most-streamed song by a female artist in a single day […]
content:
The previously unreleased song released by Taylor Swift yesterday as part of The Life of a Showgirl: Encore record has already scored some records of its own.

Spotify says that one of the four Swift songs released yesterday – “Patient Zero” – immediately became Spotify’s most-streamed song by a female artist in a single day in 2026 so far. And Swift herself became the most-streamed female artist in a single day this year.

We can expect more streamings of “Patient Zero” – along with the three other “new” songs included in The Life of a Showgirl: Encore expanded release, including “Babylon,” “Pink Clouding” and “Cleveland!” – when Swift unveils the full, world premiere music video for “Patient Zero” during Sunday night’s MTV Video Music Awards (on CBS and MTV, streaming on Paramount+ Premium in the U.S.).

A teaser clip of the “Patient Zero” video dropped Thursday, and even that brief bit seemed to provide enough clues to keep Swiftophiles scrambling for hidden messages. We know stars Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson made appearances in the clip, but that’s about all we know for sure.

Watch on Deadline

The Swifitian conjecture has been brewing since Swift appeared in a recent Law & Order: SVU-themed Emmy telecast skit with Mariska Hargitay. Some strange words spoken by Swift – “Saccharide. Aries. From the vineyard. North or south” – that have had die-hards deciphering ever since.

Maybe all will be revealed Sunday. Or maybe not.

title: Cinetic Launches Vertical Leap, Investment Vehicle & Producing Pathway For Pro Athletes — Zurich Summit
summary: John Sloss’s Cinetic Media has launched Vertical Leap, an investment vehicle and producing pathway for professional athletes. The initiative is designed to give athletes/members “a working seat inside Cinetic’s slate, with access to rough cuts, creative input, and the same industry guidance the company provides the filmmakers behind its most successful projects.” The end goal […]
content:
John Sloss’s Cinetic Media has launched Vertical Leap, an investment vehicle and producing pathway for professional athletes.

The initiative is designed to give athletes/members “a working seat inside Cinetic’s slate, with access to rough cuts, creative input, and the same industry guidance the company provides the filmmakers behind its most successful projects.”

The end goal is for member athletes to build a production career off the back of their training in the program.

Cost for athletes to become members is $25,000 per year with participants pitched a minimum of 10 documentary projects “vetted from established, profitable directors and producers”.

Investors are then able to back additional projects should they get the bug. The opportunities are in docs for now, but Sloss told Deadline that members are already asking about potential investment in non-doc projects.

Watch on Deadline

Sloss says he has signed up 10 “prominent” athletes, with plans to expand the pool up to 50 current and former players. He’s keen to attract athletes from different sports — including tennis, hockey, cricket, darts etc — but says so far the biggest demand has come from NFL and NBA. Deadline understands that three college footballers — from the Michigan Wolverines — are pooling part of their NIL together for a membership.

To fuel the new initiative two people have been repositioned from the Cinetic team and Sloss says he expects to add a few more employees for the label. The program was trailed in Puck yesterday and Sloss will discuss it publicly for the first time on stage at today’s Zurich Summit.

Said Cinetic founder and CEO, John Sloss: “Vertical Leap offers a pathway for elite athletes to support commercial, impactful documentaries, while learning the ins-and-outs of film production from the most experienced storytellers working today. It is also a way for them to build something lasting beyond their playing days, expanding their brand, deepening their creative voice, and putting real equity behind the stories they believe in.”

He continued: “For the documentary community, Vertical Leap brings the adrenaline jolt of a new class of collaborators, athletes with real creative instincts and the reach to bring documentary storytelling to audiences who might not otherwise find it.”

title: Hayley Kiyoko Wants to Make a Lesbian ‘Pirates of the Caribbean’: ‘Keira Knightley But Gay’
summary: Hayley Kiyoko wants to sail the same-sex-loving high seas. The musician, novelist and filmmaker says her dream project is a queer take on “Pirates of the Caribbean.” “I would love to do a lesbian pirate show or movie — Kiera Knightly, but gay,” she said. “Very gay and fantastical.” Kiyoko’s remarks came Thursday night during […]
content:
Hayley Kiyoko wants to sail the same-sex-loving high seas.

The musician, novelist and filmmaker says her dream project is a queer take on “Pirates of the Caribbean.” “I would love to do a lesbian pirate show or movie — Kiera Knightly, but gay,” she said. “Very gay and fantastical.”

Kiyoko’s remarks came Thursday night during a panel at UTA in Beverly Hills titled “Saving Queer Media.” The program also included filmmakers Angela Robinson, Adam Shankman and Wash Westmoreland. Moderated by Variety’s Marc Malkin and hosted by UTA Proud, the evening served as a fundraiser for the Los Angeles-based LGBTQ+ film festival Outfest.

Kiyoko made her directorial debut earlier this year with “Girls Like Girls,” a YA romance based on her novel and song of the same name. She said she tried to get the film greenlit just based on the song but said financing didn’t come through until after she wrote the novel and it became a bestseller.

Popular on Variety

She’s hoping to turn her second novel, “Where There’s Room for Us,” into a film as well. “It’s a period piece, which no one wants to pay for, but they will one day,” she said to cheers and applause from the audience.

Adam Shankman, whose directorial credits include “Hairspray,” “Rock of Ages,” “Stop! That! Train!” and the upcoming Arnold Schwarzenegger and Alan Ritchson holiday action comedy “The Man With the Bag,” said his dream project is a big-screen adaptation of “Spring Awakening,” the Tony Award-winning coming-of-age rock musical set in late 19th-century Germany.

Although he doesn’t think it could ever get the go-ahead because of its intense subject matter “where terrible things happen to these kids,” Shankman said, “I think it is such a beautiful poem and it is such a beautiful story and it lives in me in such a haunting and beautiful way. I know exactly what I would do with it, and I know exactly how I would do it. I see it completely, and I would love to make it more than any other movie. If that was my last movie, I’d be fine.”

An off-Broadway “Spring Awakening” revival begins previews on Nov. 27 ahead of opening night on Dec. 17.

Wash Westmoreland, the director behind Julianne Moore’s Oscar-winning work in “Still Alice” as well as the recent “Heartstopper Forever,” wants to adapt Chris Bryant’s 2020 book “The Glamour Boys: The Secret Story of the Rebels Who Fought for Britain to Defeat Hitler.”

“It’s a true story, and it’s set in Britain in the 1930s, where being queer was career-destroying and you’d be thrown in jail. It was absolutely illegal,” Westmoreland said. “It’s about a group of queer MPs who are very repressed and very secretive about their lives, but they go to the one place in Europe where you can have a good time and a sexy weekend, which was Berlin at the time of ‘Cabaret.’ So they went there.

“They were drinking, dancing, just having a great time. It was a true expression of freedom,” he continued. “But they saw the rise of the Nazis, and it absolutely radicalized them to go back and stand up and demand that Britain confront Germany at the time.”

Westmoreland called it a story about “queer war heroes” that resonates today. “It is a powerful analogy to what’s happening now, the authoritarians they need people to beat up on and guess who’s very easy to beat up on? LGBTQ people are,” he said. “It’s this vigilance of standing up for what we believe in and preventing the pushback of our rights.”

“Professor Marston and the Wonder Women” writer and director Angela Robinson said she’s been trying to adapt “D.E.B.S.,” her 2004 action comedy about a group of schoolgirls recruited to a secret government defense agency, as a television series. “Sometimes the stars start to align and then they don’t, but that would be really fun,” Robinson said.

title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Director James Gray Says He Doesn’t ‘Want to Preach’ Politics To Audiences: ‘Art Is Not Sunday School’
summary: “Paper Tiger” director James Gray says he doesn’t “want to preach” about politics while making the festival rounds for his latest film, starring Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller. “All movies are political in one way or another, but I like movies that exist with subtext,” Gray told Variety at the film’s New York […]
content:
“Paper Tiger” director James Gray says he doesn’t “want to preach” about politics while making the festival rounds for his latest film, starring Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller.

“All movies are political in one way or another, but I like movies that exist with subtext,” Gray told Variety at the film’s New York Film Festival premiere Friday. “I don’t want to preach to you. That’s a polemic. That’s for debate class. The reason we can watch some of those beautiful Hollywood movies from 1940 and still find them moving is because they weren’t trying to teach us a lesson. Not Sunday school. Art is not Sunday school.”

Yet “Paper Tiger” has taken on a few unexpected political parallels. Dating back to the Ming Dynasty, the Chinese used the term paper tiger to describe someone who appears powerful and intimidating but ultimately poses little threat. President Donald J. Trump has repeatedly invoked the term when discussing Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Popular on Variety

“Russia has been fighting aimlessly for three and a half years a War that should have taken a Real Military Power less than a week to win,” Trump wrote on Truth Social a year ago this week. “This is not distinguishing Russia. In fact, it is very much making them look like ‘a paper tiger.’”

Coincidentally, he only began doing so after filming wrapped on James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” a crime drama centered on a family being threatened by Russian mobsters.

“It’s very weird because I wrote and made [‘Paper Tiger’] before [Trump] ever started using that term,” Gray said. “It had nothing to do with him…. It’s sort of like half frightening, weirdly flattering. I don’t know. What would you think?”

From Gray’s early work on “The Yards” (which drew from his father’s work manufacturing subway parts and how the job led to him becoming entangled in illegal activity) to “Armageddon Time” (his autobiographical coming-of-age drama that played second fiddle to Steven Spielberg’s “The Fabelmans” on the 2022 awards circuit), each of his films chronicle deeply personal chapters of his life through the guise of genre.

“Paper Tiger” was initially conceived as a sequel to “Armageddon Time,” one that would focus on his mother’s untimely battle with glioblastoma that ultimately killed her. Gray even considered bringing back Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong as his parents, but his experience watching his father become a convicted criminal took precedence in the story.

Adam Driver stars in Gray’s latest film as Gary, a former police officer who ropes his younger brother Irwin (Miles Teller, not Strong) into a dicey business deal that lands them in trouble with the Russian mafia. Their predicament hijacks Irwin’s suburban family life, just as his wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson, not Hathaway) is diagnosed with a sudden illness. Gary dismisses the Russians as “paper tigers” (all talk, no bite), only to discover how badly he has underestimated them.

The title’s irony extends beyond the Russians. Much like “Armageddon Time” explores the complexity of the American Dream, “Paper Tiger” depicts a system that appears navigable to an ordinary American family — until, that is, it swallows them whole.

“This term was originally [popularized] by Mao Zedong in China to describe us,” Gray explains. “I always loved it because it seemed so vivid. A tiger made of paper — what is that? It’s the brittleness that’s underneath all of us no matter how tough we think we are.”

Just hours before the “Paper Tiger” premiere in New York, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Trump was setting up a trilateral peace agreement with Russia and Ukraine. But when asked if Trump himself is a paper tiger, Gray went mute.

“No comment,” he smirked.

title: Reba McEntire Says She Missed a Call from Dolly Parton Before Her Death and ‘Couldn’t’ Get Back in Touch: ‘I’ll Never Know Why She Called’
summary: Reba McEntire revealed her longtime friend Dolly Parton tried to get in touch with her just before she died. The country singer and actress shared that she missed a call from Parton, who died Aug. 25 after a “brief battle” with cancer, and was unable to get in touch with her one final time. “She […]
content:
Reba McEntire revealed her longtime friend Dolly Parton tried to get in touch with her just before she died.

The country singer and actress shared that she missed a call from Parton, who died Aug. 25 after a “brief battle” with cancer, and was unable to get in touch with her one final time.

“She did call me the last of July, and I was in a meeting and I missed her call,” McEntire told Entertainment Tonight. “I tried to get back in touch with her and I couldn’t, never made a connection. And then when my buddy called me and said, ‘Dolly’s gone,’ I thought, ‘I’ll never know why she called me.’”

Popular on Variety

McEntire added, “I’ll find out one day.”

The friends collaborated on several projects together, including their cover of “Does He Love You” for McEntire’s album in 2021 and co-hosting the 2019 CMA awards. McEntire recently performed a tribute for Parton at the Emmys with an emotional cover of “Appalachian Memories” and was one of the many people who honored Parton online after the news of her passing.

“Well, I just got the news that my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side. Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth,” McEntire wrote on X. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart. There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang.”

She added, “Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She’s gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her. I’ll never forget the first time I met you and I’ll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart. I will always love you, Reba.”

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ First Reactions Go Crazy for ‘Epic’ and ‘Jaw-Dropping’ Sequel: ‘Should Be Nominated for Best Picture’
summary: Godzilla is back and better than ever as Takashi Yamazaki’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” is earning rave first reactions after its New York Film Festival press screening. The director’s sequel to 2023’s blockbuster “Godzilla Minus One” wowed journalists with epic thrills and the first R-rated action set pieces in the long-running kaiju franchise. First reactions out […]
content:
Godzilla is back and better than ever as Takashi Yamazaki‘s “Godzilla Minus Zero” is earning rave first reactions after its New York Film Festival press screening. The director’s sequel to 2023’s blockbuster “Godzilla Minus One” wowed journalists with epic thrills and the first R-rated action set pieces in the long-running kaiju franchise. First reactions out of the festival are calling “Godzilla Minus One” a “jaw-dropping spectacle” and a “glorious continuation of the first film.”

“A truly epic cinematic feat,” writes reporter Jonathan Sim. “It takes the King of the Monsters to a whole new level while still grounding everything in human, emotional stakes. A must-see blockbuster that truly delivers. Unmatched VFX, action, and scale. Rousing, incredible filmmaking.”

Popular on Variety

“Takashi Yamazaki’s made a worthy successor to ‘Minus One’ with a family-centric story that’s also filled with thrilling action sequences and jaw-dropping monster battles,” adds Marissa Hill. “But it works in the quieter moments too… It’s still astonishing to me that these films, made on a fraction of the budget as current day blockbusters, look this good… the King of Monsters has never looked or sounded this grand.”

Film critic Edward Douglas was “completely blown away” by the sequel, while fellow critic Brandon Lewis called the movie an “overwhelming achievement of kaiju filmmaking. Aside from the jaw-dropping spectacle, Takashi Yamazaki packs in an emotional wallop.”

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is the 38th film in the “Godzilla” franchise and the 34th produced by Toho, the Japanese entertainment company that originally created the franchise. Yamazaki returns to the director’s chair after the immense success of “Godzilla Minus One,” which earned $116 million worldwide, making it the highest-grossing Japanese “Godzilla” film of all time. “Minus One” also won the Oscar for best visual effects. The sequel stars Kamiki Ryunosuke and Hamabe Minami and marks the first time a Japanese feature has been shot for Imax screens.

Per the official description, “Godzilla Minus Zero” picks up in 1949, “two years after the tumultuous events of ‘Godzilla Minus One,’ and continues the story of the Shikishima family as they face an all-new calamity.” The rampage-causing Godzilla is bigger than ever this time and heads to New York City for a global action epic.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” opens in U.S. theaters Nov. 6, three days after it begins rolling out in Japan. Check out more first reactions in the posts below.

title: Sylvester Stallone Says He ‘Became Bulimic’ After Transforming for ‘Rocky’ and Opens Up About the ‘Terrible Toll’ of Steroid Use: It Was An ‘Obsessive Body-Worship Kind of Thing’
summary: Sylvester Stallone is opening up about the less glamorous side of fame, revealing that he’s struggled with a tumultuous relationship with his body ever since he physically transformed to play the titular boxer in “Rocky.” In a recent interview with The New York Times, the famed actor delved into his “intimate” relationship with his body […]
content:
Sylvester Stallone is opening up about the less glamorous side of fame, revealing that he’s struggled with a tumultuous relationship with his body ever since he physically transformed to play the titular boxer in “Rocky.”

In a recent interview with The New York Times, the famed actor delved into his “intimate” relationship with his body and how it’s changed over time. “It was my armor. I looked at Rocky: very smooth, very normal-looking guy. And then I said, I think the character would start to become a bit more vain. And then in ‘Rambo,’ you’re playing a warrior, so you’d be a little bit more animalistic. You wouldn’t be so smooth,” he said. “So I started to think: Design your body like a jaguar, a cat. Not big like Arnold, but more feral and aggressive and very limber and athletic.”

However, Stallone admitted that this type of thinking “became an obsession.” “It got to the point where I became bulimic,” he said. “I got down to 2.6 percent body fat when I was doing ‘Rocky III,’ and I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing.”

Popular on Variety

Steroids played a role, also, he continued: “Nobody does it without additives and drugs, period. I don’t care what they say. It isn’t as though you’re a junkie, but if you’re going to work out and try to stay in shape for six months straight, and you’re eating yogurt and pudding, it’s not happening.” He noted that he’d use the drugs “in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off.” “People go, ‘Oh, you don’t get that way naturally.’ No, you don’t. But that also took a terrible toll.”

“It wasn’t until I did ‘Cop Land,’ when I had to play the weakest guy in the room — partially deaf, overweight — that I felt somewhat liberated,” he said. “But yeah, I’ve abused my body.”

Today, Stallone said he no longer sees his body as his armor, but treating it in the “masochistic” ways he did came “at a terrible price.” “If I could do it over again, I would say, ‘Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts,’” he said.

Stallone’s forthcoming memoir, “The Steps,” is available on Sept. 29.

title: “I Can Promise You, We Had No Idea That ‘Obsession’ Was Going To Become ‘Obsession'”, Says Hit Horror Film’s Seller — Zurich Summit
summary: William Goldman’s adage that “nobody knows anything” never gets old. If studios and financiers knew what was going to work every time, everyone would be rich and the industry would be a lot less interesting. The old saying reared its head today at the Zurich Summit when filmmakers and brokers behind the year’s horror phenomena […]
content:
William Goldman’s adage that “nobody knows anything” never gets old.

If studios and financiers knew what was going to work every time, everyone would be rich and the industry would be a lot less interesting.

The old saying reared its head today at the Zurich Summit when filmmakers and brokers behind the year’s horror phenomena Backrooms and Obsession admitted that they didn’t know their films were about to go stratospheric. There’s absolutely no shame in admitting that. No one knew quite how enormous both films would become, even if many clearly believed in the films and the filmmakers.

“You know, it’s funny,” CAA Media Finance Co-Head Roeg Sutherland mused during a panel on the independent business. “We have a colleague in our department who sold Obsession. I can promise you, we had no idea that Obsession was going to become Obsession.”

Watch on Deadline

CAA co-repped the domestic deal with Capstone, selling the Curry Barker-directed movie out of Toronto for around $14M to Focus. The film went on to make a staggering $264M in the U.S. alone off a $1M budget. It took $520M global.

But believing in a filmmaker is where it starts, added Sutherland.

“I think the most important thing, is less about IP and genres, though those things can be important, but it’s always about the filmmaker. Whether it’s an established filmmaker or a discovery, it has to be someone that you’re willing to go on a ride with. You never know what’s going to happen. But that’s the central element that will decide whether a movie is gonna be good or bad. The filmmaker is the person you’re betting on.”

In an earlier panel, Backrooms director Kane Parsons was asked whether he contributed to the distribution and marketing of the A24 smash. While A24 clearly mounted a brilliant campaign, Parsons admitted that there was a level of uncertainty over what the film could do and who exactly it would reach.

“The truthful answer,” the 20-year-old said about the horror film that took a whopping $400M global off a $10M budget, “is that I don’t think there was a real sense of what it would be prior to the release of the film. I don’t. Even at the height of projections.”

Parsons added that he didn’t know whether the film would truly click with fans of the creepypasta genre, but that he “liked to think we did the core idea that they were expecting.” Clearly he did, and plenty more.

Later in the day, CAA Media Finance co-head Sarah Schweitzman also noted the serendipitous element to this summer’s record-breaking $4.7BN domestic box office. But also to the success speaking to a desire for authenticity and irreverence.

“When you look at the landscape today, the movies were so amazing this year, and they’re so different to what they’ve ever been, and unexpected in achieving the success that they’ve they’ve achieved. There is no way in which you can categorize the film business as unhealthy, because it’s burgeoning, it’s booming. I think that also speaks to where we are politically. There’s a lot time for irreverence. It’s a time for saying things that are maybe unpopular or maybe scary, but there’s a real underground belief and desire to hear the truth, which is not necessarily something that everyone is encouraged to do right now.”
