content:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and more were mocked in the latest “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Weekend Update segment.

“This week, President Trump welcomed President Xi to the White House,” co-anchor Ania Magliano said. “As a sign of respect, Trump wore a bright red tie as a sign of Communist China. And Xi wore a mottled purple tie, the color of Trump’s prostate.”

Joking about Trump’s Chinese banquet for President Xi, Magliano quipped: “Trump ordered a 20, an 18 and a 21. And afterwards sat down for a Chinese-inspired banquet.”

Popular on Variety

“From Beijing to beige man, Trump met [U.K. Prime Minister] Andy Burnham” Young continued. “It wasn’t a memorable event for Trump, as he’s got dementia.”

Altman, the co-founder of OpenAI, and his appearance at the UN was also teased. “Altman, whose company launched ChatGPT, warned his creation could destroy humanity. And then he slapped his own wrists and ran out of the room saying, ‘Someone stop me!’” Magliano said.

“SNL U.K.” also took aim at Harvey Weinstein, who was sentenced to 15 years in prison in New York earlier this week.

“Me Too is now what the inmates say in the queue for Weinstein’s arsehole,” Magliano joked as the audience let out a collective “oooh.”

“Back in 2016, Weinstein hired a private intelligence firm to dig up dirt on his victims,” Young continued. “So on one side, we have a prolific rapist with paid spies. On the other, we have abuse victims who have been silenced. A conflict described by Ed Sheeran as ‘nuanced.’”

Elsewhere, Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent speech at the UN — where representatives for other nations walked out — was also mentioned. “Of course, it is easy to paint Netanyahu as the bad guy in this situation,” Young said before swiftly moving on to the next item.

title: Emmy Rossum Says Nude ‘Shameless’ Scenes Affected Her Dating Life Because Men Had ‘Preconceived Notions’ of ‘How I Was Sexually’
summary: Emmy Rossum recently revealed that playing Fiona Gallagher on “Shameless” had some lasting consequences off-screen. Rossum’s nude scenes in the show, which ran for nine seasons, made her dating life difficult because of “preconceived notions,” she said. “It got quite tricky because of the nudity on the show,” Rossum told Maria Sharapova on an episode […]
content:
Emmy Rossum recently revealed that playing Fiona Gallagher on “Shameless” had some lasting consequences off-screen.

Rossum’s nude scenes in the show, which ran for nine seasons, made her dating life difficult because of “preconceived notions,” she said. “It got quite tricky because of the nudity on the show,” Rossum told Maria Sharapova on an episode of “Pretty Tough.” “All of the guys that I would go out with had preconceived notions of who I was or how I was sexually.”

Some of the conversations were “bizarre,” Rossum said, noting one particular experience in which a man hoping to pursue a career in politics was hesitant about being associated with her because of the scenes.

Popular on Variety

“He was like, ‘I really want to be president someday.’ And I was like, ‘Wow, that’s a great goal,’” she said. “He’s like, ‘But I feel like running for office dating someone who’s been exposed in the way that you have — do you think that would be tricky for me?’ And I was like, ‘This is an insane conversation to have.’”

Rossum began “Shameless” when she was just 24, which she said was a difficult time to attempt dating as a young actress.

“You’re trying to figure out who you are,” she said. “You’re coming into your own as an artist. And there’s also all these preconceived notions about you that are out there that are associated with [you] because your body is your art, right? And people can get confused.”

Prior to “Shameless,” Rossum starred in “The Day After Tomorrow,” “Mystic River” and “The Phantom of the Opera,” the latter of which earned her a Golden Globes nomination.

title: ‘My Sad Dead’ Review: An Urban Community Gets the Haunting It Deserves in Pablo Larraín’s Superb Modern Gothic
summary: Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín’s sprawling, peculiar, terrific “My Sad Dead” is about 20 things at once in every moment. It’s a ghost story, obviously, on account of all the ghosts. It’s a droll tragicomedy, with eccentrically deadpan […]
content:
Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín‘s sprawling, peculiar, terrific “My Sad Dead” is about 20 things at once in every moment. It’s a ghost story, obviously, on account of all the ghosts. It’s a droll tragicomedy, with eccentrically deadpan characters providing both the tragedy and the jokes. It’s a nasty body-horror and a ferocious satire — in its way as scathing a portrait of modern, urban Argentina as any of Larraín’s previous Chilean films have been about his homeland. And most surprisingly, it’s a mini-treatise on hostile urban architecture and the effect it has on the human spirit to dwell in brutal, brutalist structures that quarantine their inhabitants from society, and from each other. “Rage weighs more than concrete,” sings Shakira over the closing credits, but the Piedrabuena neighborhood of Buenos Aires is heavy with both.

Ema (Mercedes Morán, in a fantastic performance of dry eyes and drier wit) is almost an emblem of Piedrabuena, though her rage has long since turned to a resilient kind of resignation, only tempered by the quick flash of amusement that often sparks up in her otherwise world-weary expression. Or should that be otherworld-weary? Ema doesn’t sleep much because of all the screaming ghosts who, for now, only she can hear.

Popular on Variety

A doctor who has been pushed into retirement, with dark mutterings going on about a trolley-problem decision she made regarding COVID treatments, Ema doesn’t technically live in Piedrabuena anymore — she has a spacious apartment in a nicer part of the city that she is looking to rent out. But she has recently moved back to care for her aged mother through the terminal stages of a painful illness. And that’s how we first see her, from above, as we hover like an angel or an overhead lamp, in the attic room of her mother’s house beside the Piedrabuena projects. Ema holds the bedridden woman’s frail, pale blue hand as, not particularly quietly nor entirely peacefully, she dies. Then her corpse opens its eyes.

It’s not her, exactly, but a fuzzy, not-quite-opaque facsimile of her. The effect that “My Sad Dead” uses to summon the dead is the more convincing for not being particularly flashy. The unusual, low-contrast color palette that Larraín and his ace regular DP Sergio Armstrong have chosen blanches the images to a flat, pinkish gray, so that those with and without heartbeats all have the pallor of a mortuary waiting room’s magnolia walls.

Yet we always know who is alive and who is, well, post-alive, and not just because the dead often have a tell, like they’ll be staggering around with half their head blown off, or bleeding copiously from a ragged, ripped-open chest wound. It’s also because of their manner. Ema tends not to encounter too many quiet, dignified, expected deaths, and those who have experienced a violent end are almost childlike in their confusion and disorientation. Often they seem trapped in a cycle, doomed to re-live (and re-die) their last moments, powerless to change the outcome.

Ema is sick of the dead and long past sick of trying to convince others that her abilities are real. So mostly she ignores the ghosts and they ignore her and that’s fine. But then her estranged sister Lidia (Alejandra Flechner) and her husband fly in for a visit from their home in Seattle, bringing with them their troubled, morbidly obese teenage daughter Julia (Carolina Álvarez), and Ema comes to realize that Julia can also commune with the dead.

And really commune: Julia, miserable and stigmatized and about to be committed to an institution by her hapless parents, loudly and lustily enjoys getting busy with the no-longer-with-us in a way that one supposes cannot technically be necrophilia, considering it’s sex with the spirits of the dead rather than with their bodies. Which doesn’t mean Larraín averts our gaze from these strangely moving copulations; the film is about the non-corporeal but it’s fascinated too by the flesh, by its gratification, its mortification and then, in an increasingly ethereal refrain, its slow putrefaction and decomposition.

With its octagonal clusters of flats arranged around a central water tower that looks like a fist raised against the sky, the neighborhood doesn’t have much spirit of community. The residents occasionally gather in a disused rec center but the meetings devolve into rants about immigrants, junkies, thugs and vigilantism. One man suggests mounting the heads of thieves on spikes, a grisly image that Larraín, for once, spares us, as opposed to the bungling burglar falling from a roof and impaling himself crunchily on a railing, or the three pretty, giggling teens who get shot and shot and shot again in a gang-related hit, or the young woman who dies agonisingly of an infected dog bite she concealed because she couldn’t afford to miss work.

Ema cannot fix these restless ghosts, but sometimes she can distract them from the shock of their painful passing, a talent which puts her in demand when the water supply becomes mysteriously contaminated, and suddenly the whole of Piedrabuena can hear what she has always heard. The screams, the gunshots and the cries for help that went unanswered.

In other hands, this would set up a supernatural TV procedural. But Ema does not solve mysteries or bring murderers to justice. “My Sad Dead” has no interest in being “Medium” and its provenance as TV — it was conceived as a Netflix miniseries but recut into this 186-minute movie for a San Sebastián competition bow — only proves that cinematic storytelling has little to do with the size of the screen on which you watch it. It is entirely cinematic, every scene loaded with texture and subtext and observational nuance. If there’s a comparison, it may be with Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog,” also nominally a television project and also one set within a single housing complex. (It feels like we’ve been talking about “Dekalog” a lot recently, given the ongoing project to remake it. Perhaps there’s something in the water.)

But really, the similarity is in mood and effect. Larraín, alongside Anastasia Ayazi and Guillermo Calderón, co-scripts with Mariana Enriquez, whose writings provide the foundational inspiration, and their outstanding screenplay tells a hundred little side-stories in addition to its main narrative. Almost all of them are harsh or gross or scary or sorrowful and yet the experience of “My Sad Dead” is mordantly funny and oddly uplifting. Maybe it’s the weirdness. Maybe it’s the way it makes a waterlogged ribbon of skin detaching from a shin and floating away seem deeply beautiful. Or maybe it’s just a reminder that being sad about death — your own or someone else’s — is simply an upside-down affirmation that you are happy to be alive.

title: ‘NAZA’ Co-Director Yuval Abraham Calls Out the U.S. Government for ‘Funding’ Israel’s Destruction of Gaza, Telling NYFF Audience: ‘This Is What Your Country Is Supporting’
summary: The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor who gave a brief Q&A with festival director Dennis Lim after the screening. Journalist and co-director Abraham told the crowd, many of whom were still drying their eyes […]
content:
The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor who gave a brief Q&A with festival director Dennis Lim after the screening. Journalist and co-director Abraham told the crowd, many of whom were still drying their eyes after bearing witness in the documentary to footage of the destruction of Gaza, that it was essential to play “NAZA” at NYFF because the U.S. is responsible for funding billions to the Israeli government and supplying military aid, which is being used against the Palestinian people.

“It’s important for us to see this film at this moment, as you were saying, because these older officials are talking about what is being done with taxpayer money from people sitting here,” said Abraham, who was met with cheers of approval from the audience. “This is what your country is supporting and funding… Part of the goal is to make denial of what’s going on in Gaza harder.”

Popular on Variety

“NAZA” first premiered at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, where it won a special jury prize and received a record-breaking 24.5-minute standing ovation. The documentary was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.” It is now set to release in more than 50 territories before becoming available to stream for free on The Guardian’s website.

Since its premiere, the directors have come under fire from a number of Israeli officials — Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the introduction of a law that would “revoke the citizenship of anyone who slanders IDF [Israeli Defense Forces] soldiers” following the film’s debut, while Israel’s Minister of Culture threatened to revoke the filmmaker’s Israeli citizenship.

Outside the festival screening, the Israeli-American Council organized a more than 50-person protest against the film, which they described as “anti-Israel,” and said “makes serious allegations about the IDF’s conduct in the Gaza Strip while ignoring findings and information that contradict its claims.” Those in attendance gathered by LED trucks that projected footage from October 7 and portraits of those who were killed that day.

“It’s completely unjustified, the massacre of October 7th,” said Abraham during the Q&A. “But it also cannot justify what you’ve seen. Does it justify the slaughter of so many civilians in Gaza?”

title: Sylvester Stallone Thought His Dad Would “Be Proud” To Make ‘Rocky’ Cameo: “It Got Really Nasty”
summary: As Sylvester Stallone made his breakout performance in Rocky, there was one person he couldn’t quite turn into a fan. While discussing his memoir The Steps, releasing Oct. 23, the 3x Oscar nominee recalled things on set getting “really nasty” after giving his real father Frank Stallone Sr. a cameo as the bell ringer in […]
content:
As Sylvester Stallone made his breakout performance in Rocky, there was one person he couldn’t quite turn into a fan.

While discussing his memoir The Steps, releasing Oct. 23, the 3x Oscar nominee recalled things on set getting “really nasty” after giving his real father Frank Stallone Sr. a cameo as the bell ringer in the 1976 boxing drama’s climactic match.

“It was like: I just want you to love me for a little bit,” Sly explained to The New York Times. “Like, look what I did! Share it with me. I know you thought I was a fool my whole life, but here we are.”

On the day of filming, Frank Sr. “didn’t ring the bell properly,” as his son “kept fighting and fighting and fighting. Everything’s choreographed. It’s one, two, three, four, bell. Not six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Carl Weathers is like, ‘What’s going on?'”

Watch on Deadline

Stallone continued, “And of course it ended up in an altercation by the end. It got really nasty. A really bad Italian drama. But for a moment I thought, Jesus, he’d be proud.”

Sylvester Stallone in ‘Rocky’ (1976) Everett Collection

In the interview, Stallone explained that his father “was very, very cold and tough” until they reconciled upon his death in 2011.

“It would be these constant bombastic explosions and then total silence,” recalled Stallone of living alone with his dad. “If he and I were talking and I said, ‘I don’t know if I agree with that,’ he’d start spinning his fork and suck his teeth, and you knew what was coming. The next thing you know, wham! He had very big hands. You learn to duck. I didn’t put a lot of stuff in the book because I didn’t want a pity party, but it was insane.”

In the biopic I Play Rocky, premiering Nov. 6 in theaters, Anthony Ippolito plays a young Stallone as he writes the first Rocky movie and fights to star as the titular boxer.

title: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham Nearly Joins Oasis, But There’s Something A Bit Off About The Gallagher Brothers In ‘SNL UK’ Cold Open
summary: There was something a bit off about Oasis’ sometimes feuding-yet-touring brothers in the Saturday Night Live UK cold open this week. SNL UK kicked off its Season 2 Episode 3 with new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, played by George Fouracres, returning to his beloved home of Manchester following a speech to the UN where […]
content:
There was something a bit off about Oasis’ sometimes feuding-yet-touring brothers in the Saturday Night Live UK cold open this week.

SNL UK kicked off its Season 2 Episode 3 with new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, played by George Fouracres, returning to his beloved home of Manchester following a speech to the UN where he socked it to Russia, according to his good pal Angela Rayner (Celeste Dring). “I’m sick of Russia trying to divide the British people. We can divide ourselves thank you very much,” jokes Burnham.

Before long, Oasis’ brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, played by Jack Shep and new cast member Freddie Meredith, arrive to offer Burnham the opportunity of a lifetime. Their guitarist has pulled out and Burnham, a guitar player himself, can step in. “Ange, cancel the budget I’m going on tour,” he tells Rayner.

But alas, Burnham is asked to input numerous personal details – a gentle poke at critiques of Oasis’ expensive and dynamically priced tickets – and once done Liam and Noel emerge as two Russian spies.

Watch on Deadline

“Oasis has always been Russian pop. All songs were made in a lab by Kremlin scientists. ‘Wonderwall’ is really ‘Wonderful Wall’ about the Berlin Wall,” says Russian spy Liam.

In the end, following an extended joke about his flip-flopping on calling a general election – “I for example could hold a general election and easily smash it, but as I announced yesterday, I want to, but I could” – Burnham orders the “Russian Mancs” to “leave Britain and go back to being Oasis.”

The cold open came in the third ep of the second season of Sky‘s SNL UK. Amelia Dimoldenberg, creator of Chicken Shop Date, which launches its final season next week, follows in the footsteps of Jeff Goldblum and Jamie Demetriou to host this week.

All of SNL UK’s cast members have returned for Season 2, including Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Dring, Fouracres, Ania Magliano, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Shep, Emma Sidi and Paddy Young, with Meredith making his debut.

SNL UK is produced by Universal Television Alternative Studio’s UK production team and Broadway Video. Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer. James Longman is lead producer.

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’
summary: “Godzilla Minus Zero” blew the roof off Alice Tully Hall during its rapturous world premiere screening at the New York Film Festival. The long-awaited sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” earned rave first reactions from the press earlier in the day, and that adoration rolled right into the world premiere. The movie was met with […]
content:
“Godzilla Minus Zero” blew the roof off Alice Tully Hall during its rapturous world premiere screening at the New York Film Festival. The long-awaited sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” earned rave first reactions from the press earlier in the day, and that adoration rolled right into the world premiere. The movie was met with multiple mid-screening applauses as the crowd went wild for all the kaiju mayhem on screen.

Ahead of its debut later this year, “Godzilla Minus Zero” has been rated R for “violent content/bloody images,” making it the first entry in the 72-year-old franchise to receive an R-rating. Director Takashi Yamazaki, returning to helm the sequel after 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” became a roaring success, says securing the rating was “essential to the film.”



“Logically, as a studio — and even as a director — you want as many people from the general public to be able to see your film,” Yamazaki told Variety at the premiere Saturday afternoon. “So, an R-rating might seem like a barrier to entry, and conversations about, ‘Hey, could we have not gotten this down to PG-13?’ of course are going to happen. In spite of that, though, there were certain scenes that, for me as a director, were so essential to the film. Censoring it or cutting it was just not an option for me.”

Under MPA guidelines, viewers under 17 cannot attend an R-rated film without a parent or guardian, a restriction that has traditionally made the rating a commercial deterrent for studios releasing big-budget, four-quadrant films. That stigma has faded over the past decade, starting with the blockbuster success of 2016’s “Deadpool” ($782 million). In 2019, “Joker” ($1.07 billion) became the first R-rated film to cross the $1 billion threshold. That record was later broken by 2024’s “Deadpool & Wolverine” ($1.33 billion) — and more recently — 2026’s “The Odyssey” ($1.72 billion), which currently stands as the 17th highest-grossing film of all time worldwide.

Popular on Variety

“I think the R-rating, at one point, carried almost a negative connotation,” Yamazaki explained. “In more modern films, it actually creates a sort of expectation and excitement of, ‘Okay, well, they’re not censoring anything. The director and the cast’s voice is there, as is.’ So it is very encouraging to see other films who have preceded us that have already found a lot of success with the R-rating at the box office. Hopefully, we can continue that trend with ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.’”

Inside the world premiere screening, New York Film Festival director Dennis Lim acknowledged that the Godzilla franchise might not be the first thing people think of playing at a major film festival. And yet, “We thought it was about time to bring a giant monster movie here.”

Yamazaki took the stage to thunderous applause from the audience both before and after the screening, where he asked the crowd not to spoil any of the sequel’s many surprises on social media.

“You are the first to see this film,” the filmmaker said. “There are a lot of ‘Godzilla’ fans around the world, so let’s work together and do not do any spoilers. No spoilers, please! I am trusting all of you guys.”

Yamazaki also had the audience laughing while explaining how he never intended to create a sequel to “Godzilla Minus One.” Executives at Toho immediately started asking him about a follow-up movie once they saw the first cut of “Minus One,” a thought that made Yamazaki instantly nervous. It wasn’t until the movie opened in theaters and started to be celebrated around the world by audiences that the director realized a sequel would be a viable option.

“Toho executives are here now,” the director said. “Hopefully all your reactions tonight don’t have them wanting a third movie.”

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Godzilla and King Ghidorah Battle to the Death in the Even Grander Follow-Up to ‘Godzilla Minus One’
summary: Yamazaki, who rebooted the genre and took it to a new peak in the revelatory 2023 retro kaiju classic "Godzilla Minus One," works with a quality that none of the filmmakers of recent decades has summoned: a fairy-tale innocence, an immersion in the annihilating heavy-metal poetry of Godzilla — the way the destruction of a city can become a spectacle out of a dream (which is to say, a national nightmare). In "Godzilla Minus Zero," when Godzilla and King Ghidorah go at it, it’s more than a WWE match of primeval rivals. It’s a clash of the titans that will reduce everyone in the audience to a wide-eyed, jaw-dropped child.
content:
Of all the criticisms leveled at Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” (apart from the one I have: that the entire movie is a frigging mess), the most resonant, to me, was the complaint that Nolan had made a mistake by leaving the Greek gods out of the story. He certainly demonstrated that you could make a version of Homer minus the gods; he didn’t necessarily show that it could be done without losing a crucial dimension. Besides, if you can’t see gods at a movie of “The Odyssey,” where are you going to see them?

The answer is: at a Japanese monster movie — more thrilling, by leagues, than “The Odyssey” — where the monsters possess an ominous majesty that’s not of this world, even as they’re in the middle of laying waste to it.

Popular on Variety

In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which premiered tonight at the New York Film Festival (it opens Nov. 6), there are two oversize mystic beasts: Godzilla, the original kaiju (the character is now 72 years old, proving that 72 is the new awesome), and King Ghidorah, the dragon hydra who made his first appearance in the 1964 kaiju classic “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster.” Each is a formidable creature, though in both cases it’s more than a matter of epic stomp or gargantuan wing power. When Godzilla tilts his head up to the sky, gathers his might, and then shoots out a blast of radioactivity that can level a city, it’s an exhibition of transcendent force. And Ghidorah’s heads — which look, up close, like costume figures out of a Golden Dragon Dance — emit orange lightning volts that extend for half a mile. These aren’t mere monsters. They’re serious movie gods.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is set in 1949, and it opens with a startling sequence in which Ghidorah, with only one head (this will change), shows up in the city of Matsumoto and destroys it. We’re given a grand vista of demolition, and also close-ups of Ghidorah seen from the point-of-view of Professor Murakami (Min Tanaka), a Hiroshima survivor who’s been doing biological creature research. Godzilla will soon turn up as well, even though he was thought to have been destroyed at the end of “Godzilla Minus One.” (It’s hard to destroy a god.) To save Japan, Kenji Noda (Hidetake Yoshioka), the high-strung, pencil-necked, Einstein-haired director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, leads his team in devising a plan that’s got a sandbox-showdown ingenuity: They will lure both creatures to a single locale and goad them into fighting each other. Whichever one remains standing will be wounded and weakened, and the human forces can then finish that monster off.

When you go to see a big visual-effects movie, like something from Marvel, the closing credits that roll on for 12 minutes will feature multiple armies of visual-effects teams (each digital company with its own general). I have no doubt that a formidable army worked on “Godzilla Minus Zero.” But it’s also a movie that features the highly unusual credit “VFX, written, and directed by Takashi Yamazaki.” That’s a sign of how much the movie’s visual effects emanate directly from the imagination of the filmmaker. He’s writing, he’s directing, and he’s orchestrating spectacular gargantuan action paintings of beasts in motion. He’s an artist of larger-than-life pop horror.

We’ve seen countless monster duels in kaiju movies (old and new, good and bad, Japanese and American), but Yamazaki, who rebooted the genre and took it to a new peak in the revelatory 2023 retro kaiju classic “Godzilla Minus One,” works with a quality that none of the filmmakers of recent decades has summoned: a fairy-tale innocence, an immersion in the annihilating heavy-metal poetry of Godzilla — the way the destruction of a city can become a spectacle out of a dream (which is to say, a national nightmare). In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” when Godzilla and King Ghidorah go at it, it’s more than a WWE match of primeval rivals. It’s a clash of the titans that will reduce everyone in the audience to a wide-eyed, jaw-dropped child.

“Godzilla Minus One” was justly celebrated for its human story, which felt like something out of a Kurosawa movie of the ’50s. In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” Yamazaki follows through on that, continuing the tale of Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), the former World War II kamikaze pilot; Noriko (Minamo Hamabe), who is now his wife; and Akiko (Sae Nagatani), their adopted daughter, who has grown into a verbally precocious seven-year-old. The fate of this family is at the heart of the film’s emotional palette. To battle the creatures, Kōichi will go back into fighter-pilot mode, but the services of Noriko will be called on as well. She’s one of the survivors of Godzilla’s 1947 attack who now has bits of Godzilla DNA embedded in her body (which is why she wears an eyepatch).

For a long time, kaiju movies were a semi-joke — a fusion of the colossal and the cheesy, and the fact that you couldn’t separate the two was part of what gave the genre its unique shlock magic. But Yamazaki transcends all that. His staging draws on our collective nostalgic memory of kaiju grandeur, and it also dignifies the genre by building it on a drama that’s staged with passion and vigor. When did anyone ever talk about performances in a Godzilla movie? But in “Godzilla Minus Zero,” one responds to the high anxiety of Yoshioka’s Noda, and to the magnetic intelligence of Masami Nagasawa as Makoto Aoyama, a meteorologist whose intuition about storms has a hint of the prophetic. Min Tanaka, who plays the professor, is an actor who was born on March 10, 1945, the day of the firebombing of Tokyo (the deadliest air raid in human history), and his courtly but simmering presence powerfully channels the film’s awareness of history. Yamazaki stages a couple of audacious sequences that feel, in their way, like his answer to “Oppenheimer.” One is a fantasy of Godzilla approaching Manhattan the way he once approached Tokyo, a chilling vision for any American to behold.

At first, when the Japanese officials think that they’re contending only with Ghidorah, the film’s battles have a tactical stateliness. Ghidorah heads off to the mountains and hibernates, curling up like a giant snake, which makes them think they can bomb him into oblivion, using planes and weapons borrowed from the U.S. But all that accomplishes is to wake the sleeping giant. The sequence in which a half dozen planes battle Ghidorah in the air is grand, eye-popping filmmaking. And that’s just the appetizer, as Godzilla’s return heralds a battle of staggering vastness.

In the final section, a plot strand or two gets a bit tangled. The professor has a hidden agenda, and how he ever meant to carry it out remains too abstract to be entirely clear. Yet as key characters are put under fire, we realize how much we’ve come to care about these creature battlers. They’re rooted in a time and place that feels all too real, and this allows the monsters to parade their primitive might in a way that means something. It was a stroke of inspiration on Yamazaki’s part to reset the kaiju genre in the late ’40s, during the Atomic Age where it is spiritually rooted (the original “Gojira” was released in 1954). The creators of the new James Bond series would do well to follow suit. (That’s how Bond could be vital again.) “Godzilla Minus Zero” is destined to connect with a huge international audience, and it’s already clear that this won’t be the last of Yamazaki’s kaiju epics. That’s because the movie proves that when you do it right, what seemed old can become timeless.

title: Robert Pattinson Says It Would Be ‘Tough’ for His Batman to Exist Within James Gunn’s DCU
summary: Superman and Batman might be one of the DC Universe’s most famous partnerships, but Robert Pattinson is officially ending speculation that his take on Bruce Wayne would fit in the cinematic world created by James Gunn. “I think it would be kind of tough to have this version of Bruce outside of that world,” Pattinson […]
content:
Superman and Batman might be one of the DC Universe’s most famous partnerships, but Robert Pattinson is officially ending speculation that his take on Bruce Wayne would fit in the cinematic world created by James Gunn.

“I think it would be kind of tough to have this version of Bruce outside of that world,” Pattinson told LADbible. “It’s one of the only characters, I guess, because of the length of the shoots, but also it’s such a specific kind of [style]; the tone of it gets inside you. I remember that happened to me the last time I did it, it took a while. You’re just in the dark the whole time. Both mood-wise and light-wise, I can’t see anything for like months. It does affect you, like you feel strange afterwards.”

Audiences were first introduced to Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” in 2022, which offered a distinctly darker take on the comic book character than previous films. “Where do you go after ‘The Dark Knight’? Ben Affleck blew it, and even Christopher Nolan, who brought unprecedented levels of realism and gravitas to that franchise-best Batman saga, couldn’t improve on what he’d created in his 2012 sequel,” wrote Variety’s Peter Debruge in his review of the film. “So what is ‘Cloverfield’ director Matt Reeves’ strategy? Answer: Go darker than ‘The Dark Knight,’ deadlier than ‘No Time to Die’ and longer than ‘Dune’ with a serious-minded Batman stand-alone of his own.”

Popular on Variety

By contrast, Gunn’s “Superman,” released in 2025, was a lighter take on the character. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman wrote that “the new movie isn’t ‘dark’ (Zack Snyder’s ambitious mistake) so much as it’s a loopy, spinning, multifaceted story with genuine emotional stakes.”

“The Batman Part II” is set to hit theaters on Feb. 18, 2028.

title: ‘Jack & Christine’ Trailer: John Hawkes Turns A Dinner Party Into A Night of Chaos – Film News in Brief
summary: “Jack & Christine,” a thriller short film starring John Hawkes, released the first trailer ahead of its world premiere at Beyond Fest on Sunday. The trailer shows married couple Jack (Luke Barnett) and Christine (Nikki Lorenzo) hosting a dinner party that suddenly spirals into an intense, chaotic evening when a guest (Hawkes) from the couple’s […]
content:
“Jack & Christine,” a thriller short film starring John Hawkes, released the first trailer ahead of its world premiere at Beyond Fest on Sunday.

The trailer shows married couple Jack (Luke Barnett) and Christine (Nikki Lorenzo) hosting a dinner party that suddenly spirals into an intense, chaotic evening when a guest (Hawkes) from the couple’s past arrives.

“I’ve always been fascinated by anxiety and paranoia, especially when they start to manifest as reality,” said Noam Kroll, the film’s writer and director. “The theme of this film can be summed up in a line from Catch-22: ‘Just because you’re paranoid doesn’t mean they aren’t after you.’ The idea had been in my head for years, and when I got the chance to work with these three incredible actors, I wrote a chamber piece tailored to each of them.”

“Jack & Christine” is produced by Kroll, Richard Handley, Sheldon Brigman, Jennifer Kroll and Dave Thies. Watch the trailer below.

Popular on Variety

Michael B. Jordan Joins CultureCon 2026 Lineup

This year’s CultureCon lineup will feature reigning best actor Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan.

Following the blockbuster and commercial success of “Sinners,” Jordan is preparing to release his second directorial effort, “The Thomas Crown Affair,” and he’s gearing up to shoot the upcoming “Miami Vice” reboot.

“Lanterns” star Aaron Pierre and musicians Wale and Tobe Nwigwe are also joining the lineup for the 2026 edition of the annual festival, designed to celebrate and empower the next generation of creators of color.

This year’s CultureCon, held October 3-4 in Brooklyn, is backed by presenting sponsor Chase Ink and a host of other companies, including Cricket Wireless, Lincoln, HBO Max, Audible and TikTok. The two-day program will also feature appearances by Oscar winners John Legend, Mahershala Ali and Daniel Kaluuya; Emmy winner Niecy Nash-Betts; and culture shifters like Colin Kaepernick, Olandria Carthen, Miles Caton, Danessa Myricks, Rajah Caruth, Scott Evans and Sherri Shepherd.

Tickets are available on CultureCon’s website.

Phil Lord, Chris Miller Named Guest Artistic Directors for AFI Fest 2026

“Project Hail Mary” filmmakers Phil Lord and Chris Miller were announced as the Guest Artistic Directors for AFI FEST 2026.

This year’s program will include “An Evening with Lord and Miller,” which features a Q&A with the directors followed by a screening of “2001: A Space Odyssey,” held at the TCL Chinese Theatre on Oct. 24.

The filmmakers have also curated a selection of films inspired by their work on “Project Hail Mary.” The slate includes “Harold and Maude” (1971), “The Muppet Movie” (1979) and “Rififi” (1955).

“After years of dragging our friends and families to screenings of films we love, we are delighted to get to do it for hundreds of strangers,” Lord and Miller said in a joint statement. “We chose four films that inspired us not only while making ‘Project Hail Mary’ but also as filmmakers and people. We stand on the shoulders of giants like Hal Ashby and Fozzie Bear.”

AFI FEST 2026 will run Oct. 21-25 at the TCL Chinese Theatre. The festival opens with the U.S. premiere of “Wildwood,” features the world premiere of “The Mosquito Bowl” and closes with “Being Heumann,” with the full lineup being announced Sept. 29.

‘Club Kid’ Gets 35mm Pre-Release Screening at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre

SFFilm will present a special preview screening A24’s “Club Kid” in 35mm at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre on Nov. 2 at 7:00 p.m. with writer, director and star Jordan Firstman making an appearance for a post-screening conversation.

“’Club Kid’ is an exhilarating introduction to Jordan Firstman as a filmmaker, with a world that feels completely specific and wonderfully alive,” SFFilm director of programming Jessie Fairbanks said. “The anarchic humor, incredible ensemble, and unexpected tenderness make this a distinctive film, elevated by needle drops that are thrillingly precise to the characters, culture, and emotional landscape of the story. Bay Area audiences will be treated to a 35mm print, a rare and special way to experience a night at the movies.”

The film follows “a hard-partying New York City club promoter sees his whirlwind lifestyle upended by the arrival of the 10-year-old son he never knew he had.”

A24 opens “Club Kid” in limited release starting on Nov. 6.

Anne Lai, SFFILM’s Executive Director, said, “One of the most exciting things we do at SFFILM is to introduce bold new filmmakers to eager and welcoming audiences. There is not a more fitting place than the iconic Castro Theatre to welcome Jordan Firstman with his feature directorial debut. For decades, gathering to see movies at The Castro has been at the heart of San Francisco’s queer culture and history. We can’t wait to share ‘Club Kid’ at this cinema sanctuary for what’s sure to become one for the ages.”

“The Debut” and “Paper Tiger” Among 2026 Virginia Film Festival Lineup, Jessica Lange and Nathan Lane to Receive Visionary Awards

The Virginia Film Festival announced the lineup for its 39th year, which will take place Oct. 21-25.

Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” starring Julianne Moore, will open the festival, while “1 15 41 Tragedy to Triumph” serves as the closing night film. The Centerpiece Film is “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” starring Amanda Seyfried, and writer, director, producer and actor Tim Blake Nelson will receive the festival’s Virtuoso Award.

In addition to appearing as keynote guests, Nathan Lane and Jessica Lange will receive Visionary Awards, and James Gray will be awarded with the Outstanding Achievement in Directing Award at a screening of “Paper Tiger.” Also screening at the festival are “14th,” “Club Kid,” “I Play Rocky,” “Ink,” “Wild Horse Nine” and “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.”

The full program will be available on the Virginia Film Festival website on Thursday.

title: Ina Garten Explains Why She’s “Always Said No” To A Biopic: “It’s My Story”
summary: After sharing her story in her 2024 memoir Be Ready When The Luck Happens, Ina Garten is reluctant to trust a filmmaker with the adaptation. The Barefoot Contessa celebrity chef recently explained why she’s “never been willing” to make a biopic about her life, despite being “approached” to adapt Be Ready for the big screen. […]
content:
After sharing her story in her 2024 memoir Be Ready When The Luck Happens, Ina Garten is reluctant to trust a filmmaker with the adaptation.

The Barefoot Contessa celebrity chef recently explained why she’s “never been willing” to make a biopic about her life, despite being “approached” to adapt Be Ready for the big screen.

“It’s funny, I don’t make long-term plans. I do what I do as well as I can, and things come along, and I say no to most of them,” she told People.

Garten added, “I’ve been approached to do a movie of my memoir, but I know that when a producer or director gets ahold of a story, they want to make it work on film and they’re going to change it. So I’ve never been willing to do that. It’s my story. I get to keep it. And I don’t want people making up things just for dramatic effect. And so I’ve always said no.”

Watch on Deadline

The 2024 memoir came after Garten ended the nearly 20-year run of her Food Network cooking show Barefoot Contessa, which ran from 2002 to 2021.

Since 2022, Garten has hosted her followup Food Network show Be My Guest, inviting friends to her dinner table in her East Hampton, New York home.

title: Robert Eggers Wants To Do ‘Romeo & Juliet’ Because Things Got “So Dark” After ‘Werwulf’, Joking: “So, I’ll Do Something About Two Teenagers Killing Themselves”
summary: SPOILER ALERT for anyone who skipped freshman English! Robert Eggers is teasing his take on William Shakespeare’s Romeo & Juliet. During a post-screening Q&A for his latest macabre title Werwulf, premiering Christmas Day, the auteur joked that the famously tragic conclusion of Shakespeare’s 16th century romance would be a welcome “break” from his usual horror […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT for anyone who skipped freshman English! Robert Eggers is teasing his take on William Shakespeare’s Romeo & Juliet.

During a post-screening Q&A for his latest macabre title Werwulf, premiering Christmas Day, the auteur joked that the famously tragic conclusion of Shakespeare’s 16th century romance would be a welcome “break” from his usual horror work.

“I was doing something else,” noted Eggers of plans for his next project in a video from the event. “But what happened was, after Werwulf, I was writing another horror movie, and it got so dark again, and I was like, ‘I need a break. So, I’ll do something about two teenagers killing themselves.'”

Earlier this week, Deadline reported that Eggers was eyeing a return to Focus Features for his take on Romeo & Juliet, which has sparked some studio competition.

Watch on Deadline

Details of Eggers’ adaptation are under wraps. His deal is not yet finalized, but we understand he’ll direct and produce this version of the classic play. The deal would reunite him with a studio with whom he’s worked across much of his body of work, including horror titles The Lighthouse (2019), Nosferatu (2024) and Werwulf.

Incredible answer from Robert Eggers about why he turned to Romeo & Juliet pic.twitter.com/003vhqRdCN — The King of Burbank @ Beyondfest (@kingofburbank2) September 26, 2026

In Werwulf, a man (Aaron Taylor-Johnson) in 14th century England finds him and his family threatened by a ravenous beast haunting the town. The film also stars Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe, Ralph Ineson and more.

title: Tucker Carlson Returns to ‘SNL’ to Review ‘The Odyssey,’ Gender-Neutral ‘Spider-Man’ and Left-Wing ‘Obsession’
summary: On the first “Weekend Update” of “Saturday Night Live” Season 52, Jeremy Culhane revived his fan-favorite impression of Tucker Carlson to offer his thoughts on some of the summer’s biggest blockbusters. On “The Odyssey,” Carlson mentioned the specialty format of Imax 70mm, saying, “The Hollywood cabal shoots its filth with millimeters — or as I […]
content:
On the first “Weekend Update” of “Saturday Night Live” Season 52, Jeremy Culhane revived his fan-favorite impression of Tucker Carlson to offer his thoughts on some of the summer’s biggest blockbusters.

On “The Odyssey,” Carlson mentioned the specialty format of Imax 70mm, saying, “The Hollywood cabal shoots its filth with millimeters — or as I like to call it, the gay inch.” He added, “I like ‘The Odyssey.’ It’s so nice to see Greek people do something other than make women feel uncomfortable.”

Carlson then turned his attention to the biggest movie of the year, saying, “Everybody loves ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Gender.'”

Popular on Variety

“That’s not what it’s called,” Colin Jost asserted, but the conservative commentator was already inventing a theme song: “Spider-They, Spider-Them uses whatever bathroom it feels like.”

Carlson then congratulated the movie’s stars on getting married, but stopped himself as he said, “I now pronounce you Mr. and Mrs. — huh? She refused to take his last name.”

As Jost reminded him that Zendaya “doesn’t have a last name,” Carlson said, “But where did it go? And who took it? And why? Sorry kids, you don’t get two names anymore. You only get one name, like a dog. That’s the rule. That’s the goal now.”

When asked about “Obsession,” Carlson said, “The left’s idea of a horror movie — that a woman is forced to love a man. Oh, no, help! I’m being chased by a heterosexual relationship! Is this what we want? I don’t. Do you? You shouldn’t. But you do. Why? Is that allowed? Maybe.”

Carlson continued on, equating “Minions and Monsters” to “Trump’s cabinet” and then saying, deadpan, “That’s right. I’ve turned on Trump. I’m so brave.”

And, finally, the pundit made a raunchy “Toy Story 5” joke. “You’ve got a friend in me?” Carlson asked. “And his name is Woody?”

Culhane debuted his Carlson impression in Season 51 of “SNL” and reprised the character on “Weekend Update.” This marks the third appearance of the character. Watch the segment below.

title: ‘SNL’ Opens Season With Mamdani Hanging Out With BFF Trump, Natalie Harp Going ‘Obsession’ Over President
summary: Season 52 of “Saturday Night Live” kicked off with its usual cold open, and it involved two unlikely political BFFs. Ramy Youssef stopped by to play New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose office was visited by James Austin Johnson’s Donald Trump. “For some reason that no one can figure out, I really, really like […]
content:
Season 52 of “Saturday Night Live” kicked off with its usual cold open, and it involved two unlikely political BFFs.

Ramy Youssef stopped by to play New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose office was visited by James Austin Johnson’s Donald Trump.

“For some reason that no one can figure out, I really, really like you,” Trump said to Mamdani.

When summing up their friendship, Trump also said, “I just love hanging out with you. We’re like one of those unlikely animal friendships, like when a tiger gets together with a baby goat. When I see stuff like that, I want to text it to you and say, ‘This could be us, but you playin’.’ Is that timely? Do people still say that? Anyway …”

Popular on Variety

The pair discussed the storm currently slamming the East Coast, the Knicks’ championship, this week’s U.N. meeting in NYC, Trump’s recent hosting of China President Xi Jinping, as well as his state dinner with Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg.

Soon enough, their discussion was interrupted by Natalie Harp, Trump’s much-discussed executive assistant. Played by Ashley Padilla, Harp evoked “Obsession” character Nikki.

Despite the storm, “I ran here from D.C., ‘Weapons’ style,” Harp said.

“She’s like the girl from ‘Obsession’ but blonde,” Trump quipped.

Harp ended the sketch by pulling Mamdani aside and threatening him, saying, “If you hurt him, I will end you.”

Jalen Brunson is hosting the season premiere with Katseye as the musical guest. The episode is also the debut of new cast members Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter.

Watch the full sketch below.

title: Jalen Brunson’s ‘SNL’ Monologue Sees Knicks Starting 5 Roasting Each Other
summary: Jalen Brunson’s “Saturday Night Live” monologue featured some familiar faces, as the remaining members of the Knicks starting five visited Studio 8H to roast their team captain. But before Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby appeared on screen, Kenan Thompson took the stage as ESPN pundit Stephen A. Smith. “Let me say […]
content:
Jalen Brunson‘s “Saturday Night Live” monologue featured some familiar faces, as the remaining members of the Knicks starting five visited Studio 8H to roast their team captain.

But before Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby appeared on screen, Kenan Thompson took the stage as ESPN pundit Stephen A. Smith.

“Let me say this, Jalen Brunson. I am man enough to admit that I was wrong,” Thompson-as-Smith said. “When the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer, nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”

After Brunson interrupted: “How long’s this going to go?” Smith replied: “About another seven minutes.” Brunson booted his “detractor” off the stage and took questions from the audience, which just so happened to include his teammates.

Popular on Variety

“I have a question. Can you foul out of ‘SNL’?” Towns asked, referencing his dismissal from Game 5 against the Spurs. “I could be here, like, the whole show?”

After Bridges and Anunoby gave Brunson a hard time, Hart asked, “Is it true that you took a $113 million pay cut just to resign with the Knicks?” Brunson said, “Yeah, that’s pretty true,” Hart responded, “Wow, so is that money, like, still up for grabs?”

The NBA stars ribbed each other a bit more, and then Brunson welcomed his teammates onstage.

Brunson opened Season 52 of “Saturday Night Live” with musical guest Katseye. The Knicks play their first season game on Oct. 20.

title: Jon Watts to Direct Next ‘Star Wars’ Movie
summary: A new “Star Wars” movie is currently in development with director Jon Watts attached. Watts is best known for directing the popular “Spider-Man” trilogy starring Tom Holland, which includes 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming,” 2019’s “Spider-Man: Far From Home,” and 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” (2026’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.) Before […]
content:
A new “Star Wars” movie is currently in development with director Jon Watts attached.

Watts is best known for directing the popular “Spider-Man” trilogy starring Tom Holland, which includes 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming,” 2019’s “Spider-Man: Far From Home,” and 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” (2026’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.) Before being selected to direct “Spider-Man,” Watts also helmed films including “Cop Car” and “Clown.” Following his involvement with the trilogy, In 2024, it was reported that Watts, his production company Freshman Year and producer Dianne McGunigle had signed a first-look feature deal with Walt Disney Studios.

In 2024, Watts co-created “Skeleton Crew” alongside Christopher Ford, a coming-of-age series set in the era of the New Republic that followed four young characters on a new adventure, per the show’s official logline. Jude Law starred as Jod Na Nawood, with Ravi Cabot-Conyers as Wim, Ryan Kiera Armstrong as Fern, Kyriana Kratter as KB and Robert Timothy Smith as Neel.

Popular on Variety

With the role, Watts joins a list of previous “Star Wars” directors that includes Irvin Kershner, Richard Marquand, J.J. Abrams, Rian Johnson and “Star Wars” creator George Lucas. Released in 2019, Abrams’ “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker” is the most recent film in the franchise to debut theatrically.

As previously reported by Variety, Simon Kinberg will pen the script for the film. Kinberg is best known for being a writer, producer and director for the “X-Men” franchise, and was considered a surprising choice at the time of the announcement.

Knight Edge Media first broke the news.

title: How ‘SNL’ Introduced Season 52’s New Cast Members Saidah Belo-Osagie & Grace Reiter
summary: For those wondering how SNL‘s new cast members factored into tonight’s season premiere, the answer was: not much. The two new featured players, Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, were introduced together, as part of an early sketch on the search for reality competition The Debut: Dream Academy‘s next breakout girl group. Belo-Osagie played Neelsa Boyce, […]
content:
For those wondering how SNL‘s new cast members factored into tonight’s season premiere, the answer was: not much.

The two new featured players, Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, were introduced together, as part of an early sketch on the search for reality competition The Debut: Dream Academy‘s next breakout girl group.

Belo-Osagie played Neelsa Boyce, a 17-year-old entrant who sought to become a pop star after playing Young Nala in The Lion King on Broadway when she was a kid.

Reiter got more screen time as Margle, who “only wear[s] flip flops because I keep passing out when I try to tie my shoes.”

Watch on Deadline

After she’s first introduced, Margle shows up fully nude to a dance choreography session. We later learn that she and another eccentric contestant named Duff (Jane Wickline) were only invited to participate after witnessing an executive behind the show, played by Ashley Padilla, committing a hit and run.

Margle is surprised to learn what Dream Academy is actually about: She says she thought it was a “show where you learned to control dreams.”

RELATED: ‘Saturday Night Live’ Season 52 Cast: Who’s Returning & Who Won’t Be Back?

Subsequently, she pitches “Moose Knuckle” as a band name and the line “Newton’s Cradle, come and get it” during a songwriting exercise.

The sketch culminates with a performance by the final girl group, featuring Margle, who performs the hot new single “Newton’s Cradle” alongside The Debut Season 1 winner Katseye (who happened to be the SNL season premiere’s musical guest).

Reiter made one other appearance in the night’s final sketch, which opens on host Jalen Brunson (of the recent NBA Finals-winning New York Knicks) in the locker room. He won’t be meeting with reporters after tonight’s game, he says — though he’s visited regardless by a grey-haired Kenan Thompson, who reveals himself to be the NBA star’s third-grade coach — you know, the one who had a “really bad drinking problem”?

Coach Dennis has come around seeking a “small loan,” and hopes to get Brunson to read his Spider-Man-themed porno screenplay. Thompson introduces Reiter as Tonya, an immigrant who came to the U.S. eight years ago with a dream — who he hopes to rope into his porn shoot. Kam Patterson also features in the sketch, which culminates in his, Reiter and Thompson’s characters stealing jerseys from the empty locker room and running away.

That was all the night had in the cards for Belo-Osagie and Reiter. Often, SNL will use its Weekend Update segment to help break in new talent, though special segments of tonight’s presentation were instead devoted to special panelists Dario Amodei (played by Wickline) and Tucker Carlson (played by Jeremy Culhane).

Before returning for the new season, SNL said goodbye to Chloe Fineman and writer-performer Martin Herlihy, who was first introduced on the show as part of the trio Please Don’t Destroy. Other returning cast includes Michael Che, Colin Jost, Mikey Day, Sarah Sherman, Marcello Hernández, James Austin Johnson, Andrew Dismukes, Ben Marshall, Tommy Brennan, and Veronika Slowikowska.

Next up this season, we’ll see episodes pairing Dakota Johnson & Turnstile (October 3), Shane Gillis & Rosalía (October 10) and Inde Navarette & Gracie Abrams (October 31).

content:
Following the Knicks’ big win at Madison Square Garden, Jalen Brunson took the stage at 30 Rockefeller Center for his Saturday Night Live hosting debut.

On Saturday’s Season 52 premiere, the NBA Finals 2026 MVP showed off some comedic chops in an otherwise business-as-usual episode of the NBC sketch comedy show, which featured Katseye as its musical guest.

Introducing new cast members Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie, Katseye returned to a parody season of The Debut: Dream Academy to crown a new girl group. The quartet also performed in a mini music video with the awkward group of ladies, also featuring Jane Wickline and Veronika Slowikowska.

The next sketch was a support group featuring Brunson as one of several men whose spouses were grinded on at Usher and Chris Brown’s The R&B Tour.

Watch on Deadline

“When I spent $1,200 on that meet-and-greet, I never expected her to actually greet his meat,” said Brunson as the other group members comforted him.

Katseye on ‘Saturday Night Live’

Jeremy Culhane and Jalen Brunson in ‘Saturday Night Live’

Jalen Brunson, Jeremy Culhane and Ben Marshall on ‘Saturday Night Live’

Brunson also starred in the parody sketch High School Musical: The New Generation as an athletically gifted new student who hilariously keeps dunking on the new Troy Bolton stand-in (Jeremy Culhane) and steals his girlfriend (Slowikowska).

As Shark Tank judge Daymond John, Brunson asked if the invention Respectacles, a pair of glasses that sounds an alarm when the wearer looks at breasts, “works for ass.” The inventors’ (Culhane and Ben Marshall) presentation keeps getting interrupted as they check out Lori Greiner.

title: ‘SNL’s Weekend Update Mocks Paramount+, ‘Spider-Man’, ‘The Odyssey’ & ‘Obsession’
summary: Saturday Night Live’s Weekend Update was back and focused on the movie business. Jeremy Culhane returned as Tucker Carlson and he was giving his thoughts on the summer’s slate of blockbusters. “It’s movie time, let’s find our seats, silence our cell phones and abandon Christian values,” he opened. “Of course, I’m talking about PAW Patrol: […]
content:
Saturday Night Live’s Weekend Update was back and focused on the movie business.

Jeremy Culhane returned as Tucker Carlson and he was giving his thoughts on the summer’s slate of blockbusters.

“It’s movie time, let’s find our seats, silence our cell phones and abandon Christian values,” he opened. “Of course, I’m talking about PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie. Let me get this right: Jesus didn’t live at the same time as the dinosaurs but PAW Patrol did? What are we doing? What’s going on?”

Other kids movies in the spotlight were Toy Story 5 and Minions and Monsters.

Watch on Deadline

“It was also a big summer for Minions and Monsters and no I’m not talking about the children’s film, I’m talking about the Trump cabinet. That’s right, I’ve turned on Trump, I’m so brave,” he said.

On the fifth installment of Disney’s Tom Hanks-narrated film, he added, “Let me understand this, you’ve got a friend in me and his name is Woody?”

It wasn’t just the kids slate that took a hit. Culhane’s Carlson also had some words for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Obsession.

“The Hollywood cabal shoots its filth with millimeters, or what I like to call it, the gay edge. I like The Odyssey, it’s so nice to see Greek people do something other than make women feel uncomfortable,” he said.

On Tom Holland’s superhero flick, he said, “Everybody loves Spider-Man: Brand New Gender. Spider-they, Spider-them, uses whatever bathroom it feels like.”

On Curry Barker’s horror movie, he added, “Obsession, the left’s idea of a horror movie is that a woman is forced to love a man. Oh no, help, I’m being chased by a heterosexual relationship.”

All of this came after Weekend Update anchor Michael Che took aim at David Ellison’s Paramount+ and Taylor Sheridan.

“The White House responded to major news networks canceling coverage of President Trump by launching a live stream called Trump TV. But if that’s Trump TV, what the hell is Paramount+?,” joked Che.

The shows on screen? Sheridan’s Yellowstone, prequel 1883, spinoff Dutton Ranch and Sylvester Stallone-led Tulsa King.

title: ‘SNL’ Season 52 Premiere Delayed In Many Areas Due To College Football
summary: It wasn’t a great start to the season for Saturday Night Live in many parts of the country after linear viewers suffered a delay thanks to college football running late. The Oregon-USC game finished just over 15 minutes late, meaning that many affiliates started after the Jalen Brunson-hosted opener with a 16-minute delay. USC hosted […]
content:
It wasn’t a great start to the season for Saturday Night Live in many parts of the country after linear viewers suffered a delay thanks to college football running late.

The Oregon-USC game finished just over 15 minutes late, meaning that many affiliates started after the Jalen Brunson-hosted opener with a 16-minute delay.

USC hosted its Big Ten rival at the L.A. Memorial Coliseum and the Ducks won 41-27, but the delay was not helped by the fact that the latter’s star quarterback Dante Moore was carted off the field and taken to hospital by ambulance after a late hit.

Many stations including in L.A., Chicago, Houston, Baltimore, Dallas and Charlotte were on the delay, while stations in New York, Boston, Washington, DC and Miami, all of which are owned and operated stations, aired it live.

Watch on Deadline

The episode was, however, live on Peacock.

The show kicked off with Ramy Youssef reprising his role as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, getting a visit from James Austin Johnson’s President Donald Trump.

Brunson then performed the monologue and was helped by a number of his teammates Mikal Bridges, Karl-Anthony Towns, Jalen Brunson, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart.

New cast members Saidah Belo-Osagie & Grace Reiter were making their debut and already starred in an early sketch.

The cast now includes Michael Che, Mikey Day, Andrew Dismukes, Marcello Hernandez, James Austin Johnson, Colin Jost, Ashley Padilla, Sarah Sherman, Kenan Thompson and Jane Wickline with Belo-Osagie, Reiter, Tommy Brennan, Jeremy Culhane, Ben Marshall, Kam Patterson and Veronika Slowikowska as featured players.

Katseye was the musical guest.

title: ‘Saturday Night Live’: Jalen Brunson’s Knicks Teammates Join Him During Opening Monologue
summary: Saturday Night Live kicked off its 52nd season with a victory lap for Knicks fans, as host Jalen Brunson was joined onstage by his teammates. The 2026 MVP swapped some quips with teammates Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart during his opening monologue on Saturday’s episode, which comes after they defeated the […]
content:
Saturday Night Live kicked off its 52nd season with a victory lap for Knicks fans, as host Jalen Brunson was joined onstage by his teammates.

The 2026 MVP swapped some quips with teammates Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart during his opening monologue on Saturday’s episode, which comes after they defeated the San Antonio Spurs in June to bring the Knicks their first NBA championship since 1973.

Calling on the group during his monologue, Brunson confirmed to Towns you can’t “foul out of SNL,” to which the center, forward excitedly responded, “So I could be here like the whole show? Nice!”

Bridges asked if his arms were “pretty long,” as Brunson validated he has a “great wingspan.” Bridges responded, “Yet, I’ll never fly.”

Watch on Deadline

Anunoby asked, “Remember in Game 4, when you took that shot at the end and missed it? Remember what happened after?”

“Yeah, you tipped it in,” said Brunson, as Anunoby replied with a laugh, “Oh yeah, that was awesome.”

Meanwhile, Hart asked if it was true that Brunson “took a $113 million pay cut just to re-sign with the Knicks,” which point guard confirmed is true. “Wow. So, is that money still up for grabs?” asked Hart.

“I don’t know. But I do have a question for you. Why did you do this to me at the cup ceremony?” asked Brunson, playing a clip of Hart poking him in the butt as the team celebrated their win.

Hart exclaimed, “Because it was funny!”

Saturday Night Live kicked off its 52nd season this weekend with host Brunson and musical guest Katseye. The season continues on NBC with guest hosts Dakota Johnson, Shane Gillis and Inde Navarrette, along with musical guests Turnstile, Rosalía and Gracie Abrams.

title: Martin McDonagh Jokes About His Past – as a Hitman – and Calls ‘Wild Horse Nine’ His Most Political Film: ‘There’s Too Much Artistic Neutrality and Too Much Saying Nothing’
summary: Martin McDonagh is taking a stand with “Wild Horse Nine.” “This is probably my most political film. That’s why I find it very exciting to be releasing this monster into the world,” he said at the Zurich Film Festival. “I feel like, in the modern day, there’s perhaps a little too much artistic neutrality, or […]
content:
Martin McDonagh is taking a stand with “Wild Horse Nine.”

“This is probably my most political film. That’s why I find it very exciting to be releasing this monster into the world,” he said at the Zurich Film Festival.

“I feel like, in the modern day, there’s perhaps a little too much artistic neutrality, or too much saying nothing, not having an opinion or being apathetic. I’m excited to be doing the opposite with this one.”

In his new black comedy, two CIA agents (played by John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) travel to Easter Island before the 1973 Chilean coup. However, it feels surprisingly timely.

Popular on Variety

“So many things in the present day mirror a lot of those types of interventions in the past. You can actually hear lines that I thought were about 1973 being interpreted by a modern audience as being about Venezuela a few months ago or other places around the world,” he noted.

“The Russia jokes in the film are about their interventions in Finland 100 years ago, but we connect them to Ukraine now. I love that it has a resonance I wasn’t necessarily aware of in the writing of it.”

McDonagh, who received A Tribute to… Award at the fest, looked back on his past during a masterclass.

“I left school very young, at 16, and was unemployed for a long time. But with the hopes of being a writer. Part of that was not wanting to have a real job or a boss. That has remained with me until now,” he said.

He wrote radio plays, all of which were rejected – “Mostly by the BBC. But I don’t bear a grudge” – and then became an acclaimed playwright.

“As a film fan, I put all that into the energy of the plays. Things would happen that you wouldn’t usually see on stage. Like cats exploding [in ‘The Lieutenant of Inishmore’].”

Seeing Al Pacino in “American Buffalo” by David Mamet was a pivotal moment.

“I can still remember it to this day. He just came on stage and blew the whole theater away. It was this combination of a play, full of energy and swearing, amazing dialogue and this movie star who, well, you’d realize what acting really was when he was on stage.”

McDonagh still writes “without the camera in mind,” but he enjoys the freedom of writing scripts.

“It’s like when you don’t go to the gym for a long time; that’s where my theater brain is at the moment. But the muscle memory is still there.”

The transition to cinema wasn’t exactly easy. “It was the bad rejections that really inspired me. Maybe I thrive not on encouragement, but anger,” he said. Still, his 2004 short “Six Shooter” won the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film.

“It was probably the scariest situation I’ve been in artistically. But the wonderful thing was having Brendan Gleeson be part of it. He protected me from any interference. I couldn’t have done it without his help and guidance,” he recalled.

He reunited with Gleeson on his hit “In Bruges,” also starring Colin Farrell, where two hitmen are forced to hide out after a mission gone wrong.

“I used to be a hit man. People don’t know that. They thought it just was plays and then films. It was plays, killing and then films,” joked McDonagh.

“I went to Bruges not knowing anything about it. I was supposed to meet a girl on the second night, and she didn’t turn up. It was this combination of thinking it was the most cinematic, undiscovered town I’d ever seen, and being bored as hell and just wanting to get drunk and get out of there.”

Once again, he felt shielded by his lead actors.

“Colin and Brendan were great partners in protecting me from any interference from the grown-ups. Who aren’t usually grown up; they’re children with a lot of money. It’s the nature of Hollywood,” he said.

“I’m going to get in so much trouble. It’s good that it’s not being filmed, right?”

McDonagh tackles serious – even shocking – topics in his films, yet somehow they still tend to be funny. But recently, he’s been noticing a change in his work.

“I’ve tried to make sure that the films aren’t just about being cool. They’re about something deeper, and I guess more tragic. I’m leaving room for more contemplative scenes where the characters are on their own and it’s not funny. They’re left to think about their lives or dwell on their regrets.”

This was the case with Frances McDormand, who played the grieving mother Mildred Hayes in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.” And now with John Malkovich in “Wild Horse Nine.”

“When they’re great actors like Frances or John, you see the sadness in their eyes, and you fill in what they’re thinking about. One of the ideas for John’s character was to give him the entire palette of emotions. You know that John can do comedy, he can do rage and he can do contemplative, quiet stuff. But I’m making sure all those things are together in one package,” he noted.

“None of my films are sort of what I would call ‘Hollywood movies.’ They’re not simple, feel-good stories. When actors of that magnitude who have maybe done some of those films, and know they’re a little empty get to work on something different, it frees them up to show their brilliance.”

McDonagh wouldn’t want to make bigger movies anyway.

“Weirdly, I’m really happy with the trajectory or the level of films that I’ve made. I don’t want a bigger budget. I don’t even want more success. I just want to continue making films completely free from any interference from anyone. That’s a perfect position to be in.”

title: Beyond Frontman Doc ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ to Open U.K.’s Odyssey Film Festival, Lands Local Distribution (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: “Because of You Ka Kui,” a documentary on the late Beyond frontman Wong Ka Kui, will open the sixth Odyssey Film Festival in the U.K., with NGO U.K.-China Film Collab also picking up the Hong Kong film for local distribution. Discussions began in March at FilMart in Hong Kong, which U.K.-China Film Collab attended with […]
content:
“Because of You Ka Kui,” a documentary on the late Beyond frontman Wong Ka Kui, will open the sixth Odyssey Film Festival in the U.K., with NGO U.K.-China Film Collab also picking up the Hong Kong film for local distribution.

Discussions began in March at FilMart in Hong Kong, which U.K.-China Film Collab attended with the U.K. Film Pavilion. The NGO deployed a similar approach last year with Robin Lee’s Hong Kong documentary “Four Trails,” which opened Odyssey and then played more widely in cinemas in 2025.

The film, from Hong Kong director Rosa Pang, revisits Wong, the singer-songwriter who drove Beyond creatively and whose songs shaped a generation of Cantonese-speaking listeners in Hong Kong and further afield. The producers are Yip Sai Wing, one of Beyond’s founding members, and Leslie Chan, the manager who is credited with finding the group.

Popular on Variety

The film is built around interviews with people who knew Wong both personally and through work. These sit alongside rare concert recordings, never-before-shown archive material from his early years and footage that has not been released until now. It follows Wong from his first brushes with music through the rise of Beyond and his growth as a songwriter and performer, looking at his approach to music, his character and his ideals. Pang and Leslie Chan described it as a dedication to “a legend, an ordinary person, through memories of those who truly knew him. The film seeks to rediscover the real Wong Ka Kui.”

Wong died in an accident in Japan in 1993, at age 31. The band’s songs have kept finding new listeners since.

There is also a U.K. link. The film’s interview with Beyond founding member William Tang was shot in London.

After an earlier theatrical run in Asia, “Because of You Ka Kui” will have its U.K. premiere as Odyssey’s opening film. The festival will run Sept. 28–Oct. 10 at a number of cinemas as well as online. Each edition is built around a different theme, and this year’s is #Fashion.

“Beyond did not simply follow the fashion of their generation, in many ways, they helped create it, like Oasis for the U.K.,” said Hiu Man Chan, Odyssey’s artistic director and founder of U.K.-China Film Collab. “Their music, image, attitude and style became part of the cultural memory of Hong Kong and influenced generations across Asia. Fashion is not only about what an era wears; it is also about how a generation chooses to see and express itself. That makes ‘Because of You Ka Kui’ a very meaningful film to launch this year’s Odyssey.”

Hiu Man Chan said the opening pick reflected the festival’s aim to treat fashion as more than clothing and catwalks, and to explore how film, music, visual identity and pop culture feed into one another. Bringing the film to the U.K. was “my true honor,” Hiu Man Chan added.

The selection also stretches the fashion theme to cover youth culture and music. Beyond’s sound and look, which mixed international rock influences with a Hong Kong that was changing fast through the 1980s and early 1990s, became bound up with a generation of young fans. Yip has called the documentary a rare chance to find the “ordinary person” behind the bandleader and icon.

Malaysian company Abnormal Studios launched “Because of You Ka Kui” internationally at FilMart in March, as the lead title of its new international sales arm.

“‘Because of You Ka Kui’ is not about nostalgia. The honesty of Wong Ka Kui as a person – in what he thought, felt and believed – continues to resonate today,” Pang said.

Leslie Chan said that after hearing all the interviews, “I really felt that I came to know Ka Kui all over again.”

Odyssey’s sixth edition will program older films alongside new ones. The festival’s opening and some of its program have backing from the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London.

title: Jia Zhangke Readies Zhao Tao Road Movie ‘Mamma Dunhuang,’ Rules Out AI in Production (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Jia Zhangke will turn his attention to location scouting and production design for his next film, road movie “Mamma Dunhuang,” once the 10th Pingyao Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon International Film Festival wraps on Sept. 30. As revealed by Variety, the film follows a woman who drives from Dunhuang, in western China near Central Asia, all […]
content:
Jia Zhangke will turn his attention to location scouting and production design for his next film, road movie “Mamma Dunhuang,” once the 10th Pingyao Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon International Film Festival wraps on Sept. 30.

As revealed by Variety, the film follows a woman who drives from Dunhuang, in western China near Central Asia, all the way to the sea. It is set to shoot in early winter.

“I really love western China, and I go to Dunhuang quite often. Dunhuang was a vital transit hub on the ancient Silk Road, keep going west and you can arrive in Rome. Yet, it is so far from the ocean,” Jia tells Variety. “So this whole film is a continental story that starts in Dunhuang and travels from the west to the eastern coastline – she drives until the sea comes into view.”

Popular on Variety

Zhao Tao, who won the David di Donatello Award for best actress for “Shun Li and the Poet,” will once again lead a Jia film, playing a homebound woman who uses AI to help her on the journey.

“I will not use AI in making ‘Mamma Dunhuang,'” Jia says. “It only plays a role in the story.”

Jia founded the Pingyao festival, which marks its 10th edition this year. He says that although it’s only been a decade, “the changes in the broader film ecosystem and the media landscape, as well as technological advancements, are drastic. Pingyao has remained nimble. We’ve been able to adapt continuously alongside the shifts in the film industry and surrounding media, capturing new developments for our curation. Looking ahead, I believe cinema will continue to evolve rapidly, so we will maintain this festival’s agility in the future. That very flexibility allows us to respond in real time to the most pressing cinematic and cultural topics on people’s minds today.”

Jia wants Pingyao to remain a haven for cinephiles rather than a hall of fame. Where most international festivals program hundreds of films, he intends to keep Pingyao’s lineup lean, built around the year’s newest boutique titles, so the spotlight falls on the selected films and helps them reach the market. This year’s official program has just 51 films.

“As a festival, not only must it have great programs, but also a vibe of equality, freedom, and ease, setting a tone where the filmmakers and audiences can merge together,” Jia says. “We put effort into bringing in films with great artistic value, and meanwhile cover as many countries and regions as possible, prioritizing regions less familiar to Chinese audiences, such as northeastern Europe and South America, hoping to introduce a broader spectrum of cinema to the Chinese audience.”

Pingyao’s online ticketing system logged more than 70 million visits this year.

Jia says part of the problem is Pingyao’s limited capacity, as the ancient city “is protected as a UNESCO World Heritage [Site]. We’ve been working on building one more theater, ideally inside the ancient city walls, with 300–500 seats to enlarge the capacity. But it is very difficult to realize this plan, we are still discussing.”

For its fifth edition, the festival partnered with visual artist Xu Bing on “AI-IF,” a project that invited audiences to make films using AI. Jia says the festival’s AI projects have all been exhibitions, and none of this year’s official selections were made with AI.

“We’ve been prudent,” Jia says. “But we maintain an open, observant, and inclusive stance toward AI. When it comes to technology advancement, each of us holds a different perspective, but there should be one fundamental attitude: we must understand and discuss it, not shy away from it. Pingyao upholds a spirit of prudent inclusivity.” Earlier this year, Jia created an AI-generated video.

Jia also co-founded Unknown Pleasures, a Chinese art-house distributor named after his 2002 film, and says the company is negotiating to acquire two Cannes titles. In June, it announced deals for Russian auteur Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” and French cinematographer Marine Atlan’s debut feature “La Gradiva.”

“We hope Unknown Pleasures’ acquired titles all have a great showcase in Pingyao,” Jia says.

title: Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit
