title: ‘School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play’ Broadway Review: When Escape Is Just A Clique Away
summary: The battle lines are drawn early and definitively in Jocelyn Bioh’s School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play. The cruelties come fast and cut deep in this Ghana school lunch room where all the unspoken rules of adolescent pick-or-be-picked-upon are as strict as they are in high schools the world over. Or in other […]
content:
The battle lines are drawn early and definitively in Jocelyn Bioh‘s School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play. The cruelties come fast and cut deep in this Ghana school lunch room where all the unspoken rules of adolescent pick-or-be-picked-upon are as strict as they are in high schools the world over. Or in other plays and TV shows the world over, whether we’re talking Heathers or Carrie or Jawbreaker. And since Stephen King didn’t write this one, we can be pretty sure there won’t blood, but gruesome playground injuries of a more psychic and soul-crushing variety are entirely on the table.

Bioh, perfectly assisted by her sympatico director Whitney White and a no-weak-link cast, has done something quite amazing with this comedy-drama, opening tonight on Broadway at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre in a first-rate Manhattan Theatre Club production. Bioh takes on the tropes and dramatic conventions of high school claustrophobia, its rebellions and savageries and tendernesses so familiar from ancestors like the franchise that gives this play its subtitle and right up through the newcomer that called John Proctor a villain, that we can only trust a writer of her depth and skills (she wrote Jaja’s African Hair Braiding, after all) to find a new path through the well-trod turf.

And she does. School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, might well come closest in approach to Kimberly Belflower’s urgent John Proctor Is The Villain in its insistence that homeroom sadism doesn’t just spring from hormones or reindeer game competition. There are larger forces at work, the stuff that hurts people who hurt people, and portraying that hurt (and its goal, escape) with understanding – not to say excuse-making – takes uncommon talent. Belflower showed it, and so does Bioh.

Watch on Deadline

The set up is simple and immediately recognizable. The year is 1986 and the place is a girls boarding school in the Aburi Mountains of Central Ghana. Five of the students – two in their final year, three a year behind – busy themselves with the gossip and whatever else passes for crucial business in the day-to-day, mostly as defined by Paulina (The Gilded Age‘s Denée Benton), the self-anointed queen of the clique by way of her looks, her force of will, her cruel streak and her much admired (if very tenuous) connection to the longed-for America by way of an aunt who lives in New York City and works in a castle there that serves unimaginable culinary delights and who sends Pauline the odd piece of designer clothing that makes her the envy of the school.

We’ll learn that Paulina, far from confident, is so self-conscious of the darkness of her Black skin that she secretly uses toxic bleach products that necessitate frequent trips to the emergency room, that her home life is so impoverished that she unleashes her frustrations on her terrified acolytes. Poor Nana (Erin Morton) gets the worst of the abuse, her large body and constant eating a source of unending bullying from Paulina, who calls her “cow.” Even Paulina’s best friend – a phrase pretty much useless in this milieu – isn’t safe. Ama (Lucia Aremu) pays dearly for the occasional hint of independence, so threatening is free thinking to Paulina.

In the grand tradition of teen movies, the equilibrium of the status quo is disrupted with the arrival of a new student. And Ericka (Jasmine Amy Rogers, all done up in big ’80s hair and a school girl uniform that leaves her unrecognizable from her flapper look in Boop) is not just any new student. She’s lived in America. She has Bobby Brown’s autograph. She has real Calvin Klein fashions, not the Chinatown knock-offs that have fooled Paulina. And she knows White Castle isn’t a white castle – it isn’t even McDonald’s.

Denée Benton and Jasmine Amy Rogers Matthew Murphy

And she has two other things going for her. She’s kind – the put-upon girls of the Aburi Girls Boarding School take to her like docile puppies to a calming stroke – and she’s naturally light-skinned. No harsh chemicals for her, much to the amazement and envy of her Ghanaian classmates. If the mixed-race Ericka doesn’t quite grasp the significance of her coloring – back home at her all-white school she was, to be sure, Black – the other girls certainly do.

And among the things all the girls seem to sense is that Paulina is no longer the shoo-in for the upcoming Miss Ghana try-outs, a realization driven home when the pageant’s recruiter – a former Aburi student who, 20 years previous, won Miss Ghana 1966 and who retains her own mean girl leanings, especially when in the company of the school’s Headmistress, a classmate from those long ago years. One of Bioh’s most telling bits of stage magic here is showing us just how long-lasting such formative role-playing can be. If the device can seem more than a little schematic in intention, its execution – a few lines of dialogue between the recruiter Eloise (Patina Miller) and the Headmistress (Heather Alicia Simms) – nonetheless conveys both the tenacity and bite of mean girldom. And did I mention School Girls is a comedy? And a very funny one at that?

Patina Miller and Heather Alicia Simms Matthew Murphy

As School Girls builds to its denouement – that pageant try-out – rest assured that Bioh and director White will not deprive us of bearing witness, and the young actors who play the school girls, some in their Broadway debuts, meet the challenge and then some. As they take turns soloing Whitney Houston’s “The Greatest Love of All” – an inspired choice not only for the technical demands that few of these hopefuls could meet, but for Houston’s haunted ending that they couldn’t possible know – the cast members imbue each character with comic ineptitude that’s as poignant as it is laugh-out-loud funny. Even the cruel Paulina’s misplaced overconfidence and comeuppance merits our charity.

Because comeuppance she gets. When the new girl Ericka takes her turn at the solo, her glorious voice rivals that of Whitney herself (as she proved in the otherwise lackluster Boop, Rogers is a talent to watch and embrace). As the greedy recruiter sees something to exploit, and the proud headmistress hears something finally worthy of pride, and the downtrodden classmates have their ding dong the witch is dead moment, poor Paulina all but crumbles into herself (Benton is a marvel in this scene).

But bullies don’t often go away easy. Her face bleeding from the corrosive bleach, her dreams of escape from poverty dashed, Paulina lashes out with ill-gotten information that will take the talented, seemingly charmed Ericka down with her. In the battle that ensues, no one will go untouched by hard truth and the realization of just how stacked the odds against triumph remain in a system where everything from the shade of one’s skin, the geography of one’s home and the capricious nature of one’s parentage determine so much, and foster all sorts of bad behavior and ruthless survivalism.

The Manhattan Theatre Club has given this excellent play the production it deserves. Costume designer Qween Jean, riding high from her Tony-winning contributions to Cats: The Jellicle Ball, delivers the perfect visuals for this tale – the conformity of school uniforms, the explosion of ’80s prom styles for the pageant auditions, the proud African ethnicity of the Headmistress’ attire and the arriviste Americanism of the made-good recruiter – while Teresa L. Williams’ cleverly efficient school cafeteria set, with its large glass windows offering quick hallway peeks at characters in their privacy – gives these school girls ample room for all their towering ambitions and their outsized insecurities.

Not enough praise can be heaped upon the excellent cast (in addition to those mentioned above, there’s the terrific Nia Otchere-Sarfo and Jordan Rice rounding out the clique). Every one of the school girls is perfectly delineated (kudos to the casting team for an exactingly chosen group), with each actor finding the humor, the humanity and, when necessary, the acidity of characters doing their best in a hothouse not of their making. Or not entirely of their making, anyway. Even the most dehumanizing of systems, from high schools to pageants to poverty and racism, require some human complicity in the building and, if we’re lucky, the undoing. The School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play all but hands us an instruction manual.

Title: School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play

Venue: Broadway’s Samuel J. Friedman Theatre

Written By: Jocelyn Bioh

Directed By: Whitney White

Cast: Lucia Aremu, Denée Benton, Patina Miller, Erin Morton, Nia Otchere-Sarfo, Jordan Rice, Jasmine Amy Rogers, Heather Alicia Simms

Running Time: 1 hr 25 min (no intermission)

title: Apple TV Claims Largest Weekly Viewership Ever With ‘Mayday’, ‘Ted Lasso’ And Post-Emmys Bump For ‘Widow’s Bay’ & ‘Pluribus’
summary: Apple TV had a record-breaking 2026 Emmys with 28 wins (29 if you include the commercials category), the most for the streamer ever and the most for any platform this year. Apple TV’s big night at the Emmys, held on September 14, was followed by a big week — the biggest in the streamer’s seven-year […]
content:
Apple TV had a record-breaking 2026 Emmys with 28 wins (29 if you include the commercials category), the most for the streamer ever and the most for any platform this year. Apple TV’s big night at the Emmys, held on September 14, was followed by a big week — the biggest in the streamer’s seven-year history, the company said Monday.

No, hell has not frozen over, and Apple did not release hard viewership numbers, just qualitative data and year-to-year and week-to-week increases. Still, they provide a glimpse into the streamer’s performance, especially when compared to existing third-party ratings information.

Per Apple, fueled by strong deliveries from the Cold War buddy comedy Mayday starring Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh, Season 4 of Ted Lasso, and a post-Emmy viewership surge for big winners Widow’s Bay and Pluribus, the service had its highest weekly viewership ever for the week of September 14, rising by 67% year-over-year.

Watch on Deadline

Released straight-to-streaming on September 4, Mayday has become Apple TV’s biggest film debut on the platform to date over its first 18 days, the company said. In the U.S., Mayday opened at No. 1 in Luminate’s September 4-10 weekly rankings with 8.7M views. It remained strong in Week 2, placing at No. 2.

Freshman horror comedy Widow’s Bay, the biggest winner at the Emmys with 14 trophies — the most ever for a comedy series in a single season — saw a massive halo effect as its viewership skyrocketed 280% week-over-week in the post-Emmys week, per Apple, with the U.S., UK, Canada, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Germany, India, Poland and Spain leading the charge.

Luminate data corroborates that claim. For the week of September 4-10, Widow’s Bay was outside of the Top 50. For the week of September 11-17, which includes the first three days after the Emmys where Widow’s Bay was crowned Outstanding Comedy Series, it jumped to No. 13.

‘Widow’s Bay’ creator Katie Dippold and cast/crew accept the Outstanding Comedy Series Award during the Primetime Emmy Awards on September 14 Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Pluribus, Apple TV’s second biggest Emmy winner with six statuettes including Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for Rhea Seehorn, experienced a 200% surge in viewership week-over-week following the ceremony, per Apple.

Since the sci-fi drama from Emmy winner Vince Gilligan wrapped its run in December, while Widow’s Bay, starring Emmy winner Matthew Rhys, was a more recent entry that didn’t launch until end of April, for Pluribus the increase was likely off a small base as the series did not reenter Luminate’s Top 50 the week of September 11.

‘Slow Horses’ Apple TV

Slow Horses, winner of one Emmy, also got a bump, getting back into Luminate’s Top 50 the week of September 11-17 at No. 43 after missing the cut the prior week. The spy thriller also posted a rare season-to-season viewership increase for a show so deep into its run, with Season 6 up 25% over Season 5 based on the first seven days of release, maintaining its position as Apple TV’s No. 1 UK title, per the company.

Nielsen’s reporting is delayed; its figures for the week of September 14 will be released this Thursday.

The most recent Nielsen weekly streaming report for the week of September 7 has one Apple TV title in the overall Top 10: Ted Lasso at No. 7 with 734 million minutes viewed. (Comedies are at a disadvantage in Nielsen’s rankings, which are based on overall watched time vs. number of views.)

With that, Jason Sudeikis’ soccer comedy was a major contributor to Apple TV’s year-over-year viewership jump in the post-Emmys week. Its fourth season, which stumbled creatively a bit before finding its footing in the second half, marks the most viewed seasons for a returning Apple TV comedy over the first 54 days, according to the streamer.

Also possibly factoring into the year-to-year gains is the iCloud+ expansion launched by Apple on September 15, which rolled out access to Apple TV at no additional cost for paid iCloud+ subscribers across more than 170 countries.

title: ‘All American’s Daniel Ezra On Directing The Series Finale & Truly Saying Goodbye To Spencer James: “He’ll Be With Me Forever”
summary: SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from the series finale of The CW’s All American. That’s a wrap on All American. The drama series, produced by Warner Bros. Television, ended its eight-season run on the CW on Monday with an emotional, moving episode directed by none other than Spencer James himself, Daniel Ezra. The rest […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from the series finale of The CW‘s All American.

That’s a wrap on All American.

The drama series, produced by Warner Bros. Television, ended its eight-season run on the CW on Monday with an emotional, moving episode directed by none other than Spencer James himself, Daniel Ezra. The rest of the Vortex had been trying to track Spencer down for the last few episodes, after Olivia (Samantha Logan) went into preterm labor with their twins. They’d thought he was tied up with a promotional photo shoot, but little did they know that Spencer was so hard to reach because he was fighting to bring his family back to Los Angeles.

He’s in a conference room urging his team’s general manager to allow his trade from New York to LA when he gets the news that his children are on the way. And, as Spencer James usually does, he finds a way. He not only makes it just in time to be there for the birth of the twins, but he also manages to persuade his team to let him go. With Jordan (Michael Evans Behling) realizing his purpose at South Crenshaw and Cassius (Osy Ikhile) sticking around Beverly, it looks like the whole family is finally back together again.

Watch on Deadline

Fast forward six years, and Coop (Bre-Z) is getting sworn in as an attorney. Amina (Alexis Chikaeze) has just successfully run a political campaign to get her dad Preach (Kareem J. Grimes) elected as a local representative. Layla (Greta Onieogou) and Jordan have a daughter of their own, and the entire crew is about to go watch Spencer play in what we come to learn is his final Super Bowl before retiring — and he’ll share the field with KJ, whose made it to the NFL as well. Coming to Olivia’s aid set Khalil on a different path, and he’s now in medical school, and Tori (Lauryn Hardy) is an assistant coach for the Lakers’ dancers.

After eight years of fighting for their dreams, the series finale of All American gives the space for these characters to finally, fully realize them.

In the interview below, Ezra spoke with Deadline about directing the final episode of a series that he credits with completely changing his life and taking Spencer James with him wherever he goes next.

DEADLINE: The finale is extremely emotional. It really made me cry.

DANIEL EZRA: It was a strange experience. It was an amazing experience, but it was a strange, because I left in Season 6, and then I came back a few times. I don’t know. In my head, when I left, it was always still there. But this was the first time where we were all saying goodbye. So yeah, very emotional.

DEADLINE: I remember when you first started directing on All American, and NK really worked to find an episode that Spencer didn’t need to be in very much so you could pull it off. I know the 100th was very Spencer-heavy, but this was too. How do you feel like you grew as a director to juggle that?

EZRA: It was one of his biggest episodes, and I’m glad that this came later. The first couple episodes I directed, we were a little more successful in finding episodes that I was at least less in. NK was very realistic. She said, ‘There’s probably never going to be an episode that you’re not in, or not at least a significant part, but we can definitely find one that’s less.’ I think the first two were that. Our 100th episode wasn’t that, and we just kind of had to accept that. But this one always made sense. The way NK pitched it to me, she actually gave me a choice, and that was the only episode I felt like I wanted to do. I felt like that’s the one that felt right to do, and so I’m glad it came later. By that point, I had directed a chunk of episodes. I directed my own short film. I had had a bit more experience, and so I felt a lot more secure in myself and more confident, I think, in what I was able to do and the speed that you wish to work at, and all those things that I felt a bit more at ease with the demands of it.

DEADLINE: You spent so many years playing this character working toward a dream, and even in the Season 6 finale the dream is only just being realized. How was it to get those flash forwards at the end of the finale to actually get to live in the version of this character that had truly accomplished everything he dreamed of?

EZRA: It was weird. That scene, you’re talking about the one with me and Mike, right?

DEADLINE: That, and before that when he is talking to Nate about retiring. The twins growing up. Everything.

EZRA: I was so grateful that, even though I had stepped away, I still got a chance to come back and film those scenes. This scene with Mike — I remember in the read through, we couldn’t get through it, me and Mike couldn’t. We were just crying in the read through. We couldn’t get through it. When we got to set and to film it, we almost had to allow extra time, because we knew it was going to be tough for me and Mike. Just the way it was written, the things we were saying, and things we were talking about, it was Spencer and Jordan talking to each other and also a bit of Mike and Daniel talking to each other as well.

As an actor, I was just super grateful that we did get that moment, because we didn’t get that before I left. It was just real serendipitous of NK to write a moment like that in, because you could have ended before that. There was there was about three points in that episode where you could have ended, and it would have been great. You could have ended after he ran off into the tunnel. That was a beautiful ending. Before that, with the babies being born. There’s a couple almost false endings in the episode that all could have worked, but that one just felt like that made it perfect. I thought when I was leaving Season 6, my story was complete. I didn’t realize it wasn’t until we got to those scenes.

DEADLINE: You also had most of the original cast on screen again, plus the new cast. That scene in the hospital room, it’s pretty packed. How did you handle that?

EZRA: My job was to not think about it being a finale in any way, because once you get into that, everyone’s going to get emotional. Everyone’s going to start reminiscing. Everyone’s going to start talking and crying. As much as you want to allow for that, you can’t really allow for that during filming. Me and out AD Steve, we had to be very deliberately kind of, not mean, but a bit like ‘We don’t have time for that.’ You know what I mean?

That’s all gonna come. We knew there was gonna be a party. We knew there was gonna be a big moment of celebration at the end. We knew all of that was coming, but there’s just no space for that when you’re filming, because you still have to get these scenes. We’ve been doing this is eight years, so they know how these things work. They know we never have enough time, and so you keep moving.

DEADLINE: So, when you do think it really hit you that this was the end?

EZRA: I was the one that got to say ‘That’s a wrap on All American.’ We finished with just a perfect scene. It was actually one of the last scenes, where everyone’s going off to see Spencer play his last game, and so I wasn’t in that scene. I had already changed, and I had shot my last scene as Spencer, but I deliberately didn’t have any fanfare for my last scene. We just kind of did it and moved on, and then it was it was Mike, Sam, Osy, and Angel in the last scene, but everyone stayed. All the actors stayed. A bunch of the cast that wasn’t even working that day had showed up, and you could start to slowly feel everyone kind of gathering and waiting for it. So I knew I was like, ‘Okay, I’m gonna have to say something.’ And then it finished. I checked in with NK. I said, ‘Are you happy? I’m happy.’ And she said she was already gone. She just kind of nodded through tears. And I said to Steve, ‘So let’s have everyone come in.’ Just seeing that room so full of people that didn’t have to be there, that all chose to be there…we packed out the Baker house. I wrapped Osy. I wrapped Angel. I wrapped Sam and Mike. I wrapped NK and Jamie as showrunners, and it just got harder and harder and harder.

Then, I finally said, ‘That’s a wrap on All American.’ I think that’s the moment where it was. I remember after that, it took forever to get everyone off to set. No one wanted to leave. Everyone was hugging and crying, and then it was probably an hour before we emptied that stage. It was very funny, because no one just wanted to leave. I think NK was the last one to leave, which felt right. She wanted a moment to herself. So probably that moment when it was time to wrap everyone and say ‘This is a wrap,’ which was a real honor for me to get to do.

DEADLINE: My very last question for you: How are you going to carry Spencer and this experience with you throughout the rest of your career?

EZRA: Spencer, he will always, always, always be with me. There’s some characters that, you know, it’s it’s a time. This is a job. At the end of the day, there’s some characters that you enjoy for a moment, and then you kind of move on. There’s a handful of characters that I think will stay with you forever. Maybe less than a handful. Maybe two or three. But Spencer’s definitely at the apex of that pyramid. I’m such a different person from when I started this to now. Every single aspect of my life has changed, and I like to think that playing him fed into that in a really, really big and profound way. It was a real honor. It changed my life in every way. I think the idea of showing up for your people, the idea of showing up the people you love and the people you care about, chasing dreams, all those things — I think he really hammered home a lot of those lessons, and he was just so fun. He’s just such a fun, real, multi-dimensional character to play. So yeah, he’ll be with me forever.

title: ‘ESPN Jeopardy!’ Renewed For Season 2 On Hulu & Disney+, Pivots From Celebrities To Sports Fans
summary: Civilian sports fans now can apply to play the latest version of Jeopardy! after it was revealed that ESPN Jeopardy! is returning for a second season. Disney+ and Hulu premiered the first season of the show in July with stars such as Jon Hamm, Hannah Storm, Manti Te’o and Adam Pally. It now will return […]
content:
Civilian sports fans now can apply to play the latest version of Jeopardy! after it was revealed that ESPN Jeopardy! is returning for a second season.

Disney+ and Hulu premiered the first season of the show in July with stars such as Jon Hamm, Hannah Storm, Manti Te’o and Adam Pally.

It now will return with everyday sports fans facing off against one another to win a $300,000 prize. In the first season, celebrities and ESPN talent competed in the tournament-style event for a $500,000 prize for the charity of their choice.

Joe Buck, who hosts the show, announced the renewal on Monday Night Football as the Philadelphia Eagles prepare to take on the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field.

Watch on Deadline

The series, which also is available to watch on the ESPN app, is the latest spinoff of the classic game show. It comes after Sports Jeopardy!, which ran for three seasons and over 100 episodes on Crackle; Rock & Roll Jeopardy!, which ran for four seasons on VH1; and, more recently, Celebrity Jeopardy! and Pop Culture Jeopardy!, which is hosted by Saturday Night Live’s Colin Jost and moved from Amazon to Netflix for its second season, which debuted in May. There was also a recent YouTube digital edition.

ESPN Jeopardy! is produced by Sony Pictures Television and Michael Davies, who exec produces the main Jeopardy!, serves as executive producer. It is shot on the Alex Trebek Stage, the official name of Stage 10 at Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City.

RELATED: Alex Trebek Dies: Longtime Host Of ‘Jeopardy!’ Was 80

title: Prime Video International Boss Urges TV Industry to Embrace AI: ‘It Doesn’t Replace Imagination, It Amplifies It’
summary: Prime Video international boss Kelly Day has urged the TV industry to embrace change, including AI. Speaking at the Royal Television Society convention in London, Day, who is VP for international at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, listed the ways that AI is being used to speed up and bring down costs throughout the […]
content:
Prime Video international boss Kelly Day has urged the TV industry to embrace change, including AI.

Speaking at the Royal Television Society convention in London, Day, who is VP for international at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, listed the ways that AI is being used to speed up and bring down costs throughout the production pipeline, from pitching to pre-production.

“For a studio like us, AI enables us to bring down the cost of production while maintaining quality, meaning more stories get made, more creative risks get taken, and more diverse voices get heard. That is not a threat to creativity. That’s creativity unleashed,” Day said, speaking to an audience of senior executives in the TV industry including BBC director general Matt Brittin and Sony Pictures TV international boss Wayne Garvie.

“AI doesn’t replace imagination, it amplifies it,” she continued. “We’re not looking for an AI model to write the next ‘Fleabag,’ and by the way, I don’t think it could. But AI might help the person who does spend less time on admin and more time on the creative vision that makes a show like that sing.”

Popular on Variety

Day pointed out that first-time filmmakers were generating concept art and short films that “bring their pitch to life” while Prime Video was using it to “transform the viewing experience” for its audiences via personalized recommendations, simplified synopses, spoiler-free summaries, audio descriptions and subtitles.

She said that Prime Video’s YA series “Maxton Hall” was now using lip sync technology to synchronize actors’ lib movements with human dubbed audio in different languages.

Most recently, we introduced lip sync technology on Maxton Hall, our most watched international original, which synchronizes actors’ lip movements with human dubbed audio.

Day added that “ethical guardrails” were required in using AI, however, saying they “cannot be an afterthought, they have to be the foundation and that’s the approach we’re taking.”

The theme of RTS’s 2026 convention, which is being hosted by Amazon, is “united in change, if not now, when?”

title: Durban FilmMart Head on Why This Year’s Event Is ‘Looking Inward’ as African Screen Industries Strive to ‘Create Solutions’ on Their Own Terms
summary: The Durban FilmMart returns for its 17th edition with a full slate of conversations and events looking to build on the legacy of innovation, disruption and industry-defining discussions at what is arguably the most influential film market on the continent. Running from Oct. 9 – 12, this year’s event is organized around the theme “Shifting […]
content:
The Durban FilmMart returns for its 17th edition with a full slate of conversations and events looking to build on the legacy of innovation, disruption and industry-defining discussions at what is arguably the most influential film market on the continent.

Running from Oct. 9 – 12, this year’s event is organized around the theme “Shifting Worlds, Turning Toward Ourselves,” a focus that Durban FilmMart Institute director Magdalene Reddy says was inspired by the pioneering Senegalese filmmaker Ousmane Sembène’s memorable assertion: “Why be a sunflower and turn towards the sun? I myself am the sun.”

“We are very much looking inward [at this year’s edition],” Reddy tells Variety. “In a world where…everything is shifting, we find that, at this time, it’s important for us as the African cinema community to look at what we need to create systems that will work for us. How can we consolidate? How can we create solutions?”

Popular on Variety

The four-day event features a wide range of panel discussions, masterclasses, one-on-one meetings and mentorship sessions designed to capitalize on a moment of unprecedented visibility — and unparalleled disruption — for the African screen industries.

In a departure from previous editions, which ran parallel to the Durban Intl. Film Festival, this year’s DFM will open with a screening, of Rwandan debutante Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Cannes Caméra d’Or winner “Ben’Imana.” The film, an alumnus of DFM’s influential pitching and finance forum, was selected to highlight the event’s outsized impact on the African filmmaking community.

“This was a DFM project. It was pitched at DFM two years ago, and they were able to win two awards at Cannes [including the FIPRESCI prize],” says Reddy. “For us, the celebration of hosting a screening at the market — which we’ve not done previously — is based on the fact that we want to show our local content in our local context.”

A crucial pillar of every DFM is its influential Think Tank strand, whose conversations and conclusions often “become a blueprint for the next DFM and the direction which the industry is going,” according to Reddy.

Central this year will be a closed-door session gathering key distributors, financiers and industry leaders looking to tackle some of the vexing challenges of film distribution on the African continent, which has been hit especially hard by successive waves of corporate consolidation in the global industry. Another session will focus on audience development, “trying to see how we can connect better with our local [audiences],” Reddy says.

A backbone of this year’s event will be a spotlight on equitable co-production, with a series of sessions organized in collaboration with the European Audiovisual Entrepreneurs network (EAVE). Tackling knotty issues such as how to best incorporate inclusivity into financing, development and production, the conversations will address the systemic imbalances that face African producers when partnering with outside co-producers, “even when they are coming with the stories, coming with the IP,” says Reddy.

“How can they go in as an equal partner? How can they sit confidently at the table, so they are engaging in a way that will benefit them? Engaging in a way where finances can still come back to Africa?” she asks.

Collaboration is a theme across the Durban FilmMart’s various strands, with the event forging a wide range of partnerships with industry bodies such as EAVE; the Nature, Environment and Wildlife Filmmakers (NEWF); the Cape Town Intl. Animation Festival (CTIAF); Documentary Africa; The StoryBoard Collective; and the Ladima Foundation, which supports African women working in the film and television industries, and will launch an initiative to push for greater gender equity at African film festivals.

“Collaboration is something that has underpinned all the work that DFM has been doing over the years,” says Reddy. “In order for the industry to survive, we need to be working together.”

This year’s Durban FilmMart unfolds at a turbulent time for the host nation, whose screen industries have been “struggling,” according to Reddy, particularly with ongoing uncertainty around South Africa’s 25% cash rebate.

To that end, leading South African policymakers are expected to be on hand at DFM, which will host a closed session for local industry to meet one-on-one with representatives of the influential Dept. of Trade, Industry and Competition, which manages the country’s rebate policy; the National Film and Video Foundation; and various local and regional film commissions.

“For us as DFM, the platform that we create is a platform for filmmakers not just to create a community for the filmmaking industry on the continent, but also a space for filmmakers to connect with policymakers,” says Reddy. “A space for policymakers to understand what are the challenges, what are the issues our filmmakers are facing. We try to bridge that gap between industry and policymakers so we can create a conducive environment and ecosystem for our filmmakers.”

That mandate, she adds, extends to DFM’s broader engagement with the African continent as a whole. “Last year’s theme was creating bridges, and that’s what we continue to do. Even though it’s challenging within the continent to work with each other, we are trying to find ways to do that.”

title: ‘The Platform’ Co-Producer David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment Spain Boards Matías Rojas’ ‘Dog Legs’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: In one of the later deals pacted at the San Sebastian Festival, Spain’s David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment boarded Matías Rojas’s adaptation of Chilean cult novel “Dog Legs” (“Patas de perro”), joining four other producers from Chile, France, Germany and Colombia. With this, “Dog Paws” enters the final phase of its financing and is expected […]
content:
In one of the later deals pacted at the San Sebastian Festival, Spain’s David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment boarded Matías Rojas’s adaptation of Chilean cult novel “Dog Legs” (“Patas de perro”), joining four other producers from Chile, France, Germany and Colombia.

With this, “Dog Paws” enters the final phase of its financing and is expected to shoot in Valdivia, Chile during the second half of next year. Chile’s ever popular Alfredo Castro (Pablo Larraín’s “The Count,” “The Club”) is attached to star.

“Spain’s involvement decisively strengthens the project and puts us in a very strong position to complete its financing,” said Federico Durán, the film’s Colombian producer through his new company El Sol Ermitaño. Durán, who has produced such notable films as “The Squad” and “Alias María,” just won a major post production award for his WIP project “Lovers Go Home!” at San Sebastián.

Popular on Variety

“’Dog Legs’ is an ambitious project, both technically and artistically, but it also aims to reach a broad audience,” he told Variety.

Matamoros, whose credits include “The Platform” and “The Virgin of the Quarry,” was also a producer at Zentropa Spain, the company founded by Lars von Trier.

Chile’s A Simple Vista, led by Tomás Gerlach, first began developing “Dog Legs” some four years ago. This year, Reality Films, the production arm of French distributor Epicentre Films, which distributes Colombia’s Cannes-winning film “A Poet” and submission to the 98th Academy Awards international feature category, came on board at the 76th Berlinale, joining German company Klinker Films, a co-producer of “A Place Called Dignity,” Rojas’ previous film.

Visual effects will be handled by French company MPC, whose credits include Thomas Cailley’s “The Animal Kingdom,” winner of Best VFX at the 2023 Sitges Film Festival and the French César Awards.

Rojas’s ties to San Sebastian run deep. He premiered his debut feature, “Root,” at the festival 13 years ago. He later returned to its Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum with his second fiction feature, “A Place Called Dignity.”

Throughout his career, he has presented his films and projects at major international festivals including Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight, the Berlinale and the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF).

Published in 1965, “Dog Legs “is a landmark of Chilean literature…radical, powerful, and still deeply unsettling. Six decades later, its themes of exclusion, abuse and violence remain strikingly relevant. The story follows Bobi, a 12-year-old boy born with literal dog’s paws, hidden away by his family until Carlos, a lonely, childless man, takes him in. His act of compassion turns the town against them, casting Carlos as a madman and Bobi as a monster and setting them on a devastating path toward violence.

title: Madrid Audiovisual Cluster Dives Deeper Into New Business Models, AI and Emerging Technologies at Iberseries & Platino Industria
summary: The Madrid Audiovisual Cluster (MAC), an economic interest group comprising close to 100 Madrid-based companies, has put together a two-day industry networking and peer-learning program at the Iberseries & Platino confab, taking place over Sept. 29 – Oct. 2 in the Spanish capital. AI takes center stage again but the program will attempt to delve […]
content:
The Madrid Audiovisual Cluster (MAC), an economic interest group comprising close to 100 Madrid-based companies, has put together a two-day industry networking and peer-learning program at the Iberseries & Platino confab, taking place over Sept. 29 – Oct. 2 in the Spanish capital.

AI takes center stage again but the program will attempt to delve deeper into the hot-button topic this year, presenting eight industry case studies examining innovation across the audiovisual value chain.

“While AI is a common thread running through the projects, the session takes a broader view of innovation, covering new business models, emerging technologies and evolving production and creative workflows,” said Teresa Azcona, managing director of the Madrid Audiovisual Cluster.

Popular on Variety

“Together, they show how innovation is transforming the industry and opening up new opportunities across the value chain.”

But as Iberseries & Platino Industria co-Director Samuel Castro pointed out: “The ability to create stories should always be based on a fully human, author-driven concept and development. AI should be used as a tool, not as an end in itself.”

Under the banner Innovation ‘Case Studies in the Audiovisual Industry: New Business Models, AI and Emerging Technologies,’ the eight case studies will illustrate how companies are applying technology to address practical challenges across the industry. Running from 12:00 noon to 2:00 p.m. on Sept. 29, the workshop will feature eight case-study presentations, with approximately 12 minutes allocated to each.

The next day, Sept. 30, takes in a conversation between producer Rosa Bosch and Tanja Meissner, Director of Berlinale Pro, which encompasses major industry platforms including the European Film Market, Co-Production Market, Berlinale Talents and World Cinema Fund.

Case Studies:

1. PLIA: Applying PLIA Technology to Script Breakdown, Pre-Production Planning and Production Tracking on “Playback”

PLIA, an AI-powered production platform for film and audiovisual projects, has developed an integrated production-management solution designed to bring the information generated across the creative and production process into a single platform.

The company will present its application on the feature film “Playback,” covering script breakdown, pre-production planning and production tracking. The platform brings together scripts, notes, budgets, location photography and production breakdowns, with the aim of streamlining information management across the production workflow.

Presenting: Jose Velasco — CEO, PLIA

2. TBS (Telefónica Broadcast Services) Tech Brand Stories: From the Physical Studio to the Virtual Production Environment: Virtual Production, AR, Motion Graphics and AI

TBS – Tech Brand Stories, formerly Telefónica Broadcast Services, is the Telefónica Group’s creative production company and audiovisual agency. The company operates across live production, broadcast services, branded content and entertainment, combining creative and technical capabilities. Its team of more than 450 professionals works across major sporting and live events as well as non-fiction, entertainment, documentary and current-affairs programming.

The case study will examine the convergence of virtual production, augmented reality, motion graphics and AI, and how these technologies are being integrated into contemporary production environments.

Alberto Gonzalo — Graphics Supervisor

Luis Miguel Boedo — Technical Coordinator

3. Hark Media – Go Global: When AI Learns to Move Us: Hybrid Dubbing for Global Distribution

Go Global specializes in localization for the entertainment industry, providing translation, subtitling, dubbing and voice-over services to streaming platforms and production companies.

The company will look at the emerging role of AI in dubbing and how hybrid workflows combining technology and human expertise could support the localization of content for international markets.

Paula Ferrari — Founder & CEO

4. Xpost Studios – Secuoya Content Group: Innovation in VFX and Post-Production Workflows

Xpost Studios, part of Secuoya Content Group, is a Madrid-based post-production and VFX facility operating from Madrid Content City. Its infrastructure includes facilities for editing, color grading, sound post-production, VFX and digital workflows.

The session will focus on the application of new technologies to VFX and post-production workflows, examining how innovation is changing the way content is processed and delivered.

Marcos Requena — Post-Production Manager

5. Story Pitcher: Connecting Audiovisual Creators and Producers Through a Digital Platform

Story Pitcher has developed a digital platform designed to connect screenwriters, directors and other audiovisual creators with production companies and content platforms.

Its model combines AI-powered matching with legal-protection tools, with the aim of facilitating more direct connections between creative talent and industry decision-makers.

Frank Belyeu — CEO, Story Pitcher

6. Mercedes Santalla: From Talent to Market: Strategy and Business for Creative and Technology Projects

Creative strategist and talent manager Mercedes Santalla works with projects and talent operating at the intersection of creative practice and technology. Her session will examine the commercial and strategic considerations involved in taking creative and technology-led projects from development to market, alongside the evolving relationship between talent, technology and business.

Mercedes Santalla — Creative Strategist & Talent Manager

7. Scoutters – Scout & Film: A Digital Platform for Location Scouting and Production

Scoutters is a digital location-search and management platform developed by Spanish company Scout & Film. Built on Scout & Film’s experience managing locations for film and advertising productions, the platform connects location scouts, agencies, production companies and film commissions with locations suited to their production requirements.

The case study will explore how digital tools are changing the traditionally location-based process of sourcing, managing and presenting filming locations.

Rubén Souto — Co-Founder, Scout & Film

Jose Díaz — Co-Founder, Scout & Film

8. HaMo – Paramotion Films: HaMo Real-Time Animation System: Digital Puppetry and Next Lab R&D

Developed by Paramotion Films through the Next Lab Generation R&D initiative, HaMo is a real-time motion-capture system designed for 3D animation and digital puppetry.

The system uses inertial sensors to capture an operator’s physical movements and Unreal Engine to transfer them in real time to a CGI character. The technology enables virtual characters to perform live alongside human presenters and audiences, with potential applications across studios, live events and social media.

This case study will look at the development and practical application of the system as an example of R&D moving from prototype to production technology.

Jose Luis Farias — CEO, HaMo

Alfonso Fulgencio — CTO, HaMo

title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani Refuses Jimmy Kimmel’s Request to Text Trump a Selfie of Them
summary: “Jimmy Kimmel Live” is back in Brooklyn. The late-night show has returned to the New York City borough for a week of shows at the Brooklyn Academy of Music. It’s Kimmel’s eighth time filming “Live” in Brooklyn, the place he was born and spent his early years, and the comic is welcoming a number of […]
content:
“Jimmy Kimmel Live” is back in Brooklyn.

The late-night show has returned to the New York City borough for a week of shows at the Brooklyn Academy of Music. It’s Kimmel’s eighth time filming “Live” in Brooklyn, the place he was born and spent his early years, and the comic is welcoming a number of heavy-hitting guests to his couch, from Howard Stern and Billy Crystal to Paul McCartney and Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT). He said the show received over 150,000 ticket requests, and kicked off his Brooklyn week with guests Pete Davidson and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, as well as a musical performance by TV on the Radio, celebrating the 20th anniversary of their celebrated album “Return to Cookie Mountain.”

While there weren’t any stories involving an Oscar-winning actor exposing himself to Kimmel in a bathroom, the host was heckled by Matt Damon in a Boston Red Sox cap — on the eve of the Yankees/Red Sox AL Wild Card Series — who was joined by Kimmel’s mother and sister, and Jon Hamm, cosplaying as an angry New York City construction worker. After his sit-down interview with Davidson, who was promoting his Netflix video podcast “The Pete Davidson Show” and upcoming film “How to Rob a Bank,” Kimmel welcomed Mayor Mamdani to the stage. He prefaced his arrival with a montage of clips of Fox News talking heads predicting that New York City would become “terrifying” under Mamdani and crime would go “through the roof.” That proved to be wrong, as murders and shootings in the city hit record lows in Mamdani’s first seven months.

Popular on Variety

“Another thing that is very unexpected is this relationship that you have with President Trump, which seems to be a very friendly relationship,” Kimmel said, adding, “Did you guys hit it off immediately or is it something that you really went into thinking, ‘OK, I need to have a relationship with the president of the United States, and I think the best way to do it is to charm him.’ How did you do that, and can you help me?”

Mamdani laughed. “Sorry brother,” he replied. “The president and I have many disagreements. One thing we do agree on is this city, how much we love this city, so from that first meeting in November of last year, I was just thinking of how we can make this meeting not about us, but about New Yorkers. How can we spend that time talking about the things that can make life in the city a little bit easier.”

Kimmel then threw to a video clip of Mamdani standing next to Trump at Gracie Mansion as the president gave a rambling speech, with the camera pressing in on Mamdani as he stood there stone-faced. “I mean, it is remarkable,” offered Kimmel. “I watch that, and I go, ‘OK, this is not a guy I’d want to play poker with.’” Mamdani said that while Trump is speaking, he’s only focused on getting federal approval for his proposed Sunnyside Yard project, a development in Queens that would feature an estimated 12,000 new homes and create approximately 30,000 jobs.

“You text with the president, I’ve read?” Kimmel pressed further.

“From time to time we’re in communication, and it’s about Sunnyside Yard, and it’s about how we can deliver for the city,” replied Mamdani. “One of the other things the president mentioned that we spoke about, that I care very deeply about, is Haitian New Yorkers. They’ve had their Protected Status ended, and I really believe we need to do whatever we can so they have stability. They’re part of the fabric of this city.”

Kimmel then asked if they could text Trump “a selfie of us right now,” only to have Mamdani shut him down: “Jimmy, I love you, but I love housing more.”

title: Amazon’s Kelly Day Says AI Will Unlock “Creative Risk” & Help Free Up Creatives Working On The Next Big Hit
summary: Amazon’s Prime Video international chief has unashamedly thrown her weight behind the power of artificial intelligence and its use in Prime Video content. Addressing the RTS London Convention, Kelly Day said the controversial tech “brings down costs meaning more stories can be made, more diverse voices can get heard and more creative risks get taken,” […]
content:
Amazon’s Prime Video international chief has unashamedly thrown her weight behind the power of artificial intelligence and its use in Prime Video content.

Addressing the RTS London Convention, Kelly Day said the controversial tech “brings down costs meaning more stories can be made, more diverse voices can get heard and more creative risks get taken,” while “transforming the viewing experience on Prime Video.”

“That is not a threat to creativity, that is creativity unleashed,” she told a room packed full of the great-and-the-good of the British TV industry.

While Day stressed “we’re not looking for an AI model to write the next Fleabag,” she said it will allow the creator of the next big hit to “spend less time on admin and more time on creative decisions that make a show like that sing.”

Watch on Deadline

Day echoed previous senior Amazon execs in backing AI. Amazon has an AI Studios division, led by Albert Cheng, which is currently being built out. Amazon MGM Studios recently dropped Luca Guadagnino’s movie Artificial, which tells of OpenAI and the company’s turbulent period in 2023 when founder Sam Altman was fired and rehired in a matter of days.

“The next generation of viewers is telling us they want more, not less,” added Day. “AI will help us get there faster. And the people who make some of the best television in the world are sitting in this room.”

Amazon is sponsoring the RTS Convention this year and Day revealed Prime Video quadrupled spend in UK TV, movies and live sport over the past five years.

Arguing that the UK TV industry should embrace change and build “for the customer,” Day said Prime Video spent £4B ($5.3B) since 2022 versus £1B the preceding five years, leading total spend to hit £5B since Prime Video moved into the territory a decade ago with Jeremy Clarkson’s motoring show The Grand Tour.

Day revealed publicly for the first time the story of how, a decade ago, Prime Video set The Grand Tour’s launch date to time with the streamer rolling out from five to more than 200 territories.

Day labeled the UK as Amazon MGM Studios’ “largest production hub outside of the U.S.,” with more than 90 productions having now filmed there in the past decade. Big hitters include the likes of Clarkson’s Farm, Last One Laughing UK and The Assassin. Upcoming are an adaptation of Stephen King’s Crouch End and Irish YA series Boys of Tommen. “We need a lot more so please call us,” said Nicole Clemens, international originals boss, who has relocated to London.

Day became the latest international head honcho to unveil a big money content spend in the UK. Both Disney+ and Netflix have laid down similar gauntlets over the past few years.

Day was speaking at RTS London alongside international originals boss Nicole Clemens before the chiefs of the BBC and Channel 4. Clarkson is speaking later, as is Steven Knight and Graham Norton.

title: Tony Robinson ‘Rewrites History’ With Debuting Radar Studios
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Here’s one for the history buffs. The newly-formed Radar Studios is teaming with British broadcaster and historian Tony Robinson for a suite of content. Tony Robinson Rewrites History will launch as a YouTube channel later this year, with an initial 12 half-hour episodes. Meanwhile, Radar Studios will debut a six-part, hour-long TV series to […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Here’s one for the history buffs. The newly-formed Radar Studios is teaming with British broadcaster and historian Tony Robinson for a suite of content.

Tony Robinson Rewrites History will launch as a YouTube channel later this year, with an initial 12 half-hour episodes. Meanwhile, Radar Studios will debut a six-part, hour-long TV series to international buyers at MIPCOM Cannes next month.

The series will see popular British personality Robinson, who is known for his role in sitcom Blackadder, revisiting defining events of the past, from ancient history through to the modern era, and explore how things might have gone differently if a single pivotal moment had gone differently. The events will range from the Spanish Armada to the advent of Covid-19.

Robinson has worked with Radar Studios parent WTFN Group in Australia for more than 15 years on TV shows such as Tony Robinson’s Time Walks and Tony Robinson’s Tour of Duty, so today’s news extends that pact.

Watch on Deadline

As we revealed last week, Radar Studios came into being when WTFN merged its digital arm Radar with its distribution business Fred Media. It aims to bring content creation, channel management and international distribution together under one roof, and already operates Robinson’s dedicated history channel Time Travels on YouTube, where it has more than 40,000 subscribers.

The new pact will see a new pipeline on original shows and digital content from Robinson roll out.

“I’ve known the team at WTFN for more than 15 years and we’ve made some terrific television together, so the opportunity to do something genuinely new with Radar Studios was irresistible,” said Robinson in a statement to Deadline.

“History is about the way things were, isn’t it? It’s written in stone and it couldn’t have happened any other way. Well, no. It’s actually full of tiny moments where everything hung in the balance. One different decision, one mistake, even a gust of wind and you have to rewrite history.

“And the great thing about this partnership is that we’re no longer thinking about history as something that has to fit into one particular television slot. We can tell stories in different ways, for different audiences and across different platforms. There is an enormous amount to explore and I’m hoping these first six hours are just the beginning.”

Radar Studios’ Chief Commercial Officer, Derek Dyson, added: “There could hardly be a better partner than Tony to lead off our originals strategy. He is one of the most recognisable and trusted faces in popular history, with an extraordinary ability to make the past entertaining, accessible and relevant to audiences around the world.

“Significantly, Tony Robinson Rewrites History demonstrates exactly why we created Radar Studios. Instead of making a series and then deciding where it might live, we are developing IP from the outset with multiple audiences, platforms and distribution opportunities in mind. We are creating original content for a dedicated, managed YouTube channel; developing additional digital opportunities around that content; and producing a standalone six-part television series for international buyers.

“One creative partnership and one piece of IP can therefore generate a whole ecosystem of content and commercial opportunities. By bringing content creation, channel management and international distribution together within Radar Studios, we can manage that entire journey ourselves.”

title: Prime Video Plots “More Feminine Point Of View” In Nordic Originals As Crime Dramas Like ‘Snake Killer’ & ‘Rinnan’ Draw In Men
summary: Prime Video’s push into Danish originals began this year with Pilou Asbæk-starring Snake Killer, which is now serving as a milestone in a charge across the Scandinavian region, according to Amazon MGM Studios Nordics originals chief Emilia Widstrand. “We’re really trying to build on that psychological thriller and crime vibe, doing it with strong creators […]
content:
Prime Video‘s push into Danish originals began this year with Pilou Asbæk-starring Snake Killer, which is now serving as a milestone in a charge across the Scandinavian region, according to Amazon MGM Studios Nordics originals chief Emilia Widstrand.

“We’re really trying to build on that psychological thriller and crime vibe, doing it with strong creators and within established Nordic genres,” she told Deadline in an interview. Looking further ahead, Widstrand will be seeking to more directly target women and younger viewers too, as the service expands.

Snake Killer launched in January, with the four-parter followings a notorious Copenhagen narcotics police unit, Uropatruljen, a heavy-handed force that operated with relative autonomy between 1965 and 2001. The story sees Brian “Smiley” Petersen (Asbæk) leading his unit in a desperate war against a brutal heroin baron. Anders Ølholm is the writer and director.

Over in Norway, drama series Rinnan, about the infamous Norwegian traitor and Gestapo agent Henry Rinnan, is also set to launch. A co-production with Norwegian broadcaster TV2, the Miso Film show points to how Amazon is willing to share rights and window originals to bolster budgets.

Watch on Deadline

Both series appeal to men, who have formed the backbone of viewing on Prime Video in the Nordics, but recent successes with unscripted shows will see the content mix changing in the future.

“Moving forward, we’ll have a more feminine point of view,” said Widstrand. “When we started out, we had a very broad audience, and we’ve really seen the appeal of female-led stories through global hits like The Idea of You and The Summer I Turned Pretty, as well as unscripted shows like LOL: Last One Laughing. We’re really building on that, alongside our crime audience.”

As such, new original out of Denmark, Murder in the Dark, a four-part series from SAM Productions and Amazon MGM Studio based upon influential Danish literary icon Dan Turèll’s book series, is designed to appeal to a broad audience. It follows a retired and hard-bitten “nameless journalist” played by Michael Falch and his daughter Sophie (Katinka Lærke Petersen), who is an ambitious police detective.

The first shot from production of ‘Murder In the Dark’ Prime Video

Widstrand became Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios Head of Nordic Originals in August last year, as we revealed at the time, to replace Karin Lindström, who later joined HBO Max. The two are credited internally with building Prime Video’s local originals team from scratch, making her the natural choice for the top post when it came available.

In January, this year, she added acquisitions duties following a restructure that saw the departure of Prime Video Nordics head Andreas Hjertø. She now works closely with the acquisitions on deals, those see does not lead specifically.

She also recently ordered a Swedish original, Sarek, a four-part psychological thriller based Ulf Kvensler’s debut novel about a group of friends on a hiking tripe that takes a dangerous turn.

That, Widstrand said, talks to a desire to age down the audience, with a cast led by Felix Sandman, Kitt Walker Johansson, Alva Bratt and Nora Rios, and to focus on well-known IP. “It really speaks to that strategy,” she added.

We sat down with Widstrand to pick her brains on the future for Prime Video Nordics and its originals slate.

DEADLINE: Emilia, you spoke at the Copenhagen TV Festival in August. What was your message to producers and the industry about what Amazon needs and is looking for from the Nordics?

Emilia Widstrand: We’ve been expanding our drama slate. It takes a long time to develop, and we wanted to take that time. Our first Danish original was Snake Killer, which was very successful, so we’re really trying to build on that psychological thriller and crime vibe, doing it with strong creators and within established Nordic genres.

Moving forward, we’ll have a more feminine point of view. When we started out, we had a very broad audience, and we’ve really seen the appeal of female-led stories through global hits like The Idea of You and The Summer I Turned Pretty, as well as unscripted shows like LOL: Last One Laughing. We’re building on that, alongside our crime audience.

DEADLINE: Can you give us an example?

EW: We have Murder in the Dark, which is based on 1980s cult movies and books that we’re bringing back for Christmas Day. That has a much more female point of view than previous drama series. We’re leaning into both the female young-adult genre, looking for local versions of the kinds of stories that have found an audience globally, as well as Nordic crime, suspense and psychological thrillers. We’re trying to find strong local IP. Sometimes, we do co-productions where we sell international rights, but the focus is very much local right now.

DEADLINE: What kinds of international co-productions are you looking at and how flexible can you be?

EW: We’re very flexible. It’s a case-by-case decision about how we can get something done, but IP is important. We’re building on existing IP or true stories, which also helps us connect locally. Obviously you work with the best local talent, and the Nordics is such an amazing place to do that – It’s really special.

DEADLINE: Sarek is based on IP and with big producers. That feels like an example of what you’re talking about.

EW: Definitely, it really speaks to that strategy. I was just back on set on the show. It’s spectacular because it’s so Nordic. We’re shooting it up in Kiruna, and the environment is really a character in the story. There, we also decided to go a bit younger with the cast.

DEADLINE: In terms of your own role, Emilia, you’ve added some responsibilities, taking on unscripted along with scripted. How has that changed what you’re doing and has it impacted the overall shape of Prime Video Nordics?

EW: Strategy and programming are still separate, but I took on the overall responsibility for our Nordic local originals. I’ve found looking after the unscripted slate, which I wasn’t familiar with before, very intriguing. We work with very talented people across both unscripted and scripted, so we can really see synergies in both the talent and the content. It’s a big responsibility, but you get a fantastic overview.

DEADLINE: What would you say you’ve learned so far? It’s been a few months since you’ve taken on the expanded role.

EW: There are differences between the territories, both in Norway and Denmark, and there are different focuses in scripted and unscripted. Denmark, for example, is very strong in comedy, and it’s very easy to find strong unscripted comedy formats there.

Norway has really surprised me with the amount of great talent. We’ve found so many strong and interesting projects that we’re developing with local talent. That’s been overwhelming in a good way, with some really good projects coming out of Norway.

‘Snake Killer’ Prime Video

DEADLINE: With that in mind, what’s a realistic number of shows that will make it onto the screen?

EW: We have a slate of around 20 to 25 local originals per year, scripted and unscripted. It’s big, but we’re still trying to grow sustainably and not take on too much, while making sure we compensate the audience for the production.

DEADLINE: When we’re looking at LOL, which has been popular in the Nordics and pretty popular all over the place, is there any difference in how it’s received across the territories you’re overseeing?

EW: LOL works really well across territories. It’s a format that’s worked in so many countries across the world, huge in Mexico and Germany. It kind of works everywhere. The local versions are very different. We have local creatives on each project, because comedy is so local – it’s very hard for someone from another territory to develop it. We have other examples of programs that work better in one territory than another, but LOL is really delivering across the region, which I’m happy to see.

DEADLINE: When you’re looking at the Nordic region at the moment, what’s the biggest challenge for you as a commissioner? Obviously, you have the Amazon machine behind you, which means there is money, but it’s not an endless pot. Is it a case of funding, or talent identification?

EW: I would say both. Talent has had a few tough years, and I think it’s hard for talent to navigate what commissioners want to commission and what their creative vision is. I’m really interested in working with creators who have a strong vision and fight for that – they don’t just deliver everything you ask for. I really value creators who want to tell you something, because that delivers the best projects.

The other thing is, of course, funding. Budgets have been kind of the same, even though there’s been inflation, so it’s really hard to adapt to that. It’s also been a challenge with the tax rebates locally, and a lot of production is shooting abroad.

‘Rinnan’ Prime Vide

DEADLINE: Where are people shooting?

EW: Eastern Europe. It’s tougher to finance locally. That’s why we try to be open. If we’re going to get something big made, we need to be collaborative with local broadcasters and find synergies.

We’ve had a fantastic collaboration with TV2 in Norway with Rinnan, a project we’re launching this fall. It’s a World War II series we’re doing with Kenneth Karlstad, and it is a fantastic example of what we can do with a local broadcaster.

They benefit from their deep understanding of the local audience, while we bring the Amazon package and the premium feeling of doing high-end drama. We do it together. We’re in the room together and we’re reacting together.

DEADLINE: It comes to you first and then TV2?

EW: Yes.

DEADLINE: Is that always the case when you do those partnership shows? I see this in lots of different territories – it tends to be the streamer goes first with an exclusive window, and then the broadcaster takes it however many months later.

EW: Yes, that’s always how we do it, because we’re also much smaller than a TV2, so it makes sense for us to go first.

DEADLINE: Broadcasters and distributors have become more and more open to these types of collaborations. That probably wasn’t the case a few years ago.

EW: I think we’re moving into a much more collaborative space with financing.

title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico Warn That Trump Will “Reinstitute A Complete Ban” Without Judge’s Injunction: “An Injury On All News Media”
summary: CNN, MS NOW and Politico are warning that the Trump administration will reimpose a “complete ban” on their access to the White House without a judge issuing a preliminary injunction. Last week, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a temporary restraining order, forcing the White House to restore access to the White House to the […]
content:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico are warning that the Trump administration will reimpose a “complete ban” on their access to the White House without a judge issuing a preliminary injunction.

Last week, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a temporary restraining order, forcing the White House to restore access to the White House to the outlets as he more fully considers the legal arguments. The TRO lasts for 14 days.

In a filing in federal court on Monday, attorneys for the three news outlets argued that the Trump White House actions since then “leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico if allowed the opportunity.”

The outlets’ legal team, led by Theodore Boutrous Jr., pointed to the White House’s restriction on CNN from access to State Dinner arrivals on Thursday evening. The network then was barred from serving as TV pooler on Air Force One on Trump’s trip to Tennessee on Saturday, with no replacement stepping in, and leaving a dearth of TV images from the trip.

Watch on Deadline

“Because the ban is an unlawful assault on the most fundamental First Amendment freedoms and will inflict irreparable harm on Plaintiffs and the public if not restrained, this Court should preliminarily enjoin its enforcement pending the resolution of this case,” the news outlets’ attorneys wrote.

Kelly cited a lack of due process by the White House when it pulled dozens of credentials of reporters from the three outlets. While the Trump DOJ has cited standards of “professionalism and decorum” and national security concerns, the media outlets’ legal team called that reasoning that “pretextual” and “post hoc,” as well as vague.

In the latest brief, CNN, MS NOW and Politico also again cited violations of the First Amendment. They noted that Trump has explained the ban by blaming their coverage as “Purposely … negative,” among other things.

“His statements also make clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from newsgathering and reporting that the President might view as negative,” the news outlets’ legal team wrote. “And his administration has continued to retaliate against Plaintiffs even after the temporary restraining order, only underscoring that Defendants’ motive is to punish and chill journalism they dislike.”

The outlets are asking the judge to prohibit the Trump team from pulling hard pass credentials, or to ensure the reporters of the White House access they had before Sept. 18. In contrast to a TRO, a preliminary injunction would sideline Trump’s ban until a trial is held, or if an appeals court rules otherwise.

Trump initially banned the three outlets on Sept. 18. When the judge granted a TRO last early Thursday, it meant that the White House had to restore hard passes, with reporters not gaining reentry until around noon that day.

The issue of whether the White House can also restrict CNN from the pool is a slightly different, but related issue. It’s also one at the center of another case, involving the Associated Press after it was banned from the pool and other White House events. That case is currently on appeal.

That said, in the latest brief, the three outlets cited the White House’s continued prohibitions on CNN as an example of White House retaliation over protected speech.

For much of last week, there was no TV network pool, meaning that there was little video coverage of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House. The four other networks in the pool — CBS News, ABC News, Fox News and NBC News — initially suspended their participation in protest of the exclusion of CNN. The networks resumed the TV pool coverage this week, but it will be put to the test again on Thursday, when CNN is assigned to that duty.

“Every day, critically important news is breaking at the White House, and the ban will substantially interfere with Plaintiffs’ ability to cover it,” the outlets brief stated. “The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable.”

The DOJ’s brief in response is due by Friday.

title: Dennis Haskins Dies: ‘Saved By The Bell’s Mr. Belding Was 75
summary: Dennis Haskins, best known for playing Mr. Belding in Saved by the Bell, has died. He was 75. His agent Jay Schachter confirmed the news to Deadline, saying in a statement, “It’s a tragic loss. Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis, loved him even more. He was a […]
content:
Dennis Haskins, best known for playing Mr. Belding in Saved by the Bell, has died. He was 75.

His agent Jay Schachter confirmed the news to Deadline, saying in a statement, “It’s a tragic loss. Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis, loved him even more. He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans.

“He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly. I’m heartbroken,” he continued.

Haskins cause of death was not disclosed.

He first played Principal Richard Belding in the Disney Channel series Good Morning, Miss Bliss, opposite Hayley Mills in 1989. After one season, the show was retooled as Saved by the Bell on NBC, where he reprised his role through its four-season run. Haskins returned as Mr. Belding for Saved by the Bell: The New Class in 1993 and played the role for seven more seasons, until the show’s finale in 2000.

Other acting credits for Haskins included Hangin’ with Mr. Cooper, Malibu, CA, The Practice, The West Wing, The Rerun Show, The Stoneman, 7th Heaven, Going Down, Red Water, Tangy Guacamole, An Ordinary Killer, JAG, Dead End Road, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, Men of a Certain Age, The Bold and the Beautiful, Victorious, Mad Men, Emerald Acres, How I Met Your Mother, Destroy the Alpha Gammas, New Girl, Hot In Cleveland, This Isn’t Working, Bill Nye Saves the World, Abstruse, Enigma, A Bennett Song Holiday, among many others.
