title: Prime Video, Sony, JioStar, Zee and NDTV Chiefs on How Connected TV Is Reshaping Indian Storytelling
summary: Connected TV is changing what Indian media companies make, not just where audiences watch it, with Prime Video now developing shows around whether audiences will watch them together, executives said at the FICCI-Frames conference in Mumbai. Streaming began as a largely solo experience, Gaurav Gandhi, VP and head of Prime Video for Asia-Pacific and Australia-New […]
content:
Connected TV is changing what Indian media companies make, not just where audiences watch it, with Prime Video now developing shows around whether audiences will watch them together, executives said at the FICCI-Frames conference in Mumbai.

Streaming began as a largely solo experience, Gaurav Gandhi, VP and head of Prime Video for Asia-Pacific and Australia-New Zealand, said during the opening presentation, “India’s Screen Economy – The Next Wave.” “So much of our time is being spent today thinking about like, hey, this is a co-viewing show compared to this is an individual-driven show first,” he said.

Gandhi said CTV combines the shared, lean-back experience of television with digital’s convenience, choice and ad targeting. “The challenge it brings up with is in that world of so much choice, when you’re in a lean-back experience, how easy do you make it for customers to be able to get to what you want to get to?” he said, adding that recommendation engines need to get much better.

Popular on Variety

Moderator Vivek Couto, co-founder, CEO and executive director of Media Partners Asia, described CTV as a screen that pairs TV’s scale with digital’s addressability and asked the panel how it would reshape the industry’s economics.

Kevin Vaz, chair of the FICCI Media & Entertainment Committee and CEO of entertainment at JioStar, said he would rather talk about the large screen than about CTV specifically. “The large screen has always been communion, the large screen has always brought families together and been a unifier,” he said. CTV keeps that and adds measurement and addressability, Vaz said, letting advertisers, most of whom prefer the bigger screen, aim their messages at specific audiences. Citing the figure presented earlier in the session, he put India’s CTV audience at nearly 200 million viewers and said it is growing fast.

Gaurav Banerjee, managing director and CEO of Sony Pictures Networks India, recalled the old marketing line “Medium is the message” and said industry discourse can get swayed by the signal rather than the substance. “So it finally doesn’t really matter how people get to that large-screen experience, but what do they do when they get there?” he said.

For Banerjee, CTV offers the same opportunity TV has offered for three decades: a family gathered around a program it can talk about over dinner. The industry’s job is to create those viewing experiences, he said, recalling watching “Nukkad” with his family as a child in the 1980s. “I think that’s something that hasn’t truly changed and should not change, and that’s something that we have to keep building and keep protecting,” he said.

For news, CTV is opening up programming that linear schedules could not justify. Rahul Kanwal, CEO and editor-in-chief of NDTV, said linear planners always worry that a show with narrow appeal will sink a channel’s ratings. On CTV, NDTV has been able to double down on “Lifeline,” about healthcare, wellness and anti-aging, and “Launchpad,” about upskilling. “News channels typically wouldn’t be able to do that kind of content because there wouldn’t be enough eyeballs in that,” Kanwal said, adding that CTV viewers open such content only if they are interested.

Vaz said the definition of a hit has shifted as screens have multiplied. Success used to be judged on a single large-screen measure, he said, but now also counts audience votes, engagement and social media trends. Technology, he added, can match each story with the viewer it suits, when and where they want it, so that one person’s flop can be another’s hit.

Punit Goenka, CEO of Zee Entertainment Enterprises, said the industry has moved beyond the TV-versus-digital split into an attention economy, where content, technology and data have to work together. Asked what makes content win amid endless choice, he kept it to a single line. “Infinite content does not mean infinite consumption,” he said.

title: ‘Digger’ Review: As a Texas Oil Tycoon, Tom Cruise Goes Over the Top in Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Bombastically Self-Important Satire
summary: "Digger" isn’t funny. It’s nervy, in your face, audacious, adventurous, and bizarro in a free-swinging, out-of-the-box way. And it feels like a comedy, since it’s fueled by the relentless overacting of a bad Coen brothers movie. But "Dr. Strangelove," built around the genius of Peter Sellers, was brilliantly funny. "Digger" borrows the doomsday architecture of "Strangelove" but leaves out the slyness, replacing it with a lavishly in-your-face spectacle of browbeating.
content:
“Digger,” starring Tom Cruise as a Texas oil tycoon who unleashes forces even more powerful than himself, is a movie that thinks it’s delivering something bigger than a mere message; it thinks it’s bringing us the word. Cruise, under pounds of jowly make-up and thinning disheveled white hair, plays Digger Rockwell, an ancient Southern fossil-fuel titan who doesn’t just lord it over his company. He’s a man who rules the oil industry, and therefore rules America and maybe the world.

Cruise, declaiming every line, acting with blind bluster and a mean gleam of good-ol’-boy joy, makes Digger a walking cartoon — a larger-than-life satire of over-the-top American arrogance, like LBJ crossed with Foghorn Leghorn. The performance is very much of a piece with what Cruise did in his fat-suit cameo as the vulgarian studio executive Les Grossman in “Tropic Thunder.” At one point, Cruise wanted to make a Les Grossman movie, and in a certain way “Digger” is that movie — a chance for him to let it rip for two hours, to give the kind of stylized hambone performance that’s essentially a “Saturday Night Live” caricature, only executed with Method fullness. On its own terms, Cruise’s acting in “Digger” is well-played and skillfully etched. It’s fun — or, theoretically, it should be — to see him cut loose. But the character of Les Grossman was a trivial showbiz lark. Alejandro G. Iñárritu, the director of “Digger,” has more serious things on his mind.

Popular on Variety

The movie is set in a not-so-distant future, where Digger wakes up in a mansion that’s as much of a gilded bunker as Charles Foster Kane’s Xanadu. (He sleeps with his fluffy white cat, who’s in the process of dying and is, for some reason, played by a fake mechanical cat.) Right off, Digger receives an alarmed communication from his henchman in Greenland, where it seems that the oil exploration has hit a snag. There’s a crack in the ice, just a few feet wide, but it’s getting larger by the minute. Digger says it’s nothing to worry about. His message is the same one he’s been running his company on for decades: Drill, baby, drill, and fuck the consequences.

Only this time the consequences aren’t cooperating. Years of climate abuse, of reckless drilling at the ends of the earth, have unleashed a wave of methane, which in terms of environmental destruction makes carbon dioxide look like laughing gas. An ice shelf, 400 miles wide, splits off from the glacier and starts floating toward Europe. It is set to collide with the continent and cause a tsunami, a mega-disaster, and mass death. Are we laughing yet?

“Digger,” with its countdown-to-Armageddon scenario, wants to be the “Dr. Strangelove” of climate change. It also wants to be the “Network” of climate change, and to radically up the ante on “Don’t Look Up,” Adam McKay’s finger-pointing satire of climate change. Did I mention that the movie is about climate change? I take that issue seriously, but at this point a movie like “Digger” is practically guilt-tripping its audience. It’s got us over an (oil) barrel: In its very extremity, the film is saying that the situation we face is so dire, so on the precipice of disaster, that if you watch this movie and somehow fail to embrace its “visionary” message of apocalypse now, you’re contributing to the problem.

But here’s the real problem: “Digger” isn’t funny. It’s nervy, in your face, adventurous, and bizarro in a free-swinging, out-of-the-box way. And it feels like a comedy, since it’s fueled by the relentless overacting of a bad Coen brothers movie. But “Dr. Strangelove,” built around the genius of Peter Sellers, was brilliantly funny. “Digger” borrows the doomsday architecture of “Strangelove” but leaves out the slyness, replacing it with a lavishly overscaled spectacle of browbeating.

Iñárritu, who wrote the script with Alexander Dinelaris, Nicolás Giacobone, and Sabina Berman, has staged the film as a baroque piece of visual fetishism, with ornately detailed sets and a showy monochromatic color scheme just this side of black-and-white. The film lets you know in every way that it’s offering audiences something different from what they’re used to seeing.

Yet I’m not sure that “Digger” is going to connect, because it’s so full of itself — so top-heavy with importance. The movie cost north of $125 million to make, and that figure is not only too big to probably justify itself; it’s a testament to the arrogance of the filmmakers — to the assumption that we’ll turn out in droves for this ponderous absurdist lecture. The movie treats Digger Rockwell as if he were a descendant of Daniel Plainview from “There Will Be Blood,” a film that was also too didactic for its own good, even as its message (capitalism: bad!) became catnip to a generation of movie buffs. “There Will Be Blood” was undeniably arresting. “Digger” is overbearing, complete with a Brechtian twist that’s both jaw-dropping and head-scratching. (You think, “Are they really doing this?” Then you think, “Why are they doing this?”)

Staging a movie of broad scolding maximalism isn’t the same thing as staging a movie of debonair satirical insanity. Along with Cruise, “Digger” features the dour theatrics of John Goodman, who glowers with one-note malevolence as the President of the United States, a character afflicted with “ass cancer” (are we laughing yet?), and also Sandra Hüller as Digger’s furious half-sister, who runs an environmental company — she’s there to symbolize the way “activism” is just a delusional bone that the oil industry throws at us. Riz Ahmed plays Ganesh, the close scientific adviser to Digger who is actually rooted in the real world, and therefore has to be the messenger of bad news. He becomes a frazzled, drunken mess.

There’s one sequence that gets your blood pumping, and that’s because of Cruise’s acting, and also because of what the scene is saying. As the world veers toward calamity, Digger stands before a global assembly (it looks like the UN of the future) and gives a speech explaining why the world has remained addicted to oil. It is, he says, because you want it that way — all of us who are hooked on 1,000 lifestyle choices, far beyond gasoline-fueled cars, that we don’t actually want to give up. It’s the film’s Howard Beale speech, and it’s bracing to see “Digger,” at least for 10 minutes, stop blaming the Usual Bad Guys, and to see Cruise deliver that message with a fire-and-brimstone glee. But then that theme slinks away, and it’s back to the accusatory disaster-movie gloom-mongering. And while I won’t reveal anything more about the film’s breaking of the fourth wall, let me just say this: It makes the movie, however unintentionally, seem to be about nothing so much as Tom Cruise taking on this role, and Iñárritu erecting the edifice for him to stand on. And that’s a tone-deaf mistake. It punches up the fact that we’re never going to solve the climate-change crisis until we disentangle it from the hot air of people celebrating themselves.

title: Premium TV and Talent ‘Will End Up on YouTube and TikTok Over Time’ Says Sister Boss and ‘Black Doves’ Producer Jane Featherstone
summary: High-end television and the talent behind it aren’t destined to only find their homes on established networks and streaming platforms, claims one of the U.K.’s most renowned producers. Speaking at the RTS London Convention on Tuesday, Jane Featherstone, co-founder of the ever-growing Sister group and producer of scripted dramas including “Black Doves,” “This is Going […]
content:
High-end television and the talent behind it aren’t destined to only find their homes on established networks and streaming platforms, claims one of the U.K.’s most renowned producers.

Speaking at the RTS London Convention on Tuesday, Jane Featherstone, co-founder of the ever-growing Sister group and producer of scripted dramas including “Black Doves,” “This is Going to Hurt” and “Chernobyl,” predicted that the sort of shows she makes will soon end up on less traditional channels.

“I think premium will end up on YouTube and TikTok over time, because great talent will jump out of the bigger mainstream organizations,” she said. “Talent is like water; they will find the the shortest way to the audience past all the obstacles.”

Popular on Variety

Featherstone said that her job as a producer was to not just find and nurture the talent, but to “make sure we’re on top of where the audiences are and where the talent want to be, and that’s what’s thrilling to me.”

Sister recently took a majority stake in fast-rising digital-first production company After Party Studios and just last week announced a strategic partnership with branded entertainment group Common Interest, two of several forward-thinking investments the company — co-founded with Elizabeth Murdoch — has made over the last few years.

“What’s fascinating to me it that we can understand how these creators have a very direct relationship with their audience — and they know what they like and what they don’t like,” said Featherstone of working with companies such as After Party. “I think it’s interesting for us as producers to be able to get access to that direct audience feedback.”

title: ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Kicks Off Broadcast’s Fall TV Premiere Week as No. 1 Show in Late Night (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: As the 2026-2027 TV season got under way last week, “Jimmy Kimmel Live” won the broadcast network premiere week in late night, both in total viewers and adults 18-49. For the week of Sept. 21, “JKL” averaged 2.29 million viewers and a 0.21 rating in adults 18-49. That’s based on live+same day big data plus […]
content:
As the 2026-2027 TV season got under way last week, “Jimmy Kimmel Live” won the broadcast network premiere week in late night, both in total viewers and adults 18-49. For the week of Sept. 21, “JKL” averaged 2.29 million viewers and a 0.21 rating in adults 18-49.

That’s based on live+same day big data plus panel ratings. “Jimmy Kimmel Live” beat NBC’s “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” (1.3 million) and CBS’ “Comics Unleashed” (704,000 for the first half hour, 521,000 for the second half hour) during the 11:35 p.m. hour.

The premiere week guests for “Jimmy Kimmel Live” included Woody Harrelson (“Brothers”), Sam Richardson (“Matchbox The Movie”) and musical guest Greta Van Fleet on Monday; Jamie Foxx (“Jamie Foxx: Take Care of Yourself”) and Ke Huy Quan (“Never Say Die”) on Tuesday; Brandi Carlile (“Returning To Myself (Sad Gay Version)”) and John Wilson (“The History of Concrete”) on Wednesday; and Ben Affleck (“Animals”) and Mo Amer (“Mo Amer One Night Only at Radio City”) on Thursday. Also, Sara Niemietz sat in with The Cletones during the week.

Popular on Variety

The reps the second year in a row that “Jimmy Kimmel Live” opened the season as the No. 1 late-night show in total viewers and adults 18-49 during premiere week; it’s also now been the No. 1 show in late night during premiere week with the 18-49 demo for the fifth consecutive year.

Premiere week was down a smidge from the previous week of Sept. 14, which repped the final week of the 2025-2026 TV season (although that was just a three-night week). With guests including Stephen Colbert, “JKL” was No. 1 with total viewers (2.34 million) and adults 18-49 (0.22 rating).

Meanwhile, with the full 2025-2026 TV season now over, “Jimmy Kimmel Live” averaged 2 million total viewers for the full season. That made it “JKL’s” most-watched season in eight years (since 2017-2018).

And in adults 18-49, “Jimmy Kimmel Live” averaged a 0.18 rating for the season, making it No. 1 across late night. That was the show’s best performance in the demo in four years (since 2021-2022).

The “Jimmy Kimmel Live” momentum comes as the show kicked off a week of episodes from Brooklyn on Monday. Guests this week include Pete Davidson (“The Pete Davidson Show,” “How To Rob A Bank”), New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and musical guest TV on the Radio on Monday. That’s followed by Howard Stern (“The Howard Stern Show”), Amy Schumer and musical guest Tom Morello on Tuesday; Billy Crystal (“860”), Mahershala Ali (“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”) and musical guest De La Soul on Wednesday; John Oliver and Seth Meyers, and Robby Hoffman (“Robby Hoffman: Wake Up”) on Thursday; and Paul McCartney (“The Boys of Dungeon Lane”), Sen. Bernie Sanders and musical guest Goose on Friday.

title: JioStar’s Kevin Vaz Urges Indian Government to Restore BARC TV Audience Ratings as Media Sector Hits $28.9 Billion
summary: Leading Indian streamer JioStar’s Kevin Vaz has called on India’s government to immediately restore BARC audience ratings, using the inaugural address at the FICCI-Frames conference to warn that the data gap is leaving broadcasters, advertisers and agencies without dependable numbers heading into the festive season. Vaz is the CEO of entertainment at JioStar and chair […]
content:
Leading Indian streamer JioStar‘s Kevin Vaz has called on India’s government to immediately restore BARC audience ratings, using the inaugural address at the FICCI-Frames conference to warn that the data gap is leaving broadcasters, advertisers and agencies without dependable numbers heading into the festive season.

Vaz is the CEO of entertainment at JioStar and chair of the FICCI Media & Entertainment Committee. He thanked India’s Ministry of Information & Broadcasting for scrapping the 10+2 advertising cap, describing the move as a step toward rules that fit how linear TV and the wider media business now operate.

The ministry first ordered BARC to stop publishing news channel ratings on March 6, citing sensationalist coverage of the Israel-Iran conflict, and extended that pause several times. In early July, it widened the freeze to all genres until BARC secures registration under the Television Ratings Policy 2026, which took effect in March. BARC applied on April 29 and has expanded its panel to 70,876 homes against the policy’s 80,000-home target, but ratings remain suspended.

Popular on Variety

“At a time of global economic uncertainty, reliable audience measurement is critical to keeping this ecosystem efficient, supporting advertisers and broadcasters, and keeping domestic economic activity moving,” Vaz said.

He also pressed for a concrete roadmap to strip away the regulatory load and costs that weigh on linear broadcasting. Forbearance has been a long-standing demand from the sector, he said, and self-regulation backed by solid industry standards should sit at the core of its next phase.

The appeal comes as the sector continues to grow. Indian media and entertainment expanded 9% in 2025 to INR2.78 trillion ($28.9 billion), Vaz said. Digital passed INR1.1 trillion ($11.5 billion), while live events jumped 47%.

Through much of its history, Vaz said, the hard limit on Indian media was distribution, with too few channels and screens for stories to reach viewers. “Attention is the new currency, and in an era where content and ideas seem endless, the magic lies in creating something that makes the ‘thumb stop!'” he said.

He pointed to Connected TV as a case where older and newer screens are converging rather than displacing each other. Citing industry estimates, Vaz put India’s CTV audience at more than 200 million viewers, with over 80% of that viewing done together with family or friends. Linear TV streaming, he added, lets viewers watch live channels on any screen and connection while opening up new options for measurement and advertising. The 2026 Indian Premier League (IPL) cricket tournament, which reached more than 1.2 billion viewers, was “perhaps the clearest expression” of that convergence, he said.

Microdrama was worth INR6.5 billion ($68 million) in 2025, and the category is expected to grow at more than 50% a year by 2028, Vaz said. JioStar has entered the format through Tadka and is working with over 50 production houses, which he said was helping to bring more creators into the business.

JioHotstar also let viewers find and buy products inside the app while they watched the IPL and a live stream of blockbuster “Dhurandhar The Revenge.” Vaz called content commerce a third “value pool” for the industry, next to advertising and subscriptions.

On AI, Vaz said the technology is reshaping production, storytelling, workflows, analytics and personalization. “But even as technology expands what is possible, the human being must remain at the center of the creative ecosystem,” he said. He called for clear rules on copyright, consent, attribution and a fair return for creators, so that technology and creativity move forward together.

Before turning to the industry’s numbers, Vaz asked the room to pause in silence for the late Leena Jaisani, FICCI’s deputy secretary general and head of media and entertainment, who helped found its Media & Entertainment Committee.

This year’s edition, held under the theme “India’s Media Moment: Creating Value in an Age of Infinite Content,” marks 26 years of the committee’s work through FICCI Frames. Vaz closed by urging the industry to judge itself on the value it creates rather than on output or reach. “Did we build intellectual property that could travel from India to the world?” he asked.

title: ‘Vintage Violence’ Producers Spacemaker & Barravento Strike Partnership With Japanese Anime Studio Genco
summary: EXCLUSIVE: U.S. indie Spacemaker Productions and its Japanese subsidiary Barravento have forged a partnership with leading anime studio Genco as they continue to build bridges between the U.S. and Japanese film industries. Spacemaker and Barravento – the Tokyo-based subsidiary that Spacemaker founded in collaboration with producer Hiroto Ogi (Drops Of God, Titanic Ocean) – recently […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: U.S. indie Spacemaker Productions and its Japanese subsidiary Barravento have forged a partnership with leading anime studio Genco as they continue to build bridges between the U.S. and Japanese film industries.

Spacemaker and Barravento – the Tokyo-based subsidiary that Spacemaker founded in collaboration with producer Hiroto Ogi (Drops Of God, Titanic Ocean) – recently launched their first project, Eugene Kotylarenko’s Vintage Violence, which received its world premiere at Toronto International Film Festival.

Tokyo-based Genco is the anime planning and production company behind acclaimed titles such as Satoshi Kon’s Millennium Actress and Tokyo Godfathers; Sunao Katabuchi’s In This Corner Of The World, and Netflix series Pluto.

Together, the companies are exploring international co-productions backed by U.S. financing, as well as live-action adaptations of Japanese source material and IP, and original projects by Japanese creators for the U.S. market.

Watch on Deadline

World premiering in TIFF’s Midnight Madness section, Vintage Violence stars Cole Sprouse and Kiko Mizuhara in the story of a disgraced livestreamer who discovers a trove of rare vintage denim in a Colorado mine, following it to Tokyo – and straight into the arms of a woman who may be using him. Caught between desire and betrayal, he soon finds himself entangled in black-market turf wars, yakuza, and a past that refuses to stay buried.

WME is handling US domestic sales for the film, with Best Friend Forever overseeing international rights. The film received the location attraction tax rebate offered by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and administered by the Visual Industry Promotion Organization (VIPO).

Spacemaker Production’s founder, Alex Hughes, said: “Spacemaker has long admired Japanese cinema and has developed projects in Japan for some time. Making Japan our principal hub for Asian production is a natural evolution of that work and we are pleased to be expanding Barravento in partnership with Hiroto. His depth of experience in international production is uncommon – he understands how films are financed and executed on both sides of the Pacific, and that understanding is precisely what foreign productions shooting in Japan most often require.”

Riccardo Maddalosso, President of Spacemaker Productions, said: “Japan is also highly competitive on cost, with a consistently high standard of crew. Taken together, we believe that represents one of the strongest production propositions in today’s market.”

Hiroto Ogi added: “We are thrilled to partner with Genco, a company behind some of Japan’s most distinctive and original works, and are confident that this new chapter of international collaboration will be an incredibly exciting journey.

“Japanese films and series are finding audiences around the world, so the way we make them should become more open and international too. Filmmakers from abroad can bring perspectives to Japan that we might not see from the inside, while Japan has extraordinary talent that deserves to be discovered beyond its borders. Barravento is about creating those encounters and seeing where they lead. For me, that sense of discovery is what makes filmmaking exciting.”

In addition to its partnership with Genco, Barravento also focuses on local productions in Japan, as well as providing production services to foreign productions seeking guidance in navigating Japan’s incentive system, and covering all aspects of production.

The company’s services also include helping foreign productions access Japanese IP for development and adaptation. Among Barravento’s additional projects in development is an English-language remake of Kanteo Shindo’s cult horror classic Onibaba.

Spacemaker’s credits include How to Blow Up A Pipeline by Daniel Goldhaber, starring Ariela Barer, Sasha Lane and Lukas Gage, which premiered at TIFF 2022; Oscar Boyson’s Our Hero, Balthazar starring Jaeden Martell and Asa Butterfield; Sebastain Silva’s Rotting In The Sun, starring Jordan Firstman, and the recently announced The Lonely Woman, directed by Boy Harsher and starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA Twigs, Sturgill Simpson and Will Oldham.

title: ‘Digger’ Review: Tom Cruise Explodes In Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Surprising And Urgent Disaster Movie Satire
summary: Digger is unlike any film coming from a major Hollywood studio in years, at least in my memory. It makes sense it comes from Warner Bros, which is the one major that seems to take real swings with big budgets, directors and stars in films you might say are risky business. Some work, some don’t: […]
content:
Digger is unlike any film coming from a major Hollywood studio in years, at least in my memory. It makes sense it comes from Warner Bros, which is the one major that seems to take real swings with big budgets, directors and stars in films you might say are risky business. Some work, some don’t: It paid off last year big time with Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another, which swept through awards season and the Oscars. But Digger, with a character-driven, head-spinning performance for the ages by the world’s biggest movie star Tom Cruise and an urgent message-laden satire about the world we are f*cking up from multiple Oscar-winning but undeniably auteurist filmmaker Alejandro G. Iñárritu, takes things much further and thus could be one of the more divisive movies for the masses in a very long time.

There is no doubt it will, and should spark conversation and, love it or hate it, it should not be ignored. For me it is like a return to the kind of adventurous films in cinema’s groundbreaking era of the 1970s, but it isn’t easily defined. Its rat-a-tat-tat dialogue could come out of a ’40s screwball comedy like Howard Hawks’ His Girl Friday, or even Billy Wilder’s 1961 One Two Three. In other ways it reminds me of the outrageous satire of Kubrick’s Dr. Strangelove (Kubrick would have loved this movie) and even Adam McKay’s more recent Don’t Look Up, the latter featuring the same kind of desperate warnings about the destruction of our planet that Digger dwells on. You can even throw in Iñárritu’s Oscar-winning Birdman which with its theatrical setting has more in common with this one than you might gather from the trailers which, for a change, don’t give you the complete picture of what you are in for with Digger. Neither will I — to a point.

Watch on Deadline

The studio is urging critics not to give away some of the twists, there is a huge one about half an hour in, so audiences can experience it with fresh eyes. However it is no spoiler alert to say it is tough to talk about this film without spilling the beans because though this movie is a comedic satire, it is also one about an impending disaster for mankind, one brought about the toll taken on our environment by greedy tech billionaires and oil barons with no goal other than building their own wealth at the expense of everyone and everything else. So this is the stuff of comedy? The aforementioned twist which may well throw audiences off, or even out, demands patience because it ultimately pays rich dividends in explaining how this tragic event could seemingly be played for laughs. Here is a clue: it all has to do with time.

Dr. Strangelove dealt in real time about the world blowing itself up in a nuclear war as it ends with Slim Pickens riding the bomb like a cowboy on a horse on its way to total annihilation. Don’t Look Up similarly takes a ticking clock real time approach to the planet’s complete obliteration by a meteor and a lament that it was just too late to do anything for humanity. Those were both comedies about seizmic events. Digger does it differently, a satire of disaster movies that says the real disaster is ourselves. The payoff, the revelation comes as the end credits roll. I won’t give it away or the complicated, sometimes frustrating (for some no doubt) journey Iñárritu and his co-writers take to get us there, but trust them. I walked away ultimately very moved but still more hopeful than in Strangelove and Don’t Look Up. Yes, it is a comedy, but the laughs mask a strong message that should be taken very seriously.

Cruise, virtually unrecognizable under prosthetic make up by Oscar winner Kazu Hiro, plays Digger Rockwell, an oil barron and obscenely rich guy who also has the ear of the U.S. President (John Goodman). We meet him in his mansion with his beloved , but near dead, cat Maggie as he goes about his daily rituals doing everything a guy that rich can do to keep his faithful companion of 30(!) years breathing (the anamatronic cat is the genius scene-stealing work of a team of puppeteers). If he has no concerns about what his drilling is doing to the earth, he does still manage to show he is human by his love for this poor creature.

Trouble though is on the horizon as an explosion on one of his oil rigs has freed a killer ice flow, setting loose Tsunamis, threatening hundreds of thousands of lives, and heading directly for Europe. What to do? “Let’s bomb the shit out them, Mr. President”, a overeager general suggests to stop it from spreading. A nightmarish product of ignored warnings of climate change and global warning, and an out of control disaster that was unleashed by Digger, now coming home to roost. He sets about to try and save the world from his own misdeeds (“Digger got us into this and now he is gonna dig ourselves out of it”, the President confidently proclaims) as the U.S. Government looks to contain the damage and not take the blame, even as they have basically been screwing over our European allies for years (sound familiar?) So this is the set up before we get to the twist and a parallel storyline that serves as a comment on the action we are watching. It is an observation on how we view reality, even when it appears to be surreality, or is it? Or was it?

Iñárritu had this idea nine years ago, in 2017 right about the time Trump got elected the first time and immediately pulled us out of the Paris Climate Agreement. It has gone through several iterations since then in a time where it has become increasingly difficult, even on a daily basis, to take a satirical look at the state of a real world and U.S. government that looks like pure satire itself. You can’t make up the real stuff coming out of D.C. so how do you keep up with dizzying ever-changing events and make this all seem relevant in a world where just a couple of weeks ago tech titans started casually mentioning man-made technology could end humanity before the decade is over? Just the new normal, right folks? That is the brilliance of this script written by Inarritu, his Birdman collaborators Alexander Dinelaris & Nicolás Giacobone, and Sabina Berman, with a story by Berman & Iñárritu and Jez Butterworth. It balances the seemingly absurd stuff of science fiction with what is becoming plausible as each day goes by and further rattles our heads. It pulls this all off by not showing the actual calamity, but something far more sobering believe it or not. In its own very different way it reminds me of Stanley Kramer’s 1959 warning of nuclear proliferation in On The Beach which ends in an empty town with a banner still waving in the wind saying ‘there is still time brother’. Between the laughs you are wondering if we are on a glide path to this becoming more fact than fiction. God knows there are already a lot of Diggers out there.

Cruise has never done a role like this one and the fact that he has spent the past several years filling theatres with the Mission: Impossibles and Top Guns, he reminds us he is also the actor who brought life to Born On The Fourth Of July, Jerry Maguire, Magnolia, Rain Man, The Color Of Money, The Last Samurai, Risky Business, Eyes Wide Shut, and so many more. His range is undeniable but here it is off the charts, especially in a stunning 10 minute monologue Digger delivers that admits guilt but seeks to place the blame collectively on all of us. There is also much more than the trailer tells you about this performance, but Cruise has surprises in store here doing something he has never before done in movies, and it is impressive indeed.

Surrounding him is an outstanding supporting cast, most notably Riz Ahmed as Ganesh as a scientist who tries to warn Digger and the President about what’s coming but fails. Goodman, who may be channeling a certain well-known President sails blissfully over the top in a rich comic turn. Sandra Huller, who seems to be in everything this year, is fine as Emma, Digger’s equally dangerous younger sister, and Michael Stuhbarg is his usual pro self as the Vice President ignored by POTUS but who isn’t as clueless as he appears. Jesse Plemons is superb as the mysterious Kenny becomes a key player in all this, and there is also exemplary work from Emma D’Arcy as Lina, Digger’s ever-faithful assistant, and Sophie Wilde who watches over the action with a keen eye.

The production values across the board are top notch, starting with cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki’s camerawork employing the rich layers of Vista Vision; editors Conor O’Neill and Stephen Mirrone given a very tall task with the shifting moods; casting director Francine Maisler ; and especially production designers Dennis Gassner and Richard Johnson who pull off Herculean work for this film shot in its entirety at Pinewood Studios in England. Composer Cosmo Sheldrake’s score also makes the grade.

From Revenant and Birdman which brought him back-to-back Oscars, to memorable films like Biutiful, Babel , and Amores Perros among others, Iñárritu again proves he is one of the most original and fascinating filmmakers working today. Digger is the kind of movie we don’t see often on this scale, an ambitious satire that entertains, takes chances, sparks arguments, but is thrillingly alive as cinema designed to make us look at ourselves, hopefully wake up before it is too late, and ask the question: ‘what the hell are we doing? ‘

Producers are Iñárritu, Cruise, and Mary Parent.

Title: Digger

Distributor: Warner Bros

Release date: October 2, 2026

Director: Alejandro G. Iñárritu

Screenwriters: Alejandro G Iñárritu & Alexander Dinelaris & Nicolás Giacobone, and Sabina Berman, story by Berman & Iñárritu and Jez Butterworth

Cast: Tom Cruise, Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons, Sophie Wilde, Emma D’Arcy

Rating: R

Running time: 2 hr 8 mins

title: Orcas Island Film Festival To Honor ‘Josephine’ Director Beth De Araújo; Killer Films’ Pamela Koffler Named Marquee Industry Guest
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Filmmaker Beth de Araújo’s breakout year is continuing with the announcement of a signature award from the upcoming Orcas Island Film Festival in Washington state. The festival announced Tuesday it will honor the director of Josephine with its Jean-Marc Vallée Vanguard Award, named for the late filmmaker and frequent guest of the Orcas Island […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Filmmaker Beth de Araújo’s breakout year is continuing with the announcement of a signature award from the upcoming Orcas Island Film Festival in Washington state.

The festival announced Tuesday it will honor the director of Josephine with its Jean-Marc Vallée Vanguard Award, named for the late filmmaker and frequent guest of the Orcas Island Film Festival. The award celebrates “bold, distinctive artists” whose work embodies Vallée’s “spirit of creative independence and discovery.”

OIFF, which runs October 14-18, also announced producer Pamela Koffler, co-founder of Killer Films, as its Marquee Industry Guest. In November, Koffler and her longtime producing partner Christine Vachon will receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award from the Motion Picture Academy’s Governors Awards. Vachon and Koffler’s extraordinary body of work includes Past Lives, Carol, May December, Boys Don’t Cry, Far from Heaven, Still Alice, First Reformed, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, Happiness, I’m Not There, Zola, A Different Man, and Materialists.

Producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler attend the 96th Annual Oscars on March 10, 2024 in Los Angeles. Alberto Rodriguez/Getty Images

Koffler will take part in a conversation about her work on Saturday, October 17, to be moderated by Gregory Ellwood of The Playlist.

Watch on Deadline

Director Beth de Araújo Presley Ann/Getty Images for Gold House

The Orcas Island Film Festival lineup features a bold slate of Oscar-contending films, among them de Araújo’s Josephine, starring Gemma Chan and Channing Tatum, which won the Grand Jury Prize: Dramatic at the Sundance Film Festival, as well as the festival’s Audience Award for U.S. Dramatic. It’s joined in the program by Fjord, the Palme d’Or winner directed by Cristian Mungiu; La Bola Negra, which won the Best Director prize at Cannes for filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, as well as the Toronto Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award for Best Film; Bitter Christmas, directed by Pedro Almodóvar; The Debut, directed by Jesse Eisenberg; Lukas Dhont’s Coward, which won acting prizes at Cannes for Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne; All of a Sudden, directed by Ryūsuke Hamaguchi, which earned Cannes Best Actress prizes for Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto; Rose, the film directed by Markus Schleinzer that won actress Sandra Hüller the Berlin Silver Bear for Best Leading Performance; Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone, which is generating Oscar buzz for lead actor Andrew Scott, and The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, directed by Noah Segan, which is attracting Oscar buzz for lead actor John Turturro.

The nonfiction lineup is similarly stacked with Oscar contenders like Once Upon a Time in Harlem, directed by David Greaves and produced by Liani Greaves; Barbara Kopple’s Union Town; Boatbuilders, directed by Luke Lorentzen; Rehearsals for a Revolution, directed by Pegah Ahangarani, and Nuisance Bear, directed by Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman.

Scroll for the full OIFF lineup.

Audiences attend the 2025 Orcas Island Film Festival Courtesy of OIFF

“This program captures what makes Orcas such a special destination for film lovers: audiences can discover some of the year’s most celebrated international films, major awards contenders and singular new voices, then meet and hear directly from the filmmakers and artists behind them,” said Carl Spence, OIFF co-founder and co-director. “From Palme d’Or and Sundance prize winners to leading international Oscar submissions, an exceptional documentary program, the Jean-Marc Vallée Vanguard Award, Pamela Koffler and our visiting filmmakers and industry guests, this is one of the strongest and most exciting festivals we’ve presented. What makes OIFF unique is the intimacy of the experience—extraordinary cinema, meaningful conversations and unforgettable celebrations, all together on Orcas Island.”

Orcas Island Film Festival Courtesy of OIFF

OIFF describes itself as a “destination festival without the lines.” Last year’s event attracted attendees from 25 U.S. states and nine countries “to experience acclaimed international cinema against the spectacular backdrop of the San Juan Islands.”

“We want the OIFF experience to feel special from the moment you arrive on Orcas—not stressful,” commented Donna Laslo, OIFF co-director. “With reserved seating for every screening, we’ve virtually eliminated the long lines and uncertainty that come with general admission. You can choose your films, select your favorite seats in advance, and then simply show up and enjoy the festival. Very few film festivals offer reserved seating, and for our guests, it makes an enormous difference.”

Industry Panel

OIFF will also host an industry panel bringing visiting filmmakers, artists and industry guests together for intimate conversations about storytelling, filmmaking and the journey from the festival circuit to awards season. True Stories, Unscripted, on Friday, October 16 at Parish Hall, will feature special guests from this year’s documentary lineup and take audiences behind the scenes of nonfiction filmmaking—from the first spark of an idea to the remarkable characters and unexpected moments that could never have been scripted.

2026 Film Lineup

ALL OF A SUDDEN | Dir. Ryûsuke Hamaguchi | France | 196 min

Oscar winner Ryûsuke Hamaguchi’s sweeping new drama stars Cannes Best Actress winners Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto in a luminous story of elder care, mortality, dignity, and unexpected human connection.

BEDFORD PARK | Dir. Stephanie Ahn | USA | 119 min

Sundance Special Jury Award winner Stephanie Ahn’s acclaimed debut stars Moon Choi and Son Suk-ku in an intimate Korean American drama about family expectations, old wounds, identity, and second chances.

BITTER CHRISTMAS | Dir. Pedro Almodóvar | Spain | 111 min

Pedro Almodóvar returns with Bárbara Lennie, Patrick Criado, and Leonardo Sbaraglia in a witty, melancholic puzzle where an actress mines real lives for a screenplay—and may herself be someone else’s character.

BOATBUILDERS | Dir. Luke Lorentzen | USA | 103 min

Documentary. Premiering at the Venice Film Festival, Sundance Award-winning director Luke Lorentzen’s beautifully observed documentary follows craftspeople of Brooklin Boat Yard across four seasons as they transform raw timber into a magnificent 56-foot sailboat—a celebration of craftsmanship, community, and purpose.

LA BOLA NEGRA | Dir. Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo | Spain | 155 min

Cannes Best Director winners Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi unite Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close in a sweeping drama linking three eras through desire, inheritance, Spanish history, and Federico García Lorca.

CARL SAGAN: WE ARE MADE OF STAR STUFF | Dir. Nanette Burstein | USA | 98 min

Documentary. With unprecedented access to Carl Sagan’s personal archive, this documentary reveals the life behind the visionary astronomer, exploring the ideas, relationships and questions that shaped his understanding of the cosmos and humanity, from Academy Award-nominated director Nanette Burstein and producer Seth MacFarlane.

CLARISSA | Dir. Arie Esiri, Chuko Esiri | Nigeria | 134 min

Oscar nominee Sophie Okonedo leads David Oyelowo, Ayo Edebiri, and a superb ensemble in this reimagining of Mrs. Dalloway, transposed to contemporary Nigeria with romance, memory, and trauma.

COWARD | Dir. Lukas Dhont | Belgium | 120 min

Cannes Acting Prize winners Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne lead Lukas Dhont’s deeply moving drama about grief, masculinity, friendship, and the pressure to become who others expect. Belgium’s official Oscar submission marks a powerful return from the acclaimed director of CLOSE and GIRL.

DAO | Dir. Alain Gomis | France | 183 min

From director Alain Gomis, this New York and Berlin Film Festival selection intercuts a memorial in Guinea-Bissau and a Paris wedding, revealing one family’s bonds across continents, generations, ritual, migration, memory, and community.

THE DEBUT | Dir. Jesse Eisenberg | USA | 105 min

Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti star in Jesse Eisenberg’s theater-world comedy about a neglected housewife who joins a community musical and discovers that losing herself onstage may help her find herself.

THE DREAMED ADVENTURE | DIR. VALESKA GRISEBACH | GERMANY | 162 MIN

Winner of the Cannes Jury Prize, Valeska Grisebach’s quietly thrilling new film about a middle-aged archaeologist searching for a missing former flame on the fragile border between Eastern and Western Europe gradually shifts into a wide-ranging crime saga.

ELSINORE | DIR. SIMON STONE | UNITED KINGDOM | 111 MIN

Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, and Johnny Flynn star in the deeply emotional and inspirational true story of Ian Charleson, a gifted actor whose greatest challenge becomes his greatest triumph. Facing his own mortality with unflinching honesty, wit, and grace, Charleson delivers a courageous performance that becomes a source of healing and inspiration for those around him.

THE ENDLESS FRONTIER | Dir. Marilyn Ness | USA | 82 min

Documentary. Emmy-winning filmmaker Marilyn Ness follows scientists confronting disease, climate change, and other urgent threats while revealing the political and financial pressures jeopardizing American research—and the discoveries, progress, and lives that depend on it.

EVERYTIME | Dir. Sandra Wollner | Austria | 121 min

Cannes Un Certain Regard Prize winner EVERYTIME, Sandra Wollner’s haunting drama (and Germany’s Oscar submission) stars Birgit Minichmayr in a dreamlike family story where grief, memory, reality, and mourning begin to blur.

FATHERLAND | Dir. Paweł Pawlikowski | Germany | 82 min

Cannes Best Director winner Paweł Pawlikowski directs Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller in a striking postwar drama about Thomas and Erika Mann confronting exile, memory, guilt, and Germany’s devastated moral landscape.

FJORD | Dir. Cristian Mungiu | Romania | 146 min

Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner stars Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as Romanian immigrants in Norway whose family is upended by abuse allegations, igniting a tense battle over trust, culture, and institutional power.

OIFF 2026 | 5GENTLE MONSTER | Dir. Marie Kreutzer | Austria | 114 min

Léa Seydoux, Jella Haase, and Catherine Deneuve lead Marie Kreutzer’s Cannes Competition thriller about a police raid, a fractured family, and one woman’s terrifying uncertainty over what to believe about her husband.

A GIRL UNKNOWN | Dir. Zou Jing | China | 125 min

Zou Jing’s intimate critics’ prize-winning coming-of-age drama follows a young girl abruptly removed from her mother and rural home, tracing abandonment, resilience, identity, and the emotional scars of growing up between families.

LA GRADIV A | Dir. Marine Atlan | France | 145 min

Cannes Critics’ Week Grand Prize winner LA GRADIVA turns a school trip to Naples into a vivid coming-of-age drama as attraction, jealousy, class tension, and longing erupt among teenagers wandering ruins and volcanic landscapes.

HUMBOLDT USA | Dir. G. Anthony Svatek | USA | 89 min

Documentary. Across three very different American places named for Alexander von Humboldt, this lively, visually inventive documentary explores nature, technology, climate, and the surprising ways our lives remain connected to the world around us. Director G. Anthony Svatek is scheduled to attend.

I PLAY ROCKY | Dir. Peter Farrelly | USA | 128 min

Oscar winner Peter Farrelly directs Anthony Ippolito, Stephan James, and Matt Dillon in the irresistible true story of Sylvester Stallone betting everything on starring in Rocky—the role that changed movie history.

IN WAVES | Dir. Phuong Mai Nguyen | France | 91 min

Lyna Khoudri, Paul Kircher, and Rio Vega voice this acclaimed graphic-novel adaptation, a visually distinctive animated romance blending surf culture, memory, young love, and grief in fluid, expressive style.

INK | Dir. Danny Boyle | United Kingdom | 116 min

Venice and Telluride Festival hit INK stars Guy Pearce, Jack O’Connell, and Claire Foy in Danny Boyle’s propulsive, darkly funny story of Rupert Murdoch, tabloid disruption, populism, ambition, and the birth of modern media culture.

IRON BOY | Dir. Louis Clichy | France | 90 min

Cannes Un Certain Regard Special Jury Prize winner IRON BOY is a tender animated adventure about a ten-year-old forced into an iron corset who discovers music, friendship, rebellion, and a new sense of self.

JOSEPHINE | Dir. Beth de Araújo | USA | 120 min

This Sundance Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award winner stars Gemma Chan and Channing Tatum and follows a young woman who is haunted by the trauma of witnessing a disturbing event that opens her eyes to the violence around her. Jean-Marc Vallee Vanguard Award Winner.

LANDSCAPES OF MEMORY | Dir. Leah Galant | USA | 77 min

Documentary. Filmmaker Leah Galant turns family history into a provocative documentary examining Holocaust memory, inherited trauma, Jewish identity, Palestinian suffering, and the political uses of remembrance across generations. Director Leah Galant is scheduled to attend.

OIFF 2026 | 6LOOK BACK | Dir. Kore-eda Hirokazu | Japan | 100 min

Visionary filmmaker Hirokazu Kore-eda brings Tatsuki Fujimoto’s acclaimed manga to life in a tender, beautifully observed story of two young artists whose friendship, rivalry, and shared passion for drawing shape their lives—and reveal creativity’s life-changing power.

A MAN OF HIS TIME | Dir. Emmanuel Marre | Belgium | 155 min

Cannes Best Screenplay winner A MAN OF HIS TIME stars ANATOMY OF A FALL’s Swann Arlaud as a Vichy civil servant whose faith in government collapses amid collaboration, bureaucracy, and moral surrender.

THE MELTDOWN | Dir. Manuela Martelli | Chile | 100 min

Cannes Un Certain Regard selection THE MELTDOWN follows a nine-year-old in the Andes after her teenage friend vanishes, with Saskia Rosendahl and Jakub Gierszał uncovering adult secrets beneath a child’s perspective.

MINOTAUR | Dir. Andrey Zvyagintsev | France | 138 min

Cannes Grand Prix winner Andrey Zvyagintsev returns with a gripping drama of jealousy, power, and corruption as a wealthy executive’s suspected affair exposes patriarchal entitlement, moral rot, and a wider political sickness.

MOUSE | Dir. Kelly O’Sullivan, Alex Thompson | USA | 120 min

MOUSE stars Katherine Mallen Kupferer, Chloe Coleman, Sophie Okonedo, David Hyde Pierce, and Iman Vellani in a tender, funny 2002-set story of friendship, family, and growing apart.

NUISANCE BEAR | Dir. Jack Weisman, Gabriela Osio Vanden | USA | 90 min

Documentary. Sundance U.S. Grand Jury Prize winner NUISANCE BEAR transforms a familiar polar-bear story into a visually daring documentary about survival, spectacle, tourism, Indigenous perspective, and human coexistence in a rapidly changing Arctic.

ONCE UPON A TIME IN HARLEM | Dir. William Greaves, David Greaves | USA | 100 min

Documentary. In 1972, filmmaker William Greaves gathered legendary Harlem Renaissance figures for an

extraordinary conversation; more than fifty years later, his son completes the cinematic time capsule—an official selection at Cannes and the New York Film Festival.

THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK | Dir. Noah Segan | USA | 88 min

John Turturro, Giancarlo Esposito, Steve Buscemi, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Tatiana Maslany headline this Sundance-premiered New York crime film about old-school street craft, a changing city, and consequences catching up.

PAPER TIGER | Dir. James Gray | USA | 115 min

This Cannes and New York Film Festival selection stars Adam Driver, Miles Teller, and Scarlett Johansson in James Gray’s gripping 1980s New York thriller about brotherhood, crime, pollution, family, and ambition’s dark side.

POSSIBLE LOVE | Dir. Lee Chang-dong | South Korea | 164 min

South Korea’s Oscar submission stars Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Cho Yeo-jeong, and Zo In-sung in Lee Chang-dong’s layered drama of class, marriage, labor conflict, ethics, and emotional betrayal.

RADIOHEART: THE DRIVE AND TIMES OF DJ KEVIN COLE | Dir. Peter Hilgendorf, Andrew Franks | USA | 83 min

Documentary. From Minneapolis dance floors to Seattle’s KEXP, legendary DJ Kevin Cole looks back on five decades of music, community, discovery, and the revolutionary power of radio. Subject Kevin Cole, Director Peter Hilgendorf, and Producer Susan Benson scheduled to attend.

REHEARSALS FOR A REVOLUTION | Dir. Pegah Ahangarani | Czech Republic | 95 min

Documentary. Winner of the Best Documentary prize at Cannes, filmmaker and actress Pegah Ahangarani turns her own family archive into a profoundly personal chronicle of Iran’s long struggle for freedom. Drawing on home movies, street-protest footage, newspapers, sketches, photographs, and recorded voices, Ahangarani intertwines her life story with more than four decades of political upheaval.

ROSE | Dir. Markus Schleinzer | Austria/Germany | 94 min

Berlin Silver Bear winner Sandra Hüller stars in Austria’s Oscar submission ROSE, a gripping black-and-white drama about a woman living as a man after the Thirty Years’ War, risking property, marriage, freedom, and survival.

TANGLES | Dir. Leah Nelson | Canada | 102 min

Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Abbi Jacobson, Bryan Cranston, and Seth Rogen lead the voice cast of this Cannes Film Festival animated adaptation about a daughter returning home to help care for her mother with Alzheimer’s.

UNION TOWN | Dir. Barbara Kopple | USA | 106 min

Documentary. Two-time Oscar winner Barbara Kopple returns to labor documentary filmmaking with a Venice Film Festival selection following UPS, Amazon, and app-based delivery workers organizing across New York in a timely fight for solidarity and power.

WE ARE THE SHAGGS | Dir. Ken Kwapis | USA | 98 min

Orcas Island’s own Ken Kwapis dramatizes the stranger-than-fiction story of The Shaggs, three sisters pushed into a band by their father whose failed musical dream later became outsider-art legend—funny, odd, and unexpectedly moving. Director Ken Kwapis is scheduled to attend.

YOU FOUND ME | Dir. Alice Vial | France | 98 min

A woman’s carefully ordered life is upended by an unexpected romantic encounter in Alice Vial’s warm French comedy about timing, vulnerability, and the surprises love still has in store.

title: Famke Janssen Inks With Buchwald
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Buchwald has signed Dutch actress Famke Janssen for representation in all areas. Janssen is best known for her role as Jean Grey/Phoenix in 20th Century Fox’s X-Men franchise, having played the part in X-Men, X2: X-Men United and X-Men: The Last Stand. She starred opposite Pierce Brosnan as Xenia Onatopp in the Bond film […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Buchwald has signed Dutch actress Famke Janssen for representation in all areas.

Janssen is best known for her role as Jean Grey/Phoenix in 20th Century Fox’s X-Men franchise, having played the part in X-Men, X2: X-Men United and X-Men: The Last Stand.

She starred opposite Pierce Brosnan as Xenia Onatopp in the Bond film GoldenEye and has appeared in a wide range of other films, including House on Haunted Hill, Hide and Seek, The Faculty, Taken, The Wolverine, Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters and Boy Kills World.

On the television side, Janssen stars in Netflix’s Dutch series Amsterdam Empire, where she also served as an executive producer. She’s also held roles on FX’s Nip/Tuck, ABC’s How to Get Away with Murder and BBC One’s The Capture, and in such series as Long Slow Exhale, When They See Us and Then You Run.

Watch on Deadline

Janssen’s upcoming projects include director Sean McEwan’s indie action dramedy Turnbuckle alongside Kate Beckinsale, Chee Keong Cheung’s The Experiment, and Scott Rogers’ thriller One Second After.

Janssen continues to be represented by The Artists Partnership and Link Entertainment.

title: ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Author To Release Book Sequel, MRC Developing Film Adaptation For Amazon
summary: There is more Olive Smith and Adam Carlsen in our future, Ali Hazelwood, author of bestseller The Love Hypothesis, announced Tuesday that she is releasing a book sequel, titled The Two-Body Problem, in February. Additionally, MRC is developing a film for Amazon MGM Studios, based on the sequel, she revealed. “I wrote a sequel to […]
content:
There is more Olive Smith and Adam Carlsen in our future, Ali Hazelwood, author of bestseller The Love Hypothesis, announced Tuesday that she is releasing a book sequel, titled The Two-Body Problem, in February. Additionally, MRC is developing a film for Amazon MGM Studios, based on the sequel, she revealed.

“I wrote a sequel to The Love Hypothesis” is not a sentence I thought I’d say a year or so ago, but now I weirdly can’t imagine a world in which The Two-Body Problem doesn’t exist,” Hazelwood wrote on Instagram alongside a photo of the book cover. “I’m really eager to talk more about this book and how it came about in the next few months. For now let me just say that the TLH movie and its cast made me fall for Adam and Olive all over again, that revisiting them was an absolute pleasure.”

She continued, “As someone who gets VERY attached to stories and characters, I know that unannounced sequels can be blindsiding, so feel free to skip this book and overwrite it with whatever headcanon you prefer, and I’ll see you on the next one! But if you want to read more about Adam and Olive, The Two-Body Problem spans a couple of years, and it’s a mix of slice of life, postdoctoral turmoil, and unflinching exploration of the hardest challenge one will face in a long-term relationship: deciding what to have for dinner.”

Watch on Deadline

Saying “nothing is guaranteed,“ Hazelwood also announced, “MRC is developing a film based on the The Two-Body Problem for Amazon MGM Studios.“

Details of the film were not revealed.

‘The Two Body Problem’ by Ali Hazelwood

Based on Hazelwood’s bestselling novel, The Love Hypothesis, which premiered September 23 on Prime Video, follows Olive (Lili Reinhart), a brilliant Ph.D. candidate focused on her future in academia, but an impulsive kiss with the intimidating professor Adam Carlsen (Tom Bateman) in front of her best friend changes the trajectory of her time at Stanford University.

There is some sort of tension after Olive hastily kisses Carlsen, who grabs her key-in badge to learn her name.



What begins as a desperate act of to prove she’s moved on spirals into a fake relationship for Olive with rules, boundaries, and a mutually beneficial agreement. When the arrangement she has with her senior colleague begins to blur the lines between performance and reality, Olive is forced to test her most daunting hypothesis yet: that love might actually be worth the risk.

The Two-Body Problem book will be published on Feb. 2, 2027.

title: Ex-‘American Idol’ Contestant Caleb Flynn Found Guilty of Murdering Wife
summary: Caleb Flynn, a former contestant on “American Idol,” was found guilty of murdering his wife in their Ohio home. A jury deliberated for around two hours on Tuesday and convicted him on all nine counts that he faced of of murder, assault and tampering with evidence. On the morning of Monday, Feb. 16, Ashley Flynn, […]
content:
Caleb Flynn, a former contestant on “American Idol,” was found guilty of murdering his wife in their Ohio home. A jury deliberated for around two hours on Tuesday and convicted him on all nine counts that he faced of of murder, assault and tampering with evidence.

On the morning of Monday, Feb. 16, Ashley Flynn, 37, was found dead in the couple’s Ohio home in Tipp City. Caleb, 40, called 911 around 2:30 a.m. and said that someone had broken into their home and shot Ashley, who was pronounced dead at the scene. According to local outlets, Caleb told police that he didn’t see anybody in the home, but his garage door was open. Police reportedly found a side door to the garage that was open and that there was fridge in front of the door that would’ve needed to be pushed to open it. Caleb was booked into the Miami County Jail on the following Thursday.

“While the defendant told law enforcement that he was sleeping, his electronic devices documented something different. They documented movement and activity in the hours leading up to Ashley’s murder,” said Matthew C. Joseph, assistant prosecuting attorney for the Miami County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office said in his closing argument. “The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving.”

Popular on Variety

The attorney added, “Being the victim allowed him to do that without being the husband who left his wife for a mistress. Instead, he’d be the husband whose wife was tragically murdered by an unknown intruder.”

Caleb was a contestant on “American Idol” in 2013. In 2013, he said in his “Road to Hollywood” interview on “American Idol” that he was a music pastor and that his wife encouraged him to audition for the singing competition show. “I absolutely love the lord and I love my wife more than anything,” he said in his interview. “She is very, very pretty. I love her. I’m just a normal person who absolutely loves to sing more than anything in the world.”

title: Ringo Starr, David Byrne, Joan Baez Donate Unqiue Items for Housing Works Auction
summary: Ringo Starr, David Byrne, Joan Baez, and more have donated items to be auction in Housing Works’ second annual Turn It Up! auction, which is open through Oct. 1. The National frontman Matt Berninger, Ani DiFranco, Richard Hell, Def Leppard’s Rick Allen, photographer Bob Gruen and others have donated items as well. Items include a […]
content:
Ringo Starr, David Byrne, Joan Baez, and more have donated items to be auction in Housing Works’ second annual Turn It Up! auction, which is open through Oct. 1.

The National frontman Matt Berninger, Ani DiFranco, Richard Hell, Def Leppard’s Rick Allen, photographer Bob Gruen and others have donated items as well.

Items include a T-shirt autographed by Starr, original artworks by Byrne and Baez, a signed drum head from Rick Allen, and a color print of Gruen’s iconic photo of John Lennon standing in front of the Statue of Liberty — see all the items and bid here.

Founded in 1990 by people living with HIV/AIDS and their allies, Housing Works emerged during the AIDS crisis in response to the urgent need for housing, healthcare, and support for people living with HIV/AIDS. Over the decades, the New York City nonprofit has expanded its work to address housing instability, homelessness, healthcare access, HIV/AIDS, and social justice.

Popular on Variety

Housing Works provides direct services including housing, healthcare, behavioral health care, and supportive services, while also advocating for policy changes affecting New Yorkers experiencing homelessness, poverty, healthcare barriers, and housing instability.

The organization’s work remains connected to New York City, where it operates programs and services while advocating for communities that have historically faced significant barriers to housing and healthcare.

Turn It Up! is open for bidding through October 1, 2026.

Of the Lennon photo, the entry reads: “The US government was trying to deport John Lennon because of his support for the peace movement during the Vietnam war so I suggested we take a picture at the Statue of Liberty to illustrate that America was supposed to welcome people. Since Lennon’s death, this photo has taken on a new meaning as people think of John Lennon in terms of personal freedom similar to the Statue of Liberty.”

Connect with Housing Works: Website

title: Curry Barker’s ‘Obsession’ Follow-Up ‘Anything But Ghosts’ Sets May 2027 Release Date From Focus Features, Blumhouse
summary: Focus Features and Blumhouse-Atomic Monster have slated Curry Barker’s upcoming horror-comedy “Anything But Ghosts” for release on May 7, 2027. Focus has worldwide rights for the film, while Universal Pictures International will handle international distribution. Barker directs “Anything But Ghosts” and co-wrote the script with his “Obsession” star and longtime collaborator Cooper Tomlinson. The pair […]
content:
Focus Features and Blumhouse-Atomic Monster have slated Curry Barker‘s upcoming horror-comedy “Anything But Ghosts” for release on May 7, 2027. Focus has worldwide rights for the film, while Universal Pictures International will handle international distribution.

Barker directs “Anything But Ghosts” and co-wrote the script with his “Obsession” star and longtime collaborator Cooper Tomlinson. The pair are also co-leads in the project, starring alongside Violet McGraw, Chris Reinacher, Bryce Dallas Howard and Aaron Paul.

The official logline for the film reads, “When a group of fame-seeking wannabe ‘ghosthunters’ find themselves in over their heads, things spiral wildly and terrifyingly out of control.”

Popular on Variety

Roy Lee, Steven Schneider, Jason Blum, Adam Hendricks and Greg Gilreath serve as producers. Executive producers include Daniel Bekerman, Barker, Tomlinson and Ben Ross. Blumhouse-Atomic Monster, Spooky Pictures, Divide/Conquer produce in association with Image Nation and That’s a Bad Idea.

Barker’s debut film “Obsession” was one of the biggest box office stories of the summer. The supernatural horror galvanized the Gen Z movie-going population and grossed $519 million worldwide against a budget of less than $1 million. It also achieved a 39% jump in earnings in its second weekend, a feat rarely seen in the current box office climate.

“Obsession” was also a critical smash, earning early Oscar buzz for Inde Navarrette, who co-starred in the project alongside Michael Johnston, Megan Lawless and Tomlinson. The film follows a hopelessly lonely young man named Bear (Johnston), who uses a mysterious toy called a “One Wish Willow” to make his crush, Nikki (Navarrette), fall for him. The wish, of course, goes terribly wrong, leading to bloody consequences for Bear, Nikki and their friends.

title: Prime ‘Big Deal Days’ 2026: What to Know About Amazon’s October Prime Day Sale
summary: Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days (a.k.a. “Fall Prime Day) is back for another season of savings, with 48 hours of Prime member-exclusive deals ahead of the holidays. This year’s Prime Big Deal Days run from October 6 to 7, with millions of deals across 35 categories, according to Amazon. Prime members will get first dibs […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Amazon‘s Prime Big Deal Days (a.k.a. “Fall Prime Day) is back for another season of savings, with 48 hours of Prime member-exclusive deals ahead of the holidays.

This year’s Prime Big Deal Days run from October 6 to 7, with millions of deals across 35 categories, according to Amazon. Prime members will get first dibs on the discounts, with fast, free shipping to have all the items delivered to their door.

Not a Prime member? Get a 30-day free trial here to shop Prime Big Deal Days and take advantage of all the other Amazon Prime member perks, like free TV shows and movies on Prime Video, free music streaming on Amazon Music and more.

Here’s what else you need to know about Amazon Prime Big Deal Days 2026.

Amazon Prime Big Deal Days 2026: Date, Time

As mentioned earlier, this year’s Amazon Prime Big Deal Days takes place over two days: October 6 and 7. The deals kick off on October 6 at 12:01 a.m. PT, though some early deals are already live on the site.

What Brands Are on Sale for Prime Big Deal Days 2026?

As always, the biggest discounts will be on Amazon devices, which now include everything from Fire TV Sticks and Fire TVs, to Ring cameras, Echo smart speakers, HD tablets, Kindle e-readers and more. Amazon’s Fire TV 4K Streaming Stick, for example, is already marked down by 64% off here.

Other brands on sale for Prime Big Deal Days include Barefoot Dreams, FAO Schwarz, NEST New York, Princess Polly, Shark, Soundcore by Anker and UGG, per Amazon. A quick search of the site also turns up deals on top-rated products from Bissell, Breville, Hisense, iRobot, KitchenAid, Samsung and TCL, among others.

Amazon says new deal drops will take place three times a day: at midnight (PT), 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. The deals will be labeled as “Today’s Big Deals,” and are all limited-time offers that will expire as soon as the items are sold out.

Do You Have to Be a Prime Member to Shop Amazon Big Deal Days?

Amazon has thousands of daily deals that are available to shop without needing a Prime membership, but the best discounts and offers will be reserved for Prime members. Make sure you’re logged into your Prime account before you start shopping as that is how you’ll see the cheapest or latest discounted price.

Prime members can also get items delivered in as fast as 30 minutes with regular delivery vehicles or through Prime Air drone delivery, which is currently available in select cities across Arizona, Florida, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas.

Millions of items are also available for free same-day or next-day delivery for Prime members in more than 10,000 cities and towns across the country.

Best Prime Membership Deals 2026: Get Free Trial

A Prime membership costs $14.99/month but you can test drive the service with a 30-day free trial here.

After that, your best bet is to sign up for an annual plan, which saves you 23% off versus paying month to month.

College students and young adults ages 18-24, meantime, can save 50% off an Amazon Prime membership. Plus, get 5% cashback on select items across beauty, fashion, electronics and other categories online.

This is the fourth annual Prime Big Deal Days event. Originally launched in 2022 as the “Prime Early Access Sale,” the name was changed in 2023 to “Prime Big Deal Days.” The event was created as a fall shopping event for Amazon and a counterpart to Prime Day in the summer.

title: Black Bear Names Dan Cohen as Head of Television Distribution, Launches Digital Networks Vertical
summary: Black Bear has named Paramount and Disney veteran Dan Cohen as its head of television distribution and will launch a digital networks vertical for the indie firm. Recruiting Cohen is a big to support Black Bear’s investment in a broad slate of independent films. The studio aims to release 10-12 titles per year, with upcoming […]
content:
Black Bear has named Paramount and Disney veteran Dan Cohen as its head of television distribution and will launch a digital networks vertical for the indie firm.

Recruiting Cohen is a big to support Black Bear’s investment in a broad slate of independent films. The studio aims to release 10-12 titles per year, with upcoming entries that include “Wicker,” “Wife and Dog,” “Jason Statham Stole My Bike,” “A Woman in the Sun,” “Jonah” and “Atmosphere.”

In the role, Cohen will oversee Black Bear’s post-theatrical licensing infrastructure. He previously served as Paramount’s chief content licensing officer and president of Republic Pictures.

Popular on Variety

He stepped down in July 2025 ahead of Paramount’s merger with David Ellison’s Skydance Media. Before joining Paramount, Cohen spent 20 years at Disney/ABC as Walt Disney Studios’ executive VP of Pay Television and Digital Sales for Home Entertainment and Television Distribution.

“Dan brings an exceptional combination of licensing expertise, industry relationships and strategic vision,” Black Bear CEO Teddy Schwarzman said. “His experience will be invaluable on multiple fronts, as we continue to invest in our U.S. distribution business, expanding our reach across the post-theatrical marketplace and as we open doors for other media entities to connect with audiences across the digital landscape.”

Cohen’s remit also includes the launch of Black Bear Digital Networks, a unit geared to help large independent content owners monetize their shows a la syndication across a range of channels. The network’s inaugural clients include Sinclair Networks, Tubi, CJ ENM and the National Wrestling Alliance.

“Black Bear has built an excellent brand over the past 15 years, with a strong track record of championing original stories that connect with both critics and audiences,” Cohen said. “I have immense confidence in what they’re building for the future. There’s a great opportunity to expand the ways Black Bear films reach audiences while also creating new avenues for third-party content owners through Black Bear Digital Networks. I look forward to helping grow both businesses and finding new ways to bring great content to audiences.”

title: Former ‘American Idol’ Contestant Caleb Flynn Found Guilty In Murder Of Wife Ashley
summary: An Ohio jury has returned multiple guilty verdicts against former American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn in the murder earlier this year of his wife Ashley Flynn. Caleb Flynn, a 40-year-old former worship pastor who competed in 2013 on American Idol, sobbed after nine guilty verdicts were read finding him guilty of aggravated murder, three counts […]
content:
An Ohio jury has returned multiple guilty verdicts against former American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn in the murder earlier this year of his wife Ashley Flynn.

Caleb Flynn, a 40-year-old former worship pastor who competed in 2013 on American Idol, sobbed after nine guilty verdicts were read finding him guilty of aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence.

The murder occurred in the Flynn’s home in Tipp City, Ohio, about 20 miles outside Dayton, in the early morning hours of February 16, 2026. The 37-year-old woman was fatally shot in the head as she slept in her bed.

Opening statements for the trial began on Friday, September 18, and closing arguments ended Tuesday, September 29. The Ohio jury deliberated for just two hours today following a week of trial testimony. During that week, Flynn’s mistress Alleigha Botner, 24, a worship leader at the same Tipp City church as Flynn, read from more than 100,000 text messages between herself and Flynn, some of which indicated Flynn’s murderous intentions.

Watch on Deadline

In one exchange, Flynn wrote, “I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail. If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat. That is how dark and how hateful I feel.”

The night before the murder, Flynn wrote to Botner, “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow, February 16, a day I’ll never forget.” Botner has not been charged with any wrongdoing.

After the murder, Flynn told police that his wife had been shot by an intruder. Police early on suspected that the crime scene had been staged to look like a burglary.

Ashley Flynn was fatally shot while the couple’s two daughters, then ages 9 and 11, were asleep in the next room.

Caleb Flynn’s appearance on American Idol is largely remembered for his emotional tributes to his wife. During his “Road To Hollywood” interview from 2013, Flynn said “music is all I know” and that he’d been encouraged to audition by Ashley. “I absolutely love the Lord, and I love my wife more than anything. She is very, very pretty. I love her. I’m just a normal person who absolutely loves to sing more than anything in the world.”

The synopsis reads: “Inspired by strange true events, a doula (Doan) arrives at an isolated mountain cabin to help with a difficult delivery, only to become trapped alongside her pregnant client (Arthur) in a sadistic, reality-bending game where escape may come at a terrible price.”

James J Yi (Gook) is producing alongside Alice Teufack, Judd Tilyard (Silent Night) and Verity Fiction.

Andrea Chung (The Card Counter) is executive-producing with Carvel Rock Pictures along with Kristine Estorninos. Nicole Arbusto is casting director.

Watch on Deadline
