title: Starz Warns It Might Go Dark On Verizon FiOS Amid Carriage Dispute
summary: Starz just issued a statement on the status of its negotiations with Verizon on a distribution agreement, warning of the potential loss of all of its channels, Starz on Demand and the Starz app through Verizon FiOs. “Starz has been negotiating in good faith with Verizon on a distribution agreement that would ensure our shared […]
content:
Starz just issued a statement on the status of its negotiations with Verizon on a distribution agreement, warning of the potential loss of all of its channels, Starz on Demand and the Starz app through Verizon FiOs.

“Starz has been negotiating in good faith with Verizon on a distribution agreement that would ensure our shared customers continue to have uninterrupted access to Starz’s premium programming,” said Alison Hoffman, President of Starz Networks. “As an independent programmer dedicated to women and underrepresented audiences, Starz is vital to a competitive media marketplace, providing diverse programming alternatives to content from larger conglomerates. Limiting access to Starz would reduce competition and consumer choice. Unless an agreement is reached imminently, our viewers should be prepared for Verizon to remove Starz.”

Starz ended 2025 with 17.6 million subscribers and is also no longer reporting subscriber numbers. Unlike other programmers carrying live sports or news, it has a streaming service that accounts for about three-quarters of its subscribers base. In prior carriage disputes, distributors have encouraged their customers to sign up for Starz on streaming platforms. That dynamic makes the current dispute less likely to rattle the broader industry than showdowns between the likes of YouTube TV or Charter and broad entertainment programmers like Disney.

Watch on Deadline

It’s worth noting that FiOS customers can sign up for Starz on streaming, which is not affected by the current dispute.

title: Ridley Scott’s ‘Treasure Island’, ‘24 Jump Street’ & Others Get 2027 Sony Release Dates
summary: At a time when the major exhibitors are in town for Cinema United’s Fall Summit, Sony made a slew of release date adds and changes Wednesday. Chief among them is that Ridley Scott’s feature take on Robert Louis Stevenson’s Treasure Island starring Hugh Jackman as Long John Silver is coming out on November 11, 2027. […]
content:
At a time when the major exhibitors are in town for Cinema United’s Fall Summit, Sony made a slew of release date adds and changes Wednesday. Chief among them is that Ridley Scott’s feature take on Robert Louis Stevenson’s Treasure Island starring Hugh Jackman as Long John Silver is coming out on November 11, 2027.

Also the reteam of Channing Tatum, Jonah Hill and Ice Cube for 24 Jump Street is driving into theaters on December 10, 2027.

Also added is Sony’s recent TIFF acquisition of Thunder Road’s Michelle Yeoh action movie The Surgeon on April 2 and the Mason Thames-Ella Bright drama Narcs on August 20.

Shifting release dates are Godzilla Minus One director Takashi Yamazaki’s Bad Robot production Grandgear, moves from February 18, 2028, to MLK weekend January 14, 2028.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office

The Justin Lin-directed Sony PlayStation production Helldivers starring Alan Ritchson is going from November 10, 2027, to June 9, 2028. That’s because Treasure Island is going into production first, hence that pic landing the Veterans Day date. Also, Helldivers is getting booked during the prime summer season.

The Surgeon comes from filmmaker Roshan Sethi and follows Yeoh as an expert surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient, only to turn 35 years of surgical expertise against her captors and outwit them in a fight for survival. The movie is produced by Basil Iwanyk, Erica Lee and Diarmaid McGrath of Thunder Road, Tango’s Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Tango’s Neil Shah, Steve Klinsky, Adam Kolbrenner of Lit Entertainment Group, John Schoenfelder and Russell Ackerman. There’s an untitled Disney and Universal feature on April 2 next year alongside Surgeon.

The John Phillips-directed Narcs is produced by Gene Stupnitsky via his Big Name Entertainment alongside Robert Lamonaca, who will executive produce. John Philips and Joseph Micucci are EPs. Also opening on Aug 20 next year is Paramount’s Get Lite from Teyana Taylor.

RELATED: The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office

Treasure Island also stars Hugh Grant and Owen Cooper. Jack Thorne adapted the new take on the classic that follows a young boy who uncovers the map to a legendary buried treasure. He embarks on a perilous sea voyage to claim a hidden fortune, only to find himself locked in a deadly battle of wits with the charismatic and treacherous pirate Long John Silver. Scott and Michael Pruss are producing via their Scott Free banner. The movie will open before Warner Bros’ Margie Claus and Paramount’s Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow.

24 Jump Street comes from filmmaker Rodney Rothman (Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse), who wrote the script with Hill and Meghan Malloy. Producers are Neal H. Moritz, Phil Lord, Chris Miller, Tatum and Hill. 24 Jump Street is the only title right now on December 10 next year.

Grandgear will go up against Paramount’s Longlegs sequel on January 14, 2028,as well as an untitled Universal movie and Amazon MGM Studio’s Alone at Dawn.

Helldivers will land on the same weekend as a united Universal event film and UA/Amazon MGM Studios/Amblin’s internet horror feature The Mandela Catalogue. PlayStation’s Helldivers received critical acclaim when the game first came out in 2015, and the sequel, Helldivers 2, sold more than 12 million units across PS5 and PC in the first four months after its launch in 2024. The game, and thus the feature, centers on an elite unit of soldiers known as Helldivers who must battle alien creatures threatening to destroy the fictional planet of Super Earth. Producers are Hutch Parker, PlayStation Productions’ Asad Qizilbash and Lin through his Perfect Storm Entertainment.

title: ‘House Of Guerrero’ Film From Gina Rodriguez Adds 7 To Cast
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The growing cast of Gina Rodriguez’s feature film directorial debut, The House of Guerrero, will now also include Lisa Vidal (Righteous Thieves, The Baker and the Beauty), Aaron Dominguez (Gossip Girl, Sitting in Bars With Cake), Jesse Garcia (The Odyssey, Flamin’ Hot), Edwin Hodge (Matlock, Tomorrow War), Emilio Rivera (Mayans M.C., On My Block), […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The growing cast of Gina Rodriguez’s feature film directorial debut, The House of Guerrero, will now also include Lisa Vidal (Righteous Thieves, The Baker and the Beauty), Aaron Dominguez (Gossip Girl, Sitting in Bars With Cake), Jesse Garcia (The Odyssey, Flamin’ Hot), Edwin Hodge (Matlock, Tomorrow War), Emilio Rivera (Mayans M.C., On My Block), Adam Rodriguez (Criminal Minds: Evolution, CSI: Miami), and Javon Walton (Euphoria, Utopia).

Production on House of Guerrero is underway in Los Angeles and California’s Imperial Valley. The previously announced cast is led by Carlos Sanson Jr., alongside Rosario Dawson, George Lopez, and Gina Rodriguez.

The original story by Gina Rodriguez and Bernardo Cubría follows Alex Guerrero (Sanson), whose promising boxing career is cut short before he gets one last shot at stepping back into the ring with his embattled ex-fighter father Alejandro (Lopez) in his corner. Struggling with the grief and loss of his mother, Elsa (Dawson), Alex turns to his older sister, Paloma (Rodriguez), a gifted boxer herself, to become his new trainer and help him rediscover the fighter he once was.

Watch on Deadline

The new cast and who they will play can be found below.

Vidal as Tia Lupe, Alex Guerrero’s aunt.

Dominguez as Perico, one of Alex’s friends in El Centro.

Garcia as Diego, Alex’s therapist.

Hodge as Malcolm, Manager of Club Crave.

Rivera as Tio Turi, Alex’s uncle and husband of Tia Lupe.

Adam Rodriguez as Ruben Chapa, a trainer at the local El Centro boxing gym.

Walton as Alex in his earlier years.

House of Guerrero is produced by Scott Budnick and Ameet Shukla from 1Community, Gina Rodriguez’s I Can And I Will Productions with Molly Breeskin, and Justin Baldoni and Calof from Wayfarer. Steve Sarowitz and Jamey Heath are executive producing for Wayfarer, with Sherrese Clarke and Niija Kuykendall from HarbourView Media Group, alongside Clare LoCicero and Alice S. Kim.

Wayfarer Studios, 1Community, HarbourView Media Group and LoCicero are co-financing the feature with tax credit financing provided by Three Point Capital. UTA Independent Film Group is representing the film for worldwide sales. Casting is by Mary Vernieu and Lindsay Graham Ahanonu. Cast deals were negotiated by Eric W. Thompson.

Vidal is repped by Pearl Wexler. Dominguez is repped by Paradigm, Canopy Media Partners and Goodman Genow Schenkman. Garcia is repped by Mosaic, Independent Artist Group, Vox, and Sloane, Offer, Weber and Dern. Hodge is repped by Vault. Rivera is repped by Amsel, Eisenstadt, Frazier & Hinojosa Inc. Adam Rodriguez is repped by A Management and Global Artists Agency. Walton is repped by Paradigm and Brillstein Entertainment Partners.

title: Ted Cruz Blocks Senators’ Effort To Pass No Fakes Act
summary: The No Fakes Act, a bill to bill to curb the use of unauthorized AI deepfakes, was blocked in the Senate on Wednesday by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who said that the legislation did not have sufficient exceptions for the use of a person’s image in satirical and political commentary. The legislation gives individuals the […]
content:
The No Fakes Act, a bill to bill to curb the use of unauthorized AI deepfakes, was blocked in the Senate on Wednesday by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who said that the legislation did not have sufficient exceptions for the use of a person’s image in satirical and political commentary.

The legislation gives individuals the right to authorize the use of their voice and likeness in digital replication. The bill includes exclusions for news, documentary and sports, as well as biographical works, or for purposes of comment, criticism, or parody, among others.

The key sponsors sought to pass the bill before the Senate leaves for the midterms, but Cruz objected, sidelining the legislation for now.

“One of my concerns about how this bill is drafted right now is it will apply to websites like the Babylon Bee or The Onion, and it leaves the decision as to whether someone’s use of a likeness falls within the exception,” Cruz said. “It creates an exception for what it calls bonafide parody, but it leaves to big tech to make the decision whether it falls in that exception or not.”

Watch on Deadline

He also raised concerns over whether the bill would apply to such things as Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt’s featuring of an AI deepfake of Karen Bass, made to look like The Joker from Batman, as well as Donald Trump’s use of AI images in political communication.

Cruz said that he wanted the bill to pass, but said that his staff should work with its sponsors over the coming weeks on strengthening free speech protections.

The bill has had broad support among many entertainment industry guilds and unions, studios and record labels, as well as tech companies OpenAI and Google/YouTube.

“This bill contains the necessary broad exceptions for entire categories of speech,” said Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), a key sponsor.

She said that the protections that Cruz wanted to see in the bill “are there.”

She said that they have tried to work with Cruz’s staff on new language. She said that it will be the courts that will be left to decisions about the First Amendment, not the tech platforms.

“We have worked with First Amendment legal experts in drafting the bill, and we are confident that it is First Amendment compliant,” she said. “We have even doubled down on this language.”

She added that under the provisions, “If someone believes their content that was removed from this bill was protected speech, they can submit a counter notice triggering judicial review within 14 days if the victim wants the material to stay down. Otherwise, the content can go right back up.”

Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), another key co-sponsor, said “We should not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.”

The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and while Cruz voted for it then, he did raise issues about whether it applied to political satire and said that he wanted them to be addressed before the legislation reached the floor.

title: Venice Golden Lion Winner Milcho Manchevski’s ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’ Heads to Tokyo for World Premiere, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” the new feature from Venice Golden Lion winner Milcho Manchevski, will world premiere in the Tokyo International Film Festival’s main competition. Variety is debuting the trailer. Francesca Breccia’s Coccinelle Film Sales is handling the film and will start selling it to international buyers during Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market. Manchevski […]
content:
“Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” the new feature from Venice Golden Lion winner Milcho Manchevski, will world premiere in the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s main competition.

Variety is debuting the trailer.

Francesca Breccia’s Coccinelle Film Sales is handling the film and will start selling it to international buyers during Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market.

Manchevski wrote and directed the dark comedy, which centers on Malina and Viktor, a sister and brother getting by hand to mouth at the edges of Macedonian society. To keep going, the pair pilfer bronze busts and manhole covers, and they do it with plenty of attitude. Their chaotic path eventually brings them to a wealthy elderly woman who is blind. Her mix of hardness and kindness pushes them to examine their own sense of right and wrong, and what it means to be devoted to someone.

Popular on Variety

“Our anti-heroes defiantly refuse to identify as victims,” Manchevski said.

Sara Klimoska and Filip Trajkovikj lead the cast, with Sonja Mihajlova also on board. Jane Kortoshev is the producer.

“I was interested in telling a story of great love and unconditional acceptance that is not erotic,” Manchevski said.

The filmmaker first drew international attention with “Before the Rain,” which took the Golden Lion at Venice along with the Fipresci Prize and went on to earn an Academy Award nomination for best foreign-language film. His later features include “Dust,” the opening-night film at Venice, as well as “Mothers” and “Willow.”

The new film brings Manchevski back to Tokyo. His last feature, “Kaymak,” also bowed in the festival’s competition as a world premiere.

title: Indonesian Director Ariani Darmawan Ends 15-Year Hiatus With ‘Jani Be Good,’ Debuts Trailer Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Indonesian director Ariani Darmawan is ending a 15-year absence from filmmaking with her debut feature, “Jani Be Good,” which will world premiere in the Asian Future competition at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival. Variety is debuting the film’s first trailer. The drama is titled “Desember Jani” in Indonesian and produced by Jakarta outfit Palari […]
content:
Indonesian director Ariani Darmawan is ending a 15-year absence from filmmaking with her debut feature, “Jani Be Good,” which will world premiere in the Asian Future competition at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival.

Variety is debuting the film’s first trailer.

The drama is titled “Desember Jani” in Indonesian and produced by Jakarta outfit Palari Films.

The story takes place over four days in December and tracks four women spanning three generations. At its center is 13-year-old Jani, the youngest in the household. She slowly comes to grasp the different parts the women around her play, while working out how to speak for herself.

Popular on Variety

Chempa Puteri plays Jani, with Sigi Wimala as Winnie, Hyori Mika as Julia and Tutie Kirana as the grandmother, Oma.

Darmawan wanted Cyntha Hariadi to write the screenplay from the outset, having read the writer’s short story collection “Manifesto Flora.” “Jani Be Good” is Hariadi’s first feature script.

“When I started thinking about this film, I was imagining the small things that happen inside a home: the conversations, the tension, and the feelings that often go unspoken. We then developed this story together over three years. Becoming a mother also changed the way I see the relationship between children and parents. From there, Jani grew into my way of looking at these four women characters from different generations, all still learning to understand one another,” said Darmawan.

The women on the film’s core creative team also span several generations.

Darmawan was a prominent figure in Indonesian short filmmaking through the late 2000s and early 2010s, and her 2008 short “Sugiharti Halim” was selected for competition at the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival.

“When I invited Ariani to make a film again three years ago, our conversation didn’t start with genre or what kind of film she wanted to make. I asked her what the most extraordinary experience in her life had been while she wasn’t making films. Her answer was becoming a mother. ‘Jani Be Good’ began from that simple conversation. For us at Palari Films, this film isn’t just about a filmmaker’s return after 15 years. It’s about giving space for the voices and experiences of women from different generations to meet in one film,” said producer Meiske Taurisia of Palari Films.

The project was presented at the Hong Kong Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF) in March this year, ahead of its Tokyo selection. After the festival, “Jani Be Good” will open in Indonesian cinemas on Dec. 10.

Palari Films, founded in 2016, is led by Taurisia and Muhammad Zaidy. The banner’s “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash” won the Golden Leopard at the 74th Locarno Film Festival. Its other credits include “Aruna and Her Palate,” “Posesif,” “Ali & Ratu Ratu Queens,” “Dear David,” the Netflix original “Borderless Fog” and this year’s “Sleep No More.”

title: Florence Pugh and Hoon Lee Form the Beating Heart of Netflix’s Rich ‘East of Eden’ Adaptation: TV Review
summary: “East of Eden,” the John Steinbeck novel, opens with a place: the author’s native Salinas Valley, the fertile terrain transitioning from the nation’s frontier to its bread basket at the turn of the 20th century. “East of Eden,” the Netflix limited series created by actor and screenwriter Zoe Kazan, opens with a person: Cathy Ames […]
content:
“East of Eden,” the John Steinbeck novel, opens with a place: the author’s native Salinas Valley, the fertile terrain transitioning from the nation’s frontier to its bread basket at the turn of the 20th century. “East of Eden,” the Netflix limited series created by actor and screenwriter Zoe Kazan, opens with a person: Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), the Eve and Satanic temptress of Steinbeck’s explicit Biblical allegory. “I believe there are monsters born to human parents,” Cathy intones — transplanting Steinbeck’s introduction of his most iconic villain into the mouth of the woman it describes.

This rearrangement doubles as a statement of purpose. Kazan’s adaptation of the literary classic, overseen in partnership with co-showrunner Jeb Stuart (writer of “Die Hard” and “The Fugitive”), is faithful — arguably even more so than the 1955 film directed by her grandfather Elia, previously the book’s best-known screen version. (The feature zeroes in on the final phase of a multigenerational epic, while this series takes on the whole thing.) But emphases and points of view are rearranged to elevate two characters in particular: Cathy, as indicated by the show’s marketing and advance press, and Lee (Hoon Lee), the Chinese American cook whose added dimensions emerge more gradually. These dual portraits aren’t consistently or equally successful, but combined with a lush production and a stellar cast, they’re a case for bringing Steinbeck’s enduring tale of free will, original sin and cyclical tragedy into the 21st century.

Popular on Variety

Pugh was an Oscar nominee by her late 20s for her performance in another high-profile adaptation, Greta Gerwig’s “Little Women.” She’s nonetheless spent the last few years without a role quite deserving of her talents. (Getting beamed up into the Marvel machine will do that to a young actor.) Though largely a film star, Pugh had previously done some of her finest work on television, in Korean auteur Park Chan-Wook’s 2018 take on John Le Carré’s “The Little Drummer Girl.” Watching “East of Eden,” which Pugh also executive produced, it’s apparent what called her back to the small screen: In Cathy, she gets a character who’s constantly calculating as her position shifts over decades, from vulnerable girl to reluctant wife to skilled prostitute to grizzled madam. And making hidden depths legible on the surface is some of what Pugh does best.

A teenage Cathy arrives, beaten and bloody, on the Connecticut doorstep of half-brothers Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles Trask (Mike Faist), whose own psychodrama is already well under way. Pit against one another by their father Cyrus (Tracy Letts), a Civil War veteran obsessed with molding his sons into a soldier (Adam) and a farmer (Charles) despite either boy’s natural instincts, the Trasks are already in possession of the emotional inheritance they’ll soon pass on to the next generation. But we see them first through Cathy’s eyes, which burn with an animal intelligence even through a mosaic of bruises and scabs. Adam, simple and trusting, is an easy mark for a desperate woman looking for a life raft. Charles, canny and discerning, is a threat — and maybe a kindred spirit.

Pugh is fantastic in these early episodes, which establish Cathy as a kind of psychopath in the clinical sense — a creature of instinct who sees any threat to her agency, from parental discipline to full-blown abuse, as a lethal attack to be repaid with interest. Watching her operate is akin to Scarlett Johansson’s performance as a man-eating alien in the 2013 film “Under the Skin”: Cathy operates less out of malice than an innate, unchangeable essence. When she likens her marriage to something that “can be slipped out of, like a poorly made knot,” we understand how inimical she is to any kind of constraint, legal or otherwise. That her means of exit is abandoning her newborn twins is less than sympathetic, but in a different era Cathy would have options beyond a domesticity that never suited her in the first place.

As the series continues, however, Kazan plays up the explanatory power of an incident from Cathy’s childhood. If Steinbeck believes monsters are born, Kazan seems to be of the school that they’re made. The origin story helps contextualize the misery and self-isolation of Cathy’s later years, as the madam of a Salinas whorehouse. But it also abates the singular ferocity of her early characterization, and concedes to the viewer’s need to find humanity in her. You don’t need to like, or even find a neat cause-and-effect, for Cathy to marvel at her claiming agency at any cost.

Kazan has said she originally intended for “East of Eden” to run for eight episodes, and there’s some palpable compression in the seven ultimately produced. (Another cost-cutting measure moved the production to New Zealand. While it’s sad to miss out on authentic California landscapes in a story so rooted in geography, cinematographer Stuart Dryburgh gets some stunning, sun-dappled vistas out of the islands’ rolling hills.) “Challengers” star Faist is a surprisingly minimal presence once newlyweds Adam and Cathy set out for Northern California; even before, we don’t get to know Charles well enough for his theory that “kind recognizes kind” in Cathy to resonate. Nor do we get much time with the teenage versions of the couple’s sons Cal (Joseph Zada) and Aaron (Joe Anders) to deepen them beyond vessels for their ancestors’ baggage.

But it’s also clear what Kazan wanted to make space for. Cathy’s ingratiation with, and eventual usurpation of, brothel owner Faye (Martha Plimpton) gets an entire episode. So does an extended interlude with Lee co-written by novelist Alexander Chee, the only installment on which Kazan does not have sole script credit. As in the novel, Lee is an educated and empathetic soul who observes society from its margins. Born in America to railroad workers, Lee speaks in a thickly accented pidgin around racist strangers who expect it of him. Behind closed doors, though, he debates philosophy with neighbor Samuel Hamilton (Ciarán Hinds, so warm you wouldn’t know his role is downsized from the text) and studies the Bible. This pursuit makes Lee the voice of the story’s central theme: timshel, a Hebrew word from the legend of Cain and Abel (or Charles and Adam, or Caleb and Aaron) that translates to “thou mayest” — not “thou shalt,” emphasizing individual choice over unalterable fate.

In keeping with the concept, this Lee gets more of his own arc, driven by his own decisions and developed enough to rival his employers for the center of the show. There are more details about his parents, a sojourn into San Francisco’s bustling Chinatown and an assertion of autonomy within the Trask household, of which Lee is an essential part. The gender dynamics of Adam and Lee’s arrangement in the season’s latter half are fascinating: as cook, gardener, bookkeeper and active parent, Lee is functionally the twins’ surrogate mother, a fact “East of Eden” never states outright but instead subtly insists on. Hoon Lee is not as famous as Pugh, nor does his character burn as brightly as Cathy’s hatred for societal norms. Yet his calm, quietly wounded demeanor is just as essential to the show, and the way Lee grows more complex over time offsets the way Cathy is somewhat simplified.

Were “East of Eden” merely a sumptuous period piece, it would still be event viewing, the kind of somber-toned release that announces the onset of Fall TV. Directors Garth Davis (“Lion”) and Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre (“The Mustang”) join a crew of artisans, including production designer Grant Major, costume designer Kirsty Cameron and score composer Laura Karpman, in conjuring a moment in time as specific as the Genesis story is universal. By the episodes’ end, I wasn’t totally convinced a narrative so dependent on the passage of time was an organic fit for the screen. (Pugh gets aged up with cosmetics, but Abbott looks as boyish as ever while Adam attempts to act as patriarch.) Still, the endeavor feels worth it for Pugh and Lee’s standout efforts, which etch their characters deep into one’s memory. Even great books can acquire dust on the shelf; an infusion of feeling helps keep them alive.

All seven episodes of “East of Eden” are now streaming on Netflix.

title: Garin Nugroho, Mishima Yukiko, Qiu Jiongjiong Titles Among 15 in Tokyo Film Festival Competition
summary: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival has unveiled its complete program, led by a 15-film main competition featuring work by Indonesian director Garin Nugroho, Japanese filmmaker Mishima Yukiko and Hong Kong-based Qiu Jiongjiong. The competition spans world and Asian premieres. Seven titles receive world premieres: “The Canary’s Lullaby,” a Taiwan-Japan co-production directed by Ikeda Akira; […]
content:
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival has unveiled its complete program, led by a 15-film main competition featuring work by Indonesian director Garin Nugroho, Japanese filmmaker Mishima Yukiko and Hong Kong-based Qiu Jiongjiong.

The competition spans world and Asian premieres. Seven titles receive world premieres: “The Canary’s Lullaby,” a Taiwan-Japan co-production directed by Ikeda Akira; Qiu Jiongjiong’s “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” produced across Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar; Yamamoto Akira’s Japanese drama “The Intertwining”; Wang Jiangyong’s France-Hong Kong co-production “The Night That Binds Us”; Nugroho’s “Red Before Dawn” from Indonesia; Milcho Manchevski’s North Macedonia-led ensemble “Sister Brother Manhole Cover”; and Mishima Yukiko’s “Two Cigarettes, Three Nights” from Japan.

The remaining eight competition titles arrive as Asian premieres. Lisandro Alonso’s Chile-Argentina co-production “Double Freedom” will screen alongside Teodora Ana Mihai’s Belgian soccer-disaster drama “Heysel 85,” Rubaiyat Hossain’s France-Bangladesh co-production “The Difficult Bride,” Samuele Rossi’s Italian film “Even If Hell Came,” Sun Xun’s Singapore title “Magic Atlas,” Sérgio Graciano’s Portuguese drama “Memories of Prison,” Iranian-Turkish director Bahman Ghobadi’s Turkey-set “Trees Are Watching” and Jelena Maksimović’s Serbian co-production “Until the Day Ends.”

Popular on Variety

The Asian Future competitive section will present 10 titles, eight of which receive world premieres. They include Navid Mohammadzadeh’s Iranian film “I’m Nothing Special Really”; Ariani Darmawan’s Indonesian title “Jani Be Good”; Cai Ronglin’s “Miracle Summer” from Japan; South Korean film “On the Heights” by Kim Hyun-min; Tamil Nadu filmmaker Chezhiyan’s Indian entry “The Paper Flower”; Kujiraoka Hironori’s Japanese film “Saravah”; Azamat Shargyn’s Kazakh film “Shyrmauyq”; and Soheil Karimi’s Iranian drama “Silver.” Katski Flores’s Filipino title “EDJOP” and Tareq Daoud’s Switzerland-Turkey co-production “Serife Tavsan” will receive international premieres.

As previously announced, the Gala selection features Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” as the opening film, while Yeon Sang-ho’s “Colony” from South Korea takes the closing slot in a Japanese premiere. Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” serves as the centerpiece. Other Gala titles include Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” Wayne Wang’s “Diary of a Mad Old Man,” Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s “The Beloved” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.”

The Nippon Cinema Now section will spotlight nine Japanese films. World premieres include Matsumura Shingo’s “Between Us,” Matsubayashi Yoju’s “Okinawa Saudade,” Saito Kisin’s “Kefi,” Ueda Shinichiro’s “Earthlings in Love,” Inudo Isshin’s “Yamazaki Riverside -Over an Actor’s Shoulder-” and “Plastic Love!,” co-directed by Sybilla Patrizia and Clementine Nuttall.

The World Focus section features titles by Valeska Grisebach, Lav Diaz, Angela Schanelec and Indonesian director Edwin, plus a Taiwan Cinema Renaissance 2026 strand, an Australia Spotlight, a Youssef Chahine centenary retrospective and a tribute program for German filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger.

The Classics section will present 4K digitally remastered versions of Naruse Mikio’s “When a Woman Ascends the Stairs” and “Scattered Clouds,” alongside a Nikkatsu Roman Porno 55th anniversary retrospective and a TIFF/National Film Archive of Japan retrospective of Mizoguchi Kenji’s work. Additional sections include Women’s Empowerment, Animation — which features a “Women Directors: Diverse Visions” strand — Crosscut Asia+ and Youth.

Programming director Ichiyama Shozo leads the selection alongside senior programmer Ishizaka Kenji, who oversees Asian Future.

The festival will run Oct. 26–Nov. 4 in Tokyo.

title: Anne Hathaway Would Rather Have Another Knicks Championship Over a Second Oscar
summary: When it comes to the New York Knicks, Anne Hathaway is their good luck charm. Let’s revisit: On April 20, the Knicks lost Game 2 of their NBA Playoffs series to the Atlanta Hawks. On May 1, Hathaway’s “The Devil Wears Prada 2” premiered and featured a scene where Hathaway’s character chats up Knicks star […]
content:
When it comes to the New York Knicks, Anne Hathaway is their good luck charm.

Let’s revisit: On April 20, the Knicks lost Game 2 of their NBA Playoffs series to the Atlanta Hawks. On May 1, Hathaway’s “The Devil Wears Prada 2” premiered and featured a scene where Hathaway’s character chats up Knicks star Karl-Anthony Towns at a Hamptons soiree. The Knicks subsequently went on a historic 13-game winning streak and did not lose again until Game 3 of the NBA Finals on June 9 (Trump attended). Hathaway, a New York City native and lifelong Knicks fan, was jokingly credited for their change in fortune by yours truly and a host of others.

And so, on Wednesday night, Hathaway visited “The Tonight Show” to promote her new erotic thriller “Verity” and host Jimmy Fallon brought up the Knicks meme before gifting “The Odyssey” star, who is five months pregnant, a signed jersey from Knicks savior OG Anunoby. (Hathaway professed her Anunoby fandom after he nearly crashed into her and her son while going into the stands for a ball during a Nov. 2024 game.)

Popular on Variety

“Are you serious? Oh my god!” exclaimed Hathaway, before putting the jersey on. The Knicks also sent Hathway a basket of gifts for her baby, replete with a card reading “All my best” signed by Anunoby. “I’m so excited about my jersey,” she said, playing with it instead of answering Fallon’s questions.

Later on in the show, Fallon tortured the pregnant Hathaway with a sadistic game called “Best Thing Ever,” forcing her to choose between two cherished things. At one point, he asked her to choose whether she’d rather win another Oscar — she’s a Best Supporting Actress frontrunner for her fiery turn in “The Odyssey” — or have the Knicks win another championship.

“I… I… OK….,” stumbled Hathaway, before choosing another Knicks title.

“I’m actually, like, the way my nervous system is reacting to that choice is really intense,” she explained.

title: Tokyo Film Festival Unveils Competition Line-up With World Premieres From Garin Nugroho, Milcho Manchevski & Qiu Jiongjiong
summary: Tokyo International Film Festival has announced its full line-up including the 15 features selected for its Competition section, seven of which are world premieres. Indonesian filmmaker Garin Nugroho’s historical drama Red Before Dawn will be receiving its world premiere at the festival, along with Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski’s Sister Brother Manhole Cover, and two Chinese […]
content:
Tokyo International Film Festival has announced its full line-up including the 15 features selected for its Competition section, seven of which are world premieres.

Indonesian filmmaker Garin Nugroho’s historical drama Red Before Dawn will be receiving its world premiere at the festival, along with Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski’s Sister Brother Manhole Cover, and two Chinese films – Wang Jiangyong’s The Night That Binds Us and Qiu Jiongjiong’s Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting.

Three Japanese features will also be world premiering at the festival – Akira Ikeda’s Taiwan-Japan co-production The Canary’s Lullaby, Akira Yamamoto’s The Intertwining and Yukiko Mishima’s Two Cigarettes, Three Nights.

The Asian Future competition for rising talents has selected ten titles, including Jani Be Good, directed by Indonesia’s Ariani Darmawan in her feature debut; Filipino filmmaker Katski Flores’s EDJOP, starring Elijah Canlas as the eponymous political activist; and two features from Iran – Soheil Karimi’s Silver and Navid Mohammadzadeh’s I’m Nothing Special Really (see full line-up for Competition & Asian Future below).

Watch on Deadline

As previously announced, the festival will open with Zeze Takahisa’s Sukiyaki and close with Yeon Sang-ho’s Colony, while Godzilla Minus Zero has been set as the Centerpiece film. The festival has also reintroduced its Crosscut Asia section, dedicated to Southeast Asian cinema, which will screen titles including Filipiñana, Four Seasons In Java and Becoming Human.

The Gala Selection will screen 14 titles, including Christian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord, Yukiko Sode’s Cannes Un Certain Regard title All The Lovers In The Night, Martin McDonagh’s Oscars-tipped Wild Horse Nine, Sabu’s Arrested Memory and Wayne Wang’s Diary Of A Mad Old Man.

Other major sections at the festival include Nippon Cinema Now, which has introduced two new awards this year, World Focus, Animation, Women’s Empowerment, Special Screenings, Japanese Classics, Youth and the Asian Students’ Film Conference.

Guests at the festival will include Cate Blanchett, in town to support the Japan premieres of five short films supported by the Displacement Film Fund (DFF); Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof and Japanese-Korean filmmaker Mipo O, who are both receiving the Kurosawa Akira Award; and Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer, who is heading the main competition jury.

Tokyo International Film Festival is taking place October 26-November 4, while the TIFFCOM contents market is scheduled for October 28-30.
