title: Ted Sarandos Has No Regrets Over WB Pursuit, Talks Netflix’s Engagement Growth Challenges, Overall Deals & Casey Bloys
summary: Appearing at Bloomberg’s Screentime hours after Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery overcame the last hurdle when a federal judge approved the settlement with the state attorneys general, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was asked whether he regretted going after Warner Bros. given the scrutiny from Wall Street the streamer has been put under since then. […]
content:
Appearing at Bloomberg’s Screentime hours after Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery overcame the last hurdle when a federal judge approved the settlement with the state attorneys general, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was asked whether he regretted going after Warner Bros. given the scrutiny from Wall Street the streamer has been put under since then.

“No, I think it was the plan was solid,” he said. “I think we won the deal at some point, so we priced it right at our scale. That was the top price point where I thought we could return value to our shareholders with that asset. Any more than that, I thought we’d be taking it into negative territory, even with our scale.”

Netflix, which always positioned itself as “a builder, not a buyer,” surprised many when it entered — and won — the bidding for Warner Bros., until the film and TV studio’s parent Warner Bros. Discovery accepted a higher offer from Paramount for the whole company.

Watch on Deadline

“When I look at that, I think the deal itself kind of threw the business narrative off, for investors, for the press, for other folks, and you have to be willing to put the business narrative at risk for something that’s good for the long term return.”

That business narrative includes questions over Netflix’s slowing growth of engagement — the time subscribers spend on the platform.

Sarandos argued that the issue was somewhat self-inflicted, stemming from Netflix’s decision almost two years ago to stop reporting subscriber growth and instead focus on engagement, publishing viewership reports twice a year (soon to be once a year).

“At the time we said that, I think we were pretty unsophisticated about how we talked about engagement. Meaning, in that world, all the revenue is equal, a profit is equal, all engagement is equal, and all engagement is not equal,” Sarandos said. “We are growing engagement, on 200 billion hours of watching, we grew 2% in our last announcement.”

While Sarandos pointed to mitigating factors — Netflix faced “incredible headwinds from things like the World Cup” during the reporting period — he admitted that “yes, overall we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster.”

One of the ways to do that is expand live programming, Sarandos said.

“When we do live programming on Netflix, which is a relatively new thing, we spend about 5% of our content budget on live events, they generate about 1% of our watching,” he said. Such programming “doesn’t necessarily bring more gross engagement, but it brings very valuable engagement. It’s not a mystery that all engagement is not equal because you probably are not surprised to know that an hour of Judge Judy in the middle of the day does not generate as much revenue as an hour of NFL football.”

Sarandos added that this past quarter, Netflix had “double-digit revenue growth in every in every region of the world, so the business is great and growing fine.”

Assessing HBO Max/Paramount+ Combo, Casey Bloys Rumors

Sarandos was cryptic when asked to assess the competition threat level of a combined HBO Max/Paramount+ streamer following the Paramount-WB acquisition.

“On paper so far, it’s one and one, so I don’t know if one and one is two, or one and one is one and a half, or one and one is three,” he said.

The merged platform will be run by Casey Bloys, Chairman and CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content.

“He’s a good guy, for some reason we had a very well publicized lunch; I mean, we have eaten together many times,” Sarandos said about the duo’s headline-making meal in March, just days after Netflix lost Warner Bros. to Paramount, triggering speculation that Bloys could defect for a job or a deal at the streamer.

Asked whether such overture happened, Sarandos simply said about Bloys, “He’s going to be in a very good position wherever he goes, he’s a super talented guy.”

Overall Deal Paradigm

There have been several high-profile talent departures from Netflix over the past year: Stranger Things creators/executive producers the Duffer Brothers, who signed a big film and TV overall deal at Paramount; the show’s director/executive producer Shawn Levy, who recently inked an overall deal at Disney’s 20th Television; filmmaker Noah Baumbach, who closed a first-look film deal at Warner Bros.; and David Fincher. The Duffers, Levy and Fincher had been under overall deals at Netflix for more than a decade.

Sarandos chalked up the exits to individual circumstances not a change in Netflix’s stance on talent. (On the flip side, Netflix in June signed an overall deal with Ryan Coogler, who had been at Disney, and recently re-upped its rich overall pact with Shonda Rhimes.)

“These deals all serve completely different purposes,” he said. “Sometimes, it’s a simple way to organize a lot of work that you’re going to do together for 10 years, and the overall deal is a good way to to package it and present it. There’s other ones, which is [that] a filmmaker, a television creator has a very specific thing that they want to do, it’s going to take them many years to develop, and the overall deal is a way to do business together.”

Sarandos went on to provide context on several departures.

Duffer Brothers:

“The Duffers have worked with us for the past decade, and they had a dream that they did not want to make more TV shows right now, they really want to make big tentpole theatrical movies. And I said to them, I told told Matt and Ross, ‘You guys are great at what you do, and I think you should go do that. You’re 40, don’t wake up when you’re 60 wishing you did that 20 years later.’ I’m thrilled for them. They’re going to have great success, and they have great success. And the Stranger Things universe, they are going to continue to be a part of forever, and that’s fantastic.”

Shawn Levy:

“Shawn also was with them, and kind of doing the same thing. The problem when you have an overall deal with someone who has commitments in other places is, you’re in constant conflict for their time. Shawn is going to be making Star Wars movies for a while, so the fact that his [TV] deal is with Disney makes a lot of sense. I’m thrilled for Shawn. We’re going to do a ton of things together, we still have shows in development together. We have a show called The Sticks coming up.”

David Fincher:

“We’ve been in business with David Fincher since 2011, he has not done a movie outside of Netflix since 2014. He doesn’t know what he’s going to do next. He’s a great guy. I love the the three films we’ve done. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is phenomenal. I’m super proud of Mindhunter, 17 Emmy wins for Love Death + Robots, House of Cards, of course. He’s one of the greatest living directors, and we plan on being in business together for a very long time. It is not like he’s leaving to go somewhere else to do something else.”

title: Ben Affleck Doesn’t “Worry About SkyNet” When It Comes To AI;  “It’s Another Form Of Computing”
summary: Donald Trump could have done a lot worse than inviting Ben Affleck to his AI lunch with tech CEOs this week at the White House. Unlike the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and more, the Oscar winner and InterPositive founder isn’t playing defense or doom and gloom when it comes to the quickly evolving technology […]
content:
Donald Trump could have done a lot worse than inviting Ben Affleck to his AI lunch with tech CEOs this week at the White House.

Unlike the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and more, the Oscar winner and InterPositive founder isn’t playing defense or doom and gloom when it comes to the quickly evolving technology – at least not in relation to Hollywood. Also, unlike the techlords, Affleck seems to have some perspective.

“When I worry about AI, I worry about like my kids in school,” Affleck told Bloomberg Screentime event this evening on AI and the entertainment business. ” worry about 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use.”

“I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over this business in any meaningful way,” he insisted with a reference to the once again much mentioned humanity killing tech from the Terminator franchise. “I feel this is one of the least likely domains to be disintermediated by AI.”

Watch on Deadline

In a wide ranging conversation Wednesday about his upcoming Netflix flick Animals (“t’s a kidnapping movie”), his years of under the radar serial entrepreneurship, various panicked calls to buddy Matt Damon over the decades, moviemaking, and lessons learned from 1998’s Armageddon, Affleck kept coming back to the fears, future and falsehoods around AI.

In that, the filmmaker got down to the brass binary tacks of the tech.

“What I find is that filmmakers and people, once they sit with it and have a sense of control and a sense of understanding what’s happening, and it moves from this nebulous, abstract, terrifying alien …it’s going to kill us all like we’re paperclips …all this propaganda, they actually see what it is,” he told the industry crowd on the last panel of the day. “It’s another form of computing that does tools, and is a technological advancement that’s really in keeping with the long-standing series of technological improvements we’ve made in the film and television business.”

After over three decades in the business, Affleck made a different sort of news earlier this year when it was revealed in the spring Netflix bought his AI firm for the very non-artificial price of what was later confirmed as $587 million. The joint, which makes AI tools developed by and intended for filmmakers from essentially open source beginnings, saw its staff of less than 20 absorbed into the streamer and Affleck on board as an advisor.

Almost as good an Ambassador for AI as he is for Dunkin Donuts, Affleck added of the tech: “Like a lot of technologies it requires sort of getting comfortable and getting familiar with, and then immediately it’s knowable. You see all the ways in which it doesn’t work, all the failures, the sort of dumb nature of it in a lot of ways, and and it becomes a knowable thing.”

In terms of knowable things, Affleck’s Artist Equity is also taking a swing at realining the economics of the industry to met the realities of changing tech and viewing habits, and keep people employed with reasonable return. Formed in 2022 with BFF Damon and the seemingly everywhere Gerry Cardinale of Redbird Capitol, AE aims to widen the scope of traditional profit participation from a bonus program to a business model.

“What I’m in the process of trying to do, is institute this as on an ongoing basis, so that people are both united,” Affleck said of the company and the notion. “We all give a shit that we do something really good. We’re going to pitch in a little bit together, and we care about this shared vision. And in success, it’s going to rain money on everyone’s head.”

Way better than SkyNet any day.

title: Universal Studios Execs Promise New Sound Barrier To Reduce Rollercoaster Noise; Angry Residents At Community Meeting Demand Fast Fix
summary: At least 350 people on Wednesday attended a meeting to address the screams coming from Universal Studio’s new Fast & Furious rollercoaster that opened Sept. 16. Neighbors of the amusement park — who were required to RSVP for the meeting that was closed to the press — were greeted at Universal’s stage 7 with slides […]
content:
At least 350 people on Wednesday attended a meeting to address the screams coming from Universal Studio’s new Fast & Furious rollercoaster that opened Sept. 16.

Neighbors of the amusement park — who were required to RSVP for the meeting that was closed to the press — were greeted at Universal’s stage 7 with slides that promised a “commitment to the community” and that “every concern reaches senior leadership and informs our planning.” No recordings of the presentation were permitted but Deadline was able to talk with attendees about the meeting that one resident described as turning “hostile.” Security was present.

A trio of executives — Steve Blum, the Executive VP of Engineering & Safety, John McReynolds, SVP of External Affairs, and Cindy Gardner of Corporate Affairs — began the presentation by promising the coaster wouldn’t operate from 8 to 9 a.m. until the end of the year. The park sometimes opens as early as 7 a.m. for thrill seekers, according to its website.

Watch on Deadline

Neighbors’ complaints have had more to do with the bloodcurdling screams coming from the riders rather than the actual sound of the coaster that moves “at speeds of up to 72 MPH and at a force of up to 3.6 Gs along 4,100 feet of elaborate aerial track.” Universal Studios has touted the coaster as “a literal game changer.”

Besides reminding the community of the steps it has already taken to reduce the noise, they promised a temporary new barrier that will add over 1,900 square feet of sound-absorbing material. Installation is planned for Oct. 1; if it’s effective, the park needs to apply for permits to make it permanent, according to one attendee.

This new barrier would be in addition to the original one that stretches longer than two fields and was made with a “state of the art sound absorbing product.”

The execs also talked about other solutions they’ve explored, like asking riders to wear helmets and face shields and fully enclosing the individual cars. Those ideas been ruled out, however, due to the possibility that people would not secure the helmets correctly and that closed cars would hinder emergency evacuations.

The park may also further tinker with the individual cars that already turn away from the Toluca Lake area during key scream moments.

Neighbors got a chance to air their grievances during the two-hour-plus meeting. They shared audio of the screams they hear on any given day, and projected a quote on the big screen from Dr. Luc Arnal, a leading expert on the science of screams. It read, “Chronic environmental noise is already recognized as a public health concern, associated with annoyance, sleep disturbance, stress-related physiological responses and increased cardiovascular risk.”

Other neighbors reminded the execs that most of their houses are older than the park. One complained he can no longer compose music from his home. Toluca Lake’s Roy P. Disney, the great-nephew of Walt Disney, said, “I would argue this is in violation of [Universal Studios’] land usage permits.”

The residents also projected a slick video (narrated by a British actor and viewed by Deadline) that talked about how the residents hear screams every 20 to 40 seconds, which averages out to 1,000 screams a day, 365,000 a year. It ended with images from the Universal lot, such as the massive acrylic dome that sits over Jurassic Park: The Ride.

The narrator says, “if you can build this, you can certainly fix this.”

Once the Q and A portion began, the temperature immediately turned hot as one resident yelled “promise the screams will be gone in a year.” As more people began to shout, Blum quipped, “we could solve this tomorrow if you all want to wear noise cancelling headphones.” Residents angrily responded with “how dare you” and “that is so insulting.”

“The burden of proof should not be entirely on us because you’re counting on our exhaustion,” said one attendee.

title: Rachel Zegler, Diego Rodriguez and James Olivas on Bringing ‘Evita’ to Broadway and Reimagining the Iconic Balcony Sequence for Times Square
summary: Rachel Zegler hesitated when “Evita” director Jamie Lloyd pitched her on his big idea for their West End revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s hit musical. Zegler was portraying Argentine first lady Eva Perón as a modern pop star, and Lloyd wanted his leading lady to perform the show’s best-known song, “Don’t Cry for Me, Argentina,” […]
content:
Rachel Zegler hesitated when “Evita” director Jamie Lloyd pitched her on his big idea for their West End revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s hit musical. Zegler was portraying Argentine first lady Eva Perón as a modern pop star, and Lloyd wanted his leading lady to perform the show’s best-known song, “Don’t Cry for Me, Argentina,” from a balcony facing the street while theatergoers inside watched on screens.

“I just remember thinking, ‘Well, it will be unbelievably embarrassing if nobody comes,’” Zegler says with a laugh. “’It would be amazing if we could have paid extras, like a film set.’”

Her concerns were for naught. “Evita” was the hottest ticket of last summer in London, and every night, hundreds of people gathered outside the Palladium for free to watch as Zegler belted the emotional ballad to the masses. Though divisive, Lloyd’s staging choice wasn’t just a gimmick; “Evita” chronicles the rags-to-riches story of Perón, and the scene symbolized her solidarity with the people.

Popular on Variety

As “Evita” prepares to transfer to Broadway in the spring, Lloyd is reimagining the iconic balcony sequence to work for Times Square — and theater fans are clamboring to find out how it’ll be staged from the Winter Garden Theatre. They’ll have to wait: Zegler isn’t about to give up the surprise.

“It’s a different city, and we’re at the heart of a completely different amount of foot traffic and actual traffic,” she says. “We are working tirelessly to bring something special for that moment.”

“Evita” marks a homecoming for the 25-year-old New Jersey native. She was plucked from obscurity as a high schooler to lead Steven Spielberg’s 2021 film adaptation of “West Side Story” and parlayed her fame into leading roles in movies (“The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” “Snow White”) and on the stage (in the Broadway revival of “Romeo + Juliet”). Helping Zegler recapture the electricity of “Evita” on Broadway are her West End co-stars Diego Andres Rodriguez and James Olivas. Rodriguez, 25, playing the everyman narrator Che, is returning to the New York stage after his turn in Lloyd’s popular “Sunset Boulevard” revival. Olivas, 29, is making his Broadway debut as President Juan Perón.

No shortage of theater luminaries and stars — from Elaine Paige and Patti LuPone to Mandy Patinkin (as well as Madonna and Antonio Banderas in the 1996 film adaptation) — have brought “Evita” to life. But as Zegler, Rodriguez and Olivas point out, Lloyd’s production is unique because all three leads are Latino — a responsibility they don’t take lightly.

“It’s too hard to comprehend what this moment will be,” Rodriguez says. “But we’re all going to enter with ganas — desire — to spread the message of why we, as Latinos, should be onstage all the time.”

Months before they reunite for Broadway rehearsals, the trio gathers via Zoom to talk about the show’s acclaimed West End run and the public’s enduring fascination with celebrity politicians.

What were your first impressions of each other?

Rachel Zegler: As soon as Diego had been cast as Che, I went to see him in “Sunset Blvd.” I was immediately taken with him. I didn’t get to meet James until our first day in London. My first impression was “He is so tall. I don’t know what I’m going to do eight times a week, having to kiss this really tall man and hurt my neck.” And then I immediately fell in love with him, just like everybody else on that job.

Diego Andres Rodriguez: I remember being 17 and watching “West Side Story” in the theaters. I was like, “This is exactly what I want to do.” It’s such a full-circle moment to take the stage with Rachel.

And I finally met James in London. I was like, “I think he’s one of those California guys.” Then he was like, “Bro, I’m from Texas.” I was like, “Bro, I’m from Texas.” We were living in the same building and were on the train every day for rehearsals, and so we had a lot of time to get to know each other. He found a brother in me.

James Olivas: Like Diego said, we immediately connected as Tejanos. It’s crazy that one of us made it; the fact that two of us made it was even wilder.

What did you learn about doing the show in London that you’ll take with you to New York?

Zegler: It requires an insane amount of stamina. Diego and I don’t leave the stage. London was amazing to understand how to pace ourselves. Theater is a sport, more vigorous than most, in the sense that most athletes aren’t playing eight games a week. We’re doing eight shows. It’s tough on the body. It’s tough on the voice. It requires an intense amount of rest. Knowing when to shut up is really the most important thing.

What was it like to have masses of people show up for the balcony sequence?

Zegler: It took one tech rehearsal for people to start paying attention. I was doing it with just a piano — we were testing the speakers and cameras. The next day, they were showing up in hordes.

Why did it become such a moment?

Zegler: It was a conversation about accessibility in theater. People were able to witness something for free on Argyll Street every night. You could hear a pin drop in that square. It was unbelievable. Something I’ll never forget is the sheer amount of people on the last night. There were more people outside than inside the theater. I couldn’t see the end of the crowd.

LONDON, ENGLAND – JUNE 30: Rachel Zegler performs “Don’t Cry For Me Argentina” live on the balcony as she plays Eva Peron in “Evita” at the London Palladium on June 30, 2025 in London, England. (Photo by Ming Yeung/Getty Images) Getty Images

Andrew Lloyd Webber had expressed a safety concern about staging the sequence on Broadway because of gun violence in the U.S. Was that a worry?

Zegler: We were very fortunate with the London Palladium to have essentially a half street that was rarely used for cars and trucks. It won’t be the same in New York.

Will the essence of it, Eva performing to the people, be preserved?

Zegler: At the core of “Evita” is that Eva Perón was for the people, and so there is always going to be an intention of incorporating a connection between Eva and her public.

Did you study any prior “Evita” performances as inspiration for your characters?

Olivas: I had to distance myself from what Peróns came before me because I can’t be a 50-year-old man doing this role; no one’s going to buy it. I took threads of what came before, but I had to surrender to the idea that it has to be so uniquely myself.

Zegler: Jamie and I had a conversation after my initial audition for the role. We talked about doing this like a Coachella set. This performance is very much like Beyoncé at Coachella and costumes inspired by Dua Lipa. We end up accentuating how we hold politicians and celebrities to similar standards in the current day and age. Eva Perón was a perfect example of a celebrity politician and how that never really changed.

Why are audiences so drawn to the intersection of celebrity and politics?

Zegler: We live in a society where everything is so immediately accessible. We know everybody’s thoughts and feelings about everything, and there-fore the line between celebrity and politician is blurred. It permeates every conversation that most socially conscious people are having these days.

Rodriguez: The show is incredibly political, this new take on it. We have this responsibility to show up as Latinos who are meeting this show at a political point. It is political for us three to be up there.

What does it mean for the three of you to transfer with the show to Broadway?

Zegler: I was born and raised in New Jersey. I moved to New York when I was 17, and I’ve spent every waking minute of my life obsessed with Broadway. Anytime I get to come back to New York theater is a huge honor, and it’s not something that I take lightly. It’s really important for young people like us to see Latin bodies onstage, experiencing joy and success. I really hope that it inspires another generation of Latin performers.

Rodriguez: It shows a turning of the tides.

Olivas: There is such a prevailing narrative in this industry and this country of what the Latino community is, who we are and the content of our character. It’s amazing to show a positive representation of our community and show that we come in all shapes and sizes and have so much to offer.

This is such a high-energy show. How do you recover after a performance?

Zegler: I become like a ravenous pubescent teenage boy. I would stage door for a while and then I would order food so it would meet me at home. I would walk the dog, eat food, take a shower and then steam [my throat] while watching “Gilmore Girls” or “How I Met Your Mother.” I would go to bed around 2 a.m. when my adrenaline would finally dissipate.

Rodriguez: I took so many showers. I take, like, four a day anyway.

title: Sia Sells 50% of Music Catalog to Pophouse in $180 Million Partnership Deal
summary: Pophouse Entertainment, the Sweden-based entertainment and music investment firm co-founded by ABBA’s Bjorn Ulvaeus, has acquired a 50% stake in the publishing and master music rights of Australian singer-songwriter, Sia, for $180 million. According to the announcement, Pophouse will support Sia in developing new creative ventures while continuing to steward her body of work. While […]
content:
Pophouse Entertainment, the Sweden-based entertainment and music investment firm co-founded by ABBA’s Bjorn Ulvaeus, has acquired a 50% stake in the publishing and master music rights of Australian singer-songwriter, Sia, for $180 million.

According to the announcement, Pophouse will support Sia in developing new creative ventures while continuing to steward her body of work.

While Pophouse announced the deal, the figure was reported by TMZ, noting that the deal is complicated by the singer-songwriter’s recent divorce from Dan Bernad. Citing legal documents, TMZ reports that Sia will receive $165 million for the songs she wrote before she married Bernad — including hits like “Chandelier,” “Titanium” and “Cheap Thrills” — for which he has waived any claims in exchange for a $1 million payment. However, the remaining $15 million, for songs she wrote during their marriage, will be held in escrow until the two agree to terms. The couple were married for less than three years before Sia filed for divorce in March of 2025.

Sia originally rose to international fame with her 2004 song “Breathe,” which was featured in the final episode of the popular HBO series “Six Feet Under.” She went on to rack up nine Grammy nominations and hits like “Unstoppable,” “Chandelier,” “Elastic Heart,” “Cheap Thrills” and, with Diplo and Labrinth as the group LSD, the 2018 hit “Thunderclouds”; she has also co-written hits for Rihanna (“Diamonds”) and Beyonce (“Pretty Hurts”).

Popular on Variety

Sia said: “I’m really excited to be working with Pophouse. These songs mean so much to me, and I love that they really understand that and want to take care of them. I’ve been making music for a very long time now, and it feels exciting to think about all the new and different ways these songs might get to live on and find people. I’m really looking forward to seeing what we can dream up together.”

Pophouse CEO, Jessica Koravos, said: “Sia is an artist whose extraordinary catalogue and unique creative identity offer exceptional opportunities to celebrate and build on her remarkable body of work. This partnership will further empower Sia with strategic support and creative resources to continue pursuing her artistic ambitions while preserving and expanding her influence. It is a privilege to partner with Sia, and we look forward to supporting her continued artistic growth and ability to inspire audiences around the world.”

Pophouse Fund Partner, Shahriar Shokofan, said: “Few artists have shaped modern pop as profoundly as Sia, whose songwriting and unmistakable voice have defined some of the most iconic records of the past few decades. Sia’s ability to balance artistic integrity with mass appeal sets her apart as a truly unstoppable force. We are delighted to partner with her at this point in her career, with a shared ambition to support the continued growth of her catalogue and to unlock new audiences around the world.”

Pophouse’s investment in the Sia catalogue is made through Pophouse Fund I, the firm’s debut fund which closed in March 2025, reaching its hard cap of €1 billion. In addition, over €200 million was secured capital through dedicated co-investment vehicles, bringing the total fundraise to over €1.2bn.

Pophouse’s holdings also include catalogs by Iron Maiden, Tina Turner, Kiss, Cyndi Lauper, Avicii, and Swedish House Mafia. It is also a major investor in such projects as the Avicii Experience, ABBA the Museum, “Mamma Mia! the Party,” and ABBA “Voyage.”

title: Screenvision Shakes Up Movie-Theater Pre Show in Bid for Gen Z Ad Dollars
summary: Some of the puzzles and trivia moviegoers see when they arrive before showtime at the cinema may be going the way of Good N’ Plenty and Jujubes. Movie screens under the aegis of movie-ad titan Screenvision will unfurl a new pre-show starting in October. The new concept tamps down on the old puzzles and behind-the-scenes […]
content:
Some of the puzzles and trivia moviegoers see when they arrive before showtime at the cinema may be going the way of Good N’ Plenty and Jujubes.

Movie screens under the aegis of movie-ad titan Screenvision will unfurl a new pre-show starting in October. The new concept tamps down on the old puzzles and behind-the-scenes format that has become such an expected part of cinema culture and instead features content blocks devoted to topics including food, sports and fashion, among others.

“It’s all built on the premise that 50% of our audience is Gen Z and they really want content that reflects who they are, not just quizzes and trivia,” says Geoff Schiller, recently installed as the company’s new CEO following a stint as chief revenue officer at Vox Media. “The audiences are hungry for more.”

Popular on Variety

They’ll get it. As part of the company’s new initiative, audiences in place ahead of a movie’s showtime, will see video content from providers including Eater, Complex and NowThis. Many of the venture’s new content partners are encouraged by projections of new spending at movie theaters, with younger consumers craving more in-person gatherings.

Recent box-office stats have been encouraging to an industry that continues to grapple with the appeal of top movies eventually turning up on widescreen home TVs thanks to premium subscription services. Even so, movies in recent months such as Universal’s “The Odyssey,” A24’s “Backrooms”: and Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” have generated impressive revenue. They will be followed at the end of the year by Warner Bros. latest piece of its “Dune” franchise and Disney’s “Avengers: Doomsday.”

PwC calls for cinema advertising to rise to climb to $2.7 billion in 2030, compared with $2.4 billion in 2026. Box office revenue, meanwhile, is seen rising to $39.5 billion in 2030 compared with $34.6 billion at the end of this year.

Some partners are eager to broaden their mix of video distribution and to get in front of younger consumers., “We need to be more diverse in the places where we put our content and to be where the Gen Z c consumer is says sharon, Complex views the alliance as a way “to get our programming in front of some of the most engaged, pop culture and entertainment obsessed consumers in North America,” says Moksha Fitzgibbons, the company’s president.

For Eater, getting recommendations and content in front of moviegoers can only help burnish the outlet’s desire to be seen as “the best trusted discovery brand for people who care about food,” says Jill Denhert, Eater’s publisher. Eater, is, like Variety, part of Penske Media.

More publishers are finding new audiences for signature video clips and programming, with major outlets like Netflix doing deals in recent months to show more short-form content on their platforms.

Screenvision’s pre-show, called “Front and Center,” will still last around 28 minutes and contain commercials. After what Schiller calls a “soft launch,” it will appear in more theaters by holiday time.

The executive says he remains mindful of a need to entertain moviegoers ahead of the main attraction, and not make them feel as if they’re a crowd being held captive in front of a long stretch of promotional messages. “’Front and Center will be a show that has advertising, not advertising that has a show,” he says. He believes ticket buyers will be happy if they are getting something of value like an interview with the cast of a current or upcoming film. “If you entertain them, they will be happy. If you don’t, then they won’t.”

Screenvision has other plans in place to lure advertising and promotional dollars. Schiller says he would like to develop a “watch party” concept that brings audiences to movie theaters to watch live events The company worked earlier this year with the BET Awards and held watch events in Atlanta, New York, and Philadelphia. “We had red carpet interviews, DJs, step and repeat, fan engagement in the theaters as they were watching us stream” the show, he says.

He also sees an opportunity to give marketers other kinds of access to movie crowds. Would an advertiser appreciate the chance to offer product samples to consumers in theaters to see movies on the last shopping weekend ahead of Christmas, he asks. With many theaters close to retail outlets, malls and shopping centers, he believes local stores may be interested in doing anything from offering coupons to making scents available to a crowd.

Schiller, a veteran of print and digital publishing, has worked at Vice, Group Nine, People, USA Today and many other outlets. He says he is “not docile” and thinks companies need to examine even years-old models like the movie pre-show to see what can be updated. And he thinks advertisers have yet to make full use of the movie house. “Our ability to create a suite of solutions that offer brand marketers the ability to influence purchase decisions I think has been untapped,” he says.

title: Dominic West and Sienna Miller Shine In HBO’s Captivating Divorce Thriller ‘War’: TV Review
summary: From “Hijack” and “Lupin” creator George Kay, HBO and Sky Television’s “War” is a thrilling legal drama highlighting a bitter, high-profile divorce. Though the couple at the center of the story are tech billionaire Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and A-list actress Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), their rapidly collapsing marriage anchors “War,” which looks well beyond […]
content:
From “Hijack” and “Lupin” creator George Kay, HBO and Sky Television’s “War” is a thrilling legal drama highlighting a bitter, high-profile divorce. Though the couple at the center of the story are tech billionaire Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and A-list actress Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), their rapidly collapsing marriage anchors “War,” which looks well beyond the emotional turmoil of a love that’s ending. Instead, by juxtaposing the opposing counsels, audiences get a peek inside the ruthless minds and tactics of the lawyers surrounding Morgan and Carla. Thoroughly captivating — with Kay’s signature twists dispersed throughout — “War” depicts the lengths people are willing to go to achieve victory and what it might cost to get there.



The eight-episode first season of “War” opens in present-day London, where Morgan is thrilled to be receiving the Pioneer of the Year Award at a prestigious ceremony. As he basks in praise and gives a heartfelt acceptance speech, he also spots a stunning young woman, Flora (Rose Williams), in the crowd. By the end of the night, the very married entrepreneur has Flora in his bed. In Paris, Morgan’s wife Carla is doing press for her latest film. Exhausted by the distance in her marriage and suspicious about Morgan’s loyalty, she has called in her lawyers, Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox) and Nick Taylor (James McArdle), law partners and a married couple who run Taylor & Byrne, to begin gearing up to serve Morgan divorce papers. Unfortunately, because of Carla’s celebrity status, photos from the meeting make the tabloids, prompting Morgan to touch base with his own representation, Beatrice “Queen Bea” Ubos (Nina Sosanya) and St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens) at Cathcarts & Sons.



Elsewhere in London, a driven young lawyer, Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) joins Taylor & Byrne, where he tries to become an invaluable asset to Serena, Nick and Carla. Desperate to reinvent himself after a major career blunder in New York City, Johnny starts working angles to stand out. What begins as a straightforward dissolution of a decade-long marriage becomes a hostile takedown exposing both Carla and Morgan’s deepest vulnerabilities. The chaos even thrusts Carla’s 16-year-old son Gabriel (Aran Murphy, a doppelgänger of his father, Cillian) into the spotlight.



“War” unpacks Morgan and Carla’s mutual backstabbing and lies, along with the lengths the lawyers will go to ensure their respective clients come out on top. Yet “War” soars because it goes beyond the obvious. The series thrives because it offers glimmers of humanity sliced between moments of sabotage and betrayal. Miller and West are highly believable as two people who once shared a deep affection for each other. Hints of this reverence shine through even during some of their worst moments. This is especially poignant in the former couple’s interactions with Gabriel. Moreover, contrasting Carla and Morgan against Serena and Nick’s own marriage showcases a different partnership, one held together by love and determination but just as vulnerable as any other, if not for the parties within it working daily to fortify the union.



From beautifully strategized crisis PR campaigns to the distinctiveness of U.K. courtrooms, the show presents the impossible choices any decent family law attorney must make, which often go directly against what most people perceive as good and righteous. As Johnny discovers at the end of Episode 6, “The Simple Act of Paying Attention,” one small mishap or turn of phrase can cause one’s destruction. Watching the inner workings of two different London law firms and all that goes into dismantling a hyper-visible relationship, particularly when the court of public opinion is at play, also makes the series distinct. There will be more of this in “War” Season 2, which will star Marisa Tomei and Kelly Macdonald and focus on the lawyers from Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne going head to head once again on an explosive defamation case.



As with the rest of Kay’s dramas, “War” builds tension brilliantly and unfolds into something far more intricate than it first appears. Dividing assets and closing a chapter becomes less about fairness and more about ambition and greed. After all, divorce is never just between two parties. When it’s all said and done, everyone it touches wants a piece of the action.

Popular on Variety

“War” debuts Oct. 1 on HBO, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Thursdays.

title: DDA Hires Luxury Hospitality Exec Keith Iddins as Longtime Event Management Boss Caroline Warburton Sets Retirement (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Marketing and communications agency DDA has hired Keith Iddins, a luxury hospitality and entertainment veteran with more than 30 years experience, to the newly created role of travel relationship director for its DDA Travel and Logistics (Live) arm. Iddins, who has worked with major hotel groups including Dorchester Collection, Maybourne and Oetker, will report to […]
content:
Marketing and communications agency DDA has hired Keith Iddins, a luxury hospitality and entertainment veteran with more than 30 years experience, to the newly created role of travel relationship director for its DDA Travel and Logistics (Live) arm.

Iddins, who has worked with major hotel groups including Dorchester Collection, Maybourne and Oetker, will report to Daniel Starmer, vice president of Live, to develop DDA’s hospitality and travel services. He will also take over responsibility for hotel logistics from longtime DDA exec Caroline Warburton, until recently CEO of DDA Event Management, as she prepares to retire at the end of 2027.

“Caroline’s reputation across the industry is unmatched, reflecting decades of exceptional leadership and the trust and affection she has earned from colleagues and clients alike,” said DDA Partners Lawrence Atkinson, Dana Archer and Neil Bhatt. “As part of our strategic planning for her retirement, we are delighted to welcome Keith, a long-time partner of DDA’s through his previous roles at some of the world’s most prestigious hotels, into the fold to help build on Caroline’s remarkable legacy.”

Popular on Variety

Recruited by Dennis Davidson in 1997 as a coordinator in what was then DDA’s Market Services division, Warburton has been central to the company’s international festival and market operations for three decades. From Cannes to Toronto, she has overseen events, logistics and hospitality for leading companies across the global entertainment industry.

The appointment of Iddins follows DDA’s recent acquisition of DDA Event Management and its integration into DDA’s Live division.

“DDA Event Management and DDA have worked as one for so long that this is more a natural evolution than a change,” said Warburton. “As I prepare to retire, I know our exceptional team and amazing clients will be in the very best hands, with Daniel leading our area of the business into its next chapter. I’m excited to watch – from afar – as the company continues to thrive for decades to come.”

DDA’s Live vice president Starmer said the company had been “searching for someone to consolidate and develop DDA’s work in the travel sector” and that Iddins’ “experience and reputation” aligned with its future goals.

“We feel uniquely placed with our ability to look after the wide range of needs of our clients as they activate and operate around the world. I am excited to continue to build on Caroline’s legacy as we head toward the 2027 season of festivals and beyond,” he added.

“I’ve had the pleasure and privilege of working with DDA and their clients on many occasions throughout my career, with so many starting their careers at DDA,” said Iddins. “To now have the opportunity to join the team myself feels particularly special, and I’m very grateful for the opportunity. I’ve always loved being in the trenches with a project and being part of what happens behind the scenes to bring an event together.”

Over the past couple of years, DDA — which has a staff or 175 across offices in Los Angeles, New York, London, and Dubai — has established U.S. Film & Series Publicity and Creative Services divisions in New York and launched its first Middle East office through a joint venture with Dubai-based brand publicity specialist Sophie Toh. In London it established a live content division to work alongside its live event production, social media content production, and design and creative team.

title: ‘Best Pancakes In The County’: IFC Picks Up Domestic Rights To Nicolas Cage, Justin Long & Shelley Hennig Action-Thriller; First Look Revealed
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Independent Film Company has acquired U.S. rights to Best Pancakes In The County, the action-thriller written and directed by Ken Sanzel (Kill Chain) and starring Nicolas Cage (Longlegs), Justin Long (Weapons) and Shelley Hennig (Unfriended). The deal was negotiated by Mark Ward, Chief Acquisitions Officer for Independent Film Company and Eduard Osipov at Beno […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Independent Film Company has acquired U.S. rights to Best Pancakes In The County, the action-thriller written and directed by Ken Sanzel (Kill Chain) and starring Nicolas Cage (Longlegs), Justin Long (Weapons) and Shelley Hennig (Unfriended).



The deal was negotiated by Mark Ward, Chief Acquisitions Officer for Independent Film Company and Eduard Osipov at Beno Films on behalf of the filmmakers. Pic will be released in theaters and on digital platforms November 20, 2026.



The synopsis reads: “Set over the course of one explosive night, Best Pancakes In The County transforms an unassuming small-town diner into the epicenter of a deadly standoff involving rogue federal agents, a fast-talking con man with a dangerous past and a waitress harboring secrets of her own. As loyalties blur and tensions erupt, survival depends on who can outthink — and outgun — everyone else.”

Cage stars as “The S.O.B., an eccentric and cunning criminal caught in the escalating confrontation”. Below is a first-look image.



The film reunites Sanzel with Cage following their collaboration on the 2019 action thriller Kill Chain. Long plays Cookie and Hennig is Dolly. The ensemble cast also includes Lauren German (Lucifer), Ravi Patel (Animal Control), Brandon Mychal Smith (Get On Up), Kelly Greyson (Sleeping Dogs), Jaylen Moore (Six), and Michael Sirow (Sleeping Dogs).



The movie was filmed in Arkansas and is produced by Eduard Osipov, Raja Collins, Eric Brenner, Niko Fomenko, Gary Preisler and R. Wesley Sierk III. Executive producers include John D. Straley, Audra Gricius, Jina Panebianco, Lance Kawas, Ahmed S. Boomrod, Eugene Pruss, and Nadine de Barros. The film is produced by Beno Films and backed by CaliWood Pictures, with Fortitude International handling international sales.



“Best Pancakes In The County is exactly the kind of eccentric and wildly entertaining ride that Nicolas Cage does better than anyone else,” said IFC Entertainment Group’s Chief Acquisition Officer, Mark Ward. “Ken has built a tense, funny and unpredictable thriller around a fantastic ensemble, and we can’t wait for audiences to experience the chaos this November.”



“Working with Nic again was an opportunity to create a character who could be funny, dangerous and completely unpredictable from one moment to the next,” said writer-director Sanzel. “And then he took it to wilder and more unexpected places than I could have imagined. We wanted to take this seemingly ordinary diner, fill it with people with dueling and hidden agendas, juxtapose the threat of violence with the urgency of getting breakfast orders right, and keep turning up the pressure until everything explodes. IFC immediately understood the fast, fun tone of the film, and I’m excited to have them bringing it to audiences.”

Nicolas Cage in Best Pancakes In The County

title: Hearst Renews CBS Weekend Series ‘The Visioneers With Zay Harding’ Through 2028
summary: Hearst Media Production Group has renewed CBS weekend educational series The Visioneers with Zay Harding for two more seasons, through 2028. The show was first announced by Hearst in March 2025. Season 3 of the 30-minute eco-adventure original, which is produced by the Hearst production division in partnership with the VoLo Foundation, will premiere on […]
content:
Hearst Media Production Group has renewed CBS weekend educational series The Visioneers with Zay Harding for two more seasons, through 2028.

The show was first announced by Hearst in March 2025.

Season 3 of the 30-minute eco-adventure original, which is produced by the Hearst production division in partnership with the VoLo Foundation, will premiere on Saturday. Hosted by Harding, an international explorer, the show features scientists, engineers and everyday people who are creating sustainable environmental solutions.

The series airs weekend mornings as part of the CBS WKND educational/informational programming block. Timeslots vary by market.

Watch on Deadline

Guests this season include actor Edward Norton; former NFL player and ocean-conservation advocate Kelvin Beachum; NASCAR driver Austin Green; and Luci Baines Johnson, daughter of Lady Bird Johnson. Episodes are set from the Great Barrier Reef to America’s ports, racetracks and wildflower fields.

“Alongside our partners at VoLo Foundation, we’re proud to bring audiences two more seasons of The Visioneers,” HMPG President Bryan Curb said in a statement. “The show has struck a real chord with viewers, sharing stories that prove environmental stewardship can take many forms – and that building a more sustainable future can be an engaging, hands-on adventure.”

Thais Lopez V., president of VoLo Foundation, said the series “shows that the solutions to our biggest challenges are already in the hands of people with the courage to imagine a better world and the determination to make it real.”

HMPG’s slate includes more than 30 original series and hundreds of hours of content annually on broadcast networks, station groups, connected-TV and streaming platforms. Its library spans 85 series and 6,000 episodes, with content across 100 countries.
