Kerry Washington co-stars as Affleck’s wife in the movie. “We keep telling him that he should, but he doesn’t want to,” she told me. “You know, we’re in a place in our politics right now where anything is possible, but I would hope that the people who are running for office want to be there and he has been very explicit in saying that he doesn’t want to run for office.”

Kerry Washington says the “Animals” cast keeps telling Ben Affleck to run for office “but he doesn’t want to.” pic.twitter.com/VBVFdokksl — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026

Luis Gerardo Méndez plays an undocumented Mexican immigrant in the film who finds himself unexpectedly — and dangerously — thrust into the mayoral hopeful’s life. “I would definitely vote for him,” Méndez said. “Go Ben Affleck! He’s smart and sexy — that’s all you need.”

Affleck, however, isn’t announcing a candidacy anytime soon.

Luis Gerardo Méndez says he'd "definitely vote" for Ben Affleck if he ran for office: "He's smart and sexy. That's all you need." pic.twitter.com/45LwB1D8Ju — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026

“We don’t ask the question of what are your qualifications to hold public office any longer,” the Oscar winner said. “It’s, ‘You wanna join the circus? Who’s the biggest carny?’ I think that there is a whatever side of the aisle you’re on, one of the interesting things that people can agree on is a collective disappointment with the way that American politics has trended.”

Affleck continued, “There’s nobody alive now who thinks, hey, we’re really doing it right and things are going great and I love this political system. And that’s a problem.”

Being in office, Affleck says, is no longer about serving the people.

“It’s just about money, raising money, it’s just about playing a sort of adolescent game of who can make fun of the other person better or be more reductive and stupid about something rather than actually trying to talk about the issues,” he said. “I think the thing that’s missing from politics, frankly, is you have to lead. You can’t just scare people. You can’t just hector them. You can’t lecture them. You can’t guilt them into it. You’ve got to inspire them. Otherwise they don’t want to vote for you.”

And then he added, “Selfishly, I just see what a difficult grind of a job it is and I’d rather make movies about it.”

Animals will be released on Netflix and in select theaters on Oct. 9.

title: Ken Urker, Gypsy-Rose Blanchard’s Partner, Dies at 34
summary: Ken Urker, the partner of Gypsy-Rose Blanchard and father of their child, was found dead Thursday in Raceland, Louisiana. He was 34. Captain Brennan Matherne of the Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Department said in a statement to Variety, “We responded to a residence at 107 Double H Drive, Lot 4, in Raceland today after receiving a […]
content:
Ken Urker, the partner of Gypsy-Rose Blanchard and father of their child, was found dead Thursday in Raceland, Louisiana. He was 34.

Captain Brennan Matherne of the Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Department said in a statement to Variety, “We responded to a residence at 107 Double H Drive, Lot 4, in Raceland today after receiving a call at 6:15 p.m. Kenan Urker, 34, was found dead upon arrival. At this time, we are continuing the death investigation.”

A source close to the family told People magazine that he was discovered unresponsive by a family member inside a home on his 34th birthday.

Popular on Variety

Urker appeared on the reality series “Gypsy Rose: Life After Lockup,” which ran for two seasons on Lifetime. Variety‘s review of the series noted, “The limelight can certainly feel glorious following a lifetime in the shadows, but it’s also a very precarious and often unsustainable place to be.”

Blanchard and Urker first got together through a penpal program when she was in prison for her role in the murder of her mother Dee Dee Blanchard. After they broke off their engagement, Blanchard married and divorced Ryan Anderson. After reconciling in 2024, Urker and Blanchard had a baby girl, Aurora, in December 2024.

After alleging that her mother abused her for many years, Blanchard pleaded guilty to second degree murder of her mother in 2015 while her boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn was sentenced to life in prison for first degree murder. She served eight and a half years in prison.

title: Oscars: Pakistan Selects Documentary ‘Hanging by a Wire’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Mohammed Ali Naqvi’s documentary thriller “Hanging by a Wire” has been selected as Pakistan’s submission for the international feature film Oscar at the 99th Academy Awards, marking the first time a documentary has represented the country in the category. The Pakistan Academy Selection Committee made the selection, calling it a historic milestone for Pakistani documentary […]
content:
Mohammed Ali Naqvi’s documentary thriller “Hanging by a Wire” has been selected as Pakistan‘s submission for the international feature film Oscar at the 99th Academy Awards, marking the first time a documentary has represented the country in the category.

The Pakistan Academy Selection Committee made the selection, calling it a historic milestone for Pakistani documentary filmmaking. The announcement was issued by Sana Zahra Jafri, deputy chair of the committee.

“Hanging by a Wire” is directed by Naqvi and written and produced by Naqvi and Bilal Sami. The film revisits the August 2023 cable car emergency in Battagram, in northern Pakistan, in which eight passengers, including six schoolboys on their way to school, were left suspended roughly 900 feet above a ravine after a cable snapped. The resulting rescue effort was followed live across Pakistan and internationally.

Popular on Variety

The film draws on footage from witnesses, testimony from survivors and staged reenactments involving people who took part in the rescue to build its account.

“Hanging by a Wire” debuted at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, in the World Cinema Documentary Competition lineup, before going on to play the Tribeca Festival.

The film is produced by EverWonder Studio, Universal Pictures Content Group, Mindhouse Productions and 64th Street Media. Dogwoof holds theatrical distribution rights in the U.K., with Abramorama handling U.S. theatrical release. The film is set for a streaming release on Paramount+ on Oct. 28.

The pick brings the Battagram rescue story into the International Feature Film Oscar race as Pakistan’s representative for this awards cycle.

Pakistan has submitted 13 films in the category since 1959 without a nomination, with Saim Sadiq’s “Joyland’ marking its only shortlist appearance, in 2022.

title: Donna Langley Says the Key to Stealing Taylor Sheridan Away From Paramount Was a Better Film Deal: ‘I Saw an Opportunity’
summary: NBCUniversal Entertainment chair Donna Langley managed to snag “Yellowstone” creator Taylor Sheridan away from Paramount after a decade at the studio. How did she do it? By putting an emphasis on the film of his lucrative long-term TV and film pact. Langley said her pursuit of Sheridan began after she “saw an opportunity” created by […]
content:
NBCUniversal Entertainment chair Donna Langley managed to snag “Yellowstone” creator Taylor Sheridan away from Paramount after a decade at the studio. How did she do it? By putting an emphasis on the film of his lucrative long-term TV and film pact.

Langley said her pursuit of Sheridan began after she “saw an opportunity” created by “disruption and instability” at Paramount. While never explicitly mentioning it, she was most likely referring to the turbulent yearlong merger process between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. News of Sheridan’s deal broke in late October of 2025, only months before David Ellison emerged victorious over Netflix in the battle for WB.

“There’s just a moment to kind of look around the marketplace and see if there’s a competitive advantage,” Langley said during her interview at Bloomberg’s Screentime event on Thursday afternoon. “But really, where I started talking to Taylor was about film, because I knew that he had a film deal at Paramount, but it was a first-look deal. Didn’t have as many teeth to it as his television deal. That’s how it started, and then we just got to talking and one thing led to another.”

Popular on Variety

The film component of Sheridan’s NBCUniversal deal is expected to take effect in 2026, while the TV component will follow after he fulfills his contractual obligations to Paramount in 2028.

Sheridan broke out as a scribe for the big screen, writing films like “Sicario,” “Hell or High Water” and “Wind River.” But in more recent years, Sheridan has built a TV empire at Paramount, starting with “Yellowstone” in 2018. The Western drama has spawned a universe of spinoffs, including “1923,” “The Madison” and “Dutton Ranch.” He also created “Lioness,” “Marshals,” “Landman” and “Mayor of Kingstown.”

Sheridan is returning to his cinema roots soon. He wrote the scripts for Paramount’s upcoming “Call of Duty Movie” and “Sicario 3.”

title: Ben Affleck Used AI For “Lots Of Things” In Netflix’s ‘Animals’: “It’s A Very Human Movie”
summary: After unloading his AI firm on Netflix earlier this year, Ben Affleck is showing off the tech in action with his latest project. The 2x Oscar winner recently revealed that he “did use” artificial intelligence “for lots of things” in the making of Animals, which he co-wrote, directed and starred in, premiering Oct. 9 in […]
content:
After unloading his AI firm on Netflix earlier this year, Ben Affleck is showing off the tech in action with his latest project.

The 2x Oscar winner recently revealed that he “did use” artificial intelligence “for lots of things” in the making of Animals, which he co-wrote, directed and starred in, premiering Oct. 9 in select theaters and on Netflix.

“I used [AI] for lots of things in that movie,” he revealed at a Q&A for Bloomberg Screentime. “I’m a little bit hesitant to point out what they are or even talk about it because, in my business, we’re trying to foster the illusion of reality, right? It’s sort of like if you went to a magic show and the magician walked out and said, ‘Just before I start, I want you to know there’s another bunny under here. This guy’s a plant.’ It sort of ruins it, right?”

Affleck continued, “But yes, we did use it. And in fact, I thought it was a good example because it’s a very human movie. It’s not in space, it doesn’t have visual effects, but it allowed us to move in some cases more quickly, really mostly in post-production, to do things that otherwise we wouldn’t have been able to do.”

Watch on Deadline

Co-written by Affleck, Connor O. McIntyre and Billy Ray, Animals stars Affleck as Los Angeles mayoral candidate Mark Kimball, whose son is kidnapped, giving him and wife Abigail (Kerry Washington) a few hours to get their hands dirty and come up with the ransom money.

Affleck’s latest Netflix film comes after the streamer bought his AI firm InterPositive in March for $587 million. He quietly founded the company in 2022 and served as CEO, taking on a senior advisor role after Netflix’s acquisition.

title: Oscars: Pakistan Picks Mo Naqvi’s Doc Thriller ‘Hanging By A Wire’ As Best International Feature Entry
summary: Pakistan has selected Mo Naqvi’s nonfiction action thriller Hanging By a Wire as its official entry for Best International Film at the Academy Awards, the first time the country has chosen a documentary for that distinction. The film captures the drama and suspense around a news event that captured the world’s attention in 2023: the […]
content:
Pakistan has selected Mo Naqvi’s nonfiction action thriller Hanging By a Wire as its official entry for Best International Film at the Academy Awards, the first time the country has chosen a documentary for that distinction.

The film captures the drama and suspense around a news event that captured the world’s attention in 2023: the desperate attempt to save six school kids and two adults stranded in a cable car 900 feet above the ground, in a remote area of Northern Pakistan. The kids and adults were nearly hurled out of the car after a cable snapped, leaving them, as the film’s title indicates, hanging by a wire.

“Directed by Naqvi, and written and produced by Naqvi and Bilal Sami, the film revisits the August 2023 cable car emergency in Battagram, northern Pakistan,” notes a release announcing the film’s selection for the Best International Film category. “Combining eyewitness footage, survivor testimony and cinematic reconstructions featuring participants in the rescue, Hanging by a Wire unfolds as a documentary thriller.”

Watch on Deadline

(L-R) EP Aloke Devichand, producer Bilal Sami, director Mohammed Ali Naqvi, and EP Aaron Fellows attend the ‘Hanging By A Wire’ premiere at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival on January 22, 2026 in Park City, Utah. Arturo Holmes/Getty Images

The documentary premiered in World Cinema Documentary competition at the Sundance Film Festival earlier this year. It has gone on to screen at Tribeca Festival, the Seattle International Film Festival, and the Sydney Film Festival in Australia. Next Friday, it plays at the 23rd annual Bend Film Festival in Oregon.

“I’m honored that Hanging by a Wire has been selected to represent Pakistan in the International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards, and grateful to the Pakistan Academy Selection Committee,” Naqvi tells Deadline exclusively. “It’s a straight-up disaster film, except it really happened, and you’re watching real footage of it unfolding live. The community on the ground filmed it themselves and trusted me with that footage, so in a real sense they co-authored this film with me. How resilient and resourceful they were, both in the rescue and in documenting it, is what the film is about, and there’s nothing more Pakistani than that.”

Hanging By a Wire is produced by EverWonder Studio, Universal Pictures Content Group, Mindhouse Productions and 64th Street Media. Its theatrical distribution is handled by Dogwoof in the U.K. and Abramorama in the U.S., with a Paramount+ streaming release set for later this month.

People watch as a soldier slings down from a helicopter during a rescue mission to recover students and adults stuck in a cable car in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, on August 22, 2023. AFP via Getty Images

There are no “proper roads” in the area where the incident took place, Naqvi explained in a Meet the Filmmaker video posted by Sundance. “The way people get around in the mountains is by using makeshift cable cars. And it is so dangerous.” His Sundance Filmmaker video showed him on board one of the cable cars, only a crisscross metal gate separating him falling to the earth below. “During location scouting, I did this stupid thing of taking one.”

“Sky pirate” Sahib Khan in ‘Hanging By a Wire’ EverWonder/Mindhouse/Universal Pictures Content Group

Hanging By a Wire foregrounds an ad hoc group of locals who attempted to stage a rescue, including Sahib Khan, a cable car repairman known in his community as a “sky pirate” for his aerial exploits. Another of the rescuers, dashing Ali Swati who had access to high-quality zipline equipment, also sprang to the aid of the cable car passengers. The Pakistani official who ultimately oversaw the operation – and the likely fall person if the mission went awry — was the forceful Sonia Shamroz, “the district’s no-nonsense head of police.”

Sana Zahra Jafri, deputy chairperson of the Pakistan Academy Selection Committee, commented, “The selection marks a historic milestone for Pakistani documentary filmmaking and brings an extraordinary story from northern Pakistan to the International Feature Film Oscar race.”

title: BTS’ RM Explores Fame, Identity & Curiosity In Debut  Art Exhibition ‘Between You And Me’ At SFMOMA
summary: When you enter RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me, it’s almost impossible not to think about the person whose name appears everywhere. RM (short for Rap Monster) is, after all, one of the most recognizable musicians in the world. As the leader of BTS, he has spent years performing on the world stage and […]
content:
When you enter RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me, it’s almost impossible not to think about the person whose name appears everywhere.

RM (short for Rap Monster) is, after all, one of the most recognizable musicians in the world. As the leader of BTS, he has spent years performing on the world stage and existing in a state of near-constant visibility. But inside the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA), the scale of that fame begins to feel almost beside the point.

What’s on display here isn’t RM the celebrity. It’s just him: Kim Namjoon, a 32-year-old private citizen from Seoul, South Korea, who happens to have a penchant for finding beauty in everyday life through art.

RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me opens on October 3 and runs until February 7, 2027. It’s his first time as a co-curator and the first museum show of 142 pieces from his own collection. Along with 36 works from SFMOMA, the exhibition brings together nearly 200 pieces by Korean and international artists, spanning centuries and many art forms—paintings, sculpture, furniture, ceramics, textiles, and animation. Artists include To Sangbong, Yun Hyong-keun, Mark Rothko, Chang Ucchin, Henri Matisse, Georgia O’Keeffe, Nam June Paik, and others.

Watch on Deadline

RM insisted on variety. “There’s not a singular style, there’s no singular medium,” SFMOMA co-curator Hyoeun Kim told Deadline. “He has a painting, sculpture, furniture, ceramic, fabric, and then animation [all in the same space].”

RM (Kim Namjoon) reflects on his love for art collecting and how he went about choosing the pieces for his @SFMOMA exhibition collaboration, #RMxSFMOMA: Between You and Me:



“In an age where everything is consumed so fast, I believe some of the attitudes of some of the past… pic.twitter.com/rZeJBBHt4l — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 30, 2026

Since the works aren’t arranged as a linear historical timeline of Korean art, it makes you wonder what RM wanted to say by mixing artists from different times and cultures. “From the beginning, we didn’t really want to highlight something that was just like, ‘Oh, this is going to be an exhibition about Korean art,’” Kim explained. “This exhibition was about good artists from Korea, and then we also added other artists from America and other international places. We wanted all of these artworks to have a conversation together.”

RM has been in conversation with art since, as he told the New York Times, a visit to The Art Institute of Chicago in 2018 during downtime while BTS was on tour. Since then, his relationship with art has extended well beyond collecting. In 2020, he donated approximately $80,000 to the Korean National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Foundation to support the production and distribution of Korean art books for public and school libraries. He later narrated an audio guide for the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s (LACMA)The Space Between: The Modern in Korean Art in 2022. And this past June, the National Museum of Korea appointed him as its first Global Public Relations Ambassador, a role focused on helping promote the value of Korean cultural heritage to audiences at home and around the world.

Wooden Geese on display at RMxSFMOMA’s Bluewater room Destiny Jackson

But Between You and Me doesn’t feel like a celebrity checking another cultural box. If anything, RM seems almost suspicious of the idea that his collection needs to make him look sophisticated. “Do I really need to carry so many unnecessary things that I don’t even need? Have I ended up becoming just a boring, rich snore?” RM said jokingly during his opening remarks to the media. “I’m always drifting and floating somewhere, whether I’m in the U.S. or even when I’m in Seoul, where I was born and raised, and it’s not a very pleasant feeling,” RM remarked. “So I think I’ve leaned on art a lot because of that feeling.”

The answer to his question, as offered by the exhibition, offers little evidence of pretentiousness. Instead, it reveals a mind constantly making connections, jumping between eras, cultural references and visual artists, finding meaning in both the grandiose and the seemingly insignificant.

Split into eight sections titled Bluewater (파아란 물), Friendscape (친구가 있는 풍경), Home (집), Photobuddha (포토붓다!), People (사람들), Passion (열정), I Don’t Know, But I Like It (말로 설명은 안 되는데, 좋아) and Umber (다색), the exhibition serves up a little bit of thought-provoking discourse about certain aspects of one’s state of being. However, during our preview, there was one room in particular that felt like the exhibition’s beating heart—a place where RM, the bombastic musician, and the more pensive Kim Namjoon meet.

RM (Kim Namjoon) of BTS reveals what his @SFMOMA exhibition collaboration, #RMxSFMOMA: Between You and Me, has in store, including 142 artworks from his personal collection:



“I tried to make this exhibition as interesting and new as I could… It makes me very happy that one… pic.twitter.com/SF0NlYGVvs — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 30, 2026

I Don’t Know Why, But I Like It is perhaps the least inclined to behave like a traditional museum gallery. The walls are a deep galaxy blue. Rock formations sit throughout the space. A small model of a modern home with boulders inside is backlit by bright white light. There’s a photograph featuring Doraemon, abstract works with warped faces and hard lines, pixelated imagery, and childlike scribblings by Cy Twombly. One seemingly unassuming portrait is simply a tidy list of anxieties a person might face in their lifetime.

Pikachu animation celluloid at RMxSFMOMA in the I Don’t Know Why, But I Like It room Destiny Jackson

The room’s title comes from RM’s inability to explain every impulse behind his collection. As you enter the room, scribbled on the wall, he explains that he was asked again and again to articulate why he liked the works gathered here, but he couldn’t convey their meaning. “So, I just made a room instead,” he wrote.

It’s an honest take to place on the walls of one of the first exhibitions of its kind inside one of the country’s most high-profile museums. The wall-scroll explanation also reads: “…They’re simply things that I like. But when you think about it, that’s how everyone lives. A captured image, a sentence that passed by, a playlist for working out, a strangely shaped pebble picked up from the beach… even a corner of the heart is, in the end, just each person’s own small exhibition. I don’t know why, I just like it. And honestly, that’s enough.”

But then in the profundity there is Pikachu.

Considering RM’s well-known love for Pokémon, it’s not exactly surprising to see it honored in some way. However, the small animated celluloid depicting the iconic yellow-and-black thunder-magic monster is one of the room’s funniest—and almost unexpected—inclusions.

While speaking to Deadline, co-curator Kim laughed while acknowledging the mouse-type Pokémon just hanging out in the room. “It’s hard for me to pick a favorite piece, but the fact that there’s a Pikachu amidst all of these other brilliant pieces too says a lot about [RM’s] mind.”

Interestingly enough, to RM, the beloved Pikachu seemingly symbolizes the way he grapples with fame, identity and isolation. “This Pikachu looks a little lonely,” RM explained on the museum marker located at the foot of the celluloid. “Usually he’s running, firing thunderbolts, always by your side—but the moment he becomes a cel he drops right out of the story. No background, no next scene, no voice. One expression. Come to think of it, this is the first time he’s ever held still. Even Pikachu needs a break.”

It’s an observation from RM that perhaps unintentionally ties this chaotic room of ideas together, as his own life has rarely afforded him much stillness. In both the literal and figurative sense, this museum stop offers a momentary pause in the middle of BTS’ current 11-month tour, with the group set to embark on its Latin American leg in just a few days. There is something cheekily fitting about an artist and a character, both defined by perpetual motion and popularity, being considered in a moment when they are finally allowed to be still.

During his speech to the media, RM also called himself “a very, very confused person.” Still, what emerges from I Don’t Know Why, But I Like It feels less like confusion than an unusually expansive curiosity. Sure, there’s no obvious linear style, as a string of lights by Felix Gonzalez-Torres sits in the same room as a ceramic vase by Yoshimoto Nara, but the room invites you to pay the same attention to each piece. “My only hope is that this exhibition can be a small but sturdy bridge for many,” RM said.

The many, no doubt, include those outside the BTS stratosphere, but it’s no secret that the exhibition will be a bridge connecting tens of thousands of fans in droves to support their favorite rapper. Even during the media and donor-only preview, BTS fans, known as ARMY, showed out at SFMOMA, handing out handmade gift bags that included stickers, bracelets, postcards, treats, and a fanzine, along with other insider references only fans with years of being entrenched in fandom can appreciate and then share with newcomers. One humorous bookmark, labeled “The Art of Namjooing,” defines this as “the act of living as Kim Namjoon,” listing things he does in his spare time, such as “taking walks through parks, admiring nature, hanging out with crabs and having fun with friends.”

This feeling of ease might be what makes Between You and Me feel so personable. The exhibition acknowledges the enormous machinery of RM’s fame without asking visitors to spend their time admiring it. Instead, it asks them to engage with all types of international art, from the well-known to the unfamiliar, with their own reactions, and perhaps to sit with the emotional and physical connections to things they’ve overlooked in their own lives.

A closer look at some of the pieces on display at @SFMOMA’s #RMxSFMOMA exhibition pic.twitter.com/r1UdwpFtnB — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 30, 2026

RM has spent much of his career creating things for other people to consume through songs, albums, dance moves and performances. Here he is providing a different type of access by showing people the things that made him look twice, evidence of a mind that is always in constant flux, moving, absorbing, questioning, connecting and changing behind all the glitz and glamour of his lifestyle. “People say this is an age when everything is connected. Yet, I still live on the boundaries. Seoul and San Francisco, onstage and beneath the stage, me in front of painting and someone behind it. I have always lived somewhere in between… it would be wonderful if this, too, is a flower blooming at a boundary. It’s OK to walk slowly. Pause wherever your heart comes to rest, catch your breath, and I hope you will take a moment to smell the flowers.” RM wrote on the exhibition wall.

RM may claim to be a little confused about why he likes some of these things. But perhaps that’s the beauty of it. He doesn’t need every piece of the world to resolve into an answer before he lets himself be moved by it telling the media: “In an age where everything is consumed so fast, I believe some of the attitudes of some of the past artists can resonate even more deeply today.”

And between you and me, that’s a message well-received.

title: Nicolas Cage Calls Current MCU A “Glorified WWE,” Wants It To Stop “Cutting To The Wrestling Match”
summary: After spinning his last web in Spider-Noir, Nicolas Cage wants to see the MCU bring better storytelling back to the superhero genre. The Oscar winner compared the MCU’s current slate of projects to “a well-funded and glorified WWE,” following its “marvelous” roots as he discussed the recent cancellation of Spider-Noir after one season at Prime […]
content:
After spinning his last web in Spider-Noir, Nicolas Cage wants to see the MCU bring better storytelling back to the superhero genre.

The Oscar winner compared the MCU’s current slate of projects to “a well-funded and glorified WWE,” following its “marvelous” roots as he discussed the recent cancellation of Spider-Noir after one season at Prime Video.

“It started out, in my view, terrific. Some of the early stories were marvelous, the way that they wove all the threads together and told the different character stories and backstories,” he said in a Q&A at Fan Expo Dallas. “But lately, I do say this with love, when I see these 50+ otherwise intelligent, remarkably gifted thespians putting on these ridiculous outfits and getting ready for the fight—let’s face it, it’s cutting all to the fight—it’s hard for me not to be reminded that the MCU is becoming a well-funded and glorified WWE.

Cage added, “And one of the things I liked about Spider-Noir, was it wasn’t cutting to the fight. It was a detective story. There was a mystery there. And I would like to see it get back to telling the stories and not just cutting to the wrestling match.”

Watch on Deadline

Last month, Prime Video opted not to renew Spider-Noir for a second season as Amazon MGM Studios and Sony Pictures Television explore other Marvel projects in their partnership.

Cage previously reacted to the show’s cancellation after what he called a “perfect” first season, praising his “dangerous, innovative, pop-art Spider-Man” from series creator Oren Uziel.

title: Aaron Sorkin Clarifies He “Was Never Asked” To Omit Trump From ‘The Social Reckoning’ But Film Is “Not A Red-Blue Thing”
summary: Although Facebook has played a big role in recent U.S. politics, Aaron Sorkin didn’t want to make The Social Reckoning a political statement. The Oscar winner noted that although he “was never asked” to omit Trump from his upcoming movie about a young Facebook whistleblower, which premieres Oct. 9, he didn’t want the film to […]
content:
Although Facebook has played a big role in recent U.S. politics, Aaron Sorkin didn’t want to make The Social Reckoning a political statement.

The Oscar winner noted that although he “was never asked” to omit Trump from his upcoming movie about a young Facebook whistleblower, which premieres Oct. 9, he didn’t want the film to become “a red-blue thing.”

“I want to be clear: I was never asked to do that, to not mention Trump by name. I turned in the script and a day or two later met with Tom Rothman, who was full speed ahead on it,” he told Vanity Fair. “And I promised him, unprovoked, that we would not see any Trump signage, no ‘Make America Great Again.'”

Sorkin continued, “The movie is about Facebook’s role and the rise of divisiveness, extremism, and hyper-partisanship in the country. It is not a red-blue thing, even though, obviously, it will be felt that way.”

Watch on Deadline

After The Social Network (2010) recounted Mark Zuckerberg’s creation of Facebook and the controversy that ensued, screenwriter Sorkin returned to write and direct the upcoming sequel, which focuses on a 2021 document leak that exposed harm Facebook caused on society.

Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning’ Leah Gallo/Columbia Pictures/Everett Collection

In The Social Reckoning, Facebook engineer Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) goes to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) with the social media platform’s most guarded secrets. Jeremy Strong, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Billy Magnussen and Betty Gilpin also star.

title: ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ Scores Record-Breaking Season 2 Premiere With Nearly 9 Million Viewers
summary: The second season of the U.K.’s “Celebrity Traitors” is off to a record-breaking start. More than 8.8 million viewers watched Thursday night’s premiere of the BBC’s devious reality show, according to overnight numbers, with viewership peaking at 9 million. In addition, over 50% of people watching TV were tuning into “The Celebrity Traitors,” making it […]
content:
The second season of the U.K.’s “Celebrity Traitors” is off to a record-breaking start.

More than 8.8 million viewers watched Thursday night’s premiere of the BBC‘s devious reality show, according to overnight numbers, with viewership peaking at 9 million. In addition, over 50% of people watching TV were tuning into “The Celebrity Traitors,” making it the top program of the evening.

This marks a new premiere record for “The Traitors” series in the U.K., drawing in around 3 million more viewers than past launches for both the inaugural season of its celebrity version last year and the most recent civilian season. The number will only get bigger as those who missed the first episode catch up in the coming days.

And what a premiere it was. This season of “The Celebrity Traitors” stars an impressive list of names joining host Claudia Winkleman, including Richard E. Grant, Bella Ramsey, Myha’la, Maya Jama, James Acaster, Jerry Hall, James Blunt, Michael Sheen and more. Grant has already proven himself to be a standout with his sheer enthusiasm for the game, immediately causing chaos in the castle. The show is set to air on BBC One and iPlayer every Thursday and Friday at 8 p.m. BST for the next month, with its second episode coming out tonight.

Popular on Variety

Season 5 of the U.K.’s civilian “Traitors” is set to premiere early next year. The franchise has also become hugely successful in the U.S., with Alan Cumming hosting a celebrity version on Peacock, as well as a civilian spinoff called “New Blood” which launched in September.

title: ‘A Talent for Murder’ Director Anton Corbijn Praises Helen Mirren’s Performance as Controversial Author Patricia Highsmith: ‘She’s a Great Jerk!’
summary: In “A Talent for Murder,” director Anton Corbijn takes a closer look at writer Patricia Highsmith. Known for creating everyone’s favorite psychopath Tom Ripley, Highsmith – played by Helen Mirren – became a controversial figure because of her antisemitic and misanthropic statements. “By all accounts, she was much worse than what we show in the […]
content:
In “A Talent for Murder,” director Anton Corbijn takes a closer look at writer Patricia Highsmith.

Known for creating everyone’s favorite psychopath Tom Ripley, Highsmith – played by Helen Mirren – became a controversial figure because of her antisemitic and misanthropic statements.

“By all accounts, she was much worse than what we show in the film. You don’t want her to be completely unlikable. It’s difficult when you don’t actually know the person and base everything on hearsay, but she was a very difficult woman. Also to herself,” he tells Variety.

He enjoyed seeing Mirren, now in her 80s, fully embrace the role of someone who can be, well, a jerk.

Popular on Variety

“She’s a great jerk! I think it’s healthy. It’s never too late to be a bitch. I’m referring to our Highsmith, of course. Luckily, she only killed fictional characters.”

In the film, previously known as “Switzerland” after Joanna Murray-Smith’s play it’s based on – “I thought it would conjure too many images of cows and mountains,” Corbijn says – Highsmith is joined in her Swiss refuge by a young man, Edward (Alden Ehrenreich), who tries to persuade her to write another novel about Ripley.

They don’t exactly bring out the best in each other. Quite the opposite.

“They’re testing how bad people can be and how far they can go. Unfortunately, it’s always further than you’d like to think. Sometimes it has to do with generational trauma that manifests itself, or with human curiosity that leads to certain behaviors. I think it happens quite often: People get curious, and they go too far. That might be the case with Ripley, too.”

Ripley is evil, but he doesn’t look it. In “The American Friend,” “The Talented Mr. Ripley” or Netflix’s show “Ripley,” he knows how to charm his victims. That’s his superpower.

“When evil is obvious, it’s not interesting because you know it’s coming. That’s his strength, and I think that’s the strength of the film. You don’t know if you should like them or not,” notes Corbijn.

“I love how Alden can change in very minimal ways. He can be this nerdy guy, and then he can be a mean killer with cold eyes. We got really lucky with this cast.”

While the film emphasizes that the portrayal of Highsmith is “entirely fictional,” this is not the first time that Corbijn has taken on a real-life protagonist. “Control,” about Joy Division’s singer Ian Curtis, was his directorial breakthrough.

“I knew the guy, so I think it’s a very truthful film. With ‘Life,’ I didn’t know James Dean. He died the same year when I was born, so we never got to meet,” he laughs.

“You just fill in the gaps. But even Helen said that there’s something more mysterious about playing real-life characters than the ones you make up. It’s more complex and more interesting.”

Mirren famously portrayed Elizabeth II in “The Queen” and former Israeli Prime Minister Golda Meir in “Golda.”

“It can be so powerful, too. Now, when I think of Ian, I think of Sam Riley in the film. I’m so much more familiar with him than with the real Ian Curtis!”

Corbijn first gained prominence as a photographer and music video director, working with the likes of Depeche Mode and U2. However, looking at what’s happening in the music and film industry, he can’t help but worry.

“I get very depressed thinking about A.I. replacing so much in cinema, but it’s the same with music. Take ABBA concerts with their ‘avatars’. Is everything really replaceable? It’s dangerous because we all prefer comfort over substance, and that will be our downfall. Needless to say, there’s no A.I. in my film.”

He adds: “I’m really worried about the immediate future because things are changing way too fast. I think we will respond badly to it. And too late.”

He says he feels “quite pessimistic about the world.” He’s not the only one, which might explain why Ripley keeps on returning.

“It’s as if he returns when the world aligns with his thinking, which is terrible. Maybe people are more accepting of murder today?”

title: Charlie Cox to Lead ‘The King’s Ransom’ Play in London
summary: “Daredevil” star Charlie Cox is returning to the London stage this winter to lead “The King’s Ransom,” a new play by Stuart Slade. World premiering at the Donmar Warehouse, “The King’s Ransom” is set in 1977 Memphis and stars Cox as Vince Black, a small-time crook who is offered the opportunity of a lifetime. “The […]
content:
“Daredevil” star Charlie Cox is returning to the London stage this winter to lead “The King’s Ransom,” a new play by Stuart Slade.

World premiering at the Donmar Warehouse, “The King’s Ransom” is set in 1977 Memphis and stars Cox as Vince Black, a small-time crook who is offered the opportunity of a lifetime. “The plan is simple: Kidnap Elvis Presley’s corpse. Stash him in a chest freezer. Collect the million-dollar ransom,” the play’s synopsis says. “Vince assembles a crack team of misfits and dropouts to attempt the heist of the century.”

The ensemble includes “The Inbetweeners” star Blake Harrison as Rusty, Tom Fletcher as Charlie, Matthew Flynn as Mr. Bluefield, Leo Patrick as Jessie Lee, Jenny Rainsford as Rhonda/ Jenny, Christopher Short as Elvis, Cherrelle Skeete as Mike and Ronnie Yorke as Red, with the role of Martha played by Ruby Barker, Eira Kay and Trixie Willis.

Popular on Variety

Matthew Dunster (“2:22: A Ghost Story,” “The Hunger Games on Stage”) directs. “The King’s Ransom” will open on Dec. 16, with previews starting Dec. 5, and runs through Feb. 6, 2027.

Cox previously starred in the 2010 production of “The Prince of Homburg” at the Donmar Warehouse. His other theater credits include the West End revival of Harold Pinter’s “Betrayal” in 2019, which he transferred with to Broadway.

“The King’s Ransom” creative team includes set designer Anna Fleischle, costume designer Jean Chan, lighting designer Sally Ferguson, sound designer Holly Khan, illusion designer Chris Cox, fight and intimacy directors Ruth Cooper-Brown and Rachel Bown-Williams of Rc-Annie, and casting director Lotte Hines CDG.

title: Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy to Depart at Warner Bros. Following Paramount Close
summary: Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy’s term as chiefs of Warner Bros. is coming to an end. Multiple sources told Variety that De Luca and Abdy will not be part of David Ellison’s management team after the merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closes. The landmark $110 billion pact is expected to be […]
content:
Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy’s term as chiefs of Warner Bros. is coming to an end.

Multiple sources told Variety that De Luca and Abdy will not be part of David Ellison’s management team after the merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closes. The landmark $110 billion pact is expected to be finalized on Oct. 6.

Paramount film heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are reported to oversee both movie studios, which will release 30 movies a year, per the provisions of the deal. It’s unclear if De Luca and Abdy will remain for a transitionary period.

The news comes almost one year to the date when WBD CEO and president David Zaslav announced De Luca and Abdy’s contracts were being renewed at the studio, following the massive box office successes of Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners,” “A Minecraft Movie” and “Weapons.” Then, Warner Bros. tied the all-time studio record with 11 Academy Awards from an industry-leading 30 nominations, including a best picture win for Paul Thomas Anderson’s “One Battle After Another.”

Popular on Variety

Ellison is keeping his new leadership structure close to the vest, and despite Cindy Holland’s exit as head of streaming for Paramount+, the company has yet to confirm Casey Bloys will ascend to the top streaming job in the new combined structure. However, it is known that Ellison tapped former Mattel CEO Ynon Kriez to serve as co-CEO, overseeing day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses.

Puck first reported news of the executives’ impending exit. Paramount and Warner Bros. did not immediately return a request for comment.

title: ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: Paul Thomas Anderson Directs a Rapturous Solo Concert Movie Built Around the Songs — and Haunting Sound — of Cameron Winter
summary: The slow rolling piano echo through the hall like a rhapsody from the deep. The sound is rich, lustrous, bottom-heavy, grand. And that voice! Winter sings in a low baritone (and occasionally a high one) of astonishing power, the notes hanging there in a suspended quaver so bold it’s hypnotic.
content:
You want a concert movie to sound great, and plenty of them do. But I don’t think I’ve encountered a concert film that casts the precise kind of sonorous spell that “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” does. Directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, the movie, which had its premiere tonight at the New York Film Festival, is a record of the solo performance that Cameron Winter gave in front of a packed audience at Carnegie Hall on Dec. 11, 2025. The movie in only 75 minutes long, and it consists entirely of Winter seated at a Steinway grand piano, singing his gorgeous meditative trance tunes, but I swear you’ve never heard a sound quite like this.

The slow rolling piano echoes through the hall like a rhapsody from the deep. The sound is rich, lustrous, bottom-heavy, grand. And that voice! Winter sings in a low baritone (and occasionally a high one) of astonishing power, the notes hanging there in a suspended quaver so bold it’s hypnotic. At different moments, he’ll remind you of a great many other singers. At times he’s a low-octave Thom Yorke, his lost-in-the-haze midnight rapture is like Tom Waits minus the gravel, and there are strong echoes of early Springsteen — the plaintive bard of “Incident on 57th Street” — in his soaring vocal caress, and the wide vibrato of it. The concert may remind you, at times, of John Cale’s great 1992 live album “Fragments of a Rainy Season.” But the artist the Cameron Winter of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” is most magically reminiscent of is Bob Dylan — the Dylan who let the words pour out of him in a blissful torrent, and sang them as if possessed. Winter, like Dylan, isn’t just singing. He’s crafting pop songs that add up to an incantation, a rhapsody, a prayer.

Popular on Variety

At the start of the concert, Winter, very tall, in a black shirt and pants, with shaggy greasy unkempt indie hair (with his thick eyebrows and doleful countenance, he suggests a solemn version of Nicolas Cage in “Leaving Las Vegas”), lopes onstage and stands in front of the piano, introducing himself with what looks like a slight bow, though it’s so reticent it might just be a hipster stoop. Winter, of course, is the frontman of Geese, the indie-band-of-the-moment who, on the tuneful/tuneless scale, reside somewhere between Wilco and Arcade Fire. Geese are okay, but they’ve been overpraised. Winter’s 2024 solo record, “Heavy Metal,” is much more compelling; it gives voice to the meditative soul inside the noise rocker. “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” is a showcase for that Cameron Winter, the chanteuse of sadness and faith.

The piano is poised at a slight angle on the bare Carnegie stage, but basically Winter has his back to the audience. It’s not a hostile gesture; it’s a sign of how much he wants the music to dominate. But a movie is a whole other thing, and Paul Thomas Anderson, directing his second music-performance film (after “Junun,” a 2015 Jonny Greenwood-goes-to-India trifle), has crafted a visually spellbinding movie that’s never showy or grandiose. He frames the piano on the stage from different angles, and he brings us up close to Cameron Winter and right into his emotional orbit. There are stage-eye-view shots of the audience (the four balconies of Carnegie Hall separated by three rows of light), and the whole movie is suffused with an orange-yellow glow, as if all of Carnegie were lit by candlelight. It’s a classical sunset church vibe, and it matches Winter’s music, which is all about mystery and heartbreak, which he sings of with a beauty that makes it inseparable from joy.

I could sit here and pretend that I know what Cameron Winter’s lyrics mean, but the truth is they’re often the kind of suggestive poetry that’s diminished by being overanalyzed. The meaning resides in how he sings them, his passion ringing out like a deep dark bell, with shades of accusation and awe running through the performance. He hooks you from the opening number, “It All Fell in the River” (which I think is about the catharsis of tears), he carries you through “If You Turn Back Now” (a relationship drama that finds room for an inquisition on the devil), and he makes you feel the emasculated belittlement of “$0,” but also the stirring declaration that “God is actually real.” The movie culminates in a performance of “Take It With You” (“I found a keepsake of you by the window in the kitchen, babe,/Take it with you when you leave”) that channels the scalded romanticism of Dylan at his most majestic.

Cameron Winter’s solo songs are often beautiful, but most of them move at the same slow tempo, and they don’t have a verse-chorus conventionality. “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” has the feel of a slow-motion song cycle, like Leonard Cohen’s first album. The movie might have been a touch lugubrious were it not for that voice of Winter’s, which is a miraculous instrument: indie in a low-slung operatic way. In “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall,” he’s possessed by the music he’s singing, so lost in it that you hope he’s never found.

title: Penelope Ann Miller, Otmara Marrero Film ‘Made Clean’ First Project For Nashville-Based Cinema Country
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Filmmaker Seth Christian, whose previous producer credits include the 2020 crime drama Echo Boomers starring Patrick Schwarzenegger and Michael Shannon, has launched Cinema Country. The Nashville-based independent production company is “dedicated to human-centered storytelling and socially impactful filmmaking” under its Films For Impact label. The company’s initial slate of features will explore addiction, obesity, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Filmmaker Seth Christian, whose previous producer credits include the 2020 crime drama Echo Boomers starring Patrick Schwarzenegger and Michael Shannon, has launched Cinema Country.

The Nashville-based independent production company is “dedicated to human-centered storytelling and socially impactful filmmaking” under its Films For Impact label.

The company’s initial slate of features will explore addiction, obesity, and social media.

“Cinema Country is committed to making ‘Films For Impact’ — films that entertain, inspire meaningful conversations, and offer value to culture and humanity,” said Christian. “We’re not chasing trends or simply looking for what’s popular. We’re looking for unique, fresh stories that connect with audiences, shine a light on important issues, and serve as a voice for healing.”

First up for development on Cinema Country’s slate is Made Clean, a faith-inspired drama already in post-production that follows a mother battling addiction while trying to raise her teenage daughter and confront generational trauma.

Watch on Deadline

Directed by D. Erik Parks (Why We Breathe), the film stars Penelope Ann Miller (Carlito’s Way), Otmara Marrero (Start Up), Glenn Morshower (Transformers: Dark of the Moon), Ava Torres (Chicago Fire), Jacob Alexander (Echo Boomers), and Cherrie McRae (Deadly Deception). Parks and Christian co-wrote the screenplay.

The synopsis reads: “Tonya (Marrero), a hardworking single mother, loses her job after failing a drug test, prompting her teenage daughter, Kimberly (Torres), to run away. Desperate to change, Tonya turns to her estranged mother, Wanda (Miller), who offers little concern and instead accuses her of repeating the same destructive patterns that shaped her own childhood.

“Horrified by the comparison, Tonya finds a new job with another cleaning service and begins rebuilding her life with the help of its compassionate business owner. But when a traumatic encounter sends Tonya spiraling back into addiction—and back into the dangerous orbit of her drug-dealing ex-husband, Ronny (Alexander)—her fragile progress begins to unravel. When Kimberly’s own hidden struggle lands her in the hospital, mother and daughter are forced to confront the pain they have both kept buried.”

On deck is Hungerland, an upcoming feature that confronts obesity and the damaging effects of America’s food system, and Extension, which examines the dangers of social media and its link to many teen suicides.

“Going through something that changes your life forces you to look at what really matters,” said Christian, who two years ago suffered a stroke. “For me, it changed the way I thought about filmmaking. I wanted to build something that reflected the kinds of movies I wanted to see and the kind of industry I wanted to be part of. Cinema Country grew out of that experience.”

On Made Clean, Christian achieved the film’s $1-2M budget by assembling a network of equity partners that included a 50-person production crew, equipment-rental companies, camper owners, restaurants and other contributors.

Rather than simply providing goods or services, participating partners received a percentage of the film’s future revenue in exchange for their contributions. The approach allowed Cinema Country to direct a greater portion of its available cash budget toward talent while building a community of stakeholders.

“The model reflects my broader vision for Cinema Country: creating a more collaborative approach to independent filmmaking in which filmmakers, businesses, service providers and community partners can all have a meaningful stake in the projects they help bring to life,” commented Christian.

title: BBC Staff Revolt Over Job Cuts By Posting Laughing Emojis During Management Call
summary: EXCLUSIVE: BBC employees expressed their defiance over job cuts by posting laughing emojis during a management call, in which the corporation’s £500 million ($660M) savings plan was discussed. In a sign of growing staff unrest over the steady stream of cost-cutting announcements across the BBC, some workers made their feelings known on a Microsoft Teams […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: BBC employees expressed their defiance over job cuts by posting laughing emojis during a management call, in which the corporation’s £500 million ($660M) savings plan was discussed.

In a sign of growing staff unrest over the steady stream of cost-cutting announcements across the BBC, some workers made their feelings known on a Microsoft Teams call earlier this week.

Leaders in BBC Media Tech, the unit that powers iPlayer and other online services, were detailing plans to slash 110 roles when employees started posting a “storm” of laughing-crying and other emojis.

The protest came as the BBC braces to announce further cuts next week, with director general Matt Brittin planning to address staff in a Town Hall on Wednesday, expected to be chaired by Radio 4 Today show host Anna Foster.

Watch on Deadline

As first revealed by Deadline, insiders expect Brittin to confirm TV and radio network closures after delaying plans to announce the changes this week. BBC Three is widely expected to be in the firing line, while there is also concern about Radio 4 Extra being among the services under threat.

Multiple sources confirmed that the emoji revolt took place this week, with one person saying it was hard for managers to ignore the characters as they drifted across the screen when they spoke. Insiders said questions and comments are usually locked down during internal calls, but the emoji function was still open to workers — and it was used.

Kelly Kowal, the BBC chief operations and portfolio officer, was interrupted by the blizzard of emojis, and she later voiced her displeasure about the events, as well as the tone of discussions in staff Slack forums.

In a Slack message, reviewed by Deadline and published in full below, Kowal said: “I want to be clear that some of the comments and behaviour during the discussion were not appropriate and fell short of the standards of respect and constructive challenge I expect from us as a team.”

She continued: “We absolutely should challenge each other, disagree and have robust conversations – that’s important. But it needs to be done respectfully and professionally.

“Personal or dismissive comments, as well as posting images or GIFs in response to what was being discussed, is not acceptable. More importantly, it was disrespectful to our colleagues who were directly affected from yesterday’s announcement and detracted from what should have been a serious and constructive discussion.”

Andy Ryan, director of technology support and engineering operations, told staff in a separate call that the emojis were “challenging behaviour” and that the BBC would confront “individuals” to discuss their actions.

The BBC Media Tech job cuts are part of a fresh £37M round of savings after the division delivered £42M of cuts earlier this year. A further £23M of savings are planned for early 2027, meaning BBC Media Tech will contribute £102M of savings to the corporation’s overall target of £500M, which the BBC must deliver because of the growing number of Brits who are refusing to pay for the licence fee.

The BBC tech division will embrace AI to reduce costs, according to Kowal. The unit is also expected to focus on fewer products and push more resource into boosting iPlayer. Brittin, the BBC director general, has been candid about the need to improve iPlayer recommendations and user experience.

The BBC declined to comment.

title: ‘Hollow Moon’: Sci-Fi With Jena Malone & Dermot Mulroney Gets Sales Deal & New Title
