It’s a classical-musician movie. It’s a mild romantic mystery. It’s Tony Gilroy fiddling around with pure movie form. (He’s a sly orchestrator of big-screen storytelling.) But 19 years after “Michael Clayton,” he’s still looking for a subject that will allow him to do what he did so masterfully in that movie: heighten our perceptions of the world along with our emotions, until they become one.

title: George Cheeks May Be Poised for Expanded TV Role at Skydance Post Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
summary: Paramount TV media chair George Cheeks, whose domain has included all of CBS in addition to the Paramount cable networks, is said to be in line for an expanded oversight at the newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity (which will be named “Skydance,” the company revealed Friday). Skydance would not comment, but Cheeks has been seen […]
content:
Paramount TV media chair George Cheeks, whose domain has included all of CBS in addition to the Paramount cable networks, is said to be in line for an expanded oversight at the newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity (which will be named “Skydance,” the company revealed Friday).

Skydance would not comment, but Cheeks has been seen as a strong lieutenant overseeing the TV properties under Paramount ever since Skydance took control of the company last August. Prior to that, Cheeks was one of the three co-CEOs of Paramount Global — and was the only one of that triumvirate to make the transition to the new company.

Speculation and rumors of how the structure on the TV network and studio side might play out have been heavy over the past few days, now that the question of how the streaming structure at the merged company has been settled (with HBO boss Casey Bloys on top and Paramount direct-to-consumer head Cindy Holland exiting).

Popular on Variety

Many of the questions in the more traditional Hollywood world of TV networks and studios — still a hefty revenue driver — have centered on what roles Skydance head David Ellison might have in mind for Warner Bros. TV Group and WBD U.S. Networks chairman/CEO Channing Dungey and Cheeks. Both execs are well-liked and respected, and both boast tremendous domains, consisting of both studios and networks.

One scenario making the rounds has Cheeks potentially overseeing all of the vast TV holdings of the combined company, but so far, there’s no firm confirmation and a final structure isn’t expected to be announced until next week.

All eyes will also be on what role Ellison picks for Dungey, whose tenure at Warner Bros. TV Group continues to be extremely successful. Under Dungey, the studio produces more than 80 original series for more than 20 platforms, including HBO, HBO Max and others, with series like “Ted Lasso,” “Abbott Elementary”, “The Bachelor” franchise, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” “The Jennifer Hudson Show,” “The Pitt,” “Running Point,” “Shrinking,” “Rooster,” “The Voice” and the upcoming “Harry Potter” series. So far this year, the division has landed 13 new series orders and 13 series renewals, while “The Pitt” just landed six Emmys — including its second for outstanding drama.

Dungey also took on oversight of WBD’s U.S. Networks in 2025, including Discovery Channel, Food Network, HGTV, Investigation Discovery, TLC, Adult Swim, Animal Planet, Cartoon Network, Cooking Channel, HLN, OWN, Science Channel, TBS, TNT, Travel Channel, Tru TV and Turner Classic Movies.

When Variety spoke to Dungey last month, she said she had met with Ellison in more of a “getting to know you” setting. Beyond that, she expressed her desire to stick with the company post-merger: “I love my team at Warner Bros. Television Group. I love our shows, our talent. And I’ve become very happy in my U.S. networks role, which was something that I didn’t see coming almost two years ago. The best-case scenario for me is something that allows me to continue to play around in both of these spaces.”

Among the possible setups that observers have spitballed was the idea of splitting their oversight between networks and studios. But if Cheeks does take control of the entire TV business, the biggest question will be whether Dungey will opt to remain and report to him. Insiders say the two have a good rapport, particularly as Warner Bros. TV has been a hefty supplier of series to CBS over the years — including the successful crop of Chuck Lorre comedies that have aired on the Eye.

Beyond that, the question also remains as to how Warner Bros. TV (run by president Brett Paul and creative affairs president Clancy Collins White), CBS Studios (run by president David Stapf), and Paramount TV Studios (run by Matt Thunell) will all be integrated.

CBS Studios is also a major enterprise, producing more than 60 series, while Paramount TV Studios has a hefty slate including the Taylor Sheridan shows.

Currently, Stapf and Thunell report to Cheeks, while Paul and Collins White report to Dungey. There could be a scenario where Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios and Paramount TV Studios continue as separate labels.

Cheeks had previously been president and CEO of CBS, having joined Paramount in March 2020. This repped his second stint there, having first joined MTV Networks (a part of the then-Viacom company) in 1998 and later taking on roles including exec VP of business affairs and general counsel for the Viacom Music and Entertainment Groups.

Cheeks later moved to NBC in 2012 as president of business operations and late-night programming, then became co-chairman of NBC Entertainment and later as vice chairman of NBCUniversal Content Studios.

Deadline was first to report of Cheeks’ potential new role at Skydance.

title: ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion)
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Digger,” in theaters now via Warner Bros. When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch? So often the kiss of death for a feature is boredom; that feeling you’ve seen the same story many times before, the actors are checked out, there’s no visual panache. That’s […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Digger,” in theaters now via Warner Bros.

When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch?

So often the kiss of death for a feature is boredom; that feeling you’ve seen the same story many times before, the actors are checked out, there’s no visual panache. That’s not the case with “Digger.” While it’s shaping up to be a box office disaster, the movie is anything but dull. Tom Cruise leads the cast in acting to the rafters, DP Emmanuel Lubezki keeps the camera moving and director Alejandro G. Iñárritu injects plenty of swagger in the proceedings.

Unfortunately, the film’s opening — an extended introduction to Cruise’s ambitious oilman Digger Rockwell — is so in-your-face that it sags under the weight. Cruise is in grotesque prosthetics, eager to show us as quickly as possible how uncouth Digger is: He eats from the same can of sardines as his beloved cat, his butt crack is seen in plain view of his maid, his comb-over wisps wildly.

Popular on Variety

It’s a clichéd character surrounded by other bobbling caricatures that enter and exit the rooms of his mansion, flailing wildly as Digger learns that his oil company might have inadvertently caused a climate-based global disaster. It’s shrill and tired, and despite the best intentions of the filmmakers to cause provocation around environmentalism, it’s about as subtle as Cruise turning to the camera and screaming, “DO YOU GET IT?!?” Ultimately, the poster’s promise of “a comedy of catastrophic proportions” seems more like a threat than a guarantee of “Dr. Strangelove”-esque genius.

But then, an interesting twist happens. No, “Digger” isn’t a musical, but rather reveals that everything we’ve seen so far is a group of actors rehearsing an ambitious play about Digger called “Fossil Fools.” We’re witnessing the tech rehearsal hours before the show is set to debut in front of an audience, and Cruise drops his broad southern accent, revealing himself as Curtis Markson, the star of the show who has difficulty finding the satirical rhythm.

It’s an engagingly meta turn, and shows much more of Cruise’s psyche than audiences might expect. During a teflon press tour hyping “Digger,” journalists weren’t able to conjure anything personal or interesting from him. But during a scene where Cruise argues with “Fossil Fools” director Hannah (Sophie Wilde) about satire versus real-world events, the artifice of Cruise’s fat suit and cowboy boots melts away, and the fire in his eyes that made iconic performances in films like “Magnolia” and “Eyes Wide Shut” blaze returns in flashes.

It also helps to contextualize Iñárritu’s vision of satire itself. Some reviews of “Digger” have knocked the very idea of satirical films in 2026. After all, how can anything feel larger-than-life in the Trump era? But given the put-on-a-show staging, the film’s structure adds further firepower to standout scenes like Digger holding court in the United Nations, tap-dancing around a global community ready to feed him to the wolves after he doubles down on his wrongdoing.

The showcase scene is emphasized by the fact that everything is underwritten by Digger’s real-life nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), who bought the rights to “Fossil Fools” and used his vast wealth to fund the production. His motivations are many, as he implies that he’s doing it out of a mix of penance, flagellation and tribute to his family name. But ultimately he’s a benefactor of the arts. The themes make it impossible to ignore the real-life soap opera currently happening at “Digger” studio Warner Bros., where new owner David Ellison swears he bought the company for all the right reasons.

“Digger” ends on a somber note, with the audience methodically putting on gas masks and emptying the gorgeous theater, stepping into the dystopian world that remains after Digger’s environmental disaster. Flooded streets, discarded cars and military police are all around, until the camera tilts to the sky and the soundtrack becomes overwhelmed with the natural noises of wild animals. It’s a chilling wrap, as well as a dour end to what appears to be the last Warner Bros. film ever released.

Not all of the elements tied to the twist work — Curtis’ search for his daughter’s missing flight during the tech rehearsal is curiously underbaked — but at least it teases a flurry of ideas instead of drowning in clumsy dialogue. At its best, it recalls Charlie Kaufman’s far superior 2008 film “Synecdoche, New York,” in which Philip Seymour Hoffman is a theater director who, in the pursuit of truth, creates a full-scale recreation of New York City in a warehouse in order to accurately reflect life. It, too, looks at the idea of understanding larger truths through a stage production, but is more clever and sincere.

Ultimately, even the decision to add another layer, becoming a story about art just as much as one about the climate crisis, doesn’t escalate “Digger” into must-see territory. But the cross section of cinephiles who will be compelled to catch it in theaters — Cruise completists, flop aficionados, rubberneckers who want to see the world burn — will have more to chew on than the artifice presented at the beginning.

title: John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’
summary: John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as he takes over the new Skydance. “Come on, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans need and what the industry needs. […]
content:
John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as he takes over the new Skydance.

“Come on, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans need and what the industry needs. Think of others for a change.”

John Leguizamo has a message for Skydance chief David Ellison:



“C’mon, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans and the industry needs. Think of others for a change.” pic.twitter.com/DjEUzXvWja — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026

Although the terms of the merger include Paramount-WBD being prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in California for at least five years. Leguizamo said “that’s still not enough.”

“You got an end date. You got an expiration date. That’s not cool,” he said. “People have to plan for the rest of their lives. They plan for five years, and then what?”

Popular on Variety

“…The industry belongs in L.A.,” Leguizamo said Friday at the Critics Choice Association’s 6th Annual Celebración of Cinema & Television, where he was honored with the Career Achievement Award. “We need to support it and grow it. Rebuild it and add to it. Not subtract.”

John Leguizamo says it’s “despicable” and “heartless” that David Ellison’s Skydance is threatening to move Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s film and TV production out of Los Angeles.



When Variety’s @marcmalkin brought up the five-year production commitment in Ellison’s… pic.twitter.com/yj2YwtwAcG — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026

In April, Leguizamo was one of more than 4,000 film and TV stars and creatives who signed an open letter opposing Paramount Skydance’s pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

“We are deeply concerned by indications of support for this merger that prioritize the interests of a small group of powerful stakeholders over the broader public good,” said the letter, which was published by the New York Times and available on the website BlocktheMerger.com. “The integrity, independence, and diversity of our industry would be grievously compromised. Competition is essential for a healthy economy and a healthy democracy. So is thoughtful regulation and enforcement.”

Other signatories included Joaquin Phoenix, Ben Stiller, Kristen Stewart, Robert De Niro, Sofia Coppola, Florence Pugh, Pedro Pascal, Edward Norton, Atsuko Okatsuka, Adam McKay, Alan Cumming, Alyssa Milano, Boots Riley, Bryan Cranston, Cynthia Nixon, Damon Lindelof, David Fincher, Denis Villeneuve, Elliot Page, Glenn Close, Jane Fonda, JJ Abrams, Jason Bateman, John Leguizamo, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Margaret Cho, Mark Ruffalo, Noah Wyle, Patti Lupone, Ramy Youssef, Rosario Dawson, Rosie O’Donnell, Ted Danson, Tiffany Haddish, Tig Notaro, Yorgos Lanthimos and Yvette Nicole Brown.

Leguizamo also talked about receiving the Career Achievement Award. “It means they five that to you when you think your career is over,” he cracked, before continuing, “I’ve been in it for four decades, a long time, a lot of sacrifices, a lot of great things, a lot of pain and it feels like, ‘Oh, wow. It was worth for something. People notice and recognize what you’ve done and contributed to cinema.’”

John Leguizamo calls “Mission: Impossible — Reckoning” a “bomb so expensive they teach it in business school.”



via The Critics Choice Association's 6th Annual Celebración Of Cinema & Television pic.twitter.com/Z7NLXqG8sW — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026

He delivered emotional remarks while accepting the award from director Gregory Nava. “I will not be finished until every Latin child in this country can turn on a screen,” he said, tearing up. “When a Latin child in this country can turn on a screen and see their own face, their own name, their grandma’s accent, not getting arrested, not dying in minute nine [of an action movie], just living, just being a whole person, that’s the dream. It’s an embarrassingly small one, but they’ve made us fight over it for over a hundred years. So keep creating. Keep failing forward and don’t’ let anyone every quiet your voice, including the one inside your head telling you that you’re not good enough. That voice is a fucking liar and it doesn’t know what the hell it’s talking about.”

Honorees also included Aimee Carrero (Supporting Actress Award – Series; “Your Friends & Neighbors”), Beth de Araújo (Breakthrough Director Award; “Josephine”), Inde Navarrette (Breakthrough Actress Award – Film; “Obsession”), James Ortiz (Innovator Award; “Project Hail Mary”), Javier Calvo & Javier Ambrossi, popularly known as “Los Javis” (Director Award; “La Bola Negra”), Judy Reyes (Trailblazer Award; “High Potential”), Laysla De Oliveira (Breakthrough Actress Award – Series; “Lioness”), Oscar Nuñez (Vanguard Award; “The Paper”), Peter Dager (Rising Star Award; “Stick”) and Rodrigo Teixeira (Producer Award; “Paper Tiger”).

title: Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’
summary: It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and preparations for the closing of Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery next week. The industry is obsessively speculating on who survives the merger to be named to David Ellison’s executive […]
content:
It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and preparations for the closing of Skydance‘s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery next week.



The industry is obsessively speculating on who survives the merger to be named to David Ellison‘s executive leadership team come Monday. But first thing’s first — Ellison addressed his troops on the combined company’s new name. It’s Skydance, same as the company Ellison founded 20 years ago, and will be the parent to existing brands like Warner Bros., Paramount and HBO.



“As we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations,” Ellison wrote to staff in a memo obtained by Variety. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.”



Remain they will, though under various layers of oversight. Paramount Pictures leaders Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein will be elevated to an expansive creative post, multiple sources tell Variety, overseeing heads of individual film labels across both companies (like New Line stalwart Richard Brener). With this week’s exit of Paramount+ streaming head Cindy Holland, Casey Bloys is the presumptive ruler of all streaming at Skydance. The company has yet to make anything official.



Variety confirmed late Thursday night that Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group heads Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca are out. The decision shocked them, insiders said, though another power player with knowledge of the duo remarked that if they were surprised, “they’re the only ones.” Their fate has been one of the biggest question marks looming over the entire deal. Timing wasn’t on their side, as the motion picture group stacked dizzying losses for WBD this year (despite a banner 2025). Another source added that Ellison personally spoke to the pair on Friday. Today is thought to be their last day on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank.



While Ellison won’t get the keys to WBD until next week’s formal close, dealmaking activity is surging. Goldberg and Greenstein have been reaching out to key talent at Warner Bros. (like Margot Robbie and her LuckyChap partners) to establish continuity. Another knowledgeable source said that wheels are already turning to lock in a sequel to Greta Gerwig‘s “Barbie,” which we previously reported had flatlined over costs. Keep in mind, Ellison just tapped former Mattel CEO Ynon Kriez to be the co-CEO at the new combined company.

“There’s no way ‘Barbie 2’ doesn’t happen,” said the source.

Popular on Variety

Read Ellison’s full Skydance memo below:

Team,



I am excited to share the new name of our combined company, Skydance.



We chose this name for a few important reasons. First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.



Of course, Skydance also carries deep meaning for me. I chose the name for my own studio 20 years ago because I wanted something truly personal that also represented limitless possibility. The personal part came from my love of flight: skydancing is another name for aerobatic flying. The possibility came from the cosmos, which to me represents boundless potential and the large-canvas storytelling of cinema. Even our original logo reflected that idea, with each letter of Skydance representing a planet revolving around the sun. From the beginning, the name was meant to capture what great storytelling can do: transport people to places they might never otherwise go and take us beyond the limits of the world we know — and even our own imaginations. That sense of scale, discovery and ambition feels especially fitting for what we are building today.



We have big goals for Skydance, and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks. At the same time, we will honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special — giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.



Welcome to Skydance. I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together.



David

title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Hits All The Right Notes In Tony Gilroy’s Lyrical Love Letter To The Music Of The Movies – New York Film Festival
summary: It has been 14 years since Tony Gilroy last directed a feature film, 2012’s The Bourne Legacy. Before that was Duplicity and in 2007 his sensational Oscar-nominated Michael Clayton. He has been busy though, notably the critically acclaimed TV series Andor, but it is good to see his rare sophisticated storytelling back on the big […]
content:
It has been 14 years since Tony Gilroy last directed a feature film, 2012’s The Bourne Legacy. Before that was Duplicity and in 2007 his sensational Oscar-nominated Michael Clayton. He has been busy though, notably the critically acclaimed TV series Andor, but it is good to see his rare sophisticated storytelling back on the big screen with the compelling journey of a lifelong cellist whose nomad-like life reaches a crescendo and turning point after years of following the music professionally and personally.

Behemoth!, which had its world premiere today at the New York Film Festival, is the rare movie set in the world of Hollywood music soundstages and it undoubtedly is a love letter to this crucial, usually final, aspect of the production process. But its central focus is on the family and romantic ties of one musician, Alex Serian (Pedro Pascal), who was born to be in an orchestra — in fact he couldn’t escape it — and that has taken its toll on this man for whom music is the one and only steady beat in his life, if not his heart.

Alex’s grandfather was a session musician for movies who died playing on one in 1959; his absent father, Peter (Hank Azaria), also was a composer for cartoons and television, if not a creatively satisfied one; his mother Ginnie (Jo Beth Williams) was a successful musician herself; as was his brother Andy (Will Arnett), who had a taste of fame in a ’90s rock band. In many ways the devotion to their professional life all took a toll on this family, and in Alex’s case turned him inward — a traveling cello player drifting from city to city, and relationship to relationship, being on the road the only real life he knew, his true potential never completely met.

Watch on Deadline

Now after 20 years he is returning to Los Angeles, getting day work on a number of movie-scoring sessions but also dealing with family issues including the failing health of his mother, his brother’s quirkiness, and perhaps the biggest lingering question he has still in his life via an encounter with a 15- year-old prodigy, Viviana Glenn (Alexa Swinton), who not only has a huge following on the pop circuit (think Billie Eilish) but who also has now been called in to replace the composer on the movie Behemoth! (a code name for the secret film the are working on).

All of this is played out in non-linear fashion as we meet Alex on a session for a movie, but as he plays the notes, Gilroy’s script goes to flashbacks of his earlier life, back and forth between present day and various years, jobs and romantic liaisons. First we get a look at his past romantic entanglements as one woman yells at him complaining about another she discovers he slept with. That one is a funny bit with a determined Carol Spedding (Olivia Wilde), with whom Alex had a fling in Chicago, but is now taking things overboard insisting he made a huge mistake breaking it off. This woman is just one boiling bunny removed from a restraining order and Wilde amusingly plays it for all its worth.

In another flashback in Dallas we meet fellow musician Nadia Hynes (Eva Victor), who is involved sexually with the emotionally reserved Alex while at the same time committed to another very wealthy man, Dennis Glenn (Matthew Lillard). Cutting to six years later she has tragically died and Alex finds himself invited to her funeral, where her very young daughter Viviana demonstrates her unique talents with a piano composition. Alex begins to get a nagging feeling this girl could actually be his daughter from that long-ago relationship. Her musical abilities are just one clue. While at the funeral he runs into an old flame and close friend of Nadia (Margarita Levieva), leading both again to the bedroom. It won’t be the last time he visits this mansion as his quest for the truth leads him back in a totally different guise.

Gilroy skillfully weaves all these vignettes in and out, each with its own particular musical theme as again it is music always leading the way through the maze of Alex Serian’s life. To do this no single composer was hired to create the all-important score, but rather nine well-known maestros with distinct talents — Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandon Roberts and Alan Silvestri — who together make up The Behemoth! Collective, and who serve up a musical score that, to my ears, is hands down the year’s best. The memorable original song written for the fictional Viviana, “Your God Is Sleeping,” could be a major hit. Combined with magnificent sound design, Behemoth! is a feast for the ears. A total of 303 AFM musicians in Los Angeles were used in the musical sequences. And for all the talk of L.A.’s sad production decline as a shooting location, Gilroy has delivered a winning antidote for that as the City Of Angels has never looked so good.

Pascal, utterly convincing as this accomplished musician, subtly plays Alex in a low-key style with no showboating or anything that rings false in a portrayal where he simply becomes this wandering soul in search of himself after years of denial. The supporting players (Carmen Cuba was casting director) could not be better. Victor (Sorry, Baby) is quite good as Nadia, nailing the complicated feelings of someone married to her music like Alex but confused in love. Kaya Ralls is a complete delight as Bronte, a young fellow musician Alex mentors; Swinton as the 15 year old Viviana is superb; Williams is equally impressive as Alex’s mother in two poignant scenes 10 years apart; Azaria as Alex’s dad is terrific, seen via a brutally honest video letter Alex discovers 25 years after it was recorded; and Wilde and Arnett are in for lighter moments that offer a nice balance to the heavier ones. Erik Griffin also has some good moments as the orchestra manager.

In the end though, Behemoth! is not just a revealing character study of a man ultimately looking for his true place in the world, but also a gorgeous and glorious tribute to those who make the music that help make movies like this one so much richer.

Producers are Gilroy, Sanne Wohlenberg and John Gilroy (who also did the complex editing for the film).

Title: Behemoth!

Festival: New York Film Festival

Distributor: Searchlight

Release date: December 4, 2026

Director-screenwriter: Tony Gilroy

Cast: Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde, Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams, Margarita Levieva, Hank Azaria, Will Arnett, Matthew Lillard

Running time: 2 hr 7 mins

title: Michael De Luca & Pamela Abdy: When They Are Leaving Warner Bros & What’s Next For Them
summary: Warner Bros Motion Picture Chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy’s last day will be Tuesday, which essentially is Day 1 of Skydance, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros company. The move ends months of speculation as to whether the duo would make the post-merger jump, given the down box office year they had with $448.4M domestic […]
content:
Warner Bros Motion Picture Chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy‘s last day will be Tuesday, which essentially is Day 1 of Skydance, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros company.

The move ends months of speculation as to whether the duo would make the post-merger jump, given the down box office year they had with $448.4M domestic for the January 1-October 1 period, off from their milestone $4.3B last year, not to mention this weekend’s $125M-$160M+ Tom Cruise bomb, Digger, which will be lucky to open even at $10M domestic.

There were some insiders who were skeptical about De Luca and Abdy. From what we’ve been told, the duo were blindsided and upset to learn about their fates from Thursday night’s reports without ever receiving a phone call from Skydance co-CEO David Ellison. There was an expectation about them that they’d at least walk into the newly combined studio, much like they did at the new Amazon MGM Studios. The notion was that De Luca and Abdy would continue to oversee edits, filmmaker relations, marketing and distribution of the prized 39 dated films that they’re delivering to the new merger, which will count 70 films between this weekend and into 2029. A dinner, we hear, between the duo and Ellison months ago provided optimism.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Paramount-WBD Will Now Be Called Skydance, David Ellison Reveals

Ellison finally caught up with De Luca and Abdy on Friday to deliver the news that they had read in the press. A decision was made by the cost-controlling co-CEO in his quest to pay down debt to keep his current Paramount Pictures Co-Chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein in charge over not just the Melrose lot but all Warner Bros theatrical brands. That structure doesn’t jibe with the current terms of De Luca and Abdy’s WBD contract, which runs through 2030 and has the duo reporting to the CEO, with marketing and distribution reporting to them.

So what now?

Ellison will need to pay out De Luca and Abdy’s contract.

But wait, what about all the places De Luca and Abdy are supposed to go?

RELATED: New Line Boss Richard Brener Poised To Jump To Merged Paramount-Warner Bros – The Dish

For now, sources say they’ll take a beat, rest and re-calibrate. The two have no competing offers from other studios. Their intent, from what we’ve heard, is to remain partnered together, presiding over a full-bodied theatrical driven motion picture studio.

Rumors have swirled about their eyeing production jobs at Netflix and Sony. The two are social with other studio bosses in town, i.e. Tom Rothman at Sony and Ted Sarandos at Netflix. No talks for jobs were ever sought, rather vernacular chats about what it would be like to work in an anomaly situation of a combined studio.

Word out there has been that Netflix Film Chairman Dan Lin is on ice, and that De Luca and Abdy are coming in. Those rumors are currently not true we understand with Lin staying in place. While Netflix is dipping their toes in theatrical with longer windows, i.e. La Bola Negra, Kpop Demon Hunters 2 and Greta Gerwig’s Narnia and more, the streamer is still nascent in the theatrical business which is Abdy and De Luca’s area of expertise.

In regards to a transition to Sony for the duo, Rothman is still riding out 17 months on his current contract, and it wouldn’t be a shocker if the 71 year-old studio boss re-ups. He already has a team in place with Sony Pictures President Sanford Panitch.

There was buzz out there that Abdy met with Apple SVP Eddy Cue, and Apple TV chiefs Jamie Erlicht and Zack Van Amburg for jobs, however, we hear that’s not true, in addition to frosh burgeoning global streamer Mubi courting the duo.

What wouldn’t be a shocker is if De Luca and Abdy, who delivered 11 Oscar wins this year to Warner Bros, and a blockbuster 2025, start their own studio.



“Do you know how much tech money is out there right now? Mike and Pam would have no problem raising capital and starting their own venture given their track record,” said one source with knowledge of their situation.

Earlier this year there was a rumor that the duo were teaming with former Paramount Pictures CEO Brian Robbins to start a new studio. However, due to the duo’s contract, they were barred from raising funds to start their own venture should WBD merge. Robbins wound up with backing from Greycroft, Sony Pictures, MarcyPen Capital Partners, ValueAct Capital, and CAA to launch his family label Big Shot Pictures.

In the meantime, many in town are flabbergasted at how the filmmaker-friendly De Luca and Abdy’s exits were first reported in the press. Even before De Luca and Abdy, and this weekend’s box office upset, Digger, the Warner Bros has historically been known for audacious, box office-risky swings, i.e. Stanley Kubrick’s A Clockwork Orange and the director’s year-long shot Eyes Wide Shut, The Wachowski Siblings’ Jupiter Ascending and Speed Racer, Tony Gilroy’s Michael Clayton, The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, heck, even the Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall movie, The Big Sleep.

There are ups and downs in the film business. Last year Warner Bros was at a high, and this year, not so much. However, Paramount is absorbing a potential $1 billion year-end tentpole in Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three, and a blockbuster 2027 shepherded by De Luca and Abdy that includes Legendary’s A Minecraft Movie Squared, Bradley Cooper’s directed and starring Ocean’s Prequel which also headlines Margot Robbie, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum, and Legendary’s Godzilla x Kong: Supernova.

The key to success for any studio boss in these days is to be backed by an entertainment conglom CEO through the good times, and the bad given the cyclical nature of the business.

The question remains that if De Luca and Abdy stayed, whether the cost efficiency Ellison would have abided by that.

title: Venice Prize-Winner ‘NAZA’ Brings Explosive Gaza Exposé to U.S. Theaters – Specialty Preview
summary: NAZA, written and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has started its U.S. run, playing at the IFC Center in New York since Wednesday. That followed fast on a New York Film Festival screening last weekend and a Special Jury Prize at its Venice world premiere last month with a record 25-minute standing ovation […]
content:
NAZA, written and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has started its U.S. run, playing at the IFC Center in New York since Wednesday. That followed fast on a New York Film Festival screening last weekend and a Special Jury Prize at its Venice world premiere last month with a record 25-minute standing ovation for the doc many have called devastating.

The film was produced by The Guardian and James Wilson’s JW Films, with his longtime collaborator Jonathan Glazer (The Zone of Interest) as executive producer. MTuckman Media is helping with U.S. bookings. As of noon Wednesday, when the run started, most shows already had been sold out through the weekend, with the doc eyeing more than $70k for its first five days. NAZA is set to expand to 60+ theaters in more than 30 markets next weekend.

Watch on Deadline

It’s sitting at 100% on Rotten Tomatoes off 32 reviews, see Deadline’s here.

RELATED: ‘NAZA’: What The Critics Are Saying About Yuval Abraham & Rachel Szor’s Israel-Gaza Documentary

French sales company mk2 films handles rest-of-world sales with deals in 56 markets. The doc opened great in Italy with €1.81 million ($2.1 million) and is moving into other territories today. In an unusual move, The Guardian plans to stream the doc internationally for free starting in six to eight weeks to make it as widely available as possible.

The setup is deceptively sparse. The film unspools at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, where Abraham interviews a stream of 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers to recount details of the destruction of residential areas in Gaza that caused massive loss of life among Palestinian civilians. The officers are filmed in silhouette, their voices digitally altered.

NAZA is an acronym used by Israel Defense Forces to signify collateral damage, specifically the degree of acceptable loss of civilian life incurred while trying to kill suspected Hamas militants. The film suggests the number is elastic, from several to a dozen to as high as 500 people who were deemed permissible collateral damage, according to Israeli military personnel interviewed in the doc.

RELATED: ‘NAZA’ Trailer: First Look At Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s Much-Talked-About Gaza Documentary

Israel has denied the claims in the film. Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu has also threatened to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship and to pass legislation making it illegal to criticize the Israeli armed forces. Abraham and Szor attended Venice and NYFF but won’t be appearing at opening Q&As. Reps said the pair is not currently either in the U.S. or in Israel.

The doc has no narration, no infographics, just testimonials, said Abraham. As the soldiers spoke, he pressed them at times but said his role was to listen and document, not scold, especially “in light of the kind of reaction” to the film — meaning the backlash.

He’s an investigative journalist who’s partnered in recent years with reporters from The Guardian to cover the destruction in Gaza after Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, where 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. The Palestinian death toll is said to surpasses 74,000, including many civilians.

RELATED: Israel’s Culture Minister Calls For Oscar-Winning Israeli Filmmakers Behind Gaza Doc ‘NAZA’ To Lose Their Citizenship

Abraham noted during a Q&A at NYFF that much of the film overlaps with previous reporting and that atrocities in Gaza have been documented for years. But “they’re allowed to continue in part because many people are denying them. Part of our hope is that by making this film, we will make that denial a little bit harder.”

Szor, the main cinematographer, said he chose Tel Aviv because it’s a considered a liberal city but no one there talks about Gaza. “Either they’re justifying it, or there’s just no place for it to even be spoken about,” he said. “So we really wanted these words, these testimonies in Hebrew, from soldiers, from officers, be spoken against the background of a city like Tel Aviv.”

Abraham and Szor were part of a film collective with Palestinian colleagues Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, behind another powerful doc, the Oscar-winning No Other Land in 2024. That followed the destruction of the occupied West Bank’s Masafer Yatta by Israeli soldiers and the alliance that develops between the Palestinian activist Adra and Abraham. It grossed $2.5 million worldwide.

Other specialty openings:

Ketchup Entertainment of Coyote vs Acme fame is releasing Rolling Loud by Jeremy Garelick, a comedy set against the backdrop of the world’s largest hip-hop festival, on 868 screens. Produced by Live Nation Studios and American High in collaboration with Rolling Loud. Owen Wilson plays an overprotective dad who sneaks his 13-year-old son (Christian Convery) into the festival. The film is coming off a smashing regional tour of 13 cities and colleges. Acts included: Swae Lee, DaBaby, Offset, A Bog Wit Da Hoodie and Young Thug, among many others.

Obscured Releasing presents Samuel Abrahams’ absurdist comedy Lady at Regal Union Square in New York and Coral Gables Art Cinema in Miami, adding the Glendale and Monica Laemmles in LA next weekend. The film follows a lonely, self-obsessed aristocrat (Sian Clifford) who dupes a struggling, opportunistic director into filming her every move. While pursuing her artistic expression, Lady Isabella’s life takes a surreal turn as she realizes if she’s not in the spotlight, she might just disappear.

Rue Dangeau debuts Victorian Gothic thriller Séance starring Vivian Kerr with a one-week run at the Laemmle Royal in Los Angeles before widening to dates in San Francisco, Phoenix, Houston, Palm Springs and Sedona, with more cities to be announced. Scottie Thompson, Jilon VanOver and Connor Paolo also star. Over the course of one night, two couples confront the deficits in their marriages, the temptation of adultery, and the disturbing possibility their house is haunted by a recently deceased loved one. The feature is inspired by the August Strindberg play Creditors.

title: Selma Blair Announces ‘Hineni’ Doc About Antisemitism After She Was “Erased” Over Islamophobic Comments
summary: More than two years later, Selma Blair is taking the fallout over her Islamophobic comments and channeling it into a documentary about antisemitism. On Thursday, the actress announced at the ADL State of the Arts Reception in New York City that she’s making a documentary entitled Hineni (Here I Am) to say what she “couldn’t […]
content:
More than two years later, Selma Blair is taking the fallout over her Islamophobic comments and channeling it into a documentary about antisemitism.

On Thursday, the actress announced at the ADL State of the Arts Reception in New York City that she’s making a documentary entitled Hineni (Here I Am) to say what she “couldn’t say two years ago” when she first apologized for her comments.

“Two years ago I learned what erased feels like, and I’ve decided the opposite of erased is making something. So I’m making a film,” she said in her remarks. “The last time I let cameras in, it was about my body. This time it’s about my people. It’s a documentary about antisemitism, and as confounding and confusing as it seems to be because no one wants to talk about geopolitics but it seems to get intermingled completely, but I wanted to make this made for the people who are not in this room.”

Blair continued, “It’s called Hineni. Here I am. The thing I couldn’t say two years ago, I’m now saying with a camera crew behind me. It goes to Israel, so people can see why that land is not an abstraction to us. And it talks to people who disagree with me, on camera, and keeps the disagreement in the cut, because you don’t change a mind by only talking to people who already agree with you.”

Watch on Deadline

Acknowledging the “ignorance and rage” of her words at the time, in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, Blair come under fire in February 2024 for writing in a comment regarding Rep. Cori Bush (D-MO) and Rep. Rashida Talib (D-MI), “Thank you so much. Deport all these terrorist supporting goons. Islam has destroyed Muslim countries and then they come here and destroyed minds. They know they are liars. Twisted justifications. May they meet their fate.”

During Thursday’s reception, Blair reflected on the moment. “It offended people, and I did apologize right away. No conditions, no fine print. I meant it then and I mean it now, and I’m leaving the comment there, because the comment was not the story,” she said.

“Here’s what happened next. I’ll try to tell it fast, because it happened fast,” added Blair. “The brands I worked with were gone within a day. A few partnerships I’d spent years building were shelved. My agency was gone. My lawyer was gone. My publicist was gone. My book agent was gone. My book publicist was gone. My social media manager was gone. My son’s godmother was gone – my best friend. While some friends in the business quietly stood by me, most of them were gone. And of course, my manager, my supposed friend of thirty years, and a Jew, was gone too. I still don’t know what any of them were thinking. No one returned my calls. I know the phone stopped. Not rang less. Just stopped.”

Following Blair’s 2024 comments, her representatives at CAA and Narrative PR parted ways with the actress known for roles in Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde, The Sweetest Thing and more.

Blair was previously the subject of the Discovery+ documentary Introducing, Selma Blair, which explored her multiple sclerosis diagnosis and how she adapted to living with the neurological disorder.

title: Mary Louise Weller Dies: ‘Animal House’s Mandy Pepperidge Was 79
summary: Mary Louise Weller, who played sorority girl Mandy Pepperidge in the 1978 comedy classic Animal House and had two dozen other film and TV credits, died October 1 after a brief illness — one day before her 80th birthday. Weller had played bit roles in a pair of movies and guested on TV dramas Kojak […]
content:
Mary Louise Weller, who played sorority girl Mandy Pepperidge in the 1978 comedy classic Animal House and had two dozen other film and TV credits, died October 1 after a brief illness — one day before her 80th birthday.

Weller had played bit roles in a pair of movies and guested on TV dramas Kojak and Baretta before landing the Mandy role in John Landis’ early-’60s college tale Animal House. It was a key supporting role, with the character being the girlfriend of Greg, president of Delta Tau Chi’s rival fraternity, and who had a fling with Delta’s Otter (Tim Matheson).

The queen bee of her Pi sorority, Mandy is riding a float during the climatic homecoming parade scene when she is abducted by pirate-clad John “Bluto” Blutarsky (John Belushi) of the Delta house. In the film’s “What became of…” epilogue, Mandy is seen snuggling with Bluto as they drive off in a convertible and ID’d as Senator and Mrs. Blutarsky.

RELATED: Donald Sutherland Dies: Revered Actor In ‘Klute’, ‘Ordinary People’, ‘Animal House’, ‘Hunger Games’ & Scores Of Others Was 88

Born on October 2, 1946, in New York City, Weller’s post-Animal House career saw her guesting on such popular TV series as Starsky & Hutch, The Hardy Boys/Nancy Drew Mysteries, B.J. and the Bear, Vega$ and twice on Fantasy Island and CHiPs. She co-starred opposite Chuck Norris in the 1982 big-screen crime thriller Forced Vengeance and also appeared that same year the features Bloodtide and Q: The Winger Serpent.

Her final credit was a 1983 episode of the Jack Klugman-led crime drama Quincy, M.E.

Information on survivors or a memorial service was not available.

title: New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: A festival launching Oct. 11 at Manhattan’s SVA Theatre is positioning itself as an answer to the flattened, stereotyped picture of Muslims Western media often traffics in. The New York Muslim Film Festival (NYMFF), billed as the city’s first for Muslim filmmakers, wants them telling their own stories. Hassan Babar, the festival’s artistic director, said […]
content:
A festival launching Oct. 11 at Manhattan’s SVA Theatre is positioning itself as an answer to the flattened, stereotyped picture of Muslims Western media often traffics in. The New York Muslim Film Festival (NYMFF), billed as the city’s first for Muslim filmmakers, wants them telling their own stories.

Hassan Babar, the festival’s artistic director, said such stories should not merely serve as counter-narratives. “They should be the establishing paradigm,” Babar said.

The one-day event will screen 12 shorts from seven countries, with documentaries, dramas, comedies, animation and experimental pieces in the mix. Women make up a majority of the program’s directors.

Popular on Variety

“This festival exists because those stories deserve a stage in this city, not on the margins of someone else’s,” said Nawal Mubin, the festival’s co-founder and director.

The day will open with a reception for filmmakers and industry guests. Two blocks of six films each, running roughly an hour apiece, will precede the awards and the jury announcement.

Emmy winner Aasif Mandvi, a longtime “The Daily Show” correspondent who also starred in Paramount+ series “Evil,” sits on the six-member jury. He is joined by Arab-American writer-director Darine Hotait, founder of Cinephilia Productions, whose shorts have aired on HBO, AMC, SundanceTV and the BBC; Munir Atalla, head of production and acquisitions at Watermelon Pictures and a former Netflix creative executive; and producer Abubakar Khan, whose resume includes “The Glassworker,” Pakistan’s entry for the 2024 Oscars, and SXSW 2023 audience award winner “Mustache.”

Rounding out the panel are Lebanese-American filmmaker Sarah Mokh, a Sundance Feature Film Fellow who recently wrapped her first feature, “The Alchemy of Being Okay,” which Khan is producing, and Egyptian-American actor Abubakr Ali. Ali has roles coming up in Bassam Tariq’s “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” opposite Mahershala Ali, and Sean Durkin’s A24 film “Deep Cuts,” and recently appeared in Kathryn Bigelow’s “A House of Dynamite.”

Streamer Watermelon+ is behind the festival’s Watermelon+ Discovery Award. Its winner, whether filmmaker or rights holder, will give the platform an exclusive license to show the film for a limited period. The Islamic Scholarship Fund, New York production and post house Lost in Space, and Aneesa Talks, which filmmaker Aneesa Khan founded to support South Asian and Muslim creatives, have also signed on as partners.

The program ranges widely in tone and subject. Justin Mashouf’s documentary “$17.74” follows a former gang member, behind bars since the 1980s, whose gesture of support for Gaza from inside prison set off a viral wave of solidarity. In Karim Emara’s Qatar-U.S. dramedy “Baba Is Melting,” a son phones his father, who is waiting in the car before Friday prayer in Doha, to challenge him over a hidden second marriage.

Zaid Ahmed Hassan’s “Ghusl” centers on a son whose dying father asks him to learn Islamic burial rites, while Basma Khalifa’s U.K. experimental piece “Henna” follows the henna plant’s life cycle alongside women from 16 African and SWANA countries. Sima Naseem’s Canada-Pakistan animation “My Friend in the Jingle Truck” combines stop-motion and 2D to tell of a Karachi girl who meets a magical bird.

In Alex Aljouni’s “Bukra,” a young Syrian refugee whose sweepstakes prize is a soccer ball rushes to collect it in time for one last match with her best friend before he is gone for good. One daring move reopens old rifts among three generations of Afghan women in Negine Jasmine Sekandari and Ayda Rojhantalab’s comedy “Haram Salami,” as they weigh who they are against what custom demands and what they want.

Maram Taibah’s Saudi fantasy “Malika” explores a girl’s bond with her grandmother, and the pull between wildness and the obedience expected of girls, through a magical-realist world spun from a child’s imagination. In Bilal Shams Khan’s Pakistani drama “Sabr O Shukar,” 10-year-old Akram learns about patience and gratitude while chasing his dream of a bicycle.

Imran J. Khan’s “The Boy With Dinosaur Head” pits a troubled boy who believes he is a dinosaur against a teacher set on pulling him back to reality, and their short encounter stays with both of them. Ilhan Abdullahi and Sherry Rashidan’s Canadian comedy “Unqualified” follows Warsan, the lone Muslim at her workplace, who is handed the job of spiritually cleansing a lunchroom said to be haunted and must clear out the spirits, armed with her faith and a string of misunderstandings, before she loses her job.

Lyna Tadount and Sofian Chouaib’s French drama “Ya Hanouni” centers on two parents vying to be their baby’s first word, until their lighthearted contest is cut short by an event that upends their lives.

Babar, a Toronto-based actor and producer, co-heads programming with Aneesa Khan, who also leads communications. Mubin, a New York director-producer, co-founded the festival with filmmaker and post-production specialist Giuseppe de Matteis. Both work at Lost in Space.

title: DOJ Argues CNN & Other Outlets Can Be Banned From White House If Trump Determines They Didn’t Meet “Minimum Requirements Of Professionalism”
summary: The Justice Department argued that Donald Trump can legally ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because he determined that they didn’t meet the “minimum requirements of professionalism.” Last month, a federal judge granted the three outlets a temporary restraining order that forced the White House to reinstate dozens of their reporters’ […]
content:
The Justice Department argued that Donald Trump can legally ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because he determined that they didn’t meet the “minimum requirements of professionalism.”

Last month, a federal judge granted the three outlets a temporary restraining order that forced the White House to reinstate dozens of their reporters’ hard passes. The outlets are now asking the judge to extend that 14-day order for a longer term via a preliminary injunction, claiming that Trump’s ban is a violation of their First and Fifth amendment rights.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, has said that he is bound by the precedent set in In a 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, in which the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.”

In a court filing on Friday, the DOJ claimed that the Sherrill case still would allow for the president to restrict the three outlets from accessing the White House grounds because the White House has a “compelling interest.”

Watch on Deadline

The DOJ lawyers claimed that the Sherrill decision does not “prevent the President from concluding that bona fide journalists would identify sources instead of relying on anonymous sources, commit to factual accuracy, and provide the White House an opportunity to comment, rather than ‘perform their duties in a way that … interfere[s] with the White House’s daily operations.’ …At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information.”

The news outlets’ legal team has rejected that assertion, writing in a filing earlier this week that Trump’s “statements also make clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from newsgathering and reporting that the President might view as negative. And his administration has continued to retaliate against Plaintiffs even after the temporary restraining order, only underscoring that Defendants’ motive is to punish and chill journalism they dislike.”

Even as access to the White House grounds has been reinstated, the White House has continued to restrict CNN from coverage of TV pool assignments, including travel with Trump on Air Force One.

The outlets’ lawyers, led by Theodore Boutrous Jr., also noted that Trump and other White House officials “overlooked that the First Amendment protects reporting on matters affecting national security.”

Kelly has set a hearing for Thursday on the news outlets’ motion for a preliminary injunction.

In granting a TRO, Kelly concluded that the White House failed to provide due process to the news outlets.

The DOJ has pointed to letters sent to the outlets as evidence that they were given due process. But those letters were sent on Sept. 22, four days after Trump’s ban was started.

The judge also has noted that some of the objectionable stories cited by the DOJ do not have to do with national security. Kelly wrote in his order that “even the justifications provided to Plaintiffs after this case was filed are ambiguous about the true purpose of the revocations: while Defendants’ letters to Plaintiffs mention national security concerns, they purport to identify reporting that ‘threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods’ leaving open the possibility that all the stories fall into the later bucket, rather than the former.”

title: Zach Bryan Dons “Free Palestine” Shirt For Concert At Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium
summary: Following Robert Kraft’s campaign against Macklemore, Zach Bryan made a statement with his performance at Gillette Stadium. During Friday’s stop at the Kraft-owned venue for his With Heaven on Tour, the Grammy winner stepped onto the stage with a “Free Palestine” shirt after Kraft and other venue owners pressured Ed Sheeran to drop Macklemore from […]
content:
Following Robert Kraft‘s campaign against Macklemore, Zach Bryan made a statement with his performance at Gillette Stadium.

During Friday’s stop at the Kraft-owned venue for his With Heaven on Tour, the Grammy winner stepped onto the stage with a “Free Palestine” shirt after Kraft and other venue owners pressured Ed Sheeran to drop Macklemore from his tour over his outspoken support for Palestinians.

With another performance scheduled at the Massachusetts venue on Saturday night, it remains to be seen if Kraft will pull the plug.

The show comes after Ed Sheeran was forced to cancel his Gillette Stadium shows last weekend amid a nor’easter headed for Boston, despite caving to Kraft’s demands.

Watch on Deadline

Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his tour last month amid an outcry around the opener’s “Free Palestine” onstage remarks. Opting to remain publicly neutral on the issue, Sheeran subsequently released a statement saying it was the “promoter’s decision” after Kraft assembled several of the tour venues to give him an ultimatum.

Zach Bryan and his band wore “Free Palestine shirts while performing at Gillette Stadium tonight. pic.twitter.com/EcMrGBxJDG — ryan 🤿 (@scubaryan_) October 3, 2026

Following the statement, fellow tour openers Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham dropped out of the tour, along with Sheeran’s backing band Beoga.

Meanwhile, Macklemore announced the Free Palestine Tour last week, which is “supporting the Palestinian people and movement,” running 10/26-10/30 in Dublin, Paris and London. He since gave an update that the tour “sold out immediately.”

title: Pedro Pascal Was Surprised Tony Gilroy Made ‘Behemoth!’ “So Intimate And Healing”: “I Thought You Were Gonna Be Mean”
summary: With the world premiere of Behemoth!, Pedro Pascal is praising Tony Gilroy for the intimate drama. During a Q&A after the film’s premiere screening at the New York Film Festival, the Golden Globe-nominated actor admitted he thought Gilroy was “gonna be kinda mean” before they worked together. “You have created this complex Jason Bourne-like puzzle […]
content:
With the world premiere of Behemoth!, Pedro Pascal is praising Tony Gilroy for the intimate drama.

During a Q&A after the film’s premiere screening at the New York Film Festival, the Golden Globe-nominated actor admitted he thought Gilroy was “gonna be kinda mean” before they worked together.

“You have created this complex Jason Bourne-like puzzle over something that is so intimate and so healing this mysterious way,” Pascal told Gilroy in a video shared by NYFF. “And I didn’t think it was gonna come from him, you know what I mean? This intimidating intellectual … you know, I thought you were gonna be kinda mean. And you thought I was gonna be a dork.

In Behemoth!, premiering Dec. 4 in theaters, Pascal stars as cellist Alex Serian, a former child prodigy who returns home to Los Angeles to compose film scores and reconnect with his family.

Watch on Deadline

Written and directed by Gilroy, the Searchlight Pictures film also stars Olivia Wilde, Eva Victor, Will Arnett, Hank Azaria, Margarita Levieva and Matthew Lillard.

title: ‘Real Time’: Bill Maher Tells New Skydance Bosses “Don’t Believe What Trump Is Tweeting About Me”
summary: As the Paramount-Warner Bros merger goes through, Bill Maher has a message for his new Skydance bosses. On Friday’s episode of Real Time, the comedian pleaded with the Ellisons not to listen to their pal Trump’s criticism of him now that they own his show’s longtime home HBO. “The merger went through. Paramount now owns […]
content:
As the Paramount-Warner Bros merger goes through, Bill Maher has a message for his new Skydance bosses.

On Friday’s episode of Real Time, the comedian pleaded with the Ellisons not to listen to their pal Trump’s criticism of him now that they own his show’s longtime home HBO.

“The merger went through. Paramount now owns Warner Discovery, which owns HBO, which owns my ass,” he said during his opening monologue. “Whoever owns me now, don’t believe what Trump is tweeting about me. Did you see what he said about me this weekend? He said my ratings are so low, ‘it’s just sad.'”

Maher continued, “You know what, Mr. President? Your insults don’t bother me. Make up whatever shit you want about me, just don’t mention I went to Cornell.”

Watch on Deadline

On Wednesday, a federal judge cleared the way for the $110 billion deal to close, approving the settlement between Paramount and a group of state AGs that filed an antitrust lawsuit to block the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition.

CEO David Ellison revealed on Friday that the combined company will now be known as Skydance, under which Paramount and Warner Bros. will supposedly remain individual entities.

title: Post-Merger Skydance Keeping Both HBO Max & Paramount+ Streaming Brands
summary: More indication that the newly-christened combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery company would bundle the two flagship streamers, Paramount+ and HBO Max, instead of merging them into one. The video released earlier today by Paramount CEO David Ellison to announce that the new company will carry the name of his old one, Skydance, ended with a slide […]
content:
More indication that the newly-christened combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery company would bundle the two flagship streamers, Paramount+ and HBO Max, instead of merging them into one.

The video released earlier today by Paramount CEO David Ellison to announce that the new company will carry the name of his old one, Skydance, ended with a slide featuring the new moniker surrounded by what were positioned as the key, most valuable brands of the merged company. (You can see it below.) It included the logos of Paramount, Warner Bros., DC, CBS, CNN, Nickelodeon, as well as both HBO Max and Paramount+.

Since Paramount was already represented, also including Paramount+ feels intentional, along with the choice of HBO Max vs. the legacy HBO brand.

Watch on Deadline

Paramount (which will become Skydance on Oct. 6 when the WBD acquisition closes) is yet to officially confirm how it will combine HBO Max and Paramount+ into a streaming operation expected to be overseen by Casey Bloys, Chairman and CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content.

Asked yesterday whether the two platforms, which are considered pretty complimentary in their offerings, would be bundled vs. fully integrated, he hinted that a bundle may be the way to go.

“I don’t want to comment on what is going to happen or anything like that, but I would point to the HBO Max-Disney bundle, which has been very successful,” he said, adding, “So, could you see something like that happening? That would make a lot of sense.”

Both streaming brands making Skydance’s MVP list would seem to support that idea too.

title: ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone
summary: It would be nice to say that Connor Storrie burns up the screen in “April X,” the star’s first film vehicle released since TV’s “Heated Rivalry” made him hot property, but it would be overstating the case. Appropriating Harrison Ford’s “Blade Runner” frown, among a few other things nicked from that sci-fi classic in this […]
content:
It would be nice to say that Connor Storrie burns up the screen in “April X,” the star’s first film vehicle released since TV’s “Heated Rivalry” made him hot property, but it would be overstating the case. Appropriating Harrison Ford’s “Blade Runner” frown, among a few other things nicked from that sci-fi classic in this sci-fi filler, Storrie capably shoulders a grim, po-faced tale of human cloning and trafficking in a greige dystopian future, but there’s not much for him to work with here — and he mostly projects the aura of a working actor dutifully waiting for something better to come along. Which it did, so job done. But you can hardly blame “April X” for riding his sudden celebrity, securing a theatrical release and escaping the straight-to-VOD morass that would appear to be its natural habitat.

Surely only Storrie’s most ardently committed new fans will venture out to see this, though: It’s hardly an embarrassing blot on his résumé, but it’ll be forgotten long before the second-season premiere of the queer hockey phenomenon. For writer-director Michel K. Parandi, making his feature-length debut, “April X” will be a more critical calling card — and duly shows off some resourceful technical ability on a cramped budget. But his script, co-written with regular collaborator Jack Coulter, is less impressive, welding together story scraps from other, better films to rather turbid, uninvolving effect. It occupies a similar genre space to the recent release “Hot Spot,” Agnieszka Smoczynska’s comparably scrappy, patched-together vision of compromised human identity in the middle-distance future; that film was a misfire, but a measure of its imaginative eccentricity would still be welcome here.

Popular on Variety

The year is unspecified, but the fatigued brutalist housing blocks of outer Bucharest are still standing: Though it doesn’t specify a location either, “April X” uses the present-day wear and tear of the Romanian capital, where the film was shot on location, as shorthand for a world collapsing into concrete ruin. The odd hi-tech drone adds some futuristic pizzazz to the film’s exterior vistas, but the new technologies defining the narrative aren’t of the gleaming, brave-new-world variety: People are being cloned in grubby, shadowed fashion, while memories and dreams can be captured and downloaded onto surprisingly retro-looking data devices.

In this grimy waking nightmare, twins Baxter (Storrie) and April (German actor Lilly Krug) barely eke out a living doing a variety of sketchy jobs, some more criminal than others. He traffics organs on the black market, while she has a special gift for dreaming: At a time, apparently, when nobody has slumber visions anymore, hers are enviably lucid and vivid, to a marketable degree. April’s selling of her dreams to others wishing to experience her sensations isn’t a fresh idea — paging “Strange Days” — but it’s one of the more fertile ones here, and goes frustratingly unexploited as the film continues to probe a single glum reality.

We’re more concerned with Baxter, whose underworld dealings eventually see him run afoul of local gangster Klein (Serban Pavlu), and the twins’ combined savings aren’t enough to allay the severe consequences. Soon April disappears, and Baxter’s desperate search for her begins. It’s ongoing when the story suddenly lurches five years into the future: The world looks much the same, but his hair is briefly longer, while April has seemingly been cloned into a number of identikit sex workers. Whether her brother can locate her soul in any one of them, or somehow implant it via her recorded memories, is the film’s big existential question — but the characters themselves aren’t drawn with enough warmth or personality for us to really care either way.

Storrie soldiers through it all with a clenched jaw and a steely gaze, but the film’s world never comes fully to life. Nathan Haugaard’s sheeny widescreen lensing and Oana Novicov’s distressed production design ensure it looks pretty good, but “April X” is missing the granular particulars and textures that might make us believe it: The narrative, likewise, is just cohesive enough, but the details of Baxter’s life and livelihood are so muddy that he doesn’t have our full attention. Parandi’s film winds up outlining a dystopia more dull than devastating — though perhaps that’s the future we should really be fearing.
