title: Projeto Paradiso Founder Olga Rabinovich to Receive Inaugural Encounters Award at the São Paulo Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Philanthropist Olga Rabinovich will receive the inaugural Prêmio Encontros (Encounters Award) at this year’s Encontro de Ideias Audiovisuais, the industry platform of the São Paulo International Film Festival. The award honors her enduring commitment to advancing Brazilian cinema and elevating the international profile of Brazilian film and talent through her work with Projeto Paradiso. The […]
content:
Philanthropist Olga Rabinovich will receive the inaugural Prêmio Encontros (Encounters Award) at this year’s Encontro de Ideias Audiovisuais, the industry platform of the São Paulo International Film Festival. The award honors her enduring commitment to advancing Brazilian cinema and elevating the international profile of Brazilian film and talent through her work with Projeto Paradiso.

The Encounters Award was created to spotlight the transformative role of private investment in culture, bringing together private funders and the creative professionals behind audiovisual productions. The inaugural honor will be bestowed upon Rabinovich during the event’s opening gala ceremony on Oct. 14 and ahead of an in-conversation event with Neon president Jeff Deutchman.

Born in São Paulo, Rabinovich spent years volunteering in hospitals, working closely with terminally ill patients. In 2018, she founded the Olga Rabinovich Institute, launching Projeto Paradiso soon after. The initiative is dedicated to the advancement of the Brazilian audiovisual sector and grew out of her belief that “stories can change the world,” as well as a decision to invest in the people who create them and want to share them with audiences worldwide.

Popular on Variety

“Olga Rabinovich is the first recipient of the newly created Prêmio Encontros, because she was the inspiration behind the award,” said Renata de Almeida, director of the São Paulo International Film Festival. I first heard Olga’s name in early 2018, when Josephine Bourgois came to see me about someone from the private sector who wanted to create an institute dedicated to cinema. The Olga Rabinovich Institute was announced during the 42nd Mostra, bringing a breath of hope at a time that promised to be particularly difficult for Brazilian film and culture.”

“Eight years later, Projeto Paradiso, an initiative of the Olga Rabinovich Institute, has already made a major contribution to discovering and championing a new generation of talent, strengthening Brazil’s audiovisual sector as a whole,” continued the director. “Projeto Paradiso has an outstanding professional team, as its results clearly demonstrate. But the image that stays with me is of a meeting with Olga, climbing the winding stairs of our little building for a somewhat chaotic coffee in the festival’s office. Because, in the end, almost everything really does begin with an encounter.”

Courtesy of Milena Palladino

Earlier this year, Variety sat down with the philanthropist ahead of the third Projeto Paradiso National Network Meeting in Brazil’s buzzy production hub of Recife. Rabinovich said she “loved the idea of supporting cinema because I feel it is a magical art form.” “You enter a screening room without knowing whether you’ll be elated or disturbed or moved. It’s a transformative experience. I think it’s incredible to have a communal artistic experience that moves you like this.”

Projeto Paradiso offers a wide range of support to Brazilian screen professionals to maximize their presence on the global stage, supporting the development of stories through fellowships, residencies, workshops, and other training and international reach initiatives. The Paradiso Talent Network now comprises 278 Brazilian professionals.

The organization also helps connect Brazilian talent and projects with the international industry through a network of more than 250 partner institutions in Brazil and abroad, including the Hubert Bals Fund, La Fabrique Cinéma de l’Institut français, TorinoFilmLab, Film Independent and the Sundance Institute.

The initiative was recently behind buzzy festival titles such as Allan Deberton’s Berlinale-winning “Gugu’s World” and Grace Passô’s “Our Secret,” and boasts a talent network of 264 professionals, including Anita Rocha da Silveira (“Medusa”), Juliana Rojas (“Good Manners”) and Dira Paes (“Manas”).

In 2025 Projeto Paradiso teamed with the Embratur Brazilian Tourism Board to launch Screen Brasil, offering four Brazilian films a year in two calls – the latest of which closed Oct. 2 supporting their international distribution campaigns, submissions being made by the international sales agent holding the film’s commercial rights. Announced at Cannes Marché du Film this May, films backed to date take in Gabriel Mascaro’s “The Blue Trail,” Rafaela Camelo’s “The Nature of Invisible Things” and animated feature “Papaya.”

Projeto Paradiso’s relationship with the São Paulo International Film Festival dates back to 2018, when the philanthropy initiatve was launched during the festival’s 42nd edition. Since then, Projeto Paradiso has steadily expanded its presence at the festival.

Since 2023, it has presented the annual Paradiso Distribution Support Award, providing a distribution grant for the theatrical release of a fiction feature. In 2024, Projeto Paradiso was also one of the driving forces behind a new partnership with the Hubert Bals Fund (HBF), which led to the creation of HBF+Brazil following initial discussions at Encontro de Ideias.

The 50th edition of the São Paulo International Film Festival runs Oct. 15-29.

title: Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly?
summary: David Ellison has emerged victorious. And he’s boldly — or arrogantly, if you prefer — decided to name the entertainment giant that he’s bolted together Skydance Corp., nodding to the original name of his film production firm that has swallowed up two Hollywood studios over the past 14 months. Defying skeptics and beating back opponents, […]
content:
David Ellison has emerged victorious. And he’s boldly — or arrogantly, if you prefer — decided to name the entertainment giant that he’s bolted together Skydance Corp., nodding to the original name of his film production firm that has swallowed up two Hollywood studios over the past 14 months.

Defying skeptics and beating back opponents, Ellison has harpooned his white whale in buying Warner Bros. Discovery. Now he has to prove that the $111 billion mega-merger can become a profitable entertainment powerhouse, and not just a vessel that will get sucked under by a massive whirlpool of debt.

As the closing of the deal — set to occur Tuesday, Oct. 6 — became a certainty, entertainment industry insiders started to come to grips with the reality that the enlarged company is a new and unpredictable force in town. The deal has been polarizing for the creative community, with many boldface names going public in their opposition to the merger. The new leadership team that Skydance is assembling under the direction of Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, just recruited from Mattel to serve as co-CEO, has to navigate that dynamic. And they must do it while walking a tightrope on Wall Street to pay down debt and grow profits across film, linear TV and streaming.

Popular on Variety

“They need to move as quickly as possible to get the leverage down,” says Jawad Hussain, managing director at S&P Global. “The biggest hurdle and the biggest thing we’re going to be keeping our eye on is integration and execution.” Two years ago, Hussain says, Skydance Meida was a small company that turned out a few films a year. “Now it’s managing one of the largest media companies. It’s not necessarily an easy task.”

It’s all been a whirlwind. On the morning of Sept. 30, Ellison still didn’t know if it was a done deal.

He had spent more than a year in his relentless pursuit of acquiring Warner Bros. and HBO. The WBD board rejected his takeover offers eight times. David Zaslav, Warner Bros. Discovery’s boss, ghosted Ellison in December 2025 after Netflix clinched a deal for WB’s streaming and studios business. But Ellison didn’t surrender; he finally outbid Netflix in February, with a $31/share offer that was nearly 2.5 times the stock price before the M&A frenzy kicked off. It was an offer WBD couldn’t refuse.

Ellison and his legal team, headed by former DOJ official Makan Delrahim, predicted the proposed Paramount-WB combo would easily clear regulatory approvals. In June, Trump’s Justice Department rubber-stamped the pact without attaching any conditions. All told, regulators in 68 jurisdictions worldwide cleared the merger with minimal pushback.

The last barricade in Ellison’s way? An antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 Democratic state attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta. Ellison believed the litigation was politically motivated, stoked by fears he would try to turn CNN into a Trump-friendly mouthpiece. (He has repeatedly promised a hands-off approach to CNN’s news coverage.) But the AGs pressed their case and a federal judge agreed that their arguments — that Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield undue power in theatrical and basic cable markets — had merit. A trial was scheduled to begin in March 2027.

Frustrated and incredulous, Ellison let it be known through press leaks in August that he would pull Paramount out of California if the state AGs didn’t let him close the WB deal. Paramount insiders continue to insist the notion of Ellison’s Golden State exit wasn’t a bluff or a threat. Bonta, seeming to realize he would gain no political capital by derailing or delaying the merger, relented. Paramount and the AGs announced a settlement of the suit on Sept. 21 — with a list of concessions so lenient that it surprised not only industry watchers but also employees at both companies.

Now all that was left was the judge’s approval of the settlement. Worryingly for Ellison, U.S. District Court Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin at a Sept. 24 hearing had left the door open to a potential further third-party review of the settlement at the behest of Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.). The groups behind the #BlockTheMerger coalition, which had amassed more than 5,700 signatories from actors, filmmakers and industry workers opposed to the deal, filed a brief with the court urging Martínez-Olguín to reject the settlement.

But on Sept. 30 at just after 12:30 p.m pacific time, the judge issued her ruling: She had approved the settlement.

The proposed consent decree, Martínez-Olguin wrote, reflects a “compromise that may leave some dissatisfaction for both sides and the public but a compromise that saves the risk, time and expense of litigating through trial.”

Boom! Teams at both companies swung into action to make the final preparations needed to close the deal. That evening, Paramount and WBD confirmed the merger’s expected closing date of Oct. 6, at which point Paramount’s common stock will move from Nasdaq to list on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock symbol will change from “PSKY” to “SKYD,” reflecting the Skydance corporate name.

Ellison is expected to lead a town hall meeting with employees next Tuesday, and Ellison and Kreiz are scheduled to host a virtual press briefing — along with the new Skydance’s executive leadership — at 7 p.m. ET on Oct. 6.

Coincidentally, on Sept. 30 Ellison had been sitting on his own bit of hot news: He was ready to announce that he recruited media vet Kreiz to be co-CEO at the combined Paramount-WBD. The merged entity’s businesses will jointly report to Ellison and Kreiz.

Word of Kreiz’s joining Paramount trickled out earlier in the day, but Ellison had already decided to wait until after market close to announce it. Paramount put the release on the wire at 1:06 p.m., a little over half an hour after the judge OK’d the antitrust settlement.

Ellison triumphantly sent Paramount employees a companywide email about Kreiz’s hiring, timestamped at 1:18 p.m., praising the exec as a “proven builder and operator.” Kreiz, during his eight years at Mattel, had helped cut costs through layoffs — and oversaw its first theatrical release, 2023 blockbuster “Barbie.” He swung the company to profitability, but revenue has stubbornly stayed flat the last four years.

Ellison wrote in his email: “Together we are well positioned to integrate, operationalize and run the businesses as we build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry’s history. Kreiz, as part of his compensation package, will receive $31.5 million in fully vested stock as a signing bonus with the merger close.

Then on Friday, Oct. 2, Ellison shared on X that the new corporation would be … Skydance. His post included a sizzle reel of the combined company’s biggest hits, leading off with a clip from “Titanic” — an inauspicious choice, perhaps, given how that infamous voyage turned out.

“Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture,” Ellison wrote. “By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.”

Three years ago, Ellison was primarily known as a rich kid — scion of Oracle billionaire Larry Ellison, one of the world’s richest people — and a semi-successful movie producer, most notably with 2022’s “Top Gun: Maverick,” which turned in a boffo $1.5 billion at the box office. Now, having bagged Warner Bros., he can lay claim to being a titan in the business and no mere nepo baby.

“Ellison stared down the attorneys general and won. He stared down the unions and won,” says Prof. Erik Gordon of University of Michigan’s Ross School of Business. “You can’t see David Ellison as daddy’s boy anymore. He’s a formidable force in the industry.”

The Paramount-WBD merger is the biggest M&A deal in Hollywood history. It brings together two of Hollywood’s biggest movie studios, HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services dand TV brands including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, Food Network and more. The new company’s entertainment franchises span Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones and other HBO hits, the DC superhero universe, “Yellowstone,” “Mission: Impossible,” “Top Gun” and the Nickelodeon kids’ empire.

“We still have work to do before the deal closes, and nothing changes until it does,” Ellison told employees in his memo about Kreiz.

But even before the deal closed, the company’s new leadership was taking shape. Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy, co-heads of Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, will leave post-merger, sources told Variety. Paramount film heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are in line to oversee both movie studios.

With the deal close, Zaslav is expected to depart — with a boatload of money. Zaslav stands to earn at least $550 million in stock and cash once the Paramount-WBD deal closes, including $34.2 million in cash severance payments, per the terms of his “golden parachute” package.

Skydance’s settlement-related obligations around theatrical film and the operation of its Paramount and Warner Bros. cable channels will undoubtedly have ripple effects in the marketplace that extend well beyond the U.S. Showbiz leaders in Europe have closely watched the transaction at a time when local-language production is at a peak thanks to the influence of Netflix, Amazon and Disney+. HBO has a growing international footprint that will be crucial to Skydance’s future growth.

Pierre-Antoine Capton, chairman of France’s Mediawan, says the broader film and TV business is in line for a bumpy few years amid the shakeout of what he calls “a period of intense consolidation” of media assets. Mediawan bought Peter Chernin’s North Road Company earlier this year. It’s also circling Lionsgate as a potential acquisition.

“Having spoken with David, I believe his vision is first and foremost an artistic, creative ambition,” Capton says of the Skydance merger. “He wants to build a more powerful group in order to invest in creation. It’s not only about making cuts. I believe in his commitment to cinema and to theatrical releases.” At the same time, “everywhere in the world we’re entering a much more difficult phase, where consolidation will be, in my view, one of the solutions to the economic problems we’re all going to face,” Capton says.

Ellison and Kreiz will also be under pressure to deliver a clear roadmap for generating bigger profits from its streaming pillars, HBO Max and Paramount+.

Casey Bloys, head of WBD’s HBO, is poised to assume oversight of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. streaming business after Cindy Holland announced on Sept. 29 to staffers that she was stepping down from her role running Paramount+ and other direct-to-consumer businesses.

Holland’s resignation blindsided some senior managers at Paramount, who thought Ellison had hired her for the long haul. “We all thought we had the home-court advantage — that David was bringing all the new people at Paramount to have them be part of Warner Bros.,” a company insider says.

Paramount+ and HBO Max will together have more than 200 million subscribers. The newly merged Skydance can save money by consolidating its back-end streaming infrastructure. But “you don’t want to immediately combine the two streaming services because people won’t pay the sum of the two subscription prices,” says Prof. Sridhar Tayur of Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business. For the foreseeable future, HBO Max and Paramount+ will continue as discrete brands.

Another area to watch: what Ellison does with CNN, which throws off operating cash that Skydance Corp. will need to bolster its finances. Ellison has held preliminary talks with CNN chief Mark Thompson about staying on after the merger, sources tell Variety. The prospect of Thompson continuing at the helm, at least for now, came as a relief to CNN personnel, who have been worried that Bari Weiss, the “anti-woke” media entrepreneur Ellison put in charge of CBS News, might extend her fiefdom to include the news cabler.

Under the settlement with the 12-state coalition, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. will be subject to monitoring by a “news editorial independence board.” The board, which will include representatives from the states, will establish which will establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles” for CNN and CBS News. But critics have dismissed this as a toothless condition. One player displeased with this outcome was Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who, although he signed off on the settlement, said afterward he had advocated for a full divestiture of CNN and CBS News.

Foes of ParaBros remain hopping mad. Actor Mark Ruffalo, one of the deal’s most strident critics, has vowed to continue the fight. “This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost people their jobs — it is a bad deal for this country and should never have been approved,” he said in a social media post Sept. 30.

Ruffalo’s feud with Paramount got ugly. On Aug. 21, he posted a message warning about the dangers of the Paramount-WB merger and alleged Larry Ellison’s Oracle was complicit in “what we now have come to see as a genocide” by the Israeli government against Palestinians. Paramount responded forcefully. A company rep asserted the “antisemitic tropes” Ruffalo invoked “aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far.” Ruffalo has been set to reprise his role as an FBI agent in a second season of HBO’s “Task” crime drama. It remains to be seen if Ellison will let bygones be bygones.

Apart from the shouting, the biggest burning questions about the new entity are about its financial condition.

How is Paramount buying Warner Bros. Discovery, which has a market cap that’s six times larger? Paramount is issuing billions in debt securities and securing new loans to help foot the bill. Larry Ellison is bankrolling the WBD merger to the tune of $46.7 billion in equity financing. Paramount also lined up about $24 billion in commitments from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. In April, Paramount said the three Middle Eastern funds will own 38.5% of the combined entity, but that they will have no board seats or governance representation.

The new company will be controlled by the Ellison family alongside Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners. Cardinale’s firm is also pitching in equity for the WBD deal, after funding Skydance’s Paramount Global takeover.

The new company’s net debt is estimated to be more than $80 billion. That staggering amount would translate into annual interest payments topping $6 billion. Add to that the fact that Paramount-WB, under the settlement with the AGs, is obligated to invest at least $300 million more on film production in the U.S. annually (above what the studios combined spent in 2025).

Paramount execs have told Wall Street they can achieve $6 billion in cost savings through the merger. But not everyone thinks there’s $6 billion in cost savings to be squeezed out without negative consequences. There are obvious areas of overlap in corporate functions like IT, marketing, procurement and legal. But a big risk in executing a media merger of this scale is cutting into bone — resulting in the loss of creative professionals who are essential to the enterprise, says Prof. Tammy Madsen, a professor of management at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business.

“Creativity matters,” Madsen says. “If you are too aggressive in eliminating redundancies in the creative parts of the company, you could kill the value.”

Ellison, after the final clearance for the merger came through, wasn’t exactly popping the Champagne just yet. But he did, apparently, pop open some breakfast burritos.

On Oct. 1 — out of nowhere — employees on the Paramount Studios lot in L.A. and at the company’s offices Burbank were welcomed with buffet breakfasts: French toast, pancakes, egg burritos, shakes, berry bowls, chia pudding and more. One insider says it was the first time they had ever seen the company put out that kind of spread.

Perhaps it was more like a peace offering, coming before the pain of a first wave of layoffs at the new Skydance expected before the end of the year. The merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone, according to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August. Insiders believe layoffs will continue with further rounds into 2027.

There’s no way around the fact that thousands of employees across the former Paramount and WBD are about to get pink-slipped. But Ellison is betting that through the crucible of consolidation, a stronger company will emerge. “We have big goals for Skydance,” he wrote in his post on X about the new name, “and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks.”

Marc Malkin, Michael Schneider, Cynthia Littleton, Elsa Keslassy, Matt Donnelly, Angelique Jackson, Brian Steinberg and Gene Maddaus contributed to this story.

title: Jerry Golod, Producer of ‘Tales From the Darkside’ and Former CBS And NBC Executive, Dies at 87
summary: Jerry Golod, the producer of “Tales From the Darkside,” died following a brief battle with cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif., on Wednesday. He was 87. Throughout his career, Golod served as an executive at CBS and NBC, later launching JayGee Productions in the early 1980s. After seeing the success of Stephen King’s […]
content:
Jerry Golod, the producer of “Tales From the Darkside,” died following a brief battle with cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif., on Wednesday. He was 87.

Throughout his career, Golod served as an executive at CBS and NBC, later launching JayGee Productions in the early 1980s. After seeing the success of Stephen King’s 1982 film “Creepshow,” Golod collaborated with director Romero and producer Richard P. Rubinstein to bring the narrative to television. The three of them went on to launch “Tales From the Darkside,” which ran for four seasons and garnered a high cult following.

He also helped launch “Adderly” after reading Elliott Baker’s 1971 book, “Pocock and Pitt,” and becoming intrigued by the secondary character of the same name. The adventure series starred Winston Rekert and ran for two seasons on CBS.

Popular on Variety

In 1975, Golod became vice president of children’s programs at CBS before moving to NBC Entertainment in 1979 as vice president and national program director. While there, he oversaw daytime and children’s programming, specials, variety and West Coast late-night programming. He later joined CBS Television Studios and The CW in developing a new revival of “Tales From the Darkside,” though the series never moved past a 2015 pilot.

Golod executive produced CBS’s “Brass” in 1985 and “Return to Green Acres,” which reunited cast members of the 1960s sitcom. He also executive produced the 1991 revival of “Land of the Lost,” which ran for two seasons.

Golod was born in the Bronx on Dec. 26, 1938, and graduated from City College of New York. He began his career at advertising agency Dancer Fitzgerald Sample and went on to become vice president and associate director of programming. He also spent three years overseeing a television production company affiliated with the agency.

In the ‘90s, Golod worked with Pet Television Network as co-chairman and co-owner of a cable and satellite service aimed toward animal enthusiasts.

Golod is survived by his wife of 59 years, Ruth; their children, Dori and Jason; son-in-law Doug; daughter-in-law Danielle; grandchildren Gavin, Ramey, Morgan and Madison; great-grandsons Everett and Winslow; and nieces and nephews Jill, David, Elise, Renee, Celia, Ari and Ava.

title: ‘Coven Academy’ Creator Breaks Down Briar’s Family Tree, Dark Magic as an Addiction Metaphor, ‘Misogyny’ Against Witches — and a Deleted Kiss Scene
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “Coven Academy,” now streaming on Disney+. “Coven Academy” was supposed to be the first true young adult drama in the history of Disney Channel. The series, set at a New Orleans boarding school for witches and warlocks, is bloodier and darker than the network ever got with other […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “Coven Academy,” now streaming on Disney+.

“Coven Academy” was supposed to be the first true young adult drama in the history of Disney Channel. The series, set at a New Orleans boarding school for witches and warlocks, is bloodier and darker than the network ever got with other magical fare like “Wizards of Waverly Place.”

Ultimately, those qualities drove Disney to decide “Coven Academy” would be more at home on Freeform. “I think this shares more DNA with a classic CW show like ‘Vampire Diaries,’ or even the ‘Sabrina’ revival on on Netflix,” says series creator Tim Federle, best known as the mind behind “High School Musical: The Musical: The Series.” “When we went to Vancouver to shoot this, I feel like I hired half the ‘Riverdale’ team and was like, ‘Let’s bring that aesthetic to this show.’ Optically and message-wise, this sits in a different space than Disney Channel. As more and more of the higher ups at the company watched the show and got excited, there was a decision made, which was that this doesn’t belong there; it’s the wrong signal.”

Popular on Variety

“And yet,” he adds, “because of the sisterhood and magic, I feel this is still classically Disney. If you’ve watched ‘Zombies’ and ‘Descendants’ and ‘Vampirina,’ and maybe you’re also dipping a toe into older genre shows, I think this is a bridge.”

“Coven Academy” stars Malina Weissman as Briar, whose grief and anger about the unsolved murder of her mother, Mary, end up revealing a part of her identity she’d never known: She’s a witch. After reluctantly starting school in New Orleans, she befriends two fellow witches, Sasha (Jordan Leftwich) and Tegan (Ora Duplass), who teach her the ways of the magical world and help her search for answers about Mary (Cecilia Grace Deacon).

That process requires the young witches to break some rules, attracting the watchful eye of the school’s headmaster, Miss Graves (Tiffani Thiessen), who they realize was close friends with Briar’s mother. Miss Graves’ secrecy, and some information shared by one of their teachers, Mr. Cole (Devon Sawa), lead them to believe that she’s the murderer. But it’s later revealed that the real Mr. Cole is locked in a basement. A shapeshifting Warlock named William — who turns out to be the father of the girls’ friend Jake (Malachi Barton) — has taken Mr. Cole’s place as part of a decades-long evil scheme. He had been friends with Mary back in school until she, Graves and their coven sister Tamora (Keegan Connor Tracy) thwarted his plan to pollute the ley lines, the mystical source of all witches’ and warlocks’ powers. The coven interrupted a spell he was casting that would have made it so that they could all use only dark magic, which would lead to the eradication of monsters like the werewolves that killed his family. Decades later, he had come out of hiding to try again, and didn’t hesitate to kill anyone in his way — including Mary.

Briar, Sasha, Tegan and Graves — with an assist from Jake — manage to stop William and save the magical world. But as everyone processes their whirlwind semester at school, Briar can’t stop thinking about the connection she felt when Graves grabbed her hand to cast the spell on William. At the same time, Graves is shown speaking to Mary’s ghost in the woods. “I wanna tell her, Mary. She needs to know why I gave her up,” Graves says. “She needs to know what happened. No more secrets.” Mary replies, “No one can ever know you’re Briar’s birth mother. If the truth ever got out, you wouldn’t be able to protect her.” As a storm rolls in and Season 1 ends, Graves says, “She deserves to know.”

Federle spoke to Variety about family secrets, the meaning behind dark magic and what’s to come for “Coven Academy.”

“Coven Academy” isn’t based on IP, but you’re pulling from preexisting lore about witches, vampires and other mystical beings. What was your research process like? Did you create a rulebook about how magic operates in the world of the show? Todd Slavkin and Darren Swimmer, my co-showrunners, ran “Shadowhunters” and “Smallville.” They really understand genre. And we staffed up the writers’ room primarily with women, and some of the younger women were on, like, their second viewing of “Vampire Diaries.” In the room, we got pretty granular about the rules, like with warlocks and teleporting. I really wanted everything to be governed by character and emotion and what their perceived faults might be. For me, everything that got me picked on in middle school gets me paid now. I just needed to get with the right group, and then they would accept it. And for Briar, she gets labeled as angry or hot-headed, but it’s actually her source of power if she can channel it. For Tegan, it’s about having ADHD. It’s her ability to morph time, though other people might call her hyperactive. For Sasha, she is so empathic and has the ability to read other people, but she is not totally in touch with her own feelings. All of those felt like metaphors for the teenage experience that could somehow be explored in magic. I wanted the magic to be driven by character.

This show was originally intended to be Disney Channel’s first YA drama. It ended up moving to Freeform, but since you were writing with a Disney Channel audience in mind, how did you approach the level of violence, romance and darkness in the show? So many young people, for better or for worse, are exposed to [mature themes]. When I was in high school myself, I was not reading the assigned reading; I was reading “The Shining.” There’s a curiosity about the darker, deeper experience of growing up. I think I have a pretty good internal barometer of what makes something Disney and appropriate for a younger audience, even if it toes the line. And when you look back, you’re like, “OK, Simba’s dad dying is traumatic.” The best Disney stories go to really genuine places, even if you’re not always seeing all the blood. But there is some blood and some making out in “Coven Academy.” I am very excited about a white space that I think exists at Disney. Disney has done the most incredible job of keeping an audience engaged through the [tween] era, but there’s this white space where I want to capture the audience — I don’t want them to go away. I’d like to see Disney really have a piece of that pie.

Devon Sawa as Mr. Cole

Let’s get into the plot now. Did you always know that the villain would be Jake’s dad, who Briar’s mom had a history with? Or were Graves or Cole ever real candidates? Cole was never going to be the murderer. Devon Sawa is such a chameleon, so it was a joy to see him play multiple roles in one season. There was some discussion about Graves, but I liked the commonality and parallelism between Jake and Briar both having this giant parental question mark around them. And I kept bringing up, “What if Ms. Graves is actually her mom?” And the more I was watching Tiffani and Malina — their physical resemblance, and how maternal Tiffani is, as someone who grew up a teen icon — the more I felt like there was a really powerful story there. The idea that if a witch is related to another witch and they are in close proximity, there’s something very dangerous and powerful about that. That became the secret of the season, which I really hope we’re able to explore.

Tell me more about William, the actual villain, and what his character represents. The best villains think they’re heroes and that the thing they want is noble. He feels this very anti-monster stance. And in Jake’s awakening as a young warlock, he’s able to ultimately summon his father. “Coven Academy” is so much about: “Who are you if your family expects something? Who are you if you’re in the shadow of a sibling? Or if your family experiences trauma or loss? How do you make something out of that?” William is what happens if you go to the dark place. Genre is a blast, because you get to experiment with so much metaphor, whether it’s substance abuse or family shame.

The characters discuss the addictive nature of dark magic multiple times. Was it meant to stand in for substance abuse? I hope the audience recognizes the idea that almost anything in moderation is OK, but be careful how deep you go. In my extended family, there’s some deep substance abuse, and I saw how it tore people apart and became a real emotional lightning rod. Dark magic is about that thing that you may be drawn to, whether it’s drinking or internet doomscrolling, that can be a perfectly benign habit, but if you go deep, it can take over.

The tension between humans and “monsters” also seems to represent something bigger. It feels wrong when the witches and warlocks talk about vampires and werewolves like they aren’t equals, but it’s based on real fears about their safety. What were you trying to say with that conflict? It’s definitely a commentary on othering. With McKenna [Sway Bhatia] getting bitten, we’re trying to figure out what that means for her story with Tegan. It’s a classic “Romeo and Juliet,” or any story about a group that feels different from you. Now more than ever, we’re so divided in so many ways, and it’s easy to write off a group of people. One of the reasons I wanted Ollie [Louis Thresher] to be a newly turned vampire was because it was truly thrust upon him. He did not walk out the door that morning and say, “I want to be a vampire.” Whereas Jake, the powerful warlock who’s got so much going for him, has darker qualities, in some ways, than Ollie, who is a genuinely great guy and is now trying to make the best of [his circumstances]. That’s the story of anybody growing up and deciding what kind of person they want to be. I don’t even think of the vampires as monsters. I keep using that word, but I think of them as just different — and aren’t we all different? I don’t like black-and-white stories. I like the gray. By the way, when Jake and Briar almost kiss in the final chapter, we also shot a version where they did kiss, and we were like, “We have to save this. This is a slow burn. We’re yearning. Don’t rush everything.” The gray is how you get 100 stories and not just 10.

Malachi Barton as Jake, Malina Weissman as Briar

There are also interesting gender politics going on. William warns Jake about witches getting together and being judgmental, and Jake has a line about how witches work together with their coven sisters, but warlocks deal with their problems on their own. I made a decision really early on to separate the witches and the warlocks. With the women, it’s about girlhood and sisterhood. They lean on each other and gossip and come back together. The guys are on this very solitary journey. In my mind — not addressed yet in the series — they all used to learn together. And then around ’98, when William made this decision that fractured the community forever, the well-meaning adults separated the genders. We are fully owning this idea that boys and men are just not as comfortable expressing themselves, and when they do, these days in particular, they’re listening to some potentially questionable sources. The young ladies in the show are calling each other out and keeping each other accountable. At the beginning of the season, Briar doesn’t think of herself as a girl’s girl, and by the end, these are her sisters. Jake was being, if not brainwashed, certainly influenced by a male figure with some misogyny here. But Jake made a better decision than I think a lot of people do in real life.

Thinking about a potential second season, how do you see Jake dealing the fact that he finally gained the father he’d been missing his whole life just to lose him again? He has some major things to face when it comes to nature vs. nurture. “Am I always going to be drawn to dark magic? Is that my genetics?” It’s the addiction metaphor. But I would like to explore Mr. Cole being a genuine mentor to Jake moving forward. Jake is somebody who has to throw himself into something, because with idle time, he gets into trouble.

What about Briar and Miss Graves? Thematically, what are you exploring by revealing they’re mother and daughter? I’m childless, and I never wanted kids, but [in my work] I can’t graduate from high school, it seems. So I was interested in telling the story of a woman who absolutely knew her life would be complete without the experience of being a capital-M “Mother.” Maybe it’s because I grew up a black sheep that I’m always drawn to stories of making your parents proud vs. following your own destiny. I liked the idea of suddenly looking at somebody anew and going, “Hold on a second. Like, if I’ve inherited X, Y and Z from you, what does that mean? Did you have anger issues too?” Secrets are a big thing in families. What you keep from your family to protect them ultimately creates bigger issues later. I don’t want to tell another straight-up mom mystery again, but I think there is something fun to explore in what makes a mother and daughter so dangerous when they’re together. And who would be most threatened by that?

Tiffani Thiessen as Miss Graves

title: Asghar Farhadi Says Films Like ‘Argo’ Perpetuate American White Savior Myth: ‘Who Asked You To Come and Save Us?’
summary: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Twice Oscar-winning filmmaker Asghar Farhadi, who is at the Rio Film Festival to present “Parallel Tales,” spoke about the perceived hegemony of American cinema and how Hollywood shouldn’t be seen as a source for faithful portrayals of foreign cultures. Asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A […]
content:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Twice Oscar-winning filmmaker Asghar Farhadi, who is at the Rio Film Festival to present “Parallel Tales,” spoke about the perceived hegemony of American cinema and how Hollywood shouldn’t be seen as a source for faithful portrayals of foreign cultures.

Asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A Separation” won Best International Film at the Oscars, Farhadi said he watched the film at the time it came out and felt it was a “Hollywood thing.” In the film, loosely based on a true story, director Ben Affleck plays a Latino exfiltration specialist who masquerades as a Hollywood producer to rescue six Americans held captive in Tehran during the U.S. hostage crisis in Iran. The moderator mentioned how Affleck’s film portrays Iran “like you’re in hell.”

“The problem with these kinds of films in Hollywood [and] some people in the United States [is that] they look at the world from up to down,” he added. “Someday you should ask them: Why do you feel you’re up and we’re down? I don’t understand why they have this ego that they’re up.” The Iranian director then said Americans often claim to “have democracy,” but they don’t. “You don’t have democracy. It’s a lie.”

Popular on Variety

Farhadi then recalled spending time in the U.S. a few years ago when working on a project and, during research, travelling to San Francisco to speak with incarcerated men. “I met some people in prison who are Black, [some who come] from other countries, and the real America was there. But people in the world don’t see that part of the United States.”

“I have this problem when they feel they are up and they think, ‘[others] should be like us,’” he continued. “Even if it’s in a good way and they want to be kind to you, they wish ‘one day you’ll become like us,’ and no, I don’t want to.”

Still on “Argo,” the director said movies like it “are not deep.” “They make these movies for money; it’s a business. And in these films it’s always a white guy from the United States saving others. My question is: Why? Why does an American go to Cuba or Iran to save people? People understand they can save themselves. Who asked you to come and save us?”

Asked about how he broaches politics in his films, the renowned filmmaker said that, whenever “you talk about society, you are talking about politics.” “Even when you talk about family life, their relationships, their difficulties and problems, indirectly you are talking about politics. In my films, I always try not to talk about politics directly because, to me, that is a bit far from cinema. The cinema that I believe is the kind of cinema that gives space to audiences to discover things about themselves.”

The director then brought up Abbas Kiarostami’s “Fellow Citizen” (“Hamshahri”) as Iran’s “most political film.” The 1983 documentary heavily trails drivers across the streets of the Iranian capital. “He made a documentary about car drivers in Tehran, but when you see people, the way they talk to the police, the layers are very political.”

“Media and cinema don’t give you a complete image of people’s ordinary life,” he added. “But the thing about empathy is that, all around the world, people are similar to each other. Cinema is based on hate and love. And [when it comes to] hate and love, everywhere is the same. A love between a mother and child in Brazil, in Tehran, is the same. The way they express it is different, but the core is the same.”

Parallel Tales Sydney Film Festival

Farhadi said that when he watches a Brazilian film, he soon forgets he is watching a story from another place in the world, and feels it is a “film about us” as people. “If one day people can travel to other countries, and if they shake hands, that’s the best way to know people, not through media. I don’t believe media can give us the whole image.”

On this, the filmmaker emphasized how his last two films, “A Hero” and “Parallel Tales,” are about how we see others and how we are seen in return. They are also heavily influenced by “how social media has shaped our lives.”

“When we see something in the media, we should be careful,” he continued, adding that most information replicated by mainstream media about Iran, for example, comes from “very simple knowledge” of real life in the country. When a singular discourse is perpetuated, the director implied, it means people are “ready to accept” when someone says “they are the enemy.” “This is something the media is doing, because the most powerful media belongs to powerful people. This is the problem.”

Farhadi spoke very briefly about his next film, reiterating it will be shot in his native language of Farsi. Enquired as to whether the film might deal with the current war in Iran and the conflict in Palestine, the director said: “Not directly,” suggesting the current political climate might have an underlying effect on the story despite not being the subject of his project.

“The Salesman” helmer also recalled how “Parallel Tales” was supposed to be shot in the U.S. “I stayed there for three years, writing, searching, casting. I did casting in the U.S. with American actors, very big names. But every day that I came back to my home, I told myself: I cannot connect with this. Something is wrong. It was a big problem. One night I decided to change.”

He said changing the film’s settings to France and moving production overseas was “not an easy decision,” but that “the DNA of this film is more European than American.”

As for the starry cast that includes Isabelle Huppert, Virginie Efira and Vincent Cassel, the director said he sent the script to “select names” upon arriving in France, and he was “so lucky” because all of them immediately said yes. Still, when he goes to set, he doesn’t “think about names.” “All of them are my team, my family, my actors. It doesn’t matter if it’s a big name or not. The way I work is the same, and they like it.”

The Rio Film Festival runs October 1-11.

title: ‘Behemoth!’: Why Tony Gilroy Needed Nine Composers to Score His Latest Film, and a Guide to Who Did What in the Film (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Behemoth!” in theaters Dec. 4 Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” bowed at the New York Film Festival Friday, and Lincoln Center’s Tully Hall seemed a fitting place to showcase a film about a musician. Written and directed by Gilroy, the film stars Pedro Pascal as a cellist who returns […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Behemoth!” in theaters Dec. 4

Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” bowed at the New York Film Festival Friday, and Lincoln Center’s Tully Hall seemed a fitting place to showcase a film about a musician.

Written and directed by Gilroy, the film stars Pedro Pascal as a cellist who returns to Los Angeles after a life on the road. Music is in his DNA — his parents were musicians, as were his grandparents. Music serves as a storytelling device, with Alex’s performances, whether on stage or in films he worked on, triggering flashbacks that reveal why he left Hollywood and what brought him back.

Popular on Variety

Gilroy wanted distinct scores for each film Alex works on. Rather than rely on a single composer, Gilroy turned to nine composers: Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandon Roberts and Alan Silvestri, known as the Behemoth Collective, to deliver distinct cues for the fictional movies Alex works on. In doing so, each composer brought their unique voices to the film.

Speaking with Variety, Gilroy explains that he had been sitting with the idea for years. He recalled the first time he walked into the John Williams Scoring Stage, steeped in Hollywood history. “You get in there, and there’s the emotional power and the smell of that room. It’s such a place of work, and then this incredible magic thing happens and there’s no place for the music to go except into the microphones and into your ears. It can’t escape that room.”

He went on to say, “It’s a vivid emotional trigger and I just kept wondering every time I went there — why didn’t anybody make a movie about this? Every time I went, I was like, ‘God, there’s got to be a movie here somewhere.’ I couldn’t figure it out.”

Eventually, he did.

He wrote a script that is a love letter to movie music and the art of scoring, carefully curating a story that allowed him to seamlessly integrate the work of the Behemoth Collective into the film.

Gilroy didn’t want one composer. “I knew I had to have different voices, and once you’re going to open it up, you want to cast it like actors,” he explains. “I made backstories for all the shows, so all the shows have a story to them and I could tell all the composers what the plots of their show were.” With that he started going out to composers. “Henry Jackman was the first one who came on, and he was so enthusiastic from the beginning. He gave me the enthusiasm to keep going forward with it. I talked to some people that I knew. I knew I wanted Michael Giacchino for the cartoon cue. I knew that I’d bring Brandon back,” and so the collective eventually came together.

Variety spoke with all nine composers to break down their cues and the key instruments they used to bring the “Behemoth!” score together.

Michael Abels

Abels was tasked with composing the music for Alex’s solo cello practice sessions. In one scene, Alex practices in a room and the music transitions into a flashback of Alex as a six-year-old prodigy performing Bach’s Cello Prelude No. 1 on “The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson.” Abels explains, “The music morphs from a warm-up exercise into the actual Bach piece.”

Emily Bear

Bear wrote the love theme for “Season of Glass.” She says, “It’s inspired by the French and Italian film scores of the ’60s: a lot of lush strings, beautiful harmonics, a lot of jazz-inspired progressions, but in an orchestral setting.”

Gilroy provided a detailed backstory for the fictional film, describing a young widow, a wealthy East Coast summer setting and a boy preparing to go to war. Bear also wrote a waltz for a scene where the young widow teaches the boy to dance. Bear notes, “It’s this very intimate, slow, tentative waltz that has some contention building underneath, so we added a lot of counterpoint and weird chromatic stuff underneath.”

Lukas Frank

Frank composed the film’s original song, “Your God Is Sleeping,” as well as the “Serian Suite,” which is tied to Alex’s character. “The suite is the underscore that opens throughout. It comes in throughout,” Frank explains.

The prepared piano was a key element of the “Serian Suite.” “There’s someone drilling on a string to make this low droning sound,” Frank notes. “The whole movie opens with the sound of the pedal coming down off the piano, and then some simple strings come in.”

Michael Giacchino

Giacchino wrote music using a standard orchestra for the cartoon “Happy & Slappy,” which Alex’s father composed during his career.

“I had to write a cue that his father wrote for these cartoons back in the ’60s cartoon, similar to ’Tom and Jerry,’” Giacchino explains. The music is used in a scene where Alex watches his brother fight while the cartoon score plays, syncing humorously with the action.

Henry Jackman

Jackman created the music for “Spies Don’t Run,” another fictional film within the story. Jackman describes it as “slightly ‘Jason Bourne-ish’, with a Middle Eastern flavor.”

Jackman’s work involved multiple scoring sessions. But for “Spies Don’t Run,” he took to it seriously and ended up scoring a six-minute suite using “a combination of orchestra, a little bit of slightly abstracted vocals, with quite a lot of heavy percussion.”

Nami Melumad

Melumad contributed the cue for one of the films within the film, “Tolerance Hill.” She explains that Gilroy’s guidance helped shape her approach. “Tony described it as a period film within the story, but it also had to emotionally lead us through Alex, the main character, as he revisits his childhood home.”

Melumad turned to the harp, an instrument Alex’s mother played, to evoke warmth, nostalgia and sadness. “It’s very delicate,” she says.

James Newton Howard

Howard composed the emotional finale of the film. “It’s pure underscore — a solo piano expressing the sadness of what’s happening in the story,” he says. Howard created multiple variations, including a piano-and-cello duet and orchestral arrangements. “It’s where everything comes together,” he notes.

Brandon Roberts

Roberts was tasked with writing “Look Away Jones,” a piece intended to sound like music Alex’s father had written for a TV show. Roberts says Gilroy described it as a “full-on smoking jazz band theme song for this make-believe show about an ex-football star turned detective.”

To prepare, Roberts listened to a lot of Quincy Jones and other theme music from that era. “It was an issue of coming up with a theme that felt like it actually existed and could have been on network television at the time,” he explains.

Roberts collaborated with renowned flute player Katisse Buckingham, who played jazz flute and Tim Liu, who assembled a group of musicians. “They knocked it out of the park,” Roberts says.

Alan Silvestri

Silvestri composed the cue that plays during the scoring session for “Open World,” a big Hollywood blockbuster and is a decoy title for a fictional production called “Behemoth.” It then bleeds from the scoring session into a sequence in the film. Silvestri describes it as a “big caper moment.” He adds, “I approached it as if it were a high-stakes adventure.”

Silvestri used a large orchestra to create a score that played the heist completely straight, despite its humorous premise.

Watch the trailer below.

title: Brilliance Of The Who’s Leader Shines In ‘Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes,’ Screening At Hamptons & Mill Valley
summary: The British invasion of the mid-1960s was a multi-pronged attack, an assault led above all by The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, and The Who. Their seismic impact on American and world culture has been well documented. But of the leaders of those three mega-bands, perhaps the most mysterious remains Pete Townshend, The Who’s songwriter and […]
content:
The British invasion of the mid-1960s was a multi-pronged attack, an assault led above all by The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, and The Who. Their seismic impact on American and world culture has been well documented. But of the leaders of those three mega-bands, perhaps the most mysterious remains Pete Townshend, The Who’s songwriter and enigmatic eminence, thrashing chords and smashing guitars while Roger Daltry handled lead vocals.

His sheer brilliance and rock innovation is captured in the documentary Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes, which held its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival. It’s directed by Frank Marshall (The Bee Gees: How Can You Mend a Broken Heart) and Nigel Sinclair (producer, Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It). Despite the enormity of The Who’s success – the rock operas Tommy and Quadrophenia, songs “Won’t Get Fooled Again,” “My Generation,” “Love Reign O’er Me” and so many others – somehow the band’s primary creative engine can remain obscured.

“A lot of people, when we say, ‘Oh, Pete wrote all the songs,’ they go, ‘What?’ They don’t understand because Pete’s also very quiet,” Marshall says in an interview at his home in Telluride. “He’s not the front man. Roger’s the front man… So, I do feel he’s underappreciated.”

Watch on Deadline

Pete Townshend in Paris, August 1972. Michael Putland/Getty Images

Key to understanding Townshend, as the film explores, is his background as an artist. He studied at Ealing Art College as a teenager and absorbed lessons from a teacher there, Roy Ascott, who propounded theories of technology and consciousness that would deeply influence Townshend. An exercise at Ealing in “auto-destruction,” where students smashed up pianos or other musical instruments, would lead to Townshend’s signature move with The Who, destroying his guitar at the end of performances.

“Actually, I have one of those smashed guitars, which I had a guitar builder lay out in an exposed frame like a skeleton,” Sinclair tells us. Smashing instruments “became a habit in shows. Obviously, in that club on Goldhawk Road, [Townshend] didn’t intend to do anything. His guitar went up into the ceiling and broke through cheap, old fashioned kind of stuff — with asbestos in those days. And it crumbled on Pete — the guitar and the neck was tipped over. So, he just threw it on the ground and smashed it. That was the first time. And the audience and Roger and the other [band members] are genuinely thinking, ‘What is he doing?’ And then [Keith] Moon, who only takes him about half a millisecond to tack, immediately started smashing his drum kit.”

The Who’s Pete Townshend smashes a guitar against an amplifier at a UK club on March 13, 1967. Chris Morphet/Redferns

More than mere theatrics, the frenetic smashing of instruments and The Who’s music itself, written by Townshend, channeled the sense of rage, frustration and angst felt by so many young British people in that post-war period of crumbled empire and dwindling opportunity.

“We see it in that first [Who] song, ‘Can’t Explain,’ when somebody said to him, ‘You’re expressing what we all feel and that connection,’” Marshall comments. “And he didn’t even know, but he was, as an artist, taking what was happening and channeling it into a song.”

Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes contains remarkable archive footage of the band in private moments and on stage, material unseen for decades. Archival producers Kate Griffiths and Catalina Curbishley were key to unearthing it.

Portrait of English rock band The Who, standing in front of flags wearing mod clothing, London, circa 1966. (L-R) Keith Moon, Pete Townshend, Roger Daltrey, John Entwistle. The Visualeyes Archive/Redferns

“The Who had actually put all of their assets in frozen storage back in the ’80s. It’s in this house, in somebody’s back garden,” says producer Cassidy Hartmann. “Our team actually went in there and sorted through everything and found this material and we were able to transfer it. And once we saw it, of course we were astounded at what was there because it’s like the dream of every documentary filmmaker to find something like this that no one’s ever seen.”

“The treasure chest,” Marshall says.

Pete Townshend of The Who pictured playing an acoustic guitar with his father Cliff Townshend (1916-1986), saxophone player with the Squadronaires, at home in London on March 30, 1966. Larry Ellis/Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images

Townshend was born in West London in May 1945, just days before Germany’s surrender, to musical parents – his father a professional saxophonist and his mother a singer. His parents’ marriage was a rocky one and as a small boy, Pete was sent to live with his maternal grandmother, a woman he would later describe as “clinically insane.” That devastating experience would unconsciously inform Tommy, the rock opera about a “deaf, dumb, and blind kid” who becomes a pinball wizard.

“A big part of our approach to the film was surrounding this idea of Pete as two people, as this divided person,” Hartmann observes. “And I think the trauma speaks to that. He says, ‘I divided then back when I was a kid and became this introverted, imaginative writer person.’ And then of course he also becomes this rock star on stage. And I think a big part of the tension in the film that we were interested in was that contradiction between those two sides of himself and his struggle to kind of reconcile those.”

Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes screens Saturday and Sunday at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York. It also screens Sunday on the other side of the country – at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Northern California. “Behind Blue Eyes,” of course, is one of Townshend’s greatest compositions, a song at times plaintive and reflective, at other moments ferocious in its anger. That, and “Going Mobile,” “Baba O’Riley,” and “Won’t Get Fooled Again” were written for Lifehouse, a kind of futuristic rock opera Townshend created after Tommy. It was his single most ambitious project (which is saying something) but never came to fruition, for reasons explored in the film. Lifehouse remains the great white whale of Townshend’s career, and a narrative thread throughout the documentary.

Director Frank Marshall on June 23, 2025 in New York City. John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images

“The engine for us was once we realized that he wants to feature this abandoned project, Lifehouse — which is quite hard to understand and of course collapsed for a number of reasons over the years — but it’s incredibly important to him,” Sinclair says. “It’s an itch that he never stops scratching… Frank said we needed to actually explore Pete as a person because what’s interesting about Lifehouse is it’s so important to him. That’s what drives [the film].”

Distribution plans for the documentary are pending. Given the track record of Marshall, Sinclair (Wilder, David Frost Vs.) and Hartmann (The Apollo, Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery), optimism on that front seems warranted. Marshall, a five-time Oscar nominee and six-time Primetime Emmy nominee is one of the top producers in motion picture history. At Telluride, the film became a hot ticket, generating interest from festival-goers including a certain Oscar-winning director, who had his own film in the festival, Ink.

Producer Cassidy Hartmann and director Nigel Sinclair attend the Telluride Film Festival on September 4, 2026. Vivien Killilea/Getty Images

“Danny Boyle was over there saying, ‘I’ve got to see the Townshend film,’” Sinclair reports. “So I spoke to him and said, ‘If you can’t see here, I’ll send you a link.’ So we’re feeling pretty good about getting it placed.”

Hartmann was born after the height of The Who’s success. “I learned a lot on this project. I developed a deep affection for Pete especially. And I did see an opportunity to introduce the band to a younger generation,” she notes. “I thought that there was an opportunity there for that to connect with a bigger audience than just The Who fan base. There was something relatable and universal in Pete’s story for anyone who’s a creative person trying to do something in the world.”

title: ‘Barbershop’ Teaser: Jermaine Fowler Struggles To Win Over Calvin’s New Barbers In Prime Video Series Adaptation
summary: Calvin’s is taking walk-ins once again as Barbershop returns to screens with a new eight-episode show. On Saturday at CultureCon, Prime Video shared the first teaser for the series adaptation of the comedy-drama film franchise that launched in 2002, revealing the barbershop’s new owner in the show, all episodes of which premiere Feb. 10, 2027 […]
content:
Calvin’s is taking walk-ins once again as Barbershop returns to screens with a new eight-episode show.

On Saturday at CultureCon, Prime Video shared the first teaser for the series adaptation of the comedy-drama film franchise that launched in 2002, revealing the barbershop’s new owner in the show, all episodes of which premiere Feb. 10, 2027 on the streaming platform.

The TV adaptation stars Jermaine Fowler as Travis “Trav” Porter, who endeavors to follow in the footsteps of his grandfather Eddie (played in the movies by Cedric the Entertainer), a legendary barber at the iconic Calvin’s barbershop in Chicago. And while the barbers are new, the shop remains just as lively, the customers just as argumentative, and the fades are still the dopest in the city — because at Calvin’s, the community comes together for way more than just a haircut.

Fowler stars in the series alongside Brett Gray, Punkie Johnson, Roy Wood Jr., E.J. Bonilla, Bresha Webb, Bokeem Woodbine, Tiana Okoye and Langston Kerman, with guest stars including Zack Fox, Ego Nwodim, Diallo Riddle, Ziwe, Tituss Burgess, Comedian CP, Devon Walker and Belmont Cameli.

Watch on Deadline

Marshall Todd, who co-wrote the original film, serves as writer, EP and co-showrunner alongside Max Searle.

Jermaine Fowler in Prime Video’s ‘Barbershop’ Elizabeth Sisson/Prime

From Amazon MGM Studios and MGM Television, producers include Kevin Hart, Bryan Smiley, Mike Stein and Tiffany Brown for Hartbeat; Bradley Gardner for Busy B Entertainment; Cameron Burnett and Autumn Bailey-Ford for Prominent Productions; and George L. Tillman and Robert Teitel for State Street Pictures; plus Fowler and director Oz Rodriguez.

Launching with 2002’s Barbershop, and featuring a star-studded ensemble led by Ice Cube as Calvin, the franchise also includes the sequels Barbershop 2: Back in Business (2004) and Barbershop: The Next Cut (2016), as well as the 2005 spin-off Beauty Shop, starring Queen Latifah.

In 2005, Showtime adapted Barbershop into a series with Omar Gooding as Calvin, but the show ended after one season.

title: Jerry Golod Dies: ‘Tales from the Darkside’ EP Was 87
summary: Jerry Golod, an executive producer behind Tales from the Darkside and Return to Green Acres, has died. He was 87. The producer’s daughter Dori Golod Howell announced that he died on Wednesday at his Rancho Mirage home, following a brief battle with cancer, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Born Dec. 26, 1938 in the Bronx, […]
content:
Jerry Golod, an executive producer behind Tales from the Darkside and Return to Green Acres, has died. He was 87.

The producer’s daughter Dori Golod Howell announced that he died on Wednesday at his Rancho Mirage home, following a brief battle with cancer, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

Born Dec. 26, 1938 in the Bronx, Golod began his career in advertising, during which he led an ad agency’s TV production company before becoming vice president of children’s programs at CBS in 1975.

Following George A. Romero’s 1982 Stephen King-penned horror anthology Creepshow, Golod helped EPs Romero and Richard P. Rubinstein bring the EC comics adaptation to TV in the form of the 1983-’88 Tales from the Darkside syndicated television show.

In 2013, Golod was part of the producing team behind CBS Television Studios and CW’s reboot of Tales from the Darkside, which ultimately did not get picked up to series.

Watch on Deadline

Golod was an EP on the 1990 CBS TV movie Return to Green Acres, reuniting Eddie Albert and Eva Gabor from the 1965-’71 series. He was also behind ABC’s 1991-’92 series remake of Land of the Lost.

Additionally, Golod served as an executive producer on the 1985 TV movies Brass and Condor, and he was instrumental in helping author Elliott Baker adapt his 1971 novel Pocock & Pitt into the Canadian series Adderly (1986-’88).

title: Guillermo Del Toro Buries ‘Digger’ In Praise, Slams “Petty” Review: “Decidedly A Theatrical Experience”
summary: Although Digger has premiered this weekend to mixed reviews, Guillermo Del Toro is a confirmed fan of the Alejandro G. Iñárritu satire. The 3x Oscar winner has taken to social media to heap praise on Tom Cruise’s latest after responding to a critic that called the film “far from a must-watch” and recommended viewers wait […]
content:
Although Digger has premiered this weekend to mixed reviews, Guillermo Del Toro is a confirmed fan of the Alejandro G. Iñárritu satire.

The 3x Oscar winner has taken to social media to heap praise on Tom Cruise‘s latest after responding to a critic that called the film “far from a must-watch” and recommended viewers wait for it to hit streaming.

“Entirely Petty headline,” wrote Del Toro in response to IGN’s review. “Love it or not. And, yes, I do. The film delivers in scale, ambition and reach at a theatrical screen level. Daring, bold and cinematically complex. Decidedly a theatrical experience.”

It turns out the algorithm was listening, as the Pan’s Labyrinth auteur has since continued reposting other fans’ praise of the Warner Bros. movie, which is now in theaters.

Watch on Deadline

“Funny, I go into the platform and without even scrolling down, these are popping at the top of my timeline…” he wrote with one repost. “So… I will just keep posting them. Tune in or drop out-“

Dig or Die – c'mon! https://t.co/NvwC826iWm — Guillermo del Toro (@RealGDT) October 2, 2026

“Dig or Die – c’mon!” Del Toro wrote with another.

Sitting at a 51% critic rating on Rotten Tomatoes with a C+ CinemaScore, Del Toro compared the bad reviews for Digger to the criticism that surrounded The King of Comedy (1982), The Big Lebowski (1998) and The Counselor (2013), all having since become appreciated by audiences years later.

In Digger, Cruise stars as the titular oil tycoon Digger Rockwell, who races to fix a catastrophe he caused so he can avoid blame and be seen as humanity’s savior.

title: ‘Verity’ Solid $33M+ Start; ‘Digger’ At $8M Is Tom Cruise’s Lowest Opening In 19 Years; Both Pics Get C+ CinemaScores – Box Office Update
summary: SATURDAY AM: Warner Bros’ very original, very expensive auteur feature, Digger, is filing an $8M opening, which is still the lowest for Tom Cruise since 2007’s much cheaper Lions for Lambs at $6.7M. In hindsight, Amazon MGM Studios was bold to date on top of a big budget Cruise movie with the big screen take […]
content:
SATURDAY AM: Warner Bros’ very original, very expensive auteur feature, Digger, is filing an $8M opening, which is still the lowest for Tom Cruise since 2007’s much cheaper Lions for Lambs at $6.7M.

In hindsight, Amazon MGM Studios was bold to date on top of a big budget Cruise movie with the big screen take of Colleen Hoover’s Verity, but they caught wind from early on that the Alejandro G. Iñárritu-directed Digger wouldn’t be a tycoon at the B.O. Verity is posting the second best opening for a Hoover novel on the big screen now at $33.6M after a better than expected Friday of $15.1M.

Here’s a coincidence; both films get a C+ CinemaScore. That’s the worst Hoover has received so far, her It Ends With Us landed an A-, while Reminders of Him and Regretting You received Bs. Typically female book adaptations file in the B-range as fans of the novel are quite critical of the theatrical take. Should Verity be concerned about buckling due to that CinemaScore? Nah, Fifty Shades of Grey filed a C+ and it was alright. The 79% female turnout here for the Dakota Johnson, Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett thriller stands at a 50% definite recommend on Screen Engine/Rentak PostTrak exits.

Watch on Deadline

Verity is playing everywhere, including the South, East, South Central and Midwest. PLFs are repping 28% of the weekend sans Imax. Adam Aron can be happy that AMC Lincoln Square is the pic’s top grossing venue with more than $36K through Friday.

On the bright side for Digger, frankly, we thought it would be worse in its CinemaScopes ala Mother! (F) or Eyes Wide Shut (D-). Cruise’s idiosyncratic turn as a charismatic self-help guru in Paul Thomas Anderson’s 1999 Magnolia (which earned Cruise a Best Supporting Oscar nom) earned a C- CinemaScore. Interestingly enough, Digger‘s RT audience score of 71% is the same as Ari Aster’s Beau Is Afraid (71%), which was another divisive film made for $50M (considered wildly expensive for the arthouse auteur, though next to Digger‘s $160M+ production cost, a very thrifty spend).

What few went to Digger? Iñárritu has said that he made the movie for the Gen Z generation (who would have thought?), and the little who bought tickets were 60% between 18-34. Largely overall male at 73%. Overall definite recommend is low at 47%. Imax and PLFs for this VistaVision-shot movie are contributing close to half of the gross. No surprise, this movie is playing strictly on the coasts which are repping 48% of its cash versus the regions’ average of 40%. AMC Lincoln Square counts the best sum for this artistic disaster at $45K.

We’ll get into the mud with Digger later, but this is, what it is: a heavy dialogue driven, political absurdist satire, and per those in tracking, satire never does well. We’re not talking The Naked Gun, rather Paramount Pictures’ Tim Robbins-directed and -starring Bob Roberts from 1992. True, not a wide release back in the day, rather an indie play, but still it only made $4.4M. There’s also Steven Soderbergh’s 2009 The Informant comedy starring Matt Damon, another Warner Bros release. Though made for $22M back in 2009, it didn’t dazzle with a $10.4M opening and final domestic of $33M. What about the Oscar winning The Big Short? (final domestic $70.2M). That was loaded up with all-stars including Ryan Gosling, Steve Carell, Christian Bale and Brad Pitt and made for a substantially lower price tag of a reported net $30M. Film finance sources will argue that originality always comes at a very low cost, however, try telling that to motion picture executives in the streaming era when Netflix and Apple are making $100M+ movies (Noah Baumbach’s Netflix movie White Noise made for well in excess of $140M).

The latter example brings up the point that some streamers can get away with making expensive movies, and showing zero gross (yes, that will soon change for Netflix as they report certain titles on their upcoming fall and 2027 slate). But when a motion picture studio rolls the dice, they’re vilified. In the current era of theatrical vs. streaming, motion picture execs are banging their heads against the wall when it comes to making original movies that set themselves apart from the hodgepodge offerings in a streaming queue. Digger was an attempt by the Warner Bros. administration of Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy to do something unseen before, a la period vampire musical pic, Sinners, and anarchist 1970s action car movie, One Battle After Another, with a big star and director, that was very much in the spirit of other ballsy Warners Bros pics (remember before it opened, Gravity took a while to get off the ground in development and was considered a gamble).

Word of mouth fell on Digger in RelishMix metrics from an 8.1 on a scale of ten on Sept. 15, to a 6.4 earlier this week. “Chatter has been mixed-negative for Digger. There’s skepticism with viewers who love the idea of Cruise, but side-eye the execution: ‘Impressive that after a nearly three-minute long trailer, I still don’t really know what this movie’s about.’ The sharpest criticism isn’t about hating the movie, it’s about distrust, suspicion that the ‘aging gracefully’ narrative is a PR construct. Comments needle at the film’s tonal identity, wondering if it’s satire or self-parody, ‘For me this looked funny at first viewing. Second time it just looks cynical and a bad Kubrick’s Dr. Strangelove rip-off. Hope my first take is right.’ Plus, ‘Why does this look like Tropic Thunder cosplay’ along with, ‘I understand even less about this movie after the full trailer than I did after the teaser.’ And, there are grumbles about the promo montage in the ‘Tom Cruise Retrospective’ trailer feeling like a premature Oscars reel,” reports RelishMix.

The other curveball with Digger is that there’s a twist. From the marketing, audiences walk into the movie thinking it’s a western apocalyptic comedy. Yes, it’s that, but it’s meta and that will no doubt confuse.

Digger‘s social media reach across Instagram, Facebook, X, TikTok and YouTube stood at 289.5M followers before opening, which is -66% less than that of Mission: Impossible The Final Reckoning (847.2M) and -28% behind Top Gun: Maverick‘s (404M).

Despite the pothole of Digger, the overall weekend is looking great with the third straight $100M+ weekend so far this fall with an estimated $101.3M, +25% from a year ago when Taylor Swift: The Official Release Party of a Showgirl opened to $34M.

As far as September at the domestic box office, it was pretty damn good. Not the best, but the second best post-Covid per Rentrak with $601.9M, +1.3% from last year, and filing behind 2024’s $606.8M when Beetlejuice Beetlejuice ruled.
