During the goodnights at the end of the episode, Swift brought a birthday cake out for Johnson.

There was no question of Swift doing a musical number on the episode, since the musical guest had long since been announced as Turnstile. But the singer turning up at some point on “SNL” this season seemed like an inevitability after Swift participated in an Easter egg-laden “Law & Order SVU” sketch on the Emmys. Behind her in the skit, a large “Saturday Night Live” emblem was tacked to a bulletin board… not her subtlest clue ever.

title: ‘SNL’s Weekend Update Tackles Cornell Controversy & Return Of ‘Glee’
summary: After cracks about Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem and President Donald Trump’s vendetta against CNN, Michael Che on Saturday Night Live‘s Weekend Update touched on the ongoing controversy at Cornell University and Ryan Murphy’s decision to bring back Glee. Che first served up a serious note by referencing the sexual assault case at Cornell and how […]
content:
After cracks about Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem and President Donald Trump’s vendetta against CNN, Michael Che on Saturday Night Live‘s Weekend Update touched on the ongoing controversy at Cornell University and Ryan Murphy’s decision to bring back Glee.

Che first served up a serious note by referencing the sexual assault case at Cornell and how “obviously we don’t want to make light of anything that happened, but it is a good time to talk about men holding other men accountable.”

As the camera panned toward to a silent Colin Jost, Che said, “Look, we all have that one friend that seems like a nice guy, but they’re definitely not. It could be someone you’re close to, or someone you work with. Maybe you can’t prove anything. You can just look at him and tell those weird, privileged Ivy League types always got some messed up stuff going on.”

Che then turned to Jost and said, “Is there anything you want to add, Colin?”



“Stop cutting to me,” Jost responded.

Watch on Deadline

Later, cast member Kam Patterson joined the desk to show his enthusiasm for the reboot of Glee. (Ryan Murphy recently said that he “just finished” a Glee reboot script). Che was a bit skeptical that Patterson is a true Gleek, despite Patterson claiming he was eager to find out if Rachel was still on Broadway and if Kurt and Blaine were still together.

But Che wasn’t convinced. “Look, I know you man. You don’t have to say yes to every day that a white writer pitches to you …. Look Kam. I’ve worked here, what, 30, 35 years. I know what this is. Two white writers came up to you in suits, pitched you an idea about Glee, and now you’re out here saying a bunch of names you’ve never heard before, right?”

Patterson admits he hasn’t and feels “pretty bad” that he “just did jazz hands on national television.”

title: ‘SNL’ Cold Open Goes Full MAGA Midterms Desperation With Hegseth’s “Schlong Donkeys”, Trump’s Rambles & A Sad VP
summary: Just a month away from the volatile midterms and a president way down in the polls, there was once again a plethora of political material ripe for this week’s SNL cold open, and the NBC late-nighter went full MAGA, with some Mitch McConnell on the side. Played by Mickey Day, the wheelchair bound 84-year-old Kentucky […]
content:
Just a month away from the volatile midterms and a president way down in the polls, there was once again a plethora of political material ripe for this week’s SNL cold open, and the NBC late-nighter went full MAGA, with some Mitch McConnell on the side.

Played by Mickey Day, the wheelchair bound 84-year-old Kentucky senator offered a premature “Live from New York” before being cut off by RNC ad consultants desperate to turn things around for the GOP. To that, there was a “He tricked us” (in Spanish) Marco Rubio, portrayed by the always on point Marcello Hernández, and a 2028 J.D. Vance (Jeremy Culhane) that no one wanted to actually put in a spot.

Then there was Colin Jost’s Pete Hegseth, putting the fun in whack job Defense Secretary once again.

Watch on Deadline

“What’s up, schlong donkeys?” the Saturday Night Live Weekend Update co-anchor began in what might have been one of the greatest campaign ads ever (we’re talking 1954 Daisy level) if it was real. “Now listen up, okay, because I need all you patriots at home to do the gayest thing ever and vote. Thanks to me, the military finally has its priorities and sexuality straight.”

Tossing in some slam poetry, Jost’s Hegseth added: “In conclusion, vote, I guess. And remember, even if you’re stationed overseas, you can still vote by mail, which is the only by mail I’m cool with.”

Of course, this being a MAGA parody and being SNL, the joke had to go further. Having said that, unlike many too-long cold opens, this semi-morbid midterm skit work at the extra length – entirely because POTUS came to cook, base loathing and all.

“I’m President Trump and I approve this ramble,” started a typically and wonderfully unhinged James Austin Johnson.

Drawing from the fiction that is so much of Trumpland’s facts, he added in the fake ad: “We’re getting mogged out there, but not for long because I have a solution. If the Republicans win, I’ll give everyone $5,000, and that is not a bribe because I have no intention of following through on that promise.’

“So, just pretend I’m on the ballot, okay? You have to use something called imagination. Imagination makes a MAGA nation. Wow, that’s pretty good. I can already see that written on the back of an obese woman’s booty shorts in dirty, disgusting Myrtle Beach. What a hell all this country is! It’s full of awful people.”

Perhaps, but not in tonight’s spot-on cold open.

Delayed a tad again on the West Coast like last week’s season opener thanks to college football, tonight’s SNL is the second show of the 52nd season.

Verity star Dakota Johnson is hosting SNL for the third time. Coming off a big box office start for the Collen Hoover thriller, Johnson is joined by Turnstile as musical guest, the Maryland rockers’ SNL debut. Next week will see one-time dumped cast member Shane Gillis back for his third time hosting. The October 10 show will see the much-acclaimed Rosalía returning for her third SNL appearance.

title: Taylor Swift Joins ‘SNL’ Host Dakota Johnson During Opening Monologue
summary: Taylor Swift gave Dakota Johnson some pretty sweet payback for appearing in her “Patient Zero” music video: the mega-star joined the Verity actress during her opening monologue tonight on Saturday Night Live. Perhaps it was just a birthday present for Johnson, who turns 37 on Sunday. Either way, Swift came in to yuk it up […]
content:
Taylor Swift gave Dakota Johnson some pretty sweet payback for appearing in her “Patient Zero” music video: the mega-star joined the Verity actress during her opening monologue tonight on Saturday Night Live.

Perhaps it was just a birthday present for Johnson, who turns 37 on Sunday. Either way, Swift came in to yuk it up with Johnson, who used her opening moment to wax on about dating musicians. Her recent beaus were Role Model and Chris Martin.

“I went through two very public, very lame breakups with two very awesome musicians,” Johnson said about what she’s been doing since the last time she hosted SNL. (This is Johnson’s third appearance on the NBC show).

“It’s not my fault, though,” Johnson continued. “Some people leave concerts with merch and I leave concerts with a two and a half year relationship. But I have really good friends. They don’t judge me for dating these men. They’re actually really supportive.”

Watch on Deadline

That’s when Swift joined her on stage. “I’m not your therapist actually,” Swift tells Johnson. “You just show up once a week at my house with an empty bottle of wine and ask if I want some.”

Swift returned at the end of the show to present her buddy with a birthday cake.

The Verity star made her SNL debut in season 40. See her monologue above.

title: Daily Wire’s Pro-ICE Film ‘Pawn Shop’ Production Temporarily Suspended
summary: Production of Daily Wire’s pro-ICE film “Pawn Shop” has been temporarily halted in Livingston, Mont., following a Special City Commission Meeting held on Saturday. The action comes as Livingston locals raised concerns about the film’s impact on local business — and notably the city’s sole food bank — as well as improper notification about hazardous […]
content:
Production of Daily Wire’s pro-ICE film “Pawn Shop” has been temporarily halted in Livingston, Mont., following a Special City Commission Meeting held on Saturday.

The action comes as Livingston locals raised concerns about the film’s impact on local business — and notably the city’s sole food bank — as well as improper notification about hazardous stunts. During the meeting, residents voiced worries about the filming, saying it made them feel unsafe. City Commission member Cindy Daniels explained that she felt that “they’ve taken advantage of the situation to make their movie… We’re not profiting off that movie. So they’re not thinking of the veterans that live on K Street. They’re not thinking of the food resource center.”

The Livingston Commission concluded: “A motion to immediately temporarily suspend Bonfire Pawn Shop LLC’s permit while seeking legal opinion from the city attorney in a timely manner to amend, suspend, or revoke the permit to come back to the commission not after 5:00pm on October 5th.”

Popular on Variety

Daily Wire did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.

The halting of filming comes days after locals in Livingston protested against the film’s production, which has been reported to include an opening scene depicting the fatal ICE shooting of Renée Good that occurred in Minnesota earlier this year.

The Livingston Food Resource Center posted a statement on Instagram on Friday, explaining how filming “Pawn Shop” has affected its clients.

“People who already face numerous obstacles to meeting their most basic needs are not facing additional completely avoidable barriers to accessing food because of how this production was permitted,” it read. “We were not notified of the plans to film,” the statement continued, noting that attendance at the pantry was down 17% on Tuesday, “an eight-week low from seeing 90-100+ households a day. That is unacceptable.”

title: ‘East of Eden’ Boss Zoe Kazan on That Devastating Ending, Why Florence Pugh’s Cathy Is Both a ‘Murderer’ and ‘Survivor’ and Making Lee a Central Character
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “East of Eden,” now streaming on Netflix. Zoe Kazan has spent much of her life thinking about family legacy on and off screen. More than 62 years after her grandfather Elia Kazan famously directed James Dean in an adaptation of the fourth and final part of John […]
content:
The combination of your writing and Florence’s performance makes your interpretation of Cathy particularly hard to pin down, because she is so mercurial by nature, especially toward the final years of her life as this madam of a brothel. How did you think about scripting Cathy’s descent into madness?

Steinbeck kept a journal while he was writing this book. He wrote longhand on these big ledger books. He wrote his pages for the day on the right-hand side, and he would write letters to his friend and editor, Pascal Covici, on the left-hand side. Those letters were published, and I weirdly had read them already when I started adapting this, but I used those letters as a real North Star for me in understanding Steinbeck’s intentions. One of the things that’s really clear to me is that his viewpoint of her changed as he wrote. He goes from saying, “Oh, I’m going to write a monster unlike any you’ve ever seen,” to saying, “I think we all have a little monster blood in us, and people will hate her not because she is foreign, but because she is familiar.”

I don’t have any proof for this, but I think he didn’t know what to do with that empathy. I think it surprised him — maybe it crept up on him. One of the things I see in the second half of the book is that he starts to really punish her. It’s like he doesn’t know what to do with her, really. He starts being really mean about her physical appearance, which I get is a manifestation of her evil. But because he’s filled with empathy and understanding for her by this point in the book, it felt to me a little bit underdeveloped. I was curious about: What’s the more fully embodied version of what happens to Cathy? Why does she kill herself? How do we get there?

One of the things that really struck me was that this character is operating from the viewpoint that the world is full of folly and evil. This is a person who’s really isolated herself, who has run from love, who has thought of love as a trap, and who has done everything in her power not to be trapped. And here she is in her 30s, and she has no one she can trust because of how she’s built her life. In the book, she builds a little gray room with no windows that she can go in and close the door. For budget reasons, I had to not have her build this little room, but I tried to turn her whole bedroom into that room for herself. I thought about a world in which this person is carrying trauma and has had no access to anyone helping her with her mental health. I was also thinking about the morphine use that is implied in the story — she carries this little bottle of morphine around her neck — and I stepped off from there.

title: Pedro Pascal in ‘Behemoth!’: The Oscar-Worthy Role That He (and Latinos) Have Been Waiting For
summary: Pedro Pascal makes his Oscar case with a cello. “Behemoth!,” Tony Gilroy’s first feature as a director since “The Bourne Legacy” in 2012, world-premiered on Friday night at Alice Tully Hall as the centerpiece selection of the New York Film Festival. Pascal plays Alex Serian, a former child prodigy from a family of Los Angeles […]
content:
Pedro Pascal makes his Oscar case with a cello.

“Behemoth!,” Tony Gilroy’s first feature as a director since “The Bourne Legacy” in 2012, world-premiered on Friday night at Alice Tully Hall as the centerpiece selection of the New York Film Festival. Pascal plays Alex Serian, a former child prodigy from a family of Los Angeles studio musicians who returns home after 20 years on tour to record Hollywood film scores.

Pascal offers a beautiful, internalized performance that ranks among his best work on film. More than that, it’s the first time a director has built a movie on the merit of what happens across Pascal’s face when nobody is talking.

Popular on Variety

Pascal did not get his fame from the movies. He was almost 40 when his “Game of Thrones” character Oberyn Martell became one of the most beloved — and most egregiously short-lived — characters In TV history. Then came more series work on “Narcos,” “The Mandalorian” and “The Last of Us.” On that ascent, Pascal became an internet boyfriend (“Daddy,” as many have called him). You can’t blame me for worrying about audiences focusing on his depth and talent amid the thirst.

It is, perhaps, why his scene-stealing performance in the 2022 action-comedy “The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent” went suspiciously ignored. He played Javi, the billionaire superfan of Nicolas Cage (and maybe a cartel kingpin), who went toe-to-toe with one of the most gloriously unhinged actors of his generation. Pascal stole every frame.

Pedro Almodóvar’s short “Strange Way of Life,” Celine Song’s “Materialists” and Ari Aster’s “Eddington” gave Pascal latitude. Gilroy and “Behemoth!” make him undeniable.

Pedro Pascal in “Behemoth!” Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures

Gilroy structures the movie around flashbacks. Each time Pascal’s Alex sits down to play the opening cue of a different movie score, the music sends him back to the people and circumstances that made him flee. Pascal doesn’t overtly articulate those memories. We feel them in looks, pauses and slight changes in his posture. The performance rises in those moments.

Pascal’s work recalls Jude Law in “Cold Mountain,” which is still my go-to example of a reserved performance surviving an Oscar season that typically rewards outsized performances. In that film, Law’s wounded soldier Inman barely speaks during his long walk home from the Civil War, yet voters noticed him anyway. There isn’t a war for Pascal to walk through unless you count the one in his mind — concerning his father (Hank Azaria) or his brother (Will Arnett).

And then there’s Olivia Wilde. Somehow, her knockout year directing and starring in “The Invite,” and reminding us all of her command and delicious appeal in “I Want Your Sex,” gets better. She devours every frame in “Behemoth!” as the ex Pascal can’t quite shake. She’s channeling a little Cameron Diaz in “Vanilla Sky,” harboring obsession with a scary fuse. Noteworthy: Diaz received a Golden Globe and a SAG nomination for that performance, but the Academy passed. This doesn’t deserve that same fate.

Nonetheless, the real star of “Behemoth!” is the music itself.

Gilroy recruited nine composers, each scoring a different fictional film within the film. The result is a soundtrack that moves across eras and genres in the same way Alex’s memory does. The team includes Michael Abels (“Get Out”) along with pianist and composer Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino (“Up”), James Newton Howard (“Michael Clayton”), Henry Jackman (“Captain America: The Winter Soldier”), Nami Melumad (Pixar’s “Dream Productions”), Brandon Roberts (“Andor”) and Alan Silvestri (“Forrest Gump”).

There’s a bit of irony for anyone who follows the score race. Giacchino already has the statuette, winning for “Up” in 2010. James Newton Howard, who scored Gilroy’s “Michael Clayton,” is one of the Academy’s great bridesmaids, with multiple nominations and no wins. Silvestri, whose noms and credits include “Forrest Gump” and “Back to the Future,” has never won either.

The title refers to the giant fake movie the story builds toward. Gilroy created a tribute to the Los Angeles scoring community he believes is disappearing. Following the film academy’s 2024 rule change, as many as three composers can receive individual statuettes for original score. However, nine still don’t fit, unless they enter as a “group” and share the nom (meaning a lone Oscar statuette). A movie about musicians, ironically, could be shut out or disqualified from the category built for them, if the music branch chooses ego over artistic merit.

Admittedly, the film won’t be for everyone. “Behemoth!” is very “Tár”-coded. It focuses on a protagonist whose gift and damage come from the same place. Some will find the fake-movie conceit too clever, and others may think the climax goes too small.

Underneath it all is a simple, aching idea about love and what we think we’re entitled to. That’s Gilroy’s brilliant screenplay at work.

“Behemoth!” premiered in the middle of Hispanic Heritage Month, and for the Latinos who have been rooting for Pascal since Oberyn, this has been a long time coming.

Look at who came before him.

José Ferrer, a Puerto Rican, won for “Cyrano de Bergerac” and became the first Latino actor to take home a best actor Oscar. Seventy-five years later, he is still the only one. Mexican Anthony Quinn, who won two supporting Oscars, received lead nominations for “Wild Is the Wind” and “Zorba the Greek” but never took home the top prize. Then came Edward James Olmos for “Stand and Deliver,” Demián Bichir for “A Better Life,” Colman Domingo for “Rustin” and “Sing Sing” and most recently, Wagner Moura, who last season became the first Brazilian ever nominated in the category, for “The Secret Agent.”

And Pascal may not be the only Latino celebrating at the upcoming 99th Academy Awards.

John Leguizamo, who received the Career Achievement Award at the Critics Choice Celebracion ceremony the same day as the “Behemoth” premiere, has been grinding for four decades. As Eumaeus, the swineherd who remains loyal, he’s the heartbeat of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.” He has never been nominated for an Oscar but that also looks to change this year.

We must sit still and hold the note for Pedro.

“Behemoth!” opens on Dec 4.

title: Zach Bryan Breaks Attendance Record at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium While Wearing ‘Free Palestine’ Shirt for Second Night in a Row
summary: Zach Bryan broke the attendance record at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium on Saturday night, performing for 73,538 fans — the largest crowd for any event in the venue’s history — while wearing a “Free Palestine” shirt for the second night in a row. The move was a statement on several levels, but was pointedly directed […]
content:
Zach Bryan broke the attendance record at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium on Saturday night, performing for 73,538 fans — the largest crowd for any event in the venue’s history — while wearing a “Free Palestine” shirt for the second night in a row.

The move was a statement on several levels, but was pointedly directed at Kraft — the billionaire, Trump-supporting owner of the Foxborough, Mass. stadium — who rallied fellow stadium owners to ban rapper Macklemore from his scheduled opening slot on the Ed Sheeran tour last month from performing at their venues, after the rapper made pro-Palestine comments onstage in New Jersey. Kraft had described Macklemore‘s comments as “hate speech,” with questionable accuracy.

The attendance record, which was broken on the second of Bryan’s two performances at the venue, was announced by tour promoter AEG on Sunday morning, and in a post on the stadium’s social media accounts. The latter announcement features photos of Bryan wearing the shirt, although the message is illegible and there was no mention of it in the post; however, it is referenced in the majority of the comments. Kraft used the Gillette Stadium account to defend his ban on Macklemore; a rep for Kraft did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

Popular on Variety

The move was both a surprise — Bryan a proud Navy veteran working in the country genre, which has a fan base that would not be universally welcoming to such a purportedly left-wing position — and not, as Bryan has traditionally and steadfastly spoken his mind, from releasing a song critical of ICE raids to a bitter online dispute with country artist Gavin Adcock. According to fan footage, at least two of Bryan’s band members were wearing Palestine jerseys as well.

Bryan was seen wearing a T-shirt (with the sleeves cut off, as is his nightly custom) bearing the logo “Free Palestine.” Beneath that on the shirt were an emblem of a pine tree and another message that read “An Appeal to Heaven.” These are references to a flag commissioned by George Washington in 1775 for a fleet of schooners sent to intercept British ships; later, it became the flag for the Massachusetts Navy — giving it a distinct historical and local connection for the Boston-area show.

Bryan’s drummer, Nate Head bore a jersey with Palestine on the front and, on the back, the numeral 5 and the name “Hind Rajab.” Rajab was a 5-year-old girl in Gaza reported to have been killed by the Israeli military’s tank fire on Jan. 24, 2024, after having been trapped with her cousin and pleading for help in a disabled car for hours.

Some news outlets ran with a widely spread and apparently false statement attributed to Bryan on Saturday. The statement, in which Bryan supposedly spoke up defending his stance from the night before, came from an X account that purports to belong to the singer but does not. (Bryan’s real X account has been deactivated for some time — it’s not clear for how long, since he had a history of saying contentious things, then deactivating, then restarting it.)

Bryan’s politics have been somewhat elusive, with the singer-songwriter posting that he finds deep problems on both sides of America’s political divides. He previously raised the ire of some on the right with a song titled “Bad News,” which among its scattershot character-study lyrics, contained a seemingly negative reference to ICE (“ICE is gonna come, bust down your door / Try and build a house no one builds no more / But I got a telephone / Kids are all scared and all alone”). Following that, many on social media threatened to “Bud Light” him — that is, subject him to a boycott. But Bryan’s stadium shows have continued to be sellouts, and the artist has remained mostly apolitical as far as taking stands on any hot-button issues.

The Foxborough shows are part of Bryan’s biggest tour yet, spanning more than 40 dates across North America and Europe starting in March 2026, and adds to a record-setting year for the artist. On September 27, 2025, he became the first artist ever to play Michigan Stadium, drawing 112,408 fans, the largest ticketed concert audience in U.S. history. That show surpassed the previous mark of 110,905, set by George Strait in Texas in 2024.

title: James Van Der Beek Was the ‘Soul’ of ‘Dawson’s Creek,’ Says Show Creator Kevin Williamson: ‘He Handled His Cancer With Such Grace and Courage’
summary: “Dawson’s Creek” creator Kevin Williamson remembered the show’s late star Jame Van Der Beek on Saturday night while being honored with a Hero Award at the Barbara Berlanti Heroes Gala, Greg Berlanti’s annual F Cancer benefit. Williams explained that the show, about a small-town high school student dreaming of becoming a Hollywood director, was inspired […]
content:
“Dawson’s Creek” creator Kevin Williamson remembered the show’s late star Jame Van Der Beek on Saturday night while being honored with a Hero Award at the Barbara Berlanti Heroes Gala, Greg Berlanti’s annual F Cancer benefit.

Williams explained that the show, about a small-town high school student dreaming of becoming a Hollywood director, was inspired by his own life.

“So when I was casting the role, I was basically looking for me, but I was looking for the good-looking, handsome, camera-ready, great jawline version of myself, someone people would actually want to see,” Williamson said, adding, “He became that person. James Van Der Beek gave voice to my childhood. He was the soul of the show. He was the ultimate upgrade.”

Van Der Beek died in February, two years after being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2023.

Popular on Variety

“I saw him go from a young kid to an extraordinary man, a husband, a father and a friend. James had a full character arc. He started out as a brat,” Williamson cracked. “He would get a script and he would call me, and he would be like, ‘Why do I have to say this word? Nobody knows what this word means.’ And I would say, ‘Well, don’t worry about it, the way you mumble nobody is going to hear it anyway.’ That was that was our relationship — Dawson talking to Dawson.”

MORE: James Van Der Beek’s Career in Photos, From ‘Dawson’s Creek’ to ‘Pose’

In September 2025, a “Dawson’s Creek” reunion was held in New York to raise funds for F Cancer and Van Der Beek’s treatment and support. Williamson, Michelle Williams, Katie Holmes, Joshua Jackson, Mary Beth Peil, John Wesley Shipp, Mary-Margaret Humes, Nina Repeta, Kerr Smith, Meredith Monroe and Busy Philipps took the stage at the Richard Rodgers Theater to read the 1998 pilot episode. Lin-Manuel Miranda stepped in for Van Der Beek because he was unable to attend due to illness.

Kevin Williamson remembered his late mom last night as well as James Van Der Beek, why he cast him in "Dawson's Creek," what their relationship was like and more.

MORE: https://t.co/HcNUJer4Eg@varety #justforvariety pic.twitter.com/NZq63MCVbN — Marc Malkin (@marcmalkin) October 4, 2026

“Losing James earlier this year really knocked me over,” Williamson said, adding, “To lose the man who gave life to your own youth, I’m still unpacking that one. He handled his cancer with such grace and courage.”

Williamson also talked about his mom, who died of lung cancer. “She was so outraged that Joey picked Pacey over Dawson,” he said. “I never heard the end of it.”

The gala, held at the Santa Monica Barker Hangar, also honored “The Pitt” star Katherine LaNasa and the late NBA player Jason Collins.

title: ‘Verity’ Lures 2nd Best Opening For Colleen Hoover Pic With $62M+ WW; ‘Digger’ DOA At $20M WW – Global Box Office
summary: Colleen Hoover can look forward to a nice brunch this morning as the feature take of her novel starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett, Verity, bowed to $62.5M worldwide, the second best start for the author at the global box office behind 2024’s It Ends With Us in like-for-likes, which was $95.6M WW. […]
content:
Colleen Hoover can look forward to a nice brunch this morning as the feature take of her novel starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett, Verity, bowed to $62.5M worldwide, the second best start for the author at the global box office behind 2024’s It Ends With Us in like-for-likes, which was $95.6M WW.

Meanwhile, Alejandro Inarritu’s $160M net costing Tom Cruise political satire, Digger, was buried with a $20M global debut ($12M abroad, $8M stateside); in no way One Battle After Another which began at $48.5M WW reported in 74 territories a year ago, that ultimate multi Oscar winner becoming Paul Thomas Anderson’s highest grossing movie ever at $213.2M WW.

Verity also had more magic than the reported global opening of Warner Bros’ Practical Magic 2 which began with $46M WW in 77 offshore territories.

Watch on Deadline

With a $40M net production cost, Verity continues to underscore Amazon MGM Studios’ mark in the female content space, their Prime side rallying with series such as Off Campus and Elle to name a few.

Verity was also more vivacious than the global starts of Hoover’s Regretting You ($23.6M in 43 markets) and Reminders of Him ($28.1M WW, 57 markets) in reported global launches. In several offshore markets, Verity was ahead of Reminders of Him and Regretting You. Housemaid, which is another global crowdpleaser by author Freida McFadden isn’t necessarily the comp here given its staggered rollout and year-end holiday boost, however, Verity slayed Housemaid in its openings in UK (No. 1 $4.5M 950 screens), Brazil ($3.8M at 715 screens, No. 1) and Australia ($3.1M 500 screens for a No. 1 rank). We told you heading into the weekend that Verity presales were already ahead of It Ends With Us in Brazil’s. Mexico’s $1.5M No. 2 rank at 1,522 screens is to be commended as the market is mostly known for the excelling of genre and family pics.

Word flowed into Amazon international from foreign offices that Verity wasn’t just a female skewing movie (in the U.S with a $32.6M start, it drew 78% female), rather pulled in non-literary lovers and dudes as well. Macho movie markets like Norway ($400K, 200 screens at No. 1), Turkey and Ukraine ($370K from 235 screens, No. 1 where it’s the biggest opening for a Hoover book adaptation) are to be commended.

Best starts for Hoover were also seen in Portugal ($575K at 60 screens, No. 1) and Hungary ($318K at 70 screens, No. 1).

Lots of No. 1s here with Germany ($3.8M at 715 screens), Netherlands ($590K at 115 screens), Austria ($380K from 68 screens), Sweden ($375K at 120 screens), Switzerland ($330K at 70 screens), Belgium ($320K at 65), Argentina ($300K from 190 screens), Greece ($245K from 106 screens), as well as Lithuania grossed ($205K from 18 screens), Finland ($190K at 110 screens) and Israel ($185K at 37 screens).

Pic was best MPA title in UAE ($670K at 91 screens) as well as India with $500K at 350 screens, just -12% behind It Ends With Us which is remarkable. U.S. genre has been working in the market with Obsession rallying there.

The Michael Showalter directed title kissed $1.7M in France at 384 screens for No. 2, Spain grossed $825K from 382 screens and ranked #4, Italy romanced $760K at 312 screens for No. 3, Saudi Arabia $535K from 105 screens and ranked #4, NZ was $370K from 110 screens No. 2, Poland was $240K from 152 screens No. 3, Colombia $238K at 140 screens No. 4, Colombia $238K from 140 screens and ranked #4 while Philippines grossed $233K from 168 screens and ranked #3.

Taiwan and the CIS region open next weekend, with Slovakia and Vietnam the weekend after. Korea opens on October 22 and Japan on November 6.

Brad Pitt and Odin in ‘Heart of the Beast’ Paramount Pictures

Paramount’s The Heart of the Beast continued to beat not just stateside with a great $11M second weekend hold, but also around the world with a $32.5M take. Of that foreign’s second frame was $21.5M in 66 territories with an overall running cume of $98.7M. China opened $2.1M at 7,300 theaters including previews while Turkey pulled in $225K at 194 sites with previews.

France’s second weekend was $3M, No. 1 in the market, -17% for a cume of $7.6M. Mexico had a second frame of $2M, also No. 1, -17% for a tally there of $5.1M. UK’s $1.6M second weekend at 554 sites ranked third, -22% for a cume of $5.5M. Spain did $1.1M second frame at 392 locations, No. 2, -25% for a local cume of $3.6M. Australia posted $1.1M No. 2 in second frame at 290, -17% for a total of $3.3M while Germany grossed $955K in second weekend at 428 theaters, No. 3, +2% for a cume of $2.3M. The Heart of the Beast storms into Korea on Oct. 29.

We’ll have more updates for you later.

title: Zach Bryan Breaks Gillette Stadium’s Attendance Record While Rocking “Free Palestine” Shirt
summary: For his second night performing at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium, Zach Bryan broke a record and made a statement. While once again wearing his “Free Palestine” shirt during Saturday’s show on his With Heaven on Tour, the Grammy winner boasted the venue’s largest ever turnout with more than 73,000 in the audience. “Tonight, Zach Bryan […]
content:
For his second night performing at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium, Zach Bryan broke a record and made a statement.

While once again wearing his “Free Palestine” shirt during Saturday’s show on his With Heaven on Tour, the Grammy winner boasted the venue’s largest ever turnout with more than 73,000 in the audience.

“Tonight, Zach Bryan broke the Gillette Stadium attendance record with 73,538 fans!” Gillette Stadium shared on Instagram.

Bryan previously made waves on Friday with his first show at Gillette, wearing his “Free Palestine” shirt on stage after Kraft and other venue owners pressured Ed Sheeran to drop Macklemore from his tour over his outspoken support for Palestinians.

Watch on Deadline

The show comes after Sheeran was forced to cancel his Gillette Stadium shows last weekend amid a nor’easter headed for Boston, despite caving to Kraft’s demands.

Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his tour last month amid an outcry around the opener’s “Free Palestine” onstage remarks. Opting to remain publicly neutral on the issue, Sheeran subsequently released a statement saying it was the “promoter’s decision” after Kraft assembled several of the tour venues to give him an ultimatum.

Following the statement, fellow tour openers Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham dropped out of the tour, along with Sheeran’s backing band Beoga.

Meanwhile, Macklemore announced the Free Palestine Tour last week, which is “supporting the Palestinian people and movement,” running 10/26-10/30 in Dublin, Paris and London. He since gave an update that the tour “sold out immediately.”

title: Daily Wire Filming Temporarily Suspended In Montana After Special City Meeting
summary: Following protest from locals, the city of Livingston, Montana has temporarily suspended production on Daily Wire’s latest film, Pawn Shop. During a special meeting on Saturday, the Livingston City Commission unanimously passed a motion raised by Commissioner Cindy Daniels in response to concerns raised by citizens over the disruption to businesses and the city’s only […]
content:
Following protest from locals, the city of Livingston, Montana has temporarily suspended production on Daily Wire‘s latest film, Pawn Shop.

During a special meeting on Saturday, the Livingston City Commission unanimously passed a motion raised by Commissioner Cindy Daniels in response to concerns raised by citizens over the disruption to businesses and the city’s only food bank, as well as lack of notice regarding some of the production’s more dangerous stunts.

“A motion to immediately temporary suspend Bonfire Pawn Shop LLC’s permit while seeking legal opinion from the city attorney in a timely matter to amend, suspend or revoke the permit to come back to the commission not after 5:00pm on October 5th,” the Commission concluded in Saturday’s meeting.

Watch on Deadline

Deadline has reached out to the film’s producers at Daily Wire and Bonfire Legend for comment.

Since filming began, locals have protested the alleged use of blank gunshots, pyrotechnics and a staged car wreck without properly notifying residents and businesses, as well as its opening scene, which appears to dramatize ICE‘s fatal shooting of Renée Good in Minnesota back in January.

Daily Wire's new pro-ICE movie production has attracted local protesters in Livingston, Montana.



Filming under the working title 'Pawn Shop', the latest project from Ben Shapiro's Daily Wire and Dallas Sonnier's Bonfire Legend has upset locals — not just because of its alleged… pic.twitter.com/LBCQh4rEkh — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 2, 2026

Meanwhile, the Livingston Food Resource Center (LFRC) released a statement explaining how the production has impacted its clients, who “already face numerous obstacles to meeting their most basic needs,” adding: “Since filming began across the street from our building, road closures and armed security guards have increased the barriers to accessing food. Our clients deserve to feel unequivocally safe accessing this essential resource.”

With dangerous stunts involving pyrotechnics, Livingston Fire Department confirmed they were on call, but some locals say they were not properly notified of the sequence taking place in their front yards. Deadline has reached out to the Montana Film Office.

Originally scheduled to film in downtown Livingston through Oct. 10, Police Chief Wayne Hard says the department has been contacted with complaints “on a daily basis” since production began, but there have been no reports of violence.

With Rust producer Carter Boehm serving on the production team, the latest collaboration between Bonfire Legend’s Sonnier and Daily Wire comes after their last film, Run Hide Fight: Infidels, was picketed by IATSE. Several crew members walked off over labor issues in South Carolina, shortly before Jonathan Majors was involved in an on-set accident that resulted in his co-star JC Kilcoyne needing stitches “all over his hands” after falling through a window.

Deadline has confirmed that the Pawn Shop production is not under an IATSE contract either, while it is under a “conditional start” with SAG-AFTRA.

A call sheet seen by Deadline lists Danny Trejo, Harvey Keitel and Henry Thomas among the cast.

The synopsis for Pawn Shop reads: “When chaos hits the streets of Minneapolis, a young federal agent is left alone after his partner is seriously hurt and must find a way to survive an increasingly dangerous situation. Seeking shelter inside a neighborhood pawn shop, he becomes trapped with a traditional Hispanic father and his progressive college-age son, forcing three very different men to confront fear, conflicting beliefs and a crisis that tests their courage and humanity.”

title: ‘Avengers: Endgame’ Overtakes ‘Avatar’ Again As Highest Grossing Movie Ever At Global Box Office
summary: Disney/Marvel Studio’s Avengers: Endgame is once again, the highest grossing movie ever, overtaking Avatar, $2.9255 billion to the latter’s $2.9237 billion. This is all due to the re-release of the Anthony and Joe Russo directed movie in the tee-up to their Avengers: Doomsday upside down multiverse movie on Dec. 18. Endgame was king of the […]
content:
Disney/Marvel Studio’s Avengers: Endgame is once again, the highest grossing movie ever, overtaking Avatar, $2.9255 billion to the latter’s $2.9237 billion.

This is all due to the re-release of the Anthony and Joe Russo directed movie in the tee-up to their Avengers: Doomsday upside down multiverse movie on Dec. 18.

Endgame was king of the world at the box office once before when it was announced at Comic-Con 2019 that the movie beaten the James Cameron Na’Vi film.

The re-release of Endgame, entitled, Avengers: Endgame Encore plummeted in its second weekend with $4.4M, -81% from its No. 1 notch last weekend with a $26.1M start. The pic’s running stateside cume is $894.6M, the No. 3 off all-time behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($954.4M) and Star Wars: Force Awakens ($936.6M).

The foreign running cume for Endgame is $2.03B, No. 2 on the all-time MPA box office list.

Watch on Deadline

Endgame Encore was the top non-local movie in China ($21.3M) as well Indonesia, Vietnam, Ecuador and Bolivia. The second global weekend for Encore was $18.8M ($14.4M coming from 52 territories). The global cume for the re-release is $126M ($36.2M stateside, and $89.8M abroad).

Endgame Encore has become the highest grossing re-release across Latin America, particularly Mexico ($6.1M), Brazil ($3.1M), Colombia, Peru, Paraguay, as well as Malaysia, India ($3.8M), and Indonesia.

In a fanboy juggernaut on Dec. 18, Doomsday will be up against Paramount/Warner Bros/Legendary’s Dune: Part Three in what is expected to be another Barbenheimer-like weekend.

title: James Gunn Confirms He’s ‘Already’ Writing His Next Film Ahead of ‘Superman: Man of Tomorrow’
summary: James Gunn announced on Threads that he is actively working on writing his next film ahead of the release of “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” due in theaters July 9, 2027. In response to a comment that asked, “Are you ready to write your next film, James, or not quite yet?” Gunn wrote, “Already in it. […]
content:
James Gunn announced on Threads that he is actively working on writing his next film ahead of the release of “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” due in theaters July 9, 2027.

In response to a comment that asked, “Are you ready to write your next film, James, or not quite yet?” Gunn wrote, “Already in it. I had to do something while I was waiting for the assembly!”

Gunn also confirmed on the platform that the assembly cut of “Superman: Man of Tomorrow” is complete. In August, he’d previously confirmed that filming of the superhero flick had wrapped.

Popular on Variety

“Superman: Man of Tomorrow” is the sequel to 2025’s “Superman,” with David Corenswet returning as the Man of Steel. In the sequel, Superman is forced to team up with his adversary Lex Luthor (Nicholas Hoult) as they work to defeat an even bigger threat: the superintelligent antagonist Brainiac (Lars Eidinger).

Rachel Brosnahan is back as Lois Lane. Other returning cast members include Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen, Sara Sampaio as Eve Teschmacher, Isabela Merced as Hawkgirl, Nathan Fillion as Guy Gardner and Edi Gathegi as Mister Terrific. Milly Alcock, who cameoed as Superman’s cousin Kara Zor-El, returns for “Man of Tomorrow” after headlining this summer’s DC tentpole, “Supergirl.” The sequel will also introduce Aaron Pierre to the big screen as John Stewart, who is debuting in the HBO Max series “Lanterns.”

Along with writing and directing his “Superman” films, Gunn began running DC Studios alongside Peter Safran in 2022.

“Peter’s the best,” Gunn told Variety in January. “He does everything I don’t do well. He keeps the ship steady, keeps everyone aligned, connects us with Jim Lee and the comics side and unifies departments that used to operate separately. What we share is a genuine love for these characters. We know what a privilege it is to help shape how people see them now — and that responsibility is something we take seriously.”

title: Gypsy-Rose Blanchard Launches Petition to ‘Fight Online Harassment’ Following Partner Ken Urker’s Death: ‘Fame Does Not Erase Humanity’
summary: Gypsy-Rose Blanchard is speaking out following the death of her partner Ken Urker and urging fans to support Kenan’s Law, a petition aimed at holding social media platforms accountable for how online harassment is handled. While a cause of death has not yet been released, Blanchard wrote that before Urker passed, the two repeatedly reported […]
content:
Gypsy-Rose Blanchard is speaking out following the death of her partner Ken Urker and urging fans to support Kenan’s Law, a petition aimed at holding social media platforms accountable for how online harassment is handled.

While a cause of death has not yet been released, Blanchard wrote that before Urker passed, the two repeatedly reported harassment and cyberbullying he received across platforms including TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Reddit. She wrote that they believed such content “crossed the line from criticism.”

Popular on Variety

“Ken was a public figure and experienced an enormous amount of public scrutiny,” she wrote. “Ken made reports. I made reports. Videos were reported. Comments were reported. Posts were reported. And many times, the answer we received was: ‘No violation.’ That is the problem I want to change.”

Blanchard continued: “Being a public figure does not mean you stop being human. Public figures read the comments. They see the videos. They have children. They have parents. They have families. They experience the consequences of what happens online. Fame does not erase humanity.”

Urker, who also fathered a baby girl, Aurora, with Blanchard, was found dead Thursday in Raceland, Louisiana. He was 34. Captain Brennan Matherne of the Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Department said in a statement to Variety, “We responded to a residence at 107 Double H Drive, Lot 4, in Raceland today after receiving a call at 6:15 p.m. Kenan Urker, 34, was found dead upon arrival. At this time, we are continuing the death investigation.”

“Ken recently died following a suspected overdose,” Blanchard wrote in the petition. “At this time, we do not know whether the overdose was intentional, and I will not speculate about circumstances that have not been determined.”

Urker appeared on the reality series “Gypsy Rose: Life After Lockup,” which ran for two seasons on Lifetime.

title: Sass Jordan, Singer and Longtime ‘Canadian Idol’ Judge, Dies at 65
summary: Sass Jordan, the singer, songwriter and longtime “Canadian Idol” judge, died on Oct. 2. She was 65. Her family confirmed her death, noting that she “died peacefully” and was “surrounded by those who loved her most.” They remembered her as “an inimitable force of nature” and “an irreplaceable being of light and joy.” Jordan began […]
content:
Sass Jordan, the singer, songwriter and longtime “Canadian Idol” judge, died on Oct. 2. She was 65.

Her family confirmed her death, noting that she “died peacefully” and was “surrounded by those who loved her most.” They remembered her as “an inimitable force of nature” and “an irreplaceable being of light and joy.”

Jordan began her recording career in 1986 as co-lead vocalist on “Come On (Baby Tonight)” from Bündock’s album “Mauve.” She quickly became a sought-after session singer in Montreal, most notably on The Box’s breakthrough “L’Affaire Dumoutier (Say To Me…)”, and appeared in the band’s video for “Closer Together.”

She was also a prominent songwriter. Michael Breen took her composition “Rain” onto the Canadian charts in 1987.

Popular on Variety

In 1989, Jordan won the Juno Award for Most Promising Female Vocalist of the Year after her debut album, “Tell Somebody.”

After moving to Los Angeles in Jan. 1990, she released “Racine” in March 1992. It became the defining album of her career, selling an estimated 450,000 copies worldwide and 100,000 in Canada on the strength of “Make You a Believer,” “I Want to Believe,” “You Don’t Have to Remind Me” and “Goin’ Back Again,” with “Who Do You Think You Are” following in 1993.

“Make You a Believer” climbed to #11 on Billboard’s Mainstream Rock chart, and Billboard named her its top female rock artist of 1992.

She joined “Canadian Idol” as a judge in 2003, the only woman on the panel, and stayed for all six seasons. She continued performing and releasing music for two decades.

“If you love music and you’ve been around as long as I have, you pretty much do what you got to do,” Jordan once said. “But I love music. I am a huge, gigantic fan.”

Born Sarah Jordan on Dec. 23, 1960, in Birmingham, England, she was the daughter of French literature professor Albert Jordan and former English ballerina Jean Lanceman. She began singing with friends at a young age and, by 16, was fronting bands in downtown Montreal clubs; later, she became singer and bassist for local favorites The Pinups.

She is survived by her husband, Derek Sharp, daughter Stella Jordan-Sharp (Daniel Yepes), stepdaughter Brianne Sharp and brother Daniel Jordan (Isabelle Courville).

title: ‘Spotlight’ Director Says The Catholic Church Hasn’t Done ‘Enough’ To Protect Children From Sexual Assault 10 Years After Film’s Best Picture Win: ‘Not Until Every Child Is Safe’
summary: Tom McCarthy’s biographical drama “Spotlight” won Best Picture at the Academy Awards in 2016. The film, featuring a stacked ensemble led by Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams and Mark Ruffalo, was widely praised for chronicling the investigative reporting by the Boston Globe that exposed the Catholic Church’s systemic cover-up of sexual abuse of children by priests. […]
content:
Tom McCarthy’s biographical drama “Spotlight” won Best Picture at the Academy Awards in 2016. The film, featuring a stacked ensemble led by Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams and Mark Ruffalo, was widely praised for chronicling the investigative reporting by the Boston Globe that exposed the Catholic Church’s systemic cover-up of sexual abuse of children by priests. A decade later, McCarthy says his influential film still hasn’t galvanized enough change within the church.

“I’ve heard from a lot of people who saw the movie. A lot of people who felt understood after the movie was released,” McCarthy told Variety Saturday night at the New York Film Festival. “Has it caused a lot of change within the Catholic Church? In my opinion, not really. Not enough. It’s not enough until every child is safe, as far as I’m concerned. And that’s a zero sum game. So, I would like to see more change.”

Popular on Variety

McCarthy’s new film, “A Statement,” could be seen as a cathartic response to the lack of institutional change that followed “Spotlight.” Bolstered by a strong ensemble led by Paul Rudd, the film follows 20 experts who attempt to reach a consensus on a statement to Congress about the effects of carbon dioxide emissions on the climate.

Based on a real-life conference that took place in St. Petersburg, Fla., in 1980, the film’s opening text calls the gathering “the first meeting dedicated to solving the climate crisis in America.” The group, ultimately, never reached a consensus — and nearly 50 years later, the debate over carbon emissions continues to divide American politics.

“I’m very proud of [‘Spotlight’],” McCarthy explained. “I think, as filmmakers, our job is to start a conversation, get people thinking about an issue, but draw a light on things. That’s what I think we’ve done with ‘Spotlight,’ and hopefully, we’ve done that with ‘A Statement.’ This movie doesn’t preach. There is a right and wrong here, but we want people to come to the table and have thaat conversation and listen.”

Coincidentally, “A Statement” premiered the same weekend Tom Cruise’s “Digger” bombed at the box office. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman panned the film as a “bombastically self-important satire” that attempts to be “the ‘Dr. Strangelove’ of climate change.” Nathaniel Rich, who wrote the 2019 nonfiction book “Losing Earth” that McCarthy based his script on, used the same adjective when describing “A Statement.” At the festival, he called McCarthy’s film the “first climate change movie written for adults” and praised it for being “not bombastic.”

“I haven’t seen [‘Digger] but I’m very curious to see it,” Rich said. “All I can say is there has not been a film like [‘A Statement’] before. There are some films like this on other social justice issues that movie beyond a kind of polemic into a deeper exploration of the material. That hasn’t happened with climate change in a feature film until now.”



On Thursday, 21 states sued the Trump administration over its repeal of federal greenhouse gas regulations for power plants. While the Trump-led EPA believes that eliminating the Biden-era limits will lower costs and boost American energy production, the Democratic-led coalition argues the rollback will set the country back decades in its fight against climate change. The back-and-forth is the latest example of how climate action, nearly half a century after the meeting depicted in “A Statement,” has become poisoned by partisan politics.

“Everything becomes politicized,” Rudd said. “This was not a politicized issue. This [gathering] was really smart people, Republicans and Democrats alike, who realized, ‘Oh, this is an existential threat and it is something that we should deal with. Now, how we go about dealing with it, we need to figure that out — but the science is there. We know.’”

But do we know? At the end of the film, Paul Giamatti’s David Slade (a government director at the Department of Energy) offers a reassuring one-liner to Tatiana Maslany’s character about the factual nature of science. The 1980 gathering took place just four days before Ronald Reagan won the presidency.

“Presidents come and go,” Slade said, “but if there’s one thing we’ll always agree on, it’s science.”

“Yeah, well,” Rudd laughed. “I think he said that with a bit of a wink.”

content:
John Wilson’s Sundance-premiering The History of Concrete from Magnolia Pictures is oh so solid, eyeing $450k on 160 screens in week three for a cume of over $1.2 million cume, making it the top grossing, platform-release doc of 2026. Acclaimed documentary NAZA is reporting a five-day gross of $86k since its theatrical debut Wednesday.

NAZA opened on one screen at the IFC Center in New York. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the Oscar-winning directors of No Other Land, have been been threatened and there were no Q&As. The film, which won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, sees the pair interview Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers (faces concealed, voices digitally altered) on rooftops in Tel Aviv about the civilian death toll in Gaza. It was made in secret and released independently with the backing of its producer The Guardian, and MK2. The cume so far has been limited mainly by theater capacity, says mTuckman Media, which is assisting with the U.S. rollout. Adds exclusive engagements in over 30 markets next week and will continue to expand through October.

Ketchup Entertainment’s Rolling Loud opened to an estimated $467k at 930 locations, as per ComScore. A father (Owen Wilson) takes his young son to a hip-hop festival, setting off a chaotic adventure through the crowds and backstage. Written and directed by Jeremy Garelick.

Watch on Deadline

Ha Chan, Shake Your Booty! from Sony Pictures Classics added $34.3k on 75 screens in week 2 for a a cume of $364.5k.

Magenta Light Studios’ horror-thriller Appofeniacs by Chris Marrs Piliero debuted to $22.7k in New York and LA. A young man’s deepfake videos unleash paranoia and violence across intersecting lives.

Cannes-premiering psychological drama Atonement from Kino Lorber opened to $18k on two screens. Reed Van Dyk.explores guilt, redemption and forgiveness in the aftermath of wartime trauma in Iraq. Stars Boyd Holbrook, Hiam Abbass and Kenneth Branagh. Expands to more markets next week.

The live transmission was directed for cinema by Gary Halvorson and hosted by soprano Christine Goerke.

Trafalgar Releasing’s music doc Linkin Park: Unshatter grossed $336.1k at 692 locations for a domestic cume of $680.4, as per Comscore. Plotline: Follow’s Linkin Park’s return, from intimate studio sessions through the release of their new album and a concert in São Paulo. Featuring Mike Shinoda, Joe Hahn and their bandmates, it combines archival footage, performances and interviews and is directed by Joe Hahn.

Bollywood Crime thriller Drishyam – The Conclusion from Zee Studios grossed $2.74 million at 541 theaters, as per Comscore. The film by by Abhishek Pathak, the third and final installment of the hit franchise, is no. 8 at the domestic box office.

title: White House Slams Chuck Lorre’s “Peanut-Sized Brain” After He Roasts Trump: “Immediately Seek Psychiatric Help”
summary: Following his blistering onstage jokes about Trump last weekend, the White House has issued a response to Chuck Lorre. On Saturday, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle trotted out another Trump Derangement Syndrome diagnosis for the 10x Emmy nominee, who recently called the POTUS a “bloated orange piece of sh*t.” “Chuck Lorre should immediately seek psychiatric […]
content:
Following his blistering onstage jokes about Trump last weekend, the White House has issued a response to Chuck Lorre.

On Saturday, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle trotted out another Trump Derangement Syndrome diagnosis for the 10x Emmy nominee, who recently called the POTUS a “bloated orange piece of sh*t.”

“Chuck Lorre should immediately seek psychiatric help to treat his severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain,” Ingle told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Last Saturday, Lorre gave Trump several shoutouts in his Founders Award acceptance speech at a Project Angel Food fundraiser in Los Angeles.

Watch on Deadline

“Sure, I’d love to stand here and talk about my deep yearning for a more compassionate government, one that prioritizes the health and welfare of its citizens,” he said, according to The Daily Beast. “But the burden of my profession demands that I take this opportunity to say a few words about that bloated orange piece of sh*t in the White House.”

Lorre continued, “I’d love to express my gratitude to all the people who’ve devoted their lives to making Project Angel Food an oasis for those in need. That would be my preference. But because I’m a comedy writer, I have no choice but to explain how I wake up every morning to turn on CNN to see if the president of the United States had a heart attack while straining to take a dump.”

The Stuart Fails to Save the Universe creator’s speech comes after the Big Bang Theory spin-off was renewed for Season 2 at HBO Max, which will bring the show back under the Paramount umbrella after Trump’s friends the Ellisons acquired Warner Bros. Discovery.

On Wednesday, a federal judge cleared the way for the $110 billion deal to close, approving the settlement between Paramount and a group of state AGs that filed an antitrust lawsuit to block the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition.

CEO David Ellison revealed on Friday that the combined company will now be known as Skydance, under which Paramount and Warner Bros. will supposedly remain individual entities.

title: ‘Reacher’ Author Explains Why He “Vetoed” Third Tom Cruise Movie, Calls Prime Series A “Fabulous Luxury”
summary: As Prime Video’s Reacher prepares a fifth and sixth season, the franchise’s creator is happy with the freedom provided by this adaptation. Author Lee Child, who penned the Jack Reacher books on which the series is based, explained why he “exercised that veto” on a third entry in the Tom Cruise movies, opting instead for […]
content:
As Prime Video’s Reacher prepares a fifth and sixth season, the franchise’s creator is happy with the freedom provided by this adaptation.

Author Lee Child, who penned the Jack Reacher books on which the series is based, explained why he “exercised that veto” on a third entry in the Tom Cruise movies, opting instead for the “fabulous luxury” of a streaming series.

“I had a clause in that movie contract that after two movies I had a veto whether we would do any more. I exercised that veto,” he told Collider. “The deal was done in 2005, and it finished in a long, long time of development. Then the two movies finished in 2017. That first movie in particular was huge. It came out in December 2012. By January 2013, like one reporting cycle later, I had eight old paperbacks in the Top 10. You cannot buy that, and you cannot turn it down.”

Cruise starred as the former army police officer in writer/director Christopher McQuarrie’s Jack Reacher (2012) and co-writer/director Edward Zwick’s Jack Reacher: Never Go Back (2016).

Watch on Deadline

Child added, “By 2017, of course, there was a whole new landscape. Binging television had been invented. Broadband was much more widespread. It was a thing now. It was not a thing in 2005. It hadn’t been invented, and nobody, I think, now would ever go for a feature film over streaming television for two reasons. First of all, the running time — it’s fabulous luxury. It really is. Eight hours, 10 hours, 12 hours, whatever you want. You can tell the whole story, all the light and shade, all the quiet parts, all the fun parts. It doesn’t have to be rammed together for 90 minutes of content.”

Alan Ritchson as Jack Reacher in ‘Reacher’ Prime

In 2022, Season 1 of Prime Video’s Reacher premiered with Alan Ritchson in the titular role. “The finances are totally different. With a feature film, the actor attracts the money. What actor is worth a $200 million investment?” explained Lee Child.

“Whereas with television, the platform pays it, and you can have anybody. You can have total unknowns,” he added. “The star on television doesn’t really attract either the audience or the money, and so we had a completely free hand for casting.”

Before Season 4 of Reacher premiered on Prime Video in August, the streamer gave it an early renewal for Season 5 back in May. The upcoming season adapts Make Me (2015), the 12th book in Child’s series, in which Reacher hitches a train to the Midwestern town of Mother’s Rest, where he helps private investigator Michelle Chang search for her missing colleague.

After Season 4 amassed 66 million viewers globally in its first 28 days on Prime Video, Amazon doubled down and gave the show an early Season 6 renewal.

title: Marvel Canceled ‘Blade,’ But the Gory Vampire Brawler ‘Half’ Will Thrill Genre Fans
summary: Marvel mastermind Kevin Feige has made some of the shrewdest financial decisions in Hollywood history, but he sure dropped the bag when he didn’t make a new “Blade.” (Just ask would-be star Mahershala Ali.) Luckily, Indian auteur Samjad has directed a film that will bring joy to fans of the battle-ready half-vampire Wesley Snipes popularized […]
content:
Marvel mastermind Kevin Feige has made some of the shrewdest financial decisions in Hollywood history, but he sure dropped the bag when he didn’t make a new “Blade.” (Just ask would-be star Mahershala Ali.)

Luckily, Indian auteur Samjad has directed a film that will bring joy to fans of the battle-ready half-vampire Wesley Snipes popularized on the big screen. Samjad’s new movie “Half,” which he co-wrote with Praveen Viswanath, has a simple concept: Twin siblings (Ranjith Sajeev and Aiswarya Raj) are robbed and left for dead on a highway, but as they are half-vampires, they recover and vow to take gruesome revenge on the gang that attacked them. From there, the film is a fantasia of blood and gore, as “The Raid 2” and “The Night Comes for Us” fight coordinator Very Tri Yulisman orchestrates creative, funny and bone-crunching action.

Samjad enjoys “Blade,” but had a different vision in mind for his film.

Popular on Variety

“What if we take a classic vampire action thriller and execute it in a completely raw, grounded way without a single frame of slow motion?” he says. “That core idea felt so much fresher and visually exciting to me.”

“Half” has been a powder keg for audiences, resulting in high-energy screenings at its TIFF Midnight Madness debut and at Fantastic Fest. It’s a brawler where the action is clear, crisp and often shot in the daytime. And while the fights feel modern, the film evokes more classic fare.

“We tried to make the film look like it was shot on an old camera in the olden way, with the old equipment and hard work,” Samjad says. “I think we have to work really hard to get one special shot, right? Now we can achieve it through robotic cams and specialized equipment. Everything is there. But in the olden days, it had to be done through manual hands and panning and zooming. We used lots of zoom lenses because I like the technique with the camera. We tried to achieve the ’80s- and ’90s-type of movie.”

Despite the zippy feature it created, when Samjad describes the “Half” shoot, it’s clear it was a miracle it got made.

“We were shooting in the middle of a desert,” he says. “It would be a very sunny day, and the heat would go up to 56 Celsius (132.8 Fahrenheit). We can barely stand in the sun. But suddenly everything will change, and clouds will come in, and in 10 to 15 minutes, rain will start and flood everywhere. We put a small shop set near a highway, and when we were shooting, we checked the weather on the internet, and everything was perfect. But suddenly a hailstorm took away all the set, including our tripods, including everything. We faced this every time we shot.”

Weather wasn’t the only challenge, as a literal war broke out during production.

“10 days of shooting were finished,” he says. “On the 11th day, there was a war going on, the India and Pakistan war. We had to go back to our home in Keralam [a state in southwestern India]. We were stuck in the middle of the desert, and we suddenly went to our rooms and were evacuated from there, but there was no vehicle, and we could see the missiles and everything going in the sky. We were in a dangerous situation, and somehow with our production’s help, we came back to our home. After the war finished, we went back to the same place and started shooting again after two months.”

Despite the challenges, Samjad says he was thrilled to play with vampire mythology and had the freedom to do so due to his protagonists’ half-vampire status.

“There is a healing factor for both of them, as normal vampires have the healing factor,” he says. “As they are half-vampires, we have done something special for them. We can do anything. That’s the power of half-vampires. Our half-vampire could be anything. When they heal, if there is sunlight, the healing will not happen. If there is no sunlight or there is a shadow, healing happens. Normal vampires, when they are exposed to the sun, will burn, right? But half-vampires will not burn, but the healing factor will not work. That’s the idea. We researched vampires, and in India, there are vampire stories from olden days. There were ’70s, ’80s, old black-and-white movies. We have vampires, but in different names. So we took some elements from the European side and mixed up everything.”

“Half” is set to play at the upcoming Sitges Film Festival and is still seeking U.S. distribution.

title: Is ‘Rubber Soul’ the Beatles’ Best Album? The Answer to That is as Malleable as the Shifting Track Lists, but This ‘Super Deluxe’ Is Super Essential: Boxed Set Review
summary: What is the Beatles’ best album? “The one you’re listening to right now” is always the correct answer, of course, and that could encompass “Meet the Beatles” or “Let It Be” at any given moment. But for most fans who aren’t just being sentimental about their first point of entry, it’s usually going to come […]
content:
What is the Beatles‘ best album? “The one you’re listening to right now” is always the correct answer, of course, and that could encompass “Meet the Beatles” or “Let It Be” at any given moment. But for most fans who aren’t just being sentimental about their first point of entry, it’s usually going to come down to a pick among five — “Rubber Soul,” “Revolver,” “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band,” “The Beatles” and “Abbey Road” — with the first-mentioned there sometimes being the last-cited, because that 1965 transitional LP isn’t as fully ambitious in scope as those that followed. “Rubber Soul” is undoubtedly among the most influential albums ever released, make no mistake. Yet it was arguably the last Beatles record (at least until “Let It Be”) that was tossed off reasonably casually, on deadline, and not consciously aiming at being some kind of tour de force.

Which is partly why I’ve suddenly joined the stubborn minority flank of fans that has always thought of “Rubber Soul” as the best all-around effort. That could change in 15 minutes, naturally, because it happens to be The One I’m Listening To Right Now — in its very expanded form as “Rubber Soul: Special Edition Super Deluxe,” a five-LP or four-CD set that finally reached the world Friday after many years of fans’ wishing and hoping. Or it might be 15 months before I switch sides on this one and go back to the White Album. Because there’s something about “Rubber Soul” in all of its released forms, including the substantially different original U.K. and U.S. versions, that makes for the Fabs’ most consistent listening experience.

Popular on Variety

It provided — provides — a different kind of joy than the kind of whiplash that the world would get when the screaming guitar of “Taxman” gave way to borrowing the “Psycho” strings to mourn all the lonely people, and other hilariously sharp juxtapositions on “Revolver” going forward. “Rubber Soul,” in contrast, catches the Beatles constantly at the glorious nexus of rocking and mature. (Or folk-rocking, but the force of the electric guitar remains strong.) It’s kind of the last bastion of Carl Perkins’ influence being stronger than the pot’s, but with the looming spectres of Dylan, the Byrds and Simon & Garfunel getting also getting their licks in before the psychedelia, orchestration and music-hall homages seriously creep in.

And it’s the sound of the Beatles almost accidentally catching lightning in a bottle, before they more deliberately put their kites way, way up in the air for just about everything that followed. There’s a shorter way to describe it: perfect.

The boxed set has four distinct components, each of them incredibly necessary, whether new or old: the requisite fresh stereo remix of the U.K. album from Giles Martin and Sam Okell; a collection of studio outtakes; the U.K. track list in mono, revisited; and the American version in stereo. So, in order not just of appearance, but of what you need:

The first thing to know is that the remix is essential… and compared to the boxed set, it can be had for cheap — free, really, in these days of streaming — and so there is little excuse to not give this piece a chance. Not surprisingly, the Beatles’ mass fandom has had mixed, if primarily positive, thoughts about past Martin/Okell full-album remixes, but it’s difficult to imagine there being very many souls out there who will not regard this as a spectacular upgrade, any passing sonic quibbles aside. No Beatles album stood in more need of their touch, arguably. When George Martin previously took a whack at a new mix, he remained largely reverent toward the panning that was done to put “Soul” in stereo in the ’60s. Revisiting that approach in the U.S. stereo reprisal here is still fun, in a quaint way: You are right in the studio with the Beatles — and half of them are on one side of you and half are on the other! But only the most perverse among us would maintain that ultra-separation is how “Rubber Soul” ought to remain forever, much less was intended as an essential part of its conception. The fresh mix is far from radical, but achieves its mission of making the album sound relevant to the ears of 2026 and 2086, while fooling you into thinking it’s just the way you’ve always heard it for years.

Some of us will leap to the cutting-room-floor section, which has 26 unreleased scraps — none of it completely revelatory, all of it a pleasure to listen to for anyone who knows the finsihed recordings by heart. Vocals and instrumental tracks were typically recorded separately at this time, so we get a lot of backing-tracks-in-progress before the lead vox and harmonies were overlaid, but there are a handful of actual demos or early scrub takes that survived being erased. Plus one never-before-reported tune that apparently surfaced only recently, a couple of minutes of a John Lennon demo of “Little Girl,” a modest charmer that probably would have seemed too impossibly old-fashioned for “Rubber Soul,” even fleshed out. It would be lying to say the world was any worse for having been denied this Lennon curio till now. But as the capper to a fairly voluminous amount of more familiar works-in-progress, “Little Girl” is a nice dessert.

Hearing so many isolated instrumental tracks does make for some discoveries that maybe were already obvious to the most attentive Beatles buffs, but might still be surprising to others of us. Like: how much of a borderline-country album “Rubber Soul” was and is. The non-vocal version of “Run for Your Life,” for instance, sounds as much like a Buck Owens track as their cover of “Act Naturally” did on the previous album, and there’s really a good deal of C&W or rockabilly throughout, for a group that was soon to be acid-tripping. You also get a version of “Michelle” with the harmonies turned up so high, it almost sounds like a barbershop-quartet homage. We get to hear “In My Life” without any solo at all, much less the George Martin piano part that was sped up x2 to become a harpichord… but there’s also a short excerpt of a version that tried out an organ solo, recorded by John on a cassette in the control room.

The most fun outtakes might be the early tries we hear of “Day Tripper” (which was never on any version of “Rubber Soul,” but on a single as part of the same era). There’s a kind of hootenanny-style recording, before the signature riff was composed, and then, once things get electric, we get delightful outtake arrangements where they tried ramping up the intensity in certain parts of the song… plus lots and lots more of the Ringo fills you know and love. And a version of “I’m Looking Through You” that goes on for about 45 seconds longer than the release version, so Beatles fans can hear more of a fairly rare example of Paul being a little mean. Part of the reason “I’m Looking Through You” runs longer in the outtake is because the parts of the song where it wants to turn into a rave-up go on for a few bars longer each time, as if they really wanted to work in a little more of the “soul” sound promised in the title. With “Norwegian Wood,” there’s a progression of different degrees of use of the sitar sound, from a take that has too much of George Harrison‘s use of the exotic instrument — it sounds like it’s about to turn right into “Within You Without You” — to a version with none at all, before they settle on a mixture that’s just right.

Having both the U.K. and U.S. editions represented here in faithful recreations of how those audiences have long heard the album allows the chance to revive the eternal debate of which track listing was better. Americans may have gotten a better idea, faster, of how strong the folk strains were on the album by it beginning with “I’ve Just Seen a Face” (which had already appeared on “Help!” in Europe), leading right into the one-night-stand reportage of “Norwegian Wood.” But of course if you forever heard it as opening with “Drive My Car,” in the U.K. (and not included at all on the U.S. version), your tendency would have been to remember it as a solid rock ‘n’ roll album. In the end, no one loses either way, but it’s fascinating to think about how these perceptions might have been forged differently by some fairly arbitrary choices at the time. Thankfully, we all have the liberty now to take the 16 songs that were included on either or both sides of the pond, add the double-A-side single “Day Tripper”/”We Can Work It Out” (included as a 7-inch single in the vinyl boxed set), and make “Rubber Soul” what it could have been in a perfect world: an 18-song masterpiece without a duff track anywhere in the mix.

The wild thing is that you can hear all of this for pennies on the dollar through your Spotify or Tidal subscription. What you can’t get, beyond the handsome packaging of the individual LP components, is the hardback coffee table book that offers a wealth of annotation on every one of these 18 songs, along with the bigger-picture perspective on where the Beatles were in this culture where they leading the cultural changing of the guard. It’s hard to imagine living without it, for the recording details but also the reminder of, say, where McCartney was at in his relationship with Jane Asher, and how that led to the hopeful “We Can Work It Out” and not-so-hopeful “I’m Looking Through You,” or whether “Drive My Car” counts in the lineage of the group’s “comedy” songs, or whether Lennon meant “Nowhere Man” as an attack on squares or on himself, and the discrepancies between the later accounts of John and Paul — never to be settled, at this late date — over who wrote the melody to “In My Life.”

All wonderful grist for the Beatlemaniac mill, but at the core of it, a singular yet malleable album that had “rubber” in the title but really put in concrete how much the Beatles would mean to us in the years and millennia to come.

title: What David Zaslav Got Wrong About ‘Coyote vs. Acme’
summary: Three years after “Coyote vs. Acme” was shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off and rescued by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment, the Looney Tunes comedy has become a box-office bright spot with more than $100 million globally. Was Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav, who deemed it financially unworthy to release on the big […]
content:
Three years after “Coyote vs. Acme” was shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off and rescued by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment, the Looney Tunes comedy has become a box-office bright spot with more than $100 million globally. Was Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav, who deemed it financially unworthy to release on the big screen, wrong to axe the film?

That answer might depend on who is doing the accounting, analysts say. “Coyote vs. Acme” is a major win for Ketchup Entertainment, which paid $50 million for distribution rights and pre-sold foreign territories to offset the cost. Those grosses might not have been as celebratory for Warner Bros., considering the film cost $70 million to produce. (Theater owners get to keep half of ticket sales.) Warner Bros. dumped the live-action animation hybrid, starring Will Forte and John Cena and produced by DC Studios co-chief James Gunn, for a $30 million tax write-down.

There’s an argument to be made that Warner Bros. would have been able to put more marketing dollars behind the release, which could have elevated global ticket sales. There’s another case that moviegoers rallied only behind “Coyote vs. Acme” to prove the studio wrong. By comparison, “Coyote vs. Acme” dramatically outperformed another recent Ketchup-distributed Looney Tunes adventure, 2024’s “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie,” after Warner Bros. Discovery quietly decided to offload that film as well. “The Day the Earth Blew Up,” whose target audience skewed much younger, grossed $15.4 million globally.

Popular on Variety

“It’s easy to opine on a decision after we’ve seen the effects,” says Shawn Robbins, founder of Box Office Theory and director of movie analytics at Fandango. “The movie did well partly because of rallying from fans. But it turned out to be a good movie.”
