We want kids to feel excited to move, try things, express themselves and, most importantly, have fun being exactly who they are.”

Dove chief growth marketing officer Marcela Melero said, “For more than 20 years, the Dove Self-Esteem Project has been helping young people build body confidence and self-esteem. And we know that work needs to start early. If we want to reach more children, we need to take body confidence education beyond the classroom and into the things they love to watch and listen to. ‘My Body Is Amazing’ with Meekah does exactly that, celebrating bodies for everything they can do, not simply how they look.”

The Blippi brand averages more than one billion monthly YouTube views and reaches more than 100 million fans worldwide, with Meekah related content averaging more than 200 million monthly YouTube views. Available in 25+ languages, including ASL, across 65+ distribution platforms, the franchise spans streaming, live experiences, products, music, publishing and gaming.

“My Body Is Amazing can be seen below and is also available on YouTube.

title: Fox News Marks 30 Years On Air: ‘We Saw an Opportunity Nobody Else Saw’
summary: Today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast takes a long look back at 30 years since the launch of Fox News Channel. Love it or hate it, Fox News has been an influential force in media and politics in the U.S. since its debut on Oct. 7, 1996. Jason Klarman, chief digital officer for Fox […]
content:
Today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast takes a long look back at 30 years since the launch of Fox News Channel.

Love it or hate it, Fox News has been an influential force in media and politics in the U.S. since its debut on Oct. 7, 1996.

Jason Klarman, chief digital officer for Fox News Media, who was part of the channel’s launch marketing team way back in the early Clinton era, discusses the milestone anniversary and the era of media in which Fox News Channel was born.

Klarman expands on how the Fox News brand built on Fox’s historical “challenger” mentality in the marketplace to eventually rise like a Phoenix to become the TV powerhouse and cultural influencer that it is today. The executive, who was named chief digital officer in 2023, details Fox News’ push over the past decade to try to expand the brand to younger audiences via the Fox Nation streaming platform and a big new podcast slate, among other efforts.

Popular on Variety

Klarman addresses the issue of Fox News evolving into a polarizing brand in the U.S. at a time of heightened partisan tensions in the body politic and ever-increasing fragmentation in TV viewing. He weighs in on how Fox is embracing the world of TikTok and other social media platforms in the quest to stay relevant and create a funnel for future viewers.

“There is a consistency to Fox that hasn’t changed from 1996 to 30 years later,” Klarman says. “A lot of channels that chased audiences and moved away from what was core to their brand and their ethos — Fox has never done that.”

Jason Klarman, chief digital officer for Fox News Media

Klarman remembers the channel’s humble beginnings, when it launched on just 10 million subscribers on John Malone’s Tele-Communications Inc. systems.

“It was a slow burn. We used to joke that we were fourth in a three-horse race. We were scrappy. And we did a lot of fun things to bring attention to ourselves,” Klarman says.

“I remember when we launched in Atlanta, we went down there, I took the two billboards opposite CNN, and I hired a high school marching band. We unveiled the billboards when we launched on Cox [cable system] in Atlanta.”

In the early years, there were a few explosive moments in culture that helped create what would become the Fox News demo were, in Klarman’s view.

“There were points along the way that we just started to see, incrementally, the distinction between us and the other news organizations. It really began to crystallize. One of those moments was certainly around Monica Lewinsky and the coverage of that. And then the election of 2000 — that was a big one. I think it was an accelerant for us. It was a very hard-fought race right down to the wire,” Klarman says. “And ultimately, it really galvanized the need for a channel called Fox News.”

(Pictured top: Fox News photos circa 1996; original on-air personalities Sean Hannity and Steve Doocy)

“Strictly Business” is Variety’s podcast featuring conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment. (Please click here to subscribe to our free newsletter.) New episodes can be downloaded at Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, Spotify, SoundCloud and more.

title: ‘The Voice’ Season 30 Premiere Hits 7.8 Million Viewers in Seven Days (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: The Season 30 premiere of “The Voice” hit 7.8 million viewers in its first seven days of availability. That total comes from a combination of Nielsen’s measurements of linear viewers on NBC and NBCUniversal’s own data regarding streams on Peacock. This marks the biggest opening audience for the singing competition series since Season 27 in […]
content:
The Season 30 premiere of “The Voice” hit 7.8 million viewers in its first seven days of availability.

That total comes from a combination of Nielsen’s measurements of linear viewers on NBC and NBCUniversal’s own data regarding streams on Peacock. This marks the biggest opening audience for the singing competition series since Season 27 in the spring of 2025, and a 5% increase compared to the seven-day total achieved by the Season 28 premiere, which aired last fall.

When measuring viewership across three days of availability, the Season 30 premiere grew 57% compared to last year and became the most-streamed episode of “The Voice” ever.

Popular on Variety

NBCUniversal also reports that in terms of reach, or the number of people who viewed any portion of the episode, the Season 30 premiere hit more than 19 million viewers across platforms. And across social media platforms, the episode garnered 337 million video views between Sept. 21 and Sept. 25, per Sprout Social.

“The Voice” is a produced by MGM Alternative, Warner Horizon Unscripted Television and ITV Studios’ The Voice USA, Inc. The series was created by John de Mol, who serves as an executive producer along with Mark Burnett, Audrey Morrissey, Amanda Zucker, Kyra Thompson, Adam H. Sher and Barry Poznick.

The Season 30 coaches include Queen Latifah, Riley Green, Kelly Clarkson and Adam Levine. New episodes debut on Mondays at 8 p.m., and for the first time, the series is simulcasting the live shows across NBC and Peacock in all time zones. Season 30 themes include Dolly Parton, Y2K and TikTok hits.

title: WBD’s JB Perrette Makes The Leap To Skydance: Here Is Why Zaslav’s Lieutenant Ended Up In Ellison’s Executive Suite
summary: When Skydance confirmed the company’s executive leadership team Monday, most industry reaction centered on elevated roles for content execs such as Casey Bloys, Channing Dungey and George Cheeks. But another exec in a key new post is JB Perrette, a veteran of streaming since its earliest days and a close associate of Warner Bros. Discovery […]
content:
When Skydance confirmed the company’s executive leadership team Monday, most industry reaction centered on elevated roles for content execs such as Casey Bloys, Channing Dungey and George Cheeks.

But another exec in a key new post is JB Perrette, a veteran of streaming since its earliest days and a close associate of Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav. He not only is making the leap to the new company from a top position at WBD — something of a surprise given that execs at the company being acquired generally head for the exits — but his turf also is expanding in some intriguing ways.

Skydance is due to close the deal Tuesday morning, and Perrette will join Co-CEOs David Ellison, Ynon Kreiz and others at a press conference later that afternoon on the Paramount lot.

Watch on Deadline

Upon the close of the $110 billion deal, Perrette will be Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance DTC and Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV. He will have direct global oversight of distribution, advertising sales, content sales, DTC strategy, marketing and business operations.

Perrette is poised to benefit handsomely from the merger. An SEC filing in March said he would receive $142 million in various deal-related proceeds, though some portion of that could be deferred given his post in the new company. One source cited the massive payday as a potential motivating factor. “He certainly didn’t need the money,” the person said. “He obviously felt compelled by the opportunity.”

RELATED: Streamer Subscription Prices And Tiers – Everything To Know As Costs Rise And Ads Abound

At WBD, Perrette was head of global streaming and gaming, leading the global rollout of HBO Max across more than 130 global markets including the UK, Germany and Italy after the end of a longtime output deal with Sky. The WBD streaming business, which includes some niche services along with mothership HBO Max, also turned profitable on Perrette’s watch. One less-desirable line on the resume is presiding with Zaslav over the inauspicious rebrand of HBO Max to Max in 2023. (After confusion and a degree of backlash among viewers, suppliers and advertisers, it reverted to its original name in 2025.)

While any exec who is in a high position long enough will have missteps, many industry and company sources Deadline spoke with described Perrette as a solid operational executive. Bloys may be the rainmaker with HBO and HBO Max content, but Perrette oversaw product design, global distribution deals and a host of other aspects of the streamer’s growth. Plus, he comes with a pedigree.

At Discovery, Perrette was head of digital and helped launch Eurosport’s streaming service as well as Discovery+, but his 11-year run at NBCUniversal yielded an industry milestone. Overlapping with Zaslav during their time at NBCU, Perrette rose to president of digital and affiliate distribution. He helped usher in the streaming era as one of the key execs behind Hulu’s launch in 2007 as a joint venture with Fox, later serving for several years on the streamer’s board.

RELATED: Channing Dungey Poised For Expanded Post-Merger Role Overseeing Paramount & WBD Cable Networks – The Dish

Company insiders describe a series of conversations between Perrette and Ellison over the past several weeks, a period when he gradually gained the confidence of the new Skydance boss and his co-CEO, Ynon Kreiz. “He is often the one asking the best questions in the room and has the most comprehensive view,” one former colleague said. Another person from the Paramount orbit said the execs had a “mind-meld” encompassing the future capabilities of streaming services in the AI age.

Perrette also has experience with the blocking and tackling of things like password sharing and other lucrative but detail-oriented operational tasks. Paramount board member and major Skydance investor Gerry Cardinale last week noted that efforts to merge the back ends and tech stacks of Paramount+, Pluto and BET+ have borne fruit. “We’ve already done a hell of a job,” he said. “Then we are going to do the same thing when we bring the HBO universe into this.”

A high-level streaming executive at another company noted that the move could save hundreds of millions of dollars in expenses at a time when Skydance will be eager to deliver on its promise of saving at least $6 billion in costs. “JB is good casting for that kind of thing because he’s willing to get into the weeds on it,” the person said.

RELATED: Mark Thompson To Remain At CNN As Chairman Under Ellison’s Skydance

While the fundamentals of streaming technology are familiar to Perrette, advertising and distribution might be a bit less so. “There was a lot of confusion when that popped up in the release because it doesn’t seem like he has a very extensive background in that,” one insider noted of the official announcement. As the former Paramount and WBD come together, there are some unanswered questions about the hierarchy of ad sales in particular, with both companies recently having gone through leadership changes. More details about the second level of top execs will be revealed in the coming days.

On second thought, noted one source, “what we took for granted all those years at the upfronts is up for grabs. Ellison is trying to turn it into a tech company. What will advertising even look like in that kind of environment?”

RELATED: Skydance Putting All 3 TV Studios Under George Cheeks: Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios, PTVS – The Dish

title: Supreme Court Justice Denies Last-Minute Effort To Halt Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
summary: UPDATED: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan denied an last-minute effort to halt Paramount’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, a transaction that is scheduled to close on Tuesday. Kagan’s denial of a petition was entered into the docket without comment. In a filing earlier on Monday, the petitioners — Pamela Faust, Len Marazzo, Lisa McCarthy, Deborah […]
content:
UPDATED: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan denied an last-minute effort to halt Paramount‘s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, a transaction that is scheduled to close on Tuesday.

Kagan’s denial of a petition was entered into the docket without comment.

In a filing earlier on Monday, the petitioners — Pamela Faust, Len Marazzo, Lisa McCarthy, Deborah Rubinsohn and Gary Talewsky — argued that the merger was still anticompetitive, even with the conditions put in place by the settlement of the state attorneys general lawsuit last month.

“The States’ settlement itself requires that the combined company not sell or close the Paramount or Warner Bros. lots during the commitment period, provides reapplication rights to employees displaced by the transaction, and creates an editorial-independence board. Those safeguards show the magnitude of the integration that closing will unleash, but they do not preserve competition between Paramount and Warner Bros.”

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Channing Dungey Poised For Expanded Post-Merger Role Overseeing Paramount & WBD Cable Networks – The Dish

The petition was a long shot, given that the plaintiffs’ efforts to stop the merger has been rejected by the district court and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

The plaintiffs, represented by Joseph M. Alioto, last month sought a temporary restraining order to block the merger. But U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin, in a ruling last week, cited the plaintiffs’ “repeated failures to advance any evidence in support of their motions for preliminary relief in this case to date.” She also cited an earlier decision in which she granted Paramount’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit, in which she wrote that she had “serious concerns” over the plaintiffs’ standing.

A federal appellate court denied their petition on Friday.

RELATED: Mark Thompson To Remain At CNN As Chairman Under Ellison’s Skydance

In their petition to the Supreme Court, the plaintiffs pointed to the record of transaction materials, CEO statements and consumer verifications.

Their brief stated, “The requested order is narrow: preserve separate ownership and prohibit integration pending disposition of the petition or further order. It does not decide final antitrust liability. It preserves the Court’s ability to decide the legal questions before the October 6 closing changes the competitive structure the Clayton Act is designed to protect.”

The plaintiffs described themselves as Paramount subscribers, viewers and cable customers. Their lawsuit was originally filed last spring, before the group of state attorneys general sued to block the deal. The settlement includes a consent decree that spells out a 30+ theatrical releases per year schedule, as well as separate negotiations for the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery cable channels.

title: Matt Vioral Heads To Brillstein In Transition To Management After Two Decades At Gersh; Jacob Elordi Among Clients Joining Him
summary: Matt Vioral, a 20-year veteran of The Gersh Agency talent department, has joined Brillstein Entertainment Partners in a transition to management, Deadline has learned. Vioral has been with Gersh since the beginning of his career, having elevated there from executive assistant to agent in 2010. Most recently, he served as Senior Partner. Clients he’ll continue […]
content:
Matt Vioral, a 20-year veteran of The Gersh Agency talent department, has joined Brillstein Entertainment Partners in a transition to management, Deadline has learned.

Vioral has been with Gersh since the beginning of his career, having elevated there from executive assistant to agent in 2010. Most recently, he served as Senior Partner. Clients he’ll continue to represent alongside Gersh include Jacob Elordi, Drew Starkey (who had already been repped by Brillstein for more than two years), and Ryan Eggold. Expect more names to come.

In a statement on Vioral’s transition, Brillstein’s Jon Liebman said, “We’re excited with Matt’s decision to join Brillstein. His incredibly sharp eye for talent coupled with strong instincts and deep relationships are a dynamic combination for artist management. We look forward to supporting him as he continues to help develop clients and their creative vision.”

Gersh President Leslie Siebert added, “We’re proud of the career he has built here and the contributions he has made to our clients and agency. He leaves with our friendship and support. We look forward to working with Matt in his new role at Brillstein, and continuing to work together with Gersh clients.”

Watch on Deadline

Vioral joined Gersh’s mailroom after graduating from UCLA. During his tenure, he helped guide the careers of a range of established and emerging actors while contributing to the agency’s broader growth.

A Los Angeles native and member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Vioral said: “Gersh has been my professional home for 20 years, and I’m grateful to Leslie, Bob, David and everyone at the agency for their support, collaboration and friendship. I’m excited to begin this next chapter at Brillstein, while continuing to work closely with the colleagues at Gersh who have been such an important part of my career.”

title: Kylie Jenner Bachelorette Weekend Thriller Getting  Hulu Series Order From Kim Kardashian, Lauren Oliver & Kapital Entertainment
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Kylie Jenner is set to headline and executive produce Bachelorette Weekend (working title), a thriller drama that is finalizing a deal for a straight-to-series order at Hulu, Deadline has learned. This marks the first major role for Jenner, who is following the career trajectory of older sister Kim Kardashian, a social media and reality […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Kylie Jenner is set to headline and executive produce Bachelorette Weekend (working title), a thriller drama that is finalizing a deal for a straight-to-series order at Hulu, Deadline has learned.

This marks the first major role for Jenner, who is following the career trajectory of older sister Kim Kardashian, a social media and reality star and business mogul branching out into acting and producing.

Kardashian is executive producing Bachelorette Weekend alongside Jenner. The project, created by author-/screenwriter Lauren Oliver, comes from Aaron Kaplan’s Kapital Entertainment.

In the series, a bachelorette weekend turns deadly when the bride (Jenner) winds up murdered in the pool, and her closest girlfriends all become suspects. Jenner’s role is described as the North Star of the series, which pieces together the events that led to the murder.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: 2026 TV Series Renewals Photo Gallery

Jenner, Kardashian and Oliver executive produce with Aaron Kaplan; Jaiden Kaplan co-executive produces. Kapital Entertainment is the co-studio alongside 20th Television.

A rep for Hulu declined comment.

Bachelorette Weekend is based on an unpublished book by Flora Collins that was developed by Oliver’s IP packaging company StoryGiants. The TV adaptation, written by Oliver, was developed internally at Kapital by Aaron Kaplan and Jaiden Kaplan.

RELATED: 2026 TV Cancellations Photo Gallery: Series Ending This Year & Beyond

The spec script was sent to Kardashian to produce. She felt it was a great starring vehicle for Jenner and passed it on to her, with both quickly coming on board. Through Kardashian’s first-look deal at 20th Television, Bachelorette Weekend was pitched to sibling Hulu, which bought it preemptively. After some back-and-forth, the Disney streamer took it off the market with a straight-to-series order, which is still being negotiated.

Jenner telegraphed her interest into acting with her buzzy cameo in the Charli xcx’s A24 movie The Moment. She has been a fixture in the movie circles over the past couple of years, attending major events with her partner Timothée Chalamet. Like the rest of the Kardashian-Jenner clan, including Kim, Jenner is a star and executive producer on the hit Hulu reality series The Kardashians, which returns for Season 8 on October 8.

RELATED: 2026 Premiere Dates For New & Returning Series On Broadcast, Streaming & Cable

Kardashian is the star and executive producer of her own scripted series on Hulu, legal drama All’s Fair. She also headlines and produces the upcoming Netflix movie The Fifth Wheel and executive produces the upcoming Netflix YA drama series Calabasas and the unscripted series Team Moms: Baseball, which just premiered on Paramount+.

Bachelorette Weekend expands Kapital’s slate at Hulu, where the company also has in the works drama series You Deserve to Know, starring The Vampire Diaries duo of Nina Dobrev and Paul Wesley, and What Remains, starring Kerry Washington. This marks the second green light for Jaiden Kaplan, who also conceived and produced Kapital’s two One Mile streaming movies starring Ryan Phillippe, which are currently topping the Paramount+ daily chart at No. 1 and No. 2.

RELATED: New Line Boss Richard Brener Poised To Jump To Merged Paramount-Warner Bros – The Dish

Oliver’s previous works include multiple bestselling YA novels including Before I Fall, the Delirium trilogy and Panic, which she later adapted into the streaming TV show on Amazon Prime of the same name. She is the author of psychological thrillers The Girl in the Lake and The Sleepwalker (June 2027), which is in feature development at Amazon MGM, with Lauren adapting and with Scarlett Johanssen and Scott Stuber attached as executive producers. The first book in Oliver’s debut cozy mystery series The Die Hards will be published under her pseudonym Oliva Lawrence by Minotaur in fall 2027.

Jenner and Kardashian are repped by WME. Oliver is repped by Verve and Jamie Feldman.

RELATED: James Gunn & Peter Safran To Stay At DC Studios After Paramount-Warner Bros Merger

title: Michael Douglas Weighs In on ‘Nepo Baby’ Debate, Says the Title ‘Really Pisses Me Off’
summary: Michael Douglas is wading into the “nepo baby” debate. The “Wall Street” actor, who is the son of the late Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas, opened up on a recent episode of the “SmartLess” podcast and said the title “really pisses” him off. While discussing his success with hosts Sean Hayes, Jason Bateman and Will Arnett, […]
content:
Michael Douglas is wading into the “nepo baby” debate.

The “Wall Street” actor, who is the son of the late Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas, opened up on a recent episode of the “SmartLess” podcast and said the title “really pisses” him off.

While discussing his success with hosts Sean Hayes, Jason Bateman and Will Arnett, Douglas said, “Well, first of all, you know, Hollywood royalty. I mean… this ‘nepo’ thing really pisses me off.” He continued: “I don’t know a career where a father or mother don’t try to help their son or daughter get into their business and this and that, and why they picked on this because of the well-known aspect of it.”

Beyond the discussion of nepotism, Douglas also noted that the best advice he could give to aspiring actors is to recognize “good material.” “The problem we all have is we don’t play an instrument, or we don’t paint, or we don’t write,” he said. “We’re standing there. But a good piece of material, man, a good piece of material helps things along well.”

Popular on Variety

His father, Kirk, died in 2020 at 103. He starred in films including “Spartacus,” “Seven Days in May,” “20,000 Leagues Under the Sea,” “Champion,” “The Bad and the Beautiful,” “Lust for Life,” “Paths of Glory” and “Lonely Are the Brave.” He earned three Oscar nominations and was awarded an honorary Oscar in 1996.

Douglas is known for his turns in “Fatal Attraction,” “Behind the Candelabra” and more films. Douglas has won one Oscar for acting and one for producing; he took home the trophy for best actor in a leading role in 1988 for “Wall Street” and best picture in 1976 as a co-producer of “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.”

Douglas’ forthcoming memoir, “One Helluva Ride,” comes out Tuesday.

title: Jon Stewart’s ‘Daily Show’ Skips David Ellison-Skydance News to Take on AI
summary: On Sunday night, John Oliver dedicated the majority of his Emmy-winning show “Last Week Tonight” to the Secret Service’s failings in recent years while declining to address the major media news of the week: David Ellison’s newly-formed Skydance Corp. swallowing up Warner Bros. Discovery — which controls Oliver’s network HBO — and merging it with […]
content:
On Sunday night, John Oliver dedicated the majority of his Emmy-winning show “Last Week Tonight” to the Secret Service’s failings in recent years while declining to address the major media news of the week: David Ellison’s newly-formed Skydance Corp. swallowing up Warner Bros. Discovery — which controls Oliver’s network HBO — and merging it with Paramount Skydance to form a mega-company.

So, would his late-night compatriot Jon Stewart give his two cents on the merger during Mondays’ episode of “The Daily Show,” since it’s also a part of Skydance Corp.?

Popular on Variety

Apparently not.

Stewart dedicated the show entirely to AI, first ripping apart AI leaders’ empty promises of job creation, economic prosperity and its ability to cure cancer while admitting that there’s a 10-25% chance it will kill us all. Currently, however, AI is primarily being used for ICE and other surveillance, drone warfare targeting and potential dynamic pricing at places like McDonald’s.

“What are we getting in exchange for this 10-25% chance at extinction?” asked Stewart, adding, “Right now it’s mostly murder, surveillance and surge pricing for the McRib? What a trade! I’m getting the sense that you guys might be full of shit.”

The comedian also pushed back at President Trump allowing these AI companies to self-regulate after his recent fawning AI summit, since the Zuckerberg’s and Musk’s of the world don’t exactly have a sterling track record when it comes to playing it safe. There’s also the matter of how many jobs AI will eliminate. Though AI leaders keep repeating over and over that the technology will lead to newer, different jobs and an economic windfall for everybody, they can’t say what jobs it would create or how it will economically benefit everyday people.

“The view of our self-policing geniuses is that the new world that we are building must continue without regulation or financial limitation because it’s important work carried out by important people,” offered Stewart. “And my guess is: They’ll still have jobs when this is done… Stop lying to us! Claims of universal high income and incredible hobbies isn’t going to paper over how frightening this future can sound.”

title: ‘Artificial’ Review: Luca Guadagnino Has Made the Real Sequel to ‘The Social Network’ — a Brain-Spinning Tech-Geek Docudrama, Brilliantly Acted by Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov
summary: "Artificial" is a brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history, that focuses on the founders of OpenAI, notably its CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield). But the tale it tells is much larger than that. "Artificial" goes back to the earliest days of AI and shows you how the technology was invented, how it was developed, how it was dreamed.
content:
Moviegoers will be thrilled to hear that the 2026 fall movie season brings with it a fantastic sequel to “The Social Network.” But I’m not talking about “The Social Reckoning” — Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network” (out this Friday), which continues the saga of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg by hanging the yoke of blame on him for everything that’s wrong with social media. No the real sequel to “The Social Network” is “Artificial,” Luca Guadagnino’s sprawling, enthralling, brain-spinning drama about the creation of artificial intelligence. (It had its world premiere tonight at the New York Film Festival.)

“Artificial” is a brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history, that focuses on the founders of OpenAI, notably its CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield). But the tale it tells is much larger than that. “Artificial” goes back to the earliest days of AI and shows you how the technology was invented, how it was developed, how it was dreamed. That turns out to be a story unlike any other, because the very nature of artificial intelligence — technology that’s as intelligent and searching as the human mind, or maybe smarter — is that even the people who invented it don’t quite know what it is or what it will do. They have an idea of its potential, but they can’t predict it — they can only let it loose and see what it’s capable of, which will probably be more than anyone bargained for. And by then, it will be impossible to put the genie back in the bottle.

Popular on Variety

“Artificial” is about how humanity invented a genie, and maybe a very dark one. Like “The Social Network,” the film shows us a digital “aha” moment that takes on an unexpected life of its own, though in this case two things about the technology are clear from the start: It will change the way we live, and it’s therefore worth a trillion zillion dollars. So this is a dawn-of-a-new-world story, as well as a backstabbing corporate business story, and also a horror movie, in which AI emerges from the lab as a sinister serpent, and the dramatic question is: Who’s going to control it, and how? Most of all, “Artificial” is a human story that shows us what it looks like when people are suddenly in charge of a force they devised that may be much more powerful than they are.

It’s been a long time since I saw a film that attained this next-level feeling of topical charge. A lot of people will go into “Artificial,” as I did, not knowing all that much about AI and feeling as if it’s a frosty and abstract frontier. Yet as you watch the film, AI comes alive as a subject. It becomes real — you touch what it is, what it means, what the stakes are. The result is a movie that’s at once inspiring and deeply chilling, and when it’s over you’re in a different place. And that is what a ripped-from-the-headlines movie should do. It shouldn’t merely be a dramatization of what we already know but, rather, a future-shock referendum on our lives and our values and maybe our souls. “Artificial” does that thing.

The screenplay, by Simon Rich, is pitched at a high-wire level of tech-geek patter, to the point that you may not follow every line. Yet that’s part of the film’s exhilaration — it keeps you on the edge of your brain — and it’s also what gives it the ring of authenticity. This is exactly how these dudes think, and how they talk. (Most of them are dudes, though not all.) The film opens in Toronto in 2003, where Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov), a 17-year-old graduate of the University of Toronto, walks into the classroom of Prof. Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance), a British-Canadian computer scientist who’s been trying to work up a model of artificial intelligence. Ilya is looking for work as an assistant, and the professor, with his dandyish nerd arrogance, tells him to look at a paper he’s written and come back in a few days. Minutes later, Ilya returns, having looked deeper into the material than the professor has, and he’s scrawling an equation on the blackboard that Hinton says “took him five years to learn.”

Ilya, you see, is a stone-cold genius. He’s like the Einstein of AI, with an ability to see models of it rotating in his head. He’s also a Russian émigré who speaks in an accent as thick as borscht and gazes out at the world with a stunted glower of beetle-browed sincerity that makes it look like it’s never occurred to him in this life to tell a joke or even to laugh. This is a personality of complete tech-geek maximalism. Yet playing this driven, earnest, possibly on-the-spectrum visionary of the computer age, Yora Borisov, the bald co-star of “Anora” (he sports short dark hair here, gathered in unkempt tufts and clumps), gives what may be the performance of the year. His Ilya can seem hard to warm up to at first, but he’s an authentic human being, who we begin to form an attachment to, especially when he starts to warn about the dangers of AI. What draws us to him is that he’s the key inventor of the brave new world, and also the only one who completely gets it. Borisov shades that with grace notes of tragedy.

By 2012, Ilya and Hinton have comes up with an AI model that’s developed enough to place in an auction. Within five seconds, there’s a bid on the table for $20 million, and the two decide to sell their knowledge to Google. They will set up a lab there, working independently, and have their research funded. This works for a while, but John (Chris O’Dowd), the Google executive in charge, doesn’t really get where they’re going with AI. He’s not onboard with the vision of it. Sam Altman, a rising star of Silicon Valley, is.

Gaudagnino’s last stab at zeitgeist topicality, “After the Hunt,” turned out to be a mixed bag, but in “Artificial” he’s at the top of his game, working with the impish human factor that was there in “Challengers,” his slyly exhilarating tennis-triangle movie. Guadagnino stages the film as an eclectic jamboree of brainstorming sessions and office showdowns and bro parties, and he gives it all a dramatic hotfoot with the scenes that include Elon Musk, played by Ike Barinholtz in an irresistible showbiz turn that lands just this side of caricature. His Elon is the god of the geeks and knows it. Dressed in black, holding his body at skewed “rock star” angles, his mouth turned down into a grimace of power, he’s the one who can make things happen. Guadagnino stages a group dinner, in which Ilya gets to know Altman and his pals (this is where it’s first revealed that Altman is gay), and Musk crashes in like the lord of the frat house. His bluster is easy to mock, but he’s quicker than anyone in the room, and he goes in with Altman on backing OpenAI.

As it turns out, Elon is too quick for his own good. He wants the AI models advanced, faster and faster, so that they can kill the competition. But with AI it’s not going to work like that. That’s why he opts out, and Altman takes over as sole CEO. There’s a way that the film catches the audience up in the booster spirit of early AI, when everyone is convinced that it’s going to be a powerful force for good. It will solve world hunger and teach the immune system how to beat cancer cells. The technology will achieve critical mass when it becomes AGI (artificial general intelligence), which means that it’s now teaching itself how to think. This first happens when AI plays — and wins — a video game with one of the OpenAI geeks, and the super-slow-motion beer-spraying party celebration that follows is bravura filmmaking, expressing how the lust for computers to take over our world has become nearly sexual. The film’s musical score, by Damon Albarn of Blur, has a haunting Bowie-like party-on-the-abyss shimmer.

At OpenAI, the bro slogan, led by Ilya, is “Feel the AGI,” which is a kind of Peter Pan mantra. It means: The technology will come to life — literally — if you believe in it. But the moment where Ilya learns that AI has become so smart that it can tell a joke, and lie…at that point, you feel the world shift. The documentary “The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist” captured many of the same issues, but to see the monster actually rise up before your eyes, to the point that its creators are terrified, gives “Artificial” an ominous power.

The movie takes us deep into the tech world and its ultimate paradox: the way our tech reality, which can seem so coldly factual, is actually shaped by personality. The performances sizzle, from Cooper Hoffman’s Adam Sandler-on-Adderall turn as the OpenAI super-geek Greg Brockman to Monica Barbaro as the ambiguously tranquil Mira Murati, who becomes the company’s chief technology officer, to Rylance’s delectably refined professor to Jason Schwartzman as an ex-academic screw-loose hippie who has foreseen all the dangers of AI. The conversation he has on a San Francisco bench with Ilya is the film’s equivalent of Donald Sutherland’s great scene in “JFK,” and it leaves a chill hanging in the air.

And then there is Sam Altman. Garfield plays him as a corporate seducer, and he does it by seducing the audience, making Altman winsome in his enthusiasm, a softly charismatic player who believes in the right things. And he really does…until he doesn’t. The central conflict in “Artificial” is this: The development of technology moves so quickly that for your company to succeed, to thrive, or simply to survive, you’ve got to win. You’ve got to be first. And that puts the emphasis on speed. But Ilya, cognizant of the profound dangers of AI, says that the new technology must be developed in tandem with an appreciation for how threatening it is. The trick is that it has to be developed through interaction with humanity…because it literally evolves by doing that. So…easy does it. Test it all out.

But that doesn’t chime with the business plan. As the film goes on, Garfield’s performance grows more layered and duplicitous in a nearly subliminal way, as we start to pick up on the priorities lurking just beneath Sam’s silky manners. He wants to advance the tech — which is what tech bros are supposed to do. But AI isn’t like other tech. Throwing safety to the winds could be throwing civilization into the trash.

Is that what’s happening now? The power of “Artificial” is that it so ominously captures the ambiguous place we’re now in with AI — on the cusp of a revolution, with warnings in place, yet no one is there to regulate it. (Obviously, that should be the U.S. government, but under the current leader we barely have one.) Garfield’s Altman becomes the seducer-as-betrayer, but the film is about something much bigger than his being the “bad guy.” In “Artificial,” everyone goes along with Altman, even after he’s fired from OpenAI, because he convinces them that if they don’t go along, the only other options are worse. The film is about the victory of greed, but also about something as sinister as “Invasion of the Body Snatchers.” What’s been snatched away is our desire to guide our own destiny, and maybe even be who we are. At the end of “Artificial,” we’ve handed that away all too eagerly, ceding our power to the ghost in the machine.

title: Andrew Garfield Says OpenAI’s Sam Altman Seemed ‘F—ing Great’ Before Playing Him in ‘Artificial’: ‘And Then You Learn More About a Person’
summary: Andrew Garfield admits he was initially charmed by Sam Altman before he portrayed the controversial CEO of OpenAI in director Luca Guadagnino’s new film “Artificial.” “I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when,” Garfield said on Monday night at the movie’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival. […]
content:
Andrew Garfield admits he was initially charmed by Sam Altman before he portrayed the controversial CEO of OpenAI in director Luca Guadagnino’s new film “Artificial.”

“I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when,” Garfield said on Monday night at the movie’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival. “I was like, ‘This guy seems fucking great. He’s honest. He’s transparent. He’s talking about regulation, and he has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in control. He’s incredibly charming and charismatic.’ And then you learn more about a person.”

Garfield, who spent “two to three months” listening and watching footage of Altman while preparing to play him, described feeling a moral responsibility to participate in a movie like “Artificial.” When they were filming, Garfield recalls, “there were news stories coming out every day” about the dangers of AI.

Popular on Variety

“I wish we could give it even more teeth in a way,” Garfield said. “We need to shine the light as bright as possible at the nooks and crannies of people we’re giving all of our autonomy and power to.”

Garfield was joined at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall by Guadagnino, writer Simon Rich and actors Yura Borisov (as OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever), Ike Barinholtz (as Elon Musk) and Cooper Hoffman (as OpenAI president Greg Brockman). Monica Barbaro, who portrays OpenAI’s chief technology officer Mira Murati, wasn’t in attendance. The movie charts the evolution of OpenAI and dramatizes the tumultuous time when Altman was controversially fired and then rehired by the AI giant.

Garfield has portrayed many real people on screen, including Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” and composer Jonathan Larson in “Tick, Tick… Boom.” It’s a responsibility the actor doesn’t take lightly.

“I feel a tremendous amount of compassion for what that must feel like, being on the inside of his soul, going like, ‘That’s not me,’” Garfield said of Altman. “I imagine it would feel confronting. I would feel that way. I’m projecting.”

In any case, the real Altman seems to be shrugging off “Artificial,” which he hasn’t seen. “I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie, and maybe it will be good,” Altman said in a wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair, adding that “it will not be good as an accurate depiction.”

Borisov, a recent Oscar nominee for “Anora,” admits he’s worried about what the real-life Sutskever — and the public — will think about the film.

“I can’t answer so beautiful like Andrew. That’s why he’s playing Sam,” Borisov joked. “I was nervous to watch this. It was our first time. [I have] so much feeling now about this. It’s like a child just being born, and you’re waiting for it to start breathing.”

Barinholtz, meanwhile, doesn’t seem too concerned about Musk’s reaction.

“When you’re playing as someone universally beloved as Elon, and who everyone admires and who is a good person and walks normally…,” Barinholtz cracked. “When I first met with Luca, I said, ‘I have very complicated opinions on Elon.’ And Luca said, ‘It’s not about what you feel about Elon. It’s about finding what he loves about himself.’

Barinholtz found it “interesting” to play Musk at that particular moment in time. “It’s not at the RNC with the chainsaw. This is him in 2014 when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy is amazing. He’s going to save you.'”

Rich, a humorist who worked at “Saturday Night Live” and penned the 2020 satire “An American Pickle,” was inadvertently motivated to write “Artificial” by his childhood friend, Danny Selsam.

“He started warning me about artificial intelligence in 2008. My friends and I were so shocked by his predictions that we actually discussed potentially doing an intervention to get him medicated, or perhaps institutionalized. We thought he lost his mind,” Rich said. “We took him a little bit more seriously when he joined this new nonprofit called OpenAI.”

A year before ChatGPT was released by OpenAI, Rich says, “Danny started showing us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people. When I told journalists what I had seen, they thought it was a hoax. They thought I was trying to prank them.”

Rich tried to vocalize his concerns, writing about the dangers in columns for outlets like Time magazine. But the public failed to take notice.

“I quickly realized there’s a limit to what I can do being a non-celebrity and not particularly charismatic or good-looking,” Rich said. “So this is kind of a last-ditch effort to warn mankind. I wrote this movie, and

I hope to God that a couple people pay attention.”

A late addition to the NYFF lineup, “Artificial” became one of the year’s buzziest releases after Amazon MGM dropped the nearly completed film, saying the movie would be “better served if it were released by a different studio.” That’s after Amazon signed a major $50 billion partnership with OpenAI. And Altman is close with Amazon chief Jeff Bezos, having attended his Venetian wedding to Lauren Sanchez in 2025.

Neon ultimately acquired “Artificial” and plans to release the film in theaters on Dec. 25.

Landing the world premiere of “Artificial” was a coup for NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim, who described the movie’s festival plans as a “genuinely up-in-the-air situation.” Lim noted that Guadagnino has a long history with New York Film Festival, having premiered movies such as “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All,” “Queer” and “After the Hunt” at prior editions.

“I thought we would be a great launchpad for the film,” Lim told Variety prior to the premiere. “This is a film that deals with a very pressing situation. AI is in the news practically daily. The film recaps this trajectory that we’ve been on with alarming clarity. And it does this in the form of an incredibly entertaining movie. It has a very dark humor, which is certainly one valid way of approaching the dystopian present.”

title: Skydance to Fully Reorganize International; Kevin MacLellan Will Not Lead Key Group
summary: Reverberations from the historic combination of Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery are now being felt overseas. Despite a Monday report claiming international executive Kevin MacLellan was close to clinching the top job outside North America, sources tell Variety he will not move forward in the role. While insiders praised him as a transformative leader, the […]
content:
Reverberations from the historic combination of Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery are now being felt overseas.

Despite a Monday report claiming international executive Kevin MacLellan was close to clinching the top job outside North America, sources tell Variety he will not move forward in the role.

While insiders praised him as a transformative leader, the source said David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are looking to thoroughly reorganize the international piece of the newly formed organization. Further information on the international leadership team is not yet available, as the transaction is set to close on Tuesday and operational fallout will continue well into the months ahead.

MacLellan currently serves as Paramount’s president of international and global content distribution, a role he assumed in 2025. Before that, he served as president of international television at NBCUniversal from 2011 to 2013, then as the company’s chairman of global distribution and international from 2013 to 2020.

Popular on Variety

In the memo announcing MacLellan’s departure from NBCUniversal in 2019, former Paramount Skydance president Jeff Shell praised him as a “trusted friend and advisor,” noting he oversaw a staff of 2,600 employees in 36 countries and advised on the acquisition of Sky.

Earlier on Monday, Variety reported that Gerhard Zeiler, president of international for Warner Bros. Discovery, is likely to leave the company ahead of the merger with Paramount after announcing his intention to enter Austrian politics, saying he would bid for leadership of Austria’s ruling Social Democratic Party.

The news follows Ellison’s announcement of the senior executives who will run the newly formed Skydance Corp. on the eve of officially closing the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

Ellison said in a statement, “I’m incredibly proud to introduce the team that will lead Skydance forward, a group that reflects the ambition behind this historic combination. Together, Paramount and Warner Bros. will form a creative-first home with the scale, imagination and technology to define entertainment for a generation.”

Kreiz commented: “Our goals as a team are to establish Skydance as the premier Hollywood content engine and home for the world’s leading storytellers, accelerate our integrated DTC platform with the best content, leading-edge technology and superior consumer experience, and optimize our highly profitable linear TV portfolio, reaching audiences globally across every entertainment vertical.”

Casey Bloys, Dana Goldberg, Josh Greenstein, James Gunn, Peter Safran, George Cheeks and JB Perrette are among those set to continue their roles. As previously reported, Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group heads Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca will not join the new company.

title: Raj Shamani, Indian Content Creator & Host Of ‘Figuring Out’ Pod, Signs With WME
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Raj Shamani, who hosts the hit Figuring Out podcast that has featured guests including Emmanuel Macron and Bill Gates, has signed with WME. The Indian entrepreneur, investor and author has signed in all areas. His pod, Figuring Out with Raj Shamani, has nearly 20 million subscribers, making it one of the world’s biggest podcasts […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Raj Shamani, who hosts the hit Figuring Out podcast that has featured guests including Emmanuel Macron and Bill Gates, has signed with WME.

The Indian entrepreneur, investor and author has signed in all areas.

His pod, Figuring Out with Raj Shamani, has nearly 20 million subscribers, making it one of the world’s biggest podcasts on YouTube, according to WME, along with being the number one ranked podcast on Spotify in India.

In Figuring Out, guests like Macron, Gates, Michael Phelps, Andrew Huberman and Sunita Williams discuss business, wealth, health, relationships and human behavior.

Shamani is also the founder of Figuring Out Media, an education-first business, along with the Figuring Out Academy. He has invested in a number of other businesses and products and is a keynote speaker including at the UN Youth Assembly and World Government Summit. In 2022 he wrote Build, Don’t Talk, a “practical guide teaching essential life skills not covered in school.”

Watch on Deadline

Shamani said: “Where you are born should never determine what knowledge you have access to or how big you’re allowed to dream. I started in a small room in Indore, India, with no network and no access, and built Figuring Out on a simple belief: the world’s most valuable knowledge shouldn’t only belong to people who can get into the right rooms. We wanted to bring that access to everyone. I believe education-led media can help billions of people think better and build extraordinary lives. By joining forces with WME, we can take this mission to the world and build a truly global institution together.”

WME has Indian mega-stars on its books including Ranveer Singh and Alia Bhatt.

title: Busan Film Festival Director Jung Hanseok Talks Oscars Pathway, New Competition Section & Korean Cinema Recovery
summary: It’s been an encouraging year for South Korea’s Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), which has received recognition from the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF) and also been designated a pathway to an Oscars’ nomination. FIAPF announced in March that BIFF has been added to its list of “A-list festivals” joining the ranks of […]
content:
It’s been an encouraging year for South Korea’s Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), which has received recognition from the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF) and also been designated a pathway to an Oscars’ nomination.

FIAPF announced in March that BIFF has been added to its list of “A-list festivals” joining the ranks of festivals such as Berlin, Venice and Cannes. A few months later, the Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) announced that the top prize winners of six international festivals, including Busan, will automatically qualify for submission to the Best International Feature Film category of the Oscars. This places BIFF in a select gathering alongside Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Toronto.

Jung Hanseok, who took up the post of BIFF festival director last year, says these developments are already “having a positive effect on both the number and quality of submissions to the festival. They give filmmakers a meaningful additional incentive to submit their work to BIFF.”

Watch on Deadline

BIFF only introduced a fully-fledged competition section last year, handing out awards in six categories, including Best Film, which has become the pathway to the Oscars, along with Best Director, Special Jury Award, Best Actor, Best Actress and an Artistic Contribution Award.

Last year, Gloaming In Luomu, from Korean-Chinese filmmaker Zhang Lu, was awarded Best Film, with Taiwan’s Shu Qi taking Best Director for Girl. The festival also has a Vision Awards ceremony – recognising films across both the ‘Vision – Korea’ and ‘Vision – Asia’ sections – in which a wide range of independent juries hand out prizes.

“Compared with the competition sections of longer-established festivals, BIFF’s Competition is still very new,” Jung cautions. “So one of our early challenges was to communicate its value and build confidence in the section as quickly as possible. I think the FIAPF recognition and the new Academy pathway have helped accelerate that process.”

Jung cites China as one territory where filmmakers’ interest in BIFF has risen, due to the fact that filmmakers invited to A-list festivals are more likely to receive attention when applying for public support.

“We’ve seen similar changes in Japan, where key industry figures have been noticeably more proactive and receptive towards BIFF’s Competition than they were last year,” he says. “Some filmmakers may now be able to envision a longer-term path that begins with winning the Busan Award for Best Film and continues into an Oscar campaign.”

He adds that Korean filmmakers are also waking up to this possibility. Korea’s Oscars committee has already submitted Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love as its official entry, which is currently receiving an Oscars-qualifying run in Korean theatres before streaming on Netflix. In theory, a Best Film Award win from Busan could make a second Korean film eligible.

However, BIFF’s Competition section embraces the whole of Asia and this year’s line-up of 14 titles also spans films from China, Taiwan, Japan, Uzbekistan, Indonesia and Iran (see here for the full line-up), so the field is wide open. Chinese director Zhang Yimou is heading the seven person jury that will decide on the awards.

Jung says he didn’t really appreciate the impact of the new Competition section last year, until he was planning this year’s festival: “We’ve sensed a much more positive and receptive atmosphere around the Competition section than we did in its first year. For that reason, our main priority this year has been the stability and consolidation of the Competition,” he says.

“In the longer term, BIFF intends to remain grounded in an Asian perspective and in values that emerge from within Asia when operating the section. At the same time, we want to continue asking ourselves what exactly ‘Asian’ should mean in that context.”

When asked about the competition selection criteria, Jung says it’s “quite simply, the quality of each individual film”. He adds that the 14 selected titles, when looked at together, “should form a compelling cinematic landscape that reveals something of contemporary Asian cinema as it exists today. One notable difference this year is that the quality is more consistent across the Competition, while the overall standard of the line-up has also risen.”

The festival opens tonight (Tuesday, October 6) with a screening of Kim Jong-kwan’s The Table: Day And Night, and with Kim Minha (Pachinko) hosting the opening ceremony. Other talent attending the festival includes Michelle Yeoh, who is being honored as Asian Filmmaker of the Year; Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui, who is receiving the Camellia Award; Maggie Gyllenhaal, presenting her short film Flesh Impact in Special Screenings; and French actress Isabelle Huppert, who will meet local audiences with her latest film, All About Corinne.

The stacked talent list also includes Iranian filmmaker Majid Majidi, who has Midday Meal in competition and will be making his first visit to the festival; Japanese anime master Rintaro, who worked in the same era as the legendary manga artist Tezuka Osamu; and Alfonso Cuaron, in town for a special IMAX screening of Gravity and the Asian Premiere of Jonás Cuarón’s Campeón Gabacho.

In total, BIFF is screening 246 films – five more than last year and marking the festival’s largest lineup since 2019 – and is opening one day earlier than in previous years. Jung explains that BIFF has also increased the number of screenings from Thursday through Sunday, when attendance is at its highest. “These were all practical improvements intended to give audiences greater convenience and more opportunities to see films,” he says. “The response so far has been very positive. Even before on-site ticket sales begin, online bookings alone suggest that this year’s total attendance could surpass last year.”

In addition to the Competition and Vision selections, the festival’s major sections include Gala Presentation, which is showing six titles including Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Look Back and Yeon Sang-ho’s Paradise Lost; and Icons, which this year is showing 16 titles including Ira Sachs’ The Man I Love, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All Of A Sudden, Pedro Almodovar’s Bitter Christmas, Christian Mungiu’s Fjord and Lav Diaz’s Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors.

On Screen is world premiering initial episodes from three highly anticipated series: Netflix’s The Blue Road and Dead-End Job and Disney’s The Remarried Empress. The Blue Road director Han Jun-hee will be on hand during Netflix’s Creative Asia day to present a masterclass entitled “Making Unexpected Stories Resonate”.

BIFF’s popular Open Cinema section, which offers free, open-air screenings at its iconic Busan Cinema Center, is showing eight films including Look Back, Banjong Pisanthanakun’s Inherit, and Ervin Han and Raúl García’s Annecy award-winning animation The Violinist.

This year’s special programmes include ‘Those Beautiful Years, Ahn Sung-ki’, focusing on the late Korean actor who helped define modern Korean cinema over a six-decade career; and a Japanese animation special: ‘Masterpieces of Madness, Exhilarating Prospects 12+1’. The annual ‘Carte Blanche’ programme invites prominent figures from the world of cinema to personally select films that have profoundly influenced them. This year’s guests include Korean filmmaker Kim Jee-woon, Chinese actress Fan Bingbing, and Korean cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo.

The Flash Forward section for non-Asian first and second-time filmmakers is screening eight titles include Stephanie Ahn’s Bedford Park and Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s La Bola Negra. Other major sections include A Window On Asian Cinema, Korean Cinema Today, World Cinema, Wide Angle, focusing on short films and documentaries, and Midnight Passion.

While BIFF prides itself on showcasing cinema from across the Asian continent, it’s also the case that many public audience members, not to mention press and industry, are attending the festival to catch up with the latest Korean cinema. In this respect, BIFF is also riding a positive trend as local cinema began to revive at the beginning of this year, following a long period of declining box office and audience apathy that held back post-pandemic recovery.

Starting from the Lunar New Year holiday in February, Korea has enjoyed a string of domestic hits including historical drama The Kings Warden, Yeon Sang-ho’s Colony, Na Hong-jin’s Hope, and horror film Salmokji: Whispering Water.

Also climbing up the 2026 Top Ten chart is Hur Jin-ho’s political thriller The Assassin(s), which premiered at Toronto International Film Festival and has so far grossed nearly $18M since its release over the recent Chuseok holiday. However, the film had to withdraw from its planned BIFF participation due to the huge row that erupted when right-wing critics accused the film of historical inaccuracy. The Directors Guild of Korea has recently come out in support of the film.

Controversy aside, however, Korean cinema currently has a lot to celebrate, and the recent success of The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day in this market have also brought relief to the territory’s beleaguered cinema operators. Jung welcomes this return of Korean audiences to physical theatres, although he cautions there’s still work to be done to return the local industry to full health.

“The fact that cinema attendance is increasing compared with last year suggests that there are encouraging signs of recovery,” he says. “In particular, several Korean films and major Hollywood releases have helped younger audiences – who make up an important part of Korea’s cinema-going public – become accustomed once again to the experience of going to a movie theatre to watch a film.

“At the same time, it remains very difficult for small and mid-budget films both to secure financing and to obtain theatrical releases,” he continues. “Government policy in this area is becoming more active, but we will need more time before we can judge its effects.”

Busan International Film Festival is taking place October 6-15 at Busan Cinema Center and multiple venues across the city. The festival’s industry platform, Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), kicks off on Saturday, October 10 and runs until Tuesday, October 13.

title: Jim Bakker Dies: Televangelist Was 86
summary: Jim Bakker, the televangelist who built a media empire with former wife Tammy Faye Bakker, has died. He was 86. In a social media post, Bakker’s wife Lori Bakker shared the news of his death. “It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with […]
content:
Jim Bakker, the televangelist who built a media empire with former wife Tammy Faye Bakker, has died. He was 86.

In a social media post, Bakker’s wife Lori Bakker shared the news of his death.

“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” read the Instagram post from Monday, October 5.

The statement continued, “For 66 years, Jim gave his life to preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry.”

Lori noted that “Jim loved people deeply,” adding, “He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world.”

Watch on Deadline

“Our family is grieving and we ask for your prayers and privacy during this time. Jim finished his race with faith. His voice, his vision, and his legacy will never be forgotten.”

Bakker founded The PTL Club, which he co-hosted with Tammy Faye from 1974 to 1987. Most recently, he was hosting The Jim Bakker Show on digital platforms.

Andrew Garfield portrayed Jim Bakker in 2021’s The Eyes of Tammy Faye. Jessica Chastain played Tammy Faye, for which she won an Oscar as Best Actress in 2022. Kevin Spacey also played Bakker in the 1990 NBC television film Fall from Grace.

title: Andrew Garfield On Playing Sam Altman, A Charismatic Leader Sucking Up “Our Autonomy, Power And Data” — NYFF
summary: Andrew Garfield says he prepared “day in and day out” for months to play Sam Altman, “listening and watching footage of him … trying to find my version of that character.” Where he landed on the co-founder and CEO of OpenAI wasn’t complimentary – calculating, manipulative and nihilistic. “There’s such a heavy responsibility … playing […]
content:
Andrew Garfield says he prepared “day in and day out” for months to play Sam Altman, “listening and watching footage of him … trying to find my version of that character.”

Where he landed on the co-founder and CEO of OpenAI wasn’t complimentary – calculating, manipulative and nihilistic.

“There’s such a heavy responsibility … playing a live person,” he told a packed Alice Tully Hall at the New York Film Festival’s world premiere of Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial Monday night. “I feel a tremendous amount of compassion for what that must [be] like” on the receiving end.

“But at the same time, the deeper responsibility, maybe, that I think we all felt is to shine [a light] to try and do some interrogation of who we are giving all of our autonomy, power, and data to. That felt like the greater the service.”

Watch on Deadline

“There’s a lot of research, there’s a lot of footage, there’s a lot of information, [on Altman] which is all grist for the mill, and then there’s your own imagination. I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when, and I was like, “This guy seems f-cking great. I was like, ‘He’s clear-eyed, he’s honest, he’s transparent, he’s talking about regulation … We need more of these people in in control, in power, and he’s incredibly charming, charismatic. And then I, you know, like all of us, we learn more about a person.”

The film, from Neon, explores the lead up and launch of the ChatGPT parent by Altman, Ilya Sutskever (played by Yura Borisov), Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz), Greg Brockman (Cooper Hoffman) and others as a nonprofit in 2015.

Sutskever is the moral center of the film and grows increasingly uncomfortable as Altman forges ahead with complicated AI models that have learned how to lie, willfully ignoring risks. Sutskeyer leads a short-lived and highly public boardroom coup that ousts Altman as CEO. But he was reinstated after Microsoft offered him a perch and hundreds of OpenAI employees threatened to quit and follow him.

Scribe Simon Rich said he wrote the movie as a “last ditch effort to warn mankind … and I hope to God that a couple of people pay attention.”

He traced the film back to grade school in New York City and a mate of “freakish intelligence” who started studying AI some years later. “My friends and I were so shocked by his predictions that we actually discussed potentially doing an intervention to get him … perhaps institutionalized. We thought he’d lost his mind. We took him a little bit more seriously when he joined this new nonprofit called OpenAI. About a year before ChatGPT was released, he showed us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people.”

Elon Musk – himself the subject of a current documentary by Alex Gibney – strides in and out of scenes. Barinholtz said at the Q&A that he told Guadagnino early on he had “very complicated opinions” about Musk and the helmer told him, “’It’s not about you loving Elon, but finding what Elon loves about himself.’” The actor reminded the audience that “this is not Musk at the RNC with a chainsaw. This is him in 2014, when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy’s gonna save us.”

They funny on stage, and the film has a healthy dose of comedy.

“I really think there’s a pretty thin line between comedy and horror, Rich said. “There are so many Simpsons episodes that are based on Twilight episodes, and Luca does a wonderful job of really straddling that line. And there are moments where you don’t really know whether to laugh or cry, and that’s often my favorite kind of art.”

Neon — which boarded the film after a controversial decision by producer Amazon MGM to bail — is releasing it theatrically on Dec. 25

title: Casey Bloys Re-Ups Contract As He Embarks On Integrating HBO Max & Paramount+ Teams
summary: Casey Bloys’ new role at a new company comes with a new contract too. Deadline has confirmed that Bloys, named earlier today Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance DTC, has signed a multi-year extension to his current Warner Bros. Discovery contract, which runs though end of 2027. Contract renewals are standard practice for hires at […]
content:
Casey Bloys‘ new role at a new company comes with a new contract too. Deadline has confirmed that Bloys, named earlier today Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance DTC, has signed a multi-year extension to his current Warner Bros. Discovery contract, which runs though end of 2027.

Contract renewals are standard practice for hires at that level. Getting a long-term commitment from Bloys was likely part of Paramount — and now Skydance — CEO David Ellison’s decision to go with the decorated HBO executive over Paramount’s DTC Chair Cindy Holland in one of the most dramatic choices he had to make while assembling the top executive suite of the combined company post-WBD merger.

Bloys, who will oversee content for both HBO Max and Paramount+, is expected to take some time and evaluate Holland’s programming team at Paramount+ before making personnel decisions. He is bringing with him his core group of HBO/HBO Max executives, HBO head of drama Francesca Orsi, HBO and HBO Max head of comedy Amy Gravitt, HBO Max head of originals Sarah Aubrey and HBO/HBO Max head of communications Jeff Cusson. Like Bloys, Orsi, Gravitt and Cusson all had been at HBO for more than 20 years.

Watch on Deadline

Bloys, who started at HBO in 2004 as a comedy executive, rose to head of comedy before being named President of Programming in 2016. He added original content responsibilities for HBO Max in 2020 and was named Chairman and CEO of HBO and Max Content in 2022.

Under his tenure, HBO has remained a powerhouse, generating hit, acclaimed series. HBO/HBO Max is coming off another strong Emmy season, winning 21 awards out of 122 nominations, including Outstanding Drama Series for The Pitt and Outstanding Limited or Anthology Series for DTF St. Louis.

The news of Bloys’ re-up was first reported by the Ankler.

title: LL Cool J Returns to the Big Apple In CBS’ Solid and Steady ‘NCIS: New York’: TV Review
summary: Three years after “NCIS: Los Angeles” wrapped its 14-season run, LL Cool J has returned to the franchise as Senior Special Agent Sam Hanna in CBS’ new “NCIS” spinoff, “NCIS: New York.” Created by R. Scott Gemmill — also the creator of “The Pitt” — the series follows Sam, who returns to his hometown after […]
content:
Three years after “NCIS: Los Angeles” wrapped its 14-season run, LL Cool J has returned to the franchise as Senior Special Agent Sam Hanna in CBS’ new “NCIS” spinoff, “NCIS: New York.” Created by R. Scott Gemmill — also the creator of “The Pitt” — the series follows Sam, who returns to his hometown after years working in the field across the globe. Though Sam is initially in New York only for one case, he finds himself drawn to the city and to a new team who are ready to defend one of the world’s most vital ports. Though critics were just given the pilot for review, the episode works fine as a new extension of one of CBS’ longest-running franchises.

The 20-episode season opens nearly 7,000 miles away from the Big Apple. Sam, who speaks Arabic fluently and whose specialties brought him to the Middle East, is working in Dubai. However, he is distracted by the repeated rings of his cellphone. An old friend, a Navy Reservist, has called him several times and left numerous voicemails. Sam notes the calls, but he keeps focusing on his case. Unfortunately, by the time he returns his friend’s phone call, the man is lying dead on a bench in Central Park.



Back stateside, Sam finds himself at the Naval Criminal Investigative Service’s New York office at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. After convincing Assistant Special Agent-in-Charge Robyn Wells (Jennifer Beals) to let him investigate what happened to his friend, Robyn partners Sam with Nick Schaeffer (Scott Caan, playing a different role from his “Hawaii Five-O” character, who’d appeared on “NCIS: Los Angeles in a crossover episode). Nick is an agent with a devil-may-care attitude, who shares Sam’s love of NYC. Rounding out the New York field office are Special Agent Addison “Addy” Ross (Jacqueline Byers), Special Agent Wyatt Sellers (Shane Harper) and Sean Sullivan (Devin Druid), a young, ill-mannered techie who’s stuck working for NCIS only because he was caught hacking the police pension fund.



“NCIS: New York” works like a well-oiled machine. Sam and Nick’s first case involves murder, a love scam, kidnapping and a massive shootout. Viewers get only glimmers of the characters’ personalities and backgrounds, but the show offers enough detail and texture to understand how Season 1 might unfold. LL Cool J’s Sam and Caan’s Nick have great chemistry and work well as a buddy-comedy duo rather than a dark, overserious pair, which adds levity to the series. Despite some corny jokes that mostly play on the two men’s height difference, their banter is all in good fun and will undoubtedly endear itself to long-time fans of the “NCIS” universe.



New York City also plays a major role in “NCIS: New York.” While trying to solve the mystery of the Navy Reservist’s death, Sam and the team journey across town, from Brooklyn to Queens and even the Diamond District in Midtown. Beyond the repartee between Nick and Sam, Addy and Wyatt share a sibling-like relationship that could turn into something more, especially since Wyatt is nursing a broken heart following the sudden end of his engagement. Moreover, “NCIS” fans will certainly be interested to see what kind of bond and connection Sam and Robyn could form, even as he still mourns his late wife.



“NCIS: New York” is a solid spinoff. Though the show (thus far) doesn’t necessarily elevate the franchise, it has all the components that have made it a staple of network television for the last two decades. With a beloved character in Sam and some brand-new faces entering the scene, the show is steady, intriguing and will likely go the distance.

Popular on Variety

“NCIS: New York” debuts Oct. 6 on CBS, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Tuesdays.

title: Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes: ‘Today Is a Historic Day, Not Just for Skydance but for Our Entire Industry,’ David Ellison Says
summary: It’s official: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are now a single company — joined together as Skydance Corp., led by chairman and CEO David Ellison. The deal, valued at $111 billion, brings together two major studios, TV networks including CBS, CNN, Comedy Central, MTV and TBS, and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max. The new […]
content:
It’s official: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are now a single company — joined together as Skydance Corp., led by chairman and CEO David Ellison.

The deal, valued at $111 billion, brings together two major studios, TV networks including CBS, CNN, Comedy Central, MTV and TBS, and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max. The new Skydance will have annual revenue of nearly $70 billion, the company says — but it also will have to wrestle with $80 billion in net debt.

The closing of the deal comes a little more than a year after Ellison’s Paramount Skydance (created in 2025 after his Skydance Media bought Paramount Global) first launched his bid for Warner Bros. Discovery. He encountered numerous obstacles on the way there — including a rival Netflix deal for WB assets and an antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 Democratic attorneys general — but has now prevailed in sealing the deal.

Popular on Variety

The Ellison family — with the multibillion-dollar backing of Larry Ellison, David’s tech-mogul father — holds the largest equity stake in Skydance. The Ellisons and investment firm RedBird Capital Partners together are the sole holders of Paramount Class A common stock, including 100% of the combined company’s voting shares.

Skydance Class B shares will begin trading today on the New York Stock Exchange under the new ticker symbol “SKYD.” Under the terms of the merger, Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders received an amount in cash equal to $31.01666668 per share. WBD shares have ceased trading on Nasdaq effective Tuesday.

“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement.

The CEO continued: “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality…. Our focus now turns to the future: building a company that empowers creatives, entertains audiences and rewards shareholders.”

The merger creating Skydance was funded with $47 billion of investment in Class B common stock, led by Larry Ellison, RedBird Capital Partners, LionTree, and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. That equity investment was priced at $12 per share. Debt financing for the transaction was led by Bank of America, Citigroup and Apollo Global Management.

Ellison has hired Ynon Kreiz, former CEO of Mattel, to run the company as co-CEO. On Monday, Ellison announced the senior leadership team for the new Skydance.

Skydance reiterated its general strategy, claiming that “consumers can expect greater innovation from a company built with technology at its core.” The company said its Paramount+ and HBO Max direct-to-consumer streaming products will be merged “into a single service over time.”

As previously stated by Paramount execs, the new Skydance is aiming for more than $6 billion in “run-rate synergies” over the next three years. The company said it will apply “the same operational playbook that allowed Paramount to exceed its synergy targets following the Skydance-Paramount merger.”

Cost savings at the merged Paramount-WBD will come “primarily” from technology, integration and procurement, marketing and real estate rationalization, according to Skydance. “That will make the company leaner and more nimble, freeing it to grow its investment in the stories, creators and technology that matter most.”

However, the new Skydance will also look to reduce expenses through mass layoffs, with thousands of employees at the former Paramount and WBD expected to be pink-slipped over the next several months.

Skydance believes it can reduce its ratio of net debt to adjusted EBITDA from around 6-7x in 2026 to a target of 3.0x by the end of 2029.

Skydance has three business segments: Studios, Direct-to-Consumer and TV Media. The company’s portfolio unites brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros., HBO and HBO Max, Paramount+, Pluto TV, CBS, CNN, CBS Sports, TNT Sports, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, MTV, Food Network, BET, HGTV and Comedy Central.

title: Hasbro Opens Third ‘Peppa Pig’-Themed Cafe in China, Unveils New Details About Brazil’s ‘Transformers’ Attraction (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Hasbro is debuting its third Peppa Pig Play Cafe location in October this month, Variety has learned exclusively, adding one more fixed attraction to the company’s growing list of in-person experiences around the globe. Opening in October in Suzhou, China, the third Peppa Pig Play Café in the region “brings the beloved preschool brand to […]
content:
