title: Na Hong-Jin Traces ‘The Chaser,’ ‘The Wailing’ and ‘Hope’ to Bar Talk, Shamans and War Fears at Busan Masterclass
summary: Na Hong-Jin told a Busan International Film Festival masterclass audience that his film “Hope” grew out of a conviction, around 2017, that war was about to break out on the Korean peninsula. At the time, Na said, news reports were describing U.S. fighter jets and bombers flying in and out over Pyongyang through the night. […]
content:
Na Hong-Jin told a Busan International Film Festival masterclass audience that his film “Hope” grew out of a conviction, around 2017, that war was about to break out on the Korean peninsula.

At the time, Na said, news reports were describing U.S. fighter jets and bombers flying in and out over Pyongyang through the night. He expected fighting to start in early 2018 or soon after the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. That sense of foreboding, he explained, is one of two ingredients he needs before he will commit to a project. The other is the unease he feels around people. He has come to see their words as a mix of truth, distortion and outright lies, regardless of whether any ill intent lies behind them.

The session at the 31st edition of the festival was billed under the title “Na Hong-Jin, A Genre of His Own.” Na planned it as an hour-long walk through his process, followed by half an hour of audience questions. He pitched it at the students he expected in the room.

Popular on Variety

He described an upbringing that fed directly into his work. His mother read horror novels, mysteries, thrillers and comic books, and sent Na and his brothers to bookstores to buy them, handing the books down once she had finished. His father’s job took him to Japan often. Na had a Walkman before he started preschool, and it kept being replaced each time older neighborhood boys took it from him. Na studied crafts at university, working with wood, metal, dyes and ceramics, because flat, two-dimensional drawing had come to bore him.

Na said he does not go hunting for material. He waits for it to find him while he spends time with all kinds of people. “The Chaser” began on a night out watching football with friends at a local bar, where he ended up drinking all night with a group of detectives at the next table. One of them, drunk, told him that serial killer Yoo Young-chul had once set a fire and escaped after being taken into custody by police in Mapo. Na said he had not known about the incident and was shocked.

“The Yellow Sea” started with reports of a killing a day, in the same place, in Garibong-dong, an area with a dense Korean-Chinese population that police struggled to control. Na’s research took him by plane to Yanbian, where he met a well-known gangster and spent long hours hearing his stories. For “The Wailing,” he grew close to a member of a shaman’s family. He then spent several months living alongside shamans at a mountain hermitage, where he said he came to feel, and even see, various things.

The fishing trips Na took with people he had never met on the east coast of Gangwon province while preparing “Hope” left a mark on the film. He gave one character the name of a friend from those trips, Yang-bae, played by Eum Moon-suk in the film

While building antagonists, Na reads widely for symbolism and metaphor but largely stays away from other people’s films, wary of borrowing from them. He also rarely sees friends in the film industry, preferring to spend free time with people and worlds he does not know.

Before writing a screenplay, Na said, he settles on a genre and, crucially, a rhythm. “Later on, there is no going back, it’s irrevocable,” he said.

Once on set, he sees himself less as an author and more as a supervisor overseeing every element in the frame for a team of 200. Space comes first. On the first day of shooting, he asks actors to arrive early, before the crew and equipment move in, so they can absorb the location. Casting follows from how each character will be framed in that space, and light comes after that.

He warned that preparing too thoroughly can leave a film rigid. Most Korean productions shoot from storyboards, but Na said he did not even look at his on “The Wailing.” Instead, he talked through each day’s shots with his cinematographer in the car every morning, breaking off to film anything striking that appeared. “It was just me and my DOP working without a tight plan,” Na said.

Na reserved his strongest words for post-production, which he believes the Korean industry undervalues and squeezes into too little time. He tells his crews that everything before it exists to serve that phase. “It is the stage that makes or breaks the film, and this is the key moment that we’ve all been working towards,” he said.

Losing control of the schedule, he warned, turns a filmmaker from hunter into prey. He added that he believes each film is born with its own fate, which often reveals itself through near-miraculous moments of weather and nature during shooting.

Na said “The Wailing” was meant to tell audiences that the misfortunes they suffer, large and small, have causes and outcomes that have nothing to do with them. He hoped they would blame themselves less and carry those burdens a little more lightly. His films have so far ended in darkness, offering only the belief that light might exist somewhere ahead. As he gets older, he said, he increasingly wants to let audiences see that light.

He has not decided how much of it his next ending will reveal.

Asked by an audience member how he would define himself as a genre, given the title of the masterclass, Na said that anyone who met him up close would find him unlike anyone they had encountered before, and that people tend to either warm to him or not. He said he used to struggle to read what lay behind people’s words, but has become more relaxed, trusting that true intentions surface eventually.

“I can tell you that I’m not an easy person to be around,” he said.

title: North Stars: How ‘Heated Rivalry’ Made Canadian TV Red Hot
summary: The mega-success of Heated Rivalry has buyers asking what is coming next from Crave, the Canadian streamer that greenlit the ice hockey romance hit. The streamer is part of Bell Media, and company President Sean Cohan is backing Canadian producers to produce the next Heated Rivalry as Canadian content becomes hot international property. The next […]
content:
The mega-success of Heated Rivalry has buyers asking what is coming next from Crave, the Canadian streamer that greenlit the ice hockey romance hit.

The streamer is part of Bell Media, and company President Sean Cohan is backing Canadian producers to produce the next Heated Rivalry as Canadian content becomes hot international property.

The next season of the sports show drops in 2027. Cast members have hinted at a third run for the steamy series, which Cohan says is “the biggest global hit that Canada’s ever produced,” and there is more source material from which to work. He is not ready to definitively confirm or deny a third outing, but there does appear to be a direction of travel. “In success, this show continues,” he says.

Cohan is more definitive on the future of Crave, which he says, historically, was an under-marketed and under-utilized gem. Offering a slate of Canadian originals differentiates Crave from the U.S.-owned streamers, and HBO programming adds premium U.S. firepower. Bell’s pact for HBO fare has been extended, and Cohan says it runs into the 2030s.

Watch on Deadline

Heated Rivalry delivered on Bell’s promise to generate shows that resonate locally and go global, with the associated financial and reputational benefits. That was one of former A+E exec Cohan’s goals when he joined the Canadian content giant in late 2023.

Sean Cohan, Bell Media President Bell Media

“We talked about making great global and profitable shows and about elevating the Canadian creative brand, which has been misunderstood or underestimated,” he says. “Bell Media spends a ton domestically on Canada-made content and the question was: Why can’t we make that in a way that exports around the world? And then we went and did it.”

Boosted by Heated Rivalry, Crave recorded just over 5 million subs in Bell’s most recent results, and is eyeing 6 million by end of 2028, but Cohan is thinking beyond that. He wants the streamer to be in half of Canadian TV homes by the end of 2029. “The new target that we have in our mind is closer to one in two,” he says. In a market with an estimated 15.8 million TV homes, that means Crave will need to continue its growth trajectory to hit its numbers.

Hudson Williams’ next turn

The next big thing in-the-making is Yaga, which features Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams alongside Carrie-Anne Moss in a witchy folklore drama set in a coastal town called Whittock. The series will be heavily promoted at MIPCOM. Other Crave shows coming to the international market include queer softball drama Slo Pitch and Meatballs, inspired by the eponymous Bill Murray movie and starring Robbie G.K., another Heated alum. There is also Bulges, set in a Hooters-like bar, but where the staff are all male, and with Saved by the Bell star Mark-Paul Gosselaar starring. Sphere Abacus, the distributor that Bell acquired last year, is selling them all.

Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss in ‘Yaga’ Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss in YAGA photo credit Crave and Christopher Lawrence

“Canadian content was already on the rise — you had shows like [Fremantle-distributed] Sullivan’s Crossing, which had gone to The CW in the U.S. and Netflix around the world,” says Sphere Abacus Managing Director Jonathan Ford. “Heated Rivalry really increased that, and that led to channels and platforms around the world always wanting to know what the next big thing is coming out of Canada and, particularly, Crave.”

Ford, an international distribution veteran, adds: “Canadian programming can fit with different audiences. Some storylines feel relevant to the U.S. market, perhaps more so than some British storylines and accents, but it’s also relevant to the U.K., Australia and New Zealand, and the quality of the shows appeals to the European markets too.”

Heated Rivalry made Williams, along with Connor Storrie, a global star and Sphere Abacus has pre-sold Yaga to AMC in the U.S., Sky in the U.K. and HBO Max in continental Europe, among others.

“The sales were done off the script and casting, partly because the storyline and casting of Yaga are so strong, but also there’s an element of having wind in the sails from Heated Rivalry,” says Ford.

While Heated Rivalry set a high benchmark, now the heat is on for Crave and Sphere Abacus to deliver more made-in-Canada hits.

title: Disneyland & Disney World Price Bumps Are The Smallest In Recent Memory, With Some Ticket Rates Unchanged
summary: Each year October brings Halloween, the turning of the leaves, the World Series and changing ticket prices at Disney’s U.S. parks. For 2026-2027, however, many ticket tiers remain unchanged, while those that are rising are seeing some of the smallest bumps in recent memory. There are good reasons for this. When Comcast reported earnings in […]
content:
Each year October brings Halloween, the turning of the leaves, the World Series and changing ticket prices at Disney‘s U.S. parks.

For 2026-2027, however, many ticket tiers remain unchanged, while those that are rising are seeing some of the smallest bumps in recent memory. There are good reasons for this.

When Comcast reported earnings in July, it noted softer attendance at its domestic parks, despite the opening of Epic Universe in Orlando.

At Disney, global guests grew 4% and attendance at domestic parks rose 3%. Disney noted continued, but moderating, headwinds from international attendance at domestic parks. The segment’s average per capita ticket revenue still rose 5%. Forward bookings remained robust. WDW specifically saw healthy core attendance increases from domestic tourists and annual passholders.

Watch on Deadline

Still, the recently announced price points indicate Disney is aware that consumers are hurting, with gas prices making it a struggle to even get to the parks.

Disneyland‘s least expensive single-day (Tier 0) ticket is still $104. That rate has remained unchanged since 2019. In line with last year, there are eight dates to get tickets at that price — all in November. See calendars below.

Another indication Disney is aware of a price pinch: Lowest-cost dates for each month are, this year, highlighted in green.

The peak 1-day (Tier 6) ticket for holiday dates in Nov.-Dec. 2026 remains $224. That price currently applies to Thanksgiving week, the days around Christmas and those leading up to New Year’s Eve. See below.

The second-highest price point, Tier 5, also remains unchanged at $199. Ditto multiday tickets, parking and annual passes. Each of the intervening tiers has only been raised $5.

The tiers and attendant cost increases (if any) break down as follows:

Tier 0 – Was $104, still $104

Tier 1 – Was $129, now $134

Tier 2 – Was $149, now $154

Tier 3 – Was $169, now $174

Tier 4 – Was $184, now $189

Tier 5 – Was $199, still $199

Tier 6 – Was $224, still $224

“Our goal is to put guests at the center of our decision making, and that starts by listening to them,” Thomas Mazloum, chairman of Disney Experiences, said of this year’s rates. “That matters more now when families are watching every dollar, and we see it in the choices they make every day — in how they plan, in how far ahead.”

Mazloum added, “We think about pricing market by market, rather than with one broad brush,” as Disneyland guests tend to be more local and those to Walt Disney World regularly travel longer distances.

Apropos of that, the company is still considering targeted offers in market, like last summer’s “Evening Ticket” at Disneyland for local residents. Those were only $59.

Over in Orlando, ticket prices are generally higher, reflecting the bigger trip Walt Disney World Resort often is for guests coming from farther away. The lowest priced offering to the Magic Kingdom remains unchanged at $119 for a single day, single park ticket, though there are none on the calendar before the end of the year. The highest-priced, Tier 6, entry is also unchanged at $209. Multiday ticket prices are not increasing.

Annual Passes at Walt Disney World are increasing by $10-$120, depending on the level. Parking prices and Lightning Lane Multi Pass pricing are not changing.

title: Alfonso Cuarón & Jonás Cuarón On Future Of Cinema: “The Theatrical Experience Will Continue, But It Will Coexist With Many Different Forms”
summary: Alfonso Cuarón and Jonás Cuarón shared their thoughts on the future of the theatrical experience, teased a few details of upcoming projects and discussed Korean cinema during their first visit to Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) today. BIFF is hosting both a special IMAX screening of Gravity, the Oscar-winning movie that the father and son […]
content:
Alfonso Cuarón and Jonás Cuarón shared their thoughts on the future of the theatrical experience, teased a few details of upcoming projects and discussed Korean cinema during their first visit to Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) today.

BIFF is hosting both a special IMAX screening of Gravity, the Oscar-winning movie that the father and son filmmakers co-wrote, and the Asian premiere of Jonas Cuarón’s most recent film, Campeon Gabacho, the story of a Mexican immigrant in New York, which premiered at this year’s SXSW.

“I believe that the theatrical experience will keep on existing, and I hope so because I love the theatrical experience, but I think it’s going to coexist with more forms,” said Alfonso Cuarón, a four-time Oscar winner for Gravity and Roma.

“And I’m very pleased about that, and I’m also very afraid,” he continued. “But I want to learn from the new generation about how they take this new world and turn it into art, and that’s at the end of the day what I’m putting my focus on.”

Watch on Deadline

Cuarón said he’s already learned from his son, despite initially trying to dissuade him from a career in cinema: “When he was growing up, I consciously pushed him away from studying or getting involved in film. We went to the movies together and he shared my love of cinema, but I told him I can’t encourage you to study film.”

Although he took that path anyway, Cuarón said: “It was very refreshing to see that he was developing a language so different from mine. Selfishly, it was a language I could learn from.

“From his first film, that was all done with still photography, and then his second film Desierto, when I read that script, I said I wanted to write something like that. So I feel in many ways, he has pushed me in my own language to explore further. He has a deep belief in audiences and a deep belief in the power of of film.”

Continuing the theme of appealing to audiences, Jonás Cuarón shared his love of genre cinema and the fact that he’s currently working on a script for a horror movie: “I like the way genre connects with an audience, like with the audience here yesterday for Gravity, you could see they were really stressed out for Dr. Ryan Stone. And horror is a really great genre in that sense of connecting with the audience. It’s similar to comedy; that when you see a horror you really get a communal reaction.”

Both father and son expressed an appreciation for Korean cinema. Jonás Cuarón said: “Something in Korean cinema that really connects with me, and that I’ve always tried to do in my films, is bringing in social semantics, but under the guise of genre and particularly also with humor.

“A lot of movies that I really respect from The Host and Parasite, to recent Korean films like Hope and No Other Choice, they all share what I love about cinema, which is that they talk about social issues but connect with the audience through genre, and a sense of humor that I really connect with.”

Speaking with Korean director Yeon Sang-ho (Colony, Paradise Lost) later today in a masterclass, Alfonso Cuarón noted how failure can be an important component in success: “I have way more projects fall apart than the projects I made; and perhaps they could be considered as failures, but thanks to those failures, I managed to do some other films that were well received in one way or the the other.”

Busan International Film Festival is taking place October 6-15 at Busan Cinema Center and multiple venues across the city. The festival’s industry platform, Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), kicks off on Saturday, October 10 and runs until Tuesday, October 13.

title: Doha Film Festival Unveils 2026 International Feature Competition Lineup
summary: Qatar’s Doha Film Festival (DFF) has unveiled the International Feature Film Competition lineup for its second edition which is due to take place this November. The fifteen titles include Hosam Abu Dan’s Gaza-shot drama Thirteen in Gaza, a coming-of-age drama about a motherless thirteen-year-old living with her father in a Gaza displacement camp without privacy […]
content:
Qatar’s Doha Film Festival (DFF) has unveiled the International Feature Film Competition lineup for its second edition which is due to take place this November.

The fifteen titles include Hosam Abu Dan’s Gaza-shot drama Thirteen in Gaza, a coming-of-age drama about a motherless thirteen-year-old living with her father in a Gaza displacement camp without privacy or protection. It won the NETPAC Award in Toronto in September.

It is among four Palestinian films in competition alongside Muayad Alayan’s Venice–selected Conversation with the Sea about a Palestinian man caught in the crosshairs of Israeli bureaucracy over a social security debt for his son who drowned in the Red Sea some two decades previously.

Watch on Deadline

They also include Rabab Khamis’ documentary Sama, which will world premiere in the festival. It revolves around a ten-year-old girl who collects plastic and cardboard in Deir al-Balah in Gaza to sell as fuel and help sustain her family.

Mohanad Yaqubi’s Revolutionaries Never Die, taking its cue from 113 reels of films preserved by Lebanese filmmaker Jocelyne Saab, will also compete. It won the Special Jury Prize in the Filmmakers of the Present competition at Locarno over the summer.

They are among 11 films in the main competition supported by the Doha Film Institute (DFI), which oversees the festival.

The unveiling of the selection is a sign that the DFI is confident the event will go ahead in spite of regional instability caused by the U.S.-Iran-Israel war.

Qatar is a key mediator in indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran, at the same time as negotiating directly with the latter for a regional non-aggression security framework.

Further titles from the Arab world include Concrete Land by Asmahan Bkerat, following an Afro-Palestinian Bedouin family on the outskirts of Amman as luxury villas close in around them. Filmed over eight years, the filmmaker’s debut feature premiered in the Semaine de la Critique at Locarno.

Moroccan director Tala Hadid will present Bardi, about the centuries-old equestrian tradition of Tbourida, which premiered in the Currents section at the New York Film Festival.

As previously announced Yemeni Scottish director Sara Ishaq’s The Station, set against the backdrop of a women-only petrol station in war-torn Yemen, both opens the festival and competes.

Out of sub-Saharan Africa, Cameroonian director Auguste Bernard Kouemo competes with House of the Wind, which debuted in the Venice Film Festival’s Orizzonti sidebar winning its Special Jury Prize and the Lion of the Future for a Debut Film.

Also out of the region, is My Semba by Hugo Salvaterra. It follows three orphaned siblings in Luanda who fight for dignity through faith, fury and verse. The film won the Feature Film Competition Award at the International Film Festival Innsbruck.

Asia is represented by Thai director Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s 9 Temples to Heaven, about a family which visits nine temples in a single day in the hope of keeping their grandmother alive. The film debuted in Cannes Directors’ Fortnight. It went on to win Best Director and Best Actor in the Asian New Talent Award at the Shanghai International Film Festival and is Thailand’s submission for the 99th Academy Awards.

Also out of Asia are Zou Jing Cannes Critics’ Week Fipresci-winner A Girl Unknown, about a girl abandoned at birth who passes between three families, and Rafael Manuel’s Filipiñana about teenage tee-girl at a Manila country club who begins to uncover the violence beneath its manicured lawns.

The latter film won the World Cinema Dramatic Special Jury Award for Creative Vision at Sundance and is Philippines submission for the 99th Academy Awards.

Further contenders include Chilean director Manuela Martelli’s The Meltdown, which premiered in Cannes Un Certain Regard and is Chile’s 99th Academy Awards entry, and Alessandra Sanguinetti’s The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer, following two cousins on the Argentine Pampas through the photographer’s lens over 25 years. It won the Golden Leopard in the Filmmakers of the Present competition at Locarno.

Rounding out the selection is Tin Castle by Alexander Murphy follows an Irish traveller family, two parents and ten children, threatened with eviction as they fight to preserve their way of life in an old caravan.

“This year’s features competition reflects great ambition. The 15 films from across the world are united by the courage, imagination and urgency of their filmmakers. Each has travelled a remarkable journey, and it is deeply meaningful that Doha is a part of that journey, ensuring that these powerful works are seen, shared and remembered,” said Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, CEO of Doha Film Institute and Director of DFF.

The competition will feature a jury of five industry experts who select winners in Best Narrative (with prize money of US$75,000), Best Documentary (US$50,000), Best Artistic Achievement for feature narrative or documentary (US$45,000), and Best Performance (US$15,000) categories. A certificate of Special Mention will also be presented to a feature narrative or documentary.

The festival expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period.

Alongside the DFI, key partners on Doha Film Festival include Katara, Media City Qatar, Film Committee and Visit Qatar.

The festival will unfold from November 19 to 27.

title: Why ‘You Can See Everything Everything’ Could Make Oscars History as First Doc Nominated for Best Picture
summary: Will the Academy’s documentary branch finally see it all? “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 doc that made for an explosive secret screening in Telluride, follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes during the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling long after. It just played the New York Film […]
content:
Will the Academy’s documentary branch finally see it all?

“You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 doc that made for an explosive secret screening in Telluride, follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes during the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling long after. It just played the New York Film Festival and carries something no nonfiction film has pulled off in 98 ceremonies: a legitimate shot at best picture.

It’s a gate that nonfiction films have been trying to storm past for years. Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s 2021 film “Flee” came closest, landing documentary, animated and international feature nods at the 94th ceremony (a first, though the film went home empty-handed).

Popular on Variety

Why might the Holmes yarn break through? It’s a movie the rest of the Academy can find without an individual branch hanging a neon sign. Cinematographer David Bolen shoots with long lenses, parking on faces well past the point of comfort, which is what made the first “You Can See Everything” trailer viral. Actors who have never opened a doc screener in their lives know Fielder from “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal.” Oppenheim has his own heat with “Primetime,” the Robert Pattinson drama also sitting in the awards mix.

The best picture category is decided by the full membership of roughly 11,000 voters. However, the doc branch alone hands out the five documentary feature slots, and its habits have driven campaigners up the wall for decades.

“Sometimes it feels less like we’re judging the work and more like we’re judging only who we know,” one documentary branch member tells Variety. “That’s frustrating. You can make the most formally ambitious documentary of the decade, but if people have already decided they love another filmmaker, or they’ve seen them at enough dinners and screenings, you don’t stand a chance.”

History has shown, however, that popularity rarely does a doc any favors. The “Hoop Dreams” omission in 1994 forced the Academy to overhaul the branch’s voting mechanism. Morgan Neville’s Mister Rogers portrait “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?” grossed more than $22 million in 2018, won the PGA and Critics Choice doc prizes but didn’t score an Oscar nom. Neville, who won for “20 Feet From Stardom” (2013), hasn’t been nominated since, which keeps a theory on the circuit alive: Win once and the branch considers you taken care of. Laura Poitras (“Citizenfour” and “All the Beauty and the Bloodshed”) is the rare exception. “There’s a popularity contest element to it now that pisses me off,” another voter says. “I don’t care how many people I know on a film or how charming somebody is at a Q&A. Did they make a great documentary? That should be the question.”

There will be other buzzy titles expected in the doc race, including Ava DuVernay’s criminal justice sequel “14th” and Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s “Naza,” the portrait of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict that stunned at Venice.

Then there’s the question of who gets a ballot in the first place. Members from any branch can opt in for international feature, animated feature and, as of last season, animated short nominating rounds. Documentary is the lone holdout, and the argument for opening it up to the wider membership comes down to math. The 98th Oscars had 201 eligible docs. Even at roughly 90 minutes a pop, that’s more than 300 hours — or about seven and a half workweeks for people with their own movies to finish. Nobody is watching everything. More members watching could provide balance.

“You Can See Everything” won’t make the branch’s life easier, because Fielder isn’t hiding behind the camera. He’s in the frame, and the film keeps circling whether Holmes is being authentic, performing for the camera or some blurry mix of both. For a branch that still prizes the fly on the wall, that’s a tough sell.

The smart money has this as the kind of movie that misses the 15-film shortlist in December. If it does, a snub that loud becomes a rallying cry, the way Ben Affleck’s directing omission for “Argo” did, and the wider membership answers in the one place it can: the best picture ballot.

title: Israel’s Oscar Contender ‘Tell Me Everything’ Dropped From Swiss Queer Film Festival After Palestinian Groups’ Boycott Threats
summary: A queer film festival in Switzerland has dropped an Israeli film from its lineup after receiving boycott threats from a collective of local groups including a Palestinian film festival. Everybody’s Perfect, which describes itself as a festival of queer cinema based in Geneva, had initially unveiled Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” as part of its […]
content:
A queer film festival in Switzerland has dropped an Israeli film from its lineup after receiving boycott threats from a collective of local groups including a Palestinian film festival.

Everybody’s Perfect, which describes itself as a festival of queer cinema based in Geneva, had initially unveiled Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” as part of its lineup. The film, which was recently selected as Israel’s submission for the Oscar’s international feature category, follows a 12-year-old boy who discovers a “devastating secret” about his father in the 1980s at the height of the HIV crisis. The film premiered at Sundance earlier this year and last month set a record for most nominations at Israel’s film academy awards.

On Monday Everybody’s Perfect cancelled two planned screenings of the film, blaming threats of a boycott after receiving an email from fellow Geneva-based festival Palestine, Filmer C’est Exister last Thursday, according to a rep for Everybody’s Perfect. “They started writing messages like ‘We’re going to boycott your festival’ — boycott, boycott, just boycott,” said Charlotte Spector, the festival’s communications lead. “When people mention boycotting a festival that is a very big threat.”

Popular on Variety

“[‘Tell Me Everything’] a beautiful film about the ’80s and AIDS/HIV,” Sector added. “There’s nothing that is remotely close to what is going on currently and what has been going on [in Israel/Gaza].”

Everybody’s Perfect, which opens Friday, Oct. 9 with the Swiss premiere of “Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror,” is part funded by the city of Geneva, as is Palestine, Filmer C’est Exister. The latter did not respond to Variety’s queries by press time. According to a post on Instagram, other groups involved in pressuring the queer festival to drop “Tell Me Everything” were Student Coordination for Palestine at the University of Geneva, BDS Geneva, CRAQ and Marad.

Variety understands that after receiving the boycott threats, Everybody’s Perfect asked Rosenthal to declare his “stance towards the current Israeli government and the war in Palestine” on Friday. Rosenthal and producers Green Productions responded the following day, saying they do not represent the Israeli government and do not finance or produce films supporting or promoting its current policies.

Despite receiving the statement, which according to Sector the festival shared with media organizations, on Monday Everybody’s Perfect decided to de-program the film. In a statement to the Swiss newspaper, the festival’s artistic director, Sylvie Cachin, said: “The cancelation isn’t related to the film itself, but to the desire to avoid controversy just days before the festival’s opening.”

This was echoed by Sector, who said: “Six days [out] from the festival they made the decision they wanted to not get into this kind of heated argument. It was a way of saying we’re all coming together, we need to come together.”

She added: “[We have] heavy hearts still now. I have friends who said ‘I really want to see that film’ and would have paid twice the price to see it. This was a three-day decision with lots and lots of heartache. It was difficult.”

Similarly, the message informing the filmmakers of the festival’s change of heart apologized for bowing to the boycotters. “Please know that we are sincerely sorry for how this has turned out,” it reads. “Once again, personally, I do not condone this backlash and this attack, but we had to make this decision for the well-being of the festival audience and to ensure that the other films in the selection could be properly showcased.”

The cancelation comes following a number of pledges to boycott Israeli film institutions signed by actors including Javier Bardem and Emma Stone. Israel’s filmmaking community, which is traditionally left-wing, has rejected such calls, pointing to films coming out of the country that are openly critical of the Israeli government, such as “Naza,” which debuted at Venice, and last year’s Israeli Oscar entry “The Sea,” about a Palestinian boy who goes to Tel Aviv.

Earlier this summer Israeli director Nadav Lapid was booted as a member of the jury at the FID Marseille international film festival despite living in self-imposed exile in France in protest at the Israeli government. His latest film, “Yes,” was described in a Variety review as a “blistering attack on Israeli nationalism.”

The producers for “Tell Me Everything” told Variety: “A film does not represent a government, and filmmakers should not be held responsible for its policies. Many of us in Israel oppose the war and are deeply critical of our government. ‘Tell Me Everything’ is a human story about love, family, identity and healing. We made it to create connection and conversation, not to represent a government. Would Iranian or American filmmakers be asked to make similar declarations about their governments before their films could be shown?”

“We care deeply about being part of an international film community where difficult questions and different perspectives can exist. Festivals should make room for that connection and conversation- not exclude artists because of where they come from.”

title: Skydance Names Jay Askinasi Head of Ad Sales, Taps David Decker to Lead Content Sales and Ray Hopkins as Distribution Chief
summary: David Ellison’s Skydance, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, continues to announce senior executive appointments for the new company: On Thursday, the company said Jay Askinasi will lead ad sales for Skydance, David Decker will head up content sales, and Ray Hopkins will oversee distribution. Askanasi and Hopkins will also serve […]
content:
David Ellison’s Skydance, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, continues to announce senior executive appointments for the new company: On Thursday, the company said Jay Askinasi will lead ad sales for Skydance, David Decker will head up content sales, and Ray Hopkins will oversee distribution.

Askanasi and Hopkins will also serve as part of the Skydance Executive Leadership Team. The announcement was made by JB Perrette, the former WBD executive who is co-chair and chief business officer of Skydance TV and Skydance DTC, to whom the executives will report.

With Askanasi taking over as head of ad sales for the combined company, Ryan Gould and Robert “Bobby” Voltaggio — who have served as presidents of U.S. advertising sales at Warner Bros. Discovery — will be leaving the company.

Popular on Variety

“By combining our strengths and uniting our teams, we will build on the incredible legacies of both companies to serve audiences and partners in new and more innovative ways and shape an even more ambitious future,” Perrette said in a statement. “Jay, David and Ray are hugely talented and respected leaders with deep experience, strong industry relationships and a shared commitment to our partners and our people. There is tremendous opportunity ahead of us, and I look forward to working closely with them as we build the next generation media and entertainment organization.”

Here are bios for each of the newly appointed execs at Skydance:

Jay Askinasi, Chief Revenue Officer – Advertising

Jay Askinasi will serve as Chief Revenue Officer Advertising. A digital-first revenue leader, Askinasi joined Paramount as Chief Revenue Officer after leading global media revenue and growth at Roku. Previously, he served as CEO of Publicis Media Exchange U.S., where he oversaw major media and advertising operations. Across his career, Askinasi has developed expertise spanning platforms, agencies, data and advertising technology, with a proven track record of modernizing underused assets into high-growth commercial businesses.

David Decker, President, Content Sales

David Decker will serve as President, Content Sales. A more than two-decade Warner Bros. Veteran, Decker has led the worldwide licensing and distribution of Warner Bros.’ film, television, animation and digital content portfolios across major global platforms. Most recently serving as President of Content Sales for Warner Bros. Discovery, Decker has built landmark deals throughout his career.

Ray Hopkins, President, Distribution

Ray Hopkins will serve as President, Distribution. Having joined CBS Corporation in 2013, Hopkins is one of the media industry’s most accomplished distribution executives, bringing more than 35 years of experience managing Paramount’s relationships with video providers, digital and streaming platforms and CBS affiliate station groups. He previously served as Chief Operating Officer of YES Network and has been inducted into the Broadcasting + Cable Hall of Fame. Hopkins is widely recognized for building durable partnerships and expanding the reach and value of premium media brands.

title: Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on ‘The Social Reckoning’: Getting Inside a Whistleblower’s Mind, Jeremy Strong’s ‘Antihero’ Zuckerberg and Why Trump is the Movie’s Voldemort
summary: SPOILER WARNING: This interview contains plot points, including some spoilers, for “The Social Reckoning,” opening in theaters on Oct. 9. “The Social Reckoning” is many things — but those expecting a direct follow-up to 2010’s “The Social Network” may be surprised. That earlier film, which earned Aaron Sorkin an Oscar for its screenplay, closely followed […]
content:
SPOILER WARNING: This interview contains plot points, including some spoilers, for “The Social Reckoning,” opening in theaters on Oct. 9.

“The Social Reckoning” is many things — but those expecting a direct follow-up to 2010’s “The Social Network” may be surprised.

That earlier film, which earned Aaron Sorkin an Oscar for its screenplay, closely followed the emotional trajectory of Mark Zuckerberg (played then by Jesse Eisenberg) as he first created Facebook and then fought to defend himself against charges of IP theft. Now, “The Social Reckoning” confronts the world Facebook has made, with Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) a supporting character in the story of Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a mid-level Facebook employee who decides to become an unlikely whistleblower.

Haugen’s charges, in our world, became “The Facebook Files,” published in 2021 by Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and sharing with the world the company’s seeming indifference to its spread of misinformation and its negative impacts on mental health among young users. (Jeremy Allen White plays Horwitz in the film.) Madison’s tracking of Haugen’s steps from believer in Facebook’s mission as a member of its do-gooding, soon-to-be-dissolved civic integrity team to burn-it-down apostate is compelling in part because of the difference between this character and the Zuck we once knew. In Sorkin’s writing, Zuckerberg sees himself as a figure with the power to shift the culture. Haugen wants no such thing — but may have ended up doing so anyway.

Popular on Variety

The film represents a hinge point for both its writer-director and its star: Sorkin takes over directing duties from “The Social Network” helmer David Fincher, and the new film is the most anticipated of his four efforts so far behind the camera. For Madison, it’s her first film since her emergence as a star (and her Oscar win) with 2024’s “Anora” — a role whose emotional arc, from brashness to shy isolation, is more or less the opposite of Frances’.

In their one interview together promoting “The Social Reckoning,” out Oct. 9, Sorkin and Madison spoke about the trickiness of trying to make a crowd-pleaser about contentious issues, Madison’s inhabiting Haugen without yet having met her, and what Madison learned sharing a scene with the famously committed Strong.

I noted that multiple politicians are part of this story — I caught references to Donald Trump (obviously, given that the film depicts the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol), and to Bernie Sanders — but that they’re never mentioned by name. What did this lack of specific reference add to the way the story was told?

Sorkin: Is it OK if I … because I was the one who did that?

Madison: Yes!

Sorkin: Just because I was the one who did that. You didn’t get to decide.

Madison: Take it.

Sorkin: Two things: I didn’t want the distraction. And I don’t like for a movie to feel timely. I want it to feel timeless, and so a few years from now, 10 years from now, 50 years from now, I don’t want it to feel like you can only appreciate this movie if you were involved with the news back in 2026.

Mikey, Aaron writes famously rhythmic dialogue meant to be delivered with verve and speed — and delivered precisely as written. What was it like immersing yourself in that?

Madison: Reading his script, I was aware of it in some way, and also because of his work that I had seen and loved. But then being on set for my first day working with Jeremy Allen White, we had this monster of a scene with a ton of dialogue. It was quite dense, and a lot of information that we were going back and forth with. That was the first day where I was really like, OK, yes, this is like a different beast than anything that I’ve experienced before, but challenging, interesting, very different. I was very welcoming toward it because as an actor, it’s interesting to be experiencing all different kinds of work.

You’re playing a real person, Frances Haugen, and you hadn’t met her when you shot the role. Have you met her by now?

Madison: I’m meeting her very soon, and I’m really looking forward to it. I think we’ll have a lot to talk about, and also I just want to share my admiration for her in person. We’ve been sending some notes to each other back and forth via email, but this will be the first time like face-to-face.

Sorkin: You’re meeting her tonight. [Haugen and Madison walked the red carpet together at the New York premiere of “The Social Reckoning” on Oct. 4, the same day this interview took place.]

Madison: Yes, I am. But then we’re also meeting another time. Yeah, I’m playing a character based off of a real person, and we’re following her story and the facts of what happened very closely and specifically and honestly.

But in terms of building a character, it was one that I built purely from the ground up. Of course I wanted to meet her — I found her to be amazing. But I was also concerned that it would interfere with Aaron’s and my vision, and I didn’t want it to alter the character that I had created. And so I decided to just hold off a little bit until I reached out to her.

This film has a similar device at its opening to “The Social Network”: A vignette plays out that informs everything that comes after. Then, it was Rooney Mara’s character dumping Mark Zuckerberg. Now, it’s a young woman [Portia Doubleday] whose routine traffic stop by the cops turns into a parable about how social media has poisoned our brains. It ends up being hugely important to the movie. What inspired this story-in-miniature?

Sorkin: I had been spending a lot of time with Frances — many hours over a period of many months, and the same thing with Jeff Horwitz. What I had was a lot of information, but I couldn’t find the shape of a movie yet, until I asked Frances what was the inciting action. One day you weren’t a Facebook whistleblower. The next day you were. What changed? And she said, “I had a friend who had been radicalized by spending too much time on Facebook.” And I began to imagine the opening scene.

I didn’t realize that was drawn from life.

Sorkin: As is the opening scene in “The Social Network,” by the way.

Frances Haugen opened up to journalists and testified before Congress, but opening up to a dramatist strikes me as a different thing altogether. What was that process like for you?

Sorkin: I really have to hand it to Frances. I don’t know how many of us would have been happy about having a movie made about us — putting our life in the hands of a complete stranger, whose wishes and agenda may not be the same as ours. I would talk to her about that from time to time. Are you OK with this? Are you OK with that? And what was important to her was getting the word out about what she had discovered.

I think of “The Social Network” as a character study of Mark Zuckerberg. Here, though, he’s such a malign presence and, for me, a lot of his complication seems to have been sanded away by his success. Aaron, how did you talk to Jeremy Strong about playing him now? No actor wants to see the person they’re playing as irredeemable.

Sorkin: Yeah, sure, and neither of us did. The character of Mark Zuckerberg has a different function in this film than he did in “The Social Network.” He was an antihero, but he was the protagonist in “The Social Network,” and Frances is the protagonist in “The Social Reckoning.” But both Jeremy and I agreed that Mark is not a villain; he’s an antihero, which is to say, his goal is good, right? He just wants to connect people. That’s good, but his methods have become perverted along the way.

I know that when I’m writing an antihero, you can’t judge the character. You have to write the character as if they’re making their case to God why they should be allowed into heaven. Jeremy felt the same way about playing the character. He was Mark Zuckerberg’s biggest defender from the beginning — before he started shooting, during his shooting, and afterward. I didn’t read it, but I know that he wrote a letter to Mark, letting him know that he planned on playing the part respectfully and in Mark’s defense.

Mikey, you have one memorable scene where Strong’s version of Mark Zuckerberg runs roughshod over your colleagues while you watch. What was it like to shoot?

Madison: I was excited for that scene and happy that I was able to work with Jeremy, even if just for a little bit — with me off in the corner. I had heard so much about his process, and as an actress, I’m very curious if there are things that I can learn from other actors’ processes.

I obviously think the result of his work is very compelling, and so I was excited. I do feel like the energy that he brought to his character and like the way in which he wanted to film the scenes brought a really specific, intense energy to the environment on the set, which I think was incredibly helpful and added another layer and depth to it. And I really got to just be an observer — that’s what I was doing — and it was fascinating.

I also noticed that — not just when the camera was on him and capturing his performance, but when it was on other people — he was still in his character, really trying to get the best performances out of everyone. That’s very generous of an actor to do that, and I really appreciated that. It was inspiring to see another actor with a process as intense and specific as that be as generous. Do you know what I mean?

I do. There are plenty of actors who’ve been working hard and don’t give everything when the camera switches over to their costar’s shots.

Madison: But it’s always disappointing, too, because I really feel like you’re only as good as your counterpart. I always want the best performance out of the people I’m working with, so I was appreciative to see that.

Sorkin: You’re the exact same way. Mikey, doing her off-camera work — you would not know that she was off-camera.

Without spoiling the plot, there’s a dispiriting note at the end of the film as text on-screen informs us that some very high percentage of Americans get their news from Facebook to this day. Aaron, I think of you as an optimist — do you think there’s a way forward here?

Sorkin: As troubling as the climax of the film is, ultimately, you feel good at the end. It’s a feeling of optimism, because David has picked up a rock and thrown it at Goliath — and, as a matter of fact, two Davids. Frances has picked up a rock, thrown it at Facebook, and print journalism [does] too.

Mikey, do you share Aaron’s optimism about pulling out from the misinformation spiral?

Madison: Yes, of course I do. I am ultimately a very optimistic person. I do believe in the good of people. I believe in rehabilitation and people’s ability to learn and be better. Maybe it’s a bit naive at times, but yeah, I do. We have to hold on to that hope, or else things just seem so bleak.

You’re not on social media. Was there ever even the most fleeting sense, preparing for this film, that you were missing out?

Madison: It wasn’t a part of my preparation to be on Instagram or Facebook. It just wasn’t a part of things, and so I never indulged in that. Hearing Aaron talk about all of the dachshund videos that he was fed during his research process, there was a part of me that was like, I think I’m missing out on something there. But I’ve maintained the same feeling that me not being on social media is right, and I didn’t feel it was necessary for me to bring this character to life.

Aaron, Paramount produced your film “The Trial of the Chicago 7,” before selling it to Netflix during the height of COVID. Now, they’re under new leadership, and subsuming Warner Bros. [This interview was conducted after the deal was announced, but before it closed on Oct. 6.] Do you think it’ll be more challenging, in an age of consolidation, to make films that address political issues directly?

Sorkin: It will be more challenging with the consolidation of Warner Bros. and Paramount. There is one less movie studio making movies, and that’s not good. Making a movie shouldn’t be considered an act of courage. It shouldn’t take bravery. But you look around, and you see studios and networks making decisions out of fear.

The big reason that Frances, at the end of the movie, implores Congress to take action and pass some laws — and the reason why that’s extremely difficult to do — is that there are tech billionaires funding the campaigns of the people who need to make the laws. For that reason, it’s going to be difficult. It’s not going to be impossible.

Mikey, you’ve said that you wanted to retreat from the spotlight somewhat after the burst of excitement and activity around “Anora.” What does it feel like to be back with your first film since winning the Oscar?

Madison: I’m very happy to be promoting this film because I really want people to go and see it, and I really believe in the story and the message. So I’m hopeful that people do go and see the movie in theaters. This was the first project I felt compelled to do after “Anora” — it felt like something very different than anything I had done before, in terms of the tone of the character and wanting to work with Aaron. It just was something that felt right.

But in terms of the big picture, I don’t know if it’s helpful for me to think about things like that. I think I’ll get too in my head and overwhelmed. I just want to keep making movies with people I admire and doing work that feels important or compelling or moving in some way. I’m just focused on that part of it.

Aaron, what made Mikey the right fit for this role? It’s so obviously different from Ani in “Anora” — and others Mikey has played, too.

Sorkin: Number one. You’re not going to like this, OK?

Madison: [laughs] OK.

Sorkin: She’s a great actor. She has world-class skills as an actor. There are certain things that an actor can’t fake. An actor can’t act smart, and an actor can’t act funny. They have to bring those things with them. Mikey has both those clubs in her golf bag. But add to that the fact that Mikey moves through the world as if everyone is right-handed and she’s left-handed. It’s just a slight … I wish I could describe it, but it’s perfect for Frances. It’s very charming. It’s very endearing. And we understand that Frances is most comfortable at her keyboard, at her computer screen. Once she has to interact face-to-face with people, it’s something she needs to make an effort to do.

Given the subject matter, are you concerned that people will have preconceptions about the movie? The very point is that we live in such divided times, but, for that reason, I wonder if a movie like this can entertain the masses broadly.

Sorkin: People, with movies, they tend to — there are people who make up their minds without seeing it. But if you come, I bet you’ll be surprised.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

title: A+E Global Media and Lifetime Expand Microdrama Slate, Announcing Mobile Launch Originals and Nearly 200 Titles Adapted for Third-Party Distribution
summary: A+E Global Media and Lifetime are dramatically expanding their output in the world of microdramas and vertical video. The company has announced that its new MyLifetime.com platform will offer three original Lifetime vertical films from Microhouse Films as well as seven titles adapted from the A+E Global Media library. The Lifetime mobile app plans to […]
content:
A+E Global Media and Lifetime are dramatically expanding their output in the world of microdramas and vertical video.

The company has announced that its new MyLifetime.com platform will offer three original Lifetime vertical films from Microhouse Films as well as seven titles adapted from the A+E Global Media library.

The Lifetime mobile app plans to add new vertical titles every two weeks (along with access on MyLifetime.com), with up to seven originals by the end of the year. Two of those will be sponsored holiday-themed verticals from vertTV.

“Microdramas are one of the most dynamic and exciting areas of growth in entertainment, and Lifetime is proud to be an early and meaningful participant in that evolution,” said Elaine Frontain Bryant, executive vice president and head of programming, A&E, Lifetime and LMN, in a statement. “Our opportunity is not simply to introduce a new format, but to define its role within the Lifetime ecosystem in a way that strengthens our brand, deepens fandom and gives audiences another way to experience the stories they already love. With original series, library titles and new brand-supported projects rolling out through the Lifetime app on mobile and MyLifetime.com, we are building a strategy that spans premium storytelling, audience engagement and global distribution.”

Popular on Variety

Also, timed to the upcoming MIPCOM market, A+E Global Media has adapted nearly 200 titles into vertical microdramas that will be available to license to other platforms.

The Microhouse Films slate for MyLifetime.com includes “Tides of Temptation,” “Matched With a Murderer” and “His Lies Taste Like Love.”

“Tides of Temptation,” which is exec produced by Taye Diggs, Autumn Federici and Shelby Stone, is a stand-alone digital companion to the Lifetime original movie “Terry McMillan Presents: Paradise with You,” which debuts Nov. 7.

Other Microhouse Films projects to come include “Reunion Island,” which debuts at the New York-based microdrama/vertical storytelling-based ALZA Festival, and “Recklessly in Love with My Daughter’s Best Man.”

The holiday-themed, sponsored vertical originals from vertTV include “Casting Christmas” and “Destination, Christmas.” Jeffrey Schenck, Barry Barnholtz, Peter Sullivan, Brian Nolan and Ben Rosenthal are the founders of vertTV.

Meanwhile, Lifetime original films that have been edited into vertical chapters for MyLifetime.com include “A Lifeguard’s Obsession,” “Burned by Love,” “Danger in the House,” “My Husband’s Worse Mistake,” “What Would You Kill For?,” “Secret of a Dean’s Wife” and “College Professor Obsession.”

As for the A+E library content that has also been cut into microseries, besides the nearly 200 Lifetime movies, it includes “Cold Case Files,” “I Survived,” “Alone,” “Ice Road Truckers,” “Forged in Fire,” “History’s Greatest Mysteries,” “Hoarders” and “Married at First Sight.”

“The expansion into vertical storytelling creates compelling new opportunities for brands to connect with audiences in highly engaging, mobile-first environments,” said Toby Byrne, A+E Global Media’s president of media solutions, in a statement. “Projects like these give advertisers the ability to participate in premium, culturally relevant storytelling while reaching audiences across the platforms where they are spending their time.”

title: Oscars: Democratic Republic Of Congo Selects ‘Rumba Royale’ For Best International Feature Film Race; The Fally Ipupa Starrer Is Country’s Second Ever Submission
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The Democratic Republic of Congo has selected historical thriller Rumba Royale as its entry for the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards. It’s a historic milestone for Congolese cinema in that the film is the second ever film submitted by the country for the category following its first submission in […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The Democratic Republic of Congo has selected historical thriller Rumba Royale as its entry for the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards. It’s a historic milestone for Congolese cinema in that the film is the second ever film submitted by the country for the category following its first submission in 1997 with Macadam Tribu.

Directed by Yohane Dean Lengol and Hamed Mobasser, Rumba Royale is set in 1959 Leopoldville, the former capital of Belgian Congo (which is now called Kinshasa), in the final months of Belgian colonial rule. It was a time when the pulsating rhythms of rumba set nightlife alight. The story takes place around the Club Rumba Royale, where white Europeans and Congolese citizens rub shoulders, and where the captivating melodies of rumba merge with aspirations and fiery debates of independence.

The story follows photographer Daniel, played by African rumba star Fally Ipupa, as political change, personal ambition and tragedy reshape the world around him.

Watch on Deadline

Produced and filmed in Kinshasa, the project brought together Congolese actors, technicians, craftspeople, musicians and emerging film professionals in an environment where the local industry continues to develop despite limited infrastructure, production resources and financing opportunities.

The project is the brainchild of writers Kevin Dwyer and Mobasser, the latter of whom is a Belgian diplomat based in Washington D.C. who also co-directs the title.

“Rumba Royale demonstrates the extraordinary stories that can emerge when local talent is given the opportunity to create at scale,” said the filmmakers. “This selection is a celebration of Congolese creativity, resilience and ambition. We hope it helps shine a light not only on this film, but on the growing community of filmmakers across the region whose work deserves greater international attention and support.”

title: Michael Douglas Was Third Choice For Gordon Gekko; How He Rode ‘Wall Street’s Slick Villain To Oscar Glory
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Editor’s note: Mike Fleming Jr. here. For the better part of last year, my day began with a 6 a.m. call and an hour with Michael Douglas for his memoir One Helluva Ride. It was early for me, but always worth catching MD someplace in Europe, where he enjoys the fruits of his long […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Editor’s note: Mike Fleming Jr. here. For the better part of last year, my day began with a 6 a.m. call and an hour with Michael Douglas for his memoir One Helluva Ride. It was early for me, but always worth catching MD someplace in Europe, where he enjoys the fruits of his long run as Hollywood superstar with his wife Catherine Zeta-Jones and their family. Written by Douglas, Shane Salerno and me, the memoir One Helluva Ride was released Tuesday by Grand Central Publishing. Details revealed by Douglas about his colorful personal life have dominated headlines this week; we thought Deadline readers would be most interested in the dissection of the seminal film that helped forge a great career.

Related Stories

News



Oliver Stone: Director’s Career In Photos



Casting



Michael Douglas, Willem Dafoe, Ellen Barkin, Homer Gere And Yvonne Chapman Join Oliver Stone’s Next Pic ‘White Lies’



Douglas started with a difficult task, trying to forge an identity out of the long shadow cast by his father, Kirk Douglas. Douglas got his first movie boost as a producer, sharing the Best Picture Oscar for One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, and capturing the Zeitgeist with The China Syndrome. His onscreen rise took longer. The producer in Douglas helped the actor in him by prizing good scripts above all else. The best of those meant playing flawed characters, and Douglas came to relish seeing how far he could push that envelope and still have audiences on his side.

Watch on Deadline

The book tells Douglas’ story through a dozen of his most memorable films – Romancing the Stone, Fatal Attraction, Basic Instinct, Traffic, Falling Down and The War of the Roses among them — and The Streets of San Francisco, the TV series with Karl Malden that helped forge Douglas’ work ethic and prepared him to produce Cuckoo’s Nest with the late Saul Zaentz. The following excerpt focuses on Wall Street, the film that emboldened Douglas to take the kind of risks many of his actor peers didn’t dare. Pushed relentlessly by Oliver Stone, Douglas turned the corporate raider Gordon Gekko into a defining villain of ’80s films. That turn paved the way for everything that followed.

As Michael writes in the book’s intro, “I can’t think about my life without thinking of my movies. Six of the eight decades I’ve lived on this planet have been spent making films—they have always been my landmarks, the way I mark time.” Here, he takes us back to Wall Street, the film that allowed him to play any role and have audiences show up on the weekend, just to see what he got himself into next, and how he was going to get out of it.

‘I had never played the bad guy’

I’d never played the bad guy. In Fatal Attraction I had played a guy who made a bad decision and spent the rest of the movie trying to make up for it. But he wasn’t a real villain.

Dad always thought I should play a part as cunning and manipulative as his famous character in The Bad and the Beautiful, the ruthless Hollywood producer Jonathan Shields. He told me, “You’re so likable, Michael, but when you finally play a bad guy, you’re going to surprise a lot of people who think you can only do the nice-guy stuff. I know the darkness under there.”

RELATED: The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office

Oliver Stone had just won best director and best picture for Platoon. Premiere magazine said, “In one short year, he has emerged as the most interesting and important director in Hollywood.”

In the early 1980s, while researching his screenplay of Scarface in Miami, Oliver noticed not only the rise of cocaine, but of a young, emerging millionaire class. Millionaires were once men in their sixties, but thanks to Wall Street, you suddenly had all these guys—kids, really—in their twenties and early thirties with tons of disposable income. They were using it to fund a decadent lifestyle of drugs and parties and flashy materialism.

Oliver saw parallels between the get-rich-quick Miami drug trade and what was taking place in the New York financial world. Oliver called Wall Street “Scarface North.” He wanted to use the backdrop of the finance world to hold a mirror up to America. Oliver was eager to prove that he could transfer his intensity from the Vietnam jungle to the concrete jungle of Manhattan’s Financial District. The title of his new project was going to be either Greed or Gekko the Great.

Wall Street follows Bud Fox, a young, ambitious stockbroker who is seduced into the ruthless, illegal world of insider trading under the dark mentorship of wealthy corporate raider Gordon Gekko. In the course of the story, Bud faces a complex moral struggle between his blue-collar roots and the seductive, corrupt power of money.

To counterbalance his protagonist, Stone needed a villain. Someone slick, charismatic, and seductive. A ruthless corporate raider.

For the part of Gekko, the studio really wanted Warren Beatty but he would not commit. Next the role was offered to Richard Gere, who turned it down.

Then Oliver sent me the screenplay. It was long, with intense industry-jargon-heavy monologues running two or three straight pages of single-spaced type. I was captivated by Gekko’s words:

Greed, for lack of a better word, is good.

Greed is right.

Greed works.

Greed clarifies, cuts through, and captures the essence of the evolutionary spirit.

Greed, in all of its forms—greed for life, for money, for love, knowledge—has marked the upward surge of mankind.

And greed, you mark my words, will not only save Teldar Paper, but that other malfunctioning corporation called the USA.

This Gordon Gekko part was fantastic and it was exactly what I was looking for. But that didn’t mean the studio wanted me.

Scott Rudin and other Fox executives said I was too young for the part, but the truth was they just didn’t believe I could pull it off. In fact, they warned Oliver that I was more of a producer than an actor and told him I’d probably be in my trailer all the time reading scripts or on the phone to LA trying to set up my own projects. Why couldn’t they accept that I was capable of both jobs, separately or at once?

There was really nothing onscreen that showed Oliver I could play Gordon Gekko. Gekko was all power, all the time. He was the puppet master. He was nasty. He was Machiavellian. He was the ultimate villain.

Rather than being turned off by the studio’s feedback, Oliver was intrigued. In fact, the more the studio executives warned Oliver about me, the more interested he was. He believed in me, not only because of my acting résumé, but because of my life. He was hiring me because I was an Oscar-winning producer who, like Gekko, knew how to make money. Four back-to-back blockbusters—One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, The China Syndrome, Romancing the Stone, Jewel of the Nile—had proven that. I was the actor who walked off a hit TV show to make an independent movie that didn’t even have a distributor. I was the Hollywood disrupter who made an indie film that beat every big studio movie, both at the box office and at the Academy Awards, as he himself had just done with Platoon. I was a maverick, an outsider, like Oliver, and, more importantly, like Gordon Gekko.

Oliver told me when we met he found “an edge” to me that he liked and felt I had the right mix of charisma and business savvy to play Gekko. He trusted that the DNA I possessed as the son of Kirk Douglas, along with the skills I had acquired as an actor over twenty years, would be enough for me to bring out the Gordon Gekko inside me. He believed there was a chord I hadn’t played because I didn’t want to be compared to my father. He gave me the role.

Now we had to build Gordon Gekko from the ground up. Building a character starts with external elements. Establishing these details always helps me figure out how my character thinks, moves, and expresses himself.

1. The name: There was nothing accidental about the name. “Gekko” was chosen to highlight Gordon’s predatory nature. He was a stealthy, cold-blooded hunter intent on killing his prey. And geckos are survivors. The more I researched and delved into the character, the harder I worked to embody these traits.

2. The clothes: Essential to the image, the persona of this man, was Gekko’s wardrobe. The suits, the suspenders, the cuff links, the shoes, all of it. Costume designer Ellen Mirojnick brought in Manhattan tailor Alan Flusser to help with the outfits. They studied the power suits of other Masters of the Universe figures like Carl Icahn, T. Boone Pickens, and even a young Manhattan real estate tycoon named Donald Trump.

3. The hair: I had a long, flowing mane, still a Santa Barbara hippie at heart. But that wouldn’t work for a shark like Gekko. I needed something slick and edgy, a look different from anything audiences had seen before. And then I thought about Pat Riley. Pat was not only one of the best coaches in NBA history, but he looked damn good doing it. This was partly because he knew he was representing the Buss family and the Lakers organization, but also Pat’s father had played and managed in the minor leagues for twenty-two years and always believed in the discipline of good grooming. When his parents went to dinner, his dad wore a sport coat, gabardine shirt, and tie. Pat took this to heart and basically put Armani on the map in Los Angeles. But he was never fussy about it. In fact, he wore the same Lorenzo Banfi shoes every night and got dressed and slicked his hair back in under five minutes.

But yeah, he did look good, and I wanted Gordon Gekko to have some of that flair. I remembered a day Pat Riley and I were together in Miami, and Pat was driving his Mercury with the top down. I was in the back seat, absolutely fixated on how his hair stayed perfectly in place despite the breeze. This was exactly the commanding look I needed for Gekko. (For years afterward, Pat would tease me, saying I stole his look, and for years I would deny knowing what he was talking about. Eventually, in 2026, I confessed the truth when the Lakers unveiled a statue of Pat in Star Plaza outside Crypto.com Arena in LA.)

4. The smoking: By design, Gekko is seen smoking during key moments in the story, including his famous “Greed is good” speech. Winston cigarettes and Davidoff cigars serve to sell an image of supreme, untouchable confidence.

5. The speech: Gekko’s biggest weapon was his ability to command a room with his words. I would have to deliver long monologues while holding not only the other characters’ attention but the audience’s as well. I worked with a speech coach on breath control and vocal rhythms. Gekko’s words stabbed the person he was tearing down.

6. The language: Beyond just the way he speaks, there’s a distinctive vocabulary that signals Gordon Gekko’s philosophy and approach to everything in life. I focused on how I would deliver these lines in a way that would show his personality and background:

Lunch is for wimps.

Wake up, will ya, pal? If you’re not inside, you’re outside, okay. What’s worth doing is worth doing for money.

You need a friend, get a dog.

It’s all about bucks, kid. The rest is conversation.

7. The trappings: Everything around me, every object, every setting, had to convey wealth. The private jets, the limos, the high-end restaurants, the big house on the beach. It was essential to Gekko’s image and character. Whenever you saw Gordon Gekko, you saw money. This included, of course, his signature Motorola DynaTAC 8000X cell phone. Wall Street was the first major studio movie to use one in a picture.

Oliver and I talked a lot about Gekko’s Long Island background. He wasn’t an Ivy Leaguer who had things handed to him by patronage and social circles. He clawed his way up to the top mercilessly. He had a street toughness you wouldn’t find in someone coming out of Harvard or Yale, and I worked on tapping into that blue-collar warrior masquerading as a white-collar titan.

I did a tremendous amount of research. I talked with a bunch of Wall Street traders, and Oliver and I met with Michael Milken at the Drexel Burnham Lambert offices in LA. While they were giving us a tour, Milken seemed a bit nervous. When Oliver said, “Can you show us the shredding machines?” Milken didn’t find it funny. He excused himself and that was the last we saw of him.

We spent time interviewing Asher Edelman. Edelman was a Wall Street wizard who taught a course at Columbia Business School called Corporate Raiding—The Art of War. He threw out the standard textbooks and assigned Sun Tzu’s The Art of War instead.

I ultimately drew from a composite of several real Wall Street titans, including Ivan Boesky, Carl Icahn, Dennis Levine, and Oliver’s friend Owen Morrissey, who had been involved in a real-life $20 million financial scandal just a couple years before. I also had my own connections on Wall Street: investment bankers I had dealt with to finance past films. I took bits and pieces from all of them. One guy’s seduction and charm. Another one’s intellect. Someone else’s killer instinct. There was a little bit of Asher Edelman, Hollywood talent agent Mike Ovitz, and Oliver himself thrown in for good measure.

I prepared for this role harder than I had for any that came before. I felt immense pressure to deliver for Oliver because he had fought hard to cast me in the film against 20th Century Fox’s objections.

We did a week of rehearsals in New York and went through the script many times. It became clear early in the process that Sean Young (who was playing my wife) and Daryl Hannah (Gekko’s former mistress turned Bud’s girlfriend) were uncomfortable and struggling with their roles. Oliver did his best to convey what the characters’ wants and needs were, but there was something they just weren’t connecting with. Especially Daryl.

On April 15, 1987, we began filming Wall Street. I got into a routine. I would show up on set, head to hair and makeup—Gordon Gekko had a year-round tan—and get dressed in expensive suits and accessories. It was my uniform, and from the moment I donned all of it, I felt different.

I went back to an old trick I had learned long before, on The Streets of San Francisco. I liked to review my lines when I was doing something else. Brushing my teeth, I’d be saying, “Now you’re not naive enough to think we’re living in a democracy, are you buddy?” While cooking, I proclaimed, “The new law of evolution in corporate America seems to be survival of the unfittest.” I’d sip my coffee and look up to declare, “Most of these Harvard MBA types, they don’t add up to dog shit. Give me guys that are poor, smart, and hungry. And no feelings.” This exercise helped me reach another level of understanding and memorization.

I need my lines to be rote, to be almost unconscious, like breathing. That helps me deliver them without sounding like I’m delivering a lecture. Once I know them at that level, I have the bandwidth to explore the other facets of the character and scene, like where I’m looking, what expressions I’m making, how I’m physically moving around the set. When the words come out naturally, without having to think about them, that is the real freedom and joy of acting. On Wall Street, I found that rhythm. But not right away. And not without a lot of pain.

I learned quickly that Oliver’s tough-guy reputation was well earned. At a time when so many of us were trying our damnedest to avoid the draft, Oliver was an idealistic dreamer whose desire for adventure led him to enlist in the army. He came back from Vietnam with scars, both physical and psychological. Wounded twice in battle, he won the Bronze Star with Valor, and the Purple Heart. He then studied film at NYU and his toughness and ferocity were evident in the scripts he wrote for Midnight Express and Scarface.

Oliver treated making movies like going to battle. One of the first scenes we filmed was with Gekko and Bud Fox in a limo, where Gekko asks Bud the difference between a well-dressed man on a street corner and a homeless man rooting through a garbage can right next to him.

It’s a crucial scene, where Bud Fox is seduced into making his Faustian bargain with Gekko. The writing was beautiful, but there was a lot of dialogue, and I was still learning Oliver’s guerrilla-style filmmaking. The cinematographer was Bobby Richardson, who is extraordinary. He had already done Salvador and Platoon and would go on to do JFK, The Doors, Born on the Fourth of July, and Quentin Tarantino’s last six movies. We shot the scene in a real limo with Bobby and his camera in the jump seat. They used a flat lens, and the camera was right in our faces. Oliver moved the camera a lot within scenes. He wanted to create the sensation of sharks during a feeding frenzy. The camera, like Gekko, was a predator. As an actor, it required a tremendous amount of concentration.

I fumbled a few lines and immediately recalled the experience with Michael Crichton on Coma, where I was unprepared, didn’t know my lines, and had to do the scene in front of an entire crew sixty-four times before I got it right. But here, as we went along, I felt that I was getting better and dialing in.

We went through the scene a few more times, then broke for lunch. Oliver knocked on my trailer door and popped his head in. “Are you okay?”

“Yeah, I’m good,” I replied.

“Are you on drugs?”

“No, I’m not on drugs. Why would you ask me that?”

“Because you look like you’ve never acted before in your life.”

Fuck.

Me.

In that moment, I heard every single person in my life who had told me I couldn’t do something. That I was just a TV actor. That I was crazy to do Cuckoo’s Nest. That I would never be a leading man. That I would never escape my father’s shadow. All the rejection, all the self-doubt, it was all there, right in front of me. And now I had to prove them wrong. Dad told me I wasn’t as sweet and charming as everyone thought I was, that I had a piece of steel inside me. I would have to summon it if I had any hope of pulling off this role.

I wasn’t a producer on Wall Street, so there was no reason for me to see the dailies. I didn’t normally watch dailies anyway because I would always beat myself up, cringing at my performance. But now I insisted. I needed to see what I was doing wrong.

I watched a rough cut of the scene. “Hey, Oliver,” I said to him. “I actually think it’s pretty good.”

“It is, isn’t it?”

What? Now he agreed? Was he just screwing with me? Well fuck you, too, Oliver. I wasn’t going to wilt. I wasn’t going to back down. I was going to show him that I was Gordon Gekko.

I realized what Oliver was doing. Some directors take a patriarchal view, putting a fatherly arm on your shoulder when you need one. But not Oliver. He challenges you. He twists your melon. He uses every trick he can to get just one percent more out of you. By summoning all the rejections and dismissals I had suffered in my career, he was making me respond to them. Right here, right now, in this role. He was tapping into corners of my personality that I didn’t even know existed.
