I’ll show him. I turned his doubt into fuel. I started rehearsing even harder on my own, using that anger as a source of energy. I thought that day and every day for the rest of the shoot: I’ll goddamn show Oliver.

Oliver treated his actors like fellow soldiers in the foxhole. There was no coddling. There was no “You did your best.” Oliver hated that style and he was not going to, as he called it, “seal clap after every scene.” You were either in the trench with him or you weren’t. And if you were, he had to know that his back was protected. Just like you had to know. So he would test you. He would find any insecurities and vulnerabilities and poke, prod, and manipulate them into peak performances.

The most famous line from Wall Street is “Greed, for lack of a better word, is good.” It encapsulates not only the thesis of the film, but the excessive materialism of the 1980s. The line is pulled from a commencement speech Ivan Boesky gave at the UC Berkeley Haas School of Business, when he said, “I think greed is healthy. You can be greedy and still feel good about yourself.” Just six months after Boesky’s arrest for insider trading, we were shooting the most iconic scene of Wall Street in the ballroom of the Roosevelt Hotel on East 45th Street. Using Oliver’s indictment of my earlier performance as fuel, I studied my ass off in preparation.

The scene takes place at the stockholders’ meeting. A giant room, with over a hundred cast members and extras, and me pacing like a lion.

It’s a three-and-a-half-minute monologue. That’s an eternity on film. Oliver’s direction, his and Stanley’s words, and my preparation almost had me believing that I was really taking over a company.

After the first take—in which I did the entire monologue in one fluid go—Oliver yelled, “Cut,” and the entire room of five-hundred-plus people stood and applauded. Cast, extras, crewmembers, everyone. I thought back to Cuckoo’s Nest, and how the cast and crew had applauded Jack’s performance on more than one occasion. A decade had passed, and it was happening to me now. It meant the world to me.

We kept going. To get the needed coverage, we shot the scene from all angles. Charlie and Sean’s close-ups. The company shareholders on the dais. The featured extras. The wide shot of the entire room. Then it was time for my close-up.

As I was doing the scene, I could see Oliver next to the camera, head down, reading the script to make sure I was following the speech as written.

He wasn’t looking at me. He wasn’t watching my performance. Take after take, he was not seeing anything I was doing. He was just reading along to make sure I got every word, every comma, right. I was getting increasingly pissed off until finally, after take five, I said into the mic, “Oliver, I’m over here.” Only then did he look up.

After one or two more takes, he said, “Print. Let’s move on.” That was it? No notes on my performance? No guidance at all? Angry, I grabbed Oliver, pulled him to a corner, and went ballistic. I was killing myself for him, and he didn’t even have the courtesy to pretend to be paying attention to my performance?

Oliver explained that he prefers to be in what’s called “video village,” the tent where producers watch the video feed of a scene. Oliver keeps away from the actors because he doesn’t want to end up in their eyeline. He wants an actor to be free to take in the whole room without being distracted by his presence or feeling like he’s judging them. He believes a script is the bible, trusts the writing, and could tell through hearing the script if it was working right tonally. He also mentioned that he was looking up, but only when he knew I wasn’t aware. He was concentrating on my performance without making me hyperaware that he was doing it.

My rising stock had helped him find financing at Fox. But the pressure for Oliver to prove himself on his first studio film, at three times the cost of Platoon, was immense.

Prior to shooting, Oliver did something truly extraordinary, and unprecedented, with Charlie. He let him choose who would play his father in the film. It came down to my old costar Jack Lemmon or Charlie’s real father, the incredible Martin Sheen.

Charlie chose his real dad.

As good as Oliver Stone is at pulling out incredible performances from his male stars, the same isn’t always true for his leading ladies.

Sean Young, who played my wife, had a terrible relationship with Charlie and pretty much everyone else besides me. She caused a lot of problems on set, and many on the crew had an issue with her. It got so bad that at one point Charlie taped a sign on her back that read “Biggest cunt in the world.” Sean did not notice the sign for some time. When I saw it, I pulled it off.

“What was that?” she asked.

“Forget it.”

It would have ended there, except the guy who furnished all the art for the film had seen it and told her. She had every right to be furious.

Daryl Hannah also continued to have a tough time. Several of Oliver’s longtime crewmembers, including cinematographer Bobby Richardson, had urged him to recast Sean and Daryl, but he stood by them until he fired Sean. Oliver would later say he wished he had fired both. He thought they were miscast.

Oliver was the first director to really test me as an actor. I’ll admit, I hated his guts while we filmed it. He continued to ride me and piss me off, risking any future relationship we might have, just to get that extra bit of anger out of me. But somehow Oliver knew that what I needed to really elevate my performance was an extra level of nastiness that I wasn’t used to. Looking back, I can never repay him for that gift.

After I finished my final scene in the film, I called Dad and said, “Boy, are you going to love me in this role. I am mean.”

Two months before our release, Black Monday happened. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped an astonishing 22.6 percent. It was the worst financial crisis since the crash of 1929, which had ignited the Great Depression.

Wall Street premiered on December 11, 1987. It instantly became part of the cultural conversation, like Fatal Attraction and The China Syndrome.

It always shocks me, even now, when people walk up to me and say, “Gordon Gekko is the reason I became a stockbroker.” What the hell?! He isn’t a hero, he’s the villain, and he ends up paying for it with a prison sentence. But they don’t care. They love the take-no-prisoners mentality. So many people took the wrong message away from the film. It’s sad, really.

As a cultural phenomenon Wall Street lasted long after it left the theaters. It became iconic among “finance bros.” In fact, there’s a scene in the 2000 film Boiler Room where eight young traders are all sitting around a TV watching Wall Street. Ben Affleck’s character starts quoting the dialogue in perfect sync with the film.

My portrayal of Gordon Gekko is the face of corporate predation to this day. But it was just a character, not something to aspire to. It is so pervasive, that in 2012, twenty-five years after the first film, the FBI recruited me to do a PSA talking directly to investment brokers about the dangers of financial fraud. I was as surprised as anyone to be working with the FBI. But the statute of limitations on my cross-country drug runs had finally expired.

Wall Street also struck a chord during award season. I was nominated by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association for a Golden Globe for Best Actor. I was staying in the Hotel Bel-Air, and as my mother and I left to go to the ceremony, we passed George Harrison. I acknowledged the lead guitarist of the Beatles with a nod and wave and went to the show.

I won that evening, gave my speech, then went through the whole press flurry afterward. When I came out, everyone had gone home. I had no one to celebrate with. I said screw it and went to Trader Vic’s for a drink, then back to the hotel, kind of excited, but feeling a little sorry for myself. I was in my room around 12:30 a.m. when the phone rang. It was George Harrison!

“Hello, Michael. I just got back to the hotel, and my mate and I thought we’d come by and say hi.”

Uh, hell yeah, George Harrison and his mate can come by.

A couple of minutes later, there was a knock on my door and in he walked, accompanied by the biggest dog I’d ever seen, and then his “mate”:

Bob Dylan.

Man, that was one of the most amazing nights of my life. We sat around and shot the shit, but the thing I remember most is the dog. There was caviar on the table and this behemoth started licking it. And no one was stopping him.

Bob said, “Far out, dog loves caviar!” but all I was thinking is, That’s gotta be like a hundred dollars per lick!

Then it was time for the Oscars. Fatal Attraction was nominated for Best Picture, along with nominations for Adrian Lyne, Glenn Close, Anne Archer, and James Dearden. Everyone but me. But I was nominated for Wall Street. And in another confusing fact, somehow, Wall Street wasn’t nominated for Best Picture, nor was Oliver Stone for directing. Fox studios had decided Broadcast News was going to be their big Oscar film that year. I was singly excluded from Fatal Attraction and singly included for Wall Street.

In the Best Actor category, I was nominated alongside my pal Jack Nicholson for Ironweed, Marcello Mastroianni for Dark Eyes, Robin Williams for Good Morning, Vietnam, and William Hurt for Broadcast News. My father has been nominated for three Oscars and lost every time.

Marlee Matlin, who’d won Best Actress the previous year for Children of a Lesser God, presented the award. As she worked her way through the category, using sign language as a translator conveyed her words, it reminded me of the night we won for Cuckoo’s Nest, when Louise gave her acceptance speech in sign language. Maybe the gods were giving me a sign.

“And the winner is, let’s see . . . Michael Douglas for Wall Street!”

After I won the Oscar, my entire group made the rounds of after-parties and the later it got, the more people peeled off, even Diandra. At five in the morning, Jann Wenner and I went to see Jack Nicholson at his place up on Mulholland. We knew he’d be up. Jack opened the door with a grin. He told me he had been rooting for me to win that night, even over himself. He said, “I wanted you to win more than anything. I even wore my lucky suspenders to help make it happen.” He already had two Oscars. Warren Beatty had one for Reds. Robert Redford had one for Ordinary People. It was official. I was one of them. We hung out with Jack until around 7:00 a.m., after the sun had risen, and the next morning, after a nap, that Oscar was still tucked under my arm when I went to my dad’s house to show him how far I had carried his legacy.

The one-two punch of Fatal Attraction and Wall Street during the same year transformed me from leading man to superstar. I was a forty-three-year-old late bloomer, and now one of maybe five or six actors who could get a movie greenlit just by agreeing to be in it.

After two decades of grinding nonstop, I finally decided to take some time off. I’d lounge around, watch my buddy Pat Riley and the Lakers, and go on vacations with Diandra and Cameron . . .

At least that was the plan.

One Helluva Ride, By Michael Douglas With Shane Salerno and Michael Fleming Jr.

title: Bebe Neuwirth, Whitney Leavitt, Reece Weaver & More Among Line-Up For One-Night-Only ‘Chicago’ Anniversary Performance On Broadway
summary: Broadway’s recording-breaking revival of Chicago will welcome back some old friends to celebrate the show’s 30th anniversary on Broadway this November, with former cast members including Bebe Neuwirth, James Naughton, Robyn Hurder, Whitney Leavitt, Ariana Madix and Alex Newell joining the current “Roxie Hart,” Reece Weaver, in the one-night-only celebration. The 30th anniversary gala performance […]
content:
Broadway‘s recording-breaking revival of Chicago will welcome back some old friends to celebrate the show’s 30th anniversary on Broadway this November, with former cast members including Bebe Neuwirth, James Naughton, Robyn Hurder, Whitney Leavitt, Ariana Madix and Alex Newell joining the current “Roxie Hart,” Reece Weaver, in the one-night-only celebration.

The 30th anniversary gala performance is set for November 16, 7 p.m./ET, at Broadway’s Ambassador Theatre.

The event will benefit the Entertainment Community Fund’s programs serving dancers. Additional celebrity guests will be announced at a later date.

Chicago, now in its 30th year, is the longest-running show on Broadway and the longest-running American musical in history. Both Neuwirth and Naughton were original cast members of the celebrated revival.

Watch on Deadline

Leavitt, best known for her participation in Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, and Weaver, of Netflix’s America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, are two of the most recent cast members and have prompted a resurgence in ticket sales this year.

Tickets for the gala go on sale on Thursday, October 15.

title: Joe Rogan Sets Multi-Year Extension With Spotify
summary: Spotify and top podcaster Joe Rogan have agreed to a multi-year contract extension. The parties declined to specify terms, including financials. The Wall Street Journal reported that Rogan could end up with an “estimated earnout” of $250 million. The new extension continues to broaden distribution of the show, which was exclusive to Spotify between 2020 […]
content:
Spotify and top podcaster Joe Rogan have agreed to a multi-year contract extension.

The parties declined to specify terms, including financials. The Wall Street Journal reported that Rogan could end up with an “estimated earnout” of $250 million.

The new extension continues to broaden distribution of the show, which was exclusive to Spotify between 2020 and 2024.

The Joe Rogan Experience launched in 2009. Its 2,500-plus episodes have featured two- to three-hour interviews with a range of actors, comedians, athletes, politicians, authors and more.

The show was the top podcast on Spotify, YouTube, and Apple Podcasts in 2025. Since starting on Spotify in 2020, the show has gained 18 million followers, making it the streamer’s most followed podcast.

Watch on Deadline

As the show’s audience has grown, so has Rogan’s clout in the political arena. His interview with Donald Trump before the 2024 election was credited with delivering a boost down the stretch, while the decision by opponent Kamala Harris not to travel to Rogan’s Austin, TX studio became a key part of autopsies of her failed campaign. Recently, Rogan has become more vocal about his skepticism about Trump, but many of his views align with those of the MAGA base.

In 2022, musician Neil Young pulled his music from Spotify over what he said was misinformation Rogan was spreading about vaccination. Spotify stood by Rogan. Young returned the music to the platform two years later.

In a statement, Rogan called the Spotify relationship “an amazing fit,” adding that he was “extremely happy and excited to continue with them for years to come.”

Jordan Newman, head of content partnerships at Spotify said Rogan “has built something incredibly enduring, and his show continues to resonate with a massive global audience because there’s simply nothing else like it.”

title: David Decker Lands Top Content Sales Role At Skydance With Jay Askinasi Overseeing Ads, Ray Hopkins Leading Distribution
summary: Skydance has named its top executives across content licensing, advertising and distribution. David Decker will become President, Content Sales, Jay Askinasi has been named Chief Revenue Officer, Advertising and Ray Hopkins has been appointed President, Distribution. The trio will report to JB Perrette, Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Skydance DTC. Decker’s appointment […]
content:
Skydance has named its top executives across content licensing, advertising and distribution.

David Decker will become President, Content Sales, Jay Askinasi has been named Chief Revenue Officer, Advertising and Ray Hopkins has been appointed President, Distribution.

The trio will report to JB Perrette, Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Skydance DTC.

Decker’s appointment is significant as the company heads into Mipcom. He was previously named President, Content Sales for Warner Bros. Discovery in 2023 and will oversee sales of the Paramount and WBD television library to international broadcasters, streamers and third-party platforms in the U.S.

It’s not clear what this move means for Kevin MacLellan, who was President, Global Content Distribution & International at Paramount or Don McGregor, who was the company’s global licensing chief.

Watch on Deadline

Askinasi was previously Chief Revenue Officer at Paramount, having joined last year from Roku. Hopkins was previously President of U.S. Networks Distribution at Paramount since 2019, having joined CBS in 2013.

“Bringing together the incomparable portfolios of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery creates an extraordinary combination of iconic brands, world-class storytelling, deep creative relationships and talented teams around the globe which offers tremendous opportunities for our commercial partners,” said Perrette. “By combining our strengths and uniting our teams, we will build on the incredible legacies of both companies to serve audiences and partners in new and more innovative ways and shape an even more ambitious future. Jay, David and Ray are hugely talented and respected leaders with deep experience, strong industry relationships and a shared commitment to our partners and our people. There is tremendous opportunity ahead of us, and I look forward to working closely with them as we build the next generation media and entertainment organization.”

title: ‘Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man’ Season 2 Sets Release Date
summary: The animated series “Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man” has set its Season 2 release date on Disney+. The second season will debut Jan. 13, 2027. Season 1 premiered in early 2025 and introduced a young, animated version of Spidey, voiced by Hudson Thames, who’s joined by some new and familiar faces in an alternate universe. The […]
content:
The animated series “Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man” has set its Season 2 release date on Disney+.

The second season will debut Jan. 13, 2027.

Season 1 premiered in early 2025 and introduced a young, animated version of Spidey, voiced by Hudson Thames, who’s joined by some new and familiar faces in an alternate universe. The show takes place in a separate world from Tom Holland’s MCU character and follows the early days of Peter Parker’s web-slinging career. Instead of Tony Stark showing Peter the superhero ropes, “Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man” puts Norman Osborn, better known in the comics as the Green Goblin and who’s voiced by Colman Domingo, in a mentor role to Spidey. And instead of Mary Jane or Ned Leeds from the MCU, Peter is joined by his friends Nico Minoru, who has mystical sorcerer abilities, and Harry Osborne, the rich son of Norman.

At the end of Season 1, Spider-Man and Doctor Strange team up to fight a mysterious symbiote alien, who leaves behind a small trace of symbiotic goo that Osborn collects and investigates. It’s revealed that one of Doctor Strange’s time-traveling portals accidentally sent the spider that bit Peter back in time, and that’s how he got his superpowers in the first place. It’s also revealed that Richard Parker, Peter’s father who was presumed dead, is in fact alive and imprisoned when Aunt May goes to visit him.

Popular on Variety

The cast includes Grace Song as Nico Minoru, Kari Wahlgren as Aunt May, Eugene Byrd as Lonnie Lincoln/Tombstone, Zeno Robinson as Harry Osborn, Hugh Dancy as Otto Octavius/Doctor Octopus, Charlie Cox as Daredevil.

title: Marvel’s ‘Zodiac’ Sets 2028 Release on Disney+ as New Details Revealed
summary: Marvel Television revealed the first logo for its new series “Zodiac,” a live-action spy thriller set for release in 2028. The series will begin shooting in London in the spring, Marvel Television chief Brad Winderbaum said during its New York Comic-Con panel, with casting beginning in the “next couple of weeks.” This marks the first new […]
content:
Marvel Television revealed the first logo for its new series “Zodiac,” a live-action spy thriller set for release in 2028.

The series will begin shooting in London in the spring, Marvel Television chief Brad Winderbaum said during its New York Comic-Con panel, with casting beginning in the “next couple of weeks.”

This marks the first new live-action show that’s been announced for Marvel since last year’s “Ironheart.” While the MCU had a massive hit on the big-screen with “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” breaking records at the box office, the TV universe had some popular shows come to an end.

Just a few months after it premiered in January, “Wonder Man” was canceled — despite being renewed for a second season and landing an Emmy nomination for lead actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. The show was critically acclaimed, and it made Abdul-Mateen II the first live-action actor to receive an Emmy nod for both a Marvel and DC series after he starred in HBO’s “Watchmen.”

Popular on Variety

Then, it was revealed that “Daredevil: Born Again” would be ending with next year’s Season 3. The series revived Charlie Cox’s popular street-level hero after he debuted in Netflix’s “Daredevil” show. Season 3 looks to be a long-awaited reunion for the Netflix “Defenders” heroes, including Krysten Ritter as Jessica Jones, Mike Colter as Luke Cage and Finn Jones as Iron First.

“VisionQuest” is set to premiere on Oct. 14 and will cap off the trilogy of shows that began with “WandaVision” and then “Agatha All Along.” After starring in “WandaVision,” Paul Bettany is back as the robot Vision, who’s been hiding out and communicating with other AI androids brought to life, like Ultron, J.A.R.V.I.S., F.R.I.D.A.Y. and more.

title: ‘Carrie’ Finale Burning Question: Who Is Adelaide? Kate Siegel on Why Her Mysterious Character ‘Controls This Story’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains major spoilers from the 2026 series “Carrie,” now streaming on Prime Video. Kate Siegel knows how to speak Stephen King. She was reading his work long before she probably should have, and has often retreated to it in times of need. “He was my dad’s favorite author, and when he […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains major spoilers from the 2026 series “Carrie,” now streaming on Prime Video. Kate Siegel knows how to speak Stephen King. She was reading his work long before she probably should have, and has often retreated to it in times of need. “He was my dad’s favorite author, and when he passed away, I must have read ‘The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon’ 50 times just to get through the grief,” Siegel tells Variety. Her familiarity with King’s vast writings also meant she knew exactly which of his characters to draw upon when asked to play something completely new within his sandbox. Prime Video’s new version of “Carrie” isn’t the first adaptation of King’s classic tale of a childhood gone wrong, nor is it Siegel’s first time working with series creator Mike Flanagan. She’s married to the fellow King whisperer, and previously starred in Flanagan’s film adaptations of “Gerald’s Game” and “The Life of Chuck” –– not to mention all of his original Netflix series. Summer H. Howell Courtesy of Prime Video

But when it comes to “Carrie,” she isn’t playing a single King creation, per se. Anyone familiar with the “Carrie” story knows exactly where the new series ends up after eight episodes. A reluctantly reclusive and telepathically gifted Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) tries to assimilate into high school, only to be ridiculed and manipulated by the savagery of her peers. When she thinks she has finally won them over by being crowned prom queen, she’s doused in pig’s blood and unleashes fiery hell on her town. Nearly all the show’s storylines and characters are pulled directly from King’s text.

But among the exceptions is Siegel’s character, who is only heard as the narrator throughout the first seven episodes before making her onscreen debut in the finale.

Popular on Variety

The character’s name is Adelaide, seemingly the headmistress of a home for gifted young women and the person behind the camera of the talking head interviews that have teased the terror to come all season. She’s interviewing the survivors of the prom night massacre, in search of the elusive culprit behind the carnage, Carrie, and her astral projecting enabler, Emaline (Thalia Dudek).

“It was an honor to step into this idea of a character that I’ve seen hints of in different stories [from King],” Siegel says. “There’s a woman like this in ‘The Institute.’ There are women like this in ‘Carrie,’ the original novel. There are some women like this in ‘Firestarter.’ But we don’t know which way Adelaide’s going to go. We don’t know whose side Adelaide is on. We don’t know a lot about her, but I’m familiar enough with the type of women that Stephen King likes to write that I could sort of hum the melody of who she is.”

Courtesy of Prime Video

Siegel and Flanagan spent plenty of time discussing the character, but he initially held back anything that might reveal who he wants her to become should the series continue.

“One of his favorite answers when I would ask about her past or her future or who she is, would just be, ‘Yeah, it’s crazy, right? Great question,’” she says. “And then he’d just move on!”

Siegel has since been clued in on Adelaide’s potential, and she’s gotten quite skilled at the art of the dodge as the series leaves viewers with few answers. “The questions people should be asking are, why is Adelaide filming these interviews and who is she telling this story to?” Siegel says, teasingly. “Of course she is interested in Carrie and wants to know everything about her, but to what end? We don’t want to give away too much, even though right now it’s only Season 1 — and we don’t know if anything else will happen.”

The other major clue viewers get about Adelaide is that she is also gifted, and she’s not afraid to wield those gifts as she sees fit. In the final moments of the season, she interviews Margaret White (Samantha Sloyan), Carrie’s religious mother who, in this version, survives her daughter’s prom night wrath thanks to her own repressed telekinetic abilities. But when Margaret refuses to even consider exploring these newly rekindled gifts further, Adelaide deems her unworthy of this unexpected second chance. Using telepathy, she instructs Maragret’s mind to slowly stop her own heartbeat, ultimately killing her. It’s a calculated act that lets Adelaide flex her own powers.

Samantha Sloyan Courtesy of Robert Falconer/Prime Video

Siegel says that scene is key, not just because of what Adelaide does, but how she does it –– or rather, says it. Siegel narrates the cold opens of each episode, but she was very mindful of Adelaide’s onscreen voice, which is measured and changes its cadence when she goes from interviewing Maragret to killing her. She found inspiration for that voice in an unexpected place.

“You know the show ‘Couples Therapy’ on Showtime?” Siegel says. “The therapist who runs that program, Dr. Orna [Guralnik], has a very neutral kind of questioning tone until she gets to something that she’d like to dig a little deeper on. She’s also always touching her face while she’s listening. I just love the way she does it. That was the beginning of putting on Adelaide, as if it was just gently suggesting that we go a little deeper.”

One such instance is when Adelaide casually drops the word that will send King fans into a frenzy. Speaking to Margaret, she says, “A lot of people have a little bit of shine and don’t even know it.” That, of course, is a reference to the psychic abilities featured in “The Shining” and other King books. But the word “shine” isn’t in the original “Carrie” novel.

“I was so happy that we were allowed to have that word, because Adelaide sits there on a throne of chaotic neutral,” Siegel says. “She doesn’t care if you’re good or bad. She’s really looking for this one thing, and she believes every woman could have it. She’s waiting, and she’s thinking, and she’s seeing. And then she says that word. I think Adelaide’s voice has a lot of power, so she’s very careful with it.”

While the series has not yet been renewed for Season 2, if this is all “Carrie” gets, it has been a family affair for the entire Siegel/Flanagan household. In addition to Siegel’s debut in the finale, the episode also features their daughter Theo as a young Margaret, during a flashback to the first time she conjures her gifts. Episode 3 also marks the first time Siegel has directed an episode of television (she previously made her directorial debut on a segment of “V/H/S/Beyond”).

Her episode, titled “Social Studies,” is among the season’s most important, as it depicts Carrie’s first high school party, a rite of passage that has ripple effects all the way to the finale. But due to the production schedule, it actually shot after her onscreen debut as Adelaide. Episodes 1, 2, 7 and 8, all directed by Flanagan, were shot as a super block at the top of production. Then, Siegel was up next to direct Episode 3.

To prepare, she plastered her workspace with photos of her and her friends at high school parties in the early 2000s for inspiration. It also gave her an excuse to revisit the classic ‘90s parties depicted in movies “Can’t Hardly Wait” and “10 Things I Hate About You.”

Summer H. Howell, Joel Oulette Courtesy of Prime Video

“It’s a very specific type of joy, because there’s anticipation, right?” Siegel says. “And nine times out of 10, a house party doesn’t quite deliver. But when a house party does deliver after the whole day of anticipation, and you’re a teenager and you’ve never really experienced this joy, it is so magical. That is what I wanted for Carrie.”

Not only does Carrie dance with her classmates, but also has an intoxicated (and intoxicatingly) platonic bonding moment with Tommy (Joel Oulette), the dreamy boy who genuinely befriends her as they lay on the front lawn of the party and talk about the stars. When Tommy dies as collateral damage of Carrie’s violence in the finale, his final words will be about those same stars. Having seen the finale before she got behind the camera, Siegel was able to consciously stitch these moments together.

After leaving the party, Tommy drives Carrie home and the bliss of experiencing a good night out after a life of captivity literally causes her to levitate his car off the road.

“One of Amazon’s favorite moments in the script was that car lift, and same for me,” Siegel says. “There’s a beautiful dichotomy in Episode 3, where with Carrie’s confusion and frustration and concern, she can lift a raindrop. But with her joy, she can float a car. It has a built-in melancholy, because we all know how this story ends. We know it ends in the death of Tommy. We know it ends in carnage, and it makes it even worse to see them that happy and that joyful.”

One of Siegel’s proudest directorial decisions was this scene’s other half. At the same party, Chris (Alison Thornton), the chief designer of Carrie’s torment, has the worst party of her life. As Carrie hangs her head out Tommy’s window to take in every last euphoric second of the night, a blacked-out Chris stares blankly into the future.

“That back-and-forth shot between them was not in the original script,” she says. “That was something I pitched to Mike. The weight of Chris’ grief and sadness about her parents’ divorce and being replaced, and all these concerns about who she is and who she will be, cut with the lightness of Carrie feeling like she found her people. We really need that as we move forward in the story, and see these two butt heads.”

Because she played Adelaide first and then went behind the camera, Siegel held a great deal of power in guiding the viewer from the best night of Carrie’s life to the worst. In a way, she shares that bit of control with her character, whoever she is.

“Adelaide is the narrator of this story,” she says. “And the reason I like that is because it means one thing for the first seven episodes. But once you realize what she’s doing in the eighth, you see she’s been molding and framing this story. Adelaide controls this story — and never let it be said that Kate Siegel doesn’t love control.”

title: Rodrigo Santoro and Camila Pitanga to Star in Marcelo Gomes’ ‘Garota da Urca’ From a Script by Luciana Paes and Leonardo Moreira (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Two of Brazil’s biggest screen stars, Rodrigo Santoro (“The Blue Trail”) and Camila Pitanga (“Basic Sanitation, the Movie”), are set to star in “Garota da Urca” (“Girl From Urca”), the new film by renowned director Marcelo Gomes. “Oxygen Masks Will Not Drop Automatically” writer Leonardo Moreira and veteran writer-actor Luciana […]
content:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Two of Brazil’s biggest screen stars, Rodrigo Santoro (“The Blue Trail”) and Camila Pitanga (“Basic Sanitation, the Movie”), are set to star in “Garota da Urca” (“Girl From Urca”), the new film by renowned director Marcelo Gomes. “Oxygen Masks Will Not Drop Automatically” writer Leonardo Moreira and veteran writer-actor Luciana Paes are now confirmed to write the script. “Garota da Urca” is a co-production between Matizar Filmes and Misti Filmes.

Gomes and Santoro sat down with Variety after a lengthy conversation at the Rio Film Festival, where they expressed their mutual admiration and discussed their decades in film. Santoro, who recently starred in Gabriel Mascaro’s Berlin-winning “The Blue Trail,” is one of Brazil’s most successful screen exports, having starred in major Hollywood productions such as Richard Curtis’s “Love Actually” and Zack Snyder’s “300.” Gomes broke out into the international scene with “Cinema, Aspirins and Vultures,” which screened at Cannes’s Un Certain Regard in 2005, and has since directed major films such as “I Travel Because I Have to, I Come Back Because I Love You,” “Joaquim,” and “Paloma.”

Popular on Variety

As for Pitanga, the actress is one of Brazil’s most popular telenovela stars, as well as having starred in films such as “I’d Receive the Worst News from Your Beautiful Lips” and “Basic Sanitation, The Movie,” which saw her share the screen with Oscar nominees Fernanda Torres (“I’m Still Here”) and Wagner Moura (“The Secret Agent”).

Gomes prefers to keep the finer details of “Garota da Urca” under wraps, but says it is about a married couple approaching their 50s and dealing with the existential questions that come with middle age. Gomes proves ahead of the curve in his desire to tell an adult comedy about sex and love, working on his latest at a time when films like Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite” are proving greatly successful with audiences. “We’ve been working on this project for over three years, so this has been a very happy coincidence,” he says of the momentum.

‘Oxygen Masks Will (Not) Drop Automatically’ Courtesy of HBO/Max

“Cinema, as Tarkovsky once said, is space and time,” he adds. “This is precisely what I want to broach with the film: the space of Rio de Janeiro beyond Ipanema, and time, with people in constant dialogue about the effects of the passage of time, of how time affects the maturing of feelings.”

The director adds that “Garota da Urca” is about “understanding how we can preserve those emotions from a first date as time goes on.” “It’s not about whether or not love resists the passage of time; it’s about facing how we change over time,” he goes on. “This is the idea of the film, and we wanted to invite actors who were at the same point in life as the characters and able to lend some of this existential crisis to the people they’ll play on screen. That’s how we got to Camila and Rodrigo, and I am thrilled to be undergoing this journey with such talented actors.”

Santoro echoes this feeling of admiration, saying he has been a fan of the director for over 20 years and an admirer of how Gomes is a “filmmaker who loves his characters.”

“I feel very grateful for the opportunity to make this film with him because I can already imagine the process of making the film, which, to me, is the most precious thing,” he adds.

“I don’t pay much mind to the taboos around turning 50, but I acknowledge they exist,” continues the actor. “There is this social construct and mythology around 50, but there is also something that happens within us: you have lived a long life and acquired great experience while, at the same time, there is still so much ahead and you still feel such energy for living. I think it’s a very interesting moment of life, but I want to make known I am not facing a crisis in my marriage [laughs]. I have a wonderful marriage, two beautiful, healthy daughters, and all is well.”

“Still, I am a man, an actor, who is in my early 50s and questioning things related to being a 50-year-old man in the world of today,” he notes. “I always say the work of an actor is very therapeutic, because I end up examining my own questions through my characters. This character will deal with the obscure, and it’s an opportunity I find very precious. I feel very intrigued.”

Seeing Santoro and Pitanga share the screen is also a highly enticing prospect to Brazilian audiences, who last saw the duo together in the immensely popular 2004 telenovela “Mulheres Apaixonadas.”

“This thing with Camila is curious because we had a moment during the novela despite not being a couple,” says Santoro. “That moment did so well with audiences; the characters were so well-received, and now, with the digital phenomenon of our era, social media has resurrected that novela and one of our scenes together. I thought it was curious, but also great timing, when Marcelo told me he had both of us in mind. I’m very much looking forward to working together.”

title: ‘Furiosa’ Duo Alyla Browne & Elsa Pataky Lead Cast In ‘Chiquita’; Screen Australia, Umbrella & Essential Film Group Among Partners
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga duo Alyla Browne and Elsa Pataky are among the ensemble cast for Australian feature Chiquita, which has started production in Byron Bay, Australia. Set against the world of endurance horse riding, the movie is described as “an uplifting family adventure about two outsiders; a rebellious teenage girl and a […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga duo Alyla Browne and Elsa Pataky are among the ensemble cast for Australian feature Chiquita, which has started production in Byron Bay, Australia.

Set against the world of endurance horse riding, the movie is described as “an uplifting family adventure about two outsiders; a rebellious teenage girl and a mistreated rescue horse who form an unlikely bond at a pivotal moment in their lives.”

Australian distributor Umbrella will release the film in the 2027 summer school holiday corridor.

Written and directed by Kiah Roache-Turner, based on a story by Mark Morrissey, the feature is produced by Blake Northfield and Michelle Krumm for Bronte Studios and Mark Morrissey for First Option Pictures.

Watch on Deadline

Also starring are Michael Caton (The Castle), Stephen Peacocke (The Newsreader), Martin Sacks (Blue Heelers) and rising Australian actor Aswan Reid (The New Boy).

Production investment comes from Screen Australia, in association with Screen NSW. International sales are being handled by Essential Film Group. Additional financing comes from Obsidian Creek Capital.

Director of photography is Jonathan Baker and first assistant director is Jamie Crooks, while production designer is Tylah Pratt, and costume designer Tracey Rose. Hair and makeup designer is Nele Pandis, and editor Gabriella Muir. Sandra Tahmasby Baxter serves as Head of Production for Bronte Studios.

“What I love about Chiquita is that underneath this big, cinematic adventure is a really simple relationship between a girl and a horse,” said Roache-Turner. “They’re both outsiders, they’re both pretty wild, and neither of them has much interest in doing what they’re told. Somehow they find each other. That gives us the heart of the movie, and then we get to surround it with galloping horses, endurance racing and these huge Australian landscapes. It’s a proper big screen family film with real scale.”

“From the beginning, we saw Chiquita as an Australian story with the ability to travel,” added Northfield and Krumm. “It has all the ingredients of a great family adventure with an extraordinary young protagonist, humour, heart, horses and a spectacular landscape but underneath that is a deeply relatable story about grief, family and finding where you belong. With this cast, Kiah’s vision and Essential Film Group taking the film to the international market, we’re incredibly excited about the audience this film can reach.”

title: Skydance’s JB Perrette Makes First Moves After Re-Upping Contract
summary: JB Perrette has moved quickly to put together the executives that will report to him at Skydance. Perrette, who is Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance Direct-To-Consumer, oversees global distribution, advertising sales, content sales, DTC strategy, marketing and business operations across Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s new […]
content:
JB Perrette has moved quickly to put together the executives that will report to him at Skydance.

Perrette, who is Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance Direct-To-Consumer, oversees global distribution, advertising sales, content sales, DTC strategy, marketing and business operations across Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s new owner.

Deadline understands that Perrette has signed a new contract, like a number of David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz’s top team. It’s not clear how long Perrette has signed up for, but his colleagues Casey Bloys, who he worked closely with at WBD, signed a five-year deal earlier this month.

He has gotten straight to work; earlier today, he named three executives to oversee content sales, advertising and distribution for him.

Watch on Deadline

David Decker has been named President, Content Sales, coming ahead of the Mipcom international TV market, Jay Askinasi is Chief Revenue Officer, Advertising and Ray Hopkins is President, Distribution.

Decker’s appointment has also led to the first executive from this group to depart following the merger; Kevin MacLellan, who was President of International and Global Content Distribution at Paramount, is exiting, as a result.

Insiders told Deadline that it was important for the divisions that bring in revenue to Skydance to get their houses in order sooner rather than later, compared to the content divisions that are still working out personnel decisions.

Perrette is an interesting case; he was previously CEO and President of Global Streaming and Games for Warner Bros. Discovery and one of David Zaslav’s key lieutenants. But over the last few years, he has built up a key partnership with Bloys as the pair oversaw the growth of the HBO Max streaming service, Bloys on the content side, and Perrette on the business side. He will also now work closely with George Cheeks, who is Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance TV.

title: Colin Jost & Danny Chun To Launch New Comedy Series ‘6 Bed 1 Bath’
summary: Colin Jost and Danny Chun are launching a new comedy series they created in a unique way. 6 Bed 1 Bath was made through a brand-supported model designed to give creators greater creative freedom and bring their work directly to audiences for free. The series was independently financed by Revue, which provided the upfront capital […]
content:
Colin Jost and Danny Chun are launching a new comedy series they created in a unique way.

6 Bed 1 Bath was made through a brand-supported model designed to give creators greater creative freedom and bring their work directly to audiences for free. The series was independently financed by Revue, which provided the upfront capital and production infrastructure, which enabled Jost and Chun to bring their comedy to the screen.

The show will be streamed via free and ad-supported AVOD platforms.

6 Bed 1 Bath follows a group of five roommates in their twenties who share an apartment with a man who’s lived there since 1982 and kept building new bedrooms every time his rent increased. The series recently wrapped production in New York City and will premiere across free, ad-supported video-on-demand platforms.

“Danny and I just wanted to make a show we thought was funny and somehow those are the hardest shows to get made,” Jost shared. “So we found a new, innovative way to do it outside of the normal studio system and we feel very lucky about how the cast and the crew came together. We’re excited for everyone to see it.”

Watch on Deadline

The series reunites Jost and Chun, who first wrote together at the Harvard Lampoon.

Executive producers include Colin Jost, Scarlett Johansson, Danny Chun, Andrew Singer, Jeff Grosvenor, Jonathan Lia, Ryan Case, Molly McMillen and Jon Liebman.

title: Anne Hathaway Calls Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ “Brilliant”: “It’s Worth Making The Time See & Decide For Yourself”
summary: Anne Hathaway is a fan of Tom Cruise’s Digger and just made that clear. The Verity star took to Letterboxd to praise the satirical comedy written and directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu. “I loved this brilliant movie. It’s smart and trippy and aggressive and funny and ambitious,” Hathaway wrote on the social media platform. “It’s […]
content:
Anne Hathaway is a fan of Tom Cruise‘s Digger and just made that clear.

The Verity star took to Letterboxd to praise the satirical comedy written and directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu.

“I loved this brilliant movie. It’s smart and trippy and aggressive and funny and ambitious,” Hathaway wrote on the social media platform. “It’s worth making the time see and decide for yourself what you make of it. For me? 10/10 🪏.”

Hathaway gave Digger five stars in her first Letterboxd review. Other films she has listed as her favorite include Moonstruck, It Happened One Night, Mirror and Phantom Thread.

Watch on Deadline

Digger opened in theaters to an $8 million domestic debut, a $20M global start, and a C+ CinemaScore. Deadline reported that the film could lose around $150M.

Cruise, who also produced the film, stars as Digger Rockwell, an aging oil magnate whose drilling sets off an ecological disaster. The film’s cast also includes Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons, Teddy Hawley, Robert John Burke, Emma D’Arcy, Burn Gorman, Sophie Wilde, among others.

RELATED: ‘Digger’ World Premiere Red Carpet Photos: Tom Cruise, Sandra Hüller, Riz Ahmed, Emma D’Arcy & More At London Premiere

After the opening, Cruise said he was “proud” of the film despite the lackluster box office results.

“I am so honored to have had the opportunity to create this film alongside such talented artists,” Cruise posted on Instagram. “Thank you to the entire cast and crew for your dedication, hard work, and joy. The experience was truly unforgettable and I’m so proud of what we created.”

RELATED: Guillermo Del Toro Buries ‘Digger’ In Praise, Slams “Petty” Review: “Decidedly A Theatrical Experience”

title: ‘Lanterns’ Season Finale Sets Series’ New Audience Record With Over 10 Million Global Viewers
summary: HBO’s Lanterns season finale attracted 10.5 million global viewers in its first three days, marking a new series-best. The episode, which debuted on October 4, was up 13% globally compared to the series premiere in L3. It tallied 7.2 million viewers in the U.S. alone, per the latest data from Skydance-owned HBO. Overall, the season […]
content:
HBO’s Lanterns season finale attracted 10.5 million global viewers in its first three days, marking a new series-best.

The episode, which debuted on October 4, was up 13% globally compared to the series premiere in L3. It tallied 7.2 million viewers in the U.S. alone, per the latest data from Skydance-owned HBO.

Overall, the season is averaging 19.3 million global viewers and growing, maintaining its place among the top five HBO series launches in platform history. HBO says that viewership for the series premiere is now approaching 30 million.

This bodes well for a Season 2 renewal, which Deadline understands is pending.

Watch on Deadline

Lanterns, from DC Studios and Warner Bros. Television, launched in August with 9.3 million global cross-platform viewers and 6.6 million in the U.S. in its first three days of availability on HBO and HBO Max. The company confirmed at the time that it outperformed the premieres of several tentpole series including IT: Welcome to Derry, The Penguin and True Detective: Night Country. Those went on to average 27.1M, 19.8M, and 17.5M global viewers, respectively, which already made a good case for the trajectory of Lanterns.

Lanterns is from co-creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King. The series follows new recruit John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) and Lantern legend Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler), two intergalactic cops drawn into a dark, earth-based mystery with cosmic ties as they investigate a murder in the American heartland.

title: Michael Ovitz Ordered to Complete Deposition in Julia Ormond Case After Storming Out Over Jeffrey Epstein Questions
summary: A judge on Thursday ordered CAA co-founder Michael Ovitz to complete his deposition in the Julia Ormond sexual assault lawsuit, months after storming out when he was asked about Jeffrey Epstein. Ormond is suing CAA for arranging a meeting for her with Harvey Weinstein in December 1995, after which Weinstein allegedly sexually assaulted her. Ovitz […]
content:
A judge on Thursday ordered CAA co-founder Michael Ovitz to complete his deposition in the Julia Ormond sexual assault lawsuit, months after storming out when he was asked about Jeffrey Epstein.

Ormond is suing CAA for arranging a meeting for her with Harvey Weinstein in December 1995, after which Weinstein allegedly sexually assaulted her. Ovitz had already left the agency at that point, but Ormond’s lawyers have sought to question him about the agency’s relationship with Weinstein and about how it handled sexual misconduct issues.

At a deposition on June 1, Ovitz grew irate when Ormond’s lawyers asked him if he was friendly with Epstein, the notorious sex criminal.

Popular on Variety

“What does this got to do with Harvey Weinstein?” Ovitz asked, before taking off his microphone and storming out.

Ormond’s lawyers asked the judge in the case to issue an arrest warrant and to hold Ovitz in contempt. Ovitz, meanwhile, asked to be excused from further questioning on the grounds that Ormond’s lawyers were trying to harass him with irrelevant questions.

In his ruling on Thursday, Judge Adam Silvera ordered Ovitz to complete his deposition by Dec. 18. He denied the requests for an arrest warrant and a contempt finding, but also refused to rule out further questions about Epstein.

“The Court finds that the deposition of non-party Ovitz was not completed but, rather was inappropriately terminated by non-party Ovitz,” the judge ruled.

Ormond’s lawyers issued a statement on Thursday applauding the ruling.

“We are pleased that the Court has held that Michael Ovitz ‘inappropriately terminated’ the deposition, required him to return and answer all of our questions, and ‘warned’ him to follow the Court’s rules,” said the attorneys, Kevin Mintzer, Meredith Firetog, and Effie Blassberger. “The decision makes clear that Mr. Ovitz was not entitled to storm out of the deposition, and that he is not above the law. We look forward to resuming the deposition and trust that Mr. Ovitz will behave himself.”

Emails between Ovitz and Epstein were disclosed earlier this year as part of the Epstein files. In one email, Ovitz states that he was looking forward to seeing Epstein at St. Barts, and in another he writes, “I would love to see you.”

CAA’s lawyers argued that Ovitz had been ambushed with material designed to smear his character rather than reveal anything relevant to the case.

title: Hugh Hefner’s Widow Crystal Harris Asks Jessica Biel to ‘Please Reconsider’ Playing His Wife: ‘I Experienced Sexual, Emotional…Physical Abuse’
summary: Crystal Harris, who was married to Playboy founder Hugh Hefner until his death in 2017, is asking Jessica Biel to reconsider playing a fictional version of Hefner’s wife in the upcoming film “Playmates.” After Biel’s casting was announced, Harris posted her message to Biel on Instagram, saying “Please reconsider playing Hugh Hefner’s wife if this […]
content:
Crystal Harris, who was married to Playboy founder Hugh Hefner until his death in 2017, is asking Jessica Biel to reconsider playing a fictional version of Hefner’s wife in the upcoming film “Playmates.”

After Biel’s casting was announced, Harris posted her message to Biel on Instagram, saying “Please reconsider playing Hugh Hefner’s wife if this film intends to romanticize him or the Playboy world. I was actually his wife, and I experienced sexual, emotional, financial and physical abuse in that relationship.”

Lorraine Nicholson, the daughter of Jack Nicholson, is writing and directing the Searchlight film that also stars Bill Pullman as Hefner as well as Lily-Rose Depp and “The HousemaidIndiana Elle.

Popular on Variety

“Many other woman have come forward with allegations of rape, coercion, drugging and exploitation as well,” Harris wrote, “There are also deeply troubling concerns involving minors. I hope everyone involved this film takes the time to listen the women who lived it before helping Hollywood turn it back into nostalgia.”

After Hefner’s death, Harris revealed her experiences at the “toxic” Playboy mansion in her 2024 memoir “Only Say Good Things: Surviving Playboy and Finding Myself.”

According to the synopsis, the “Playmates” movie revolves around “Elle (Elle), a 13-year-old know-it-all who considers the Playboy Mansion her second home, and meets Anna (Depp), one of seven hopefuls vying to be Playmate of the Month. The two form an unlikely friendship and try to help each other get what the other wants most, a magazine cover and a boy.” Nicholson has written for magazines about her childhood experiences at the Playboy Mansion.

title: ‘Angel and the Badman’ Review: Zachary Levi Leads Angel Studios’ Fitfully Engaging Remake of a John Wayne Vehicle
summary: Inevitably the Angel media company and streaming platform, rebranded from Angel Studios in 2025, has remade the 1947 John Wayne project “Angel and the Badman,” and not just for the angelic title. It’s actually the third iteration; a 2009 Hallmark Channel adaptation, shot in wintry British Columbia instead of the dusty, sandy American West, starred […]
content:
Inevitably the Angel media company and streaming platform, rebranded from Angel Studios in 2025, has remade the 1947 John Wayne project “Angel and the Badman,” and not just for the angelic title. It’s actually the third iteration; a 2009 Hallmark Channel adaptation, shot in wintry British Columbia instead of the dusty, sandy American West, starred Lou Diamond Phillips and Deborah Kara Unger. The latest, directed by Julio Quintana, stars Zachary Levi and is fitfully diverting, draped with calming New Mexico scenery.

The first version, Wayne’s self-financed debut as producer as well as star, came from Republic Pictures and veteran screenwriter James Edward Grant, who went on to write another 11 Wayne films. The gamble was in Wayne’s decision to hire Grant as a first-time director. Intriguingly balanced sagebrush-and-six-gun romcom one minute, leisurely drama of redemption the next, “Angel and the Badman” presented Wayne as Quirt Evans, a gunman and cattle rustler saved from his violent past and and varmint future by a chance encounter with a Quaker frontier family. The Worth clan, especially the demure yet hungry-eyed adult daughter Penny, played by Gail Russell, nurses Quirt back to health after his opening-credits shootout with the Laredo gang — of which Quirt’s a member, looking to get out.

Popular on Variety

Of the three, the first movie remains the most compelling. It wasn’t the first Quaker oater — “The Lady from Cheyenne” preceded it, and “High Noon” and “Cheyenne Autumn” followed, along with the not-actual-Western “Friendly Persuasion” — but it’s most character-specific and flavorful of the versions. The new film, with its blend of Christian virtues and righteous bloodshed, may well connect with audiences hip to distributor Angel’s business model guided by “values-based” stories (per the website language) that “amplify light and bring more goodness into the world,” and “reintroduce positive values to the entertainment industry.”

What works here? Tommy Lee Jones certainly does, in the old Harry Carey role of the wily, philosophical U.S. Marshall who has his eye on Quirt and the Laredo gang. He’s 80 years old, and thankfully Jones hasn’t done anything to look otherwise. But his voice is higher now, and his delivery of even the cardboard-iest of lines offers witty little payoffs. The downside of Jones being the upside of his own movie is simple: There are times when you’d rather be watching a whole movie about this guy.

As Quirt, Zachary Levi is, well, a number of different things. A lot of his role, as written, leans into anachronistic wisenheimer mode, with rejoinders like “goodbyes ain’t never really been my thing” or, when rescuing the woman he loves from a fate worse than death, a quippy “Sorry I’m late!” Elsewhere in the film, Quirt must reckon with the legacy of brutality left to him by his father, and by his own livelihood in recent years. Levi can’t reconcile the tonal swings, but he’s proficient, if more in the vein of Jason Sudekis/Ted Lasso than in the creation of dimensional dark angel. (That title always referred to two angels, not one.)

The Quaker religion has been replaced here by all-purpose Christian belief and believers represented, variously, by the townsfolk — it’s a very small town with very few extras — and this remake’s depiction of the Worth family. Meg Fraser’s scrappy, yearning Penny works well enough, though visually and in terms of character, “Angel and the Badman” smoothes much of the western texture and atmosphere. Allowing for the notion of brand new towns uneasily sprouting alongside the railroad tracks, the film shows us little of life, and stuff, as it might have looked in the 19th-century west. Every belt buckle looks freshly yanked off the rack; every speck of signage resembles something painted 45 minutes before filming commenced that day.

Cinematographer and editor Alex Quintana’s lighting, cutting and shot design — to the degree he worked with the director on the third element — gets the job done without fuss but also without distinction, or surprises. Frustratingly, the first shot of the film is the strongest: a well-judged long-distance view of a lone rider on the horizon, after we’ve heard gunshots from off-screen, soon joined by horsemen in pursuit. We’ve seen a few like it before, but this one’s framed judiciously, and doesn’t look or feel like just another reenactment of a cliche.

The frustration arrives all too soon. There’s very little piety in the 1947 film, and there’s serious chemistry between Wayne and Russell. The new “Angel and the Badman” trades those virtues for plenty of sanctimony and not much of a spark.

title: Ice-T on ‘Law & Order: SVU’s’ Longevity and Cultural Impact: ‘I’m on a Good Treadmill, and I Want to Stay on It’
summary: “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” has been running since 1999, and Ice-T has been there since almost the beginning. The rapper turned a four-episode stint in the show’s second season into a permanent role as Detective Odafin “Fin” Tutuola. Nearly 30 years later, as the show gears up for the premiere of its 28th […]
content:
“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” has been running since 1999, and Ice-T has been there since almost the beginning.

The rapper turned a four-episode stint in the show’s second season into a permanent role as Detective Odafin “Fin” Tutuola. Nearly 30 years later, as the show gears up for the premiere of its 28th season, Ice-T sat down to talk about his career and the cultural impact of “Law & Order: SVU” at the Variety Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage presented by OUTFRONT.

Ice-T recalled being told he was the longest-running actor in U.S. television history after 21 seasons of “SVU.” He attributed the show’s staying power to the nature of the series: “First off, it’s a whodunit. Everybody loves a whodunit. Secondly, it’s not only entertainment; it’s also therapy.”

His co-star Mariska Hargitay created the Joyful Heart Foundation in 2004 to support survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence and child abuse. Ice-T described the thank-yous he has received from women who saw justice served on the show that they might not have seen in real life, and said he was proud to be part of something that has been so impactful.

Ice-T credits his musician background as helping him know how to interact with fans. Music is also where his passion still lies. “For me to be in films and television is fun, but doing music is a whole ‘nother thing because I write, produce and direct the whole thing.”

He and Hargitay branched out into another realm with a Capital One commercial that aired during the Emmys — which Hargitay hosted. It was something Ice-T had done before, but his co-star had not. Still, he joked that she was “the star of the show” while filming the spot.

The “SVU” crew also pretaped an Emmys sketch with Taylor Swift, which Ice-T likened to filming with then-Vice President Joe Biden during Season 18. “When you meet — I hate to say the word — the stars, you can tell they’re special,” he said. Swift’s cat, named after Hargitay’s Olivia Benson character, also made a cameo in the sketch. Ice-T joked that the cat must have been high on catnip, but both star and feline were “mad cool.”

After so many years in the industry, Ice-T said what keeps him engaged is seeing his family happy. “All this other stuff, I’ve kind of been there, done that. Got the T-shirt,” he said. “I’ve achieved the accolades. I’ve done all this stuff.” He added, “I’m on a treadmill, but I’m on a good treadmill, and I want to stay on it.”

The conversation with Ice-T was preceded by a panel discussing the power of culture and NBC’s 100th anniversary, moderated by Savannah Sellers, NBC News NOW anchor and NBC News correspondent. Joining Sellers were Mark Marshall, chairman of advertising and partnerships at NBCUniversal; Rachael Zaluzec, chief marketing officer at Volkswagen and Julie Scelzo, chief creative officer at Xfinity.

For Marshall, the compelling part of the brand equity that comes with an anniversary like NBC’s centennial is the generational aspect. “We have 22-year-olds who start every week at our company, and they all get in the elevator and take a picture of the peacock carpeting,” he said. Although people consume NBC’s content in different ways than in 1926, they still consume it.

It’s a cultural moment like this that makes Zaluzec eager to get involved. Volkswagen created a commercial in partnership with “SNL’s” 50th anniversary last year in a spin on the classic “The Californians” sketch.

At Xfinity, Scelzo sees these moments as an avenue to tap into culture in a relevant way: “When I really look beyond the idea of connecting you to stories of love throughout 100 years, we are literally the connection into your home to connect you to culture.”

Zaluzec emphasized the importance of maintaining authenticity while capitalizing on cultural moments. Following up the “SNL” 50 ad, she said, was about creating something that served VW’s needs now.

“You can’t force yourself into the moment, right?” Scelzo echoed. “You’re going to have to earn your right to be there.”

Xfinity sponsored a countdown clock to NBCUniversal’s 100th anniversary special on Dec. 10. “It’s one thing to capitalize on the moment,” Szelco said of the activation. “It’s another way to show up in a way that feels meaningful.”

Marshall emphasized the unique nature of a collective experience, particularly across generations. “Streaming had become kind of a siloed event,” he said. “Part of the reason live is having this rebirth is it’s a communal experience.”

title: ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck Returns to the Director’s Chair for a Nasty, Compulsive Kidnapping Thriller
summary: It’s for the best that “Animals,” actor Ben Affleck’s sixth outing behind the camera, is being released directly to Netflix — not that this slick, pacy serving of all-star pulp couldn’t or wouldn’t hold one’s attention in the multiplex. But ever since Affleck’s rousing, enjoyable political drama “Argo” won a Best Picture Oscar that it […]
content:
It’s for the best that “Animals,” actor Ben Affleck‘s sixth outing behind the camera, is being released directly to Netflix — not that this slick, pacy serving of all-star pulp couldn’t or wouldn’t hold one’s attention in the multiplex. But ever since Affleck’s rousing, enjoyable political drama “Argo” won a Best Picture Oscar that it perhaps didn’t entirely need, his subsequent efforts have been burdened with the weighty expectations of a prestige filmmaker — the noirish, overbaked flop “Live by Night” certainly didn’t benefit from those, and while the fleet-footed crowdpleaser “Air” rallied nicely, it wasn’t a major work either. Affleck is, at heart, an audience-minded journeyman: Screwy and silly when it doesn’t sporadically hit you with a stray hard truth, “Animals” is disposable pulp, but it benefits from its director-star’s unassuming professionalism.

“He can’t enforce laws that he doesn’t abide,” says Abigail (Kerry Washington), the perfectly put-together wife of Affleck’s character Mark Kimball, a wealthy Los Angeles attorney now pivoting to politics with a well-funded mayoral run. The second she says it, mere minutes into proceedings, is when you know we’re about to wade through some extreme moral murk — heavily contrived by Affleck with co-writers Billy Ray and Connor O. McIntyre. At its most incisive, the film hits the pressure points of good, needling political satire, and if it pressed them just a little longer and harder, we could have had something quite potent here. But “Animals” also has other, more lurid matters to attend to — some heated marital melodrama, some hollow “what would you do” button-pushing — and if these high-low tonal extremes strip the film of some gravitas, they keep it plenty gripping.

Popular on Variety

“Animals” opens with one of Mark’s extended campaign ads — a knowingly smarmy compilation of buzzwords and patently false man-of-the-people imagery, hitting all the necessary demographic targets, and working awfully hard to conceal the fact that the former lawyer and his family occupy an enviable Beverly Hills property worth over $10 million. So far, the people aren’t quite buying it: As Mark’s all-business campaign manager Sam (a disappointingly flat role for Steven Yeun) informs him, he’s still lagging in the polls, with the city’s Latin vote especially far from his grasp. How can that be, when he and Abigail are so good to their Mexican nanny Cecilia (“Emilia Pérez” standout Adriana Paz)?

Well, good within legal limits: When Cecilia asks if they could possibly offer some work to her boyfriend, illegal immigrant Ramon (Luis Gerardo Méndez), Abigail briskly explains that doing so could endanger her husband’s campaign. Still, it’s Halloween, and she and Mark trust Ramon enough to take their son Denny (Christopher Woodley) out trick-or-treating with his own, while they attend to more important matters: more campaign prep for Mark, and an online tryst with an extramarital lover for Abigail. So when Mark gets a call from a malevolent mystery predator, claiming that he’s taken Denny and demanding a $7 million ransom, multiple streams of guilt come into play.

What begins as a fairly straightforward kidnapping thriller is ratcheted by turns into something more complicated, if not exactly complex, by a neat series of twists. A couple of those are easily forecast, but the crucial one is fiendishly spring-loaded, deftly shifting the stakes of the whole enterprise, and testing Mark’s integrity both as a man and as a politician. Affleck, always at his best in roles that place his all-American alpha qualities under a harsh, sweat-inducing spotlight, has cast himself ideally here. His performance, at first glib, is so convincingly unnerved that you almost don’t need the faintly absurd foil character of Dayle Burton (Gillian Anderson) to tighten the screws.

An enigmatic British fixer called on by Sam to secure the ransom — since Mark’s fortune has largely been sunk into his campaign — Dayle’s purpose is mainly to strut around the place with intimidating serenity in a crisp white pantsuit, and to deliver dialogue like “Everyone’s beholden to something, that’s big boy life” in a cut-glass accent that only renders it more ludicrous. Her arrival is most entertaining, and also a clear signal of the film’s imminent takeover by its own trashiest instincts: Little in “Animals” rings true from here on out, but you still want to know where it’s heading, and how snakily it’s going to get there.

Still, for a few tantalizing minutes after its biggest bombshell, the film dangles the possibility of something starkly and breathtakingly true: a glimpse of America at its cruellest and most unequal. It never matches that — despite a broadly satirical and rather amusing coda that deservedly pokes fun at a national tradition of macho personality politics. The rest of the filmmaking, too, is content to coast at a lower difficulty setting, from the proficient but anonymously taupe lensing by master DP Robert Elswit to an untested ensemble of ever-watchable actors playing capably to type. “Animals” is a tart, nasty diversion, where it could be something uglier and more lingering. But you can’t blame Affleck for instead just getting the job coolly and efficiently done.

title: Universal Studios Hollywood Is Already Making Holiday Plans With The Grinch, Minions & Warm Butterbeer
summary: Halloween Horror Nights are still scaring visitors to Universal Studios Hollywood, but the park is already making holiday plans. Its annual holiday celebration will feature the return of “Grinchmas” and “Christmas in The Wizarding World of Harry Potter,” along with the debut of “Illumination’s Merry Minions” and seasonal surprises at Super Nintendo World. The holiday […]
content:
Halloween Horror Nights are still scaring visitors to Universal Studios Hollywood, but the park is already making holiday plans.

Its annual holiday celebration will feature the return of “Grinchmas” and “Christmas in The Wizarding World of Harry Potter,” along with the debut of “Illumination’s Merry Minions” and seasonal surprises at Super Nintendo World.

The holiday festivities run from Nov. 21 through Jan. 3, 2027, and are included with regular theme park admission.

Grinchmas will transform Universal Plaza, into a holiday-themed Who-ville featuring a 65-foot Christmas tree decorated with hundreds of ornaments and 200,000 LED lights. The 5 Towers stage will feature live music, DJs and street performers on select evenings. The Grinch, his dog Max and residents of Who-ville will be on hand to greet visitors. Tree-lighting ceremonies each evening will feature snowfall effects. There will also be Cindy-Lou Who reading How the Grinch Stole Christmas.

The park’s Minion Land will feature Illumination’s Merry Minions, with the animated characters arrayed in holiday attire for meet-and-greet opportunities. The area will also offer seasonal decorations, themed food at Minion Cafe and holiday merchandise.

Watch on Deadline

In The Wizarding World of Harry Potter, Hogsmeade village will be decorated with lights, garlands and wreaths, while the Frog Choir performs holiday music several times a day, according to the park. A nighttime show, The Magic of Christmas at Hogwarts Castle, will feature holiday-themed projections and music from the films. Hot Butterbeer will also be available.

Super Nintendo World will feature decorations, including Mario and Luigi snowmen near a Christmas tree topped with a Super Star at the entrance to the Mushroom Kingdom.

City News Service contributed to this report.

title: Natasha Rothwell Joins V’s ‘This Is Crazy!’ NAMI Benefit Performance In L.A.
summary: Following the show’s one-night-only debut last year in New York City, This Is Crazy! is coming to Los Angeles with some new faces for a performance benefitting the National Alliance on Mental Illness. Natasha Rothwell is the latest to join the star-studded cast of the play by V (formerly Eve Ensler), honoring the late talent […]
content:
Following the show’s one-night-only debut last year in New York City, This Is Crazy! is coming to Los Angeles with some new faces for a performance benefitting the National Alliance on Mental Illness.

Natasha Rothwell is the latest to join the star-studded cast of the play by V (formerly Eve Ensler), honoring the late talent manager Chris Huvane, which bows on Tuesday, October 13 at the Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts in Beverly Hills.

The three-time Emmy nominee joins an ensemble that includes Marisa Tomei, Rosanna Arquette, Lois Smith, Rudy Pankow, Rob Morrow, Rachel Hilson, Colette Hayes, Luke Ferrari, Olivia Oguma, Milo Maharlika and Michael Goven Hackett.

Written and directed by Vagina Monologues creator V and developed with CAA’s Community & Impact, This is Crazy! is series of original monologues exploring mental illness, family, survival and the complexity of the human experience.

Watch on Deadline

Following Huvane’s death by suicide in 2022, the show is produced by his former sister-in-law Ruth-Ann Huvane, a mental health advocate and NAMI National Board Member; and Tony Montenieri, executive producer of Lotus Productions. All proceeds will benefit NAMI.

“Chris was adored by all who had the honor of knowing him. He was outspoken about living with and battling depression for years before he died by suicide. His experience taught us the importance of providing help and support for people and families affected by mental illness,” said Ruth-Ann Huvane in a statement. “To honor the life and legacy of Chris, my family and I are committed to supporting NAMI’s mission to provide advocacy, education, support, and public awareness about mental illness. We are eternally grateful to NAMI, V, and CAA Community & Impact for embarking on this journey to help pay tribute to our brother Chris.”

Premiering last October at NYC’s Symphony Space, that cast included Jane Fonda, Edie Falco, Mark Ruffalo, Sanaa Lathan and more.

title: Greg Lombardo Leaving As Netflix Head Of Live Experiences After 7 Years
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Netflix is making a major change in its live experiences operations. Greg Lombardo, who led the streamer’s foray into the arena and the subsequent expansion, has exited after more than seven years, most recently as of VP Creative and Production, Global Experiences, Deadline has learned. One of Lombardo’s main initiatives since joining Netflix in […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Netflix is making a major change in its live experiences operations. Greg Lombardo, who led the streamer’s foray into the arena and the subsequent expansion, has exited after more than seven years, most recently as of VP Creative and Production, Global Experiences, Deadline has learned.

One of Lombardo’s main initiatives since joining Netflix in July 2019 as VP, Head of Live Experiences was the creation of Netflix Houses, brick-and-mortar locations in Philadelphia and Dallas offering live and dining experiences built around some of the platform’s biggest titles such as Stranger Things, Wednesday, Squid Game, Bridgerton and KPop Demon Hunters, along with branded merchandise.

Lombardo also spearheaded Queen’s Ball: A Bridgerton Experience and, most recently, the upcoming KPop Demon Hunters world tour.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: ’Bridgerton’ Spinoff About Young Lady Violet Greenlit At Netflix With Shonda Rhimes Writing

This marks the second high-profile Netflix marketing executive departure in the past week, along with the exit of Marketing & Publicity VP Pam Levine.

Lombardo’s resume includes stints as CEO of Offshore Surf and SVP Global Location Based Entertainment for Fox Filmed Entertainment.

title: Hong Kong’s Point Five Creations Readies ‘Blacky The Metal Arm Cat’, Plots Webtoon Extension Of ‘Another World’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The creative team behind Hong Kong breakout animated feature Another World are developing a second theatrical feature together, Blacky the Metal Arm Cat, which they’re presenting to potential partners at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market. Produced by two Hong Kong animation outfits – Another World producer Point Five Creations and rising animation house […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The creative team behind Hong Kong breakout animated feature Another World are developing a second theatrical feature together, Blacky the Metal Arm Cat, which they’re presenting to potential partners at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market.

Produced by two Hong Kong animation outfits – Another World producer Point Five Creations and rising animation house Intoxic Studio – the 2D project is written and directed by veteran animator Nic Ho (Mountains and Seas) based on his acclaimed short film.

The project is spearheaded by Point Five’s Polly Yeung, with Another World director Tommy Ng Kai-chung on board as art director. Intoxic Studio’s Ivana Lai is co-producing the film.

Watch on Deadline

The creative team describe the project as blending “high-stakes action, urban fantasy and imaginative world-building to explore identity, resilience and human purpose.”

Set in the ancient metropolis of Golden City, the film tells the story of a legendary warrior, once known as “Golden Claw,” who suffers a fall from grace following a devastating betrayal. He is saved by an enigmatic young mechanic who equips him with a custom mechanical arm. But when the mechanic suddenly disappears, he is forced to descend into a mysterious underworld and confront an alien presence in order to bring her back.

“Blacky is not a story about becoming a hero; it is a story about rediscovering yourself after loss,” Ho said. “We live in an era where technology and society shift rapidly – where the skills or identities we took pride in can feel obsolete overnight. This film reflects that generation-wide feeling of loss through modern, action-packed storytelling, showing what it means to find a reason to keep moving forward.”

Yeung also guided Another World from its roots as a short film into a theatrical feature. The film, released in 2025, became Hong Kong’s highest-grossing local animated feature of all time and scooped Best Animated Feature at Taiwan’s prestigious Golden Horse Awards. Yeung will be introducing Blacky the Metal Arm Cat to potential co-producers, financiers and sales agents at ACFM.

Point Five Creations has also partnered with Korean webtoon studio Creative SUMM to produce a webtoon expansion of Another World, with support from Hong Kong’s CreateSmart Initiative.

Produced by Yeung in collaboration with Creative SUMM, and with SuperString Inc producer BeeWon Lee on board as co-producer, the webtoon serves as a launchpad for a broader transmedia expansion of Another World.
