content:
Robby Hoffman is returning to Netflix with another stand-up comedy special.

Premiering sometime in 2027, it will mark Hoffman’s second hour for the streamer, following her 2025 special “Robby Hoffman: Wake Up,” which was directed by John Mulaney.

Hoffman has become a force in stand-up comedy, her observational wit and riled-up kvetching drawing comparisons to a young, queer Larry David. In 2025, she was named one of Variety‘s 10 Comics to Watch.

Outside of her stand-up career, Hoffman is best known for starring in the last two seasons of HBO’s “Hacks,” for which she earned an Emmy nomination for outstanding guest actress in a comedy series.

Popular on Variety

Hoffman’s next special will be produced by Rotten Science.

title: Gunna Launches SB the Label in Partnership With Atlantic Music Group
summary: Gunna has announced the launch of a new company, SB the Label, in partnership with Atlantic Music Group. The four-time Grammy nominee, born Sergio Giavanni Kitchens, will serve as CEO of the label, with three artists from the Atlanta area already signed. The deal follows a string of successes from the Atlanta rapper, with his […]
content:
Gunna has announced the launch of a new company, SB the Label, in partnership with Atlantic Music Group. The four-time Grammy nominee, born Sergio Giavanni Kitchens, will serve as CEO of the label, with three artists from the Atlanta area already signed.

The deal follows a string of successes from the Atlanta rapper, with his last three albums each peaking within the top three on the Billboard 200. He scored No. 1 debuts with both “Wunna” (2020) and “DS4EVER” (2022).

“SB the Label represents the beginning of a new chapter for me,” Gunna tells Variety. “It only felt right to start that chapter alongside my brothers Casper Bluff, Nechie, and Dracc, who are the first artists signed to the label.”

Popular on Variety

He adds, “For me, this is about stepping into a new role, expanding what I can create, and building something that represents where I’m headed next.”

Alongside the new partnership, he has released his new single, “Pop It,” after teasing a new studio album, “Splurge,” with an accompanying music video directed by Spike Jordan.

The new partnership builds on Gunna’s longstanding relationship with Warner Music Group, dating back to his early signing with Young Thug’s YSL Records, an imprint of 300 Entertainment, and Atlantic Records. Key executives, including 300 Entertainment and Atlantic Records Hip-Hop, R&B and Global Music Co-Presidents Rayna Bass and Selim Bouab, remain in the fold.

“We’ve watched Gunna grow into not only one of his generation’s defining artists, but also a true leader as an entrepreneur and executive,” the pair said in a statement. “SB the Label is a natural extension of his vision, and we’re honored that he’s entrusted 300 Entertainment/Atlantic Music Group as his partner.”

Atlantic Music Group Chairman and CEO Elliot Grainge adds, “It’s impossible to overstate Gunna’s influence on this generation of hip-hop and music as a whole. We’re grateful and honored that he’s chosen AMG as his partner to bring this endeavor to music fans.”

The label is another element of Gunna’s executive ambitions and brand expansion. In August, Under Armour named the rapper its global brand ambassador and creative director of P-Star, a new platform spanning apparel, footwear and community initiatives.

The new partnership also comes amid a series of leadership shifts across Warner Music Group. In September, WMG announced that Grainge would expand his responsibilities to become chairman of independent distribution arm ADA in the U.S., while Atlantic Music Group COO Zach Friedman would take on the additional role of ADA vice chairman. The changes are part of a broader realignment under WMG CEO Robert Kyncl, which has also seen new leadership appointments across the company’s international divisions.

title: Hollywood Defends ‘Digger’: Anne Hathaway and More Praise Tom Cruise’s Flop as Guillermo del Toro Says ‘Love the Arts. F— the Charts’
summary: Hollywood is coming to the defense of Tom Cruise as “Digger” becomes one of the biggest studio bombs in movie history. In the week since “Digger” opened in theaters to a disastrous $8 million domestically, industry names such as Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Guillermo del Toro, Mandy Patinkin, Glen Powell and more have used social […]
content:
Hollywood is coming to the defense of Tom Cruise as “Digger” becomes one of the biggest studio bombs in movie history. In the week since “Digger” opened in theaters to a disastrous $8 million domestically, industry names such as Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Guillermo del Toro, Mandy Patinkin, Glen Powell and more have used social media to champion the movie. As del Toro bluntly put it on X: “Love the arts. Fuck the charts.”

“I loved this brilliant movie. It’s smart and trippy and aggressive and funny and ambitious,” Hathaway wrote on Letterboxd. “It’s worth making the time see and decide for yourself what you make of it. For me? 10/10.”

Popular on Variety

Patinkin was even more effusive in his praise for “Digger,” hailing Cruise’s latest as an “instant classic” and “one of the greatest pieces of film I have ever seen in my entire life,” adding: “This is an incredible piece of work. It puts the heart and soul back into the cinema. Everything we all love about cinema, this is it. Please, please, please, run! Don’t walk, run, and see this film.”

Fonda encouraged Cruise and director Alejandro G. Iñárritu to “keep being brave.”

“The film allows us to witness another side of Tom Cruise’s courage,” Fonda wrote on Instagram. “It was a big, brave risk for him to take on this role and he was very good in it and very brave. He went all out, 100% owning the part… The film finds an original and, yes, risky way to wake us up about the climate crisis and I hope and pray word of mouth will bring folks into this film because it is far out creatively and closer to the truth than any such film made thus far. Hugs, kisses and bravissimo to all involved.”

“Digger” was widely touted as Cruise’s first non-action movie role in nearly a decade. He stars in the movie as Digger Rockwell, an oil tycoon who is faced with the end of the world after one of his rigs in Antartica malfunctions and sends ice caps hurtling towards Europe and more. Reviews for “Digger” were sharply divided, with some hailing it as a masterpiece and others panning it as an insufferable misfire.

As reported by Variety, the production budget for “Digger” ended up being between $160 million and $180 million. Throw on top of that a $100 million marketing budget and “Digger” would need to gross $350 million in theaters worldwide just to break even at the box office. That figure will be impossible to hit after the movie’s $20 million global start. The movie is now primed to lose at least $150 million to $200 million theatrically.

Cruise also took to his social media pages during the opening weekend for “Digger” to tell his fans that it was an honor to make the movie, adding: “Thank you to the entire cast and crew for your dedication, hard work and joy. The experience was truly unforgettable and I’m so proud of what we created.”

title: Nintendo of America Chief Breaks Down Her First Year: ‘Zelda’ Live-Action Movie, ‘GTA 6,’ Third-Party Game Goals and More
summary: After just under a year in her new role as president of Nintendo of America, Devon Pritchard is ready to share elements of her master plan for the beloved Japanese gaming company. At the center of her strategy is the relative youth of Nintendo’s Switch 2, which undeniably puts the company ahead of gaming console […]
content:
After just under a year in her new role as president of Nintendo of America, Devon Pritchard is ready to share elements of her master plan for the beloved Japanese gaming company. At the center of her strategy is the relative youth of Nintendo’s Switch 2, which undeniably puts the company ahead of gaming console competitors (Xbox and PlayStation) that are still stuck at the end of their older-model life cycles.

“We’re just at the beginning of seeing what Nintendo Switch 2 can do,” says Pritchard, who took over for longtime Nintendo of America chief Doug Bowser in January.

Compared with its first-generation predecessor, the Switch 2 has improved graphics and better processing power, allowing for new styles of play. “That opens up a number of different ways for the developers to create experiences that can only be found on Nintendo Switch 2,” she explains.

Popular on Variety

Devon Pritchard at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY held at Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles on September 17, 2026 in Beverly Hills, California. JC Olivera/Variety

Switch 2’s more powerful capabilities are among the reasons Microsoft’s Activision is bringing the “Call of Duty” franchise back to Nintendo consoles for the first time in more than a decade. This fall, it will launch “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” on Switch 2, in addition to its releases on Xbox and PlayStation systems — a clear signal that Nintendo’s latest system can hold its own in fast-paced action games.

Sales of Switch 2, released in June 2025, have topped more than 23 million units to date. Nintendo has released hundreds of titles for the platform, ranging from first-party hits like “Mario Kart World” to third-party games like “Resident Evil Requiem.”

“We have historically said that Nintendo is for ages 5 to 95, and that continues to be true,” Pritchard says. “We want to provide a diversity in terms of the types of experiences that you can have on the game system, and that’s really important for us.” Some gamers are excited about role-playing game “Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave”; others want to talk about the cozy “Pokémon Pokopia.” “So we want to make sure we’re a platform where people can come in and have those different types of creative experiences and have fun,” she says.

Is the Switch 2 tent big enough to accommodate “Grand Theft Auto VI” (with its M rating for adult content and themes), due out in November and the most anticipated gaming title of the year? The console certainly has the horsepower to host the M-rated “GTA 6,” but for now Pritchard won’t say if the title is coming to the platform.

“That’s going to be a conversation for Take Two and Rockstar, but nothing to announce on my end at this time,” Pritchard says.

Alongside the plan to make the most out Switch 2’s just-beginning life cycle, Pritchard has one big Nintendo milestone that’s already setting her team up for success: the 40th anniversary of the “Legend of Zelda” franchise. The moment will be marked with the release of a remake of the beloved “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” (which is the only high-profile game brave enough to go up against the November launch window for “GTA 6”), a “Zelda”-inspired live concert series, and culminate with the debut next April of the live-action “Zelda” movie made in collaboration with Sony. But Nintendo is walking a fine line with an anniversary of this magnitude as it looks to please both diehards and newcomers.

“I think it’s really about the celebration of ‘Zelda’ and the ‘Zelda’ universe in its entirety,” Pritchard says. “It’s Link, it’s Zelda, and all the other characters. I think it’s more about, how do we create a celebration that everyone can come in and join and connect with that world?”

That also means the company has the potential to update Universal’s Super Nintendo World locations with limited-time “Zelda” tie-ins — but Pritchard is mindful of how that could affect established “very immersive experiences” that are already packed with Mario and Donkey Kong rides. For Nintendo, it cannot be additive if it’s not organic.

Says Pritchard: “Whether it’s the theme park, whether it’s movies, anything we’re going to do is going to be deliberate and thoughtful about that experience that you’re having.”

title: Robby Hoffman Sets Second Netflix Special
summary: Comedian Robby Hoffman is set to return to Netflix next year with a second hour-long special. This follows Wake Up, her hour directed by John Mulaney that released globally last December. It’s early days here; there are no other details available yet on the special. Netflix is clearly high on Hoffman, which previously had her […]
content:
Comedian Robby Hoffman is set to return to Netflix next year with a second hour-long special.

This follows Wake Up, her hour directed by John Mulaney that released globally last December.

It’s early days here; there are no other details available yet on the special. Netflix is clearly high on Hoffman, which previously had her showcasing on Verified Stand-Up, writing on Workin’ Moms, dropping in on Everybody’s Live with John Mulaney, and headlining Netflix Is a Joke Fest.

Named one of Deadline’s Comics Who Won 2025, Hoffman is a queer ex-Hasidic comic from Brooklyn, beloved for her intense, direct comedic style. An Emmy-nominated actor and Emmy-winning writer, she made waves with a standout role on HBO Max’s Hacks and has also been seen on HBO’s Rooster, opposite Steve Carell, and FX’s Dying for Sex opposite Michelle Williams.

Hoffman began her career as a writer, earning a 2019 Daytime Emmy for her work on the PBS series Odd Squad before going on to work on series like Workin’ Moms, Baroness Von Sketch Show, and The Chris Gethard Show. She debuted her first critically acclaimed special, I’m Nervous, on CraveTV in 2019.

Watch on Deadline

Hoffman hosts the podcast Too Far with Robby Hoffman and is currently developing an HBO series called UnEntitled, where she’ll serve as writer, exec producer and star. She is repped by UTA, OPE Partners, and Schreck Rose Dapello.

title: Netflix Eyes Major Layoffs – The Dish
summary: Layoffs are coming to Netflix. Word about imminent cuts at the streamer started circulating Thursday afternoon, with sources describing the expected reduction as a big one. Netflix declined comment. The exact timing of the layoffs is unclear. Some expected them to start as early as Friday, with next week also a possibility. Speculation about the […]
content:
Layoffs are coming to Netflix. Word about imminent cuts at the streamer started circulating Thursday afternoon, with sources describing the expected reduction as a big one. Netflix declined comment.

The exact timing of the layoffs is unclear. Some expected them to start as early as Friday, with next week also a possibility. Speculation about the exact size of the cuts also varies, Puck pegs it at 5% of the company workforce.

Layoffs have become a regular occurrence in the media business.

Netflix has not undergone major cuts since the big staff reduction of 2022, with the February product division layoffs of several dozen employees among the most notable ones.

The streamer’s stock has dropped more than 40% over the past year as Wall Street has increasingly scrutinized its viewer engagement, which increased only 2% over the first half of the year.

Watch on Deadline

Netflix’s co-CEO Ted Sarandos addressed the topic last week at a Bloomberg conference. “Overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said.

title: ‘Paranormal Activity’ To Haunt Broadway For Eight Additional Weeks
summary: Paranormal Activity, Levi Holloway’s hit, critically acclaimed stage chiller inspired by the famous Paramount film franchise, has been extended for eight additional weeks at Broadway’s August Wilson Theatre. The play, directed by Felix Barrett will now play through February 28, 2027. Since beginning previews on August 14 and opening August 25, Paranormal Activity, starring Cher […]
content:
Paranormal Activity, Levi Holloway’s hit, critically acclaimed stage chiller inspired by the famous Paramount film franchise, has been extended for eight additional weeks at Broadway‘s August Wilson Theatre. The play, directed by Felix Barrett will now play through February 28, 2027.

Since beginning previews on August 14 and opening August 25, Paranormal Activity, starring Cher Álvarez and Travis A. Knight as the spooked couple, has been playing to full or nearly full houses. Last week, the show was at 98% of capacity and grossed $910,556.

The crowd-pleaser arrived on Broadway directly from a limited pre-Broadway engagement in Boston at the Emerson Colonial Theatre in July, and prior to Boston had played sold-out engagements at Chicago Shakespeare Theater in Chicago, Center Theatre Group at The Ahmanson Theatre in Los Angeles, Shakespeare Theatre Company in Washington D.C., and American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco.

Watch on Deadline

A production in Toronto at the CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre began on June 9 and ran through July 5. The production premiered at the Leeds Playhouse in the UK before transferring to the Ambassadors Theatre in the West End, where it is currently selling tickets through Saturday, November 7.

The synopsis: “James and Lou move from Chicago to London to escape their past, but they soon discover that places aren’t haunted, people are… With an original story inspired by the film franchise, Paranormal Activity reimagines the modern ghost story with an intimacy that only live theatre can provide.”

Paranormal Activity is a Melting Pot production in association with Paramount Pictures.

title: Venice Winner ‘A Day In The Life Of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Gets North American Deal With 1-2 Special
summary: EXCLUSIVE: 1-2 Special has acquired all North American rights to Jacqueline Lentzou’s A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra, which had its world premiere at the 2026 Venice Film Festival in Orizzonti, where it was awarded the Best Director Prize. The film, which is among the first films to score a domestic deal […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: 1-2 Special has acquired all North American rights to Jacqueline Lentzou’s A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra, which had its world premiere at the 2026 Venice Film Festival in Orizzonti, where it was awarded the Best Director Prize.

The film, which is among the first films to score a domestic deal out of Venice, recently had its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival, with upcoming appearances set for the BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in theaters next year.

Inspired by true events from 2008, the well-received Greek drama “follows Jo (Evita Andriopoulou)—wild, melancholic, and only 15—whose ordinary life is about to be altered forever. Throughout the day, as she misses the school bus, attends class, and finds a new friend in classmate Phaedra, subtle signs and symbols from the dream world quietly surface around her, but she fails to recognize them before a shocking incident forces Jo to undergo an ethereal transformation.”

Watch on Deadline

The deal was negotiated by Ola Byszuk of Lucky Number on behalf of the filmmakers with 1-2 Special.

The film is Jacqueline Lentzou’s second feature following Moon, 66 Questions, which played at the 2021 Berlinale and New Directors/New Films and which was awarded a Critic’s Pick by the New York Times.

Pic was produced by Avion Films (Annabelle Aronis), Atalante Productions (Ioanna Bolomyti), Kelek Film (Arda Çiltepe, Steffen Goldkamp), 4A4 Productions (Andrea Queralt), Haris & Co (Elli Papadiamanti), and Jacqueline Lentzou.

title: John Leguizamo Boards Colombian Cycling Documentary ‘Cyclovia’ As EP
summary: EXCLUSIVE: While riding awards-season surf in the wake of his performance as swineherd Eumaeus in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, John Leguizamo has signed on as executive producer for Cyclovia, a new feature doc from BAFTA-winning director Finlay Pretsell shot across five regions of Colombia with the producing team behind The Look of Silence, A House […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: While riding awards-season surf in the wake of his performance as swineherd Eumaeus in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, John Leguizamo has signed on as executive producer for Cyclovia, a new feature doc from BAFTA-winning director Finlay Pretsell shot across five regions of Colombia with the producing team behind The Look of Silence, A House Made of Splinters and Alis.

Speaking to Deadline at the Edinburgh Film Festival, where his latest film Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon was screening, Pretsell explained that this new project had been in development for quite some time.

“It’s a project about Columbia’s obsession with the bicycle,” he said, “which is so deep-rooted in their culture. It kind of follows on from my film Time Trial [2017], which is about professional cycling, and I kept on noticing the Colombians were these amazing riders winning the Tour de France. But I didn’t really want to make another film about cycling per se. And when I started going to Columbia, I started to notice that it’s in their DNA, and I wondered, why hasn’t there been a film made about this before? Because there’s so many different facets to it. You’ve got these amazing gravity bikers in Medellín who go down these swooping dual carriageways at 100km an hour, in and out of traffic, and all these young guys from the comunas. It’s outrageously cinematic and wild.”

Watch on Deadline

Leguizamo expressed his enthusiastic support for both the project and the sport. “I love cycling,” he said. “I’ve tried it. Alas, the pros have nothing to worry about from me. But I love Latin content, and I love stories about Latin excellence, and this is both. Colombia’s relationship with the bicycle is unlike anywhere else on earth, and Finlay and this team are telling that story with the scale and the soul it deserves. I’m thrilled to be on board.”

Said Pretsell: “John getting behind this film is a gift. Cyclovia is about people who have turned a simple machine into a way of surviving, celebrating and dreaming, and John’s whole body of work is about pulling Latin stories out of the margins and into the centre of the culture. That’s exactly where this film belongs.”

Producer Sonja Henrici added, “Documentaries from Latin America still get made largely for European festival audiences. We want this one to also play in Bogotá and in the Bronx. John gives us a route to both, and he arrives at the stage where it actually changes what the film can be.”

The international co-production is backed by broadcaster commitments from SVT (Sweden) and YLE (Finland), with UK and Colombian tax credits. Public funders include Screen Scotland, the Swedish Film Institute, Film i Väst, AVEK and the Finnish Film Foundation.

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Star Anthony Ippolito on Sylvester Stallone’s Reaction, Drinking Raw Eggs and Why Hollywood Needs ‘More Raw, Human Stories’
summary: The first time you hear Anthony Ippolito’s voice in the trailer for “I Play Rocky,” you can’t help but gasp. The unmistakable Sylvester Stallone drawl is there, but something harder to convey than an impression is, too: the hunger of a young man Hollywood didn’t believe in yet. Ippolito knows that feeling better than most. […]
content:
The first time you hear Anthony Ippolito’s voice in the trailer for “I Play Rocky,” you can’t help but gasp. The unmistakable Sylvester Stallone drawl is there, but something harder to convey than an impression is, too: the hunger of a young man Hollywood didn’t believe in yet.

Ippolito knows that feeling better than most.

When he learned that Peter Farrelly was making a film about an unknown Stallone who willed his screenplay “Rocky” into existence, he also heard that bigger names were circling the part. Some people told him not to bother. Instead, he hung a heavy bag from a wooden beam in his grandmother’s basement, a room he says is “very much stuck in the ’70s,” pulled on vintage boxing gloves and shot an audition tape with no script and no invitation.

“I was like, ‘I gotta try something,’” he says.

Popular on Variety

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Ippolito discusses landing the leading role in the making of a legend, getting his start in the business, and his thoughts on a changing Hollywood.

Listen below!

It’s a fitting origin story for a film about a man who turned down life-changing money rather than let anyone else play the character he wrote. The Amazon MGM Studios release, written by Peter Gamble and directed by Farrelly, finished as first runner-up for the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival.

In a sense, Ippolito has been preparing since he was 3, when neighbors noticed he was “oddly good at baseball.” The novelty landed him on the local news and the TV series “Ripley’s Believe It or Not!,” and a commercial agent suggested his mother start a college fund. Later credits include the Adam Sandler film “Pixels,” the Netflix drama series “Grand Army” and the Paramount+ limited series “The Offer,” in which he played Al Pacino.

His work on Stallone bordered on obsession. He listened to every scrap of footage he could find, including “Rebel,” an early Stallone film he ordered from a Japanese website and waited two months to receive. He studied the handwritten first draft of “Rocky,” scrawled in a red Mead notebook. He spent nearly two years bulking up from about 150 pounds to roughly 180 while training at Gleason’s Gym in Brooklyn. Yes, he drank the raw eggs. Once.

What stays with me is how Ippolito reads this moment. With AI-generated performers entering the conversation, he argues that actors “have to be humanists” and that the image of a young writer drafting his future longhand with a Bic pen has never felt more urgent. He wants raw, character-driven films in the vein of John Cassavetes.

Hollywood should take note. The next Stallone may not look like a movie star yet. He may be in his grandmother’s basement.

This interview has edited and condensed for clarity.

Anthony Ippolito in “I Play Rocky” Amazon MGM Studios

Before acting, you were a lefty center fielder and pitcher who wanted to make the Yankees. How did baseball turn into acting?

That was the initial goal: to try to make it as a baseball player. That’s how I got into acting, though. When I was 3 years old, I was oddly good at baseball. I was playing outside with my dad, and my neighbors saw and were like, “This is weird. You’re too good at this for a young kid.” I was on the local news first, then “Ripley’s Believe It or Not!,” “Regis and Kelly,” all that stuff. I was 3, so that took me in a completely different direction. A commercial agent talked to my mom and said, “Hey, build a college fund for your kid and that was the entry point.

I have a friend who is a producer at ABC, and he sent me a photo of you as a kid with a bowl cut, in a Boy Scout uniform, on John Quiñones’ hidden-camera series “What Would You Do?” How did you get wrapped up in that? [Shows Ippolito the picture.]

That was Amarillo, Texas. I was really young when I got my first one of those. If the producers liked you, they kept including you. It’s a difficult environment because you have an earpiece in and real people around, so you have to toe the line. If you can do it, and they identify that, they’ll keep putting you in. A couple of people have made it out. One of the guys from “Stranger Things” was in one, and my friend David Iacono was in one with me. We met when we were like 15.

A few versions of how you landed this role are floating around. What’s the real story?

The kitchen sink. That’s the answer. Everything you hear is hard to communicate concisely. It was a bit of a messy process. I saw this was happening and thought, “OK, how do I get in the conversation for this?” I heard other names were floating around, bigger celebrity names and that was a little discouraging. I was hearing from some people, “Maybe it’s not even worth it. If it gets dropped in front of you, then you know.” But I was like, “No, I gotta try something.”

So without a script, I took that opportunity to shoot this thing in my grandma’s basement, which is very much stuck in the ’70s. I got the look, got a heavy bag, did some construction, hung it from a wooden beam and grabbed some vintage boxing gloves that matched the vibe. I always thought one of the most interesting parts of Rocky was his movement, his body rhythm, especially when he’s fighting. It’s almost an extension of his normal rhythm. So I felt that if I could capture that and show them I was interested, that might help. That’s how I got the script.

By the way, nobody’s asking for an audition scene at this point. They’re just like, “Here’s the script.” But I was like, “OK, I’m gonna audition for this.” I picked the scenes I thought were best, put an audition together, threw it at them, threw a couple more things at them and eventually I heard it was looking good.

Do you remember the first time you saw “Rocky?”

It’s hard to put my finger on the first time. I remember seeing “Rocky Balboa” in the movie theater when I was maybe eight years old. I was sitting real close to the screen. The first one, I couldn’t tell you. It was probably a year or two before that.

Stallone’s signature drawl comes from partial facial paralysis caused by a forceps accident at birth. How did you capture that without tipping into a generic impression?

It was a lot of listening first. I listened to him over and over again, almost obsessively. Everything I could find: “Rocky” interviews, but also other parts he played, because he was an unknown actor at the time. He had only done small parts, but he had a lot of great stuff. There’s this movie he did called “Rebel” that I ordered from a Japanese website, and it took two months to get to my place. Then he did “The Lords of Flatbush,” “Police Story,” “The Prisoner of Second Avenue,” “Capone,” but we’re talking two or three scenes. So you’re taking these little pieces and saying, “What is he doing here? What is he doing over here?”

He’s playing characters, but as an actor he’s also trying to tell the truth, right? He’s being truthful in his work. So you take everything you can and ask, “Who’s the guy here?” Hearing it from as many different directions as possible was very helpful. Then you have the burden of finding it within yourself in a way that feels honest and not forced or heavy-handed.

You spoke with Stallone before filming. What did he give you that you couldn’t have gotten from a tape?

Just his firsthand experience of being in those rooms with those producers, and what that dynamic is like. Everything going on in the background of his life in the context of those negotiations, and the toll that takes through this middle period of trying to stick to your guns. Hearing him recount that was really a privilege, because it’s something I’d been thinking about so much for over a year before talking to him.

Has he seen the finished film?

He did see the movie, and he had a very positive reaction. Thankfully, I got to speak to him. If you’re doing a biopic about, say, a musician or a political figure, the idea of them watching your acting from a technical perspective is a little different. But this is what he does. He’s an actor, so he’s watching me do what he does. I was just nervous in general, because seeing a cinematic telling of the inflection point in your life is probably a wild experience in and of itself. So I was hoping he’d have a positive reaction, and he did. He told me he really loved the film, and he’s really excited for more people to see it.

Stallone famously wrote the “Rocky” script in three and a half days. Did you read that original draft?

Absolutely. There’s some really cool stuff in there. There are a lot of KFC buckets in the original. Some of that made it into the movie, in the background of Rocky’s apartment. What was really cool is that he wrote it longhand. You can find the red Mead notebook he wrote in, and for the dialogue, it’s “R,” underlined and then Rocky’s lines and “P,” underlined, for Paulie. You can see his handwriting. You can see he’s blazing through this, crossing stuff out. It’s very raw.

And I think it’s important to point this out: It was a first draft. It’s nuts to say that the polished, finished, beautiful art that “Rocky” is was made in three and a half days total. Things were thrown around. Mickey had a different kind of personality. Things came together over time, but a lot of it was there in the beginning.

Let’s talk about the physical transformation. Did you actually drink the raw eggs?

I actually did it once, while I was training at Gleason’s Gym in Brooklyn. I had a hotel that didn’t have a microwave or anything, and I was having to get in crazy macros every day, a lot of protein. I was jerry-rigging it for a while, and then I was like, “All right, this is a good excuse, a good reason to do it.” I learned from that for sure.

It was a really large undertaking and took a very long time. Your body doesn’t really want to change, or at least mine didn’t in the beginning. When I played Pacino, I intentionally didn’t change my body very much. I was about the same size as him. But Pete told me he wanted that look, and I agreed. I think it was important to get that silhouette. It’s integral to the character and to Stallone himself. There’s something very interesting about the juxtaposition of his muscular, stocky physique and the fact that he’s trying to sell his intellectual property. That’s part of what made Stallone so interesting to me. So I had to gain a considerable amount of weight, which required an entire lifestyle shift.

How long did it take, and how much weight did you put on?

Almost two years. I started somewhere around 145 or 150, and I read that Stallone was about 180 in the movie, so I got up to that.

Peter Farrelly won best picture for “Green Book.” What surprised you about working with him?

Honestly, I was pretty surprised by how much room and freedom he gave me to play, to find things and explore moments. He’s such a veteran that a lot of the time I’m just trusting him, and that was a huge luxury for me. For him to take this chance on me in the first place is amazing and incredible. But to give me the room to take certain risks and bring in ideas on top of that is a whole other thing. He also has that incredible comedic sensibility, so there will be moments that aren’t in the script and if he sees something pop up through the blocking or whatever, he’ll hop all over it.

What was it like watching the film for the first time at TIFF, with your family and a full audience?

It was the most surreal thing ever. It really hit me during the introduction. Pete went up and spoke, and then there were maybe 15 minutes where they were showing the intro stuff and those 15 minutes felt like an hour. I was like, “Oh man, people are gonna get restless.” I was going a little nutty in my seat, to be honest with you. But hearing the audience respond throughout the movie the way they did exceeded anything I could have expected.

What if the room had gone the other way?

Every room’s different. You never know. People could collectively have been in a bad mood that day for some reason. It’s never a be-all-and-end-all, but it would have been discouraging, for sure.

Stallone earned Oscar nominations for best actor and original screenplay as a total unknown. What does it mean for your name to be in that conversation 50 years later?

It’s really overwhelming. This whole experience has been that way. But I think the great thing about this movie, and the way movies are going right now, is that we’re having a great year and these awards shows can serve to promote every film and celebrate the work all these fantastic artists have done over the last year. So to just be in that conversation and to help get more people excited about the movie is really all you could ask for.

You’ve now played the young version of Adam Sandler’s character in “Pixels,” Al Pacino in “The Offer” and now Stallone. Are you worried about becoming the guy Hollywood calls to play legends?

I’m not somebody who does impressions at all. I also did a show called “Grand Army” on Netflix, where I played a fictional character, which was great. And in some ways, even approaching these projects, you have to take those same liberties and approach it as a fictional character. There’s a respect and responsibility that comes with the fact that they are real people, and there are certain things you want to include. But at the same time, we’re doing an interpretation of a story. We’re condensing this incredible period of this guy’s life into a two-hour film, so we’re taking certain leaps anyway. There’s some freedom there as well.

So are you done playing Italian American actors for a while?

I feel like I’ve been spoiled. I don’t know who else would be in that conversation. But I think it would be nice to eventually play somebody who doesn’t have so many pieces of footage of them in the public eye. Just be a little different.

This awards season has a striking number of films that are love letters to acting itself, and I think it’s hard not to draw a line to AI and the creation of Tilly Norwood. Why do you think Hollywood is telling so many stories about actors right now?

I think actors on some level have to be humanists. What’s interesting about the Stallone story in the context of “I Play Rocky” is that he wrote the script longhand with a Bic pen in a red Mead notebook. There’s something intimate and tangible about that process, especially when you juxtapose it with the life we’re in now, with all these forms of tech and things writing for you, things thinking for you. I think we really need more stories about people doing things themselves, thinking for themselves and taking agency over their lives, especially the younger generation coming up.

What’s your read on the current state of Hollywood? Fix it for us.

I don’t know if I can fix it. And not that it needs to be completely fixed. There are a lot of good things happening. A lot of smaller-budget movies are getting a little more exposure, and there are more opportunities for that. Maybe the internet allows for that. But I do think more small- to midbudget movies should be funded. They have the problem of getting exposure, reaching audiences, marketing, because I think those are a lot of the best films. I’m a big fan of John Cassavetes, and I think we need more movies on that kind of scale, that are raw and human.

Sometimes if they throw too much money at something, a $100 million or $200 million movie, there’s a gloss over the whole thing. Especially now, younger kids are so immersed in social media and people are trying to fabricate themselves or polish and airbrush their lives and appearances. I really think there’s more of a need for raw, human stories than ever before. So hopefully that makes a resurgence.

Do you think a younger audience that has never seen “Rocky” can still access this film?

I think this film stands on its own in a lot of ways. It’s a somewhat separate story. It’s kind of an origin story, the inception of the character and it’s about a struggling writer, a struggling creative person trying to make a living doing it. That’s its own standalone piece. But at the same time, hopefully it acts as a bridge to “Rocky” for people who haven’t seen it and makes them curious about the original film and maybe even the rest of the franchise, because I think it’s a really, really important character in cinema history.

Assuming “I Play Rocky” goes great and the meetings start happening, what’s the project you want?

Something that feels not necessarily small, but intimate and character-driven. The bigger stuff, the explosions and the CGI monsters, it’s cool. I’m not saying those things are bad. I liked “Power Rangers” growing up. But more human, character-driven storytelling. That’s the game plan.

Any director you’d drop everything for?

I met Wim Wenders in Zurich, and it was maybe the coolest experience I’ve ever had. I saw “Perfect Days.”

10 QUESTIONS WITH ANTHONY IPPOLITO:

Childhood nickname?

“Ant,” honestly. They just cut it in half.

Favorite Yankee of all time?

A dark-horse choice of mine is Roger Maris. “61*” is what really put me on to him.

Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into?

I was modifying Nerf guns when I was a little kid. I’d break into them and spray WD-40 on the cylinders. It was pretty dangerous. We had to wear glasses.

Go-to karaoke or shower song?

This is gonna expose the Italian in me, but Sinatra. Most Sinatra.

Give me an alternate title for “I Play Rocky.”

You could just call the movie “Stallone,” I guess.

Your secret talent?

I like to paint. I draw, too. Drawing’s a bit more practical, like on a plane.

Favorite ice cream flavor?

Van Leeuwen. Black cherry chip, and then vanilla honeycomb.

The one item you couldn’t live without?

A pen.

What film or TV show in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of?

“Wings of Desire.”

Fictional character you most relate to or admire?

Quint in “Jaws.” I don’t know if I relate to him at all, but I admire that character. There’s something about Robert Shaw in that part.

Favorite piece of advice you’ve given or received?

It’s from “The Four Agreements”: Be impeccable with your word. And I think that also relates to yourself. When you say you’re going to do something, you’re making little agreements with yourself. If you follow through on it and don’t give up on yourself or abandon your plan for yourself, it’s ultimately good for you.

title: ‘WandaVision’ Creator Jac Schaeffer to Develop ‘Stargate’ Series at Amazon (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Jac Schaeffer is developing a new “Stargate” TV series for Amazon MGM Studios, Variety has learned exclusively from sources. The project falls under Schaeffer’s overall deal with Amazon MGM, which was announced earlier this year. According to sources, a writers’ room is expected to open in the near future. Along with Schaeffer, Joby Harold and […]
content:
Jac Schaeffer is developing a new “Stargate” TV series for Amazon MGM Studios, Variety has learned exclusively from sources.

The project falls under Schaeffer’s overall deal with Amazon MGM, which was announced earlier this year. According to sources, a writers’ room is expected to open in the near future. Along with Schaeffer, Joby Harold and Tory Tunnell for Safehouse Pictures will executive produce the project.

Reps for Amazon and Schaeffer declined to comment.

Popular on Variety

This will be Amazon’s second attempt at a new “Stargate” series. It was previously reported that Martin Gero was working on a new TV entry in the sci-fi franchise, but that project ultimately did not move forward.

Schaeffer is no stranger to the genre world, given her previous success with the smash hit series “WandaVision” for Marvel Studios and Disney+. The show was the first Marvel Cinematic Universe series to premiere on Disney+, with Marvel stars Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany reprising their roles as Wanda and Vision from the Marvel films. It went on to earn 23 Primetime Emmy Awards nominations as well as numerous other accolades. It was one of the most well-reviewed and highly-praised TV shows of 2021.

Schaeffer then went on to create the “WandaVision” spinoff “Agatha All Along” starring Kathryn Hahn as Agatha Harkness, reprising her role from “WandaVision.” Schaeffer was the showrunner, writer, and executive producer on that show in addition to directing. Prior to her time with Marvel, she wrote the screenplay for the Disney animated featurette “Olaf’s Frozen Adventure” as well as the 2019 Anne Hathaway-Rebel Wilson comedy “The Hustle,” which was a remake of the 1980s comedy feature “Dirty Rotten Scoundrels.”

She is repped by Curate, CAA, and attorney Erik Hyman.

“Stargate” originally launched as a 1994 movie starring James Spader and Kurt Russell. The film was followed by the hit series “Stargate SG-1,” which aired for 10 seasons and starred Richard Dean Anderson, Michael Shanks, Amanda Tapping, and Christopher Judge among others. The spinoff “Stargate Atlantis” then aired for five more seasons between 2004 and 2008.

title: Variety Toasts Pete Davidson at The New York Party With Gayle King, Ana Navarro and Kareem Rahma
summary: New York is having a moment. In June, the Knicks pulled off the impossible and won their first NBA championship in 53 years, sending the city into a frenzy of infectious energy. “I was at my friend Justin’s house with a bunch of straight people, which was fun,” Nicky Campbell, fashion TikTok star and one […]
content:
New York is having a moment. In June, the Knicks pulled off the impossible and won their first NBA championship in 53 years, sending the city into a frenzy of infectious energy.

“I was at my friend Justin’s house with a bunch of straight people, which was fun,” Nicky Campbell, fashion TikTok star and one of Variety’s first 10 Creators to Watch, recalled of the night the Knicks won. “We all started screaming, and then we ran out to meet all my other friends at Times Square. I was there for hours.”



For Campbell, who has called New York home for 12 years, the championship celebrations that erupted on the streets were unlike anything he’d witnessed before. “It was wild. People were on cars!” he exclaimed, admitting, “I might have jumped on one at one point, too.”

To celebrate the city that never sleeps, Variety threw The New York Party Thursday night at Living Room Bar & Lounge in the Flatiron District. The event honored Staten Island’s own Pete Davidson, who graced the cover of Variety’s New York issue. In a career-spanning interview with chief correspondent Marlow Stern, the comedian opened up about leaving “Saturday Night Live,” his famous exes and the concussion he suffered while shooting the film “Tommy Karate.”

Popular on Variety

Ramin Setoodeh and Pete Davidson at Variety’s New York Party. Variety via Getty Images

Still recovering from the injury, Davidson wore a pair of blacked-out sunglasses while driving himself to the Living Room Bar & Lounge. Decked out in an oversized chocolate-brown leather jacket, Davidson posed on the red carpet and embraced Variety’s co-presidents Ramin Setoodeh (also the publication’s co-editor-in-chief) and Dea Lawrence. He was later spotted mingling with fellow comedian Matt Friend, news icon Gayle King, “The View’s” Ana Navarro and “Subway Takes” host Kareem Rahma.

Gilded Age glamour met modern Manhattan nightlife inside the grand lounge, where guests were greeted with glasses of champagne. As they noshed on lobster rolls and tuna tartare, the evening gave the mix of media personalities a chance to toast the city and reflect on what makes New York so special.

“It all started for me with these interviews I did on the streets of New York and doing impressions,” Friend said. ”There’s nothing like this city.”
