title: How Skydance Will Remake the Illustrious Culture of Warner Bros. Pictures More Than Any Owner Before
summary: There have been many quiet Mondays at the Burbank offices of Warner Bros. Pictures, usually following a bomb like the one the studio just suffered with Tom Cruise’s “Digger.” The cryptic eco-disaster project will represent a loss of hundreds of millions when all is said and done. But the silence this past Monday was compounded […]
content:
There have been many quiet Mondays at the Burbank offices of Warner Bros. Pictures, usually following a bomb like the one the studio just suffered with Tom Cruise’s “Digger.” The cryptic eco-disaster project will represent a loss of hundreds of millions when all is said and done.

But the silence this past Monday was compounded by a familiar wave of merger-induced grief, multiple sources told Variety, especially as employees observed WB Motion Picture Group co-head Pamela Abdy packing up her office in boxes. In a move that shocked some, Abdy and co-head Michael De Luca were dismissed last week as David Ellison finally homed in on his acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. De Luca and Abdy had been at the head of Warner’s film business for four years, delivering a wild series of strikes (“A Minecraft Movie”) and gutters (“The Bride!”). In addition to family photos and movie props, Abdy may have boxed up the remnants of a workplace tradition diluted by acquisitions and corporate unions over the past three decades.

Warner Bros. Pictures is poised to undergo its most dramatic cultural transformation since the 1980s under the new leadership of Skydance CEO Ellison — and specifically, his motion picture group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. The Ellison regime has revealed itself thus far as a shirtsleeve operation, one zeroed in on lowering costs and boosting profits. The preciousness and luxuries that made Warner Bros. a desirable home for creatives will be rightsized with tech ruthlessness, multiple high-level sources suggest.

Popular on Variety

Goldberg and Greenstein had only spent a year (albeit a productive one) as the heads of Paramount Pictures before this week’s announcement that they will preside over all film labels at the combined company. This means that De Luca and Abdy’s replacement will report into Goldberg and Greenstein, not the office of the CEO (as was the case under David Zaslav’s Discovery and John Stankey’s AT&T, for example).

“On the film side, the scale of this combination, particularly its commitment to theatrical, puts Dana and Josh at the center of the movie business,” Richard Weitz, co-chairman of WME Group, says. The power agent is alluding to Ellison’s commitment to release 30 theatrical films per year across both studios, an agreement he had to put in writing to get his merger over the finish line.

Lorenzo Di Bonaventura, who served as a top WB film executive from 1989 to 2002 before moving to Paramount to produce huge IP like “Transformers,” says the Skydance team’s dedication to movies is not just on paper.

“Looking at the two companies and their slates, I don’t think they have done 30 movies between the two in a very long time,” he says. “That is a net plus for our business, because that means more movies are getting made and more capital is being expended in creating them.”

Goldberg and Greenstein are respected by industry peers, hailing from Village Roadshow (“The Matrix,” “Ocean’s Eleven” series) and Sony Pictures, respectively. They’re now faced with the daunting task of further defining distinct identities for multiple WB labels like New Line and Clockwork.

“I worked with Josh for more than a decade, and I have a great deal of respect for him,” says Tom Rothman, Sony Pictures chief and Greenstein’s former boss. “What you need in that job is a combination of IQ and EQ. It’s managing capital allocation, but in a much more important sense, it’s managing artistic temperaments. He’s extremely capable in both regards.”

While detractors of Goldberg and Greenstein say they do not enjoy the kind of profile some competitors do on the byways of Los Angeles and in coastal elite circles, they’ve greenlit 20 films since taking office at Paramount. They’ve also signed talent deals with the Duffer Brothers, Will Smith, James Mangold, Jon M. Chu and Issa Rae (on top of a distribution pact with Legendary Entertainment).

Any successful film executive’s job comes down to superior talent relations and responsible budgeting. De Luca and Abdy certainly had the former covered (De Luca was a groomsman in Paul Thomas Anderson’s wedding; Abdy was considered a whisperer to filmmakers like Alejandro Iñárritu). “Irresponsible” spending is likely what helped them court the premium filmmakers for which Warner Bros. is renowned, one source says. “It’s easy to say yes when you don’t care what the price is,” they add.

With some $80 billion in debt on the Skydance balance sheet, carte blanche is over. But it’s not just about fiscal prudence. Unlike “carpetbaggers” Zaslav and Stankey, as another top industry player calls them, Ellison and his team consider themselves obsessed lovers of film. The pomp and “platinum” aura of Warner Bros., as one former WB exec phrases it, may be sacrificed quickly.

The lingering magic (and occasional arrogance) of Warner Bros. were holdovers from a culture built by Bob Daly and Terry Semel, insiders say. They ran the company as co-CEOs for almost two decades starting in 1980. The pair prioritized elevated popcorn hits made by substantial filmmakers. Clint Eastwood and Christopher Nolan kept bungalows on the WB lot without having overall deals. “They just wanted to be there,” one former employee says.

While the TV group at WB often was peeved that it brought in all the revenue while the film group got all the attention, the pecking order remained. A collection of Warner vets, many now in high-ranking posts elsewhere, describe a kind of “heart pull” that the studio inspires in its graduates. A crowded text chain of former employees called the “Gate 4 Club” (referring to the entrance many used to access the lot) is active across the industry. They wistfully discuss the days of Daly and Semel parking a row of brand-new Range Rovers as gifts to the cast and filmmakers of “Lethal Weapon” after a sequel hit big.

It’s doubtful any shiny SUVs will be wrapped in ribbons at Warner Bros. anytime soon. Besides, Ellison prefers the sky.

title: Remi Wolf on the Meaning Behind Her New Album ‘Mud,’ Her ‘Off Campus’ Cameo and Friendship with Hayley Williams
summary: Remi Wolf hasn’t landed a spot on “Survivor,” one of her favorite shows she’s always wanted to be on, so she instead put her mental fortitude to the test by rolling around in a makeshift mud pit. She quickly realized she’s “never gonna make it on that show if I can’t handle this in such […]
content:
Remi Wolf hasn’t landed a spot on “Survivor,” one of her favorite shows she’s always wanted to be on, so she instead put her mental fortitude to the test by rolling around in a makeshift mud pit. She quickly realized she’s “never gonna make it on that show if I can’t handle this in such a controlled setting,” she tells Variety. But her foray into the earthy substance was more than just a mental experiment; it was a musical one, too: “Mud” is the name and driving imagery of her third studio album, which was released today.

For Wolf, frolicking in mud is both literal and metaphorical. On the album, she revels in “brutal” emotions, allows herself to feel the pain and discomfort they cause, and realizes the beauty of moving through it. Or, as she likes to call it, the “mudding and sudsing.”

Popular on Variety

“Once you get past the point where you’re disgusted that you’re so dirty and unknown Earth is inside of all your crevices, you can start to have fun in there,” she says. “If you kind of let yourself surrender to the mud, it can be a really fun and beautiful and freeing experience. I felt like making this album, I went through all the phases of being in mud.”

Wolf was “in the shit” and wanted audiences to know it. The 10-track album chronicles her emotional turmoil, pivoting off of vibrant anthems like “Photo ID” that helped launch her popularity or sing-alongs like “Soup.” Instead, she’s become more diaristic, grappling with the ugly emotions that come with what appears to be a breakup. She belts lyrics like “I can be your favorite track, I know I can,” and yells “Why don’t you want me back?” on her third single “I Won’t Cry.” On “Bottle,” she confesses, “The dam broke when we said goodbye / Darling I can’t think about it ’cause it makes me cry.” Wolf always aims to be honest in her work, but this time she got vulnerable in a way that allowed her to create what she says is her “strongest” body of work yet.

“People want to cry,” Wolf says. “I feel like we’re all pent up and everything’s so crazy. I want to take people to church a little bit with this album and give them a space to let it all out.”

For “Mud,” Wolf worked with a close-knit group of friends and collaborators — Jared Solomon, Jack Demeo and Gigi Grombacher, among others. On her earlier albums, 2021’s “Juno” and 2024’s “Big Ideas,” she brought her visions to life with the help of hired creative directors, but wanted to tighten the circle with her latest. “I was so vulnerable and broken down that I was like, I can’t even fathom going into the studio with people that aren’t automatically going to be chill with me being this way,” she says. The crew decamped to Joshua Tree, jamming around a campfire and recording in a makeshift studio in their Airbnb. “I was just like ‘fuck all the bullshit! I’m bringing in my homies, and we’re homieing down so hard.”

Next came visuals. She led the charge as the creative director and knew the mud pit was “a necessity” for the album’s imagery, that the video for “Bottle” should feel “claustrophobic” and that the visuals for “I Won’t Cry” would represent “the cleansing.” “I also just wanted to stand on the car and be in a bikini and wash it,” says Wolf, who is celebrating the release of her album on Friday at a Los Angeles car wash.

She’s also been able to work out songs for the first time at live shows, including one with her longtime influence Hayley Williams. She debuted her lead single “Twiggy” at the Newport Folk Festival in July with Williams and the pair performed Williams’ track “Parachute” in Los Angeles during night two of her show at the Hollywood Bowl on Tuesday. They first met when Wolf opened for Paramore back in 2023, and they’ve maintained a friendship ever since.

“She’s so fucking awesome,” Wolf says. “I love her and respect her, and she’s just the best singer and such a unique artist and very beautiful person.”

Wolf also graced the stage with a cameo on Amazon Prime’s hit hockey series “Off Campus,” performing at a fictitious schoolwide block party. “It was an amazing day on set meeting the cast,” she says. “They all seem like they like each other, and they actually do. It was a fun set to be on. I’d never been on a set like that; it was cool to just watch the village work.”

But now, she says, her focus is on “Mud” and putting it all out there, no matter how messy things may get. “I was crossing my fingers that people would ride with me,” she says, “and I really think they are.”

title: Skydance TV: George Cheeks’ Evolution From The Business Guy To Chief Content Officer & JB Perrette’s Linear-Streaming Job Bundle
summary: Skydance’s CEO Business Leadership Team unveiled on Monday features only Co-Chairs, with everyone in the group sharing oversight of a division alongside someone else. All pairs come from the same side of the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery company (WBD’s Casey Bloys & JB Perrette for DTC and James Gunn & Peter Safran for DC; Paramount’s […]
content:
Skydance‘s CEO Business Leadership Team unveiled on Monday features only Co-Chairs, with everyone in the group sharing oversight of a division alongside someone else. All pairs come from the same side of the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery company (WBD’s Casey Bloys & JB Perrette for DTC and James Gunn & Peter Safran for DC; Paramount’s Dana Goldberg & Josh Greenstein for film) except for one crossover duo: Paramount’s George Cheeks and WBD’s Perrette, who will serve as co-Chairs of Skydance TV.

The move marks the latest shared leadership position for Cheeks and also a new role he has not been in yet — at least by title — as Chief Content Officer of Skydance TV, a unit spanning Skydance’s three TV studios, Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios and Paramount TV Studios, CBS and about 30 basic cable networks. As Skydance TV Chief Business officer, Perrette will oversee the division’s ad sales, distribution, content sales and international operations.

For a decade now, Harvard Law graduate Cheeks has been the business partner to a creative executive, whether it was as Co-President of Universal Cable Prods. and Wilshire Studios alongside Dawn Olmstead or as NBC Entertainment Co-Chairman alongside Paul Telegdy. Now he is the creative executive alongside Perrette with a title matching that of Skydance DTC Chief Content Officer Bloys, one of TV industry’s most accomplished development executives.

Watch on Deadline

That caps a long evolution for Cheeks that can be traced back to one of his first Hollywood jobs, while having Perrette as Chief Business Officer across DTC as well as TV Studios and linear networks corrects a structural flow that existed at both Paramount and WBD.

The Business Guy

After stints at entertainment law firms Loeb & Loeb and Hansen Jacobson Teller and the BA & legal department of Castle Rock Entertainment early on, Cheeks landed a business and legal affairs job at MTV Networks. There, along with drafting deal memos, he also started doing script coverage for then-top programming executives Tony DiSanto and Liz Gateley.

Cheeks got his first formal assignment on the creative side — and showed his talent relations skills — when, as EVP Business Operations for NBC and Universal TV, he was put in charge of NBC Late Night in 2014. Lorne Michaels took a liking to him (while disliking his predecessor) and took him under his wing, valuing his creative sense by asking for his feedback on writer packages and taking him to auditions.

Cheeks has acknowledged that getting the NBC Late Night gig changed his career, fueling his aspirations to straddle business and creative. He would later be handpicked as the main liaison to NBCUniversal’s other uber TV producer, Dick Wolf, for similar reasons (the procedural king wanted to switch executives), proving that he can work well with top-level talent.

Still, when Bonnie Hammer announced Cheeks and Olmstead’s appointment as UCP co-Presidents in early 2018, she called Olmstead a “talented creative executive” while praising Cheeks’ “business savvy” as “second to none.” Similarly, Steve Burke’s statement about Cheeks’ promotion as NBC Entertainment co-Chairman alongside Telegdy later that year called him “a strategist and masterful dealmaker.”

That is a perception Cheeks carried over in his 2020 move to then-ViacomCBS as President and CEO of CBS Entertainment, with David Nevins initially serving as the division’s Chief Content Officer. That changed in 2021. Overseeing CBS-branded operations in various roles over the past five years — including another shared one as co-CEO of Paramount Global — varnished Cheeks’ creative credentials as he worked closely with such executives as CBS Entertainment President Amy Reisenbach and CBS Studios President David Stapf.

Now Cheeks, who also has been overseeing Paramount’s basic cable networks, will be focusing on programming and marketing content while expanding his portfolio to include Warner Bros. TV, Paramount TV Studios as WBD’s cable brands, leaving most of the business areas to Perrette. (Given his business background, Cheeks is still expected to get involved in some decisions.)

Bundling Linear & Streaming Business Ops

Legacy media companies such as Skydance are faced with managing the transition from linear TV to streaming, and Perrette serving as Chief Business Officer across both direct-to-consumer and linear networks/TV studios will help facilitate that as the two areas have become intertwined in many key areas such as carriage agreements, ad and content sales.

For instance, in affiliate distribution deals for linear networks, carriers increasingly insist on bundling the streaming service. The same goes for ad buyers who package ad time across linear and digital.

And then there is content licensing, which could be a lot more efficient if the studios’ distribution divisions and their sibling streamers are overseen by the same business op executive. For instance, CBS and Paramount+ had been siloed, with Paramount+ automatically asking for exclusivity on virtually all CBS series. A holistic approach would help determine whether certain shows need to stream exclusively on Paramount+ or, based on their engagement and other metrics, they could be licensed to other platforms too, bringing in revenue that can be used to produce more shows.

Straddling both areas will also give the business executive in charge more ownership over next-day CBS series to better integrate them into the platform alongside the Paramount+ originals. (CBS fare, a big viewership driver in-season, is expected to stay largely on Paramount+ until the streamer’s merger with HBO Max is completed within the next couple of years.)

Additionally, the new streamlined structure with Perrette across both linear and streaming business ops makes for simplified and expedited decision-making. At WBD, where he was CEO of global streaming, it was a quartet of executives collaborating on these decisions: Perrette, CFO Gunnar Wiedenfels, Chief Revenue and Strategy Officer Bruce Campbell and President of International Gerhard Zeiler.

‘The Odd Couple’ 2.0?

In addition to being the only cross-company pair in the top Skydance executive echelon, Cheeks and Perrette share another distinction — Cheeks is the only former Paramount Global and Perrette the only former Discovery executive in the group.

As for compatibility, both are bringing in good track record. Perrette already has his successful partnership with Bloys, and Cheeks has showed that he could work with anyone.

Cheeks joked about it when asked in 2019 how he gets along with Telegdy, a flamboyant, larger-than-life personality.

“We literally could not be more different. It’s like Casting 101: ‘Let’s cast this dude and that dude and they’re so different, they’re an odd couple,’” he said at NATPE.

Cheeks clearly impressed Hollywood moguls with his performance as he keeps getting cast as half of executive couples.

title: ‘All The Little Houses’ Series Adaptation In The Works At Apple From ‘The Hunting Wives’ Author May Cobb, Naomi Sheldon & Fifth Season
summary: EXCLUSIVE: In a highly competitive situation, Apple TV has landed the rights to develop All the Little Houses, a drama series based on the recently published novel from The Hunting Wives’ May Cobb. Cobb is co-creating the show with Naomi Sheldon, of Prime Video’s The Girlfriend, who will be its writer. Fifth Season will serve […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: In a highly competitive situation, Apple TV has landed the rights to develop All the Little Houses, a drama series based on the recently published novel from The Hunting Wives’ May Cobb.

Cobb is co-creating the show with Naomi Sheldon, of Prime Video’s The Girlfriend, who will be its writer. Fifth Season will serve as the studio and Kristen Campo’s Campout Productions and Linden Entertainment will serve as executive producers.

All the Little Houses is set in the wealthy enclave of Longview, Texas, where Charleigh Anderson has clawed her way from outcast to undisputed queen bee. But when a seemingly perfect, prairie-kissed family arrives in town — complete with a trad-wife mother, woodworking father, and wholesome daughter — Charleigh finds her carefully constructed world under threat. As two formidable women go head-to-head, their battle for the soul of Longview exposes the secrets, resentments, and desires lurking beneath its picture-perfect surface.

A native Texan screenwriter and bestselling author of page-turners, Cobb is best known for The Hunting Wives, which served as the basis for the hit Southern gothic Netflix series, on which she’s an executive producer. The show premiered last summer as the third most popular on the global English-language chart, hitting the Top 10 list in 40 countries and reaching No. 1 in 10, including the U.S, with billions of minutes viewed. Starring the likes of Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman, The Hunting Wives returns for its second season on November 26.

Watch on Deadline

Cobb released All the Little Houses in January; its sequel, All the Little Secrets, is out November 17. She is repped by Victoria Sanders Agency, Jordan Cerf of Linden Productions and Darren Trattner from Jackoway.

Sheldon is a playwright, screenwriter, and actress known for co-creating The Girlfriend, a limited series based on the thriller novel by Michelle Frances, for Amazon and Imaginarium. Starring Robin Wright and Olivia Cooke, and directed by Wright, the show premiered last fall and was nominated for Best Limited Series at both the Golden Globe and Critics’ Choice Awards.

In a multi-studio bidding war, Sheldon sold her next project, an original erotic thriller, to Netflix with Media Res. Most recently, she wrapped the writers’ room for The Spot, Ed Solomon’s Hulu/A24 crime drama series starring Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor. Currently developing original projects with Carnival, Firebird, and David Jonsson’s Grey Area, she is represented by CAA, Independent Talent, and Ziffren Brittenham.

title: Sony’s Screen Gems Sets YouTube Exec Fede Goldenberg To Top Genre Label; Ashley Brucks Segues To Producer Role
summary: Sony Pictures Entertainment said Friday that it has tapped Fede Goldenberg, a veteran YouTube content partnership exec, as head of Screen Gems. He replaces Ashley Brucks, who had been President of Screen Gems since 2023. Sony said today that she will segue to a producing role on some upcoming Screen Gems projects, which were not […]
content:
Sony Pictures Entertainment said Friday that it has tapped Fede Goldenberg, a veteran YouTube content partnership exec, as head of Screen Gems.

He replaces Ashley Brucks, who had been President of Screen Gems since 2023. Sony said today that she will segue to a producing role on some upcoming Screen Gems projects, which were not named in today’s release announcing the exec shuffle.

Goldenberg will report to Sanford Panitch, President of Sony Pictures’ Motion Picture Group, who announced the hire.

The change comes amid a wave of content creator-driven genre hits at the summer box office, with Curry Barker’s Obsession, Kane Parsons’ Backrooms and Markiplier’s Iron Lung leading the way. Sony said the change atop its genre label marks a new creative strategy, saying it will “expand its longstanding focus on traditional genre films to include theatrical projects from the next generation of digital-native storytellers.”

Goldenberg has developed strong relationships in the content creator space via spending the past 15 years at YouTube after stints ant MCNs like Maker Studios and Fullscreen. Most recently at YouTube he was Head of TV & Film Content Partnerships, working with studios to boots their global footprints across the platform. He also helped drive major creator initiatives including Markiplier’s exclusive digital release of Iron Lung.

Watch on Deadline

Screen Gems’ most recently releases were Insidious: Out of the Further, which has earned $169.5 million globally after its mid-August release, and before that July’s Evil Dead: Burn in a team-up with New Line and Ghost House that grossed $72.4 million worldwide.

Brucks had arrived at Screen Gems after a tenure at Paramount that included bringing in the original Paranormal Activity. She also helped to relaunch the Scream franchise in 2022, and oversaw A Quiet Place and A Quiet Place Part II.

THR reported the Goldenberg hire earlier today.

title: Francis Coppola’s ‘Megalopolis’ Back In Theaters
summary: EXCLUSIVE: For the first time since its 2024 launch, Francis Ford Coppola’s Megalopolis will return to theaters in a limited engagement that will allow audiences to interact with the iconic director. Coppola decided when he self-financed and shot the provocative film that it would not be put through any domestic-based streaming services or DVDs produced […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: For the first time since its 2024 launch, Francis Ford Coppola’s Megalopolis will return to theaters in a limited engagement that will allow audiences to interact with the iconic director.

Coppola decided when he self-financed and shot the provocative film that it would not be put through any domestic-based streaming services or DVDs produced for the U.S. market. He felt it was now time to put it back out.

Reading International Inc. has booked the film in many its cinemas around the country, from New York to Hawaii, to screen simultaneously on October 24. Venues will include Village East Cinemas in New York City. This will be followed by a livestreamed Q&A with Coppola, moderated by his son and collaborator, Roman Coppola, who was second unit director on the picture. Audience members will be able to text their questions before, during and after the film. The filmmaker will answer the best ones live during the presentation.

“Megalopolis is back in its rightful place, theaters, and the interest in seeing it as was intended is growing,” said Coppola. “I am excited to take part in an interactive Q&A across multiple theaters simultaneously.”

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Francis Ford Coppola Reveals The Movie He Is Most Proud Of … The Answer May Surprise

Coppola spent a fortune to personally stake a film that became one of the most expensive indies ever, one he’d been dreaming about for decades. Much the way that audiences continue to discover his other films, Coppola hoped Megalopolis would follow a similar track, and that it will be viewed and debated long after he has passed away. He believes its themes of rebuilding cities and the polarizing political factions will be continually relevant. The film’s ensemble cast is headed by Adam Driver, Shia LaBeouf, Dustin Hoffman, Jon Voight, Nathalie Emmanuel, Laurence Fishburne, Aubrey Plaza and Giancarlo Esposito.

Each screening also will include hard-copy letters from Coppola given to each audience member, containing his official director’s statement about Megalopolis for audience members to read before watching the film. Each screening will also include the famed unique “Live Element,” which was only available at select screenings when the film was first released.

Megalopolis will find its way back in theaters periodically going forward, including the tradition of the film screening at multiple theaters every New Year’s Day. This fulfills a wish from Coppola to have the film be shown on this day as a symbol of coming together and discussing ideas for improvement as a society.

RELATED: Francis Coppola & ‘Megalopolis’ Star Adam Driver On “The Death Of Journalism & The Death Of The Hollywood Studio System”

title: Bill Burr on ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Sparring With Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg and Why Tech CEOs are ‘Leading Us to Ruin’
summary: Over three decades in stand-up comedy, Bill Burr has gained a reputation for saying, with gruff conviction and political fire, the thing on everyone’s mind. In Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning,” Burr gets to aim that unfiltered attitude at Mark Zuckerberg. Burr plays Charlie Garrigan in the follow-up to “The Social Network,” which […]
content:
Over three decades in stand-up comedy, Bill Burr has gained a reputation for saying, with gruff conviction and political fire, the thing on everyone’s mind. In Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning,” Burr gets to aim that unfiltered attitude at Mark Zuckerberg.

Burr plays Charlie Garrigan in the follow-up to “The Social Network,” which follows the Facebook founder during the pandemic, as an investigative journalist threatens to lay bare his company’s misdeeds while Zuckerberg, played by Jeremy Strong, grapples with his own role in fueling the Jan. 6 Capitol insurrection. Charlie, a Facebook investor-turned-critic, fictionalized for the film, shows the tech titan tough love as he helps him prepare to testify before Congress.

Burr was offered the part after Sorkin saw him in David Mamet’s Broadway production of “Glengarry Glen Ross,” in which the comic played angry salesman Dave Moss. Shortly after that performance, Burr received a call from his agent: Sorkin wanted to pitch him a movie role.

Popular on Variety

“I thought that was hilarious, because it’s like, ‘Dude, you’re Aaron Sorkin. I’d put up staging in the background with no lines to be in a movie that you’re doing,’” Burr says. “He was so humble, and he was taking the time to pitch me the role like I’m somebody. It made me feel good.”

Your character is fictional, or an amalgamation of figures from Zuckerberg’s past. Was it freeing to not have to tie your performance to a real person, or did that make things more challenging?

It eliminated the steps of me having to try to become a specific person. Although, I have to tell you, I’m still trying to get better at acting, so I would have been up for it if that was on the table. With Charlie and Zuckerberg, so much going on between these two guys. There’s a business relationship, a friendship, a falling out. I’m catching him in the crosshairs right before he goes in front of Congress, and half of the room is just teaching him how to talk to Congress so he doesn’t have to change the damage that he’s doing.

I get to say the thing that everybody is talking around, which is a very stand-up thing. So much of comedy is you just say the thing, and then it releases all of this tension. But unlike a comedy show like I do, where I’m just messing around, this is legit. This is a big problem that Facebook had. So it was definitely challenging in a really fun way.

What was it like acting opposite Jeremy Strong? I imagine his process is unlike some of the scene partners you’ve had in the past.

Well, everybody’s process is different, so it was just working across from another actor that had a different process. But we were all thrown in there together, and it was interesting because we worked six days in a row, so it really felt like we were doing the thing that [Zuckerberg and the crisis PR team] was doing.

Had you met “Jeremy” before the movie wrapped, or were you only dealing with “Zuckerberg”?

I had gone to a Broadway play he did, “An Enemy of the People,” and met him there. But that whole mystique around [Method acting] — you know, they’re playing Winnie the Pooh and they were Winnie the Pooh the whole time. Was that weird? I mean, I don’t need to be playing hacky sack with somebody in between takes. Some people are gregarious and they shoot the breeze with you right up until they say their lines. Other people get quiet. Other people go talk to a wall. At this point, I’ve been doing it long enough.

I wondered if his process helped create that sense of distance and conflict between your characters.

I think the blocking helped make that work — I was way up in the bleachers, and he was down there. That worked. In general, I was very adversarial with everybody in the room. I was interrupting the smooth speak they were giving Zuckerberg. I love all the dialogue Wunmi Mosaku has, where she tells him, “Don’t say humans.” It’s almost like being a defense attorney for an ax murderer, and you know he did it.

All these years making fun of corporations, I’ve secretly always wanted to be in a conference room. How do they talk around the fact that they know there’s lead in their toothpaste? It reminded me of that movie “Zone of Interest.” When the Nazis are talking about the victims, they call them “cargo” or something. They can’t even say what they’re doing. I find that fascinating.

Or like in “Succession,” when a low-level employee is abused they call it “NRPI”: No Real Person Involved.

The thing about these corporations is it’s nameless and faceless. The general public will get mad at a singer or a golfer or a comedian, and it’s like: “All right, buddy. Name the top 10 CEOs.” They can’t do it. But if you’re an individual who hoards hand sanitizer during a pandemic, everybody knows who you are and where you live.

Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning” ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection

I’ve heard you talk about these “nerds with apps” sort of ruining the country —

Not sort of! They are absolutely doing it. And they’re closing the door behind them and putting a tremendous amount of people out of work. Economically — forget environmentally — they’re leading us to ruin. When it’s just you making the money, how’s somebody going to buy the widget you’re making? Capitalism is great. Unregulated capitalism is frightening.

You said recently that while preparing for a scene in “The Social Reckoning,” you got emotional to the point of tears. What made you so emotional? Did the material hit close to home?

It wasn’t the material. No, that was from being walled off emotionally. This has happened to me throughout my acting career. Occasionally I will get a scene, and if my character feels a feeling that is on the spectrum of vulnerable, I can all of a sudden well up like I’m at a funeral, and I never understood what it was. The way they raised boys to be men, you weren’t allowed to feel any of those feelings, so I have walled those off for so long that I don’t feel those feelings. And when I act, these characters do. So then I have to open the vault to go in there to get disappointed or whatever. And when I open the door, what happens is literally a cry from 40 years ago gets out.

And the scene didn’t call for crying?

I forget what scene it was, but it didn’t call for crying. It’s bizarre. Instead of misdirected anger, it’s like misdirected crying. I had to cry this out by myself in a hotel room, and then the next day I was able to do the scene. I finally figured out why it was happening. When I act, all of a sudden I would just feel alive, and it was because I was opening that door that I had closed off for protection when I was a kid a long time ago.

Were you worried you might not be able to execute the scene?

I was in a sheer panic that I was going to go to set and fall apart, and it would not have made sense. Because some people think if you’re acting and you’re crying, you must be doing a good job. Well, not if it doesn’t call for that. Then it’s weird.

It’s fascinating that acting has had such a therapeutic effect on you.

Yeah, it does. I also have been doing these breathwork massages and have finally gotten rid of 90% of my childhood anger. I can say now that I’m not an angry person. I mean, I still can get angry, but it’s just another emotion. I’m not bringing my entire life experience with it, which is what I used to do. I used to walk around at an eight, and now I start at zero.

It’s like in pickup sports, when everyone’s trying to have a good time and burn some calories, and there’s always that one person bringing Game 7 energy. And you’re like, “Come on, man! I’m not trying to get my knee blown out here. There are no scouts in the stands.” My anger was like that. And getting it all out is something I’m really dedicated to.

title: Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC
summary: Jason Blum and James Wan aren’t paying much attention to the bad reviews (but massive box office success!) for “Other Mommy.” Instead, the horror maestros spent Friday night looking ahead at what’s next, unveiling Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s upcoming slate of films during the 90-minute presentation at New York Comic-Con. In the next year, the horror […]
content:
Jason Blum and James Wan aren’t paying much attention to the bad reviews (but massive box office success!) for “Other Mommy.” Instead, the horror maestros spent Friday night looking ahead at what’s next, unveiling Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s upcoming slate of films during the 90-minute presentation at New York Comic-Con.

In the next year, the horror house will launch a new installment of the “Exorcist” franchise starring Scarlett Johansson, “Violent Night 2” with Kristen Bell, new collaborations with MatPat and a revamped “Blair Witch Project.”

If you couldn’t make it to the horror-filled presentation, read below for the major takeaways from the Blumhouse panel at NYCC.

Popular on Variety

Jason Blum Addresses the Doppelganger Elephant In The Room

Despite its major box office success, “Other Mommy” debuted this weekend to an onslaught of negative reviews. One of the things that was picked apart online was the title of the film itself, particularly why it wasn’t named “Other Mother” both for the sake of the rhyme and to further the parallels between “Coraline.”

“Well, funnily enough, my partner James Wan wanted to call it ‘Other Mother,’ and he got outvoted,” Blum revealed during the panel. “This is probably why we should always listen to James Wan.”

Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ As Mrs. Clause

Kristen Bell is getting into the Christmas spirit, and no, it isn’t with “Frozen.”

The actress is joining David Harbour in “Violent Night 2,” stepping into the jolly-but-deadly shoes of Mrs. Clause.

“It was thrilling to get this call from David. I think I was so confused when he called, because I didn’t even know the were making a second one,” Bell said during the panel. “David called and said, ‘I need you to come to Winnipeg.’ And I was like, ‘What? No.'”

As a big fan of the first film, Bell shared that once she learned it was for “Violent Night 2,” she was in. She revealed David told her she would play Mrs. Clause, who is a “‘badass, and she’s every bit as capable as Santa is.’ And I said, ‘Say more.’ And we made it work.”

‘Paranormal Activity,’ ‘Blair Witch’ and ‘Saw 11’ Teased

The fan-favorite film “Paranormal Activity” is getting a modern makeover and is set to release in theaters May 21, coming alongside the news of the Broadway play’s extension into February.

“‘Parnaormal Activity’ is such an emotional movie for me, because it’s really how Blumhouse started,” Blum shared. “It really gave birth to everything that we’ve done.”

Wan and Blum announced the news with a teaser video of director Ian Tuason reenacting the infamous at-home footage of becoming posessed while sleeping overnight before turning to the camera to share the film is currently in production.

Craig Zobel Is Directing Adaptation of Comic Book Horror ‘Something Is Killing The Children’

Director Craig Zobel announced he will direct the adaptation of James Tynion IV and Werther Dell’Edera’s “Something is Killing the Children.”

Blumhouse is developing the franchise both as a live-action film and an adult animated television series, with Tynion IV spearheading the latter. Stephen Christy and James Tynion IV will produce the film for BOOM! Studios and Penguin Random House, alongside Jason Blum for Blumhouse. Shaun Sutton, Ryan Turek, Adam Yoelin and Mette Norkjaer will executive produce. Dell’Edera will as co-produce.

Blumhouse Is Making More Than Just Movies

The production company’s horror game, “Grave Seasons” is officially launching March 9, following years of teasing the game’s arrival. Blum shared they will also share prize packs that include Fortnite codes that celebrate the Purge’s Lady Liberty as part of Fortnightmares.

title: ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Producer Backs Park Syeyoung’s Memory-Bending Love Motel Drama ‘Satellite of Love’ at Busan Asian Project Market
summary: A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging her love life all along in “Satellite of Love,” the fourth feature from South Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung (“The Fin”). The project is part of […]
content:
A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging her love life all along in “Satellite of Love,” the fourth feature from South Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung (“The Fin”).

The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

The motel sits among reed beds and woods, its rooms echoing with lovers every night. When her lover walks out, the woman insists he come back in 10 years, to the day and the hour. He says no. She stays put regardless, never leaving the room and cycling through the same chores – eating, washing up, laundering the sheets – while guests check in and out around her.

Popular on Variety

A decade on, a man turns up saying he is the one who left. She doesn’t know his face, but he keeps at it, and slowly they fall in love. Then the cracks show. Their conversations start to loop. When he pleads with her to run away with him, the motel’s managers take him away.

The truth is that the motel exists to keep the woman’s feelings alive and replay them. Men brought in from outside are coached to act out romances with her again and again, performing love, regret and guilt while their tears are gathered. Once she knows this, she goes back to her routine and turns her eyes to the door, waiting again for someone to come back.

“I hope to convey the way in which our memories are so volatile and how the present can keep altering what has happened in the past,” Park says. “How nothing is definite and every memory is subject to change.”

Park has been working on his third feature, “Who Stole My Cross?,” which is now in post-production. His first two features followed groups of characters from the outside, without digging into their inner wants, while “Who Stole My Cross?” centers on a single figure. That shift pushed him further, and he wants “Satellite of Love” to be driven entirely by its character. The script is in development.

The film is produced by Coproduction Office’s Philippe Bober and creative producer Sylvain Cruiziat. The company has worked with Park on “The Masked Monster” and “The Fin,” which played Locarno in 2024 and 2025, respectively, and on “Who Stole My Cross?” Bober, who founded the company, produced Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or winners “Triangle of Sadness” and “The Square.”

The producers rank Park as a singular voice in present-day Korean cinema. “Satellite of Love” will be their fourth film together. “We are thrilled to continue supporting Syeyoung on his path as an auteur, and to accompany him on this next chapter,” they say.

At the APM, the team wants to meet potential Asian co-production partners and financiers and to put Park’s next film in front of the industry early.

Beyond “Satellite of Love,” Park is writing several commercial features he hopes to shoot in Korea alongside more personal projects he will make independently. “I will make films till I die, and I want to explore a range of financing approaches along the way,” he says.

title: LaKeith Stanfield Previews ‘Molepeople’ Movie From Paramount Primal, Blumhouse Atomic Monster at New York Comic-Con
summary: Oscar nominee LaKeith Stanfield previewed his next movie, “Molepeople,” during a special appearance at New York Comic-Con on Friday evening. Stanfield and Emmy winner Ben Mendelsohn star in the horror movie, about a man who descends into the abandoned tunnels beneath New York City, where he discovers a “twisted society lurking beneath the streets.” The […]
content:
Oscar nominee LaKeith Stanfield previewed his next movie, “Molepeople,” during a special appearance at New York Comic-Con on Friday evening.

Stanfield and Emmy winner Ben Mendelsohn star in the horror movie, about a man who descends into the abandoned tunnels beneath New York City, where he discovers a “twisted society lurking beneath the streets.”

The film — directed by Rob Savage from a script by Nathan Elston — will be co-financed and co-produced by Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Paramount Primal, with Paramount handling worldwide distribution. Onstage, Stanfield announced that “Molepeople” has been set for theatrical release on Aug. 27, 2027.

Producers include Blumhouse Atomic Monster chief Jason Blum; Paramount Primal heads J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules; and James Harris. Elston and Savage are executive producers alongside Ryan Turek and Tracy Rosenblum.

Popular on Variety

The project represents a merging between Paramount Primal — one of the key specialty labels in Skydance’s film division, specializing in “smartly budgeted” projects with a distinct point of view and “pulp sensibility” — and Blumhouse Atomic Monster — which spent two decades innovated that methodology of churning out low-budget horror hits.

Paramount Primal’s upcoming slate includes “Boys for Life,” with Alex Wolff, set for theatrical release on April 9, 2027; “Sweet Spot,” a high-concept thriller spec from writing duo Nic Curcio and Kirby Gladstein; and “The Troop,” based on the acclaimed horror novel by Nick Cutter. The label also recently acquired the U.S. rights to adapt the original screenplay for “A Nightmare on Elm Street” from the Wes Craven estate, and is developing the R-rated fantasy “Tower Defense” from writer Evan Daugherty.

In 2024, Blum’s Blumhouse merged with James Wan’s Atomic Monster; the combined company has grossed more than $10 billion in worldwide box office and has represented approximately half of the horror market over the last decade.

Blumhouse Atomic Monster has produced over 250 movies and television series, including the “Conjuring” universe, the most successful horror franchise in history; additional franchises include “Halloween,” “The Purge,” “The Black Phone,” “Annabelle,” “Paranormal Activity,” “The Exorcist,” “Insidious,” “The Nun,” “M3GAN” and “Five Nights at Freddy’s.” This year, “Obsession” and “Backrooms” became the highest-grossing films ever for Focus Features and A24, respectively, and helped Blumhouse Atomic Monster hit $1 billion in worldwide box office for the second year in a row. The company’s latest film “Other Mommy” is expected to top this week’s box office charts, despite negative reviews.

“Molepeople” marks Stanfield’s third movie with Blumhouse, following a bit part in 2014’s “The Purge: Anarchy” and a key role in Jordan Peele’s Oscar-winning 2017 film “Get Out.”

More to come…

title: ‘Below’ Creator Breaks Down the Finale’s Last Shot, Josh Hartnett’s Accent and Season 2 Clues
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the first season of “Below,” now streaming on Netflix. Netflix’s new mystery series “Below” has arrived, and audiences are being transported to the beautiful and dangerous Newfoundland town of Snook’s Arm. Josh Hartnett stars as fisherman Calvin Penney, who, alongside Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis), is investigating a […]
content:
How did you come up with the look of the giant squid?

McKeown: There was a lot of research that we did ahead of time. We talked to some experts. One was sort of like a real-life Fonda. Her name is Dr. Annie Mercier, and she works at that actual building, the Ocean Sciences Centre, which is a real place in Newfoundland. We’d talk to her just about cephalopods and how they behave. There’s a long and rich history of Architeuthis dux, the North Atlantic giant squid, in that area of Newfoundland. That’s where all the original discoveries happened. So the giant squid is very important to the history and mythology of Newfoundland. Once you open your eyes for that, you’ll see it everywhere. There’s statues of the giant squid, there’s museums dedicated to it, you see it everywhere. So it really had to be that creature for Newfoundland. But we wanted it to be more than just the North Atlantic giant squid. We want it to be something even more unknown and something more mysterious. So we talked to experts about what would plausibly be a previously undetected ancestor of the giant squid that we know, and then so we worked backward and extrapolated from that.

Rhoades: There is so much time modeling and doing scales and being able to figure out boats, houses, ships, all of those things. It was a really complex multiteam. Obviously, it was our VFX team, but it was also an SFX team. It’s everyone working with production design. Everything had to be so precise to get the scale of her right. You don’t want it to be silly, obviously, but you want it to be fun, but it had to be scary. I think one of our biggest challenges was like the scope of the eye outside of the submersible, just getting those things right.

content:
As The Exorcist makes its way back to theaters, a first look at Mike Flanagan‘s new chilling take on the horror classic has been unveiled.

On Friday, Blumhouse released the first trailer for The Exorcist: Martyrs, which premieres March 12, 2027, revealing Scarlett Johansson’s Detective Judy Miller and the demonic homicide case at the center.

In The Exorcist: Martyrs, Detective Julie Miller (Johansson) ends the killing spree of satanic Father Sunday (John Leguizamo), only for a new serial killer to drag her back into the darkness 13 years later when her name is written in the blood of a murdered altar boy on the walls of a church crypt.

Teaming up with former prison chaplain Father William (Chiwetel Ejiofor) and rookie Detective Gina Restrepo (Sasha Calle), Detective Miller discovers an ancient evil that has linked killers like H.H. Holmes, the Night Stalker and the Zodiac for generations.

Watch on Deadline

Written and directed by Flanagan, and based on characters created by The Exorcist author William Peter Blatty, the cast also includes Diane Lane, Jacobi Jupe, Scoot McNairy, Gil Bellows and Laurence Fishburne.

Producers include David Robinson and Jason Blum, with executive producers Alexandra Magistro and Ryan Turek.

title: ACFM Chief Ellen YD Kim Talks AI Development; Korean Recovery; Market Spotlights On Thailand & Japan
summary: Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the industry platform of Busan International Film Festival, launched three new programs last year, which are starting to yield results as they move into their second edition. Among these, InnoAsia hosts a range of panels, workshops and other events focusing on advanced technologies and innovative business strategies, including AI, […]
content:
Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the industry platform of Busan International Film Festival, launched three new programs last year, which are starting to yield results as they move into their second edition.

Among these, InnoAsia hosts a range of panels, workshops and other events focusing on advanced technologies and innovative business strategies, including AI, Virtual Production, microdrama, VR & AR and branded content. As ACFM market director Ellen YD Kim explains below, projects introduced through InnoAsia’s AI works-in-progress showcase last year have already gone on to raise finance and reach the international market.

Companies attending this segment of the market include Google DeepMind, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Kling AI and Alibaba Group. Kling AI, the AI video arm of China’s Kuaishou, is hosting a panel on the second day of the market, New Cinematic Possibilities: Reimagining Filmmaking, with speakers including Korean director Kim Sungsoo (12.12: The Day) and Lee Sangwook, a producer at MBC C&I AI Contents Lab.

Watch on Deadline

In addition, ACFM is hosting the second edition of DocSquare, which brings together Asian documentary filmmakers, distributors, festivals and funders. This year, the market is hosting an ‘Impact Asia Day’, during which a study of documentaries in Korea, Japan and Taiwan will be released.

Another initiative entering its second year is ‘The A’, a conference summit and in-depth report covering 15 Asian territories. This year’s panels include a session on Asian film distribution, with speakers from companies including Korea’s Noori Pictures, Thailand’s Chada Entertainment and Mongolia’s Filmbridge; and an investor panel, featuring Solaire Partners, Pathe Films and Hive Media Corp, among other speakers.

All the market’s other long-running programs are also returning – Asian Project Market (APM), which this year has selected 30 projects from 20 countries; Busan Story Market, which is presenting 25 pieces of IP from Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Indonesia; Asian Cinema Fund; Producers Hub, and Platform Busan.

Two Asian film industries will be under the spotlight at this year’s ACFM – Thailand has been anointed the first ever ‘Country of Honor’, while Japan is the ‘Focus Country’ in the Producers Hub.

Speaking to Deadline in the run-up to ACFM, Kim explains that the market aims to help the industry navigate one of its most turbulent periods – a time of mergers, shrinking capital, restructuring of platforms and the disruptions of microdrama and AI – by providing a platform to “Connect, Strengthen, and Expand”.

ACFM is taking place at BEXCO from October 10-13, during Busan International Film Festival (October 6-15).

DEADLINE: How was InnoAsia received by the Asian industry last year and what results have you seen so far?

ELLEN YD KIM: InnoAsia has established itself as the place in Asia to see where generative AI filmmaking actually stands. The industry values it for bringing together in one place the AI production tools and pipelines that global tech companies and creators are working with today.

AI projects introduced at last year’s Work-in-Progress Showcase have gone on to raise production financing and participate in the Cannes Marché du Film. Mateo AI Studio signed a promotional partnership with Kling AI; was presented at Kling AI’s session in Cannes; and raised $1.5m (KRW2bn) in pre-Series A funding. The company’s fully AI-generated feature Raphael is now being readied for release.

Producer Ham Seul-gi and director Seol Woo-in, who took part last year with an AI short, founded AIKNOW Studio and completed an AI feature, Steelay, which they will preview at this year’s WIP before it opens in Korean theaters on October 20.

Inshorts, an AI upscaling company, went from InnoAsia’s start-up strand to being presented as Korea’s representative at EFM Startups in Berlin and at Cannes Next, and has since been expanding its business with contracts in Japan, China and other Asian markets. The company returns to InnoAsia this year as an exhibitor.

DEADLINE: How are ACFM exhibitor numbers tracking this year compared to last year? Any new participants?

KIM: This year 339 institutions and companies from 32 countries and territories are exhibiting, including four with online-only booths. That is up 17% from 289 exhibitors from 31 countries last year, and the fourth consecutive year of growth, from 264 in 2023 and 275 in 2024.

The strongest interest has come from Thailand, this year’s Country of Honor, which has grown from 17 exhibitors to 28. Japan, the Producer Hub Focus Country, is now the largest international presence with 46 exhibitors. Growth across Southeast Asia is also clear: the Philippines is up from 15 to 21 exhibitors, and Cambodia from one to nine.

Europe’s presence is also notable. The UK has grown from one exhibitor last year to seven this year, with companies such as Protagonist Pictures and Cornerstone Films under the UK Film stand. Leading European sales companies including Goodfellas and Le Pacte from France, Pluto Film from Germany and Heretic from Greece. And more countries are joining for the first time or returning, among them the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Bangladesh and Kazakhstan.

The mix has changed too. Tech exhibitors have increased from seven to 18, and national agencies and film commissions from 62 to 79. The market is broadening from trading finished films into a place where technology, co-production, location attraction and the promotion of national industries feed into one another.

DEADLINE: Why did ACFM decide to spotlight Thailand and Japan this year? What strengths do these markets currently have? And what can other markets learn from them?

KIM: The two countries are taking part at different levels. Thailand is the ‘Country of Honor’ of the market as a whole. Launched this year, Country of Honor is the highest tier of ACFM’s country partnerships, and it presents a country’s industry as a whole across a wide range of ACFM’s programs. Japan is the Focus Country of Producer Hub, which works on a different scale. It concentrates on producers, and through them on the driving force of production: their projects, their co-production experience and the environment they work in.

Thailand has been developing content as a key pillar of its national soft power strategy. In 2025, the country hosted more than 540 foreign productions, and it offers eligible foreign productions cash rebates of up to 30%. At the same time, Thai titles have entered the Netflix Global Top 10, proving the competitiveness of its own content. Its strength is that it is both an international production base and a market with competitive local content.

This year Thailand presents five features as the inaugural line-up of the Busan Story Market’s new ‘Remake IP’ section; co-hosts our opening reception, and is bringing 28 exhibitors. The ties with Busan also run deep: from Pen-ek Ratanaruang’s Ploy in 2006 to last year’s APM selection, Thai projects have been traveling to the world through Busan for 20 years.

Japan today is Asia’s most dynamic co-production partner. On top of its longstanding strength in independent and arthouse cinema, bold policies centered on grants and incentives are expanding international collaboration into commercial films and series. This year ten Japanese producers will pitch their projects in Busan, including co-productions with Korea, Canada, Indonesia and France. Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunka-cho) is taking part directly for the first time.

Our focus on these two countries is the result of two governments’ determination to take their content industries overseas and meeting the partnership efforts ACFM has been steadily making. Thailand needed a market that could turn its soft power strategy into real business, and ACFM proposed the Country of Honor program. Japan, backed by new support policies, was looking for a place to meet international partners, and came to us first to say it wanted to take part as the Producer Hub Focus Country. The lesson for other markets is that a government’s commitment produces results when it meets a concrete platform ready to put it to work.

DEADLINE: The Korean industry appears to have picked up this year – at least with some big box office hits and titles selected for major festivals. What are your thoughts on the current health of the industry?

KIM: The recovery is real. Box office for the first half of this year reached $431m (KRW 579bn), up 42% on the same period last year, while admissions rose 34% to 57.05 million. Korean films led that recovery taking 64% of first-half revenue, with The King’s Warden becoming the highest-grossing film in Korean box office history.

What interests me more is the breadth. Success was not limited to period dramas and action tentpoles. Mid-sized films such as the romance Once We Were Us and horror film Salmokji: Whispering Water also succeeded, and audiences in their twenties were at the heart of it. A film’s strength and word of mouth, not its release date, are now deciding the box office. We have been reminded that audiences never left the cinema.

I also do not think the health of Korean cinema should be measured by the domestic box office alone. Korean IP and production know-how are at work inside local hits across Asia. But it’s too early to say the industry has regained its health. The King’s Warden alone accounted for 28% of first-half revenue, and a single distributor took close to half the market.

While the theatrical market grew, the number of Korean releases fell by 22. The average return on Korean commercial films in 2025 was minus 33%, the lowest since the pandemic, and in June one of the major cinema chains filed for corporate rehabilitation. A recovery that leans on one hit is not unique to Korea either: this year’s The A Report shows the same pattern in India, China and Taiwan.

So I see this as a rebound, not yet a structural recovery. Audience demand has been confirmed, and so has the strength of Korean IP. The task now is to rebuild a production base that can steadily supply films of varied scale to meet that demand.

DEADLINE: Has the Korean government introduced any new policies to support the industry since ACFM took place last year?

KIM: There has clearly been policy change over the past year – in three directions. First, production support has grown sharply. The Mid-Budget Film Production Support Program, introduced last year, supported nine films with $7.5m (KRW10bn) in its first year. This year the main budget of about $15m (KRW20bn) was joined by a supplementary budget of about $19m (KRW25.8bn), supporting 32 films in total.

In a single year the budget has more than quadrupled and the number of films has more than tripled. The cap on support per film rose from $1.2m (KRW1.5bn) to $1.9m (KRW2.5bn). The selections include new films by Byun Young-joo, Lee Joon-ik and Um Tae-hwa. Development funding rose by more than 80% and the government’s contribution to the film account of the Fund of Funds increased to $36.5m (KRW49bn). Public money is filling the space that private investment has left.

Second, international co-production and technology have become policy priorities. A new international co-production category within the mid-budget program selected Bound, by Australian director Eddy Bell, which on completion will be the first Korea-Australia co-production. The supplementary-budget selections include a new film by Japanese director Koji Fukada, which is also a recipient of this year’s Co-Production Support Fund from ACFM’s Asian Cinema Fund.

The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has separately launched a pilot program for co-productions and Korea and Canada signed an audiovisual co-production treaty this year. The AI-related budget has tripled and a new AI Film Production Support Program has been introduced.

Third, this direction continues into next year. In the government’s 2027 budget proposal, announced in September, film support is set at $128.6m (KRW172.6bn), about 30% more than this year. Support for international co-productions would rise from six films to 14, and a new program would support foreign productions shooting in Korea.

There are also issues still under debate. On the issue of holdbacks, the window between theatrical release and online release, the government and the industry had aimed to reach a voluntary agreement by August, but did not. Discussion also continues on bringing streaming platforms into the legal framework for the audiovisual industry, and on requiring them to contribute to the film fund.

That said, a bigger budget does not by itself solve the problem. Policy funding also grew last year, yet actual investment was slow to follow. Investors say there are too few projects worth investing in, while producers say they cannot find money. Closing that gap is the next task, and it is the reason we created the Investor Summit within The A Summit this year.

title: ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Other Performers Injured On Set
summary: EXCLUSIVE: A number of recent injuries on the set of Season 10 of ABC’s 9-1-1 has put the production’s safety protocols under scrutiny again. Deadline understands that four performers, including star Oliver Stark, have sustained stunt-related injuries to varying degrees in recent months. While the incidents do not seem to be connected, the unfortunate timing […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: A number of recent injuries on the set of Season 10 of ABC‘s 9-1-1 has put the production’s safety protocols under scrutiny again.

Deadline understands that four performers, including star Oliver Stark, have sustained stunt-related injuries to varying degrees in recent months. While the incidents do not seem to be connected, the unfortunate timing does highlight the challenges with making a stunt-heavy show like 9-1-1 on a broadcast network schedule.

A spokesperson for 20th Television, which produces the series, declined to comment for this story.

In late August, Stark broke his ankle while performing a stunt and required surgery. Sources close to production say that production continued in the wake of the incident and Stark has since returned to work. While reports of the injury surfaced online, the details of the incident have not yet been shared.

Watch on Deadline

Sources tell Deadline that the stunt involved a firefighter swinging from a car over a set piece to the ladder truck. We understand that, during rehearsals, a stunt double sprained an ankle performing the same stunt and declined medical treatment, so no injury report was submitted to production.

On the 9-1-1 set, production sources say it is typical for stunts to be practiced first with heavyweight bags so the stunt coordinators and other crew members can better understand the necessary weight distribution, etc. Then, the set piece is rehearsed with stunt doubles to work out any issues before the actors come in for their own rehearsal.

In Stark’s case, we’re told the mechanics of the stunt were adjusted after the stunt double was injured. Sources indicate that, still, Stark rolled his ankle over another performer in the scene.

Two other injuries followed in subsequent weeks. In one incident, a stunt person injured their arm on a piece of the set that had jagged metal on it, requiring a hospital visit and stitches. Within the last two weeks, another stunt performer was sent to the hospital after a stunt gone wrong. Sources close to production say the hospital trip was “precautionary” after an “awkward landing” on a platform designed to simulate a ground collapse resulted in a broken rib and minor compressed lung. It’s unclear whether this performer has returned to work.

All SAG-AFTRA signatories, including 20th Television owner Disney, are required to follow certain on-set safety protocols. Stunt performers and coordinators are required to complete a general safety and injury prevention program in order to remain eligible for employment on union productions.

The standards and practices for set safety are developed by Contract Services’ industry wide safety committee. The general guidelines for stunts task production management with ensuring they “allow enough time for rehearsals, training, equipment preparations, and inspections,” per the company’s latest stunt safety bulletin. Contract Services also has more detailed guidelines for specific stunt work.

Typically, the stunt coordinator leads all stunt-related preparations including script review, planning, site selection, preparation, testing, rehearsal, modification, and recommendation of the qualified personnel and equipment to be utilized to perform the stunt. The first assistant director is responsible for holding an on-set safety meeting prior to any stunt work so all involved personnel can see a walk-through of the maneuver and discuss protocol in detail. Another safety meeting is required if there are any “substantive changes” to the stunt.

A concentration of injuries on a single season of television doesn’t necessarily indicate negligence, especially on a high-octane show like 9-1-1. However, it is ambitious for a series like 9-1-1 to pull off massive stunt sequences on a regular basis given the restraints of working within the relatively tight production schedule required of broadcast shows, making it more likely for problems to occur.

Two years ago, a crew member died from a cardiac event while driving home from set after the workday ballooned to 14 hours due to complications with a controlled burn that was being used for a stunt. Still, a production source told Deadline at the time that 9-1-1 was “one of the safest that I’ve ever worked on.”

title: Ella Langley Cancels Tulsa Show Over “Serious Security Threat”
summary: UPDATED with Tulsa PD’s statement: Ella Langley has been forced to skip the Tulsa, Oklahoma stop on her Dandelion Tour for the safety of herself and fans. Hours before the chart-topping “Choosin’ Texas” artist was set to take the stage at BOK Center, she announced the concert’s cancellation over a “serious security threat” posed to […]
content:
UPDATED with Tulsa PD’s statement: Ella Langley has been forced to skip the Tulsa, Oklahoma stop on her Dandelion Tour for the safety of herself and fans.

Hours before the chart-topping “Choosin’ Texas” artist was set to take the stage at BOK Center, she announced the concert’s cancellation over a “serious security threat” posed to the event.

“Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show,” she wrote on her Instagram Story. “This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team.”

Langley added, “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.”

Watch on Deadline

Tulsa PD’s Captain Richard G. Meulenberg IV noted in a statement that it was Langley’s team who made the decision to cancel the show.

After doing a standard pre-sweep with BOK Center and bomb-sniffing dogs, Meulenberg explained “a call came in saying that someone’s going to do great harm to the people here at this event,” which could include gunshots or an explosion.

“So, we came out again in an over abundance of caution, used our bomb dogs again, searched the entire area,” said Meulenberg. “We could not find a credible threat here at the BOK Center.”

The venue confirmed the cancellation on their own social media, noting that details regarding ticket refunds “will be shared as soon as possible.”

“The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed,” said the BOK Center. “We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first.”

Langley’s Dandelion Tour, accompanying her sophomore studio album, comes after the lead single “Choosin’ Texas” became the longest-running No. 1 song on the Billboard Hot 100. The tour is scheduled to continue on Saturday at the United Supermarkets Arena in Lubbock, Texas.

title: ‘Stargate’ Series From ‘WandaVision’ Creator Jac Schaeffer In Works At Amazon
summary: A new Stargate series is in the works at Amazon MGM Studios. WandaVision creator Jac Schaeffer is developing the series under her overall deal with the studio, sources confirmed to Deadline. Joby Harold and Tory Tunnell also will executive produce the project, along with Schaeffer. A writers room has opened in New York, we’re told. […]
content:
A new Stargate series is in the works at Amazon MGM Studios. WandaVision creator Jac Schaeffer is developing the series under her overall deal with the studio, sources confirmed to Deadline.

Joby Harold and Tory Tunnell also will executive produce the project, along with Schaeffer. A writers room has opened in New York, we’re told.

Amazon declined to comment.

This is the second try at a new Stargate series. A reboot of the popular MGM IP from Stargate veteran Martin Gero received a series order by Prime Video in November 2025, but it June it was revealed that the project would not be moving forward. The show had completed a 20-week writers room and was in pre-production in the UK when it was pulled, sources told Deadline at the time.

Stargate was among the first MGM titles identified for series or film adaptations following Amazon’s $8.5B acquisition of the storied Hollywood studio in 2022.

Watch on Deadline

The franchise launched in 1994 with the feature film Stargate, created by Roland Emmerich and Dean Devlin. The film spawned several Stargate series – Stargate SG-1, which aired from 1997–2007, spinoff Stargate Atlantis, from 2004-2009 and Stargate Universe from 2009-2011. Animated series Stargate Infinity aired from 2002-2003.

Variety was first to report the news.

title: Vietnamese Horror ‘Arithmadtic’ Leads Bee Entertainment’s Busan Market Slate, With New Film From ‘The Corpse’ Director
summary: Psychological horror “Arithmadtic,” set in an elite international school, leads a genre-heavy slate that Vietnam’s Bee Entertainment is presenting to buyers at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM). Vietnamese films grossed more than VND3 trillion ($114 million) at home in 2025, outperforming international titles in the local market for the first time. Bee is […]
content:
Psychological horror “Arithmadtic,” set in an elite international school, leads a genre-heavy slate that Vietnam’s Bee Entertainment is presenting to buyers at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

Vietnamese films grossed more than VND3 trillion ($114 million) at home in 2025, outperforming international titles in the local market for the first time. Bee is aiming to take that momentum abroad.

Its slate pairs four features, all set for release in 2027, with three long-form TV dramas at various stages of production. The company is using the market to find partners for investment, co-development and distribution, as well as rights licensing deals.

Popular on Variety

Anh Thu, known for the 2007 Vietnam-South Korea co-production “Muoi: The Legend of a Portrait,” and Lam Thanh My (“Yellow Flowers on the Green Grass”) star in “Arithmadtic,” or “Cong Tru Nhan Chia” in Vietnamese. The film’s campus is styled after the Dark Academia aesthetic. The story centers on a transfer student’s enigmatic bond with a teacher, as a string of unexplained, supernatural incidents cracks the school’s polished facade.

Phuong Tra My, who played the lead in “The Third Wife,” which premiered at Toronto and won the NETPAC Award, joins the cast alongside Chu Anh Tuan, Cong Ninh, Hoang Minh Hung and Dac Thang. The film is directed by Irving Ly, whose short “Close the Eye to See” played BFI Flare and the Korea Queer Film Festival and won a Silver Kite at Vietnam’s 2025 Golden Kite Awards. It opens in January 2027.

Three more features are set for release across 2027. Tran Nhan Kien, who trained at the Asian Film School and took part in the Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival’s B.I.G NAFF Fantastic Film School, directs “The Step-Mother.” It follows a boy who has lost his father, as his relationship with his stepmother moves from conflict and misunderstanding to the blurry line between strictness and care. It is dated for the second quarter.

Pom Nguyen directed “The Corpse” franchise, whose first two installments grossed more than VND280 billion ($10.7 million) combined. Next up from Pom Nguyen is “How to Find a Fortune in 60 Days,” which combines action, comedy and family drama, due in the third quarter. Le Ha Nguyen’s “Dealing With a Ghost,” a horror romantic comedy, closes the film slate with a fourth-quarter release.

On the series side, “The Unrecognized Heir,” an 80-episode family drama directed by Trac Huynh Nhat Tan, began airing on VTV9 in December 2025 and has already drawn 1 billion views across social media platforms, according to the company. “A Deal With God,” a 65-episode series directed by Dang Minh Quoc, mixes family drama with comedy and fantasy. Trac also directs “Destined to Find You,” an 80-episode romance now in post-production.

A subsidiary of Bee Comm, Bee Entertainment invests in, produces, releases and sells both Vietnamese and foreign films. Founded in 2009, Bee Comm produces the Vietnamese edition of “Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?” and the social-impact program “Mai Am Gia Dinh Viet” (“The Vietnamese Family Shelter”).

The ACFM runs through Oct. The 31st Busan International Film Festival closes Oct. 15.

title: Cambodian Remake of Korean Mother-Daughter Drama ‘Wedding Dress’ Leads Abnormal Studios’ Busan Market Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: A Phnom Penh-set reworking of Kwon Hyung-jin’s 2010 South Korean drama “Wedding Dress” is the lead title for Malaysia’s Abnormal Studios at this year’s Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, where the company is selling the film ahead of its local release. The new version centers on Dalin, a single mother who designs bridal […]
content:
A Phnom Penh-set reworking of Kwon Hyung-jin’s 2010 South Korean drama “Wedding Dress” is the lead title for Malaysia’s Abnormal Studios at this year’s Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, where the company is selling the film ahead of its local release.

The new version centers on Dalin, a single mother who designs bridal gowns and whose devotion to her job has opened a gap between her and her 10-year-old daughter Mina. A terminal diagnosis shifts her priorities, and she sets about readying everything she thinks the girl will need for a happy life once she has died.

The Cambodian adaptation is the first feature from Huang Han, whose earlier work has screened at the Berlin, Busan and Pingyao film festivals. It keeps the core of the mother-daughter story while anchoring it in the day-to-day life and emotional textures of the region.

Popular on Variety

Also on the slate is “The Hungry One,” Venezuelan horror director Alejandro Hidalgo’s upcoming feature. His credits include “No Voltees” (2024); “The Exorcism of God” (2021), which was distributed in more than 150 countries; and his 2013 breakout “The House at the End of Time,” Venezuela’s top-grossing horror film.

The story follows Emily, a white American woman whose Chinese husband takes her to visit his relatives’ ancestral home in Malaysia over the 15-day Hungry Ghost Festival, when the boundary with the underworld is lifted and ghosts wander among the living. A mounting series of eerie encounters puts everything she cares about at risk.

The film is in pre-production, and its producers are working to close the last round of financing.

The company is also handling “Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,” an independent cannibal black comedy-horror from Feisal and Iskander Azizuddin. In it, two friends with nothing to lose become hooked on power after hitting on a winning spicy beef jerky recipe made with human flesh.

From Malaysia comes sci-fi fantasy “Mimpi Kita: Castle in the Air,” which pits a simulated world against a dystopian real one as it asks what children owe their parents. The project took part in the It Project section of the NAFF Project Market at Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival this year.

The wider pan-Asian lineup features “Because of You Ka Kui,” a film celebrating Canto rock frontman Wong Ka Kui which, according to the company, has drawn strong fan support in select territories, and “Next Stop, Somewhere,” a drama led by Hong Kong veteran Anthony Wong. From Cambodia comes fish-out-of-water rom-com “Far Away Close to You,” which plays on the might-have-beens of youthful romance.
