Doubleday may be best known for her work on USA’s Emmy-winning drama “Mr. Robot,” in which she played a conflicted employee at the series’ central villainous tech concern, E Corp. As she tells Variety, on the week of “The Social Reckoning’s” release, the way technology affects our cognition is a live concern for her, and has had direct consequences in her own life.

When you first read the script, did you have a vision for Kaylee? Did she remind you of anyone or anything that you thought you might draw on?

I live in Los Angeles, and I know what’s going on in the world. And I actually have known a couple of people who were radicalized, and they actually came to mind. During COVID, I was actually pre-med for like three seconds.

Whoa! What?

Yeah, there was nothing to do. But that’s a big thing to do. It was actually really difficult — cell bio is just excruciating. But I actually knew a couple people that were in the pre-med track and who were radicalized. And to know them so well and find that out was … I didn’t really understand. I think I still don’t quite understand how that happens. How can you understand the organelles of a human cell and understand what the scientific method is and how important facts are, and yet still believe that COVID can come from a 5G tower?

I remember they were showing me these videos, and I couldn’t make sense of it. And so that’s kind of where I started with my own personal experience of what happens to a person. Repeated exposure can start to make extreme ideas feel normal. I kept thinking, “They’re in an echo chamber, and they’re seeing these really bizarre videos that look like they’re made in a basement, and they’re seeing them so often that I think they just have acclimated to the fact that there are these possibilities that they want to be in on.” They want to be cracking the conspiracy or these other truths that are not being examined.

So I started there, and built from that place. I started to better understand how does a seemingly normal person turn out to be the one that you see in the beginning of the movie. What is that process like?

That’s an interesting perspective, and one that I think is important in contemporary life and for this movie — that the radicalized are not some strange, naive other people, but people like you or I who fell prey to incredibly powerful technology.

I think it’s the important perspective to have, because often I think that people see these videos and they think, “Oh, that’s a very faraway person. Something is wrong with them. They were raised and born that way.” That’s how I viewed it. You know, I viewed it as really away from me, and that’s not what happened. And so, having close relationships with people who were lovely and finding this out about believing in Pizzagate, I was really interested in the social science perspective of that. You know, what does gaslighting look like in human form?

And I think that that’s also what [Kaylee] is in the movie, right? She’s the human component. What happens up close when one human is affected by this huge company’s massive influence? Or what can happen when you have that much power to influence the way that people think, especially when you’re giving them repeated exposure to certain ways of thinking?

I interviewed Aaron Sorkin for a different story, and he mentioned that he’d had conversations with Frances Haugen, and that the character you play is drawn from a real story from Frances’ life. What were the conversations you had with him about Kaylee like?

I think Aaron wanted it to be really grounded. That was really important, especially because — and we talked about this a lot — we didn’t want the moment to be about being under the influence, [as if] that is why this person is acting this way, but that this is actually how she feels. So we spent a lot of time grounding it and making sure that you saw what Frances saw with her friend, what we see online, and what my experience was with people that I’ve met that have just fallen into QAnon radicalization. It was really important that it felt real.

A couple of things are happening that I think are easy to see: the entitlement and the victimization. Like she’s the victim in that moment; she feels perpetrated. And why is that? To dumb it down to “She’s a racist” would be reductive of what’s going on. That’s not really what that moment’s about. It’s: How do people, over time, change — especially with repeated exposure and influence? I remember watching these videos and thinking there’s something so emotional about it. It’s almost like an emotional addiction, and you become a part of a group, or you become a part of some way to vindicate yourself from your own pain or your own victimization by making somebody else the enemy to sort of justify the anger that you have within yourself. Those are the things that I brainstormed with him about because I was concerned [that it might] fall into this trap of “Oh, this drunk girl that’s just super erratic.”

I want to talk about the nuts and bolts of acting the scene. Sorkin writes very rhythmic dialogue that is meant to be delivered note-perfect down to the comma. And, in the scene, you’re slurring your words. Did this present a special challenge?

I was scared about that, actually. I remember Aaron sort of said this when we were rehearsing. He was like, “Just trust the words. They’ll save you.” Trust that you can land on them — and that is true. I don’t know how to explain it, but there is something unbelievably comforting, and I knew it when I read it, when I first got it … It infects your body, that rhythm. If you can get that rhythm in your body, it just feels like molasses. It just sort of runs together because he’s so brilliant. It affords the actor, actually, the ability to live within the constraints of words that you know are going to catch you. So instead of feeling like you might have to add or create a beat or figure out how to pull your truth out of a moment, he makes that process unbelievably effortless.

We actually shot it in two days, which was lovely, because it was a pretty heavy scene, you know.

How did you feel at the halfway mark, walking into night two?

When the stakes feel this high when you’re working with someone, I just let myself feel. Because I trust him to know how to direct me, and he’s approachable and really funny and really warm, and what a joy to feel like “Hey, this lands.” I felt like I had the liberty to play a little bit. It was more about finding the level that he wanted. Where does that escalation begin, and why? Like, where is the moment where this person decides that they’re going to turn this night into what you saw? And I think that there is that moment where she’s sort of calculating; there’s like a moment where it turns, and I think he was really specific about that. I’m always nervous, but thankfully, he’s a great director, so that gave me the liberty to try different levels and see what worked and what didn’t.

I’ve been comparing your work here to Rooney Mara’s at the start of “The Social Network”: It’s a one-scene performance, but it defines everything that follows, and we briefly glimpse each character again. In your case, you had to act as Kaylee storming the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. How did that feel to shoot?

I remember Jan. 6 and how I felt that day, and … I never thought that I would be doing this. I never thought I would actually have to put myself in those shoes. And it made me really, really sad. I don’t want to get too emotional. It just made me really sad, because I had some space from it — especially given how loud things are, and there’s constant stuff going on every single day. But to actually be in that, there’s just something so tragic.

That’s why I appreciated playing this character so much — because she’s a human consequence. She is the one who would be there. Behind amplifying extremism and misinformation and Facebook’s hand in this: What is this doing to one person that ends up being there? I was grateful to examine someone who has been part of what I’ve criticized — but it was really challenging. I had mixed feelings about it. Even that day, [Sorkin] kept saying, “Turn around and take in where you are, and [take in] that those people really believed it.” That’s what’s so gut-wrenching: [they’re] really believing that they’re doing the right thing. And that is what produces, for me, the anger and the rage and the sadness. That they feel how I feel when I’m standing up for something that I believe in. It’s the same.

I first saw you on “Mr. Robot,” which was a show all about how the digital world is not separate from our real lives — it’s hopelessly intertwined with them, redefining reality. “The Social Reckoning” has similar concerns. Do you spend a lot of time thinking about these issues?

Yeah, of course. I don’t really share too much online. I just talk to myself about how angry I am about things that are going on. And it’s interesting how people feel about AI, because watching this film, you see this person who may have had a good idea to connect people, and the consequences of it being this massive, and having this much influence and the ability to radicalize small groups of people who can actually cause a lot of harm. Where we’re at with AI, I feel like it’s really comparable. I don’t really think we fully understand the implications of what this is going to do to the world, and we’re sort of at the precipice. As a ’90s child, I’m just like, what is happening? The entire world is just going to massively change, and there’s going to be huge consequences to these changes. And who’s thinking about that? You know, like who’s ensuring that we’re actually going to be OK?

That’s what I’ve been thinking about the most after “Robot.” I spend time concerned about it — I’m sure you do too. A lot of people do. Look what happened at Facebook. So what’s going to happen now with OpenAI? What is our future going to look like?

We could discuss that for hours, and I think we’d emerge pretty dispirited. But I wanted to close the loop: What ended up happening with your pre-med studies?

It was like the most incredible experience I’ve ever had. To be honest, taking the bio classes I took opened my brain to a whole different world. But I just was like, I still want to be an actress, and I don’t know if I can make a 20-year commitment. You know what I mean? I don’t know. Can I go 16 hours and just eat Top Ramen?

I still think about it, though. It took me 20 years to finish my degree because my parents didn’t want me to become an actor. My dad was all about, you know, “If you’re stupid, you’re going to be evil, and you have to be smart.” And so it took me 20 years, but I got my B.A. — I took a little pre-med journey, and I finished! I’m not actually pre-med. But who knows what will happen?

This interview has been condensed and edited.

title: ‘Squadron 42’ Release Nears as Cloud Imperium Opens Steam Wishlist
summary: Cloud Imperium Games’ “Squadron 42” is now available to wishlist on Steam ahead of its planned Q2 2027 release. The single-player sci-fi adventure game is set in the year 2945, as the United Empire of Earth is threatened by outlaws and hostile aliens alike. Players enlist as a rookie in the UEE Navy and embark […]
content:
Cloud Imperium Games’ “Squadron 42” is now available to wishlist on Steam ahead of its planned Q2 2027 release.

The single-player sci-fi adventure game is set in the year 2945, as the United Empire of Earth is threatened by outlaws and hostile aliens alike. Players enlist as a rookie in the UEE Navy and embark on a dangerous journey through the galactic war. Aboard a massive capital ship, players work alongside a dynamic crew to earn their rank.

The game takes place within the universe of “Star Citizen,” Cloud Imperium Games’ multiplayer online experience that has been gestating for nearly 15 years. The CIG team has been developing “Star Citizen” simultaneously with “Squadron 42,” which follows a focused single-player narrative adventure rather than a multiplayer game style. Much of the technology and game systems utilized in “Star Citizen” is repurposed for “Squadron 42,” game designer and CIG founder Chris Roberts told Variety in May.

Popular on Variety

Its star-studded cast includes Mark Hamill, Gary Oldman, Gillian Anderson, Ben Mendelsohn, Henry Cavill, Andy Serkis, John Rhys-Davies, Jonathan Bailey, Mark Strong, Alix Wilton Reagan, Ben Mendelsohn, Damson Idris, Liam Cunningham, Jane Perry and more.

“Squadron 42” is powered by StarEngine proprietary technology, which has been developed in-house at Cloud Imperium Games. The independent studio was co-founded in 2012 by game designer Roberts, the mind behind the ‘90s PC game “Wing Commander,” alongside wife Sandi Roberts.

“Squadron 42” is slated for release in Q2 2027. Players can now wishlist the game on Steam.

title: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Warns A.I. Models Are “Being Trained To Hijack Your Intimacy”
summary: In a new video interview for The New York Times, actor Joseph Gordon-Levitt, serving as the United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance, has some concerning words about the impact of artificial intelligence. Things like the “decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy” and the hijacking “of your intimacy.” The video interview takes […]
content:
In a new video interview for The New York Times, actor Joseph Gordon-Levitt, serving as the United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance, has some concerning words about the impact of artificial intelligence. Things like the “decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy” and the hijacking “of your intimacy.”

The video interview takes place as Gordon-Levitt is in en route to address world leaders and officials gathered at the U.N. on the impact of A.I.

Watch the full video below.

First question: Why should the public listen to an actor on A.I. safety?

“Very fair question,” Gordon-Levitt responds. “Why listen to an actor? Don’t listen to an actor. You should read Human Compatible by Stuart Russell. Go look up Yoshua Bengio. Read posts by people who work in alignment and safety and policy. You don’t want to read all those things? Well, I did! So, you know, if you want to listen to me, that’s a shortcut.”

Watch on Deadline

Gordon-Levitt continues, “What we don’t want is a bunch of people confused or apathetic while these very fast-moving businesses design the future by themselves, just in the interests of their own profits. A lot of what needs to happen, I think, has to do with communication, which is ultimately kind of what acting or filmmaking is.”

At one point in the direct-to-cell phone-camera interview, Gordon-Levitt is asked what he fears most about A.I.

“At the risk of annoying The New York Times,” he responds, “I would object to that question just because reducing these concerns into one sound bite of fear — that’s one of the problems. To me, saying: Oh, I’m scared that A.I. could exterminate all of humanity — that doesn’t really get at the substance of the concern. There’s real validity to that concern. But that’s not the thing that really worries me.

“The thing that worries me is a lot more complicated and a lot more boring to talk about, because it’s a lot more dense. The decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy. These companies are betting on the notion that they’re going to take over the entire economy. That would be totalitarianism, and that would be really bad.”

He continues, “Simultaneously, these models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it. We shouldn’t be scared of an A.I. We should be concerned about the people building A.I.”

When Gordon-Levitt, a co-founder of Creators Coalition on A.I. and recently named one of Time magazine’s 100 most influential “innovators, leaders, and thinkers” on the topic, is asked to explain the “human-centric digital governance” phrase in his U.N. title, the actor concedes “it’s sort of a mouthful.”

“It just means that digital technology should be governed by people and for people,” he says. “’A.I.’ is nothing but algorithmically recombined, human-produced data. It’s humans. Calling it artificial intelligence sort of decenters humans. It offers this kind of magical fictitious character, this A.I. that we’ve seen in various sci-fi movies, but really — really all it is is us. It’s us.”

On whether the “slow-moving” U.N. can force a “fast-moving” Silicon Valley to play by certain rules, Gordon-Levitt responds, “To be honest, this is one of the things that I have found sort of daunting or troubling. I don’t know the answer. I think if it does take, say, seven years for the U.N. to put together an internationally agreed upon regulatory framework for A.I., then seven years from now we’ll be glad that we started now.”

title: Oscars: UK Selects ‘Rehearsals For A Revolution’ For Best International Feature Film
summary: The UK has selected Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals For A Revolution as its entry to the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards. The film explores Iranian filmmaker Ahangarani’s experience of exile as she rebuilds her life and creative practice in London, through five portraits of relatives and mentors, which are also expressions […]
content:
The UK has selected Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals For A Revolution as its entry to the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards.

The film explores Iranian filmmaker Ahangarani’s experience of exile as she rebuilds her life and creative practice in London, through five portraits of relatives and mentors, which are also expressions of resistance. The UK played an integral role in the film’s journey, serving as the base where it was written.

Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, Ahangaran retraces more than 40 years of Iran’s history. From the early days of 1979, until the war that began in 2026, she pieces together intimate and collective memories, forming the portrait of a country shaped by political repression and in constant hope for a revolution.

Sony Pictures Classics, which acquired North America, Latin America, Asia (except Japan), New Zealand, Turkey Portugal, and global airlines out of Cannes, announced the selection of the film as the UK’s entry and also detailed release plans.

Watch on Deadline

The distributor said it will give the film qualifying runs in New York and L.A. in December. It will then open it exclusively at Landmark’s Nuart Theatre in L.A. and the Film Forum in New York on January 8, 2027, before rolling it out across the country over the following weeks.

The deeply personal debut feature premiered as a Special Screening at the Cannes Film Festival where it won the L’Oeil d’Or (Golden Eye), and played last month at the Telluride Film Festival and Toronto International Film Festival.

It was recently honored with an Albie Award from the Maysles Documentary Center, an award honoring those who inspire, not only through their work, but also through their roles as mentors, role models, and champions of social justice.

“How extraordinary to see Pegah’s remarkable film recognized in this category. From winning the L’Oeil d’Or at Cannes to the standing ovations at TIFF and now this recognition, Rehearsals For A Revolution is building incredible momentum and marking a significant moment for a formidable female filmmaker creating in exile from her home country,” said SPC in a statement.

“This selection in the Best International Feature category has the potential to be truly transformative for the film, opening doors to audiences around the world while shining a spotlight on Pegah’s extraordinary talent and her vital voice. It’s a recognition that will have a lasting impact not only on the life of this film, but on Pegah’s future career as a filmmaker.”

title: Netflix’s ‘The Blue Road’ Director Han Jun-hee On Taking Risks With Stories & Shooting In Japan
summary: Korean writer-director Han Jun-hee talked strategies for getting audiences to respond to risky or unfamiliar material in a masterclass at Netflix’s Creative Asia day at Busan International Film Festival. “There has to be risk for something to be interesting. Only if you take risks can you tell an interesting story. Trying to play it safe […]
content:
Korean writer-director Han Jun-hee talked strategies for getting audiences to respond to risky or unfamiliar material in a masterclass at Netflix’s Creative Asia day at Busan International Film Festival.

“There has to be risk for something to be interesting. Only if you take risks can you tell an interesting story. Trying to play it safe all the time, especially in Korea, is a risk in itself,” said Han, who is involved in two series premiering in Busan’s On Screen section – The Blue Road, which he wrote and directed, and Dead-End Job, which he created.

In a talk moderated by Netflix Korea content manager Kim Kijae, Han explained how he approached his breakout hit series D.P. (2021), about Korean military police on a mission to catch deserters, and Weak Hero Class (2022), about bullying and high school violence. Han wrote and directed D.P. while he served as creative director on Weak Hero Class.

Watch on Deadline

“When it comes to army stories, some people think only guys can relate; but for female audience, they all have fathers or brothers who might have been in the army. If you think outside of the box, it could be an interesting story,” Han said.

In the case of Weak Hero Class, which revolved around a group of male friends and features a lot of fighting, Han said: “In Korea, the perception is that this genre can only be made into a film with a small budget. And again, the story looks like it might only appeal to guys. But we all went through high school; met friends there, got jealous of someone, wanted to be someone; these are universal feelings. Then we also added action to the story.”

Half joking, Han also said that casting a trio of hot, young actors – Park Ji-hoon, Choi Hyun-wook and Hong Kyung – was a conscious decision to draw in female audiences. But he also noted that all three have gone on to prove themselves as talented actors and big stars. Park starred in The King’s Warden, released earlier this year, which has become the highest-grossing Korean film of all time.

Han also talked about the importance of working with new directors as he stepped back from the directing role for Weak Hero Class: “We have so many new talents emerging, so we can help them make something great, and by bringing in an emerging director, I knew Weak Hero Class would really shine.”

Moving on to 2024 feature Pilot, Han described how he used genre, in this case comedy, to convey a message to the audience. Directed by Kim Han-gyul, the film is an adaptation of 2012 Swedish film Cockpit about a pilot who pretends to be his own younger sister after being fired from his job.

“When we gave the script to the main actor [Jo Jung-suk], he responded in just three days. He said he wanted to try different things in comedy and felt this part could go deeper than being a superficial comedy role,” Han recalled.

“With all the writers and directors I work with, if we take on something we’re not familiar with, we have to show that we understand it,” he added. “We can’t be prejudiced or biased. Whatever the story, I don’t think there’s a topic we can’t cover in a series or film. I don’t think you can say, ‘This isn’t commercial enough.’ If you have a message you want to convey to the audience, what is it you want to say? That is the most important part of filmmaking.”

He took a similar approach when creating Dead-End Job, directed by Kim Da-min, which deals with a serious subject, the vagaries of the labor market, but also uses genre to convey a message: “When the scriptwriters first brought this to me, Netflix said it’s either going to be a short film or not work out at all. The story needed to be told in a familiar way to resonate with people, so that’s why we thought a fantasy element would be interesting.”

Han also talked about The Blue Road, his return to directing, based on a manhwa about two detectives from Korea and Japan who form an alliance to track down a serial killer staging high-profile murders in both countries. While the two detectives have to navigate different working styles and jurisdictional hurdles, Han said the crews in the two countries also found they had to overcome cultural differences.

“Korean crews are very fast and flexible, while Japanese teams are meticulous and prepare everything very carefully. Neither way is better or worse; just different,” Han said.

“Japanese crew members all have unique roles to play and focus on getting everything perfect, while in Korean teams, we all help out on everything and do it quickly. If it doesn’t work out, we just try it again. At first, there were lots of misunderstandings, but we found we had a lot to learn from each other and eventually found a way to make it all work.”

The Blue Road is streaming on Netflix from November 20, while Dead-End Job is scheduled for October 30. The third series premiering in Busan’s On Screen section, Disney+’s The Remarried Empress, is streaming from November 4.

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London
summary: Spanish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi delved into the generational trauma behind award-winning film La Bola Negra at Deadline’s Contenders London. The feature – revolving around the interconnected stories of three gay men in 1932, 1937 and 2017 – took its cue from Alberto Conejero’s 2013 play La piedra oscura, which in turn was […]
content:
Spanish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi delved into the generational trauma behind award-winning film La Bola Negra at Deadline’s Contenders London.

The feature – revolving around the interconnected stories of three gay men in 1932, 1937 and 2017 – took its cue from Alberto Conejero’s 2013 play La piedra oscura, which in turn was inspired by García Lorca’s unfinished play La Bola Negra.

At the heart of the La piedra oscura is the love story between real-life football player Rafael Rodríguez Rapún and Lorca during the Spanish Civil War. The work is spun into another story in the film about a young trumpeter called Sebastián, played by singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente.

“When I read in the plane the first monologue, I started to cry… something touched deep inside, like a wound I didn’t know I had about like my country and what happened like 90 years ago,” he said.

Watch on Deadline

He and Javier Ambrossi then investigated Lorca’s play and discovered it was unfinished.

“We realized it was the first play he was going to portray a gay character, so it was going to be revolutionary. But he was murdered. He couldn’t do it, and we were like, ‘What a loss!’”

The directorial duo went to Granada to consult the screenplay which is preserved at the Centro Federico Garcia Lorca.

“We got to see the four pages and there was like a power in those pages, like art as a physical thing, because the niece of Lorca said that fascism wanted to destroy all the manuscripts when the war started, but everyone hid it. So, it felt like a weapon that fascism wanted to destroy. We start from there, imagining what ‘La Bola Nera’ could have been, mixing it with ‘La pieda scura’, and then we had our present timeline.”

Ambrossi said the four pages had acted as a character blueprint for their film.

“The beautiful thing about the four pages that exist of the unfinished work by Federico Garcia Lorca is that the first page is a list of characters he was going use,” he said. “It was like a challenge, you know. I was like, oh my god, if we reimagine this world, it could be something very beautiful.”

Penélope Cruz, who has a small role as Nené Romero, a Cuplé singer entertaining soldiers during the Spanish Civil War, also joined the conversation.

Cruz said she was a big fan of the directors’ work – which includes The Messiah and Veneno – and instructed her to set up a lunch.

“Like after 10 minutes we were friends and then they told me they were writing this movie, and there was a character that they thought about sending, but they thought it was too short. And I told them never worry about that with me. Like I don’t choose the material based on how many minutes the character is on screen,” she recounted.

“A few days later they sent it, and I completely fell in love with the Nené, and I was blown away by this script. I thought I don’t know if they realize how incredible and powerful this is what they have in their hands.”

title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird’s Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup – London Film Festival
summary: If David Ellison wants a ticket to the Oscars this year it most likely won’t be with anything from Paramount or even (so far) from Warner Bros, but if you said Netflix you might be on the right track. Ray Gunn, from Oscar-winning filmmaker Brad Bird (Ratatouille, The Incredibles), comes out of Skydance Animation’s original […]
content:
If David Ellison wants a ticket to the Oscars this year it most likely won’t be with anything from Paramount or even (so far) from Warner Bros, but if you said Netflix you might be on the right track. Ray Gunn, from Oscar-winning filmmaker Brad Bird (Ratatouille, The Incredibles), comes out of Skydance Animation‘s original deal with the streamer, counts Ellison among its producers, and is the kind of smart, visually sumptuous and clever ‘toon that is ripe for the Best Animated Feature category.

Having its world premiere Saturday at the London Film Festival, Ray Gunn is a throwback to Bogart-style film noir detective classics like The Maltese Falcon, The Big Sleep and other ’40s gems of the Dashiell Hammett, Raymond Chandler and Sam Spade mode. Throw in a little Chinatown via Jack Nicholson or Altman’s The Long Goodbye, or Robert Mitchum in Farewell My Lovely, and you get the idea, and then think elements of The Jetsons or Who Framed Roger Rabbit animated hits, marry them with Blade Runner, and then toss in a bit of Madonna in Dick Tracy, take a visit to the Star Wars bar, stir them all together and you have something approximating the world Bird has cooked up here.

In other words it is a love letter to the movies past and futuristic. They call its main setting, Metropia, an “alternate future” channeling 1939, and that seems about right.

Watch on Deadline

No matter what the inspirations, and there were clearly many, they all come from cinema and that’s a delicious thing here. Bird, who also wrote the nifty script with Matthew Robbins, has been blessed to collect a sensational voice cast to match an intriguing bunch of characters who make up this mashup.

Chief among them is Sam Rockwell‘s Ray Gunn, an analog private dick in a digital planet. The methods he uses are mainly all AI’ed in this futureworld, but he operates like its San Francisco circa 1941, handling cases with his partner in grime Eye Ra Kadock (a wonderful Tom Waits), a cyclopian alien at the ready for any assignment that comes their way. And boy do they get a doozy when sultry Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), a troubled pop superstar, walks in the door. Of course its all about a murder she is accused of, one of her ex-husbands, and the timing couldn’t be worse for her beleaguered record company Megamax, now run by her first hubby and manager Barry Vogel (Alan Tudyk). Gunn is hired to keep her out of trouble, something she constantly finds herself in. Could there also be an instant attraction here? They don’t need the scandal or the nagging competition from Slugsy (Matt Berry), an alien mob boss who would like to bring Venus back under his purview. There are all sorts of sides to Venus, a lot of shady characters complicating things, and in pure Bogie-Bacall fashion Ray gets to sort them all out while dealing with this colorful group.

Using vibarant CGI techniques to bring this world to life, Bird and his talented artisans manage to successfully merge two very different worlds, centuries apart in a cohesive and viable original universe that somehow seems right. You don’t have to be a fan of noir and Dark City detective yarns to appreciate the story, and it doesn’t matter if you aren’t a sci-fi aficionado either. The human/alien blend blends and helps to make this Skydance Animation production an entertaining proposition for adults and even their kids who get dragged to see it, rather than the usual other way around for ‘toons.

RELATED: The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office

Rockwell is the perfect lead here, his voice work right on target as a guy who is trying to hang on in a world passing his old-school style right by. Johansson, as the PR nightmare pop diva, matches him and even gets to show off her musical chops in a couple of the songs provided by New Zealand’s Kimba. Among the rest of the cast, Bobby Cannavale scores as Arnold Dam, co-owner of the Moon Room, the place where Venus sound-alike Levity Love (Kether Donohue) performs covers of her hits. Working the cop beat is Police Capt. Roz Drexler, nicely etched by Michelle Rodriguez. There’s also former cop Sam Stelfreeze (Michael Chernus) in the mix, and among others the slimy ralien smuggler Vanzine Kaluta (Kathryn Hunter).

Setting the shifting moods expertly is Michael Giacchino’s score that nicely avoids the clichés of the genre(s) while still honoring them.

Producers are John Lasseter, Bird, Lisa Beroud, David Ellison and Dana Goldberg.

Title: Ray Gunn

Festival: London Film Festival

Distributor: Netflix

Release date: December 4, 2026 (theatrical); December 18 (streaming)

Director: Brad Bird

Screenwriters: Brad Bird and Matthew Robbins

Cast: Sam Rockwell, Scarlett Johansson, Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, Michelle Rodriguez

Rating: PG

Running time: 1 hr 59 mins

title: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Says A.I. Is Being Trained to ‘Hijack Your Intimacy’: ‘We Should Be Concerned’
summary: Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who has added United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance to his resumé, has warned the public to be “concerned about the people building A.I.” and how the technology is being trained to “hijack your intimacy” in a vlog-style video interview with The New York Times published on Saturday. When the outlet […]
content:
Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who has added United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance to his resumé, has warned the public to be “concerned about the people building A.I.” and how the technology is being trained to “hijack your intimacy” in a vlog-style video interview with The New York Times published on Saturday.

When the outlet asked what he fears most about AI, the “500 Days of Summer” actor said he doesn’t want to reduce “these concerns into one sound bite of fear.” “That’s one of the problems. To me, saying: Oh, I’m scared that A.I. could exterminate all of humanity — that doesn’t really get at the substance of the concern. There’s real validity to that concern. But that’s not the thing that really worries me,” Gordon-Levitt said.

He continued, saying what worries him is the “decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy.” “These companies are betting on the notion that they’re going to take over the entire economy. That would be totalitarianism, and that would be really bad… Simultaneously, these models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it. We shouldn’t be scared of an A.I. We should be concerned about the people building A.I.”

Popular on Variety

Gordon-Levitt was appointed to a brand-new United Nations position in March. At the time, the organization defined it as “a newly established role designed to strengthen public understanding of how digital technologies shape everyday life, rights and opportunities.”

The actor and director has long been outspoken about A.I., and in January, joined more than 700 artists, writers and creators, including Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, in supporting an anti-AI campaign calling out tech companies exploiting copyrighted work without permission.

title: ‘Tenzing’ Review: A Remarkable Adventure That Puts the Audience Right Up on Mount Everest, Along with the First Two Men — One a Sherpa, Overlooked by History — to Scale It
summary: "Tenzing" earns its inspirational fervor, but the reason it fits into the new wave of mountain-climbing movies is that the director, Jennifer Peedom, an Australian who’s been making documentaries about mountain-climbing for 18 years, has staged the film with a you-are-there authenticity that’s breathtaking but never showy. She’s a classicist; this is a movie that, in spirit, you could imagine John Huston or Howard Hawks having directed.
content:
The movies are having a mountain-climbing moment. More than a moment, really — it’s been building since 2018, the year that saw the release of not one but two jaw-dropping, vertigo-inducing, heart-in-the-throat documentaries, “Free Solo” and “The Dawn Wall,” that took you right up to the places that climbers crave and that most of us wouldn’t dare to go near. But as these films demonstrate, we might well dream of it. The new mountaineering movies are delirious vicarious cinema, employing technological means and a filmmaking bravado that comes with them that would have been unimaginable three or four decades ago. Movies like “14 Peaks” and “The Alpinist” — or “Skywalkers: A Love Story,” the great documentary about rooftoppers — chart the impossible, and the very fact that the films exist can seem part of the impossible. That’s an element of their scary exhilaration.

“Tenzing” fits into the genre, though in a far more traditional way. It’s not a documentary. It’s a drama, and a rather old-school one: the story of the first climb to reach the peak of Mount Everest, which happened in 1953. It’s a tale of courage, ambition, arrogance, death, and triumph, and it’s also a story of embattled national pride and ethnic identity. The team that scaled Everest in 1953 was led by the British, who were in the last throes of trying to stake out their empire. No one had ever made it to the top of Mount Everest (there had been eight previous attempts), and this team barely did either. The elements were too forbidding: the chasms and vertical rock faces, the wind and the storms, and the air — so thin it could kill you. The Brits were ready to conquer, but they couldn’t have made the climb without their team of Sherpa, the Tibetan ethnic group native to the area, who had mountaineering in their blood. The Sherpa were officially the “guides,” but they knew what they were doing far more than the British did.

Popular on Variety

On that revolutionary trek, the first two people to reach the summit of Everest were Edmund Hillary, who was a New Zealander, and Tenzing Norgay, a Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who’d been dreaming of scaling Everest ever since he was a boy. These two were the Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of mountaineering. But for decades, because of his ethnicity, Tenzing’s role in the mission was understated by history; he was treated as Hillary’s noble assistant. “Tenzing” celebrates his rightful place as a mountaineering visionary — and it does so by dramatizing this climb with a filmmaking rigor that’s stately and inviting and, at moments, ominous and casually miraculous. (When a vast plain of snow suddenly collapses, you feel like a hole just opened up in the earth.) “Tenzing” earns its inspirational fervor, but the reason it fits into the new wave of mountain-climbing movies is that the director, Jennifer Peedom, an Australian who’s been making documentaries about mountain-climbing for 18 years, has staged it with a you-are-there authenticity that’s breathtaking but never showy. She’s a classicist; this is a movie that, in spirit, you could imagine John Huston or Howard Hawks having directed.

The film opens with Tenzing as a boy, gawking at Mount Everest, which looms across the valley like Godzilla. It sits on the border of Nepal and China in the Himalayas, and Tenzing grows up in the shadow of its awe. He calls the mountain by its Tibetan name, Chomolungma, and early on has an encounter with the legendary British alpinist George Mallory (Johnny Flynn), who was part of the first three Everest expeditions in the 1920s. So from the start, the spirit of this endeavor will be global.

Peedom isn’t just a filmmaking wizard. She’s a humanist who dramatizes the intricate politics of the 1953 Everest climb, which was led by John Hunt, a British colonel (played with stiff-upper-lip exuberance by Willem Dafoe) who believes that the entire mission should be run in a strict military manner. He’s right in certain ways, but the trouble is that his outlook prioritizes hierarchy, which places the Sherpa at the bottom of the pecking order.

The film flashes back, maybe a little too much, to key periods of Tenzing’s life (his boyhood, his meeting of the woman he’ll marry). But it’s most interesting when he has to fight and cajole his way onto the expedition. Genden Phunstok, the Tibetan actor who plays Tenzing, is disarmingly handsome, and in his quiet way he’s a star. Dealing with the British, his Tenzing is scrupulous and honorable, but don’t confuse that with subservience. He’s got a will of iron, and a velvet wit, and something else the British don’t have: a faith in the power of Everest that allows him to see the mountain as an ally rather than an adversary. He’s not trying to conquer the mountain; he’s trying to fuse with it. That gives him a whole different outlook as a climber.

As the mission goes on, Tenzing forms a connection with Edmund Hillary, played with frosty empathetic reserve by Tom Hiddleston. The two men have much in common; they are fearless but modest. “Tenzing” captures the sometimes prickly camaraderie of the team members, a drama that feeds into the logistics of the climb, which the movie dramatizes with a stunning existential flair. You literally watch “Tenzing” and think, “How on earth did they film this?” It’s the living definition of an adventure movie, but without adventure-movie corniness. The film never overhypes the danger or the dread, and it cuts no dramatic corners. It knows that the real story is gripping enough.

As the men draw closer to the peak, the likelihood of reaching it actually grows more distant. The weather is too forbidding; the window of time gets smaller. Tenzing is promoted to being an official team member, and when he and Hillary are finally tapped as the two who will make the last leg of the trek, that’s because it’s now clear that they’re the only two who can do it. Even then, their triumph is far from assured; the climb becomes more unreal in its harshness. The pull of “Tenzing” is that we in the audience are right there, along with them, every snowy, icy, impossible step of the way.

title: ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ Live-Action TV Series to Begin Shooting in 2027, More Details Coming ‘Very Soon’
summary: Peacock’s “Dungeon Crawler Carl” live-action TV series will begin shooting next year, author Matt Dinniman and Universal TV execs revealed Saturday. “We are starting to see drafts and outlines, and we’ve gotten the whole series pitch, which is really exciting, but it’s continued to evolve,” Universal Global Television scripted series chief Kelsey Balance said during […]
content:
Peacock’s “Dungeon Crawler Carl” live-action TV series will begin shooting next year, author Matt Dinniman and Universal TV execs revealed Saturday.

“We are starting to see drafts and outlines, and we’ve gotten the whole series pitch, which is really exciting, but it’s continued to evolve,” Universal Global Television scripted series chief Kelsey Balance said during a New York Comic Con panel hosted by Dinniman. “While that’s happening, we are building the ship, or building the plane, as we fly. So that’s happening, and that drives everything. At the same time, we’re into soft prep. So we’re hiring HODs. We’re finding great line producers, production designers, directors, casting — all of it is kind of happening right now, which is fun.”

Based on Matt Dinniman’s best-selling LitRPG novel series, the “Dungeon Crawler Carl” TV show will be led by Chris Yost and Eric Heisserer, who will executive produce alongside Seth MacFarlane, Erica Huggins, and Rachel Hargreaves-Heald for MacFarlane’s banner, Fuzzy Door. Dinniman is co-executive producer. The adaptation hails from Universal Global Television.

Popular on Variety

Here’s the official logline for the “Dungeon Crawler Carl” TV series: “An alien invasion has wiped out most of humanity, and any survivors are forced to fight for their lives on a sadistic intergalactic game show. Sounds bad, right? Now try doing it with bare feet and a stuck-up, self-centered, tiara-wearing talking cat as your partner. Welcome to Dungeon Crawler World: Earth, where the apocalypse will be televised … and Coast Guard vet Carl finds himself stuck with his ex-girlfriend’s award-winning show cat, Princess Donut the Queen Anne Chonk, as they try to survive the end of the world, fighting monsters, aliens, an insane A.I. and even other survivors … all for the sake of good TV. Survival is optional. Entertainment is not.”

Balance noted the “DCC” TV series team was “hopeful we’d be able to announce something today” during Saturday’s NYCC panel, but the project is “just in the middle of the chaos of the storm that not all of that has landed officially yet.” However, Balance says additional details are coming “very soon, within the next few weeks.”

“We’re going to be locking in all of those key things, which will be fun to share with you guys,” the Universal TV exec said. “Then we’ll start actual real prep in the new year and shooting next year. So, the plan is to have all scripts written before production starts, which is great. We’re on track for that and then we’ll start shooting it, which is exciting. We’re constantly brainstorming all the time on when and how we can share things.”

For now, Dinniman and the execs say they can’t give an update on when the show might premiere, though the author did try to get an answer out of them while moderating the panel. Along with Balance, panelists included Jordan Moblo, EVP, Creative Acquisitions & IP Management, Universal Studio Group, and Vivian Cannon, EVP, Drama Development, Universal Television. The panel was an event for NYCC press and professional badge-holders and offered a behind-the-scenes look at how Universal Studios Group identifies promising IP, partners with creators and shepherds adaptations through the development process.

Dinniman also said that, aside from the reveal that “Carl” audiobook narrator Jeff Hays will voice Princess Donut for the TV series, no other casting decisions have been made, including who will play Carl.

“We were just discussing this backstage. Carl’s not been cast. And we don’t have a specific answer for that,” Dinniman said when asked by an audience member what actor he’d like to take on the role. “I want Carl to be played by someone who embodies the role and someone who can be both goofy and give off that really, really scary vibe. When Carl’s upset, he’s a very scary person.”

title: ‘Star Trek: Starfleet Academy: Season 2 Release Date & Photos; Bill Nighy & Rosemarie DeWitt To Guest Star

content:
We have a release date for the second and final season of Star Trek: Starfleet Academy. The sophomore season will premiere in March 2027, it was announced Saturday during the Star Trek Universe panel at New York Comic Con. The panel included series star Holly Hunter, along with Sandro Rosta, Bella Shepard, Karim Diané, Robert Picardo and co-showrunners and executive producers Alex Kurtzman and Noga Landau.

It also was revealed that Bill Nighy (Living, About Time) and Rosemarie DeWitt (Untamed, The Staircase) will guest star in the upcoming season. Nighy will play Nahla’s estranged father, Nyk Ake, and DeWitt will play Tarima’s mother, Laytha Sadal, the First Lady of Betazed. You can see both in some just-released photos below.

Produced by CBS Studios in association with Alex Kurtzman’s Secret Hideout and Roddenberry Entertainment, Star Trek: Starfleet Academy follows the adventures of a new class of Starfleet cadets as they come of age in one of the most legendary places in the galaxy. Under the watchful and demanding eyes of their instructors, they will discover what it takes to become Starfleet officers as they navigate blossoming friendships, explosive rivalries, first loves and a new enemy that threatens both the Academy and the Federation itself.

Watch on Deadline

Season two of Star Trek: Starfleet Academy follows our cadets into their second year aboard the USS Athena. There, their ideals of leadership, friendship, romance and morality are put to the test as they navigate budding rivalries, shaky diplomatic negotiations, a fiercely competitive schoolwide tournament, and the arrival of a mysterious new cadet whose existence raises questions that could have consequences far beyond the classroom.

Several first-look Season 2 photos also were released, which you can see below.
