title: DOJ Launches Investigation Of Networks For Suspending TV Pool Amid Trump’s Ban On CNN
summary: The Justice Department has launched an investigation into whether the five major networks violated antitrust laws when they suspended participation in the White House TV pool in protest of Donald Trump’s ban on CNN. Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the Justice Department, said in a statement, “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering […]
content:
The Justice Department has launched an investigation into whether the five major networks violated antitrust laws when they suspended participation in the White House TV pool in protest of Donald Trump‘s ban on CNN.

Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the Justice Department, said in a statement, “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.” The New York Times first reported on the investigation.

After Trump announced his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds on Sept. 18, CNN also was restricted from the TV pool. As part of a long-running arrangement, CNN, CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News rotate pool duty providing technical, video and reporting coverage of the president, with feeds then distributed to other networks and news organizations. The pool is necessary because of the space limitations of areas of the White House, like the Oval Office, or on Air Force One.

Watch on Deadline

After the CNN freeze out, the other members of the TV pool jointly announced on Sept. 21 that they would refrain from their rotation turn, a move made to protest the White House effort to block the news network.

“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the five networks said in a statement at the time.

The suspension lasted for about four days, but it came during the White House visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping. The suspension of the TV pool meant that there was much less video coverage of major ceremonies and other events surrounding his visit. Trump later complained that CNN and MS NOW did not cover Xi’s visit, without mentioning his efforts to ban the two outlets from the White House grounds.

ABC confirmed that it has not received any notification of the investigation but it expects to. A CNN spokesperson declined to comment. Other networks in the pool did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The White House has continued to restrict CNN from certain assignments, including flying on Air Force One on presidential trip.

After Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House grounds, those three media outlets sued, claiming violations of their First Amendment and due process rights. A federal judge imposed a temporary restraining order, which last until Tuesday, that has forced the White House to renew access to dozens of reporters. The judge, Timothy Kelly, is expected to rule by then on whether to grant the news outlets a preliminary injunction, something that would prevent the White House from denying access on a longer term.

The issue of access to the White House grounds is separate, yet related, to the issue of whether the administration can also freeze out members of the pool because the president does not approve of their editorial decisions. A different case, involving the Associated Press, is on appeal in the D.C. Circuit. The AP was barred from the White House pool because its style guidance did not adhere to Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for the Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the investigation “appears to be a pretext for seeking records from the networks about how they are covering daily White House events during a media ban the president himself put in place. The decisions news organizations make about coverage are protected by the First Amendment, and summoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”

The administration has been rebuffed in the federal courts in another effort to seek materials from media organizations as part of an antitrust investigation. Last year, a federal judge barred the Federal Trade Commission from issuing a civil investigative demand to Media Matters for America, the progressive watchdog group, as part of an antitrust investigation of an advertiser boycott of Elon Musk’s X.

Media Matters later said that a settlement with the FTC required that the agency forgo issuing such a civil investigation demand. They also said that the “agreement — and the decisions Media Matters won in the district court and the court of appeals — offers a roadmap for other newsgathering and nonprofit organizations facing, or at risk of, government retaliation.” Three advertising holding companies, WPP, Dentsu and Publicis, also reached a settlement with the FTC.

title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Trailer: Hunter Schafer Teams Up With Michelle Yeoh To Find “Cure For All Replicants” — NYCC
summary: Nearly 45 years later, a new Blade Runner is back to make the Ridley Scott franchise “more human than human” once again. On Saturday at New York Comic-Con, Prime Video released key art and a new trailer for the eight-episode limited series created by Silka Luisa with Amazon MGM Studios and Alcon Television Group, premiering […]
content:
Nearly 45 years later, a new Blade Runner is back to make the Ridley Scott franchise “more human than human” once again.

On Saturday at New York Comic-Con, Prime Video released key art and a new trailer for the eight-episode limited series created by Silka Luisa with Amazon MGM Studios and Alcon Television Group, premiering in full Nov. 25 on the streamer.

Set 50 years after the events of Blade Runner 2049, Los Angeles has been reborn, just not by humanity. Cora (Hunter Schafer), a fugitive in a final bid to stop running, takes on one last identity: a Blade Runner. Forced to partner with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant days from dying, she hunts down a runaway hiding a truth that could collapse a fragile city.

Luisa, Yeoh and Schafer took the stage at Prime Video’s NYCC panel on Sunday, along with cast members Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben and Matthew Needham, as well as executive producers Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson.

Watch on Deadline

The series also stars Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Tom Burke and Maurizio Lombardi.

Luisa serves as showrunner, creator and executive producer. Additional EPs include Ridley Scott, Alcon Entertainment co-founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, Alcon’s President of Television Ben Roberts, Steven Johnson, David W. Zucker and Clayton Krueger from Scott Free Productions, Richard Sharkey, Tom Spezialy, Michael Green, Cynthia Yorkin, Frank Giustra, Tim Gable, Isa Dick Hackett and Jonathan van Tulleken, who directed the first two episodes.

Directed by Scott, the original Blade Runner premiered in 1982, starring Harrison Ford and Sean Young. In 2017, Ford reprised his role as Rick Deckard in Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049, starring alongside Ryan Gosling.

title: ‘In a Violent Nature: Part 2’ Gets 2027 Premiere Date With IFC & Shudder — NYCC
summary: Johnny is back for more first-person POV blood and carnage as Chris Nash’s In a Violent Nature: Part 2 heads to theaters on Valentine’s Day weekend. On Saturday at New York Comic-Con, actor Ry Barrett, who reprises his role as the undead firefighter mask-clad killer, announced that the Independent Film Company/Shudder slasher sequel will premiere […]
content:
Johnny is back for more first-person POV blood and carnage as Chris Nash‘s In a Violent Nature: Part 2 heads to theaters on Valentine’s Day weekend.

On Saturday at New York Comic-Con, actor Ry Barrett, who reprises his role as the undead firefighter mask-clad killer, announced that the Independent Film Company/Shudder slasher sequel will premiere in theaters on Feb. 12, 2027, following the original’s breakout at Sundance’s Midnight program in 2024.

In a Violent Nature: Part 2 picks up where the first left off as Johnny (Barrett) continues his violent rampage at an Ontario summer camp, where a young outcast camper is forced to spend the night with his counselor sister and her friends at their annual end-of-season party.

Following the original movie’s unique approach to the slasher genre that put the audience in the killer’s perspective, the sequel will expand on Johnny’s lore and deliver more brutally extreme and creative kills.

Watch on Deadline

The sequel, which made its world premiere last month at Fantastic Fest, is co-directed by Nate Wilson and Chris Nash, who also penned the script. The film is produced by Peter Kuplowsky, Shannon Hanmer and Nash.

title: Globo and Endemol Shine Brasil Pact to Forge Global Entertainment IP Powerhouse (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Brazilian media behemoth Globo and Endemol Shine Brasil, part of Banijay Latin America, have forged a non-scripted IP strategic partnership to develop and produce a next generation of franchises from Brazil, with the aim of jointly crafting original IP with global appeal, as well as of course local relevance. The ambitious pact will further the […]
content:
Brazilian media behemoth Globo and Endemol Shine Brasil, part of Banijay Latin America, have forged a non-scripted IP strategic partnership to develop and produce a next generation of franchises from Brazil, with the aim of jointly crafting original IP with global appeal, as well as of course local relevance.

The ambitious pact will further the partners’ previous collaborative efforts, which has produced the likes of such mega hits as “Big Brother Brasil,” “No Limite” (“Survivor”),” “The Masked Singer,” “Dança dos Famosos” (“Dance of the Famous”) and “The Wall,” among others. Both companies will have a hefty presence at Mipcom.

Globo’s proven ability to create and produce Brazilian content that reaches and engages more than 70 million people daily, combined with Endemol Shine Brasil’s knowhow and access to the global reach of parent company Banijay Entertainment, makes this a formidable pairing.

Popular on Variety

Said Nani Freitas, CEO of Endemol Shine Brasil: “Our partnership with Globo goes back many years, all the way to Endemol’s arrival in Brazil. The combination of our expertise creates a highly powerful environment for developing culture-defining entertainment. That is why it is especially meaningful to take another step forward in this relationship and join forces in the creation of new entertainment formats from the very beginning of the development process, with the potential to connect audiences far beyond our market.”

Amauri Soares, Executive Director of Globo Studios, concurred: “Globo has been expanding investments in creative development hubs, connecting our talent with strategic partners to accelerate the creation of original formats. By bringing together Globo’s creativity with the international expertise of Endemol Shine Brasil and Banijay Entertainment, we are taking another step toward transforming our studios into a hub for developing Brazilian intellectual properties with global reach.”

Under the agreement, Globo will have priority rights to exploit the new formats across its channels and platforms, while Endemol Shine Brasil will spearhead international expansion through Banijay Entertainment’s worldwide network of more than 170 labels across 25 territories, opening a direct route to international markets.

“Everyone knows launching new original programming in our markets is no easy task, which makes this partnership all the more significant. I’m very excited and proud Endemol Shine Brasil has possibility to do exactly that with a major player like Globo. I can’t thank Amauri enough for this great opportunity to collaborate,” said Laurens Drillich, CEO, Banijay Latin America.

Endemol Shine Brasil has been aggressively expanding its production footprint across traditional, digital and vertical microdramas.

In April, it teamed up with ReelShort on the Brazilian version of the microdrama platform’s biggest hit, “Married at First Sight.” It also formed a partnership with A Fábrica, a Banijay Americas company, to create a slate of vertical-format microdramas.

Its new docu-reality series “Underground City” (“Cidade Subterrânea”), an original format it created, which delves into São Paulo’s subway system, premiered on GNT and Globo’s streaming platform, Globoplay, and also aired on TV Globo’s Fantástico.

Mipcom runs over Oct. 10-15.

title: ‘Squid Game’ Producer Reads Founding Declaration as Asian Independent Producers Form Cross-Border Alliance at Busan
summary: Independent producers from five Asian territories joined forces on Sunday, launching the Asian Producers Alliance (APA) at the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market to push for cross-border co-production and stronger protection of creators’ rights. “Squid Game” producer Kim Ji-yeon, a board member of the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK), read the […]
content:
Independent producers from five Asian territories joined forces on Sunday, launching the Asian Producers Alliance (APA) at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market to push for cross-border co-production and stronger protection of creators’ rights.

“Squid Game” producer Kim Ji-yeon, a board member of the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK), read the founding declaration as representatives of the five organizations took the stage. “For years, we have faced the same changes alone – in our own markets, in our own languages. Today we choose to face them together,” the declaration read. “We will advance co-production across Asia, so that our stories can be made together and travel further.”

The coalition brings together PGK, the Indonesian Film Producers Association (APROFI), the Philippine Independent Producers Group (PIPG), the Hong Kong Movie Production Executives Association (HKMPEA) and the Taiwan Producers Association (TPA). Its members are independent producers, with no studios, conglomerates or state bodies involved. PGK and APROFI initiated the group, whose formation was approved online by all five organizations.

Popular on Variety

The announcement came at the close of “Empowering Asian Cinema: Solidarity and Creative Alliance,” a seminar hosted by PGK at the ACFM Producers Hub. Moderated by PGK International Committee director Han Jin, the panel brought together producers Yulia Evina Bhara of Indonesia’s KawanKawan Media, Rhee Handae, CEO of Korea’s Sidus, Yamaguchi Shin of Tokyo-based Knockonwood and Bianca Balbuena, co-founder and COO of the Philippines’ Epicmedia Productions, to discuss co-production in an industry upended by streaming and short-form content.

Yamaguchi offered a concise direction for the conversation: “Think globally.” As producers in each market face the realities of cross-border production, he said, international co-production is becoming an unavoidable part of the industry’s future.

That shift is already reflected in the panelists’ work. Yamaguchi has spent more than two decades structuring international co-productions across Asia, Europe and North America. Rhee leads Sidus’s Korea-Vietnam co-productions, including projects developed through a joint venture with director Phan Gia Nhat Linh. Bhara’s credits include Cannes winner “Tiger Stripes” and Venice-winning “Autobiography,” while Balbuena has produced films that have screened at major festivals including Sundance, Venice, Cannes and Berlin.

APA will begin as a consultative coalition, with co-production across Asia and creators’ IP rights among its priorities, and aims to develop into a body with a formal decision-making structure. Producer organizations across Asia can join during its first year, and more than one organization per territory may join. Members plan to meet online quarterly and hold an annual general assembly during ACFM.

PGK president Lee Dong-ha and APROFI chair Edwin Nazir are the alliance’s inaugural co-representatives, with Han Jin and Bhara leading its secretariat as co-secretary generals. All four serve one-year terms, with elections held at each year’s general assembly.

“APA is not a declaration – it is a practice of solidarity that begins now,” Lee said.

HKMPEA chair Johnny Wang said producers had long been accustomed to following paths paved by their predecessors. “Now, with the birth of the APA, we are embarking on an entirely new and unprecedented journey,” he said.

APA will hold its second seminar at the JAFF Market in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, in December, hosted by APROFI and focused on creators’ IP.

title: Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal
summary: LYON, France — Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi, Daniel Brühl, Tsui Hark and Andrey Zvyagintsev attended the opening gala of France’s Lumière Festival Saturday night where Haynes teased his anticipated ‘De Noche,’ starring Pedro Pascal. It also saw Lumière Fest chief Thierry Frémaux, also head of the Cannes Festival, take a well-received swing at U.S. President […]
content:
LYON, France — Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi, Daniel Brühl, Tsui Hark and Andrey Zvyagintsev attended the opening gala of France’s Lumière Festival Saturday night where Haynes teased his anticipated ‘De Noche,’ starring Pedro Pascal. It also saw Lumière Fest chief Thierry Frémaux, also head of the Cannes Festival, take a well-received swing at U.S. President Donald Trump.

“Donald Trump has protested that he wasn’t given the Nobel Peace Prize. The Lumière Award is the only prize we think he won’t ask for,” Frémaux told the crowd of the fest’s top honor. “In any case, we won’t give it to him,” Frémaux added, referring to the fest’s top honor at Lyon’s cavernous Halle Tony Garnier, a 5,000-seat concert hall, at a gala where he acted as ever as host.

Joel and Ethan Coen will accept this year’s Lumière Award later in the festival. The opening night, however, belonged very much to Haynes, in Lyon for a masterclass and a retrospective featuring “Poison,” “Safe,” “Far from Heaven” and “I’m Not There.”

Popular on Variety

Todd Haynes Credit: Lea Rener

On stage at the Halle Tony Garnier, he offered an update on his upcoming “De Noche,” the Pedro Pascal-Danny Ramirez romance revived after Joaquin Phoenix exited the project in 2024.

With filming now completed and a release date yet to be announced, Haynes said the film will “most likely be an R-rated film,” although he saw no need to make its visual language “prurient.”

“What’s going on between the two men is so complex and so moving, but ultimately, it’s a love story,” he said. “They’re exposing themselves to each other, and they’re exploring things about their masculinity, their vulnerability.”

Set in 1938, the film shares its historical backdrop with Ettore Scola’s “A Special Day,” the opening-night screening introduced by Haynes. Starring Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni, the 1977 classic follows an encounter between a housewife and a gay man in Fascist Rome on the day of Hitler’s visit to Mussolini.

“Anyone can identify with what’s happening,” Haynes said of “De Noche.” “The sort of armor of masculinity is particular to men.” The film’s 1938 setting, he added, brings its own cultural barriers.

Joel and Ethan Coen will accept the fest’s Lumière Award at its climax on Oct. 16. “We like cinema brothers in Lyon,” Frémaux said, referring to Auguste and Louis Lumière, the Lyon-born cinema founders, as well as two-time Palme d’Or winners Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, who received the prize in 2020.

The Coens join a roll call of previous recipients including Clint Eastwood, Quentin Tarantino, Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Wong Kar-wai, Jane Fonda, Tim Burton, Jane Campion and Michael Mann.

Walking an improvised red carpet inside the Halle Tony Garnier, guests also included Andrey Zvyagintsev, Fatih Akin and Abel Ferrara. They helped launch the nine-day celebration of cinema, with 163 films and more than 400 screenings across dozens of venues in and around Lyon.

Daniel Brühl, Zhang Ziyi, Fatih Akin Credit: Sarana Lafont

Zhang Ziyi is in town to introduce the first French screening of a 4K restoration of Ang Lee’s “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon” (2000), which was shown out of competition at Cannes, won four Oscars and launched her internationally. Asked whether a film like that could be made today, she answered: “I don’t think so.” Digital tools might mean crews no longer need “50 people to pull the wire,” she said. “Maybe things get easier, but the feeling has changed.”

Frémaux also turned the opening ceremony into his customary crash course in Lyon cinema history.

This year he showcased the Lumière brothers’ autochrome color process through vivid early photographs and newly restored experimental footage, once again asserting the city’s claim as cinema’s birthplace.

The ceremony ended with the assembled guests delivering the traditional declaration that the festival was open, before Zhang obliged when asked to improvise a Chinese version.

At the gala dinner, cinema history gave way to another Lumière tradition: a full-volume blast of “Allumer le feu,” the exuberant anthem by late French rock idol Johnny Hallyday, a perennial favorite of Frémaux’s. French actress Alexandra Lamy and Brühl were among those dancing on their chairs.

The Lumière Film Festival runs through Oct. 18.

title: Journey Drummer Deen Castronovo Returns to the Stage to Play Full Show, Two Nights After Medical Scare
summary: No one is saying what caused Journey drummer Deen Castronovo to have been assisted off stage after two songs and admitted to a Tulsa hospital Thursday night. What they were saying, though, was that he had recovered from whatever hit him and was ready to resume action. That seemed to hold true Saturday night, as […]
content:
No one is saying what caused Journey drummer Deen Castronovo to have been assisted off stage after two songs and admitted to a Tulsa hospital Thursday night. What they were saying, though, was that he had recovered from whatever hit him and was ready to resume action. That seemed to hold true Saturday night, as Deen played a full 29-song show with the band in San Antonio, as promised earlier in group members’ social feeds.

“He crushed last night,” guitarist Neal Schon said in a comment on his Facebook feed early Sunday morning, in response to a fan query about how Castronovo weathered his return to the stage at Texas’ Frost Bank Center. On X, Schon said the drummer was “back in rare form.”

San Antonio last night. Amazing crowd ! You Rocked ! Deen was back in rare form 🙌🏽 pic.twitter.com/q2AUhuuud5 — NEAL SCHON MUSIC (@NealSchonMusic) October 11, 2026

Not only did he perform the full show on drums, but — seeming to bat down rumors that he was suffering from pneumonia — Castronovo sang lead vocals on the same five songs he usually takes the lead on every night on tour. Saturday in San Antonio, according to user contributions on Setlists,fm, he sang the sole lead on three numbers, “Lights,” “Keep on Runnin'” and “Precious Time,” and also shared lead vocals with Jonathan Cain on two more, “Just the Same Way” and “Anytime,” as has been the norm on this tour.

Popular on Variety

On his own Facebook page, Castronovo posted a message to fans Saturday prior to the concert. “Thank you all for the overwhelming love, concern, well wishes, messages and texts over the past couple of days. While I haven’t been able to respond to everyone personally, please know how much your kindness and support mean to me. Tulsa, I’m so sorry I couldn’t finish the show with you all. Thank you to Jonathan Cain, Neal Schon and everyone at the BOK Center for lifting me up in prayer that night. Hearing about that touched my heart deeply. I’ll be joining Journey on stage in San Antonio tonight. Much love to you all!.”

Great to see and hear Journey drummer Deen Castronovo back with the band after his medical scare at a concert in Oklahoma recently. Deen sounds amazing.

Sorry for some of the fidgeting on the video. pic.twitter.com/lSHBKMqBSP — Raul Dominguez Jr. (@DominguezCinco) October 11, 2026

On Friday, Schon had assured fans that the drummer would be be back for the San Antonio show. “Deen is doing great” the guitarist testified at the time. “Come out and help welcome him back! Your prayers truly worked.”

When the drummer was compelled the leave the stage Thursday in Tulsa, there was some confusion during an approximate 25-minute break before the music resumed with Journey’s drum tech, Steve Toomey, taking over. “Get your prayers ready for Deen Castronovo, folks,” Cain asked of the crowd before they resumed. That night’s show was reduced from 29 to 19 songs, between the concert running late from the interruption and Toomey likely not being able to duplicate Castronovo’s lead singing moments as well as his drumming.

title: Taiwan’s Sole Busan Competition Title ‘To Be Ordinary’ Marks Lee Yun Chan’s Return to Features After Two Decades
summary: Taiwanese director Lee Yun Chan has returned to feature filmmaking after two decades away with “To Be Ordinary,” the only Taiwanese film in competition at the Busan International Film Festival. Lee made her feature debut with 2005’s “The Shoe Fairy” and more recently directed the Disney+ series “Women in Taipei.” The Mandarin title literally means […]
content:
Taiwanese director Lee Yun Chan has returned to feature filmmaking after two decades away with “To Be Ordinary,” the only Taiwanese film in competition at the Busan International Film Festival.

Lee made her feature debut with 2005’s “The Shoe Fairy” and more recently directed the Disney+ series “Women in Taipei.”

The Mandarin title literally means “a useful person.” “To make a film again after all this time, have it selected for competition and bring the cast to Busan – I feel really useful,” Lee tells Variety.

The film follows Yu Jie, a college student and web designer, whose motorcycle is hit by a car as he rides home one night from a part-time job. The elderly driver, consumed by guilt, signs his house over to Yu Jie and covers his medical and living costs each month. Yu Jie’s family, close to breaking point financially and emotionally, slowly reconnects over shared dinners, while Yu Jie grows close to his physical therapist, Yi-han. The fragile happiness does not last.

Popular on Variety

Lee says the story began taking shape about 10 years ago, as she was raising her family. After the cast began training, the film was shot over 42 days. For cast members Weber Yang, Chang Shih Ying and Junior Hsieh, Busan is a first. Before filming, the actors playing the family spent time grocery shopping and cooking together, and even went hiking with a wheelchair, building the ease and affection Lee wanted to bring to the screen.

“I wanted to tell the story of an ordinary family in the city, trying to live their own small lives, and what happens when one of them has an accident,” Lee says. She grounded the film in the rhythms of everyday life in Taipei, from the familiar music of garbage trucks to the daily MRT commute. “These are things we encounter in our everyday lives,” she says.

Yang, who plays the taciturn father, unemployed for three years, says he first encountered the script while going through a midlife crisis. “I felt I had everything, but I was lost and anxious, unsure what came next,” he says. The role also showed him how universal some of the film’s situations are, from a couple’s difficulty communicating to the pressure of social expectations and the questions people ask themselves about their place in the world.

Chang, who plays the mother, says the role’s emotional complexity gave her new ways to look at family, marriage and herself. “I’m lucky that every different role lets me live a different life,” she tells Variety.

Hsieh, who plays a young man left disabled after a car accident, prepared by borrowing a wheelchair from his school and adjusting his eye level in daily life to better understand the world from a wheelchair user’s perspective. The experience, he says, gave him a deeper understanding of acting. He hopes to take on a role with action or martial arts in the future.

Asked about the kinds of roles he hopes to play next, Yang says he would like to portray a homeless person, showing what it means to hit rock bottom and reflecting the realities of contemporary society.

Lee says she simply wanted to honestly document what happens when an ordinary family is hit by an accident. “Because it’s an ordinary story, like the lives we all lead, I think it can move people,” she says.

Producer Inch Lin and Mandarin Vision world sales representative Desmond Yang say that while the film may not be aimed at mainstream audiences, its universal theme of repairing family relationships can help it find viewers. After its Busan world premiere, the film is set to screen at the Tokyo International Film Festival and the Golden Horse Film Festival, before opening theatrically in Taiwan on Nov. 13.

title: Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation
summary: Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui, who received the Camellia Award at the opening of Busan International Film Festival, shared her experiences of being a woman filmmaker in a male-dominated industry at a festival press conference, along with her thoughts on how Hong Kong cinema has evolved. When asked how other women had helped shape her […]
content:
Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui, who received the Camellia Award at the opening of Busan International Film Festival, shared her experiences of being a woman filmmaker in a male-dominated industry at a festival press conference, along with her thoughts on how Hong Kong cinema has evolved.

When asked how other women had helped shape her career, Hui said she’d had five women bosses when she entered the industry back in the ‘70s who had welcomed her and helped her to become established as a filmmaker.

“I was lucky because my first five bosses really supported me, gave me freedom and support, and allowed me to do what I wanted with the TV programs I was making. They were only criticizing me to make my work better,” Hui said.

“Afterwards I met people who were not so nice, so I really want to talk about these five women in my masterclass. Some were company bosses and there were some actresses as well. It’s true that I seem to learn much less from men. I don’t know why because I’m not unfriendly with them, but perhaps it’s like karma in Buddhism, I don’t work with them as well.”

Watch on Deadline

Hui started her career working for Hong Kong broadcaster TVB, back then an incubator for Hong Kong’s new wave of pioneering filmmakers, before moving into features, many of which have won awards at major festivals, spanning the ‘80s to the present day.

Her body of work includes an early trilogy about the Vietnamese boat people – Below The Lion Rock, The Story Of Woo Viet and Boat People – which was followed by films in a variety of genres including The Romance Of Book And Sword, Eighteen Springs, All About Love, A Simple Life, which won best actress in Venice, and The Golden Era, which won best director at Taiwan’s Golden Horse. Her most recent work, Elegies (2023), a documentary about Hong Kong poetry, opened Hong Kong International Film Festival and was nominated for the Golden Horse Awards.

Looking back at developments in the Hong Kong film industry since the ‘70s, Hui also talked about the changing status of female filmmakers. “When I worked in TV in the ‘70s, and later when I made my first film, I tried my best to work on subjects like cops and robbers that men do,” Hui remembered. “I wanted to prove that women can do what men do.”

“But once I’d fulfilled that intention, I got back to subjects that really interest me; about the predicament of people in modern-day society, which is also quite a lot about women. It wasn’t intentional to make women’s stories, that’s just the way it turned out.”

She also observed that when she started her career, there were many women directors in television, but only two or three in the film industry. Now there are about 10-20 women directors actively working in the Hong Kong industry, she observed (including many that have had films screen in Busan, Hong Kong and Tokyo film festivals, including Norris Wong, Oliver Chan, Heiward Mak, Jessey Tsang and Cheuk Wan-chi).

“Nowadays their position has become much better,” she continued. “Back in the ‘70s, I felt under pressure to have very masculine habits and dress like a man. It was almost like pretending to be a man when I’m on set. But nowadays, the female directors do not hide their gender when they’re working, and don’t mind coming across as quite feminine. They’re also much more conscious in the way they’re trying to make films telling women’s stories, which I think is totally legitimate.”

While saying that she felt “very jealous” of developments in Korean cinema, Hui said she’s also encouraged by the new generation of Hong Kong filmmakers, who have a different approach to the freewheeling and commercially driven filmmakers of the ‘80s and ‘90s.

“Despite the lack of investment, the young filmmakers in Hong Kong are still very dedicated, hardworking, and talented. I feel that if they have an opening, they will be able to make better films than we did, because in the ‘80s and ‘90s it was all about entertainment. There was a lot of volume but very little content.

“But now the filmmakers are trying their best, perhaps because it’s so difficult to raise investment, they put a lot of effort into the planning and some of the films are really good.”

She also mentioned the big improvements in acting in Hong Kong cinema. “Back in our era, most of the actors and actresses came from soap operas or beauty pageants. Now they all come from the Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts, so they have a really solid foundation in acting. They also have really professional ethics.”

While accepting the Camellia Award at Busan’s opening ceremony, Hui mentioned that it was getting “more difficult” for her to make films as she turns eighty next year. She joked in the press conference about being worried that she’d trip on the red carpet because she’s not so steady on her feet these days.

But she also said that she still enjoys making movies and is currently developing some ideas, so she’s not ready to announce her retirement just yet. “My judgment and understanding has not been reduced, in fact experience gives you a deeper understanding. So I still want to make films because I want to convey this new understanding that I have now in my work.”

Jointly presented by BIFF and Chanel, the festival’s Camellia Award honors pioneering women filmmakers who advance the role of women in Asian cinema. Previous recipients have included Korean production designer Ryu Seong-hie (Decision To Leave) and Taiwanese filmmaker and actress Sylvia Chang (Love Education, Daughter’s Daughter).

title: Fox Launching ‘Extracted’ International Production Hub In Malaysia
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Fox Entertainment Global (FEG) is hoping to take Extracted worldwide via a new production hub in Malaysia, its first international hub. With MIPCOM kicking off today in Cannes, sales execs at FEG will be sitting down with buyers to unveil the Malaysian hub, which qualifies for local tax incentives. Numerous international versions of the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Fox Entertainment Global (FEG) is hoping to take Extracted worldwide via a new production hub in Malaysia, its first international hub.

With MIPCOM kicking off today in Cannes, sales execs at FEG will be sitting down with buyers to unveil the Malaysian hub, which qualifies for local tax incentives.

Numerous international versions of the survival competition format can be filmed at the hub, which is based in the wilderness of Lake Kenyir replete with jaguars and pythons. The turnkey hub has a permanent headquarters and sets. Fox stressed it gives access to local crews and tax incentives, and said it has “more cameras than the Super Bowl.”

Extracted launched last year and has been a big hit for Fox, landing 45 million viewers across its first two seasons and already greenlit for ea third. Exec produced by Sylvester Stallone and filmed in British Columbia, the show challenges ordinary people to survive alone in an unforgiving wilderness with no training, no supplies, and no contact with the outside world. Watching every moment from a remote headquarters are their loved ones, who ultimately decide whether to let them continue or press the ever-present “EXTRACT” button, ending both the contestant’s journey and their family’s chance at the grand prize. Season 2 wrapped in April and was won by RJ Reynolds, a Project Manager from Texas.

Watch on Deadline

The hub is Fox’s first internationally, although it does have a Next Level Chef hub in Ireland for the Gordon Ramsay series.

“Extracted has all the ingredients of a universally resonant format: a powerful premise, stunning visuals, unforgettable family dynamics, and incredibly high stakes,” said FEG President Prentiss Fraser. “The infrastructure we’ve built in this Malaysia hub accelerates the series’ international expansion, offering licensees the infrastructure and expertise to create their own versions more efficiently, while delivering the scale and intensity that make the show so compelling.”

Fox execs are out in full force in Cannes this week, with the network’s Baywatch reboot set to be one of the hot shows on the Croisette.

title: ‘Saturday Night Live’: Shane Gillis’ Third Time Hosting Is Saved By Cast Newbie Grace Reiter
summary: In his third time hosting Saturday Night Live, Shane Gillis isn’t making the case for a triumphant return to the cast. On this weekend’s episode, which also featured musical guest Rosalía, the comedian delivered several on-brand sketches that featured his signature everyman sense of humor, but no water cooler moments worth meme-ifying. Gillis’ opening monologue […]
content:
In his third time hosting Saturday Night Live, Shane Gillis isn’t making the case for a triumphant return to the cast.

On this weekend’s episode, which also featured musical guest Rosalía, the comedian delivered several on-brand sketches that featured his signature everyman sense of humor, but no water cooler moments worth meme-ifying.

Gillis’ opening monologue was a tight five about his Bud Light commercials and getting into shape with workout buddies Joe Rogan and Theo Von, during which he put on his best femme voice to mimic gym gays and complained that “women just dress like whores now” at the gym.

The comedian also noted that he’s “balded directly into an Adolph Hitler haircut,” and the only other option is looking gay. “That’s it, you’re either gay or Hitler. And isn’t that where we’re at as a country?” he quipped.

Watch on Deadline

In the first sketch, Gillis played the host of a cop talk show, in which he just arrested his various guests.

Gillis then appeared in a country song music video, playing the father of a bride who imagines what he’ll do with her room when she moves out, only to end up hooking up with Ms. Pac-Man in a cloud of black mold.

In a Green Eggs and Ham sketch, featuring Mikey Day as the Cat in the Hat and Gillis as his defensive son who thinks his dad is being scammed, the host made things interesting when he accidentally dropped an F-bomb.

A History Channel sketch about WWII-time inventors patenting quiet shoes saw Gillis’ character finding them handy for “sneaking” around his wife, hence the name “sneakers.”

Gillis also led a heating/AC commercial that’s honest about how much of a nightmare of a process is, complete with workers making fun of you, smoking in your doorway and staring through your windows.

Meanwhile, new cast member Grace Reiter continued to prove her chops as she played problem child Coco in a “Weekend Update” segment in which her mom (Ashley Padilla) can’t find a babysitter. She was a perfect match for Padilla as the bratty daughter publicly embarrassing her mom.

Reiter also shared a couple of sketches with Gillis, playing his elderly mother as a hospice nurse (Sarah Sherman) tells him she only has a few days, which conflicts with his plans to see Jelly Roll in Vegas. The sketch also features a cameo from Ben Marshall as Jelly Roll, Marcello Hernandez as Jesus and Rosalía as a horny divorcee, egging him on to make the concert.

Rosalía, Marcello Hernandez, Grace Reiter, Ben Marshall and Shane Gillis on ‘Saturday Night Live’

The final sketch of the episode was set in a kid’s chess tournament, where young TJ (Jeremy Culhane) tries to ignore his parents (Gillis and Reiter) in the stands, where they go from arguing exes to inappropriate flirtation. Saving the best for last, Reiter was certainly a bright spot on an otherwise dull episode.

Gillis’ latest hosting gig on SNL comes after he hosted in 2024 and 2025, following his removal from the NBC sketch comedy‘s featured cast days after he was announced. The decision came in response to resurfaced videos of Gillis mocking Asian accents, in addition to using ethnic and gay slurs.

title: Shane Gillis Drops F-Bomb In ‘SNL’ “Green Eggs & Ham” Sketch, Apologizes
summary: Shane Gillis’ return to Saturday Night Live featured a not-safe-to-air slip in a Dr. Seuss-inspired sketch. On this weekend’s episode, the comedian accidentally dropped an F-bomb while playing the Cat in the Hat’s (Mikey Day) defensive son who is suspicious of Sam I Am (Andrew Dismukes) pressuring him to eat green eggs and ham. “Hey, […]
content:
Shane Gillis‘ return to Saturday Night Live featured a not-safe-to-air slip in a Dr. Seuss-inspired sketch.

On this weekend’s episode, the comedian accidentally dropped an F-bomb while playing the Cat in the Hat’s (Mikey Day) defensive son who is suspicious of Sam I Am (Andrew Dismukes) pressuring him to eat green eggs and ham.

“Hey, what the hell is wrong with you? My dad said he doesn’t like them. Walk away,” said Gillis.

“Bro, it’s a non-starter. He said he doesn’t f*cking,” he added, immediately covering his mouth. “Jeez! — like ’em.”

Although Gillis moved on in the sketch, Day called back to the expletive later. “Zachary’s the one who’s going. I want you out of this house. You’re a loser, and you said a bad word!” he said.

Watch on Deadline

Gillis acknowledged, “Yes I did.”

He can be heard saying “sorry about earlier” at the very end of the sketch. (You can watch it above.)

While censors didn’t catch the F-bomb on the live broadcast and stream, SNL posted the sketch to social media later that night with the word muted. (The expletive is audible in the recorded show on Peacock.)

Gillis referenced the incident during the curtain call at the end of the episode. “And sorry about earlier,” he said before thanking everyone. (You can watch a video below.)

Gillis was removed from SNL’s featured cast in 2019, shortly after he was announced. He’s since hosted the show three times, including in 2024 and 2025.

title: ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution
summary: Saturday Night Live once again returned Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost) to its opener, this time with Donald Trump’s secretary of defense addressing the crew of the beleaguered USS Lincoln. The ship was at sea for 265 days with no port call, and reports of poor conditions and demoralized sailors, but concerns over their plight were […]
content:
Saturday Night Live once again returned Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost) to its opener, this time with Donald Trump’s secretary of defense addressing the crew of the beleaguered USS Lincoln.

The ship was at sea for 265 days with no port call, and reports of poor conditions and demoralized sailors, but concerns over their plight were dismissed by Donald Trump.

At one point in tonight’s skit, Jost’s Hegseth tells the crew of his plans to stream a live execution. In reality, the Pentagon confirmed plans to stream the December execution of Nidal Hassan, sentenced to death for killing 13 people and injuring dozens more in a rampage at Fort Hood.

“As we get into the Christmas spirit, we’re going to execute a guy on live TV,” Jost said. “Yeah, that’s right. Public executions are back.”

Watch on Deadline

“And if the guy somehow survives the firing squad, then he’s got to fight Jake Paul. So check that out.”

Hegseth’s plans for a livestream of the execution have generated a backlash, with lawmakers in both parties condemning it and the president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops calling it a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”

Jost has played Hegseth with an ever-present focus on acting tough, yet clearly overcompensating as one of the least qualified individuals to hold the post.

Wearing a sash containing small bottles of Fireball whiskey, Jost’s Hegseth told the Navy crew, “I’m wearing an ammunition belt made of Fireball cinnamon whiskey — the only alcohol designed to taste better on the way back up.”

Jost’s Hegseth also stood in front of the new logo for the Department of War — the Trump team’s preferred name for the Defense Department — with looks like it has a Third Reich influence.

One of the sailors asked, “Sorry, is that a Nazi eagle?”

“It’s an American eagle with a Nazi vibe,” Hegseth responded.

Last week, after Hegseth gave a speech to the Air Force Academy, there was extensive social media attention to the revised eagle design used as a backdrop and its similarities to one used by the Nazi regime.

Tonight’s cold open also featured a cameo by Robert Kennedy Jr, played by James Austin Johnson, who tried to mimic the gravelly voice of the secretary of health and human services.

Johnson’s RFK Jr. told the sailors, “Yes, 200,000 pounds of pork, beef and goat meat have been recalled. But I just want to stress that catfish, pony and cricket are viable proteins for any American family.”

He added, “But I want to thank you. We were able to spot those recalls early by testing the meats on your ship. The research you provided on Operations Hell Cruise will be vital for many years to come.”

Hegseth finished up by quoting Lincoln — actually Linkin Park. “You strive so hard, and got so far, but in the end, it doesn’t even matter.“

He added, “Thank you for all being willing to go down with the ship — even though it breaks my personal rule of never going down on anyone.”

title: Javier Bardem on Adding Homoeroticism to 007 and Telling Sam Mendes That His ‘Skyfall’ Villain Should Be Someone Who ‘Wants to Have Sex With Bond’
summary: Javier Bardem’s “Skyfall” villain Raoul Silva is widely considered to be one of the best James Bond baddies across the entire franchise, a sadistic and flirtatious cyber-terrorist with bleached-blond locks who gave 007 arguably his most homoerotic scene to date. “We are the last two rats. We can either eat each other, or eat everyone […]
content:
Javier Bardem‘s “Skyfall” villain Raoul Silva is widely considered to be one of the best James Bond baddies across the entire franchise, a sadistic and flirtatious cyber-terrorist with bleached-blond locks who gave 007 arguably his most homoerotic scene to date.

“We are the last two rats. We can either eat each other, or eat everyone else,” Silva says as he unbuttons the shirt of Daniel Craig’s Bond, tied to a chair. He then moves his hands down Bond’s thighs, offering “Well, there’s a first time for everything” (to which Bond famously replies “What makes you think this is my first time?”)

As it happens, it was Bardem himself who wanted to dial up the sexuality of his character, and found a willing director in Sam Mendes.

Popular on Variety

“We went through the reading of it and [Mendes] was so open to what I was proposing to do with the sexuality of the character,” Bardem revealed at a special Screen Talk at the BFI London Film Festival on Sunday. “Because I said, ‘Listen, all the villains have done everything to destroy the world, but what about something person? What about something like, besides destroying the world, he wants to have sex with Bond.'”

According to Bardem, Mendes’ first response was was “‘Let me talk to the studio’… and the studio was very brave!” The scene, he noted was one that “now lasts in the memory of the audience” because it “put Bond out of his place in a moment with a situation that he’s not been to before — and the way he comes out of it is brilliant.”

Bardem also revealed that in the prison cell scene in “Skyfall” with Craig (who he said was “adorable”) and Judi Dench as M (“what a gift!”), he was so overcome that he forgot his lines.

“Sam said action and then [Dench] comes in and nobody talks… I forgot the lines!,” he said, to which Mendes asked him what was going on. “I’m sorry, I just realized that I’m in a James Bond movie. Excuse me, I just saw Judi Dench as M and James Bond looking at me and thought ‘Fuck, I’m in a James Bond movie!’ Sorry, let’s do it again!”

Across a wide-ranging conversation about his career and craft, Bardem — the first Spanish actor to win the best actor Oscar (for “No Country for Old Men”), holder of a record 5 Goya leading actor awards and one of a select group to have won Venice’s Volpi Cup twice — discussed a selection of his more than 65 screens credits and collaborations with numerous filmmakers. But he even went as far back as his first brush with acting as a five year old in the 1974 Spanish TV series “El Picaro,” which starred his mother, the late actress Pilar Bardem.

“My mother was in the show and this kid got sick and she said, ‘Don’t worry. I have my my kid,'” he revealed. In the scene, he said he started to cry. “And [the director] said ‘I love it, I love it, he’s a dramatic actor!’ And he was right!”

Bardem also joked that for “many years” until his mother passed away in 2021, he wondered “where is my salary” for his appearance. “Still today, I don’t know what she did with my money.”

Alongside his screen talk, Bardem has two films at the London Film Festival, which runs until Oct. 17, including Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” alongside his wife Penelope Cruz and Esteban Martinez’ “The Beloved.”

title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Flops With $5.5 Million Debut, ‘Other Mommy’ Tops Box Office With $27.5 Million
summary: “Other Mommy,” a horror movie starring Jessica Chastain as a double-jointed doppelgänger from hell, scared up $27.5 million in its box office debut. Those ticket sales were enough to lead in North America over this weekend’s other new release, “The Social Reckoning,” which crumbled in fifth place with $5.5 million. “Other Mommy” landed above expectations […]
content:
“Other Mommy,” a horror movie starring Jessica Chastain as a double-jointed doppelgänger from hell, scared up $27.5 million in its box office debut. Those ticket sales were enough to lead in North America over this weekend’s other new release, “The Social Reckoning,” which crumbled in fifth place with $5.5 million.

“Other Mommy” landed above expectations despite being one of the worst-reviewed movies of the year. Universal and Blumhouse’s campy thriller, about a sinister paranormal entity who takes on the appearance of a young girl’s mother, was saddled with a 19% on Rotten Tomatoes and tragic “D+” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. (Even last weekend’s bomb “Digger” earned a “C+” grade on exit polls.) Those marks don’t bode well for box office longevity, though “Other Mommy” is well-positioned financially against a modest $18 million budget. The movie collected $17.69 million at the international box office, bringing its global tally to $45.19 million.

“Horror movies are generally immune to a negative reception, but this is extreme,” says analyst David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Business is going to drop sharply.”

Popular on Variety

“The Social Reckoning,” too, will have to combat poor word-of-mouth in the coming weeks. That’s a problem because Sony’s Facebook drama didn’t incentivize crowds in the first place. The R-rated movie, written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, was projected to open to $7 million to $8 million. Even those returns wouldn’t have come close to 2010’s “The Social Network,” which opened almost exactly 16 years ago to $22 million, not adjusted for inflation. Critics and audiences were mixed on “The Social Reckoning,” which holds a 54% on Rotten Tomatoes and tepid “B-” grade on CinemaScore. The movie, picking up years after the first, follows a Facebook engineer (Mikey Madison) who leaks thousands of internal documents to a reporter (Jeremy Allen White) to blow the whistle on the company’s dark practices. Ticket buyers were mostly older males, a demographic that’s been slow to return to theaters since the pandemic.

Comparisons between the two films were always going to be tough because “The Social Network” is widely considered one of the best films of the 2010s. That film, directed by David Fincher, written by Sorkin and starring Jessie Eisenberg as Zuckerberg, ended up earning $224 million globally and won four Oscars (including one for Sorkin’s screenplay). Because of the first film’s pedigree, and the fact that Fincher and Eisenberg didn’t return for the second, Sony tried to distance the association between the movies and called the follow-up a “companion piece” rather than a sequel. That’s also likely why the studio economized on the budget; “The Social Reckoning” carries a $30 million price tag while “The Social Network” cost $40 million.

“The production cost was reasonable,” says Gross. “But it’s still a lot of money to recoup at these box office levels.”

Meanwhile, “Digger” cratered in its second weekend with $2.9 million from 3,321 theaters, a 64% decline from its dismal $8 million debut. So far, the Tom Cruise satire has limped to $14 million domestically and $30 million globally. Warner Bros. spent above $160 million to produce the film, which is shaping up to be one of the biggest bombs ever, with losses that could top $200 million theatrically. Given the scale of the disaster, Hollywood stars have been coming to the defense of “Digger,” with bold-faced names like Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Guillermo del Toro and Mandy Patinkin praising the film and encouraging audiences to go to theaters.

Elsewhere, holdovers including Amazon MGM’s Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity,” Sony’s “Resident Evil” reboot and Paramount’s Brad Pitt-led “Heart of the Beast” rounded box office charts.

Second place went to “Verity” with $11.4 million from 3,572 theaters, a harsh 64% decline from its opening weekend. The psychological thriller, starring Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson, will wind up as a win for Amazon MGM, having grossed $53 million in North America and more than $80 million worldwide to date against a $40 million budget.

“Resident Evil” dropped to second place with $8.3 million in its fourth weekend. So far, the R-rated video game remake has generated a strong $138.5 million domestically and more than $260 million globally against a $75 million budget.

“Heart of the Beast,” a survival thriller about a man who survives a plane crash with his dog, was No. 4 with $7.1 million from 3,365 theaters in its third frame. The film has earned $49.6 million in North America and $131.3 million worldwide. It will need to keep chugging along in theaters to justify its $82 million production budget.

More to come…

title: John Malkovich Says the Oscars Race Was a ‘Different World’ When He Was Last on the Campaign Trail: ‘Now, That’s the Only Way to Get People to Go to Theaters’
summary: John Malkovich has been highly tipped for an Oscar nomination for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s CIA black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” making it his first real shot at an Academy Award in three decades. The 72-year-old actor was previously nominated for best supporting actor in “Places in the Heart” (1984) and “In the Line […]
content:
John Malkovich has been highly tipped for an Oscar nomination for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s CIA black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” making it his first real shot at an Academy Award in three decades. The 72-year-old actor was previously nominated for best supporting actor in “Places in the Heart” (1984) and “In the Line of Fire” (1993), but never won.

Speaking at a London Film Festival Screen Talk on Sunday, Malkovich said he views awards buzz “probably differently than I did then, because the movie business existed.”

“It maintained an — undeserved, in my opinion, but nevertheless — a very, very high position in the culture. And when I say ‘undeserved,’ meaning there weren’t that many ‘Chinatowns’ or ‘Godfathers’ or ‘Godfathers II,'” Malkovich said. “So now, that’s the only way to get people to go to the theaters, the whole thing. And that’s months and months and months.”

Popular on Variety

Reflecting on the last time he was up for an Oscar over 30 years ago, Malkovich said the campaigning was not so intense. “When I was nominated for an Academy Award, someone said, ‘You’re nominated for an Academy Award,'” he said.

However, Malkovich has never been a huge fan of awards ceremonies anyway, and only attended the Oscars once, when he was nominated for “Places in the Heart.” He told the London crowd that he felt quite overwhelmed by the experience.

“I had a manager called Phyllis Carlyle, and we were on our way to the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion, and she was a little bit… bossy. She said, ‘Now honey, when we get there, there’s gonna be a lot of people,'” he recalled. “And I said, ‘OK, but we can just go in a side door, right?’ And she, right in my face, goes ‘Honey! It’s the Oscars, there’s no side door!’ So, I mean, that’s kind of my native personality in the face of that kind of onslaught.”

Malkovich acknowledged that Hollywood as a whole has changed quite a lot since the last time he was on the awards trail, with the advent of streaming taking over theaters. Often, he said, campaigning for a film is the only way to make the public go see it in theaters.

“Both ‘The Killing Fields,’ which was a 1984 Oscars film I think, and ‘Places in the Heart,’ they’re already been out, they’d already made their money, they were already successful. The same with ‘In the Line of Fire,'” he said. “It was really a different world. Now, that kind of seems to be the only way to get people to actually go to a theater.”

He isn’t too bothered by it, though. “I’m 72 years old, things change,” he said. “I don’t really like thinking things aren’t what they used to be. They just change, and you either change with them or die. And I prefer to change with them. I’ll die, anyway.”

“Wild Horse Nine,” in which he stars opposite Sam Rockwell as a veteran CIA agent, held its U.K. premiere at London Film Festival on Friday. Set shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup d’etat, the two are dispatched to Easter Island, where they must confront both their dark pasts and present conspiracies.

“Wild Horse Nine” first premiered at Venice Film Festival in September, where it received rave reviews and Malkovich took home the best actor prize. At a Venice press conference, Malkovich humbly shrugged off the praise, saying: “That is incredibly kind. I’ve had a long career, and I’ve had spectacular collaborations with writers, directors and actors. I never feel in competition with any of them. For me, it’s a very nice thing. But the nicest thing is the film getting attention. And the film has several terrific performers, and it’s beautifully written and directed. That’s what matters to me.”

title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight Reflects on Animated Feature’s 16-Year Journey at London Premiere: ‘When We Started This, Barack Obama Was a Fresh-Faced President’
summary: Stop-motion animation is a notoriously time-consuming method to make a film, with most features taking several years of painstakingly detailed work by vast teams of creatives. But few have likely taken as long as Laika’s sweeping fantasy epic “Wildwood,” which had its world premiere at the BFI London Film Festival on Sunday. Speaking on stage […]
content:
Stop-motion animation is a notoriously time-consuming method to make a film, with most features taking several years of painstakingly detailed work by vast teams of creatives.

But few have likely taken as long as Laika‘s sweeping fantasy epic “Wildwood,” which had its world premiere at the BFI London Film Festival on Sunday.

Speaking on stage at the premiere alongside voice stars Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay, director Travis Knight explained the stop-motion process to the audience at the Royal Festival Hall.

“Basically we build thousands and thousands of this tiny little objects, we put them in front of a camera and set lights and we take a picture, we move them a microscopic distance, we take another picture, we move them another microscopic distance, we take another picture,” he said. “And we repeat that process over and over until either the film emerges or society collapses.”

Popular on Variety

On “Wildwood,” — which Knight had previously acknowledged was the most ambitious Laika had ever attempted — production started in 2021 in the midst of COVID, but the development had actually begun some 10 years earlier, when Laika optioned the book by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis.

“This movie took us 16 years to make,” Knight explains. When we started Barack Obama was a fresh-faced president in his very first term. I could have become a medical doctor twice in the time it took us to make this movie. A child who was born when we started this could have driven me to the premiere.”

Following its world premiere at the London Film Festival, which runs until Oct. 17, “Laika” is due to be released on Oct. 23 by Fathom Entertainment in the U.S. and by Black Bear in the U.K. The film marks the first by Laika to receive a PG-13 rating.

title: James Gray Says He Considers ‘Two Lovers’ His First Successful Feature: “I Don’t Regard The Films I Made Before This Very Highly”
summary: Filmmaker James Gray told a London Film Festival audience this morning during a career Q&A that he believes Two Lovers, his fourth feature, starring Joaquin Phoenix and Gwyneth Paltrow, was the first time he successfully executed his artistic vision as a director. “This movie was very important to me. It was the first time I […]
content:
Filmmaker James Gray told a London Film Festival audience this morning during a career Q&A that he believes Two Lovers, his fourth feature, starring Joaquin Phoenix and Gwyneth Paltrow, was the first time he successfully executed his artistic vision as a director.

“This movie was very important to me. It was the first time I had creative control. The work took on another character,” Gray said after the LFF crowd was shown a clip from the 2008 film.

“I don’t regard the films I made before this very highly. I hope people like them, but I don’t think of them as truly mine. I was still trying to do something. Two Lovers was the first film that felt like who I was trying to be, if that makes sense, because I had total freedom.”

Gray added that Two Lovers was a relatively “cheap movie,” costing around $9.5 million.

Watch on Deadline

“I was left alone. The actors were great. I made exactly what I wanted,” he said. “I don’t know if the film is great, good, or terrible, but my emotional connection to it is profound because it was a beautiful time in my life.”

Directed by Gray from a screenplay he co-wrote with Ric Menello, Two Lovers tells the story of Leonard (Phoenix), an aspiring photographer and introvert who has moved back into his parents’ home following a recent heartbreak. His concerned parents try to set him up with Sandra (Vinessa Shaw), the daughter of a family friend. But Leonard meets Michelle (Paltrow), the beautiful but volatile mistress of a wealthy married man who has recently moved into an apartment in his family’s building. He becomes caught between the two women.

Gray is at the LFF with his latest feature, Paper Tiger. The film screened last night in London.

Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller star in the pic set in 1986 Queens, NY, in which two brothers become entangled in a scheme that ends up involving the Russian mafia, putting their family at risk. The film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May. Neon will release the film theatrically on November 13.

The LFF runs until October 18.

title: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Carey Mulligan Leads Voice Cast Of Laika’s Ambitious And Visually Stunning Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic – London Film Festival
summary: Laika, the Oregon animation house that specializes in stop motion, has a perfect track record of landing Best Animated Feature Oscar nominations for all four of its first films: Coraline, ParaNorman, Missing Link, and Kubo and the Two Strings. With its latest and unquestionably most ambitious project Wildwood, the streak could well continue. This film […]
content:
Laika, the Oregon animation house that specializes in stop motion, has a perfect track record of landing Best Animated Feature Oscar nominations for all four of its first films: Coraline, ParaNorman, Missing Link, and Kubo and the Two Strings. With its latest and unquestionably most ambitious project Wildwood, the streak could well continue. This film has been gestating at Laika for 16 years, finally starting production in 2021, and now having its world premiere today at the London Film Festival. It is also slated to open AFI Fest later this month for its North American premiere in Hollywood.

For director-producer Travis Knight, who is also CEO of Laika, this adaptation of Colin Meloy’s book has been a personal dream, especially since the setting of the book, and now the film, is right in his hometown of Portland, OR. How could he resist? A sweeping fantasy right in your own backyard featuring a magical forbidden forest of talking animals mixed with humans? It all becomes the center of a truly epic story that feels born to be on the big screen. The painstaking stop-motion animation process applied to a tale on a scale rarely seen on this level is a visual knockout, and the story is a compelling one focused on a scrappy young heroine determined to fight back and save her baby brother after he is harrowingly abducted from the streets of Portland by a murder of crows.

Watch on Deadline

Prue McKeel (nicely voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) is a loyal and loving teen girl who promises her parents she will take good care of her baby brother Mac on a normal sunny day outing. It turns out to be a frightening one when Mac is snatched up by a menacing swarm of black crows who swoop down in unison from the sky and fly away with him. Her frantic efforts to catch up fail and she sees the birds disappear into the adjoining forbidden forest known to allow no outsiders. Unable to go back home and explain to her parents (Maya Erskine and Jake Johnson), she sets off to find Mac and bring him back. No easy task, but her rather awkward and far less adventurous classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay) offers any help he can supply, which isn’t much. Still, he sets out to follow her into the forest where after an encounter with the imposing uniformed coyotes who patrol the place gets separated from Prue.

Soon both are swept up, on individual tracks into this world like something out of Lewis Carroll, as they go down the rabbit hole into a society like no other — a land of talking animals, bandits, wise owls, even a loyal rat and more. For Curtis it is meeting the evil Dowager Governess Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) who attempts to bring him into her fold. She is a woman devastated by the death of her only son, so much so she can’t function and turns her grief into no good, with the coyote force in lockstep for her dark ambitions. When Curtis sees what she is up to he refuses and is tossed into a prison with other rejects.

Meanwhile, Prue, meeting The General (Angela Bassett), the wise Great Eagle leader of the Avian Principality, as well as Brendan, the empathetic leader of the outcast Bandits, uses every intuition she has to navigate this dense landscape. Eventually all roads lead her to Alexandra, who lies to her. She encourages her to go home to her parents, saying it is better for a grieving mother to know the truth of what happened to her child. Prue follows the advice, confesses what happened to Mac, and discovers the secret her parents have been keeping from her all along.

There is much more to come in this two-hour-plus adaptation including a battle royale that will see Prue returning for a massive fight to the finish, still hoping to navigate a happy ending.

With six-time Oscar-nominated cinematographer Caleb Deschanel (The Black Stallion) working for the first time on an animated film, the visual palette based in part on the book’s gorgeous illustrations by Caron Ellis is breathtaking. Deschanel makes the stop-motion process feel like live action, the camera picking up character heartache and triumph in ways I haven’t quite seen before in this form. Knight is a born storyteller so the emphasis is always on that, and even though the visuals are quite awesome in their own right, they never overwhelm. Character development is key here, as it was in the book, and each is fully fleshed out. Among them is Bassett’s commanding eagle, the General; Brendan (powerfully voiced by Mahershala Ali), leader of the Bandits; Maksim (Tom Waits), loyal coyote foot soldier to the Dowager Governess; regal Iphigenia (Tantoo Cardinal); bumbling coyote Dmitri (Charlie Day); reclusive aging owl Rex (Richard E. Grant); and Septima, a little rat who rises to the occasion and will break your heart (wonderfully voiced by Awkwafina).

There can be no doubt Meloy created this sweeping story in the tradition of other epics like Lord of the Rings and Chronicles of Narnia, and though Wildwood isn’t quite up on that mountain it ably marches to its own drummer, a story of grief, courage, determination and triumph, and yet another Laika stop-motion gem that stays in the heart.

Producers are Knight and Sam Wilson.

Title: Wildwood

Festival: London

Distributor: Fathom

Release date: October 23, 2026

Director: Travis Knight

Screenwriter: Chris Butler

Cast: Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Tom Waits, Richard E. Grant, Amanda Stenberg, Tantoo Cardinal, Len Cariou, Marc Evan Jackson

Rating: PG-13

Running time: 2 hr 12 mins

title: ‘Shy & Lola’: How Bel Powley, Hayley Squires &  Amanda Coe Brought A Coen Brothers Vibe To BBC Thriller In UK Port Town
summary: EXCLUSIVE: What would happen if you took the “visual reference” of the Coen brothers and transported this vibe to the UK’s port town of Grimsby. That question is posed in Shy & Lola, a BBC drama starring Harry Potter’s Bel Powley and The Night Manager’s Hayley Squires, which will be taken to buyers at MIPCOM […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: What would happen if you took the “visual reference” of the Coen brothers and transported this vibe to the UK’s port town of Grimsby.

That question is posed in Shy & Lola, a BBC drama starring Harry Potter’s Bel Powley and The Night Manager’s Hayley Squires, which will be taken to buyers at MIPCOM next week before launching on the BBC.

In an interview with Deadline, Powley and Squires stressed the highly original nature of the Amanda Coe-penned series from Baby Reindeer maker Clerkenwell Films, but they did say the work of the Coen brothers influenced its look and tone.

“The Coen brothers often explore incredibly dark subjects, such as murder, death, blood and guns, but they shoot them in a way that gives the material a sense of levity and lightness,” said Powley. “I think that’s what the cinematographer was looking for visually.”

Watch on Deadline

Squires said the “Coen brothers’ influence probably comes through in the humor” of Shy & Lola, which also “comes out in the geography where the stories take place and the things that are specific to that place.”

Revealed by Deadline several months back, Shy & Lola spotlights its protagonists, two very different women who are forced to become allies when a murder entangles them in the criminal underworld operating in Grimsby. Shy is a cleaner, scraping by and dreaming of a new life in Portugal. Lola is an ex-model-turned-grifter who arrives in town with trouble at her heels. The unlikely pair build an operation that threatens to blow the local bad guys out of the water, as opposing futures beckon.

Coe, whose credits include Apple TV’s Dior series The New Look and the BBC’s Apple Tree Yard, was inspired by Fargo.

“I love the idea that you can create a world of its own that resonates with the real world but is very heightened and blackly comic,” added Coe. “We use violence sparingly but in an interesting way. There’s a theme of violence going through the show without glorifying it.”

Shy & Lola is based on the French show Cheyenne & Lola starring Charlotte Le Bon and Veerle Baetens. BBC Studios approached Clerkenwell with the idea to adapt the French show and the indie immediately saw an opportunity to add its own twist. “It has that mix we love at Clerkenwell,” said Petra Fried, who runs the indie and is an EP on Shy & Lola. “It’s a darkly comic, propulsive story with real emotional depth underneath it. It’s funny and entertaining, but the stakes are very real, so you never stop caring about these women.”

Coe, who said she has a track record of making “female-led shows,” noted that there are major distinctions between Cheyenne & Lola and her version. “The French version starts with a character in their underwear looking amazing,” she added. “That is not the vibe of our show.”

“I’ve never witnessed that in a chemistry read before”

Image: BBC/Clerkenwell Films Ltd./Kerry Spicer BBC/Clerkenwell Films Ltd./Matt Towers

In order for this “vibe” to work, the chemistry between the leads had to impeccable. Luckily, they matched perfectly. Powley and Squires are two actors at the top of their game, with BAFTA nominee Powley about to be seen as Aunt Petunia in HBO’s eye-catching Harry Potter, and Squires, who wowed in Ken Loach’s I, Daniel Blake a decade ago, playing a big role in the BBC and Prime Video’s The Night Manager.

“I’ve never witnessed that in a chemisty read before where you just go ‘wow’ after 10 seconds,” said Coe. “Together they were more than the sum of their parts.”

Squires admired Powley from when she had a small part in one of her breakout hits, Julia Jarrold’s rom-com A Royal Night Out. She said the pair quickly made a “silent pact to find the best version” of the characters they were playing. “We are quite different people but have a real understanding of each other,” she added. “That mirrors the characters of Shy and Lola. They essentially fall platonically in love with each other on screen, which was a beautiful relationship to play out.”

Powley also spoke to Shy and Lola’s “unlikely charm” and praised Squires for bringing “such gravity and being so grounded in her performances.”

Another “character” in Shy & Lola, according to Powley, is the port town of Grimsby, a place rarely represented in British TV or movies, although it is the home of Sacha Baron Cohen’s ill-fated 2016 comedy that bears its name.

Squires, who joked that when she first read the scripts she simply thought to herself, “How am I going to master the Grimsby accent,?” something she eventually did with the help of Grimsby-born Shy & Lola co-star Thomas Turgoose, said the setting brings with it a “sense of community.”

“There’s an ensemble of characters who make up the community where they work and live, and it has a real richness to it,” she added. “These aren’t people who despise where they come from or hate where they live. The majority of working-class people actually don’t [hate where they live].”

Squires thinks this “richness” has been lost somewhat in the recent depiction of working class communities, as she harks back to successful, multi-faceted 1990s shows like Our Friends in the North. “I feel as though that trend might have changed,” she added. “It’s the same with anything to do with class or culture; if your writer has knowledge of that community then it comes through.”

She is enthused by the success of shows like the BBC’s Sherwood, however, and throws her weight behind the national broadcaster as an “organization that has had to battle to hold its ground, and I think it has.”

BBC Studios will be selling Shy & Lola at MIPCOM this week.

title: AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same”
summary: Is the world ready for a giant worm going to work on the subway? Korean director Kim Sung-soo thinks so and is making a film on this very subject, Worm Train, inspired by Franz Kafka’s short story Metamorphosis. Kim, whose credits include major Korean blockbusters such as Asura: The City Of Madness and 12.12: The […]
content:
Is the world ready for a giant worm going to work on the subway? Korean director Kim Sung-soo thinks so and is making a film on this very subject, Worm Train, inspired by Franz Kafka’s short story Metamorphosis.

Kim, whose credits include major Korean blockbusters such as Asura: The City Of Madness and 12.12: The Day, talked about how he’s using Kling AI tools to make the short film on a panel at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) today.

Kling AI, which recently released its 4.0 image generation model, also invited Chinese animation filmmaker Li Wei (Big Fish & Begonia); Harry Hyun, a director and CEO of Korea’s MooAm Co; and Lee Sang-wook, a producer and team manager at Korea’s MBC C&I AI Contents Lab, to present recent projects made using Kling AI tools, as well as discuss the latest trends in this new mode of filmmaking.

After presenting a teaser for Worm Train, Kim said AI has changed the way he thinks about filmmaking, but that “one thing never changes, which is what makes a film cinematic”.

Watch on Deadline

“Now everyone has similar tools and anyone can access Kling, but while some will make a masterpiece, others will make a film that is mediocre,” Kim said. “Initially, I thought AI would destroy the industry, but I don’t think so any more, because technology does not replace creativity. The value of images still comes from human intervention.”

Hyun, who has made AI films including Crypto Man and Genfluencer, expanded on this topic. “I don’t think AI production compared to traditional production is really that different – the difference is efficiency and simplicity – but if you don’t have experienced filmmakers on set, everything can end up looking the same.

“That’s why AI images may look impressive at first, but not later, because everyone is using the same lighting, same everything,” Hyun continued. “You need an art director who can do the fine tuning, a director and cinematographer who have really studied and learned when to use a close shot, wide shot, how to frame an image. These are long discussions we have on set, they’re not random decisions. Only when you’re working with experts will you be able to create something different with AI – not just cookie cutter deliverables.”
