title: ‘Bedford Park’ Star and Busan Juror Moon Choi on Locking Away Her Trophies and Plotting a Screen Version of a Molière-Winning Play
summary: For several years after the biggest run of her career, Moon Choi, known in Korea as Choi Hee-seo, kept her trophies out of sight. The haul was substantial. Her turn as Japanese anarchist Kaneko Fumiko in “Anarchist from Colony” swept Korea’s new actress prizes, and her lead role in independent feature “Our Body,” which bowed […]
content:
For several years after the biggest run of her career, Moon Choi, known in Korea as Choi Hee-seo, kept her trophies out of sight.

The haul was substantial. Her turn as Japanese anarchist Kaneko Fumiko in “Anarchist from Colony” swept Korea’s new actress prizes, and her lead role in independent feature “Our Body,” which bowed in Toronto, earned her Busan International Film Festival’s Actress of the Year honor in 2018. By her own count, two films brought her 14 awards in a single year. She was around 30.

“Some years passed, and I put the trophies in the cabinet. I didn’t want to have them displayed because whenever I saw them displayed somewhere, I kind of felt pressure,” Choi tells Variety. “I felt like I had to prove something to show them that I was worth it.”

Popular on Variety

“I felt that being successful at a young age can do some bad things to you. It didn’t make me feel proud, but it actually kind of made me feel crestfallen because I felt like I had to reach a height that goes beyond those awards,” she says.

What followed was a stretch she describes candidly: more independent films, Korean TV series that “flopped really badly” and film “A Girl with Closed Eyes” with Kim Minha that still has no release date two years after its Busan premiere. Through all of it, she was waiting for “Bedford Park.”

Choi is now back in Busan in a different role, sitting on the seven-member jury for the festival’s competition section, which is only in its second year. Zhang Yimou presides over a panel that also includes Bi Gan, Kei Ishikawa, July Jung, Vietnamese producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc and Kazakh actor Samal Yeslyamova. “Bedford Park” is also in town, screening in the Flash Forward section.

“I don’t have the pressure that I need to prove anything to anybody,” Choi says of returning as a juror. “I’m kind of feeling like a student trying to learn from all these films that I’m going to be watching alongside amazing people like Zhang Yimou and Bi Gan.”

Her yardstick for the competition comes from Asghar Farhadi’s idea that a good film begins once the audience leaves the cinema. Two days before heading to Busan, she watched Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love,” starring her friend and stage partner Jeon Do-yeon, on the big screen with her father. Outside the theater, the pair argued over whether the film’s final shot of a full moon offers hope. Her father read the title as a paradox pointing to an impossible love; she saw the opposite.

“I just felt so fulfilled because of those conversations I had with my father, which is rare,” Choi says. “I want to look for the films that leave us with these amazing questions as we exit the theater, rather than the films that I feel like that give us definitive answers.”

As an actor, she adds, she will be watching for performances that linger “not because they were so perfect, but because they were so truthful in the moment.”

Written and directed by Stephanie Ahn, “Bedford Park” follows Audrey (Choi), a Korean American physical therapist in New Jersey caught between her immigrant parents’ expectations and her own life. After her mother is hurt in a car accident, Audrey forms an unlikely bond with Eli (Son Suk-ku), the former wrestler who was behind the wheel. The film world premiered in Sundance’s U.S. Dramatic competition in January and won the Special Jury Award for Debut Feature. Sony Pictures Classics picked up worldwide rights during the festival, and the film has since played Toronto’s Discovery program.

Choi auditioned seven years ago. Ahn sent her the full screenplay in advance, which she says is rare, and she finished it on her phone in one sitting. Audrey’s tug-of-war between being a dutiful Korean daughter and living for herself mirrored her own upbringing: Japan from the ages of nine to 12, two years in Seoul, then three in New Jersey. Back in Korea, classmates teased her as “the Japanese kid.”

“It seemed like wherever I went, I didn’t belong anywhere because when I came back to Seoul from Japan or the U.S., people would view me as that girl from Japan, that girl from the U.S.,” Choi says. “Although I’m not a Korean American immigrant, I thought that I could resonate with that.”

Audrey’s profession gave Choi another way into the character. “I felt like she had such a warm heart for others, but she didn’t know how to do that for herself,” she says, linking that to the value Korean and Japanese families place on self-sacrifice. “I think Audrey was fighting against that.”

The film took years to finance. Choi was unknown in the U.S., Ahn was a first-time director coming from editing, and Eli was originally written as a white character, with names like Tom Hardy and Jake Gyllenhaal floated as a dream. COVID shut everything down. Four years in, the team shot a 15-minute short as a proof of concept for financiers.

Choi showed it to Son, a friend of a decade from the days when they would drop off casting resumes together. By then he had broken out as a star, and he told her he would want the role if Eli were Korean American. She pitched the idea of rewriting Eli as a Korean American adoptee to Ahn, who met Son over Zoom and reworked the script for him. Son in turn brought in Hyundai Motor Company, which backed the film as its first investment in an independent feature, and Foster and Ahn made Choi an executive producer. Foster produces alongside Russ Krasnoff, Chris S. Lee, Theresa Kang, Son and Nina Yang Bongiovi, whose earlier Sundance launches include “Sorry to Bother You” and Rebecca Hall’s “Passing.”

“They were kind enough and generous enough for me to be able to focus on acting on set,” Choi says. Post-production brought three-hour Zoom calls over cuts and music cues. “That was, I think, when I felt like, ‘Oh, this is what producing feels like.’”

Watching the finished film at Sundance, she says, felt like “giving birth to something so valuable,” a sentiment Son shared.

Choi has rarely followed the conventional path for a Korean actor. A voracious reader as a child, she kept looking for scripts that could surprise her. That didn’t always sit well with K-dramas and Korean commercial films, where with some scripts, she says, you know exactly what will happen on the next page. That choosiness earned her a reputation for “independent and artsy movies.” After New Jersey, she enrolled at Seoul’s Yonsei University to read journalism and English literature, spending her evenings training as an actor with its student theater club, and later took a year of acting courses at UC Berkeley on an exchange program. She is also the author of a collection of short stories and poems. Along the way she appeared in Bong Joon Ho’s “Okja” and shot a two-hour feature in Gangneung with Japanese actor Joe Odagiri, who she says came to Korea and worked for next to nothing.

Choi recalls a conversation with Jeon in New York, where the pair recently closed the final leg of Simon Stone’s staging of “The Cherry Orchard.” The production premiered in Seoul in 2024 with Jeon and “Squid Game” actor Park Hae-soo, then toured Hong Kong, Singapore and Adelaide before landing at New York’s Park Avenue Armory in September.

“She just held my hands, and she said, ‘Moon … I’m so happy for you, and just know that you are greater than what you think you are,’” Choi says.

Choi already has one directing credit, “Bandi,” her short for the 2021 “Unframed” anthology, in which she, Son, Park Jeong-min and Lee Je-hoon each directed a short. Choi and Son also wrote theirs. She says she never set out to direct and writes screenplays mainly for the pleasure of it.

A new project may change that. Choi has signed on to lead a Korean stage adaptation of “Une histoire d’amour,” the play by French writer-director and actor Alexis Michalik that follows a lesbian couple’s attempt to have a child. The play premiered in 2020, picked up a Molière for its staging that year, and Michalik has since made it into a film. Choi will perform it in Seoul next year, and after a Zoom call with Michalik she has his blessing to option it for a screen version she pictures in Brooklyn.

“Should I direct it, produce it? I’m not sure,” Choi says. What she does know is that she wants to write the screenplay herself, which she says “would kind of give me an idea if I want to produce it, or act in it, or direct it.”

The global reach of K-pop and series like “Squid Game” has opened doors for Korean actors abroad, Choi says, but whether they can act in English remains the limit. Choi now acts in English, Korean and Japanese, but she only started learning English at 15, and Ahn hired a dialect coach for both leads so they would sound like Korean Americans from New Jersey. “I know I can do it because I’ve done it once,” she says.

At home, she sees Korean cinema in recovery but leaning hard on genre, particularly horror, a pattern she also noticed in Los Angeles meetings. Park Chan-wook and Lee Chang-dong have delivered new films in back-to-back years, and she points to Na Hong-Jin and Byun Sung-hyun among those who followed them. But she wants more filmmakers her own age, in their late 30s or early 40s, and singles out Son, who runs his own production company and is writing his first feature.

She feels a responsibility there too, she says, “because I produce now as well, I can probably be the forefront of that, because it’s generation, right? Who do we have after Lee Chang-dong and Park Chan-wook?”

For now, Choi is on the festival circuit with “Bedford Park” and hunting for an English-language role. She signed with Gersh and management company Cognition six months ago and has been auditioning and sending self-tapes since.

“I am a total newcomer in Hollywood,” she says.

And the screen version of “Une histoire d’amour”? “I don’t know, it’s going to take 10 years, maybe.”

title: How Busan Title ‘Selvi’ Turns a Nurse’s Working Hours Into an Endurance Test
summary: A homecare nurse whose working day stretches from 12 hours to 72 sits at the center of “Selvi,” the first feature from Tamil filmmaker Sailesh Rathnakumar, which premieres in the Busan International Film Festival’s Vision–Asia section. Anjali Patil plays the title role and produces through her banner Anahat Films. Rathnakumar wrote the screenplay with cinematographer […]
content:
A homecare nurse whose working day stretches from 12 hours to 72 sits at the center of “Selvi,” the first feature from Tamil filmmaker Sailesh Rathnakumar, which premieres in the Busan International Film Festival’s Vision–Asia section.

Anjali Patil plays the title role and produces through her banner Anahat Films. Rathnakumar wrote the screenplay with cinematographer Bargav Sridhar, and Sreekar Prasad edited the film.

Selvi hopes to qualify as a nurse and eventually work in Singapore. When Kavitha, a friend since childhood, attempts suicide, Selvi takes over her shifts on top of her own and spends her days moving between private homes, caring for families who know little about her.

Popular on Variety

“For someone like Selvi, a crisis doesn’t necessarily arrive as one dramatic event,” Rathnakumar tells Variety. “It develops through a series of working hours, additional responsibilities and small compromises that gradually become unbearable.”

The jump from 12 to 24, 48 and then 72 hours gave the story its shape, he says. As the clock runs, Selvi is always on hand for someone else and has less and less time to be a person in her own right.

The film opens on a beach, with Selvi and her friends flying kites, before moving into domestic interiors where her world narrows. “With the kites, I wanted to show the possibility of looking upwards, of imagining something beyond the immediate circumstances of one’s life,” Rathnakumar says.

The production took its time finding homes that felt lived in and signaled the class of the families inside them. “Selvi can be essential to a family’s everyday life without ever being treated as someone who belongs to it,” he says.

Most of the nurses the director has met came from rural villages to the cities for work. He sees a pecking order within the care sector, where some workers have the training and means to go abroad while others stay stuck in insecure jobs doing intimate, demanding work with little recognition.

Because Sridhar co-wrote the script, the camera plan was baked in from the writing stage. The film never leaves Selvi’s point of view, and the audience learns things only when she does.

Prasad came aboard at the script stage. At their first meeting, the editor flagged scenes that could go without harming the story, which saved the production time and money, Rathnakumar says. The director shot some of them anyway. None made the final cut.

A Prague Film School alumnus, Rathnakumar began his career doing sound and music supervision for veteran Indian editor B. Lenin.

For Patil, Selvi’s habit of putting her own plans on hold struck close to home. After finishing her postgraduate studies in design and direction at the National School of Drama in 2010, she drifted into acting and became one of her family’s main earners. She launched Anahat Films in 2021 intending to write and direct, then spent its first five years producing for other filmmakers.

“Somehow our ambitions grow around circumstances like fungi,” Patil says. “Also, culturally, in Indian society, this behavior is celebrated. Keeping others before oneself to the point of absolute exhaustion. We are surrounded by so many Selvis, men and women alike.”

The shoot couldn’t run in sequence and was organized by location instead, so Patil tracked her own makeup, hair, body and voice continuity across Selvi’s decline, leaning on continuity photos and long rehearsals with the ensemble. “I love being that human thermostat for the film,” she says.

Wearing both hats came at a cost. The final scene was shot on Marina Beach at the end of a rough day, in a window of just a few hours. Patil was preoccupied with whether the production could afford to return if they missed it, and by the last take the light had gone. Rathnakumar and Sridhar told her they had what they needed, but she wasn’t satisfied.

“I remember walking away hurriedly on Marina Beach, sobbing in frustration, hiding from the crew, thinking that, as a producer, I couldn’t even afford to give myself a proper time for the film’s end close-up shot,” Patil says.

The actor, whose credits include “Naa Bangaaru Talli,” “Newton” and “Kaala,” co-produced “The Moogai,” which played Sundance in 2024, and “The Shadowbox,” which played Berlin in 2025. “Selvi” was presented as a work-in-progress at the Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum in March and drew backing from the Red Sea Fund.

International funding, Patil says, means long waits, complicated contracts and co-production treaties, and Indian filmmakers end up chasing the same grants as professionals from wealthier countries. “There is already an undisclosed disparity right there that nobody can talk about,” she says. “And honestly, a lot of times, I feel people still don’t know how to distribute independent Indian films in many parts of the world.”

Rathnakumar points to character-led Tamil films such as “Maharaja,” “Meiyazhagan,” “Vaazhai” and “Lubber Pandhu,” which found audiences alongside star vehicles like “Amaran.” “I think the challenge for independent cinema is not necessarily whether audiences are willing to watch these films, but whether the films can reach them,” he says.

Patil, who has worked in Hindi, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil-language cinema, says Tamil filmmaking has made room for independent voices over the past two to three years, calling it “very, very hopeful for all of us.”

Next up, Rathnakumar is producing Patil’s feature “Average Girl,” the short “Florescence” and Sridhar’s directing effort “Goliath.” He is also developing “Uneventful Death of Mr. Srinivasan,” a comedy about a family whose celebrations turn to mourning when a 70-year-old man dies a day after his Bheema Radha Shanthi ceremony.

Patil, meanwhile, plans to disappear after Busan to work full-time on a speculative sci-fi script she has been developing for six years. “I won’t be postponing my ambitions like Selvi,” she says.

title: Box Office Boom for China’s Women Directors Feeds New Parallax Films Pickups From Shao Yihui, Yin Lichuan and Yang Lina (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Three filmmakers at the forefront of China’s women-led cinema boom – Shao Yihui, Yang Lina and Yin Lichuan – have new titles on the slate of sales agent Parallax Films, which is shopping them to buyers at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) in Busan. In the short “Winning at Sleep,” Shao turns her […]
content:
Three filmmakers at the forefront of China’s women-led cinema boom – Shao Yihui, Yang Lina and Yin Lichuan – have new titles on the slate of sales agent Parallax Films, which is shopping them to buyers at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) in Busan.

In the short “Winning at Sleep,” Shao turns her satirical eye on meritocracy and the culture of constant competition. The story centers on an everyday girl who is handed an unlikely chance at glory through an unusual contest.

“It’s OK” reteams Yang with Golden Horse winner Wen Qi (“Angels Wear White,” “The Bold, the Corrupt and the Beautiful”). Wen plays a young teacher dealing with an urgent health crisis, all while managing the unspoken connection she shares with her traditional mother. The dramedy takes on questions of womanhood and a woman’s control over her own body.

Popular on Variety

Veteran director Yin’s “A Joke” is billed as the first Chinese feature to tackle sexual harassment in the workplace. It follows a sanitation worker who spends three years quietly collecting proof against her abusive boss, then joins forces with a young lawyer to expose him.

The pickups ride a wave that began in 2021 with Shao’s breakout “B for Busy,” which opened the door for female-centered stories in China. Three years later, Yin’s “Like a Rolling Stone” and Shao’s second feature “Her Story” grossed more than RMB845 million ($118 million) combined at the domestic box office.

“Her Story” went on to win best picture, best actress and best supporting actress at the 38th Golden Rooster Awards, mainland China’s government-backed film honors. Films by women directors have historically won few opportunities at the awards, making the haul a landmark for feminist filmmaking in the country.

On the festival circuit, Luka Yuanyuan Yang’s documentary hybrid “Chinatown Cha-Cha” found similar success. Parallax credits a young female audience with growing clout for proving that films about gender roles, relationships and social pressure can pull in big numbers. Investors, studios and producers have since backed a broader range of women-led projects.

A generation of female directors now works across both commercial and indie filmmaking, chasing box office and festival prestige at once. Alongside Shao and Yin, the group includes Yang (“Spring Tide,” “Song of Spring”), Teng Congcong (“Send Me to the Clouds,” series “To the Wonder”) and Vivian Qu (“Angels Wear White,” “Girls on Wire”).

Parallax’s short film lineup also features “Our Secrets,” which took the Lights On Women’s Worth Award at Cannes’ La Cinef. “Scorching,” “Thirteenth Night” and “Fishtank” turn to fantasy to chart their characters’ interior lives. “Orlo With Karma” is a Tibetan coming-of-age romance from Kangdrun, director of “Linka Linka.”

“Linka Linka,” which won the Firebird and Fipresci prizes at the Hong Kong International Film Festival, explores urban Tibetan youth culture today, while “100 Sunset” looks at the Tibetan diaspora in Canada. Anuparna Roy’s “Lovers in the Blue Night” won the Netpac Award at Venice. Documentary and hybrid titles about identity and family include “Masayume,” Visions du Réel winner “From Dawn to Dawn” and docufiction “Shanghai Daughter.” “Now I Met Her” and “Embers” sit at the commercial end of the slate.

title: Locarno Title ‘Rapture’ Director Dominic Sangma Confronts Unregulated Stone Mining in Busan Asian Project Market Drama ‘Veil of Dust’
summary: A villager maimed by a mining blast and his wife’s fight for compensation open up a story of exploitation, complicity and indigenous belief in “Veil of Dust,” the new project from “Rapture” director Dominic Sangma. The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & […]
content:
A villager maimed by a mining blast and his wife’s fight for compensation open up a story of exploitation, complicity and indigenous belief in “Veil of Dust,” the new project from “Rapture” director Dominic Sangma.

The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

When an explosion rips through the hills, 35-year-old Nengsal is dug out of the debris having lost a leg. His wife Ajin, 32, sets out to win compensation but runs into a system that thrives on exploiting people and keeping them quiet. The headman is compromised, an NGO in the area is pursuing its own politics, and the man running the mine discloses that Nengsal was never on the books, leaving workers like him invisible on their own land. Through the couple’s children, 12-year-old Kasanchi and 10-year-old Miklu, the film moves into a mystical realm rooted in indigenous belief, as healer Rengin leads Miklu through an unsettling ritual on a bird meant to “transfer” his father’s wound. When an unplanned blast kills a boy from the village, the elders take advance compensation to keep the peace. With Nengsal pleading with Ajin to end his pain and her fight for justice going nowhere, she turns to the rare herbs in her garden, which can both heal and harm.

Stone mining has surfaced in Sangma’s earlier films, but here it takes center stage, and the urgency of the subject led him to pause the final film of his village trilogy. The blasts, the shaking ground, wrecked homes and farms, and villagers killed in mine accidents are part of his childhood memories, and the mining is still going on. It had been normal for so long that he never felt the need to address it, he says, until a recent stay in the village, where he saw landslides, cracked houses and mining edging closer to the main settlement.

Popular on Variety

“To an outsider, unregulated mining might seem like a mere environmental issue. But to those of us who live in its shadow, it doesn’t just erode the soil – it erodes the soul,” Sangma says.

The father of a young daughter, Sangma says he hopes speaking out will make the village a slightly better home for her. The elders have stayed quiet, perhaps because they never saw mining as a problem or because it has fed many of them, and the deeper he went, the more tangled it became. “In a way villagers were the part of the reason why it continues for so long,” he says.

Sangma calls the film “a microcosm to what we are doing to the mother earth with our greed” and hopes it will nudge audiences to care a little more for the planet.

Producer Xu Jianshang, who produced Sangma’s debut “Ma’ama” and “Rapture,” says the director is moved by his community’s suffering and that his very local concerns speak to the wider world. “There is beauty and grace in his image making and as a producer I feel we need to support more such voices,” she says.

“Rapture,” the second film in Sangma’s trilogy, premiered at Locarno in 2023 and won the cultural diversity award at the Asia Pacific Screen Awards. “Ma’ama” won best cinematography at the Shanghai International Film Festival and best film at the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival.

“Veil of Dust” is in development, and in Busan the team is raising money and seeking co-production partners and backers who share the director’s vision.

title: Pat McAfee Joins ESPN’s In-Game Super Bowl LXI Coverage & Expands MNF Role
summary: Pat McAfee is taking his Field Pass show from college football to the NFL. The network’s marquee talk show talent will be doing a version of Field Pass with the Pat McAfee Show during next year’s Super Bowl LXI. It will be one of three alternate telecasts for the big game. The others are Super […]
content:
Pat McAfee is taking his Field Pass show from college football to the NFL.

The network’s marquee talk show talent will be doing a version of Field Pass with the Pat McAfee Show during next year’s Super Bowl LXI. It will be one of three alternate telecasts for the big game. The others are Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats and the venerable Manningcast. Field Pass will air on ESPNU while Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats will air on NFL Network and Manningcast will be on its usual home, ESPN2.

Additionally, Field Pass with the Pat McAfee Show will become an alternate telecast for a number of this season’s Monday Night Football games. It will debut in Week 6 for Washington Commanders and San Francisco 49ers, the first of five Monday Night Football editions. The stint will conclude during Week 18 on January 9.

Watch on Deadline

McAfee will remain in his field level position with Dan Orlovsky and Darius Butler, while Connor Campbell, Ty Schmit and Tone Digs will join from an in-stadium suite.

On NFL Network, MNF Playbook with Next Gen Stats begins a week earlier, in Week 5, for Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams, its first of seven Monday editions.

title: Five Organizations Launch Asian Producers Alliance In Busan Market
summary: Five independent producer organizations from Korea, Indonesia, Philippines, Hong Kong and Taiwan launched a coalition, the Asian Producers Alliance (APA), at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM). The five bodies include the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK), Indonesian Film Producers Association (APROFI), Philippine Independent Producers Group (PIPG), Hong Kong Movie Production Executives Association (HKMPEA) […]
content:
Five independent producer organizations from Korea, Indonesia, Philippines, Hong Kong and Taiwan launched a coalition, the Asian Producers Alliance (APA), at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

The five bodies include the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK), Indonesian Film Producers Association (APROFI), Philippine Independent Producers Group (PIPG), Hong Kong Movie Production Executives Association (HKMPEA) and the Taiwan Producers Association (TPA).

In the initial stages, the alliance aims to support regional and international co-production and protect creators’ intellectual property, while evolving into a consensus body with a formal decision-making structure.

Its founding declaration reads: “We, independent film producers from Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines, Hong Kong and Taiwan, gathered today in Busan, declare the formation of the Asian Producers Alliance. For years, we have faced the same changes alone – in our own markets, in our own languages. Today we choose to face them together. We will advance co-production across Asia, so that our stories can be made together and travel further.”

Watch on Deadline

The alliance was launched at the close of a seminar entitled ‘Empowering Asian Cinema: Solidarity and Creative Alliance’, hosted by PGK at the ACFM Producers Hub.

Moderated by Han Jin, Director of PGK’s International Committee, the panel brought together producers Yulia Evina Bhara (Indonesia’s KawanKawan Media), Rhee Handae (CEO of Korea’s Sidus) and Shin Yamaguchi (Japan’s Knockonwood) to discuss the state of their industries and the possibilities of co-production in an environment reshaped by streaming platforms and short-form content.

APA’s inaugural team includes PGK President Lee Dong-ha and APROFI Chairman Edwin Nazir as Co-Representatives, with Han Jin and Yulia Evina Bhara as Co-Sectretary Generals. The Representatives and Secretary Generals willserve one-year terms and are elected each year at the General Assembly held during ACFM.

PGK President Lee Dong-ha said: “Asian producers have faced the same challenges separately, market by market. Starting today, we face them together. APA is not a declaration – it is a practice of solidarity that begins now.”

APROFI Chairman Edwin Nazir said: “APA gives Asian producers a foundation to connect and collaborate. Stronger together, we reach further.”

PIPG Founder Member Bianca Balbuena said: “In a time where divisiveness has dominance, the creation of APA signals a safe space for producers in Asia where we cultivate harmony and collaboration in the film industry, and where collective resources, expertise and vision are shared in solidarity.”

HKMPEA Chairman Johnny Wang said: “In the past, we as producers were accustomed to following the paths paved by our predecessors. Now, with the birth of the APA, we are embarking on an entirely new and unprecedented journey. We believe that in today’s globalized context, international co-productions will bring powerful synergies to every APA member.”

TPA Chairperson Yating Chang said: “It is truly our honor to participate in APA. We are really looking forward to connecting with other producers’ associations around Asia.”

APA will hold regular online meetings every quarter, with a General Assembly convening each year during ACFM in Busan. The alliance is welcoming other producers bodies across the region to join and stress that membership is not limited to one organization per territory.

APA’s next gathering will be at the JAFF Market in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, in December, under the theme of creators’ IP.

title: Sacha Baron Cohen Confirmed To Star In Quentin Tarantino’s ‘The Popinjay Cavalier’ West End Stage Play With Dates & On Sale Window Announced
summary: UPDATED with official statements & dates: Producers of Quentin Tarantino’s stage play The Popinjay Cavalier today confirmed what Deadline reported a month ago: Sacha Baron Cohen will star in the director’s first stage play, which will premiere on the West End next spring. The venue and opening date were also revealed. Previews begin on February 23 […]
content:
UPDATED with official statements & dates: Producers of Quentin Tarantino‘s stage play The Popinjay Cavalier today confirmed what Deadline reported a month ago: Sacha Baron Cohen will star in the director’s first stage play, which will premiere on the West End next spring.

The venue and opening date were also revealed. Previews begin on February 23 and the production opens March 18 at London’s Phoenix Theatre.

According to an announcement on the play’s website, tickets go on sale tomorrow with priority access beginning at 9 a.m. BST and GP kicking off at 12 p.m. BST.

Baron Cohen who, like Tarantino, will make his West End debut with the project, said in a statement: “Quentin called, I said yes before he even got to say his first ‘motherfxxxer.’ When the best director in the world calls, you don’t ask questions, I am beyond delighted that we will be losing our West End virginity together, I have made him promise not to be gentle.”

Watch on Deadline

The remaining cast is yet to be revealed.

As reported by Deadline in March, the new stage play, produced by Sonia Friedman Productions and Sony Pictures Entertainment, will be a “swashbuckling comedy” set in 1830s Europe.

Tom Rothman, the chairman and chief executive of Sony Pictures Entertainment’s Motion Picture Group, and Friedman, said in a dual statement, “It is a joy and an honour to be developing this play with Quentin — and obviously quite an adventure. How lucky we are that one of the great storytellers of our time has chosen to make his theatrical debut.

“To see Quentin in action in a rehearsal room is extraordinary. His delight in working with actors, fencers, acrobats, musicians and our creative team is infectious, and there is such pleasure in hearing his delicious language come alive and discovering what his world can become on stage.

“And now we have Sacha Baron Cohen at the heart of it all: a fearless, brilliantly inventive actor with the wit, mischief and daring this role demands. We feel immensely fortunate to be producing this show. Audiences are in for a tremendous treat.”

PREVIOUSLY on September 10: Sacha Baron Cohen will star in an upcoming West End production of Quentin Tarantino’s stage play The Popinjay Cavalier, Deadline hears.

According to sources close to the project, Cohen will portray the title character when The Popinjay Cavalier lands at an as-yet-undisclosed West End venue in spring 2027.

As reported by Deadline in March, the new stage play, produced by Sonia Friedman Productions and Sony Pictures Entertainment, will be a “swashbuckling comedy” set in 1830s Europe.

RELATED: Quentin Tarantino Ranks His Top 20 Favorite Films Of 21st Century: From ‘Black Hawk Down’ To Steven Spielberg’s ‘West Side Story’

The synopsis: “The Popinjay Cavalier is a rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen. A sweeping celebration of theatre and its heightened romance, told with Tarantino’s signature style and unmistakable wit.”

Among Sonia Friedman Productions’ credits are Paddington: The Musical and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.

RELATED: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Trailer: Sacha Baron Cohen Reprises A Modern Classic Character In New Film From Amazon MGM Studios

Tarantino revealed last year that he was working on a play. At the time, he said: “The play is written. It is absolutely the next thing I’m going to do. We’ll start the ball rolling on it in January. … It’s probably going to take up a year and a half to two years of my life.”

Zac Ntim contributed to this report.

title: Dan Levy Calls Out Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ Monologue and Says ‘More Men Need to Be Standing Up’: ‘Speechless That Something Like That Can Exist on Live National Television’
summary: “Schitt’s Creek” star Dan Levy is calling out Shane Gillis’ “Saturday Night Live” monologue, saying that “more men need to be standing up in opposition to it.” Gillis, who hosted “SNL” over the weekend, has generated heated backlash for his comments about women in his opener. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, […]
content:
“Schitt’s Creek” star Dan Levy is calling out Shane Gillis‘ “Saturday Night Live” monologue, saying that “more men need to be standing up in opposition to it.”

Gillis, who hosted “SNL” over the weekend, has generated heated backlash for his comments about women in his opener. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” he said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.”

Levy posted an Instagram Reel on Sunday night reacting to Gillis’ monologue in disbelief. “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists,” Levy began. “There’s a difference there. By the way, I’ve seen more men’s nipples at the gym than I’ve ever seen women showing their bodies off.”

Popular on Variety

Levy continued, “But I’m speechless that something like that can exist on live national television. And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime.'”

The Emmy-winning actor and writer, who hosted “SNL” himself in 2021, emphasized that “men need to be defending women more.”

“This is not a women’s issue, this is an everybody issue. Because the more that men objectify women in the media, the more that other men see them as objects and treat them as objects,” he concluded. “They are not objects. They are superior human beings to men, OK? And I’m sorry if this gets me in trouble with the internet, but fuck.”

Levy received plenty of celebrity support in the comments, with Elizabeth Banks writing “Nailed it” and Broadway actor Barrett Wilbert Weed commenting “I love you, Dan.”

Gillis also dropped the f-bomb during his hosting stint on Saturday, a big faux pas for live television. That and his monologue mark the latest development in the comedian’s complicated history with “SNL.” Back in 2019, he was hired as a featured player and fired days later when podcast clips resurfaced in which he made racist and homophobic comments. He later returned as a host in February 2024 and helmed the show a second time in March 2025, making Saturday’s episode his third time hosting.

Representatives for “Saturday Night Live” and Gillis did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

title: Cannes Festival Winning Producer Quijote Films Launches In-House Scripted Series Division (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Chile’s Quijote Films, behind Cannes Un Certain Regard prizewinners “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo” and “The Settlers,” is venturing into scripted series with the launch of a new in-house series development arm. Based out of Chile and Los Angeles, the company has already invested up to $250,000 in development ahead of Mipcom, which Quijote […]
content:
Chile’s Quijote Films, behind Cannes Un Certain Regard prizewinners “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo” and “The Settlers,” is venturing into scripted series with the launch of a new in-house series development arm.

Based out of Chile and Los Angeles, the company has already invested up to $250,000 in development ahead of Mipcom, which Quijote head of strategy Sergio Karmy is attending.

Known for its savvy assembling of multiple territories to co-produce auteur projects, Quijote Films has lead produced or participated in close to 30 international co-productions to date, including Chile’s first co-production pacts with Ukraine (“Pamfir”) and South Africa (“The Smell of Apples”).

Popular on Variety

“We’ve shown that independent, auteur-driven cinema can be a viable business. I’m proud that at Quijote we’ve reversed the usual formula: our arthouse films are allowing us to finance our expansion into new genres, formats and more commercial audiences,” said Quijote CEO Giancarlo Nasi.

The company’s roughly $250,000 investment in 2026 supports creative personnel and project-specific costs aimed at building a sustainable pipeline of original series. It has established an in-house screenwriting and external development team to originate original series and partner with third-party creators, studios and production companies as an executive producer.

Buttressing its co-production efforts in Chile is the country’s cash rebate incentive that reimburses between 30% and 40% of expenses incurred by international productions filmed in Chile.

It applies to feature films and series with a minimum investment of $400,000, allowing productions to recover between $120,000 and $3 million.

“Our mission is clear: to create high-quality content in partnership with key players across different regions, while preserving the identity and reputation that independent cinema has helped Quijote build over the years. We’re incredibly excited about where we stand today, how far Quijote has come, and the opportunities that lie ahead,” said Karmy, who joined Quijote from Fabula, run by director Pablo Larrain (“My Sad Dead,” “The Count”) and his producing partner Juan de Dios Larrain.

At Mipcom, Quijote is seeking international co-development and co-financing partnerships with streaming platforms, studios and production companies. Combining original IP development with executive production and international co-production expertise, the company aims to expand its global footprint and build a pipeline of premium scripted series for worldwide audiences.

Looking ahead to 2027, Quijote welcomes co-development opportunities across territories and languages, with no geographical or linguistic boundaries.

“We, independent producers, have a lot to bring to the table: we have a meticulous eye for detail, know how to produce efficiently, put together co-financing structures, and work with teams across countries and cultures,” said Nasi, who in his recent Masterclass at the Vancouver Film Festival, stressed that the best-co-productions are those that make both creative and financial sense.

“We’re still Quijote. We’re looking to replicate our co-production experience by looking for international partners who can help us bring out the best in every story, with the same exacting creative and production standards that define our work, whatever the genre or format.”

title: Why the Boss of Leonine, Germany’s Top Indie Film and TV Company, Is Backing Skydance: ‘David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz Are a Very Strong Team’
summary: Fred Kogel, chief executive of Leonine Studios, Germany’s leading independent distribution and production company, is upbeat about the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, now part of Skydance. Variety spoke to him about how the merger is likely to affect the film and TV landscape in German-language territories. One of the commitments made by […]
content:
Fred Kogel, chief executive of Leonine Studios, Germany’s leading independent distribution and production company, is upbeat about the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, now part of Skydance. Variety spoke to him about how the merger is likely to affect the film and TV landscape in German-language territories.

One of the commitments made by Skydance chief David Ellison when he was pushing for the merger was to produce 30-plus movies a year. Kogel is confident that Ellison will deliver.

“What gives me confidence that the number [of movies] will be delivered is that David Ellison comes from a content background and produced great movies with Skydance in the past,” Kogel says. “He is a businessman and a creative guy. He loves the business and he loves making movies.”

Popular on Variety

Kogel points to Ellison’s track record as a producer as evidence to support this. “Knowing the production business and knowing the theatrical business, I know what it means to increase the number of theatrical movies,” he says. “It’s a hard feat to achieve. You need long-term development. You need enough projects in the pipeline to build that number up. So, I’m optimistic with him and the management that they will deliver on the number of films.”

Does Kogel have any concerns about Skydance’s viability, in light of its sizable debt burden?

“In my opinion, Skydance is a group with extraordinary assets, IPs and possibilities,” he says. “I have complete trust in the people running Skydance. I admire David Ellison because he is an entrepreneur and has proven [his abilities] in the past. I think David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are a very strong team. I also have great respect for Ynon. It requires a vision, a lot of strength and courage, and a great team to achieve what they already have achieved. Of course, it’s a tough market, but it’s a great business to be in. And being the managers they are, I have complete trust that they and their teams can handle this. So, I’m positive. I’m totally positive.”

Kogel sees opportunities for Leonine to produce films for Skydance. “If there is IP that is convincing and that can be produced by us, it could be a natural fit to work with another distributor. That’s what we have already done in the past,” he says.

Leonine could also produce TV drama series for Skydance. “We are already doing good business with HBO Max as a production unit,” he says. “So, for us, it’s always interesting to be a local producer of premium content and to be aligned with a studio like Skydance, and of course we could help.”

He adds, “In general, with production, I think it’s a good development. If you come at it from the side of television production, I think it’s also a positive development for us. I mean, we are doing very good business with HBO Max in Germany.

“HBO Max started [in Germany] at the beginning of the year, and just two weeks ago, we started the first major German original together with HBO Max, ‘Four Blocks Zero’ — the prequel to our very successful TNT series ‘Four Blocks.’ It’s a great production by our banner Wiedemann & Berg Television. It’s a very good collaboration, and additionally we delivered a production by the Beetz Brothers — ‘Clangold,’ the first documentary commissioned by HBO Max in Germany. I see them as a major force in the German commissioning market.

“Local German productions are very important for all streamers and broadcasters to create a long-term commitment from the German audience. Germany is the biggest TV market in Europe and one of the most important markets in the world. And Skydance as a content powerhouse, with its strong services HBO Max and Paramount+, has the power to invest.”

The 30-plus movies a year coming from Skydance could be seen as increased competition for Leonine’s distribution business, but Kogel doesn’t see it that way.

“For me, having been in the distribution business for such a long time, distribution has always been hugely competitive. So, it’s not major news for us,” he says.

“We are a very competitive local distributor that tries to be at eye level with the international majors, so we are accustomed to a lot of competition. In my opinion, every good movie that enters the German market helps the German market, and the theatrical market in general.

“I don’t see it as a major problem. I think as long as the movies are of high quality — and that’s what I expect — then it’s good for the market. And I mean, we see a big trend, especially in Germany, where the 20-25 best films of the year account for the vast majority of the year’s business. And you simply have to be competitive, and, better still, have one or more of the 25 best films of the year, and that also applies to us. That applies to everybody: Warner, Paramount, Sony, Universal — to everybody. So, it’s a competitive market, and as long as there is really good competition, I’m happy. We have to face that competition. So, I don’t mind getting 10 more films a year in Germany. I would be happy if these are the right films, because we need films that draw the audience to the theatrical market.

“We are a strong supporter of the theatrical release market, as Leonine, and I’m really very happy if anybody in the business has that commitment.

“So, our goal is to make the right films that draw people to the cinemas. I think that, with David Ellison and his team’s plans to increase the volume, make quality films, and make audience-pleasing films, we are totally aligned on that.”

So, is it the quality, not the quantity, of the Skydance films that is important?

“Yes, it’s the quality. But in the end, I think in most cases the right films will find their way to the market, and that’s the reason why I answer it from the German perspective,” Kogel says. “You must see that, of the approximately 650 films released in Germany each year, at least 200 are German movies, which means 450 are international movies. So, if 10 more international movies were to find their way to the theaters, and if they were the right movies, it would be good for the theaters.

“For me, it’s a crowded market anyway, and finding the release dates is the most difficult task for our distribution team, as is supporting the films so that they find their way to the audience. We definitely see in the German market that, if we have strong films, other films benefit from that because people will then go to the cinemas. For me, the worst situation is that we have 200 German films and 450 international films and too few must-see movies, which often is the problem, especially with the German productions. So, the discussion for me is not about having 10 more films or 10 fewer films; it’s about having the right films, and if they draw the audience, then that’s a good thing for all of us.”

There may be an opportunity for Leonine to distribute Paramount and Warner Bros. films in German-language countries.

“That could be a possibility. We buy at least 25 international movies and sometimes carve out an international studio movie and release it in Germany,” Kogel says. “I mean, that’s the kind of business we do, but normally it doesn’t happen if a major studio has a huge distribution operation in Germany — as Warner Bros. has — because then they can release it themselves and don’t need us. But sometimes it happens.”

There are advantages to having a merged Paramount+/HBO Max streaming group, Kogel says.

“In the end, I always say it’s good for the whole business if we have strong partners. So, for Leonine, it’s good to have a strong Skydance group in the German market because we can do business with both services. In my opinion in our competitive market the setup will strengthen Paramount+ and that in the end Paramount+ may become a stronger partner under the Skydance banner – at least in the next years. For the moment it’s too early to predict a long-term strategy. But that’s not possible anyway in our business.

“Competition will increase when it comes to the streamers because a strong HBO Max and a strong Paramount+ are stronger contenders against the other streamers than either would be under separate roofs. For example, if they increase the number of movies to 30-plus, there will be more movies on their platforms. We don’t know yet what will happen in the end. But it will, of course, increase competition, which is generally a good thing for everybody who is in the content business and who wants to produce and license great content. So, for me, it’s a good thing.”

Leonine has an advantage over other independents in that it is part of a large group, Mediawan, which is headed by Pierre-Antoine Capton, and also includes Plan B.

“There are, of course, advantages and you have to distinguish between distribution and production. So, in production, we are cooperating in many ways, as we are part of the Mediawan Group, and certain production companies of ours are working closely with production companies within the Mediawan Group. For example: When we produced and released a highly successful German movie called ‘Weekend Rebels,’ it was noticed by Plan B, and together we developed a U.S. version with Plan B, which has now gone directly to Apple. It’s a remake. We work together on co-productions. So, these are very interesting opportunities that Pierre-Antoine Capton and I regularly discuss. What can we do together in non-fiction and fiction, and how can we join forces better?

“When it comes to distribution, I think it’s a different business because distribution is very different from market to market.

“We are constantly talking about possible future cooperations when it comes to movies: If Mediawan has a successful French movie, we are talking about distributing it in Germany.

“It’s good that Leonine, as one of Germany’s biggest distributors, is within the Mediawan group. It’s interesting to look at every movie that comes out of the group to see if we can release it or do a carve-out for Germany, Austria and Switzerland.”

If Warner Bros. and Paramount want to bring more of their production business to Germany, they’ll find that the German production incentive is not as attractive as it could be, Kogel cautions.

“We are not yet where I want Germany to be in the end, where we could benefit from U.S. studios producing more projects in Germany. Why? It’s easy: We don’t have a tax credit system here that meets the standards of other European countries or of possible future U.S. tax credits, under the new plan.

“That’s the missing link for Germany to be truly competitive with the other European territories, which already have a tax credit.”

title: Story of Jackson Brothers Jackie, Jermaine, Tito and Marlon to Be Told in New Documentary Launching at MIPCOM (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: The four founding members of The Jackson 5 not named Michael are coming together for their own documentary for the first time. Workerbee (part of Banijay UK) and Paper Route Studios have secured exclusive access to Jackie, Jermaine, Tito and Marlon Jackson for a 90’ feature-length film, also available as a three-part doc series, set […]
content:
The four founding members of The Jackson 5 not named Michael are coming together for their own documentary for the first time.

Workerbee (part of Banijay UK) and Paper Route Studios have secured exclusive access to Jackie, Jermaine, Tito and Marlon Jackson for a 90’ feature-length film, also available as a three-part doc series, set for global release. Mediawan is set to to handle international distribution and launch a sales push at MIPCOM.

The as-yet-unnamed film is, according to the description, the story of “four brothers and their journey as part of one of the world’s earliest and most successful and influential boy bands of all time and the various roads each of their lives took.”

Popular on Variety

Three years in the making, the film, directed by Benjamin Hirsch (“Janet Jackson”), chronicles the “extraordinary rise, triumph, fractures and reunion,” from their beginnings in Gary, Indiana, through their transformation into global superstars. The film also features the final interview Tito Jackson gave before his death in 2024.

The film uses observational filming, rare archive footage, unseen material and recollections from the four brothers to explore how they were shaped by their father Joe Jackson, whose “uncompromising determination turned family rehearsals into a relentless training ground,” adds the description. “The four remember those early rehearsals differently — the pressure, the competition, the laughter between takes and the sense that, even as children, something extraordinary might be happening. They also remember their mother Katherine at the heart of the family operation, as they began to venture out beyond Gary.”

“When Marc Pos came to us about working with The Jacksons it was an instant ‘yes’. The Jackson 5 are one of the most influential musical acts of all time,” said Rick Murray, CEO Workerbee Group.

“This film tells the story of the four remaining members of the original band from their perspective, offering an unprecedented insight into their rise from humble beginnings to global superstardom and their lives through today. We’re incredibly grateful to them for their trust and for allowing us to tell their story.”

Added director Hirsch: “Following our work with Janet Jackson, having the opportunity to work with the Jackson brothers is a huge privilege. From listening to their untold and amazing stories, delving into their rare and often unseen archival footage and rediscovering their incredible back catalogue of hits, this film has been a real treat to put together.”

The film is directed by Hirsch, with Simon Stanley as film editor, Dorothea Sterian as producer, Sam Newman-Butler as archive producer and Sophie White as production manager. Yessica De Brouwer is associate producer, with Murray and Marc Pos as executive producers.

“It is a true honour to be a part of the team to bring this story to life after all of these years,” said Corey Russell, co-founder, Paper Route Studios. “The Jacksons are a music royalty and deserve to have their story told. Working with the team at Workerbee has been an absolute pleasure. Ben is a real talent and will craft a beautiful and compelling documentary. We can’t wait for audiences to see this film.”

Added Benjamin Lepetit, VP of content, Mediawan Rights: “We are delighted to accompany the film on its international journey. This is a powerful story of family, ambition and music, centered on artists whose influence has resonated across generations and around the world. The never-seen-before access to the family archives and the ambition of the project make it the defining documentary on the Jacksons. We look forward to introducing this exceptional documentary to international buyers at MIPCOM.”

Banijay Entertainment supported the film through early-stage development investment via its Creative Fund.

title: ITV Studios Revs Up Scripted Dramas and Format Deals Amid Media Arm Sale Process
summary: Andrea Riseborough is heading to the moon, “The Voice” is bound for Estonia and a much-loved U.K. natural history host is coming back to tell more fish stories. ITV Studios kicked off the Mipcom market in Cannes on Monday morning with a breakfast gathering to show off its broad slate of new and returning scripted […]
content:
Andrea Riseborough is heading to the moon, “The Voice” is bound for Estonia and a much-loved U.K. natural history host is coming back to tell more fish stories.

ITV Studios kicked off the Mipcom market in Cannes on Monday morning with a breakfast gathering to show off its broad slate of new and returning scripted and unscripted series.

Ruth Berry, ITV Studios’ president of global partnerships and its Zoo 55 digital content arm, noted that ITV Studios is representing no less than 11 fresh original formats at this year’s Mipcom gathering — a feat amid the global downturn in traditional series commissioning and the general disruption among large production groups.

“We’re feeling very positive about what it means for the evolution of both studios,” Berry told a group of journalists on Monday morning. Asked by Variety if the M&A fever gripping the global content marketplace had impacted ITV’s operations, Berry didn’t hesitate: “In a word, no,” she said, pointing to the ambitious slate. “Absolute corkers,” she said of ITV’s lineup.

Popular on Variety

Mike Beale, ITV Studios’ managing director of creative networks, emphasized that the company is “pairing broadcasters and streams to co-commission” new shows, which opens opportunities for fresh formats.

ITV itself is in the process of being cleaved into two separate firms. NBCUniversal’s Sky is in the midst of acquiring the ITV broadcast and digital platform while ITV Studios will remain a standalone entity, although acquisition rumors won’t quit. ITV Studios is in a strong position to shape these days with the worldwide success of “Love Island.” Berry noted that the U.S. edition of the series ranks as the most-watched program ever on NBCUniversal’s Peacock streamer.

Among the projects that got a push from ITV Studios on Monday was the return of Jeremy Wade, host of “River Monsters,” in a video podcast series in which he recounts tales of his fresh-water exploits. “Fish On! With Jeremy Wade” launches Oct. 20 on Patreon and via the RiverMonsters.TV. The “River Monsters” series that premiered on the Animal Planet cabler in 2009 has found new life on social media platforms with younger viewers.

“You’ll hear that young people don’t want to watch long-form content — not true,” Berry told the crowd, citing the average watch time of 90 minutes for “River Monsters” episodes on YouTube.

Other shows highlighted at the session include “First Woman,” which stars Riseborough as the first woman to walk on the moon — and the first to go missing on the lunar surface; and “Number 10,” a soapy look behind the scenes at the real-life personal and political pressures that surround the occupants of 10 Downing Street.

“Number 10″ series creator Stephen Moffat was on hand to add his perspective on the show. “Every other country is run from big palace or a big building — ours is run from a house on a shabby little street with a big black door,” he joked.

Among other news shared during the hourlong session:

ITV’s enduring format “The Voice” has reached its 80th territory commission thanks to a deal in Estonia.

ITV has picked up distribution rights to Channel 4’s unscripted series “Incognito.” The series brings 10 strangers together in an institutional setting for seven days, with each person trying to guess the true occupations of the others while hiding their own identities.

ITV has struck a deal with former Endemol Shine Australia executive Sara Richardson to launch a drama label. She’ll work with the existing Lingo Pictures to develop new projects for Australia and beyond.

ITV’s cold case drama “Karen Pirie” has been renewed for a third season.

Hit drama series “Line of Duty” will return for Season 7 next year.

(Pictured: “Fish On!” host Jeremy Wade)

title: ‘Gnome Alone’ Sequel ‘Game Of Gnomes’ From ‘The Nut Job’ Director Launching Ahead Of AFM
summary: EXCLUSIVE: SC Films International has started production on Gnome Alone: Game of Gnomes, the sequel to its animated family movie from 2017. Peter Lepeniotis (The Nut Job) is returning to write and direct. SC Films is producing and will launch worldwide sales at the American Film Market next month. The film marks the first collaboration […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: SC Films International has started production on Gnome Alone: Game of Gnomes, the sequel to its animated family movie from 2017.

Peter Lepeniotis (The Nut Job) is returning to write and direct. SC Films is producing and will launch worldwide sales at the American Film Market next month.

The film marks the first collaboration under a multi-picture, multi-year deal between SC Films International, SiXiTZ Studios and Magieva.

In the sequel, “Chloe and Liam travel back in time to save mankind from warring families and the dreaded Troggs, with their gnome allies Quicksilver, Zook and Zamfeer at their side”.

Simon Crowe and Matthew Joynes produce for SC Films alongside Lepeniotis, Kevin Hicks, Nathaniel Hunter and Euan Macdonald. Production is being split between California and Toronto. Animation is being produced by SiXiTZ Studios, the animation and media studio founded and led by Macdonald, using workflows and technologies built in partnership with Magieva. Hunter and Macdonald have built film and animation pipelines for Disney, Lucasfilm and Apple, and won an Emmy together in 2022 for the animation studio they co-founded.

Watch on Deadline

The original Gnome Alone played theatrically worldwide, with Netflix taking North America. The Nut Job grossed $120M worldwide.

“Gnome Alone is one of our most successful titles, and we’ve always wanted a sequel,” said Crowe. “Peter has built a whole new world full of great characters, fun and action.”

“This time we’re sending Chloe and the gnomes back in time,” said Lepeniotis. “It’s the biggest canvas this world has had.”

SC Films’ AFM slate also includes the animated features Girl in the Clouds and Zsazsa Zaturnnah, and the live-action features Breeder (IFC) and Cotton Eye Joe (in post).

title: Evan Shapiro Pegs Skydance Value At Only $29B As His Media Universe Map Updates
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The new-look Skydance is worth just $29B due to its huge debt pile, according to media analyst Evan Shapiro. The former NBC, Participant Media and IFC exec, who now maps the media landscape through his ESHAP business, said the valuation was down to both the $81B debt that Skydance assumed on day one of […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The new-look Skydance is worth just $29B due to its huge debt pile, according to media analyst Evan Shapiro.

The former NBC, Participant Media and IFC exec, who now maps the media landscape through his ESHAP business, said the valuation was down to both the $81B debt that Skydance assumed on day one of trading and its links to major shareholder Oracle, which is has long-term debts of over $160B due to investments in AI.

Shapiro is talking at MIPCOM Cannes this week, where he will unveil the latest edition of his Media Universe Map, which will be the first that is interactive and allows users to compare entertainment and tech ecosystems of the past to 2026.

“One of the puzzles we needed to solve in making this map was figuring out what the name of Paramount/WBD would be and, more importantly, WTF Skydance is actually worth,” he said ahead of his talk. “No one in their right mind would buy the $81B in debt they are carrying and no one who isn’t high as a kite would buy Skydance for the $111B price that was just paid for WBD.

Watch on Deadline

“One of the biggest reasons for that is that the fortunes of Skydance and Oracle are now intrinsically intertwined, and combined they have $240B of debt, a good portion of which is either junk or a millimeter above junk. To put that in perspective the Ellisons now carry more in debt than all of Disney is worth.”

Shapiro claimed this meant his team had to determine a net asset value for Skydance, which came in at just $29B, far below the value David Ellison’s Paramount paid for WBD.

We have reached out to Skydance for comment.

The latest Media Universe Map highlights the dominance of tech companies, with Nvidia’s value the largest at $5.3T, followed by Apple ($4.9T), Alphabet ($4.3T), Microsoft ($3.8T), Amazon ($2.8T) and Meta ($1.8T). Larry Ellison’s Oracle, which is a major shareholder in the American version of Chinese social platform business Bytedance, was valued at $429B.

Of the pureplay media and entertainment businesses, Netflix was the largest with a valuation of $293B, ahead of Disney ($187B). Comcast was at $73B, while Fox was just $25B, though this is set to almost double when it completes its deal for Roku, which is valued at $23B.

India’s Reliance, which houses Disney-backed streamer JioHotstar, was at $164B, Sony came in at $144B. Both companies have assets well beyond the media space.

Shapiro, who describes his role as a media cartographer, has been rolling out his media maps for six years and is unveiling the first interactive version this week in Cannes. As he has described in the past, he claims there had been a fundamental shift in media ownership in recent years, which the map demonstrates.

“The biggest change in the Media Universe since I started mapping it is the shift from an industry controlled by C-suites to an ecosystem controlled by the consumers,” he said. “We are now in the ‘user-centric era,’ so I felt it was only fitting to put control of my map in the hands of the users. This new Media Universe Map App does just that – allowing you to drive the map yourself, on desktop or mobile, and double click on anything and everything you want more of.”

He added that the functionality would allow users of his program to compare today’s landscape with those of yesteryear.

“One of the things I get asked for most in my map, is a way back machine to compare years past to today’s map,” he said. “This new user-driven map does just that – we’ve included a time machine to allow you to compare and contract the media universe from years and eras gone by to the latest landscape.”

title: Russell Brand Rape Trial Gets Underway In London
summary: Russell Brand’s rape trial has officially commenced. Brand entered Southwark Crown Court on Monday wearing a gray suit, an open-neck white shirt, and a patterned cravat. He was accompanied by his wife, Laura, clasping her hand as he entered the building. Brand faces three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault, and one charge […]
content:
Russell Brand‘s rape trial has officially commenced.

Brand entered Southwark Crown Court on Monday wearing a gray suit, an open-neck white shirt, and a patterned cravat. He was accompanied by his wife, Laura, clasping her hand as he entered the building.

Brand faces three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault, and one charge of indecent assault. The allegations come from six women and span a decade from 1999 to 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges and has consistently denied wrongdoing.

The opening day of Brand’s trial will likely focus on jury selection and other administrative matters, with the Crown Prosecution Service expected to start making its case from Tuesday at the earliest.

The trial, which could last 10 weeks, is being overseen by Mr Justice Bennathan, who has presided over high-profile cases during his time as a judge, including the conviction of Kyle Clifford, who killed his ex-girlfriend, her sister and her mother in a crossbow attack. The women were the wife and daughters of BBC horse racing commentator John Hunt.

Watch on Deadline

Brand appeared in Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek. Before his work in Hollywood, he was a regular fixture on British television, hosting Big Brother’s Big Mouth and other series.

The actor and comedian, who was married to Katy Perry, has reinvented himself as a Christian convert who evangelizes about free speech and free thinking in MAGA America.

title: Disney+ Hires Amazon’s Philip Pratt To Run Originals In Germany, Switzerland & Austria
summary: Philip Pratt, the former Amazon Germany originals boss who oversaw the likes of Maxton Hall, has moved over to Disney+. Pratt has taken on the VP, Original Production post in Germany, Switzerland and Austria and will join Disney in early 2027 to oversee commissioning in the region, based out of Munich. He is effectively replacing […]
content:
Philip Pratt, the former Amazon Germany originals boss who oversaw the likes of Maxton Hall, has moved over to Disney+.

Pratt has taken on the VP, Original Production post in Germany, Switzerland and Austria and will join Disney in early 2027 to oversee commissioning in the region, based out of Munich. He is effectively replacing Benjamina Mirnik-Voges, who is leaving.

Reporting to EMEA content boss Angela Jain, he will contribute to a Disney international commissioning team that is aiming to triple its number of originals over the next three years. Previous Disney Germany shows nclude Call my Agent Berlin, Jörg Winger’s Sam – A Saxon and The Interpreter of Silence, while upcoming is Austrian satire Vienna Game, thriller Nele Neuhaus Monster and Swiss production Under the Ice.

Pratt spent 11 years at Amazon MGM Studios, where he was Head of Original Productions working across huge hits like Maxton Hall – The World Between Us, war movie The Tank and a local version of LOL: Last One Laughing.

Watch on Deadline

Jain said Pratt’s “creative track record and experience make him the perfect person to lead [Disney’s] work across Germany, Switzerland and Austria, partnering with exceptional producers and talent to build a slate that gets audiences talking.”

Pratt added: “I look forward to working with incredibly creative talent to bring stories to Disney+ that entertain, resonate and reach millions of viewers across Germany, Switzerland, Austria and beyond. I envision Disney+ to be a creative home where producers and talent come together, take bold ideas forward and create extraordinary entertainment.”

Pratt’s hire follows that of My Brilliant Friend producer Sonia Rovai’s recent appointment as Disney’s VP of Original Production in Italy. Under CEO Josh D’Amaro the Mouse House is looking to triple international originals and Jain has previously said she has been given an expanded budget.

title: Marina Hyde Begins Her Post-Guardian Era With Goalhanger-Backed Creator Venture Always On
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Marina Hyde, whose sharp and incisive columns have called out many public figures in British and U.S. society, is going solo – and it looks like she’ll be Always On. We can reveal the broadcaster, podcaster and writer, who contributed to Apple TV series The Studio, is teaming up with Gary Lineker’s Goalhanger to […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Marina Hyde, whose sharp and incisive columns have called out many public figures in British and U.S. society, is going solo – and it looks like she’ll be Always On.

We can reveal the broadcaster, podcaster and writer, who contributed to Apple TV series The Studio, is teaming up with Gary Lineker’s Goalhanger to launch Always On With Marina Hyde. This comes after she last month announced her exit from The Guardian newspaper after 26 years.

The brand is designed to bring her writing together with formats on YouTube and social media, and is being framed as “a window into the stories that Marina finds interesting – the details, performances and absurdities that catch her attention, and the connections only she can make.”

Expect interviews and collabs with influential British voices across a multitude of formats. On day one, Hyde will provide a regular written column, a YouTube show and original social content, and in “over time,” will push into “further audio, video and digital formats.”

Watch on Deadline

Hyde is no stranger to her new home at Goalhanger, which produces her popular entertainment podcast, The Rest is Entertainment. She co-hosts the entertainment industry digest with Richard Osman. Hyde is expected provide more detail on the venture in the latest episode of the show.

“This is going to be so much fun,” said Hyde. “I’m hugely excited to be launching Always On in partnership with the brilliant team at Goalhanger, and to be able to respond to the news batsignal in whatever format feels right – written/video/podcast/social/costumed vigilantism. I’m also thrilled we’ve named it in tribute to the nervous breakdown it’s going to give me. Thanks guys – means a lot.”

For Goalhanger, Always On is the first launch from its Goalhanger X initiative, which aims on building creator-led media ventures. Hyde becomes the latest figure from British journalism branching out on their own, with The Traitors contestant and broadcaster Amol Rajan recently exiting the BBC to launch his own operation and the likes of former BBC staples Emily Maitlis and Jon Sopel now well established with the Global-produced podcast The News Agents.

Jack Davenport, co-founder at Goalhanger, said of Always On: “We love Marina. At Goalhanger, our shows span sport, politics, history and entertainment, but the truth is Marina could host them all. There’s no one else who can bring together so many different strands and make sense of the world quite like she can.

“Partnering with her to launch Always On is the start of something really exciting for us as a business. Goalhanger X is built around unique personalities: people with a distinctive voice, an incredibly loyal audience and the ability to create far beyond any single format.”

Davenport said Always On would give Hyde Marina “the freedom to build a world around everything she finds interesting, funny or important, and to connect directly with audiences through writing, video, social, podcasts and whatever comes next.”

Goalhanger’s role would be providing the “creative, audience and commercial infrastructure around that vision so it can grow, while keeping Marina firmly at the centre.”

title: TV Cooking Shows Get Spicy With Food Influencers in the Mix: ‘It Has to Hook You In’
summary: Gordon Ramsay is on set in Ireland when we speak. It’s a hot, sunny day but he is surrounded by Christmas trees and elves as he’s shooting the “Next Level Baker” holiday special for Fox. It’s very festive, which seems appropriate as he’s recently uncorked the 25th season of “Hell’s Kitchen,” and earlier this year […]
content:
Gordon Ramsay is on set in Ireland when we speak. It’s a hot, sunny day but he is surrounded by Christmas trees and elves as he’s shooting the “Next Level Baker” holiday special for Fox.

It’s very festive, which seems appropriate as he’s recently uncorked the 25th season of “Hell’s Kitchen,” and earlier this year unwrapped the 10th season of “Kitchen Nightmares,” while also serving up the 16th season of the U.S. version of “MasterChef.”

But despite the continued popularity of his shows, reinforced by the Netflix series about him, some in the industry are starting to ask: Have TV audiences started to lose their appetite for food shows?

Popular on Variety

Natalie Cruz, an analyst for Ampere Analysis, says, “Globally, the commissions of reality-food shows have shown a consistent downward trend since 2022, with the highest decrease of 16% lower global commissioning volumes between 2024 to 2025, from 663 to 555 titles. This trend continues into 2026, with commissioning volumes falling by 13% between the second half of last year and the first half of this year from 282 to 245 titles.”

Cookery shows need to add some spice to pique the hunger of audiences, according to TV sales executives. Take “The Heat,” part of the offering from international distribution and production giant ITV Studios, which folds the ingredients of a high-end cooking format in with those of a dating show. “It’s very aspirational, very glossy and escapist,” Tom Clark, ITV Studios’ executive VP global sales and commercial strategy, says.

“The Heat” is set in a real restaurant in sun-drenched Barcelona where a group of young chefs battle it out under the supervision of a world-class Michelin chef. “The chefs are working together during the day and they’re competing, but they’re also living together at night; so they’re working hard and they’re partying hard,” Clark explains.

“And what that means is the stress and the ambition for winning the cooking contest meets the relationships and the night lives that go alongside of that. What you then see is the romances, the rivalries, the flirtations, the fallouts — they all make their way back into the kitchen in the daytime.”

Ramsay has watched the show, and he’s not impressed. “I think ‘The Heat’ is a bit of a hotch-potch … sort of ‘Big Brother’ meets ‘Top Chef.’ I was cringing watching some of the early episodes, and it just had no narrative.”

The U.K. broadcaster ITV appeared to agree. After its first season, the show was axed.

“The Heat” was a blend of cooking contest and dating show. “The Heat” (Courtesy of ITV Studios)

Ramsay attributes the popularity of his own shows to their “live aspect,” and underscores the need to “keep things incredibly fresh.” Referring to “Hell’s Kitchen,” he says, “There’s a format, but each and every season, we rip up the rule book and rewrite the challenges.”

The secret to its success, Ramsay says, is that he runs it like a live restaurant. “There is something magical about going into the unknown when that first ticket arrives. We train and train and train those individuals, put them through this incredible boot camp before we go live, and each and every night is a live performance, like you’d go to see in a theater,” he says.

Lucas Green, chief content officer, operations, at Banijay Entertainment, another global TV distribution and production titan, acknowledges there has been a shift in audience tastes as food content on social media proliferates. “People love watching recipes and food porn on Instagram and TikTok, and I think that’s probably replaced the instructional cooking shows,” he says.

“MasterChef” was the most adapted format in the world last year. Courtesy of Banijay

That said, Banijay’s “MasterChef” was the most adapted format in the world last year, with versions on air in 38 territories (the total is now 41 territories), and similar formats, like “Top Chef,” are also going strong, which Green ascribes to their narrative structure.

“[‘MasterChef’ has] got that light-touch reality storyline with people coming back week to week, and they’re very, very determined to win,” he says. “[The show] changes people’s lives. Lots of winners have gone on to get Michelin stars. It’s very aspirational.”

The blending in of a story arc boosts the audience’s desire for more, encouraging binge-viewing, says Mike Beale, managing director, creative network, at ITV Studios, which has “Hell’s Kitchen” on air in 26 territories and “Come Dine With Me” in 50. “You need to take the viewer from one episode to another.
