Just seeing five people cook, and there’s one winner at the end of the competition, and then next week, you do the same competition again with five new people, isn’t going to do that anymore,” Beale says. “It has to hook you in and take you there, and streaming has driven that behavior.”

Meanwhile, the networks continue to bring new zest to old favorites, such as the launch last year of “Gordon Ramsay’s Secret Service” on Fox, reinventing the “Kitchen Nightmares” formula, Olivier Levet at TV consultancy The Wit says.

YouTube is proving to be a fertile seedbed for new cooking show concepts, Levet adds. “Content creators are experimenting with new formulas, such as battles over iconic cartoon dishes, seen in Joshua Weissman’s ‘I Tried Every Famous Cartoon Food,’ or global tournaments between typical breakfasts, with Ibai Llanos’ ‘El mundial de los desayunos,’” he says.

Joshua Weissman Courtesy of Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for NYCWFF

Meanwhile, Levet notes that the streamers have developed their own taste for cookery shows like “Dinner Time Live With David Chang,” “Culinary Class Wars,” “Iron Chef: Quest for an Iron Legend” and “The Final Table” on Netflix, and “The World Cook” on Prime Video.

And online and linear can feed off each other, Green argues. “MasterChef” has a spin-off in Brazil, “MasterChef Creators,” which streams on YouTube, and casts only digital influencers, which has brought a younger audience to the show.

Whatever exotic recipes the latest generation of celebrity chefs throw together, for Ramsay, his approach is simple, “I suppose I just work at keeping it fresh, and I take criticism, but I don’t sit there and self-absorb and self-obsess about how good we are. I treat every season like it’s the first.”

And sometimes the greatest drama stirred up by Ramsay’s shows occurs after they have aired, he observes, and it’s down to a mistaken view of the realities of running a restaurant.

Referring to some misguided folk on “Kitchen Nightmares,” he says, “The biggest issue I’ve got is when the program goes out and they get that fanfare and attention, especially in the media. They then get a little bit carried away with the fame. And there’s nothing famous in running a restaurant. It’s hard, brutal work that needs to be disciplined and focused on, so you can’t start indulging in success by running a restaurant and sitting down with customers and having the odd glass of champagne or drinking a martini before you start running your dining room.”

title: ’30 Rock’ 20th Anniversary Reunion: Tina Fey and Tracy Morgan Try to Remember Their Lines, Alec Baldwin Riffs as Jack Donaghy and More Best Moments
summary: Conan O’Brien did little to manage expectations as he kicked off Sunday evening’s “30 Rock” reunion, a one-night-only benefit at Radio City Music Hall to celebrate the beloved sitcom’s 20th anniversary. “Welcome to the greatest night in the history of entertainment!” he said from the stage to raucous applause. “I’m Conan O’Brien, and I’m known […]
content:
Conan O’Brien did little to manage expectations as he kicked off Sunday evening’s “30 Rock” reunion, a one-night-only benefit at Radio City Music Hall to celebrate the beloved sitcom’s 20th anniversary.

“Welcome to the greatest night in the history of entertainment!” he said from the stage to raucous applause. “I’m Conan O’Brien, and I’m known to exaggerate.”

His comments didn’t seem hyperbolic to the 5,000 rowdy fans in the audience, who spent a pretty penny and braved a rainstorm for a chance to witness the live, never-to-be-televised event. Cheers from the crowd were near-deafening as O’Brien introduced the cast — Tina Fey, Alec Baldwin, Tracy Morgan and Jane Krakowski — and they kept up the enthusiasm for surprise guests like Jon Hamm, Tom Hanks, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Will Forte and Brian Williams.

“What you will see tonight is, in “30 Rock” fashion, an overly ambitious grab bag of nonsense,” Fey said. Created by Fey, “30 Rock,” which ran for seven seasons on NBC from 2006-2013, takes place behind the scenes of a fictional “Saturday Night Live”-esque sketch comedy show called “TGS With Tracy Jordan.” Fey plays head writer Liz Lemon, Baldwin portrays NBC boss Jack Donaghy and Krakowski and Morgan star as cast members Jenna Maroney and Tracey Jordan.

Popular on Variety

The cast reunion doubled as a charity fundraiser for the Boys and Girls Club of Harlem, an organization they wanted to honor for two specific reasons. “We chose the Boys and Girls of Harlem because they are a great New York institution,” Fey said. “But also because we figured we kind of owed them something because of how much Tracy Jordan struggled to shoot the commercial he did.” (In one memorable episode from Season 5, Tracy couldn’t remember his lines as he filmed a public service announcement for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America.)

Fey revealed that Jack McBrayer was the one to suggest a 20th anniversary reunion. “He probably meant a cast dinner. But I’m not a good listener, so here we are,” Fey said. “I wanted to celebrate at Radio City because I like to feel tiny.”

She designed the evening to be “more than just a Q&A,” stuffing the 90-minute event with elaborate musical numbers, game show sketches and other “30 Rock”-themed skits.

“No one has ever seen this show before, including us, because we have not rehearsed it,” Fey said. “But one thing I can promise you, from the bottom of my heart, we will have microphone problems.”

If you couldn’t “go to there,” as Liz Lemon would say, Variety has compiled the best moments from the night:

Tom Hanks accepts best guest star award on behalf of Elaine Stritch

“30 Rock” had no shortage of A-list guest stars, from Carrie Fisher (as fictional comedy writer Rosemary Howard) to Steve Martin (as Jack’s neurotic friend Gavin Volure) to Oprah Winfrey (as herself). “It was pretty wild,” said Judah Friedlander, who played “TGS” writer Frank Rossitano. “You never knew who would show up. One week it was Al Gore, and the next it could be Queen Latifah.” Katrina Bowden, who portrayed Liz’s beautiful assistant Cerie, asked: “Wait, are those real people who lived?”

But only one bold-faced name could win the coveted “best guest star” prize, which went to Elaine Stritch as Jack’s overbearing mother Colleen Donaghy. She was (posthumously) nominated against Marcella Roy as young Liz Lemon, Sherri Shephard as Tracy’s wife Angie Jordan and Kelsey Grammer as his heist-wielding alter ego “Frajer.”

“Unfortunately, Elaine can’t be here tonight to accept her award because she’s dead,” Bowden deadpanned. (Strich died in 2014 at age 89.) “So here to accept on her behalf is two-time Academy Award winner Tom Hanks.”

Hanks was apparently tricked into attending the evening while he was one block up, near 30 Rockefeller Plaza. “I was on my way to dinner at the Rainbow Room,” Hanks said. “I eat there every night to avoid Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax.”

’30 Rock’-stradomus

“30 Rock” is famous for predicting a bunch of stuff that proved to be bizarrely accurate. “Even though we were exhausted and writing absurdist nonsense, so much of what we wrote actually came true,” the show’s writers said from the stage. Highlights in a montage of prescient jokes include Jenna’s “free Lyle Menendez” tattoo (the brothers were recently granted an early parole hearing) and Tracy’s call with someone pretending to be Bill Cosby — “You’ve got a lot of nerve getting on the phone with me after what you did to my Aunt Paulette!” — way before the comedian was accused of drugging and sexually assaulting women. Then there was Jenna’s weight-gaining role in the fictional “Mystic Pizza: The Musical” (which now exists and began a national tour this fall) and the iconic show-within-a-show “MILF Island,” which paved the way for the very real HBO Max reality dating series “FBoy Island.”

Tina and Tracy play ‘What’s my next line?’

McBrayer put Fey and Morgan’s memories to the test, feeding them niche quotes from the show to see if they could remember the wacky things their characters said over the course of seven seasons. They started strong; Fey knew the reason there “ain’t no party like a Liz Lemon party” because “a Liz Lemon party is mandatory.” And Morgan remembered the seminal “advice I wish I woulda got when I was your age” which was to “live every week like it’s Shark Week.”

And then things took a turn. Fey was stumped by a clip of Liz, dressed as Princess Leia from “Star Wars” to try to get out of jury duty. “Because I can read minds?” Fey guessed. (Her actual line was “Because I’m a hologram.”) But she rebounded with her character’s memory of participating in the “Big Sister” program. (“That little girl taught me how to use a tampon.”)

When Morgan couldn’t think of the punchline to “What is this, horseville?” he turned to the audience to supply the answer. Everyone shouted: “Because I’m surrounded by naysayers. Wordplay!” Morgan couldn’t recall other Tracy-isms, like, “I don’t get why people like brunch. What’s the benefit of combining breakdancing and lunch?” and “I was just thinking about how weird it is that we eat birds.” But he had a good excuse.

“I’m supposed to remember that?” Morgan said. “You gotta give me a break. I got hit by a truck!”

Dr. Leo Spaceman doles out medical advice

Chris Parnell’s wacky doctor Leo Spaceman, who gets promoted to Surgeon General of the United States at the end of the series, was on hand to “clear up any confusion about our official health recommendations.” A sampling of his frequently asked questions: “Do vaccines cause autism? Or, does autism cause billionaires?” (“Either way, you’re in trouble, fam.”) “Is it safe to eat lettuce yet?” (“Nope, it never was. Stick to the paleo food groups: Beef, meat, and Zyns.”) “Can I give my spouse a GLP-1 without them knowing?” (“Now, any doctor will tell you: If you don’t know the law, you can’t break it.”) That should clear a few things up!

‘What would Jack Donaghy say?’

Since the series went off the air in 2013, “30 Rock” guest star and former “NBC Nightly News” anchor Brian Williams admitted he’s been missing Jack Donaghy’s pithy advice and commentary on the state of the world. One of the night’s sharpest sketches — introduced by Williams — involved Jack responding to major news events of the last 13 years.

— In 2014, Jack’s assistant Jonathan (Maulik Pancholy) told his boss that his emails were leaked in the infamous Sony hack. “The one where I tried to get Tracy in drag in the female ‘Ghostbusters’?” Jack asks, to which Jonathan replies, “No, I never sent that one. It’s the one where you offer to give Jenna to Kim Jong Un if it would help.”

— In 2017, Kenneth, the eager page played by McBrayer, reveals he was “#MeToo’d by a lady on the camera crew.” He elaborates, saying, “She asked me what my ideal last meal would be, and I said chickpeas and Mountain Dew.’ She said, ‘Me too!’ And then we high-fived so hard, my pants fell down.”

— In 2021, Jack shamed the insurrectionists who stormed the capitol on Jan. 6. “When I defecated on Nancy Pelosi’s desk,” he said, “I looked in her straight in the eye like a man.”

— In 2023, Jonathan celebrated a box office rebound — “Sir, ‘Barbie’ and ‘Oppenheimer’ were a huge success. The movie business is back! — and Jack retorts: “And more importantly, now when you Google “Barbenheimer,” that’s what comes up, and not Cody Barbenheimer, the young man who mysteriously drowned in Lindsey Graham’s bathtub over Memorial Day weekend.”

Jane Krakowski’s musical medley

Fresh off her run in “Oh, Mary!” on Broadway, Krakowski wowed the room by performing several of the attention-seeking Maroney’s greatest hits. Wearing a sparkly silver dress and flanked by dancers in page uniforms, she opened with “That’s Her,” the opening theme song from “The Girlie Show” and masterfully pivoted into the feminist anthem “Muffin Top” before transitioning to Jackie Jormp-Jomp’s classic “Chunk of My Lung,” a parody of Janis Joplin’s “Piece of my Heart.” (Jenna was cast to play the music icon in an unlicensed biopic that never got off the ground.)

The already giddy crowd erupted when Krakowski was joined by John McEnroe to belt the “Sunday Night Football”-inspired “Tennis Night in America” and later by Forte, dressed as an angel in character as Jenna’s beau Paul L’astnamé, for a duet of the Christmas carol “O Holy Night.” Marceline Hugot, who plays Kathy Geiss, the mute daughter of GE’s boss Don Geiss, made a brief but thrilling appearance on trumpet.

title: Like Its Hero, Marvel’s ‘VisionQuest’ Struggles to Connect Emotionally: TV Review
summary: Partway through “VisionQuest,” the titular android Vision (Paul Bettany) attempts to help a British teenager named Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) understand the precise nature of their relationship. The truth goes something like this: Vision is a reconstituted version of his former self, who was killed by Thanos in “Avengers: Infinity War” and then kinda-sorta brought back […]
content:
Partway through “VisionQuest,” the titular android Vision (Paul Bettany) attempts to help a British teenager named Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) understand the precise nature of their relationship. The truth goes something like this: Vision is a reconstituted version of his former self, who was killed by Thanos in “Avengers: Infinity War” and then kinda-sorta brought back sans memories by his wife Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen), a grieving witch, in the 2021 series “WandaVision”; Tommy is an ordinary person suddenly imbued with the consciousness and abilities of a child Wanda invented with magic, which survived the collapse of his mother’s suburban simulation and crossed the pond in search of a host.

Vision runs a simulation where he struggles, over and over again, to condense all this lore and explain it to Tommy in a way that doesn’t overwhelm him with anger and confusion. There’s not a single version that doesn’t end with Tommy storming out of the room.

Popular on Variety

This is more or less how it feels to watch “VisionQuest,” an eight-episode Marvel Studios series that’s positioned as a sequel of sorts to “WandaVision.” The show plays with some clever concepts, particularly in its visual presentation; as the simulation scenarios pile up, so do Vision clones until a dozen exhausted, exasperated Bettanys all collapse on a hotel floor. (Much of “VisionQuest” strips away the monochrome coating to show Vision as an ordinary human, allowing Bettany to flex his fusty charm.) But this imagery is larded with so much convoluted backstory and abstract concepts that “VisionQuest” ends up in the exact same predicament as Vision himself, a synthetic being trying and mostly failing to connect with his emotions.

Artificial intelligence has long been a staple of comics and other forms of science fiction, but as real-life AI companies talk seriously about potential sentience, there’s a topical slant to Vision’s preferred strategy for getting in touch with his feelings. He’s created and/or convened a bunch of autonomous AIs — what we would now call “agents,” though creator Terry Matalas may have overseen the scripts before that term fully entered the popular lexicon — to help him with various tasks. There’s F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), who helps decode social interactions, and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), who’s a proponent of fun. Mechanics D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis) and U (Jonathan Sayer) tend to the more mundane work of keeping internal systems in shape. Finally, there are more familiar figures from earlier stages of the MCU: Tony Stark’s old pal J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy) is on hand; most intriguingly, so is Ultron (James Spader), the namesake antagonist of the second “Avengers” film.

All these assistants take corporeal form in Vision’s so-called Mindspace, a virtual and psychological plane that takes the shape of a quirky Victorian mansion. Here, Ultron looks not like a menacing CGI robot but the 66-year-old Spader himself: a schlubby guy with a flowing beard and a trenchcoat whose menacing, purple-prosed monologues (“It feels to me like your Greek tragedy has a deuteragonist”) are undercut by his appearance. To the show’s credit, this Ultron is a highly entertaining creation, allowing Spader to layer some of his signature sardonic air to a character who’s still cynical, but much humbled from his supervillain days. Without access to the real world, Ultron has to settle for being the devil on Vision’s shoulder rather than an actor in his own right.

It’s when the Mindspace intersects with said real world that “VisionQuest” gets overly complicated. Directors Christopher J. Byrne, Gandja Monteiro and Vincenzo Natali — along with Matalas, who helms the final pair of episodes — have some fun inside that mutable dimension: When a hostile android’s neural network connects with Vision’s, the episode becomes a riff on possession and exorcism (“The power of code compels you!”), and when Ultron begs Vision to let him “take the wheel,” it’s a literal ship’s wheel buffeted by stormwinds. But apart from having the AIs appear and speak to Vision as a kind of imaginary friend, invisible to everyone else, “VisionQuest” never lands on a consistent or legible way to map the relationship between the two realms, or how events in one affect the material reality of the other.

Constantly toggling between the Mindspace and meatspace (sorry, it’s right there!) inevitably takes a toll on Tommy, who only exists in the latter. Even by the fantastical standards of comics-based storytelling, the tenuousness of Tommy’s nature — he’s kind of another incarnation of Quicksilver, played by Evan Peters in “WandaVision,” but also kind of not? — makes him a difficult protagonist to map onto. That straining to comprehend the irrational fog of human emotions is the show’s explicit subject only clarifies the problem rather than neutralizing it. As Vision wonders what his purpose is without Wanda or the Avengers, we do, too.

“VisionQuest” tries to balance such philosophical questions about consciousness (yes, the Ship of Theseus metaphor comes back) with more active conflicts. At the behest of a mysterious client, the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) is on Vision’s trail, as is the aforementioned android (T’Nia Miller). Evading them provides some momentum, though not enough to propel an entire cast so massive I haven’t even mentioned Diane “Philomena Cunk” Morgan, who plays the Paladin’s assistant, yet. Before long, “VisionQuest” is trying to stitch all its unwieldy threads together with basic clichés about chosen family. “VisionQuest” often tells the audience what we’re supposed to be feeling, yet rarely achieves its stated aim.

“WandaVision” was the first Marvel Studios show to air on Disney+, and with its shapeshifting sitcom homage as an allegory for grief, that series has remained a high bar to beat amid the MCU’s oversaturation era. This remains the case for the direct sequel. “VisionQuest” rehashes many of the same themes about recovering from loss — there is, of course, a flashback to the famous line about love persevering — with a hero who is, by definition, much less accessible. (And given AI’s alarming trajectory toward mass job replacement and/or civilizational destruction, I didn’t feel especially inclined to empathize with a bunch of digital entities.) “VisionQuest” can be enjoyable in its comfort zone of zanily tweaking the Mindspace. But when it’s time to venture out into the tactile world, the show doesn’t leave a lasting mark.

The first two episodes of “VisionQuest” will premiere on Disney+ on Oct. 14, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Wednesdays.

title: Tilly Nollywood? African Filmmakers — Ready or Not — Get Set for the AI Revolution
summary: The world premiere of what’s been billed as the first photorealistic, AI-generated feature film in the Yoruba language fizzled out last week when user demand overwhelmed the servers of Docuth, the streaming platform that hosted the launch. After months of hype building to the release of “Asiri Ilu Awon Osu” (Mystery of Osu Land), the […]
content:
The world premiere of what’s been billed as the first photorealistic, AI-generated feature film in the Yoruba language fizzled out last week when user demand overwhelmed the servers of Docuth, the streaming platform that hosted the launch.

After months of hype building to the release of “Asiri Ilu Awon Osu” (Mystery of Osu Land), the film’s Nigerian producers, Mysterious Tech Studio, took to social media to apologize for the glitch, telling their followers: “To everyone at home and abroad who has tried to watch and could not get through, please do not be offended or discouraged.”

The episode felt somehow symbolic for this moment in the history of AI in Africa, where excitement over the technology’s transformative potential for the continent’s filmmakers often runs counter to the practical realities on the ground.

Popular on Variety

As African industry professionals convened at this year’s Durban FilmMart, both the potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence were high on the agenda.

Among the chief concerns for many stakeholders are the barriers to entry. AI tools that are widely available elsewhere in the world face unique challenges in reaching African consumers, from high data costs and low broadband speeds to payment-processing headaches.

Tamara Dawit, of Ethiopian Canadian production company Gobez Media, noted that those challenges represent significant “systemic barriers” to the adoption of the latest tech tools on the African continent.

“How do we address those issues so that everyone is benefitting from the advancements in technology?” she said. “If these are great opportunities for the industry, can everybody actually access them?”

Zukisani Karabo Mabece, of media-tech and production company Digicine Motion Picture, agreed.

“AI isn’t necessarily a magic pill,” said Mabece, whose Johannesburg-based company has leaned into generative AI with a host of digital tools designed to democratize access to cutting-edge technology for African filmmakers.

“It’s very biased. It’s very Western,” he said. “We’re having to build our own language models to accommodate the languages that we have here locally. We took it upon ourselves to build models that serve our market and our geography.”

In some instances, the rapid adoption of AI technology has had unintended consequences that aren’t unique to Africa.

Earlier this year, the South African government drafted an ambitious AI policy that was summarily withdrawn when journalists discovered that at least six of its 67 academic citations were the by-products of AI hallucinations, referring to journals and authors that did not exist. The drafters appeared to have used a large-language model to compose the policy without verifying its claims.

While the blunder was a PR disaster for South African policymakers, Amilcar Patel, who serves as co-chair of the South African Screen Federation (SASFED), noted that there are more pernicious dangers lurking for Africans when it comes to using AI tools developed in the Global North.

“We need to be very careful when we’re using AI in our work, especially in our policy and legal work, because we’re infusing a very different culture that doesn’t protect women, that doesn’t protect the poor, that doesn’t protect the vulnerable, into our legislative framework,” said Patel. “And then it becomes law.”

For African creatives, there are additional ethical factors to consider.

“AI mirrors society,” said Dawit. “Society has a lot of systemic inequities within it, and those show up [in AI models].”

“Those that are building AI don’t look like us. Biases are already built into the AI systems,” added Samantha Kaine, of the Independent Media Producers Assn. of Creative Talent (I.M.P.A.C.T.). “When the major AI models are trained largely on Western data and Western culture, what does it take to use these tools without importing someone else’s aesthetic or erasing who we are — erasing our own identity?”

Such concerns are likely to be on the agenda next month when Cape Town plays host to the Africa AI Summit, a three-day event that gathers heads of state and global tech and business leaders to draw up a roadmap that will shape the future of AI across Africa and the Global South.

Backed by partners including the World Bank, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Nvidia, the event is built around a billion-dollar AI initiative that’s designed to accelerate the deployment of artificial intelligence across the continent.

In the meantime, African filmmakers will continue to find uses for AI tools, even as the continent’s digital infrastructure and policy frameworks are forced to play catch-up.

One week after the failed rollout of “Mystery of Osu Land,” Kafilat Yusuff, of Mysterious Tech Studio, told Variety that after “viewers experienced intermittent access due to high traffic at launch,” the platform “has now been stabilized.” The film, which incorporated roughly 80% AI-assisted scenes with 20% live-action scenes utilizing real actors and their voices, is now available to stream on Docuth.

“Our experience has shown us that AI offers independent African filmmakers new ways to explore ambitious stories and visual worlds,” Yusuff said. “However, it also raises important questions about the role of human performers, consent, compensation, creative ownership and how audiences receive AI-assisted films.”

As for future plans, she said that the company is holding off on a follow-up until “Mystery of Osu Land” has had time to enjoy a “full run.”

“We spent a lot of time building this, and with the premiere traffic we just saw on Docuth, it’s clear there’s a lot of global curiosity. So our focus now is festivals, wider press and securing a stable global streaming release so everyone who wants to see it can,” she said.

“We are documenting everything we learned from this hybrid 80% AI-20% live-action pipeline, which will eventually help us and other African filmmakers make future projects at lower cost.”

The Durban FilmMart runs Oct. 9 – 12 in Durban, South Africa.

title: How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’
summary: The long nightmare might be over for South African producers, whose industry has been crippled for more than two years by the paralysis of a rebate program that for all intents and purposes had ceased to function. Speaking this week at the Durban FilmMart, Nelly Molokoane, director of film and television production at the Dept. […]
content:
The long nightmare might be over for South African producers, whose industry has been crippled for more than two years by the paralysis of a rebate program that for all intents and purposes had ceased to function.

Speaking this week at the Durban FilmMart, Nelly Molokoane, director of film and television production at the Dept. of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC), insisted that the government body tasked with administering the country’s 25% cash rebate has finally turned a corner. “The department is back in business,” Molokoane said.

After months of political pressure from industry bodies that rallied under the banner of the Save SA Film and TV Jobs Coalition, the DTIC is now working through a backlog of applications and rebate claims dating back to 2024, with Molokoane counseling patience as the embattled department attempts to right the ship.

Popular on Variety

“We know that the industry now is bleeding, but we are doing our best,” she said.

The news sparked a collective sigh of relief from the filmmakers and industry groups gathered in Durban, who have locked horns with South African officials over delays in processing rebate claims, bureaucratic bottlenecks, a lack of transparency from their counterparts in government, and overall questions about the future of the once-thriving incentive program.

“The worst is over,” said producer Delon Bakker, who serves as chairperson of the Independent Producers Organization. “We’re very confident that we’re now moving in the right direction. We’re not sure at what pace, but we are definitely making progress.”

The crisis dealt a devastating blow to a South African industry that was already feeling the squeeze, with the exhibition sector floundering, global streaming networks scaling back their investments in local production and domestic broadcasters — including the struggling public broadcaster, SABC — unable to keep the industry afloat.

“We’re talking thousands of jobs. We’re talking hundreds of companies that have suffered losses because of this. We’re talking projects that have made claims that have not been paid two, three, four years later,” said producer Paul Buys, of Rose and Oaks Media. “It’s really pushed everybody to the limits.”

The DTIC has made significant strides in paying off most of the nearly 2-billion-rand ($121 million) backlog in unpaid rebate claims and shored up roughly 1.5 billion rand ($91 million) to fund the rebate through 2029.

While those producers who spoke to Variety were cautiously optimistic that the industry has finally turned the page, there remains much work to be done. Chief among their concerns is what shape the incentive program will take moving forward, whether it’s a modified version of the existing cash rebate program, a tax credit scheme, or some alternate proposal.

Still, after months of often contentious dialogue with government officials, local producers are grateful that both sides have found a way through the impasse. “Ultimately, everyone wants this to work, and ultimately, we want to work with the department,” said Bakker. “We want peace. We want a period of prosperity.”

For her part, the polarizing Molokoane — who has faced calls for her resignation from industry bodies — struck a conciliatory tone in Durban.

“We’ve been engaging the industry since last year to say, ‘How best can we support this industry?’ And I know maybe the industry has been informed that the DTIC is not on board,” she said. “We are on board…. We would like to work with you in order to ensure that we’ve got a sustainable industry.”

For now, local producers are guardedly optimistic that such political goodwill will last, while their foreign counterparts will look for reassurances that the rebate is back on solid footing. “It’s going to take some time to get that certainty back…and build trust internationally,” said Big World Cinema producer Steven Markovitz.

In spite of the challenges, South African filmmakers say the rebate crisis has been a wake-up call that has not only galvanized the industry but bolstered their resolve to build a sustainable film and TV business — with or without a functioning incentive program.

“There’s a willingness to try and do things in this crisis,” said Markovitz. “I do think that we’re going to come out of it looking at other ways to try and break that dependency on DTI subsidies for every film that we do.”

“These obstacles and challenges constantly force us to rethink different ways to do things and different ways to still get our films made and our stories told,” added Yellowbone Entertainment’s Layla Swart. “And I think despite everything, that’s always what we do. We’re fighters and we’re constantly advocating for the things that work with us.”

The Durban FilmMart runs Oct. 9 – 12 in Durban, South Africa.

title: ‘Line Of Fire’ Gets Backup Script Order As Lisa Katz Talks NBC Fall Rollout, ‘Newlyweds’ Exit, 2027 Pilot Season, Peacock Strategy & ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: NBC’s fall 2026 scripted lineup kicked off with the Sept. 21 series premiere of Line Of Fire, starring Peter Krause and Hope Davis. After a strong launch and week-to-week ratings gains, the drama about a family of federal law enforcement agents entangled in a mystery has become the first new 2026-27 broadcast series to […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: NBC‘s fall 2026 scripted lineup kicked off with the Sept. 21 series premiere of Line Of Fire, starring Peter Krause and Hope Davis. After a strong launch and week-to-week ratings gains, the drama about a family of federal law enforcement agents entangled in a mystery has become the first new 2026-27 broadcast series to get a back order as NBC has picked up 5 additional scripts.

The premiere episode’s multi-platform viewership has grown to nearly 12M (including encores) so far, improving the Monday 10 PM time period by +48% in Live+3 MP total viewers vs. last fall.

“We’re so excited that the audience seems to be responding as we did, we think it’s such a special show,” NBC and Peacock Scripted Content President Lisa Katz said. “What I love most about it is you have a show that has so many different access points: you have the cases, then you have the family drama and the mystery. It’s a very ambitious idea, and I think that [creator] Josh Safran’s done a wonderful job of balancing it in a way. I think we got so lucky with this incredible cast led by Peter and Hope and sophisticated storytelling that I feel like reminds me of some shows we did in NBC in the past.”

Watch on Deadline

If the extra scripts get converted to an episodic order, that would bring Line of Fire‘s first season to 18 episodes, which would match the season length of a recent NBC drama known for its sophisticated storytelling, This Is Us.

“I think for this show, given the storytelling, 18 feels the sweet spot, and also with what our Monday night schedule looks like and where the opportunities are,” Katz said of the newcomer. “So that would be the goal.”

As a 10 PM drama, Line Of Fire is posting strong DVR numbers and it also is doing well on Peacock. What’s more, Episode 2 grew a whopping 47% among Live+Same Day adults 18-49 on NBC.

“It’s continuing to gain momentum, it’s grown week over week, which I haven’t seen happen in so long, so clearly, people are responding and telling people, and they’re watching,” Katz said.

To further fuel word of mouth, in a synergy move, the Line of Fire pilot episode will be getting a promo run on sibling cable network Bravo on Oct. 14. Episode 4 premieres on NBC tonight.

Mariska Hargitay & Chrisopher Meloni will reunite on ‘Law & Order: SVU’s 600th episode airing Nov. 12 NBC

Don’t Call It A (Broadcast) Comeback

There seems to be something in the water this fall with venerable franchises defying their age as CBS’ NCIS dramas and ABC’s Dancing With the Stars all returned up from their most recent season premieres and NBC’s Chicago Med won the night in total viewers with its season opener last week. Is broadcast television back?

“I hope so, it was never gone for me, but I think that people, with these shows that you get to watch weekly for multiple episodes, and you get to spend time and revisit these characters and their stories week after week, year after year, I think is meaningful, so I’ve believed in broadcast all along,” Katz said. “I’m fortunate enough to be able to do streaming and broadcast, and I think that broadcast shows and that cadence and that rhythm and the ability to air weekly is just something that people value, and I’m glad to see that. Seems like other people agree with me right now.”

In addition to their continuous linear strength, Wolf Entertainment’s Chicago and Law & Order series have been big next-day-on-Peacock draws, with all five series, along with Line Of Fire, firmly in the streamer’s Top 10 since their premieres.

“It’s great that they’re coming back,” Katz said. “And Chicago Fire is going to be 300th episode, SVU 600 episodes, and people aren’t tired of it, they’re eating it up. We’re very fortunate with Dick Wolf and the showrunners and the cast, and the storytelling I think is as strong if not better, so it’s great that people are continuing to watch.”

Any plans to end any of the two long-running shows hitting milestone episodes this season?

“No plans, they’re going strong,” Katz said

Ashley Michel Hoban and Taylor Schilling Courtesy/Getty

NBC’s 2027 Pilot Season & Dick Wolf’s Next Franchise

Dick Wolf came close to expanding his NBC footprint again this season with the pilot What the Dead Know. It didn’t get picked up to series in May but was put in redevelopment, with star Taylor Schilling’s option extended and a new writer, Dr. Death co-creator Ashley Michel Hoban, currently co-executive producer on Fox’s Doc, brought in to pen a new script.

“That pilot’s in contention, and we’ve bought some other development from Wolf Entertainment, continuing to try to find the next franchise. Because, as you know, Dick doesn’t do pilots or series; he does franchises. So we’re trying to find what will be the next one, and What the Dead Know is definitely one of them.”

The new Wolf Entertainment hopefuls are among the crop of projects NBC has in the works as part of the 2026-27 development cycle.

“We’re still doing the (typical) broadcast cycle, so we’ve been hearing pitches the last few months, and we’ve bought a few projects from them that will be on the cycle to hopefully develop, shoot,” Katz said of Wolf’s team. “This pilot season proved very successful in terms of helping us find the right shows, and with Line of Fire‘s performance, I feel very good about it and eager to do it again.”

NBC surprised some when it brought back the January-May pilot season by ordering eight pilots — five dramas, three comedies — earlier this year. The network bet on TV stars as leads of all of them, including David Boreanaz headlining The Rockford Files reboot, which is going into production for a January launch. It’s a strategy NBC plans to continue.

“The goal is to make great shows that break through, and how’s that going to happen? If you don’t have the IP in the case of Line of Fire, but you have a really compelling, well-executed show, then how can we stack the deck? By bringing in Peter and bringing in Hope — both of them are associated with such high caliber projects, I think it gave it a legitimacy, and also bringing in their fans. And then also we have these younger cast members,” Katz said. “Rockford is IP, people know it and are familiar with it, but might not exactly know what it is. And then you have David, a tried and true television star who starred in three long-running successful series, so I feel like it’s about the balance between fresh and familiar, proven stars and new stars, and just being able to find that alchemy.”

NBC’s version of pilot season is set to return in 2027 with similar number of pilots to 2026, Katz said.

“In the early days when I used to do pilots, we were doing 20-25 comedy and drama pilots a year, and that feels maybe excessive,” she said. “I think it’s about doing the right number and the right ones that really feel like you want to be able to see the chemistry of the cast, to see if the concept works. But I would also say we’re open to, if something came that was a bigger idea that we wanted to go, which we did with The Hunting Party where we did script-to-series. That’s also on the table, and it really just depends on what the right model is. But I think for us it’s similar to last year, and then seeing how the new shows perform and what the needs are, and being able to respond accordingly.”

Newlyweds ‘ and ‘Happy’s Place’ NBC

‘Newlyweds’ Shakeup & Multi-Cams’ Older Viewer Skew

Going through a pilot as proof of concept sometimes may not be enough. New multi-camera comedy Newlyweds, headlined by Téa Leoni and Tim Daly, which did a pilot, is undergoing a change at the helm as Gail Lerner, who co-created the series with co-star Jamie Lee Curtis, announced on Friday that she had been fired as showrunner amid production. What happened?

“That truly was an instance of creative differences, and we feel like that concept of a romantic comedy in a multi-cam format was very winning. And that cast is phenomenal with Téa, Tim, and Jamie,” Katz said. “So, we’re working to find the right person and move forward, and we’re still really, really invested and committed to it, and feel like it’s a great companion to Happy’s Place too. Both multi-cam shows, and we love that Tim and Téa are married, and [Happy’s Place co-stars] Rex [Linn] and Reba [McEntire] are a couple; we’ve got some real-life couples.”

Newlyweds, which filmed the eighth episode of its 13-episode order on Friday, was scheduled to go on hiatus this week as search is underway for a new showrunner. Could that be extended if a new person is not found quickly or they need more time to get up to speed?

“We don’t know yet, but because we’re not premiering till later, we feel like we can stay on schedule,” Katz said. Newlyweds and Season 3 of Happy’s Place debut Oct. 23.

With the exception of Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, which is an extension of an established comedy franchise, all multi-camera comedies that are working these days seem to be centered on characters of a certain age played by stars such as Leoni & Daly, McEntire, Shifting Gears‘ Tim Allen and Leanne‘s Leanne Morgan. NBC is developing a sitcom headlined by Frasier alum David Hyde Pierce for next season. Is the multi-cam genre that gave us Friends and The Big Bang Theory now only working for older people?

“It’s interesting. I think for us we try to center it around a star and a voice, and I think also it’s such a specific form,” Katz said. “Multi-cam is a very different format than a single-cam, and I think some of the people that have experience in it tend to be older. That seems how it’s worked for us when we look at Reba or Tim and Téa or George Lopez [star of NBC’s Lopez vs Lopez], but it’s also people that have a strong point of view and voice or experience to share. So I think that’s been really helpful in terms of how we’re building those.”

Taylor Kinney, Jason Beghe, S. Epatha Merkerson, Miranda Mayo and Oliver Platt

NBC

NBC’s Staggered Fall 2026 Rollout & Peacock Collab

For decades, broadcast networks lived and died by Premiere Week in September when all new and returning series debuted, all vying for attention. That tradition is gone, with the networks opting for more strategic rollouts. NBC’s this season is particularly spread out as scheduling has to work around NBA games and the network’s post-season baseball coverage. Only one scripted series, Line of Fire, opened in September; it launched behind the season premiere of The Voice on Sept. 21. There was one other entertainment series, The Traitors: New Blood, a civilian version of the hit Peacock reality hit, that started off in September, with One Chicago and the Law & Order franchise joining last week.

What are the advantages and disadvantages of such a staggared rollout?

“I’m really grateful to our scheduling and marketing teams and the collaboration because it feels like we were able to focus on a few things at once, and by using The Voice, which — I don’t work on The Voice or Traitors: New Blood but I am watching them live or on Peacock next day — I think they’re so great this season,” Katz said. “So by having those, Line of Fire, now we have the Chicagos back, in a few weeks, we’ll have the comedies back. It feels like we’re able to focus on a couple priorities, then launch those and move on to the next. I know everybody used to get so excited about Premiere Week, and it’s all happening. It feels like this strategy has proven, particularly this year, to be working, so I think it’s a good one.”

NBC’s new and returning scripted series are premiering alongside the debuts of Peacock originals — the combined fall rollout kicked off with The Paper Season 2 release on Peacock Sept. 9 and ends with the Dig premiere on the platform Nov. 23, with network and streaming debuts in-between. Scheduling was done holistically across linear and streaming.

“I think that we’ve become over the past few seasons much more aligned in terms of using the NBC next day as another programming move on Peacock,” Katz said. “So, we’re not trying to launch a Peacock original at the same time as we’re launching a new NBC show because we want to be able to platform and highlight each show and give it its due, and also looking at what might be a handoff to something else and which shows can benefit from being scheduled around them, even though they’re on different platforms. I think that that’s also been really successful, how they can be complementary.”

‘The Paper’ Season 2 (L-R) Domhnall Gleeson as Ned, Chelsea Frei as Mare, Melvin Gregg as Detrick, Eric Rahill as Travis John P. Fleenor/Peacock

‘The Paper’ Renewal & ‘FNL’ Reboot Status Updates

The first of NBCU’s fall premieres was Season 2 of The Paper. There hasn’t been a lot of information about its performance. Is it possible for it to get a third season?

“Yeah, we have a writers’ room that has been working for Season 3. It only launched a month ago, so it’s still newer, but we thought the second season was great, the audience response and consumer response has been really good, saying as good or better than the first season,” Katz said. “And speaking about our strategy of NBC and Peacock complementing each other, we haven’t had the NBC comedies on yet, so we’re hopeful getting those comedies back on NBC will help the engagement on Peacock and bring more comedy viewers. We are eager to see how The Paper performs once St. Dennis and Reggie come back and when we launch Happy’s Place in Newlyweds.

The Paper is a successor to one beloved NBC series, The Office. Peacock has been developing a reboot of another, Friday Night Lights. Not at the moment, though.

“It’s on pause,” Katz said about the new FNL.

Also on indefinite hold is the live-action Ted series after creator Seth MacFarlane said earlier this year that there are no plans for a third season of the pricey endeavor.

“Right now, we are focusing on the animated version,” Katz said.

(l-r) Duke McCloud, Sarah Snook in ‘All Her Fault’ Sarah Enticknap/Peacock

Peacock Programming Strategy: White Wine Thrillers, 101 Studios

NBCUniversal’s $27 billion NBA deal and the push for Peacock profitability, achieved for the first time in Q2 2026, has put some constraints on the streamer’s slate, with room for 12 scripted originals a year in addition to Peacock’s sizable unscripted portfolio. The platform went through 13 months without a new scripted series greenlight from May 2025 until June 2026. There have been several pickups since, including The Break-In, Dungeon Crawler Carl, Before I Let Go and The Fast & the Furious series.

“Part of it is, we’ve had some leadership changes, so we spent the past year or so really trying to be incredibly thoughtful and intentional about the kinds of shows and what will work,” Katz said. “And I think when you look at the things that we’ve picked up — and we’ve renewed some shows as well, like Five Star Weekend –– I feel really excited that they feel like we’re really catering to some specific fandoms and things that can help hopefully break through. Whether it be Dungeon Crawler Carl, which has this enormous rabid fan base, or it’s Fast and Furious, where we have the opportunity to tap into that franchise, or Before I Let Go, Kennedy Ryan’s book which she has, again, this really passionate fan base.”

The pending spinoff of Peacock’s parent NBCUniversal from Comcast has not had an impact on its programming strategy so far but the timing of the streamer’s launch has, Katz said.

“Peacock was one of the later to market streamers, and we’re catching up a bit, so I think a way to do it is to find things that people have to tune into, and we love doing things that are original, like All Her Fault, or we like doing things that can tap into a fan base that we can explore,” she said. “So I think that we’ve come up with a great strategy. It took a minute to get there and find the right things but now I think we’re in a really good rhythm.”

Peacock’s All Her Fault helped is part of a wave of female-focused mystery series dubbed white wine thrillers. The streamer has stayed on trend with The Break-In, from the All Her Fault team, as well other female-skewing dramas, including The Five Star Weekend, which had a mystery element, and Before I Let Go.

“I think people really turn up for these shows that have some mystery, suspense thrillers, a relatable theme,” Katz said. “I think when you talk about All Her Fault, and you just say the first sentence of what happens, a mom went to pick up her son and he wasn’t there, and also the husband was like, ‘Why didn’t you check the number?’ I think that resonates with people in a way that is really powerful. Plus, you have incredible writing, direction, casting — all the elements came together. I would say Five Star Weekend is not a thriller and just a story about female friendship and a bit of, again, something that felt emotional, relatable, had food and Nantucket scenery and things that you wanted to spend time there. I know people like to categorize things, so yes, that’s one of the things. But I think we’re open to all different kinds of ways to reach the audience.”

Universal IP-based series such as Fast and the Furious and Ted notwithstanding, Peacock has been buying, developing and greenlighting quite a few female-leaning series. The industry speculation has been that the focus is informed by the arrival of Taylor Sheridan collaborators David Glasser, whose 101 Studios produces all Sheridan series, and Chris McCarthy, as well as the Jan. 1, 2029 move from Skydance to NBCU by Sheridan himself. Sherdan and 101 Studios are known for their lineup of male-skewing hit series such as Yellowstone, which streams on Peacock, Landman, Tulsa King and MobLand.

Indeed, the first Peacock project recently announced from 101 Studios and McCarthy under their NBCU deals is The Chairman, a Matthew Weiner drama starring Eddie Murphy in his scripted series debut. Is Peacock’s development designed to accommodate the output coming from 101 Studios — and soon Sheridan?

“We’re really excited to be working with them and hope they can bring some of the success that they’ve had elsewhere,” Katz said. “And when you have people that are so great at what they do, you’re like, how can we supplement that? Like on NBC, if it’s something that Wolf Entertainment can do, they’re going to do it, and they’re gonna be the best at it. So we look for things that are different than a Wolf show. And I think similarly, knowing the kinds of shows that 101 and Taylor do, I think there’s plenty of other shows, like all the ones I just listed, I think Dungeon Crawler Carl, Before I Let Go, Ted animated, Five Star. Those aren’t the shows that they’re going to be doing. So it’s like taking advantage of what they’re bringing. But there’s so many other audiences that we can serve, and so we’re focusing on that as well.”

‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’, Seth MacFarlane Ace Books/Josh Telles/Deadline

‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’: Production Update On TV’s Hottest IP

One of the most anticipated upcoming series on any platform is Peacock’s adaptation of Matt Dinniman‘s hugely popular novel Dungeon Crawler Carl, from showrunners Chris Yost and Eric Heisserer, Seth MacFarlane’s Fuzzy Door and Universal Global Television. Its progress is being closely watched by fans since the series’ June greenlight.

“We are currently in the process of meeting with directors, and then we’ll move on to casting, but the room started about a month ago, and we’re getting material and underway,” Katz said of the series, which is targeting a 2027 production start.

Not long after Universal Studio Group poached Jordan Moblo from Netflix to run Creative Acquisitions and IP Management for the studio, he optioned Dungeon Crawler Carl when it was still self-published.

“Jordan Moblo in IP fell in love with it and got it. And then when we heard it, everybody — when these special things come and they’re so original and so unique, you just jump on,” Katz said. “So we’re so grateful that we got in at the right time, and we’re so excited about that one.

Katz has been able to witness first-hand Dungeon Crawler Carl‘s immense popularity.

“I was taking my son to camp, and he had it in his backpack, I sent it with him, I’m like, you’re not going to be on screens, you should read this book,” she said. “And then we got to the airport, and there were two people in the boarding area that were both reading. Once you are aware of it, It’s everywhere.”

Katz and her team quickly jumped on the sister studio’s TV adaptation to set it up at Peacock. Had they waited, the project may have gone on the open market, with everyone pursuing the now white-hot IP.

“I feel like the goal is always to find the best stories and that one, we all were like, we have to do this,” she said. “So we’re really excited.”

title: Maddie Hasson Joins Julia Garner & Lewis Pullman In Apple TV’s ‘Guilty Creatures’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Maddie Hasson (Bone Lake, The Recruit) is set as a series regular opposite Julia Garner in Apple TV’s thriller drama Guilty Creatures, from director Craig Gillespie, showrunner Stuart Zicherman and Tomorrow Studios. In addition to Garner, Hasson joins previously announced Lewis Pullman. Adapted for the screen by Sarah DeLappe from Mikita Brottman‘s true-crime book […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Maddie Hasson (Bone Lake, The Recruit) is set as a series regular opposite Julia Garner in Apple TV‘s thriller drama Guilty Creatures, from director Craig Gillespie, showrunner Stuart Zicherman and Tomorrow Studios.

In addition to Garner, Hasson joins previously announced Lewis Pullman.

Adapted for the screen by Sarah DeLappe from Mikita Brottman‘s true-crime book Guilty Creatures: Sex, God, and Murder in Tallahassee, Florida, the series is set against a backdrop of sex and and murder in the Florida panhandle. It delves into the psyche of a torrid romance and subsequent act of murder between two young, adulterous but God-fearing lovers — believed to be played by Garner and Pullman — unraveling their complex lives and the emotional toll of living as killers for 18 years.

Guilty Creatures is produced by Tomorrow Studios (One Piece), an ITV Studios partner, and developed through the studios’ first-look deals with Garner’s Alma Margo and Gillespie’s Fortunate Jack Productions. Marty Adelstein, Becky Clements and Alissa Bachner executive produce through Tomorrow Studios, along with Garner through Alma Margo. Zicherman also serves as executive producer alongside DeLappe. Gillespie and Annie Marter executive produce through Fortunate Jack Productions. Brottman also serves as an executive producer.

Watch on Deadline

Hasson can most recently be seen leading Mercedes Bryce Morgan’s survival thriller Bone Lake. She was a series regular in Netflix’s The Recruit and starred in James Wan’s New Line horror film Malignant, Taurus opposite Machine Gun Kelly, Scoot McNairy, and Megan Fox, and Sony Classics’ Novitiate, opposite Margaret Qualley and Melissa Leo. She’ll next be seen starring in the limited series The Altruists from Obamas’ Higher Ground productions. Hasson is repped by UTA, Brillstein Entertainment Partners and Yorn Levine Barnes et al.

title: Monarch Media To Produce First-Time Feature Scribe Jonathan Yu’s Coming-Of-Age Dramedy ‘Goldfish’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: In his first outing as screenwriter, Jonathan Yu is already on his way toward a produced script: Monarch Media has announced that it will be producing his coming-of-age feature dramedy, Goldfish. Goldfish centers on a 17-year-old high school senior who presents as detached, ironic and emotionally armored, but underneath is quietly paralyzed by fear […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: In his first outing as screenwriter, Jonathan Yu is already on his way toward a produced script: Monarch Media has announced that it will be producing his coming-of-age feature dramedy, Goldfish.

Goldfish centers on a 17-year-old high school senior who presents as detached, ironic and emotionally armored, but underneath is quietly paralyzed by fear of failure, abandonment and becoming his parents.

Set to produce for Monarch, Steve Barnett, Alan Powell and Vicky Patel are currently in search of a director for the project.

Patel, who was contacted by Yu via cold-email, was hooked after reading his script and immediately brought it to her colleagues.

Watch on Deadline

“Every once in a great while, you pick up a wholly original coming-of-age script that’s filled with humor, heart and teenage angst, and this is one of those screenplays,” Patel said. “Jonathan has done an incredible job of crafting a story we can all relate to, and we can’t wait to bring it to life.”

A human biology major at UC San Diego, Yu has had a love of storytelling ever since discovering the Harry Potter books, and films like Jurassic Park and Good Will Hunting, early in life. He didn’t come to recognize screenwriting as a career option until well into college. While Goldfish is not autobiographical, the script draws on his years on his high school swim team. He is repped by 831 Entertainment.

Monarch Media is best known for its work on the acclaimed Richard Linklater film Hit Man, starring Glen Powell. The company’s adult animated feature film Tangles, starring Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Seth Rogen and Bryan Cranston, is vying for Oscar consideration after premiering to critical acclaim at Cannes. More recently, the company launched its comedy Babies, starring Rogen and Anna Kendrick, out of the Toronto Film Festival. They’re currently prepping a feature reboot of A Walk to Remember, as well as an untitled Nick Jonas rom-com for Netflix, which begins production in January.

title: Amber Siyavus Dies: ‘Big Brother’ Season 8 Contestant Was 46
summary: Amber Siyavus, who competed on Season 8 of Big Brother, has died, the Clark County medical examiner in Nevada confirmed to Deadline. She was 46. According to her death records, Siyavus died October 9 at a residence in Las Vegas. The cause and manner of death are pending. Longtime Big Brother host Julie Chen Moonves […]
content:
Amber Siyavus, who competed on Season 8 of Big Brother, has died, the Clark County medical examiner in Nevada confirmed to Deadline. She was 46.

According to her death records, Siyavus died October 9 at a residence in Las Vegas. The cause and manner of death are pending.

Longtime Big Brother host Julie Chen Moonves posted a remembrance to Siyavus on Instagram reels Monday, alongside a clip of Siyavus’ Big Brother post-eviction interview: “Rest in Peace Amber. Hard to believe but I know you are back in our eternal home with our Creator. Thank you for your heart and honesty. We will remember you with love.”

Siyavus competed on season 8 of Big Brother in 2007. During her time on the show, she became close to her fellow housemates, Jameka Cameron and Dustin Erikstrup, and was known for some emotional and quite often tearful moments, earning the nickname “Whamber.”

Siyavus was evicted eighth and finished in seventh place. Dick “Evel Dick” Donato went on to win the season.

In January 2018, Siyavus’ 18-year-old daughter, Lexi Tomcavage, died in an apparent suicide, according to TMZ, which was first to report Siyavus’ death.

title: ‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death Confirmed as Suicide
summary: RJ Mitte died by suicide, his rep has confirmed. The actor’s rep confirmed his cause of death to People magazine Monday evening. Mitte died Monday at 34. He was best known for his role in the Vince Gilligan-created drama “Breaking Bad,” in which he played Walter White Jr., the son of Walter White (Bryan Cranston) […]
content:
RJ Mitte died by suicide, his rep has confirmed.

The actor’s rep confirmed his cause of death to People magazine Monday evening.

Mitte died Monday at 34. He was best known for his role in the Vince Gilligan-created drama “Breaking Bad,” in which he played Walter White Jr., the son of Walter White (Bryan Cranston) and Holly White (Anna Gunn). Like his “Breaking Bad” character Walt Jr., Mitte had cerebral palsy.

The Brownsville Police Department received a call at 12:50 p.m. local time and found Mitte dead at his home, People reported. “The cause and manner of death are still pending, as there is currently an ongoing investigation,” the BPD.



Mitte appeared in all five seasons of the show, which ran from 2008 to 2013.

Popular on Variety

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his rep said in a statement earlier Monday. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”

After “Breaking Bad,” he had roles on “Switched at Birth,” “Robot Chicken,” “On Hiatus with Monty Geer,” “This Close,” “Now Apocalypse” and “The Guardians of Justice (Will Save You!)” among others. He also appeared in films including “Dixieland,” “Who’s Driving Doug,” “The Recall,” “Mower Boy,” “Time Share,” “The Oak Room” and more.

Before starring on “Breaking Bad,” the actor appeared in short films including “Stump” and “Weird Science 2: Strange Chemistry,” as well as the film “House of Last Things.” At the time of his death, he had a handful of projects in pre-production and production phases, and was actively promoting his new movie, “Talking to Strangers.”

If you or anyone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline by dialing 988 or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: Selma Blair Charged with Second-Degree Assault Following Plane Incident, Released on $20,000 Bail
summary: Selma Blair has been charged with second-degree assault after being arrested following a violent incident on a Delta flight on Sunday, according to Queens Criminal Court. The actress posted $20,000 in bail, paid by credit card, and was released on Monday. Blair was arrested after she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another on […]
content:
Selma Blair has been charged with second-degree assault after being arrested following a violent incident on a Delta flight on Sunday, according to Queens Criminal Court. The actress posted $20,000 in bail, paid by credit card, and was released on Monday.

Blair was arrested after she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another on a Delta plane heading from Los Angeles to New York. Blair also attempted to open the plane door while in the air. Law enforcement was waiting for the 54-year-old “Legally Blonde” actress at John F. Kennedy airport, where police took her into custody and transported her to a hospital for evaluation. Two flight attendants reported injuries, with one receiving treatment at a hospital.

A representative for Blair told Variety: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

Popular on Variety

Following the altercation on Sunday, the “Cruel Intentions” actress was arrested on Monday by a Port Authority police officer. She appeared in Queens Criminal Court Monday evening, where she appeared before Judge Indira D. Khan, per court documents viewed by Variety.

In 2016, Blair experienced a previous outburst while on a plane, during which she was removed from a flight on a stretcher while traveling with her then 4-year-old son after she “had a total psychotic blackout,” as she described it. Blair attributed the incident to drinking a glass of wine and taking a pill. “It was horrible and frightening, and I had empathy for myself actually afterward because it was actually so out of character for me, especially because I’m a mother,” she said at the time.

More to come…

title: ‘High Potential’ Lands Post-Super Bowl LXI Slot on ABC Next February
summary: ABC will take advantage of the post-Super Bowl glow to promote the Kaitlin Olson drama “High Potential,” the network announced Monday. That means the show will air immediately following Super Bowl LXI on ABC and Disney+ on Sunday, Feb. 14, 2027. That’s not the only show that Disney hopes to give a Super Bowl halo […]
content:
ABC will take advantage of the post-Super Bowl glow to promote the Kaitlin Olson drama “High Potential,” the network announced Monday. That means the show will air immediately following Super Bowl LXI on ABC and Disney+ on Sunday, Feb. 14, 2027.

That’s not the only show that Disney hopes to give a Super Bowl halo effect. As Variety previously reported, Hulu plans to launch the new Dan Fogelman-produced football drama “The Land” on Super Bowl Sunday as well.

This reps the first time ABC has aired the Super Bowl since 2006. That year, the network ran an episode of “Grey’s Anatomy” behind Super Bowl XL. Before that, in 2003, it ran an episode of “Alias” after Super Bowl XXXVII.

Popular on Variety

Other ABC shows that have received the Super Bowl lead-out slot include “The Practice” (2000, Super Bowl XXXIV). In 1995, the network used the slot to launch the pilot episode of a long-forgotten series titled “Extreme.” (The James Brolin adventure drama was canceled after seven episodes.) It ran the comedy pilot “Davis Rules” in 1991; and most successfully, launched the series “The Wonder Years” behind Super Bowl XXII in 1988.

Last year, NBC didn’t schedule a lead-out behind the Super Bowl, instead sticking with Winter Olympics coverage (which it also did in 2022). In 2025, Fox ran the game show “The Floor” behind Super Bowl LIX, and in 2024, CBS aired the series premiere of “Tracker” after Super Bowl LVIII, attracting 18.44 million viewers. That reps the last scripted show to air after the Big Game.

“High Potential” is set to return for Season 3 in early 2027 on Tuesday nights (streaming the next day on Hulu), the network noted. “High Potential” ended the 2025-2026 broadcast season as the No. 1 show among adults 18-49, according to the Alphabet net, with a 3.35 rating after 35 days of viewing on ABC, Hulu, Hulu on Disney+ and digital platforms. In viewers, the show averaged 16.01 million viewers in the same multiplatform, 35-day results.

“High Potential” stars Kaitlin Olson as Morgan, Daniel Sunjata as Karadec, Javicia Leslie as Daphne, Deniz Akdeniz as Lev “Oz” Ozdil, Amirah J as Ava, Matthew Lamb as Elliot and Judy Reyes as Selena.

20th Television is behind “High Potential,” which is based on the French series “Haut Potentiel Intellectuel (HPI)” and was created in the U.S. by Drew Goddard. Goddard and Sarah Esberg of Goddard Textiles, Nora and Lilla Zuckerman and Kaitlin Olson serve as executive producers. Andrea Massaro (Goddard Textiles) serves as co-executive producer.

Here’s the announcement of the post-Super Bowl move, as revealed during Monday night’s “Monday Night Football” game:

title: Kacey Musgraves Fires Back After Kristi Noem Disses Her: You Don’t ‘Have a Dog in This Fight, but If You Did You Would’ve Shot It’
summary: Kristi Noem might have thought twice before initiating a war of words with Kacey Musgraves, who had a mic-drop of a comeback post after the ousted Secretary of Homeland Security went on X to pick a fight with the country-pop star. Because when things get rough in a Noem feud, it’s always going to wind […]
content:
Kristi Noem might have thought twice before initiating a war of words with Kacey Musgraves, who had a mic-drop of a comeback post after the ousted Secretary of Homeland Security went on X to pick a fight with the country-pop star. Because when things get rough in a Noem feud, it’s always going to wind up going to the dogs.

Noem didn’t like it that Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico, a Democrat who is leading in polls in the red state, attended the concert by fellow Texan Musgraves over the weekend and was warmly received, as captured in photos and video. “Thank you for having me last night, Kacey Musgraves!” he wrote on social media, alongside a photo of the singer taking a photo of the two of them.

That led Noem to attempt to not just badger Musgraves for associating with Talarico but to set up a feud with “Choosin’ Texas” hitmaker Ella Langley (who, for what it’s worth, is from Alabama).

“I’ll take Ella Langley over Kacey Musgraves any day,” tweeted the Republican firebrand. “And if I’m choosin’ Texas, I’ll take Ken Paxton over James Talarico.”

Musgraves quote-tweeted Noem and responded: “I don’t think you have a dog in this fight but if you did you would have shot it.”

Langley appeared not to welcome Noem pitting her against Musgraves, as she or her team quickly moved to untag her X moniker from the politician’s tweet.

I don’t think you have a dog in this fight but if you did you would have shot it. https://t.co/bI50bahJZu — K A C E Y (@KaceyMusgraves) October 12, 2026

Noem has not returned to X for any more posts since Musgraves’ sardonic comeback, as of this writing.

Noem became famous for an anecdote in her memoir about shooting her 14-month-old dog, Cricket, to death in a gravel pit after she deemed the animal too troublesome. The story was intended to be an example of the one-time South Dakota governor’s firm resolve to do tough things, but it was seen as derailing her chances at becoming Donald Trump’s vice presidential pick during the 2024 campaign.

title: Jessica Lange Says FX Was ‘Too F—ing Cheap’ to Pay for Cars Home From ‘American Horror Story’ Set, So ‘We Had to Drive Ourselves’
summary: Jessica Lange shaded “American Horror Story” network FX during a panel at PaleyFest (via Entertainment Weekly) in which she remembered having to drive herself home from the anthology series’ set during production on previous seasons. The Oscar and Emmy-winning icon currently stars in “AHS 13,” marking her first appearance on the show since 2018’s “AHS: […]
content:
Jessica Lange shaded “American Horror Story” network FX during a panel at PaleyFest (via Entertainment Weekly) in which she remembered having to drive herself home from the anthology series’ set during production on previous seasons. The Oscar and Emmy-winning icon currently stars in “AHS 13,” marking her first appearance on the show since 2018’s “AHS: Apocalypse.”

“We had to drive ourselves,” Lange said during the panel discussion alongside franchise co-star Sarah Paulson. “We would drive ourselves home at like 4 or 5 in the morning, park on some street in the French Quarter, and find our way home.”

Lange added that it’s “still a bone of contention for her” as Paulson laughed in approval next to her. The actor, who filmed the show’s third season “Coven” in New Orleans, said FX was “too fucking cheap” to provide cars or drivers for the stars at the time.

Popular on Variety

Over the course of the show’s first four seasons, Lange helped propel “American Horror Story” to become one of TV’s buzziest shows. She headlined the Season 1 as Constance Langdon, Season 2 as Sister Jude Martin, Season 3 as Cordelia Goode and Season 4’s Elsa Mars, all of whom she is playing again in “AHS: 13.” Lange won Emmys for her roles in the show’s first and third seasons.

Lange told “Good Morning America” before the new season kicked off that the chance to play her old characters is why she returned after a yearslong hiatus away from the franchise, explaining: “It really was just the idea of bringing those four characters back — and one mystery character that I’m not going to [spoil].”

“First, [Ryan Murphy] talked to me about playing [season 1’s] Constance, which I think was his favorite character that I did. But I said I’ll come back if I can do all four characters,” Lange also said on “Live With Kelly and Mark” before the season premiered.

title: ‘High Potential’ Gets Post-Super Bowl Slot, Eyes ‘Grey’s Anatomy’-Style 2-Parter On ABC & Disney+
summary: ABC’s last time carrying the Super Bowl in February 2006 was a memorable one, with then-hot sophomore drama Grey’s Anatomy delivering one of the most talked about lead-out programs in the history of the Big Game, Part 1 of a bomb-themed two-episode arc that drew 38.1 million viewers. Twenty years later, ABC is picking up […]
content:
ABC‘s last time carrying the Super Bowl in February 2006 was a memorable one, with then-hot sophomore drama Grey’s Anatomy delivering one of the most talked about lead-out programs in the history of the Big Game, Part 1 of a bomb-themed two-episode arc that drew 38.1 million viewers.

Twenty years later, ABC is picking up where it left off, slotting its flagship series that is also early in its run, High Potential, immediately following Super Bowl LXI on ABC and Disney+ on Sunday, Feb. 14, 2027. Like Grey’s Anatomy, I hear High Potential is planning a two-parter, with the special post-Super Bowl episode as Part 1, ending on a cliffhanger that will be resolved in Part 2 airing in the show’s regular time slot the following Tuesday.

The upcoming Season 3 of High Potential will not launch after the Super Bowl; the series starring Kaitlin Olson is expected to return earlier, likely in January. (For the first time in its run, High Potential is not on the fall schedule this season.)

Watch on Deadline

Olson — as her character Morgan in front of High Potential‘s signature murger board — announced the news of the special post-Super Bowl episode Monday night in a promo that ran on-air and online during Monday Night Football.

Super Bowl LXI will air on ABC, ESPN and Disney+, which explains why High Potential will stream on Disney+ for the first time outside of the bundle. Its streaming home is on fellow Disney platform Hulu, both for next day episodes and previous seasons.

In 2000, ABC also aired Part 1 of a two-part episode of a popular drama series, The Practice, after the Super Bowl.

High Potential finished the 2025/2026 broadcast season as the No. 1 show in adults 18-49 (3.35 rating) and the No. 3 show among total viewers (16.01 million) over 35 days of viewing on ABC, Hulu, Hulu on Disney+ and digital platforms.

The series follows a single mom with an exceptional mind (Olson), whose unconventional knack for solving crimes leads to an unusual and unstoppable partnership with a by-the-book seasoned detective.

High Potential stars Olson as Morgan, Daniel Sunjata as Karadec, Javicia Leslie as Daphne, Deniz Akdeniz as Lev “Oz” Ozdil, Amirah J as Ava, Matthew Lamb as Elliot, and Judy Reyes as Selena. 20th Television produces the series, which is based on the French format Haut Potentiel Intellectuel (HPI) and was created in the U.S. by Drew Goddard.

Goddard and Sarah Esberg of Goddard Textiles, new showrunners Nora and Lilla Zuckerman and Olson serve as executive producers. Andrea Massaro (Goddard Textiles) is a co-executive producer.

title: Antitrust Experts Doubt Donald Trump’s DOJ Has A Case In Going After Networks For Suspending White House TV Pool
summary: News that the Justice Department is investigating five major networks for suspending the White House TV pool last month was met with outcry that it was another example of Trump administration retaliation against the media. Alarming as it may be to First Amendment groups, among antitrust experts, there are doubts that the DOJ would have […]
content:
News that the Justice Department is investigating five major networks for suspending the White House TV pool last month was met with outcry that it was another example of Trump administration retaliation against the media.

Alarming as it may be to First Amendment groups, among antitrust experts, there are doubts that the DOJ would have much of a case.

Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act restricts competitors that restrain competition. In this case, the five networks that make up the TV pool — CNN, Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — last month withheld their participation to protest the White House’s exclusion of CNN. For about four days, that meant fewer video images and other coverage of Trump that week, including the ceremonies surrounding the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping.

William Kovacic, global competition professor of law and policy at George Washington University, said, “I think you have to take any lawsuit from the Department of Justice seriously.”

Watch on Deadline

But he said an antitrust claim against the networks likely would have a “very remote prospect of success.”

At issue is “what is the predominant character of the behavior: Is it a commercial interest or is it designed to achieve some form of First Amendment expression?”

“To me, if there is a commercial aim to this, it is well hidden,” said Kovacic, a former chairman of the Federal Trade Commission.

Diana Moss, vice president and director of competition policy at the Progressive Policy Institute, said via email, “Group boycotts are illegal when they stifle competition, such as forcing a competitor(s) out of the market.”

She added, “Presumably, the arrangement among the five networks is designed to increase coordination and efficiency in the distribution of news footage. There is no anti-competitive intent or effect. The networks were responding in solidarity to repression of a free press (1st Amendment).”

Court Precedence

The lines between commercial conduct and protected First Amendment activity can be blurred, but courts have sided with boycotting parties even then.

Sam Weinstein, professor at Cardozo School of Law and former attorney in the DOJ’s Antitrust Division, said that “typically a non commercial boycott is protected by the First Amendment.”

“It would seem to be a non starter,” he said.

He cited the Supreme Court’s 1982 decision in NAACP vs. Claiborne Hardware Co., involving an organized 1960s-era boycott of white-owned businesses in Mississippi. The justices held that the state could not hold the protesters liable for damages when they engage in lawful activity protected by the First Amendment.

Weinstein also referred to another Supreme Court case, FTC vs. Superior Court Trial Lawyers, when the justices ruled that a boycott by court-appointed lawyers for indigent defendants violated antitrust law, as its purpose was to to gain increased compensation. The majority compared it to horizontal price fixing.

The latter case, Weinstein said, is different from what happened with the TV pool. Prices and compensation were not at issue.

It’s still unclear whether the networks will comply with the DOJ investigative request, but the networks already made it clear that they were jointly suspending participation in the pool, releasing a statement that “no administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

“The real question is a question of law, not a question of fact,” Weinstein said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the DOJ said over the weekend, “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”

“An End Run Around”

Democrats already have accused the Trump administration of politicizing the Antitrust Division, violating the norms that have separated the White House from the DOJ since the Nixon era. The investigation of the networks is likely to add another example to their arguments.

Bob Corn-Revere, chief counsel for the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said via email, “Threatening an antitrust investigation is just another example of this Administration misusing regulatory authority to punish the media for doing something the President dislikes. Political boycotts are part of a longstanding American tradition and are protected under First Amendment law.”

He added, “Whether the government’s excuses are dressed up as ‘national security’ or antitrust law, this is another attempt by the Administration trying to make an end run around the First Amendment to control news coverage.”
