title: ‘Half’ Review: Hip-Hop Beats & Brutal Beatings In Samjad’s Fast, Fun, Super-Violent Indian Vampire Horror Movie – Sitges Film Festival
summary: Two halves make a satisfying whole in this lean, mean action-horror, in which twin vampires stalk a scorching-hot Madras Max: Fury Road dystopia in the none-too-distant future. The 1996 Robert Rodriguez/Quentin Tarantino collaboration From Dusk Till Dawn springs immediately to mind, but, compared to that, director Samjad sinks his teeth into the meat of his […]
content:
Two halves make a satisfying whole in this lean, mean action-horror, in which twin vampires stalk a scorching-hot Madras Max: Fury Road dystopia in the none-too-distant future. The 1996 Robert Rodriguez/Quentin Tarantino collaboration From Dusk Till Dawn springs immediately to mind, but, compared to that, director Samjad sinks his teeth into the meat of his movie in next to no time. Scored with an urgent techno-bhangra beat by Midhun Mukundan, the result is a violent revenge thriller that has been lapped up on the genre circuit since it premiered in the Midnight Madness strand at TIFF this year.

The film starts with the minimum of backstory, which is at odds not only with the norms of Indian cinema but also the press book, which suggests that a whole lot of exposition about the genesis of the story’s two siblings has been cut. This might be for the better; our introduction to Ethan and Ivy (Ranjith Sajeev and Aiswarya Raj) is brief but suitably ominous. “Born of mortal dust and vampire blood, the twins walk in darkness,” a title card tells us, before we’re shown a brief flashback to their seemingly idyllic childhood where the two fight like cat and dog (“Raising you two will be the end of me,” says their mother).

Cut to the present, where the two are taking a road trip to the much busier Mumbai district of Pai Nagar in shades that not only protect them from the sun but, conveniently, make them also look very, very cool. As they make their way, we cut to a family of four making the same trip across the desert, passing Babu’s Puncture Shop, whose owner makes a phone call. Soon the family is being tailed by a couple on a scooter, carrying what appears to be a baby and yelling, “Sir! Sir! Oil leak!” The father pulls over, and the car is immediately swarmed over by bandits, who brutally kill him — plus his wife and two kids — with no mercy.

Watch on Deadline

The aftermath of the crime is cleaned up with ruthless efficiency, the gang hauling off the car, stripping it for parts and burning the bodies of the victims, a process that threatens to rinse and repeat when Ethan and Ivy follow almost immediately in the same slipway. The murder of the family is graphic enough, but what happens to Ethan and Ivy is far more perverse, especially when Ivy’s apparently dead body is defiled by one of the feral desert gang members. Samjad keeps the twins’ superpowers under wraps for an agonizingly long time, until the sun goes down and their bodies are able to regenerate.

The wait is worth it; when Ethan and Ivy finally take their revenge on this criminal outfit — one by one, piece by piece — it’s with a satisfying sense of bone-cracking justice, orchestrated like S. S. Rajamouli’s 2022 breakout hit RRR at 200mph. The genius of Samjad’s conceit, however, is that, for all their superhuman abilities, the twins are vulnerable — not only is sunlight their only weakness, Ivy also is deaf and non-verbal, which adds a real sense of threat towards the end, when things look very bleak indeed.

Part of this is down to Samjad’s fantastic sense of world-building; like Peter Weir’s 1974 black comedy The Cars That Ate Paris, Half is a sardonic comment on the sleazy eco-system of crime: Babu’s Puncture Shop is just one layer in a pyramid that goes surprisingly high and eclipses even the bumbling, paid-off police force, which willfully sees no evil and nervously treats each investigation as “extra paperwork.” There’s also a twitchy paranoia at play, since Ethan and Ivy, as outsiders, inevitably spark a turf war as various warring factions try to figure out who is killing their men.

There aren’t too many directors that can sustain this level of inventive carnage — even Takashi Miike has yet to show a man choking to death on the stump of his own severed hand — but Samjad directs the action with clarity and skill, helped immeasurably by Very Tri Yulisman’s incredible fight choreography. A puzzling coda means the film ends later than it probably should, but Samjad already has established his impressive cult bona fides: If you only see one gory Malayalam neo-noir spaghetti western vampire beat-’em-up in your life, make it this one.

Title: Half

Festival: Sitges, TIFF

Director: Samjad

Screenwriters: Praveen Viswanath, Samjad

Cast: Ranjith Sajeev, Aiswarya Raj, Amala Paul, Abbas, Sreekanth Murali

International sales: Best Friend Forever, Fragrant Nature Film Creations

Running time: 1 hr 36 mins

title: RJ Mitte Remembered By ‘Breaking Bad’ Co-Stars: “This Is So Heartbreaking”
summary: RJ Mitte, the Breaking Bad actor, died at 34, and his co-stars are mourning his loss. Dean Norris, who played DEA agent Hank Schrader on the AMC series, took to social media to remember Mitte. “Oh my God! Was working just found out about RJ. I am heartbroken,” he wrote. “Though RJ didn’t play my […]
content:
RJ Mitte, the Breaking Bad actor, died at 34, and his co-stars are mourning his loss.

Dean Norris, who played DEA agent Hank Schrader on the AMC series, took to social media to remember Mitte.

“Oh my God! Was working just found out about RJ. I am heartbroken,” he wrote. “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed.”

Norries continued, “This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”

Mitte played the son of Bryan Cranston’s Walter White in the AMC series. The actor’s character, Walter Jr., also had Cerebral palsy, and he used his platform on the show to raise disability awareness and become an advocate.

Watch on Deadline

Mitte’s reps confirmed news of his death with the following statement: “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte.”

Other actors have also taken to social media to express their thoughts on Mitte, with Lou Diamond Phillips sharing on X, “I just found out, Brian. Absolutely heartbreaking. What a wonderful young man. My heart goes out to his family and friends.”

title: Ben Affleck Says ‘Justice League’ Was A “Low Point” In His Career
summary: Ben Affleck is getting real about the “low point” of his career, pinpointing it to the time he was filming Justice League. In a new interview, the actor opened up about the reshoots and how Warner Bros. handled the whole situation. “The truth is, the experience of Justice League was so, so negative for lots of […]
content:
Ben Affleck is getting real about the “low point” of his career, pinpointing it to the time he was filming Justice League.

In a new interview, the actor opened up about the reshoots and how Warner Bros. handled the whole situation.

“The truth is, the experience of Justice League was so, so negative for lots of different reasons,” Affleck said on the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “Some of which having to do with where I was personally, some of which having to do with the tragedy that happened during the time, and also the fact that I really saw how not to make a movie like that when the studio is at odds with the filmmaker. You’re really making a mistake. That was what really doomed that.”

After Batman v Superman disappointed at the box office, the studio felt pressure to make Zack Snyder’s Justice League lighter and more appealing to audiences. During post-production, Snyder experienced a family tragedy, and Warner Bros. hired Joss Whedon to oversee reshoots, which drastically shifted the film’s storyline and tone.

Watch on Deadline

“Boy, that was shitty,” he said. “Him being taken off that movie, and the reshoots that we did–if you want the low point of my career, [it] was that.”

Affleck noted that “Somebody’s death by suicide, that eclipses everything. And the way that was, I thought, frankly, used as an excuse… I just thought that was one of the shittiest things I’ve ever seen. It was so gross. And then the whole environment and vibe, much of which I wasn’t privy to, but that I sort of heard about secondhand in terms of Ray [Fisher] and Gal [Gadot] and other people’s experiences. It was just like ‘Wow, this is about as gross as it gets.'”

Watch Affleck’s full interview in the video below.

title: Whistleblowing Portal Launches in U.K. for Entertainment Industry Workers to Report Abuse, Harassment and Discrimination
summary: Workers across the U.K.’s film, TV, music and theater sectors are now able to report whistleblowing concerns, including those relating to harassment and abuse, following the launch of a new portal by the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA). As an officially designated whistleblowing body, people will now be able to report concerns to CIISA […]
content:
Workers across the U.K.’s film, TV, music and theater sectors are now able to report whistleblowing concerns, including those relating to harassment and abuse, following the launch of a new portal by the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA).

As an officially designated whistleblowing body, people will now be able to report concerns to CIISA about experiences that relate to the CIISA Standards, and which may have a wider impact on others. Reports are made in confidence, with CIISA saying it will take “careful steps to protect the identity of individuals who come forward.”

The launch comes just as a the U.K. legal system grapples with one of the entertainment industry’s most high-profile cases of alleged abuse, with Russell Brand currently in court charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. According to reports and investigations into the allegations, a culture of fear and intimidation by Brand’s fame and influence allowed the alleged behaviour to persist for many years.

Popular on Variety

The launch also comes following a soft-launch of the reporting service in June. After its recognition in Parliament as an official whistleblowing entity, CIISA has since received around 30 reports (as of 1 October) and now anticipates an increase in the volume.

“There is absolutely no place for abuse, harassment or discrimination in the workplace, and it is crucial that people have a confidential place to report any concerns so that action can be taken,” said culture secretary Lisa Nandy.

“CIISA’s new reporting portal is an important step in tackling this issue, and this government will continue to back them every step of the way. Safety at work is non-negotiable, and we expect employers across the creative industries to work with CIISA and uphold the very highest standards.”

Added Helena Kennedy KC, chair of CIISA: “This marks an important milestone for CIISA and the creative industries. The creative sector is a UK success story and protecting the people who power that success is at the heart of CIISA’s ambitions; I’d like to thank the Government and industry for their support in getting us to this place. However, as an industry-funded organisation CIISA requires the full backing of the sector if it is to continue to meet the clear demand for its services.”

Philippa Childs, head of entertainment workers union Bectu said that CIISA was create because “extreme power imbalances, the preponderance of freelance employment, and the short-term nature of projects have meant that the creative industries were a place where sexual predators and bullies could hide in plain sight.”

She added: “Giving workers an anonymous, industry-wide, recognised platform to blow the whistle on bad behaviour is a crucial next step along the path to address bullying and harassment.”

Workers who report concerns to the CIISA may be entitled to additional legal protections under U.K. whistleblowing law, including where they may have previously signed NDAs. However, CIISA’s first-stage reporting service is initially focussed on building what it describes as a “clearer picture of the behaviours and practices affecting people across the sector,” rather than acting on individual cases.

title: ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference
summary: James Cameron’s “Avatar” technology helped shape the look of Sony Santa Monica Studio’s “God of War” games, game director Bruno Velazquez revealed at View Conference in Turin on Monday during a discussion of how increasingly intertwined filmmaking and video game production have become. Velazquez said the studio sought to present the two most recent mainline […]
content:
James Cameron’s “Avatar” technology helped shape the look of Sony Santa Monica Studio’s “God of War” games, game director Bruno Velazquez revealed at View Conference in Turin on Monday during a discussion of how increasingly intertwined filmmaking and video game production have become.

Velazquez said the studio sought to present the two most recent mainline “God of War” games as uninterrupted single takes, borrowing techniques from cinema to give the virtual camera a handheld feel. “We take inspiration from films,” he said, recalling that the developers obtained one of the cameras used by Cameron on “Avatar” and brought it onto their motion-capture set to shoot scenes alongside the performers.

The comments came during an “Ask Me Anything about Games, VFX and Animation” session featuring Industrial Light & Magic animation director Hal Hickel, Guerrilla Games studio director Jan-Bart van Beek, Paramount VFX supervisor Tara DeMarco, Lola Visual Effects supervisor Trent Claus and Skydance Animation production designer Noelle Triaureau. The discussion was moderated by Wieke Schrakamp.

Popular on Variety

“Arguably, it’s almost the same job these days,” said van Beek, whose studio is behind the “Horizon” franchise, pointing to shared rendering and motion-capture technology and the migration of talent between the two industries. He cited the LED volume used in virtual production as one example of game technology influencing filmmaking, although he noted that games remain fundamentally different because of player choice and agency.

The traffic also runs in the other direction. DeMarco said her current Paramount project, “Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow,” is drawing on gaming historians and consultants to recreate the look and play of video games from the 1990s and early 2000s, rather than simply applying present-day technology to period material. The team is preparing a guide to pixel art, resolution and gameplay, she said.

The movie, directed by Siân Heder and starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, adapts Gabrielle Zevin’s best-selling novel about game developers.

Van Beek pointed to the success of “The Last of Us” and “Fallout” as evidence of the growing flow of video game intellectual property into film and television. “The other way around, it almost doesn’t really happen anymore,” he said, recalling the proliferation of movie-based games in the 1990s. However, he cautioned that adaptations remain challenging because much of the original interactive experience can be lost.

The convergence also extends to how studios assess audience reactions. In detail, Velazquez revealed that “God of War” development incorporates scheduled play-tests, facial recordings, eye tracking and detailed surveys examining narrative comprehension and difficulty. “We actually have eye tracking software where we actually see where their eyes are going,” he explained. “Are they looking at where we want them to look at certain moments?” Such feedback has become integral to the production process.

For Hickel, technological sophistication does not necessarily guarantee a better character performance. Discussing “The Mandalorian and Grogu,” he explained how ILM determines when to retain Grogu as a physical puppet and when digital intervention is necessary. “Sometimes the puppetiness is exactly the effect you want on the audience’s brain,” he said, noting that viewers appreciate the character’s “muppety quality,” even if certain movements require digital corrections.

Hickel also described how the production used virtual reality to scout digital environments and simulate different seating positions inside an IMAX auditorium. Apple Vision Pro proved particularly useful for judging the scale of sets before physical construction. “We could really understand the space and know how big it was, and which parts were going to be built practically,” he recalled.

The conversation also addressed AI, with Velazquez comparing current anxieties to earlier fears that computer animation and motion capture would eliminate traditional animation jobs. Both technologies ultimately expanded artists’ capabilities, he argued. “You still need that creative mind. You still need a team of creatives to come together and use these tools,” he said. “But if you don’t have the soul behind it, it’s not going to matter.”

Van Beek took a more cautious position, warning about the potential misuse of AI and the appropriation of other artists’ work. “People are going to use it for really great things and really terrible things,” he underscored. Hickel, meanwhile, distinguished the uncertainty facing professional employment from the enduring ability to create art. “There’s no technical innovation that’s going to stop people from making art and finding ways to make art,” he argued, suggesting that new types of animation and VFX companies may eventually emerge.

Despite increasingly sophisticated tools, the panelists stressed that technology alone will not secure a career. Velazquez said he would rather recruit someone who collaborates effectively than a technically stronger candidate with a poor attitude, while DeMarco emphasized the importance of communication, constructive feedback and adaptability when moving between disciplines.

title: Sony Pictures Imageworks’ Michelle Grady and ILM’s Janet Lewin on Bad Bosses and Changing Studio Culture: ‘Culture Is What You Tolerate’
summary: TURIN, Italy — “Culture is what you tolerate,” said Sony Pictures Imageworks president Michelle Grady, reflecting on bad bosses and how studios build a workplace where people can thrive. “You work, you put a lot of energy into building it, emulating it, encouraging people to understand what it is, and then, you know, make some […]
content:
TURIN, Italy — “Culture is what you tolerate,” said Sony Pictures Imageworks president Michelle Grady, reflecting on bad bosses and how studios build a workplace where people can thrive.

“You work, you put a lot of energy into building it, emulating it, encouraging people to understand what it is, and then, you know, make some hard decisions along the way,” said Grady, who admitted it is a phrase she probably overuses.

Speaking Monday at Turin’s View Conference on the Leadership & Mentoring: Training the Next Generation of Leaders panel, moderated by the University of Hertfordshire’s Saint John Walker, Grady joined Janet Lewin senior VP, general manager and head of ILM, Skydance Animation president Holly Edwards, Pixar’s head of RenderMan creative engagement Dylan Sisson, Guerrilla Games studio director Jan-Bart van Beek and the National Film Board of Canada’s Eloi Champagne to discuss changing expectations of studio leadership and the challenges of developing talent.

Popular on Variety

Asked by an audience member about “anti-mentors,” Grady acknowledged that difficult experiences can offer valuable lessons.

“We’ve all probably had pretty tough bosses at a certain point in our lives,” she said. “You understand what you want in a boss and what you really don’t appreciate in a boss.”

Lewin agreed that companies must be deliberate about the leaders they appoint and the behavior they accept.

“It’s our job as leaders of a company to create the culture and exhibit the values that we want to see in other leaders within the organization,” she said.

At ILM, that means coaching, mentoring and intervening when managers struggle, rather than simply hoping problems resolve themselves.

Younger Staff Want a Voice

But studio culture is also being reshaped by changing expectations among younger employees.

“This business used to be so top down,” Grady said. “It didn’t work then particularly well, but that democratic participatory leadership is the way. It’s a better way.”

“I think this generation wants to have a voice,” she added.

Lewin described ILM’s employee forums, town halls and open-door policies, designed to give executives access to perspectives that might otherwise be filtered through layers of management.

“A good idea can come from anywhere,” she said, citing ILM veteran John Knoll. But collaboration has its limits: “It’s wonderful to encourage participation and hear different perspectives, but someone’s got to make a decision.”

Leaders Make the Hard Calls

Leadership also means making painful decisions. Asked about the most difficult decision of her career, Lewin pointed to the closure of ILM’s Singapore studio, which ILM announced in August 2023 and which employed more than 300 people. She said it was a business decision, made with others, about staying cost competitive.

“It had nothing to do with the talent that was there at the studio. They were doing incredible work,” she said.

Lewin went to Singapore to meet with staff. “It was heartbreaking,” she said, adding that ILM retained around 60% of the talent through moves to its other locations.

Studios Rethink Leadership Training

The industry has also had to rethink how it prepares people for leadership in the first place.

For decades, Grady said, studios routinely promoted exceptional artists into management without providing adequate training.

“We’d take them off the box and make them leaders and just shove them into the chair and let them figure it out on their own.”

Formal programs are now helping address that problem. ILM has introduced a six-month mentorship initiative pairing aspiring leaders with senior executives. Imageworks’ mentorship program, which began as a diversity initiative with about 30 participants, is now oversubscribed every year, Grady said.

“What’s been really interesting is it’s a two-way street,” Lewin said. “Getting the younger generation to participate has been super beneficial to me and to ILM because it’s a different point of view and a different vantage point.”

Sisson said he never really had a mentor. “When I was a kid, Pixar didn’t exist,” he said, so his generation largely figured things out as it went. Pixar has since built a mentorship program into its RenderMan Challenge, which he said has “helped change people’s trajectories and their careers.”

Edwards, who began her career as a production assistant, recalled learning from a producer over several films, absorbing lessons about both the leader she wanted to become and the behaviors she wanted to avoid.

Champagne described a turning point at the NFB. Frustrated with how things were run, he wrote a manifesto listing what needed to change and gave it to his boss — “risking potentially my job,” he said. “From that point on, the answer was, ‘O.K., now you’re going to be part of the decision, and you’re going to help us fix those things.’ So sometimes complaining can pay.”

Games Can’t Gamble on Talent

Opportunities to develop emerging talent are becoming harder to find, particularly in video games, van Beek said.

“Maybe you can’t gamble on talent anymore,” he said, noting that major projects can take six to eight years to complete. He pointed to Pixar’s animated shorts as a model for allowing new directors to gain experience on smaller, less commercially risky productions.

The Next Generation Steps Up

Sharing the stage with the executives were two members of the generation the panel was discussing. ILM concept artist Emily Bland and concept artist Isobel Hine each founded organizations to address a lack of representation and mentorship in their field. Bland’s Women in Concept Art connects junior artists with professionals. Hine’s Women’s Concept Art Association runs studio-style training through its Studio Jam program and includes artists at every career stage, from students up, on its core team.

Both urged studios to push younger staff, particularly women, into leadership sooner. “We have a habit of self-selecting out if we do not fit every single point within criteria to a T,” Hine said.

“I think it’s our role as leaders to kind of help lower the ladder for the next generation,” she added.

title: ‘Bloodsuckers’ Team Reunites on ‘Body in the Closet’ on Warner Bros. Title With Comedian Axel Åhman Eyed for the Lead Role (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Axel Åhman is set to star in the upcoming series “Body in the Closet” produced for Warner Bros. International Television Production Finland. He’ll play Staffan, an audience services employee at a theatre. A country boy, he has found his way into a big-city cultural institution and knows its history by heart. He also has a […]
content:
Axel Åhman is set to star in the upcoming series “Body in the Closet” produced for Warner Bros. International Television Production Finland.

He’ll play Staffan, an audience services employee at a theatre. A country boy, he has found his way into a big-city cultural institution and knows its history by heart. He also has a crush on Betty but is painfully clumsy and tactless in his attempts to approach her.

This leads to… his accidental death by chainsaw. However, it’s not the end for Staffan, as he returns to haunt Betty throughout the series.

Popular on Variety

“I found it funny to play a murder victim. I like it when characters meet an unexpected end, and when writers dare to go darker,” Åhman told Variety.

“Comedy is at its funniest when it dances on the borderline of darkness,” he added. “We don’t see much dark comedy in the Nordics. When I got the chance to participate, I just had to tag along and see where it headed. It’s also a nice challenge to play someone else’s script. I have mainly played characters from my own writing.”

As pointed out by producer Mia Oikarinen, Åhman is best known as a member of the hugely popular comedy group KAJ, but he’s also a writer, screenwriter, comedian, musician and actor.

“His comic timing and background in writing make him a particularly strong fit for Staffan and for the series’ darkly comic tone. He was very happy that we thought of him for the role – and amused that we immediately pictured him as Staffan.”

Elin Grönblom directs. She co-wrote the show with Josefin Sonck, who will play the lead. Grönblom and Sonck are already known for “Bloodsuckers.”

“I like the genre because it allows you to play and have fun. Horror, or in this case, dark comedy with some killing, is also a welcome form of escapism. We like to see characters do things that we ourselves don’t dare to do, and probably shouldn’t,” said Grönblom.

Sonck agreed: Comedy and horror are closely related.

“Both rely on surprise and playing with the audience’s expectations. But this isn’t a ‘horror comedy.’ It’s more about one person’s increasingly desperate life situation, told through dark humor and supernatural elements.”

“Body in the Closet” will start shooting next autumn, and Svenska YLE, the Swedish-language division of Finland’s public broadcaster YLE, is already on board.

“Josefin and I are both drawn to dark humor. It allows us to take a serious topic – in this case, egocentrism and the relationship between a narcissistic parent and child – and show its absurdity through humor,” said Grönblom.

“When you can laugh, perhaps uncomfortably, you can also shine a light on something serious from another angle. [The show] is set in a visually realistic world: the gray Helsinki autumn. But we exaggerate the characters and the action to create a fast-paced, humorous tone.”

The story follows the Swedish-speaking minority in Finland.

“We belong to this minority as well, but it’s a world that can be recognized anywhere. Especially the theatre world with its prejudiced, grandiose characters. Since the theme of the series is egocentrism, what better stage to put them on?,” wondered Grönblom.

The team believes in the show’s “strong international potential.”

“All our characters are driven by their own egos and needs, and often fail to see others around them. We laugh at the increasingly absurd situations these horrible people put each other through,” observed Oikarinen.

She added: “Sometimes we need to laugh at them to cope with what’s happening around us, especially in this increasingly egocentric – and frankly quite frightening – world.”

According to Sonck, the show combines three elements: a universal and timely theme, a suspenseful plot with twists and cliffhangers, and a cast of “funny, quirky characters who act out the things we all secretly think but would never admit.”

“Our series explores self-absorption, the quest for validation, and our attempts to control how we present ourselves to the world. The theater becomes a symbolic setting for these themes. But it’s also a place where secrets are brought into the spotlight.”

title: Toni Collette’s Directorial Debut ‘The Best Of’ Among 75 Projects Backed by Screen Australia
summary: Toni Collette will make her feature directing debut with “The Best Of,” her screen version of Graeme Simsion’s bestselling novel, which is one of 75 projects sharing more than AUD16.9 million ($11.7 million) in production and development money from Screen Australia. Collette, an Emmy and Golden Globe winner, produces alongside Christopher Simon. The story centers […]
content:
Toni Collette will make her feature directing debut with “The Best Of,” her screen version of Graeme Simsion’s bestselling novel, which is one of 75 projects sharing more than AUD16.9 million ($11.7 million) in production and development money from Screen Australia.

Collette, an Emmy and Golden Globe winner, produces alongside Christopher Simon. The story centers on two ex-lovers who come back into each other’s lives after spending decades apart, only to find old feelings stirring with messy and mixed results. Screen Australia made a major production investment in association with Screen NSW. Kismet handles local distribution and Cornerstone holds international sales.

The round, announced Tuesday, covers features, series and shorts.

Popular on Variety

“Australian storytellers continue to captivate audiences with their creativity, originality and distinctive perspectives. This latest round of funding supports an exciting range of projects from emerging creatives forging new paths to established voices exploring new creative territory. Screen Currency 2026 found that local stories matter deeply to Australians, and these projects will deliver on the authenticity and ambition that audiences have come to expect,” said Louise Gough, Screen Australia’s director of narrative content.

Brouhaha Entertainment, the company behind “Boy Swallows Universe,” is making “The Dark Lake,” a series based on Sarah Bailey’s award-winning novel. Tonkin plays a detective in a rural town whose investigation into the killing of a former high school classmate forces her to face buried secrets of her own. Troy Lum and Andrew Mason produce, with Becca Johnstone writing and executive producing. Giorgia Stawaruk, Tonkin and Katarina Mandic are also executive producers. Screenwest partners on the major production investment, with additional financing from Screen NSW.

Jeffrey Walker (“The Artful Dodger,” “Fing!”) directs “Bull” (working title), a feature from Infin8 Studios and Total Fiction Films. Drawn from a true story, it follows a smooth-talking prisoner who signs up for a debating team inside Tasmania’s harshest jail, hoping to change course and finally give his mother a reason to be proud. George Pullar stars, co-writes with Taylor Danworth and produces with Michael Lawrence, John Molloy and Suzanne Walker. Richard Roxburgh, Robyn Malcolm, Teresa Palmer, Thomas M Wright and Harrison Gilbertson round out the cast. Screen Queensland is on board, with Kismet distributing locally and Cornerstone handling international sales.

Sooshi Mango’s untitled feature debut follows three obstinate Italian immigrants who mobilize their multicultural neighborhood when a mysterious wellness club puts their cherished social club at risk. Nick Kozakis (“Kick On”) directs from a script by the group’s Joe Salanitri, Carlo Salanitri and Andrew Manfre with Declan Fay. Paul Dainty and Cathy Rodda produce, with Timothy Whiting as co-producer. VicScreen partners, and Roadshow has local distribution.

Rodd Rathjen directs “No Friend But the Mountains,” adapted from Behrouz Boochani’s acclaimed memoir, from a screenplay he co-wrote with Boochani. The Kurdish journalist, fleeing persecution, is intercepted at sea and sent to Manus Island, where he documents the gradual breakdown of the men held there. Gal Greenspan, Sharlene George, Amy Parry, Arkos Armont, Katy Roberts, Boochani and Antony Waddington produce. The New Zealand Film Commission, Screen Queensland and VicScreen are partners, with Madman distributing in Australia.

On the development side, Mithila Gupta’s “Desi Down Under” will turn her coming-of-age Indian-Australian audio series into a romantic comedy feature about three misfits who head from Kerala to the beach at Coogee, where they hope to pick up surf-lifesaving skills they can use to help their compatriots. Gupta writes and produces with Nina Aujla, Smriti Mundhra and Maya Gnyp.

Goalpost Pictures’ series “The Caretaker,” adapted from Gabriel Bergmoser’s bestselling novel by Alexei Mizin and Ryan van Dijk, both members of Screen Australia’s 2026 Talent Gateway cohort, also landed development backing. The thriller centers on a woman hiding out as caretaker of a ski resort out of season, who goes to ever more extreme lengths to hold on to the life she has built.

Among the shorts, BAFTA-nominated Rosie Westhoff (“The Main Part”) writes and directs “Solastalgia,” in which a young girl tries to reassemble scattered memories of the bushfire that destroyed her home while looking for connection in a transformed place. Chloe Brennan (“We Used to Own Houses”), Amanda Browne and Ashlee Russell (both “Mothmama”) produce, with Kitty Green (“The Royal Hotel”) as mentor.

Green also mentors the team behind a family short from Pasifika-led Mana Film Productions that mixes live action and animation, “My Life as a 12-Year-Old Demon Hunter… With Great Hair!” It tracks 12-year-old Tala over a single day as she fends off demons out to steal her powers – a bigger headache than her homework. AWGIE winner and bestselling author Maria Lewis writes, directs and co-produces, with Shonee Samia co-producing and Herbert Leota animating. Animator Jake Duczynski (“Magic Beach”) joins Green as mentor. Both shorts received principal production funding.

Full lists of production, development and short film approvals are on Screen Australia’s website. The agency will reveal more recently funded projects alongside the ABC Media Showcase on Oct. 21.

title: How Steven Moffat & Sue Vertue Obsessively Recreated 10 Downing Street For Channel 4’s ‘Number 10’
summary: Steven Moffat and Sue Vertue went into an “obsessive level of detail” when reconstructing the UK Prime Minister’s 10 Downing Street home for buzzy Channel 4 series Number 10. The storied showrunner and producer talked Deadline through how the reconstruction for the Rafe Spall-starring series stretched all the way to “the right door handles, the […]
content:
Steven Moffat and Sue Vertue went into an “obsessive level of detail” when reconstructing the UK Prime Minister’s 10 Downing Street home for buzzy Channel 4 series Number 10.

The storied showrunner and producer talked Deadline through how the reconstruction for the Rafe Spall-starring series stretched all the way to “the right door handles, the right flower pots, the paintings on the correct walls, the precise colours – everything.”

Channel 4’s Number 10 is one of the big shows being sold by ITV Studios at MIPCOM this year and follows a fictional UK Prime Minister doing his day job behind one of the most famous doors in the country. Jenna Coleman and Katherine Kelly also star. Hartswood Films is producing.

The Prime Minister’s home was recreated at Bray Studios for the interior shots but Vertue revealed that exterior shots were taken outside the actual building itself in Central London, with filming taking place across a weekend when the Prime Minister, his family and staff were away.

Watch on Deadline

“The first five minutes [of the show] involve the Prime Minister walking down Downing Street and through the front door,” said Vertue. “I said, ‘Leave it with me’. We didn’t know until the day itself whether something might happen and the filming would be stopped. Obviously we didn’t have access to the most sensitive security areas, but it was still an amazing opportunity.”

The rest of the interior scenes were shot with an “obsessive level of detail,” Moffat explained, including commissioning the person who had originally made the Number 10 fireplace to reconstruct another. The reconstruction was made trickier, however, by the fact that the crew weren’t allowed to take photographs inside Downing Street and there aren’t diagrams online.

“But if you’re selling a show on the idea that audiences will see what happens behind that door, then you have to get what’s behind it right,” added Moffat.

A Number 10 trailer was shown to press and buyers yesterday, spotlighting a tone that seems to sit somewhere in between iconic British comedy The Thick of It and a high-end thriller, with plenty of “gallows humor,” Moffat said. He is a huge fan of political biographies and said his research process was obsessive, although he is keeping schtum on which political bigwigs he spoke with when putting together the scripts.

‘Number 10’ is “ultimately an office comedy”

The UK has had seven Prime Ministers in a decade during a time of political turmoil but Moffat said he wants his show to humanize not demonize, hence why he deliberately doesn’t name the fictional Prime Minister’s party or allegiance.

“It’s a monstrous job,” he added. “If Prime Ministers were simply lazy, ineffective or dishonest, why do they all appear to age 20 years while they’re in office? Look at what the job did to Tony Blair. He still looks haunted.”

Number 10 has already sold to European buyers and Moffat and Vertue are now hopeful a U.S. deal can be brokered.

“Americans tend to like things that are distinctly British,” added Moffat. “Sherlock and Doctor Who are two of the most British shows ever made, and they travelled very well. This is a political show, but ultimately it’s also an office comedy—or perhaps an office comedy-drama. I think that gives it broad appeal.”

title: Who Is In Charge At Skydance International – For Now At Least
summary: When the Skydance C-suite started being unveiled last week featuring Davis Ellison’s key lieutenants, the international piece of the puzzle was largely left unsolved. The list of senior executives did not answer the question of who would oversee the old Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s (WBD) considerable presences outside of the U.S., which incorporates hundreds […]
content:
When the Skydance C-suite started being unveiled last week featuring Davis Ellison’s key lieutenants, the international piece of the puzzle was largely left unsolved.

The list of senior executives did not answer the question of who would oversee the old Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s (WBD) considerable presences outside of the U.S., which incorporates hundreds of staffers around the world in streaming, TV networks like the UK’s 5 and Australia’s Network Ten, and distribution of some of the biggest movie franchises and TV shows out there.

That left international insiders we spoke with through last week feeling a bit lost, and they were none the wiser following the Ellison town hall that took place Wednesday. “Everyone is in the dark at the moment, and I think that’s probably true for almost everyone globally,” said one such Warner insider late on that day.

Slowly over the past few days, the question in terms of at least the very top of the chain has been answered but with some caveats.

Watch on Deadline

JB Perrette, one of the big winners of the $110B merger, will take on streaming and networks outside of the U.S. as part of his tongue-twisting new role: Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance Direct-To-Consumer. One insider we’ve spoken to described his role as one of the most important at the new-look Skydance, given the scope of the role.

Perrette is well known in international circles and has spent much time abroad over the past 15 years, first at Discovery where he rose up to President and CEO of Discovery Networks International, and then at the merged WBD, where as part of his President and CEO of Global Streaming & Games role he led the global rollout of HBO Max, navigating the knotty exit of HBO’s long-term output deal with Sky in the UK, Germany and Italy, for example. That one has now been resolved and HBO Max is busy building around the world and commissioning local originals under Sarah Aubrey and a team of commissioners in different countries.

Sales & Free-To-Air Chiefs Installed

Perrette’s new role does technically incorporate global distribution, but it will be his trusted new lieutenant, David Decker, who is at this particular coalface, as he has taken on the post of President of Content Sales, shopping huge franchises from the Paramount and Warner libraries including NCIS, The Big Bang Theory, The Bachelor and Star Trek around the world.

The timing is good for former WBD content sales boss Decker, with the biggest international TV market of the year, MIPCOM Cannes, well underway. He has had a packed schedule this week as buyers get their heads around the ways of the new Skydance content sales team, and we hear he is encouraging a business-as-usual approach with his sellers.

Decker is one of three new reports to Perrette, alongside Chief Revenue Officer Jay Askinasi and President, Distribution Ray Hopkins. Yet Perrette and Decker’s meaty roles still leave gaps – slightly lower down the international chain, questions remain over how territories are divided up and who looks after what.

We can today reveal that CBS Chief Operating Officer Bryon Rubin is at least temporarily taking charge of free-to-air networks 5 and Network Ten, although an announcement on a more permanent future for these nets is expected over the next few weeks.

Rubin, who has been COO and CFO of CBS since 2020, reports into new Skydance TV boss George Cheeks.

With more announcements expected shortly, it could well be that Perrette, Rubin and co are planning to install a longer-term head of free-to-air networks or a separate head of international streaming (those who could be in the frame include the likes of Paramount+ EVP Marco Nobili and 5 boss Reemah Sakaan), while it remains to be seen how the world will be divided up in terms of territory.

A week is a long time in the world of entertainment and just a few days ago it felt as though things could have panned out oh so differently. It initially appeared that the top international job would be a direct run-off between Paramount’s Kevin MacLellan and WBD’s long-serving Gerhard Zeiler.

However, Zeiler has lofty political ambitions, which could even see him become Chancellor of his native Austria, and both Zeiler and MacLellan have now confirmed their exits. MacLellan’s came just a few weeks after he detailed at a London convention how Ellison had sold him the Skydance dream. Such is the way of C-suite politics.

In the meantime, the deep-lying concerns raised by Ellison’s planned $6B synergies are of course reverberating internationally and sources we speak with are quietly cognisant that big changes could be afoot. As MIPCOM moves into day two, more international clarity is desired following a week that will go down in the annals of entertainment industry history.

Skydance declined comment.

title: Cold War Thriller ‘Honey’ Scores First Sales After Cannes World Premiere
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The first sales for Honey have rolled in as the darkly comedic thriller had its world premiere in Cannes. The Cold War drama is for the BBC and ZDF. It has been pre-bought by Australian streamer Stan and Sky in New Zealand. Fifth Season is distributing the show and has also sealed presales with […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The first sales for Honey have rolled in as the darkly comedic thriller had its world premiere in Cannes.

The Cold War drama is for the BBC and ZDF. It has been pre-bought by Australian streamer Stan and Sky in New Zealand. Fifth Season is distributing the show and has also sealed presales with OSN+ for the Middle East and North Africa and Hot in Israel.

The deals come in the wake of a glitzy premiere for the series at MIPCOM in Cannes. The sunny setting on the Côte d’Azur was far removed from the icy East Berlin backdrop of the opening episode of the show. It follows Martha, played by Ann Skelly (House of Guinness), a deep cover agent in 1982 Germany. She explores a shadowy world of counterespionage and finds herself blindsided by desire in a Cold War ménage à trois.

Skelly, Sally Woodward Gentle, the series executive producer at Sid Gentle Films, lead writer and EP Emma Moran and Jennifer Ebell, EVP, Television Distribution at Fifth Season all spoke about the show before the first episode rolled.

Watch on Deadline

Skelly appears alongside Nate Mann, Jannis Niewöhner and Rory Kinnear in the series.

“Seeing a character so brazen and bold and full of want, that’s really fun because I didn’t really grow up with many female characters like that,” Skelly said of playing Martha. “She’s just incredibly ambitious and totally backs herself and is full of confidence, but not quite the experience, which is, I think, so much fun to watch a character like that.”

The Martha character is one that went on to appear in Killing Eve. Fiona Shaw played the character latterly known as Carolyn Martens. The team behind Honey, however, have been at pains to stress that while it is the same universe, it is not a prequel.

The series has elements of spy thriller, romance, comedy and drama, and Moran said that was what drew her in. “The tone was what excited me about the idea, I loved smashing together romance and spy [genres],” she said.

“We’re in semi-totalitarian society [in the series] where you have to watch yourself, and desires have to be restrained. With the love triangle that dominates the show, it was so satisfying play with those two poles of, ‘I can’t say who I am, I can’t do this’ but then to have desire crash into that.”

title: Propagate Content Adds Four Docuseries From Monster Films
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Ben Silverman and Howard T. Owens’s Propagate Content has acquired true crime shows and a history-murder title from UK producer Monster Films. Sky History’s The Real X-Files, True Crime’s Almost Perfect Murders and The Secret World of Forensics and the BBC’s Dark Land: The Hunt for a Killer have joined the Propagate library following […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Ben Silverman and Howard T. Owens’s Propagate Content has acquired true crime shows and a history-murder title from UK producer Monster Films.

Sky History’s The Real X-Files, True Crime’s Almost Perfect Murders and The Secret World of Forensics and the BBC’s Dark Land: The Hunt for a Killer have joined the Propagate library following a deal negotiated by the company’s CFO, Noah Nusinow and Jimmy Humphrey of Marmalade Sky, who reps the shows.

Each series is 10 60-minute episodes, which Daniel Thunell, Head of International at Propagate, said “delivers a distinct lens on true crime and the unexplained, while delivering the kind of premium, character-driven storytelling that resonates with international audiences.”

The Real X-Files explores once-classified files buried beneath London’s public records office that document decades of military, intelligence and police investigations into the paranormal — from the Bermuda Triangle to recovered alien spacecraft.

Watch on Deadline

Almost Perfect Murders follows ten British cases in which killers were caught after committing seemingly unsolvable crimes, while The Secret World of Forensics pulls back the curtain on ten murder investigations, spotlighting forensic pioneers and revealing how science lead to the truth.

Dark Land explores cold cases in in Wales related to more than 100 unsolved murders, and brings in investigators from policing and psychology to revisit them.

“We are super excited to be working with Propagate Content on these four titles,” said David Howard and Rik Hall, founders of Monster Films. “Having admired their ambitious and wide-ranging slate from a distance, we thought they were perfectly suited to bring these series to market.

Propagate’s acclaimed documentaries include The Last First: Winter K2 for Apple TV, I’m Chevy Chase and You’re Not for CNN, Untold for Netflix, Emmy-nominated Hillary for Hulu, LFG for HBO Max and Jerry West: The Logo for Prime Video.

title: ITV Buys ‘The Galway Bay Murders’ Thriller Starring Kate Mulgrew & Colm Meaney
summary: ITV has bought upcoming Irish thriller The Galway Bay Murders starring Star Trek icon Kate Mulgrew and Colm Meaney. The show from new TV writer Eithne Verling follows seasoned NYPD detective Nora Savage (Mulgrew), who arrives in the west of Ireland hoping to escape a traumatic past and find a quieter life. However, her plans […]
content:
ITV has bought upcoming Irish thriller The Galway Bay Murders starring Star Trek icon Kate Mulgrew and Colm Meaney.

The show from new TV writer Eithne Verling follows seasoned NYPD detective Nora Savage (Mulgrew), who arrives in the west of Ireland hoping to escape a traumatic past and find a quieter life. However, her plans are shattered when the body of a young woman is discovered in a bog, drawing Nora into a complex murder investigation alongside the local Garda team. The ensemble cast also includes John Connors (The Gentlemen, Irish Blood), India Mullen (Normal People, Under Salt Marsh), Cillian O’Sullivan (Daredevil: Born Again, Star Trek: Strange New Worlds) and Jack Rowan (A Town Called Malice, Wreck).

Mulgrew is playing the lead and the show was born out of a conversation she had with Verling after the pair had a chance meeting in Galway while the Star Trek actor was on holiday.

Watch on Deadline

Irish broadcaster RTÉ is already aboard and the news was revealed at MIPCOM Cannes, where ITV Studios, which is distributing the show, also unveiled a new Australian TV drama label under Sara Richardson, along with a slew of sales for shows like Steven Moffat’s Number 10.

Two Cities Television is producing The Galway Bay Murders, which was previously called The Yank. Bosses at Two Cities recently told us the series, which has deficit financing from distributor ITV Studios, is an example of the indie “taking a bit more control of our own destiny” by making a lower-budget show for which they have almost total editorial control.

Darren Nartey, Head of Content Acquisitions at ITV, said: “The Galway Bay Murders is precisely the kind of bold, high-calibre drama our audiences love. Eithne Verling has crafted a completely magnetic crime thriller, with an outstanding cast led by Kate Mulgrew and Colm Meaney, a compelling central mystery and the stunning backdrop of Ireland’s west coast. We’re thrilled to partner with ITV Studios, Two Cities Television and RTÉ to bring this captivating new series to the ITV audience”

The series is directed by Joe Lawlor and Christine Molloy (Baltimore, Kin) and produced by STV Studios-backed Two Cities, Keeper Pictures and AS I AM Productions. The Galway Bay Murders is made in association with and distributed internationally by ITV Studios.

title: Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan Team Up for ‘Expectations’ Remix and Music Video
summary: Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan are officially teaming up on an “Expectations” remix and music video. Rodrigo confirmed the news on Instagram Tuesday, sharing a photo of her and Roan posing on a yellow car with the license plate “XPECT8NS.” The uptempo song is the 12th track on Rodrigo’s recent third album, “You Seem Pretty […]
content:
Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan are officially teaming up on an “Expectations” remix and music video.

Rodrigo confirmed the news on Instagram Tuesday, sharing a photo of her and Roan posing on a yellow car with the license plate “XPECT8NS.” The uptempo song is the 12th track on Rodrigo’s recent third album, “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love.”

“Beyond excited to announce ‘expectations’ featuring Chappell Roan!!! song and video out Thursday!!!!” Rodrigo wrote in the caption.

Rumors of an “Expectations” remix started circulating on Sunday after a German retailer put the single on sale, then quickly took it down. The next day, Rodrigo posted a quick audio clip to her Instagram story of a female voice saying, “Ooh, Olivia does remixes now,” which some fans suspected was Roan.

Popular on Variety

Rodrigo and Roan go back some years, as the latter supported the former on both her “Sour” and “Guts” tours. Beyond sharing the stage, they also consistently collaborated with the same producer, Dan Nigro, and have connective tissue as respective winners of the Grammy for best new artist.

Roan recently graced the stage at Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival, which took place in Irvine, California, in late August. Rodrigo personally curated the all-female lineup for the inaugural event including Doechii, Mitski, Garbage, the Breeders and many more. Roan performed just before Rodrigo’s headlining set, which featured guest appearances from Sarah McLachlan, Alanis Morissette and Stevie Nicks. Daisy Chain Fields raised $10 million that was then matched by philanthropist Melinda French Gates to bring the total to $20 million.

Roan is staging her own two-day fundraiser in Los Angeles on October 21-22 to benefit trans youth and LGBTQ+ communities. The event, taking place at the Shrine, will have performances from Lola Young, Caroline Polachek, Tinashe and Muna.

Rodrigo, meanwhile, is currently on her “Unraveled” tour in support of “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love.” The trek is currently making its way across North America before heading overseas in March for dates in London, Barcelona and Amsterdam, among other cities.

title: Lucian Piane, ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race’ Music Producer, Dies at 46
summary: Lucian Piane, a music producer on “RuPaul’s Drag Race” has died. He was 46. According to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records, Piane died on Monday after reportedly being struck by a car in Glendale, Calif. Piane worked on the main “Drag Race” show from Seasons 1-8 and composed the music and the Rusical numbers […]
content:
Lucian Piane, a music producer on “RuPaul’s Drag Race” has died. He was 46.

According to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records, Piane died on Monday after reportedly being struck by a car in Glendale, Calif.

Piane worked on the main “Drag Race” show from Seasons 1-8 and composed the music and the Rusical numbers during that time. He also worked on “Drag Race: All Stars.” In addition, Piane also collaborated with RuPaul and wrote some of the host’s biggest songs including “Cover Girl,” “Sissy That Walk,” “Jealous of My Boogie,” “Born Naked,” “Champion” and “Main Event.”

He also earned a Grammy nomination for his work on the soundtrack to the 2007 “Hairspray” film.

Popular on Variety

Before his death, Piane battled with substance abuse and mental health issues. Fans and friends had been voicing concern for Piane online after he posted a series of alarming videos on Instagram. Many were asking him to “get sober and stay sober” and writing “This is so sad to see. Lucian please seek help.”

Journalist Larry Flick wrote a tribute to Piane, writing, “Lucian was my friend. It wasn’t always easy. He was troubled, complicated, and filled with rage that he didn’t know how to manage. Like many, I tried to help until he made it impossible. Guilt right now is real. The way he left this life was tragic and brutal. But I pray rest and peace await him on the other side.”

Piane was born on Oct. 4 in Kansas City, Mo. Variety has reached out to representatives at “RuPaul’s Drag Race” for comment.

title: Louis Malle’s ‘Elevator to the Gallows’ Set for 70th Anniversary 4K Release as Jean-Jacques Beineix’s ‘Betty Blue’ Hits Big Screen After 35 Years
summary: French giant Gaumont is launching a new 4K restoration of Louis Malle’s 1958 classic crime thriller “Elevator to the Gallows,” starring Jeanne Moreau. The special edition is being released in celebration of this year’s 70th anniversary of the French New Wave, the upcoming 70th anniversary of the film in 2028 and, in the same year, […]
content:
French giant Gaumont is launching a new 4K restoration of Louis Malle‘s 1958 classic crime thriller “Elevator to the Gallows,” starring Jeanne Moreau.

The special edition is being released in celebration of this year’s 70th anniversary of the French New Wave, the upcoming 70th anniversary of the film in 2028 and, in the same year, the centenary of Moreau’s birth.

Released 1958, “Elevator to the Gallows” marked the directorial debut for the young Malle, who was 25 years old at the time.

Set in Paris over the course of a night, the film stars Moreau and Maurice Ronet as lovers who set out to murder her husband and his boss (played by Jean Wall), only for the plan to go awry. Distinguished by Miles Davis’ award-winning jazz score, the film established both Malle and Moreau as verifiable talents.

Popular on Variety

Betty Blue Courtesy of Gaumont

Another Gaumont classic, “Betty Blue,” Jean-Jacques Beineix’s iconic tale of amour fou run rampant, is making its long-awaited return to the big screen at this year’s Lumière Film Festival.

Originally released in 1986 as “37°2 le matin,” the award-winning erotic drama chronicles the doomed romance between Zorg (Jean-Hugues Anglade), a handyman and aspiring writer in his 30s, and the volatile, impulsive and fragile 19-year-old Betty (Béatrice Dalle).

The film is also one of this year’s highlights for Gaumont, which is presenting the new 4K master of the full 185-minute version — “a film that has been invisible in theaters in this version since 1991,” noted Jérôme Soulet, head of catalogue at Gaumont.

The 4K restoration of “Betty Blue” was carried out by Gaumont at the GP Archives laboratory.

The film screens this year as part of the Lumière Festival’s Big Films on the Big Screen sidebar that offers the opportunity to rediscover cinematic masterpieces in their intended format.

Soulet will also be on hand at the Lumière Festival’s International Classic Film Market in Lyon to present the company’s lineup of new releases at the annual Catalogue Holders’ Premiere Presentation on Wednesday.

title: Taiwan Gets Its Own Spotlight at Lumière, Led by Restored ‘Osmanthus Alley’ in Its Original Language
summary: Taiwan is getting a dedicated national focus at the International Classic Film Market (MIFC), the industry arm of Lyon’s Lumière Festival, the first for a non-European country, according to the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute (TFAI). A new 4K restoration of Chen Kun-hou’s “Osmanthus Alley” leads the Taiwan in Focus program, which runs alongside this […]
content:
Taiwan is getting a dedicated national focus at the International Classic Film Market (MIFC), the industry arm of Lyon’s Lumière Festival, the first for a non-European country, according to the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute (TFAI).

A new 4K restoration of Chen Kun-hou’s “Osmanthus Alley” leads the Taiwan in Focus program, which runs alongside this year’s guest country, Greece.

TFAI is using the showcase to seek international distribution and programming partners for the island’s restored classics. “Osmanthus Alley” made its world premiere at the festival on Oct. 12, with Chen and star Lu Hsiao-fen in attendance. TFAI says distributors it has previously worked with have expressed interest, with release terms and timing still under negotiation.

Adapted from Hsiao Li-hung’s novel, the film follows Thik-hông (Lu), an orphan who marries into a wealthy family, is widowed young and sees her son sent away to Japan, leaving her isolated behind the walls of the family estate. Simon Yam and Tuo Tsung-hua appear in guest roles. Lu won best actress at the 1987 Asia Pacific Film Festival, and the theme song, with lyrics by Wu Nien-jen, took the Golden Horse for best original film song.

Popular on Variety

The restoration also brings back the film’s original Taiwanese soundtrack. Chen insisted on shooting in Taiwanese, but state-run Central Motion Picture Corporation (CMPC) chose to release the film in Mandarin, in line with the government’s policy of promoting the language at the time. Chen eventually persuaded the studio to produce a Taiwanese version, but it played in only a limited number of theaters and gradually faded from view.

Its selection coincides with the 70th anniversary of Taiwanese-language cinema, which TFAI traces to 1956’s “Xue Pinggui yu Wang Baochuan.” An estimated 1,200 Taiwanese-language films were made between the 1960s and 1981, but only about 200 survive in TFAI’s collection. The restoration also anticipates TFAI’s 2027 focus on literary adaptations, while Chen’s lifetime achievement award at the 2023 Golden Horse Awards prompted renewed interest in his work.

Chen began as a cinematographer, winning a Golden Horse for “He Never Gives Up” (1978), and from 1979 worked closely with Hou Hsiao-hsien, the pair often trading roles behind the camera. Chen’s “Growing Up” won him the Golden Horse for best director in 1983.

TFAI restored “Osmanthus Alley” from its original 35mm negative, filling missing frames from an interpositive, with audio drawn from the 35mm Taiwanese sound negative. The source was generally in good condition, but mold spots and dense clusters of small white specks required careful treatment. Aggressive cleaning settings risked erasing image detail, so technicians used masks and adjusted processing settings before completing frame-by-frame manual repairs.

In line with FIAF’s code of ethics, Chen was repeatedly consulted. An intermediate version had more saturated, vibrant colors, but discussions with the director led to a more subdued final grade, closer to the original photography.

Tu Duu-chih, who handled the film’s original sound mix, returned to help restore the Taiwanese soundtrack from six primary audio reels. The team synchronized the material, repaired damaged sections and reduced noise through multiple passes using light processing settings.

The soundtrack holds another connection to Taiwanese cinema history. Cast members who did not speak Taiwanese were dubbed in post-production: co-star Lin Hsiu-ling voiced Lu’s dialogue, while Hou provided the voice for Tuo.

TFAI, which holds about 20,000 film titles, restores 10 to 12 films a year and has restored more than 100 since 2013. Physical deterioration prompts climate control and emergency digitization, but a full restoration depends on whether a film has “a clear purpose and an audience ready to experience it right now,” the institute says. Recent restorations include Tsai Ming-liang’s “Vive L’Amour,” which screened in Venice Classics in 2025, and “The Dull Ice Flower,” chosen by Taiwanese audiences in a public poll and selected for Cannes Classics this year. Taiwanese-language titles “Love Never Ceases” and “Zhang Di Seeks A-Zu” were restored for the anniversary.

Overseas, TFAI prioritizes in-person screenings to introduce lesser-known titles before pursuing distribution and streaming partnerships.

“We want audiences to discover Taiwan cinema beyond Taiwan New Cinema and see the many different facets of Taiwan,” TFAI tells Variety.

TFAI will also pitch its ongoing restoration of Yao Feng-pan’s “All in the Dim Cold Night” (1974) at MIFC’s Re>birth program on Oct. 15, seeking distributors and festival slots for the horror film. Often called Taiwan’s “King of Horror,” Yao built the film’s eerie atmosphere without modern visual effects, relying on practical techniques such as low-angle green lighting and burning straw on location.

Taiwan in Focus also includes a round table with TFAI chair Arthur Chu and programmer Howard Yang, a networking event and an exhibition of original Taiwanese film posters.

The institute hopes to build longer-term programming partnerships with international archives, giving restored Taiwanese films a life beyond their festival premieres. For “Osmanthus Alley,” the next step is securing overseas releases following its return to the screen.

title: ’14th,’ ‘You Can See Everything’ and ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ Lead Critics Choice Documentary Awards Nominations
summary: Ava DuVernay’s timely and viscerally moving “14th” leads this year’s Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations with six, including best documentary feature. Close behind with five nominations apiece are Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s examination of Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything”; Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman’s polar bear migration story, “Nuisance Bear”; David Greaves’ […]
content:
Ava DuVernay’s timely and viscerally moving “14th” leads this year’s Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations with six, including best documentary feature. Close behind with five nominations apiece are Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s examination of Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything”; Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman’s polar bear migration story, “Nuisance Bear”; David Greaves’ archival portrait of Black cultural history, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and Pegah Ahangarani’s Iranian historical documentary, “Rehearsals for a Revolution.”

Netflix led all distributors with 17 nominations, nearly double the nine earned by runner-up Neon.

Popular on Variety

DuVernay, Fielder and Oppenheim are among the directing nominees, alongside Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor for “NAZA,” Felipe Bustos Sierra for “Everybody to Kenmure Street,” Ross McElwee for “Remake” and Orlando von Einsiedel for “The Cycle of Love,” the only directing nominee whose film did not land a documentary feature nom.

Now in its 11th year, the Critics Choice Documentary Awards will take place Nov. 8 at the Edison Ballroom in New York City, with television host and producer Ross Matthews serving as host. The awards celebrate excellence in nonfiction filmmaking.

The organization’s track record of predicting Oscar success has been mixed over the years. Its inaugural top prize winner, “O.J.: Made in America” (2016), went on to win the Academy Award for documentary feature. Since then, only three other top prize winners or nominees have crossed over to the Oscars: winner “Summer of Soul (…Or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised)” (2021) and nominees “Will & Harper” (2024) and last year’s “The Perfect Neighbor” (2025). All others failed to be nominated, or in some cases, not even make the preliminary shortlist (i.e., 2022’s “Good Night Oppy”).

As previously announced, Ron Howard will receive the Critics Choice Impact Award. Visionary filmmaker Jehane Noujaim will receive the CCA’s Pennebaker Award, presented by Chris Hegedus, Pennebaker’s widow and longtime collaborator. Named in honor of trailblazing documentarian D.A. Pennebaker, the award, formerly known as the Critics Choice Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizes filmmakers whose careers have made a profound and lasting contribution to documentary storytelling.

Feature-length documentaries, two-part documentaries and short-form documentaries are eligible for nomination if they were first released commercially in the U.S. between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2026.

title: Live-Action ‘Moana’ With Dwayne Johnson & Catherine Lagaʻaia Gets Disney+ Premiere Date
summary: The new live-action film Moana will stream exclusively on Disney+ October 21, the streamer announced today. The new interpretation builds on the original animated film, which Disney+ says is the most watched movie of all time on the streamer with over 1.5 billion hours streamed globally. Dwayne Johnson reprises his role as the demigod Maui […]
content:
The new live-action film Moana will stream exclusively on Disney+ October 21, the streamer announced today.

The new interpretation builds on the original animated film, which Disney+ says is the most watched movie of all time on the streamer with over 1.5 billion hours streamed globally.

Dwayne Johnson reprises his role as the demigod Maui in the new film, while Catherine Lagaʻaia stars as the “courageous wayfinder” Moana.

The synopsis: “In Disney’s live-action reimagining of the beloved animated adventure, Moana (Catherine Lagaʻaia) answers the Ocean’s call and, for the first time, voyages beyond the reef of her island of Motunui with the infamous demigod Maui (Dwayne Johnson) on an unforgettable journey to restore prosperity to her people.”

The movie features Moana song classics including “How Far I’ll Go”‘ and “I Am Moana” to the new song “Along The Way.” To celebrate the premiere, Disney+, Disney and Heal the Bay — a nonprofit environmental organization dedicated to making the coastal waters and watersheds of Greater Los Angeles safe, healthy and clean — are teaming up for a special community beach cleanup on Saturday, October 17.

title: Fox Boss Rob Wade Commits Long Term To Creator Studios: “We’re Not Here To Flip A House”
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Fox Entertainment CEO Rob Wade has committed long into the future to his company’s creator studio, telling Deadline: “We’re not here to flip a house.” Fox Creator Studios (FCS), a “digital-first division,” was unveiled at the start of this year with partnerships including a food roster headed by Gordon Ramsay, but the idea had […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Fox Entertainment CEO Rob Wade has committed long into the future to his company’s creator studio, telling Deadline: “We’re not here to flip a house.”

Fox Creator Studios (FCS), a “digital-first division,” was unveiled at the start of this year with partnerships including a food roster headed by Gordon Ramsay, but the idea had been percolating in Wade’s mind for more than a decade.

Wade feels that plenty of big companies are investing in the creator, AI and tech space simply in order to “sell for hundreds of millions and get out,” but Fox won’t be following suit. “The game is built around that, which is not a recipe for long-term success,” said Wade. “But we’re in it for the long term. We’re not here to flip a house. If I want to invest in something, my bosses and board will say that if it’s successful they want to build on it. We will never sell [Fox Creator Studios].”

Wade was speaking to Deadline in the days leading up to MIPCOM, where he has just been joined on a Deadline-hosted panel by FCS boss Billy Parks, Prentiss Fraser, who runs distributor Fox Entertainment Global (FEG), and Fox-backed creators Josh Richards and Chris Sawtelle.

Watch on Deadline

Wade, Parks and Fraser have grand plans, with the former positioning the main goal as “creating a path to IP creation on the internet.”

In this vein, FCS is doing things a bit differently to its rivals in what is becoming an increasingly crowded space both in the U.S. and internationally, with content creators one of the big topics at this year’s MIPCOM, a traditional TV sales market.

FCS is seeking to tie with content creators across a whole range of genres but won’t necessarily air their work solely on Fox or Fox-owned platforms like Tubi. Instead, it will leverage resources and advertising infrastructure to create content spanning different platforms and territories. Content creators can then diversify revenue streams, while FEG boss Fraser and her team shop their wares around the world. The studio has so far struck deals with long-time Fox collaborator Ramsay, comedian Tom Segura and creators like Richards, who makes YouTube sketch comedy Read the Room.

This approach sets Fox apart from its competitors in two key ways, Wade believes, “going direct and investing in original content by creating finance for new shows,” and providing “very significant advertising infrastructure” via an ad sales division that has the likes of the NFL and World Cup in its portfolio.

Parks, who joined Fox from The Chernin Group, said the studio offers hands-off support to creators who are “being pulled in many different directions.”

“We’re not greenlighting their ideas through a long, traditional development process,” he added. “Instead, we’re available for notes and feedback in an equitable way, without approaching the relationship as a top-down studio-to-creative model.”

In this way, Parks said creators “who are trying to do something outside their comfort zone” can be supported with capital and an IP-sharing vision.

“Many platforms that work with creators option their libraries or make shows with them to drive audiences to their own platforms,” he added. “That’s how companies such as Netflix, Amazon and Hulu are structured to work. That isn’t necessarily better or worse. Every creator will make different choices at different points in their career. But those platforms are primarily built to acquire subscribers, and that’s what they do with creators.”

Parks was recently at creator economy market VidSummit, where he said bosses at CAA, UTA and WME were all present along with leaders from platforms like Netflix and Tubi. “Everyone is thinking about the different types of deals available to creators, whether that involves investment, production or intellectual property,” he added.

All started with ‘Dancing With The Stars’

But while creators may be the talk of today, Wade and Parks have been thinking about this for a long while.

Wade says FCS’ inception harks back more than 15 years to when he was a producer on Dancing with the Stars and booked the show’s first ever YouTuber, Bethany Mota.

“She did very well but we learned a few things,” he added. “I was expecting an avalanche of YouTube views and imagined the votes for her would heavily skew young but there was no sudden mass of views or a sudden mass on YouTube. Our knowledge of the internet back then was very different.”

He realized that YouTube success does not always translate to traditional TV in obvious ways and figured out over the years that a studio’s infrastructure could be used in smart ways in this space. Things solidified with the success of Prime Video and A24’s Hazbin Hotel, which was produced by Fox-owned Bento Box and started life on YouTube via its creator Vivienne Medrano.

“We thought to ourselves, ‘We’re not a library, we’re a studio’,” added Wade. “What a studio does is back creators and put bets on them. That is something we know how to do.”

title: Katherine Waterston Joins Post-9/11 Limited Series ‘The Best Of Us’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Katherine Waterston (The Agency, The Uprising) is the latest star to join the cast of Paramount+’s limited series The Best of Us, which has been shooting in New York City since last month. She will star opposite Jeremy Strong in the upcoming six-episode limited series inspired by the David vs. Goliath fight that won […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Katherine Waterston (The Agency, The Uprising) is the latest star to join the cast of Paramount+‘s limited series The Best of Us, which has been shooting in New York City since last month. She will star opposite Jeremy Strong in the upcoming six-episode limited series inspired by the David vs. Goliath fight that won justice for 9/11’s ailing heroes.

Waterston will play Amy Smith, a lawyer and the soon-to-be ex-wife of Jason (Strong).

From writers Tobias Lindholm and Frank Pugliese, the 6-episode series The Best of Us dramatizes a landmark case that reshaped the fight for accountability: a relentless legal war that stretched nearly a decade to secure almost $1 billion in compensation for first responders who fell gravely ill in the wake of 9/11.

Strong leads the cast as renowned class action lawyer Jason Smith, who risked everything to take on entrenched institutions, exposing the politics, greed, corruption, and betrayal that compounded tragedy, set against the emergency workers’ remarkable unity and bravery as the World Trade Center was collapsing.

Watch on Deadline

In addition to Strong, the previously announced cast also includes Barry Pepper as Coach, a former NYPD police officer and 9/11 first responder suffering from leukemia due to his work at Ground Zero; Andrea Riseborough as Molly, Coach’s resilient wife; Neal Huff as Peter Allen, Jason’s pragmatic colleague at the law firm; Gaby Hoffmann as Kathleen McCormick, a seasoned FDNY firefighter and activist; Sky Yang as The Lost Son, a young and mysterious homeless man; and John Slattery as James Leavitt, a highly experienced and formidable defense lawyer.

The guest cast includes LaChanze, Richard Schiff, Elizabeth Rodriguez, Joe Morton, Jen Tullock, William Baldwin, and Keith W. Richards.

Produced by Paramount Television Studios and Sister, the limited series is written, directed, and executive produced by Lindholm and written and executive produced by Pugliese. Strong is also an executive producer, along with Tony Hernandez.

Waterston was recently seen in Paul Greengrass’ The Uprising and in the Paramount+ series The Agency alongside Michael Fassbender. Before that, she starred in Fackham Hall, a British Period Comedy written by Jimmy Carr. Additional credits include the latest installment in the Fear Street franchise, Prom Queen, The End We Start From, Slow Horses, Perry Mason, They Listen, Babylon, Inherent Vice, Alien: Covenant, and the Fantastic Beasts film series. Waterston is represented by UTA, Strand Entertainment, LARK Management, and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller.

title: Critics Choice Documentary Awards Nominations: ‘14th’ Nabs 6; Elizabeth Holmes Doc, ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’, ‘Nuisance Bear’ Land 5 Each
summary: 14th is coming out of the gate strong.
