title: The Black List Names 2026 Writers Lab Participants
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The Black List has named the six writers and projects chosen for its 2026 Writers Lab. They are Elton de Almeida (A Mark of Kin), Yasmin DeWinter (Guillaume), Scott Leddy (Nightwatch), Marcelle Pallais (One Last Summer), Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz (Depths) and Emma Taylor Stock (Denial). The program, now in its 13th year, […]
content:
E XCLUSIVE : The Black List has named the six writers and projects chosen for its 2026 Writers Lab. They are Elton de Almeida (A Mark of Kin), Yasmin DeWinter (Guillaume), Scott Leddy (Nightwatch), Marcelle Pallais (One Last Summer), Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz (Depths) and Emma Taylor Stock (Denial).

The program, now in its 13th year, provides creative mentorship and professional support to promising feature writers as they further develop their selected project during a weeklong workshop in Ojai, CA.

The Black List’s Annual Lab program supports two distinct cohorts: writers and ﬁlmmakers. The Writers Lab focuses on developing feature scripts to be sold in the studio system and/or used as voice samples. The Projects Lab, which will be announced in November, offers writer-directors the chance to develop a screenplay that they intend to direct.

Watch on Deadline

During the Lab, each writer will develop their screenplay through peer workshops and one-on-one sessions with working professional screenwriters, including returning mentors Travis Braun (One Night Only), Stephany Folsom (Toy Story 4, The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power), Katie Silberman (Set It Up, Don’t Worry Darling), Victoria Strouse (Seekers of Infinite Love, Finding Dory) and Christina Hodson (Birds of Prey, Bumblebee).

Black List Annual Lab alumna Savion Einstein (A Cuban Girl’s Guide To Tea and Tomorrow) will also join as a session mentor. After the lab concludes, the writers cohort will participate in a yearlong support program involving monthly meetings with screenwriters, agents, managers, producers, and executives.

“We’re excited to welcome the latest cohort of screenwriters to the Black List Lab fold. At a time when the industry can seem particularly challenging and harder than ever to break into, we’re thrilled to be able to support projects that make us excited to go to the movies. These writers are bringing distinctive voices, bold points of view, and stories that deserve to be heard to the Lab and we’re privileged to be able to give them space to take risks, challenge themselves, and build community with other writers, in Ojai and beyond,” said Megan Halpern, Black List SVP.

Submissions for the 2027 Labs are now open on the Black List website .

Previous Black List Lab alumni include Claire Ayoub (Empire Waist), Minhal Baig (We Grown Now), Tom Dean (Carolina, Caroline), Gia Gordon (Law and Order), Danny Hogan (The Pitt), Jimmy Keyrouz (Broken Keys), Dagny Looper (The Resort), Alexandra Qin (ThirstyGirl), Michelle Steffes (For When You Get Lost), and Jason Young (The Magic Flute).

Learn more about the 2026 Writers Lab projects, and the creatives behind them, below.

2026 Writers Lab Projects:

Elton de Almeida – A MARK OF KIN

Haunted by her family’s tragic past, a cunning scammer seeks revenge on the uncle who abandoned her decades ago — only to be trapped by a demonic curse that feeds off her bloodline.

Yasmin DeWinter – GUILLAUME

Paris, 1898. Two American brothers walk into a brothel. One vomits on a girl. The other pulls a knife. Within the hour, they owe a madam five thousand francs they don’t have. Their ship sails at dawn. The elder just had a seizure in a piss-soaked alley – and if anyone finds out, he loses his wife, his childen, and his name.

Scott Leddy – NIGHTWATCH

In the midst of an apparent nuclear attack on NATO and the US, a communications blackout with the President places the Defense Secretary in the hot seat on America’s Doomsday Plane, but with the minutes ticking down, a comms expert discovers an anomaly that could change everything.

Marcelle Pallais – ONE LAST SUMMER

A restless, sharp-witted teen aching for meaning and adventure escapes to a wealthy beach town, only to be pulled toward a charming boy and his family’s deadly secret. Adapted from NORTHANGER ABBEY by Jane Austen.

Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz – DEPTHS

Trapped aboard a US nuclear submarine, a former priest turned navy engineer must stop a demon-possessed Soviet defector before she turns the Cold War hot.

Emma Taylor Stock – DENIAL

When a health insurance giant denies their bestie’s cancer treatment, three friends attempt to approve the claim themselves. But their plan spirals when they accidentally kidnap the CEO and must expose his fraud to save themselves.

title: ‘Below’ Attracts Record Debut For A Netflix Canadian Series
summary: Below attracted a record audience on Netflix over the weekend. The limited series about a fisherman (Josh Hartnett) whose small Newfoundland hometown is terrorized by a mysterious sea creature baited 17 million views from its debut on October 8 through Sunday evening, marking the most-viewed debut ever for a Netflix Canadian title, per the streamer. […]
content:
Below attracted a record audience on Netflix over the weekend.

The limited series about a fisherman (Josh Hartnett) whose small Newfoundland hometown is terrorized by a mysterious sea creature baited 17 million views from its debut on October 8 through Sunday evening, marking the most-viewed debut ever for a Netflix Canadian title, per the streamer.

Below also handily secured the top spot on the English TV list for the week of October 5-11.

Second place went to East of Eden, which nearly doubled its viewership from its opening weekend with 12.6 million views. Zoe Kazan’s adaptation of John Steinbeck’s classic novel had an underwhelming launch with just 6.5 million views — Netflix’s lowest No. 1 opening since March.

Interestingly, third place went to Disney’s Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 1, which landed on Netflix last week and tallied 4.1 million views as it found a new audience. The series’ third season will premiere on Disney+ next month.

Watch on Deadline

Elsewhere, Mojo Brookz: I Know You Lying, the debut Netflix special from the stand-up comedian, nabbed the No. 4 spot on the English TV list with 3.3 million views, and Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story claimed fifth place with 3 million views. The Gentlemen Season 2 nabbed the No. 8 spot with 2 million views, and reality competition series Wonka’s The Golden Ticket won No. 9 on the list with 1.9 million views. A Different World, which has already been renewed, clocked in at No. 10 spot, also with 1.9 million views.

On the film side of things, Ben Affleck’s Animals launched at No. 1 with 23.8 million views. Tyler Perry’s Doing Life rose to second place with 18.2 million views. Unabomber, in which Jacob Tremblay portrays domestic terrorist Ted Kaczynski, seized No. 7 with 7.3 million views.

title: BAFTA Winner Narges Rashidi Signs With TFC Management
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Narges Rashidi, who recently won the BAFTA for Leading Actress for her portrayal of Nazanin Zaghari Ratcliffe in BBC’s Prisoner 951, has signed with TFC Management. The series, directed by Phillipa Lowthorpe and also starring Joseph Fiennes, told the true story of Zaghari Ratfcliffe’s wrongful seven-year imprisonment in Iran and her husband’s subsequent fight […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Narges Rashidi, who recently won the BAFTA for Leading Actress for her portrayal of Nazanin Zaghari Ratcliffe in BBC’s Prisoner 951, has signed with TFC Management.

The series, directed by Phillipa Lowthorpe and also starring Joseph Fiennes, told the true story of Zaghari Ratfcliffe’s wrongful seven-year imprisonment in Iran and her husband’s subsequent fight for her release. In addition to the BAFTA, Narges also received two Royal Television Society Awards along with several other award nominations for her portrayal of Nazanin.

Narges is perhaps best known in the U.S. and the UK for her role as fearless mobster Lale in Gangs of London for Sky/AMC, which is heading into its fourth and final season in 2027. Narges also performs the majority of her own stunts across the series.

Her breakthrough role was leading Babak Anvari’s 2016 acclaimed and award-winning Persian-language film Under the Shadow, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival. For her performance, Narges received a nomination for Best Actress at the BIFAs, a well as the Breakthrough Actress award at the New York International Film Festival.

Watch on Deadline

Narges’ other credits include Netflix feature Havoc opposite Tom Hardy and indie feature Last Swim, which won at Berlinale 2025. Narges has a long list of German credits including series The Allegation, which won the Dior Grand Prize at Canneseries in 2021.

Founded in 2020 by David Stone and Ben Jacobson, TFC Management reps on-camera talents such as Dakota and Elle Fanning, Shira Haas, Lashana Lynch, JD Pardo, Dan Ings and Josh Hutcherson, as well as such creators, filmmakers, novelists and producers as Warren Littlefield, Brian Yorkey, Megan Park, Adam Reed, Akiva Goldsman, Courtney Lilly, Josh & Jonas Pate and Rebecca Serle.

TFC’s sister company, TFC Productions, most recently produced the Apple series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, created by David E. Kelley and starring Elle Fanning, which recently received eight Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Comedy Series.

Rashidi will continue to be repped by The Artists Partnership in all areas.

title: ‘Elsinore’ And ‘La Bola Negra’ Continue Awards Momentum With Wins At Hamptons Film Festival
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Elsinore and La Bola Negra were two of the standout films to collect awards at the just-concluded 34th edition of the Hamptons Film Festival. Audiences who attended 205 screenings of the fest’s 140-plus features and shorts from October 2-11 selected La Bola Negra as Best Narrative Feature. The film, directed by Javier Calvo and […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Elsinore and La Bola Negra were two of the standout films to collect awards at the just-concluded 34th edition of the Hamptons Film Festival.

Audiences who attended 205 screenings of the fest’s 140-plus features and shorts from October 2-11 selected La Bola Negra as Best Narrative Feature. The film, directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, is Spain’s official submission for the Best International Feature Film category at the upcoming Oscars. It emerged from the Toronto Film Festival with heat after winning the TIFF People’s Choice award, often an Oscar bellwether.

Another hopeful with a presence at the Hamptons is Elsinore, which made its East Coast premiere at the event. Directed by Simon Stone, the film starring Andrew Scott won the international people’s choice award at Toronto, along with prizes at other festivals in recent weeks.

Watch on Deadline

Because of its timing in between larger fall festivals and the surge of campaign season later in the year, the Hamptons has built a reputation as a fest of note. It doesn’t hurt that it takes place near the beaches of Long Island’s East End about 90 miles from New York City, long a vacation destination and a place to see and be seen.

NAZA, which has drawn packed screenings and ovations but also protests and controversy for its documentary portrait of Israeli military attacks on Palestinian communities, also collected an award. The film, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, received the Victor Rabinowitz & Joanne Grant Award for Social Justice. The film recognizes a film that exemplifies the values of peace, equality, global justice and civil liberties.

Burgundy, directed by Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, captured HIFF’s documentary audience award.

La Bola Negra was described in a statement by HIFF Narrative Competition jury members Cara Cusumano, Jeremy O. Harris and David Rooney as a “triptych of queer desire, queer memory and queer resistance weaves together an epic story using revisionist history and builds to an emotional climax that rips to the core.”

The narrative jury also gave a Special Mention to The Guest, which is directed by Mads Mengel.

Best Documentary Feature honors went to If Pigeons Turned to Gold. Documentary Competition Jury members Carlos A. Gutiérrez, Mark Obenhaus and Sky Sitney called it “a bold, deeply personal story of the filmmaker’s own family struggles with addiction. It is told with provocative rawness and inventiveness.”

Other HIFF honors included the Junior Jury Award, from a panel of East Hampton High School students, given to Mouse; the Artemis Rising Foundation Raise the Vibration Award for Social Impact, to The Drug in Our Pocket and A Song for the Snow Lion; the Peter Macgregor-Scott Memorial Award, to Laser-Gato; the Sherzum Award, for films tackling LGBTQ+ people, issues and concerns, to What Will I Become? and Welcome to Paris; the Brizzolara Family Foundation Award for Films of Conflict & Resolution to The Choice; the Suffolk County Next Exposure Grant to Barbizon; and the Zelda Penzel “Giving Voice to the Voiceless” Award, to Wild Inside.

Ben’Imana and The Drug in Our Pocket won the documentary and narrative categories, respectively, of the New York Women in Film & Television’s awards for excellence.

title: ‘Clean Hands’ Review: Zach Braff Is a Cop on a Crusade to Save His Addict Daughter in an Uneasy Fact-Based Crime Drama
summary: When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “Clean Hands” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior […]
content:
When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “Clean Hands” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior actually is. Written, produced and directed by Jake Allyn (“Ride”), the film chronicles the relationship between real-life Hagerstown, MD narcotics officer Kevin Simmers (Zach Braff) and his efforts to rescue his daughter Brooke (Esther McGregor) from the grip of drug abuse. But while the “happening right under his nose” details lend a heartbreaking edge to a sadly familiar story, the script’s argument against criminalizing addiction reconciles uneasily with its portrayal of Simmers’ determination to save Brooke by any means necessary.

Simmers is a hero cop, looked up to by his colleagues and liked better than one might expect by the local townspeople, given his by-the-book approach. Though he maintains a close relationship with 19-year-old Brooke, he’s blindsided when he learns that she’s addicted to Percocet and has been consorting with abusive dealer Brick (Kraig Dane). After unsuccessfully trying to enroll her in a private rehab facility, Simmers learns that she’s moved on to heroin; he takes a tough-love approach to let her get arrested, hoping to scare her straight. But when even that fails, he becomes determined to cut off her supply at the source, pursuing local addicts in the hopes of apprehending anyone who might deal her drugs.

Popular on Variety

Despite the support of his religious wife Dana (Abigail Spencer) and colleagues on the police force, including an ambitious deputy (Lucas Till) eager to succeed him as the precinct’s role model, Simmers’ efforts to help get Brooke clean fail over and over again. As he faces the prospect of losing her to addiction, he begins to conceive an alternative path for struggling drug abusers, even while witnessing members of the Hagerstown community — including some of his fellow officers — exploiting addicts instead of helping them.

Given the infomercial pasted at the top of the closing credits for Brooke’s House, the rehab facility Simmers created in response to his daughter’s addiction, it feels safe to assume that the former police officer fully endorsed this portrait of him and his family’s struggles. Yet the typical disclaimer absolving the filmmakers of responsibility for dramatizing these real people’s lives is oddly posted at the beginning of the closing credits rather than at the very end, suggesting that some of the narrative leaps taken here by the filmmakers are bigger than usual. To that end, one can understand why Allyn wouldn’t want to risk misrepresenting Hagerstown law enforcement. But should audiences accept at face value every action taken by Simmers in his crusade to save his daughter?

By all accounts, he was a dedicated cop with honed instincts as an investigator, and a loving father to Brooke — so much so that, in the film, Dana accuses the two of them of being addicted to each other. But the character’s compassion towards perpetrators and his cool detachment under pressure seem only to apply when he doesn’t have an active stake in a crime. When he does, he seems willing to abuse his power and take any measures that he thinks will result in whatever he’s already decided the outcome should be — whether that’s lying to a healthcare provider to get his daughter treatment, or arresting an individual he deems complicit in Brooke’s condition.

As the film tells it, Simmers eventually learns that waging war against dealers and community enablers makes less of an impact on people who are addicted than providing them consistent, patient, loving support. But the character is so relentless for so long with his methods that it’s hard not to pin a portion of the blame for Brooke’s addiction on him.

Again, that seems distantly like the point (or at least one point) of “Clean Hands.” But Allyn is entirely too interested in Simmers’ police work, meaning high-pitched chases and strong-arm interrogations, to strike the right balance between his day job and his earnest efforts to help his daughter. As a viewer, it’s possible to forgive a character who’s so determined to protect his daughter that he takes overbearing or inappropriate measures, but when the film wants the crime stuff to be tense and exciting — amplified with music by instrumental rock act Those Who Ride With Giants — it undercuts the humanity of what that character is facing.

Simmers marks a departure from the kinds of roles for which Braff is best known, and the actor commits to the character’s tenacity and determination in a way that suggests he’s either prioritizing authenticity regardless of how the character is perceived, or he misunderstands how sympathetic Allyn’s version of Simmers can be. The problem is the contrast between his well-meaning actions and their impact on others: Brooke faces beatings in jail because her father antagonizes the guards and other inmates, God-fearing Dana flinches every time he drops an f-bomb or angrily dresses down a rehab administrator, and until the very last scene in the film, he ignores or dismisses the addiction, poverty or desperation of anyone he encounters who’s struggling.

McGregor offers a welcome counterbalance as Brooke, whose general disposition emanates from her relationship with her father, even as it’s hobbled by troubles the script pinpoints with delicacy. Though the film doesn’t quite know what to do with Dana as Simmers bulldozes his way to a cure for Brooke, Spencer similarly offers grace — or at least a less rigid form of support — that hints at how his initial way of helping may not be the most effective one.

To whatever extent this story is told accurately, Simmers was of course doing the best that he could to reckon with a challenge he’d dealt with in the line of duty, but never with a person so close to him — and years of repetition reinforced a one-size-fits-all reaction to an affliction that must be addressed individually. But the film builds to the founding of Brooke’s House and its immediate, overwhelming success, indicating that all Simmers needed to do was change his tactics, instead of the more meaningful, moving change in his perception of addiction as something to be mechanically repaired. A handful of appealing performances aside, “Clean Hands” ignores too many messy realities in favor of quick solutions; the stuff that gives a true story like this power is the hard work and struggle that happens between an epiphany about oneself and the reality of implementing its lessons in the world.

title: ‘Tommy & Tuppence’ Stars Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas on That ‘Intense’ Finale, Why the Detective Duo ‘Keep Missing Each Other’ Romantically and a Potential Season 2
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of “Tommy & Tuppence,” now streaming on BritBox. The finale of “Tommy & Tuppence” finds the Agatha Christie detective duo, played by Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas, on the verge of a new chapter. The BritBox Original series brings the classic characters into the modern day, […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of “Tommy & Tuppence,” now streaming on BritBox.

The finale of “Tommy & Tuppence” finds the Agatha Christie detective duo, played by Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas, on the verge of a new chapter.

The BritBox Original series brings the classic characters into the modern day, where Tommy and Tuppence are exes instead of a married couple (as Christie originally wrote). A decade after dating at university, they bump into each other at a wedding and soon become embroiled in a murder mystery. The two have an exciting will they-won’t they chemistry as they solve cases around London (with the help of Tommy’s Aunt Ada, played by Imelda Staunton), begin their own private detective business and start getting closer. But there’s just one problem — Tuppence is married to a director back in L.A.

The series’ sixth episode sees Tommy and Tuppence solve a cold case surrounding harrowing child murders in the countryside, just as Tuppence at last acknowledges her feelings for Tommy and decides to divorce her husband. In classic rom-com fashion, just as Tuppence bursts through Tommy’s door with the news, she sees him kissing police detective Draper (Callie Cooke). Then, Tuppence’s sister presents them with their biggest mission yet: helping the U.K. government with a major case.

Popular on Variety

“Finally, it clicks and she realizes — but is she just a bit too late?” Thomas tells Variety over Zoom.

“Much of their relationship is characterized by sliding doors moments and missing each other just by a hair’s breath, which is in part infuriating but also kind of tantalizing,” Dylan adds. “It’s like, when are they going to get it out?!”

Below, Dylan and Thomas break down the finale episode, reveal how they established Tommy and Tuppence’s chemistry and discuss a potential Season 2.

First of all, what made you want to come on board the series?

Dylan: Obviously, Agatha Christie is untouchable in so many ways — incomparable rather, because she’s the Queen of Crime and it’s beloved by people. But when I read the scripts I felt like, here’s an opportunity to do something that I don’t think I’ve seen before, which is blending that cozy crime world, that Agatha Christie world, with an opportunity to make this feel really grounded and naturalistic and real.

Thomas: Tommy and Tuppence are amateurs anyway, so it lends itself really well to the more modern-day idea of being a sleuth and listening to a podcast and trying to figure something out yourself. Like we can all relate to that; I love a true crime podcast. And the way that [Christie] wrote those characters was quite modern actually, for the time. Particularly Tuppence being a pretty outspoken, front-footed woman, she was very modern in the way that she behaved. So that felt like a very easy transfer.

Tommy and Tuppence are married in Christie’s stories, but in this adaptation they’re exes in this sort of will they-won’t they phase. How did you establish that chemistry?

Thomas: Josh and I did a lot of meeting up and trying to work on the relationship and find a colloquial shorthand in and amongst the text. I certainly was quite daunted by the scenes where there’s quite a lot of exposition and they’re going through and trying to figure out the crime. I remember being like, “I don’t know how to do this!” And Josh was like, “I think these are the moments that they’re having the most fun and also when they as characters are connecting the most.” And as soon as you said that, it totally unlocked it for me. Because there’s two things going on, which is really fun about Tommy and Tuppence — the relationship between them and the crimes that they’re solving. So to use the crime-solving as a way to become closer was so fun. And then [writer] Phoebe [Eclair-Powell] was really open with allowing us to be freer with some of those bits to make it feel more modern.

Dylan: Yeah, and moments where it allowed for a little bit of improvisation. They let us get away with some of that, which was kind of them.

Antonia Thomas and Josh Dylan in “Tommy & Tuppence.” Lara Cornell/LOOKOUT POINT / BRI

What were the conversations you had about Tommy and Tuppence’s history?

Dylan: We’re still piecing bits together, to be honest. I think the idea is that they met at university and were together and obviously had an amazing connection, but the details, the reason why they split up is still a bit contentious. They get along and they have this care for each other, but you grow up a lot in 10 years. So at the top of the series and throughout, you’re seeing these people that have this core chemistry and connection, but they’re realizing the ways in which they’ve changed and the ways they’re still the same. And that feels really human and real and truthful to me, and was really interesting to play.



Thomas: And also, as much as they have changed, they’re still the same. It’s like that idea of a leopard doesn’t change its spots. The thing that was the problem last time, 10 years ago, is still basically the problem. It’s just, are they more mature? Can they address things differently?



Dylan: But on the flip side, the spark that drew them together in the first place is also still there, in exactly the same way.

What makes them work so well together in a more professional sense, as a detective duo?

Thomas: I think the fact that they’re quite opposites. They’re the yin and yang, they complement each other. Tuppence is pretty impulsive, she’s very instinctual and has often a strong gut feeling about things and is quite ballsy. So she’ll want to attack things head on, and then Tommy is much more thoughtful and precise and forensic often about things, which is really needed. The push and pull between them I think keeps them steady and in the middle.

And I have to ask, what was it like working with Imelda Staunton as Aunt Ada?

Dylan: What a legend. She’s cool as hell and very twinkly and magical. And seems to kind of be the perfect Aunt Ada.



Thomas: There’s so much fun to her, like she brought such a fun, almost impish, brilliant side to Ada. And working with her and just watching her work, she’s such a seasoned veteran. It was a brilliant.

Let’s get into the final episode. It’s quite intense — you’re hunting down Jane Lancaster, a child murderer who then sets the house you’re all in on fire, and then Tuppence finally confesses her feelings to Tommy while he’s unconscious. What was that like to film?

Dylan: Oh my god, that’s actually a bit triggering. I just got flashbacks to being in that cottage and being in the room with the wonderful actress Alice Krige as Jane Lancaster — being in this tiny little bedroom with her for like, two days. It was so intense.

Thomas: You had to do your big ol’ speech, didn’t you?

Dylan: Absolutely glorious monologue. And then being carried out of the fire, I remember Antonia — she’s an incredible actress anyway, full stop the end, but I remember this particular take where I was a dead weight on the floor like, succumbed to the flames, and she was over my face and then a tear fell in my mouth.

Thomas: [Laughs] And then we were also really tired because that was the end of the shoot. I don’t know if I’ve done a job as intense because we’re basically in every scene, bar a few. And so by the time we got to Episodes 5 and 6, we’d been going for a few months. And then those two episodes just ramped up and it’s just really dark, isn’t it? It’s about child murder and kidnapping and Ada dies and that’s really sad. And then between the two of them as well, they’re not in a good place.

Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas in “Tommy & Tuppence.” Lara Cornell/LOOKOUT POINT / BRI

Do you think Tommy heard Tuppence’s confession? At the end, he seems to be moving on with Draper…

Thomas: No, I don’t think he does. I think that’s what’s sort of sad about it, in a way. And about the ending altogether. Finally, it clicks and she realizes — but is she just a bit too late?



Dylan: Much of their relationship is characterized by sliding doors moments and kind of missing each other just by a hair’s breath, which is in part infuriating but also kind of tantalizing. And they’re not always the best — shock, horror – at expressing themselves. They clearly feel a huge amount, they’re very sensitive and very compassionate and feeling, but they just keep missing each other. It’s like, when are they going to get it out?!

It’s almost like we need a second season! And the ending sets that up quite well, with an offer for the duo to help the government on a case. What would you want to see from a potential Season 2?

Thomas: Would love a second season.



Dylan: I would love to do one.



Thomas: Also, can we do it somewhere exotic?



Dylan: Yeah, the Caribbean? We’ll take Spain! No, to be fair, we’d love to do it. These characters have so much scope and potential and range to go on so many more adventures, and we love the creative team. It does feel like Season 1 ends at a very exciting junction, and they grow a lot as well. What I love about this show is that it’s grounded and funny and doesn’t take itself too seriously a lot of the time, but then I do think it has the capacity in moments to go to some darker places and stretch. So I think that would be quite nice, to continue that theme.

This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

title: Why the ‘Girls’ Revival Is Such an Exciting Idea
summary: The return of “Girls” for a five-episode limited run won’t just be interesting because of how Hannah Horvath has or has not changed. It’ll be a litmus test for how we at home have, as well. After all, Lena Dunham has at times struggled to distinguish herself from her most famous creation. At the height […]
content:
The return of “Girls” for a five-episode limited run won’t just be interesting because of how Hannah Horvath has or has not changed. It’ll be a litmus test for how we at home have, as well.

After all, Lena Dunham has at times struggled to distinguish herself from her most famous creation. At the height of HBO’s “Girls,” the op-ed-generating machine that, incidentally, was a very good TV show, journalists wrote about and addressed Dunham as if she literally were the narcissistic writer she portrayed onscreen. A general consensus seemed to have formed that Dunham could not possibly understand the ways in which Horvath was flawed and annoying — despite the fact that Dunham had written her. And, in the years after “Girls” wrapped up in 2017, Dunham struggled to step out of the show’s shadow with new work, in part due to medical and substance issues she documented in her recent memoir “Famesick.”

As proven by “Famesick” and her 2025 Netflix series “Too Much” — a wistful, surprisingly mature story of attempting to move on from romantic disappointment — Dunham is in a different place now, and so, maybe, is her audience. Her book was received with warm nostalgia and appreciation for Dunham’s lacerating understanding of herself and the web of misunderstandings that surround her.

Popular on Variety

So — while it’s obviously too early even to speculate about what a late-2020s “Girls” might look like, aside from its cast, with Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells confirmed to return — there’s hope that it might cut through some of the clutter that came to define the show as it ran on. It’s also reasonable to assume that “Girls” 2 might more fully reflect Dunham’s perspective than did the show we now remember fondly: Part of the tension and drama of “Famesick” is its depiction of “Girls” as the product of a vexed series of compromises with Dunham’s then-creative partner Jenni Konner, brought in to teach the raw writing-directing talent behind the indie film “Tiny Furniture” how to make conventionally structured TV. Judd Apatow returns to this iteration “Girls” as an executive producer, but Konner does not.

The Dunham-Konner breakup — Dunham’s side of which is painstakingly reconstructed in “Famesick” — lends the idea of a “Girls” revival an intriguingly meta aspect. Wherever Hannah is now, she’ll likely be written by a person newly working on her own terms. (Along with co-writers, Dunham is credited as a writer on every episode of “Too Much,” which was not true of the first six seasons of “Girls.”) And the information Dunham has shared about her inner life lends the revival the feeling of a reclamation, as well. Hannah’s ending on the series — isolated from many of her friends and raising a child as a single mother — was, we now know, written at a time when Dunham was physically ill and addicted to drugs. Making the series in what seems to be a happier and stabler moment in her life — including with a new perspective on parenthood, as Dunham, having written about her grief following her hysterectomy, is now a mother — allows the possibility of Hannah finding a deeper, richer ending.

Or… not an ending, but a stopping point. As this news proves once again, nothing in TV is ever really final — does anyone believe, for instance, that we’ll actually never see Carrie Bradshaw again? But the Carrie example gives a sense of the potential, and pitfalls, of a “Girls” revival. It was joyful and heartening for fans of that show to check in with Carrie and her friends on the streets of New York in the 2008 sequel film and 2020s HBO Max revival “And Just Like That.” (I use “streets of New York” advisedly — note that I am avoiding mentioning the words “Abu Dhabi.”) And these new projects allowed Michael Patrick King to test out how the characters of “Sex and the City” might move through passages of life as they grew into late middle age — a genuinely radical project. But as “And Just Like That” ran on, Carrie could at times feel less like the living, breathing person she once had and more like an accumulation of narrative contrivances — back with Aidan, again! — and opportunities to comment on changing social mores.

In all, though, it was invigorating to see Carrie Bradshaw ripped out of her moment and placed into contemporaneity. And Hannah Horvath has similar promise. Since “Girls” ended, she’s been frozen in time — our reactions to her may have shifted, but she remains a creature of the late Obama era, as emblematic of old-millennial mores and ways of speaking as Carrie Bradshaw was of turn-of-the-century Gen X fabulosity. How has Hannah’s perspective shifted since we left her — and what parts of her remain irreducibly herself? Much in the same way that I’ve loved watching Dunham coming into herself in recent years, I can’t wait to find out.

title: ‘Just Dance: Decades of Hits’ Costume Designer Breaks Down the New Game’s Look and Not Using AI: ‘It’s Our Art’
summary: At a time when AI is increasingly being used to replace human creativity, “Just Dance” is refusing to change its hands-on approach. The Ubisoft dance game, which just launched “Just Dance: Decades of Hits” on Tuesday, brings on-screen characters to life through a process rooted in human labor. Real dancers wear handmade costumes, wigs and […]
content:
At a time when AI is increasingly being used to replace human creativity, “Just Dance” is refusing to change its hands-on approach.

The Ubisoft dance game, which just launched “Just Dance: Decades of Hits” on Tuesday, brings on-screen characters to life through a process rooted in human labor. Real dancers wear handmade costumes, wigs and makeup before being filmed against a green screen and integrated into the game.

“We are really loving what we do. It’s our art. It’s what we love,” Benjamin Jouffret, the game’s costume designer and character lead, tells Variety. “We are proud of working, sketching ourselves, creating what is in our minds and making real costumes with real costume makers.”

Popular on Variety

Jouffret says his team is committed to creating its characters without AI. Having studied fashion and previously working as a stylist, Jouffret has spent the past eight years overseeing the costumes and characters that appear on-screen.

The process begins with a brainstorming session, during which the creative team listens to a song and watches its music video to determine the direction of a character. Sometimes the team draws inspiration directly from the artist, other times opting to take the concept in a completely different direction.

The concept art and finished product for Zara Larsson’s “Midnight Sun” for “Just Dance: Decades of Hits.”

These decisions also inform the game’s maps, which combine the characters with their backgrounds and surrounding environments. “If you want to create a map for the community or the hardcore players, we know that they will really want to have a connection with the singers,” Jouffret explains. “If you have a Lady Gaga song, you want Easter eggs. For that, we are really inspired by the artists.”

From there, the team determines whether the dance will feature a solo performer or a duo or trio, as well as the type of character that fits best. Sometimes, up to 10 characters will be featured in one dance.

“We also decide if you want a casual costume, or an alien or a mascot or a nonbinary character,” Joufrett says. “We do a lot of things.”

His team then assembles mood boards using references from films, music videos and other media before developing sketches and finalizing designs. Once a concept is approved, the team consults its roster of dancers to find someone who can embody the character and complement the choreographer’s vision.

Overall, the timeline is relatively short. After a one-day brainstorming session, the team typically spends two to three weeks designing a character, followed by roughly four weeks of production. That period includes fittings, hair and makeup tests and rehearsals to ensure the costumes work with the choreography. Filming takes place over a single day.

The sketch and final product of the costume for Bad Bunny’s “Nuevayol” in “Just Dance: Decades of Hits.”

Across the game’s Paris-based lead studio and its partner studio in Shanghai, the team creates roughly 100 costumes per installment, balancing visual appeal with practicality.

“We can’t make beautiful costumes if they can’t be used by the dancers,” Jouffret explains. “We can do what we want, but we have to do it smartly.”

The team previously experimented with 3D printing, but the materials proved too heavy for dancers to move comfortably in. Today, that technique is reserved for accessories requiring smaller, intricate details.

For Jouffret, the trial and error of the process is part of what makes the game so special. “We really love to create and make things by ourselves,” he says.

The sketch for the costume for Billy Joel’s “Uptown Girl” in “Just Dance: Decades of Hits.”

His team collaborates with costume makers and other specialists, each bringing expertise in areas such as mascots, corsets and casual wear. The team’s commitment to representation is also reflected in the game itself, which features dancers with different backgrounds and abilities. In one installment, the team worked with dancer Jana Bruno, who has one arm, earning recognition for its diversity efforts.

“Just Dance” releases a new installment every year, sometimes revisiting characters and storylines from previous games. For “Decades of Hits,” one new character, Lyra, is the daughter of a character introduced in a previous game. Players will follow her storyline of searching for her father through dance.

Meanwhile, hundreds of costumes from the franchise’s 17-year history remain in storage in Paris, forming a physical archive of the work behind the game’s characters. Jouffret says the team hopes to showcase the creations through a potential exhibition or runway presentation, although some pieces would need repairs after the wear and tear of filming.

title: ‘Once Upon in the Middle East’ Review: China’s Oscar Entry Is a Breakneck Blockbuster That Mixes Food Porn With Wartime Devastation
summary: Not since Zhang Yimou’s 2002 wuxia spectacle “Hero” has China landed an Oscar nomination for Best International Feature — and this dry spell surely won’t be broken with this year’s bombastic submission “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Like most of the country’s entries over the past decade, this blockbuster epic — a […]
content:
Not since Zhang Yimou’s 2002 wuxia spectacle “Hero” has China landed an Oscar nomination for Best International Feature — and this dry spell surely won’t be broken with this year’s bombastic submission “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Like most of the country’s entries over the past decade, this blockbuster epic — a summer box office hit at home — makes for an extravagant display of the strength of the nation’s commercial film industry. Strength, in the sense that no modest operation could conceivably pull off the technical wizardry and large-scale worldbuilding showcased here, where an entire city is at one point turned into an inferno of crumbling buildings, and a massive military base is, in a later scene, ambushed in a rain of blazing pyrotechnics.

The film is also, as expected from this state-backed production, blatantly propagandistic — but in a way that is particularly baffling, and shockingly tasteless. If those sound like the elements for a good time, in the B-movie sense, then you are also correct. Against the odds, “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is also, both regrettably and miraculously, extremely watchable. The Jekyll part of your brain will tell you to leave but the Hyde-side will keep you seated in morbid, twitchy-eyed fascination over the film’s two-and-a-half hour runtime.

Popular on Variety

To cut straight to the point, this is a film in which China symbolically emerges from the rubble of the Iraq War as a pacifistic patriarch and guardian of all the world’s children. Director Wen Muyue delivers this subtext through the story of Xu Fu (Shen Teng), a debt-ridden chef who agrees to temporarily take over a Chinese restaurant in the fictional Gulf-region city of Bahata, intending to return to his daughter and mother in China in two years time.

Flash-forwards to an elder Xu Fu with liver spots and a conspicuous scar on his cheek tell us that he will indeed make it back to his family, but it’ll take much longer than a few years — the frankly absurd reasons for his delay a consequence of his, let’s say, geopolitical misfortunes. He’s a man in the wrong place at the wrong time, though, cleverly, the film makes the point that a good Chinese meal is never unwelcome. In fact it’s globally in demand — a lifeline that ensures Xu Fu’s survival through the film’s whirlwind of events.

Before we get to the grisly images of dead children covered in ash, the film starts out as a feel-good dramedy in which Xu Fu adapts to his new surroundings. Frazzled softie Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), the restaurant manager, is our hero’s bridge between China and his new home, translating for Xu Fu between Arabic and Chinese during tense but diplomatic discussions with the restaurant owner Zaid (Sherif Sabby). Glossy, mouthwatering closeups of grilled meats and bubbling stone-pot stews testify to the success of Xu Fu’s kitchen takeover. Nurturing local talent is also on the agenda when he takes on a mentee, Seif (Omar Sharif — no, not that one), an angsty orphan who learns to sublimate his rage into the art of Chinese cooking. Though as the film goes on, this anger grows into a furious, war-hardened desire for retribution. Does a delicious roasted duck stand a chance? It does, in this film’s mind, with the help of the preternaturally compassionate Xu Fu.

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is something of a both-sides film in that both the Americans and the not-so-thinly-veiled Iraqis are gross caricatures of themselves, and there’s particular ire reserved for that most treacherous of abominations: Chinese-American … food. In epic-handshake-meme solidarity, Xu Fu and Zaid agree that their restaurant will never serve U.S.-style Chinese dishes like General Tso’s chicken; and when the US troops bomb Bahata to smithereens and occupy the city, a crass Chinese-American private (Aarif Lee Zhi-ting) bullies his way into free meals at Xu Fu’s restaurant. Not a pushover but a practical-minded realist, the chef takes the punches, striking up a booze-smuggling deal with the Americans to keep the orphans living in his restaurant safe.

The maddening implausibility that sustains the film’s relentless, weirdly hypnotizing forward momentum means we’re never in one place — or one mood — for too long. Zaid’s home is bombed in one intensely melodramatic sequence that culminates in a slow zoom over Zaid cradling his dead wife and child. Next thing we know, he’s radicalized and joins a terrorist group. Xu Fu, Ma Junsheng and Seif — the cooking trio — are promptly captured by the U.S. Army and forced to preside over the kitchen on base. This allows for more sumptuous shots of delicious food while Xu Fu is, for whatever reason, targeted by an aggro, block-jawed American soldier. Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng also play surrogate dads to Seif, whose increasingly violent eruptions threaten to change the course of his life more than once.

For all its dewy-eyed sentimentality, the film is also startlingly brutal and bloody, making for a deranged whiplash effect that’s felt most powerfully in the film’s final act, which is set in a terrorist stronghold where pipsqueaks are brainwashed into becoming suicide bombers. Cozy, brotherly scenes (as when Ma Junsheng slips Seif a smuggled can of soda) are directly followed by executions and montages of plush-bear-wielding kiddies invoking jihad. There’s a slickness to the carnage that rubs uncomfortably against the film’s humanist ethos, rendering artificial (for all Shen Teng’s trembling and mouth-contorting labors) the horrific tragedies that befall its characters. It’s a vision of wartime brutality that’s both blithely matter-of-fact and desperate to pull at our heartstrings; utterly delusional, in other words, and hard to look away from.

title: Drake Bell Calls Out SAG-AFTRA After Losing Health Insurance & Urges People To “Not Become An Actor” Or “Join SAG”
summary: Drake Bell is calling out SAG-AFTRA after revealing he didn’t have health insurance because he didn’t qualify. The Drake & Josh alum took to social media to share a screenshot from the actors’ guild website where it read, “You do not qualify for Health Plan coverage at this time.” “Your reported covered earnings from July […]
content:
Drake Bell is calling out SAG-AFTRA after revealing he didn’t have health insurance because he didn’t qualify.

The Drake & Josh alum took to social media to share a screenshot from the actors’ guild website where it read, “You do not qualify for Health Plan coverage at this time.”

“Your reported covered earnings from July 2025 – June 2026 did not meet minimum eligibility requirements, or you did not qualify under other eligibility rules,” the portal read.

A second notice on the website stated that Bell had earned $17,480.53 so far and needed $11,452.47 more to reach $28,933 and qualify for health coverage.

“Do not become an actor. Do not join SAG,” Bell captioned his Instagram Stories post. “You can work steadily for 35 years and they will say [middle finger emoji].”

Watch on Deadline

Bell also tagged the guild and SAG-AFTRA president Sean Astin, saying “you’re doing a bang up job,” and adding, “How about stop using actors to run things maybe? They literally just know how to say words in front of a camera.”

Drake Bell’s Instagram post Instagram / drakebell

RELATED: SAG-AFTRA Responds To AI Actress Tilly Norwood Furor: “Creativity Is & Should Remain Human-Centered”

The actor is best known for starring in Nickelodeon shows like The Amanda Show (1999), All That (2004), and Drake & Josh, a sitcom that ran on the children’s network for four seasons.

In recent years, Bell has taken on voice roles like Spider-Man in Ultimate Spider-Man (2012). He would reprise the superhero role in Phineas and Ferb (2013), Avengers Assemble (2013), and Hulk and the Agents of S.M.A.S.H. (2013).

title: ‘The White Lotus’ Filming In Cannes As Season 4 Production Enters Final Stretch, Hôtel Martinez Transformation Confirms New Resort Logo
summary: The White Lotus‘ Cannes takeover continues. As Season 4 of Mike White’s HBO series is headed into the final stretch on its lengthy shoot, the mystery series has camped out at the famous Hôtel Martinez on Promenade de la Croisette six months after production on the new installment began at the French Riviera and five […]
content:
The White Lotus‘ Cannes takeover continues. As Season 4 of Mike White‘s HBO series is headed into the final stretch on its lengthy shoot, the mystery series has camped out at the famous Hôtel Martinez on Promenade de la Croisette six months after production on the new installment began at the French Riviera and five months after the show filmed scenes during the Cannes Film Festival.

Deadline reported in April that two hotels will be featured in the new season: Airelles Château de la Messardière in Saint-Tropez as the White Lotus du Cap and the Hôtel Martinez as the White Lotus Cannes. With filming underway, Hôtel Martinez has been transformed, and many set pieces and props are still displayed in the lobby. The White Lotus logo can also be seen everywhere, from furniture to windows and carpets.

Matching the art deco style of the Hôtel Martinez (with the font mimicking that of the actual marquee), the new While Lotus logo is a major departure from the ornate flowers featured in the first seasons. There had been small tweaks season to season as the series traveled to different locations — all of them telegraphed in the start-of-production slate photos that stealthily revealed the new logo (including the Season 4 one). You can see below how The White Lotus hotel logo has evolved over the seasons.

Watch on Deadline

White reportedly is shooting at Palm Beach this week, before a rumored weeklong shoot at the Martinez, which may have been booked out for the occasion.

Sets at the Martinez are blocked off with a sign that reads, “This is a fragile movie set, please do not touch or move any set elements.” This includes golden palm trees, a fake elevator, a replica of a check-in desk, a circular sofa and two blue armchairs with a blue painting of a man hanging on the wall. White Lotus props like caps, towels, bags and scarves also can be found in the hotel lobby. You can see photos and videos in the Instagram post below.

A doorman at the Martinez beamed while speaking to Deadline about the hotel hosting The White Lotus, noting that it will “surely get us more customers,” once the season premieres next year.

The Season 4 cast includes Laura Dern, Steve Coogan, Vincent Cassel, Caleb Jonte Edwards, Ben Kingsley, Dylan Ennis, Corentin Fila, Ari Graynor, Marissa Long, Alexander Ludwig, Chris Messina, AJ Michalka, Kumail Nanjiani, Nadia Tereszkiewicz, Kumail Nanjiani and Max Greenfield.

Written and directed by series creator White, Season 4 is executive produced by White, David Bernad and Mark Kamine.

title: Golden Globes Vs Golden Globe: Infringement & Money Are Latest Legal Battlefields In Shindig Skirmish
summary: The 84th annual Golden Globes Awards are months away, but the once boozy and sometimes unhinged ceremony is front and center right now, at least in the court dockets. Two months after the remnants of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association sued Penske Media Corporation for its part in Dick Clark Productions’ purchase of the Golden […]
content:
The 84th annual Golden Globes Awards are months away, but the once boozy and sometimes unhinged ceremony is front and center right now, at least in the court dockets.

Two months after the remnants of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association sued Penske Media Corporation for its part in Dick Clark Productions‘ purchase of the Golden Globes in 2023 with allegations of monopolization and fraudulent misrepresentation, the Penske-controlled Golden Globes is going after the Golden Globe Foundation for trademark infringement and unfair competition.

Now, if you need to take a moment and re-read that to separate the Globes from the Globe, we get that — it’s a lot. It also might be a good time to remind that PMC is the parent company of Deadline owners PMX.

Watch on Deadline

In this particular point of legal loggerheads, the Golden Globes says it needs a jury to step in and get the foundation to stop trying to muddy the waters around its brand.

Putting emphasis on Golden Globe Foundation board boss Raffi Boghosian, the Golden Globes’ four-claim complaint details: “Defendant has adopted and continued using the GOLDEN GLOBE mark as part of its corporate name and in connection with a broad array of activities, including hosting events, conducting auctions, awarding grants, publishing materials, and developing merchandise—activities that are confusingly similar to Plaintiff’s business and have caused and threaten to continue to cause consumer confusion—without authorization from Plaintiff and over Plaintiff’s express demand that Defendant cease such use.”

The Globes and its Sidley Austin attorneys are seeking an injunction to stop the GGF from using said mark and a trophy cabinet of unspecified damages to make sure they don’t try to do it again.

The filing also alleges that “GGF’s activities and use of the GOLDEN GLOBE Mark have also expanded well beyond its stated charitable mission” to now engage “in other commercial and quasi-commercial activities.” In fact, the September 30 filing in federal court insists the non-plural foundation rejected a 2025 cease-and-desist letter and cut off licensing negotiations in July when Boghosian took over the GGF.

As well as listing the HFPA scandals over the years and the havoc and near death they brought to the Golden Globe Awards’ lucrative TV rights, the complaint says the “GGF’s unauthorized and expanding use of the GOLDEN GLOBE Mark is part of a broader pattern of coordination between GGF and the HFPA directed against Plaintiff and its affiliates.”

Then there’s that previous lawsuit. As always, there’s also the money.

“On information and belief, GGF and the HFPA have since entered into or are in the process of finalizing a settlement of the HFPA’s claims against GGF that would result in GGF transferring charitable funds to the HFPA,” the Golden Globes filing asserts.

“On information and belief, the HFPA’s inclusion of GGF as a defendant was a pretext designed to facilitate this transfer, and the settlement is intended to redirect charitable funds to finance the HFPA’s lawsuit and other private disputes against Plaintiff. This coordination between GGF and the HFPA further demonstrates that GGF’s continued use of the GOLDEN GLOBE Mark is not undertaken in good faith, but rather as part of a concerted effort to trade on the goodwill of Plaintiff’s mark while acting in alignment with the HFPA against Plaintiff’s interests.”

Guess what? The GGF doesn’t see it that way, or at least not with that characterization.

“The Golden Globe Foundation was created in 2023 as part of the same deal that sold the Golden Globes to the company now suing us,” GGF spokesman Nate Miller said in a statement Tuesday. “That company then promoted our name. The Golden Globes’ president welcomed guests to our first grants dinner, where we gave $5 million to 96 organizations, and publicly thanked Penske Media’s own Robb Report for supporting the Foundation.

They went on to say: “Now that company, owned by Penske Media and billionaire Todd Boehly’s Eldridge, is suing a nonprofit that supports schools and press freedom over the same name it once celebrated. This lawsuit is a transparent attempt to pressure the Foundation, and we will answer it in court.”

As these lawsuits ramp up, so does awards season.

To that, the submission deadline for the 2027 Golden Globes is October 30. Nikki Glaser will be back for a third time hosting the ceremony when it airs on January 10 live on CBS and streaming on Paramount+.

title: Doc Talk Podcast: David And Liani Greaves On Their Oscar Contender ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’
summary: Once Upon a Time in Harlem is continuing its strong push for Oscar recognition, earning five nominations Tuesday for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards. That’s added to the distinction of premiering at Sundance, and being honored with berths at the Cannes, Telluride, Toronto and New York film festivals – the only documentary to do so […]
content:
Once Upon a Time in Harlem is continuing its strong push for Oscar recognition, earning five nominations Tuesday for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards. That’s added to the distinction of premiering at Sundance, and being honored with berths at the Cannes, Telluride, Toronto and New York film festivals – the only documentary to do so this year.

The film directed by David Greaves and produced by Liani Greaves (David’s daughter) is based on extraordinary footage from an event in 1972 – a reunion for one afternoon only of the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance. They gathered at the home of Duke Ellington for what would be a final opportunity to renew friendships, share stories and engage in vigorous debate about the Harlem Renaissance, its artists and scholars, and Black cultural and political life in America.

Watch on Deadline

The documentary, based on material shot by William Greaves – David’s father and Liani’s grandfather – opens theatrically in New York this Friday and in Los Angeles on October 23. David and Liani join the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss their remarkable nonfiction feature and how they crafted it from almost 30 hours of raw footage.

David was one of the original cameramen on the 1972 shoot. He recalls working with his father to capture the once-in-a-lifetime gathering and how William wanted the finished film “to be a theatrical experience that moves at a snappy pace.” Liani reflects on her grandfather who was a true Renaissance man himself: actor, sculptor, poet, dancer, songwriter and filmmaker.

RELATED: ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’ Trailer: Oscar Contender Reveals Extraordinary Reunion Of Harlem Renaissance Leaders

The Greaves also explore the interpersonal dynamics at play in the reunion of so many artists and thinkers who gathered that day in Harlem. Disagreements emerged among the group on how to define the Harlem Renaissance and whether its legacy would continue or be lost. The Greaves speak to the importance of women to the Harlem Renaissance and how their integral role is sometimes overlooked.

Certain frictions or frustrations became apparent during the reunion as some of those women tried to make their voices heard in the din of lively conversation.

Liani Greaves reveals why the presence of George Schuyler at the gathering triggered strong emotions among some of the attendees (having to do with his contrarian politics). She also relates one unflattering remark aimed at Schuyler — a moment not included in the documentary. Doc Talk co-host John Ridley explains why he particularly identified with comments made in the film by Richard Bruce Nugent, one of those fascinating living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance featured in the documentary.

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

title: Bay Theater In Pacific Palisades To Reopen For First Time Since 2025 Fires As Paramount Takes Over Venue
summary: Going on two years after the wildfires that devastated Pacific Palisades and other Los Angeles-area neighborhoods, a popular moviehouse is ready for its closeup. Paramount Pictures and real estate developer Rick Caruso said Tuesday that the Bay Theater in Palisades Village will reopen before year’s end. The high-end five-screen venue at 1035 N. Swarthmore Ave., […]
content:
Going on two years after the wildfires that devastated Pacific Palisades and other Los Angeles-area neighborhoods, a popular moviehouse is ready for its closeup. Paramount Pictures and real estate developer Rick Caruso said Tuesday that the Bay Theater in Palisades Village will reopen before year’s end.

The high-end five-screen venue at 1035 N. Swarthmore Ave., shuttered since the Palisades Fire in early January 2025, is being restored, and luxury cinema operator The Lot will manage it. Along with first-run movies and classics, the Bay will host special screenings and immersive theatrical experiences, said Paramount, which is taking over the theater formerly operated by Netflix and Cinepolis before that.

“Together with Caruso, we are proud to help bring the Bay back to life as a place for the Pacific Palisades community to gather around the shared experience of cinema,” said David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance. “This theater has always meant more than movies alone — it’s woven into the fabric of this neighborhood, and helping restore it is a privilege. We’re inspired by the resilience of Pacific Palisades residents, and we’re honored to help support this community’s comeback.”

Watch on Deadline

The surrounding Caruso-owned Palisades Village reopened during the summer, and now the Bay Theater is set open its doors by the end of 2026, though no date is set.

The original Bay Theater opened down the road on Sunset Boulevard in 1949 before closing in 1978. The venue’s current iteration debuted in 2018.

“The Bay has always been at the heart of the Palisades,” said Caruso, who was runner-up in the race for Los Angeles mayor in 2022, “and its return is one of the most meaningful signs yet that this community … is coming back stronger than ever.”

The Lot, which will oversee operations for the Bay, runs luxury dine-in theaters in La Jolla, Newport Beach and other California cities.

title: Judge Extends Block on Trump’s White House Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
summary: Following President Donald Trump’s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico last month, a federal judge has once again blocked him from doing so. U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly wrote in the ruling issued Tuesday evening that the outlets are “likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also […]
content:
Following President Donald Trump‘s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico last month, a federal judge has once again blocked him from doing so.

U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly wrote in the ruling issued Tuesday evening that the outlets are “likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims.” Thus, the Court granted their motion for a preliminary injunction and extended the previously awarded relief, which will continue to preserve the status quo as the case proceeds.

“Still, no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed,” the judge noted.

Popular on Variety

The judge previously ordered the White House to immediately reinstate access to the news organizations on Sept. 24 after the president banned them initially. At the time, Kelly granted the news orgs’ motion for a temporary restraining order in their lawsuit against Trump and three White House officials, alleging the ban violated the First Amendment.

The White House must “immediately return, reinstate, and restore the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO that were revoked on or about September 18, 2026, until further Order of the Court or the expiration of this Temporary Restraining Order,” Kelly wrote in the ruling.

In September, Trump posted on social media that he was “proud to announce that, effective immediately,” he was “banning” the three outlets from the White House. When reporters from those news organizations arrived the following day, they were denied entry despite holding “hard passes.” CNN, MS NOW and Politico then sued Trump and three White House officials over the ban, alleging it violates the First Amendment and “brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint.”

title: Martha Plimpton Slams Shane Gillis’ ‘Really F—g Stupid’ ‘SNL’ Monologue: ‘He Deserves a Spanking From His Mom’
summary: Martha Plimpton has joined the list of stars speaking out over Shane Gillis’ poorly received “Saturday Night Live” opening monologue. “There’s this Shane Gillis guy who I’ve never heard of who said some really fucking stupid shit on live on air on ‘SNL’ on Saturday,” the “Goonies” star said in a video posted to her […]
content:
Martha Plimpton has joined the list of stars speaking out over Shane Gillis’ poorly received “Saturday Night Live” opening monologue.

“There’s this Shane Gillis guy who I’ve never heard of who said some really fucking stupid shit on live on air on ‘SNL’ on Saturday,” the “Goonies” star said in a video posted to her Instagram. “It’s like really stupid shit. He deserves a spanking from his mom.”

Plimpton also spoke about watching a documentary about Lore Michaels, who created and executive produced the sketch comedy show. “There was one scene that took place in Lorne’s office where in between the rehearsal taping and the live show, a bunch of people gather in Lorne’s office to decide what’s gonna get cut and what’s gonna make it to air. It was all white men in the room deciding. All white men. And maybe even all straight white men,” she said. “I think Lorne needs some more women in that room making decisions. Don’t you? Yeah, I think so.” She continued to shout out her love of ‘SNL’ mainstay Kenan Thompson, who commented on the video. “Shane Who?” her caption read.

Popular on Variety

Gillis sparked outrage over his misogynistic opening monologue nearly immediately after he took the stage on Saturday night. The bulk of the criticism he’s faced is the result of a joke about women’s workout clothes. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” he said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.”

Dan Levy shared an Instagram Reel on Sunday reacting to the monologue in disbelief. “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists,” he said. “There’s a difference there. By the way, I’ve seen more men’s nipples at the gym than I’ve ever seen women showing their bodies off.”

title: ‘All About Corinne’ Review: Isabelle Huppert Stalks Sandrine Kiberlain in a Witty, Deliciously Acted French Industry Satire
summary: As one of the select few French actresses who has earned definite-article status in her homeland — referred to routinely as La Huppert, alongside the likes of La Binoche and La Deneuve — it’s immediately, amusingly jarring to see Isabelle Huppert cast as a thoroughly indefinite article: a jobbing movie extra whose name nobody recalls, […]
content:
As one of the select few French actresses who has earned definite-article status in her homeland — referred to routinely as La Huppert, alongside the likes of La Binoche and La Deneuve — it’s immediately, amusingly jarring to see Isabelle Huppert cast as a thoroughly indefinite article: a jobbing movie extra whose name nobody recalls, no matter how many headshots and résumés she desperately forces into the hands of higher-ups on set. Casting Huppert as an industry nobody is the chief gag of “All About Corinne,” Marc Fitoussi‘s winningly droll film-biz comedy, but there turns out to be a lot of mileage in it, particularly with co-star Sandrine Kiberlain — cast not just as an industry somebody, but as Sandrine Kiberlain herself — as her imperious foil.

Both sending themselves up in contrasting ways, the stars’ perceptive, vanity-free performances lend some weight and feeling to what is otherwise a frothy exercise — as is to be expected from Fitoussi, a specialist in female-driven French divertissements, including the uncharacteristically chipper Huppert vehicle “Copacabana” and the recent Laure Calamy hit “Two Tickets to Greece.” Given its starry, easy-breezy charms and accessibly inside-baseball humor, “All About Corinne” should have little trouble securing global arthouse distribution following a festival run that began as Locarno’s closing night selection, continuing through gala slots in Toronto and Busan; audiences au fait with “Call Your Agent!” and its good-humored brand of industry satire will feel right at home.

Popular on Variety

“You might want to ask yourself why you’re still in the same place at your age,” says a colleague, with casual cruelty, to Corinne Maclou (Huppert), an actress who, for decades, has been steadily and invisibly working at the least glamorous end of the business — and who, in her sixties, hasn’t yet given up hope of stardom. In fringe theater, at least, she’s had the odd inspired moment in the spotlight; in film, she’s lumped with countless other, younger extras and bit players, fighting for the rare gift of a single line.

Not for lack of ability — Huppert may dim her light a bit, but doesn’t stretch so far as to play a bad actor — she’s simply never had the break, and while Corinne’s efforts to ingratiate herself with A-listers are played for squirm-inducing comedy, there’s also gentle pathos to her desperation, underlined by the ironic star casting. She knows, and we know, that she’s a Huppert-level talent. Why can no one else see it?

Corinne’s standard line to try curry favor with bigger-name actresses is to cheerfully remark on their physical resemblance to each other, noting that they could play sisters — an approach that doesn’t get the diminutive redhead far with the tall, beachy-haired Kiberlain when they share a scene (or at least occupy the same frame) together. But Corinne’s persistence coincides with a sudden phase of insecurity for the soignée leading lady, who’s trying to cultivate a more down-to-earth image after her agent pithily tells her that “even Cotillard is less detached from reality.” And so she pityingly takes Corinne’s CV, as well as the proferred recording of an obscure Chilean play which Corinne believes to be her finest hour.

Nothing comes of it, of course, until months later, when Corinne sees the news that Kiberlain is taking to the Paris stage in a production of the very same play, and bitterly confronts her outside the theater. Out of resentment and shamefaced guilt, a highly conditional friendship is forged, as each actress uses the other to very different ends: In Kiberlain, Corinne sees her long-awaited connection to the top; through Corinne, Kiberlain believes she can keep it real. Fitoussi’s writing is fizzy and lightly bitchy throughout, but it’s the stars, playing freely with their respective screen personae, who make it genuinely funny. In a more obvious iteration of this story, their roles might be swapped: There’s as much inherent comedy in Huppert playing a spiraling, faintly tragic rube as in Kiberlain, best known for her neurotic comic work, revealing the brittle hauteur of her “real” self.

Other good sports turning up as themselves, to wickedly unflattering effect, include Emmanuelle Bercot, tetchily directing a big-budget period drama that could turn things around for Corinne, and Diane Kruger — hilariously glamazonian as she competes with Kiberlain for maximum miscasting in a new Dardenne Brothers film about a tiler in Liège. If that raises a chuckle from you, as it certainly did from this critic, then consider yourself squarely in the film’s target audience. You can cut precisely without cutting too deep: More sweet than scathing, “All About Corinne” loves its stars too much to really draw blood. We love them too, so that’s just fine.

title: Kelly Clarkson vs. Art of Play: Footage Revealed of Singer’s Visit to Brooklyn Novelty Store She Slammed for ‘Pretty Woman’ Treatment
summary: Footage of Kelly Clarkson visiting the Brooklyn novelty store she slammed on Saturday has now been acquired and released by Pablo Torre, the host and executive editor of the investigative podcast, “Pablo Torre Finds Out.” The video offers another perspective to the ongoing drama between Clarkson and Art of Play, the Brooklyn local business she […]
content:
Footage of Kelly Clarkson visiting the Brooklyn novelty store she slammed on Saturday has now been acquired and released by Pablo Torre, the host and executive editor of the investigative podcast, “Pablo Torre Finds Out.”

The video offers another perspective to the ongoing drama between Clarkson and Art of Play, the Brooklyn local business she alleged gave her the “Pretty Woman” treatment when an employee looked at the singer as though she “couldn’t afford” Molly, the $15,000 bird automaton she inquired about purchasing. “Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote on X before naming the store.

Clarkson can be seen wearing a baseball hat, bright yellow T-shirt, baggy jeans and a backpack in the video. She enters the store with her children, browses and picks up a few items as more shoppers continue to enter. From footage from an alternative camera angle, we can see Clarkson then find herself standing in front of the automaton bird, where she then gets the attention of a store employee, who can be seen speaking with the musician and pointing at something by the bird, though it is not clear from the video what he was pointing at.

Popular on Variety

After Art of Play shared a statement in response on Sunday, writing that the bird is “permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale” and “plays an important role in the magic shows we host here,” a skeptical Clarkson responded once again, describing the interaction now seen on video and writing: “Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍 so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.’”

At this point in the footage, Clarkson and the employee part ways as he begins helping other customers in the store. Clarkson then puts back the items she was holding, but before she leaves, she turns around and speaks to another employee behind the counter, gesticulating, seemingly upset about the earlier interaction. Other shoppers in the store can be seen looking back at Clarkson, whose entire visit to the store lasted less than five minutes. Her first tweet about the interaction was posted 15 minutes after she left.

While some are staunchly pro-Clarkson in the debate that has since taken over the internet, others have questioned the singer’s motives for calling out the small business across her social media accounts. In an interview with Inside Edition on Tuesday, store owner Adam Rubin said that his store has been review-bombed since Clarkson took to social media and named the store, and employees and surrounding businesses have been harassed. “We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger… Things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It’s just social warfare,” he said. Rubin also offered an explanation for why Clarkson might have felt she received subpar treatment: “When Kelly came in, the shop was crowded. She was dressed like everybody else in the shop. We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that did not live up to her expectations.”

Art of Play is described as a specialty curiosity shop and online retailer.

Watch the full footage here.

title: ‘A Chronicle Of Minor Things’ & ‘Goldfish’ Among Award Winners At Busan’s Asian Project Market
summary: A Chronicle Of Minor Things, from Indian filmmaker Tribeny Rai, picked up the APM Busan Award and the Sorfond Award at the close of this year’s Asian Project Market in Busan. The jury said the project stood out for its original story and narrative structure, and for the director’s ability to weave a social issue […]
content:
A Chronicle Of Minor Things, from Indian filmmaker Tribeny Rai, picked up the APM Busan Award and the Sorfond Award at the close of this year’s Asian Project Market in Busan.

The jury said the project stood out for its original story and narrative structure, and for the director’s ability to weave a social issue subtly into the story, while the project’s distinctive landscape and themes were also recognized for their potential to appeal to international audiences.

Casparina, from Indonesian filmmaker Reza Rahadian, received the CJ ENM Award for transforming the director’s most personal story into a family drama with universal emotional resonance.

Goldfish from Indonesia’s Aditya Ahmad picked up three awards: the VIPO Award, the Kongchak Studio Award and the QCinema Special Award. VIPO recognized the project for its “fresh exploration of identity against a changing environment and the production feasibility demonstrated by the close collaboration between its director and producer”.

Watch on Deadline

E Del Mundo’s Once Upon a Time in the Philippines received the ArteKino International Award for its “original analysis of structural violence and the individual’s capacity to resist it”. Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung’s Satellite Of Love received the Songwon Award for its original story, strong visual vision, and ability to contain the complex dimensions of love within a simple narrative.

The CathayPlay Award went to Taiwanese director Yen Hao-hsuan’s Uncle, which draws on Yen’s personal experience to explore family, shame and belonging in a rapidly changing Taiwan.

The Kantana Picture Award went to Korean filmmaker Kim Jinyeong’s Red Hunger for its strong storytelling and visual potential, while Fatimah, from Thailand’s Panu Aree, received the Kantana Virtual Production Award for its story spanning dual identities, long-buried family secrets, and a journey across both geographic and internal landscapes.

This year’s APM, which takes place as part of Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), received a record 604 submissions from 48 countries, with 30 projects from 17 countries participating as official selections. Eight projects received awards across 11 categories. See below for the full list of award winners.
