title: Aaron Paul Mourns ‘Breaking Bad’ Co-Star RJ Mitte: “I Am So Sorry You Were Hurting, My Friend”
summary: Aaron Paul paid tribute to his Breaking Bad co-star RJ Mitte after his death at 34. The actor, who played Jesse Pinkman in the AMC series, took to social media to memorialize Mitte. “RJ, You have always been an inspiration for so many. I am so sorry you were hurting my friend. I wish we knew,” Paul wrote. […]
content:
Aaron Paul paid tribute to his Breaking Bad co-star RJ Mitte after his death at 34.

The actor, who played Jesse Pinkman in the AMC series, took to social media to memorialize Mitte.

“RJ, You have always been an inspiration for so many. I am so sorry you were hurting my friend. I wish we knew,” Paul wrote. “You constantly had a smile on your face and you took every single challenge that was given to you with such confidence and grace.”

He continued, “I met you when you were a little boy and watched you grow into a beautiful young man. Taking on every challenge head on.”

Watch on Deadline

Paul noted that the last time he saw Mitte he kept calling him Superman, adding, “You reminded me of him. You reminded me of him because you always led with kindness and strength. It was blinding. You were born into a world with challenges but you never let any of that stand in your way.”

The actor called Mitte’s death “an absolute tragic loss” and made a note to anyone in a difficult situation.

“I hope whoever is reading this note that feels lost or sad or uncertain about the future please say something. Life is so damn special,” he wrote. “It’s impossible that we exist, but yet we all are here. There is so much going on in all of our lives but far too much beauty in this world to ignore. We need to focus on that. We must suffocate the noise and focus on each other. Hold each other up. That’s what this life is all about. Connect with someone you care about and say I love you.”

Mitte’s reps confirmed the news, saying he died by suicide in Brownsville, Texas.

Paul ended his post saying, “RJ, love you my friend. I’m so sorry.”

If you or anyone you know is having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.

Read Paul’s complete message below.

title: Ashley Blaine Featherson-Jenkins & Christina Elmore Launch Tomorrow/Today, Acquire ‘Black Girl, Jump’ For TV Development
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Actor-producers Ashley Blaine Featherson-Jenkins & Christina Elmore are making it official: with the pre-emptive acquisition of TV rights to Black Girl, Jump, a young adult horror novel from Charlene Thomas, they announce the launch of their new production banner, Tomorrow/Today. Featherson-Jenkins and Elmore are on a mission, per the former, “to center voices that […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Actor-producers Ashley Blaine Featherson-Jenkins & Christina Elmore are making it official: with the pre-emptive acquisition of TV rights to Black Girl, Jump, a young adult horror novel from Charlene Thomas, they announce the launch of their new production banner, Tomorrow/Today.

Featherson-Jenkins and Elmore are on a mission, per the former, “to center voices that have been siloed and celebrate talent that’s been sidelined.” They launched Tomorrow/Today — quietly, in 2025 — after deciding they were no longer interested in waiting for permission to make the art they craved.

“The name says it plainly: no day is promised, so tomorrow has to be today, and bold stories that are worth telling should be made now instead of someday,” Featherson-Jenkins said

Watch on Deadline

Elmore said the duo aims “to elevate artists and storytellers with urgent stories they just can’t shake.”

Tomorrow/Today’s first major acquisition, Black Girl, Jump, is billed as Bunny meets Get Out. It’s a surreal speculative novel centered on a popular cosmetic that makes all girls shine, except for Black girls. That is, until Bryn — the only Black girl invited to attend an exclusive summer retreat — discovers a skin-boiling river in the woods that makes her sparkle, too, and reveals the lengths the girls and the town will go to in order to steal her shine.

The novel, from the author of Seton Girls and It’s You Every Time, is slated for publication by Dutton on June 8, 2027.

Featherson-Jenkins is best known as Joelle in Netflix’s Dear White People, and co-created web series Hello Cupid with Lena Waithe. She also hosts OWN’s podcast Trials to Triumphs and has appeared in Run the World, Grand Crew, Ghosts and the documentary Black Barbie. She is repped by Vault Entertainment and Fox Rothschild.

Elmore was a five-season regular on TNT’s The Last Ship and played Marie in Lena Waithe’s Twenties. She received an NAACP Image Award nomination for a guest turn on HBO’s Insecure and was a lead in HBO Max’s The Girls on the Bus. She is repped by Gersh, OPE Partners and Hansen, Jacobsen, Teller.

Author Thomas is represented by IAG and Ann Rose at Marsal Lyon Literary Agency (formerly of The Tobias Literary Agency at the time of sale).

title: ‘Abbott Elementary’ Star William Stanford Davis Sets Memoir ‘Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” via BenBella Books. “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” will dive into Davis’ life and career — including struggles such as addiction and rejection — and the experience of nabbing his […]
content:
William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” via BenBella Books.

“Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” will dive into Davis’ life and career — including struggles such as addiction and rejection — and the experience of nabbing his breakout role at age 70. Per the official description, Davis’ story is written in three parts: “The first will chronicle Davis’ childhood in the 1960s in the Ville, a predominantly Black neighborhood in St. Louis. The second will follow him as a young man, fresh off the bus in ‘country-ass’ Jefferson City in the early 1970s. The final section will chronicle Davis’ journey, well into his forties, from addict to working actor, and the years of perseverance, rejection and hard-earned experience that ultimately led to the biggest role of his career.”

“Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” was sold to BenBella Books editor and CEO Glen Yeffeth by Miles Blim at Aevitas Creative Management in association with Innovative Artists. It will be released in hardcover, e-book, and audiobook formats.

Popular on Variety

Besides “Abbott Elementary,” Davis’ credits include the Wanda Sykes film “Undercard,” Apple TV’s “Swagger,” HBO’s “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Showtime’s “Ray Donovan” and ABC’s “Lincoln Heights.”

“I’ve wanted to write this memoir for a long time, to honor the road I’ve taken to get here and to connect with folks who are still on their way,” Davis said in a statement. “People know me as Mr. Johnson from ‘Abbott Elementary,’ and while that’s the biggest role of my career so far, it’s not the whole story. I’m excited to finally share the full story: the struggles, the setbacks, the second chances and the perseverance it took to keep going and get to where I am today. It took me a long time to get here, and the beautiful thing is, I’m just getting started.”

title: ‘Lanterns’ Season 2 Won’t Be Greenlit Until the Writers’ Room ‘Comes Up With a Worthy Successor to a Great First Season’
summary: While HBO’s “Lanterns” hasn’t yet scored a second season renewal, one could be on the way depending on how things go in the writers’ room, according to DC Studios co-chief Peter Safran. While he didn’t confirm an exact date fans can expect an announcement to come on, Safran did note that news on whether “Lanterns” […]
content:
While HBO’s “Lanterns” hasn’t yet scored a second season renewal, one could be on the way depending on how things go in the writers’ room, according to DC Studios co-chief Peter Safran.

While he didn’t confirm an exact date fans can expect an announcement to come on, Safran did note that news on whether “Lanterns” will get a second season should arrive “before the end of the year” in a recent interview with Collider. Safran also noted that Season 2 would need to be up to par with Season 1, which enjoyed a massively successful premiere and run. “If we’re able to come up with what we believe to be a worthy successor to a beloved and great first season, that’s what’s going to dictate whether there’s a second season,” he said.

Safran added that the most rewarding part of Season 1’s success has been seeing the “Green Lantern” property back in the cultural conversation. (“Lanterns” was adapted from DC Comics’ “Green Lantern” franchise, which follows an intergalactic police force.)

Popular on Variety

The eight-episode show’s season finale aired on Oct. 4, and wrapped up the central mystery of who killed Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and revealed the identity of the second Manhunter, plus how John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) becomes Earth’s sole Green Lantern in DC Studios’ forthcoming “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”

Before the finale, Variety reported that the show’s seventh episode reached 7 million viewers in the U.S. in its first three days of availability. Previous episodes had averaged over 12 million viewers per episode in the U.S. to date and nearly 19 million when factoring in international viewing.

title: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes
summary: Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profound diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day — saying much in the process about the voices, inner and otherwise, that we grant most control in our lives, for […]
content:
Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profound diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day — saying much in the process about the voices, inner and otherwise, that we grant most control in our lives, for better or worse. Though its structuring principle of a single day playing out twice consecutively to differing effect (as opposed to braiding its alternate timelines like “Sliding Doors” or “Blind Chance”) explicitly recalls Hong Sangsoo’s “Right Now, Wrong Then,” this chicly poised debut feature by fellow South Korean Lim Hayeon has a style, tone and outlook of its own, maintained with impressive control over a surprisingly breezy-feeling 145 minutes.

One of the real discoveries in this year’s main competition at the Busan Film Festival, “Beach Fictions” should have little difficulty charming other programmers on the international fest circuit following its world premiere — while only its running time, manageable but unexpectedly robust for a film this light on its feet, presents an obstacle to global arthouse distribution, or at least specialist streaming exposure. Either way, this graduation project (produced by the Korean Academy of Film Arts) announces its writer-director-editor as one to watch, should her future films match this one’s warmth and formal elegance; in only her second big-screen outing after years of TV work, winsome lead Hansol Park also feels like a breakout talent.

Popular on Variety

“Beach Fictions” pulls you in from its first iridescent frame, as Sinuk Park’s camera glides serenely from a bejeweled nighttime view of Incheon through the chattery hubbub of a mood-lit restaurant where Tae-ju (Park), seen only from behind, is dining with friends, their conversation seemingly more animated than hers. Even without the detached voiceover — which turns out to belong to perceptive novelist Ewha (Sujeong Ye), describing the superficial response of Tae-ju’s friends to an anecdote she shares — we’d sense her loneliness amid company. Later, when her friends abandon her at the table to smoke outside, she’s crushed to find them gossiping about her; shortly afterwards, in a never-rains-but-pours development, she breaks up with her casual boyfriend Hyun-jin after he expresses scant interest in taking the relationship further.

With her social life in tatters and a world of her anxieties realized, Tae-ju rashly skips town, heading for the tranquil coastal guesthouse of another friend. On the train there, she encounters Ewha, whom we’ve already seen observing her from afar at the restaurant, and confides in the kindly, silver-haired older woman — who says Tae-ju resembles the protagonist of the novel she’s currently writing. But is she the writer’s inspiration or her creation, an incomplete fiction who has somehow taken on an agency of her own? From here on out, the authorship of Tae-ju’s life is ambiguous, as well as constantly in flux, buffeted by the whims and suggestions of others, as well as by her own impulses.

In the sleepy beach town, she meets and is immediately entranced by charismatic street magician Manhyuk (Kim Wookyum, delightful), only to later be warned off him by her hostess, who claims he’s a local lothario and sometime sex worker. A day in his company turns sour but when, in the film’s deftly shuffled second half, she meets him in slightly different circumstances, and the day’s events take on a different chain of connections, the potential romantic outcome differs too.

Her nascent relationship with Manhyuk is the chief variable of Tae-ju’s two stories, but other, slighter factors push it this way and that: a water-damaged phone in need of repair; a hangout with fellow guesthouse patrons that echoes or corrects her earlier social fallout; and a consultation with a psychic, recommended by Ehwa, whose counsel also shifts her fate. The contrasts between the two tales are never drastic; the gradations are sometimes as fine as those between warm and cool melancholy. The camerawork is consistently, richly sun-flooded, but some compositions isolate Tae-ju more than others; Wonhong Lee’s delicate jazz piano score can similarly tilt a situation from cozy to nervy.

But both gently lolloping narratives hold the attention, in large part thanks to Park’s deeply sympathetic performance as Hae-ju, simultaneously played as a fragile, will-o’-the-wisp go-alonger — or perhaps just an author’s as-yet-unformed blank canvas — and a wounded flesh-and-blood human now guarding her emotions more carefully. It’s a canny turn completely in synch with Lim’s complex, metatextual script, which brims with ideas about the fictional construction process, as well the real-life bind felt by vulnerable young women expected to bend to others’ desires and expectations. Is life itself not just a series of drafts and redrafts, with notes we either learn from or don’t, our characters never not in progress? Wry and wise and happy-sad, “Beach Fictions” crosses nothing out, alive to all possibilities.

title: Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning)
summary: Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing. Luca Guadagnino’s genre-blending movie about the evils of artificial intelligence (and one of its fathers, Sam Altman) had a triumphant U.K. premiere at the London Film Festival on Sunday. The director, standing beside key cast members Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov, received thunderous applause at Royal Festival Hall. […]
content:
Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing.

Luca Guadagnino’s genre-blending movie about the evils of artificial intelligence (and one of its fathers, Sam Altman) had a triumphant U.K. premiere at the London Film Festival on Sunday. The director, standing beside key cast members Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov, received thunderous applause at Royal Festival Hall.

The British event followed the world premiere of “Artificial” a week earlier at the New York Film Festival. It was a make-or-break moment for a project plagued by scandal after Amazon MGM punted the film off its summer slate. Worse was what came after: an odious whisper campaign saying the film stank (anonymous sources dismissed it as only worthy of a streaming release, according to a July report). But the Big Apple swallowed the film with rapture.

“So this is a dawn-of-a-new-world story, as well as a backstabbing corporate business story, and also a horror movie, in which AI emerges from the lab as a sinister serpent,” wrote Variety chief critic Owen Gleiberman in his review, calling the movie a “brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history.”

Popular on Variety

Others agree. The title has a 96% Fresh rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, representing the highest score of Guadagnino’s career across 11 feature film releases. Garfield has been catapulted to the front of the best supporting actor race, thanks to a performance that delivers “a masterclass in diabolical villainy,” according to another review.

The notices, the standing ovations, the awards buzz — all of it represents a stunning reversal of fortune for Guadagnino after the Amazon debacle in June. It was highly uncommon, in Hollywood terms, for even a tech-owned content studio to kill a project it had cradled since infancy. Neon rescued the movie with a global rights deal shortly after the Amazon rift.

“We believe that ‘Artificial’ will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” the e-commerce giant said at the time. Global press almost unanimously noted that the decision to jettison the movie came only three months after Amazon signed a significant partnership with Altman’s OpenAI (including a $50 billion investment in the company).

But, per Variety’s sources, the writing is on the wall. Nothing was wrong with “Artificial,” and the response underlines the dubiousness of Amazon’s decision to drop it.

“Wasn’t this supposed to be god-awful?” wondered one film executive at a rival studio. The exec didn’t just raise an eyebrow at Amazon MGM, but at other legacy distributors who were in the mix to take the project before Neon won out. “A reaction this strong just shows you, every studio pretending the film wasn’t releasable is just conflicted out by their own investments in AI.”

In July, New York magazine published a piece citing individuals close to the project as saying it “lacked theater-worthy criteria.” That doesn’t quite track with early audience response. In fact, the critical consensus is that “Artificial” — not Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” which debuted last weekend via Sony Pictures — is a worthy spiritual successor to David Fincher’s “The Social Network.” It’s hard to imagine Amazon not being pleased with this response had it kept “Artificial.”

Interestingly, Amazon’s headaches at the intersection of talent and AI are not exclusive to the Guadagnino movie. At New York Comic Con last weekend, actor Nicolas Cage made waves when he disclosed that he refused to sign a document permitting the studio to use AI in and around his likeness on its now-canceled original series “Spider-Noir.”

“I am not an AI-friendly actor. I’m not a member of their club. I didn’t sign the waiver,” Cage said. “I’m probably not going to be working with that studio again.” There’s a bit more to this story, insiders close to “Spider-Noir” said. Cage was referring to a form from the show’s producer, Sony Pictures Television, considered “industry standard” on content shoots. The waiver gives the studio permission to create a duplicate of an actor in costume, which aids in VFX work during postproduction. Actors are free to opt out, and the form is said to be in line with SAG-AFTRA guidelines.

But it won’t be the end of talent bristling over the coming AI revolution — at Amazon or elsewhere. One creative team member on an Amazon MGM series tells Variety that AI training is a requirement on the lot these days.

The source describes a “mandatory and perfunctory meeting” with the company’s AI team, billed as standard workplace education that corporations regularly hold around sexual harassment and fire safety. The AI group spent an hour pitching the creatives on a suite of products it referred to as “tools.” Our source says, however, it became clear that these tools could “eliminate entire jobs” on the production. Amazon MGM declined to comment on the matter.

More telling, per the source, is that the show’s corporate stewards from Amazon also sat through the training “stone-faced.” While the individual won’t name the execs in attendance, they found it “collectively embarrassing for everyone to be doing this, including on the Amazon side.” A source with direct knowledge of Amazon’s process said such meetings are not mandatory, and humans guide every part of the process related to the tools.

And so begins the great sacrifice the major studios are about to make in service of computer-based cost efficiencies and the “move fast and break things” bravado of Silicon Valley. Time will tell if a prompt can make content that’s as buzzy and well positioned as “Artificial.”

title: Shareholders Approve Fox’s $22 Billion Roku Acquisition
summary: With media M&A in the air, shareholders of both companies have approved Fox’s planned cash and stock acquisition of Roku at special meetings today. The approvals were expected. The deal announced in June – which will turbocharge Fox’s streaming capabilities – calls for the company run by Lachlan Murdoch to acquire Roku for $160 a […]
content:
With media M&A in the air, shareholders of both companies have approved Fox’s planned cash and stock acquisition of Roku at special meetings today.

The approvals were expected.

The deal announced in June – which will turbocharge Fox’s streaming capabilities – calls for the company run by Lachlan Murdoch to acquire Roku for $160 a share through a combination of cash and Fox Class A stock, giving Roku an enterprise valuation of $22 billion. On closing, Fox shareholders will own about 73% of the merged business, with Roku shareholders taking the other 27%.

Roku, founded in 2002, reaches around 100 million global streaming homes through its connected TV platform, and is in more than half of all U.S. broadband households. Fox operates its namesake broadcast network, a large local station portfolio, cable networks Fox News and Fox Business, subscription streamer Fox One, and a sports rights portfolio including the NFL, MLB, NASCAR, Big Ten and the FIFA World Cup.

Watch on Deadline

Fox said at the announcement that the Roku purchase would “create a scaled next-generation media and technology company positioned at the intersection of two of the most important forces reshaping video consumption: the enduring primacy of live sports and news, and the continued rise of streaming.”

Roku founder, chairman and CEO Anthony Wood will have an ongoing role at the combined company and will join the Fox board.

Fox Corp. President and Chief Operating Officer John Nallen told investors at a media conference last month that the deal is on track to close in the first half of next year despite a new request for information from regulators. He called the request by the U.S. Department of Justice “entirely expected.”

It’s the latest transformative deal in a rapidly transforming media landscape that just saw Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery close their merger, creating the new Skydance.

In an SEC filing today, Fox noted nearly 100% of votes in favor of the deal. Roku’s tally will come in a filing Thursday.

title: Kelsey Grammer Returning To NBC As Star Of EMT Drama In Development From ‘Chicago Med’ Alum
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Twenty two years after the end of Frasier, Kelsey Grammer is set to star in another potential NBC series, this time a drama. Grammer is headlining and executive producing Pops, which has entered development at the network. It is written by longtime Chicago Med writer-produced Danny Weiss. In Pops, Grammer plays the title character, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Twenty two years after the end of Frasier, Kelsey Grammer is set to star in another potential NBC series, this time a drama. Grammer is headlining and executive producing Pops, which has entered development at the network. It is written by longtime Chicago Med writer-produced Danny Weiss.

In Pops, Grammer plays the title character, a man aged out of a successful career who, in desperate need of a fresh start, jumps into the chaotic world of emergency medicine alongside first responders half his age.

The project is based on the true-life story of Ed Levien, a Maryland resident who became a volunteer EMT in his 60s after a successful career in advertising. Nicknamed “Pops” by his younger co-workers, he spent 12 years as EMT until returning last fall at the age of 76.

Pops draws parallels to ABC’s The Rookie, about LAPD’s oldest rookie, which also was based on a real person changing careers midlife. It also shares some similarities with the CBS sitcom Carol’s Second Act, starring Kelsey’s Back To Your co-lead Patricia Heaton as a divorced mom with adult children who goes to med school and becomes a 50-something medical intern. (Grammer guest starred alongside Heaton.)

Watch on Deadline

Weiss and Levien executive produce Pops alongside Grammer and Jordan McMahon via Grammer’s Grammnet NH Productions and 3 Arts Entertainment. Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group, is the studio.

Grammer has straddled comedy and drama throughout his career. His hourlong series credits include Starz’s Boss and Amazon’s The Last Tycoon. At NBC, he is reunited with his Frasier co-star David Hyde Pierce, who is starring in a multi-camera comedy in development.

Grammer was a fixture on NBC for more than two decades playing psychiatrist Dr. Frasier Crane across three series, Cheers, spinoff Frasier and Wings. The role, which he recently revisited for Paramount+’s Frasier revival, earned him four of his five Emmys.

Grammer will be seen in the upcoming film Avengers: Doomsday, out in December, reprising his MCU role as Dr. Henry “Hank” McCoy. His Grammnet company has produced such series as Medium and The Game. Grammer is repped by UTA and Vault Entertainment.

Weiss, a former US Marine, spent 10 seasons on NBC/Universal TV’s Chicago Med, rising through the ranks from staff writer to co-executive producer. His medical drama experience also includes writing a freelance episode of Fox/Universal TV’s House, M.D., where he spent four seasons as the in-house medical researcher. Weiss is repped by Echo Lake Entertainment and Frankfurt Kurnit Klein & Selz.

title: YouTube Puts AI Labels On Songs That Use The Tech For Vocals Or Composition
summary: The debate over whether Kanye used AI on his latest album Bully just got more interesting. YouTube Music today announced it “is rolling out labels to make it easier to see when a song was created primarily using generative AI.” An example the company gives is “using a generative model to create the composition and […]
content:
The debate over whether Kanye used AI on his latest album Bully just got more interesting.

YouTube Music today announced it “is rolling out labels to make it easier to see when a song was created primarily using generative AI.” An example the company gives is “using a generative model to create the composition and vocals.” It also noted that the music-related labeling will occur on the main YouTube app, apparently to identify when such a song is used.

“When you listen to a track on YouTube Music where AI played a significant role, you’ll see a label directly on the player page. Tapping the label opens a simple menu that shares more information,” the video giant indicated in a blog post. It also shared a sample layout of the label in action.

A 2026 report from The Business of Apps notes that YouTube is “Far ahead of all others in total usage with two billion users, but behind Spotify and Apple in paid subscribers.” That number is specific to music streaming.

Watch on Deadline

YouTube says it will use a combination of its own tech and info from its “music partners” to ID such tracks. The goal is to offer users “clarity when it comes to the music they listen to.”

Spotify initiated a AI tag earlier this year with is voluntary at the discretion of the music label or artist. The service also indictaed that it wouldn’t favor songs from “AI personas.” Apple Music is also reportedly getting an AI label.

title: Kathy Griffin Slams Shane Gillis & Other “Hacks” Under “Joe Rogan’s Influence”: “They All Tell The Same Jokes”
summary: As Saturday Night Live fans eviscerate Shane Gillis’ third hosting attempt, Kathy Griffin is weighing in on his controversial monologue. Following last weekend’s episode, the 2x Emmy winning comedian called out Gillis and other “hacks” under “Joe Rogan’s influence,” following backlash to Gillis calling women “whores” for wearing shorts at the gym. “I think as […]
content:
As Saturday Night Live fans eviscerate Shane Gillis‘ third hosting attempt, Kathy Griffin is weighing in on his controversial monologue.

Following last weekend’s episode, the 2x Emmy winning comedian called out Gillis and other “hacks” under “Joe Rogan‘s influence,” following backlash to Gillis calling women “whores” for wearing shorts at the gym.

“I think as a comic I’m always going to fight for the First Amendment and his right to say it and yet I don’t have to like it,” Griffin told the Page Six. “So, I defend his right to say it, and I also defend everyone else’s right to think less of him.

Gillis’ opening monologue during SNL was a tight five about getting into shape with workout buddies Rogan and Theo Von, during which he put on his best femme voice to mimic gym gays and complained that “women just dress like whores now” at the gym.

Watch on Deadline

While Gillis’ brief set bombed on Saturday, it also drew backlash from fellow comedians and fans alike, especially in the wake of an alleged gang rape by fraternity members known as the Cornell 7.

Griffin sees Rogan’s comedian manosphere as the issue, explaining “they all tell the same jokes,” often at the expense of women.

“There are a lot of hacks who are doing very well, and they come from TikTok or the podcast world,” she noted. “He’s not the only guy to break out from Joe Rogan’s influence.”

Griffin continued, “There are so many; they all look alike to me. They all look like they can’t get laid; they all sound alike to me; they all tell the same jokes… and they tell these jokes about women that are from like 100 years ago, like women should be in the kitchen and shut up and all this other stuff.”

Gillis’ latest hosting gig on SNL comes after he hosted in 2024 and 2025, following his removal from the NBC sketch comedy‘s featured cast days after he was announced in 2019. The decision came in response to resurfaced videos of Gillis mocking Asian accents, in addition to using ethnic and gay slurs.

title: MS NOW Corrects Report On FBI Director Kash Patel Landing In Russia: “We Regret This Error”
summary: FBI Director Kash Patel called on MS NOW to apologize to the agency after an erroneous report that he had landed in Russia. Citing two unnamed sources, the network’s Ken Dilanian reported during Peter Alexander’s show in the 11 a.m. ET hour that Patel had landed in the country for a meeting. The FBI’s Rapid […]
content:
FBI Director Kash Patel called on MS NOW to apologize to the agency after an erroneous report that he had landed in Russia.

Citing two unnamed sources, the network’s Ken Dilanian reported during Peter Alexander’s show in the 11 a.m. ET hour that Patel had landed in the country for a meeting.

The FBI’s Rapid Response account pushed back, posting video of Patel at Liberty University in Virginia.

Two hours later, during Alicia Menendez’s show in the 1 p.m. ET hour, Dilanian appeared on air again to said that he as correcting the report.

“We’ve since learned that Patel did not, in fact, land in Russia today and remains in the U.S. The FBI did not answer our questions when we asked them about it,” he said.

Watch on Deadline

Dilanian noted that there already had been reports that a Patel meeting in Russia was planned. Those reports raised “serious concerns, including among Democratic lawmakers who had urged Patel to call off the meeting which, according to published reports, was supposed to be happening today. But we do know now that he has not already landed in Russia, as we reported earlier. The timing of any potential trip remains unclear. Again, we regret this error, and we are transparent about when we make errors.”

Patel posted on X that MS NOW owes “an apology to this FBI, the men and women of law enforcement, and to the American people.” But he also focused on a separate MS NOW report that the FBI under his leadership had brought thousands fewer criminal cases than previous administration, despite Patel’s claims.

MS NOW just reported I had “landed in Russia” for meetings with the FSB. The same outlet constantly tells lies about this FBI and law enforcement’s historic achievements in safeguarding the American people.



The results speak for themselves:

• 53,969+ violent crime arrests (up… — FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) October 14, 2026

Dilanian defended that reporting, writing on X, “There has been a lot of commentary about this story. But no one at the FBI or anywhere else has disputed the DOJ data showing FBI criminal referrals down 15%. That’s thousands fewer criminal cases under @FBIDirectorKash, @dbongino and @FBIDDRaia than during the same period in the Biden Administration.”

An MS NOW spokesperson referred to Dilanian’s on air correction.

title: Anthony Edwards Names Justin Bieber ‘White Boy of the Year’ in Satirical Believe That Awards (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Move over, Chalamet — there’s a new white boy of the year. Minnesota Timberwolves player Anthony Edwards has brought back his satirical Believe That Awards, which went viral in 2025 — reaching 150 million cross-platform views — for crowning Timothée Chalamet white boy of the year. In the 2026 edition, that honorific went to Justin […]
content:
Move over, Chalamet — there’s a new white boy of the year.

Minnesota Timberwolves player Anthony Edwards has brought back his satirical Believe That Awards, which went viral in 2025 — reaching 150 million cross-platform views — for crowning Timothée Chalamet white boy of the year. In the 2026 edition, that honorific went to Justin Bieber, who beat out fellow nominees Tom Holland, Erling Haaland, Robert Pattinson and Travis Kelce. Bieber made an appearance in the awards special alongside fellow winners Michael B. Jordan, Druski, Coco Gauff, 50 Cent and more.

The Believe That Awards, now live on Edwards’ YouTube channel and social media profiles and presented by PrizePicks, are produced by Edwards through his Three Fifths Media banner alongside Wheelhouse and Portal A. The special is meant to “celebrates standout moments, cultural disruptors and iconic achievements across sports and entertainment, filtered through the unapologetic and uncensored lens of Edwards.”

Popular on Variety

The second annual Believe That Awards starring Anthony Edwards

“We’re back, and we raised the bar across the board this year,” Edwards said in a statement. “You know me, which means you know we have the same unfiltered, totally unpredictable energy that is always built for and aimed directly at the culture. We brought together the biggest names in the game to chop it up, have fun and celebrate real greatness on our own terms. You’re not getting this vibe anywhere else.”

“From day one, our mission at Three Fifths Media has been to create content that remains fiercely authentic to Anthony and the community that moves with him,” said Justin Holland, who is Edwards’ business manager and co-founder of Three Fifths Media. “The Believe That Awards sits at the true epicenter of sports, entertainment and culture. Year 2 proves that when you give creators and athletes the room to be themselves, audiences show up in a massive way.”

title: ‘Full House’ Star Jodie Sweetin Says Dave Coulier is ‘Doing Great’ Following ‘Tough Battle’ with Cancer
summary: Jodie Sweetin is giving fans a health update on her “Full House” co-star Dave Coulier, eight months after the actor announced he was in remission from tongue cancer. Speaking with People, Sweetin said Coulier is doing “really well,” and she’d just spent a weekend at his house with Andrea Barber, who played Kimmy Gibler on […]
content:
Jodie Sweetin is giving fans a health update on her “Full House” co-star Dave Coulier, eight months after the actor announced he was in remission from tongue cancer.

Speaking with People, Sweetin said Coulier is doing “really well,” and she’d just spent a weekend at his house with Andrea Barber, who played Kimmy Gibler on the ABC sitcom. The actress agreed Coulier has had “such a tough battle,” explaining that “sitting around and having coffee with him in the morning meant so much.” The two recently connected at an arts fundraiser in Detroit, which was “so much fun,” she added. “He’s doing great.”

Sweetin also noted their bond has lasted since acting on-screen together more than 30 years ago. “We’re still super close,” she said. “We’re all doing 90s Con in Hartford this coming weekend. Yeah, we’re like obnoxiously annoyingly close… We’re a family.”

Popular on Variety

Sweetin played Stephanie Tanner on the beloved sitcom, while Coulier played Joey Gladstone, Danny Tanner’s best friend (though he’s referred to as “Uncle Joey” on the show). “Full House” ran for eight seasons, from 1987 to 1995.

In Feb., Coulier revealed he was in remission after undergoing treatment for tongue cancer, a diagnosis he had shared in December. He had beaten Stage 3 non-Hodgkin Lymphoma nearly a year before that. “It’s been a roller coaster ride for sure,” Coulier said during an appearance on “Good Morning America.” “I’m in remission with both cancers. And what a journey this has been.”

Three months later, the actor took to social media to respond to fans who pointed out his changing appearance following both cancers, sharing on Instgram that he hadn’t been able to eat solid food in months and lost 45 pounds.

“Hi everyone, it’s me Dave, and I haven’t posted in quite a while and the last time I did some of you said that I look differently, and I sound differently, and I do,” he began the video. “And what you’re seeing is the side effects of extensive radiation that I went through for carcinoma in my throat… It’s affected my ability to speak, some of you have said that I speak differently. So you’re right on with what you’re seeing and what you’re hearing.”

title: FBI Adds Ex-Bellum Entertainment CEO To Most Wanted Fraudsters List; Offering $150K Reward For Info On Fugitive Mary Carole McDonnell
summary: In a true turn of events that would seem almost incredulous in a Hollywood script, the boss of a now defunct production company that specialized in true crime is wanted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Almost a decade after things started to go badly very quickly financially and otherwise for Bellum Entertainment, ex-CEO Mary […]
content:
In a true turn of events that would seem almost incredulous in a Hollywood script, the boss of a now defunct production company that specialized in true crime is wanted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Almost a decade after things started to go badly very quickly financially and otherwise for Bellum Entertainment, ex-CEO Mary Carole McDonnell has been placed on the FBI‘s Most Wanted Fraudsters list.

Assumed to be overseas in Dubai, UAE for the past few years, the 75-year old is accused of ripping California banks off to the tune of more than $29 million starting in 2017.

The feds are offering $150,000 for information that leads to McDonnell’s arrest and conviction.

Watch on Deadline

If found guilty on the five counts of bank fraud (which have maximum sentences of 30 years each), and the ID theft she was charged with in 2018, McDonnell could be facing 154 years behind bars. Though she would likely receive less than the max, it is clear former reality TV producer McDonnell would be going away for likely the rest of her life if convicted.

Now, if you think there is typo with that Most Wanted Fraudsters list, you’d be incorrect. More supplementing than replacing the famous FBI’s Most Wanted list, the currently 13 crook strong Most Wanted Fraudsters list was launched on June 4, 2026 to focus on white-collar crimes.

“The FBI’s historic Top 10 list focuses on violent criminals,” John Kent, Assistant Special Agent in Charge, FBI L.A. told Deadline today. “The Most Wanted Fraudsters list is a new way to elevate the focus on fugitives wanted for financial crimes.”

As far as McDonnell goes, the FBI does not tolerate the theft of 15 million dollars,” Kent added. “This woman was a Hollywood executive specializing in true crime content and allegedly crossed over into actual true crime. She conned her victims into believing she was an old money heiress when in reality she was a common thief.

To be specific, McDonnell convinced the banks that she was, according to the FBI, an “heir to the McDonnell Aircraft Family, with an $80 million secret trust to which she will have access.” Which makes it kinda clear why Bank of California and others would hand over millions to her without seemingly asking too many questions.

BTW – 2017, the year McDonnell allegedly scammed the banks was the same year that the Missouri-born exec, who also went by various aliases and is facing identity theft charges too, saw It Takes a Killer and Corrupt Crimes producer Bellum start to go belly-up. At the time, Bellum owed over $1 million to creditors, with more debts looming.

As Deadline’s late great David Robb reported in November 2017, the 2004 formed Bellum (originally called LongNeedle Entertainment) was sued separately by Armageddon Media and by Adirondack Entertainment for non-payment. Both companies claimed they made a 104-episode true crime series for Bellum that the company agreed to pay $3,097,000 for, but never did.

The non-paying Bellum was already under investigation at the time by the California Labor Commission for alleged nonpayment to former workers – including ex-cops and FBI agents who appeared as experts on the company’s shows. To make matters even more messy, round the same time, CEO McDonnell told current staff, including her company VP nephew, that a “significant bank fraud” was the reason no one was getting paid.

We may now have a better sense of what that “significant bank fraud” really was – though probably not how McDonnell intended.

title: ‘Crystal Lake’ Pays Tribute To Snake Killed In Making Of ‘Friday the 13th’: “A Direct Nod”
summary: More than 45 years after the first Friday the 13th, Brad Caleb Kane is righting a wrong from the set of the 1980 slasher. Ahead of Friday’s Crystal Lake premiere on Peacock, the series creator noted that a snake Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini) sets free after finding it in the camp pantry in the first […]
content:
More than 45 years after the first Friday the 13th, Brad Caleb Kane is righting a wrong from the set of the 1980 slasher.

Ahead of Friday’s Crystal Lake premiere on Peacock, the series creator noted that a snake Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini) sets free after finding it in the camp pantry in the first episode is “a direct nod” to a trained serpent that was actually killed while filming the original movie.

“But [Pam’s] a different person in the first episode than the kids are [in the movie],” he explained. “Yes, it’s a direct nod, but then it goes to the place of the first movie.”

Kane clarified: “But we don’t actually kill a snake in ours. No, no animals were harmed in the making of Crystal Lake. Some hippies might have been harmed in the making of Crystal Lake, but no animals.”

Watch on Deadline

During the filming of the original 1980 slasher Friday the 13th, a domesticated bull snake was infamously killed in real life while shooting the scene in which “final girl” Alice (Adrienne King) finds the reptile slithering around her cabin and calls for her fellow counselors to come help.

RELATED: 2026-27 Premiere Dates For New & Returning Series On Broadcast, Streaming & Cable

In the scene, Bill (Harry Crosby) runs in with a machete and kills the snake, before it’s shown writhing and dying on the floor. Cast and crew have since revealed that the sequence was real, noting that the snake’s handler was unaware of the film’s intentions and was “inconsolable” afterward.

With PETA launching two months before Friday the 13th‘s premiere in 1980, there were no animal protection laws in place yet during the filming of the Sean S. Cunningham-helmed movie.

Streaming Friday on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. As two strangers begin digging into her mysterious past, Pam goes to murderous lengths to keep her secrets buried.

title: Teenager Sues CBS News Over Story On Reflecting Pool Vandalism Arrests
summary: A Maryland teenager filed defamation suit against CBS News over a report his attorneys say falsely linked him as one of those arrested for alleged vandalism of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool last summer. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in the District of Columbia, seeks at least $20 million in damages. The plaintiff, […]
content:
A Maryland teenager filed defamation suit against CBS News over a report his attorneys say falsely linked him as one of those arrested for alleged vandalism of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool last summer.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in the District of Columbia, seeks at least $20 million in damages.

The plaintiff, identified as “JV” and as a 15-year old high school student, was riding his e-dirt bike past the National Mall on June 20, according to the suit. He was briefly detained and handcuffed over the use of the e-bike, and released without charges, per the suit.

The lawsuit claimed that in a June 21 report on the CBS Evening News, a story “falsely asserted that JV was arrested for engaging in vandalism towards the Reflecting Pool.” The broadcast story did not show his face, but the lawsuit claimed that “it showed video of him from the rear while he was briefly handcuffed, and he was readily identifiable because of his hair and because of the distinctive nature of the logo on the black hoodie that he was wearing (which he routinely wears and is known to wear).”

Watch on Deadline

CBS News also published the story on its website and in social media accounts with some modifications, according to the suit. In that version, anchor Jericka Duncan was talking about the reflecting pool arrests, naming only Olympian David Hearn. The online video showed the image of JV from behind, but his face was visible as he turned around, per the lawsuit.

“JV was readily recognized by friends and acquaintances. In fact, it was a family friend who first notified JV and/or his family about the report,” the lawsuit stated, while claiming that it was viewed 1.8 million times across Facebook, TikTok and Instagram.

The lawsuit claimed that JV has “suffered embarrassment, humiliation, anxiety, loss of sleep, emotional distress, and continuing fear that CBS’s false accusation will follow him through high school and affect his college admissions, athletic opportunities, employment, and future career.”

On Aug. 21, according to the lawsuit, Duncan issued a retraction and said, “We never should have published this story.”

A CBS News spokesperson declined to comment. The lawsuit was first reported by TheDesk.net.

Meanwhile, the allegations of vandalism to the reflecting pool have fallen apart.

Besides Hearn, no other figures were charged. Hearn’s case was dismissed after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro acknowledged that the damage to the reflecting pool was due to faulty work on the part of the contractor. The Washington Post reported on Wednesday that an inspection report concluded that the blue coating applied to the pool failed in at least 85 places.

title: Dodgers-Brewers & Rays-Guardians MLB Playoff Game Times For Thursday Changed
summary: Want to watch the back-to-back World Series Champion Dodgers fight for their lives tomorrow? You’ll have to tune in a little bit earlier than expected. The threat of rain in Cleveland has led Major League Baseball to move Game 3 of the American League Championship Series between the Rays and Guardians on Thursday ahead to […]
content:
Want to watch the back-to-back World Series Champion Dodgers fight for their lives tomorrow? You’ll have to tune in a little bit earlier than expected.

The threat of rain in Cleveland has led Major League Baseball to move Game 3 of the American League Championship Series between the Rays and Guardians on Thursday ahead to 1 p.m. ET from the previously scheduled 6 p.m. ET start time. The ALCS is tied 1-1.

That change has allowed the league to shift Thursday’s Game 4 of the National League Championship Series between the Brewers and Dodgers further into primetime for East Coasters. It has been moved from 9 p.m. ET to 8 p.m. ET. (For Angelenos not good with time zone calculations, this means Game 4 of the Dodgers-Braves in Los Angeles will now air Thursday at 5 p.m. PT.)

That Game 4 is a potential do-or-die for L.A.’s season. With the Brewers up 2-0, if Milwaukee wins tonight, the Dodgers will face elimination tomorrow. On the positive side for L.A., Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said slumping superstar Shohei Ohtani, who will be batting sixth Wednesday, has indicated he is “close to finding something” in batting practice that will help him end his postseason struggles.

Watch on Deadline

All ALCS games are telecast on TNT Sports platforms, while and Fox/FS1/Fox One carries the NLCS. They are also available to MLB.TV subscribers. ESPN Radio provides live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games.

title: ‘South Park’: Stan Discovers Sephora’s Backrooms Before Ike Aura Battles a Looksmaxxing Chad
summary: In the third episode of “South Park” Season 29, the gang gets stuck in Sephora’s “Backroom,” Stan’s dad shrinks himself using products from the beauty chain and aura battles take over South America (the newly named mountain town), meaning internet lingo like “mogging,” “maxxing” and “mewing” (along with “chad,” “cringe” and “rizz”) are plentiful. In […]
content:
In the third episode of “South Park” Season 29, the gang gets stuck in Sephora’s “Backroom,” Stan’s dad shrinks himself using products from the beauty chain and aura battles take over South America (the newly named mountain town), meaning internet lingo like “mogging,” “maxxing” and “mewing” (along with “chad,” “cringe” and “rizz”) are plentiful.

In the episode, titled “You Like That On Your Face,” Kyle must try to help his little brother, Ike, win his live-streamed aura battle at school against Chad, though his concern over the practice means he isn’t of much assistance. (Kyle calls aura battling and looksmaxxing a “bad combination.”)

Popular on Variety

But it’s Ike’s lucky day as Cartman steps up to help him prepare. “I’m sure that deep down your brother wants to help. Okay? Maybe he just he just doesn’t know how,” says Cartman while comforting Ike ahead of the battle. “If I had a little brother, he’d be my special little guy.” So, Cartman takes Ike to Sephora, which the kids of South Park have overrun, to pick up some products to help. (It’s a nod to the ongoing joke that tweens spend ages in the beauty store; “Something not right in there,” says a man sitting in front of the store. “My granddaughter wanted to go to Brandy Melville. Then she asked if she could just stop in the Sephora. That was six and a half years ago. There’s something in there men can’t understand.”)

But while Cartman and Ike are in Sephora, they get enticed into going into the backrooms with an employee, which look straight out of Kane Parsons’ horror film. Earlier in the episode, Stan wandered into the backrooms himself, so he knows how to get them both out before the aura battle begins. All the effort to get them out was for naught, though, because Ike doesn’t win the battle — Stan’s dad, Randy (who is now the size of his son after going to Sephora and thus is forced to enroll back in school) does beat up Ike’s opponent, though, meaning his looksmaxxed face is no longer.

This episode notably lacked any nod to Trump, though mentions of the president as a whole have been brief compared to the previous season, when the president was the show’s focal point for absurd antics. Some examples include plot points like JD Vance seducing Donald Trump in order to dodge punishment for trying to kill his unborn baby with Satan, among a long list of others.

The premiere episode of the show, which aired last month, centered around Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Kenny’s newfound love of e-bikes, while the second episode was a full-on phallic fest as Butters set out to rid South America of “billionaire weenies” — which, as it turns out, are literal penises — and their data centers that are affecting the area’s electricity. The episode also went in on anti-vaxxers, as Butters’ parents blame his anti-billionaire and AI beliefs on the measles vaccine he got. “I knew what that vaccination would do to him because I listened to podcasts,” yelled his dad. “But you couldn’t take time out of your precious day to listen to podcasts, could you? And now your son is a libtard.”

With Season 29, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone are going full steam ahead with the “South America” name change, which was announced earlier this month ahead of the Season 29 premiere. The premiere — the first episode since taking on the name “South America” — hit 4.2 million viewers in three days, as previously reported by Variety.

title: ‘To Be Ordinary’ Review: A Compassionate, Even-Handed Taiwanese Family Melodrama
summary: A high-speed traffic accident leaves a college student in a wheelchair for life, but that’s merely the starting point of the narrative in “To Be Ordinary,” a sensitive, slowly enveloping film with scant interest in disability-drama cliché — instead offering an expansive portrait of how the young man’s entire family is affected by his accident […]
content:
A high-speed traffic accident leaves a college student in a wheelchair for life, but that’s merely the starting point of the narrative in “To Be Ordinary,” a sensitive, slowly enveloping film with scant interest in disability-drama cliché — instead offering an expansive portrait of how the young man’s entire family is affected by his accident over the course of more than a decade. Spanning marital strife, economic upheaval, coming-of-age pains and moral crisis, Taiwanese writer-director Lee Yun Chan‘s fourth feature — her first since 2010’s “Dancing Without You” — has a lot of story to wrangle, but does so with a mostly delicate, empathetic touch, with a script that treats all individuals in this unhappy scenario with equal care and interest.

Since her last film, Lee has done mostly small-screen work — directing, among other things, the 2022 Disney+ series “Women in Taipei” — and if a certain televisual strain of melodrama occasional creeps into “To Be Ordinary,” the film’s sturdy formal restraint and expansive story scope should still serve it well in cinemas. Following its premiere as the only Taiwanese production in Busan’s main competition, the film will play at the Tokyo Film Festival later this month, opening theatrically in Taiwan in mid-November. Further festival play is likely, particularly in Asian-focused programs, and the film is accessible and moving enough for limited global distribution, though specialist streaming platforms may be its best bet.

Popular on Variety

Lee, who co-wrote the screenplay with “Women in Taipei” scribe Ginger Wang, wastes little time setting the story into motion, opening on a lovely, gliding nighttime tracking shot of 22-year-old Yu-jie (Junior Hsieh) on his moped, cruising the rain-slicked roads of suburban Taipei, as the grandiose strings of Cicada’s score conjure a false feeling of serenity. DP Ming Lee’s camera will certainly never be this free again; the reverie stops short when, at an intersection, Yu-jie is struck by a car, driven by the wealthy, elderly Mr Ma (Hsiu Shen Liang), who’s immediately beset with irremediable guilt.

Yu-jie survives the accident but soon learns, in hospital, that he’ll never walk again; a college student who has already started his own web design business, he accepts the bad news with remarkable stoicism, quickly adapting to life in a wheelchair and seeking ways to live the most normal, productive life possible — which includes a budding relationship with young hospital physiotherapist Yi-Han (Phoebe Chu).

If anything, the rest of his family has a harder time adjusting. His mother (Chang Shih Ying) and father (Weber Yang) were already at a fraught point in their marriage, and their son’s plight only drives them further apart, the situation exacerbated by Dad’s longtime unemployment. Meanwhile, Yu-jie’s younger sister Yu-ching (Pin Hsuan Chen), already facing the hormonal turmoil of early adolescence, feels sidelined by the tragedy — pressured to look after herself while, as her mother puts it, “there’s enough going on at home” — and begins to lash out.

At a pragmatic level, the family is aided by Mr Ma’s crushing conscience: In addition to the required legal settlement, he transfers ownership of his entire house to Yu-jie, and continues to contribute generously toward his medical bills and living expenses. But such generosity can itself become a burden of sorts to the benefactor, particularly as Mr Ma retreats into old age and ill health; avoiding drawing its characters along victims-and-villains lines, “To Be Ordinary” reserves compassion for all in this wretched turn of events, which gives it welcome dramatic complexity and maturity, particularly as the story spans 11 years of evolving consequences.

Thoughtful, closely-knit ensemble playing keeps the family dynamic believable even when the script takes a few convenient short cuts: Chen is especially affecting and volatile as a young woman growing up both as a kind of afterthought, and as a support system to her flailing parents. Lee directs proceedings with a handsome sobriety that befits the material, though between the persistently overcast visuals and the solemnly emotive writing, “To Be Ordinary” could stand an occasional injection of tonal surprise — an acknowledgement of the absurdity, hilarity or small domestic joys that sometimes disrupt hard times. Still, the film is never glib or unconsidered. There’s unassuming beauty in its even-handed, fair-minded worldview, and the space it gives its characters to reckon with sorrow, and find their own way out of it.

title: Sylvester Stallone Has ‘Millions of Regrets’ About Doing His Own Stunts: ‘I’m An Idiot for Doing That’
summary: Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how decades of daredevilry have affected him—and why he considers himself an “idiot” for continuing to do his own stunts year after year. In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the “Rocky” actor said he has “millions, millions of regrets” about his action career. “I could literally spend […]
content:
Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how decades of daredevilry have affected him—and why he considers himself an “idiot” for continuing to do his own stunts year after year.

In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the “Rocky” actor said he has “millions, millions of regrets” about his action career. “I could literally spend a half hour talking about injuries, the amount, not even like one, I’m talking about 30 hours, 30 minutes of just individual ones, because it becomes compounded. I have been injured many, many times, but after ‘Expendables,’ I ended up with nine back operations, three neck fusions. Both shoulders ripped out, eye, you know, all kinds of lens put … it’s been brutal,” he said, adding that he’s never been “quite the same” since the surgeries.

Stallone starred in — and also directed — the action thriller “The Expendables” in 2010 alongside Jason Statham, Mickey Rourke and more. While filming a scene where Stallone got tackled by WWE legend Steve Austin, the stunt went wrong and left Stallone with dislocated shoulders and a fractured neck that required more than seven back surgeries. The “Rambo” actor needed a metal plate inserted into his neck and spinal fusions.

Popular on Variety

Stallone’s moral of the story is to “let other people do their job.” “Don’t be a stage hawk, or whatever you call it, a showboat. I know a lot of people are thinking about doing stunts … don’t. Don’t. Let the pro do it,” Stallone said. “You cannot beat gravity; when you hit the ground, you lose, and it’s going to come back.”

He continued, “I mean, just ask every football player in the world. So yeah, and people go, ‘Aren’t you proud of them?’ No. I think I’m an idiot for doing that. I’m proud that I broke myself in pieces. Like, duh, no.”

The actor shared a similar piece of advice ahead of the release of his memoir, “The Steps,” last month; Stallone told The New York Times that treating his body in the “masochistic” ways he did came “at a terrible price.” “If I could do it over again, I would say, ‘Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts.”

title: ‘The Lowdown’ Creator Sterlin Harjo on the Films That Inspired Season 2, and What Convinced Tommy Lee Jones to Join the Show
summary: As “The Lowdown” Season 2 opens, citizen journalist (or “truthstorian”) Lee Raybon (Ethan Hawke) is in a completely uncomfortable position: success. He’s about accept a local media award for a piece he wrote about the death of Dale Washberg (as detailed in Season 1 of the series), but isn’t happy about it. Rather than accept […]
content:
As “The Lowdown” Season 2 opens, citizen journalist (or “truthstorian”) Lee Raybon (Ethan Hawke) is in a completely uncomfortable position: success. He’s about accept a local media award for a piece he wrote about the death of Dale Washberg (as detailed in Season 1 of the series), but isn’t happy about it.

Rather than accept his acclaim, a boozy Lee gets on stage and immediately tears into the crowd for being sellouts. It doesn’t go well. Series creator Sterlin Harjo admits to Variety that Lee’s inability to deal with a bit of acclaim comes directly from his own experience after the launch of his previous FX series, “Reservation Dogs.”

“I was living in a studio loft in downtown Tulsa, and all of a sudden I had a TV show,” he says. “I had been a kind of quiet independent filmmaker hoping to get some attention from anyone in this industry with my films. But then, ‘Reservation Dogs’ Season 1 truly changed my whole life. And I didn’t handle it well at first. You don’t know what to do. All of a sudden, there’s articles, and there’s all this stuff and you’re very exposed. It was fun thinking of that as Lee Raybon, because how does he handle the little recognition that he got? I bet he handles it really wrong, and I bet that there is a knee-jerk reaction to reject it.”

Popular on Variety

The theme of Season 2, Harjo says, is to figure out how to love yourself — and how that love will extend to everyone else in your life. After that initial shock of his “Reservation Dogs” success, Harjo is getting there. It helps that he has another critically acclaimed series on his hands.

Conceivably, “The Lowdown” could go on forever, given that there’s no shortage of story fodder about the amount of profligacy that exists in the world. After Season 1, “I wasn’t finished telling the story,” he says. “There was more of the corruption that I could tell.”

As Season 2 premieres on Oct. 14 on FX, Lee is soon recruited by public defender Ginger (Betty Gilpin) to investigate a new mystery: the disappearance of her client inside the Oklahoma prison system.

This time out, Harjo says he was inspired by the 1972 Lee Marvin/Gene Hackman film “Prime Cut,” 1981’s “Cutter’s Way” and the 1949 noir “The Third Man” to come up with the underlying concept.

“This idea of a missing man, I was like, how do we amp this up a little bit?” he says. “Well, it’s really hard to go missing in prison. There’s a sign-in sheet. How do you go missing from prison? That was such an intriguing question.”

Harjo says he, fellow exec producer Duffy Boudreau and Hawke began brainstorming the idea while doing their press tour for Season 1 of “The Lowdown.”

“That’s when we came up with kind of the bones of the plot,” he says. “Through lots of influences, and also just Oklahoma.”

Harjo says they also got to know Hawke’s cousin, a public defender in Ft. Worth, who shared stories about her experiences. “And I grew up in a town with a prison, and I saw how that affects a town,” he adds. “You really saw this shift in the town, and not a positive one. Because you have drugs, you have trafficking, you have drug trafficking of guards and prisoners.”

For inspiration, Harjo also remembers visiting his uncle as a kid in a McAlester, Oklahoma, prison, where he was doing time for repeat alcohol offenses. “The Lowdown” wound up shooting in that very same institution this season.

But that’s just one half of Season 2. The show’s other bombshell comes at the end of the opening episode: Tommy Lee Jones shows up as Lee’s estranged father.

“We talked a lot about being a father in Season 1. What’s it like being a son? And how do you forgive your father or a parent?” Harjo says. But just as Lee Sr. neglected his son growing up, Lee Jr. continues to mess things up with his own daughter, Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong).

“He’s trying to not make bad decisions [like his father],” Harjo says. “And at the same time, he’s neglecting his daughter, which is a bad decision. And then, his father, who was a bad father, is connecting with his granddaughter.”

“The more complicated you can make all that stuff, the better, because you’ve got to fight your way out of it as a writer,” Harjo says. “It was a very painful writing experience, more painful than anything, because I had written myself into so many corners. There was stuff that I was writing, there was episodes being written deep into production. I hope I never have to do that again!”

After writing the first episode of Season 2, Harjo immediately thought of Jones for the part as Lee’s father. Both he and Jones are both represented by CAA — and once Jones read it, the actor wanted in. Jones had already watched Season 1 — and told Harjo that he specifically loved the bookstore security guards Waylon (Cody Lightning) and Cousin Henry (Jude Barnett), who provide some comic relief.

“He wanted to be with them, which that told me everything I needed to know,” Harjo says. “If you love the security guards, you love me and the show and the vibe. Because those characters wouldn’t necessarily be on a lot of shows. You would cut that. After the premiere the other day, [Jones] says, ‘Thanks for paying attention to the character Waylon, because most people wouldn’t. It’s characters and storylines like that I think make the show what it is.’”

Harjo also excitedly notes that Jones started watching “Reservation Dogs” while shooting “The Lowdown.”

“There was something amazing about every day coming to work and having Tommy Lee Jones describe an episode of the show that I created,” he says. “He’d be talking to Ethan or me about it, and it was nice that he appreciated it so much. ‘Reservation Dogs’ is the type of show that you might think someone like Tommy Lee Jones could miss and not get it, but he’s a sophisticated, really smart artist and he loved it. It was amazing every day.”

As for the character of Ginger, she’s clearly a love interest for Lee — a tough character who can go toe-to-toe with him, but has a humor to her as well. Once Gilpin came on board, Harjo says she helped redefine who Ginger could be.

“Lee can be a bit wild, and I needed someone to match that energy,” Harjo says. “Betty can do anything, and I already knew that she was great. And then she came, and it was like another level. All of a sudden she’s doing things in the first scene that I’m filming with her, and there’s things happening that I did not write. From that day forward, I’m trying to write toward her voice and what she’s bringing to that character.”

Harjo says he aimed to make Season 2 “go harder and faster with everything that we have established. It’s kind of like ‘Reservation Dog’ Season 2 as well. I’ve established the world. I feel like people that like the show will come with me. I have a meter of what feels real and what doesn’t, so I always sort of adhere to that. Let’s make ‘Empire Strikes Back,’ where it’s great and it stands on its own, but you also want more by the end. Gods of TV willing, we’ll be making a Season 3 of this show.”

The first two episodes of “The Lowdown” Season 2 premiere on FX and Hulu on Oct. 14 at 9 p.m. ET, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Wednesdays

title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer to Head to Tokyo for Leadership Award and Onstage Summit With Toho Boss Matsuoka Hiro
summary: Academy CEO Bill Kramer is set to make his first trip to Asia later this month. He will collect a leadership award at the Tokyo International Film Festival and also sit down with Toho president and CEO Matsuoka Hiro for a public conversation. The festival’s 39th edition runs Oct. 26–Nov. 4 and has built a […]
content:
Academy CEO Bill Kramer is set to make his first trip to Asia later this month. He will collect a leadership award at the Tokyo International Film Festival and also sit down with Toho president and CEO Matsuoka Hiro for a public conversation.

The festival’s 39th edition runs Oct. 26–Nov. 4 and has built a program titled Academy in Tokyo around the visit. Two colleagues will join Kramer in the Japanese capital: Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and Meredith Shea, the organization’s chief membership, impact and industry officer.

The three executives will share a stage on Oct. 28 at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya Hall for a 90-minute panel moderated by TIFF festival director Hisamatsu Takeo. They will take the audience behind the curtain of the Oscars and outline the Academy’s international initiatives and membership programs. The conversation will also turn to how the organization views international cinema today and where it is heading.

Popular on Variety

Once the panel wraps, Kramer will receive TIFF’s Global Cinema Leadership Special Award. The festival said the honor recognizes his contribution to the growth of the worldwide film business and to film culture. Later that day, the Academy will hold a private reception for its members from across the globe.

Other senior Academy figures will also be in Tokyo for the festival and the member reception. Among them are Amy Homma, who oversees the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and the Academy Collection as director and president; Jenny Galante, the Academy’s chief revenue and business development officer; and Jennifer Davidson, its chief marketing, communications and content officer.

Kramer returns to the same venue on Oct. 29 to sit down with Matsuoka. Their session will look at the state of the global film landscape and the outlook for theatrical and streaming distribution, along with ways to deepen cross-border partnerships. Both public events are free, though advance reservations are required. Booking details have yet to be released.

Kramer took the Academy’s top job in 2022. Before that, he ran the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures as its director and president. The museum opened its doors in September 2021. As CEO, Kramer has pushed to broaden the Academy’s 11,000-strong membership and give it a more international makeup. He runs the organization’s global operations, from the Oscars and the Academy Foundation to the $500 million Academy100 campaign.

Howell Taylor is in her second term as president. She is an Oscar-nominated producer whose credits include “A Star Is Born,” “The Accountant,” “Captain Fantastic” and “Blue Valentine.” She joined the Academy’s Producers Branch in 2014. She also co-produced the 92nd Oscars telecast in 2020, which earned her an Emmy nomination.

Shea is the first person to hold her post. Her remit covers membership, awards administration and talent development. It also includes the Academy’s outreach to film festivals and international territories.

Matsuoka has steered Toho’s expansion overseas, including its acquisitions of Gkids and Anime Limited. He also oversaw the production of Oscar winner “Godzilla Minus One.” In 2025, Toho posted its best-ever results at the Japanese box office. Matsuoka also sits on the board of trustees of the Academy Museum.

TIFFCOM, the content market that runs alongside the festival, takes place Oct. 28–30.

title: Sharon Osbourne Says Ozzy’s Final Concert Film Was “Very Hard To Watch,” Would Have Made Him Feel Like A “Lucky Son Of A Bitch”
summary: More than a year after his death, Ozzy Osbourne’s fans can relive his final performance through an upcoming concert film. Sharon Osbourne recently shared her reaction to Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning, premiering Oct. 25 in theaters, adding that her late husband would feel like “one lucky son of a bitch” after […]
content:
More than a year after his death, Ozzy Osbourne‘s fans can relive his final performance through an upcoming concert film.

Sharon Osbourne recently shared her reaction to Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning, premiering Oct. 25 in theaters, adding that her late husband would feel like “one lucky son of a bitch” after seeing the documentary from director Ben Wainwright-Pearce (Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, George Michael: The Faith Tour).

“It was very hard to watch a lot of this film. I had to, but it was very, very hard,” Osbourne told Rolling Stone. “It’s bittersweet. It’s amazing. Everything about the show was amazing and just a joyous occasion and one that will go down in music history. I’m proud of that and that it was for my husband, and I’m so thankful to everyone that took part in it, for their time, their effort, their giving.”

Noting that Ozzy “was in hospital for a week in England” before the July 5, 2025 concert, Sharon recalled his doctors “advised us not to do the show,” but he was determined.

Watch on Deadline

“They said it would kill him. We were all together and Ozzy said, ‘It’s not an option. It’s what I want,'” she revealed. “He said, ‘I know I’m dying. If I miss a few months of my life, I want to go this way. This is what I want.’ It was his wishes and we went through it. He said to me, ‘Another six months, what’s it going to do for me?'”

Ozzy died at age 76 weeks later on July 22, 2025, suffering a heart attack after living with coronary artery’s disease and Parkinson’s disease.

When asked what Ozzy would think of the concert film, Sharon surmised, “He would say, ‘How lucky am I?’ He goes, ‘I’m one lucky son of a bitch.’ And he knew it. He never took anything for granted, ever.”

The late Black Sabbath frontman’s family is also developing a biopic about him, five years after Sony Pictures and Polygram Entertainment were said to be in the works on a project.

title: How LaRoyce Hawkins Exits ‘Chicago P.D.’ In Season 14
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The following reveals major plot points from tonight’s episode of NBC’s Chicago P.D. It’s the end of an era as LaRoyce Hawkins makes his final appearance as Kevin Atwater on NBC’s Chicago P.D. as a series regular. As many of you are fully aware, when people leave any of the One Chicago franchise […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The following reveals major plot points from tonight’s episode of NBC’s Chicago P.D.

It’s the end of an era as LaRoyce Hawkins makes his final appearance as Kevin Atwater on NBC’s Chicago P.D. as a series regular. As many of you are fully aware, when people leave any of the One Chicago franchise shows, it’s not beyond belief that they could be back one day.

In fact, tonight’s episode titled “Don’t Blink” was directed by Jesse Lee Soffer, an original cast member who has returned to direct his former castmates, as well as reprise his role of Jay Halstead in last year’s major crossover event.

So how did Atwater ride off into the sunset? In the final moments of the Season 14 premiere, he gets a call learning that Tasha Fox (Karen Obilom) is in labor. He freaked out a bit, but he was ready and excited to welcome their first child together.

Watch on Deadline

Viewers meet the adorable Atwater baby boy, Malcolm Atwater, the little guy whose tough-guy dad misses being with his family when he has to return to work. He got some important advice from Kim Burgess (Marina Squerciati), a more experienced parent, who tells him that being away from his family gets easier with time. In another adorable moment, Burgess and Adam Ruzek’s (Patrick Flueger) daughter Makayla sends baby Malcolm a little stuffed toy.

(l-r) Shane Richlen as Steve, LaRoyce Hawkins as Officer Kevin Atwater

In a scary moment, Atwater is shot while on duty, but he was wearing a bulletproof vest that saved his life. The case helps Atwater realize that being a parent is the most important job there is; he speaks with Voight (Jason Beghe) about a possible career change.

Without confirming a solid plan, he says goodbye to his family, the crew that he’s been with through the good, bad, and worse, with a toast. He reveals he and Tasha will be looking for a new home to get a fresh start. Atwater and Voight spoke about the possibility of him becoming a teacher at the Academy. Voight encouraged him to look into it, saying also that they’ve been looking for good officers in the Atlanta office. No matter what choice they make, the Atwaters get their happy ending.

The story is left open for a potential return should that happen one day, giving the fans their own happy ending for a beloved actor and the character he’s played since Season 1.

“Knowing that we were in this position and trying to figure out in the room what’s the best way we can do this… Like, how can we send him off in a positive way, optimistically?” said showrunner Gwen Sigan about what it was like in the writers’ room planning for Kevin’s exit.

She continued, “Is there a way that we can send him off that feels like it’s his choice, and he’s authoring it, and that feels like a pivotal move for the character? We didn’t want it to be something that comes out of left field. So that’s what we focused on. We wanted it to feel really organic to him, and feel like we were giving him the best send-off we could. So I think we’ve done that. I’m very proud of the episode. I’m proud of his performance in it. I think he killed it.”

(l-r) Patrick John Flueger as Officer Adam Ruzek, Marina Squerciati as Officer Kim Burgess, LaRoyce Hawkins as Officer Kevin Atwater, Benjamin Levy Aguilar as Dante Torres, Jason Beghe as Sgt. Hank Voight

Sigan also opened up about Hawkins and Soffer’s reunion.

“It was just really nice that the two of them got to do that together. And I hope you can feel that on screen. I know that they put so much care into it,” she said.

Chicago P.D. returns with new stories from Season 14 on Wednesdays at 10 p.m.

title: AMPAS To Attend Tokyo Film Festival; Program Includes Special Talk Session With Bill Kramer & Toho CEO Hiro Matsuoka
summary: This year’s Tokyo International Film Festival will host ‘Academy in Tokyo’, a special program welcoming top executives from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS).
