Academy CEO Bill Kramer, President Lynette Howell Taylor, and Chief Membership, Impact and Industry Officer Meredith Shea will visit Japan for the program. On October 28, the three […]
content:
This year’s Tokyo International Film Festival will host ‘Academy in Tokyo’, a special program welcoming top executives from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS).

Academy CEO Bill Kramer, President Lynette Howell Taylor, and Chief Membership, Impact and Industry Officer Meredith Shea will visit Japan for the program. On October 28, the three will participate in a panel discussion, followed by the presentation of a leadership award to Kramer and a gathering for Academy members.

On October 29, Kramer will take part in a conversation with Hiro Matsuoka, President and CEO of Toho Co, during which they will discuss the global cinematic landscape, the future of theatrical and streaming distribution, and next steps for international collaboration.

Kramer, who is making his first visit to Asia, will receive the Global Cinema Leadership Special Award in recognition of his significant contributions to the development of the global film industry and the advancement of film culture.

Watch on Deadline

Since becoming Academy CEO in 2022, Kramer has worked to further diversify and globalize the Academy’s membership. He oversees all of the Academy’s global operations and programs, including the Oscars, the Academy Foundation, and services for the organization’s 11,000 global members.

The panel on that day will offer a behind-the-scenes look at the Oscars as well as insights into the Academy’s global initiatives and membership programs. The discussion will also explore the Academy’s perspective on the current state and future of international cinema.

On October 28, the festival will host a private reception for Academy members from around the world.

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ VFX Boss Jerome Chen on Hulk’s Redesign, Finishing 445 Shots in a Week
summary: Marvel and Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” involved nearly 2,000 VFX shots and just 24 weeks of post-production, with 445 shots delivered in a single week, overall VFX supervisor Jerome Chen revealed at View Conference in Turin on Wednesday. “In one week, we did about 445 shots,” Chen said, comparing the feat with his first […]
content:
Marvel and Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” involved nearly 2,000 VFX shots and just 24 weeks of post-production, with 445 shots delivered in a single week, overall VFX supervisor Jerome Chen revealed at View Conference in Turin on Wednesday.

“In one week, we did about 445 shots,” Chen said, comparing the feat with his first film as a supervisor in 1999, which contained 450 shots in total and took two years to complete.

About three-quarters of “Brand New Day’s” VFX work was delivered during the final six weeks, he added, making an already demanding schedule even more intense.

Popular on Variety

Next, Chen recalled that preparations began with a scouting trip to New York in December 2024, before he had received a finished script. Director Destin Daniel Cretton wanted a more grounded, street-level Spider-Man, with the city itself integral to the story. But most filming would take place in the U.K., where Pinewood Studios, London and Glasgow doubled for New York. Production designer Charles Wood’s concept art helped establish a relatively restrained palette, punctuated by saturated colors at key emotional moments.

The team preserved usable street-level photography and digitally replaced or extended much of what lay above it. “We just found basically a recipe of a half dozen or so things that tell you that it’s New York,” Chen said. Those included hanging traffic signals, scaffolding, water towers and the correct power lines. Even the yellow markings along British curbs had to disappear.

Small pieces of script could produce enormous technical assignments. An introduction involving Spider-Man and a tank expanded from a handful of words into 11 shots and roughly 52 seconds of footage. Physical tabletop models helped the crew determine how a vehicle should crash through a building when there was no time for elaborate previws. In another sequence, a compact camera rig mounted on a helmet captured Tom Holland’s performance from near his face, with a blurry red shape added in compositing to suggest the inside of his mask. “Sometimes the easiest tricks are the most effective,” Chen said.

The movie also gave Chen his first opportunity to work on Mark Ruffalo’s Hulk. Because the character appears in a more savage, telepathically controlled state, the team explored a different physique from earlier Marvel outings, adjusting his proportions, muscular definition, hair color and the relative size of his hands and feet. Chen consulted Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige about how Hulk’s appearance had evolved across the franchise.

“I realized that nobody had ever looked closely at Hulk’s toenails before,” Chen joked. “That was something that we had to do.” Earlier versions looked unnaturally green, while the team also considered how the character’s skin would react to different lighting. They lengthened his arms, reduced his body fat and gave him grayer hair. A subtle shift in eye color, from green to brown, signals a moment when Hulk regains his humanity. Full-scale, 10-foot Hulk standins helped actors and camera crews judge his dimensions on set, and even his pants required careful attention.

A climactic energy wave involving Jean Grey proved harder to solve creatively. Chen initially resisted the rainbow-like chromatic aberration familiar from other screen depictions of superpowers. But with five weeks remaining, he reversed course, deciding the established visual vocabulary served the film better than something overly electronic. “I thought it was the weakest part of the film,” he admitted. “I wish we had come up with something better.”

Time, he argued, often determines the quality of VFX more than the artists’ abilities. “If you go to a movie and you see that there’s a visual effects shot that doesn’t look that good, it’s not because there are bad artists on it,” he said. “You can tell they just ran out of time.” Chen advised supervisors facing decision fatigue to review shots within their sequences rather than obsess over individual frames.

Finishing so rapidly could also have consequences for the industry: “We may have done ourselves a disfavor by actually finishing this movie in 24 weeks because once again we’ve proven that it can be done on time.”

The final challenge was unexpectedly modest. With the vendors already finished, a last-minute review revealed a sweat stain under Spider-Man’s arm. “You can’t have superheroes sweating into their suit,” Chen recalled. A small team at Marvel’s Burbank offices removed it in about 47 minutes, delivered the corrected shot and sent Chen home from a nearly empty parking garage beneath the studio.

title: MK2 Films Scores Brady Corbet, Kleber Mendonça Filho, Céline Sciamma Shorts (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: LYON, France — Short films by Brady Corbet, Kleber Mendonça Filho and Céline Sciamma are joining the international sales catalogue of Paris-based MK2 Films, which is expanding its collection of lesser-seen works by established filmmakers. The acquisitions, unveiled during Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival, headed by Cannes director Thierry Frémaux, and its International Classic Film Market […]
content:
LYON, France — Short films by Brady Corbet, Kleber Mendonça Filho and Céline Sciamma are joining the international sales catalogue of Paris-based MK2 Films, which is expanding its collection of lesser-seen works by established filmmakers.

The acquisitions, unveiled during Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival, headed by Cannes director Thierry Frémaux, and its International Classic Film Market (MIFC), span nearly two decades, from Corbet’s 2008 “Protect You + Me” to two recent works: Sciamma’s “Tutti Frutti” and Mendonça Filho’s “South of Tehran.”

The acquisitions are part of a broader push by MK2 Films to develop its short-film catalogue alongside its established feature film business.

Popular on Variety

“These short films create a dialogue with the feature films of iconic filmmakers represented in the MK2 Films collection, offering a different perspective on their creative vision and cinematic language,” said Frédérique Rouault, head of collections at MK2 Films. “They also open up new programming opportunities for festivals and cinemas, allowing audiences to discover rarely seen works by some of today’s most influential directors.”

The new acquisitions join Jia Zhangke’s “Torino Shadow,” which screened at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival and in the New York Film Festival’s Spotlight Shorts program. The catalogue also includes early works by two-time Palme d’Or winners Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, notably “Le Chant du Rossignol,” acquired through MK2 Films’ recently announced deal with their production company Les Films du Fleuve.

Sciamma’s 44-minute “Tutti Frutti” draws on personal footage she had shot since 2022, exploring filmmaking as a solitary practice. Commissioned by the Centre Pompidou and produced by Lilies Films, it premiered in Paris in June during a retrospective devoted to the director of “Portrait of a Lady on Fire” and won the Jury Prize at the 2026 Villa Medici Film Festival.

MK2’s catalogue already includes Sciamma’s 2023 short “This Is How a Child Becomes a Poet,” a tribute to Italian poet Patrizia Cavalli that premiered at Venice Days. The company also represents her complete feature filmography, including “Petite Maman” and new 2026 cuts of “Tomboy” and “Girlhood.”

South of Tehran Courtesy of MK2 Films

Mendonça Filho’s nine-minute “South of Tehran” features Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi recalling his earliest encounters with cinema. Produced by Emilie Lesclaux and Film at Lincoln Center, it was shot during the 2025 New York Film Festival, where the two directors were presenting their latest features, and grew out of conversations between them. It premiered at the New York fest earlier this year as the inaugural project of NYFF Encounters, an annual initiative commissioning filmmakers to shoot shorts during the festival.

MK2 already handled international sales on Panahi’s “It Was Just an Accident,” winner of the 2025 Cannes Palme d’Or, and Mendonça Filho’s “The Secret Agent,” which earned the Brazilian director Best Director and Wagner Moura Best Actor the same year in Cannes.

Protect You + Me Courtesy of MK2 Films

The third acquisition looks further back in its director’s career. Shot by cinematographer Darius Khondji, Corbet’s “Protect You + Me” offers audiences an opportunity to discover the director’s early work, long before his mainstream breakthrough with “The Brutalist,” the acclaimed historical drama that won three Oscars, including Best Actor for Adrien Brody, and earned Corbet the Silver Lion for Best Director at Venice in 2024.

Back in 2009, the short received an Honorable Mention at the Sundance Film Festival.

The acquisition strengthens MK2 Films’ ties with Corbet, who appeared as an actor in Michael Haneke’s “Funny Games,” recently added to the company’s catalogue, and Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” which MK2 is preparing to re-release theatrically in a new 4K restoration.

The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through Oct. 18 with the MIFC wrapping on Oct. 16.

title: FlyDubai Hijacking Incident Set for Development as an Inspirational Movie by Dori Media Group and India’s Sphereorigin
summary: The harrowing but ultimately hopeful story of the FlyDubai airline hijacking incident last month is being developed as a narrative film by Dori Media Group and India’s Sphereorigin. The Sept. 30 incident is believed to have been a terror plot by the co-pilot of the FlyDubai plane that was bound for Ben-Gurion International Airport in […]
content:
The harrowing but ultimately hopeful story of the FlyDubai airline hijacking incident last month is being developed as a narrative film by Dori Media Group and India’s Sphereorigin.

The Sept. 30 incident is believed to have been a terror plot by the co-pilot of the FlyDubai plane that was bound for Ben-Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv. The flight was primarily full of Israeli citizens traveling home after visiting in Dubai. The co-pilot is alleged to have stabbed the plane’s captain and taken over the flight controls with the intention of crashing it into Ben-Gurion airport. The flight is reported to have plummeted more than 14,000 feet for about 30 seconds until valiant efforts by the injured pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, allowed passengers to overpower the suspected pilot in the cockpit.

The extraordinary circumstances have turned Machchhar into a national hero in his native India as well as in Israel. Dori Media, which produces film and TV out of Tel Aviv, Zurich and Buenos Aires, was approached by representatives for Sphereorigin about working together on a film. The project came together in record time in old-school fashion at the Mipcom content market and conference in Cannes.

Popular on Variety

“We were approached by streaming platforms and broadcasters in India expressing interest to tell the heroic story of the Indian pilot and the courageous Israeli passengers on that recent flight,” said Sunjoy Waddhwa, managing director at Mumbai-based Sphereorigins. “We are privileged to collaborate with Dori Media on this premium project as we have known and worked with them for a long time and together with Subh (Subhadarshi Tripathy) felt they’d be the ideal partner to produce a film of this caliber.”

Tripathy brokered the deal on behalf of Dori Media and Sphereorigin.

Dori Media chief Nadav Palti was surprised and energized to get a phone call from the parties on Oct. 11, on the eve of Mipcom opening. The sides met in the Dori Media booth at the Palais and hammered out the terms of the development pact by the afternoon of Oct. 14. Palti told Variety the speed of the deal coming together indicated the desire by the companies to tell the story of the incident that could have been a devastating tragedy but instead became a triumph that demonstrated the skill and the courage of Machchhar, who is recovering from his injuries. The co-pilot accused of carrying out the attack is under arrest and facing prosecution by UAE authorities.

“We are honored to jointly produce this special film with the team at Sphereorigins,” said Palti. “What happened on that flight was nothing short of a miracle and we will approach this film by looking to tell the heroic story of the pilot and those brave passengers who helped save the lives of many aboard that historic flight.”

Dori Media Group’s Nadav Palti and Sphereorigin’s Sunjoy Waddhwa Adi Gilad

In the narrative to has unfolded from authorities and passenger accounts, Machchhar had the presence of mind to open the locked door of the cockpit after he was stabbed. That allowed passengers to hear the commotion and discover what was happening. Machchhar tried to fight to retain control of the plane and amid that noise, a group of passengers were able to subdue the suspected assailant. Two other pilots who happened to be traveling on the flight then took over and were able to safely land the plane at the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The ability to do so marked a gesture of kindness from the Saudi kingdom that does not otherwise allow Israel-affiliated aircraft to land in its borders.

“I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside,” Machchhar said recently in a highly publicized video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. “I was of course fighting for my own life but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die.”

Waddhwa moved to strike a film development deal around the incident after getting unsolicited inquiries from Indian media firms. The sides are still looking for a writer and director. The hope is to release it on an accelerated timetable next year.

“We were approached by streaming platforms and broadcasters in India expressing interest to tell the heroic story of the Indian pilot and the courageous Israeli passengers on that recent flight,” Waddhwa said. “We are privileged to collaborate with Dori Media on this premium project as we have known and worked with them for a long time and together with Subh (Subhadarshi Tripathy) felt they’d be the ideal partner to produce a film of this caliber.”

Sphereorigin was founded by Waddhwa and others in 2002. Dori Media Group has grown to rank among Israel’s largest independent producers since its launch in 1996. The company had its largest slate of offerings — from documentary features and docuseries to game and competition series to scripted dramas — at Mipcom. It produces a wide slate of Spanish-language content for Argentina and other Latin American markets.

(Pictured: A tribute to Capt. Smit Machchhar is crafted out of sand on India’s Puri beach)

title: What’s Driving Spanish TV? Spanish Drama Originals on Platforms, Renewals and Crossover Genres
summary: What’s trending in Spanish drama series and how the sector fares abroad and at home were some of the points briefly outlined by Gloria Saló from Spanish consultancy firm GECA on Tuesday during a Mipcom presentation sponsored by Audiovisual from Spain. The report “Spanish Fiction 2026, Between New Stories and New Seasons,” which covers data […]
content:
What’s trending in Spanish drama series and how the sector fares abroad and at home were some of the points briefly outlined by Gloria Saló from Spanish consultancy firm GECA on Tuesday during a Mipcom presentation sponsored by Audiovisual from Spain.



The report “Spanish Fiction 2026, Between New Stories and New Seasons,” which covers data from Jan. 1 through June 2026, confirms the strong position of Spanish fiction worldwide — seventh among top 10 global fiction premieres — plus the Spanish appetite for dramas, comedies, trending genre crossovers and the consolidation of platforms that are sustaining the fiction series boom.



“At a time when Spanish fiction is thriving both creatively and structurally, and reaching out to the rest of the world, it’s hugely important for us to investigate new trends,” Saló told Variety at the Mip Creative Hub.

The data analyst pointed out three factors behind the success of Spanish drama which saw Spanish fiction premieres jump 83% between 2021-2025: risk-taking creators, a willing to challenge genre boundaries and themes, the creative use of strong IPs “reinvented to the upmost efficiency and performing extremely well at home” and scripted shows with returning potential. “All this contributes to a highly dynamic drama sector, crucial for the entire audiovisual ecosystem,” she said.



Four takeaways from the GECA research:

Popular on Variety

Spain No. 7 in a Top 10 of Global Premieres

In a highly concentrated market where three countries — the U.S., Japan and South Korea accounted for 55% of the 857 fiction premieres during the first semester 2026; Spain ranked seventh with a 5.2% share from 30 new titles released domestically. The U.S. took the top spot with a 31.8% share from 177 titles.



Sustained Spanish Boom

Spanish premieres at home jumped a record 83% between 2021-2025, from 40 to 73 local fiction premieres. The output for H1 2026 remained relatively stable with 30 new titles versus 33 the same period 2025. Another 24 new releases are lined up for the rest of the year; most of them originals (20) followed by new seasons (3) and a saga.



Hottest genres in Spain

As in the rest of the world, dramas – across a wide spectrum of crime, suspense and fantasy to family drama – proved the hottest genre, weighing in as half the premieres during that period (15 titles). Titles ranged from Atresplayer’s “33 Days” created by renowned true-crime investigative journalist Carles Porta and Netflix’ mystery thriller “Oasis” to SkyShowtime’s thriller “The Tribute” (“El homenaje”) and Prime Video thriller “Day One,” about new technology threats.

Next up were comedies and dramedies with eight and four new releases (26.7% and 13.3% of premieres respectively), followed by mini-series (two or 6.7%) and animation with one title. Reflecting the breath and variety of narratives, attractive premieres took in Prime Video’s “Naughty Business” (“Cochinas”), a comedy in which a woman starts a porn business after her husband’s death. Disney + offered comedy through the thriller lens with “If It’s Tuesday, It’s Murder” (“Si es martes, es asesinato”), Prime Video the sketch comedy “Vida Perra” created by Rafel Barceló and Enric Pardo, and Movistar Plus+ the comedy drama “I Always Sometimes” (“Yo sempre a veces”) which bagged best screenplay at Canneseries.



Worth highlighting says the report is the value of returnable potential to maintain the production output. As many as nine renewals were released in Spain in the first half of 2026, such as Seasons 4-5 of Netflix’s “Alfa Males” (“Machos Alfa”). Several new seasons posted new storylines for familiar characters, such as the latest instalment of “Berlin and the Lady with an Ermine” (“Berlin y la dama de armiño”) from Netflix, Movistar Plus+’s mob thriller “El Inmortal,” and “Marbella: Expediente judicial.”



Drama for Streaming

Proof of streamers’ leading position for drama content in Spain, 27 out of 30 premieres launched digitally (90%) and only three on linear TV. SVOD players accounted for two-third of the titles and a mix of U.S. and leading Spanish streamers released most shows, with four each: Atresmedia’s Atresplayer, Movistar Plus+, Netflix and Prime Video.

The free VOD service Primeran from Basque pubcaster EITB launched three shows, Telecinco 2, and 10 local and global players, including Disney +HBO Max premiered only one new title. “The absence of a clear market leader and the limited weight of linear television reflect a market geared towards on-demand consumption,” said the GECA study.

title: YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom
summary: A new virtuous circle is emerging for media and entertainment giants that promises to harness the advantages of disparate platforms, digital and linear, powered by the connective tissue of YouTube. This was one of the dominant themes that emerged in four whirlwind days of panel sessions, closed door meetings, networking and schmoozing events up and […]
content:
A new virtuous circle is emerging for media and entertainment giants that promises to harness the advantages of disparate platforms, digital and linear, powered by the connective tissue of YouTube.

This was one of the dominant themes that emerged in four whirlwind days of panel sessions, closed door meetings, networking and schmoozing events up and down the Croisette as top industry players from Europe and beyond gathered in Cannes for the annual Mipcom content market and conference.

The growing muscle that YouTube flexes as the video crossroads of the world was a near-constant subject of conversation. Google’s streaming behemoth is becoming ever more integral to media development, distribution and marketing plans for most contenders in media, from the biggest Hollywood studios to indie startups.

Popular on Variety

Evan Shapiro, the respected industry analyst who is often billed as a “media cartographer,” gave a well-attended presentation on Wednesday morning that drew together threads probed in various tracks of the conference. Shapiro’s session offered sobering stats about the changing nature of viewing audiences. The older contingent of media and entertainment leaders have to come to grips with the fact that the world’s population is getting younger. That means they need to cater to consumers who have come of age with technology in their pockets and a very different worldview on how, when and why they consume media in across different mediums and platforms.

At the same time, Shapiro pointed to hope on the horizon for legacy media outlets.

“We believed television would be replaced by streaming 1 for 1 — that didn’t happen,” he said. Streaming and social video have augmented viewing time and even more important, they help deepen fan connection to their favorite shows. Shapiro emphasized more than once that media giants courting audiences need to think in terms of generations and affinity groups, not the age and gender demos of yore.

“Now consumers have an infinite number of channels. Every human with a phone is a channel,” Shapiro said. It’s the age of “personalized television through a combination of your phone and your television set.”

Matt Schnaars, president of platform distribution and partnerships for NBCUniversal, reinforced Shapiro’s observations in a separate session.

“The embracing of social media platforms, starting with YouTube, to drive people back to live viewing, we see that in results. We see that in audiences,” Schnaars said. “When we look at YouTube … [they] are an example of somebody who’s in really every business that we’re in, but not in a way that’s competitive. It’s accretive and incremental. And so we get excited.”

NBCUniversal is windowing some of its most prized, fan-favorite content – college football – on YouTube. The Peacock streaming platform shares its weekly exclusive games on YouTube. In the old days, that would have been unheard of. Today, it’s about reaching fans where they live. Peacock earlier this year struck an innovative distribution pact to be bundled as part of a YouTube TV premium tier.

“It can build habituation, and then ultimately, hopefully, a purchase of Peacock or going to YouTube TV even to go experience the full slate,” Schnaars said.

Like NBCU, the BBC sees enormous potential in the Beeb’s experiments to date with the FAST channels that are fast becoming a new form of syndication.

“YouTube for me is exciting because it’s where a lot of the audience are now,” said Kate Phillips, chief content officer at BBC Studios. She noted that the Beeb now has 34channels on YouTube, increasing to 50 by the end of 2028.

Leaders from Germany’s RTL Deutschland unpacked their partnership with YouTube at a Mipcom session. Executives said the free streaming platform has given new life to its long-running action series “Cobra 11.” After uploading more than 200 episodes, RTL generated 30 million views on YouTube, helping drive a 123% increase in first video views for the series on RTL+ and a 26% rise in subscriptions linked to the show. ITV has also partnered with YouTube, while France’s TF1, M6 and France Télévisions have struck distribution deals with global streaming giants, including Netflix and Amazon.

Justin Connolly, YouTube’s global head of media and sports, stressed that YouTube is prospering as it becomes more intertwined in the pay-TV eco system through YouTube TV. And YouTube (as well as TikTok) is essential to most of the creator-led content ventures that are proliferating.

“We only win when our partners win,” Connolly said.

In addition to exploring the new nexus of streaming and linear, Mipcom delivered some classic moments. Christie Brinkley, the 1980s supermodel, was here to pitch her docu-series “Uptown Girl: The Christie Brinkley Story” for Fox Global Distribution. The revival of “Baywatch” made a splash on the Cote d’Azur with the photo call featuring Stephen Amell and his shapely costar Brooks Nader.

Here are other trends and themes that emerged from this year’s conference:

Consolidation

As Hollywood grapples with consolidation, cost-cutting and a slowdown in production, French entertainment giants are seizing the opportunity to expand their footprint in the U.S., either through acquisitions or by exploring new investments.

Fresh off its merger with British powerhouse All3Media, Banijay Entertainment is eyeing an expansion into the U.S. scripted market. Speaking at Mipcom, CEO Marco Bassetti and chairman Jeff Zucker said the newly enlarged group had the financial firepower to pursue opportunities in Hollywood, where it has yet to establish a major scripted production business.

Mediawan, meanwhile, is already making moves. After acquiring Peter Chernin’s North Road Company earlier this year, the Paris-based group has teamed with Reese Witherspoon to buy Hello Sunshine from Blackstone-backed Candle Media at a steep discount to its $900 million valuation in 2021. The deal further expands Mediawan’s Hollywood portfolio, which also includes Brad Pitt’s Plan B.

Latin America’s Growth Spurt

Beyond microdramas, where on earth can growth come from in the current TV landscape? With a swing to far-right populism, local production is being put through a political grinder, first in Javier Milei’s Argentina who decimated public-sector subsidies. Now Brazilian cinema is at risk. As a market, however, Latin America paints a different picture. The region is forecast to grow by 15.4% to $62 billion in revenues, exceeding the U.S. growth rate of 10.2%, Omdia’s María Rua Aguete, announced at Mipcom, presenting research and calling Latin America “one of the most exciting growth opportunities in global media and entertainment.” The driver?: online video, led by Netflix. The challenge? Connectivity.

Global Political Peril

For all the talk of consolidation and streaming at Mipcom, another major concern was looming over the television industry: the changing political landscape and the rise of far-right parties that are challenging public broadcasters across Europe.

In France, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally is leading presidential polls ahead of the 2027 election and has called for a sweeping overhaul of public broadcasting, including privatization. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is also gaining ground and wants to abolish the license fee that finances public broadcasters ARD and ZDF. Meanwhile, Brazil is heading into a fiercely contested presidential runoff between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

Against this backdrop, public broadcasters are stepping up efforts to defend their relevance, reach younger audiences and strengthen their presence on digital platforms, where a growing share of voters get their news.

France Télévisions has forged a major partnership with YouTube, where its franceinfo news channel generated 110 million views in September, eight times its audience a year earlier. In Germany, ARD’s Tagesschau and ZDF’s ZDFheute are also distributing news on YouTube and developing formats aimed at younger viewers.

The stakes go well beyond audience figures. At a time of growing political polarization and disinformation, public broadcasters are seeking to reinforce their role as trusted, independent sources of news — while ensuring they remain relevant to the next generation.

Creators Gonna Create

Prolific creator Dhar Mann – who has more than 170 million followers across all social platforms – spoke about his vision for Creator City in Los Angeles, which will open in February when L.A. hosts the NFL’s Super Bowl at SoFi Stadium. The four-acre campus will house nine sound stages. “We’re going to have about 175 sets. It’s going to be able to have about 15 concurrent productions happening at the same time,” he explained. “All the sets are actual brands. So, when you see content being created, it’s not just a random coffee shop – it could be a Starbucks. It’s not just a random retail store – it could be a Target.”

True Crime is Killing it

In “Killing a Bear,” a true-facts based murder mystery at Mipcom, the victim is a Pyrenean brown bear whose death sparks the first criminal investigation in Spain for an animal’s suspected slaughter. Crime repped 27% of scripted TV orders globally, first half 2026 – the single most commissioned TV genre, estimates Ampere Analysis, and a whopping 61% of the No 1 series at Mipcom from many of the world’s biggest players. Whether “Cupertino’s” “whip-smart tour of AI insanity” or John Hannah as a crimebuster in sunny but shady Benidorm, some shows at least aim to stand out from the crowd.

title: ‘Lupin’ Star Omar Sy Voices Support For French High School Protests; Decries Authoritarian Response
summary: French star Omar Sy has voiced his support for high school student protests sweeping France and decried the authoritarian crackdown which has seen one teenager lose their hand and more than 6,000 youngsters taken into temporary police custody. The protests have been building since late September, sparked by complaints of staff shortages and dilapidated schools. […]
content:
French star Omar Sy has voiced his support for high school student protests sweeping France and decried the authoritarian crackdown which has seen one teenager lose their hand and more than 6,000 youngsters taken into temporary police custody.

The protests have been building since late September, sparked by complaints of staff shortages and dilapidated schools. Social commentators suggest they also point to deeper anxieties over the future direction of the country amid a cost of living crisis and fears over the future of work as AI threatens jobs.



Initially driven by high school pupils, teachers, higher education students and trade unions have since joined the ranks of the protests. A major countrywide mobilisation is due to take place this Saturday with supporters of the “yellow vest” movement also joining and more than half a million people expected to take to the streets.



“The high school students’ movement is a small beacon of light,” Sy said in an interview with French state radio station France Inter on Wednesday.



“It is the future of our country telling a nation that is completely adrift: ‘We have a sense of direction, listen to us. We have a pretty clear idea of where we want to go, because this country will one day be ours’. When I see that there’s no reaction to this, that the immediate reflex is to silence them, lash out at them, or even pit them against each other like children in a fight, I find it pathetic,” he said.



“And I ask myself: where are the adults in charge? What is our role, as adults, as parents? What are we actually doing to our children?,” he continued.



“Instead of jumping straight to reprimanding, punishing, or correcting them, or forcing them to face off against one another, we aren’t listening to them at all. In fact, it’s even worse. We tell them to be quiet, and then we expect them to reach an agreement on their own. We don’t even know what they have to say.”



Sy is currently doing the media rounds in France ahead of the launch on October 23 of the fourth series of Netflix hit series Lupin in which he is the titular star.



The French-born star, who brokeout internationally with his role in 2011 comedy-drama The Intouchables, has been living in the U.S. with his family for the last 14 years but retains strong connections with France where he remains a household name.



Sy was asked whether he still enjoyed living in the U.S. given it was “very different” from when he took up residence there 14 years ago, with the country “hardening considerably.”



“Yes, because today it’s home, but it’s true America has hardened, there’s no question,” he said. “But it’s not just America unfortunately… the whole world has hardened in the same way, with the same intensity.”



“It’s no better when I come back here. I see things as being just as harsh. I see the same violence, the same tensions, the same misguided questions, and, ultimately, the same misguided answers. One can observe the same tendency to retreat, the same xenophobia. In fact, what’s happening here is a global phenomenon.”



Sy is not the only French star voicing support for the high school movement.



Last week, Cannes Best Actor winner Vincent Lindon also revealed his thoughts during an interview on the upcoming feature adaptation of Les Misérables in which he plays Jean Valjean.



“In May 1968, it was a rejection of consumer society,” he told France Inter. “People were fighting against abundance. Today, it is a crisis born of scarcity. These are young people who want chairs to sit on… decent, functional sanitary facilities, and a fair distribution of resources, and therefore opportunities.”

“I have children who went through middle school, high school, and so on, and it is true that this is one of the first times the younger generation is legitimately asserting demands and rights in the face of a state that currently lacks the funds to buy social peace.”

title: Radial Entertainment Completes Busy MIPCOM Week With ‘Making A Serial Killer’ Season 3 Order
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Radial Entertainment has had a busy week on the Croisette and just finished it off with another order. The global distribution biz has greenlit a third season of its original series Making a Serial Killer, the true-crime series that looks at what shaped the world’s most notorious serial killers. It unravels the chilling backstories […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Radial Entertainment has had a busy week on the Croisette and just finished it off with another order.

The global distribution biz has greenlit a third season of its original series Making a Serial Killer, the true-crime series that looks at what shaped the world’s most notorious serial killers. It unravels the chilling backstories of murderers through testimony from those affected and law enforcement officers who stopped them.

Season is being produced in partnership with the UK’s FirstLook Studios (fka FirstLook TV), with Radial taking rights in the U.S., Canada, Germany, Switzerland and Austria. The ten-part series will premiere on December 1 on FilmRise channels and other platforms stateside.

“We’re focused on building lasting true crime franchises with international appeal, and FirstLookStudios has been a fantastic partner in bringing that vision to life,” said Cristina Guggino, VP, Originals & Content Partnerships at Radial Entertainment.

Watch on Deadline

“Making a Serial Killer delivers on that strategy by examining the mind of the killer without losing sight of the human impact. We’re excited to bring a third season to audiences across the U.S., Canada, Germany, Austria and Switzerland.”

“Making a Serial Killer is about the ‘why’ as much as it is about the ‘how and how were they caught,” added Will Hanrahan of FirstLook Studios. “It’s a proven winner with True Crime audiences and our partnership with Radial is one we value as an example of fantastic editorial, commercial and strategic collaboration.”

Katie Carroll and Guggino are serving as executive producers for Radial, with Hanrahan as executive producer from FirstLook Studios alongside series producers Graham Smiles and Rachel Bowering.

This multi-territory deal was negotiated by Carroll, who is Director, Originals & Business Development at Radial, and Lucy Middelboe, Director of Business at FirstLook Studios. The pair has shepherded the partnership since its inception.

For Radial, the news is a third announcement this MIPCOM Cannes week. Yesterday, it ordered new episodes of Forensic Files from ITV Studios America and Content Partners, news that came after it had bagged Season 4 rights to World’s Most Evil Prisoners and revived New Dominion Pictures title A Haunting for an updated run.

MIPCOM ends today.

title: SXSW London Sets 2027 Festival Theme
summary: SXSW London 2027, which is set to run from 24–29 May, will do so under the theme of “The Power of Human Potential.” Festival organizers have also confirmed the form of the 2027 conference programme. The 2027 edition will be organised into 14 thematic tracks. These include: AI & Experience, Frontier Technologies, Health & Longevity, […]
content:
SXSW London 2027, which is set to run from 24–29 May, will do so under the theme of “The Power of Human Potential.”

Festival organizers have also confirmed the form of the 2027 conference programme. The 2027 edition will be organised into 14 thematic tracks. These include: AI & Experience, Frontier Technologies, Health & Longevity, and Society Rewired, as well as new tracks such as Future Earth and Sports.

“The 2027 theme, ‘The Power of Human Potential’, is as much a call to action as it is a programming theme,” Katy Arnander, Chief Programming Officer at SXSW London, said in a statement. “SXSW London is the global festival for the convergence of business, tech, creativity and culture. The conversations on our stages, at our parties and in our networking sessions shape what happens in the year ahead.”

SXSW London reported more than 20,000 festivalgoers in 2026. The festival hosted 863 speakers, including Michelle Obama, the Russo brothers, and Neon Founder Tom Quinn. Other previous speakers include Sir Tim Berners-Lee, Demis Hassabis, Esther Perel, Idris Elba and the late Dr Jane Goodall.

Watch on Deadline

The festival’s screen strand hosted 100 screenings in 2026. Those included the UK premiere of Sex and Death in Camp Miasma, and the world premieres of the animated series Get Jiro and the feature film Savage House. The music programme featured performances by Rachel Chinouriri, Tiwa Savage, Shame, Pete Tong and Gilles Peterson.

Arnander added: “In our third year, we look forward to once again welcoming artists, inventors, leaders, founders and policymakers to lead conversations, make connections, and bring curiosity and practical optimism to the future of their industries and our collective society.”

title: MIPCOM 2026 Takeaways: Surfing The New Wave Of TV With YouTube, ‘Baywatch’, Skydance, Banijay & More
summary: MIPCOM is the biggest gathering in international TV. This year there were 10,000 attendees and over 3,000 buyers. The organizers have thrown open the doors to the wider world of content and distribution – and nowadays YouTube execs and creator businesses mingle with TV buyers and sellers. Deadline was out in force and here are […]
content:
MIPCOM is the biggest gathering in international TV. This year there were 10,000 attendees and over 3,000 buyers. The organizers have thrown open the doors to the wider world of content and distribution – and nowadays YouTube execs and creator businesses mingle with TV buyers and sellers. Deadline was out in force and here are the team’s takeaways.

Surfing To Cannes

MIPCOM always needs a bit of glitz and glamor and this year that largely came in the form of those beloved red shorts and swimsuits. Yes folks, Baywatch is back, and co-stars Stephen Amell and Brooks Nader were on board to tell us all about the reboot. Shepherded by execs from Fox and Fremantle, the pair could be seen at many of the most glamorous events along the Croisette throughout the week, while a fun stunt involving superbikes took place Monday night. They weren’t the only big stars in town, however, with Christie Brinkley around to talk up her new docuseries, Stephen Fry spotted at Monday drinks promoting Fox’s The Interrogator and the likes of Rafe Spall, Robbie GK and Luke Evans chatting with press.

Will Skydance Open Up Or Keep The Good Stuff?

The different program sales operations of Skydance hit the Côte d’Azur under their pre-existing Paramount and WB brands. Some higher ups at other distribs questioned how open for business the combined operation will be. New Skydance content sales chief David Decker was all smiles at the WBD stand, able to look over and see his new Paramount colleagues just along the beachfront. With a huge debt pile, the parts of the Skydance business that are revenue generating – such as program sales – are under pressure to deliver. With huge streamers to nurture, however, will some content stay in the family and not make it to market? Disney and others went through periods of holding back shows to bolster their SVODs. But, per the big Disney stand in the Palais des Festivals this year, they are fully back into the program sales biz. Let’s see how Skydance turns up at MIPCOM 2027.

Watch on Deadline

YouTube Dividing Lines Drawn

The inseparable relationship between YouTube and TV was clear for all to see at MIPCOM Cannes but serious concerns from the latter remain. Traditional TV folk, who are very much on board the YouTube train, were drawing dividing lines, both privately when we chatted with sources, and on stage. BBC content boss Kate Phillips drew cheers from a packed auditorium when she said algorithms can’t create great content, noting: “If you commission based on algorithms you are literally a creative carcass.” YouTube Europe boss Pedro Pina, a fixture at these events, reminded producers that the platform won’t take work away from them by entering the production game. At times, however, it felt like the traditional players were looking to remind the world that YouTube has its limits.

Banijay Wants More Drama In The U.S.

The new, bigger Banijay was in town. There was a swanky post All3Media-Banijay wedding party in Cannes’ iconic Carlton Hotel and Jeff Zucker and Marco Bassetti took to the MIPCOM stage. Banijay was big already, and after merging with All3Media, has a 265,000-hour library and is huge. In Europe, that is taken as read in industry circles. Internally, the company thinks of itself as having the heft of a Lionsgate or even a Sony. That’s not, however, the perception Stateside. Fremantle, ITV Studios and others have sunk cash into scripted plays in the U.S. with varying levels of success. How Banijay cracks scripted there is a big agenda point for Bassetti, Jane Turton and Banijay Americas topper Ben Samek. Expect news.

AI: From Headlines To The Bottom Line

A lot of newbie AI businesses were at MIPCOM to convince the content buyers and sellers they could help streamline or monetize what they do. The focus was how AI can be integrated and optimize the existing business – rather than presentation of noisy (and controversial) slates of AI TV shows and movies. The reality of such optimization is likely fewer jobs. But there was an acceptance of another reality – AI isn’t going away. It is already part of TV production and distribution. MIPCOM is a great example of how and why humans want and need to meet, talk, network and socialize, but the question is now how, not if, AI fits into the picture.

Creators Drop The Pranks And Get Serious

MIPCOM was a conduit for the developing creator economy this year, with the focus switching to those YouTube and digital stars who are actually building businesses. Dhar Mann’s (pre-)opening night keynote was full of passion and promise, but most notable was how he has gone from producing from iPhones in his bedroom to owning a four-acre production campus, Creator City. It will house productions, creators and A-list brands in one place. “Five years ago nobody was taking me seriously,” he said. Creator deals unveiled at the market included Endemol Shine Brasil’s pact with Latino creator house Grupo Podpah.

Microdrama Mania

Plenty remain sceptical on microdrama, but this week proved there’s no doubt it’s here for the long haul. Reps from pioneers such as ReelShort were in town pressing the flesh, while a global microdrama leaders’ summit brought together the likes of COL Group, Roseberry, RJ RisingJoy and NetShort. The room was packed, which shows seriously established players are thinking about it – and traditional players such as Germany’s ZDF, Chile’s TVN and Turkey’s Kanal later engaged in a vertical video matchmaking session. TikTok, a first-time attendee, struck arguably the biggest vertical deal for microdramas, from U.S. creator house Made By Us.

New Entrants Welcomed To The Club

Though MIPCOM is still the domain of the distribution biz, the number of players from outside TV land and sessions on branded content and other adjacent video spaces ramped up again. The likes of TikTok, ad giant WPP and live streaming business Upstream made their event debuts, eager to speak with the increasing numbers of producers, sellers and financiers who are broadening their horizons in a tough landscape for independent players. “I’ve been hugely impressed by how much momentum there is around driving collaboration from across the disciplines both on and off the Croisette,” Jason Hughes from Sky Media, the ad arm of Sky, told us.

title: Multitude Media Restructures Leader Team & Prepares Live Entertainment Push
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Multitude Media has promoted Gem Pinkney to the newly-created role of managing director and plans a push into live entertainment. The agency, which reps for PR the likes of Danny Dyer, Lolly Adefope and Shazad Latif along with BAFTA and numerous production companies, has a new senior leader team led by founder and CEO […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Multitude Media has promoted Gem Pinkney to the newly-created role of managing director and plans a push into live entertainment.

The agency, which reps for PR the likes of Danny Dyer, Lolly Adefope and Shazad Latif along with BAFTA and numerous production companies, has a new senior leader team led by founder and CEO Will Wood.

Former Director of TV Pinkney is now MD and Multitude’s TV division will be led by a senior team made up of Nicole Campbell (Senior PR Lead – Scripted & Ents), Sal Porter (Senior PR Lead – Unscripted & Factual) and Jess Molyneux (Senior PR Lead – Corporate and Special Projects), who have all been promoted.

Longstanding Multitude team member Charlotte Kershaw, who has been with the company since 2019, will return from maternity leave in January as Strategy & Creative Director across TV, Culture and Live Entertainment, leading on Multitude’s expansion into new areas and identifying new business across TV, Culture and Live Entertainment.

Watch on Deadline

Emily Hargreaves, who has been at Multitude for nearly a decade, continues to lead the personal PR biz including Dyer, Adefope and Latif.

A live and entertainment push is also planned with hires incoming over the next few months.

Wood said: “I’ve watched with admiration as Gem has redefined our TV business and helped secure the calibre of work I’ve always wanted us to work on. We’re seeing growth across all of our divisions and now’s the time to bolster our senior team to ensure we can capitalise on the opportunities in front of us. I’m incredibly proud to have such a brilliant team working for Multitude, some of whom are now approaching 10 years with us, and these changes should set us up for many years to come.”

title: ‘Love of Your Life’ Director Rachel Morrison on  Margaret Qualley’s ‘Wild Range,’ Confronting COVID-19 and Subverting Romantic Drama Expectations: ‘Finding Herself Is Enough’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for “Love of Your Life,” now streaming on Prime Video. When Rachel Morrison read the script for “Love of Your Life,” it stuck with her. Penned by “Nyad” writer Julia Cox, the story follows Maya, a 20-something emergency room nurse living in Boston without much family to call her […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for “Love of Your Life,” now streaming on Prime Video.

When Rachel Morrison read the script for “Love of Your Life,” it stuck with her.

Penned by “Nyad” writer Julia Cox, the story follows Maya, a 20-something emergency room nurse living in Boston without much family to call her own. When she meets the nerdy but charming Charlie, the two start building a life together — until tragedy during the COVID-19 pandemic causes it to fall apart. Maya runs away from her pain by traveling the world, first to Portugal and then to London and Japan, but an unexpected romance forces her to confront her past and realize that there may be more than one love of her life.

Morrison, who has already had an illustrious career as a director of photography — she was the first woman to be nominated for the best cinematography Oscar for her work on 2017’s “Mudbound” — made her directorial debut two years ago with the sports drama “The Fire Inside.” For her follow-up, she’d been thinking about the intersection of love and loss.

Popular on Variety

“I obviously was drawn to the script, but didn’t immediately think, ‘This is my next project,'” Morrison tells Variety over Zoom. “It really was just, this is good writing and I want to talk about it with this writer.”

Morrison and Cox really connected. “There was a deep sense of mutual respect, but also, for this script that was incredibly well received and jumped off the page, she was not precious about it,” Morrison says. “The more I sat with it, the more it sort of got under my skin.”

The same was true for the film’s cast, an all-star ensemble led by Margaret Qualley as Maya and including Gabriel Basso as Charlie; Aaron Pierre as Felix, a handsome stranger she meets abroad; Patrick Schwarzenegger as her best friend Jason; and Catherine Keener in a scene-stealing performance as Charlie’s mother Ruth.

“We have leading actors playing supporting roles, and I think that’s because this really spoke to them,” Morrison says.

Below, the director speaks more with Variety about working with Qualley, putting the COVID-19 pandemic on screen and why they didn’t go with the obvious ending.

What was it about the script that struck you?

I think there were two prominent things. One is that it’s sadly rare to have features where particularly female characters are layered and complex and flawed and messy and aren’t sort of reduced to just a plot engine, but actually have a lot of nuance and growth to do within the script. And I thought that was really exciting to see a character who could make some really questionable decisions, but you’re still rooting for her.

And then I think the reason why I was interested in the cross-section between love and loss is because of how personal it is to me. I’m somebody who was shaped from some pretty significant early loss that really transformed who I became. And I went through the same kind of messy tumult that Maya’s character did, where you’re trying to make sense of your life after something so devastating, and you’re moving through the world without actually engaging in it. These guardrails come up because you don’t ever want to be hurt again, and it’s a real process to take those down. So I think I saw myself in Maya and in the script, and felt like I could be additive to it. The more I sat with it, the more I realized how personal it was and therefore how right I would be to tell it.

Tell me about finding your leading lady in Margaret Qualley.

Margaret had read the script — I mean, many actresses had read the script and kind of raised their hand. A few names stood out, Margaret’s in particular, where I knew she could be a real ally and partner in this. As somebody who’s going to have to anchor the entire thing, it’s critical that your actress wants to be there and really understands the film that you’re trying to make. We sat down and really talked about it, and it was clear we both wanted to make the same film. I’ve been a big fan of hers for a long time, and part of what I’m a fan of is this wild range she has. Her character choices are sometimes from one thing to the next, just these really bold characters. And I was excited that I don’t feel like in a feature sense, I’ve seen — maybe on “Maid” on TV — a really foot-on-the-ground, relatable performance that I knew she was capable of. And I was excited to see what the girl-next-door version could be.

How about the men in Maya’s life: Gabriel Basso, Aaron Pierre and Patrick Schwarzenegger?

The biggest goal was for there to be variation between them. Each character had specificity as scripted, and actually as we cast the roles, they started to inform each other. Aaron is maybe a little more stoic than his character is written, which then allowed Gabe [to have] this kinetic, golden retriever energy. And then, obviously, doing chemistry reads with Margaret and Patrick too, and making sure that each of their chemistry was palpable but unique unto itself. And certainly Gabe brought out a different quality in Margaret than Aaron did and Patrick did, and you can feel it throughout the film.

How has your career as a cinematographer informed your directing style?

First and foremost was the desire to shoot on real locations. People have different methodologies, but for me it was almost a non-starter. I really wanted to go to the spaces where this film existed, and not try to create them in a soundstage. And there are other directors who probably would skew towards the soundstage version, and so I commend Amazon MGM for actually letting me do it that way, because that’s not really how movies get made anymore. It’s actually really unusual to go to two cities, let alone four.

And then, I can’t turn off the DP in me, which I think is actually a real asset to my cinematographers because I’m scouting from the beginning. Even before the DP comes on, I’m looking at how the location interacts with light, how I can block a scene within a space to move the camera in such a way. So it’s sort of ingrained in how I visualize things, even probably from the page. And then [cinematographer] Todd [Banhazi], we had such a lovely collaboration. He’s amazing. But he kind of would light the world and then let me exist, which is how I like to work.

Margaret Qualley and Gabriel Basso in “Love of Your Life.” ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection

The COVID-19 pandemic is a central part of the story. How did you go about portraying that and addressing our collective trauma from it, given that it wasn’t that long ago? Not many films have attempted to put it on screen.

I think for us, the most important thing was to get it right. Because this isn’t just the pandemic, it’s the pandemic as experienced through a first responder. And so we did a lot of consulting, both myself and Margaret, with nurses and doctors and just the medical profession during that time and the different stages of it. And then the lasting effects of it, of course. But I think just looking for little things that we would all relate to, even like “Tiger King,” wiping down the groceries with Clorox. The goal was really to recreate it in a way that feels both like yesterday and also like a lifetime ago, but that everyone would fully relate to. And not make it sensationalized. I think that’s the thing about the whole movie — I’m always trying to make it the grounded, relatable version of itself and not the cinema version of itself. So it’s never the extreme, it’s always the recognizable.

Margaret has some very heavy emotional scenes. How did you work together to get her to that place?

Margaret had really great instincts. You have this character who spends a lot of the movie not actively grieving — it’s manifesting in these other ways, but she’s not actually releasing the emotion. Obviously, she’s feeling all the things and is traumatized, but she doesn’t quite know how to express it. On the day, there are things that happen always with good actors where they’re feeling the feel and there’s a reaction that isn’t even performative, it’s so from the body and the heart and the soul. So like, Margaret heaving trying to get the words out to Ruth on the phone, it was actually scripted that she got it all out and then lost it — but she couldn’t find the words. And I think she was right. It was a much more honest portrayal of what Maya would have been going through. I think my approach is you go in with a plan, but you’re always looking to pivot or react to what’s in front of you and not what you’d imagine. You have to be open to that, otherwise I think you can really stifle the process.

At the end of the film when Maya flees the airport, I expected her to run back to Jason, but she actually goes to visit Ruth. Tell me about the decision for her not to end up with him.

You just touched on the other thing that drew me to this script, which is that we’re taking these genres that have a set of expectations and completely subverting them. It was very much by design that the audience thinks she’s going back to Jason for a moment, and then realizes she’s going to Ruth. And that’s because this genre is set up for the happily ever after romantic ending. And I am just so profoundly grateful and thrilled that that’s not how this film ends and that it really is so much more about finding her way back to life and to herself. The hope is now she will be open to all the possibilities in front of her — and will probably find the right person again someday and maybe still have kids and all the things — but we’re not spelling it out or buttoning it up for people and know that just finding herself is enough.

Aaron Pierre and Margaret Qualley in “Love of Your Life.” ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection

“Love of Your Life” got a one-week theatrical release before dropping on Prime. Why was this important for you?

I mean, I’m somebody that came from a time when dramas were in theaters. I made this film knowing it was always destined for Prime, [but] I made it for the theatrical experience anyway. I don’t know that I would ever shoot something differently because of the platform, but I’ve definitely been encouraging anyone and everyone to see it in theaters while they can because I do think there’s something so immersive about that experience for a number of reasons. There’s something very special about an engaged audience sharing an emotional experience together too, which is something that we just don’t get that much anymore because most movies in theaters these days are horror or action. The idea of all having a good cry together is quite rare. But, thankfully, I think it plays very well on Prime, too. And one thing that we learned just through the testing process is that — shocker — men feel more comfortable emoting at home. And so, it may actually play better for the male gender to just, in the comfort and privacy of their own home, really let it go.

Any idea what your next film will be?

I’m interested in grounded sci-fi. I’m always looking for a device to hide the drama because I do want to make movies for the theater if possible. Because unless you’re Nolan or now maybe Coogler, we can’t get audiences to dramas anymore. I mean, even when you look at most of these films, like an “Arrival” or a “Blade Runner” or “Dune,” often they’re just simple [stories]. “Star Wars” is a father-son story, but it exists in space and therefore people are excited to go to the theater for the spectacle of it. So one bucket would be a big, world-building spectacle-y sci-fi drama. And I guess there’s another version where I make something smaller in the A24/Neon space where, by virtue of not making it for as much money, it gets a theatrical release because it can exist in a smaller space. But my goal right now would be to do something that’s undeniably theatrical and to do something that I haven’t done before. I’m always trying to push myself and challenge myself, hence the pivot from cinematography at the top of my game to starting completely over as a director. It’s to keep growing and evolving. So whatever’s least expected of me, that’s probably what I’ll do next.

This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Soundtrack Features New Music From Composer Raül Refree
summary: “La Bola Negra” soundtrack, featuring music by composer Raül Refree, is set to be released on Oct. 16 by Lakeshore Records. Taking its name from an unfinished play by Lorca and drawing on his writings and legacy, “La Bola Negra” is directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi better known as Los Javis. It stars […]
content:
“La Bola Negra” soundtrack, featuring music by composer Raül Refree, is set to be released on Oct. 16 by Lakeshore Records.

Taking its name from an unfinished play by Lorca and drawing on his writings and legacy, “La Bola Negra” is directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi better known as Los Javis. It stars Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes, Lola Dueñas, Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close. It spans three generations and pivotal moments in Spanish history. In 1932, Carlos (Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. In 1937, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. And in 2017, Alberto (González) uncovers a long-buried family secret that gives voice to truths the past tried to erase.

When scoring Netflix’s “La Bola Negra,” Refree knew he wanted to pursue a timeless, orchestral and avant-garde sound.

Popular on Variety

It’s an intense score that grows along with the film and with the different protagonists as their stories unfold.

Refree, who is one of Variety’s 10 artisans to watch, tied his instrumentation to the characters rather than the eras. “Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) plays the trumpet, so his scenes rely heavily on the brass section. Carlos (Milo Quifes) plays the piano, so his music features the piano alongside the string section. Finally, Alberto’s (González) story takes place in the present day, and because he is going through a personal crisis, his music relies much more on silence,” Refree says.

As the film progresses and the paths of the three protagonists cross in one way or another, the timbres and instrumental approach also begin to blend. “Mira que nos acechan” is where all the concepts come together, carrying the meaning that we are all one.

Listen to the first of two cues from the film’s score, exclusive to Variety, below.

“En España Empieza a Amanecer”





This scene begins abruptly with a hard cut and marks a crucial moment towards the end of the film. Refree says, “I wanted the music to have a strong impact, with the brass section playing severely loud, and in sharply cut clusters that intensify the shock of this unexpected turn of events.”



It’s a scene where the prisoners are forced out of their rooms, taken to their cells, and are later executed. “I imagined this procession of frightened prisoners and violent soldiers through a rhythmic pattern played by the strings – loud, aggressive pizzicatos. I thought the wood creaking quality of the strings created a sense of unease, almost as if the music itself were giving voice to the prisoners’ fear as they are led to their deaths. At the same time, I used electronic sounds, almost like a distorted form of tinnitus, to convey the disorientation the prisoners experience after being abruptly woken up.”



The final melody is a minuet that Sebastián plays on the trumpet earlier in the film. Refree says, “It is a childlike piece that, for me, becomes the central theme of the score – a reflection of the fear and fragility of the film’s characters.”

“Enfermería”



“This was one of the first pieces I composed for the film, and it remains one of my favourites. This is the scene where Sebastián first sees Rafael. It begins with a relaxed, beautiful musical landscape led by the horns, evoking a sense of everyday life and daylight in a military hospital during wartime. The staccato trumpets add a touch of understated, almost casual heroism, as if suggesting the ordinary routines of soldiers living through extraordinary circumstances.”

As the scene unfolds, however, the music begins to empty out, giving way to darker, lower melodic textures. “The bass trombone gradually takes the lead, and the intensity builds as Sebastián becomes increasingly overwhelmed by the sight of this beautiful, and injured body,” he says. “Musically, everything grows wilder and more dissonant, reflecting his inability to control what he is feeling. His attention drifts towards intimate details – the bare armpit, the small hollow at the base of Rafael’s neck – and the music follows him into this increasingly private, almost obsessive fascination. What begins as a beautiful, peaceful morning at the front gradually transforms into an intense, almost concealed intimate desire for which Sebastián has no control.”

The film opens in New York City and Los Angeles on Oct. 16 before expanding to additional theaters across the United States and Canada. Select theaters will present it in 35mm. “La Bola Negra” will debut on Netflix in the United States and Canada on Dec. 2.

title: Bollywood Actor Imran Khan Heads to High Court to Fight Order to Leave India Over Election Protest
summary: Imran Khan is preparing a court challenge to an order that gives the Bollywood actor until Oct. 28 to leave India, after he attended a demonstration demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down. Khan, a Bollywood superstar and Aamir Khan’s nephew, is an American national who lives in India on an Overseas Citizen […]
content:
Imran Khan is preparing a court challenge to an order that gives the Bollywood actor until Oct. 28 to leave India, after he attended a demonstration demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down.

Khan, a Bollywood superstar and Aamir Khan‘s nephew, is an American national who lives in India on an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card. It was at his home in Mumbai’s Khar neighborhood that the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) delivered the notice, a police officer said.

A petition calling the Leave India Notice “drastic” is expected to reach the Bombay High Court as early as Friday. Its central argument is that nothing in Indian law or the OCI regulations bars a cardholder from attending a protest. Zulfiquar Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik of MZM Legal LLP are handling the case.

Popular on Variety

Police rounded up upwards of 400 people across Mumbai on Oct. 10, many of them at August Kranti Maidan, where demonstrators had gathered in solidarity with a Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi. The Delhi agitation centers on allegations that voter lists were manipulated during the Special Intensive Revision exercise. According to police, nobody had sought permission for the Mumbai event, and Azad Maidan is the sole venue where the Bombay High Court permits protests in the city.

Speaking to reporters before he was detained, Khan said he had no demands. “I am here as a citizen, as someone who lives in this city,” he said.

Police also picked up his girlfriend, actor Lekha Washington, and his cousin Zayn Marie Khan. From inside the van, Khan shared an Instagram selfie captioned “Apparently I’m going for a drive.” He had also taken part in CJP’s July demonstrations.

Gamdevi police have since filed a First Information Report listing Khan among the accused. Kirit Somaiya, a former MP from the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), took a complaint to the same station claiming that Khan’s presence at the protest broke the terms of his OCI status and visa, and police passed it on to the FRRO. Somaiya, who wants Khan arrested and deported and has accused him of “political extremism,” separately asked Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan on Oct. 13 for a Look Out Circular that would flag any attempt by Khan to exit India.

No OCI rule addresses whether cardholders can protest, and stripping someone of OCI status is a separate process from a Leave India Notice. The Union Home Ministry has used that power before, revoking the OCI card of Kannada cinema actor Chetan A Kumar, also a U.S. citizen, over “anti-India activities.”

Khan stepped back from acting after a run of films that included “Delhi Belly,” “Mere Brother Ki Dulhan” and “I Hate Luv Storys,” which followed his 2008 lead debut in the Aamir Khan-produced “Jaane Tu Ya Jaane Na.” He also directed the 2018 documentary short “Mission Mars: Keep Walking India.” He is due to make an acting comeback with “Adhure Hum Adhure Tum.”

title: Guillermo del Toro Pays Tribute to Late ‘E.T.’ Designer Carlo Rambaldi Ahead of Hollywood Walk of Fame Honor: ‘A Worldwide Maestro of Magic’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Guillermo del Toro is paying tribute to Italian special effects master Carlo Rambaldi, who is being honored today with a posthumous Hollywood Walk of Fame star. Rambaldi, best known for designing the iconic title character in Steven Spielberg’s “E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial,” died in 2012 at age 86. He was a three-time Academy Award winner for […]
content:
Guillermo del Toro is paying tribute to Italian special effects master Carlo Rambaldi, who is being honored today with a posthumous Hollywood Walk of Fame star.

Rambaldi, best known for designing the iconic title character in Steven Spielberg’s “E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial,” died in 2012 at age 86. He was a three-time Academy Award winner for his work in special effects, having won Oscars for “King Kong” (1976), “Alien” (1979) and “E.T” (1983).

Prior to “E.T.,” Rambaldi had already collaborated with Spielberg on “Close Encounters of the Third Kind.” He subsequently worked with David Lynch on the cult classic “Dune.” The long list of top directors whom Rambaldi worked with over the course of his glorious career include Federico Fellini, Luchino Visconti, Pier Paolo Pasolini, Marco Ferreri, Mario Bava, Dario Argento, Lucio Fulci, John Huston, Ridley Scott and Oliver Stone.

Popular on Variety

Rambaldi was born in the village of Vigarano Mainarda, outside the city of Ferrara, in the northern Italian region of Emilia-Romagna. The son of a bicycle mechanic, he graduated from the Academy of Fine Arts in Bologna in 1951 and, though he dreamed of becoming an artist, was drawn into the world of cinema when he was asked to create a dragon for a low-budget science fiction movie in 1956.

Del Toro has been known to share a deep passion with Rambaldi for creatures used in contemporary fantasy and horror cinema made through the artisanal use of animatronics.

“Carlo Rambaldi changed the world of special effects, makeup and puppetry,” del Toro says in a video message shared exclusively with Variety. “He brought a know-how and a finesse and a great sense of character and design that can only be described as being the heir of the old world craftsmanship and beauty that comes with a country with a great theatrical tradition and a great artistic tradition.”

Del Toro added: “Without him, it’s absolutely impossible to imagine the daring, beautiful work that is being done now and in the last few decades. He is not only a great Italian effect master, but a worldwide maestro of magic.”

As previously announced, Rambaldi’s Walk of Fame ceremony is taking place on Thursday at 1611 Vine Street in Hollywood, attended by Cinecittà studios president Antonio Saccone, several of Rambaldi’s family members and Matt Winston, son of Stan Winston, the Oscar-winning special effects master who designed the dinosaurs for “Jurassic Park.”

title: How Do You Get ‘Friday the 13th’ Fans to Care About Jason’s Mom? ‘Crystal Lake’ Team on Their Ambitious Attempt and Decision to Leave Out the Hockey Mask
summary: “You should know that Jason’s mother, Mrs. Voorhees, was the original killer.” That quote from “Scream,” in which Ghostface trips up Casey (Drew Barrymore) while asking her about scary movies, is a reminder that for many modern audiences, “Friday the 13th” matriarch Pamela Voorhees exists as little more than a trivia question. Yet Peacock and […]
content:
“You should know that Jason’s mother, Mrs. Voorhees, was the original killer.”

That quote from “Scream,” in which Ghostface trips up Casey (Drew Barrymore) while asking her about scary movies, is a reminder that for many modern audiences, “Friday the 13th” matriarch Pamela Voorhees exists as little more than a trivia question. Yet Peacock and A24 are betting big on audiences’ interest in an epic tale about the murderous mother.

“Crystal Lake” drops all eight episodes of the first season today, and creator and showrunner Brad Caleb Kane knows that slasher audiences might not initially be interested in an hours-long backstory of a woman on the edge in the ’70s, played here by recent Emmy winner Linda Cardellini.

Popular on Variety

“I’m an old school slasher fan. I certainly didn’t get into [1981 summer camp slasher] ‘The Burning’ to hear about [the killer] Cropsy’s long backstory,” Kane says. “You get into it for visceral thrills, and for how those movies make us feel — especially as kids, when most of us experience them for the first time. But in doing TV, and I’ve done a lot of TV up to this point, there really is a lot you can do delving into character and motivations and transformation.”

For the uninitiated, 1980’s “Friday the 13th” is about the young counselors of Camp Crystal Lake getting murdered as they try to reopen the property years after a tragic incident. In the end, the killer is revealed to be Mrs. Voorhees (Betsy Palmer), who blamed her son Jason’s drowning years earlier on counselors hooking up when they should have been watching him, and she decided to teach this new batch of horny teens a lesson.

The “Friday” franchise swelled into a dependable moneymaker, with 11 more films, a TV show, video games and merch galore following the original indie slasher. The focus shifted to Jason — now a hulking, undead killer — as the antagonist, leaving Mrs. Voorhees as little more than a footnote in the series. But with “Crystal Lake,” Kane, who is also the showrunner of horror prequel series “It: Welcome to Derry,” was interested in creating a fully realized antihero with a strong sense of time and place.

“We knew we were going to do the Pamela Voorhees story, but there’s very little known about her, except what we know from the first movie,” he says. “Betsy Palmer had her ideas about Pamela’s backstory if you read her interviews, and some ‘Friday the 13th’ comics dove into the backstory a bit and went in different directions. But when you get into television storytelling, people come to TV for character. We didn’t know much about the town of Crystal Lake, even though it’s fun to see in the movie. Where we started was, ‘What decade are we telling the story?’ And obviously, before the events of the first movie that take place in 1980, what was happening in that decade in America? Can we start with those thematics and somehow parallel the story of America in the ’70s and all the changes that were happening? There were a lot of changes that were happening for Pamela Voorhees and how she became the mother of all slashers that we ultimately know.”

Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in “Crystal Lake.” Matt Infante/PEACOCK

Cardellini, who has had key roles on critically acclaimed series from “Freaks and Geeks” and “ER” to “Mad Men” and “DTF St. Louis,” was excited to work on an ambitious project which had a broad canvas for her character and an opportunity for her to contribute to its success.

“It was really fun to talk to Brad about the show,” she says. “I also felt like he was excited to talk about it with me and to hear what I had to say. It wasn’t something where I was going to be shut out and just told what to do. The collaboration of it was exciting. The fact that I had never played anything like that draws me too. There’re so many things going for the show. Pam, she’s a singer and she’s a murderer. She’s also having sexual relationships with these men. There were so many different facets that, as a woman of a certain age, there is not that much to do in any given role. There was so much to do. There was so much to uncover. It was such a wild ride that it was just irresistible to me.”

Cardellini was also intrigued by the chance to develop Pamela’s unique motivation throughout the series.

“For Pam, everything is about Jason, which is great because the franchise is about Jason, and it’s wonderful that you get to meet her and understand her, because she is the original killer, but she’s only doing it because of Jason,” she says. “Everything relates back to her joining with Jason. So even what looks like a selfless move or like a move to help somebody else is really in service of her reconnecting with him.
