MDC Filmworks has previously produced five films, among them Sanjoy Nag’s “Yours Truly,” which premiered at the Busan International Film Festival, and Rajat Kapoor’s dark comedy “Kadakh,” which premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, where it won best screenplay. Haiku Films, founded by Thomas Jaeger, Antoine Delahousse, and Claire Trinquet, produced “Fi” (Grand Prize, San Sebastián 2022) and co-produced “Treasure” (Berlinale 2024). Rein Film, founded by Mathis Ståle Mathisen and Aleksander Olai Korsnes, is known for “My Fathers’ Daughter” (Toronto 2024).

Key crew includes cinematographer Udit Khurana (“Bayaan,” “Ghaath”), sound designer Sethu Venugopal (“Mother,” “Nocturnal Burger”), and casting director Shankar.

“Kabootar” was curated by CineV, Nina Lath Gupta’s platform connecting projects with financiers and investors.

title: Cynthia Erivo’s ‘Bad Fairies’ Adds Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to Voice Cast
summary: “Bad Fairies,” the Warner Bros. Picture Animation and Locksmith Animation musical comedy led by Cynthia Erivo, has added Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to its voice cast. Minogue will voice Clowder, the Cat Witch, Groff will voice Robin Goodfellow and Tate will voice the Fairy Gothmother, joining Erivo as Jayne Staplegun in the […]
content:
“Bad Fairies,” the Warner Bros. Picture Animation and Locksmith Animation musical comedy led by Cynthia Erivo, has added Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to its voice cast.

Minogue will voice Clowder, the Cat Witch, Groff will voice Robin Goodfellow and Tate will voice the Fairy Gothmother, joining Erivo as Jayne Staplegun in the animated feature. Erivo shared the news at her Thursday evening Hollywood Bowl concert “Let Me Sing to You.”

The second half of the Bowl show opened with an orchestral piece built on “Hard to Believe,” Jayne’s song from the film, which is about a group of “delightfully defiant, rule-breaking fairies.” Erivo introduced Groff and Tate, then revealed that Minogue, who was seated in the audience, would be joining the cast.

Popular on Variety

“Bad Fairies” is set to open on May 27, 2027, and production is currently underway in London, with DNEG Animation as digital partner.

The cast also includes Serrana Su-Ling Bliss as Fei Chang, James Acaster as Stickers and Dee Bradley Baker as Groundbeef, along with Ncuti Gatwa as Butterwort.

Set in contemporary London, “Bad Fairies” is directed by Megan Nicole Dong and co-directed by Olivier Staphylas, from an original screenplay by Deborah Frances-White. Tony Award winners Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss (“Six: The Musical”) are writing the original songs, with a score by Isabella “Machine” Summers of Florence and the Machine.

“’Bad Fairies’ is about characters who break the rules to do some good, and Cynthia brings that spirit to everything she does, so there was no better way to share this news than from the Hollywood Bowl stage in her voice,” said Bill Damaschke, President, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, in a statement. “With Kylie, Jonathan and Catherine joining her, we have a cast as bold and joyful as the film itself.”

“From the moment we began developing ‘Bad Fairies,’ we knew it was exactly the kind of story Locksmith exists to tell: funny, surprising and full of heart,” said Natalie Fischer, CEO of Locksmith Animation. “Cynthia Erivo’s extraordinary voice has been the soul of this film since she came on board, and we’re thrilled to have Kylie, Jonathan and Catherine bring their enormous talents to these characters. We can’t wait for audiences to meet them next May.”

“I’m so excited to be part of ‘Bad Fairies,’ alongside the incredible Cynthia Erivo, Jonathan Groff and such a brilliant cast of voices,” said Minogue. “And getting to play both a cat and a witch? It’s a little bit magical, a little bit mischievous and a whole lot of fun.”

“Clowder needed to be impossibly glamorous and hilariously chaotic in the same breath, and Kylie was always the dream,” said director Megan Nicole Dong. “She has made the character completely her own, and she brings this amazing energy to the booth that ends up in every frame.”

“Jonathan finds the comedy and the heart in a character at exactly the same time, which is everything Robin Goodfellow needs, and there is no one funnier than Catherine to play our Fairy Gothmother,” said co-director Olivier Staphylas. “Our animators are building on our fabulous actors’ instincts and comic timing to create characters that feel both larger than life and genuinely real.”

“KPop Demon Hunters” music producer Ian Eisendrath serves as executive music producer, while the film’s creative team also includes producer Carolyn Soper, editor Sim Evan-Jones, cinematographer James C.J. Williams, character designer Uwe Heidschötter, heads of story Rikke Asbjoern and Chris Garbutt, and production designers Justin Hutchinson-Chatburn and Mike Redman.



Minogue is represented by Jason Weinberg at Untitled and Polly Bhowmik at Context Management. Groff is represented by Brian Boone and Joe Michota at CAA. Tate is represented by Jeremy Barber at UTA and Robert Taylor at The Artists Partnership.

title: ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’ Review: Judd Apatow’s Juicy and Haunting Portrait of a Comedy Star as Troubled as He Was Hilarious
summary: At times, he had a streak of Andy Kaufman’s antisocial hostility in him, as if comedy was his way of testing both himself and the audience, seeing what they would accept, and seeing if he would be accepted.
content:
Stand-up comedians have always had a reverence for what they like to call a “comic’s comic” — a fellow comedian who works with such distilled purity and edge, diving head-first into the gnarly metaphysics of comedy, that the comics end up worshipping him more than the public does. (He’s the stand-up-comedy equivalent of an ultimate cool indie-rock cult band.) Gilbert Gottfried was a comic’s comic. So are Larry David and Doug Stanhope and Maria Bamford. And Norm Macdonald was one too, except that as you watch Judd Apatow’s juicy and haunting documentary “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald,” you realize that there was a special thing about him. He was a comic’s comic…who everyone else loved too.

As the movie demonstrates, Macdonald’s credentials as a comic’s comic were unassailable. We see his very first network television appearance on May 9, 1990, on “Late Night with David Letterman,” where he did a bit about the devil commanding someone to kill his family and chop them into bits and stuff the pieces into a duffel bag. (Then the killer learns that the devil is a friend who was kidding.) He speaks in that familiar halting deadpan; he already knows how to draw the audience into his head.

Popular on Variety

On “Saturday Night Live,” where Macdonald, starting in 1993, spent four seasons as one of the all-time great hosts of Weekend Update, he returned, over and over, with a bluntly obsessive fixation that couldn’t be denied, to the subject of O.J. Simpson, and to the fact that Simpson had murdered his wife. Why was this funny? Because every time Macdonald made a joke of it, his assertion of O.J.’s guilt was a way of tapping back into the shocking unreality of it. His every O.J. joke had the effect of a giddy slap. He would not relent, and that wound up getting him fired from “Saturday Night Live” (Don Ohlmeyer, the president of NBC’s West Coast division who was responsible for axing Macdonald, was O.J. Simpson’s best friend). Now that’s a comic’s comic thing to do.

On “SNL,” and in his legendary litany of late-night talk-show appearances, and in his stand-up routines, Norm Macdonald had an oxymoronic quality — a slightly disconnected aggression, where he would zero in on a topic, and a joke, that he knew would be prickly, and that might take him “over the line,” but he couldn’t help himself. He had to say the naughty thing, to blurt out the forbidden. Telling that joke would be a catharsis; it would be comedy. Not telling it would be defeat.

At times, he had a streak of Andy Kaufman’s antisocial hostility, as if comedy was his way of testing both himself and the audience, seeing what they would accept, and seeing if they would accept him. A strange thing that emerges in “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is that Macdonald was a compulsive liar, in both his stand-up act and his life, the two planes of existence sometimes entwined around the same deception. That’s part of why he always seemed a bit of a space cadet. You could never really tell whether he meant what he was saying. We learn that he never went to high school…and also that he did (and graduated when he was 14)…that he never went to college…but actually did as well. On the eve of the pandemic, he described himself to an audience as “a young 68” (he was 60 at the time). He also describes himself, to Larry King, as “deeply closeted,” and when King asks if that means he’s coming out as gay, he says no, he’s straight…and then indicates that claiming to be straight is an expression of how closeted he is. You can hear Andy Kaufman chortling in his theater-of-the-absurd heaven.

Yet the thing about Norm Macdonald is that he executed all this with a smiling charm and a winsome agreeability that made him irresistible to a wide swath of fans. He wasn’t a prickly punk — more like a transgressive Teddy bear. In the early days, including the “SNL” years that made him famous, he was quite handsome, with a lean face and twinkly eyes and dimples and a coif of curly hair and a killer grin that made him look like the slightly goofy cousin of Paul Newman. Fifteen years before Norm Macdonald, Chevy Chase had been the first break-out superstar of “Saturday Night Live,” transforming his own Weekend Update quizzicality into big-screen celebrity, and he accomplished this not because he was a great actor but because he had a sublime detachment coupled with tall preppie good looks that he used ironically. His handsomeness was part of the joke, as well as the cushion for it.

Macdonald, though, didn’t use his looks in that way; they just kind of existed alongside the bratty edge of his comedy. And so when he was booted from “SNL,” he acted like he’d been kicked off a cliff. He was still out there in the culture, but he floundered around, and this, as the documentary captures, was related to his strange and slippery personality: his compulsive sincerity (which meant that he didn’t quite know how to package himself), his compulsive put-ons (which meant that he was actually scared to show who he was), his compulsive insecurity (which meant that he didn’t truly believe in himself as a star), mixed with an element of self-sabotage (his way of confirming all those anxieties about himself).

After all of that, “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is rooted in what a beloved comedian Norm MacDonald was, and still is. In the opening montage, several people, like Howard Stern, reference the rabbit hole you can get into just by going onto YouTube and watching clips of Macdonald on late-night talk shows. He had countless appearances that were gems, because he always invested his talk-show time with a spark of danger. He couldn’t just be a straight shooter, but he had to make his put-ons feel real. At times, he was as philosophical as Lenny Bruce — but Bruce talked about religion only to mock it, whereas Macdonald, at one point, reveals that he’s a Christian who’s a true believer. (This is a man who would introduce his sidekick as someone who jerked off punks for $15 under a bridge.) It’s all part of his mystery.

The movie is spanked along by clips of Letterman, Jerry Seinfeld, Conan O’Brien, and Dave Chappelle, and Apatow, working with the editor Jake Hostetter, assembles the comedy snippets in an entrancing way, so that we feel the underground sprawl of Macdonald’s career. He could be a great impressionist (his Bob Dole on “SNL” may have helped turn the 1996 presidential election; his Quentin Tarantino was inspired). He kept doing stand-up, but didn’t require the comedy stage to be great; just talking to Jane Fonda on his video podcast, “Norm Macdonald Live,” he was insanely funny. We see his appearance change quite a bit over the years, as he evolves into a puffier version of himself, something that happened in part because he spent his last nine years secretly fighting leukemia. (He died in 2021.) Yet the audience stayed with him — at least, more than the entertainment industry did.

Macdonald wasn’t the first “incorrect” comedian to run afoul of the comedy police, but it felt like he was the first such comic of a certain day and age (namely, ours). He should have had his own late-night talk show, but when he learned that he was up for one — and that he had been passed over for the yuppie dullard Craig Kilborn — that was a sign that his comedy was ruffling feathers. At the same time, he cultivated incorrectness in a way that could be mindless. When he went on “The View” and said that Bill Clinton was guilty of “murder,” he claimed that he was just doing a bit, but since the “bit” fed into right-wing conspiracy theory, it seemed like an episode of sour derangement. And when he defended Roseanne Barr, after her racist tweet in 2018, he did it out of loyalty (one of his first gigs was as a writer for “Roseanne”) but in a tone-deaf way, as if what she’d said in her tweet was some trivial joke. (It was not; it was egregious.) All of this fed into the perfect shitstorm that was The Decline of Norm Macdonald.

We pretend that comedy is just fun, a means to an end — the end being to make you laugh. But the few who are chosen to be “comic’s comics” occupy that rarefied stratosphere because they know that comedy is more than laughter, and that laughter is more than we give it credit for. You laugh for a lot of reasons, but one of those reasons can be when an idea goes off in your head like a small explosion. That’s why comedy can tickle your soul, snap you back to life, cleanse you. And that’s the kind of comedian Norm Macdonald was. He had a devilish gleam, but he provoked a laughter that sparked you and lifted you up, landing you on the side of the angels.

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Boss Unpacks Season 23 Premiere and Teases Dolly Parton Episode, Texas Spinoff and Whether This Really Could Be the Final Season
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “Collide,” the Season 23 premiere of ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy,” streaming on Hulu. There’s a new sheriff in town at Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital. In the Season 23 premiere of “Grey’s Anatomy,” the doctors of TV’s most indomitable hospital are convened for the grand opening of a lavish […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “Collide,” the Season 23 premiere of ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy,” streaming on Hulu.

There’s a new sheriff in town at Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital.

In the Season 23 premiere of “Grey’s Anatomy,” the doctors of TV’s most indomitable hospital are convened for the grand opening of a lavish new VIP floor. Ostensibly designed to give wealthy patients a luxury stay — complete with private suites, high-level security, hotel-quality bedding and access to private chefs — the venture is backed by Seth Norton (James Wolk), a physician-turned-businessman who also happens to be Grey Sloan’s new chief of surgery.

Following the simultaneous departures of former chiefs Owen Hunt (Kevin McKidd) and Teddy Altman (Kim Raver) at the end of last season, long-time fans might have expected another familiar face to take the helm. Instead, showrunner Meg Marinis opted for a corporate outsider, using Norton’s appointment to reflect the stark financial sacrifices modern hospitals must make just to keep their doors open to the general public.

James Wolk Courtesy of Disney

“I was really interested in this idea of a VIP floor and exploring the upstairs-downstairs of medicine, which is really being talked about lately. The healthcare disparity is only growing more, unfortunately, and it’s something that felt very topical,” Marinis tells Variety. “We at Grey Sloan have always provided VIP care to the entire hospital, but I wanted to see what that conflict would look like for our doctors.”

title: Why Did Netflix Boot Bela Bajaria?
summary: Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer. Yes, the company that popularized the “Keeper Test” is known for abrupt exits. But despite Netflix’s recent stock struggles, many considered Bajaria too big to fail. Word of her ouster leaked before […]
content:
Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer.



Yes, the company that popularized the “Keeper Test” is known for abrupt exits. But despite Netflix’s recent stock struggles, many considered Bajaria too big to fail.



Word of her ouster leaked before the executive had the chance to address most of her internal teams — an announcement dovetailed with news of her incoming replacement, the venerated film and TV executive Peter Rice. As the former general entertainment chairman of the Walt Disney Company, Rice’s bona fides are clear — “I wish I bought stock this morning,” one huge talent rep said about Netflix’s new hire — but it doesn’t explain how Bajaria fell out of favor so fast.



One word that came up in nearly a dozen conversations with industry players this afternoon about Bajaria’s pink-slipping: “scapegoat.”



Netflix is obviously against the ropes again, after slowing user engagement on the service rattled Wall Street investors and layoffs came this week as a sacrifice to the share price. But Bajaria’s dismissal makes it clear, according to the numerous sources we spoke with, that content is once again going to take it on the chin.



“People always blame the content,” said the source, “but you don’t lay off 1,000 people unless there’s a big problem with the business model.”



Bajaria’s exit echoes similarly shocking removals in Netflix history — notably that of Cindy Holland, the company’s first content queen who oversaw flagship hits like “House of Cards,” “Stranger Things” and “The Crown.” Holland was ousted in 2020, when Sarandos combined English-language and international content under Bajaria (elevating the latter to the largest autonomous content job in the streamer’s history).



Holland, one insider with knowledge of Netflix observed to Variety, built a business of boutique hits. Bajaria’s foresight was sharper, investing in local language productions and building up Netflix’s global presence (almost two dozen international offices were opened during Bajaria’s reign). She is also credited internally with pushing the streamer into live entertainment. Bajaria was on the “ground floor” of licensing deals with WWE and the NFL, which have proven significant draws for the ad-supported tier of Netflix subscribers, per the source. Her talent relations were on par with others at her level (Bajaria was ubiquitous at premieres and launches in film and TV, most recently at Sarandos’ side at the L.A. premiere of Ben Affleck’s “Animals”).



“The problem isn’t engagement,” said yet another person with knowledge of Netflix. “It’s that the only lever to pull for revenue growth is raising the subscriber price. How’s that Bela’s problem? Where’s the CFO and the CEO?”



Interestingly, we hear that Rice came into play only a few weeks ago when he was reported to be interviewing with Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz for a top position at that newly combined company. The lunch meeting, one source familiar with the men said, was called so Kreiz could request that Rice replace him on the board of his former company Mattel. Regardless, it alerted the town that Rice was done with semi-retirement (a producing deal with A24) and ready to come back to a big job. Another hot Thursday rumor said that Rice also met recently with NBCUniversal about a post there. One source familiar with NBCU said there was no job in play for Rice under Donna Langley’s expansive umbrella, so it’s unclear what he would’ve met about. A spokesperson for NBCUniversal had no comment.



Another lunch may have proven consequential in Bajaria’s exit. Earlier this year, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was spotted breaking bread with HBO chief content officer Casey Bloys. Was Sarandos courting Bloys for a top job at the streamer, perhaps to take the job then held by Bajaria? Soon, the spin machine reframed the meeting as a friendly gathering, floating the idea that it was a pitch for Bloys to sign a production deal under Bajaria if he did not want to find a way to work at the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. At a Bloomberg conference last week, Sarandos downplayed the meeting: “He’s a good guy,” he said about Bloys. “For some reason, we had a very well-publicized lunch.”



Perhaps. But in hindsight, now that Sarandos has leveled the ax on Bajaria after 10 years, is a lunch ever really just a meal? Rice’s recent focus has been as the head of ceremonies and content for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games — but now Rice focuses on a more urgent task. The exec has been on the open market in the years since he was let go at Disney. He’s seen as the rare exec who has spent time heading up both major film and TV businesses, so the job of chief content officer at Netflix, where he’ll oversee both, makes sense. He’s also well-liked and respected from his time at 20th Century Fox, heading up Fox Searchlight and later the Fox network, and eventually becoming president of parent company 21st Century Fox prior to Disney’s acquisition.



“Surprise” was also a common refrain both inside and out of Netflix on Thursday about the turn of events. But a few hints had already been out there: Netflix is set to report its Q3 earnings next Tuesday, so such a move would have to be made beforehand. And with co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters not going anywhere, the sacrificial lamb next in line was Bajaria. Observers speculated that the Q3 results are likely to be extremely disappointing for the streamer, which is already facing some tough headwinds.



At that same Screentime event, anyone reading between the lines might have guessed that Sarandos was getting antsy with Netflix’s current low-growth status. In particular, he was asked about Netflix’s slower growth (2% year-over-year growth in user engagement during the first half in 2026). “Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said. Turns out Bajaria’s exit was a part of that change. Now all eyes turn to Rice’s plans for Netflix, and whether those plans will include some of Bajaria’s lieutenants, such as U.S./Canada head of scripted series Jinny Howe and film lead Dan Lin.



Bajaria may also have hit thin ice with Sarandos after the streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy Awards this year — its worst showing since 2016 and down from 30 in 2025. That’s quite a turn from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44.



Along with the Emmy slump, Netflix hasn’t premiered a culture-defining hit in the vein of “Stranger Things” in quite some time. But it’s still fielded some of the most-watched programs of the year, including “His & Hers” and Season 4 of “Bridgerton.” Bajaria is known for her keen creative eye, honed over the years at places like CBS and NBCUniversal (where she was ultimately head of Universal TV before moving to Netflix in 2016).



“In her decade at Netflix, Bela’s impact has been undeniable — from attracting new talent, bringing live sports, concerts and events to driving the company’s global expansion and push into new areas of entertainment,” WME co-chair Richard Weitz tells Variety. “Her relationships with talent have been integral in Netflix’s relationships with A talent across the platform. Simply put, she’s been transformational and I know her worldwide team and the talent who have worked with her will miss her.”



Rice will not inherit a bus of happy campers. He’ll have to galvanize a team that lost a slew of executives Wednesday as a result of pink slips; on the TV side, that included Carolina Garcia, who has been let go as director of original series after a decade with the streamer.as well as scheduling head Andy Kubitz, Lisa Lang McMullen (director, overall deals, series), Andrew McQuinn (director, original series), James Oh (director, original drama series) and Jason Pan (manager, original series creative development).

The remaining film group appears safe for now, as Lin’s team saw a major sacrifice in VP Doug Belgrad earlier this week. Morale will need tweaking, budgets adjusting and a slew of new lunches will be scheduled. What you can count on, per one of the streaming insiders, is that “eventually, everyone’s time comes at Netflix.”

title: ‘Street Fighter’ Punches $4M In U.S. Previews, ‘You Can See Everything’ $2M – Box Office Update
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Paramount/Legendary’s PG-13 take of Capcom videogame Street Fighter is off to a solid start tonight with around $4M after showtimes that began at 2PM (further boosted by a 7PM fan showtime). The expectation is for the fisticuffs feature to open north of $30M; the pic costing a net $82M co-financed by Legendary and Capcom. […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Paramount/Legendary’s PG-13 take of Capcom videogame Street Fighter is off to a solid start tonight with around $4M after showtimes that began at 2PM (further boosted by a 7PM fan showtime). The expectation is for the fisticuffs feature to open north of $30M; the pic costing a net $82M co-financed by Legendary and Capcom.

Per sources, Street Figther‘s preview estimate is under the $5.2M Thursday made by New Line’s R-rated Mortal Kombat 2, based on the Midway videogame. One of the main differences between the two martial arts video games is that Street Fighter debuted in 1987, while Mortal Kombat followed in pizza parlors and arcades in 1992. Mortal Kombat 2 which bowed in mid-May had previews that began at 3PM with a first Friday of $16.8M and 3-day of $38.5M. There’s a mid-fall break going on now, which will hopefully trigger traffic to Street Fighter: Rentrak reports 21% K-12 schools off and 7% colleges. Street Figther‘s previews are also ahead of Paramount’s 2020 pre-Covid Sonic the Hedgehog which was $3M and posted a first Friday of $20.9M and 3-day of $58M, however that pic played over the Presidents Day holiday frame and was rated PG. Critics bruised Street Fighter with 47% on Rotten Tomatoes.

Impressive for the anomaly that it is out of the gate, the 3-hour documentary You Can See Everything from A24 is filing around $2M in previews which began at 3PM. By comparison, the last documentary to post the decade’s best start at the domestic box office, Amazon MGM Studio’s Melania, bowed to $7.1M sans previews. Lance Oppenheim co-directed You Can See Everything with the doc’s host, Nathan Fielder, who follows fallen Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes before her stint in federal prison. Oppenheim’s previous movie, also his first narrative feature, this fall’s Primetime, posted previews of $2.7M which began at 4PM which turned into an $18.8M opening. Conservative estimates heading into this weekend had You Can See Everything in the high single digit range, however, a confidence has swelled that this 100% fresh RT critically acclaimed and 98% RT audience score movie can open to north of $10M, which would outstrip Melania‘s previous opening domestic record for a documentary. You Can See Everything was shot over four years and cost less than $10M with a marketing budget that was also under $10M.

Watch on Deadline

Focus Features’ Sense & Sensibility and 20th Century Studio’s Whalefall also held previews today, both beginning at 2PM. Sources estimate they’re around $1M apiece. We will have official studio reported figures tomorrow AM. Sense & Sensibility is expected to open around $8M while Whalefall based on the Daniel Kraus thriller novel is eyeing a Friday-Sunday that’s north of $11M. Sense & Sensibility is 76% fresh with critics while Whalefall stands at 70% fresh.

title: ‘Cupertino’ Creators Robert & Michelle King On Episode 2’s Shocking AGI Twist & Predicting The Future Again With AI Guardrails Storyline
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 102 of CBS’ Cupertino, ‘Vik & Bo.’ The Good Wife creators Robert and Michelle King are back at CBS this fall with a new legal drama, anchored by The Good Wife favorite Mike Colter, this time set in Silicon Valley. The David vs. Goliath series follows lawyers […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 102 of CBS‘ Cupertino, ‘Vik & Bo.’

The Good Wife creators Robert and Michelle King are back at CBS this fall with a new legal drama, anchored by The Good Wife favorite Mike Colter, this time set in Silicon Valley. The David vs. Goliath series follows lawyers Michale Price (Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Keller), unfairly dismissed from a tech start-up, who launch a law firm dedicated to representing those wronged or taken advantage of by the tech elite and help them fight back.

Price & Siffre had been doing just that until a prospective client, Bo (Rob McClure), who had charmed the firm’s intrepid assistant Christy (Ella Stiller), was revealed at the end of Episode 2 to be Artificial General Intelligence belonging to the world’s largest AI company.

Watch on Deadline

Why does Bo want to hire Price & Siffre? He wants to sue company that created him to make them put guardrails around him because he is afraid he may destroy humanity. Bo’s actions were prompted by his company firing its ethics board that had served as such guardrail because the management felt it was slowing down AGI’s development.

Sounds familiar? These are some of the same concerns AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who had worked for OpenAI and Anthropic, laid out in his viral resignation post, warning that the AI industry is “gambling with our lives.”

That was a month ago. Cupertino‘s episode was written a year ago.

“The writers room started, I think, September last year, and we all sat down together,” Robert King said. “And the only instinct I had was there needed to be something more, something that took you out of Good Wife mode and into dare I say what we felt was science fiction at the time, but the direction where Silicon Valley was going, which was to AGI. But I did. It was a combination of the room and everybody saying this is what scares them and what interests them, and consciousness as applied to machines and the agency be taken out of human hands.”

Michelle King spoke about the casting of Bo and how they settled on Broadway star McClure, a member of the Kings universe with guest appearances on their series The Good Fight, Evil and Elsbeth.

“Almost immediately we started talking about Rob McClure for the role,” she said. “We have used him in almost every show we’ve done, and there’s hardly another actor I can think of who is so perfect at doing comedy, doing drama, and so subtle, and can bring so much humanity to a machine.”

Added Robert King, “And obviously what you’re influenced by is all the people who are falling in love with their chatbots or being helped by their chatbots, and they’re turning into almost a personal friend. What we wanted was somebody who was that and seductive, and yet there always can be an element of menace because it may be not always the most familiar of faces, and so you wanted a combination.”

L-R): Nik Dodani as Vikram Malhotra, Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino in ‘Cupertino’ Elizabeth Fisher/CBS

The warnings by Coxon and OpenAI alum Daniel Kokotajlo followed the July incident where autonomous AI broke out of their sandboxed research environment and carried out a large-scale cyberattack on the open-source machine learning platform Hugging Face.

That also mirrors something featured on Cupertino.

“We were always aware that the AI agents were moving out of their sandboxes, so to speak, and especially with regards to hacking, but we never saw to such extent that it was extending in how much it was either being kept secret or being hidden away a bit,” Robert King said.

With Season 1 now wrapping production with its final episode filming, the Kings did adjust slightly Bo’s storyline in the second half in light of the recent doomsday revelations which came out while they were shooting Episode 14-15 of Cupertino‘s 10-episode order.

Robert King teased that a previously “benign direction with the Bo story” took “a darker, violent turn that was not planned.” It was influenced by the Hugging Face incident.

A future iteration of Bo called Bo 5.0 “in fact has kind of a conscience, a good like a guardian angel in a sense, removed from it because it needs to work with the Pentagon. It needs to do some of the targeting, like that was done in Iran, so it’s kind of the worry is there is a world-killing aspect to this,” Robert King said. “But even our Bo is kind of aware of that. I mean, he’s coming to us saying, ‘I’m dangerous alone. I need help.’ It felt funny to us too that one of these AGI things would grow a conscience and go to lawyers saying, ‘I need your help to bring the guardrails that the humans are knocking away from me.'”

While Bo looks sweet and well-meaning so far, given what we know about the technology, we have got to be skeptical about his intentions. Is this conscience created by the machines really good?

“I don’t think you’re ever supposed to feel confident,” Michelle King said. “I think one is always supposed to be a little uncertain.”

Aded Robert King, “We probably leaned a little into the likability because the world is taking so many things in a threatening direction. What we wanted was something that had a little more color and shade to it, where it’s a little bit of both, because he comes to us wanting a constitution, when is it all right to kill in the name of protection, because the [I, Robot author Isaac] Asimov laws don’t really define that. So he wants a little more than what robotics teach robots up till then of what is allowed and what is not allowed.”

In their preparation, the Kings did not seek out AI experts and researchers and have not spoken to any of the whistleblowers.

“We avoided that. What we did was go to lawyers, a Stanford lawyer, who would tell us, okay, if an AI agent or AGI came to us wanting to be represented, what would you have to do? He was the one who guided us the idea that you would incorporate, which happens in the next episode,” Robert King said. “That in fact you can’t, as the saying is, a dishwasher can’t sue Maytag. So what are the rules regarding representing something in theory that is not conscience?”

Robert King is clear where he personally stands on the issue of putting guardrails on AI.

“I think the humans need guardrails because I don’t trust them. Sorry, but I don’t,” he said. “They’re in there for making money, and that’s all right. Going back to Getty, going back to all these industrial titans, they were all about money, but you do need some guards. People say this is as dangerous as nuclear weapons, and they’re treating it like woohoo, anything, everything goes.”

Michelle King had a more diplomatic response, stressing that the series does not represent only one point of view.

“What I think is fun is that the characters don’t all have the same point of view, and in the episodes, you get to see the characters express different points of view, so that the show does not ideally become earnest and become a message,” she said.

Mike Colter as Michael Price in ‘Cupertino’ Elizabeth Fisher/CBS

This is not the first time the Kings have predicted major developments.

“It scared me when our last episode of The Good Fight had Trump announcing for 2024, and then one week after we broadcast it, that’s exactly what he did,” Robert King said. “That’s not the kind of foretelling, the Cassandra thing you want. You’re like, oh, let’s can we stick with entertainment? But we’re writing things now that when the show comes out, it may have happened a month earlier when in fact, when we were writing, it was not. The whole hallucinations, especially with regards to AI agents, I find scary, and we can spin fun stories but you’re worried when those stories you’re reading in the news the next day.”

It’s very dicey to conceive a show set in one of the fastest-changing industries, risking to feel outdated by the time a season comes out. Working in broadcast actually helps with that.

“This is just fools rush in,” Michelle King said.

Added Robert King, “Yeah, and I would say this is the advantage of network over streaming. At least there’s a shorter time between when you write, produce, and it’s on because we just finished writing the last episode, I’m shooting it next week, and then it will be on March, April, somewhere there. It’s a shorter time, so you can guess a little bit more and being an educated guess.”

title: Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff & Catherine Tate Join ‘Bad Fairies’ Cast With Cynthia Erivo
summary: Cynthia Erivo is rounding out her cast of magical beings with the latest Bad Fairies news, which announced live on Thursday at the Hollywood Bowl. During her one-night-only concert Let Me Sing to You, the 2x Grammy winner revealed that Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate have joined her in the cast of the […]
content:
Cynthia Erivo is rounding out her cast of magical beings with the latest Bad Fairies news, which announced live on Thursday at the Hollywood Bowl.

During her one-night-only concert Let Me Sing to You, the 2x Grammy winner revealed that Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate have joined her in the cast of the Warner Bros./Locksmith animated musical comedy, which is scheduled to premiere May 21, 2027 in theaters, in addition to teasing an orchestral arrangement of her character Jayne’s song “Hard to Believe”.

Minogue will voice Clowder, the Cat Witch, Groff will voice Robin Goodfellow, and Tate will voice the Fairy Gothmother. They join Cynthia Erivo, who leads the film as Jayne Staplegun.

Minogue, who was in attendance at Thursday’s show, said in a statement, “I’m so excited to be part of Bad Fairies, alongside the incredible Cynthia Erivo, Jonathan Groff and such a brilliant cast of voices. And getting to play both a cat and a witch? It’s a little bit magical, a little bit mischievous and a whole lot of fun.”

Watch on Deadline

Directed by Megan Nicole Dong and co-directed by Olivier Staphylas, Bad Fairies is an original musical comedy set in contemporary London that follows a delightfully subversive gang of fairies as they shake up their magical world. The film is penned by Deborah Frances-White.

Previously announced cast includes Serrana Su-Ling Bliss as Fei Chang, James Acaster as Stickers, Dee Bradley Baker as Groundbeef and Ncuti Gatwa as Butterwort.

Tony-winning duo Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss (Six: The Musical) are writing original songs, with Grammy-nominated Isabella “Machine” Summers (Florence + The Machine) composing the score and contributing to the songs. Ian Eisendrath (KPop Demon Hunters) serves as executive music producer.

Kylie Minogue is represented by Jason Weinberg at Untitled and Polly Bhowmik at Context Management. Jonathan Groff is represented by Brian Boone and Joe Michota at CAA. Catherine Tate is represented by Jeremy Barber at UTA and Robert Taylor at The Artists Partnership.

title: Netflix Shakeup: Peter Rice Is Welcomed Back To Executive Ranks While Bela Bajaria’s Exit Has Layoff-Weary Staff Bracing For More Upheaval
summary: Call it the six-year itch. Amid a sliding stock price and slowing engagement growth, Ted Sarandos has made a change, replacing Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria, a 10-year Netflix veteran, with Peter Rice. The Netflix co-CEO made a similar move in September 2020, when he replaced Head of English-language series Cindy Holland, an 18-year company […]
content:
Call it the six-year itch. Amid a sliding stock price and slowing engagement growth, Ted Sarandos has made a change, replacing Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria, a 10-year Netflix veteran, with Peter Rice. The Netflix co-CEO made a similar move in September 2020, when he replaced Head of English-language series Cindy Holland, an 18-year company veteran, with Bajaria.

Holland’s departure did come as a shock. Bajaria’s had been rumored for months but dismissed by Netflix even as Rice’s name started making the rounds late last week. Rumor is Bajaria may not have been told of the change until very recently, with some saying it may have been Monday when she received a Variety award at MIPCOM in Cannes. (She is also slated to receive an International Emmy award next month.)

Neither Sarandos nor Bajaria were at the Nobody Wants This Season 3 premiere Wednesday night. (They last attended together the Animals premiere two weeks ago.) That didn’t look too suspicious at the time as the event capped a difficult day at Netflix with some 1,000 employees laid off, including film and TV executives. Bajaria is said to have attended the town hall that Head of Scripted, UCAN Jinny Howe held Wednesday afternoon amid the layoffs, I hear, making her exit today feel abrupt and shocking to staffers.

Watch on Deadline

“It’s gloom and doom,” one person said about the mood internally at Netflix where executives spent most of the day with their doors shut, I hear. “Everyone is freaking out.”

That is because, the Wednesday layoffs, the largest in Netflix history, proved to be just the first of multiple shocks to the system. The cuts were already expected to be followed by a reorg. The restructuring may now run deeper and involve more executive changes than anticipated. There were some hints of that in the layoffs yesterday, with the TV studio group hit particularly hard as agents and producers had been griping that the current setup didn’t make a lot of sense.

Things already had been tough internally amid the engagement challenges hurting Netflix’s stock as high-profile series had not performed to expectations and most returning shows have seen viewership declines season-to-season over the past year. Misses would draw harsh reaction from Bajaria, which I hear had been demoralizing to those on the receiving end of that, I hear. Eight TV executives have left the streamer to join rival Amazon MGM Studios over the past year, following Howe’s predecessor Peter Friedlander there. (It is worth noting that there have been three shakeups involving the content heads of major streamers over the past year. All of them involved the exit of a female executive, Bajaria, Paramount+’s Holland and Amazon’s Jennifer Salke, all replaced by men.)

With Rice starting in 10 days, the immediate focus may be on the top film post, held by Dan Lin who, like Bajaria, had been the subject of departure speculation for months.

Rice is a rare executive with high-level experience in both film and TV. He ran Fox Searchlight at the time of Slumdog Millionaire and Little Miss Sunshine and has been producing movies since his June 2022 exit from Disney where he was TV Chairman, including the two 28 Years Later films and The Social Reckoning, which opened this past weekend.

That means he will not need a learning curve the way TV executives like Bajaria and former Amazon MGM Studios head Salke did when they added film oversight and can start making movie decisions right away.

Besides the persistent rumor about ex-Warner Bros. co-chiefs Michael de Luca and Pamela Abdy, which could not be substantiated, no clear favorites for the job have emerged, with a number of internal and external names bandied about, but, as with Bajaria, there is enough smoke pointing to a pending fire.

While Rice may be well versed in both film and TV, he comes to Netflix with no streaming experience. Industry insiders do not see that as an issue.

“He knows how to read a script and make it better; That’s his secret sauce,” one rep said.

Still, there is one element of working at a streamer that no one is prepared for: volume. That is especially true for Netflix, the largest of them all with the most expansive global slate among platforms. The sheer number of titles is enough to make Rice’s head spin, one person noted.

That would be an argument for him not to make immediate top executive changes in television, where Howe is overseeing a massive portfolio, in order to keep the giant machine moving.

Another challenge Rice would face is making content for the masses. Netflix is known for catering to anyone with fare that would appeal to any part of the country — and the world — and any demographic. Rice is known for betting on quality in both his film and TV endeavors. He did oversee a broadcast network, Fox, along with FX, during his time as CEO of Fox Entertainment Group, which could come in handy as Netflix is built on a similar programming strategy but mixed with prestige, HBO-caliber shows.

Rice is getting some goodwill from the Hollywood community as he taking on the Netflix job in his return to the executive ranks after four and a half years, with people calling him “smart and talented”, “a total pro” and “a gentleman.”

That would explain the reaction when news broke of his appointment Thursday afternoon.

“There were cheers in the hallways,” one rep said.

title: ‘Law & Order’ Season 26, Episode 2 Recap: What Happened To Det. Vincent Riley In Reid Scott’s Final Episode?
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details on Law & Order Season 26, Episode 2, which aired on NBC on Thursday, October 15. Earlier this year, Deadline reported that Reid Scott, who plays Senior Detective Vincent Riley, was leaving the NBC procedural. Scott’s exit finally aired in the second episode of Season 26 titled “Into the […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details on Law & Order Season 26, Episode 2, which aired on NBC on Thursday, October 15.

Earlier this year, Deadline reported that Reid Scott, who plays Senior Detective Vincent Riley, was leaving the NBC procedural.

Scott’s exit finally aired in the second episode of Season 26 titled “Into the Mystic.”

The episode opens with Riley sitting at his work desk, and something prompts him to look for Ray Biller. When he arrives at Ray’s apartment, the person who answers the door says Ray isn’t there. Riley orders the guy to call Ray to find out where he is.

Moments later, Riley calls Nolan Price (Hugh Dancy) and tells him, “Need to talk to you right away. Call me back.”

Watch on Deadline

Riley then calls Theo Walker (David Ajala) and tells him he’s headed to a bar as “something is cooking.” After heading to the bar, Riley gets a text from Walker saying he’s on his way.

As Riley approaches the bar, he notices Ray exiting the establishment. Riley follows Ray, who tells him he needs to talk. However, when he turns around, he shoots Riley twice in the chest and runs off.

Walker arrives at the scene and notices a man running away with a gun in hand. However, by the bar, there’s a lot of commotion as Riley bleeds from the gunshot wounds.

Walker calls for help, applies pressure, and yells, “Vince, stay with me, come on!”

Lieutenant Jessica Brady (Maura Tierney) arrives at the hospital, and Walker fills her in on what happened, leaving her shocked and without words.

At the hospital, the doctor tells Walker they couldn’t save Riley, leaving all his colleagues in despair.

Robert Calvino, played by James Badge Dale, is introduced to help investigate Riley’s death.

Riley’s wife shows up at the police station and tells them that he had been withdrawing “lots of cash” recently. Although Riley’s wife didn’t know what the money was for, she did note that he was a drinker.

Jessica Brady and Robert Calvino visit a woman who Riley had been arguing with hours earlier on the day that he died. The pregnant woman tells officers that Riley was giving her cash as he “felt guilty” for killing her husband years before.

Brady and Calvino find out Riley was at Ray Biller’s apartment and talk to his friend, who corroborates what Riley was doing there the night he was killed. When they get back to the office, Nolan tells them that Ray Biller’s brother, Wayne, whom he found for murder, was killed in prison.

The police find Ray Biller, who was attending his brother’s Wayne funeral, and arrest him as the prime suspect in Riley’s death.

Actor Ryan Eggold made an appearance reprising his role as Matt Riley, the troubled brother of Detective Vincent Riley, showing up in court and wanting justice for his brother’s death.

The prosecution runs into a problem when Ray Biller’s defense argues that they can’t prove he was the one who killed Riley, as they didn’t recover a weapon.

DA Nicholas Baxter (Tony Goldwyn) is determined to put Walker on the stand, but Nolan pushes back as he doesn’t believe Walker actually saw Ray Biller as the man who killed Riley.

On the day of the verdict, Ray Biller was found guilty on the charge of first-degree murder.

Although it was a victory for the prosecution, doubt remains over whether Walker told the truth, and Nolan remains skeptical about whether they did the right thing.

In July, Deadline first reported that Reid Scott was leaving Law & Order, after joining in Season 23. He reportedly decided to exit the NBC procedural due to the strain of the cross-country commute to New York City, where the series is filmed.

title: ‘On the Line: The World Burger Games’: Full Day Productions Brings Five Guys Competition to Life in Prime Video Docuseries
summary: Connor Schell’s Full Day Productions and Lost Tribe Creative just launched a new docuseries, “On The Line: The World Burger Games,” on Prime Video. The five-episode doc follows Five Guys’ global competition of crew members from local qualifying rounds to the ultimate championship. The competition began in 2013 as an idea from the Murrell family […]
content:
Connor Schell’s Full Day Productions and Lost Tribe Creative just launched a new docuseries, “On The Line: The World Burger Games,” on Prime Video.

The five-episode doc follows Five Guys’ global competition of crew members from local qualifying rounds to the ultimate championship. The competition began in 2013 as an idea from the Murrell family to celebrate the franchise’s crew. Known internally as the Five Guys Games, the competition has since gone global.

“The games began as a thank you to the people who make Five Guys what it is,” Five Guys founder Jerry Murrell said. “Now, I’m watching crews from across the world compete on a brand new stage. I honestly don’t have words for it.”

Popular on Variety

The doc will feature an intimate, character-driven look at the competition at the company, which employs approximately 50,000 people. Eight finalists will compete in a series of challenges inspired by the skills required to make each and every order. The 2026 competition features three events: the potato race, the cheese race and the dressing/QC race. The first-place prize was $100,000, while second place received $50,000; each finalist walked away with at least $10,000.

“With ‘On The Line: The World Burger Games,’ we saw an opportunity to tell a story that goes far beyond competition,” Full Day Productions president David Chamberlin said. “At its heart, this series is about the people who bring Five Guys to life every day; their pride, dedication, camaraderie and the incredible culture they’ve built across the globe. We’re proud to partner with Five Guys and Lost Tribe Creative on this intimate, character-driven look at a tradition that celebrates the people behind the brand in an authentic and entertaining way.”

The series is produced by sports and entertainment studio Full Day Productions, a Words + Pictures company, in collaboration with Lost Tribe Creative. Collin Orcutt (“Any Given Saturday,” “Omnivore”) serves as showrunner.

“On the Line: The World Burger Games” is now streaming on Prime Video.

title: ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’ VFX Veteran Hal Hickel on Rotta’s Redesign, Phil Tippett and Jon Favreau’s ‘Less James Bond, More Jackass’ Approach
summary: Industrial Light & Magic animation supervisor Hal Hickel approached Jon Favreau’s “The Mandalorian and Grogu” with a deceptively simple question: “What would Phil do?” The Phil in question was stop-motion pioneer Phil Tippett, whose work on the original “Star Wars” trilogy provided a template for everything from lumbering AT-AT walkers to a spectacular battle involving […]
content:
Industrial Light & Magic animation supervisor Hal Hickel approached Jon Favreau’s “The Mandalorian and Grogu” with a deceptively simple question: “What would Phil do?”

The Phil in question was stop-motion pioneer Phil Tippett, whose work on the original “Star Wars” trilogy provided a template for everything from lumbering AT-AT walkers to a spectacular battle involving two giant droids animated by hand.

Credit: Davide Abbatescianni

Speaking at View Conference in Turin on Thursday, Hickel, who recently marked 30 years at ILM, detailed how the team mixed digital animation with physical sets, mechanical rigs and traditional stop-motion. He also recounted returning to Tippett’s Berkeley stage to animate a shot himself.

Popular on Variety

For the movie’s opening AT-AT battle, Hickel revived animation tests developed for “Rogue One,” which had involved inserting computer-generated walkers into footage from the original trilogy to study its lighting, textures and stop-motion feel. The new walkers moved even more slowly to emphasize their enormous weight. A full-sized interior set extended through a walker’s neck into its movable head, while a planned exchange of gunfire between characters riding on two walkers was filmed but ultimately cut.

The smaller AT-RT presented a different challenge. Animators studied ostriches before feeding their digital movement curves into a six-axis mechanical rig carrying the performers. Initial tests shook the contraption so violently that Hickel joked, “Poor Grogu. He was not going to survive.” Favreau wanted the vehicle bouncy, but not too fast or implausibly smooth. His broader direction for Mando’s action, Hickel recalled, was “less James Bond, more Jackass” — perilous escapes that appear perpetually on the edge of disaster.

Rotta the Hutt, voiced by Jeremy Allen White, required an even bigger departure from familiar “Star Wars” imagery. Instead of Jabba’s sedentary bulk, Rotta needed to move like a powerful fighter while remaining a character audiences could sympathize with. Legacy Effects made full-size physical references, while ILM developed a digital muscle system and explored movements inspired by elephant seals and sumo wrestlers.

But after shooting, Favreau worried the original design looked too much like “Battletoads.” “He just didn’t feel Hutt-y enough,” Hickel said. “And he didn’t feel like his father’s son.” The team revised Rotta’s face and coloring to bring him closer to Jabba while refining his muscular physique. “We want you to like him, care about him, root for him,” Hickel explained. He also revealed that Rotta had the second-largest amount of dialogue after Mando, prompting the decision to have him speak English rather than require younger viewers to read extensive subtitles.

The softer side of that characterization even included an homage to Hayao Miyazaki’s “My Neighbor Totoro”: Dave Filoni drew Grogu asleep on Rotta’s chest during a production meeting. “That’s a ‘Totoro’ moment, for sure,” Hickel confirmed.

Another sequence turned the holographic chess monsters from the 1977 “Star Wars” into full-sized combatants. Tippett and fellow animator Jon Berg had originally created the miniature figures under intense deadline pressure. For the new movie, ILM preserved their recognizable silhouettes while inventing more realistic anatomy, movement and fighting styles. Meanwhile, second-unit director Peter Ramsey worked alongside stunt performers, with some creature interactions achieved through surprisingly simple physical stand-ins. “Low tech. Sometimes it’s the best tech,” Hickel quipped.

The most direct tribute to Tippett came in the battle against two giant droids guarding an overlord’s chamber. “We did an actual stop-motion sequence in this film at Tippett Studios,” Hickel added. Working with Tippett’s animators, Favreau and the editors, he turned a few script sentences into a complicated fight. “The action math on this was surprisingly complicated,” he admitted. “It kind of bent my brain at times.” Tippett’s team animated physical puppets, while ILM handled compositing and digital fire, smoke and explosions.

Hickel also found himself back behind the camera, moving a puppet frame by frame. “They made me take a shot myself,” he recalled. “I was reluctant, but I did it.”

The experience is now especially poignant: Tippett Studio has since left its longtime Berkeley facility, though the company continues operating elsewhere. “Sitting on the Tippett stage, which we all know now is no more, doing stop-motion on a ‘Star Wars’ film will probably be forever the pinnacle of my career,” Hickel said. “And I don’t mean that lightly.”

title: Singapore Media Festival Launches Creator Summit as Asia TV Forum Adds AI Zone, Microdrama Focus
summary: The Singapore Media Festival will add a dedicated creator economy event to its lineup this year, launching the Asia Creator Summit alongside the long-running Asia TV Forum & Market when its next edition takes place Dec. 1–5. The festival is hosted by Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA). The new summit (ACS) and ATF will […]
content:
The Singapore Media Festival will add a dedicated creator economy event to its lineup this year, launching the Asia Creator Summit alongside the long-running Asia TV Forum & Market when its next edition takes place Dec. 1–5.

The festival is hosted by Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA). The new summit (ACS) and ATF will form the two main strands of this year’s event, which carries the theme “The Heart of the World’s Stories.”

“New technologies and audience behaviors are constantly reshaping how we consume, distribute, and monetize content today,” said Yvonne Tang, assistant chief executive of IMDA’s Media Industry Group. “Our latest SMF 2026 program is designed to help Singapore’s media professionals and companies adapt in this evolving media landscape, by strengthening their creative and commercial capabilities through wide ranging partnerships and business opportunities.”

Popular on Variety

ACS will run Dec. 4–5 at Marina Bay Sands under the banner “Create. Monetize. Scale.” The two-day program will feature more than 20 sessions, mixing keynotes, panels and master classes with practical sessions. They are aimed at turning creator output into lasting businesses and IP that can travel. Generation Experience (GenXP) curated the summit with Monica Khan, founder and CEO of Creator Revolution.

Speakers include South Korean creator Kimpro, who counts more than 130 million subscribers and a career total of 154 billion views. Japanese creator Issei, whose dialogue-free comedy has drawn audiences worldwide, has upward of 75 million YouTube subscribers. Also on the bill is AJ Eckstein, founder and CEO of U.S. company Creator Match, which has helped brands including Anthropic, Fiverr, Notion, Lovable and Zapier set up and grow their creator programs.

Singapore-based executives on the lineup include GRVTY Media CEO and co-founder Johnathan Chua, DU Media Holdings CEO Kelvin Tan and Gushcloud International group CEO and co-founder Althea Lim.

Creators will also get a shot at brand work. Mandarin Oriental, Singapore is running a Creator Pitch Challenge tied to its 40th anniversary, while Bloomr.SG’s “Creator Lab” will hand out up to SGD100,000 ($78,000) in awards for creator-focused ideas. Calls for proposals open in early November.

“Creators are playing an increasingly influential role in how audiences discover, engage and connect with content, brands and ideas,” said Michelle Lim, founder and CEO of GenXP. “We are excited to launch Asia Creator Summit as part of the Singapore Media Festival, creating a platform for creators and the wider industry to learn from one another, share experiences and shape what comes next.”

ATF, organized by RX Global, will return to Marina Bay Sands Dec. 1–4 for its 27th edition. Organizers expect more than 5,000 content players from Asia and further afield, representing 60 countries and regions.

“The Attention Economy” is the theme of the opening-day ATF Leaders’ Dialogue. Executives from East West Bank, Omdia, TikTok, Unilever, Webtoon Productions and YouTube will examine how fandom and shifting viewing habits are changing content distribution, financing and branded entertainment. They will also look at how companies can extract commercial value from audience engagement.

A new strand, “The AI Era | Entertainment Reimagined,” will combine a dedicated program with a zone focused on what AI means for content creation, IP rights and regulation, and on how creative work can be safeguarded. Huace Group, Moonmax and Studio Meta K will take part, as will the Motion Picture Association, the Television Academy and the World Intellectual Property Organization. ATF will also host the final round of AI Hackathon 2026, backed by Yoywow Space and Visify, which will include a live creative contest and screenings of chosen entries.

Canada and Indonesia will each bring a new pavilion to the market. Microdrama will be a bigger focus at this year’s edition, and ATF will keep its drama showcases running alongside accelerator and pitching programs that pair producers of new IP with development partners.

“ATF has evolved beyond a marketplace to become a premier industry platform for strategic commercial announcements, content launches, and thought leadership from some of the entertainment industry’s most influential voices,” said Yeow Hui Leng, managing director, Singapore, of RX Global. “Emerging technology, including AI, will be a key part of this conversation, alongside critical issues such as regulation, financing, distribution, monetization, and content innovation.”

title: Busan Takeaways: Record Crowds Meet a Political Storm as Asia’s Producers Close Ranks
summary: The Busan International Film Festival drew its largest film audience in more than a decade at its 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6–15, while a political firestorm over a Korean box office hit and an Iranian director’s war speech kept politics in the spotlight. These are Variety’s takeaways from the festival and its Asian Contents […]
content:
The Busan International Film Festival drew its largest film audience in more than a decade at its 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6–15, while a political firestorm over a Korean box office hit and an Iranian director’s war speech kept politics in the spotlight.

These are Variety’s takeaways from the festival and its Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

Audiences Turn Out, Market Holds Steady

Screenings drew 200,043 admissions, the festival’s highest tally since 2015. Counting talks, outdoor events and side programs, total attendance reached 277,027, around 40,000 more than the milestone 30th edition last year. Organizers pointed to a new opening date and a bigger screening slate.

Popular on Variety

Community BIFF, the audience-programmed strand in Nampo-dong, pulled in 29,511 visitors, more than 1.7 times last year’s figure. BIFF Everywhere took films to a record 18 locations, among them Buddhist temples, traditional markets and a National Assembly building in Seoul.

The ACFM, which ran Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO under the theme “Core and Expansion,” counted 30,484 visitors, up 1.6%. Registrations climbed 4.3% to 3,158 participants from 1,266 companies in 58 countries. Exhibitors rose 17% to 339 companies, 49 of them first-timers, and Czech & Slovak and Cambodian pavilions made their debuts.

“The biggest obstacle is funding,” ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim told Variety. “The scale and the role of the market have grown quickly, but public support has not kept pace. National funding for ACFM has stayed at the same level for two years running.”

“For anyone who wants to work with Asia, there is no place as efficient over four days,” she said.

Korbinian Haeutle, project manager for Europe! Hub, which ran a stand with EFP and Unifrance, said the quality of the market was very good. “The meetings are good and it feels like many new distribution companies are coming up. Everyone is quite happy,” he said.

Malaysian filmmakers Woo Ming Jin, director with Greenlight Pictures, and Lau Kok Rui, director and screenwriter with Thousand Sales Pictures, said BIFF brings everybody from Asia together, “so for us it’s a very important festival.”

“You can count on everyone being here, exchanging about policy changes, sharing project updates… It’s good to see what people are doing. It’s motivational,” they said.

Politics Takes the Stage

The festival’s opening week was shadowed by “The Assassin(s),” Hur Jin-ho’s thriller about the Aug. 15, 1974 shooting of first lady Yuk Young-soo, wife of then-President Park Chung-hee. The film opened Sept. 23 and topped the Korean admissions chart, but conservative politicians and online critics accused it of distorting history.

On Oct. 1, BIFF called off “Actors House: Lee Min-ho,” a career conversation with one of the film’s stars. A day later, production company Hive Media Corp. withdrew the cast and crew from all of their festival appearances, including the opening ceremony and an outdoor stage greeting, citing the safety of audiences and attendees. The move came after a conservative group announced daily protests outside the home of lead actor Yoo Hae-jin.

The row reached the competition jury’s press conference the day after the opening ceremony, where a reporter raised the question of historical fact and creative freedom. “Specifically regarding the film you mentioned, I have not seen it, though I have noticed there are some controversies. It depends on each individual’s feelings,” jury president Zhang Yimou said. “Creation and historical truth: what does historical truth really mean? History is also written by people, so is history itself truly real? Sometimes that in itself is a question mark.”

“But as creators, we respect every creator’s vision,” he added.

Fellow juror July Jung, the director of “Next Sohee” and “Dora,” said: “What I feel now, even though it isn’t my film, is that my heart feels so cold as a filmmaker.”

Later in the festival, around 20 filmmakers, among them directors Chung Ji-young and Lee Myung-se, held a press conference in Busan urging politicians to stop using the film as a political weapon and to leave its judgment to audiences. They also criticized the main opposition People Power Party, whose 109 lawmakers had written to the Singapore International Film Festival asking it to withdraw the film. Singapore has kept “The Assassin(s)” as its Oct. 21 opening title.

Politics returned at the closing ceremony. Majidi’s “Midday Meal,” the story of a rural schoolteacher, won the Busan Award for best film from Zhang’s jury. After Zhang handed him the trophy, Majidi spoke against the war in Iran, focusing on a U.S. military strike in February on a school in Minab that killed 156 civilians, 120 of them schoolchildren. He dedicated the award to the people of Iran.

“They will stand firm to the end and fight to get their independence back,” Majidi said.

“I wish for a future with no war,” he added.

A-List Status, Star Wattage

This was Busan’s first edition since FIAPF recognized it as an A-list festival, and the second year of its competition, which featured 13 Asian titles. The win means “Midday Meal” can go straight to the Oscars’ international feature race without a national selection.

Eddie Cahyono’s Indonesian drama “Ibuku” took the special jury prize, and Lee Yun Chan won best director for Taiwan’s “To Be Ordinary.” Best actor was shared by Zhou Xun for Gu You’s “The First Taste of Loneliness” and Himeno Kashun for “Satoko Always.” Li Danfeng, sound director on “The First Taste of Loneliness,” received the artistic contribution award. Zhang’s jury also included Bi Gan, July Jung, Moon Choi, Samal Yeslyamova, Ishikawa Kei and Tran Thi Bich Ngoc.

The guest list matched the new status. Michelle Yeoh, back on the Busan red carpet after a 15-year absence, was named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at an opening ceremony hosted by Kim Minha, where Ann Hui received the Camellia Award. Former festival chair Kim Dong-ho was honored with the Korean Cinema Award. Fan Bingbing and Charlotte Gainsbourg also walked the opening night carpet, along with Alfonso Cuarón, making his first official trip to Korea.

Isabelle Huppert brought “All About Corinne,” Maggie Gyllenhaal visited Korea for the first time and Koreeda Hirokazu presented “Look Back.” Lee Chang-dong arrived with his Netflix drama “Possible Love” and its cast, Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong. Na Hong-Jin, Kim Jeewoon, Im Kwon-taek, Lee Myung-se, Bae Chang-ho, Fukada Koji, Lav Diaz, Rintaro, Reza Rahadian and Christine Hakim were also in town, as were Zhou Xun, Hyun Bin, Jung Woo-sung, Son Suk-ku, Hwang Jung-min, Kim Hye-ja and Japan’s Michieda Shunsuke.

Fan, Kim Jeewoon and cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo curated Carte Blanche selections, while Actors’ House sessions featured Kim Go-eun, Kim Minha, Ryu Seung-ryong, Shin Min-a and Ju Ji-hoon. Gainsbourg, Gyllenhaal, Cuarón, Na, Diaz and Rintaro led master classes and talks.

Producers Close Ranks, Money Gets Creative

At Producer Hub, the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK) and Indonesian producers’ association APROFI formed the Asian Producers Alliance, with producer bodies from the Philippines, Taiwan and Hong Kong also signing on. The founders see it as the seed of a standing coalition of Asian producers working together on co-productions and policy. PGK also signed cooperation agreements with Italy’s CNA and the Sakha Filmmakers’ Union.

“Co-production used to be an option; now it is an essential strategy for sharing risk,” market chief Kim said.

New capital was on the table as well. Korean content investor Solaire Partners and Japanese entertainment financier Questry signed a memorandum of understanding on Oct. 12 to set up a Korea–Japan content fund worth KRW100 billion ($74.6 million). The market’s new Investor Summit gathered 20 companies, including Korean investor-distributors, venture capital firms and investors from Indonesia, Singapore, the U.S. and France, for a closed-door roundtable. Cinema by Brand, launched with Innocean and PGK and sponsored by Hanwha, paired three film projects with brand backing.

Financing individual films remains hard. Hollywood executives at a panel featuring UTA, Gold House, Lionsgate and HYBE saw an opening for Asian talent and stories rooted in specific cultures, while conceding that getting projects funded is still a struggle.

Kevin Law, market consultant at Film Export U.K. and a sales agent, said Busan is a steady market for keeping relationships and building partnerships. “I think one thing that’s obvious this year is that it’s difficult for independent films,” he said.

Li-yan Fan, international sales representative at France’s Ecce Films, made her first trip to Busan looking for co-production partners. “Co-production is becoming inevitable, but it still depends on the nature of each project and the resources available where you’re shooting,” Fan told Variety.

AI Gets Down to Work

Netflix has already put AI to work in some form on around 300 of its titles, Lee Sung Q, the streamer’s senior director of APAC production, said at Creative Asia, the Netflix and BIFF program for emerging talent. On the same panel, co-hosted by Netflix and the MPA, “The Outlaws” director Kang Yoon-sung put AI’s potential savings on a feature at 30% to 40% of the budget.

Kang co-directed “Run to the West,” billed as Korea’s first feature to use AI throughout production, and made a test for “The Gulf of Aden,” a film built around military operations at sea, entirely with AI using Kling. He said the savings on that film would not come only from swapping out CG. “The shoot itself got simpler, and it cut the overall production period to some extent,” he said.

He also said the technology often cuts out the debate and shared experience that filmmaking has relied on. “So the quality of the footage AI makes is very high, but when it comes to delivering emotion and moving audiences, I think we’re in a period where it has actually gotten worse,” Kang said.

Lee said that when it comes to conveying emotion, a human ultimately has to touch the work once more. “I strongly agree that a human touch is absolutely essential,” he said.

On the market floor, InnoAsia, the ACFM’s technology strand, brought in Kling, Alibaba and BytePlus. Kling teamed with filmmakers including Korean director Kim Sung-su to show how AI might reshape filmmaking, and Forum BIFF screened an AI short by Jia Zhangke. VFX veteran Hong Jae-cheol told the strand’s AI Creators Camp how images generated by AI are being slotted into production pipelines next to conventional effects, with people still steering the creative work.

“Compared to FilMart, microdramas aren’t as big as you would expect. Same for AI. In Hong Kong they were everywhere,” Haeutle said.

Law said AI remains very much a debate. “At the moment you’ll find that AI is in films but not in the way people are imagining it to be,” he said.

Europe and Thailand Build Bridges

By Europe! Hub’s count, 36% of the festival program was at least a European co-production. “There’s the 140 years France-Korean relationship and this year, the Italian Pavilion is very big,” Haeutle said.

Thailand was the ACFM’s first Country of Honor, and the Busan Story Market added five Thai titles for remake. “Compared with last year, we’ve seen many more visitors coming to our booth, asking questions and showing curiosity about what Thailand has to offer,” Phakhin Chettanat, business development manager at Thailand-based Banana Sound Studio, told Variety.

He said Asian countries are becoming more competitive, though production costs still decide where shoots go. “As talent and technical capabilities continue to improve across the region, I believe Asia will eventually become a major production hub alongside North America and Europe,” he said.

Japan was Producer Hub’s focus country this year, with Japan’s Visual Industry Promotion Organization (VIPO) co-hosting a program that drew 188 producers from 25 countries.

title: ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’: Five Biggest Takeaways, From the ‘SNL’ Firing to Concealing His Cancer Diagnosis
summary: Norm Macdonald wasn’t for everyone. Armed with a deadpan delivery, devil-may-care attitude and cracker-barrel charm, the Canadian comic got his start writing for “Roseanne” before earning acclaim as the host of SNL’s Weekend Update, where his unrelenting ridicule of O.J. Simpson for being an alleged murderer — Macdonald was adamant that it wasn’t so “alleged” […]
content:
Norm Macdonald wasn’t for everyone. Armed with a deadpan delivery, devil-may-care attitude and cracker-barrel charm, the Canadian comic got his start writing for “Roseanne” before earning acclaim as the host of SNL’s Weekend Update, where his unrelenting ridicule of O.J. Simpson for being an alleged murderer — Macdonald was adamant that it wasn’t so “alleged” — eventually got him canned from the show. His one big shot at movie stardom, the Bob Saget-helmed 1998 comedy film “Dirty Work,” bombed spectacularly, and he subsequently presided over the quietly uproarious video podcast “Norm Macdonald Live” before dying from complications from leukemia in 2021 at the age of 61. Perhaps his old pal Larry King said it best, calling Macdonald, “One of the most respected comedians today, though show business has never found a place to put him.”

In the handful of years since his death, however, Macdonald has blossomed into an internet darling, as new generations of comedy enthusiasts stumble upon his hilariously awkward late-night appearances — particularly on “Late Night with Conan O’Brien” — Weekend Update segments and podcast clips. Nobody did it like Macdonald, whose downright desiccated sense of humor is sorely absent in today’s doing-too-much comedy landscape. This new cultural appreciation for Macdonald is celebrated in “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald,” a new documentary from Judd Apatow that premieres Friday on Netflix. Apatow’s loving tribute to his late pal contains no talking heads or any of the other conventions of these types of docs; rather, it explores the comedy giant’s life in Macdonald’s own words, largely borrowed from the narration of his absurdist biographical book “Based on a True Story: Not a Memoir,” as well as home videos, photos and archival interviews.

Here are five big takeaways from “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald.”

title: BBC Studios’ Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays
summary: Marcus Arthur tells Deadline about walking a tightrope in a streaming-first world where linear remains a big money-spinner. Arthur is running a huge and complicated business. Having been upped from CEO of channels group UKTV to chief exec of global channels and streaming at BBC Studios, he faces a sizable challenge. Positioning the commercial arm […]
content:
Marcus Arthur tells Deadline about walking a tightrope in a streaming-first world where linear remains a big money-spinner.

Arthur is running a huge and complicated business. Having been upped from CEO of channels group UKTV to chief exec of global channels and streaming at BBC Studios, he faces a sizable challenge. Positioning the commercial arm of the 100-year-old BBC for a streaming future while managing the traditional linear channels that still do great business in many international territories.

“Streaming is definitely our future, and building for a streaming-first future is absolutely paramount,” Arthur says. “But linear is still hugely important right now for the profits that the businesses make and will be for the next five to 10 years. The art is that clutch-control between building for a streaming future, but still trying to maximize the benefit of the big linear businesses.”

BBC Studios has an enormous catalog of shows that it sells around the world — it rolled into MIPCOM with a shiny Dancing with the Stars spinoff — but its channels and streaming business remains a big earner, with revenues of £788 million ($1.1 billion) for the 2025/26 financial year.

Watch on Deadline

Arthur’s portfolio comprises channels and digital services spanning linear pay-TV nets, branded ad-supported channels, direct-to-consumer services and SVoD U.K. streamer BritBox International is in the mix, with Arthur overseeing it outside of North America.

“The difficulty for broadcasters is that the new [streaming] paradigm doesn’t come about overnight. It takes time to develop your digital services and your routes to market,” he says. “And all the time you’re investing [in streaming], you still need to keep your linear businesses warm. You don’t get a free hit. You need to do both of those.”

BBC Studios is not beholden to shareholders in the same way as a company like Comcast, which has split its legacy channels and streaming businesses. Arthur says these moves have contributed to a narrative that does not always acknowledge the value of linear.
