“People don’t always recognize that there’s still growth in linear in places like South Africa, or that you can still grow your linear share in Poland and other markets that we are in, like Turkey, because they have read about a few of the big broadcasters that have decided to bifurcate their linear and streaming businesses. There’s an equally long list of people who have decided to keep those assets together, whether that’s Fox, ITV or AMC.

“The businesses that decide to keep them together are the ones who believe that they can still benefit from those linear sides of their business for a long period of time for their future profitability, and most of them are using those profits to invest in the digital side.”

With a smorgasbord of channels, meanwhile, there will always be fine-tuning and rebrands. Drama network BBC First is an example: It was rebranded as BBC Belgium in that European country and there has since been an uptick in viewership with a launch lineup that included the likes of Wild Cherry, Foyle’s War and Call the Midwife. That rebrand followed a similar move in the Netherlands where BBC First was rebadged BBC NL.

Major Player

Last year, BBC Studios teamed with CosmoBlue to distribute channels and launch a new general entertainment network across the Middle East and North Africa regions and Turkey. Part of the deal was also the integration of the BBC Player service into the CosmoGO streaming app.

TheBBC Player on-demand services can bridge the traditional and the new, providing a streaming service that can sit next to regular channels.

“We’ve grown that to 21 products in the EMEA region,” Arthur says. “We have taken the existing channels’ businesses and put the very best digital product alongside it. When we’re speaking to the pay platforms we have relationships with, we’re now talking to them about a linear business that has a really strong digital future.”

BBC Player is multi-genre, including drama, and there is also the scripted-focused BritBox service. In line with the plethora of business models within the BBC Studios channels and streaming business, BritBox runs as an SVoD proposition in Australia, going direct to consumers, while it operates in conjunction with regional pay TV platforms in the Nordics.

Elsewhere, BBC Studios-owned channel group UKTV did a deal last year to launch content from its ‘U’-branded on-demand service on Channel 4’s streaming platform. It meant Channel 4 bolstered its streaming offering with UKTV programs including the Bergerac reboot, as well as classic BBC shows that air on UKTV channels including The Office and Red Dwarf.

Arthur offers a progress report: “We have experienced very healthy growth and we have managed not to cannibalize our standalone service. That deal was great for Channel 4 because it got really good content from the BBC, the archive, and the UKTV originals. For UKTV, it took us onto a platform that, by nature, is younger and exposed us to a whole load of new people.”

FAST Facts

Free Ad-supported Streaming TV (FAST) is a smart way to make the most of a big catalog and BBC Studios has been steadily launching channels. Arthur tells us that it is about to launch a suite of new channels in the U.K., pegged to some big-ticket brands.

The services will carry the aforementioned U branding from UKTV, with Top Gear on U, EastEnders on U and Antiques Roadshow on U among eight launches.

“You can test and learn with FAST,” Arthur says. “You can get channels up and see if they grow, and then move and change.”

Across EMEA, BBC Studios said there were 53.6 million hours of viewing of its FAST channels in the first seven months of this year, a year-on-year increase of more than 50%.

FAST can also plug the gaps where BBC Studios does not have services. “They’ve done exceptionally well for us where we don’t have any big pay deals or our own channels. It’s a very effective way to launch into marketplaces.”

BBC Studios

Charter For Change

Outside of the commercial Studios business, pubcaster BBC is making eye-watering cuts. For BBC Studios, the knock-on effect is a greater recognition of the importance of the cash it returns to the public service mothership.

BBC Studios has argued that U.K. regulations are putting its operations at a disadvantage compared to its peers in the international business. One bone of contention is its borrowing cap, which will sit at £750 million ($1 billion) in 2027.

“We have a good track record, when we do have funds, of spending them well and getting returns, but whether we get more cash availability as part of the Charter is for the government and for [BBC director general] Matt Brittin,” Arthur says.

Looking ahead for the next year, Arthur says the BBC iPlayer service will be modernized in terms of look and feel. And, of course, his channels and streaming division needs to make money.

“We need to grow our revenues,” he says. “Despite the fact that advertising in the U.K. might be incredibly challenged, I want to grow our EMEA revenues. I want to grow our APAC revenues and our revenues in both Australia and New Zealand.

“We want this to be a growth business, and to show that we have things in place that can make that true,” he continues. “I don’t want to just be managing businesses where the revenue is flat and all you’re doing is looking at costs. I mean, life’s too short.”

title: Layoffs Take Place At ‘The Repair Shop’ Producer Ricochet
summary: EXCLUSIVE: A number of staffers including creative chief Damon Pattison have been laid off at Ricochet, the Skydance UK-owned indie that produces hit BBC show The Repair Shop. We understand around 10 staff left several weeks back including Pattison and Rob Butterfield, who was running the indie’s Scotland office. This represents just under a third […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: A number of staffers including creative chief Damon Pattison have been laid off at Ricochet, the Skydance UK-owned indie that produces hit BBC show The Repair Shop.

We understand around 10 staff left several weeks back including Pattison and Rob Butterfield, who was running the indie’s Scotland office. This represents just under a third of overall staff numbers, which now stands at 24 across offices in Brighton and Glasgow, according to Ricochet’s website. Joanna Ball remains MD.

We understand the decision was made as a response to market conditions and was decided upon long before the Skydance deal closed. A Ricochet spokeswoman confirmed the layoffs had already taken place but declined further comment.

Ricochet is best known for The Repair Shop, a heartwarming BBC series that has been running for a decade and spawned several spin-offs. Each episode of the ratings smash follows professional craftspeople from around the country who restore family heirlooms that have sentimental value for their owners.

Watch on Deadline

Ricochet’s other credits include Guz Khan’s Custom Cars, Ben Fogle’s New Lives in the Wild and Sun, Sea & Selling Houses.

Pattison joined Ricochet more than two years ago after leaving the UK arm of Pooch Perfect outfit Beyond Productions. During his time there, the experienced UK producer picked up the rights to Australian series Muster Dogs and landed the Guz Khan commission.

The news comes with TV industry layoffs a reality in the UK. The BBC and Channel 4 are making hundreds redundant while sales executives have left the newly-merged Banijay outfit since the All3Media deal closed.

Along with Who Do You Think You Are? indie Wall to Wall Media and First Dates producer Twenty Twenty, Ricochet is one of a trio of UK indies owned by Warner that now fall under the Skydance banner.

The Ricochet layoffs, however, are not as a result of the Skydance deal and insiders at the production outfits have said they are currently none the wiser about what their future holds under David Ellison. For the most part, Skydance international currently falls under JB Perrette, with more executive names expected to be announced in the coming weeks.

title: 10 Films to Track at El Gouna, From Cannes and Berlin Standouts to Rising Arab Filmmakers
summary: The ninth edition of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival brings together a strong showing of Arab cinema to the Red Sea, with a lineup spanning emerging regional voices, established filmmakers, and prize-winning titles from Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Shanghai. Across its narrative, documentary and short-film competitions, this year’s selection features stories of love, memory […]
content:
The ninth edition of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival brings together a strong showing of Arab cinema to the Red Sea, with a lineup spanning emerging regional voices, established filmmakers, and prize-winning titles from Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Shanghai.

Across its narrative, documentary and short-film competitions, this year’s selection features stories of love, memory and family, as well as war and displacement, while offering glimpses of communities navigating political, social and economic upheaval. Several titles also underscore El Gouna’s growing role in nurturing projects before they reach the screen, with filmmakers and projects previously supported through CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm, returning with completed works.

Here are 10 titles to keep an eye on at this year’s festival.

Popular on Variety

Feature Narrative Competition

“Safe Exit” (2026)

(Mohammed Hammad, Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Qatar, Germany. Produced by Kholoud Saad, Dora Bouchoucha, Dina Farouk, Ibrahim El-Batout, and May Odeh)

A decade after his feature debut, Egyptian filmmaker Mohammed Hammad delivers his sophomore film, “Safe Exit,” which premiered at this year’s Berlinale. Set in downtown Cairo, it centers on Samaan, a Coptic Christian security guard haunted by his father’s murder by extremists, whose life changes when he meets Fatma, an impoverished sex worker facing struggles of her own. Hammad explores faith, isolation, and some of the contradictions of contemporary Egyptian society. His debut, “Withered Green,” screened at El Gouna’s inaugural edition in 2017.

“Only Rebels Win” (2026)

(Danielle Arbid, France, Lebanon, Qatar. Produced by Omar El Kadi, Nadia Turincev and Georges Schoucair)

Widowed and with her children now grown, Suzanne (Hiam Abbass), a Lebanese woman of Palestinian origin, finds herself free to put herself first. When she falls for Osmane, a younger undocumented Sudanese migrant in Beirut, their relationship puts that newfound independence to the test. When the war made shooting in Lebanon impossible, director Danielle Arbid had a local crew film the Beirut locations without actors, then used the footage as rear projections while shooting in a Paris studio. “Only Rebels Win” opened the Panorama section at this year’s Berlinale.

“3 Weeks After” (2026)

(Miroslav Terzić, Serbia, Bulgaria, Italy, Croatia, Luxembourg. Produced by Snežana van Houwelingen and Branislav Trifunović)

Fresh off of winning the Europa Cinemas Label at Karlovy Vary, Miroslav Terzić’s “3 Weeks After” centers on a group of students stranded at an isolated mountain hotel three weeks after a classmate dies by suicide. Questions soon emerge about the bullying that preceded his death, and about how many of them knew what was happening. Rather than concentrating solely on those responsible, Terzić widens the circle to the classmates who were silent bystanders who never intervened.

“Halima” (2026)

(Yassine El Idrissi, Morocco. Produced by Yassine El Idrissi)

Best director and best actress winner (Khadija Amari) at the Shanghai International Film Festival, “Halima” marks Moroccan filmmaker Yassine El Idrissi’s fiction feature debut. Moving between Halima’s present-day life on the Moroccan coast and her past in the Rif mountains, the film traces how the widow, threatened with displacement from her land and struggling to support herself, became involved in the illegal cannabis trade. Drawing on El Idrissi’s years as a photojournalist and his encounters with marginalized communities across Morocco, “Halima” looks at the region’s hidden cannabis economy while resisting easy judgments about the people whose livelihoods depend on it.

Feature Documentary Competition

“Citizen Osama” (2026)

(Ahmed Hassouna, Palestine, France. Produced by Laura Nikolov and Rashid Masharawi. Co-produced by Ahmed Hassouna)

In northern Gaza, photojournalist Osama Al-Ashi is documenting a war while trying to survive it. A Venice premiere, Ahmed Hassouna’s documentary follows Al-Ashi as his work to record the devastation all around him collides with the responsibility of keeping his wife and newborn son out of harm’s way. The film has been selected as Palestine’s official entry for Best International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards.

“The Return of Captain Kabonga” (2026)

(Amir El-Shenawy, Egypt. Produced by Ahmed Abdelsalam)

In Ismailia, a city along Egypt’s Suez Canal, veteran street wrestler Ashraf “Kabonga” Mahrous is trying to revive the WWE-inspired wrestling shows he once staged with a group of local amateurs. Amir El-Shenawy tracks that effort alongside Kabonga’s more immediate struggle to make ends meet and support his family while Egypt grapples with economic crisis. “The Return of Captain Kabonga” makes its world premiere at El Gouna after participating in CineGouna Funding in 2025 where the project picked up several cash and in-kind post-production awards.

“Whispers in May” (2026)

(Dongnan Chen, Hong Kong, Netherlands, South Korea, Sweden. Produced by Jia Zhao and Kay Xu. Co-produced by Heejung Oh and Malin Hüber)

Fourteen-year-old Qihuo gets her first period and sets out with her friends to find a traditional skirt for her coming-of-age ceremony in China’s remote Liangshan Mountains. With her parents away working in the city, her journey captures how life is changing for young people even as long-held customs remain firmly rooted. Blending documentary with fictional and mythical elements, Dongnan Chen’s “Whispers in May” won the top DOX:AWARD at this year’s CPH:DOX.

“Nuisance Bear” (2026)

(Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman, Canada, U.S., U.K. Produced by Michael Code, Teddy Leifer and Will N. Miller)

Winner of the Grand Jury Prize in the U.S. Documentary Competition at Sundance, “Nuisance Bear” follows polar bears along their centuries-old migration route through Manitoba, Canada, where they increasingly cross paths with tourists, wildlife officers and hunters. Directors Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman expand their Oscar-shortlisted 2021 short of the same name into a feature that shifts the usual nature-documentary perspective, showing the bears’ migration from their point of view, with humans and the town itself becoming the intruders.

Short Film Competition

“My Village Blamed Women for the End of Mankind” (Al Khabith) (2026)

(Jad Chahine, Egypt, United Kingdom. Produced by Yara Goubran)

When a mysterious epidemic begins infecting women in a remote fishing village, fear quickly turns the community against them. “At its core, the film is about a man trying to protect three women from death, only to discover that protection itself can become part of the violence inflicted upon them,” director Jad Chahine explains. That contradiction feeds into a larger question Chahine poses to the audience, and perhaps to himself: “If the end is inevitable, what gives us the right to decide when it begins? And when does our fear of it make us create it with our own hands?” Making its world premiere at El Gouna, the film follows Chahine’s Cannes La Cinef-selected “The Call of the Brook.”

“Disquiet” (Irtibak) (2026)

(Mariam Abdelgaber, Egypt. Produced by Tamer Ashry, Zeina Eissa, Alia El Shahbour and Mariam Abdelgaber)

A young supermarket cashier is given a key by an elderly regular who asks her to check on her apartment if she ever disappears. When the woman stops coming to the store, the cashier decides to use it, drawing her into the private life of someone she barely knew. “Disquiet” marks Mariam Abdelgaber’s debut in narrative filmmaking and stars Rakeen Saad and Menha El Batraoui. The film makes its world premiere at El Gouna.

title: Kenny Ortega Says His New Lego Friends ‘Heartlake’ Movie Brings the Bricks to Life ‘in the Most Wonderful Musical Capacity’
summary: Kenny Ortega is the talent behind iconic films ranging from “Hocus Pocus” to “High School Musical” not to mention dozens of music videos, concerts and two Olympics opening ceremonies. So it’s unsurprising he was the top choice when Lego were thinking about making their first musical feature based on the Lego Friends line. Ortega, who […]
content:
Kenny Ortega is the talent behind iconic films ranging from “Hocus Pocus” to “High School Musical” not to mention dozens of music videos, concerts and two Olympics opening ceremonies. So it’s unsurprising he was the top choice when Lego were thinking about making their first musical feature based on the Lego Friends line.

Ortega, who says Lego has been “part of my life for over 30 years,” was brought on to executive produce “Lego Friends: Heartlake the Musical,” shaping the story and choreography as well as picking the director (his longtime collaborator Paul Becker), location (London, U.K.) and actors. He calls the all-British cast “triple threats” who could sing, dance and act, saying they reminded him of working with a 15-year-old Christian Bale on “Newsies.”

The 50-minute film, which is set to premiere Oct. 16 on Lego’s YouTube channel, as well as Peacock and Netflix, follows a young girl, Daisy (Jada Langley) as she is magically transported into the world of Heartlake City where she makes some fast friends and helps them save a special landmark.

Popular on Variety

Ahead of the film’s launch, Ortega sat down with Variety to talk about how he ended up working on the project, whether he has ideas for a sequel and his plans for the L.A. Olympics.

How did you come on board “Lego Friends: Heartlake the Musical”?

Hannah Draper and Michael McKenna [from production company Final Pixel] reached out to me and said, “Do you like Lego?” I was like, “Lego’s been part of my life for over 30 years.” I’ve got a nephew — every birthday, every holiday, every special occasion [it’s] Lego, Lego, Lego. I was like, “We love Legos!” So it was easy for me to say, “I’d love to take a meeting, I’d love to hear more about it,” and that’s how it began.

How did they pitch it to you?

Final Pixel is an award-winning global creative virtual production innovation studio and so the way they pitched it to me was [they would] basically create a 3D virtual world that we would build sets in front of and on this giant curved LED screen. And that right away was it for me. Because I mean, I’ve been making films since virtual reality didn’t exist. Visual effects were painted on glass, or you know, wire removal, and so this was an opportunity for me as a producer and storyteller to work in a capacity that I hadn’t before, and that really excited me.

Jada Langley in “Lego Friends: Heartlake the Musical” (Courtesy of The Lego Group) The Lego Group

Did you work closely with screenwriters Kirk R. Thatcher and Jeremy Adams on shaping the story?

Oh yeah. I was brought in primarily in the beginning as an executive producer to develop the story and help the writers come to understand how music, song and dance production can move character and story forward in the storytelling of our movie.

How much did the story change from first draft to final cut?

My work skews older than what this project set out to accomplish. Where the Lego Friends universe is like, six years-old and up, mine is a little older than that with Disney, with “High School Musical” and “Descendants,” “Cheetah Girls,” and “Julie and the Phantoms” at Netflix, and so I thought that’s what they wanted. So in the beginning I would say what changed was that I had to sort of age down, and to put on a new thinking cap and to go, “Okay, I’m now creating something for maybe five years-old.” So that was fun, that was different, that was unique.

How long was the shoot?

We came back and did a few reshoots, so the total, I would say maybe — under 30 days? Like 25, 26, days.

We had a lot of fun, deciding on how to build Heartlake, what to incorporate in it, what characters would take on the main roles in a first little musical. I mean, this was all a test. We came at it with a modest amount of money and time because they had never done it, and this was an experiment, sort of. Let’s see what we can accomplish here, and then maybe this gives us an opportunity to go bigger and beyond this, and I hope that that will be the story.

Do you already have some ideas for a sequel?

Heck yeah! It was a lot of fun.

You’ve previously produced two Olympic ceremonies, for the 1996 Summer Olympics in Atlanta and the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City. Are you involved in the L.A. Olympics in 2028?

I’m not. I’m so excited about it though, I hope to be invited to opening and closing ceremonies. I want to get tickets to see the events. I was an athlete growing up. My father was an Olympic athlete, track and field athlete. I have not been invited. I don’t even know who is creatively going to be running that aspect of the Olympics, the ceremonies. But it was the time of my life working with Don Mischer and Mitt Romney in Salt Lake and the folks in Atlanta for the Summer Games and I would love to at least be there to witness what comes to Los Angeles.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: Iron Maiden Announce 2027 North American Tour Dates

content:
Long-running British heavy metal titans Iron Maiden will return to North America for a third and final leg of their 50th anniversary “Run for Your Lives” tour.

The band, which are 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees, will conclude this leg with two festival headline performances at Sonic Temple and Boardwalk Rock.

Bassist and founder Steve Harris says, “As many of our fans know, Maiden were planning on taking a break from live performances in 2027, but we’ve been enjoying this last leg in the USA and Canada so much that we all had a chat and decided we should take the show to parts we missed, particularly the North West and South East. It just seems fair to our many fans there who have given us tremendous support for so many years. We can’t get everywhere but we can try!

Popular on Variety

“Also, we have always enjoyed playing the many great festivals that are in Europe and wanted to experience a couple more in the USA which we will do at the end of the tour in Columbus and Maryland. At festivals you are not just playing to your own fans so it’s always a challenge and we all love a challenge!”

title: David Surkamp, Pavlov’s Dog Singer, Dies at 73
summary: David Surkamp, frontman for the long-running progressive-rock band Pavlov’s Dog, has died at age 73, according to a social media post on the band’s social media accounts. No cause of death was announced. While the band, which formed in St. Louis in the early 1970s, was not and arena-filling progressive rock group like Yes, Genesis […]
content:
David Surkamp, frontman for the long-running progressive-rock band Pavlov’s Dog, has died at age 73, according to a social media post on the band’s social media accounts. No cause of death was announced.

While the band, which formed in St. Louis in the early 1970s, was not and arena-filling progressive rock group like Yes, Genesis and Emerson Lake & Palmer, they enjoyed a long career and a fervent fan base. Their at-times symphonic sound included violin and flute, and Surkamp’s high voice put them in a similar category as Yes.

“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the unexpected passing of our creative force, lead singer, and dear friend, David Surkamp, on October 13th,” bandmember Abbie Steiling wrote.

Popular on Variety

“There are no words sufficient for a loss of this magnitude. We are heartbroken. We are grateful. We will carry David, his music, and the memories created with us always. Our deepest condolences are with Saylor, Evan, and the Surkamp family as well as the Pavlov’s Dog family as we walk together through this difficult time of grief.” She added that Surkamp’s wife, Sara, died last November, and hoped he “has found peace with the love he has missed so dearly.”

The band released its debut album, “Pampered Menial” — produced by Sandy Pearlman and Murray Krugman, who helmed hit albums for Blue Oyster Cult — in 1975 and followed with “At the Sound of the Bell” the following year; the latter album featured guest appearances from such luminaries as Roxy Music saxophonist Andy Mackay and Yes/King Crimson drummer Bill Bruford.

However, with the rise of disco and punk in the latter half of the decade, progressive rock fell out of fashion. The band recorded a third album in 1977 but its label, Columbia, was unimpressed and declined to release it and Pavlov’s Dog split (the album was final issued by German label Rockville some 30 years later).

During the 1980s, Surkamp relocated to Seattle and formed Hi-Fi with former Fairport Convention singer Ian Matthews, before reuniting Pavlov’s Dog in 1990 for the album “Lost in America.” The band continued off and on over the following years, with Sara Surkamp joining on acoustic guitar and vocals in 2006. The band released its final album with David Surkamp, “Wonderlust,” last year.

title: Lucky Daye on Creating His New Album ‘Aloud’ and Collaborating With Pusha T and Muni Long: ‘It’s About the Magic’
summary: Lucky Daye is in a season of change. Ahead of the release of “Aloud,” out today, the Grammy-winning singer-songwriter is settling into a new label home at Warner Records, working with a wider circle of collaborators and taking more control of his creative process. Even his look signals a shift: When Variety meets him for […]
content:
Lucky Daye is in a season of change. Ahead of the release of “Aloud,” out today, the Grammy-winning singer-songwriter is settling into a new label home at Warner Records, working with a wider circle of collaborators and taking more control of his creative process. Even his look signals a shift: When Variety meets him for lunch at Nobu in Atlanta, his hair is styled into a bold, sculptural frohawk that he’s described as part of the album’s new era.

The day before, on the set of the video for “Knockin,” his collaboration with Muni Long and the Black punk band Paradox, that era was taking shape in real time. Two of his managers are on set, along with his chief of staff and Susan “Susy” Oludele, the celebrated natural hair artist responsible for Daye’s evolving look. They’re part of a larger creative ecosystem that, notably, includes a team of predominantly Black women. Daye says being surrounded by them makes him “very, very happy.”

Popular on Variety

“I feel nurtured,” he says, quickly making clear the relationship works both ways. “I feel like they let me care for them the way that I want to care for them… It’s a back and forth.” Later, he puts it more simply: “Really a team. It’s not one of them fake teams.”

That sense of support has extended to Warner. Daye had already begun “Aloud” before signing with the label, but when asked how the new deal affected the album, he doesn’t hesitate: “Every feature.” He credits the label with taking “a huge load” off him and his management team while helping facilitate an eclectic guest list that includes Leon Thomas, Pusha T and Akeem Ali. Still, Daye insists the machinery around the music isn’t what drives it. “It’s not about the deal. It’s not about the money,” he says. “It’s really about the magic.”

“Aloud” finds Daye chasing that magic from a different emotional place. He calls himself “Lucky 2.0” — more sensitive to love, compassion and his own feelings, more willing to say what he’s thinking and, perhaps most significantly, less interested in making music rooted in pain. “This is from truth,” he says of the new album. “It hurts worse.”

Across “Aloud,” that truth arrives with a surprising amount of playfulness, from current single “Talk to Me,” one of Daye’s favorites, to the quirky interludes he describes as “commercial breaks.” Daye spoke with Variety about loosening up without losing depth, working with Thomas amid inevitable comparisons, bringing Muni Long and Pusha T into his world, and learning to trust himself without leaning quite so heavily on longtime collaborator D’Mile.

You asked me what my favorite song was, and I said “Talk to Me.” Then I asked you yours and you picked the same song. What is it about that record for you?

It’s a very catchy hook. Then you got like.. cadences on verses, which I love, and a simple concept. The concept of the album – direct concepts and drums, punchlines, ’cause I’m gonna bar things up, so I got to punchline it. But it’s just an infectious melody that I want. I want everybody to just feel.

There’s a playfulness throughout “Aloud,” even in the intros and skits. “Intro to Down” is funny and a little quirky. Was that intentional?

In my mind, the world forgets fast. So I wanted to create quick commercial breaks to throw them off a little bit. The name of the album is to be “Aloud,” is to be confident, to be happy. So if anything’s holding you down, get rid of it.

Was this the most fun you’ve had making an album?

For sure. This is the most fun because I’m hands-on the whole time. Other albums, I would have someone listening as I go along, giving input. But this one was like, hold on. It’s no relying. God was like, “You’re actually the guy. So do it.” It was just fun working with so many people, seeing the finished product of different pieces you pull together and getting to know people around me at the same time.

“Knockin” had some of the strongest storytelling on the album. How did you approach that song?

That song was special mainly because it was all emotion. I put the singing last and I put the emotions in front and started telling the story. I miss when people told stories. And I guess it’s not that easy to tell stories. [With “Knockin”], I wanted to put myself in the place of going to college, being in dorm rooms. I never had the opportunity to. [The subject of the song is] your friend is really hot. [Laughs] But as a man, you don’t want to cross that line. But it’s still those thoughts like, dang. I just want to tell you. The perspective of this album is from a man. I’ve never done it from that angle before. Every other album stemmed from pain. This is from truth. It hurts worse.

Muni Long adds another perspective to “Knockin.” How did she end up on the record?

Muni was in the studio next door, and I had just finished doing a feature with her that she needed on her album. It was a no-brainer. Like, who’s going to talk shit? Nobody can really talk at that level. She’s not going to apologize. She means it.

Another collaboration people have been waiting for is you and Leon Thomas on “Fly You Out.” There have also been a lot of comparisons between the two of you. How do those land with you?

I expect comparisons. That’s part of the game. That’s why it’s a game. Give people something to talk about. I think our job is not to let it get to us and take it to heart.

The collaboration came easily. Once the label came in, it was like, “Whatever you want, you’re getting it.” They asked, “If this song should have a feature, who would you get if it was anybody?” Of course I’m going to think Leon. He’s one of my favorite R&B artists right now. When it comes to creativity, when it comes to male artistry, he’s the first person I’m going to mention. We brown skin, we out here, we hustling, we singing and we tap into our emotions at the same time. But we still men that like girls. So I felt like it was a good match.

I sent him the song, he sent the idea back…We got in the studio and put the bow on the whole thing. He’s self-sufficient. It was great seeing him work. It was great sharing my ideas with him. I think the fans wanted it.

You also have Pusha T on “Mouf Say.” What made him the right person for that record?

Pusha is a hip-hop legend. When I hear Pusha T’s name, I just connect with so many names that I respect and the people that motivated me to want to be successful. Pusha’s worked with Pharrell, Jay-Z, Kanye. So for him to even be in the conversation was an automatic yes. His voice is iconic. Clipse is iconic. And he’s a Gemini. I’m a Libra, so it works.

D’Mile has been such an important collaborator throughout your career, and he’s here again on “Nowhere Fast.” But you’ve talked about relying more on yourself this time. How has that relationship evolved?

Me and D’Mile love each other, and we respect each other. I think we’re both like, “Damn, I wish I could be working with you right now.” But we also understand life has its processes. I don’t know what God’s doing with him; you don’t know what God’s doing with me. At the end of the day, I can always know that’s my brother. If I wanted to make a whole album with him, I could make a whole album with him. But I think on this album, God wanted me to look inside myself. This is a feeling that you’ve got to be sensitive to. I’m just trying to catch it. I think I caught it.

title: Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In ‘The Death Of Sherlock Holmes’: “This Is A Clean Slate”
summary: Rafe Spall was one of the biggest names at MIPCOM Cannes this week where he gave Deadline his take on playing super sleuth Sherlock Holmes. The Trying star is leading The Death of Sherlock Holmes, which fills the gap between the detective’s apparent death at the Reichenbach Falls in 1891 and his reappearance in The […]
content:
Rafe Spall was one of the biggest names at MIPCOM Cannes this week where he gave Deadline his take on playing super sleuth Sherlock Holmes.

The Trying star is leading The Death of Sherlock Holmes, which fills the gap between the detective’s apparent death at the Reichenbach Falls in 1891 and his reappearance in The Adventure of the Empty House three years later.

Set against the Swiss Alps, the story follows an Englishman (Spall) found barely alive in an icy mountain stream by local woman Alma (Deleila Piasko) and her young son, Franz. When the village doctor is found murdered, villagers turn on the boy – leaving the amnesiac stranger, who is experiencing flashbacks to a previous life in England, as his only hope as his powers of deduction return.

“What makes it original is the fact that he’s someone who has no idea who he is,” Spall told us at the Majestic Hotel on the Croisette. “He gets these flashes of brilliant deduction that lead him toward understanding what kind of person he is, and eventually perhaps figuring out that he’s the most famous detective in the world.”

Watch on Deadline

Piasko said the relationship between Holmes and Alma is central to the story. “What’s very special is that this Englishman doesn’t judge her,” she added. “She’s a single mother living in a small village, and she’s treated with contempt, experiencing a kind of exclusion. With him, it’s different.”

Spall said these circumstances of amnesia allowed him to create a fresh take on the character and freed him from comparison to other Sherlocks.

“It’s a clean slate in a way. I didn’t feel like I was following in a long line of great actors who have played him in the past — Benedict Cumberbatch, Jeremy Brett, Basil Rathbone, Robert Downey Jr. and all these amazing people.”

The show is a co-production between Sky and SRF in Switzerland, Germany’s ARD Degeto and the Bell Media-owned Sphere Abacus, which brought Spall to Cannes this week. The series will broadcast on Sky in the U.K. and Ireland and also goes out on Sky in Switzerland and Germany. FFF Bayern from Germany and Italy’s IDM Film Commission are supporting the series.

Spall’s face was all over town given he’s also starring in Channel 4 drama Number 10, which ITV Studios has been shopping. He talked about playing a British Prime Minister – revealing he actually met one in the research phase – and addressed his role as Arthur Weasley in the upcoming HBO TV series Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone – chuckling as he compared his role with that of his dad, Timothy Spall, in the movie series.

Here’s the full interview with Spall and Piasko.

DEADLINE: Rafe, There are lots of different versions of Sherlock coming through at any one time. This one is slightly unique in that he is suffering from amnesia and doesn’t know who he is. How did that color what you wanted to bring to the character? What did you think was the core of this version of Sherlock?

RAFE SPALL: What makes it original is the fact that he’s someone who has no idea who he is. He gets these flashes of brilliant deduction that lead him toward understanding what kind of person he is, and eventually perhaps figuring out that he’s the most famous detective in the world.

It’s a clean slate in a way. I didn’t feel like I was following in a long line of great actors who have played him in the past — Benedict Cumberbatch, Jeremy Brett, Basil Rathbone, Robert Downey Jr. and all these amazing people. The comparison is somewhat taken away by the fact that I can say, if people think I’m rubbish in it, that it’s a different Sherlock Holmes. It was completely different.

I would have been much more frightened if it had been one of the Conan Doyle novels, which is what Steven Moffat adapted. But the great characters in the modern Western canon are always ripe for interpretation. Hamlet gets done every year, and so does Sherlock Holmes, because they’re great pieces of work and great characters that can sustain different shapes and approaches.

DEADLINE: Deleila, when Sherlock — or whoever he is at the start of the show — comes into Alma’s life, what does she make of this man who seems to have come from nowhere? He could be helpful, or he could be a disaster for her.

DELEILA PIASKO: They are strangers, and they become partners in crime. We tell the story of them getting to know each other. They are both lost in the world, so their relationship is really at the core of the show. It’s about the relationship between the Englishman and Alma. It’s a journey with them. Alma realizes that she needs him. She’s a lone wolf, but at one point she needs a partner — somebody to help her.

What’s very special is that this Englishman doesn’t judge her. She’s a single mother living in a small village, and she’s treated with contempt. She’s experiencing a kind of exclusion. With him, it’s different. It’s the beginning of a friendship — or whatever it becomes.

DEADLINE: Most Sherlock Holmes stories are mysteries – intricate, complex and brilliantly written. Would you describe this series as a mystery, or does it fit somewhere else tonally?

SPALL: Fans of the genre will be satisfied by the whodunit – the question of how something happened and the mysterious nature of it. They’ll also get a thrill from seeing flashes of this famous character’s powers of deduction.

What’s interesting is that Conan Doyle got sick of writing Sherlock Holmes. He killed him off, with Holmes and Moriarty falling off the Reichenbach Falls. Then, I think, he missed the money, so three years later he brought him back. This is the first attempt I can think of to fill in the gap of what happened, so it isn’t based on a Conan Doyle novel. It’s a new story that, hopefully, fulfils people’s expectations of a Sherlock Holmes story. There’s a lot of mystery and a classic Holmes whodunit at its heart.

DEADLINE: When did you first hear about the project, and what drew you to it?

SPALL: My agent called and said they were doing a new version of Sherlock Holmes and asked if I’d like to speak to the people making it. I found it very charming and nice, and I thought it was really original. I was asked, I said yes, and here we are. It was probably about a year ago that it came to me, although I think the project had been around for a while and was then pulled together quite rapidly.

DEADLINE: Deleila, was it a similar process for you?

PIASKO: Yes, pretty much the same time. I read the script and thought it was fantastic. I was very lucky.

SPALL: We had a fun time because we were filming in some pretty rough-and-ready places — the Swiss Alps, the Italian Alps and a great town called Regensburg in Bavaria. We were in fairly remote locations, so it was very important to be surrounded by nice people. We really got on with each other and had a good time making it.

DEADLINE: With European co-productions, different parties can sometimes pull in different directions to serve their respective audiences. Did this feel more holistic and complete?

PIASKO: There were many different approaches. Our show is about cultural clashes, and of course there are different experiences. It’s also a multilingual show, so behind the scenes you have to communicate somehow, but I think that’s the beauty of it. It makes the world bigger and fleshes it out, especially when you have different languages. It was very free creatively. We were very welcome to bring our nerves and our ideas into it.

SPALL: From a trade point of view, it’s an interesting example of a new way of putting together big television in Europe. The bottom has fallen out of the American co-production market and a new way needed to be found.

I can only speak from an English point of view, or as someone who predominantly makes British film and television, but I think there have been some very successful examples of this new model. This series is an example of the way the industry has changed and evolved. When it came to me, I knew Sky Switzerland and Sky Germany were putting up the initial money, and it was then acquired by Sky UK, which I had previously worked with. I was the only English person involved, which felt appropriate because Sherlock Holmes is in the Swiss Alps.

DEADLINE: Rafe, you’re doing a lot of work at the moment. What does the next year or two look like for you?

SPALL: I’m doing Harry Potter at the moment. If people like it, I’ll be doing that for a long time. Then I’m going to do Under Salt Marsh Season 2 next year. I’ve got Number 10, which I think is coming soon, and ITV Studios is selling that. Maybe there’ll be another season of Trying — we’ll see. Who knows? I’m very lucky to be paid to do a job I love. It’s the only skill I could possibly exchange for cash. No one else would accept money for anything else I could offer.

DEADLINE: And what does the next couple of years look like for you, Deleila?

PIASKO: There are some things in the pipeline, but I can’t share them yet. Maybe there will be in a second season of The Death of Sherlock Holmes — we’ll see. There are also some other projects, including the German TV show Zweifel, which won Best Series at the Cannes Series festival in 2024. The second season will air next January.

DEADLINE: Are you nervous about Harry Potter, Rafe? We’re hearing the sets are looking amazing, like nothing else.

SPALL: I’ve never seen production values like it. I’ve been lucky enough to do things such as Prometheus and Jurassic World, big franchise projects, but I’ve never seen sets like these. Kate Hall, who does the hair and make up and worked on The Crown, is extraordinary. Holly Waddington, who won an Oscar for Poor Things, is doing the costumes. I’ve never come out of costume fittings feeling so excited. I was around true genius — a costume designer who just blows my mind.

So I’m not nervous about it. I’m just really enjoying it. It’s funny that my dad played Ron’s rat and now I’m playing Arthur Weasley. The other day I was on set and Ron’s rat was there. I took a photograph next to it. If I had social media, I would post it.

DEADLINE: Talking of which, do you worry about the social media reaction, given the controversy surrounding J.K. Rowling?

SPALL: I’m mercifully not on any form of social media, and I don’t feel I have anything further to contribute to that debate. I’m just feeling really lucky to be part of something full of amazingly creative, brilliant people, all working at the top of their game. There are fabulous actors involved. Katherine Parkinson and I play the Weasley parents, and to my mind, she’s one of the best actors in the world. She’s phenomenal. The other day it was me, her, Kit Harington and Johnny Flynn. It was just fun.

DEADLINE: You’ve said you’re hoping for a second season of The Death of Sherlock Holmes…

SPALL: If people like it, we’ll do more of it. There are more stories to tell.

WHITTOCK: I also wanted to ask you about Number 10. The British prime minister is obviously never just one person and can be whoever you want him to be. But there is a picture in people’s minds of what the prime minister is. What was your take on playing that character?

SPALL: It was pretty thrilling. It was one of the most challenging things I’ve ever done because Steven Moffat writes 10-page scenes, which is rare in modern television. And for a writer of Stephen’s quality, every comma needs to be observed. If it isn’t, you soon get reminded where it needs to be.

It was technically pretty full-on, but wonderful. We built the entirety of the downstairs of Number 10, and it became one of my favourite things I’ve ever done. I’m playing a fictional prime minister. I was lucky enough to meet a real former prime minister to talk about who he could be. In a way, it could be anyone — practically anyone you meet on the street these days. They were very charming and generous.

I loved doing it, and I hope people enjoy it. Stephen and Sue — his producing partner and wife — are powerhouses. Sue is one of the best producers the country has ever produced, and Stephen is one of the best writers.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: ‘Dear William:’ Film Adaptation Of David D. Magee’s Memoir Underway
summary: EXCLUSIVE: A big-screen adaptation of David D. Magee’s memoir Dear William: A Father’s Memoir of Addiction, Recovery, Love, and Loss has been greenlit, with production underway in Mississippi, and Andrew Hyatt (The Blind and Paul) directing. Hyatt has also written the film’s screenplay. Matt Passmore, Emily Rose, Gabriel Nagy and Hudson Macready star in the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: A big-screen adaptation of David D. Magee’s memoir Dear William: A Father’s Memoir of Addiction, Recovery, Love, and Loss has been greenlit, with production underway in Mississippi, and Andrew Hyatt (The Blind and Paul) directing.

Hyatt has also written the film’s screenplay. Matt Passmore, Emily Rose, Gabriel Nagy and Hudson Macready star in the film, which tells the true story of a family confronting addiction and loss while finding its way back to one another. Magee is also producing the film, alongside Cory Pyke.

Passmore plays David, a divorced, broke, and unraveling father who sets out for California with his oldest son, William (Nagy), on a two-thousand-mile drive. Along the way, he discovers that they are both struggling with addiction. The synopsis continues: With Rose portraying Kent and Macready playing Hudson, the story expands beyond father and son to follow a family reckoning with the truths it has kept hidden, navigating marriage, loss, and faith, and discovering the possibility of hope and joy on the other side. At its heart is a son’s final request that gives his father a lifelong purpose.

Passmore is best known for his leading roles as detective Jim Longworth in A&E’s The Glades and Neil Truman in USA Network’s Satisfaction. His additional television credits include McLeod’s Daughters, Frayed, and Netflix’s 13 Reasons Why, while his film work includes Jigsaw.

Watch on Deadline

Rose starred as Audrey Parker in Syfy’s Haven. Her television credits also include Brothers & Sisters, Jericho, and ER. Macready is an actor, singer-songwriter, and guitarist whose screen credits include a recurring role on ABC’s High Potential.

title: Russell Brand Accuser Argues He Wanted To Assault Her When Trying To Drag Her Into A Toilet: “The Intent Was There”
summary: Russell Brand’s second accuser in his trial has argued “intent was there” to assault her when the presenter allegedly tried to drag her into a toilet at the MTV offices in London 25 years ago. The accuser, who we are calling C2, said Brand went from “affable, jovial and friendly” to “suddenly turning into a […]
content:
Russell Brand‘s second accuser in his trial has argued “intent was there” to assault her when the presenter allegedly tried to drag her into a toilet at the MTV offices in London 25 years ago.

The accuser, who we are calling C2, said Brand went from “affable, jovial and friendly” to “suddenly turning into a wild-eyed maniac, trying to pull me into the toilet.”

She was working for MTV in London at the time and had been showing Brand where the toilet was, she said. Once she showed him, C2 alleged Brand “was trying to pull me into the bathroom.”

“I said, ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go’, and then he started to plead almost, saying, ‘Go on, go on, come in,'” added C2. “He had hold of my arm hard in a grip and I’m pulling back out towards the corridor.”

Watch on Deadline

After about 20 seconds, C2, who described herself as “physically stronger than the average woman,” said she was able to “wrench herself away.” She added that she subsequently told two colleagues but didn’t tell her employers as she was “scared” and thought it would be “my word against his.”

Brand faces seven charges, encompassing three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault, and one of indecent assault. The charges pertain to allegations made by six women, spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges and has consistently denied wrongdoing.

Under cross-examination from Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter, C2 was questioned over whether at the time she could have actually felt that Brand wanted consensual sex, and it was only after she watched the 2023 documentary Russell Brand: In Plain Sight that she changed her view.

C2 denied this. “Why would you drag someone into a toilet if you didn’t want to assault them?,” she added. “You don’t drag someone by the arm. You don’t grip someone and try and pull them. That’s not consensual. The intent was there. It could have been very different.”

As they were walking towards the toilet before the incident, C2 said “nothing was suggested about romance, not a word.” She added that even though he was one of the flagship MTV presenters at the time, she did not see Brand again while working at the network.

She did not come forward before seeing the documentary because “in 2001, it would have been my word against his,” C2 said, adding: “I had a job to consider, [and] came away relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me, and I managed to get myself out the situation. I just wanted a quiet life. I didn’t need this.”

“Sex was a huge preoccupation for him”

Yesterday, a police interview was played to the court from complainant C1, who alleged Brand raped her in his hotel room during the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth after he posed for semi-nude photos from her. He was appearing in a play at the time on the fringes of the conference.

Today, a number of witnesses gave evidence supporting C1. John Rogers, who wrote a play Brand appeared in at the Labour conference, said the presenter had told him he had had an “encounter” with a woman that week. Brand’s “reaction was a bit odd” and “he was a bit flustered” when telling the story, according to Rogers.

A flatmate of Brand’s during the Bournemouth conference, Andrew Dobson, alleged Brand wanted to leave hurriedly the morning after the alleged assault took place. “He came in and there was suddenly an urgency,” added Dobson. “It felt tense and confusing. I didn’t understand why.”

Dobson said “sex was a huge preoccupation” for the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star. Before finding fame, he described Brand as “vibrant, egotistical, lively, demanding, persuasive and erratic.”

Two acquaintances of C1’s also told the court via witness statement that she had told them about her alleged rape after watching the Brand documentary in 2023.

One said C1 had told her she had been raped previously by her husband “and felt as if she were reliving this and completely froze” during the alleged assault. C1 told her she was worried about backlash from her community if she reported Brand at the time, this acquaintance said.

The other said she was told by C1 over WhatsApp after C1 had reported Brand to the police. The police had told her she should only share the information with “trusted persons,” this witness said, via a pre-written statement.

The trial continues.

title: From ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ To Scottish Indie Boss: Kevin McKidd On Ferryman Films & His New Show ‘The Only Suspect’
summary: Scottish multi-hyphenate Kevin McKidd has launched an indie on home turf, and says he’s using his Hollywood experience to make it work. When Deadline speaks with him in his New York hotel, McKidd is in the throes of filming Conviction, the Elisabeth Moss-starring Hulu legal drama from House creator David Shore. After that, he’s headed […]
content:
Scottish multi-hyphenate Kevin McKidd has launched an indie on home turf, and says he’s using his Hollywood experience to make it work.

When Deadline speaks with him in his New York hotel, McKidd is in the throes of filming Conviction, the Elisabeth Moss-starring Hulu legal drama from House creator David Shore. After that, he’s headed to L.A. to direct some episodes of ABC’s Grey’s Anatomy, the show in which he starred as Dr. Owen Hunt before he said goodbye to the role in 2026 after almost two decades. Meanwhile, he’s recently wrapped on UK drama The Only Suspect.

In Conviction McKidd plays the husband of Moss’ Neve Harper, a confident lawyer who finally has her shot at a career-making case: a high-profile murder where the husband is accused of killing his wife by setting their home on fire.

Watch on Deadline

The conversation, however, quickly turns to his native Scotland. McKidd is using the smarts he learned in the U.S. business to power up Ferryman Films, his indie label out of Edinburgh. “I’ve got access to this American skillset and these people who’ve been showrunners on big shows,” he says, “and then there are these Scottish writers with all this potential. It’s really been fun to see that cross-pollination.”

One project he’s working on but keeping mum about is Troubadour. “We’re developing that with Bruno Heller (Rome) who is the chieftain of it, but Kieran Hurley, who’s quite an accomplished Scottish playwright, is co-writing with him,” McKidd says.

His new indie banner has partnered with STV Studios, the production and distribution arm of Scottish broadcaster STV run by former NBCUniversal exec David Mortimer. An adaptation of William Shaw detective novel The Red Shore is the first collaboration resulting from the deal.

There’s also Friends Like These for the BBC in the works, a female-led show about a group of 30-something friends. Gillian McCormack (Counsels) is writing.

A Guilty Secret

One thing that has wrapped is psychological drama The Only Suspect, adapted by Simon Ashdown (Trigger Point) from the novel by Louise Candlish. It is for ITV in the U.K., with Farren Blackburn directing. Moving between the present day and mid-1990s London, it follows Alex (McKidd) and his wife, Beth, played by Amaka Okafor (Black Rabbit). The devoted couple’s seemingly picture-perfect suburban life hides a devastating truth linked to a dead body—Alex, it transpires, is the man who buried that body, and has been harboring the dark secret ever since.

The Only Suspect Red Planet Pictures, David Hindley

“He’s very much a kind of antihero,” McKidd says of his character. “That’s a really delicious challenge—to have an audience root for a character while also having major mixed feelings about them. I find those characters a fantastic knot to untie.”

The setting for the 1990s part of the series is Camden, London, which was very much the epicenter of the U.K.’s Cool Britannia movement. It struck a chord with McKidd, given he was one of the stars of Trainspotting, a defining movie of that era. He played the memorable and tragic character of Tommy in the Danny Boyle film and recently attended a 30th anniversary screening of the film in Edinburgh.

“I spent my formative years exactly in the period of time in which we see the younger versions of these characters,” McKidd says.

“I didn’t kill anyone, thankfully,” he quips. “But there are those mistakes that you make in your twenties as you’re figuring out life, which is what this show is all about. I was able to get into that character because it weirdly reflected my own life, going back to this place in the same way as Alex as he has to go back and face what happened in the 90s.”

McKidd says viewers should buckle up for twists and turns. “Every episode keeps you guessing. Just when you think you know what’s happening, they pull the rug from under you. It has quite a dark psychology, but there’s a lot of humor in it too.”

Red Planet Pictures is producing. The venerable U.K. label is majority-owned by Fremantle, which is handling international sales and will be pushing at MIPCOM. It is Red Planet’s second Candlish adaptation after Our House, one of ITV’s biggest new drama launches back in 2022.

Explaining why McKidd was such a good fit for The Only Suspect, Red Planet’s Tom Mullens, who is an exec producer on the show, says: “He’s such a clever actor with great dramatic range and a chameleon-like versatility, which was essential for the part of Alex, a deeply complex character who goes on a cathartic journey across the four episodes.

“Not only do we see a charming and manipulative Alex as he protects his secret, but we also see a man who loves his wife and is faced with an impossible choice, knowing that by confronting his guilt and telling the truth, he might also destroy his life and marriage.”

Heading Home

McKidd starred in several U.K.-produced shows during his time on Grey’s Anatomy but still noticed a change when it came to filming The Only Suspect.

Grey’s Anatomy ABC, Scott Everett White

“On [Grey’s Anatomy] we have three cameras rolling all the time, every take. But with The Only Suspect it was a single camera, which is pretty much where I started, in indie films in the ’90s and the early 2000s.

“With three cameras, it can dilute what you’re doing. [Director] Farren Blackburn and the DP did such a good job at using that one camera and always placing it in the optimal position to get the most intense version of that setup.”

McKidd’s own directing work has made him more of a team player. “Before, I was probably a bit of a pain in the arse. I was like ‘You know, my character wouldn’t do that.’ Now I’m much more accommodating. I know what it is like to sit in that director’s chair.”

With experience in front of and behind the camera, he says he’s also happy to relinquish control when an acting gig comes up. “When I worked with Ben Williams, who was brilliant [as the director of Hideo Yokoyama adaptation Six Four], and Farren, the first thing I said to them was, ‘I’m not going to come in as this actor-director who’s going to be rolling his eyes at your choices. I can take that chip in my brain out and just focus on being an actor. I’m just going to put my complete trust in you.’”

Being an indie boss, meanwhile, is another skillset. It requires patience as the options are picked up, writers are attached and pitches made to buyers.

“I’ve got this underpinning of being a theater actor, really, who fell into all this TV and film,” McKidd says. “Then I was plugged into the Hollywood system, having come from very independent grassroots. I’ve got one foot in both camps, and that can benefit my acting, but also the company.”

With Conviction calling, McKidd signs off: “I’m always trying to be a moving target. That’s what I want for the company. I want to keep people guessing.”

title: International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview
summary: Welcome back Insiders, glad to have you here after a busy week in Cannes and plenty else going on. Sign up here and whatever you do, read on. Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes Newly minteds: At this year’s MIPCOM there was a little bit of surf and a whole lot of shine as the edition was […]
content:
Welcome back Insiders, glad to have you here after a busy week in Cannes and plenty else going on. Sign up here and whatever you do, read on.

Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes

Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images

Newly minteds: At this year’s MIPCOM there was a little bit of surf and a whole lot of shine as the edition was dominated by Fox and Fremantle’s Baywatch reboot, along with two newly-minted players emerging at their first big international market. While Baywatch stars Stephen Amell and Brooks Nader (pictured) were given the champagne treatment, execs from the newly-minted Banijay and Skydance were setting out stalls for the first time. Both behemoths (Skydance sales teams have retained their pre-existing Paramount and WB brands for now) had plenty to say to press and hosted swanky events, with many arriving Sunday afternoon in good time for Banijay’s glitzy do in the interior garden of the Hotel Carlton. Banijay bosses Jeff Zucker, Marco Bassetti and Jane Turton were in Cannes along with David Decker, the executive handed the Skydance content sales keys by David Ellison. Both have more to do in terms of reorg and there is still some confusion about how things will shake out at Skydance internationally. We’ve got the lowdown on all that went down in Cannes in our annual takeaways, which reveals the big stars who were in town, the shows making waves and the intriguing questions that hang over the future relationship between traditional TV folk and YouTube, plus plenty more. On the ground, there was an air of determined positivity, with sources we spoke with over the week acknowledging the tricky tightrope of today’s TV industry yet appreciating there are plenty opportunities out there. For now, the tide goes out on another edition of the biggest international sales market in the world. Find all coverage here and read a digital version of our MIPCOM magazine here.

Russell Brand Trial Begins

Watch on Deadline

Getty

“Indiscriminate and voracious”: One of the biggest UK entertainment trials in a generation began in earnest Monday, with Russell Brand entering the courtroom to face three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault from six women. Unsurprisingly, there has been an enormous amount of press interest over a figure who used to be a fixture on the big and small screen both in the UK and around the world. Jake has been at Southwark Crown Court and reported in depth as the prosecution first set out opening arguments about the Despicable Me star’s “indiscriminate and voracious” appetite for sexual contact that led to a decade of criminal offending, and then explained each allegation in detail. Some of the women have since been taking the stand. The allegations are wide-ranging, varied and horrific, and Brand will have the chance to defend himself likely in a few weeks’ time. He has always denied all allegations. The trial is expected to last six to eight weeks and we will be reporting frequently from the courtroom.

The Deadline Interview: Nicole Wallace



Nicole Wallace, a streaming phenomenon who broke out in the Culpables trilogy, was our Deadline International MIPCOM magazine cover star this year, and she was more than worthy. Wallace’s star is on the rise and she is shifting gears, with starring roles in Prime Video’s Postcards From Italy and motor-racing drama Throttled upcoming. We chatted to the actress about her next steps, switching languages and her defining Culpables scenes. >>> Nicole Wallace, a streaming phenomenon who broke out in the Culpables trilogy, was our Deadline International MIPCOM magazine cover star this year, and she was more than worthy. Wallace’s star is on the rise and she is shifting gears, with starring roles in Prime Video’s Postcards From Italy and motor-racing drama Throttled upcoming. We chatted to the actress about her next steps, switching languages and her defining Culpables scenes. >>> Read The Interview Photo courtesy of Violeta Sofia

Global Breakout: India’s ‘Hunkkaar’

We love spotlighting Indian streaming hits via Global Breakouts and Hunkkaar felt a shoo-in. This “algorithm-breaking” hit exec produced by Priyanka Chopra is about a teenage girl who accuses a powerful spiritual leader of sexual assault, triggering a chain of reaction that becomes a national story. JioHotstar’s show landed binge audiences, quite the feat for subject matter so dark. “I’m always drawn to stories that have depth and meaning, and Hunkkaar is one such story,” says Chopra. >>>Read The Breakout

The Essentials

Lea Meienberg/Getty

🌶️ Hot One: Ralph Fiennes, Tessa Ross and Studiocanal are behind Unbeaten, a biopic of legendary British horse racing trainer Henry Cecil.

🌶️ Another: Ridley Scott collaborator Alexander Witt is directing Feathering the Wind, a coming-of-age feature set against the high-speed world of competitive youth sailboat racing.

🇺🇸 Shocker in the States: Netflix’s content chief Bela Bajaria has been replaced by Peter Rice. Our editor-in-chief Nellie Andreeva’s analysis here.

⛺ Festival latest: Mel had this rundown of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival, with local breakouts, Oscar contenders and emerging talents.

🏆 Awards latest: The European Film Awards shortlisted La Bola Negra, Woman Unknown and NAZA for big prizes.

🌆 Skydancing: We had this rundown of the who’s who (for now) at Skydance’s international business, and then broke news that Skydance UK network 5’s much-loved content boss Ben Frow is leaving.

⚽ Goaaaaal: Before news of 1,000 layoffs broke, Netflix struck an intriguing deal to show World Cup soccer in Spain and Andorra.

🌐 YouTube: Meet the content creators making waves in Europe.

🤝 Done deal: Mediawan partnered with Reese Witherspoon to buy her Hello Sunshine outfit from Candle Media.

🏪 Setting up shop: Lionsgate Play boss Rohit Jain launched Hindi and Punjabi streamer Tiger TV in India.

🪧 Protest: Lupin star Omar Sy voiced his support for high school student protests sweeping France.

🍿 Box office: The first two movies under Skydance – Legendary’s Street Fighter and Clockwork’s limited re-release of The Devils – hit theaters around the world this weekend.

🎥 Trail: Check out A Long Winter, the Andrew Haigh adaptation of Colm Tóibín’s short story starring Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitriona Balfe, Kit Connor and D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai.

title: Kate Berlant on Her HBO Special ‘Parmesan,’ the Joke That Made a Man Flip Her Off and Her Next Project With John Early
summary: There’s a throughline in Kate Berlant’s new HBO special “Parmesan,” and it’s not cheese. “My addiction? My phone,” the comedian says at the beginning of the hour. With slapstick style and performative haughtiness, Berlant yearns for a time before cellphones in the special, out Oct. 16. Chronicling the hyper-niche behaviors that define our online existence, […]
content:
There’s a throughline in Kate Berlant’s new HBO special “Parmesan,” and it’s not cheese.

“My addiction? My phone,” the comedian says at the beginning of the hour.

With slapstick style and performative haughtiness, Berlant yearns for a time before cellphones in the special, out Oct. 16. Chronicling the hyper-niche behaviors that define our online existence, Berlant describes the seemingly inescapable embarrassment of wasting one’s life away in an endless scroll. She delivers verdicts on the great issues of our time, like whether to cover a baby’s face with an emoji or comment “PARMESAN” to receive a link to a pasta recipe. In one of the funniest bits, she talks about watching videos of “unspeakable violence” to “unwind,” like “gorillas fistfighting zookeepers, tourists being eaten by sharks.”

“It makes me long for the past, when maybe you’d numb yourself at the local watering hole,” Berlant tells Variety. “That suddenly feels so quaint. You’d be with your community, and some people would be abusing alcohol in terrifying ways, but at least you’d be together, and you’d be forced to interact with other people.”

Popular on Variety

She’s in an Airbnb in San Diego, ripping the “Home Sweet Home” pillows off the bed and couch because “they have hepatitis.”

“There is this loneliness, which is palpable, and I do think it will drive people into community,” Berlant continues, “because we’ll realize that that’s what we need.”

The first two words of your special are “world’s ending.” Yeah.

Would you describe yourself as a pessimist? You know what’s funny? When I was going to shoot the special, I was like, “I’m not gonna talk about the world ending.” Do I really want to dwell in that fear that we’re all so drenched in? I am not a pessimist, I would say, but I think fear is the appropriate response to the times in which we live, so I would say I have fear.

Fear of what? Generally, I have hope and optimism, and I think there’s a lot of beauty in the world. But I think that we live in a kind of undeniably existentially terrifying moment, and so it felt like it would be insincere or bizarre to not address that ultimately, because I think it is the water that we’re swimming in right now. It’s a strange time, and that also has pulled me toward how lucky I feel to be doing live performance. To me, the beauty of standup is that it is an encounter with actual people, and we are seeing the death of the living arts across all areas of life right now. So I don’t think the special is dark, but I think it acknowledges some of the themes that dominate contemporary life.

I don’t think people will be watching AI comedians. I agree. It will never die. People are always going to want people. I was on a six-week social media cleanse, so I was off for the latest [round of AI paranoia]. I logged back on because my special was announced, and I wanted the dopamine hit. When I was on social media, I saw all the AI stuff, and it really pulled my feet under. And then I deleted it again last night, because I just can’t do it.

EMILIO MADRID

You said you just went on a social media cleanse. To what extent is your phone an obstacle to creativity? How do we defeat the endless scroll?

We are in the fight for our lives. As far as it being an obstacle to creativity — well it’s complicated. There’s part of me that’s like, “I want to understand the culture.” I love the youth. I don’t want to lose track of where they are, of what they’re looking at. I think that’s really essential. I haven’t figured out how to have an ambient relationship, where you kind of understand, but it’s not completely overtaking your consciousness.

It’s an obstacle for all of us, whether or not you consider yourself a creative person. It prevents your relationship with yourself and with others. Certainly I procrastinate. My focus has been ravaged by this thing, so I have to reorient myself, and it takes a lot of discipline. I was in school for many years, and I always loved school, and I don’t think I could be in school now.

You joke about having chronic back pain from being an “emerging talent.” Are there other descriptors that have been thrown at you that you’ve grown to resent? Oh my God. I understand why people have said this, but I’ve certainly been branded a “weird comedian” or an “alt comedian,” “left of center.” Sometimes that confuses me, because I have always considered myself quite broad. I cross my goddamn eyes. I identify almost primarily as a physical comedian, and so my act, I hope, is broad. I hope I can reach all different kinds of people.

How do you feel about “character actress”? I think it should be an Oscar category! “Character actress” I embrace with everything I have. I was always going to be a character actress because I have curly hair and I cross my eyes. You’re either an ingénue or a character actress.

You do a bit about incest material being too edgy for the audience. Have you ever told a joke that you felt actually did break a taboo? No. I’ve never been drawn to being perceived as edgy, or in doing edgy material. I don’t think I’ve ever thought, “I went too far.”

I find it interesting that when you ask comedians about their edgiest material, it’s often not what you’d predict. Sometimes it’s not racial or sexual material but, like, some random thing you didn’t realize was touchy. This is really interesting to me: There is a piece of material in this hour that did anger someone, and I was shocked. There’s a joke I have about fathers being like a family friend. I was doing that joke, and I noticed two people get up and leave — center audience. I saw it, but I just thought, “Certainly it’s not about what I’m doing.” And then later I was told it was a man and his wife or partner. And he flipped me off when I said, “A father is a family friend.” And then in the lobby, he threw a glass of wine. I touched a nerve, and I was amazed by that.

That’s wild. Do you know why? Probably he’s feeling a lot of shame or guilt around his parenting.

You talk about your sexuality a lot in the special, saying you’ve “succumbed to a homosexual lifestyle” in recent years. Is it harder to write material when it’s personal? My comedy has always obliquely referenced myself; I’ve never spoken autobiographically about myself. The [off-Broadway] show I did before this, “Kate,” was a send-up of that. So this was my first time ever doing autobiographical material, or actually trying to work through questions about myself that I actually had. Was it harder? No, it just was the only thing I could do. I had done “Kate,” and that consumed my life for a couple of years. And then I was like, “I guess I’m going to try to write stand-up again.” I thought, “So much has changed in my life and in the world. I can’t just pick up where I left off and do that again. I can’t just free-associate and present these caricatures of a person without addressing what was actually going on for me.” So it wasn’t harder or easier. It was just the logical next step, because I had just spent two years doing something that was specifically not about myself. Well, it’s all about yourself, always, of course, but I just mean — I created a person who isn’t me. I have an Irish, abusive mother in that show, and that’s not true. So now I was like, “OK, I think I actually have to talk about myself.”

Talk to me about the anti-closer. You hilariously refuse to deliver one final punchline, instead remaining on stage while the audience leaves the room. I chronically struggle to get off stage with stand-up. There’s this pressure of doing a big closer, everyone goes ballistic, and you leave. There’s something inherently embarrassing about it, because you’re reducing yourself to this expectation of the form. It makes sense that you would want to go out on a huge laugh, or that you would tie things up and then leave. That’s logical. But something about it has always … I can’t do it. I was doing shows in New York, and one of my oldest friends, Doron Hagay, who directed the special, said, “You need a big closer.” I was thinking about that, and I was like, “It would be funny if I never left.”

You say something like, “I’m gonna watch you for once,” and it reminded me of “Kate,” when you would linger in the lobby before the show with a sign that said “Ignore me.”

I know. It’s so funny because I forgot. You can just never get away from yourself. The same questions and ideas and motifs haunt you for the rest of your life. I hadn’t even considered that for my last show I was in the lobby as everyone came in, and now I’m on stage while everyone leaves.

Clearly there’s something about the relationship between audience and performer that interests you. Yeah, what is that? Performance is so strange. It’s such a strange encounter. You come on stage, everyone’s like “yay,” and then you leave. It’s so satisfying. I love it so much. It’s funny how everyone knows their role, which I think is really comforting about seeing something live. For me, the most interesting thing is disrupting that expectation. I’d be remiss if I didn’t admit that I went to a master’s program called Performance Studies, where questions about relationships between audience and performer are investigated.

EMILIO MADRID

What is your relationship to fame?

I can’t wait to experience being famous.

Oh, stop! As an emerging talent, I feel — listen, I am a ham, and always will be one, and so I love any opportunity to be a goof or put on a little show. If somebody comes up to me and likes my comedy, that only makes me excited. I’m not Mariah Carey. My life has not been interrupted by people enjoying my comedy. It’s been enriched by that. But having a persona, being aware of one’s persona — this has all been so chronically amplified by social media. I feel no issue being out in the world, flesh and blood. That’s fine. That’s not complicated for me at all, because I’m not Mariah Carey. Where it’s complicated is navigating that persona and being watched and performing online. That’s this new thing. It’s not so new, but it’s pretty new. That’s what can confuse me or shut me down: how to continue that performance on the internet.

When you were workshopping the act and doing the anti-closer, was it ever difficult logistically? I would imagine that some people wouldn’t want to leave the room because they just want to watch you on stage. People are remarkably respectful and understand it. People are smart. People know what to do. When you say that you’re a stand-up comedian, often one of the first questions you’ll get is, “Oh, do you get heckled?” And that essentially doesn’t exist. That’s a new, perverse obsession of stand-up clips, but that’s not real. It doesn’t really happen. Sure, it has happened in the history of comedy, and I’ve had it a couple of times. I actually had somebody kind of heckling my taping. There was a woman in the front row talking to me, and I had to be like, “Please stop talking to me!” That was hysterical, because it never happens except for that night.

I think the heckling thing has almost been encouraged by the comedians who are putting out the clips. I went to the Comedy Cellar recently and was like, “This is not a participatory art form!” And people are engaging.

Yes. I suppose at many clubs, they have a warm-up act that does almost exclusively crowd work every night. And crowd work is such an art form. I want to be clear: Todd Barry, Moshe Kasher, they’re comedians that do that so beautifully. That’s a different category. That really does exist. But what you’re talking about is a direct symptom of social media and of those clips, and people thinking that’s what going to see comedy is. But even if I perform at a club, most people aren’t doing that to me.

You and John Early have a very beloved creative relationship. This year you starred in his film “Maddie’s Secret.” What are you two working on next?

Let’s just say we are ready to have a television show, and I’ll leave it at that. We’ve had a couple of — I don’t want to use the word “failed”: TV things that didn’t happen. Pilots that didn’t go, or we were actually in pre-production on a pilot when COVID hit, and then it went away. So we are back in the workshop, and we’re doing some writing right now.

The desired medium for you guys is a television show.

Movies absolutely, and John is such a brilliant director and writer, and I’m so glad that he’s finally being seen as the filmmaker that he really is. But we’re currently investigating television as a medium that could work for us.
