title: Diddy Moved to New Prison Days After Being Hospitalized for Alleged Head Injury
summary: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs has been transferred from his New Jersey prison to a new one in Pennsylvania, officials and his spokesperson confirmed on Friday, days after he was hospitalized for an alleged head injury. Combs, 56, was serving out his 50-month sentence at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey when he was rushed to the […]
content:
Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs has been transferred from his New Jersey prison to a new one in Pennsylvania, officials and his spokesperson confirmed on Friday, days after he was hospitalized for an alleged head injury.

Combs, 56, was serving out his 50-month sentence at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey when he was rushed to the hospital on Saturday “non-life-threatening injury,” the Los Angeles Times reported. Other reports blamed the injury on an alleged prison fight, an account the Bureau of Prisons denied. Combs returned to the prison later that day — but that return stint was short-lived, as Combs was transferred on Friday to the minimum-security FCI Allenwood Low in Allenwood, Pennsylvania.

“We can confirm that Sean Combs transferred to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, October 16, 2026,” a Bureau of Prisons spokesperson confirmed on Friday. “For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not discuss the conditions of confinement for any individual in our custody, including reasons for transfer.”

Popular on Variety

A spokesperson for Combs said in a statement that the mogul’s team appreciated the bureau “taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously.”

“His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction, and while we cannot speak to the BOP’s specific reasons for the move, it is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind,” the spokesperson added. “We are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption.”

Combs’ time at Fort Dix was turbulent, particulalry after an NBC News report in late September claimed he has access to contraband cellphones to “scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him.” On weekends, he has access to liquor that was smuggled in by guards.

Combs was sanctioned by prison guards after the report came out for “disruptive conduct” and was stripped of 41 days of good-conduct time, delaying his release from January to March 2028.

The musician is currently serving a four-year sentence after he was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution in October 2025. His legal troubles have continued during his incarceration. Just last week, he was ordered to pay NBCUniversal $477,700 in legal fees after losing a $100 million defamation suit over the documentary “Diddy: The Making of a Bad Boy.”

title: Katie Zacharia, Trump’s Press Secretary, Is Out After Five Days
summary: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out after just five days on the job. President Trump told reporters Friday that he would talk to Zacharia about a new role. “I said, ‘When I get back we’re going to talk,'” Trump said, “because I don’t think that Katie should be made to suffer like she’s […]
content:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out after just five days on the job.

President Trump told reporters Friday that he would talk to Zacharia about a new role.

“I said, ‘When I get back we’re going to talk,'” Trump said, “because I don’t think that Katie should be made to suffer like she’s suffering at the hands of the press.”

Zacharia, a commentator who had appeared on Fox News, had a brutal week after being appointed by the president on Oct. 9. She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who left to join Fox News as a contributor.

Popular on Variety

Though Zacharia has styled herself as an “attorney,” she has since acknowledged that she did not pass the bar exam and is not licensed to practice law. She had a brief 14-minute press conference on Tuesday, taking only three questions, and on Thursday endured a grilling from Fox host Sean Hannity.

“What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference, Sean, with very little prep time,” she said. “Given the fact I had been on the job less than maybe eight hours, and had a briefing book in the morning, I feel like I did my very best, Sean, to deliver for the American people that day.”

Hannity followed up with a series of skeptical questions about her credentials. Zacharia defended calling herself a “lawyer” because she had a valid law degree.

Her faltering performance led to speculation about whether she would outlast Anthony Scaramucci, the press secretary who survived just 11 days in Trump’s first term.

In the end, she did not.

“Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci quipped on X. “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

Fox News reported Friday that Zacharia would be “transitioning out” of the job.

title: Eight VIFF Films That Deserve a Closer Look
summary: The 45th Vancouver International Film Festival (VIFF) featured some high-profile titles, including Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” which has been generating awards buzz for star Julianne Moore, and Martin McDonagh’s closing-night black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” took home the Audience Award in the Special Presentations […]
content:
The 45th Vancouver International Film Festival (VIFF) featured some high-profile titles, including Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” which has been generating awards buzz for star Julianne Moore, and Martin McDonagh’s closing-night black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” took home the Audience Award in the Special Presentations category.

Yet beyond the marquee titles, VIFF’s lineup spanned 76 countries and offered plenty of discoveries from established auteurs and emerging filmmakers alike. From Matthew Rankin’s experimental take on Brian Mulroney to Tizza Covi’s portrait of an aging blues musician facing eviction, these eight narrative and documentary films approached familiar subjects from unexpected angles or offered a glimpse into lives rarely captured on film.

“The Loneliest Man in Town” (Tizza Covi and Rainer Frimmel, Be For Films, Austria, Panorama)

Popular on Variety

Courtesy of the Berlinale

A melancholy and deeply nostalgic portrait of an aging Vienna-based blues musician who is the only holdout tenant of an about-to-be-demolished apartment building where he had spent his entire life. As he says goodbye to his home and possessions — which include vintage blues records, memorabilia and an out-of-tune piano — he ponders the prospects of a new beginning elsewhere, even as he’s firmly in the last chapter of his life.

“Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney” (Matthew Rankin, NFB, Canada, Showcase)

Courtesy of VIFF

Probably one of the most psychedelic and unconventional historical documentaries in recent memory. Rankin forgoes talking heads entirely, instead remixing archival footage, animation, and music to trace Mulroney’s rise to power in what feels like an experimental vintage fever dream. Rather than examine the late Canadian prime minister’s political impact and legacy, the film explores how his image was built and how his party transformed along the way.

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” (Noah Segan, Sony Pictures Classics, U.S., Special Presentations)

Courtesy of Sony Pictures Classics

John Turturro plays an aging pickpocket whose old-school craft is becoming obsolete in a cashless world. After targeting the wrong mark, he finds himself entangled in a dangerous situation with a crime family and is forced to race against a clock to save his disabled wife. Segan uses the crime thriller genre to tell a deeper story about the nature of progress and how the world moves on, leaving certain people behind along with the shared values, ways of life and technologies they once trusted. With its melancholy jazz score, it’s an elegy to a New York that’s slipping away.

“School for Defectors” (Jeremy Workman, South Korea, U.S., Showcase)

Courtesy of VIFF

This hopeful documentary follows teenagers attending Jangdaehyun School in Busan, which helps the children of North Korean defectors to navigate life in South Korea. As they struggle to adjust, many deal with insecurity, shame, trauma and discrimination. The school works to give them confidence, purpose, meaning and a sense of belonging, while also helping them understand what their parents fled. For a number of students, the full story of their family’s escape is revealed for the first time on camera.

“Minotaur” (Andrey Zvyagintsev, Mubi, France, Germany, Latvia, Special Presentations)

Courtesy of MK2 Films

Zvyagintsev meticulously constructs a window into the life of Gleb, the CEO of a Russian transport company who occupies a sleek modern home with his wife and son, but there’s a clear disconnect between them. When Gleb discovers his wife’s infidelity, it sends him on a particularly dark path, with moments of morbid humor intertwined. In the background, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is on-going, and the military is scrambling for recruits. The town’s mayor pressures Gleb and other executives to hand over employees for the draft. His household becomes a microcosm of a broader societal moral decay, fuelled by detachment, indifference, corruption, complacency and the pursuit of comfort. A Cannes Festival Grand Prix winner.

“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” (William Greaves, David Greaves, Neon, U.S., Insights)

Courtesy of William Greaves Productions

Imagine being a fly on the wall at a dinner party attended by some of the most influential figures in Black cultural life. In 1972, filmmaker William Greaves gathered artists and intellectuals associated with the Harlem Renaissance for an intimate dinner party at Duke Ellington’s home, capturing their conversations on 16mm. Now completed by his son, David Greaves, this documentary offers an intimate time capsule of a generation’s wit, debates and unmistakable style — inviting audiences to spend an evening in the company of history.

“The Flight” (Soran Mardookhi, NFB, Canada, Showcase)

Courtesy of VIFF

The downing of Ukraine International Airlines Flight PS752 in January 2020 killed all 176 people aboard, many of them Iranian Canadians. The incident devastated the families of the victims and shook the Iranian diaspora. Mardookhi follows three grieving Iranian-Canadian families who seeking answers and accountability from the Islamic Republic of Iran years after tragedy. Through stories the victims become more than just names in a news report or a statistic, but rather individuals whose absence continues to affect those left behind.

“Diary of a Chambermaid” (Radu Jude, Ritual Films, France, Romania, Showcase)

Courtesy of Film Movement

Jude’s modern twist on Octave Mirbeau’s novel follows Gianina (Ana Dumitrașcu), a Romanian migrant working as a live-in housekeeper and nanny for a wealthy family in present-day Bordeaux. Her young daughter waits at home in Romania, growing more upset with each video call and each postponed promise of a return. At her employers’ recommendation, Gianina also joins an amateur stage production of “The Diary of a Chambermaid,” with scenes from its rehearsals interspersed throughout the film. The film is built on juxtapositions: the care she gives her employers’ son versus the FaceTime sessions she can offer her own daughter. An elegant French home against rural Romania. The performative progressive speeches by her employers in contrast to how Gianina is actually viewed. And her outwardly warm, accommodating demeanour while the thoughts she shares with her mother or mutters under her breath are rather different.

title: ‘The Julia Set,’ Starring Chase Infiniti, Lands at Sony Pictures Classics Following TIFF Premiere
summary: Sony Pictures Classics has acquired rights to Niki Byrne’s “The Julia Set,” starring Chase Infiniti, following the film’s world premiere at TIFF. The film, written and directed by Byrne, was one of the festival’s breakouts, thanks in large part to Infiniti’s commanding performance. The “One Battle After Another” and “The Testaments” star earned rave reviews […]
content:
Sony Pictures Classics has acquired rights to Niki Byrne’s “The Julia Set,” starring Chase Infiniti, following the film’s world premiere at TIFF.

The film, written and directed by Byrne, was one of the festival’s breakouts, thanks in large part to Infiniti’s commanding performance. The “One Battle After Another” and “The Testaments” star earned rave reviews — including in Variety — for her turn as Julia Fischer, a math prodigy navigating being the youngest, most gifted student in her elite prep course, while falling into an abusive romantic relationship with her teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney). Amid those pressures, the film’s synopsis explains, “Julia must find the strength to follow the path she was destined to take.”

Jason Isaacs and Gillian Anderson also star as Pascal’s parents, with Nina Hoss, Carmen Ejogo, Chloe Bailey, Nico Hiraga, Liz Lin and Alex Dillard rounding out the acclaimed cast.

Popular on Variety

“Growing up, I didn’t understand that people made movies. I thought they were the purview of the gods, that they fell out of the sky, and if we were lucky, we caught them,” Byrne said in a statement. “For 35 years, my entire lifetime, Michael Barker, Tom Bernard and their team at Sony Pictures Classics have made sure audiences catch the movies worth catching. I couldn’t be prouder to add ‘The Julia Set’ to their extraordinary library, and to know it will be seen the way movies are meant to be seen: in a darkened theater, together.”

Sony Pictures Classics, led by Michael Barker and Tom Bernard, will distribute the film in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore). The studio is planning a theatrical release next year.

“With subjects as wide-ranging as feminism, romantic infatuation, class differences, familial conflict, bullying and love, and even what it means to be a math prodigy, Niki Byrne’s emotionally engaging and impressive directorial debut gives meaning to living in the modern world,” the Sony Pictures Classics team added.

“Seeing the enthusiastic response at TIFF confirms what promises to be a great theatrical success as well as cements that Chase Infiniti’s much-lauded performance in ‘One Battle After Another’ was no accident,” the studio’s statement continued. “She is at the center of this deeply rich, even suspensefully entertaining film supported by an amazing cast.”

The deal was negotiated between Sony Pictures Classics and Gersh.

title: A Different World: Tom Werner Wants To Make An Impact On Screen, Stage & In The Stadium
summary: Tom Werner has been involved in a lot of hit television shows, from working on Mork & Mindy and Taxi when he was at ABC to producing series including The Cosby Show, Roseanne, 3rd Rock From The Sun and That ‘70s Show at Carsey-Werner. When he moved into sports ownership as part of the group […]
content:
Tom Werner has been involved in a lot of hit television shows, from working on Mork & Mindy and Taxi when he was at ABC to producing series including The Cosby Show, Roseanne, 3rd Rock From The Sun and That ‘70s Show at Carsey-Werner.

When he moved into sports ownership as part of the group that acquired the Boston Red Sox in 2001 and soccer club Liverpool FC in 2010, he wanted to help these teams find their form on the field and bring them back to greatness.

Liverpool FC’s greatness started with manager Bill Shankly in the 1960s and, in a wide-ranging interview, Chairman Werner revealed that he has tapped Jude Law to play the legendary soccer coach in a new series.

This was the same goal with Netflix’s recent reboot of A Different World, a series that he originally produced for NBC starting in 1987, that was handed a second season renewal by the streamer just over a week after its September premiere.

Watch on Deadline

“When Fenway Sports Group got involved with the Red Sox, they had not won a World Series in 84 years, and we felt, in a world in which we were good stewards, that we could restore the legacy and the luster of the Red Sox,” Werner told Deadline. “As it relates to A Different World, I’m not really interested in Emmys or economics right now, I am interested in impact.”

Werner and Debbie Allen, who directed over half of the episodes of A Different World’s original 144 episodes, had been working on bringing the show back for some time before pairing with showrunner Felicia Pride, who has written on series including Queen Sugar, Grey’s Anatomy and Bel-Air.

“The reason that we wanted to bring it back really had to do with the fact that I felt like at its best it would have impact,” he said.

When A Different World first premiered, admissions to historic black colleges and universities (HCBUs) rose around 25%, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.

A Different World Daniel Delgado Jr/Netflix

Over the last couple of years, HCBUs are also seeing a rise in enrollments with Howard University receiving record applications in 2024.

“It was my hope that this reboot, done well, would not just talk about relevant social issues, which it does… but that there was something where we could have similar impact,” he added. “This is very different than if you had said, ‘Why don’t we do a show about freshmen at Purdue?’”

Netflix’s A Different World is centered around Deborah, played by Maleah Joi Moon, the free-spirited, well-intentioned yet rebellious youngest child of the original show’s Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison) and Whitley Gilbert (Jasmine Guy), during her freshman year at Hillman College alongside a whole new generation of Hillman’s best and brightest.

The ten-part series features topics such as a situation with ICE, sexual assault and college funding issues, all current issues that colleges and college students now have to deal with. “I’m very proud of the impact and I’m delighted that it seems the audience has responded,” Werner added.

The show debuted at number four in Netflix’s top ten chart with 4.2M views in its opening few days and reached number one in 12 countries.

Werner, who has been Chairman of Liverpool FC since 2010, is also hoping a project about his favorite football club can have a similar impact.

The club is working with Beef studio A24, Drive To Survive producer Box to Box Films and Adolescence writer Jack Thorne on a series initially centered around legendary manager Bill Shankly, who helped turn the club into a global powerhouse.

He believes the series could become like The Crown. “It’s a story about family and relationships through the lens of a football club,” he said. “My feeling is, if you do nothing more in that first episode than show 50,000 people singing “You’ll Never Walk Alone”, I defy anyone who won’t be moved by that one scene,” he added.

Werner also revealed that Black Rabbit star Jude Law was attached to star as Shankly.

Elsewhere, he is also working with Lionsgate on a television project that he is financing. “I always figured out when we sold The Cosby Show, the money was secondary. What was important was that we were actually telling stories that hopefully resonated, and I still think I’m doing that. Sometimes, I’m putting my own capital into it. We’re going to finance it and then we’ll sell it afterwards and have a distributor. It’s a way of getting stories to the audience that you know otherwise might not have been told,” he added.

Sarah Snook winning a Tony for The Picture of Dorian Gray Getty

In recent years, Werner has also gotten heavily involved in theater. He produced the Sarah Snook-led solo adaptation of Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray, adapted and directed by Kip Williams, which saw the Succession star win a Tony Award and the Laurence Olivier Award. He also produced a stage adaptation of 1952 western High Noon, starring Billy Crudup as Marshal Will Kane, which premiered earlier this year at London’s Harold Pinter Theatre.

The High Noon adaptation was written by Eric Roth, who wrote the screenplays for films including Forrest Gump, The Insider, Munich and Dune. Roth and Werner, along with Rob Ashford, the choreographer of Frozen, are now working on a musical event featuring pop group Imagine Dragons in Las Vegas.

“Eric had written this script, which was a film script for Netflix. This project has morphed into something that is a musical/concert performance piece. It’s exciting because it’s going to be more than a than a concert because it’s a terrific love story between two people who fall in love in college and it follows their journey,” he said.

Werner also has a one-man theatrical event based on Rodney Dangerfield’s life that he is developing with Joan Dangerfield for Broadway or off Broadway with Danny Goldstein

On the television side, Werner said that while he has no interest in selling Carsey-Werner’s library, which one would imagine is very valuable in today’s IP-obsessed landscape, he has received calls about a reboot of 3rd Rock From The Sun. “That was one of my favorite shows because working with John Lithgow was just a dream,” he said. “I’m calling [a potential reboot] 4th Rock.”

“I’m a storyteller, and I love telling and reading and being involved with good stories,” Werner concluded.

title: Jude Law Set To Play Legendary Liverpool Manager Bill Shankly In A24 Series From Jack Thorne
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Jude Law might be a Tottenham Hotspur fan but he’s potentially heading to Anfield for his next role. The Black Rabbit star is set to star as legendary Liverpool FC manager Bill Shankly in a series from Adolescence writer Jack Thorne and A24. The soccer club revealed in 2024 that it was working with […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Jude Law might be a Tottenham Hotspur fan but he’s potentially heading to Anfield for his next role.

The Black Rabbit star is set to star as legendary Liverpool FC manager Bill Shankly in a series from Adolescence writer Jack Thorne and A24.

The soccer club revealed in 2024 that it was working with the Beef and Margo’s Got Money Troubles producer A24 and Drive To Survive producer Box To Box Films on the project.

The series will chart Shankly’s rise, helping the club achieve promotion from the old Second Division before winning three First Division Championships, two FA Cups, four Charity Shields and the UEFA Cup. Set against the vibrant backdrop of Liverpool’s 1960s with the boom of music and culture, the drama will explore a pivotal period in the club’s history, charting its journey from a team struggling to a global powerhouse with now over 400 million followers across the world, and recognized as one of the most renowned sporting institutions.

Watch on Deadline

Tom Werner, best known for producing series such as Roseanne, The Cosby Show and Netflix’s recent A Different World reboot, has been Chairman of Liverpool FC since 2010.

He told Deadline that he believes the series could become like The Crown. “It’s a story about family and relationships through the lens of a football club,” he said.

Shankly, or Shanks as he was commonly known, became Liverpool manager in December 1959. He was also responsible for “You’ll Never Walk Alone” being its anthem. He stepped down in 1974 after winning the 1974 FA Cup and died seven years later at the age of 68.

“Bill Shankly understood that it wasn’t just about finding the best talent on the team. It was about forging a connection with a fan base, and the reason that Liverpool is so special to me, besides the fact that you could say it’s got a billion fans worldwide, is that the relationship between the club and its supporters is really unique. If we can articulate that in a mini-series that starts with Bill Shankly and continues through its journey, we can touch on things like the Beatles,” he added.

Shankly’s granddaughter Karen Gill, who is the author of The Real Bill Shankly, is also involved in the project, which will be filmed in Liverpool and at Anfield, the club’s longtime home.

Werner added that, in success, the second batch of episodes would touch on the Hillsborough disaster, the deadliest disaster in British sporting history that saw 97 people die and over 750 injured as Liverpool played Nottingham Forest at the Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield in 1989.

Thorne, himself a Liverpool fan, has written the first two episodes, and Werner and his team have begun talks with broadcasters and streamers. “My feeling is, if you do nothing more in that first episode than show 50,000 people singing “You’ll Never Walk Alone”, I defy anyone who won’t be moved by that one scene,” he added.

title: ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Scores 9-Year Ratings High Among Adults 18-49 On Super Bowl Night
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Dancing with the Stars is still having its moment. Tuesday night’s episode drew 6.59 million live + same-day viewers, according to Nielsen’s Big Data + Panel, up 2% from the week prior. Dancing with the Stars led primetime on Tuesday across the major broadcasters. Super Bowl night also posted an 11% ratings increase among […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Dancing with the Stars is still having its moment.

Tuesday night’s episode drew 6.59 million live + same-day viewers, according to Nielsen’s Big Data + Panel, up 2% from the week prior. Dancing with the Stars led primetime on Tuesday across the major broadcasters.

Super Bowl night also posted an 11% ratings increase among adults 18-49, growing to a 1.56, Nielsen reports. That marks the fourth week of growth in a row to hit not only a season high but also the show’s best non-finale episode in over nine years, since “A Night at the Movies” in May 2017.

Tuesday night’s episode saw the remaining couples compete to songs from past Super Bowl halftime performers. The show, where ESPN Monday Night Football’s Joe Buck joined the judges table as well, collected 70 million fan votes cast throughout the night.

Watch on Deadline

Next week in the ballroom, the competitors are getting personal on Dedication Night. Special guest judge Kym Johnson returns to offer her expert insights. Dancing with the Stars is produced by BBC Studios.

title: Michael Che’s Awkward Interview Over Shane Gillis’ Joke Backlash On ‘SNL’: “I Didn’t Think About It, Honestly”
summary: Michael Che gave an awkward interview on the Today Show as he tried to avoid talking about the controversial Shane Gillis joke on Saturday Night Live. The “Weekend Update” host already knew he’d be grilled about the Gillis backlash and took to social media to joke about it. “Gotta do more press this week to promote […]
content:
Michael Che gave an awkward interview on the Today Show as he tried to avoid talking about the controversial Shane Gillis joke on Saturday Night Live.

The “Weekend Update” host already knew he’d be grilled about the Gillis backlash and took to social media to joke about it.

“Gotta do more press this week to promote the special. wonder what every f***ing questions gonna be about. thanks a lot shane,” Che shared on Instagram

Today host Laura Jarrett asked Che if he had seen the pushback over Gillis’ sexist joke, and he said, “That’s comedy. It’s like, you think it’s funny and then some people don’t.”

Jarrett followed up by asking whether he had laughed at the joke, and he said, “I was at cue cards, actually, thinking about what I was going to say that was going to make people upset, so I didn’t even see it until, like, the next day.”

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Dan Levy Slams Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ Monologue: “Speechless That Something Like That Can Exist On Live National Television”

Unsatisfied with the answer, Jarrett pressed Che on what he thought of the joke after hearing it, and the comedian said, “I didn’t think about it, honestly.”

“There’s so much going on. It’s really hard to see what everyone is doing, especially for me. I’m not what they call ‘good at my job,’ so I don’t pay attention to that,” he replied to questions if he had seen the joke during rehearsals. “That’s why I focus on ‘Update,’ because it’s not something that I’m natural at, so I got to really, really work at it. I got to study it.”

Gillis hosted SNL on Saturday, October 10, and made a joke during his monologue that has gotten everyone abuzz.

“I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” Gillis said on the late-night show.

He continued, “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts? Those neon, they’re like artificial bait-colored. And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combined at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now.”

Following the interview on Today, Che took to Threads to clarify his stance.

“Folks, I just wanna make one thing abundantly clear… i did NOT laugh,” he wrote. “Also, I NEVER laugh. NONE of this sh** is funny to me. I haven’t actually laughed at comedy in about 11 yrs, ever since I figured out how to do it. Even if it looks like I’m laughing, I’m not really laughing. I’m just being polite.”

He would also add, “Please. Stop saying I hate women. I only hate like 6 of them. (and THEY KNOW WHAT THEY DID!) The other 4,049,999,994 is alright with me. Wear whatever the f**k you want. Squat nekkid!”

Watch Michael Che on the Today show in the video below.

title: Chase Infiniti-Starring ‘The Julia Set’ Acquired By Sony Pictures Classics After TIFF Premiere
summary: Sony Pictures Classics has taken U.S. and key international territory rights to the student drama The Julia Set starring Chase Infiniti. The movie, directed by Niki Byrne, drew headlines at the Toronto Film Festival as it repped Infiniti’s next feature outing following the multi-Oscar winning One Battle After Another. The Julia Set stands at 70% […]
content:
Sony Pictures Classics has taken U.S. and key international territory rights to the student drama The Julia Set starring Chase Infiniti.

The movie, directed by Niki Byrne, drew headlines at the Toronto Film Festival as it repped Infiniti’s next feature outing following the multi-Oscar winning One Battle After Another. The Julia Set stands at 70% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes with critics.

Infiniti plays math prodigy Julia Fischer, who is recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics. At the same time, she begins to fall for her charismatic teaching assistant Pascal (Christopher Briney). As Pascal crumbles under the weight of his overbearing father Aleksander’s (Jason Isaacs) suffocating expectations, it is Pascal’s mother, Anne (Gillian Anderson), who helps Julia recognize and seize a moment of opportunity that will help to define her future.

Sony Pictures Classics

SPC is buying rights in the U.S., Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, the UK, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore).

Byrne said, “Growing up, I didn’t understand that people made movies. I thought they were the purview of the gods, that they fell out of the sky, and if we were lucky, we caught them. For 35 years, my entire lifetime, Michael Barker, Tom Bernard and their team at Sony Pictures Classics have made sure audiences catch the movies worth catching. I couldn’t be prouder to add The Julia Set to their extraordinary library, and to know it will be seen the way movies are meant to be seen: in a darkened theater, together.”

Sony Pictures Classics added, “With subjects as wide ranging as feminism, romantic infatuation, class differences, familial conflict, bullying and love, and even what it means to be a math prodigy, Niki Byrne’s emotionally engaging and impressive directorial début gives meaning to living in the modern world. Seeing the enthusiastic response at TIFF confirms what promises to be a great theatrical success as well as cements that Chase Infiniti’s much lauded performance in One Battle After Another was no accident. She is at the center of this deeply rich, even suspensefully entertaining film supported by an amazing cast that includes Christopher Briney, Gillian Anderson, Nina Hoss, Jason Isaacs.”

Pic also stars Nina Hoss, Carmen Ejogo, Chloe Bailey, Nico Hiraga, Liz Lin and Alex Dillard.

title: ‘Red Rising’ Movie in the Works at Paramount With ‘Hunger Games’ Director Francis Lawrence
summary: Hail Reaper! The rights to the popular “Red Rising” book series have been picked up at Paramount with “Hunger Games” director Francis Lawrence attached to a movie based on the first novel. Justin Rhodes will write the script, based on the original 2014 novel by author Pierce Brown. Lawrence and Cameron MacConomy will produce for […]
content:
Hail Reaper! The rights to the popular “Red Rising” book series have been picked up at Paramount with “Hunger Games” director Francis Lawrence attached to a movie based on the first novel.

Justin Rhodes will write the script, based on the original 2014 novel by author Pierce Brown. Lawrence and Cameron MacConomy will produce for About.Blank, alongside Francesco Goedhuis. Brown will executive produce.

“Red Rising” takes place in a sci-fi future where planets have been colonized and society has been separated into a color-coded caste system. The impoverished Reds work as slave labor in the mines of Mars, while the super-strong Golds rule the solar system and war on each other. The books follow Darrow of Lykos, a miner who suffers a great loss and is thrust into a rebellion’s revenge plot against the Golds. He undergoes a brutal transformation to become a Gold himself and enrolls at a military school alongside other young adults who are tested before joining the highest Gold ranks. There are currently six books in the series, including “Golden Son,” “Morning Star,” “Iron Gold,” “Dark Age” and “Lightbringer,” with a seventh and final novel, “Red God,” on the way.

Popular on Variety

Lawrence is no stranger to adapting popular young adult novels. He’s directed every “Hunger Games” movie, including next month’s prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping” and 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” He also directed last year’s Stephen King adaptation “The Long Walk.”

Lawrence is repped by CAA, Gretchen Rush at Hansen Jacobson and ID. Brown is repped by CAA, Hannah Bowman at Liza Dawson Associates for publishin and Dave Feldman at Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver & Thompson. Rhodes is repped by CAA, Adam Kolbrenner at Lit Entertainment and Eric Suddleson at Toczek Suddleson.

The Hollywood Reporter first broke the news.

title: Timothy Busfield Indictment on Child Sex Abuse Charges Thrown Out by Judge
summary: A New Mexico judge on Friday threw out an indictment against actor Timothy Busfield, finding that prosecutors failed to act in an impartial manner during the grand jury proceedings. Busfield was indicted in February on charges of groping a 7-year-old boy on the set of “The Cleaning Lady,” a Fox show on which he worked […]
content:
A New Mexico judge on Friday threw out an indictment against actor Timothy Busfield, finding that prosecutors failed to act in an impartial manner during the grand jury proceedings.

Busfield was indicted in February on charges of groping a 7-year-old boy on the set of “The Cleaning Lady,” a Fox show on which he worked as a director. He maintains his innocence.

In his ruling, Judge Joseph Montano found that prosecutors had impeded grand jurors who wanted to hear from defense witnesses. Some eight potential witnesses were sitting in the hallway outside, but were not called to appear.

Popular on Variety

“The prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner, including the failure to properly instruct the grand jury on the law for calling witnesses and in instructing the grand jurors on a procedure that effectively withheld requested witnesses,” the judge wrote. “In doing so, the grand jury proceedings were conducted in a manner that violated grand jury statutes designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system and the presumption of prejudice applies.”

Prosecutors have the option of seeking another indictment, but have yet to decide whether to do that.

“Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed,” said a spokesperson for the Second Judicial District Attorney in Albuquerque.

Busfield, best known as a star of “The West Wing” and “Thirtysomething,” was accused of groping a boy who worked as a child actor on “The Cleaning Lady” in 2022. In an interview with investigators, Busfield said that the boys’ parents were seeking “revenge” after the boys were not hired for the show’s final season.

Busfield’s attorneys had him take a polygraph test, which he passed. Warner Bros. TV, which produced the show, conducted its own investigation after a separate allegation was raised through SAG-AFTRA in late 2024. The WBTV investigation was unable to substantiate the claim.

Busfield and an Albuquerque police detective were the only two witnesses to appear before the grand jury. During his testimony, Busfield cited the WBTV investigation and said that other witnesses would be able to testify.

According to the ruling, some of the grand jurors asked to hear from additional witnesses on three occasions. However, the prosecutor told them that at least eight of them would have to agree in order for a subpoena to be issued, and that all 12 would have to return on a later date to hear that testimony.

The judge stated that no such requirements exist, noting that the witnesses were in the hall. The judge found that this had “the practical effect of unilaterally withholding witnesses requested by the grand jurors.”

“These actions are not in line with either the letter or the spirit of the grand jury laws,” Montano concluded.

Amber Feyerberg, Busfield’s attorney, said that he is “relieved and grateful today.”

“The grand jurors kept asking to hear from the people who were on set with him,” she said. “Those witnesses were sitting in the hallway, ready to tell the grand jury what they saw, and what they saw shows that Tim is innocent. The prosecution would not let them in, and the Court saw that for what it was: a violation of the grand jury laws that protect the integrity of our justice system. We know this may not be the end. If the State chooses to try again, Tim is ready, and so are those witnesses.”

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival
summary: London Film Festival’s surprise film on Friday night was “I Play Rocky,” Peter Farrelly’s biographical drama about the beginnings of Sylvester Stallone’s beloved boxing franchise. Farrelly was on hand to introduce the movie and shouted out his star, newcomer Anthony Ippolito, who has already earned praise for his portrayal of Stallone. “I could do a […]
content:
London Film Festival‘s surprise film on Friday night was “I Play Rocky,” Peter Farrelly’s biographical drama about the beginnings of Sylvester Stallone‘s beloved boxing franchise.

Farrelly was on hand to introduce the movie and shouted out his star, newcomer Anthony Ippolito, who has already earned praise for his portrayal of Stallone. “I could do a TED talk about Anthony Ippolito. This kid is ridiculous,” Farrelly said, adding that the 27-year-old sent in a self-tape before the film team even began what was meant to be a “worldwide search” for who would play Stallone.

“He heard about the movie, tracked down the script, shot three scenes in his grandmother’s basement on Long Island and sent it to us,” Farrelly continued. “I looked at it like, ‘That’s it.’ We never looked past him.”

Popular on Variety

“I Play Rocky” tells the true story of how Stallone, then a young small-time actor, overcame obstacles to both write and star in the 1976 classic. Alongside Ippolito, it stars AnnSophia Robb as Sasha Czack, Stallone’s wife; Matt Dillon as his father, Frank Stallone Sr.; P.J. Byrne as “Rocky” producer Irwin Winkler; Jay Duplass as director John G. Avildsen and more.

Farrelly added that he’s most proud of the fact that Stallone himself is pleased with the movie. “No matter how well the movie does, how many people like it, if Stallone said, ‘I don’t like it,’ I would be really disappointed,” he said. “And he loved it.”

The film first premiered at Toronto Film Festival last month, where it was up for the People’s Choice Award and generated positive reviews. Variety‘s chief film critic Owen Gleiberman called the film a “cleverly-crafted crowd pleaser” and praised Ippolito for getting his portrayal of Stallone “just right,” writing: “Watching and listening to Anthony Ippolito, we can believe that Sylvester Stallone is standing right in front of us, though the performance is more than just an awesome impersonation. He’s truly playing Stallone — the sweetly stubborn and dogged person he was at the time.”

“I Play Rocky” is set to hit U.S. and U.K. theaters on Nov. 6.

title: 7 Movies Finished by Second Directors: From ‘Batman 2’ to ‘Spartacus’
summary: Hollywood is a business of people. Yesterday, the industry got a reminder of that when Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced that Steven Soderbergh will help director Matt Reeves finish production on “The Batman Part II” while Reeves deals with a family matter. “Just to be clear, I am not leaving ‘The Batman Part II,'” […]
content:
Hollywood is a business of people. Yesterday, the industry got a reminder of that when Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced that Steven Soderbergh will help director Matt Reeves finish production on “The Batman Part II” while Reeves deals with a family matter.

“Just to be clear, I am not leaving ‘The Batman Part II,'” Reeves wrote on X shortly after the news broke.

“I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes.”

This, of course, is not the first time in the history of popular cinema that an outside director stepped in to take a project over the finish line. However, few of the other switches were done with friendship, collaboration and support, as is the case with Soderbergh and Reeves. Whether it was ballooning budgets, off-camera scandal, or personal differences, Hollywood has no shortage of studios scrambling to replace their director when disaster struck.

Here is a list of seven instances in movie history where a film had to be finished by a second director.

title: Francis Lawrence To Direct Sci-Fi Film ‘Red Rising’ For Paramount
summary: Paramount has acquired film rights to Pierce Brown’s New York Times bestselling sci-fi book series Red Rising, enlisting Francis Lawrence to direct an adaptation of the first installment, Deadline can confirm. Justin Rhodes, a writer-producer with credits like Terminator: Dark Fate and the Prime Video series Secret Level, will write the script. Lawrence and Cameron […]
content:
Paramount has acquired film rights to Pierce Brown‘s New York Times bestselling sci-fi book series Red Rising, enlisting Francis Lawrence to direct an adaptation of the first installment, Deadline can confirm.

Justin Rhodes, a writer-producer with credits like Terminator: Dark Fate and the Prime Video series Secret Level, will write the script. Lawrence and Cameron MacConomy will produce for about.blank alongside Francesco Goedhuis, with author Brown executive producing.

Red Rising follows Darrow, a “Red” miner on Mars who discovers his people have been enslaved by the ruling Gold caste. After being remade to infiltrate Gold society, he joins a rebellion seeking to overthrow his world’s color-based hierarchy.

The deal marks the latest high-profile book adaptation set up at Paramount, which releases a big-budget take on Tomi Adeyemi’s YA romantic fantasy novel Children of Blood and Bone on January 15, 2027. Others upcoming include Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow — in theaters November 12, 2027 — and The Midnight Library.

Watch on Deadline

Best known for directing five Hunger Games films — including The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, out November 20 — Lawrence is coming off the Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk for Lionsgate. Most recently, he inked a deal with the same studio for Carry Me to My Grave, an adaptation of a recently published horror novel by Christopher Golden that he’s eyeing to direct and produce.

THR was first to the news of Red Rising.

title: ‘Whalefall’ Review: Austin Abrams Wrestles With Grief, Toxic Masculinity & Grotesque Whale Innards In Emotionally Gutsy Body Horror
summary: Austin Abrams’ ascension to “scream king” status has resulted in an emotionally raw survival/body horror based on Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel. In Whalefall, written and directed by Brian Duffield, Jay (Abrams) goes diving in the Pacific Ocean to find the remains of his late father Mitt (Josh Brolin), who took his own life a year […]
content:
Austin Abrams‘ ascension to “scream king” status has resulted in an emotionally raw survival/body horror based on Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel.

In Whalefall, written and directed by Brian Duffield, Jay (Abrams) goes diving in the Pacific Ocean to find the remains of his late father Mitt (Josh Brolin), who took his own life a year before amid a terminal illness. When Jay and a giant squid are devoured by a whale, he has an hour of oxygen left to find a way out of the giant mammal’s stomach, while unpacking his grief around his dad.

The film is steeped in beautiful coastlines and underwater shots by cinematographer Aaron Morton, all of which he filmed in California thanks to the state’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program.

Meanwhile, the natural beauty of the Golden State is offset by the graphic body horror of the whale’s innards, built on practical sets by production designer Ramsey Avery and lit by bioluminescence. It’s like watching a really gross car wash while dropping acid, which is sure to be a fun time for any gore fans, reminiscent of the alien abduction scene in Jordan Peele’s Nope (2022).

Watch on Deadline

Even in the confines of an artificial stomach, with an oxygen hose shoved in his mouth, Abrams manages to exude humor through the physical comedy of being trapped in the most bizarre of situations, as well as some quippy dialogue with a jellyfish that tugs on the same heartstrings Tom Hanks did when he befriended a volleyball named Wilson.

At times, the dynamic between father and son can feel drowned in melodrama, but Abrams and Brolin are able to reel in their gutsy performances to portray a troubled relationship that’s still grounded in love.

Despite some definite womb symbolism in the unexpected fleeting comfort Jay finds in the stomach, symbolizing his emotional regression in order to process some heavy unresolved issues with his late dad, I didn’t immediately get that Jay was projecting his dead father onto the whale through his inner dialogue.

While the point of their relationship appears to have been the surfer bum Mitt wanting to prepare his son for the hardships of the world through many a whale metaphor, masked in some light toxic masculinity, but no real communication about the important things weighing on Jay, Dad was somewhat conveniently prepared for the circumstances of being trapped in a whale’s stomach, which is illustrated through multiple emotional flashback scenes.

“That’s called whale fall,” said Brolin in a ridiculously on-the-nose line reading, which for many will evoke the Ladybird GIF of Beanie Feldstein declaring, “It’s the titular role!”

One whale metaphor that lands quite nicely is how the sperm whale calls out for help when in distress, which inspires a Hail Mary plan in Jay’s fight for freedom from the belly of the beast. In addition to its literal implications in his survival, it serves as a symbol of the protagonist’s inability to communicate his own grief to those who love him most.

While Duffield’s adaptation of Kraus’ Whalefall is not subtle on the metaphors and melodrama, it’s an enjoyable gross-out genre film charged with raw, relatable emotion, and featuring strong performances from Abrams and Brolin as well as Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily Rudd.

Title: Whalefall

Distributor: 20th Century Studios

Release date: October 16, 2026

Director: Brian Duffield

Screenwriters: Brian Duffield, Daniel Kraus

Cast: Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy, Emily Rudd

Rating: PG-13

Running time: 1 hr 46 mins

title: Timothy Busfield Gets Sexual Abuse Indictment Tossed Over Prosecutors Failing “To Act In A Fair & Impartial Manner”; DA “Evaluating Our Options”
summary: Almost a year after Timothy Busfield was charged with two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and child abuse stemming from alleged incidents involving two minor boys on the New Mexico set of the Fox/Warner Bros TV series The Cleaning Lady, the Emmy winner has seen the case against him dismissed. “The prosecuting […]
content:
Almost a year after Timothy Busfield was charged with two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and child abuse stemming from alleged incidents involving two minor boys on the New Mexico set of the Fox/Warner Bros TV series The Cleaning Lady, the Emmy winner has seen the case against him dismissed.

“The prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner, including the failure to properly instruct the grand jury on the law for calling witnesses and in instructing the grand jurors on a procedure that effectively withheld requested witnesses,” Land of Enchantment Judge Joseph Montano wrote Friday in an order on the thirtysomething actor’s move to quash the indictment against him. “In doing so, the grand jury proceedings were conducted in a manner that violated grand jury statutes designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system and the presumption of prejudice applies.”

Busfield directed several episodes of the Élodie Yung starrer during its four-season run from 2022-25. Being held without bond at the Bernalillo County Metropolitan Detention Center after being arrested and booked, Busfield appeared briefly in Judge Felicia Blea-Rivera’s courtroom remotely January 14. On January 20, just a few days after the actor-director turned himself in, New Mexico Judge David Murphy rejected flight concerns by Bernalillo County District Attorney Sam Bregman and past (never charged) accusations against The West Wing actor. At the time, insisting on his innocence, Busfield was released from custody pending trial.

Watch on Deadline

Since then he has said that the claims are “absolutely one gazillion percent untrue. Never ever.”

A sometime caustic hearing was held in Albuquerque on September 25 on Busfield’s motion to have the indictment thrown out.

Now, with the indictment actually dismissed, Judge Montano has given DA Bregman’s office to “institute new criminal proceedings” against Busfield. Each count in the now tossed indictment carries a maximum sentence of six years behind bars – which could have added up to over a decade in state prison for Busfield if the DA refiles and he is found guilty. With that said, the reality is today’s order is a pretty damning indictment of its own against the one-time Gubernatorial hopeful and his office’s rush to judgement.

“The issue presented is that once alerted, the grand jurors requested to hear from witnesses not presented by the State, and the prosecutor used an unexplained procedure and an incomplete explanation of the subpoena requirement to unilaterally withhold evidence from the grand jury,” Judge Montano added in his six-page order. “These actions are not in line with either the letter or the spirit of the grand jury laws. To the extent delays may result when the prosecutor disputes evidence requested by grand jurors-after they have been alerted to the evidence without objection-the Court finds the reliability of the grand jury system and the intent that grand jurors be given access to more evidence-as long as it complies with the evidentiary standard ­outweighs the potential delay in proceedings.”

Reached by Deadline Friday after the dismissal order was made public, DA Bergman’s office said: “Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed.”

The brevity reads volumes.

Reps for Busfield, who has been out on bond and mainly on the East Coast since the beginning of the year, and his main lawyer Larry Stein did not respond to Deadline’s request for comment on their big win today

title: Netflix Enters Box Office Era With ‘La Bola Negra’; ‘You Can See Everything’ & ‘Musk’ Face Off – Specialty Preview
summary: Opening this weekend, Cannes’ award-winning La Bola Negra, Spain’s Oscar entry for Best International Feature inspired by an unfinished Federico García Lorca play, marks a milestone for Netflix. A24 debuts the buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, on 855 screens — about double the number as Musk, with Bleecker Street expanding that Alex […]
content:
Opening this weekend, Cannes’ award-winning La Bola Negra, Spain’s Oscar entry for Best International Feature inspired by an unfinished Federico García Lorca play, marks a milestone for Netflix.

A24 debuts the buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, on 855 screens — about double the number as Musk, with Bleecker Street expanding that Alex Gibney doc to 472 locations after a limited opening last week on four screens, with showtimes clipped by a nearly four-hour run time including intermission.

The Holmes doc (almost three hours) is off to a strong start with $1.75 million in previews and great exits, as in a 92% definite recommend and 100% positive score.

Watch on Deadline

Neon meanwhile launches David Greaves’ prize-winning documentary Once Upon A time In Harlem in two NYC theaters.

RELATED: Doc Talk Podcast: David And Liani Greaves On Their Oscar Contender ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’

La Bola Negra: Netflix is giving this festival favorite a 47-day theatrical window and the streamer’s first-ever Sunday box office gross report as it tees up a a string of films for a more traditional release: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth by David Fincher hits Imax over Thanksgiving, Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is getting a wide release in February with a 45-day theatrical window, Taika Waititi’s animated feature Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory is scheduled to hit theaters November 5, 2027 with a 47-day window. The Mosquito Bowl by Peter Berg, opening in limited release October 30, and Danny Boyle’s Rupert Murdoch biographical drama Ink on December 11, both will have approximate 30-day theatrical windows. All will report grosses.

The planned sequel to smash hit KPop Demon Hunters will also receive a broad theatrical release, said Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos recently.

La Bola Negra follows three gay men whose lives interconnect across three different eras. In a decorated festival run, helmers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi shared Best Director at Cannes (see Deadline review). It nabbed the TIFF People’s Choice Award for Best Film, Audience Awards at San Sebastian and Sydney, and Best Narrative Feature at the Hamptons Film Festival. Stars musician Guitarricadelafuente in his acting debut, Milo Quifes and Carlos González. Glenn Close and Penélope Cruz make appearances.

Netflix operates the historic Paris Theater in NYC and owns the Egyptian Theatre in Hollywood. It has opened films theatrically, making a splash with some, like the Knives Out franchise, or Frankenstein, which lingered in theaters well beyond its streamer debut. Usually the footprint is limited, the window short and official box office intel zero.

La Bola Negra opened NewFest in New York on Thursday. Screenings with director Q&As in New York today, and Saturday in L.A. Netflix will add select cities over the next several weeks ahead of a moderate nationwide jump.

Netflix early this year lost its bid to buy Warner Bros., a move that ramped up industry speculation around the streamer’s theatrical plans. More recently, a shakeup this week saw 1,000 job cuts and the exit of content chief Bela Bajaria as the company looks to boost engagement and grow in an increasingly competitive landscape.

A24’s You Can See Everything by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim launches at 855+ theaters ahead of a wider, nationwide release next week for the unusual documentary that was a secret for years before blasting off at Telluride with a surprise screening, then heading to the New York Film Festival. It’s 100% Certified Fresh with Rotten Tomatoes critics. See Deadline review.

A24 financed this verité project four years ago in secret and it flows from the San Diego home of disgraced biotech entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes in the 45-day period just before she entered the Bryan Federal Prison in Texas. Holmes granted the directors unfettered access to the house she shared with her partner and two young children, eventually inviting the filmmakers to live with them.

The Stanford dropout and founder of biotech startup Theranos was charged with fraud for lying about the technology and financial health of her company. It claimed to revolutionize blood-testing with a proprietary device that could run dozens of comprehensive medical tests from a single drop of blood obtained by a simple finger prick. She always insisted she had done nothing wrong, including in circular conversations with Fielder in the doc. She was convicted in a Northern California court in early 2022 after a highly public trial and reported to serve a 10-year sentence in May 2023.

A24 is approaching the film more as a kind of genre-bending cultural phenomenon than a traditional doc with runtime comps more similar to live event concert films like Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé, and BTS: Permission to Dance on Stage – Live. A recent documentary comp, Melania, did about $7 million at 1,700 theaters.

Alamo Drafthouse said You Can See Everything has racked up the highest presales for any A24 title and of any documentary in the circuit’s history by tickets sold. It’s currently Alamo’s No. 2 presales title behind only Avengers: Doomsday.

New, Limited

Neon opens David Greaves’ prize-winning documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem at two theaters in New York (Film Society of Lincoln Center and Film Forum), with an Los Angeles expansion October 23. The doc world premiered at Sundance and screened at Cannes Directors’ Fortnight, Telluride, Toronto and New York Film Festival, where it won the Library of Congress Lavine/Ken Burns Prize for Film. At 100% on Rotten Tomatoes (45 reviews), it has five nominations for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards including Best Documentary Feature.

The project was completed by David Greaves but conceived of and compiled by his father, the late William Greaves, who captured on film a 1972 cocktail party he hosted at Duke Ellington’s house with living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group, many of whom had not seen each other in 50 years, reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. The doc is shot on 16mm film and newly restored. In-person Q&A’s with David Greaves and producer Liani Greaves in NYC this weekend, and L.A. next weekend.

Dominik Moll’s French crime drama Case 137 from Film Movement opens at The Quad in NYC, adding Laemmle Glendale on October 30 before heading to San Francisco, D.C. and other markets. Written by Moll (The Night Of The 12tth) with Giles Marchand. Following the Yellow Vest protests of Paris in 2018, internal affairs officer Stéphanie Bertrand (Léa Drucker) must investigate the conduct of her fellow police officers during the demonstrations. Striving to remain objective, her position leaves her at stark odds with the rest of the force as she scrutinizes the near-fatal assault of a teenage protester from her hometown. Premiered at Cannes in 2025. Drucker won the Best Actress César Award for the role.

New, moderate/wide

Briarcliff Entertainment’s biographical comedy-drama Trust Me I’m a Doctor directed by Thane Economou and starring Kal Penn opens at 491 theaters. The film follows Dr. Sandeep Kapoor (Penn), whose life is turned upside down when he’s implicated in the death of a former patient, model and reality television star Anna Nicole Smith (Abbie Cornish). Set against the height of the early 2000s tabloid era, the film chronicles Kapoor’s fight to clear his name as paparazzi descend on his office, police raid his home, private journals are leaked, and every aspect of his personal life becomes public. He must navigate a high-stakes drug conspiracy trial while confronting the intersection of celebrity, justice, politics and personal redemption. Based on Kapoor’s 2017 book Trust Me, I’m a Doctor.: My Life Before, During and After Anna Nicole Smith.

Spider horror Crawlers from Roadside Attractions debuts on 1,037 screens. A catastrophic infestation of venomous spiders sends an apartment building into lockdown. Trapped inside by a police-mandated quarantine, building manager Serena (Matilda Lutz) and her residents battle to survive as the creatures multiply by the second. Directed by Angel Gómez Hernández, written by Jayson Rothwell.

Focus Features’ Sense and Sensibility, director Georgia Oakley’s fresh take on Jane Austen’s iconic novel, opens wide in 2,436 locations. The film reunites Focus and Working Title following their acclaimed collaborations on Joe Wright’s Pride & Prejudice (2005) and Autumn de Wilde’s Emma. (2020). Screenplay by Diana Reid based on the 1811 novel, the latest nod to the author whose social satire continues to allure readers and viewers over generations. Stars Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe and Frank Dillane, with George MacKay and Fiona Shaw. See Deadline review.

The lead-up included book club partners Vogue and Reese’s Book Club; slumber-party screenings; Alamo Q+A screenings; candlelight concerts; and brand partnerships with Estée Lauder, Paper Source, Coach, Butter London and Crate & Barrel.

title: The Impossible ‘Whalefall’: Director Brian Duffield Wanted a Challenge, So He Discovered a Way to Crush Austin Abrams in a Whale Stomach That Left Onlookers ‘Baffled’
summary: Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach. “Whalefall” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay (Austin Abrams) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, […]
content:
Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach.

“Whalefall” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay (Austin Abrams) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, ends up in its stomach and must escape before his tank of oxygen runs out. It’s a lean idea, but required an innovative and energetic leader like Duffield to get the claustrophobic shots done on practical sets.

“It’s such a small space and essentially a 360-degree set,” he says. “There’s a couple portals you can kind of shove a camera through, but it’s also somewhat full of water. All the lighting of the coil is inside the set. Basically everything that you would have on a normal movie set, we’re putting inside of a very small space. It’s also on a gimbal that’s rocking and rolling. So you take your normal film set footprint and then you put it into a bag. And then you also put Austin Abrams into the bag, and then sometimes other animals. If Austin’s wrong an inch, it doesn’t really work. Everyone’s cramped in this little doorway. But he can’t hear us, because the rubber is so thick inside.”

Popular on Variety

Duffield smiles at the outrageous setup.

“I was talking to a director,” he says. “He had a question and I sent him pictures of the set. And he was just like, ‘You’ve got to be joking.’ From when the whale is chewing Austin, it’s just a bunch of big, burly men jumping on the set and crushing down on him. And he’s in there, screaming and drowning with a real oxygen tank. I’m looking at this little monitor and if he needs help, it’s going to sound the exact same. Every time you call cut, you’re just hoping that the screaming stops. We had the studio come to set and watch this thing. From the outside it just looked so silly. I remember Disney safety reps would come and just be watching it, saying, ‘I genuinely don’t know if this is safe.’ But we worked hard, really hard to make sure Austin was safe.”

Brian Duffield photographed at the PMC Studio in Los Angeles. Dan Doperalski for Variety

Everyone made it out of the shoot unharmed, but the finished product is filled with harrowing set-pieces that are sure to push audiences to the brink. Duffield understood the vision early on, as he reached out to novelist Daniel Kraus on social media when he first heard the premise of the novel of the same name, before it was even published. He read an advance copy of the 2023 book, and was quickly swept away with the cinematic promise it held. Duffield ended up co-writing the “Whalefall” script with Kraus.

“You get the initial ‘boy inside a whale’ story, which definitely tickled all the genre parts of my brain,” Duffield says. “The idea of making a movie that had never been made before is always really appealing to me. It’s instantly clear how challenging that was, and I was really looking for a challenge. I was hungry to just keep pushing myself and the crew that I had consistently been working with. I think we just had the appetite at the time to take a big swing.”

Duffield is no stranger to ambitious projects. He began his Hollywood career as a writer with a disparate group of scripts, including a big-budget sequel (2015’s “The Divergent Series: Insurgent”), a Western (2015’s “Jane Got a Gun”), a slasher (2017’s “The Babysitter”) and a sci-fi action movie (2020’s “Underwater”). He transitioned into an idiosyncratic directing career with 2020’s “Spontaneous” (logline: a romance is shaded by the fact that people start spontaneously combusting) and 2023’s “No One Will Save You,” a nearly dialogue-free alien invasion movie.

Beyond their high concepts, Duffield’s works are marked by an emotional heft, which is no different in “Whalefall.” Jay’s diving trip is prompted by him trying to locate the body of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) after he dies by suicide. He’d never be able make amends with, or come to an understanding with his father, a theme that resonates through much of the story.

“I don’t think I was looking for a father-son story, but I think I needed a father-son story,” Duffield, a parent himself, says. “As soon as I was reading it, I couldn’t stop thinking about … not the whale, but about Jay and Mitt in that relationship. I thought, ‘That was the magic trick of the book.’ You’re forgetting about squids and acid and you’re thinking more about how these two guys are thinking they want nothing more than to spend time together, but they can’t quite express how they need to spend time in a different way.”

Brian Duffield photographed at the PMC Studio in Los Angeles in October 2026. Dan Doperalski for Variety

While Abrams and Brolin were able to bring the emotional gravitas to flashback scenes chronicling key moments in their frayed relationship, shooting the in-whale scenes was the overarching creative challenge.

“I had plenty of directors come and visit and all of them just looked so baffled,” Duffield says. “I had general confusion about how we were doing what we were doing. The thing I’ve learned the most is the joy of making movies for me is the crew and getting to hire a lot of the same people over and over again. I think if I have any gift as a director, it’s hiring people that are extremely talented, Oscar winners and whatnot. I like spending time with them and feel comfortable asking advice. I trust them if I feel like they have a note or an idea — it’s probably good.”

It’s part of a larger ethos Duffield brings to every project.

“I want to feel the effort, and I want to feel like I’m becoming a better filmmaker because of it,” he says.

title: The Hiring of Peter Rice at Netflix Could Set the Stage for a Corporate Culture Clash About the Future of Movies
summary: The profile of what a Hollywood executive is — the role, the methods, the priorities — is now in the midst of a transformation. The old definition of a successful studio executive was someone who’s commercially victorious, with a track record of great movies. But what we once called a movie executive might now be […]
content:
The profile of what a Hollywood executive is — the role, the methods, the priorities — is now in the midst of a transformation. The old definition of a successful studio executive was someone who’s commercially victorious, with a track record of great movies. But what we once called a movie executive might now be called a content officer, and there’s a larger change as well. Where film executives used to have to follow the numbers, now they follow the algorithms. And here’s the difference: Numbers are something you’re in charge of, while algorithms have a way of taking charge of you.

Peter Rice, the former president of 21st Century Fox and former chairman of Walt Disney Television who was just hired to be the chief content officer of Netflix (replacing Bela Bajaria, who was ousted in a dramatic shake-up), has worked in Hollywood C-suites for 15 years. But his roots are in the world of old-school movie-executive passion. In his new position, he’ll oversee both movies and television, which is a perfect role for him, since he has worked on the small-screen side ever since he was promoted to chairman and CEO of the Fox Networks Group back in 2012. But when he was president of Fox Searchlight, from 2000 to 2009, Rice was one of the most revered movie executives of his time, overseeing titles like “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Juno,” “Little Miss Sunshine” and “Sideways,” to name just a few. His only competition as the consummate movie-executive maven might be Tom Rothman, the original head of Fox Searchlight. These two sustained the single best model for how to expand the independent film revolution as a mainstream movement beyond the Harvey Weinstein model.

Popular on Variety

In recent years, Rice, born in the U.K. and now 60, has been semi-retired, or maybe just in a holding pattern. But Ted Sarandos, the Netflix co-CEO, having now given the ax to Bela Bajaria (there’s speculation that she was let go as a scapegoat for the company’s current growth squeeze), made an incredibly smart move in hiring Rice to be his chief content officer. Recently, there had been rumors that Rice was going to be offered a major position within Skydance. His ascension into the Netflix brain trust is every bit as significant, and given his historical tendency to rise in a company (without, somehow, making enemies), one could see that happening over the next five years at Netflix. Being the chief content officer at Netflix is like being in charge of hamburgers and fries at McDonald’s. In his new role, Rice will help to shape the company’s spirit and aesthetic. The question is, how?

Sarandos is a hands-on CEO — a visionary, if you will — who likes to have things his way. (Apologies for the switched-up burger-chain metaphor.) He must have a good idea of what he wants from Rice. Right now, that could be: more of what Netflix has been doing. Except that Netflix is now flirting with what may be the biggest change in its business plan since the company stopped mailing physical media to consumers.

Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” — the “Forget ‘Harry Potter,’ ‘Lord of the Rings,’ and ‘Dune!’ This is your new global-conquest fantasy franchise!” adaptation of C.S. Lewis’s sixth “Narnia” book — has been conceived from minute one to be a game-changer. The movie cost $280 million (hello, budget that makes “Digger’s” look like chump change!). And Gerwig, operating off the uber-A-list power she acquired after the megasuccess of “Barbie,” insisted that the film receive a full-scale theatrical release. (It will open on the world’s Imax screens, and many other screens as well, on Feb. 10, 2027.) Even after that agreement was made, Gerwig had to fight battles to ensure it would happen.

But she prevailed, and Netflix, with “Narnia,” will now be in the movies-released-in-actual-theaters business in a way that is hasn’t been … ever. (I’ve written about how a token Netflix theatrical release inevitably gets covered by the media as if it were bigger than it is, because critics and entertainment reporters tend to live near the few theaters in New York and L.A. where Netflix movies are playing.) As if in acknowledgment of what a profound change all this represents, Netflix recently announced that it would be taking greater general strides into the theatrical realm. (“La Bola Negra,” its big 2026 Oscar hopeful, will receive the longest theatrical rollout Netflix has given any film to date.) The company will also now report box-office numbers, a major change for the transparency-shy Sarandos.

As someone who’s been highly critical of what I’ve characterized as Netflix’s master plan to convert the world of movies into glorified home viewing, I applaud these developments. I hope they become part of the larger “comeback” of movies that everyone, in 2026, is talking about. This is pure speculation on my part (I’m a critic, so I’m allowed to speculate), but Netflix’s hiring of Peter Rice, at this moment, does not feel disconnected to any of this. Rice, in his heart, is a movie guy. I don’t care how much small-screen content one has greenlit — you can’t take that cinematic DNA out of someone. If Netflix’s new movie plan is successful, I could foresee that precipitating Rice’s rise within the company.

But what if the “Narnia” film, which only this week has been plagued by rumors of an underwhelming test screening, turns out to be a flawed blockbuster that doesn’t cut the commercial mustard? (I want the film to be great; I’m just floating the possibility.) What then? Will Netflix’s plan to expand into theatrical distribution be threatened? That depends on what Sarandos wants. And I could easily see him buckling on that. But if Rice becomes the voice of theatrical movie passion within Netflix, then that could lead to a major corporate clash. Or maybe he’ll be the one to help Sarandos see the light! Tuning into the offscreen drama of Netflix, it will be fascinating, and maybe an indicator of where the future of movies is going, to see who brings who into the stream of things.

title: ‘Street Fighter’ Cast Guide: All the WWE Stars, UFC Champs and Celebs Playing Video Game Fighters in the Live-Action Movie
summary: Round one…fight! “Street Fighter” is back on the big screen for a new take on the popular fighting game video series that started back in arcades in the 1980s and is still popular today. Paramount and Legendary’s live-action movie takes place in the ’90s and follows a worldwide fighting tournament that brings together challengers from […]
content:
Round one…fight!

“Street Fighter” is back on the big screen for a new take on the popular fighting game video series that started back in arcades in the 1980s and is still popular today.

Paramount and Legendary’s live-action movie takes place in the ’90s and follows a worldwide fighting tournament that brings together challengers from around the world. The roster includes Ken Masters (Noah Centineo) and his childhood friend and training partner Ryu (Andrew Koji), who have appeared in every “Street Fighter” video game. There’s a colorful cast of fellow characters like Chun-Li (Callina Liang), M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), Cammy (Mel Jarnson), Vega (Orville Peck) and more. The cast also has several real-life martial arts fighters, WWE stars and wrestlers, like Roman Reigns as Akuma, Cody Rhodes as Guile and Oliver Richters as Zangief.

Kitao Sakurai, who’s helmed episodes of “Beef,” “Dave” and the “Eric Andre Show,” directs the movie, which previously had Danny and Michael Philippou (“Talk to Me,” “Bring Her Back) attached. It’s actually the third “Street Fighter” movie, following 1994’s self-titled film and the 2009 release “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li.” The 1994 “Street Fighter” had a cast with Jean-Claude Van Damme as Guile, Ming-Na Wen as Chun-Li, Damian Chapa as Ken, Byron Mann as Ryu and Kylie Minogue as Cammy. “The Legend of Chun-Li” was a notorious flop and included Kristin Kreuk as Chun-Li, Neal McDonough as M. Bison, Michael Clarke Duncan as Balrog and Black Eyed Peas singer Taboo as Vega.

See the full cast of the new “Street Fighter” movie and how they compare to their video game counterparts below.

title: Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Admits ‘She Looks Insane’ in ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer but Defends Making the Doc: ‘Make Up Your Own Mind’
summary: Elizabeth Holmes’ partner Billy Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast just as Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everything” started its theatrical release to explain why the couple allowed a camera crew inside their home in the days leading up to Holmes going to prison. Evans has not yet seen the movie, […]
content:
Elizabeth Holmes‘ partner Billy Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast just as Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everything” started its theatrical release to explain why the couple allowed a camera crew inside their home in the days leading up to Holmes going to prison. Evans has not yet seen the movie, which has earned universal acclaim and Oscar buzz since world premiering at the Telluride Film Festival last month.

“[The context going in] is Elizabeth is facing an 11-year sentence. She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape or form and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” Evans said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”

“It was to have people see who she is,” he continued. “I have gone through this consistent experience with the people who love me most, from my grandmother to my best friends. They’d hear I knew [Elizabeth Holmes] or I was falling for this person and now we’re going to have a kid… in the beginning, every single one of these people thought I was crazy. ‘Do you know who she is?’ I would tell them, ‘I understand why you feel that way but just meet her.’ And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift. That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”

Popular on Variety
