However, it would appear Holmes and Evans’ decision is backfiring. “You Can See Everything” has only amplified the backlash against and the distrust of former Theranos CEO Holmes. Even before the movie screened for press, A24 dropped a chilling teaser trailer that had many viewers disturbed by Holmes’ demeanor and claims that she did not do anything wrong at Theronos.

“I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said on the podcast, admitting that Holmes “looks insane” in the trailer and acknowledging that “especially the music” in the clip has an anti-Holmes bent.

“Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure,” Evans said. “With this there’s certainly concern but it’s ultimately our decision.”

Holmes and Evans met in 2017 and had their first child, William, in 2021. Their daughter, Invicta, was born in 2023. Watch Evans’ full interview on the “All-In” podcast in the video below.

title: How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story spoils the plot of the film Whalefall, now out in theaters, based on Daniel Kraus’ novel. A running joke Whalefall director Brian Duffield had going to summarize the film hailing from 20th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment and hitting theaters this week was that “men would rather get swallowed by a […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story spoils the plot of the film Whalefall, now out in theaters, based on Daniel Kraus‘ novel.

A running joke Whalefall director Brian Duffield had going to summarize the film hailing from 20th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment and hitting theaters this week was that “men would rather get swallowed by a sperm whale than go to therapy.”

Just as Austin Abrams’ Jay Gardiner finds himself in quite the harrowing predicament trapped in a whale’s stomach after a tangle with a squid, the cast, crew and filmmakers of Whalefall also found themselves in the tricky situation of bringing the premise of Daniel Kraus’ novel to the big screen.

To back up, Jay’s decision to seek out the remains of his dead father Mitt Gardiner (Josh Brolin), who has committed suicide by drowning in the Pacific Ocean following a diagnosis of mesothelioma, is what really landed him in this situation. Just as he has to get scrappy and use anything he can find to escape, those behind the making of the movie had to be in constant communication about what it would take to pull off such intense scenes, many of which took place inside a life-sized whale stomach built specifically for the film.

Watch on Deadline

“It takes a village to build a whale, and I think it takes a really great village to survive it. And that’s been really one of the most gratifying parts of [production],” Duffield said when Deadline visited the set of the movie at Radford Studios in L.A. in September, during an early tank scene where Abrams encountered the whale for the first time. “It’s such a new and unique challenge that I think we hired the right people, because it was a lot of us all banging our heads together trying to figure out how to shoot every day.”

Multiple whale stomach models were built by Weta Workshop in New Zealand, with the head, throat, esophagus and larynx constructed in California because they were too big to ship to set on time. The 12-foot-tall, 18-foot-long whale head was manufactured by StudioArt & Technology.

Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios’ ‘Whalefall’ 20th Century Studios

“It’s such an interlocked set. I’ve never made a movie, and I can’t imagine ever making a movie where every single department really has to be talking to each other every step of the way,” Duffield said. “For the stomach, Ramsey [Avery] our production designer [had] to figure out how to build it, and then we [had] to figure out how to put cameras in it, but then also we had to figure out how to light it, and then the lights become bioluminescence.

Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron, who worked on Jordan Peele’s Nope, rigged the LED lighting in the stomach to eventually render as the bioluminescence that then helps illuminate Jay’s environment.

“Some colors do not show up the same color in LED lights. So, our costume designer had to build Austin’s costume around what the LEDs would show up with,” Duffield added. “So we would take neoprene samples to New Zealand, where we built the stomachs, to show them under the lights, against the whale skin, to see what colors show up.”

Cameras and lenses were broken “nonstop” during filming; the crew ultimately constructed scenes around the one spot the camera could actually fit into the cramped space and worked backwards from that vantage point. If that weren’t claustrophobic enough, Abrams also faced the added challenge of emoting behind a facemask and the diving equipment Jay uses.

“We redesigned the regulator to make it as small as possible, because regulators are not really meant to be worn outside of water. And yet, the air inside the whale stomach is toxic. It won’t kill him, necessarily, but it’s full of methane and things that make him a little high,” Duffield said. “So we redesigned the regulator to give him as much mouth shape as possible. He actually does talk throughout the movie to himself or to other characters in the stomach. That has been a challenging learning curve.”

Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner 20th Century Studios

These formidable aspects of the film’s creation echoe Kraus’ general approach to writing books; he now has 30-plus under his belt.

“I like to create new problems and have to fight through the solutions — I try to start with an impossible [conceit] where I just throw hurdles in front of me of things that I don’t know,” Kraus told Deadline on set. “So I have to relearn how to write a book every time.”

The impetus for Whalefall came from a viral video in which a kayaker ended up in the mouth of a whale. Once Kraus heard about the clip, it spawned discussions with friends about whether it could actually happen. He could not stop thinking about it.

Following an email to author friend Mary Roach, author of Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal (2013), and correspondence with three whale experts she recommended, Kraus had found the “high concept” hook for the book, which hit shelves in 2023.

“I didn’t want to do it if it couldn’t really happen — being swallowed by a whale has been treated like a fable and Biblical stories forever. My interest was, could you do it scientifically accurately?” Kraus said. “And by the end of the day, I was all systems go. All the whale experts were super-excited to help, and they think about whales all day, but never in this context. We were off to the races.”

Both Duffield and Kraus drew connections to the science fiction genre in different ways, with Kraus developing an interest in whales during the frontloaded research process for the book, which took about three months.

“I became more and more … obsessed, you might say, with whales,” he said. “There’s a lot of what I was doing with this biology of a whale, but I also unexpectedly started to get really enamored of whales as a being, as a force of nature.

“Sperm whales are extraordinarily intelligent. They’re one of the most mysterious animals on the planet. Everything about them is strange. They really feel like aliens. Even in the deep ocean, which is filled with alien-like creatures, the whales almost feel like a master alien. They’re not aggressors. They’re very peaceful animals. Sperm whales have been witnessed helping humans many, many times, like divers in trouble.”

Experiencing a whale from the inside out adds complicated layers to Whalefall‘s story, even when it comes to the father-son relationship at its heart.

“How do you fall in love with a character through its guts, basically? It’s definitely gross, but what are the ways that we can fall in love with this animal, because Austin is in such a unique situation, and I think there’s something interesting about his character, who is very fond of of animals and nature,” Duffield said. “One of the things that differentiates his character and Josh’s character is Josh is very hard and Austin’s very soft. But they both have this love of nature, and so giving Austin moments that he can really, for lack of a better way to put it, appreciate how cool the situation is — while also being scared sh*tless and thinking he’s going to die pretty much at any given moment — that was part of the craft of it, too.”

Duffield evidently shared a similar awe. For him, the trick with the stomach being the setting for a majority of the movie was balancing the claustrophobic feeling of Jay’s plight with breaks from the cramped space.

“It’s challenging for a couple reasons. One, it’s such a long stretch of the movie, and quite a lot happens while he’s in in the stomach, but it was also about keeping it fresh and interesting so [that] after 30 minutes, people weren’t just like, ‘Alright, I’m sick of this stomach,’” Duffield said. “[Jay] does have different little side adventures. He spends some time in the second stomach, which is very visually different, and then in the esophagus of the whale as well. Different animals that are also in the stomachs, and different problems he has to MacGyver his way out of, so it’s just trying to figure out how to keep it fresh visually, which Daniel honestly just did a lot of in the book.”

Whalefall executive prodcuer Doug Merrifield, whose credits include the Free Willy films, joined Duffield, Kraus and Imagine Entertainment’s Allen Mandelbaum in emphasizing that the whale is not the villain in the movie. It’s orcas that attack Jay’s sperm whale that ultimately provide the antagonists and the catalyst for the film’s climax.

“The whale is not a bad guy. The whale is just an animal that’s doing what it’s meant to be doing. The whale is not interested in [Jay]. It’s trying to get a squid, and Austin is in the way,” Duffield said. “The movie makes a very direct correlation, eventually, between Josh Brolin and and the whale, and part of Austin’s journey is making peace with his dad, who is dead at the start of the movie.”

L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios

One of the main threads of the book that drew Duffield to directing the adaptation was the father-son relationship at its core; his own son was 4 at the time of the set visit. In Whalefall, Mitt and Jay didn’t always know how best to communicate with each other; the ocean is where they find common ground.

“The miracle of the book and hopefully of the movie is, when it ends, you primarily are talking about the relationships, and then the whale is third or fourth build, which for a movie that’s set almost entirely inside of a whale feels impossible, but somehow [Kraus] pulls it off,” Duffield said. “As you age up, you start viewing things from different perspectives. I think before I was a dad, I probably would have been firmly in Jay’s point of view, and then now being on the other side of it and having a son — granted, my son just turned 4, so it’s a very different than the relationship between [Jay] and [Mitt] — [I’m] really starting to feel for Brolin’s character, and understand him to some extent.”

Kraus, who grew up in conservative small-town Iowa, leaned into the personal when it came to building the tension of Mitt and Jay’s relationship. His father was a hunter, not as extreme as Mitt, but still an inspiration for the character.

“I’m a product of [where I grew up], which is to say, I have avoided getting therapy. I’m a product of that culture where you don’t express yourself and you don’t show your feelings when it comes to interpersonal things,” Kraus said. “Mitt is a very emotional guy when it comes to the ocean, like he will fight tooth and nail for every living creature in there. He’ll do whatever it takes to protect the ocean. But when it comes to dealing with his son, he’s absolutely clueless. He would be much better at interacting with a whale than he would be his son. And ultimately, Mitt becomes the whale, in a sense, and through the whale, they are able to have the conversation.”

As Jay fights nitrogen narcosis — a condition in divers in which certain gases take on an anesthetic effect in the nervous system, resulting in a kind of high — and the methane in the whale’s stomach, he has flashbacks that help him piece together info he needs for his survival. The memories often involve his father imparting pearls of wisdom, regardless of whether Jay though of them that way at the time.

“The challenge really was, the book has probably 50 flashbacks where it’s constantly hopping back and forth. In the movie, [we had] to take all that information that Jay needs to know scattered across all those flashbacks, and find ways to pack them into vastly fewer flashbacks,” Kraus said. “That was really the biggest challenge.”

A small creative detail further merges Mitt and the whale, who speak as one character in Kraus’ book.

“The whale’s heart is beating, and the stomach is reacting to the beats of the whale’s heart. So that’s sound puppeteering the stomach. There’s water in it, which is moving from that. And then, on top of all of that, just to show how full circle it starts to go, the whale’s heart is Josh Brolin’s heartbeat,” explained Duffield, who came up with the idea. “We’ve recorded Josh’s heartbeat, and then our sound guys made it a whale heartbeat that is playing.”

L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios

This detail also fits in with Kraus’ thematic vision.

“When I came across the concept of a whalefall, which is when a whale dies and its corpse sinks to the bottom of the ocean, and its body, as it decomposes, sets off a shock wave of life, generations of life are born from its remains,” Kraus said. “ I found that very emotional and touching to the idea that when a whale dies, or somebody we know and love dies, that their death sort of begets life, the memory of them, the influence of them. It goes on, and it goes on for generations, and even when I talk about it now, I get goosebumps, it’s just such a beautiful thought.”

Sometimes it takes getting stuck inside a whale to provide some perspective.

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became “The Journey Of Our Lives”
summary: Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra, an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for […]
content:
Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra, an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar.

“I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she?!’ ”

Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother. “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power, there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.”

Watch on Deadline

Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra, the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close, speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.

RELATED: Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release

Cruz’s character, one Nené Romero, performs for the troops in a series of beautifully choreographed, risqué numbers that the boys, far from home, lap up with hunger in their eyes. Los Javis say that Nené was inspired by La Fornarina, a cupletista, a Spanish singer of cuplé songs — bawdy numbers about “sex and drugs,” as Calvo explains it — who performed in theaters in Madrid around the turn of the last century.

Their research included the study of the erotic novels penned by Spanish writer and fashion designer Álvaro Retana, who also wrote lyrics for saucy songs of the type that Cruz performs in La Bola Negra. “They would be singing all over Madrid. They were so funny, they were unleashed — and they thought they were going to be free forever,” says Calvo when we meet in a suite at the swanky Corinthia Hotel during the London Film Festival. “But these singers and their gay friends, all the people in that circle, they were all incarcerated, persecuted, killed or disappeared. They’re forgotten, kind of. So we wanted to bring them back.”

Cruz was already a fan of Los Javis having been gripped by their outrageously captivating 2023 TV drama miniseries La Mesías, a hit for Moviestar+ in Spain, which is now available via Mubi in the UK, Canada Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Australia, and will soon be streaming in France. “They are so talented,” I recall an ecstatic Cruz telling me at the closing-night party in Cannes. “I saw their first television show Veneno as well,” she said, “and now they’ve won the directing prize at Cannes.”

The next time they work with Cruz, says Ambrossi, they plan to create “a whole film around her,” but that will be be after what they hope will be their next feature project, a movie that they claim will be “90% in English.” That movie, whenever it’s made, will likely have a larger budget than Los Javis spent on La Bola Negra. Ambrossi says that its roughly $15 million budget was tight but it’s “big for a Spanish movie.”

The ‘La Bola Negra’ team at the Deadline Studio during the Toronto Film Festival Deadline

With time and the right people on La Bola Negra, Ambrossi adds, “we knew we could do it big. The scope is not always about big landscapes; it’s about how you position people, so you get the sense that it’s bigger, and taking the time to find the right locations, because these are all natural locations.“ They also insisted on making time for proper rehearsals before the 12-week shoot (“Because it’s a deep story and the actors needed time”).

Calvo explains that with the purse strings being so tight they had to find “creative solutions.” They didn’t, for example, have a room in which to shoot all the soldiers having dinner. “We’re like, “OK, then we’ll compose a beautiful shot with everyone outside with tables, and we’ll just imagine they went out to have dinner there,” he explains.

They also turned to “the godfathers of cinema,” as Calvo refers to such legendary directors as Thodōros Angelopoulos (Alexander the Great) and Andrei Tarkovsky (Solaris), who, “with just with a landscape, mist and composing the humans in a proper way” were able to conjure up scenes of movie magic.

Working with the sublime cinematographer Gris Jordana — a frequent collaborator, as are the film’s editor, production designer, hair and makeup designer, costume designer, composer, and many other key creatives — Los Javis sought to bring some of that “godfathers of cinema” magic to their own film. “They’re part of our team,” Amborossi says. “We have been growing together. In every project we learn together. So that’s why the movie is so big, even if the budget is not. They put a lot of effort because it’s a collective experience. It’s like they put in their souls.”

“This is a movie about poetry,” says Calvo, “and there’s also a poetry in images. You don’t have to show everything. You can give something, and the viewer will leave it to their imagination.”

RELATED: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London

Ambrosssi jumps in. “If you don’t have the money, just don’t do it badly,” he says. “Cut it, and someone can talk about it in the next scene. Sometimes we needed a natural beauty location. For example, we didn’t have an office for the general lieutenant featured in the film, so we found an empty space with a nice view — you can see the sea — and we composed it with people and a table and a small framed picture of Franco, and that was it. And that’s not expensive.”

The main point, Calvo believes — as the likes of David Lean found while directing Lawrence of Arabia — is that it was necessary to find intimacy within such an epic story.

Los Javis were helped in that endeavor, Calvo adds, because the film is loosely based on Alberto Conejero’s one-act play La Piedra Oscura, which deals only with the relationship between Rafael and Sebastian, a play that is “so intimate and delicate” that they wanted to expand it into a triptych. ”Like, a big movie,” says Calvo, spreading his arms wide, “and an intimate movie at the same time. You have the fragility and the the war, so it’s about contrast. And it was so nice to create that, because sometimes it’s more difficult to create the relationship of Rafael and Sebastian, with all the tension, than a bombing scene.”

L-R: Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau) in ‘La Bola Negra’ Carla Oset/Netflix

Countless meetings with key creatives were held in pre-production to map out the movie, and the more mistakes they made the better, because it meant they’d go out and get it right during the shoot, says Ambrossi. “It’s like, work, work, work, work, make a mistake, then try again,” he says, smiling. The work, however, didn’t feel like work. ”I always go back and say, ‘Oh, wow, it was the journey of our lives,’” Calvo declares.

RELATED: Netflix Enters Box Office Era With ‘La Bola Negra’; ‘You Can See Everything’ & ‘Musk’ Face Off – Specialty Preview

Ambrossi contends that the film is proudly gay, whether that puts it in a niche box or not; it’s “a gay movie” and “I love to keep it that way,” he says. “I want people to have an experience that is universal. But I don’t want them to miss that it’s gay.”

It’s certainly unusual to see a gay story against the backdrop of war. Calvo cites Tarkovsky’s classic Ivan’s Childhood, Elem Klimov’s harrowing Come and See and Francis Ford Coppola’s Apocalypse Now as being amongst his favorite war movies. “So, I have those references,” he says, “but my emotion is another thing, and my sensitivity is what we’re portraying. Why shouldn’t I make a movie the same way the people that made war movies I admire made, but telling my own story and using my own feelings? For me, it was natural to just talk about myself through my references. And why can’t we have it all?”

Ambrossi laughs. “It’s great that we told everyone it is a gay film with — mostly — gay actors portraying gay characters, directed by gay people about the queer experience, and it’s hitting the No. 1 spot at the box office every single night in Spain. I like that. I think it’s cool, because it really represents two things; one, that the world is going in a direction that we are not always aware, and also that the industry has to understand that gay stories are not niche.”

La Bola Negra is a starting point for the next conversation, Ambrosssi continues, and that “once we try, once we prove them wrong, then we can have the conversation about universal stories. But we had to tell them, ‘You don’t have to change the lead and put a straight star in it to get the audience.’ They just go, “Ah, it’s a gay story.’”

Were they pressured in any way to compromise? “They don’t even try to do it with us, because we write, direct and produce. It’s our movie,” Ambrossi responds with gusto. He allows, however, that they encountered difficulties making the 2020 miniseries Veneno. “It was a show with trans actresses, and everyone was like, ‘You won’t find that many trans actresses to put in a show in Spain.’ And we were like, ‘We’ll do it.’ And we did.”

RELATED: ‘La Bola Negra’s Los Javis On Completing The Final Work Of Gay Poet “Murdered By Fascism” In 1936 Spain — Toronto Studio

During their travels promoting the movie — at Cannes (where Los Javis shared the best director prize with Fatherland’s Pawel Pawlikowski), Telluride, Toronto (where it won the People’s Choice Award for best film), San Sebastián (where the film was honored with the festival’s Audience Award) and here in London — the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. “The feedback from non-gay people, non-LGBTQ people, is the same. This idea of wanting to be yourself, being rejected, a lot of women get that. It gets everyone. At some point, it’s about family, about motherhood, about brotherhood, about friendship. It’s a war movie. It’s about being different, but it’s about art and the power of art.”

Calvo, listening intently, jumps in, pointing out that the film is “about understanding and seeing the other as a human being. Which is, I think, important.”

xxx

When it came to casting the male leads, they chose singer-musician Guitarricadelafuente because they were drawn to the “magnetism, the sadness” in his eyes. “He had to be the eyes of the viewer,” says Calvo, “and he has eyes that you can rely on, and he had this shyness, but also this bravery, this strength, but then this subtleness. We just knew it was for him.”

Ambrossi, meanwhile, hails Bernardeau (Elite) as being “one of the best of his generation.” “We needed his technique,” he explains, “because Guitarricadelafuente is new, so we needed the balance to play off each other.” The same goes for González. “He’s so flamboyant and fun in real life,” Ambrossi says. “Here, he’s doing a job that you cannot imagine. If you were to meet him, you would be like, ‘Are you the same person?’”

Indeed, I spoke with González at a soirée following a special screening of La Bola Negra at Tate Modern, and he was an absolute hoot. He vowed to do anything for the film “with its big black balls.” My eyes widened at that remark and our dirty laughter nearly got us turned outta the party.

As for Carlos, they were looking for Andalusian guys, and the moment they saw Quifes’ audition, they shut down the search.

The roles played by Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau are the heart of the film, providing its most tender, heartfelt moments. They met for the first time at rehearsals, where Guitarricadelfuente, who’d never acted before, says he felt “100 percent safe” because he was working opposite a professional actor. “It was a very special moment meeting Miguel,” he says.

Having someone like Miguel “really helped me out in this in this journey,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “There was something very special about the way that our characters grew up together, and the development of that intimacy, that way of nonverbal communication, those gestures that communicated so much. I’m grateful for the time that we spent at that room rehearsing.”

Los Javis were “democratic with us,” he notes, because “they let us express ourselves freely, and if there was maybe sometimes in the dialogue something that maybe didn’t resound that much in ourselves, they would say, ‘What would you say? What would you do?’ They let us roll on and magical things happened.”

Were they able to improvise? Bernardeau shakes his head and notes that it wasn’t so much improvisation because of how much thought went into every scene, what with how the three stories intertwine. “You need to be careful with what you change. There’s a lot of detail, so you cannot improvise. But they were very free with us in changing smaller stuff. I did feel very free to try different ways and paths into the scenes.”

The ‘La Bola Negra’ team on the red carpet in Cannes Kate Green/Getty Images

I remember covering the film’s ecstatic 20-minute ovation at Cannes in the Grand Théâtre Lumière and watching the faces of this new generation of filmmakers and actors. Bernardeau was holding back tears. “I knew that once I start crying I would not stop,” he admits.

In front of him, he recalls, was the festival’s camera team “and Tilda Swinton clapping and looking at us.” Swinton introduced Bernardeau to her agent Christian Hodell, chief executive of Hamilton Hodell, who now represents him. Now the actor will soon be moving from Spain to live in London.

Guitarricadelafuente remembers looking up to the Lumière’s second tier to see so many young people who’d clearly connected with the film: “That made me feel as if we were at a concert.” He notes that he’s been astonished by how audiences in Spain have flocked to see the picture. Los Javis were known to young people, he says. “Like, there are people in my family that haven’t been to the cinema in 10 years. They feel like they’re missing out on something, because there’s been like a consensus between everybody to see it. It’s not a film about civil war, it’s not a film about Lorca. It’s is a film about life.”

It sure is.

Culturally, Spain’s on a roll. Singer-songwriter Rosalía took the International Artist of the Year at the Brit Awards; La Bola Negra won a major prize at Cannes; and, of course, Spain won the World Cup. Calvo beams a full-wattage smile. “We’re just getting out there.”

Netflix releases the film in theaters Friday in New York City and Los Angeles ahead of a wider release over coming weeks before debuting on streaming in the U.S. and Canada on December 2. Altitude opens the film in the UK on November 6.

title: ‘Crystal Lake’s Gwendolyn Sundstrom On Grace’s Friendship With Jason, “Learning A Lot” From Linda Cardellini & That Killer Twist
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details about Peacock’s series Crystal Lake. While Crystal Lake revisits several familiar locals from the Friday the 13th franchise, Gwendolyn Sundstrom brings a fresh role to the slasher prequel series. Now available to stream on Peacock, Sundstrom told Deadline that Jason Voorhees’ (Callum Vinson) childhood friend Grace has been her […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details about Peacock‘s series Crystal Lake.

While Crystal Lake revisits several familiar locals from the Friday the 13th franchise, Gwendolyn Sundstrom brings a fresh role to the slasher prequel series.

Now available to stream on Peacock, Sundstrom told Deadline that Jason Voorhees’ (Callum Vinson) childhood friend Grace has been her “favorite character so far” to play, filming the Brad Caleb Kane series in New Jersey when she was only 13.

“It was fun, ’cause in real life I don’t really relate to Grace that much, but it was fun to try and find things from my life that I could put into Grace and really play her,” explained Sundstrom. “But I had a great day every day on set, it was amazing.”

Watch on Deadline

As the series recounts the accidental drowning of young Jason that was first mentioned in the original 1980 movie, the opening scene of the first episode reveals Grace throwing a bully’s ball out into the lake after he was teasing Jason. While counselors Claudette (Danielle Kotch) and Barry (Phoenix Parnevik) sneak off to hook up, Jason goes after the ball, only to drown in the depths of Crystal Lake.

Jason and Grace’s endearing adolescent friendship continues to play out through flashbacks as she struggles to mourn his death amid the usual complications of growing up.

“I think it was really helpful that Callum and I had really good chemistry in real life too, but I think building Grace as a character, she’s also kind of an underdog,” explained Sundstrom. “She also doesn’t have very many friends, so I think we could kind of work off each other and portray that kind of character cause we’re so similar.”

With nowhere to put her maternal love after the loss of her son Jason, Pam Voorhees (Linda Cardellini) soon takes an interest in Grace, whose own mom appears to be abusive and neglectful.

“I loved working with Linda. She was so nice,” Sundstrom said. “I definitely learned a lot from her. I think when Pam takes on kind of this maternal role, I think that’s something Grace, first of all, isn’t really used to, and also doesn’t really want. I think she’s trying to push Pam away, and Pam only wants to get even closer and even more protective, and I think that’s kind of a conflict that the two characters have.”

After finding a new “family” in a pack of traveling hippies, Grace ends up on a drug trip that results in a deconstruction of the very first kill in the Friday the 13th franchise. But instead of Pam, it’s revealed that Grace was the person to kill Claudette and Barry in that first-person POV sequence.

Callum Vinson as Jason Voorhees and Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in ‘Crystal Lake’

“I had a lot of fun with that scene,” said Sundstrom. “I definitely like filming more dramatic, gritty, emotional things, so that was really fun for me.”

And while diehard fans of the franchise might not be down with the retcon of such an iconic kill scene, Kane explained he wanted to “blow people’s minds” and “give the audience something different to chew on.”

“You have to re-contextualize it, and you want a shock,” explained Kane. “We come to these movies for the rollercoaster ride of it, we come to these movies for the jaw-drop of it. If you think you know everything from the movie coming into the TV series, and then we just go, ‘yeah, it’s exactly as you thought it was,’ that’s no fun.”

Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees and Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in ‘Crystal Lake’

Now streaming on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. As two strangers begin digging into her mysterious past, Pam goes to murderous lengths to keep her secrets buried and find her son, whom she’s convinced is still alive after his body was never recovered.

title: Miley Cyrus Setlist: Every Song Played at ‘Bass Persuades – Live at the Hollywood Bowl’ (UPDATING LIVE)
summary: Miley Cyrus kicked off her “Miley: Bass Persuades – Live at the Hollywood Bowl” shows on Friday night at the famed Los Angeles venue, giving her first headlining performance in years. The pop star, who is going mononomously as just Miley for this era, announced this pair of Friday and Sunday shows in early September […]
content:
Miley Cyrus kicked off her “Miley: Bass Persuades – Live at the Hollywood Bowl” shows on Friday night at the famed Los Angeles venue, giving her first headlining performance in years.

The pop star, who is going mononomously as just Miley for this era, announced this pair of Friday and Sunday shows in early September along with the news that her new album, “Bass Persuades,” would be released on September 18 via Atlantic Records. “It’s been a while,” said Cyrus of the shows at the time on Instagram. “The Hollywood Bowl is my favorite place to experience music and see my favorite artists. I’ve sat in those seats many times, but I’ve never taken the stage. LA is my heart and I’m bringing it home. See you there. ❤️ Miley.”

Indeed, it has been a while since Cyrus graced the stage as a headliner outside of festivals. The closest approximation was a performance earlier this year at the taping for the “Hannah Montana” 20th anniversary special, and before that with “Spotify’s Billions Club Live” in Paris last June for a select group of fans. The month before that, she debuted her new album “Something Beautiful” with a fan-only TikTok event at Los Angeles’ Chateau Marmont. The last time she did a full-fledged tour was for “Bangerz” in 2014.

Popular on Variety

Cyrus has been open about her decision not to tour, telling British Vogue in 2023 that after the “Bangerz” tour, she decided to take a break from it. “It’s been a minute,” she said at the time. After the last [headline arena] show I did [in 2014], I kind of looked at it as more of a question. And I can’t. Not only ‘can’t,’ because can’t is your capability, but my desire. Do I want to live my life for anyone else’s pleasure or fulfillment other than my own?”

Last month, Cyrus clarified her stance on live performances during an interview with Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, explaining that she’d be more open to doing residencies. “This is the ultimate dress rehearsal,” she said of her Bowl shows. “I’ve learned now through the queue that my calculations are correct and people will come to me. I don’t need to drive to you. Proven, that was a quick test. I win. So this is perfect because people like to see me perform and I like to sleep in my marshmallow bed so we can both be happy.”
