title: Paul Bettany Says He and Johnny Depp ‘Hadn’t Spoken’ in Years When Their Texts Were Read During Libel Trial: ‘I Was Being Painted As This Close Friend’
summary: Paul Bettany opened up in a recent interview with The Times about the public’s misconception of his relationship with Johnny Depp after text messages between the two actors were used in court during Depp’s libel lawsuit against The Sun. “I hadn’t spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven’t spoken to him […]
content:
Paul Bettany opened up in a recent interview with The Times about the public’s misconception of his relationship with Johnny Depp after text messages between the two actors were used in court during Depp’s libel lawsuit against The Sun.

“I hadn’t spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven’t spoken to him since. I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn’t spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the shit two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd,” Paul told the publication.

Popular on Variety

“So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me,” he continued. “I’ve been married 23 years and, for what I do, I live an incredibly quiet life. Everybody kind of thought this is probably a nothing burger – and left it alone.”

In 2013, a controversial text exchange between Depp and Bettany became public when it was read during a Feb. 2020 trial hearing. “Let’s burn Amber!!!” wrote Depp, to which Bettany responded: “Having thought it through I don’t think we should burn Amber – she’s delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I’m not sure she’s a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments ­– we do a drowning test. Thoughts?” Depp responded that they should “drown her before we burn her!!! I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she’s dead.”

The two actors worked together on multiple films, including 2010’s “The Tourist,” 2014’s “Transcendence” and 2015’s “Mortdecai.”

Depp initially sued News Group Newspapers (NGN) (which publishes The Sun) for libel after an article was published by the publication titled “Gone Potty – How can JK Rowling be ‘genuinely happy’ casting wife beater Johnny Depp in the new ‘Fantastic Beasts’ film?” Depp alleged that the article “caused serious harm to (his) personal and professional reputation” and also caused him “significant distress and embarrassment.” In 2020, Judge Andrew Nicol ruled against Depp.

title: ‘Klara and the Sun’ Review: There’s No Life — Intelligent, Artificial or Otherwise — in Taika Waititi’s Calamitous Android Fantasy
summary: Adapting a solemnly complex, questioning novel as a cockeyed child’s-eye comedy worked once before for Taika Waititi — which is to say that “Jojo Rabbit,” his crass, mawkish “anti-hate satire” about a Hitler Youth member’s personal and political awakening, won him an Oscar and grossed nearly $100 million, in spite of its manifold artistic and […]
content:
Adapting a solemnly complex, questioning novel as a cockeyed child’s-eye comedy worked once before for Taika Waititi — which is to say that “Jojo Rabbit,” his crass, mawkish “anti-hate satire” about a Hitler Youth member’s personal and political awakening, won him an Oscar and grossed nearly $100 million, in spite of its manifold artistic and ethical shortcomings. But even that film’s many defenders are unlikely to be moved in sizable numbers by his twee, pulseless fantasy “Klara and the Sun” — such a hopeless mismatch of filmmaker and source material, it appears to be have been assembled as a kind of perverse defy-the-odds challenge. Whether there was ever a successful movie to be made of Kazuo Ishiguro’s finespun, melancholic, almost brittly interior study of android consciousness is open to question, but Waititi should reasonably be in the bottom tier of auteurs you’d enlist to try, maybe just ahead of Baz Luhrmann, but a notch below Quentin Tarantino.

Published in 2021, “Klara and the Sun” is a confidently delicate novel, skirting slightness — as well as a bit of thematic recycling — in the way that a recent Nobel laureate can afford to do. It reads as something of a companion piece to “Never Let Me Go,” Ishiguro’s sober, mournful study of a human clone reflecting on her place in a hostile universe; swap in AI robots for clones, and “Klara” plows much the same field. “Never Let Me Go” got a fitting adaptation in Mark Romanek’s chilly, elegant 2010 drama of the same title; that film couldn’t have been more stylistically coordinated to the author’s voice, and you’d hardly expect the director of “What We Do in the Shadows” and two “Thor” movies to take the same approach.

Popular on Variety

But from the very first tinkly strains of Michael Giacchino’s overbearingly precious score, it’s obvious that moist-eyed whimsy is an ill-chosen path; the filmmaker’s variously cutesy, kooky affectations fight the stoic sadness of Ishiguro’s storytelling at every turn. (The author takes an executive producer credit, and one would give several pennies for his thoughts.) Having premiered at London after being conspicuously absent from September’s season-launching festivals, “Klara and the Sun” will open in theaters on October 23, and looks to have all the cultural staying power of a standard ChatGPT conversation — with any audiences that do turn up likely to be nonplussed by a fable that’s pitched too juvenile for adults, and way too dull for children.

The comedy is broadest, and therefore most strikingly unfunny, in an opening section that plays as a ghastly dystopian update of “Annie” — introducing Ortega’s perma-sparkly Klara as one of several lonely humanoid AFs (artificial friends) awaiting human purchase in a store managed in tough-love fashion by a hard-mugging Natasha Lyonne. We are some way into a post-Third World War future where the internet has collapsed and people are largely housebound; the wealthy buy AFs to keep their isolated, unsocialized children company. Not that you get much sense of this reality — or any reality at all, really — from Michael Berlucchi’s textureless, aggressively gold-filtered lensing or Ra Vincent’s daintily retro production design, least of all in Lyonne’s midcentury-style Friend Store: Humanity already appears to be occupying a floaty simulacrum of the way things were.

Ortega, button-cute amid the eeriness of everything else, never bursts into a rendition of “Tomorrow,” but she does open the film with a winsome monologue thanking the sun for her existence — she is solar-powered, after all — and praying to the godly orb for a loving buyer, so close enough. She finally gets her wish when sullen teen Josie (promising British talent Mia Tharia, recently seen in “The Education of Jane Cumming”) spots her in the shop window, is beguiled by her visible quirkiness (she stands on one leg, for starters) and persuades her uptight mother Chrissy (Amy Adams, as prim and hard as the string of pearls around her neck) to bring the robot girl home to their isolated and wholly unbelievable Midwest-ish farmhouse.

There, Klara’s attempts to fit into a dysfunctional human household yield some halting fish-out-of-water hijinks, as she rubs both Chrissy and brusque Kiwi housekeeper Melania (Rachel House) the wrong way, while enchanting Josie with her open heart and ingenuous curiosity. But here, the film’s tonal balance begins tipping toward tragedy, over which Waititi has no more command than its flatlining comedy: Josie, it emerges, has a life-threatening illness, which puts Klara in a rather more crucial position in the family than anyone initially dared to admit. And so the script — written by Waititi with TV vet Dahvi Waller (“Mrs. America”) in her first big-screen credit — blunders into existential explorations of artificial life and afterlife that any number of recent, comparably lo-fi works, from “Ex Machina” to “Marjorie Prime” to “Her” to “Robot Dreams,” have probed with more nuance and wit.

Ortega, innately charismatic as ever, tries to make Klara enough of a life force to give these conflicts and considerations some weight, but is defeated by the one-note writing of her character as a relentlessly hopeful, Pollyanna-esque naif. The story’s later stages hinge on Klara’s faltering, increasingly shattered digital memory, but save for some glitching, strikingly pixelated graphics, we never get a vivid sense of how she actually sees the world. Not that her human counterparts feel any richer or realer, with Adams particularly script-trapped as the stiffly guarded Chrissy, who shoulders enough grief, both lingering and preemptive, to match the actor’s “Arrival” character, yet never gets to give it satisfying expression.

Ishiguro’s novel was plainspoken in its pathos, as has always been the author’s gift: His characters carry the disappointments and more crushing losses of their lives as part of their everyday routine, often acknowledging and dismissing them in the same simple sentence. Waititi’s writing, even in its best vehicles, has no such piercing gift. He aims to smuggle feeling in through irony and farce, intrusions that here curdle unhappily with the heartsore earnestness of the source. If there were any more life to the filmmaking, this tension could least be interesting, but the results are both perky and inert, unreal but entirely unmoored in time and space. As desperate to be loved as its beaming heroine, but far more knowingly so, Waititi’s “Klara and the Sun” is a warmly worded Hallmark card from an artificial friend.

title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Pulls Val Chmerkovskiy After ‘Inappropriate’ Carrie Ann Inaba Slap Joke: ‘The Well-Being’ of Our Staff Is ‘Non-Negotiable’
summary: “Dancing With the Stars” is benching Val Chmerkovskiy after his recent joke about judge Carrie Ann Inaba. “The well-being of everyone who works on ‘Dancing with the Stars’ is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show,” BBC Studios said in […]
content:
“Dancing With the Stars” is benching Val Chmerkovskiy after his recent joke about judge Carrie Ann Inaba.

“The well-being of everyone who works on ‘Dancing with the Stars’ is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show,” BBC Studios said in a statement on Saturday. “As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.”

Chmerkovskiy shared a statement of his own following the announcement that he will not be in the ballroom, writing on Instagram, “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”

Popular on Variety

He continued, “The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in. Please send Carrie Ann, Jenna, and the whole DWTS family lots of love during Dedication Night. I’ll be watching and cheering everyone on!!”

Disney

For context, during the Oct. 13 episode of “Dancing With the Stars,” judge Carrie Ann Inaba critiqued Jenna Johnson (who is married to Chmerkovskiy) for having a lift in her routine, and read her the definition of said lift. Afterward, Chmerkovskiy posted to his TikTok story, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” seemingly referencing Will Smith slapping Chris Rock at the 2022 Oscars, after saying, “Keep my wife’s name out of your fucking mouth.”

The post was quickly deleted, but Inaba saw it and commented on her own Instagram, thanking the media for alerting her to his remark.

Chmerkovskiy, who has appeared on “Dancing With the Stars” since the second season, later apologized to Inaba and the viewers he upset, posting the following message on his Instagram Story on Thursday: “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post. I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family. I recognize that l am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who l am, and who I want to be for you all. I am truly sorry to Carrie Ann, and everyone who I hurt with my careless post. I will do better moving forward.”

Jenna Dewan, Chermkovskiy’s partner, will still dance at dedication week, Variety confirms, and will be paired with Alan Bersten, who was eliminated in week three. Dewan will be dancing a Viennese waltz to “Unchained Melody,” dedicated to her mother.

“Jenna Dewan is aware and has continued to be a true professional and respectful of the process,” the source tells Variety. “Jenna is a beloved part of the ‘Dancing with the Stars’ family, and we are grateful for the joy and positivity she brings to the show.”

During Season 34, Inaba opened up to Variety about the criticism and constant booing she receives in the ballroom — something the male judges, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli, do not.

“It used to really affect me. I have been targeted with this kind of negativity since the show began, back when we had chat rooms. I remember seeing some horrible words written about me, and I was shocked,” she shared. “Sometimes the things they say are cruel, and that has affected me. It’s made me scared. It’s not so much that I get hurt as I get afraid, because it feels like they’re attacking me verbally, so I shrink down a little during the season, especially after week five or six.”

title: Harry Styles ‘Together, Together’ Tour Doc Coming From John Wilson, Universal Pictures Content Group (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Harry Styles has invited one of the buzziest documentary filmmakers on the market behind the curtain of his historic Madison Square Garden residency. John Wilson, the director behind indie box-office surprise “The History of Concrete” and HBO’s “How To with John Wilson,” has been rolling cameras on Styles at MSG since August, two sources with […]
content:
Harry Styles has invited one of the buzziest documentary filmmakers on the market behind the curtain of his historic Madison Square Garden residency.

John Wilson, the director behind indie box-office surprise “The History of Concrete” and HBO’s “How To with John Wilson,” has been rolling cameras on Styles at MSG since August, two sources with knowledge of the project said.

Wilson is capturing footage for a doc expected to be a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world. One source described it as featuring authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.

Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles produced the project. UPCG will own global rights to the film. Though distribution plans are still being worked out, insiders said the doc may be positioned for a theatrical release via Universal.

Popular on Variety

Styles is currently in the midst of the largest single-engagement residency ever at MSG, part of his “Together, Together” tour. It began in late August and is set to run through the end of October. The show has created plenty of viral moments and provided ample short-shorts. Reps for the singer, Wilson, and Universal had no immediate comment. Social media lit up over the weekend thanks to a fan-snapped photo of Wilson trailing styles with a camera.

Wilson’s got a knack for interrogating the mundane, as well as highlighting the absurdity of humans and the levers that make them work. He may seem an out-of-the-box choice for a glossy pop music documentary, but not if you’re paying attention to current sensibilities. Look at Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, whose Elizabeth Holmes project “You Can See Everything” is burning up the specialty box office this weekend. Fielder started in the realm of absurdist comedy, and with the Holmes project moves into a world of watercooler high crimes and compelling fourth-wall breaking. Billie Eilish recruited “Titanic ” and “Avatar” mastermind James Cameron to direct her own theatrical concert opus “Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour,” which was released in theaters this summer.

Wilson began his career directing music videos. He is repped by UTA.

title: ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Suspends Val Chmerkovskiy For TikTok Referencing Will Smith Oscar Moment; Dancer Responds, “Instinct Was To Defend My Wife”
summary: UDPATED with Chmerkovskiy response: Val Chmerkovskiy is being suspended from Dancing with the Stars for a week after he posted a controversial TikTok message that seemed to reference Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap. In a statement released today, producer BBC Studios said, “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing with the Stars is non-negotiable. […]
content:
UDPATED with Chmerkovskiy response: Val Chmerkovskiy is being suspended from Dancing with the Stars for a week after he posted a controversial TikTok message that seemed to reference Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap.

In a statement released today, producer BBC Studios said, “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing with the Stars is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.”

Chmerkovskiy sparked the controversy the day after the show’s first “Super Bowl Night,” during which judge Carrie Ann Inaba offered a withering critique of the performance of Chmerkovskiy’s wife, DWTS dance pro Jenna Johnson. Wrote Chmerkovskiy in the since-deleted post, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.”

In a response to the suspension, Chmerkovskiy issued a statement through his rep, acknowledging his “poor decision” and “bad judgment,” saying he hadn’t thought through his TikTok comment before posting.

Watch on Deadline

Chmerkovskiy’s statement reads: “Hi everyone. As you may have seen in the news, I won’t be in the ballroom this week.

“In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.

“The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in.

“Please send Carrie Ann, Jenna, and the whole DWTS family lots of love during Dedication Night. I’ll be watching and cheering everyone on!!”

Chmerkovskiy’s scrutinized post came in response to Inaba’s on-air critique of a lift move made by Johnson, in which she read the definition of a lift and suggested Johnson should know better.

The Fresh Prince comment referred, unintentionally or not, to the infamous 2022 Oscar-night moment when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock across the face after the latter made a joke about Smith’s wife Jada Pinkett Smith. Chmerkovskiy’s TikTok comment was widely interpreted to suggest, however jokingly, that he had considered taking action similar to Smith’s, though the dancer later said he hadn’t thought that far.

In any case, the joke was apparently lost on Inaba, who on Thursday posted a message on Instagram saying, “So this is what we are doing now?” Her post showed photos of Chmerkovskiy and Smith, and in the text of her message she thanked the New York Post and Entertainment Weekly “for bringing this to my attention.” (See it below.)

After he posted the TikTok, Chmerkovskiy apologized, writing on Instagram, “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post. I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family. I should have never made the reference that I did and I deeply regret it. I recognize that I am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who I am, and who I want to be for you all.”

Chmerkovskiy’s celebrity partner Jenna Dewan is apparently aware of the pro’s temporary suspension and will dance with pro Alan Bersten next week in a performance dedicated to her mother.

title: Paul McCartney Was Concerned Paul Mescal Is “Markedly Shorter” Than ‘The Beatles’ Co-Stars
summary: As Beatles fans are transported back to Abbey Road for Sam Mendes’ upcoming biopic, Paul McCartney has some thoughts on the casting. The Beatles alum said he was concerned that Paul Mescal looks “markedly shorter” compared to his co-stars, and he even reached out to Mendes about it, but doesn’t know how the director is […]
content:
As Beatles fans are transported back to Abbey Road for Sam Mendes‘ upcoming biopic, Paul McCartney has some thoughts on the casting.

The Beatles alum said he was concerned that Paul Mescal looks “markedly shorter” compared to his co-stars, and he even reached out to Mendes about it, but doesn’t know how the director is “gonna deal with it” in the four-film cinematic event.

“Yeah, and guess what? He’s smaller than the guy who’s playing John [Lennon],” explained McCartney on the Good Hang with Amy Poehler podcast. “Sam Mendes is making the film. I heard Sam Mendes is making the film. I said, ‘Sam, I’ve got just one thing that I need to say to you. Paul’s a bit smaller.'”

After the movies’ cast re-created the iconic Abbey Road (1969) album cover while filming in London back in August, McCartney said his concerns worsened.

Watch on Deadline

“So, I don’t know how Sam’s gonna deal with it, but he sent me a picture, a still from the filming they were doing,” he recalled. “They were crossing the Abbey Road crossing, and the Paul character is markedly smaller.”

McCartney continued, “So, I texted him, ‘Sam! Smaller! Don’t do this! You said you wouldn’t do it.’ He said, ‘No, it’s ok. It’s just the stride.’ And he sent me another one where they were equal.”

Last February, Deadline exclusively revealed that Mendes is set to direct each installment of The Beatles — A Four-Film Cinematic Event, through his Neal Street Productions and Sony Pictures Entertainment. Each film will connect, telling the band’s story from each member’s point of view.

The film has since cast Mescal as Paul McCartney, Joseph Quinn as George Harrison, Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr and Harris Dickinson as John Lennon.

title: Donald Trump Finally Arrives On ‘SNL UK’ In Job Swap Cold Open With Andy Burnham & Volodymyr Zelenskyy
summary: Donald Trump has spent some time in the UK these past few years but tonight he finally made his debut on Saturday Night Live UK. James Austin Johnson brought his POTUS to Sky’s hit UK version of the NBC show in a job swap cold open alongside Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) and Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Freddie […]
content:
Donald Trump has spent some time in the UK these past few years but tonight he finally made his debut on Saturday Night Live UK.

James Austin Johnson brought his POTUS to Sky’s hit UK version of the NBC show in a job swap cold open alongside Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) and Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Freddie Meredith).

“I will raise with Trump at the first opportunity,” said Burnham to Zelenskyy over issues the Ukrainian leader had been having in his home country, at which point Trump appeared.

“You say my name and I appear,” said Trump. “I got the idea from my very close friend Beetlejuice, the great Beetlejuice. It’s one of the two reasons I like him. The other is that he’s a sex pest… It’s alleged, they can’t prove that stuff.”

Trump went on to give Burnham an offer, that they do a job swap. “It’s an awful job,” he said of being President of the U.S. “It’s a terrible place full of disgusting people. I don’t know why I do it.”

Watch on Deadline

Trump went on to poke fun at big UK news stories including Manchester City soccer club’s controversy, the small boats crisis and the recent mauling to death of a man by a tiger.

He also had some comedy reserved for an acquaintance, Russell Brand, who is currently on trial for rape and sexual assault.

“I’m in town to see my favorite comedian. He’s performing live at the High Court in the role of defendant.”

Before signing off, he said British comedy is in a “bad situation” because SNL UK “doesn’t have anyone who can play Trump.” (You can watch the sketch below.)

Austin Johnson has been playing Trump on SNL for five years, having replaced Alec Baldwin.

Trump has been referenced plenty in SNL UK but hadn’t appeared until tonight.

James Norton is hosting tonight’s SNL UK, the fifth episode of the first half of Season 2. Music comes from The Streets. Next week, this tranche of Season 2 episodes will conclude with Cynthia Erivo.

All of SNL UK’s cast members have returned for Season 2, including Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Dring, Fouracres, Ania Magliano, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Shep, Emma Sidi and Paddy Young, with James Meredith making his debut.

SNL UK is produced by Universal Television Alternative Studio’s UK production team and Broadway Video. Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer. James Longman is lead producer.

title: ‘Street Fighter’s Orville Peck Tried To “Orchestrate” Kylie Minogue Cameo: “Guys, I Can Text Her”
summary: More than 30 years later after she blew away Street Fighter fans as bazooka-toting Cammy, Kylie Minogue nearly returned for a cameo in the latest feature adaptation. The 2x Grammy-winning Australian pop icon’s friend and collaborator Orville Peck, who stars as Vega in the newly released Paramount video game movie, revealed that he “was trying […]
content:
More than 30 years later after she blew away Street Fighter fans as bazooka-toting Cammy, Kylie Minogue nearly returned for a cameo in the latest feature adaptation.

The 2x Grammy-winning Australian pop icon’s friend and collaborator Orville Peck, who stars as Vega in the newly released Paramount video game movie, revealed that he “was trying to orchestrate” her return, but scheduling conflicts ultimately stood in the way.

“They were trying to get Kylie to do a cameo in our Street Fighter,” he told Queerty. “They were having a hard time getting ahold of her or whatever, and I was like, ‘Guys, I can text her.’ So, I was trying to orchestrate this whole thing, and it didn’t work out with timing. She was gonna be so down to do it.”

Peck added, “But of course, I immediately told Kylie when I got cast. She told me how filming their Street Fighter was one of the most fun experiences of her life, and she was like, ‘I’m so excited for you to get to do that.'”

Watch on Deadline

The Mule artist said he’s “still trying to orchestrate” a meeting between Minogue and Mel Jarnson, who plays Cammy in the Kitao Sakurai-helmed adaptation of the Capcom game.

@queerty This week, Orville Peck makes the jump from country crooner to action star in Street Fighter. But he’s not the first icon of music to do so: Back in 1994, his friend & collaborator Kylie Minogue starred in the original big-screen adaptation of the video game, and he says he texted her immediately when he got the part. And he’s got some tea, too: Apparently they tried to get Kylie to make a cameo in this Street Fighter! While Orville reveals she was “so down to do it,” timing just didn’t align, but he’s still hoping to orchestrate a photo op with his movie’s Cammy—actress Mel Jarnson—or maybe leave the door open for something in a potential sequel. Regardless, Kylie told Orville filming the ‘94 Street Fighter was “one of the most fun experiences of her life,” and it sounds like he felt the same this go-around, especially because he was emboldened to bring his full self to the project, leaning into queer energy to his portrayal of the masked character Vega. For our full conversation with @orvillepeck about @streetfightermovie, his latest album MULE and more, head to the link in our bio. @kylieminogue queerty #orvillepeck #streetfighter #streetfightermovie #kylieminogue ♬ original sound – Queerty* – Queerty*

“Maybe the sequel, we’ll see,” teased Peck of a potential Minogue cameo.

In 2024, Peck featured Minogue and Diplo on his song “Midnight Ride”, released as a single on his third studio album Stampede.

title: Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’
summary: Quentin Tarantino has long said he’ll be retiring after his 10th feature film, but fans shouldn’t worry yet. While the “Pulp Fiction” director confirmed he’d finished penning the script for his final project, he won’t be getting much further with it until his newly opened play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” closes. Tarantino made the statement on […]
content:
Quentin Tarantino has long said he’ll be retiring after his 10th feature film, but fans shouldn’t worry yet. While the “Pulp Fiction” director confirmed he’d finished penning the script for his final project, he won’t be getting much further with it until his newly opened play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” closes.

Tarantino made the statement on a recent episode of “The Graham Norton Show,” where he joined the host alongside fellow guests Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan. It was his first appearance on the show in more than a decade.

“I’ve written a script that I really like, but I want to do the play and see who I am; then I’ll then go back and spend time with my family and live a little and then see what I want to do,” Tarantino said.

Popular on Variety

He also gave audiences more insight into “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which he said started as a screenplay before the director realized “it really worked as a play.” “I think it will be thrilling,” he said.

Starring Sacha Baron Cohen, “The Popinjay Cavalier” will open at London’s Phoenix Theatre next March, following previews in late Feb. The play, described as a “swashbuckling comedy,” is set to run for three months, closing on June 13. “I’m keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out,” Tarantino said in a statement when the show was announced.

Tarantino’s most recent release remains “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which came out in 2019 and starred Brad Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Margaret Qualley and more. Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor that year, as did Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for best production design. Tarantino was also nominated for best picture and best director, while DiCaprio was nominated for best actor.

title: James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’
summary: James McAvoy has starred in films including “Speak No Evil,” “Atonement” and “X-Men: First Class,” but he recently revealed the “only” film he still consistently receives residuals from is M. Night Shyamalan’s 2016 horror “Split.” “You get the odd check for, you know, a couple 100 quid here or sometimes you get checks for, like, […]
content:
James McAvoy has starred in films including “Speak No Evil,” “Atonement” and “X-Men: First Class,” but he recently revealed the “only” film he still consistently receives residuals from is M. Night Shyamalan’s 2016 horror “Split.”

“You get the odd check for, you know, a couple 100 quid here or sometimes you get checks for, like, 25 cents and you’re like, ‘It literally costs more to post this than it did for me to cash it,’” McAvoy said during a recent episode of the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “But the only one that really consistently pays me is ‘Split.’”

“I think it was made for like $6 million or something like that? And let’s say they spent 30 advertising it. In our first weekend, we made 40, so we were in profit,” McAvoy continued. “Our first residual check came at the end of the first weekend. It was bonkers.”

Popular on Variety

In “Split,” three girls are kidnapped by a man with a diagnosed 23 distinct personalities (McAvoy). “They must try to escape before the apparent emergence of a frightful new 24th,” per the film’s official description. Anya Taylor-Joy, Haley Lu Richardson and Jessica Sula starred alongside McAvoy. The film, which cost just $6 million to make, went on to gross $138.29 million domestically and $140.16 million internationally for a $278.45 million worldwide total.

McAvoy also spoke about Shyamalan and his experience working with the director.

“I very consciously took from many of the directors that I worked with, and subconsciously as well, but the thing I took away from him is his preparedness,” McAvoy said. “He made that film, and [sequel] ‘Glass,’ on incredibly modest budgets, and very focused on how he would maximize his day and maximize his shots and maximize what he got out of the story by just being incredibly well-prepared and being able to share that and communicate that with the crew.”

title: Here’s Where to Buy New York Knicks Home Opener Tickets at Madison Square Garden Online
summary: With the start of the NBA only a few days away, the hottest ticket in New York City is to the Knicks home opener at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Since winning the NBA Finals against the San Antonio Spurs back in June, the Knicks have become the toast of New York with […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

With the start of the NBA only a few days away, the hottest ticket in New York City is to the Knicks home opener at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Since winning the NBA Finals against the San Antonio Spurs back in June, the Knicks have become the toast of New York with good vibes around the city, massive TV ratings and even Jalen Brunson hosting the premiere episode of “Saturday Night Live.”

The home opener for the Knicks just isn’t the first game of the 2026-2027 season, but it’s also when the team gets to raise their championship banner in MSG and the players get their championship rings. In addition, this is the first championship ceremony for the Knicks since 1973 — that’s 53 years without a banner. It’s a historic event in the NBA and no Knicks fan should miss it.

However, with pricing difficulties that led the organization to pause ticket sales temporarily, tickets to the home opener are very much sought-after and tough to get. Plus, the NBA scheduled the first game of the season against the new hot team in the league, the new look Philadelphia 76ers with the addition of former-Boston Celtic Jaylen Brown and former-L.A. Laker LeBron James joining the squad.

Meanwhile, the Knicks resurgence in New York has attracted a slew of attention from celebrities and sports fans alike, drawing in the likes of Spike Lee, Timothee Chalamet, Kylie Jenner, Tracy Morgan, Ben Stiller, Taylor Swift, Este and Alana Haim, Mariska Hargitay and others.

Tickets for the game, which is completely sold out, can still be found on third-party tickets sites, such as Ticketmaster, StubHub, Vivid Seats and others. Plus, hotel rooms in New York are available, including hotels near MSG, on TripAdvisor, Hotels.com, Expedia, Kayak and other booking platforms.

Below, check out some of the best places to buy tickets for the Knicks home opener, below:

Ticketmaster has tickets to the MSG home opener: Philadelphia 76ers vs. New York Knicks. The retailer is the official ticket seller of the pro league, so one of the best ways to buy and sell NBA tickets is through Ticketmaster.

We found tickets for Philadelphia 76ers vs. New York Knicks at the resale site StubHub starting at $1,069 for two tickets, at the time of publishing. We like the retailer because of their “FanProtect Guarantee,” which means all tickets sold are authentic, valid and delivered to your email inbox before tipoff.

title: James McAvoy Pitched ‘Star Trek’ Series About “Young Picard,” Jokes “All I Really Want To Do” Is Play Young Patrick Stewart
summary: After putting in his tenure in the X-Men franchise, James McAvoy had his sights set on another iconic character originated by Patrick Stewart. The Golden Globe nominee recently revealed that he pitched a Star Trek series about “young Picard” that was titled Mutiny On the Stargazer, noting that he nearly “made” the limited series. “That […]
content:
After putting in his tenure in the X-Men franchise, James McAvoy had his sights set on another iconic character originated by Patrick Stewart.

The Golden Globe nominee recently revealed that he pitched a Star Trek series about “young Picard” that was titled Mutiny On the Stargazer, noting that he nearly “made” the limited series.

“That was a whole idea I had I pitched to the Star Trek people as well, and we nearly did it,” said McAvoy on the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “I’ve got a whole story about an early Picard. All I really want to do in my career is play young versions of Patrick [Stewart].”

The interview came after McAvoy took over the role of Professor Charles Xavier from Stewart in the X-Men prequel movies First Class (2011), Days of Future Past (2014), Apocalypse (2016) and Dark Phoenix (2019). Stewart originated the live-action role in X-Men (2000), reprising him in the sequels X2 (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009), The Wolverine (2013), Logan (2017) and Days of Future Past, and again in the upcoming MCU title Avengers: Doomsday, premiering Dec. 18 in theaters.

Watch on Deadline

McAvoy continued, “I had this whole story of a young Picard that I love. I pitched, it was like a one-off standalone season … when he took over as captain of the Stargazer and what actually happened, and the secret he’s been holding his entire career. I just pitched it to them, talking to them, and they were into it, but we had logistical issues that meant we couldn’t do it. But I love that story that I just got to bed and think about it at night.”

Running for seven seasons in syndication from 1987 to 1994, Stewart starred in Star Trek: The Next Generation as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, commanding officer on the USS Enterprise-D. He reprised the role in Star Trek: Picard, running for three seasons from 2020 to ’23.

Picard’s first command was explored in author Michael Jan Friedman’s six-part Star Trek: Stargazer book series, which was published between 2002 and 2004.

title: Jaime Pressly Defends ‘Mom’ Co-Stars As “Beautifully Flawed” After Chuck Lorre Memoir: “Incredible Cast Of Women”
summary: After Anna Faris responded to Mom co-creator Chuck Lorre’s professional criticisms, Jaime Pressly has chimed in. The actress, who played recovering addict Jill Kendall on the CBS sitcom, defended her co-stars as “an incredible cast of women” after Lorre wrote in his memoir Sitcom that he “was, in fact, right” about his reluctance to cast […]
content:
After Anna Faris responded to Mom co-creator Chuck Lorre‘s professional criticisms, Jaime Pressly has chimed in.

The actress, who played recovering addict Jill Kendall on the CBS sitcom, defended her co-stars as “an incredible cast of women” after Lorre wrote in his memoir Sitcom that he “was, in fact, right” about his reluctance to cast Anna Faris in the lead as Christy Plunkett.

“I was there for seven years, but there [were] eight seasons,” she told E! News. “I came on in the second season, but I had seven wonderful years of working with an incredible crew and an incredible cast of women, who were, all of us, just as beautifully flawed as our characters on the show were.”

Pressly continued, “And I think I just really thoroughly enjoyed being able to go to work with girlfriends every day. All of us of a certain age, it was nice. It was refreshing.”

Watch on Deadline

In an excerpt from Sitcom, Lorre wrote: “I wasn’t sure Anna would be appropriate for this kind of material. Then I thought about how badly I’d bungled my working relationship with Charlie Sheen.”

Allison Janney, Mimi Kennedy, Beth Hall, Jaime Pressly and Anna Faris in ‘Mom’ Cliff Lipson/CBS/Courtesy Everett Collection

After his experience with Sheen on Two and a Half Men, Lorre recalled conceding, “Someone’s personal life is none of my business. The mom in Mom would be, and should be, Anna Faris.”

Lorre added: “As the years went by, it became apparent that my initial reluctance to hire Anna was, in fact, correct. After six years, she left the show for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show.”

Premiering in 2013, Faris starred in the first seven seasons of Mom as Christy, a recovering alcoholic who struggles to maintain a job, her family and her sobriety as her mom Bonnie (Allison Janney), who’s also in recovery, moves in with her.

Faris left the show in 2020 to “pursue new opportunities,” leaving Janney as the sole lead for the eighth and final season, which ended in 2021.

Following Lorre’s comments, Faris shared her response Thursday on Instagram. “Yikes. Yes, I read a few things. I really didn’t see that coming. Of course it hurts. Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted. I’m proud of what we made together, and nothing changes how grateful I am for those people and those years,” she wrote.

“I’ve been sober for a year and a half. I was on a show about recovery, and then I lived it. Now I’m healthy, I’m working, and I’m happier than I’ve been in a long time,” Faris continued. “If anyone reading this is where I was, I hope that’s useful. It gets better. I’m proof.”

In addition to Faris and Janney, Pressly starred in the series alongside Mimi Kennedy, Beth Hall and Kristen Johnston, playing their supportive group of friends from Alcoholics Anonymous.

title: Clive Barker Teases ‘Hellraiser: Revival’ Video Game Has Reignited “Many Ideas” For Film Franchise: “Planning To Keep My Fingers In That Pie”
summary: Nearly 40 years after first opening the Lament Configuration on screen, Clive Barker is ready to explore pain and pleasure again in the Hellraiser film franchise. With the recent release of the Saber Interactive’s Hellraiser: Revival video game, the writer/director of the original 1987 horror movie, which was based on his own book, teased that […]
content:
Nearly 40 years after first opening the Lament Configuration on screen, Clive Barker is ready to explore pain and pleasure again in the Hellraiser film franchise.

With the recent release of the Saber Interactive’s Hellraiser: Revival video game, the writer/director of the original 1987 horror movie, which was based on his own book, teased that he has “many ideas” of where to take the franchise next.

“I think what was achieved in the game is a wake-up call to anyone who’s been involved in the making of a franchise like Hellraiser,” he told Dread Central.

“It says to get your ideas warmed over so you can go back into existing worlds in a brand new way,” added Barker. “I have many ideas that I’d like to see realized in the Hellraiser universe, and I’m planning to keep my fingers in that pie.”

Watch on Deadline

Based on his 1986 novella The Hellbound Heart, Barker wrote and directed the first Hellraiser movie the following year, introducing audiences to Pinhead (Doug Bradley) and his Cenobites. The franchise has since sparked 11 movies, multiple books, comics, video games and more.

HELLRAISER, Clive Barker, 1987

Barker successfully reclaimed U.S. rights to the Hellraiser franchise in 2020, joining the 2022 David-Bruckner helmed Hulu reboot as a producer.

title: James Austin Johnson’s Trump Stops by ‘SNL U.K.’ for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: ‘You Don’t Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?’
summary: Donald Trump made his first appearance on “SNL U.K.,” courtesy of “SNL” cast member James Austin Johnson. Saturday night’s cold open recreated U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) meeting with Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy (Freddie Meredith) to reaffirm Britain’s support in their war with Russia. “We need America to restore the Starlink internet. Without it, […]
content:
Donald Trump made his first appearance on “SNL U.K.,” courtesy of “SNL” cast member James Austin Johnson.

Saturday night’s cold open recreated U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) meeting with Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy (Freddie Meredith) to reaffirm Britain’s support in their war with Russia.

“We need America to restore the Starlink internet. Without it, we are vulnerable to drone strikes,” Meredith’s Zelenskyy said. “Also, it is very difficult to stream ‘Celebrity Traitors.’ I’m very behind, no spoilers, but I think Richard E. Grant is going to go all the way.”

Replied Fouracres as Burnham, “Well, I can promise you now that I’ll raise all of this with President Trump at the first opportunity.”

Popular on Variety

Johnson then appeared with his spot-on Trump impression, marking the first crossover between the “SNL U.K.” and “SNL” casts. “Did somebody say Richard E. Grant?” he said.

“President Trump?!” Fouracres’ Burnham exclaimed.

“That’s right, you say my name and I appear,” Johnson’s Trump sad. “I got the idea from my very close friend Beetlejuice, the late, great Beetlejuice. It’s one of the two ways I am like him, the other is sex pest — alleged, they can’t prove he did that stuff.”

When asked why he’s in the U.K., Johnson as Trump said he’s been in town “to see my favorite comedian” who is “performing live at high court in the role of defendant,” referencing the Russell Brand trial.

Johnson’s Trump then explained that he is hoping to do a job swap with Burnham. “I take over the U.K., you take over America,” he said. “I tell ya, that place is a real mess, you’re going to hate it. It’s an awful, awful job. It’s a terrible place full of disgusting people, I don’t know what the hell happened. C’mon, job swap with me!”

Fouracres as Burnham replied, “I can’t swap jobs with you now, cocker! I’ve barely gotten started. People don’t even hate me yet!”

Johnson’s Trump then went on a rant about things he could fix in Britain, including that M&S have too many variations of Percy Pigs.

“And how about British comedy, folks? What a bad situation, it’s not doing well,” he continued. “‘SNL U.K.,’ you’re telling me you don’t have a guy — the whole cast, you don’t have one guy who can play Trump? What an awful situation. Some of these people went to RADA! What is that, the Royal Academy of Dogshit Actors? Ooh, you can say shit on this one! That felt really good.”

Johnson as Trump finally gave up on the job swap, saying: “Fine, I’ll go home. And Zelenskyy, let me know if you need anything, anything at all. Provided it’s not help with war.”

Added Fouracres as Burnham, “Sorry Zelenskyy, me old mocker. But as dire as things might be, what matters most is that we all be nice to this insane man.”

After cracking jokes about everything from U.S. President Donald Trump’s recently fired press secretary to ridiculous claims that King Charles might be Muslim, co-host Ania Magliano turned her attention to Gillis. The comedian caused quite the stir last weekend for making misogynistic comments in his opening monologue as well as dropping the f-bomb live on air, which is not allowed per NBC guidelines.

“I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” Gillis said during his monologue. “You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.”

Popular on Variety

Magliano riffed on this by saying: “A ride operator at Munich Oktoberfest was praised for giving out free cycling shorts to female riders. Wearing the gym shorts will protect women from being upskirted, but it does make them vulnerable to something much worse.”

A photo of Gillis during his monologue then appeared on screen, sparking laughter from the live audience.

Magliano then took aim at Gillis’ accidental f-bomb, subtly pointing out the fact that “SNL U.K.” is allowed to swear on air.

“Last week on ‘SNL,’ comedian Shane Gillis also caused controversy by dropping the f-bomb,” she said. “Oh, Shane. You’re not allowed to say that, you stupid fucking cunt.”

title: Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’
summary: Walking through Turin with his wife and creative partner James Ellis Deakins, Roger Deakins found himself thinking about Giorgio de Chirico. The Italian painter, one of his favorites, had drawn inspiration from the city’s vast squares, long arcades and unusual arrangements of light and shadow. Deakins was noticing the relationship for himself. It’s characteristic of […]
content:
Walking through Turin with his wife and creative partner James Ellis Deakins, Roger Deakins found himself thinking about Giorgio de Chirico. The Italian painter, one of his favorites, had drawn inspiration from the city’s vast squares, long arcades and unusual arrangements of light and shadow. Deakins was noticing the relationship for himself.

It’s characteristic of a man who has spent much of his life looking at the world, yet remains somewhat at a loss to explain precisely how he sees it.

“Somebody asked the other day, what is a cinematographer? I mean, I still can’t answer that,” he says.

Popular on Variety

It’s an uncommon admission from someone whose images have helped define contemporary cinema, from “No Country for Old Men” to “Blade Runner 2049” and “1917.” But for Deakins, the work is too dependent on the circumstances of a story, and the people telling it, to be reduced to any one method.

“It’s your emotional reaction to things that’s important,” he says. Technical considerations can be discussed, but the decisions that shape an image ultimately arise from something inexplicable.

Perhaps his relationship with looking began as something more personal. As a young man, Deakins, born in the southern English resort of Torquay, discovered that the camera offered a kind of confidence, a way of approaching a world in which he hadn’t always felt comfortable.

“I was kind of hiding behind the camera to a certain degree,” he recalls. “I had confidence because there was something between me and reality.”

He could scarcely have imagined where that camera would take him. Only in retrospect has he come to appreciate the significance of experiences whose importance wasn’t apparent at the time.

“If you don’t experience things, then what have you got to contribute?”

It’s a conviction he shares with Ellis Deakins, his wife and essential collaborator on every project since they met on Michael Apted’s “Thunderheart.” For her, experience gives a filmmaker more than a collection of visual references. It provides different ways of understanding the people and specifics of a story.

“If you’re going to tell a story, having had many different experiences gives you many different points of view,” she says. “You’re able to actually add more to the story.”

Deakins worries that cinema can become too inward-looking, with filmmakers drawing inspiration primarily from other films.

“I rarely, if ever, do that,” he says of referencing earlier movies. “You bring all the things that you experienced in your life to something.”

Their Team Deakins podcast often explores the myriad routes people have taken into filmmaking. There is no repeatable path, just as there is no formula for a good image. James encourages the aspiring to experiment, examine their photographs and footage, and ask themselves why something works or doesn’t. It’s how they develop an eye, or what Roger calls a personal sensibility.

Deakins, however, is less inclined to analyze his own.

When asked about the relationship of shapes and forms in his still photography, he struggles to explain what draws him to a composition. He tends to see the whole image, he says, rather than its individual elements.

Ellis Deakins is more definite. Looking at his photographs, she notices how shapes intersect and contrast.

“You may not be aware of it, but you are interconnecting shapes,” she tells him. “But I know it’s instinctual.”

The distinction between conscious intention and instinct becomes more intriguing when we discuss Andrew Dominik’s “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford.” Much of the film contrasts light and dark, yet the scene depicting Robert Ford’s murder takes place in a bar housed in a tent, surrounded by snow, its interior swathed in flat, even light. The violence, and Casey Affleck’s Robert Ford, seem jarringly exposed.

Was the contrast deliberate?

Deakins considers the question. The appearance arose partly from the circumstances of the set: the tent, the snow outside, the whiteness of the surroundings. Whether the scene had been staged there for its visual effect or because of its historical circumstances, he cannot entirely say.

But there were choices to be made. They could have introduced stronger shadows, allowing the light to fall on only part of the tent. Instead, they chose to preserve the evenness of the illumination.

“I think it was a very conscious decision to have almost a sort of documentary feel about it, as opposed to the rest of the film.”

He thinks the scene is stronger for it.

How much is planned varies from one director to the next. With Sam Mendes on “Jarhead,” he worked largely handheld, responding to actors as they performed. With Joel and Ethan Coen, the process was often meticulously planned. Different ways, he suggests, of reaching the same place.

The common concern is what matters in the scene, and where the audience should be as that part of the story unfolds. For James, that requires entering someone else’s imagination. She recalls her early work as a script supervisor, when understanding what a director wanted meant learning to see through another person’s eyes.

It is a reminder that, however personal Deakins’ instincts may be, the images are not made in isolation. His way of seeing must always attempt to meet the director’s vision, the actors’ performances and the needs of the film.

Harrison Ford once described what it feels like to work with Deakins. Discussing “Blade Runner 2049” alongside Ryan Gosling, Ford observed that Deakins’ approach to lighting proceeds from the story, leaving an actor feeling supported.

It’s a quality Deakins himself describes as the product of collaboration. He particularly misses the intimacy of operating a camera with a director standing beside him, rather than watching from a monitor elsewhere.

After a take, the director might turn and ask, “How was that for you?”

“Then there was that sense of trust,” he remembers. He misses, he says, that “intense collaboration and trust.”

He and Ellis Deakins are careful to distinguish digital technology from the working habits it can encourage. They have always embraced whatever technology best serves the storytelling, and have a long and fruitful history of shooting digitally. But Roger remembers the particular discipline of working on low-budget film productions, when stock and time were precious and rolling the camera was consequential.

“You kind of had to figure out what was the essence of the scene and what was the shot that was going to give you that.”

Finding the essence of a scene does not always mean moving closer or showing more. Ellis Deakins points out that holding back from an actor can itself create a feeling, leaving the audience uneasy because they want a closer view.

Deakins recalls admiring Andrei Tarkovsky’s long takes. “They would hold shots, and the shot would become something else. It would be saying something else.”

He finds another kind of patience in his still photography, where a single image can hold the viewer’s attention indefinitely. And he has spent a lifetime fishing. A couple of days before our conversation, he had been out in his boat off the Devon coast catching mackerel. Enough for supper, anyway.

“You never know what might happen,” he says, “and you’ve got to sort of change your approach constantly to adapt to the sort of tide and the weather and the way the fish are running.”

He acknowledges the parallels with filmmaking, without wanting to make too much of them. Both involve waiting, observation and a willingness to respond to the world as it is rather than impose a fixed plan.

At View Conference in Turin, I later spot the partners attending a number of technical talks themselves. For all their insistence that filmmaking depends on instinct and experience rather than formulas, they remain curious about what others are making and discovering. There is something fitting about seeing Deakins, whose work is so often studied and dissected by others, sitting among the audience, still looking and listening.

During our conversation, he had recalled a remark by the photographer Raymond Depardon: if he knew how to take a good photograph, every photograph he took would be good.

I had also mentioned “Moby-Dick,” the novel Deakins chose to take to the island on a recent episode of “Desert Island Discs.” Did he identify more with Ishmael, the observer, or Captain Ahab, the obsessive pursuer?

“I’m definitely Ahab,” he replied.

“Isn’t Ahab the captain?” Ellis Deakins asked.

“Yeah, he goes down with a whale.”

“A crazy captain,” she said.

“Searching for something he doesn’t really understand, fighting something he doesn’t really understand,” Deakins replied.

“I’ve always felt an affinity with Ahab for sure.”

title: Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors
summary: For Oscar-winning VFX supervisor Paul Lambert Lambert, of all the huge challenges presented by Ryan Gosling space epic “Project Hail Mary,” the most daunting was creating convincing zero gravity. “Zero-G was probably my personal biggest concern going into the movie,” he said at View Conference in Turin, Italy, drilling down on its VFX. “We tried […]
content:
For Oscar-winning VFX supervisor Paul Lambert Lambert, of all the huge challenges presented by Ryan Gosling space epic “Project Hail Mary,” the most daunting was creating convincing zero gravity.

“Zero-G was probably my personal biggest concern going into the movie,” he said at View Conference in Turin, Italy, drilling down on its VFX.

“We tried very hard to convince the production to use the vomit comet,” he added, referring to aircraft maneuvers that briefly generate weightlessness. But the spacecraft sets were too elaborate to recreate onboard, so Gosling performed on wire rigs, including a rotating harness.

Removing the wires was only the beginning. When a suspended body still appeared to be hanging rather than floating, VFX artists adjusted the position of Gosling’s legs, arms or torso and added drifting objects to reinforce the illusion. Lambert said the actor was committed to performing his own stunt work, including demanding spacewalk material.

Popular on Variety

Other experiments were deliberately hands-on. Fraser used an infrared-modified camera, programmable IR lights and water running in front of the lens to develop some of the film’s stranger imagery. “It was literally a mad science lab,” Lambert recalled. Burning fireballs, liquids, lasers and ferrofluid were also filmed to provide starting points for the microscopic effects.

The DP returned during postproduction to work with ILM’s Helios virtual-camera system on the sequence near Adrian. Artists tracked Gosling’s on-set performance and recreated it within digital environments, allowing Fraser to choose new camera positions without discarding the original acting.

Across those techniques, the supervisors’ ambition remained consistent: to make even the most elaborate effects obey a recognizable physical logic while ensuring Rocky felt as present beside Gosling as any human scene partner.

The visual effects team behind “Project Hail Mary” started its journey through space, however, by making an unexpected discovery: much of the sky would look surprisingly familiar. Rather than fill Ryan Gosling’s interstellar adventure with colorful nebulae, Lambert and co-supervisor Mag Sarnowska used astronomical data, practical puppetry and carefully controlled cinematography to keep its science-fiction imagery grounded in reality.

“We had visions of all these beautiful nebulae, but in the end, the skies were pretty much as we see them today, from Earth,” Lambert told View Conference in Turin on Friday, describing research conducted for directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel.

The team drew on data from the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission to map the stars between Earth and Tau Ceti, some 11.9 light-years away, while studying NASA footage and raw images from the International Space Station to establish how cameras behave in orbit. Exposure became a guiding principle. “If you were to take a movie camera up to space and try to shoot something, you wouldn’t see the stars,” Lambert explained.

Near the brightly illuminated planet Adrian, background stars were therefore largely absent. Farther from Tau Ceti, where the light was weaker, a hypothetical high-sensitivity camera could reveal them. “Rather than simply choosing when to show stars with dramatic effects, we wanted their visibility to follow the actual lighting and exposure conditions,” Lambert said.

DP Greig Fraser extended that philosophy into the film’s texture. Digitally captured footage was printed onto Kodak film and scanned back: 5254, with silver retention, for a relatively smooth, subdued Earth, and grainier 5203 for space. Two months of virtual-production exploration before filming also allowed Fraser and the directors to test lighting, camera movements and the scale of spacecraft interiors.

Rather than dictate final shots, those sessions let the filmmakers experiment with digital environments and camera positions early, with the resulting camera data helping guide the physical shoot and subsequent VFX work.

Rocky, the alien companion performed by James Ortiz and a team of puppeteers, posed a different problem: making a physically present character indistinguishable from his digital counterpart. Sarnowska described three practical versions, including an animatronic and a smaller reference puppet. Framestore scanned the physical creation and studied hours of performance footage, reproducing the puppeteers’ movement when the cramped spaceship sets made practical operation impossible.

“Our full CG Rocky got really good at mimicking the puppeteers,” Sarnowska said. “In the end, half of the Rocky shots were puppet and the other half CG.” She added that the team sometimes struggled to distinguish the versions during internal reviews. The effects crew also rebuilt Rocky’s transparent xenonite barriers digitally to remove reflections, hide operators and maintain the complicated play of light through the set.

For Rocky’s sonar-based point of view, the filmmakers also experimented with printing the images onto different film formats, ultimately using 10mm and 16mm for selected shots to give them a more organic texture, to bring a larger credibility to a moving tale of interstellar friendship which proved one of this year’s box office hits.

title: NFL Introduces Celebrity Guest Cheerleaders: On the Sidelines With Comedian Atsuko Okatsuka and the L.A. Rams (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: It’s just before halftime of the Los Angeles Rams’ Monday Night Football matchup with the Buffalo Bills, and comedian Atsuko Okatsuka is standing in the tunnel, hyping herself up. In less than a minute, the comedian, actress and native Angeleno will strut onto the field at SoFi Stadium to perform with the Rams cheerleaders. Okatsuka […]
content:
It’s just before halftime of the Los Angeles Rams’ Monday Night Football matchup with the Buffalo Bills, and comedian Atsuko Okatsuka is standing in the tunnel, hyping herself up.

In less than a minute, the comedian, actress and native Angeleno will strut onto the field at SoFi Stadium to perform with the Rams cheerleaders. Okatsuka hides behind a bright smile while marking her dance moves, but she’ll later admit to being “super nervous.” Sure, she’ll only be dancing for about 45 seconds, but it’s been nearly 20 years since she last shook her poms.

Fortunately, when Okatsuka cartwheels into the center of the formation, muscle memory takes over. Her Venice High School cheer skills come rushing back. (She was voted “Most Spirited,” after all!) The sold-out crowd cheers while the newest Rams cheerleader grooves to the high-tempo beat of Katseye’s “Animal” and, then, in an instant, her big moment is over. When the music ends, Okatsuka strikes her final pose — she crushed it — and now, she runs back toward the tunnel with the rest of her new squad.

Popular on Variety

Okatsuka stops to share her instant reaction with Variety: “I’m so old,” she cracks.

A few minutes later, she sinks into a lounge chair in the green room to reflect on becoming the NFL’s inaugural Celebrity Guest Cheerleader.

“The middle part I crushed,” Okatsuka says, beaming with pride. “It was so fun. It takes me back to performing good spirits through dance. I haven’t done that in a minute.”

Atsuko Okatsuka during the regular season game against the Buffalo Bills on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Ryan Hadji /Los Angeles Rams) Ryan Hadji /Los Angeles Rams

The NFL’s Celebrity Guest Cheerleader initiative is the latest extension of the league’s successful “Celebrity Guest” series, which launched last year with pro athletes, actors and musicians — including Jerry Rice, Simone Biles, Suni Lee, Method Man, Common, Joel McHale, Ken Griffey Jr., Benson Boone and Marshawn Lynch — working as sideline photographers during games.

“Our approach to fan engagement is rooted in finding new ways to bring the NFL into the broader cultural conversation, connecting audiences to the game through the voices, experiences and stories that resonate with them,” says Rob Santini, NFL VP, global culture, social and entertainment.

“The Celebrity Guest programs are a natural evolution of that strategy: creating opportunities for entertainers and cultural voices to experience the NFL in unexpected ways,” Santini explains. “We couldn’t have asked for better partners than Atsuko and the Los Angeles Rams to bring this to life.”

The idea for Okatsuka to join the Rams squad came from a popular bit in her 2025 Hulu stand-up comedy special “Father,” where she jokes about how former cheerleaders, like her, are hiding in plain sight. Then, she does a special “roll call” to call them out in the audience. (“Ready?” Okatsuka yells into the mic, as her audience echoes back, “OK!”) The bit continues, breaking down the hype woman mindset that cheerleaders must adopt, pumping up the team even when they have no idea if they’re going to win, and how that positivity manifests in everyday life.

“We’re always looking for ways to bring the Rams brand to the intersection of sports and culture,” adds Kurt Gies, director, social media and influencers for the Los Angeles Rams. “When the NFL introduced us to Atsuko, we knew it would be a great fit, particularly given her roots in Los Angeles and her background as a former cheerleader.”

The announcement on the Rams’ Instagram about Okatsuka’s performance generated more than 1 million views. Her performance is one of the team’s top-performing pieces of content this season, with more than 4 million views and 200,000 engagements. “The response reinforced the power of blending sports and culture to connect with new audiences,” Gies says.

To prepare for the performance, Okatsuka studied the choreography at home before meeting with the Rams cheerleaders to run the routine at their weekly rehearsals.

“Stand-up comedy is so different. So, I was like prepping like I’m going to the Olympics or something,” she says. “Once I was there, they were so patient with me. They’re cheerleaders — they’re really good at making you feel good. Not to a fault, but they kept going, ‘You’re doing good,’ and then you start to believe it.”

The Rams also gifted Okatsuka with a customized uniform for game day. “My stylist and I thought about how it might cut for me to have shoulders, kind of like the players,” Okatsuka says, joking about how she wanted to show a little less skin than her squamates. “I was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think I could wear that,’” she says, laughing. “‘Can I be covered neck down?’”

Okatsuka gets to keep the suit, but she’s not quite sure where she’ll wear it next. It’s a little too much for her next comedy special, which will also shoot at the United Theater in Downtown L.A. “I’ll wear it before, backstage,” she jokes.

Look for the next Celebrity Guest Cheerleader to take the field during the NFL holiday games. And Okatsuka has a few ideas for who should take part.

“Shapel Lacey is a stand-up comedian, and he was a competitive cheerleader. It’d be cool to normalize having guys do it. Maybe one of the Backstreet Boys — AJ McLean,” Okatsuka says. “Lil Jon — he was a lot of people’s first cheerleader. At least music-wise, all he does is positive affirmations, so it’d be cool to see him perform with NFL cheerleaders.”

title: Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ Wins Best Film at BFI London Film Festival
summary: Sergei Loznitsa’s “Imperium,” which revisits the Soviet Union of the early 1970s through footage shot by Italian cameramen, has won the best film award at the 70th BFI London Film Festival competition. The prizes were unveiled Sunday as the festival drew to a close. The competition jury was led by filmmaker Sam Pollard, whose credits […]
content:
Sergei Loznitsa’s “Imperium,” which revisits the Soviet Union of the early 1970s through footage shot by Italian cameramen, has won the best film award at the 70th BFI London Film Festival competition.

The prizes were unveiled Sunday as the festival drew to a close. The competition jury was led by filmmaker Sam Pollard, whose credits include “MLK/FBI” and “Citizen Ashe,” and also featured “Life of Jorge Luis Borges” filmmaker Mariano Llinás and DDA chief strategy officer Julie La Bassiere.

“The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart,” the jury said.

Popular on Variety

In the first feature competition, the Sutherland Award went to Thailand’s Oscar submission “9 Temples to Heaven,” the first fiction feature from Sompot Chidgasornpongse. The film reflects on faith, kinship and the passage from life to death. Actor Amir El-Masry (“Giant,” “Limbo”) presided over that jury, joined by “Moonglow” producer Alemberg Ang and sales, distribution and awards strategist Rosa Bosch.

“An accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region,” the jury said.

Bertil Nilsson’s “Masc” received a special mention in the same section. The debut tracks Robin, who drifts between short-term jobs and uncertain relationships while looking for somewhere he fits. The jury singled out Nilsson as a fresh British talent with an unusual concept and a funny script.

The Grierson Award for documentary went to Asmahan Bkerat’s feature directorial debut “Concrete Land,” which spends time with several generations of a mixed-race family in Jordan as they resist displacement and hostility. “Santosh” director Sandhya Suri headed the documentary jury, alongside Melbourne International Film Festival senior programmer Kate Fitzpatrick and BAFTA and Emmy-winning producer Andee Ryder.

“In a noisy and often polemical world it was refreshing, humbling and deeply relevant to see the quiet resilience and dignity of this family in the face of the erasure of their culture and traditions,” the jury said.

Theo Rollason’s “Queer Edward II,” assembled entirely from archive material, earned a special mention. It goes behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s “Edward II,” set against the anti-LGBTQIA+ laws Britain passed in the 1980s, and the jury praised it as a portrait of Jarman the artist and Jarman the activist.

Rahul Roye’s “Aman” won the Short Film Award. The film centers on a trans man who learns he is pregnant the night before his gender-affirming surgery, upending his sense of who he is as a man and as a father. It is streaming free on BFI Player until Oct. 25.

Writer-producer Helen Simmons (“100 Nights of Hero”) led the shorts jury, which also included comedian Leo Reich and script editor Jack Casey.

“We were struck by the film’s painterly cinematography, and expansive and assured storytelling, which guided us through the world with care,” the jury said.

Elizabeth Hobbs’ “Daughters of the Late Colonel,” about two middle-aged sisters left adrift after the death of their domineering father, took a special mention for its inventive visual style.

Audience voting for the festival’s best feature film and best British discovery prizes closes Oct. 21, with winners to be named later. Last year, Chloé Zhao’s “Hamnet” took the audience prize for best feature, while Yemi Bamiro’s “Black Is Beautiful: The Kwame Brathwaite Story” won British discovery.

title: London Film Festival: Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ & Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s ‘9 Temples To Heaven’ Among Big Winners — Full List
summary: Ukrainian filmmaker Sergei Loznitsa’s latest feature Imperium has won the Best Film Award in the Official Competition at this year’s London Film Festival. The winners were announced this afternoon, the last day of the LFF. The LFF Official Competition jury was led by documentary filmmaker Sam Pollard. Discussing why they chose Imperium, the jury described […]
content:
Ukrainian filmmaker Sergei Loznitsa’s latest feature Imperium has won the Best Film Award in the Official Competition at this year’s London Film Festival.

The winners were announced this afternoon, the last day of the LFF.

The LFF Official Competition jury was led by documentary filmmaker Sam Pollard. Discussing why they chose Imperium, the jury described the picture as an “extraordinary film that explores the Soviet Union in the early 1970’s from a rich archive with a wide-ranging perspective that looks at life in a country with an extraordinary social and cultural landscape that has rarely been seen.”

The jury added: “The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels, giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart. Our jury is immensely proud to honour such a powerful and singular piece of work.”

Watch on Deadline

Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse won the coveted Sutherland Award in the First Feature Competition with 9 Temples To Heaven. The film, which debuted at Cannes, follows Sakol, who, after hearing a prophecy that his elderly mother may die soon, sets out on a one-day pilgrimage to nine temples as a remedy.

Kissada Kamyoung and Palme d’Or winner Apichatpong Weerasethakul (Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives) produced the film alongside co-producers Thomas Hakim and Julien Graff of petit chaos, the company behind Payal Kapadia’s award-winning All We Imagine as Light.

Discussing their decision, the first feature jury, led by Amir El-Masry, said the film was an “accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region. The film is visually outstanding, spiritual, and meditative, where a story about life and death transcends borders and generations.”

Elsewhere, Concrete Land, directed by Asmahan Bkerat, won the Grierson Award in the Documentary Competition, and Rahul Roye’s Aman won the Short Film Award.

The LFF ends this evening with a screening of The Debut, directed by Jesse Eisenberg.

title: El Gouna Unveils Third Cohort Of CineGouna Emerge Program’s Rising Stars
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival has announced the third cohort of emerging talents from across the Arab world selected for its Rising Stars program. They are Egyptian director Abdallah Dnewar, Saudi Arabian writer-director Razan AlSoghayer, Palestinian filmmaker Omar Rammal, Palestinian Jordanian director-producer Asmahan Bkerat and Syrian DoP, editor and director Rama Abdi. Launched in […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival has announced the third cohort of emerging talents from across the Arab world selected for its Rising Stars program.

They are Egyptian director Abdallah Dnewar, Saudi Arabian writer-director Razan AlSoghayer, Palestinian filmmaker Omar Rammal, Palestinian Jordanian director-producer Asmahan Bkerat and Syrian DoP, editor and director Rama Abdi.

Launched in 2024, the initiative is part of El Gouna’s CineGouna Emerge program aimed at nurturing the next generation of MENA film professionals. CineGouna Emerge in turn is a strand of El Gouna’s CineGouna industry program alongside the Forum talks lineup, Funding project showcase, Market and new Series focus.

“This year’s Rising Stars are already leaving their mark, each in their own corner of the industry,” said Hayat Aljowaily, Director of CineGouna Emerge & International Engagement, who spearheaded the Rising Stars program.

Watch on Deadline

Cairo-based Dnewar produced the critically acclaimed Rotterdam-selected animated short My Brother, My Brother, and Locarno-selected Khufu, and been a script consultant on several short films. He is currently Head of Specials at Egyptian media company Zest. There, he oversaw the Eish Short Film Competition, a joint initiative between the El Gouna Film Festival and United Nations World Food Programme (WFP).

Based between Saudi Arabia and The Netherlands, AlSoghayer’s work explores womanhood, memory, friendship, patriarchy and growing up within a rapidly changing society. Drawing from personal experience and everyday life, she creates intimate, nostalgic stories rooted in Saudi culture and the complexities of change. Her debut short Son Of Badriyah plays in this edition of El Gouna.

West Bank-born Rammal has carving out a unique path between digital storytelling and independent cinema, with his visual style and deeply human storytelling racking up hundreds of millions of views across digital platforms.

He made waves this year with Everyday in Gaza, which won the best short documentary award in the 2026 edition of Italy’s David di Donatello awards. His debut fiction short, Kentucky Gaza makes its MENA premiere at the El Gouna, having premiered in the International Competition at Clermont-Ferrand in France. He is currently developing his first feature film.

Bkerat ,whose work explores themes of displacement, identity, and cultural heritage, is currently on the festival circuit with her debut feature documentary Concrete Land, which premiered at the Locarno Film Festival and won the Insights Audience Award at VIFF (Vancouver).

It recently played to sold-out screenings at the BFI London Film Festival and is now on a major festival tour, including Dok Leipzig, IDFA, and Doha. She is currently producing the feature documentaries If These Stones Could Talk and Landwards, and is in early production on her next directorial feature.

Damascus-based Abdi began her filmmaking journey in 2018, working across commercial, journalistic and cinematic productions as a camerawoman and director.
