In 2022 she directed her first short Fish Dance, and is now working on her first feature-length documentary House Number 7, which she is presenting in the CineGouna Funding project showcase.

Through the program, this year’s Rising Stars will connect with industry leaders and take part in the festival’s main activities, from panel discussions and media engagements to the red carpet. The experience is curated to give each of them the visibility their work has earned.

“What we offer them is not a beginning, but a moment of recognition: a chance to be seen, to be heard, and to find one another,” said Aljowaily. “Our role is simply to bring them into the same room, and into the light, at a moment when their work is ready to be seen.

Amr Mansi, Co-Founder and Executive Director of El Gouna Film Festival added: “We need to ensure that stories from this region are shared with the rest of the world. We strongly believe that our participants will be the dominant voice in telling these stories.”

Andrew Mohsen, Artistic Director of El Gouna Film Festival, emphasized the fact that the participants are fully integrated into the festival program.

“What makes Rising Stars meaningful is that it does not stand apart from the rest of the festival,” he said. “Many of these filmmakers are here with projects they are pitching at CineGouna Funding, or with films that are competing, or have competed, in our official selection. The program recognizes talent we are already invested in, and whose work we have watched grow from one edition to the next.”

title: Jaime Pressly Defends ‘Mom’ Co-Stars as ‘Beautifully Flawed’ After Creator Chuck Lorre Revealed His ‘Reluctance to Hire’ Anna Faris
summary: Jaime Pressly has joined former “Mom” co-star Anna Faris in responding to show co-creator Chuck Lorre’s professional criticism. In his recent memoir “Sitcom,” Lorre wrote that he “was, in fact, right” to be hesitant to cast Faris as the lead character, Christy Plunkett. Pressly, who joined the CBS sitcom in its second season as recovering […]
content:
Jaime Pressly has joined former “Mom” co-star Anna Faris in responding to show co-creator Chuck Lorre’s professional criticism.

In his recent memoir “Sitcom,” Lorre wrote that he “was, in fact, right” to be hesitant to cast Faris as the lead character, Christy Plunkett. Pressly, who joined the CBS sitcom in its second season as recovering addict Jill Kendall, came to the defense of her “incredible cast of women” co-stars.

“I was there for seven years, but there [were] eight seasons,” Pressly told E! News. “I came on in the second season, but I had seven wonderful years of working with an incredible crew and an incredible cast of women, who were, all of us, just as beautifully flawed as our characters on the show were.”

Popular on Variety

“And I think I just really thoroughly enjoyed being able to go to work with girlfriends every day,” she added. “All of us of a certain age, it was nice. It was refreshing.”

Faris left “Mom” in 2020 ahead of its final season. At the time, she said she wanted to open herself up to other opportunities.

“I wasn’t sure Anna would be appropriate for this kind of material,” Lorre wrote in his book. “Then I thought about how badly I’d bungled my working relationship with Charlie Sheen.” Lorre and Sheen had a public feud toward the end of “Two and a Half Men,” which led to the actor being fired from the hit sitcom in 2011.

“As the years went by, it became apparent that my initial reluctance to hire Anna was, in fact, correct,” Lorre added about Faris. “After six years, she left the show for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show.”

Faris addressed Lorre’s comments on Instagram on Oct. 15: “Of course it hurts. Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted. I’m proud of what we made together, and nothing changes how grateful I am for those people and those years.”

She continued, “I’ve been sober for a year and a half. I was on a show about recovery and then I lived it. Now I’m healthy, I’m working, and I’m happier than I’ve been in a long time.”

After Faris left the show, Pressly starred as the main lead in the final season. “Mom” also starred Allison Janney, Mimi Kennedy, Beth Hall and Kristen Johnston.

title: Box Office: ‘La Bola Negra’ Scores $277,500 From Four Theaters as Netflix Reports Grosses for First Time Ever
summary: In a major shift in the theatrical tides, Netflix has reported box office grosses for the first time ever. The streamer’s awards hopeful “La Bola Negra” scored $277,500 from just four theaters, averaging $69,375 per location. Those ticket sales are notable as the second-highest screen average ever for a non-English language film behind 2019’s “Parasite,” […]
content:
In a major shift in the theatrical tides, Netflix has reported box office grosses for the first time ever.

The streamer’s awards hopeful “La Bola Negra” scored $277,500 from just four theaters, averaging $69,375 per location. Those ticket sales are notable as the second-highest screen average ever for a non-English language film behind 2019’s “Parasite,” which opened to $393,216 from three theaters, averaging $131,072 per location. It’s also the highest-ever PSA — the key metric for arthouse releases — for a Spanish language film. By comparison, Neon’s multilingual legal thriller “Fjord,” another Oscar contender, debuted last weekend to $124,000 from four theaters, translating to $31,000 per location.

Now the test is whether “La Bola Negra” can sustain momentum as Netflix slowly expands the movie’s footprint in the weeks to come. The streamer plans to keep the film in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times and the company’s longest theatrical rollout to date, before its Netflix release on Dec. 2. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known as Los Javis, “La Bola Negra” is a generation-spanning queer epic that chronicles the interconnected story of three men. After the drama was embraced at Cannes Film Festival with a 16-minute standing ovation, Netflix acquired the movie for around $5 million. “La Bola Negra” tied for the Cannes best director prize and won Toronto Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award, which has historically been a reliable indicator of Academy Awards attention.

Popular on Variety

Netflix has long been viewed as a major big-screen adversary, probably because the company’s co-CEO Ted Sarandos has frequently dismissed movie theaters as an “outmoded idea.” And while the streamer has been warming to theaters beyond just Oscar-qualifying runs, with token releases for 2022’s “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Story” and last year’s”Kpop Demon Hunters” re-release and the “Stranger Things” series finale, Netflix has never disclosed how much those movies made in cinemas.

In the past, Netflix has viewed multiplexes, not as a financial strategy, but rather as a marketing stunt to drive interest pack to the platform. But there are other benefits to box office reporting for Netflix, which has never won the coveted best picture Oscar. Unlike streaming metrics, which can be twisted and touted in any which way, box office dollars are uniformly reported — meaning there’s no denying a hit (or a miss). Netflix’s change in strategy comes as the streamer’s stock has been languishing. Last week, the company laid off 1,000 employees and replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Disney veteran Peter Rice.

Moving forward, Netflix plans to disclose grosses for upcoming releases such as David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” around Thanksgiving and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and Taika Waititi’s animated “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory” in 2027. Whether those buzzy projects achieve breakout status, Netflix’s new attention toward theatrical is a win for exhibitors, who are already celebrating the biggest post-COVID year at the box office.

title: Georgina Cates, ‘An Awfully Big Adventure’ and ‘2point4 Children’ Actress, Dies at 51
summary: Georgina Cates, the British actress who appeared in films including “An Awfully Big Adventure” and the TV series “2point4 Children,” has died. She was 51. Cates’s death was announced by her daughter, Naiia, on Instagram in June, though it had not been reported until now. “My beautiful, free-spirited mom lived a hard life and still […]
content:
Georgina Cates, the British actress who appeared in films including “An Awfully Big Adventure” and the TV series “2point4 Children,” has died. She was 51.

Cates’s death was announced by her daughter, Naiia, on Instagram in June, though it had not been reported until now.

“My beautiful, free-spirited mom lived a hard life and still found ways to make herself and others laugh and smile <3 now she can rest easy,” Naiia wrote. “I will always see you in black and white photos, Virginia slims, baggy clothes, no bras, big sunglasses, doodling while talking, pleasers, and flip flops and everything in between. I love you, thank you for your creativity, curiosity and your bravery to always be true to yourself — no matter what.”

Cates began her career on “2point4 Children” in 1991, in which she played the character of Jenny Porter. She went on to appear in TV shows including “Casualty,” “An Exchange of Fire,” “Chris Cross,” “Crimewatch File” and “The Bill” through the early 1990s before making her feature film debut in “Au Pair” in 1994, which followed a young Welsh woman as she leaves her quiet country for Germany in search of adventure.

Popular on Variety

In 1995, she starred in “An Awfully Big Adventure” alongside Hugh Grant and Alan Rickman. She also appeared in 1998’s “Clay Pigeons” with Joaquin Phoenix, Vince Vaughn and Janaene Garofalo, in addition to “Jackass Presents: Bad Grandpa” and “Everlasting,” among other projects.

Georgina Cates was born on Jan. 14, 1975 in Colchester, England, and moved to Los Angeles to pursue acting. From 1997 to 2005, Cates was married to Skeet Ulrich, whom she met at an Oscars party, and the couple had twins, Naiia and Jakob. On Naiia’s Instagram post, Ulrich commented “I love you more than words can say sweetheart ❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️”

Cates is survived by her daughter, Naiia, and son, Jakob.

title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Stuns With $15 Million Debut, ‘Street Fighter’ Leads With $31 Million
summary: “You Can See Everything” accomplished a true box office feat, becoming the rare must-see documentary on the big screen. Director Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-hyped look at Elizabeth Holmes has generated a massive $15 million from just 855 theaters. Those ticket sales were enough for second place behind another newcomer, Paramount’s video game adaptation […]
content:
“You Can See Everything” accomplished a true box office feat, becoming the rare must-see documentary on the big screen.

Director Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-hyped look at Elizabeth Holmes has generated a massive $15 million from just 855 theaters. Those ticket sales were enough for second place behind another newcomer, Paramount’s video game adaptation “Street Fighter,” which opened to $30 million from 3,575 venues. Heading into the weekend, “You Can See Everything” was aiming for $7 million to $8 million, which would have been remarkable for a documentary, especially one that doesn’t involve music or capture a wildly popular concert. Not to mention, this one runs at nearly three hours and wasn’t on anyone’s radar until two months ago.

After a surprise world premiere at Telluride Film Festival, “You Can See Everything” became a word-of-mouth sensation, bolstered by some of the best reviews of the year. A24, which produced the movie in secret over three years for roughly $7 million, reported more than 2,000 sold-out screenings as audiences rushed to theaters to avoid spoilers on the stranger-than-fiction story about the Theranos founder before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. People are clearly captivated by the drama surrounding Holmes, whose rise and spectacular fall from grace was depicted in the Hulu series “The Dropout,” starring Amanda Seyfried. But the turnout for “You Can See Everything” also speaks to the commercial appeal of Fielder, who has developed a flair for blending reality and fiction through works like HBO’s “The Rehearsal” and Comedy Central’s “Nathan For You.” Oppenheim, his co-director, recently helmed another A24 hit, the Robert Pattinson-led “Primetime,” which has earned nearly $50 million against a $15 million budget.

Popular on Variety

Around 70% of opening weekend crowds were under 35 years old, and they liked what they saw onscreen. According to exit polls, 90% of ticket buyers would “definitely recommend” the film and 80% said it was “even better than expected.” Those reactions signal a long theatrical life for the movie, which is expanding nationwide in the weeks to come.

“This is a giant weekend for the genre,” says analyst David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Documentaries rarely receive a wide release — there’s only one every other year — and they average $3 million over their first three days.”

This year has been an exception with two major docs, the other being Amazon MGM’s “Melania,” a $40-million-budgeted glimpse at first lady Melania Trump. That film opened to $7.1 million from 1,778 theaters — at the time registering as the biggest opening for a non-music or concert doc in over a decade — and ended its run with $16.3 million. (“You Can See Everything” carries a budget in the single digits and will be much more profitable than “Melania.”)

Among its opening weekend bona fides, “You Can See Everything” secured the largest debut for any film playing on under 1,000 screens since 2006’s “Borat,” which ignited to $26 million from 837 theaters (not adjusted for inflation). And it’s the biggest opening for a documentary in over 20 years, since 2004’s seminal “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which premiered to $24 million from 868 theaters (not adjusted for inflation). Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are notable, not just for a documentary, but any arthouse release these days. By comparison, A24’s box office winner “The Drama,” anchored by two of Hollywood’s biggest stars in Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, opened earlier this year to $14.3 million from 3,087 theaters.

Elsewhere at the box office, “Street Fighter” collected another $20.1 million overseas for a decent global start of $51.1 million. Critics and audiences were lukewarm on the video game reboot, which landed a “B-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls and a 42% on Rotten Tomatoes. Directed by Kitao Sakurai and starring Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji, “Street Fighter” follows two estranged fighters who are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed “Street Fighter” for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution. The long-gestating film was originally set at Sony as part of Legendary’s pact with the studio and moved to Paramount once the initial deal expired. It’s the third movie based on the Capcom video game series following 1994’s box office winner “Street Fighter,” starring Jean-Claude Van Damme, and 2009’s misfire “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li.”

“Whalefall” and “Sense and Sensibility,” two other newcomers, launched in fourth and fifth place, respectively. Disney and 20th Century’s “Whalefall,” a survival thriller starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver swallowed by a sperm whale, missed expectations with $8 million from 3,065 locations. The movie also floundered at the international box office with $9.5 million from 51 territories for a global total of $17.5 million. Reception was mixed, with audiences bestowing a “B” grade on CinemaScore and critics’ reviews averaging a 71% on Rotten Tomatoes. “Whalefall” cost $60 million and requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales.

“Sense and Sensibility,” the latest remake of Jane Austen’s classic, opened to $7.2 million from 2,545 screens. The well-reviewed movie has earned $11 million internationally, bringing its worldwide tally to $18.5 million. Led by Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, the Focus Features film carries a $25 million budget and doesn’t have as high a hurdle to get out of the red.

Neither film was able to outperform Universal’s horror film “Other Mommy,” which claimed the No. 3 spot with $8.3 million in its second weekend. Despite a painful 70% decline from its debut, “Other Mommy” is already a hit with $44.8 million domestically and $78.7 million globally against a modest $18 million budget.

Among specialty releases, Netflix’s generation-spanning drama “La Bola Negra” collected $277,500 from four theaters in Los Angeles and New York — averaging $69,375 per location. Those returns stand as the second-highest screen average ever for a non-English language film behind 2019’s “Parasite,” which captured $393,216 from three theaters — averaging $131,072 per location. For a more recent comparison, Neon’s multilingual legal thriller “Fjord” debuted last weekend to $124,000 from four theaters — translating to $31,000 per location.

This weekend is notable because it’s the first time Netflix has ever reported box office grosses. The streamer plans to keep “La Bola Negra” in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times, before the film’s Netflix release on Dec. 2. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known as Los Javis, “La Bola Negra” was embraced at Cannes Film Festival with a 16-minute standing ovation and won Toronto Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award, which has become an Oscar precursor.

title: Inside ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment,’ Netflix’s Controversial Reality Series: ‘People Are Going to Have Very Strong Feelings’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: It is one of the most notorious social experiments ever conducted, inspiring numerous films, documentaries and psychological studies. In August of 1971, Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo recruited 24 male college students to participate in a study — funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research — about antisocial behavior and the effects of imprisonment. […]
content:
It is one of the most notorious social experiments ever conducted, inspiring numerous films, documentaries and psychological studies. In August of 1971, Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo recruited 24 male college students to participate in a study — funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research — about antisocial behavior and the effects of imprisonment. Selected students passed a psych screening and didn’t have criminal records or medical conditions. The psychology department was transformed into a mock prison replete with small cells, a corridor doubling as a prison yard and a closet for “solitary confinement, and for two weeks, at a rate of $15 a day ($124.79 in 2026), participants would be dropped into a simulated prison environment and assigned randomly to the role of prison guard or prisoner. They were referred to only by the number on their prison uniform as a form of dehumanization, and guards were encouraged to maintain order by any means necessary.

By Day 2 of the study, the inmates had staged a rebellion against the guards, using their beds to barricade themselves inside their cells; the guards responded by spraying the prisoners with fire extinguishers, forcing them to strip and sleep on the cold concrete floor. As the situation worsened, with guards exhibiting increasingly cruel forms of punishment and several prisoners suffering mental breakdowns, the Stanford prison experiment was ended on the sixth day. It’s now considered a colossal ethical failure due to its lack of safeguards for participants, neglecting to properly inform partakers of the parameters, poor oversight and the fact that the man conducting the experiment, Dr. Zimbardo, also served as the “prison” superintendent.

Popular on Variety

So, now would be the perfect time for a redo, right? Right?!

“The New Stanford Prison Experiment”, debuting Oct. 21 on Netflix, is meant to serve as a cultural corrective of sorts — an attempt to see if the Stanford prison experiment could actually yield valuable insights into the human condition if done correctly. It seeks to answer the question, “Does power corrupt?” And raises additional ones about conformity, dominance/submission, voyeurism and the bounds of reality television.

Executive produced by Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth (“Top Chef,” “Project Runway”) via their production company Alfred Street Industries, “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” takes thirty participants from diverse backgrounds, transports them to a decommissioned section of a real working prison — the Adult Detention Center in Cherokee County, Georgia — and simulates a prison environment over two weeks, assigning eight as guards (splitting them up between separate day shift and night shift teams) and 22 as prisoners.

“We were definitely nervous to take on something that has already failed — that is a nerve-wracking place to be — but we felt the question it was asking was very relevant and important today,” Lipsitz tells Variety. “Still, there were moments where we thought it would end on the same day that the original experiment did.” (More on that later.)

Whereas the original study was comprised of all white male college students (and one Asian American) from similar economic backgrounds, this new iteration features folks of all races and walks of life, including three women. Furthermore, the crew took pains to make sure the inmates or guards weren’t aware of the production, so as not to influence their decision-making, by having no crew members in the pod and everything shot on Robocam.

Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026

The show implemented a number of safeguards to ensure that things never went haywire, including “extensive background checks and psychological testing” for all participants, informed consent, medics and psychologists on call 24/7, a safe word (“pineapple”) if they ever felt they needed to leave or wanted to talk to a therapist and/or producer and a series of confessional interviews throughout the experiment. “The production paid for off-duty guards to be on hand in case anything got out of hand, so there were trained professionals on the spot who could handle anything that went awry,” explains Cutforth, including Major Boughner, who served as commander of both the real side of the correctional facility and the experimental pod.

There was also a panel of experts observing the inmates and guards at all times, and advising production on the ethics of the undertaking: Alison Wood Brooks, a behavioral scientist who teaches a course called “How to talk gooder in business and life” at Harvard Business School; Michael Cantrell, a former federal corrections officer; and Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist. And yes, participants in the experiment/reality show were paid, though Lipsitz and Cutforth were unable to disclose just how much.

“We did not want to pay them enough that they were doing this for the money because then it defeats the purpose of the experiment,” offers Lipsitz. “We were surprised by how many people wanted to do it. There’s no big prize at the end and you’re not meeting the love of your life. I think people wanted to understand what they were capable of and were interested in the concept of power, and what kinds of decisions they would make under these circumstances.”

“People wanted to challenge their own integrity and morality, and some people just wanted to see if they could stay in there for 14 days and eat prison food,” adds Cutforth.

Dan Cutforth and Jane Lipsitz. Getty Images

“The New Stanford Prison Experiment” establishes its uneasy tone early on. Upon entering the prison, the 22 inmates hear loud yelling and heckling through the walls, since there are real prisoners on the other side of them. “That was real,” maintains Lipsitz. “The moment when they were in there and the real inmates started to scream, it really did have a big effect on the people as they came in, and I think it was a contributing factor to some people dropping out,” says Cutforth. “It made them aware that this is not a joke.”

According to Lipsitz and Cutforth, six people ended up dropping out of the show after it became too intense for them, though not all of these people made the final cut. And unlike the original experiment, the Netflix series allowed those with criminal pasts to participate, such as “Scary” Larry Foy who, by his estimation, had spent over 300 days in jail and tells his cellmate that he’d tried to kill his brother. “Scary” Larry seems to not take well to being back behind bars from the get-go, but the show’s producers insist that everything remained safe. “There were definitely participants who had been to jail,” admits Lipsitz. “But we did very extensive background checks and psychological testing, and Larry had done a lot of recovery work and works as an advocate now for reform. He had changed his life pattern. It was very important to us to not put people into the population who posed a threat.”

Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026

Without giving too much away, the experiment takes a dark turn on day six — the same day the original experiment was terminated — as one team of guards quells a potential uprising by imposing a form of punishment seen as extreme by even the other guard shift. Things devolve from there, as the show implements several “interventions,” from asserting the hierarchy to a staggering role-reversal, that drastically alters the dynamic amongst the group. But Lipsitz and Cutforth are adamant that things never got too out of hand. “I would say that it was much more emotionally intense than physically intense,” she states. “There were moments of real concern, but the actual prison guards never had to go in and intercede.”

Overall, Lipsitz and Cutforth say they’re happy with the way “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” concludes and what the show reveals about its participants.

“This could have gone a million ways, but I think what it proved is that the question of, ‘Does power corrupt?’ wasn’t actually the right question to be asking,” Lipsitz says. “There were a lot of questions that this answered, but everyone is going to have their own POVs based on their own experiences and we want to leave it up to the viewers to decide.”

Cutforth concurs: “It’s going to cause conversations and people are going to have very strong feelings.”

title: ‘Dreadline Express’ Game Developer David Konecny Talks Stressful Player Choice & The Art Of Building A Psychological Horror
summary: For Czech developer David Konecny, Dreadline Express brings together a lifelong fascination with trains, psychological horror, and stories shaped by difficult choices. His debut game takes players aboard a train at the end of the world, where a distinctive card-based system lets them explore the lives of its varied passengers and see how their stories […]
content:
For Czech developer David Konecny, Dreadline Express brings together a lifelong fascination with trains, psychological horror, and stories shaped by difficult choices. His debut game takes players aboard a train at the end of the world, where a distinctive card-based system lets them explore the lives of its varied passengers and see how their stories and fates unfold. Drawing inspiration from games like Duke Nukem 3D and SOMA, as well as films made by Ari Aster, Konecny has created an unsettling world that challenges players to trust their instincts and confront morally complicated decisions.

Below, Konecy spoke to Deadline about his journey into game development, childhood influences, and the challenge of giving players the freedom to discover its secrets.

DEADLINE: You’re a solo game developer in the Czech Republic; this is the first game that you’re putting out, right?

Watch on Deadline

DAVID KONECNY: The situation is a little more complicated. It’s a solo project, but I have some coworkers who help me with art and audio because those are areas where I’m not as fluent as I’d like to be. I’m still developing the art direction, giving them concepts, drawing level layouts, and providing inspiration. Then we discuss the results. Everything comes from my head, but they help me bring it to life.

It’s my first commercial game. I’ve made some free titles, participated in game jams, and worked on a lot of projects that never saw the light of day because something always went terribly wrong and I couldn’t finish them. But, yeah, this is the first one.

DEADLINE: You’ve also been working in software development as your main job. But how long have you been making games, and how did you get started?

KONECNY: When I was little, we didn’t have computers, and I kept begging my parents to buy me magazines about games. I read about them without having any way to play them. I would look at the images and imagine how the games worked. I begged my parents to get me a computer or a game console.

I was also a tech-savvy child and interested in anything technological, so I asked them to sign me up for a children’s programming group. That’s where I gradually started to understand how things worked. I made my first little games, including text adventures in HTML. Later, I went to university to study programming and software development. That’s my career now. Thanks to games, I’m a software developer, and I think I’m a good one [laughs].

There weren’t any universities for game development at the time, so there wasn’t a way to learn it as a main career. The two big centers of game development in the Czech Republic were studios such as Altar and Bohemia Interactive, which made games like Operation Flashpoint. They were nowhere near my city, so there was no way for me to learn anything there. That’s why I started working in software development as my main career. But I always wanted to make games, and making games is different from making regular software. I kept learning about games in my free time, always creating and writing something.

Dreadline Express Shoreline Games

DEADLINE: What games did you play growing up that influenced how you think about game development?

KONECNY: The good thing was that every computer lab had a bunch of games installed on the computers. When the teacher wasn’t looking, we were all playing. I remember Warcraft II being a regular choice, but probably the most influential game for me was Duke Nukem 3D.

I really loved the world and all the little details that made the experience feel real. When you killed a monster, and it was under those doors that opened and closed, the door would crush the monster. When it opened again, you could see its innards stretched across the door. It was an immersive experience for me. I thought, “This is the best we can get. The game cannot be more realistic than this. This is it, guys. This is the stuff.”

I also loved how some levels changed. There was a level where you had to start a demolition, and the whole building collapsed, opening a new way forward. That was so innovative to me. Those experiences stayed with me, and I want to create a world that feels alive and real. That was huge for me.

DEADLINE: Let’s talk about Dreadline Express. It’s a train at the end of the world. When we spoke at Gamescom, you mentioned that people had compared it to Snowpiercer, although that wasn’t necessarily an inspiration you had in mind. Where did the idea originate, and how long had you been thinking about it?

KONECNY: There are a lot of inspirations, but I like trains. I think it all began when my great-grandmother used to take me to watch trains while she was looking after me. We’d go to an overpass and watch them from above. That’s one of my core memories.

The game itself came about during a period when I was having a crisis in game development. I stopped making games for two or three years and started writing short stories and novels. Nothing was ever published, but I was developing these stories, and eventually I came up with one about this train. I love trains, and I love Lovecraft. I also wanted to incorporate a totalitarian regime because it’s something that’s in our DNA as Czechs.

I put all these elements together and realized I wasn’t sure how I wanted the story to unfold, because everything seemed interesting and there were so many possible directions. The only logical decision was to make it a game so players could decide which path to take and which character’s story interested them most. That was the beginning of Dreadline Express. The card mechanics came later, and that’s a completely different story.

DEADLINE: Talk about the card mechanics. Players have a lot of control over what they discover, and this system is a distinctive way to approach storytelling. Why did you decide to use cards?

KONECNY: Originally, it came from Steam Trading Cards, the cards you get for playing games that you can sell or combine. It’s a dopamine mechanism that Steam has built in. I always found it a little strange. I wondered, “Why is it there? I’m playing games, and I don’t need another reward for playing because the game itself is a reward.” It’s not like you’re doing your taxes and get a card. That would be cool, actually. If you filled out your taxes and got something, that would be nice [laughs]. I started thinking about how to take these cards, which people obviously love collecting, and turn them into a proper game mechanic. Completing a full set feels good, but I wanted the cards to give players more than the satisfaction of unlocking something. I wanted them to provide options. That’s how the idea was born.

I wanted to create a gameplay loop where you get a card, discover something, and immediately start thinking: “OK, I have this new item, this new thing. How can I use it? What can I combine it with? What possibilities will it open up for me?”That’s why I chose cards. They’re cool; they let us create really nice illustrations, and a lot of love goes into them.

Dreadline Express Shoreline Games

DEADLINE: Let’s talk about the art design, both the cards and the game itself. The characters have these angular pixelated features that give them an unsettling quality. What look were you and the art team going for, and why?

KONECNY: One consideration was that we’re not a huge team with a huge budget, so we need to make things quickly and work within our limitations. This PS1-style, low-resolution, pixelated graphics approach is great for horror because it leaves something to the player’s imagination. It suits these stories much better than photorealistic graphics do because players can fill in the gaps, making the experience more immersive.

I also really wanted the characters to be distinctive, so we went a little over the top with their designs. We gave them really sharp features, which become even more pronounced with that low-resolution style. You really see those edges, and that makes them more memorable. I wanted the characters to be a little horrifying. The idea was to show how the train had taken something from them, a part of their humanity. They’re sitting there, and you can see how crumbled they are and how they don’t blink.

DEADLINE: They look a little gothic and spooky. What did you want players to feel when they first encountered these characters?

KONECNY: I wanted players to feel a little afraid of the characters when they first meet them, when they stare at you with those dead eyes. Then, as you start talking to them and gradually understand their stories, I wanted you to find your way toward them. You might initially feel repulsed by them or genuinely afraid, but eventually you might feel sorry for them or find some connection with them.

DEADLINE: What other games, films or filmmakers influenced the horror in Dreadline Express?

KONECNY: I really love good psychological horror. Off the top of my head, I can think of Ari Aster’s Hereditary and Midsommar. The Menu is also great horror. I like it when it’s about the story rather than jump scares or a monster that’s simply bad because it’s bad. I love it when everything has layers.

We have antagonists on the train, of course, but even they have their own stories. I love the ambiguity of it, where nothing is entirely good or bad, and you have to decide for yourself. Another example is Hellraiser, because I really love the Cenobites. They’re not bad guys. They want to show you something incredible from their perspective, but it might not be so incredible for humans. It’s really interesting to look at something from different points of view. The psychological aspect is even more interesting than the body horror. If you look at something from different perspectives, it becomes really compelling. That’s what I wanted to put into this game.

In terms of games, Frictional Games is probably my favorite horror studio, especially because of SOMA. It’s psychological horror, and it connects to some of your internal fears. It makes you think about your life in different contexts. For me, it was a life-changing experience. I always wanted to make something that could stick in people’s minds and make them think about the game or the story after they finish it. That’s really important to me.

Dreadline Express Shoreline Games

DEADLINE: What was the biggest challenge in developing the game, whether narratively, in terms of level design or otherwise?

KONECNY: The first thing is that I’m making a horror game in which you cannot die. That’s unusual compared with games like Resident Evil, Silent Hill and Dead Space. The biggest challenge, though, is that I’m putting a lot of trust in the player. I let them discover clues and figure out how to play for themselves. That’s a big part of the experience. Players need to feel clever, like, “I did this. I figured it out. The developer didn’t tell me anything, and I managed to find a way.”

It’s hard to strike the right balance. You want to provide just enough clues without making things too obvious. That was a huge challenge. I traveled with the game to different conventions and game development events for a year and a half, collecting data and asking people questions to find the right balance. That was a huge part of development. I hope I nailed it, but we’ll see.

DEADLINE: What do you hope players take away from Dreadline Express?

KONECNY: I hope they find a game that values their time, doesn’t overstay its welcome, and gives them exactly the experience they want to have. I’m especially looking forward to seeing players talk to each other about their different experiences with the game. I hope it creates conversations and discoveries, maybe even brings some people together. I’m excited about that sense of discovery.

Maybe someone will learn something about themselves based on the choices they make, who they sacrifice, or how they approach different situations. I think we have something quite big prepared for the ending, and I hope as many people as possible will really appreciate it. Maybe if it makes someone cry, I’ll be happy [laughs].

Dreadline Express is now available on Steam.

title: ‘Street Fighter’ Rings Up No. 1 $51M+ WW Opening, Largely Driven By Fans – Global Box Office Update
summary: With the Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes documentary craze currently a stateside thing, Paramount/Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter was the ringleader at the worldwide weekend B.O. with a $51.1M global opening. Of that $20.1M came from 65 markets with the lionshare stateside with $31M. Again, this is several kicks up from what Street Fighter did in its […]
content:
With the Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes documentary craze currently a stateside thing, Paramount/Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter was the ringleader at the worldwide weekend B.O. with a $51.1M global opening. Of that $20.1M came from 65 markets with the lionshare stateside with $31M.

Again, this is several kicks up from what Street Fighter did in its last big-screen appearance with Jean- Claude Van Damme in 1994, that pic opening to $6.8M domestic, and ending its run at $33.4M stateside, and $99.4M global (all unadjusted for inflation and currency swings).

Though Street Figther‘s opening round is lower than expected (a $70M worldwide opening was hoped for), I understand that this $82M net production will be fine in the end after all ancillaries per those in the know. For the Skydance owned Paramount, this is a distribution deal. Capcom and Legendary co-funded the movie.

Watch on Deadline

Why the lower then anticipated opening? It was essentially the older fans who showed up and nobody else. Also, with a PG-13 rating, the hope is that an expanded family audience would come out for Street Fighter in a way that they couldn’t for the R-rated Mortal Kombat, based on another Gen X videogame.

The reported opening on Mortal Kombat II was $63M WW with $23M from 78 territories on 31K screens. In like-for-likes, Street Fighter‘s foreign start of $20.1M is 4% ahead of Mortal Kombat 2 and 2% ahead of Free Guy.

Street Fighter was shot for Imax, which did $7.7M in its global network; broken out that’s $5.4M in North America (18% of the weekend) and $2.3M from 471 screens offshore.

The No. 1 openings were in UK ($3.3M at 593 sites), Mexico ($1.8M at 865 sites), Australia ($1.6M at 260 locations), Panama ($228K) and Taiwan ($235K at 90 locations) and Indonesia with $384K at 480 theaters.

No. 2s were Brazil ($1.2M at 726 locations), Malaysia ($491K at 138 locations), Hong Kong ($201K at 55 sites), Thailand ($200K at 257 locations) as well as UAE with $705K at 58 locations. Overall, the total Middle East region grossed $1.4M.

The Kitao Sakurai directed movie was No. 3 in Germany ($850K at 436 theaters), Philippines with $275K at 206 theaters, and Colombia with $227K.

The raging riots against the police curbed moviegoing in France where Street Fighter was No. 4 with $1.1M at 355 locations. Spain was also 4th with $550K at 298 locations in addition to Netherlands with $314K at 86 locales.

In Japan, Street Fighter was the second MPA title in the market with $875K at 333 locations for a No. 5 rank. Also, the movie swung low in Italy with $451K at 250 locations. Korea didn’t have a front seat to the movie with a No. 8 $242K opening at 435 locations. Meanwhile in India, Street Fighter did $431K at 1,064 locations; that’s where the Nelson Dilipkumar directed action title Jailer 2 reigned with an estimated $18M (and global around $32M for a No. 2 rank). We’ll have more official figures on Jailer 2 from Rentrak later.

RESIDENT EVIL , Austin Abrams, 2026. © Sony Pictures Releasing / Courtesy Everett Collection

Austin Abrams is more popular in his Sony/Constantin movie Resident Evil than Disney/20th Century Studio’s Whalefall, a $22.6M WW fifth weekend (3rd place) to awful $17.5M global bow (6th place)

The second big screen take of a Capcom game in the market, Resident Evil, saw $17.1M (-36%) from overseas at 67 markets and 31K screens with $5.5M domestic. Running global cume is $361.1M ($212.7M of that from foreign). Top-performing markets by cume are China $56.0M, UK $18.2M, Mexico $12.4M, Australia $9.1M, Japan $8.5M, France $8.5M, Germany $8.2M, and Spain $7.7M. Constantin has Germany speaking territories with Metropolitan handling France and Sony the rest of the world.

Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios’ WHALEFALL. © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved. 20th Century Studios

It was one of the best thrillers of 2023 on the New York Times list, which is why 20th made it. Some rival distribution sources believe that Disney would have best positioned Whalefall as a genre film so that it could over perform, however, they couldn’t alienate the book’s fans. While Whalefall on its net $60M production cost tanked with a No. 4 opening, somewhere in the world it was No. 1 and that was in Bosnia, Kuwait and Sauda Arabia ($400K). UK was high at $700K. The pic was No. 2 in China ($700K), Korea (wow, beating Street Fighter with $400K), Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Bahrain, Croatia, Iraq, Jordan, Lithuania, Oman, Qatar and UAE ($400K). The Brian Duffield directed movie was No. 3 in Japan ($500K) as well as Philippines Lebanon, Serbia, Slovenia and Ecuador. Disney says Whalefall opened within the top 5 US films in Mexico ($800K, best territory for the movie), Germany ($500K), Italy ($400K), Spain, and Brazil. France did $500K.

Universal/Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s second weekend of Other Mommy was fourth with a $17.9M WW take ($9.5M int’l at 65 territories, $8.3M domestic, -70% on that D+ CinemaScore). Big running global cume at $78.7M ($33.9M foreign, $44.8M domestic) off that net $19M production price tag. That beats the reported cume of Jessica Chastain’s spooky movie Crimson Peak ($74.6M WW), but it still has a way to go if it’s going to overtake her Mama ($146.4M WW).

Other Mommy in France did $1.2M at 264 screens which included $118K previews. The standard opening was above Speak No Evil. Belgium bowed to $170K, No. 2 in the market behind The Odyssey, across 70 screens. An opening at this level is above The Black Phone and well above Black Phone 2. Holdovers included UK/Ireland with $1.2M in weekend 2 and a $5M cume, ahead of Black Phone. Italy delivered a second frame of $1M for a No. 2 behind a local title and a $3.7M cume, ahead of the lifetimes of Weapons and Evil Dead Rise. Mexico minted $900K with a $3.4M cume. Spain did $600K for a $2.3M running cume, ahead of Black Phone and Speak No Evil. Australia was $500K for $1.9M cume, in line with Black Phone 2.

Fifth around the globe was Amazon MGM Studio’s third weekend of Colleen Hoover’s Verity with $17.6M WW ($11.4M int’l and $6.2M domestic). Worldwide stands at $145.3M ($79.2M offshore, $66.2M North America). The movie clicked past Regretting You ($90.4M WW) as Hoover’s second best around the world a while ago, and it will remain that way as It Ends With Us is such high bar at $351.4M WW.

Dakota Johnson, Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett are still No. 1 in Germany with $1.9M (-27%) at 685 screens and a near $10M cume. Slovakia opened to $140K from 80 screens for a No. 1 rank, by far the biggest opening for a Hoover book adaptation there. Brazil still great with a No. 2 of $1.2M at 1,000 screens, -40% for a $9.1M cume. UK posted $1.5M at 657 screens, down -43% and a No. 3 rank for a running tally of $12.6M.

title: Curtain Up: ‘La Bola Negra’ Shines As Netflix Shares Grosses In Historic First — Specialty Box Office
summary: Netflix’s Spanish drama La Bola Negra debuted to $277.5k on four screens – these numbers coming directly from the giant streamer Sunday in its first ever official box office grosses. The TIFF audience award-winner saw $108.3k Friday and $84.6k on Saturday leading into a strong three-day per screen average of $69.4k for the company’s inaugural […]
content:
Netflix‘s Spanish drama La Bola Negra debuted to $277.5k on four screens – these numbers coming directly from the giant streamer Sunday in its first ever official box office grosses.

The TIFF audience award-winner saw $108.3k Friday and $84.6k on Saturday leading into a strong three-day per screen average of $69.4k for the company’s inaugural report.

The film, based on an unfinished play of the same name by Federico García Lorca, launched at the Paris Theater and Angelika in New York, and AMC Century City and Burbank in LA. Netflix is giving the festival favorite a 45-day theatrical window in a new era of box office reporting overseen by global theatrical distribution head Spencer Klein. It will expand in NY/LA and add major markets over the next few weeks ahead of a wider break 11/6.

House records, as per Netflix, reflect the highest opening gross for a non-English language film at the Angelika, The Paris and AMC Century City (excluding dubbed anime) and, more broadly, the second-highest per-screen average for a non-English language film of all time. And the highest per-screen average ever for a Spanish film.

Watch on Deadline

Buzz for the film began at its Cannes world premiere where helmers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi shared Best Director for the R-rated, era-spanning story that went on to beguile the festival circuit. Spain’s Oscar entry for Best International Feature follows the interconnected lives of three gay men.

Netflix gave the film a full theatrical marketing campaign including out-of-home, social, standees, trailers and community screenings, along with bespoke elements. A poetry salon hosted by John Cameron Mitchell and modeled on Lorca’s secret 1930s intellectual gatherings, brought filmmakers and cast together to honor Lorca’s lasting influence on queer art and culture ahead of the NYC premiere last Thursday at NewFest. Marketing will be key for and upcoming titles as the company seeks to draw moviegoers into seats.

The streamer release Guitarricadelafuente’s single from the film, ‘La Nieve,’ (The Snow) on Sept. 18. The musician made his acting debut in the film, which also stars Milo Quifes and Carlos González., with Glenn Close and Penélope Cruz.

Reactions from in-theater audience exit surveys were strong with 96% rating La Bola Negra Excellent or Very Good (80% Excellent), and 87% giving it a Definite Recommend. The film skewed male (66%) and young, with 51% under 35 and 25 to 34 year-olds the largest age group at 39%.

It’s Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh with critics at 87%.

Upcoming Netflix releases set for wider theatrical release and significant windows include The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth by David Fincher; Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew; animated feature Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory: by Taika Waititi; The Mosquito Bowl by Peter Berg and Danny Boyle’s Ink.

More to come

title: Georgina Cates Dead: BBC Star & ‘Clay Pigeons’ Actress Was 51
summary: Georgina Cates, the actress known for her roles in Clay Pigeons (1998) and several BBC projects, has died. She was 51. On Saturday, BBC’s 2point4 Children creator Andrew Marshall announced Cates’ passing, years after her breakout role as Jenny Porter on the sitcom when she was 16 years old. She had reportedly died in May, […]
content:
Georgina Cates, the actress known for her roles in Clay Pigeons (1998) and several BBC projects, has died. She was 51.

On Saturday, BBC’s 2point4 Children creator Andrew Marshall announced Cates’ passing, years after her breakout role as Jenny Porter on the sitcom when she was 16 years old. She had reportedly died in May, and a cause of death was not immediately made available.

“I’m very sad to report, I have just discovered, that lovely and talented Claire Woodgate aka Georgina Cates, our first Jenny in 2p4 died last May,” wrote Marshall on X. “I have no other details than than on IMDb. Sympathies to her family and children. If anyone has further details to share, please do.”

Marshall’s post comes after Cates and ex-husband Skeet Ulrich’s daughter Naiia announced her mother’s death in June.

Watch on Deadline

“My beautiful, free-spirited mom lived a hard life and still found ways to make herself and others laugh and smile <3 now she can rest easy,” she wrote on Instagram. “I will always see you in black and white photos, Virginia slims, baggy clothes, no bras, big sunglasses, doodling while talking, pleasers, and flip flops and everything in between.”

I’m very sad to report, I have just discovered, that lovely and talented Claire Woodgate aka Georgina Cates, our 1st Jenny in 2p4 died last May. I have no other details than than on IMDb. Sympathies to her family and children. If anyone has further details to share, please do. — Andrew Marshall (@AndrewM2p4c) October 17, 2026

Naiia continued, “I love you, thank you for your creativity, curiosity and your bravery to always be true to yourself – no matter what.”

Born Claire Elaine Woodgate on April 4, 1975 in Colchester, Essex, England, Cates broke out in the first two seasons of 2point4, before appearing in such shows as The Ruth Rendell Mysteries, The Bill and Chris Cross, in addition to roles in movies like An Exchange of Fire (1993), Au Pair (1994), An Awfully Big Adventure (1995), Frankie Starlight (1995), Big City Blues (1997) and A Soldier’s Sweetheart (1998).

Also in 1998, Cates earned acclaim for her performance as Amanda in the Ridley Scott-produced Clay Pigeons, also starring Vince Vaughn and Joaquin Pheonix.

In 2007, following a years-long hiatus from acting, Cates won the Best Actress in a Leading Role award for her performance in Sinner during the 41st Brooklyn Arts Council International Film & Video Festival.

Cates is survived by her children Naiia and Jakob, whom she shared with ex-husband Skeet Ulrich.

title: ‘Monday Night’ Friction? ESPN NFL Broadcasters Joe Buck & Troy Aikman Have Noisy Start To Super Bowl Year
summary: NFL announcing duo Joe Buck and Troy Aikman, who helped revive Monday Night Football after moving to ESPN in 2022, now find themselves at the center of one of the NFL’s dishiest off-field dramas. Money, as usual, is seen as the root cause. Buck last month agreed to a contract renewal with ESPN parent Disney, […]
content:
NFL announcing duo Joe Buck and Troy Aikman, who helped revive after moving to ESPN in 2022, now find themselves at the center of one of the NFL’s dishiest off-field dramas.

Money, as usual, is seen as the root cause.

Buck last month agreed to a contract renewal with ESPN parent Disney, with the 5-year deal reportedly worth $108 million. He has branched out to non-sports fare, guest-hosting Good Morning America and hosting streaming quiz show Sports Jeopardy!

Aikman, meanwhile, has yet to re-sign, with his current contract set to expire after the Super Bowl, which ESPN will carry for the first time next February. (Sibling broadcast network ABC will have the big game for the first time since 2006.)

Watch on Deadline

The pair, who called games together on Fox for 20 years, are said to have clashed over the differing contract status. Front Office Sports last week detailed a heated exchange between the two witnessed by a number of colleagues prior to last Monday’s L.A. Rams-Buffalo Bills game.

Aikman did not push back on the report when asked about it during an appearance on Dallas-Fort worth radio station KTCK-FM. “Well, I think there’s probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed,” he said with a chuckle. “I don’t know if now is the time. I don’t know that it’s hard to figure out kind of what happened.”

The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback said he plans to continue as MNF analyst through the end of the season. “I’ll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens,” he said. “But I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold, with the Super Bowl and all that and where my next landing spot may be.”

Meadowlark Media co-founder Dan Le Batard, who had his own stormy relationship with ESPN during a decade as a host there, said on his daily podcast Friday that he was stunned by Aikman’s comments. He said he interpreted them as “‘I’m not coming back.’ And it’s before the Super Bowl! They’ve got to work together!” Le Batard also blamed Buck for the reported sequence of events. “I can understand where Troy would be very upset if Joe Buck just negotiated his own deal.”

Disney put Buck and Aikman onstage last May toward the top of its upfront presentation to advertisers, an event that also featured remarks from Josh D’Amaro, who succeeded Bob Iger as CEO last February. As chief exec, D’Amaro has reaffirmed that ESPN, rumored over the years to be a spinoff candidate, is very much a part of the corporate portfolio.

Prior to the past week’s bumps, Buck and Aikman had been having a smooth ride. The pair’s jump from Fox injected restored energy and credibility to MNF, with many sports media pundits reaffirming their view that the duo is the best in the business. Before 2022, the onetime prime-time pioneer cycled through a succession of announcers and received increasingly middling games on the NFL schedule, which led to stagnating ratings and frustrated ad buyers.

Times have changed at ESPN, however, thanks to a sweeping deal with the NFL that exchanged a 10% stake in the network for control of media assets including NFL Network. The ownership ties open up intriguing possibilities, with speculation centering on numerous candidates to succeed Aikman.

Two of the most intriguing names being bandied about are Peyton Manning and Travis Kelce. The former’s company, Omaha Productions, is part-owned by the NFL and Manning is a ubiquitous media presence on top of his Hall of Fame playing credentials. Kelce is still playing for the Kansas City Chiefs but is of course even better known to the masses as Taylor Swift’s ball and chain.

An ESPN rep declined to comment when contacted by Deadline. After news of Buck’s re-upping surfaced last month, the company issued a statement saying it was determined to focus on its historic Super Bowl broadcast, which Disney is hyping with a year-long promotional blitz. “To that end, we won’t be addressing talent contract specifics publicly before the Super Bowl,” the statement said.

Deadline encountered the same sentiment from multiple sources in the ESPN orbit in recent days, who noted that the big game is nearly four months away, leaving time for some climate change. “A lot can happen between now and then,” one said.

Despite those efforts to calm the waters, a fairly broad consensus has formed that Aikman is a short-timer at ESPN.

“It sure feels like goodbye, doesn’t it?” said Bryan Curtis of the Ringer during an appearance on Jimmy Traina’s Underscore Media podcast Friday. “It sure does,” Traina replied.

They both went on to marvel at the turn of events for MNF and the tensions in the broadcast booth “spilling out into the public in this weird, weird way,” as Curtis put it. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro’s “biggest win before he resigned the NFL deal,” he added, was “getting Joe and Troy away from Fox because it solved the problem. It was over. … And for the drama to be located over there now, what a turnaround that is.”

title: Jesse Eisenberg Says He ‘Couldn’t Get Movie Studio Parts Anymore’ After Winning A Razzie For ‘Batman v Superman’: ‘The Industry Did Not Want Me to Be in a Superhero Movie’
summary: Jesse Eisenberg has said he was frozen out of studio movies after winning a Razzie for Zack Snyder’s “Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice.” The Razzies — short for Golden Raspberry Awards — are a tongue-in-cheek ceremony that “honor” the supposedly worst films of the year. They are traditionally handed out the night before the […]
content:
Jesse Eisenberg has said he was frozen out of studio movies after winning a Razzie for Zack Snyder’s “Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice.”

The Razzies — short for Golden Raspberry Awards — are a tongue-in-cheek ceremony that “honor” the supposedly worst films of the year. They are traditionally handed out the night before the Oscars.

Eisenberg, who played arch villain Lex Luther opposite Henry Cavill and Ben Affleck, was allocated a worst supporting actor Razzie for his part in the 2016 superhero flick.

Although supposedly lighthearted, the “award” damaged his acting career, Eisenberg admitted during a screen talk Sunday as part of the BFI London Film Festival, causing him to step back from acting and instead lean in to writing and directing. (Eisenberg’s latest directorial effort, “The Debut” starring Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, is closing LFF Sunday night).

Popular on Variety

“Listen, a lot of it just came from fear,” he said of his career pivot. “I couldn’t get into movie studio parts anymore because I had won a Raspberry Award from [being in the] ‘Batman’ movie … and I saw the trajectory.”

“If you’re an actor, you’re constantly panicked about ‘Am I on an upslope or a downslope?’” he explained. “Because there’s no plateau. Acting is just this unstable, awful industry where you are either on the treadmill and you’re doing okay and you’re running up or you are yesterday’s news and it’s awful. And if you’re a paranoid person like me, you see it way in advance.”

“So I was like, I’ve got to direct movies. That’s why I started writing them, just to kind of keep my career afloat, really.”

“Batman v Superman,” which opened globally with an impressive $424.1 million box office, took home four Razzies overall, including for worst screenplay, worst sequel and worst screen combo for Cavill and Affleck. Eisenberg has previously said the film’s “poor” reception damaged his career.

At the BFI talk, the actor said his takeaway from the experience was that he shouldn’t star in any more superhero films. “The industry tells you what they want from you,” Eisenberg said. “The industry did not want me to be in a superhero movie, and if you’re smart and self-aware, you learn that quickly. And you know, it’s the unsuccessful actor that goes ‘No, I want to be in more of those.’ It’s not going to happen and they don’t want you there and they wouldn’t have given you a Raspberry Award if they wanted you there. That’s an award for bad acting. And so the industry tells you what it wants and if you want a career in the arts you have to follow the things that you’re being told are liked.”

One role the industry did want to see him reprise was that of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, given Eisenberg was nominated for a best actor Oscar for playing the tech titan in 2010’s “The Social Network,” penned by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher.

Despite that, the actor has been adamant he did not want to return in the recently-released follow-up “The Social Reckoning,” which Sorkin both wrote and directed. He didn’t expand on that decision during his LFF talk, other than to say the “companion movie,” as it has been dubbed, “is quite different.”

He was more open about working with Kieran Culkin in Eisenberg’s sophomore directorial effort “A Real Pain,” which was released in 2024. The movie scored Eisenberg a nod for best screenplay and Culkin a best supporting actor win at last year’s Oscars, but the film could have turned out very differently.

“We didn’t know if Kieran was ever going to show up to Poland,” Eisenberg revealed. “Emma Stone is producing the movie. She personally took him on the plane to Poland [where it was shooting] because we didn’t know if he was going to show up. She sent me a video of him going through customs, saying ‘We are here!’ and then he still was late.”

And Culkin, who’d recently come off HBO’s mega-hit “Succession,” was adamant he wanted Eisenberg to use a similar “spontaneous” shooting style, which had not been part of the plan. “We’re like, what’s best for the movie?” the actor/director recalled as he tried to work out what to do. “And I guess what’s best for the movie is probably following this live wire around because that’s the engine of the movie anyway. If he had a small part, you’d be like, ‘We just have to tell this guy to shut up,’ you know? But he’s the lead… So it was a real learning curve.”

title: ‘Capturing Bigfoot’ Review: An Astounding Documentary Uncovers the Truth
summary: "Capturing Bigfoot" is an amazing documentary about the legend of Bigfoot — about how it was born, how it took hold, and how that iconic piece of film footage came to be. It’s a documentary that answers all the questions and solves all the mysteries. Unlike your typical film about UFOs, it doesn’t leave you with that vague feeling of "The truth is still out there, and I’m not sure what it is." "Capturing Bigfoot" shows you the truth, but what it really shows you is what that truth says about us, a society that went down the rabbit hole of wanting to believe and now, increasingly, lives there.
content:
“ ” doesn’t waste time getting to the hairy meat of the matter. It opens with the shaky, grainy 16mm footage that’s the most widely viewed piece of cinéma vérité in history apart from the Zapruder film. It even looks like the Zapruder film — though the setting, in this case, is a woods, full of birch trees and sunlight and vivid autumn color. For a few moments, the image jerks around in a raw amateur way. Then it grows steadier, and there, about 100 feet away from the camera, an ape-like figure walks along in front of the forest foliage, turning its head for an instant to look at the cameraman, then continuing on its way.

This famous evidence of the creature known as Bigfoot was shot by a man named Roger Patterson in Northern California on Oct. 20, 1967. The footage lasts just 59 seconds. We don’t get to spend much time gawking at the creature (it’s only a tantalizing glimpse), but he’s there just long enough for us to notice several things. The hair on his back looks a bit shiny. And is it our imagination, or is this primitive creature not just walking but strolling, with a rather jaunty sense of purpose?

Popular on Variety

Why did this footage possess the world? As an opening title informs us, “No one has ever been able to determine whether the film is real or a hoax.” Then it adds, “Until now.” “Capturing Bigfoot” is an astounding documentary about the legend of Bigfoot — about how it was born, how it took hold, and how that iconic piece of film footage came to be. It’s a documentary that answers all the questions and solves all the mysteries. Unlike your typical film about UFOs, it doesn’t leave you with that vague feeling of “The truth is still out there, and I’m still not sure what it is.” “Capturing Bigfoot” shows you the truth, but what it really shows you is what that truth says about us, a society that went down the rabbit hole of wanting to believe and now, increasingly, lives there.

“Capturing Bigfoot” is being released at the perfect moment, when belief in the uncanny has been given a new “credibility” by the testimony of select U.S. military officials about the reality of UAPs — but, at the same time, certain legendary mythologies about an existence beyond ours have now been unmasked as hoaxes. For decades, the 1934 photograph of the Loch Ness Monster was a haunting image of a lost world. In 1994, it was revealed that two men had created that image out of woody putty attached to a toy submarine. And in 1991, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley explained that they created the crop-circle phenomenon by going into a field and making one, in 1978, after an evening spent at a pub. As someone who’d spent many hours gawking in wonder at photographs of crop circles, I greeted the revelation of that hoax with a crestfallen fascination. I no longer flirted with the teasing possibility that crop circles could have been created by a force from another world. Somehow, though, the melting down of that possibility made our own world seem smaller.

But the Bigfoot legend never loomed in that way, at least not for me, because there was always something fishy about it. Starting with this: If there was a “Bigfoot” living in the woods of Northern California in the late 1960s, wouldn’t it have been seen by someone other than Roger Patterson and his camera? Marq Evans, the director of “Capturing Bigfoot,” digs into the Bigfoot legend with an investigator’s wide-eyed curiosity and cunning. For a while, he zeroes in on Patterson, the Zapruder of the saga, who died in 1972. The film goes back to paint a portrait of this eccentric resident of Yakima, Wash., who became obsessed with the idea of oversize simian humanoids going back to the late ’50s.

Patterson, with his light drawl and camera-ready affability, might have stepped out of the ancient version of an Errol Morris film, back when Morris was the snarkster of “Gates of Heaven.” His obsession was touched off by an article in True magazine in 1959 (we see the article; it was entitled “America’s Abominable Snowman”). And, of course, the legend that Bigfoot emerged from had actually been around for centuries, going back to the Himalayan myth of the Yeti (in British Columbia, it became the Sasquatch).

Patterson would take his young son on camping trips in a VW van into the mountains of Northern California, on the lookout for Bigfoot. He would stuff two live horses into the van — an indication, right there, that he had a bit of a screw loose. But he was cosplaying at being a cowboy. He was a rodeo rider, and with his rifle and cowboy hat and drawling aw-shucks attitude, he made himself into a camera-ready character. His ingenuity was tapping into what we might, at the time, have called National Enquirer culture: its tall tales and its legion of readers. This was the true silent majority of the new America. We see old footage of interviews with people who claim to have had Bigfoot sightings, which are just like the interviews with people who claim to have had alien encounters.

Patterson’s son, Clint, now in his late 60s, is the documentary’s central figure. He resembles Bill Paxton, and he’s like a Bill Paxton character. “When I came out of my mom’s vagina,” says Clint, “they put a cowboy hat on me.” He means that literally. (It tells you what you need to know about this family.) Clint, for most of “Capturing Bigfoot,” remains a true believer in his dad’s 59-second Bigfoot film. And there are expert witnesses who testify as to why it has to be authentic. One is Dr. Jeff Meldrum, a professor of anatomy at Idaho State University, where he’s got an “Evolutionary Morphology Laboratory” that’s essentially a Bigfoot room, with models, evidence, and an example of the 16mm camera Roger Patterson used. Meldrum says that watching the footage, he can identify detailed muscle groups in Bigfoot, and that the creature is clearly real. (One interesting detail: The Bigfoot we see in the footage is female. She has mammary glands.) And Bill Munns, who worked as a make-up artist at Universal Studios starting in 1969, explains that the image of Bigfoot in the footage could not have been a man in a costume. Even Hollywood, he says, did not have the technology at the time to make an ape-man look that good.

But then the movie starts to piece together the story of how the footage came into existence. Roger Patterson was, among other things, a canny DIY visual artist who, in 1966, wrote and published a book about Bigfoot entitled “Do Abominable Snowmen of America Really Exist.” It was illustrated with his lavish drawings. And Clint Patterson talks about how as a boy, he once went into his father’s shed, which was usually locked, and found a pile of second-hand fur coats.

Using his 59-second film, Roger Patterson was able to turn Bigfoot into a phenomenon. He went on the talk-show circuit (Johnny Carson, Merv Griffin, Art Linklater), making himself into a found-object celebrity. The Bigfoot footage, as Clint puts it, “went viral before the word viral even existed.” It was given credibility by being featured in scientific magazines, as if it were an anthropological discovery. And the film, in its Zapruder-like “authenticity,” was seen, in its very semiotics, as a document of something real. Patterson played it in movie theaters, on a road-show tour, charging $2 a ticket, then moving on to the next town. In the Salt Palace in Salt Lake City, one of his associates recalls that “We played two weeks after Simon and Garfunkel, and took more money out of the building than they did.”

The money, which added up to many millions in today’s dollars, was a blessing and a curse. Much of it went, mysteriously, to Patterson’s brother-in-law, Al DeAtly, who used it to rescue his construction company, fashioning himself into the lead contractor in the state of Washington (where he built a country mansion as large and gaudy as Mar-A-Lago). But one of Patterson’s most loyal associates, Bob Gimlin (interviewed in the documentary), got nothing. That said, he is still on the Bigfoot convention circuit.

On the dark underside of the 59-second Bigfoot film lies a tawdry family drama. There is greed and infighting, all buried in the murk of a secret that must be maintained at all costs. Marq Evans uncovers the secret. He has assembled the documentary with resounding suspense, and he finds the smoking gun. It is a lost piece of 16mm film footage shot in 1966, the year before the famous Bigfoot footage, and what it shows is a kind of rehearsal for it. We also meet an associate of Patterson’s, a man named Bob Hieronymus, who has a familiar loping walk.

“Capturing Bigfoot” reveals that the 1967 footage of Bigfoot was a hoax, and in that sense you could say that the story is over and done with. Roger Patterson was a classic American snake-oil salesman who figured out how to con the media age. But one of the key themes of the documentary is that Patterson, with his ingenious little fake film, didn’t just create an outlandish legend. He created a reality that took on a life of its own. He created the “evidence” to make magical thinking real, and I don’t think it’s overstating things to say that you can draw a direct line from the true-believer world of Bigfoot to the true-believer world that so many exist in today, whether its UAP obsession or the wacked conspiracy theory that says the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Bigfoot or no Bigfoot, we’re all living on the Planet of the Ape Believers.

title: Taylor Swift Fires Up Academy Gala With Four Songs in Her First Band Performance Since the Eras Tour
summary: Taylor Swift got some of the old gang back together for her first full-band performance since the Eras Tour, delivering a four-song set to a black-tie audience Saturday night at the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala. Conan O’Brien introduced her by saying, “It’s an insane, unprecedented honor to introduce a cherished member of our little […]
content:
Taylor Swift got some of the old gang back together for her first full-band performance since the Eras Tour, delivering a four-song set to a black-tie audience Saturday night at the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala.

Conan O’Brien introduced her by saying, “It’s an insane, unprecedented honor to introduce a cherished member of our little ‘Toy Story 5‘ family. She’s John, Paul, George and Ringo all in one.”

As an indicator of just how long she’s been off any kind of regular performance circuit, the gala-capping show included Swift’s first-ever live rendering of “The Fate of Ophelia,” the smash hit single she released just over a year ago, on Oct. 3, 2025. The song is expected to be a leading contender for record of the year and other categories at the 2027 Grammys, for which Recording Academy voters just received their first ballots.

Popular on Variety

🚨| Taylor Swift performing "The Fate of Ophelia" for the very first time at the Academy Museum Gala! pic.twitter.com/w1Pidc32mh — The Eras Tour (@tswifterastour) October 18, 2026

As expected, she also sang her contender for the 2027 Oscars, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” from the Pixar film “Toy Story 5.” It wasn’t her first live performance ever of that song — she did it at the Grammy Museum and at a private Ross House FYC showcase — but it was her first time singing it live with a full band, and not as part of a mash-up. Besides its Oscar eligibility, the song is also in contention at the Grammys, entered in the song of the year category as well as film soundtrack and country divisions.

Taylor Swift performs “I Knew It, I Knew You” at the #AcademyMuseumGala pic.twitter.com/23reYW7dBU — Variety (@Variety) October 18, 2026

For the remaining two slots in her set, Swift dug farther back into the past, covering both her cynical and romantic bases, opening with “Blank Space” and ending with “Love Story.”

Taylor Swift performs onstage during the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala in Partnership with Rolex at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Stefanie Keenan/Oscars/Getty Images for Academy Museum Foundation) Getty Images for Academy Museum

Wearing a Ralph Lauren gown for her performance, Swift invited the formally clad gathering to dance along with her set, saying, “Dancing is absolutely allowed. It’s not mandatory, but it’s more fun.”

Her backing crew had some singers and players who would be familiar to Swifties, but also some differences in the lineup, which was stripped down in some regards and packed out in others, namely with a horn section. She was joined by two sax players — not a regular staple of her touring outfit — as well as four singers and a guitarist, bassist, keyboard player and drummer.

Among the regular band members participating was Paul Sidoti, who wrote on Instagram, “Great to be playing music with my onstage partner of 19 years for the first time since The Eras Tour at a little party last night in Hollywood.”

Taylor Swift performs onstage during the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala in Partnership with Rolex at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Emma McIntyre/Oscars/Getty Images for Academy Museum Foundation) Getty Images for Academy Museum

Swift posed for photos with attendees including “Toy Story 5” voice actors Joan Cusack and Conan O’Brian and celebs like Cara Delevingne, Sabrina Carpenter, Eli Roth, Charlize Theron, Colman Domingo, John Carpenter, Hannah Waddingham, Dakota and Elle Fanning.

Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift attend the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala in Partnership with Rolex at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Stefanie Keenan/Oscars/Getty Images for Academy Museum Foundation) Getty Images for Academy Museum

Taylor Swift performs onstage during the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala in Partnership with Rolex at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Stefanie Keenan/Oscars/Getty Images for Academy Museum Foundation) Getty Images for Academy Museum

Taylor Swift performs “The Fate of Ophelia” live for the first time at the Academy Museum Gala. pic.twitter.com/Y58dJKtp20 — Variety (@Variety) October 18, 2026

🎥| Taylor inviting the gala attendees to dance along with her performance 🥰🤏 pic.twitter.com/6kHvkVfo05 — Taylor Swift Updates 💎 (@swifferupdates) October 18, 2026

(L-R) Charlize Theron, Amy Homma, Director and President, Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection, Colman Domingo, Taylor Swift, and John Carpenter attend the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala in Partnership with Rolex at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.
