content:
The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call will be back in the emergency room for Seasons 2 and 3.

The Korean Netflix drama series has gone into production on the second and third runs of the show, with stars Ju Ji-hoon (Kingdom) and Choo Young-woo (The Tale of Lady Ok) returning.

Also back in the cast are Yoon Kyung-ho (Husbands in Action) and Jeong Jae-kwang (Take Charge of My Heart), while Park Gyeong-won, and Jeong Ye-in have come through a “rigorous audition process” to join the ensemble.

The new seasons will see Baek Kang-hyuk (Ju Ji-hoon), a genius surgeon returning alongside his protégé, Yang Jae-won (Choo), Han Yu-rim (Yoon Kyung-ho), who originally opposed Kang-hyuk but is now his trusted partner and the chief of planning and coordination at Hankuk National University Hospital and anesthesiologist Park Gyeong-won (Jeong Jae-kwang). Nurse Cheon Jang-mi (Jeong Ye-in) joins the team.

Watch on Deadline

Director Lee Do-yun will again helm the series, and is also penning the scripts.

The show is based on the webttoon Trauma Center: Golden Hour, with Studio N and Mays Entertainment attached as co-producers. Season 1 was a hit for Netflix, hitting Top 10 lists in 63 countries last year, and topping the list in 18 countries worldwide.

title: ‘Other Desert Cities’ Broadway Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris and Allison Janney Lead a Resounding Family Drama
summary: Families are interesting. They all come with their own unique histories, prejudices and mysteries. Jon Robin Baitz’s Pulitzer Prize-nominated play “Other Desert Cities,” set in the years following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, explores harmful ideologies, grief, depression, memory and how secrets can wrap themselves around a family, slowly choking it from the inside out. […]
content:
Families are interesting. They all come with their own unique histories, prejudices and mysteries. Jon Robin Baitz’s Pulitzer Prize-nominated play “Other Desert Cities,” set in the years following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, explores harmful ideologies, grief, depression, memory and how secrets can wrap themselves around a family, slowly choking it from the inside out. Revived for the first time since 2011, this production, directed by John Benjamin Hickey, is gutting, witty and painfully timely.



“Other Desert Cities” opens on Christmas Eve 2004, at the Wyeths’ palatial Palm Springs home. Polly (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) and Lyman (Ed Harris), a former film writer and old Hollywood movie star, respectively, are thrilled to have their adult children home for the holidays. Their son, Trip (Joe Keery), resides in Los Angeles and works as a producer for early-aughts reality TV shows. Their daughter, Brooke (Lily Rabe), is a writer emerging from a near-decade-long battle with debilitating depression. Until now, she has remained sequestered on the East Coast. The Wyeths have an especially full house since Polly’s sister, Silda (Allison Janney), is living with them following yet another stint in rehab for her alcohol addiction.



The play opens in a sprawling, spotless beige living room adorned with a massive Christmas tree topped with a Star of David (honoring Polly’s heritage), courtesy of scenic designer Scott Pask. Polly, Lyman and the kids return from a game of tennis at the nearby country club. The foursome fret and fuss over one another, mostly because of their opposing political views. The elder Wyeths are staunch Republicans. Trip and Brooke cringe at their parents’ casual racism as they decide together how to spend the rest of the day before planning to indulge in a lobster Christmas Eve dinner back at the club.



Though Brooke has finally ventured to the West Coast after a six-year absence, her motivation isn’t just a friendly visit. Instead, she anxiously reveals to her parents that her second book is set to be published in the new year. And it’s not a work of fiction, as Lyman and Polly expected. Instead, it is a memoir that chronicles the most tragic event in the family’s history. Brooke has written about her older brother Henry, who died by suicide decades prior following his involvement in a cult bombing which left a man dead. It was such a horrific incident in the Wyeths’ lives that neither Lyman nor Polly can bear to speak their eldest son’s name. In fact, they fled Los Angeles after his death to hide in the desert.



Brooke’s revelation effectively ends the merriment. Lyman initially tries to be a peacemaker, saying he will not read the book, but he asks that Brooke refrain from publishing it until his and Polly’s deaths. Polly, by contrast, reads the manuscript and is immediately filled with anguish and all-consuming fury. Her solution is to disown Brooke, should the memoir ever see the light of day. What commences is a series of violent screaming matches between the mother and daughter before Lyman eventually reveals a long-held secret, bringing Brooke to her knees. After all, the truth often depends on who tells it.



“Other Desert Cities” is a resounding piece of theater, not simply because of the subject matter but because of the performances. The entire cast works as a seamless ensemble, switching from quippy wit, including Polly’s assertion that sarcasm is “only for teenagers and homosexuals,” to heartbreaking and volatile outbursts rife with the pain of a family standing on a foundation of lies and hypocrisy.



An exquisite portrait of 21st-century Americana, centering on a family divided by politics, ideology and a hidden history, “Other Desert Cities” is smart, authentic and deeply satisfying. Dark and haunting in one breath and hilariously raw in the next, it’s a play whose intensity has never felt more profound.

title: Inde Navarrette on Meeting Pamela Anderson, Hosting ‘SNL’ and X-Men Stunt Training
summary: “Obsession” star Inde Navarrette had quite the busy weekend, going from the Academy Museum Gala on Saturday to the Newport Beach Film Festival on Sunday. Navarrette attended the festival, which runs until Thursday in Newport Beach, as one of Variety’s 10 Actors to Watch, who were celebrated during the festival’s Honor Brunch. While speaking with […]
content:
“Obsession” star Inde Navarrette had quite the busy weekend, going from the Academy Museum Gala on Saturday to the Newport Beach Film Festival on Sunday.

Navarrette attended the festival, which runs until Thursday in Newport Beach, as one of Variety’s 10 Actors to Watch, who were celebrated during the festival’s Honor Brunch.

While speaking with Variety’s Marc Malkin at the festival’s carpet, Navarrette said attending the gala was “amazing.” “I mean, you’re just overwhelmed and kind of drowning in everybody that you have looked up to, possibly ever, and it’s just so lovely meeting people and the reception that ‘Obsession’ has been getting… I’m just so honored to go and be with the members of the Academy and just get an inside scoop on what that magnificent world is like.”

Popular on Variety

Jessica Lange and Pamela Anderson were two of the actresses Navarrette was excited to see Saturday night. “I spoke to Jessica Lange, who is an icon,” she said. “[And] the way that Pamela carries herself with such grace and honesty and just pure creativity and love is just exactly who I want to be.”

And Navarrette’s schedule isn’t slowing down just yet — she’s set to host this year’s “Saturday Night Live” Halloween episode with musical guest Gracie Abrams.

“I literally I feel like I snuck in,” joked the actress. “I’m super excited to keep everything under wraps because I really truly want to make this super fun for the audience. And what I love is when I don’t know anything. So I’m really excited to be working with the writers.”

Also on the horizon is the MCU’s forthcoming “X-Men” film, in which she’ll play Rogue. Navarrette told Malkin she hasn’t corresponded directly with Anna Paquin, who originated the role, but feels “the correspondence started when I was younger, when I really fell in love with the ‘X-Men’ movies in the first place.”

On the topic of stunt training for the superhero film, Navarrette said it’s a good excuse to get herself in the gym. “I’ve always wanted to take part in that sort of a thing,” she said. “I think it’s also a really good excuse to get in the gym. I’m the laziest person, and I am very excited to get up and move my body.”

title: ‘The Simpsons’ Surprise: Apu Is Heard for the First Time in Nearly a Decade, as Sunil Malhotra Takes Over for Hank Azaria (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the Oct. 18 episode of “The Simpsons,” “The Revengening,” which aired Sunday night on Fox. “The Simpsons” has pulled off its own October surprise: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon is back. The fan favorite character finally spoke again for the first time in nearly a decade on Sunday night’s episode, […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the Oct. 18 episode of “The Simpsons,” “The Revengening,” which aired Sunday night on Fox.

“The Simpsons” has pulled off its own October surprise: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon is back. The fan favorite character finally spoke again for the first time in nearly a decade on Sunday night’s episode, “The Revengening.” Variety has exclusively learned who is behind Apu’s new voice: actor and voice-over vet Sunil Malhotra (“Grey’s Anatomy,” “The Legend of Korra”).

Malhotra’s hiring and the return of Apu — who has been seen, but not heard on “The Simpsons” since the October 2017 episode “The Serfsons” — was a closely guarded secret inside “The Simpsons” universe. Fox didn’t share a screener for “The Revengening,” and producers kept both the episode’s table read and its subsequent production under tight protocols (including NDAs for all involved).

Popular on Variety

Also heard on Sunday’s episode was the debut of Janina Gavankar (“The Morning Show”) as Apu’s wife, Manjula. And now that Apu is back and the Kwik-E-Mart has reopened, executive producer Matt Selman said both characters and the Nahasapeemapetilon family will once again be seen (and heard) on “The Simpsons” more often.

“We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, ‘Simpsons’-y way that allowed him to evolve,” Selman said. “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role, and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”

Hank Azaria previously voiced Apu, a character that has been controversial over the years due to its stereotypical portrayal of a South Asian convenience store clerk. The issue of Apu was the centerpiece of the 2017 documentary “The Problem With Apu,” in which comedian Hari Kondabolu discussed the impact the character has had on people of South Asian descent.

After that doc made waves — including in “The Simpsons” writers’ room, where it was screened and discussed — Azaria announced that he would no longer voice Apu. “I apologize for my part in creating that and participating in that,” Azaria said in 2021 on Dax Shepard’s podcast “Armchair Expert.” “Part of me feels like I need to go to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologize. And sometimes I do.”

In the aftermath, Apu was shifted to the background on “The Simpsons,” as producers decided how to handle the character going forward. For years, that meant Apu would still occasionally be seen in Springfield, but never heard.

Until now. The idea of bringing back Apu this way, as one of this year’s Halloween-themed episodes, came from staffer Nick Dahan (who’s the credited writer on “The Revengening”) and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos. After hearing their pitch, Selman said he thought it was “a brilliant way” to bring Apu back and reference the entire situation.

Voice actor Malhotra said he took time to look into what it would mean to take over Apu and talked to the producers to make sure the character was more culturally appropriate.

“When my agent called me about a ‘Simpsons’ audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink,” he said. “But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers’ room look different now? Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologized for past mistakes? Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably ‘Simpsons’ way that didn’t disappoint fans?

“Whether the producers knew it or not, I was prepared to walk away,” he continued. Malhotra said that he declined his very first “professional job offer 28 years ago” because it would have required him to play a stereotypical “Hindu guy,” adding that playing such a caricature “to be the butt of the joke wasn’t something I was willing to do, and I’ve turned down similar work multiple times since.”

But as Malhotra got further down the road with “The Simpsons,” he said, he began engaging with the producers about their plans for Apu before he would commit to the role, where he was promised that the return of Apu was being handled with the utmost care.

“My callback was the first of many times that no one at ‘The Simpsons’ let me down,” he said. “I told casting that I’d only consider an offer if I could meet showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos, both of whom gladly did so. It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for longtime fans of ‘The Simpsons’ and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way.”

In “The Revengening,” a spooky lead-up to next week’s “Treehouse of Horror XXXVII,” a man in a “Daft Monk” Halloween costume (as in, a Daft Punk helmet and monastic robe — wordplay!) is accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents all over town. A year later, “Daft Monk” is still alive, and getting his revenge by taking out his would-be killers, one by one.

Eventually “Daft Monk” summons the townspeople to Springfield City Hall, where he takes his helmet off and reveals that he’s actually Apu.

“I’d be lying if I didn’t say that the sweetest part of all was unleashing that righteously rage-fueled “I AM APU!” — on behalf of so many of us — over and over in the studio until we got it just right,” Malhotra said. “I really feel like we did and I can’t wait for fans to see more Apu.”

Apu then shares his backstory: After he was nearly killed dozens of times, he wound up on “The Island of Forgotten Garbage,” where he’s healed by “The Simpsons” quack Dr. Nick (who also has been seen sparingly in recent years, and is now voiced by Eric Lopez, who previously also took over as Bumblebee Man).

“All the junk Springfield gets rid of winds up here,” he tells Apu, “like you … If you wound up here, it’s for a reason, right, Leon?” (Out pops the character that Michael Jackson played in the Season 3 episode “Stark Raving Mad,” which was pulled from “Simpsons” rotation in 2019 after the doc “Leaving Neverland” showcased more allegations against the late pop star.)

Says Apu before he reveals himself: “I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed!”

Then, unmasked, he tells the Springfield crowd: “It would have been so easy to bring me back. I immediately ran home to my family, but they were gone. Then I went to the Kwik-E-Mart, and was shocked to find it abandoned. As I wandered aimlessly through town, no one even noticed me. It was as if I was invisible. That was when I vowed to take my revenge on Springfield.”

He’s about to light City Hall on fire, but Marge Simpson pipes up — representing the Springfield citizens, but also clearly serving as a mouthpiece for the show’s producers: “Apu, we’re so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing.”

Bart adds: “But we were so scared, and just didn’t know what to do.”

Lenny also chimes in, in a nod to the debates inside “The Simpsons” writers’ room: “If it’s any consolation, we had so many internal conversations about it.”

But, Carl finishes, “Ahh, they kind of just didn’t go anywhere.” (And for almost a decade, that’s how “The Simpsons” never got around to bringing back Apu.)

Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, and offers this penance to Apu, while reminding viewers how important Apu has been to the makeup of Springfield: “I’m just doing what the old Apu would have done. The guy who loved this town and everyone in it. You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands. We took you for granted. I took you for granted.”

But before Apu can blow up the town, he wakes up. It turns out it was a nightmare; no one is dead. He’s back in the Kwik E-Mart, and Manjula is there too. So is his No. 1 customer, Homer, who invites him to a Halloween party.

“What the heck? I’ll do it,” Apu says. “A Halloween party sounds kind of fun. Plus, I feel like I haven’t seen everyone in ages. Oh, but I wish I had a costume.”

But he actually does: There’s a “Daft Monk” costume stashed under the cash register. So was it really a dream? And that’s the end of the episode — but Apu is back!

This isn’t the first time “The Simpsons” writers used their characters to allude to their indecisiveness on what to do with Apu. In the 2018 episode “No Good Read Goes Unpunished,” Marge begins reading her favorite childhood novel to Lisa, but quickly realizes the old book was a lot more offensive and racist than she remembered. She tries to sanitize it, but “now it’s as inoffensive as a Sunday in Cincinnati … what am I supposed to do?”

Lisa then looks at the audience, seemingly addressing “Simpsons” fans: “It’s hard to say. Something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. What can you do?”

The scene pulls back to reveal a photo of Apu near Lisa’s bed, and it’s obvious they’re no longer talking about a book, but their own show. With Marge also looking straight at viewers, the two suggest that “Some things will be dealt with at a later date … if at all.” (It should be noted that Apu and his children also appeared in the episode, but did not speak.)

In June 2020, during the post-George Floyd reckoning on race, “The Simpsons” announced that moving forward, its characters of color would be voiced by culturally appropriate actors. Among the major changes, Alex Désert took over as Carl Carlson from Azaria, and Kevin Michael Richardson (who had already been a part of the series cast) became Dr. Julius Hibbert, which was previously Harry Shearer. Now, Apu, with Malhotra taking over, joins that list as well.

And for several years, the creative team promised that they would address Apu at some point. In 2021, series creator Matt Groening told USA Today that the producers were first seeing if they could make new Apu stories work. “I think the Apu stories are fantastic, and he’s one of the most nuanced characters on a silly two-dimensional cartoon show,” Groening said in the interview.

Early reactions on social media about the return of Apu has already been positive: “Apu is back thank you Simpsons,” said one. Another: “The Simpsons reveals the new voice for Apu. Representation for Indian Americans. Well played Matt Groening and Dan Castellaneta, Hank Azaria, Nancy Cartwright, Harry Shearer, Julie Kavner and Yeardley Smith.” Wrote a third: “Apu reveal is the greatest thing to happen on the Simpsons in a long time. I missed that genius character!”

Meanwhile, Malhotra and Gavankar jointly posted this reveal on their Instagram pages:

Malhotra’s recent voice credits include “The Legend of Vox Machina,” “The Loud House,” “Monster High,” “The Casagrandes” and “Star Wars: Tales of the Jedi.” He’s also been heard on video games including “Mortal Kombat 1,” “Avatar: The Last Airbender – Quest of Balance” and “Marvel’s Avengers.” In TV, besides “Grey’s Anatomy,” he’s also appeared on “ER,” “NCIS: New Orleans,” “MacGyver” and “Maron.”

title: ‘Other Desert Cities’ Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Gets Seriously Funny For Broadway Debut
summary: It’s hard to imagine any secrets or hints of repressed trauma surviving long in the glare of Palm Springs sunshine that keeps things bright in the airy, open-floor, large windowed home of the moneyed family at the center of Jon Robin Baitz’ Other Desert Cities, but survive those secrets do, at least until they don’t. […]
content:
It’s hard to imagine any secrets or hints of repressed trauma surviving long in the glare of Palm Springs sunshine that keeps things bright in the airy, open-floor, large windowed home of the moneyed family at the center of Jon Robin Baitz’ Other Desert Cities, but survive those secrets do, at least until they don’t.

Director John Benjamin Hickey’s revival of this ever-captivating play, in a production opening at Broadway‘s Hudson Theatre tonight, features a must-see cast of Julia Louis-Dreyfus (in her Broadway debut), Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Joe Keery and Lily Rabe, but the bold names aren’t the only things that justify Other Desert Cities‘ hot ticket status. Though it can feel, in tone and performance, altogether different than the acclaimed original 2011 production – of course comparisons will be made, and not always to the benefit of the new take – Baitz’ play seems just as vital in today’s bitterly divisive political and social environment.

Don’t let that description suggest a stuffy, joyless evening in the theater – as if anything associated with the endlessly appealing Louis-Dreyfus could ever be joyless. The Seinfeld and VEEP star brings an inexhaustible supply of audience good will to everything she does, and if her performance as this wealthy, unbending disciple of Reagan Republicanism is short on the studied patrician steeliness that Stockard Channing made a delicious meal of, Louis-Dreyfus’ more amiable (at least initially) interpretation is no less thoughtful if bit less impactful.

Watch on Deadline

Louis-Dreyfus plays Polly Wyeth, a former screenwriter of popular if slight movies about a spunky teen girl (I’m picturing Gidget) married to a former Hollywood hunk-turned-ambassador Lyman (Ed Harris, but I’m picturing John Gavin) whose rightward drift over the years (the Wyeths are longtime friends of Ron and Nancy and various assorted Bushes) leaves her at odds with her liberal, recently sober sister (and former writing partner) Silda (Allison Janney) and the Wyeths’ two adult children – Trip (Joe Keery), the LA-based producer of a cheesy Judge Judy-esque courtroom show (with celebrity juries, no less) and Brooke (Lily Rabe), the black sheep Sag Harbor-ensconced author given to deep depressions and pervasive gloom and anger.

No one could blame Brooke (though they do anyway): The Wyeth children used to be three, cut by one with the suicide of eldest son Henry years ago.

Set in the gorgeous, no-detail-out-of-place Mid-Century modern Palm Springs home to which the elder Wyeths retreated in the scandalous aftermath of Henry’s suicide (he was, we learn, a left-wing radical somehow connected to a deadly Weather Underground-style bombing), the family has gathered for a rare reunion to celebrate Christmas 2004. The big, tastefully decorated Christmas tree is more than mere decoration: It’s a big, white-lighted rebuke to the Texas-Jewish upbringing that Polly has worked so hard to squelch through Nancy-esque poise and the refined tones that seemed more natural to Pat Buckley. Any wonder our first glimpse of Polly is après-tennis in chic little blue and white (and no-doubt-tailored) athletic ensemble, her beautifully highlighted, jawline-skimming bob absolutely unmussed by whatever feats of country club athletics she’s almost certainly just won.

Ed Harris, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Joe Keery Emilio Madrid

But even that huge tannenbaum is no match for Silda, whose bohemian panache – she wears discount Pucci – and show-biz (read Jewish) inclinations (she quotes Totie Fields) clearly grates on the disdainful Polly. So ungiving is Polly that we instantly side with Silda (and, of course, Janney, one of few performers who can go head-to-head with Louis-Dreyfus in the likability department and who is greeted with wild applause upon her delayed entrance on stage).

In the choose-sides battleground that is the Wyeth home, daughter Brooke is defintely on Team Silda. In fact, she’s Silda Plus. Rueful and, in her own way, as caustic as her mother, Brooke has temporarily returned to the fold following months of serious depression and years of a writer’s block that had even her family suspecting she was a one-hit wonder after the publication of her celebrated debut novel.

Well, surprise and Merry Christmas: Brooke has come bearing gifts – her new, soon-to-be-published novel (and sooner to be excerpted in The New Yorker) that isn’t a novel at all. It’s a family memoir, stuffed with the details of the troubled Henry’s suicide and the parental abandonment that led to it.

If the play’s first act is loaded with some comparatively light intra-family needling (Polly upbraids Brooke – with Louis-Dreyfus’ immediately recognizable comic delivery – by proclaiming “sarcasm is the purview of teenagers and homosexuals”) – Act II goes for the jugular. Mom and dad have flipped out over the soon-to-be spilled secrets that they believe will be nothing less than cruel public humiliation and an attempted discrediting of all the family values on which they (and their Republican friends and colleagues) have built lives and staked reputations.

Polly, in particular, is enraged (the more easy-going Lyman is, at least initially, more even-handed – he simply refuses to read, or comment on, the hefty manuscript plunked before him.) As accusations and remembered psychic injuries pile up, the story of Henry – where he went wrong, why he went wrong and who was to blame – slowly emerges.

Without spoiling the big second-act reveal, no one in this play – or in the audience – has an unchallengeable claim on the truth. Even the proudly-forthright Silda shares only what she wants to share, and conciliatory son Trip, occupying a middle-ground (or rather a no-man’s-land) between parents and sister, can’t possibly establish anything like a separate peace when he can’t possibly know the full details of this war.

Keery and Lily Rabe Emilio Madrid

Whether or not Baitz’ writing (or Hickey’s direction) can wholly support the major leap we’re eventually expected to take will be determined by each person in a Hudson Theatre seat. Mine was occupied by someone not entirely convinced, and I left the theater questioning the tale’s credibility to a degree I don’t recall asking when I saw the original production 15 years ago (the play or my memory? who’s to say). There are a few clues along the way that, in retrospect, support the big twist, but nothing fully persuaded me of the overall credibility of the secrets exposed, or their plausibility beyond the dramatic demands of plot.

Still, there’s no doubt that we want to follow this cast wherever it asks us to go, even when that’s a pretty big ask. The cast itself can occasionally seem tentative, particularly Dreyfus during the heavy second act. At a few points during the play an otherwise winning Harris, at the reviewed performance, still seemed to be finding his way through the character and the script. Fortunately we’re all more than willing to cut him some slack after a wonderful scene in the first act in which his former-actor character recreates an old B-movie death scene that suggest Harris has played more than a few of these himself.

Indeed, no actor as familiar and, yes, beloved as so many in this cast can completely escape their own histories, and why should they? We want to give Louis-Dreyfus’ Polly a certain benefit of the doubt because we still love Elaine Benes, an affection that well-serves the play’s dynamic and tensions, and we take to Janney’s Silda not only because of the character’s humanist politics (though there’s certainly that too – some of her lines about the cruelties of a certain political party ring truer in this era than the play’s in-universe post-9/11 setting) but also because we’ve followed Janney since The West Wing.

The two younger actors might not have those lengthy careers but their talent easily justifies their growing reputations (Keery from Stranger Things, Rabe from, among other credits, American Horror Story and a fine roster of stage performances). Keery’s charming delivery of several truth-telling speeches proves that villains don’t get all the juicy, crowd-pleasing moments.

Harris and Rabe Emilio Madrid

Indeed, Rabe might just have the toughest job of all, and not because she is regularly called upon to joust (sometimes loudly) with performers as skilled and, to repeat, beloved as Louis-Dreyfus and Harris. If some will see Rabe’s righteously angry, often anguished characterization of the wounded Brooke as, well, a bit much, a fairer way is to say we’re bearing witness to the explosions (outward-directed and inward) of a young woman who bears all the pent-up rage of an imperfect child long-smothered by the surface perfectionism of a tyrannical mother. (And kudos to Scott Pask for a set-designed Palm Springs interior that pretty much defines perfectionism with its smug, moderne, desert elegance).

Rabe also beautifully carries the significant weight of the play’s famously ambiguous epilogue, to which director Hickey has added a blink-and-miss-it grace note that poses more questions than it answers. That’s an absolutely legitimate, if superfluous, directorial choice, and one that the playwright surely must have okayed. Yes, it’s a bit frustrating in the fleetness of its execution and vague reverberations, but Other Desert Cities is nothing if not an exquisitely designed study of the malleability of truths long believed settled. Of course it demands reconsiderations, right up to the very end.

Title: Other Desert Cities

Venue: Broadway’s Hudson Theater

Written By: Jon Robin Baitz

Directed By: John Benjamin Hickey

Cast: Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Joe Keery, Lily Rabe

Running Time: 2 hr 30 min (including intermission)

title: Jason Sudeikis Gives Update On Potential ‘Ted Lasso’ Seasons 5 & 6
summary: Never count Ted Lasso out. After all, show co-creator Jason Sudeikis thought the series would end with Season 3. Then came Season 4. Sudeikis held forth recently on the podcast Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso about the prospects for Seasons 5 and 6. Sudeikis indicated he “would like to” do more seasons but, he said, […]
content:
Never count Ted Lasso out.

After all, show co-creator Jason Sudeikis thought the series would end with Season 3. Then came Season 4.

Sudeikis held forth recently on the podcast Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso about the prospects for Seasons 5 and 6.

Sudeikis indicated he “would like to” do more seasons but, he said, “it takes a village.”

Asked if he thinks Apple would be open to more Ted, Sudeikis ventured, “I would assume so.”

Pressed on whether there would, in fact, be more to the show, the actor admitted, “I just don’t know,” before offering more definitively, “We haven’t started a writers’ room or anything like that.”

Watch on Deadline

Fragoso pointed out that Sudeikis had no concept for a fourth season before creating it, and he was at that point drained, with an empty cup, creatively. The host asked if a similar process could produce two more installments.

“Um, we’re going to need a bigger cup,” the actor joked.

But he did not rule it out, at one point describing how, after a log post-Season 3 hiatus, he kept hearing the voices of the characters in his head. “Then, he said, “other new voices started to show up.” Those were the voices of the women on the team in Season 3.

“I think it’d be fun,” said Sudeikis.

title: Yeon Sang-ho’s ‘Paradise Lost’ Sells To 118 Territories; Sets U.S. Premiere At Hawaii International Film Festival
summary: Korea’s CJ ENM has sold Paradise Lost, the psychological thriller from Train To Busan director Yeon Sang-ho, to 118 countries worldwide, including Twin for Japan, The Jokers Films for France, and Well Go USA for North America. The film is also set to receive its US premiere in the ‘Spotlight on Korea’ section of this […]
content:
Korea’s CJ ENM has sold Paradise Lost, the psychological thriller from Train To Busan director Yeon Sang-ho, to 118 countries worldwide, including Twin for Japan, The Jokers Films for France, and Well Go USA for North America.

The film is also set to receive its US premiere in the ‘Spotlight on Korea’ section of this year’s Hawaii International Film Festival (HIFF) on November 1 and 4, following sold-out screenings at Toronto and Busan film festivals. The film screened in the Special Presentations section at Toronto, followed by the Gala Presentation section of Busan.

Among other territories that have acquired the film are Taiwan (Long Shong), Singapore (Shaw), Spain (Youplanet Pictures), Benelux (18K Film), Mongolia (Content Distribution), Philippines (Pioneer Films), Middle East (Gulf Film) and Cambodia (Westec Media), while Emphasis has inflight rights.

Watch on Deadline

CJ ENM said the film’s international sales revenue has exceeded its net production budget. Yeon is well known internationally through films such as Train To Busan, Peninsula, and Colony, which premiered Out of Competition at this year’s Cannes film festival.

Starring Hyun-joo Kim and Hyeon-seong Bae, Paradise Lost follows a mother whose son disappeared nine years earlier when a bus carrying children to a camp mysteriously vanished. Her life takes an unexpected turn when her son, long presumed dead, returns alive.

This year’s HIFF runs from October 21 through November 15 across the Hawaiian Islands. The festival showcases films from around the world, with a particular focus on Asia and the Pacific.

Commenting on the sales success, CJ ENM said: “The film combines a distinctive premise with a deeply felt exploration of family and motherhood. These universal emotions are resonating across cultures and generating strong interest in international markets.”

Presented by Wowpoint and CJ ENM, Paradise Lost opens in South Korean theaters on October 21, 2026, with distribution handled by CJ ENM.

International theatrical releases are scheduled for Taiwan on October 23 and Singapore on November 5, followed by North America and Vietnam on November 6 and Indonesia on November 13.

title: The New Apu Makes His Debut Tonight On ‘The Simpsons’
summary: Apu has found his voice again on The Simpsons. Hank Azaria voiced the character for close to 30 years until a 2017 documentary ignited a backlash over how the character represented South Asians. Since then, the fan favorite has been seen on the show, but not heard. Until now. Tonight’s episode, “The Revengening,” is a […]
content:
Apu has found his voice again on The Simpsons.

Hank Azaria voiced the character for close to 30 years until a 2017 documentary ignited a backlash over how the character represented South Asians. Since then, the fan favorite has been seen on the show, but not heard. Until now.

Tonight’s episode, “The Revengening,” is a prelude to next week’s annual “Treehouse of Horror” frightfest. It centers on a mysterious figure and a plot out of the Scream movies. When the mystery man finally reveals himself, it turns out he is none other than Apu Nahasapeemapetilon.

Apu not only has a new lease on life in Springfield, he has a new actor voicing him: Sunil Malhotra. Malhotra has a long list of voice credits, including in massively popular video games such as World of Warcraft, League of Legends, Halo: Reach, Fallout 4, Mortal Kombat 1 and many more. On TV, he has appeared on ER, Grey’s Anatomy, Cold Case, House, NCIS: New Orleans, The Loud House, Monster High and Star Wars: Tales of the Jedi.

Watch on Deadline

Sunil Malhotra (Paul Smith)

“When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink,” said Malhotra. “But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking. Did the writers room look different now? Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologized for past mistakes? Could I make the character my own and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn’t disappoint fans?”

The actor said he was prepared to walk away from the role on TV’s longest-running primetime show if he felt the intentions were not respectful.

“My callback was the first of many times that no one at The Simpsons let me down,” he continued. “I told Casting that I’d only consider an offer if I could meet showrunner Matt Selman and Co-Executive Producer Cesar Mazariegos, both of whom gladly did so. It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for longtime fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way. I’d be lying if I didn’t say that the sweetest part of all was unleashing that righteously rage-fueled “I AM APU!” [in tonight’s episode] — on behalf of so many of us — over and over in the studio until we got it just right. I really feel like we did and I can’t wait for fans to see more Apu.”

Selman was equally enthusiastic, saying in a statement, “We love this character and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve. We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”

title: Lucca Comics Chief Emanuele Vietina on Celebrating the Crossover Between Movies and Video Games: ‘It’s All Part of a Specific Vision’
summary: Lucca Comics and Games director Emanuele Vietina is understandably proud of the lineup he’s assembled for the 60th edition of this unique event, to be held Oct. 28-Nov. 1 in the Tuscan town of Lucca, which seamlessly spans the full gamut of geek culture and pop entertainment. It also attracts more than 200,000 fans a […]
content:
Lucca Comics and Games director Emanuele Vietina is understandably proud of the lineup he’s assembled for the 60th edition of this unique event, to be held Oct. 28-Nov. 1 in the Tuscan town of Lucca, which seamlessly spans the full gamut of geek culture and pop entertainment.

It also attracts more than 200,000 fans a day – many of which cosplayers – within its medieval ramparts.

As previously announced, highlights of this year’s edition include a sneak peak of Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians,” with talents in tow and the presence of Aardman Animations’ founder Peter Lord and director Peter Walker for the Italian premiere of “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.” In a major coup, Japanese filmmaker Kore-eda Hirokazu will be making the trek to Lucca to meet fans and discuss adapting Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga “Look Back,” which blends live-action realism with the creative process behind the manga genre.



To mark its 60th anniversary, Lucca will feature “Lucca Legacy: A Comics and Games Story” exhibition in the 14th century Palazzo Guinigi, which will dig into the archival vaults to “tell a seminal story that was made by [Marvel legend] Stan Lee, [‘Iron Man,’ ‘Black Panther’ and ‘The X-Men’] creator Jack Kirby, [iconic Hearst cartoonist] Lee Falk and all the great American artists comics that found a home in Lucca in the 70s,” says Vietina.

The Lucca Comics chief speaks to Variety about pulling out all the stops to celebrate the crossover between different forms of geek culture, in particular between movies and video games.

Popular on Variety

How does the “Percy Jackson” world tie in with Lucca’s theme this year which is “Legacy”?

The “Legacy” theme represents, if you will, the heritage of what has become one of the world’s major comic conventions. The way film and TV series at Lucca engage with the great fantasy storytelling of Percy Jackson is that the book’s author, Rick Riordan, is essentially bringing things up to date. We often talk about “contemporary mythology.” With Percy Jackson, which features Olympus and the Olympian gods, he revitalizes the great heritage of classical Greco-Roman culture, making it accessible to young people today.

An event like ours deals with contemporary mythologies, yet it remains firmly anchored in the mythology of the past. This year, however, is particularly emblematic. For the movie world, Lucca is not merely the oldest comics convention in existence, or even the only one to feature a formal red carpet in front of an opera house that dates back to the turn of the 20th century.

On top of these aspects, we will also have a special fan screening of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” which is the latest entry in the “Hunger Games” film franchise, based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel. Warner Bros. will bring the world of “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” [known as “Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone” in the U.S.] to Lucca in an immersive pavilion while we wait for the new HBO series. So with Riordan, Collins and J. K. Rowling, Lucca will become, above all, the realm where great literature meets great cinema.

What are other aspects of Lucca this year that you are particularly proud of?

Another aspect that characterizes Lucca is the exhibition side. In Lucca, we have the big premieres with talents, but there are also big stands for fans. So “Percy Jackson” will have a dedicated experience space, the same goes with “Harry Potter,” but there is also “Dexter” and others. This year we have set the all-time record of investments from the studios and streamers.

This helps attract the thousands of cosplayers that pour into town. What else is in store for them?

There is plenty of room for the world of cosplay, with a particular focus on crossovers between the cinematic realm and the video game world. We’ll see a significant presence from [Polish video game developer] CD Projekt Red, featuring “Cyberpunk 2077” and the “Cyberpunk Edgerunners” animation, as well as “The Witcher,” which will be represented alongside its latest downloadable content (DLC). It’s clear that this European studio has truly embraced the crossover concept, especially given the news surrounding a cinematic expansion for “Cyberpunk 2077.”

Tell me more about how Lucca reflects the crossover between video games and movies

For us, the strong focus that Lucca Comics and Games places on video games, specifically from a cinematic perspective, is very important. In this context, I want to point out that we will have Hideki Kamiya [the legendary game director behind “Resident Evil 2,” “Devil May Cry” and “Okami”], and also [director and producer] Yoshinori Kitase, who will revitalize the connection with Square Enix and the “Final Fantasy” fan base. Then there is the presence of the creators of “Alien: Isolation 2,” a game that is very strongly driven by movies. It’s all part of a specific vision.

Animation, of course, plays a big role. Talk to me about that aspect

In terms of legacy, this 60th edition of Lucca marks a great return to a major focus on animation. I’ve already mentioned CD Projekt Red, with Bartosz Sztybor and Saya Elder, who are the producer and showrunner of “Edgerunners” coming to Lucca. Just as importantly, we have [Cartoon Network Studio’s] “Adventure Time” with one of its co-creators Victor Cartwright on hand. Then we will have Aardman Animations represented by its founder Peter Lord. They will be coming for the Italian premiere of “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.” Lord, who, of course, is beloved by everyone, will be honored on our “Walk of Fame,” as he represents one of the most significant legacies in the field. He’ll be joined by Matthew Walker, the film’s director. For us, Peter’s presence is truly meaningful.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

title: Ju Ji-hoon, Choo Young-woo Return for Netflix’s ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call’ Seasons 2 and 3
summary: Netflix is bringing back Korean medical drama “The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call” for two more rounds, with the streamer confirming that Seasons 2 and 3 are in production. In 2025, the show’s first season made the Top 10 charts in 63 countries and reached No. 1 in 18 of them. Ju Ji-hoon (“Kingdom”) is […]
content:
Netflix is bringing back Korean medical drama “The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call” for two more rounds, with the streamer confirming that Seasons 2 and 3 are in production.

In 2025, the show’s first season made the Top 10 charts in 63 countries and reached No. 1 in 18 of them.

Ju Ji-hoon (“Kingdom”) is back in the lead as Baek Kang-hyuk, a brilliant surgeon who will go to any length to keep a patient alive.

Choo Young-woo (“The Tale of Lady Ok”) also returns as Yang Jae-won. The character was the first protégé Baek took under his wing and has since followed his mentor’s path onto the trauma team.

Popular on Variety

Yoon Kyung-ho (“Husbands in Action”) reprises the role of Han Yu-rim. Once Baek’s adversary, Han is now a partner he relies on and heads planning and coordination for Hankuk National University Hospital.

Jeong Jae-kwang (“Take Charge of My Heart”) also comes back, stepping into the scrubs of anesthesiologist Park Gyeong-won once more.

Newcomer Jeong Ye-in, who landed the part after a demanding audition, plays nurse Cheon Jang-mi.

Lee Do-yun, who directed the first season, is back at the helm and is also penning the scripts.

The show is adapted from the webtoon “Trauma Center: Golden Hour.” Studio N and Mays Entertainment are producing, and Netflix is presenting.

Both new seasons will stream exclusively on Netflix. The streamer did not announce premiere dates for either installment.

Two of the show’s returning cast members also feature in Netflix’s current Korean lineup. Jeong Jae-kwang appears in romance series “Take Charge of My Heart,” which launched on the streamer Oct. 9. Yoon Kyung-ho is part of the ensemble of horror series “Dead-End Job,” led by Lee Jae-wook, which premieres Oct. 30.

title: ‘The Secret Agent’ Director Kleber Mendonça Filho to Be Patron of Marrakech Film Festival’s Atlas Workshops
summary: Brazilian filmmaker Kleber Mendonça Filho, best known for “The Secret Agent,” will be the patron – serving as a mentor to the filmmakers – of the 9th edition of the Atlas Workshops, the Marrakech Film Festival’s professional platform dedicated to the development of Moroccan, Arab and African cinema, which takes place from Nov. 22 to […]
content:
Brazilian filmmaker Kleber Mendonça Filho, best known for “The Secret Agent,” will be the patron – serving as a mentor to the filmmakers – of the 9th edition of the Atlas Workshops, the Marrakech Film Festival’s professional platform dedicated to the development of Moroccan, Arab and African cinema, which takes place from Nov. 22 to 26.

Mendonça Filho made his mark on the international scene with “Neighboring Sounds” (2012), “Aquarius” (2016) and “Bacurau on the Map” (2019), which won the Jury Prize at Cannes. His most recent film, “The Secret Agent” (2025), won the award for best director at Cannes before going on to win two Golden Globes and receive four Academy Award nominations this year.

Mendonça Filho said, “Listening to new ideas and understanding the aspirations of new generations of filmmakers is a source of inspiration for my own work.

Popular on Variety

“And all of this in Marrakech, such a fascinating city, which hosts such an exceptional film festival. Last year, during my Conversation at the festival, I was asked whether I had ever planned to shoot a film in this city. Serving as the patron of the Atlas Workshops makes me feel as though I’m witnessing, right before my eyes, the birth of new films.”

Selected from among 320 projects in development and 90 films in production or post-production, this edition’s 30 projects and films fall into three categories: 14 projects in development, 11 films in production or post-production, and five projects in the Atlas Close-Ups section, which is dedicated to Moroccan cinema.

The 14 countries that are represented are Algeria, Cabo Verde, Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine, Rwanda, Senegal, Sudan, Syria and Tunisia.

The selection of projects in development includes 12 fiction films and two documentaries, of which six are debut feature-length films.

Several of the projects are headed by filmmakers who have already won attention with their previous films: Amjad Abu Alala (“You Will Die at Twenty”), Laila Abbas (“Thank You for Banking With Us”), Meryem Benm’Barek (“Sofia,” “Behind the Palm Trees”), Sofia Alaoui (“Animalia”) and Yasmine Benkiran (“Queens”).

Of the 11 films in production or post-production—including five debut feature-length films—four received development support from the Atlas Workshops: Samuel Ishimwe’s “Seasons of the Weary Kind” (Rwanda), selected in 2019; Alaa Eddine Aljem’s “Eldorado” (Morocco), selected in 2020; Yoro Mbaye’s “Fagadaga” (Senegal), selected in 2022; and Ismaël El Iraki’s “Wolfmother” (Morocco), selected in 2023.

The Atlas Close-Ups program features five Moroccan projects, including four fiction films and one documentary.

Atlas Station: A selection of producers and short films in post-production from Morocco

Conceived to support young Moroccan professionals, this year’s Atlas Station welcomes eight filmmakers selected from among 30 applicants. In meetings and exchanges with international professionals, these four women and four men will participate in a professional development program focused on various aspects of film production.

The program also provides support for five Moroccan short films in post-production—four fiction and one documentary—selected from among 24 submissions. The selected filmmaking teams will receive support tailored to the needs of their film, particularly in terms of final editing and distribution.

The Atlas Programs—an initiative supporting Moroccan, Arab, and African cinema

Founded in 2018, the Atlas Workshops now fall under the Atlas Programs, which gathers together the professional initiatives of the Marrakech Film Festival.

Atlas Press, Atlas Distribution Meetings

Atlas Press supports the development of film criticism, while the Atlas Distribution Meetings brings together some 60 professionals from Africa, the Arab world and Europe to foster networking and the circulation of films. The Atlas Distribution Awards rounds out this initiative by providing support for the distribution of films.

The Atlas Workshops, Atlas Station and Atlas Distribution Meetings take place in Marrakech from Nov. 22 to 26, while Atlas Press takes place from Nov. 23 to 27.

title: Selena Gomez Reveals Vaping Nicotine Changed Her Voice: ‘It’s Not Worth It’
summary: Selena Gomez said heavy nicotine vaping has changed her voice, and told fans she has now quit the habit. The singer, actor and Rare Beauty founder, 34, spoke about it in a video of roughly a minute posted to her Instagram Story on Sunday. “I’m not going to be able to change my voice,” Gomez […]
content:
Selena Gomez said heavy nicotine vaping has changed her voice, and told fans she has now quit the habit.

The singer, actor and Rare Beauty founder, 34, spoke about it in a video of roughly a minute posted to her Instagram Story on Sunday.

“I’m not going to be able to change my voice,” Gomez said. “I vaped nicotine a lot. Nicotine is so hard to quit, and I think I just wanted to say, if you’re going through it, or if you’re even trying to vape, it’s just not worth it. It’s so stupid, and it’s changed my voice.”

Gomez added that she understood if some fans didn’t like listening to her voice, and told them they were free to tune out.

Popular on Variety

She said she was excited to have stopped and hoped she could keep it up, though it was hard.

“But I know if you are going through something, you can get through it too,” she said. “It sucks.”

Gomez did not cite vaping when she answered repeated fan questions about her voice during an Instagram Live session last December. At the time, she said her throat sometimes swells on the inside.

Gomez has been open about her health over the years. She has lupus and received a kidney transplant in 2017, and she has spoken publicly about her bipolar disorder diagnosis, including in the 2022 documentary “Selena Gomez: My Mind & Me.”

She stars in and executive produces the Hulu comedy series “Only Murders in the Building” alongside Steve Martin and Martin Short. The show returns Dec. 8 for its sixth season, which moves the action to London under the title “Only Murders in London.” She launched her cosmetics brand Rare Beauty in 2020.

title: Seventeen’s Jeonghan and Joshua Find Their JxJ Duo Sound on ‘Dreamscape’: ‘Right in the Middle Between Strong and Subtle’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: For more than a decade, Seventeen’s Jeonghan and Joshua have shared the spotlight with 11 bandmates in one of K-pop’s best-selling groups. Now they get it to themselves with “Dreamscape,” their first album as the duo JxJ. The record is also Jeonghan’s first new music since he completed South Korea’s mandatory military service this summer. […]
content:
For more than a decade, Seventeen’s Jeonghan and Joshua have shared the spotlight with 11 bandmates in one of K-pop’s best-selling groups. Now they get it to themselves with “Dreamscape,” their first album as the duo JxJ.

The record is also Jeonghan’s first new music since he completed South Korea’s mandatory military service this summer. While he served, Seventeen kept performing without him, and at times he watched his bandmates from the audience, among the group’s fans, known as Carats. Joshua spent the same stretch producing songs of his own and sending them to their company.

The pair met as trainees and recorded the duet “Falling for U” for the 2018 special album “Director’s Cut,” but JxJ is the first project built entirely around the two of them.

Popular on Variety

Joshua says their company first suggested they collaborate together. “After giving it some thought, we’ve been together for so long, and we really wanted to show a different side to ourselves,” he says. “Sides that we haven’t shown as a whole group, as Seventeen, so we thought it was going to be fun. And a lot of our fans actually like our chemistry, the chemistry that the two of us have.”

Jeonghan says that with several members away on military service, those who remained talked with the company about how to keep bringing Carats new music. “We thought that it would be a really exciting project, so that’s how it came to life.”

Seventeen debuted in 2015 under Pledis Entertainment, now part of Hybe, with 13 members split into hip-hop, vocal and performance teams. It holds the record for the highest-selling K-pop album, “FML,” and was the first K-pop act to sell more than 5 million copies of an album in its first week. All 13 members renewed their Pledis contracts this summer, the second time the full group has re-signed. Military service has thinned the lineup, though. Six members are currently serving, and Seungkwan and Dino enlist together on Oct. 26. That leaves five active members: Jeonghan, Joshua, S.Coups, Jun and The8. Jeonghan and Joshua both sing in the vocal team, and JxJ is the group’s seventh unit.

“The exhilaration and the Carats screaming, cheering, their love, the spotlight – everything is something that you can only enjoy on stage,” Jeonghan tells Variety. “So I missed those moments on stage. I just wanted to get ready after finishing my military service, prep myself, and get back on there as soon as possible.”

He says he came out of the service having grown more as a person than as an artist. “When I was in the military, in my workplace, I felt so much love, consideration, respect, and those heartfelt feelings for other people. I just wanted to weave that into the music, and I just hope that that will show when the listeners and our beloved Carats are listening to our music.”

Of everything he felt in that time, warmth struck him hardest, and he came to see it as “a form of love.” It is the one thing, he says, he doesn’t want to lose sight of.

The songs Joshua handed over made an impression. “They were really surprised with the work that I’ve done,” he says of the company. “I think my company knew more about my personal taste after I gave them what I produced.”

Jeonghan hadn’t known that Joshua was so interested in producing. “When we started working on this album, I was amazed by how clear an idea he had in his mind about the musical direction that we should have moving forward. It seemed like he gave it a lot of thought and has confidence in it.”

The credits bear that out. Joshua co-wrote and co-composed his solo track, the alternative rock song “Not Personal,” and has a lyric credit on the closer, “No Looking Back.” Jeonghan co-wrote the lyrics for his own solo, the electro-house track “Coloring.”

Joshua had his own surprise. With a tour to follow the album’s promotions, Jeonghan had been mapping out the stage show. “I didn’t know he was thinking that much about the concert performances and how we should showcase our abilities through the concerts,” Joshua says. “So that was really interesting.”

The two didn’t start out agreeing on what JxJ should sound like. “He wanted to showcase a more… what would you call it? A more aggressive… well, not aggressive, but a stronger side, and I wanted to show a subtle, mature version of ourselves,” Joshua says. “Eventually, we met at the middle and came out with the song ‘12 O’Clock,’ which is right in the middle between strong and subtle.”

Getting there took three or four candidates for the title track. One started out as a house song and was then reworked as a band track. The final pick sits between the two. “I think this album was more meaningful, not so much in that we were attempting new tries, but in that we were able to expand our spectrum and touch on different genres that we didn’t explore in the past,” Jeonghan says.

“12 O’Clock” is a dance-rock track built on ’70s and ’80s disco and funk. Its title plays on noon and midnight: one hour for chasing goals in waking life, the other for the fantasies of sleep. In the video, the pair wander through warped train carriages and rooms with no way out, following a mythical creature that is part peacock, part Ouroboros. The seven-track album opens with the house song “Like You,” passes through R&B and soul, and ends on the raw band sound of “No Looking Back.” Jeonghan says that range gives the record an immersive, dreamlike feel, and the choreography is being built to match. “We just really wanted the whole album to feel like a journey between traveling through dreams and reality,” Joshua says.

For Joshua, the bigger change from Seventeen is how much he gets to sing. Within a 13-member group, and a five-member vocal team, his parts are short. “Even if it lasts long, it’s like five seconds. But as a unit, we could show more of our vocals.”

Making his career far from home was its own adjustment. Joshua grew up in Los Angeles. When he first arrived in Korea, he struggled with customs such as bowing and speaking in honorifics to elders. Thirteen years on, Korea feels like home, and he has watched the world catch up with it. “Even if I was American in America, it was really hard for me to fit in at first because of the differences and nobody knew anything about Korea at that time,” he says. “But now, it’s the new cool thing.”

Jeonghan says Seventeen’s global scale brings freedom and pressure hand in hand. “Of course, there’s the faith and the trust that our fans place in us, and this helps us explore various genres and take on new challenges. But at the same time, there’s the pressure to live up to their expectations. The pressure is always there, and that’s why we’re always trying harder and having so many meetings and practicing really hard.”

Joshua is waiting to see how fans respond before saying whether JxJ goes beyond one album. “We won’t know where this will take us until we get there” he says. Jeonghan sounds more sure. He says the pair saw the unit’s potential while preparing “Dreamscape” and came away feeling “this unit will definitely have something else to offer, something new to bring to the table.”

The album may be named for dreams, but Jeonghan says he didn’t make it to chase one. He sees it as the pair’s first album since entering their 30s. “I just wanted to showcase myself as a grown, more mature artist,” he says.

Working on JxJ showed Joshua how much he likes having a hand in his own music, and he says he can’t wait to make more personal work of his own. He has other plans too. “I’m also taking acting classes, so hopefully in the future I could be in a future acting project,” Joshua says. “That’d be really cool.”

Jeonghan says he thinks less about a next goal than about the fans already there. “I am just so grateful for all the love and support that our fans, Carats, are sending. So I just want to show them great music, bring them good music, and share great moments with them, and just keep growing together.”

title: Huw Edwards Drama For Skydance UK Network 5 Being Probed By Ofcom
summary: Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards is being probed by Ofcom over “fairness and privacy.” An investigation has been launched into the two-part series for Skydance UK network 5 under the “fairness and privacy” section of the regulator’s Broadcasting Code. No more detail was forthcoming. “We are investigating a fairness and privacy complaint about this […]
content:
Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards is being probed by Ofcom over “fairness and privacy.”

An investigation has been launched into the two-part series for Skydance UK network 5 under the “fairness and privacy” section of the regulator’s Broadcasting Code. No more detail was forthcoming. “We are investigating a fairness and privacy complaint about this programme,” said an Ofcom spokeswoman.

Starring Martin Clunes as Edwards, Power explored the allegations around the relationship between the BBC news anchor and a vulnerable teenager. Edwards rose to become one of the UK’s best-known news anchors before workplace misconduct allegations and a child pornography conviction ruined his reputation. In 2024, he pled guilty to making indecent images of children and was given a suspended sentence.

Edwards has been publicly critical of the 5 drama, saying the team behind it “made no attempt” to verify its story.

Watch on Deadline

“Fairness and privacy complaints” are complaints about “unjust or unfair treatment in programmes, or about unwarranted infringements of privacy in programmes.”

Edwards has not publicly said he made the complaint but these type of complaints must either come from the “‘person affected’ or by a person authorised by ‘the person affected’,” according to the Ofcom code.

Produced by Wonderhood Studios, 5 has always said Power was based on “extensive interviews with the victim and his family” as well as court reporting.

When Edwards published his critique six months ago, 5 said: “It has been produced in accordance with Ofcom’s Broadcasting Code. All allegations made in the film were put to Huw Edwards via his solicitors six weeks before transmission.”

Ofcom will now examine the series under the “fairness and privacy” section of the Broacasting Code and could dish out a range of punishments if it is found to have broken the code.

Deadline has reached out to 5 for comment.

title: ‘Tall Tales & Murder’ Scores New International Deals As Season 2 Takes Shape
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Crime caper Tall Tales & Murder has racked up more international sales as the team behind the show turn their attention to Season 2. The series bowed on RTÉ in Ireland last month to critical acclaim, and it will soon be on the BBC in the UK. Filmin has now nabbed the Avalon-distributed show […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Crime caper Tall Tales & Murder has racked up more international sales as the team behind the show turn their attention to Season 2. The series bowed on RTÉ in Ireland last month to critical acclaim, and it will soon be on the BBC in the UK.

Filmin has now nabbed the Avalon-distributed show for Portugal and Spain, while Picbox has snagged it for Central and Eastern Europe.

Tall Tales & Murder is based upon the ‘Dublin Trilogy’ by Caimh McDonnell and landed a two-season order off the bat. Avalon produces the series with Metropolitan Pictures. It is written by Stuart Carolan (Love/Hate).

Co-creator Chris Addison (Veep), was in Cannes last week at MIPCOM, meeting with international execs as Avalon keeps up its distribution push on the series.

Watch on Deadline

He told Deadline how the show has evolved from the books, as he starts to think about the show’s sophomore run.

“Any adaptation is going to be different from the source material, it’s just the degree to which it’s different. We left the source material so far behind in the first season that coming into Season 2, you’re off the rock. It’s a whole other world at that point.

“The first season starts out slightly odd and goes slowly bananas, so that means the pickup point of Season 2 is bananas.”

The Tall Tales & Murder cast includes Ella Lily Hyland (Black Doves), Aidan Gillen (Game of Thrones) and Philippa Dunne (Amandaland).

Addison said the show had been built around Hyland, who plays Bridget. “She’s the most naturally talented actor I’ve ever worked with,” he said.

Hyland was also in Cannes. The Irish star said Tall Tales & Murder marked her first time shooting on home turf with a local crew.

“There was a love on set that is rare,” she said. “Everyone worked really hard. It’s fair to say we had limited time to do all of the ambitious things that we wanted to do, so there was a sense of everyone being in it together. It meant a lot to everyone.”

The Iberia and CEE sales on Tall Tales & Murder follow earlier deals with international buyers, including SBS in Australia and ZDF in Germany.

title: Kleber Mendonça Filho To Mentor Marrakech’s Atlas Workshops As 30-Project Selection Unveiled
summary: The Atlas Workshops, Marrakech Film Festival’s project development platform, has named Brazilian director Kleber Mendonça Filho as the patron of its 9th edition and unveiled the 30 projects invited to participate. The award-winning The Secret Agent filmmaker follows in the footsteps of Cristian Mungiu and Jeff Nichols, in a role which will see him mentor […]
content:
The Atlas Workshops, Marrakech Film Festival’s project development platform, has named Brazilian director Kleber Mendonça Filho as the patron of its 9th edition and unveiled the 30 projects invited to participate.

The award-winning The Secret Agent filmmaker follows in the footsteps of Cristian Mungiu and Jeff Nichols, in a role which will see him mentor the filmmakers in attendance.

Mendonça Filho was at Marrakech last year while on the awards trail with The Secret Agent, which won best director in Cannes and then went on to clinch two Golden Globes and four Oscar nominations.

Watch on Deadline

“Last year, during my Conversation at the festival, I was asked whether I had ever planned to shoot a film in this city. Serving as the patron of the Atlas Workshops makes me feel as though I’m witnessing, right before my eyes, the birth of new films,” said the director, whose credits also include Aquarius (2016), and Bacurau on the Map (2019).

“I am delighted to receive this invitation. Listening to new ideas and understanding the aspirations of new generations of filmmakers is a source of inspiration for my own work.”

Selected from 410 submitted projects, the workshops will present 30 projects hailing from 14 countries, spanning Algeria, Cabo Verde, Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine, Rwanda, Senegal, Sudan, Syria, and Tunisia.

The lineup is split between 14 projects in development, 11 films in production or post-production, and five projects in the Atlas Close-Ups section, which is dedicated to Moroccan cinema. (scroll down for full list)

The projects in development include new projects from a host of directors who have already made their mark, including Amjad Abu Alala (You Will Die at Twenty), Laila Abbas (Thank You for Banking with Us), Meryem Benm’Barek (Sofia; Behind the Palm Trees), Sofia Alaoui (Animalia), and Yasmine Benkiran (Queens).

“We have a strong presence of strong female Moroccan directors,” said Atlas Workshops head Hédi Zardi, referring to Benm’Barek, Alaoui and Benkiran.

There are also first features by buzzy newcomers including Sarra Ryma, whose short film What Do The Maknines Dream Of played in Cannes Critics’ Week this year, while Zardi also noted the presence of French Senegalese filmmaker Dyana Gaye, with her first film in a decade, a Dakar-set musical entitled Studio Kébé.

“The aim is to have a good mix of discoveries and features by more established directors,” said Zardi.

Four of the 11 projects in the production or post-production selection previously participated in the Atlas Workshops at the development stage: Samuel Ishimwe’s Seasons of the Weary Kind (Rwanda), Alaa Eddine Aljem’s Eldorado (Morocco), Yoro Mbaye’s Fagadaga (Senegal), and Ismaël El Iraki’s Wolfmother (Morocco).

“It shows a continuity in our work,” commented Zardi, noting the presence of emerging talents such as Lebanese director Jessy Moussallem, who will attend with Faux Bijoux, an extension of her award-winning short of the same name.

“She has just started shooting and will show us the first images straight from the shoot at Atlas,” said Hardi.

Commenting on the Atlas Close-Ups lineup focused purely on Moroccan films, Hardi highlighted to the diversity of the selection, ranging from hybrid documentary Amar Made His Dream Come True, to audience-driven B512, The Man Who Forgot To Die and poetic drama The Cemetery’s Birds.

Atlas Station, supporting emerging Moroccan producers and directors, will support eight local producers and showcase five short film projects.

Founded in 2018, the Atlas Workshops is enjoying a vintage year on the festival front thanks to past participants such as Congo Boy and Strawberries, which premiered in Cannes Un Certain Regard; Furies, which played in Venice; Bardi, which debuted in New York; and Ego Reach We All, which screened in Locarno.

Atlas Workshops is one prong of Marrakech’s Atlas Programs banner, which gathers the professional initiatives of the Marrakech International Film Festival.

Alongside the Atlas Workshops and Atlas Station, Atlas Press supports the development of film criticism, while the Atlas Distribution Meetings bring together some 60 professionals from Africa, the Arab world, and Europe to foster networking and the circulation of films. The Atlas Distribution Awards round out this initiative by providing support for the distribution of films.

The Atlas Workshops, Atlas Station, and Atlas Distribution Meetings take place in Marrakech from November 22 to 26, while Atlas Press takes place from November 23 to 27, 2026.

Prior to the physical meeting in Marrakech, the Atlas Workshops will hold online sessions from November 2 to 6 to get the participants up to date with the latest industry developments and trends for independent film.
