title: ‘The Celebrity Traitors’: BBC Says It’s “Categorically Untrue” James Acaster Made Complaint About Co-Stars’ “Macho Banter”
summary: The BBC has firmly denied that James Acaster complained about the behavior of fellow comedians, Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan, during The Celebrity Traitors. The Mail on Sunday reported over the weekend that Acaster, who starred in Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire, raised his concerns with producers at Studio Lambert after he became “uncomfortable” with the “macho […]
content:
The BBC has firmly denied that James Acaster complained about the behavior of fellow comedians, Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan, during The Celebrity Traitors.

The Mail on Sunday reported over the weekend that Acaster, who starred in Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire, raised his concerns with producers at Studio Lambert after he became “uncomfortable” with the “macho banter” of Beckett and Ranganathan.

In a story splashed on the front page of the Mail on Sunday, the newspaper quoted a “snitch” on the show as saying: “Rob and Romesh clearly thought they were having a bit of a laugh, but James began to feel quite a lot of it was at his expense, and away from the cameras he started to get annoyed and upset by it. In the end, he spoke to the production team about it, saying he was unhappy and felt like he was being singled out.”

The BBC has since issued a forceful denial. A spokesperson said: “Claims of teasing amongst the cast on the show and claims of complaints about teasing are categorically untrue. There were no incidents of this nature and there is no evidence to support these allegations.”

Watch on Deadline

The Celebrity Traitors has become the subject of intense press speculation after dominating television ratings in the UK. The series is averaging nearly 9.3 million live viewers, which is almost unheard of outside of sport and major national events.

title: Sue Perkins Exploring ADHD Diagnosis For First Time In Audible Podcast ‘Attention, Please! Tales From A Distracted Mind’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Former Great British Bake Off host Sue Perkins is exploring her late-in-life ADHD diagnosis for the first time in an Audible podcast. Perkins was diagnosed with ADHD just a few years ago, in her 50s, and says she has since been on a journey. Landing today, Attention, Please! Tales From a Distracted Mind will […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Former Great British Bake Off host Sue Perkins is exploring her late-in-life ADHD diagnosis for the first time in an Audible podcast.

Perkins was diagnosed with ADHD just a few years ago, in her 50s, and says she has since been on a journey.

Landing today, Attention, Please! Tales From a Distracted Mind will see Perkins take audiences inside her head via dramatic recreations, live conversations and specially composed music by Joe Zeitlin. She speaks with psychologist Dr Tara Quinn-Cirillo, neuroscience expert Professor Ellie Dommett, and endocrinologist Professor Niamh Martin, who share their expertise and tackle some of her most pressing questions, drawing on the latest research and understanding.

Perkins is a former Great British Bake Off and comedian who has fronted numerous British TV shows.

Watch on Deadline

Perkins said: “I’ve spent most of my adult life feeling like I’m wired slightly wrong. Like everyone else got an instruction manual and mine got lost in the post. Getting an ADHD diagnosis later in life was equal parts relief and ‘Oh God, now what?’ This audio memoir is me finally having a proper look at my gloriously chaotic brain and trying to work out how to actually live with it rather than despite it. Fair warning: there’s laughter, there’s crying, there’s an inner voice that won’t shut up (also me), and at one point I end up doing equine therapy in the rain. It’s been quite the journey, and I’m chuffed it exists in audio because honestly, reading it back would have done my head in.”

title: Agents and Indie Producers Argue Incentives Alone Won’t Fix Hollywood’s Ills
summary: It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV. The FCC’s “financial interest and syndication” rules forced TV networks to buy shows from superproducers like Norman Lear and Grant Tinker rather than making them in-house. And […]
content:
It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV.

The FCC’s “financial interest and syndication” rules forced TV networks to buy shows from superproducers like Norman Lear and Grant Tinker rather than making them in-house. And ever since the FCC did away with fin-syn 30 years ago, producers and agents have been longing for its return.

Now, with momentum building behind a U.S. film incentive, they are hoping the moment is ripe to recreate fin-syn for the streaming era. They argue it would bring a jolt of creativity and a spirit of enterprise to a business stuck in a creative slump.

Popular on Variety

The major agencies — WME, CAA and UTA — announced last week that they are forming a coalition with production companies including Imagine Entertainment and Legendary to push for legislation that would force streamers to buy at least 50% of their original content from independent producers. The legislation would also limit the length of licensing terms, reviving secondary markets that have largely withered away.

Their message is that Hollywood ails not only from runaway production, but also from a consolidated ecosystem that limits creativity and makes it harder for producers, writers and actors to profit from their labor.

“The tax incentive may change where the production shoots, but it doesn’t change who owns and profits from it,” argued Ken Ziffren, co-founder of Ziffren Brittenham LLP, who has been campaigning for a restoration of fin-syn for decades. “We think the tax legislation only goes so far to help our industry and it’s not a complete effort, and it can’t be a complete effort, unless it’s paired with a modernized ownership framework.”

Jeff Sagansky, a producer, investor and longtime fin-syn supporter, argued that overseas incentives are not the only reason that U.S. production jobs are going away.

“They’re also going away because of the way the streaming business has consolidated around four players,” he said. “They act as an oligopoly. They’ve got incredible pricing power,” saying the streamers are ordering 30-40% fewer hours of programming than they were a few years ago.

Getting the idea through Congress will be an uphill battle, and will face adamant opposition from Netflix, Amazon and the other streaming platforms. The effort also has the potential to sow division within an industry that has united behind the goal of passing the first-ever federal film incentive.

Supporters wanted to some version of their ideas into the tax credit bill that was introduced to much fanfare in September. But while they had some positive meetings, they were ultimately rebuffed. They are now aiming for 2027, when Democrats are expected to take control of at least one of the houses of Congress.

Rep. Laura Friedman, a co-author of the tax incentive as well as a former producer, said in a statement that she sympathizes with producers’ concerns about industry consolidation and the threat to diverse voices in entertainment.

“My focus right now is on passing our bipartisan national film tax credit bill to put film and television workers back on the job, but I look forward to continuing to work with stakeholders to ensure the industry is vibrant for the future,” she said.

The Streaming Innovation Alliance, which includes Netflix and other streamers, issued a statement on Thursday calling the proposal a package of “blunt government mandates” that would “only dampen production and discourage creative risk-taking.”

The Federal Communications Commission adopted the fin-syn rules in 1970, when there were only three TV networks. The rules prevented networks from owning syndication rights in their shows, and later, from owning shows that aired in primetime. The rules are credited with leading to an era of groundbreaking TV, including “All in the Family,” “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and “The Cosby Show.”

The repeal of the rules in the mid-90s spurred a wave of vertical integration, as Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC and Viacom acquired CBS.

Arguing that the end of fin-syn had killed off independent production, a group called the Coalition for Program Diversity urged the FCC to reinstate a version of it. In 2002, the coalition — led by Ziffren — sought a new regulation that 25% of primetime programming come from independent producers. In a deregulatory era, such pleas fell on deaf ears.

Nowadays, streamers typically either make shows themselves or buy from the handful of other major studios. When they do buy from indie producers, they typically take all rights for 10-20 years, locking the producers out of the option of selling into secondary markets.

Mark Vahradian, producer of the “Transformers” franchise and other films, argued that streamers are so powerful that they can dictate those terms, and that dynamic ultimately hurts consumers.

“There’s no incentive for the creators to go out and build something brand new,” said Vahradian, a founding member of Producers United. “That’s why they’re only making sequels and franchise titles. They own those and have no motivation to say ‘Why don’t we do something new?’”

For years there wasn’t much opportunity to do anything about it. But with President Trump vowing to “save” Hollywood from a dramatic downturn, fin-syn supporters see an opening.

The initiative would require an act of Congress, as the FCC’s ambit is limited to the public airwaves.

Andrew Long, a senior fellow at the Free State Foundation, a free-market think tank, argued that the streaming marketplace is far more diversified now than the three-network era of the 1970s.

“It’s hard to find factual predicate that would justify this kind of government intervention in the video distribution marketplace in 2026,” Long said, adding that it could raise First Amendment concerns. “I think there would be high scrutiny, and I think that given the state of the marketplace and the options available, it might not pass muster.”

But Rich Shuter, head of business affairs at UTA, argued that consolidation leaves his agency’s clients without much leverage — and viewers without much choice.

“We’re going back to a situation where you have these streaming conglomerates controlling all the content the country is viewing,” Shuter said. “They’re determining what is being produced.”

Shuter said that more risk-taking will lead to a more vibrant ecosystem.

“We don’t want to stall the federal tax credit from being passed as quickly as possible,” he said. “We hope the administration and Congress recognize this is a supplemental benefit.”

title: Collage, a New Management and Investment Company, Launches as a Bridge Between AI-First Studios and Hollywood (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: As Hollywood continues to navigate the plethora of questions surrounding AI and its place in the industry, one former talent agent hopes to be the link between everyone involved. Enter Collage, a new management and investment company aimed at helping AI-first production companies navigate the Hollywood pipeline. Founded in July by former UTA agent Dante […]
content:
As Hollywood continues to navigate the plethora of questions surrounding AI and its place in the industry, one former talent agent hopes to be the link between everyone involved.

Enter Collage, a new management and investment company aimed at helping AI-first production companies navigate the Hollywood pipeline. Founded in July by former UTA agent Dante DeSario and media investor Michael Lambert, who worked within the talent agency’s independent film group before leaving in March, the company has completed a seed funding round — the amount of which DeSario would not disclose — backed by a suite of investors and advisers: Black Bear and Fundamental Films, Dennis Miller, Blue Deer Media, GOAL Ventures, AGC Studios, Roy Lee, Marty Bowen, Todd Lieberman, Todd Garner, Barry Porter, George Huber, Max Michael and Ric Roman Waugh, among others. The firm, based in Beverly Hills, currently has five full-time employees and roughly a dozen part-time staffers.

The earliest inklings for Collage came in February 2024, after DeSario got his hands on an early demo of OpenAI’s short-lived video generator Sora. After meeting with — and signing — some filmmakers who played with the generator and seeing them build their own companies focused on AI productions, DeSario realized that his own venture could “support these artists in a way that they needed help in various degrees” while helping “Hollywood navigate this, frankly, incredibly sensitive time over AI.”

Popular on Variety

Much of DeSario’s work includes aiding the initial batch of companies — which includes AI studios like Asteria, Native Foreign, Obsidian, and Jason Zada’s Secret Level — as they navigate Hollywood guilds, “studio bureaucrats,” copyright issues and demonstrations of the technology’s capabilities. DeSario’s firm also acts as an investment company, though he would not disclose which companies he’s invested in. “We’re here to offer the menu of things to what this new category needs,” he says.

On the Hollywood side, DeSario wants to demonstrate to studios which companies are making human-led work and “who to stay away from” in an era of seemingly never-ending upstarts.

Collage’s model comes as legacy Hollywood companies figure out how to engage with AI at a time when consternation persists among both creatives and audiences over issues surrounding jobs, slop content and the impact on creativity. DeSario hopes Collage can act as “infrastructure,” a bridge between the various stakeholders in the industry that allows more stories to be told while encouraging acceptance of the technology.

“I’m an independent film guy,” he said. “I just want to help filmmakers get their projects made. That was my whole intention, and realizing that this is something that is unlike what a lot of people think. There’s a lot of fallacy. It’s not pushing a button. There’s real craft and real differentiation between those who can have taste and want to tell stories and helping them get out there.”

He’s also hoping that, as more of these companies emerge, they’ll be able to compete with and complement the companies that have maintained footprints in Hollywood through their traditional filmmaking offerings. “The legacy system should be inviting them because they’re incredible craftspeople to work with all of the various people who are already working on films,” DeSario says.

A goal for him, he says, is to help audiences witness the AI version of a “Toy Story” moment, or a film developed with AI that breaks through with general moviegoers.

“I’ve personally seen work that has made me feel something,” he says. “You want to feel something. I’ve had that experience. I think a lot of people haven’t had that experience, and because it’s hard to feel something when there’s so much fear in the air. I want to help show the general audiences and help facilitate what I’ve seen to everyone else because it’s pretty potent.”

title: Sony Pictures Television Hires Lauren Glaubach, Former YouTube and Pinterest Exec, to Lead Digital and Social Distribution Strategy
summary: Sony Pictures Television hired Lauren Glaubach, a former YouTube and Pinterest content exec, in the newly created role of executive vice president, distribution, digital and social platforms. Glaubach will head up Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and other digital platforms, reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, presidents of distribution and networks at […]
content:
Sony Pictures Television hired Lauren Glaubach, a former YouTube and Pinterest content exec, in the newly created role of executive vice president, distribution, digital and social platforms.

Glaubach will head up Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and other digital platforms, reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, presidents of distribution and networks at SPT. She’s tasked with unlocking “new opportunities” for the company’s film and television library and “maximizing” the value of its IP, Sony Pictures Television said.

Glaubach joins the company as Sony Pictures Television has stepped up efforts to boost revenue from digital platforms. Recent initiatives include the announcement of “Jeopardy! YouTube Edition Volume 2”; the launch of “Reading Rainbow” on YouTube; and a newly announced partnership with Prof. Brian Cox, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester, to develop premium original content for digital audiences.

Popular on Variety

“Lauren has spent her career working at the intersection of content, platforms, and audiences, and has a proven track record of building and growing digital businesses,” Spivak and Littmann said in a joint statement. “We’re very pleased to have her join SPT and are excited about what we can accomplish together.”

Glaubach most recently was at Pinterest, where she served as VP, head of global content partnerships, leading a team responsible for overseeing the platform’s content producer network and creator communities. Prior to Pinterest, she spent more than a decade at YouTube in senior strategy, programming, partnerships and operations roles, most recently serving as director, global head of kids and family content partnerships and programming. During her tenure at YouTube, Glaubach managed a partner portfolio of more than 500 channels spanning traditional media and YouTube-first creators.

Earlier in her career, Glaubach held strategy, brand management and marketing roles at Disney and BloomSpot, an e-commerce marketplace. She earned a bachelor or arts degree in psychology from Princeton University and an MBA from Harvard Business School.

Glaubach, in a statement provided by SPT, said: “The ways audiences engage with entertainment continue to evolve, creating meaningful opportunities to extend the reach and impact of the stories and franchises they love. I’m excited to join Sony Pictures and work with this talented team to develop digital experiences that meet audiences where they are, deepen their connection to our content, and open up new possibilities for our iconic brands.”

title: Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer
summary: Bot attacks have plagued Ticketmaster for years, so to combat it, the ticketing service is shaking up its executive ranks and going all-in on AI. Ticketmaster has hired Jim Freeman as its chief technology officer, filling a slot left vacant since February after its London-based chief technology officer, Carlos Alvarez-Coch, departed ahead of a deposition […]
content:
Bot attacks have plagued Ticketmaster for years, so to combat it, the ticketing service is shaking up its executive ranks and going all-in on AI.

Ticketmaster has hired Jim Freeman as its chief technology officer, filling a slot left vacant since February after its London-based chief technology officer, Carlos Alvarez-Coch, departed ahead of a deposition in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against parent company Live Nation. It has also appointed Rachel Smith, a veteran of Block (owner of music service Tidal), to be its first senior vice president of data science and machine learning, and Disney and Stripe product veteran Chuck Mortimore as its next senior vice president of product.

As part of the AI push, Ticketmaster has also brought on the team from Raige.ai, an AI startup the company acquired in July. The team will boost Ticketmaster’s adoption of AI tools across the company while also building out the platform’s AI infrastructure.

Popular on Variety

“Reliable, secure and personalized experiences depend on how effectively we use technology and data,” Saumil Mehta, Ticketmaster’s global president, said in a statement. “Jim, Rachel, Chuck and the Ragie.ai team will help us move faster, build better tools and deliver better outcomes for fans, artists, venues and clients.”

Freeman’s remit as chief technology officer will tackle all things AI: building AI tools, using the technology to power fan experiences and ensuring its adoption across Ticketmaster’s organization. Freeman joined the company after a stint as senior adviser at Permira, though he formerly worked as a vice president at Amazon to build and launch Prime Video and its respective device and distribution partnerships.

Smith’s work will include an expanded focus on data science and analytics, including tightening integration between data and the company’s broader product development, while Mortimore will help lead product strategy to help combat the company’s bot issues and ensure fans have easier access to both their accounts and their tickets.

Pictured top (l. to r.): Jim Freeman, Rachel Smith, Chuck Mortimore

title: Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’
summary: The 9th edition of El Gouna Film Festival (Oct. 15-23) may be celebrating Mona Zaki’s past, but the Egyptian film star is far more interested in what she’s yet to do. Honored with the festival’s Career Achievement Award at the opening ceremony, Zaki, who has already built a career spanning more than three decades, hasn’t […]
content:
The 9th edition of El Gouna Film Festival (Oct. 15-23) may be celebrating Mona Zaki’s past, but the Egyptian film star is far more interested in what she’s yet to do.

Honored with the festival’s Career Achievement Award at the opening ceremony, Zaki, who has already built a career spanning more than three decades, hasn’t even turned 50. Sitting down with Variety on the shores of the Red Sea, she speaks about that prolific career less as a completed body of work than a continuous process of reinvention. That ongoing transformation has required her to repeatedly shed audiences’ expectations of who Mona Zaki should be. “I get bored easily with myself,” she shares.

Looking back, Zaki says two lessons in particular stand out: learning the power of saying “no” and finding the confidence and willingness to express herself, both personally and emotionally. The latter, she confides, was something acting itself helped teach her.

Popular on Variety

“You just have to open up,” she reflects. “Your emotions are important to be heard, and it’s okay. Part of your healing is saying what you feel.”

Zaki entered the industry young, first in theater, before moving into television and, ultimately, the silver screen. Early on, she became closely associated with the “girl next door,” an image that increasingly felt at odds with both the woman she was becoming and the kinds of characters she wanted to explore.

“I started to kind of feel like I’m going there doing the same thing in every different project,” she recalls. “How boring is that? I needed to shift.”

That turning point came with Yousry Nasrallah’s 2009 drama “Scheherazade, Tell Me a Story” (Ehky Ya Shahrazad), written by the late Wahid Hamed, which saw Zaki take on the role of a television host whose program examines the experiences of women navigating romance, health, everyday life, and the expectations placed upon them by Egyptian society.

The departure from Zaki’s familiar screen persona drew intense backlash, with audiences questioning what had happened to the “girl next door” they had come to know. The response shook her enough that she turned to Hamed with concerns about facing the film’s promotional tour. He encouraged her to stand behind a choice she had made out of love for the work, advice that helped Zaki confront the resistance to seeing her move beyond the roles that had defined her early career.

For Zaki, the experience marked the beginning of a struggle that has followed her throughout her career, that of finding roles that allow women to address subjects Egyptian cinema has historically treated as difficult or off-limits. “Censorship, talking about taboos, things that are not okay most of the time, especially for women to talk about,” remain among the challenges she continues to face. “I’m still living in that struggle even now. It can be very difficult to find a meaningful script.”

While she believes the landscape has advanced over more than 30 years, Zaki remains deeply frustrated by the gap between the talent of Egypt’s actresses and the opportunities afforded them. “It breaks my heart that most of them are not taking the chances they deserve and the topics they would love to talk about and the rights they want to stand for.”

Her own connection with audiences is something she has learned to negotiate over time. “It’s a relationship. You work on it like any other relationship in your life,” she explains. Part of that relationship, she believes, means establishing boundaries around her freedom to evolve as an artist.

“I have the right not to feel bored and sick of myself doing the same thing because I’m not corporate, I’m an artist,” she stresses. “Art is about freedom, it’s about change, it’s about trial and error.”

With each role, Zaki starts by building a life for the character beyond what exists in the script. She works with an acting coach on every project, drawing on different techniques to construct the character’s history.

One of the most important parts of that process, she explains, is imagining a character’s life before the audience ever meets her. Zaki might close her eyes and picture the woman she’s playing at seven years old, in her childhood home with her mother, building memories and emotional associations that will never appear on screen but are critical to the performance. “I don’t have to say it, but I can make people feel it the way I felt it.”

That method was put to a different test with “El Sett,” Marwan Hamed’s biopic of Umm Kulthum. This time, Zaki was building a character from the life of one of the Arab world’s most revered cultural figures, with decades of history and public memory with which to contend. She plunged into what she calls “crazy research,” watching every piece of footage she could find and repeatedly listening to a rare two-hour radio interview that became one of her most important references.

“The whole internal emotions are the imagination of the writer and me.” While the facts of Umm Kulthum’s life are immutable, Zaki still had to find the woman behind them.

To bridge that gap, Zaki imagined the parts of Kulthum’s life no archive could relate: the emotions, relationships and private struggles that might have shaped her from childhood. The character stayed with Zaki long after cameras stopped rolling, and she found it difficult to sever that connection after filming wrapped.

“I came out of the project feeling that I’m a 70-year-old woman. I’m serious, this was not a joke.” For months, she had taken on not only the physical transformation into Kulthum, but also the emotions and experiences of a woman decades older than herself. Fully returning to Mona Zaki proved disorienting. “I think my whole face changed after that,” she recalls. “I couldn’t accept myself in the mirror.”

Some of Kulthum has proven difficult to shake. “I’m trying to get rid of her,” Zaki muses. “I only have a few leftovers, gladly. Honestly, I don’t want to feel like I’m 70 and I’m not there yet.”

Asked what she looks for in a role now, after more than three decades of acting, Zaki doesn’t hesitate. “Reality. Honesty. That would just take my heart.”

title: Sony Pictures Television Names Lauren Glaubach EVP Distribution, Digital & Social Platforms
summary: Sony Pictures Television has tapped Lauren Glaubach for the newly created role of EVP, Distribution, Digital and Social Platforms. Reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, Presidents of Distribution & Networks, SPT, Glaubach will help drive Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and digital platform for both film and television content, “while building connections […]
content:
Sony Pictures Television has tapped Lauren Glaubach for the newly created role of EVP, Distribution, Digital and Social Platforms.

Reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, Presidents of Distribution & Networks, SPT, Glaubach will help drive Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and digital platform for both film and television content, “while building connections with audiences and creating opportunities for sustained engagement and revenue.”

The hiring of Glaubach follows news earlier this month that SPT distribution and networks co-president Mike Wald would be retiring at year-end after 32 years with the company, and the naming of Spivak and LIttman as Presidents of Distribution & Networks,

Leading Sony Pictures’ global strategy on social and digital platforms, Glaubach will shape and drive a comprehensive growth and monetization strategy that balances long-term brand stewardship with revenue generation, per SPT. She will oversee efforts to deepen audience engagement, extend the reach of the studio’s marketing and promotional initiatives, and unlock new opportunities across the company’s film and television library. She also will lead the continued growth of Sony Pictures’ digital channel portfolio, maximizing the value of the studio’s extensive collection of franchises, brands, and intellectual property across social and digital platforms.

Watch on Deadline

“Lauren has spent her career working at the intersection of content, platforms, and audiences, and has a proven track record of building and growing digital businesses,” said Spivak and Littmann. “We’re very pleased to have her join SPT and are excited about what we can accomplish together.”

Glaubach joins SPT from Pinterest, where she served as Vice President, Head of Global Content Partnerships, leading an international team responsible for overseeing the platform’s content producer network and growing creator communities. Prior to Pinterest, she spent more than a decade at YouTube in senior strategy, programming, partnerships and operations roles, most recently serving as Director, Global Head of Kids & Family Content Partnerships & Programming. During her tenure at YouTube, Glaubach managed a partner portfolio of more than 500 channels spanning traditional media and YouTube-first creators, and built a creator ecosystem across YouTube Kids, Supervised Experiences and the main YouTube app.

“The ways audiences engage with entertainment continue to evolve, creating meaningful opportunities to extend the reach and impact of the stories and franchises they love,” said Glaubach. “I’m excited to join Sony Pictures and work with this talented team to develop digital experiences that meet audiences where they are, deepen their connection to our content, and open up new possibilities for our iconic brands.”

Her appointment comes at a time of significant momentum across Sony Pictures Television’s digital business. Recent initiatives include the announcement of Jeopardy! YouTube Edition Volume 2, the launch of Reading Rainbow on YouTube, and a newly announced partnership with Professor Brian Cox to develop premium original content for global digital audiences.

Earlier in her career, Glaubach held strategy, brand management and marketing roles at The Walt Disney Company and BloomSpot. She earned an MBA from Harvard Business School and a B.A. from Princeton University.

title: Tom Holland And Drew Pearce Team On Sony Thriller ‘Penthouse’ With Billy17 And Point Of No Return Producing
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures has pre-emptively bought Penthouse, an original idea by Drew Pearce, with Tom Holland’s production company Billy17 and Pearce’s Point Of No Return producing. The film is being developed as a starring vehicle for Holland. Pearce (The Thomas Crown Affair, The Fall Guy, Iron Man 3) will be writing the script, with Holland […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures has pre-emptively bought Penthouse, an original idea by Drew Pearce, with Tom Holland’s production company Billy17 and Pearce’s Point Of No Return producing. The film is being developed as a starring vehicle for Holland.

Pearce (The Thomas Crown Affair, The Fall Guy, Iron Man 3) will be writing the script, with Holland and his Billy17 partners playing an instrumental role in its development alongside Pearce.

The plot is under wraps, but Penthouse described as a thriller. Tom Holland, Harry Holland and Will South will produce on behalf of Billy17 alongside Pearce on behalf of Point of Not Return. Ian Fisher will executive produce for Point of No Return.

Following the record-breaking success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Penthouse builds on the already strong relationship between Sony and Holland, whose Billy17 has a producing deal with Sony Pictures. Holland is still on screens with Sony Pictures’ Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which counts a worldwide gross of more than $2 billion.

Watch on Deadline

Holland will also star in Sony Pictures’ upcoming film about Fred Astaire, which recently announced Margaret Qualley, Sabrina Carpenter and Talia Ryder as co-stars; Holland and Billy17 also serve as producers of the pic.

Additionally, Holland recently starred in The Odyssey. He is repped by WME and Sloane Offer.

Pearce’s writing credits include Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw and Hotel Artemis, which he also directed. The Thomas Crown Affair, starring and directed by Michael B. Jordan, hits theaters in March 2027. Pearce is repped by WME and Sloane Offer.

title: Steven Crowder Files Trademark Lawsuit Against CNN And Jubilee Over Use Of “Change My Mind” In James Talarico Town Hall
summary: Conservative comedian and commentator Steven Crowder has filed a trademark infringement lawsuit against CNN and co-producer Jubilee Media, claiming that their recent town hall with James Talarico was an unauthorized use of his “Change My Mind” format. In the lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Fort Worth, TX, Crowder’s LWC IP claimed that the […]
content:
Conservative comedian and commentator Steven Crowder has filed a trademark infringement lawsuit against CNN and co-producer Jubilee Media, claiming that their recent town hall with James Talarico was an unauthorized use of his “Change My Mind” format.

In the lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Fort Worth, TX, Crowder’s LWC IP claimed that the October 14 town hall “appropriated” his series, in which he sits at a table on college campuses with banners that display topics like, “I’m Pro-Gun. Change My Mind.” The series features debates with figures with alternative views.

The CNN/Jubilee town hall featured Talarico answering questions from moderator Erin Burnett and audience members, as well as a portion of the event where he sat and conversed with Texans who didn’t share his views. The lawsuit claimed that the format was “intentionally modeled after LWC’s ‘Change My Mind’ series.” The suit included screenshots of the event featuring the phrase “Change My Mind.”

Watch on Deadline

The lawsuit also claimed trademark counterfeit and trademark dilution. It seeks an injunction prohibiting the use of the trademark, as well as unspecified damages.

“In a nationally televised town hall, Defendants appropriated LWC IP’s mark and signature format to leverage the goodwill and credibility Steven Crowder and Louder with Crowder have cultivated among conservative and Republican audiences over nearly a decade. Defendants did so in the midst of a closely watched Texas Senate race, seeking to benefit from the public association between the Mark and conservative political discourse while creating a likelihood that viewers would perceive endorsement, sponsorship, or affiliation where none existed.”

Spokespersons for CNN and Jubilee did not immediately return requests for comment.

title: Ashley Avis Helming Film Adaptation Of Joanne Greenberg’s ‘I Never Promised You A Rose Garden’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: After a decade-long effort to secure the film rights to I Never Promised You a Rose Garden —Joanne Greenberg’s classic 1964 novel, which she calls “one of the most arresting and authentic explorations of mental illness ever written” — Ashley Avis has done it. The rising filmmaker, whose credits include Disney+’s Black Beauty, will […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: After a decade-long effort to secure the film rights to I Never Promised You a Rose Garden —Joanne Greenberg’s classic 1964 novel, which she calls “one of the most arresting and authentic explorations of mental illness ever written” — Ashley Avis has done it.

The rising filmmaker, whose credits include Disney+’s Black Beauty, will direct from her own script and produce alongside Edward Winters through her Winterstone Pictures banner.

Inspired by Greenberg’s experiences as a young woman diagnosed with schizophrenia, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden follows Deborah Blau, a brilliant and deeply troubled Jewish teenager who retreats into an elaborate kingdom she has constructed within her own mind.

As Deborah loses her grip on reality, she’s admitted to Chestnut Lodge, where she forms an unlikely bond with renowned German psychiatrist Dr. Clara Fried, whose own past remains shrouded in unresolved trauma and mystery. In the years following World War II, these two women must navigate the fragile boundary between reality and fantasy, forging a unique relationship that challenges the fabric of mental health as we know it.

Watch on Deadline

Regarded as a seminal work on mental health, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden has sold millions of copies worldwide and previously inspired an Academy Award-nominated 1977 film, directed by Anthony Page and starring Kathleen Quinlan.

Avis told us of the novel, “Joanne Greenberg crafted a story that is at once deeply intimate and breathtakingly imaginative, because it is courageously personal. She invites us into the Kingdom of Yr, into all of its seduction, and beauty along with its violence – and we will question, along with Deborah, whether it is possible to give it up.”

What moved Avis most about the book “was the true story tucked between the pages of Rose Garden; the relationship between two very real women who inspired these characters. Deborah Blau and Dr. Fried become mirrors for one another as they navigate darkness, trauma, healing, and the question of what it means to truly live in, and accept, reality.”

A great lover of animals — and horses, in particular — Avis channeled that passion into the two films for which she’s best known: a Disney+ adaptation of Anna Sewell’s classic 1877 novel Black Beauty, starring Kate Winslet and Mackenzie Foy, and the Critics Choice Award-nominated documentary Wild Beauty: Mustang Spirit of the West. Currently, Avis is developing American Wolf — a film on the wolves of Yellowstone, based on the novel by Nate Blakeslee — with Appian Way. Additionally, she has set up a reimagining of Wim Wenders’ romance City of Angels at Warner Bros. She is represented by CAA and Ryan Goodell of Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

title: Armie Hammer Wraps Under-The-Radar Action-Thriller ‘Tokyo Blitz’, Film Heads To AFM For Sales
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Armie Hammer is starring in under-the-radar action-thriller Tokyo Blitz, which recently wrapped in Los Angeles. This marks the Call Me By Your Name and The Social Network actor’s first announced project since his controversial Citizen Vigilante film caused a stir this summer after getting the backing of Elon Musk. Hammer continues to rebuild after […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Armie Hammer is starring in under-the-radar action-thriller Tokyo Blitz, which recently wrapped in Los Angeles.

This marks the Call Me By Your Name and The Social Network actor’s first announced project since his controversial Citizen Vigilante film caused a stir this summer after getting the backing of Elon Musk.

Hammer continues to rebuild after years in the wilderness. CAA helped broker the deal for him to join Tokyo Blitz, but agency sources tell us CAA isn’t repping the actor who hasn’t had agency representation since he was dropped by WME in 2021.

Film Mode Entertainment has boarded worldwide sales on Tokyo Blitz and will be showing a first look to buyers at next month’s American Film Market.

Watch on Deadline

Written and directed by Garrett Glassell (Kade), the movie “follows a ruthless Yakuza enforcer (Joey Chase) who’s trying to save his fractured family when he’s drawn into a deadly war for control of Tokyo’s first legal casino, putting him on a collision course with Rick (Armie Hammer), an elite American hitman who never misses his mark.”

The film also stars Kooper Seewald, Yuwi, Nobuaki Shimamoto, and John Kim.

Keli Price produced under his Price Productions banner, alongside Tommy Anderson of Charthouse Films and Liam S. Terlecki. Executive producers include Clay Epstein of Film Mode Entertainment, Christopher Manalo, and Mike Levenson.

“Tokyo Blitz is an action-thriller with real heart at its core, and Garrett has created a distinctive world that feels both visceral and deeply personal. He has a unique style and vision, and pairing that vision with Armie couldn’t have been a better fit,” said Keli Price.

“Armie brought tremendous intensity and commitment to the role. We’re thrilled to have Film Mode bringing Tokyo Blitz to the international marketplace and giving buyers their first look at AFM,” said Clay Epstein.

Price negotiated Hammer’s deal with CAA and brokered the Film Mode pact. Hammer is repped by law firm Yorn Levine. Chase is repped by NTA; Seewald by Elégance; Yuwi by Park Noack; and Shimamoto by Minc.

title: Michael Douglas Says Marvel ‘Wouldn’t Let Me’ Quit After Asking Studio for ‘Ant-Man’ Character to Be Killed Off
summary: Michael Douglas reached his limit playing Hank Pym (the original Ant-Man) after two Marvel movies, but the studio refused to grant him his wish when he asked for the character to be killed off. The Oscar winner was asked during a recent “Happy Sad Confused” interview if the stories were true about him wanting to […]
content:
Michael Douglas reached his limit playing Hank Pym (the original Ant-Man) after two Marvel movies, but the studio refused to grant him his wish when he asked for the character to be killed off. The Oscar winner was asked during a recent “Happy Sad Confused” interview if the stories were true about him wanting to be killed off from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, to which he responded: “I would have been killed off after the second one, but they wouldn’t let me.”

Appearing on “The View” in 2024, Douglas said he asked Marvel to kill him off in the third standalone “Ant-Man” movie, “Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania,” and even pitched an idea of how to do it that included a special effects bonanza.

“[Getting killed off] actually was my request for the third one,” Douglas said at the time. “I said I’d like to have a serious [death], with all these great special effects. There’s got to be some fantastic way where I can shrink to an ant size and explode, whatever it is. I want to use all those effects. But that was on the last one. Now, I don’t think I’m going to show up [for a fourth].”

Popular on Variety

Douglas debuted as Hank Pym in 2015’s “Ant-Man” and returned in three follow-up appearances: 2018’s “Ant-Man and the Wasp,” 2019’s “Avengers: Endgame” and 2023’s “Quantumania.”

“I said, ‘I’ve never done a green screen movie,’” Douglas said on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast about wanting to join Marvel “I [told] all my agents, ‘I’d like to do one of these green screen movies to see what they’re like,’ you know? Because it’s amazing. It’s nothing, just a green screen and they show you the pictures of what it’s gonna look like when it’s all finished.”

“It’s hard acting, man,” he added. “It’s coming at you here, this and that, you know… We did ‘Ant-Man’ and Paul Rudd was a wonderful actor — a lovely group — but then you can’t get out of it.”

Watch Douglas’ full appearance on “Happy Sad Confused” in the video below.

title: Jaafar Jackson on Playing His Uncle in ‘Michael,’ Losing the Original Third Act and the Upcoming Sequel: ‘My Job Is to Come Prepared’
summary: Two years before a frame of “Michael” was shot, Jaafar Jackson wrote down a list of goals. One was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross $1 billion at the worldwide box office. He did both. Antoine Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion worldwide and Lionsgate’s […]
content:
Two years before a frame of “Michael” was shot, Jaafar Jackson wrote down a list of goals. One was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross $1 billion at the worldwide box office.

He did both.

Antoine Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion worldwide and Lionsgate’s biggest release ever. It also made a star of Jackson, who had never acted professionally before.

“I was pretty emotional,” he tells Variety. “I know how proud Michael would be of that, because he was someone who wanted to break many records.”

Popular on Variety

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Jackson opens up about leading the blockbuster “Michael,” navigating the Oscar buzz surrounding his performance and what he hopes comes next after a career-defining year.

Listen below.

Jackson, 30, is sitting down with Variety just two days after wrapping his second film, “Supermax,” opposite Will Smith, following 40 days of shooting in Australia. He’s candid about the life that led him here. Growing up in a house filled with 30 or 40 relatives every holiday, he dreamed of becoming a golfer, not a performer. He didn’t fully grasp the weight of his last name until he was about six, watching his father and uncles take the stage as the Jackson 5 at a reunion concert in New York and hearing the crowd erupt.

He has fond memories of his family, especially his late uncle. One of his earliest recollections of Michael is asking him for Starbursts — specifically the pink and red ones, his favorite flavors.

Bringing Michael to life, however, took two years of preparation before Jackson officially landed the role: building his own archive of songs, demos, journals, rehearsals and performances; working with acting coach Angela Gibbs; and immersing himself in the techniques of Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen. Nailing his signature voice and tone came first. After the young Jackson sent producer Graham King an unsolicited voice note speaking as Michael, he had a coach the next day. The hardest part came with learning his signature movies, particularly when performing the footwork for “Bad,” which is what closes out the film.

But what does it mean to reenact your own family’s history?

Colman Domingo plays a grandfather who, Jackson says, was gentler with him than with his father, Jermaine. Nia Long, who plays his grandmother Katherine, would touch his hand in certain scenes the way his grandmother did in real life. His father Jermaine insisted on watching the film for the first time at its Berlin premiere, surrounded by an audience. And the next day, he called his son and told him, he couldn’t tell him apart from his late brother.

Jaafar is just trying to take this all in.

Read excerpts from his episode below.

The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson, “Michael” (Glen Wilson / Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection) ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection

You’re here two days after wrapping a movie with Will Smith. Is that correct?

That’s correct. I was in Australia for about 40 days, an incredible experience, to shoot my second film and to shoot outside the country, since we shot all of “Michael” in Los Angeles. It was a whole new experience, with a new crew, a new cast and a character completely different from Michael. That excited me.

So you didn’t dance or sing in this movie?

No, no, not at all. It’s completely different.

You were born in Los Angeles in 1996. What was your childhood like growing up as a Jackson, and when did you first understand what that name meant to the world?

I grew up with a lot of siblings and cousins who visited on weekends and every holiday. About 30 to 40 family members were at the house, so we had lots of game nights and family cookouts, with music playing. I didn’t really realize who my family was until I was around six, when I saw them perform in New York for their 30th anniversary. Hearing the fans scream, I was scared because I didn’t understand how intense it was to see people react to someone like that.

I first saw that when my dad and uncles came out on stage as the Jackson 5, and that’s the first memory I can recall of, “Oh, they’re important in some way. They have a huge fan base.”

A very important follow-up. What games did you play on family game night, and how competitive does it get in the Jackson household?

It was always Pictionary. Boys versus girls, no doubt. It was pretty competitive, because the boys always like to brag. I think our streak was like 15 years. I think it was unfair. There are a lot more boys in the family.

You started making music around 12, and your debut single, “Got Me Singing,” came out in 2019. Did you always see yourself as a musician first?

No. Growing up, I was only focused on golf. I started playing when I was around 4. My dad gave me golf balls to throw before I could properly swing a club, because I was so young. I fell in love with it. He got me a coach to train with once a week, then I joined a young golf club and started playing tournaments and did some charity tournaments with my father. I committed to it full time, every day, until he brought me to a recording studio and had me sit and watch him create from scratch. That shifted what I wanted to do. That was the turning point.

What’s your earliest memory of your Uncle Michael? Not the icon. Just Uncle Michael.

Asking him for candy. He always had candy machines or stacks of candy in the movie theater, and I had a problem with an addiction to Starbursts at that age. Pink and red. I would eat too many as a kid. I remember always asking him for candy and wanting to play. He always had the latest games and game consoles, and we’d play hide-and-seek.

In that house, it must have been impossible to find him.

He was the best at it. It was just fun, free-roaming and a blast all the time.

“Michael” became the first biopic to cross $1 billion worldwide, and it’s Lionsgate’s biggest film ever. Sorry you set that bar for yourself. Do you remember where you were when you heard and who called to tell you?

I was at home, and I spoke with Antoine [Fuqua] and Graham King individually. We were discussing how crazy a milestone that is. Going into it, you hope and dream it’ll be that successful. I remember that two years before production even started, I wrote down a list of goals I wanted to accomplish and one was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross the $1 billion mark. When it did that, I was pretty emotional. I was proud of it, because I know how proud Michael would be. He wanted to break many records, and I couldn’t be more grateful that this did.

I imagine you walking the earth, stalking Rami Malek. “I’m coming for your record, man.”

No, he’s great. I actually got to meet him in Paris during Fashion Week. He couldn’t have been nicer.

Let’s talk about “Michael” Part 2. Lionsgate’s Adam Fogelson has said production could start at the end of this year or early next, with a release targeted for 2027 or ’28. Where do things officially stand? Is anything on your schedule?

I haven’t been told anything concrete, but whatever decision is made, I’m more than ready to get back into it and excited for where that goes. I haven’t been told a date or anything solid yet. As far as my schedule, it’s open.

Leading up to the release, there was a lot of reporting about the original third act, which dealt with some sensitive subject matter. What was it like, as an actor, to lose material you had already shot and performed, knowing that footage would never see the light of day?

It was a massive shoot. I’ve heard many stories from other actors about how much you shoot on a project that doesn’t make it into the final picture. In the editing room, you go through scenes looking for specific performances or takes and things change constantly. So going in, I knew not everything we shot would make it into the final picture. But for me, it was the most rewarding experience because even the things that weren’t used, the experience I got from them, made me a better actor. I feel like that will happen many more times with other projects. You wish a certain performance was in there and it’s not. That’s something you have to deal with when making a film.

You’re in a best actor conversation with some people like Ryan Gosling, Pedro Pascal, Matt Damon and John Malkovich. How are you approaching your first Oscar campaign? Even the movie’s detractors seem to agree: “But Jaafar is great.”

It’s been a crazy and surreal experience, and it’s all gone so fast. I’m taking it a day at a time. Having those conversations and being here speaking with you has been a great honor, and I’m learning so much. Whatever the studio has in mind, I’ll be there to support the film in any way I need to and I’ll be happy to do that. It’s an exciting time, and it inspires me to want to do more work and challenge myself in many different ways. To be in that conversation is definitely an honor.

Did you know awards season was like this? That you’d have to go through all these campaign stops?

Not to that extent. You hear stories, but it’s a great experience to feel it and see it firsthand.

What did you have to learn from scratch, and who taught you the Michael-isms and the Michael moves?

It started with dissecting and creating a library of footage of Michael. A library of all his songs, demos, writings and journaling, performances and rehearsals. I immersed myself in that every day. It became a full-time job, while I also worked on acting with Angela Gibbs, my head coach, who steered me in the right direction, put me in acting classes and brought in other coaches. I read books on classic teachers like Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen and studied different approaches, because there are many tools you can use, but they don’t work for every actor. I researched different ways to approach a scene, picked my favorites and then developed new ones that might work for Michael, like the dancing. It was a full immersion, a process that took about two years until I actually knew I had the role. Then it was a different energy and confidence, knowing I had it.

Our chief film critic, Owen Gleiberman, wrote in his review that you got Michael’s tentative, high, sugary voice just right. Did you find the voice first or the movement first?

The voice came first. The movement was harder. I believe the voice was the first thing that convinced Graham because I sent him a voice note out of nowhere, over text, of me speaking as Michael. He called me and said, “Getting you a coach tomorrow.” That was the turning point.

Fans keep circulating the side-by-side of your “Bad” tour rehearsal with the 1988 concert. What was the hardest move to replicate?

The hardest thing was feeling that true freedom on stage, so it didn’t feel rehearsed or choreographed. It’s very fluid, and that came from repetition, doing it over and over in rehearsal, so when I shot it that day, I could be completely free. I wasn’t thinking about the next move. I was present in the moment. That was the most fun part. But in rehearsal, the most challenging thing was going up on your toes, because doing it over and over hurts you. I did, many times. That move was a problem for me. I had a whole new respect for ballet dancers. Their toes are probably the strongest part of the body.

Colman Domingo plays your grandfather, Joe Jackson. What was it like to film those scenes, knowing your own father lived through many of those tougher moments?

It was eye-opening to act alongside Colman, then see him as my grandfather and have that full-circle moment. It was so seamless. He’d arrive on set, I’d arrive and we’d get right into it. No rehearsals. I loved that, because we discovered things with every new take and Antoine would guide it or let us play. I grew up with a different side of my grandfather, a softer side. He was strict here and there. If you didn’t put your dishes away, he’d make sure you did or finish all your cereal. But the grandfather my father grew up with was more strict and disciplinary and wanted to keep them together as a group. It was a different time, growing up in the ’60s and parents disciplined their kids differently. Seeing how Colman channeled that, telling so much through his stillness, his eyes and the tone of his voice, was amazing to witness.

Seeing it brought to life on screen would be difficult for anyone. How did it feel to be in a scene recreating something that, in theory, could be traumatic for your dad and your whole family?

Of course it’d be very personal, making a film about your own family and then having them watch it. I remember being really nervous about my family going to see it. I didn’t know if I wanted to sit there with them, because I didn’t want to be in my own head about what they thought of my performance. I just wanted them to enjoy it for themselves. Seeing a film about your own family can make a lot of people uncomfortable because you have your own idea of what that is, and it’s hard to capture it in a two-hour film. But the response I got from my family was incredible, and it made me emotional to get those phone calls from my cousins, even my younger cousins who are 12 and 13 and my uncles and aunts. They were so supportive, and I was happy I could bring that emotion out in them and bring them together to experience it.

What did your father say when he saw the film for the first time?

I saw him get emotional because he first saw it at the Berlin premiere, with the crowd, with the fans. I said, “Dad, you sure you want to wait to see it there?” He said, “I’m sure.” He wanted to see it with the audience. I felt a little nervous for him, but he loved it. He had tears when he got on stage afterward. He called me later that night or the next day to say how incredible it was to see his son playing his brother and not be able to tell the difference in so many moments. I told him how high a compliment that is, if I can convince him, me being his son, that I’m actually his brother in that film. It brought back a lot of memories. He said how much he misses Michael and his smile, and that seeing me on screen brought back the presence I brought to some of those quiet moments, especially the energy in the “Bad” performance. He was incredibly proud. That’s the highest reward, to get that from your parents and your family.

We’re at the tail end of Hispanic Heritage Month. In a clip that went viral earlier this year, you said, “I’m half Colombian and a lot of people don’t even know that.” Your mother, Alejandra, was born in Bogotá and you’ve talked about weaving Latin music into your early songs. What does being half Latino mean to you, and how have Latino audiences responded?

The response from the Latin audience has been amazing. I wish I’d had a chance to go down to South America or Mexico City, where I know the response to “Michael” was through the roof. As someone half Colombian, I sometimes feel embarrassed that I don’t know any Spanish. It’s not too late to learn. My mom still has a full Colombian accent, which I love. Every time I call her, I tease her about it. My Colombian side of the family is fairly small compared to my father’s side, and they’re still in Bogotá. I have some family in Mexico I don’t see often, but we keep in touch. My mom makes Colombian food every now and then. That’s a reminder, with the holidays coming up. I haven’t been to Colombia since I was 14, so I plan on going soon. The last time I was in South America was Brazil in 2019. It’s beautiful, and I love that part of the world.

There are complicated feelings around this movie, about where it ends and where part two should go. As a family member who sees Michael through that lens, what’s your message to people who have their own idea of what Michael was about, including the more complicated discussions and allegations from his life?

Finding out who Michael was is in his music. It’s in his lyrics. It’s in the poems he wrote, the videos, the messages he put out, the talks he gave on panels and at universities. It’s in what he devoted so much time to: charities, visiting other countries and visiting countless children. Part two, I can’t say, because I don’t know. It’s not up to me. My job is to come prepared and deliver the best performance I can. But to know Michael, it starts with the music.

10 QUESTIONS WITH JAAFAR JACKSON

Childhood nickname? Art. Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into? Tarantulas. I have one as a pet now. And toy soldiers. I used to imagine battles with toy soldiers. Karaoke song or shower song? I’ve never done karaoke. I’m too shy. I feel like I’d be judged completely. In the shower, I don’t have a favorite. I hum different melodies or make weird instrument sounds if there’s an echo. Alternate title for “Michael?” It’d have to be a song title. I’m going to go with “Man in the Mirror.” Secret talent? Juggling. Favorite ice cream flavor? Easily McConnell’s Sea Salt Cream & Cookies. The one item you couldn’t live without? I can live without my phone. Maybe Apple TV, for my movies. I have a big movie collection. What TV show or film in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of? “Troy.” Not Brad Pitt’s role, because he played that so well. Hector. Fictional character you most relate to or admire? I’m going with Black Panther. Favorite piece of advice you’ve received? Not to be jaded. To enjoy the most simple things in life, and that there’s beauty in front of you at all times. Just being present to look at it, not getting taken away by the illusion of what’s in front of a screen, that dopamine intake. Be present, find beauty everywhere and stay curious, with wonderment. You find happiness and joy there a lot more than in other places.

Do you remember who told you that?

It wasn’t told to me verbally. It was through a note I found that was written by Michael. The way I found it, I felt like I was supposed to hear that.

Enjoy the ride, man.

Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more. title: Elizabeth Holmes Exposé Book ‘Bad Blood’ Returns to Bestseller Lists Following Nathan Fielder Doc
summary: Eight years after its publication, John Carreyrou’s “Bad Blood” is getting another moment in the spotlight — this time courtesy of Nathan Fielder. The Wall Street Journal reporter’s bestselling exposé of Elizabeth Holmes and her fraudulent blood-testing startup Theranos has climbed back up Amazon’s book charts following the release of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Eight years after its publication, John Carreyrou’s “Bad Blood” is getting another moment in the spotlight — this time courtesy of Nathan Fielder.

The Wall Street Journal reporter’s bestselling exposé of Elizabeth Holmes and her fraudulent blood-testing startup Theranos has climbed back up Amazon’s book charts following the release of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s buzzy new documentary about the disgraced Silicon Valley founder.

As of Monday, the 2018 book ranks No. 1 in three of Amazon’s bestseller categories — biomedical engineering, business infrastructure and venture capital — and No. 3,048 among all books on the retailer’s website.

Popular on Variety

NO. 1 BESTSELLER Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup Buy Now On Amazon $9.79

The renewed interest comes amid a huge theatrical debut for “You Can See Everything,” which opened nationwide on Oct. 16 and earned $15 million domestically over its first weekend. The nearly three-hour A24 release, filmed largely in secret, follows Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their two children during the final weeks before Holmes reported to federal prison in May 2023.

Published in 2018, “Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup” remains the definitive account of Theranos’ rise and collapse. Carreyrou, whose reporting for The Wall Street Journal first exposed serious problems with the company’s technology in 2015, traces how Holmes convinced some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful investors that she had developed a revolutionary blood-testing machine capable of running hundreds of tests using just a few drops of blood.

Of course, the technology never worked as advertised. By the time Theranos dissolved in 2018, its onetime $9 billion valuation had evaporated, Holmes had become the face of Silicon Valley excess, and Carreyrou’s investigation had helped turn one of the tech industry’s most celebrated startups into one of its biggest scandals.

“Bad Blood” became a No. 1 New York Times bestseller following its release and spent more than 100 weeks across the newspaper’s bestseller lists. Carreyrou himself has praised the documentary, suggesting that Fielder and Oppenheim’s approach deserves Oscar recognition.

Holmes was convicted in 2022 of four counts of wire fraud and conspiracy related to Theranos and subsequently sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. She has continued to maintain her innocence, a position that becomes a recurring point of tension in the new film.

title: Fox Corp. Top Lawyer Adam Ciongoli Is Exiting, Nick Trutanich to Take Over as General Counsel
summary: Fox Corp. said Adam Ciongoli, chief legal and policy officer, will not renew his contract — and that he will step down from the role effective Dec. 1. Ciongoli will serve as a special adviser to Fox through June 2028. Nicholas Trutanich, currently Fox Corp.’s executive vice president, principal deputy general counsel, will become general […]
content:
Fox Corp. said Adam Ciongoli, chief legal and policy officer, will not renew his contract — and that he will step down from the role effective Dec. 1. Ciongoli will serve as a special adviser to Fox through June 2028.

Nicholas Trutanich, currently Fox Corp.’s executive vice president, principal deputy general counsel, will become general counsel of the company with Ciongoli stepping down. Trutanich will report directly to executive chair and CEO Lachlan Murdoch.

The changeover comes as Fox Corp.’s $22 billion deal to buy streaming-platform company Roku remains pending. The companies expect the deal to close in the first half of 2027. Shareholders of both Fox and Roku approved the agreement, which is still pending Justice Department clearance.

Popular on Variety

Before joining Fox in 2023, Ciongoli was general counsel and chief sustainability, corporate responsibility and governance officer for Campbell Soup Co. He previously was general counsel of Lincoln Financial Group, Willis Group Holdings PLC and Time Warner Europe. Before moving into the private sector, Ciongoli served as counselor to John Ashcroft when he was U.S. attorney general; as chief counsel to the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on the Constitution, Federalism and Property Rights; and as law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.

“I’d like to thank Adam for his many immense contributions over the last three years,” Lachlan Murdoch said in a prepared statement. “I deeply appreciate his service to Fox and am grateful that he will continue to serve Fox as a special adviser. Nick Trutanich has been a critical member of the Fox team since joining the company five years ago and will bring deep legal, litigation and compliance experience to this expanded role.”

Ciongoli, in a statement provided by Fox Corp., said: “It has been a privilege and an honor to be a part of the Fox family, and I have especially valued my relationships with Lachlan and our talented colleagues. I look forward to continuing to work with Lachlan and Fox as a special advisor to help this great company in its continued successes.”

Prior to joining Fox, Trutanich served as the U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada from 2019-21 and previously held senior roles at the Nevada attorney general’s office and served as a federal prosecutor within the DOJ. Earlier in his career, Trutanich was a litigator in private practice and a federal law clerk. “I will be honored to serve as general counsel and grateful for the opportunity to lead such a talented legal team,” Trutanich said. “It is an exciting time of growth and innovation at Fox, and I look forward to working with colleagues across the company to advance our goals.”

Also as part of the transition, the company announced that Kristopher Jones, EVP and head of government relations, will report directly to John Nallen, president and COO of Fox Corp., effective Dec. 1.

Fox Corp.’s brands include Fox News Media, Fox Sports, Tubi Media Group, Fox Entertainment and Fox Television Stations.

Pictured above: Adam Ciongoli (left), Nick Trutanich

title: Kris Bowers Set to Compose Original Score For Disney’s Animated Feature ‘Hexed’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Academy Award winning composer Kris Bowers is set to score the music for the upcoming Disney animated feature “Hexed.” The film stars Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones, Jodie Foster and Walton Goggins in a magical coming-of-age saga. “Hexed” follows an unconventional teenage girl who discovers secret magical abilities which, once unleashed, hurtle her into a spectacle-filled […]
content:
Academy Award winning composer Kris Bowers is set to score the music for the upcoming Disney animated feature “Hexed.”

The film stars Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones, Jodie Foster and Walton Goggins in a magical coming-of-age saga. “Hexed” follows an unconventional teenage girl who discovers secret magical abilities which, once unleashed, hurtle her into a spectacle-filled journey through a hidden realm of witches.

“Hexed” is set to hit theaters on Nov. 25.

Popular on Variety

Bowers said, “Creating the score for ‘Hexed’ was all about exploration and experimentation. Inspired by a young woman who dreams of flying, both literally and metaphorically, I began exploring unusual ways of making music with air: bird call whistles, wind wand, nose flutes, bottles, kazoos, air sirens and even recordings of actual birds transformed into instruments.” He added, “The film’s unique take on a magical realm inspired a sound that blends orchestra, an effected chamber woodwind ensemble, synths and natural sound elements, often blurring the line between acoustic and electronic textures. At its core, this is a deeply emotional mother-daughter journey and I wanted the music to capture both that intimacy and the wonder and adventure of this world. I’m so grateful for the incredibly engaging collaboration with Fawn, Jason, Jared and the entire Disney Animation filmmaking team.”

Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand direct the film, with Roy Conli and Yvett Merino on board as producers.

In addition to scoring “Hexed,” Bowers also composed the music for Netflix’s animated film “Steps.” Additionally, he scored the upcoming Paramount/Skydance sports drama, “Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story, which premieres on Dec. 25.

Bowers will also reunite with filmmaker Ben Proudfoot. He composed the score for Breakwater Studios’ documentary “The Eyes Of Ghana.”

title: Ex-UTA Agent Dante DeSario Launches Collage, A Management Firm For AI-Native Production
summary: Former UTA film agent Dante DeSario has launched Collage, a management company devoted to AI-native production. The new firm has closed a seed funding round, with Black Bear and Fundamental Films investing. Other investors and senior advisors include Dennis Miller, Blue Deer Media, GOAL Ventures, AGC Studios, Roy Lee, Marty Bowen, Todd Lieberman, Todd Garner, […]
content:
Former UTA film agent Dante DeSario has launched Collage, a management company devoted to AI-native production.

The new firm has closed a seed funding round, with Black Bear and Fundamental Films investing. Other investors and senior advisors include Dennis Miller, Blue Deer Media, GOAL Ventures, AGC Studios, Roy Lee, Marty Bowen, Todd Lieberman, Todd Garner, Barry Porter, George Huber, Max Michael, and Ric Roman Waugh.

Clients of the L.A.-based company at launch include a number of top-shelf names in the emerging arena of AI. On the roster are Asteria, the studio behind software platform Continuum and recent festival feature selections like Alpha Gang and Chikaboom!; real-time 3D animation studio Defect; Berlin-based AI studio Lipstick; Matriarch, the AI-native and hybrid production company from ex-Luma Dream Lab L.A. chief Verena Puhm; Native Foreign, creator of the OpenAI-backed franchise Critterz; Obsidian, Wes Walker’s studio partnership with Imagine Entertainment; Secret Level, the studio behind hybrid horror feature Terrarium; and Lux Meridian, the generative production arm of Territory Group whose work includes Dune, The Martian, and Guardians of the Galaxy.

The stated goal of Collage is to build a bridge between AI-native production companies and Hollywood studios, streamers, filmmakers, and brands. Once connected, the company’s thesis holds, the parties will build their respective businesses, expand their reach, and develop commercial relationships.

Watch on Deadline

After a couple of years of high anxiety over how the influx of AI could reshape the production process and possibly eliminate jobs, the entertainment business has generally settled into a more pragmatic phase. On a macro level, the AI boom is contiuning apace, and against that backdrop a growing number of traditional players have been reaching across the aisle to Silicon Valley.

As a member of UTA’s independent film group, DeSario worked with filmmakers and packaged and arranged financing for hundreds of films, including Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid. The well-received Cannes title fetched a UTA-record in the high-teens millions in a sale to A24. Other films in DeSario’s portfolio included Damian McCarthy’s Hokum (Neon), Jennifer Peedom’s Tenzing (Apple), and Alex Ullom’s upcoming 4 x 4 (Neon).

Collage’s role in the emerging ecosystem of AI will be to help organize it by identifying top suppliers; matching production methods to projects; pricing and sizing projects; and helping to ensure proper management of the quality, legal and delivery aspects of production. The company will also invest selectively in companies, either directly or down the line through dedicated investment vehicles managed by Collage Capital.

“We saw extraordinary creative companies emerging around generative production, but very little infrastructure around them,” DeSario said in a statement. “Hollywood needed a trusted way to find and work with the best of these companies, while the companies themselves needed help with business development and operations, technology relationships, and capital. We built Collage to connect the two and give great creative companies the support they need to grow.”

title: Richard Riehle Dies: ‘Office Space’ & ‘Bridesmaids’ Actor Was 78
summary: Richard Riehle, an actor in Office Space, Bridesmaids, Casino, Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo, and The Man From Earth, has died. He was 78. Riehle played Tom Smykowski, a cynical Initech product manager, in the Mike Judge satirical comedy, sharing credits with Ron Livingston, Jennifer Aniston, Stephen Root, and Gary Cole.
