content:
Richard Riehle, an actor in Office Space, Bridesmaids, Casino, Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo, and The Man From Earth, has died. He was 78.

Riehle played Tom Smykowski, a cynical Initech product manager, in the Mike Judge satirical comedy, sharing credits with Ron Livingston, Jennifer Aniston, Stephen Root, and Gary Cole.

The actor died of natural causes in Los Angeles last Thursday, October 15, according to a TMZ report.

Riehle was born on May 12, 1948, in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin. He first entered the entertainment industry in the John Wayne-starring western film Rooster Cogburn in 1975.

Watch on Deadline

Films in which Riehle was credited include Joyride (1977), Black Rain (1989), Of Mice and Men (1992), Free Willy (1993), The Fugitive (1993), Lightning Jack (1994), Casino (1995), Ghosts of Mississippi (1996), The Odd Couple II (1998), Lethal Weapon 4 (1998), Office Space (1999), Deuce Bigalo: Make Gigolo (1999), Joe Dirt (2001), Beethoven’s 5th (2003), Wedding Crashers (2005), National Lampoon’s Dom Daze 2 (2006), Red (2008), Halloween II (2009), Bridesmaids (2011), A Very Harold & Kumar 3D Christmas (2011), Texas Chainsaw 3D (2013), Lovesick (2014). His last film credit was in 2026, in The Cowboy Killer.

On television, Riehle first appeared in the TV film The Other Side of Hell. The actor would go on to appear in My Two Dads (1989), Dragnet (1989), and Falcon Crest (1989).

Other television shows in which Riehle appears include Quantum Leap, Murder, Show Wrote, L.A. Law, Ferris Bueller, The Golden Girls, Roseanne, Star Trek: The Next Generation, Ally McBeal, The Practice, Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Chicago Hope, Home Improvement, Columbo, Star Trek: Voyager, Sabrina, the Teenage Witch, The West Wing, ER, Grounded for Life, The Laramie Project, Married to the Kellys, Star Trek: Enterprise, Boston Legal, George Lopez, 7th Heaven, The Young and the Restless, Psych, Better Off Ted, The Client List, The Mindy Project, The Legend of Korra, Mom, Two and a Half Men, Black-ish, NCIS, The Middle, and Another Period.

Riehle’s latest television credits include American Housewife (2019) and Fuller House (2020), and his last role was Warden Reynolds in HBO’s Barry (2023).

title: Chelsey Summey Departs As Warner Bros Head Of Communications
summary: EXCLUSIVE: With more exits expected later this week as Paramount seizes Warner Bros, we hear that the latter’s Head of Communications, Chelsey Summey, has departed the Burbank, CA lot. Summey first joined Warner Bros as SVP Communications in January 2024 and was later named Head of Communications reporting to Motion Picture bosses Michael De Luca […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: With more exits expected later this week as Paramount seizes Warner Bros, we hear that the latter’s Head of Communications, Chelsey Summey, has departed the Burbank, CA lot.

Summey first joined Warner Bros as SVP Communications in January 2024 and was later named Head of Communications reporting to Motion Picture bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy. During her tenure she oversaw strategic communications across Warner Bros. Pictures, New Line Cinema, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, Warner Bros. Clockwork and Warner Bros. Theatre Ventures. In this capacity, she led internal and external communications strategy, advising studio leaders on high-profile business and reputational matters while shaping the narrative around Warner Bros.’ films, talent, and broader business priorities.

Summey came to Warner Bros from Amazon MGM Studios, where she served as Head of Corporate Communications for the studio’s film group.

Watch on Deadline

Before that, Summey spent nearly a decade at 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios), where she rose to SVP Corporate Communications overseeing media relations, executive communications, corporate events, talent relations and awards-campaign strategy for the studio as well as the daily operations of the global communications team.

While at Fox, she worked on several award-winning and blockbuster movies including Bohemian Rhapsody, the Deadpool franchise, The Greatest Showman, The Martian, The Revenant, Hidden Figures, Life of Pi and the Ice Age franchise among others. During her tenure, she played an integral role in developing and leading the studio’s crisis communications strategy.

Before Fox, Summey held corporate communications and publicity roles at both Paramount Pictures and CAA.

title: We Can See Oscar Possibilities For A24’s Hit Documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ – And That Includes An Acting Category
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains details about storylines and characters/actors in A24’s documentary You Can See Everything. Ever since its super-secret onetime screening at the Telluride Film Festival over Labor Day weekend, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, near three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything has been one of the most talked […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains details about storylines and characters/actors in A24‘s documentary You Can See Everything.

Ever since its super-secret onetime screening at the Telluride Film Festival over Labor Day weekend, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s brilliant, near three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything has been one of the most talked about films of the fall season — if not the entire year.

Now, after this past weekend’s sensational opening in about 800 theaters, where it grossed $15 million-plus to become the highest-grossing debut in under 1000 theaters in more than two decades (and the biggest non-music documentary opening since Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004), it is white hot and bound to accelerate.

Watch on Deadline

With all that in mind, it is never too early to start talking Oscar, even for a film that might break the mold for a documentary in several categories, and uniquely a possible acting nomination.

A24 held screenings on Saturday at the DGA for members of the documentary branch, and on Sunday afternoon for its official AMPAS screening at the Academy’s Samuel Goldwyn Theater, where an estimated 530 people showed up — one of the best turnouts this season. That screening drew lots of audible reaction to the film’s twists and turns, as well as enthusiastic applause during end credits and for directors Fielder and Oppenheim, who appeared for the Q&A afterwards (which I moderated). I am told the packed Saturday DGA screening was similarly enthusiastic.

Pundits are already speculating on the movie’s Oscar chances in the Best Picture category, where no documentary has ever been nominated before. But I have to say there never has been one quite like You Can See Everything, in which Fielder and Oppenheim see, well, everything about disgraced Theranos founder Holmes, who invited them to document her life just a month before reporting to prison.

Fielder, whose works include HBO’s The Rehearsal and Comedy Central’s Nathan For You, often blurs the line between reality and fiction but here puts himself in the center of the story in order to see a side of Holmes like never before. If you ask me, what he achieves here is as robust an example of strong journalism, however gonzo, as many more traditional documentaries. It is an important point since the AMPAS Documentary Branch is not known for thinking out of the box and generally rejects any film with connections to the entertainment side of things. The reaction though from Academy screenings (there was a previous one at the Academy Museum shortly before the film played the New York Film Festival) indicate we may be into a precedent-shattering moment.

In addition to Best Picture — which oddly may be an even more realistic goal than Documentary Feature, which has drifted more international in scope recently — You Can See Everything deserves strong consideration for Best Directing, David Bolen’s exceptional cinematography, Ari Balouzian’s haunting music and Adam Locke-Norton’s editing, the latter particularly impressive since he had 700 (!) hours of footage to shape into a 2-hour and 54-minute movie.

As for the category that would really be earth-shattering? Best Supporting Actress. The studio and filmmakers have been successful (save for one trade critic who gave it away instantly in Telluride) in keeping the identity of the Oscar-nominated and Emmy-winning star who shows up in the second half of the film after Holmes reports to prison. One pundit actually had her lead his list of possible nominees by saying “Redacted” and then the name of the film. Clever.

The appearance is an astounding twist and should be enjoyed by audiences just discovering the film for the first time, so I am not going to reveal just what happens. But in the interest of talking all things Oscar here, I will refer to whom we are discussing. And in fact, [SPOILER ALERT, second warning!], Amanda Seyfried was on the press line at Saturday’s Academy Museum Gala being coy and evasive when asked by reporters about Holmes and/or her participation in the film (Fielder and Oppenheim were also at the gala). Seyfried of course played Holmes and won an Emmy for the TV film The Dropout. How she figures into this film — well, you’ll have to go see it. But ever since I saw the movie at Telluride I have wondered: Could there ever be someone nominated for acting in a documentary, and if so, could it be her?

At Telluride I even popped the question to A24 sources who were already looking into that possibility. They still are in the process, but I am told they believe she is eligible and are definitely mulling the possibility of campaigning her. There is nothing in Academy rules for actors that suggests documentaries are verboten, only “uncredited” performances are. Seyfried and the others are fully credited at the end of the film, and in fact IMDb has just begun listing her (and others on camera in the film including actor Christopher Abbott and Fielder) on their official page for the movie.

I am told A24 is exploring other awards possibilities as well, even though the Golden Globes and SAG-AFTRA’s Actor Awards explicitly rule out documentaries in their competitions. To get into consideration at either of those you would have to petition to change the rules; I hear there is some sort of effort to try to do that for SAG-AFTRA, but deadline for submissions is November 1 and the guild would have to upend their rules — not likely. The Critics Choice Association on the other hand has already nominated You Can See Everything for its separate Critics Choice Documentary Awards ceremony taking place November 8. It is up for five awards including Best Documentary Feature, but there is no performance category (other than narration). The CCA confirmed to me that despite the separate ceremony, all documentaries, and by extension performances in them that apply, could be nominated for Critics Choice Awards.

No actor has ever been nominated for appearing in a documentary in the 99-year history of the Academy Awards. The closest I could find might be Maria Bakalova in 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, but in that movie, which is not a documentary despite featuring some real-life people (can you say Rudy Giuliani?), Bakalova is playing a character and not herself.

For that matter, no actor has ever been nominated for an Oscar in a movie in which they play themselves. The closest was ironically this year’s Wild Horse Nine Best Actor frontrunner John Malkovich, who played himself in 1999’s Being John Malkovich. Though that film was up for three Oscars, he was overlooked for a nomination, though he was SAG-nominated as part of the ensemble cast; he actually was named Best Supporting Actor by the New York Film Critics that year and was runner-up with the L.A. Film Critics. A critics organization like those could also be the way I see a realistic Seyfried march to the Oscars gaining steam.

Stay tuned.

title: Why Netflix Fired Dan Lin (and the Truth About His Tension With Greta Gerwig Over ‘Narnia’)
summary: “Everyone is collateral damage.” That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the company’s head of film. Following last week’s 6% workforce reduction at Netflix – which claimed victims including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and Lin’s right-hand Doug Belgrad – consensus said it […]
content:
“Everyone is collateral damage.”



That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the company’s head of film.



Following last week’s 6% workforce reduction at Netflix – which claimed victims including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and Lin’s right-hand Doug Belgrad – consensus said it was a matter of time before co-CEO Ted Sarandos would show Lin the door.



It took a day. On the heels of the Bajaria news on Thursday, Sarandos rang Lin on Friday to tell him he’d been dismissed, three sources told Variety. The exec kept his head up and pressed on through the weekend, appearing at Saturday’s Academy Gala (in the same room as Sarandos) and at a Sunday tastemaker screening to support the filmmakers of “La Bola Negra.” As has been summarized in many articles about the Netflix purge, creative leadership at the company is being overhauled amid poor stock performance and declining user engagement on the platform. Peter Rice, the veteran film and TV executive, will now preside over and shake up the platform’s content.



Competing narratives are flying about why Lin was let go, but they arrive at the same conclusion: In the end, it wasn’t working. Some say Sarandos is desperate to sell a story about growth to Wall Street (Netflix’s quarterly earnings report drops Tuesday). Others say Lin could not dance fast enough to find the balance between sticky streaming titles and theatrical release experiments (in fairness, he made it halfway through a five-year deal, barely enough time to get a casting announcement together by today’s standards). There are also some interesting leaks around tension he’s said to have with A-list filmmakers like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck, which we’ll get to.



The Lin era at Netflix was framed around austerity, both by the town and in some ways by “The Lego Movie” producer himself. A June profile in the New York Times declared Lin was done “coddling” Hollywood, bragging he did not “fawn over stars or write blank checks.” The implication was that his predecessor Scott Stuber had overpaid for talent and too-ambitiously committed to a new Netflix movie release every week in 2022. Those efforts scaled back gradually until Stuber exited in mid-2024.



Lin entered with a red pen and a machete, the lore goes, in hopes of emphasizing quality over quantity. Some find it convenient that Stuber’s legacy is still being kicked up, perhaps to provide cloud cover for decisions made by Lin and his former boss Bajaria. Amid the noise of the current Netflix layoffs, it’s important to remember that the prevailing logic at Netflix for a long, long time was “we don’t give a shit about theatrical,” said one colorful studio source. Releasing movies in theaters was never part of the Netflix business model. Stuber paid premiums to get filmmakers like Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón and Rian Johnson on the service. He also worked with fervor to make the theatrical exhibitors accept Netflix titles in any capacity. While they refused at the time, individuals familiar with Sarandos said Stuber laid the groundwork for the inevitable – that the only way to create value around movies is to put them in theaters first.



Lin brought this logic to fruition in convincing Sarandos that family-driven IP should receive robust, exclusive theatrical windows before moving on to streaming, individuals with knowledge of Lin said. We’ll see the results next year when Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” come to cineplexes.



Where Netflix once organized its internal film teams by the budget range of projects they worked on, Lin grouped his executives according to genre expertise. He also moved swiftly to program release windows left empty by Stuber’s exit (“Nonnas,” “Happy Gilmore 2,” “The Thursday Murder Club”). He spent one day of his work week with the Netflix animation team, where he installed Hannah Minghella as a leader. For the core slate, Lin is credited with wooing Alan Ritchson (“War Machine”), Matthew McConaughey and Ben Stiller for upcoming projects.



In the weeks before his exit, reports said Lin clashed with filmmaker Affleck over the just-released “Animals,” and perhaps more consequentially with Gerwig this summer over the upcoming “Narnia.” The latter represents a $250 million theatrical-first gamble.



Four sources with knowledge of the matter said that, indeed, Lin and Gerwig had a falling out during a Zoom call about the project earlier this year. On a virtual meeting populated by numerous Netflix executives, Lin is said to have been “dismissive” to the director in conversations about the progress of the film. Lin is known in town to be incredibly fair, but at times obtuse in his frankness. Word travelled fast around Netflix that the meeting had gone south, at which point sources said Bajaria called Gerwig’s producer Amy Pascal to smooth things over. Two sources also said that Gerwig’s new, all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd went to Sarandos directly over the faux pas. Lin was subsequently disappeared from the film, all sources concurred, and Belgrad stepped in as the primary Netflix exec overseeing the project (until, of course, he was laid off last week).



None of the sources suggested the incident led to Lin’s firing. One Lin defender said he’s never “afraid to talk about how to make a movie better.” Another person familiar with the company said there are any number of filmmakers who could say the same about Lin’s delivery. While it may be juicy to speculate that Gerwig’s follow-up to the game changer “Barbie” could be troubled, don’t forget that the industry doubted that Margot Robbie film right up to opening weekend. “Barbie” grossed $1.44 billion at the worldwide box office and became the highest-earning release in the history of Warner Bros. Pictures.



While talk will instantly turn to Lin’s replacement (is it Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy? “Probably,” said one high-placed source), don’t shed too many tears for Lin. He ascended to Netflix from a successful, self-made business in Rideback, where he’s likely to return.



“When I took this job, Bela gave me a simple piece of advice: Be yourself,” Lin wrote in a Monday memo obtained by Variety. “You work here because it’s personal. Because of that unspoken pact between your individual passion for movies and the audiences we serve. To them, movies aren’t about business. They’re about feeling something.”

title: Tim O’Donnell, Veteran TV Comedy Writer-Director Known for ‘Growing Pains’ and ‘Dave’s World,’ Dies at 77
summary: Tim O’Donnell, the veteran comedy writer-director known for his work on sitcoms including “Growing Pains,” “Dave’s World” and “Phil of the Future,” has died. He was 77. O’Donnell died at his home in Glendale, Calif. on July 27. He had struggled with bladder cancer for three years. A memorial service will be held at 2 […]
content:
Tim O’Donnell, the veteran comedy writer-director known for his work on sitcoms including “Growing Pains,” “Dave’s World” and “Phil of the Future,” has died. He was 77.

O’Donnell died at his home in Glendale, Calif. on July 27. He had struggled with bladder cancer for three years. A memorial service will be held at 2 p.m. on Oct. 25 at the Writers Guild Theater in Beverly Hills.

O’Donnell was known for his versatility and skill at shaping network TV comedies during the modern heyday of sitcoms. He was also active with the Writers Guild of America West, serving twice on contract negotiating committees and as a board member.

More recently, O’Donnell had worked with Sony Pictures on the studio’s efforts to develop local-language adaptations of sitcoms. He traveled to Russia and China in the 2000s to help instruct local producers on how to craft American-style sitcoms.

Popular on Variety

“Tim knew everybody, and he was an astute observer of the business,” said Brian Lowry, a Variety alum and media biz commentator. “As a former news guy, he also recognized the absurdities that populated his new sphere and had the ability not only to laugh at them, but to make others laugh at them as well.”

O’Donnell grew up in the South Bay area of Los Angeles County and attended Loyola University. His career as a scribe began in local news in Chicago, working for CBS-owned radio and TV stations. He earned local Emmy Awards for his news writing and on-air editorials. He then moved to the West Coast to work for KCBS-TV Los Angeles, where he wrote for the legendary reporter Bill Stout.

O’Donnell eventually moved into narrative TV, serving as a writer, producer and director on such series as ABC’s “Growing Pains” and “Clueless,” CBS’ “Dave’s World” and the short-lived TV adaptation of the 1989 John Candy film “Uncle Buck,” also for CBS. He worked on ABC’s “Home Free,” an early role for Matthew Perry, and Disney Channel’s live-action comedy “Phil of the Future.”

O’Donnell was married to Cara O’Donnell for nearly 39 years. His survivors include four children: daughter Kit Michelle O’Donnell Sparke, and three daughters from his first marriage to Vicki Marshall: Shannon O’Donnell Provatas, Carrie O’Donnell VanAckeren and Bridget Morpurgo. He is also survived by four grandchildren.

The family requests that RSVPs for the Oct. 25 memorial service be sent to jmtsutsui@gmail.com. There will also be a livestream available at this link.

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters. “You Can See Everything” may rewrite the rules of the Oscar season. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary, which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

“You Can See Everything” may rewrite the rules of the Oscar season.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary, which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to a staggering $15 million over the weekend, a number most nonfiction films never see in a full run. It’s also boasting a record-setting 99 on Metacritic, 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and holding a 4.7 (out of 5) on Letterboxd and 9.4 on IMDb (as of Monday, Oct. 19). If the IMDb score holds, it will surpass the longstanding No. 1 “The Shawshank Redemption” (1994) as the highest-rated film of all time.

In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture (Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose and Jack Davis), director (Fielder and Oppenheim), production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian).

Popular on Variety

Variety confirmed exclusively after the film made its surprise world premiere (and general existence became known) at the Telluride Film Festival that Amanda Seyfried, credited in the film as Elizabeth Holmes, is eligible for the Academy Awards in the acting categories. Seyfried, who also appears as herself while reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. If she lands the nomination, it would be her second, following “Mank” (2020). She would get there for playing two people at once: herself and the woman she already won an Emmy statue for playing.

Fielder may also be eligible to submit as a performer, although he is credited as himself. If he was eligible and submitted, the logical home would be lead actor. No actor has ever been nominated for playing themself. The closest we came to seeing this was a person from another A24 film, “Sing Sing” (2023), which had cowriter and star Clarence Maclin vying for consideration in the best supporting actor race, but was ultimately overlooked.

Christopher Abbott, who also appears in the film as Holmes’ spouse, Billy Evans, in recreated scenes, is also eligible for acting consideration in the supporting actor category.

Sources close to the awards campaign say the acting push will center on Seyfried regardless.

No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture in 98 ceremonies. The zeitgeist says this one can be. The awards circuit that usually paves the way is another matter.

We are in uncharted waters.

Courtesy Everett Collection

Golden Globes: Not eligible based on current written rules, but there could be an avenue.

The Globes don’t recognize documentaries, which means no picture, no director and no Seyfried. The film cannot be submitted in any category. However, with the acting eligibilities lingering, sources share the group may consider it for this upcoming run. That doesn’t mean it can be eligible across the board. And then in that case, do they consider it a drama or comedy/musical?

Critics Choice Awards: Eligible across the board, including the acting races.

That makes Critics Choice the only major stop this season where the performances in “You Can See Everything” could get significant recognition before Oscar nominations.

Actor Awards: Not eligible but could they make an exception?

The ceremony formerly known as the SAG Awards does not recognize documentaries, since they aren’t narrative films, even with the narrative recreations woven throughout this one. Seyfried’s path to a supporting actress nomination looked like it would skip the precursor vote by her fellow actors. However, the committee that rules on films is said to be looking at the film to see if it can, in fact, be eligible.

BAFTA: Still a bit of a question mark but it doesn’t look promising.

The current rules and guidelines indicate the film can submit in the top categories, but sources say BAFTA may not go for it. Whether Seyfried and Fielder can enter the acting races is less clear. However, indications suggest it may ultimately be eligible for recognition if the voters choose to go for it.

Writers Guild of America: Not eligible.

The film has no credited screenplay, which isn’t unusual for a documentary but isn’t universal either. Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” famously won the WGA’s original screenplay prize more than 20 years ago. That won’t be the case here, so “You Can See Everything” won’t be eligible for the Oscars‘ original or adapted screenplay categories.

Directors Guild of America: Eligible in both top categories.

This is where it gets interesting. The DGA has a separate documentary category, and its top prize is labeled for directors of a theatrically released feature film. Questions began percolating because of RaMell Ross, whose “Hale County This Morning, This Evening” was nominated for documentary feature at the Oscars before his narrative debut, “Nickel Boys,” was entered in first-time feature director at the DGA, a category he went on to win.

This is Fielder’s first directorial credit for a documentary feature, but that isn’t the case for Oppenheim, who helmed “Spermworld” (2024) and “Some Kind of Heaven” (2020). Therefore, the film won’t be eligible for first-time feature director. However, Oppenheim makes his narrative feature directorial debut with the A24 thriller “Primetime” starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. He will be vying for one of the five slots in that category.

More importantly, under the forward-facing rules, Fielder and Oppenheim are eligible for the DGA’s top award in addition to the documentary prize. That means they could take a slot otherwise slotted for Christopher Nolan (“The Odyssey”) or the other directing duos in the race, including Los Javis (“La Bola Negra”) and Phil Lord and Chris Miller (“Project Hail Mary”).

ACE Eddies: Eligible

The guild that represents film editing separates theatrical feature films into four categories: drama, comedy, documentary and animated. Per the rules, “You Can See Everything” would have to choose a category to submit to. A similar situation occurred with Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s animated nonfiction film “Flee” (2021), which was submitted to the guild as a documentary and nominated by ACE Eddie.

ASC (American Society of Cinematographers): Eligible, but only as a documentary.

Per the rules for the highest award for cinematographers, “All Documentary Feature Films and Documentary Series Episodes must be submitted in the Documentary Award category.”

Producers Guild of America: Eligible for both the theatrical motion picture award and the documentary prize.

Add it up and you get a contender with no conventional map. Best picture winners typically announce themselves through the guilds, with a PGA win, a DGA nod, an Actor Awards ensemble slot and a Globe or two along the way. “You Can See Everything” likely won’t be at the Globes. The actors can’t nominate it. BAFTA would be a stop if the rules hold. That leaves the DGA, PGA and Critics Choice as the only places the film can win a top prize and signal whether it’s a historic nominee or something bigger.

And this raises a bigger question: What if the first documentary nominated for best picture goes all the way to the top prize?

A few studios are trying to frame the race as David vs. Goliath regarding how they can possibly topple Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar sensation “The Odyssey.” What if this is actually Odysseus vs. Elizabeth Holmes?

A caveat that applies to all of the above: every voting body and guild writes its own rules, and any of them can convene a committee to revisit eligibility. So all of these are subject to change.

Holmes built a company on the promise that one test could see everything. Awards season has at least six major contests, and as of now, none of them can agree on what they’re actually looking at.

title: Rita Wilson Says She’s Returning for Lena Dunham’s ‘Girls’ Revival: ‘I Would Do Anything for Her’
summary: Evie Michaels is back! Rita Wilson is teasing plans to reprise her “Girls” role as Marnie Michael’s eccentric mother in Lena Dunham’s much-anticipated revival. When asked by People if she’ll be returning for the new iteration of the hit show, Wilson told the publication, “That is what I’m hearing, so I don’t think Lena would […]
content:
Evie Michaels is back! Rita Wilson is teasing plans to reprise her “Girls” role as Marnie Michael’s eccentric mother in Lena Dunham’s much-anticipated revival.

When asked by People if she’ll be returning for the new iteration of the hit show, Wilson told the publication, “That is what I’m hearing, so I don’t think Lena would be lying about that.” The actress went on to say that she is “so excited” about the series return, Wilson first joined the show during Season 2 and made guest appearances throughout the show’s run.

“Oh my gosh, yes. I mean, Lena is one of the most talented people I’ve ever worked with. I would do anything for her,” she continued. “I would bend over backward. And then I love Allison Williams who, you know, I was lucky enough to play her mom.” She added: “I know Lena’s gotta be cooking up something very good.”

Popular on Variety

Earlier this month, it was announced that HBO had greenlit a revival of “Girls,” the dramedy created by Dunham. The series will return for a limited, five-episode run with production beginning in 2027 — a decade after the Season 6 finale.

With Dunham as creator, showrunner and star, the original series ran from 2012 to 2017 and followed a group of friends through the misery and dysfunction of their 20s in New York City. All four core cast members are returning for the revival: Dunham as Hannah Horvath, Allison Williams as Marnie Michaels, Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro. Additionally, Andrew Rannells reprises the role of Elijah Krantz.

Wilson first joined the show during Season 2 and made guest appearances throughout the show’s run.

Judd Apatow returns as executive producer on behalf of Apatow Productions alongside Dunham, Ilene S. Landress and Michael P. Cohen of Dunham’s Good Thing Going banner. Williams, Kirke, Mamet and Rannells serve as co-executive producers.

title: Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83
summary: Bob Buziak, former president of both RCA Records and Sony’s TriStar Music Group, died on October 19, a rep confirms to Variety. No cause of death was announced; he was 83. Buziak was best known for reviving RCA’s fortunes in the 1980s with hit albums by Bruce Hornsby, Eurythmics and Love and Rockets, not to […]
content:
Bob Buziak, former president of both RCA Records and Sony’s TriStar Music Group, died on October 19, a rep confirms to Variety. No cause of death was announced; he was 83.

Buziak was best known for reviving RCA’s fortunes in the 1980s with hit albums by Bruce Hornsby, Eurythmics and Love and Rockets, not to mention the blockbuster soundtracks to the “Dirty Dancing” films, which spawned a No. 1 single with Eric Carmen’s “Hungry Eyes” and an Oscar- and Grammy-winner with Bill Medley and Jennifer Warnes’ “(I’ve Had) The Time of My Life.”

He left a job at the Ford Motor Company in 1968 to work in the music business, taking on distribution and promotion roles in Detroit and San Francisco before joining Capitol/EMI Records in Los Angeles. He held promotion and A&R roles at that label before joining Arista Records, where he thrived as head of West Coast operations and, later, managing director in the U.K. His performance at that label led directly to his being named president of RCA in 1986.

Popular on Variety

While there, Buziak’s distribution deals with indie labels like Beggars Banquet (which brought Love and Rockets and others) and Jive helped expand and modernize the label’s roster.

He left the label in 1990 to serve as president of Sony’s TriStar Music Group and later founded Chameleon Entertainment as a joint venture with Time Warner. In 1995, he launched Buziak & Company LLC, which consulted for telecom and cable companies, and played a key role in the sale of Paradigm Music Entertainment to Liberty Media.

He was a board member of inVentures a U.K. investment group and initiated a merger with Redwood Partners a U.S. corporate search firm to create a multi-platform international consulting and venture group.

title: Disney Appoints Carol Choi As Asia Pacific President Following Luke Kang’s Retirement
summary: The Walt Disney Company said that Carol Choi, currently Executive Vice President of Disney Asia Pacific, will succeed Luke Kang as President, APAC following his decision to retire after 16 years with the company. In her new role, effective December 1, Choi will lead Disney Entertainment’s portfolio of businesses across Asia Pacific including studios, Disney+, […]
content:
The Walt Disney Company said that Carol Choi, currently Executive Vice President of Disney Asia Pacific, will succeed Luke Kang as President, APAC following his decision to retire after 16 years with the company.

In her new role, effective December 1, Choi will lead Disney Entertainment’s portfolio of businesses across Asia Pacific including studios, Disney+, local original content production, consumer products, media networks and content sales.

Her remit spans Greater China, Japan, South Korea, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand.

“Luke Kang has been an exceptional leader and a driving force behind Disney’s growth and transformation across Asia Pacific,” said Alan Bergman, Chairman, Disney Entertainment, Studios, and Jimmy Pitaro, Chairman, ESPN.

Watch on Deadline

“He has strengthened our businesses, built outstanding teams and deepened Disney’s connection with fans across the region, and we are grateful for his many contributions.

Carol Choi is a proven Disney leader with broad operating experience, strong creative instincts, and a deep understanding of the region, and she is the perfect person to lead the organization into its next chapter.”

Kang commented: “It has been an extraordinary privilege to lead Disney in Asia Pacific through a period of significant growth and transformation. Together, we have strengthened our businesses, expanded the reach of Disney’s stories and brands, and built new ways to serve our fans across one of the world’s most dynamic regions. Carol is an exceptional leader whose deep knowledge of our businesses, creative ambition, and instinct for consumers make her uniquely positioned to build on this momentum and lead APAC into its next phase of growth.”

Choi said: “I am honored to take on this role and grateful to Luke for the strong foundation he has built,” said Choi. “Asia Pacific is home to some of the world’s most passionate fans and dynamic creative communities. I look forward to working with our teams and partners to bring exceptional stories and experiences to audiences, grow our businesses, and deepen Disney’s connection with fans across the region.”

In the EVP role, Choi, a 20-year Disney veteran, led the region’s studios business, original content strategy and integrated marketing. She previously served as Managing Director of Disney in Japan and Korea and held senior leadership roles in Greater China.

During her tenure, Choi helped launch and grow Disney+, expand the studios business, and build long-term collaborations with leading filmmakers and talent across the region.

Kang joined Disney in 2011 as Managing Director of Korea and subsequently ran the Greater China and North Asia businesses, expanding Disney’s presence through localization, digital innovation and consumer engagement. During his tenure as APAC president he oversaw the launch of Disney+ across the region and the studio’s entry into local-language content in several markets, including Korea and Japan.

title: Rita Wilson Teases Return In Lena Dunham’s ‘Girls’ Revival On HBO: “I Would Do Anything For Her”
summary: Rita Wilson says she “would do anything” for Lena Dunham after confirming the Girls revival. HBO and Dunham announced the comedy would return for five episodes in 2027, and Wilson teased she would reprise her role. “That is what I’m hearing, so I don’t think Lena would be lying about that,” Wilson told People about […]
content:
Rita Wilson says she “would do anything” for Lena Dunham after confirming the Girls revival.

HBO and Dunham announced the comedy would return for five episodes in 2027, and Wilson teased she would reprise her role.

“That is what I’m hearing, so I don’t think Lena would be lying about that,” Wilson told People about the show’s revival.

Wilson noted that she was “so excited” about the reunion and added, “I mean, Lena is one of the most talented people I’ve ever worked with. I would do anything for her. I would bend over backwards. And then I love Allison Williams who, you know, I was lucky enough to play her mom. I know Lena’s gotta be cooking up something very good.”

Watch on Deadline

In the HBO series, Wilson played Evie Michaels, the mother of Allison Williams’ Marnie.

Girls ran for six seasons on HBO from 2012 to 2017. Created by Lena Dunham and produced by Judd Apatow, the series will return with five new episodes. Production for the limited-run series will begin in 2027, 10 years after the show’s last original episode.

RELATED: Lena Dunham Has Idea For ‘Girls’ Movie, Jokingly Tries To Force HBO Max’s Hand

Returning cast will include Dunham as Hannah, Allison Williams as Marnie, Jemima Kirke as Jessa, Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna, and Andrew Rannells as Elijah.

Dunham created, wrote, and directed Girls, and executive produced these episodes alongside Judd Apatow for Apatow Productions, Ilene S. Landress, and Michael P. Cohen for Good Thing Going. Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells serve as co-executive producers.

title: ‘Lizard Music’ Starring Dwayne Johnson And Directed By Benny Safdie To Tune Up Christmas Day 2027 Via Amazon MGM
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Amazon MGM Studios has set the theatrical release date for the live-action/CGI hybrid Lizard Music, starring Dwayne Johnson and directed by Benny Safdie, for December 25, 2027. Lizard Music follows a boy (Theo Clark Leber) left to his own devices who stumbles upon a secret late-night broadcast of lizards playing otherworldly music, and a […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Amazon MGM Studios has set the theatrical release date for the live-action/CGI hybrid Lizard Music, starring Dwayne Johnson and directed by Benny Safdie, for December 25, 2027.

Lizard Music follows a boy (Theo Clark Leber) left to his own devices who stumbles upon a secret late-night broadcast of lizards playing otherworldly music, and a hidden door to the extraordinary swings open. His search for answers leads him to an eccentric and whimsical old man nicknamed The Chicken Man (Johnson) and his beloved companion, an 85-year-old chicken named Claudia – the boy and the old man become kindred spirits who find each other at just the right time.

United by a shared vision, they set off on an adventure that begins as a hunt for a hidden society but blossoms into something far greater: a voyage through invisible worlds, unexpected harmonies, and the unbreakable bond between lost souls who discover magic not only in what they find, but also in each other.

Watch on Deadline

The project is billed as being another transformative role for Johnson, with extensive makeup and prosthetics used to turn him into the eccentric septuagenarian Chicken Man. Alicia Silverstone, Tim Heidecker, Arya Parvathi, Regina Hall, Colman Domingo, Jeff Goldblum, Rachel McAdams, Andrew Dice Clay and David Krumholtz also star.

Safdie adapted the screenplay off Daniel Pinkwater’s novel of the same name. Producers include UA’s Scott Stuber and Nick Nesbitt, Out for the Count Productions’ Safdie, Seven Bucks Productions’ Johnson, and Magnetic Fields Entertainment’s David Koplan.

Given the fantasy and wonder nature of the project, a Christmas launchpad is ideal in reaching family audiences. Lizard Music will arrive in theaters next year following the December 17 release of Disney/Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Secret Wars, New Line’s Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum and Lionsgate’s sequel The Housemaid’s Secret.

Also opening on Christmas Day 2027 so far are Amazon MGM Studios’ Ron Howard-directed actioner Alone at Dawn starring Adam Driver and Anne Hathaway, and a Warner Bros’ movie being directed by Nancy Meyers.

title: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Stars Hit The Field To Aid James Talarico’s Smashmouth Attempt To Score A Texas Senate Race Win
summary: “It’s time to leave it all on the field.” That’s the message Friday Night Lights series stars Connie Britton, Jesse Plemons and Adrianne Palicki are pitching to Texans in the final push for U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico in an ad the Democrat dropped over the weekend. Repurposing the fictional Dillon High School football team’s […]
content:
“It’s time to leave it all on the field.” That’s the message Friday Night Lights series stars Connie Britton, Jesse Plemons and Adrianne Palicki are pitching to Texans in the final push for U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico in an ad the Democrat dropped over the weekend.

Repurposing the fictional Dillon High School football team’s battle cry of “Clear eyes, full hearts, can’t lose” from NBC’s hit 2005-2011 drama series starring Britton and Kyle Chandler, the spot kicks off Talarico’s Lone Star state tour heading towards Election Day on November 3.

Along with the FNL crew (blandly called “Friday Night Leftists” on Laura Ingraham’s Fox News show Monday) in attendance, don’t blink at the 0:56 mark or you may miss Kacey Musgraves giving the candidate a front-row greeting.

Tied in the polls with GOP Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who has been the subject of legal and ethical scandals over the years, Talarico has attracted a galaxy of star power in his bid to become the first Democrat to hold state office in usually red Texas since 1994.

Watch on Deadline

In addition to controversies over sit-downs with late-night hosts Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel and earning the wrath of Elon Musk, Talarico, a four-term member of the Texas House of Representatives, has been in Los Angeles repeatedly for a series of big-money fundraisers. The soirées have been hosted by seasoned Dem donors like Damon Lindelof and ex-HBO exec and Obama-era Ambassador to Spain James Costos.

In addition, Willie Nelson and Bill Nye the Science Guy have joined the Talarico hayride, and The Chicks welcomed the candidate on stage with them October 17 in San Antonio.

Still, for all the hopes, dreams and big names Talarico is bringing to the final weeks before the midterms, his MAGA rival Paxton has received backing from Donald Trump and the well-watched Fox News. Even more important than Trump, Paxton is the beneficiary of more than $190 million from Musk in the race.

With control of the Senate in reach for the Dems and Trump’s polls in the toilet, the race between Paxton and Talarico is not only the most star-studded on the midterms but also the most expensive, with more than $500 million in ad buys alone.

Talarico is in Fort Worth tonight and Tyler, TX on Tuesday as both campaigns head to the finish line next month.

title: ‘The Gilded Age’: 2 Supporting Characters Not Returning For Season 4
summary: The sprawling cast of HBO’s period drama The Gilded Age gets larger every season. With so many characters to service, some are being taken out of rotation. In Season 4, that will include George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) secretary Richard Clay, played by Patrick Page, and New York Globe publisher T. Thomas Fortune (Sullivan Jones). Both […]
content:
The sprawling cast of HBO‘s period drama The Gilded Age gets larger every season. With so many characters to service, some are being taken out of rotation.

In Season 4, that will include George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) secretary Richard Clay, played by Patrick Page, and New York Globe publisher T. Thomas Fortune (Sullivan Jones). Both characters were introduced in Season 1 as recurring. Page and Jones were promoted to series regular for Season 2 before reverting to a recurring status in Season 3. It is possible that one or both are brought back in future seasons for guest appearances.

Both Richard Clay and Thomas Fortune had eventful Season 3 arcs. Clay was fired by George (Spector) for failing to close a major deal, aligned with a top rival to get back at his former boss and became a prime suspect in George’s shooting at the end of the season.

Watch on Deadline

An editor of aspiring writer Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), Thomas Fortune was her mentor before he crossed a line, pursuing a romantic relationship with her in Season 2 despite being married. In Season 3, he gave Peggy another out-of-town assignment and tried to tag along uninvited until Peggy’s new suitor (and future husband) Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), stepped in and took him down in a fistfight.

Sullivan Jones and Patrick Page in ‘The Guilded Age’ HBO

New cast additions for Season 4 of The Gilded Age include Taylor Trensch, James Scully, Dennis Haysbert, Maggie Kuntz, Neal Huff, Bonnie Milligan, Jim Gaffigan, Dallas Roberts, Andrew Burnap, Elizabeth Marvel and Adrienne Warren.

They join returning cast members Carrie Coon, Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Louisa Jacobson, Blake Ritson, Denée Benton, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, Kristine Nielsen, Kelli O’Hara, Taylor Richardson, Douglas Sills, Erin Wilhelmi, John Douglas Thompson, with Bill Camp and Phylicia Rashad.

Season 4, which premieres Nov. 1, is getting a lot of interest from fans, with its trailer amassing 43M views on YouTube alone since its release last week. The trailer raised some concern about the Russell’s daughter Gladys (Farmiga) who is not in it but she is on the list of returning cast and was featured in the first Season 4 teaser.

Both the teaser and the trailer end on a memorable line by Baranski’s Agnes van Rhijn. You can watch the trailer below.

Created, written and executive produced by Julian Fellowes, The Gilded Age is also produced by director Salli Richardson-Whitfield, written and executive produced by Sonja Warfield and executive produced by Gareth Neame, David Crockett, Bob Greenblatt, Kate Churchill, Davita Scarlett and Elaine Aronson. Armstrong Dunbar and Holly Rymon serve as co-executive producers. The historical drama is a co-production between HBO and Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

title: Anurag Kashyap and Vasan Bala Present Mumbai Cab Thriller ‘Aakhri Ride’ for Halloween Release (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Indian filmmakers Anurag Kashyap and Vasan Bala have come on board to present “Aakhri Ride,” a short thriller set over a single Halloween night in Mumbai, which will release worldwide on Oct. 31. The film will go out on Oh Short Flips, a YouTube channel curated by Kashyap. Vijesh Rajan and Yashoda Parthasarthy wrote and […]
content:
Indian filmmakers Anurag Kashyap and Vasan Bala have come on board to present “Aakhri Ride,” a short thriller set over a single Halloween night in Mumbai, which will release worldwide on Oct. 31.

The film will go out on Oh Short Flips, a YouTube channel curated by Kashyap.

Vijesh Rajan and Yashoda Parthasarthy wrote and directed the short, their first film. It follows a Mumbai ride-share driver who is driven to breaking point during one frightening night.

Kashyap said he had worked with the pair since the “Gangs of Wasseypur” days and “always believed they are excellent storytellers with a unique visual language. So when they finally decided to turn writer-directors, it was an easy decision to back them. And now, I am quite excited to see the audience’s response to their first film – ‘Aakhri Ride,’ when it releases on Halloween Day.”

Popular on Variety

Chandan Roy (“Panchayat”) and Aamir Dalvi (“Kennedy”) head the cast, and Faisal Malik (“Panchayat”) also appears. Ranjan Singh, Vishesh Agrawal, Rajan EPK and Kashyap produced, with Navaras Pictures backing the project in association with Plexus Motion Pictures and Flip Films.

Bala described Rajan as the “Wiz Kid” that filmmaker Srinivas had introduced him and his colleagues to. “We were always in awe of what he could do with his VFX skills but there was always a sensitive and fun storyteller in him. When he and Yashoda went to make the film, we all rooted for them. I was beyond excited to watch their short film. It’s sharp, fun, quirky and with a beating heart. So coming on board was a nano second decision, a no brainer,” Bala said.

The directors traced the idea back to long taxi rides home after meetings around the city. “We’d be sitting in the back seat, talking about work or sitting in silence, while the driver was often carrying a completely different world on his phone: family back home, money worries, things we may never fully know. We began to notice an invisible social divide: we were enjoying the comfort of being driven home, while he was trying to make ends meet. We shared a small space, but knew so little about each other’s lives,” they said.

The pair set out to examine that gap through a mix of horror and comedy, built around a man so weighed down by daily problems that he fails to see what he has picked up. “We hope viewers laugh, get spooked, and maybe think a little about the person driving them home,” they said.

The film began its festival run in the Short Film Market Picks at Clermont-Ferrand, then landed selections at three genre events: BIFAN in Bucheon, Fantasia International Film Festival and Fantastic Fest. Its circuit, which includes Oscar- and BAFTA-qualifying festivals, also took in Florida Film Festival, Austin After Dark, Wench, Fantaspoa, events in Rhode Island and San Jose, Italy’s Absurd Film Festival, France’s Red Movie Awards, Cannes Indie Shorts and New York Indie Shorts Awards.

At Fantasia, the short won the Silver Audience Award for best Asian short. It also picked up best film at the Dada Saheb Phalke Film Festival and best Indian short at the Indo Dubai International Film Festival, and finished as second runner-up at BISFF.

title: Jon Stewart Jokes Skydance Has ‘Pulled Our Renewal’ Before Slamming JD Vance, Trump and Emmanuel Macron
summary: Jon Stewart was back behind the desk of “The Daily Show” Monday night and went all in on Vice President JD Vance, President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron — but not before cracking a joke about his recent renewal. Kicking off the show, Stewart introduced guest David Corn, “who you know the Native […]
content:
Jon Stewart was back behind the desk of “The Daily Show” Monday night and went all in on Vice President JD Vance, President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron — but not before cracking a joke about his recent renewal.

Kicking off the show, Stewart introduced guest David Corn, “who you know the Native Americans used to refer to as David Maize,” he said. “And they’ve just pulled our renewal! I’m sorry.”

Vance, or “Vice President Jeffrey Dahmer Vance,” as Stewart referred to him, was up first, with the host cutting to a recent clip of Vance apologizing to a woman for using “imperfect” rhetoric. “Sometimes you incite violence against vulnerable communities, and then later on you apologize,” said Stewart. “So the dehumanizing rhetoric against immigrants, which all of us thought was a cornerstone and intentional strategy of both Donald Trump and JD Vance’s rise to power… actually, that wasn’t intentional. It was all just sloppy word choice. That was all on him.”

Popular on Variety

Stewart then moved on to France — “where Paris is burning, and not in the not in that way, not in the good, fun way,” said the host — where riots exploded in the past weekend, which French officials have said had nothing to do with immigration, Islam, or Muslim communities. However, that didn’t stop Vance from tweeting that “western liberals imported the third world into France.” “Are you seriously suggesting that immigrants have brought a culture of revolution and protest to France? What are you talking about? Have you ever been to the theater? Can you not hear the people sing?” said Stewart.

And yet, despite the riots in France, Emmanuel Macron attended a Celine Dion concert with his wife, a decision Stewart called out. “First of all, who goes to a concert with their actual wife?” joked Stewart, referencing the viral Coldplay cheating scandal. “And second of all, Celine Dion concert — a little on the metaphorical nose, yeah, Mr. President? As your country falls apart, you stand on the deck, enjoying the dulcet tones of the theme song from ‘Titanic.’”

Stewart went on to explain that people in France were rioting over the rising cost of living and fuel prices, a result of the conflict in the Persian Gulf. “Holy shit! In France, they’ve burned down an entire city because of a war they didn’t start and aren’t even any part of,” he joked. “And here in the country that started the war, we’re not even sure we’re going to get to take back the house… I mean, we’re so mad about this war, we might vote,” he said. “Our country happens to be flame retardant. Or one of those two,” he continued, laughing. “Even I would cancel me for that one.”

He then got into Trump, calling out the president for saying that high gas prices are the result of the war in “Ukraine that Russia started” and joking about his instated and then promptly waived sanctions on Russian fuel sales. “We will not waver, but we will waive,” said Stewart. The host went on to have a fake phone call with Trump, during which he asked if he knew who cut off Ukraine’s access to “Starlink or Star Shield, whatever it’s called.” “I didn’t do that,” Trump said. “No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t know where it is. I don’t even think it was slowed down.”

Ahead of Stewart’s Monday show, it was announced that he would remain the host of “The Daily Show” through 2028. Stewart’s contract was set to end at the end of 2026 after signing a one-year renewal in November 2025. Stewart made his hosting debut on “The Daily Show” in 1999, left in 2015, and returned in February 2024. Upon his return, “The Daily Show” ratings went up.

“Jon Stewart is a generational talent and ‘The Daily Show’ continues to be one of the most influential franchises on television and a cornerstone of Comedy Central. We are excited to continue our partnership with Jon and his award-winning news team,” said George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV.

Check out the entire monologue below.

title: Judi Dench Says Panned ‘Cats’ Film Was a ‘Waste’ of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s ‘Goodwill and Talent’: ‘Oh God, I Can’t Bear It’
summary: Judi Dench, who played Old Deuteronomy in Tom Hooper’s “Cats,” is reflecting on the universally panned film in her forthcoming memoir, “Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It?” Released in 2019, the film adapted Andrew Lloyd Webber’s hugely successful musical of the same name. But despite its stacked cast — which also […]
content:
Judi Dench, who played Old Deuteronomy in Tom Hooper’s “Cats,” is reflecting on the universally panned film in her forthcoming memoir, “Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It?”

Released in 2019, the film adapted Andrew Lloyd Webber’s hugely successful musical of the same name. But despite its stacked cast — which also included James Corden, Idris Elba, Taylor Swift and others among Dench — the film was considered a critical and commercial failure.

“Oh God, I can’t bear it – and [Lloyd Webber] had waited so long for it to be made,” she wrote. “What a waste of all that goodwill and talent. I understand the critics were rather hostile to the film. I never saw the final cut so I can’t judge. All I’ll say is nobody sets out to give a poor performance or make a bad film. You do your best, offer something up and hope that people will get on board and join the party.” (Dench was nominated for a Razzie award for her performance in the film.)

Popular on Variety

She also added, “It’s a miracle that anything is ever made – films, plays, TV – let alone turn out to be a success, because there are so many moving parts,” speaking about the industry at large.

“Sometimes things just don’t work out: the timing’s wrong, the cast don’t gel, the elements don’t coalesce,” she wrote. “But people’s intentions are mostly honorable. There were no villains in the making of Cats. And if something isn’t a success, then there are always things you can say you’ve learnt.”

“Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It?” hits shelves Nov. 3.

title: Why Daisy Edgar-Jones Listened to Dolly Parton to Prep for ‘Sense and Sensibility’
summary: Daisy Edgar-Jones is no stranger to starring in a book-to-screen adaptation. She knows how to please hardcore fans while offering a fresh take on the material. (See the success of “Normal People” and “Where the Crawdads Are” or the upcoming “Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow” as proof.) That said, starring in a Jane Austen adaptation […]
content:
Daisy Edgar-Jones is no stranger to starring in a book-to-screen adaptation.

She knows how to please hardcore fans while offering a fresh take on the material. (See the success of “Normal People” and “Where the Crawdads Are” or the upcoming “Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow” as proof.) That said, starring in a Jane Austen adaptation is a different beast altogether — but Edgar-Jones has been an Austen admirer from an early age.

“My mum gave me all the books when I was at a very formative age,” Edgar-Jones told Variety at the Los Angeles premiere of “Sense and Sensibility,” in which she stars as Elinor Dashwood. “It’s a rite of passage to read them all when you’re a teenager, and you’re finding yourself and falling in love for the first time and experience that personal growth. So, yeah, I read them in one fell swoop.”

Popular on Variety

Even then, Edgar-Jones connected with the eldest Dashwood daughter, known for her good sense — certainly more so than her passionate sister Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles).

“I really enjoy playing characters that have a deep well inside that maybe other people overlook, and finding ways in which to express that,” Edgar-Jones explained. “She’s somebody that has such a strength and this deep well of emotion that she’s learned to button up. And I love the journey she goes on where she becomes more comfortable with embracing that wilder side of herself. I was just so excited to sink my teeth into playing her.

To prepare for her roles, Edgar-Jones listens to songs that get her into the character’s headspace. To promote the film release, Edgar-Jones shared her “Sense and Sensibility” playlist, which ranges from legends like Billie Holiday, Minnie Riperton and Dolly Parton to contemporary artists like Alice Phoebe Lou, Julia Jacklin and Jessica Pratt.

Why include Parton’s “Here You Come Again?” Well, Edgar-Jones used to belt that track in the car on the way home from school.

“It just epitomizes what it is to like love somebody — that heartbreak and slight female rage inside that you just want to let out. I really could imagine, if Eleanor lived in a time with Dolly Parton, she’d be belting that around her bedroom in Barton [Cottage].”

Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe and Daisy Edgar-Jones at the “Sense & Sensibility” Los Angeles premiere. Michael Buckner

At the Oct. 7 premiere, held at the United Theatre in Downtown L.A., Edgar-Jones was joined by her film family, including Caitríona Balfe, who plays their mother, Mrs. Dashwood, and Creed-Miles, who was named one of Variety’s 10 Actors to Watch earlier that day.

“It’s a bit scary,” Creed-Miles said about having so many eyes on her work. “I just really care about filmmakers, and Georgia [Oakley] is a really special one. I was a big fan of “Blue Jean,” so going into this, I wasn’t thinking about that side of it. I’ve never experienced anything on this level of like support, and that’s really special.”

Creed-Miles also reflected on the amplified sisterhood narrative in the film, as screenwriter Diana Reid (also a Variety 10 to Watch honoree) adapted the script to center more on the relationship between Elinor and Marianne.

“I’m family with these women: Georgia, Diana, Daisy is one of my absolute best friends, everyone,” Creed-Miles said. “Amazing women were involved in the making of this film. There was something cathartic and really rewarding about having a family making something — and a family of sisters, as well.”

title: Why ‘Office Space’ Actor Richard Riehle Was the Quintessential Actor’s Actor (Guest Column)
summary: The first time I met Richard Riehle, I was making one of the first things I’d ever made. It was a Funny or Die video, and my friend Tanner Thomason and I were trying to figure out how to get an actual actor to be in it. Someone suggested Richard. “Just offer it to him. […]
content:
The first time I met Richard Riehle, I was making one of the first things I’d ever made. It was a Funny or Die video, and my friend Tanner Thomason and I were trying to figure out how to get an actual actor to be in it. Someone suggested Richard. “Just offer it to him. I bet he’ll be down.” So we wrote him a nice letter, offered him the enormous sum of $250, and a week later we were working with a legend.

I remember arriving on set that morning and finding Richard already there, sitting by himself, reading the newspaper and drinking a root beer. He’d beaten the crew there. He didn’t need anything, didn’t seem particularly concerned that he was an actor with hundreds of credits doing a little internet video for two guys who had never really made anything before. He was just happy to be there.

That was about 13 years ago. I spent a lot of the next 13 years trying to find reasons to work with him again. If I wrote something with a part Richard could play, I offered it to him. Sometimes I probably wrote the part because I wanted an excuse to hear his stories. We ended up acting in several other projects together, too, and over the years we became friends.

Popular on Variety

He was also, without question, one of the best actors I’ve ever worked with. I know that might sound like the sort of thing people say when someone dies, but I mean it. Richard was astonishingly good. He could make a line funny just by deciding not to make it funny. He could steal a scene without seeming to do much of anything. And every once in a while he’d remind you that underneath the familiar face and the wonderful mustache was an actor with a range most people never got to see.

Years ago, we were doing a table read for a movie called “Fear, Inc.” We’d cast Richard as the funny neighbor. The actor who was supposed to read the villain couldn’t make it that night, so Richard offered to fill in. No big deal. Just reading a few extra lines. Then he started doing the role, which he had literally worked on at home. He knew the lines of a role he wasn’t even going to play for the table read. The sweet, funny neighbor we’d all been laughing at was suddenly terrifying. I remember looking around the room and seeing jaws drop. People were genuinely stunned. It was like we’d all forgotten, for a moment, who we were sitting across from.

Richard had more than 400 acting credits, which is an almost ridiculous number until you understand the man. More than anything, he just loved being on set. Student films, tiny independent movies, major blockbusters, network sitcoms. I honestly don’t think he cared all that much about the difference. If he could hang out on set instead of in his trailer, that’s where you’d find him. And if you worked with him once, you had a friend. Invite him to a screening a year later, some random improv show, or a backyard barbecue, and if he was free, he’d show up.

A couple of years ago, we were in Dallas shooting a movie called Tonic. One night over beers, Richard told me how excited he was to have been asked to reunite with his old “Office Space” pal, Stephen Root, on an episode of “Barry.” We got to talking about his career, and he said something I’ve thought about a lot since. Richard suspected that taking so many small independent projects over the years had probably hurt his chances of getting certain television or studio jobs. Maybe people saw the sheer volume of credits and made assumptions. Maybe he’d have been better off being more selective. But he wasn’t going to change anything.

He wanted to act. As much as he could, for as long as he could. If saying yes to some tiny movie meant missing out on a bigger one, well, that was fine with him. He’d rather spend his Tuesday on a set somewhere, even a tiny set, than sit around waiting for a more prestigious phone call. I loved that about him. I think a lot of us could learn something from it.

Richard lived in the same Los Feliz spot for years. He liked being able to walk around Hillhurst and Vermont, to get out and be part of the neighborhood. He drove a Honda Civic that was something like 25 years old. Why get a new car? This one worked. It got him to set and back. That was Richard.

And he had that mustache. I’m actually wearing a mustache today partially because of Richard Riehle. Six years ago, I grew one for a movie we made together called “Faith Based.” I wasn’t sure I was going to keep it. Richard told me I should. He said growing his own mustache was one of the best decisions he’d ever made. It fit his face, he explained, and gave him something distinctive. Coming from a man whose mustache belongs in the same conversation as Sam Elliott’s and Burt Reynolds’, I took that advice pretty seriously. I haven’t shaved it since. I suppose that’s a pretty small thing to carry forward from a friendship, but I like knowing that a little piece of Richard will be looking back at me in the mirror every morning.

When I think about Richard now, I don’t really think about his filmography, impressive as it is. I think about that first morning. The newspaper and the root beer. A man who’d already been in more movies than I could count, sitting patiently on the set of a $250 internet video in Canoga Park, ready to give it everything he had for a comedy sketch.

He gave that little project just as much as he would have given a studio movie. I don’t think it ever occurred to him to do otherwise. Richard just loved being an actor.

Luke Barnett is an actor, writer, and filmmaker whose credits include AMC’s “Dark Winds,” Apple TV+’s “For All Mankind” and Peacock’s “The Burbs.” His recent filmmaking work includes the viral short “The Crossing Over Express,” currently being developed as a feature, and the Fangoria-produced “Goodbye, Monster,” which just premiered at Fantastic Fest. He has also worked on nearly a dozen projects with the late Richard Riehle, though not nearly enough.

title: Michael Douglas Asked To Be Killed Off Marvel’s ‘Ant-Man’: “They Wouldn’t Let Me”
summary: If Michael Douglas had his way, he would’ve left the Marvel Cinematic Universe after starring in 2015’s Ant-Man and its sequel. In a new interview, the actor got real about his time in the MCU and asked the studio to kill off his character. “I would have been killed off after the second one, but […]
content:
If Michael Douglas had his way, he would’ve left the Marvel Cinematic Universe after starring in 2015’s Ant-Man and its sequel.

In a new interview, the actor got real about his time in the MCU and asked the studio to kill off his character.

“I would have been killed off after the second one, but they wouldn’t let me,” Douglas said on the Happy Sad Confused podcast.

Douglas shared that he wanted to star in a CGI-heavy film, adding, “I said, ‘I’ve never done a green screen movie.’ I [told] all my agents, ‘I’d like to do one of these green screen movies to see what they’re like,’ you know? Because it’s amazing. It’s nothing, just a green screen, and they show you the pictures of what it’s gonna look like when it’s all finished.”

After starring in the MCU, Douglas said, “It’s hard acting, man,” adding, “It’s coming at you here, this and that, you know.”

Watch on Deadline

Douglas joked about reading the “fine print” of his contract, saying that Ant-Man star Paul Rudd “was a wonderful actor” and the cast was “a lovely group,” noting, “but then you can’t get out of it.”

After starring in Ant-Man in 2015 as Hank Pym, Douglas would reprise the role on several other occasions. Douglas reprised his role in 2018’s Ant-Man and the Wasp, 2019’s Avengers: Endgame, and 2023’s Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania. He also voiced the character in several episodes of the Disney+ animated series What If…?, between 2021 and 2023.

Watch Michael Douglas’ full interview in the video below.

title: ‘Star Wars’ Headed To Super Bowl LXI For Animated Altcast On Disney+, Disney Channel and Disney XD
summary: Characters from “A Galaxy Far, Far Away” are headed to Super Bowl LXI as ESPN, Lucasfilm and the NFL team up for a Star Wars alternative telecast. On Sunday, February 14, Disney+, Disney Channel, and Disney XD will air an alternate telecast featuring iconic characters from across the Lucasfilm franchise alongside the AFC and NFC champions, including […]
content:
Characters from “A Galaxy Far, Far Away” are headed to Super Bowl LXI as ESPN, Lucasfilm and the NFL team up for a Star Wars alternative telecast.

On Sunday, February 14, Disney+, Disney Channel, and Disney XD will air an alternate telecast featuring iconic characters from across the Lucasfilm franchise alongside the AFC and NFC champions, including C-3PO, voiced by original Star Wars cast member Anthony Daniels.

The Star Wars animated telecast will recreate every play of Super Bowl LXI in real time, transforming players on the field into animated avatars, while Star Wars characters sub in during key moments and various Easter eggs appear throughout the game.

Star Wars Funday Football will air alongside the traditional telecast with Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters, and Laura Rutledge on ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ from SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. ESPN’s Spanish-language telecast will be available on Disney+ and ESPN Deportes, with a separate Spanish-language presentation on Univision.

Watch on Deadline

This is the first animated alternative presentation of a Super Bowl. The Star Wars Funday Football altcast follows others from ESPN, Disney, and the NFL, including Toy Story Funday Football (October 2023, Falcons-Jaguars), The Simpsons Funday Football (December 2024, Bengals-Cowboys), and Monsters Funday Football (December 2025, Eagles-Chargers).

ESPN will produce Star Wars Funday Football using data visualization technology from Sony’s Beyond Sports.

Beginning Tuesday, Oct. 20, SC+, ESPN’s daily SportsCenter show on Disney+, will feature Star Wars “Hyperspace Highlights” with plays from Monday Night Football presented with a Star Wars visual theme. Also, starting October 26, SC+ will showcase on Mondays an animated Darth Vader interviewing an NFL player participating in that night’s Monday Night Football game.

title: Quinta Brunson Shares Update On Betty Boop Film Development: “The Story Will Be Unlike Anything Anyone Expects”
summary: Quinta Brunson is sharing an update on the Betty Boop film she is developing and starring in. While appearing on Good Morning America, the Abbott Elementary creator and star teased that she is “creating a really incredible movie” and is still “in process right now,” so she couldn’t share many details. “I think the story will be unlike […]
content:
Quinta Brunson is sharing an update on the Betty Boop film she is developing and starring in.

While appearing on Good Morning America, the Abbott Elementary creator and star teased that she is “creating a really incredible movie” and is still “in process right now,” so she couldn’t share many details.

“I think the story will be unlike anything anyone expects,” she said on the ABC morning show. “It’s not just about Betty herself but an era of animation.”

When GMA host Robin Roberts asked Brunson what it was about Betty Boop that made her want to make a film about her, she said, “It was the story about her creation, honestly. It’s just not that simple, and it shines a light on way more than you would ever think in America’s history. So it’s really cool.”

Brunson said she is working with Fleischer Studios, the company that owns the animated character Max Fleischer created. Brunson’s own Fifth Chance Productions is also producing the film.

Watch on Deadline

In addition to working on the Betty Boop film, Brunson stars in ABC’s Abbott Elementary, which entered its sixth season earlier this month. Brunson recently voiced the character of Dr. Fuzzby in Disney’s Zootopia 2.

In the coming weeks, Brunson will voice Sherri in the upcoming animated film The Cat in the Hat, set to open in theaters on November 6. Playing the HR director at the I.I.I.I. (Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC), Brunson shared credits with Bill Hader (the Cat in the Hat), Matt Berry, Xochitl Gómez, Giancarlo Esposito, America Ferrera, Tiago Martinez, Bowen Yang, Paula Pell, and Titus Burgess.

Watch Quinta Brunson in the video below.

title: Awards Go To ‘Mayilaa,’ ‘The Gymnasts Of Fisherman Colony’ And More At Seattle’s Tasveer film Festival
summary: The Tasveer Film Festival in Seattle has wrapped its 21st edition with the announcement of awards in multiple categories. Mayilaa, a drama directed by Semmalar Annam, won the Jury Award for Best Feature Narrative. The film starring P. Melody Dorcas, Geetha Kailasam, Shudar Kodi, and Sathya Maruthani tells a mother-daughter tale of “a novice saleswoman […]
content:
The Tasveer Film Festival in Seattle has wrapped its 21st edition with the announcement of awards in multiple categories.

Mayilaa, a drama directed by Semmalar Annam, won the Jury Award for Best Feature Narrative. The film starring P. Melody Dorcas, Geetha Kailasam, Shudar Kodi, and Sathya Maruthani tells a mother-daughter tale of “a novice saleswoman [who] travels South India to meet financial needs, despite having no sales experience.”

Mayilaa has also screened at Dharamshala International Film Festival in northern India, the Singapore International Film Festival, and International Film Festival Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony‘ Courtesy of Akelo Media

The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony, directed by Habiba Nosheen, won the Jury Award for Best Feature Documentary. The film centers on young women pursuing gymnastics in an area of Pakistan where such an athletic activity is uncommon for girls. As Deadline reported earlier this month, the documentary is executive produced by Mariska Hargitay, Trish Adlesic, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Malala Yousafzai. Hargitay noted, “When we first learned about these young girls and their lives from director Habiba Nosheen, my producing partner, Trish Adlesic, and I knew we wanted to help ensure that their story would reach audiences around the world.”

Watch on Deadline

Autumn Pictures

The Jury Award for Best Short went to The Last Glance, directed by Kamran Faiq and starring Adnan Shah Tipu and Areej Ayub Hussain.

Tasveer, which ran from October 13–18, showcased 136 films from 16 countries across more than 25 languages, including 20 World Premieres, 4 North American Premieres, and 4 U.S. Premieres. The festival notes, “The 2026 program included powerful storytelling by female directors, groundbreaking animation, an impressive slate of sports-centric cinema, and one of the festival’s strongest LGBTQ+ lineups to date.”

“Each film in this year’s lineup came to us carrying someone’s whole world,” noted Tasveer Executive Director Rita Meher. “Our role is to welcome it home, with a stage, a room full of industry, and real opportunities to go further. Watching filmmakers meet their audience and the people who can champion their work is exactly why we do this.”

Juried award winners were selected by a panel including Jury Lead Aparna Purohit (CEO of Aamir Khan Productions); James Longley (two-time Academy Award-nominated documentary filmmaker); Nekisa Cooper (former Head of Content at MasterClass, and president of the board of directors at Chicken & Egg Films), and Warren Etheredge (producer, film educator at the University of Washington, and co-founder of the Walla Walla Movie Crush).

“Some stories move us through their intimacy; others through their reflection of the world around us,” commented Jury Lead Aparna Purohit. “The films we considered at Tasveer did both, confronting the socio-political realities of our time with courage, sensitivity and remarkable cinematic vision.

“As Head of the Jury, it was a privilege and responsibility to engage with such a rich range of perspectives. I was deeply moved by the filmmakers’ honesty, diversity and ambition, and grateful to my fellow jurors for the thoughtful, open conversations that shaped our deliberations.
