I am delighted that Tasveer continues to give South Asian stories a platform to cross borders and resonate with audiences and communities worldwide. This experience reaffirmed why cinema matters: it reflects our world, challenges our assumptions and brings us closer to lives beyond our own, fostering greater empathy.”

Tasveer Film Festival

The third annual Tasveer Film Market, “North America’s only industry platform dedicated to South Asian and diasporic cinema,” distributed $170,000 in awards across three competitive pitch events.

In its seventh year, the Tasveer Film Fund awarded $35,000 each to four original short film projects:

The Blue House – Red Reddy

Friendforhire.com – Nishanth R

Ghusl – Ambarien Alqadar

Planned Parenthood – Rahul Chaturvedi

The closing ceremony featured the announcement of the following award winners:

Jury Awards

Best Short: The Last Glance

Best Feature Narrative: Mayilaa

Best Feature Documentary: The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony

Audience Choice Awards

Best Documentary Short: Salam Shalom

Best Documentary Feature: 49-51

Best Narrative Short: We Were Here

Best Narrative Feature: Never Had a Chance

Choice Awards

Best Social Justice Film: Flowers of Acacia

Best Animation: The Hidden Side of the Moon

Best LGBTQIA+: Aman

Best Editing: Upon Starvation

Best Director (Priyankar Patra): Early Days

Best Actor (Male) (Chiranjit Biswas): Delupi Best Actor (Female) (Mahek): Mother Tongue

title: Jakarta Pitches Itself as Regional Film Hub, Points to Busan as Model
summary: Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung Wibowo kicked off the Jakarta Film Summit 2026 on Tuesday with a pitch for the Indonesian capital as a regional film hub, making the case that the city is equipped to draw more shoots, filmmakers and investors from across the region. Speaking at the Royal Glass House at Park Hyatt Jakarta, […]
content:
Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung Wibowo kicked off the Jakarta Film Summit 2026 on Tuesday with a pitch for the Indonesian capital as a regional film hub, making the case that the city is equipped to draw more shoots, filmmakers and investors from across the region.

Speaking at the Royal Glass House at Park Hyatt Jakarta, Pramono built his argument around the city’s infrastructure, its economy and its transit system. He held up Busan, the South Korean port city that is home to the Busan International Film Festival, as an example Jakarta could learn from as it grows its own industry.

The governor cited economic growth of 5.52% and inflation of 2.7%. Jakarta has climbed from 17th to 15th place in a global transport ranking, according to the figures he presented, and public transit now connects 93% of the city.

Popular on Variety

The summit, hosted by the Jakarta Film Commission with the Indonesian Film Agency (Badan Perfilman Indonesia, or BPI), runs through Oct. 22, with the first two days given over to production policy, filming permits, incentives, financing and investment. Upward of 500 attendees from 10 countries are taking part, with 40 speakers on the bill. Government officials and financial institutions are in the room alongside investors, streamers and industry professionals.

Tuesday’s sessions dealt with how government can back productions, including opening up shooting locations around Jakarta. An ASEAN Film Alliance Network panel examined how to nurture talent, raise money and set up co-productions across the region.

The focus will shift to money on Oct. 21. Panels will cover how to get a project ready for funding, what role banks can play, and how audience data can help investors gauge risk.

The final day, Jakarta Scouting Day, will take film commissioners and production companies out to prospective locations including Pasar Rumput, Muara Angke Harbor, Kota Tua and the Bundaran HI Skydeck. Also on the schedule is “The Two Cities,” which will pair Jakarta with Hong Kong to explore ways the two might work together.

Organizers hope the event will yield policy recommendations, build up industry capacity and lift Jakarta’s international standing as a filming destination.

Fauzan Zidni, chair of BPI, said: “Jakarta Film Summit shows that local government can be a strategic partner for the film industry. When policy, permits, and financing are discussed at the same table with filmmakers, we are no longer working in silos. BPI is ready to make sure the recommendations from this forum are translated into policies that filmmakers can feel on the ground.”

title: Russell Brand Trial: Fourth Woman Alleges ‘Violent’ Sexual Assault While Working at Capital Radio
summary: Russell Brand’s criminal trial continued in London on Tuesday with testimony from his fourth accuser, who alleged the actor and comedian violently assaulted her while she was working at Capital Radio in the early 2000s. Brand has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault […]
content:
Russell Brand‘s criminal trial continued in London on Tuesday with testimony from his fourth accuser, who alleged the actor and comedian violently assaulted her while she was working at Capital Radio in the early 2000s.

Brand has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to incidents with six women spanning from 1999 to 2009. He has pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations against him.

Speaking from behind a blue screen — all alleged victims of sexual assault cases are granted lifelong anonymity in the U.K. — at Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday, Brand’s fourth accuser detailed the alleged assault, which she said occurred during the summer of 2004 or 2005.

Popular on Variety

As reported by Sky News, the woman said she was having a “normal day” at work when she ran into Brand at the Capital offices, who then “just leapt on me” after she left a room. Brand, who the accuser said was accompanied by one woman and three men, “grabbed my face, and was pushing his body against mine, literally walking me backwards,” she alleged.

She claimed he pushed her against a wall and began kissing her, describing the alleged attack as “violent,” “sloppy” and “frenzied.”

“He touched my bum, my breast, his hand on my waist and his other hand was just pinning me against the wall, and his body was just pressed up against me,” she said, according to Sky News. Asked by prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC how forceful Brand was, the woman said: “It was rough, his whole body was pressed against me… his hands were moving up and down so much it was violent. It was hard, and he just wasn’t stopping.”

The alleged victim said the woman and three men who were with Brand didn’t intervene. “They didn’t say anything; they didn’t move,” she said. “It was the middle of the working day, and they just didn’t say anything.”

The woman eventually pushed Brand away and told him to “fuck off,” she said, according to Sky News. Brand fell back, she claimed, and let out a laugh, causing one of the men to start laughing as well.

She then left the building to smoke a cigarette, telling the court she felt “dirty, shocked, stunned and shaken.” She did not tell anyone about the alleged incident at the time, but reported it in 2023 after watching few minutes of Channel 4’s documentary about the allegations surrounding Brand.

Questioned by Brand’s defense lawyer Ian Winter KC about her uncertainty of the exact year the alleged incident occurred, the woman said: “It was over 20 years ago.”

Winter questioned how she was certain the man who allegedly attacked her was Brand. The woman said she had never met him before but was aware of who he was: “The person who assaulted me was Russell Brand. I can’t forge that.”

She tearfully added, “This is a situation I did not want to be in. I don’t gain a single thing by saying what happened to me.”

Brand’s trial is expected to last six weeks.

title: ‘The Debut,’ ‘Ink’ Among Evolution Mallorca Highlights as Festival Celebrates 15th Edition: ‘We Want the Island to Be a Thriving Film Destination’
summary: Back in 2012, actress-turned-director Sandra Lipski wanted to crown a successful festival run for her debut short film “Going Down” with a screening in her hometown of Mallorca, but was surprised to realize the thriving island did not have its own film festival. Rather than wait for it to happen, she decided to start one […]
content:
Back in 2012, actress-turned-director Sandra Lipski wanted to crown a successful festival run for her debut short film “Going Down” with a screening in her hometown of Mallorca, but was surprised to realize the thriving island did not have its own film festival. Rather than wait for it to happen, she decided to start one herself. The result is Evolution Mallorca, celebrating its landmark 15th edition this year and taking place between Oct. 28 and Nov. 4.

Lipski was born in Germany, but moved to her family on the Spanish island as a young girl, later heading to Los Angeles to pursue a career as an actor. When the 2008 writers’ strike hit Hollywood, the actress was on the cusp of a big break. “That was very frustrating for me as an actress because that was the year I had a lot of big things coming out,” she tells Variety when recalling the origins of the festival. “I then said I would just do my own short film, which I did. Then I spent 2010 travelling to a lot of festivals.”

“I was so confused about Mallorca not having a film festival,” she adds. “Living in the U.S., there was a film festival in every tiny town, and it felt obvious to me the island would have one because it felt like the perfect festival location. I was very young at the time and just decided to try it and see what happens. I pulled some friends together, many Europeans who, like me, were born somewhere else but grew up here, and we created a very well-rounded team.”

Popular on Variety

In the years since its inception, Evolution Mallorca ballooned into a destination festival showcasing the best of cinema produced in the region but also attracting major international names. Guests who have attended previous editions include Danny DeVito, Annette Bening, Paul Haggis and Jessica Hausner. This year’s edition is set to be another glitzy one, with the festival honoring “Conclave” director Edward Berger, “Black Swan” cinematographer Matthew Libatique, “Inglourious Basterds” actress Diane Kruger, and “Triangle of Sadness” star Iris Berben.

club kid A24

This year’s line-up will feature over 100 projects across its program, with the festival boasting its largest feature film selection to date. International highlights include Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” and the opening gala in Jordan Firstman’s Cannes-dazzler “Club Kid.”

“We try having more glamorous, notable films in our international feature film section, films that have won awards from other festivals and already have a strong seal of approval,” says Lipski. “We need this section as it works as a helium balloon lifting the festival towards a wider audience. But, just a millimeter away, we are pushing the debut feature section and Made in Baleares, which is what Evolution is all about: giving a platform to and celebrating upcoming filmmakers.”

Notable films amongst the Made in Baleares section, which celebrates local cinema, include the world premiere of Juan Sut’s “Torna,” a co-production between Mexico and Mallorca following a young man who learns the house his dad left him in Mallorca is inhabited; Danna Ayelén Bosch García’s doc “Un Darrer Capfico,” exploring the intimate bond between Mallorcans and the sea; and Marga Melià’s “Putting Up With Paradise,” which revisits talks with Mallorcan artists to provide a critical, human look at the island’s past and future.

“What makes Evolution special is that these films all stand next to each other,” emphasizes the festival director. “They are all equally important to us and give the festival its soul of diversity and inclusion, reaffirming our mission of giving a platform to new voices.”

The director also says she has seen certain themes emerge in the section: overcrowded islands, housing issues for the local younger generation and finding a balance with tourism. “I don’t think it can go away; I think we just need to find a way to deal with it,” she says. “The island needs tourism as it is a main source of income, but we need to contain it so that local life is not forgotten.”

Lipski also notes the festival’s continued mission of platforming short films, which speaks directly to Evolution’s origins. “These are important filmmakers because they will be the future of the industry. And we have names like Renée Zellweger and Michael Keaton in the program, directing their first shorts. I always say: Don’t underestimate the power of a short film.”

Sandra Huller in “Fatherland” Courtesy of Agata Grzybowska

Evolution also has a key differentiator with its Cinematography Focus, a section celebrating the art, vision, and craft of cinematography. This year’s program will be led by Cinematography Icon Awardee Matthew Libatique and delivered in collaboration with British Cinematographer and Camera & Light Magazine. Activities include a hands-on lighting workshop, an exclusive Icon Talk with Libatique, and a timely panel discussion on the female gaze in cinematography. Previous editions have welcomed and honored some of the world’s most influential cinematographers, including Ed Lachman, Erik Messerschmidt, Anthony Dod Mantle, Phedon Papamichael and Oona Menges.

Speaking about the origins of the section, Lipski says that, on the festival’s 10th anniversary, she sat down with her team – which includes her husband, cinematographer Rainer Lipski – to understand how they could celebrate the craft within Evolution. The director says there are festivals dedicated to cinematography, like Cameraimage, but she couldn’t find other film festivals with intensive programs focused on professionals. “It has really grown into a meeting point for cinematographers from all around the world,” she notes.

The festival director is also a big supporter of promoting Mallorca as a shooting destination, as well as underscoring how great a location it is to host a film festival. “In the last decade, Mallorca has really boomed in terms of production,” she says. “It’s also a sanctuary for celebrities, which is not why I do the festival here, but it’s a helpful point in showing how accessible the island is from all over the world. We are very well-connected and in a very desirable place in the south of the Mediterranean. It’s very similar climate-wise to Los Angeles, and that’s how the industry started in LA, because the climate was so perfect.”

“People just love to come,” she adds. “The island has amazing infrastructure in terms of hotels, production companies, equipment… You can find everything here. I think it’s time to give it more of a push to show that to people. We have an event called Mallorca Go, which happens on the last weekend of the festival, where we take the visiting producers and filmmakers somewhere on the island. This year we are taking them to Calvià, a municipality in the southwest that has proclaimed this year to be its year of cinema and is inviting more film shoots. We want the island to be a thriving film destination.”

title: ‘Goodbye Julia’ Director on Reaching for ‘Wider Audiences’ in Sudanese Period Drama ‘About Love & September Laws’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Sudanese filmmaker Mohamed Kordofani, whose debut feature “Goodbye Julia” premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard sidebar, has attracted a raft of partners for his follow-up “About Love & September Laws,” which he’ll be taking to Rome’s MIA Market, running from Oct. 19-23. Produced by Klozium Studios, the production outfit he launched in 2020 with “Goodbye […]
content:
Sudanese filmmaker Mohamed Kordofani, whose debut feature “Goodbye Julia” premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard sidebar, has attracted a raft of partners for his follow-up “About Love & September Laws,” which he’ll be taking to Rome’s MIA Market, running from Oct. 19-23.

Produced by Klozium Studios, the production outfit he launched in 2020 with “Goodbye Julia” co-producer Khalid Awad, the film will reunite the core creative team behind Kordofani’s acclaimed debut, including co-producers Marc Irmer, of France’s Dolce Vita; Michael Henrichs, of German production company DGS; and Issraa Elkogali, of Sweden’s RiverFlower. Also on board are “Goodbye Julia” cinematographer Pierre De Villiers, editor Heba Osman, sound designer Rana Eid and co-writer Khaled Alwaleed.

“About Love & September Laws” is the second installment in a planned trilogy that tells the modern history of Sudan. Set in 1983, it follows an African American journalist, Carter, who arrives in Khartoum on a mission to revive a struggling newspaper. There he reunites with Nouri, an old friend he hasn’t seen in 10 years, now an idealistic doctor who serves as an ideological counterpoint to the jaded reporter.

Popular on Variety

Things grow complicated when Carter falls for Fatin, his newly hired translator, unaware that she is Nouri’s ex-wife. The fragile romance collides with the sudden weight of politics when Sharia law is imposed across Sudan, and Nouri finds himself facing the death sentence when he refuses a court order to amputate a thief’s hand.

When Carter uncovers a story that could expose the regime’s hypocrisy and save Nouri’s life, he’s forced to choose between the career he came to rebuild, the friendship that gave him a home in Sudan and a love he is only beginning to realize he can’t afford to lose.

Speaking to Variety ahead of MIA, Kordofani explains that while “About Love & September Laws” is set against the backdrop of a pivotal moment in Sudanese history, at its core “it’s a story about three people who are entangled in different kinds of love.”

The director’s groundbreaking debut was the first Sudanese feature to make the official selection at the Cannes Film Festival. Executive produced by Academy Award winner Lupita N’yongo, the film won the Un Certain Regard section’s Freedom Prize along with 65 other international plaudits, including audience awards at El Gouna and Singapore. In a rave review, Variety’s Jessica Kiang praised the “engrossing” drama as a “well-performed deep cut into Sudan’s recent history [that] unfolds like a morality thriller.”

As with “Goodbye Julia,” which takes place in Khartoum during the six years prior to the 2011 secession of South Sudan, Kordofani’s latest again looks to “bridge the personal and the political, the local and the global, the past and the present,” he says. However, after his first feature struggled to break into the U.S. and U.K. markets, the director says he’s determined to “reach even wider audiences.”

“Even before ‘Goodbye Julia,’ I’ve always wanted to make films that are for the mainstream but still hold artistic value, educational value — [sharing] something about my country that people don’t know,” he says. “I still want to do the things I want to do, but I want to make the film more accessible. The wider the reach, the better.”

“Goodbye Julia” won the Freedom Prize in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard

Last December, “About Love & September Laws” scooped a trio of prizes at the Red Sea Film Festival’s industry Souk Awards. In Rome, where it’s among the 12 projects taking part in MIA’s Film Co-Production Market, Kordofani said he’s particularly “looking for partners that can [build a] bridge to the United States.”

“It’s a film with an American lead. It’s predominantly English. I think, in the development stage, I should start building these bridges, not only for casting but also for the journey of the film and presenting the film [to a U.S. audience],” he says.

Central to that will be the lead role of Carter, a former Black Panther and disillusioned reporter who’s “lost faith in bigger causes and bigger movements,” says Kordofani. Opposite him is Nouri, the idealistic doctor, whose refusal to enforce a Sharia court order puts his life in jeopardy. “There’s this clash of personalities,” says the director, characterizing the film as a “moral drama” where “slowly, the politics will seep into their story and guide how the story unfolds.”

A winner of Variety’s MENA Talent of the Year Award in 2023, Kordofani is among the many Sudanese who were forced to flee the country amid the ongoing war. Now based in Nairobi, where he and Awad have established their production shingle Klozium Studios, he nevertheless feels an obligation to his homeland, saying, “I do feel a responsibility to talk about Sudan.”

“Living apart from my family, I continue to…search for purpose through filmmaking,” he says. “And especially now, as war rages on, I feel an urgent responsibility to preserve and create our own narrative — before it is stolen, silenced or rewritten by others.”

“About Love & September Laws,” he adds, offers “a platform to engage directly with the Western world, not as an outsider telling Sudan’s story, but as someone inviting them into a shared conversation about freedom, sacrifice, love and truth-seeking.”

title: ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Director Muhammad Mustapha Talks Masculinity Ahead of El Gouna Premiere: ‘The Only Emotion Men Are Allowed to Express Is Anger’
summary: Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how men understand and perform masculinity. The documentary, which had its world premiere in the Feature Documentary Competition at Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival, grew out of Mustapha’s curiosity about this particular group of […]
content:
Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how men understand and perform masculinity.

The documentary, which had its world premiere in the Feature Documentary Competition at Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival, grew out of Mustapha’s curiosity about this particular group of men and questions about his own understanding of masculinity.

“I’m a feminist. I’m intellectual. I find myself very drawn to this hyper-masculine performance,” he tells Variety. “I should know better, right? And so this was the question: Why am I so intrigued?”

Popular on Variety

Mustapha distinguishes that curiosity from a desire to investigate something he saw as inherently wrong. When he began the project in 2016, he approached it as an anthropological and sociological study of masculinity and how it is expressed in different contexts.

His own upbringing gave him a point of reference. Mustapha grew up in what he describes as a “local” Cairo neighborhood, where he was surrounded by its masculine codes. As a studious “nerd,” he could be seen as less masculine there. But when he entered dental school, the same behavior could instead make him appear loud or vulgar.

That contrast helped him recognize how masculinity could shift according to context, a fact he also saw among the men he was observing.

“How they perform their masculinity on stage is different than in front of the pub, is different than when he is addressing a problem, different than when he is with his family,” he says.

It took roughly three years for that initial exploration to develop into a film, as Mustapha’s relationship with the men deepened and he was forced to examine his own views of masculinity.

That relationship also informed how “Big Boys Don’t Cry” was made. Mustapha rejects the idea that documentary filmmaking can ever be entirely observational, arguing that a camera inevitably changes what happens in front of it. The men became collaborators, at times proposing situations themselves.

“I wouldn’t say I made this film alone. I would say I made it with the characters. We made it together.”

One of the film’s central figures is Abdallah, with whom Mustapha spent a year before filming began. Mustapha initially believed the film would be driven by its ideas about masculinity, only to discover in the edit that their friendship had become its emotional throughline.

Muhammad Mustapha Courtesy of Hassala Films

“I thought there was no emotional arc in the film. It was very theme-driven, and it was very intellectual,” he recalls. “At the end, while we were editing, I discovered that the emotional core of the film is actually our friendship.”

Building that relationship also meant giving the men control over what they shared. Participants could ask for material to be removed throughout the process, including during the final edit.

“I earned their trust. It was not given to me,” he affirms.

The absence of women is equally intentional. Mustapha wanted to observe the men in an exclusively male environment, which he compares to peeking into a gym locker room. Introducing women, he believed, would “change the equation.”

For Mustapha, the questions at the heart of “Big Boys Don’t Cry” extend far beyond Egypt. While masculinity takes different forms across cultures, he sees restrictions on men’s emotional expression as painfully universal.

“The only emotion men are allowed to express is anger,” he argues. “Imagine how distorted the male psyche is because of all this suppression of emotions.”

The El Gouna premiere brings “Big Boys Don’t Cry” back to a major stop in its development. Mustapha brought the project to CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm, in 2020 before it went on to receive support from the Doha Film Institute, Red Sea Film Fund and Germany’s Robert Bosch Foundation.

“It’s a full circle moment,” he reflects. “I’m very excited to show it to people in Egypt, though I’m slightly nervous.”

The film’s decade-long development has also led Mustapha to reflect on how independent films are made in Egypt and the region. He wants filmmakers to take more artistic risks and focus on local audiences rather than on the whims of international festivals and programmers.

“We need to work with less budget, with less financial risk, and more artistic risks.”

And above all: “Tell our stories to our audience.”

title: British Council’s Film Lab Africa Previews ‘TABOO’ Anthology Series At London Screening
summary: Film Lab Africa, the British Council’s film and TV accelerator programme in Nigeria, hosted a preview screening of TABOO, a new seven-part Nigerian anthology series, during the London Film Festival. The preview screening was held at EbonyLife Place London, a new African arts and cultural centre in south-west London. Comprising seven 20-minute episodes, TABOO is […]
content:
Film Lab Africa, the British Council’s film and TV accelerator programme in Nigeria, hosted a preview screening of TABOO, a new seven-part Nigerian anthology series, during the London Film Festival.

The preview screening was held at EbonyLife Place London, a new African arts and cultural centre in south-west London. Comprising seven 20-minute episodes, TABOO is said to explore “cultural beliefs, societal expectations and contemporary African experiences.” The anthology addresses themes such as identity, tradition, gender, family and mental health.

The seven Nigerian producers presented teasers of their films to UK film industry professionals, including distributors, sales agents, production companies and talent reps. The event was held in collaboration with T A P E Collective.

The seven productions are:

Watch on Deadline

They Will Teach You Silence

Emmanuel ‘Story Priest’ Adejo

After her brother’s suicide leads to his body being denied burial rites and her mother’s subsequent mental collapse, Ejura, a young woman, must commit the ultimate cultural taboo – stealing and wearing a sacred masquerade costume – to bury her brother and save her mother, but at a devastating cost.

Where’s The Gizzard?

Aghogho ‘Tega’ Onobrakpeya

An Urhobo wife sparks outrage in her village when she allegedly eats the chicken gizzard reserved for the male head of the household, forcing her to confront a patriarchal tradition built on oppression and control.

Generation to Generation

Setemi Ayodele Oni

During the Ife-Modakeke conflict, one of Nigeria’s longest running intra-tribal wars, an orphaned teen militia who lures vulnerable runaways to their deaths forms an unexpected bond with two brothers from the rival community, forcing him to choose between saving them or saving himself.

àzén! (Witch)

Enimien Aziegbe

Branded a witch for his vitiligo, a father must decide to risk facing the community that rejects him or miss the most important moment of his beloved daughter’s life.

Omorogun

Odaro Ehide Eguavoen

Through the eyes of four-year-old Adedayo, a household taboo about wooden cooking utensils unmaking a boy leads him to wonder whether it can unmake a man.

Hysteria

Dimeji Ogunranti

When a Nigerian woman chooses to end her painful cycle of hereditary fibroids and miscarriages by seeking a hysterectomy, she becomes haunted by a choir quartet exposing the taboo of a woman rejecting motherhood until her body and mind become a battleground over who controls her future.

Something in The Blood

Sally Kenneth Dadzie

When a prominent imam’s youngest son begins showing signs of mental illness, the father’s refusal to seek medical help, choosing instead to blame demons and confine the boy to rigorous deliverance sessions, leads to the son’s death. Afterward, the father begins experiencing the same symptoms, trapped in a haunting he cannot escape.

title: Domingo Corral Urges Commissioners To Ditch Conservative Thinking Or Risk Missing Next ‘La Bola Negra’: “You Cannot Reject The Other Way”
summary: Those holding the purse strings in Spanish film and TV must not “reject” ambitious projects or they could miss the next La Bola Negra or Sîrat, according to the influential former content chief at Movistar Plus+. Domingo Corral whipped a partisan audience into something of a frenzy at the MIA Market in Rome yesterday when […]
content:
Those holding the purse strings in Spanish film and TV must not “reject” ambitious projects or they could miss the next La Bola Negra or Sîrat, according to the influential former content chief at Movistar Plus+.

Domingo Corral whipped a partisan audience into something of a frenzy at the MIA Market in Rome yesterday when he passionately called on TV and film commissioners to do away with safety-first tendencies and embrace the spirit that he attempted to install at Movistar Plus+, the pay TV and streaming arm of Telefonica-owned Spanish telco Movistar.

Corral was joined on the MIA panel by Maria Zamora from Elastica Films, Belén Atienza from Suspense Entertainment and Fernando Bovaira from Mod Producciones, who all agreed that recent upticks at the Spanish box office could be attributed to ambitious but mainstream movies.

“Formulaic, conservative proposals will always be there, but you cannot reject the other way,” said Corral. Bovaira, who has produced films such as Agora and Vanilla Sky, added: “We need commissioners who are willing to go the casino and gamble.”

Watch on Deadline

Recalling his strategy during his 11-year spell at Movistar, Corral added: “If there was ambition with the producer, we had to make sure the vision became a reality. We wanted vision and passion for something original, and the role of the commissioner was key. As an independent producer now, if you don’t have a strong commissioner who promotes the strategy, it’s very difficult.”

Corral and his team were axed from Movistar Plus+ last year, prompting an outcry from the creative community, who saw his outlook as the main preserve of ambitious but popular storytelling. His track record included La Bola Negra, which has just released in four screens in the U.S. to $278,000 ahead of its streaming launch.

Corral also greenlit Cannes title Sîrat from Oliver Laxe, Los Tigres from Alberto Rodríguez, Alauda Ruiz de Azúa’s Los Domingos, and Cinco Minutos Más, starring and written by Berto Romero and helmed by Javier Ruiz Calder.

Soon after news of his axing got out, Around 150 creatives, heavyweights Pedro Almodóvar, Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruzan, signed an open letter thanking Corral and his team for championing high-end original film and TV and asking for those efforts to continue and standards be maintained.

Movistar Plus+’s Head of Original Films & Spanish Cinema, Guillermo Farré, later told Deadline he was committed to staying the course on original Spanish films, but not everyone is convinced yet.

During the MIA panel, Zamora from Elastica, which is selling La Bola Negra, said: “When you want to make authors grow with you, it’s difficult to raise the funding you need for them to really perform internationally. We don’t know if Movistar will keep doing it. We hope they will.”

Corral was keen to push the concept of ‘quality mainstream,’ which is predicated on the idea that ambitious concepts will attract audiences on the strength of the content.

“When I was at Movistar Plus our obsession was how to be and how to stay relevant in a context where there are so many films and series that get made,” he said. “If you follow the algorithm it’s a surefire way of not being relevant, in my opinion.

“The strategy we followed may not work for everyone but it worked for us. We had three films in Cannes in three years, and we had the support of the entire industry and without the producers we could not have done it.”

Corral has since struck a production deal with HBO Max, and this week told Deadline why he believes his vision of ambition production aligns with that of Sarah Aubrey and Casey Bloys at the top of the merger Skydance commissioning tree. The debut show from the pact, about the disappearance of Spanish petty criminal El Nani, remains in development, Corral confirmed.

The MIA Market in Rome runs through Friday.

title: Ex-MTV Worker Didn’t Report Alleged Russell Brand Rape Because “Media Industry Protects Its Own”
summary: Editor’s note: This story contains details of alleged sexual offenses that some readers may find distressing. A former MTV employee has said she didn’t initially report her allegation of rape against Russell Brand because she feared being “seen as trouble.” Giving evidence at Brand’s trial at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, the woman alleged […]
content:
Editor’s note: This story contains details of alleged sexual offenses that some readers may find distressing.

A former MTV employee has said she didn’t initially report her allegation of rape against Russell Brand because she feared being “seen as trouble.”

Giving evidence at Brand’s trial at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Monday, the woman alleged that she was orally raped by the Despicable Me star in July 2004 when attending the birthday party of a TV producer. Brand denies all charges and has pleaded not guilty.

The woman, whom we are calling Complainant 3 (C3) because she has a lifelong right to anonymity, claimed that Brand dragged her into the toilet of Soho’s Nordic Bar and forced his penis into her mouth. She further alleged that Brand grabbed her breasts while chatting to her at the bar.

Watch on Deadline

Under cross-examination from Brand’s barrister, C3 was grilled about why she did not report the alleged rape until 2023, when she became aware of The Times of London and Channel 4’s investigation into Brand’s conduct around women.

C3, who gave evidence from behind a screen so Brand could not see her in the courtroom, said she feared that filing a police complaint about the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star in 2004 could have led to her being “seen as trouble” in the TV industry.

When Ian Winter KC asked whether she was concerned for her job, she replied that the “media industry protects its own,” but stressed that her employment was “way down my list of concerns” at the time. Earlier, she said: “I wanted to change the narrative, so I wasn’t the victim.”

Winter, Brand’s barrister, pressed C3 on why she did not report the star to MTV. C3 replied that Brand was not employed by the now-Skydance-owned network when the alleged rape occurred. At the time of the incident, Brand was hosting Channel 4 show Big Brother’s EFourum, later renamed Big Brother’s Big Mouth.

Her testimony echoed evidence from another woman, Complainant 2 (C2), who also worked at MTV in the noughties and did not complain about her interaction with Brand in 2001. C2 — who has never met C3 — alleged that Brand attempted to pull her into the restroom at MTV’s offices and had a “desperate, wild-eyed look.”

C2 told Southwark Crown Court last week: “I spoke to colleagues but never mentioned it to employers because I was scared, and I had got away. I thought it would be my word against his. He is a big asset [for MTV] and I just work there, and I’ve got a mortgage to pay, so what is the point in making life hard for myself.”

C3 claimed that she phoned the TV producer “a couple of days” after the alleged toilet incident at his birthday party and warned him that Brand was a “sexual predator” who attempted to sexually assault her. She stopped short of alleging she was orally raped, however.

In a witness statement to the police in 2023, the producer recalled the 2004 phone call. He said C3 told him that Brand got “pushy,” “aggressive,” and that she was “scared.” The producer alleged that he “made contact” with Brand’s associates and told them his behavior was “not acceptable,” according to the statement, which was read out in court by prosecution barrister Riel Karmy-Jones.

During cross-examination, Brand’s barrister repeatedly insisted that the toilet incident was consensual and that C3 was a willing participant. C3, who became audibly emotional during her testimony, denied that it was consensual.

Brand faces three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of indecent assault based on allegations made by six women. Brand will set out his defense later in the trial.

The court was told repeatedly that Brand declined to answer questions when interviewed by police. He instead relied on a prepared statement, in which he claimed that he did not recall meeting the women and did not remember their names. He said any sexual contact was consensual.

The trial continues.

Max Goldbart contributed to this report

title: Former A24 Docs Chief Joins ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger’ Outfit Magna Studios
summary: Former A24 docs chief Nicole Stott has joined Magna Studios, the production outfit behind Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger. Stott becomes an executive producer in Magna’s non-fiction division and will collaborate closely with SVP, Non-Fiction, Oliver Calleja, Creative Director Louis Mole, and the wider team across Magna’s documentary features and limited series. A24 shuttered […]
content:
Former A24 docs chief Nicole Stott has joined Magna Studios, the production outfit behind Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Stott becomes an executive producer in Magna’s non-fiction division and will collaborate closely with SVP, Non-Fiction, Oliver Calleja, Creative Director Louis Mole, and the wider team across Magna’s documentary features and limited series.

A24 shuttered its documentary hub last year but prior to this Stott had been division head, working across the likes of The Yogurt Shop Murders and Sundance Grand Jury Prize-winner Nuisance Bear. A24 was in production on smash Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything at the time, although she didn’t work directly across the movie. She is a former co-head of non fiction at Concordia Studio and headed up London’s Passion Pictures docs for a decade.

Magna Studios is run by former Pulse Films execs Marisa Clifford and Davud Karbassioun, and is owned by Lumina Media, the next-gen company founded by Pulse founder Thomas Benski.

Watch on Deadline

It has made the likes of Disney+’s Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, Sky’s The Pembrokeshire Murders and the upcoming Lily Allen feature for Prime Video.

Clifford said: “Nicole is a perfect fit for the world-class team we’ve assembled here at Magna. Her outstanding body of work and creative vision make her an invaluable asset as we push boundaries and scale our studio globally.”

title: Banijay Entertainment Confirms Post-Merger Leadership Structure
summary: The newly-minted Banijay Entertainment has set out its senior leadership team following the merger with All3Media. The Survivor and The Traitors company had already installed RedBird IMI CEO Jeff Zucker as Chairman, Marco Bassetti as CEO and Jane Turton as Deputy CEO, and today confirmed the next tier of management in an internal note to […]
content:
The newly-minted Banijay Entertainment has set out its senior leadership team following the merger with All3Media.

The Survivor and The Traitors company had already installed RedBird IMI CEO Jeff Zucker as Chairman, Marco Bassetti as CEO and Jane Turton as Deputy CEO, and today confirmed the next tier of management in an internal note to staff seen by Deadline.

There are no major surprises among the execs, who all report into Bassetti. Fred Balmary becomes Chief Business Officer; Nicolas Chazarain is Chief Legal Officer; Thomas Gousset is Chief Finance Officer; Lucas Green becomes Chief Content Officer, Operations; Kate Humphreys is Chief Communications Officer; James Townley is named Chief Content Officer, Development; and Anne Van Sprang is Chief Human Resources Officer.

There have been several major personnel changes since All3 owner RedBird IMI and Banijay Group merged their entertainment assets to form the $8B behemoth Banijay Entertainment. Primarily impacted have been execs on the distribution side, where Cathy Payne is CEO of Banijay Rights. All3 group COO Sara Geater also exited in the wake of the merger.

Watch on Deadline

In his note to staff, Bassetti wrote: “Since their appointments, this group has made a significant contribution to the business, with many playing an integral role in delivering the merger and advancing the current integration – please join me in congratulating them as we embark on this next chapter.”

He added that Turton, Balmary, Chazarain, Gousset, Van Sprang and Payne were also joining the Banijay executive team. “We will formally introduce the team across the business as the integration progresses. In the meantime, we appreciate your patience as we continue through this period of change,” he added.

The news comes a week Banijay unveiled its supercharged business to the international market at MIPCOM Cannes last week, with Zucker and Bassetti taking to the stage to set out their plans. A push into U.S. scripted appears likely, along with more European co-productions and further entertainment launches.

title: Patrick Dempsey Signs With Gersh (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Patrick Dempsey has signed with Gersh for representation. The Emmy and Golden Globe Award-nominated actor is a big get for the company, which is the fourth largest talent and literary agency in the world. Dempsey currently stars in and executive produces the Fox series “Memory of a Killer,” which streams on Hulu. Season 2 of […]
content:
Patrick Dempsey has signed with Gersh for representation.

The Emmy and Golden Globe Award-nominated actor is a big get for the company, which is the fourth largest talent and literary agency in the world.

Dempsey currently stars in and executive produces the Fox series “Memory of a Killer,” which streams on Hulu. Season 2 of the drama is currently in production in Toronto, with filming expected to wrap at the end of the year.

Dempsey is, of course, best known for his portrayal of Dr. Derek Shepherd aka “McDreamy” on ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy,” which earned him two Golden Globe nominations and a Screen Actors Guild Award as part of the ensemble cast. Dempsey appeared in 262 episodes across 12 seasons of the medical procedural, leaving midway through Season 11 in 2014 and then coming back for a run of episodes six years later, in Season 17.

Popular on Variety

Dempsey, he himself a race car driver, also starred in Michael Mann’s biopic “Ferrari” opposite Adam Driver and Penélope Cruz, as well as Eli Roth’s “Thanksgiving.” He is also known for his romantic lead turn opposite Amy Adams in 2007’s “Enchanted,” and he reprised the role in the 2022 sequel, “Disenchanted.”

On the small screen, Dempsey recently starred as Captain Aaron Spencer in “Dexter: Original Sin.” His additional television credits include the international drama series “Devils” and the limited series “The Truth About the Harry Quebert Affair.”

Dempsey first rose to prominence with “Can’t Buy Me Love” and “Loverboy,” and his additional film credits include “Sweet Home Alabama,” “Made of Honor,” “Bridget Jones’s Baby,” “Transformers: Dark of the Moon,” “Valentine’s Day,” “Freedom Writers” and “Scream 3.”

In 2023, Dempsey was bestowed the great honor of People’s Sexiest Man Alive.

He continues to be represented by attorney Mitch Smelkinson.

title: The Beatles Immersive Experience, Featuring Sets and Props From Sam Mendes’ Biopics, Set for Liverpool
summary: Once the cameras stop rolling on Sam Mendes’ epic four-part biopic series about the members of the Beatles, many of the sets and props are going to have a new life celebrating the band in their native home. A 100,000 sq. ft Beatles experience has been announced for Liverpool, moving the existing The Beatles Story […]
content:
Once the cameras stop rolling on Sam Mendes‘ epic four-part biopic series about the members of the Beatles, many of the sets and props are going to have a new life celebrating the band in their native home.

A 100,000 sq. ft Beatles experience has been announced for Liverpool, moving the existing The Beatles Story to a new location in the heart of the city more than four times the size of its current site in Albert Docks.

The experience will take fans from the bands’ post-war childhoods in Liverpool through Hamburg, The Cavern, Beatlemania, Abbey Road, Shea Stadium, Savile Row and beyond. A number of these immersive locations will be created using sets and props from “The Beatles: A Four-Film Cinematic Event.”

Popular on Variety

Capitalizing on the noise from the movies, the experience is due to open in 2028, shortly after their release worldwide by Sony Pictures in April of the same year (current reported plans have the four films releasing simultaneously).

‘Filming recently in Liverpool for our four Beatles movies brought home just how extraordinary the band’s legacy in the city is,” said Mendes. “Their imprint can be felt everywhere. It’s particularly fitting that this new Beatles experience will be helping to support the next generation of talent coming from this extraordinary city.”

The ambitious plan was announced by Apple Corps, the company founded in 1968 to oversee the Beatles’ creative and business interests, and will mark the first official fan experience to be operated in Liverpool by the company. Apple Corps will take over running of the current The Beatles Story in 2027, before moving to the attraction to the new site in 2028. It will also take over Liverpool’s 400ft St Johns Beacon tower for the Yellow Submarine experience.

“I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it’s very exciting to me that The Beatles Story and The Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city,” said Paul McCartney. “I love Liverpool. It’s part of who I am, it’s part of who The Beatles are. If you’d told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started we’d never have believed it. The extraordinary plans the Apple Corps team have shown me for The Beatles Story take me right back to that journey, from Liverpool to the world and back home again. It couldn’t have happened without Liverpool and I can’t wait for people to be able to step into our story and share the experience.”

The new Beatles Story in Liverpool will be only the second permanent Beatles experience ever operated by Apple Corps, following the forthcoming attraction at 3 Savile Row in London, which is due to open at the end of 2027.

Each film in “The Beatles: A Four-Film Cinematic Event” will be from the perspective of a different band member, and are being led by Paul Mescal as McCartney, Joseph Quinn as George Harrison, Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr and Harris Dickinson as John Lennon.

title: Atlanta Hawks Strike Streaming Alliance With Amazon’s Prime Video
summary: The Atlanta Hawks are just the latest sports team to figure out the best way for their games to stream. Local Hawks games will be made available to Prime Video subscribers across a five-state region starting in the 2026-2027 season, according to Andrew Saltzman, president of business enterprise and chief commercial officer of the Atlanta […]
content:
The Atlanta Hawks are just the latest sports team to figure out the best way for their games to stream.

Local Hawks games will be made available to Prime Video subscribers across a five-state region starting in the 2026-2027 season, according to Andrew Saltzman, president of business enterprise and chief commercial officer of the Atlanta Hawks and State Farm Arena. Prime Video will make all broadcasts that are not exclusive to national outlets available in Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, South Carolina, and Mississippi — at no additional cost.

“Getting maximum reach was paramount in our decision making,” says Saltzman, during a recent interview,

Popular on Variety

The Hawks were just one of 13 NBA teams forced to dribble in a new direction following the bankruptcy of Main Street Sports Group, the regional-sports media company that previously held regional Hawks rights, but could not overcome subscriber losses to stay solvent. In July, the Hawks struck a deal for over-the-air broadcast of its in-market games with Gray Media that will have all non-nationally televised regular-season games air on WANF and the Peachtree Sports Network.

Under terms of the deals, the Hawks are scheduled to air 74 games on over-the-air television or stream via Prime Video. The games are produced by Gray’s Raycom Sports.

All the NBA teams that relied on Main Street Sports “had different decisions to make, had unique scenarios,” says Saltzman. The alliance with Amazon will have Hawks games available for viewing in cities likes Nashville, Charlotte and Charleston. “It gives us arguably one of the largest footprints,” he says.

The Hawks begin the 2026-27 regular season on Wednesday, Oct. 21 at the Orlando Magic.

“Exclusively streaming the Atlanta Hawks as part of our growing local sports portfolio is another step forward in providing fans an easy, one-stop destination to watch the teams they love,” said Charlie Neiman, head of sports partnerships for Prime Video, in a prepared statement. “The Hawks have demonstrated a forward-thinking approach to reaching and engaging their fans and share the same commitment to innovation that drives our organization. Together, we’re making it easier than ever for fans across the Southeast to watch their team.”

title: U2 to Play Halftime Show for NFL’s Thanksgiving Eve Game in What League Calls ‘a New NFL Holiday Tradition’
summary: Although Thanksgiving Eve has not yet been recognized by everyone as a holiday in its own right, the National Football League is instituting what it calls “a new NFL holiday tradition” — a halftime performance by a major musical act for the game streaming on Netflix the night before turkey day. The artist selected for […]
content:
Although Thanksgiving Eve has not yet been recognized by everyone as a holiday in its own right, the National Football League is instituting what it calls “a new NFL holiday tradition” — a halftime performance by a major musical act for the game streaming on Netflix the night before turkey day. The artist selected for this year’s inaugural halftime blowout: U2.

Being Irish, the members of U2 will probably not be expected to be back in Dublin for any family Thanksgiving dinners, which will make it all the easier for them to be on the 50-yard line at SoFi Stadium on Nov. 25. The Los Angeles-area stadium will be the site of a matchup between the hometown Rams and the Green Bay Packers, with kickoff scheduled for 5 p.m. PT/8 p.m. ET.

U2, of course, has some halftime experience on its resume, having performed at the Super Bowl in February 2002.

Popular on Variety

This NFL performance will follow shortly after the release of the band’s first album of new material in nine years, “Carnaval De Luz.”

The NFL and Netflix have already been looking to make a bigger deal out of non-Super Bowl halftime shows, putting on Christmas Day halftime shows the previous two years. The 2025 performance, billed as Snoop’s Holiday Halftime Party, featured Snoop Dogg, Lainey Wilson, Huntr/X and Andrea Bocelli participating in a Dec. 25, 2025 show at Minneapolis’ U.S. Bank Stadium. The previous year, it was Beyoncé on the big day for the “Beyoncé Bowl.” No plans for a 2026 Christmas halftime show have yet been announced.

Jesse Collins Entertainment is producing the U2 halftime show for Netflix and the NFL.

“There’s a reason U2 has headlined stadiums for decades: they don’t just perform, they deliver iconic moments audiences remember forever,” said Ted Sarandos, co-CEO of Netflix, in a statement. “We’re thrilled that they’ll bring that same magic to the NFL stage on Netflix. It’s going to be an unforgettable night for football fans and Netflix members worldwide.”

After winning the NBA Finals for the first time in 53 years back in June, the New York Knicks are at the top of the pro basketball league. With so many storylines, drama on and off the court and high championship expectations for all 30 leagues in the league, the 2026-27 NBA season officially tips off with a triple-header in Detroit, New York City and San Antonio.

Starting on Tuesday, Oct. 20, the season is tips off with an exciting start, as the Boston Celtics taking on the Detroit Pistons at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit at 3 p.m. ET/12 p.m. PT, followed by the Philadelphia 76ers vs. the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Manhattan at 7 p.m. ET/4 p.m. PT. All three of Tuesday’s games broadcast exclusively on NBC and livestream on Peacock, with a variety of ways to stream the action live online without cable.

When Does the 2026-27 NBA Season Begin?

The NBA season officially tips off on Tuesday, Oct. 20 with games scheduled until the NBA Finals in June 2027.

How to Watch the 2026-27 NBA on TV

Regular season game coverage is split across four networks: NBC, NBA TV, ESPN and ABC. If you don’t have cable, there are still plenty of ways stream the game live online on streamers such as DirecTV, Sling TV, Hulu+ Live TV and others.

If ratings are any indicator of success for the league, the NBA Finals between the San Antonio Spurs, led by French superstar Victor Wembanyama, and New York Knicks, led by the King of New York Jalen Brunson, drew in an average of more than 20 million viewers per game for ABC and ESPN.
