content:
Amazon MGM Studios is revamping its film division, with Julie Rapaport and Alana Mayo each being tapped as as Head of Film, Production & Development.

Both will report to Courtenay Valenti, Head of Film, Streaming and Theatrical at Amazon MGM. Valenti revealed the restructuring Tuesday and sent a note to staff.

“Julie and Alana will each oversee approximately half of our film slate — spanning all genres across theatrical and streaming — with each managing roughly 15 films per year,” she wrote. “It’s important to note that we are not creating separate pods or siloed teams, as our senior production & development team members will all work with both Julie and Alana across the entire slate, regardless of specific reporting lines.”

Read her full memo below.

Watch on Deadline

Valenti said Mayo will continue continue to lead Orion Pictures, which she has overseen since 2020. Rapaport has been with Amazon since 2015 and most recently was had the title of Head of Film, Production & Development.

Here is the memo.

title: Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Prestige’ Sets 20th Anniversary Re-Release For 2027
summary: Christopher Nolan’s thriller The Prestige will to return theaters on January 29, 2027, in celebration of the film’s 20th anniversary. Walt Disney Studios will re-release the film that stars Hugh Jackman, Christian Bale, Michael Caine and Scarlett Johansson, and features the late David Bowie as physicist Nikola Tesla. The re-release will give audiences the chance […]
content:
Christopher Nolan’s thriller The Prestige will to return theaters on January 29, 2027, in celebration of the film’s 20th anniversary.

Walt Disney Studios will re-release the film that stars Hugh Jackman, Christian Bale, Michael Caine and Scarlett Johansson, and features the late David Bowie as physicist Nikola Tesla.

The re-release will give audiences the chance to see the film on 70mm and IMAX for the first time, and it will also be presented in 35mm and Digital 2D formats.

See a new teaser trailer above and new poster art below.

Today’s announcement comes 20 years to the day after the film’s original release in U.S. theaters on October 20, 2006. The film earned two Academy Award nominations, for Best Cinematography and Best Art Direction.

Watch on Deadline

“I’m very excited to bring The Prestige back to the big screen,” said Nolan, whose most recent film is The Odyssey, “and particularly thrilled to offer audiences the chance to see it on 70mm film, and on IMAX for the first time.”

The film’s official synopsis describes it as a “twisting, turning story that, like all great magic tricks, stays with you long after the final reveal.”

“Robert Angier (Jackman), a charismatic showman, and Alfred Borden (Bale), a gifted illusionist, are two young, passionate magicians – friends and partners until one fateful night when their biggest trick goes terribly wrong. Now the bitterest of enemies, they will stop at nothing to learn each other’s secrets. As their rivalry escalates into a total obsession full of deceit and sabotage, they risk everything to become the greatest magician of all time. But nothing is as it seems, so watch closely.”

The Prestige is directed by Christopher Nolan from a screenplay by Jonathan Nolan and Christopher Nolan, based on the novel by Christopher Priest. The film was produced by Emma Thomas, Aaron Ryder and Christopher Nolan.

title: Costume Designer Sandy Powell to Present Film London Jarman Award – Film News in Brief
summary: Oscar-winning costume designer Sandy Powell is set to present this year’s Film London Jarman Award on Nov. 24, where she will also be the guest of honor. Powell frequently collaborated and was mentored by Derek Jarman, whom the award was established in honor of in 2008 to celebrate U.K.-based artist-filmmakers in the film industry. Throughout […]
content:
Oscar-winning costume designer Sandy Powell is set to present this year’s Film London Jarman Award on Nov. 24, where she will also be the guest of honor.

Powell frequently collaborated and was mentored by Derek Jarman, whom the award was established in honor of in 2008 to celebrate U.K.-based artist-filmmakers in the film industry. Throughout her career, Powell has also worked with Martin Scorsese, Neil Jordan, Todd Haynes and Yorgos Lanthimos.

“Sandy’s remarkable career speaks to a truly remarkable talent. From her days collaborating with Derek Jarman on films like ‘Caravaggio’ and ‘Edward II’ to the peerless design she has brought to a staggering array of modern classics, her work is bold, beautiful and boundlessly creative,” said Adrian Wootton, OBE, the chief executive of Film London. “She has long been vocal in her support of Derek’s cultural legacy, and, as such, I don’t think we could ask for a more fitting guest of honor for this year’s Film London Jarman Award.”

Popular on Variety

Also working on “Cinderella,” “The Wolf of Wall Street” and “Mary Poppins Returns,” Powell received the Academy Award for Best Costume Design for “Shakespeare in Love,” “The Aviator” and “The Young Victoria.” This year’s Film London Jarman Award nominees are Sadia Pineda Hameed, Ilona Sagar, Rhea Storr and Alia Syed.

Tuesday, October 20

Molly Shannon Joins “Summer 2000: The X-Cetra Story” as Executive Producer

Molly Shannon has joined “Summer 2000: The X-Cetra Story” as an executive producer before the film’s Los Angeles premiere at the AFI Fest on Oct. 24.

After the screening, the Emmy-nominated actress and bestselling author will moderate a Q&A with director, writer and producer Ayden Mayeri, writer, producer and cinematographer Barry Rothbart, producer Rachael Fung and subjects Janet Kariuki, Mary Washburn, Jessica Hall and Robin O’Brien.

“Summer 2000: The X-Cetra Story” follows a group of friends as they reunite when the album they made as pre-teens becomes a cult online hit 20 years later.

“I was so deeply moved by this beautiful film and its reminder of how easy it is to lose track of that free-spirited, dreaming little girl inside all of us,” Shannon said. “It’s a wonderful reminder to keep making room for the things that bring us joy, no matter how much time has passed. I’m so excited to be part of this project and to help share X-Cetra’s story with audiences.”

The film made its world premiere at SXSW and won the Documentary Feature Jury Award. Since then, it has screened at the Sydney Film Festival, Melbourne International Film Festival and the Bentonville Film Festival. After AFI Fest, it will screen at DOC NYC.

title: ‘Princess Diaries’ Actor Erik von Detten Accused of Elder Abuse and Fraud in Gold Scheme
summary: Erik von Detten, the former Disney star known for his roles in “The Princess Diaries” and “Brink!” is facing a lawsuit alleging elder abuse and fraud after an elderly couple claimed he persuaded them to invest more than $2 million of their retirement savings in significantly overpriced gold coins. The lawsuit, filed in California in […]
content:
Erik von Detten, the former Disney star known for his roles in “The Princess Diaries” and “Brink!” is facing a lawsuit alleging elder abuse and fraud after an elderly couple claimed he persuaded them to invest more than $2 million of their retirement savings in significantly overpriced gold coins.

The lawsuit, filed in California in May, names von Detten, 44, and his employer, precious metals company Rosland Capital, as defendants. Sheila Greenberg, 85, and her husband, Norman Greenberg, 97, allege they lost approximately $900,000 after purchasing gold coins through the company.

Rosland Capital has ceased operations and declared bankruptcy in July, listing some $64 million in liabilities and just $500,000 in assets. According to filings in the bankruptcy case, the company has faced scrutiny from the New York Attorney General’s Office and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Popular on Variety

The creditors’ committee is seeking to subpoena Von Detten as it investigates the failure of the company, saying it appears he “played an instrumental part in the Debtor’s business and its financial collapse.”

“The Greenbergs’ story is not unique,” the creditors’ committee alleges. “It is one of hundreds. Creditors, including the other Committee members, have described remarkably similar experiences: trust cultivated, expertise professed, reliance encouraged, and substantial savings ultimately lost with zero information about where their money has gone.”

Rosland advertised on Fox News and Newsmax with spots starring actor William Devane, who pitched gold coins as a hedge against inflation and other sources of instability. Retirees were encouraged to convert their IRAs into gold-backed funds, and were offered “a free safe to store your gold.”

According to their lawsuit, the Greenbergs contacted Rosland Capital in 2020 after seeing an ad on TV. They were connected with von Detten, who had joined the company in 2018 after largely stepping away from acting.

The Greenbergs say they told von Detten they had limited knowledge of the gold market but approximately $2 million available in retirement savings. They allege that von Detten presented himself as an experienced adviser and encouraged them to purchase Lady Liberty gold coins as an investment.

Von Detten did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Rosland reported $151 million in revenues in 2021. But according to the company’s first-day filing in bankruptcy court, the company suffered “excessive cash outflows” and racked up net losses of $24 million from 2022-25. The rising cost of gold also put a strain on the company’s business, as it was unable to keep up with customer demand, resulting in a months-long backlog in orders.

“During this interval, the price of gold usually increased dramatically such that Debtor ended up paying more for the gold product than the customer paid Debtor for that product,” the company’s accountants reported. “This situation was not sustainable and the Debtor lost money rapidly.”

Sales reps were paid 15%-35% of the profit on each order, regardless of whether that order was later refunded. When the company ceased operations, there were about 470 messages and voicemails either demanding refunds or demanding delivery of gold products, according to the first-day motion.

The creditors’ committee, however, does not appear to believe that the business simply failed due to deteriorating market conditions.

“The Committee believes the facts point to something far more troubling: a business that preyed on a vulnerable population, stole customer money while its ability to perform was collapsing, lied to its own customers about what their money would be used for, and ultimately left creditors to ask whether those funds were misused, diverted, transferred to insiders or affiliates, or simply consumed to keep the scheme alive,” the committee’s attorneys wrote.

Von Detten was a familiar face in Disney productions throughout he late 1990s and early 2000s. He starred as the title character in the 1998 Disney original movie “Brink!” and played Josh Bryant, the love interest of Anne Hathaway’s Mia Thermopolis, in 2001’s “The Princess Diaries.”

He also voiced Sid Phillips, the toy-destroying neighbor in “Toy Story” and Erwin Lawson in Disney’s animated series “Recess.” His other credits include “Escape to Witch Mountain,” “So Weird” and “Complete Savages.”

Von Detten largely retired from acting around 2010, later transitioning into sales and financial services. He briefly reprised his role as Sid in “Toy Story 4.”

title: Music Industry Moves: Barbara Cane, BMI’s VP of Worldwide Creative, to Retire After Five Decades
summary: After a five-decade career with BMI, Barbara Cane has announced that she will retire from the company at the end of this year. While she is leaving her current role as BMI’s Vice President of Worldwide Creative, Cane has agreed to serve in an advisory capacity to BMI, working directly with CEO Mike O’Neill. “After […]
content:
After a five-decade career with BMI, Barbara Cane has announced that she will retire from the company at the end of this year. While she is leaving her current role as BMI’s Vice President of Worldwide Creative, Cane has agreed to serve in an advisory capacity to BMI, working directly with CEO Mike O’Neill.

“After more than five decades, BMI is not simply where I have built my career — it is part of who I am,” Cane said. “It gave me the opportunity to grow, to discover, and, most importantly, to uncover the soul within the songwriter. Through every chapter of my journey, I have come to understand that creativity is not simply a profession; it is the heart of who songwriters are and the force that moves our industry forward. What has made this journey so meaningful is that my own values remain deeply aligned with those of BMI – to believe in creators, to nurture their gifts, and to create an environment in which their careers can flourish. After fifty years, that purpose still lives in my heart—and it is why this work has never felt simply like a career, but like a calling.”

O’Neill added, “Barbara is one of the first people I met when I joined BMI almost 32 years ago, and her kindness, caring nature and warm welcome showed me exactly why she is so loved by so many in our industry. She has demonstrated that same care and attention time and again to the many songwriters she worked with, nurtured and supported, and it’s why her relationships in this industry have endured. While Barbara and I started out as colleagues, we’ve ended up as family, and I don’t know many who can say that about the people they work with. The beautiful thing for me is that Barbara has agreed to continue working with me as an advisor, allowing BMI and our writers to still have her insight and counsel, while also allowing her to enjoy some time away from us for the first time in fifty years.”

Popular on Variety

Cane began working at BMI part-time in 1970 while she was still in high school and has dedicated her entire professional career to the company. She held numerous roles throughout her tenure, starting in BMI’s “Song Research” department and holding a number of creative roles including General Manager of the Los Angeles office as well as Vice President of Creative in New York, Los Angeles and London, directing the creative activities for BMI’s Pop, Rock and Indie teams.

+ Electric Feel Publishing has signed songwriter and producer Naila to the company’s UK roster.

Naila is a London-based, multilingual writer, producer and multi-instrumentalist from Barcelona who has worked with Joel Compass, H.lls, P2J, Gabzy, Moon Willis, Rimon, BenjiFlow, Mahalia, AoD, Dinos, JJ and ColeYoursTruly, among others. She has worked closely with and developed Spanish artists Violeta, Paula Cendejas, Chiara Oliver and Olivia Bay, as well as French artist Anaïs Cardot.

“I am incredibly excited to become a part of the amazing team at Electric Feel, it’s a blessing to be surrounded by this amount of talent and skill and I cannot wait for the music and experience ahead with the EF family!” said Naila.

+ Warner Chappell Music Nashville has struck a global publishing deal with Kentucky-reared singer-songwriter Elizabeth Nichols, known for her breakout single, “I Got a New One.” She made her Grand Ole Opry debut last November and has performed at Stagecoach, Lollapalooza, C2C and CMC festivals and has opened for Little Big Town, Jason Aldean, Russell Dickerson, and Jordan Davis.

“I’m very excited to join Warner Chappell, where I can finally monetize my questionable taste in men. I have the best team in the world. Here’s to many more songs.”

Katy Wolaver, SVP, A&R, Warner Chappell Music, shared: “Elizabeth is a breath of fresh air… witty, clever, and unabashed in taking authentic life experiences and turning them into irresistible lyrics and melodies. Her songs embrace a wide range of moods and emotions, from unique takes on relationships to political satire. In just a short time on the country landscape, she’s moved her career into high gear, and all of us at Warner Chappell are delighted to join her on what is sure to be an incredible ride.”

+ Sony Music Publishing Nashville, in partnership with Taycan Entertainment, has signed rising songwriter and producer Jared Conrad to a worldwide publishing deal. Conrad has earned cuts with Cody Johnson, Lee Brice, Brothers Osborne, Ian Munsick, Randall King, Mitchell Tenpenny and Austin Snell, among many others. His credits also include co-writing Pentatonix and Meghan Trainor’s “Kid On Christmas” from Pentatonix’s Grammy-nominated album “Holidays Around the World.”

+ Columbia Records has announced the expanded role of Manos Xanthogeorgis as Executive Vice President, Creative & Digital, leading a newly formed creative team while continuing to oversee digital across the labe

In his expanded role, Xanthogeorgis will oversee creative and art direction, short- and long-form content, and the label’s digital functions, including audience development, viral marketing and social.

“What I love about music is that something deeply personal to an artist can become just as personal to someone they’ve never met. Finding new ways to help that happen is what keeps this work so exciting for me,” said Xanthogeorgis.

title: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win Best Picture at the Oscars
summary: The word disruptor is a vividly descriptive one, and it’s almost always applied to an individual. But it doesn’t have to be. Take the rule-busting, category-smashing, one-of-a-kind-because-you’ve-never-seen-anything-of-its-kind “You Can See Everything,” a movie that in one weekend has turned the movie landscape topsy-turvy. “You Can See Everything” is such an unprecedented cinematic wild card that […]
content:
The word disruptor is a vividly descriptive one, and it’s almost always applied to an individual. But it doesn’t have to be. Take the rule-busting, category-smashing, one-of-a-kind-because-you’ve-never-seen-anything-of-its-kind “You Can See Everything,” a movie that in one weekend has turned the movie landscape topsy-turvy.

“You Can See Everything” is such an unprecedented cinematic wild card that as you watch it, the very question of what it is makes the movie itself a disruptor. It’s a documentary…made by a prankish cringe comedian…about a notorious white-collar criminal…that plays as a piece of hangout-movie vérité…until the actress who played the white-collar criminal in a TV series actually shows up…at which point the psychodramatic circus is just getting started.

This past weekend, “You Can See Everything” made $15 million on 800 screens (complete with 2,000 sold-out shows). That made it the most successful opening for a non-music documentary since Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” 22 years ago. Yet even those numbers don’t tell the story of how “You Can See Everything” has injected itself into the cultural bloodstream — and is reconfiguring the movie world. People are rushing to see it almost as a kind of mission. Audiences are alive to it; the film is so full of revelation and new-paradigm entertainment value that people often say it exceeds their expectations. This, in a word, is everything a great movie should be: an experience unlike one you’ve had before, one that lures and enthralls you, and that leaves you feeling different when it’s over.

Popular on Variety

The film’s box-office numbers are likely to shoot up in its second weekend, when it expands to a full national release. And there’s every chance that the numbers could continue to go up for a week or two after that, the way they did with “Obsession.” The excitement that surrounds “You Can See Everything” rhymes with the out-of-the-box quality that drew people in hordes over the summer to see “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” This was a new kind of audience: a new demo, a new consciousness, a crystalization of the possibility that we might be on the cusp of a new “film generation.” That’s an old term (from the 1970s), one that desribed how the first generation to grow up with movies as their transcendent art form embraced them in a new way, like rock ‘n’ roll — not just as entertainment or even as art but as a fundamental expression of who they were.

Watching “You Can See Everything,” people see themselves reflected in the post-ironic deadpan of Nathan Fielder, who is 42 and represents, from his television shows, a novel mode of fucking with people that’s intricate in its cleverness yet bizarrely honest. Having his close-up conversations with Elizabeth Holmes, he’s wily and detached, but he’s also a straight-shooter, asking rigorous questions about what we want to know: how Holmes could have lied the way she did, and, if she claims (as she does throughout the film) that she wasn’t lying, how she could possibly believe that. The movie, in a sense, is a cosmic meditation on lying. (Holmes sounds as monomaniacal, and as hard to fathom, in her systematic delusions as Donald Trump.) I think the Elizabeth Holmes showcased in “You Can See Everything” is a quintessential example of the human being as corporate performer — she’s doing a dance of put-on earnestness, and her act is so good that Fielder meets his match in attempting to unmask it. The film is an almost dreamlike duel of egos.

By making a movie in which he and his directing partner, Lance Oppenheim, literally didn’t know where they were going, Nathan Fielder has given us a documentary drama that’s all about discovery. That’s what gives “You Can See Everything” its cathartic existential entertainment value. Like “Pulp Fiction,” it seems to be doing nothing less than reinventing what a movie can be. And the outpouring of adoration — and ticket sales — is already so undeniable that I think it’s all but certain that “You Can See Everything” will wind up being the first documentary to be nominated for best picture at the Oscars.

Here’s how that would work. Right now, the film is still forging its path, but I’d wager that it has a solid shot of being named best picture by one or more of the critics’ groups (the New York Film Critics Circle, the Los Angeles Film Critics Association, the National Board of Review, and so on). That would establish its credibility as a work of cinematic art. The Oscar voters aren’t beholden to the critics, but they often follow their lead. It’s been a long time, in fact, since these two pools of tastemakers existed in any true opposition. (I know more than one critic who thinks that it’s the job of year-end critics’ voting to move the needle on the Oscars.) Voting aside, the movie is sure to top many critics’ 10 Best lists, and by the time that happens it will likely have made $100 million at the box office. Its mainstream cultural status as one of the best pictures of the year will, at that point, be undeniable. And if and when it’s nominated for best picture, that will be a ground-shifting moment.

But here’s why I think “You Can See Everything” is also a serious contender to win. This is not an Oscar odds column, and I’m not going to try and parse the chances of “You Can See Everything” next to every film that’s been floated as a contender, from “La Bola Negra” to “Artificial” to “Project Hail Mary” to “I Play Rocky” to the yet-to-be-seen “Dune: Part Three.” But I will use “The Odyssey” as a front-running standard bearer.

In many quarters, “The Odyssey” has acquired an aura of inevitability. It’s the big-vision version of what movies can be, and at a casual glance it connected on every level: with the critics, at the box office, as a must-see cultural phenomenon. At the same time, I think it’s a vulnerable front-runner (in a way that the last Christopher Nolan Oscar movie, “Oppenheimer,” was not), because there are a great many people who are less than in love with it.

If “The Odyssey” wins, it will not be a surprise. It will feel very much like a traditional Oscar victory, the least disruptive one possible. But we are now in an era of disruption — and, quite strikingly, we’re in a year when disruption (from AI or wherever) isn’t just threatening the film industry. It’s looming up as one of the forces that could save it. By the time of Oscar night, “You Can See Everything” may have emerged as the year’s quintessential example of what a movie can be: an ecstatic disruption, an adventure of the spirit, one that wakes you up and startles you, that makes you want to see it again (I’m still working up the courage to go a second round with “The Odyssey”), and one that unites the audience in the feeling of having experienced something uncanny. Something we haven’t seen before. The reason I predict “You Can See Everything” will triumph at the Oscars is that anyone who votes for it won’t just be voting for best picture — they’ll be voting for the future.

title: Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’
summary: Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content. Last week, amid its layoff of 1,000 employees, Netflix ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and has tapped veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her. The company also let go head of […]
content:
Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.

Last week, amid its layoff of 1,000 employees, Netflix ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and has tapped veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her. The company also let go head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia.

On the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos — who had previously led Netflix’s content operations for over 20 years — explained the decision to install a new team overseeing its programming lineup led by Rice.

Popular on Variety

“I know that we could do better, and we want to build on that momentum,” Sarandos said, when asked about the leadership change on the content side.

Sarandos started by praising Bajaria “for all of her incredible contributions to Netflix. Bela had an incredible decade-long run here. She put a lot of great hits on the board. She led the teams through a lot of expansions of new types of content. She also did the hard work of building this incredible international team, who’s been making local content around the world, which has become a great competitive differentiator for us over the last decade.”

That said, Sarandos continued, “Now we’ve seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the U.S. where we can have an outsized impact when we create a big buzzy show that members love and talk about all over the world.”

Sarandos said he has known Rice, a former Disney and 21st Century Fox television and movie exec, for about 15 years. At Disney, he was chairman of Walt Disney Television before he was ousted by former CEO Bob Chapek in 2022.

“And I’ve got to tell you the outpouring of excitement about him coming to Netflix from across the industry and from the creative community has been nothing short of overwhelming. He’s one of the really rare people in the industry who’s led TV networks, movie studios, streaming services,” Sarandos said. “His creative instinct and his business acumen are remarkable. He’s really an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment. You know, network [television], prestige cable, streaming, theatrical and TV films, and live sports.”

Sarandos said, “most importantly… Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.”

A bit later in the call, Sarandos again sang Rice’s praises.

“Peter brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s kind of that exact balance skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter,” Sarandos told Wall Street analysts. “Now, there’s a ton to be excited about in our Q4 slate, and a ton to be excited about in 2027. And I believe that Peter will actually be able to have an impact on those projects that are in the works, even in the short term.”

title: Versant Unlikely To Acquire Skydance Cable Networks If They Hit The Market, CEO Mark Lazarus Says
summary: Versant Media CEO Mark Lazarus said the company spun off by Comcast/NBCUniversal earlier this year is unlikely to be a buyer if Skydance looks to shop some of its dozens of cable TV networks. “Buying more cable assets on a large scale would prolong our life but not necessarily make our life better because we […]
content:
Versant Media CEO Mark Lazarus said the company spun off by Comcast/NBCUniversal earlier this year is unlikely to be a buyer if Skydance looks to shop some of its dozens of cable TV networks.

“Buying more cable assets on a large scale would prolong our life but not necessarily make our life better because we would still have the secular decline,” Lazarus said Tuesday at the Axios Media Trends Live conference in New York. “Might there be some interest in another vertical that we could create around a pay television business? Yes, but just buying big networks or a bunch of networks that don’t necessarily change our trajectory is probably not in our short-term future.”

Versant owns a swath of former NBCU cable networks like MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), CNBC and USA. It also has a portfolio of digital properties like movie ticketing service Fandango and tee-time reservation platform Golf Now.

Watch on Deadline

Executives have said they hope to make digital the primary source of total company revenue in the coming years, a time horizon Lazarus estimated at three to five years. Currently, he said, digital is less than 25% of the whole pie.

The merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery into Skydance closed earlier this month and created a media giant with more than 50 cable networks. Given the ongoing downturn of viewing and advertising on cable, speculation has continued that Skydance could try to offload some of its cable. The company has said it is aiming not to shed any networks, instead using their cash flow to pay down debt and invest in other areas.

Versant has faced skepticism since its January debut, with its stock price falling 29%. Lazarus conceded that the company still needs to “prove out our thesis.”

Asked about Comcast’s plan to spin out NBCUniversal and whether Versant would ever consider a reunion with NBCU down the road, Lazarus hedged a bit. “Our cash flow is really strong, and I think we will find our path, whether it’s on our own transformation or alongside someone else, but no, that wouldn’t be the plan to necessarily go back to them,” he said.

Lazarus said Versant is considering renewing its deal with NBCU to handle its advertising sales as well as options like outsourcing it to another big media company or bringing it in-house.

“So far, it’s going very well,” the former NBCU exec said of the sales arrangement. “We provide scale and reach and efficient media to their big, big fancy sports stuff. We know that salesforce well, I oversaw that for a long time. So it’s going very well. You know, at some point, you know, in the next a year from now or so, as we get to a natural window, we’ll sit down with them and decide if it should go on or not. But if we both agree, it should go on, we would do that.”

title: ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ Trailer Clocks Massive 481M+ First-Week Views, More Than ‘Barbie’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: We just got wind after the Netflix earnings call that the viewership for the trailer of the streamer’s mega-wide theatrical release Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew from Greta Gerwig garnered more than 481.3 million views in its first seven days, according to WaveMetrix. That seven-day traffic bests that of Gerwig’s Barbie (240M views), Wonka (237.2M […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: We just got wind after the Netflix earnings call that the viewership for the trailer of the streamer’s mega-wide theatrical release Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew from Greta Gerwig garnered more than 481.3 million views in its first seven days, according to WaveMetrix.

That seven-day traffic bests that of Gerwig’s Barbie (240M views), Wonka (237.2M views) and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie (281.6M views).

Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew trended at No. 1 on X and is still the No. 1 trending movie trailer on YouTube and NarniaFilm.com, which briefly crashed due to the influx of visits.

Watch on Deadline

Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew hits theaters on Feb. 12 stateside in what is an exclusive 45-day theatrical window to streaming. Sony is handling theatrical for the film overseas. The movie is one of many seismic movies for Netflix as they embrace theatrical further, look to longer windows, in addition to reporting grosses. Their limited four-theater release of La Bola Negra in NYC and LA scored the second best opening theater average ever for a non-English movie after Parasite with $69K+

Gerwig debuted the Narnia trailer on Oct. 13 in NYC at an exclusive Imax sneak peek event. In conversation with Late Show host Stephen Colbert, she reflected on her lifelong connection to C. S. Lewis, her vision for the film, and the groundbreaking artistry behind the first screen adaptation of Narnia’s origin story.

The Magician’s Nephew trailer also made music history, as it marked the first time Led Zeppelin ever granted a sync for “Stairway To Heaven” to be used in a film or trailer, a milestone that drove headlines from Deadline, Billboard, Rolling Stone and more.

Led Zeppelin posted the trailer on IG and guitarist / songwriter Jimmy Page praised Greta as “a powerhouse in the world of cinema,” adding, “I am thrilled that she chose ‘Stairway to Heaven’ in the trailer for her film.”

In her conversation with Colbert, Greta talked about meeting the band, who are C.S. Lewis fans that saw the heart of the story in the film. “I was so moved that they allowed me to use the song,” she said.

“The whole thing was very fortuitous. It is about a spiritual journey. It’s about the true path of enlightenment and spirituality, and then this sort of path of false idols and the wrong roads you can go down. And I was like, this is exactly the story of this movie. It really is a spiritual quest and a spiritual journey. So to me, this was the song that made sense to introduce this into the world. But, they have not let it be used in anything, so I was so moved that they allowed me to use the song and, and they did it because they saw the heart of the story in the film. And they too love C.S. Lewis and they have a reverence for his work. So it, it was very, it was the whole thing was very fortuitous. But I’m so happy that it got to be this song,” said the 4x Oscar nominated filmmaker.

o support the trailer launch, Netflix ran global paid media across social, linear + connected TV, and out-of-home. The trailer had a presence across TikTok, Reddit, Meta, X, Snap, Pinterest & YouTube. Linear included moments across early morning, late night and Sunday NFL.

Beamed Saranados on today’s earnings call about Netflix’s new era of box office reporting and theatrical, “We’re really excited about where we sit now, of course, we have one week of public reporting of box office under our belt, and we’re real happy about it. So let’s check in again in about six months.”

“Our theatrical strategy has evolved.”

Narnia stars Emma Mackey, Daniel Craig, Carey Mulligan, Meryl Streep, Denise Gough and Ciarán Hinds. Gerwig adapted. Pic is produced by Amy Pascal, Mark Gordon, Vincent Sieber and Gerwig.

Gerwig’s Barbie opened to $162M domestic, and $356.3M WW and wound up becoming Warner Bros’ highest grossing movie ever with $1.44 billion at the global box office.

title: Denzel Washington And Christopher McQuarrie Team On New Thriller At United Artists And Amazon MGM Studios
summary: EXCLUSIVE: United Artists isn’t done adding to an already loaded film slate as sources tell Deadline that Scott Stuber’s company and Amazon MGM Studios have greenlit an untitled thriller with Denzel Washington set to star Christopher McQuarrie on board to direct. Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner penned the script. The film will bow in theaters […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: United Artists isn’t done adding to an already loaded film slate as sources tell Deadline that Scott Stuber’s company and Amazon MGM Studios have greenlit an untitled thriller with Denzel Washington set to star Christopher McQuarrie on board to direct. Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner penned the script.

The film will bow in theaters on October 1, 2027.

The plot centers on a former police detective serving a life sentence who is diagnosed with terminal brain cancer. Granted compassionate release with six months to live, he returns home to the estranged daughter he left behind and a grandson he never knew existed. He only wants to make amends and forget his dark past, but his dark past has not forgotten him.

McQuarrie will also produce alongside Heather McQuarrie along with Stuber and Nick Nesbitt, who produce through United Artists; Joseph Restaino for Hungry Bull Productions; Reza Moheet and Norman Aladjem for Mainstay Entertainment; Katia Washington; and Tommy Harper. Hungry Bull’s Tony Stopperan, Mainstay’s Tim Honigman and Joe Guest will serve as executive producers

Watch on Deadline

As for Washington, the two-time Oscar winner had been planning to reunite with Antoine Fuqua this fall for the Netflix epic about ancient Carthaginian general Hannibal. Those plans were put on pause when pre-production was halted following budgetary issues. The stoppage allowed Washington to refocus on other projects, with this film moving to the top of the list following meetings with McQuarrie that ultimately led to Washington giving the thumbs-up. Producers will now look to fill the role of Washington’s daughter.

Most recently, Washington has made his return to the Broadway stage in Othello alongside Jake Gyllenhaal, and starred in Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest. Up next, he will star in Netflix’s The Take (formerly titled Here Comes the Flood) alongside Robert Pattinson and Daisy Edgar-Jones. That film is slated to release in 2027.

After a decade redefining the modern action spectacle with Mission: Impossible, Oscar winner McQuarrie returns to the crime genre he helped define with films like Jack Reacher, The Way of the Gun and The Usual Suspects. He most recently helped helm the last four Mission: Impossible films including the most recent Mission: Impossible -The Final Reckoning.

With UA, Stuber is now in production on Lizard Music, the next collaboration between Dwayne Johnson and Benny Safdie. It is also in post-production on a new version of Highlander starring Henry Cavill, and is prepping Michael Mann’s Heat 2 starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Christian Bale, and The Mandela Catalogue, the analog horror adaptation with Steven Spielberg’s Amblin Entertainment to be directed by series creator Alex Kister.

In partnership with Ben Affleck and Matt Damon’s Artist Equity Independent Pictures, Hungry Bull recently wrapped production on Downriver starring Jessica Biel, Garrett Hedlund and Jake Lacy.

Next up for Mainstay on the big screen is the genre-bending vampire western The Sun Always Sets in the West at Lionsgate, set for a 2027 start date. On TV, Mainstay recently produced The Matchmaker with Patti Stanger at the CW.

Washington is represented by WME. McQuarrie is represented by CAA and Greenberg Glusker. Barkan and Zehentner are represented by Mainstay Entertainment and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, Gellman, Meigs & Fox.

title: Netflix’s Greg Peters Calls Layoffs Hard Tradeoff For Long-Term Growth
summary: Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said the giant streamer’s move to cut 1,000 jobs last week reflects a fast-changing media landscape that requires hard questions about “where we can trim or redirect how we’re investing.” “We do not take these decisions lightly, but we also believe we have a responsibility to make hard trade-offs in service […]
content:
Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said the giant streamer’s move to cut 1,000 jobs last week reflects a fast-changing media landscape that requires hard questions about “where we can trim or redirect how we’re investing.”

“We do not take these decisions lightly, but we also believe we have a responsibility to make hard trade-offs in service of our members, our partners, our employees, our investors, and ultimately our long-term growth,” he told investors Tuesday during a video conference after the streamer reported quarterly earnings.

“We’ve got a big and ambitious mission. We aspire to entertain literally the whole world. Now, fulfilling on that big mission requires us to be incredibly disciplined about where we focus, where we invest, how our people work, where our resources go. And when you’ve driven considerable top line growth, as we have over the last several years, and you’re in a highly dynamic market that’s constantly changing, I don’t think it’s unusual then to find that there are some areas that we built quickly and we ended up over-invested in, or there are opportunities to adjust how we are operating to best drive the business through the next stage of growth,” he added.

Watch on Deadline

“We prefer to make these adjustments organically and iteratively. That’s the best way to do it. We think it’s our mission basically to constantly be trying to tune and adjust. But sometimes the team needs a forcing function. The company needs a mandate that requires the whole organization to ask hard questions about where can we be more efficient, where can we make tough decisions about where we can trim or redirect how we’re investing … And that was the simple thinking behind it and what motivated these recent changes.”

The layoffs of about 6% of the company’s workforce were followed in short order by the ouster of content chief Bela Bajaria and film boss Dan Lin. Netflix tapped former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice to replace Bajaria.

title: ‘The Cycle Of Love’ To Return To Cinemas For One-Day Only Engagement: Extraordinary Romantic Tale From Director Orlando Von Einsiedel
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Fresh from earning two nominations for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, The Cycle of Love is cycling back into theaters. The romantic documentary directed by Oscar winner Orlando von Einsiedel and executive produced by Priyanka Chopra Jonas will play for one-day only on November 1, which the distributor is calling a special “date night” […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Fresh from earning two nominations for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, The Cycle of Love is cycling back into theaters.

The romantic documentary directed by Oscar winner Orlando von Einsiedel and executive produced by Priyanka Chopra Jonas will play for one-day only on November 1, which the distributor is calling a special “date night” screening event. It’s booked in locations nationwide from New York to Los Angeles, and even further west to Hawaii. The film, which recounts the extraordinary love story of PK — an “untouchable” young Indian artist — and Lotta, “a Swedish adventurer in search of magic, whose meeting was written in the stars from [PK’s] birth,” becomes available on TVOD starting November 2, on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV, and YouTube.

The Cyle of Love won the Artemis Rising Foundation Award for Social Impact at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York and audience awards at the Middleburg Film Festival in Virginia and the Indie Meme Film Festival in Austin, TX. At the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, it’s nominated for Best Director, recognizing von Einsiedel, and Best Cinematography, recognizing DoP Franklin Dow.

Watch on Deadline

Chirag Lobo as young PK in ‘The Cycle Of Love’ Courtesy of Franklin Dow

“In 1977, PK, a 23-year-old Delhi street artist from a poor, ‘untouchable’ family, picked up a handful of paintbrushes and a second-hand bicycle and set off across 6000 miles and nearly a dozen countries,” notes a synopsis. “His mission: to find Lotta, the woman who had captured his heart on a visit to India.

“PK knew their meeting was fate. When he was still a baby, an astrologer left his parents with a prophecy: ‘You will marry a girl who is not from the village, not even from this country, she will be musical, own a jungle and be born under the sign of the ox.’ Lotta was born in May and she played the recorder and piano. When PK asked her if she owned a jungle, she replied, ‘not a jungle, but a forest.’ He knew this was his destiny. Charmed by his smile, creativity and gentleness, Lotta accepted his offer to show her around India and, over her two-month visit, they fell hopelessly in love, despite caste, nationality, and everything else.”

(L-R) Actor Chirag Lobo, director Orlando von Einsiedel, and actress Mina Dale attend ‘The Cycle Of Love’ UK premiere at The Curzon Mayfair on September 17, 2026 in London. Jo Hale/WireImage

Von Einsiedel won his Academy Award for The White Helmets (2016) and earned an Academy Award nomination for Virunga (2014). His additional directing credits include The Lost Children (2024), co-directed by Jorge Duran and Lali Houghton; the documentary series Heart of Invictus (2023), and the short film Lost and Found (2019).

In a recent interview with Deadline, von Einsiedel told us about the origins of The Cycle of Love.

“I was in Sweden and I was giving a talk at an event and two young people, very smiley young people, came up to me and handed me a book and said, ‘This is a book about our parents’ story and we know your work a little bit. And if you like this story and are interested, would you consider making a film about it?’” the filmmaker recalled. “When somebody approaches you cold and says, ‘This is a great story,’ it sadly isn’t always a great story. So, I didn’t have the highest hopes in the world, but I read the book a number of weeks later and immediately knew I’d been an idiot for not being more enthusiastic. And the story blew my mind and it’s about magic and destiny and love and adventure and the kindness of strangers. And I immediately got back in touch and said, ‘Hello, do you remember me?’ And luckily, they did remember me.”

Grain MediaKalabati Pictures

The film includes extensive dramatizations immersing viewers in this almost unimaginable story. Von Einsiedel cast actor Chirag Lobo as young PK, and actress Mina Dale as young Lotta.

“I learned very quickly there wasn’t much archive footage… PK unfortunately didn’t have a documentary crew following him in 1977,” von Einsiedel said. “Normally, that [cuts] a documentary off at its knees. And I found that very scary, but it was kind of freeing and wonderful in a way to try and problem-solve how to overcome this.”

The film becomes a road movie, with the director casting people he met in the course of filming — non-professional actors — to take part in it. Von Einsiedel says his approach was inspired by several acclaimed directors.

“I suppose I’ve borrowed enormously from amazing filmmakers like Abbas Kiarostami, Chloé Zhao, Jonas Poher Rasmussen and the Ross Brothers, all these brilliant people who blended documentary and scripted,” he said. “I’ve tried to stand on their shoulders and try something different.”

PK Mahanandia in ‘The Cycle of Love’ Courtesy of Franklin Dow

PK’s story of perseverance — receiving a sign about his future and then undertaking a journey to make that vision a reality — has touched audiences around the world.

“We don’t all have destiny written for us or given a prophecy as children, but we all have hopes and dreams and ambitions,” von Einsiedel observed. “But to make those happen, you have to work at them. And I think that’s a really inspiring message at the heart of this film. Here’s a man who had a very difficult life and he decided he was going to change it and took an enormous risk. And we might not be able to cycle 6,000 miles to change our lives, but we can all do something to achieve our dreams.”

He added, “There’s a line PK says as well: ‘We can choose which story to believe about ourselves.’ I think that’s such a powerful line because PK had been told all his life that he was polluted, he was dirty, he was nothing, and he chose not to believe any of that and achieved extraordinary things because of that.”

The Cycle of Love is a Grain Media and Kalabati Pictures production, in Association with BD4, Tudip Entertainment and AMPL, Artemis Rising Foundation, Grace Labs, Waldesfriede Films and Purple Pebble Pictures. The film is produced by Harri Grace, Chloe Leland, Emelie Mahanandia von Schedvin, and Karl Mahanandia von Schedvin.

Executive producers are Priyanka Chopra Jonas, Anne Carey, Adriana Banta, Jorge Villon, Abhijeet Chhabra, Dan Silver, Ryan Harrington, Geralyn Dreyfous, Emily Goldner, Chris Silvestri, Mark Roden, Melony and Adam Lewis, Michael Humphries, Regina K. Scully, Lekha Singh, Cristina Ljungberg, Victoria Steventon, The Reilly Family, Danielle Turkov, and Amy Shepherd.

title: Netflix Chiefs Concede That Slowdown in U.S. Viewing Sparked the Content Leadership Shakeup: ‘We’re Focusing on Execution,’ Ted Sarandos Says
summary: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters nodded to slowdown in U.S. viewing and ad sales that spurred the radical shake-up of the streamer’s content leadership during Tuesday’s conversation with Wall Street analysts after its third-quarter earnings release. Sarandos and Peters had to address the situation that led to the dramatic decision to oust chief […]
content:
Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters nodded to slowdown in U.S. viewing and ad sales that spurred the radical shake-up of the streamer’s content leadership during Tuesday’s conversation with Wall Street analysts after its third-quarter earnings release.

Sarandos and Peters had to address the situation that led to the dramatic decision to oust chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin. Former Fox and Disney executive Peter Rice was appointed Oct. 15 as Bajaria’s successor, starting next week.

Peters sought to assure analysts that while Netflix is going through a soft period in the U.S., its underlying fundamentals are strong. As ever, when the going gets tough in pay TV, executives point to positive signs when it comes to churn — or the lack thereof. Peters emphasized that the churn rate of subscribers moving on and off the platform was better than expected in the U.S. and elsewhere for the quarter, especially after the streamer initiated a price hike.

Popular on Variety

Peters emphasized that “the quality, quantity and variety of viewing remains healthy and it drives our business model. And the best evidence that we’ve got that we’re delivering that value is churn. We’ve got healthy retention in every region,” he said. For the quarter ended Sept. 30, the level of churn improved on a global basis and in the U.S.

“The ultimate determinant of are we delivering that value is the reaction to price changes. And those recent price changes that we did, including in the United States, have gone well. We’ve seen results that are consistent with past changes,” Peters said.

Most of the regions outside the U.S. delivered strong viewing and engagement, he added.

“Our local titles from those regions are driving engagement and they’re driving business growth. And you can see how our business model works here. We specifically highlighted India, which had a strong slate with a couple titles really, really performing. And as a result, view hours in Q3 in India grew 24% on an absolute basis,” Peters said. “They were also up on a per-member basis, all of which drives membership.”

As the dust settles on the management shake-up, Sarandos told analysts that they are laser-focused on nurturing shows to stand out as hits.

“We had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world. We’re focusing on that execution,” Sarandos said. “India is a great example, but that success is also happening in Korea and Japan. And when you look to [Europe, the Middle East and Africa], when we look to the Nordics, which is a very mature market for us, that content slate is killing it there. And it’s proof that when we have the right focus, make the right choices and deliver creatively, we can drive outsize impact on the business around the world.”

Rice, Sarandos added, “brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s that exact skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter.”

Spencer Neumann, Netflix’s chief financial officer, chimed in with his observation that while Netflix does need big, noisy hits, it is not overly dependent on any one genre or format of content.

“Even with modest view-hour growth that we’re delivering, we’re delivering that increasing value to our members across quality, quantity and variety viewing with a steady drumbeat of big hits in most regions,” Neumann said. “That’s really the great thing about our model — the stability of our growth engine. We’re not overly dependent on any kind of one title, nor outsized performance by any one region to deliver healthy growth.”

(Pictured: Netflix co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos)

title: Kurosawa Kiyoshi, Shimizu Takashi Among Directors of Disney+, Hulu Japanese Horror Series ‘Night Tales Club’
summary: Kurosawa Kiyoshi and “Ju-on” director Shimizu Takashi are among the seven filmmakers behind “Night Tales Club,” a six-part Japanese supernatural anthology series set to premiere on Disney+ and Hulu in January 2027. Yamada Takayuki leads the series as Hojo, a high-flying businessman fixated on the unexplained who acts as its storyteller. Each episode adapts a […]
content:
Kurosawa Kiyoshi and “Ju-on” director Shimizu Takashi are among the seven filmmakers behind “Night Tales Club,” a six-part Japanese supernatural anthology series set to premiere on Disney+ and Hulu in January 2027.

Yamada Takayuki leads the series as Hojo, a high-flying businessman fixated on the unexplained who acts as its storyteller. Each episode adapts a different tale from author Sawamura Ichi’s collection of short horror stories. Sawamura also adapted the material for the screen.

Hojo is convinced that ghosts, curses and other paranormal events are “bugs” – glitches that point to a hidden conspiracy. To get to the bottom of it, he offers JPY20 million ($126,000) in gold to anyone willing to come to his gathering, the Night Tales Club, and present a firsthand account of the supernatural along with proof. Six such accounts make up the series as Hojo chases the truth behind them.

Popular on Variety

Kurosawa, whose credits include “Cure” and “Wife of a Spy,” and Shimizu, known for “Ju-on” and “The Inugami Family,” each take one episode. So do Katayama Shinzo (“Gannibal,” “The Human Vapor”), Sode Yukiko (“Aristocrats,” “All the Lovers in the Night”), Sakashita Yuichiro (“I Can’t Cry With Your Face,” “Blonde”) and Nakamura Yosuke (“Higuma!!,” “Poison Girl”). Nakajima Kenji (“The Naked Director,” “Tokyo Swindlers”) directs the Hojo sequences.

Wakabayashi Yusuke and Yamamoto Teruhisa produce.

“As the original author of these stories, I feel an enormous sense of surprise and joy that they will soon be available on screen to scare audiences around the world.” Sawamura said.

The show joins a growing lineup of Japanese series on the streamer. Disney+ already carries “Gannibal,” in which a police officer stumbles on something sinister in a remote village, and “Land of Tanabata,” about a college student with an apparently pointless power who looks into a murder. Lighter fare includes cross-cultural romantic comedy “Merry Berry Love” and comedy variety show “The One Shot.”

title: Access: Horror Virtual Film Festival Sheds Light on Disability by ‘Centering Ableism as the Horror Rather Than Disability’
summary: When Ariel Baska traded her 15-year career teaching Latin for the film industry, they were instantly faced with a series of unexpected guardrails. “I found that all of these doors were closed to me because I could not literally walk in the front door,” Baska tells Variety. “As someone who is on the deaf-blind spectrum […]
content:
When Ariel Baska traded her 15-year career teaching Latin for the film industry, they were instantly faced with a series of unexpected guardrails.

“I found that all of these doors were closed to me because I could not literally walk in the front door,” Baska tells Variety. “As someone who is on the deaf-blind spectrum and has mobility impairments as well, it makes it very difficult when you literally just can’t access the networking spots where everyone is gathered.”

So, Baska decided to take matters into their own hands as the founder and co-director of Access: Horror, a disability-led horror and experimental virtual film festival. Access: Horror aims to provide access and representation to people with disabilities behind and in front of the camera. The organization brings awareness to how disability is portrayed in film while also making movies more accessible by adding content warnings, captions and audio descriptions.

Popular on Variety

The festival runs online from Oct. 4 to Nov. 1 with a large slate of films from emerging filmmakers, as well as a series of panels and filmmaker Q&As. Baska and co-director Heather Petrocelli focused their festival on the horror genre because of the fact that “ableism” and “disabled and disfigured bodies have been at the heart of horror from the beginning.”

The lineup is separated into three blocks of programming: Edibles, The Body Keeps the Score and Dead Darlings. Among the titles featured in this year’s festival is Lee Cleaveland’s “Everhand,” where a one-armed farmer orders a mysterious machine, and he and his wife must face off with a company rep in order to reclaim their humanity. Another is Charlie Gillette’s “Tal,” which translates to ‘mask’ in English, which is a claustrophobic meditation on immigrant identity and familial expectations. “A Fermenting Woman” from Priscilla Galvez follows a peculiar chef and fermentation expert as they prepare a career-saving meal using a very special ingredient.

Petrocelli and Baska’s goal in curating the festival lineup was to find films that align with their mission and reclaim disability’s role in the genre.

“That reclaiming is entirely about centering ableism as the horror rather than disability as the horror,” Baska says. “Every James Bond villain, every Captain Hook character that you have in the world has made people afraid of difference, but if we turn that fear and that expectation into the horror, rather than the physical difference, whatever it may happen to be, whether it’s a limb difference, whether it’s a wheelchair, reframing the monster is the thing that is most essential for me and for the festival.”

Along with their organization’s missions, the pair picked horror because of the conversations the genre provokes.

“Horror is the most honest genre because that is what we are living through right now,” Baska says. “I feel like if we want to find ourselves, we have to find ways of engaging with the trauma that we’re all in at the moment. There’s a beating heart to horror. There’s an opera. There’s a frequency that horror nerds are attuned to that no one else is.”

By giving a voice to novice filmmakers, they also ensure their goals of making films more accessible are heard.

“The understanding is that if you are a filmmaker who plays with Access: Horror, we give you those assets [of content warnings, captions and audio descriptions] so you can play with them in future,” Petrocelli says. “But the expectation is that you will budget for them appropriately moving forward in your career, so it’s a way to both teach early-stage filmmakers about accessibility while also creating a better space for our audiences.”

Created in 2023, Access: Horror is still finding its footing in the film festival world with the goal of continuing to grow and garner support.

“We’re still kind of finding our way and negotiating as best we can in the way that accessibility is always kind of a negotiation, and you’re constantly trying to find your way between things,” Baska says. “At the same time, we just would ask that people consider the broader landscape that we are living in and make a real pitch for people to engage.”

title: Charli xcx Cancels ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ Show in Arizona Due to Illness: ‘It Breaks Me That I Can’t Be With You’
summary: Charli xcx has announced that she has canceled tomorrow night’s “Music, Fashion, Film” performance in Arizona due to illness. The pop singer is currently on her “Music, Fashion, Film” tour across North America and, after two shows in Los Angeles over the weekend, was slated to appear at Glendale’s Desert Diamond Arena on Wednesday. But […]
content:
Charli xcx has announced that she has canceled tomorrow night’s “Music, Fashion, Film” performance in Arizona due to illness.

The pop singer is currently on her “Music, Fashion, Film” tour across North America and, after two shows in Los Angeles over the weekend, was slated to appear at Glendale’s Desert Diamond Arena on Wednesday. But in a social media post, she said she’s been fighting sickness through this run of shows and has completely lost her voice.

“I put absolutely everything I have into my performances, both physically and emotionally, and it breaks me that I can’t be with you tomorrow,” she wrote. “My team worked hard to find a new date but ultimately were unable to. I’m so disappointed, but promise to return to AZ in the future.”

Popular on Variety

She continued, “Again, I’m sorry to the angels who had made plans to be there tomorrow. I know how much time, planning and care it takes to come to concerts and appreciate everyone’s support immensely.”

Refunds for those who purchased tickets through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded. All other tickets will be refunded at the point of purchase.

Charli kicked off her 12-date “Music, Fashion, Film” tour in early September with an opener in Philadelphia before heading to Brooklyn for two nights at Barclays Center, followed by subsequent shows in Toronto, Atlanta and San Diego. In Los Angeles this past weekend, she brought out a handful of guests, including Chappell Roan for a rendition of “Boom Clap” and PinkPantheress for her own song “Stateside.” Charli will conclude the tour on Friday at Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena.

title: David Fincher Scrapped 60 Pages Of Tarantino’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Script: “It Was Essentially Two Movies”
summary: David Fincher directed The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood follow-up written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt. With Tarantino penning the script, Fincher had to make some sacrifices and cut 60 pages. “The first draft I read was 230 pages. It was essentially two movies,” Fincher told Empire in a […]
content:
David Fincher directed The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood follow-up written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt.

With Tarantino penning the script, Fincher had to make some sacrifices and cut 60 pages.

“The first draft I read was 230 pages. It was essentially two movies,” Fincher told Empire in a joint interview with Tarantino. “Somewhere in there was the Venn diagram of what Brad wanted to do, what I want to do, what Quentin wanted to do. Not ‘want to do,’ but the areas we would focus on.”

With the cuts, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, which follows Pitt reprising his role as stuntman Cliff Booth, ended up having a runtime of around 2 hours and 20 minutes.

Watch on Deadline

The film, which is slated to premiere in Imax on November 25, followed by the Netflix release on December 23, also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller.

Tarantino explained that he doesn’t think of TFMAOCB as a “hangout movie at all,” adding, “Once Upon A Time In Hollywood was a hangout movie, but you know you’re going to Cielo Drive (site of the Manson murders). It has this force, thus I didn’t need a lot of plot. This script was very different.”

Once Upon a Time in Hollywood premiered in 2019 and was written and directed by Tarantino. The film featured a cast that included Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Austin Butler, Dakota Fanning, Timothy Olyphant, Mike Moh, Margaret Qualley, Al Pacino, Emile Hirsch, Bruce Dern and Luke Perry.

summary: Disney+’s latest Japanese original is supernatural thriller series Night Tales Club. Six-part series will launch in January 2027 and is based on […]
content:
Disney+’s latest Japanese original is supernatural thriller series Night Tales Club.

A teaser trailer has dropped for the show, which follows a successful businessman, Hojo, obsessed with the inexplicable who turns his attention to solving life’s biggest mysteries, unleashing all manner of bizarre horrors.

Six-part series will launch in January 2027 and is based on a short horror story collection from Ichi Sawamura. Each episode will see Hojo sharing a different mysterious story. He is convinced that ghost stories, monsters and other supernatural anomalies are “bugs” in an underlying conspiracy, so begins inviting people to share their experiences and evidence at his Night Tales Club in exchange for 20 million yen.

Takayuki Yamada has been cast as Hojo, the storyteller, with each episode directed by a different director, including Kiyoshi Kurosawa (Cure), Takashi Shimizu (Ju-On), Shinzo Katayama (Gannibal), Yukiko Sode (Aristocrats), Yuichiro Sakashita (I Can’t Cry With Your Face) and Yosuke Nakamura (Higuma!!), with Kenji Nakajima (The Naked Director) directing the Hojo sequences.

Watch on Deadline

The series is produced by Yusuke Wakabayashi and Teruhisa Yamamoto and adapted for the screen by the original writer, Sawamura, who said: “As the original author of these stories, I feel an enormous sense of surprise and joy that they will soon be available on screen to scare audiences around the world.”

Disney+ has to date launched Japanese originals such as Gannibal, about a police officer who discovers a horrifying secret in his sleepy rural village, and Land of Tanabata, about a university student with a seemingly useless ability who investigates a murder, along with lighter fare such as cross-cultural romcom Merry Berry Love and comedic variety show The One Shot.

The news comes a day after Carol Choi replaced the retiring Luke Kang as President of The Walt Disney Company APAC.

title: Ted Sarandos Insists Netflix “Strategy Is Unchanged” As Execs Are Pressed About Growth
summary: “Our business and our business flywheel are working. There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working,” Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos insisted Tuesday as analysts lobbed question upon question about what the company is doing to address […]
content:
“Our business and our business flywheel are working. There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working,” Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos insisted Tuesday as analysts lobbed question upon question about what the company is doing to address a slowdown in growth.

In other words, strong titles in global territories from Asia Pacific to Latin America are driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue and profit. “The U.S. is also working, it’s just not growing as fast as it could, or as fast as we’d like. We had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world,” he said on a call after quarterly earnings. “We’re focusing on that execution.”

He’ll be leaning for that in large part on new chief content officer Peter Rice to lead that charge.

Watch on Deadline

“Our strategy is unchanged,” he said at another point, focused on originals combined with licensed fare and a growing live business. He somewhat dismissed short-form video and third-party or user-generated content that some Wall Streeters think could help boost engagement as “early-stage initiatives” with limited investment.

He did say to expect more deals like the one with TF1 network in France that brings strong local programming onto the platform.

The job of co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters on the video call today was to reassure investors – who have bid the stock down over 40% in the last year – that there’s a path to long-term growth. On one hand, the streamer’s bid for Warner Bros., massive job cuts and C-suite changes indicate a recognition that change is needed in a fiercely competitive market. On the other, the CEOs reassured the Street that the solution is, while not easy, rather simple, that it mostly needs to deliver enough “quality and quantity” of programming consistently. That’s the slate, and they said it looks stronger this fall and into next year and that Netflix aims to keep it that way.

Sarandos said the streamer sees overall engagement “as the sum total of actual value that we are delivering to members… And the best evidence that we’ve got that we’re delivering that value is churn.” Netflix in fact leads all of its rivals in customer retention.

“Q3 churn, both globally and in the United States, improved year on year. It’s better than forecast. It’s already industry leading. And the ultimate determinant of whether we are delivering that value is the reaction to price changes” – meaning the streamer’s recent subscription price hikes have gone well.

Netflix CFO Spencer Neumann said the focus is firmly on the key metrics of member growth, pricing, and ads. “And we expect to deliver strong revenue growth into 2027 as well with those same three levers. The ad side led to softer-than-anticipated revenue guidance for full-year 2026 that dinged the shares today, when they fell 6% after the close.

Theatrical is another area but the strategy there is still a bit confusing. Netflix is planning to release 30 films theatrically this year from small platform releases with long windows, to wide family films. It just started reporting box office with La Bola Negra this past weekend.

“We are a streaming-first business. That is our core. But we consider every time we have a new film, the film itself, the audience for the film, and the filmmaker when we’re trying to come up with the release plan,” Sarandos said.

“We start off by looking at the project we have, asking ourselves how do we best serve movie lovers, many of whom are our members, who want to see that movie in a theater, and how do we do it without actually harming the view value on Netflix?”

La Bola Negra opened well in limited release. “We’re really excited about where we sit now, of course, we have one week of public reporting of box office under our belt, and we’re real happy about it. Let’s check in again in about six months,” Sarandos said.

title: Doc Talk Podcast Live From Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival With Makers Of Four Oscar-Contending Films
summary: Oscar documentary favorites are starting to emerge as critics and other arbiters begin to announce their nominees and shortlists, bringing some clarity to a wide-open awards race. Four of the documentary features gaining traction: American Doctor, To Hold a Mountain, Closure and Once Upon a Time in Harlem. Filmmakers behind those distinguished productions assembled at […]
content:
Oscar documentary favorites are starting to emerge as critics and other arbiters begin to announce their nominees and shortlists, bringing some clarity to a wide-open awards race. Four of the documentary features gaining traction: American Doctor, To Hold a Mountain, Closure and Once Upon a Time in Harlem.

Filmmakers behind those distinguished productions assembled at the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival in Arkansas last week for HSDFF’s inaugural roundtable of Oscar contenders, an event held in partnership with Deadline. On the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast, we share the conversation with you, recorded live with an audience at the Arlington Hotel in Hot Springs.

To Hold a Mountain, the Sundance Grand Jury Award winner filmed in Montenegro, was represented on the panel by co-director Biljana Tutorov. She told us why she, co-director Petar Glomazić and their protagonist Gara Jovanović became, in her words, “enemies of the state” while they were making the film.

Watch on Deadline

Michał Marczak, who won the Golden Alexander at the Thessaloniki International Documentary Festival in Greece for Closure, tells us how making the film unexpectedly helped him deal with postponed grief from losing his father when Michał was just 11.

American Doctor’s Poh Si Teng explains why one of her protagonists “ghosted” her at a key stage of production and how she managed to overcome that hurdle.

Once Upon a Time in Harlem producer Liani Greaves, who made the award-winning film with her father David Greaves, shares insights on their father-daughter cinematic collaboration and how they crafted the story from material shot in 1972 by William Greaves (David’s father and Liani’s grandfather). It’s the only documentary this year to screen at Sundance, Cannes, Telluride, TIFF and the New York Film Festival – a testament to the extraordinary reception for the film.

The filmmakers tell us what they value most about finding themselves so prominently in Oscar contention – and, candidly, what’s not so great. Constant worldwide travel – that would be one downside; another, for Marczak, has to do with promoting the film through social media. Teng poignantly speaks to her filmmaking colleagues in Gaza who cannot leave the occupied territory even as Palestinians continue to lose their lives to Israeli military attacks.

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

title: Julia Stiles ‘Bawled’ Before Heath Ledger Tribute, Breaks Down ’10 Things I Hate About You’ Cast Reunion on ‘Dancing With the Stars’
summary: Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.” During Dedication Night, she performed a contemporary routine with her partner Ezra Sosa to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You”; in the 1999 film “10 Things I Hate About You,” Ledger’s character, Patrick, sang the Frankie Valli […]
content:
Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.”

During Dedication Night, she performed a contemporary routine with her partner Ezra Sosa to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You”; in the 1999 film “10 Things I Hate About You,” Ledger’s character, Patrick, sang the Frankie Valli number to Stiles’ Kat Stratford from the bleachers while she was at soccer practice.

©Touchstone Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection

“I said, if we had to have someone with us on stage representing Heath’s legacy or the film, I said it had to be the whole cast. I begged them, each and every one of them, and they all rallied. They really did,” Stiles told Variety after the routine. She said that it was “really trippy” to see herself in the blue dress, similar to what she wore in the film, and her hair done in a similar style. “At 17 years old, I never would have thought that here I’d be at 45, celebrating my body, dancing on the show that I absolutely love and that fans are still interested in this movie and still moved and touched by this movie.”

Earlier in the week, Stiles opened up to Variety about the emotional rehearsals.

“I know that Dedication Night is emotional, but I thought I was distanced from it enough. Like, oh, it was so many years ago. Something about seeing clips from that movie and images and hearing my voice and hearing his voice is bringing back so many memories. It’s a lot,” she said, noting that she started crying while practicing. “One of the things that we really hope to do as performers is to make people feel something and have people care about the work that you do, and his memory lives on because it was such an incredible performance.”

Ledger died in January 2008 at the age of 28.

title: ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’
summary: “Young Sheldon” actor Iain Armitage might’ve become a star thanks to the hit CBS sitcom, but when it came time to call it quits on the seven-season series in 2024, he admits he was the cast member “the most happy about the show ending.” In an interview featured in Jessica Radloff’s oral history, “Young Sheldon: […]
content:
“Young Sheldon” actor Iain Armitage might’ve become a star thanks to the hit CBS sitcom, but when it came time to call it quits on the seven-season series in 2024, he admits he was the cast member “the most happy about the show ending.”

In an interview featured in Jessica Radloff’s oral history, “Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy” (via US Weekly), Armitage, who played the titular character, said he wasn’t “going home and crying all day” like some of his co-workers at the news of the series ending. He also added that it was “heavy and annoying and weird” to be in a state of mourning around “Young Sheldon,” and he refused to “stay in that heaviness forever.”

“Plus, I wanted to be in Virginia. I wanted to be traveling, and I’m happy to do whatever movie comes up. And my mom has always imbued me with a very healthy sense of ephemerality, and the fact that nothing good can last and everything changes, and that’s a good thing,” he said. “I would hate to be on a show playing 23-year-old Sheldon. That would suck. I wouldn’t want to do that.”

Popular on Variety

Armitage was just eight years old when the series began, and now, two years since it ended, he said he it’s “nostalgic sad” to look back. “I miss working at Warner Bros., I miss the crew and the people I love. I love the act of acting. I love doing it. It’s fun. But not really specific moments. More the overall thing.”

“And Iain was ready, too … to move on to something else, artistically, and maybe personally … with things that boiled up a little bit toward the end of the season,” said Lance Barber, who played George Sr., Sheldon’s dad, in the book. “I think a lot of people felt there were certain elements of the show that they were ready to move on from.”

In a previously released excerpt of Radloff’s novel, Armitage said that while it was a “complete privilege” to be on the show, it was a “big undertaking for an 8-year-old.” “I always did the best that I could, and sometimes kids are not perfect,” he continued. “I was grateful to the people who understood that and gave me grace.”

“Young Sheldon” was so successful that the Sheldon Cooper-focused “Big Bang Theory” prequel inspired its own spinoff, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” which premiered in 2024.

title: Leica and Formula 1 Team Up on $9,950 Camera Inspired by the Racetrack (Featuring Exclusive F1 Photo Setting)
summary: Formula 1’s luxury ambitions are extending to the camera business.
