“Netflix is consistently hitting its straps in Southeast Asia but still has a long way to go there as it leans into free-to-air style local programming. Korea is the mature market, and its next leg of growth is advertising,” he said.

According to Media Partners Asia estimates, the third quarter was Netflix’s strongest ever for paid subscriber additions in India. Local unscripted programming has been particularly successful, with “Lock Upp” becoming the streamer’s most-watched title in the country, while distribution arrangements such as its Flipkart bundle have helped broaden its reach.

Peters grouped India, Indonesia and Colombia among markets where Netflix still has considerable room to add subscribers and plans to maintain accessible entry-level prices.

In more mature markets such as the U.S., U.K. and Australia, revenue growth is expected to come primarily from pricing and advertising. Japan and Mexico fall somewhere in between, offering opportunities for both subscriber growth and higher revenue per member.

Given Netflix is also looking to expand its advertising tier into 15 additional countries in 2027, marking its first expansion into new advertising markets since launching the offering, it’s unlikely seismic changes are on the horizon, but it remains to be seen how far the aftershock’s from last week’s U.S. shake up will reverberate.

title: Thirty Tigers President David Macias Previews His First Book, ‘Circulation,’ a Look at What Gets Lost When the Algorithm Dominates Music Consumption (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Have you been listening to more music and enjoying it less? David Macias thinks he knows what might ail you: an over-reliance on the algorithm in the modern music industry. It’s a system that the Thirty Tigers president believes keeps feeding music fans more of what they want, or are presumed to want, until they […]
content:
Have you been listening to more music and enjoying it less? David Macias thinks he knows what might ail you: an over-reliance on the algorithm in the modern music industry. It’s a system that the Thirty Tigers president believes keeps feeding music fans more of what they want, or are presumed to want, until they get burned out on the safe and overly familiar. This problem is something Macias diagnoses — along with some ideas for creative fixes — in his first book, “Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm,” which comes out Jan. 14 from Whitefox Publishing.

Macias brings some visionary credentials to the project, having been lauded for how his company Thirty Tigers, which he co-founded in 2001, has thrived in the world of independent music. It operates under a unique model, being a music distribution, label services and management company that lets artists maintain ownership over the records that are released under its umbrella. So he had a good track record of observation and innovation when he started having thoughts about how algorithm-based music consumption, which theoretically should help listeners discover new music, might actually be walling them off from discovering scenes beyond the ones they already know.

Popular on Variety

“Circulation” can be pre-ordered here, and previews of passages from its pages will soon be going up on Macias’ Substack, here. In the meantime, in a recent sit-down in Nashville during AmericanaFest, he talked with Variety about some of the key ideas in the book.

“Around two years ago, the business just started feeling worse, and I couldn’t quite figure out why it felt harder,” Macias says. “People felt more adrift. And I think that it’s because the things that we know to do were mattering less and less, and because the logic of the algorithm has just sort of taken hold. I mean, I’ve seen estimates of anywhere from 70-80% of all the media that we consume is now recommended to us by an algorithm, which includes social media and things like that…

“Honestly, I was kind of at a… I don’t want to say crisis point. It wasn’t like I had to drop employees or thought, ‘This isn’t fun anymore. I’m leaving.’ But also, you know, I’m now in my sixties, and I was kind of like, if this is what it’s going to be, then maybe there’s better people than me to do that.” He thinks he’s far from alone in that. “What’s happening is fueling an engine of cultural alienation, I think. How many people do you know that feel fantastic about their relationship with culture these days? How many people in the music industry do you know that are like, ‘I don’t know why, but I don’t feel great. This doesn’t feel as fun as it used to feel’?” But rather than give in to that, Macias says he “wanted to really figure out what was going on first — like, what is really happening, down to the cellular level.”

Macias emphasizes that this is not an old-man-yells-at-cloud book… or, specifically, an old-man-yells-at-Spotify book. “If you call somebody the devil, it makes it really hard to go in and figure out a common solution,” he says. “And if I felt like somebody was the devil, I’d call them the devil. But I don’t know — every person I’ve ever met at Spotify is pretty nice, and they just seem interested in getting people a good tune to listen to. I don’t think that there’s this evil intent out there. But the end result is that how things are going creates a sclerotic music ecosystem. And down the road of a sclerotic ecosystem is cultural tune-out, because we’re gonna just keep getting fed the same tunes again and again. But down this other road is a chance for vibrancy and creating more touchpoints for community.”

Macias says he’s “read a lot about business theories and all that kind of stuff, but it was like, OK, but why does Spotify make the choices that they make in terms of how they orient the algorithm? Businesses are oriented around customer retention, and a 5% increase in customer retention can have exponential values in terms of long-tail capital. So Spotify’s not trying to fuck us. They’re just trying to please us, right? But if you look at what is it that we as people want, then, what are we asking for? And you explore the psychological terrain about our relationship with comfort and reassurance. … There’s been a massive spike in nostalgia — music that was from our childhood. In the Luminate studies, in 2024, I think 49% of all streams came from music released in the last five years. Last year, that dropped to 43.6%. So people are comforting themselves with music that comes from a time when they felt like they had it figured out a little bit more than they do now. The algorithm reads it like, ‘Oh, you want more of that? Y I’ll give you more.’ That can only be regressive, and what is happening is that with the industry being so algorithmically addicted, we just keep feeding the same emotional cues back into the system again and again and again. … We can only be fed the same emotional cues before we become desensitized to it over time.”

He has his own nostalgia for a youthful time, but a youthful time when musical revolutions were being fostered by cross-breeding. “I start out the book talking about Fab 5 Freddy and how he was friends with Blondie, Grandmaster Flash, Andy Warhol and all these people… this agent to bring all kinds of things together. The song ‘Rapture’ happened because he had a cassette of Grandmaster Flash’s music when he went to dinner at Debbie Harry and Chris Stein’s house. He played it, they thought it was cool; next time they were recording, they remembered that, and ‘Rapture’ was the first No. 1 pop hit to ever have rapping in it. II’m 14 years old and sitting in Lakeland, Florida, watching ‘Friday Night Videos’ and I’m seeing shit that I’ve never seen before that’s cool, different and exciting…

“And we’re losing that kind of vibrancy because we’re not prioritizing it at all as an industry. So ultimately, what the book is doing is laying out, how do we add the vibrancy and the friction back into the mix? I’m not saying ‘Don’t do the algorithmic thing,’ because I’m gonna do the algorithmic thing, and there’s times when it really makes sense. But we also have to do this thing too, which is to invest in nascent and emerging music cultures that we have every reason to think might grow.”

Macias lays out in the book three sort of niche music communities that he feels have considerable potential but are not getting enough music biz attention because the algorithm is not rewarding them. One is queer music. Another is the Big Ears community, based around an eclectic festival that takes place in Knoxville every year. And the third is music that appeals to progressive Christians. “I don’t know if any of those are necessarily gonna wind up in the mainstream, but I think that they could all go from here to here,” he says, raising his hand, “if the proper investments were made, with people coming together to build more architecture around them.”

David Macias speaks onstage during the 14th Annual Thirty Tigers Gospel Brunch at City Winery as part of AmericanaFest 2026 on September 19, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. Getty Images

“I was talking to somebody higher up in the Christian business and I was like, ‘Do you guys just not platform kind of more liberal things because there’s this patina of fear out there?’ And he just laughed at me, and he was like, ‘No, if we thought we’d make money doing that, we’d do it.’ But praise music became the thing. More and more artists said, ‘If we don’t do praise music, we’re not gonna be able to get on the radio or tour,’ and then pretty soon that’s all there was. You know, we signed Amy Grant, and she doesn’t really match up with that… she’s not doing praise music, either.”

Macias keeps coming back to Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico as a marker of the hunger he believes exists for a different kind of faith-informed music. “You know, before he even was running for Senate, he took off like a rocket. He was in seven figures on TikTok and Instagram because there were people that were hungry for expressions of their faith that led to the idea of service. He is definitely more in the school of the Jesus that they recognize as the one who washed the feet of the disciples prior to the Last Supper, rather than this muscular Jesus who’s got a six-pack and is guarding the border. There’s no architecture to get songs to them, though. It can’t happen through the Christian business. Again, nobody’s trying to be an asshole; they just perceive there’s no money in it…

“I’ve gone to talk to Live Nation, and I talked to the managers of a couple bands that are not considered Christian bands, but they’re very faith informed in their music. I asked Live Nation, ‘Hey, if we bring all of these people together, do you think we could sell out a minor league stadium?’ And they were like, ‘Yeah, we do.’ So we’re talking about maybe doing something. But it takes somebody like me who knows those people and has the motivation to go build these structures. And if all of a sudden we have a festival and come up with some media properties that are sustainable, then all of a sudden we have enough points of contact for those 2 million people that are following James Talarico and want to hear songs and develop relationships with personalities that share their value system.”

And this isn’t just a new thing he’s seeing with Talarico. “Do you know the writer Rachel Held Evans?” he says, mentioning a late author who was a heroine to many feminist or progressive-leaning Christians. “Basically my premise there is, what if Rachel Held Evans were a music genre?”

Picking a different area of opportunity, he talks about wanting “to go build a queer version of AfroPunk,” and says he has talked to a major promoter and even city officials about a vision of setting up a festival to showcase it on the west coast. “I want to operationalize what I’m talking about in the book and not just be like, ‘Somebody should do this.'”

If any of that sounds like pie in the sky for admittedly niche genres or audiences, it’s worth noting how much Thirty Tigers has been aligned with the growth industry that is Americana music, a loose genre that now claims some of the biggest acts in music.

With Americana, “I and many, many other people showed up, and there was no data to tell us that we should, because we loved the music and understood its emotional value. We built festivals and conferences and radio stations and all that kind of stuff, and because I think we were good at that, it built and built and built and then it got to the point where a Zach Bryan happens. And then major labels come along and sign a bunch of stuff and just kind of feed those same things back into the system with an incredible velocity until it just chokes the system… But I’ve seen what happens, building architecture around a community where the data doesn’t necessarily suggest that ‘Here’s how we’re all gonna get rich,’ and we just have to apply that to other music scenes that we believe in.”

With all this talk of festivals, what about confronting the dominance of the algorithm on its home turf —streaming? Macias has ideas for that as well.

“One suggestion I make in the book has to do with the heart of the Big Ears fan, who is a person who cares deeply about being a seeker. They want to find things that are new and novel, and the importance they place on that is outsized compared to most people. So, just as a suggestion off the top of my head, I (wrote about how) I’d like to go to Spotify and say: Let’s build a room that’s like a museum. Let’s take 200 classic albums of experimental music from the past, like Brian Eno’s ‘Music for Airports’ and Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel,’ and put them in with new things, and have artists from that community that are making things on the cutting edge that have broken through tell us their 20 favorite records at the moment. Put them all in a room and tell the people that are there, ‘We’re gonna invite you here, and in this room you won’t be tracked. The algorithm will be turned off. It will be pure discovery.'” If you hit the the scan button, things are gonna pop up, and it’s just gonna be random out of those thousand albums. Now, if you want to go outside of the room and listen to it and be recommended some more, that we will do, but here we’re gonna honor your ethic of discovery.”

Convincing a DSP to have a room where users could be promised they won’t be tracked might come the closest Macias comes to having an impossible dream. But his ideas for how to zap music lovers into going beyond their self-proscribed tastes are boundless, and he feels rejuvenated after working on “Circulation” over the past two years.

“I’ve gone from being where I felt like I don’t know what the fuck is going on, and it feels bad — that’s all I know, and other people in the industry feel bad, and they feel adrift — to being more excited about what I’m doing than maybe ever. Because there’s a problem, and maybe we can solve this problem. It’s a really important problem to solve, people’s relationship with art. They use it to process. They use it to learn about their neighbors. And the world is safer and less scary if you know the stories of other people that aren’t quite like you. But that is not what’s happening as we build this infrastructure around things that are comfortable to us where nothing else really gets in.

“But for those people who think that AI is gonna kill us, I’m like, ‘Well, right before they end us, I’m just gonna go over and unplug the machine,’ you know? We still have choices about how we interact with technology. The agency is with us.”

title: Talent Agent Matt Shaffer Exits Innovative After Nearly Two Decades
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Matt Shaffer, a talent agent who has been with Innovative Artists Entertainment for nearly 20 years, has exited the firm, Deadline has learned. Sources described this as a mutual parting of ways. No word yet on Shaffer’s next destination or clients he’ll be bringing with him, but expect more information soon. With Innovative Artists […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Matt Shaffer, a talent agent who has been with Innovative Artists Entertainment for nearly 20 years, has exited the firm, Deadline has learned.

Sources described this as a mutual parting of ways. No word yet on Shaffer’s next destination or clients he’ll be bringing with him, but expect more information soon.

With Innovative Artists since May 2007, Shaffer has worked over the years with clients including Abigail Cowen, Sofia Pernas, Jennifer Esposito, Moon Bloodgood, Raoul Trujillo, David Lim, Denim Richards, Lavel Schley, and Aaron Jennings.

Prior to his time at Innovative, he worked as a talent agent at Endeavor for more than five years. He holds a J.D. from the South Texas College of Law and, prior to law school, completed a Bachelor of Business Administration at Southern Methodist University.

Watch on Deadline

This week, Innovative welcomed actress and singer Tisha Campbell to its roster, as we first reported. The agency recently hired talent agents Amanda Glazer and Brian Sacripanti and promoted Celine Biancardi to the same role.

title: ‘Coach’ Single-Cam Reboot With Ty Burrell In Works At NBC From ‘Mr. Throwback’ Duo
summary: EXCLUSIVE: NBC is giving a 2020s reboot to one of the top sitcoms of the 1990s with a star from one of the biggest comedies of the 2000s. Modern Family alum Ty Burrell is set to executive produce with the intention to star in Coach, a single-camera take on the 1989 ABC multi-camera comedy, which […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: NBC is giving a 2020s reboot to one of the top sitcoms of the 1990s with a star from one of the biggest comedies of the 2000s. Modern Family alum Ty Burrell is set to executive produce with the intention to star in Coach, a single-camera take on the 1989 ABC multi-camera comedy, which starred Craig T. Nelson. The new incarnation comes from Daniel Libman and Matthew Libman, co-creators of Peacock’s Mr. Throwback, Davis Entertainment and Universal Television.

Written by the Libman brothers, Coach centers on a legendary coach — the role earmarked for Burrell — who returns home to Minnesota to rebuild his alma mater’s basketball program and reconnect with his community.

Burrell, Daniel Libman and Matthew Libman executive produce alongside John Davis and John Fox of Davis Entertainment. Universal Television, part of Universal Studio Group, is the studio.

Watch on Deadline

Created by Barry Kemp, the original Coach aired on ABC for nine seasons. It starred Nelson as Hayden Fox, head coach of the fictional NCAA Division I-A Minnesota State University Screaming Eagles football team and subsequently the Orlando Breakers, a fictional National Football League expansion team.

In 2015, NBC gave a 13-episode order to a sequel series from Kemp set 18 years later, with the title character Fox (Nelson) called back from retirement to become assistant coach to his grown son, Tim (Andrew Ridings) at an Ivy League school in Pennsylvania. After filming one episode, NBC opted to not move forward with the revival that also featured original cast member Bill Fagerbakke.

Burrell is best known for playing dad Phil Dunphy on the ABC comedy series Modern Family, which earned him eight consecutive Emmy nominations and two wins as well as a SAG Award. Coach would mark Burrell’s first on-screen role since the end of Modern Family; he was recently part of the voice cast of the Fox animated series Duncanville. Burrell is repped by Gersh and Goodman Genow Schenkman.

Matthew and Daniel Libman co-created with Adam Pally and David Caspe the 2024 Peacock comedy series Mr. Throwback, which was headlined by Pally and NBA star Stephen Curry and, like Coach, had a sports theme. The brothers also co-created the YouTube Premium series Champaign ILL with Caspe and Jordan Cahan. The Libmans, who also worked on Happy Endings and Black Monday, both created/co-created by Caspe, are repped by UTA, TFC Management and Hansen Jacobson Teller.

title: Anonymous Content Signs Canadian Actress Bella Neuspiel
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Anonymous Content has signed Bella Neuspiel, a rising Canadian actress currently based in New York, for representation. Neuspiel will next be seen recurring in The Body, Netflix’s eight-episode thriller from Under the Bridge‘s Quinn Shephard, premiering November 11. The series follows a group of misbehaving Catholic school girls who experience prophetic visions after a […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Anonymous Content has signed Bella Neuspiel, a rising Canadian actress currently based in New York, for representation.

Neuspiel will next be seen recurring in The Body, Netflix’s eight-episode thriller from Under the Bridge‘s Quinn Shephard, premiering November 11. The series follows a group of misbehaving Catholic school girls who experience prophetic visions after a dance-team initiation goes wrong, triggering mass hysteria throughout their town. Others in the cast include Kristina Bogic, Sara Boustany, Geena Meszaros, Nnamdi Asomugha, Louisa Krause, Shirley Chen, Jackson Kelly, Sofia Wylie and Gabby Windey.

Previously, Neuspiel appeared in Carly May Borgstrom’s 2024 film Spirit in the Blood, a supernatural coming-of-age thriller starring the new Carrie TV series’ Summer H. Howell, along with Sarah-Maxine Racicot and Greg Bryk.

Watch on Deadline

An accomplished dancer, Neuspiel has trained extensively in ballet, contemporary and jazz, and was previously a company member of the Toronto-based Canadian Contemporary Dance Theatre. Additional training includes National Ballet of Canada, Steps on Broadway and PMT House of Dance. Outside of acting and dance, her multidisciplinary background includes writing, comedy/sketch comedy, gymnastics, acrobatics, singing and playing multiple musical instruments.

Neuspiel continues to be represented by Element Artist Management and Viewpoint.

title: FCC Chairman Warns Broadcasters That Airing “Fake Polls” Could Run Afoul Of “Regulatory Obligations”
summary: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr warned broadcasters on Wednesday about airing “fake polls” or “suppression polls,” once again threatening regulatory action for news content. Carr has talked previously about the media’s reliance on poll information, as President Donald Trump, who appointed him to the top FCC post, has often dismissed survey results that are unfavorable to […]
content:
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr warned broadcasters on Wednesday about airing “fake polls” or “suppression polls,” once again threatening regulatory action for news content.

Carr has talked previously about the media’s reliance on poll information, as President Donald Trump, who appointed him to the top FCC post, has often dismissed survey results that are unfavorable to him as “fake.”

Carr wrote, “Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis.”

He added, “The FCC takes these issues seriously. Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes. It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations. After all, the country benefits greatly when Americans can trust and rely on the media to report the news fairly and accurately.”

Watch on Deadline

During this election season, there has been a significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls designed to do nothing more than interfere with the regular functioning of the electoral process and alter the normal patterns of voter turnout and enthusiasm.



Many… — Brendan Carr (@BrendanCarrFCC) October 21, 2026

He did not cite specific examples. But on Tuesday, Wedgewood Polls released a statement admitting that it had fabricated results, even though its data had been used in polling averages by a number of outlets.

“Wedgewood Polling was never intended to sway an election or permanently mislead the public; it was designed as a wake-up call,” the company said in a statement. “If a fictional entity run by a small group of industry veterans can be integrated into major polling averages and cited by major news organizations, the standards for how polling data is vetted, aggregated and reported must change.”

Wedgewood released the statement after the site FiftyPlusOne contacted them about a story that questioned the authenticity of its polls.

The New York Times said that it included 15 polls released by Wedgewood from June to October.

The Times said in an editor’s note, “Before adding polls to its database, The New York Times seeks to confirm the validity of all new pollsters. In this case, the group answered a series of questions regarding the identities of the pollsters; the methods they were using to draw their sample, contact respondents and weight their polls; and the source of their funding. The group also responded to similar vetting questions from FiftyPlusOne and VoteHub, both of which subsequently included Wedgewood’s releases in their trackers.”

The FCC does not regulate print or digital media, and has limited authority over cable and streaming. It also was unclear which broadcasters featured Wedgewood polling. Carr wrote, “If broadcasters believe they should provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered, they can now take those actions consistent with FCC regulations.”

In explaining its news distortion policy, the FCC states that its authority over news content is “narrow,” given the First Amendment. The FCC states that when it comes to news distortion, broadcasters “are only subject to enforcement if it can be proven that they have deliberately distorted a factual news report. Expressions of opinion or errors stemming from mistakes are not actionable.” The agency’s broadcast hoax policy prohibits stations from broadcasting false information about a crime or catastrophe. The licensee had to have known that the information was false.

Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the FCC, wrote on X following Carr’s comment, “Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong. FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”

title: Janine Harouni Dates New YouTube Stand-Up Special ‘Man’oushe’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Comedian Janine Harouni will release her next special, Man’oushe, on YouTube on October 25th. Centered on the miscarriage of her first pregnancy, Man’oushe releases to coincide with Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month. The special also weaves together threads about Harouni’s Arab heritage, a surprising family DNA test, and the death of the show’s […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Comedian Janine Harouni will release her next special, Man’oushe, on YouTube on October 25th.

Centered on the miscarriage of her first pregnancy, Man’oushe releases to coincide with Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month. The special also weaves together threads about Harouni’s Arab heritage, a surprising family DNA test, and the death of the show’s director Adam Brace, who passed away suddenly during its creation.

Brace was an Olivier-nominated director, best known for his work on recent UK hits including Liz Kingsman’s One Woman Show, Leo Reich’s Literally, Who Cares, and Alex Edelman’s Emmy and Tony Award winner Just For Us.

Harouni performed Man’oushe at the Edinburgh Fringe while nine months pregnant, earning her second Edinburgh Comedy Award nomination. This made her one of the few comedians to receive back-to-back noms. Whereas Man’oushe was nominated for Best Show, her debut hour, Stand Up with Janine Harouni (Please Remain Seated), earned her a nomination for Best Newcomer.

Watch on Deadline

Harouni also performed Man’oushe Off-Broadway at the SoHo Playhouse in New York City. In addition to writing and performing, Harouni exec produced the special alongside husband Andrew Nolan. The show was directed for stage by Brace and Jon Brittian. This is the second special from Bad George, Harouni’s production company owned with Nolan, following Larry Dean’s Dafty, which sold to Sky One earlier this year.

A UK-based American stand-up, Harouni was named Comedy Champion on Netflix’s reboot of Star Search earlier this year. Her stand-up has been viewed over 250 million times on social media and gained her a following of over 850K.

Recently, Harouni wrapped a series regular role opposite James McAvoy in the Sky Original series Meantime, based on the novel by Frankie Boyle, which is slated for release in early 2027. She’s also appeared in Trying (Apple TV), Twenty Twenty Six (BBC), Bob’s Burgers (Fox), and The Batman (Warner Bros.), and is a regular on UK panel shows like Mock the Week, The Last Leg, and The Russell Howard Hour.

Touring the U.S. beginning in December, Harouni is repped by Curtis Brown and Levity Talent.

title: Meta’s Almost $10 Billion Legal Costs Take Huge Toll on Q3 Earnings, Wall Street Shrugs
summary: Meta’s $18 billion nationwide settlement with state attorneys general forced nearly $10 billion in additional costs for the company during its third quarter in 2026, missing Wall Street expectations even as its quarterly revenue was up 28%. The company’s revenue for the quarter hit $64.6 billion, up 26%, while its net income was $9.86 billion, […]
content:
’s $18 billion nationwide settlement with state attorneys general forced nearly $10 billion in additional costs for the company during its third quarter in 2026, missing Wall Street expectations even as its quarterly revenue was up 28%.

The company’s revenue for the quarter hit $64.6 billion, up 26%, while its net income was $9.86 billion, up 264%. Its earnings per share hit $3.83. Analysts polled by LSEG Data & Analytics expected the company’s revenue to hit $63.4 billion and earnings per share of $5.46.

Wall Street analysts didn’t seem to mind the lower EPS, however, as its share price was up 2% after market close.

Popular on Variety

“We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone – including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in a statement. “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board.”

The earnings report came hours after a New Mexico state judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company liable last month for deceiving users about Facebook‘s data privacy and content moderation policies. That ruling came after Meta reached an $18 billion settlement with 52 state attorneys general in August over claims that it designed Instagram with addictive features, knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms, and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms, among other claims.

The settlement saw Meta’s costs for the quarter balloon to $51.6 billion. The company said in its earnings release that its operating income would have jumped from $12.98 billion to $22.88 billion — had it not had $9.89 billion in costs from the settlement.

Meta’s third quarter saw the company effectively relaunch its AI efforts, including the introduction of its AI agent Muse, a Muse-infused gadget and a new suite of Meta-branded eyeglasses.

Meta introduced Muse last month, touting the agent as “the world’s first personal AI agent built for everyone.” The agent took center stage at its Meta Connect event last month, where it was given both an animated character to represent it and an infusion into several of the company’s software and hardware offerings.

More to come…

title: ‘ComicView: Rooftop Series’ Renewed for Season 2 at BET (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Keep on laughing: BET’s “ComicView” reboot has been renewed for Season 2. BET has ordered 20 more episodes of the revived stand-up franchise, which premiered in June as “ComicView: Rooftop Series.” Chris “CP” Powell returns as host of the program, which will see 60 comedians performing on a Hollywood rooftop. Veteran comics Affion Crockett, Cocoa […]
content:
Keep on laughing: BET’s “ComicView” reboot has been renewed for Season 2.

BET has ordered 20 more episodes of the revived stand-up franchise, which premiered in June as “ComicView: Rooftop Series.” Chris “CP” Powell returns as host of the program, which will see 60 comedians performing on a Hollywood rooftop.

Veteran comics Affion Crockett, Cocoa Brown, Lavell Crawford and Luenell join the Season 2 lineup alongside rising talent.

“I’m beyond proud and excited to be back at the helm for Season 2 of ‘ComicView: Rooftop Series,’” Powell said. “Season 1 was amazing, and this season promises to be even better, with bigger comics and even bigger laughs. BET being back at the forefront of stand-up comedy just feels right!”

Popular on Variety

“ComicView” first aired in 1992 as a nationally broadcast showcase for up-and-coming comics. The show became a pillar of Black comedy and a launchpad for talent that would go on to become huge names in stand-up, including D.L. Hughley, Sommore, Cedric the Entertainer and Bruce Bruce.

The series rotated hosts throughout its initial run from 1992 to 2008, and it was briefly revived in 2014. After a nine-year absence, the show returned in 2024 as a four-episode series hosted by Mike Epps, taped at Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat Weekend in Las Vegas.

“‘ComicView’ is part of BET’s DNA, and this rooftop proved our audience is still hungry for it,” said Aisha Summers-Burke, EVP, head of creative, BET Studios. “Season 2 puts a whole new class of comics in front of them, and there’s no one better than CP to hand them the mic.”

“ComicView: Rooftop Series” is executive produced by Jeru Tillman for Southfield Village Entertainment.

title: Poison Ivy DC Series in the Works at HBO With ‘The Penguin’ Exec Lauren LeFranc
summary: Another Batman villain may be getting their own TV series. A Poison Ivy TV show is in the works at HBO with “The Penguin” showrunner Lauren LeFranc as a producer, Variety has confirmed. LeFranc’s “The Penguin” marked the first live-action spinoff from a Batman movie, after Colin Farrell originated his villain in Matt Reeves’ “The […]
content:
Another Batman villain may be getting their own TV series.

A Poison Ivy TV show is in the works at HBO with “The Penguin” showrunner Lauren LeFranc as a producer, Variety has confirmed.

LeFranc’s “The Penguin” marked the first live-action spinoff from a Batman movie, after Colin Farrell originated his villain in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” in 2022. It aired on HBO in 2024 and became a hit with critics and fans for its gritty, gangster story. Farrell won an Emmy and Golden Globe for his lead performance, and the show nabbed several best limited series nominations.

Poison Ivy, the green femme fatale from the Batman comics, has never been the main focus of a movie or TV show, but she’s appeared in several live-action and animated DC titles. The classic villain has the ability to control plants and often controls people’s minds using seductive pheromones. She first arrived on the big screen in 1997’s “Batman & Robin” and was played by Uma Thurman. In live-action TV, she also appeared in “Gotham” and “Batwoman,” and she’s popped up in several animated shows like “Batman: The Brave and the Bold,” “The New Batman Adventures,” “Young Justice” and more. Recently, she was voiced by Lake Bell in “Harley Quinn” and played the titular character’s girlfriend.

Popular on Variety

The DC Universe is expanding this weekend with “Clayface,” focused on the shape-shifting Batman villain. It’s unconnected to Robert Pattinson and Reeves’ world, which is continuing in 2028 with “The Batman Part 2.” HBO will also air “The People vs. Gorilla Grodd,” a comedic, villain-focused spinoff from James Gunn’s “Superman” movie, sometime in 2027.

title: Anna Marsh on How Canal+ Group’s M&A Activity Helps ‘Challenge the Status Quo’ and Why ‘There’s Just No Room for Error’ in Fast-Moving Business
summary: After a busy year that’s seen the Canal+ Group complete a wave of acquisitions across two continents, Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+, insisted such moves have been instrumental in strengthening the position of the French media giant at a time of unprecedented industry disruption. […]
content:
After a busy year that’s seen the Canal+ Group complete a wave of acquisitions across two continents, Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+, insisted such moves have been instrumental in strengthening the position of the French media giant at a time of unprecedented industry disruption.

“It’s really important to have a fresh perspective. People that are going to challenge the status quo. Because the business is moving so fast,” said the New Zealand-born exec, who appeared in conversation at Rome’s MIA Market on Wednesday with MIA head Gaia Tridente.

“The audience is so tough that we constantly need to be looking at ourselves in the mirror. AI is emerging right now. We’ve got enormous consolidation in the U.S. Looking at the different ways that the borders between pay TV and free TV are colliding,” Marsh continued.

Popular on Variety

“There are so many questions to ask. Nobody has all the answers. When we’re able to expand, when we’re able to acquire new companies and enter into new territories, it’s truly enriching.”

Marsh was speaking in Rome on the heels of GREENLit, MIA’s flagship drama showcase, which offered an exclusive first look at four upcoming international series, among them “Gucci: Game Over,” a six-episode miniseries based on Allegra Gucci’s memoir that’s co-produced by Sky Studios and Lucky Red and distributed internationally by Studiocanal.

Marsh praised the series as a testament to “the culture, the courage, the history that Europe’s been blessed with,” while insisting to the assembled industry professionals in the room, “I think Europe has a great future when it comes to storytelling. And the depth of the stories that we can tell here is absolutely endless.”

The Canal+ Group acquired a majority stake in Lucky Red, the Rome-based distribution and production company, in February. It was the latest in a series of moves made by the French media conglomerate to expand its growing footprint. Earlier this year, the group acquired a 34-percent stake in UGC, the Paris-headquartered film studio that operates one of France’s leading cinema chains, and also completed a $2 billion takeover of South African pay-TV company MultiChoice.

That move helped to boost the Canal+ subscriber base to north of 40 million, more than half of whom are English-speaking, thanks to MultiChoice’s reach across the African continent.

“That just opens a wealth of opportunity,” said Marsh, who touted recent Canal+ and Studiocanal projects like “The Road Home,” an apartheid-era drama starring Cynthia Erivo, Thabo Rametsi and Guy Pearce which recently wrapped shooting in South Africa, and “Shadow Has Fallen,” a Canal+ original action series, whose third season wrapped in Cape Town.

“That’s a really strategic part of the group’s focus right now,” she said, of the company’s Africa expansion. “And you can really see how Studiocanal is at the heart of that strategy. If we, as Canal+, enter a new market with so much potential as South Africa, we have to have a strong content strategy.”

Another pillar in that strategy is Studiocanal Stories, a specialty label launched in 2024 that’s dedicated to book adaptations. Pointing to the blockbuster “Paddington” franchise as the company’s “biggest, most successful IP” to date — and one that “started as a book,” as she noted — Marsh stressed how optioning existing IP “allows us to relax a little bit” because it comes with a built-in audience.

“It does give confidence,” she said, “and it does allow us to put more money and more data behind the decision-making.”

Of course, when it comes to decision-making, some of the old metrics still apply — chief among them talent. That was certainly the case with “What Happens at Night,” an upcoming psychological horror adapted from Peter Cameron’s 2020 novel that’s produced by Apple Studios in partnership with Studiocanal.

Directed by Martin Scorsese — “one of the greatest cineastes of all time,” according to Marsh — and starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, Marsh said the film is as close as one can get in these uncertain times to what she described as “a bit of a slam dunk.”

Still, nothing is guaranteed, with Marsh admitting, “It is harder and harder to hit the bull’s eye.” “Audiences are becoming more and more difficult and their standards are constantly raising,” she said. Especially with Gen Z audiences, “there’s just no room for error.”

The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market runs Oct. 19 – 23.

title: Brandi Carlile to Receive Humanitarian Honor at National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards
summary: Brandi Carlile will be the recipient of the Los Angeles Press Club’s annual Visionary Award for Humanitarian Work, to be given out at the National Arts and Entertainment Journalism Awards Gala in December, the organization has announced. Carlile’s honor will be part of the dinner and awards show that takes place Dec. 6 at downtown […]
content:
Brandi Carlile will be the recipient of the Los Angeles Press Club‘s annual Visionary Award for Humanitarian Work, to be given out at the National Arts and Entertainment Journalism Awards Gala in December, the organization has announced.

Carlile’s honor will be part of the dinner and awards show that takes place Dec. 6 at downtown L.A.’s Millennium Biltmore. About 800 working journalists and guests gather in the historic Crystal Ballroom for a night in which competitive awards are given out to reporters, critics and photographers covering the arts, along with a handful of lifetime achievement honors for major arts figures as well as journalists.

Also set to be celebrated that night is KCRW’s Madeleine Brand, who will receive the Luminary Award for Career Achievement in Media. Brand has hosted the popular “Press Play” for the station since 2014 and has worked in the public radio sphere for more than 30 years. Other honorees will be announced in the days to come, the Press Club said.

Popular on Variety

The Visionary Award was first given out at the National A&E Journalism Awards Gala in 2012, to Jane Fonda, with Robert Redford presenting it to her. Last year, it went to Seth Rogan and Lauren Miller Rogen in honor of their charitable work. Others who have received it over the years include Quincy Jones, Tiffany Haddish, Diane Warren and Forest Whitaker.

“We are excited to have Brandi Carlile as this year’s Visionary Awardee,” said Los Angeles Press Club President Danny Bakewell, Jr. “Her work is amazing and, during these troubling times, desperately needed. Topical songs like ‘The Joke,’ ‘Human’ and ‘Church & State’ have spoken to her vision for social justice, as well as providing a showcase for one of the great voices in contemporary music. Her eagerness to reach out has led her to collaborate closely with figures like Elton John and Joni Mitchell, but that spirit isn’t just reserved for her heroes; it’s her compassion for society’s underdogs that has most touched millions of listeners.”

Earlier in October, Carlile appeared at the Grammy Museum in L.A. for a conversation with Cameron Crowe and a full-band performance to mark the one-year anniversary of her eighth studio album, “Returning to Myself.” She just released a deluxe companion version of the album with all of the original tracks reimagined in stripped-down arrangements, archly titled “Returning to Myself (Sad Gay Version).” Carlile and her longtime band members Phil and Tim Hanseroth recently wrapped up their first headlining tour in U.S. arenas, named the “Human Tour” after one of the key songs on the latest album. In November, they will briefly move back into theaters for the immediately sold-out tour dubbed “Burn the Setlist (The All-Request Tour)” before resuming the “Human Tour” in Europe in early 2027.

On the philanthropic side, Carlile has dedicated a portion of her ticket sales to fund her grassroots organization, the Looking Out Foundation, which has granted more than $10 million to community-based nonprofit organizations working to support humanitarian causes across the globe. Carlile has bolstered these efforts through the creation of her wine club, XOBC Cellars, which was created in part to send proceeds to the Looking Out Foundation, “helping them to defend the rights and joys of refugees, immigrants, the LGBTQIA2S+ community and more.” Early in the “Human Tour,” she livestreamed “Be Human: A Concert for Minneapolis” (now viewable on YouTube), which raised over $750,000 for Minnesota’s The Advocates for Human Rights to help families and individuals affected by ICE.

title: Meta Tops Q3 Revenue Estimates, But Earnings Hit By Teen Lawsuit Settlement; Stock Split Creates Class C Shares
summary: Meta’s third-quarter revenue beat Wall Street expectations, but earnings took a hit from the company’s settlement of a lawsuit filed on behalf of teenage social media users. Revenue for the July-to-September period set a new record at $64 billion, beating the consensus forecast of analysts of $63.3 billion. Earnings per share of $3.83 also beat […]
content:
‘s third-quarter revenue beat Wall Street expectations, but earnings took a hit from the company’s settlement of a lawsuit filed on behalf of teenage social media users.

Revenue for the July-to-September period set a new record at $64 billion, beating the consensus forecast of analysts of $63.3 billion. Earnings per share of $3.83 also beat estimates, but without the legal expenses they would have surged to $7.40.

The settlement in the case, reached last August, provides for payments to the plaintiffs and others of up to about $18.59 billion. For the quarter, the company said its report of costs and expenses includes a $9.89 billion charge related to the agreement.

Along with the financial results, the company said it is effecting a 2-for-1 stock split and creating a new set of Class C shares. The new stock will start trading in January 2027 and will be offered to existing shareholders. Proceeds from the new issue will help fund the company’s aggressive spending on artificial intelligence.

Watch on Deadline

After long struggling to assert the same dominance it has in social media in the booming field of AI, Meta has finally gained traction with the recent launch of the well-received virtual assistant Muse. It also launched a frontier model, Muse Wonder, designed to help the offering gain more scale.

title: Everything We Know About Greta Gerwig’s ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ So Far
summary: A new Narnia movie approaches, directed by none other than Barbie (2023) helmer Greta Gerwig. The film will adapt The Magician’s Nephew, the first book in C.S. Lewis’ beloved series, The Chronicles of Narnia. It will first arrive in theaters before streaming on Netflix later next year. Read on for everything we know about Greta […]
content:
A new Narnia movie approaches, directed by none other than Barbie (2023) helmer Greta Gerwig.

The film will adapt The Magician’s Nephew, the first book in C.S. Lewis’ beloved series, The Chronicles of Narnia. It will first arrive in theaters before streaming on Netflix later next year.

Read on for everything we know about Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew film:

When will Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew come out in theaters?

The film is slated to release in theaters February 12, 2027. It was originally going to go theatrical in November 2026 over Thanksgiving weekend, but then Netflix moved to give the film a wide release ahead of its arrival on the streamer April 2.

Watch on Deadline

Is there a trailer for Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew?

Yes, a trailer has been released, watching Campbell and McKenna hop worlds set to Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven” in the first successful licensing for the rock song. The duo meets Jadis, dressed in a silvery disco ball-like dress. Viewers see Aslan, but Streep’s voice is not heard in the trailer. Another voice opens the trailer and closes it, sounding like that of Irish actor Ciarán Hinds.

RELATED: ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ Trailer Clocks 481M+ First-Week Views, More Than ‘Barbie’

Deadline exclusively reported the views clocked by the first clip, which add up to more than 481.3 million, in its first week.

Who is in the cast of Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew?

Newcomers David McKenna (Netflix’s Lord of the Flies) and Beatrice Campbell will star as Digory Kirke and Polly Plummer, the two children at the center of the story. Daniel Craig will portray Uncle Andrew Ketterly, the eccentric uncle who identifies as a magician. Carey Mulligan will play Mabel Kirke, mother of Digory and sister to Andrew. Emma Mackey will portray Jadis, who eventually becomes the White Witch originally portrayed by Tilda Swinton in the 2005 The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion The Witch & The Wardrobe.

Emma Mackey in ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ Netflix

Meryl Streep will, in fact, voice Aslan the lion, which had been rumored for some time.

“I wanted someone who was profound but not pretentious, who had gravitas but not morose self-seriousness,” Greta Gerwig told Empire of her decision in casting Aslan. “Someone who could communicate depth and pathos as well as joy and delight.”

RELATED: Greta Gerwig On Why She Chose Meryl Streep To Voice Aslan In ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’

“I wanted someone who was older than 70, so there was a wisdom of experience, but who also had the capacity of fresh wonder, like a child. And also to be one of the greatest actors to ever do it. That list is not a long one,” Gerwig added.

What is The Magician’s Nephew about?

The 1955 novel is the origin story of The Chronicles of Narnia, in which Digory and Beatrice get tricked into using magic rings by Uncle Andrew. The rings transport them between worlds where they witness the birth of Narnia by Aslan as well as accidentally awaken the White Witch, Jadis.

Who else is behind Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew movie?

The film is produced by Mark Gordon, Amy Pascal, Vincent Sieber-Smith and Gerwig. The executive producers are Patricia Whitcher and Douglas Gresham and Melvin Adams for the C. S. Lewis Estate. The film is co-produced by Christine Crais.

RELATED: Greta Gerwig On Securing Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven” For ‘Narnia’ Trailer: “They Too Love C.S. Lewis”

title: Kid Cudi To Direct, Write & Star In Basquiat Movie: “A Love Letter To Jean, The 80s & NY City”
summary: One of the greatest artists of the 20th century is coming to the big screen again from one of the 21st century’s true hyphenates. Kid Cudi revealed on his Instagram on Wednesday that he will write, direct and star in a film about the life of Jean-Michel Basquiat. “For years people have asked me about […]
content:
One of the greatest artists of the 20th century is coming to the big screen again from one of the 21st century’s true hyphenates.

Kid Cudi revealed on his Instagram on Wednesday that he will write, direct and star in a film about the life of Jean-Michel Basquiat.

“For years people have asked me about playing Jean Michel Basquiat in a film,” the Man on the Moon performer posted this morning. “But no project actually came to be. This year, I finally said f*ck it, ima write it myself.”

“This film will be a love letter to Jean, the 80s and NY city,” Cudi added of the acclaimed (and now bestselling) Basquiat, who died in 1988 at age 27. “Jean has inspired me all through out my career, and it will be the biggest honor to tell his story in a way we haven’t seen before.”

The still-unreleased The Collaboration from director Kwame Kwei-Armah notwithstanding, it’s not like we haven’t seen a plethora of Basquiat documentaries and features over the decades.

Watch on Deadline

At the same time, with support from the likes of Jay-Z and other deep-pocket collectors, we’ve also seen Basquiat’s work rocket to the top of the sales charts. Not that Basquiat wasn’t successful during his lifetime, but that was nothing compared to what his paintings and other works rake in nowadays. In 2017, Basquiat’s Untitled from 1982 was sold for a then-record $110.5 million.

More recently, Andy Warhol and Jackson Pollack pieces have sold for more, but Basquiat remains a key and pricey American artist for collectors and museums.

In that context, not only did Grammy winner and Doe director Cudi (aka Scott Mescudi) unveil the “filming 2027” Jean, but also revealed some starling wardrobe takes of himself as Basquiat. No disrespect to Jeffrey Wright’s breakout performance in 1996’s Basquiat from Julian Schnabel, but Cudi clearly captures the essence of the artist — as the pics he posted show.

Already having announced a “horror/thriller” sophomore directorial feature in August, Cudi faced backlash last month after appearing onstage in Chicago with old pal Kanye West. In response, Cudi defended himself and to some degree West, who among antisemitic statements and other controversies released a pro-Hitler song last year.

“He was dealing w mental health struggles for years and now he’s good,” Cudi posted in the early hours of September 4. “Everyone deserves some grace when they family. I was the hardest on him out of anybody. I held him accountable. He apologized and it was sincere.”

On the flip side, Cudi was quick to cut M.I.A. loose in May from his tour in support of his Free album. At the Dallas stop of the tour, M.I.A. complained about being “canceled for being a brown Republican voter,” and then added, “I can’t do ‘illegal,’ though some of you could be in the audience.”

Cudi said in the aftermath: “I didn’t want anything offensive at my shows,” and M.I.A was M.I.A.

Back on the big screen, we now know Cudi’s second film as a director is entitled Wrong Number. In production in L.A., the Cudi-penned project co-stars Mile End Kicks alum Barbie Ferreira as Deadline’s Matt Grober exclusively reported last month.

As for Jean, take a look at Cudi’s post from today below.

title: Los Angeles On-Location Production Declines Again Even As California’s Tax Incentive Heavily Backs Remaining Projects
summary: On-location production is still declining in the Los Angeles area, even if California’s Film & Television Tax Credit Program is propping up much of what’s left. Per the latest report from FilmLA, on-location filming accounted for 4,171 shoot days from July through September 2026, which is a 4.8% decrease from the same period last year. […]
content:
On-location production is still declining in the Los Angeles area, even if California’s Film & Television Tax Credit Program is propping up much of what’s left.

Per the latest report from FilmLA, on-location filming accounted for 4,171 shoot days from July through September 2026, which is a 4.8% decrease from the same period last year. However, the organization also finds that the state’s tax incentive is accounting for about 40.3% of scripted, on-location production during that time — nearly doubling the share from a year ago.

Television is benefitting the most from incentivized productions. Projects that were accepted into the program made up 62% of all TV comedy shoot days and 49.4% of TV drama shoot days (up from 19% and 20.6%, respectively) during the same time last year.

This doesn’t quite tell the full story, since television production, particularly on comedies, often largely takes place on soundstages, which are not captured in this data. Soundstage occupancy also remains far below the levels it once maintained a decade ago.

Watch on Deadline

Incentivized TV series that shot in L.A. last quarter included A Hundred Percent (Netflix), Baywatch (Fox), Mr & Mrs. Smith (Amazon), Shrinking (Warner Bros. TV/Apple TV+), High Potential (ABC), The Night Agent (Sony Pictures Television/Netflix), Tracker (CBS), I Love LA (HBO), and Rooster (HBO).

Feature films finished the third quarter with 533 shoot days, a marginal 2.1% increase from the same period last year. Incentivized projects account for 24.4% of that total, the majority of which are independent. However, there are a few studio films in the mix including 13 Going on 30 (Netflix), Cut Off (Warner Bros.) and They Follow (Neon).

Commercials marked the largest decline, down 15.9% to on-location 562 shoot days during the third quarter, although those are not covered by California’s tax credit program.

On-location production in Los Angeles has been on a decline for years, and the trend has continued despite California’s massive efforts to expand the state’s tax incentive program last year. Not only did lawmakers raise the cap to $750 million annually, the revamped bill also significantly expanded program eligibility. Granted, this quarter’s decline is smaller than Q2’s 13% slip.

title: Hur Jin-ho Thanks Singapore Festival for Protecting Freedom of Expression as ‘The Assassin(s)’ Opens, SGIFF Chair Boo Junfeng Says: ‘We Refuse to Show Anything That Has Been Censored’
summary: South Korean director Hur Jin-ho thanked the Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) for defending freedom of expression as his political thriller “The Assassin(s)” opened the festival’s 37th edition on Wednesday, two weeks after the Korea’s conservative opposition asked SGIFF to pull it. “I am truly grateful to the film festival for protecting artistic freedom and […]
content:
South Korean director Hur Jin-ho thanked the Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) for defending freedom of expression as his political thriller “The Assassin(s)” opened the festival’s 37th edition on Wednesday, two weeks after the Korea’s conservative opposition asked SGIFF to pull it.

“I am truly grateful to the film festival for protecting artistic freedom and the freedom of expression in cinema, and I believe this decision by the festival will give great courage to those of us who made this film, including myself, the staff, and the actors,” Hur said as the end credits rolled.

The gala screening took place at the Sands Theatre at Marina Bay Sands, as the smoke haze that has hung over Singapore in recent weeks, carried from fires in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan, lifted slightly.

Popular on Variety

On Oct. 6, the People Power Party (PPP) wrote to SGIFF executive director Jeremy Chua on behalf of all 109 of its lawmakers, asking the festival to reverse the selection. The festival kept the film, and in an Oct. 7 statement said it had been chosen “through SGIFF’s independent curatorial process for its artistic merit and contribution to contemporary Asian cinema.”

Festival chair Boo Junfeng, the Singaporean director of Cannes selections “Sandcastle” and “Apprentice,” told the opening-night audience that the team had been flooded with messages from a group in South Korea pressing it to cancel the screening, and had also received many notes of support. “SGIFF has carefully considered the various arguments put forth, and we see the film as an artistic interpretation of historical events, and we respect the creative vision of the makers behind it. Therefore, we stand by our decision to have the film as our opening,” Boo said.

He also thanked Hur and his team “for making their way here to join us despite the pressures back at home.”

“We have a no-cut policy. We refuse to show anything that has been censored, because we believe films should be seen as their makers had intended, and nothing should alter their vision,” Boo said.

Boo called the direct link between a filmmaker’s vision and a paying audience a legacy that the festival’s founders fought to secure and that the current team means to protect.

“It is not always easy to remain steadfast in the face of pressure, but I suppose choosing the path of least resistance isn’t quite in our DNA,” he added.

“The Assassin(s),” which opened in Korea on Sept. 23, returns to Aug. 15, 1974, when first lady Yuk Young-soo, wife of then-President Park Chung-hee, was shot dead at the National Theater during a Liberation Day ceremony. Yoo Hae-jin stars as a police inspector who sees the attack and heads the inquiry. Park Hae-il plays a senior newspaper editor and Lee Min-ho a cub reporter. Investigators at the time held gunman Mun Se-gwang solely responsible, claiming he was working for North Korea and for Chongryon, the Japan-based association of pro-Pyongyang Korean residents. Hur’s film stops short of naming a culprit, and its critics argue that the open ending implicates Park or his government.

In its letter, the PPP argued the film distorts history “in a manner that runs deeply counter to public sentiment in the Republic of Korea.” The party cited a survey in which 58.2% of respondents said the film distorts history, along with objections from Park Ji-man, the son of Park and Yuk, and from foundations linked to the couple.

“Nowhere in the film is any specific individual defined as being behind the incident, and the film’s hypotheses and dramatic settings are not presented as historical fact,” the film’s producers said in a Sept. 28 statement.

The dispute had already disrupted the film’s festival outing at home. The Busan International Film Festival called off a career talk with star Lee Min-ho, and distributor Hive Media Corp. pulled the cast and crew from all Busan appearances on safety grounds, while a conservative activist group said it would picket Yoo’s home every day. A former PPP Seoul city councilor has also asked police to investigate Hur, Hive Media CEO Kim Won-kuk and the film’s two writers for defamation, and the Directors Guild of Korea and Producers Guild of Korea have both spoken out against the targeting of those who worked on the film.

On stage in Singapore, Hur said the 1974 shooting took place when he was in fifth grade and had stayed with him as among the darkest chapters of Korea’s modern history. “Regarding that incident, there were discrepancies between what was officially announced at the time and the actual facts that came to light later on. I wanted to craft that aspect into a pursuit thriller format, which is why I chose to make this film,” he said.

Kim, who joined Hur on stage, has worked on four consecutive films with the director: “The Last Princess,” “Forbidden Dream,” “A Normal Family” and “The Assassin(s).” He said Hur’s “Christmas in August” was one of his favorite films long before the two met. “Whenever we work together, he is a director who places immense value on details – details regarding human nature as well as the details of the incidents,” Kim said.

Present in the audience were Indian superstar and filmmaker Aamir Khan, and celebrated Asian director Peter Chan Ho-sun, both of whom will deliver masterclasses at the festival on Thursday.

SGIFF runs through Nov. 1.

title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Producer Rodrigo Teixeira Set for GLAFF’s First Visionary Award, Presented by Wagner Moura (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Two-time Oscar-nominated producer Rodrigo Teixeira will receive the inaugural Árbol de la Vida Visionary Award at the GuadaLAjara Film Festival (GLAFF), the Los Angeles offshoot of the Guadalajara International Film Festival, on Nov. 6. The honor will be presented by Oscar-nominated actor Wagner Moura ahead of a screening of James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which Teixeira […]
content:
Two-time Oscar-nominated producer Rodrigo Teixeira will receive the inaugural Árbol de la Vida Visionary Award at the GuadaLAjara Film Festival (GLAFF), the Los Angeles offshoot of the Guadalajara International Film Festival, on Nov. 6.

The honor will be presented by Oscar-nominated actor Wagner Moura ahead of a screening of James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which Teixeira produced. The award recognizes individuals who have made a lasting impact on cinema and strengthened the ties between Latin America and the international film industry.

Teixeira will also serve as the first mentor of the GLAFF Co-Production Lab, a new industry initiative developed with the Guadalajara International Film Festival (FICG) to foster co-productions between Mexico and the United States.

Popular on Variety

“Rodrigo Teixeira has built a career defined by bold storytelling and a true commitment to artists across the border,” says Ximena Urrutia, executive director of GLAFF. “As inaugural mentor of our New Mexico-U. S. co-production lab, he will help emerging filmmakers turn ambitious cross-border projects into lasting partnerships.”

For more than two decades, Teixeira has bridged Latin American and global filmmaking through his production company RT Features, whose credits include “Call Me by Your Name,” “The Lighthouse,” “The Witch” and “Invisible Life.” He earned best picture nominations for “Call Me by Your Name” and Walter Salles’ “I’m Still Here,” which won the Oscar for international feature. Films from his banner have collected nine Oscar nominations and six Golden Globe nominations.

“Paper Tiger” marks the third collaboration between Teixeira and Gray, following “Ad Astra” and “Armageddon Time.”

The 16th edition of GLAFF runs Nov. 5-7 in Los Angeles, opening with Diego Luna’s “Ashes” and closing with Eddie Sánchez’s “Mexicanamerican.”

title: Olivia Cooke on Returning to ‘Slow Horses,’ On-Set Injuries and That Shocking Finale Cliffhanger: ‘I Want a Showdown!’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains plot details from “Judgement Day,” the Season 6 finale of “Slow Horses,” now streaming on Apple TV. “Hello, River.” Those two fateful words announced Olivia Cooke’s return to “Slow Horses” after a four-season absence from the Apple TV spy drama. Cooke’s MI5 agent Sidonie Baker made a brief but […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains plot details from “Judgement Day,” the Season 6 finale of “Slow Horses,” now streaming on Apple TV.

“Hello, River.”

Those two fateful words announced Olivia Cooke’s return to “Slow Horses” after a four-season absence from the Apple TV spy drama. Cooke’s MI5 agent Sidonie Baker made a brief but memorable appearance in Season 1, forging a flirty chemistry with inept spy River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) before dying from a gunshot wound to the head — or so River thinks.

Sid’s resurrection wasn’t a total surprise to “Slow Horses” fans: the character comes back in author Mick Herron’s namesake novels, and Apple made little secret of her storyline in the advance promotion for Season 6, which concluded this week. But enough has changed since Cooke’s first stint on the show to make her re-joining the ensemble an event in itself. First, “Slow Horses” itself grew into a hit, with a raft of Emmy nominations (plus a few wins) and an avid audience to show for it; meanwhile, Cooke’s own career has taken off thanks to a leading role in the fantasy epic “House of the Dragon.”

Popular on Variety

That star power is on full display throughout Season 6, which sees Sid and River on the run from Russian sleeper agents over one incredibly stressful night. Icy MI5 head Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas) — who once planted her favored mentee Sid in Slough House, a kind of purgatory for screwup agents, as her eyes and ears — used Sid’s identity as a cover for an off-the-books assassination on Russian soil, and now the Kremlin is out for revenge. All of the Slow Horses (a not-so-affectionate nickname for Slough House employees), past and present, are targeted, and Sid goes to River for help.

The pair’s winding route from River’s late grandfather’s country house to Diana’s beach retreat, which Slough House head Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) cheekily appropriates as a safe house, is a winding one. Sid and River barrel through a barn, an arcade, and finally an airstrip where Sid is nearly shipped off to Russia as an unwilling sacrifice on their way to a long-awaited first kiss. This being “Slow Horses,” though, their triumph is short-lived: River helps Sid escape and nearly reunites with her at his grandfather’s house, but collapses from an apparent poisoning in the kitchen while she showers upstairs in the season’s final moments.

“River has kept her going, in a sense,” Cooke says now of the star-crossed lovers. Speaking with Variety from the U.K., the actor shared what it’s been like to dive back into the deep end with over a month of night shoots, from an unlikely injury to her collaboration with Lowden.

Courtesy of Apple TV

Your character comes back in the books, but I’m sure when you were first filming, it wasn’t certain we would get to this point. Did you know there was a chance you would return?

We shot [Season 1] towards the end of 2020. It was one of the first projects back after lockdown. I don’t know if the book had come out yet where I make my return, but there were whispers of it. I don’t know. It was such an uncertain time, and it was the first series as well. It just felt, like, an eon away. Who would have thought it would have gone on for so long?

But they kept me abreast of all the things that were going on story-wise over the years. I’ve been admiring from afar, and biding my time. I’d get messages from Jack being like, “You’re coming back!” and I’m like, “Fantastic, when?” And no one could really give me a clear answer. I remember seeing Saskia [Reeves], who plays Standish, at the theater, and she was like, “You coming back? And I was like, “I would love to. I just don’t know. I have no clear answers.” We were all just in a cloud of mystery for a bit.

During that time, what was it like for you to watch this show that you were once a part of, but weren’t for a while?

Really fun, but tinged with jealousy. Because I experienced it, you know? Even though we were all masked up and socially distanced from each other and the crew when we weren’t in the scenes, it was such a fun, charmed environment that I was just desperate to get back to. And it’s so palpable — watching Season 2, 3, 4, 5 — just how much fun everyone’s having on set. It really just glows through the screen. So it’s always bittersweet. I love watching them, and I love seeing how good all my friends are, but I’m also incredibly jealous as well that they’re all having fun without me.

I imagine that, as an actor, having to return to a character that you left behind is a challenge. Is there any work or preparation that you did to reassume this role?

I had to remind myself how I sounded, like what accent I was doing. I had to check back in with that. But also, it was quite nice, because Sid is coming back in a very jaded way. Both her and River have grown up mentally in the interim. They’ve been away from each other, and the events that led up to Sid’s disappearance were really traumatic. So I had a bit of rope to not honor the more jovial, happy-go-lucky version of Sid that we saw in the first season.

We don’t get a lot of detail about what the last three years were like for Sid, because there’s a lot happening in the present. Do you have your own sense of that backstory?

I was asking Adam [Randall], the director, a lot about that. We thought that she’d been in a rehabilitation facility that is kept under wraps by MI5. It’s for ex-spies, ex-Joes, and she’s had to learn how to walk and talk again, basically. It’s been an incredibly lonely process that has, I think, cauterized a part of her, in some non-descript location. We were thinking maybe Cumbria, if you know of it. Sort of like the the Vermont of England — very green, but you can get lost in the landscape. I think it’s just been a very long road of recovery, and also of introspection for her.

You mentioned the FOMO earlier, so I’m also interested in what it was like for you to actually step back into the set. I’m sure the non-COVID version of the show feels different.

Well, it was pretty much the same crew, and also it’s a lot of the same crew that does “House the Dragon” as well. Like on off seasons with “Slow Horses,” there’ll be people that do dailies and things on “House the Dragon” and vice versa. So I know everyone quite well. It was really lovely. It’s like the best high-school reunion possible. As if you went to a high school and everyone’s your friend, which I don’t think is a reality for anyone. It was just really joyous, even though we shot it right before the December break, in the middle of winter, all night shoots for five weeks, because they truncated all my stuff.

Courtesy of Apple TV

I was going to ask about that too — the nocturnal nature of it. I sort of loved it. Adam has this energy about him where it sometimes feels a bit run-and-gun, which I love. And if a particular stunt doesn’t work out, or when we get to the set, the material doesn’t quite match with how the workings of the set are, he’s like, “All right, let’s figure this out. Let’s improvise.” It’s so lovely for me as an actor, too, because I feel like there’s a real energy to that. It did just feel like we were making an independent film for five weeks, because the majority of my stuff was just with Jack and Adam.

Your storyline this season is almost entirely two-handers with Jack. What’s he like as a collaborator?

He’s my favorite type of man, which is a very silly man. It’s wonderful acting with him, because he just chucks you a curveball, and then you try and grab it. It makes me feel like I’m stretching my mind in ways that I don’t usually get to do with doing this job. And he’s so fun! He wears it very lightly. He’s such a good actor. He’s very funny, and doesn’t take it too seriously either. Which I love, because sometimes, with other male actors, they take it very serious.

In addition to the night shoots of it all, there’s a lot of action on the show. Were there any particularly tricky sequences?

There were, but the one thing that actually did me in was just running. There’s a lot of scenes where I’m just running alongside Jack, who is twice as tall as me, and my 5-foot-5 arse is just desperately trying to keep up. It was like 2 in the morning, and we were being chased by a Land Rover. You’re stretching, you’re trying to keep warm, but I think I’d been a bit static for too long, and we set off and I just felt both thighs go snap. I pulled both of my quad muscles really, really badly. For two weeks, I was hobbling around. Just from a run! But then I thought to myself, “When was the last time I got chased?” Since I was like 12!

You’ve gotta have your people page Tom Cruise’s people and be like, “How do I run onscreen?”

Literally! Climbing fences, shooting, being on the back of a moving truck while there’s all these fire and gas canisters going off — but just running really, really did me in.

I was curious about the barn interlude. I can’t imagine being in a barn full of smelly cattle for hours on end.

The thing is, you can’t really do anything about it. You just have full acceptance 20 minutes in, and get used to it. But we were moving around in and amongst a lot of cows, which was quite scary, actually. They’re really big, and they can kick! I was just remembering old horror stories about people being killed by a stampede of cows, just walking across a field, and I was like, “I’m so close to them!” But it was fine, no one died.

The other action moment that really stood out for me is when you’re on the truck and kicking the oil drum, and it explodes. That looks tricky.

That was a crazy, crazy sequence, just trying to dispose of the Russian agents who had come to collect me, and running and jumping on the truck and then Jack just doing donuts around a plane. And you know, Jack does all his own driving stunts! It was very impressive. That was so fun, so cathartic. I love kicking things, and then having this big old stunt where it blows up — it felt like our own Jason Bourne moment.

Courtesy of Apple TV

In addition to the action, Sid has a whole emotional trajectory. She seems reluctant for most of the season to accept just how ruthless Diana Taverner has been with her. Why do you think Sid clings to that so much?

Because Sid thinks, ultimately, that Diana saved her by getting her out of the hospital, by putting her into some specialized rehab. I think she does genuinely think that she’s only here, she’s only alive because of Diana Taverner. So there’s, I think, some real Stockholm syndrome going on with her. Also, she’s only ever experienced one side of Diana, which has always been very collegial. I think Sid has liked how impressed Diana’s been with her in the past, and hasn’t seen this steely, ruthless side to her that everyone else has experienced.

How do you think she feels once she speaks to Diana on the phone and can’t deny what’s happening anymore?

It’s incredibly clarifying, and almost a relief to know that this is the truth — the cold, hard truth. This person thinks that I’m dispensable, that I’m a pawn in whatever game that Diana is trying to play. Knowing that her life could be forfeit so easily — I think through the shock of it — she’s almost giddy. Like, “Oh shit, this is all so obvious to me now.” She kind of has nothing to lose from that point on, because it’s like, “Well, I’m gonna die regardless, going on this plane with these people, so I might as well just try to get out of here.”

You and Jack have great comedic chemistry. But because it’s a spy show, and especially because of what happens at the end of the season, you’re also meant to be questioning everyone’s motivations all the time. Do you have your own read on how Sid feels about River, and how sincere those emotions are?

I think despite herself, especially in the first season, her feelings for River have really caught her off guard. I think there’s a genuine connection — this tiny little pinhole of light. River has kept her going, in a sense. Even if they didn’t really get to know each other that well, whatever she’s projected onto River, and the reason why she seeks him out, is because there is something there that has been fizzing for a very, very long time. Especially in the absence. I think those things only get bigger when they’re unresolved, and she’s been so adrift for so long.

I was devastated by the cliffhanger. I can’t believe I have to wait an entire year to find out what happened.

I know, I know!

Are you someone who reads the books, both to find out what happens with your character and maybe see what happens down the road?

In the interim, I hadn’t read the books, but I read for the season that is about to come out, just because I was like, “Surely I’m coming back!” But [Mick Herron] is such a brilliant writer, and he’s so acerbic, and sometimes it’s not faithfully adapted, but they’re really good companions to each other.

Obviously, you can’t tell me anything too specific about the future on the show, but the one thing I was very bummed out by is that we actually don’t get you and Diana face to face in this season. Do we think that might happen in the future?

I hope so! I want a showdown. With Kristin Scott Thomas, I think she’s a wonderful actor. I could watch her endlessly. So selfishly, I want that for me, for my dear diary. But yes, it feels like that is a very cathartic thing that must happen.

title: ‘Glee’ Reboot: Who’s Coming Back? Will Rachel Sing Olivia Rodrigo? How MAGA Is Sue? And More Fan Questions
summary: What have we missed on “Glee”? For six glorious, terrifying seasons from 2009 to 2015, we witnessed Ryan Murphy bring a fever dream to life. With each new episode, the musical dramedy series’ unique blend of satire and earnestness had girls, the gays and their allies pondering: What song that should be sung by Mercedes […]
content:
