A lot can happen in a decade – and it’s likely that not all our beloved Gleeks will be returning to William McKinley High’s dingy halls. But it seems that Lea Michele wouldn’t miss this opportunity for the world, especially since reviving her career from bullying allegations with rave reviews in “Funny Girl” (just as Rachel Berry would do). Though Disney hasn’t officially confirmed it, Variety has learned from multiple sources that Michele’s return is already guaranteed. Additionally, Heather Morris and Chord Overstreet, who play Brittany Pierce and Sam Evans, have made social media posts that seem to indicate they’ll be back as well.

For everyone else’s fate, here are our best educated guesses.

Naturally, Jonathan Groff will make a cameo as Jesse St. James, as he is Michele’s real-life bestie. Darren Criss is probably another sure get, given that he still performs much of Blaine Anderson’s “Glee” material live. Chris Colfer, who played Blaine’s beau Kurt Hummel, said two weeks ago that he’d “heard nothing” about a potential reboot — but then, over the weekend, Colfer and Criss reunited to sing the “Glee” version of “Baby It’s Cold Outside” in London. Coincidence? We think not. Though Colfer has kept quite a low profile since the series, finding success as a bestselling children’s book author instead of pursuing showbiz, now could be the time for him to shimmy back into the spotlight.

Elsewhere, Harry Shum Jr. (who played Mike Chang), seems to be a lock as he is currently enjoying a renaissance tearing up the dance floor on “Dancing With the Stars” — another Disney-produced show, and perhaps an intentional tie-in. And Matthew Morrison, who has become a TikTok meme with his hilariously earnest cameos, would probably love nothing more than to reprise Mr. Schue.

We’d say the same of Jane Lynch, though it may depend on the direction of her character – is the political incorrectness of Sue Sylvester too much for these dark times? (More on that later.)

Speaking of which, Kevin McHale has previously expressed hesitancy to reprise his role of Artie Abrams as he “shouldn’t be playing a character in a wheelchair.” However, as news of a reboot began bubbling up in recent weeks, McHale has appeared more open, telling People: “I could never say no to that.”

What about Dianna Agron, who played pregnant and slightly evil cheerleader Quinn Fabray? While she hasn’t been very present on TV since “Glee,” Agron is making her return on HBO’s upcoming final season of “Industry.” It again may come down to character direction, as we could see Agron wanting to leave Quinn in the past in favor of more mature roles — and there were rumors back in the day of a feud between her and series creator Murphy.

Also more uncertain are Amber Riley (Mercedes Jones) and Jenna Ushkowitz (Tina Cohen-Chang). Riley has also kept fairly out of the spotlight and hasn’t publicly spoken about a potential reboot (though we would love to hear her voice again, trust). Ushkowitz still attends “Glee” conventions and speaks about her time on the series, so she seems more likely.

title: Alexander Skarsgård on His Wacky ‘Wicker’ Red Carpet Looks: From Clear Shoes and a Multicolored Skirt to a Gray Wig Inspired by Co-Star Olivia Colman
summary: Alexander Skarsgård knows how to make an entrance. The Swedish actor has been turning heads with his wacky red carpet looks while promoting his new fantasy romance “Wicker.” At the London premiere earlier this month, he donned a metallic gold Saint Laurent suit. If that wasn’t bold enough, he slipped into a pair of clear […]
content:
Alexander Skarsgård knows how to make an entrance.

The Swedish actor has been turning heads with his wacky red carpet looks while promoting his new fantasy romance “Wicker.”

At the London premiere earlier this month, he donned a metallic gold Saint Laurent suit. If that wasn’t bold enough, he slipped into a pair of clear plastic lace-up shoes.

“They were surprisingly comfortable, and I was worried that they would steam up in five minutes, but that actually didn’t happen,” Skarsgård told me Saturday at the Academy Museum Gala. “But I’ve been getting a lot of comments from friends and family about my little piglets sticking out. They make fun of me. They make fun of my feet.”

Popular on Variety

Alexander Skarsgård says his clear shoes at the “Wicker” premiere were “surprisingly comfortable”: “I was worried they were going to steam up in five minutes.”#AcademyMuseumGala pic.twitter.com/EBivFxYpnU — Variety (@Variety) October 18, 2026

At the “Wicker” premiere in Los Angeles on Tuesday, Skarsgård wore a multicolored skirt and a whimsical black shirt adorned with his co-star Olivia Colman’s face from London fashion house Chopova Lowena. “We’ve been on a press tour for a couple of weeks, and now we’re in L.A., and it’s our final big premiere before the movie opens on Friday,” he said. “I wanted to wear something special for this lovely lady over here, Olivia, whom I adore.”

As for the purple and green skirt, Skarsgård said, “It’s very comfortable. It’s quite a hot night, and it’s light and breezy. I’m enjoying it.”

Earlier in the day, he shocked attendees at a SAG-AFTRA screening and Q&A when he arrived in a long gray wig. “I got a little jealous because everyone is complimenting Olivia on her beautiful hair and beautiful hair color,” Skarsgård said. “I got no love for my hair. As a narcissistic actor, I need a little bit of attention, so I threw on a beautiful gray wig to match Olivia today.”

“Wicker” co-star Elizabeth Debicki praised Skarsgård’s fashion choices. “He can do no wrong,” she said. “I love the man. What can I say? I’m biased.”

In “Wicker,” Colman plays an outcast in a medieval town who falls in love with a man made of wicker (Skarsgård). Debicki plays a housewife who burns with jealousy over the attention the townspeople give to Colman and Skarsgård’s characters.

Skarsgård’s wicker look was a practical costume created by the Wētā Workshop in New Zealand, with lead makeup effects artist Sarah Rubano, prosthetic designer Joe Dunckley and lead weaver Jasmin van Lith.

“Amazing,” Colman said of seeing Skarsgård in the costume for the first time. “We’d seen backward and forwards from Weta Workshop in New Zealand images for about 18 months, and so suddenly he puts it on, and we were all going, ‘Oh God, I hope it works.’ And he came out of the makeup trailer and went, ‘Oh God, it’s beautiful.’”

Olivia Colman says it was “amazing” to see Alexander Skarsgård in his wicker costume: “It’s beautiful.” pic.twitter.com/lFnjEnvZ5p — Variety (@Variety) October 21, 2026

“Wicker” is in limited release starting Oct. 23 before expanding on Oct. 30.

title: Oscar Nuñez, Marlene Forte, Otmara Marrero & Vivian Ruiz To Star In Adrian Cardenas’ Directorial Debut ‘In An Orderly Fashion’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Writer Adrian Cardenas is making his directorial debut with the film In an Orderly Fashion, which just completed production in Miami with Oscar Nuñez (The Office, The Paper), Marlene Forte (The Rookie, Star Trek), Otmara Marrero (Florida Man, StartUp), and Vivian Ruiz (Bloodline, Pain & Gain) in lead roles. In an Orderly Fashion follows Rafa […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Writer Adrian Cardenas is making his directorial debut with the film In an Orderly Fashion, which just completed production in Miami with Oscar Nuñez (The Office, The Paper), Marlene Forte (The Rookie, Star Trek), Otmara Marrero (Florida Man, StartUp), and Vivian Ruiz (Bloodline, Pain & Gain) in lead roles.

In an Orderly Fashion follows Rafa (Nuñez), a devoted physical therapist who dreams of traveling the world in retirement. But on the first day of freedom, he’s rewarded with a terminal illness. Chaos ensues when he asks the unthinkable of his beloved nurse wife, Aida (Forte): to put him out of his misery, so long as he doesn’t know when it’s coming.

Marrero stars as Gabriela and Ruiz as Maria.

Watch on Deadline

“Making this movie in my hometown of Miami with Oscar, Marlene, Vivian, and Otmara was a dream,” shared Cardenas, who before taking his talents to Hollywood was a Major League Baseball player for the Chicago Cubs. “I’m grateful the script resonated with them and that they trusted me to guide them as they so skillfully navigated the tonal tightrope between dark comedy and drama. Their talent and generosity extended beyond their performances, setting the tone for a cast and crew that became family in the process.”

Adrian Cardenas Ricardo Betancourt

In an Orderly Fashion is produced by Maria Altamirano and executive produced by Heidi Stolte, Chris Stolte, Sven Voelcker, Ann Lewnes, Daniel Weiser, Sharon Greene, Nuñez and Forte. Tyler Bagley, Barker Carlock, and Derrick Nevot co-produce.

Nuñez is represented by Omnipop Talent Group and Artists & Representatives. Forte is represented by BRS/Gage and Rothman Andres Entertainment. Marrero is represented by Luber Roklin Entertainment. Cardenas is repped by Range Media Partners.

title: Mark Kermode & Daphne Dentz On Restoring ‘Ken Russell’s The Devils’: “There’s A Balance Between The Grain, The Dirt, The Vibe And The Look”
summary: If you don’t ask, you don’t get, and that’s what Mark Kermode discovered over 20 years ago while trying to put together the definitive version of Ken Russell’s badly butchered 1971 film The Devils. Thanks to Kermode’s sleuthing, not only did the missing moments turn up, but it also resulted in the one of the […]
content:
If you don’t ask, you don’t get, and that’s what Mark Kermode discovered over 20 years ago while trying to put together the definitive version of Ken Russell’s badly butchered 1971 film The Devils. Thanks to Kermode’s sleuthing, not only did the missing moments turn up, but it also resulted in the one of the surprise hits of the year; this week the film expands on its planned one-week run after taking $1,725m — a $4,925 per-screen-average — from 350 locations across North America. Next weekend, it opens in its native UK just in time for Halloween.

Unusually for a restoration project, The Devils wasn’t just given a hi-res make-over, it was restored to the original version that Russell handed to Warner Bros. and never saw again, first thanks to the timorous British censor and then the much more scissor-happy MPAA. Based on Aldous Huxley’s 1952 non-fiction book The Devils of Loudon, about a notorious series of demonic possessions alleged to have occurred in the French town in 1634, it was controversial enough for its time, even though nobody ever got to see its most infamous scene, in which naked, rampaging nuns run riot and defile a statue of Jesus Christ.

Russell always believed the scene was missing, never to be found, and, for a time, so did Kermode, until, while snooping around in the Warners archive, he came across a set of shipping logs. One stood out: It was labeled “C-cut 86”.

Watch on Deadline

“At that point,” says Kermode, “I thought that the missing sequence was maybe 86 seconds long and maybe ‘C-cut’ meant ‘Censor cut’.” The archivist, however, wasn’t so sure. “He said, ‘I don’t know, but I’m pretty certain it’s not what you’re looking for.’ I said, “OK. I’ll make you a deal. If you call it in and it isn’t what we’re looking for, I’ll never bother you ever again.’ God bless him, he called it in, and then I got a phone call. He said, ‘OK. The canister came in. We opened it. It smelt of vinegar, so we’ve sent it to be washed. But I looked at the first frame, and it’s just a huge crucifix and there’s a load of nuns…’”

Grandier and Sister Jeanne in ‘Ken Russell’s The Devils’ Warner Bros. Clockwork

In 1971, Ken Russell’s name was synonymous with controversy, and for years the missing scene was presumed to be an act of gratuitous provocation. But in 2004, when Kermode — with the help of the film’s original editor, Michael Bradsell — put together a very rough DigiBeta Director’s Cut, with Russell’s blessing, audiences saw that the scene was far from gratuitous. Rather, it is pivotal to the film’s story, in which rival political forces manipulate the fantasies of a disturbed nun, Sister Jeanne (Vanessa Redgrave), to discredit Loudon’s popular incumbent priest Urbain Grandier (a literally smoldering Oliver Reed).

Notes Kermode, “Ken had always said that the whole point of the film is that it’s a film about brainwashing. It’s about the use of hysteria as a political tool, and the film is very clear about that. I think, as people recognize today, it’s very satirical in the way that it deals with politics and it’s incredibly contemporary. But that sequence was really important to him, because what it was demonstrating was that, in the middle of this apparently religious enclave, all this is being played out for the simple political end of getting Grandier out and getting the walls of the city knocked down. He said the whole point is that it’s a kind of a pantomime of blasphemy, and if you take it out, you never quite get that point across.’ That sequence is, in the very best sense of the word, hysterical.”

So, how did Mark Kermode’s rough-edged DigiBeta assembly become the luminous restoration that proved to be the hottest ticket in Cannes this year? And where does Guillermo Del Toro come into it?

To find out, Deadline spoke to Daphne Dentz, Senior Vice President of Post-Production Creative Services at Warner Bros. Discovery.

DEADLINE: When did you come on board with this project?

DAPHNE DENTZ: I guess it was January [2026], when Christian Parkes reached out to me. I’d never met him before. He was like, “We really want to restore The Devils and do the Director’s Cut. What do you think about that?” There was also the content licensing team; there’s a woman named Robyn Sklaren over there, and she was a huge proponent of getting this greenlit. I think it was sort of a combination of that and Christian’s enthusiasm, which is completely infectious. He’s incredible. It was like the stars aligned, and that was it. Then my team — the preservation team started researching and looking for assets. Luckily, we had everything — so we just went for it.

DEADLINE: What do you mean by assets?

DENTZ: We have a preservation services team, and they’re really experts as regards everything that relates to film assets and sound and audio assets. They went into the archive and scoured for every piece of film. Luckily we had the original camera negative. We had separation masters. We also had deleted scene reels, A/B reels, and that was the piece that was needed. Initially, we weren’t sure we had everything, but we did.

DEADLINE: Is that common? Mark Kermode was saying even Ken Russell didn’t think these things existed…

DENTZ: Well, I oversee the Global Media Archive, and I have to say that Warner Bros. — and this is just not me touting the Warner Brothers philosophy — our archive is pretty solid. We’ve spent 100 years preserving our assets, and I would say that over the last 10, 15 years, there’s been an even more aggressive attitude around preserving and archiving our assets. We’ve got good tools in place to search. We have a film prep team that literally sits in a room on the studio lot and goes through camera negatives and documents every frame and shot that exists in the OCN [Original Camera Negative]. Essentially, what we did was we pulled the original camera negative and those deleted scenes or those reels, and they went through it, frame by frame, identifying what we had. Then with, the 2004 DigiBeta that we received, our digital conform operator Katie Largay, frame by frame, rebuilt this film.

Derek Jarman’s set design for ‘Ken Russell’s The Devils’ Warner Bros. Clockwork

DEADLINE: What’s the first thing you do in approaching a project like this?

DENTZ: Well, the first part of the process is the research. The second part is the film prep and the sound prep. Then, once we have what we think is all the elements, we start scanning. We’ve got the best scanners in the world. We scanned at full 4K 16-bit, and our colorist, Andrea Kleebach, is amazing. All those scans went into our digital intermediate bay at Water Tower Color, and we just started analyzing it shot by shot. I have to say, when we saw those first scenes, we cried. We couldn’t believe our eyes. The original camera negative was in such good shape. People have never seen this film look as good as it does today.

DEADLINE: Did you refer to Ken Russell’s other films? How much was he a part of this reconstruction?

DENTZ: Well, it’s an interesting question — may I read something to you? Really, the best way to describe it is the way the colorist described it, because the real challenge was honoring the film’s original aesthetic. We didn’t have a clean visual record of what this film looked like on its first day in the theater. The way she described it is so perfect. She said, “The previous restoration we don’t believe reflected Ken Russell’s or [cinematographer] David Watkins’ intent. It couldn’t serve as a North Star… Reference materials couldn’t be trusted. Colorists look for a fingerprint of the filmmaker across other works.”

It’s detective work. Then, she said, she basically read descriptions about how the film felt to watch [at the time]. Words like, “hallucinogenic”, “bleached” and “Caravaggio” became creative parameters. I mean, this is one of those very special cases where you have a cinematographer who’s shot the most beautiful scenes and composed the most beautiful aspects. Every shot looks like a museum portrait. At least to me, that’s how it felt. And Derek Jarman’s production design is spectacular.

DEADLINE: Did you reconstruct it strictly according to the template of what Ken Russell had laid down with the DigiBeta version? Or were there other things — like a shooting schedule or a continuity schedule — that you were looking at as well?

DENTZ: We looked at everything we had. It’s interesting, because our original camera negative was sort of an auto-select, and in the 2004 version, there were a lot of changes. I can get into that a little bit here, which may be helpful. Here’s what our conform artist said. She said, “Multiple reels contained redundant or alternate version scenes that differed from the approved director’s cut reference.” The Rape of Christ sequence, for example, was discovered on a separate role labeled “Deleted scenes” and substantially overlapped with Reel 5 of the OCN while also containing extraneous material not present in the director’s cut and omitting certain shots included in that version. All scanned OCN materials were systematically lined up against the director’s cut reference to identify editorial variances and maintain a comprehensive inventory of missing footage.

DEADLINE: Do you approach a project like this in chronological order? Or is there an element of just taking things as you find them?

DENTZ: Well, the reels are conformed, and it’s typical that you would start from Reel 1 and then just work through. All the material is sent for dirt cleanup, but we also are very sensitive around making the film look new. There’s a balance between the grain and the dirt and the vibe and the look of the film, in terms of keeping it authentic while creating an asset that’s modern — 4K, HDR, SDR, or for digital cinema — because we didn’t have digital cinema back in ’71. Keeping all those elements balanced is an art.

DEADLINE: Is that the case with all restorations? How do you calibrate the amount of grain and the amount of dirt that you allow back in?

DENTZ: Well, it’s a great question, and it varies. We think we’re experts at our scan department. They really know film stock, and so there’s an element of understanding what the film stock of the day would look like, and the grain structure of a film from the ’70s versus the ’80s and ’90s. I mean, we do so many films at Warner Bros. from the ’30s, like The Wizard of Oz, to The Devils, and then to things that are a little bit more recent, like Se7en, for example. Now, in this particular case, we didn’t have [the original] filmmakers to come in and tell us, “This is what the film should look like.” But Guillermo [Del Toro] did come and sit with us. I don’t want to speak for him, but he was very enthusiastic about what he was seeing.

DEADLINE: Could you expand? What was Guillermo’s role?

DENTZ: He came in and reviewed the work with our colorist. We always need help. We always are looking for some direction. Andrea is really, like I said, a detective. We looked for one-sheets and things that were on the internet. Then Guillermo came in, and one of the things he was very interested in was the tiles in Derek Jarman’s production design — the whites, and how difficult it is to achieve the whites in a film like this. He blessed it. He came in and he said, “Yep. You’re on the right track — this looks the way that it should look.”

DEADLINE: The print that was screened in Cannes looked like a movie one might have watched in the ‘70s before the print became degraded after doing the rounds of too many cinemas.

DENTZ: That’s so wonderful to hear, because we’re so close to it now, it’s hard for us to see. The goal is always to honor the aesthetic, the creative intent, and to not waver in that and to stay true to what we think Ken Russell would’ve wanted. We’re really careful.

DEADLINE: What appeals to you about this work?

DENTZ: This particular film appeals to me on so many levels. I mean, the first thing is just from the most basic sense of the beauty of it. I felt like every shot — even the ones that are kind of grotesque — is incredible. It’s a beautifully shot film, and I have spent my whole career looking at images in dark rooms. When the first shot opens, you’re just pulled right into this world of incredible cinematography and incredible production design. The first film I ever saw that I can remember was Ken Russell’s film Women in Love. [Laughs.] I was probably three or four years old, and my mother took me to the theater! She probably shouldn’t have, but it was late at night, and I think she thought I was going to sleep through it. She just recently passed away, and I wish that she could have seen this. She didn’t know that we were going to do The Devils, and I think she would’ve been thrilled.

DEADLINE: Do you have a dream project that you’d like to restore?

DENTZ: This was a dream project. This really is a dream project because it has all the elements of never been seen or haven’t been seen in this form ever really. I mean, the folks at Cannes, they saw this film in a way that I don’t think anyone had ever really seen this film before, in 4K resolution. For sound, we had only a mono track, and we’ve done our best with that — in some cases, we had to create sound using multiple assets and elements. But for sure, seeing it in the theater is spectacular, it really is.

title: Cory Michael Smith Joins Scarlett Johansson In ‘Scapegoat’ At Square Peg And A24
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Cory Michael Smith is the latest to join the ensemble cast of Ari Aster’s next thriller Scapegoat, starring Scarlett Johansson. The film also stars Jacob Elordi, Jude Law, Ella Purnell, Caleb Landry Jones and Samba Schutte. Aster is directing from a script he wrote. A24, who has released Aster’s past four films, is the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Cory Michael Smith is the latest to join the ensemble cast of Ari Aster‘s next thriller Scapegoat, starring Scarlett Johansson. The film also stars Jacob Elordi, Jude Law, Ella Purnell, Caleb Landry Jones and Samba Schutte. Aster is directing from a script he wrote. A24, who has released Aster’s past four films, is the distributor.

Aster and partner Lars Knudsen will produce through their Square Peg banner.

While the plot is being kept under wraps, some have speculated it’s about a doctor who operates on an internet-famous person. Others say it’s sci-fi romance, and some have said it’s more of a traditional drama for Aster. As of now, there is no consensus on the movie’s details, according to insiders.

Deadline first reported earlier this year that this would be Aster’s next film after the director had taken his time deciding on what would be his follow-up to Eddington.

Watch on Deadline

Smith is coming off his acclaimed performance in the HBO movie Mountatinhead, which also starred Steve Carell and Ramy Youssef. He can currently be seen opposite Dakota Fanning and Jake Johnson in The Sun Never Sets.

Next up, he has the A24 pic Slayground from director Jeremy Saulnier. That film bows January 29. He Is repped by UTA and Circel M&P.

title: Jane Levy Temp-Checks ‘Evil Dead’ Fans About Potential Franchise Return: “Let’s Call Sam Raimi Right Now”
summary: Three movies later, Jane Levy is teasing Evil Dead fans about a potential return for her character Mia Allen after she survived the bloody events of the 2013 reboot. During a post-screening Q&A for the Fede Álvarez-written/directed horror film, which was hosted by Contra Celluloid, the actress appeared to fuel recent rumors that she will […]
content:
Three movies later, Jane Levy is teasing Evil Dead fans about a potential return for her character Mia Allen after she survived the bloody events of the 2013 reboot.

During a post-screening Q&A for the Fede Álvarez-written/directed horror film, which was hosted by Contra Celluloid, the actress appeared to fuel recent rumors that she will reprise her character for the 2028 prequel Evil Dead Wrath or a future installment in the Sam Raimi franchise.

“I have a question. Do you guys think Mia should come back to Evil Dead?” she asked in a video from the Q&A, igniting applause from the audience. “OK, I was just checking. That’s all.”

Levy then joked, “Let’s call Sam’s Skype number right now and see if he wants Mia to come back.”

Watch on Deadline

Raimi’s original trilogy included The Evil Dead (1981), Evil Dead II (1987) and Army of Darkness (1993), with star Bruce Campbell reprising his role as Ash for a cameo in Álvarez’s 2013 reboot, in addition to leading the Starz series spin-off Ash vs Evil Dead (2015-’18).

With Lee Cronin’s Evil Dead Rise (2023) steering the franchise in a new darker direction, the horror continued this summer with Sébastien Vaniček’s Evil Dead Burn.

Next, Francis Galluppi’s Evil Dead Wrath will premiere April 7, 2028. The film is a prequel to the original movie, set in 1972, which producer Robert Tapert described as “another great departure” from the franchise.

title: ‘Petal Dance’ Director Ishikawa Hiroshi Ends 13-Year Feature Hiatus With ‘The Blue We Touch’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Japanese filmmaker Ishikawa Hiroshi, whose credits include “Tokyo.sora,” “Su-ki-da.” and “Petal Dance,” is back with his first feature in 13 years. His new film, “the blue we touch” (original title: “Awo no Jo”), is in post-production and will be released in Japan in 2027 by Bitters End, which unveiled the project ahead of the Tokyo […]
content:
Japanese filmmaker Ishikawa Hiroshi, whose credits include “Tokyo.sora,” “Su-ki-da.” and “Petal Dance,” is back with his first feature in 13 years. His new film, “the blue we touch” (original title: “Awo no Jo”), is in post-production and will be released in Japan in 2027 by Bitters End, which unveiled the project ahead of the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s TIFFCOM market.

The ensemble drama centers on a pair of former friends and traces the hard-to-name feelings that pass between people. Nao heads the cast as Mitsu, 29, who does contract web design and wants a permanent job, along with a chance to make work that connects with an audience. She is drawn to Fujino (Nakajima Ayumu), who runs HR at her firm, and slowly starts to share grievances she has kept quiet about for a long time.

Karata Erika plays Ayane, who works nights while preparing for a career as a public prosecutor. She crosses paths with Tomoki (Aoki Yuzu), an art student who can’t get his figure drawing right, and agrees to sit for him as a model. The arrangement opens up Tomoki’s work, while Ayane finds her way back to memories she treasures.

Popular on Variety

Nakano Arisa, who made her screen debut in Wim Wenders’ “Perfect Days,” plays Nozomi, a classmate of Tomoki’s who watches him change up close.

Ishikawa handled writing, directing and editing duties. He won awards as a commercials director before moving into features with “Tokyo.sora” in 2002. “Su-ki-da.” followed in 2006 and earned him best director at the New Montreal FilmFest, with “Petal Dance” arriving in 2013. His work is known for its careful handling of color and its feel for the mood of ordinary days.

Nao’s earlier films include “The Last 10 Years” and “Sensei’s Pious Lie.” Karata has appeared in “Asako I & II,” “Desert of Namibia” and Netflix’s “The Queen of Villains,” while Nakajima’s credits span TBS’ “Until the T-Shirt Dries,” “Happyend” and “Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy.” Aoki’s résumé includes “5 Centimeters per Second,” “Blue Lock” and “Minamata.”

Bitters End has been active for more than three decades, releasing films in Japan by Hamaguchi Ryusuke, Bong Joon-ho, the Dardenne brothers, Jia Zhangke, Roy Andersson and Gianfranco Rosi. Its recent releases include “Below the Clouds,” “Young Mothers” and “The Odyssey.”

On the production side, the company’s credits include Oscar winner “Drive My Car” and Locarno Golden Leopard recipient “Two Seasons, Two Strangers.” This year, “All of a Sudden,” which took a prize at Cannes and is Japan’s Oscar submission for international feature, played in competition, and “All the Lovers in the Night” made the Un Certain Regard lineup.

Bitters End is now growing its international sales operation. “In My Father’s Room” competed at San Sebastián, where it took the Fipresci Prize and the Ateneo Guipuzcoano Award.

title: Ranbir Kapoor, Yash Epic ‘Ramayana: Part One’ Sets Pay-Per-View Release on JioHotstar After Theatrical Run
summary: Nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana: Part One,” starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, will be available to buy on demand from streamer JioHotstar in India after its theatrical run. The deal between JioHotstar and Prime Focus Studios will see the film sold as a separate on-demand purchase on the platform. The companies described it as the first pay-per-view […]
content:
Nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana: Part One,” starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, will be available to buy on demand from streamer JioHotstar in India after its theatrical run.

The deal between JioHotstar and Prime Focus Studios will see the film sold as a separate on-demand purchase on the platform. The companies described it as the first pay-per-view offering of its kind on JioHotstar. The film will stream in the best quality each supported device can handle.

The epic, starring Ranbir Kapoor, Yash and Sai Pallavi, follows exiled prince Rama (Kapoor) and his consort Sita (Pallavi) through exile into catastrophe, as Sita’s abduction at the hands of Ravana (Yash) sets in motion an epic war between righteousness and evil. Sunny Deol plays Hanuman and Ravie Dubey Lakshman. Arun Govil, Lara Dutta, Rakul Preet Singh, Vivek Oberoi, Kunal Kapoor and Kajal Aggarwal round out the cast.

Popular on Variety

The film opens worldwide on Nov. 5, in time for the Diwali festival holiday, in the Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and English languages. Imax 3D is among its formats. Sony Pictures Entertainment is releasing the film globally. The film’s Indian distribution will be handled by media personality Karan Johar’s Dharma Productions.

“’Ramayana’ is one of India’s greatest civilizational treasures – a story that has shaped our conscience, inspired our imagination, and guided the way we live for centuries,” said Nita M. Ambani, chair of JioStar. “As India enters a new era of storytelling, we have an extraordinary opportunity to carry our cultural legacy forward. At JioHotstar, our vision is to use technology to bring the finest stories within reach of every Indian. It is our privilege to present this grand cinematic vision of ‘Ramayana’ to families across the country, and introduce a new generation to its eternal values of duty, love, courage, and goodness.”

Prime Focus Studios is producing with DNEG, the visual effects and production company that has won eight Oscars, and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations. “Ramayana” is a live-action project in two parts, with Shridhar Raghavan adapting Valmiki’s epic for the screen.

Namit Malhotra, the producer and filmmaker who founded DNEG and serves as its CEO, said he believes the film should be watched on the largest screen available, in Imax 3D.

“But our country’s cinema infrastructure cannot reach everyone who holds this epic close,” Malhotra said. “’Ramayana’ belongs to every Indian, and our ambition must reflect that. JioHotstar has time and again shown how technology can bring a nation together through its sports and entertainment offering. That made them a natural partner to take Ramayana into people’s hands and living rooms, after its theatrical run.”

The film brings in Oscar winners Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman as composers. Ravi Bansal and Ramsey Avery handled production design, and Terry Notary and Guy Norris oversaw the action. The film was designed with Imax and other premium large formats in mind, and the production mixes Indian and international talent.

title: Vietnamese Whodunit ‘Karaoke Murder’ Sets Record With Same-Weekend Opening on Four Continents (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Vietnamese whodunit “Karaoke Murder” will open in cinemas across North America, Europe, Australia and Asia on the same weekend, a first for a film from Vietnam, according to its backers. The film, titled “Án Mạng Karaoke” in Vietnamese, will bow nationwide at home on Oct. 30. U.S.-based specialty distributor 3388 Films will release it that […]
content:
Vietnamese whodunit “Karaoke Murder” will open in cinemas across North America, Europe, Australia and Asia on the same weekend, a first for a film from Vietnam, according to its backers.

The film, titled “Án Mạng Karaoke” in Vietnamese, will bow nationwide at home on Oct. 30. U.S.-based specialty distributor 3388 Films will release it that same weekend in the U.S., Canada, the U.K., France, Germany, Norway, Australia and New Zealand, landing in time for Halloween. 3388 Films holds exclusive international rights in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, Japan and Taiwan.

“Karaoke Murder” is Hoang Le’s first film as director. Director-producer Vo Thanh Hoa of 89s Group serves as creative director, with Mai Bao Ngoc producing. 89s Group and F35 Studio are the production companies. The ensemble cast includes Doan Thien An, Thanh Son, Dai Nghia, Van Dung, Phuong Dung, Tieu Bao Ngoc, Tuyen Map, Quynh Ly, Ta Lam and Trinh Thao.

Popular on Variety

Set on a mountain pilgrimage taken by a group of neighbors, the film follows a former journalist who has to put her old investigative skills back to work after a widely loathed, karaoke-obsessed tycoon is killed overnight. With the group cut off from the outside world, suspicion falls on everyone.

Thien A. Pham, founder of 3388 Films, said the company had previously distributed titles on four continents as part of their international rollouts. “Aligning an international release with a film’s local date is a significant breakthrough moment. It’s what we’ve advocated for years because we believe greater momentum can be generated for international films when local and international release dates sync up,” Pham said. “It’s energizing to have gutsy partners, like the producers of ‘Karaoke Murder,’ as 3388 Films continues to redefine possibilities for Asian films.”

The producers said they built the story around karaoke because of the place it holds in Vietnamese life. Singing sessions are part of weddings, birthdays and Lunar New Year, as well as ordinary Sunday afternoons, and nearly every household owns a speaker and microphone. The pastime also causes friction. Vietnam penalizes noise after 10 p.m., karaoke ranks among the most common causes of rows between neighbors and news outlets report karaoke disputes ending in tragedy every year, according to the producers.

“We’re proud – but above all, grateful,” said Vo. “For years, our belief has been simple: ‘win at home first – then travel with your own voice.’ We make films for Vietnamese audiences before anyone else.”

Vo said 89s Group’s films had grossed more than VND600 billion ($23 million) at the Vietnamese box office between 2023 and 2026. “That foundation gives us the confidence to step onto the world stage – not by imitating others, but with our own voice,” Vo said. “I hope the Vietnamese diaspora will feel a little piece of home when they watch ‘Karaoke Murder.’ And I hope international audiences leave the theater a little more curious about Vietnamese cinema – and perhaps a little more careful the next time they pick up a microphone.”

3388 Films has specialized in Asian content for more than 20 years. Its recent releases include “Mai,” the first Vietnamese film to cross $2 million at the North American and European box office.

title: Iron Maiden’s Nicko McBrain Rejected an Invite to Golf With Trump, Says He Should Be ‘Put in Jail’: ‘I’m Not Amused by the Narcissism’
summary: Nicko McBrain, the long-time drummer for heavy metal band Iron Maiden, recently admitted he’d been invited to play golf with Donald Trump, but turned down the offer because of his staunch anti-MAGA beliefs — and that the president and his “bunch of cronies,” in McBrain’s words, “should be put in jail.” Like Trump, McBrain resides […]
content:
Nicko McBrain, the long-time drummer for heavy metal band Iron Maiden, recently admitted he’d been invited to play golf with Donald Trump, but turned down the offer because of his staunch anti-MAGA beliefs — and that the president and his “bunch of cronies,” in McBrain’s words, “should be put in jail.”

Like Trump, McBrain resides in Florida, and in a recent interview with the Telegraph, said a friend of his “who’s a massive Republican” asked, “‘Oh, do you want to come and play golf with us? With the president,’” said McBrain. “And I said, ‘You fucking what?’… and I just said, ‘No.’ No mate.”

He continued: “I’m not politically inclined, although I must be because I have my thoughts about him. I’m not amused by the narcissism, and all this kerfuffle about the Epstein files and whatnot, and especially the debauched war that he’s put on Iran.” McBrain went on to add that Pete Hegseth is “going to be put in prison.” “My last word on Trump and his bunch of cronies is, they should be put in jail,” he concluded.

Popular on Variety

McBrain’s autobiography “Hello Boys and Girls!” hits shelves Thursday, and is described as a “thrilling, hilarious and deeply personal autobiography,” per publisher HarperCollins. “With trademark humor and heart, Nicko takes readers behind the scenes of one of Britain’s biggest ever bands… This is the story of what it feels like to remain not just relevant but more loved than ever after decades at the top, and to live a life transformed by music, brotherhood and belief.”

The band announced earlier this month it will set off on the third and final leg of its 50th-anniversary “Run for Your Lives” tour, beginning in April and concluding in May. They will close this leg with two festival headlining performances at Sonic Temple and Boardwalk Rock.

In April, Iron Maiden was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as part of the class of 2026. The official induction ceremony is set for Nov. 14 at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

title: White House Correspondents’ Association Decries Trump Team’s “Retaliation” After POTUS Lashes Out At Reporter
summary: White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich said that the Trump administration was engaged in retaliation by blocking a journalist’s access because the president was upset over his questions. Heinrich, senior White House correspondent for Fox News, said in a statement on Wednesday, “The White House Correspondents’ Association strongly objects to the decision to restrict […]
content:
White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich said that the Trump administration was engaged in retaliation by blocking a journalist’s access because the president was upset over his questions.

Heinrich, senior White House correspondent for Fox News, said in a statement on Wednesday, “The White House Correspondents’ Association strongly objects to the decision to restrict a journalist’s coverage simply because the president didn’t care for their questioning. That is retaliation. The American public’s right to an independent press depends on reporters being able to do their jobs without fear that challenging the president will cut off their access.”

Heinrich’s statement followed a Semafor report that Andrew Feinberg, correspondent for The Independent, had been told by the White House that he no longer would be print pooler on Trump’s trip to South Carolina on Wednesday evening.

Watch on Deadline

On Tuesday, Feinberg was part of the pool in the Oval Office as Trump took questions from reporters following his announcement of a new fraud tip line where whistleblowers could collect up to $30,000, or 1% on commissioners, for exposing government fraud. He asked Trump about the False Claims Act, a law that has been on the books since the 1800s that allows them to collect much higher sums, up to 25%.

When Feinberg tried to ask additional questions, Trump lashed out at him. He said to Feinberg at one point, “What is wrong with you? Are you a sick person?” Vice President JD Vance posted on X that Feinberg was an “imbecile” and the White House rapid response account called him a “mongoloid moron,” a slur. Feinberg did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump lashed out again on Wednesday when taking questions on his way to Marine One heading to the South Carolina trip. He called CNN’s Kaitlan Collins “a low-IQ person” and told her, “You’re a dummy.” He also called a reporter for ABC News “a stupid person.”

A White House spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Feinberg defended his questions in an account posted on The Independent website and wrote, “For the record, I had an annual physical earlier this month, and I can report I’m in perfect health. I was doing my job, and I’ll be right back at it tomorrow.”

Last year, the White House took control of who was selected to be in the press pool rotation after years in which the WHCA determined the scheduling.

title: Netflix Co-CEOs Address Executive Shakeup & Layoffs In Town Hall, Talk Up New CCO Peter Rice’s Experience Across Platforms — Including Streaming
summary: A day after Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters faced anxious investors on the company’s Q3 earnings call after reporting mixed financial results, the duo on Wednesday faced anxious staffers at a town hall meeting after laying off 1,000 and shaking up the executive ranks by replacing Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria with Peter […]
content:
A day after Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters faced anxious investors on the company’s Q3 earnings call after reporting mixed financial results, the duo on Wednesday faced anxious staffers at a town hall meeting after laying off 1,000 and shaking up the executive ranks by replacing Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice and also ousting head of film Dan Lin.

The one-two punch of the layoffs on Wednesday, followed by the Bajaria exit on Thursday, which Netflix employees found out about from the press before the news could be communicated internally, was reportedly brought up at the town hall meeting, with Peters indicating job cuts were over for the foreseeable future.

Watch on Deadline

Like on the earnings call the day before, Sarandos touted incoming CCO Rice, who we hear was not at today’s town hall as he officially starts next week.

In his absence, Sarandos spoke enthusiastically about Rice’s background, echoing his comments on the earning call.

“He’s one of the really rare people in the industry who’s led TV networks, movie studios, streaming services. His creative instinct and his business acumen are remarkable. He’s really an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment, network, prestige cable, streaming, theatrical and TV films and live sports,” Sarandos said Tuesday, making a point to stress twice that Rice’s background extends beyond film and TV — areas he is mostly known for through his stints as President of Fox Searchlight Pictures during the era of Slumdog Millionaire and Little Miss Sunshine, CEO of Fox Networks Group and Chairman of Walt Disney Television.

That general perception led to some comments following Rice’s appointment last week about him coming from traditional media to the largest streamer without streaming experience.

While it is not extensive, Rice does have some streaming background. His experience is more extensive than Bajaria’s when she originally joined Netflix, Zack Van Amburg and Jamie Erlicht’s when they took over Apple TV, and Jennifer Salke’s when she took the reins of Amazon MGM Studios.

Rice spent time on the Hulu board. And, for almost three years, from 2019 when his top lieutenant at the time (and eventual successor) Dana Walden took oversight of Hulu Originals until his 2022 ouster, he also signed off on greenlight decisions for a string of buzzy Hulu series such as Only Murders in the Building, Dopesick, The Dropout and The Great. In that role, he also worked with FX topper John Landgraf on transitioning the cable brand to streaming with viral series like The Bear and backed risky big-budget bets that became streaming hits in FX’s Shōgun and Disney+’s Percy Jackson, while also using his Searchlight connections to get the Summer of Soul documentary on Hulu ahead of its awards run, an effort capped by an Oscar win.

Even if Rice didn’t have streaming experience, his hire has still been cheered by producers and talent reps due to his creative credentials and Hollywood relationships. The latter has become a top talking point for Sarandos when explaining the reason for the executive change.

“Most importantly, Peter Rice understands talent relations,” he said on the earnings call Tuesday and reiterated again at the town hall. Similar to the reaction of those watching the earnings webcast, people attending the town hall perceived the comments as praise for Rice but also a slight to Bajaria and her talent relations, though she was thanked for her 10 years at Netflix both on the call at and the town hall, I hear.

Attendees of the town hall also got the impression that concerns over the prospects of Netflix’s current pipeline producing a massive hit may have contributed to the regime change, with Sarandos suggesting on the call that he expects Rice to put his stamp and “have an impact on those projects that are in the works even in the short term.

“I know that we could do better, especially in the U.S.,” Sarandos said Tuesday.

At both forums, he spoke about Netflix’s “business flywheel” fundamentally working but in need of better execution, including refocusing on making shows that can work globally.

The reset comes amid a major stock slide and flashing red light on Wall Street as engagement growth has slowed amid “really solid doubles and triples” but no home runs this year, as Sarandos acknowledged Tuesday.

The reset may include going back to basics.

During the town hall, Sarandos reportedly spoke about getting back to “member joy,” which had been a key part of Netflix’s corporate philosophy and so important to co-founder Reed Hastings that he listed it as one of his biggest contributions to the company when he left earlier this year.

Echoing that at the town hall, Sarandos stressed the importance of members and how that should inform everything they do, I hear.

title: Sebastian Koch Joins Apple TV’s ‘Disavowed’ As Series Regular
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Sebastian Koch (Never Look Away, Black Book) has joined the cast of Apple TV’s Disavowed, the upcoming action-thriller created by Art Marcum and Matt Holloway. Koch will play a series regular role, though details are under wraps. He joins the previously announced stars, led by James Marsden, Norman Reedus, Sylvia Hoeks, Bokeem Woodbine, Noma […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Sebastian Koch (Never Look Away, Black Book) has joined the cast of Apple TV‘s Disavowed, the upcoming action-thriller created by Art Marcum and Matt Holloway.

Koch will play a series regular role, though details are under wraps. He joins the previously announced stars, led by James Marsden, Norman Reedus, Sylvia Hoeks, Bokeem Woodbine, Noma Dumezweni, Daniel Zovatto, Mia Tharia and Sonita Henry.

Disavowed follows legendary CIA Case Officer Brad Griffin (Marsden), who is abruptly fired in the middle of a global hunt for an elusive assassin responsible for killing his colleague. Disgraced and outcast from the world of intelligence, all bets are off when Brad decides to go after the $15 million federal bounty on the assassin’s head.

Hailing from Apple Studios, the series is executive produced by Marcum & Holloway, Tom Spezialy, Michelle MacLaren, Rebecca Hobbs and Marsden. Blue Marble Pictures (Pachinko) produces, with Theresa Kang and Caroline Garity serving as executive producers. MacLaren (The Morning Show, Breaking Bad) will direct the first two episodes and serve as executive producer alongside Hobbs under her overall deal with Apple TV.

Watch on Deadline

Koch’s credits include Paul Verhoeven’s Black Book (2006), Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies (2015), Tom Hooper’s The Danish Girl (2015) and Paul Weitz’s Bel Canto (2017). In the fifth and sixth seasons of Showtime’s Homeland, he played the German entrepreneur Otto Düring. His upcoming projects include Matt Reeves’ The Batman: Part II and Gabriele Salvatores’ The Luneberg Variant.

He is repped by The Artist Partnership (UK) and Agentur Schlag (Germany).

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Winning Wednesday With $2.3M; Can Elizabeth Holmes Melt ‘Clayface’ In U.S.? DC Villain Eyes $45M+ WW
summary: WEDNESDAY PM UPDATE: Nathan Fielder and Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes are banking an estimated $2.3 million Wednesday (that’s real box office money by the way, not a false-positive blood test result) with A24’s three-hour documentary You Can See Everything winning the day. However, the googly-eyed interviewer and subject didn’t win Tuesday as discount tickets for […]
content:
WEDNESDAY PM UPDATE: Nathan Fielder and Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes are banking an estimated $2.3 million Wednesday (that’s real box office money by the way, not a false-positive blood test result) with A24’s three-hour documentary You Can See Everything winning the day.

However, the googly-eyed interviewer and subject didn’t win Tuesday as discount tickets for Street Fighter were the testosterone for that Paramount/Legendary movie, the latter besting the documentary Tuesday $2.8M-$2.6M. Street Fighter is looking at an estimated $1.7M today with a $37.2M running domestic take. You Can See Everything‘s five-day cume is looking like $23.1M.

Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen in ‘ Clayface Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection

So will DC genre movie Clayface be kicked out of No. 1 by a three-hour documentary? Too close to call as the latter expands to 2,600 theaters. Clayface is heading into the weekend with presales that indicate $20M+, but also a Rotten Tomatoes critical score of 75% certified fresh (that’s better than The Flash‘s 63% and Supergirl‘s 52% Rotten), while You Can See Everything could emulate a mid- to high-teens-plus second weekend. It’s impossible to find a good seat for the documentary co-directed by Lance Oppenheim and Fielder at the Alamo Drafthouse LA this weekend.

Watch on Deadline

The R-rated Clayface begins previews tomorrow at 2 p.m. and is booked at 3,400 sites Friday in Dolby Cinema, PLFs and Motion Seats. Foreign footprint is 76 territories including France, Korea, Germany, Italy, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Spain and the UK, with an outlook of $20M-$25M for a $45M+ global bow. Supergirl posted a $30M foreign opening in 77 territories, but she had Japan and China in her opening suite.

Fathom Entertainment’s theatrical release of Laika’s Wildwood could over-index, we hear, with a $12M-$15M U.S. take in 2,718 theaters. Heading into the weekend it’s 100% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes with a 98% audience score. The stop-motion animated feature from Travis Knight follows a girl’s desperate quest to save her baby brother in a forbidden forest full of enchanted creatures, endearing allies, formidable adversaries and a hidden realm.

Olivia Colman in ‘ Wicker Black Bear

Black Bear could have an adult-pleasing upscale success in its Sundance acquisition of period sex comedy Wicker, from Topic Studios, which stars Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman who upon asking the gifted basketweaver (Peter Dinklage) for a Wicker-husband gets one — a loyal and sexy one in Alexander Skarsgård. Booked at 1,471 theaters, the pic has as shot at hitting $5M off reviews that are 95% certified fresh and a trailer that went crazy viral for an indie film.

Jenna Ortega stars in ‘ Klara and the Sun Sony 3000 Pictures

The Sony/Spyglass/TSG co-financed feature take of Kazuo Ishiguro’s Booker Prize long-listed Klara and the Sun from Oscar winner Taika Waititi is platforming in 850-890 locations in hopes that Jenna Ortega fans find it and spread good word of mouth for this moving sci-fi dystopian tale about an AI robot who befriends a dying a young girl. Low single digits expected right now. Sony says the movie cost a net $20M, but we’ve heard it’s close to double that after it was mired in post-production. Thirty-three critics weren’t sympathetic at 27% Rotten on Rotten Tomatoes.

A Talent For Murder‘ Bleecker Street/LD Entertainment

Bleecker Street has A Talent for Murder at 876 locations with an eye at low-single digits. The Anton Corbijn-directed thriller starring Helen Mirren, Olivia Cooke and Alden Ehrenreich follows a mysterious young man from a New York publisher who is sent to Switzerland to persuade renowned novelist Patricia Highsmith to write one final installment of the Ripley anthology. The Bleecker Street movie world premiered at TIFF and it counts 84% fresh from 32 reviews.

RELATED: ‘A Talent For Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren Is Mesmerizing As Tortured Genius Crime Writer Patricia Highsmith – Toronto Film Festival

TUESDAY AM: Look out Clayface, because Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes are out for blood. And not the Theranos kind. Like box office blood.

After overperforming this past weekend with $15.6 million and a No. 2 opening, A24’s Gen Z-skewing feature documentary You Can See Everything won Monday at the domestic box office with $2.57M, clocking Paramount/Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter into second with $1.9M.

The documentary, made for less than $10M, now counts a running North American tally of $18.1M. Street Fighter stands at $32.6M through four days.

Next to other recent Gen Z fare, You Can See Everything‘s Monday ain’t that far from Obsession‘s first Monday of $2.9M. It’s also higher than the first Monday of Markiplier’s Iron Lung which was $2.05M, though it is behind A24 sensation Backrooms‘ first Monday ($7.6M; no big deal there).

You Can See Everything, directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is going wide this weekend with at least 2,600 theaters and counting, and early speculation is it has a shot at taking down Warner Bros/DC’s lower-budget genre movie debut Clayface (a character from the Batman Gotham universe in which the Dark Knight isn’t ever referenced).

‘Clayface’ says “Please don’t hurt me, Elizabeth Holmes” Warner Bros. Pictures

Calm down, newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros distribution and marketing execs: right now the domestic forecast has Clayface at north of $20M this weekend. We’ve heard presales have picked up for the film in the past two days, with the battle between Clayface and Holmes and Fielder boiling down to a market-by-market fight almost like a Red vs. Blue election. Note that advance ticket sales can jump significantly in the next three days as A24 adds showtimes for You Can See Everything. Major circuits’ presales for Clayface are wavering; some indicate an $18M opening, while others see it in the mid-$20Ms. What’s working here in the James Watkins-directed movie? That trailer scene where Clayface is cutting his face with scissors.

EntTelligence has the average general ticket price for Clayface at $14.65 versus $12.88 for You Can See Everything. Also Clayface‘s in-theater campaign is bigger with 34.1M impressions to 2.3M.

As a three-hour documentary, You Can See Everything is in rare air at the box office. But that runtime didn’t stop it from over-indexing from a high-single-digits forecast last weekend to the $15M+ it notched. Couples are going to You Can See Everything at 44%. Obsession was also a Gen Z couples pic, and that jumped 39% in its second weekend to $23.9M from a $17.1M opening. Unheard of.

Many have comped You Can See Everything, given its fewer-than-1,000-screen engagement launch, to 2006’s Borat. That Sacha Baron Cohen movie opened to $26.4M at 837 locations and surged 7% in its second weekend in a 2,566 wide break that earned $28.2M.

When the final box office analysis is run, it wouldn’t be a shocker if You Can See Everything‘s weekend results are near to even with Clayface‘s. And that’s not with the use of a Theranos machine.

title: Meta Ordered To Pay New Mexico $25 Billion For Deceiving Facebook Users About Privacy
summary: A judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in civil penalties for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook. The ruling Wednesday by state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew came in the state’s landmark Cambridge Analytica case against Facebook for violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. It is the largest […]
content:
A judge in New Mexico has ordered to pay $25 billion in civil penalties for deceiving users about privacy on .

The ruling Wednesday by state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew came in the state’s landmark Cambridge Analytica case against Facebook for violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. It is the largest penalty against the tech giant to date.

The judge’s order followed a civil case in September in which jurors found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. The company was accused of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica used Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.

“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” Mathew wrote in his ruling as reported by The Associated Press.

Watch on Deadline

“Facebook’s wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Mathew wrote.

“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference following Mathew’s ruling.

Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement to media outlets, “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will win on appeal.”

The U.S. Federal Trade Commission previously levied a $5 billion penalty against Meta in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

title: Netflix, Bengali Streamer Hoichoi Partner to Bring Series to Hindi, Tamil and Telugu Audiences
summary: Every series Bengali streamer Hoichoi launches over the next two years will get Hindi, Tamil and Telugu-language versions streaming exclusively on Netflix, under a partnership the two companies unveiled in Mumbai on Thursday. New titles will arrive on Netflix in the three languages at the same time as their Bengali debut on Hoichoi. The first […]
content:
Every series Bengali streamer Hoichoi launches over the next two years will get Hindi, Tamil and Telugu-language versions streaming exclusively on Netflix, under a partnership the two companies unveiled in Mumbai on Thursday.

New titles will arrive on Netflix in the three languages at the same time as their Bengali debut on Hoichoi. The first is “The Cursed Temple of Kauriburi,” a horror series rooted in folklore that bows Nov. 6, with Jeetu Kamal, Solanki Roy and Paoli Dam in the leads. More releases will follow over the coming months.

Netflix will also carry 14 existing Hoichoi series. The lineup comprises “Madam Inspector,” “Sampurna,” “Lajja,” “Eken Sirji,” “Anjaan Saaye,” “The Curse of Parnashavari,” “Bloodlines,” “The Adventures of Daadi & Jagga,” “Raat Abhi Baaki Hain,” “Achinta: Trial By Law,” “Shaadi Ka Siyappa,” “Queens,” “Parineeta: A Love Story” and “Mahanagar.” Genres run from crime thrillers and detective mysteries to folklore horror, social and courtroom drama, and romance.

Popular on Variety

The two companies will also make new shows together. Netflix and Hoichoi will work on original series that rework selected Hoichoi stories, with Hoichoi Studios producing. The companies said each adaptation would bring in new creative voices. Further details have yet to be revealed.

For Netflix, the pact is part of a wider effort to supplement its originals with more licensed programming from outside producers. The streamer said its global audience, which it puts at close to a billion people, gives studios, networks and creators a strong reason to work with it.

The Hoichoi pact follows two other high-profile licensing moves. In France, Netflix now carries the full programming lineup of broadcaster TF1. In Brazil, Netflix struck a deal earlier this month with broadcaster Globo, which had long held out from licensing to the streamer in its home market even as its content appeared on Netflix elsewhere in Latin America and around the world.

Hoichoi launched in 2017 as the first venture from SVF’s new media arm and is run by co-founder Vishnu Mohta, also SVF’s executive director. The platform hosts more than 2,000 hours of programming, among them over 100 original series, films, shorts and docuseries, and says it reaches more than 250 million Bengalis around the world. It moved into theatrical production in 2023, setting up Hoichoi Studios as its film production arm.

title: Indonesia Drafts New Film Law as Jakarta, Home to Four Netflix Productions, Courts International Shoots (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Indonesia’s film agency is helping draft a revised Film Law that would reshape its powers, while Jakarta, where Netflix now has four titles in production, is working to become a regional film hub. Fauzan Zidni, chair of the Indonesian Film Agency (BPI), tells Variety the first draft, prepared with the Ministry of Culture, has taken […]
content:
Indonesia’s film agency is helping draft a revised Film Law that would reshape its powers, while Jakarta, where Netflix now has four titles in production, is working to become a regional film hub.

Fauzan Zidni, chair of the Indonesian Film Agency (BPI), tells Variety the first draft, prepared with the Ministry of Culture, has taken shape since Cannes. “It is still in discussion, and I will say more when the moment is right, but the direction is right and the momentum is there,” he says.

The Jakarta Film Commission launched in June alongside Filming in Jakarta, a one-stop service for producers. Karno says production companies from Malaysia and India have since come to the city to shoot films and series.

Popular on Variety

In the capital, Netflix’s latest slate follows “Tygo,” the streamer’s “Extraction” spinoff. “We’re very happy to say that Netflix now is doing [four] titles … through Filming in Jakarta,” says Vice Governor Rano Karno. Under a memorandum of understanding tied to the inaugural Jakarta Film Summit, Netflix will also help develop local film talent, he adds.

Governor Pramono Anung has set the goal of making Jakarta a film hub on the scale of Busan, and Karno, a veteran actor and filmmaker, has driven much of the city’s film policy. Over the next five years, he says, Jakarta wants to settle the full ecosystem, from production through financing and market access, and build Busan-style infrastructure. Post-production facilities, soundstages and studios are the biggest gaps, which the city aims to fill within three to five years.

Jakarta has cut certain location fees by 50% and introduced a 50% tax concession on cinema admissions for qualifying Indonesian films. Karno says the city has barely scratched the surface on production incentives and is working to improve them, learning from Thailand and Malaysia as it tries to grow the industry faster.

Busan has been a close partner. Karno credits the Busan Film Commission with helping the Jakarta Film Commission become an official member of AFCNet, the Asian Film Commissions Network. “It’s a momentum for us to be known [as the] future film hub in the region,” he says.

To spread the benefits beyond the capital, the city is working with Bank Indonesia’s Jakarta representative office on the film and creative economy sectors, and is inviting filmmakers and industry players to its film summit and festival. Its Jaksinema initiative, which brings cinemas into public markets, offers cheaper tickets aimed at lower- and middle-income audiences.

Karno, who says he has spent more than 50 years understanding the industry’s problems, expects the summit to become an essential date on the calendar, with the city government fully committed to making Jakarta a City of Cinema.

The summit will also take on what Zidni sees as the core barrier to institutional investment. Banks lend against physical assets such as land, buildings and machinery, which production houses can’t offer. Film IP, including copyright and broadcast and distribution rights, has no valuation method that banks or the Financial Services Authority (OJK) will accept.

Government Regulation No. 24 of 2022 on the Creative Economy already allows for IP-based financing. What’s missing are technical guidelines from OJK and a revision of OJK Regulation No. 40 of 2019 on asset quality so that IP can formally count as collateral. The summit is bringing OJK, the Ministry of Creative Economy, the Directorate General of Intellectual Property (DJKI), banks and the Indonesian Appraisers Association together to agree on a standard IP valuation method, a pilot financing scheme and a regulatory path.

At the national level, Indonesia has no equivalent of France’s CNC, Korea’s KOFIC or Singapore’s IMDA. BPI can convene, advocate and coordinate, but it cannot fund films on its own or mandate policy. Zidni wants the revised law to give the agency statutory authority and ring-fenced funding.

Two ministries currently oversee film in Indonesia, and Zidni says BPI is not trying to replace either of them. “That coordination problem is as much political as it is institutional, and solving it is part of the work,” he says. He calls the Minister of Culture’s support the strongest it has been in years, but gives no date for getting the law through parliament.

Local productions took roughly 67% of Indonesia’s box office last year, though Zidni says 2026 is tracking at slower growth amid global economic pressures. “What we have not built is the bridge that carries those stories outward,” he says.

At the Lumière Summit, Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture announced a new international co-production fund, developed with CNC support and open to filmmakers worldwide working with Indonesian partners. It sits alongside a matching fund, under which the government contributes up to a set ceiling per project for producers who land international financing. Zidni concedes that the matching fund on its own won’t help independent producers who lack overseas contacts.

“What it does is create a concrete incentive to invest in building those relationships, the payoff is now tangible and government-backed, not hypothetical,” he says.

Indonesia signed its first audiovisual co-production agreement, with the Netherlands, at JAFF Market in 2024. Talks on a bilateral treaty with France are active. Korean producers are looking hard at Southeast Asia, and Zidni calls Indonesia the obvious partner by scale, though he can’t give a precise timeline. “We are no longer asking partners to believe in our intentions,” he says.

Zidni, who previously worked at Disney, watched global streamers pull back from Southeast Asian originals after 2023. “A platform can change its content strategy, exit a market, or deprioritize Indonesian content, and we have no recourse,” he says. BPI is pushing for closer ties with international sales agents and regional distribution within Southeast Asia, and is exploring whether Indonesian producers can build a shared market presence.

Talent is another pressure point. Indonesia’s film schools, spread across 27 campuses, turn out around 1,200 graduates a year, but most are not absorbed by the industry and turnover runs at about 60%, Zidni says.

His mandate runs to 2030. By then, he wants at least two bilateral co-production treaties in force, a financing system with a track record, and Indonesian producers attending the major international markets as regulars.

“When the system works routinely, not heroically, that is when I will know we have built something that lasts,” he says.

title: Chris Pratt Confirms Star-Lord Will Return to the MCU, Says ‘Hard Action’ Has Been Taken to Make It Happen
summary: Good news, “Guardians of the Galaxy” fans. Chris Pratt, who has played superhero Star-Lord across six films, recently confirmed that his character will return to the MCU and that the studio has already taken “hard action” to make it happen. “I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been […]
content:
Good news, “Guardians of the Galaxy” fans. Chris Pratt, who has played superhero Star-Lord across six films, recently confirmed that his character will return to the MCU and that the studio has already taken “hard action” to make it happen.

“I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” said Pratt on The Playlist’s “Bingeworthy” podcast while discussing Star-Lord’s comeback.

He continued: “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.”

Popular on Variety

The news comes months after Pratt admitted he pitched Marvel an idea for bringing Star-Lord back into the MCU. “I’m happy to do anything they want me to do and will,” Pratt said about Marvel when on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast. “And also, I personally have a really strong vision of what I would want him to do. And I think it’s fucking great.”

When asked if he pitched this idea already to Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige, Pratt responded: “Yep. And I think that, you know, I’m down to contribute any way I can to them setting up the next 10 years of storytelling, you know? And also, I have a pretty strong idea of how I think I could contribute to that.”

Pratt’s Star-Lord has appeared in “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” “Avengers: Infinity War,” “Avengers: Endgame,” “Thor: Love and Thunder” and “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3,” the latter of which promised via credits scene text that Star-Lord would return.

The next installment in the MCU, “Avengers: Doomsday,” hits theaters on Dec. 18.

title: Dolly Parton CMA Tribute: Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts, Oprah and More Remember the Country Icon as the ‘Great Unifier’
summary: Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts and Oprah were among the stars who paid tribute to Dolly Parton during the Country Music Association’s celebration of the late country icon Wednesday night. Oprah, who appeared in a pre-recorded video at the beginning of the broadcast, shared what Dolly meant to her. “We’re both Tennessee girls, and she represented […]
content:
Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts and Oprah were among the stars who paid tribute to Dolly Parton during the Country Music Association’s celebration of the late country icon Wednesday night.

Oprah, who appeared in a pre-recorded video at the beginning of the broadcast, shared what Dolly meant to her. “We’re both Tennessee girls, and she represented to me the essence of being 100% who you see yourself to be. Authentic all the time, and I just loved her for it,” she said. “I love that she had such grace and such tenacity. I mean, listen, if she put her mind to something, that was it. And I love that she was so generous of heart and generous of spirit, and her presence here on Earth will be felt for forever because the spirit that is so strong that was hers is actually everlasting.”

Roberts, who starred alongside Parton in 1989’s “Steel Magnolias,” reflected on the experience of filming with the performer. “Dolly came into my life when I was in my early 20s, and it was magical to see someone so alive, so present,” the actress shared in a pre-recorded video. “She really was a shining example of remembering who you are, where you came from, and what it means to be kind. We love her.”

Popular on Variety

Katy Perry took the stage to remember Parton as a woman who “masterfully toyed with the power of her femininity.” “Devastatingly sharp and equally as sweet, she could read you for filth with a wink and a smile, and then make sure that your children learn to read too. That’s a mother,” she continued. “Beneath the decades of dazzle was an extraordinary generosity of spirit. Some called her the Great Unifier because she had this ability to bring people together from all walks of life, political perspectives and sexual orientations. She saw beyond those labels because she saw the humanity in everyone. For me, Dolly is the blueprint.”

Carpenter, who, before Parton’s passing, had collaborated with her on a remix of “Please Please Please,” said that the “I Will Always Love You” singer “meant lightness” as she began her recorded tribute. “She meant kindness, joy, quick comebacks, rhinestones, big hair, family, radiance, and love. I think Dolly was one of the only people on planet Earth that everyone could universally agree on, which I think is very special in any artist. But there’s nobody like Dolly.”

Carol Burnett, who first met Parton while filming the 1979 CBS television variety special “Dolly & Carol in Nashville,” recalled an early memory of the star while on set. “When I talk about thoughtful, I remember there was one night I was in my hotel room getting ready to go out to dinner to a restaurant, and there was a knock at the door, and I opened it, and there was Dolly with a home-cooked meal for me, so that I wouldn’t have to go out to a restaurant, and to top it off, that home-cooked meal was home-cooked by Dolly herself.”

Bono, Goldie Hawn and other stars also paid tribute to Parton during the show.

The special was a “joyful, emotional celebration of the artist, songwriter, entertainer, humanitarian and entrepreneur whose music and generosity carried her from the mountains of East Tennessee into the hearts of generations around the world, told through performances, archival footage and personal stories that trace her extraordinary journey to becoming one of the most beloved entertainers and philanthropists in American history,” per the evening’s official logline.

The singer-songwriter-actress died in August at the age of 80 following a “brief battle” with cancer.

Over the course of the evening, more than 20 performers took the stage, including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Reba McEntire, Carrie Underwood, Vince Gill, Kristen Bell, Molly Tuttle and Carly Pearce, as well as Kelsea Ballerini, Brad Paisley, Zac Brown, Ashley McBryde, Bela Fleck, Kristin Chenoweth, Lady A, Ricky Skaggs, Sierra Hull, Little Big Town, Lukas Nelson and Darius Rucker.

The special aired live on ABC and Disney+ on Wednesday and will stream on Hulu the following day.

title: John Anderson, Country Hall of Famer Whose Hits Included ‘Seminole Wind’ and ‘Swingin’,’ Dies at 71
summary: John Anderson, the country Hall of Famer behind hits like “Seminole Wind” and “Swingin’,” has died. He was 71. Anderson’s death was announced by his family across his social media accounts on Wednesday. No cause of death or further information was noted. “It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of […]
content:
John Anderson, the country Hall of Famer behind hits like “Seminole Wind” and “Swingin’,” has died. He was 71.

Anderson’s death was announced by his family across his social media accounts on Wednesday. No cause of death or further information was noted.

“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend,” read the statement. “To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special.”

It continued: “We are completely heartbroken. His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever. Please keep our family in your thoughts and prayers as we grieve this unimaginable loss.”

Popular on Variety

Over Anderson’s nearly five-decade career, he earned 20 Top Ten country hits, with five reaching the top spot on the charts — “Wild and Blue,” “Black Sheep” and “Swingin’” were among his most notable hits, as were “Straight Tequila Night,” “Money in the Bank” and “Seminole Wind.” From his first, the self-titled debut “John Anderson” in 1980, to his last, “Years,” released in 2020, the country singer released 22 studio albums.

Anderson was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024 and previously into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2014. He won the Academy of Country Music Career Achievement Award in 1993.

“John Anderson was a one-of-a-kind song stylist who proved that fresh innovations were best born from time-honored traditions,” said Kyle Young, CEO of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, in a statement. “Whether he borrowed inspiration from Lefty Frizzell’s vocal bends or the Florida swamp land, he brought dynamic distinction and creative soul to a world that needed to hear his voice. In 1981, John famously gave life to Billy Joe Shaver’s lyric, ‘I’m just an old chunk of coal, but I’ll be a diamond someday.’ He was already a diamond then, and a diamond he always will be.”

Anderson was born Dec. 13, 1954, in Orlando. He grew up in Apopka, Fla., and knew by age twelve that he wanted to pursue music. After graduating from high school, he moved to Nashville, began performing regularly, and ultimately signed a recording contract with Warner Bros. Records in 1976.

He is survived by his wife, Jamie, their two daughters, Alexa Kate and Brionna Cheri, and his grandchildren.

title: BBC Merges TV & Audio Commissioning Teams Amid Plan To Cut 100 Content Roles
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The BBC will merge TV and audio commissioning teams across comedy and other genres amid plans to close around 100 roles in its content unit.
