The new single arrives at DSPs at the usual midnight hour as Thursday turns into Friday, but listeners to the artist’s SiriusXM channel, Life With John Mayer, will get a preview throughout the day Thursday. The song was produced by Blake Slatkin with Mayer and mixed by Serban Genhea.

It almost goes without saying that the credits acknowledge the song was recorded at Chaplin Studios. One of Mayer’s biggest endeavors in the past couple of years was joining forces with the film director McG to purchase the Hollywood lot that started as Charlie Chaplin’s studio and eventually became the home of A&M, then Henson Studios. Mayer and McG shared their experience with taking the reins of the studio with Variety at the top of 2026; read about that here.

The singer-songwriter-guitarist indicated then that 2026 would mark a turn back toward his solo recording career after several years of focusing on his role as co-frontman of Dead & Company, including being the primary designer of both of that group’s residencies at Sphere in 2024 and 2025.

Mayer was already known to be coming back as a live performing artist in a big way with a run of shows booked for Sphere in Las Vegas next year. He currently has concerts at the venue booked for April 8 through June 12, all of them in a configuration that will see him doing separate sets with his full band, with the John Mayer Trio and as a solo performer.

title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: ‘An Amazing Piece of Technology’ But ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’
summary: “Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI. “I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI Fest’s opening night U.S. premiere of “Wildwood.” “I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer […]
content:
“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI Fest’s opening night U.S. premiere of “Wildwood.” “I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is a computer is technology. Technology is useful when you put it in the hands of people, when you put it in the hands of artists who can amplify their voice.

“Technology is not useful when it takes the place of the artist, and that’s the concern with generative AI,” he continued. “It’s an amazing piece of technology, but the concern is that when it supplants the artist, then we have an issue because the computer cannot speak about humanity at all. It doesn’t know what it feels like.”

Popular on Variety

“Wildwood” is a stop-motion fantasy feature about a young girl (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) who travels into a forbidden forest when her baby brother is kidnapped by a murder of crows. It took 16 years to complete the film, Knight said.

“Sixteen years is a long time,” Knight said. “As I’ve said before, this film is old enough to have driven me to the premiere tonight. But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big sweeping adventure story. It’s a beautiful extravaganza. It’s an epic, but that’s not something that sustains you for 16 years.

He continued, “At the heart of it, it has to be something that means something to you and that’s the thing I’m most proud of is that underneath it all, it is something that is really heartfelt, it’s beautiful, it’s emotional and that’s the thing I hope audiences take away from this.”

Knight doesn’t believe that AI could have helped speed up the process — at least not if he wanted to maintain the highest quality. “That very notion fills me with rage,” he said. “Look, that’s the world we live in and the technology seems like it’s only pushing us in one direction, which is everything is going to be simpler. Everything is going to be automated; everything is going to be easier. What I would say to that is that there is something special about the human touch. There is something beautiful about humanity. And that’s one thing that stop motion represents. Stop-motion represents humanity at its finest creativity, emotion, care, devotion, time.

“That’s something that AI could never do because a computer has never felt anything,” Knight added. “It’s never felt loss or love or pain, and that’s something that people can feel and that’s something you feel in something that was made by people.”

“Wildwood” Courtesy of Laika

The cast of “Wildwood” also includes Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Jake Johnson, Carey Mulligan, Maya Erskine, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg and Tantoo Cardinal.

Bassett talked about recording her work during COVID. “I wanted to get out of the house, get creative again,” she told me. “It was just right on time.”

title: Laika’s First PG-13 Film, Brad Bird’s Neo-Noir and an Alzheimer’s Memoir: Animation’s Revolution Isn’t for Kids
summary: The MPA gave “Wildwood” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and language,” which is a mouthful for any movie and an especially wild one for a stop-motion picture about a girl hunting for her kidnapped baby brother. It’s the first PG-13 in Laika’s 17 years as a […]
content:
The MPA gave “Wildwood” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and language,” which is a mouthful for any movie and an especially wild one for a stop-motion picture about a girl hunting for her kidnapped baby brother.

It’s the first PG-13 in Laika’s 17 years as a feature studio, and at 140 minutes, it ties the record for the longest English-language animated film ever made. Travis Knight, who runs the Portland, Ore., studio and directed “Wildwood,” didn’t land there by accident. Anyone who remembers how dark the back half of “Kubo and the Two Strings” got probably isn’t shocked he went this far.

Knight is one of the filmmakers taking part in this year’s Pixels and Pencils panel, Variety’s animation directors conversation at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, now in its fifth year. Joining Knight at the event are Brad Bird (“Ray Gunn”), Daniel Chong (“Hoppers”), Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado (“Forgotten Island”) and Leah Nelson (“Tangles”).

Popular on Variety

The SCAD Savannah Film Festival runs Oct. 24-31.

The panel has turned into a decent crystal ball leading to the Academy Awards. The director of “Flow,” Gints Zilbalodis, participated in 2024 before the little indie feature that could upset the big studios for the animated feature Oscar and last year, four of the eventual five nominees at the 98th Academy Awards, including winner “KPop Demon Hunters,” spoke at the event.

Since “Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio” won the animated feature Oscar the 95th ceremony, the trophy hasn’t gone back to Disney or Pixar (“The Boy and the Heron,” “Flow” and “KPop” followed), which is a real shift for a category those two studios have owned since “Shrek” took the first trophy in the category in 2002.

But this year, animation’s auteurs are making the movies they want to make.

RAY GUNN — Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) and Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson). ‘Ray Gunn’ ©2026 Skydance Animation

Bird’s “Ray Gunn” is the easiest place to start, partly because the man has been chasing it since 1996, when a B-52s song and a Henry Mancini tune got tangled in his head and spit out a title. That was three years before “The Iron Giant” bombed at the box office (still a masterpiece, by the way) and then spent the next 25 years becoming the movie an entire generation of dads can’t get through without tearing up.

He’s pitched his new film as “The Maltese Falcon” meets “Buck Rogers.” Sam Rockwell is Raymond Gunn, a gumshoe working a murder in Metropia, a version of 1939 that never happened, where humans and aliens share the same smoky streets. Netflix will release it Dec. 18, after London Film Festival screenings and a limited 70mm run. The PG rating comes with a note about “suggestive material,” which, if you know Bird’s work, tracks. Indeed, the Pixar licensing cash cow and family-friendly adventure “The Incredibles” was about a guy who hates his insurance job and misses his glory days.

Chong’s “Hoppers” is the on the list our nieces and nephews have already watched twice on Disney+. The Pixar original opened to $46 million in March, the best start for an original since “Coco” in 2017 and cleared $500 million worldwide in about five weeks, which felt like the whole studio exhaling after “Elemental” and “Elio” stumbled out of the gate. Chong, who created “We Bare Bears” for Cartoon Network, made his feature directing debut with the story of Mabel (Piper Curda), a college student who uploads her mind into a robot beaver so she can talk to animals and keep developers from bulldozing their forest.

It’s a family movie, sure. It’s also about habitat loss and how much people are willing to give up to stop it, and there’s a robot face removal scene that has reportedly sent some of the younger audience members out to the lobby. Timely, no?

Crawford was on our very first panel back in 2022 with “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” the Oscar-nominated sequel nobody asked for that turned out to be a pretty frank movie about a cat who’s afraid to die. And people loved it. Mercado, his best friend in real life, co-directed that one too and their friendship, which goes back to “Kung Fu Panda 2,” is the seed of “Forgotten Island.”

In the film, Jo (H.E.R.) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) grew up together in the Philippines in the 1990s and are about to be pulled apart, with Raissa off to Caltech and Jo staying home. Then they get stuck in Nakali, a place out of Philippine folklore that eats memories and if they don’t find a way out, they’ll forget each other entirely. You don’t need to have been 18 years old in Manila in the 1990s to feel that one. So seeing DreamWorks throw this kind of muscle behind a Filipino story with universal appeal means something.

As for Laika, the studio is five for five in animated feature nominations, from “Coraline” to “Missing Link” and zero for five in wins, although “Missing Link” beat “Toy Story 4” and “Frozen II” at the Golden Globes.

Knight, who got his own nomination for “Kubo,” directs the Chris Butler adaptation of Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis’ 2011 novel. In the stop-motion feature, Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) goes into the forbidden woods outside Portland after her brother is taken and stumbles into a war. The Laika crew built 136 sets and 231 puppets to get her there. Fathom releases “Wildwood” on Oct. 23, the day before Savannah kicks off.

IFC

Then there’s “Tangles,” which isn’t pretending to be anything other than a movie for adults. Nelson, a first-time feature director, wrote it with Sarah Leavitt, adapting Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s in the late 1990s. Abbi Jacobson voices Sarah, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus plays her mom and is among the producers with Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen.

It got a seven-minute ovation at Cannes before Independent Film Company picked it up, and the charcoal-heavy animation does something with memory that live action could not pull off. The jokes are there early but the tears come fast and furious by credits roll.

Both “Tangles” and “Wildwood” are also going drama at the Golden Globes, where animated titles have usually defaulted to comedy. It’s category paperwork, technically, but it says a lot about how these teams want their films seen.

None of this is exactly new, by the way. “Persepolis” and “Anomalisa” were nominated by the Oscars years ago, and Japanese studios have been making animation for grown-ups for as long as we’ve been watching movies. Only three animated films, “Beauty and the Beast,” “Up” and “Toy Story 3,” have ever been nominated for best picture and the last of those was 15 years ago. What feels different in 2026 is the confidence. Nobody on this panel seems to be asking whether their story is “allowed” to be animated.

They grew up on Saturday morning cartoons. Now they’re making them for Saturday night.

title: Chaka Khan to Be Honored at Soul Train Awards (TV News Roundup)
summary: Chaka Khan will receive the Classic Soul Honor at the 2026 Soul Train Awards, celebrating the singer-songwriter’s influence on R&B. Across her career, which spans more than five decades, Khan helped shape the sound of soul, funk and R&B with her music, including hits like “Tell Me Something Good,” “Sweet Thing,” “Ain’t Nobody,” “I’m Every […]
content:
Chaka Khan will receive the Classic Soul Honor at the 2026 Soul Train Awards, celebrating the singer-songwriter’s influence on R&B.

Across her career, which spans more than five decades, Khan helped shape the sound of soul, funk and R&B with her music, including hits like “Tell Me Something Good,” “Sweet Thing,” “Ain’t Nobody,” “I’m Every Woman” and “I Feel for You.” She received 11 Grammys, including the Recording Academy’s Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award, and was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2023 with the Musical Excellence Award.

“Chaka Khan is the embodiment of soul music,” said Louis Carr, the president of BET. “From her groundbreaking work with Rufus to a solo career that has produced some of the most iconic records in music history, she has continually expanded the possibilities of R&B and soul while inspiring generations of artists to find and own their voices. Honoring Chaka is a celebration of the music and cultural legacy that Soul Train has always embodied.”

Popular on Variety

Airing Nov. 27 on BET and CBS, the Soul Train Awards are executive produced by Jesse Collins. Dionne Harmon and Jeannae Rouzan-Clay also serve as executive producers, with Jesse Collins Entertainment as the production company for the show. Connie Orlando is the exec producer for BET.

In other TV roundup news:

First Looks/Trailers

National Geographic revealed the trailer for “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” which premieres Nov. 13.

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho (“Moana”), the one-hour special showcases the National Geographic and Rolex Perpetual Planet Ocean Expeditions documenting the impact of rapid environmental change on all five ocean basins. The documentary follows teams of National Geographic explorers investigating the ocean.

In the Southern Ocean, three new discoveries surface, including the first-known live sighting of a giant Antarctic gonate squid. Two teams work to understand the impact of rising temperatures on Pacific Ocean ecosystems. The first deep-sea scientist from the Seychelles dives below the surface of the Indian Ocean. Local students train to measure the Atlantic Ocean’s depth along the Gambian coastline. A team works to study the Arctic Ocean, warming at four times the rate of the rest of the planet.

The documentary is presented by the National Geographic Society in partnership with Rolex and produced by Offspring Films. Katharine Arthy is director. Executive producers include Sam Hodgson for Offspring Films, Vanessa Serrao and Kaitlin Yarnall for National Geographic Society and Tracy Rudolph Jackson for National Geographic.

“Expedition: Saving Our Seas” premieres Nov. 13 at 9 p.m. EST on National Geographic and will stream the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Watch the trailer below.

Programming

Five bonus episodes of “Lot Patrol,” from Manny Halley Productions, will debut on BET on Nov. 3.

“Lot Patrol” looks at Hollywood through the lens of an eccentric group of security guards as they patrol a major studio backlot. The comedy series will round out its first season at 10 full episodes after the special premiere.

The series features DeRay Davis (“21 Jump Street,” “Semi-Pro”), Carl Anthony Payne II (“Martin,” “House Party”), Tamera Kissen (“White Men Can’t Jump,” “House Party”) and comedians Skeet Carter, TK Kirkland, Alex Thomas, Tanjareen Thomas, Lionell Dalton, Nick Nervies, Dawn Raven, Iyana Halley and G Thang.

“’Lot Patrol’ is a fresh, culturally rooted take on the industry. People inside and outside entertainment are realizing that the business of Hollywood is actually quite comical through a certain lens,” creator Manny Halley said. “It’s OK to laugh at how things in this town operate — particularly through an urban lens, which is a fresh angle. With this unbelievable ensemble of comedic talent, audiences get exactly what they’re looking for: a unique, genuine tone that is refreshingly different.”

“Lot Patrol” is produced by Manny Halley Productions, a division of Imani Media Group. The series is created and written by Halley and Ernest L. Dancy. Manny Halley Jr., Maureen Pierre and DeRay Davis are producers. Erik White is director.

*

“The Biggest Little Farm Series,” a 12-part docuseries and sequel to the documentary “The Biggest Little Farm,” premieres Nov. 8 on YouTube.

The original film follows John and Molly Chester and their team as they transform a depleted farm into a thriving ecosystem. Eight years later, their experiment has become far more wild than they had ever imagined. The series will “dive deeper into the lives of the creatures. It will shed light on the battle between predator and prey, farmer and pest, and reminds audiences that Nature has its own way. To balance the chaos, there’s one question the stewards cannot escape: Can a farm become too feral for its own good?”

“The Biggest Little Farm Series” is presented by the Artemis Rising Foundation. It is directed by John Chester and is produced by Tom Quinn, Paul Gurinas, Jessica Gurinas and Shannon Green. John Chester, Erica Messer, Regina K. Scully and Sandra Keats are executive producers while Amy Overbeck and Ali Galante are co-executive producers.

Watch the full trailer here:

*

Hearst Media Production Group has announced a second season of “Home for Good.” The series will return to ABC stations nationwide on Saturday, Jan. 9 as part of the “Weekend Adventure” educational informational programming block.

Hosted by Art Edmonds, “Home for Good” is a “home renovation series honoring people who make a difference in their communities. Each half-hour episode transforms a room or personal space to better serve people who dedicate their lives to helping others. Season 2 will continue to feature first responders while bringing more community champions and service workers into the spotlight, including educators, mentors and volunteers who serve families in need.”

“We’re excited to bring Home for Good back for a second season,” Bryan Curb, president of HMPG, said. “The series shows what giving back looks like through the people who serve their communities, while giving viewers practical fire and CO safety information they can use at home. That combination reflects the value of E/I programming: stories that educate, inform and offer a meaningful benefit to audiences.”

Specials

“The Pursuit: F1 Academy” documentary special will premiere Nov. 19 on Disney+.

The special follows F1 Academy, the all-female racing series created by Formula 1 to prepare young women for higher levels of motorsport. Fans will get behind-the-scenes access to the 2025 Academy season, following a group of elite drivers including Doriane Pin, Maya Weug, Chloe Chambers and Alisha Palmowski.

“The Pursuit: F1 Academy” was filmed across global locations during the 2025 racing season and will also provide insight into the teams and leadership shaping F1 Academy, including managing director Susie Wolff.

The documentary special was produced in association with ESPN as the latest extension of the “Fuel the Magic” partnership between Disney, Formula 1 and F1 Academy. The collaboration was first launched at the Formula 1 Chinese Grand Prix 2026 and expanded to the Grand Prix Du Canada 2026 to include the Academy with classic Disney icons Minnie Mouse and Daisy Duck.

“The Pursuit: F1 Academy” will air ahead of the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix 2026 on Nov. 19-21. The special will also be available to stream on the ESPN app later this year.

title: ‘Line of Fire’ Gets Full 18-Episode Season Order at NBC
summary: “Line of Fire” has been given a full 18-episode season order at NBC. The freshman action thriller series is one of the fall season’s breakout hits, with NBC’s best delayed-viewing lift in more than three years. Initially slated for 13 episodes, NBC gave a back order to five additional scripts with the hope of extending […]
content:
“Line of Fire” has been given a full 18-episode season order at NBC.

The freshman action thriller series is one of the fall season’s breakout hits, with NBC’s best delayed-viewing lift in more than three years.

Initially slated for 13 episodes, NBC gave a back order to five additional scripts with the hope of extending the season as a result of sustained viewership. Now, the first season is officially getting 18 total episodes and will extend into 2027.

“Line of Fire” follows a family of agents from various branches of federal law enforcement who find themselves tangled in a deadly conspiracy. They bridge personal differences and cross professional boundaries “as they tackle cases for the FBI, US Marshals, Secret Service and Department of Justice,” per the logline. “After a seemingly cut-and-dry case turns into a deadly conspiracy, they must use the expertise from a lifetime of protecting civilians and politicians to protect one another and bring the killer to justice … even if it means betraying their sworn code.”

Popular on Variety

Peter Krause stars in the series alongside Hope Davis, Kat Cunning, Tommy O’Brien, Taylor Bloom and Charlie Barnett. Creator and writer Joshua Safran executive produces with Jenna Bush Hager and Ben Spector. The series is produced by Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

“Line of Fire” airs on Mondays at 10 p.m. and streams the next day on Peacock.

Variety TV critic Aramide Tinubu praised the show in her review, saying it “has all the makings of becoming a classic in the canon of beloved police procedurals.”

title: Rebel Wilson Trial Over ‘The Deb’ Producers’ Defamation Claims Looks To Be Delayed
summary: Years in the making, the L.A. courtroom showdown between Rebel Wilson and The Deb producers is not going to trial as scheduled. In a filing Wednesday that has been agreed upon by all the principals, Wilson’s lead lawyer Allyson K. Thompson has asked for the long set January 19, 2027 trial to be pushed back […]
content:
Years in the making, the L.A. courtroom showdown between Rebel Wilson and The Deb producers is not going to trial as scheduled.

In a filing Wednesday that has been agreed upon by all the principals, Wilson’s lead lawyer Allyson K. Thompson has asked for the long set January 19, 2027 trial to be pushed back over two months. In fact, the Hart Kienle Pentecost attorney has also requested to LA Superior Court Judge Thomas Long that summary judgement hearings currently scheduled for December also be pushed back.

A hearing in downtown L.A. is on the books for Friday to address the requests. The parties are aiming to have the trial moved to March 22 next year.

Out of what has been an extremely contentious battle even by Hollywood standards between producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden and Deb director Wilson over allegations of misconduct on the film, this latest twist has a much more personal origin.

Watch on Deadline

“Counsel for Ms. Wilson, Ms. Allyson Thompson, was recently diagnosed with breast cancer,” the 24-page ex parte application filing states.

“Ms. Thompon (sic) has been placed on a medical leave for surgery from November 30, 2026, through January 4, 2027, and is currently working reduced hours due to side effects of the disease,” it continues. “The doctor’s note was shared with all counsel for purposes of meeting and conferring. Ms. Thompson would prefer not to have to attach the doctor’s note to the moving papers but will provide the Court with a copy should it require review.”

The document goes on to say: After notifying all counsel of the issue, the parties held a scheduled telephonic meet and confer on Friday, October 16, 2026, to address this and other discovery matters. During the call, the parties agreed in principle to continue the trial to March 22, 2027, or a later date mutually acceptable to the parties and the Court. They also agreed that the expert-discovery deadlines could be continued with the trial date.”

Even with the usually packed LASC calendar, it is almost a certainty that Judge Long will sign off on the request tomorrow.

The October 21 filing and the public announcement of Thompson’s heath issues come as Wilson scored successful reviews (read Deadline’s Glenn Garner’s here) last month at TIFF for her latest big screen effort Girl Group. Unlike the 2024 Great North debut of The Deb, there were no legal dark clouds hanging over the Randall Park and Jennifer Coolidge co-starrer. On the other side of the Pacific, Deb actress Charlotte MacInnes appeal over an Australian court’s decision earlier this year that Wilson did not defame her in a series of social media posts continues.

Still, buried in the finger pointing, hyperboles, and connections to the Blake Lively vs. Justin Baldoni It Ends With Us saga with ongoing claims of dark arts PR moves and smear sites, The Deb sunk from view pretty swiftly after it was finally released by Sunrise Films in late August

According to the American Cancer Society, 1 in 8 American women will have “invasive breast cancer.” Approximately 320,000 cases are anticipated to be identified in 2026. While breast cancer is the second most common form of death from cancer after lung cancer, the ACS also notes “breast cancer death rates have been decreasing steadily since 1989, for an overall decline of 44% through 2023.” They add: :This is most likely the result of finding breast cancer earlier through screening and increased awareness, as well as better treatments.”

title: ‘Line Of Fire’ Gets Full 18-Episode Season Order At NBC
summary: NBC has handed a full 18-episode season order to its Monday night freshman drama hit Line of Fire. It’s not a surprise. The drama, starring Peter Krause and Hope Davis, about a family of federal law enforcement agents entangled in a mystery, is one of the breakout stories of the fall. After a strong launch […]
content:
NBC has handed a full 18-episode season order to its Monday night freshman drama hit Line of Fire.

It’s not a surprise. The drama, starring Peter Krause and Hope Davis, about a family of federal law enforcement agents entangled in a mystery, is one of the breakout stories of the fall. After a strong launch and week-to-week ratings gains following its Sept. 21 premiere, it became the first new 2026-27 broadcast series to get a back order of 5 additional scripts earlier this month.

The drama drew strong cross-platform average viewership of more than 14 million to the Sept. 21 pilot. It increased its demo rating by 47% in week 2 and rose to a season-high demo in the most recent Oct. 19 episode in live + same day, according to the network and Nielsen stats.

Watch on Deadline

Line of Fire also has seen NBC’s best DVR lift for a premiere episode in more than three years, since the Night Court reboot in January 2023, according to the network.

Created and written by Joshua Safran, in Line of Fire, a family of law enforcement agents bridges personal differences and crosses professional boundaries as they tackle cases for the FBI, US Marshals, Secret Service and Department of Justice. After a seemingly cut-and-dry case turns into a deadly conspiracy, they must use the expertise from a lifetime of protecting civilians and politicians to protect one another and bring the killer to justice … even if it means betraying their sworn code.

In addition to Krause and Davis, cast includes Kat Cunning, Tommy O’Brien, Taylor Bloom, and Charlie Barnett.

Safran executive produces with Jenna Bush Hager and Ben Spector. The series is produced by Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

Line of Fire airs on Mondays at 10 p.m. ET/PT and next day on Peacock.

title: Jenna Ortega Plans To “Be Off The TV For A While” After ‘Wednesday’ Season 3
summary: After wrapping production on Season 3 of Wednesday last month, Jenna Ortega is looking forward to exploring new roles. The Emmy nominee explained that she will “probably be off the TV for a while” after completing the third season of the Tim Burton-created Netflix series, noting that she wants “to leave time” for other opportunities. […]
content:
After wrapping production on Season 3 of Wednesday last month, Jenna Ortega is looking forward to exploring new roles.

The Emmy nominee explained that she will “probably be off the TV for a while” after completing the third season of the Tim Burton-created Netflix series, noting that she wants “to leave time” for other opportunities.

“I actually haven’t had a lot of franchise conversations. I haven’t,” noted Ortega on the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “But what I’m meant to do will come and find me. I think after Wednesday, I’ll probably be off the TV for a while. You know, I had many years doing that. I was bouncing from show to show as a kid, this to this, and I want to leave time for new things.”

In the podcast, Ortega also admitted that she’s still “a little confused” by the show’s popularity, explaining that it “felt like some sick mind game” when she got recognized for her role.

Watch on Deadline

Last month, Netflix announced that production wrapped on Season 3 of Wednesday, sharing a first-look image of Ortega as the titular Addams Family daughter.

Scheduled to premiere in 2027, the returning cast also includes Catherine Zeta-Jones as Morticia Addams, Luis Guzmán as Gomez Addams, Isaac Ordonez as Pugsley Addams, Emma Myers as Enid Sinclair, Hunter Doohan as Tyler Galpin, Joy Sunday as Bianca Barclay, Moosa Mostafa as Eugene Ottinger, Georgie Farmer as Ajax Petropolus, Billie Piper as Isadora Capri, Luyanda Unati Lewis-Nyawo as Sheriff Ritchie Santiago, Victor Dorobantu as Thing, Evie Templeton as Agnes DeMille and Fred Armisen as Uncle Fester.

Previously announced new Season 3 cast includes Eva Green as Aunt Ophelia, Winona Ryder as Tabitha, Chris Sarandon, Noah Tayler, Oscar Morgan, Kennedy Moyer, Lena Headey, Andrew McCarthy and James Lance. Joanna Lumley has been upped to series regular.

title: Amazon Cornered The YA Market, Now It’s Coming For New Adult Stories
summary: Amazon Prime Video has found much success in the YA space with series such as The Summer I Turned Pretty, We Were Liars, Elle and Sterling Point. Now, the streamer is turning its attention to a similar but slightly older and raunchier audience for its next batch of programming: the New Adult. It has already […]
content:
Amazon Prime Video has found much success in the YA space with series such as The Summer I Turned Pretty, We Were Liars, Elle and Sterling Point.

Now, the streamer is turning its attention to a similar but slightly older and raunchier audience for its next batch of programming: the New Adult.

It has already had hits in this space, which features characters aged 18-29 rather than younger teenagers between ages 12-18, with shows such as its adaptations of Elle Kennedy’s Off Campus and Carley Fortune’s Every Summer After. It has also lined up a show based on Elsie Silver’s Rose Hill book series and a TV adaptation of Lucy Score’s Things We Never Got Over that dovetail into the growing tier.

New Adult, which is thought to have emerged as a term in the late 2000s thanks to publisher St. Martin’s Press, aims to bridge the gap between Young Adult (YA) fiction and Adult fiction.

Watch on Deadline

New Adult also offers explicit sex scenes (hello, Off Campus). The online book community calls this spice, and it ranks how high each book’s spice level is depending on the amount of explicit sexual scenes. For instance, a story with less detail is sometimes called a “closed-door” romance because, like in movies or TV, the act is merely alluded to and not fully shown.

RELATED: Prime Video Teases Summer Slate Of YA Originals, Book Adaptations & More From ‘The Love Hypothesis’ To ‘Clashing Through The Snow’

Off Campus, often labeled a YA series, fits into New Adult. The first season follows the romance between Briar University’s hockey captain Garrett Graham (Belmont Cameli) and quiet songwriter and college junior Hannah Wells (Ella Bright). It launched in May and became Prime Video’s third most-viewed debut season ever behind The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Fallout, and was renewed for a second season ahead of its launch.

Similarly, Every Year After was renewed for a second season after its June bow. The TV series, which comes from Amy B. Harris and Leila Gerstein, is based on Carley Fortune’s eponymous book, the sequel of which will serve as the basis of Season 2. While the first book starts with Sam Florek (Matt Cornett) and Persephone “Percy” Fraser (Sadie Soverall) meeting in their adolescence, the time jump in the show’s first season includes the characters in their late 20s. The second book, One Golden Summer, tells the love story of Sam’s brother Charlie Florek (Michael Bradway), who is 35; his love interest Alice Everly, who has yet to be cast for Season 2 of the show, is 33 in the book.

“We’re always coming of age, and I love that. I see it in my mom’s generation, I see it with people in their 80s still entering new phases of what life looks like,” Fortune told Deadline in an interview tied to Every Year After‘s release. “I think the 30s are particularly interesting because you have made so many decisions that have set you up for where you are, and it is a great time to sit back or be forced to take a look at what those decisions, where they have put you, and is that where you [want to] be? The stakes go higher.”

Next up are Rose Hill and Things We Got Over. Rose Hill is a series of four contemporary romance novels — Wild Love, Wild Eyes, Wild Side and Wild Card — that feature interconnected stories set in the same fictional town.

RELATED: Everything We Know About Prime Video’s ‘Rose Hill’ Series Adaptation So Far

The first season of Rose Hill will follow the story from the first novel Wild Love, which centers on best friends and neighbors West Belmont (Jake Weary), a rancher with commitment issues, and brooding record label owner Ford Grant (Sean O’Pry), who’s long carried a torch for West’s sister, Rosie (Hannah Galway). And when country-pop star Skylar Stone (Sadie Dickerson) breezes into their rugged mountain town, the heat gets turned way up in this romantic family drama.

The streamer is already casting the Rose Hill series in anticipation of success: O’Pry, Galway, Weary and Dickerson have already been cast as the couples that lead the first two books. A few key characters from the latter half of the quartet have also been cast. Prime Video has a history with this strategy, having also banked on buzz around Off Campus by intertwining the love stories of the main four hockey teammates from the beginning of the series. While Season 1 focuses on Hannah and Garrett, Stephen Kalyn’s Dean DiLaurentis and Mika Abdalla’s Allie Hayes were heavily teed up to take over for Season 2, and Easter eggs were planted for the other two teammates’ love stories in Season 1.

The same pattern applies to Things We Got Over, based on the first novel in Lucy Score’s trilogy of romances. While the first installment features a love triangle between Naomi Witt (Molly Griggs) and the Morgan brothers Nash (Tommy Martinez) and Knox (Matthew Noszka), the following two books delineate to center two more Knockemout romances (Knockemout is the small town in Virginia where the series is set). Soft spoiler alert: the second book features the romance of the brother Naomi doesn’t end up with, and the third features local librarian Sloane (Sarah Jeffery) and Lucian (Sean Teale).

RELATED: Everything We Know About Prime Video’s ‘Things We Never Got Over’ Adaptation So Far

While Rose Hill is marketed as a series of single dad romances, and the Knockemout trilogy follows two brothers and their best friend, these two series are considered women-led — a genre that remains undersupplied across film and television, according to a report from Luminate.

Rose Hill and Things We Never Got Over also both deal with more mature themes including parenthood. In Wild Love, the first Rose Hill book, O’Pry’s character Ford realizes he has a biological child after sperm donation on a whim to get concert tickets. Things We Never Got Over forces parenthood on Naomi, whose twin sister Tina leaves her daughter Waylay (Megan Stott) behind for her more responsible sister to take care of. While Off Campus is set in college, the book series still deals with heavier topics as well, like Hannah’s rape and Garrett’s father’s abuse in Season 1.

It’s not a coincidence that Off Campus, the Rose Hill books and Things We Got Over trilogy all come from the same romance publisher: Bloom Books. The imprint even uses obsession in its marketing for books it brings to life.

RELATED: The Summer Fiftysomething Female Friendships Took Over Streaming With ‘Five Star Weekend’ & ‘Ride Or Die’s Surprise Success

Rose Hill leans western like Netflix’s recently cancelled Ransom Canyon, and Prime Video is aiming to rope in more than if not the same audience that fell in love with Off Campus. These shows should also appeal to older millennials given that a number of the characters in these books skew older. That being said, the New Adult category strikes a balance between those not yet old enough to pay for their own Prime Video or Amazon Prime accounts (new subscribers) and audiences of older women who may already have said subscriptions, which may have factored into the cancellation of female friendship-centered buddy comedy Ride Or Die.

Should the streamer continue with Obsessed Fest, it will be interesting to see how it markets its expanding slate of book adaptation romances. It will also be interesting to see if social media fan edits, which Head of Marketing for Amazon and MGM Studios Sue Kroll admitted to staying up late watching at the inaugural festival, will diverge when more of the New Adult shows arrive on Prime Video.

Amazon is also leaning into New Adult on the film side: Ana Huang’s Gods of the Game trilogy has been optioned for a trio of film adaptations by Amazon MGM Studios, and Lauren Asher’s Throttled will get a feature adaptation from the studio as well. Both Huang’s and Asher’s books are published by Bloom.

RELATED: Which Ali Hazelwood Books Are Becoming Movies? ‘The Love Hypothesis,’ ‘Deep End’ & More

They follow successful film adaptations of non-Bloom books like Casey McQuiston’s college-set Red, White & Royal Blue — which is getting a sequel film — starring Taylor Zakar-Perez as 21 year-old Alex Claremont-Diaz and Nicholas Galitzine as the slightly older Prince Henry; Ali Hazelwood’s The Love Hypothesis starring Lili Reinhart and Tom Benton, which is set in graduate school at Stanford University; and Hazelwood’s Love, Theoretically.

Then, there’s Fourth Wing, a romantasy series based on Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean series, which centers 20-year-old Violet Sorrengail (to be portrayed by Esther McGregor). A huge book in the romantasy genre, Fourth Wing does fall into the New Adult age-range category, but romantasy — a combination of romance and fantasy — often includes much more elaborate world-building. Amazon MGM Studios will also stretch its film romance offerings with the dark romance adaptation of Butcher & Blackbird, which has just set its lead cast.

Amazon is not alone in spotting the growing New Adult trend. Netflix, which has been in on the YA trend for many years, has lined up an adaptation of Fortune’s This Summer Will Be Different, and Shawn Levy is developing a series based on Elsie Silver’s Chestnut Springs novels. The streamer has also optioned the rights to Huang’s Twisted Love and its sequels for a TV series adaptation.

RELATED: Co-Founders Of Magic Hour Entertainment And Rebelle Media Plus Author Duo Christina Lauren Advise Studios & Streamers To Devote Resources To “Elevated” And “Prestige” Romance Through Casting, Chemistry & More

On the film side, Netflix also has Guarding Stars, based on Katherine Center’s The Bodyguard, and In a Holidaze, based on the book by Christina Lauren, coming out in November and December, respectively. The two holiday stories feature characters in the older New Adult age bracket. Shawn Levy’s 21 Laps and Alex Cooper’s Unwell Productions are also behind a feature film adaptation of Hazelwood’s Deep End.

Apple TV’s got The Buccaneers going for it, but that book adaptation falls more in the vein of period romances like Bridgerton. Apple TV also recently won rights to Yarros’ upcoming novel Peculiar Stars, which publishes November 17. Hulu took a big swing with an attempt to adapt Sarah J. Maas’ A Court of Thorns and Roses, but the rights have reverted back to Maas, who has two more books in that romantasy series on the way.

Ahead of Amazon’s Obsessed Fest over the summer, Peter Friedlander, Head of Global TV, Amazon MGM Studios, said there was a halo effect from Off Campus on Every Year After. “One success begets another,” he said just a day before Every Year After received its second-season renewal, like Off Campus had done. Sterling Point’s Season 2 renewal signals continued domination in the YA space for the streamer too, as do the upcoming second seasons of We Were Liars and Elle and The Summer I Turned Pretty‘s concluding film.

RELATED: Prime Video Flexes YA Synergy As ‘Elle’, ‘Off Campus’ & ‘Every Year After’ Stars Turn Out For Inaugural Fan Event Obsessed Fest

title: Becca Tobin On ‘Glee’ Reboot: “This Gives Me Diarrhea”
summary: Becca Tobin has had quite a reaction to the news that Glee is getting a revival on Disney+ and Hulu. Tobin joined the Ryan Murphy series in Season 4 as Kitty Wilde, a bully and a member of the McKinley High cheerleader squad who channeled an early Quinn Fabray. The actress recurred in Season 4 and became […]
content:
Becca Tobin has had quite a reaction to the news that Glee is getting a revival on Disney+ and Hulu.

Tobin joined the Ryan Murphy series in Season 4 as Kitty Wilde, a bully and a member of the McKinley High cheerleader squad who channeled an early Quinn Fabray. The actress recurred in Season 4 and became a series regular in Season 5. She reprised the role in Season 6.

“This gives me diarrhea,” Tobin said on the LadyGang podcast about the show’s revival. “It’s a situation where I’m not an original cast member. I was not in season 1. I came in three seasons in. So, there’s no guarantee.”

She added, “There’s no guarantee for anyone, anything, anywhere ever, right? But it’s the type of thing where you just sit, and you wait, and you’re like, ‘Okay, is he going to decide to invite, ask, whatever?’ It’s such a weird feeling.”

Watch on Deadline

Earlier this week, Deadline reported that Glee was getting a reboot, with Disney+ and Hulu ordering it as a series. Although no talent is attached to the revival, the show’s co-creator said he had finished a script for the new series.

On the LadyGang podcast, Tobin continued to express her thoughts over the Glee announcement, adding, “You know when you get that kind of anxiety where you’re like, oh God, is this going to be the type of thing where it comes back and everywhere I go, and I’m not doing anything, not even like one scene of one episode, and then everybody’s talking to me and asking me about it.”

Although not much was said about what the Glee revival would be about, Tobin acknowledged how “challenging it’s going to be for them to weave in already these original cast members and the new people and the whatever. I don’t know what the plan is. I do know the original people will most likely be coming back. It’s not a mystery that Ryan has spoken to them.”

title: Michael Gray, Star of ‘Shazam!’ TV Series, Dies at 75
summary: Michael Gray, the star of the 1970s “Shazam!” television series, died on Friday in Palm Desert from natural causes. He was 75. Gray first got his break in television in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s “The Little People” alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares. Early in his career, he held several supporting roles […]
content:
Michael Gray, the star of the 1970s “Shazam!” television series, died on Friday in Palm Desert from natural causes. He was 75.

Gray first got his break in television in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s “The Little People” alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares. Early in his career, he held several supporting roles across series including playing Marcia’s boyfriend Jeff on “The Brady Bunch” as well as appearing on “Dynasty,” “Marcus Welby, M.D.,” “Room 222” and “The Flying Nun,” as well in films such as “Run, Simon, Run,” “Beyond the Valley of the Dolls” and “Myra Breckinridge.”

In 1974, he joined the cast of “Shazam!” as Billy Batson, starring alongside John Davey and Les Tremayne in the series, which ran for three seasons until 1976. Gray became a teen idol, frequently appearing on the covers of Tiger Beat and other teen magazines.

Popular on Variety

“From my very first day on ‘Shazam!,’ Mike and Les [Tremayne] welcomed me like a king,” Davey said about Gray. “Mike was just a loving, sweet guy with a great sense of humor. He loved acting, loved doing the show and, in recent years, loved appearing at comic cons. He really enjoyed meeting and chatting with the fans. Mike was a wonderful man. I don’t think he ever stopped smiling.”

“Shazam!” was remastered in 2012 for distribution on DVD, which sparked a career resurgence for Gray. In recent years, he appeared in several episodes of the FX series “Archer” as one of the titular character’s boyhood idols, as well as appearing in “Surge of Power” on AMC’s “Comic Book Men.” When “Shazam! Fury of the Gods” released in 2023, Gray made a brief cameo where he interacted with Zachary Levi’s Captain Marvel as a nod to the original series.

Gray was born in Chicago on Sept. 2, 1951, and was raised in Miami Beach, Florida, before moving to Los Angeles to study acting at the Pasadena Playhouse and pursue his career in entertainment. After landing his role in “Shazam!,” Gray began to feel typecast and took a hiatus from acting. During this time, he worked in children’s theater education and men’s fashion, as well as owning and operating a floral business with his wife, Stacy.

Following the 2012 resurgence of “Shazam!,” Gray frequently attended fan conventions and reconnected with his fanbase while also pursuing roles in projects such as the “Surge of Power” franchise.

“I meet people [everyday] who say, ‘You have no idea what you did for me as a child.’ ‘You helped me get through life.’ ‘You made me the better man, or woman, that I am today,’” Gray told Fanboy Planet in 2012. “And that’s a nice feeling. I didn’t know the show had that much strength and power back then.”

Gray is survived by his wife, Stacy Benon Gray, whom he married in 1994; step-children Ryan Cooper and Laurel Cooper; and son-in-law Lee Barker.

title: CBS Premiere Week Multiplatform Ratings See Big Year-Over-Year Increases (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: CBS kicked off its fall 2026 TV season the week of Oct. 4 with a strong performance for its new and returning series, according to Nielsen live+7 multiplatform data. Per that data, CBS’ premiere week averaged 8.63 million viewers — up 14% from its premiere week in 2025 (the week of Oct. 12). Leading the […]
content:
CBS kicked off its fall 2026 TV season the week of Oct. 4 with a strong performance for its new and returning series, according to Nielsen live+7 multiplatform data.

Per that data, CBS’ premiere week averaged 8.63 million viewers — up 14% from its premiere week in 2025 (the week of Oct. 12). Leading the charge was the return of “Marshals,” which was the No. 1 entertainment show for the week (15.14 million viewers) in both linear and streaming. That was followed by “Tracker,” with 13.86 million viewers. “Marshals” and “Tracker” were also the week’s two most-watched shows in streaming alone.

Meanwhile, “Sheriff Country,” returning for a second season, hit a new series high, with 10.518 viewers — up 27% from its series premiere last year — and “NCIS” returned with 10.59 million viewers for its Season 24 premiere, up 23% from its season premiere last year.

Popular on Variety

Overall, if you take out sports, CBS reports pulling off seven of the week’s top 10 series in L+7 multiplatform viewing across linear and streaming. That includes “Marshals,” “Tracker,” “60 Minutes,” “NCIS,” “Sheriff Country,” “NCIS: New York” and “FBI.” When just broadcast is tallied, CBS has eight of the top 10 shows, with “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” also in the mix.

Besides “NCIS” and “Sheriff Country,” other shows with year-to-year growth during CBS’ premiere week included “NCIS: New York” (up 58% from last year’s time period premiere for “NCIS: Origins,” to 10.52 million), “FBI” (up 18% to 8.93 million), “Georgie & Mandy’s First Wedding” (up 11% to 8.70 million), “Fire Country” (up 7% to 7.96 million), “Survivor” (up 13% to 7.94 million), “NCIS: Origins” (up 19% to 7.75 million), “Elsbeth” (up 5% to 7.69 million), “The Amazing Race” (up 6% to 4.82 million) and “Harlan Coben’s Final Twist” (up 29% to 3.15 million).

Meanwhile, among new series, “Cupertino” saw a big lift in delayed viewing, averaging 7.17 million viewers in L+7 multiplatform — up from 3.19 million in live+same day.

title: Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year
summary: Singer-songwriter and Variety Hitmakers 2024 honoree Raye has won the 2026 Mercury prize for her epic second studio album, “This Music May Contain Hope,” beating out Olivia Dean, Paul McCartney and others for the prize. The Mercury Prize has no real equivalent in the U.S., and is intended to recognize music from the U.K. and […]
content:
Singer-songwriter and Variety Hitmakers 2024 honoree Raye has won the 2026 Mercury prize for her epic second studio album, “This Music May Contain Hope,” beating out Olivia Dean, Paul McCartney and others for the prize.

The Mercury Prize has no real equivalent in the U.S., and is intended to recognize music from the U.K. and Ireland; the Brit Awards are more of a British equivalent to the Grammys. Past Mercury Prize best album winners include Arlo Parks, Little Simz, the XX, James Blake and others.

Raye’s album topped fellow nominees Dave (for “The Boy Who Played the Harp”), Dove Ellis (“Blizzard”). Florence + the Machine (“Everybody Scream”), Jade (“That’s Showbiz Baby!”), Knats (“A Great Day in Newcastle”), Kojey Radical (“Don’t Look Down”), Nia Archives (“Emotional Junglist”), Olivia Dean (“The Art of Loving”), Paul McCartney (“The Boys of Dungeon Lane”), Suede (“Antidepressants”) and the War Child “Help(2)” compilation.

Popular on Variety

Variety wrote of Raye’s album: “Suffice it to say, the album does not lack for ambition: Divided into four sections based on the seasons, it sprawls across a surprisingly fast-moving 70 minutes, 17 songs and nearly as many styles. Inevitably, it runs the risk of being too much for some listeners: too many songs, too many stylistic pivots, too much of… well, basically everything. This is not an album for background listening — it basically demands your attention.

“But as artists from Queen to Beyoncé have proven, ambition and excess can be glorious things when deployed with intelligence and humor, and while we’re not equating Raye with either of the above, there’s a similar sense here of trusting the artist to take you on an interesting voyage without wasting your time.”

Performers at the show included Suede, Pulp, and others.

title: Heather Morris & Chord Overstreet In Talks To Return For ‘Glee’ Reboot
summary: Two more original Glee cast members are eyeing a return for the Disney+/Hulu reboot. Heather Morris, who portrayed ditzy, high-spirited cheerleader Brittany, and Chord Overstreet, who played Sam Evans in the original series are in talks to return for the reboot, sources have confirmed to Deadline. Overstreet’s Sam Evans was a transfer student to William […]
content:
Two more original Glee cast members are eyeing a return for the Disney+/Hulu reboot. Heather Morris, who portrayed ditzy, high-spirited cheerleader Brittany, and Chord Overstreet, who played Sam Evans in the original series are in talks to return for the reboot, sources have confirmed to Deadline.

Overstreet’s Sam Evans was a transfer student to William McKinley High School, who joined the football team and the school’s glee club, New Directions.

They join Lea Michele, who we reported Wednesday is in talks to reprise her Rachel Berry character from the OG.

Disney+ and Hulu announced a series order for the reboot earlier this week.

Watch on Deadline

Co-creator Ryan Murphy said last month that he had been in touch with “around 10 of the original cast members” of the show, though no casting was announced as part of the series order.

The original Glee cast included Chris Colfer, Jane Lynch, Kevin McHale and Matthew Morrison as well as Dianna Agron, Cory Monteith, Amber Riley, Mark Salling, the late Naya Rivera and Darren Criss.

Set at William McKinley High School in Lima, Ohio, Glee followed the members of the New Directions, a glee club competing in the show choir circuit, while dealing with social issues. Each episode featured a musical performance.

The reboot hails from original show producer 20th Television.

The original Glee, created by Murphy, Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan, aired for six seasons from 2009-2015, on Fox. It won six Emmys, including for Murphy and Lynch as well as guest stars such as Neil Patrick Harris and Gwyneth Paltrow, and currently streams on Hulu.

Rosy Cordero contributed to this report.

title: Chris Jericho To Play Gorgeous George In Prime Video’s Muhammad Ali Limited Series ‘The Greatest’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Chris Jericho will be portraying legendary wrestling pioneer Gorgeous George in Ben Watkin’s upcoming historical drama, The Greatest, a Prime Video limited series that chronicles the life of Muhammad Ali. All eight episodes will be released on Wednesday, November 4. One of wrestling’s first true mainstream celebrities, Gorgeous George became a television sensation whose […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Chris Jericho will be portraying legendary wrestling pioneer Gorgeous George in Ben Watkin’s upcoming historical drama, The Greatest, a Prime Video limited series that chronicles the life of Muhammad Ali. All eight episodes will be released on Wednesday, November 4.

One of wrestling’s first true mainstream celebrities, Gorgeous George became a television sensation whose flamboyance, swagger, and mastery of self-promotion famously influenced a young Muhammad Ali. Jericho, curls and all, makes his first appearance in the show’s fourth episode.

The Greatest features defining moments in Ali’s life and career, both in and out of the ring, that have been well documented, and moments that took place outside the spotlight. The world remembers an icon, but The Greatest is about a man, a husband, a father, a brother, and a son.

Watch on Deadline

Jaalen Best leads the cast in the role of Ali, and he stars alongside Omari Hardwick and Dana Gourrier, who star as Cassius “Cash” Clay Sr. and his wife Odessa “Bird” Clay, respectively, parents of Muhammad Ali and Rudy Clay (Kai Parham). Amin Joseph plays Sonny Liston, Ali’s rival and the heavyweight champion, and Giovanni Ribisi plays Angelo Dundee. In a recurring role, Michael Ealy plays Malcolm X.

The Greatest is created, executive produced, and created by Watkins and is the first authorized scripted series about the life of Ali. Ali’s widow, Lonnie Ali, also executive produced alongside Michael B. Jordan’s Outlier Society, Authentic Studios, Roc Nation, Shawn Carter, Polygram Entertainment, and Grace: A Storytelling Company.

Similar to Gorgeous George, Jericho is best known for entertaining fans in the ring as a wrestler for WWE, then for AEW, where he continues to fight on occasion. His recent acting credits include CBS’ Tracker and Apple TV’s Margo’s Got Money Troubles. Up next, he will appear on Dexter: Resurrection‘s second season, premiering October 30 on Paramount+. Behind the camera, he executive produced Vietslam: Squashing the Cultural Gap, which explores professional wrestling’s unexpected cultural footprint in Vietnam, and the upcoming horror film Dead of Night, set for a limited theatrical release on November 13. Jericho is repped by agent Alison Little and manager Barry Bloom.

title: Michael Gray Dies: ‘Shazam!’ Star Was 75
summary: Michael Gray, star of the 1970s CBS live-action series Shazam! died of natural causes on Friday, October 16 in Palm Desert, CA, his rep confirmed to Deadline. He was 75. One of Gray’s early television roles came in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s The Little People, alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares. But […]
content:
Michael Gray, star of the 1970s CBS live-action series Shazam! died of natural causes on Friday, October 16 in Palm Desert, CA, his rep confirmed to Deadline. He was 75.

One of Gray’s early television roles came in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s The Little People, alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares. But his big break came a couple years later when he landed the role of Billy Batson in the Saturday morning live-action show Shazam!

Gray’s Billy Batson was a teenage boy who could transform into the superhero Captain Marvel by speaking the magic word “Shazam!” With his guardian “Mentor” (Les Tremayne), Billy traveled the country in a 1973 Dodge Open Road motorhome, looking for injustices to resolve. The role originally was played by Jackson Bostwick and later by John Davey.

“I didn’t know the character or the story when I was initially cast, so I had to be a quick study – so it was fun and exhausting, challenging and thrilling, all at once,” Gray said during a Comic-Con panel in 2012. “It didn’t matter that it was on Saturday morning or prime time – though the fact that it was one of the first few live-action shows on Saturday morning was exciting. It truly was a thrilling show to work.”

Shazam! aired on CBS from 1974-1976.

During the ’70s Gray also became a teen idol, frequently appearing on the covers of Tiger Beat and other popular teen magazines.

His early career also included guest roles in primetime series such as The Brady Bunch (as Marcia’s boyfriend in a 1973 episode), Dynasty, Marcus Welby, M.D., Room 222 and The Flying Nun. He also played Burt Reynolds’ younger brother in the TV movie Run, Simon, Run, and appeared in the 1970 films Beyond the Valley of the Dolls and Myra Breckinridge.

His more recent credits include a four-episode arc on the FX comedy Archer as the voice of one of Sterling Archer’s boyhood idols, portraying “TV’s Michael Gray.” He also appeared in the Surge of Power film franchise, on AMC’s Comic Book Men, and had a fun cameo in Shazam! Fury of the Gods, where he interacted with Zachary Levi’s Captain Marvel in a wink to the original series.

Gray is survived by his wife Stacy Benon Gray, whom he married in 1994, his stepchildren Ryan Cooper and Laurel Cooper and son-in-law Lee Barker.

title: Marvel’s ‘Zodiac’ Spy Series To Be Written By Amit Cohen & Ron Leshem
summary: Following the news that Marvel has the spy thriller series Zodiac in the works at Disney+, Amit Cohen and Ron Leshem have been set as the show’s writers, we hear. When the new show was announced on October 8, details were scant. The story will follow a pair of spies who are chasing targets who […]
content:
Following the news that Marvel has the spy thriller series Zodiac in the works at Disney+, Amit Cohen and Ron Leshem have been set as the show’s writers, we hear.

When the new show was announced on October 8, details were scant. The story will follow a pair of spies who are chasing targets who have special abilities, sources tell Deadline. As we previously reported, the show is expected to premiere in 2028, with production beginning in 2027.

Leshem served as a creator of the original Israeli Euphoria series and its HBO adaptation from Sam Levin starring Zendaya. Alongside Cohen, they created and executive produced multiple Israeli shows, including Trust No One, Bad Boy, 8200, Red Skies, and Traitor. For the U.S. market, the writing partners created the Hulu drama series No Man’s Land.

Zodiac will join a waning live-action TV slate at Marvel, where many of the franchise’s most popular titles have either already ended or soon will. The WandaVision trilogy is coming to its conclusion later this month with VisionQuest, which premiered on October 13 and will continue to air weekly until all 8 episodes are dropped on November 10.

Watch on Deadline

Daredevil: Born Again, which welcomed several beloved characters back into the MCU, including Charlie Cox as Matt Murdock and Krysten Ritter as Jessica Jones, will end with Season 3 next year. Wonder Man was a one-season series, as Marvel opted not to renew the series for a second season. Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, who played the titular superhero, received an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series. The nod was the first for Marvel since the studio’s success with WandaVision.

Katie Campione contributed to this report.

title: Tony Lipp And Dara Gordon Join Entertainment 360 As Partners
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Tony Lipp and Dara Gordon have joined Entertainment 360 as partners. Lipp will also join the management board, and Gordon will lead the New York office. The hirings are a major win for the company, with Lipp and Gordon drawing interest from several management companies after the pair recently left Anonymous Content. Lipp started […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Tony Lipp and Dara Gordon have joined Entertainment 360 as partners. Lipp will also join the management board, and Gordon will lead the New York office.

The hirings are a major win for the company, with Lipp and Gordon drawing interest from several management companies after the pair recently left Anonymous Content.

Lipp started his career as a talent agent at CAA where he worked from 1996-2011. In 2011, he made the transition to management and film and TV production when he joined Anonymous Content. A partner in the company, he also served as Head of the Talent Department during his tenure.

His current clients include John Lithgow, Sally Field, Patrick Wilson, Jonathan Bailey, Michelle Monaghan, Kate O’Flynn, Betty Gilpin, Patrick Stewart, Lewis Pullman, Joshua Jackson, Matt Bomer, Max Minghella, Jack Quaid, Patricia Clarkson, Beth Behrs, Justin Kirk, Cush Jumbo, Lauren Cohan and André Holland.

Watch on Deadline

While at Anonymous Content, Lipp produced various film and television projects most recently the Netflix film Remarkably Bright Creatures, starring Field and based on Shelby Van Pelt’s New York Times bestselling novel. The pic won an Emmy Award for Best Original Movie.

He also was an executive producer on the 2018 Focus Features film Boy Erased, which starred Lucas Hedges, Nicole Kidman and Joel Edgerton.

“For over 20 years I have admired the managers and leaders of Entertainment 360 enormously. Their dedication to the artists they represent is best in class and I feel so lucky to be able to join them,” Lipp said. “I am incredibly excited to start this next chapter in my career with such thoughtful and inspiring colleagues and I am especially thrilled to be doing it alongside my dear friend, Dara Gordon.”

Gordon joined Anonymous Content in 2015 where she was a partner in the Talent Department, based in New York City.

She started her career at CAA in Los Angeles, then moved to work at Warner Bros in feature development. In 2009 she became a manager in at Authentic Talent & Literary Management in New York.

“Tony and Dara are exactly the kind of people you build a company around. Beyond their exceptional clients, they bring the experience, relationships and leadership to help shape our future. Tony has built an extraordinary career as a manager, producer and leader, and brings a depth of experience and perspective that will be invaluable to our management board,” a statement from Entertainment 360 partners reads. “Dara is equally accomplished, with tremendous instincts, an entrepreneurial spirit and a genuine passion for the artists she represents. We are thrilled to welcome them both as partners, and particularly excited for Dara to lead the expansion of our New York office, a major priority for the company.”

Gordon’s clients include Aaron Pierre, Adria Arjona, Betty Gilpin, Billy Magnussen, Caitlin FitzGerald, Danny Ramirez, Emma Laird, Havana Rose Liu, Ismael Cruz Cordova, Julia Butters, Kristine Froseth, Leo Woodall, Lewis Pullman, Lili Reinhart, Melissa Benoist, Micah Stock, Orlando Norman, Rightor Doyle, Sadie Soverall and Winona Ryder.

She executive produced two seasons of the Netflix series Bonding, created by her client Doyle, as well as the Amazon feature film Birds of Paradise, directed by Sarah Adina Smith and starring Froseth.

“I have always loved being a manager, but the process of getting to know the people at Entertainment 360 has made me even more enamored by and excited about this profession,” she said. “I feel lucky to be joining this formidable group, whom I have long admired from afar, and look forward to growing together. As a fourth generation New Yorker, the opportunity to help ramp up New York office of this company is a true honor, especially at a time when this city feels even more dynamic than ever.”

title: Biographies of John Williams and Bernard Herrmann Among Honored Works in ASCAP’s Awards for Music Writing and Broadcasts
summary: The winners of annual awards given out by ASCAP for the year’s most outstanding music writing and broadcasts include biographies of film composers John Williams and Bernard Herrmann, as well as a documentary about cult R&B artist Swamp Dogg, liner notes for an archival release from Frank Zappa, Rick Beato’s YouTube podcasts, and books about […]
content:
The winners of annual awards given out by ASCAP for the year’s most outstanding music writing and broadcasts include biographies of film composers John Williams and Bernard Herrmann, as well as a documentary about cult R&B artist Swamp Dogg, liner notes for an archival release from Frank Zappa, Rick Beato’s YouTube podcasts, and books about Broadway musicals and Black opera innovators.

These disparate writings are among the recipients of the 77th annual ASCAP Foundation Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Awards, voted on by a select committee of four ASCAP members to recognize the best in books, articles, liner notes and broadcast programs about all forms of music.

The film composer biographies being recognized were Tim Greiving‘s “John Williams: A Composer’s Life,” the first-ever biography about Hollywood’s most successful living composer, which got a Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Award in the field of concert music, and Steven C. Smith‘s “Hitchcock and Herrmann: The Friendship and Film Scores that Changed Cinema,” the author’s second book about Herrmann (with a twist that makes it dually the story of his greatest filmmaker collaborator), which was given a special recognition award in the same category.

Popular on Variety

Another book award in the concert music field, this one outside the realm of film music, went to Lucy Caplan for “Dreaming in Ensemble: How Black Artists Transformed American Opera.” Awards for books in the pop music field were given to Gayle Wald for “This Is Rhythm: Ella Jenkins, Children’s Music, and the Long Civil Rights Movement” and James O’Leary for The Middlebrow Musical: Between Broadway and Opera in 1940s America.”

Among the articles that won recognition from the ASCAP judges were a piece by the New York Times’ Ben Sisario about efforts to rescue decaying master tapes, a story by Esteban Meneses about Mexican symphonic composers and an article by the New York Times’ Max Keller about cellists debating the right way to hold their instruments. A piece in the Atlantic by Gabriel Kahana won for outstanding music criticism.

The top broadcast award went to Gail Wein for her podcast series “Classical Gas,” with a special recognition honor for Beato for his YouTube series “Everything Music.”

A liner notes award was given to percussionist Ruth Komanoff Underwood for her personal essay contained in the boxed set for “Cheaper than Cheep,” a live 1974 concert film by Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention.

A broadcast/media award in the pop field went to directors Isaac Gale, Ryan Olson and David McMurry for their documentary “Swamp Dogg Gets His Pool Pained.”

The judges for this year’s honors were Robbie Fulks, Julie Flanders, Carman Moore and Betsy Schramm.

The full list of winners, as provided by ASCAP:

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Broadcast/Media Award in pop music recognizes directors Isaac Gale, Ryan Olson and David McMurry for their documentary film “Swamp Dogg Gets His Pool Painted,” released in 2025, a unique storytelling of the legendary cult R&B musician Jerry “Swamp Dogg” Williams’s and his housemates’ musical creative life in Los Angeles surrounding his pool.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Broadcast/Media Award in concert music recognizes radio host and producer Gail Wein for “Classical Gas,” produced by Classical Voice North America, the 2025 podcast series of interviews with classical musicians available on multiple platforms.

A Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Rick Beato for his 2025 YouTube series, “Everything Music,” exploring music, technology and issues facing music creators in today’s industry.

The ASCAP Foundation Paul Williams “Loved the Liner Notes” Award honors percussionist Ruth Komanoff Underwood for her personal essay for “Cheaper than Cheep,” the live box set from the 1974 concert film by Frank Zappa and The Mothers of Invention, on ZAPPA RECORDS/UMe.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Awards in pop music are presented to: Gayle Wald for “This Is Rhythm: Ella Jenkins, Children’s Music, and the Long Civil Rights Movement,” the life story of “the first lady of children’s music,” published by University of Chicago Press.

James O’Leary for “The Middlebrow Musical: Between Broadway and Opera in 1940s America,” an exploration of how musicals such as Oklahoma!, Beggar’s Holiday, and Street Scene embraced weighty stories in ways not seen before 1943, published by Oxford University Press.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Awards in concert music go to:

Lucy Caplan for “Dreaming in Ensemble: How Black Artists Transformed American Opera,” an account of Black innovation in American opera during the Harlem Renaissance, published by Harvard University Press.

Tim Greiving for “John Williams: A Composer’s Life,” the first biography of one of the most important film composers of all time, published by Oxford University Press.

Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Steven C. Smith for “Hitchcock and Herrmann: The Friendship and Film Scores that Changed Cinema,” published by Oxford University Press.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award recipients for articles published in 2025 are as follows:

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award for an article in the pop music field goes to Ben Sisario, “The ‘Race Against Time’ to Save Music Legends’ Decaying Tapes,” on the intricate efforts to restore analog tapes with original recordings from Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan and more, published by The New York Times.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award for an article in the concert music field goes to Esteban Meneses, “Revolución: Mexican Composers on the Rise,” a look at Mexican composers whose works are being performed, commissioned, and recorded by orchestras around the world, published by Symphony Magazine.

Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Max Keller, “Does It Matter How A Cello Is Held? It’s a Centuries-Old Debate,“ published by The New York Times.

The Virgil Thomson Award for Outstanding Music Criticism is presented to Gabriel Kahane for his article, “A Love Letter to Music Listings,” published by The Atlantic.

title: Richard Gadd, Bill Camp and Ray McKinnon Join Michael Keaton-Directed Western ‘Rode to Ruin’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Emmy Award-winning actor and writer Richard Gadd, multi-Emmy and SAG nominated actor Bill Camp and Oscar-nominated filmmaker and actor Ray McKinnon are joining “Rode to Ruin,” a Western thriller directed by Michael Keaton. Keaton also stars in the film, which is now in production in Santa Fe, New Mexico, along with Morgan Freeman and Laura […]
content:
Emmy Award-winning actor and writer Richard Gadd, multi-Emmy and SAG nominated actor Bill Camp and Oscar-nominated filmmaker and actor Ray McKinnon are joining “Rode to Ruin,” a Western thriller directed by Michael Keaton.

Keaton also stars in the film, which is now in production in Santa Fe, New Mexico, along with Morgan Freeman and Laura Linney. Angel acquired worldwide rights and will release “Rode to Ruin” in theaters in 2027.

Also joining the cast are Chris Candy, Travis Hammer, Thom Rivera and Derek Hinkey.

Popular on Variety

“Richard, Ray and Bill are the kind of actors who make every scene better simply by being in it,” said producer Lori McCreary. “They each bring such specificity, humanity and truth to their work, and seeing them alongside Michael, Morgan and Laura is incredibly exciting. Avy Kaufman has helped us make this cast something very special.”

The story follows a retired U.S. Marshal whose 40-year search for his wife’s killer leads him to an aging outlaw losing his memory, and to a buried truth neither man may survive, according to the synopsis.

Gadd plays Clive McKinney, the young, dangerous, and charismatic head of an outlaw gang riding the territory in search of a rumored fortune and the man who destroyed his family.

“Rode to Ruin” is produced by McCreary, Keaton, Kelly Mendelsohn, Gary Lucchesi and Richard Gray for Freeman and McCreary’s Revelations Entertainment and Keaton’s George and Leona Productions.

R. Dean McCreary wrote the screenplay, and executive producers include Steve Sarowitz, Carter Boehm, Skip Herman, Blake Johnson, Randall Emmett and John Bommarito.

Gadd is represented by UTA, Individual Artist Management and Casarotto and Markham, Froggatt & Irwin. Camp is represented by UTA and Franklin, Weinrib, Rudell & Vassallo, P.C. McKinnon is represented by Paradigm, Anonymous Content and Skrzyniarz & Mallean.

Linney is represented by CAA, Lighthouse Management + Media, and Kevin Yorn; Keaton is represented by CAA and JSSK and Morgan Freeman is represented by CAA and Sloane, Offer, Weber and Dern.

title: Peter Chan Rules Out AI-Generated Content, Says Feature Films Will Survive the Rise of Vertical Dramas
summary: Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun, director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his filmmaking but “definitely not AIGC,” or AI-generated content, and that the two-hour feature will hold its ground against short-form and vertical dramas, at least in his lifetime. Speaking at an In […]
content:
Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun, director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his filmmaking but “definitely not AIGC,” or AI-generated content, and that the two-hour feature will hold its ground against short-form and vertical dramas, at least in his lifetime.

Speaking at an In Conversation event at the Singapore International Film Festival, Chan was asked by an audience member whether he had ever doubted his decision to go into the film industry. His advice to aspiring filmmakers: “This is probably the toughest time for film, but do I believe this medium is going to be lost and gone to short-form entertainment? No.”

He said he would probably use AI as a technique, the way the industry already uses CGI and special effects, noting that CGI has relied on AI for years without calling it that. “Anything that helps me make movies, I welcome. But they won’t know art. Movies are still made by people,” Chan said.

Popular on Variety

Young audiences’ shrinking attention spans have them turning to short and vertical dramas, Chan said, while at the other end, people are listening to podcasts that run for hours, and Christopher Nolan did podcasts around the world to explain his purist approach of making “Oppenheimer” the way movies were made in the ’50s. “So there are two completely opposite ends of the spectrum that are surviving and thriving simultaneously. So I believe that movie will be around for a long, long time,” he told a rapt audience at the Grand Ballroom, Marina Bay Sands.

Chan’s latest film, “The Road Not Taken,” premiered in Toronto. “My new movie is about Alzheimer’s, but it’s really not just about Alzheimer’s. It’s about a broken family that has all sorts of problems a family could have,” he said.

The story centers on a couple in the middle of divorce proceedings when the wife, who has early-onset Alzheimer’s, no longer remembers the divorce and drifts back in her mind to the time they fell in love in their 20s. A harsh grandfather and the couple’s relationship with their Gen Z daughter complete the picture. The daughter in the film is 20, the same age as Chan’s own daughter, who is training to become an actor. Chan’s partner is actor Sandra Ng.

The English title comes from the Robert Frost poem, which Chan called his life motto, while the Chinese title, “Ming Tian Hui Geng Hao,” translates as “Tomorrow Will Be Better.” “There’s really no right path,” he said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, it’s all about how you walk it. You make it right.”

While researching the film, Chan visited an Alzheimer’s care institution in Chengdu, in China’s Sichuan province, where he picked up an eight-word Mandarin phrase that he used to sum up his career: go with the flow, and know when to stop. In the ’90s, when he was making romantic comedies at United Filmmakers Organization (UFO), the company he co-founded, gangster pictures and wuxia ruled Hong Kong screens. “We were not exactly going with the flow, but we did make the flow, somehow,” he said.

That same flow later carried him to “The Warlords,” which he described as his biggest film. “Never had I thought that I would ever make a historical epic battle movie with Jet Li. That was never, ever in my agenda for my entire life,” Chan said.

This year marks the 30th anniversary of “Comrades,” which Chan made at 34 as his seventh feature and which captures Hong Kong between 1985 and 1995. He left Hong Kong on Christmas Eve 1996, and only after returning from America around two and a half years later did he grasp how deeply the film had affected filmmakers in mainland China, South Korea and Southeast Asia, even though, he said, it probably only barely recouped its investment.

“That movie gave me a lease of movie life for the next 30 years, until now,” Chan said.

He said 90% of people remember him for that single film, “as if I have not done better afterwards,” calling it a blessing but also a spell he wanted to break.

Chan, who also said the ’90s marked the start of Hong Kong cinema’s decline rather than its golden age, described his DreamWorks film “The Love Letter” as a difficult experience. He was not thrown by working across cultures, he said, having grown up Thai-Chinese and feeling like an outsider even in Hong Kong. What he struggled with was a corporate system where it was unclear who called the shots, and a reliance on test screenings that he likened to today’s algorithms.
