title: British Filmmaker Joanna Hogg on the Struggle to Turn Personal Stories Into Fiction: ‘Each Time I’m Learning From Scratch’
summary: British filmmaker Joanna Hogg, who has been serving as president of the Feature Narrative Competition jury at the ninth edition of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival this week, tells Variety she prefers to know as little as possible about a film before watching it, “not even a synopsis of the story.” “I prefer to go […]
content:
British filmmaker Joanna Hogg, who has been serving as president of the Feature Narrative Competition jury at the ninth edition of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival this week, tells Variety she prefers to know as little as possible about a film before watching it, “not even a synopsis of the story.”

“I prefer to go in with no criteria and a very open mind,” she explains. “I am looking for something that moves me, but it also can be something that strikes me in a particular way. It doesn’t have to reduce me to tears, but just something that’s maybe got a clarity about it, a feeling that the filmmaker has ideas and a vision.”

With films from both first-time and established directors, a range of genres and stories from different parts of the world, Hogg sees little sense in applying the same criteria to each. “I really feel like I’ve travelled, even though I’ve been here in El Gouna. I’ve really travelled all over the place.”

Popular on Variety

It is Hogg’s first visit to Egypt, and she describes herself as something of an outsider on a jury that includes filmmakers from Egypt, Iraq and Turkey. Listening to their perspectives, she notes, has “whetted my appetite to discover films, actually not just from Egypt, but the Middle East in general.”

The experience also marks a return to watching films after months spent largely immersed in her own writing. “I’ve been stuck at home for quite a few months writing and actually not watching any films,” Hogg explains. “It’s been really nice to come here with a sort of clear mind, not having been watching cinema at all. Reading a lot, but not watching. And so I think it made me more receptive to the films.”

Hogg is currently writing her next film, which once again has her grappling with the line between lived experience and fiction. The director’s work, which includes “The Souvenir,” “The Souvenir Part II” and “The Eternal Daughter,” is deeply personal.

“I’m very interested in the sort of tension between what’s personal and a real experience that I’ve had and turning that into cinema and into fiction,” she goes on.

Despite drawing on her own experiences across several films, Hogg doesn’t feel the process has become any easier. “It’s a different story that I’m telling with this film. Each time I’m learning from scratch in a way, which I quite like,” she says.

Hogg graduated from film school, but found herself working in television rather than making films, an experience she remembers with little fondness.

“It was a disappointment in a way that I went into television,” she acknowledges. “I went into it because I needed to work and it wasn’t as easy as I thought making a first feature film.”

The turning point came, she remembers, while she was directing a television episode to which she felt little connection. “I almost can remember where I was standing when I thought this,” Hogg recalls. “I was rehearsing a scene with these actors. It was very much television and it was not a story that I had any relationship to. I hadn’t written the script.”

Her realization was simple. “I thought, I really must tell something personal.”

The late American film producer Barbara Stone, a friend of Hogg’s who would go on to produce “Unrelated,” her 2007 debut film, supplied the final push. When Hogg told her she intended to make a short, Stone challenged her, asking, “Why make a short film? Make a feature.”

Hogg’s working relationship, and friendship, with Tilda Swinton dates back even further, to her 1986 graduation film, “Caprice.” Their career paths diverged creatively for decades before they reunited on “The Souvenir” films and later “The Eternal Daughter.”

“We talk about this sometimes and we said, ‘Well, actually, maybe it’s not a bad thing. We both developed our own way first,’” Hogg reflects. “Then when we came together with ‘The Souvenir,’ which was many years later, it was such a pleasure. We did think, well, ‘Why the hell have we taken this long to do another piece of work? We’ll do more work together.’”

For now, however, Hogg’s attention is on the still-unannounced film waiting for her back home. After days immersed in the work of other filmmakers at El Gouna, she anticipates some difficulty returning to the world of her own film.

“I’ll have to decompress,” she explains, allowing the films she has been watching to settle before she can “come quietly back to my story.”

title: As Uncensored Re-Release of Ken Russell’s ‘The Devils’ Shocks Audiences, Director’s Son Preps Doc Feature ‘Mad Dad’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Considered one of the most controversial films of all time for its graphic, blasphemous, and sexually provocative imagery, Ken Russell’s “The Devils” is now back in cinemas uncut and uncensored. Re-released in 4K by Warner Bros. imprint Clockwork some 55 years after its controversial debut, the new director’s cut of the film — which premiered this […]
content:
Considered one of the most controversial films of all time for its graphic, blasphemous, and sexually provocative imagery, Ken Russell‘s “The Devils” is now back in cinemas uncut and uncensored.

Re-released in 4K by Warner Bros. imprint Clockwork some 55 years after its controversial debut, the new director’s cut of the film — which premiered this year in Cannes and later the London Film Festival — has given an entirely new generation the chance to discover Russell, often considered the overlooked “wild man” of British cinema.

Timed to the release — and an upcoming retrospective of his work being presented next year by the British Film Institute — the director’s son and fellow filmmaker Rupert Russell has unveiled “Mad Dad,” a feature documentary described as the “definitive portrait of Ken Russell.” Russell teamed up with Anna Hashmi, producer and founder of The Corner Shop on the project, which is also being produced by Andy Starke of Anti-Worlds Films and Sam Cryer of Intermission Films, with Daniel Bergmann of Stink Films as executive producer.

Popular on Variety

In “Mad Dad,” Rupert sets out on a tragicomic journey to discover who his enigmatic father really was: the dad and the director, the art and the artist, the myth and the man, the accolades and the absurdity. At the heart of the story are the unseen family archives, featuring hundreds of personal letters, thousands of photographs, and several home movies – not to mention Russell senior’s own autobiographical docudrama “A British Picture,” in which Ken played his own antagonists and Rupert, aged four, played the young Ken.

Contributors to the doc include family members who have never spoken publicly before and legends of

film and music such as Guillermo del Toro, Steven Soderbergh, Kathleen Turner, Pete Townshend,

Oliver Stone, Twiggy, Ann-Margret and many more.

Rupert Russell’s other works include “Freedom for the Wolf,” which won the Audience Award at

Slamdance Film Festival and was nominated for the Cinema for Peace Most Valuable Film of the

Year Award during Berlinale 2019. His second documentary, “Price Wars” — which he also wrote as a book, published by Doubeday, aired on ARTE. His most recent film, “The Last Sacrifice,” received a theatrical release in 2025 and was acquired by the horror streamer Shudder.

The Corner Shop continues to expand its film production slate. It recently received BFI funding for “The Mammoths That Escaped the Kingdom of Erlik Khan” with two-time Oscar-nominated director Tamara Kotevska. Last year saw the release of another feature with Kotevska, “The Tale of Silyan,” which premiered at Venice and TIFF, sold to Nat Geo, won awards at IDA, Cinema Eye, Venice, Humanitas and Chicago, and received two Emmy nominations.

title: Meghan Markle ‘Deeply Distressed’ by Allegations Her Father Possessed Child Sex Abuse Images
summary: Meghan Markle has shared a statement saying she is “deeply distressed” by allegations that her estranged father, Thomas Markle, possessed child sex abuse images. A report in The Sun claimed on Friday that child sex abuse images had allegedly been found in 82-year-old Thomas Markle’s former home in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle […]
content:
Meghan Markle has shared a statement saying she is “deeply distressed” by allegations that her estranged father, Thomas Markle, possessed child sex abuse images.

A report in The Sun claimed on Friday that child sex abuse images had allegedly been found in 82-year-old Thomas Markle’s former home in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. Variety has not been able to verify if there is currently an investigation underway. Thomas Markle — who now reportedly lives in Florida — vehemently denied the allegations to the Daily Mail, calling them “a bunch of lies” and adding: “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

In a statement shared with Variety, the Duchess of Sussex said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.” She claimed that in 2018, a letter about her father was sent to the Metropolitan Police and its Royalty and Specialist Protection unit and was “subsequently shared” with her.

Popular on Variety

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

The Metropolitan Police said in a statement to Variety: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. We are undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.” It is understood that the Met has not and is not currently investigating Thomas Markle.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he failed to walk her down the aisle at her wedding. She was escorted by King Charles instead. Thomas Markle has never met her and Prince Harry‘s two children. Last year, she sent a letter to him while he was in the hospital getting his left lower leg amputated due to a blood clot.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan concluded.

Representatives for the FBI and local police in the Philippines did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment. Variety has made attempts to reach Thomas Markle and Thomas Markle Jr.

According to the BBC, the undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, confirmed that “the matter is currently being investigated” by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force. The national police are in possession of Thomas Markle’s computer, Philippines interior minister Jonvic Remulla told the outlet, to conduct a digital forensic examination.

Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the U.K. after living in California for six years. Speaking to GQ about the move, Prince Harry revealed that he still has hopes of reconnecting with his father, King Charles, and brother Prince William.

“Some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out,” Harry said. “With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile — that’s the key point.”

title: Jon Tower Named Permanent Executive Producer Of ‘CBS Mornings’
summary: Jon Tower has been named the permanent executive producer of CBS Mornings, having served in the role on an interim basis since earlier this year. Tower succeeds Shawna Thomas, who left the show in March. The morning show recently went through a revamp, with Norah O’Donnell returning as co-host in September, joining Nate Burleson and […]
content:
Jon Tower has been named the permanent executive producer of CBS Mornings, having served in the role on an interim basis since earlier this year.

Tower succeeds Shawna Thomas, who left the show in March.

The morning show recently went through a revamp, with Norah O’Donnell returning as co-host in September, joining Nate Burleson and Gayle King.

CBS News president Tom Cibrowski and editor in chief Bari Weiss wrote in a memo that Tower “has brought steady leadership, sharp editorial instincts and a clear vision for the future of the broadcast. He is a thoughtful journalist, a creative storyteller, and a collaborative leader who understands both the urgency of the news and the importance of the stories that resonate with the morning audience.”

Watch on Deadline

Tower joined CBS News in 2014 and has served as senior broadcast producer of the morning show. He previously was senior producer at Morning Joe, where he worked for a decade. Variety first reported on Tower’s appointment.

title: Jonathan Groff Returning To Broadway In Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’
summary: Tony Award winner Jonathan Groff will return to Broadway this winter in The Amish Project, a solo play written by Jessica Dickey and directed by Sarna Lapine. Performances begin Wednesday, February 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre. Producers Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy announced the show and its star today. An official opening night is […]
content:
Tony Award winner Jonathan Groff will return to Broadway this winter in The Amish Project, a solo play written by Jessica Dickey and directed by Sarna Lapine. Performances begin Wednesday, February 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre.

Producers Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy announced the show and its star today. An official opening night is yet to be announced, and the design team will be announced shortly.

Coming off two very successful big-cast Broadway projects – Merrily We Roll Along and Just In Time – Groff will now go solo in The Amish Project, a play described by the production as “a deeply moving solo play about the astonishing power of compassion in the face of unimaginable loss.”

The synopsis: “When tragedy shatters a close-knit Amish community, what follows is an extraordinary act of grace that challenges everything we think we know about forgiveness. Inspired by true events that unfolded just minutes from where Groff grew up, The Amish Project is an intimate portrait of a place and a community channeled through a single performer. Written by acclaimed playwright Jessica Dickey (The Rembrandt, The Convent) and directed by Sarna Lapine (Call Me Izzy, Sunday in the Park with George), this remarkable story invites us to reflect on how, even in the darkest of hours, our shared humanity endures.”

Watch on Deadline

Said Groff, “Twenty years ago this month, an unimaginable tragedy happened in a one room Amish schoolhouse in Lancaster, Pennsylvania and Jessica Dickey wrote an astounding work of art in response. Sarna Lapine sent me The Amish Project last year and I was floored by the urgency and potent poetry of Jessica’s writing as she dives headfirst into the many aftershocks of this horrific event and explores the idea that sometimes the most radical human act is forgiveness. I am profoundly grateful to be bringing Jessica’s play to Broadway alongside Sarna and this incredible team.”

The Amish Project debuted to critical acclaim at the New York International Fringe Festival and was developed at the Cherry Lane Theatre before premiering Off Broadway at the Rattlestick Playwrights Theater in 2009. It has since become Dickey’s most-produced play, with productions at the Guthrie Theater (Minneapolis), Milwaukee Rep, American Theater Company (Chicago) and City Theatre (Pittsburgh), among others at theaters around the world.

Producers Ahrens and Kirdahy said in a statement, “We are honored to bring Jessica Dickey’s stirring and luminous play to Broadway, under the direction of the visionary Sarna Lapine. There is nothing quite like experiencing the singular Jonathan Groff live, and his humanity, generosity and gift for storytelling make this a deeply transporting night of theater that we are proud to share with audiences.”

Playwright Dickey said, “I wrote The Amish Project in the heartbreak of my twenties, grappling with how to make a meaningful life as an artist in a world capable of such violence. The play launched my writing career and changed my life. To return to it now, all these years later, when its questions feel as urgent as ever, is profoundly moving. And to do so alongside Jonathan Groff, whose personal connection to this story is matched by his staggering talent, and the extraordinary Sarna Lapine, with the steadfast belief and care of Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy, is a gift I could never have imagined. I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to see it—I’ll be the playwright in the back laughing and crying.”

Director Lapine said, “When I first read Jessie’s play, I was blown away by it. She has channeled something extraordinary about a community, a community in mourning, a community in conversation. It is a piece that stays with you for days, weeks, months, years after you’ve sat with it. Like the framework of a well-built one-room schoolhouse, the writing is precise, lean, and strong, illuminating resilience in the face of fragility, and asks, how does one forgive the unforgivable?”

title: ‘The Gentlemen’ Season 3 Cast Additions Include Orlando Bloom, Robert Carlyle & Elijah Wood But No Meghan Markle; Here’s Who’s Not Coming Back
summary: Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen is adding a few more gentlemen (and ladies) for its third season, which has started production in UK and Morocco. Joining the Theo James-starring series are The Lord of the Rings movie franchise stars Orlando Bloom and Elijah Wood, Robert Carlyle (Line of Duty), Dexter Fletcher (Ritchie’s Lock, Stock and Two […]
content:
Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen is adding a few more gentlemen (and ladies) for its third season, which has started production in UK and Morocco. Joining the Theo James-starring series are The Lord of the Rings movie franchise stars Orlando Bloom and Elijah Wood, Robert Carlyle (Line of Duty), Dexter Fletcher (Ritchie’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels), and Bruna Marquezine (Blue Beetle), as well as Ed Speleers (You), Saffron Burrows (You), and Bugzy Malone (Operation Fortune: Ruse de Guerre).

The Middle East-set new season will not feature Suits alumna Meghan Markle who had had conversations about a role but that is no longer in the cards.

Watch on Deadline

James leads The Gentlemen‘s returning cast alongside Kaya Scodelario, Ray Winstone, Joely Richardson, Vinnie Jones, Jasmine Blackborow, Harry Goodwins and Benjamin Clementine — who all have been on the show since Season 1 — as well as Maya Jama, who made her debut in Season 2 playing the glamorous and well-connected fixer, Aisha.

Not returning for Season 3 are two core cast members who had been with The Gentlemen since the start, Daniel Ings, who plays Lord Frederick “Freddy” Horniman, Eddie’s (James) cocaine-addicted older brother, and Giancarlo Esposito as American billionaire and drug kingpin Stanley Johnston.

Freddy was last seen in the Season 2 finale bloodied and traumatized, holding Gospel John Dixon’s severed head after he had been forced by Eddie to decapitate him as punishment for helping Dixon carry on the plane explosion that killed Eddie’s wife, Bella. Meanwhile, Stanley was arrested over his illegal dealings.

“I’m not in the next one, so that’s a fun sense of closure,” Ings recently told HATC Magazine. “I see it as closure for the character in a way; it just ends as this wild, broken, crazy, probably mumbling into the ether somewhere in the British countryside.”

Theo James & Kaya Scodelario in Season 3 of ‘The Gentlemen.’ Netflix

In Season 3, Eddie (James) and Susie (Scodelario) embark upon their most audacious project yet: building a casino in the Middle East. But with danger lurking around every corner, has the Duke’s unchecked ambition finally gone too far? (You can see a video of the duo on set below.)

The Gentlemen‘s eight-episode Season 3 is written by Ritchie and Matthew Read, directed by Ritchie and Eran Creevy and executive produced by Ritchie, Ivan Atkinson, Read, Will Gould, Simon Crawford Collins and Frith Tiplady for Moonage Pictures alongside Jonathan Glickman and Alix Jaffe for Miramax TV, and James. The series is produced by Moonage Pictures for Netflix and Miramax TV.

title: International Insider: Turmoil At Netflix; MIA Market Report; Patrick Brammall Interview
summary: Welcome, once again. This week, Insiders, it’s Jesse Whittock taking you through seven days in international film and TV that spans everything from major corporate layoffs to Italian festivals. On we go, and sign up for the newsletter here for the full Insider experience. Turmoil At Netflix IInternational light shines in dark: The crisis engulfing […]
content:
Welcome, once again. This week, Insiders, it’s Jesse Whittock taking you through seven days in international film and TV that spans everything from major corporate layoffs to Italian festivals. On we go, and sign up for the newsletter here for the full Insider experience.

Turmoil At Netflix

Mario Tama/Getty Images

IInternational light shines in dark: The crisis engulfing Netflix has seen the end of global content chief Bela Bajaria and film boss Dan Lim, and the introduction of former Fox and Disney TV studio topper Peter Rice. Though the company is still throwing off bundles of cash, the profits aren’t good enough for a ravenous Wall Street, and the blood of 1,000 staff has been let as Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters attempt to change the record. However, amid the ongoing troubles, the international side of the Netflix business has quietly bolstered its reputation. Though Netflix stock skidded on soft quarterly results and the lack of bonafide U.S.-made hits in 2026 has been a big problem, the streamer talked up local breakouts such as Japan’s Plastic Beauty, Denmark’s The Secret Woman, Mexico’s El Chapo and The Perfect Lie out of the Netherlands. The success of carrying the channel suite of France’s TF1 should lead to more deals of the same nature, Netflix execs added. It should be noted that none of the non-U.S. titles referenced this week could be considered global hits just yet, but there’s no doubt territory managers and regional bosses will have been heartened they’d been singled out for praise. Bajaria was popular with them, and her legacy will include the huge growth at international Netflix hubs over the past six years. As for Netflix’s new Chief Content Officer, Rice, well, there’s an international story to tell there as well. He was born and raised in the UK, studying at the University of Nottingham before beginning his media career at Twentieth Century Fox in 1989. Though his career has almost entirely been working for the U.S. studios, he has been known to attend the Edinburgh TV Festival and other European events, bringing hope that his strategy will continue the local-to-global model that has seen investment hit so many markets. Read Nellie Andreeva’s excellent report on his career and prospects here.

When in Rome…

From MIA to you: The latest edition of Rome’s MIA Market has been taking place this week, and I made the journey to the Italian capital for the first portion of the five-day event. Edward Berger, whose papal selection movie Conclave was set within the walls of Vatican City, opened the conference and market with a fascinating look into his filmmaking process and views on how the movie business has evolved. Berger put forwards the theory that the U.S. studios had needed the arrival of Netflix to “wake” them from a slumber, but that, given current circumstances, it might be the turn of Skydances, Disneys and NBCUniversals to inspire the streamer. MIA also heard more from Banijay Entertainment boss Marco Bassetti, speaking publicly for the second time in a week following MIPCOM in Cannes, and from Domingo Corral, the widely-respected former content boss at Spain’s Movistar Plus+, who passionately argued gatekeepers must take risks – his version of this led to greenlights for the likes of La Bola Negra and Sîrat. Elsewhere, we got a snapshot of the Italian entertainment (‘audiovisual’) market, where inward investment fell for the first time since 2018. MIA has turned itself into an important co-production and financial market – this year’s launch of the European Investment Hub track was a sign of that – and besides the fact you can eat fabulously well in Rome (my new tip is Francesco Panella’s Antica Pesa in Trastevere), the content on offer makes it a worthy addition to an entertainment player’s schedule. More MIA here.

Watch on Deadline

The Deadline Interview: Patrick Brammall

Apple TV

Patrick Brammall was in reflective mood when Deadline spoke to him about his Apple TV thriller series Last Seen. The Australian actor and Harriet Dyer – his real-life wife and on-screen partner – had over the summer said goodbye to romantic sitcom Colin From Accounts and were contemplating their next steps while raising a young family in Los Angeles. Brammall opened up about what attracted him to a dramatic role in Last Seen, how he feels about leaving behind an injured dog in an Aussie comedy, and his role in The Devil Wears Prada 2. He also gave his views on the changing shape of the Australian production scene and sent love to Brian Walsh, the late Binge commissioner who backed Colin in the first place. >>>Read The Interview

Bye Bye, BBC Three… Again

‘Fleabag’ net on the scrapheap: How many TV channels have been axed twice in 10 years? There can’t be many, but BBC Three is now one of them. The youth-skewing network is the highest-profile casualty of the BBC‘s massive cost-cutting operation. Deadline was the first to tip the plan last month, and this week it became reality, as the axe also swung for BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra. There have been many who claim BBC Three doesn’t need a linear identity to survive given most of its target audience prefers online content, but it’s still a downer for a channel that has spawned genre-smashing shows such as Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey. In another depressing week for the UK’s public broadcaster, there were more cuts, talk of even more cuts and programs scrapped, as the BBC’s desperate bid to make the books work continues under former Google EMEA chief Matt Brittin.

The Essentials

Fernando Marrero/Travers Jacobs

🌶️ Hot One: J.A. Bayona, Javier Bardem and Laurent Bouzereau are teaming for Néstor, a feature doc about the life of legendary Spanish cinematographer Néstor Almendros.

🌶️ Another: Gianni Nunnari, producer on movies including the 300 franchise, is bringing Brian Selznick’s young adult novel Run Away With Me to the screen, with the author adapting his own novel.

🔥 Hot, Hot, Hot: Kari Skogland will direct Vigilant, a crime thriller based on a Skúli Sigurðsson novel and adapted for TV by Severance star Ólafur Darri Ólafsson.

🤝 New job: Carol Choi succeeded the retiring Luke Kang as President of The Walt Disney Company in Asia Pacific.

⛺ Fest latest: Walter Thompson-Hernández’s buzzy indie feature If I Go Will They Miss Me is among 10 titles screening in the International Competition at this year’s Thessaloniki Film Festival.

🏆 Interview: The story of how Olivia Colman-starrer Wicker went from an unpublished short story to a big-screen feminist romantasy, as told by the producers behind it.

⚖️ Legal: The latest from the Russell Brand trial in London. Brand denies all charges.

🌐 YouTube: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s manager, Rebecca Dowell, is spearheading an Entertainment and New Media division at her international management outfit Three Six Zero.

🇯🇵 TIFF talk: Liz Shackleton set the seen for next week’s Tokyo International Film Festival through a chat with its leaders and an interview with TIFFCOM CEO Yasushi Shiina.

😎 Madchester: Dates for the first post-Edinburgh TV Festival in Greater Manchester were announced.

🪧 Protest: Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones signed an open letter in support of their Normal People scribe Sally Rooney, whose books are banned in the UK.

👀 First look: At Minnie Driver in Paramount+ heist drama The Day.

Photo of the Week

Joe Maher/Getty Images

Claymation – Naomi Ackie and Tom Rhys Harries at the European premiere of Clayface at the Curzon Mayfair in London.

title: Meghan Markle “Deeply Distressed” Over Allegation Her Father Possessed Child Abuse Images
summary: Meghan Markle has said she is “deeply distressed” by explosive allegations reported by The Sun newspaper that her estranged father, Thomas Markle, has possessed child abuse images. In a front-page story on Friday, the Rupert Murdoch-owned tabloid newspaper claimed that Thomas Markle is being investigated over child abuse images after being reported to the FBI […]
content:
Meghan Markle has said she is “deeply distressed” by explosive allegations reported by The Sun newspaper that her estranged father, Thomas Markle, has possessed child abuse images.

In a front-page story on Friday, the Rupert Murdoch-owned tabloid newspaper claimed that Thomas Markle is being investigated over child abuse images after being reported to the FBI by his own son.

Thomas Markle has denied the allegations, telling The Daily Mail that it was “a bunch of lies.” He added: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me.”

In her statement, which was shared with Deadline, Markle said she became aware of unspecified allegations against her father in 2018. Markle said she decided at that time to deny him access to her children so she could “protect” them.

Watch on Deadline

The Duchess of Sussex said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.

“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

Thomas Markle Jr. told The Sun that he discovered a stash of “hundreds” of images and videos on computers and a cellphone at his father’s home in the Philippines.

“When I found this material I was horrified and I had no option but to report my dad. I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now,” he said. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”

‘The Sun’ front page

Thomas Markle Sr. denied his son’s account, claiming that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines.

“Those computers were boxed up in Mexico and put on a cargo ship which took months to get to the Philippines. I kept asking Tom for my computers but he wouldn’t give them to me,” he said.

The Sun story goes into detail about what was discovered and the nature of the images, reporting that they included toddlers “either captured nude or engaged in horrifying sex acts.”

Markle Sr., who won an Emmy for his work in the camera and electrical department on ABC’s General Hospital, is currently in a rehab centre in Florida after having his leg amputated below the knee following a blood clot.

He has regularly given interviews in the British and American press since his daughter became part of the British royal family. Markle Sr. appeared in the 2020 feature-length documentary, Thomas Markle: My Story, which aired on Skydance-owned UK network 5.

title: Hunter Biden Signs With CAA
summary: CAA has signed a deal to represent Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden, in a pact that could have the storied talent agency seeking out new ways for the former attorney and current painter to promote himself or tell stories in a variety of ventures. CAA has had a long relationship with […]
content:
CAA has signed a deal to represent Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden, in a pact that could have the storied talent agency seeking out new ways for the former attorney and current painter to promote himself or tell stories in a variety of ventures.

CAA has had a long relationship with the Biden family. The agency unveiled an agreement to represent President Joseph Biden in 2025, and had previously represented him between 2017 and 2020.

Hunter Biden, who was at the center of several controversies as Republicans sought to link work he did overseas Biden works primarily in abstract, mixed-media pieces exploring themes of memory, transformation, and the natural world. He works mostly from his studio in Los Angeles, where he tries to utilize “bold chromatic choices, layered textures, and an intuitive approach to composition,” according to a biographical sketch provided by the agency.

Popular on Variety

Over the course of his life, Biden has tried to forge his own path with investing and lobbying activities, and has served as an advisor to his father. The federal government probed his tax affairs and allegations he possessed a gun while using drugs. President Biden pardoned his son in early 2024 before leaving office. In 2026, Hunter Biden tried his hand at cryptocurrency, launching a meme coin called $LAPTOP.

Hunter Biden has spoken candidly about his history with alcohol and drug addiction, and detailed his path to sobriety in his 2021 memoir “Beautiful Things.” He has tried to use his own experience to press for greater understanding and support around addiction treatment.

In 2026, he launched, “Where’s Hunter,” a Substack column, in which he focuses on art commentary, memoir-style essays, and further reflection on his recovery journey.

title: IATSE Names Video Engineer Jillian Arnold First Labor and Technology Officer
summary: The International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees has become the latest entertainment organization to appoint a technology chief, naming video engineer Jillian Arnold as the union’s first labor and technology intelligence officer. In this role, Arnold will shepherd how IATSE navigates new technologies and their impact on the organization’s entertainment workers and their crafts. She […]
content:
The International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees has become the latest entertainment organization to appoint a technology chief, naming video engineer Jillian Arnold as the union’s first labor and technology intelligence officer.

In this role, Arnold will shepherd how IATSE navigates new technologies and their impact on the organization’s entertainment workers and their crafts. She previously chaired the union’s AI subcommittee during its 2024 negotiations with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers and, in 2020, became the first woman and first video engineer to lead IATSE Local 695 in its 90-year history.

“Jillian has been a leader on artificial intelligence and its impact on the labor movement,” IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb said in a statement. “In this new role, she’ll be a resource and a voice representing members on both sides of the border as we navigate public policy and workplace challenges relating to the development and implementation of these new tools.”

Popular on Variety

“Technology has been a defining part of my entire career,” Arnold said. “I’ve seen firsthand how technological innovation can expand what workers are capable of achieving. I’ve also seen why workers need a meaningful voice in determining how technologies are developed and integrated into the workplace. I’m excited to bring those experiences together in this new role and help ensure that technological progress strengthens our crafts and the people who perform them.”

Arnold’s appointment is the latest in a series of new roles across the entertainment industry focused on technology in the AI era. Disney hired Karandeep Anaud as its first chief technology officer last month, while Ticketmaster hired its first senior vice president of data science and machine learning as the company embraced the technology. Amazon MGM and Lionsgate also both hired their first AI leaders in the last two years.

title: ‘Dance of the Souls,’ Unspooling at Morelia, Explores Oaxaca’s Muerteadas, Celebrating the End and the Beginning
summary: In “Dance of the Souls,” Mexican filmmaker Ramón Llaven returns to his native Oaxaca in southern Mexico to observe a unique event held in the local communities of the Etla Valley. Produced by Fata Morgana and Eudiamonía Films in co-production with Estudios Churubusco Azteca and Lost Time Media, “Dance of the Souls” screens at Mexico’s […]
content:
In “Dance of the Souls,” Mexican filmmaker Ramón Llaven returns to his native Oaxaca in southern Mexico to observe a unique event held in the local communities of the Etla Valley.

Produced by Fata Morgana and Eudiamonía Films in co-production with Estudios Churubusco Azteca and Lost Time Media, “Dance of the Souls” screens at Mexico’s Morelia Film Festival and also unspools at Mexico City’s DocsMX and the Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival.

Employing a mystical narrative device, the film follows a wandering soul as it returns on the Day of the Dead to visit the places it used to inhabit and the people it once loved, and accompany locals as they prepare for one of Oaxaca’s most important celebrations. The event brings together masked revelers in elaborate costumes who dance in remembrance of lost loved ones while also celebrating life.

Popular on Variety

“My intention was to create a documentary about the muerteadas — a Oaxacan tradition in which we dance for over 12 hours, accompanied by a brass band and wearing costumes adorned with bells and mirrors,” Llaven tells Variety.

“I also wanted to weave in my childhood memories of Doña Julia, a spiritual healer whose healing sessions I had the chance to witness. This served as the starting point for the film.”

The idea of incorporating the perspective of a spirit, Llaven adds, “gives rise to a question: If you could return, which places would you visit?”

Courtesy of Fata Morgana

The filmmaker returned to his Oaxaca after spending nearly 15 years away.

“This time apart allowed me to return and observe my community from a fresh perspective. It was important to me to tell the story from within, and the figure of the returning spirit — traversing the spaces it once occupied — provided the perfect lens for this.

“The people and landscapes featured in the documentary are close to me and belong to this region.”

The film recounts the untimely deaths of several of young men from the town, including Ricardo, a friend of Llevan, whose loss deeply affected the director. “It also allowed me to learn about the region’s funeral rituals and their connection to the natural world,” he explains.

While Llevan’s past links to the region made the process easier, gaining the trust of the community and the individuals featured in the film nevertheless proved the most difficult part of the production, the director recalls.

Another major challenge when he began shooting was the pandemic — “due to the necessary safety precautions and the apprehension felt by the participants given the situation. This also delayed the filming of the muerteada: we began shooting in 2021, but we were only able to film this celebration in 2023 and 2024, once large-scale public gatherings resumed in the community.”

When he finally got the chance, Llevan sought to convey “the physical experience of dancing for hours during the muerteada, until reaching a state of ecstasy. The carnival allows us to adopt the perspective of the spirit, moving among the dancers and becoming part of the community.”

A distinctive feature of the murteada, he notes, “are the costumes adorned with bells and mirrors — which can weigh up to 20 kilograms — worn during dances that, in some villages, last as long as 18 hours. This celebration allows us to welcome death with joy.”

While there are numerous Day of the Dead celebrations throughout Mexico, the origins of the Oaxacan muerteada remain uncertain, Llaven explains. Some accounts trace the tradition to two possible Oaxacan regions: Cañada or Mixteca. In some communities in the Etla Valley the muerteada is even more significant than both the new year and the patron saint’s feast day, he adds.

“Unlike other traditions that also involve welcoming the spirits of the departed, the muerteada also serves as a reflection of life itself. … It represents the end of one cycle and the beginning of another. It is a way to celebrate the fact that we are still alive, which enables us to carry on.”

title: Pedro Pascal on Learning Cello for ‘Behemoth!,’ Why ‘You’ve Got to Eat S—’ to Make It in Hollywood and the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Line His Character Says
summary: “If you could hear it, you would think I was killing an animal.” That’s Pedro Pascal on his cello playing, more than a year after he started lessons for a movie that hadn’t been greenlit yet. The star first had lunch with Tony Gilroy in late July 2025 about taking on the lead role of […]
content:
“If you could hear it, you would think I was killing an animal.”

That’s Pedro Pascal on his cello playing, more than a year after he started lessons for a movie that hadn’t been greenlit yet. The star first had lunch with Tony Gilroy in late July 2025 about taking on the lead role of his latest movie, “Behemoth!.” But even before anything was signed, and before he knew whether the project would hold together, Pascal went straight to cellists Timothy Loo and Charlie Tyler and got to work.

Cameras would eventually roll across Los Angeles at the end of that October, with a final day in Vienna. Every lunch break and short weekend went to “the next thing, and the next thing.” Pascal calls it “a highly intense lip sync” that left him back-footed for the entire shoot, and “the hardest thing that I’ve ever done.”

Popular on Variety

It was also his favorite filmmaking experience ever. “I miss ‘Behemoth!’ more than I miss anything I’ve ever done,” he tells Variety. “I miss the character.”

We’ve waited a long time for Pascal to play a part like Alex Serian. I suspect a lot of Latinos felt the same.

Pascal, 51, spent two decades in small roles onstage and on television before HBO’s fantasy epic “Game of Thrones” changed his life at 39. He then became the internet’s shared boyfriend through Disney+’s “Star Wars” series “The Mandalorian” and HBO’s post-apocalyptic drama “The Last of Us.” No one gave him a part worthy of what he can do with his face when he has no lines.

Alex, a gifted cellist who comes home to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road, is that part. The Searchlight Pictures film, written and directed by Gilroy, premiered as the centerpiece selection of the New York Film Festival on Oct. 2 and opens Dec. 4. It refuses to reveal what it’s actually about until well past the midpoint.

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Pascal digs into Gilroy’s ode to movie composers and a character who says more with a bow than he ever does with words. He also coughs up a line from the upcoming “Avengers: Doomsday,” teases his role in Todd Haynes’ anticipated “De Noche” and sends a message to his friend and favorite awards-season foe, Kieran Culkin.

Before that, the return of the Awards Circuit roundtable looks at this season’s Oscars contenders, including whether Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything” is taking on frontrunner status over “The Odyssey.”

Listen below.

The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

See all Academy Awards predictions

Variety Awards Circuit: Oscars





Pedro Pascal in “Behemoth!” Justin Lubin

I wrote that this is the role I’ve waited a long time for you to play. Thank God Tony Gilroy is alive and well.

He is a spy for the rebellion. Tony kind of blows my mind. He’s so skilled at so many classical elements, classical music being a huge part of this movie and he’s so innovative and progressive in the way he deals with narrative structure while painting completely whole human beings. In my research, and in my love of him now that I’ve gotten to work with him, there’s something I pay even more attention to as I revisit everything he’s written. “Dolores Claiborne,” in 1995, is a manifesto on misogyny. At the time that didn’t feel new, but within the thriller genre, its intelligence around such a real issue left a mark on me. It’s like school in a way. As personal and intimate as this story is, there’s something really rebellious about it and a little anarchistic, in insisting that you pay such close attention to this life puzzle that anyone can have if they want to reflect on their own lives and hear the music of it and let the music guide you into revelations about yourself.

The film doesn’t reveal what it’s really about until maybe 65 or 70% in, and it subverts every expectation of what a drama about classical music could be. You do so much acting with your face. I cried at the end because of a face you make in a pivotal scene. Was it harder to go through this story without a lot of words to show what you’re feeling?

I loved it more than anything I’ve gotten to do. I guess because there are fewer lines to learn. [laughs]

There was so much language in the cello playing that speaks for the character. He’s very obviously someone who expresses himself through his music and fails at so many things in life because he doesn’t know how to speak the language of human relationships. He knows how to navigate his own life and express himself through playing the cello. That was something I understood really deeply and had empathy for. I’m somebody who talks a lot and uses a lot of words and loves language, but I related to this untethered, nomadic person whose skill beyond playing the cello is adaptability to survive. That was a deep connection for me.

The homework, beyond the insane technical challenge of looking like I played the cello convincingly, was understanding Tony and the story he was telling. It’s funny, because we recently noticed, while taking the train together, that we’re talking a lot more about Alex Serian than we ever did while shooting the movie.

That happened organically?

Completely organically. Tony puts so much faith in the people he hires, and I think that faith is a form of leadership that invites your most devoted work. He’ll say it’s pragmatic, which I totally understand, because as a leader you want your crew and your cast to give you their best. At the same time, it’s this very warm and exciting invitation to be inside the story without having to talk about it too much. I was given all this permission to step into a day of shooting, into a scene, into pivotal or subtle moments of this very interesting arc the character is on, without talking to Tony about it first. The only time he’d come in and make little adjustments, suggestions even, he would always start with, “I don’t want to fuck with this. But do you think maybe we can put a smile on this?” And he didn’t mean my face. He meant internally, energetically. It was a fascinating dance of trust.

I would say it’s the hardest thing I’ve ever done, because of the cello. But it was also the most nurturing and rewarding experience: playing someone so private, with a camera on him and knowing that everything he doesn’t share with the people orbiting him in the story is being shared with the audience. It’s an interesting kind of present vulnerability that you had to show up for all the time. As recessive as he may feel, the audience is with him. I can’t hide anything from you guys. Anything he doesn’t understand himself, even if he’s looking at something that’s a big reveal and we as an audience aren’t meant to know what he’s seeing, because he doesn’t know how to process what he’s seeing in that moment.

Olivia Wilde slays in this movie. I thought she was going to murder you.

She was my favorite character on the page, and that we got Olivia was, as Tony would say, the movie gods smiling upon us. Coming in and slaying the hell out of the scene.

How much did you see of yourself in Alex? You’re famous, you’re surrounded by people constantly. Did you feel a connection to what it’s like to be lonely?

This is what I find so fascinating, and it’s why I’m talking so much more about him now. I don’t want to use the word “defending” him, but I’m sharing what I understand of him, because I don’t believe he lacks connections or doesn’t know how to connect. What he cannot meet in many of his relationships is a certain expectation of him that goes beyond the realm of a language he knows how to speak. Without it being calculating, he does choose to be in relationships that have their guardrails set in place. Love with a woman who is in a relationship. Nonattachments. Out of his own fear of bringing anyone into his inherited pain and his inherited dysfunction. He’s not somebody to blame his parents. He just is who he is, and he’s doing his best.

The second language he’s very good at is intimacy. Not emotional intimacy, but he can express himself through, I guess, lovemaking. That’s why there are so many relationships in the movie that I feel have very real connections. It just doesn’t come into commitment. There are people who, let’s say, put a demand on him: “I need you to say something, because I’m not willing to say it.” He doesn’t know how to say it, but it isn’t necessarily fair to demand that he be the one to say it.

You had never picked up a cello. Why are you good at everything?

I’m bad at a lot of things. If you could hear it, you would think I was killing an animal.

You can’t just let the bow slide up and down the strings. It has to be primed to press against the string and attempt to play the note. But to marry all of it, the bowing with the fingering and the different positions and the vibrato, is a lifelong endeavor that lifelong cellists are struggling with to this very day. My teachers suffer at the hands of it even now. So it was a highly, highly, highly intense lipsync, shatteringly difficult and I felt back-footed the entire time.

I had an intensive period before we started shooting. I had lunch with Tony in late July, and we started toward the end of October. Before anything was signed, as soon as I understood there was a green light, whether it would fall apart or not, I didn’t care. I went straight into my lessons with Timothy Loo and Charlie Tyler, these incredible musicians. Then when we started shooting, whatever window we had, whatever lunch, whatever short day, weekend, I was learning the next thing and the next thing and the next thing. It was crazy. The very last day of shooting was in Vienna, but we spent every day of the shoot all over Los Angeles, which had its own magic.

What a concept, to shoot a movie about L.A. in L.A …

So many locations. We were in Pasadena. We were in Studio City. We were in Malibu. We were in the Arts District. We were downtown. Getting to take a break and feel integrated into the city, then go home at the end of the day, was a dream experience. Everyone felt it. The whole crew was local. Damián García, our brilliant cinematographer, lives in Barcelona and our incredible producer Sanne Wohlenberg lives in London, but everyone else, all the department heads, were Los Angeles, if not Angelenos. Major legacy industry people who had worked on the most incredible things. We were all very in love.

Tony told me it would’ve been a lie to make this movie about the business and not shoot it here.

When you talk about Olivia Wilde tearing into the movie the instant she steps on-screen, that’s a perfect example of movie magic we haven’t talked about enough. That scene takes place in Chicago, but we shot it in downtown Los Angeles. It was not cold, and it was not snowing. It is an operatic blizzard happening in this movie. That’s down to our incredible camera department and production design. And Mary Zophres, the costume designer, picked out that emerald green dress for Olivia and worked with me on every detail. What Alex is wearing isn’t necessarily something you notice, but it has everything to do with the gentle nature in which he tries to exist in the world.

The last scene we see of him, in the cathedral, that sweater. He seems so calm, so at peace. And when he’s running through the house, the white shirt and the bow tie, he feels like a man on a mission. As close as we’ll get to you playing James Bond.

The white shirt and bow tie don’t hurt. It’s all so intentional. Everything I wore was this collaborative, gorgeous conversation with Mary. I can’t say enough about everybody who worked on the movie.

You spent about two decades taking small roles onstage and on television before “Game of Thrones” changed everything. You were 39. Someone out there is in those forming years, waiting for that moment. What do you wish someone had told you back then?

I was thinking about a different version of this today, weirdly. One of the first things I got to do when the season was airing was go back to my roots and play Don John in “Much Ado About Nothing” at Shakespeare in the Park, which Jack O’Brien directed. I caught myself thinking about that very, very pivotal year of my life, one I’d been waiting for ever since I left high school and how much I missed it. Then I was thinking about how much I missed shooting “The Last of Us” in Alberta and sharing “The Last of Us” with the world. And then: I miss “Behemoth!” I miss “Behemoth!” more than I miss anything I’ve ever done. I miss the character. I miss being with everyone every day. I miss Tony. And I was thinking, you’re going to look back, so be very present today, because it’s only going to take a couple of years to miss this. Pay attention. Enjoy it.

What I would tell anyone is that if you’re waking up every day and trying, and some days that means not doing anything at all, but you have intention behind your pursuit, you’re in love with what you’re pursuing and you’re pursuing it in your own way, you are exactly where you’re supposed to be. Have faith in that. I think it’s a huge mistake if you feel like you need to mold yourself into something that doesn’t feel true to yourself, or meet an expectation that even fractionally feels like some kind of internal betrayal.

You’ve got to eat shit, and you’ve got to take a lot of shit. That’s part of it. It’s a huge part of it for me, because it forms character, hopefully in the direction of knowing how to treat other people and protecting the value of generosity, because it comes around. There isn’t any way I would be here were it not for the generosity of others who have been there for me. I owe it to all the people in my life. I wouldn’t know where to begin. It’s a population of people that I owe things to.

It makes me think of the finale of “The Office,” when Andy says “I wish there was a way to know you’re in ‘the good old days’, before you’ve actually left them.”

That’s exactly what I was thinking about today.

I was in bed, and I saw the premiere of “Smells Like Teen Spirit” on MTV and I just didn’t blink. “What is this?” I remember the first time I saw Tracy Chapman. I remember the first time I saw Sinéad O’Connor’s “Nothing Compares 2 U” and just being changed.

When I was a kid, I was so into Motown. I was so into classic rock. I had my whole period with Bob Dylan and the Doors and Led Zeppelin and the Rolling Stones. God, Roberta Flack. I walked two miles to get the 1978 self-titled album once I’d heard “The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face.” But through the lens of my nephews, I see how much access the young generation has to express themselves through social media, which has its advantages and its dangers. Major dangers. But it’s also a very important tool of expression, or at least, for older people like us, a way of bearing witness to what their experience is, what their needs are. I’m really excited about young people seeing this movie, even though it’s old farts making it, because there’s something so relatable about evaluating your own life and realizing it has its own music, its own movie. If you follow that music, there are surprises.

Behemoth! Screenshot courtesy YouTube/Searchlight Pictures

You’re famously generous on red carpets and in interviews. When people ask what it’s like to interview you, I say you’re exactly the way you imagine him to be. The internet has turned you into a kind of “shared boyfriend.” Uly Morazan, who’s a content creator and makes videos about you, is a great example of that. Everyone feels they can connect with you. Does that version of Pedro make it harder to disappear into someone like Alex?

Oh my god, I love Uly. It’s not harder for me at all, because I think so dramaturgically about work. That’s my training and the way my brain works. There are so many different types of actors. There are actors who can live in the perspective of their character so completely that I envy them sometimes. There are actors who are writers, even though they don’t write and can save a character and elevate a character through their own contributions of language. There are actors who think producerially and see the whole picture and their place in it. The challenge would come from anyone who sees me in a particular way and hasn’t seen me do something like this. But something like this is a thing I’ve been dreaming about my whole life.

And in its own tiny way, I’ve gotten to play very rich roles in tiny theaters all around the country through my theater career and my years as a member of Labyrinth Theater Company in New York. So the short answer is no. It’s a lot harder to step into Marvel or a beloved video game. You have to be realistic about those expectations and also protect the personal authorship you’re ultimately going to want to share with an audience that’s either new to the project or beloved fans of it. That’s a fascinating balance to understand and study, because you can’t betray anything about yourself. It just won’t be true. You have to accept that you’re not going to meet everybody’s expectations, but you do have to take expectation into account, because these are people who understand the material in a way that’s very important for you to understand when you go into it.

I was told you can tell me almost everything about “Avengers” and the Todd Haynes film. So tell me everything.

You want me to tell you everything about “Doomsday” and “Secret Wars” together? They are about the Avengers and major events that all of us are a part of.

I asked David Harbour, who sat in that very spot, for one line his character says, completely out of context. Give me a line from “Avengers.”

I’m trying not to pick the line that’s in the trailer … “It’s good to see you again.”

And Todd Haynes’ “De Noche?”

“De Noche” has its own movie gods, one of them being Todd Haynes. It’s a sister film for me, emotionally anyway, in terms of how special it is to me. For both of them, there were only these windows for them to be made and to be able to fly in through that window together is its own sort of magic. To me, it was a movie that had to be made, a Todd Haynes movie that had to be made, just like this is a Tony Gilroy movie that had to be made.

Kieran Culkin isn’t in a film this year, and I’m going to miss the banter you both shared during “The Last of Us” and while he was on the circuit for “Succession.” If you had a message for Mr. Culkin, what would it be?

Oh, Kieran … He’s not going to listen to this, so I’ll text it to him.

“Come here, Kieran. Let’s cuddle.”

Pedro Pascal in “Behemoth!” Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures

10 QUESTIONS WITH PEDRO PASCAL

What’s your childhood nickname?

“Pepelo.” If I had grown up in Chile, I would be Papelo.

Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into?

I think I love everything I was into. But I fell for Cabbage Patch Kids, and now I’m like, why?

My father-in-law fell for the Beanie Babies revolution. Thought they’d be worth a gazillion dollars.

That was a craze, though. I moved on to Garbage Pail Kids, and I don’t regret that at all.

Go-to karaoke or shower song?

“La Bamba.” But I don’t do karaoke.

Not even at a friend’s house?

I’ve done “La Bamba” for friends.

So I just need to get invited. Secret talent?

I have few secrets and very, very few talents. I used to know how to juggle. Can’t juggle anymore. Just tried. Big mistake. I’m good at laundry.

You fold well?

Fold well.

Favorite ice cream flavor?

Chocolate Häagen-Dazs. Without question.

Mine is cookies and cream Häagen-Dazs.

That’s my second, bro. If it’s not chocolate, the closest second is cookies and cream Häagen-Dazs.

The one item you can’t live without?

Something my mother made me.

What TV show or film in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of?

I wish I was in “The Lost Boys.” Can I also say “Twin Peaks?”

Did you see “The Lost Boys” musical?

No, but I heard it’s amazing. Michael Arden is a friend of mine. We worked together on “King Lear,” and he’s an incredible director.

Fictional character you most relate to or admire?

Did you ever see “My Life as a Dog?” Ingemar, in Lasse Hallström’s movie.

I had chills for a second, because my answer to that is usually “My Life,” with Michael Keaton and Nicole Kidman. Nobody talks about that movie. I think it’s Keaton’s finest hour. Favorite piece of advice, given or received?

It’s corny as hell, and it’s a verse from Shakespeare. But to thine own self be true.

title: Joel McHale to Star in Short Film From ‘Open Door’ Director Kevin Cate (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Joel McHale’s next move could be a viral sensation. McHale is set to star in the next short film from director Kevin Cate, the pair confirmed in a collaborative video on Oct. 23. No information outside of McHale’s casting is known about the short film, but Cate is set to collaborate again with the same […]
content:
Joel McHale’s next move could be a viral sensation.

McHale is set to star in the next short film from director Kevin Cate, the pair confirmed in a collaborative video on Oct. 23. No information outside of McHale’s casting is known about the short film, but Cate is set to collaborate again with the same core team that made “Open Door,” “Birthday Flight” and “Unbearable Christmas” under his Clinging Vine Films banner.

Cate’s 2023 sci-fi short “Open Door” received over 33 million views across YouTube shorts, TikTok and Instagram, and is going to be adapted into a feature.

Popular on Variety

Cate has also been busy directing his first feature, “Unbearable Christmas,” starring Julia Stiles, Alex Moffat, David Cross and Stephen Root. He also released his latest short film, “Birthday Flight,” in Sept. That work, which follows a man who dozes off on a plane and wakes up to find it empty, has hit a million views on various platforms.

McHale is best known as a host and comedic ringer on scores of shows, known for his acerbic wit on current series like “The 1% Club,” “House of Villains” and “Crime Scene Kitchen.” He also stars on the Fox sitcom “Animal Control,” which is now in its fifth season. Previously, he hosted the cult favorite clip show “The Soup” and was the star of the gone-too-soon sitcom “Community.”

In film, McHale appeared this year in “Scream 7” and the satire “Stop! That! Train!” He’s also had roles in “Spider-Man 2,” “Ted,” “Becky” and “Blended.”

Watch McHale in the announcement video that Cate posted to Instagram below.

title: Leslie Bibb Boards Amazon MGM Studios’ ‘Upgraded 2’ Opposite Camila Mendes
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Leslie Bibb is set to star in Upgraded 2 from director Becca Gleason, joining the previously announced returning star and producer Camila Mendes. Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews, who penned the first film, wrote the screenplay. Story details are under wraps, but the first movie starred Mendes as Ana, an ambitious intern at an […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Leslie Bibb is set to star in Upgraded 2 from director Becca Gleason, joining the previously announced returning star and producer Camila Mendes.

Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews, who penned the first film, wrote the screenplay. Story details are under wraps, but the first movie starred Mendes as Ana, an ambitious intern at an art auction house in New York City who misrepresents herself to a handsome wealthy man as the house’s director. As their romance develops, her deception creates challenges that threaten her career and relationship.

Gulfstream Pictures financed the original 2024 film. Amazon MGM Studios landed worldwide distribution rights to the sequel, which will be available in more than 240 countries and territories on Prime Video. It begins production this month in Italy.

Producers include Gulfstream’s Mike Karz and Bill Bindley, Honor Role’s Mendes and Rachel Matthews, Luber Roklin Entertainment’s Lena Roklin, and Tempo Productions’ Piers Tempest.

Watch on Deadline

Bibb most recently guest starred in Season 5 of HBO’s Hacks opposite Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder, earning an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy Series for the finale season. She also returned for the second season of Apple TV’s Emmy-nominated Palm Royale alongside Kristin Wiig, Allison Janney,and Laura Dern. Last year, Bibb starred in Season 3 of Mike White’s HBO drama The White Lotus and the ensemble earned an Actor Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

Recently, it was announced that Bibb will star in and executive produce dark comedy series The Rush Whisperer for HBO. Also upcoming, she will star in Brett Goldstein’s romantic comedy series Escorted for Prime Video opposite Goldstein and Lesley Manville. Additional TV credits include Netflix’s original comedy God’s Favorite Idiot, Netflix’s superhero series Jupiter’s Legacy, ABC’s dramedy GCB, ABC’s American Housewife, TV Land’s Nobodies, NBC’s Crossing Jordan and the ninth season of NBC’s ER.

On the film side, her credits include Clint Eastwood’s Juror #2; Lionsgate’s About My Father; The Lost Husband, which she also produced; Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby; Iron Man and Iron Man 2; Warner Bros’ comedy Tag; Netflix’s To the Bone; Jared Hess’ Don Verdeen; No Good Deed; Hell Baby; Sony’s Zookeeper; Take Care; Confessions of a Shopaholic; Law Abiding Citizen; A Good Old Fashioned Orgy; and Miss Nobody.

Bibb is represented by UTA, LBI and JSSK.

title: Casey Bloys Unveils His Skydance DTC Content Team Featuring All HBO Max Execs: Francesca Orsi, Sarah Aubrey, Amy Gravitt & More
summary: Casey Bloys, Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance DTC, has officially revealed his leadership team of senior executives — and it is the same team he had in his previous role as Chairman and CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content: Francesca Orsi, Amy Gravitt, Sarah Aubrey, Nina Rosenstein, Glenn Whitehead, Nancy Abraham & Lisa […]
content:
Casey Bloys, Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance DTC, has officially revealed his leadership team of senior executives — and it is the same team he had in his previous role as Chairman and CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content: Francesca Orsi, Amy Gravitt, Sarah Aubrey, Nina Rosenstein, Glenn Whitehead, Nancy Abraham & Lisa Heller and Jeff Cusson.

The announcement Friday comes two and a half weeks after Bloys took over content for the combined HBO Max-Paramount+ streaming operation following the October 6 closing of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

As Deadline reported earlier today, Jane Wiseman is leaving as EVP and Head of Originals for Paramount+ and her team will now report to Aubrey, whose new title is Head of Paramount+, Max Originals and International Programming.

Watch on Deadline

Orsi has been promoted to President, HBO Drama Series and Films, from EVP, HBO Programming, Head of HBO Drama Series and Films. In her expanded new role, she will work with Bloys on determining which drama projects are best suited for HBO.

Gravitt, EVP, HBO Programming, Head of HBO & HBO Max Comedy Series, and Nancy Abraham and Lisa Heller, Co-EVPs, HBO Documentary Programming, will continue in their current roles.

Expanding their duties across both HBO Max and Paramount+ are Whitehead, who will serve as President & COO, HBO and Paramount+, and Cusson, now EVP and Head of Communications, Skydance DTC.

Bloys laid out the new structure in an internal memo, which you can read below.

“These leaders and their teams have a long history of delivering consistently on the main metrics of viewership, awards and critical response. No doubt they will continue to do so across Skydance DTC,” Bloys said about his senior executives.

With HBO Max and Paramount+ destined to combine into a single platform, Aubrey will “work closely with me and Skydance leadership on the iteration of Paramount+ as we look to align with HBO Max,” Bloys said. The platforms’ merger will follow a “short-term” phase of them being separate-but-bundled services, Skydance CEO David Ellison said earlier this month. That transition period of HBO Max Paramount+ co-existing together is believed to be 1-2 years.

In his email, Bloys also thanked Wiseman for having done “amazing work” as EVP and Head of Originals for Paramount+.

“The development slate is incredibly impressive, and Jane has graciously offered to help with the transition,” Bloys said. “She is an extraordinarily talented executive.”

title: Donald Trump Lashes Out At NBC News Reporter As She Presses Him On Why He Supports Ad That Has Been Condemned By Democrats And Republicans
summary: President Donald Trump again lashed out at a reporter, this time an NBC News correspondent who pressed him about his support for a Vivek Ramaswamy ad that has been condemned by Democrats and Republicans. Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, is behind a new spot that debuted this week featuring the estranged mother […]
content:
President Donald Trump again lashed out at a reporter, this time an NBC News correspondent who pressed him about his support for a Vivek Ramaswamy ad that has been condemned by Democrats and Republicans.

Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, is behind a new spot that debuted this week featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. In the ad, Acton’s mother says that she doesn’t trust her daughter, saying she “lies about her past.”

Unmentioned in the spot are allegations that Acton’s stepfather, now deceased, sexually abused her when she was a child. According to the AP, the stepfather was charged with raping her but did not show up at a court hearing and was deemed a fugitive. Acton’s brother said that at the time, he and his sister were removed from their mother’s custody as she remained with their stepfather.

Referring to the Ramaswany ad, Trump said, “A mother is saying, ‘Don’t put my daughter there because she’s a terrible person and she’s a liar. Why shouldn’t somebody use that?”

Watch on Deadline

NBC News’ Monica Alba then asked him, “But do the sexual abuse allegations mean nothing to you?” Trump went on, but Alba continued to ask the question.

“Who are you with?” he asked her.

“I am with NBC sir,” she responded.

“One of the worst networks you have,” he said.

She continued to ask about the sexual abuse allegations, and Trump told her, “Quiet.”

“Isn’t she a fresh person? You’re a horrible little reporter, aren’t you?” Trump said.

Trump said, “If my mother said bad things about me, do you think the Democrats would put it up? I think so. But my mother thought I was wonderful.” He looked up in the air and said, “Thank you, Mom.”

He said of Acton’s mother, “She said her daughter is a disaster. Her daughter is a liar. And she felt she had a obligation…I should be so lucky to have an ad like that.”

He then asked Alba, “Why wouldn’t you listen to a mother that says that? Why? Miss NBC, why wouldn’t you, listen.”

Alba responded, “She stayed with her stepfather.”

“I don’t know anything about her stepfather,” Trump said.

President Trump on political ad against Amy Acton (D-OH): "If my mother said bad things about me, do you think the Democrats would put it up? I think so — but my mother thought I was wonderful… Why wouldn't you listen to a mother who says that?" pic.twitter.com/mrfuigQbEH — CSPAN (@cspan) October 23, 2026

Republicans including the state’s current governor, Mike DeWine, have said that Ramaswamy should pull the spot. “It’s wrong. It needs to be taken down,” DeWine said of the ad on Thursday. Nikki Haley, who clashed with Ramaswamy during the 2024 GOP presidential debates, posted on X, “Just seeing what we tried to tell everyone back then. He’s a bad guy. It’s a shame he continues to get away with it.”

Trump’s outburst at a reporter is only the latest this week. He berated Andrew Feinberg, correspondent for The Independent, and later the White House pulled him from travel pool duty. Trump also lashed out at CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and a reporter for ABC News as they asked him questions.

title: IATSE Taps Jillian Arnold As Union’s First Labor & Technology Intelligence Officer
summary: Jillian Arnold will be guiding the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees on new and emerging tech going forward. Arnold was appointed on Friday as the union’s first Labor & Technology Intelligence Officer, a newly created role to focus on how emerging technologies (read: artificial intelligence) will impact the craft and working conditions of its […]
content:
Jillian Arnold will be guiding the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees on new and emerging tech going forward.

Arnold was appointed on Friday as the union’s first Labor & Technology Intelligence Officer, a newly created role to focus on how emerging technologies (read: artificial intelligence) will impact the craft and working conditions of its members in the U.S. and Canada.

In the role, Arnold will continue work she’s already begun within IATSE in various capacities over the years. In 2020, she became the first woman and the first video engineer elected president of IATSE Local 695 in the union’s 90-year history, representing production sound, video, and projection workers in the Hollywood jurisdiction. She was elected to a second term in 2023.

She also previously served as chair of the IATSE AI sub-committee during the union’s 2024 negotiations with the AMPTP.

Watch on Deadline

“Technology has been a defining part of my entire career,” Arnold said in a statement on Friday. “I’ve seen firsthand how technological innovation can expand what workers are capable of achieving. I’ve also seen why workers need a meaningful voice in determining how technologies are developed and integrated into the workplace. I’m excited to bring those experiences together in this new role and help ensure that technological progress strengthens our crafts and the people who perform them.”

Added IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb: “Jillian has been a leader on artificial intelligence and its impact on the labor movement. In this new role, she’ll be a resource and a voice representing members on both sides of the border as we navigate public policy and workplace challenges relating to the development and implementation of these new tools.”



IATSE Director of Canadian Affairs John M. Lewis said: “Companies that employ members on both sides of the border may choose to deploy certain AI technologies in different jurisdictions but not in others. With the creation of this new role, members in Canada and United States will have the benefit of an expert voice who can help ensure their interests are protected at the bargaining table.”

content:
Assistant district attorney Alexandra Cabot is back.

Stephanie March will appear in the ninth episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” Season 28 to reprise the role she has played in more than 100 episodes. March was a member of the main “Special Victims Unit” cast from Season 2 in 2000 to Season 5 in 2003, when Cabot had to fake her own death and enter a witness protection program. She has returned to the series as a guest several times over the years across Seasons 6, 10, 11, 13 and most recently Season 19 in 2018. She also played Cabot in the 2006 legal drama “Conviction,” a short-lived “SVU” spinoff.

Besides “SVU,” March’s prominent credits include Ricky Gervais’ 2009 comedy film “The Invention of Lying,” Matthew Newton’s 2017 indie film “Who We Are Now,” Laura Kosann 2019 mockumentary “The Social Ones” and Ava Duvernay’s 2023 film “Origin.” She also collaborated with Duvernay on her 2022 series “Naomi.” In 2023, she was in the Amazon Prime Video series “Harlan Coben’s Shelter.” She is repped by Paradigm and Navigation Media Group.

Popular on Variety

Created by Dick Wolf, “SVU” is the longest-running primetime drama in the history of American Television.
