title: Why Olivia Colman Didn’t Get Splinters From Getting Intimate With Alexander Skarsgård’s ‘Wicker’ Costume
summary: Believe the hype. “Wicker,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe. Olivia Colman plays a spinster fisherwoman in a medieval community where marriage is what gives a woman worth. Although she is a fierce independent woman, the village mocks her as she goes about […]
content:
Believe the hype. “Wicker,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe.

Olivia Colman plays a spinster fisherwoman in a medieval community where marriage is what gives a woman worth. Although she is a fierce independent woman, the village mocks her as she goes about making her living. One day she goes to the local basket weaver, played by Peter Dinklage, and asks him to make her a wicker husband.

Enter Alexander Skarsgård — yes, that is him under all that makeup — wearing a practical suit and prosthetic makeup to transform him into a basket man.

Popular on Variety

It began with Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, who were adapting Ursula Wills’ short story “The Wicker Husband.” Weta Workshop artists, prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley and lead makeup FX artist Sarah Rubano received the script and a call from the writers and directors who told them, “We want to make this practically,” says Dunckley. “They wanted a piece of beautiful concept art that showed their vision.”

The pair spent 18 months in research and development alone. Because prosthetic makeup materials are manufactured to imitate human flesh and skin, it posed a challenge. “This guy is made of wicker, so we had to do it a different way,” Dunckley says. He continues, “We tested our theory. We thought that if we could get the strands of the weave to be individual and get them to move as if they were individual muscle fibers that drove his movement, then he could be a believable sentient wicker being.”

But they couldn’t mold it, so the pair were pushed toward modern innovation using 3D digital sculpting and 3D printing.

They began with a full-body scan of Skarsgård so they could sculpt pieces specific to him.

The intricate basket weave was created using a relatively new powder-bed laser-sintered printing process. Dunckley explains, “It’s a volume of thermoplastic elastomer; you shoot a laser into it and where that focal point of the laser is, it fuses the powder and you can build intricate weave and complex geometry. The powder in the bed holds the strands apart while they set.”

And why didn’t Colman get splinters during the film’s steamy bonking scenes?

Nearly all of Skarsgård’s costume was made up of 50 individual 3D-printed appliances that were painted to look like wicker before being stitched onto a suit made out of soft, flexible spandex — so no actual straw was involved.

Dunckley says, “It’s a semiflexible material, not too dissimilar to the feeling of touching proper wicker weave.”

As for the prosthetics, Rubano focused on the makeup, which comprised 10 individual pieces.

Rubano says, “He would get into this very fitted suit and we would bounce between the makeup chair and getting him ready in the suit, depending on the different stages.” She goes on to say, “We had ears, eye bags and lips. We had an underlip piece and a jaw piece, and the larger forehead, nose, cheekbones and there was lots of hand painting around his eyes.”

His facial hair — beard, hair and eyelashes — was constructed from muka, a silky-soft fiber extracted from the harakeke plant. This material allowed them to knot the individual strands onto the weave itself so they could cut and style it like human hair.

The key was not to lose Skarsgård under the makeup. Dunckley says the team used 3D animation software: “We could track the expressive range of the face so that we could engineer into the weave the ability to move for his expression.”

In all, it took under two hours to transform Skarsgård into the wicker husband. “90 minutes is where we were by the end of it,” Rubano says.

Dunckley adds, “The other big piece to the puzzle was Alexander himself. What a wonderful collaborator and team player! He was resilient. He was funny. He was so invested. He would sit as still as a statue in the chair.”

They encountered one small issue. Rubano reveals, “He runs hot; the suit’s kind of hot and it was a hot Hungarian spring.”

And what about the wicker penis?

“There’s been a lot of speculation about just the mechanics of how this would work and about the potential danger of a wicker penis,” Dunckley says. “I think the basket maker, he’s skilled. He’s traveled the world. He’s learned from every culture how to weave, and I think he would know exactly how to weave a wicker ween so it’s user-friendly.”

Rubano credits the film’s costume designers András Dániel Tóth and Attila Godena-Juhász for that detail. “They fabricated the wicker ween for the full-body river shot. They did such a great job because it was very last minute, but it’s puff spandex. The weave was 3D, so there was dimension to it. From a distance, they color-matched it so beautifully.”

title: Ethan Klein Reacts to Hila Klein’s Cheating Allegations Amid ‘H3 Podcast’ Fallout: ‘Please Respect My Family’s Privacy … They Have Nothing to Do With This’
summary: Ethan Klein has spoken out after the implosion of his marriage and the “H3 Podcast” due to cheating allegations from his wife, Hila Klein, who publicly accused him of having a six-month romantic affair. “I know a lot of people are understandably looking for a comment from me, but I ask that you please respect […]
content:
Ethan Klein has spoken out after the implosion of his marriage and the “H3 Podcast” due to cheating allegations from his wife, Hila Klein, who publicly accused him of having a six-month romantic affair.

“I know a lot of people are understandably looking for a comment from me, but I ask that you please respect my family’s privacy and do not contact them looking for me or asking for their comments,” Klein wrote in an Instagram Story on Friday. “They have nothing to do with this and share in your outrage and disappointment. Thank you.”

After meeting in 2007, Ethan and Hila built their YouTube careers together and got married in 2012. The Los Angeles-based couple have three children together. They launched the “H3 Podcast” in 2016. On YouTube, it currently has 2.5 million subscribers.

Popular on Variety

In response to the cheating allegations, the podcast production crew sided with Hila and unanimously agreed that they would cut ties with Ethan.

In an Instagram post late Thursday night, Hila wrote, “I am living a nightmare I can’t wake up from. My husband has been having an affair. I have been fed lie after lie after lie for months. Here is the truth.”

She continued: “I could sense something was wrong. I tried to ask him questions and share my concerns and hurt feelings. But I was met with dismissive answers and no action. Things that bothered me continued to bother me, and he did nothing about it. So I trusted him. Because I loved him. I stopped questioning him and began to question myself, my own instincts. My sanity.”



According to Hila Klein, “Eventually, he was caught in a lie, and I knew I was done. But the lies continued. ‘It was just a kiss’ became ‘it was emotional cheating.’ After I dragged these lies from him, he finally admitted he’d been in an affair for over 6 months, the extent of which I’m sure I still don’t know.”

“The betrayal I feel is immeasurable. The person I loved and trusted for 20 years evaporated overnight. He was my safe place, my partner in marriage, parenting, and business,” Hila wrote. “My only family on this side of the world. How do I even begin to make sense of this?”

She concluded, “I don’t know what comes next; I’ve never been here before. I am in survival mode, trying to navigate separation, co-parenting, and unthinkable heartbreak. All I can do right now is focus on taking care of myself and my children, one day at a time. You’re not crazy. Trust your instincts. Trust yourself. If you’re not being treated right, get up and leave.”

The “H3” crew, in a statement posted on Instagram, said, “We stand with Hila and will support her every step of the way. We’re disgusted by Ethan’s actions and the hurt he has caused. We all deserved better: Hila, us, and you.”

“We are all shocked, angry, and heartbroken to learn about Ethan’s ongoing affair,” the H3 team said. “As soon as we found out, we all agreed: we would not continue working with Ethan involved or profiting in any way. We don’t yet know what that means for the future. There’s a lot to work through, and we wish we had more answers for you.”

The “H3 Podcast” crew’s statement concluded, “Please know that we’re safe, we’re sticking together, and we’re looking after each other. We’ve put so much of ourselves into this show, and it’s hard to find the words for what we’re feeling right now. Thank you for giving us some time to figure things out, and for all the love you’ve shown us. We love you, and we miss you already.”

title: ‘The Cycle’ Is a Surprising New Take on the Police Procedural, With a Huge Twist and an Emotional Resonance the Director Didn’t Expect
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “The Cycle,” now streaming on Shudder. What if a werewolf continued to transform even after its death? This light bulb idea came to frequent collaborators Jordan Downey and Kevin Stewart as they were sketching out a TV treatment for their 2018 film “The Head Hunter.” “We both […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “The Cycle,” now streaming on Shudder.

What if a werewolf continued to transform even after its death?

This light bulb idea came to frequent collaborators Jordan Downey and Kevin Stewart as they were sketching out a TV treatment for their 2018 film “The Head Hunter.”

“We both looked at each other and stopped and were like, ‘Wait, that’s a really cool, fun idea and a take on werewolves that we’ve never seen before,’” Downey says. “Being the horror cinephiles that we are, we were like, ‘I don’t think anyone’s done that. I can’t think of a movie or a show.’ We Googled it and realized, no, it hasn’t been done. What do you do with that idea?”

Popular on Variety

The result is “The Cycle,” a handsomely shot detective story following Meg (Deborah Ann Woll) and Marks (Jeffrey Donovan) as experts trying to solve a lycanthropic murder mystery — although the film largely keeps the exact supernatural entity a mystery, until the third act goes full creature feature.

Downey, who co-wrote the film with Stewart and directed it, thought that outsized hook would benefit from a recognizable framing.

“Right away, it felt like it fit best into a crime mystery, a police procedural,” he says. “Ultimately, if you have this werewolf that is going to reanimate and then at dawn turn back into a man — but in this case it’s a deceased man who doesn’t move, walk, talk, has no life — that would just be dumbfounding to police. They would come into this crime scene and they would see these victims, but then they’d find this naked dead guy not knowing that he’s harboring something supernatural. So it made sense that there really wasn’t another package to put it into.”

“The Cycle” ©AMC/courtesy Everett Collection

Once the case is cracked, the third act shifts hard into monster movie mode, complete with plenty of practical blood, guts and werewolf nastiness.

“I love creature features,” Downey says. “I didn’t want it to be this ‘elevated,’ pretentious experience that didn’t give monster movie fans the proper experience. You go into ‘The Cycle’ not knowing that’s what’s coming. I thought what would happen is the characters would be thrust into a completely crazy change in their lives, that they now exist in a world where werewolves can be real and there’s one in proximity to them. That change would be as shocking to them as it hopefully would be to the audience. So we were aware of trying to do things early in the movie, so when that tonal shift happens, it felt earned but also surprising.”

Ushering in the change of pace was the transformation scene, which is one of the most loved traditions in werewolf movies and was exciting for the team to plan for, along with key special effects artist and supervisor Patrick Magee.

“The first thing was acknowledging that if you’re going to make a werewolf movie, we didn’t want to run from that challenge,” Downey says. “In the ’80s, Rob Bottin and Rick Baker nailed it with ‘The Howling’ and ‘An American Werewolf in London.’ In the years since, people have shied away from it because either it’s too expensive, too time-consuming or maybe there’s a clever new way of doing it. But we just felt like enough time had gone where we hadn’t seen that done very well for so many years. So we said right away, ‘If we’re going to do this, we have to do a proper werewolf transformation. We have to nail it.’ We storyboarded it a lot. We talked about it a lot. We broke down the best scenes that had been done and thought about … Do we want to see foot? Do we want to see hands? Do we want to see eyes, teeth? Is it a spinal cord? All of the different things that we wanted to see in our scene, and then how it would apply to an undead corpse version of a transformation.

Beyond the horror element, the film examines the complex choices that can come with fatherhood, which comes most notably via Meg, who learns that her long-lost parent is the werewolf at the heart of the story.

“It wasn’t in the first drafts, to be honest,” Downey says. “In our initial treatments, Meg was investigating a stranger. It was the same concept that a man’s body was discovered, the police didn’t know how he was tied to these murders, and they went to her because she was an expert in her field, but he wasn’t her father. We got her into Act Three, when she went to the house, just like in the movie where they go to investigate his whereabouts and the life of the recluse. We felt like she was putting herself in this really dangerous position, without some kind of an emotional tie to that character. I told Kevin that I don’t believe that the character would do this given the circumstances. We were also missing something that I thought is really important in horror films, which is the heart and the pathos of a monster movie and the tragedy. So then, we came up with the idea that, ‘OK, what if this is her father?’ So now we’ve anchored something to her emotionally. We can work in the tragedy of this man who left, but it was in her mind for a terrible reason, a father walking out on their children. In his mind, it was to protect them. And once we had that for her father, then we started to apply that theme to some of the other characters.”

Much like the cycle of undead werewolves, it’s easy to see this story carry on through new chapters. Downey says he’s happy keeping “The Cycle” as a single story, but has also mulled over what a larger scope could be.

“I think this movie is self-contained and there’s versions of it that I would probably not be interested in,” Downey says. “But we did talk a lot about different stories. I think there’s a great prequel in the original werewolf that came from over the sea. There’s an aquatic, boat-set version of this story that I think would be interesting. You could do a TV series about the life and the trials of [Meg’s father] Peter Stump and all of the different things that he was doing while isolated for those 30 years. I think it’d be interesting to see … because she’s so good at her job, and in the final scene of the movie so confident that she’s gonna get this figured out. But what if she didn’t? What if 10, 15, 20 years goes by and she has not solved it and she is now facing the same dilemma her dad was, which was, ‘This fucking thing can’t be stopped.’ But by killing herself, that does nothing. Finding her at a point of quit would be really interesting. I’d only want to do stuff if Deborah and Jeffrey wanted to come back and work on it again, and if there were fans that wanted it to happen, but I would never say no.”

title: Aaron Guzikowski Tapped To Pen New ‘Alien’ Movie For 20th, Scott Free
summary: Aaron Guzikowski, creator of the Scott Free-produced HBO Max sci-fi series Raised by Wolves, is scripting a new Alien movie for 20th Century Studios, Deadline can confirm. Not much else is known about the project though sources described it as the next in the franchise. Scott and Michael Pruss will produce for Scott Free, with, […]
content:
Aaron Guzikowski, creator of the Scott Free-produced HBO Max sci-fi series Raised by Wolves, is scripting a new Alien movie for 20th Century Studios, Deadline can confirm.

Not much else is known about the project though sources described it as the next in the franchise. Scott and Michael Pruss will produce for Scott Free, with, J.R. Young overseeing for the studio.

An American screenwriter and showrunner, Guzikowski’s Raised by Wolves — following two androids raising human children following the destruction of the Earth in a great war — aired for two seasons. He’s otherwise best known for penning Prisoners, Warner Bros.’ lauded 2013 crime thriller directed by Denis Villeneuve.

An iconic sci-fi horror series, Alien revolves around humanity’s deadly and terrifying encounters with the extraterrestrial species known as the Xenomorph. Fede Álvarez directed the most recent installment, 2024’s Alien Romulus, which grossed over $350 million worldwide.

Watch on Deadline

title: Renate Reinsve On Making Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Winner ‘Fjord’: “I Knew I Was Going Into A Completely Different World”
summary: By now, Renate Reinsve is no stranger to the closing-night pomp of the Cannes Film Festival, having won the best actress trophy in 2021 for Joachim Trier’s The Worst Person in the World, her first ever leading role. Since then, she’s clearly mastered the art of capturing souls; after reteaming with Trier for last year’s […]
content:
By now, Renate Reinsve is no stranger to the closing-night pomp of the Cannes Film Festival, having won the best actress trophy in 2021 for Joachim Trier’s The Worst Person in the World, her first ever leading role. Since then, she’s clearly mastered the art of capturing souls; after reteaming with Trier for last year’s Cannes triumph Sentimental Value, which brought her a nomination for Best Supporting Actress at the Oscars, Reinsve returned to the festival with Romanian director Cristian Mungiu, where Fjord, the film they made in collaboration with American star Sebastian Stan, won the Palme d’Or, the director’s second.

In Mungius film — which has officially been selected by Romania as its Oscar hopeful in the Best International Feature Film race — Reinsve plays Lisbet, the wife of a Romanian educator (Stan) who has travelled with his family to live in her Norwegian hometown. After local title-tattle amongst the townsfolk, who deplore the family’s chosen Romanian Christian evangelism, there are accusations that the couple are harming their five children, which leads the state authorities to take the kids into care.

Watch on Deadline

It’s unusual for lightning to strike so many times, especially in Cannes, but Reinsve remembers having a dream — or maybe it was a premonition.

“Joachim was there,” she recalls, “and then there was this Romanian bear, and that kind of represented my transition from Joachim to Cristian.”

I’m eager to learn what kind of bear it was. Male or female? And will it go to the Oscars?

“Male, brown, and the bear was taking me to the forest, like, to another realm,” she says brightly. “Interesting, right?”

Totally, I concur. I love bear tales, having roared at one that had entered a restaurant in Telluride a few years back. In fact, when we bumped into each other at the very same restaurant two years ago, we chuckled about it.

We ponder a moment over what the psychology of the bear and the other stuff in the dream could’ve meant. “I think it’s about the fact that I feel so connected to Joachim, and about going into another movie after a movie that meant so much to me. I knew that this movie would mean a lot, going into these huge themes, and playing a character that I knew was gonna be very challenging to do.

“Of course, [the two directors] are not similar at all,” she adds. “But they do have some similarities, in terms of being so certain of their way of making a movie, and they hold onto their ideals so strongly. So, I knew that I was going from one person’s world, into a completely different world, with another person. I think that was the dream.”

‘Fjord’ Tudor Pandura/Neon

Unlike the contemporary women of Trier’s world, Lisbet, the mother of five that she plays in Fjord, is devoid of vanity, favoring drab long skirts and black coats. No make-up. Her physicality is that of a -longsuffering, exhausted parent.

During early conversations with Mungiu she learned that his camera was “really far away” and that he wanted to remove any kind of manipulation. “Like, you weren’t supposed to lead the audience to any emotional state or lead them to an opinion about the person. So, we had strip away the emotion.”

She shrugs. “I thought, How can you see what she’s going through?”

The prospect frightened her, because she was playing a character having to endure something “so dramatic and so strong” that she was scared the audience wouldn’t connect to what she was going through. As a classically trained actress, she was used to giving the audience “just enough to connect, but still leaving it open to their interpretation”. Now, she says, she was being asked to “leave it very open”.

As Reinsve mulled over the situation, a picture entered her mind about how we react when we drive past an accident on the side of the road.

“In one second, you know how severe it is, because you see how the people move from a distance, and you see how they hold themselves, and you see how if they move slowly or if they move fast, and you know what’s happened. So, I kind of had that image when going through and trying to trust and stay true to Lisbet.”

Having worked in the theater for two decades she enjoys the task of breaking down a character’s mindset and their physicality. In particular, she loves characters “that are quite a lot.” However, she admits to feeling “a bit provoked” that there was this dynamic “where her husband spoke on her behalf, and I had to really find a way for her to do that in a way I could have compassion and understanding with.”

The task was, she continues, “to be very specific at the same time as not judging them, and that was a really hard balance to do.”

I frown at the idea that Lisbet’s husband spoke for her for. However, Reinsve argues that there’s a lot of trust within the relationship “so he knows exactly what she wants and feels” and she’s comfortable with it. In fact, it’s all there up on the screen in her performance, where she captures the character’s empathy and compassion by conveying incredibly subtle — but at the same time very specific — gestures.

Reinsve says that Mungiu likes to shoot a lot of takes. “His poetry really lies within the mise en scène,” she says, in the way that he builds the movements within the frame little by little. The actor recalls standing by the monitor watching him, “and I could see how it really changed how you saw the character, informing you, in a subliminal way, how everything moves within the frame.”

She marvels at his ability, while suggesting that the filmmaker “does so many takes because he builds that poetry of the image slowly from the first take. So, he doesn’t necessarily want you to know your lines from the beginning, you can actually shape it with him while he works on it.”

‘Fjord’ Tudor Pandura/Neon

Reinsve smiles at this, explaining that she didn’t know Mungiu’s shooting methods “from the beginning, so I gave it my all”, and she punches the palm of her hand for emphasis. “The first three takes we ever did in the movie were when she’s told that her kids are going to be taken away. But he gave me the script a week before. It’s 12 minutes, that scene, and I didn’t know his acting style that well yet, so that was a really hard first day. I gave it my all for the first three takes, and then we kept on going for 17 takes while he built it. And then I had to, like, really observe him and learn when he started getting ready. When he’s happy, he rubs his hands, and then I know now I can give it my all,” she says, as she merrily rubs her own hands together.

Reinsve was challenged by Mungiu’s way of working, but, at the same time, found it refreshing. “He’s very specific on rhythm and movement, and then he doesn’t really want to judge the character. So, I had to throw everything I knew out the window and kind of start over, just adapting to what he wanted. And then, of course, when I had gotten his method under the skin, I could slowly start adding elements that I felt were right. Not manipulating them, but adding specific little things that I could kind of enjoy doing.”

Having to learn something new, she says, is “always a little bit humiliating. But then you actually have the opportunity to transform, and I really feel that I have learned so much as an actress going through that process and really opening up to that process, because if I’d just done things I already know… That way, you limit your ability to learn new things.”

In any case, she concedes, working in the theater means that no two performances are the same anyway; and she’s used to performing disparate roles. On the Norwegian stage she has performed much of Ibsen’s canon and more contemporary works such as Simon Stephens’ adaptation of Mark Hadden’s best-seller The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time.

However, she remarks that if she’d started her career in movies — her screen debut was a small part in Trier’s 2011 film Oslo, August 31st — “maybe it would be more natural to go into something again and again that was more me. But now I have this already kind of an approach where I love going into different styles of directing and different characters.”

Mungiu mixed it up from the get-go, she says. When they first met he asked her to read another role, the part of Mia, a liberal minded neighbour — “because he thought that would be the one that I connected to” — but he allowed her to read for Lisbet as well. And as she studied the part, she felt an “overwhelming” connection to Lisbet, both in the “curiosity” of who she was “but also in being a mother myself. Her having her kids taken away was devastating. And I told Cristian that I really had the strongest feeling reading Lisbet, and I felt he was surprised. So, I was already a bit heartbroken because I thought he would give me Mia. It would be more obvious, and I was so happy when I could play Lisbet.”

Immediately, she began a deep dive into matters theological, which meant exploring the rituals of the Pentecostal Church and mingling with congregations. She keenly observed, she says, the connection they had to singing, giving each other food, and how they greeted each other at services held in their homes and official places of worship.

Reinsve familiarised herself with all details of their faith. In so doing, she was struck by how congregants would hold their hands towards God the way they dressed, and the detail of women wearing headbands.,

At times she felt conflicted as she dug into a person “who has different values and different opinions [to me]” and she suggests that the situation was especially challenging because Lisbet’s actions were informed “by values that I don’t believe in myself, but I had to find compassion for those values and why they came to be.”

She laments not having had enough time to further explore Lisbet’s perspective. Put together, there were six months spent on research and shooting. “And I was still not knowing enough,” she sighs.

Seeing as Reinsve is Norwegian herself, I ask if she recognized those people who were so zealous in wanting to take those kids from their parents.

Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve in ‘Fjord’ Tudor Pandura/Neon

“Well, I’ve heard stories about big mistakes being made in child services in Norway, which is mainly a really good institution and has saved a lot of kids and is doing so many great things. But there have been horror stories of misunderstandings and also, like this, a collision of values.”

She has since talked to people in child services in Norway who have seen the movie, and they are really happy “to have another perspective, a starting point for a conversation. It’s always healthy, even though it is a well-functioning service. Mostly, it’s important to notice when something is off,” she cautions.

Similarly, in the U.S., where Neon released Fjord earlier in October, people are having heated conversations about it, which delights her. “It’s a big debate, and that’s amazing,” she cries. It’s what Mungiu wanted, Reinsve suggests. “Like, to open a conversation, and not only about the themes in the movie, but also having a movie that divides people, and that your empathy for the characters are actually shifting during the movie, and it really is open for everyone’s opinion.”

There was a comfort, Reinsve relates, in having worked with Stan three years prior on A Different Man, “especially here, because the technique of acting was so new in a way, because there were so many elements that were new.” Also, because the two actors are old friends, “You don’t have to warm up. It’s very quiet the way they are together. So, to have to have that familiarity also, I think, made them seem like they had a warmer relationship than their physicality implies.”

The movie shot in a remote Norwegian village of 25 people who were swamped by cast and crew. The nearest food store was miles away, and getting food for everyone was a production in itself, especially when avalanches blocked the roads “so all the crew, all the gear, all the cast needed to go on a boat to get to se. We had a very strong bond in the end. It was really just us and these… ghosts,” she says, dropping a shocker.

What? The rooms at the hotel were haunted, Reinsve says, in a tone of such eeriness that any shadow of doubt on my part was wiped from my face. I shift my chair closer to get the skinny on the specter. “Ghosts definitely haunted that hotel,” she declares. “Everyone had knocking on their doors at night. Everyone had that, and other different experiences too, and it made the stay even more mystical. I don’t think I slept very well for two months. I was so scared,” she says of the phantom menace that lurked in the remote locale, way up in mountains reachable by hops on two planes and then boat or car.

The locals were aware of the apparitions because “it was a thing there.” Some nights, she reveals, “the ghost would knock on my door for, like, two hours, from 1.30am. When I looked… no one was there,” she says adding a ghostly wail for added effect.

Did she turn to drink? Shaking her head, she guffaws and says she didn’t. “We had some parties with food and dancing in circles, Romanian-style, and, well, OK, a little drinking,” she confesses. “It was it was so much fun. The Romanians from the production were very good hosting and singing.” Stan joined in too, she says.

Reinsve admired watching him work. “I’ve seen him close up into production, and he really enjoys it. Like, I can see the joy on his face, thinking about how he can change and going through the process. It’s so fascinating to watch him, because a big part of of acting for him is of course the change on the inside, but also building something from the outside, where he doesn’t even recognize himself.”

Right in the middle of the last awards season, Reinsve was filming Alexander Payne’s Somewhere Out There, and through this one she’ll be portraying visionary feminist and author Mary Wollstonecraft in filmmaker Mia Hansen-Løve’s If Love Should Die, a movie that will jump back and forth in time to explore 12 years of her life in England, Revolutionary France and elsewhere in Europe. It’s a co-production involving many locations — “We’re in six countries,” she notes — and she has spent time researching in some of them, including here in Blighty.

She speaks of visiting the Stoke Newington district of north London where Wollstonecraft — mother of Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein — founded a school and worshipped at a church on Newington Green. The actor has walked the streets that Wollstonecraft trod over two centuries ago, taking in museums that now celebrate her life. Reinsve took a similar tour around the philosopher’s Parisian haunts, including the spot where she witnessed Louis XVI attending his trial and “going towards death” by guillotine. “I really love that part of the process. Just the research and trying to get as close to her as possible,” Reinsve says. She really is living her dreams.

title: ‘Overcompensating’s Benito Skinner Reveals Season 2 Hookup That Fans “Ask About Everyday”
summary: As Benito Skinner heads back to campus for Season 2 of Overcompensating, he’s giving the fans what they want. The series creator, EP and star revealed that the upcoming sophomore season of the Prime Video college series features lots of nudity and a hookup scene that fans ask about “everyday.” “I was half-naked,” he told […]
content:
As Benito Skinner heads back to campus for Season 2 of Overcompensating, he’s giving the fans what they want.

The series creator, EP and star revealed that the upcoming sophomore season of the Prime Video college series features lots of nudity and a hookup scene that fans ask about “everyday.”

“I was half-naked,” he told co-star Owen Thiele on his In Your Dreams podcast. “I wear like 12 jock straps this season.”

Skinner continued, “I will say one thing, because I just think it’s fun and it’s coming, and I can’t hold things anymore. But Benny [Skinner] does hook up with Miles [Rish Shah] in Season 2. You will see that, is what I’m gonna say, because I get asked that everyday.

“That’s one thing, and obviously George [Thiele] is a much bigger character in Season 2,” he added.

Watch on Deadline

Inspired by his journey to coming out of the closet as a college jock, Skinner’s semi-autobiographical series was renewed for Season 2 at Prime Video last September.

With Holmes upped to series regular as hilarious party girl Hailee, Season 2 guest appearances include Tom Francis as Declan Bishop, Aisha Dee as Naomi and AnnaSophia Robb as Chels.

Also reprising their recurring roles from Season 1 are Connie Britton, Kyle MacLachlan, Lukas Gage, Andrea Martin, Julia Shiplett, Nell Verlaque, Danielle Perez, Yasmine Sahid, Boman Martinez-Reid, Tomaso Sanelli and Austin Lindsay.

title: Weekly World News Comedy Series From ‘Reno 911!’ Co-Creator Robert Ben Garant Raises $2.5M To Film Full Season Independently In California
summary: After three decades in the Hollywood system, Reno 911! co-creator Robert Ben Garant is venturing outside of it for his next series, set in the world of satirical tabloid fixture Weekly World News. The project, on which Garant will serve as co-showrunner/executive producer alongside frequent collaborator fellow Reno 911! alumna Cathy Shim, will film a […]
content:
After three decades in the Hollywood system, Reno 911! co-creator Robert Ben Garant is venturing outside of it for his next series, set in the world of satirical tabloid fixture Weekly World News.

The project, on which Garant will serve as co-showrunner/executive producer alongside frequent collaborator fellow Reno 911! alumna Cathy Shim, will film a six-episode season commissioned by Weekly World News Studios, which raised $2.5 million from six private investors to finance it. WWN Editor-In-Chief Greg D’Alessandro serves as writer and executive producer on the series, which is set to start production the first week of February in Simi Valley, California.

Shot in the improvised mockumentary style of Reno 911!, the comedy follows the reporters of Weekly World News, known for Bat Boy, alien encounters and Elvis sightings, as they track down stories too outside-the-box for “legacy” media. The reporters treat every assignment with complete seriousness, even as their compelling personalities and professional ambitions collide on the job. Through it all, they stay committed to delivering “The World’s Only Reliable News.”

Watch on Deadline

This marks the first series for Garant since the Reno 911! revival for Quibi/Roku six years ago. He and Shim came close with workplace comedy Movers, which got a pilot order at FX last year but ultimately didn’t go to series. It was their third produced pilot since Reno 911! to not go the distance following Seoul Hunters for TruTV and Chasers for Comedy Central.

Amid a shrinking comedy space with few opportunities, the duo are looking to create one for themselves following the example of comedian Shane Gillis who also shot a six-episode season of his comedy Tiers independently before selling it to Netflix.

The producers of the WWN series plan to start pitching the series to platforms and other distributors once there is filmed footage. The series’ price point would make it suitable for any outlet, including basic cable networks which operate under financial constraints when picking up original programming.

Because of its improv nature, the series will be working off “scriptments,” which have been written. Based on the amount of improvisation, the season may go beyond six episodes. Because of the current minimum budget threshold of $1M an episode, the WWN series does not qualify for a California tax credit, but its producers wanted to use Los Angeles cast and crew instead of going to New Mexico or New Jersey.

“I grew up with Weekly World News. It’s made me laugh for a long time. Our take is that every story in the Weekly World News is true. If it made the paper, it happened.” Garant said. “So our reporters are busting their ass to report these incredible stories, but they all have chips on their shoulders because everyone thinks their paper is a joke.”

Adam Kolbrenner of Lit Entertainment produces alongside Joe Corcoran and Ken Denison, who will produce for Weekly World News Studios. Patrick White of Lit Entertainment will serve as co-producer and Grace Lovret of Weekly World News Studios will serve as executive producer.



“In a world where nobody knows what to believe, the reporters at Weekly World News have the advantage of believing absolutely everything,” D’Alessandro said. “Ben has an extraordinary ability to make absurd situations feel completely real, which makes him the perfect creative partner. Ben, Cathy and I want the audience to believe in these characters, even when they can’t believe what’s happening around them. And it’s all fact-checked by Bat Boy.”



Weekly World News Studios produced The Zombie Wedding, released in 2024, and is working on a documentary and a slate of film and television projects drawn from the Weekly World News library, including a live-action Bat Boy series, that was previously set up at Netflix.

The Weekly World News supermarket tabloid was published in print from 1979 to 2007. The brand has stayed live on social media since then.

Garant is repped by CAA, Artists First, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. Shim is repped by Global Artists Agency, Artists First, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. Weekly World News Studios and D’Alessandro are repped by Adam Kolbrenner of Lit Entertainment Group and Elsa Ramo of Ramo Law.

content:
Laika’s latest animated stop-motion story explores a fictional, mysterious, unurbanized stretch of land outside the city of Portland, Oregon.

The Impassable Wilderness, as it is called, has many lessons to teach heroine Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) when she drags her classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay) into the woods shrouded in ivy to save her younger brother Mac (Arthur Knight) after a murder of crows swoops in and steals him away. The magical ivy that surrounds Wildwood isn’t supposed to let any Outsiders in, but Prue’s blood hints at a connection she and her brother have to the world without knowing it.

Based on the book of the same name written by The Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy, the Wildwood film brought about three new songs from Portland-based band, one of which plays during the credits of the movie. Meloy also wrote some songs sung by the Wildwood voice cast at various parts in the film.

title: Sacha Baron Cohen Says Donald Trump Has ‘Elements of Brilliance’ and ‘We Were Too Easy to Dismiss Him as a Nincompoop’
summary: 20 years after retiring Ali G, Sacha Baron Cohen has dusted off his tracksuit collection and reprised the character for “Ali G: Who Iz I?,” now open in theaters before coming to Amazon Prime Oct. 30. The comedian first brought Ali G to audiences at the turn of the century with “Da Ali G Show,” […]
content:
20 years after retiring Ali G, Sacha Baron Cohen has dusted off his tracksuit collection and reprised the character for “Ali G: Who Iz I?,” now open in theaters before coming to Amazon Prime Oct. 30. The comedian first brought Ali G to audiences at the turn of the century with “Da Ali G Show,” where he interviewed some of the world’s most powerful figures (and, more often than not, made fools of them in the process).

“As Ali G, I had the privilege of sitting with some of the smartest and most powerful people in the world, and all of them were punctual,” Baron Cohen told Josh Horowitz Wednesday night during a live taping of “Happy Sad Confused” at New York’s 92nd Street Y. After a lengthy pause, he turned his attention to the one exception: “Donald Trump kept us waiting for about 40 minutes.”

Baron Cohen recalled feeling “intimidated” upon entering Trump Tower with director James Bobin, where they waited in a room while Trump shouted a string of expletives “not for the likes of delicate Jewish ears” at Rudy Giuliani over the phone.

Popular on Variety

“Later on, I heard that he used to do that with other people,” Baron Cohen said. “It really was a power move.”

Trump appeared taken with Bobin, who Baron Cohen described as a “very handsome, blond, Oxford-educated” Englishman. But when he realized he’d be sitting down with Ali G instead, his demeanor “immediately” changed.

“I actually met a woman who was in the car with him after that interview, and he was apparently furious,” Baron Cohen said. “He actually went out publicly a couple of times to criticize me. And in the end, we used all those clips and used them to advertise another show that I did.”

Baron Cohen’s interview with Trump aired in 2003, back when the future president was best known as a New York real estate mogul, before going on to host NBC’s “The Apprentice.” Looking back at their encounter, Baron Cohen said he could understand how Trump won a second term in the White House, pointing to the president’s “elements of brilliance.”

“I mean, how has he survived a second term? People underestimated him,” Baron Cohen said. “We were too easy to dismiss him as a nincompoop. There are elements of brilliance to him, otherwise. And that explains his appeal with the fact that he’s there for a second term, the fact that he’s transforming this country. I won’t say positively or negatively.”

This was not the only time Baron Cohen reflected on Trump’s one-of-a-kind characteristics on his latest press tour. He told Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway on the Pivot podcast that the president is “amusing” and that there’s “a huge amount of comedy in the way he speaks.”

“He’s intentionally being funny,” Baron Cohen explained. “And if you have a look on the far right, they use comedy and sarcasm as an engaging way to dismiss criticisms.”

Baron Cohen suggests that Trump’s popularity, perhaps, reflects a broader theme explored through his own collection of provocative characters: “In the black and white, the world is a little bit complicated.”

title: Sandra Hüller Joins ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ in Cameo Role
summary: Oscar nominee Sandra Hüller will make a cameo in Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday.” News of Hüller’s top-secret role comes as directors Anthony and Joe Russo are in post-production on the project, ahead of its Dec. 18 release date. The superhero movie is already stuffed to the gills with award-winning actors and massive movie stars, including Chris […]
content:
Oscar nominee Sandra Hüller will make a cameo in Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday.”

News of Hüller’s top-secret role comes as directors Anthony and Joe Russo are in post-production on the project, ahead of its Dec. 18 release date. The superhero movie is already stuffed to the gills with award-winning actors and massive movie stars, including Chris Hemsworth, Pedro Pascal, Paul Rudd, Anthony Mackie, Florence Pugh, Vanessa Kirby, Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, Tom Hiddleston and Channing Tatum, plus more “Black Panther,” “Thunderbolts,” “Fantastic Four” and “X-Men” actors. The movie also features the much-anticipated returns of Chris Evans as Steve Rogers and Oscar winner Robert Downey Jr. as Victor von Doom, taking on the villainous role instead of Iron Man/Tony Stark.

Not much has been revealed about the plot for “Avengers: Doomsday,” except for the fact that Downey’s Doctor Doom represents the superheroes’ most dangerous foe yet. Rumors about Hüller’s involvement began swirling a couple of weeks ago, with some fans speculating she could be tied to Downey’s Doom (perhaps his mother) or that she might play another of the Latverian Witches (who don the colorful robes Marvel displayed at this year’s Comic-Con).

Popular on Variety

The Marvel cameo also marks Hüller’s fifth major feature in 2026, following “Project Hail Mary” (with newly announced Marvel superhero Ryan Gosling, who’ll play Ghost Rider), “Rose,” “Fatherland” and “Digger,” all of which are players in this year’s awards race. In 2024, the German star earned her first best actress Oscar nomination for “Anatomy of a Fall,” one of two best picture nominees in which she starred that year. (The other film was “The Zone of Interest,” which won two Oscars, including best international feature; “Anatomy of a Fall” won the Oscar for best original screenplay.)

The Hollywood Reporter first reported Hüller’s involvement. Marvel Studios does not comment on casting.

title: Awards Season Heats Up With ‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York,’ ‘Fatherland’ & More — Specialty Preview
summary: The weekend feels awards-y with John Turturro tugging the heartstrings in The Only Living Pickpocket In New York, Oliva Coleman (Wicker) and Helen Mirren (A Talent For Murder) in the house, and Hans Zischler and Sandra Hüller playing Thomas Mann and his daughter on a road trip (Fatherland). The A24 You Can See Everything phenomenon […]
content:
The weekend feels awards-y with John Turturro tugging the heartstrings in The Only Living Pickpocket In New York, Oliva Coleman (Wicker) and Helen Mirren (A Talent For Murder) in the house, and Hans Zischler and Sandra Hüller playing Thomas Mann and his daughter on a road trip (Fatherland). The A24 You Can See Everything phenomenon goes wide. Netflix expands TIFF audience award-winner La Bola Negra.

Sony Pictures Classics opens Turturro-starring Pickpocket by Noah Segan in limited release on six screens in NY (AMC Lincoln Square, Angelika Film Center, Bam Rose) and LA (AMC Burbank, AMC Grove, Laemmle Royal). He plays Harry Lehman, an aging pickpocket who plies his trade with ever-diminishing returns in a drastically changed New York. Turturro took the Zurich Film Festival’s Golden Eye Award for his performance in the film — Segan’s directorial debut — with Steve Buscemi as Harry’s regular fence, Tatiana Maslany as his estranged daughter and Will Price as the arrogant, heat-packing scion of a Manhattan crime family also starring. A favorite out of where Sundance where it premiered, the film is Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 97%, see Deadline’s review, which calls it mesmerizing.

Mubi is out with Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, also limited, at four theaters in New York (Film Forum, Film at Lincoln Center) and Los Angeles (AMC Burbank, Laemmle Royal). World premiered at Cannes to critical acclaim and the Best Director award for Pawlikowski. At 91% Certified Fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, see Deadline review. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann (Hans Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) embark on a challenging and emotional road trip across a Germany in ruins, from U.S. dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Mann, who had returned home after sixteen years in exile in the U.S., faced not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family. Pawlikowski picks up here where he left off with his award-winning Ida and Cold War, exploring themes of identity, family, love and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

Watch on Deadline

Mubi also debuts Making Marie Antionette, the late filmmaker Eleanor Coppola’s behind-the-scenes documentation of her daughter Sofia Coppola directing 2006 film Marie Antoinette. Premiered at Telluride, Deadline review here. Opens on 20 screens nationally including NY and LA.

Moderate/wide: Bleecker Street, in partnership with longtime collaborator LD Entertainment, releases Anton Corbijn thriller A Talent For Murder on 876 screens with Helen Mirren starring as celebrated crime novelist Patricia Highsmith. World premiered at TIFF, see Deadline review. Based on Joanna Murray-Smith’s acclaimed 2014 play Switzerland, the film follows a young literary agent from New York (Ehrenreich), who travels to Switzerland on a mission to convince the famously reclusive Highsmith to write one final installment in her iconic Ripley series. What begins as a seemingly straightforward assignment soon takes an unexpected turn.

Black Bear launches Wicker, the Sundance breakout from Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, at 1,471 theaters. A lusty comedic fable about sex, marriage and social convention centered around a lonely Fisherwoman, Olivia Colman, who commissions a wicker husband from the local Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy and threatens the village’s social order. The Tailor’s Wife/bullying local queen bee (Elizabeth Debicki ) sets out to sabotage the romance. Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 92% with critics. Audience score of 93%. Deadline review here.

Black Bear’s teaser poster/social campaign highlighted an unconventional leading man turned object of desire — aka:” What is MARRIAGE MATERIAL, and why is it a basket?” Off that, self-described “basketheads” spread Wicker fandom across the film’s social channels. It had a stunt screening at Beyond Fest, targeted events with Feeld, Letterboxd and Vanity Fair, and events at the 92nd Street Y and Vidiots culminating in the LA premiere at the DGA. Fans have been sharing sightings of six feet tall Wicker Husband standees in bookstores and theaters. On Oct. 25, it will play in Dolby Cinema at AMC locations nationwide for a daylong event. Black Bear will host a special one-night Wicker 4DX event Oct. 28.

TIFF-premiering documentary Nuns Vs The Vatican by Lorena Luciano debuts at LA’s Laemmle Monica Film Center, with a national rollout to follow. Mariska Hargitay, Trish Adlesic, Lauran Bromley, Regina K. Scully and Amanda Stephens are executive producers. In the shadows of the Catholic church, nuns and women have long endured abuse at the hands of priests — insidious and tactful grooming, silenced by confession, and hidden through systemic cover-ups. This investigative documentary uncovers the harrowing details and institutional indifference as nuns start to break decades of silence, exposing a system built to protect power. Self-distributed.

title: Everything We Know About Universal’s ‘Miami Vice ’85’ Movie So Far
summary: Universal has a new Miami Vice film in the works with a cast that grows more star-studded by the day. Preceded by Michael Mann’s 1980s TV series, the dynamic duo of James “Sonny” Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs will reunite once more. Titled Miami Vice ’85, the film will be shot for Imax. For everything we […]
content:
Universal has a new Miami Vice film in the works with a cast that grows more star-studded by the day.

Preceded by Michael Mann’s 1980s TV series, the dynamic duo of James “Sonny” Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs will reunite once more. Titled Miami Vice ’85, the film will be shot for Imax.

For everything we know about Miami Vice ’85, read on.

When will Miami Vice ’85 come out in theaters?

At first, the action film was set for August 6, 2027, but now it will bow May 19, 2028.

Watch on Deadline

Has Miami Vice ’85 started production?

Yes, production has begun, with shots of Michael B Jordan in character as Tubbs making the rounds on social media.

Who will play Tubbs and Crockett in the new Miami Vice movie?

Deadline first reported that Jordan was in talks to portray Ricardo Tubbs. Next came Austin Butler’s circling the role of detective James “Sonny” Crockett.

Late in the summer, the cast behind Jordan and Butler began to assemble, starting with Alden Ehrenreich (Weapons, A Talent for Murdre) joining the pair first. Then came Whitney Peak, who will portray Lenore Dove in the upcoming The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (2026) film.

Deadline broke the news of Camila Morrone’s and Danny Ramirez’s castings next. John Leguizamo will portray the villain in the flick.

Next came Andrew Schulz and Walton Goggins’ boarding the project, as first reported by Deadline. We also broke the news of André Holland’s joining the film in addition to Michael Irby’s casting as Lt. Lou Rodriguez.

And last, but certainly not least, we first reported Haley Lu Richardson’s casting.

Who else is behind the new Miami Vice movie?

Joseph Kosinski (Top Gun: Maverick, Tron: Legacy) will direct the reboot. Dan Gilroy rewrote a first draft script by Eric Warren Singer. Dylan Clark is producing along with Kosinski. The script is based on characters created by Yerkovich from the series executive produced by Yerkovich and Michael Mann. EVP Production Development Sara Scott and Creative Executive of Production Development Christina Hoffrogge are overseeing the project for Universal.

What will the new Miami Vice movie be about?

The film will draw on the NBC series pilot episode, titled “Brother’s Keeper” as well as the first season of the television series, which ran from 1984-1989 and centered Tubbs and Crockett, two undercover detectives investigating South Florida’s criminal underbelly.

Taika Waititi’s Klara and the Sun, based on the book by Kazuo Ishiguro, stars Jenna Ortega as the titular robotic Artificial Friend.

The film follows Klara as she wishes for a charge or owner to claim her from the Friend Store, where she gets a limited amount of time in the front alcove to show off and garner attention. Then she is chosen by Josie (Mia Tharia), whose mother Chrissy (Amy Adams) is reluctant to purchase an older model of the product when the newer ones are being sold at Fancy Friends down the street. But Klara and Josie’s bond is solid from the moment they meet eye contact. Though Josie is “lifted,” or genetically enhanced, she is also gravely ill, and Klara does her best to cheer her up as well as her mother. The film also features Natasha Lyonne, Aran Murphy, Steve Buscemi and Rachel House.

title: ‘Crazy Rich Asians’ Star Constance Wu Teases “Really Funny” HBO Series Filming In NYC
summary: After eight years, Constance Wu is reuniting with the Young family for the Crazy Rich Asians HBO sequel series. On Friday, the Golden Globe nominee teased the “really funny” script from the 2018 film’s co-writer Adele Lim, revealing the filming is taking place in New York City for the one-hour drama series, which got a […]
content:
After eight years, Constance Wu is reuniting with the Young family for the Crazy Rich Asians HBO sequel series.

On Friday, the Golden Globe nominee teased the “really funny” script from the 2018 film’s co-writer Adele Lim, revealing the filming is taking place in New York City for the one-hour drama series, which got a series order from HBO earlier this month.

“Well, I mean, the first movie is based on the book by Kevin Kwan,” she explained on Today. “And he actually has a whole bunch of books in the Crazy Rich Asians world, and so a lot of it follows that. I could tell you that we’re all excited to be coming back. It’s filming here in New York where I live, so I’m thrilled about that. And I think it’s really funny.

Wu confirmed that production starts next year on the eight-episode series, and she’s read a script. “It’s very funny. I think it’s really good,” she said.

Watch on Deadline

“We’re in great hands because Adele is showrunning and writing and she did the original [film], and she’s just so smart and good and talented that I feel just great with her at the helm,” added Wu

Earlier this month, we reported that HBO gave the series a green light after about two years of development from Lim, the movie’s director Jon M. Chu, Nina Jacobson and Brad Simpson.

Wu is set to reprise her role Rachel Chu in the series, alongside Henry Golding as Nick Young and Ronny Chieng as Eddie Chang, with Michelle Yeoh recurring as Eleanor Sung-Young.

title: Bill Maher’s Embarrassing Karoline Leavitt Interview on ‘Real Time’
summary: Bill Maher appears to be on good terms with Trumpworld. The 70-year-old HBO host joined Kid Rock and Stephen A. Smith as President Trump’s White House dinner guests earlier this month, and, following the dinner, Trump intimated to reporters that Maher’s criticisms of him on his late-night program are mostly bluster, and he “likes me […]
content:
Bill Maher appears to be on good terms with Trumpworld.

The 70-year-old HBO host joined Kid Rock and Stephen A. Smith as President Trump’s White House dinner guests earlier this month, and, following the dinner, Trump intimated to reporters that Maher’s criticisms of him on his late-night program are mostly bluster, and he “likes me a lot more than people understand.”

“Yeah, I did it again, bitches,” Maher said about his four-hour dinner with Trump during his opening monologue on “Real Time” Friday night, adding, “You know what? Fuck you. I like these dinners.”

Maher then managed to land Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary who left the post in August, as an interview guest on his show “Real Time.” It’s a curious pairing given that Maher had previously attacked Leavitt on his program following the then-press secretary’s defense of Trump shouting, “Quiet, piggy!” to Bloomberg News reporter Catherine Lucey when she questioned him about Jeffrey Epstein aboard Air Force One. Leavitt spun the incident by claiming, “It’s actually admirable. It’s the president being frank, open, and honest. It’s actually good,’” prompting Maher to jokingly remark to Leavitt, “Well, in that case: Shut up, bitch.”

Popular on Variety

And so, Maher welcomed Leavitt to “Real Time” Friday night where he mostly treated her with kid gloves and poked fun at her successor, Katie Zacharia, for only lasting five days on the job.

“The president sends his regards,” Leavitt told Maher. “I told him I was coming on the show and he said, ‘Tell him he loved that dinner and he knows it.’”

“I do like it,” Maher admitted, before turning the talk back to Leavitt. “You were the youngest one to do this job… So what are you going to do now?”

Leavitt said she left the job to take care of her two young children, who are 2 and six months, and then said she’ll be starting as a Fox News pundit on Nov. 1. No follow-up from Maher about the Trump-Fox News pipeline, but instead a silly rejoinder about how Trump wants to turn the White House press pool into an actual swimming pool.

Cue Maher: “You know what? This is the one thing that people get mad at me [about]… I don’t give a shit about any of this. I like the ballroom! America does need a ballroom. It’s the United States of America.”

The softball questions and flattery didn’t stop there, as Maher asked Leavitt about her penchant for being “sarcastic” and didn’t ask any follow-up questions when she touted Trump’s war with Iran.

Maher delivered a litany of compliments about Trump, saying he “gets it” and, when Leavitt claimed Trump was “far more sane than the last [president]” who was “a mental patient,” Maher replied, “He’s far more energetic.”

It’s another reminder that Maher isn’t a journalist and refuses to challenge the conservative guests on his show. He’s just happy for them to be there.

title: Kartik Aaryan’s ‘Captain India’ Set Amid Houthi Conflict in Yemen (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Kartik Aaryan’s upcoming action drama “Captain India” is set amid the Houthi conflict in Yemen, Variety understands. The film marks Aaryan’s first turn as a pilot. Shimit Amin directs the project, which is based on a real humanitarian evacuation. Aaryan’s character leads the rescue effort. That conflict is central to the story and adds a […]
content:
Kartik Aaryan’s upcoming action drama “Captain India” is set amid the Houthi conflict in Yemen, Variety understands.

The film marks Aaryan’s first turn as a pilot. Shimit Amin directs the project, which is based on a real humanitarian evacuation. Aaryan’s character leads the rescue effort.

That conflict is central to the story and adds a geopolitical dimension to the drama. How exactly the fighting figures in the plot has not been disclosed. The film is expected to follow the obstacles of carrying out a humanitarian mission as tensions rise.

The Saudi-Houthi confrontation that continues today dates to 2015, when Houthi forces took the Yemeni capital of Sanaa and Saudi Arabia began a military campaign. Variety understands that “Captain India” draws on what was among the hardest rescue operations India has carried out, in Yemen that same year, when the country evacuated its own citizens along with people from around the world.

Popular on Variety

T-Series and Baweja Studios produce “Captain India” in association with Dopamine Studios, Aaryan’s banner. Bhushan Kumar of T-Series is among the producers, and S B Films handles production. Nash Vazifdar, Sanchit Gupta and Priyadarshee Shrivastava wrote the screenplay.

Aaryan most recently starred in “Tu Meri Main Tera Main Tera Tu Meri” and “Bhool Bhulaiyaa 3,” and has “Naagzilla” and other projects currently in the pipeline. Amin, meanwhile, is best known for directing “Chak De! India” and “Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year” (2009), both for Yash Raj Films, and has largely stayed away from feature directing in the years since. He directed an episode of BBC/Netflix’s “A Suitable Boy” (2020).

The film is currently shooting in the U.K. “Captain India” will open in theaters on Aug. 13, 2027, over the Independence Day weekend in India.

title: Ken Atchity, ‘The Meg’ Producer and Literary Agent, Dies at 82
summary: Kenneth Atchity, “The Meg” producer and literary agent, died on Monday. He was 82. Across his career as a literary manager, producer and writer, Atchity produced more than 30 films; wrote over 20 books; negotiated publishing and entertainment deals; and published hundreds of additional titles through his own imprint, Story Merchant Books. In addition to […]
content:
Kenneth Atchity, “The Meg” producer and literary agent, died on Monday. He was 82.

Across his career as a literary manager, producer and writer, Atchity produced more than 30 films; wrote over 20 books; negotiated publishing and entertainment deals; and published hundreds of additional titles through his own imprint, Story Merchant Books. In addition to producing “The Meg” films with his business and producing partner Chi-Li Wong, he had credits on “Gambino,” “The Kennedy Detail,” “The Lost Valentine,” “The Amityville Horror: The Evil Escapes,” “Joe Somebody” and “Life Or Something Like It.”

Prior to working in Hollywood, Atchity served as an assistant professor of English and comparative literature at Occidental College before earning tenure and becoming a full-time professor. During his 17 years at the college, he became a Fulbright professor of American literature at the University of Bologna; founded and edited two magazines; and was awarded Occidental’s faculty achievement award and the UCLA Writers Program’s distinguished instructor award.

Popular on Variety

Atchity also worked as a communication engineer at AT&T Long Lines, where he designed and implemented the Green Network, which connects NASA’s 26 research centers. He decided to change careers to produce “Shades of Love,” a set of 16 films which were broadcast on HBO and Cinemax and were internationally distributed by Warner Bros..

Born in Eunice, La., in 1944, Atchity was raised in Kansas City, Mo., and attended Georgetown University before entering Yale as a Woodrow Wilson Fellow, where he earned a masters in philosophy and a PhD. While there, his doctoral dissertation won the John Addison Porter prize, the university’s highest academic award, and was published with an introduction by novelist John Gardner.

Atchity is survived by his wife, Kayoko Mitsumatsu; his son, Vincent Atchity; his daughter, Rosemary Atchity; his five grandchildren, Margaret D. McKenna, Edward J. McKenna, Oliver D. Atchity, Eliot J. Atchity and Louis M. Atchity; and his sisters, Mary Calhoun and Laurie Dressman..

Donations may be made to Yoga Gives Back, an organization empowering women and children in India which Atchity served on the board for.

title: Karoline Leavitt Compares Katie Zacharia’s Abrupt Exit As Trump’s Press Secretary To ‘The Apprentice’: “He’s Known For … Moving On From People”
summary: Karoline Leavitt appeared on HBO’s Real Time with Bill Maher on Friday and was questioned about the short stint of her successor as Donald Trump’s White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia. After doing just one briefing that lasted 14 minutes, Zacharia was ousted last Friday, after less than a week in the job. Leavitt told […]
content:
Karoline Leavitt appeared on HBO’s Real Time with Bill Maher on Friday and was questioned about the short stint of her successor as Donald Trump‘s White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia.

After doing just one briefing that lasted 14 minutes, Zacharia was ousted last Friday, after less than a week in the job.

Leavitt told Maher that “it’s a tough job” and one of the “hardest” in Washington.

“That pressure in that room is enormous,” Leavitt said. “The press are vicious, and you know I give her credit for standing up there. And as the president said, it wasn’t a good fit, and that’s okay. I wish her well, and we’re on to the next. And he has a lot of options.”

Maher, though, said that that “sometimes you give up a home run at the first inning. They don’t usually go to the bullpen that quick.”

Watch on Deadline

Leavitt responded, “Look, I mean, the president did have a hit show called The Apprentice, where he’s known for, you know, moving on from people. So hey, it’s in his nature to do that type of thing, I guess.”

Earlier, Maher quipped that Zacharia’s tenure was shorter than the dinner he had with Trump last week that lasted for four hours. At that sitdown at the White House, Maher was joined by Stephen A. Smith and Kid Rock. The HBO host credited Trump with listening to him as he challenged him on certain issues, like ICE, degrading Ukraine’s Starlink access, as well as telling the president that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “is dragging you down.”

“There are so many moments where he gets it,” Maher said. “Like I said to him, ‘You know, when you said the Supreme Court, they’re voting against me? You know that’s not how the Supreme Court is supposed to work, right? They’re not voting for or against you. You appoint them and they make decisions.’ And he went, ‘Yeah, I took that one too personally.'”

Maher added, “He gets it and then he doesn’t get it. Now I’m an optimist. I prefer to think of the president as half sane.”

In response, Leavitt tried for a bit of whataboutism, telling Maher that Trump is “very sane. He’s a lot more, I think we can agree, he is far more sane than the last one. We had a mental patient.”

“He’s far more energetic,” Maher said.

But Maher returned to what happened during the dinner with Trump. “We have a nice conversation and he goes, ‘You’re my enemy. Pass the peas.’ I mean, he will say that, ‘You’re my enemy,’ and then a minute later, we’re just talking normally, and we don’t act like enemies.”

Maher also told Leavitt that he was worried over what Trump will do if the midterms go bad for Trump and Republicans. “We know he likes vengeance,” he said. Leavitt, though, said that she doesn’t “worry about the president. Look, he loves our country very much, and he wants to make it right.” She even suggested that he would work with Democrats, noting that he has worked with D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser.

During her tenure, Leavitt was known for her steadfast defense of the president, even if that meant delivering regular lectures to the media on their coverage of the administration. Even though she was highly praised for her performance, it didn’t stop the fall in Trump’s approval rating, which has dropped to an average of 38.8% from 50.5% at the start of his term, per Real Clear Politics.

Maher pressed Leavitt on Trump’s recent moves to waive sanctions on Russia, calling it “unconscionable,” along with “basically putting a knife in the back of [Ukraine’s president] Zelensky.”

Maher asked, “Is there anything that could make you, because a lot of Republicans now say we’ve had enough, make you not be loyal to whatever he was doing?”

Leavitt, who is soon to become a commentator for Fox News, gave no indication that there was anything. “He was my boss, but to me, he’s also a friend, and he gave me the opportunity of a lifetime.”

title: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins Explains Aaron Paul’s Cameo: “A Real Brief Easter Egg”
summary: In DC Studios’ Clayface, Tom Rhys Harries’ titular shape-shifting Batman villain takes multiple forms, including a surprising familiar face. Following murmurs of a cameo, director James Watkins confirmed that Aaron Paul makes a brief appearance in the DCU movie as Matt’s (Harries) father, who raised him in the slums of Gotham City. “He has a […]
content:
In DC Studios‘ Clayface, Tom Rhys Harries’ titular shape-shifting Batman villain takes multiple forms, including a surprising familiar face.

Following murmurs of a cameo, director James Watkins confirmed that Aaron Paul makes a brief appearance in the DCU movie as Matt’s (Harries) father, who raised him in the slums of Gotham City.

“He has a real brief Easter egg kind of moment,” Watkins told Entertainment Weekly.

While flashbacks of Paul as Matt’s father were ultimately cut from the film, the Breaking Bad alum makes a quick appearance in the action-packed Club Vesuvius scene, in which Matt shape-shifts into multiple people to take on Szabo’s (David Dencik) goons before taking has dad’s form to kill Jimmy “One Nut” (Enzo Squillino Jr.), the gangster who took his father’s life years before.

Watch on Deadline

“In terms of trying to figure out the character, it was, How much is Matt defined by his past and how much is he an everyman?” the director explained. “At one point, we were looking at it and thinking, Is it the ‘sins of the father’?”

Watkins continued, “But actually, as we worked on the script, I thought that notion of revenge was more universal and more relatable to all of us. It doesn’t matter whether you’re carrying a trauma or any of that. If we’re slighted, we carry this sense of being wronged and we all want to do something, but generally in life we can’t do anything about it and we’re powerless.”

Now playing in theaters, Clayface stars Harries as rising actor Matt Hagen, who suffers gruesome wounds after the brutal mafioso Szabo (Dencik) cuts up his face, resulting in the downfall of his career. But when he discovers the groundbreaking nanotech research of Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), Matt convinces her to restore his face to its former glory, only to result in terrifying side effects and a bloody quest for revenge.

title: Billy Corgan Backs Marilyn Manson Over Sex Abuse Claims, Citing Inside Knowledge Of Case: “I Personally Didn’t Feel He Was Guilty”
summary: “I personally didn’t feel he was guilty of the things he was being charged with,” Billy Corgan says of his old friend Marilyn Manson, who was accused of sexual abuse, domestic violence and more by Evan Rachel Wood and other women. “Ultimately the fact (is) that the D.A. didn’t pursue,” the Smashing Pumpkins leader added. […]
content:
“I personally didn’t feel he was guilty of the things he was being charged with,” Billy Corgan says of his old friend Marilyn Manson, who was accused of sexual abuse, domestic violence and more by Evan Rachel Wood and other women. “Ultimately the fact (is) that the D.A. didn’t pursue,” the Smashing Pumpkins leader added.

“So, basically, the person that I knew, and the way it all kind of went down, even though it was an elongated process, was commensurate with the person that I knew,” Corgan went on to say on a just released episode of the New York Times podcast Popcast. “I don’t want the world to tell me who my friends are and who I should associate with.”

It is a fact that back in January 2025, newly sworn in L.A. District Attorney Nathan Hochman closed the four-year long probe his office and the Sheriff’s department had been conducting into Manson. “We have determined that allegations of domestic violence fall outside of the statute of limitations, and we cannot prove charges of sexual assault beyond a reasonable doubt,” Hochman said of the much accused shock rocker born Brian Warner.

Watch on Deadline

At the time, current The Shards star Wood, who had been engaged to Manson during their tumultuous 2007 – 2010 relationship, stated that she and her lawyer were told by “Deputy District Attorneys and the Sheriff deputies who investigated the case that there was compelling evidence to support our claims, but that the statute of limitations prevents many of those crimes from being prosecuted.” Writing online, Wood, who had testified before California’s state Senate on sexual and domestic violence and was a booster of the non-retroactive statute of limitations extending 2024 Phoenix Act, tersely noted “violent crimes should not have an expiration date.”

In his Popcast appearance, Corgan didn’t address the specifics of why the D.A. dropped the case and never mentioned Wood, Game of Thrones actress Esmé Bianco ( who settled her sexual assault and battery claims with the ‘Beautiful People’ singer in 2023), or other Manson accusers by name. He did however pull back the Gen X rockstar curtain a bit in offering his POV.

“The other thing that people should know, and it may gets lost in the gloss here, is Manson’s wife, Lindsay, is a twin, and her twin is Ashley, and Ashley is married to James Iha of the Pumpkins,” the Grammy winning guitarist explained to Popcast hosts Jon Caramanica and Joe Coscarelli. “So, Manson’s basically a part of our family. Anybody in that situation struggles with the accusations, the seriousness of the accusations.”

“I also knew the inside baseball of the case. I knew certain people who were involved, and so you make those evaluations.”

Despite the Popcast sit-down proving wide-ranging on a number of professional and personal subjects, Corgan, who had Manson as a guest at his birthday party earlier this year, did not elaborate on the aforementioned “inside baseball” nor who the other individuals involved were besides obviously Manson himself. Shifting his perspective somewhat, Corgan went on to say of Manson and the very high profile situation: “If he’s guilty or anybody in that situation is guilty, they should go to jail. I’m not saying I have any moral supremacy here. I’m saying it’s a case by case basis. This kind of witch mob thing bothers me.”

In the aftermath of allegations from Wood and then others, Manson was dumped by CAA as a client and lost acting roles in American Gods and Creepshow. From 2020 to 2025 and beyond, Manson has decried the claims from various women as “horrible distortions of reality. Even though he was ordered in late 2024 to pay Wood nearly $327,000 in legal fees from suing her for defamation in 2022, the now 57-year old Manson has insisted that his past relationships were “entirely consensual with like-minded partners.”

As he has for many years, accusations and otherwise, Manson is out playing gigs to a loyal fanbase. He will be playing L.A.’s Wiltern on Halloween and on November 1, with a show at London’s Wembley Stadium set for May next year. This weekend finds Manson on-stage at Fort Worth’s Texas Motor Speedway on October 24.

“Something’s coming …” the league’s post teased with a clip of the Avengers logo appearing in the green-tinted sky above Milwaukee’s American Family Field.

Worlds collide ⚾
