title: Jay-Z Brings Out Blue Ivy Carter, DJ Khaled and John Legend During the First of Two Nights at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium
summary: “Can I take you to my home for a second?” asked Jay-Z as he led into “Empire State of Mind” during the first of two headlining shows at Inglewood, California’s SoFi Stadium. Thus, he did, as he’d been doing for the past hour-and-a-half, bringing Brooklyn to Los Angeles as he traced the corners of his […]
content:
“Can I take you to my home for a second?” asked Jay-Z as he led into “Empire State of Mind” during the first of two headlining shows at Inglewood, California’s SoFi Stadium. Thus, he did, as he’d been doing for the past hour-and-a-half, bringing Brooklyn to Los Angeles as he traced the corners of his vast discography, the backbone of a career that stretches 30 years with countless hits to match.

Jay touched down on the West Coast for an invigorated set Friday night as part of his yearlong “Jay-Z 30” celebration, which began with a one-off headlining show at Philadelphia’s Roots Picnic in late May. What followed were three back-to-back sold-out nights at Yankee Stadium, plus shows in London and Paris, and a robust eight-episode HBO docuseries breaking down the finer points of his catalog. Given all the chatter that Jay may have booked himself for Super Bowl 2027 as the Halftime Show performer — which would make sense, considering a year of unusually high activity nearly a decade after he released his last album — it was hard not to consider Friday’s concert as a test run for what could potentially be the biggest performance on the biggest stage this coming February. (After all, the Super Bowl is taking place in the same venue where he performed.)

As he’s consistently shown, Jay was in mint condition as he ran through hit after hit after hit at SoFi across a two-hour set, toggling the setlist of previous shows while keeping the focus centered on the electricity between himself, the audience and his band. Fans have, of course, come to expect high-wattage surprise stars: At his Yankee Stadium shows, he coronated the 25th and 30th anniversaries of “The Blueprint” and “Reasonable Doubt,” respectively, with cameos from his wife Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and his daughter Blue Ivy Carter, to name just a few.

Popular on Variety

Blue Ivy Carter plays the keys with her dad Jay-Z at the first of two shows at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium pic.twitter.com/7h5kZzNA1p — Variety (@Variety) October 24, 2026

His SoFi show, meanwhile, felt pared-down with purpose. There were few guest stars throughout the night, with Blue Ivy playing the keys on “The Story of OJ” and “Dead Presidents,” a shift from when she tickled the ivories on “Feelin’ It” at Yankee Stadium. Scarface came out for “This Can’t Be Life” as well as his own classic “Mind Playing Tricks on Me.” John Legend and DJ Khaled emerged for the night’s closer, “God Did,” a song that originally also featured Fridayy, Lil Wayne and Rick Ross.

(As an aside, having witnessed the very rare performance of “This Can’t Be Life,” I can’t help but note that Scarface’s verse is one of the most moving I’ve ever heard on a rap song. Listen if you haven’t, immediately.)

Amid the talking points surrounding Jay’s potential Halftime Show has been the question of whether or not he can carry a performance of that magnitude without bringing out guests. And by the sheer propulsion of the evening, plus the hits lining it, Jay once again reinforced that he’s the star of his own show, no matter which direction it points. At 56, he is a seasoned veteran, one of the few hip-hop acts who can book stadium shows across the world after such long periods of dormancy. Consider him an elder statesman, if you will, but the bravado and showmanship that he continues to exhibit feel like more than a decent justification for his continued relevance, despite what any detractor on the Internet might deign to claim.

Jay-Z brings out Scarface for “This Can’t Be Life” in Los Angeles pic.twitter.com/bp2BwcLKI1 — Variety (@Variety) October 24, 2026

Jay comes from a time when success was predicated mainly on skill, with business acumen running hand in hand alongside it. It’s why he managed to build an empire around his own talents, and why fans continue to show up by the thousands to behold them. The SoFi show was no exception, a dexterous display of lyrical acuity and magnetism that jolted to life with opener “Hovi Baby” and gave way to tracks like “Izzo (H.O.V.A.)” and “Run This Town.” Many of the visuals were the same as his Yankee Stadium shows, right down to the opening shot of Beyoncé shaving his head, yet they still felt elevated and unique to his performance, building out the world of tracks like “Song Cry” and “Lucifer.”

It’s likely that Jay will pull out all the stops for the final night of his “Jay-Z 30” tour on Saturday night. (Fans clocked Beyoncé, Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams having a Destiny’s Child reunion in one of the SoFi suites on Friday.) But if his first performance was any indication, Jay is up to the task, no matter how big the platform.

title: Kore-eda Hirokazu Explains Why He Never Films Children Crying – and What Ken Loach and Hou Hsiao-hsien Taught Him
summary: Japanese auteur Kore-eda Hirokazu, whose films are known for their natural performances from child actors, said there is one thing he has decided never to put on screen: a child crying. “It’s not that I can’t, or that it’s difficult. I don’t shoot it,” the Japanese director said at an In Conversation event at the […]
content:
Japanese auteur Kore-eda Hirokazu, whose films are known for their natural performances from child actors, said there is one thing he has decided never to put on screen: a child crying.

“It’s not that I can’t, or that it’s difficult. I don’t shoot it,” the Japanese director said at an In Conversation event at the the Singapore International Film Festival on Saturday. “The ideal is that after viewers finish watching, they remember that child’s smile and cry.”

The festival presented Kore-eda with its Cinema Honorary Award at the National Museum of Singapore before an onstage conversation with festival chair Boo Junfeng, the filmmaker behind “Apprentice.” Introduced in 2014, the award is the festival’s top honor and recognizes lasting contributions to Asian cinema. Previous recipients include Im Kwon-taek, Garin Nugroho, Jafar Panahi and Deepa Mehta.

Popular on Variety

Kore-eda said his methods with children have grown more flexible. Through “Shoplifters” and the films he made abroad, “The Truth” and “Broker,” he did not hand children scripts. Instead, he rewrote dialogue around the personality and vocabulary of the children he met at auditions, so that they only spoke lines they could say with conviction, and then fed them lines on set or described a situation and let them talk freely.

On “Monster,” he gave the young cast scripts, judging that the subject was risky enough that separating the children from their roles was safer. He now decides child by child and film by film, he said.

Two directors shaped that approach. Hou Hsiao-hsien, Kore-eda said, joins in when children are playing in a scene, slips out once the camera is rolling and lets them keep going – a trick Kore-eda now uses himself.

From Ken Loach, he took a lesson about judgment. In Loach’s “Kes,” a boy discovers the bird he has raised dumped in a trash can after his brother kills it, and the young actor’s reaction looks nothing like a performance. When Kore-eda met Loach about 20 years ago, while he was making “Nobody Knows” and wrestling with similar questions, Loach told him he had only instructed the boy to go and look for the missing bird. Asked how he had weighed the ethics of that, Loach said he understood the risk but was confident that his relationship with the boy could repair any hurt. Kore-eda said the lesson was that Loach was weighing each shot as he went.

“I keep it firmly in mind that judging things that way – it worked on the last shoot so it will work this time, or a method that worked with the last child will work with this one – is the most dangerous thing in directing children,” he said.

He never gets angry with children or rushes them, he said, and he doesn’t lie to them. “The ideal is that a child ends the day saying, ‘Today’s shoot was fun, I’m looking forward to tomorrow,’” he said.

Some children simply won’t listen, he added, in which case he turns that into the role. During auditions for “Like Father, Like Son,” one boy answered every question, including his name and where he was from, with “Why?” Staff thought communication was impossible, but Kore-eda was drawn to him and wrote a character who answers everything with “Why?”

Kore-eda called himself a fan of Hou rather than someone he was influenced by, but the Taiwanese director also changed how he approaches a scene. Hou read the script for Kore-eda’s 1995 debut “Maborosi,” which won the Golden Osella in Venice, and introduced him to a composer, so Kore-eda showed him the finished film. Hou critiqued it severely, he said. “I was deflated. But what he told me was absolutely right.”

Kore-eda said he had drawn up a meticulous blueprint and that his crew did professional work to realize it, but he failed to update the plan on set. Hou asked whether he had storyboarded every scene and shot it exactly as drawn. He had.

“Where you shoot a scene from – you go into the location, feel the space, see the light falling there, and that’s when you first decide how the actors move,” Kore-eda recalled Hou telling him. “Once the actors’ movements are decided, only then do you decide the camera position. You have to do it in that order. You know that, you made documentaries.”

“Now I’m truly grateful he said that to me, but at the time it really got to me,” Kore-eda said. “I swore I’d never draw storyboards again.”

Kore-eda said he sees his two 2026 films, “Sheep in the Box” and “Look Back,” as a return to his roots. “Sheep in the Box,” which competed in Cannes, follows a couple whose 7-year-old son died two years earlier and who take in a humanoid robot built from his data. Despite the AI element, Kore-eda said, the film is about grief work.

“It’s a story about how to properly say goodbye to the dead, so I feel it actually ended up closest to what I tried to do in my debut,” he said.

“Look Back,” his live-action adaptation of Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga about two girls bound by a love of drawing manga, played in competition at Venice and opens in Singapore on Oct. 29 after playing at the festival. On it, he said, he went back to the documentary thinking of his early films, treating the camera as an eye and simply asking where to watch the subject from.

“So I think the second half of my career probably starts next year,” he said.

Kore-eda said he writes best on long flights and in spare hours at hotels abroad, and has been writing on his current trip from London to Thailand and Singapore. He hopes to be shooting one project around this time next year at the earliest, or the year after if that proves difficult.

Thirty years after he started making films, the growing number of career awards leaves him uneasy, he said. “I feel like I still have about half my career left, and yet it kind of feels like I’m being told it’s time to graduate,” he said.

Kore-eda said he has little interest in AI, even though “Sheep in the Box” features a child brought back through generative AI. At a producer’s suggestion, he let an AI read his script for the first time. “At first it told me, ‘This is wonderful, it’s a sure thing for the Cannes Film Festival,’” he said. He ended the exercise after concluding the AI had probably never had a film experience big enough to change its life.

Kore-eda said he never tries to work out what audiences want, citing advice from a senior colleague he admired in his television days, when ratings were treated as everything. “He told me, ‘If you think of them as viewers, it won’t reach anyone,’” Kore-eda said. “He said to picture one person’s face and make it for them.”

Asked what dish he would choose for the afterlife, a nod to his 1998 film “After Life,” Kore-eda said he probably wouldn’t eat anything once he was dead. His last meal before dying, though, is already decided: the tenzaru soba at Sunaba, a noodle restaurant in Tokyo’s Akasaka district, where a senior producer took him when he was a young assistant director who had gone days without going home.

“The soba I ate there was the best I’ve had in my life, and it still is,” he said. “I want to eat that one more time at the end.”

title: Impulso Morelia: Tatiana Huezo’s ‘Galerna’ Takes Top José María Riba Award, With ‘Homeboys’ Another Key Winner
summary: “Galerna,” a fiction feature from Mexico’s Tatiana Huezo, has snagged the top prize at Impulso Morelia, the pix-in-post industry section of the 10-day Morelia Film Festival, which wraps Oct. 25. The José Maria Riba Award, presented by Cinépolis Distribution and Profest 2026, bestows $14,740. (250,000 pesos) toward outstanding post-production needs and/or promotional activities. Only her […]
content:
“Galerna,” a fiction feature from Mexico’s Tatiana Huezo, has snagged the top prize at Impulso Morelia, the pix-in-post industry section of the 10-day Morelia Film Festival, which wraps Oct. 25. The José Maria Riba Award, presented by Cinépolis Distribution and Profest 2026, bestows $14,740. (250,000 pesos) toward outstanding post-production needs and/or promotional activities.

Only her second fiction outing, following “Prayers for the Stolen,” Huezo first received critical acclaim for her documentaries, led by “Tempestad” and “The Tiniest Place,” both produced by Pimienta Films (“Roma”). “Galerna” recently won the coveted Egeda Platino Industria Award at the San Sebastian Festival where it participated in the festival’s WIP Latin America competition showcase.

Popular on Variety

The road movie follows two casting directors into the remote reaches of Mexico, where their search for natural actors for a sci-fi film becomes an unsettling journey into their own fears, biases and preconceptions.

Following close behind with a Special Mention from the panel and a post-production award in kind from Caffeine was “Homeboys,” a documentary by Alonso Garibay and Alejandro Bernal which centers on Roberto Hernández, “Mr. Lucky,” who was deported to a country he barely knew and who later founded a shelter for those with similar experiences. “Homeboys” also took home the Eugenio Polgovsky award of $5,340.83 (100,000 pesos), created in memory of the beloved filmmaker.

“Tatiana’s ‘Galerna’ represents a new exciting direction for one of the best filmmakers working today, and I’m certain it will be a watershed moment in Mexico cinema when it is finally released to the public. I couldn’t be more thrilled than it is being recognized with the top prize. This year’s selection was fantastic, and I’m sure we’ll see these films succeed with audiences and critics,” said Piano’s Julio Chavezmontes, one of the jurors in the international panel.

“On a personal note, it was deeply moving to see the inaugural Eugenio Polgovsky award go to “Homeboys”. This is a film that shares Eugenio’s fearless humanism, and I have no doubt he would have championed it, if he was still with us today,” said Chavezmontes.

For fellow juror Mauricio Durán Ortega, president of National Film Industry Chamber, Canacine, “Impulso’s selection was outstanding, as always.”

“All the projects deserved support and having a film reach that stage is already a major achievement. The award makes a real difference in helping filmmakers complete their work. Since most projects are already in post-production, our recommendations focus on what can still be refined. This year, the decision was unanimous – ‘Galerna’ stood out so clearly that no further debate was needed.”

Post-production house Caffeine, selected “Galerna,” “All the Water in the World” and “Homeboys” to receive in-kind services valued at over $20,000 (387,000 pesos) in total.

For Caffeine CEO Adrian Geyer, all three “show the range of Mexican cinema right now.”

“Tatiana Huezo’s road movie takes us down paths that feel supernatural without ever becoming so, with images that tell so much they let us travel alongside the characters; Diego del Río and Diana Bracho’s ‘All the Water in the World’ dares to explore aging and family from a place Mexican cinema rarely goes, with an honesty that unsettles us because it confronts us, as viewers, with ourselves; and Alonso Garibay and Alejandro Bernal’s ‘Homeboys’ gives a voice, in their debut documentary, to people both countries have tried to forget.”

Fernanda Garduño of Estudios Splendor Omnia chose documentaries “Raká,” and “Katechon” as winners of its in-kind services at the studios’ facilities in Tepoztlán, Morelos, which are valid for two years.

“I chose Teresa Camou’s “Raká” for its sensitive direction, intimate storytelling and striking images. By letting its subjects speak for themselves without imposing judgments, the film offers a poetic view of alternative ways of life. Support for sound design will help bring its full potential to life.”

For Garduño, Javier Toscano’s “Katechon” stands out for its “compelling portrayal of hope as a disciplined way of life rather than a cliché. Despite some familiar documentary tropes, its exceptional archival footage and creative storytelling make it visually distinctive and deserving of the award to support its color grading and finalization.”

The 12th Impulso Morelia unspooled Oct. 18-20 during the festival. Below are the prizewinners.

INTERNATIONAL PANEL

Jurors: Cara Cusumano, Carlos Rodríguez Ríos, Julio Chavezmontes, Mauricio Durán and Sandrine Dumas

José Marià Riba Award

“Galerna,” Tatiana Huezo (Pimienta Films, Elastica Films)

Special Mention

“Homeboys,” Alonso Garibay and Alejandro Bernal (Norteña del Sur, Documotora)

AMBULANTE–EUGENIO POLGOVSKY AWARD

“Homeboys,” Alonso Garibay and Alejandro Bernal (Norteña del Sur, Documotora)

CHURUBUSCO AWARD, image and post services in kind split evenly between two projects

“Legit, Elisa Miller (Pimienta Films, UMI Films).

“All the Water in the World (“Toda el agua del mundo,”Diego del Río)

SPLENDOR OMNIA STUDIOS AWARD

“Raká,”Teresa Camou (Fontana Films, Oriente Cine)

CAFFEINE POST-PRODUCTION AWARDS

title: Vino G. Bastian, Pevita Pearce, Faradina Mufti, Indra Jegel Lead ‘Miracle in Cell No. 7’ Director Lee Hwan-kyung’s Indonesian Father-Son Drama ‘Gasigogi’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Korean filmmaker Lee Hwan-kyung, director of “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” has assembled an Indonesian ensemble led by Vino G. Bastian, Pevita Pearce, Faradina Mufti and Indra Jegel for “Gasigogi,” a father-son drama now in production with Falcon Pictures. The film follows Jiwa, a father who sacrifices everything in a fight to save Juna, his […]
content:
Korean filmmaker Lee Hwan-kyung, director of “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” has assembled an Indonesian ensemble led by Vino G. Bastian, Pevita Pearce, Faradina Mufti and Indra Jegel for “Gasigogi,” a father-son drama now in production with Falcon Pictures.

The film follows Jiwa, a father who sacrifices everything in a fight to save Juna, his son, who has blood cancer. Bastian plays the lead, with Pearce as co-lead and Mufti as Chitra. Falcon Pictures unveiled the cast together with Hwantasy Entertainment.

Bastian starred in the Indonesian remake of “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” while Pearce is known for “5 cm” and Mufti for “Impetigore.” The supporting cast includes Altaaf Akavi (“Tunggu Aku Sukses Nanti”), Indro Warkop (“Miracle in Cell No. 7”), Dea Panendra (“Marlina the Murderer in Four Acts”), Sadana Agung (“Agak Laen”), Irma Novita Rihi (“Women From Rote Island”), Luisa Adreena (“Na Willa”), Pritt Timothy (“Ayah, Aku Mau Cerita”), Verdi Solaiman (“The Raid”) and Kiki Narendra (“Ghost in the Cell”).

Popular on Variety

The working title takes its inspiration from the stickleback fish. The male of the species remains alone with the eggs and fights off predators until his body gives out, at which point his flesh becomes the hatchlings’ first food. Lee uses the image as a metaphor for fatherhood and the sacrifices parents make for their children.

The project marks Lee’s return to directing following the success of the Indonesian version of his earlier phenomenon, and he has called it the most emotionally taxing film he has taken on. He made “Miracle in Cell No. 7” as a gift for his daughter. “Gasigogi” is dedicated to his son.

By shooting in Indonesia, Lee wants to draw on the country’s strong attachment to family, faith and community. He said the film is an original work rather than a transplant of Korean feeling, one that “breathes with Indonesian lungs.”

“Just as a father gives everything to his child, I want to pour everything I have into creating a precious gift for this family,” Lee said. “The name of that gift is ‘Gasigogi.’ The goal is simple: I want to create a film so honest and resonant that when the credits roll, the first thing the audience wants to do is call their father.”

“To be trusted with a story of this magnitude is both an incredible honor and a tremendous emotional challenge,” Bastian added. “Director Lee has crafted a raw, devastating, and beautiful narrative about what a father will endure for his child.”

Mufti said she was grateful to Falcon and Lee for entrusting her with Chitra. “As a mother myself, this story feels very close to my heart,” she said. “It reminds me that love isn’t always expressed through words, but often through the things we do and the sacrifices we make for our children.”

Falcon producer Frederica added, “The unparalleled dedication of our brilliant cast and crew, combined with Director Lee’s masterful storytelling, makes ‘Gasigogi’ a truly special project. We believe this film will leave a lasting, emotional legacy for Indonesian cinema and audiences everywhere.”

title: Inside The BBC Cuts: Painful Service Closures Begin, But Worse Could Be To Come
summary: “The world needs the BBC more than ever. It might be a different size and shape. It’s not going to be a so-so Netflix or a me-too YouTube. It’s going to be a better BBC.” That was the message Matt Brittin left ringing in the ears of BBC staff when concluding a town hall last […]
content:
“The world needs the BBC more than ever. It might be a different size and shape. It’s not going to be a so-so Netflix or a me-too YouTube. It’s going to be a better BBC.”

That was the message Matt Brittin left ringing in the ears of BBC staff when concluding a town hall last month. The director general was attempting to lift the gloom after being beset with questions from anxious employees about job losses, service reductions, and general retrenchment.

He has an uneviable task. Brittin is grappling with a financial crisis that is precipitating some of the most painful cuts in the BBC’s history. He is also attempting to cement the BBC’s position as Britain’s premium media brand in an era of unprecedented competition.

These two objectives are not obviously compatible, but Brittin’s pitch to staff is that they are not incompatible. It’s why, when he announced the closure of linear networks BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra on Tuesday, he said the decisions were necessary to both “respond to immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world.”

Watch on Deadline

It’s not an easy sell to an unsettled workforce that is all too aware that worse is yet to come. The BBC must save £500 million ($670M) by 2028 after hemorrhaging more than two million licence fee payers since 2020. Despite relentless internal memos about layoffs and content cuts since the summer, the BBC has only announced £200M of its half-billion goal. In other words, it’s not even halfway through the cuts.

Closing BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra may seem substantial, but the reality is that switching off these services in spring 2027 will only save around £10M, according to two insiders. In the case of BBC Three, the network spectrum from which the channel broadcasts will continue to be an expense because it also houses CBBC, the children’s network that airs between 7AM and 7PM.

Deadline can reveal that BBC leaders did discuss merging CBBC with the corporation’s other children’s network, CBeebies. The BBC would have banked a more significant saving alongside the closure of BBC Three, but executives dismissed the idea because they did not wish to call into question the corporation’s commitment to kids’ public service media.

CBBC series ‘The Worst Witch’ starred Bella Ramsey

A senior insider, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the closure of CBBC was deemed too “politically dangerous” when the BBC is negotiating its funding settlement and charter with the UK government. A second source added that Lisa Nandy believes BBC children’s services should be protected — perhaps unsurprising after her first visit to the BBC as culture secretary involved meeting Hacker T Dog, CBBC’s resident puppet.

BBC Sounds Under Threat?

That the BBC even contemplated CBBC’s future is revealing of the agonizing decisions facing Brittin as he attempts to put the broadcaster on a surer financial footing.

Speculation internally has turned to the future of another service: BBC Sounds, the radio and podcast streaming service launched in 2018. Deadline hears that the BBC has held tentative discussions about whether Sounds could be folded in with iPlayer to create a single streaming service for video and audio, not unlike Netflix and YouTube. A BBC insider said it is symptomatic of the BBC “having to dig much deeper and be more radical to find savings.”

Although no decisions have been made and Sounds is not under immediate threat, there are signals that point in this direction. During an internal all-staff call earlier this month, Brittin said he wanted iPlayer to be an “entertainment destination,” and asked Manon Dave, a product designer, to demonstrate a reimagined iPlayer where audio and video dovetailed. A further clue came this week, when BBC content chief Kate Phillips merged TV and audio commissioning teams in comedy and arts.

Somewhat counterintuitively, BBC Media Tech, the division that powers online platforms, is among the hardest hit by the cuts. The unit must save £102M by next year, but the talk is that a smaller team will focus on fewer products, which also fits with the emerging narrative around a single streaming service.

BBC News BBC

The BBC has announced around 1,200 job cuts in recent months, which is 800 shy of its intended target. Some think the BBC could exceed 2,000 redundancies. Few are immune. On-screen presenters like health editor Hugh Pym are expected to leave the building as BBC News contributes at least £51M to the savings pot.

Staff morale is low amid the drip-drip of redundancy announcements, which follows the BBC’s workforce contracting by 10% since 2020. The BBC is also navigating fraught negotiations over a staff pay deal, with the corporation infuriating unions by bundling in changes to terms and conditions, such as curbing cab usage for night shift workers. Many think industrial action is likely.

“There’s a lot of anger and bitterness,” said one insider. “If we all took work-to-rule [industrial action] and refused to do overtime, and turned our phones off for our lunch break, it would cause them a real headache.” Another spoke of a “f**k it feeling” internally: “The longer cuts get drawn out, the more uncertain everything feels. You think, God, do I really want to be sticking around for whatever this might end up being?”

A former Google executive, Brittin is trying to inject more Silicon Valley spirit and speed into the BBC’s culture. He is known to be disarmingly direct in meetings, unapologetically taking team members to task if they do not support their assumptions with audience data. “I’d like us to celebrate activity less, and outcomes more,” he told colleagues this month.

BBC Three Not Mourned

The closure of BBC Three, BBC Scotland, and Radio 4 Extra has not provoked significant backlash. When BBC Three was first taken off air in 2016, campaigners rallied to save the channel and two producers, Hat Trick boss Jimmy Mulville and Avalon co-founder Jon Thoday, made a serious offer to acquire the network. A decade on, Thoday is unmoved by the switch-off.

“I don’t think the BBC should have got rid of BBC Three in the first place. I don’t think they should have brought it back in the second place. And I’m not going to lose any sleep over them getting rid of it now,” said Thoday, who produces HBO’s Last Week Tonight with John Oliver.

“All I hope is that the cancelation of BBC Three for the second time results in the BBC increasing its spend on content for young people. It’s really important that the BBC increases and leads on comedy investment and lets comedy bring young viewers to the BBC.”

A former BBC executive added that the “terrible” decision to reinstate the channel in 2022 had harmed BBC Three, which was hit by low linear ratings for flagship shows. “It killed it,” they said. RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, The Rap Game and I Kissed a Girl/Boy have all been cancelled recently, meaning there is space for a creative refresh of the brand on iPlayer. The BBC has committed to increasing investment for younger audiences, but offered no detail on the value and scope of this ambition.

‘RuPaul’s Drag Race UK’ airs on BBC Three BBC/World of Wonder

Perhaps the most ominous thing for the BBC is that it is not in control of what comes next. Funding talks with the government are progressing slowly, despite Westminster press briefings about enthusiasm for a so-called “Netflix tax,” which would involve charging consumers extra for subscription streaming services to help pay for the BBC. Ministers like this idea, and the BBC has not dismissed the solution, but there are those at the corporation who are skeptical that it will solve its funding crisis.

The protracted talks leave the BBC with no visibility over its finances beyond the end of next year, an extraordinary situation for any organization that relies on £3.9 billion of public income. The BBC expects the government to publish its policy position before the end of the year. As director-general Matt Brittin looks to forge a “sovereign” streaming service from a smaller BBC, clarity can’t come soon enough.

title: Quentin Tarantino Wraps His AFI Fest Q&A By Showing Crowd First 17 Minutes Of ‘Cliff Booth’
summary: Quentin Tarantino surprised the crowd during a Q&A and screening of his 10-time Oscar-nominated Once Upon a Time in Hollywood on Friday night at AFI Fest in Los Angeles by screening the first 17 minutes of its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. It marks the first public look at the film, a follow-up […]
content:
Quentin Tarantino surprised the crowd during a Q&A and screening of his 10-time Oscar-nominated Once Upon a Time in Hollywood on Friday night at AFI Fest in Los Angeles by screening the first 17 minutes of its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

It marks the first public look at the film, a follow-up to Hollywood that Tarantino scripted and David Fincher directed. Brad Pitt revises his Oscar-winning role as Booth, a stuntman and sidekick to Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton in the original 2019 film.

Netflix is gearing up for the Cliff Booth theatrical release November 25 in Imax before hitting the streamer beginning December 23.

Watch on Deadline

“Well, I could talk a little bit about The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, or I could show you the first 17 minutes,” Tarantino said at the end of his special-event Q&A session at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. He had just been asked about the film and how it came about, and if he had anything else to say before the conversation wrapped.

He then stood up as the crowd began to figure out what was coming.

Here’s the moment:

Quentin Tarantino reflects on the decision to revisit Cliff Booth as he introduces the first 17 minutes of ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ at AFI Fest pic.twitter.com/0flrYw0J73 — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 24, 2026

Cliff Booth fast-forwards to 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The new logline: Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.

The pic also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis and Karren Karagulian.

Buzz for the film has been building since it was announced in 2024 that Pitt and Fincher were teaming on the project that Tarantino originally wanted to direct. Fincher said earlier this week that he had to cut 60 pages from Tarantino’s script, after he said the first draft he read was 230 pages. “It was essentially two movies,” Fincher told Empire.

The final cut of the film, Fincher said, has a runtime of around 2 1/2 hours.

During tonight’s AFI Fest event, Tarantino also talked about his upcoming play The Popinjay Cavalier, which will premiere in London’s West End next spring. Sacha Baron Cohen will star in the director’s first stage play, which begins previews February 23 and opens March 18 at the Phoenix Theatre.

Quentin Tarantino on his debut stage play, which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and will open on the West End next year pic.twitter.com/jMUAJpEuCN — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 24, 2026

Patrick Hipes contributed to this report.

title: Morelia Film Festival Prizes: ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building,’ an ‘Expression of Pure, Unbound Beauty,’ Wins Top ‘Ojo’ Award
summary: Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo award at the 24th Morelia Film Festival (FICM), which wraps Oct. 25. Hailed by Variety as a “lush, poetic film rooted in memories,” it became the first Mexican feature to […]
content:
Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo award at the 24th Morelia Film Festival (FICM), which wraps Oct. 25.

Hailed by Variety as a “lush, poetic film rooted in memories,” it became the first Mexican feature to compete at Cannes’ Critics Week in 20 years.

Morelia’s international jury, led by J.A. Bayona (“Society of the Snow”), praised the coming-of-age film for “courageously exploring the past, embracing pain and transforming it …into an expression of pure, unbound beauty.”

Popular on Variety

Drawing on the filmmaker’s own experiences, the drama traces back to a defining moment in his childhood: the year he turned eleven and when his father was diagnosed with HIV.

“Six Months…” also nabbed the Audience Award for fiction films, a strong indication of its box office potential.

Alejandro Ramírez, Cinépolis CEO and FICM president, described the festival’s 24th edition as a particularly Mexican celebration as it welcomed some of Mexico’s finest filmmakers and actors, including Guillermo del Toro, Alfonso Cuarón, Carlos Reygadas, Jonás Cuarón, Diego Luna, Gael García Bernal, Demián Bichir, Diego Boneta and Luis Gerardo Méndez.

With James Gray in town to present his crime drama “Paper Tiger” and J.A. Bayona serving as jury president, the festival has enjoyed a standout edition, he noted. Bayona also presented “Beyond Society,” a three-part documentary about the making of “Society of the Snow.”

“I think the films this year represent the wide diversity of Mexican cinematic imagination,” festival director Daniel Michel observed.

“There are many different and fascinating stories covering the breadth of experiences in our country which, we hope, will find a home in cinemas, as well as a large spectatorship. We’re also very proud to represent very different regions; Mexico is not a country one can easily summarize, but, rather, a vast territory with many differences which, I believe, our official selection has tried to gather in a single place.”

Meanwhile, Joaquin del Paso’s “The Garden We Dreamed,” which turns on a Haitian family traveling north in search of a better future, snagged two awards: a Special Mention and Best Cinematography for its DP, Gökhan Tiryaki.

“Sad Girlz,” a buzz film at the fest, was recognized as the best fiction debut with the Casa Wabis-Escine award, lauded by the jury for its “genuine performances” and “impeccable exploration of a young modern teen’s life, with all its complexities and contradictions.”

The rest of the awards were quite evenly distributed. Santiago Maza, whose “Black Shine” competed among the short films, won the ECAM award, a scholarship for a Master’s degree in distribution from the prestigious Madrid Film School (ECAM).

Nicolas Pereda snapped up the Best Director award with his absurdist comedy “Everything Else Is Noise,” which also snagged his lead Teresa Sanchez (“Flies”) a Best Actress Ojo prize for her performance as Tere, a cello musician-composer in whose apartment her colleague Rosa arranges her first television interview.

Sam Louwyck won the Best Actor prize for his portrayal of a gay hairdresser in Nathalia Acevedo’s “Beauty Salon,” where his salon serves as a refuge for marginalized people.

Noted Michel: “We’re also very pleased to have had directors from very different backgrounds and identities who have brought their perspectives and very singular ideas on filmmaking to our festival.”

Next year, the festival will be moving its dates back to the last week before the Day of the Dead. FICM is already gearing up for its 25th anniversary, promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup.

Among the highlights of the 10-day festival:

“Naza”

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary “Naza” – which means collateral damage – played to a packed Teatro Matamoros after which it unsurprisingly won an audience award. Unlike its reception at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, where it won the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking standing ovation, it was met with stunned silence as the credits rolled.

Presenting the documentary beforehand was festival VP Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Batel who underscored the importance of the screening to help audiences understand such a complex conflict. He noted that the Israeli filmmakers have been unable to return to their country after being accused of treason, adding that such accusations by a “criminal government” are a source of pride for those working toward peaceful solutions.

He reaffirmed the festival’s commitment to peace, dialogue and ending violence worldwide, calling for an end to the ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people.

Film critic Alonso Díaz de la Vega, also spoke, describing Naza as a “deeply moving” film that exposes not only the genocide in Gaza but also the global implications of military technology, artificial intelligence and surveillance.

“The most important thing this screening can inspire is not silence, but the words ‘Free Palestine,’” Díaz de la Vega concluded. The film opens in select theaters in Mexico on Oct. 22.

Guillermo del Toro Rules

At the festival to present the 3D re-release of his much-lauded “Pan’s Labyrinth,” the anti-authoritarian theme of his Oscar-winning fable hit home even harder this time, given the rise of right-wing governments across the region and the world at large.

Speaking to hordes of mostly young fans at his Masterclass and later at a press conference and multiple one-on-one interviews, the indefatigable filmmaker reflected on the current state of affairs in the world.

He grew emotional at the presser when he said: “The state of our species and society today goes beyond anything we could have imagined back then. But I recognize the same sadness and despair. It pains me deeply to see one, two, or three generations fail the next. We’re handing down a world in ruins, morally, socially and spiritually fractured, with the very fabric that once allowed us to tell fables and parables falling apart.”

French-Mexican Alliance

As part of the partnership established in 2003 between FICM and Cannes Critics’ Week, this year’s edition presented a selection of eight films and one short that screened at the sidebar last May. Ava Cahen, artistic director of the Cannes Film Festival’s parallel section, led the screenings, which included such titles as Aina Clotet’s “Viva,” Alexander Murphy’s “Tin Castle” and Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown.”

Toasting Mexico and France’s 200 years of diplomatic relations this year, French ambassador to Mexico Delphine Borione awarded Alfonso Cuarón the insignia of Officer of the Order of Arts and Letters during the fest to honor his “extraordinary contribution to contemporary cinema, singular vision, artistic reinvention and role in bringing Mexican culture to global audiences.”

Calling Cuarón “one of the greatest filmmakers of our time,” she praised his universal vision and the cultural ties his work has forged between Mexico and France. “To speak to the world, one must never stop being oneself,” she said, reflecting on his films, from “Y Tu Mamá También” to “Roma.”

Reflecting on France’s deep influence on his filmmaking, Cuarón described cinema as “not a narrative art, but a musical art” – a rhythmic, organic creation with its own heartbeat and a direct image of time.

He closed by addressing France’s current political turmoil, expressing hope that young people’s calls for change would be heard rather than co-opted by opportunism. Quoting French writer Pascal Quignard, he concluded: “I do not believe art can ever be negative. It ignores negation because it ignores time.”

Special Mention

title: El Gouna Takeaways: ‘Safe Exit’ Wins Top Prize, Arab TV Seeks New Talent and Egyptian Filmmakers Push Boundaries
summary: Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival wrapped its ninth edition Friday after nine days of screenings, industry activity and a closing night that spread its top prizes across the Middle East and beyond. Mohammed Hammad’s “Safe Exit,” a psychological drama about a young Coptic security guard in Cairo confronting trauma rooted in religious violence, won the […]
content:
Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival wrapped its ninth edition Friday after nine days of screenings, industry activity and a closing night that spread its top prizes across the Middle East and beyond.

Mohammed Hammad’s “Safe Exit,” a psychological drama about a young Coptic security guard in Cairo confronting trauma rooted in religious violence, won the Golden Star for best narrative feature. Ahmed Hassouna’s “Citizen Osama,” following a Gaza photojournalist balancing his work with family life amid war, took both the Golden Star for documentary and best Arab documentary. Anders Davidsen’s “Stolen Memories,” in which the discovery of childhood photographs leads an 18-year-old to question his past, won the Golden Star for short film. Rakan Mayasi’s Bekaa Valley-set “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep” was named best Arab narrative, while Marie Rose Ousta’s “One Day Born,” about an 11-year-old boy living under the constant threat of warplanes in Lebanon, took best Arab short.

Jordan’s Rakeen Saad won best actress for Zaid Abu Hamdan’s “Boomah,” while Jovan Ginić took best actor for Miroslav Terzić’s “3 Weeks After.”

Popular on Variety

Here are five takeaways from this year’s festival.

CineGouna, the Industry Platform, Is Becoming the Main Event

“We want the industry to be our hero,” El Gouna co-founder and executive director Amr Mansi told Variety ahead of this year’s festival.

The ninth edition made good on that ambition. More than 320 projects applied to CineGouna Funding, with 19 selected projects ultimately receiving more than $350,000 across 40 awards, while participants held more than 140 one-on-one meetings with companies, institutions and international festivals.

The activity extended beyond financing. CineGouna now encompasses Funding; Forum, a program of panels, masterclasses and industry discussions; Market, which connects filmmakers with companies and institutions; and Emerge, its initiative for young and emerging talent. This year also brought Egyptian Voices, a development program for Egyptian filmmakers, and an inaugural Series lab for Arab television projects into the fold. CineGouna is becoming as central to El Gouna’s identity as the films it screens.

Arab TV Is Searching for a Development Pipeline

CineGouna’s expansion into television also highlighted a wider problem confronting Arab television: there’s an abundance of talent, but opportunities to develop and sell new shows are sorely lacking.

Veteran Egyptian screenwriter and producer Mariam Naoum, who spearheaded the six-week CineGouna Series development lab, told Variety there are “great, great talents” in the region, but only “three or four platforms,” leaving creators competing for limited outlets.

Producer and screenwriter Haitham Dabbour similarly noted that fewer platforms make buyers more cautious, while director Mariam Abou Ouf warned that the business is “approaching a deadlock.” The six projects selected for the inaugural lab came to El Gouna to pitch their series and meet potential industry partners, with the aim of moving the projects closer to production.

Displaced Filmmakers Need More Than a Platform

War and displacement continue to shape filmmaking across the Arab world, affecting not only the stories reaching screens but the filmmakers trying to build careers.

The first Safe Harbour MENA, launched with the International Film Festival Rotterdam and the International Emerging Film Talent Association, brought four filmmakers displaced within the region into a program of training, project development and industry networking.

The initiative reframed support less as simply offering filmmakers a platform to tell stories about displacement than giving them the professional connections needed to continue working. “Citizen Osama’s” double win offered a potent reminder of the circumstances confronting filmmakers in the region: director Ahmed Hassouna remains in Gaza.

Egyptian Filmmakers Are Pushing for More Creative Freedom

“Safe Exit’s” top prize landed amid a broader conversation at El Gouna about an Egyptian industry in transition.

Producer Mohammad Mashish pointed to a younger generation with “more freedom than before” and audiences increasingly exposed to international cinema, but argued that the industry needs more time for development and screenwriting.

Producer-distributor Ziad Srouji put the challenge more succinctly: “Specificity travels, generic does not.” Muhammad Mustapha, whose documentary “Big Boys Don’t Cry” premiered at El Gouna, similarly argued for models that lower financial risk while allowing filmmakers to take greater artistic risks.

The tension is increasingly clear: Egyptian filmmakers are looking outward while asking for enough room to make work rooted firmly at home.

El Gouna Looks Beyond El Gouna

One of the festival’s most locally significant launches will take place largely after its guests have gone home.

Cinema on Wheels is taking three shorts from this year’s lineup on a free screening tour through Hurghada, Minya, Qena, Luxor and Aswan before concluding in Cairo, accompanied by discussions with audiences.

“We’re always exploring ways to increase the reach of El Gouna Film Festival beyond just its duration and the town of El Gouna,” artistic director Andrew Mohsen explained.

For a festival built in an affluent Red Sea resort, the effort to bring its programming to audiences elsewhere in Egypt significantly expands its reach. As Mansi put it: “Cinema on Wheels is our way of connecting El Gouna to the rest of the country.”

title: Anika Rashaun Dies: ‘Real World’, ‘The Challenge’ Alum Was 34
summary: Anika Rashaun, the Reality TV star who appeared and competed on MTV’s The Real World and The Challenge and later became a professional matchmaker, advice columnist and dating coach, died October 1 of breast cancer. She was 34. Rashaun’s death was announced by friends on social media. Cyndi Rich wrote on Facebook, “Anika shined so […]
content:
Anika Rashaun, the Reality TV star who appeared and competed on MTV’s The Real World and The Challenge and later became a professional matchmaker, advice columnist and dating coach, died October 1 of breast cancer. She was 34.

Rashaun’s death was announced by friends on social media. Cyndi Rich wrote on Facebook, “Anika shined so bright. Being close to that light as one of her closest friends was a true blessing. She is a vibrant soul. I’ll love her and treasure the 16 years of memories forever.”

In a Substack tribute, Rashaun’s friend Tiara Ramos wrote that Rashaun was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer last summer. “My world already feels dulled and blurred without her,” Ramos writes. “The urge to pick up the phone and FaceTime her is a reflex I can’t shake. Knowing the pain her husband, her parents, her loved ones, and her community are feeling right now makes me sick. I am angry. I am heartbroken. I am devastated.”

Watch on Deadline

Rashaun first appeared at age 24 on MTV’s The Real World Seattle: Bad Blood in 2016 and, the following year, returned to take part in The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions.

For The Real World 2016-2017 “bad blood” season, in which Real World housemates were eventually joined by people they considered nemeses, Rashaun was paired with her ex-boyfriend Will. The synopsis for that season notes, “Ex-lovers Anika and Will go together like oil and water: The yin yang pair dated for three years, and during that time Anika was constantly annoyed that Will couldn’t match her dominance.”

After the season ended, Rashaun, a New York City native, moved to Los Angeles and, building on the social media following she attained through the series, built a lifestyle brand that would eventually include matchmaking and dating advice. She remained cordial with Will, though lost touch after the show.

In 2017, Rashaun returned to the MTV universe for The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions. She was eliminated in the third episode.

Theo King-Bradley, who appeared in both of Rashaun’s seasons on Real World and The Challenge, posted a tribute on Instagram (see it below). “I’ve been doing everything else to keep my mind off the fact that you’re not here. I’ve genuinely been sad as hell since hearing you passed. I’m sad I didn’t get to see you one last time. But the last time and conversation we had with each other I can cherish and play it back in my mind to smile.”

After her stint on The Challenge, Rashaun returned to her career as dating coach and lifestyle podcast host. According to her Instagram, she attended school to become a licensed marriage and family therapist.

Rashaun married her boyfriend Kyle Rehn on Valentine’s Day this year. Complete information on survivors was not immediately available.

title: The Surprise Guest in ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win an Oscar. Should They?
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters. The question that’s consumed the awards-pundit class since “You Can See Everything” exploded into theaters last week is whether Amanda Seyfried, the unlikely linchpin of this hybrid documentary, can be nominated for or win an acting Oscar. A24 is planning […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

The question that’s consumed the awards-pundit class since “You Can See Everything” exploded into theaters last week is whether Amanda Seyfried, the unlikely linchpin of this hybrid documentary, can be nominated for or win an acting Oscar. A24 is planning to campaign her for one. Much of her time onscreen is as herself, reacting in real time — but she does, eventually, re-enact co-director Nathan Fielder’s remembered interactions with disgraced tech founder Elizabeth Holmes.

In this, she’s reprising a role that, with the 2022 Hulu series “The Dropout,” already won her an Emmy and a Golden Globe. It’s the role, now that “You Can See Everything” is on track to become one of the most financially successful documentaries in history, that’s become Seyfried’s signature. To this viewer, the question is at once an amusing thought experiment (sure, why not?), and a testament to Seyfried’s compelling screen presence — and more than a little beside the point. For once, an Oscar seems minimizing. What Seyfried’s doing in her most compelling screen work ever is something other, or more, than simply acting.

Popular on Variety

To be clear, the parts of “You Can See Everything” when she is literally acting are riveting on their own terms. Seyfried simply wears the role of Holmes easily. She’s doubly disadvantaged — in that we’ve just spent 90 minutes with the real Holmes, against whom we can compare Seyfried, and in that we’ve also spent time absorbing just how little Seyfried understands the enigma of Holmes’ motivations. And yet Seyfried somehow creates a coherent and compelling version of a woman we don’t understand, and we know she doesn’t, really, either.

To pigeonhole Seyfried’s appearance in “You Can See Everything” as, solely, an acting performance misses the rawness of Seyfried’s presence here. She allows herself to be seen thinking through a conundrum, as herself, and falling short of finding answers — in other words, after Holmes and husband Billy Evans, she’s the documentary’s other subject. Seyfried delivers a painful and unresolved excavation of the mind of an actor, seeming to land in a place of uncertainty as to how her own past work as Holmes has changed the story even as she willingly takes on the part once more.

Consider, for instance, the scene in which Seyfried visits Evans at home, after Holmes’ incarceration. This is impressively game and daring. And Seyfried is, I suppose, “acting,” both in the theorist’s sense that all of us are acting our way through life and in the particular that Seyfried has set out to lure information out of Evans to better understand the seemingly bizarre arrangement Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim had been excavating before Holmes went to prison. But is she acting, in the traditional sense, when she meets and interacts with Holmes and Evans’ two children, or when she defends her social media post criticizing the late Charlie Kirk against Evans’ mockery? Alternately tender and outraged, Seyfried allows us into her world, just as Holmes tried to. But Holmes, talking past real questioning, couldn’t get there, no matter how all-access her invitation to Fielder had been. Seyfried, by contrast, seems deeply in touch with emotions lying just under the surface. And her increasing befuddlement both matches our own and raises the question of just how deeply an actor can ever understand their subject.

Seyfried, just as Holmes and Evans do in their askew manner, knows her angles. It wasn’t lost on me that within the frame as Fielder speaks to her at her home is a miniature playhouse, of the sort her company Make It Cute sells. That the computer on which she and Fielder watch video of Holmes watching “The Dropout” is propped on coffee table books about Seyfried’s great passion, dogs, and that she and Fielder discuss Holmes while feeding her photogenic horses on her photogenic farm only burnish her brand further. And yet she cannot help but exposing more than she may mean to.

A conversation about the ethics of “The Dropout” — a drama based on real events that, as with any dramatization, used creative license, and that many viewers took as fact — places Seyfried in a surprisingly exposed position. Holmes did not, literally, say and do all the things that Seyfried says and does in the role, Seyfried admits, but she may well have, and the performance overall conjures the sense of a person who is unconcerned with scientific accuracy or with the truth. Shouldn’t that be enough? “I didn’t do that to her,” Seyfried concludes, after attempting to walk herself through a justification of “The Dropout” as plainly not depicting objective reality, no matter what viewers think. “She did that to herself.” She seems to be convincing herself not to feel guilty, up until her final line, delivered with a “It’s Chinatown”-style futility. “It’s very complicated,” she says, having indulged the complications long enough.

Coming into “You Can See Everything,” this viewer saw Elizabeth Holmes’ Theranos as transparently fraudulent and “The Dropout” as an excellent TV show that was in no need of moral justification. Leaving the theater, nothing about those beliefs had changed, but engaging the question of what Seyfried might have owed to Holmes allowed both women to be seen in intriguing new lights. Seyfried, painfully aware of the existence of the two young children she’d met, twists around the question of whether her past work might have been unfair, or have been presented as possessed of a truth its creators didn’t actually know. And in this moment, she seems less to be acting than to be, in a moment of painful frankness I admire her for allowing herself to experience on-camera, acted upon.

Say this much: “You Can See Everything” is undeniably a career high for an actor who has seemed at times in her career like an underdog. (A sliding-doors scenario for the ages: The role of Elizabeth Holmes originally went to sketch comedian Kate McKinnon, and Seyfried got the role only after McKinnon dropped out and Seyfried got a career-boosting Oscar nomination for 2020’s “Mank.”) Amiably loopy in interviews — including in red-carpet appearances at this year’s Academy Museum Gala, where Seyfried sidestepped discussing the film in favor of free-associative Dada — and impressively shifting between genres to avoid being pigeonholed, Seyfried is easy to root for, but can seem hard to know.

Which makes the Oscar talk make perfect sense. Seyfried has gone to a very raw place in “You Can See Everything” — and, not for nothing, has delivered some of the most memorable humor in its second half. (Her growing scandalization at Evans’ control over Holmes’ image and her life allows the viewer a compelling way to stay engaged with the story once Holmes herself leaves it.) But whether or not she can break through in what would, despite vaguely similar precedent — Maria Bakalova in the 2020 “Borat” sequel was nominated for reacting against real life — be close to an unprecedented case, Seyfried has done something more impressive than earning any award. She’s opened up her work as an actor — both her preparation and the moral question of what it means to play a living person — to careful scrutiny, and was vulnerable enough to attempt to talk it through, and to be shown to be uncertain. This appearance, or performance, or whatever, will be discussed far beyond Oscar season. It situates Seyfried as what we ought to have known she was all along: Among the most daring stars of her generation.

title: New York’s AMC Kips Bay Theater Closes on Jan. 3; CEO Says ‘AMC Wants to Stay’ but NYU Langone ‘Wants Us Gone’
summary: AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3. Aron wrote a letter to the Kips Bay community and addressed how the nearby hospital NYU Langone, which plans to grow its medical facility, has not engaged with […]
content:
AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3.

Aron wrote a letter to the Kips Bay community and addressed how the nearby hospital NYU Langone, which plans to grow its medical facility, has not engaged with any of AMC’s alternatives to share the space. In addition to the 15-screen AMC theater, the building also houses a Fairway supermarket and bank, which are also expected to close.

“Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease,” Aron writes. “We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.”

Popular on Variety

On Aug. 24, Variety reported that the Kips Bay theater would close at the end of 2026, ending a 27-year run at the location. AMC took over the theater in 2006, which became the chain’s second-largest multiplex in the city (after Times Square’s Empire 25 theater). The Kips Bay location has become adored by local residents, who staged a protest in September in an attempt to stop the closure.

“Every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15,” Aron wrote. “It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theaters across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theaters operated by AMC nationally.”

The theater closure comes after a record-breaking summer box office, which saw movies like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5” and more collectively gross $4.67 billion domestically. There are also major upcoming movies like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part III,” which Kips Bay residents will now still get a chance to see at their beloved theater before it closes for good.

Read Aron’s full letter below.

“To the Kips Bay Community,

Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.

So many moviegoers and neighbors, and importantly so many of your elected officials, have rallied around our theatre. (Given the central role that movie theatres play in the lives of so many New Yorkers, perhaps it is much better and more accurate to say that so many of you have rallied around YOUR theatre.)

On behalf of everyone at AMC, thank you. Your support means a great deal to us, and especially to our theatre team members at AMC Kips Bay 15 who work tirelessly day-in and day-out to put smiles on your faces.

In thinking about this theatre, which has been a cultural icon and entertainment lifeline to so many nearby residents for decades and decades since its opening on May 14 1999, I want to make one thing absolutely clear:

AMC Theatres does not want to go. Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay.

Operating under long term leases, there was a time that the monies headed each month to the theatre’s landlord had risen to become so high that the theatre’s long-term viability was uncertain. But, we were fortunate to have been successful in addressing those concerns in recent years. Today this theatre (one which has been in continuous operation for more than 25 years) has a bright future — if we would be allowed to keep it.

Indeed, every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15. It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theatres across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theatres operated by AMC nationally.

In that light, this is a theatre that should not be even close to a permanent shutting off of its lights.

Of course, AMC wants this AMC movie theatre to stay in place.

And remembering how much and how often Americans love watching movies in theatres, a tradition in Manhattan that dates back more than a full century, we have heard from so many of you that you too want us to stay open for your benefit.

Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours.

Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.

We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.

We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.

It isn’t true that New Yorkers can be prevented from having your cake and eating it too. Indeed you can. But only if people of goodwill think out of the box a bit. After all, the ubiquitous proverb “where there is a will, there is a way” is one that is believed to have first been published in the year 1640 — that’s three hundred eighty six years back to be precise.

Speaking of people of goodwill, I especially want to express gratitude to Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal and New York State Assembly Member Keith Powers, for their leadership and tireless advocacy on this matter. Reinforcing and speaking for the local community’s clear desire, they have energetically brought attention to the importance of keeping an AMC movie theatre open and operating in Kips Bay.

In summary, this is a theatre that you in Kips Bay want to continue to be at your beck and call, and one that we at AMC unequivocally also want to be allowed to continue within our theatrical fleet.

But time is short. Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.

Hopefully, there is an outcome in which a wise workable solution is devised, one that will benefit and please the entire neighborhood. What say you NYU Langone Health?

Whatever happens, I want you to know how much AMC appreciates your support, your efforts and your voice. We are proud to have been part of the Kips Bay community since 1999, and I sincerely hope that we can continue to be part of it for years to come.

Sincerely,

Adam Aron, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer AMC Entertainment

title: Box Office: ‘Clayface’ Lands at No. 1 with $10.4 Million Debut, ‘You Can See Everything’ Adds $6.14 Million on Friday
summary: Clayface might have been a considerably nicher choice for a feature film than DC’s “Supergirl” and “Superman,” but that didn’t stop audiences from showing out to catch the Batman supervillain’s gory, nightmare-inducing origin story at the box office this weekend. The new release generated $10.4 million from 3,458 North American theaters on Friday, taking the […]
content:
Clayface might have been a considerably nicher choice for a feature film than DC’s “Supergirl” and “Superman,” but that didn’t stop audiences from showing out to catch the Batman supervillain’s gory, nightmare-inducing origin story at the box office this weekend.

The new release generated $10.4 million from 3,458 North American theaters on Friday, taking the No. 1 spot. It’s a strong start for the film, which looks to pull in $24 million by Sunday.

Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star. Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”

Popular on Variety

Fellow DC films like “Superman,” produced for nearly $230 million, brought in $618.72 million worldwide over the course of its 2025 theatrical run, while “Supergirl” was considered a bomb with $126 million against a $170 million budget earlier this year. In comparison, “Clayface” cost $44 million to produce.

A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” landed in second place on Friday, making $6.14 million from 2,655 North American theaters, up from 855 at opening weekend. The buzzy doc has made $31.7 million domestically so far. Rival estimates suggest the film will gross another $20 million by Sunday.

Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

Laika’s “Wildwood,” another new release, landed in third place on Friday, grossing $4.28 million from 2,942 North American theaters. Featuring a voice cast that includes Carey Mulligan, Jacob Tremblay and others, the stop-motion film looks to bring in $11.2 million by Sunday.

Directed by Travis Knight, “Wildwood” revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted. Strong reviews should continue to propel the lavish film at the box office, which carries a substantial $100 million price tag.

Black Bear’s “Wicker” followed in fourth place, earning $2.36 million on Friday from 1,471 North American theaters. The offbeat romantic comedy, directed by Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, is targeting a $5.5 million opening weekend.

Described as an “audacious comedic fable,” “Wicker” tells the love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband from the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Alexander Skarsgård plays said husband. Elizabeth Debicki also stars.

Coming in fifth was Legendary Entertainment’s “Street Fighter.” The action film grossed $2.34 million on Friday and should add another $8.4 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $46.7 million.

“Street Fighter,” directed by Kitao Sakurai, stars Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji as two estranged fighters in the 90s who are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

title: Quentin Tarantino Surprises Fans With 17 Minutes of ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ at AFI Fest
summary: Quentin Tarantino surprised audiences on Friday night at AFI Fest when he shared the first 17 minutes of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino made a special appearance at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood, following a screening of “Once Upon a Time … In Hollywood.” Following the Q&A moderated by Rotten Tomatoes’ Jacqueline […]
content:
Quentin Tarantino surprised audiences on Friday night at AFI Fest when he shared the first 17 minutes of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

Tarantino made a special appearance at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood, following a screening of “Once Upon a Time … In Hollywood.” Following the Q&A moderated by Rotten Tomatoes’ Jacqueline Coley, the filmmaker said, “Well, I could talk a little bit about ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ or I could show you the first 17 minutes.”

Directed by David Fincher, who was also in attendance, the film sees the return of Cliff Booth played by Brad Pitt. The film picks up in 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The logline reads: “Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.”

Popular on Variety

He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition and desire that could only happen in LA.

Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, shared his decision to revisit Cliff Booth. He said, “I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ was, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in’ and there is that aspect; I loved the Cliff Booth character,” Tarantino said. “I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”

While further plot details can’t be spoiled, the opening sequence has Tarantino’s distinguished style of writing and visually, the Hollywood of 1977 is, in true Fincher style, gritty and dark.

The Netflix film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller and is set to premiere in Imax theaters on Nov. 25, before hitting the streamer Dec. 23.

The evening kicked off with Tarantino introducing the film and shared that had not seen the film at that theater.

In the Q&A, Tarantino shared how he had spoken with Burt Reynolds about playing the George Spahn character. Tarantino recalled, “He said yes and we became friendly, but he passed away before we could make the film. But we did get to rehearse with him and do the script reading with him, so actually, the last performance Burt Reynolds ever gave was as George Spahn in the script reading.”

The character would be played by Bruce Dern.

He also talked about his upcoming play “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and is set to premiere in London’s West End next year. “I’m not going to talk a whole lot about that, but our previews are in February. In November we’ll start rehearsals.” He went on to say, “I’m just a writer and that’s just kind of what I do. I’m always writing.”

title: AMC Theatres Wants NYC’s Endangered Kips Bay Multiplex To Remain But Decision “Not Ours To Make”; Scheduled Closing Date Announced

content:
AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron has issued an open letter to New York City residents reiterating the company’s desire to continue operating its longstanding Kips Bay 15 multiplex in the Manhattan neighborhood of that name, but concedes the decision is not AMC’s to make.

Neighbors of the Kips Bay-Murray Hill section of Manhattan along Second Avenue near the East River have been vocal about the planned closure of the multiplex that’s been a central commercial hub since 1999 (AMC took over the venue in 2006). The property on which the multiplex sits was privately purchased last year by NYU Langone, one of New York’s major health care systems.

AMC announced in August that the purchase would likely mean the closure of the multiplex by the end of this year, prompting an outcry and protests from residents and other businesses in the area.

Watch on Deadline

Following “direct engagement” from Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal, AMC’s Aron issued the open letter concurring with Hoylman-Sigal that the neighborhood needs such amenities as a movie theater, supermarket and housing.

Writes Aron, “Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.”

Read the entire statement below.

“AMC Theatres does not want to go,” Aron writes. “Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay….Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours. Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make.”

According to Aron, the NYU Langone Health facility “wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.”

Aron notes that AMC has “engaged” with NYU Langone to suggest various alternatives that would allow the multiplex to continue operating in some form. “Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds,” he writes, adding, “We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.”

The AMC chief warns that time is running out for the venue. “Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.”
