title: ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ Gets a Fittingly Sexy Fashion Collection Ahead of Sarah J. Maas’s Latest Book
summary: In an age of endless brand partnerships and collaborations, it always feels good seeing a team-up that doesn’t feel forced. Such is the case with For Love & Lemons very sexy collaboration with “A Court of Thorns and Roses” — a collection of corsetry, lace, romantic florals and embellished evening wear that just makes sense. […]
content:
In an age of endless brand partnerships and collaborations, it always feels good seeing a team-up that doesn’t feel forced. Such is the case with For Love & Lemons very sexy collaboration with “A Court of Thorns and Roses” — a collection of corsetry, lace, romantic florals and embellished evening wear that just makes sense.

The collaboration, which launched Oct. 22, arrives just days before the Oct. 27 release of “A Court of Splintered Harmony,” the sixth installment in Sarah J. Maas’ wildly popular romantasy series. Rather than relying on book-cover graphics and branded sweatshirts, the LA-based brand infused the aesthetic of Maas’ fictional world of Prythian into four mini collections based on themes from the books: “The First Bloom of Spring,” “Welcome to the Night Court,” “Under Starfall Skies” and “A Dance of Silver Flames.”

ACOTAR x For Love & Lemons SHOP ONLINE

The Spring Court-inspired pieces feature pastel florals and delicate lace, including the $639 Rose of the Manor Gown, while the darker Night Court assortment includes the $629 Night Court Mini Dress and $829 Moonveil Gown. Elsewhere, celestial-inspired Starfall designs and nods to characters like Nesta and the Valkyries round out the collection, with pieces ranging from a $398 beaded mini skirt to a $729 gown.

“This collection has been over a year in the making, and it was born out of true passion,” For Love & Lemons co-founder Gillian Kern said of the partnership. “We love the way Sarah J. Maas uses fashion to evoke a mood.”

The collection also includes several pieces featuring custom embroidery, hand-beaded detailing and intricate embellishments. Produced in limited quantities, the designs will not be restocked once sold out, according to the brand. Several styles, including the Storykeeper Dress and Dance with Fire Gown, have already sold out, while other pieces remain listed as coming soon.

The launch is part of a broader merchandising blitz surrounding the highly anticipated next “ACOTAR” novel. Knix recently debuted a collection of lingerie, sleepwear and underwear inspired by the series, while fragrance brand Fine’ry released four ACOTAR-themed scents. Funko Pop and Loungefly have also rolled out character figurines and accessories, respectively. Meanwhile, Target has launched an extensive assortment of merchandise spanning jewelry, apparel and collectibles, with midnight release celebrations planned at approximately 250 stores on Oct. 26. Barnes & Noble will host similar events at more than 500 locations nationwide.

title: Serielizados Prizes: Hagai Levi’s ‘Etty’ and ‘Astonishing’ ‘Killing a Bear’ Win Big as ‘El Observatorio’ Bags the Mind the Gap Pitch Prize
summary: Influential Israeli creator Hagai Levi (“The Affair,” “Scenes From a Marriage”) and prominent Spanish TV-making duo Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo (“La Zona”) won best international and national series at Barcelona’s Serielizados for “Etty” and “Killing a Bear” respectively. The prizes for Serielizados two competitive sections were announced Saturday night at a Serielizados awards ceremony. Both […]
content:
Influential Israeli creator Hagai Levi (“The Affair,” “Scenes From a Marriage”) and prominent Spanish TV-making duo Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo (“La Zona”) won best international and national series at Barcelona’s Serielizados for “Etty” and “Killing a Bear” respectively.

The prizes for Serielizados two competitive sections were announced Saturday night at a Serielizados awards ceremony.

Popular on Variety

Both series in six-parts reflect the boldness of their respective creators, who broke new ground within traditional genres.

In the French-Dutch-German show “Etty,” based on Dutch Jewish author Etty Hillesum’s diaries, Levi deliberately opted for a modern spin to the period piece in which we follow the passionate 27-year-old Etty as she embarks on a spiritual and emotional journey in a Nazi-occupied Amsterdam.

In the Spanish show “Killing a Bear” (“Matar a un oso”) the Sánchez-Cabezudo brothers brought innovation to the crime genre, making a bear the victim, relating the crime from the POV of multiple characters, and expanding the number of prime suspects to a tight community of 262 Anti-Bears chat room in Spain’s idyllic high-Pyrenean Val d’Arán.

“With this series, we felt really lucky to have been invited into a world so fully realised, so distinctly Catalan but portrayed with a confidence and a muscularity that left us astonished,” said Finnish producer Roosa Toivonen, also Tallinn TV Beats co-head, who sat on the national competition jury with Canneseries’ Claire-Marine Pietriga and the Berlinale’s Rowan Woods.

‘Kiling a Bear’

Both series also stand out among the best shows that Europe currently has to offer, with the stamp of approval from quality-maker Arte France.

Indeed, the European cultural channel was a major backer of Levi’s historical drama – conceived as a feature film in six episodes – which world-premiered out of competition in Venice, was highlighted at Series Mania, and bowed in French cinemas May 6 before launching on Arte.tv on May 16. Shepherded by Les Films du Poisson, “Etty” is sold internationally by Studio TF1.

“Killing a Bear” which had its Catalan premiered at Serielizados fast on the heels of its world premiere at Spain’s Valladolid Film Festival, is the latest prime example of Arte France’s successful collaboration with the largest Spanish pay-TV/SVOD operator Movistar Plus. The Movistar Plus Original, produced by the Sánchez-Cabezudo brothers’ Studio TF1-owned Kubik Films, will bow in Spain Dec. 1.

Besides the top win for “Etty,” Arte France also scooped best screenplay at Serielizados’ official International Selection Awards for the French comedy “Camarades” co-created and co-penned by Benjamin Charbit (“Under Control”) and Dominique Baumart (“The Bureau”).

Another comedy wooed the international jury: BBC’s hit show “Ann Droid” for which its creator, Bafta-nominated Diane Morgan (“Mandy,” “Cun”), won best performance for her turn as the second-hand robot Linda.

On the national competition front, all four selected series won accolades. Next to “Killing a Bear,” the anticipated drama “Segunda Temporada” from the hot creators of Filmin’s “Autodefensa” – writer-director Miguel Ángel Blanca and co-writers Berta Prieto and Víctor Diago – scooped best screenplay. Bringing together a washed-up ghost-writer and a fading trap legend fresh out of jail, the show was developed as part of Serielizados Kick talent lab, before making it as a 7-30-minute drama produced by Barcelona-based Boogaloo Films and Canada. Paris-based Oble handles sales.

Beloved Spanish-acting queen Carmen Machi (“Aida,” “La Mesías”), bagged a fresh best actress nod for her performance as tax inspector Sara Santano in the Movistar Plus-100 Balas’ “Celeste” Season 2 which bowed as a world premiere in Barcelona. Last year the show’s creator Diego San José and helmer Elena Trapé scooped two Serielizados wins for “Yakarta,” another example of their inimitable downbeat but sharply observant humor.

Elsewhere, the buzzy HBO Max-3Cat co-commissioned dramedy “In Vitro” which offers a witty and heart-warming look at fertility treatments, received a Special Mention. “This [show] really stood out to us for its global appeal and international remake potential,” said the jurors.

The series, created by Marc Crehuet with Alejandra Guimerà, was co-penned by Crehuet with Carmen Marfá, Natalia Boadas and Serielizados co-founder Víctor Sala. The latter said the show ,which launched simultaneously Oct. 19 in Spain on HBO Max and 3Cat, garnered an excellent 18.2% share on the Catalan pubcaster.

“Many countries could be jealous of the creative courage the Spanish commissioners have shown, as they have helped equally bold producers to greenlight shows of this caliber!” said the jurors of the Spanish competition, who highlighted the central female-characters of different ages in each of the four series.

The jurors added: “Serializados is one of these tremendous gems – smaller events where you can see that the content is lovingly hand-picked and curated out of pure passion for the art and craft of series, and the atmosphere is convivial with a lovely team that truly cares about everyone’s experience and hospitality. We, the jury members, had a great time and watching the four nominated shows was a lot of fun, as they are each so brilliant and original in their very unique ways.”

Although Serielizados has another few days to run – until Oct. 28 – across various Barcelona venues, co-founder and festival programmer Betu Martínez Molero was pleased with this 13th edition, led by masterclasses with Levi, Steven Moffat and Sue Vertue, a full day of the Miniput -quality TV festival showcase, and the second edition of the Mind the Gap pitch competition.

Mind the Gap

The top €5,500 ($6,100) Mind the Gap Award was handed out to the creators of the Spanish show “El Observatorio,” from Laura Roqué, Luis Sorolla and Eloy Zamora. Set in a small village from Sierra Morena, the story turns on a group of astrophysicists investigating mysterious flickering lights, until one of them-Sara starts to believe the light might be her deceased father trying to communicate.

“After a great deliberation we’ve decided to award new talent who need to be discovered,” said Arte France’s Alexios Kastrissianakis, co-juror with Mubi’s Ben Driscoll, Movistar Plus’ Laura Escrivá, ZDF Studios’ Susanne Frank and Beta Film’s Peter Lohner. First pitched at the ECAM Forum 2026 where it earned the Serilizados award, the project, in early development, is looking for a producer.

The jury also gave two honorable mentions to two female-led series about abuse: the Finnish psychological drama “Dangerous Woman,” produced by Gutsy Pictures for MTV Finland and TV4 Sweden, and the Spanish drama “Callback” created by sisters Joana and Mireia Vilapuig for “This is Not Sweden” producer Funicular Films, with Left Tackle Films.

“Callback” was also bestowed the €2,000 ($2,200) Konga Music Agency award.

Martínez Molero said: “This year we solidified our position as the leading international TV series festival in Spain and one of the most prominent in Southern Europe, reaching 18.000 attendees across more than 60 activities, including more than 30 national and international premieres.”

He added: “We’ve seen a growing interest from both media and audiences for our National and International Competitions, packing our main venues. It’s also been great to see how presenting non-distributed international shows helps put them on the radar of Spanish platforms looking to acquire new series, while also helping local creators connect with key international players in the TV industry.”

Following its onsite showcase in Barcelona, Serielizados will bow on line on the streamer Filmin over Nov. 10-22.

title: Elon Musk’s Grok Releases First AI-Generated ‘Odyssey’ Episode, Months After Promising ‘Historically Accurate’ Full-Length Film
summary: Months after Elon Musk promised that his AI tool Grok Imagine would create an entirely AI-generated, feature-length version of “The Odyssey,” the tech mogul has partially followed through on the claim. On Friday, the company shared the first 7-minute, AI-generated episode of the “Odyssey” series on X. The account also credited the “creative collaboration” to […]
content:
Months after Elon Musk promised that his AI tool Grok Imagine would create an entirely AI-generated, feature-length version of “The Odyssey,” the tech mogul has partially followed through on the claim.

On Friday, the company shared the first 7-minute, AI-generated episode of the “Odyssey” series on X. The account also credited the “creative collaboration” to Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, both of which specialize in AI filmmaking.

In July, Musk announced plans to make a “historically accurate” full-length feature version of Homer’s ancient Greek poem. He noted that his AI “The Odyssey” would be ready by the end of 2026.

Popular on Variety

“Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer,” he wrote, together with an AI-generated 3-minute short of “The Odyssey” posted by an X user.

At the time, “Doctor Strange” and “The Black Phone” director Scott Derrickson pulled no punches and addressed Musk directly on social media to call out the absurdity of the project. “Clearly @elonmusk doesn’t know shit about cinema & he stopped reading in his 20s,” Derrickson wrote on Musk’s social media platform, X. “His opinions on art are worthless.”

While no further statement accompanied the AI-generated episode — or Musk’s original tweet about creating a “historically accurate” version of “The Odyssey” — the move comes after the tech trillionaire repeatedly criticized the film ahead of its release, especially the casting of Elliot Page as Achilles’ Ghost and Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy.

Musk claimed that Nolan cast both actors to satisfy the Academy’s representation and inclusion standards for Oscar eligibility; in March, he wrote that “Chris Nolan is an anti-White racist,” saying he cast Nyong’o only because “He wants the awards.”

See the first episode of the series here.

title: DJ Pikachu: Pokémon Goes EDM With Lasers, Battles and Marshmello in 30th Anniversary Concert at Intuit Dome
summary: Gotta rave ’em all! Pokémon celebrated its 30th anniversary with an epic EDM concert at LA’s Intuit Dome with DJs Marshmello and Alison Wonderland on Saturday night. Billed as Pokémon Night Out, the show mixed together the creatures from the popular video games and trading cards with the lasers, pyrotechnics and mind-blowing visuals of EDM […]
content:
Gotta rave ’em all! Pokémon celebrated its 30th anniversary with an epic EDM concert at LA’s Intuit Dome with DJs Marshmello and Alison Wonderland on Saturday night.

Billed as Pokémon Night Out, the show mixed together the creatures from the popular video games and trading cards with the lasers, pyrotechnics and mind-blowing visuals of EDM music. The event was livestreamed online for fans who couldn’t attend in person, and there’s a second show at London’s O2 Arena on Nov. 10.

But why EDM music? At first, there doesn’t seem to be much of a connection between the colorful, family-friendly world of Pokémon and the loud, head-banging techno genre. However, the two communities have a surprising number of similarities.

Popular on Variety

“Folks who are big fans of EDM, there are four principles that they all subscribe to: peace, love, unity and respect. PLUR. That notion is so aligned with the values of Pokémon in so many ways. We have a mission of bringing the world together through Pokémon. This seemed like a really natural way to be able to bring those worlds together and to be able to find that middle ground,” said Narbeh Minasians, senior director of brand communications and digital marketing for The Pokémon Company International. “We’ve never done anything like this before. This is brand new for us. This is a true celebration of 30 years of our brand, and it’s being done in the most incredible, original fashion that you can imagine.”

Ken Lew Photography

After launching 30 years ago and growing into a worldwide phenomenon across entertainment, gaming and merchandise, Pokémon ended its banner year in style with Marshmello and Alison Wonderland, two fans of the brand themselves. And LA’s high-tech Intuit Dome was the perfect venue for the one-of-a-kind show.

With 30 years of history and more than 1,000 Pokémon to choose from, Marshmello and Alison Wonderland crafted two sets that blew the minds of Pokémon fans and EDM ravers alike. Alison Wonderland kicked things off with a countdown of nearly every Pokémon while she DJ’ed in front of a massive video wall with vibrant images of the video game creatures. She played to the crowd’s nostalgia with a remix of the classic theme song from the “Pokémon” TV show, then brought out a neon-covered Pikachu on stage with her. The yellow Pokémon mascot had glowing glasses and ears that changed colors along with the set. One of the standout moments of the entire concert was Alison Wonderland’s remix of the eerie theme from the creepy Lavender Town in the original “Pokémon” games. Footage from the pixelated “Pokémon Red and Blue” played on screen along with her haunting beat from the ghost-filled town that has creeped out Pokémon trainers for decades.

Marshmello then took the stage and appeared as if his DJ booth was floating in the center of the video wall as Pokémon-themed visuals swirled all around him. Smoothly animated Pokémon that looked like they were ripped straight from the latest games flew, danced and battled right next to the DJ as he performed. The masked DJ played to both fans of his own EDM style and Pokémon gamers with eye-popping lasers that criss-crossed through Intuit Dome and fan-favorite Pokémon that appeared in short vignettes on screen.

In one section, a sleek Corviknight soared through a city as chill, beats thumped through the landscape. In another, the punk rock-inspired Toxtricity jammed on some projected scaffolding alongside Marshmello as his song “Come & Go” with Juice Wrld played. After that, the video wall froze over as white mist floated above it and snowflakes fell from the ceiling. Two fighters, Lucario and Greninja, appeared, broke through the frozen screen and fought on the shattered ice blocks in an epic battle. Every type of Pokémon was well represented: a creepy Gengar floated above Marshmello as he played in a crumbling, haunted castle before adorable critters like Eevee, Pikachu, Charmander, Squirtle and Bulbasaur frolicked in the tall grass.

Ken Lew Photography

The most jaw-dropping moment of the show came with a showdown between two beloved Pokémon foes: the earth-shaking Groudon and Kyogre, master of the seas. The “Ruby and Sapphire” legendaries faced off as the screen split between erupting volcanoes and crashing tsunami waves. For a second, everything went from color to black-and-white as the drama intensified and the two powerful Pokémon blasted each other with a hyper beam and hydro pump. The pumped-up crowd lost its mind as a real-life Pokémon battle unfolded in front of their eyes.

The show came to a close with one more appearance from a legendary Pokémon: Mewtwo from the original games. The all-powerful, psychic Pokémon loomed large on the screen then telekinetically lifted rocks and even a mini, animated Marshmello as the beats played. The DJ then closed his set with his song “Happier” as a montage of Pokémon danced the night away.

In its 30 years, Pokémon has never attempted a large-scale concert like this, but it proved to be a hit for both longtime fans and EDM ravers. Cosplayers packed Intuit Dome dressed as their favorite Pokémon and trainers from the TV show, ready to jam all night. Hopefully the success of the Intuit Dome show and the upcoming London concert pave the way for more musical Pokémon events as the franchise looks ahead to its next 30 years.

title: Jessica Biel Says ‘7th Heaven’ Reboot Will ‘Modernize’ the Show Now That TV Has ‘Less Limitations’: ‘We Were Very Careful About What Our Audience Wanted’
summary: Nearly 20 years since the conclusion of “7th Heaven,” and over a year since the news broke about its reboot, original star Jessica Biel is giving fans an update on the new iteration of the show, including how she plans to “modernize” it for today’s audience and what she hopes to accomplish on set as […]
content:
Nearly 20 years since the conclusion of “7th Heaven,” and over a year since the news broke about its reboot, original star Jessica Biel is giving fans an update on the new iteration of the show, including how she plans to “modernize” it for today’s audience and what she hopes to accomplish on set as a producer.

“What we want to create, how we want to modernize it, is really the things that are happening for teenagers and families that have teenagers all the way down to the youngest child — technology-based issues, school stuff, bullying stuff, drugs, alcohol,” Biel said on a recent episode of Collider Ladies Night. “All of those things we want to address in a very real way, which is, I think, what the original kind of gently touched on, but we were very careful about what our audience wanted. We had a lot of limitations. We have less limitations now.”

Created by Brenda Hampton and produced by Aaron Spelling, “7th Heaven” debuted on The WB (later The CW) in 1996 and concluded in 2007. The show proved to be a major early hit for the network, ultimately airing for 11 seasons and nearly 250 episodes. The show followed the Camden family and their seven children in the fictional town of Glen Oak, Calif., where Eric was a Protestant minister. In addition to Biel, the cast also included Stephen Collins, Catherine Hicks, Barry Watson, David Gallagher, Beverley Mitchell, Mackenzie Rosman, Nikolas Brino, and Lorenzo Brino.

Popular on Variety

When asked if the original show could withstand the test of time, Biel explained that the core theme — family — was “what was working back then.” “I’m looking for what I can watch with my kids on television. It’s limited. I cannot watch a lot of these things with them, and they love TV, and it’s my business. My husband and I are in this business together doing these things, and we can’t share a lot of that with our kids,” she continued. “So, I think the idea of whatever faith you want to have, that’s important. That we don’t have a lot on television, whether you believe that or go down that road or not. There are a lot of people that really do want to walk down that road, so I think some kind of faith, some kind of family, community, and maybe something not so jaded, like something a little bit more glass-half-full. It’s not that it’s soft, because it’s realistic.”

As a producer, Biel plans to create a “safe place for people to be really creative and really vulnerable,” she explained.

“When I’m on set as a producer, I’m always thinking about the safety net of the set and the communication that you hope you can have — free-flowing communication with your actors and your crew,” she added. “You just want to create a safe place for people to be really creative and really vulnerable, because a lot of the stuff that I’m doing now, the content that I’m doing now, it’s emotional stuff. It’s people really putting themselves out there on the chopping block emotionally, and if you don’t have that space protected, I think it’s hard. It’s hard to give those kinds of performances.”

Variety exclusively broke the news of the “7th Heaven” reboot back in May 2025. At the time, sources said that the new iteration of the show would focus on a diverse family, and that none of the original cast members would appear.

title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores $19.5 Million in Huge Second Weekend, ‘Clayface’ Leads With $24 Million Debut
summary: Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office. Although Warner Bros. and DC’s R-rated “Clayface” was comfortably at No. 1 with $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, A24’s […]
content:
Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office.

Although Warner Bros. and DC’s R-rated “Clayface” was comfortably at No. 1 with $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, A24’s buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc “You Can See Everything” was surprisingly close after defying box office expectations again. The stranger-than-fiction film collected a spectacular $19.5 million while expanding to 2,655 venues in its sophomore outing.

Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are 28% above its launch of $15.6 million from 855 theaters, which marked the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years. So far, the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed movie has earned a huge $45.1 million domestically to date. After capturing the zeitgeist and selling out screenings across the coasts, awards sages are predicting it could become the first documentary to ever score a best picture nomination at the Oscars.

Popular on Variety

“Opening ‘You Can See Everything’ in 855 theaters was a really smart move, allowing the film to establish itself and build momentum before going much wider,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “The fact that we’re seeing a documentary deliver such a significant second-weekend increase is remarkable.”

“Clayface” arrived on the lower end of the studio’s expectations of $25 million to $35 million. The antihero adaptation earned another $19 million overseas from 76 markets for a global tally of $43 million. Along with a positive reception, the film seems well-positioned theatrically because it cost just $44 million to produce. That’s a way smaller budget compared to DC’s other recent tentpoles, including this July’s “Supergirl” and 2025’s “Superman.” Although “Superman” was a decent hit with $618 million against a $225 million budget, “Supergirl” was a setback for the newly relaunched comic book studio after bombing with $126 million against a $170 million budget. Meanwhile, DC has found success on streaming with its “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns” shows for HBO Max. DC wanted to keep costs low on “Clayface” because it’s a body-horror thriller that’s much darker than those family-friendly adventures. Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Audiences enjoyed the film, which holds an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.

“Over the years, there have been a dozen spinoffs of superhero villains and antiheroes, from ‘Joker’ to ‘Venom’ to ‘Kraven the Hunter,'” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This picture was wisely conceived as something different, costing a fraction of what those films cost, and it should be profitable when it finishes all ancillary business.”

“Clayface” opened alongside a smattering of new releases, including Laika’s stop-motion animated “Wildwood,” Black Bear’s offbeat romantic comedy “Wicker” and Sony’s literary adaptation “Klara and the Sun,” starring Jenna Ortega.

“Wildwood” debuted at No. 3 with $11 million from 2,718 venues, launched above projections of $6 million to $8 million. It’s a promising start for original animation, which has been challenged in the years following the pandemic. And “Wildwood” has the benefit of sterling reviews (a rare 100% on Rotten Tomatoes) and audience scores (an “A” grade on CinemaScore exit polls), which should help the film stick around beyond its opening weekend. However, this movie carries a hefty $100 million price tag (stop-motion animation is labor-intensive and takes years to produce) and likely won’t turn a theatrical profit.

“This is a very good opening for a new animated film from outside of the studio development and distribution system,” says Gross. “Audiences love this movie, but it needs a very long run to recoup its costs.”

So far, “Wildwood” has collected just $3 million internationally from 11 markets. The movie hails from Laika Studios, best known for making the 2009 stop-motion fantasy “Coraline.” This is the company’s first release since 2019’s “Missing Link,” which opened to $6 million from 3,413 theaters and ended its run with $26 million globally. “Wildwood” was directed by Laika’s CEO Travis Knight and revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted.

“Wicker” captured fifth place with $5.75 million from 1,471 locations, a strong start for the low-budget film. Black Bear acquired the well-reviewed movie after Sundance for $2.5 million. Olivia Colman stars as an ostracized woman who commissions a local basketmaker to weave her a husband. Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy in the village.

“It is fantastic to see that the film is truly resonating with the audiences,” says Black Bear’s head of domestic theatrical distribution David Spitz. “This is a true testament to the filmmakers, cast, our innovative marketing, and our partnership with exhibition whose support proves that these types of films are what audiences want in their mix of movie-going experiences.”

“Klara and the Sun” collapsed at No. 15 with $720,000 from 880 locations. Sony scaled back the theatrical footprint after reviews panned the movie as “calamitous” and “confoundingly awful.” Luckily, the Taika Waititi-directed adaptation had a modest $20 million budget, so the studio’s inevitable box office losses won’t be too painful. Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel, “Klara and the Sun” takes place in the dystopian future as an obsolete companion android (Ortega) tries to bond with her new owner, a young sick girl named Josie.

Meanwhile Amazon MGM didn’t report grosses for Sacha Baron Cohen’s mockumentary “Ali G: Who Iz I?” after dialing down the release to just 125 theaters for two days. It’ll premiere soon on Prime Video.

Paramount’s video game reboot “Street Fighter” landed in fourth place with $8.6 million from 3,575 theaters in its second weekend, a painful 72% drop from its debut. The movie has generated $46.9 million in North America and $79.6 million worldwide to date. Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed “Street Fighter” for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution.

Disney and 20th Century’s “Whalefall,” too, took a tumble in its sophomore outing with $3.2 million from 3,065 theaters. The survival thriller, starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver swallowed by a sperm whale, dropped to 10th place on weekend charts and has earned $14.1 million domestically and $31.1 million globally to date. “Whalefall” cost $60 million and requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales.

Elsewhere, Netflix’s generation-spanning drama “La Bola Negra” earned $245,000 from nine locations — a decline of 12% despite expanding its theater count. So far, the streamer’s awards hopeful has collected $650,000 from two weekends in limited release. Netflix plans to keep “La Bola Negra” in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times, before the film’s Netflix release on Dec. 2.

title: ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers from “The New Stanford Prison Experiment,” now streaming on Netflix. “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” ends on a far more hopeful note than Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo’s original 1971 trial. The first iteration of the Stanford prison experiment took 24 white male college students (save one Asian American) […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers from “The New Stanford Prison Experiment,” now streaming on Netflix.

“The New Stanford Prison Experiment” ends on a far more hopeful note than Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo’s original 1971 trial.

The first iteration of the Stanford prison experiment took 24 white male college students (save one Asian American) and paid them $15 a day to participate in a two-week simulated prison environment in order to study the effects of incarceration. Students were randomly assigned to the roles of guards or inmates, with the guards pressured to maintain order by any means necessary. Participants fell into their roles a little too well and, after a prisoner rebellion, increasingly cruel forms of punishment from the guards and a number of students suffering mental breakdowns, the experiment was ended on the sixth day. It’s widely considered one of the most notorious, ethically compromised psychological studies in history.

Popular on Variety

And so, on Oct. 21, Netflix debuted “The New Stanford Prison Experiment,” a six-episode reality-TV version from executive producers Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth (“Top Chef”) that saw thirty entrants of various racial, geographical and economic backgrounds — including three women — partake in a two-week simulated prison environment, only this time in the decommissioned cell block of an actual working prison. Eight of them were assigned as guards, working in two separate shifts, and the other 22 as prisoners. Unlike the 1971 version, the show implemented safeguards to ensure protection, including background checks and psychological testing for all involved; informed consent; medics, psychologists and off-duty guards on call 24/7; a safe word (“pineapple”) if participants ever felt they needed to leave or talk to a therapist and/or producer; and conducted regular interviews with participants throughout. There was also a team of three experts on hand observing the proceedings: Alison Wood Brooks, a behavioral scientist who teaches at Harvard Business School; Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist; and Michael Cantrell, a former federal corrections officer.

Over the course of the experiment, five people bow out — the first, Larry Foy, a former convict who goes by the nickname “Scary Larry,” gets severely triggered by being in a prison environment again and demands to be removed. “Nobody thought it would affect him in the way that it did, but we knew he could make the decision for himself and relieve himself of the experiment if it became too much, which he in fact did,” Lipsitz explains to Variety. “I think he was surprised by how much it affected him.”

The experiment nearly unravels by day six (again) when two prisoners, Pete and Brandon, are placed in “23 and 1” for conspiring against the guards, meaning they must remain locked in their cell for 23 hours a day and are given 1 hour a day outside it for showering and recreation. Brandon nearly bails, but decides to stay after an emotional phone call with his mother. “We thought it would end on the same day that the original experiment did,” admits Lipsitz, adding that the Pete and Brandon predicament raises an interesting question for audiences: “Do you see them as ridiculous pains in the ass or antiheroes?”

To complicate matters further, producers implemented four “phases”: Transformation, Hierarchy, Role-Reversal and Self-Governance. During the Role-Reversal phase, the most punished inmates — Pete and Brandon among them — are made guards while the most power-obsessed guards, such as Chet Hudson, an oil rigger from Mississippi who put Pete and Brandon in “23 and 1,” and Chris Lee, a 41-year-old startup CEO with a more kumbaya approach, are converted to inmates. Chet, uncomfortable with being powerless, quits after a day; meanwhile, the inmates who’d been fed up with Pete and Brandon for their mischief-making in their previous role begin crowding the duo and come perilously close to attacking them when the three female guards from the other shift intervene to stop it. They’re led by Laura Berens, a CEO and entrepreneur, who emerges as the finest leader of the experiment with her firm-but-fair methods.

“As a woman running the show, it was important to reflect the female experience as well and look at that in terms of power dynamics,” offers Lipsitz. “I think that Laura really emerged as the strongest leader of the whole series when they’d ended their shift and checked on them to see how it was going to go. It was almost motherly concern. They did not want a prison riot.”

Laura Berens has the guards’ attention in “The Stanford Prison Experiment.” Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026

As for that hopeful ending, during the final Self-Governance phase, all of the rules are thrown out the window, and the prisoners are allowed to do as they please. Though some inmates, including Lee, demand to stay and finish the experiment, a fellow prisoner, the Black comedian Mike Paramore, convinces him that it would be far more powerful if all the prisoners walked out of the facility together, arm-in-arm, suggesting an image of racial unity. And that’s what they do, ending the experiment on the thirteenth day.

“We felt it was really powerful and did not see that coming at all,” says Lipsitz. “I would hesitate to come to any conclusions about race and gender, but I think it holds up a mirror to a lot of those issues and is very revealing,” Cutforth remarks. “It’s something me and Jane are particularly proud of and felt privileged to be able to make the show.”

“One really fascinating thing about it is, there’s a lot of talk about the manosphere and the ‘male loneliness epidemic,’ and having those men together with no phones, alcohol or women, these men from all different backgrounds really bonded in an amazing way,” Lipsitz adds. “There were conversations in there where you could hear that they’d learned from each other and were fascinated by other people’s POVs — people they would have never come across in society except for here. It seemed like a very positive experience for them, and for the women as well.”

Will there be a second season of “The New Stanford Prison Experiment?” Lipsitz and Cutforth hope so.

“I would love to have the opportunity to do it again, for sure,” shares Cutforth. “That prison setting is an incredible petri dish, and I would love to see more things play out there.”

“Obviously, we couldn’t do it the same way,” says Lipstiz. “I think it would be interesting to do it with women and ask some different questions or frame it differently. But we’re really proud of it and hope people watch, debate and think about what it means in modern society. That’s the most you can ask for.”

title: Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love’ Returns to No. 1 on Albums Chart Following ‘Expectations’ Remix
summary: Following the release of her “Expectations” remix with Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo returns to the top of the Billboard 200 with “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” earning a third total week at No. 1. Rodrigo initially released “You Seem Pretty Sad” back in June, bowing atop the chart and remaining […]
content:
Following the release of her “Expectations” remix with Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo returns to the top of the Billboard 200 with “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” earning a third total week at No. 1.

Rodrigo initially released “You Seem Pretty Sad” back in June, bowing atop the chart and remaining there for another week. On October 15, she put out her first-ever remix of “Expectations” with Roan, who also made her feature debut, sending the album back to the top with 75,000 equivalent album units and bumping Taylor Swift’s “The Life of a Showgirl” from the summit.

Popular on Variety

Zach Bryan enters the chart at No. 2 with his latest “Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs,” which earned 65,500 equivalent album units. It marks his sixth album to break the top 10 and his second release this year following “With Heaven on Top,” which landed at No. 1 in January. “Young Manhood” arrived with just a few days’ notice, touting guest appearances from Lana Del Rey and Turnpike Troubadours and building momentum towards his tour that kicks off in April 2027.

Elsewhere, Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem” remains at No. 3, while Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” holds at No. 4. Rounding out the top 10 are Noah Kahan’s “The Great Divide,” followed by Drake’s “Habibti” at No. 7, Kahan’s “Stick Season” at No. 8, Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” at No. 9 and SZA’s “SOS,” which returns to the top 10 nearly four years after its initial release in December 2022.

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Star Stephan James on Paying Tribute to Carl Weathers with His Red Carpet Look: ‘I Can Literally Walk in His Shoes Yet Again’
summary: Stephan James paid tribute to Carl Weathers by donning a white suit on Saturday at the AFI Fest screening of his new movie, “I Play Rocky.” James plays the late actor in the Peter Farrelly film, which chronicles the making of Sylvester Stallone’s “Rocky” in 1976. ” “This is a three-piece custom King & Bay […]
content:
Stephan James paid tribute to Carl Weathers by donning a white suit on Saturday at the AFI Fest screening of his new movie, “I Play Rocky.”

James plays the late actor in the Peter Farrelly film, which chronicles the making of Sylvester Stallone’s “Rocky” in 1976. ”

“This is a three-piece custom King & Bay bespoke suit,” James told me while walking the red carpet at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. “My friends in Toronto at King & Bay remade this suit for me because Carl Weathers wore the exact same suit to the ‘Rocky II’ premiere in Philadelphia. It was a three-piece white suit, and I had them remake it so I can literally walk in his shoes yet again.”

Stephan James at the “I Play Rocky” screening during AFI Fest at the TCL Chinese Theatre on Oct. 24 in Hollywood. Variety via Getty Images

The idea came from James’ publicist Samantha Hill. He accessorized with a rose brooch. “Carl had an actual rose, so this is my little twist on it,” James said. “I’m doing something a little more timeless with a brooch.”

Popular on Variety

Weathers played fighter Apollo Creed, who fought Rocky Balboa in the first two “Rocky” movies before becoming his coach in the third installment, and died in “Rocky IV” during a match against Ivan Drago (Dolph Lundgren). Weathers passed away in 2024.

James also told me he had a little chat with Michael B. Jordan after he was cast as Weathers. Jordan played Apollo’s son in the three “Creed” movies. “‘Hey, I’m gonna be your daddy, Mike. I’m gonna be your daddy,’” James said. “So yeah, we had to talk.”

Stephan James as Carl Weathers in “I Play Rocky” and Michael B. Jordan as Apollo Creed in 2023’s “Creed III.” ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection

“I Play Rocky” stars Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone. The film has been earning critical raves — and Oscar buzz — since its premiere in early September at the Toronto International Film Festival.

The movie, from Amazon MGM, will be released in limited theaters on Nov. 6, followed by a wider release on Nov. 20.

title: Holland Taylor Says She Was ‘Never Paid Very Well’ on ‘Two and a Half Men’: ‘I Got Four Emmy Nominations, and They Never Gave Me a Raise’
summary: Holland Taylor is speaking out about why she didn’t renew her contract on “Two and a Half Men.” The actress spent six years as Evelyn Harper, the mother of Charlie (Charlie Sheen) and Alan (Jon Cryer), on the CBS sitcom. She recently revealed that part of the reason she left the show was due to […]
content:
Holland Taylor is speaking out about why she didn’t renew her contract on “Two and a Half Men.”

The actress spent six years as Evelyn Harper, the mother of Charlie (Charlie Sheen) and Alan (Jon Cryer), on the CBS sitcom. She recently revealed that part of the reason she left the show was due to the small paycheck.

“They never paid me very well on that show. I was paid on that show what I had made on a series like eight years before or something,” Taylor said on the “Alchemy with Anthony Mason” podcast. “And I got four Emmy nominations, and they never gave me a raise. They usually do.”

Taylor was nominated four times for supporting actress during her time on the sitcom. After the sixth season, she declined to renew her contract and instead returned occasionally as a guest star.

Popular on Variety

“I stopped being under contract. So, in other words, they would say, ‘Can you do a guest appearance at the end of March?’ And I would say, ‘No, I cannot,’” she said. “I only did it if I wanted to do it.”

Taylor said the producers were “astonished” by her decision, but she appreciated having flexibility in scheduling.

“I loved a lot about that show, but they were not full of courtesies,” Taylor added. “In any case, when the six years were up, I said, ‘I don’t want to be on a contract anymore, but I will visit the show occasionally if you want.’ I mean, I did play the boys’ mother.”

The actress said the team thought she was negotiating and told her they could not afford to pay her more. “I said, ‘You could actually pay me the cost of this building, but don’t bother because I don’t want to continue on under contract,'” she said. “And they said, ‘But we can’t afford to give you more.’ I said, ‘I’m cool with it. I just will come back as a guest from time to time.'”

“Two and a Half Men” ran for 12 seasons from 2003 to 2015. In 2011, Sheen left the show after public struggles with substance abuse.

title: Man Arrested on ‘Miami Vice ‘85’ Brooklyn Set After Brandishing a Knife
summary: The Brooklyn set of “Miami Vice ‘85” was disrupted when a man was arrested after brandishing a knife around crew members on Friday. The man, whom the New York Police Department confirmed as 23-year-old Alex Perez of Brooklyn, was charged with menacing and criminal possession of a weapon after being arrested around 11 p.m. The […]
content:
The Brooklyn set of “Miami Vice ‘85” was disrupted when a man was arrested after brandishing a knife around crew members on Friday.

The man, whom the New York Police Department confirmed as 23-year-old Alex Perez of Brooklyn, was charged with menacing and criminal possession of a weapon after being arrested around 11 p.m. The NYPD also confirmed to Variety that the event took place on the film set, near Washington Cemetery. No injuries were reported.

TMZ first released footage of the incident, which showed Perez being handcuffed before a large butcher knife was removed from his sweatshirt pocket by a police officer. The outlet reported that Perez has 5 prior arrests, including for alleged gang-related activities, assault with a firearm and burglary.

Popular on Variety

Variety first reported that a “Miami Vice” reboot was in the works with Austin Butler and Michael B. Jordan back in Oct. 2025 before the film got an official title in April 2026. Jordan will star as Ricardo “Rico” Tubbs with Butler playing James “Sonny” Crockett. First look images of the two in character dropped earlier this month when filming began.

Per the film’s logline, Kosinski’s “Miami Vice ’85” will explore “the glamour and corruption of mid-80’s Miami” and is “inspired by the pilot episode and first season of the landmark television series that influenced culture and set the style of everything from fashion to filmmaking.” Dan Gilroy penned the film’s script, based on characters created by Anthony Yerkovich from the TV series.

“Miami Vice ‘85” is scheduled for an Aug. 6, 2027 theatrical release.

content:
Documentary NAZA, recently acquired by Neon mid-theatrical rollout, passed the $1 million mark this weekend. The Venice-premiering film, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (two of the Oscar winning directors of No Other Land) is eyeing $74.5k on 73 screens in week 4, for a cume of $1.07 million. Producer The Guardian had been self-distributing the explosive Israel-Gaza doc, which will continue to add more cities throughout October and November.

It’s a crowded specialty market. Neon‘s Once Upon A Time In Harlem is eyeing an estimated $50.2k for its second weekend on three screens. That’s a $157.3k cume for the generation-spanning documentary. The distributor’s Cannes Palme d’Or-winning drama Fjord is at a $333k weekend (in week 3) for a cume of $694k.

Other limited releases: La Bola Negra from Netflix had a limited expansion to nine theaters for a solid 3-day gross of $245k in week 2 for cume of $650k. Alamo Brooklyn was a top theater for the TIFF Audience Award-winner and these are solid numbers following a muscular debut last weekend. It’s the very first film the giant streamer is accompanying into theaters with official box office grosses.

Watch on Deadline

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York from Sony Pictures Classics, critically acclaimed and starring John Turturro, opened in 6 theaters to $156k. AMC Lincoln Square led with $33k, boosted by Q&As.

Mubi released Cannes Best Director-winner, Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, at 4 theaters in New York and Los Angeles to an $83.8k opening weekend. Mubi noted strong audience demand with sold out shows across all four locations.

Moderate: Black Bear’s Wicker starring Olivia Coleman and Alexander Skarsgard is striking a chord with women, debuting to $5.75 million on $1,417 screens and a no. 5 spot.

Klara and the Sun (Sony) opened to $725k at 880 locations.

A Talent for Murder from Bleecker Street starring Helen Mirren as Patricia Highsmith debuted at 876 locations for a 3-day gross of $717.8k. Bleecker’s Alex Gibny’s doc Musk grossed $71k at 63 theaters for a $643k cume.

Jailer 2 from Shloka Entertainments hit $1.16 million in week 2 from 262 theaters for a cume of $7.2 million, as per Rentrak. By Nelson Dilipkumar. Stars Rajinikanth, Hrithik Roshan.

Wide: The fall indie crown continues to travel with A24’s You Can See Everything, at no. 2 this weekend in an expansion to 2,655 screens for an estimated gross of $19.5 million and cume of $45.1 million.

Fathom Entertainment’ presentation of Laika’s beautifully crafted stop-motion animation Wildwood followed at no. 3 on 2,779 screens with an $11.78 million debut.

Focus Features Sense and Sensibility, the latest adaptation of the beloved Jane Austen novel, on 2,572 screens in week 2, is at a $3.4 million weekend and a $16.7 million cume.

title: Man Arrested On ‘Miami Vice 85’ Brooklyn Set After Threatening Crew With Butcher Knife
summary: Filming on Miami Vice ’85 was disrupted on Friday night when a man threatened a member of the production with a butcher knife. According to an NYPD spokesperson, 23-year-old Alex Perez of Brooklyn was arrested at around 11:15pm on charges of menacing and criminal possession of a weapon after police were called to the vicinity […]
content:
Filming on Miami Vice ’85 was disrupted on Friday night when a man threatened a member of the production with a butcher knife.

According to an NYPD spokesperson, 23-year-old Alex Perez of Brooklyn was arrested at around 11:15pm on charges of menacing and criminal possession of a weapon after police were called to the vicinity of Avenue N and McDonald Avenue.

A member of the production team told police that Perez drew the knife after a verbal dispute, “causing him to become fearful for his safety.”

Perez was taken into custody and the knife was recovered with no injuries. Deadline has reached out to Universal for a comment.

Filming began this month on Miami Vice ’85 around New Jersey and New York City, where Michael B. Jordan has been seen shooting in character as Ricardo Tubbs.

Watch on Deadline

Last year, Universal set a reboot of the 1980s NBC series from director Joseph Kosinski and a script by Dan Gilroy and Eric Warren Singer. Jordan was cast as Tubbs in the movie, with Austin Butler taking on the role of Sonny Crockett.

The cast also includes Alden Ehrenreich, Whitney Peak, Camila Morrone, Danny Ramirez, John Leguizamo, Andrew Schulz, Walton Goggins, André Holland, Michael Irby and Haley Lu Richardson.

title: Hudson Williams Is Writing A Film, “Getting Tripped Up” Over Ex-Hockey Player Character
summary: In addition to Season 2 of Heated Rivalry, Hudson Williams is taking some inspiration from the ice for another future project. […]
content:
In addition to Season 2 of Heated Rivalry, Hudson Williams is taking some inspiration from the ice for another future project.

The actor recently admitted he’s “getting tripped up” on a script he’s writing, which includes a character who is an ex-hockey player, similar to his Ottawa Centaurs player role Shane Hollander on Heated Rivalry.

“I’m writing a movie right now, but one character is an ex-hockey player,” he noted to Entertainment Weekly. “We were like, ‘But if we have this hockey player and then you’ve done a hockey show…'”

Williams continued, “We’re getting tripped up on it and we’re considering other sports, but for some reason this character just made way more sense being an ex-hockey player. It’s almost like you have to bust through the prison of your own mind or construct of your own mind.”

Watch on Deadline

With Rachel Reid’s Game Changer novel The Long Game serving as the basis for Season 2 of Heated Rivalry, production began on the sophomore season of Jacob Tierney’s Crave Original series adaptation in Canada in August.

Deadline recently reported that Justice Smith, Charlie Gillespie, Daniel Diemer, Shaheen Jafargholi, Emily Hampshire, Edvin Ryding, Robert Naylor, Sabrina Jalees, Priyanka, Brendan Morgan, David Tomlinson, Gerry Dee, Michelle Mylett, Lauren Chan and Nick Stahl have been cast in Season 2, which is set to premiere in spring 2027.

title: ‘Clayface’ Beams $43M WW Opening, Delivers Paramount-Warner Bros. Second No. 1 Weekend Win Since Merger – Global Box Office
summary: The newly combined Paramount-Warner Bros merger (aka Skydance) saw its second back-to-back No. 1 weekend win at the global box office with DC’s Clayface which filed $43M WW. Is this the new norm? A consecutive weekend win by Skydance? Should the platinum studio Disney be worried? Even if A24’s You Can See Everything pops to […]
content:
The newly combined Paramount-Warner Bros merger (aka Skydance) saw its second back-to-back No. 1 weekend win at the global box office with DC’s Clayface which filed $43M WW.

Is this the new norm? A consecutive weekend win by Skydance? Should the platinum studio Disney be worried?

Even if A24’s You Can See Everything pops to No. 1 over the dead zone of Halloween stateside, Warner Bros Animation’s The Cat in the Hat will bring Skydance back to No. 1 over the first frame in November.

Though the global opening here for Clayface is under the $45M hoped for, it’s still solid for the net $44M costing feature (before P&A), especially given its excellent audience exits. That A- is one of a few earned by horror titles, the others being Get Out, Weapons and Obsession. DC Bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran reportedly covered their faces after watching Clayface for the first time, literally scared by all the gross scenes. That’s what fanboys and moviegoers are responding to in the movie.

Watch on Deadline

The global opening here in pure dollars isn’t far from what Universal’s Other Mommy from Blumhouse Atomic Monster did a couple of weeks ago, that being a $45.6M start (but in 50 territories). The foreign start for that D+ horror movie was $17.8M while Clayface here was $19M from 76 territories. Domestic was No. 1 with $24M, over A24’s second frame of 3-hour documentary You Can See Everything. By the way, that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim co-directed nonfiction film doesn’t start opening abroad until Nov. 12 in Australia, followed by UK on Nov. 20 via A24. Sony is handling the bulk of foreign as Deadline first told you with translated prints being prepped at the time of this report. We hear that Palace Cinemas in Australia just broke the record for their biggest single day of pre-sales ever thanks to You Can See Everything, doubling the chain’s previous record held by Taylor Swift: Eras Tour.

In regards to Clayface‘s territory grosses, it exceeded or met Other Mommy‘s first weekend in the UK ($2.6M), Australia ($1.3M versus $1.1M), France ($1.2M) and Brazil ($879K vs. $751K). Clayface was under Other Mommy in Mexico ($1.4M to $1.9M), Italy ($873K vs $2.2M), Spain ($721K vs. $986K), UAE ($626K versus $658K), Saudi Arabia ($561K versus $601K) and Taiwan ($404K vs. $424K). Other Mommy didn’t open in Germany or Korea yet as it respectively opens there on Oct. 29 and Nov. 18, but Clayface did $593K in Germany and $589K in Korea.

Meanwhile, in reported grosses, Clayface‘s opening in Italy beat Supergirl‘s first weekend of $717,7K and Korea’s first weekend of $422K.

Arabella Olivia Clark in ‘Other Mommy’ Universal Pictures/Everett Collection

Speaking of Other Mommy, the Universal title’s third global weekend came in at $9.2M WW in 68 territories ($5.3M int’l, $3.85M domestic) with a strong No. 2 opening in Poland of $464K behind local hit Lalka and ahead of Black Phone 2, Smile and M3GAN. Also, France had a solid hold of $900K for a cume of $2.5M above Black Phone at the same point in time. Global running cume is $94.8M with $43.3M from offshore and $51.5M stateside.

Andrew Koji as Ryu in ‘Street Fighter’ Paramount Pictures

Paramount Warner Bros can call dibs on No. 2 at the global weekend B.O. with the second frame of Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter with $16.8M WW ($8.2M from 65 markets for a foreign cume of $32.7M) and running global cume of $76.3M. As we told you, North America ate floor with a -72% plummet of $8.6M. The feature take of the hit 1980s video game held onto its Imax screens around the globe which delivered $2.5M for a near $12M running circuit cume. Top second frame holdovers for Street Fighter were UK ($1.3M, -58%, No. 4, $5.6M cume); Australia ($800K, -45%, No. 2 and $2.6M cume), France ($744K, -33%, No. 9 and $2.2M cume), Mexico ($659K, -63%, No. 4 and near $3M cume) and Germany ($485K, -42%, No. 9 and running cume of $1.6M).

L-R: Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) and Mac McKeel (Arthur Knight in ‘ Wildwood Courtesy of Laika

Laika’s stop-motion animated pic Wildwood minted $11.3M stateside with another $3M in its foreign launch from 11 territories via FilmNation for a $14.3M WW start. UK looks to be landing an opening around $1.4M after a Friday-Saturday take of $931K that’s 15% ahead of Kubo and the Two Strings, and 22% ahead of The Boy and the Heron. Black Bear is handling the UK release. Kismet has Australia which is shaping up for a $567K opening, ahead of Laika’s Missing Link, Kubo and the Two String and The Boxtrolls. NZ is filing $58K. Notorious in Italy is looking at a $393K opening, with a Saturday $142,5K take ahead of Missing Link, Kubo and Boxtrolls. Wildwood via Beta Film in Spain is seeing a $292K opening from 232 cinemas, with an 8.4 rating on FilmAffinity, making it the highest rated release YTD on the platform. Netherlands via The Searchers is looking at $168K with a Saturday gross ahead of ParaNorman, Kubo, Missing Link and Coraline. Croatia is $25K, Serbia $6K, South Africa $33K, Singapore $29K and Italian speaking Switzerland is $2K. Wildwood‘s foreign rollout continues next weekend across Latin America, the Middle East, the Nordics and additional Eastern European markets. Mexico alone was Laika’s second-largest grossing market for the 2024 re-release of Coraline.



Sony/Constantin’s Resident Evil posted a sixth global weekend of $13.3M WW ($10.3M foreign, $3M stateside), and a running global of $384.5M. Foreign gross alone is $230.8M. China alone counts $65M. Pic is still in play at 67 markets on 26,400 screens.

Josh Hartnett and Dakota Johnson in ‘Verity’

Amazon MGM Studio’s Verity saw $7.2M abroad from 79 markets and another $3M stateside for a $10.2M WW for fourth frame that takes the worldwide tally to $162.7M ($91.2M foreign, $71.5M domestic). Newest opening was in South Korea with $179K at 445 screens, surpassing the lifetime of It Ends With Us ($124K) there to become the biggest Colleen Hoover feature adaptation of all-time. Holdovers include Germany ($1.3M at 626 screens, -30% ranked No. 2 with cume near $12M), UK ($861K at 531 screens, -41%, with a $14.4M tally), Australia ($577K this weekend from 274 screens, down -38% and ranked #3. The cume is now $8.1M) and Brazil ($525K from 900 screens, -56% for a No. 2 rank and near $10M cume).

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Director Lance Oppenheim Says Billy Evans ‘Didn’t Care About Being Seen Naked’; Evans Asked, ‘Want to Film Me Showering?’
summary: “You Can See Everything” audiences were expecting to be taken aback for a variety of reasons when watching the documentary, but a full-frontal shot of Elizabeth Holmes’ partner Billy Evans wasn’t something many foresaw experiencing in the theater. Lance Oppenheim, who co-directed the buzzy A24 doc with Nathan Fielder, has now revealed just how that […]
content:
“You Can See Everything” audiences were expecting to be taken aback for a variety of reasons when watching the documentary, but a full-frontal shot of Elizabeth Holmes’ partner Billy Evans wasn’t something many foresaw experiencing in the theater. Lance Oppenheim, who co-directed the buzzy A24 doc with Nathan Fielder, has now revealed just how that jarring shower scene came to be — and why Evans might have been fine with revealing all to begin with.

“I honestly don’t know,” Oppnehim said when asked why Evans would agree to appear naked in a recent GQ interview. “It’s beyond me, but I’ve heard interesting theories that people have when they see it,” he said, before getting into the technical details of how they shot it. “There’s a camera in the bathroom, there’s a camera that was on Nathan, there’s a camera outside the bathroom, and there’s an interaction that we see after Billy leaves where he sort of looks at the camera and smiles.”

Popular on Variety

“So I don’t know what that means, but I feel like there’s enough stuff in there that gives me the impression that maybe he was excited that people could see everything and that there was full access, I guess,” Oppenheim continued. “But it really beats me, honestly. We were in the car ride on the way back from the gym, and I said to Billy, ‘We will give you some time to shower.’ And Billy responded, ‘Want to film me showering?’ I offered to film him in a way that could avoid seeing his genitals, but Billy said he didn’t care about being seen naked.”

Ahead of the film’s release earlier this month, Evans admitted he hadn’t seen the doc while appearing on the “All-In” podcast. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said on the podcast, admitting that Holmes “looks insane” in the trailer.

Before hitting theaters on Oct. 16, “You Can See Everything” had been quietly in the works from Fielder and Oppenheim for more than three years. The doc offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

The film has been a major hit with audiences, bringing in $15.6 million from 855 theaters in its opening weekend (the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years) and adding another $19.5 million after expanding to 2,655 venues for its sophomore outing.

title: Peggy King, ‘George Gobel Show’ Actress and Singer of the ’50s, Dies at 96
summary: Peggy King, a 1950s television and recording star, died Sunday following a battle with Alzheimer’s at the Saunders House Assisted Living facility in Wynnewood, Pa. She was 96. King’s publicist, Alan Eicher, confirmed her death. King was a regular on the “George Gobel Show” from 1954-57. Gobel dubbed her “Pretty Perky Peggy King,” a nickname […]
content:
Peggy King, a 1950s television and recording star, died Sunday following a battle with Alzheimer’s at the Saunders House Assisted Living facility in Wynnewood, Pa. She was 96.

King’s publicist, Alan Eicher, confirmed her death.

King was a regular on the “George Gobel Show” from 1954-57. Gobel dubbed her “Pretty Perky Peggy King,” a nickname that stuck for the rest of her career. She was nominated for an Emmy Award for best female singer in 1955. She performed “Count Your Blessings” at the 1955 Academy Awards and co-hosted the Emmys in 1958.

King appeared on shows including Bob Hope’s “Chevy Show,” “American Bandstand,” “The Steve Allen Show,” “The Kraft Music Hall with Milton Berle,” “What’s My Line?,” “The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson,” “The Perry Como Show,” “The Garry Moore Show” and “The Jack Benny Program.” Her dramatic credits include roles on “Maverick” and “Dragnet.”

Popular on Variety

In 1952, she signed to an MGM contract, which led to a cameo in Vincente Minnelli’s “The Bad and the Beautiful,” in which she sang on the soundtrack album. She also appeared in “Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy.”

Mitch Miller signed her to a long-term contract with Columbia Records, where she made two best-selling albums. She had a string of hit singles, and composer Arthur Hamilton wrote “Cry Me a River” for her but Miller would not let her record the song.

King starred with Tab Hunter in the television musical “Hans Brinker or the Silver Skates.” She also starred in a TV musical version of “Jack and the Beanstalk” with Joel Grey, Celeste Holm and Cyril Ritchard. She played a stewardess in the 1957 thriller “Zero Hour!” with Dana Andrews and Linda Danell.

She was inducted into the Broadcast Pioneers Hall of Fame in 2010 and was among the first celebrities honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. King’s last released recording was the album “Songs a la King,” released in 2016. She performed regularly in the Philadelphia area, New York and Los Angeles as late as 2014.

King was born Feb. 16, 1930, to Floyd Henry King and Margaret Finan in Greensburg, Pennsylvania. She graduated from Ravenna High School and sang on radio in Cleveland. She was a regular on “The Mel Torme Show” for CBS and had a successful commercial jingle for Hunt’s Tomato Sauce.

King is survived by her daughter, Suzy Rudofker, and son-in-law, Dwain Goforth.

title: Hudson Williams Says He’s Writing a Film Featuring an ‘Ex-Hockey Player’ and Is ‘Getting Tripped Up’ by ‘Heated Rivalry’ Parallels
summary: Hudson Williams is working on a new film and is “getting tripped up” over a “Heated Rivalry” parallel. Prior to the success of the Canadian queer hockey romance that catapulted the actor to fame over the past year, Williams wrote and directed several short films, including “Soakers,” “Buttons” and “Inside Augustine Mendoza’s Quotidian Apartment.” Now, […]
content:
Hudson Williams is working on a new film and is “getting tripped up” over a “Heated Rivalry” parallel.

Prior to the success of the Canadian queer hockey romance that catapulted the actor to fame over the past year, Williams wrote and directed several short films, including “Soakers,” “Buttons” and “Inside Augustine Mendoza’s Quotidian Apartment.” Now, the actor says he is writing a new project where one character is a former hockey player.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly for “Yaga,” the Canadian witchy detective-thriller Williams stars in, the actor responded to co-star Carrie-Anne Moss’ hang-up over referencing real-life friend Keanu Reeves’ “John Wick” franchise in the show.

Popular on Variety

“I’m writing a movie right now, but one character is an ex-hockey player,” he said. “We were like, ‘But if we have this hockey player and then you’ve done a hockey show…’ We’re getting tripped up on it and we’re considering other sports, but for some reason this character just made way more sense being an ex-hockey player. It’s almost like you have to bust through the prison of your own mind or construct of your own mind.”

The actor did not elaborate on the nature of the project. It’s far from the only thing Williams is currently or recently working on: “Yaga” premiered on Oct. 23, and production began on the second season of “Heated Rivalry” in August. He will also appear in the dark comedic thriller “Apparatus” opposite Dylan O’Brien, and in the ensemble culinary thriller “Tyrant” with Charlize Theron, Julia Garner, Demi Moore and Omar Apollo.

title: ‘Wicker’ Stars Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Elizabeth Debicki on Making the ‘Very Silly,’ ‘Really Heartbreaking’ Film: ‘It’s Not Just a Slapstick or Sex Comedy’
summary: When Elizabeth Debicki arrived on set for “Wicker,” the first thing she saw was Alexander Skarsgård wading through water — full-frontal. But it wasn’t Skarsgård in the flesh; he was “stark naked as wicker.” “I turned the corner, and I was like, ‘Hi, Alex!’ and I went bright red because my brain couldn’t compute what […]
content:
When Elizabeth Debicki arrived on set for “Wicker,” the first thing she saw was Alexander Skarsgård wading through water — full-frontal. But it wasn’t Skarsgård in the flesh; he was “stark naked as wicker.”

“I turned the corner, and I was like, ‘Hi, Alex!’ and I went bright red because my brain couldn’t compute what it was seeing,” Debicki tells Variety, sitting alongside Skarsgård and their co-star Olivia Colman in a hotel suite at the Chateau Marmont in L.A. “I was just like ‘Oh my God! Welcome to Budapest, I guess.’”

From married filmmakers Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, “Wicker” follows the relationship between an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) and her fantastical husband (Skarsgård), who is handcrafted for her by the local basket weaver (Peter Dinklage). When the wicker husband proves to be a better man and partner than the rest of the married men in the village, jealousy erupts, and the unlikely couple must figure out how to preserve their simple life amid the chaos and vitriol. (And yes, Straw-Skarsgård is on full display in the Black Bear film, now playing in theaters.)

Popular on Variety

While Debicki needed a moment to grapple with the sight of a naked wicker man, Colman’s reaction mirrored her character falling in love at first sight.

“It was amazing because we’d all been looking at images for 18 months or so, and then to see it in the flesh, it was amazing,” Colman said. “That [feeling] of, ‘Oh my god, it’s going to work!’

The Oscar winner was the first to see Skarsgård in his full wicker suit and prosthetic makeup. The prototype had been sculpted after Skarsgård’s features, but when the Weta Workshop artists tried it on someone else in New Zealand, it almost worked, but not quite.

“If it doesn’t quite work, it looks like a horror film because it looks like you cut someone’s face off and glued it onto your own, and that wasn’t quite the tone we wanted to go for here,” Skarsgård explains. “So, it was a lot of anticipation and excitement and a lot of nerves because it was like, ‘Oh shit! If it doesn’t work, then we’re kind of screwed.”

Thankfully, Colman’s exuberant reaction eased any of Skarsgård’s fears. “It was an incredible day that I’ll never forget. Putting it on and then it helped me find the physicality of the character and then stepping out of the trailer and having Olivia outside going [gasps],” he recalls. “You can see how intricate and how beautiful the work was, and the fact that once it was glued onto my face, it actually moved with my movements. It’s even better than we imagined.”

The cast’s multilayered reaction is exactly what moviegoers can expect when watching “Wicker.” The film is intended to warm your heart and make you laugh, but it’s also guaranteed to make you blush. Audiences got their first peek at the film with a steamy three-minute trailer filled with sexual innuendo and hard-as-wood jokes. Since then, the marketing for the Black Bear film has taken on a life of its own, with playful promotional products like hand-woven nipple pasties, a popcorn bucket shaped like the wicker man’s torso and splinter removal kits.

But the film itself dares to go much deeper. “It’s not just a slapstick or sex comedy,” Skarsgård says. “They did an amazing job with this, and I hope and think and believe that people will go on this journey, be excited with all the twists and turns.”

In an era of box-office unpredictability, the “Wicker” cast isn’t worried about moviegoers embracing the film’s big swing. The stars believe the fanciful romance’s originality is enough to attract moviegoers to the theater — as evidenced by the post-trailer buzz. “Wicker” captured fifth place with $5.75 million from 1,471 locations, a “strong start” for the low-budget indie, according to Variety‘s Rebecca Rubin. (Black Bear acquired the movie for $2.5 million after it generated buzz at Sundance Film Festival earlier this year.)

The movie is so much fun, but there’s also a lot of serious moments, and a good balance of raw emotional scenes. I wasn’t expecting it to be such a tender love story. How did you establish that balance?

Colman: That was all in El and Al’s [Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s] beautiful script. They just got the tone. So, you just had to follow it, and you couldn’t really go wrong. It can be hard to go from very silly to really heartbreaking, but because it was all done with realism, it worked better.

In my saddest moments in my life, I’ve definitely found myself laughing hysterically as well, which is a very human thing, pain and recovery, all those things. And El and Al just nailed it. It made our journey, our job easier.

What message about marriage and romance do you want audiences to take away from this?

Colman: Think wisely. Hopefully, the love you choose enhances your life, not diminishes it.

Debicki: It’s such a beautiful examination of the idea that loving someone is really looking in a mirror of yourself. You know that’s what’s so frightening. But I always think of the line when Olivia said, “Well, what does he know about love?” And the basket maker says, “Well, I imagine he learned it from you.” That’s what we do in life. We are constantly learning from each other. It’s also a really beautiful examination of the institution of marriage.

And a lot of this film is looking at what patriarchy does to women, the messaging of women needing to compete. That there’s a kind of scarcity complex that you must do it this way, and she rethinks the system and creates it in the image of herself that’s authentic, and in that she thrives, and that’s a really good conversation to have for women.”

Elizabeth Debicki on the “Wicker” set with directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer.

What do you think it says about audiences that they’re willing to come out and root for a wicker husband and a wife?

Colman: I think people are excited about something that’s original and different. I think audiences get patronized a bit like, “Oh, they like that film. We’ll do another five like that,” and there’s space for that. But there’s also space for something totally original and different. And El and Al had control of this.

Skarsgård: The fact that they did have complete creative control and they could have the freedom to make their own movie the way they wanted to make, without lots of chefs in the kitchen or with lots of nervous financiers being like, “Well, are we sure this is going to work?” It was really exciting to be part of that journey. Like we’re making something quite unique here. There’s freedom in that.

Debicki: We’re in a very difficult time for women. If you look at women in this country and patriarchal systems, a woman’s right to choose what they do with their bodies, and how they live their lives, and just pay disparity in general since the dawn of time. I mean, women rightfully are questioning things, and this movie is refreshing because it’s looking at these issues in a way that’s really accessible and entertaining, but there’s some serious conversations in this movie. I think it’s important to talk about that.

People have been having so much fun with their promo and the products that they’re making. What fun merch have you guys been into or seen recently?

Skarsgård: We got a splinter removal kit. And those 3D-printed wicker husband torsos. They’re popcorn buckets, and then you fill them with popcorn, popcorn out of like a wicker basket.

What about all the wicker puns? When have we reached the end?

Skarsgård: We have a good one.

Colman: 50 Shades of Hay.

Skarsgård: It’s been a lot of fun watching this. We all love the film and were very excited when the trailer came out, but you never ever expect that kind of reaction. I’ve never had a movie with that kind of reaction. It’s been really thrilling, and we’re excited to now share the whole movie, more than just those three minutes, with the world.

title: Amanda Seyfried Explains Turning Down ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ For Family: “Just Not For Me”
summary: After 12 years, three standalone movies and a holiday special, Amanda Seyfried appears to have no regrets turning down a Guardians of the Galaxy lead role. The Oscar nominee explained that the MCU role of Gamora was “just not for me,” noting she made the decision “for my family” to not take on the character, […]
content:
After 12 years, three standalone movies and a holiday special, Amanda Seyfried appears to have no regrets turning down a Guardians of the Galaxy lead role.

The Oscar nominee explained that the MCU role of Gamora was “just not for me,” noting she made the decision “for my family” to not take on the character, which was ultimately played by Zoe Saldaña.

“I think turning down Guardians of the Galaxy was just so obvious to me at the time,” she explained in a Q&A with SAG-AFTRA Foundation. “I’m like, ‘This is not going to be a hit. The tree and the raccoon are talking to each other. And also they’re all in space.’ And I was just like, ‘This will ruin my career if this is bad. And there’s a high chance that this could be bad.'”

Seyfried continued, “I mean, obviously I was wrong. But I still don’t take back that decision. I made it for myself. I made it for my family that I knew I wanted to have. And I just don’t want to spend all the time in the makeup trailer. I just can’t sit still anyway. I really don’t like stunts, and I don’t like heights, and I don’t like pretending the entire world. I need something to hold on to.”

Watch on Deadline

Starring opposite Chris Pratt’s Star-Lord, Saldaña starred as the green-skinned alien assassin in Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (2017) and Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 (2023), as well as 2022’s The Guardian of the Galaxy Holiday Special. She also played the character in Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and Avengers: Endgame (2019).

title: From ‘Hoop Dreams’ to ‘Flee’: The 20 Documentaries That Deserved a Best Picture Oscar Nomination
summary: In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case. While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been excluded from the top category […]
content:
In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case.

While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been excluded from the top category meant to honor the year’s best filmmaking. When the Academy expanded the Best Picture lineup from five to 10 after the snub of “The Dark Knight” (2008), the press release led with the possibility of a documentary getting recognized. That has yet to happen … perhaps until now?

That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.
