He was 90. A couple of years ago, Walter gave us a nice interview for the Roddenberry Archive.”

Koenig’s reps said in a statement, “Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece.

“Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in ‘Star Trek: The Original Series,’ Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond ‘Star Trek,’ his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film ‘Mr. Fleischmann,’ for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards — a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft…

“Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”

title: Damson Idris And Jonathan Levine Team On Apple And Chernin Thriller ‘Sacrament’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Following the global success of F1, Apple and Damson Idris have found their next high-profile project on which to team. Sources tell Deadline that Apple Original Films is coming on to develop Sacrament, a new feature with Jonathan Levine attached to direct and Idris attached to produce. Insiders add that film remains in early […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Following the global success of F1, Apple and Damson Idris have found their next high-profile project on which to team. Sources tell Deadline that Apple Original Films is coming on to develop Sacrament, a new feature with Jonathan Levine attached to direct and Idris attached to produce.

Insiders add that film remains in early development, though the plan is to develop the film as a starring vehicle for Idris, the F1 star. The project will hail from Apple Studios, and Chernin Entertainment will produce via its first-look feature deal with Apple.

Written by Enzo Mileti & Scott Wilson, the film follows two Chicago cops-turned-contractors who track a runaway thief to a remote and fortified township in Sacrament, UT. What begins as a routine job escalates into a battle where they are outnumbered, outgunned and forced to become better partners.

Watch on Deadline

Peter Chernin and David Ready will produce for Chernin Entertainment. Idris will produce under his Keep Quiet Productions banner, and Levine will produce alongside Gillian Bohrer through their company MegaMix.

Following the success of F1: The Movie, which grossed $634 million worldwide and scored multiple Oscar nominations including Best Picture, Idris and Apple were looking to partner again. It was Chernin that approached Idris with the script.

Idris is currently filming the the Miles Davis pic Miles & Juliette from director Bill Pohlad and also has the Netflix series The Lords’ Day, which he also executive produced.

As for Levine, the director has become sought after with buzz growing on his upcoming sports drama Mr. Irrelevant, which bows on Christmas Day. That buzz was so loud that Tom Cruise asked to see the film; he was so impressed he tapped Levine to helm his sequel to the hit Paramount sports pic Days of Thunder.

Sacrament marks the latest feature development for Apple and Chernin Entertainment, joining titles including One Month Mark, Last Flight Out and Five Secrets. Chernin Entertainment has also produced multiple projects for Apple TV including the epic Chief of War and the Emmy-nominated See both with Jason Momoa, Truth Be Told starring Octavia Spencer and Gabrielle Union, and Emmy-winning documentary series The War for Football.

Idris is repped by CAA, M88 and attorney John Meigs. Levine is repped by Goodman, Genow, Schenkman, Smelkinson & Christopher.

title: Microsoft Offers Buyouts To 60,000, A Quarter Of Its Workforce
summary: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to more than a quarter of its staff, some 60,000 people, as it looks to defray the cost of AI and data center spending. The buyouts will be offered to staffers at the vice president level or below in the U.S., Canada, India and the U.K. The Xbox, Windows, Copilot […]
content:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to more than a quarter of its staff, some 60,000 people, as it looks to defray the cost of AI and data center spending.

The buyouts will be offered to staffers at the vice president level or below in the U.S., Canada, India and the U.K. The Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance divisions could be impacted.

Workers who accept the buyouts will receive benefits similar to a standard severance package. Employees have until early December to decide if they want to offer, and would exit Dec. 31 if they do.

Microsoft, which reports quarterly earnings Wednesday, has a total workforce of about 223,000.

Watch on Deadline

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees on the company’s blog. “This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.”

The tech giant has been chipping away at its staff and Coleman is referring to the company’s first-ever voluntary retirement program offered to around 7% of U.S. employees, or 8,700 people, at the senior director level and below. About 30% of eligible employees took the buyout. The company apparently heard from others who might have taken the deal if they’d been eligible, so it’s offering a redo.

Between 3% to 5% of tech world employees offered buyouts usually take them.

The in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees, including a large number at its Xbox gaming unit.

The company has projected 2025 capital spending at some $190 billion, mostly on AI-related data centers and chips.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program,” Coleman said.

Earlier today, the co-CEOS of the newly created Skydance also announced voluntary buyouts for staff.

title: Anthropic Board Member Reed Hastings Says “Creative Destruction” Is The Main AI Risk
summary: Amid a flood of AI news Monday, Anthropic board member Reed Hastings expressed his view that artificial intelligence will threaten many companies but not likely the human race. Hastings, co-founder and former CEO of Netflix, joined the Claude maker’s board last year. In an appearance on the podcast On with Kara Swisher, Hastings addressed Anthropic […]
content:
Amid a flood of AI news Monday, Anthropic board member Reed Hastings expressed his view that artificial intelligence will threaten many companies but not likely the human race.

Hastings, co-founder and former CEO of Netflix, joined the Claude maker’s board last year. In an appearance on the podcast On with Kara Swisher, Hastings addressed Anthropic and the broader AI landscape in addition to weighing in on his alma mater’s recent struggles.

Multiple former Anthropic and OpenAI staffers made news in recent weeks by warning that there is a greater than 10% chance of human extinction within the next decade. Researcher Jacob Coxon, who did a flurry of media appearances after his doomsday prediction went viral on social media, “is not the ideal messenger,” Hastings said, but the message still “resonates” with the public.

“We lived through a terrible era with nuclear weapons where we could have blown each other up and there were times when it was close and I don’t want to repeat it,” Hastings said. “I don’t want to just because we can, get through a 10% chance of nuclear holocaust, let’s not do that again. So let’s keep the odds way, way low about what it can do. But on the same lens, you can get a lot of attention by saying the world’s going to end tomorrow. We humans, we’re very focused on Armageddon.”

Watch on Deadline

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, recently joined a chorus of top executives warning about the risk of harm from AI as it grows rapidly and becomes more sophisticated.

Anthropic, meanwhile, is looking to vault to the top ranks of companies by total valuation when it goes public, likely by mid-to-late-November. A prospectus it filed Monday with the SEC summarizing operating results, business risks, strategic goals and other information in a 400-page overview for investors, laid out a number of financials. Revenue grew 14-fold in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period of 2025, reaching $16.3 billion. Due in large part to a one-time charge, the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion.

The valuation of the company after the IPO on the Nasdaq, under the ticker symbol ANT, is in flux, but is estimated to be between $1.5 trillion-$2 trillion.

Hastings sees “creative destruction” as far more of a risk than anything apocalytpic about humanity itself. “Companies are going to get very competitive,” he said. “Take Oracle. There’ll be an Oracle challenger that will use AI and build an incredible database or set of applications that will be much lower cost. And that’s the creative destruction. It’s going to speed up capitalism and give entrepreneurs … [a way to] compete with everybody.”

Along with the blitz of Anthropic coverage, there were also major announcements from Meta and Microsoft. The former said it intends to raise $95 billion in equity financing aimed at helping it push deeper into AI, while the latter tech giant said it was offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as it shifts resources toward AI.

title: CNN And Politico Again Are Barred From Air Force One
summary: CNN and Politico again were restricted from traveling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One on Monday, only the latest effort by the White House to punish outlets for content it does not like. CNN was scheduled to be the TV pool and Politico the print pool on Trump’s trip to Mississippi, where he […]
content:
CNN and Politico again were restricted from traveling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One on Monday, only the latest effort by the White House to punish outlets for content it does not like.

CNN was scheduled to be the TV pool and Politico the print pool on Trump’s trip to Mississippi, where he is making a midterm campaign swing. As the secondary print pooler, Axios stepped in to provide updates via its reporter Hans Nichols.

A White House spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment.

On September 18, Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds, but a federal judge later put that restriction on hold, finding that the outlets were likely to succeed in their claims that their due process and First Amendment rights were violated. But the administration has continued to restrict the outlets from travel when they are they are the assigned poolers on the trips. Because of space limitations in smaller areas like Air Force One and the Oval Office, media outlets take turns serving as pool reporters, with their notes and images distributed to the rest of the press corps.

Last week, attorney Theodore Boutrous Jr. wrote a letter on behalf of CNN, warning that they would “return to court” unless access is restored.

Watch on Deadline

“These efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage are mistaken, counterproductive and unlawful,” Boutrous wrote in a letter to Michael Velchik, DOJ senior counsel representing the Trump administration. They have not responded, Boutrous said.

Politico was previously blocked from Air Force One pool duty on October 5. CNN is part of a five-network rotation for the TV pool, and was previously restricted from travel on September 21, September 26, October 1 and October 16.

title: Less Than 1% Of SAG-AFTRA Members Have Qualified For Streaming Bonus So Far As Union Faces Reckoning Over Post-Strike Conditions
summary: SAG-AFTRA is doing damage control as the actors’ union is forced to confront how the ongoing domestic production decline has crippled its membership. The union revealed some sobering numbers over the weekend during the national board’s in-person plenary, including the fact that less than 1% of its members will so far stand to benefit from […]
content:
SAG-AFTRA is doing damage control as the actors’ union is forced to confront how the ongoing domestic production decline has crippled its membership.

The union revealed some sobering numbers over the weekend during the national board’s in-person plenary, including the fact that less than 1% of its members will so far stand to benefit from the bonus distribution fund that the above-the-line guilds pushed for during the 2023 negotiations with the AMPTP.

Roughly $1.5 million will soon roll out from the fund to about 700 performers for work on high-budget SVOD projects released in 2024, the guild said Monday in its overview of the in-person meeting. That comes out to about 0.4% of the guild’s 160,000+ members, more than 100,000 of which are considered actors and performers.

Details for those who will benefit are expected to go out in the coming weeks, as are some changes to the union’s health plan, which has also been ruffling feathers since SAG-AFTRA agreed to deep cuts in exchange for a much-needed infusion to the health fund in negotiations with the studios earlier this year.

Watch on Deadline

In a video message Monday, SAG-AFTRA president Sean Astin tried to assuage concerns, admitting to “a palpable disconnect between the work of this union and the lived experience of too many of our members.”

“I find myself thinking a great deal about the working-class actor who used to get hired consistently enough to build a life, someone who could earn a living, raise a family, maintain health coverage, and perhaps even retire with some measure of security,” he said. “Part of what once made that possible was residual income. For decades, it sustained actors and their families through the inevitable periods between jobs. Cable and then streaming steadily dismantled that system, and we’ve spent years fighting to reclaim it. What we’ve won back is substantial, but it’s nowhere near what it was.”

SAG-AFTRA was bullish about implementing a streaming success bonus in 2023, as was the Writers Guild of America. It is one of several hot-button issues that led to a historically long, dual strike that lasted half the year. Since that contract was finalized, the unions have spent the last several years trying to actually put that bonus distribution into action, which is why performers are just now receiving checks from work released two years ago.

As Deadline reported at the time, the success bonus has a very high threshold that makes it difficult for most projects to qualify. For SAG-AFTRA, any title that surpasses the viewership threshold will trigger a payment to each principal performer equivalent to 100% of the fixed residual. However, the performer will only receive 75% of that payment; the other 25% will be funneled into a fund controlled by both SAG-AFTRA and AMPTP trustees to be distributed among the rest of the union’s members. There’s still no details, exactly, on how that 25% is being distributed and to whom — nor whether these distributions are included in the figures from SAG-AFTRA on Monday.

Astin spent most of his 12-minute speech asking members to hold on a little longer, particularly in the face of some brutal upcoming maneuvers. At the end of October, SAG-AFTRA is returning to its regular membership policy, meaning members who are not caught up on their dues will be terminated.

However, despite acknowledging that “few issues weigh more heavily on our members than health care,” Astin had little else to say about that topic. In its memo about the national board plenary, the union noted some improvements for senior members with extensive retiree health credits, though it did not have anything to say about the mounting complaints from high-profile members about their difficulties qualifying and affording services in the first place.

Last week, actor Drake Bell called out the union after revealing he didn’t have health insurance because he didn’t qualify, having not hit the required $28,933 in annual union-contracted income.

“Do not become an actor. Do not join SAG,” Bell captioned his Instagram Stories post. “You can work steadily for 35 years and they will say [middle finger emoji].”

Bell is not alone. Cecily Strong also recently lamented hikes in mental health coverage prices via the union’s insurance plans earlier this year. Atypical actor Jack Haven and Princess Diaries star Heather Matarazzo also recently revealed they would lose their health insurance if they did not get more work soon.

After nearly losing access to his own insurance (and getting an unnamed role on CBS’ Matlock to boost himself over the threshold), actor Cheyenne Jackson launched a social media initiative to spotlight other SAG-AFTRA performers at risk of losing their coverage.

“I’m starting a little series called ONE JOB AWAY, spotlighting fellow actors who are close to qualifying for their SAG health insurance and could use a little help with that next booking,” Jackson wrote in an Instagram post Monday. “I’ll share their faces, their work, and how to reach them. Casting directors, producers, friends making things… maybe your next hire is someone you meet here. Actors… DM me your info if you want to be featured.”

He says he’s already received “hundreds” of submissions.

title: Hubert de la Bouillerie, Editor on ‘Woodstock,’ ‘Witches of Eastwick,’ Dies at 75
summary: Hubert de la Bouillerie, who edited films including George Miller’s “The Witches of Eastwick” and “Tango & Cash,” died Aug. 8 in Los Angeles. He was 75. Among his credits was additional editing on the 1970 documentary “Woodstock,” along with “Highlander II: The Quickening,” “Mo’ Money,” “Doin’ Time,” “Blank Check” and “Celtic Pride.” He also […]
content:
Hubert de la Bouillerie, who edited films including George Miller’s “The Witches of Eastwick” and “Tango & Cash,” died Aug. 8 in Los Angeles. He was 75.

Among his credits was additional editing on the 1970 documentary “Woodstock,” along with “Highlander II: The Quickening,” “Mo’ Money,” “Doin’ Time,” “Blank Check” and “Celtic Pride.”

He also served as editor on “Police Academy 5” and “Police Academy 6.”

De la Bouillerie also moved behind the camera as a director. His directing credits included the 1996 television film “The Right to Remain Silent,” whose ensemble cast included Lea Thompson, LL Cool J, Patrick Dempsey, Christopher Lloyd, Amanda Plummer and Carl Reiner, as well as the 1997 science-fiction film “The Apocalypse.”

His wife, Debbie Robins de la Bouillerie, pre-deceased him. Earlier in his life, Hubert was married to Hilary Saltzman, daughter of film producer Harry Saltzman, who, together with Albert R. Broccoli, brought the original James Bond film series to the screen.

Later in his career, Hubert continued to develop his own projects as a writer and producer, reflecting the breadth of his interests and his lifelong commitment to storytelling.

He was also an accomplished photographer and writer. He published a novel, “Of Love and Evil: The Birth,” a gothic story weaving history, love, mystery and the supernatural.

Hubert’s family describes him as a storyteller at heart. “Whether working with moving images in an editing room, directing actors, developing a screenplay, looking through the lens of his camera or putting words onto a page, he was drawn throughout his life to creativity and artistic expression,” the family wrote in a statement.

De la Bouillerie is survived by his two children, Jacqueline Bell and Alexandre de la Bouillerie, as well as his sister Annie Goeke and his siblings Caroline Gruber, Juliette Glazebrook, Diane Cottrell, Helie de la Bouillerie and Alban de la Bouillerie.

title: Netflix Hires Steve Wilson to Lead Podcast Content Acquisition
summary: Netflix has hired Steve Wilson to head its podcast expansion, Variety has confirmed. Wilson will lead the company’s podcast content acquisitions on a contract basis. Before heading to Netflix, Wilson spent 15 years at Apple, where he most recently headed marketing for Apple Podcasts and partnered with podcasters and networks. He left Apple in December […]
content:
Netflix has hired Steve Wilson to head its podcast expansion, Variety has confirmed.

Wilson will lead the company’s podcast content acquisitions on a contract basis. Before heading to Netflix, Wilson spent 15 years at Apple, where he most recently headed marketing for Apple Podcasts and partnered with podcasters and networks. He left Apple in December 2020, and spent nearly six years at podcast studio QCode as chief strategy officer before joining Daylight Media in the same position.

As reported in September, Netflix now offers more than 60 video podcasts on its service, and has continued to lean into expanding its catalog. The streamer’s original lineup of video podcasts currently includes true-crime show “Murder With My Husband”; talk show “The Pete Davidson Show” hosted by the “Saturday Night Live” alum; pop-culture interview show “Shut Up Evan” hosted by Evan Ross Katz; “The Puzzle Room With David Kwong”; and “Allegedly,” a true-crime podcast from NBC News correspondent Ellison Barber.

Wilson joins Netflix at a tumultuous time, two weeks after the company announced layoffs of 6% of employees, equating to about 1,000 jobs. The cut was the biggest to date, and primarily affected workers in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and HR teams, according to an email to employees written by co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters.

“Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the co-CEOs said in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Variety.

Amid the layoffs, Netflix also ousted a number of chief executives, including chief content officer Bela Bajaria, head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia. Veteran TV exec Peter Rice was tapped to replace Bajaria.

When asked about the leadership change on the content side during the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos said, “I know that we could do better, and we want to build on that momentum.”

title: Neil Young Files $10 Million Suit Against Trump for Using ‘Rockin’ in the Free World,’ Six Years After a Prior Settlement Over the Same Song
summary: Neil Young has filed a $10 million lawsuit Monday against Donald J. Trump’s political action committee, Trump 47 Committee Inc., alleging copyright infringement for the ongoing use of Young’s song “Rockin’ in the Free World” as the president’s walkup music at midterm election rallies. If it feels like (to quote a Crosby, Stills, Nash & […]
content:
Neil Young has filed a $10 million lawsuit Monday against Donald J. Trump‘s political action committee, Trump 47 Committee Inc., alleging copyright infringement for the ongoing use of Young’s song “Rockin’ in the Free World” as the president’s walkup music at midterm election rallies.

If it feels like (to quote a Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song) “we have all been here before,” the deja vu comes from the fact that this is Young’s second time filing suit against Trump over his unlicensed appropriation of “Rockin’ in the Free World.” The first was in 2020, and that lawsuit was settled, only for Trump to continue to play it again now, against the terms of the prior settlement, according to Young’s suit.

The suit says the classic 1989 song is “a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten. The lyrics pain vivid street-level portraits — a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.”

Variety has reviewed the suit, which was filed by Young against the Trump 47 Committee Monday in the U.S. district court for the eastern district of Virginia. It specifically cites the playing of the song at the president’s rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Oct. 12, although it notes that the recording has also been played “numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections.” It asks for an injunction against further public performance for political purposes as well as the $10 million in damages for the existing use.

It says that Trump “is now and at the time of all rallies this year was personally aware that a license would be required to play the song at rallies and that Young has not, and would not, grant the required license.” The suit then goes on to state that in 2020 Young sued a different corporation formed by the president, Donald J. Trump for President Inc,, for copyright infringement of “Rock'” plus another song of Young’s.

“Donald J. Trump for President Inct. asserted no defense and immediate;y settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ without a license and permission from Young.” This new lawsuit does not specify any financial or other terms of the 2020 settlement.

“Among other things, Young has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way,” the suit contends.

Young has been among the most vocal of all musicians going public with vociferous opposition to Trump, making it difficult to know whether the president’s ongoing use of Young’s most famously anti-Republican song is being done out of ignorance or as a deliberate finger in the rocker’s face.

Of course, the White House has often deliberately trolled pop stars this year by using their songs in videos promoting ICE or the war in Iran, then mocking the musicians when they speak up on social media.

The current leading headline on Young’s Archives website is “The Tragic Death of the Republican Party,” over a reprinted column by writer Robert Reich. The musician’s site is filled with similar signed and unsigned columns, some written by Young himself. An unsigned editorial posted on his front page Oct. 1 begins, “Trump by any standards has been the most corrupt president in the history of the United States. What’s remarkable is that it’s done with little effort to hide it. It’s this corruption that appears to finally be motivating his supporters to turn against him.”

title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Star Tovah Feldshuh Responds to Adam Brody’s Palestine Support: ‘To Accuse the Jewish People of Genocide’ Is ‘Right Out of Hitler’s Playbook’
summary: “Nobody Wants This” star Tovah Feldshuh has weighed in after Adam Brody called for a “Free Palestine” during a GQ interview last month. At the time, the actor, who plays Rabbi Noah Roklov on the Netflix show, explained that while he hadn’t spoken publicly about the Israel-Gaza issue before, it comes up “a lot” for […]
content:
“Nobody Wants This” star Tovah Feldshuh has weighed in after Adam Brody called for a “Free Palestine” during a GQ interview last month.

At the time, the actor, who plays Rabbi Noah Roklov on the Netflix show, explained that while he hadn’t spoken publicly about the Israel-Gaza issue before, it comes up “a lot” for him in private. He then made his stance on the conflict clear: “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide,” he said. “Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”

On Sunday, speaking about Brody, Feldshuh told The New York Post that “to accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild. It’s right out of Hitler’s playbook. You take the victim, and you make the victim the perpetrator.” When these accusations come from Jewish people themselves, it “makes a difference to the [Jewish] community,” she added.

She continued: “I believe that the perseverance of the existence of the state of Israel is crucial to the well-being of the democratic world and of the free world… Of course, Israel needs the United States, [but] the United States needs Israel, believe me.” “We’re in a time where we have the ‘horseshoe effect,’ where socialism and antisemitism are trying to meet,” she said.

Feldshuh plays Bina Roklov in “Nobody Wants This,” the mother of Brody’s character. “My job, as Bina but also as Tovah, is to love the people on set at my place of work, to be kind,” she said.

Earlier this month, “Nobody Wants This” creator Erin Foster responded to Brody’s support for Palestine, saying: “I disagree with him, and that’s OK.”

“You know, it’s complicated,” Foster said of Brody’s comments while a guest on the “Not Skinny but Not Fat” podcast. “I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing. And, you know, while I love Adam, I also disagree with him, and that’s OK.”

title: Macklemore Calls for Unity During First ‘Free Palestine’ Show as Hozier, Kneecap and Mark Ruffalo Support: ‘Those Two Words Are So Threatening to Some People’
summary: Macklemore dedicated his first “Free Palestine” tour date in Dublin, Ireland to “love and liberation,” just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage. 3Arena was dotted with keffiyehs and Palestinian flags on Monday night as Dubliners young and old gathered to back the […]
content:
Macklemore dedicated his first “Free Palestine” tour date in Dublin, Ireland to “love and liberation,” just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage.

3Arena was dotted with keffiyehs and Palestinian flags on Monday night as Dubliners young and old gathered to back the “Thrift Shop” rapper at the start of the three-show stint, which will also see him play Paris and London this week alongside special guests. All proceeds are going to charities supporting Palestine, and Macklemore also donated his $1 million salary from Sheeran’s tour to the cause.

To recap, on Sept. 14 Macklemore was dropped from the remainder of Sheeran’s U.S. “Loop” tour after he said “free Palestine” on stage and gave political speeches over two concerts at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sept. 4 and 5. The speeches went viral, sparking backlash from pop star Pink and a petition from the Israeli American Council calling for Macklemore to be removed from Sheeran’s tour. In solidarity with Macklemore, Sheeran’s other opening acts — including Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe — and his backing band, Beoga, also dropped out.

Beoga was there to support Macklemore on Monday, alongside surprise guests including Hozier and Kneecap. During his set, Mackelmore took a moment to share what the evening meant to him in the wake of the controversy. “Six weeks ago, it was two words. Two words is all that it took. Two words that are rooted in love and liberation,” he said. “Not against anybody, not divisive. Not a call for hatred. But a call to recognize our shared humanity. Free Palestine. I said, free Palestine! The same thing that I want for all of us, freedom, dignity, the right to exist without fear. Being able to raise our children in the homes that we grew up in, not having to prove our humanity to the rest of the world.

“And yet,” he continued, “those two words are so threatening to some people. They would rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean. Because freedom that requires another person’s oppression is not freedom at all. And while the world debates those words, we see the videos, we see the footage, we see parents pulling their children out of the rubble. Families erased. Devastation beyond our imagination. And somehow, those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary. That’s why we are here tonight. That is why we are here, because throughout history, music has given people a place to resist, to come together as a collective, to share our grief, to share our stories, to move from the heart, to mobilize people with the frequency of love. The heartbeat in our drum that makes us feel alive, that makes us feel connected.”

But before Macklemore took the stage, the night kicked off with an introduction from Liam Cunningham of “Game of Thrones” fame. “Tonight, we celebrate life. We honor resilience. We stand with Gaza!” he said. The music then began with Palestinian-Israeli singer Lina Makoul, who delivered a powerful song without words “because anything she said could have severely affected her freedom,” as Cunningham noted. Beoga was next, performing several traditional Irish jigs after percussionist Eamon Murray told the crowd, “Don’t fuck with the Irish!”

The first heavyweight guest was none other than Hozier, who got the crowd crooning along with “Too Sweet,” “From Eden,” and “Work Song.” The Irishman said he is “so proud of my country and the way they’re showing up,” and highlighted that 55 students in Gaza are waiting to have their visas approved by the Irish government so that they can study there. “This has happened before. It happened last year, and this can be solved with ministerial discretion,” he continued. “It’s an absolute wonder, it’s baffling how it hasn’t been solved yet.”

Seeming uncharacteristically nervous, Hozier then announced that he was going to perform a tune that he’d “never sang live before.” It was “The Prayer of Shields,” an 18th-century folk song written by John Shield that hoped for equality for all people. “The Jew he is me fellow man/ The Muslim the same indeed, sir,” he sang in a haunting tone. “To the infidel I’d wish him well/And help him in his need, sir.”

As the stage was reset, the crowd was treated to a series of video messages from celebrities who couldn’t be there but wanted to show their support. “Thanks to Macklemore for doing this,” The Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas said. “Take care of each other and the innocents, and continue standing up in this struggle towards a just world system.”

Added “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, “We are all together in this fight to help free Palestine. Keep speaking up and using your voice, it’s working.”

“Keep fighting for a free Palestine and humanity all over the world and amongst the people. There will be no peace until there’s equality,” Mark Ruffalo said to enthusiastic applause throughout the stadium. “Lots of love, have a good show. Keep fighting the good fight.”

Irish rap trio Kneecap then stormed the arena, injecting a dose of energy by getting mosh pits going in the crowd as they ran through hits like “Fenian” and “H.O.O.D.” “We wanna thank Macklemore for organizing this concert. We wanna thank Ed Sheeran for helping to organize this concert,” member Móglaí Bap cheekily said as the crowd erupted in cheers.

It was then finally time for Macklemore’s set. The rapper was greeted with enormous applause as he emerged in a green-and-orange keffiyeh to “Chant,” with Australian singer Tones and I joining him to sing the chorus. Supported by a six-piece band, Macklemore rapped with conviction: “This is my moment/ They can’t take my talent/ They can’t take my stripes.” He addressed the crowd for the first time as the song finished, looking overwhelmed and wiping tears from his eyes. Before he could begin to speak, a “free Palestine” chant broke out in the audience.

“It has been a crazy six weeks,” he said. “We took my shortest tour of all time, which was two nights at MetLife Stadium, and we turned that shit into this right here.” He added, “We’re gonna start with an anti-capitalist anthem,” as his hit “Thrift Shop” rang out and a pair of peppy dancers two-stepped on stage.

A run-down of Macklemore’s greatest hits ensued, including “Same Love” with Mary Lambert joining him; “These Days”; “Glorious”; and “Good Old Days,” with Tones and I reemerging to sing Kesha’s part on the track. He then surprised the audience with a new song that “he wrote this last week,” titled “Where Is Our Love?” In the political yet soft-spoken rap, Macklemore says “free Palestine” and speaks about “America being terrorized by ICE agents” as well as mentioning Congo and Sudan.

The set ended on a high note with his 2012 hit “Can’t Hold Us,” during which Macklemore climbed into the crowd and had them literally hold him up. As confetti exploded in the air, Macklemore left the audience with one last message: “I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people. We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath,” he said before leading one final “free Palestine” chant.

Macklemore’s “Free Palestine” tour continues in Paris on Thursday and London on Friday.

title: Milcho Manchevski Talks ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’, His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia’s Film Agency — Tokyo
summary: This week, Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski returns with Sister Brother Manhole Cover, his second feature of the year, which screens in competition at the Tokyo Film Festival. Directed by Manchevski from a screenplay he also wrote, Sister Brother Manhole Cover follows siblings Malina and Viktor, who live on the outskirts of post-Communist Macedonia. They make […]
content:
This week, Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski returns with Sister Brother Manhole Cover, his second feature of the year, which screens in competition at the Tokyo Film Festival.

Directed by Manchevski from a screenplay he also wrote, Sister Brother Manhole Cover follows siblings Malina and Viktor, who live on the outskirts of post-Communist Macedonia. They make their living stealing bronze busts and manhole covers, which line their city’s streets. When a routine theft goes wrong and Viktor is badly injured, Malina strikes a desperate deal with a corrupt doctor, forcing them into a dangerous journey through Macedonia’s underworld. Their journey leads to an unexpected refuge: the opulent home of the doctor’s blind mother.

Sister Brother Manhole Cover is Manchevski’s ninth feature. The filmmaker debuted his first documentary, Good People, earlier this year at the Sarajevo Film Festival.

Watch on Deadline

“It’s unusual to have two films come out at the same time, but better two than zero,” Manchevski joked in an interview with Deadline ahead of his trip to Tokyo for Sister Brother, adding that he is enjoying this productive period after spending many years being barred from producing films in his home country.

Manchevski, who won the Golden Lion at Venice with his debut feature Before the Rain (1994), was blacklisted and had several projects halted by the Macedonian Film Agency after he reported corruption at the organization. Manchevski’s accusations were later upheld by Macedonia’s Anti-Corruption Commission after an investigation.

Below, the veteran filmmaker, who lives between New York and Macedonia, speaks with Deadline about the extensive witch hunt he endured after exposing corruption at the Macedonian Film Agency, finally getting to make Sister Brother Manhole Cover, and why he believes the Tokyo Film Festival is the perfect launchpad for movies.

Sister Brother Manhole Cover is a Banana Film production, in co-production with Gala Film (Bulgaria), Sense Production (Serbia), Tirana Film Institute (Albania), Berkeley Media Group (UK), Amarcord Production in association with Augustus Color (Italy) with the support of North Macedonia Film Agency, the Bulgarian National Film Center, Film Center Serbia, the Albanian National Center of Cinematography, and Italy’s Direzione Generale Cinema e Audiovisivo – Ministero della Cultura.

The Rome-based Coccinelle Film is handling world sales on the title.

DEADLINE: Milcho, where did this idea come from?

MILCHO MANCHEVSKI: I wanted to make a film about sisterly and brotherly love—something we rarely see in movies or even in literature. It was also partly inspired by Macedonian folk songs and folk literature, which often include the theme of sisterly love. Sometimes it turns shocking and dark, but it is always fully dedicated. That was the initial embryo. Then I wanted to talk about inequality and wealth inequality. I think that’s the premier issue of today. So many problems in the world go back to this sense of unfairness and inequality. That feeling festers in people. But I didn’t want to turn it into an exclusively dark story. I thought it should be told through defiance and humor, because Victor and Marlena don’t see themselves as victims. They see themselves as people with agency—people who do things. Unfortunately, pretty much the only thing they can do is petty crime.

DEADLINE: Yeah, I loved the idea of people stealing the busts. It’s so European.

MANCHEVSKI: People actually do it. It’s three euros a kilo for the metal. I did a little research. There was an explosion of new monuments in Macedonia in the early 2010s, because the nationalist government decided to reintroduce us to our past. There was plenty of cash just lying around. And the manhole covers, they cover the underground and the septic part of us that we don’t really want to smell or see. Then our heroes take them off, and you can smell the reek.

DEADLINE: I read this film was previously titled Leaving Copacabana?

MANCHEVSKI: Yes. The title was Leaving Copacabana. Copacabana was their slum, which we constructed for the film. The little shacks you see are leaning on an ancient aqueduct. We got permission from the government to work there because it’s a national monument. We constructed the shacks for two reasons: first, to have full control; and second, so we wouldn’t go into somebody’s home—somebody’s slum—and disrupt their life. The slum was jokingly called Copacabana, as if they were in Brazil. The tagline was “sister, brother, manhole cover.” But that title somehow took over because it’s more irreverent and catchier, and I think it describes the film better. It’s not so much about leaving one place and going to a richer place; it’s about their relationship and society.

DEADLINE: Where did you shoot this film? There are a lot of locations.

MANCHEVSKI: Everything was done on location. There was no studio. And even on location, we didn’t want to change too much. The exception was the slum, which we constructed based on actual slums in Skopje. Most are inhabited by Roma, but not exclusively. We built it around the aqueduct because I liked the graphic quality, but also because it incorporated the ancient past into the very prosaic present of the characters and the whole community. Everything else was scouted around Skopje. We looked for actual places that had a certain smell, places where you could feel the underbelly, but also places that could give us a cross-section of society. For example, you have the illegal dump, which we had to sanitize so people could work there.

DEADLINE: That was a real dump?

MANCHEVSKI: That was a real dump. We took over a corner of it, sanitized the area, and brought in our own paper and cloth—things that didn’t stink too much. We had to ward off dogs. We liked that particular dump because you could see the highway below. Again, there was this contrast: here and there, us and them. That’s necessary when you’re telling a drama. The house was a real house, too. We didn’t do much to it; we brought in the piano and the busts, which we created, of course. I’m taking one of the manhole covers to the red carpet in Tokyo next week.

DEADLINE: You’ve become a regular at Tokyo Film Festival. Why do you screen your films here?

MANCHEVSKI: It’s an old love story. Before the Rain, my first film, played Tokyo. Going there and spending time there was so nice. I like how people in Japan, and especially at the festival, appreciate films. They take special care with them; they create new posters and trailers. It’s not just a run-of-the-mill place or festival. Then Dust played there, and then Kaymak. Now, I want to go there—it is at the top of my list.

DEADLINE: This is your second film of the year. You were in Sarajevo with the doc Good People. I read that this was mostly because for years you were unable to produce anything?

MANCHEVSKI: Yes, for a while, I wasn’t able to work because I reported corruption at the film agency in Macedonia. I did it twice, and it was eventually confirmed by the Anti-Corruption Commission and the State Audit Office. As retaliation, they blacklisted me, filed criminal charges against me, launched a smear campaign, and blocked my previous films and films in progress. Eventually I won two court cases against the agency, and the dam broke. This film was initially approved in 2022, and then, at the same time, the tragedy in Kočani happened. I felt I should make a documentary about it. The two films are completely different stylistically. There’s a lot of humor in Sister Brother; there’s no humor in Good People. It’s somber, with a glimmer of hope at the end. The overlap mostly happened in the edit, where you can shuttle between the two. I know it’s unusual to have two films come out at the same time, but better two than zero.

DEADLINE: You’ve worked across the United States and Europe and have been able to make many different kinds of things. Many European and American filmmakers now talk about how difficult it is to make work. How do you feel about the industry today?

MANCHEVSKI: I’m always an outsider, and I like it that way. I’ve lived in New York since 1985, but recently I’ve mostly been making films in Europe because of the general attitude toward filmmaking and the arts. Financing is always tough. It’s the curse of filmmaking. I’m jealous of painters and poets: you sit down, do your work, and it’s done. Maybe nobody will see it or like it, but at least it’s finished. With film, you first have to sell it and then make it. Filmmaking involves a lot of money, technology, and egos. Working in Europe has advantages, but distribution is not as muscular as in Hollywood. But nobody tells you how to end the film, whom to cast, or whether you need to reshoot a scene. You want feedback and collaboration, but it’s not a situation where the money dictates what the art will look like. That’s why I prefer Europe to Hollywood.

I’ve worked in the United States—I worked on The Wire for HBO, made an independent film, developed films with studios, and even started a studio film. But in the last decade or so, there has been pressure to conform ideologically and make films with messages. I think every film has a message by default. The question is whether it offers more: Is there beauty in the film? Is there something profound? Does it talk about a bigger truth rather than just a message? The pressure—from festivals and film funds—to be message-driven and ideological comes at the expense of everything else. Even when I agree with the message, it’s a pity that so much contemporary cinema turns into two-dimensional pamphlets.

title: Searchlight Pictures Marketing EVP Michelle Hooper Leaving Studio
summary: EXCLUSIVE: We hear that Searchlight Pictures’ EVP of Marketing Michelle Hooper, who delivered the specialty label numerous Oscar nominations and wins during her two-decade tenure, is exiting. Hooper led publicity, awards and creative marketing operations, earning the studio 21 Best Picture Oscar nominations — including Best Picture winners Slumdog Millionaire, 12 Years a Slave, Birdman, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: We hear that Searchlight Pictures‘ EVP of Marketing Michelle Hooper, who delivered the specialty label numerous Oscar nominations and wins during her two-decade tenure, is exiting.

Hooper led publicity, awards and creative marketing operations, earning the studio 21 Best Picture Oscar nominations — including Best Picture winners Slumdog Millionaire, 12 Years a Slave, Birdman, The Shape of Water and Nomadland; a total of 183 Oscar nominations; and 49 wins.

As far as Golden Globes go, her work delivered 32 awards from 133 nominations, including 20 Best Picture noms and eight wins.



Hooper, who joined Searchlight in 2006, is respected by her peers for her taste, whip-smart instincts, creativity and ingenuity in marketing, and was internally known as “the closer,” bringing a film’s campaign home in its final stretch. Her campaigns for various Oscar winners often dialed into the cultural zeitgeist, from understanding how Nomadland would resonate in the context of the pandemic, to spotting the cultural relevance of Slumdog Millionaire in the Obama era, and appreciating the historical significance of 12 Years a Slave, which was closely followed by Birdman.

This season, Hooper’s awards campaigns include for Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine (93% certified fresh) and Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth! (87% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes).

Watch on Deadline

Prior to joining Searchlight, Hooper spent four years at Fox Broadcasting where she was VP of Entertainment Publicity. While at Fox, Hooper spearheaded the implementation of national publicity campaigns for multiple series such as launching American Idol, 24, Arrested Development, Family Guy and The Simpsons. Prior to joining Fox, Hooper was the Director of Entertainment Communications at CBS Entertainment in New York, where she was part of the team that launched and created the publicity campaign for Survivor.

After Disney acquired 20th Century Fox in March 2019, Hooper made the jump. I understand that Hooper’s departure is part of the cuts that occurred at the Disney studio earlier this month.



Other notable releases during Hooper’s Searchlight administration include James Mangold’s eight-time Oscar-nominated A Complete Unknown, starring Timothée Chalamet as Bob Dylan; Jesse Eisenberg’s A Real Pain, which won an Oscar for Kieran Culkin; Marielle Heller’s Nightbitch starring Amy Adams; Yorgos Lanthimos’ four-time Academy Award winner Poor Things, starring and produced by Emma Stone; Lanthimos’ follow-up Kinds of Kindness, also starring Stone with Jesse Plemons, Hong Chau and Margaret Qualley; and Andrew Haigh’s romantic drama All of Us Strangers starring Andrew Scott, Paul Mescal, Jamie Bell and Claire Foy.

She also oversaw the marketing on streaming originals such as Tina Mabry’s The Supremes at Earl’s All-You-Can-Eat starring Uzo Aduba, Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor and Sanaa Lathan; Karrie Crouse and Will Joines’ Hold Your Breath starring Sarah Paulson; and Eva Longoria’s Oscar-nominated Flamin’ Hot, which became the first original film to debut simultaneously on both Hulu and Disney+ and is Searchlight’s most-watched streaming motion picture of all time.



Other past successful films during Hooper’s reign include The Favourite, Can You Ever Forgive Me?, Isle of Dogs, Super Troopers 2, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, Gifted, Jackie, Brooklyn, Wild, The Grand Budapest Hotel, Beasts of the Southern Wild, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, The Descendants, The Tree of Life, Black Swan, 127 Hours, Crazy Heart, 500 Days of Summer, The Wrestler, Juno, Once, Little Miss Sunshine and The Last King of Scotland.



Hooper shared the Publicist Guild of America’s Maxwell Weinberg Showmanship Award for her work on Survivor. She is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and BAFTA.

title: Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK
summary: Disney and Channel 4 have struck a landmark UK content deal that will also see the Channel 4 linear network become available on Disney+, a UK first. In one of the biggest deals of its kind in UK TV history, shows like Channel 4 stalwart Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins and upcoming Bella Ramsey-starrer Maya […]
content:
Disney and Channel 4 have struck a landmark UK content deal that will also see the Channel 4 linear network become available on Disney+, a UK first.

In one of the biggest deals of its kind in UK TV history, shows like Channel 4 stalwart Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins and upcoming Bella Ramsey-starrer Maya will drop on Disney+ at the start of next year in the UK and Ireland.

From there, Disney+ EMEA general manager Karl Holmes told Deadline there will be a “regular tempo” of new Channel 4 shows entering the Mouse House, although he wouldn’t put an exact figure on this.

From the start of next year, Disney+ UK and Ireland subs will be able to watch these shows day-and-date plus hundreds of hours of on-demand content like Russell T. Davies’ Tip Toe and Nicola Coughlan’s Big Mood. And in a UK first, Channel 4’s linear channel will also become available in its entirety on Disney+.

Watch on Deadline

Speaking alongside Holmes, Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra claimed the Gogglebox network and Disney+ don’t have much overlap in terms of audience and the deal can be complementary. Channel 4 already licenses Disney content like Abbott Elementary, The X Files and Scandal for its VoD player.

“From our perspective, people develop viewing habits in different places,” said Dogra. “There are a number of services they may use to discover content, and we need to make sure Channel 4 is available on those platforms.”

Holmes said Disney+ viewing skews younger than public service broadcasters like Channel 4, adding that around 40% of Disney+ viewing over the past year has come from 16-34 year olds. “There is a genuinely complementary relationship here,” added Holmes. “We’re not competing with free-to-air partners; we’re helping them reach a broader audience.”

The news comes more than a year after Disney+ kicked off a strategy of partnering with local European networks by striking a content-swapping deal with ITV that has seen shows like The Bear and The Kardashians head to ITVX, while Love Island and Mr Bates vs the Post Office went in the opposite direction. This preceded Disney deals with the likes of Germany’s ZDF and Spain’s Atresmedia. Netflix has simultaneously struck a high-profile pact with France’s TF1 that was recently talked up by Ted Sarandos.

Holmes said the Disney-Channel 4 pact is broader in scope than Disney-ITV and his team learned from the latter when executing the former. “One clear lesson is that a focus on shows that are current, big, bold and buzzy – and available day-and-date – works particularly well with our audience,” he added. “That’s what we’ve prioritised in this collaboration. We’d like to build on it further in the future.”

For Dogra, who has been in post less than a year, the deal is the latest landmark agreement she has helped mastermind following the once-in-a-generation ads deal inked with Skydance UK network 5. She has talked up collaboration opportunites including putting Channel 4 shows on BBC iPlayer, while downplaying the idea of a BBC-Channel 4 merger.

While the Paramount deal “gives us scale from an advertising perspective,” today’s agreement “allows us to maximise our impact by reaching as many people as possible across the UK and Ireland, including people who may not currently be using Channel 4 services,” Dogra added.

“The premise is that we need to lean into the wider ecosystem,” said the CEO, a former Sky and Warner Bros. Discovery executive. “We’re not going to build scale in every area ourselves, so we need to work with like-minded organizations.”

More details on the Disney-Channel 4 deal will be incoming in due course.

title: ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Release Schedule: When Do New Episodes Come Out?
summary: The turn between the 18th and 19th centuries draws closer with the next season of The Gilded Age, which will grace the small screen at the end of the year. Season 4 of the period drama, co-showrun by creator Julian Fellowes and Sonja Warfield, the series tackles the results of growth in industry, accumulation of […]
content:
The turn between the 18th and 19th centuries draws closer with the next season of The Gilded Age, which will grace the small screen at the end of the year.

Season 4 of the period drama, co-showrun by creator Julian Fellowes and Sonja Warfield, the series tackles the results of growth in industry, accumulation of mass wealth and drastic societal changes as well as new inventions that sped civilization along to where it is today.

For the full release schedule of The Gilded Age Season 4, read on.

When does The Gilded Age Season 4 premiere?

Watch on Deadline

Season 4 of the period drama premieres Sunday, November 1.

How many episodes are in Season 4 of The Gilded Age? Do they arrive weekly or all at once?

There will be eight episodes in the fourth season of The Gilded Age. After the first one premieres Sunday, November 1 in the popular 9 p.m. slot on HBO and HBO Max, new episodes will come out one per week through December 20.

See the full release schedule below:

Sunday, November 1: Episode 1

Episode 1 Sunday, November 8: Episode 2

Episode 2 Sunday, November 15: Episode 3

Episode 3 Sunday, November 22: Episode 4

Episode 4 Sunday, November 29: Episode 5

Episode 5 Sunday, December 6: Episode 6

Episode 6 Sunday, December 13: Episode 7

Episode 7 Sunday, December 20: Episode 8 (FINALE)

Who is in the cast of Season 4 of The Gilded Age?

Most of the core ensemble will return for Season 4. Louisa Jacobson portrays Marian Brooke, niece of Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) and Ada Brooke now Forte (Cynthia Nixon, who married the Reverend Luke Forte (Robert Sean Leonard) only to have him pass away from cancer.

Carrie Coon and Morgan Spector will be back as the ambitious social climber Bertha Russell and her railroad tycoon husband George Russell, though their relationship hit some rough waters in Season 3. Harry Richardson plays their son Larry Russell, and Taissa Farmiga portrays their daughter Gladys, who married the Duke of Buckingham (Ben Lamb) in Season 3 through arrangement by her mother.

L-R: Denée Benton and Jordan Donica in ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Karolina Wojtasik/HBO

Denée Benton stars as Peggy Scott, a journalist and writer who met her match in Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) last season. Audra McDonald portray’s Peggy’s mother Dorothy, and John Doughlas Thompson portrays her father Arthur Scott.

Blake Ritson plays Agnes van Rhijn’s son Oscar. Kelley Curran plays Enid Winterton, formerly known as Turner because she served as Bertha’s maid. Ashlie Atkinson plays Mamie Fish, socialite who is close with Mrs. Astor (Donna Murphy). Ben Ahlers plays Jack Trotter, formerly the van Rhijn footman and now a man of means since his clock invention patent was sold. Also on the van Rhijn household side, Debra Monk plays Agnes’ lady’s maid Ms. Armstrong. Taylor Richardson plays Bridget. Kristine Nielsen plays Mrs. Bauer who cooks for Ada and Agnes. Simon Jones plays the van Rhijn butler, Bannister.

Celia Keenan-Bolger plays Mrs. Bruce, housekeeper for the Russell family. Erin Wilhelmi plays Adelheid Weber, Gladys’ lady’s maid. Douglas Sills portrays Chef Borden, who cooks for the Russells. Jack Gilpin is the Russell butler.

George Russell’s secretary Richard Clay (Patrick Page) and New York Globe publisher T. Thomas Fortune (Sullivan Jones), will not appear in the rotation of Season 4.

RELATED: ‘Gilded Age’ Christmas Album To Feature Carrie Coon, Laura Benanti, Audra McDonald, Adrienne Warren & Other Cast Members And Broadway Stars

Newcomers to the fourth season include Jim Gaffigan, who will portray President Grover Cleveland, Dallas Roberts as Secretary of the Treasury Daniel Manning, Elizabeth Marvel as Nurse Virginia Saville and Andrew Burnap as Ivy League graduate Porter.

Taylor Trensch (Bat Boy: The Musical), James Scully (You), Dennis Haysbert (24), Maggie Kuntz (John Proctor is the Villain), Neal Huff (Mare of Easttown), and Tony Award-winner Bonnie Milligan (Search Party) have also boarded Season 4 in recurring roles.

What is Season 4 of The Gilded Age about?

The logline warns to “be careful what you wish for” as Bertha Russell’s family deals with consequences to her changing society. Agnes van Rhijn sees an opening to re-elevate herself to her former position in society and Marian forges a new path for herself. Peggy has an uphill battle working to be accepted by her future in-laws as well.
