title: Carrie Ann Inaba Speaks Out After Val Chmerkovskiy’s ‘DWTS’ Suspension, Requests Show to Add ‘New Lift Rule’ Next Season
summary: Carrie Ann Inaba is speaking out about the recent drama surrounding “Dancing With the Stars,” including her controversial comments about lifts. “I have not spoken about what happened because of professional courtesy for those who are still competing, and we actually have standards and practices that keep us separated,” Inaba began in a comment on […]
content:
Carrie Ann Inaba is speaking out about the recent drama surrounding “Dancing With the Stars,” including her controversial comments about lifts.

“I have not spoken about what happened because of professional courtesy for those who are still competing, and we actually have standards and practices that keep us separated,” Inaba began in a comment on her recent Instagram carousel.

In one photo, she’s hugging Jenna Johnson during the Oct. 20 show, which was the episode Johnson’s husband, Val Chmerkovskiy, was benched after making an inappropriate comment toward Inaba. During that episode, Inaba called out Johnson’s lifts and when she pushed back, the judge read her the definition.

“But I think a part of this ‘headline’ has missed a few important parts of what happened,” Inaba continued. “I think it’s important for everyone to know that Jenna and I hugged it out after the Super Bowl show. Jenna was an absolute professional about it, and two women worked through the moment. It came to my attention later that Jenna was deeply hurt. So I also offered to speak with her at anytime. I have also offered to discuss the lift rule and how I enforce it. @sharnaburgess made a great video explaining lifts, assists and which dances allow and don’t allow them.”

The judge has always docked a point from dancers who do lifts, but has faced criticism over the last few seasons from those who feel that she picks and chooses whose lifts she points out and which she lets slide.

She continued in her comments, sharing that she hopes a change is made going forward.

“I think in the future, a new lift rule should be created for next season. I think a session of with all the dancers and the judges in a room together to discuss the history of how and why Len Goodman, our original producers and I defined the lift rule and the what the purpose is which is safety and fairness,” Inaba wrote. “The show has evolved tremendously, the way the show is cast has also changed, and so has our audience and the way they consume the show. So, working together to create a better understanding between the dancers and the judges and our audience is important to me, as we move forward and is something I have asked for.”

The ballroom has been tense since the lift comment was made by Inaba on Oct. 20. After the episode, Chmerkovskiy posted on TikTok, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” which most assumed was a reference to Will Smith slapping Chris Rock at the Oscars in 2022, after saying, “Keep my wife’s name out of your fucking mouth.” Chmerkovskiy quickly deleted the status, but not before many fans saw it.

Before last week’s Dedication Night, BBC Studios announced that he would not be competing that week.

“The well-being of everyone who works on ‘Dancing with the Stars’ is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show,” BBC Studios said in a statement released on Saturday. “As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.”

The professional dancer shared an apology on Instagram and said he personally reached out to Inaba as well. “

“In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention,” he wrote on Saturday. “Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”

title: Jennifer Lawrence Did Not Start Her Beauty Brand Because of Hollywood Instability: ‘A Smarter Exit Plan Would Be Signing Up for a Big Franchise’
summary: Jennifer Lawrence has officially entered the celebrity beauty game with the launch of her haircare brand Mes, but the Oscar winner’s career pivot is not a reaction to Hollywood instability. Speaking to The Cut, Lawrence said that if she worried about the money Hollywood could bring in then “a smarter exit plan would be signing […]
content:
Jennifer Lawrence has officially entered the celebrity beauty game with the launch of her haircare brand Mes, but the Oscar winner’s career pivot is not a reaction to Hollywood instability. Speaking to The Cut, Lawrence said that if she worried about the money Hollywood could bring in then “a smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise.”

“Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door,” the actor added.

Mes, per The Cut, is a “biodesigned haircare” company that is “selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. [Lawrence] partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can.”

Lawrence explained that moving from acting into the haircare space felt like a natural extension of her interests as a performer because “there is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product. I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, ‘Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.'”

So what is Lawrence most nervous about as she launches a beauty brand? She told The Cut she hopes people stick with the products and don’t grow impatient.

“If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” Lawrence explained. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.”

Lawrence added of waiting to see the reception, “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension. I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

Read Lawrence’s full interview with The Cut here.

title: Donnie Iris Dies: ‘Ah! Leah!’, ‘The Rapper’ Singer Was 83
summary: Donnie Iris, the pop-rock singer who first came to widespread attention with the group the Jaggerz and their 1970 hit “The Rapper” and later had a 1980 solo hit in “Ah, Leah!,” died Monday, October 26, in Pittsburgh three years after being diagnosed with bladder cancer. He was 83. His death was announced on Facebook […]
content:
Donnie Iris, the pop-rock singer who first came to widespread attention with the group the Jaggerz and their 1970 hit “The Rapper” and later had a 1980 solo hit in “Ah, Leah!,” died Monday, October 26, in Pittsburgh three years after being diagnosed with bladder cancer. He was 83.

His death was announced on Facebook by bandmate and drummer Joe Vitale Jr. A cause of death was not specified, but earlier this month on October 9 Iris announced his retirement from concert performing due to “recent health issues.”

“While I will no longer be performing live,” Iris wrote to fans, “the memories, the music, and the connections we have built together will always remain close to my heart. Thank you for your loyalty, your energy, and your love through all the years. It has been my great honor to make music for you.”

Watch on Deadline

In the post from Vitale, Iris’ drummer in the band Donnie Iris & the Cruisers, writes, “I have some very sad news to share. Many of you may already know about this, but today my boss and friend Donnie Iris passed away at the age of 83. I have had the honor and blessing of playing drums for Donnie Iris and the Cruisers for the past 5 years and it has been an extraordinary journey….My deepest condolences to Donnie’s daughters and family. To the band and crew, you are all so wonderful and loved working with all of you all these years. Donnie, love ya brother RIP my friend.”

Born Dominic Ierace in New Castle, Pennsylvania, on February 28, 1943, Iris began singing at an early age at weddings and talent shows, eventually pivoting toward rock and roll and doo-wop as he formed bands with high school and college friends in the early and mid ’60s. One of those groups called themselves the Jaggers, in a nod to their favorite singer, but quickly changed the spelling to Jaggerz.

The group’s first album, Introducing the Jaggerz, was released in 1969, was a modest success at best, but the band’s sophomore effort, 1970’s We Went to Different Schools Together on the Kama Sutra label included the song “The Rapper,” written and sung by Iris, which fit right in with the bubblegum music fad and soared to No. 2 on the charts. The catchy song featured a rather ominous chorus in which Iris warned a young woman against a smooth talking man (i.e., a “rapper”) with the repeated lyrics: “Rap, rap, rap, they call him the rapper/Rap, rap, rap, you know what he’s after.”

Although the Jaggerz failed to release a notable follow-up to “The Rapper,” the group stayed together until 1977. From there, Iris joined the band Wild Cherry, who had already had a hit record with “Play that Funky Music,” and the band was past its peak popularity during Iris’ tenure.

Iris left the band in 1979, forming Donnie Iris and the Cruisers, and in 1980 that group released its first album Back on the Streets, which included the Iris-co-written song “Ah! Leah!” The single began receiving local airplay in the Boston-Cleveland-Pittsburgh markets, and within months had gone nationwide. “Ah, Leah!” peaked at No. 29 on the Billboard Hot 100 but became ubiquitous as an album-oriented-rock track on rock stations. The band toured extensively, their video of “Ah, Leah!” became a staple on early MTV.

The group scored a more modest hit with “Love Is Like A Rock,” from the 1981 album King Cool. Other singles and tours followed but none matched the success of the band’s “Ah, Leah!” heyday.

Iris himself continued to record and perform until his recent retirement. He remained a beloved, favorite-son performer in the Pittsburgh area.

Complete survivor information was not immediately available.

title: ‘Fear Factor’ Vertical Scripted Spinoff Set To Launch On Holywater Tech’s My Drama From Fox & Endemol Shine North America
summary: Fear Factor: House Of Fear is making the first-ever leap from an established unscripted television franchise to an original scripted series. The as-yet untitled Fear Factor vertical spinoff, from Fox Entertainment Studios and Endemol Shine North America, a Banijay America company, will debut on Holywater Tech’s My Drama platform. Date TBA. The series, which will […]
content:
Fear Factor: House Of Fear is making the first-ever leap from an established unscripted television franchise to an original scripted series. The as-yet untitled Fear Factor vertical spinoff, from Fox Entertainment Studios and Endemol Shine North America, a Banijay America company, will debut on Holywater Tech‘s My Drama platform. Date TBA.

The series, which will consist of 30 three-minute episodes, is created from the ground up for mobile-first audiences, per Fox and Endemol Shine NA, “taking the thrills, tension, and terror synonymous with Fear Factor and reimagining the franchise as an entirely original fictional horror story.”

The vertical series takes place during prep week on a remote horror television set, where a practical-effects artist and her crew unleash a haunted fortune-telling machine that forces them into personalized death trials, leaving the survivors to uncover its tragic origins before it claims everyone they love.

Watch on Deadline

The project also marks a move into scripted horror by My Drama.

“Fear Factor has always tapped into something primal: what scares us, how far we’ll go and what happens when we’re forced to confront our fears,” said Hannah Pillemer, Head of Scripted, Fox Entertainment Studios. “Michael Thorn and his network team saw the opportunity to bring this iconic franchise to Fox in a bold new way, successfully introducing House of Fear and the outrageous Johnny Knoxville to a whole new generation of fans. That tremendous response has opened the door to take Fear Factor somewhere it has never gone before: becoming the first unscripted television franchise to make the leap into original scripted storytelling. Our friends at Endemol Shine came to us with an inspired way to do exactly that, turning everything audiences love about Fear Factor into the foundation for a completely original horror story.”

“Few franchises are as naturally built for vertical as Fear Factor,” said Michael Heyerman, EVP, Unscripted Series, Endemol Shine North America. “Vertical storytelling is creating a new language for entertainment, one built on immediacy, intimacy, and serialized discovery, and Fear Factor already speaks it fluently. Our partners at Fox gave the franchise a powerful new life with House of Fear, and we’re proud to build on that momentum. Alongside Holywater, together we’re creating a new generation of horror that doesn’t just fit the mobile screen but uses it as part of the experience.”

The scripted spinoff comes on the heels of a Season 2 renewal for the Johnny Knoxville-hosted Fear Factor: House of Fear, which will premiere during the 2026-27 season. The reality competition series debuted on Fox and Hulu to 17.5 million multiplatform viewers, ranking as the season’s highest-rated broadcast debut and No. 1 new unscripted series among Adults 18-49, per Fox and Nielsen.

Fear Factor, a Banijay Entertainment format, has become a global television phenomenon with 32 adaptations worldwide.

The untitled Fear Factor scripted vertical series is produced by Fox Entertainment Studios and Endemol Shine North America. Written by Thom Woodley and Andrew Beck, the series is directed by Gabriel Caste and produced by Ian Nsenga and Yuliia Vyshnevska. It will debut on Holywater Tech’s My Drama platform with worldwide distribution managed by Fox Entertainment Global.

title: LDNDOCS Festival Announces 2026 Lineup Stacked With Documentary Luminaries And Rising Talents
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Oscar winners, Oscar nominees and Oscar hopefuls will be assembling in the UK capital next month for one of the newest film festivals on the planet. The second edition of LDNDOCS, set to unfold from November 20-22 in central London, will present “14 new, award-winning documentary features from some of the world’s most acclaimed […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Oscar winners, Oscar nominees and Oscar hopefuls will be assembling in the UK capital next month for one of the newest film festivals on the planet.

The second edition of LDNDOCS, set to unfold from November 20-22 in central London, will present “14 new, award-winning documentary features from some of the world’s most acclaimed and exciting documentary filmmakers.” The lineup announced Tuesday boasts two-time Oscar winner Barbara Kopple, presenting her film Union Town; Emmy winner Amir Bar-Lev with The Last First: Winter K2; Emmy winner Stephen Maing and Emmy nominee Eric Daniel Metzgar with The Great Experiment, and Oscar nominee Sara Dosa with her latest, Time and Water.

Scroll for the full LDNDOCS lineup.

Watch on Deadline

‘Rehearsals for a Revolution’ Sony Pictures Classics

Oscar nominee Poh Si Teng will present her directorial debut, American Doctor, while Iranian-born director Pegah Ahangarani will screen her documentary Rehearsals for a Revolution, winner of the L’Oeil d’or prize at Cannes and recently selected as the official British entry for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards. LDNDOCS will kick off with Once Upon a Time in Harlem, the award-winning film about an extraordinary reunion in 1972 of surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance. The documentary was conceived and shot by the late William Greaves, and realized over 50 years later by his son, David. David’s daughter Liani (William’s granddaughter) produced the film along with Anne de Mare.

Ben Fowlie , founder of LDNDOCS Matthew Carey

Creative executive and producer Ben Fowlie (Queer Edward II, Boatbuilders) founded LDNDOCS. He previously founded the prestigious Camden International Film Festival in Maine, which recently held its 22nd edition. Regarding the LDNDOCS lineup, he noted, “2026 has been an incredibly exciting year for documentaries, both in terms of the range of the work and also in how nonfiction films are resonating with audiences, especially within a theatrical setting. This year’s program highlights that. It is full of bold, ambitious nonfiction films and filmmakers who are continuing to push cinematic nonfiction in new and powerful ways.”

Screenings for LDNDOCS will take place at the Curzon Bloomsbury Cinema, Bertha DocHouse, and Garden Cinema and will be followed by discussions with the visiting directors and special guests. LDNDOCS says its mission “is simple: to bring extraordinary stories to the big screen, because we believe the future of cinema is cinema. Our goal is to help the documentary form thrive, building audiences one screening at a time.”

This is the 2026 lineup for LDNDOCS:

American Doctor

Directed by Poh Si Teng | USA, State of Palestine, Malaysia, Qatar, Denmark | 2026 | 93 min

Three American medics return home from working in hospitals in Gaza, determined to fight for the patients and colleagues they left behind.

Bleeding Hearts

Directed by Andrew Morgan | USA | 2026 | 97 min

A music-driven love story about real-life couple Zella Day and Jesse Woods, two musicians chasing a shared dream while navigating pressures that could spark their breakup—or their breakthrough.

A Fox Under A Pink Moon

Directed by Mehrdad Oskouei and Soraya Akhalaghi | Iran, France | 2025 | 76 min

Five years, one smartphone, two directors — a long-distance self-portrait of an emigrant’s journey.

The Great Experiment

Directed by Stephen Maing and Eric Daniel Metzgar | USA | 2025 | 100 min

THE GREAT EXPERIMENT is an epic poem in documentary form – a mirror held to a nation at war with its own reflection, asking not who is right, but whether the experiment itself can survive.‍

The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer

Directed by Alessandra Sanguinetti | Argentina | 2026 | 96 min

Spanning more than 20 years, this intimate portrait of two girls, their everyday lives, fantasies and dreams explores their realities and inequalities of growing up female in rural Argentina.

Jean-Michel Basquiat

Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman | USA | 2026 | 95 min

Through untold memories from close friends and family and rare archival imagery, this film demystifies the story of Basquiat and discovers the man behind it all, Jean-Michel.

Khosha: The New Land

Directed by Gakemotho Satau and Zander Booth | Botswana, USA | 2026 | 67 min

Near the beautiful and mysterious Okavango Delta in the heart of Africa, eight members of the Khwe Bushman tribe – descendants of the oldest living human culture – embark on a long journey to find a new homeland.

The Last First: Winter K2

Directed by Amir Bar-Lev | USA, UK | 2026 | 98 min

A historic race to become the first to summit K2 in winter unravels into tragedy, exposing how ambition, ego, and the pursuit of glory can be as dangerous as the mountain itself.

Nuisance Bear

Directed by Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman | USA | 2026 | 90 min

A polar bear is forced to navigate a human world of tourists, wildlife officers, and hunters as its ancient migration collides with modern life. When a sacred predator is branded a nuisance, it becomes unclear who truly belongs in this shared landscape.

Once Upon A Time in Harlem

Directed by David Greaves | USA | 2026 | 100 min

A decade after his death, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves has one last trick up his sleeve with what he considered the most important event he captured on film: a 1972 party he engineered with the living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance.

Rehearsals for a Revolution

Directed by Pegah Ahangarani | USA | 2026 | 95 min

Through five portraits of relatives and mentors, five expressions of resistance, Pegah Ahangarani sketches her life story. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protests footage, newspapers, and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran’s history.

To Hold A Mountain

Directed by Biljana Tuturov and Petar Glomazić | Serbia, France, Montenegro, Slovenia, Croatia| 2026 | 82 min

In the remote highlands of Montenegro, a shepherd mother and daughter proudly defend their ancestral mountain from the threat of becoming a NATO military training ground, stirring memories of the violence that shattered their family.

Time and Water

Directed by Sara Dosa | USA, Iceland | 2026 | 90 min

Facing the death of his country’s glaciers and the loss of his beloved grandparents, Icelandic writer Andri Snær Magnason turns his archives into a time capsule to hold what is slipping away — family, memory, time, and water.

Union Town

Directed by Barbara Kopple | USA | 2025 | 106 min UNION TOWN completes Barbara Kopple’s trilogy on labor rights following her Oscar-winning HARLAN COUNTY, USA and AMERICAN DREAM, two landmark cinéma vérité documentaries.

title: Donald Trump Says He’ll Ban The Use Of The Term “Artificial Intelligence” In “All Relevant Documents” And “Everything Else”
summary: Donald Trump took another stab at an AI rebrand on Tuesday, this time vowing to ban the use of the term “artificial intelligence” in “all relevant documents” and “everything else.” The president’s preferred name is “super intelligence,” something he emphasized when meeting with Elon Musk and other tech executives at the White House last month. […]
content:
Donald Trump took another stab at an AI rebrand on Tuesday, this time vowing to ban the use of the term “artificial intelligence” in “all relevant documents” and “everything else.”

The president’s preferred name is “super intelligence,” something he emphasized when meeting with Elon Musk and other tech executives at the White House last month.

But the use of the term AI goes back decades, and the Trump White House previously referred to it that way, releasing an “AI Action Plan” last year. Polling, though, shows significant concern about the impact of AI, and negative views of data centers.

Trump posted on Truth Social, “When will The Wall Street Journal start calling Artificial Intelligence (AI), a very bad and inaccurate name, SI (Super Intelligence), the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be. In short order, we will be officially BANNING the term, ‘AI/Artificial Intelligence,’ in all relevant documents, and everything else, due to its inaccuracy. Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP”

Watch on Deadline

Trump signed an executive order on Sept. 29 that directs federal agencies to use the term “super intelligence,” with figures like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang going along with it. But media outlets have continued to use the term “AI,” given the widespread adoption of it that goes back decades.

Although the president’s authority to force public adoption of “super intelligence” is limited, the White House has tried to enforce previous rebrands. It banned the Associated Press from the Oval Office and removed it from the White House pool because the news organization did not change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The AP sued, and a federal judge ruled that the White House likely was violating the First Amendment. The judge’s decision is on appeal. Steven Spielberg’s A.I. Artificial Intelligence dates to 2001.

title: Celine Dion To Perform Paul McCartney’s Original Songs For Animated Feature ‘High In The Clouds’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Celine Dion will perform original songs written and composed by Paul McCartney for the upcoming 3D animated feature High in the Clouds, adapted from his children’s novel, with the soundtrack to be released worldwide by Universal Music Group. Dion already has been announced as member of the voice cast topped by Himesh Patel and […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Celine Dion will perform original songs written and composed by Paul McCartney for the upcoming 3D animated feature High in the Clouds, adapted from his children’s novel, with the soundtrack to be released worldwide by Universal Music Group.

Dion already has been announced as member of the voice cast topped by Himesh Patel and Hannah Waddingham and also featuring McCartney, Idris Elba, Lionel Richie, Ringo Starr and Jimmy Fallon, among many others.

Waddingham, Patel and McCartney also will lend their voices to original musical performances throughout the picture.

RELATED: The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office

Watch on Deadline

High in the Clouds follows the adventures of teenage squirrel Wirral (Patel) as he accidentally sparks a revolution against Gretsch (Waddingham), the bossy diva-owl who has banned all music from his town, and embarks on an extraordinary journey to set music free. Dion voices Wirral’s mother, Sugartail.

Up Oscar winner Michael Giacchino, who also worked on Ratatouille, Inside Out, Coco, Klara and the Sun and many others, has composed the original score based on McCartney themes.

News that Dion is recording the original songs comes just 10 days after “The Power of Love” singer completed the first of her comeback concert residency in Paris, which drew some 550,000 spectators across 16 shows.

It was Dion’s first major concert program since being forced to abandon her Courage World Tour in 2020 due to the pandemic, followed by health struggles.

McCartney posted about his joy at seeing Dion back on the concert circuit on social media back in September.

“It’s been so great to see the amazing reaction to Céline’s comeback in Paris. There’s so much love out there for her,” he wrote.

“I’m so excited that she’s part of our High in the Clouds film. I’ve just been listening to some of her parts, and I’m blown away by it. Wow, what a talent. We are very lucky to have her as part of the team. Can’t wait to share it with the world.”

High in the Clouds is adapted from McCartney’s 2005 novel, co-written with Philip Ardagh and illustrated by Geoff Dunbar. An earlier iteration of the animated film dating back to 2015 saw the Beatles star McCartney collaborate briefly with Lady Gaga on one of the tracks.

The picture is directed by animation filmmaker Toby Genkel (The Amazing Maurice) from a screenplay by Oscar winner Jon Crocker (Paddington 2), with production design by Patrick Hanenberger (Rise of the Guardians, The Lego Movie 2).

The film is produced by McCartney (MPL Communications), Robert Shaye and Michael Lynne (Unique Features), and by Sidonie Dumas, Nicolas Atlan, and Terry Kalagian for Gaumont, in association with MPL Communications, Michele Anthony and David Blackman for Polygram Entertainment, Lemoko Investments, Sky, and James L. Nederlander Productions.

Award-winning Gaumont Animation is producing the feature and partnering with the team at 88 Pictures (The Bad Guys: A Very Bad Holiday, Spirit Untamed), which is handling key animation elements of the film.

Gaumont will present an exclusive work-in-progress screening of High in the Clouds during the upcoming American Film Market (AFM).

The film already has been sold in major territories to UK (Sky UK Ltd.), German-speaking territories (Constantin Film), Eastern Europe (Vertical/Monolith/AQS), Latin America (Imagem), CIS (Mint Films), Middle East (Four Star), South-East Asia/Taiwan/HK (A Really Good Film), Greece (Tanweer), Portugal (Cinemundo), Israel (Lev), Baltics (Acme), South Africa (Sun)

CAA Media Finance is handling North America

title: Japan Must Follow Hollywood’s Distribution Playbook, Says Tokyo Market Chief Shiina Yasushi, Who Eyes Major Expansion by 2030
summary: Japan’s entertainment business has to adopt the model that made Hollywood studios global players if the country wants to reach its content export targets, according to Shiina Yasushi, CEO of TIFFCOM, the Tokyo International Film Festival’s content market now heading into its 23rd edition. The Japanese government has set a target of JPY20 trillion ($126.6 […]
content:
Japan’s entertainment business has to adopt the model that made Hollywood studios global players if the country wants to reach its content export targets, according to Shiina Yasushi, CEO of TIFFCOM, the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s content market now heading into its 23rd edition.

The Japanese government has set a target of JPY20 trillion ($126.6 billion) in overseas content sales by 2033, and expects anime to bring in JPY6 trillion ($38 billion) of that. Shiina argues that looking abroad won’t be enough without a change in how Japanese companies operate.

“Historically, Japanese companies have often licensed content rights abroad and left local distribution and marketing to their licensees. Going forward, companies should retain ownership of their IP, be actively involved in international distribution, and maximize the revenue generated from their properties,” Shiina tells Variety.

He points out that Hollywood studios reached global scale by setting up their own distribution operations country by country and dealing with each market directly. Japan should take the same route, he says. With that base in place, a property can then be spread across film, games, streaming and merchandise. Shiina sees this as the shift to the “IP-driven industry” the government has called for.

Japanese companies have begun rethinking how they handle IP. TBS is working with Legendary Entertainment, Nippon TV is expanding internationally and publishers are looking at overseas adaptations. Shiina says a fundamental shift is under way. “In the past, the very concept of the long-term value of IP was not widely considered,” he says. Talent agencies have also started paying attention to IP, he adds, because the IP a performer worked on can live on long after they retire.

According to Shiina, the market itself has changed most in who attends. TIFFCOM used to be mainly a place where international sales agents traded finished content. Once producers arrived, it became a more creative market. Streamers now attend next to film and TV companies, and the IP holders on the floor include anime studios, publishers, game companies and toy makers.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM) is now big enough to build programs around specific regions and genres, Shiina says. Alongside its Asian focus, it has a collaboration with Italy and, this year, a partnership with Canada’s genre outfit Frontières. When TGFM started, it simply picked projects that met its eligibility rules.

The aim is to make Tokyo a key stop for developing and financing projects, as well as for selling finished ones. “While traditional markets centered on sellers and buyers, our vision is a marketplace where everyone involved in production comes together – from producers, directors, and screenwriters to studios and investors providing capital,” Shiina says.

Taking the Tokyo IP Market to the Cannes Film Market raised TIFFCOM’s profile. Even so, Shiina says the goal isn’t simply to repeat that move at other overseas markets. The priority is still getting international professionals to come to Japan.

“Japan possesses such compelling IP that creators and producers around the world want to collaborate with us. By coming to Japan, international partners can engage in direct, face-to-face dialogue with creators – including original authors, directors, and screenwriters,” he says.

At Cannes, Japan was Country of Honor. Its delegation included sales executives, directors, producers, studios and senior company leaders. Because the program featured anime studios and IP as well as live-action, publishers went too. For Shiina, the biggest result was a change in attitude. Japanese executives who used to see festival markets only as places to buy and sell finished films found out they could take part themselves.

He wants to keep that from being a one-time event. “If Cannes was the first step, this edition of Tokyo represents the second step, and we are still just at the beginning. By sustaining this virtuous cycle, we aim to build a lasting, sustainable business,” Shiina says.

TIFFCOM’s technology keynote this year features AGBO executives speaking about AI and storytelling. Shiina won’t predict which part of the business AI will change first. He is sure, though, that it will reshape production by lowering costs and shortening turnaround. Rights are his main worry, and he says the whole industry needs to work on frameworks for them.

“The critical priority is how to protect creators. This year’s keynote features AGBO – a studio founded by film directors – speaking on how to leverage AI and technology in a creator-led manner, which I believe is precisely the topic the industry wants to hear right now,” he says.

Shiina doesn’t think Japan can settle the AI question alone. Both the technology and the rights involved cross borders, and he says opting out of AI is no longer realistic.

On anime’s long-running problems with costs, working conditions and creators’ share of profits, Shiina says things are getting better, though slowly. He cites work-style reforms, a new law protecting freelancers, and joint government and industry efforts on working conditions. Studios are also starting to keep their IP and build their own businesses instead of working only as subcontractors, and live-action producers are doing the same. “I believe anime is leading the way worldwide, with live-action following in its footsteps,” he says.

Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market and Hong Kong FilMart are also chasing international growth. Shiina says a market should be judged on quality, not numbers. “When industry professionals plan their annual calendars, Tokyo remains an unmissable destination because it allows them to connect directly with Japanese rights holders and creators,” he says. Getting more Japanese companies to take part is the key, he adds, because international attendance follows Japanese participation.

Looking ahead, Shiina wants to expand TIFFCOM’s capacity across its whole operation, not just its floor space. “By around 2030, including venue expansion, we envision growing TIFFCOM into a significantly expanded marketplace,” he says.

title: ’60 Minutes’ Audience Sinks to Surprising Low Without Football
summary: It’s not surprising to see ratings at “60 Minutes” slump when CBS doesn’t air a strong football game before the start of the show. But the program’s performance on Sunday, which lacked exactly that kind of NFL lead-in, is alarming nonetheless. The fifth episode of this season’s cycle of the venerable CBS newsmagazine drew only […]
content:
It’s not surprising to see ratings at “60 Minutes” slump when CBS doesn’t air a strong football game before the start of the show. But the program’s performance on Sunday, which lacked exactly that kind of NFL lead-in, is alarming nonetheless.

The fifth episode of this season’s cycle of the venerable CBS newsmagazine drew only 5.64 million viewers, one of the smallest audiences for the program in years, according to data from Nielsen. The show captured a mere 558,000 among viewers between 25 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers in news programming.

Since 2000, “60 Minutes” has never failed to capture less than seven million viewers overall and less than one million viewers in the advertiser category.

CBS News declined to make executives available for comment, and the network had not released the Nielsen data itself publicly as of Tuesday evening. The Nielsen numbers were confirmed by four people familiar with the information. For the night, “60 Minutes” was the second-most-watched non-sports program on broadcast TV, behind CBS dramas “Tracker” and “Marshals.” Typically, “60 Minutes” finishes first in that category.

Such numbers may be cause for consternation at CBS News, the CBS television network and corporate parent Skydance. “60 Minutes” has long stood as one of the most-watched programs on TV that isn’t tied to sports, and is supposed to funnel viewers from the NFL into the rest of the CBS Sunday primetime lineup. Compared to the year-earlier telecast of the newsmagazine, which had a more robust football lead-in, Sunday’s telecast of “60 Minutes” fell 60% in overall viewership and a whopping 81% among viewers between 25 and 54.

CBS News remains under intense pressure to demonstrate stability at the program, which was overhauled in chaotic fashion at the end of last season, despite mustering a notable 9% uptick in overall viewership. Bari Weiss, CBS News’ editor in chief, ousted Tanya Simon, an executive producer with years of history working at the show, in favor of Nick Bilton, a journalist and screenwriter with less formal TV experience. Also pushed out were correspondents Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi. Anderson Cooper left of his own volition following the end of his contract. Their replacements, which include Ross Douthat and contributors like Ariel Levy and Sebastian Junger, have top-shelf backgrounds, but also little experience working on a weekly TV program that emphasizes long-form enterprise journalism.

Sunday’s telecast faced competition from a late football game on Fox.

The program featured a probe into the Trump administration’s efforts to deport people to countries where they have no ties, and the show’s investigation revealed how some deportees are being subsequently forced back to the nations they originally fled. The segment echoed one from last season during which correspondent Alfonsi examined the deportation of some migrants to harsh prisons in El Salvador, a story that generated controversy because Weiss asked it for it be held at a late stage in production. The show also featured interviews with Colorado Governor Jared Polis and Tina Peters, a top election official whose sentence tied to a conviction of breaching her county’s election system he commuted.

title: Barry Keoghan Undergoes Skin-Tightening Cosmetic Treatment in Video Posted Months After He Called Out Online Abuse Over ‘How I Look’
summary: Barry Keoghan is making headlines for appearing in a new social media video shared by U.K. celebrity facial expert and Dermaspa founder Nilam Holmes, who posted a behind-the-scenes look at the Oscar nominee’s Xerf treatment. Per Dermaspa’s website, Xerf forgoes injections and uses radio-frequency technology to tighten the skin and renew collagen. The treatment costs […]
content:
Barry Keoghan is making headlines for appearing in a new social media video shared by U.K. celebrity facial expert and Dermaspa founder Nilam Holmes, who posted a behind-the-scenes look at the Oscar nominee’s Xerf treatment. Per Dermaspa’s website, Xerf forgoes injections and uses radio-frequency technology to tighten the skin and renew collagen. The treatment costs around $3,500 for a face and neck session.

“I’ve been working with Barry for a while now, looking after his skin through different movies, campaigns and projects and the trust he places in me means a lot,” Holmes wrote in a caption accompanying the video. “His skin has really improved over the last few years and he looks great. Today we did his [second Xerf] skin-tightening treatment. I was running late filming some Xerf content, so rather than make me rush what I was doing, he offered to let me film him having it.”

Keoghan narrates the video, saying: “I’ve been hearing a lot about it, and Nilam is very excited about it, and she’s great at what she does. I really mean that, and again, every time I come in, it’s very relaxing and therapeutic. I feel better about myself, I look better. I think it’s important to look after yourself inside and outside.”

As seen on Holmes’ social media pages, her other clients who have undergone Xerf treatment include Chris Appleton, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Joe Alwyn and Nicole Scherzinger. She’s also worked with Pink and Joe Alwyn and has posted regularly about treating Keoghan in the past, giving him facials before various photo shoots.

“Working on multiple projects at a time; movies, campaigns, interviews, press and philanthropy projects means unstructured routine, travel, make up, and disrupted sleep patterns, which all take a toll on the skin,” Holmes posted in March 2025 about treating Keoghan for his Wonderland magazine cover. “So we have regular skin sessions which consist of fixing up problematic skin, calming down inflammation, maintaining the skin when it’s great and trying to get that healthy, rested look. On top of that Barry is like a little student for me. Passionate about everything, he likes to know everything about everything which I love and he brings the fun when he visits.”

Earlier this year, Keoghan went viral for telling SiriusXM’s “The Morning Mash Up” that the online “abuse” about his appearance had gotten so bad that he no longer wanted to “go outside.”

“There’s a lot of hate online,” Keoghan explained at the time. “There’s a lot of abuse of how I look, and it’s kind of past the point of — you know, everyone goes through that… but it’s made me shy away. It’s made me really go inside myself, not want to attend places, not want to go outside. I say this being absolute pure and honest to you. It’s becoming a problem.”

Keoghan noted that he removed himself from social media to avoid nasty comments about himself, but occasionally, after a premiere or event, he would go online to see “how he’s received.” Unfortunately, he said most of the time, the reaction is “not nice.”

title: Elmo Is Going as Meryl Streep’s Evil Fashion Editor Miranda Priestly for Halloween This Year
summary: This Halloween, “Sesame Street’s” beloved furry red monster is trading crayons for couture. In a somewhat unexpected cultural crossover, Elmo for Halloween 2026 is dressing as fashion magazine editor-in-chief-from-hell Miranda Priestly, archly portrayed in the “The Devil Wears Prada” movies by Oscar-winner Meryl Streep. “Guess who Elmo is?” he says in a video released by […]
content:
This Halloween, “Sesame Street‘s” beloved furry red monster is trading crayons for couture.

In a somewhat unexpected cultural crossover, Elmo for Halloween 2026 is dressing as fashion magazine editor-in-chief-from-hell Miranda Priestly, archly portrayed in the “The Devil Wears Prada” movies by Oscar-winner Meryl Streep.

“Guess who Elmo is?” he says in a video released by “Sesame Street,” before revealing his Miranda Priestly look.

In the video, a sentient pumpkin strolls in front of Elmo, prompting him to crack in character as Priestly: “Pumpkins. For fall. How groundbreaking.” Then Cookie Monster appears, prompting Elmo to snark about Cookie’s blue fur color: “Well, it’s not cerulean. But, it works.” To which Cookie Monster responds: “Uh, thanks? Me think?”

Watch the video below — which will certainly fly right over the heads of Elmo’s preschool fans.

In years past, Elmo in different “Sesame Street” segments has dressed for Halloween as a spaceman known as “Galactic Stan,” as well as a pirate and a witch. Meanwhile, Elmo himself continues to be a popular Halloween costume selection for kids and adults alike.

Streep starred in the original 2006 “The Devil Wear’s Prada” movie alongside Anne Hathaway, Emily Blunt and Stanley Tucci. The movie is based on the novel of the same name by Lauren Weisberger, who once worked at Vogue and modeled the Miranda character on real-life fashion editor Anna Wintour. The quartet of actors reprised their characters in this year’s sequel, “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” from 20th Century Studios.

title: Jafar Panahi Now Faces a Five-Year Prison Term in New Ruling on Top of His Previous One-Year Conviction
summary: Cannes Palme d’Or-winning Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi – who was facing a one-year prison sentence – has now been sentenced by a Tehran Revolutionary Court to five years and one month in jail in a separate ruling, according to the Emtedad News Agency, an online Iranian reformist media outlet. Panahi’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad […]
content:
Cannes Palme d’Or-winning Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi – who was facing a one-year prison sentence – has now been sentenced by a Tehran Revolutionary Court to five years and one month in jail in a separate ruling, according to the Emtedad News Agency, an online Iranian reformist media outlet.

Panahi’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad that the court has now sentenced his client in absentia to five years and one month of imprisonment – though implementation of both rulings is discretionary – and issued an order for the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, plus a two-year ban on using social media a two-year travel ban. It is unclear what the charges against Panahi are in this case.

The lawyer said that after Panahi’s bank accounts were suddenly frozen last week, he went to the prosecutor’s Tehran office with his client and learned of the verdict which has been issued in absentia. According to Nili, the case file stated that Panahi was living outside Iran, though the director had returned to Iran on March 30, 2026 shortly after the ceremony for the 98th Academy Awards, in which his latest film ”It Was Just an Accident” made it to the nomination stage as France’s candidate in the Best International Feature Film Category.

Over the past two decades, Panahi has had frequent run-ins with the Iranian authorities.

In 2010, the revered auteur — known globally also for other prize-winning works such as “The Circle,” “Offside,” “This is Not a Film,” “Taxi” and “No Bears” — was banned from making movies, speaking to the press and traveling, though he surreptitiously kept making them anyway.

In 2022, Panahi was arrested in connection with protests by a group of filmmakers but was released about seven months later.

The ban was lifted in April 2023, and Iranian authorities allowed Panahi to travel to Cannes to launch “It Was Just an Accident.” Panahi subsequently traveled widely to promote the drama, which centers around an outpouring of strong feelings by a group of former prisoners toward a torturous guard and stems from his incarceration.

But he returned to Iran despite the fact that, at that point, he faced a one-year prison sentence in his home country and a climate of escalating tension that made his return very risky.

“I am the kind of person who needs to be in his country,” Panahi told Variety. “I need to breathe there and work there. And even if they want to go ahead with that prison sentence, they can go ahead. Nothing will change my mind about going back.”

title: ‘DWTS’ Judge Carrie Ann Inaba Speaks Out After Val Chmerkovskiy Suspension & Calls For “New Lift Rule”
summary: Carrie Ann Inaba is finally addressing the Dancing with the Stars drama after Val Chmerkovskiy was suspended and is calling for a “new lift rule.” The DWTS judge made controversial comments on the October 13 episode and called out pro dancer Jenna Johnson for a lift, which is severely frowned upon in the ballroom dancing […]
content:
Carrie Ann Inaba is finally addressing the Dancing with the Stars drama after Val Chmerkovskiy was suspended and is calling for a “new lift rule.”

The DWTS judge made controversial comments on the October 13 episode and called out pro dancer Jenna Johnson for a lift, which is severely frowned upon in the ballroom dancing competition.

“I have not spoken about what happened because of professional courtesy for those who are still competing, and we actually have standards and practices that keep us separated,” Inaba said in an Instagram post on Tuesday, October 27.

During the episode, Inaba and Johnson had a tense exchange about the definition of a lift. Chmerkovskiy, who is married to Johnson, posted a shady comment on social media saying, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” The comment referenced Will Smith taking the Oscar stage and slapping Chris Rock to defend his wife. After the comment, Chmerkovskiy earned a one-week suspension, with BBC Studios calling the pro-dancer’s social media post “inappropriate” and not reflecting “the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show.”

Watch on Deadline

Inaba shared in her new social media post that she had squashed the beef with Johnson.

“I think a part of this ‘headline’ has missed a few important parts of what happened,” Inaba said. “I think it’s important for everyone to know that Jenna and I hugged it out after the Super Bowl show. Jenna was an absolute professional about it, and two women worked through the moment. It came to my attention later that Jenna was deeply hurt. So I also offered to speak with her at anytime. I have also offered to discuss the lift rule and how I enforce it. @sharnaburgess made a great video explaining lifts, assists and which dances allow and don’t allow them.”

In the comments, Inaba continued, “I think in the future, a new lift rule should be created for next season. I think a session of with all the dancers and the judges in a room together to discuss the history of how and why Len Goodman, our original producers and I defined the lift rule and the what the purpose is which is safety and fairness. The show has evolved tremendously, the way the show is cast has also changed, and so has our audience and the way they consume the show. So, working together to create a better understanding between the dancers and the judges and our audience is important to me, as we move forward and is something I have asked for.”

Chmerkovskiy has since then deleted his social media comment and apologized to Inaba, saying, “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”

title: Banijay & Don’t Tell Comedy Strike Strategic Partnership
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Banijay America has made a strategic move into creator-led comedy through a partnership with Don’t Tell Comedy, one of the fastest-growing stand-up brands in the United States. Together with Banijay Rights, the global distribution arm of Banijay Entertainment, the deal brings Don’t Tell Comedy’s 14 million followers and 115 hours of stand-up content to […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Banijay America has made a strategic move into creator-led comedy through a partnership with Don’t Tell Comedy, one of the fastest-growing stand-up brands in the United States.

Together with Banijay Rights, the global distribution arm of Banijay Entertainment, the deal brings Don’t Tell Comedy’s 14 million followers and 115 hours of stand-up content to streaming and digital platforms worldwide, while creating new opportunities for talent, formats and brand partnerships. Don’t Tell will benefit from access to Banijay Entertainment’s global network, digital channel expertise and production resources, helping monetize a growing content library, reach new audiences and create opportunities for its comedians through longer-form programming.

Under the agreement, Don’t Tell’s stand-up library will be distributed across AVOD, FAST and SVOD platforms internationally, including Prime Video Direct. In an effort to tap into YouTube’s rapid growth on living room screens, Banijay will launch all-new dedicated channels for Don’t Tell Comedy on the platform. They’ll also support the development of new projects, brand partnerships and financing opportunities to expand Don’t Tell Comedy’s digital reach, with curated longer-form compilations, specials designed for different streaming audiences, and more.

Watch on Deadline

“This partnership marks another leap into the creator landscape for Banijay America,” said their CEO, Ben Samek. “Don’t Tell Comedy has built an exceptional platform for discovering and developing talent, and Kyle Kazanjian-Amory, Brett Kusher and the team have an unmatched eye for the next generation of comedy stars. By pairing that creative strength with Banijay Rights’ global reach, our existing partnership with YouTube and overall expertise in entertainment, we can help its comedians reach broader audiences, while expanding the brand across new formats, new screens and new audiences worldwide.”

Shaun Keeble, SVP Monetisation for Banijay Rights, added: “Don’t Tell Comedy has built something incredibly compelling by putting emerging comedians at the centre of a digital-first entertainment brand. With them we intend to extend that ecosystem across streaming and digital platforms, from AVOD and FAST to SVOD and new audience-focused YouTube channels. Through curated, longer-form programming and distribution windows, we can unlock further value from the catalogue while introducing emerging comedy talent to audiences around the world.”

Founded in a Los Angeles backyard in 2017, Don’t Tell Comedy is a live stand-up producer with a unique hook: Each year, they stage more than 5,000 secret-location shows worldwide, with the U.S. as their biggest market. With their underground comedy experiences, helping to spotlight new generations of comedic talent, the intention has been to create the feeling of a house party. Subsequently, Don’t Tell has furthered the reach of its brand with short taped comedy specials released online, which now accrue over 1.5B views annually across YouTube and other platforms. Comics who have gotten their start on Don’t Tell’s stages include Ralph Barbosa, Robby Hoffman, SNL‘s Michael Longfellow, Katherine Blanford and Malik Elassal, to name a few.

“Our mission is simple: to make comedy more accessible,” said CEO Kazanjian-Amory. “Nine years ago, we started by organizing affordable live shows in areas without good options for live stand-up. In 2022, we expanded to producing short-form stand-up specials and distributing them for free across social media. Now, with Banijay, we are excited to continue creating opportunities for emerging talent, connecting them with global audiences, and finding new formats to expand the Don’t Tell Comedy ecosystem where we shine a light on amazing talent from anywhere around the world.”

Banijay Entertainment operates across 25 territories and delivers an average of 19,000 hours of content and 3,000 live events globally each year. The Don’t Tell deal is just the latest big digital initiative for the company, which recently relocated Phil Rosenthal’s popular culinary series Somebody Feed Phil from Netflix to YouTube and has also worked with him on digital hub Phil Rosenthal World. Other initiatives include the Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party vodcast, and its subsequent Bundesliga rights package, and the ongoing development of creator-led formats like Stop the Train and Let’s Play Ball.

title: Bridget Moynahan Reflects On Career, Industry Change At North Fork TV Festival Deadline Dinner
summary: As one of the leads on CBS mainstay Blue Bloods, which ended its 14-season run in 2024, Bridget Moynahan enjoyed a run of rare stability in a rapidly evolving TV industry. The actor reflected on the environment of change and disruption during the latest installment of the Deadline Dinners series, which was held October 21 […]
content:
As one of the leads on CBS mainstay Blue Bloods, which ended its 14-season run in 2024, Bridget Moynahan enjoyed a run of rare stability in a rapidly evolving TV industry.

The actor reflected on the environment of change and disruption during the latest installment of the Deadline Dinners series, which was held October 21 at the North Fork Television Festival. Along with streaming’s rise to dominance, more recently the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger (forming Skydance) and a big shakeup at Netflix have added to uncertainty about the industry’s future.

Don’t count Moynahan among the skeptics, however. “I still feel optimistic about great stories and creativity being able to break through,” Moynahan said. “Despite all of the changes, people will always gravitate toward stories, so I do feel hopeful. You have to have hope.”

The conversation, moderated by Deadline New York Business Editor Dade Hayes, touched on various points in Moynahan’s career. Her signature roles have been on shows like Sex and the City (and followup And Just Like That) as well as the John Wick films. She is starring opposite Christopher Meloni in Hulu’s The Land, a scripted drama about the NFL’s Cleveland Browns that will premiere after Disney’s Super Bowl coverage next February.

Watch on Deadline

American Beech Hotel in Greenport, NY, hosted the dinner, an intimate gathering of two dozen people in the boutique hotel’s ground-floor boite. Attendees included fellow actors Kate Walsh (Grey’s Anatomy) and Michael Nathanson (The Knick) as well as festival stakeholders from the legal, industry and sponsorship realms.

Now in its 11th year, the festival has leaned into its setting on Long Island’s East End, about 90 miles from New York City. The region is notably more tranquil than its glitzier sibling to the south, the Hamptons. While it may be quieter on the North Fork, some major figures in finance, media and technology have homes there, and Greenport has evolved from its roots as a remote fishing village into a significant cultural hub.

A separate festival-curated conversation on October 21 featured actor Kelly AuCoin from Billions. On the following night, Walsh, Anthony Anderson and Kelsey Grammer received awards at a gala dinner. The festival also screened independent pilots and convened a panel about how artificial intelligence is reshaping the TV business.

Moynahan, who produced an indie pilot that premiered at the 2025 North Fork fest, said she has enjoyed her chances to get behind the camera. She directed three episodes of Blue Bloods and another of spinoff Boston Blue. Asked about genres or areas she hopes to explore next, Moynahan said, “There are a lot of shows I am watching now” with that in mind. One example is Youth, the HBO series created by Sharon Horgan, which Moynahan considers an ideal blend of entertainment and serious purpose.

When Moynahan asked the table if they had watched Youth, several guests loudly chimed in, adding their own favorites and comparing notes. As the free-flowing conversation continued, it wound up illustrating Moynahan’s point about the eternal hunger for stories well told.

title: Connor Storrie Circling Role In Marvel’s ‘Ghost Rider’ Opposite Ryan Gosling
summary: Connor Storrie is circling a role opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel Studios’ Ghost Rider, sources have confirmed to Deadline. Reps for Marvel declined to comment. There’s word yet on the role to be played by Storrie, though he’s reportedly the film’s villain. Reuniting Gosling with his Star Wars: Starfighter director Shawn Levy and that film’s […]
content:
Connor Storrie is circling a role opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel Studios‘ Ghost Rider, sources have confirmed to Deadline.

Reps for Marvel declined to comment. There’s word yet on the role to be played by Storrie, though he’s reportedly the film’s villain. Reuniting Gosling with his Star Wars: Starfighter director Shawn Levy and that film’s writer, Jonathan Tropper, the comic book movie is slated for release on July 28, 2028. Marvel dropped the bombshell of its announcement at this year’s San Diego Comic-Con, with production slated for 2027.

Ghost Rider is the alter ego of Johnny Blaze, a stunt motorcyclist who, in Marvel comics, makes a deal with the demon Mephisto to save his adoptive father and becomes bound to the Spirit of Vengeance. Created by writer Gary Friedrich, artist Mike Ploog, and Roy Thomas — Stan Lee’s first successor as editor-in-chief of Marvel Comics — he first appeared in Marvel Spotlight #5 in 1972. Nicolas Cage famously brought the character to screens in a pair of earlier Marvel films, 2007’s Ghost Rider and 2011’s Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance.

Storrie has broken out as one of the buzziest names of the moment with Heated Rivalry, Crave/HBO Max’s queer hockey romance based on the Game Changers book series by Rachel Reid, where he stars opposite Hudson Williams. The show is presently heading into its second season.

Watch on Deadline

Since the show’s November 2025 debut, Storrie has had his pick of projects. Others upcoming for him include Craig Zobel’s thriller Turpentine opposite Melissa McCarthy, A24’s Please from Halina Reijn and Peaked from Molly Gordon, and Sarah Polley’s The Bell Jar for Focus Features. Notably, following his Heated Rivalry breakout, he also earned an Emmy nomination for a hosting appearance on Saturday Night Live.

THR was first to the news of the actor’s big new gig.

title: Jack Champion, Owen Patrick Joyner, Grace Van Dien & Georgie Murphy Lead YA Romance ‘The One Before The One’ After Cast Switch
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Jack Champion (Avatar franchise), Owen Patrick Joyner (Final Destination: Bloodlines), Grace Van Dien (Stranger Things) and Georgie Murphy (Stumble) are now leading the YA romance The One Before The One, which Blue Fox Entertainment launched at the Cannes market earlier this year. Production wrapped in Austin, Texas last month, on the movie written and […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Jack Champion (Avatar franchise), Owen Patrick Joyner (Final Destination: Bloodlines), Grace Van Dien (Stranger Things) and Georgie Murphy (Stumble) are now leading the YA romance The One Before The One, which Blue Fox Entertainment launched at the Cannes market earlier this year.

Production wrapped in Austin, Texas last month, on the movie written and directed by Brittany Sarkisian, based on a story by John E Clark. The film is produced by Sarkisian and Jaylen Moore for Showmance Productions, along with Raja Collins, Dan Sheldon and Tara Pirnia.

The synopsis reads: “When burned-out Wall Street analyst Steven (Champion) returns to his hometown for his twentieth high school reunion, he is inexplicably transported back to his senior year and reunited with his lost love, Beth (Van Dien). Steven becomes determined to rewrite history, but the version of Beth he spent twenty years idolizing may not be the soulmate he remembered. While trying to ensure his best friend Brian (Joyner) doesn’t once again miss the opportunity to play college football and rebuilding his relationship with his longtime friend and songwriter, Katie (Murphy), Steven slowly comes to realize that the life and love he always wished for might not be the one that got away.”

Watch on Deadline

The film was previously set to star Charlie Gillespie, Sara Waisglass, and Siena Augudong, but scheduling conflicts led to the new cast being drafted in soon over the summer.

The film is said to be “set against the backdrop of late-90s nostalgia: nokia phones, house parties, alt rock, and the looming panic surrounding Y2K”.

Champion is represented by UTA, Amplifed, and Goodman, Genow. Joyner is repped by Prototype Talent Agency, Protégé Entertainment and Myman Greenspan. Murphy is repped by Gersh, Link Entertainment, and Play Management. Van Dien is repped by Innovative Artists and Link Entertainment.

title: Melanie Lynskey to Play Erin Patterson in ‘Mushroom Murders’ Limited Series at Paramount+
summary: Melanie Lynskey is set to star in the limited series “Mushroom Murders,” which has been greenlit at Paramount+. The show is based on the now-infamous case of Erin Patterson, the Australian woman who was convicted on multiple counts of murder and attempted murder after allegedly preparing food for guests containing toxic death cap mushrooms. The […]
content:
Melanie Lynskey is set to star in the limited series “Mushroom Murders,” which has been greenlit at Paramount+.

The show is based on the now-infamous case of Erin Patterson, the Australian woman who was convicted on multiple counts of murder and attempted murder after allegedly preparing food for guests containing toxic death cap mushrooms. The show will depict the 97 days between the meal and Patterson’s arrest.

Lynskey will executive produce in addition to starring. Anya Beyersdorf (“Fake,” “Apple Cider Vinegar,” “Fires”), Daina Reid (“The Handmaid’s Tale,” “Shining Girl,” “Run Rabbit Run”) and Deb Balderstone (“Dustfall”, “Ticket to Paradise,” “Palm Beach”) created the series, all three serving as executive producers. Reid will also direct all six episodes.

Beyersdord will write along with Dianne Taylor (“Dustfall,” “After the Party”) and Belinda Chayko (“Dustfall,” “Fires”). Xavier Marchand also executive produces, as does Sophia Mogford for Paramount+. Soapbox Pictures will produce.

“This is an ambitious series that brings a gripping real-life story that captivated Australia and the world to the screen with the scale, quality and creative vision audiences expect from Paramount+,” said Beverley McGarvey, president of Network 10 and head of streaming for Paramount Australia. “It is a powerful addition to our growing slate of premium storytelling, and we are delighted to partner with such an exceptional creative team to share it with viewers around the world. We are also thrilled to welcome Melanie Lynskey, whose remarkable talent will be integral to the series both on screen and as an Executive Producer.”

Lynskey currently stars in the Paramount+ series “Yellowjackets,” which is going into its fourth and final season. She has received two Emmy nominations for outstanding lead actress in a drama for her work in the series. She was also nominated in 2023 for guest starring in the hit HBO series “The Last of Us.” Her other TV credits include “Two and a Half Men,” the true crime drama “Candy,” “Togetherness,” and “Mrs. America.”

She is repped by Gersh.

title: Tokyo Opener ‘Sukiyaki’ Director Zeze Takahisa on the Protest Roots of a Global Japanese Pop Hit: ‘The Culture Used to Be Wide Open – Now It’s Become Narrower’
summary: The opening film of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” tells the story of how the title tune became a worldwide hit in 1963 as well as a beloved standard that has been recorded in foreign-language versions that have also topped charts. The film goes beyond the song itself to delve into […]
content:
The opening film of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” tells the story of how the title tune became a worldwide hit in 1963 as well as a beloved standard that has been recorded in foreign-language versions that have also topped charts.

The film goes beyond the song itself to delve into the lives and careers of its makers: lyricist Ei Roksuke (Matsuzaka Tori), composer Nakamura Hachidai (Okada Junichi), and singer Sakamoto Kyu (Nakano Taiga). They became known in Japan as the “689 trio” with the unusual moniker coming from the “number” characters in their names: Hachi (8), Roku (6) and Kyu (9). But as the film shows in scene after highly charged dramatic scene, their professional and personal relationships were not always harmonious.

Interviewed at the headquarters of Toho, the film’s Japan distributor, Zeze stressed the film’s relevance, six decades after “Sukiyaki,” known locally as “Ue o Muite Aruko” (I’ll Walk with My Head Up”), first hit the charts. “Back then the country was recovering from the war and all sorts of influences were flooding in from abroad,” Zeze said. “Those influences created an energy that propelled the popular culture here. Now Japan is absorbing fewer influences from abroad. The culture used to be wide open – now it’s become narrower.”

But younger Japanese are now discovering that energy from the Showa Era (1926-1989), the period of Emperor Showa’s reign, when Japanese pop culture was at a fertile peak. Together with nostalgic Boomers, they could be found in the audience of “Godzilla Minus One,” the 2023 smash hit Godzilla series installment set in the early postwar period . The follow-up by director Yamazaki Takashi, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is also at TIFF as the festival’s Centerpiece screening, “It’s a kind of Showa boom,” joked Zeze.

In casting “Sukiyaki,” he says, the main criterion was not a physical resemblance to its main characters, though Nakano Taiga channels Sakamoto’s exuberant stage persona with an uncanny precision. “It was more about the feeling the actors projected,” Zeze explains. “But Taiga comes from a show business family with roots in film’s period so he had a natural affinity for the role. Also, when Sakamoto sings in the film, it’s Taiga’s voice you’re hearing – he has an amazing talent as a vocalist.”

The film’s drama, though, centers more on Nakamura and Ei, who joined forces to compose a series of hits in the 1960s but quarreled and parted as Nakamura spiraled into alcoholism. “ Nakamura went through a tough period after ‘Sukiyaki’ became a hit so we show that,” says Zeze. “If the film were just a success story, it wouldn’t be interesting – it has to have both ups and downs.”

None of this drama had much to do with “Sukiyaki” becoming a hit abroad, but the film also delves into the sources of its creation, from Nakamura’s mastery of the jazz piano, which he displayed in New York clubs, to Sakamoto’s roots into early rock – he was a big Elvis fan – and Ei’s composition of the poignant Japanese lyrics,

“Of course people abroad didn’t understand the lyrics, but the song’s energy came across to them,” says Zeze. “The lyrics reflect what was happening in Japan at that time.” Ei Rokusuke, the lyricist, was inspired by the demonstrations against the Japan-US Security Treaty in 1960. “ The demonstrators called for peace, but failed to stop the treaty ratification. “He wanted them to ‘walk with their heads up,’ despite their defeat,” says Zeze. “So the song has depth – it ‘s not just a cheery pop tune.”

title: Hasan Piker Sues Scott Jennings for $72 Million Over Out-of-Context Lynching Quote
summary: Twitch streamer Hasan Piker sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday, alleging that Jennings had defamed him by misconstruing a quote to make it sound like Piker endorsed lynchings. On his own podcast on Aug. 11, Jennings played a mashup of clips of Piker, including one in which Piker referenced going “back to a better […]
content:
Twitch streamer Hasan Piker sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday, alleging that Jennings had defamed him by misconstruing a quote to make it sound like Piker endorsed lynchings.

On his own podcast on Aug. 11, Jennings played a mashup of clips of Piker, including one in which Piker referenced going “back to a better time when lynchings were happening.” Jennings denounced the commentary and warned Black voters of the “Piker plan of returning our country to lynchings.”

In the lawsuit, Piker’s attorneys state that it was clear that Piker was mocking another person’s argument — not offering his own support for lynchings — and that Jennings repeatedly contorted Piker’s words to convey the opposite of his actual meaning.

“These were not expressions of disagreement with Mr. Piker’s politics,” the lawsuit states. “Nor were they rhetorical characterizations of an admittedly controversial commentator. They were factual assertions about what Mr. Piker had said and advocated in his work. Each statement was demonstrably false.”

The suit seeks $72.5 million in damages.

Piker threatened to sue Jennings, who appears frequently on CNN, within a couple of days of the original comments. The controversy has already been adjudicated by Snopes, the myth-busting site, which came down on Piker’s side.

“A full review of Piker’s unedited remarks confirms Jennings falsely claimed Piker said he was in favor of bringing back lynchings,” the site concluded. “In the original stream, Piker’s remarks on lynchings were sarcastic reactions to a user’s chat comment and opinions expressed by someone else in a separate video.”

As a public figure, Piker would have to show that Jennings either knew what he was saying was false or that he acted with reckless disregard for the truth of the statements. He would also have to demonstrate that the comments were provably false statements of fact and not Jennings’ opinions.

“Mr. Jennings was not simply expressing an opinion,” the lawsuit states. “He was falsely asserting that Mr. Piker had advocated racial violence against Black Americans.”

Piker also asserts that he suffered harm to his reputation as a result of Jennings’ comments that damaged his ability to make a living.

According to the complaint, Piker’s lawyers submitted a retraction demand to Jennings on Aug. 31, but they have not received a substantive response.

The mashup of Piker clips had been circulated a few days before Jennings’ commentary by the National Republican Senatorial Committee. The compilation appeared intended to damage Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, who has appeared with Piker.

“How does Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign surrogate Hasan Piker feel about Black Americans?” the NRSC asked on X. “Watch for yourself.”

title: Horror Film ‘The Land of Jinn’ Is First Indonesia-Kyrgyzstan Co-Production, Unveiled at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
summary: Indonesia and Kyrgyzstan have made their first film together. “The Land of Jinn,” a supernatural horror feature directed by Kevin Rahardjo (“Smothered”), was unveiled at the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market as the first co-production between the two countries. The story centers on a young Indonesian woman who journeys to Kyrgyzstan in search of a mystical healer […]
content:
Indonesia and Kyrgyzstan have made their first film together. “The Land of Jinn,” a supernatural horror feature directed by Kevin Rahardjo (“Smothered”), was unveiled at the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market as the first co-production between the two countries.

The story centers on a young Indonesian woman who journeys to Kyrgyzstan in search of a mystical healer who might save the baby she is carrying. Along the way, she unwittingly ties her child’s destiny to the jinn that roam the region. The film draws on the story of King Solomon, said in legend to have commanded the jinn.

Makbul Mubarak (“Autobiography”) and Tumpal Tampubolon (“Crocodile Tears”) wrote the screenplay.

“I’ve always been fascinated by the lengths someone might go to in pursuit of what society tells us is a ‘complete’ life, and what drew me to this project was the chance to translate that desire into the language of horror,” Rahardjo said.

The journey takes the protagonist to Kyrgyzstan’s frozen, snowbound mountains. “The landscape is more than a backdrop. It becomes part of her obsession, beautiful and unforgiving, and almost indifferent to human desire,” Rahardjo said.

Cameras rolled in Kyrgyzstan’s Issyk-Kul region and in Jakarta. The film, in English, Indonesian and Kyrgyz, is now in post-production, with a release planned for 2027.

Yulia Evina Bhara and Amerta Kusuma produce for Jakarta-based KawanKawan Media, while Sultan Pirzhan and Elvira Sarieva of FreeMinds and Maksat Bolotbek of Bairak Group produce on the Kyrgyz side.

“I think fear is universal, but ghosts are local,” Bhara said.

She noted that people in both countries live alongside the unseen world, and that children in each grow up hearing their grandparents’ warnings not to venture out after Maghrib, the sunset prayer. “In Indonesia we have 17,000 islands and 17,000 ghosts. In Kyrgyzstan, the mountains and steppes have their own Jinns,” she said.

She pointed to the complementary strengths of the two industries, with Kyrgyzstan offering auteur talent, unspoiled scenery and a door into markets across Central Asia and Eurasia, and Indonesia bringing a proven horror market, a 65% local market share and a profitable model for the genre.

“This project was an incredible start to what will hopefully be a long lasting creative collaboration between Indonesian and Kyrgyz filmmakers,” Sarieva said.

Also on board as a producer and delegate is Nazira C. Noer, CEO and co-founder of film marketing and publicity firm Poplicist, whose clients have included “Jumbo,” “Agak Laen” and “Ghost in the Cell.” She is also Navvaros Entertainment’s chief marketing officer and serves as secretary general of the Indonesian Film Agency.

In Tokyo, the producers want to find partners to close the film’s financing gap and handle distribution, with the goal of locking in pre-sales or a festival route for 2027. Bhara also hopes to present the film as a template for co-productions within Asia.

Rahardjo’s next project is a creature feature unfolding in a countryside village in Indonesia.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

title: Variety Nominated for 62 Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards
summary: Variety has amassed 62 nominations for the Los Angeles Press Club’s 19th annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards, including nods for Print Journalist of the Year for Chris Willman and Online Journalist of the Year for Ethan Shanfeld. In the criticism category, Owen Gleiberman was nominated for film critic (over 1,000 words) as well […]
content:
Variety has amassed 62 nominations for the Los Angeles Press Club‘s 19th annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards, including nods for Print Journalist of the Year for Chris Willman and Online Journalist of the Year for Ethan Shanfeld.

In the criticism category, Owen Gleiberman was nominated for film critic (over 1,000 words) as well as music critic and Daniel D’Addario was nominated for theater/performing arts critic. Willman was nominated for music critic, online columnist of the year and print columnist of the year, among other nods.

Several Variety cover stories were recognized as finalists, including Daniel D’Addario’s Jodie Foster cover, Trish Deitch’s Jamie Lee Curtis cover, Shanfeld’s Miley Cyrus cover and D’Addario’s Charlie Hunnam cover.

In the art and photography category, Daniel Doperalski was nominated in the portrait photo, music/theater/arts category for his photo for Variety’s “KPop Demon Hunters” cover.

Shanfeld was also nominated for several other reported features; his Baywatch casting story is up for TV Industry Feature (Over 1,000 Words) while his his investigation into the Diddy Trial “circus” is up for Music/Performing Arts Industry Feature (Over 1,000 Words).

Winners will be revealed at the Art & Entertainment Journalism Awards on Dec. 6 at the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles, where Brandi Carlile will be honored with the Humanitarian Award. Variety won 20 prizes at last year’s Arts & Entertainment Awards.
