title: William Shatner Remembers ‘Star Trek’ Co-Star Walter Koenig
summary: William Shatner today paid tribute to his Star Trek co-star Walter Koenig after news of the latter’s recent death. The actor who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the sci-fi series died at 90, and his former co-star, who played Captain Kirk, took to social media to remember him. Shatner expressed sadness at […]
content:
William Shatner today paid tribute to his Star Trek co-star Walter Koenig after news of the latter’s recent death.

The actor who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the sci-fi series died at 90, and his former co-star, who played Captain Kirk, took to social media to remember him.

Shatner expressed sadness at Keonig’s passing, even while admitting they didn’t know each other well. That did not keep the captain from praising the kindness of one of the longest-serving members of the Enterprise crew.

“What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years,” wrote Shatner, “was a man who genuinely loved the Star Trek community. At conventions, Walter was rarely content to remain behind a signing table. He preferred to be among the people who had kept Star Trek alive for so many decades. That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him.”

Watch on Deadline

Shatner concluded with condolences to Koenig’s “family, his friends, and the countless fans whose lives he touched.”

I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig’s passing.

Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original Star Trek series and the six films that followed.

What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the… — William Shatner (@WilliamShatner) October 27, 2026

Yesterday George Takei, who as Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu sat at the navigation controls with Koenig’s Chekov, shared his own thoughts.

“Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades,” wrote Takei. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”

title: IDA Documentary Awards Shortlists: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘To Hold A Mountain,’ ‘Nuisance Bear’ Make Features Cut, But What Got Snubbed?
summary: The IDA Documentary Awards announced its shortlists of the year’s top documentaries Tuesday, boosting Oscar prospects for a select group of feature films and shorts. Some of the most touted documentaries of the year made the cut, but the list is equally newsworthy for what got left out. In the features categories, 16 films will […]
content:
The IDA Documentary Awards announced its shortlists of the year’s top documentaries Tuesday, boosting Oscar prospects for a select group of feature films and shorts.

Some of the most touted documentaries of the year made the cut, but the list is equally newsworthy for what got left out. In the features categories, 16 films will compete for Best Documentary at the awards show set for December 4 in Los Angeles, among them: A Fox Under a Pink Moon, A Life Illuminated, Birds of War, Nuestra Tierra, Nuisance Bear, One in a Million, and You Can See Everything – the Elizabeth Holmes documentary that has become a runaway box office hit.

Also making the list – Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, the follow up to her Oscar-shortlisted My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow. Two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot earned a spot on the list with his feature The Eyes of Ghana, and Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals for a Revolution, winner of the L’Oeil d’or prize at Cannes, also made the list.

Watch on Deadline

But there were some shocking snubs in that category: no love for Musk, 14th, nor two prominent Gaza-themed films – American Doctor and NAZA. Also missing out was Once Upon a Time in Harlem, one of the most honored documentaries of the year. The shortlist selection committee favored some comparatively obscure titles, like Concrete Land, directed by Asmahan Bkerat; Filthy, directed by Bàrbara Mestanza and Marc Pujolar; Silver, directed by Natalia Koniarz, and The Fabulous Time Machine, directed by Eliza Capai.

Scroll for the complete lists.

An ICE deportation flight seen in ‘They’re Here.’ Arte France

On the shortlist of short films, a dozen documentaries made the cut, including They’re Here, directed by Oscar winner Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller. That timely documentary, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival, examines the deadly ICE occupation of Minneapolis, MN. Bill Morrison, Oscar-nominated last year for Incident, made the list with his latest short, Sawyer Avenue, Sunday Afternoon. That documentary also centers on ICE, in this case, the seizure of a man by federal agents “without a warrant on a residential street in Chicago.”

Remarkably, four New York Times Op-Docs films made the shorts shortlist: A Wolf in the Suburbs, directed by Amélie Hardy; Sanyi Kakas (Sanyi the Rooster), directed by Lotte Salomons; Son, directed by Leona Cauklija, and Stalin Boys, directed by Bianca Giaever and Ora DeKornfeld.

Director Yoruba Richen also made the shorts shortlist with Free Joan Little, as did Oscar-nominated filmmaker Waad Al-Kateab with Maybe Tomorrow, co-directed with Wafa Mustafa. But in a surprise, two-time Oscar nominee Joshua Oppenheimer didn’t get recognized for his new short, The Revolution Against Death (recently acquired by the New York Times Op-Docs).

IDA

The 42nd IDA Documentary Awards will be presented on Friday, December 4 at The Ebell of Los Angeles. Tabitha Jackson, director of Film Forum in New York City and former director of the Sundance Film Festival, will host the ceremony. In a release, the nonprofit IDA said, “At a time when filmmakers face critical distribution and funding challenges, IDA looks forward to gathering and uplifting this irrepressible global community and introducing their work to new audiences.”

The five nominees for the Best Feature and Best Short categories will be selected from the shortlists that were revealed Tuesday, with nominations set to be announced on November 17. “IDA members from 100 countries will view and vote for the Best Feature and Best Short category winners until voting closes on November 29.”

Additional IDA Awards will be presented in the following categories with winners selected by jurors consisting of 200+ documentary professionals from 60+ countries: Best Director, Best Cinematography, Best Editing, Best Original Music Score, Best Production, Best Sound Design, Best Writing, Best Curated Series, Best Episodic Series, Best Documentary Not in the English Language, Best Music Documentary, Best Student Documentary Award, the ABC News VideoSource Award, and the Pare Lorentz Award.

These are the films that made the shortlists announced Tuesday:

title: Melanie Lynskey Stars In ‘Mushroom Murders’ Australian True Crime Limited Series Ordered By Paramount+
summary: Paramount+ has greenlit Mushroom Murders, a six-episode limited drama series out of Australia starring and executive produced by Melanie Lynskey (Yellowjackets, Don’t Say Good Luck). It is based on Australia’s infamous Leongatha mushroom murders, with New Zealand actress Lynskey playing Erin Patterson who had been convicted in the case. The series, created by Anya Beyersdorf […]
content:
Paramount+ has greenlit Mushroom Murders, a six-episode limited drama series out of Australia starring and executive produced by Melanie Lynskey (Yellowjackets, Don’t Say Good Luck). It is based on Australia’s infamous Leongatha mushroom murders, with New Zealand actress Lynskey playing Erin Patterson who had been convicted in the case.

The series, created by Anya Beyersdorf (Fake, Apple Cider Vinegar, Fires), Daina Reid (The Handmaid’s Tale, Shining Girl) and Deb Balderstone (Dustfall, Ticket to Paradise), is being announced today at the Australian TV upfronts. Its green light was initiated by the previous Paramount+ regime prior to the Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

In 2023, Erin Patterson (Lynskey) served individual beef wellingtons to her estranged in-laws and their relatives at a lunch in her Victoria home in Australia. Unbeknownst to her guests, Patterson allegedly prepared the food with highly toxic death cap mushrooms, resulting in the deaths of three guests. The limited series depicts the 97 days between the now infamous lunch and Patterson’s subsequent arrest.

Watch on Deadline

Patterson’s trial drew nationwide attention, with her 2025 sentencing broadcast live. She is appealing her sentence of at least 33 years in prison.

Australia has emerged as a top market for Paramount+ that has delivered such breakout series as comedy Colin From Accounts and NCIS: Sydney.

Mushroom Murders is produced by Soapbox Pictures and executive produced by Balderstone, Xavier Marchand (Dustfall, A Gentleman in Moscow) and executive produced by Sophia Mogford. Beyersdorf is writer-executive producer, Reid will direct all six episodes and also executive produce. Dianne Taylor (Dustfall, After the Party) and Belinda Chayko (Dustfall, Fires) are writers alongside Beyersdorf.

“This is an ambitious series that brings a gripping real-life story, that captivated Australia and the world, to the screen with the scale, quality and creative vision audiences expect from Paramount+,” said Beverley McGarvey, President Network 10 and Head of Streaming, Paramount Australia. “It is a powerful addition to our growing slate of premium storytelling, and we are delighted to partner with such an exceptional creative team to share it with viewers around the world.”

Lynskey, Emmy nominee for Showtime’s Yellowjackets (twice) and HBO’s The Last Of Us, most recently starred in the Netflix film Don’t Say Good Luck. She is repped by Gersh.

title: How ‘Klara And The Sun’ Got Blotted Out At the Box Office
summary: At a time when the box office is rebounding, and embracing auteur-driven fare (i.e. Christopher Nolan’s near $1.8B grossing The Odyssey) as well as originality (a three-hour documentary about a delusional, scandalous tech titan called You Can See Everything), the star studded Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams starring Klara and the Sun failed to shine […]
content:
At a time when the box office is rebounding, and embracing auteur-driven fare (i.e. Christopher Nolan’s near $1.8B grossing The Odyssey) as well as originality (a three-hour documentary about a delusional, scandalous tech titan called You Can See Everything), the star studded Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams starring Klara and the Sun failed to shine with a $701K domestic opening last weekend. The movie, booked at 880 locations, posted a theater average that was less than $800.

The Sony theatrical release, based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 Booker Prize long-listed novel, comes from absurdist auteur Taika Waititi who after glamming, joking and grossing up Marvel’s Mightiest Avenger with Thor: Ragnarok in 2017 (the superhoe’s top earner with $855.3M WW), went on to win an adapted screenplay Oscar for the Hitler-adjacent politically offbeat comedy Jojo Rabbit in 2019. A niche New Zealand filmmaker known for his witty humor and heart, Waititi received the phone call to come work at Marvel following the 2016 Sundance world premiere of his movie The Hunt for the Wilderpeople. Waititi also delivered the second highest-grossing Thor movie in Thor: Love and Thunder in 2022 ($760M).

Director Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega, on the ‘Klara and the Sun’ set Sony Pictures Releasing/Everett Collection

Last Monday we walked into an AMC Century City press screening for Klara and the Sun with a tremendous amount of bias: We heard that the movie sat around for two years with Sony befuddled as to how to release it. We heard rumors about Sony being at odds with Waititi’s “free jazz” and “instinctual” auteur stylings on set (those are adjectives used by rival studio executives who adore and have worked with Waititi). Then there were the bloody reviews out of the London Film Festival (The Guardian called Klara and the Sun “a sentimental mess”).

Watch on Deadline

I cried three times during the movie in which Ortega stars as the title character, a later-edition artificial robot. After wallowing unbought with her fellow robots in a gloomy city storefront, Klara is finally purchased by a sickly young girl, Josie (Mia Tharia), and her dominant mother, Chrissy (Amy Adams). The plan is for Klara to bring joy to Josie while looking out for her safety. They live in a bright sunny country home surrounded by golden wheat where Klara finds her footing in the real world; She is continually energized, bedazzled and worshiping the sun. Along the way, Chrissy comes to blows with Klara, but then learns the robot is the best thing in her daughter’s life. There’s also a bit of a twist in this emotional dystopian feature about how precious life can be.

How did a movie led by famous YA star Ortega (39M followers on social) and directed by an Oscar-winning filmmaker, lose its way in a booming box office?

The industry continually calls for more movies aimed at women. Here was one.

‘Jojo Rabbit’ Fox Searchlight

And how ironic: When Searchlight first rolled out Jojo Rabbit, there was concern over Waititi starring as Adolf Hitler in the movie, and befriending a young boy. A TIFF world premiere paved the way for the movie’s Oscar run, winning the festival’s awards-bellwether prize, the Grolsch People’s Choice Award, and goosestepping to 81% certified fresh with critics on Rotten Tomatoes and 94% with audiences. Audiences ultimately realized with Jojo Rabbit that the movie wasn’t an affront and that it had something smart to say in divided political times. The final global box office was $93M.

We’ve seen pre-finance package documents on Klara and the Sun which showed a direct cost for the pic of $44.3M with a $4.4M contingency and anticipated New Zealand subsidies of $7.55M. Sony insiders swear the movie cost a net high $20M before global P&A spend. At either budget point, for an audacious movie, Klara and the Sun was economically priced with Spyglass and TSG covering 50% of the budget. The losses here on Klara and the Sun are ulimately minimal next to the $150M-plus that’s out there on the $160M net priced Tom Cruise starring Digger, which Alejandro Inarritu directed. Likewise, Sony minimized its exposure on the $30M-$42M costing Aaron Sorkin directed Mark Zuckerberg follow-up, The Social Reckoning, which was 50% co-funded by Alcon. We hear that movie, which grossed around $17M WW to date, will lose the Culver City studio a result in the single millions after all ancillaries.

The book Klara and the Sun was championed by Sony-based 3000 Pictures producer Elizabeth Gabler back in 2023. Waititi would discover the novel in an airport book store, and was wowed. That was serendipitous, as his moving sense of whimsy was the right fit for the novel. (Or was it?) The novel was quite melancholic and subtle; Ishiguro’s tomes are challenging to adapt (i.e. his dsytopian novel Never Let Me Go didn’t translate at the B.O. grossing $2.4M domestic and less than $10M WW). We’re told that Ishiguro even encouraged and supported Waititi throughout to make his own version of Klara and the Sun.

When there’s a box office misfire, the media quite often likes to uncover some sort of major mishap on set. Truth be told, Waititi turned the film in under his allotted shoot time and under budget. The pic began lensing in February 2024 at Silverlight Studios in Wānaka, NZ and continued in Auckland, wrapping April of that year.

The original ending of the movie described by one source close to the testing was “a bummer” and more faithful to the book’s ending. Waititi worked with Gabler in reshoots (which occurred in April 2025 with Ortega) to get the ending to a significantly more positive place. We’ve heard myriad reports about the pic’s testing; that the movie with the original ending came in at an 83% positive and with the revised upbeat ending, went up to 87% positive. Other sources in the know tell us that the test scores were “just fine” and that audiences didn’t buy into the tonality nor did they connect with the characters.

The minus of Klara and the Sun, per marketing sources, is that it’s not a widely-read book. Thus, there wasn’t a massive appeal for the IP. On the plus side, that provided more liberties for Waititi and Dahvi Waller in adapting.

Some have told us that Klara and the Sun sat around for two years with Sony up in arms about how they wanted to release it. Studio insiders counter that Klara and the Sun only sat around for a year. There was a discussion at one point to send it to Cannes back in May. However, Ortega’s production commitment on Season 3 of Netflix’s Wednesday was busy, lasting from late February this year through Sept. 30. We hear the actress — along with Waititi — were involved with marketing; Ortega suggested the light blue color background in the one-sheet.

The movie was finally dated for Oct. 23 as wide in Rentrak back in mid-April. Early tracking wasn’t promising. It landed in the low single digits when the film hit six weeks out before its release.

After Wednesday wrapped, Ortega became fully available to promote the film, traveling with Waititi and Adams to the London Film Festival, Rome Film Festival and a New York premiere. Ortega, Adams and Waititi also did the Drew Barrymore Show where the host championed the movie.

Ortega appeared on Seth Meyers, as well as the Today Show, alongside Adams. Ortega also posted about the film and her red carpet appearances in London and Rome on her IG.

But then the reviews hit out of London on Oct. 15 like a swat of hand ninjas out of Spider-Man: Brand New Day slicing down Klara and the Sun for its sentimentality. Ot has a current Rotten Tomatoes critical score of 25%. “Klara and the Sun is Waste for Jenna Ortega” was Vulture’s headline, while other critics slammed it as “emotionally manipulative” and “meandering.” The whole situation was reminiscent of the 2016 Will Smith weeper, Collateral Beauty, which after getting pummeled by critics at 14% on Rotten Tomatoes, had an ugly cry at the box office with a $7.1M domestic opening and $31M final.

Seeing the reviews, Sony waved the white flag, reducing Klara and the Sun‘s theatrical release from wide to moderate on Rentrak. With such retreats come organic marketing budget cuts, and this one was significantly less than $30M worldwide. Given its sophisticated patina, Klara and the Sun is movie that lives and dies by reviews in regards to finding an audience. It’s not a popcorn movie like Street Fighter which overcome bad reviews (41%) and still opened at the box office ($31M).

We heard audiences hit the exits over the weekend, further supporting the concerns that were raised by testing on Klara and the Sun. It came in at a 69% positive score and 48% definite recommend (not very good), with women over 25 showing up at 33% but not in bulk, with 19% under 25.

“The Jenna Ortega fans were not seeing this as their movie. They might have expected one thing, but didn’t get it,” says one source with knowledge of the pic’s pulse. An RT audience score went missing throughout the weekend before appearing yesterday at 78%, worlds above the critical rating.

While A24 has been able to capture the Gen Z audience in the noir stylings of You Can See Everything, a movie whose box office success has been propelled by several fan memes parodying Elizabeth Holmes and co-director/doc interviewer Nathan Fielder, another marketing source observes that Klara and the Sun‘s misfire at the B.O. with that demo stems from not being FUBU (“For Us, By Us”). That was the secret of success for A24’s highest-grossing movie this year, Backrooms, which finaled with $400.6M WW.

At a time when the box office is winning against streaming, the sad takeaway here with Klara and the Sun is that no matter how much TLC a studio provides a production to get it in its best possible shape, even with decent-to-above average test scores; the pack nature of critics continues to have the power to thwart the best of commercial cinematic intentions.

Klara and the Sun is one of many examples in a flourishing box office of just how fickle the theatrical marketplace can be.

title: ‘The Kitchen’ Sets Food Network Return Date For Special Episode
summary: The Kitchen is returning to the Food Network less than a year after its cancellation. Garden Slate Productions, which produced the show for the network, shared a behind-the-scenes teaser of some of the hosts filming a special episode. The new episode airs Saturday, October 31, at 11 a.m. ET on the Food Network. The video […]
content:
The Kitchen is returning to the Food Network less than a year after its cancellation.

Garden Slate Productions, which produced the show for the network, shared a behind-the-scenes teaser of some of the hosts filming a special episode.

The new episode airs Saturday, October 31, at 11 a.m. ET on the Food Network.

The video features four hosts: Katie Lee Biegel, Geoffrey Zakarian, Alex Guarnaschelli, and Jeff Mauro. Sunny Anderson, who was part of the core cast when the show went off the air, was not on the set. It is unknown if she will be part of the special.

Earlier this year, Mauro, Zakarian, and Biegel teased that they had filmed a special episode of The Kitchen.

Watch on Deadline

In October 2025, Food Network confirmed it had canceled The Kitchen after more than 10 years on the air and a couple of Daytime Emmy nominations. The last episode of the cooking talk show would air in December of that same year.

“The last episode of The Kitchen @foodnetwork is this morning! Thank you so much for 12 great years and over 500 episodes!!! I will miss our crew so much and so appreciate all of you for letting us do what we love to do for so long. What an amazing ride!!!” Katie Lee posted on Instagram on the show’s last day on the air.

Sunny Anderson shared a couple of posts, starting with a reflection on her time on the show.

“Is it the end? Or the beginning? This is how you must look at all change in LIFE…cuz we are still living, it’s not the end until it’s over,” Anderson posted. “Still thankful!!! Today is the last ep!! 40 seasons just doesn’t happen to many in this game…ya never gonna catch me mad or sad about this win!!!! Today on #thekitchen…huevos rancheros in an edible vessel and i just booked a holiday vacay 80% on points!? I’m unstoppable!!!”

title: Korean Webtoon Adaptations, ‘The Vanishing Act’ Lead 2027 Vertical Slate Unveiled by COL Group, V47 and Virtue Asia
summary: Adaptations of Korean webtoons and web novels developed with CJ Group and a batch of new originals headline the 2027 vertical slate unveiled in Singapore on Wednesday by FlareFlow parent COL Group, V47 Entertainment and Virtue Asia. The lineup was presented at Inside Microdramas, which organizers described as an upfront without precedent. The Korean titles, […]
content:
Adaptations of Korean webtoons and web novels developed with CJ Group and a batch of new originals headline the 2027 vertical slate unveiled in Singapore on Wednesday by FlareFlow parent COL Group, V47 Entertainment and Virtue Asia.

The lineup was presented at Inside Microdramas, which organizers described as an upfront without precedent.

The Korean titles, developed with CJ Group, include “Idol Once Again,” a fantasy in which a washed-up idol travels back in time for a second shot at fame, and “Genius Doctor Lee Mu-jin,” based on a popular webtoon about a street fighter coached by the ghost of a brilliant physician. Also on the Korean slate is “The Exclusive Secretary,” adapted from a web novel, in which a corporate heir and the secretary who lives with him grow closer while a perilous fight over the family succession plays out.

On the originals side, COL Group and V47 are developing “The Vanishing Act,” a mystery about a magician who disappears on air during the final of an international talent contest, and “Fortune Chasers,” which mixes a scripted reality competition with thriller beats. “1% Better,” a reality format set in the world of sports and fitness, pits unlikely rivals against each other.

The slate also carries over three of COL’s best-performing existing microdramas – “Oops, I Married My Bestie’s Brother!,” “My Sweetheart’s a Gangster” and “From Janitor to Mrs. Billionaire” – as IP the companies aim to extend through wider distribution, adaptation and commercial tie-ups. They did not specify what form those follow-ups will take.

COL Group’s FlareFlow has passed 52 million registered users and carries close to 7,000 short-drama titles, reaching viewers in upward of 200 countries and regions. The platform topped all rights holders in TikTok’s short-drama revenue-share rankings for the first quarter of 2026.

The three companies also launched Story Engine, an operating model that ties together development, production, financing and worldwide distribution. It pools V47’s development and production arm, Virtue Asia’s expertise in cultural strategy and integrating brands, and COL Group’s genre know-how and international distribution reach. Brands can go past product placement and sponsorship to come aboard as development partners, executive producers or financiers, with a possible stake in the resulting IP.

“We see a real opportunity for brands to go beyond traditional advertising and become part of the entertainment audiences actively choose to watch,” said Timothy Oh, chief marketing officer of FlareFlow and general manager of COL Group International. “By bringing together our genre expertise and international distribution network with the creative strengths of V47 and Virtue, we’re helping brands develop original entertainment IP that can build lasting audience connections and grow across platforms and markets.”

V47 was formed by Virtue Asia and Goldfinch International, the U.K.-based Goldfinch Group’s international expansion vehicle, which targets MENA, Asia and Africa.

V47 Entertainment chair David Webster said the opportunity lay in developing entertainment that could grow into something larger than one production. “By bringing brands into the development and financing process, we can give ambitious original ideas the backing they need to reach audiences, while creating opportunities to build franchises and valuable IP over time. The story must always come first, but we’re opening up new ways for brands to become meaningful partners in creating the entertainment people want to watch.”

Virtue Asia, a strategic and creative agency, counts Disney, Google, Spotify, Toyota, Diageo and Shiseido among its clients. Its CEO, Lesley John, said brands could no longer get noticed by interrupting culture and instead had to earn a place within it. “Microdramas offer an exciting opportunity, but success depends on understanding the culture, the audience, and the storytelling that makes people want to keep watching. Our role is to bring those worlds together – translating cultural insight into creative integration that feels native to the story and adds value to the audience experience, not just visibility for the brand.”

title: Thai Forest Spirit Horror ‘Cher,’ First Thai Winner at Frontières, Joins Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
summary: A Thai horror film built on the folklore of the Nang Mai, the forest nymphs of Thai myth, is the only Thai entry in the 2026 Tokyo Gap-Financing Market lineup. “Cher” arrives in Tokyo after becoming the first Thai project selected for, and awarded a top prize at, Canada’s Frontières Co-Production Market. Benetone Films and […]
content:
A Thai horror film built on the folklore of the Nang Mai, the forest nymphs of Thai myth, is the only Thai entry in the 2026 Tokyo Gap-Financing Market lineup.

“Cher” arrives in Tokyo after becoming the first Thai project selected for, and awarded a top prize at, Canada’s Frontières Co-Production Market.

Benetone Films and Fearfolks are producing the feature, which Songsak Mongkolthong (“Graveyard Horror,” “School Tales the Series”) directs from a screenplay by Patrick Graham, writer of Netflix’s “Ghoul” and “Betaal.”

Rattanawadee “Mim” Wongthong (“Death Whisperer”) heads the cast, with Pae Arak and Weir Sukollawat (“4 Tigers”). Vikash Nowlakha, who shot the “Dhurandhar” duology, is the cinematographer. The producers said those two Indian films earned a combined $330 million at the global box office.

Mongkolthong said the story raises the possibility that the Nang Mai, long part of Thai belief, may have different origins from the ones taught in Thailand.

“The idea of starting a new life begins with confronting our own prejudices, anger, and hatred. When we learn to move beyond anger and hatred, a new life can begin,” he said.

Benetone Films CEO Rachvin Narula and COO Kulthep Narula said the company backed the project from the outset and treated it, as the studio’s first tentpole, differently from the approach of other Thai studios.

“We are absolutely thrilled it is getting the global recognition it deserves so early on,” they said.

Tokyo is the latest stop on a market run for the film. It was selected for the It Project market at the Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF), part of South Korea’s Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival (BIFAN), and won at Frontières in July.

“We are extremely grateful to BIFAN, Frontières and TIFFCOM for giving Thai films a voice on this global stage, and for allowing us to bear these great honors,” said Fearfolks CEO Hans Audric Estialbo. “Prestigious markets like TIFFCOM allow the film to build momentum and a community of followers early, which is what most successful IPs need now.”

Filming is due to start in the first three months of 2027, ahead of a global release in 2028.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

title: Val Chmerkovskiy Says He Wants ‘Nothing But Love’ for Carrie Ann Inaba Following ‘DWTS’ Suspension, Apologizes to Jenna Dewan: ‘I Am So Sorry for All the Chaos’
summary: “Dancing With the Stars” pro Val Chmerkovskiy and judge Carrie Ann Inaba have made amends, concluding the hectic saga that has ensued since Chmerkovskiy made an “inappropriate” joke about Inaba earlier this month that resulted in his getting benched from the competition. On Tuesday night’s episode of the dance competition series, Chmerkovskiy was back in […]
content:
“Dancing With the Stars” pro Val Chmerkovskiy and judge Carrie Ann Inaba have made amends, concluding the hectic saga that has ensued since Chmerkovskiy made an “inappropriate” joke about Inaba earlier this month that resulted in his getting benched from the competition.

On Tuesday night’s episode of the dance competition series, Chmerkovskiy was back in the ballroom following a one-week suspension from the show. The decision by the show to remove him from the competition temporarily was made after Chmerkovskiy posted to his TikTok story, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” after his wife, fellow judge Jenna Johnson, was critiqued by Inaba during the Oct. 13 episode of the show. The TikTok was interpreted as a reference to Will Smith’s infamous slap at the 2022 Oscars, and deemed “inappropriate” by BBC Studios.

While Chmerkovskiy’s absence was not touched upon in last week’s episode, this week, as Val returned, audiences saw the pro apologize to his partner, Jenna Dewan. “We are back together. I am so sorry for all the chaos. You did not sign up for that, and I feel awful,” Chmerkovskiy said during their pre-dance package, to which Dewan responded: “I forgive you…I missed you.”

Following Tuesday’s show, Chmerkovskiy and Inaba embraced one another, as caught on camera across social media. “It felt [like] cathartic relief, you know?” Chmerkovskiy told People about speaking with Inaba. “I think it was just really important for me to make sure that she feels safe and knows that, firsthand from me, I want nothing but love for her.”

He continued: “I want nothing but joy for her and as much as the world might say otherwise, I want her to know how I feel, not how others want me to feel, but how I genuinely feel. I will have nothing but love for Carrie Ann. I have nothing but respect for what she has to say.”

Earlier on Tuesday, Inaba posted a lengthy statement to Instagram about the saga. “I have not spoken about what happened because of professional courtesy for those who are still competing, and we actually have standards and practices that keep us separated,” Inaba began.

“But I think a part of this ‘headline’ has missed a few important parts of what happened,” Inaba continued. “I think it’s important for everyone to know that Jenna and I hugged it out after the Super Bowl show. Jenna was an absolute professional about it, and two women worked through the moment. It came to my attention later that Jenna was deeply hurt. So I also offered to speak with her at any time. I have also offered to discuss the lift rule and how I enforce it. @sharnaburgess made a great video explaining lifts, assists and which dances allow and don’t allow them.”

“I think in the future, a new lift rule should be created for next season,” she concluded. “Working together to create a better understanding between the dancers and the judges and our audience is important to me, as we move forward and is something I have asked for.”

title: Kore-eda Hirokazu Hails Japanese Cinema’s Global Moment as Ninomiya Kazunari, Academy’s Amy Homma and ‘Kokuho’ Producer Murata Chieko Take Stage at Kering Women in Motion Tokyo Event
summary: Kering Women in Motion, an allied program of the Tokyo International Film Festival, held a talk event on Tuesday at Toho Cinemas Roppongi Hills for a packed crowd. Director Kore-eda Hirokazu (“Shoplifters”) opened the event with brief remarks. “In recent years, I’ve been hearing people at international film festivals say, ‘Japanese films are really interesting […]
content:
Kering Women in Motion, an allied program of the Tokyo International Film Festival, held a talk event on Tuesday at Toho Cinemas Roppongi Hills for a packed crowd.

Director Kore-eda Hirokazu (“Shoplifters”) opened the event with brief remarks. “In recent years, I’ve been hearing people at international film festivals say, ‘Japanese films are really interesting right now.’ That’s a sentiment we didn’t hear 10 years ago,” he said. “Led by Hamaguchi Ryusuke and Fukada Koji, directors in their 20s and 30s have been taking their works overseas, and through their accumulated efforts and recognition, the attention given to Japanese films has been increasing. How to pass this on to the next generation and spread it further is a challenge for the older generation, and I think it’s also very important for film fans who are exposed to these works.”

The panelists – Arashi singer and actor Ninomiya Kazunari, producer Murata Chieko and Amy Homma, director and president of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection – spoke about the present and future of Japanese cinema, as well as diversity and inclusion in the industry, with journalist Tatsuta Atsuko serving as facilitator.

“I’m a Japanese-American woman and I’m a Jewish American woman – and both of those cultures and ethnicities carry deeply long lineages of history,” Homma said. “I’m very lucky to have been raised with the awareness that multiple truths can exist at the same time.”

National cinemas also exist parallel to each other, she added, but “that does not make one more important or one more harder than the other,” she said. “American film history is just as important as Japanese film history and just as important as French film history.”

By taking a broad view of film history and experiencing different types of cinema, she said, “We allow ourselves to learn so much more about a lived experience that’s outside of our own, because there’s no better way to develop empathy to develop cultural understanding than through watching a movie.”

Ninomiya, who first came to international attention for his starring role in Clint Eastwood’s Academy Award-winning World War II drama “Letters from Iwo Jima,” said that working on an international production “presented both differences and learning opportunities for me as an actor.” One difference, he found, was the staff’s tendency “to ask more questions” than they would on a Japanese set. “They ask things like, ‘What is this?’ or ‘How do you use this?’” The result, he said, was a conversation leading to solutions, instead of a top-down explanation that might result in confusion.

Murata, the producer of the 2025 smash-hit kabuki-themed drama “Kokuho,” which received rave reviews abroad and was nominated for a Best Makeup and Hairstyling Oscar, said she wanted to “create something that will move as many people as possible, make as many people laugh as possible, and make as many people cry as possible.”

For that to happen, she added, tolerance of varying cultural perspectives is essential. “The worst case is a world in which that becomes difficult,” she said.

Homma commented that as a museum director in charge of various teams doing everything from research to marketing, “It’s always about who the best person would be.” Her aim, she added, was “for many people to bring their own cultural differences or their own unique qualities and have that be seen as a strength. I don’t want anyone to shy or hide their individualism.”

Diversity “across gender expression, across ethnicity and across ages,” she said, “is what makes for a great team,” adding, “It’s about plural thinking, not individual thinking.”

title: Jessica Biel Says She Won’t Hand Her Son Acting Roles Just ‘Because You’re Part of This Family’: ‘We’re Not Doing That’
summary: With parents like Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake, it might not be entirely possible to avoid being labeled a nepo baby in totality — but that isn’t stopping Biel from making it explicitly clear to her son that he “can’t just take a part” from someone because of who his parents are. On a recent […]
content:
With parents like Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake, it might not be entirely possible to avoid being labeled a nepo baby in totality — but that isn’t stopping Biel from making it explicitly clear to her son that he “can’t just take a part” from someone because of who his parents are.

On a recent episode of the “Great Chat Show” podcast, Biel told host Josh Smith that she’s been discussing the business of acting with her oldest son, 11-year-old Silas, who recently made an appearance in “Matchbox: The Movie,” in which Biel starred.

“He’s a DJ, he’s incredible [at] music, he’s doing such cool things with music — he just has that, right? He just has that innately and is interested in that,” she said. “And also has this comedy streak and this theatrical kind of funny, silly quality. And he’s been talking to us about, yeah, wanting to be an actor. So, this is coming up a lot.”

She explained that when Silas’ name came up for the role in “Matchbox,” she was initially unsure of moving forward, given that she and Timberlake try to keep their kids “away from all of this.” But, she said, “you don’t want to squash their dreams, even though I kind of want to squash this one. I’m like, ‘Please don’t do this! Anything but this! It’s really hard!’”

Biel continued: “Because the other thing I was talking to him, Silas, about is, there are kids who work really hard, and they go to acting class, and they’re in theater class, and they’re doing all the work,” Biel explained. “You can’t just take a part from that person just because you’re my son. Like, that’s not cool. We’re not doing that. So this is a special opportunity because it’s really teeny tiny. And, if you had a big monologue, I wouldn’t let him do it… You would have to earn that part because we’re not starting that. We’re not starting, ‘Oh, you just get handed a bunch of opportunities because you’re part of this family.’ Mm-mm, we’re not doing that.”

Biel first broke into Hollywood as Mary Camden on the long-running family drama “7th Heaven.” She’s currently a producer on a reboot of the show, which she said will “modernize it” and focus on “the things that are happening for teenagers and families that have teenagers all the way down to the youngest child — technology-based issues, school stuff, bullying stuff, drugs, alcohol.”

She is also set to star in the forthcoming Searchlight film “Playmates” as Hugh Hefner’s wife.

title: Amazon MGM Studios Japan To Double Investment In Original Content; ‘One Piece’ & ‘Kingdom’ Producers Talk IP Strategies – TIFFCOM
summary: Buddy Marini, Amazon MGM Studios’ new head of Japan, says the company has doubled its investment in original Japanese content, including an expanded slate of live-action films and series. Marini was speaking on a panel on the opening day of TIFFCOM, which also featured One Piece showrunner Steven Maeda and Kingdom producer Shinzo Matsuhashi, outlining […]
content:
Buddy Marini, Amazon MGM Studios‘ new head of Japan, says the company has doubled its investment in original Japanese content, including an expanded slate of live-action films and series. Marini was speaking on a panel on the opening day of TIFFCOM, which also featured One Piece showrunner Steven Maeda and Kingdom producer Shinzo Matsuhashi, outlining their strategies for adapting valuable IP from Japan.

While he didn’t put a number on the investment, Marini explained how Amazon MGM is working with partners including Korea’s Studio Dragon and Japan’s Credeus, Toho, TV Tokyo and Wowow to ramp up production of Japanese live-action and anime content. While the slate is primarily made for Japanese audiences, the intention is that it will also travel globally.

“Amazon Prime has been acting as an aggregator for content, and we grew that business very successfully, but going forward we wanted to focus more on original content – not just in Japan but worldwide,” said Marini, a former head of Warner Bros Japan who has been in his new post since March.

Watch on Deadline

“We’re seeking to appeal to a wide audience so we’re producing content across diversified genres, and across different formats including drama, anime and theatrical films.”

Marini also introduced several live-action titles that the studio has been working on, including an adaptation of popular light novel series, The Apothecary Diaries, which will star Mana Ashida as the protagonist Maomao. Co-produced by Amazon MGM Studios and Toho, the series will stream exclusively worldwide on Prime Video in 2028.

“While the anime is popular worldwide, this has been entirely produced in Japan by Japanese staff members and cast. We’re aiming for global audiences, although there are not so many cases like this,” Marini explained.

Amazon MGM Studios also recently teamed with Wowow to produce Chloe And Emma, a live-action adaptation of a manga that has been streaming on Prime Video since June 2026, and with TV Tokyo on Criminal (Hanzaisha), directed by Daishi Matsunaga, which dropped on the streamer in March.

Older titles include a Japanese version of Korean series Marry My Husband, produced with Korea’s Studio Dragon; manga adaptation The Silent Service, produced with Credeus, which was released as a series and theatrical feature, and Japan-U.S. live action crime drama series Like a Dragon: Yakuza, adapted from Sega’s video game series, which was produced with The Fool, Wild Sheep Content and 1212 Entertainment.

“High-quality content is in demand so we’re going to double our investment to reach an international standard and attract global audiences,” Marini said.

“Our long-term goal is to work with Japanese creators to make content that appeals to the world. From this perspective, script is the most important element, and we have creative executives in our team, along with writers and development executives, to help us to come up with scripts that have global appeal. We’re also flexible on whether projects are released through theatrical or streaming.”

The panel Marini was speaking on, ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’, organized by the Motion Picture Association and UniJapan, also featured fireside chats with Matsuhashi and Maeda, followed by a Q&A session.

Matshashi, CEO of Japanese production outfit Credeus, which has credits including the Sony-backed blockbuster Kingdom franchise and last year’s Oscar submission Kokuho, explained how the company has been working to retain IP on some of its projects.

For the Blue Lock feature, based on a popular manga, Credeus set up a rights holding company, CK Works, as a joint venture with the publisher of the manga, Kodansha.

“It’s rare for production companies to be involved in holding IP rights, but it’s starting to become more standardized and practiced globally,” said Matshashi.

“Production cost very high and this can’t be covered fully by production companies, who are usually seen as contractors who create, deliver and are left with nothing at the end. We were frustrated with this system, so we hope that by retaining rights, we can build structures like those in Hollywood.”

Maeda, showrunner on Netflix’s live action adaptation of Japan’s iconic One Piece manga, talked through the logistics of adapting a long-running manga with hundreds of installments into an eight-episode series, and ensuring it had the budget level to do the original work justice.

“We had a lot of discussions and push and pull on what the budget was going to be. So we wrote three versions of the show,” Maeda explained. “The first version was going to be very expensive and Netflix asked us if we would do a version that was much less expensive.

“The problem with that was, if we did that version, it was not going to be the One Piece show that the fans were going to love, and the first step for One Piece was to make sure that the fans got on board.

“That’s the big battle with global IP: you’re going to have people who love the show, and they want the faithful adaptation, and you’re going to have people who have never heard of the show, and you still need to bring those people in. If you succeed, you can have international success. And if you fail, everyone hates you,” Maeda said.

TIFFCOM is running for three days (October 28-30) at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho.

title: Carrie Ann Inaba & Val Chmerkovskiy Hug It Out After ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Suspension Drama
summary: It was all professional between Carrie Ann Inaba and pro dancer Val Chmerkovskiy on the Dancing with the Stars set after all the drama. The judge and the contestant hugged it out on the set of the ABC dance competition, a moment that has now gone viral, which you can see at the end of […]
content:
It was all professional between Carrie Ann Inaba and pro dancer Val Chmerkovskiy on the Dancing with the Stars set after all the drama.

The judge and the contestant hugged it out on the set of the ABC dance competition, a moment that has now gone viral, which you can see at the end of this post.

It was Chmerkovskiy’s first week back on the show after his week’s suspension following comments directed at Inaba.

On the October 13 episode, Inaba pointed out lifts in Jenna Johnson’s performance. During the episode, Inaba and Johnson had a tense exchange about the definition of a lift.

Chmerkovskiy, who is married to Johnson, posted a shady comment on social media saying, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” The comment referenced Will Smith taking the Oscar stage and slapping Chris Rock to defend his wife.

Watch on Deadline

After the comment, Chmerkovskiy earned a one-week suspension, with BBC Studios calling the pro-dancer’s social media post “inappropriate” and not reflecting “the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show.”

Chmerkovskiy has since then deleted his social media comment and apologized to Inaba, saying, “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”

As for Inaba, she shared a social media post recently where she said that “Jenna and I hugged it out after the Super Bowl show,” adding, “Jenna was an absolute professional about it, and two women worked through the moment. It came to my attention later that Jenna was deeply hurt. So I also offered to speak with her at anytime. I have also offered to discuss the lift rule and how I enforce it.”

title: Entertainment Hits $332.5B To Become World’s Second Most Valuable Sector As Netflix, YouTube & Spotify Fly – Interbrand Report
summary: Hollywood is struggling with layoffs and budget cuts, but entertainment just overtook the automotive industry to become the world’s second-largest business sector. That’s according to consultancy Interbrand, whose latest Best Global Brands report pegs the cumulative value of entertainment companies at $332.5B, an increase of 12.4% year-on-year. Within that, Netflix’s brand value grew 22%, which […]
content:
Hollywood is struggling with layoffs and budget cuts, but entertainment just overtook the automotive industry to become the world’s second-largest business sector.

That’s according to consultancy Interbrand, whose latest Best Global Brands report pegs the cumulative value of entertainment companies at $332.5B, an increase of 12.4% year-on-year.

Within that, Netflix‘s brand value grew 22%, which Interbrand considers as reflecting pushes into live entertainment, sport and advertising. That should be soothing mood music to Netflix execs, who’ve been under fire from Wall Street over its latest round of financials and for a lack of user engagement.

Netflix is ranked the 23rd most-value brand in the world, with Instagram, at seven, and YouTube, tenth, the only entertainment brands in the top ten overall. Disney is 23rd and Sony 35th, while Spotify is ranked 39th. Interbrand’s assessment is each has moved beyond their original role as a content platform and become businesses that shape consumer behavior.

Watch on Deadline

According to Gonzalo Brujó, Global CEO at Interbrand, “Entertainment’s growth reinforces one of the defining themes of this year’s ranking: Growth comes not from doing more, but from making stronger choices about where and how a brand creates value. In an industry where content is abundant and consumer attention is fragmented, competitive advantage is shifting from the scale of content to the strength of the brand.”

Brujó told Deadline that as AI “transforms how entertainment is created, distributed and consumed, technology alone will be an increasingly weaker source of differentiation,” and that “the brands that win will be those that understand the role of brand in driving choice, identify new arenas for growth, and consistently give people reasons to come back, creating habits, not just moments.”

Interbrand’s list was dominated by tech giants, with Apple top, Microsoft second, Google third, Amazon fourth and Samsung fifth. Other consumer brands such as McDonald’s, Toyota and Coca-Cola ranked highly, with Larry Ellison’s Oracle 13th. Gaming brands such as Nintendo and PlayStation also increased their brand values.

Omnicom-owned Interbrand’s annual report weights companies based on available financial data and requires them to have significant revenues outside their home territories, along with predictions of profits over the long-term and a ‘Brand Strenth Score’ equal to 50 or above. Research was conducted by Paradigm Sample.

title: Yuriko Gamo Romer & Marc Smolowitz On The 12 Year Journey Behind Their Japanese-U.S. History Baseball Doc ‘Diamond Diplomacy’ — Tokyo
summary: After a year on the U.S. festival circuit, with buzzy stops at Mill Valley and Hot Springs, Diamond Diplomacy, the feature documentary from San Francisco-based filmmaker Yuriko Gamo Romer, receives its first international screening this week at the Tokyo Film Festival. The screening will serve as a unique homecoming for Gamo Romer and the doc. […]
content:
After a year on the U.S. festival circuit, with buzzy stops at Mill Valley and Hot Springs, Diamond Diplomacy, the feature documentary from San Francisco-based filmmaker Yuriko Gamo Romer, receives its first international screening this week at the Tokyo Film Festival.

The screening will serve as a unique homecoming for Gamo Romer and the doc. Produced between the United States and Japan, Diamond Diplomacy traces more than 150 years of shared baseball history between the two nations.

Using rare archival footage, the film explores baseball’s arrival in Meiji-era Japan through Babe Ruth’s 1934 tour and World War II to the modern era of Japanese stars such as Ichiro Suzuki and Shohei Ohtani. Using the sport, the doc examines the history of diplomacy, racism, war, reconciliation, and cultural exchange between the two countries. The story centers on Masanori “Mashi” Murakami, the first Japanese player in Major League Baseball, and Warren Cromartie, who starred for the Yomiuri Giants.

Gamo Romer previously directed and produced MRS JUDO: Be Strong, Be Gentle, Be Beautiful (2012), a feature documentary about Keiko Fukuda, the first woman to attain the 10th-degree black belt in judo. Her other credits include the shorts Baseball Behind Barbed Wire (2023) and My Immigrant Story (2018). Readers may also recognize her name from media reports about the Trump administration’s brutal cuts to the National Endowment for the Humanities. Gamo Romer was one of the few NEH recipients who spoke publicly about how the wide-scale cuts affected her work. Diamond Diplomacy had received substantial grants from the NEH. Overall, the Trump administration canceled more than 1,400 previously approved NEH grants. The cuts were later ruled unconstitutional by a U.S. court.

Watch on Deadline

Gamo Romer’s public advocacy attracted new funders and partners. U.S.-Japanese diplomat Glenn S. Fukushima boarded the project as an executive producer after hearing Gamo Romer on NPR. He was later joined by Steven Okazaki, Jacqueline Glover, and Mari Nakachi, who helped to fill gaps in the film’s funding. Strand acquired North American distribution rights in May, and the film heads to Tokyo with a freshly minted local distribution deal with Wondergenic. Producers on the doc are Gamo Romer, Marc Smolowitz, and Loi Ameera Almeron.

Below, Gamo Romer and Smolowitz speak with Deadline in depth ahead of their Tokyo screening about how they rebuilt their production after Trump’s NEH cuts and how they dug into the MLB archives to explore U.S.-Japanese history.

The Tokyo Film Festival runs until November 4.

DEADLINE: Yuriko, this film began as a short?

YURIKO GAMO ROMER: The initial spark was the 1949 San Francisco Seals coming to Japan during the postwar occupation. General MacArthur sent the baseball team to Japan as a goodwill gesture. That was the story I was drawn to. It turned out my friend’s father had been a pitcher on the Seals and had a movie camera with him when he went to Japan. That’s how the project started. I started opening history books and meeting people, and the project got longer and bigger. We did release a short focused more on the World War II Japanese American incarceration story. It came out a couple of years ago.

MARC SMOLOWITZ: The short, called Baseball Behind Barbed Wire, was a big festival success. It allowed Yuriko to talk about Diamond Diplomacy and gave us a way to keep communicating to funders and supporters that the feature was coming. The short helped the project pick up momentum, and the feature scaled up after that, around 2023. We got a grant that made the short possible. We were strategic about making clear that the short and feature were part of the same film enterprise, even though the short came out first.

DEADLINE: Yuriko, talk me through the research process. Was it easy to uncover this story? I only fairly recently learned about the internment camps in California. You don’t learn about that in the U.K., where I went to school.

GAMO ROMER: I’m old enough that when I went through the California school system, it wasn’t taught at all. I didn’t learn about it until the 1980s, when there was a movement to get reparations for people—especially American citizens—who were suddenly thrown into prison, basically. For the film’s research, I started coming across books. Historian Rob Fitts, who is in the film, has written several books on this area. I met him about a year into the research, and he had written a biography about Masanori “Mashi” Murakami, the first Japanese player to play in the major leagues. I went on a book tour with Rob, met a lot of people, and learned much more.

The history isn’t covered extensively, but the Babe Ruth tour comes up right away. Rob wrote a book about that; it’s a dramatic story. You bump into all these connected stories, but they aren’t covered in depth. Some are only in Japanese-language books. There are a few books around. I probably have most of them in my library now. I’ve been working on this film for more than 12 years. Through the research and meeting people, I kept discovering stories. It just kept getting bigger. One of the challenges was keeping the film short enough for people to sit down and watch it.

DEADLINE: Marc, there are a lot of great producers and executive producers on the film. We know how difficult it is to get documentaries off the ground. Could you talk about how you built this production?

SMOLOWITZ: I’ve been with Yuriko on this since the beginning, so we’ve built a long partnership. I always tell the story about the National Endowment for the Humanities funding because it’s important. We first received development funding, which was a big milestone. Later, we received a larger amount. Ultimately, that money was taken away during the DODGE controversy. We were on a trajectory to finish the film and had enough money at that point, with other funders who had stepped up. The cuts happened in the final year of making the film. We couldn’t have predicted that it would become one of the biggest gifts to the film’s story: it led us to our largest supporter. Yuriko was brave enough to speak out about the controversy. It became a case study in crisis PR—something terrible happens, and you communicate it publicly in a way that can turn into a win.

She went on NPR, and Glen Fukushima found us. Over several months, he became the perfect executive producer—not only filling the funding gap, but bringing a high-level diplomatic connection between the U.S. and Japan. He understood the film’s value as a cultural product that could encourage dialogue. Then we found Mari, Jackie, and Steven. These people became building blocks that gave the film credibility with funders. That’s how you do it: nurture the project for years.

DEADLINE: Trump’s NEH cuts have been so devastating. I did a panel recently with Rita Coburn. She directed a great film about W. E. B. Du Bois. She told me that during the production, she could sense that their NEH funding was about to be cut, so she told her crew to get their invoices in quickly.

SMOLOWITZ: We could report the same kind of thing. Rumors were coming down. When we were cut, about 14 people were working on the movie. It was a real hit to people’s livelihoods. We recovered pretty quickly—within about three months we were back at full pace. We shifted our delivery target by about one festival season. Many filmmakers weren’t able to solve their crisis that way. It has created a lot of discussion in the nonfiction field about how we value the humanities and how we’ll fund films if those kinds of funds aren’t available. There has been some recovery. California Humanities, for example, recently re-announced grants that had been on pause for about a year and a half. It’s looking up, but it’s tricky for filmmakers who have worked for years on important projects and then get cut off.

DEADLINE: Yuriko, where did you find all the great archival baseball footage? Does the MLB have a robust archive?

GAMO ROMER: Very early on, Marc helped a lot with negotiating a licensing agreement. It was a huge line item, and I wondered how I’d ever pay for it. Fortunately, they let us pay over several years. In retrospect, it was a wonderful deal. It was a blanket agreement, and they did all the research. The MLB asked me to send a list of what I wanted, along with a script, treatment, or rough cut. That helped them think beyond what I knew to ask for. They provided things that shocked me. A lot of footage in the film that you wouldn’t expect to come from MLB archives did come from there. The archive team knew where everything was and what the stories were. Ken, the editor, and I would receive material and ask, “What is this?” It was incredible.

DEADLINE: When you came to Japan to shoot, how were you and the project received? It’s not the easiest material for people involved in the story to relive.

GAMO ROMER: I shot twice at the Yokohama Country and Athletic Club, which is essentially an expatriate club filled with Americans and Brits. Some people knew bits and pieces of the story. But there’s a general interest. The story is less known among the broader population, especially younger people. We had a press screening last week. Mashi and I spoke and answered questions afterward. He gave a heartfelt speech about how grateful he was that I made the film. He feels people don’t know or appreciate baseball history, and that knowing more might help them appreciate it. The hope is that younger people will see the film, learn, and expand their horizons. Part of the problem is that there hasn’t been much access to this information and history.

DEADLINE: So how are you thinking about the release?

SMOLOWITZ: Strand is handling the U.S. release. Wondergenic Films is our Japanese distributor. They’re essentially a distribution startup. One partner is a Japanese distributor who has acquired individual films at Venice and released them in Japan when they otherwise wouldn’t have had a Japanese release. His young business partner, Michael, is binational and bilingual; he grew up in the U.S. and now lives here in Japan. They’re interesting young partners, and our film is their prototype—the first one they’re giving this kind of commercially oriented launch. They’re both huge baseball fans. Michael, the American-side CEO, is the grandson of Cappy Harada, which is a remarkable personal connection. For them, it will be about seeing which exhibitors come on board. They’re reasonably confident in predicting at least 60 screens, but it could be more. They haven’t officially announced the start date, but the plan is April.

title: CNN’s Scott Jennings Hit With $72.5M Suit By Hasan Piker Over “Manipulated” Lynching Misquote
summary: In a blistering response to Scott Jennings allegedly using “a false, fabricated, and manipulated video” claiming Hasan Piker wants to bring back lynching of Black Americans, the left-wing streamer plans to take the CNN MAGA talking head to the courtroom cleaners for $72.5 million. “The accusation was especially calculated to provoke outrage because it invoked […]
content:
In a blistering response to Scott Jennings allegedly using “a false, fabricated, and manipulated video” claiming Hasan Piker wants to bring back lynching of Black Americans, the left-wing streamer plans to take the CNN MAGA talking head to the courtroom cleaners for $72.5 million.

“The accusation was especially calculated to provoke outrage because it invoked one of the most shameful chapters in American history,” the 38-page complaint filed Tuesday in federal court in DC states. “Mr. Jennings did not merely suggest that Mr. Piker held objectionable political views. He falsely told Black Americans that Mr. Piker wanted them lynched for exercising their right to vote. He used the history of racial terror as the premise for a political attack built on views Mr. Piker never expressed.”

Take a look at the still CNN paid Jennings in action here with the very video Piker says was altered. Remember, please, the language he uses refers to one of the most evil aspects of America’s history.

Watch on Deadline

Abdul El-Sayed’s best pal and campaign partner says the USA should resume lynchings against black people.



Listen for yourself and understand what the socialists have in store for the black community pic.twitter.com/N3ntbIHefw — Scott Jennings (@ScottJenningsKY) August 12, 2026

Pointing out that former Mitch McConnell aide Jennings traffics in “political controversy” for listeners and advertising, Piker’s Meier Watkins Phillips Pusch legal team spotlight the defendant on his August 11 podcast ‘falsely told his listeners that Mr. Piker had a ‘plan of returning our country to lynchings …then he falsely told his social media followers that Mr. Piker says the USA should resume lynchings against black people.'”

With the fiercely fought midterms just a week away, and Piker supported candidates like Michigan Senate contender Abdul El-Sayed moving ahead in the polls, the defamation action reflects the very different sense of reality that has come to bring a constant wrecking ball of hatefulness to the body politic.

Still, nothing says FAFO like prying cold hard cash out of an enemy’s bank account – no matter if you are MAGA, DSA or something in-between.

To that, Piker wants Jennings, who was and is again openly angling for Donald Trump to award him the once again open White House press secretary gig, to feel some pain for his “financial, professional, and political incentives to publish sensational accusations against Mr. Piker.” Specifically, after unsuccessfully attempting to get Jennings in late August to cop to the misquote and retract it, Piker, in his three-count lawsuit, is looking for “compensatory damages in an amount not less than $27,500,000.” He also seeks “punitive damages in the amount of $45,000,000,” plus fees and interest for “the reputational, professional, economic, and emotional injuries” Piker says he’s suffered.

In a move sure to harden ideological underpinnings and supporters of two provocative pundits in our divided America, Piker points out the edited and apparently fake clips came from a two year old segment where the influential Twitch star was actually mocking racism, not advocating for it — and Jennings must have known it.

“The distinction matters,” today’s complaint notes. “Mr. Jennings was free to criticize Mr. Piker, to condemn his political positions, or to argue that his commentary was offensive,” it continues “Mr. Jennings was also free to play Mr. Piker’s actual words, and provide his own commentary on what Mr. Piker actually said. Mr. Jennings was not free to do what he did: knowingly attribute to Mr. Piker statements that Mr. Piker never made, and then present those invented statements as evidence that Mr. Piker supports the racially motivated murder of Black Americans.”

A regular at the table on Abby Phillip’s primetime CNN show, Jennings is nowhere to be seen tonight.

title: Jamie Dornan Says There’s ‘Pressure’ to Taking Over Aragorn Role in ‘Lord of the Rings: Hunt for Gollum’: I’m Not ‘Trying to Outdo’ Viggo Mortensen
summary: Jamie Dornan is stepping into the shoes of Aragorn in “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” after the hero was famously played by Viggo Mortensen in the original “LOTR” trilogy. Dornan spoke to L’Officiel (translated by Slash Film) about taking on the role and playing a younger version in the prequel. “There’s […]
content:
Jamie Dornan is stepping into the shoes of Aragorn in “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” after the hero was famously played by Viggo Mortensen in the original “LOTR” trilogy. Dornan spoke to L’Officiel (translated by Slash Film) about taking on the role and playing a younger version in the prequel.

“There’s pressure when you’re trying to follow in those footsteps. I’ve been asked to play a super iconic role, and I’ll do my best. But for me, Aragorn will always be just Viggo. His performance is one of my all-time favorites, and I feel honored to try to recapture at least some of the energy he originally brought to the character. There’s no part of me that’s trying to outdo him,” Dornan said.

“The Hunt for Gollum” is directed by and stars Andy Serkis, who provided the voice and motion capture for the CGI hobbit in the original trilogy. Serkis, who has also helmed “Mowgli: Legend of the Jungle,” “Venom: Let There Be Carnage” and more, was the second unit director on Peter Jackson’s “The Hobbit” trilogy. “The Hunt for Gollum,” a standalone film, will be his first time as the main director on one of the fantasy franchise’s entries.

In addition to Serkis returning to Middle-Earth, “The Hunt for Gollum” brings back Ian McKellen as Gandalf and Elijah Wood as Frodo. Newcomers include Kate Winslet, Leo Woodall, Lee Pace and Anya Taylor-Joy. The new film will be told from Gollum’s perspective as Gandalf sends a young Aragorn out to find the corrupted hobbit. Before coming rising to fame as Aragorn, heir to the throne of Gondor, the hero is a lonely hunter known as Strider in “The Hunt for Gollum.”

title: Versant Expands Suite of FAST Channels With 4 New Selections From CNBC, E!, Oxygen
summary: Versant may best be known for the cable channels that provide the bulk of its revenue, but the company continues to build out new-media extensions. The owner of MS NOW, CNBC and USA is launching four new free ad-supported streaming networks based on programming franchises from CNBC, Oxygen and E!. When these new options debut, […]
content:
Versant may best be known for the cable channels that provide the bulk of its revenue, but the company continues to build out new-media extensions.

The owner of MS NOW, CNBC and USA is launching four new free ad-supported streaming networks based on programming franchises from CNBC, Oxygen and E!. When these new options debut, Versant will have a portfolio of 13 FAST outlets.

The new quarter consists of Snapped, a program that chronicles the life of a women charged with murder and which began airing on Oxygen in 2004; Botched, a selection from E! that examines the highs and lows of plastic surgery; Oxygen Murders of America, a true-crime documentary series; and CNBC Ambition, which offers stories of entrepreneurship, innovation, wealth creation, and success and relies on a bevy of primetime series that previously aired on the business-news cable outlet.

All four new channels will be available on Prime Video in the U.S. beginning October 27, with staggered launches on The Roku Channel starting November 3. Versant said it expects to continue to launch FAST channels with additional platforms in the coming months.

“Growing our digital platforms and reaching new audiences are central to Versant’s strategy,” said Dave Pietrycha, chief revenue and business officer of Versant, in a statement. “Bringing more of our programming to Prime Video and The Roku Channel extends the reach of our iconic brands and provides audiences with more ways to discover content they value wherever they watch.”

Versant has been working to diversify its operations and streams of revenue, in many cases by developing direct-to-consumer services associated with its mainstay cable networks, and in others by acquiring businesses that might augment current operations. Versant’s FAST portfolio began with six channels. amd the company added three more with its January 2026 acquisition of Free TV Networks. Prime Video and The Roku Channel already offer Pam Grier’s Soul Flix, American Crimes, Oxygen True Crime Archives, E! Keeping Up, Bad Girls Club, GolfPass, and Prime Video also offers 365BLK and Outlaw.

title: Peter Medak, Director of ‘The Changeling’ and ‘The Krays,’ Dies at 88
summary: Peter Medak, the Hungarian-born director and actor best known for films including “The Changeling,” “The Krays” and “The Ruling Class” died Tuesday in Los Angeles. He was 88. Over a career spanning six decades, Medak directed 27 feature films, moving between psychological horror, black comedy and crime dramas. His 1980 supernatural thriller “The Changeling,” starring […]
content:
Peter Medak, the Hungarian-born director and actor best known for films including “The Changeling,” “The Krays” and “The Ruling Class” died Tuesday in Los Angeles. He was 88.

Over a career spanning six decades, Medak directed 27 feature films, moving between psychological horror, black comedy and crime dramas. His 1980 supernatural thriller “The Changeling,” starring George C. Scott, won eight Genie Awards including best motion picture. He also directed the 1990 British gangster drama “The Krays,” for which he received the Evening Standard Award for best director.

Born in Budapest in 1937, Medak spent part of World War II in hiding with his family. Under Hungary’s Communist regime, his father was imprisoned and Medak was barred from attending school. He fled to England during the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and began working in the British film industry, eventually serving as assistant director before moving to Hollywood.

He made his feature directorial debut with 1968’s “Negatives,” starring Glenda Jackson. His 1972 satire “The Ruling Class,” starring Peter O’ Toole, competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes and earned an Oscar nomination for Toole. Other credits include “A Day in the Death of Joe Egg,” “Let Him Have It” and the Gary Oldman-led “Romeo Is Bleeding.”

Medak also worked extensively in television, directing episodes of “Homocide: Life on the Street,” “The Wire,” “Breaking Bad” and “House.” His 2018 documentary “The Ghost of Peter Sellars” revisited his troubled production of the 1970s comedy “Ghost in the Noonday Sun.”

He is survived by his four children, Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornela, and five grandchildren.

title: Oscar Contender ‘Shame and Money’ Acquired in North America by Oscilloscope (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Oscilloscope Laboratories has acquired North American rights to Visar Morina’s “Shame and Money.” The film won the Grand Jury Prize in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival, which qualifies it to compete for the Oscar for international feature film under new Academy rules. Oscilloscope is planning a theatrical release in early […]
content:
Oscilloscope Laboratories has acquired North American rights to Visar Morina’s “Shame and Money.” The film won the Grand Jury Prize in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival, which qualifies it to compete for the Oscar for international feature film under new Academy rules.

Oscilloscope is planning a theatrical release in early 2027.

The film, which stars Astrit Kabashi, Flonja Kodheli, Kumrije Hoxa, Fiona Gllavica and Alban Ukaj, was co-written by Morina with Doruntina Basha.

The film centers on a couple in their 40s who live with their extended family in rural Kosovo making a modest living on their farm. Following a familial dispute, their livelihood is lost. They are forced to move to Pristina where the pressure to provide for their family weighs heavily on the parents as they do their best to find work and a place to stay.

Morina said: “In times when the majority of people worldwide are finding it increasingly difficult to make ends meet, I believe we need a kind of class consciousness, and I hope our film makes a small contribution toward that.”

Oscilloscope president Dan Berger said, “Visar’s has drawn a portrait of a family that is subtle, searingly real and ultimately humane. We feel as one with the characters and their struggles, fully signed on for this indictment of an economic system constructed to keep too many people down.”

The producers are Fabian Altenried, Sophie Ahrens and Kristof Gerega from Schuldenberg Films (“Objet a,” “Strange River,” “Life Is Not a Competition but I’m Winning”), along with Pia Hellenthal (“Searching Eva”) and Morina.

Rights have also been acquired via international sales agency The Yellow Affair for France (Arizona Distribution), Indonesia (Falcon), Spain (Mirror Audiovisual), Switzerland (Trigon) and Filmarti (Turkey) with further deals expected to close soon. Eksystent Filmverleih released the film theatrically in Germany in September.

“Shame and Money” has won a plethora of awards since Sundance including the Cinemasters Jury Prize at FilmFest Munich, best film and best actor at Prifest Kosovo and four awards at ODA Film Festival – best movie, actress, actor and script.

“Shame and Money” is Morina’s third feature, following “Exile” and “Babai.” He is represented by Cinetic Media.

title: Jennifer Lawrence Says Playing Katniss Again After 11 Years in ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Was ‘Crazy,’ ‘Unbelievable’ and ‘So Beautiful’
summary: Jennifer Lawrence appeared on the latest episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast and spoke out for the first time about what it was like to reprise Katniss Everdeen for the first time in 11 years. The Oscar winner is back as her iconic “Hunger Games” character in the upcoming prequel movie “Sunrise on the […]
content:
Jennifer Lawrence appeared on the latest episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast and spoke out for the first time about what it was like to reprise Katniss Everdeen for the first time in 11 years. The Oscar winner is back as her iconic “Hunger Games” character in the upcoming prequel movie “Sunrise on the Reaping,” in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate.

“It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said about reprising Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful. And Woody, obviously, came through the window of my hotel room uninvited. It wouldn’t be the same if he listened to boundaries or used a door.”

Variety reported last December that Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson were returning as Katniss and Peeta Mellark for a scene in “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Lawrence has now let it slip that Woody Harrelson will also be back as Haymitch. The new prequel movie centers on a young Haymitch (played by Joseph Zada) as he competes in the 50th Hunger Games. Book readers know that Suzanne Collins’ “Sunrise on the Reaping” novel ends with a flash-forward epilogue featuring Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch, so it appears the film adpatation is following suit.

Lawrence told Variety during her “No Hard Feelings” press tour in 2023 that she was “totally” open to reprising her “Hunger Games” role of Katniss Everdeen should the right opportunity arise. She added at the time, “If Katniss ever could ever come back into my life, 100 percent.”

As Katniss, Lawrence headlined four “Hunger Games” movies between 2012 and 2015. The franchise (which also includes the Rachel Zegler-led 2023 prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes”) has grossed $3.3 billion to date at the worldwide box office.
