“Executor has violated the Court’s April 24, 2026 order by failing to meet his own self-selected, and then extended, deadline,” states the 12-page motion. “Despite having years to prepare these already belated accountings, Executor quietly filed incomplete documents styled as putative accounts current for 2023 and 2024. The 2023 filing expressly notes the material ways in which it is incomplete. As for 2024, it is nothing more than a placeholder. Neither of these defective filings provides a basis on which the Court could give its approval. Executor, however, neither sought relief from the Court nor committed to filing complete and accurate 2023 or 2024 accountings on any particular date.”

The filing is full of citations of alleged past violations of disclosures and obligations in what has become a very public and dragged out conflict between Michael Jackson and Debbie Rowe’s second child and the controversial Thriller superstar’s on-again/off-again lawyer.

However, one figure in this latest document stands out.

“This instance, however, is particularly offensive in that Executor’s defective filings include a request for approval of more than one hundred million dollars ($100,000,000) in compensation for the co-executors and the Ziffren firm,” the October 23 motion says. To rub that in, the document adds with barely veiled sarcasm: “It is unclear how Executor could calculate and distribute such an amount with any confidence and yet be unable to file complete and accurate accountings years later.”

Put in that context, and with the history between the parties (blockbuster biopic and all), “difficult” may be the kindest term one could use.

The motion from Paris Jackson goes on to declare: “Paris therefore requests that the Court reduce the compensation to Co-Executors for 2023, 2024 and each consecutive year until such time as Executor files a complete and accurate 2026 account current, by five percentage points, i.e., from 15% to 10% of the gross entertainment-related income.”

While 28-year-old Paris Jackson has reportedly received about $65 million from her late father’s now multi-billion dollar estate, which was over $500 million in debt at the time of MJ’s 2009 prescription drug OD death, she has been demanding a deeper dive into the books from Branca and now dead co-executor John McClain for a while. Claiming sweetheart deals, bonuses and payouts for no or little work, legal fees, and swaths of unnecessary expenses (like the tens of millions in reshoots for a near completed Antoine Fuqua-directed Michael after the unearthing of a very restrictive 1994 deal — along with a $20 million-plus settlement — with the family of then-underaged Jordan Chandler), Paris has had some wins and losses in what is pretty obviously a long term goal of taking control of the estate itself.

Or not, according to the MJ Estate itself today.

“It is an understatement to say that this motion is completely without merit, nor is it argued on facts, the estate’s spokesperson told Deadline Wednesday. “Plaintiff’s attorneys have motioned for a reduction in executor compensation, when in fact the executors waived that from the estate’s beginning, and have never taken any executor compensation. They are paid a separate, court-ordered management fee for operating the hugely successful Michael Jackson business.”

Not mentioning that $100 million, Team Branca add: “It is also nonsensical that the motion seeks absurd penalties for the 2023 and 2024 accountings which have already been filed or for the 2025 and 2026 accountings which are not required to be filed for another six and 14 months, respectively.”

BTW – whatever goes down on December 4, with a sequel to the $1.02 billon and more box office busting Michael in the works, don’t for one second think this de facto Jackson civil war is anywhere near over.

title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Creator Teases “Pivotal & Important” Role Written For Dax Shepard
summary: In latest Nobody Wants This news, Erin Foster is preparing to bring Kristen Bell’s real-life husband into the onscreen family. Although Netflix has not yet renewed the Jewish romantic-comedy for Season 4, the series creator/executive producer told Dax Shepard that she and the show’s writers have “been writing you into the season,” asking the actor […]
content:
In latest Nobody Wants This news, Erin Foster is preparing to bring Kristen Bell’s real-life husband into the onscreen family.

Although Netflix has not yet renewed the Jewish romantic-comedy for Season 4, the series creator/executive producer told Dax Shepard that she and the show’s writers have “been writing you into the season,” asking the actor if he would “say yes.”

“I was watching Season 3, which I love, and I jokingly said … ‘I think Season 4, I should come in and f*ck this whole perfect party up,'” joked Shepard on his Armchair Expert podcast as he interviewed Erin and sister/EP Sara Foster.

Erin teased, “We have an idea that was formed a few weeks ago. We put your name on the board, thinking about it. And then today, we were in the room and this idea for you actually pivoted and switched into something bigger.

Watch on Deadline

“And then, what we said was, ‘Well, let’s ask him how many episodes he would actually wanna be in before we make this choice,'” she added. “Because it’s not like you have to be there all season or anything, but it would be pivotal, and an important role. And we felt like it would be a very fun, interesting thing to do.”

Although Shepard has gone without an onscreen acting role since 2020’s Buddy Games, he recently broke his hiatus for a role in the upcoming second season of Apple TV’s Bad Monkey.

“You know what’s funny? If you had asked me last year, I would’ve said no, ’cause I had not acted in six years, and I was very happy to not act. And then Bill Lawrence was in here, and he said, ‘I’m gonna make you act on one of my shows.’ And I was like, ‘I don’t really wanna do it.’ And he said, ‘What if every scene’s with Vince [Vaughn]?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah, I’ve always wanted to do that,'” he explained.

“So, I just did this, and I loved it. I ended that experience, and I was like, ‘Oh, I’m more open to that than I thought I was,'” added Shepard, to which Foster quipped, “So we’re catching you at the right time.”

In Nobody Wants This, inspired by Foster’s relationship with her music exec husband Simon Tikhman, agnostic podcaster Joanne Williams (Bell) begins an unexpected romance with progressive Rabbi Noah Roklov (Adam Brody), which shakes both their families as Joanne immerses herself in Noah’s culture and decides to convert to Judaism.

While Foster has said she has “more story to tell” in a potential Season 4 of Nobody Wants This, the show has become the subject of discourse since star Adam Brody publicly shared his support for “Free Palestine” amid the Israel-Hamas conflict’s ongoing impact on Gaza.

title: Barbara Barrie Dies: Star Of Broadway And ‘Barney Miller’ Was 95
summary: Barbara Barrie, who received a Tony nomination for her role in Broadway’s original Company, an Oscar nomination for her performance in Breaking Away and wide recognition as the wife of Hal Linden’s police captain on TV’s Barney Miller, died October 28 at her home in Manhattan. She was 95. Her death was reported to The […]
content:
Barbara Barrie, who received a Tony nomination for her role in Broadway’s original Company, an Oscar nomination for her performance in Breaking Away and wide recognition as the wife of Hal Linden’s police captain on TV’s Barney Miller, died October 28 at her home in Manhattan. She was 95.

Her death was reported to The New York Times by her daughter Jane Harnick, who said Barrie’s death was medically assisted and that the actor had been diagnosed with terminal cancer.

Following her breakthrough Cannes Film Festival award-winning performance in 1964’s One Potato, Two Potato, Barrie built a career that encompassed the stage, film and television, making marked contributions to all. She appeared in 11 Broadway productions, including original stagings of Stephen Sondheim’s Company, Neil Simon’s The Prisoner of Second Avenue and California Suite, Harvey Fierstein’s Torch Song Trilogy and a 2004 revival of Fiddler on the Roof.

In addition to 1979’s Breaking Away, her film credits included an uncredited role in the classic 1956 drama Giant and as the mother of Goldie Hawn’s character in 1980’s Private Benjamin.

Barrie was most prolific on television, with credits stretching back to the 1950s anthology dramas and such popular 1960s series as Route 66, The Twilight Zone, The Fugitive, Ben Casey and Ironside, among many others. In 1974 she flirted with Gavin MacLeod’s Murray Slaughter on a memorable episode of The Mary Tyler Moore Show and began her five-season recurring role on Barney Miller the following year. Her character largely was absent beyond the first season as the ABC sitcom increasingly focused on the police precinct workplace comedy rather than the title character’s domestic life.

The cast of ‘Barney Miller’, clockwise from top left: Max Gail, Gregory Sierra, Jack Soo, Ron Glass, Abe Vigoda, Hal Linden and Barbara Barrie Everett Collection

In addition to her portrayal of Barney Miller‘s Liz Miller, Barrie probably is best known to TV audiences for her series regular role on the 1996-2000 sitcom Suddenly Susan, in which she portrayed “Nana” Keane, grandmother of Brooke Shields’ title character. Barrie appeared in 92 episodes during the show’s five-season NBC run.

Born Barbara Ann Berman on May 23, 1931, in Chicago, Barrie was moved to New York City after college to launch her show business career. She made her Broadway debut in the 1955 play The Wooden Dish, returning four years later in The Beaux Stratagem by George Farquhar. She also appeared in various Off Broadway productions, including 1958’s The Crucible, as well as regional and touring productions.

Her signature stage role arrived in 1970 when she originated the character of Sarah in Company, starring opposite Elaine Stritch, Dean Jones and Beth Howland, among others. She was nominated for a Tony Award for the performance in what would prove to be a seminal Broadway musical.

Barrie’s most recent Broadway role was in Joshua Harmon’s Significant Other in 2017.

In film, Barrie landed her first leading role in 1964’s groundbreaking One Potato, Two Potato, portraying a divorced woman who marries a Black man and in so doing risks losing custody of her child. Both the film and Barrie’s performance were acclaimed highlights of the year’s Cannes Film Festival.

Bernie Hamilton and Barbara Barrie in ‘One Potato, Two Potato’ (1964) Everett Collection

Perhaps Barrie’s most beloved and memorable film performance came in Breaking Away, when she portrayed the mother of the main character played by Dennis Christopher, a small-town young man who dreams of becoming a competitive bicycle racer. Barrie received an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress for her performance but lost to Meryl Streep in Kramer vs. Kramer. Barrie would reprise the Breaking Away role for a TV series adaptation, earning an Emmy nomination.

Among her numerous other TV credits, Barrie appeared in Family Ties, Law & Order, Pushing Daisies, Nurse Jackie, Kate & Allie, Once and Again and Army Wives. She was Emmy nominated three times, for Breaking Away, Law & Order and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.

RELATED: Susan Saint James Dies: ‘McMillan & Wife’, ‘Kate & Allie’ Actor Was 80

Barrie was the author of two children’s books: 1990’s Lone Star and 1994’s Adam ZigZag. She also wrote two memoirs following her diagnosis of colorectal cancer: Second Act in 1997 and Don’t Die of Embarrassment in 1999.

Barrie was married to Jay Harnick, the founder and artistic director of TheaterWorksUSA, from 1964 until his death in 2007. In addition to her daughter Jane Harnick, she is survived by son Aaron Harnick and three granddaughters.

title: Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis Transform Into Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes to Spoof ‘You Can See Everything’
summary: On Wednesday night’s episode of “The Tonight Show,” host Jimmy Fallon went full Nathan Fielder while guest Jamie Lee Curtis played Elizabeth Holmes to spoof A24’s buzzy documentary, “You Can See Everything.” “Now, be honest. Do you really want to be on the show tonight?” asks Fallon, doing his best Fielder impression. “Of course I […]
content:
On Wednesday night’s episode of “The Tonight Show,” host Jimmy Fallon went full Nathan Fielder while guest Jamie Lee Curtis played Elizabeth Holmes to spoof A24’s buzzy documentary, “You Can See Everything.”

“Now, be honest. Do you really want to be on the show tonight?” asks Fallon, doing his best Fielder impression. “Of course I do. I love talking to you,” responded Curtis with her best Holmes-like voice while donning a blonde wig and looking deeply into the late-night host’s eyes. “So, you’re not just here to promote your new show. ‘Newlyweds’?” “No, I’m engaging with you as a human being,” said Curtis. “Why would I deceive you? There’s no reason for me to do that. There’s nothing for me to deceive you on.”

“Good chat,” concluded Fallon, but not before one last question: “You’re being real right now?” “I’m always being real,” responded Curtis. As Fallon leaves, she yells, “Thank God! Fuck, what an asshole!”

As mentioned in the cold open, Curtis was on the show to promote “Newlyweds,” her new NBC sitcom that premiered on Oct. 23. The logline for the show, starring Téa Leoni and Tim Daly, describes it as “a later-in-life love story about a free-spirited woman and a buttoned-up professor who marry impetuously after a whirlwind courtship.”

Curtis will appear on the show in a recurring guest star role, and also co-created it with Gail Lerner, who was fired from the show earlier this month for “creative differences.” In Lerner’s statement when the news broke, she described the experience working on the show as “the most joyous TV experience of my life.”

“You Can See Everything,” which debuted in theaters earlier this month on Oct. 16, has been a hit both critically and at the box office, where it’s already grossed $45.1 million domestically to date. Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

Watch the full cold open here.

title: James Gunn Calls Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman the DCU’s ‘Diamond Characters,’ Says Krypto, John Stewart and Peacemaker Could ‘Turn Into Diamonds’
summary: James Gunn has once again taken to Threads in defense of his DC universe, and this time, is clarifying his previously proposed eight- to 10-year roadmap for the fictional world and making it clearer where each character stands within it. “You can look at my quotes from January ’23 when we started and I said […]
content:
James Gunn has once again taken to Threads in defense of his DC universe, and this time, is clarifying his previously proposed eight- to 10-year roadmap for the fictional world and making it clearer where each character stands within it.

“You can look at my quotes from January ’23 when we started and I said we were going to do exactly what we’re doing,” the DC Studios co-head wrote responding to a now-deleted post. “I said some stories would be standalone like the Guardians movies were (which is what Clayface is) and some stories would have part of a larger narrative structure, which is what the Superman Saga is. All that said, each piece of the larger story should work on its own with or without having to see everything else.”

He continued in a second post: “ALSO, some things get conflated here. The often cited ‘8 to 10 year roadmap’ originally pitched wasn’t only story points (although that was a part of it), but also the plan for DC as a whole, including focusing on diamond characters (Superman, Batman, WW) as well as smaller characters we could turn into diamonds (Krypto, John Stewart, Peacemaker), how we would foster filmmaker freedom & allow for multiple tones & ratings, the influences of Star Wars & George RR Martin, and so much more.”

Gunn’s note about the “8 to 10 year roadmap” refers to his and fellow co-head Peter Safran’s 2022 remarks during a virtual Warner Bros. Discovery town hall, during which he’d said they’d mapped out an 8- to ten-year plan for DC. In a third post, he added: “It’s exciting seeing things START to come together and all that makes me even more excited for what we have in store for everyone in Man of Tomorrow.”

On Saturday, Gunn took to the social media platform to defend his decision to expand the DC universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his films aren’t building toward a major crossover event.

Responding to a commenter who pointed out that Gunn doesn’t necessarily need to lay the foundation for one totally interconnected universe, he wrote, “I couldn’t agree more.” “DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else. People not understanding this is strange to me, because ‘Star Wars’ has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books, admittedly without the tonal variety,” he wrote.

Gunn’s next film, “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” hits theaters July 9, 2027.

title: ‘South Park’: Cartman, Stan and Kyle Must Solve South America’s Beef Crisis in Halloween Week Episode
summary: In the fourth episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America’s beef has surprisingly become a hot commodity — and Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Randy won’t let their lunch-of-choice get taken away from the local mountain town without a fight. The episode, titled, fittingly, “Guinea Pig on a Stick,” opens with Cartman eager to get […]
content:
In the fourth episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America’s beef has surprisingly become a hot commodity — and Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Randy won’t let their lunch-of-choice get taken away from the local mountain town without a fight.

The episode, titled, fittingly, “Guinea Pig on a Stick,” opens with Cartman eager to get a sloppy joe for lunch at South America Elementary. But to his horror, he learns there’s a national beef crisis, so the government is taking it from South America, and he and the gang will have to eat different versions of the four-legged rodent instead. But the kids (and Randy, who remains shrunken) won’t stand for this, and set off to find a solution after reflecting on what Kenny (who got blown up by an e-bike in the first episode of Season 29) would have done: not stand for this.

They visit the local ranch, where they learn that the suddenly premier, in-demand South American beef is just “the same cows that have always been here.” But, as the ranch worker responds, “Now we have a much higher clientele, you know, and all the rich people in other states want a premium experience.” He’s referring to national clientele outside of South America — specifically the chain Ruth’s Chris Steak House — despite the fact that every person who indulges in the meat literally explodes with diarrhea.

Those eating the beef don’t care, though, as it’s become a symbol of “who’s more patriotic,” explains Randy, with politicians wanting to prove they support local South American beef. Plus, in the end, another chain, Sizzler, swoops in and steals all the cows. With no beef left, Stan has an epiphany: “They said nobody even really cares about our cows… So then, this rancher could inject anything with lard and butter, and people would be just as obsessed with it. That’s it, dude. That’s it. We can have all our cows back.” Indeed, it works, as the episode ends back at Ruth’s Chris Steak House, where a waiter is serving diners their new “patriotic meals”: flame-seared guinea pig on a stick.

This week’s episode was decidedly not a Halloween special, despite the show’s storied history of spooky holiday episodes and its airing just a few days earlier. Thus, it appears creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone are skipping the holiday altogether. And though last year’s episode, titled “The Woman in the Hat,” wasn’t advertised as a Halloween episode ahead of its air date, it did come two days later than normal, timed to fall on the spooky night of Oct. 31.

So far, Season 29 has centered a range of much-talked-about topics, including e-bikes, data centers, billionaires and anti-vaxxeres. In the third episode, the crew found themselves stuck in Sephora’s “backroom,” a nod to the joke that tweens spend ages in the beauty store, and dove into the internet-era term aura battles (meaning lingo like “mogging,” “maxxing” and “mewing” were plentiful).

With Season 29, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone are going full steam ahead with the “South America” name change, which was announced earlier this month ahead of the Season 29 premiere. The premiere — the first episode since taking on the name “South America” — hit 4.2 million viewers in three days, as previously reported by Variety, and even featured an updated theme song to ring in the name change (and a Donald Trump cameo).

title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Football Heroes Take to the Battlefield in Peter Berg’s Emptily Macho WWII Epic
summary: No one familiar with the oeuvre of Peter Berg — the action merchant behind the Afghanistan war drama “Lone Survivor” and the improbably pumped-up boardgame adaptation “Battleship” — should approach “The Mosquito Bowl” expecting great restraint or good taste. Ostensibly, Berg’s Netflix-backed combat epic is fighting the same fight as Terrence Malick’s “The Thin Red […]
content:
No one familiar with the oeuvre of Peter Berg — the action merchant behind the Afghanistan war drama “Lone Survivor” and the improbably pumped-up boardgame adaptation “Battleship” — should approach “The Mosquito Bowl” expecting great restraint or good taste. Ostensibly, Berg’s Netflix-backed combat epic is fighting the same fight as Terrence Malick’s “The Thin Red Line,” likewise charting the physical and psychological torment of American soldiers in Guadalcanal during the Pacific Theater of the Second World War. But they are two very different history lessons. There’s not a hint of Malick’s poetic anti-war melancholy in Berg’s brawny, cacophonous Semper Fi salute to American military brotherhood, which certainly doesn’t stray from standard war-is-hell sentiment — rarely, in fact, has war been depicted as more loudly ruinous — but positively revels in onscreen carnage, as if to underline the mettle of its Marine heroes.

Not that said mettle is in any danger of going unnoticed. For the four men at the pretty hollow center of “The Mosquito Bowl” aren’t just soldiers but sportsmen — stars of the college football circuit who bring their strength and smarts from the field to the battlefield. And if that comparison sounds glib to you, then buckle up, because the film has plenty more: “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in the history of football,” says one character, a sentiment that sounds sort of rousing without making much sense. That goes for much of the script by Berg and Mark L. Smith, which is drawn from a popular 2022 historical novel by Buzz Bissinger — the journalist whose 1990 bestseller “Friday Night Lights” became the basis of Berg’s sturdy 2004 football drama and the more popular TV series spun off from it.

Berg and Bissinger are cousins; the screen adaptation of “The Mosquito Bowl” was likely a fait accompli all along. Yet while the book’s ennobling mixture of Greatest Generation portraiture and brutal evocation of the rigors of combat is perfectly tailored to the filmmaker’s interests, it also hands the screenwriters a bit of a structural red herring. The title refers to a football game that the principals were tasked with organizing on Guadalcanal; it was played on Christmas Eve 1944 between the 4th and 29th regiments of the 6th Marine Division, and featured a wealth of drafted football talents who had set aside their sporting careers to serve their country. Outwardly, the book and film both seek to imbue this event with the significance of the famed Christmas truce soccer matches between British and German forces in the no-man’s-land of the First World War.

When push comes to shove, however, the game simply isn’t all that consequential. It’s skipped over surprisingly swiftly on the page, and despite much anticipatory buildup, the film, too, struggles to make a climactic set-piece of an event that has considerably less visceral impact than the various juddering, blood-on-the-lens battle scenes on either side of it. Nor does it work as a human interlude, because the human dimension of “The Mosquito Bowl” is so flimsy. Its four principals are colorless, interchangeable alpha males, uniformly stout of build and square of jaw; they’re granted mildly differing character attributes by the script, but even as the closing credits roll, you’d be hard pressed to remember who was who.

John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), a graduate (and future football coach) of Brown University, is given the leading perspective — which is to say he occupies the framing scenes that have him visiting a college football field years after the war with a stoic, misty gaze, and reflecting vaguely on all that has been won and lost. We rewind to 1941, when the earnest young man’s budding future with the New York Giants is put on ice by a surge of patriotic duty in the wake of Pearl Harbor; the same goes for jocular Purdue grad Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, appropriating his father Jack’s rakish perma-grin), soulfully withdrawn Wisconsin Badgers star Dave Schreiner (stage star Tom Francis, a Tony nominee for “Sunset Blvd.”), and fellow Wisconsin grad Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), whose personality lands somewhere between those last two — the writers having run out of all-American archetypes quite early on.

Historical dates are lightly fudged to give the four men a shared soldierly narrative, and so they collectively endure the grueling trials of Parris Island basic training, horrible but familiar from many a military drama, before shipping out to the Pacific, where the shattering, deafening mayhem that awaits them is horrible but familiar from many a war movie. Knowing that he has nothing new to show us, Berg’s solution is to show us ever more of the same, ladling on the frank images of death and devastating injury with relentless rat-a-tat-tat sound design to the point that the film does attain a blunt sensory force.

The aesthetic, with DP Jacques Jouffret’s aggressively desaturated palette and nauseous POV shooting coupled with antsy, abrasive editing, is ripped from “Saving Private Ryan,” but cranked up to video game levels, with a grinding, guitar-heavy score by post-rock band Explosions in the Sky; the film’s technical proficiency so overwhelms its slender character-building that it begins to feel almost heartless.

The actors, all talented, are given no scope to be any more than capable. There’s scant room for inner life here, nor for reflection on anything more specific than war’s general cruelty — though, needless to say, the enemy gets even shorter shrift. There’s a jingoistic undertow to “The Mosquito Bowl,” with its flag-waving celebration of football and Marine fortitude, that sits queasily with decontextualized shots of Japanese soldiers committing ritual seppuku or being summarily executed by American captors, or the main characters’ repeated gung-ho statements about “killing the Japanese.” The film strains to say something about the morally corrupting effects of warfare, but doesn’t challenge its heroic leads on the racist invective they parrot, or circle back to any regret they may feel deeper into their service. Trivial and shoehorned in as it seems, when the titular football game rolls along, you can practically feel the film’s sigh of relief: at last, a blessed few minutes of macho combat without consequences — or politics.

title: From Carlos Reygadas to Hamaguchi’s Cinematographer, Tokyo’s Nippon Cinema Now Directors on Unexpected Connections
summary: A first-time director who messaged Oscar winner Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s cinematographer directly, and a former hunter whose film led Carlos Reygadas to float a collaboration, were among five Nippon Cinema Now filmmakers who shared the unexpected connections behind their work at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF). The “How We Make Films” panel at Tokyo […]
content:
A first-time director who messaged Oscar winner Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s cinematographer directly, and a former hunter whose film led Carlos Reygadas to float a collaboration, were among five Nippon Cinema Now filmmakers who shared the unexpected connections behind their work at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF).

The “How We Make Films” panel at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, moderated by TIFF programming director Ichiyama Shozo, brought together Ueda Shinichiro (“Earthlings in Love”), Saito Kisin (“Kefi”), Natori Satoshi (“Chihiro | Akemi”), Matsumura Shingo (“Between Us”) and Yaza Takenoshin (“Hinotama: Ball of Fire”) to discuss the making of their radically different features.

As he introduced the participants, Ichiyama noted that although the selection typically focuses on newer directors in Japanese cinema, he was interested in bringing Ueda in because of the unique vertical format of his latest film, “Earthlings in Love.” Ueda explained that the film was an adaptation of sorts, born from a 30-episode microdrama series designed for social media, hence the vertical aspect ratio. Its budget, though, was “equivalent to a regular independent film,” he said. That already sets it apart from most microdramas, which are typically very low-budget. “I’m from the theatrical film world, so we were making it as if it were a film to start with […] so it became appropriate for a theatrical release,” Ueda said.

Ichiyama then introduced “Kefi,” a debut feature by young cinematographer Saito, which he described as “a very unique, strange film,” one where “you never know what’s happening, but at the end, it all comes together.” Asked how such a film came about, Saito said he had met a producer in charge of production and movie advertising, who found a sponsor for the project. “And so the sponsor had a theme for us, and based on that theme, we were going to make a film, and I agreed to it. But as we continued our discussion, the sponsor said that we could make it as we like. So it turned out to be a very strange film,” Saito said.

The original theme, he said, was “maternal love, being a mother.” The finished film instead follows three sisters after they receive the news of their father’s passing. “They kind of left it to us, so I kind of just added my preferences,” Saito said.

Moving on to “Chihiro | Akemi,” Natori spoke about a key location in the film, a house in eastern Hokkaido.

“I wanted to shoot a film that is basically about the distance between the woods and the house, just going back and forth from the house. I myself used to be a hunter, and with the experiences from hunting, I came up with all these ideas, and I tried to put them in this film. You go out hunting, you look for prey, and then you hunt, and then you eat the meat. And you continue this over and over again,” Natori said. “And I kind of compared that life and the life that I have in Tokyo.”

Natori, who used to work as a director at an advertising company, said that in the Hokkaido wilderness, those social roles were stripped away. “I really felt like my personality changed, and I was really interested in that shift, as if there was another person inside me. I fully felt this uncanny feeling of somebody else emerging from inside me, and I felt like this would be a really terrifying idea.” Nawata Canon, an actor and producer on the film, also incorporated her own experience of giving birth into it, Natori said.

Discussing his influences, Natori cited Andrei Tarkovsky’s “Nostalghia,” calling it “foundational” because it taught him that “the plot is secondary.” To him, the texture of a film matters more, and color and style are equivalent to story.

Natori also spoke about the film’s festival run, including the Split Film Festival in Croatia, where it won the Grand Prix in the feature film competition. That led to a meeting with Mexican director Carlos Reygadas, who was on the jury. “He came up to me and he said, ‘Your film is crazy. What’s going on here?’ So he personally talked to me and wanted to collaborate with me. So for the next one, potentially it’s going to be a Japan-Mexico collaboration,” Natori said.

A common theme of the panel was the freedom to make the kind of film each director wanted. Speaking about “Between Us,” Matsumura said that “it was very much free in terms of what I could do with the concepts” in a film that “focused on theater and how the theater and reality overlap.”

The conversation turned to taking a chance on approaching collaborators, with Yaza describing how he came to work with cinematographer Kitagawa Yoshio, known for his work with Hamaguchi.

“I had never done a feature-length film or anything that required a budget, so I didn’t really know how much it would cost or what the budget would look like,” Yaza said. “But then I messaged [Kitagawa] directly. He has also done many low-budget films, and so I was curious.”

He never imagined, he said, that “the cinematographer for Hamaguchi’s film would be able to join my project,” and assumed “there must be some kind of trick to make films with a low budget like Hamaguchi does.”

Yaza asked Kitagawa about making films on a tight budget. That eventually led to a call in which the cinematographer offered to shoot the film and connected him with a producer, who began approaching financiers. “It was my first set because I’ve never been on a film set before,” Yaza said. “I was also the youngest person on set, and it was a very generous environment, [one] with an open mind, and we were able to enjoy ourselves until the end.”

Natori’s thoughts on what matters most in feature filmmaking seemed to capture the idiosyncratic appeal of the Nippon Cinema Now selection as a whole. “I think it’s important for you to make a feature-length film that you will be satisfied by,” he said, “that you can only do because it’s your first time.”

title: Milwaukee Brewers Win First World Series In Franchise History
summary: Somewhere up in heaven, Bob Uecker is cracking open a cold Miller Lite. The now-departed Uecker, more famous for his beer commercials than he ever was for his modest career as a MLB catcher, was the Milwaukee Brewers’ radio announcer until 2024. And tonight, as the team won its first-ever World Series, his 54 years […]
content:
Somewhere up in heaven, Bob Uecker is cracking open a cold Miller Lite.

The now-departed Uecker, more famous for his beer commercials than he ever was for his modest career as a MLB catcher, was the Milwaukee Brewers’ radio announcer until 2024. And tonight, as the team won its first-ever World Series, his 54 years in the booth were not forgotten.

In his postgame locker room speech tonight, Brewers’ manager Pat Murphy carried on his schtick of delivering Uecker’s “messages” to the team from the great beyond.

Here is the mesage, per The Athletic:

Watch on Deadline

“So, Ueck sent me a text today. He said, ‘Look, I helped you against the Padres. And I messed with the Dodgers a little bit. And then you came here, and you were on your own, because we had a doubleheader and they actually let me catch the last three innings of the game. But you did it for the city, you did it for the state, and you boys oughta be awfully proud to know that you’re the first-ever Milwaukee Brewer team to be world champions.'”

Not that the Brewers needed any help. They were clearly the best team in Major League Baseball all season. They had the best record and stormed through the postseason, sweeping the two-time defending champion L.A. Dodgers to win the NLCS and beating the Tampa Bay Rays in a gentleman’s sweep, four games to one, in the World Series. In that’s quite a feat for the team from the league’s smallest market especially since, in its 57 years of existence, the club had never won the final game of the season.

After taking each of the first two games in this year’s World Series by one run, the Brewers destroyed the Rays 10-0 in Game 3. Tampa Bay regained some dignity last night with a 4-3 win before being dominated again tonight.

Milwaukee led from the second inning on. They went up 4-0 in the 6th when Brewers catcher William Contreras (later named series MVP) drove in Christian Yelich to score the team’s final run. Tampa Bay got some consolation in the bottom of the 9th when Chandler Simpson doubled to deep right field and brought Liam Hicks in to score. But it was Milwaukee’s night — and year.

title: ‘Merry Berry Love’ Producers Nippon TV & CJ ENM Talk Korea-Japan Collaboration To Boost J-Drama – TIFFCOM
summary: Japanese broadcaster Nippon TV and Korean studio CJ ENM described how they’re combining the strengths of their respective industries to create drama series that can appeal to global audiences, during a TIFFCOM presentation. The two broadcast giants worked together on ten-part series Merry Berry Love, which started streaming worldwide on Disney+ on October 7. The […]
content:
Japanese broadcaster Nippon TV and Korean studio CJ ENM described how they’re combining the strengths of their respective industries to create drama series that can appeal to global audiences, during a TIFFCOM presentation.

The two broadcast giants worked together on ten-part series Merry Berry Love, which started streaming worldwide on Disney+ on October 7. The series stars Korea’s Ji Chang Wook (The Worst Of Evil), playing a spatial designer, and Japan’s Mio Imada (Tokyo Revengers), playing a strawberry farmer, who find love on a remote Japanese island.

Shinji Enari, Nippon TV’s Executive Vice President, Content Business, explained how the show marks the first time the company has worked with CJ ENM: “We delegated leadership to CJ ENM and have been supporting the production while following their lead”.

Watch on Deadline

Directed by Kim Soojung (Semantic Error) and written by Lee Jaeyoon (Divorce Insurance), Merry Berry Love was developed and produced by CJ ENM and co-produced by Nippon TV. Weekly episodes are streaming on Disney+ immediately following linear broadcast on Nippon TV in Japan.

Disney+ reports that, just 14 days following launch, the show is the number one most viewed Japanese live-action title premiere on Disney+ globally in 2026, and the number one most viewed Japanese title premiere in the APAC region.

Giyoung Choi, CEO of CJ ENM Japan, said the cooperation made sense because Korean companies have many years experience in distributing dramas globally, while Japan has previously been stronger in format sales.

“Nippon TV wants to offer Japanese drama to the global market by taking advantage of our expertise in this area,” said Choi, who is of Korean origin and speaks fluent Japanese. He then outlined some of the differences between the Korean and Japanese drama industries.

“The way the Korean industry approaches the task is different. In Korea, they think about how to be successful, but in Japan they think more about how to avoid mistakes and failures. One approach is not better than the other; they are just different.

“The key is to try to reach out to each other to understand the good points of the Korean and the Japanese systems. At first, Japanese and Korean staff face some communication difficulties, but by observing each other, we can learn how to work together successfully. And based on the experience we gained working on this show, we’re really looking forward to working on more joint productions.”

Korea-Japan collaborations on drama series is a growing trend with multiple shows recently combining actors, crew, storylines and locations from both markets. Other recent examples include Netflix crime thriller Blue Road, based on a manhwa about detectives in Korea and Japan tracking down a serial killer committing murders in both countries; and Fuji TV’s Kidnap Game, a thriller with talent and production partners from Japan, Korea and Hong Kong.

Also in the TIFFCOM presentation, Nippon TV presented the 11 unscripted shows that have been produced by Gyokuro Studio over the past year, including Love On The Menu, Never Look Back, Majority Rules, Ultra Mission, Mega Catch and Secret Little Assistant.

Launched in June 2025, Gyokuro Studio was established to produce unscripted shows targeting global format sales. Nippon TV has also opened a Los Angeles office to expand its global infrastructure, which also includes outposts in New York, London, Amsterdam, China and Southeast Asia.

Gyokuro Studio head Ken Akiyama said: “We’ve had offers from multiple companies for shows including Majority Rules, Ultra Mission and Never Look Back. We thought this would take more time, but we’re negotiating multiple contracts within one year of launching the studio.”

TIFFCOM is running for three days (October 28-30) at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho.

title: ‘South Park’ Parodies ‘GTA VI’ Hype With Dog Poop Gameplay
summary: As gamers await the release of Grand Theft Auto VI next month, South Park once again took aim at the upcoming game, this time armed with dog poop. On Wednesday’s episode of the Comedy Central show (currently rebranded as South America for Season 29), the gang visits the local cattle ranch and gets a sneak […]
content:
As gamers await the release of Grand Theft Auto VI next month, South Park once again took aim at the upcoming game, this time armed with dog poop.

On Wednesday’s episode of the Comedy Central show (currently rebranded as South America for Season 29), the gang visits the local cattle ranch and gets a sneak peek at the video game, featuring a new gameplay in which Jason fights an NPC on Vice Beach with a bag of dog poop.

“Look at that, the graphics are seriously next level. You see the world-building?” an insider teases. “It’s a dog taking a poop. And people can pick up the dog poop. You can throw things at the person with dog poop, and if they choose to fight back, you can pick up the dog poop and actually attack them with the dog poop. That is what’s coming in November.”

The kids are in amazement as Cartman declares, “Dude, that game looks fucking tits!”

Watch on Deadline

Wednesday’s South Park episode “Guinea Pig on a Stick” comes ahead of the highly-anticipated Nov. 19 release of Grand Theft Auto VI from Rockstar Games, the first GTA installment since 2013.

As the show refers to the game’s release as the “big change” coming in November, it also serves as Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s satirical reminder of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

title: ‘Tonight Show’: Jimmy Fallon & Jamie Lee Curtis Channel Fielder & Holmes In Cold Open
summary: As Jimmy Fallon gears up for Halloween, he and his latest talk show guest nailed their take on You Can See Everything. On Wednesday’s episode of The Tonight Show, the 6x Emmy-winning host channeled his inner Nathan Fielder to grill Jamie Lee Curtis as Elizabeth Holmes during the NBC talk show’s cold open. “Be honest, […]
content:
As Jimmy Fallon gears up for Halloween, he and his latest talk show guest nailed their take on You Can See Everything.

On Wednesday’s episode of The Tonight Show, the 6x Emmy-winning host channeled his inner Nathan Fielder to grill Jamie Lee Curtis as Elizabeth Holmes during the NBC talk show’s cold open.

“Be honest, do you really want to be on the show tonight,” asked Fallon, mimicking Fielder’s line of questioning in the much meme-ified teaser, as Curtis responded in her most convincing Holmes voice, “Of course I do. I love talking to you.”

Fallon asked, “So, you’re not just here to promote your new show Newlyweds?”

Watch on Deadline

As the pair continued to reenact the You Can See Everything scene, Fallon seemed satisfied with her answers before giving her some privacy. “Thank god! Fuck, what an asshole,” said Curtis, breaking Holmes’ stiff facade.

The late-night parody of You Can See Everything comes as the Lance Oppenheim-helmed doc surpasses $45M worldwide in A24’s slow-burn expanding release, building buzz for its acclaimed portrait of the incarcerated Theranos founder.

title: How A Former Senior Netflix Staffer Launched One Of Japan’s Buzziest Indie Cinemas
summary: Director Lee Chang-dong’s beautiful genre mash-up, Possible Love; Dario Argento’s Giallo classic, Suspiria; and Sophy Romvari’s accomplished debut, Blue Heron, are some of the titles Japanese cinephiles can catch this week at Cineyama, one of the country’s buzziest new indie cinema venues. Located in Yamanashi Prefecture, just outside Tokyo, CineYama is a unique proposition in […]
content:
Director Lee Chang-dong’s beautiful genre mash-up, Possible Love; Dario Argento’s Giallo classic, Suspiria; and Sophy Romvari’s accomplished debut, Blue Heron, are some of the titles Japanese cinephiles can catch this week at Cineyama, one of the country’s buzziest new indie cinema venues.

Located in Yamanashi Prefecture, just outside Tokyo, CineYama is a unique proposition in Japan’s indie film scene: The venue sits at the site of a former kindergarten, and its founder, Matt Kelson, is American. He is also a former senior Netflix staffer.

“I worked there about 11 years in total,” Kelson explains of his lengthy Netflix tenure. “In LA, I started on the product team and was responsible for all the artwork you’d see on the service. We worked with design agencies around the world. Netflix then opened a screenings team with the advent of Netflix Originals. I joined and was responsible for film festival screenings. Eventually, I moved to Japan to manage screenings across APAC.”

After a series of regional cuts, Kelson was laid off from Netflix, but was keen to stay in Japan with his family. The Michigan native had previously run an indie film space in Detroit and decided he would begin to look for a suitable venue where he could launch a similar project in Japan.

Watch on Deadline

Kelson landed at the former Sawamatsu Kindergarten in Uenohara City, Yamanashi Prefecture. The building had been abandoned for 10 years and had the perfect amount of space to build upon.

“Finding the space was pretty quick,” he explains. “I met someone who owned another business in town, and she introduced me to the city government. They were really excited to show me different buildings, including a couple of old schools.”

CineYama. Credit: Matt Kelson.

“I had to pitch the idea to the city government. They thought it was interesting, and then, to make the process fair, they created an open call so anyone could pitch to use the space,” Kelson adds.

“A group of about 12 people in the city government judged the proposals. No one else applied—it was just me. The whole process took about three months of back-and-forth meetings before they gave me the stamp of approval.”

Kelson was then tasked with pitching his idea to the local residents’ council, which had to give unanimous approval.

“It took two sessions before everyone was on board,” he says. “The first one was a little contentious, but I was able to calm people down and explain what I was doing.”

Kelson says residents of the suburban neighborhood were afraid the cinema would attract too much traffic and disrupt local life.

“I reassured them that it was only 43 seats and wouldn’t be that disruptive. I was able to get everyone on board,” Kelson explains.

After a full year of renovations and consultations, the cinema officially opened its doors in the Spring as a 43-seat venue with digital, 35 and 16mm projection.

“We’ve had over 3,000 people come since opening, which was a lot more than I expected in the first six months. I’ve been really happy with that,” Kelson explains.

CineYama. Credit: Matt Kelson.

Kelson describes the cinema’s current programming as “experimental.”

“We’re seeing what works and what doesn’t. For the most part, I’m trying to show more international titles, because a lot of Japanese cinemas have moved toward showing mostly Japanese content,” he says. “As a foreigner here, I want to show other cultures and ways of life, and keep CineYama’s perspective very international, while also showing some Japanese films—usually more independent ones.”

In recent years, Uenohara City, which sits just an hour west of Tokyo, has become an increasingly popular destination for young families looking to escape the speed and cost of the capital. As such, Kelson explains that some of CineYama’s best-performing titles have been children’s films.

“I played the new Bluey movie not too long ago, and it did really well,” he explains, adding he has been pleasantly surprised by the interest in arthouse titles.

“In June, I did a whole Tarkovsky series, showing six of his films. We got 160 people to come, which amazed me out here in Yamanashi,” Kelson says.

In the new year, CineYama and Kelson will begin a new challenge: distribution. Kelson plans to launch a location distribution outfit, based out of the cinema.

“The first title will be Burden of Dreams, Les Blank’s film about Werner Herzog making Fitzcarraldo,” Kelson says.

“It was surprisingly never released in Japan, so I reached out to Les Blank’s son and found the rights. I’m going to show it. It’s a film I thought about throughout the whole building process: this wild story about a guy in the jungle trying to build an opera house.”

The film will begin its first local run at CineYama before rolling out nationwide to other smaller theaters.

When asked what advice he would give to other film exhibition upstarts, Kelson says everything “starts with the location.”

“You need to find somewhere that works as a cinema and has the specifications for a big screen, but can also tell a story,” he says.

“With any location I’ve looked at, it’s been important that it’s already part of the community—somewhere that can get people excited to visit. A box that’s just a cinema isn’t exciting for people anymore. You can watch films in your room at home. It has to be an experience people can form memories around.”

title: ‘Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting’ Review: Qiu Jiongjiong Returns With a Sensory Banquet
summary: Lauded for the stylized studio environments of his debut fiction feature, 2021’s Locarno prizewinner “A New Old Play,” Qiu Jiongjiong returns to the soundstage for a second helping in his follow-up, “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting.” “A New Old Play” told the story of an actor who played different roles in successive epochs of Chinese […]
content:
Lauded for the stylized studio environments of his debut fiction feature, 2021’s Locarno prizewinner “A New Old Play,” Qiu Jiongjiong returns to the soundstage for a second helping in his follow-up, “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting.” “A New Old Play” told the story of an actor who played different roles in successive epochs of Chinese history, and made his life into a three-hour pageant by using stage techniques: rippling bedsheets dyed a watery blue for ocean waves; fake plastic trees for nature. “Fuxi” has no such neat thematic relation between subject and style, but it’s a joy to be back on the soundstage with Qiu regardless.

Now acting as his own production designer as well, writer-director-editor Qiu serves up more painted backdrops and practical theatrical effects, this time in an anthology film in which a cast toplined by Lee Kang-sheng play multiple roles in rhyming chapters centered around food. It’s a four-course feast for the eyes, even if “A New Old Play’s” intertwined themes of art, memory, and China’s tumultuous 20th century offered more food for thought.

“Fuxi” — a word translated by an opening title card as “a tasty delicacy, or the act of eating it” — circles ideas of ritual and community, embodied by tasty-looking Sichuan food and, at times, fairly detailed instructions for cooking it. The appeal to arthouse audiences is obvious, though the international critics and programmers who compared “A New Old Play” to Jia Zhangke’s politically ambitious “Platform” may find “Fuxi” less substantial. Qiu operates in a more folkloric mode, beginning with the film’s first segment, “The Ancestors’ Fuxi,” set among a prehistoric tribe whose members are recognizably human, except for their tails. As a member of the tribe approaches the end of her life, it is explained, she cuts off her own tail, and prepares it as a soup, to feed her descendants as part of her burial rites.

The dying granny, who chops away at her appendage with a prop hatchet, is played by Lee, sporting a silver wig seemingly fashioned of rope. Famous as Tsai Ming-liang’s longtime muse, Lee has a sly charisma that peeks out at the edges of even his most morose roles, as it does here. Lee reappears as another female elder in “The King’s Fuxi,” which jumps ahead by at least one millennium — people no longer have tails, and their diet has diversified. There’s agriculture now — villagers toil behind tiered hillsides fashioned from flat boards painted with abstract green swirls — and animal husbandry.

In the “Ancestors” segment, wild dogs, played by actors in masks and black unitards, howl on the village outskirts; by the second segment, they’re kept as pets, and one (voiced by Qiu himself) even narrates the story. Society has become more hierarchical: The food Lee’s character serves is an offering to her king, who has abdicated in order to live as a bird (he floats through hand-painted clouds and smoke-machine haze on digitally removed wires), but still returns once a year to taste the tribute of his subjects.

This king is based on Duyu, a figure from Sichuan legend (“Duyu” means “cuckoo”), and one who may be inspired by a real figure who introduced the core principles of farming to the region. But even as “Fuxi” moves into recorded history, it remains in a liminal space between textbook and myth, material world and spirit world. In the third, most substantial segment, “The Litterateur’s Fuxi,” four spirits — including one played by Xue Xuchun, who portrayed a similar underworld guide in “A New Old Play” — assemble in a 1997 represented by cutouts of skyscrapers backlit through lighting-gel windows. They’re gathering to share a festive banquet at which each course triggers a memory from the life of the Song dynasty dissident poet Su Dongpo (Lee Hong-chi); amid the artifice of Qiu’s mise-en-scène, overhead shots of pork belly browning on a bubbling skillet, or fish steaming in chilis, stand out for their earthiness, and the use of offcuts such as a lamb’s spine makes a stark commentary on the pains of exile.

If “Fuxi” has a political agenda, it’s to be found in this section’s look at the responsibilities of an artist, though the fourth section, “Sworn Brothers’ Fuxi,” set at the dawn of the 20th century, is much more typical in its oblique and disguised musings on the promises and disappointments of modernity. A boy (Zhou Jiarui, one of the great-grandsons in “The Ancestors’ Fuxi”) runs away from servitude in a kitchen and, pursued by officers of the dying Qing dynasty, falls in with three of the spirits from the previous chapter, a motley gang of outlaws or ghosts who teach him to make congee, and about the virtues it requires — patience when preparing a meal, camaraderie when sharing it. The film’s overarching philosophy, as summed up in its final sequences, is stoic, bawdy and not particularly deep: “We eat, we shit, and that’s it, as of old.”

Freedom, for Qiu, seems to mean the freedom, in his storytelling, to repeatedly cross borders between life and death, and between different layers of fiction. “Fuxi” has a frame story, but it’s hard to tell where the frame ends and the story begins: Sol (Wen Ke) and Luna (Xiao Luxi), wearing respective sun and moon headpieces, look down on the feasting mortals, occasionally falling to earth but also appearing in interstitial sequences tinted, like a silent movie, either sepia or steel-blue, in which a film crew preps the Fuxi sequences.

In a recurring image, Sol and Luna seesaw on a foam mountain, rising and falling in turn as the days and centuries flow by below. Qiu’s eloquence lies in such playful gestures, which are pleasurable for their own sake. “Fuxi” takes place on sets with the heightened artificiality of a Hollywood backlot; Qiu’s handcraft is so sumptuous and elaborate that “resourceful” doesn’t cover it. In an era when digital effects work — and, increasingly, gen-AI imagery — is used as a quick fix for corner-cutting productions at all budget levels, every one of “Fuxi’s” intricately wrought tactile flourishes is a luxury good.

title: ‘Between Us’ Review: Estranged Teenagers Process Past Tragedy Through High School Theater in Fitfully Ambitious Japanese Drama
summary: The lingering trauma shared by two middle-class families, once friendly but now estranged following a tragic camping incident, is finally addressed through the unlikely prism of a high-school drama club production in “Between Us,” Shingo Matsumura’s well-intentioned, yet only fitfully successful, exploration of unprocessed grief. The writer-director’s fourth feature film premieres as part of the […]
content:
The lingering trauma shared by two middle-class families, once friendly but now estranged following a tragic camping incident, is finally addressed through the unlikely prism of a high-school drama club production in “Between Us,” Shingo Matsumura’s well-intentioned, yet only fitfully successful, exploration of unprocessed grief. The writer-director’s fourth feature film premieres as part of the Tokyo Film Festival’s revamped and newly competitive Nippon Cinema Now section and is bolstered by a quartet of assured performances from its female leads.

Ririka Kawashima is most impressive as the shellshocked teenager Makoto in a story that sees mothers and daughters emerge from the emotional fallout of losing a loved one to shoulder the burden of recovery and reconciliation. Never lacking in ambition, yet left somewhat wanting in execution, commercial prospects for “Between Us” may well be limited to specialist showcases with a particular focus on nurturing emerging voices still honing their craft.

In a brief yet crucial prologue, 10-year-old Kasumi and her parents set out on a countryside camping trip. They were set to be joined by Kasumi’s classmate Makoto and her family, but she is sick and her father is called into the office unexpectedly. As a result, only Makoto’s eight-year-old brother Kenji goes with the other family, and upon arrival at the campsite, scampers around excitedly with a butterfly net, while being warned not to wander too far.

Six years later, and the domestic landscape has changed dramatically for both households. High-schooler Makoto (Kawashima) lives with her mother, Emi (Akiko Kikuchi) — who is now an emotional wreck — while her father (Yoichiro Saito) has moved out, lost his office job, and now scrapes together a living as a delivery driver. Makoto bristles when an elderly neighbor casually mentions her brother, while Emi becomes all but catatonic when a colleague at the library where she works asks after her “little one.”

Kasumi (Anna Kurasawa) and her family appear to be faring somewhat better. They are still together and have added a now five-year-old daughter, Chika, to their brood. But when mother Fumiko (Asami Usuda) comments that their youngest was complaining about never seeing her father (Takahiro Miura) smile, the cracks beneath this veneer of domestic bliss quickly become apparent.

These early sequences display a keen ability from Matsumura to paint a tragic picture of malignant, festering grief from a past tragedy, without the need for any overt explanation. However, in a frustrating and unnecessary misstep, an out-of-place news report on a car radio confirms that Kenji disappeared on a camping trip with family friends six years earlier, and that the police have not ruled out the possibility of foul play. Not only does this heavy-handed over-clarification — beyond earshot of any character and included solely for the benefit of the audience — erase any sense of mystery surrounding what has happened, but it also suggests a forthcoming procedural element to the narrative that never materializes.

Instead, the film turns its attention to Makoto and Kasumi, who find themselves not only attending the same high school, but enrolled as sole members of the school’s struggling drama club. Simultaneously, Fumiko and Emi cross paths at the library, where the revelation that the family at least tangentially responsible for her son’s death now have an adorable little sprog of their own, threatens to send Emi into an emotional tailspin.

While both patriarchs prove utterly ineffectual in processing what has happened, and their wives reluctant to engage, it falls to the younger generation to acknowledge the suffocating sense of loss that has smothered and crippled both families. Makoto and Kasumi resolve to produce a play dramatizing precisely this decision to reconcile, leaning into the residual affection they still hold for each other and, unlike their parents, a desire to process the hostility that has manifested in the hope of letting go and moving forward.

As it crawls timidly towards its climactic performance, “Between Us” frustrates as frequently as it impresses, teasing at promises of meta-textual experimentation or cathartic revelations, precious few of which come to fruition. In many ways, Matsumura’s film recalls Lee Jong-un’s 2019 Korean drama “Birthday,” which observed the paralyzing impact of the 2014 Sewol ferry disaster, in which more than 300 people died, without ever reenacting the event itself.

The director’s resolve to leave crucial questions unanswered is bold and praiseworthy, but he might have gone further still. Similarly, his stance that his teenage heroines are more willing and better equipped emotionally to forgive, heal and reconcile than their parents might have benefited from a modicum of conflict or pushback from the older generation. Nevertheless, despite these shortcomings, “Between Us” remains a tidily assembled little package that brandishes a welcome glimmer of dramatic ambition, and at the very least, provides its female cast with a stage on which to shine.

title: ‘Paddington the Musical’ Extends West End Run Through 2028 After Olivier Awards Sweep
summary: “Paddington the Musical” is sticking around London a little longer. The hit stage adaptation of Michael Bond’s beloved children’s books has extended its West End run through June 25, 2028, as the production approaches its first anniversary at the Savoy Theatre. The extension comes following a record-tying seven wins at the 2026 Olivier Awards, including […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

“Paddington the Musical” is sticking around London a little longer. The hit stage adaptation of Michael Bond’s beloved children’s books has extended its West End run through June 25, 2028, as the production approaches its first anniversary at the Savoy Theatre.

The extension comes following a record-tying seven wins at the 2026 Olivier Awards, including best new musical, best director for Luke Sheppard and best actor in a musical for James Hameed and Arti Shah, who jointly portrayed the titular bear. The production also took home nine WhatsOnStage Awards, tying the record for the most wins in the ceremony’s history, as well as the Critics’ Circle Award for best new musical.

Based on Bond’s 1958 book “A Bear Called Paddington” and StudioCanal’s 2014 film, the musical follows the marmalade-loving Peruvian bear as he arrives in London and finds a home with the Brown family, whose lives are upended when a mysterious villain sets her sights on their new houseguest. The production features music and lyrics by McFly singer Tom Fletcher, a book by Jessica Swale and direction by Sheppard, whose credits include “& Juliet.”

The show has drawn particular attention for its elaborate staging of Paddington himself, brought to life through a combination of a full-body bear costume and remote puppetry. Original performers Shah and Hameed spent three years developing the character through workshops, with Shah physically embodying Paddington onstage while Hameed provided his voice and remotely controlled his facial expressions.

The extension also coincides with the arrival of a new West End cast, which began performances Oct. 28. Abbie Purvis and Hassan Taj now alternate as Paddington’s onstage performers, with Sonny Monaghan providing his voice and remote puppetry. The new cast also includes Haydn Oakley and Charlotte Wakefield as Mr. and Mrs. Brown, Cassidy Janson as Millicent Clyde and Linzi Hateley as Mrs. Bird.

The musical’s success has already prompted an international expansion. A Broadway production is set to begin previews March 30, 2027, at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre, ahead of an official opening April 18. Another production will open at Sydney’s Capitol Theatre in September 2027.

“Paddington the Musical” is produced by Sonia Friedman Productions, StudioCanal and Eliza Lumley Productions on behalf of Universal Music UK. Tickets for the extended London run are now on sale, with the best availability beginning in summer 2027.

title: Tahmima Anam’s New Novel ‘Good Books’ Being Adapted for TV With Pacesetter, Kudos and ‘Emily in Paris’ Writer (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: The next novel by Tahmima Anam, the author of acclaimed and award-winning books “A Golden Age” and “The Good Muslim,” is being adapted for TV, Variety has learned. According to sources, “Good Books,” set behind the scenes in the world of publishing, is being developed for screen by Pacesetter Productions and Kudos. Anam is adapting […]
content:
The next novel by Tahmima Anam, the author of acclaimed and award-winning books “A Golden Age” and “The Good Muslim,” is being adapted for TV, Variety has learned.

According to sources, “Good Books,” set behind the scenes in the world of publishing, is being developed for screen by Pacesetter Productions and Kudos. Anam is adapting with writer Alison Brown, the Emmy-nominated writer and producer whose credits include “Emily in Paris,” “Younger” and “Upload.”

“Good Books” was first announced at the Edinburgh Book Festival where Anam sat on multiple panels. During the festival it was announced that U.K. publisher Cannongate had signed the book, with publication set for 2028. Cannongate’s frequent U.S. collaborator Scribner bought North American rights.

At the time of the deal, the publisher described the book as “The Devil Wears Prada” meets “Yellowface,” and about “how books get made and who gets to make them, imposter syndrome and what one needs to rise above it, and most of all about mothers, daughters and the people who stand in for them.”

The “Good Books” synopsis reads: “When Raya Chatterji meets Prue McNeill, London’s most respected

literary agent, at the New York bookshop where she works, she has no idea what this encounter will bring: a new career; a return to the city of her birth; and the secrets she left behind.”

Pacesetter Productions, founded by Jessica Rhoades, produced Peacock’s recent spy thriller series “Ponies” and has partnered with Charlie Brooker as producers on both his hit series “Black Mirror” and the upcoming Philomena Cunk comedy “Cunk on Cinema.” Kudos, part of Banijay, is among the U.K.’s most respected names in TV, behind shows including “House of Guinness,” “SAS: Rogue Heroes” and “Grantchester.”

Anam is the author of the Bengal trilogy and a recipient of the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize for Best First Book and the O. Henry Award. Her novel “Uprising” was shortlisted for the Orwell Prize for Political Fiction. She is a Granta Best of Young British Novelist and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. Born in Dhaka, Bangladesh, she trained as an anthropologist at Harvard University.

title: Russell Brand’s Wife Calls Him an ‘Amazing Husband’ at Rape Trial: ‘I Feel Very Seen by Him’
summary: Russell Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, took the stand to defend her husband at his rape and sexual assault trial in London on Thursday, calling him an “amazing husband.” Gallacher’s testimony comes after the former actor and comedian said in court on Wednesday that no one with relevant evidence to the alleged incidents being discussed in […]
content:
Russell Brand‘s wife, Laura Gallacher, took the stand to defend her husband at his rape and sexual assault trial in London on Thursday, calling him an “amazing husband.”

Gallacher’s testimony comes after the former actor and comedian said in court on Wednesday that no one with relevant evidence to the alleged incidents being discussed in the trial had agreed to testify on his behalf. Gallacher is appearing in court as a character witness for Brand. “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations,” Brand said. “I have devoted myself to these matters.”

Brand has been charged with with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges. The case involves six female plaintiffs, all of whom are given automatic lifelong anonymity according to U.K. law, and relates to alleged offenses that occurred between 1999 and 2009.

Speaking in court on Thursday, Gallacher — who has been married to Brand since 2017 and shares three children with him — recalled how the two first met at his “highly explicit” comedy show in 2006, when she was 19 and he was 31, according to Sky News. They began dating and told each other they loved each other, but it was “difficult for him to be monogamous,” she said. They then split in 2007.

Brand went on to marry pop star Katy Perry, but Gallacher said she “had not seen him during the marriage,” which lasted from 2010 to 2012. Brand and Gallacher reconnected in 2014.

Asked by defense lawyer Ian Winter KC about their marriage, Gallacher — who has been by Brand’s side nearly every day of the trial so far — called him “caring and kind,” an “amazing husband” and a “wonderful father.”

“I feel very seen by him,” she said (via Sky News), adding: “We have a very honest, frank and clear relationship and marriage… our relationship has always been [about] honesty.”

On the stand Wednesday, Brand was questioned by both the defense and prosecution about each alleged offense. He denied the claims, telling the jury: “I’m innocent.” However, he admitted that some of his past behavior was “wrong in retrospect.”

“As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong,” he said. “I do recognize I have been a very determined and focused man … With women — of course, which is the subject of my trial — I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering and idiocy.”

The jury is expected to start deliberating a verdict as soon as Tuesday.

title: European Production Association CEPI Welcomes Canadian Bodies As First International Members
summary: Canada and Europe have been moving closer together politically, and now their media production bodies are doing the same. CEPI, the European Audiovisual Production Association, has welcomed the Canadian Media Producers Association (CMPA) and the Association Québécoise de la Production Médiatique (AQPM) as its first international observer members. CEPI represents 3,000 independent production companies in […]
content:
Canada and Europe have been moving closer together politically, and now their media production bodies are doing the same.

CEPI, the European Audiovisual Production Association, has welcomed the Canadian Media Producers Association (CMPA) and the Association Québécoise de la Production Médiatique (AQPM) as its first international observer members.

CEPI represents 3,000 independent production companies in 17 countries through 19 national associations and one European association, and now counts the two Canadian bodies among its ranks.

The European Union and Canada have moved closer politically together during the Trump Presidency, and their media bodies have followed suit, with CBC/Radio-Canada the first non-European network to become a full member of the European Broadcasting Union over the summer and Canada set to compete in the next Eurovision Song Contest.

Watch on Deadline

CEPI will work with the CMPA and AQPM to strengthen dialog and coordinate on shared advocacy issues such as regulation of streaming services, domestic production requirements, IP and rights, and co-productions.

The news comes after the three bodes and other producer associations from Australia and across Europe signed a joint statement calling on governments to protect domestic production and local storytelling at the Toronto International Film Festival last month.

“The arrival of CMPA and AQPM as CEPI’s first international observer members reflects the increasingly international nature of the audiovisual industry,” said Anthony Muldoon, President of CEPI. “While Europe and Canada may be an ocean apart, the challenges and opportunities facing our independent production sectors are remarkably similar. We share a commitment to supporting independent producers and creating original stories that reflect our respective cultural realities.”

CMPA President and CEO Reynolds Mastin added: “Canadian and European independent producers face many of the same challenges, from modernizing regulations for the digital age to ensuring that local stories continue to be told, and to making sure domestic producers have a fair opportunity to own their work. We are stronger when we tackle these challenges together.”

Hélène Messier, President and Executive Director at AQPM, called joining CEPI “a great privilege,” as she flagged challenges such as generative AI, diversity of cultural expression and preservation of cultural sovereignty.

title: Disney+ & Netflix Hoover Up Non-English Acquisitions As Fervor For Japanese & Korean Content Continues – Ampere
summary: Disney+ and Netflix’s buying habits appear to be dispelling the notion that non-English-language acquisitions aren’t on their agendas. Research from Ampere Analysis shows that non-English content now accounts for at least half of acquisitions at both global streamers. As of September, non-English content accounted for 65% of Netflix acquisitions, with the figure at Disney+ hitting […]
content:
Disney+ and Netflix‘s buying habits appear to be dispelling the notion that non-English-language acquisitions aren’t on their agendas.

Research from Ampere Analysis shows that non-English content now accounts for at least half of acquisitions at both global streamers. As of September, non-English content accounted for 65% of Netflix acquisitions, with the figure at Disney+ hitting 50%.

Japan and Korea were the leading source for Netflix acquisitions, with German and Japanese content topping Disney+’s list.

Ampere noted its research had identified Japanese, French, South Korean and Turkish as the biggest acquisition opportunities moving forwards if high demand and relatively low export volume was considered.

Just 40% of Japanese streaming content is available worldwide, with the U.S. and South Korea the biggest buyers of what can be bought, though France and Germany also show relatively high interest.

Watch on Deadline

It’s a similar story for South Korean content – despite the global popularity of K-drama, only 45% of the country’s titles are available only on its own streaming services. The Middle East and Southeast Asia appear most likely to bite on its romantic-themed films and shows, Ampere claimed.

“Non-English content remains underexploited despite growing global demand. In recent years, Amazon Prime Video, HBO Max and Disney+ have increasingly expanded non-English-language title licensing in multiple markets,” said Tingting Li, Research Manager at Ampere.

“Japanese, South Korean, French and Turkish content present the top opportunities for international licensing, with strong audience appeal but still gaps in cross-border availability. For content owners and platforms, buying this content can bridge the gap between audience demand and international distribution.”

title: Russell Brand’s Wife Says Star Was “Caring” Lover At Time Of Rape Allegations
summary: Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that the Despicable Me star was a caring and considerate lover during the period in which he has been accused of rape. Laura Brand took to the witness stand on Thursday at London’s Southwark Crown Court, giving evidence in support of her husband, who faces three charges of […]
content:
Russell Brand‘s wife has told a court that the Despicable Me star was a caring and considerate lover during the period in which he has been accused of rape.

Laura Brand took to the witness stand on Thursday at London’s Southwark Crown Court, giving evidence in support of her husband, who faces three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one of attempted indecent assault.

The charges span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009. Laura Brand told the court that she first met Russell in August 2006 after a gig in Edinburgh, and they began a sexual relationship a month later. Asked what kind of lover Russell was, Laura said he was “very caring” and went at “my pace.” She added: “I felt entirely cared for and looked after by Russell.”

The pair broke up in February 2007 after Russell was unfaithful. “I was not interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people — it was really difficult for him to be in a monogamous relationship,” Laura said. “I was a little heartbroken.”

Watch on Deadline

Riel Karmy-Jones, the prosecution barrister, pointed out that Laura was not in a relationship with Russell in 2009, when Complainant 5 alleged that she was anally raped by the Forgetting Sarah Marshall actor. Deadline has been reporting daily from a live video feed of the courtroom since the trial began.

Russell and Laura reconnected a decade later, marrying in 2017 near Henley-on-Thames in Oxfordshire. They have three children together. Laura, who has been in court most days, described her husband as being “amazingly attentive” and “kind,” telling jurors: “I love him very much.”

Two of Brand’s ex-girlfriends also gave evidence through witness statements that were read out in court by a defense lawyer. One woman, who dated Brand between 1996 and 1999, said he was “gentle and loving.” The second, who had an open relationship with Brand from 1999, added: “He never engaged in an intimate act without mutual consent.” Both said he was promiscuous, with the second noting that “women would circle like birds” around Brand as he became more famous.

The prosecution and defense have now made their case to the jury. Closing arguments are expected tomorrow. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, expects the jury to begin verdict deliberations next Tuesday, November 3.

The trial continues.

title: ‘The Cube’ Creator Adam Adler Joins Channel 4’s Production Biz As Creative Director
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Sarah Dillistone has made her first big hire at Channel 4’s in-house production biz. Dillistone has snapped up The Cube creator Adam Adler as Creative Director and he will lead on the creation of new shows for the nascent unit. Adler is a highly-regarded British formats executive who is best known as creator of […]
content:
